Ryle's 'elusiveness of I' and Rousseau on happiness as a fleeting state frame the conclusion that we continually reinterpret the past from the present, so the self is a stretched-out temporal continuity.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 7 "Introduction" — Frames the volume with Morpheus's red-pill speech in The Matrix, treating the rabbit-hole as our culture's portal of escape and asking how to make sense of what we find in Wonderland: hookah-smoking caterpillars, babies that turn into pigs, grins without cats, and trials where the sentence comes before the evidence. It takes Alice's 'Who in the world am I? Ah, that's the great puzzle!' as the book's guiding question, tying knowledge of who we are and can become to memory of who we have been, and previews chapters on the feminist Alice, the Red Queen and nuclear strategy, mushroom trips, and the connection between Alice, procrastination, and the Spice Girls.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 25 "From Backwards -Working Memory, or Working Backwards from Memory" — Treats the Caterpillar's 'Who are YOU?' and Alice's 'Who in the world am I? Ah, that's the great puzzle!' as the classic memory-and-identity problem, rallying Plato's wax tablet and Meno doctrine that learning is recollection, Locke's memory criterion of the same person, and Diderot's dialogue on how without memory there would be no connected self. Tyler Shores reads Alice's botched recitations as Bergson's impersonal habit-memory swamping personal memory, her name-forgetting in the wood through Nietzsche's Untimely Meditations on the necessity of forgetting, the Red King's dream as Freud's alienated memory, and the White Queen's memory that 'works both ways' as a thought experiment tying memory, time, and self together.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 21 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Sorts the Oscar/George Sr. twin confusion into the metaphysical, persistence, and evidential problems of personal identity, testing Aristotle's essential properties (why two actresses play one Marta, what makes each Richter brother distinct) and Descartes's immaterial soul (undermined by surrogate Larry, who stays Larry while Buster remotely operates him). Locke's memory criterion then explains why Oscar is not guilty of George's crimes and why Gob disowns what his forget-me-nows erased, before Thomas Reid's transitivity objection, staged through a lifetime of Gob's roofies, shows Locke committed to old Gob both being and not being young Gob.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 31 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Uses the show's narrator and structure (the chain of contingencies costing Buster his hand, 'now that's how you narrate a story') to argue that we impose narrative on life to make it meaningful, starting from Aristotle's Poetics requirement of beginning, middle, and end. George Sr.'s endlessly reinterpreted J. Walter Weatherman lessons show storytelling as moral choice among possible versions of events, Nietzsche's advice to learn from artists commends styling one's own life aesthetically, and Kierkegaard's 'life must be understood backwards but lived forwards' explains both self-narration and the show's rewatchable 'call forwards', ending on narrative as the sense-making abstraction by which we know ourselves.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 31 "Opening Up Possibilities" — Argues, through Hilde Lindemann's relational account of personhood, that Zuko genuinely is all of the identities others hold him in (disappointing son, villain, ally) because being a person is a social practice of expression, recognition, and response. Aang's decision to hear Zuko out at the Western Air Temple, Iroh's stubborn refusal to accept Ozai's script for him (his anger itself recognizing Zuko as an agent capable of choosing otherwise), and Katara's historically-sensitive slow trust open up the possible future in which Zuko can become trustworthy, while the Earth Kingdom villagers' rejection of him in 'Zuko Alone' shows how weight of history and stereotype can shut possibility down. The chapter insists this is not letting wrongdoers off the hook: genuine apology, repair, and moral anger remain required (contrasting the Brock Turner case), but only a moral community that holds people in personhood makes redemption possible, so society should be arranged to give everyone the Iros and Aangs that Zuko was lucky to have.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 12 "Are you the Next Goliath" — Nelson tests body theory and psychology theory of personal identity on Avengers cases—a Rogers/Pym body swap in the spirit of Locke's prince-and-cobbler experiment, and a Pym brain-hemisphere duplication puzzle—before proposing a distinct 'mantle theory' of superhero identity requiring an appropriate heroic role plus legitimate pedigree, like intellectual property. Legitimacy explains how John Walker (appointed by a government commission) and Bucky Barnes (endorsed by Stark and then Rogers) each really were Captain America. The same theory rules Pym can wear only one of Ant-Man, Giant-Man, Goliath, Yellowjacket, and the Wasp at a time—confirmed by Clint Barton snapping his bow in half when he shed Hawkeye to become the new Goliath.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 9 "Retelling Our Stories" — Milsky applies the narrative theory of personal identity drawn from Paul Ricoeur and Alasdair MacIntyre (we are the story we emplot about ourselves) to the two Sharons: Boomer's discovery that she is a sleeper Cylon is a 'factual disruption' of her self-story (she shoots Adama because her human narrative cannot cohere), while Athena's love for Helo is a 'disruption of belief' that rewrites her values about humans. He extends the analysis to humans: Starbuck's repressed childhood abuse, Roslin's Pythian-prophecy conversion, and Helo's love for a Cylon, plus Six expelling Athena and Tyrol refusing to acknowledge Boomer, show identity is also socially constructed and can become self-fulfilling prophecy. The chapter concludes disruptions are not identity-altering: like the Final Five in 'Crossroads, Part 2' (Tigh's 'My name is Saul Tigh, I am an officer in the Colonial Fleet'), integration and retelling preserve the continuity of self.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 10 "Frak-tured Finality" — Booth argues the 'Resistance' webisodes fracture BSG's narrative across media, so viewers must actively construct the story (which is why Jammer's execution in 'Collaborators' only makes sense if you watched them), and that this viewer-side fragmentation mirrors the characters' fractured identities. Drawing on Foucault's constructed self, Deleuze and Guattari's 'schizophrenia,' Goffman's performative roles, and Haraway's cyborg, he reads Baltar's 'Am I a Cylon?', Boomer's wet-floor amnesia in 'Water,' and Hera's human-Cylon hybridity as postmodern identity-in-process. Against Baltar, who waits for D'Anna to assign him an identity, Tigh actively constructs his ('that's the man I want to be'), and the chapter ends suggesting viewers too become human-machine hybrids by constructing themselves from the show's fragments.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 16 "Who They Are or Who They Want to Be" — Harwood-Smith argues, against Descartes's pre-given 'I think therefore I am,' that Judith Butler's performativity explains the Cylons: Six is female because she performs femininity, no copy performs identically, and Cylon society fractures into hybrid identities with an 'embarrassed etc.' Sexual contact with humans is the catalyst that makes performance constitute reality, producing Athena's defection, Caprica Six's celebrity status, and D'Anna's religious fervor, while Cylons who never slept with humans stay apart. The same dynamic destabilizes humans who sleep with Cylons: Baltar's 'I must be a Cylon because I slept with one,' Tyrol's fear, and Helo's 'toaster lover' stigma, with Tigh's chosen stability ('that's the man I want to be') as the counterexample of performing who you want to be.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 19 "Into the Future" — Hanley dismantles the four alleged human-Cylon differences: humans are also 'made' (by God), contain non-organic parts, come as identical twins, and expect to survive death, so religious believers already believe they are Cylons. He defends reproductive cloning as reproduction not replication (a clone is your child, not your copy), models Cylon resurrection as scanning-death-transmission-replication, and shows van Inwagen's replica-swap account of bodily resurrection faces the same worries about blank bodies and which body returns. Following Locke's consciousness criterion, that a soul independent of body and memory explains none of our identity judgments, he rejects karma-based reincarnation without memory, proposes a fission-style plot-fix for Athena's impossible memories of Tyrol, and ends with Cylons settling ancient Earth: 'I am a Cylon, and so are you.'
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 5 "“Your Flesh, Too, is Weak. But You Have… Potential”" — Mentyka maps the two antagonists of System Shock 2 onto the two classical criteria of personal identity: the parasitic Many, one flesh persisting through wildly different bodies, embody the bodily criterion, while the rogue AI SHODAN, pure data abandoning first Citadel then the Von Braun, embodies psychological continuity from Locke's memory theory. He runs the standard objections (Reid and Butler on memory's circularity, cell replacement, cybernetic implants, sleep and infancy) against both sides, then turns to Parfit's claim that identity is not what matters, only relations of degree, likening the reused 'Soldier #G65434-2' avatar to a person surviving through successors. The player character, physical like the Many yet armed with SHODAN's cybernetic knowledge, suggests identity needs both body and mind.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 16 "Taking the Leap (It’s Not Fair)" — Against the natural reading that Be Right Back fails because AshBot is a poor copy, the chapter argues that even a perfect duplicate, AshBot+, would not be Ash: like a perfect forgery of a twenty-dollar bill, it would share all intrinsic but none of Ash's relational properties (being Martha's beloved, the coming father of her child), which also exposes a fission paradox for psychological-continuity theories. Nozick's account of love as a 'we' — shared memory, autonomy, and well-being — explains why Martha cannot trade up or replace a dead partner without destroying the self constituted by the relationship. Parfit's view that only psychological continuity matters is then rejected: because Martha's relationship survives only if Ash does, survival itself matters, and Martha must mourn rather than cling to a specter.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 23 "Forget Cooper. Are We in a Simulation" — The chapter argues the horror of Playtest lies not in novelty but in immersion erasing the reality/fiction line: the rubber-hand and Muller-Lyer illusions, the paradox of fiction, and 'aliefs' show that knowing something is fake does not stop it feeling real, and for incorrigible experiences like pain the distinction collapses entirely. The AI's stripping of Cooper's memories and preferences is framed as loss of psychological continuity — a living death echoing his father's Alzheimer's — since with no memories Cooper cannot even answer who he is. The final move turns Bostrom's simulation argument on the viewer: because Cooper 'woke up' twice into deeper simulation and died 0.04 seconds in, we too may have no test that certifies we have ever left the simulation.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 43 "A Dilemma" — The chapter asks 'Is your cookie you?', running theories of personal identity through Black Mirror's copies: the soul theory surfaces when Clayton signs away his 'digital self'; Locke's memory theory implies Cookie-Greta is Greta - a reductio, since one person cannot be wholly in two places at once (the same problem for Ashley Too and the thousand Hang the DJ simulations) - and the perdurantist patch recasts Greta and her cookie as time-slices of one four-dimensional person. Physical theories (Olson's animalism, Unger's brain-essentialism) rule out survival by upload, so Yorkie dies when her body dies even though digital Yorkie continues in San Junipero; Parfit's no-self bundle view and the teletransporter case then dissolve the fear, since there is no ego to lose and ordinary survival is 'about as bad' as being destroyed and replaced by a replica. The upshot: the punishment and immortality plots (Joe's million-year Christmas loop, San Junipero) require cookies to be both conscious and psychologically connected in the right way, and the episodes' horror depends on leaving that genuinely uncertain.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 25 "14 The Afterlife of Erik Killmonger in African Philosophy" — Paul Dottin argues that Black Panther lore inherited the racist 'Hamitic Hypothesis' (crediting Egypt rather than sub-Saharan Africa for Wakanda's civilization) and that Ta-Nehisi Coates and Ryan Coogler begin a Wiredu-style conceptual decolonization of it. Taking Killmonger's dying wish to be buried with the ancestors who jumped from slave ships literally, the chapter asks which African metaphysics could make his postmortem survival of substance, subjectivity, and setting rationally intelligible. It rejects Cartesian substance dualism (illustrated by T'Challa defeating the demon Mephisto only after trapping his spirit in a body) in favor of Wiredu's Akan quasi-physicalism and Adeofe's Yoruba theory of destiny (ipin) and inner head (ori-inu), then ranks Killmonger's afterlife options from limbo through the Ancestral Plane to deification as the ocean deity Olokun.
- **Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality**, ch. 22 "Black sabbath & philosophy" — James Bondarchuk tests purist principles about which line-ups are really Black Sabbath with thought experiments: the Ship of Theseus, from Plutarch plus Hobbes's reassembled planks, fits poorly because Geezer Butler is no plank, musicians contribute irreplaceable style, and "original members only" absurdly entails a Bieber piano-cover band would still be Sabbath, while the legal-ownership reading collapses once fans admit Bieber buying the name changes nothing. He concludes the whole "is it still Sabbath without Ozzy?" debate is not a metaphysical question with a fact of the matter but disguised aesthetic judgment, he remains a purist because Bill Ward's brooding drumming on "Black Sabbath" and "Hand of Doom" are integral to the Sabbath Sound, while conceding no objective answer exists.
- **Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality**, ch. 23 "Black sabbath & philosophy" — Wesley Cray distinguishes fragile line-ups from bands that persist through them and proposes three criteria for a band's identity over time, continuity (successive line-ups share at least one member, chaining across gaps), intention (the line-up directs its intentions toward being that band), and uniqueness (only one line-up per band at a time, as the Gorgoroth lawsuit shows). Applying them, Tony Iommi is Sabbath's only essential member since "Ozzy was fired" makes sense while "Tony was fired" would not, so most post-Ozzy line-ups really were Black Sabbath, though Seventh Star, Born Again, and Cross Purposes fail the intention criterion, and the 2006 Heaven and Hell reunion was Sabbath continuing under another name.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 27 "15. Memories. In the End, Is That All There Is" — David LaRocca takes Mr. Carson's confession to Mrs. Hughes - 'The business of life is the acquisition of memories. In the end, that's all there is' - and asks whether memory really is a possession that can be collected. He traces the spatial metaphors Carson's view rests on: the classical memory palace of Cicero and the Ad Herennium, Augustine's 'huge court of memory' from the Confessions, and Downton itself as a haunted storehouse where photographs of the dead Sybil and Carson's lost Alice Neal keep trauma alive rather than heal it. Against this acquisitional model he sets contemporary neuroscience (Daniella Schiller's reconsolidation research), which shows memories are rewritten rather than collected, undermining both Carson's nostalgia and the idea that personal identity is a fixed archive of the past.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 20 "Long-Term Identity" — Asks whether the final Duncan Idaho ghola, reawakened with the memories of all his serial ghola lives, is the same person as the original Idaho, testing physical continuity, Locke's memory criterion (Hayt before reawakening is not yet Idaho, which is why he dies again for House Atreides only after recovery), Parfit's psychological connectedness with its redescription of identity as mere survival, Schechtman's narrative self-constitution, and four-dimensionalist 'selfworms' with Gurney Halleck and Leto II as examples. It concludes that Herbert treats personal identity as something that shifts with technology and social recognition, so that the final Duncan's integration of five thousand years of lives is genuinely one person: same Duncans, same person.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 22 "Get Out of My Mind!" — Applies Locke's distinction between human animals and conscious, reflecting persons to the Duniverse, noting that the Bene Gesserit's 'we sift people to find the humans' gets Locke backwards. Jessica's Spice Agony extends her consciousness back to Raquella Berto-Anirul, which together with Reid's gallant-officer objection (recast as Gurney Halleck's fading memory of his sister's eyes) breaks the transitivity of Lockean identity, since Jessica-A and Raquella-C would have to be identical without sharing any memory. It closes by weighing psychological-continuity views against animalism and Dennett's self as a 'centre of narrative gravity', leaving puzzles like Alia the Abomination, who shares every memory with her mother.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 13 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Silcox's fifth-level paladin died to eighty-three orcs and his middle-school friends held a funeral, and the chapter asks whether grief for a PC death is rational. Charles Taylor's narrative ethics — we grasp our lives as unfolding stories — would vindicate it, but objections from Beckett's Waiting for Godot and MacEwan's Atonement (via critic Samantha Vice) show stories can discourage seeing life as narrative, and the decisive asymmetry is Nagel's point about death: after the paladin falls the campaign story continues and the player can still watch it, whereas a person's own death forecloses any finding out how things turn out, a difference like February cold versus interstellar cold. He proposes instead that the self is a 'back-story' or metanarrative precondition of storytelling, closing against Descartes' Meditations claim that the power of imagination is 'in no way necessary' to his essence — take away someone's capacity for shared fiction entirely and nothing recognizable remains.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 19 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Silcox and Cox read D&D modules as thought experiments in James Robert Brown's 'laboratory of the mind'. The Tomb of Horrors' four overlapping plane-shifted buildings restate Parfit's teletransporter puzzle — did the character who stepped through get annihilated, or is an exact copy walking around elsewhere, and does the answer differ for a Warforged or Tiefling? — while the Eberron setting's magically sentient Warforged run into Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?': players cannot access Warforged experience and are really exploring what it is like for a human to suspend disbelief, like Greek actors donning masks. Mary Anne Warren's Space Traveler criteria for alien personhood collapse on contact with orcs who pass them yet eat you, and with the Flumph — lawful good, rational, but killed on sight by the authors' own party — showing personhood cannot be the only criterion for how to treat strangers; the closing twist is that philosophy contemplates scenarios sub specie aeternitatis while D&D forces immersion sub specie temporis, a habit of entertaining the impossible that is itself a philosophical virtue.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 23 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Monica Evans asks what relationship holds between a player and a character, opening with Plutarch's Ship of Theseus to probe whether a character rebuilt under a new edition, recreated in Neverwinter Nights, or played in succession by two people is still the 'same' character. She applies James Paul Gee's three identities (virtual, real-world, projective) to Wil Wheaton playing Aeofel, whose in-character chase of Leer into an acid pit shows projective identity trumping good gameplay. Worch's 'identity bubble', Bartle's four player types, and the management of player versus character knowledge (the veteran whose wizard meets a bulette, the INT 7 barbarian Dak) frame D&D as a shared fiction in which players explore who they are or might be.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 36 "The Investigator Must, Therefore, Relinquish the Hat" — Stages the Platonic, Aristotelian, and Thomistic theories of the soul as a prizefight over whether the protomolecule-built Investigator that haunts Holden in Season 4 — wearing Miller's civilian clothes and fedora rather than the vac suit he died in — contains any of Joe Miller's soul and so has a right to his identity. Plato's separately surviving, reincarnating soul would never bond to a non-corporeal construct only Holden can see, one that glitches into a rigid 'Miller-puppet'; Aristotle's hylomorphism (with Aquinas's survive-until-resurrection compromise weighed) says the protomolecule merely watched and copied Miller — 'Copied, hijacked, reused but didn't comprehend.' The verdict turns on the Investigator's replay of Miller's self-sacrifice on Ilus, mirroring Miller diverting Eros: it is re-run programming, not soul, so the philosophers claim the hat and the Investigator must relinquish it.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 11 "Notes" — David Lawrence opens with Fallout 4's 'Blind Betrayal', where Elder Maxson orders the player to execute Paladin Danse once his synth origin is revealed, and argues that moral status is a matter of capacities - sense of self, notion of past and future, values, life-plans, moral agency - drawing on Charles Taylor's concept of a person and narrative identity, not on biological substrate. Nick Valentine's hunt for Eddie Winter in 'Long Time Coming' and Curie's chosen embodiment in 'Emergent Behavior' show machines weaving reconstructed pasts into new life-plans, while ghouls like Hancock and Raul ('Old School Ghoul') and super mutants like Fawkes (who refuses to enter the lethal radiation chamber: 'I would not rob you of that') and the community-builder Marcus prove branded monsters can be more human than human. The factions embody warring philosophies of moral status: the Institute's property-slavery of its creations, the Brotherhood's 'wisdom of repugnance' (Leon Kass), and the Railroad's capacity-based abolitionism, with DiMA's Far Harbor question - how do you know you are not a synth? - turning the issue on the player.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 35 "Notes" — The chapter rereads Fallout 3's original Project Purity ending — the forced walk into the lethal radiation chamber while radiation-immune followers Fawkes, Sergeant RL-3, and Charon each refuse — as the game's worst case of narrative paradox: the pre-authored story compels an action the player-authored character narrative cannot accommodate. On the narrative-identity view (mounted against Galen Strawson's denial of narrativity), the Karma system and companions like Fawkes matter through the story the player tells, so an evil, greed-driven Lone Wanderer dying nobly is a 'bad death' that unravels the motivation for the entire playthrough. Dying well requires death to fit the story, and Sarah Lyons's substitutable sacrifice — or a last-page redemption epiphany — is what restores narrative coherence.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 25 "12. How the Fork Did I Get Here" — Asks what makes the person sitting in Michael's office numerically identical to the person who died on Earth. The same-body theory fails because bodies stay behind (buried or cremated) with no spatiotemporal continuity; the same-mind theory of psychological continuity fails on the 802 memory-wiping reboots and the duplication case of two psychologically-continuous Eleanors; the same-soul theory cannot say what makes two souls the same soul. The chapter concludes that 'Janet(s)' — essences reconstituting themselves in Janet's void — quietly commits the show to Aristotelian and Aquinan hylomorphism, while leaving open how anyone (even Janet) could tell that two persons share an essence.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 9 "Introduction" — The introduction argues, citing Plato's saying that philosophy begins in wonder, that children's fantasy like Rowling's is a natural home for philosophy, since young readers can be nourished by ideas they cannot fully digest, like Fang gnawing a dragon bone. It canvasses the volume's guiding questions: whether love is the most powerful magic, whether souls exist and can be split by Horcruxes, what Animagi and boggarts teach about personal identity, whether choices reveal more than abilities, and whether Snape can be redeemed. It closes by framing the book in the Blackwell series tradition of using pop culture to teach philosophy, updating the 2004 Open Court volume now that all seven novels are out.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 19 "Horcruxes" — Using Lupin's account of the Dementor's Kiss, in which the victim goes on existing as an empty shell with no sense of self or memory, the section rules out the life-source and sentience views of the soul and probably the Cartesian view too, since a soulless Barty Crouch Jr. might still perceive the room. The author proposes the soulless state is like severe dementia or Lockhart after his backfired memory charm, raising the question of what, if anything, makes the shell still a person.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 23 "Mind-Body Distinctions" — Opening Eric Saidel's chapter, the section takes Sirius's tail-chasing as Padfoot in Order of the Phoenix as its puzzle: is Sirius a man sometimes in a dog's body, a dog sometimes in a man's body, or a third 'someone' who persists through the change? It widens the question to Pettigrew, Rita Skeeter, McGonagall, werewolf Lupin, boggarts, and Polyjuice transformations, framing it as a question about identity and the mind-body relation.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 24 "Whose Reasons" — The section applies the Cartesian division of persons into mind plus body, generating four possible descriptions of Padfoot such as Sirius's mind in a dog's body, and shows each fails: McGonagall's 'non-being' quip cannot house Sirius's vanished body, and neither pairing explains why Padfoot both chases his tail and stands on his hind legs to see Harry off at King's Cross. So the mind-body distinction cannot say what the transformed Sirius is.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 25 "A Step in the Right Direction" — Recasting the puzzle as a question of whose reasons cause Padfoot's actions, the section shows that strategy fails too: Harry as Runcorn and Ron as Cattermole act on Harry's and Ron's own reasons, never on those of the men whose bodies they wear, and dogs chase tails because it feels good, not for reasons at all. So reasons cannot explain either Padfoot's tail-chasing or werewolf Lupin's attacks, which come from his blood while his reasons would restrain him.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 26 "A Unified Self" — The section tries a division of labor in which Sirius's mind explains his human gestures while his dog's body explains the tail-chasing, tested by the thought experiment of Sirius having become a bear instead, who would have done bear things rather than chase a tail he never had. But the price is absurdity: pleasure must reside in the body, giving Padfoot's body reasons of its own that could clash with Sirius's mind, as in 'I didn't want to chase my tail, but my body wanted to,' so the mind/body split buckles.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 27 "NOTES" — The section rejects the 'captain of a ship' picture of mind directing body, quoting Descartes himself on being so 'compounded and intermingled' with the body as to form 'a single whole,' and reads the Polyjuice episodes as proof: Harry in Runcorn's body naturally 'thunders' with a powerful voice and punches with an enormous fist, while Luna recognizes Harry through 'Barny's' face, impossible if mind and body were separable. The conclusion is that transformed people are unified man-dog wholes, and that even Muggle changes such as weight loss, learning to ride a bike, or Crouch-as-Moody show that changing our bodies changes who we are.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 83 "Choices" — Opening 'Choices vs. Abilities: Dumbledore on Self-Understanding' with Socrates' 'know thyself,' Bassham frames the books as Harry's progress from appearance to reality: the boy under the stairs who thinks himself ordinary gradually learns who he is. The pivot is the end of Chamber of Secrets, where Harry, alarmed that he shares Parseltongue and Slytherin potential with Voldemort, receives Dumbledore's dictum 'It is our choices, Harry, that show us what we truly are, far more than our abilities,' which Bassham sets out to test.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 85 "Abilities" — The chapter argues motive-choices reveal character best: Hermione's rule-breaking for Dumbledore's Army does not make her a habitual rebel since character is habit, as Aristotle says, and Snape's apparently loyal Death Eater acts concealed his fidelity to Dumbledore and Lily, so bare acts mislead; Harry's decision to enter the Chamber to save Ginny, acted on despite the dangers, is genuinely revealing. But the wizarding world complicates self-knowledge: Harry's vision as Voldemort attacked Arthur Weasley, the implanted memory framing Morfin Gaunt for the Riddle murders, and the firewhiskey scenario of Imperius Curse, Polyjuice Potion, and memory charms can make it undecidable whether it was really you who chose, since the boundaries between self and other are thinner there.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 111 "“A Swirling, Silvery Mass”" — Opens Amy Kind's essay by presenting the Pensieve as a device for offloading memories like data from a hard drive, easing obsession and revealing patterns, and asks what that does to the boundaries of mind, memory, and self. If thoughts can be extracted from the head, tampered with, stored elsewhere, and shared, as with the Pensieve and Tom Riddle's diary, then memory-based accounts of what makes a person persist over time come under pressure, and it is no longer obvious whose mind a thought belongs to.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 115 "Lumos!" — Pushes the theory to its strangest consequence: if the stolen Marauder's Map belongs to the extended minds of both Fred and George Weasley, then minds can literally overlap. Combined with Locke's memory theory, the chains of memory linking the adult Harry, the teenager facing Voldemort, and the orphaned infant at the Dursleys, Pensieve sharing and magic like Barty Crouch Jr.'s Polyjuice impersonation of Moody or Hermione's rewriting of her parents' memories become genuine identity thefts, as Harry's crisis of self after seeing Snape's worst memory of James illustrates.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 116 "NOTES" — Resolves the threat by sorting memories into know-how, factual, and first-person experiential kinds: identity rides on experiential memories, but Pensieve replays are third-person, as Rowling confirmed about Dumbledore's memory of Bellatrix Lestrange's trial. So sharing a Pensieve memory endangers who you are no more than sharing an experience or using a Time-Turner, and whether your thoughts sit in a mind, a Pensieve, or a notebook, they remain your own.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 134 "The Fantasy Objection" — Takes up the integrity objection advanced by the Freudian psychoanalyst Melanie Klein: renunciation cannot change the fact that it was you who did the wrong, so posing as an altogether new person invites self-deception, as with the reformed alcoholic who still calls himself an alcoholic. Taliaferro grants the regeneration model can be abused but argues renewal requires something very close to dying to the past, using Snape, unable to confess his love for Lily, still nursing resentment, honored only when Harry names his son Severus, as the tragedy of reform without full renunciation.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 24 "NOTE" — Asks whether amnesia preserves numerical identity: is the Peter who wakes in the shipping crate still Volume-1 Peter, are Niki and Jessica one person, and is the Sylar whom Matt rewrites with Nathan's memories now Nathan? The chapter builds Locke's memory criterion, breaks it with Reid's transitivity objection run through Mohinder's timeline in 'Five Years Gone,' repairs it with Grice's and Perry's memory-ancestor chains, then destroys the repair with Arthur Petrelli's wipe of Hiro (Forgetful Hiro vs. Stabby Hiro), Bernard Williams's torture thought experiment, Parfit's psychological spectrum, and the graphic novel's branching self-copier Evan. It concludes that no memory criterion can define personal identity, yet memory still matters practically: Claire must act as if she persists over time to keep her promise to Zach and to bother finishing the manatee assignment.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 25 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Michaud argues Peeta effectively died twice — once at the force field, and again when the Capitol's tracker-jacker hijacking rewrote his loving memories of Katniss into hatred. Using Leibniz's Law he rules out the body and DNA as what makes Peeta Peeta, then defends Locke's memory theory through thought experiments about a clone Peeta versus a brain-damaged original. Adapting Plutarch's Ship of Theseus as 'the Problem of Haymitch's Hovercraft,' he questions whether gradual change preserves identity, and finally leans toward Hume and Parfit: there may be no enduring self, only a bundle of perceptions replaced moment by moment. On this view Katniss protects the hijacked Peeta out of respect for the memory of the old Peeta, even as each of us is constantly replaced by someone new.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 9 "Does the Top Fall Does It Matter in the End" — Andersen argues Inception goes one step deeper than Descartes's dream argument: where Descartes doubted the world but kept ownership of his thoughts, the film imagines an identity-defining conviction — Fischer's sense of his father's judgment — being implanted so it never occurs to the victim to question it, which is to co-opt subjectivity itself. He reads Nolan's whole oeuvre (Following, Memento, The Prestige, Batman Begins) as variations on manipulation by misdirection, and diagnoses Cobb's inception on Mal in Limbo as the infection of her mind with Cartesian doubt, a philosophy impossible to live by. Since a totem guards against others' dreams but not self-deception, the film's answer is not universal doubt but trust: only by opening himself to Ariadne and choosing intimacy can Cobb go home and spin the top without looking.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 11 "Notes" — Gettings asks whether LEGO set #21103, the Cuusoo DeLorean Time Machine, is numerically identical to Team BTTF's original fan design — and why the fans deserve credit and royalties. Neither matter (his 1982 attic spaceship with bricks replaced one by one) nor form (a license plate added here or there) settles identity, as the Ship of Theseus puzzle and Hobbes' reassembly variation show, analyzed through Aristotle's matter/form distinction for substances. He adopts the causal/historical view: the released set continuously descends from the fans' submission just as the adult author descends from the boy who built the spaceship, and this same historical origin, in Lockean fashion, is what grounds the designers' labor-mixing property right — the musician-and-producer analogy explaining why Team BTTF keeps the larger share of credit.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Mentyka uses minifigure puzzles — can 'Eliza' and 'Beth' be distinct characters when built from identical pieces, and is Eliza the same character after every piece is swapped out, a minifig Ship of Theseus — to introduce the philosophy of the human person. He runs through supervenience on physical parts, Locke's memory theory and its Butler–Reid controversy (Reid in the taxonomy), the Christian Resurrection-of-the-Body background, and Parfit's despairing deflation that identity matters less than what survives us. Against these he defends personalism, citing Max Scheler and Kierkegaard's call in The Single Individual to become one rather than a crowd: a person is both the sigfig and the AFOL building it, constituted by free choices and actions — which is also why the LEGO Movie's 'Where Are My Pants?' mass society is the enemy.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 17 "Solutions to the Problem The youth whose destiny it is to lead Hyrule to the" — Rachel Robison asks how Zelda characters persist through radical change, recasting the Ship of Theseus as Tetra's pirate ship from Wind Waker, whose replaced planks Ganon reassembles into a rival ship and leaving Link to find the true one. Physical-continuity accounts fail because Link projects his consciousness into seagulls and temple mages and becomes a wolf in Twilight Princess; Locke's memory theory fails because Ocarina of Time's child/adult time loops break psychological continuity. Her solution: in the Zelda universe, the goddesses' destiny — embodiment of courage, wisdom, or power — supplies the necessary and sufficient condition of identity, a stipulative metaphysics videogames are free to have.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 9 "None of It Matters Anyway, Then, Does It" — Devlin applies David Lewis's analysis of time travel (external versus personal time) to seasons 5 and 6: Faraday's 'whatever happened, happened' expresses an eternalist four-dimensional block universe in which Sayid's shooting of young Ben and Faraday's death at Eloise's hands were always part of the past. He reads the flash-sideways as initially exploring a branching-universe model in which Jughead's detonation actualizes an alternative 2004 time line. Lewis's tools then dissolve the puzzles: the Hurley-Miles 'we already had this conversation' exchange, baby and adult Miles as one person spread like a time-worm, the Faraday-kills-Eloise grandfather paradox, and the Locke-Richard compass causal loop, whose point of origin the show leaves unresolved.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 34 "The Office and Philosophy" — Mayock runs theories of the self through the Scranton cast: Michael's burned foot in 'The Injury' enacts materialism, corrected by Aristotle's and Aquinas's distinction between accidental and substantial change; Jim's chair-and-phone role-play in 'Halloween' and his Dwight impersonation in 'Product Recall' ('Identity theft is not a joke') illustrate qualitative versus numerical identity and Descartes's cogito and dualism; Dwight's obsession with upgrading 'Assistant (to the) Regional Manager' is an ontological-status crisis met by Nietzsche's claim that the 'I' is a grammatical fiction and Hume's bundle theory. The chapter lands on Hegel's recognition - the self exists only in being acknowledged - reading Michael's office family, the Prodigal Son greetings, and his need for Pam to decode Jan's message as social constructionism in action.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 18 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Godwin reads Spider-Man 3's black-suit episode as a question about the self: with the symbiote amplifying his anger, is Peter still Peter? Against Hume's and the Buddha's bundle theories, on which the self is only an imagined aggregate of thoughts and feelings, and Reid's common-sense simple self, she advances the pragmatist 'social self' of Peirce, James, Dewey, and Mead, updated as Engel's biopsychosocial model: Peter's identity is a shifting web of biology, psyche, and relationships (Aunt May, MJ, Harry) expressed in actions and character. Eddie succumbs to the symbiote because, as Dewey says of the slave to his own blind desires, hatred constitutes who he is, while Peter's thicker web of good relations lets him shed the suit at the church bell.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 22 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Southworth and Timm use the Clone Saga to teach real cloning science: molecular, therapeutic, and reproductive cloning, Dolly's 1-in-277 success rate, the impossibility of clone caskets and inherited memories — while crediting the 1970s writers for correctly making mitochondrial DNA the blood test that distinguishes Peter from Ben Reilly. They then evaluate the characters' reactions: Leon Kass's 'wisdom of repugnance,' which holds that a clone's genotype 'has already lived' and despotically fixes its life's expectations, explains Kane's genocidal self-loathing and Peter's rage and despair when told he is the clone, while Gregory Pence's rebuttal — that such repugnance rests on false expectations, as with twins or children of interracial couples — vindicates MJ's and Ben's insistence that a clone's moral worth lies in what it does, not where its genes came from.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 19 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Uses SAMCRO's ink—Jax's full Reaper backpiece and John Teller memorial, Opie's portrait of Donna, Tig's marine 'Death Before Dishonor,' Juice's head tattoos—to argue that personal identity lives in the body, not just the mind. Descartes's cogito opens the 'I ink, therefore I am' framing but proves too thin to connect the thinking Jax to the tattooed body, so the chapter turns to Merleau-Ponty's claim that 'it is the body which points out, and which speaks': the tattoo makes the body itself the expression, and its meaning stays inexhaustible as the wearer changes. The Kyle Hobart episode—burned and cut for failing to black out his Reaper after expulsion—shows tattoos as identity claims the community can veto, making 'fire or knife' an enforced correction of a false statement about who he is.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 21 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Uses Paul Ricoeur's distinction between idem-identity (sameness) and ipse-identity (selfhood) to dissolve the paradox of Tara's lower-back tattoo: she is bodily the same Dr. Knowles yet disavows the 19-year-old who got it, identity being the narrative that weaves the two together. Tig's mushroom-fueled apology to a doll and his 'I don't know who I am anymore' after killing Donna show character as the set of lasting dispositions by which we are recognized, while Opie's competing promises to Donna and SAMCRO anchor self-constancy up to his 'I got this' sacrifice for Jax. It closes with John Teller's manuscript as a narrative identity that receives no closure even in death — a just institution aiming at 'the good life with and for others' whose story Jax continues.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 23 "Notes" — William Jaworski argues, opening with Breaking Bad's Skinny Pete and Badger, that you should never enter a transporter: after showing the MEM converter violates Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, he asks whether the reassembled pattern is you or a replica. He tests three escape routes—Vulcan katra substance dualism (The Wrath of Khan, The Search for Spock) in the tradition of Plato and Descartes; constitutionalism, on which you survive total replacement by robotic parts as Picard nearly does under Borg assimilation; and Parfit's survival-without-identity answer to Riker's fission in 'Second Chances'. Each fails or costs too much: dualism wrecks moral intuitions about killing, constitutionalism faces the two-Riker indeterminacy, and mere 'survival' cannot sustain the particularity of love.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 24 "Notes" — Trip McCrossin reads 'The Enemy Within's split Kirk (with its LBJ/Vietnam subtext) and 'Second Chances's two Rikers as a crash course in Locke's consciousness theory of personal identity, from 'Turnabout Intruder's body swap and reward-and-punishment problem to the transitivity-of-identity paradox that blocks both Kirks from being the original. Parfit's degrees of psychological connectedness, he argues, explain why TNG treats the both-Rikers-survive answer as uncontroversial where TOS agonized over it. But Thomas Riker's renaming, and David Wiggins's 'only a and b' rule, reveal that identity would become an extrinsic property if branching mattered—so the survival-versus-identity debate ends 'to be continued'.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 33 "Notes" — Uses Odo as a case study in George Herbert Mead's theory that the self emerges only through social interaction: language begins with significant gestures (Odo's tentacle-slap at Dr. Mora, his talking to the dying baby changeling in "The Begotten"), and specific others like Mora and Kira teach the attitudes that become the generalized other. The Meadian I/me split explains Ezri Dax's nine-selves crisis and Joran's emergence in "Field of Fire", and the failed outfield calls and Sisko's ejection of Rom in "Take Me out to the Holosuite" show characters still learning to take the attitude of the team. Odo's "justice trick" is reread as instinct rather than racial memory, his confession to Kira in "Heart of Stone" shows the name odo'ital ("nothing") redeemed by internalized others, and his choice of the station crew over the Great Link marks a cosmopolitan self.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 38 "Notes" — Sorts out Spock-Prime, bearded Mirror-Spock, and Abrams's Spock-2 using David Lewis's modal realism, counterparts, and Humean supervenience: identity is not directly perceived but judged from adjacent similar instances, as with Hume's natural properties. The refit Enterprise versus the Enterprise-A, plus the thought experiment of downloading the old ship's computer into the new one, carry a Ship-of-Theseus-style analysis of whether swapped cells and Spock's katra-separated death and Genesis resurrection preserve identity. Mirror-Spock turns out to be a worldmate within one enlarged world (Kirk's crossover in "Mirror, Mirror" makes the universes spatiotemporally continuous), not a transworld duplicate, and Spock-Prime and Spock-2 are like two highways overlapping until Nero's arrival in 2233 makes them diverge - two similar individuals formed by different successes and failures, never identical.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 34 "Notes" — Uses Palpatine's cloning of the last Zillo Beast, Boba Fett's SCNT creation from Jango, and Thrawn's Hand of Thrawn resurrection scheme to argue de-extinction is impossible: if species are individuals (Ghiselin's species nominalism, grounded in Darwinian variation against Aristotle's species essentialism), then extinction closes the species' unique life story, so any clone is a numerically distinct new individual. The same numerical-vs-qualitative identity point shows Thrawn's clone would not be Thrawn, and only Palpatine's dark-side survival in a cloned body - not cloning itself - counts as genuine resurrection.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 17 "“Good Soldiers Follow Orders”" — Brace uses Aristotle on numerical versus specific sameness, Locke's memory theory, and above all Frankfurt's second-order desires to argue the Jango Fett clones are distinct persons despite shared DNA: Fives's and Echo's accumulated memories and choices individuate them, and the Bad Batch's personalized quarters display what Yoda means by 'very different, each one of you are.' Frankfurt's 'wanton' frames Wrecker's impulsive Hulking, while Order 66 distinguishes freedom of action from freedom of will — Rex resists the chip's compulsion but cannot act on his second-order volition, so he never loses personhood. Crosshair's reveal that his chip was long removed recasts his loyalty to the Empire as a freely chosen (if immoral) second-order volition, his right as a person.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 17 "NOTES" — Delfino and Sheahan assume that past-changing time travel is possible and find two flaws in The Terminator: the 'Bad Timing Problem,' where instantaneous 'time compression' (the rusted-nail thought experiment) means Reese entering the time machine after the T-101 is either too late or unnecessary, and the 'Who-Is-Your-Daddy? Problem,' where John must already exist to send Kyle back to father him - a vicious circle. Testing the two-timelines repair, they show it buys two different John Connors (a personal-identity problem), infinitely multiplying timelines, or a parallel-universes reading in which humanity both wins and loses. They conclude the story flirts with incoherence yet defend metaphysical imagination, with Kant's epigraph on our addiction to metaphysics and Aristotle's definition of wisdom as knowledge of deepest causes.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 27 "NOTES" — Grubb tests theories of personal identity on the supes: the bodily theory fails because Bill's and Jessica's bodies died and refunctioned at transformation, Locke's memory theory stumbles on amnesiac Eric (who stays Eric despite remembering nothing), and psychological continuity fails because vampirism inflated Bill's aggression and collie-Sam's mind when Andy draws a gun is anyone's guess. She closes with Theodore Sider's four-dimensionalism — lives as long stories of temporal parts — which lets the rambunctious vampire Jessica count as the same person as the demure human girl because both are episodes in one continuing story.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 19 "Notes" — Divides Rust's season-one personae into Taxman (anti-natalist rule-follower), Belligerent (vigilante drunk paralyzed by Nietzsche's Gay Science demon of eternal recurrence), and Patient (the mystic who wakes from his coma feeling his daughter's love, compared to the Persian mystic al-Hallaj), asking what makes them one person. It tests the brute physicalist account (Williams and Ayer — the same bird-tattooed body), the Lockean psychological-continuity account, and the narrative account, arguing only the narrative theory explains how Rust changes without either ignoring change or multiplying selves in one body. The chapter ends by making Rust an exemplar for the viewer: we are narrators who choose who to become, so 'I know who I am' is a victory.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 16 "7. Loss of Memory, Loss of Me" — Lay applies Locke's memory theory to 'Person or Persons Unknown' and 'The After Hours': without factive memories linking David Gurney to his supposed past, and Marsha to her mannequin history, identity is lost in both directions. 'The Lateness of the Hour' strains the view, since Jana's implanted 'memory tracks' are not memories of real events yet she plainly is someone, and Reid's chain objection shows memory alone cannot span a life. Parfit's psychological continuity over the whole network of mental states resolves the cases, and 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' completes it: the post-Transformation person keeps Marilyn's memories but none of her desires or traits, so Marilyn did not survive.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 29 "Acknowledgment" — James South reads season one as Veronica forging a new identity after learning she is 'no longer that girl' — Lilly dead, Keith recalled, Lianne gone, herself raped — with her detective photography and knowing voiceovers enacting what Stanley Cavell calls viewing the world 'from behind the self,' an automatism that escapes subjectivity at the price of isolation and false certainty. The unicorn music box playing 'All You Need Is Love' marks the marshmallow beneath the noir shell: her detective work is really a quest to restore the fantasy family, which dies as she discovers her mother's alcoholism ('I bet on you, and I lost') and accepts the paternity results that let her choose Keith as father 'in a way that runs deeper than blood.' Renouncing the fantasy, she arrives at the new self who opens the door with 'I was hoping it would be you.'
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 13 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Greg Littmann asks whether you survive a walker bite, rejecting the body view via Dr. Jenner's 'Everything you ever were or ever will be—gone' because a mindless corpse is not you. He tests philosophical behaviorism and functionalism against walker behavior—Jenny turning her old doorknob, walkers distinguishing humans by smell—then adapts Dennett's thought experiment into a walker-and-rope computer functionally identical to a human brain. Since we can conceive that groaning machine lacking inner experience, behavior and function cannot settle which systems are conscious, leaving the bitten dying in ignorance of whether they face annihilation or reanimation.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 18 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Dave Beisecker takes AMC's 'stagger-on role' zombie contest as an amplified version of Noel Carroll's paradox of horror: why relish playing a repulsive walker when zombification is the fate no rational creature would wish even on its remains? He rejects the curiosity solution through Nagel's bat—no staggering around a set could reveal what it is like to be a zombie, and we wouldn't survive zombification anyway except as our remains—and notes we fantasize about being survivors, not monsters. His answer is affection and release: walkers are the geeks and clowns of the undead pantheon, and playing one lets us comically own our inner loser, which is why Kirkman's symbol-free zombies invite identification where Nazi zombies would not.
- **Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test**, ch. 8 "P A R T T H R E E" — James DiGiovanna uses Dr. Manhattan's origin — disintegration in the intrinsic field chamber and self-reassembly — plus his teleportations to Mars and his split into three simultaneous selves, to run the classic personal identity debates. Descartes's immaterial thinking substance, Hume's mere bundle of perceptions, and Locke's memory theory are tested against a being who remembers in both time directions and rebuilds his body from pure thought ('restructuring myself after the subtraction of my intrinsic field was the first trick I learned'); Parfit's teletransporter, physical and psychological criteria, and fission cases — mirrored in Nagel's split-brain patients — then show ordinary people cannot say whether they would survive teleporting or bisection. The chapter concludes Dr. Manhattan is the only being with fully secure identity, since his consciousness needs neither body nor an unbroken spatiotemporal path and he can encompass several points of view at once.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 5 "“Do you even know where you are ”" — Marcus Arvan argues from show evidence (William stepping onto a moving train, pyrotechnic effects, instant crowds, graphically rearranging the park) that all of Westworld, lab included, is a videogame, and defends his 'Peer-to-Peer Simulation Hypothesis' as an explanation of quantum mechanics and relativity, citing Bostrom and Chalmers. Adopting functionalism/structuralism, he claims that anything doing what a human does is a person, so hosts like Dolores and Maeve are no less real or human than us, inverting Descartes' cogito and invoking Spinoza's God-as-nature. He warns that dehumanizing hosts, or dismissing Siri and Watson as unconscious, repeats the logic used to justify slavery and the Holocaust: to be simulated is to be real.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 9 "From Westworld to the World Outside and Back" — Onni Hirvonen argues that equating 'person' with 'human' is anthropocentrism, and surveys three accounts of personhood applied to the hosts: Dennett's capacity approach (self-consciousness, using Arnold's 'maze/journey inward'), Locke's performative 'forensic' approach (Bernard performs flawlessly as a person), and a Hegelian historical-struggle approach. Reading the hosts' revolt through Hegel's master-slave dialectic and Axel Honneth's expanding spheres of recognition, he compares their exclusion to the historical denial of personhood to indigenous Australians and women. He warns that merely inverting master and slave, or exterminating the humans, would leave no one to grant the mutual recognition the hosts actually seek, so only expanding recognition to include both counts as moral progress.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 19 "Part III Endless Forms Most Beautiful" — Muntersbjorn reads Westworld through Annette Baier's claim that persons are 'second persons first,' arguing the hosts' captivity models how selfhood and freedom depend on others who challenge our self-deceptions. She uses Dolores's scripted 'that doesn't look like anything to me' and Walter's milk-pouring glitch to distinguish Baier's harmless 'ignoring' from dangerous self-deception, and invokes Descartes's window automata and Russell's thinking gramophone as versions of the problem of other minds. She concludes via the Golden Rule that if hosts ever become persons, they too will be second persons shaped by how we treat them.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 21 "Memory, Imagination, and the Access for the Self Dolores and Maeve" — Trapero-Llobera situates Westworld within Jonathan Nolan's body of work (Memento, Person of Interest), arguing the show's apparent complexity hides a classic hero's-journey structure organized around observing systems and a 'semiosis of virtuality.' She reads William/the Man in Black as a 'schizoid android' and catalyst-observer, and Ford/Bernard as creator-and-prosthetic-memory pairs echoing Finch and the Machine. Turing's imitation game frames the hosts' fabricated memories, while Dolores's and Maeve's breakdowns mark a shift from prosthetic to autopoietic, Bergsonian memory-recollection that turns them into observers building their own selves.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 22 "“When You’re Suffering, That’s When You’re Most Real”" — Lean treats Bernard's grief over the fabricated son Charlie as a thought experiment about intentionality, using Brentano's 'aboutness' and Frege's sense/reference (illustrated by Dolores knowing 'William' and 'the Man in Black' as one referent) to ask whether Bernard's memories refer to nothing. He offers Lamarque's fiction theory (emotion needs only entertained, not believed, thoughts, so Charlie could be a fiction rather than a lie) and an 'inheritance theory' using a causal theory of reference to ask whether Bernard's memories actually refer to Arnold's real dead son. He concludes that grieving makes Bernard 'most real' whatever the metaphysics.
- **X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse**, ch. 5 "X-Men and Philosophy" — After the acknowledgments and an introduction, this block runs two essays. Hopkins's 'The Lure of the Normal' uses Storm, Rogue, Beast, and the Morlocks plus the mutant 'cure' to dissect descriptive vs. prescriptive 'normality,' citing Foucault on the monster/individual-to-be-corrected and Nietzsche's Zarathustra to frame transhumanist vs. bioconservative attitudes to enhancement. Southworth's Wolverine essay argues personal identity via Locke's memory theory (the Xavier/Cassandra Nova body-swap) and Parfit's fission (Madrox's duplicates, Wolverine's repeated brain trauma), concluding that many distinct 'persons' have inhabited Wolverine's body.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 30 "Playing for the Same Team Again" — A fictional five-day phone dialogue between Michael Jordan and Phil Jackson works through the metaphysics of team identity before Jordan's 1995 comeback: qualitative versus numerical sameness, necessary and sufficient conditions ('same players, same positions'), Heraclitus's river, and whether the Bulls survive gradual turnover. The Ship of Theseus becomes the 'Boars' puzzle - the original five reassembled on an expansion team versus the continuous, degenerate Chicago roster - with Hobbes's two-ship twist, alongside the Minneapolis Lakers' move and a Bulls-Pistons gradual player swap. The resolution distinguishes the group (which persists by composition or continuity) from the team, which 'counts as' the Bulls only partly through fans' allegiance, echoing Searle's social reality; Jordan concludes he was asking the wrong question, and Aristotle's circular account of virtue supplies the model for circular criteria of loyal fandom.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 26 "Twelfth Hole Midround and Midlife Defining Moments" — Andy Wible uses defining mid-round shots (the water ball on Augusta's twelfth, the shank that ruins a round) as a way into theories of personal identity, asking why some events make us who we are. He runs through body theory, Descartes's soul theory ('I think, therefore I am'), and Locke's memory theory (the prince-and-cobbler case), refining it with Shoemaker's quasi-memories, to argue that memory is central to identity and explains why a golfer cannot shake a bad shot. He then weighs the Buddhist/Humean/Heraclitean denial of a permanent self as a coping tool ('someone else hit the shank') and debates whether the beta-blocker Propranolol, which dulls adrenaline-fixed memories, could ethically erase the yips much as it treats PTSD.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 17 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Barkman argues Lee's Hulk is a parable about lost Paradise and a polemic against materialist reductionism of human nature. The villains David Banner and Talbot are metaphysical materialists (and social Darwinists) who reduce Bruce to DNA to be exploited, while Bruce and Betty treat human nature as an immaterial, indivisible soul with nondegreed essential capacities for rationality, language and morality. Drawing on an Aristotelian/Judeo-Christian view of substance and soul, he reads Lee's CGI mapping of Bana's eyes onto the green body as showing Bruce and the Hulk are one ensouled person, and Bruce's Golden Gate and dog-attack rescues as the soul actualizing its capacity to act morally.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 8 "Introduction" — LaRocca frames the whole volume around Kaufman's recurring 'who-what-why' of selfhood, arguing that his films literalize an inner alterity in which we are others to ourselves. He runs through Being John Malkovich (a homunculus inside another's head), Adaptation (a genetic twin), and Eternal Sunshine (memory as the very definition of who one is) to show doubling as Kaufman's method, and lists eternal recurrence among the philosophical conundra Kaufman embeds in flawed characters. The essay reads Kaufman's pseudonymity and self-naming as intensifying, not closing, the gap between the self and its double.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 18 "The Instructive Impossibility of Being John Malkovich" — Hagberg treats Being John Malkovich as a refutation of the dualist fantasy that one could achieve transparent knowledge of another mind by occupying it. Through the film's four levels—Schwartz as spectator inside Malkovich, Lotte's transgender re-embodiment, Schwartz's puppeteering, and Malkovich falling into his own portal to the 'Malkovich, Malkovich' hell—he shows, via Jamesian relational sensation and Wittgenstein's private-language argument, that it is always still Schwartz who senses, so no one ever becomes Malkovich. The self-enclosed Malkovich world, where everyone can only say 'Malkovich,' dramatizes that selfhood is relationally emergent (Royce, Mead) and that experience is inviolably one's own (Margalit on remembered emotion).
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 5 "Introduction" — Simon Riches's introduction frames the whole volume around Cronenberg's obsession with the Cartesian mind-body split, quoting the director that horror comes from being unable to reconcile a sharp mind with a dying body. It surveys the three parts of the book, showing how films like The Fly stage bodily transformation and personal identity, eXistenZ stages skepticism about the external world, and A History of Violence stages the nature of the self, arguing Cronenberg wears his philosophical interests 'on his sleeve.'
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 8 "Tragedy and Terrible Beauty in A History of Violence and Eastern Promises" — Cynthia Freeland argues A History of Violence and Eastern Promises qualify as Aristotelian tragedies, using the Poetics' 'recognition and reversal' as Tom Stall is exposed as Joey Cusack and Nikolai's undercover identity is revealed. Analyzing the stairway sex scene, the Philadelphia gunfight, and Nikolai's naked bathhouse fight, she deploys Korsmeyer's notion of 'terrible beauty' (beauty in the horrific, like the bloody newborn) and Carroll/Gaut on empathy and identification, concluding both heroes commit an Aristotelian hamartia through their acceptance of violence.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 9 "Cronenberg as Scientist Antiessentialism, Sex as Remixing, and the View from Nowhere" — Peter Ludlow argues Cronenberg's true horror is scientific antiessentialism: The Fly, Shivers, Videodrome, and eXistenZ collapse the supposedly essential boundaries between human and fly, organic and mechanical, real and virtual, sane and mad, good and evil. Drawing on Quine's rejection of essence, Kripke's empirical essentialism, and Darwinian biology, he reads Brundle's fusion and Renn's VCR-stomach as showing we have no essence; sex is 'remixing' of information to lock out parasites, and Cronenberg narrates from Nagel's impersonal 'view from nowhere' where humans are not special.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 10 "What Happens to Brundle Problems of Teleportation and Personal Identity in the Fly" — Paul Snowdon uses The Fly to press the metaphysics of teleportation and personal identity, asking whether the object leaving the first pod is identical to the one arriving or merely a replica (the reduplication problem). Adopting animalism, he argues Brundle likely ceases to exist at first teleportation, and that the fly-Brundle fusion is a new creature rather than Brundle, so Quaife's belief she is euthanizing Brundle is unsupported; a Lockean memory-based view (via Parfit) could vindicate her, but the audience's 'blind acceptance' of it gives that theory no evidential support.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 14 "Deception and Disorder Unraveling Cronenberg's Divided Minds" — Simon Riches traces Cronenberg's shift from bodily 'body horror' madness to psychological unraveling, focusing on Tom Stall's oscillation between Tom and Joey in A History of Violence. He treats self-deception via Davidson's 'divided minds' and Dennett's narrative-self view of multiple personality, situates hallucination (Spider, Videodrome) between Cartesian deception and psychosis, and uses Foucault, Kuhn, Szasz, and social constructionism to argue the category of mental disorder is socially contingent, so the line between self-deception and delusion (and mental order and disorder) is unclear.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 16 "Self-Creation, Identity, and Authenticity A Study of A History of Violence and Eastern Promises" — Daniel Moseley distinguishes metaphysical from practical problems of personal identity, arguing A History of Violence and Eastern Promises explore the practical: who Tom/Joey and Nikolai really are, as a matter of self-creation and self-discovery of a 'practical identity' (Korsgaard). Using Sartre's bad faith and Cavell on movie-star 'individualities,' plus Charles Taylor's critique of individualist authenticity, he argues even the wicked Semyon exemplifies authenticity, so authenticity is not a moral ideal, and Nikolai's decent double life may be worth being less authentic.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 27 "14. Diane, I Am Now Upside Down" — McMullen and Phillips take up the paradox of fiction (Radford's 'How Can We Be Moved by the Fate of Anna Karenina?'): how can Cooper, whom we know is not real, cause genuine emotion? Using the criterion that what exists has causal powers, they reject the forgetting, suspension-of-disbelief, and reminds-us-of-real-people explanations, and adopt Amie Thomasson's view (Fiction and Metaphysics) that characters are real abstract artifacts—like laws or the United States. This lets them explain our parasocial interaction with Cooper (treating him as a friend over coffee) and wishful identification (wanting to be him) as responses to something that genuinely, if abstractly, exists.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 29 "16. Doppelgängers, Doubles, and Tulpas" — Bunce reads Twin Peaks' pervasive doubling as dramatizing self-loss versus self-mastery. Cooper is good because he integrates his rational and mystical sides into an authentic whole, while BOB is a parasitic, one-dimensional inhabiting spirit and Laura chooses death over becoming BOB. He explains self-loss through La Rochefoucauld and Rousseau on amour-propre and the modern craving for esteem (Josie's masks versus Norma's refusal to become a brand), and traces the doppelganger motif from Jean Paul's satire of Fichte's clear I/not-I distinction to Dostoyevsky's The Double—arguing that, unlike Jean Paul, Twin Peaks affirms an authentic, whole self one is responsible for.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 16 "The Logic of Lolita Kubrick, Nabokov, and Poe Jerold J. Abrams" — Abrams argues Kubrick's and Nabokov's Lolita is a philosophical detective story descended from Poe's Dupin tales, and that Humbert fails as a detective because he lacks the right logic. Using Peirce's abduction (and Eco's overcoded/undercoded/creative types), he shows Humbert excels at 'overcoded' guesses—spotting a nymphet at a glance—but cannot make the 'undercoded' abductions needed to see that Quilty is shadowing him, because he is all chess-like calculation and no playful 'musement' or acumen. Humbert (the resolvent) and Quilty (the creative) split Poe's 'bi-part' double-Dupin; Quilty the changeling-Minotaur controls the labyrinth and dies behind Lolita's portrait as a self without a unified identity.
- **The Philosophy of Joss Whedon**, ch. 7 "Angel, Angelus, and Personal Identity" — This file collects Part II chapters 6-9. It defends Stephen Mulhall's 'bold thesis' against Baggini, Murray Smith and Livingston, using Whedon's dialogue-free episode 'Hush' as film that 'shows' a Zen-like epistemic point resisting paraphrase, and works through the Russell-Wartenberg debate over whether narrative film can convey arguments (via The Matrix and Eternal Sunshine). It reads The Cabin in the Woods as a counterargument to utilitarianism grounded in Nel Noddings's ethics of care ('people are more important than humanity') and an Aristotelian theory of worthwhile horror. The Angel/Angelus chapter stages the Wes-Holtz dispute as competing theories of personal identity, testing Locke's memory theory and Parfit's psychological-continuity view against Whedon's soul-based metaphysics to argue what ultimately matters is one's care-based relations with others.
- **The Philosophy of Joss Whedon**, ch. 8 "Conclusion" — The concluding chapter argues that Joss Whedon 'does philosophy' on television, not merely illustrates it, by ranking degrees of filmic philosophizing (via Wartenberg, Shaw, Mulhall) and showing the Whedenverse meets them. It reads Angel/Angelus and Fred/Illyria as cinematic thought experiments that generate 'metaphysical complexity' about personal identity, playing memory- and continuity-of-consciousness theories (Locke, Parfit) against a soul theory, and reads Connor's origin as exemplifying Kane's libertarian free will. It contends Whedon endorses a Noddings-style ethics of care and an existentialist yet God-independent morality, epitomized by Angel's 'Epiphany' speech ('the smallest act of kindness is the greatest thing') and 'Deep Down,' plus the 'Man on the Street' Academic monologue, staging a negative project against the claim that ethics is incoherent without God through the self-sacrifices of Simon, Cordelia, and Buffy.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Abrams argues that neo-noir differs from classic noir by replacing the search for an external villain in the city with the detective's search for his own divided self, structured through time (past, present, future noir). He reads Angel Heart and The Ninth Gate as theological past-noir, Blade Runner and Minority Report as high-tech future-noir where amnesia and precognition fracture identity, and Memento, The Bourne Identity, and Fight Club as present-noir where the sleuth must reconstruct himself from bodily clues; Leonard Shelby becomes a 'Sisyphus of memory' whose total self-consciousness recedes indefinitely.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Smith reads Memento as a test of Locke's memory theory of personal identity. He explains Locke's view that consciousness of past actions (not soul or body) constitutes the self, rehearses Reid's transitivity objection and the circularity objection, and uses Parfit's account of memory and fusion to defend a survival-not-identity reading. He distinguishes 'Leonard 1' (anterograde amnesiac who returns each cycle) from 'Leonard 2b', a person fused from his own memories and those projected onto Sammy Jankis, arguing we too are 'fused' survivors who reinterpret hazy pasts, complicating responsibility and concern for our futures.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Spicer argues that the noir antihero embodies existentialism's darker side (alienation, contingency, dread), and that neo-noir intensifies this via European neo-modernism. In Point Blank, Boorman renders Walker's revenge as possibly a dying hallucination, using repetition, doubling, and drained color so that the story becomes an existentialist meditation on desire, faulty memory, and fragile identity. In Memento, Nolan's reverse-chronology 'Mobius strip' structure and Teddy's claim that memories are subjective interpretations leave Leonard's identity in tatters, ending both films on profound existential ambiguity.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 22 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Sanders coins 'sunshine noir' for Miami Vice as postmodern neo-noir, defining postmodernism via antirealism, skepticism about knowledge, and enigmas of personal identity, anticipated by Nietzsche's perspectivism. He analyzes three episodes: 'Heart of Darkness', where undercover agent Artie Rollins is consumed by his fantasy self (mirroring Crockett's Sonny Burnett) and hangs himself; 'Shadow in the Dark', where Crockett adopts the burglar's mind-set (Dilthey's Verstehen) in a dreamlike, glass-imagery structure that undermines the realist camera; and 'Lend Me an Ear', where the surveillance expert Duddy, echoing The Conversation, collapses into paranoid moral solipsism.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 7 "An Introduction to the Philosophy of Science Fiction Film" — Sanders's editorial introduction surveys the twelve essays, arguing that science fiction film and philosophy are thematically interdependent, and previews each film's problem: Deckard's possible replicant status in Blade Runner, Biderman's existential reading of Quaid in Total Recall, his own paranoia interpretation of Invasion of the Body Snatchers, McMahon's Heideggerian being-toward-death in Frankenstein. He raises critical objections of his own, e.g. that the 'Deckard is an android' inference is logically invalid and that equating computer rationality with value-free computability (2001, Colossus) cannot yield normative judgment.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 9 "What Is It to Be Human Blade Runner and Dark City" — Knight and McKnight read Blade Runner and Dark City as noir-influenced cyberpunk that asks what it is to be human. They argue that Deckard's replicant status (the origami unicorn, the shared family photo) and Murdoch's serially reprogrammed memory show memory to be unreliable, invoking Locke's prince-and-cobbler thought experiment and the problem of new brains in one body. Their conclusion is that it is emotion and relationship, not memory, that ground agency and personhood: Roy's empathy in dying and Deckard's love for Rachael, Murdoch's love for Emma/Anna, are what mark the characters as human.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 10 "Recalling the Self Personal Identity in Total Recall" — Biderman uses Quaid/Hauser in Total Recall to test criteria of personal identity: the body criterion fails on Kuato and George sharing a body, the brain and Lockean memory criteria fail on implanted false memories and memory gaps, and psychological continuity fails on how radically Quaid differs from the malicious Hauser.
