Facing Hume's conclusion that the self is a fiction (echoed by Wittgenstein and Derrida's deconstruction), he argues Quaid escapes it through the Sartrean existential route: thrown into existence, he takes a stance toward his facticity and, following Kuato's 'you are what you do,' authentically creates himself by rejecting Hauser and saving Mars.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 11 "Picturing Paranoia Interpreting Invasion of the Body Snatchers" — Sanders rejects the standard Cold War-allegory and feminist readings of Invasion of the Body Snatchers and argues the film is best understood as film noir dramatizing paranoia. He shows that the mechanics of pod duplication are riddled with incoherence (multiple duplicates, location, timing, matching), then reads the frame story as evidence that Miles's whole account is a delusional psychosis. Dr. Hill's acceptance of the wild story on flimsy evidence violates Hume's maxim that a rational person proportions belief to evidence, making the film an ironic meditation on the philosophical significance of paranoia and lost humanity.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 15 "Some Paradoxes of Time Travel in The Terminator and 12 Monkeys" — Devlin uses The Terminator and 12 Monkeys to work through time-travel paradoxes with David Lewis's framework. He resolves the personal-identity paradox of the two James Coles at the airport via Lewis's distinction between personal and external time, and treats the grandfather paradox differently for each film: 12 Monkeys holds a possibilist growing-universe model in which the fixed past cannot be changed (Cole cannot kill his younger self), while The Terminator adopts a branching-universe model allowing the past to change into an alternate timeline. He closes on the causal loop of the Army of the 12 Monkeys message, which lacks an origin unless uncaused causes are allowed.
- **The Philosophy of Spike Lee**, ch. 24 "Rethinking the First Person Autobiography, Authorship, and the Contested Self in Malcolm X" — LaRocca uses Lee's Malcolm X and Haley's 'as told to' Autobiography to probe personal identity and authorship: since Haley (not X) authored the book and Lee/Washington perform Haley's literary X, he asks whether one can write another's autobiography and what becomes of the self. He surveys Locke's memory theory of identity, Descartes's thinking subject, Hume's bundle of perceptions, and Wittgenstein's denial of a thinking subject to frame X's serial renamings (Malcolm Little, Detroit Red, Malcolm X, El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz) as a 'ceaselessly evolving,' unfinished identity. He reads Lee's techniques—nondiegetic gunshots, the spinning camera, the gliding sidewalk shot ('the eye that can finally see itself'), and the framing Rodney King and Mandela footage ending on 'by any means necessary'—as arguments that the self is a contested literary and cinematic creation.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 25 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Eberl compares HAL in 2001 and David in A.I. to ask whether an artificially created being can be a person meriting respect and rights. He runs both through criteria of personhood—self-consciousness, rationality, social activity, autonomy—and Turing's imitation game/behaviorism, concluding their responses give sufficient evidence of personhood even if the soul question is open. He uses Hegel's master–slave dialectic of recognition to explain the deadly struggle between humans and their creations (Bowman disconnecting HAL; the Flesh Fair destroying Mechas), warning against a moral crime of 'biological supremacy,' and invokes Aristotle's telos/virtue to argue Flesh Fairs wrongly preclude Mechas from fulfilling their function, while David's Pinocchio 'leap of faith' and cry 'I'm special, I'm David!' mark his approach to personhood.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — The editors' introduction surveys the volume and frames Soderbergh as a maker of 'philosophical cinema' whose films engage epistemology, metaphysics, and ethics. It previews the essays' claims: that sex, lies, and videotape and Schizopolis stage epistemological questions of truth, evidence, and skepticism; that The Underneath and The Limey use Bergson's durée to explore time and self-understanding; that Traffic tests Kant's ethics against Sartrean individual decision; and that Solaris recasts memory and authenticity via Augustine and Baudrillard's simulacra. It positions Soderbergh within Indiewood filmmaking after Welles as a self-reflexive artist.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Tzioumakis reads sex, lies, and videotape through Lyotard's The Postmodern Condition, arguing the film is contradictory as a 'postmodern' text. Its four characters (Graham, Ann, Cynthia, John) acquire self-knowledge not from the celebrated video camera but through what Lyotard calls the flexible networks of language games: Graham's 'unexpected moves' displace Ann and Cynthia, who then master his interrogative game, while John's reactive lying dooms him. Tzioumakis contends the film's neat character transformations are legitimated by this agonistic network yet remain wedded to a strong emancipation 'master narrative' plus heterosexuality and patriarchy, undercutting its reputation as exemplary postmodern cinema and linking it back to modernity.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Palmer argues that The Underneath and The Limey fuse film noir's obsession with the untranscendable past with Alain Resnais's Bergsonism, mediated by Deleuze's account of the time-image. In The Limey, career criminal Wilson's consciousness accumulates recollection-images (including Poor Cow footage of a young Stamp) and prospective imaginings (the two visualized shootings), building toward a Bergsonian intuition: confronting Terry Valentine, Wilson recognizes himself as the same kind of selfish betrayer and spares him, achieving a redemption denied noir predecessors like Get Carter's Carter and Point Blank's Walker. The Underneath, by contrast, uses achronic color-coded structure only to define Michael from the outside, which Palmer counts a partial failure of the same interior ambition.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — King analyzes The Limey as 'Get Carter as made by Alain Resnais,' using Bordwell's fabula/syuzhet distinction to show how its nonlinear editing renders what Soderbergh calls the nonlinear nature of thought. Dialogue continuity is stretched across discontinuous spaces (the Wilson-Elaine 'embarrassed/ashamed/disappointed' exchange), flash-forwards precede events, and the party shooting is replayed three times as Wilson's fantasy. King argues the whole film reads as Wilson's subjective reconstruction on the plane home, grounded in Bergson (via Deleuze's time-image) yet, unlike Resnais's Marienbad, never producing real ontological or epistemological doubt because the revenge-thriller backbone and color-coding keep it legible. The film's dominant note is nostalgia for a past that, because of Wilson's imprisonments, never really was.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 19 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Ritzer reads Kafka through Deleuze (and Guattari), Jameson, Barthes, and Lacan as a self-reflexive, schizophrenic pastiche. The film's shift from black-and-white to color as Kafka enters the castle is analyzed via Deleuze's 'colour-image' and Barthes on color as artifice, using color's sensual materiality rather than realism. Its dense allusions to Wiene, Murnau, Lang, Welles's The Trial, and German expressionism make it, in Jameson's terms, a postmodern pastiche marking the waning of historicity, while Lacanian schizophrenia (the breakdown of the signifying chain) models Kafka's paranoia about power structures controlling the individual. Ritzer finally argues the film approaches Deleuze and Guattari's 'minor cinema,' deterritorializing classical Hollywood's realism through intensity and the supremacy of sign over referent.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 21 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Morton reads Schizopolis as Soderbergh's philosophical autobiography of identity, quoting Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding on memory as the ground of personal continuity to interpret Fletcher Munson's 'transmigration' into the doppelganger Dr. Korchek. Because Fletcher carries his own memory and nature into Korchek, he cannot escape his failed marriage (Korchek is sleeping with Fletcher's wife), confirming Lockean continuity: he 'cannot escape his own nature.' Morton ties the film's decayed language games and Elmo Oxygen's gibberish to a view that language masks action, and reads Fletcher's fate-frozen ending as identity surrendered to outside forces.
- **The Philosophy of Tim Burton**, ch. 5 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" — The editor's introduction frames the whole collection around three topics in Burton's corpus—identity, authority, and aesthetics—and previews each essay. On identity it contrasts an essentialist "core self" with an empirical, experience-built self, using Big Fish and Batman Returns as test cases; on authority it surveys Mars Attacks!, Sleepy Hollow, and Batman; on aesthetics it points to Sweeney Todd, death, and color. It functions as a roadmap that argues Burton's films merit philosophical reading rather than advancing one philosopher's thesis.
- **The Philosophy of Tim Burton**, ch. 7 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" — Ken Hada argues that Big Fish dramatizes a narrative, intersubjective account of the self against essentialist and Cartesian views. Dying storyteller Ed Bloom builds his identity through fantastic tales (the giant catfish, the Witch), while his journalist son Will—who dismisses the stories as lies—illustrates a 'circumscribed self' that refuses the social shaping every self undergoes. Drawing on Sartre's consciousness-as-nothingness and 'the Other teaches who I am,' Mead's generalized other, Aboulafia's mediating self, and Benjamin's 'The Storyteller,' Hada reads Will's climactic act of telling his father's death-scene as his becoming a mediating storyteller and granting Ed narrative immortality. Hume's 'bundle'/self-as-fiction and Descartes' cogito are invoked as the poles Ed's storied self transcends.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 13 "A.I. Artificial Intelligence and the Tragic Sense of Life" — Dunn interprets A.I. as a meditation on the 'tragic sense of life': treating David as a person, he argues the film dramatizes three doomed human desires (love, uniqueness, immortality) and tests two failed escapes from mortality, science (Professor Hobby, the Flesh Fair, David's suicide leap) and religious faith (the fraudulent Blue Fairy at drowned Coney Island). Defending the maligned finale, he reads the simulated Blue Fairy and the one-day resurrection of Monica as raising whether a perfect simulation of love can be 'real enough,' with David achieving a sober humanistic acceptance of impermanence.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 16 "7 Memory and Relationships in the Work and Music of Neil Young" — Sizer analyzes how memory shapes Young's songwriting: childhood trauma (polio, his parents' divorce, Omemee) fueling "Sugar Mountain," "Helpless" and "I Am a Child"; the "use and lose" pattern of collaborators and the ghost of Danny Whitten in Crazy Horse; and his late-life dread of memory loss watching his father's dementia. He frames this with Hobbes and Hume on memory-as-imagery, Wittgenstein's associative memory, and Locke's memory theory of personal identity (with Dennett on writing as a means to reconstruct and preserve the self).
- **Joss Whedon as Philosopher**, ch. 7 "Angel, Angelus, and Personal Identity" — This file gathers Part II, arguing Whedon actually philosophizes through film. It works through the film-as-philosophy debate (Mulhall's 'bold thesis' and its critics Baggini, Smith, Livingston, Russell, and Wartenberg), using 'Hush' as a Zen-like case that resists linguistic paraphrase and The Cabin in the Woods to pit Mill's utilitarianism against Noddings's ethics of care (Dana refusing to kill Marty to save the world). Its capstone treats the Angel/Angelus problem as a personal-identity thought experiment, staging the soul theory (Plato), body theory (Hobbes/Holtz), and Locke's and Parfit's memory/psychological-continuity theories, and arguing Whedon's eight-season Angel-Angelus and Fred-Illyria cases serve as a cinematic counterexample to Neo-Lockean continuity, ultimately endorsing a care-based view of what matters in identity.
- **Joss Whedon as Philosopher**, ch. 8 "Conclusion" — The concluding chapter argues that Joss Whedon 'does philosophy' through the Whedonverse, building on Mulhall, Wartenberg and Shaw's hierarchy of filmic philosophizing. It reads Angel's 'Deep Down' and 'Epiphany' speeches as endorsing that kindness is a self-standing good regardless of God, framing sacrifices by Simon (for River), Cordy (for Angel) and Buffy (for Dawn) as a cinematic thought experiment refuting the claim that ethics is incoherent without God. It reads Connor as exemplifying Kane's libertarian free will (Darla and faux-Cordelia 'stir up' quantum indeterminacy), Angel/Angelus as a years-long test of memory-continuity personal identity against Parfit's Neo-Lockean view, and 'The Cabin in the Woods' plus Dollhouse's 'Man on the Street' as endorsing a Noddings-style ethics of care and Whedon's religious non-realism, with Angel offered as a Socrates-like moral exemplar.
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 3 "Introduction" — The editors' introduction surveys Nolan's oeuvre chronologically to argue that a recurring theme of self-destruction and unstable self-identity runs through every film. It reads Following's needy Young Man through Buber's I/Thou (existing fully only when a Thou acknowledges you) and Hegel's master/slave dependence between Cobb and his mark, casts Inception's spinning top as a version of Descartes's dream argument about telling the real from the constructed, and invokes Hobbes when the Joker introduces 'a little anarchy' into Gotham. It frames Doodlebug as Nolan's most Freudian film and Interstellar as uniting personal identity, moral choice, and epistemology in Cooper's self-sacrifice.
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 7 "We Are the Change That We Seek" — These essays treat time, selfhood and substance across Nolan's films. Fosl argues Nolan's selves (Leonard, Bill in Following, the Borden twins, Bruce Wayne) are unstable narratives signified through manipulable objects, invoking Locke on memory-based identity, Augustine on memoria, Nietzsche on forgetting and Sartre/Gadamer on the manipulable past. LaRocca applies Clark and Chalmers's Extended Mind Thesis to Memento, arguing Leonard's tattoos and Polaroids are literal external memories whose deliberate falsification ('Don't believe his lies') makes him morally culpable for murder. Willis uses Lacan's gaze and objet a to read Following's voyeur-becomes-viewed structure and 'the box' as a lure. McGowan reads Interstellar through Hegel: the mysterious 'they' who opened the wormhole are revealed as future humanity, dissolving substance into subject and licensing Cooper's retroactive causality as the 'ghost' who saves Murph.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 7 "A Dead End" — Patrick Stokes uses the Doctor's regeneration and the multi-Doctor stories ("The Five Doctors," "The Caves of Androzani") to test theories of personal identity. He runs Locke's memory criterion against Reid's transitivity objection, Parfit's Branch-Line teleportation case (a Gallifrey-to-Skaro replica), Nozick's Closest Continuer schema applied to the Valeyard, four-dimensional person-stages, animalism, and narrative identity, showing each fails to explain regeneration. He gestures that identity may lie in a subjective self-appropriation, the Doctor taking ownership of his incarnations.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 8 "Doctor Who and the Ultimate Answer" — Greg Littmann uses regeneration and dozens of Doctor Who transformations (doubles like the Abbot of Amboise, disembodied brains, transmats, Eldrad's body-hopping, Cassandra's possession) as hypotheticals to test criteria for personal identity. He shows bodily identity, spatiotemporal continuity of the body, the memory criterion (undercut by Donna and John Smith cases), and psychological/personality similarity each face counterexamples, deliberately leaving the question open so readers judge for themselves.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 9 "What’s Persistence Without Identity" — Richard Hanley asks what counts as personal survival for a Time Lord, distinguishing body, mind, and soul theories. Using the Tenth Doctor's "every single cell" regeneration, the severed hand grown into a Doctor in "Journey's End," John Smith's Chameleon-Arch amnesia, and Jackson Lake's infostamp fugue, he argues bodily and soul continuity fail and defends a neo-Lockean mental-continuity criterion refined by Nozick's closest-continuer schema, concluding with Parfit that persistence may not be what matters in survival.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 10 "I Think, Therefore I Exist . . . I Think" — David Kyle Johnson uses regeneration and the DoctorDonna to ask what makes the First and Tenth Doctor the same person. He debunks the Platonic/Cartesian soul via Phineas Gage and brain science, refutes Locke's memory criterion with Reid's transitivity and the amnesia/John Smith cases, questions Parfit's causal-chain view via the "Journey's End" meta-crisis, then argues persons are four-dimensional "time worms" (sets of stages) before pushing to the deflationary conclusion that, like a "heap," a person may not exist as a discrete entity at all.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 16 "They May Not Be Human, but Could Daleks Be People Too" — Bonnie Green and Chris Willmott use the Daleks' human-factor experiments ("The Evil of the Daleks," "Dalek," "Daleks in Manhattan") to lay out the philosophy-of-biology "species problem": are species natural kinds, individuals, or sets? They trace essentialism from an Aristotelian God-given essence through Darwin's overthrow of it to modern genetic essentialism (the humanizing Dalek DNA), then use the Dalek/Thal split to survey biological species concepts and monism versus pluralism. They close with personhood and Peter Singer's speciesism, asking whether human-Dalek Sec would deserve rights.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 28 "Here They Are ... Ready to Outsit Eternity" — Michael Hand uses the Doctor's regeneration to argue that life after death is logically possible. Because the First-through-Tenth Doctors are the same person despite total personality change (a dandy becoming a clown), identity is distinct from personality, so a god perfecting flawed Joe for heaven need not make him someone else. He then tests the replica theory against 'Journey's End' (the metacrisis Doctor) and 'Human Nature' (John Smith), concluding we favor bodily continuity, and endorses van Inwagen's 'divine cryonicist' solution to the unavailability-of-atoms problem, echoing the Doctor's 'ready to outsit eternity' praise of frozen humanity in 'The Ark in Space'.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 29 "Love and Doctors" — Paul Dawson asks whether the Doctor dies when he regenerates by separating body, organism, and person. Using Kripke's rigid vs non-rigid designators he weighs whether 'the Doctor' names one individual or a role (the numbered Doctors, 'my replacements'), then applies Locke's memory criterion and Reid's transitivity objection, adopting Parfit's psychological-connectedness chain (via Sarah Jane's overlapping memories). He concludes the organism survives regeneration necessarily while the person survives only if psychological continuity holds, and argues the 'Journey's End' metacrisis Doctor Two is genuinely the person Rose loved through branching/fission.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 36 "One More Thing, Don’t Blink!" — Michelle Saint and Peter French explain why 'Blink' is horrifying despite the Weeping Angels being beautiful, not disgusting. Using Noël Carroll's fear-plus-disgust theory of art-horror as a foil, they draw on Frankfurt's account of caring and MacIntyre's narrative identity to argue the Angels destroy personhood: by hurling Kathy Nightingale out of her time and place they strip away everything she cares about and the narrative that constitutes her self. They then revise Carroll, proposing horror is fear plus impotence: the Angels weaponize the impossible task of not blinking, exposing our powerlessness to protect our own identity.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 14 "5. Could Hell Be Any Worse than Doc Benton’s Immortality" — Hellwig uses Dean's choice of Hell over Doc Benton's organ-replacement immortality in 'Time Is on My Side' to examine medical immortality. He pairs Dean's worry—that maiming and replacing your body makes you unrecognizably human—with Bernard Williams's Makropulos argument that immortality ends in categorical-desire-exhausting boredom, adding a third condition to Williams: a recognizably human life requires being able to self-identify with one's own body, illustrated by real disfigurement cases and Aubrey de Grey's biogerontology.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 25 "14. Baby’s Identity" — Doll uses the Winchesters' Impala 'Baby'—repeatedly totaled and rebuilt from replaced parts—as a running Ship of Theseus (from Plutarch) to probe what makes an object or person the same over time. She tests Aristotle's four causes (favoring the formal cause) and Theodore Sider's four-dimensionalism, both of which falter, then notes Supernatural's souls solve personal identity for the resurrected Winchesters and alternate-universe doubles; since soulless Baby has no such thread, her identity rests on the subjective, family meaning the Winchesters invest in her.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 17 "8. Self-Hatred as Identity" — Cash argues that Jimmy and Mike become their Breaking Bad selves through a 'negative self-relation' (a term from Martin Hägglund) rather than Walt's outward resentment. Mike's 'I broke my boy' speech in 'Five-O' shows him internalizing guilt for making Matty 'debase' himself, leaving nothing to live for but stashing money for Kaylee; Jimmy internalizes Chuck's verdict that he is 'Slippin' Jimmy with a law degree, a chimp with a machine gun,' so each success as Saul only confirms the worst image of himself. Cash uses Sartre's Being and Nothingness—that one cannot truly be evil 'for myself' without judging oneself as an other—to argue Jimmy's self-hatred must become unconscious for the Saul mask to become his face.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 19 "10. Slippin’ Identity" — Šekrst uses Jimmy's many personas—Slippin' Jimmy, James McGill, Saul Goodman, Viktor St. Clair, Gene Takavic—to survey theories of personal identity. She shows psychological continuity (Locke's memory-based view) falters on sleep, comas, and Chuck's apparent dementia, and the brute-physical/bodily view falters on brain-transplant thought experiments and the Phineas Gage case ('no longer Gage'). She defends a narrativist account with a reality constraint: identity is the story one is disposed to tell about oneself, so Jimmy can disown Slippin' Jimmy and reidentify as Saul, and Gene can recall his Saul self—narrative being sufficient though perhaps not necessary for persistence, with others' stories contributing but the protagonist's being authoritative.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 31 "19. Cleons and Cloning" — Heter examines the Cleon Dynasty's clones (Brothers Dawn, Day, Dusk) to ask what a clone actually is, rejecting definitions built on identity. He distinguishes numerical identity (the Mule just is Magnifico Giganticus) from qualitative identity (two copies of a book), then shows the Cleons fail to be qualitatively identical because of age, psychology, perceptual perspective, and even drifting genetics over time—so grounding cloning in shared qualitative/genetic identity yields the odd result that clones could gain or lose clone-status as their genes change. He instead proposes a causal definition: a clone is an organism whose genetic information results from an (imperfect) copying process originating in a donor, so Cleon I is not a clone but every later Cleon is.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 18 "Be Slow to Judge" — Southworth uses Wolverine and other X-Men to examine personal identity. Locke's memory criterion (illustrated by the Cassandra Nova/Xavier mind-swap and connected memories) implies that Wolverine's repeated amnesia makes him literally several successive persons until House of M restores all his memories. Jamie Madrox's up-to-100 duplicates function as a real-world version of Parfit's fission thought experiment, showing sameness of memory is insufficient for identity. Southworth applies Parfit's brain-based, seven-year view to Wolverine's constant healed head trauma and concludes we should be slow to judge characters as the 'same' culpable person.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 20 "“Cyborgs Don’t Feel Pain. I Do.”" — Littmann uses the Terminator films to ask whether machines can be persons. The Terminators clearly pass the Turing Test by convincingly passing for human, giving behavioral evidence that they think. Littmann then presses Searle's Chinese Room, reworked as a tiny non-English-speaking Austrian inside the T-101 reciting phonetic lines, to argue that behavior alone cannot prove genuine understanding or feeling. He concludes that the films' 'Terminator's-eye-view' shots, showing the world from the machine's perspective, are the strongest evidence that the machines are conscious and so may count as people surviving humanity's extinction.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 9 "None of It Matters Anyway, Then, Does It" — William J. Devlin applies David Lewis's distinction between external time and the traveler's personal time to Lost's season 5-6 time jumps, showing how Faraday's eternalist 'whatever happened, happened' (Chang's unbreakable rules) contrasts with the branching-universe model that Faraday later embraces with 'we're the variables.' Lewis's account resolves specific puzzles: why baby Miles and adult Miles can coexist without violating the indiscernibility of identicals, whether Faraday could kill his mother Eloise (the grandfather paradox), and the uncaused causal loop of the compass Locke and Richard pass between 1954 and 2007.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 15 "6. In a Mirror Is Our Image" — Karavitis arranges thirteen Twilight Zone android/machine episodes on a moral spectrum from simple machines ('The Brain Center at Whipple's,' 'Steel') to indistinguishable androids ('The Lonely,' 'I Sing the Body Electric,' 'The Lateness of the Hour') to fully synthetic humans ('The Trade-Ins'). Using personhood, moral-agent/moral-patient distinctions, Aristotle's and Kant's views on animals, Singer and Regan on degrees not kinds, and Locke's memory theory of identity, he argues that if body-swapped Holts remain persons then scratch-built androids are persons too—so the destroyed androids were murdered, and evil is treating persons as disposable objects.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 16 "7. Loss of Memory, Loss of Me" — Lay contrasts Locke's memory theory of personal identity with Parfit's psychological-continuity view across several episodes. Locke's factive-memory account explains 'The After Hours' (Marsha the mannequin) and 'Person or Persons Unknown' (David Gurney's non-factive memories), but fails for 'The Lateness of the Hour' (android Jana has installed beliefs, not memories) and especially 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You,' where post-Transformation Marilyn keeps all her memories yet is a different person. Using a Reid-flavored chain of episodes, Lay argues Parfit gets it right: a whole overlapping network of mental states, not memory alone, individuates the self.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 20 "10. Memories Are Made of This" — Nisley reads two episodes through Hume's skepticism about the continued existence of objects and selves, which rests on memory, resemblance, and imagination rather than proof. In 'And When the Sky Was Opened,' three spacemen (Forbes, Harrington, Gart) progressively vanish as memory and corroborating testimony fail, dramatizing Hume's point that belief in continued existence needs more than force and vivacity of ideas. In 'The Trouble with Templeton,' Booth's dead wife Laura reappears but behaves unlike his memories, showing the imagination 'feigns' continuity; both episodes undermine memory as the foundation of rational belief.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 31 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Holdier asks how the many rival Elizabeth Bennets (Austen's, P.D. James's Death Comes to Pemberley, Grahame-Smith's zombie killer) can share an identity. He rejects the Cartesian cogito for ignoring circumstance and adopts Paul Ricoeur's ipse/idem distinction: the three Elizabeths may share the same ipse (moment-to-moment self and personality) while their different worlds produce distinct idem (narrative) identities. He then applies David Lewis's possible-world semantics and modal realism, arguing each Elizabeth is 'world-bound' and the others are her equally real 'counterparts,' sufficiently similar to be compared across worlds without being identical, so 'Elizabeth Bennet' can name both a single ipse and many idem narratives.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 14 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Fink-Jensen, an anthropologist, uses narrative analysis and rites-of-passage theory (Van Gennep's separation/liminal/reincorporation stages) to examine how men construct the internal identity of 'father.' Drawing on interviews with first-time dads (Marc, Jim, Craig, Steve), she argues that because men lack the biological markers of pregnancy they feel alienated from the transition, and that Western 'couvade' activities – attending prenatal classes and appointments, hearing the heartbeat – plus telling birth stories function as rituals that cement fatherhood as an identity.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 29 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Carreras, writing as a son, examines the ethical tension in the father-son relationship between using a father's inevitable influence and fostering the son's autonomy. Opening with Aristotle on parents loving children as 'something of himself,' he uses the case of Jerry (a lawyer) pressuring his son Jose (who loves 18th-century English literature) to argue for a 'foundational view' of autonomy – that the best life is one embraced 'from the inside,' likened to seeing without a value-blindfold – and advises fathers to ask 'Is this what he truly wants, or what I want?'
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 8 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Robert Arp's introduction takes Descartes' 'I think, therefore I am' and its mind–body dualism (the conceivability argument that mind is distinct from body) and inverts it into the book's motto 'I am, therefore I ink': the tattooed person insists identity is bodily-based self-expression, challenging the Cartesian idea that the essential self is a non-bodily thinking thing. Arp flags Descartes' possible question-begging, then previews each chapter, framing tattoos as fertile ground for the philosophy of the person, personal identity over time, and self-expression.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 20 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Kyle Fruh and Emily Thomas use tattoos to attack two questions of personal identity. Against Locke's dominant psychological (memory) account and for the unpopular somatic (bodily) account defended by Judith Thomson and Eric Olson, they argue the depth of people's attachment to their tattoos – individuating them or marking group membership – shows we identify with our bodies. On the 'Who am I?' question they argue tattoos have an 'anchoring effect' in narrative identity: permanent, irremovable ink (contrasted with new laser-removable ink, and with dehumanizing forced Auschwitz numbers) fixes a commitment 'come what may,' echoing Quine's phrase, so that 'when you get a tattoo, you tattoo you.'
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 21 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Rachel Falkenstern argues that although tattoos seem permanent, the embodied self is changing and finite, so tattoos are 'illusions of permanence.' Using Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology she dissolves the mind/body and self/tattoo boundary (we are our bodies, the world shapes us and we shape it); using the German aesthetic tradition from Kant to Hegel she reads a tattoo as a sensuous 'appearance of freedom' and links the Romantic notion of Bildung (self-formation) to choosing ink. She adds Foucault's aesthetic self-transformation and Shusterman's somaesthetics/Deweyan pragmatism to cast tattooing as reciprocal self-expression and self-creation that offers a glimpse of infinity within finitude.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 28 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Decker reads Ray Bradbury's 'The Illustrated Man' (William Phelps, whose witch-inked tattoo of murdering his wife Lisabeth becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy) and 'The Illustrated Woman' (Emma and Willy Fleet's shared delusion of an invisible masterpiece) to ask whether 'the body is our fate.' He aligns Phelps's predetermined tattoo with Alvin Goldman's 'Book of Life' thought experiment about foreknowledge and lost free will, and with Foucault's claim that power socially constructs docile bodies. Against this fatalism he sets George Herbert Mead's creative social self, 'taking the attitude of the other,' arguing tattooing is a plural renegotiation of identity rather than a fixed inscription.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 17 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Kristie Miller asks whether any dating behavior—dating a sibling, a gorilla, or a blow-up doll—is genuinely 'taboo' in the prudential (self-interested, utility-maximizing) rather than ethical sense, using decision theory's notion of maximizing expected utility. She sorts behaviors labeled 'pathological' into merely conventionally pathological, pseudo-pathological (e.g., polyandry explained by resource scarcity and childrearing), and genuinely pathological (arising from malfunctioning evolved mate-selection modules like symmetry or MHC-odor detection). Because inclusive fitness and utility diverge, and using future-selves discounting and weakness of will (the stable partner vs. the bad-boy biker), she concludes that in some circumstances even dating a sibling or a gorilla can be the utility-maximizing, and thus rational, choice.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 13 "The Vampire with a Soul Angel and the Quest for Identity" — Amy Kind uses Joss Whedon's Angel/Angelus to test theories of personal identity and moral responsibility. Body-swap episodes support the Lockean/Parfitian psychological (memory) theory over Olson's biological theory, and shared memories make Angel psychologically continuous with, hence identical to, Angelus. But Kind invokes Parfit's distinction between continuity and connectedness (with real cases like Katherine Power and Sara Jane Olson) to argue identity is not what matters: the ensouled Angel's radical break in psychological connectedness means he should not be held morally responsible for Angelus's atrocities. She closes with Mill that it is better to be Angel burdened by a soul than Angelus unburdened.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 10 "4. Total Recall & The Sixth Day" — Rowlands treats Total Recall as a defence of the memory (psychological-continuity) theory of personal identity: erasing Quaid's memories and restoring Hauser's is an essential change that ends Quaid, so he fights for his existence. He works through and rejects the soul theory (dualism's problems) and body/brain theories via head-transplant and neuron-replacement thought experiments, distinguishing Aristotle's essential/accidental change and Heraclitus's river. The Sixth Day's cloning raises Parfit's fission/duplication problem: a double success cannot be a failure, driving him to abandon identity for a Heraclitean 'river of selves' bound by survival, not identity.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 15 "9. Blade Runner" — Using Blade Runner's replicants ('I want more life, fucker!') and Roy's dying soliloquy, Rowlands asks how death can harm the one who dies. He states the Epicurean argument (while we live death is not yet; when dead there is no one to harm) and answers via harms of deprivation, illustrated by Tyrell's imagined brain damage. Drawing on Wittgenstein (death as the limit of life) and Heidegger's being-towards-death/being-towards-a-future, he distinguishes weak (non-conceptual) from strong (conceptual) possession of a future, arguing death harms more those with more invested. Linear time and the ultimate horizon of death are what let a life have meaning at all.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 24 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Bill Davis explains why Arwen relinquishes elvish immortality and why Aragorn and Frodo accept death as a 'gift,' contrasting the Ringwraiths' cursed undeath (an Aristotelian frustration of their mortal nature) with genuine mortality. He surveys real-world responses to death: Socrates' calm confidence in the soul, Lucretius's and the existentialists' liberation through annihilation, and worries from Bernard Williams and others about the tedium of immortality, which Boethius answers with a timeless heaven. Davis argues Arwen chooses a finite life of deep love over deathless boredom, and that all three accept death trusting Iluvatar's love promises a world remade beyond the circles of the world.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 13 "Who is Who" — On regeneration and personal identity, the chapter runs Doctor Who through Leibniz's law of identity and soul-based individuation, Locke's memory criterion of personhood, and Hume's bundle theory, testing them against multi-Doctor stories, the Ganger duplicates ('The Almost People'), 'The Girl Who Waited' (closest-continuer theory) and 'City of Death.' It then shifts to physicalism (the Morbius brain) and to a pragmatist, social theory of the self (James, Dewey, Mead's 'taking the attitude of the other,' Dennett's intentional stance), reading the reintegration of identity in 'The Doctor Dances.'
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 18 "Be Slow to Judge" — Jason Southworth uses Wolverine's repeated memory erasures to test Locke's memory (and connected-memory) criterion of personal identity, arguing that on Locke's view a new 'person' inhabits Wolverine's body each time his memories are wiped, until House of M restores them all. He then deploys Jamie Madrox, whose duplicates share and re-merge memories yet act as distinct agents, as a real-comics version of Parfit's fission case, pushing Parfit's conclusion that identity requires physical (brain) continuity. Because Wolverine's healing factor constantly rebuilds his brain, the moral is to 'be slow to judge' whether a character is the same person who acted before.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 7 "5. Battlestar Galactica as Philosophy Breaking the Biopolitical Cycle" — Eberl and Bishop read the reimagined Battlestar Galactica and Caprica through the biopolitics of Foucault and Agamben, tracing 'biopower' across four phases from Zoe Graystone's avatar to the arrival at Earth. They argue the show asks whether artificial Cylons are persons (Zoe's avatar exhibits Baker's first-person perspective and Buber's I-Thou recognition), and use Agamben's zoe/bios/'bare life' and Homo sacer plus Roslin's population control and abortion ban to show sovereign power over life. The Cylon occupation of New Caprica is read through Arendt's three stages of totalitarian dehumanization, and Lee Adama's plea to 'break the cycle' offers a fragile hope undercut by the finale's flash-forward to present-day robotics, showing humanity forgetting the lesson.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 20 "18. Russian Doll as Philosophy Life Is Like a Box of Timelines" — The chapter treats Russian Doll's time loops (Season One) and time portals (Season Two) as vehicles for the metaphysics of time, comparing them to Groundhog Day and canvassing presentism, eternalism, and the growing-block theory. It argues the show is committed to a Parfit-style 'multiple timelines' solution to the problem of whether looped characters are numerically identical, and rejects a Berkeleyan idealist alternative. Its climax reads Nadia through Camus's Myth of Sisyphus: unable to change significant past events, she becomes an 'absurd hero' who embraces her family and lot in life, smiling in the mirror, so Season Two's lesson (echoing Nietzsche's eternal recurrence) is that meaning comes from owning one's circumstances.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 44 "41. Blade Runner as Philosophy What Does It Mean to Be Human" — Shanahan argues Blade Runner is philosophical despite Ridley Scott's denial, using the replicants (Roy Batty, Rachael, Leon) as defamiliarizing 'mirrors' for the human condition. He shows the Nexus-6 replicants satisfy Descartes' two criteria for a thinking soul (linguistic flexibility, novel problem-solving) while human characters like Deckard prove as cold and empathy-deficient as the machines, collapsing the human/replicant distinction the Voight-Kampff test presumes. He then reads Rachael's implanted memories through Locke's memory theory of personal identity, Roy's 'tears in rain' death through Epicurean worries about finitude, and frames the whole via Plato's Cave line 'they are like us' — the replicants model our own concerns with memory, death, and the meaning of a temporally bounded life.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 58 "55. Avatar as Philosophy The Metaphysics of Switching Bodies" — Tepley asks whether Jake Sully's final body-switch with his avatar in Cameron's Avatar is metaphysically possible without brain transplant or souls. Using Locke's definition of a person and the transitivity of numerical identity, he shows animalism forbids body-switching, substance dualism (Descartes/Plato) is unavailable in the film's materialist world, and merely copying a brain pattern creates a duplicate, not the same person. His positive solution uses the constitution view (Aristotelian in origin) plus Clark's extended-mind idea to argue Jake literally extends into his avatar, then—via an analogy with split-brain corpus-callosum cases discussed by Nagel, Parfit, and van Inwagen—shrinks back so long as no second stream of consciousness forms, a model he extends to secular survival of death by mind-uploading.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 84 "79. Cyberpunk 2077 as Philosophy Balancing the (Mystical) Ghost in the (Transhuman) Machine" — Lay reads Cyberpunk 2077's transhuman Night City against the enhancement debate. Using the Ship of Theseus, Parfit's continuity plus fission/fusion (V and Johnny 'fusing,' the Delamain AIs) and Clark and Chalmers's extended mind, he argues enhancement neither destroys personal identity (which Parfit says doesn't matter) nor dehumanizes users — it may be the purest expression of Clark's cyborg humanity. The real danger is corporate exploitation of bodies, explained via Adorno's culture industry and Arendt's banality of evil. Buddhist nonattachment (Nagarjuna's emptiness, echoed by a Schopenhauer shard) grounds each ending's pacification-versus-attachment theme, but Lay corrects it with Weil's critique of power and Buber's I-Thou, concluding the game urges transcending the boundary between 'me' and 'you' through mystical interpersonal relation.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 90 "85. Persona 5 Royal as Philosophy Unmasking (Persona)l Identity and Reality" — Lopez and Marquez use Persona 5 Royal's Phantom Thieves to explore Schechtman's 'characterization' question of personal identity ('Who am I?') via three bases: qualia (the privately felt sense of self expressed when Ryuji names himself a 'troublemaker' and Morgana insists he is 'NOT a cat'), Wittgensteinian hinge propositions, and language-games in which identity and 'justice' get their meaning through use. Ryle and Wittgenstein's behaviorist worries about private language are set against Nagel's bat and Chalmers's qualia. The Maruki arc—offering a pain-free false utopia and Sumire living as her dead twin Kasumi—poses whether Bentham's utilitarianism, James's pragmatism, or Baudrillard's hyperreality could justify a blissful simulacrum, which the game's 'true ending' rejects for painful reality.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 12 "3. What Is Who" — The chapter runs the Doctor's regenerations and the 'Timeless Child' reveal through competing theories of personal identity: Plato's soul/Forms, Locke's memory continuity, and bodily continuity, all of which the Doctor's body-swaps and forgotten lifetimes defeat (the Twelfth Doctor's 'you are a broom' speech recasts the Ship of Theseus). It endorses an existentialist answer—personal identity is chosen and constantly 'becoming,' as the Thirteenth Doctor declares 'I know exactly who I am. I'm the Doctor'—and uses Sartre against Freud to explain how the Doctor and the Whovian fandom reconcile internal and external selves in a community of acceptance. It closes arguing that only an 'objective' immortality (memories preserved in the Matrix) survives death, not a subjective self.

### Atman and Brahman

Atman and Brahman are the twin poles of much of classical Indian metaphysics: atman is the innermost self or consciousness, while Brahman is the ultimate, unconditioned ground of all reality. In the Advaita Vedanta system articulated by Shankara, the deepest teaching of the Upanishads is that these two are not different but identical, so that the true self is nothing other than the absolute. Ordinary experience of a separate, individual self is traced to ignorance, and liberation comes through the direct realization of this underlying unity. The position is a rigorous nondualism, holding that plurality and separateness are ultimately appearance rather than final truth.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 78 "Unknown" — The chapter reinterprets Kant's second postulate: God is not the external distributor of justice whose theological counterpart is our sense of powerlessness before the all-powerful machines, but the power of united humanity - 'one for all and all for one', the third, still-unfinished Matrix of Zion. The spoon-bending boy supplies the illustration: we cannot bend the spoon so long as we believe reality is a separate material substance, but recognizing its unity with us, 'it is only yourself' that bends - and Neo's real lesson is not that he is a special being but that he is One with all existence.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 14 "Mind the Mindfulness" — Reads The Meaning of Life as a sustained reductio of transcendentalism — the two-world metaphysics shared by Plato, Augustine, and Vedanta's Brahman/atman — arguing that the film's dehumanizing sketches (the machine that goes 'ping,' the 'every sperm is sacred' father selling his children, the Vegas-style Christmas in Heaven) show how otherworldly belief overrides this-worldly compassion. It parallels the Buddha's scriptural critiques: the Agganna sutta against caste, the no-self (anatta) doctrine against the Bhagavad Gita's soul that licenses Krishna to tell Arjuna killing is a favor, and impermanence (anicca) against the fantasy of eternal bliss. Python's grotesque — Creosote's explosion, the organ-donor lady's 'Galaxy Song' despair — matches Buddhist corpse meditations, while the film steers between hedonism (Creosote) and nihilism (the housewife who surrenders her liver) toward the Buddha's Middle Way and, against everyday distraction (the boardroom's 'people are not wearing enough hats,' the couple who think Schopenhauer begins with an S), toward mindfulness (sati).
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 32 "Who Wants to Be Human Anyway" — Reads Kenji Kawai's thrice-repeated minyo 'Ghost theme' as the key to Major Kusanagi's quest in Ghost in the Shell and Innocence: each richer orchestration tracks her progress from manufactured shell, through the diving-scene worry that only others' treatment makes her human, to merging with the Puppet Master. Using Koestler's holons — individuals preserved while functioning within an evolving whole — and his view of consciousness as emergent (itself a rejection of both Descartes's immaterial soul and Ryle's dismissal of the 'ghost in the machine'), the chapter argues Oshii first celebrates the Major's Atman-like self-transcendence, then subverts Koestler in Innocence by making machines human: the ghost-dubbed gynoids act as a voiceless pack while the Major, still recognizably herself, aids Batou from the net — and Kawai's music literally gives the dolls a voice.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 36 "22. The Many-Faced God and Indian Philosophy" — Van Eyghen maps the Faceless Men onto Indian philosophy: their one God of many faces parallels Vedanta's Brahman in personal form as Ishvara, and Arya's training to become 'no one' parallels shedding the ego toward identity with Brahman - with Jaqen as guru and the stick-beating ritual as an example of identity fusion in Harvey Whitehouse's cognitive science of religion. But the Faceless Men may go further than Vedanta toward Buddhism, since they worship a god with no face of his own and aim at no-self rather than union, while Arya's pragmatic adoption of the shellfish-merchant disguise echoes the Bhagavad Gita's Krishna: perform your duty without attachment to any self.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 12 "2. Know Thyself, Agent Cooper!" — Reads the Season Two Black Lodge finale as Cooper's failed journey of self-knowledge, framed by Socrates' Delphic "know thyself" and the unexamined life. Against Hume's bundle theory — when Hume looks inward he only ever finds particular perceptions, never a self — the chapter sets the Vedanta/Tibetan Buddhist ideal of knowing the true Self beyond thought (the ocean versus its waves), with the Black Lodge as the place Hawk calls a passage "every soul must pass on its way to perfection." Cooper's screaming white-eyed Laura, the flickering Caroline/Annie corpse, and his grinning doppelgänger are Jungian shadow-projections paralleled scene-by-scene with the wrathful visions of the Tibetan Book of the Dead; entering with imperfect courage, he flees his fears instead of integrating them, splitting into trapped good Dale and the rampaging Mr. C of The Return.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 34 "19. Hinduism Gets More than Five Percent Right" — Kaur and Gupta argue Hinduism got far more than five percent right, mapping the show's points onto karmic theory and the Bhagavad Gita's three kinds of action: right action, inaction, and wrong action. Eleanor's fruitless point-grubbing and selfless departure exemplify nishkama karma, desire-less action, while the 802 reboots and Janet's memory-wiped revivals mirror the birth-death-rebirth cycle on the way to self-realization. Ranking the cast on the Gita's ladder of unfoldment, desire-driven Eleanor and Jason below Tahani and knowledgeable Chidi, with Michael straying from his dharma and detached, duty-bound Janet nearest to Brahman, they show the series dramatizes the Gita's teaching that motivation, not the deed itself, determines an act's worth.
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 24 "The Danger of Thinking “Science Is Whatever We Want It to Be”; or, the" — Barkman reads the 30 Rock cast as prisoners who prefer delusion, using Plato's allegory of the cave and the Upanishadic scheme of samsara, karma, maya, and moksha, in which Atman is realized as one with Brahman, as twin diagnoses. Drew's 'bubble' of good looks, Liz's false memory of being a harmless nerd in 'Reunion' and her belief she can have it all, Jack's pride about his terrible sketch ideas, Kenneth's unexamined dogma ('I can't handle the truth!'), Jenna's age-hiding, and Tracy's white myths about diabetes and Colorado all illustrate ignorance of reality that costs happiness. The Hindu-Platonic lesson is that knowledge of reality, not Dr. Spaceman's 'science is whatever we want it to be', is the route to happiness, because ignorance is not bliss.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 34 "19. Hinduism Gets More than Five Percent Right" — Argues Hinduism 'gets more than five percent right' via the Bhagavad Gita: the show's point system mirrors karma, Eleanor's failed point-chasing and quiet departure for the Bad Place enact nishkama karma (desire-less action), and the 802 reboots are rebirths without memory. The characters form a ladder of unfoldment — Jason's unknowing wrong action below Eleanor's knowing one, Tahani's corruptly motivated good deeds, Chidi's knowledge without decision, Michael swerving from his demonic dharma, and Janet highest: desireless, rebooting like cyclical rebirth, her void echoing boundless Brahman. Chidi's logic-bound indecision versus Eleanor's knowledge-producing logic completes the Gita reading.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 18 "Notes" — Reads Rust's 'dream inside a locked room' and 'everybody is nobody' monologues through the dream-argument and illusion-of-self traditions: the Upanishads and Advaita's atman/brahman, Vasubandhu's Buddhist non-self, Zhuangzi's butterfly dream, Plato's Theaetetus, and Descartes' dream doubt, plus Metzinger's self-model neuroscience. It diagnoses Rust as a neuro-nihilist in Metzinger's sense and defines his predicament with Nietzsche's nihilist, who judges the world as it is that it ought not to be, while noting Schopenhauer misread India's religions as pessimistic. Thompson argues nihilism is a deep insight gone awry — the self is not a thing but an enacted process like dancing — and reads Rust's final near-death experience of love as proof that transcendence of the dream of being a person is possible.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 22 "Spontaneity, Immediacy, and Difference Philosophy, Being in Time, and Creativity in the Aesthetics of Jack Ker" — David Need contrasts three theories of 'being in time' behind the aesthetics of spontaneity: Kerouac's debt to Spengler's organic cycles of civilization (a stereoscopic, dualist view where an arbitrary measure like a candle or page limns deep being), Olson's use of Whitehead's 'concrescence' in 'Projective Verse' (a monist, all-at-once projection of new monads), and Cage's use of Coomaraswamy's Vedanta, where silence is sabdabrahman and chance imitates Nature. He argues the real fault line is the old monist-vs-dualist divide (Advaita brahman vs. Cartesian dualism), and that each artist's notion of creative freedom follows from which metaphysical schema he borrowed, so our quarrels with the Beats reflect our own metaphysical stakes.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 12 "2. Know Thyself, Agent Cooper!" — De Carvalho reads Cooper's ordeal in the Black Lodge as a journey of self-knowledge, distinguishing 'knowing yourself' (your feelings, as Laura sought with Dr. Jacoby) from 'knowing your Self' in the deep sense of Vedanta's Brahman and Tibetan Buddhism's Mind. He sets Hume's bundle theory—the failure to catch a self behind the perceptions—against the Hindu Swami's ocean-and-waves image of an eternal Self beyond thought, and reads Cooper's confrontation with his screaming-Laura and doppelganger visions via the Tibetan Book of the Dead and Jung's shadow: facing his fears with imperfect courage, Cooper fails to integrate his shadow and is split in two.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 26 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — LoPresti uses the 'This Week in God' segments (the God Machine, Ed Helms's Hindu-vs-Mayan 'faith-off,' Colbert's inclusivist White House roast) to lay out three responses to religious diversity—exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism—and defends John Cobb's Whiteheadian process-metaphysics pluralism. He insists the distinct concepts of religions be respected rather than collapsed, citing Buddhist impermanence and no-Self and the South Asian Atman/Brahman as unique and non-reducible, and closes by reading the show's turn to political framing of religion through Marx's claim that religion is a mechanism for controlling the masses.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 8 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — John Friend's foreword surveys yoga's three classical philosophical systems and connects them to how modern Hatha yoga is practiced: Classical (Patanjali) yoga as separating purusha (spirit) from prakriti (matter) to reach kaivalya; Vedanta as neutralizing maya to realize the unity of atman with the supreme; and non-dual Tantra, from which Hatha yoga derives, treating body and mind as frequencies of one divine Shiva-Shakti energy. It argues yoga's enduring claim is that the essential self is free, and that direct lived experience of that freedom outranks merely intellectual knowledge of the texts.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 18 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Ken Burak describes teaching yoga in his philosophy class — a 'three wheels' exercise moving from the true self behind our masks to the Upanishadic identity of Atman and Brahman ('Thou Art That') — to give students embodied access to the universal/particular problem. He reads Western philosophy from Plato's Phaedo (Socrates seeking death as liberation of soul from body) through Descartes' doubt as a 2500-year practice of pratyahara (sense-withdrawal), one limb mistaken for the whole journey, and asks what asana and this long retreat could each bring the other.

### The Tao (the Way)

The Tao, or the Way, is the central notion of Daoism: the nameless, formless source and ordering principle from which all things arise and to which they return. In the Daodejing, associated with Laozi, the Tao is said to be beyond full description or definition—"the Tao that can be spoken is not the eternal Tao"—yet it can be sensed and followed by those who cultivate stillness and simplicity. Living well means aligning oneself with this natural course rather than resisting it through force, ambition, or excessive contrivance.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 14 "Was it a Show about Nothing" — Eric Bronson takes George's NBC pitch for 'a show about nothing' as a live philosophical problem: Parmenides argued we cannot meaningfully speak of what-is-not (so Art Vandelay is unsayable), but Plato's Sophist answers that nothing is 'otherness' with real power - the puffy shirt is something other than beautiful, and 'The Parking Garage' is doing something other than what is interesting or useful. Lao Tzu's Tao Te Ching goes further: the nameless Tao begets the ten thousand things, and wei wu wei (action through non-action) conquers, as in 'The Chinese Restaurant', where a whole episode of standing in line doing nothing is itself something happening.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 29 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Jennifer McMahon and Steve Csaki compare Tolkien with Zen Buddhism and Taoism on four themes while insisting on the real differences. Tolkien's talking trees (Old Man Willow, Treebeard's 'half awake' forest) invite comparison with Buddhist universal sentience and Dogen's walking mountains, but Tolkien anthropomorphizes where Buddhism grants non-human modes of sentience; the hobbits' ties to the Shire echo dependent origination, though Tolkien's stewardship and preference for the domesticated Shire over sinister wild nature remain Western. Frodo's succession of mentors (Bilbo, Gandalf, Aragorn, and the unlikely 'Master Samwise') parallels the Zen master-student relation, while Tolkien's war of light against darkness - nine Walkers against nine Riders - is decisively not the Taoist balance of yin and yang, for Taoists destroying either cosmic force would itself produce evil.
- **The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am**, ch. 14 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" — Argues Tony misappropriates Sun Tzu's Art of War: he applies tactical precepts like deception, formlessness and 'Balk the enemy's power' (citing the book in 'He Is Risen' after Melfi's jab in 'Big Girls Don't Cry'), but ignores the philosophical core. The chapter contrasts Sun Tzu's monistic one-world view of yin-yang interdependence, harmony and winning without fighting with the Greek two-world dualism of Plato and with the Christianity that lets Tony tell Melfi 'soldiers don't go to hell' in 'From Where to Eternity'. Tony's sausage panic attacks in 'Fortunate Son' show his failure to see how his crimes ripple through his family, and because he lacks the commander's exemplary character and harmony, Tony is 'just a soldier', not a ruler.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 29 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Jones narrates a day riding a customized Sportster around O'ahu as a lived Daoism that heals the Platonic-Cartesian mind-body split: the ride enacts Zhuangzi's 'rambling without destination' and Cook Ding's effortless wu-wei, rider li (the low hand-greeting among riders) is Confucian ritual propriety, and the island's dry and wet ranges embody yin and yang through whose flow the rider blends. Heraclitus's 'expect the unexpected' and 'the sun is new every day' are vindicated when a container truck stops short and only the disciplined, ego-less low-side, dropping the beloved bike while riding the skid, saves the rider's life, sealing the day's lesson that there is never freedom without discipline. Sartre's hell of other people appears in the cagers' compartmentalized inattention, and the chapter closes with Zhuangzi: 'The way is made by walking it.'
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 46 "Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat" — In a fictional interview with the Taoist sage "Bat-Tzu," Mark White explains Taoism through Batman's circle: Bruce's yang-dominated life of vengeance and paranoia needs the yin that Dick and Tim supply, shown by his forgiveness of Zatanna and tenderness toward Helena's baby, while Jason Todd illustrates the fate of the unbalanced who cannot accept death. Alfred emerges as the Taoist sage practicing wei-wu-wei, effortless service like Chuang Tzu's butcher, balancing right and wrong in Bruce, and the Batman-Joker duality shows yin and yang defining each other. Lao Tzu's sayings on balance, complementary opposites, and water-like yielding organize the whole reading.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 10 "I Still Miss Someone The Self and Its Travels Along the Way" — Geisz explains the Confucian social dao of ritual (li), humaneness (ren), filial piety and the junzi, the Daodejing's metaphysical Dao with its unity of opposites, and Zhuangzi's tales of free wandering, then maps all three onto Cash's songs. Zhuangzi's "Free and Easy Wandering" answers Cash's road songs ("I've Been Everywhere," "The Wanderer"), Cook Ding's effortless carving answers John Henry's hammering in "The Legend of John Henry's Hammer," and the scrambled countdown of "Twenty-Five Minutes to Go" echoes Zhuangzi's logic-bending humor. The payoff is Cash's own country Yin-Yang of interdependent opposites, freedom chained to imprisonment ("Folsom Prison Blues"), sin twinned with redemption ("I Hung My Head"), fidelity with betrayal ("Jackson," "Cocaine Blues"), and a self that, unlike Zhuangzi's self-forgetting sage, must travel a temporal path carrying its guilt, yet stays on what Geisz calls a very wide superhighway of a Dao.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 38 "Teddy Baseball" — Lee reads Ted Williams's The Science of Hitting as a Daoist skill story from the Zhuangzi: 'get a good ball to hit' matches the cicada-catcher's total absorption in the cicada's wings, hitting 'by feel' like the carpenter's hammer matches Cook Ding carving without looking, and Williams's midnight batting practice after Korea matches the wheelwright grown old at his craft—effortless spontaneity produced by disciplined practice and unified attention, not mere mechanics. Williams's 'proper thinking' is Daoist sorting of objective conditions rather than abstract disputation. The closing tale of the old woman who cannot teach the Way to someone lacking the stuff explains why Williams failed as Senators manager: his players did not have the native talent to receive it.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 20 "The End" — Chan contrasts Zhuangzi's butterfly dream, where dream and reality form one transformable whole and the self is forgotten, with Inception's dreams, which are rigidly structured and must be kept strictly separate from reality for Cobb to function. She shows that the film's motifs (the dream machine, the spinning top, the faceless children) work as narrative codes marking each dream layer, making Inception an example of 'dream explaining' rather than Tarkovsky-style 'dream worshipping'. The chapter concludes that Inception's 'dreams' are really a meta-space narrative device, as in Nolan's short Doodlebug, and that the film lacks the Daoist sense of the whole, so Cobb can never transform into the butterfly.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 36 "Psych and Philosophy" — John Thompson argues Psych embodies the Daoist Way of reversal from the Daodejing and Zhuangzi: every episode begins with a death that triggers Shawn and Gus's irreverent, backwards-tracing investigation, their untrained spontaneous 'gifts' exemplify wu wei like Cook Ding carving an ox, and their bickering partnership is yin-yang interplay (as when Gus leads the joking in 'An Evening with Mr. Yang'). Zhuangzi singing at his wife's funeral parallels the Shabby the Sea Lion and 'Dust in the Wind' funeral parodies, the show's blurred TV-versus-fandom reality echoes the butterfly dream, Lassiter succeeds when he relaxes into wu wei ('Feet Don't Kill Me Now'), and the closing bloopers enact Dao's endless reversal - though the chapter ends by conceding Dao defies the very label 'Daoist show.'
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 36 "22. The Dao of Master Westley" — Doll tests each character against the Dao: Confucius's identification of the Dao with tradition and ritual fails because Florinese tradition is exactly what enables Humperdinck's murder and war plans, so she turns to Laozi's De and wu-wei, diagnosing Vizzini's fatal overconfidence (he lacked Socratic knowledge of his own ignorance), Humperdinck's paranoia, and Buttercup's passivity as failures to sense when to act and when to refrain. Westley emerges as Zhuangzi's ideal - like Cook Ting the butcher, mastering skills until instinct suffices: adapting through the Fire Swamp, treating Vizzini's death as 'an appropriate death', yet sparing Inigo and Fezzik because killing them would be against nature, which is why the giant and the Spaniard accept him as their sage.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 42 "27. The Mystic with the Mouth" — In a lecture Deadpool keeps interrupting, the chapter reads the Merc's violence through Bataille's Theory of Religion: sacrifice as the search for lost intimacy, killing as the moment sacrificer and victim escape the profane world of mere things into sacred immanence, and sovereignty as the freedom glimpsed in destruction, with Rudolf Otto's mysterium tremendum et fascinans naming the awe Deadpool's massacres (the Circle Chase nunchuks, the Ultimate cartoon, the movie's highway slaughter) provoke. His 'dark Dao' of unhappy wandering is then set against the playful ways of the Zhuangzi - Cook Ding's ox-butchering, the Peng bird, the maimed teacher Wang Tai - as a Daoist path of inner-worldly transcendence that is amoral and gore-soaked. The payoff is the human tension of being both animal and angel: Deadpool is 'a savage god of mystical mayhem.'
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 27 "15. Farts, Butterflies, and Inner Truth" — Franklin Perkins reads Frank's fear that his jewelry business might start World War III — 'you can't fart without changing the balance in the universe' — as the butterfly-effect problem of acting inside a complexity we cannot grasp, from the Roosevelt assassination down to Tagomi's Colt .44. Against the Germans' fatal flight into abstraction (Volk, Blut, Ehre), the chapter presents the I Ching, read through Chinese correlative cosmology of the Tao and yin-yang, as a manual for mole-like, concrete, adaptive interpretation in which each casting (hexagram 11's 'wall falls back into the moat,' the purple knee bands) means only through creative engagement, ending with hexagram 61: our world arose as contingently as a throw of the yarrow stalks.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 27 "The Way of the Archer" — White reads Clint Barton through the Tao Te Ching and Chuang Tzu: Hawkeye's instinctive archery—'use your bow gently, naturally, instinctively'—is wei wu wei, while his bragging, his glory-chasing failure against Iron Man, and his attempt to become Goliath all violate it by striving against his own nature, until the Kree-Skrull War teaches him the bow is his way. Chuang Tzu's butcher carves the lesson that the effortless path (the straightforward shot) is the skilled one, and Lao Tzu's sage-leadership—lowering oneself, deflecting praise—is exactly how Captain America handles Clint's insurrections. Lao Tzu on sages putting themselves last illuminates Hawkeye's sacrificial death and his legacy passed to Kate Bishop, while the butterfly dream frames his resurrection and the House of M's rewritten reality: with no way to compare the states, life and death are both to be welcomed as parts of the Way.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 34 "NOTES" — The book's final chapter is a mock interview in which 'Bat-Tzu' applies Taoism to Bruce Wayne's life: his yang (hard, retributive crime-fighting) has dominated his yin (his tenderness toward Dick, Tim, and Helena), and Robin has always been the yin balancing the Dark Knight. Quoting Lao-Tzu's Tao Te Ching and Chuang-Tzu on duality, acceptance of death (Jason Todd's resurrection), and effortlessness, the piece casts Alfred as the Taoist sage whose help exemplifies wu-wei, like Chuang-Tzu's butcher who cuts without dulling his blade. It even reads Batman's most intimidating feature, his absent shadow, as proof that nothingness can matter more than substance.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 15 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Lynch tests the fan claims that the Dude is 'the Duddha' or a practicing Daoist: the Dude has wu wei in his effortless arts of bowling and abiding and shares Zhuangzi's withdrawal from society (the Nixon bowling poster, learning from drunks, Donny's ashes scattered with naturalistic acceptance), but lacks Daoist metaphysics, the Dao's inexpressibility, and any articulated views. The Buddha parallels are real — nonattachment, practice over theory (the poisoned-arrow parable), compassion for Bunny — yet Gautama's radical discipline and middle path are the opposite of the Dude's laziness, so Dudeism emerges as an undisciplined American cousin, and the Dude follows 'just his way and his alone'.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 14 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Morgan Deane reads Ender's tactics as Sunzi's Art of War in action: winning all future fights by terror, exploiting Bonzo's hot anger, 'fatal terrain' when Graff stacks hopeless odds, formlessness that hides intent, and fluid toon formations that move like water — all grounded in Daoist harmony with the Way and the Confucian role-duty of the general-as-father who throws soldiers into hopeless positions to win their devotion. He also finds Legalist rewards-and-punishments in Ender's command of Dragon Army, concluding Ender qualifies as a Sunzi-style military genius whose empathy is the steep moral price of victory.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 10 "a3.xhtml" — Brannigan reads Bilbo's tug-of-war between Baggins security and Took adventure through Taoism: the two desires are not contradictory but the interplay of yin and yang, and true dwelling is found in the journey itself, as the 'Roads go ever on' song says. Greed is the great weight - Thorin enslaved by the treasure he 'never forgot', Smaug hoarding for hoarding's sake, even the orc-loving of machines - and the cure is the mirror-mind of Empty Mind that reflects without grasping, illustrated by the Taoist masters tale of 'Gold-Is-Heavy' and 'Empty-Mind'. Beorn, who lives on honey indifferent to gold, and Bilbo, who in the spirit of wu-wei sheds his desire for the Arkenstone and finally lets go of the Ring, embody life in harmony with the Tao.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 20 "The End" — Hiu M. Chan contrasts Zhuangzi's butterfly dream with Inception's plot: Zhuangzi forgets his self, dreams without planning, and ends in the 'transformation and unity' of dreamer and butterfly, whereas Cobb's self is constantly highlighted — he plans missions, codes his dreams with motifs (the spinning top, the dream machine, the faceless children, distinct locations, weather, crosscutting), and can never fuse dream and reality. The chapter maps the film's four-layer 'meta-space' narrative structure (exposition through resolution distributed across dream layers) and argues the 'dreams' are really programmed, coded narrative devices, the opposite of the Daoist 'whole' in which reality itself is the biggest dream and a true person no longer dreams. Against semiotic 'dream explaining' (the top means dreaming), she holds that in Daoism the top would mean nothing beyond a spinning top, and contrasts Nolan with Tarkovsky's 'dream worshipping' films like The Mirror. The ending's reunion is thus only apparent: Inception lacks the Daoist harmony that would let Cobb 'become the butterfly.'
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 28 "Notes" — Bein reads the LEGO brick as the Daodejing's 'uncarved block': a single brick is an invitation rather than a toy, and precisely because it is empty of meaning (and mostly empty of plastic — the stud-and-tube marriage of yin and yang) it can become anything, whereas printed, specialized pieces 'are diminished by being added to'. Against the Greek obsession with definition — Socrates refusing sophistry while insisting one cannot rule justly without defining justice, Plato's definition dialogues, Aristotle's inheritance of the precision ideal, and William James's 'think clearly' — Daoist imprecision is defended as a philosophical stance: dao is a way, an activity, not a thing. Wei wu wei ('doing without doing') explains Emmet's winning plan of building the utterly ordinary Octan spaceship, why Lord Business's penny-throw is genius without sagacity (coercive, not water-like), and why governing should be like cooking a small fish — minimal, attentive intervention.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 29 "NOTE" — Shai Biderman and William Devlin argue the character John Locke begins as an empiricist in the mold of his philosophical namesake - his boar hunting, tracking, and trebuchet-building against the hatch all follow the scientific method befitting a tabula rasa mind furnished by experience - but the miracle of his healed legs poses a 'why' that empirical explanation of 'how' cannot answer. He therefore converts to the Taoism of the Tao Te Ching: the moth-cocoon lesson to Charlie, 'I stopped looking' for Sun's ring, reading dreams and signs from the island, and finally his self-sacrifice to stop the time flashes all enact following the Way. The chapter reads the black-and-white backgammon stones, Locke's one-black-one-white eyes in Claire's dream, and Jacob versus the Man in Black as yin-yang complementarity, with empiricism and Taoism finally interdependent like the dots in each half.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 30 "Keep the Needle on the Record" — Donavan Muir argues Lost's narrative world, unlike Jane Eyre's, requires its own metaphysics, and that this metaphysics is an order of balanced binary oppositions: Jacob and the Man in Black as twins diverged at birth, the cave scale's light and dark stones that Locke knocks out of balance in 'The Substitute,' science/faith, with characters like Jack converting from one pole into its opposite. The proper model is the yin-yang in motion - the Tao as a balanced ontological flow in which interdependent opposites wax and wane - so that treating the poles as independent is the delusion that threatens the island's order. The finale, where both Jacob and the Man in Black cease to exist and the castaways are freed, enacts the Mahayana Buddhist Middle Way: enlightenment as letting go of rigid oppositions that interdependence double-negates.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 12 "Notes" — Decker parallels the Republic's fall into Palpatine's Empire with the Zhou dynasty's collapse that birthed Chinese philosophy, reading three Jedi from the Dark Times comics through it. K'Kruhk, guided by the Zatoichi-like Master Zao, learns wu-wei - following the Force rather than forcing outcomes, with Laozi's Dao as the Force's Chinese analogue. Dass Jennir's struggle over what 'Jedi' means after killing a slaver becomes Confucian rectification of names and the cultivation of ren, while Kai Hudorra's loss of faith, withdrawal to a casino, and final sacrificial stand against Vader embody Mozi-style pragmatic minimalism redeemed by Jennir's virtuous example.
