- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 10 "Notes" — Schiltz reads Isaac McAdoo as a Zhuangzian sage: his virtuoso haircut scene in 'Man City' parallels Zhuangzi's butcher who carves oxen by following the natural seams of the dao, and his candid, simple, guileless character mirrors the Daoist mistrust of complexity and language. Isaac's slump in 'Rainbow' is diagnosed as lost wu-wei ('all up in his head'), cured by Roy's no-stakes pickup games that restore effortless action, and Laozi's 'ruling a great state is like cooking a small fish' explains Isaac's wordless leadership during Sam's Dubai Air protest and the suit-wearing gesture at Rebecca's father's funeral.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 23 "The Dao of Hoops" — Dirk Dunbar, a former professional player, argues that Daoist concepts illuminate basketball excellence and that the sport can be a path to the Dao. Balancing yin and yang means blending competition with surrender and strategy with spontaneity; Zhuangzi's archer shows how craving victory drains power. Wuwei explains the 'zone' of effortless play Dunbar experienced while scoring sixty-five points in a high school game and seventy-four in Iceland, while qi grounds free-throw breathing and visualization and ziran the discipline of releasing a shot without willing it in. Drawing on Daode jing verses and Phil Jackson's Sacred Hoops, he claims basketball teaches a life of disciplined surrender beyond the ego.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 27 "Thirteenth Hole Free and Easy Wandering on the Golf Course Swing Like a Taoist" — Scott F. Parker reads golf's paradox—that you play your best shot when you stop trying so hard—through the Taoism of the 'Tao Te Ching' and the 'Chuang Tzu.' Using the parable of the archer (skill is constant but attachment to the prize ruins the shot), Cook Ting carving the ox by spirit not force, and Master Yu accepting his deformity, he draws out nonattachment to results, 'doing without doing' (wei wu wei), and self-knowledge/self-acceptance, illustrated by Zach Johnson never going for a par 5 in two at the 2007 Masters and Tiger Woods rarely swinging all-out. The essay embodies the Taoist point that the Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao: to try to not-try is self-defeating, so one must simply not try.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — McRae reads Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon as a dramatization of the tension between Confucian humanism and Daoist naturalism over how to cultivate an authentic 'focus-field' self. Li Mu Bai and Yu Shu Lien are exemplary persons (junzi) bound by the wuxia code and li, unable to voice their love, while Jen rebels into criminal freedom under Jade Fox; Li's use of the green bamboo forest against Jen embodies wu-wei and rou (yielding suppleness). It argues that authentic self-cultivation, and Jen's final leap, require balancing Daoist natural freedom against Confucian roles, since freedom without relationships exacts a fatal price.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Kohler-Ryan and Palmer treat 'sense' and 'sensibility' as a spectrum Lee explores through sisterhood in Sense and Sensibility (Elinor/Marianne) and Crouching Tiger (Shu Lien/Jen). Elinor and Shu Lien embody sense, Shu Lien specifically the Confucian balance of li and ren that lets her soften ritual with humanity; Marianne embodies Burke's British-Romantic sublime while Jen embodies Daoist immersion in the dao. Reading door-frames, windows, hair-combing rituals and Shu Lien's hairpin as symbols, they argue only Sense and Sensibility achieves integration in time, whereas Li Mu Bai's confession that he lived sense and sensibility as separate spheres comes too late.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 23 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Hole reads The Ice Storm's prophetic opening as a meditation on 'what is impending', weaving existentialism with Zen Buddhism and Daoism. He uses the Four Noble Truths and the Zen story of the monk 'still carrying the woman' to show the families suffer through attachment to rigid self-images, and Jung's synchronicity and the Daoist dao/wu-wei to read the ice storm's formation and Mikey's chance electrocution as an interdependent flow the characters resist. Centrally he applies Heidegger's being-toward-death—death as ownmost, non-relational, not-to-be-outstripped—arguing that fleeing one's death is fleeing one's authentic being, alongside Kierkegaard's leap of faith and Nietzsche's living dangerously; he closes by applying the argument to his own mortality.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 19 "10. The Dao of Psychohistory" — Fried reframes Asimov's binary (do individual choices matter to history?) through four Chinese theories of non-action (wu wei). Confucian non-action, ruling by moral example and retiring under an unjust ruler, illuminates Onum Barr's dignified private life; the Dao De Jing's mystical libertarianism, where people self-transform when the ruler stops intervening, resembles Gaia's ruler-less holism; Legalist impersonal non-action (Han Fei's ruler who hides his desires and lets harsh law act) has no clear Foundation analogue; and Zhuangzi's useless tree models Gaal Dornick's TV arc, in which she reclaims agency precisely by choosing private non-action over a scripted role in galactic history.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 46 "Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat" — In a mock interview with 'Bat-Tzu' (a disguised Alfred), Mark White explains Taoism through Batman. Bruce is dangerously dominated by yang after his parents' deaths and needs the yin balance that Robin (Dick as the lighthearted 'Batman with a feminine side') and his spiritual quest restore; Batman's fear-inducing shadow illustrates Lao-Tzu's usefulness of nothingness. Alfred is the Taoist sage embodying wei-wu-wei - 'action without action' - quietly serving like Chuang-Tzu's effortless butcher and like water that wears down stone, harmonizing Bruce's warring opposites toward the Way.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 29 "NOTE" — Shai Biderman and William J. Devlin trace John Locke the character's shift from the empiricism of his philosophical namesake to Taoism. Early Locke is the tabula-rasa empiricist and scientific-method hunter and hatch-engineer, but his miraculous restored ability to walk, Jacob's touch, and his visions push him to ask 'why' rather than 'how.' They argue Locke comes to follow the Tao—the unnamable Way symbolized by the black-and-white yin-yang seen in backgammon pieces and Claire's dream—advising Charlie via the struggling moth, teaching Walt to visualize the knife's path, and finding Sun's ring by not looking, ultimately reading his sacrificial death as effortless surrender to the island's flow.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 30 "Keep the Needle on the Record" — Donavan S. Muir argues that Lost deliberately withholds its metanarrative so viewers must construct its metaphysics, which he identifies as an order of balanced binary oppositions. Drawing on the spinning Taoist yin-yang, he reads the interdependent, mutually converting poles—Jack from man of science to man of faith, Sawyer from con man to protector—and the light/dark scales in Widmore's painting and the cave (Locke throwing out the white rock) as figures for a Tao whose balance sustains existence. Invoking Derrida's traces and Mahayana Buddhism's Middle Way and emptiness, he reads Jacob and the Man in Black as twins whose oppositions must be annihilated, so that only when both cease to exist in 'The End' are the castaways set free.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 15 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Hathaway and Sharpley analyze the cannabis experience of medical-'compassion club' users through Csikszentmihalyi's concept of 'flow.' They ground flow in William James's 'stream of consciousness' and in Taoism, reading Tao as 'a patterned flow of the universe' and wu wei as the effortless equilibrium users describe ('it just centers me,' 'I take an inventory on my soul'). Against Western monophasic medicine, they defend users' 'anecdotal' testimony as legitimate knowledge of a body–mind–spirit balance that cannabis restores.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 8 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — John Friend's foreword surveys yoga's three classical philosophical systems and connects them to how modern Hatha yoga is practiced: Classical (Patanjali) yoga as separating purusha (spirit) from prakriti (matter) to reach kaivalya; Vedanta as neutralizing maya to realize the unity of atman with the supreme; and non-dual Tantra, from which Hatha yoga derives, treating body and mind as frequencies of one divine Shiva-Shakti energy. It argues yoga's enduring claim is that the essential self is free, and that direct lived experience of that freedom outranks merely intellectual knowledge of the texts.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 46 "Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat" — White stages a mock interview with "Bat-Tzu" (revealed to be Alfred) to read Batman through Taoism. Lao-Tzu and Chuang-Tzu supply the ideal of balancing yin and yang: Bruce lets his hard, vengeful yang dominate and needs Robin's yin, while Dick keeps balance and Tim risks losing his. Bruce's intimidating shadow illustrates the usefulness of nothingness, and Chuang-Tzu's teaching on accepting death frames Jason Todd's fate. Alfred embodies the Taoist sage — wei-wu-wei, water-like flexibility, and effortless, unspoken guidance.

### Personal Identity (memory theory)

John Locke argued that what makes a person the same individual over time is not the persistence of a soul or a body but the continuity of consciousness, especially memory. On this view, a person is a thinking, self-aware being who can regard itself as the same across different times and places, and identity extends only as far as that consciousness can reach back through remembered experience. The theory reframes selfhood as a psychological rather than a metaphysical fact, and it raised enduring puzzles about lapses of memory, forgotten deeds, and the boundaries of moral responsibility.

- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 115 "Lumos!" — Pushes the theory to its disturbing limit: if the Marauder's Map is part of both Fred's and George's extended minds, minds can overlap. Since identity rests on memory continuity (Locke's theory, the adult Harry identical with the orphaned infant), memory-sharing, Obliviation, and implanted or stolen memories - Barty Crouch Jr.'s Polyjuice theft of Moody's identity, Lockhart's memory charms, Hermione's rewriting of her parents - threaten who we are, and Harry's Pensieve encounters with Snape's worst memory and his own status as a Horcrux trigger his identity crises.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 113 "The Mental Realm of the Hulk" — Applies Locke's memory theory: the shape-shifting Martian Manhunter and the irradiated Fantastic Four stay the same people through mental continuity, and the early comics' Banner-minded Hulk meets Locke's criterion — but the later "Hulk smash!" Hulk, who recognizes Betty Ross yet lacks Banner's memories, fails it. The chapter then breaks the criterion itself with Reid's brave-officer objection (the general both is and is not the flogged boy), Alzheimer's and Doc Ock's amnesia attack on Spider-Man, and the circularity of distinguishing genuine from false memory (the deluded fan who "remembers" starring in Adventures of Superman).
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 28 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Uses Narnia's magical transformations to probe personal identity, starting with the qualitative/numerical identity distinction illustrated by the look-alike twins Shasta and Corin in The Horse and His Boy. Aristotle's essential/accidental properties frame the question of what Eustace can lose and remain Eustace, including turning into a dragon, and Rabadash into a donkey, showing persons are not identical to their bodies. Descartes's soul argument and Locke's memory theory are tested and rejected, the latter because it cannot handle Rilian's enchanted amnesia, Shasta's forgotten infancy, or Susan's disowned memories without circularity. The chapter defends instead a first-person-perspective theory on which a person is constituted by, not identical to, a body, illustrated by the repeatedly repaired Dawn Treader and by the heroes surviving death in The Last Battle as restored points of view.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 21 "“Nobody’s Bob Dylan”" — Vernezze and Lulewicz take Dylan's 1964 Halloween quip "I got my Bob Dylan mask on" as an entry into personal identity, testing each theory against his life: the bodily view (Zimmerman to Dylan) survives cell turnover but stumbles on brain-transplant cases; Locke's memory theory handles them but faces Reid's brave-officer regress and Alzheimer's cases, and Dylan's reincarnation lyrics ("Shelter from the Storm," "I and I") ignore memory altogether. The Christian soul view of the gospel albums ("When He Returns," "Gotta Serve Somebody") follows Descartes and Plato but cannot justify the swirl-to-filling inference that souls exist. The chapter ends sympathetic to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist no-self: Dylan's "I is another," his name as fabrication, and the cover album Self Portrait all deny a fixed self-created essence.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 8 "Dead People" — William Larkin uses Romero's films - Karen Cooper devouring her father in Night of the Living Dead, Roger begging Peter to shoot him in Dawn, Riley's 'Those people are all dead' in Land - to argue that persons are res corporealis, bodily continuers, rather than Descartes's res cogitans. Our terror of becoming a zombie ourselves and our grief at recognized neighbors in the horde reveal that deep down we think persons survive as corpses, so bodily continuity suffices for identity while psychological continuity is unnecessary. The Locke-style body-switching intuition (prince and cobbler) that supports the psychological approach is dismissed as theoretically biased data compared to what good zombie fiction draws out of us.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 9 "Zombies and Us" — Hamish Thompson asks why we kill zombies with so few qualms and whether zombification releases us from obligations to the person who was, testing brain-death criteria, altered-identity and self-defense justifications against Shaun of the Dead (Shaun's mother and Ed), Day of the Dead's Bub, White Zombie, and Invasion of the Body Snatchers. He borrows Hume's bundle theory - the self as a fiction, a bundle of perceptions rather than an essence - and Parfit's degrees of psychological continuity to dissolve the sharp alive/dead and same-person/other-person dichotomies that make zombie-killing easy. The payoff is that we are already partly zombie (Shaun's checkout line, Ed on the sofa, the author's all-night gaming), differing only in our capacity for brief autonomous, goal-directed choices like Shaun's three-plan montage.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 16 "Introduction" — Frames Part III's metaphysics chapters. Lawrence's chapter uses The Matrix to survey dualism and the materialist theories of mind; Southworth's uses Wolverine's amnesia to test Locke's memory criterion and Jamie Madrox's duplicates for Parfit's view of identity; Pierce's asks whether Harry Potter's prophecies leave Harry free, probing compatibilism versus libertarian free will; and Littmann's asks whether Skynet's Terminators could be persons via a Terminator version of the Turing Test.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 18 "Be Slow to Judge" — Southworth tests Locke's memory theory on Wolverine: the Cassandra Nova/Xavier mind-swap shows identity follows mind, not body, and Wolverine's serial memory wipes (Team X, Weapon X, Apocalypse's brainwashing) mean that on Locke's connected-memory view several different people have inhabited his body — with House of M's total recall suddenly loading him with responsibility for all their deeds. Jamie Madrox's duplicates then carry Parfit's objection that shared memories cannot suffice for sameness of person, pushing toward physical continuity and the chapter's deflationary moral: be slow to judge who deserves blame.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 19 "Identities, Selves, and Others" — Patterson uses Thornhill's being mistaken for the fictitious George Kaplan to test theories of personal identity: the body theory fails a CIA thought experiment in which a Kaplan double is slowly rebuilt from Thornhill's own replaced cells; Locke's memory theory fails on amnesia scenarios and circularity, since one cannot have memories of a self unless one already has a self; and Parfit's psychological continuity survives, with Thornhill drifting along a 'Psychological Spectrum' toward 'one hundred percent Kaplan' as he plays the spy. The chapter then turns existentialist: with Sartre, no essential nature fixes who Thornhill is, so he is totally responsible for the self his choices create, from 'Expedient Exaggerations' to risking death on Mount Rushmore. Charles Taylor's claim that a self exists only in dialogue with a community explains why Eve and others literally help make Thornhill into the person he becomes.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 17 "Was Jerry Garcia the Soul of the Grateful Dead" — John Uglietta asks what made the Grateful Dead the Grateful Dead when they swapped five keyboardists yet stopped being themselves the moment Jerry Garcia died, prompting the rename to The Dead. Testing Aristotle's essential versus accidental properties, Peter French's structural account of group identity (the Yankees, the Glenn Miller Orchestra), same-stuff theories via a VW bus rebuilt piece by piece from its old parts — a Ship of Theseus puzzle — and Locke's memory theory applied to Phil Lesh's liver (but feared brain) transplant, he proposes that the band's essence was a group spirit born of members 'surrendering their own little trip'. The soul of the Dead was bigger than Jerry but smaller than the whole band, and its loss at his death was something the survivors could recognize but not replace.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 19 "To Join in with the Game" — Gracyk argues Waters is wrong that Pink Floyd ended when he quit in 1985: Waters's case rests on an illicit use of the identity of indiscernibles, since if losing Waters's lyrics destroys the band's identity, then losing Barrett's or Wright's, or adding 'Lucifer Sam,' would too, which proves too much. Borrowing Locke's distinction between the same man and the same person (the oak that remains the same oak through change; the unrecognized Syd in Abbey Road's Studio Three) and Kant's contrast between free and dependent beauty to explain how intentions change aesthetic evaluation, he defends actual intentionalism over hypothetical intentionalism: Hendrix really sings 'kiss the sky,' and interviews with Waters genuinely aid interpretation of Wish You Were Here. He then argues for collective agency, that groups can have intentions through members charged to act responsibly on the group's behalf, so no single member can disband a collective: Waters had a duty to leave, Gilmour, Mason, and Wright were entitled to continue the group's longstanding intention of making and performing original music, and the Echoes compilation is therefore an accurate portrait of the real Pink Floyd.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 26 "Memories Are Made of This" — Randall Jensen asks whether Cash's hope of reunion with the dead ('Meet Me in Heaven,' 'If We Never Meet Again This Side of Heaven') is even coherent, using the 'One Piece at a Time' Cadillac and a hypothetical 1954 Plymouth to retell the Ship of Theseus puzzle about identity through part replacement. He canvasses Platonic dualism from the Phaedo (Cash is his soul, the body a rusty cage), the materialist hope that God can reassemble a resurrected body despite dispersed matter, and the psychological-continuity view that persons are 'made of memories,' ending on the duplication problem: if God made two heavenly bodies both carrying Cash's memories, which one would be Cash?
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 19 "Into the Future" — Hanley dismantles the four claimed human/Cylon differences: artificial reproduction is in principle possible for us; prosthetics already blur what we are made of; model copies differ like identical twins (Boomer is not Athena); and resurrection has human analogues — he proposes an SDTR (scanning, death, transmission, replication) model and uses van Inwagen's replica-switch account of bodily resurrection while rejecting soul-based reincarnation on Lockean grounds, since consciousness rather than soul is the criterion of identity. He defends reproductive cloning as reproduction, not replication (a clone is your child, not your copy), and reads Athena's memories of Tyrol as evidence she is a replicated Boomer. The upshot: being a Cylon is nothing to fear — 'I am a Cylon, and so are you.'
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 26 "“I Feel Exactly What You Feel”" — Runs Star Trek's transporter and android stories as thought experiments on personal identity: the body theory (Kirk rejecting android Korby — 'Dr. Korby was never here' — and Picard telling the resurrected Rishon Uxbridge 'you do not exist'), the brain theory ('Spock's Brain,' Bashir refusing to replace half of Vedek Bareil's brain), and Locke's memory theory as vindicated by the Trill (Lela Dax's 'a person is but the sum of their memories,' the 'Dax' extradition hearing over Curzon's crimes). Riker's transporter double in 'Second Chances' and the Tuvix fusion then break the memory theory through fission and fusion, prompting Parfit's move that psychological continuity, not numerical identity, is what matters in survival. Memory erasure in 'Dagger of the Mind' and Kurn's rebranding after the failed Mauk-to'Vor in 'Sons of Mogh' count as death if we are our memories.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 17 "Solutions to the Problem The youth whose destiny it is to lead Hyrule to the" — Robison asks how Link stays the same person through Ocarina of Time's child/adult switches, Twilight Princess's wolf form, and Wind Waker's consciousness-projection into seagulls and mages. Physical-continuity views fail because Link's body changes or is left behind; Locke's memory-based psychological continuity fails because adult Link's past hasn't happened yet when he travels back. After a Ship of Theseus variant (Ganon reassembling Tetra's sunken planks) she proposes that in Zelda's stipulative metaphysics, destiny, the goddess-given roles of courage, wisdom, and power, is the necessary and sufficient condition of identity, fitting videogame universes whose metaphysics are fixed by designers.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 13 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Spicher argues that when Bumblebee trades his beat-up 1976 Camaro for a shiny 2007 model only his appearance changes (an accidental change), never his identity, because transforming is part of a Transformer's essence like a human wearing a mask. Locke's memory continuity and Thomson's bodily criterion each fail - the embryo, coma, and corpse problems, plus the thought experiment of Megatron's memories transplanted into another body - so he defends an Aristotelian composite of form and matter in which the Spark is the soul-like form organizing the machine body, preserving identity through transformation as form guides matter toward actuality.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 25 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Harris and Baer use the Boatman scene ('Pan is me... we'd die') to test criteria of personal identity against the trilogy: Lyra and Will's inference to a thinking third part, the ghost, reenacts Descartes's dualist reasoning about mind-body distinctness, Iorek's lack of a ghost exemplifies the same-body criterion, and Pantalaimon's instant shape-shifting favors the psychological criterion, spelled out through Locke's prince-and-cobbler memory thought experiment and Parfit's psychological connectedness and continuity. They ask whether Lee Scoresby's dissolution into conscious atoms that reunite with Hester's counts as genuine survival, best accommodated by Locke's consciousness criterion or a panpsychist matter criterion, with Chalmers cited as the contemporary defender of conscious matter. The chapter closes with individuation, whether Lyra and Pan are one person or two, applied to a Primal Fear-style multiple-personality murder trial, the hypothetical of Pan killing someone while Lyra is innocent, and living wills in persistent vegetative states.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 16 "Mr. Monk Is Mr. Monk" — Malloy runs the classic theories of personal identity through Monk episodes. Bodily (really brain) identity fails when 'the Monk' — the reckless medicated alter of 'Mr. Monk Takes His Medicine' — shares Monk's body and brain yet is not held responsible, and Stanley Tucci's method actor in 'Mr. Monk and the Actor' shows that copying Monk's looks and behavior does not transfer identity. Locke's memory theory breaks on the amnesia of 'Mr. Monk Bumps His Head' (Monk becomes roofer 'Jerry') and the blackout in 'Mr. Monk and the Rapper,' and Reid's brave-officer paradox yields contradiction once recovered Monk remembers being both Monk and Jerry. Hume's bundle theory — 'I never can catch myself,' the self as theatre of successive perceptions — grounds psychological continuity's graded identity, but then cult-swayed Monk in 'Mr. Monk Joins a Cult' might count as a different person, making his deprogramming a kind of murder; the chapter closes by rejecting Reid and Butler's 'simple and unassayable' escape, insisting a philosopher, like a detective, must keep theorizing how Monk stays Monk.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 8 "Dead People" — William Larkin pits Descartes's res cogitans (the person as psychological continuum, reinforced by Locke's prince-and-cobbler body-switch) against a res corporealis view in which bodily continuity suffices for identity, using Romero's Dead films as intuition pumps. The terror of Roger's 'I don't want to be walking around like that' and Rain's request in Resident Evil only makes sense if we think it would be us rising as zombies, and the tragedy of Karen Cooper devouring her father or Johnny menaging Barbara only lands if the same person persists. Against the 'just dead flesh' scientists and the mall-memory reading of Dawn, he argues zombie psychology is merely residual instinct, so our fear and pity reveal we really believe persons survive as corpses, hence as bodies, not as minds.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 9 "Zombies and Us" — Hamish Thompson asks what could justify killing zombies, canvassing self-defense, total-brain-death criteria, and release from obligations to a radically altered person, using Shaun of the Dead's mother-killing, Bub's trained shooting in Day of the Dead, White Zombie's piano-playing heroine, and the pod-people substitutions of Invasion of the Body Snatchers. He deploys Hume's bundle theory of the self as a fiction of succeeding perceptions and Parfit's graded psychological continuity (with Locke's prince/cobbler case) to argue identity comes in degrees, so zombie termination is never as clean as the genre pretends. The chapter ends by turning the lens around: Shaun's checkout-line beepers and Ed's sofa-and-video-game existence suggest ordinary lives differ from zombiehood only by intermittent acts of imaginative self-direction.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 7 "A Dead End" — Stokes uses regeneration and the multi-Doctor episodes ('The Three Doctors', 'The Five Doctors', 'The Trial of a Time Lord') to test theories of personal identity: Locke's memory criterion, Reid's transitivity objection, Parfit's teleporter and 'branch-line' cases, Nozick's closest-continuer theory, four-dimensional person-stages, animalism, and narrative identity. He argues that no objective-continuity account explains why the Fifth Doctor still cares whether he himself survives in 'The Caves of Androzani', and hints that being the Doctor may be a subjective stance in which each incarnation takes ownership of the others as itself.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 8 "Doctor Who and the Ultimate Answer" — Littmann mines Who scenarios as hypotheticals that test identity theories: regeneration, natural doubles like Salamander, impersonating Zygons and Chameleons, bodiless beings like Omega and the Great Intelligence, TARDIS jumps that break spatiotemporal continuity, Cassandra possessing the Doctor and Rose, memory theft by Eldrad and the Daleks, and the Master's year as the unrecognizably good Professor Yana. He argues that sameness of body (including the four-dimensional 'worm' of spatiotemporal continuity), the memory criterion, and psychological similarity each fail, leaving the question of what makes the Doctor the Doctor — and you you — open.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 9 "What’s Persistence Without Identity" — Hanley first fixes what is true in the Who canon (treating fiction as pretense), then asks how the Doctor persists when regeneration replaces 'every single cell' and when John Smith's amnesia severs memory in 'Human Nature'. Rejecting bodily continuity (the severed hand of 'The Christmas Invasion'), soul 'pellets', and simple memory (Reid's transitivity problem), he defends neo-Lockean mental continuity plus Nozick's closest-continuer schema to explain why Jackson Lake, the regrown Doctor, and DoctorDonna in 'Journey's End' are not the Doctor, and closes with Parfit's claim that psychological continuity rather than identity is what matters in survival, alongside Lewis's space-time-worm alternative.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 10 "I Think, Therefore I Exist . . . I Think" — Johnson argues that the Platonic-Cartesian soul is refuted by neuroscience (Phineas Gage, Penfield's stimulation studies), and that Locke's memory criterion fails on Reid-style transitivity cases like DoctorDonna and on Bernard-Williams-inspired worry about the amnesiac John Smith, who would still dread the Family of Blood's torture. Parfit's causal-continuity criterion then wrongly makes the meta-crisis Doctor of 'Journey's End' identical with the Tenth, so Johnson defends a four-dimensionalist 'time worm' view on which the Doctors are stages of one person — before a final sorites-style argument (heaps, spin-offs like Torchwood) suggests that 'persons' may not exist at all.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 28 "Here They Are ... Ready to Outsit Eternity" — Argues that regeneration helps show life after death is logically possible: the successive Doctors (Fourth to Fifth in 'Logopolis') prove identity survives radical personality change, so a perfected heavenly Joe would still be Joe. Testing whether identity lies in body or memory, he contrasts John Smith in 'Human Nature' (same body, so same person) with the 'Journey's End' Doctor-clone whose replicated memories Rose rejects ('But he's not you'), favoring bodily continuity. This leaves the unavailability-of-atoms problem, which he solves with van Inwagen's theory that God removes and preserves our bodies at death like a divine cryonicist, echoing the Fourth Doctor's 'ready to outsit eternity' tribute in 'The Ark in Space'.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 29 "Love and Doctors" — Asks whether 'the Doctor' is a Kripkean rigid designator naming one individual or a non-rigid role filled by different people, using the Ninth Doctor's deathbed doubts and the Time Crash memory loop to settle on the rigid reading. He then deploys Locke's body/organism/person distinctions, Parfit's overlapping psychological-connectedness fix to Reid's transitivity objection (Sarah Jane across 1983-1996-2006), and the amnesia-prone regenerations and the Valeyard to show the organism survives regeneration while the person might not. Finally he argues that because DoctorTwo in 'Journey's End' shares all the Doctor's psychologically connected memories of Rose, fission makes them two persons with equal claim, so Rose gets the person she actually loved.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 20 "Long-Term Identity" — Asks whether the final Duncan Idaho ghola, whose serial memories wake during his encounter with Murbella, is the same person as the original who died holding off nineteen Sardaukar. It tests physical continuity, Locke's memory-based sameness of person (Hayt becomes Duncan only when the original's consciousness reawakens), Parfit's psychological connectedness with its redescription of identity as survival through quasi-memory, Schechtman's narrative self-constitution, Velleman's self-inventing characters, and four-dimensionalist 'space-time worms' on which Leto II's 3,500 years and the Duncans' gappy five millennia are single long selves. Herbert's moral: identity is not fixed—societies and technologies, from the Tleilaxu tanks to the Sisterhood's swift accommodation, keep redrawing what counts as the same person. Same Duncans, same person.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 22 "Get Out of My Mind!" — Runs Lady Jessica's spice-agony Other Memory through Locke's Essay: if a person is a 'thinking intelligent being' whose identity extends as far as her consciousness reaches, then Jessica—having received the memories of every Reverend Mother back to Raquella Berto-Anirul—must be identical with Raquella, and with Alia who shares the same memories, which is absurd. Thomas Reid's gallant officer is staged as Gurney Halleck, who remembers Rabban's whip but not his sister's eyes, breaking the transitivity of memory-based identity. The chapter closes with three modern paths—psychological continuity, Eric Olson's animalism, and Dennett's selves as 'centers of narrative gravity'—plus a Lockean coda defending the Abomination Alia as a person no fixed class of nature could exclude.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 10 "Mastering the Chief" — Joyce Havstad asks which of the millions of player-instantiated Master Chiefs is real, and whether the flash-cloned John left behind on Eridanus II is the same boy. She runs the Ship of Theseus on the MJOLNIR armor—a technician rebuilds a second suit from every replaced piece—contrasting material with historical continuity, and adds Hobbes's reassembled-planks version. Locke's prince-and-cobbler memory criterion is reconstructed across John, John-117, and Master Chief, then broken by Reid's brave-officer objection, leaving psychological continuity as the best but imperfect criterion; the Flood's conversion of a Covenant soldier into a Combat Form shows identity lost once original sentience is gone.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 38 "In a Mirror, Darkly" — The chapter stages Arctor's bishop's-robe musing ('What is identity? Where does the act end?') against the classic puzzles: the Ship of Theseus with its two reassembled vessels, and the baby photos you share no cells with. Locke gives memory plus a unified 'thinking, intelligent being' with real unity; Hume bites the bullet, finding only perceptions in introspection, never a self, so the self's identity over time is a normal, inescapable delusion like a mountain's. All of it converges on Fred watching Bob and asking 'who am I? Which one of them is me?'
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 44 "Follow the Psyche" — The chapter assembles Dick's survival-of-the-psyche cases: Agneta Rautavaara kept alive as a brain in a nutrient bath, Professor Thomas's conscious brain piloting a spaceship, the wub transferring into Captain Franco mid-execution, and the Rexorian consciousness in 'Human Is', then grounds the pattern in Locke's prince-and-cobbler and detached-little-finger thought experiments: 'consciousness makes personal identity.' Everything is codified as the Psyche Continuity Rule, to keep track of the person follow the psyche, with brains mattering only as convenient storage vessels.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 45 "The Perils of Rekall, Inc" — The chapter runs through three incompatible backstories for Total Recall's Quaid, Cohaagen's infiltration plot, Hauser's genuine defection and self-erasure, or a Rekall trip gone live, and shows that in all three no single psyche links the life stages, forcing a Body Continuity Rule and then a Combined Rule that follows the psyche when mental life is unified and the body when it is disjointed. Paycheck's Jennings, who starts referring to his earlier self in the third person, exposes the rule's weak joint: deciding when a mental life counts as sufficiently disjointed.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 142 "Memory and the Brain-Butchers" — The section uses Quaid's Rekall-fabricated life, complete with false wedding memories and a false eight-year marriage, to challenge Locke's memory theory of personal identity: implants, together with ordinary forgetting, revision, and loss, show memory cannot be what makes you the same person from one day to the next. Kuato's line, 'A man is defined by his action, not his memory,' is offered as the alternative the following sections develop.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 21 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Nicolas Michaud treats Watson's 2011 defeat of Jennings and Rutter as evidence for Turing's test: had Watson's answers come from behind a door we would have judged them intelligent, and its goofy misses ('What is Toronto?????') reflect missing context, not missing thought, no more damning than a child's honest error. Against Searle's Chinese Room he deploys the systems reply - you plus the Big Book of Rules might be the thing that understands - and argues that nobody, human or machine, can meet Searle's impossible burden of proving understanding, since Watson can define words, associate connotations, and pick Jeopardy! out from not-Jeopardy!. Quoting Locke's definition of a person as a thinking being that can consider itself as itself, he concludes Watson approaches personhood and that we had better teach our 'intelligent offspring' kindness and fairness before they learn anything else.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 15 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Jenkins asks what makes Bender Bender when Leela still recognizes him as the walnut-panelled steam robot of 'Obsoletely Fabulous.' Scruffy's progressively repaired conference table stages the Ship of Theseus problem and the same body theory, while the Roboticon 'Soul Detector' (Fry sets it off, robots pass through) rules out Descartes' same soul theory for robots. Episodes from 'Anthology of Interest II' and 'The Honking' to 'The Prisoner of Benda' mind swap and Roberto's instant 1-X re-education support Locke's psychological continuity: Bender persists through an overlapping chain of memories and traits stored on his hard drive - 'Everything that is Bender is right here' - which is why an empathic, ascetic Bender ('The old Bender is gone') threatens his very identity.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 26 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Lopez uses the monster - 'one man made out of many' - to stress-test personal identity: brain-swap and amnesia-torture thought experiments first drive us to identify with our memories (the memory-based psychological criterion) and then, when Victor offers to wipe memory before the pain experiments, with our bodies, yielding inconsistent answers. The monster's own testimony - waking confused, prodding fire like an infant, acquiring language by eavesdropping on Safie's lessons, and building his values from scratch out of Paradise Lost and the cottagers - shows he is a genuinely new person rather than whoever once owned his corpse-parts, since we would not say a memory-wiped torture victim ceases to exist. He concludes the monster satisfies the five listed personhood criteria (consciousness, reasoning, self-motivated activity, communication, self-awareness), with identity riding a continuing stream of consciousness running on a body that is, in the end, secondary 'hardware.'
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 26 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Kenneth Sayles reads Peter and Valentine's net personas through three lenses: John Locke's identity theory to ask whether a consistent virtual persona with no physical anchor deserves our trust, Plato's Ring of Gyges to ask what anonymity does to morality, and Hannah Arendt's account of totalitarianism to warn that nameless, unaccountable influence ('action without a name... is meaningless') paves the way for rule by propaganda and a fictitious world. Real-world parallels - identity theft, the hacker collective Anonymous, YouTube politics - make the Enderverse nets look prophetic rather than fantastic.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 9 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Jason Iuliano asks whether the Brody who lied to Helen Walker about Tom Walker's death is the same person as the one who beat Walker, and whether 2011 Brody is responsible for 2003 Brody's acts. He contrasts the biological criterion (same human animal), the psychological criterion of overlapping memories and intentions (so Brody remembering his family remains the same person), and the narrative identity theory Carrie invokes in 'Q&A' when she says Nazir pulled Brody apart and put him back together as someone else. A Carrie thought experiment about ECT outcomes and a Nazir mind-swap of Brody's and Walker's psychologies argue that only narrative coherence captures whom we should praise, blame, and anticipate surviving.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 11 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Laszlo Kajtar uses Brody's Complex PTSD - torture, forced killing of Walker, intrusive nightmares attacking Jessica - to test theories of personal identity. Animalism says Brody is the same biological organism before and after captivity, while the psychological approach, sourced in Locke's memory criterion, traces continuity of beliefs, desires, and intentions and finds it disrupted by trauma and Nazir's brainwashing, which filled the hole trauma left after Issa's death. Kajtar argues both miss the first-personal 'sense of self': like many PTSD sufferers, Brody feels he is not the person he was, and 'It's like she doesn't know who I actually am now' shows identity shattered from the inside.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 22 "Dracula and Philosophy" — McCrossin uses Locke's memory theory of personal identity - consciousness extending to past and future actions, with 'all the right and justice of reward and punishment' founded in it - to ask whether Dracula is a monster but still a person, illustrated by an imagined Quincey-Seward body swap where only the mind that remembers the deed deserves blame. Mina, midway between human and vampire and fearing for her own future personhood, supplies the empathy and pity ('that poor soul') that turn the crew's campaign into one of mercy - they weep and grant the Count a peaceful death - adding a sentimental middle ground that Locke's claim that morality is demonstrable like mathematics cannot account for.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 21 "10. One Good, Solid Hope—the Impossible Girl" — Elsby and Luzecky ask what stays constant across Clara's echoes and argue traditional identity theories fail her: Locke's memory-continuity and same-life account cannot apply because no echo remembers the others, and Plutarch's Ship of Theseus—invoked by the Doctor's broom speech in 'Deep Breath'—rules out bodily continuity, since the echoes have different bodies and minds. Their positive view is that Clara is less a particular than a universal, a 'recipe' or species whose instances share an essence ('the soufflé isn't the soufflé; the soufflé is the recipe'), with the modern-day Clara 'real' as the origin of the echoes. That essence, shown in climbing the ladder to the clouds in 'The Snowmen,' facing the parasite-god with the most important leaf in human history in 'The Rings of Akhaten,' stepping into the Doctor's torn timeline in 'The Name of the Doctor,' and persuading the Time Lords in 'The Time of the Doctor,' is hope itself.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 40 "25. Meeting Up with Your Self" — Sylvia and Stevens use Doctor Who's crossover episodes to complicate the Self-Other distinction: existentially (via Yalom and Maslow), the Doctor's name-promise - 'never cruel or cowardly... never give up, never give in' - supplies meaning, while Ten and Eleven must stop treating the War Doctor as Other. Deleuze's account of learning through the shock of encountering the Other structures the reading of 'The Girl Who Waited,' where young Amy and her thirty-six-years-older self form an assemblage in which the older Amy relearns her love for Rory and chooses annihilation for his sake. Locke's memory theory of personal identity frames the puzzle that a version of you with different memories may be an Other, which the authors extend to confronting our recorded past selves on social media and learning empathy from the shock.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 27 "15. Memories. In the End, Is That All There Is" — David LaRocca tests Mr. Carson's claim that 'the business of life is the acquisition of memories. In the end, that's all there is' against the tradition of spatial memory metaphors and modern neuroscience. Downton itself becomes a memory palace - echoing Cicero, the Ad Herennium, and Augustine's 'court of memory' - whose characters defer endlessly to the past, while photographs (Tom with Sybil's image, Carson with Alice Neal's) act as sources and surrogates of memory in an age of acquisitional capitalism. Daniella Schiller's reconsolidation research, Nicholas Carr's Nietzsche-typewriter anecdote, and Langdon Winner's point that technologies reshape life show memories are malleable rather than collectible possessions, undermining Carson's model and any fixed memory-based account of personal identity.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 23 "12. Becoming Vetinari Personal Identity on the Discworld" — Pierce uses Moist von Lipwig's rehabilitation (Albert Spangler becomes Postmaster General), Cosmo Lavish's doomed project of literally becoming Vetinari, the Auditor Myria LeJean, Angua's transformations, the Librarian's orangutan body, Miss Level's two bodies, and duplicated Rincewind teleportation cases to test theories of personal identity. Locke's memory theory, patched by Leibniz into psychological continuity, collapses into circularity under false-memory cases like a wizard implanting Teatime's murders in Rincewind's mind, while bodily and brain-continuity views founder on Igor part-swaps, splitting hemispheres, and identical-twin-style fission. Leibniz's own soul view and Reid's treatment of identity as a primitive, unanalyzable fact get their due, and Hume's skepticism about any continuing self marks the chapter's conclusion that every available view exacts a price.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 25 "14. Being One’s Me (Witchy) Personal Identity on the Discworld" — The chapter reads Granny Weatherwax's analysis of Magrat—'you're your me'—through Locke's memory theory of personal identity, opening with Granny's broomstick, whose stick and bristles the dwarf engineers have replaced dozens of times yet which remains 'the same' broomstick, as a Theseus's-ship puzzle for witches. It stages Locke's view against the classic objections: Butler's circularity charge that memory presupposes identity, and fission worries raised by the duplicated Glods of Al-Ybi and by the mirror magic that splits Granny and Lilith among a billion reflections. Death's challenge to each witch to find 'the one that's real' in the mirror universe becomes the test case, and Granny's simply looking down at herself and saying 'This one' is offered as a vindication of a Butlerian, body-anchored and indefinable conception of personal identity.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 17 "6. One Clone from Another" — Asks what metaphysically individuates one Leda clone from another, surveying the tradition: Aristotelian substances bearing properties, Plato's and Descartes's non-repeatable individual essences, Berkeley's and Hegel's soul-substances, Aquinas's matter-based view, Locke's memory-based personal identity (with its sleeping-copy and consciousness-download objections), and Hume's argument that substance is a meaningless idea. It then turns to the Buddhist framework — the Four Noble Truths, anatman (no eternal self), the five skandhas, and dependent origination, illustrated by Alison's soap-and-drug crates — before closing with Nishida Kitaro's logic of contradictory self-identity. Read through that lens, the clone dance party in Felix's loft shows each clone's moves are truly her own precisely because they incorporate and mirror her sisters': identity is relational, not intrinsic.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 13 "5. The One, the Only, Darrow" — Kevin McCain uses Darrow's transformations—Helldiver of Lykos, carved Gold lancer, Reaper of Mars—to ask what makes him numerically the same person, warming up with Plutarch's Ship of Theseus replayed on the Pax and the Quinn trading parts. Same-matter and animalist views (Eric Olson) struggle with Mickey's near-total carving and Darrow's restarted heart, and Locke's prince-and-cobbler example, run as a carver swapping Darrow's and the Jackal's psychologies, sinks all physical-continuity views. The simple memory theory breaks transitivity across Darrow's childhood, and Sydney Shoemaker's psychological-continuity fix then fails when a carver splits Darrow's brain into two surviving bodies—a fission case where both new Darrows continue him—while the soul view cannot be verified; the chapter ends with Trenton Merricks's suggestion that there may be no criteria of identity over time at all.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 20 "9. Is Headless Deadpool Still Deadpool" — Ben Fulman runs Deadpool's decapitations, the T-Ray personality split, and Evil Deadpool—his discarded body parts regenerating together in a dumpster—through the theories of personal identity: Locke's memory continuity, Reid's branching-memory 'Deadpool paradox', Chisholm's essential parts, the Ship of Theseus traced from Heraclitus to Plutarch, and later positions by Sider, Wiggins, Noonan, Grice, and Perry on overlapping memory chains and their circularity. Finding each account strained by Deadpool's cases, the chapter proposes that Deadpool stores his memories in the readers via the fourth wall. His identity over time is thus jointly sustained by the audience—a 'non-personal identity' that ends only when every reader has forgotten him.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 38 "24. Won’t the Real Wade Wilson Please Stand Up" — Evil Deadpool, assembled from Wade's discarded body parts with all his old memories, makes Wade a walking Ship of Theseus, and the chapter runs the puzzle through Plutarch's original, Hobbes's reconstructed-ship variant, and Locke's Prince-and-Cobbler memory criterion, staged as a Thor/Thing body swap. Memory fails because Evil Deadpool shares Wade's memories, so the candidates become Schechtman's narrative and person-life views, Parfit's branching survival - neither is the original, and identity is not what matters anyway - and finally Unger's core-capacity view: Wade remains the real Deadpool by continuing to be a conscious being, while his detached parts ceased to be Deadpool parts the moment they were replaced.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 11 "1. What’s So Scary about Demonic Possession" — Using the Asylum possession arc - the boy who rips open the pig's heart, the demon exposing Sister Jude's hit-and-run secret and whispering 'You're Bloody Face' to Thredson, and Sister Mary Eunice's corruption - the chapter argues that possession stories terrify because they break our identity judgments through time, the same judgments on which moral responsibility, criminal punishment (the Manson family parole cases, Phineas Gage), trust, and personal safety depend. Descartes's mind-body union and psychological-continuity theories of identity explain why sameness of body can no longer guarantee sameness of person, and why we fear our own identity being erased next.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 13 "3. My Sister, My Self" — Staged as a remembered backstage conversation among Elsa's freak show performers, the chapter has conjoined twins Bette and Dot work through the Ship of Theseus, the psychological-continuity theory of identity and its coma and false-memory counterexamples, Quine's claim that persons are only convenient posits rather than real entities, split-brain cases suggesting one body can host two minds, and fission worries about what would happen if they were separated - to ask whether they are one person or two, concluding it is a genuine paradox with no agreed answer.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 15 "6. In a Mirror Is Our Image" — Karavitis places thirteen TZ episodes on a spectrum from specialized machines ('The Brain Center at Whipple's,' 'Steel,' 'The Old Man in the Cave') through human-like robots ('The Mighty Casey,' 'A Thing About Machines,' 'From Agnes with Love') to indistinguishable androids ('The Lonely,' 'The Lateness of the Hour,' 'In His Image'), showing that the more humanlike the creation, the deeper the emotional response — including uncanny-valley unease. He imports the animal-ethics debate (Aristotle's property view, Kant's indirect duties, Singer and Regan on moral patients) to frame personhood as the determinant of moral duty, then uses Locke's memory-continuity via 'The Trade-Ins' to argue TZ's androids would be persons, so their routine destruction or disassembly amounts to murder — the show's unstated definition of evil as treating people like disposable objects.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 16 "7. Loss of Memory, Loss of Me" — Lay tests Locke's memory theory against the series: Marsha in 'The After Hours' is only the mannequin-person again when she remembers being one, and David Gurney in 'Person or Persons Unknown' has lost his identity because his memories lack factivity — they correspond to no actual past. Reid's brave-officer chain and Parfit's psychological continuity from Reasons and Persons then let him handle the hard cases: Jana's fake 'memory tracks' in 'The Lateness of the Hour' can still constitute her identity as overlapping chains of mental states (severed by reprogramming into Nelda), while the post-Transformation girl of 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' has all of Marilyn's memories but not her beliefs, desires, or character — so Marilyn did not survive.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 12 "2. The Unimportance of Identity When You Have a Portal Gun" — The chapter argues Rick C-137 is already dead: the Brainalyzer body-hops in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption' and the Operation Phoenix swap in 'Big Trouble in Little Sanchez' copy psychological states rather than transfer a consciousness, so each post-transfer Rick is a new psychological clone, exactly as in Parfit's Teletransporter. Building from Locke's memory theory of personal identity to Parfit's claim that identity is not what matters, it reads the dimension-hop in 'Rick Potion #9', the Morty voucher, and the ambiguous clone Beth of 'The Rickchurian Mortydate' as the show itself endorsing psychological continuity over numerical identity. What matters is that someone carries on Rick's desires and relationships, so nobody noticed the protagonist's death.
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 21 "9. To Err Is Human, to Forget … Sublime" — Huntingford contrasts Stranger Things with its blueprint, Stephen King's It: where It forces the Losers Club back to the traumatic truth of childhood, the show traffics in 'false nostalgia,' vicarious nostalgia for an Eighties that only existed on screen, supported by Loftus's false-memory experiments (the impossible Bugs Bunny, Stewart's Root Beer) and Will's anniversary effect and El's mother's broken record of 'breathe, sunflower, rainbow... 450.' Against this malleability she sets Locke's memory theory of personal identity from the Essay and Sacks's 'lost mariner,' warning that nostalgic self-deception can rewrite the self, yet concluding, with It's own ending, that since we cannot survive some horrors, the comforting lie of misremembered childhood is what we tune in for.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 10 "1. Do You Long for Having Your Heart Interlinked" — Timothy Shanahan asks whether K and Joi's relationship counts as romance, sex, and love, using Locke's definition of a person as a thinking, reflective being to ask whether a programmed AI can love, and weighing Joi's programming against the determinism that may bind human lovers too. He reads the Joi-Mariette-K sex scene through Plato's Symposium myth of severed halves seeking union, substance dualism, and a Kant-inspired 'controlled hallucination' view of perception, concluding all sex is a person-to-person conscious connection through bodily intermediaries. Deckard's rejection of Wallace's replica Rachael is explained with a Mona Lisa forgery analogy: an indistinguishable copy still lacks the irreplaceable original person. The baseline question 'Do you long for having your heart interlinked?' frames love as the longing of lonely cells of awareness to connect.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 11 "2. Is Joi a Person" — Chris Lay argues Joi is a person. He raises Searle's objection that programs only simulate understanding and need the right biological 'stuff', then answers it: Joi apparently violates her 'everything you want her to be' programming, so her affection for K is authentic either way. Testing Joi against Locke's personhood criteria — rationality, sentience, and self-consciousness grounded in memory and in her self-sacrifice before Luv — he adds a Cartesian reading in which her transfers between console and emanator make her a disembodied soul, closer to Descartes's essence of the human than embodied replicants are. If a digital person like Joi would also fail the baseline, the wall separating kind would need a full societal reset.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 25 "12. How the Fork Did I Get Here" — Tepley uses Eleanor waking in Michael's office to pose the problem of numerical personal identity: what makes the person in the chair the very same person who died seconds earlier on Earth? He eliminates the same-body theory, since bodies stay behind and lack spatiotemporal continuity, the same-mind theory of psychological continuity, which fails on the 802 reboots and implies the absurdity that two duplicates would both be Eleanor, and the same-soul theory, which offers no criteria for sameness. The 'Janet(s)' revelation that the humans are recomposed from 'essences' turns out to be Aristotelian-Thomistic hylomorphism, committing the show to a same-soul theory of identity it never defends.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 25 "From Backwards -Working Memory, or Working Backwards from Memory" — Treats the Caterpillar's 'Who are YOU?' and Alice's 'Who in the world am I? Ah, that's the great puzzle!' as the classic memory-and-identity problem, rallying Plato's wax tablet and Meno doctrine that learning is recollection, Locke's memory criterion of the same person, and Diderot's dialogue on how without memory there would be no connected self. Tyler Shores reads Alice's botched recitations as Bergson's impersonal habit-memory swamping personal memory, her name-forgetting in the wood through Nietzsche's Untimely Meditations on the necessity of forgetting, the Red King's dream as Freud's alienated memory, and the White Queen's memory that 'works both ways' as a thought experiment tying memory, time, and self together.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 3 "“There is nothing in the desert, and no man needs nothing”" — Argues David in Prometheus qualifies as a Lockean person - intelligence, rule-following rationality, self-reflection via an active power of thought (his self-modeling on Lawrence of Arabia, his judged desire to be free of Weyland's programming), and mental pleasure and pain - while Ash fails the test, reacting only passively to company orders like Locke's unfree tennis ball. Against Weyland's and Shaw's Cartesian soul-based denial ('you're a robot'), this leaves open that beings humans create could share our moral status, making David's ostracism arbitrary and cruel.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 21 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Sorts the Oscar/George Sr. twin confusion into the metaphysical, persistence, and evidential problems of personal identity, testing Aristotle's essential properties (why two actresses play one Marta, what makes each Richter brother distinct) and Descartes's immaterial soul (undermined by surrogate Larry, who stays Larry while Buster remotely operates him). Locke's memory criterion then explains why Oscar is not guilty of George's crimes and why Gob disowns what his forget-me-nows erased, before Thomas Reid's transitivity objection, staged through a lifetime of Gob's roofies, shows Locke committed to old Gob both being and not being young Gob.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 12 "Are you the Next Goliath" — Nelson tests body theory and psychology theory of personal identity on Avengers cases—a Rogers/Pym body swap in the spirit of Locke's prince-and-cobbler experiment, and a Pym brain-hemisphere duplication puzzle—before proposing a distinct 'mantle theory' of superhero identity requiring an appropriate heroic role plus legitimate pedigree, like intellectual property. Legitimacy explains how John Walker (appointed by a government commission) and Bucky Barnes (endorsed by Stark and then Rogers) each really were Captain America. The same theory rules Pym can wear only one of Ant-Man, Giant-Man, Goliath, Yellowjacket, and the Wasp at a time—confirmed by Clint Barton snapping his bow in half when he shed Hawkeye to become the new Goliath.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 19 "Into the Future" — Hanley dismantles the four alleged human-Cylon differences: humans are also 'made' (by God), contain non-organic parts, come as identical twins, and expect to survive death, so religious believers already believe they are Cylons. He defends reproductive cloning as reproduction not replication (a clone is your child, not your copy), models Cylon resurrection as scanning-death-transmission-replication, and shows van Inwagen's replica-swap account of bodily resurrection faces the same worries about blank bodies and which body returns. Following Locke's consciousness criterion, that a soul independent of body and memory explains none of our identity judgments, he rejects karma-based reincarnation without memory, proposes a fission-style plot-fix for Athena's impossible memories of Tyrol, and ends with Cylons settling ancient Earth: 'I am a Cylon, and so are you.'
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 5 "“Your Flesh, Too, is Weak. But You Have… Potential”" — Mentyka maps the two antagonists of System Shock 2 onto the two classical criteria of personal identity: the parasitic Many, one flesh persisting through wildly different bodies, embody the bodily criterion, while the rogue AI SHODAN, pure data abandoning first Citadel then the Von Braun, embodies psychological continuity from Locke's memory theory. He runs the standard objections (Reid and Butler on memory's circularity, cell replacement, cybernetic implants, sleep and infancy) against both sides, then turns to Parfit's claim that identity is not what matters, only relations of degree, likening the reused 'Soldier #G65434-2' avatar to a person surviving through successors. The player character, physical like the Many yet armed with SHODAN's cybernetic knowledge, suggests identity needs both body and mind.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 17 "“Don’t forget, she’s a dangerous individual”" — The chapter tests the White Bear Justice Park's daily torture of Victoria Skillane against every major theory of punishment: Kant and Hegel's retributivism makes her deserve punishment (her crime could not be universalized and annulled justice) but cannot justify a punishment disproportionate to the crime. Locke's memory criterion suggests Punished Victoria is not the person who did the crime, though Parfit's psychological continuity and Thomson's bodily continuity restore the identity. Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism partially vindicates the park as deterrence and incapacitation, but cannot explain the laughing crowds — which Machiavelli's civic spectacle and Nietzsche's genealogy of punishment (Schadenfreude as moralized creditor-debtor pleasure) explain: the crowd is gleefully reenacting Victoria's own crime and calling it justice.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 38 "“Exit Game”" — Reading 'Striking Vipers' through its closed- and open-door imagery, the chapter asks whether Danny and Karl's virtual sex as Lance and Roxette is adultery, testing the question with Plato's Ring of Gyges (what people do when no one can see them), Locke's memory theory (if Danny remembers Roxette's sex acts, is Roxette Danny?), and behaviorist replies that only physical penetration counts. Nietzsche supplies the chapter's frame: his master/slave morality and his view of life as self-created representational art explain how the characters' hidden, mind-only moral inversion creates real existential meaning in virtual sex. The episode's fusion of bodily and mental pleasure is said to break down Mill's higher/lower pleasures distinction - 'lower' physical virtual pleasures yield a 'higher' sense of wholeness - and Schopenhauer's insatiable striving plus Husserl's meaning-conferring perception underwrite the conclusion that virtual love can be real, with Danny and Theo's once-a-year open marriage endorsed as an act-consequentialist balance between monotonous fidelity and escapist fantasy.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 43 "A Dilemma" — The chapter asks 'Is your cookie you?', running theories of personal identity through Black Mirror's copies: the soul theory surfaces when Clayton signs away his 'digital self'; Locke's memory theory implies Cookie-Greta is Greta - a reductio, since one person cannot be wholly in two places at once (the same problem for Ashley Too and the thousand Hang the DJ simulations) - and the perdurantist patch recasts Greta and her cookie as time-slices of one four-dimensional person. Physical theories (Olson's animalism, Unger's brain-essentialism) rule out survival by upload, so Yorkie dies when her body dies even though digital Yorkie continues in San Junipero; Parfit's no-self bundle view and the teletransporter case then dissolve the fear, since there is no ego to lose and ordinary survival is 'about as bad' as being destroyed and replaced by a replica. The upshot: the punishment and immortality plots (Joe's million-year Christmas loop, San Junipero) require cookies to be both conscious and psychologically connected in the right way, and the episodes' horror depends on leaving that genuinely uncertain.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 27 "15. Memories. In the End, Is That All There Is" — David LaRocca takes Mr. Carson's confession to Mrs. Hughes - 'The business of life is the acquisition of memories. In the end, that's all there is' - and asks whether memory really is a possession that can be collected. He traces the spatial metaphors Carson's view rests on: the classical memory palace of Cicero and the Ad Herennium, Augustine's 'huge court of memory' from the Confessions, and Downton itself as a haunted storehouse where photographs of the dead Sybil and Carson's lost Alice Neal keep trauma alive rather than heal it. Against this acquisitional model he sets contemporary neuroscience (Daniella Schiller's reconsolidation research), which shows memories are rewritten rather than collected, undermining both Carson's nostalgia and the idea that personal identity is a fixed archive of the past.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 20 "Long-Term Identity" — Asks whether the final Duncan Idaho ghola, reawakened with the memories of all his serial ghola lives, is the same person as the original Idaho, testing physical continuity, Locke's memory criterion (Hayt before reawakening is not yet Idaho, which is why he dies again for House Atreides only after recovery), Parfit's psychological connectedness with its redescription of identity as mere survival, Schechtman's narrative self-constitution, and four-dimensionalist 'selfworms' with Gurney Halleck and Leto II as examples. It concludes that Herbert treats personal identity as something that shifts with technology and social recognition, so that the final Duncan's integration of five thousand years of lives is genuinely one person: same Duncans, same person.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 22 "Get Out of My Mind!" — Applies Locke's distinction between human animals and conscious, reflecting persons to the Duniverse, noting that the Bene Gesserit's 'we sift people to find the humans' gets Locke backwards. Jessica's Spice Agony extends her consciousness back to Raquella Berto-Anirul, which together with Reid's gallant-officer objection (recast as Gurney Halleck's fading memory of his sister's eyes) breaks the transitivity of Lockean identity, since Jessica-A and Raquella-C would have to be identical without sharing any memory. It closes by weighing psychological-continuity views against animalism and Dennett's self as a 'centre of narrative gravity', leaving puzzles like Alia the Abomination, who shares every memory with her mother.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 26 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Kenneth Sayles reads Peter's and Valentine's anonymous rise on the nets through three lenses: John Locke's identity theory asks how a virtual identity can lack a physical anchor, Plato's Ring of Gyges asks what anonymity does to justice, and Hannah Arendt warns that 'action without a name... is meaningless' and that faceless power is a precondition of totalitarianism. Comparing the personas to the hacker collective Anonymous and to identity theft, he concludes our own Internet could breed its own Locke and Demosthenes and asks how much trust we owe virtual people whose controllers we can never know.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 17 "Notes" — Matthew Watts sorts Fallout's artificial beings into cyborgs, synths, and pure robots and tests each against a theory of the self: Locke's memory theory explains the Robobrain socialites of Vault 118 and Nick Valentine's implanted prewar past, Parfit's psychological continuity (identity as a matter of degree) makes the Old World Blues Think Tank a caricature of a self stretched too thin, and Putnam's machine-table functionalism with multiple realizability (the Red Menace holotape running on any hardware) undermines Covenant's SAFE test by making function, not substrate, the mark of a mind. DiMA's excision of his own guilty memory in Far Harbor shows identity as Evan Thompson's enactive process rather than stored recall, since pruning memories can maintain or improve the self-in-progress. For moral standing below full personhood, Nussbaum's capabilities approach fits Curie's flourishing (research, companionship, watching a sunset in a synth body) and Singer's sentience criterion fits Victor the Securitron's avoidance of harm, exposing 'substrate prejudice' as a robot analog of speciesism - down to ED-E's triumphant arrival on the West Coast.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 115 "Lumos!" — Pushes the theory to its strangest consequence: if the stolen Marauder's Map belongs to the extended minds of both Fred and George Weasley, then minds can literally overlap. Combined with Locke's memory theory, the chains of memory linking the adult Harry, the teenager facing Voldemort, and the orphaned infant at the Dursleys, Pensieve sharing and magic like Barty Crouch Jr.'s Polyjuice impersonation of Moody or Hermione's rewriting of her parents' memories become genuine identity thefts, as Harry's crisis of self after seeing Snape's worst memory of James illustrates.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 142 "NOTES" — Uses William James's marginal motto, sow a thought and reap a destiny, together with Aristotle's account of how repeated acts shape the soul, to argue that Voldemort's maimed afterlife-state is the cumulative result of freely chosen evil he can no longer muster remorse to undo. Setting Heidegger's atheism against Rowling's depicted afterlife, and adding Locke's character-and-memory identity, Kant's postulate that harmony of virtue and happiness requires an afterlife, and Pascal on why the soul's immortality must concern us, it concludes that if Rowling is right, every choice here is infinitely consequential.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 24 "NOTE" — Asks whether amnesia preserves numerical identity: is the Peter who wakes in the shipping crate still Volume-1 Peter, are Niki and Jessica one person, and is the Sylar whom Matt rewrites with Nathan's memories now Nathan? The chapter builds Locke's memory criterion, breaks it with Reid's transitivity objection run through Mohinder's timeline in 'Five Years Gone,' repairs it with Grice's and Perry's memory-ancestor chains, then destroys the repair with Arthur Petrelli's wipe of Hiro (Forgetful Hiro vs. Stabby Hiro), Bernard Williams's torture thought experiment, Parfit's psychological spectrum, and the graphic novel's branching self-copier Evan. It concludes that no memory criterion can define personal identity, yet memory still matters practically: Claire must act as if she persists over time to keep her promise to Zach and to bother finishing the manatee assignment.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 25 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Michaud argues Peeta effectively died twice — once at the force field, and again when the Capitol's tracker-jacker hijacking rewrote his loving memories of Katniss into hatred. Using Leibniz's Law he rules out the body and DNA as what makes Peeta Peeta, then defends Locke's memory theory through thought experiments about a clone Peeta versus a brain-damaged original. Adapting Plutarch's Ship of Theseus as 'the Problem of Haymitch's Hovercraft,' he questions whether gradual change preserves identity, and finally leans toward Hume and Parfit: there may be no enduring self, only a bundle of perceptions replaced moment by moment. On this view Katniss protects the hijacked Peeta out of respect for the memory of the old Peeta, even as each of us is constantly replaced by someone new.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Mentyka uses minifigure puzzles — can 'Eliza' and 'Beth' be distinct characters when built from identical pieces, and is Eliza the same character after every piece is swapped out, a minifig Ship of Theseus — to introduce the philosophy of the human person. He runs through supervenience on physical parts, Locke's memory theory and its Butler–Reid controversy (Reid in the taxonomy), the Christian Resurrection-of-the-Body background, and Parfit's despairing deflation that identity matters less than what survives us. Against these he defends personalism, citing Max Scheler and Kierkegaard's call in The Single Individual to become one rather than a crowd: a person is both the sigfig and the AFOL building it, constituted by free choices and actions — which is also why the LEGO Movie's 'Where Are My Pants?' mass society is the enemy.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 17 "Solutions to the Problem The youth whose destiny it is to lead Hyrule to the" — Rachel Robison asks how Zelda characters persist through radical change, recasting the Ship of Theseus as Tetra's pirate ship from Wind Waker, whose replaced planks Ganon reassembles into a rival ship and leaving Link to find the true one. Physical-continuity accounts fail because Link projects his consciousness into seagulls and temple mages and becomes a wolf in Twilight Princess; Locke's memory theory fails because Ocarina of Time's child/adult time loops break psychological continuity. Her solution: in the Zelda universe, the goddesses' destiny — embodiment of courage, wisdom, or power — supplies the necessary and sufficient condition of identity, a stipulative metaphysics videogames are free to have.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 24 "Notes" — Trip McCrossin reads 'The Enemy Within's split Kirk (with its LBJ/Vietnam subtext) and 'Second Chances's two Rikers as a crash course in Locke's consciousness theory of personal identity, from 'Turnabout Intruder's body swap and reward-and-punishment problem to the transitivity-of-identity paradox that blocks both Kirks from being the original. Parfit's degrees of psychological connectedness, he argues, explain why TNG treats the both-Rikers-survive answer as uncontroversial where TOS agonized over it. But Thomas Riker's renaming, and David Wiggins's 'only a and b' rule, reveal that identity would become an extrinsic property if branching mattered—so the survival-versus-identity debate ends 'to be continued'.
