- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 17 "“Good Soldiers Follow Orders”" — Brace uses Aristotle on numerical versus specific sameness, Locke's memory theory, and above all Frankfurt's second-order desires to argue the Jango Fett clones are distinct persons despite shared DNA: Fives's and Echo's accumulated memories and choices individuate them, and the Bad Batch's personalized quarters display what Yoda means by 'very different, each one of you are.' Frankfurt's 'wanton' frames Wrecker's impulsive Hulking, while Order 66 distinguishes freedom of action from freedom of will — Rex resists the chip's compulsion but cannot act on his second-order volition, so he never loses personhood. Crosshair's reveal that his chip was long removed recasts his loyalty to the Empire as a freely chosen (if immoral) second-order volition, his right as a person.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 27 "NOTES" — Grubb tests theories of personal identity on the supes: the bodily theory fails because Bill's and Jessica's bodies died and refunctioned at transformation, Locke's memory theory stumbles on amnesiac Eric (who stays Eric despite remembering nothing), and psychological continuity fails because vampirism inflated Bill's aggression and collie-Sam's mind when Andy draws a gun is anyone's guess. She closes with Theodore Sider's four-dimensionalism — lives as long stories of temporal parts — which lets the rambunctious vampire Jessica count as the same person as the demure human girl because both are episodes in one continuing story.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 19 "Notes" — Divides Rust's season-one personae into Taxman (anti-natalist rule-follower), Belligerent (vigilante drunk paralyzed by Nietzsche's Gay Science demon of eternal recurrence), and Patient (the mystic who wakes from his coma feeling his daughter's love, compared to the Persian mystic al-Hallaj), asking what makes them one person. It tests the brute physicalist account (Williams and Ayer — the same bird-tattooed body), the Lockean psychological-continuity account, and the narrative account, arguing only the narrative theory explains how Rust changes without either ignoring change or multiplying selves in one body. The chapter ends by making Rust an exemplar for the viewer: we are narrators who choose who to become, so 'I know who I am' is a victory.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 15 "6. In a Mirror Is Our Image" — Karavitis places thirteen robot and android episodes on a spectrum from the X109B14 computer of 'The Brain Center at Whipple's' to indistinguishable androids like Alicia, arguing that the moral duties we owe artificial creations depend on personhood. By Locke's memory-continuity account of identity, the mind-transferred couple of 'The Trade-Ins' remain persons, and so would androids created from scratch, which makes the routine destruction of Alicia, Grandma, and Jana murder. The animal-ethics tradition from Aristotle's property view through Kant's indirect duties to Singer and Regan's moral patients supplies the analogy, and the show's unstated definition of evil is treating persons as disposable objects.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 16 "7. Loss of Memory, Loss of Me" — Lay applies Locke's memory theory to 'Person or Persons Unknown' and 'The After Hours': without factive memories linking David Gurney to his supposed past, and Marsha to her mannequin history, identity is lost in both directions. 'The Lateness of the Hour' strains the view, since Jana's implanted 'memory tracks' are not memories of real events yet she plainly is someone, and Reid's chain objection shows memory alone cannot span a life. Parfit's psychological continuity over the whole network of mental states resolves the cases, and 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' completes it: the post-Transformation person keeps Marilyn's memories but none of her desires or traits, so Marilyn did not survive.
- **Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test**, ch. 8 "P A R T T H R E E" — James DiGiovanna uses Dr. Manhattan's origin — disintegration in the intrinsic field chamber and self-reassembly — plus his teleportations to Mars and his split into three simultaneous selves, to run the classic personal identity debates. Descartes's immaterial thinking substance, Hume's mere bundle of perceptions, and Locke's memory theory are tested against a being who remembers in both time directions and rebuilds his body from pure thought ('restructuring myself after the subtraction of my intrinsic field was the first trick I learned'); Parfit's teletransporter, physical and psychological criteria, and fission cases — mirrored in Nagel's split-brain patients — then show ordinary people cannot say whether they would survive teleporting or bisection. The chapter concludes Dr. Manhattan is the only being with fully secure identity, since his consciousness needs neither body nor an unbroken spatiotemporal path and he can encompass several points of view at once.
- **X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse**, ch. 5 "X-Men and Philosophy" — After the acknowledgments and an introduction, this block runs two essays. Hopkins's 'The Lure of the Normal' uses Storm, Rogue, Beast, and the Morlocks plus the mutant 'cure' to dissect descriptive vs. prescriptive 'normality,' citing Foucault on the monster/individual-to-be-corrected and Nietzsche's Zarathustra to frame transhumanist vs. bioconservative attitudes to enhancement. Southworth's Wolverine essay argues personal identity via Locke's memory theory (the Xavier/Cassandra Nova body-swap) and Parfit's fission (Madrox's duplicates, Wolverine's repeated brain trauma), concluding that many distinct 'persons' have inhabited Wolverine's body.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 26 "Twelfth Hole Midround and Midlife Defining Moments" — Andy Wible uses defining mid-round shots (the water ball on Augusta's twelfth, the shank that ruins a round) as a way into theories of personal identity, asking why some events make us who we are. He runs through body theory, Descartes's soul theory ('I think, therefore I am'), and Locke's memory theory (the prince-and-cobbler case), refining it with Shoemaker's quasi-memories, to argue that memory is central to identity and explains why a golfer cannot shake a bad shot. He then weighs the Buddhist/Humean/Heraclitean denial of a permanent self as a coping tool ('someone else hit the shank') and debates whether the beta-blocker Propranolol, which dulls adrenaline-fixed memories, could ethically erase the yips much as it treats PTSD.
- **The Philosophy of Joss Whedon**, ch. 7 "Angel, Angelus, and Personal Identity" — This file collects Part II chapters 6-9. It defends Stephen Mulhall's 'bold thesis' against Baggini, Murray Smith and Livingston, using Whedon's dialogue-free episode 'Hush' as film that 'shows' a Zen-like epistemic point resisting paraphrase, and works through the Russell-Wartenberg debate over whether narrative film can convey arguments (via The Matrix and Eternal Sunshine). It reads The Cabin in the Woods as a counterargument to utilitarianism grounded in Nel Noddings's ethics of care ('people are more important than humanity') and an Aristotelian theory of worthwhile horror. The Angel/Angelus chapter stages the Wes-Holtz dispute as competing theories of personal identity, testing Locke's memory theory and Parfit's psychological-continuity view against Whedon's soul-based metaphysics to argue what ultimately matters is one's care-based relations with others.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Smith reads Memento as a test of Locke's memory theory of personal identity. He explains Locke's view that consciousness of past actions (not soul or body) constitutes the self, rehearses Reid's transitivity objection and the circularity objection, and uses Parfit's account of memory and fusion to defend a survival-not-identity reading. He distinguishes 'Leonard 1' (anterograde amnesiac who returns each cycle) from 'Leonard 2b', a person fused from his own memories and those projected onto Sammy Jankis, arguing we too are 'fused' survivors who reinterpret hazy pasts, complicating responsibility and concern for our futures.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 9 "What Is It to Be Human Blade Runner and Dark City" — Knight and McKnight read Blade Runner and Dark City as noir-influenced cyberpunk that asks what it is to be human. They argue that Deckard's replicant status (the origami unicorn, the shared family photo) and Murdoch's serially reprogrammed memory show memory to be unreliable, invoking Locke's prince-and-cobbler thought experiment and the problem of new brains in one body. Their conclusion is that it is emotion and relationship, not memory, that ground agency and personhood: Roy's empathy in dying and Deckard's love for Rachael, Murdoch's love for Emma/Anna, are what mark the characters as human.
- **The Philosophy of Spike Lee**, ch. 24 "Rethinking the First Person Autobiography, Authorship, and the Contested Self in Malcolm X" — LaRocca uses Lee's Malcolm X and Haley's 'as told to' Autobiography to probe personal identity and authorship: since Haley (not X) authored the book and Lee/Washington perform Haley's literary X, he asks whether one can write another's autobiography and what becomes of the self. He surveys Locke's memory theory of identity, Descartes's thinking subject, Hume's bundle of perceptions, and Wittgenstein's denial of a thinking subject to frame X's serial renamings (Malcolm Little, Detroit Red, Malcolm X, El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz) as a 'ceaselessly evolving,' unfinished identity. He reads Lee's techniques—nondiegetic gunshots, the spinning camera, the gliding sidewalk shot ('the eye that can finally see itself'), and the framing Rodney King and Mandela footage ending on 'by any means necessary'—as arguments that the self is a contested literary and cinematic creation.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 21 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Morton reads Schizopolis as Soderbergh's philosophical autobiography of identity, quoting Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding on memory as the ground of personal continuity to interpret Fletcher Munson's 'transmigration' into the doppelganger Dr. Korchek. Because Fletcher carries his own memory and nature into Korchek, he cannot escape his failed marriage (Korchek is sleeping with Fletcher's wife), confirming Lockean continuity: he 'cannot escape his own nature.' Morton ties the film's decayed language games and Elmo Oxygen's gibberish to a view that language masks action, and reads Fletcher's fate-frozen ending as identity surrendered to outside forces.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 16 "7 Memory and Relationships in the Work and Music of Neil Young" — Sizer analyzes how memory shapes Young's songwriting: childhood trauma (polio, his parents' divorce, Omemee) fueling "Sugar Mountain," "Helpless" and "I Am a Child"; the "use and lose" pattern of collaborators and the ghost of Danny Whitten in Crazy Horse; and his late-life dread of memory loss watching his father's dementia. He frames this with Hobbes and Hume on memory-as-imagery, Wittgenstein's associative memory, and Locke's memory theory of personal identity (with Dennett on writing as a means to reconstruct and preserve the self).
- **Joss Whedon as Philosopher**, ch. 7 "Angel, Angelus, and Personal Identity" — This file gathers Part II, arguing Whedon actually philosophizes through film. It works through the film-as-philosophy debate (Mulhall's 'bold thesis' and its critics Baggini, Smith, Livingston, Russell, and Wartenberg), using 'Hush' as a Zen-like case that resists linguistic paraphrase and The Cabin in the Woods to pit Mill's utilitarianism against Noddings's ethics of care (Dana refusing to kill Marty to save the world). Its capstone treats the Angel/Angelus problem as a personal-identity thought experiment, staging the soul theory (Plato), body theory (Hobbes/Holtz), and Locke's and Parfit's memory/psychological-continuity theories, and arguing Whedon's eight-season Angel-Angelus and Fred-Illyria cases serve as a cinematic counterexample to Neo-Lockean continuity, ultimately endorsing a care-based view of what matters in identity.
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 7 "We Are the Change That We Seek" — These essays treat time, selfhood and substance across Nolan's films. Fosl argues Nolan's selves (Leonard, Bill in Following, the Borden twins, Bruce Wayne) are unstable narratives signified through manipulable objects, invoking Locke on memory-based identity, Augustine on memoria, Nietzsche on forgetting and Sartre/Gadamer on the manipulable past. LaRocca applies Clark and Chalmers's Extended Mind Thesis to Memento, arguing Leonard's tattoos and Polaroids are literal external memories whose deliberate falsification ('Don't believe his lies') makes him morally culpable for murder. Willis uses Lacan's gaze and objet a to read Following's voyeur-becomes-viewed structure and 'the box' as a lure. McGowan reads Interstellar through Hegel: the mysterious 'they' who opened the wormhole are revealed as future humanity, dissolving substance into subject and licensing Cooper's retroactive causality as the 'ghost' who saves Murph.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 7 "A Dead End" — Patrick Stokes uses the Doctor's regeneration and the multi-Doctor stories ("The Five Doctors," "The Caves of Androzani") to test theories of personal identity. He runs Locke's memory criterion against Reid's transitivity objection, Parfit's Branch-Line teleportation case (a Gallifrey-to-Skaro replica), Nozick's Closest Continuer schema applied to the Valeyard, four-dimensional person-stages, animalism, and narrative identity, showing each fails to explain regeneration. He gestures that identity may lie in a subjective self-appropriation, the Doctor taking ownership of his incarnations.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 8 "Doctor Who and the Ultimate Answer" — Greg Littmann uses regeneration and dozens of Doctor Who transformations (doubles like the Abbot of Amboise, disembodied brains, transmats, Eldrad's body-hopping, Cassandra's possession) as hypotheticals to test criteria for personal identity. He shows bodily identity, spatiotemporal continuity of the body, the memory criterion (undercut by Donna and John Smith cases), and psychological/personality similarity each face counterexamples, deliberately leaving the question open so readers judge for themselves.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 9 "What’s Persistence Without Identity" — Richard Hanley asks what counts as personal survival for a Time Lord, distinguishing body, mind, and soul theories. Using the Tenth Doctor's "every single cell" regeneration, the severed hand grown into a Doctor in "Journey's End," John Smith's Chameleon-Arch amnesia, and Jackson Lake's infostamp fugue, he argues bodily and soul continuity fail and defends a neo-Lockean mental-continuity criterion refined by Nozick's closest-continuer schema, concluding with Parfit that persistence may not be what matters in survival.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 10 "I Think, Therefore I Exist . . . I Think" — David Kyle Johnson uses regeneration and the DoctorDonna to ask what makes the First and Tenth Doctor the same person. He debunks the Platonic/Cartesian soul via Phineas Gage and brain science, refutes Locke's memory criterion with Reid's transitivity and the amnesia/John Smith cases, questions Parfit's causal-chain view via the "Journey's End" meta-crisis, then argues persons are four-dimensional "time worms" (sets of stages) before pushing to the deflationary conclusion that, like a "heap," a person may not exist as a discrete entity at all.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 29 "Love and Doctors" — Paul Dawson asks whether the Doctor dies when he regenerates by separating body, organism, and person. Using Kripke's rigid vs non-rigid designators he weighs whether 'the Doctor' names one individual or a role (the numbered Doctors, 'my replacements'), then applies Locke's memory criterion and Reid's transitivity objection, adopting Parfit's psychological-connectedness chain (via Sarah Jane's overlapping memories). He concludes the organism survives regeneration necessarily while the person survives only if psychological continuity holds, and argues the 'Journey's End' metacrisis Doctor Two is genuinely the person Rose loved through branching/fission.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 19 "10. Slippin’ Identity" — Šekrst uses Jimmy's many personas—Slippin' Jimmy, James McGill, Saul Goodman, Viktor St. Clair, Gene Takavic—to survey theories of personal identity. She shows psychological continuity (Locke's memory-based view) falters on sleep, comas, and Chuck's apparent dementia, and the brute-physical/bodily view falters on brain-transplant thought experiments and the Phineas Gage case ('no longer Gage'). She defends a narrativist account with a reality constraint: identity is the story one is disposed to tell about oneself, so Jimmy can disown Slippin' Jimmy and reidentify as Saul, and Gene can recall his Saul self—narrative being sufficient though perhaps not necessary for persistence, with others' stories contributing but the protagonist's being authoritative.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 18 "Be Slow to Judge" — Southworth uses Wolverine and other X-Men to examine personal identity. Locke's memory criterion (illustrated by the Cassandra Nova/Xavier mind-swap and connected memories) implies that Wolverine's repeated amnesia makes him literally several successive persons until House of M restores all his memories. Jamie Madrox's up-to-100 duplicates function as a real-world version of Parfit's fission thought experiment, showing sameness of memory is insufficient for identity. Southworth applies Parfit's brain-based, seven-year view to Wolverine's constant healed head trauma and concludes we should be slow to judge characters as the 'same' culpable person.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 15 "6. In a Mirror Is Our Image" — Karavitis arranges thirteen Twilight Zone android/machine episodes on a moral spectrum from simple machines ('The Brain Center at Whipple's,' 'Steel') to indistinguishable androids ('The Lonely,' 'I Sing the Body Electric,' 'The Lateness of the Hour') to fully synthetic humans ('The Trade-Ins'). Using personhood, moral-agent/moral-patient distinctions, Aristotle's and Kant's views on animals, Singer and Regan on degrees not kinds, and Locke's memory theory of identity, he argues that if body-swapped Holts remain persons then scratch-built androids are persons too—so the destroyed androids were murdered, and evil is treating persons as disposable objects.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 16 "7. Loss of Memory, Loss of Me" — Lay contrasts Locke's memory theory of personal identity with Parfit's psychological-continuity view across several episodes. Locke's factive-memory account explains 'The After Hours' (Marsha the mannequin) and 'Person or Persons Unknown' (David Gurney's non-factive memories), but fails for 'The Lateness of the Hour' (android Jana has installed beliefs, not memories) and especially 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You,' where post-Transformation Marilyn keeps all her memories yet is a different person. Using a Reid-flavored chain of episodes, Lay argues Parfit gets it right: a whole overlapping network of mental states, not memory alone, individuates the self.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 20 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Kyle Fruh and Emily Thomas use tattoos to attack two questions of personal identity. Against Locke's dominant psychological (memory) account and for the unpopular somatic (bodily) account defended by Judith Thomson and Eric Olson, they argue the depth of people's attachment to their tattoos – individuating them or marking group membership – shows we identify with our bodies. On the 'Who am I?' question they argue tattoos have an 'anchoring effect' in narrative identity: permanent, irremovable ink (contrasted with new laser-removable ink, and with dehumanizing forced Auschwitz numbers) fixes a commitment 'come what may,' echoing Quine's phrase, so that 'when you get a tattoo, you tattoo you.'
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 13 "The Vampire with a Soul Angel and the Quest for Identity" — Amy Kind uses Joss Whedon's Angel/Angelus to test theories of personal identity and moral responsibility. Body-swap episodes support the Lockean/Parfitian psychological (memory) theory over Olson's biological theory, and shared memories make Angel psychologically continuous with, hence identical to, Angelus. But Kind invokes Parfit's distinction between continuity and connectedness (with real cases like Katherine Power and Sara Jane Olson) to argue identity is not what matters: the ensouled Angel's radical break in psychological connectedness means he should not be held morally responsible for Angelus's atrocities. She closes with Mill that it is better to be Angel burdened by a soul than Angelus unburdened.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 10 "4. Total Recall & The Sixth Day" — Rowlands treats Total Recall as a defence of the memory (psychological-continuity) theory of personal identity: erasing Quaid's memories and restoring Hauser's is an essential change that ends Quaid, so he fights for his existence. He works through and rejects the soul theory (dualism's problems) and body/brain theories via head-transplant and neuron-replacement thought experiments, distinguishing Aristotle's essential/accidental change and Heraclitus's river. The Sixth Day's cloning raises Parfit's fission/duplication problem: a double success cannot be a failure, driving him to abandon identity for a Heraclitean 'river of selves' bound by survival, not identity.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 13 "Who is Who" — On regeneration and personal identity, the chapter runs Doctor Who through Leibniz's law of identity and soul-based individuation, Locke's memory criterion of personhood, and Hume's bundle theory, testing them against multi-Doctor stories, the Ganger duplicates ('The Almost People'), 'The Girl Who Waited' (closest-continuer theory) and 'City of Death.' It then shifts to physicalism (the Morbius brain) and to a pragmatist, social theory of the self (James, Dewey, Mead's 'taking the attitude of the other,' Dennett's intentional stance), reading the reintegration of identity in 'The Doctor Dances.'
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 18 "Be Slow to Judge" — Jason Southworth uses Wolverine's repeated memory erasures to test Locke's memory (and connected-memory) criterion of personal identity, arguing that on Locke's view a new 'person' inhabits Wolverine's body each time his memories are wiped, until House of M restores them all. He then deploys Jamie Madrox, whose duplicates share and re-merge memories yet act as distinct agents, as a real-comics version of Parfit's fission case, pushing Parfit's conclusion that identity requires physical (brain) continuity. Because Wolverine's healing factor constantly rebuilds his brain, the moral is to 'be slow to judge' whether a character is the same person who acted before.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 12 "3. What Is Who" — The chapter runs the Doctor's regenerations and the 'Timeless Child' reveal through competing theories of personal identity: Plato's soul/Forms, Locke's memory continuity, and bodily continuity, all of which the Doctor's body-swaps and forgotten lifetimes defeat (the Twelfth Doctor's 'you are a broom' speech recasts the Ship of Theseus). It endorses an existentialist answer—personal identity is chosen and constantly 'becoming,' as the Thirteenth Doctor declares 'I know exactly who I am. I'm the Doctor'—and uses Sartre against Freud to explain how the Doctor and the Whovian fandom reconcile internal and external selves in a community of acceptance. It closes arguing that only an 'objective' immortality (memories preserved in the Matrix) survives death, not a subjective self.

### The Death of God

"God is dead" is Nietzsche's diagnosis, most famously voiced by a madman in The Gay Science, that belief in the Christian God and the moral and metaphysical order it underwrote has lost its hold on Western culture. He does not mean it as a triumphant slogan but as an event of enormous consequence: without a divine guarantor of meaning and value, humanity risks sliding into nihilism unless it can create new values for itself. The phrase names both a cultural crisis and an opportunity, marking the loss of an absolute foundation and the task of finding meaning without one.

- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 20 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Douglas Blount tests Nietzsche against Sauron, whose forging and grasp of the One Ring - even striving to supplant Ilúvatar - enacts the will to power, exploitation, the death of God, and the ideal of the Übermensch. He argues that in Middle-earth the naked will to power appears not as a brave new humanity but as plain evil, and that Tolkien answers Nietzsche not with argument but with a rival portrait: Gandalf's self-sacrifice on the Bridge of Khazad-dûm, Frodo's mercy to Gollum that becomes Middle-earth's salvation, and Sam's humble refusal of 'Samwise the Strong'. Judged by Nietzsche's own aesthetic criterion of taste, Tolkien's vision of community, humility, and abnegation is the more beautiful - and therefore the more compelling - portrait of reality.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 25 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Joe Kraus argues Tolkien wrote The Lord of the Rings in part as a protest against modernism - the post-WWI mood (Berman, Marx's 'all that is solid melts into air', Nietzsche's 'God is dead') that tradition is obsolete and whatever can be done must be done. The heroes win by remembering: Gandalf alone thinks to watch the Shire, Sam's book-learning about elves and the password 'Elbereth' saves the day at Cirith Ungol, while Saruman and Denethor fall into modern despair through the palantír and Pippin's stone dropped in Moria brings Gandalf down. The Ring itself is modernism's false promise of remaking the world, and Tolkien answers it with a fantasy where ancient lore has tangible power - sealed by Pippin's maturing into one of Middle-earth's great librarians.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 17 "And There Is No Escape" — Abrams reads Allen through Foucault's panopticon: modern society is unlimited voyeurism in which the medieval God whose 'eyes are on us always' has been replaced by the omniscient gaze of Film — Cliff's exposé documentary forcing Lester to watch his own life in Crimes and Misdemeanors, Tom Baxter stepping off the screen in The Purple Rose of Cairo, and the nested eavesdropping layers of Another Woman, which he counts to infinity via Noël Carroll's 'mass art'. Against Mary Nichols's virtue-ethics reading, he argues Allen's ethics is Nietzschean self-fashioning: Judah lives 'beyond good and evil' where Raskolnikov failed, Allan Felix sheds the Bogart alter ego and 'gives style' to his character in Play It Again, Sam, while Eve in Interiors stages Hegel's master–slave dialectic, the 'master' artist dependent for her identity on those she objectifies.
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 20 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Bamford argues that Atkins's insistence that dieters evaluate the plan for their individual needs parallels Nietzsche's cultural therapy: as the death of God left modern culture nihilistic, so a processed-food culture suffers 'nutritional nihilism,' and the 'mega-orthodox' doctors who worship medical consensus with 'religious fervor' treat science as a replacement religion. Reading Ecce Homo's 'question of nutriment' alongside Twilight of the Idols, she shows that Nietzsche's perspectivism — no uninterpreted facts, only interpretations from physiological perspectives — makes each dieter fully responsible for interpretation, which is why Atkins must ask us to think for ourselves. The limit: where Atkins keeps an 'absolute faith in empirical science' (and Atkins Nutritionals mass-markets processed low-carb products), a properly Nietzschean therapy would question that faith too.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 12 "Getting Right with Brian (Just in Case)" — Reads Life of Brian through Nietzsche's madman: the crowd's laughter at Brian's market sermons ('consider the lilies... have the birds got jobs?') enacts the death of the cheerless, pathos-soaked God, with Brian as a sincere 'divine idiot' who escapes ressentiment by falling idiotically below the dialectic rather than rising above it as an Übermensch. Bergson's account of the comic — rigidity invisible to its bearer, 'as though wearing the ring of Gyges with reverse effect' — explains why the Pythons' straight men, British class consciousness, and the Roman/British empires ('Romani ite domum,' the centurion's Latin lesson) are funny, and why Britons and Romans can laugh at themselves while Americans cannot. Pivoting from Jorge's war on laughter in Eco's The Name of the Rose, the chapter closes with a Pascal's-wager parody: having laughed at Brian, you have already wagered your immortal soul on God being British — the sort of God who can take a joke.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 15 "And Now for . . . Comedic Eliminativism" — Argues The Meaning of Life dismantles the 'axial' picture of life as a journey toward a salvific destination (Jaspers's Axial Age thinking), instanced in the headmaster who announces Jenkins's mother's death between Empire Day announcements, the tank fish who never connect Howard's being eaten to their own fate, and the restaurant couple ordering 'philosophy for two' with no appetite for wisdom. The classical answers all fail as delivered: Socrates's philosophy as learning how to die, Heidegger's claim that facing death reveals one's own unique possibilities, and Kant's three questions (What can I know? What should I do? For what may I hope?) collapse into the question of life's meaning, but religion has gone stale and philosophy has become detached trivia. The Pythons instead accomplish the user-friendly domestication of the death of God — the hearty laughter Nietzsche and Derrida counsel — and the chapter coins 'comedic eliminativism' on the model of eliminative materialism's dissolution of Descartes's mind-body problem: replace the yearning for the meaning of life with altered reactions, laughter itself as the solution to the riddle.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 20 "Knowledge and Nihilism Science and Monty Python’s The Meaning of Life" — Croskery tours the social institutions that promise guidance for a good life, pairing each with a Python work: Adam Smith's invisible hand and Bentham's greatest-happiness utilitarianism fail in the 'Merchant Banker' sketch, where charity leaves the banker 'a pound down on the whole deal', while Marxist market ideology and alienation surface in the Communist Quiz and the accountant who longs to be a lion tamer. In The Holy Grail, Aristotle's doctrine of the mean sorts Brave Sir Robin's cowardly flight from Sir Lancelot's rash slaughter of a wedding party and Galahad's desire-distorted chastity at Castle Anthrax, with Bedevere's duck-weighing witch logic showing reasoning without judgment, and Arthur's quest collapses because 'strange women lying in ponds handing out swords is no basis for a system of government'. Life of Brian's 'blessed are the cheesemakers' and the 'You're all individuals!' crowd ground a Kantian demand for autonomy against blind obedience to religious rules. The Meaning of Life's 'Galaxy Song' and 'spiraling coils of self-replicating DNA' pose Nietzschean nihilism — science dissolving the highest values — which the film's closing advice to be nice to people and keep a sense of humor answers with a modest, livable meaning.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 13 "U2 and Philosophy" — Malpas takes The Joshua Tree as an album about place: its desert imagery and restless movement ('Where the Streets Have No Name', 'I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For' as 'an anthem of doubt more than faith') carry the listener from Ireland to Reagan's America to Pinochet's Chile, while its political references - Ethiopian famine, El Salvador, Dublin high-rises - always work through concrete locations rather than abstract ideals. Using Heidegger on homelessness as the inability to dwell, and Marx and Engels' 'all that is solid melts into air', he argues that modernity has not erased our relatedness to place but covered it over. The album's desolation is therefore readable the other way: belonging is constituted through care, commitment and uncertain journeying in the places we already are ('Heartland').
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 11 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Butterfield takes Bond's answer to Elektra in The World Is Not Enough - he survives by 'tak[ing] pleasure in great beauty' - and asks whether hedonism can answer the problem of suffering and death. She reads Bond through Heidegger's being-towards-death (quoting Live and Let Die's 'You start to die the moment you are born'), then diagnoses him as Kierkegaard's aesthetic 'seducer', an immature escapist who dreads boredom and flees commitment, before rehabilitating him with Nietzsche and Camus: Bond flushing the cyanide pill down the toilet in From Russia with Love and Mathis's advice in Casino Royale to make evil 'personal' show Bond creating his own values beyond good and evil, surviving the absurd through style and personal vendetta. Bond emerges as an existentialist role model for courage and creativity, though we should not copy his hedonism or lawlessness.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 31 "Metallica, Nihilism, and Nostalgia" — Peter Fosl reads Metallica's lyrics ("Leper Messiah," "The God That Failed," "One," "To Live Is to Die," "Escape") as extending Nietzsche's and Marx's critiques of Christianity: religion as slave morality born of ressentiment and as opium deadening the oppressed, illustrated by the landmine veteran of "One" pleading with a silent God and Hetfield's abandoned-childhood grief. He argues the band often falls into the "incomplete nihilism" Nietzsche predicted, lamenting God's failure and longing nostalgically for the Christian meaning it can no longer believe in rather than transvaluating values. Yet the defiance of "The Four Horsemen" and "Escape" and the band's creative power show it also working toward an overcoming of Christian nihilism, confirmed for Fosl by Hetfield's post-rehab health.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 10 "Rupert’s Response and Responsibility" — Biderman and Jacobowitz read Rope through Nietzsche: Brandon and Philip strangle their classmate David as would-be Nietzschean supermen, acting on mentor Rupert Cadell's cocktail-party theory that murder can be an art for a superior few. The chapter explains the will to power, the Ubermensch, and the death of God, then argues Brandon is no superman: he kills from weakness and a bully's need for an audience, mistaking crass destruction for the refined self-creation Nietzsche demanded, just as the fascist appropriation of Nietzsche fails. Rupert's horrified final speech, renouncing 'superior or inferior beings' and insisting each of us is 'a separate human being,' raises whether a teacher can disavow responsibility when students act out his provocative ideas: ideas have consequences, and the only true test of a philosophy is whether we can live by it.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 24 "Kill Bill Volume 2 Mommy Kills Daddy" — Mark Conard reads the two Kill Bill volumes as Tarantino's Oedipal play and self-therapy: Volume 1 fuses the movie genres of his childhood with women in the lead roles while Bill lurks as the absent, godlike father, and the Bride's empowerment is traced from the Pussy Wagon through the Hanzo sword—a transformation from 'pussy to cock'. In Volume 2, Pai Mei teaches her that her strength lies in her own hands, freeing her from a masculine conception of power, while Bill is humanized—sandwiches, flute-playing, a heart that can break—so that killing him means killing the father's God-like hold, explicitly glossed through Nietzsche's death of God. The final duel's sheathed sword lets the woman, as woman, defeat the man, and the Oedipal act succeeds where Oedipus himself had to go blind.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 25 "Like Caine in Kung Fu" — Bence Nanay and Ian Schnee argue Pulp Fiction is genuinely Nietzschean, but not by celebrating violence: the film stages the crisis of meaning after God's death through two reactions to chance. Vincent is the passive nihilist—dogmatically insisting the six bullets mean nothing, inheriting gangster values unquestioned, modeling himself on Elvis—while Jules's 'moment of clarity' makes him a Nietzschean free spirit who creates perspective-relative meaning and breaks the cycle of violence by buying Ringo and Honey Bunny's lives. His plan to 'walk the earth, like Caine in Kung Fu' reworks Zarathustra's wandering, and the running toilets gag marks Vincent's blindness to the significance of events, which is why only one of them survives.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 17 "There is No Dark Side of the Moon Really. Matter of Fact It’s All Dark" — Johnston reads The Dark Side of the Moon through Buber's I and Thou: modern life traps us in the I-It mode of experience, from 'Welcome to the Machine' to teachers who treat students as replaceable Its ('Hey, teacher, leave us kids alone!') and Horkheimer's instrumental reason that turns personnel into 'human resources,' while the album repeatedly calls us to the I-You encounter, from 'Echoes'' strangers whose glances meet ('I am you and what I see is me,' Waters's origin of empathy) to 'Breathe''s 'don't be afraid to care.' He links the opening heartbeat and the breath of 'Breathe' to Buber's eternal You, defends Buddhism against Buber's charge that enlightenment is worldless monologue (the Buddha becomes one with the world, a perfect reciprocity like the innate You of the womb), and accepts Nietzsche's point that the Enlightenment's abstract God is dead while insisting, with Buber, that encounter with the eternal You remains possible. The album itself, he concludes, resists degenerating into an It: even if 'the sun is eclipsed by the moon,' the light persists and Dark Side can be the antidote to the It-world.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 11 "Meaning The Final Frontier" — Biderman and Devlin read The Wrath of Khan as a Nietzschean test of whether revenge can ground a meaningful life after the death of God: Kirk, stuck 'flying a goddamn computer console' as an admiral, and the Genesis project seek meaning through creation without God, while Khan, broken by exile on Ceti Alpha V, chooses vengeance. Using Nozick's contrast between impartial retribution and personally satisfying revenge, and Nietzsche's will to power, master-slave morality, and ressentiment, they argue Khan had the superhuman gifts and independence from herd morality of a candidate Overman, but let revenge enslave him — culminating in Genesis turned weapon and his dying 'For hate's sake . . . I spit my last breath at thee,' a resounding No to life. Spock's mirror-image self-sacrifice, which affirms life, is offered as the better Nietzschean Overman.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 13 "Why I Can Play Zelda for Four Hours Straight" — Fellela reads Link's endless drudgery (slashing grass for rupees, collecting bottles, leaving the final Ganon fight at a 'permanent pause') through existentialism: Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' is dramatized in Ocarina of Time's opening, where Link must acquire sword, fairy, and skills to make himself the hero, and Nietzsche's 'God is dead' call to become gods is answered by Link restoring meaning to a hostile Hyrule. Camus' Sisyphus figures the repetitive world-saving quest as an absurd hero's owned task, and Frankl's logotherapy (meaning as the tension between what one is and what one should become) explains why humiliating menial tasks, in camp or in laundromats or in Zelda, become bearable and even meaningful. Link's fixed options even illustrate Frankl's point that freedom is the stance we take toward conditions, not freedom from them.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 14 "Game Over" — Janssen argues Zelda is quietly obsessed with death: turning the console off models death as pure absence of experience, which we cannot otherwise comprehend, and gives the gamer a comforting structured formula in place of a chaotic universe. Link, resurrected endlessly to serve the player, is condemned to Hegelian purgatory and what Bernard Williams called the tedium of immortality, while dungeon bosses, who die once and stay dead, are the only genuinely mortal, hence most human, beings in Hyrule. The Wind Waker prologue's eternally returning Hero does suggest Plato-style dualism with an immortal soul, but the chapter notes that Nietzsche's assault on faith destroyed dualism's credibility, leaving the series as a vessel for both materialist nothingness and romantic reincarnation.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 20 "Brush the Cobwebs from the Sky, Let the Genie Out from the Bottle" — Lougheed reads OK Computer, Kid A, and Amnesiac as portraits of Nietzsche's Last Humans: passive, resentful denizens of the world after the death of God, from the 'No Surprises' narrator begging for his quiet life of carbon monoxide to the 'Everything in Its Right Place' man sucking a lemon over the loss of objective right and wrong, whose isolated malice ('when I am king you will be first against the wall') is perspectivism collapsed into passive nihilism. Hail to the Thief then breaks from this landscape: its protagonists risk transcendence as Over Humans who create new, life-affirming values ('2 + 2 = 5'''s 'don't question my authority', 'Backdrifts''' 'nothing more to lose'), keep a critical distance from society's nihilistic sickness ('Where I End and You Begin'), and test their lives against eternal recurrence ('Sail to the Moon'''s 'know right from wrong', '15 Step'''s ending up where you started). The chapter closes by weighing Nietzsche's over-human project against critics who prefer gradual, generational self-overcoming for everyone.
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 15 "The Missionary" — Christopher Hoyt reads Buffett's escape from Catholicism as a case study in secular meaning-making after Nietzsche's death of God, taking the Mardi Gras ritual of Folly swatting Death out of town as Buffett's core spiritual attitude — interpreted the way Wittgenstein criticized Frazer, as an expression of our stance toward death rather than mere magic. Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' frames the post-1960s task of self-definition without God, while Marx's alienation explains what the persona of *Jimmy* refuses: the impersonal work and borrowed values that leave moderns living an alien narrative, like McGuane's character Skelton in Ninety-Two in the Shade. The twist is that *Jimmy*'s pop-culture vocabulary — Tully Mars built from Donovan's Reef and Slim Pickens, Bogart, the Brylcreem jingle — is itself authentic, and the 'semi-true story' of the myth tells deeper truths than a literal biography could, making Buffett something like a pop prophet for late modernity.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 11 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Auxier argues the trilogy is narrated on a Nietzschean lattice rather than being a mere inverted Milton: after tracing the Paradise Lost, Genesis 6, and Pseudepigrapha sources (Azazel as the model for Asriel, Metatron from Third Enoch, Dust from Milton's warring particles), he reads Mrs. Coulter's speech to Father MacPhail about seeking God out and giving him 'the gift of death' as Nietzsche's death of God fused with a description of Nietzsche's own final dementia. Will and Lyra become overman and overwoman beyond good and evil: Will rises by his will and his willingness to kill (the alethiometer's verdict 'He is a murderer' makes him a worthy companion), while Lyra commands both truth and lies, the alethiometer embodying truth as 'a mobile army of metaphors.' But the chapter's payoff is critical: Pullman does not endorse Nietzsche, since in a world where the will to power dominates, the overwoman Mrs. Coulter has no place and falls with Asriel and Metatron into the Abyss, while Xaphania's teaching offers a disciplined, workful imagination as an alternative.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 13 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Fairweather casts the campaign against Pullman's books as Socrates's trial rerun (impiety plus corrupting the young) and asks whether legally protected speech can still be morally wrong, weighing Mill's On Liberty point that children lack the 'maturity of their faculties' against the charge that Pullman's 'killing God' rhetoric inflicts spiritual violence on young believers, by his own image of intercision. The answer comes through Nietzsche's Three Metamorphoses: Asriel, Will, and Lyra play the lion that slays the great 'thou shalt' of the Authority, but the lion's destruction is only the possibility of freedom, since full freedom is Nietzsche's child creating its own values rather than lapsing into nihilism or Sartrean bad faith. Pullman's Republic of Heaven, with its virtues of courage, compassion, love, kindness, and curiosity held in community, is a social ideal rather than a radically Nietzschean one, so the charge of corrupting young readers is deflated.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 12 "Death Knight as Overman" — Luke Cuddy asks whether playing WoW can answer nihilism, using Schopenhauer's bleak remark on our sudden existence and Nietzsche's death of God to set up the problem — King Bangalash dies and WoW goes on, just as humans die and the universe continues. Entering Huizinga's Magic Circle gives Azeroth its meanings, but the player must then dissolve the circle, recognize that the game itself is meaningless, and keep playing anyway — creating the toon as a work of art in the Dionysian spirit. A maxed Death Knight still is not Nietzsche's Overman, because the player affirms only her in-game existence; the fifth step is carrying that self-creation back into real life.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 12 "Oh to Be a Gooner" — Kilpatrick reads Nietzsche's madman's question 'what sacred games shall we have to invent?' as answered by the stadium: after the death of God, soccer has replaced religion as the shared narrative where modern communities make and worship heroes. Using The Birth of Tragedy, he reads a goal as an Apollonian–Dionysian fusion—the scorer's individuated ecstasy merging with the collective joy of teammates and fans—and, on Nietzsche's claim that existence is justified only as an aesthetic phenomenon, argues the game is defensible only when played creatively and artistically rather than by negative, win-at-all-costs tactics. Nietzsche's rejection of nationalism (the state as 'the new idol', the 'good European', Zarathustra's 'children's land') means club over country, and Wenger's Arsenal—with its dietary and training laboratory at London Colney cultivating an Overman, its Invincibles season, and its young, passport-blind signings—emerges as the club Nietzsche would support through its very will-to-power.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 20 "Gene For Pedantry Same As Gene For Philosophy" — Loader's chapter is a spread of fake 'Existential Times' news parodies: an uncompliant student who answers every robot thought experiment with 'But you're not' drives his professor to swearing over the problem of other minds; Wisconsin scientists find the self as a half-centimeter of Silly Putty in the neck, joking that Hume 'may simply have been looking in the wrong place' when introspection found only a bundle of perceptions; a poll finds not one American philosopher has read Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit beyond 'the bit about the master and the slave'; and a student essay on Sartre's Existentialism and Humanism wanders off into Planet of the Apes and calls Sartre 'Mr Horse.' The Philososcope prescribes page 232 of Heidegger's Being and Time, a movie loser quotes Nietzsche ('There is always some madness in love') before falling into a pond, an archaeology department's found remains of God back Nietzsche's 'God is dead,' and a Marxist begs capitalism to hold off collapsing until her book is published—philosophy satirized as pedantry, posing, and self-importance.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 28 "Get Serious" — David Kyle Johnson takes Nietzsche's suggestion that God is slowly dying and reads The Onion's religion stories — the faith healer who loses a patient during a routine miracle, Kansas fundamentalists lobbying to overturn the Second Law of Thermodynamics, and 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' — as evidence of secularization. He splits blind faith (irrational belief despite evidence, as with Bush's 'Blind-Faith-Based Initiatives') from genuine faith as belief without sufficient evidence, arguing religion does science badly whenever it shields creationism from falsification. But science rests on unproven assumptions too, he shows via Hume's problem of induction, Descartes' skeptical problem, and Wittgenstein's charge that naming a 'strong nuclear force' explains no more than God pushing things down. Ockham's razor then decides for atheism — an unexplained universe is simpler than God plus a universe — though William James's will to believe leaves a door open for faith where evidence is impossible, qualified by Clifford's warning that beliefs likely to harm others are never permissible.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 30 "I Thought It Was Just the Doctor that We Needed, but It’s Both of You" — Reads the Doctor as a Christ-figure and savior (the 'Voyage of the Damned' ascension that drew Christian Voice protests, Martha's year of gospel-telling in 'The Last of the Time Lords'), applying Feuerbach's claim that humanity projects its ideals onto God. But the show under Russell T Davies also distrusts godlike power: Davros's 'you made this' accusation, the Racnoss massacre, and Joan Redfern's question in 'The Family of Blood' show the lonely god's devastation. Against this, companions like Donna embody Nietzsche's Übermensch ('There's no such thing as an ordinary human'), so the chapter concludes the Doctor and ordinary humans need each other, mutually overcoming their weaknesses.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 35 "The Ethics of Dexter’s Appeal" — James F. Pontuso reconstructs Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals - promise-keeping, the unpayable debt to ancestor-founders that becomes God, cruelty turned inward as bad conscience, and Christianity's divine self-ransom that only deepens guilt - to explain why Dexter, who feels no guilt, is not abnormal but a man before morality. Following Gibbon's picture of Roman soldiers whose civil religion justified slaughter without remorse, he imagines Dexter thriving in the legions ('Dexter SPQR') rather than hiding behind Harry's Code, and argues the show appeals because Aristotle's ethics concerned outward conduct and justice rather than inner conscience. In our levelled age we secretly crave what Nietzsche craved: the sight of 'something perfect... still capable of inspiring fear.'
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 7 "His Work Is Its Own Reward" — Timothy Sexton argues the real Overman is not Doyle's flat 'calculating machine' but Jeremy Brett's Granada Holmes: the sneer with which he frees the Blue Carbuncle thief and the 'I am not retained by the police' outburst show him stepping beyond the herd's good-and-evil after the death of God. Brett's theatrical style, from the pivot before Lady Brackenstall in 'The Abbey Grange' to 'Gentlemen, we can do better than that' in 'The Norwood Builder', enacts Nietzsche's grand art of giving style to one's character, sublimating nihilistic dread into the pleasure of proving superiority. Where Rathbone-era Sherlocks solve crimes for truth, justice and the Victorian Way, Brett's Holmes makes the work its own reward, satisfying Nietzsche's demand that the Overman 'attain satisfaction with himself'.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 29 "The New Man or the Old" — Marks reads Holmes as the paragon Victorian whose faith in reason mirrors his era's confidence and, underneath it, its anxiety: Holmes's outburst in 'The Cardboard Box' ('What is the object of this circle of misery and violence and fear?... That is humanity's great problem to which Reason, so far, has no answer') appears the same year Nietzsche published 'Gott ist tot' in The Gay Science, amid Marx's 'opium of the people' and Darwin's displacement of religion. Reinterpreting the 2009 Ritchie film, he rejects the obvious religion-versus-reason reading of Lord Blackwood: Blackwood's 'magic' is really chemistry and machinery (technocracy), Holmes's science serves the military (dictatorship), and Moriarty (terrorism) defeats both, dramatizing post-9/11 fears about the militarized fruits of Reason. He concludes that Holmes straddles the Victorian and postmodern divide and that replacing religion with science is Rationalism's 'siren song.'
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 23 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Brandon Kempner reads Gaiman's Batman: Whatever Happened to the Caped Crusader? as Nietzschean eternal recurrence: Batman dies and is reborn as the infant Bruce Wayne to repeat his life exactly, because Gaiman first strips away every teleological ending, Catwoman kills Batman, Alfred reveals he invented the Joker, and the Moore-style domestic bliss of the Superman farewell is denied. With God dead there is no Heaven, telos, or external reward, so, like Nietzsche's Overman who creates values above the city's conventional morality, Batman's meaning can lie only in the lived repetition itself: 'the only reward you get for being Batman? You get to be Batman,' the highest formula of life-affirmation. Kempner extends the pattern to the funeral-framed rebirth of a new Dream in Sandman: The Wake, showing Gaiman's recurring obsession with cycles that have 'no endings' across his work.
- **Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within**, ch. 18 "Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy" — Zanelotti takes up the charge that Larry is a self-hating Jew, from whistling Wagner to 'The End,' where learning he is a gentile turns him into a churchgoing enthusiast who sings 'Go Tell It on the Mountain' and gives Richard Lewis his kidney. Sartre's bad faith diagnoses both poles: Larry denying his facticity by imagining he can simply shed his Jewish past and re-adopt it at will, and critics who demand he live up to an 'authentic' Jewish essence; Marx's false consciousness, meanwhile, explains the self-hating baldy who buys into the haired agenda. Using Ronald de Sousa's rejection of the 'Just Joking Defense'—we are accountable for laughter because we let ourselves become people who cannot restrain it—the chapter argues the show sets a comic frame that mocks bad faith rather than Judaism. Its deeper target, via Nietzsche's death of God, is the overenthusiastic meaning we manufacture when faith is 'curbed,' which is why Larry ridicules only public displays of religion, not belief itself.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 13 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Greene asks whether Nucky is Nietzsche's Ubermensch and works through each criterion. Nucky, Gyp Rosetti, and the other mobsters are passionate, active shapers of their world (Van Alden fails here), and Nucky is a genuine creator of values after the death of God - his whopper to the Temperance League, his flip-flopping sermons to black and white congregations, and his 'I. Am. Not. Seeking. Forgiveness.' over Jimmy's body reject slave morality where the other gangsters merely follow the objective moral code of omerta. He sacrifices lesser lives (Hans Schroeder, Gillian) and has the required dark side, but he fails the final test of teaching the eternal recurrence, so he remains only 'well on his way' to Superman - a status the show's women (Margaret, Lucy, Gillian) never approach, hovering closer to the last man.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 17 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Ketcham reads the monster as Zarathustra's dark double: both are exiled 'godless men' who begin their journeys at a cottager's door, but where Nietzsche's prophet preaches the Übermensch, the will to power, and living so one could will eternal recurrence, the monster traverses the three metamorphoses in reverse - born the innocent child, becoming the lion who tells Victor 'you are my creator, but I am your master,' and ending the camel carrying his maker's corpse to a self-immolating pyre in the polar dark. Shelley's abyss is science usurping God and drawing Promethean punishment; Nietzsche's abyss is the shadow of the dead God (The Gay Science) that keeps humanity from the great noontide and traps Frankenstein as a 'last man' whose will is subjugated to pleasant happiness. The monster, bastard of a godless man and bridge to neither animal nor Übermensch, shows a will that is sheer power without any foundation for overcoming man - 'whither humanity?'
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 32 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Kenn Fisher reads the franchise as the extinction of the Great Chain of Being: from Plato's humans mid-way between gods and beasts, through Genesis dominion and Descartes's non-conscious animals, to Malcolm's 'God creates man. Man destroys God. Man creates dinosaurs' - with computers (Hammond's control room, Wikipedia, Google) replacing God at the top. He then tracks animals' ascent from property: Francione on welfare versus personhood, Bentham's 'Can they suffer?', and Singer's equality-as-prescription, applied to Dieter Stark tasering a compy (punished by the compys) versus the unexamined electric fences that keep InGen's 'zoo animals' caged. He closes with Carol Adams's meat-masculinity link - Roland Tembo will hunt only a male T. rex, the dinosaurs are all female - and holds up vegetarian Lex as hope that the Chain bends into a Circle.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 20 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Namvol argues that 'Glob' is the post-apocalyptic corpse of the Christian God: combining Don Cupitt's claim that gods live only in worship and practice with Nietzsche's 'God is dead,' he traces how the Mushroom War destroyed the believers, churches, and rituals that kept God alive, leaving Ooo an empty exclamation. Pantheism fails as a rescue because evil is native to Ooo's nature (Gunter, the eternally self-existing Abadeer), so God cannot simply have become the land. Against Dostoevsky's 'without God all things are permitted,' the chapter sides with Žižek—that morality's shadow, guilt, outlives God—as when Finn's self-regulation kicks in after 'All the Little People' and 'Dungeon Train,' making Finn, not Glob, the true savior of a godless world.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 19 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Michaud reads the novel through Nietzsche: the Crew of Light are resentful sheep banding together to kill a lion, damning Dracula not for wrongdoing but for his will-to-power, his hunting, and his reproduction - things humans do daily to animals - while the tale's enduring popularity over Nietzsche's heresy proves the death of God never happened, since we still use religion to console ourselves about dying. Following Ernest Becker's Denial of Death, he argues Dracula stories are humanity's immortality project: we must narrate the destruction of physical immortality to persuade ourselves it is a curse ('it would suck to be immortal') and that heroic, spiritual salvation in heaven is the better eternity.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 29 "17. Downton Abbey as Eternal Recurrence" — Christopher Ketcham asks whether primogeniture and entail make Downton Abbey a social embodiment of Nietzsche's eternal recurrence - the same estate, without revision, turned over generation after generation like the eternal hourglass of existence. Working through Lawrence Hatab's five interpretations of the doctrine, he tests royal continuity against death duties, the nihilism of industrial capitalism, and the Great War that killed heirs and empires, and borrows Kant's categorical imperative as an analogy for Britain's uniquely preserved 'royal categorical imperative' of continuity. The Abbey's recurrence survives only anthropomorphically - Violet, the family, the servants, and the tenants as its living organs - and the chapter wonders whether such ossified continuity, like dinosaur bones, is really eternal.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 22 "10. The Light from Friendship" — Pavelich sets Aristotle's account of friendship - recognized and reciprocated goodwill between equals, perfected in the friendship of the good who 'share our souls', a standard met only by Jack and Bella Crawford - against Nietzsche's friendship as striving between overmen, who honor 'one's best enemy' in the friend and grow through conflict. He reads Hannibal's treatment of Will (hiding the encephalitis, framing him, serving the Nietzschean trout) as Nietzschean friend-making - Lies that are supposed to spur Will's growth, consistent with an Übermensch who tells Will 'Killing must feel good to God' and says 'I don't hide from God' - while Will's masquerade of friendship is betrayal in both senses, since Will seeks an Aristotelian soulmate and finds a killer he must stop. Because each betrays the other, neither Aristotelian nor Nietzschean friendship survives, though the moments before the Mizumono bloodbath - Hannibal inviting Will to just walk away - glimpse a real friendship already made impossible.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 12 "1. Reading the Signs" — Di Bernardo reads the religious language of The Walking Dead as sustained irony - a 'doubleness of sense' - arguing that the walkers, churches, and signs comment critically on faith rather than endorse it. He tracks the church scenes (the Southern Baptist church of 2.1 'What Lies Ahead' with its timed bells and sitting-dead congregation, Gabriel's Saint Sarah's where Maggie answers that it is 'just four walls and a roof'), the ambiguous 'sanctuary' and Terminus signs, and the comic-book Jesus (Paul Monroe) as a machine-gun savior, concluding that the scriptural promise of eternal life through consuming flesh and blood yields only undead life. Against Epicurus's consolation that death is nothing to us, and in the shadow of Nietzsche's madman announcing the death of God, the chapter warns against investing absolute trust in any signs - religious or secular - a warning capped by Rick biting out Joe's throat as his own 'day of reckoning.'
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 12 "1. Everything’s Amazing and Nobody’s Happy" — Max Elder reads Louis through Nietzsche's Gay Science claim that all philosophy is unconscious memoir, arguing Louis's confession-like comedy reveals dark truths we would rather flee - the Conan 'everything's amazing and nobody's happy' bit, the 'I know the darkness' exchange with the Christian woman, and the Subway/Pamela scene where a homeless man bathes behind a subway violinist. Using Nietzsche's line that man alone laughs because he suffers so deeply, and The Birth of Tragedy's comic as the artistic discharge of the nausea of absurdity, the chapter argues Louis's laughter performs a gestalt switch that ties the ugly to the beautiful and so redeems it. It reads the religions-supply-meaning argument - God's mockery-laughter versus Nietzsche's holy laughter - as the reason redemption now happens in comedy clubs rather than churches, and closes with Louie's 'Country Drive' scolding of Jane ('you don't get to be bored') as Nietzschean embrace of the amazing fact of being alive.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 9 "1. Where Have All the Supermen Gone" — Holdier argues that neither hero is Nietzsche's Übermensch: Superman's servile mild-mannered Clark Kent guise would strike Nietzsche as slave morality, while Batman's self-loathing (his Hush confession that deep down he is not a good person) and breakable human body disqualify him too. Instead, reading them through The Birth of Tragedy and Grant Morrison's Supergods, Superman embodies the Apollonian force of order, sunlight, and rationality and Batman the Dionysian force of chaos and passion, so their battles (The Dark Knight Returns, Batman v Superman) are the inevitable but never-final friction of art's twin poles. The fight's real winner is the reader, who gets both deities at once.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 14 "5. How Heroes Argue" — LaBauve opens with a staged Justice League debate over rescuing the Joker's hostages, where Batman's emotional, vengeance-tinged appeal loses to Superman's trust-based plea, and reads it through Aristotle's On Rhetoric: Batman persuades almost entirely by pathos (the relatable brokenness of Nolan's trilogy) with detective's logos, while Superman balances pathos, logos, and above all ethos, since Aristotle calls the speaker's character the strongest appeal. Against Max Landis's claim that Superman is irrelevant, he pairs the Death of Superman with Nietzsche's "God is dead" parable and the Kill Bill monologue to argue that Superman is a mythology of virtue - alongside real moral heroes like Gandhi, King, and Jesus - showing humans the ideal they ought to become, so Superman not only wins but must win.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 16 "6. The God We Need Now" — Ketcham stages the essay as a 1939 diary (a boyhood piece longing for a new god now that the biblical God has, he feels, abandoned the Depression-era world) followed by an old man's reread: America made Superman its messiah - born in a flash of light like the star of Bethlehem, canonized by DC's "publishing synod" much as the church redacted the New Testament - but he suspects the god will age as badly as the God of Abraham. Rereading after Korea, Vietnam, and Wall Street scandals, he argues we now need and worship a darker god modeled on Hades: the rich, hidden, vengeful billionaire Bruce Wayne, whose subterranean mansion, Cerberus-like Alfred, and tax-break tributes from citizens mirror the underworld god and Greek sacrifice. He ends imagining our grandchildren's next god as a cyber-god of AI, and declares Batman, not Superman, the god we need now.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 20 "10. Gods Are Overrated" — Michaud grants that Superman is godlike and turns Hume's problem of evil on him: if Superman is all-powerful, all-knowing, and good, why does suffering persist that he could prevent at super-speed - the desert animal dying painfully for no purpose, the crimes that happen while he picnics with Lois - and the free-will defense and "it's all part of the plan" excuses fail him even worse than they fail God. Superman then becomes our excuse for doing nothing, and like belief in immortality and the afterlife (holy wars where no one "really" dies, prayers instead of feeding the starving) he dulls our sense that this life is all we get. Reading Nietzsche's "God is dead" as the discovery that we keep gods only to feel special and saved, Michaud concludes we would live more meaningful, Batman-like self-reliant lives if the savior-Superman were dead to us.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 31 "18. Thus Slaughtered Deadpool" — The chapter argues Deadpool is neither hero nor anti-hero but Nietzsche's Ubermensch beyond good and evil: perceiving the writers as the 'man at the typewriter' who keeps the Marvel cast as unwitting sheep under a slave morality, he kills the Marvel Universe in Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe to free them from their creators. In Deadpool Killustrated he murders the literary archetypes (Moby-Dick, the Little Mermaid, Tom Sawyer) so the heroes they inspired can never be written, compared to the Overman demolishing inherited values before they corrupt the next generation, and in Deadpool Kills Deadpool he slaughters every version of himself to force the creator-god into the open. Since 'good' and 'bad' are categories of the herd whose very source is corrupt, the author declines to judge the slaughter at all.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 21 "8. Mr. Robot, Mad Son of Noir" — Hoyt places Mr. Robot in the film noir tradition born when world war proved Nietzsche's point that God is dead: as with Bogart's Spade turning in Brigid in The Maltese Falcon, the noir hero's task is existential self-definition - guarding integrity in a world without truth, justice, or absolute meaning. But where classic noir blamed gangsters, neo-noir from Chinatown through Fight Club to Mr. Robot points at capitalism and unbeatable conspiracies (Price apparently able to bend the federal government itself), and the show's cold blue offices and 'shortsighting' framings show characters breaking under the pressure of choices no space protects.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 25 "11. The Gods Are Dead and Elliot Has Killed Them" — Robison-Greene reads Elliot's chapel monologue - 'If I don't listen to my imaginary friend, why the fuck should I listen to yours?' - as a Problem of Evil argument: an omniscient, omnipotent, omnibenevolent God is incompatible with the unnecessary suffering of his father's death and of massive income inequality. The 'gods' Elliot kills are also Mr. Robot ('like all gods their madness takes you prisoner') and the religion of materialism, and Nietzsche supplies the blueprint for what follows: the Genealogy's slave revolt in values as the model for fsociety's uprising, and the Parable of the Madman plus the Ubermensch to cast Elliot-as-Mr. Robot as the creator of new values - though unlike Nietzsche's slaves, the oppressed here are complicit in their own subordination.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 11 "3. Mermen and Dismemberment" — Contends that Hendrix's discord is philosophy-as-discord: 'I Don't Live Today' (the Native American dead-in-life), the Woodstock 'Star-Spangled Banner' with its bombs and sirens against sporting-event sentimentality, 'Machine Gun,' and 'House Burning Down' lacerate listeners so they actually feel war's atrocities instead of parroting patriotic clichés. Against this the chapter sets the oceanic, womb-like escape fantasies of '1983 (A Merman I Should Turn to Be)' and 'Valleys of Neptune,' treating them through Schopenhauer as metaphysical consolation, Marx's opiate, and Nietzsche's 'hangman's metaphysics,' and concludes that Hendrix finally refuses such world-denying illusions — and Heideggerian inauthentic withdrawal — in favor of existential engagement with suffering here and now.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 23 "11. 999 Fingers" — Voiced by a composite being shredded together from every AHS character, the chapter retells the Buddha's path - Siddhartha sheltered from suffering like a pampered prince, enlightenment as watching 'every episode of American Horror Story', Mara's temptations, and Angulimala with his garland of 999 fingers converted to monkhood - to read Briarcliff's cruelty, Sister Jude's devil, and Bloody Face's son Johnny as suffering born of clinging, in a contingent, moment-to-moment world of karma and rebirth, while Nietzsche's killed God, eternal recurrence, and ressentiment frame the question of who is to blame when there is no creator.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 31 "19. Nineteen Eighty-Four’s Religion" — Crossley and Markou trace Orwell's ambivalence about religion — a lifelong atheist who loved the Church of England's liturgy — into the novel: Goldstein's book repeats the socialist critique of priests who 'softened by promises of compensation in an imaginary world beyond the grave' propped up hierarchy, yet the Party then occupies religion's vacant place itself, with O'Brien as 'priest of power', Goldstein as arch-heretic, and 'Thou art' replacing the old despotisms' 'Thou shalt not'. They argue Orwell thought a purer socialism needed the communal goods of religion, from the proles' fuzzy 'Christianness' to the radical Christian tradition of the Diggers and Levellers, and read Ingsoc as that utopian tradition betrayed. The novel's warning is therefore double: what fills the gap when religion dies, and how religion itself can be a blueprint for totalitarianism.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 9 "Scientifically, Introductions Are an Idiot Thing" — The introduction frames the whole book through the Rick/Jerry opposition: Rick is a Nietzschean artist-creator who insists the world is objectively meaningless and Godless yet keeps choosing his family, while Jerry is the herd-animal chasing socially approved values. It claims the show, like Nietzsche's deliberately difficult writing, sorts its audience into Jerrys who enjoy the dick jokes and Ricks who do the hard philosophical work of finding microscopic meaning in a meaningless cosmos. It closes with Socrates's 'unexamined life is not worth living' to justify submitting to philosophy's perplexity even if the Eyehole Man kicks the shit out of you.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 19 "8. Neither the Hero You Deserve Nor the Hero You Need" — Reading 'Vindicators 3' through Nietzsche, the chapter argues the superhero team are slave-morality charlatans whose duty to protect the weak is the herd's imaginary revenge, while Rick, who defeated Worldender drunk, embodies master morality and honest will to power, against Jerry's dishonest version in the Pluto-not-a-planet fight of 'Something Ricked This Way Comes'. Rick's casual destruction of Worldender becomes Nietzsche's death of God, the collapse of the value-source that gave the Vindicators' lives meaning, which Vance Maximus denies at the cost of his life. The chapter then tests Rick against the Ubermensch via the camel-lion-child metaphor and concludes he is at best Nietzsche's lion, tainted by resentment over his lost family rather than the value-creating child, leaving Morty and Simple Rick as long-shot candidates.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 25 "14. After the Blackout" — Martin Muchall treats the offscreen Blackout as an emblem of the moral catastrophe diagnosed in MacIntyre's After Virtue: our moral vocabulary has shattered into emotivist hissing and clapping, with Roy's murder of Tyrell, his 'God of biomechanics', staging the death of God and the 'everything is permitted' that follows. Utilitarian pleasure and Kantian cold reason (Spock, who must tell the truth to the murderer at the door) have both failed, leaving neoliberal hypercapitalism — corporate psychopathy, the orphanage sweatshop, the Baseline as workplace performance review — as the real villain. Against this, K's ending models the Buddha: everything is impermanent, there is no self to defend, and his selfless, empathetic death points to a morality grounded in evolved and cultivable altruism.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 15 "5. RuPaul versus Zarathustra" — The van der Wielen sisters read RuPaul against Nietzsche's Zarathustra: both are outcasts who descend from solitude bearing a spiritual teaching in a marketplace that mocks them, and both announce that inherited values are ungrounded — Zarathustra through the death of God and the call to become the over-man, Ru through 'we're all born naked and the rest is drag' and the cosmic life force that makes every identity a costume. But where Zarathustra refuses followers and shuns the people's values, Ru's creed polices female stereotypes (long hair, breasts, heels) and pulls the cart of consumerist values — money, fame, individualism — so that she comes to resemble the priests and wise men Zarathustra condemns. Her openly admitted fakeness and opportunism (the Wigstock 'gender fuck' abandoned for the glamazon brand) leave the chapter asking who flies higher: the tragic free spirit or the pragmatic, honestly dishonest superstar.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 19 "8. The Death of God and the Death of Meaning" — Montoya reads Chidi's breakdown upon learning he has been tortured for three hundred years as Nietzsche's death of God, quoting the Parable of the Madman from 'Jeremy Bearimy' to show how the guaranteed meaning of Chidi's worldview collapses into nihilism. Michael's midlife-crisis makeover and partying embody Camus's embrace of the absurd, while Sartre's existence precedes essence, abandonment, and anguish explain why Eleanor's confession to Michael and her sacrifice in the Judge's test count as authentic choices. With the Judge's verdict stripping away any hope of reward, the humans finally choose goodness for its own sake, which the chapter presents as the show's answer to nihilism.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 10 "2. What Does Life Mean after the Snap" — This chapter reads four post-Snap Avengers as existentialist answers to how life keeps meaning after catastrophe.
