- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 54 "The Triumph of Love" — Reading the series' set pieces as the triumph of traditionally feminine values over masculine aggression, the section moves from Lily's sacrificial love burning Quirrell, through Harry sparing Pettigrew for Lupin's and Sirius's sake, to love expelling Voldemort during the Ministry possession, where 'it was your heart that saved you' and Dumbledore names a force 'more wonderful and more terrible than death.' Harry's kindness to Kreacher, Griphook, and Dobby pays off in the Horcrux hunt, his plea that Voldemort 'try for some remorse' redefines true manhood as incorporating the feminine, and the Forest sacrifice wins the war with a defensive Expelliarmus rather than a duel, showing love more important than aggression.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 131 "Remorse and Death" — Opens Charles Taliaferro's essay by reading Fawkes's burning and rebirth as a clue to a philosophical model of moral repair: the wrongdoer must confess, feel sincere remorse, repudiate the pleasure or gain of the wrongdoing, and form new intentions, a kind of death to the old self like Christian baptism, after which the repaired relationship is reborn and the friend is seen in a new light. It then sets up Voldemort as the perversion of this pattern, spreading death by clinging to life while Harry and Dumbledore move to deeper life by accepting death.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 132 "The Inversion of Voldemort" — Sharpens the remorse-versus-regret contrast through Voldemort's cold regret after having Nagini kill Snape, and shows true remorse at work in Dumbledore's confession about the Resurrection Stone ring, his arranged death at Snape's hand, and his tearful self-disclosure to Harry at King's Cross. Harry too must die to be regenerated: letting Voldemort strike him destroys the Horcrux inside so that his soul becomes whole and completely his own, while lesser purgings, like his furious outburst at Ron and Hermione, and his love for Ginny complete the pattern of dying to the old self.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 133 "The Integrity Objection" — Completes the inversion: each Horcrux rips and destabilizes Voldemort's soul, and only excruciating remorse could put it back together, something he will never attempt, while his evil literally disembodies him until he lives parasitically on the blood and limbs of others. Against this, Hermione's gloss on the Potters' gravestone, the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death, means the soul survives whatever happens to the body, grounding the contrast between Voldemort's pathetic, unmourned end and the honored deaths of Dobby, Fred, Lupin, Tonks, and Colin Creevey.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 134 "The Fantasy Objection" — Takes up the integrity objection advanced by the Freudian psychoanalyst Melanie Klein: renunciation cannot change the fact that it was you who did the wrong, so posing as an altogether new person invites self-deception, as with the reformed alcoholic who still calls himself an alcoholic. Taliaferro grants the regeneration model can be abused but argues renewal requires something very close to dying to the past, using Snape, unable to confess his love for Lily, still nursing resentment, honored only when Harry names his son Severus, as the tragedy of reform without full renunciation.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 135 "Fawkes’s Secret" — Answers the fantasy objection, that ethics drawn from a world of spells and talking portraits is escapist make-believe, by noting that Rowling's moral insight does not depend on the magic: loyalty, friendship, romantic love, fairness, opposition to enslavement, free the house-elves, and the roles of remorse, forgiveness, and reform are values of our own Muggle world. In the name of realism, the objector merely fails to engage the imagination.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 136 "NOTES" — Closes the essay by asking why Fawkes never cured Dumbledore's ring-curse or blocked Snape's killing curse, and answers that the phoenix may have left Hogwarts only because his work was done: rupture, betrayal, and vice are healed by a death and rebirth in which one rises from the flames of remorseful confession a new person, with radically new desires, ready to rejoin relationships and community.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 12 "The Guilt Never Goes Away" — Robichaud asks whether Iron Man can atone for Tony Stark's wrongs, using the Iron Monger's reprogrammed-suit example to distinguish causal from moral responsibility and to argue that omissions can be causes. Tony's negligence in running Stark Industries is blameworthy because his playboy ignorance was itself negligent (as with the Mandarin's willful ignorance), and via T. M. Scanlon's account of blame the families harmed by the illegal weapons sales are the ones most warranted in blaming him. Since 'I'm sorry' is not enough for wrongs this serious and Tony never submits to punishment, the chapter concludes that even his crusade as Iron Man to 'right the wrongs' — crushing Raza's group and collecting rogue weapons — may not yet warrant forgiveness.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 24 "NOTES" — Becky Vartabedian applies W. D. Ross's agent-specific ethic of prima facie duties to Michael: at the dock his actual duty of beneficence toward the kidnapped Walt overrides fidelity and noninjury to Jack, Kate, and Sawyer, but does not erase his responsibility for Ana Lucia's and Libby's murders. Because Ross requires amends rather than giving a blank check, the chapter asks whether Michael's spying as 'Kevin Johnson' aboard the Kahana - culminating in giving Jin time to escape the bomb - repairs his wrongs, or whether Walt's rejection and Michael's exile from the closing church scene show he failed to make things right on the terms of those he wronged.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 10 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Kukkonen reads Peter's never-extinguished guilt over Uncle Ben as an 'infinite debt' modeled on Anselm's atonement theology: no good deed repays the primal transgression, so even the heroic serum rescue for Aunt May in 'The Final Chapter' (Amazing Spider-Man #33) leaves the debt intact. Against the Nietzschean escape into self-sufficient magnanimity (Ben's ghostly blessing in 'Doom Service!'), he argues via Levinas and Derrida that Peter's responsibility extends to every stranger, as when a rescued policeman with Uncle Ben's face calls him back in 'Spider-Man No More!' (#50). Following Kierkegaard's Works of Love, the chapter concludes that Peter's heroics do not pay off but deepen his debt of love, since every choice heeds one call while unavoidably failing others.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 13 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Barkman argues that Spider-Man's ethics, while universal enough for Jews, Platonists, and Confucians, are specifically Christian in emphasis: God creates for friendship, which requires free choice, so 'with great power comes great responsibility' restates Luke 12:48 — the more one is given, the more justice is required, as Peter's refusal of MJ and Octavius's wasted intelligence in Spider-Man 2 show. The free-will solution to the problem of evil (chosen evil, fallen angels, Adam's curse, a law-governed physical world) is read through Peter's questioning God in 'The Big Question' (Peter Parker: Spider-Man #48). The chapter culminates with Spider-Man 3, where the symbiote inflames Peter's grief into revenge against Sandman — a perversion of justice — until Peter forgives Flint Marko, enacting mercy as the perfection rather than the absence of justice.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 23 "12. Vigilante Wanted" — Ketcham writes a fictional Dust Bowl kid's 1940 diary: facing bank foreclosure, he weighs which comic to keep as the vigilante who would burn down the bank — Superman, the Kansas farm boy gone Metropolis-insider, or Batman, rich like the bankers yet a fellow avenger who only fights 'carnival freaks'. Testing each against Hamlet's paralysis, Henry V at Agincourt, Tom Joad's 'I'll be ever'where' promise, and a Lex-Luthor pact with the devil, he burns the Batman comics and keeps Superman — realizing he is really giving up his own hate and the preacher's unforgiveness, though even Superman begins to fade 'like dust in that wind'.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 21 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Chaib takes Ruby's line that Hell is 'forgetting what you are' and reads God's character through early modern philosophy: Descartes' supremely real being and deceiving demon frame Castiel's delusion of godhood and Ruby's manipulation of Sam, Spinoza's denial that evil exists (it is 'inadequate knowledge') explains the comprehensible motives of Crowley and Lucifer, Berkeley's claim that things persist only because God perceives them makes a dead God an existential threat, and Kant's 'moral theism' rebuts dogmatic atheism. With Hegel and Fromm, Hell becomes self-forgetting and communion with God becomes self-knowledge achieved through knowing others, the opposite of Ruby's Hell. The chapter concludes via Locke that closing Hell's gates would deny once-human demons the redemption tied to our very idea of God, so the brothers' forgiving love, unlike Michael and Lucifer's rigidity, reflects God's nature.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 31 "Notes" — Mills asks why Nate is more hurt than relieved when Roy declines to headbutt him over kissing Keeley, while Jamie had to fight for forgiveness. Using Strawson's reactive attitudes - anger is how we take someone seriously as a member of the moral community - plus Nussbaum's Anger and Forgiveness and Radzik's transactional account of amends, she argues Roy's instant absolution dismisses Nate as a pitiable non-agent rather than a culpable moral equal. The chapter contrasts this with earned, transactional forgiveness across Season 3 (Nate apologizing to Will and Ted, Beard's own story of betrayal and forgiveness), showing the headbutt as the recognition Nate needed.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 32 "Notes" — Baggett asks whether Rupert is beyond the grace the show extends to everyone else. She surveys theories of forgiveness - Butler's change of emotion, treatment and performative accounts, and Stump's Aquinas-based framework grounding forgiveness in the love that desires another's good and union, separable from reconciliation - then applies Aristotle's corrupted bad person whose vice 'makes moral truths invisible' as Rupert's limit case. Ted's darts-based tough love is contrasted with Sassy's vengeful certainty and Deborah's cheap grace, and the chapter leaves Rupert's turnaround possible but entirely his choice, while his choices have already been making him.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 21 "NOTES" — Corn and Dunn read Maryann's takeover of Bon Temps through René Girard's scapegoat theory: mimetic desire breeds the resentments Sookie hears all day, the crowd's 'wild energy' dissolves the Apollonian individual into Dionysian self-forgetfulness (Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy, Plato's assembly that echoes blame until judgment drowns), and the town and the Fellowship of the Sun alike restore solidarity by uniting against vampires — or against Sam on the sacrificial oak. Godric's self-delivery to the Newlins is a failed Christlike sacrifice, so the chapter ends with Sookie's 'God doesn't punish, God forgives' as Girard's alternative to founding community on sacrificial violence.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 15 "Basketball, Violence, Forgiveness, and Healing" — Witte recounts the 1972 Ohio State-Minnesota brawl in which he was beaten unconscious, and reflects on his decades-long path from 'moral hatred' (a concept he draws from Murphy and Hampton) to forgiveness. Using Anne Minas's four senses of 'forgive,' he identifies his task as the fourth: giving up resentment without condoning the act, excusing punishment, or reversing his judgment. He frames forgiveness as 'setting it right,' the first step in a healing process, and narrates his eventual reconciliation with attackers Corky Taylor and Clyde Turner as evidence that no game is worth the loss of a relationship.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 33 "Hoosiers and the Meaning of Life" — Michael Peterson argues that Hoosiers is a microcosm of life's meaning: Aristotle's eudaimonia frames the characters' searches (Norman Dale rebuilding his career, Shooter his self-esteem and his bond with son Everett), and Dale's 'in my book, we're going to be winners' speech shows that character, unselfish teamwork, and playing to potential - virtue learned by doing, as coaching models moral instruction - matter more than the scoreboard against South Bend Central. The film's second chances (Principal Summers's clean slate, Whit's return, Dale's hiring of the town drunk Shooter) reveal that character alone is insufficient: mercy and forgiveness, which Hannah Arendt traces to Jesus, reframe an unchangeable past and open a future. Peterson then surveys worldviews - naturalism (Bertrand Russell's 'accidental collocations of atoms'), postmodernism (Derrida's deconstruction), Hinduism's Atman-Brahman - and argues only Christian theism, in which God's nature is love (Aquinas), can ground the character and forgiveness the film dramatizes.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — D'Aries and Hirsch read Paul Thomas Anderson's Hard Eight as a neo-noir moral inversion: the aging criminal Sydney seeks atonement not through religious penance but through selfless love, rescuing John and Clementine while removing the loathsome Jimmy (who knows Sydney killed John's father). They contrast him with Melville's Bob le flambeur and Besson's The Professional, where convention demands the criminal be punished. Sydney escapes formal justice but is sentenced to a 'prison without bars' of self-loathing (the bloodstained cuff), and the authors warn that such sympathy-for-the-devil inversions verge on nihilistic moral relativism.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 17 "The Power of Memory and the Memory of Power Wars and Graves in Westerns and Jidaigeki" — Brodey compares John Ford's Westerns (My Darling Clementine, She Wore a Yellow Ribbon, The Searchers, The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance) with Kurosawa's jidaigeki (Seven Samurai, Throne of Blood, Hidden Fortress, Yôjimbô) as postwar mythmaking that both buries and builds national identity after military defeat. She argues graves and gravestones are bivalent symbols—commemorating loss while risking perpetuating revenge—and that both directors oscillate between Rousseauean nostalgia for a nobler past and Hobbesian frontier brutality that must be tamed. Ford trusts that memory of past wrongs can spur a better future and enable forgiveness, while Kurosawa, more pessimistic and drawing on Buddhist cyclical detachment in Throne of Blood, warns of the dangers of both remembering and forgetting trauma.

### Eternal Recurrence

Eternal recurrence is Nietzsche's thought that one's life, and indeed the whole of existence, repeats identically an infinite number of times. He offers it less as a cosmological claim than as a test of one's attitude toward life: could you will to live this same life, with all its pain and triviality, over and over forever? To embrace the prospect joyfully rather than with despair is, for Nietzsche, the mark of a life fully affirmed, and the idea is closely tied to his call to love existence exactly as it is.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 15 "The Seinfeldians as Fixed Essences" — Mark Conard notes the show's relentless recurrences - Kramer sliding through the door, 'Newman!', George's firings, the Puddy on-again-off-again loop - and asks whether this is Nietzsche's eternal recurrence. It cannot be, since Nietzsche's cosmos is a flux of recombining centers of force; things recur in Seinfeld precisely because nothing changes. The Seinfeldians are instead fixed Platonic Forms or essences: 'The Bizarro Jerry' proves it, since only an unchanging archetype can have an exact opposite (Kevin, Gene, Feldman, Vargas), and the backwards episode 'The Betrayal' works only because characters exempt from time and change cannot develop.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 20 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Douglas Blount tests Nietzsche against Sauron, whose forging and grasp of the One Ring - even striving to supplant Ilúvatar - enacts the will to power, exploitation, the death of God, and the ideal of the Übermensch. He argues that in Middle-earth the naked will to power appears not as a brave new humanity but as plain evil, and that Tolkien answers Nietzsche not with argument but with a rival portrait: Gandalf's self-sacrifice on the Bridge of Khazad-dûm, Frodo's mercy to Gollum that becomes Middle-earth's salvation, and Sam's humble refusal of 'Samwise the Strong'. Judged by Nietzsche's own aesthetic criterion of taste, Tolkien's vision of community, humility, and abnegation is the more beautiful - and therefore the more compelling - portrait of reality.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 12 "In the End, It’s Only Round and Round (and Round)" — Steiff argues Pink Floyd's music is cinematic in itself: like film it unfolds in time and uses foreshadowing ('Speak to Me'), dynamic contrast, and Kuleshov-effect juxtaposition, which explains why the Wizard of Oz mashup creates any meaning at all, though she finds that mashup a novelty compared to 'Echoes' over the ending of Kubrick's 2001. The heart of the chapter is circularity: the heartbeat that both opens and closes Dark Side, The Wall's interlocking 'isn't this where / we came in,' and the fish bowl of 'Wish You Were Here' make the listener see, not merely be told, that life is a maze of metaphysical necessity, doomed to repeat the same round. Compared to Waters's doggerel 'Free-Four,' which says the same thing about death, Dark Side's forty-three-minute loop lets you live a microcosmic life, and that shown-rather-than-said quality gave a lonely listener the dark hope of knowing he was not alone.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 19 "The Doors Are Never Locked" — Held reads Cash's Walk the Line retort "Well, they're not Christians then" as a thesis about redemption: since, with Augustine, we rejoice most at the sinner saved, and since the Sermon on the Mount forbids judging what we cannot know (anyone's deep character), humility demands withholding condemnation and hoping even the worst can change. He contrasts Christian redemption, a revaluation of the person that needs outside grace (Cash needed June and the Carters; nobody is self-made), with Nietzsche's attack on redemption as slave-morality self-hatred, granting that Nietzsche's eternal recurrence also revalues the past but objecting that self-revaluation collapses into rationalization, as Cash's Saul in Man in White shows. Forgiveness proper requires repentance and a solvent character, like paying off a debt; the shame of the "Long Black Veil" woman shows why; and because we see "through a glass darkly," nobody, not the Reno murderer, not Joe Bean, is beyond hope, which is why the doors are never locked and why execution or life without parole claims a judgment of moral worth that is not ours to make.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 22 "The Triforce Holds a Prosperous Future" — Sherlock reads Majora's Mask's repeating three days as Nietzsche's eternal recurrence from The Gay Science, the demon's demand that we affirm the same life 'innumerable times more', but then shows the Ocarina disrupts the mapping: the Inverted Song of Time and Song of Double Time make each cycle a non-repetition, dissolving the recurrence test's existential weight into a new anxiety about fragmented time. Items that survive the reset and rupees banked in Clock Town give time a material value, while the Deku Scrub transformation scene ('You'll stay looking that way forever') is analyzed as uncanny temporality via Freud's Das Unheimliche, with Derrida's claim that there is no non-metaphysical concept of time framing the conclusion that even game time cannot be separated from its representation.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 29 "Will You Say Yes" — Bruce finds Nietzsche's eternal return in the NES Zelda's clockless, endlessly restartable structure: the same game recurs every time you press start, yet since the player changes, each playthrough manifests the forces anew, and the demon's question 'do you desire this once more?' becomes 'do you will to play once more?'. Link's growth through eight dungeons to face Ganon is read as will-to-power, personal strength and self-overcoming rather than mere domination, and saying yes to the struggle is amor fati. Against Plato's two-worlds doctrine of Forms and the Christian after-worldly (both Nietzsche's targets), the original Zelda offers no guide, no Bible, and no linear time to a final judgment: this looped world is the only one, so it must be affirmed.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 20 "Brush the Cobwebs from the Sky, Let the Genie Out from the Bottle" — Lougheed reads OK Computer, Kid A, and Amnesiac as portraits of Nietzsche's Last Humans: passive, resentful denizens of the world after the death of God, from the 'No Surprises' narrator begging for his quiet life of carbon monoxide to the 'Everything in Its Right Place' man sucking a lemon over the loss of objective right and wrong, whose isolated malice ('when I am king you will be first against the wall') is perspectivism collapsed into passive nihilism. Hail to the Thief then breaks from this landscape: its protagonists risk transcendence as Over Humans who create new, life-affirming values ('2 + 2 = 5'''s 'don't question my authority', 'Backdrifts''' 'nothing more to lose'), keep a critical distance from society's nihilistic sickness ('Where I End and You Begin'), and test their lives against eternal recurrence ('Sail to the Moon'''s 'know right from wrong', '15 Step'''s ending up where you started). The chapter closes by weighing Nietzsche's over-human project against critics who prefer gradual, generational self-overcoming for everyone.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 25 "Philosopher of the Dangerous Perhaps" — Argues that Herbert is a genuine philosopher extending Nietzsche's Zarathustra into the twentieth century, via three narrative parallels: the Preacher entering Arrakeen mirrors Zarathustra's first down-going into the town with its tightrope walker and mocking buffoon; Paul's empire of water-fat Fremen and Alia's orthodoxy realizes the 'Ultimate Man' whom the crowd begs for instead of the Superman; and prescience reworks eternal recurrence's gateway 'Moment,' where every timeline ends in Krazilec. Reading Paul's sixty-five-billion-death jihad through Arendt's banality of evil and Herbert's 'superheroes are disastrous' thesis, the chapter concludes Paul is the failed tightrope walker and Leto II the goad—'not lightning, but lightning rod'—pushing humanity beyond man toward the Superman, with Spannungsbogen naming the tension of the drawn bow between animal and Overman.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 161 "Chapter 25 - Untimely Speculations" — Heath Massey's introduction to Chapter 25 opens with Nietzsche's Gay Science passage on intellects that might experience time backward, then stages the demon of eternal recurrence: every pain and joy returning in the same sequence in a world without aim, which either crushes you or becomes 'the highest formula of affirmation', amor fati. Eternal recurrence is a test of the will separating 'man' from 'overman', since one could not celebrate it while believing the world needs a divine purpose. The chapter then maps Dick's imaginative variations of temporality onto two Nietzschean tendencies - disruptions of time-sense that render characters powerless, and extraordinary temporalities that liberate them beyond finite human time, culminating in Dick's theory of supertemporality.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 162 "Human, All Too Human" — This section collects Dick's incapacitating temporalities. In Martian Time-Slip, repairman Jack Bohlen relapses into schizophrenia while trying to slow autistic Manfred Steiner's accelerated time-sense, concluding that psychosis is 'the utter alienation of perception from the objects of the outside world', which would also explain the fine line between prophecy and psychosis. In 'Your Appointment Will Be Yesterday' the Hobart Phase reverses time - libraries eradicate books, authors unwrite their manuscripts - and threatens a closed loop of Eng's swabble until crank Lance Arbuthnot has his own manuscript eradicated to keep the reversal in place. In Ubik, Joe Chip watches cigarettes, milk and TVs regress to prior 'templates' as the world decays; in all three, altered time crushes rather than elevates, leaving characters struggling not to be overcome by the inexorability of time.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 163 "Preparatory Human Beings" — The counter-tendency gathers Dick's empowering temporalities. 'The Golden Man' presents Cris Johnson, a golden-haired mutant with virtually no frontal cortex, who survives a random-firing gun by 'pre-thinking' a panorama of possible futures - Homo superior as superhuman beast, by instinct rather than intelligence. In Now Wait for Last Year, General Molinari uses the drug JJ-180 to trip sideways into parallel presents and recruit healthy duplicates of himself, virtually overcoming mortality with 'a dynasty consisting of himself'. And in The Man in the High Castle, Abendsen's The Grasshopper Lies Heavy, Frank Frink's handwrought jewelry and Tagomi's meditative slip all point toward an alternate present - ours - where the Allies won, making art and the I Ching oracles of resistance to totalitarian domination.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 164 "On the Advantage and Disadvantage of Eternity for Life" — The essay's close presents Dick's own 'wicked thought' from 'If You Find This World Bad, You Should See Some of the Others': a plurality of universes arranged laterally to linear time, 'ten thousand bodies of God' hung like suits, including one where Germany and Japan won World War II. It asks whether lateral change might explain schizophrenic experience and whether eternity, in Dick's phrase being 'free from and somehow out of and above time', is supertemporality - occupying multiple time sequences at will. Like Nietzsche's eternal recurrence, Dick's multiverse is a test rather than a doctrine: those crushed by an aimless universe remain merely human, while those who can affirm endless strife or tap parallel presents are virtually superhuman, resisting time's supposedly inexorable march.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 23 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Brandon Kempner reads Gaiman's Batman: Whatever Happened to the Caped Crusader? as Nietzschean eternal recurrence: Batman dies and is reborn as the infant Bruce Wayne to repeat his life exactly, because Gaiman first strips away every teleological ending, Catwoman kills Batman, Alfred reveals he invented the Joker, and the Moore-style domestic bliss of the Superman farewell is denied. With God dead there is no Heaven, telos, or external reward, so, like Nietzsche's Overman who creates values above the city's conventional morality, Batman's meaning can lie only in the lived repetition itself: 'the only reward you get for being Batman? You get to be Batman,' the highest formula of life-affirmation. Kempner extends the pattern to the funeral-framed rebirth of a new Dream in Sandman: The Wake, showing Gaiman's recurring obsession with cycles that have 'no endings' across his work.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 18 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Scores Walt and Mad Men's Don Draper against Nietzsche's Overman and Last Man: Roger Sterling (and the early, passive Jesse) are Last Men, while Walt moves from weak negation of the status quo to genuine self-affirmation - 'going under' in the 'Crawl Space' crawl hole and emerging in 'Face Off' having poisoned Brock and out-created Gus, which the chapter takes as proof that in a capitalist world two creators cannot coexist. Killing Gus is framed as accepting the eternal recurrence of joy and sorrow, willing even his own bad acts. Don, by contrast, negates far more than he creates, and the chapter ends by asking why viewers empathize with the one failed Overman and find the other inspiring.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 13 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Greene asks whether Nucky is Nietzsche's Ubermensch and works through each criterion. Nucky, Gyp Rosetti, and the other mobsters are passionate, active shapers of their world (Van Alden fails here), and Nucky is a genuine creator of values after the death of God - his whopper to the Temperance League, his flip-flopping sermons to black and white congregations, and his 'I. Am. Not. Seeking. Forgiveness.' over Jimmy's body reject slave morality where the other gangsters merely follow the objective moral code of omerta. He sacrifices lesser lives (Hans Schroeder, Gillian) and has the required dark side, but he fails the final test of teaching the eternal recurrence, so he remains only 'well on his way' to Superman - a status the show's women (Margaret, Lucy, Gillian) never approach, hovering closer to the last man.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 28 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Laderoute reads 'The Late Philip J. Fry' - the forward-only time machine overshooting past the year one billion and the last protons to a second Big Bang and an identical universe (ten feet lower, conveniently crushing its duplicates) - as a tour of cosmology from Aristotle's static, eternal, Earth-centered heavens through the Stoics' providential determinism and fiery ekpyrosis to Big Bang cosmology and heat death, which is why the Professor is so shocked. Nietzsche's Gay Science 341 supplies the existential payoff: faced with living identically forever, one can react with horror or delight, and eternal recurrence becomes a challenge to become the person you want to be. Fry, a billion years late for his Cavern on the Green dinner, reads Leela's message carved in stone, and in the repeated universe finally arrives on time - 'That was the old Fry... he's dead now' - amor fati enacted.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 17 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Ketcham reads the monster as Zarathustra's dark double: both are exiled 'godless men' who begin their journeys at a cottager's door, but where Nietzsche's prophet preaches the Übermensch, the will to power, and living so one could will eternal recurrence, the monster traverses the three metamorphoses in reverse - born the innocent child, becoming the lion who tells Victor 'you are my creator, but I am your master,' and ending the camel carrying his maker's corpse to a self-immolating pyre in the polar dark. Shelley's abyss is science usurping God and drawing Promethean punishment; Nietzsche's abyss is the shadow of the dead God (The Gay Science) that keeps humanity from the great noontide and traps Frankenstein as a 'last man' whose will is subjugated to pleasant happiness. The monster, bastard of a godless man and bridge to neither animal nor Übermensch, shows a will that is sheer power without any foundation for overcoming man - 'whither humanity?'
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 45 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Steven Neumann reads the sold-my-soul legends around Led Zeppelin ('here's to my sweet Satan' backwards on 'Stairway to Heaven'), Black Sabbath, and bluesman Robert Johnson at the Clarksdale crossroads as a parable of Nietzsche's amor fati: every joy comes bundled with suffering, so greatness means affirming the whole package. He deploys the eternal recurrence thought experiment - would you will your life, Plant's dead son and Bonham's fatal bender included, to repeat eternally? - and contrasts the ascetic denial of pleasure with Nietzsche's claim in Ecce Homo that his own sickness and obscurity made him love fate all the more.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 27 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Martyn Jones stages a fictional Nietzsche telling Mac, Dennis, and Charlie the plot of 'The Gang Solves the Gas Crisis' as a parable of metaphysics gone wrong. Mac and Dennis's scheming is Apollonian - imposing logical order and 'paradigms' on a recalcitrant world - while Charlie is Dionysian, the designated wildcard whose uncontainable energy (sabotaging the van and ripping out the brakes) dooms every plan that tries to harness him, since Apollonian schemes fatally imagine they can contain Dionysian force. Reason is a gloss, not a truth-tracker: like every theology and philosophy it is an expression of will, a survival tool serving selfish ends, so the delusional gas scheme needs no truth to serve its purpose. Charlie alone is praised as a proto-Übermensch - innocent, creative, founding his own values without resentment - and the tale closes musing that even an eternal recurrence of their botched schemes might be willed all over again.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 29 "17. Downton Abbey as Eternal Recurrence" — Christopher Ketcham asks whether primogeniture and entail make Downton Abbey a social embodiment of Nietzsche's eternal recurrence - the same estate, without revision, turned over generation after generation like the eternal hourglass of existence. Working through Lawrence Hatab's five interpretations of the doctrine, he tests royal continuity against death duties, the nihilism of industrial capitalism, and the Great War that killed heirs and empires, and borrows Kant's categorical imperative as an analogy for Britain's uniquely preserved 'royal categorical imperative' of continuity. The Abbey's recurrence survives only anthropomorphically - Violet, the family, the servants, and the tenants as its living organs - and the chapter wonders whether such ossified continuity, like dinosaur bones, is really eternal.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 33 "21. Batman Is Superman" — The chapter argues that Bale's Batman, not the alien Superman, is Nietzsche's Übermensch: a mortal whose identity is forged in the unreconciled struggle between Dionysian emotion and Apollonian reason - vengeance against justice in Batman Begins - and who relives his traumas as Nietzschean eternal recurrence, from the bat-filled well to the prison leap of The Dark Knight Rises. The Joker is his dark double, whose will to power and ferry-boat experiment nearly extinguish Gotham's hope, but Batman absorbs the chaos and sacrifices his heroic name, whereas Superman in Injustice, losing Lois, falls into a vengeful Dionysian abyss he cannot master. Only a mortal who extends his limits without succumbing to the herd's 'gravity of madness' can be Nietzsche's superman, so the mortal, conflicted, imitable Batman is the true superman.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 17 "5. Rhapsody on a Theme by Schroeder" — The chapter argues Schroeder's monomaniacal devotion to his toy piano and Beethoven is a Nietzschean way of life: he refuses the herd's path and the self-denying 'priestly' values of ordinary childhood, and treats music as the highest creative force, as The Birth of Tragedy claims. Nietzsche's demon of eternal recurrence becomes a test Schroeder passes - he lives for this life and could will its exact repetition - while Schopenhauer backs the claim that music discloses the world's inner nature as language cannot, and the Christmas-dance scene shows the communal fusion Nietzsche heard in song and dance. Strips about Lucy on the piano, his 'grown accustomed to that face' shock when she moves away, and the Beethoven's-birthday holiday cast Lucy as his unsuspecting muse; but as a would-be Ubermensch he must go beyond playing Beethoven and create his own compositions.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 21 "9. My Dharma Is the Road that Never Ends" — Reads Twin Peaks: The Return as a commitment to Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and amor fati: Cooper is trapped in an existential time loop (Dougie's relearning, Wally's Part 4 Dharma speech, the final-episode Cooper/Richard do-over) and must learn to love every horrific repetition, quoting the Gay Science demon passage and Nietzsche's Will to Power on enduring recurrence. The chapter frames Lynch and Frost as Romantics — Novalis on wonder, Isaiah Berlin's Roots of Romanticism on the artist's inner vision — who break three storytelling rules (authors create stories, protagonists solve problems, stories have endings), so that Laura's mystery stays a living Jack-the-Ripper-style mystery and the story becomes a meta-narrative co-created with viewers, echoing Buddhist pratityasamutpada and Russell's beginningless world. Cooper's finale is a Sisyphean task he accepts, making his integrity the audience's own test.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 14 "5. The Funny Thing about Being Yourself" — Reads Schumer's comedy as Nietzschean self-creation: like the tightrope walker over the abyss she confronts who she is, says 'Yes' to life in the spirit of the eternal recurrence and amor fati, and 'gives style' to her character by wearing mistakes as badges of honor, notably reclaiming her paparazzi photos in the Leather Special. Balke then casts her as Rorty's ironist, whose continual burning of old material keeps her free of a 'final vocabulary' in a contingent world, with 'Amy Goes Deep' doing the Rortian work of testing herself against others. He closes with George Herbert Mead's account of a self formed through social interaction with significant others.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 39 "27. I Am Inevitable" — Reads Thanos's 'I am inevitable' (his name echoing thanatos) as death personified, then asks 'whose death?' through Heidegger — 'people die' is the evasive 'one dies,' and Tony's final snap and 'I am Iron Man' figure an authentic appropriation of being-toward-death that redeems his guilt — before Blanchot's reversal and Lacan's symbolic death dissolve that authenticity into impersonal, language-borne dying (Loki's 'No resurrections this time' as the meta-textual murder of comic-book death). It ends with Deleuze's Nietzschean eternal return as the empty form of time that the time heist and quantum multiverse enact, concluding the real inevitability 'engraved in the very fabric of reality' belongs to Steve Rogers and Peggy Carter's dance, not to Thanos or Iron Man.
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 17 "8. Philosophy and the Personae" — Randall Auxier builds a characterology of the four personae using Aristotle's methods (endoxa and aporia) and the band's wealth hierarchy as his map. The Demon is Nietzsche — an uninhibited cosmopolitan beyond good and evil who philosophizes with a hammer and whispers eternal recurrence; the Starchild is Epicurus — Paul's microtia and bullied childhood formed the detached soul that Plato's Republic ties to being a philosopher, yielding ataraxia, aponia, therapy, and disciplined long-term pleasures; the Catman has Kundera's lightness of being around 'Beth'; and the Spaceman's otherworldly detachment explains both his guitar genius and the Nazi-regalia incident. The chapter's thesis: KISS succeeded because Gene and Paul's detached, centered self-knowledge let them give fans exactly what they secretly wanted.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 22 "Can You Face the Bat" — Sarah Donovan and Nicholas Richardson use Nietzsche and Foucault to present Batman as a self-constructed identity: across Batman: Year One, Arkham Asylum, and The Dark Knight Returns, Bruce consciously builds the persona ('Yes, Father, I shall become a bat') rather than revealing a deeper true self. Foucault's constructed categories of normal and abnormal surface in Arkham Asylum's 'super-sane' Joker and the Alice in Wonderland parallels that put Batman's own sanity in question alongside Amadeus Arkham's madness. Nietzsche's will to power and eternal recurrence, via the shepherd biting the snake in Zarathustra, explain why Bruce can face the bat that others flee, becoming heroic where Arkham and Dr. Cavendish go insane.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 22 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Brown and Fosl read the twin Lebowskis as America's post-1960s despair: the Big Lebowski is Kierkegaard's failed Caesar who despairs because he cannot rid himself of the self that did not become Caesar (a fake achiever living on an allowance), while the Dude is the failed leftist whose revolutions collapsed. Against nihilism Walter pulverizes with Nietzschean will, Kierkegaard prescribes the leap of faith, and Camus revolt — but the Dude offers a distinctly American answer, abiding repetition: rolling balls frame after frame like Camus's happy Sisyphus, repeating phrases and roles (Butlerian performativity) so that re-creating himself is his victory over meaninglessness, with No Country for Old Men as the dark twin where nihilism may be winning.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 3 "A Strange Realization" — Dunn argues that Strange begins as a foot soldier of the Baconian project (Bacon and Descartes' program of conquering nature and treating death as an enemy to be subdued, embodied in his surgical God-complex and neurogenesis research), and that its shipwreck drives him to Kamar-Taj. Using Nietzsche, he reads both Strange and Kaecilius as sick with the 'spirit of revenge against time' — Kaecilius fleeing into Dormammu's timeless Dark Dimension as Nietzsche's Hinterweltler, Strange clinging to his unrecoverable past. The climactic 'Dormammu, I've come to bargain' time loop is interpreted as Nietzsche's eternal return weaponized, and Strange's 'Pain's an old friend' as his achievement of amor fati, echoing the Ancient One's dying claim that death is what gives life meaning.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 6 "The Existential Redefinition of Doctor Strange" — DiGeorgio traces Strange's 'existential conversion' from scientific nihilism ('matter and nothing more') through Sartrean bad faith — playing the brilliant surgeon while not really believing life meaningless, refusing the Ancient One's widened keyhole — to authenticity. His hesitation to stay and fight after killing a zealot, and the Ancient One's 'it's not about you,' set up his choice to defend humanity as Sartre's universal decree, choosing for all humankind in anguish and freedom. The endless time loop imposed on Dormammu is read as Nietzsche's eternal recurrence demanding total commitment to one's choices, so that by the end Strange lives existence-precedes-essence: what he does, not his 'brilliant surgeon' essence, defines him.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 29 "17. Downton Abbey as Eternal Recurrence" — Christopher Ketcham provocatively equates primogeniture and entail - the legal machinery that returns Downton intact to each generation - with Nietzsche's 'greatest weight,' the eternal recurrence. Working through Lawrence Hatab's five interpretations of the doctrine, he asks whether the Abbey's continuity is cosmological (it is not, since estate taxes and squandering heirs keep chipping away), a Zarathustra-style life-affirming yes to the agrarian world against the 'nihilism' of capitalist fashion, or merely symbolic like a listing in Burke's Peerage beside fossilized dinosaur bones. His answer comes via Violet, the family, and the servants, who have 'become one with the property': the Abbey recurs only anthropomorphically, and even that stickiness is dissolving under industrialization, the death tax, and the war that killed off three royal cousins' empires.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 25 "Philosopher of the Dangerous Perhaps" — Claims Herbert is a philosopher whose Dune saga is a novelistic thought experiment extending Nietzsche's Zarathustra in the light of twentieth-century horrors: the Preacher's entry into Arrakeen parallels Zarathustra's first discourse on the Ubermensch at the tightrope, Paul is the failed tightrope-walker while Leto II is both devil-buffoon and goad toward the Superman, and the empire of Dune Messiah is enumerated trait by trait as Nietzsche's realm of the Ultimate Man. Eternal recurrence is paralleled with prescience as both the trap of destiny and the gateway 'Moment' that frees humanity from apparent necessity, and Arendt's banality of evil frames Paul's sixty-five billion jihad deaths as an ordinary, human result rather than demonic villainy.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 14 "NOTES" — Shores reads Volume 1 through Nietzsche's eternal recurrence as a self-test of life-affirmation: Adam sealed in a coffin embodies recurrence in its 'most terrible form,' Future Hiro's string map dramatizes Nietzsche's claim that every action is indissolubly tied to all others, and Linderman's speech divorcing happiness from meaning is answered by Nietzsche's demand to crave nothing more fervently than the eternal return. The chapter stresses where the show diverges: Claire insists 'the future is not written in stone' and the heroes rewrite destiny, while Arthur Petrelli ironically holds a copy of Thus Spoke Zarathustra while contradicting it. Hiro's failed attempts to save Charlie and his father (Kaito's 'we cannot play God') frame the amor fati question of whether free will means changing events or willing them eternally.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 17 "7 Indiana Jones and Existential Self-Affirmation" — Daniel Tilsley reads The Last Crusade as an excavation of identity: the fedora Fedora bestows after young Indy's defeat, the twenty-six-year quest for the Cross of Coronado ('All my life'), and the chosen name 'Indiana' (taken from the family dog) are acts of Nietzschean self-affirmation — amor fati and the willingness to will the Eternal Recurrence of one's life. The villains fail because they seek external artifacts to patch deficient lives, whereas the Grail Knight, like Camus's Sisyphus, authentically affirms his endless task of guarding the cup. The arc completes when Henry Sr. finally calls his son 'Indiana' while hanging from the abyss, recognizing the man he chose to become, and Crystal Skull repeats the pattern with Mutt and the fedora's eventual inheritance.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 22 "The Triforce Holds a Prosperous Future" — Lee Sherlock reads Majora's Mask's repeating three-day cycle against Nietzsche's eternal recurrence from The Gay Science, noting that the Ocarina's Inverted Song of Time and Song of Double Time destabilize exact repetition and so dissolve the 'greatest weight' of the demon's question. Items carried across cycles and rupees banked in Clock Town give time a material value — some things survive the reset and some do not — which supports Derrida's denial of a non-metaphysical concept of time. Finally, Freud's das Unheimliche explains the game's 'uncanny temporality': the Skull Kid's transformation of Link into a Deku Scrub ('You'll stay looking that way forever') makes the familiar strange and fuses loss of body with loss of time.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 29 "Will You Say Yes" — Michael Bruce ('Zeldathustra') reads the original Legend of Zelda through Nietzsche's thought of eternal recurrence: with no game clock, the ability to save, and looped enemy patterns, every playthrough repeats the same structure, and the player faces the demon's question — do you will to play once more and innumerable times more? The Triforce's split between Wisdom and Power becomes Nietzsche's opposition of the will-to-truth and the will-to-power, with Link's dungeon-by-dungeon self-overcoming enacting amor fati. Against Plato's two-world doctrine of Forms and the Christian after-worldly, the chapter insists the game (like life) gets its meaning from this world only — experimentation, repetition as training, and saying yes.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 33 "21. Batman Is Superman" — Argues that Christian Bale's Batman, not the alien Superman, embodies Nietzsche's Übermensch: a mortal, flawed, lonely hero whose identity is forged in the unreconciled struggle between Dionysian vengeance and Apollonian reason across Nolan's trilogy. Batman Begins enacts eternal recurrence as Bruce repeatedly relives and integrates the well, the opera, and his parents' murder; The Dark Knight's Joker is Batman's Janus-faced shadow whose ferry experiment nearly proves the herd's 'gravity of madness,' and Dent's fall shows what Batman resists becoming. Superman II's temporarily mortal Superman is beaten by a truck driver and retreats to invincibility, proving the immortal alien can never overreach mortal limits as the Übermensch must.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 8 "Notes" — Reads Carcosa, the Yellow King, and Ledoux's 'time is a flat circle' as cosmic horror in the lineage of Lovecraft and Ligotti, arguing that the genre's dread — that monsters exist and the fixed laws of nature may fail — is a metaphor for realizing Schopenhauer's blind will, with Rust's car monologues in 'The Long Bright Dark' presented as a beginner's guide to Schopenhauer. It notes Rust inverts the usual Lovecraft protagonist by starting the story already horrified, and that eternal recurrence framed through Schopenhauer's sphere-of-time makes even the rescued children's torment maddeningly endless. The chapter closes by complaining that the finale 'Form and Void' betrays both genres: the occult becomes ordinary crime and Rust's 'light is winning' star-field reverses Schopenhauer's pessimistic cosmology.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 9 "Notes" — Distinguishes philosophical pessimism (Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Camus, Unamuno) — the denial that the universe is an ordered place whose laws human reason can grasp — from mere gloominess, and reads Rust's 'time is a flat circle' as Nietzschean anti-metaphysics of a world going nowhere. It argues pessimism makes Rust the better detective because, expecting no rational order, he sees what is actually there, while optimist Marty's illusions about family and career multiply his losses and end with him losing both. Against conflating pessimism with despair, the chapter splits ideas (pessimism) from attitudes (hope), showing how Hart's heart and Cohle's clear sight combine into the show's ideal of hopeful pessimism.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 13 "Notes" — Takes Nietzsche's 'man is the cruelest animal' and argues the show's real exploration of cruelty lies not in the cult's crimes, which stay mysterious, but in the Cohle–Hart relationship, whose private cruelties are closer to the human condition. It explains human cruelty through theory of mind — knowing we make others suffer — and through the moral vocabulary of desert, karma, and Schadenfreude (Nietzsche's slave morality inventing hell) that hides our pleasure in suffering, which Nietzsche sees as the key to life-affirmation against Buddhist and Christian world-denial. The chapter maps Hart as Dionysian energy and Cohle as Apollonian form, and reads Rust's 2012 talk of eternal recurrence as a ruse concealing his search for a Nietzschean moment of ecstatic affirmation of all the cruelty he has caused and endured.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 19 "Notes" — Divides Rust's season-one personae into Taxman (anti-natalist rule-follower), Belligerent (vigilante drunk paralyzed by Nietzsche's Gay Science demon of eternal recurrence), and Patient (the mystic who wakes from his coma feeling his daughter's love, compared to the Persian mystic al-Hallaj), asking what makes them one person. It tests the brute physicalist account (Williams and Ayer — the same bird-tattooed body), the Lockean psychological-continuity account, and the narrative account, arguing only the narrative theory explains how Rust changes without either ignoring change or multiplying selves in one body. The chapter ends by making Rust an exemplar for the viewer: we are narrators who choose who to become, so 'I know who I am' is a victory.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Reads Cohle's arc as an existentialist passage toward authenticity, using Sartre's being-for-itself to explain why Hart's 'family man' identity is bad faith — a clinging to social roles that denies the freedom of a consciousness that is an activity, not a thing. Beauvoir's analysis of women as the passive, objectified Other illuminates why Rust, despite his nihilism, persistently protects vulnerable women and children such as Sophia, Dora Lange, and Marie Fontenot: threats to others' freedom threaten our own. Nietzsche's Silenus wisdom, the spirit of gravity on the tightrope, and the shepherd who bites the head off the snake frame Ledoux's and Childress' warped eternal return as the poison Cohle must overcome before he can will life eternally and declare 'the light is winning.'
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Traces Cohle's opening monologue directly to Schopenhauer — reality as a purposeless will whose satisfied desires breed only boredom, answered by ascetic denial of the will-to-live rather than suicide. It then explains Nietzsche's eternal recurrence as the true test of life-affirmation, via the Gay Science demon and Zarathustra's ordeal with the Small Man, and interprets will to power as finding meaning in overcoming resisting conditions, so that affirmation does not mean approving everything that happens. Hatab argues the show's horrified version of the flat circle is Schopenhauerian rather than Nietzschean, and that Cohle's 'light is winning' ending is ambiguous — if it rests on a supernatural reunion with Sophia, it would betray Nietzsche's this-worldly affirmation.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 28 "Notes" — Argues 'time is a flat circle' means neither a metaphysical cosmology nor M-theory physics nor reincarnation, but is Nietzsche's eternal recurrence as a thought experiment about how to live. Tracing Rust's pessimism and his lack of the 'constitution for suicide' (echoing Schopenhauer's claim that suicide affirms the will-to-live, with starvation as its only true denial), it shows the flat circle operating as both trap and cure: obsessing over it keeps Rust on the Yellow King case until his near-death experience becomes the 'tremendous moment' of amor fati. Heidegger's view in Being and Time that anxiety before death can empower meaningful existence frames Rust's final affirmation — escaping the flat circle by faithfully acknowledging it, through sacrifice.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 15 "Notes" — Michels reads the Amazon series' first two seasons as a Nietzschean tale organized around eternal recurrence, treating the turning Wheel as Nietzsche's 'existential imperative' and greatest weight: the ferryman who dies vainly saving his son fails the test, while Loial urges the heroes to make themselves unforgettable. He maps Nietzsche's monumental, antiquarian, and critical uses of history onto Moiraine's lesson about the song of Manetheren, contrasts the Ubermensch with the 'last man,' and reads Moiraine's will to power against the ascetic, life-denying Way of the Leaf of the Tuatha'an. Lanfear and Ishamael embody nihilism and resentment, while amor fati names the life-affirming embrace of fate Nietzsche prized.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 16 "Notes" — Silver argues WoT gives a new spin on the free-will defense to the problem of evil: when Rand weaves a world without Shai'tan in A Memory of Light, Elayne appears as if turned, robbed of the ability to be an individual, showing that freedom's value lies in authentic individuality and that abolishing evil equals a world run entirely from the Dark One's single perspective. On fate, he reads ta'veren as freedom-affirming rather than controlling and defends Rand's Dragonmount epiphany via 'deep self' compatibilist views (Frankfurt, Watson) while calling it partly bad faith. On the Wheel's eternal recurrence he sets Nietzsche's amor fati against Adorno's charge that it is a failure of hope, arguing Rand's 'do better next time' is hope, not acceptance.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 19 "Wholly Communion Poetry, Philosophy, and Spontaneous Bop Cinema" — Sterritt reads Peter Whitehead's 1965 film 'Wholly Communion,' shot at London's International Poetry Incarnation, as 'spontaneous bop cinema' embodying Beat poetics through Bakhtin's dialogic/carnivalesque and the schizoanalysis of Deleuze and Guattari. Ginsberg's drunken recitation of 'The Change' becomes a 'body without organs' entering the 'chaosmos' on the plane of immanence; Jandl's sound poetry is pure Deleuzian sensation. Adrian Mitchell's anti-Vietnam 'To Whom It May Concern' is read through Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and amor fati and Deleuze's 'difference in repetition,' its incantatory counter-words a materialist line of flight against the order-words of war.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 8 "Introduction" — LaRocca frames the whole volume around Kaufman's recurring 'who-what-why' of selfhood, arguing that his films literalize an inner alterity in which we are others to ourselves. He runs through Being John Malkovich (a homunculus inside another's head), Adaptation (a genetic twin), and Eternal Sunshine (memory as the very definition of who one is) to show doubling as Kaufman's method, and lists eternal recurrence among the philosophical conundra Kaufman embeds in flawed characters. The essay reads Kaufman's pseudonymity and self-naming as intensifying, not closing, the gap between the self and its double.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 16 "I Don’t Know, Just Wait Remembering Remarriage in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind" — Day reads Eternal Sunshine as Cavell's Hollywood comedy of remarriage: the kaleidoscopic middle in 'Joel's head' is the couple's remarriage conversation, a 'green world' where they invent a shared childhood and learn what it means to have memories together. Against a tape-recorder model of memory, he invokes the later Wittgenstein's private-language argument to argue there is no private memory — what Joel remembers he can return to Clementine in conversation. He rereads Mary's Nietzsche, the eternal recurrence, not as the end of regret but as affirming it (Joel's 'I wish I'd stayed. I do.'), and claims viewers themselves remember the erased past for the pair across the hallway's ten seconds of waiting.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 24 "Nietzschean Themes in the Films of Charlie Kaufman" — Shaw argues Kaufman's films embody a Nietzschean 'Dionysian pessimism' organized around the will to power, eternal recurrence, perspectivism, and a bundle-theory of the self. He reads Being John Malkovich through the bundle self: personal identity is the dominant drive that acts, so Malkovich 'becomes' Lester/Mertin, the will that controls the vessel. Adaptation's Laroche voices Nietzsche's plastic power of forgetting, and Eternal Sunshine dramatizes eternal recurrence and amor fati as Joel and Clementine choose to repeat their doomed love. Synecdoche, New York, by contrast, Shaw judges a failure of passive nihilism—Caden as the fly who never leaves the bottle—deadening rather than life-affirming.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 21 "9. My Dharma Is the Road that Never Ends" — Potter and Cobb argue that Twin Peaks is a Romantic refusal of resolution: mysteries live by not being solved, so Lynch and Frost break the rules that stories need authors, protagonists who solve problems, and endings. They read Cooper's entrapment in a time loop through Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and amor fati (quoting The Gay Science and The Will to Power), tie Wally Brando's Dharma speech and Isaiah Berlin's Roots of Romanticism to the theme, and argue the real 'story' is the endless meta-narrative co-created between the show and each viewer—Life itself as process without endpoint.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 32 "18. Repeating Twin Peaks" — Komel argues repetition is both a structural principle of the TV series (every show repeats its pilot) and the key to Twin Peaks, invoking Nietzsche's eternal recurrence, Kierkegaard, and Lacan/Žižek. Using Lacan's aim-versus-goal of desire and Žižek's 'coffee without milk' as a positive absence, he reads Laura Palmer as a 'positive absence' around which the series turns, and shows the murder repetitions are out of order—Maddy's on-screen death precedes and retroactively produces Laura's in Fire Walk with Me. Laura's final scream in The Return, unlike its predecessors, subversively rewrites the original, so 'The Return' is really 'The Repetition' that undoes its origin.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Arnett reads Mann's 'modern crime films' through Nietzsche and Marc Augé's 'nonplace,' arguing Mann is a director-architect who exerts a will to power over institutional space (Atlanta's High Museum becomes Lecktor's prison in Manhunter; Neil's glass beach house in Heat). Mann's heroes are Nietzsche's 'godless' who refuse the herd, becoming Dionysian figures who redefine space—Neil and Vincent as Dionysian/Apollonian artists whose LAX showdown is a 'frenzy' of convergence. The endless recurrence of place-versus-nonplace, and Vincent killing Neil only to be trapped in supermodernity himself, dramatizes Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and Dionysian pessimism.
- **The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute**, ch. 15 "3. Experiences with Nietzsche" — Müller-Lauter interweaves memoir—hearing 'Praised be what makes hard!' and 'What does not kill me makes me stronger' torn from context in Nazi Weimar—with a systematic account of Nietzsche's nihilism as the devaluation of the highest values following the death of God. He traces the move from 'incomplete' to 'perfect' nihilism and the revaluation of values through the free spirit and the legislating Dionysian philosopher, insisting (against Bäumler's and Lukács's systematizations of the unauthorized Will to Power) that Nietzsche's experimental, fragmentary thought resists both fascist and Marxist appropriation.
- **The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute**, ch. 22 "9. A Question of Responsibility Nietzsche with Hölderlin at War, 1914 –1946" — Corngold and Waite argue Nietzsche programmed a deliberately esoteric doctrine of 'order of rank' (Rangordnung) and will to power meant to work as a delayed actio in distans across centuries, taking responsibility ('Ich bin verantwortlich') even for what followed. They trace how the Nietzsche-Hölderlin nexus—Hölderlin's 'Thought' as father to Nietzsche's/Hitler's 'Deed'—was cultivated from George's circle through Heidegger's wartime lectures to Rosenberg's 1944 Weimar address, showing the Nazis staged a controlled 'debate' over Nietzsche while treating Hölderlin as untouchable, so the nexus itself functioned as Gramscian non-coercive hegemony.
- **The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute**, ch. 25 "12. Nietzsche and the Fascist Dimension The Case of Ernst Jünger" — Ohana locates fascism's 'nihilistic-totalitarian syndrome' in the Janus-faced combination of Nietzschean nihilism and the Overman's will to power, whereby ethics is replaced by aesthetics and the self-creating 'new man' shapes reality ex nihilo. He reads Ernst Jünger's Stahlgewittern, Der Arbeiter and 'Total Mobilization' as the aestheticization of war and technology into a work-state, and traces Heidegger's fascination with Jünger's 'will to will' back to Nietzsche and Hölderlin—arguing that, following Camus, one cannot ignore the directionless dynamism leading from Nietzschean perspectivism toward Rosenberg's marching-column politics.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 11 "My Troubles Are Going to Have Troubles with Me Schopenhauer, Pessimism, and Nietzsche" — Jacob Held pits Schopenhauer's pessimism against Nietzschean affirmation using I Had Trouble in Getting to Solla Sollew. He reads Schopenhauer's will-to-life and 'pendulum between pain and boredom' into Seuss's endlessly striving characters, and treats the mirage-towns Solla Sollew and Boola Boo Ball as proof there is no escape from suffering. The protagonist's final line, 'I've bought a big bat... now my troubles are going to have troubles with me,' becomes Nietzsche's yes-saying: instead of the ascetic renunciation Schopenhauer prescribes, Seuss's child-hero affirms life, redeeming its accidents the way Nietzsche's eternal-recurrence thought experiment and 'become a child' passage in Zarathustra demand.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 7 "“Gan Is Dead”" — Garret Merriam reads the ending of The Dark Tower—Roland scaling the Tower only to be flung back to the Mohaine Desert to repeat his quest—as a literal enactment of Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and its demon's test. Roland fails the test ('Please, not again!') because he treats his life as a teleological quest ('all things serve the beam') rather than embracing that 'ka is a wheel'; the Horn of Eld and Furth's hope of 'escaping the trap' miss the point. Merriam argues that once Roland accepts 'Gan is dead'—that meaning must be self-made, not bestowed from the Tower—he could achieve amor fati, and closes with Camus's Sisyphus: we must imagine Roland happy.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 26 "GARDENING" — Mara Miller argues gardens do not merely sit inside time but actively structure six kinds of time (scientific, objective/shared, kairos, subjective, temporality, historical), opening with Augustine's puzzle that he knows what time is until asked to explain it. She contrasts Greek chronos with kairos (the right moment to plant after the last frost), shows how Versailles propagated a shared time (eternal, historic, recurring) and eighteenth-century English landscape gardens taught the long-range vision capitalism needed, and describes cyclical 'eternal recurrence' (Eliade). Watching a dry Zen garden or fireflies, the visitor becomes the constant who notices—reworking Descartes's cogito as 'I notice, therefore I am'—while Japanese stepping-stones enforce a Buddhist mindfulness of impermanence in the present moment.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 40 "37. Groundhog Day as Philosophy Phil Connors Says “No” to Eternal Return" — Blessing argues that Groundhog Day, despite frequent comparisons to Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and Camus's Myth of Sisyphus, actually rejects both. Phil Connors does not say the Nietzschean 'yes' to reliving the same day (his attitude is odium fati, not amor fati), nor does he find Camusian happiness by embracing absurdity; instead he keeps changing, striving toward a better tomorrow. She reads his transformation from misanthropic hedonist on a hedonic treadmill into a kind, generous, self-actualized man as a vindication of Aristotle's virtue ethics: happiness comes from habitually doing the right thing (saving the falling boy, learning piano, serving others), pursuing objective and intrinsic goods rather than mere meaning-subjectivism, so redemption is not 'looking at things differently' but becoming a better person.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 89 "84. The Legend of Zelda Breath of the Wild as Philosophy Teaching the Player to Be Comfortable Being Alone" — Lay argues that Breath of the Wild teaches, chiefly through design rather than plot, that solitude is good for the player. He tests eternal return (the recurring Ganon-Zelda-Link cycle across the series), Sartrean absolute freedom and Kierkegaardian anxiety of choice (BotW's Korok-dung 'reward' and refusal to attach external meaning push players to make their own meaning), and Kierkegaard's inward 'repetition.' He lands on Mill's and Schopenhauer's defense of solitude-in-nature as self-actualizing rather than isolating, and reads sequence-breaking exploits as Marx-style spontaneous creative activity, concluding the game frames solitude as a path to eudaimonia and human flourishing.

### Utilitarianism

Utilitarianism is the moral theory holding that the right action is the one that produces the greatest overall balance of well-being, or happiness, considered impartially across everyone affected. It emerged in Britain through the work of Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill as a reforming answer to moral systems grounded in tradition, intuition, or divine command, offering instead a single measurable standard for evaluating laws and conduct. Because it judges acts by their consequences rather than by intentions or rules, it counts each person's happiness equally and treats the good of the many as the aim of morality.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 11 "“The Graduation” Autonomy and the Relational Self" — Jessica Prata Miller reads Buffy through Carol Gilligan's care perspective: Buffy's self is relational (the Scooby Gang, 'Dawn is a part of me' in 'The Gift'), her moral reasoning contextual rather than rule-bound (caging Oz instead of killing the werewolf, rejecting Riley's Initiative 'demons bad' abstraction), and her emotions a moral resource ('My emotions give me power'). She also weighs the criticisms — Buffy's secret harboring of Angel exposed in 'Revelations,' and Faith's utilitarian 'plus column' defense of hiding a killing, which Buffy rejects ('I am' the one who cries over the bystander). Comparing the three Slayers, Miller argues only Buffy attains moral autonomy: Kendra's unquestioning obedience and Faith's hyper-individualistic action-hero isolation both fail, while Buffy's 'I like to think of it as graduation' break from the Watchers' Council shows autonomy achieved within, not against, relationships.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 28 "Buffy Should’ve Killed Ben" — Jacob Held pits retributivism against utilitarian theories of punishment using three Buffyverse cases: vengeance demons Anya and Halfrek show that 'just desert' is arbitrary, relative, and subjective; Angel's gypsy curse (punishment as desert) secures society less reliably than Spike's Initiative chip (pure deterrence), while Oz's preventive caging raises the problem of punishing the innocent. The hard case is 'The Gift': Buffy refuses to kill the innocent Ben, but Held sides with Giles, who strangles him — arguing that since the state's end is security and freedom, one life may rightly be traded for six billion.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 11 "The Obligation to Play Baseball" — Horan and Solomon examine the 2001-02 contraction fight in which Judge Harry Crump ordered the Minnesota Twins to honor their Metrodome lease and play the 2002 season. They argue the Minnesota courts smuggled Bentham-Mill utilitarian reasoning about the public good into contract law, which normally awards only money damages, because baseball's antitrust exemption (from Justice Holmes's 1922 ruling through Justice Blackmun's 1972 opinion) had always treated the game as more than a business. Having long profited from special treatment, the owners lost when Bud Selig's plan to eliminate the Twins collided with the same 'greatest good for the greatest number' logic.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 37 "19b" — A paired debate on whether Pete Rose belongs in the Hall of Fame despite his lifetime ban for betting on the Reds, framed by retributive versus utilitarian theories of punishment. Aeon Skoble argues yes: betting on one's own team to win commits no fraud like throwing games, and Cooperstown honors baseball excellence, not moral perfection — the Hall already enshrines racists, adulterers, and cheats. Mark Hamilton answers no with the Dowd Report's evidence, Rule 21(d), and Giamatti's banishment statement: a managing gambler may sacrifice the season to settle tonight's debt, and reinstatement without remorse would declare the game's rules toothless.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 22 "The Dangers of Hedonism" — Sander Lee reads A Midsummer Night's Sex Comedy as Allen's warning against hedonism, tracing that ethos to empiricist thought from Hobbes and Locke through Bentham's utilitarianism to American pragmatism, embodied in Leopold Sturgis, an Ayer-style positivist philosopher who denies everything unprovable yet dies of passion with Dulcy and is deified by Andrew's spirit ball as pagan 'pure essence'. Using Sartre's Nausea, the chapter shows Andrew and Ariel's attempt to recreate their lost 'perfect moment' by the brook failing on every count, proving such moments inauthentic fantasies that ignore freedom, responsibility, and the passage of time. Through Bazin's Nietzschean reading of Renoir (Apollonian order versus Dionysian impulse), it argues that unlike Isaac Davis in Manhattan, the film's characters end more committed to hedonism than they began, with no character left qualified to condemn it.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 60 "The Sorting Hat Speaks Division and Divisiveness" — This section argues that patriotism violates the principle of equal moral worth shared by utilitarians and Kantians alike: Bentham's 'each to count for one, and none for more than one' means the Minister of Magic's pain counts no more than a house-elf's, while Kant's formula forbids treating anyone (Muggle or wizard) merely as a means. It reads Death Eater pureblood ideology as ordinary racism and sexism, cites Potterwatch's 'every human life is worth the same, and worth saving' and Hermione's S.P.E.W. campaign against 'slave labor,' and asks how preferring countrymen over foreigners differs from preferring people of one's race or gender, since neither is something a person controls.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 32 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Anna Lännström runs a full moral-responsibility audit on Gibson's tormented, remorseful Judas: Aristotle's analysis of excusing conditions (insanity, Satanic possession, ignorance) partly alleviates his guilt as it does Peter's denial; Boethius's timelessly eternal God is deployed against the foreknowledge problem and then criticized as self-defeating; and the Edwards/Frankfurt compatibilist solution is applied — Judas could not have done otherwise because God would not have permitted it, yet acted freely since he did what he wanted. Consequentialism (Mill) oddly makes the betrayal nearly harmless or even salvific, Kantian intention-analysis turns on whether Judas was a greedy embezzler or a Zealot trying to force a revolt, and virtue ethics weighs his immediate remorse and attempt to return the silver against the habitual greed John and Matthew attribute to him.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 33 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Bassham and Bagget observe that amid the film's unscriptural brutality Jesus never resists — he stops Peter's sword, heals Malchus's ear, and climbs back up for a second scourging — and ask whether this nonviolence can be rationally grounded without theological premises. They reject four classic readings of 'resist not evil' (Catholic counels-of-perfection, Schweitzer's interim ethics, Luther's penitential ethic, Tolstoy's absolute pacifism, noting Jesus himself used force against the money-changers) in favor of a hyperbole-plus-implicit-qualifier reading; then they show act utilitarianism licenses atrocities, rule utilitarianism at best yields an unpalatable absolute pacifism, and Kantian single-principle deontology preserves a right of self-defense Jesus's ethic calls us to lay aside — closing with a 'character model' of the Passion (duty vs freedom vs character) on which nonviolence is becoming the kind of person for whom violence is no longer an option, justified ultimately only by the cross.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 12 "“You Know . . . What They’re Up Against”" — Dees finds moral ambiguity lurking in Star Wars' black-and-white universe: Han Solo's Hobbesian ethical egoism ('I take orders from just one person - me') is shown to be coherent and gradually transformed by friendship with Luke and Leia into commitment to a cause. Lando's betrayal of Han on Bespin is defended as a straightforward Mill-Bentham utilitarian choice by a responsible official, weighed against Bernard Williams's Jim-and-the-commandant integrity objection, which the author rejects as moral vanity. Count Dooku's apparent idealism is exposed as evil's tool, and Anakin's massacre of the Sand People is condemned as non-ambiguous barbarity via Kant's formula of humanity (and Hume on reason's role with the passions), leaving only late Vader as genuinely morally ambiguous.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 27 "“Trust Your Feelings”" — Fader tackles the paradox that Jedi lie while Sith tell the truth: Obi-Wan's 'Darth Vader betrayed and murdered your father,' Yoda's trickster masquerade on Dagobah, the Council's cover-up of its waning powers, against Vader's brutal truth at Cloud City and Palpatine's technically honest 'I love democracy.' Kant's absolute prohibition of lying is set against the utilitarian's greatest-good lie and Nietzsche's claim that truth is the accepted set of social lies; Obi-Wan's deception is then defended through Plato's noble lie and the Buddha's Parable of the House on Fire, where 'expedients' to save the oblivious are no falsehood, while Vader and Dooku wield literal truths as weapons without compassion. Luke's answer is to stop accepting anyone's version and build his own green lightsaber: truth as perspective, intention, and finally the heart's understanding that redeems Anakin.
