- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 37 "Notes" — Asks who is morally worse by three standards-what each has done, is doing, and would do in the future subjunctive-and answers that Frank and Claire are far worse together, read symbolically as the US Constitution itself: Frank is the mercurial House, Claire the deliberate, more ambitious Senate, and Meechum the loyal military they seduce and underestimate at the republic's peril. Working from Plato's and Aristotle's claim that democracy declines into tyranny, Niebuhr's 'moral mediocrity' of nations, and the Welch-McCarthy 'have you no decency' moment, it asks whether a system that produced them is one 'we the people' deserve.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 14 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Andrew Shaffer imagines Capitol patrons at Caesar's Bar & Grill cheering the Quarter Quell bloodbath and asks what makes their enjoyment possible, answering with Schopenhauer's 'devilish' verdict on Schadenfreude as the mark of a worthless heart, Kant's calling it a 'diabolical' vice, and Nietzsche's account of another's misfortune as the social equalizer that appeases envy. He argues the spectators need dehumanization, from Effie's 'savages' rhetoric and the prep team's scrubbing to the wolf mutts wearing Glimmer's eyes, to enjoy innocent children dying, and that the star-crossed-lovers story humanizes the tributes enough to force the unprecedented double-victor rule change. The chapter closes by turning the diagnosis on us: readers thrill to the arena too, the whole trilogy arguably runs on Schadenfreude, and even Snow's execution is staged as a spectacle of righteous pleasure in a villain's death.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 17 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Abigail Mann argues that the Games only look like 'survival of the fittest': Darwinian natural selection runs on chance ('one slip in thousands') and explicitly rejects the social-Darwinist use of 'unfit' against the poor, while Darwin's Descent of Man explains the tributes' kindness through kin and group selection and an evolved moral sense, so Katniss's unhesitating volunteering for Prim is kin selection and Thresh's conflicted sparing of her shows conscience overriding self-preservation. She tests this against Kant, for whom only duty-motivated action is truly moral, which would make Thresh's inner struggle the more moral act and Katniss's instinctive sacrifice mere animal impulse, and against the egoism of Hobbes (giving to a beggar to relieve one's own distress) and Dawkins's selfish gene, answering with Hume and psychologist Daniel Batson that genuine altruism is real. Her coda: Katniss ultimately rejects Gale not only because his firebomb killed Prim but because it was engineered to trap and kill altruists, and her closing habit of listing 'every act of goodness' is the trilogy's verdict that simple kindness is not an illusion.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 15 "Does This Matter" — Garvin asks whether anything done in a dream can be right or wrong. He argues that in Inception's shared dreams ordinary ethics fully applies: the team really lies to Fischer (shared-dream communication is morally like waking communication), and the projections they mow down are, by a Turing-test-style argument, indistinguishable within the dream from persons — so either projections deserve rights or the dreamers can never know whom they are killing. For ordinary unshared dreams he engages Augustine's worry about nocturnal lust, concluding that mental acts like lust and lying are not excused by the dream state, though actions outside the dreamer's control are not blameworthy — dream wrongdoing being something to avoid repeating rather than to atone for.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 12 "The Guilt Never Goes Away" — Robichaud asks whether Iron Man can atone for Tony Stark's wrongs, using the Iron Monger's reprogrammed-suit example to distinguish causal from moral responsibility and to argue that omissions can be causes. Tony's negligence in running Stark Industries is blameworthy because his playboy ignorance was itself negligent (as with the Mandarin's willful ignorance), and via T. M. Scanlon's account of blame the families harmed by the illegal weapons sales are the ones most warranted in blaming him. Since 'I'm sorry' is not enough for wrongs this serious and Tony never submits to punishment, the chapter concludes that even his crusade as Iron Man to 'right the wrongs' — crushing Raza's group and collecting rogue weapons — may not yet warrant forgiveness.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 13 "The Hero’s Responsibility" — White defends Tony against blame for Captain America's assassination: spearheading registration in Civil War was a tragic dilemma, and Tony took the least bad option because 'if not me, who?' — telling Cap's corpse he sacrificed their friendship to save lives. Cap's death traces through Crossbones, the mind-controlled Sharon Carter, Dr. Faustus, and the Red Skull, not any direct act of Tony's; without foreseeability or wrongdoing, the chain of 'might haves' does not add up to responsibility, just as pushing someone out of a truck's path does not make you liable for the manhole they fall into. The motivation-centered lens of Kantian deontology and Aristotelian virtue ethics supports Tony (he gave up status, friends, and Cap himself), and living with tragic choices, as he does facing the Hulk, is itself heroic.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 14 "Drying Out" — Novy weighs the choice model against the disease model of Tony's alcoholism in 'Demon in a Bottle.' Frankfurt's principle that a person is not responsible for what he did only because he could not have done otherwise — tested by an imagined Dr. Doom brain-worm that would force Tony to drink — plus Plato's Protagoras claim that no one willingly chooses evil set up the puzzle of akrasia at the bottom of the bottle. Causal determinism would excuse Tony as a marionette, yet Mike Martin defines alcoholism as disordered agency and Jeffrey Smith pictures free will as an organ that disease can compromise, leaving Tony responsible for the first drink but not for the binges; sobriety is 'the drink or the dream' chosen one day at a time.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 22 "Amazing and Inspiring" — White explains Tony's drinking as weakness of will: Davidson's denial that akrasia is possible (Black Widow skipping Fury's spying order for a visit to Stark would have to have revised her judgment) is set against Searle's 'gaps,' where a person freely chooses against her all-things-considered judgment and nothing fills the gap. Frankfurt's wanton and second-order desires sharpen the picture — Tony wants a drink but does not want to want it, unlike the unreflective heroin addict — and volitionists like Wallace and Holton (the will as a muscle that Stane's orchestrated disasters exhaust) explain both his lapses and his daily resistance. If Searle is right, Tony's struggle with the bottle is not a defect of rationality but proof of it: akrasia is a symptom of freedom, which is what makes Iron Man amazing and inspiring.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 10 "NOTES" — Pierce argues that Lost's time travel runs on a fixed-time model in which nothing that happened can be undone, so the live question is ethical: Kate insists saving young Ben is still obligatory and Sayid remains responsible for shooting him, while Jack's plan to detonate Jughead at the Swan shows that trying to change the past can cause the very evil it targets, the Incident. Using Carneades' distinction between truth and necessity - future-tense truths made true by our own free choices - he shows that 'whatever happened, happened' does not abolish moral responsibility, applying the point to the Man in Black's causal-loop manipulation of Locke, Richard, and Ben. Desmond's consciousness travel in 'The Constant' is treated as the exception requiring hyper-time or alternate realities, and Pierce concludes that morality in time travel is simply ordinary morality, with Kate offering the most balanced view of the characters' choices.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 21 "Nonetheless, Don Can Be a Real Heel" — Terjesen asks whether Don is a good man, testing his mixed record (egalitarian instincts, loyalty to Mohawk Airlines, protecting Horace Jr., against habitual adultery and the stolen identity) through Aristotle's habituation, Plato's Protagoras unity-of-virtues theses, Hume's sensible knave, and John Doris's situationist attack on global character traits. The unity theses imply Don's vices undermine his virtues (affairs make him unavailable when Betty crashes; evasions about his past block honesty), and Doris's dime-in-the-payphone literature suggests even Don's reliability may be circumstance-bound, as with Pete's weddings-and-vacations-only philandering. Against full situationism, Don's consistent rules (never forcing women, valuing women he genuinely finds interesting) point to 'regional' traits, yet Roger's verdict stands: 'You're no good with relationships because you don't value them,' since Don runs family on a business code, from Adam's bribe to 'that's what people do' consolation for Pete.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 10 "The Office and Philosophy" — Argues that the standard trio of moral failure - malice (Creed ogling Pam, Andy sabotaging Dwight with the toll-receipt trick), weakness of will (Jan returning to Michael, Meredith relapsing with alcohol), and ignorance (Pam trading away Jim's teapot in 'Christmas Party') - misses a fourth category: moral blindness, embodied by Michael Scott, who can recite moral rules but cannot see when they apply (his Martin Luther King name tag on Diversity Day, defending Phyllis from Todd Packer with a harassing kiss, the fake-firing prank on Pam). Against Plato's view that all wrongdoing is ignorance, the chapter claims knowledge of rules neither helps nor harms decency; what matters is moral perception - seeing what a situation requires - shown by Jim getting Dwight to the hospital and rescuing the Dundies, Pam protecting the Dwight-Angela secret, and Toby patiently answering Dwight's anatomy questions.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 12 "The Office and Philosophy" — Asks whether Michael can (not will) ever learn empathy, distinguishing cognitive empathy - explained via Russell's argument-by-analogy account of other minds, which Michael manages only with people like himself, hence his sales success in 'The Client' - from affective empathy, which he lacks (Kevin's possible skin cancer is 'terrible news for both of us'; he cannot read Phyllis's oven mitt in Yankee Swap). Traces his cluelessness to egocentrism, and following Hume and Smith's sentimentalist account of morals - decentring the ego toward the impartial spectator via emotional contagion - argues his only hope is a real friendship (Jim's) that could drag him outside himself, since sycophantic Dwight and one-sided Todd Packer never will.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 13 "The Office and Philosophy" — Reads Tim Canterbury of the UK Wernham-Hogg as an autonomous moral agent who nonetheless cannot act on his own judgments: Kant's categorical imperative is applied to Tim's stapler-through-the-window prank (universalizing the maxim of disposing of disputed objects passes the test, so Tim is in the clear), before the chapter diagnoses the office's pointlessness with Durkheim, Fromm and Merton's notion of anomie - David Brent's management produces moral lawlessness and boredom. Tim's dice speech, his swallowed resignation and accepted promotion, and his last-second failed dash to Dawn in the finale show a weak-willed conscience: he knows what he should do but lacks the conviction, making him the moral conscience of the show without being its moral hero.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 19 "The Office and Philosophy" — Against Hobbes's view that laughter expresses superiority and Bergson's that comedy humiliates the socially disruptive into conformity, argues that viewers of The Office feel humiliation 'by proxy': Michael Scott is immune to humiliation because his narcissism blocks the minimal condition for feeling it - recognizing he could do wrong (Prison Mike, his MLK name tag while stereotyping Kelly, reneging on the pledge to Oscar's nephew, Carol's rejection at Diwali). We blush, look away, and feel his shame in his place, which transforms neither Michael nor us but reaffirms our own decency, compassion, and grip on values like self-awareness - and the chapter answers the worry that this merely endorses 'Hollywood' values by noting the standards Michael violates (moral sight, honesty with oneself) cross value systems.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 17 "And in the End" — Irwin and addictions specialist Lombardo ask where comic inspiration comes from, using Socrates' discovery that poets do not know the meaning of their own work, Hume's account of creativity as recombining materials of experience, and Nietzsche's point that inspiration is really continuous production sifted by judgment, to explain why Belushi and Farley treated cocaine and alcohol as muses. They contrast Belushi's fatal 'I use drugs' hubris, which no one around him challenged, with Farley's genuine twelve-step recovery, three sober years, and relapses. Stuart Smalley's affirmations, which bullshit himself into feeling 'good enough,' spoof recovery culture's cliches while Farley's story shows what actual recovery demands, ending with the advice to look elsewhere for the muse.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 33 "Where Do We Go from Here – Buh‐Bye!" — Southworth asks whether SNL's dumb characters, the Ladies Man, Celebrity Jeopardy's Burt Reynolds, Ferrell's Bush, can be too stupid for moral responsibility. Aristotle's capacity for decision grounds moral agency; the Merit View, sharpened by Williams's constitutive moral luck and the Control Principle, blames Ferrell's deliberately nasty Connery but not the hapless Reynolds; and Mill's consequentialist view of praise and blame as nudges for 'progressive beings' explains Stuart Smalley's affirmations and Gilly's scoldings. Strawson's reactive attitudes finally resolve the puzzle: pitiable Bush is no proper target of blame, which is why we love him, though making him so lovable may have helped the real Bush escape accountability.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 15 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Tallon uses the problem of moral luck (Williams and Nagel) to ask how blameworthy Peter really is for Uncle Ben's death: the Peter who let the thief go and the counterfactual Peter whose thief was caught at the elevator act identically, yet outcome luck makes the first feel like a murderer, clashing with Kant's Control Principle that only the good will has moral worth. Drawing on Williams's 'agent regret' and Susan Wolf's 'nameless virtue' of taking responsibility for consequences, the chapter separates culpability — Peter is guilty only of letting a thief go, with the intervening agency of the criminal breaking the causal chain — from responsibility for damage. Aunt May's own misguided confession that she caused Ben's death by arguing with him (Amazing Spider-Man #479) shows how virtuous people confuse involvement in a causal chain with guilt.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 29 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — White examines the fan fury over 'One More Day,' in which Peter and MJ trade their marriage to Mephisto to save Aunt May's life. Virtue ethics evaluates people by stable character traits, but situationist psychology (the pay-phone coin experiments, Doris's Lack of Character) argues behavior tracks trivial situational details, not traits — while fictional characters like Captain America and Peter Parker are written with simpler, firmer traits, so making a deal with the devil reads as glaringly out of character and betrays the audience's trust. Since the true agents were editor Joe Quesada and the writers, White asks whether creators owe fans fidelity to a character's established identity, and closes by arguing that even if real character is situational, integrity — being the same person across situations — remains a virtue worth aspiring to, including toward ourselves.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 10 "Notes" — Tim Challans treats Kirk, Picard, Archer, and Janeway as case studies in moral psychology, with the captain as Plato's charioteer balancing the horses of Spock's logic and McCoy's feeling. He reads Picard's 'there are four lights' coercion in 'Chain of Command' and his Locutus guilt in 'Family' through Rawls's shame/guilt distinction and Nancy Sherman's 'moral injury', while Kirk's 'I need my pain' refusal of Sybok and Archer's Xindi-era regrets show commanders owning guilt, regret, and remorse. Drawing on Nussbaum's 'upheavals of thought' and Hume's passions, he argues that a rare, well-integrated moral psychology—pride tempered by humility, as Q's lesson in 'Tapestry' demonstrates—is what qualifies the one-in-a-million starship captain.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Malloy argues loyalty's moral value is exaggerated, asking what loyalty is via Royce's cause-loyalty, Fletcher's historical self, and Keller's thin motive theory, applied to Leia torn between Alderaan and the Alliance and to Luke's emotional flight from Dagobah. The Sith embody a paradox: under the Rule of Two a loyal Sith must betray, so Vader's final turn on Palpatine was loyalty to Luke and thus betrayal of the Sith itself, while stormtrooper-style loyalty shows devotion is only as good as its object. Betrayal wrongs because it irreversibly alters a relationship - which is why Lando's Bespin gamble was right - and loyalty's real value is the commitment, dedication, and selflessness behind it.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 18 "Do Not Ask Him to Be Rational" — The Rochas argue the Jedi Council's conduct across the Temple-bombing arc — letting Tarkin take jurisdiction, then expelling Ahsoka and handing her over for trial on flimsy evidence in 'The Wrong Jedi' — exposes a Jedi ethics corrupted by deference to hierarchy. Ahsoka's decision to walk away enacts Kantian moral autonomy (self-legislation) against the Council's heteronomy, while Anakin, despite sharing her doubts, seeks another master in Palpatine and falls into heteronomy instead. Using Baier's account of trust and Iris Marion Young on social roles, they contend the Jedi's repudiation of feeling was the real failure: emotions like Ahsoka's fear rightly guided her to distrust the Council and even to trust Ventress.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 35 "“So, What Happens If You Take That Thing Off ”" — Ebner charts Din Djarin's moral development from a rights-based frame - hierarchy, Guild rules, 'I can bring you in warm, or I can bring you in cold' - to Carol Gilligan's ethics of care, a shift catalyzed by Kuiil's lessons ('You can trade', 'I have spoken') and completed by the Child. He re-reads Gilligan's pharmacy dilemma through 'The Sin', where Mando hijacks a speeder droid at gunpoint, and 'The Marshal', where trading with Cobb Vanth recasts the armor dispute as responsibility toward a threatened town rather than a contest of rights. Djarin's helmet decisions - refusing Omera, unmasking for Mayfeld's facial scan, and finally removing the helmet to say goodbye to Grogu - track his metamorphosis from rules and entitlements to responsibilities and relationships.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 37 "24. The Fifty-Third Card" — Written in the Joker's voice, it plays the fifty-third card no other contributor considered: maybe both 'heroes' are the villains—Superman's public saves are attention-seeking ego when he could help unseen, and Batman selfishly pours billions into Bat-toys instead of donating it to save millions of dying children. Its deeper target is our hypocrisy: the Dark Knight ferry scene is unbelievable because in reality we would climb over each other to push the button, since we are only as moral as our circumstances allow while buying sweatshop chocolate and bacon and calling ourselves good. The genuine 'super-man' would drop the pretense of morality altogether, live by his own lights before dancing with the devil, and laugh as the world burns.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 8 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Nathan Stout uses P.F. Strawson's account of moral responsibility through 'reactive attitudes' to ask when Sam and Dean are justified in killing what they hunt. Monsters sort into three groups: low-functioning animal killers like the wendigo and 'Heart''s werewolf Madison, intelligent but conscienceless 'antisocial' monsters like demons and leviathans, and 'moral monsters' like the cow-blood-drinking vampires of 'Bloodlust' and the kitsune Amy from 'The Girl Next Door,' who can understand and be motivated by moral reasons. Because Group 3 monsters are members of the moral community, Dean's 'if it's supernatural, we kill it' bigotry and his secret killing of Amy make the supposedly good hunters morally suspect, since killing a fellow member of the moral community ought to weigh on them.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 10 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Shannon Ford reconstructs the Winchesters' ethics of killing: self-defense and defense of others justify lethal force, as when Sam kills Jeremy in 'Dream a Little Dream of Me' and Andy shoots Ansem to save Dean in 'Simon Said,' while Dean's refusal of Ruby's virgin-sacrifice spell in 'Jus in Bello' and sparing the disarmed Pa Bender mark lines they will not cross even when the math favors killing. Killing possessed innocents like Meg is treated as permissible only under necessity and with regret. The chapter then argues that once the brothers hunt to banish all demons from the world, their conflict is war rather than hunting, so just war theory (jus ad bellum and jus in bello) might license killings ordinary morality forbids, a slippage dramatized by Gordon's enjoyment of killing and Dean's unjustifiable killing of Amy.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 31 "Notes" — Mills asks why Nate is more hurt than relieved when Roy declines to headbutt him over kissing Keeley, while Jamie had to fight for forgiveness. Using Strawson's reactive attitudes - anger is how we take someone seriously as a member of the moral community - plus Nussbaum's Anger and Forgiveness and Radzik's transactional account of amends, she argues Roy's instant absolution dismisses Nate as a pitiable non-agent rather than a culpable moral equal. The chapter contrasts this with earned, transactional forgiveness across Season 3 (Nate apologizing to Will and Ted, Beard's own story of betrayal and forgiveness), showing the headbutt as the recognition Nate needed.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 32 "Notes" — Baggett asks whether Rupert is beyond the grace the show extends to everyone else. She surveys theories of forgiveness - Butler's change of emotion, treatment and performative accounts, and Stump's Aquinas-based framework grounding forgiveness in the love that desires another's good and union, separable from reconciliation - then applies Aristotle's corrupted bad person whose vice 'makes moral truths invisible' as Rupert's limit case. Ted's darts-based tough love is contrasted with Sassy's vengeful certainty and Deborah's cheap grace, and the chapter leaves Rupert's turnaround possible but entirely his choice, while his choices have already been making him.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 15 "Notes" — Confronts a puzzle in Rust's naturalism: he dismisses the occult, yet talks freely of monsters and evil, concepts often thought irredeemably supernatural. The chapter distinguishes natural from supernatural senses of 'monster' (Aristotle's explicable hybrids versus Carroll's order-violating beings) to argue Errol Childress is a monster consistent with naturalism, then defends a 'modest proposal' — the evil person just is the morally worst sort of person, whose vices are extreme in both intensity and object. Betty's line that Childress is 'worse than anybody' and his extreme cruelty and callousness fit this account, teaching that recognizing creatures like us can be evil, not positing inhuman monsters, is the first step to combating evil.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 13 "“Haven’t Thought of You Lately at All”" — George Dunn uses Dr. Kinny's mock-prison experiment at Hearst — where 'cool guy' Rafe torments Horshack, even gentle Wallace turns taunting guard, and Mercer perhaps first bonded with his future victim Moe — as a rerun of Zimbardo's Stanford prison experiment, arguing that bad situations and corrupting power, not just bad apples, produce Neptune's villains. Against pure situationism he sets Hannah Arendt's diagnosis that great evil usually requires not wicked hearts but an 'inability to think': Woody Goodman's rehearsed excuses about neglected boys and Mercer's 'I'm just taking what you would have happily given' show wrongdoers rationalizing rather than reflecting. The chapter ends by suggesting the town's gulf between 09-ers and everyone else may be the situational 'apple barrel' breeding the arrogance, entitlement, resentment, and envy behind Neptune's crime wave.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 17 "“Do You Not Instinctively Fear Me ”" — George Dunn weighs Veronica's creed that 'someone's always supposed to pay' — Carrie Bishop destroying Mr. Rooks for her friend, Logan getting himself jailed to beat Mercer, Veronica forfeiting the Kane Scholarship to watch Aaron Echolls convicted — against the case against vengeance running from Socrates' 'one must never do wrong in return' through Seneca's claim that the angry are insane and Plato's subordination of thumos to reason, with the ultimatum game showing people pay to punish even at their own expense. Nietzsche's creditor-debtor account explains the payoff: punishing the offender restores the status and self-esteem that humiliation stole, turning passive grief into an active grievance like Madison's crushed-and-cubed Mercedes. Yet Machiavelli's 'much safer to be feared than loved' finally vindicates a measure of payback, since Veronica's threats are how a disgraced outsider demands the respect fickle Neptune withholds from Meg.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 14 "Fifth Hole How Golf Builds and Shapes Moral Character" — Beller and Stoll ask why empirical moral-reasoning research finds that sport generally does not build character, yet golfers score highest of all athletes. Using Aristotle's account of right conduct and Lickona's triad of moral knowing, feeling, and acting, they argue character forms through role models, social environment, and cognitive dissonance, supported by neuroplasticity research on the brain's capacity for moral growth. They contrast golf's self-policing tradition (Bobby Jones, Meg Mallon, Greg Norman, the film Bagger Vance) with the gamesmanship coached in team sports, and address Gilligan's 'different voice' by reporting that female golfers reason at least as highly as males, concluding that golf's honor-bound moral community sets it apart.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 17 "Seventh Hole Cheating and Gamesmanship among Amateur and Professional Golfers" — Lumpkin argues that amateur golfers routinely cheat while professionals do not, and dissects four rationalizations amateurs use: appeal to ignorance, appeal to popularity, appeal to tradition (Callahan's 'cheating culture'), and the belief that 'no one will ever know' — a golf-course version of Plato's Ring of Gyges where invisibility dissolves restraint. Drawing on Kohlberg's stages of moral development, she claims professionals reason at higher levels because officials, peers, and disqualification (e.g., J. P. Hayes) enforce the sport's social contract, whereas amateurs face no punishment. She concludes casual golfers would do better not to keep score than to keep a 'mythical' one, earning the right to score only once they follow the rules.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 14 "Excuses, Excuses Inside the Mind of a Complainer" — Kevin Kinghorn, drawing on interviews with coach Brad Gilbert, dissects why tennis players and their parents complain and make excuses. He catalogs cognitive biases and the vividness effect (why a bad call, like McEnroe's 'You cannot be serious!' outburst, sticks and feels like persecution) as forms of irrationality, and notes Stoicism (which he attributes to Zeno) as a philosophy that would suppress the complaining temperament. His central mechanism is Freudian self-deception: citing Freud's hypnotized-umbrella subject who invents a reason for his own behavior, he argues tennis parents pretend their child is destined for greatness and then genuinely come to believe the lie, so excuse-making becomes a self-destructive sign a player will never be a champion. He also reads Andrea Jaeger's ambivalence about winning as evidence of mixed, partly unconscious motivations.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Couch reads two Eastwood gestures — Josey Wales's spitting and the Man with No Name's smiling — as expressions of self-reliance that generate a 'motivational polarity,' simultaneously repelling and attracting others. Drawing on Miller and Mason on contempt and disgust as moral attitudes, and on evolutionary coalitional psychology, he argues Wales's 'contemptuous disgust' (spitting on dead bounty hunters, at the Comancheros) marks moral boundaries and forms surrogate-family coalitions, while the Man with No Name's deceptive non-Duchenne smile in the Dollars trilogy conceals lethal intent yet occasionally shows genuine compassion (freeing Tuco). The self-reliant individual, adhering to his own moral compass, inevitably divides others into allies and foes.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Karen Hoffman traces the gun across Eastwood's career as an evolving argument about violence: Dirty Harry's .44 Magnum ends violence without cost to the shooter, High Plains Drifter and Pale Rider treat the gun as righteous retribution and a proof of masculine honor, but Unforgiven shows William Munny killing men who may not deserve it and dwelling on how killing brutalizes the shooter. In Gran Torino Walt Kowalski finally gives up the gun entirely, walking unarmed into Spider's gang and being gunned down in a Christlike pose so that Thao is spared both victimhood and the guilt of killing. The chapter argues Eastwood shifts from celebrating the gun as physical protection to warning of the psychological damage violence inflicts on its user.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 14 "“And It’s Such a Beautiful Day!” shame and Fargo" — Hanrahan and Stearns read Fargo through Aristotle's theory of shame and its link to friendship, sorting the characters into his moral hierarchy: Gaear is the shameless self-indulgent man, Jerry is the morally incontinent one whose flickers of shame (before Scotty, before the swindled customer) stay inert against his greed, and Marge is the exemplar of excellence. They argue that a capacity for shame requires valuing others non-instrumentally, which the co-conspirators cannot do because they relate only through friendships of utility (Carl and the prostitute, Jerry using his son). Marge's friendship-of-the-good with Norm grounds both her decency and her ability to mediate others' shame, and her 'it's such a beautiful day' expresses the same noninstrumental valuing that makes moral concern possible.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 14 "Deception and Disorder Unraveling Cronenberg's Divided Minds" — Simon Riches traces Cronenberg's shift from bodily 'body horror' madness to psychological unraveling, focusing on Tom Stall's oscillation between Tom and Joey in A History of Violence. He treats self-deception via Davidson's 'divided minds' and Dennett's narrative-self view of multiple personality, situates hallucination (Spider, Videodrome) between Cartesian deception and psychosis, and uses Foucault, Kuhn, Szasz, and social constructionism to argue the category of mental disorder is socially contingent, so the line between self-deception and delusion (and mental order and disorder) is unclear.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 15 "Psychological Determinism in the Films of David Cronenberg" — Daniel Shaw argues Cronenberg's oeuvre embodies psychological determinism (in Skinner's and Freudian terms), reading Dead Ringers as his masterpiece: Beverly Mantle's drug-fueled disintegration and murder of Elliot flow from an ambivalence and symbiotic bond he cannot escape, analyzed through Freud's Little Hans conflict of ambivalence and dream-as-wish. Surveying Shivers, The Brood, The Fly, and Crash as portraits of characters helplessly driven by parasites, disease, instinct, or trauma, he holds Eastern Promises (with its in-control hero Nikolai) is the pointed exception that proves Cronenberg's pessimistic determinist rule.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 28 "15. The Evil in These Woods" — Rose-Barry surveys how Twin Peaks conceives evil—as Augustine's privation of good, as the Manichean clash of White and Black Lodges, and as Ricoeur's defilement (the sooty Woodsmen, BOB entering hosts)—then uses Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics distinction of vice, incontinence, and bestiality to argue Windom Earle is a better example of an evil person than BOB. Because BOB is all appetite ('I don't need—I want'), a beast lacking reason, he is like Aristotle's bestial man whose best part is merely absent; the vicious, rational Earle, who relishes wickedness and invents ever-crueler torments, has the worse condition of character—and evil, being human, can be fought.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Skoble examines evil in Manhunter through the film's Nietzsche epigraph—'whoever fights monsters should see to it that in the process he does not become a monster'—as profiler Will Graham must 'become' Lecktor and Dollarhyde to catch them, risking his own psyche. Lecktor's claim that killing feels good because doing 'what God does' makes one godlike frames the killers' evil as a will to power. Skoble invokes the Socratic dictum that to know the good is to do the good, asking whether Dollarhyde's murderous 'becoming the Red Dragon' is a large-scale delusion, and warns that truly seeing the killer's fantasy risks adopting it.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Berger uses Harold Becker's The Onion Field to challenge Kant's moral idealism. Kant held that any rational being can deduce categorical imperatives and that conscience necessarily convicts the guilty and vindicates the innocent. Yet the killers Powell and Smith feel no guilt for murdering Kant-admiring cop Ian Campbell (Smith calls guilt a trick 'rich white guys dreamed up'), while the innocent, blameless Hettinger is destroyed by shame, thievery, and near-suicide. Berger weighs Schopenhauer's 'evil genius' objection and the sociopathy explanation, concluding Hettinger's guilt is a doomed attempt to preserve moral meaning.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 14 "Passionate Objectivity in Sherlock Holmes" — Taliaferro and Le Gall pose the ethical clash between impartial detachment and partial loyalty, situating Holmes between Simon Keller (loyalty as a threat to being a 'good believer,' echoed by Holmes's 'Sign of Four' rejection of emotion) and Bernard Williams and Susan Wolf (who defend priority for loved ones—Williams's 'one thought too many'). Using Watson's shooting in 'The Three Garridebs,' Holmes's weaning off drugs, and 'perverted love' in the Sussex Vampire and Thor Bridge cases, they argue loyalty rightly understood as seeking the friend's good aids clear reasoning, and that Holmes exhibits a 'passionate objectivity' in which some acquaintance with passion is essential to being genuinely objective.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 15 "The Industrious Sherlock Holmes" — Bassham diagnoses Holmes as a workaholic against clinical criteria (obsessive work, few relationships, perfectionism, health neglect through fasting and cocaine), then traces the rise of the Protestant work ethic (Calvin, Weber, Carlyle) and its modern decline. Drawing on Thoreau's Walden critique of 'lives of quiet desperation,' Pieper on leisure, and the 'affluenza' literature, he distinguishes pathological from benign workaholism by warning signs and by motivation. He concludes Holmes is a pathological workaholic in his symptoms but redeemed by his noble, non-materialistic motive of fighting crime and achieving justice.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 40 "Bunker Mentality or Love" — Robin Bunce recovers how Terry Nation's original 1963 'The Daleks' encodes evil, reading the script in its Cold War, post-Cuban-Missile-Crisis context. He argues Nation dehumanizes the Daleks not by making them less rational but MORE rational: they embody the unfeeling reason of the neutron bomb that destroyed Skaro, having lost individuality, laughter, and the capacity to feel. Drawing on Richard Rorty's claim that our humanity lies in feeling for one another rather than in reason (and on Wells's Morlocks), he concludes the Daleks are the dreaded post-nuclear human future, and Ian teaches the Thals that love and empathy, not abstract moralizing, resist evil.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 11 "3. Why Do I Have to Be Some Kind of Hero" — Zanin reads the Winchesters' sense of moral responsibility through Dostoevsky's The Karamazov Brothers, mapping Dean onto the sensualist/atheist Dmitri-Ivan and Sam onto the faithful Alyosha. Via Father Zossima's dictum that we are 'responsible to all for all,' she argues Sam and Dean's brotherhood is Christian self-sacrificial 'love in action'—shown in Dean choosing Sam over a normal life in 'Bad Boys' and the djinn world—which grounds why they keep saving strangers even after rejecting God's plan.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 18 "8. Which Brother Is the Good One" — Browning contrasts the brothers' ethics: Dean is a consequentialist who judges hunts by outcomes ('the ends justify the means,' killing werewolf Madison or faith-healer Roy for the greater good), while Sam is a deontologist who treats lying, stealing, and killing as wrong in themselves. Tracking episodes like 'Bloodlust,' 'Croatoan,' and 'Fresh Blood,' he argues the murder-versus-kill distinction and the blurring line between human and monster show Dean's darker consequentialism is better suited to the Hunter's war, though both are driven to do good.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 21 "11. Why Sacrifice Yourself" — Browning interrogates the nobility of the Winchesters' repeated self-sacrifice, asking whether their deals (Dean's soul for Sam, John's soul for Dean) are selfless or selfish—driven by codependency, fear of being alone, and ego. He weighs utilitarian justification (sacrificing one who saves the world) against the trickster's 'Mystery Spot' lesson that 'nothing good comes' of it, and invokes Kant's notion of a true gift expecting nothing in return, alongside Milbank on life-as-gift, to question whether self-sacrifice is the 'ultimate ethical agent' when death isn't final.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 8 "1. Scamming for Fun" — Clipsham distinguishes Jimmy and Kim's 'scamming for fun' (deceiving Ken over rare tequila in 'Switch', or a montage of pointless cons in 'Marco') from the 'scheming for benefits' of Mike, Gus, and Chuck, who lie only to secure a specific end. Using Kant's prohibition on treating people merely as means, he argues that scheming for a benefit is more disrespectful than scamming for its own sake, because the latter treats a mark as an unwitting player in a game rather than a tool. He also rejects the worry that fun-scamming corrupts character, noting Jimmy was already dishonest and that Gus and Lalo's worst vices have no root in playful deception.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 9 "2. Don’t Go to Lawyers for Moral Guidance" — Ralston reads Jimmy McGill's slide into Saul Goodman as a study in moral decline, using Dewey's (and Bourdieu's) theory of habit to explain why a person capable of right action repeatedly chooses the wrong path—the pressures of criminal clients, Chuck's contempt, and HHM's rejection wear down his will as an ingrained disposition. He contrasts Kant's categorical imperative with mere 'imperatives of prudence' (rules of thumb for achieving any end), arguing Jimmy consistently follows the latter, as when he unhinges Chuck at the disbarment hearing to win. Invoking Hart's separability of law and morality and Singer on the ethicist's training, he concludes lawyers like Saul make poor moral guides.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 20 "11. The Self-Deception Road" — Doll analyzes self-deception across the series using Gregg Ten Elshof's four mechanisms—attention management, procrastination, perspective shifting, and rationalization. Chuck's electromagnetic hypersensitivity is a real psychological condition about which he deceives himself as to its physical cause, reinforced by everyone accommodating him; his refusal to see Jimmy as anything but 'Slippin' Jimmy' is rationalized as protecting others while sabotaging his brother. Jimmy, via perspective-shifting through Chuck's eyes, comes to believe he can only be Slippin' Jimmy, then rationalizes the Saul persona. Drawing on Joseph Butler and Adam Smith, Doll argues self-deception blinds moral judgment and is ultimately Saul's undoing, leaving him alone in hiding.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 24 "14. Salvaging Sunk Costs" — Using Jimmy's wish to quit law despite years of study, and Kim's objection, the chapter examines whether the 'sunk cost fallacy' is always a fallacy. It grants that unrecoverable past investments are irrelevant to a narrow cost-benefit goal, but argues via Nozick's opera-ticket case and Thomas Kelly that reflecting on sunk costs can be rational for habit formation, regret avoidance, and signaling resolve to opponents (illustrated by Mesa Verde's land, Jimmy and Kim's office lease, and Jimmy re-scamming Irene). It concludes that a complex career choice legitimately weighs a wider range of psychological, social, and moral costs than the relentless gambler's simple case.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 29 "18. Dissenting Opinions" — Framing Kim and Jimmy's clashes as a problem in the epistemology of peer disagreement, the chapter asks whether learning an epistemic peer disagrees should make you suspend judgment (the conciliatory view) or stay steadfast, using a tip-calculation dispute and their office-versus-practice compromise. It argues moral disagreements differ because we rarely count someone who disagrees on one moral question as a genuine peer, and rejects 'no fact of the matter' relativism for implying slavery could be permissible. It then reads Kim's arc, including 'Wouldn't I?', as her moral beliefs genuinely shifting toward Jimmy's, complicated by self-interested and self-deceiving reasons for holding beliefs.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 33 "21. Finding the Good in Nacho" — The chapter uses Kant to argue that Nacho Varga, though a genuinely bad drug dealer, can perform morally worthy acts in isolated moments. Because Kant locates morality in the rational will and intention rather than accomplishment, it treats Nacho's attempts on the Salamancas and his desire to leave the game as evidence of active moral reasoning, while conceding his motives are muddied by self-interest and love for his father (the shopkeeper example warns against acts done for loved ones). Its clean case is the phone call in 'Something Unforgivable,' where Nacho risks everything to plead for Lalo's near-innocent staff, doing the right thing purely because it is right.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 34 "22. Breaking Bad Promises" — The first half of this chapter lays out the moral paradox of 'bad' promises through Better Call Saul: Jimmy's payment to the Lindholm twins for the staged accident, the Kettlemans' bribe for silence, Nacho and Mike's hit contract on Tuco, Gus and Mike's criminal alliance, and Jimmy and Ira's Hummel heist. It stresses Mike's code ('if you make a deal, you keep your word') and his refund to Nacho when the hit fails, then builds a taxonomy of illicit promises as legal or illegal crossed with moral or immoral, setting up the question of whether we may break promises that are wrongful.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 10 "NOTES" — Jeremy Pierce argues that Lost mostly assumes fixed (eternalist) time and moves from its metaphysics to its ethics: even if 'whatever happened, happened,' ordinary morality still applies, so Sayid's shooting young Ben is wrong regardless of his good intentions and Jack is responsible for detonating Jughead even though he causes the very Incident he meant to prevent. Invoking Carneades' distinction between truth and necessity, Pierce holds that foreknowledge (the Man in Black's manipulation, Desmond's course-corrected saving of Charlie) does not erase free choice, concluding via Kate that morality in time travel is 'simply morality, period.'
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 33 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Griffioen dissects Colbert's 'truthiness' as two forms of motivated epistemic irrationality—preferring what one wishes true (wishful thinking) and intuiting truth from the gut over facts (self-deception). Using a running example of Samantha Bee believing in Jason Jones's fidelity against the evidence, she rejects Freud-style divided-mind accounts (with their static and dynamic paradoxes) in favor of self-deception as an attention-directing process, and skewers Colbert's circular 'truthinessiness' (proving truthiness with more truthiness). She argues gut feelings only justify belief when they implicitly track relevant facts, proposing a fallacy of 'argumentum ad ventrem.'
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 31 "18. War Means Fighting and Fighting Includes Philosophizing" — Vuckovich analyzes 'Still Valley,' where Confederate Sergeant Paradine can win the Civil War using a witchcraft handbook that freezes Union troops but only by renouncing God. He reads Paradine's temptation through Glaucon's Ring of Gyges myth in Plato's Republic (the committed unjust man who outdoes enemies without scruple) and Aristotle's friendships of shared pleasure (Paradine and the witchman Teague bonded by hatred of the enemy). Paradine burns the handbook rather than damn the Confederacy, preserving a core principle of fairness even at the cost of an easy victory—winning isn't everything.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 21 "The Grinch’s Change of Heart Whodunit" — Cunningham asks whether the Grinch's sudden metanoia is a matter of head or heart, staging a debate between Kant and Hume. A Kantian reading treats the change as reason reasserting the moral law after the Grinch's inclinations (envy, resentment) hijacked it, so he realizes stealing Christmas disrespects the Whos as ends in themselves. A Humean reading, favored by the author given that the Grinch's 'small heart grew three sizes,' treats it as a new sentiment of sympathy rather than a rational apprehension, invoking Hume's claim that reason is the slave of the passions.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 16 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Potzsch reads Emma as an Aristotelian study of eudaimonia, arguing Emma's self-deception and the flattery of those around her block her from true happiness, which for Aristotle is activity of the soul in accordance with reason and virtue. She diagnoses Emma's cruelty to Miss Bates at Box Hill as Aristotelian akrasia (moral weakness): Emma knows better but is overpowered by the desire to shine, showing virtue has not yet become her second nature. She contrasts Emma and Mrs. Elton's pursuit of honor (which Aristotle deems superficial, illustrated via Plato's Euthyphro) with Knightley's genuine virtue, and closes on Aristotle's ranking of the contemplative over the political life.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 22 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Cantwell reads Emma through 'perfectionism' and parody, arguing that Cassandra and later readers turned Jane Austen into a 'picture of perfection' while Emma herself is a flawed paragon. Drawing on Andrew Miller's Burdens of Perfection, she treats moral improvement as socially constructed and responsive to exemplars, set against Highbury's upward mobility (the Westons, Coles, Martins destabilizing class lines). Emma's attempt to remake Harriet Smith in her own image is a parody of the gentlewoman (Bakhtin on parody) that exposes Emma's own vanity; the crisis of imagining Harriet marrying Knightley forces the self-knowledge that lets Emma finally pursue genuine, socially situated perfection.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 25 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Olson and Taliaferro examine the ethics of secrets in Austen, refining Sissela Bok's definition so that a secret conceals what convention would normally make public. They argue secrets in Austen are usually corrosive (Wickham and Lydia's elopement endangering the Bennets, Brandon's silence about Willoughby harming Marianne, Lucy Steele's engagement binding Elinor) yet can be virtuous, as when Darcy secretly funds Lydia's marriage to avoid self-aggrandizement. They propose an 'ideal observer' standpoint (an all-knowing, impartial, affective narrator) for judging when a secret is honorable, and argue the Emma-Miss Bates incident is not a failure to keep a secret but a genuine vice of contempt Austen condemns.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 8 "Introduction" — Alan Goldman's editorial introduction previews the volume's essays, framing Twain as a serious philosopher hidden behind humor and irony. It lays out the Huckleberry Finn debate over whether Huck's refusal to turn in Jim is weak-willed conscience versus reason-bearing sympathy (Bennett, Goldman, Fudge, Lyons, Gehrman), then Twain's late attacks on religion via Letters from the Earth and the problem of evil, plus essays on lying, animal rights, humor, and comparisons to Diogenes, the Epicureans, Nietzsche, and Hume. It treats these as genuine philosophical stakes drawn from Twain's fiction and late writings.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 10 "Chapter 1 The Conscience of Huckleberry Finn" — Jonathan Bennett reads the chapter 16 raft episode as a clash between 'bad morality' and sympathy: Huck's conscience (slave-owning principles telling him to return Jim to Miss Watson) supplies all the reasons, while his sympathy for Jim is a bare, reasonless feeling that wins by weakness of will, so Huck does right while believing he does wrong. He contrasts Huck with Himmler, whose bad morality overrode his surviving sympathy, and Jonathan Edwards, whose Calvinist approval of eternal damnation left no sympathy to conflict. The lesson is that principles should be kept open to revision under pressure from sympathy, since one cannot declare one's own morality bad but should stay open to correction.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 11 "Chapter 2 Huckleberry Finn and Moral Motivation" — Alan Goldman argues against Bennett and against Arpaly and Schroeder that Huck is not weak-willed or irrational: his sympathy for Jim is an intentional emotion containing implicit judgments and awareness of the genuine moral reasons to help Jim, so Huck acts on his strongest reasons and is courageous rather than akratic. Because Huck is rational yet not motivated by his explicit (corrupt) moral judgments, and his real motivation comes only through emotional attachment, Goldman concludes against Kant that moral motivation is not rationally required. He uses Huck's failure to extend concern to other slaves, and analogies to meat-eaters and arbitrary aesthetic taste, to show moral inconsistency is not practical irrationality.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 12 "Chapter 3 Sympathy, Principles, and Conscience" — Robert Fudge uses Adam Smith to reinterpret Huck's conscience and praiseworthiness. Against Bennett (conscience as accepted principles) and Arpaly-Schroeder (inverse akrasia via a whole-self theory), Fudge argues, following Smith, that conscience is the sentiment-based judgment of the 'man within the breast,' the impartial spectator, and that propriety rests on sympathetic 'feeling with' others rather than abstract principle. Huck's sympathy for Jim in the chapter 16 raft scene is a reason-bearing emotion, so he is not acting akratically or against his true conscience; instead he is growing morally, molding his conscience toward the loyalty and friendship that already constitute his core self.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 13 "Chapter 4 Huckleberry Finn’s Struggle between Sympathy and Moral Principle Reconsidered" — Michael Lyons defends the 'pedestal' of moral principles against Bennett's chapter 16 reading. He accepts that sympathy rightly saved Jim and that Edwards's principled cruelty and Himmler's suppressed sympathy show principles must be revisable, but rejects the stronger claim that sympathy should override conduct while leaving conflicting principles intact. Reconstructing Bennett's argument into 'stronger' and 'adjusted' versions, Lyons argues principles remain the best primary guide once corrected by sympathy, and that Twain shows Huck retaining a natural, humanity-grounded morality even after rejecting society's 'deformed conscience.' He prizes incorruptibility, sticking to correct principles, as the mark of the highest heroism Huck could aspire to.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 27 "Chapter 14 Moral Value and Moral Psychology in Twain’s “Carnival of Crime”" — Boardman treats Twain's 'The Facts Concerning the Recent Carnival of Crime in Connecticut'—in which a narrator kills his personified conscience (a shabby dwarf) and gleefully commits a spree of crimes—as staging an 'exasperating metaphysical question' about the value and psychology of morality. On a Nietzschean reading the narrator becomes an Overman revaluing values, seeing conscience as the internalized lie of slave morality; on a Humean reading conscience is moral feeling (not reason), so once it is destroyed the narrator can still reason about right yet has no motive to act morally, illustrating the oak-tree and willful-murder arguments that vice lies in sentiment, not relations or facts. Boardman concludes both interpretations fit yet neither settles whether Twain endorses or lampoons the result—our horror at the crimes is what makes the story funny.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 19 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Florell and Wilson, psychologists, survey parenting through the nature–nurture debate, casting Locke's tabula rasa against Rousseau's noble-savage view of children, alongside Piaget and Kohlberg on moral development and Walter Mischel's marshmallow experiment on impulse control. They map the four parenting styles (authoritarian, permissive, uninvolved, authoritative) on responsiveness and control, argue authoritative parenting is optimal, and advise fathers to adjust discipline to each child's innate temperament rather than enforce rigid gender roles.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 11 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Gary Jobson, writing from a long racing career with no philosophical vocabulary, offers practical wisdom on generating the inner strength and courage to win: focus on the task at hand rather than the outcome, visualize the race, stay calm under adversity, and 'have fun.' Through stories of Buddy Melges, Ted Turner's Fastnet, and Dennis Conner's America's Cup comeback, plus his own collegiate turnaround under coach Graham Hall, he argues resolve (not luck) drives comebacks, and he treats leadership, mentorship, patience, and consistency as cultivated traits of character — an implicit account of the virtues a competitive sailor must build.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 24 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Geist, a conservation biologist, argues from physiology (elastin-digesting enzymes, B12 need), athletics (one-legged balancing for stalking, precision throwing), and the herbivore-like pattern of human speciation that humans evolved as hunters — a 'carnivorous herbivore.' He contends morality itself was born from hunting: because tools-as-weapons (clubs, spears) let an aggressor kill without retaliation, escaping natural selection's check, early humans had to invent social taboos distinguishing right from wrong. He contrasts Neanderthal 'rodeo' close-quarters spearing with Cro-Magnon distance throwing, linking spear-tracking to endurance running, language, and art — concluding that questioning hunting's morality questions our humanity.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 20 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Deal and Waller use Lakoff and Johnson's conceptual-metaphor theory to explain how we grasp Santa's God-like moral omniscience through human metaphors. Santa 'sees from above' (North Pole, flight), judges with 'cool' reason yet remains jolly, and – echoing Plato's Phaedrus charioteer and Descartes' solitary reasoner – masters his appetites and decides free of bias. His gift-giving runs on a 'moral accounting' metaphor where good deeds are commodities exchanged for presents and 'moral authority is parental authority'; they read A Christmas Story's BB-gun lesson through this frame and finally liken Santa's impartial, dispassionate sorting of naughty and nice to the impersonal law of karma.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 32 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Funke examines how the 'gateway' argument is supposed to work by treating it as a claim about weakness of will, split into two mechanisms. Motivational externalism—illustrated by Milgram's obedience experiments and Doris's situationism—holds that the illicit-market situation, not the drug, pushes users toward hard drugs, which implies legalization, not prohibition. Motivational internalism, using Michael Smith's contest between normative and motivational reasons and second-order desires, locates the risk in cannabis's creative 'analysis paralysis' and idealizing imagination; Funke argues that this imaginative value, like religion, is worth its risk and that neuropharmacology (THC's distinct cannabinoid mechanism) undercuts the internalist gateway claim.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 13 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Alfano uses the trial of 'Sunset Strip Killer' Doug Clark to argue that situational forces and attribution biases may have swayed his jury regardless of the actual evidence. Drawing on Milgram's obedience study, Zimbardo's prison simulation, Knobe's intentionality vignettes, and Haidt's disgust experiments, he shows how gender bias, pretrial media, and revulsion at Clark's necrophilia could distort judgments of guilt. He closes with Nozick's truth-tracking account of knowledge to press whether a juror who would have convicted anyway can be said to know Clark is guilty.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 15 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Howard surveys serial killers from Liu Pengli and Locusta through Gilles de Rais, Bathory, Bichel, Panzram, and modern killers she interviewed (Bobby Joe Long, Shawcross, Milat, Birnie) to illustrate 'practical moral skepticism': the thesis that one can know right from wrong yet feel no motivation to be good. She distinguishes this from epistemic moral skepticism and argues that many killers, often privileged or unconstrained, understood moral codes but were driven instead by power, sadism, fatigue, or anger, showing that a failure of moral motivation is ancient rather than modern.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 16 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Vargas argues that a psychopathic serial killer can be profoundly evil yet not morally responsible. Reviewing the clinical literature (Hare, the moral/conventional rule distinction, the 'mrah'/harm thought experiment), he holds that psychopaths are blind to moral rules and so, since blame requires understanding wrongdoing, cannot be blamed — the appropriate response is quarantine rather than resentment. He then separates evil from responsibility: to be evil is to desire others' harm for its own sake, and such evil, like being a jerk, need not be something one is responsible for, which is why psychopathic killers can be genuinely evil though not blameworthy.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 19 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Dietrich and Hall explain why fictional serial killers (Hannibal, the Joker, Dexter, Grendel) allure us. Curiosity drives us to seek explanations for the mysterious, but the deeper pull comes from 'co-activation' of fear and pleasure inside a 'protective frame' (the screen or page) that strips away empathy for victims. They argue humans are rule-following creatures who must assert selfhood through rule-breaking to secure freedom, so the serial killer becomes an alluring avatar of ultimate freedom — the idea of the killer, safely framed, lets us test how thin the veneer of morality really is, as the Joker taunts.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 22 "SERIAL KILLERS" — The Schechters contrast John Wayne Gacy with Jane Toppan and other female killers (Lydia Sherman, Carol Bundy) to ask what female serial murder reveals about human nature and the nativism/empiricism (nature/nurture) debate. They argue women tend to kill through poisoning and 'lethal nurturing' of intimates rather than phallic-aggressive stranger-murder, so female killers form a 'natural kind' that both violates and grotesquely exaggerates stereotypes of femininity. They conclude that serial killers, male and female, are also a single kind whose ruthlessness and egotism are a monstrous but recognizably human — and partly innate — reflection of our common nature.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 23 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Keegan analyzes Buffalo Bill's line from Silence of the Lambs ('It puts the lotion in the basket') to ask why it repulses us. He argues clinical labels like antisocial personality disorder smuggle in unexamined norms and focus only on behaviors, missing the deep-seated traits behind them, so psychopathy should be distinguished from ASPD. Using Habermas's communicative rationality — grounded in perspective-taking and reciprocity and, via de Waal, in our evolved primate sociality — he contends that psychopaths like Buffalo Bill, Ramirez, and Kemper have lost the communicative capacity underlying empathy, and our revulsion is our own communicative rationality registering that violation.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 24 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Terjesen critiques the 'lack of empathy' explanation of serial killing by disentangling empathy into understanding, vicarious feeling, and connection, and showing each either is possessed by killers or leads to circular reasoning (citing Deigh's 'mature empathy' and autism as a counterexample). Real killers like Dahmer, Rader, and 'Angels of Death' such as Cullen and Harvey act from sexual desire, rage, or even excessive empathy, so empathy shapes how they kill (intimate vs. distancing methods, echoing Greene's trolley/footbridge study) rather than whether they kill. He favors Kennett's lack-of-impulse-control and poor risk-assessment account instead.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 29 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Iyengar-tradition teacher Jeff Logan argues that yoga philosophy — mythology such as the warrior Virabhadra behind virabhadrasana and Hanuman behind hanumanasana — must be taught alongside asana, or practice becomes 'mere acrobatics.' Using the parking-lot and door-cutting anecdotes to show yamas like non-harm and selflessness ignored, and citing a childhood-diet study, he contends teachers should not preach the eight limbs but embed subliminal precepts in physical cues ('extend your legs straight and true'), so students come to live rather than merely know yoga's virtue ethics.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 17 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Kristie Miller asks whether any dating behavior—dating a sibling, a gorilla, or a blow-up doll—is genuinely 'taboo' in the prudential (self-interested, utility-maximizing) rather than ethical sense, using decision theory's notion of maximizing expected utility. She sorts behaviors labeled 'pathological' into merely conventionally pathological, pseudo-pathological (e.g., polyandry explained by resource scarcity and childrearing), and genuinely pathological (arising from malfunctioning evolved mate-selection modules like symmetry or MHC-odor detection). Because inclusive fitness and utility diverge, and using future-selves discounting and weakness of will (the stable partner vs. the bad-boy biker), she concludes that in some circumstances even dating a sibling or a gorilla can be the utility-maximizing, and thus rational, choice.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 7 "Introduction" — Thomas Fahy's editorial introduction frames the volume by comparing horror to his skydiving experience: both offer the thrill of confronting danger within a promise of safety. He organizes the collection's essays around morality, identity, cultural history, and aesthetics, previewing how each contributor yokes a pop-culture horror text to a philosopher (Nickel's skeptical reading of Psycho/The Birds, Morris on Kant and torture-horror, his own Hobbes reading of In Cold Blood, Lutz's Marx and Land of the Dead). He argues horror's 'play,' hybridity, and repetition let it raise questions about fear, suffering, justice, and the human capacity for violence.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 39 "36. The Godfather as Philosophy Honor, Power, Family, and Evil" — Belliotti reads The Godfather as a study of the irresolvable conflict between a nineteenth-century Sicilian value system, l'ordine della famiglia, grounded in honor and the accumulation of power within a fixed family order, and a twentieth-century American ethic of individualism and commercial success, arguing the Sicilian vision must wither in the US for lack of its sustaining conditions. He offers a four-part philosophical analysis of honor (a binding code, group affiliation, internalization, and disproportionate redress) that explains Don Vito's contempt for the assimilationist undertaker Bonasera and his willingness to risk everything (the severed horse head sent to Woltz) on a matter of principle, insisting through Michael that 'it's all personal.' He supplements this with a taxonomy of power-over as oppression, paternalism, and empowerment, and argues Don Vito's evils are morally sanitized so viewers cheer his revenge.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 85 "80. Detroit Become Human as Philosophy Moral Reasoning Through Gameplay" — Engels and Evans argue that Detroit: Become Human stages moral reasoning through the interactive stories of the androids Connor, Kara, and Markus, whose 'deviant' awakening they read through Frankfurt's distinction between wantons and persons with second-order desires and through Kant's requirement of the ability to do otherwise. Scenes like Markus scavenging a pump regulator from a dying android, the blood-on-hands visualization after his speech, and Kara protecting Alice force players to weigh Kantian, utilitarian, virtue, and Gilligan-style care frameworks. Through Alice's reveal as an android and the grieving-widower scene, the game makes an implicit anti-speciesist argument (via Singer) that beings who can suffer are morally considerable, and that agency and responsibility emerge through suffering and struggle.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 14 "5. Monsters and Evil in Doctor Who" — The chapter defines a 'moral monster' as one who delights in evil acts, arguing (via Jonathan Glover and Laurence Thomas) that Hitler-style evil is all-too-human, not alien. Using Hume's claim that action springs from passion, it contends the emotionless Cybermen are a mere force of nature (bad but not evil), whereas the Daleks, driven by hatred, tribalism, and a closed belief system, are genuinely evil monsters; the manipulating Master mirrors our everyday lying. It then examines retributive justice through Solomon's execution in 'Dinosaurs on a Spaceship' and 'A Town Called Mercy,' rejecting purely backward- or forward-looking punishment (citing Rawls on utilitarianism's injustice) in favor of the Doctor's needs-based, 'reprobative' punishment, mercy, and self-forgiveness over the Time War.

### The Noble Lie

The noble lie is a myth that Plato, in the Republic, proposes rulers might tell citizens to promote social harmony and loyalty to the just city. In his example, the people are to be told that they were born from the earth and that a god mixed different metals into their souls, marking each for a particular station. Plato presents this founding fiction as beneficial rather than malicious, intended to bind the community and reconcile people to their roles. The idea raises enduring questions about whether useful falsehoods can be justified in politics and about the tension between truth and stability in a well-ordered society.

- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 14 "The Jedi Model" — Barad presents a handbook of Jedi virtue modeled on Plato's Republic: the Jedi are Plato's Guardians, trained through physical exercise and Socratic questioning to guard peace and justice. Aristotle's golden mean explains courage as the balance between Chewbacca's cowardly fear and Anakin's rash rush at Dooku, with Luke's decision to leave Dagobah counting as courage because it has just cause. Luke's Dagobah cave vision (Vader's mask opening to reveal his own face) is read as Plato's Cave allegory turned inward - self-knowledge of one's fear of becoming evil - while compassion and forgiveness, not forbidden attachment, complete the Jedi character. The chapter even defends Jedi mind tricks via Plato's noble lie (the myth of the metals) as manipulation of the weak-minded for the common good.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 27 "“Trust Your Feelings”" — Fader tackles the paradox that Jedi lie while Sith tell the truth: Obi-Wan's 'Darth Vader betrayed and murdered your father,' Yoda's trickster masquerade on Dagobah, the Council's cover-up of its waning powers, against Vader's brutal truth at Cloud City and Palpatine's technically honest 'I love democracy.' Kant's absolute prohibition of lying is set against the utilitarian's greatest-good lie and Nietzsche's claim that truth is the accepted set of social lies; Obi-Wan's deception is then defended through Plato's noble lie and the Buddha's Parable of the House on Fire, where 'expedients' to save the oblivious are no falsehood, while Vader and Dooku wield literal truths as weapons without compassion. Luke's answer is to stop accepting anyone's version and build his own green lightsaber: truth as perspective, intention, and finally the heart's understanding that redeems Anakin.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 24 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Rollin opposes mandatory helmet laws by contrasting two conceptions of freedom: the Hobbesian absence-of-constraint view ('go to hell in my own way', from Pinocchio's 'no strings on me' to the trapped coyote) and the rational-order view running from Plato (ranked classes, noble lies, censorship, contempt for democracy) through Rousseau's 'forced to be free', which Popper already identified as the enemy of the open society. Since, as the obesity-as-disease example and Robert Paul Wolff's expert-government argument show, we cannot claim certainty about value judgments the way we can about fractures, paternalism fails: if danger justified coercion we would have to ban motorcycles, skiing, parachuting, and bull-riding alike. Helmet laws in effect claim society knows what you ought to want better than you do, and Rollin's answer to his British colleague's 'what will you do if you injure your brain?' is to join the Department of Food Science and Nutrition.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 16 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Vaclavik follows Lyra's career as liar and trickster, from the Silvertongue performance that goads Iofur Raknison into fighting Iorek Byrnison, up to the reversal in the Land of the Dead where the harpy screams 'Liar!' and only true stories can feed the ghosts. She frames Lyra's boast that she is the best liar there ever was yet is not lying as a version of the Liar Paradox, then dissolves the puzzle by showing that lies continue after the katabasis (Will's comforting fib, Mrs. Coulter's noble treachery with Metatron) just as truth-telling appeared before it. Truth triumphs in the underworld not for its own sake but because it suits the audience: the dead need the world they have lost, so storytelling, truthful or invented, is judged by what it does for its listeners.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 85 "The Ugly" — Argues eugenics forces us to discard the 'noble lie' of egalitarian democracy we teach children for their own good, and shows the cost in Jason and Heather's contempt for 'ordinaries,' Jason's aging-obsessed narcissism, and the 'aristocratic values' that let him condemn his lover Heather to a labor camp without qualm. Police general Felix Buckman, demoted for compassion toward labor-camp inmates and later assassinated for criticizing the regime, embodies the democratic values the sixes' elitism destroys, with Marvel's X-Men as the analogy for a fractured next-generation humanity.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 100 "The Epistemology of Deception" — Shifts from the ethics of deception (Kant's near-absolute condemnation of lying versus Plato's morally justified governmental lies) to its epistemology, defining deception as intentionally causing a false belief. This definition explains why Cohaagen deceives Quaid, who falsely believes he is a construction worker, while Rekall cannot deceive the Quaid who really is a secret agent, and why the Zoner Cale merely misleads Spencer Olham in Impostor without deceiving him — with Hume's reasoning about miracle testimony modeling when to believe a probable deceiver.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 24 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Greg Littmann maps Ape City onto Plato's Republic class by class: orangutan rulers who legislate, censor, and propagandize; gorilla warriors who enforce; chimpanzee producers who do all the work - including, pointedly, the science Plato made no provision for; and humans as the 'barbarians' Plato says may be enslaved or exterminated. The overlaps are detailed: the Sacred Scrolls' first article of faith functions as the noble lie's myth of the metals, orangutan funerals promise heaven to keep gorillas unafraid of death, and Zaius's erasing of Taylor's dust-writing and blowing up of the archaeological cave enact the rulers' duty to supervise stories. But the films also refute Plato: hereditary orangutans show that power corrupts philosopher kings, Dr. Honorius's 'reason' is dogma serving the faith, the gelding threat that finally breaks Taylor cracks the tripartite-soul analogy of justice, and democracy's rough virtue is that it lets us remove rulers 'without sticking anybody with iron spears.'
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 32 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Tom McBride reads the film through Wittgenstein's On Certainty: Dr. Zaius's certainties (flight is impossible, humans come from the forests) are hinge or riverbed propositions that cannot be doubted within the ape form of life, so Taylor's true story sounds not false but insane, like claiming to have slept on the moon. Speaking and able to prompt empirical investigation, Taylor fractures a foundational principle where G.E. Moore, facing a 'wild tribe' playing a different language game, could only confess that things 'stand fast' with him; and Zaius's explicit origin myth, a parallel to Plato's Myth of the Metals, is flimsy precisely because rulers who must insist on rules are not potent and are reduced to destroying the cave evidence. The genre's appeal is Margaret Atwood's 'controlled hallucination': crazy doors that swing on safe hinges, rivers that still have stable beds.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 25 "Psych and Philosophy" — Stephenson tests Shawn's ruse against the major theories of justified deceit and finds it wanting: Plato's Myth of the Metals excuses paternalistic noble lies for social harmony that Shawn's self-aggrandizing motives cannot claim, utilitarianism collapses on the long-term costs of exposure (Gus, Juliet, Henry, and the SBPD condemned by association; clients betrayed; trust in law enforcement eroded), Kant's universalizability test sinks maxims like 'lie whenever a career opportunity is at stake,' and Popper's open society condemns just the deceit on which the psychic brand runs. Even the mutual-deceit analogy to poker and Sissela Bok's reasonable-person publicity test fail, since no public forum of reasonable people would bless duping paying private clients. The escape is extra-moral: Shawn's mischievous hokum is the socially necessary boundary-pusher, whose lesson against unreflective occult belief lands best when delivered with a laugh.
