- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 7 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Cam Cobb weighs Battle School against competing philosophies of education: Plato's Republic supplies vocational sorting by natural aptitude (complete with the myth of the metals as a 'noble lie'), while Socratic dialogue and Paulo Freire's problem-posing pedagogy demand the shared critical inquiry Ender never gets. He argues Graff's curriculum is almost purely vocational - military history, tactics, the Giant's Drink, battleroom drills - leaving no liberal paideia, and that the teachers' constant rule-changing leaves Ender feeling like 'someone's pawn,' exactly the banking-style teacher domination Freire warned against.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 28 "15. The Way of the Doctor Is Deception" — Dodge takes Rule #1 - the Doctor lies - through the major theories of lying: Bernard Williams's definition (asserting what you believe false with intent to deceive), Aristotle's claim that all lies are base, Kant's categorical imperative and respect for persons (even the Vinvocci's shimmer disguises in 'The End of Time' abuse trust), and Bentham's pleasure-pain calculus, which condemns the faked death at Lake Silencio ('The Impossible Astronaut') for the grief it caused Amy and Rory yet rewards the greater happiness it made possible. Against the absolutists he sets Plato's Noble Lie from the Republic - the elite falsehood that keeps society functioning - as what the Doctor emulates by deceiving the universe into thinking him dead ('The Wedding of River Song'), and Nietzsche's point in Human, All Too Human that lying is ethically neutral when the pretense is sustainable, as when the Doctor hides the ganger-Amy switch from Rory ('The Almost People'). The upshot: the Doctor's lies are wrong in themselves but routinely justified by the good they do, which is why sometimes the hero lies.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 35 "20. The Doctor Lies" — McCain distinguishes lying (directly asserting what you believe false to make another believe it) from mere deception - the Sixth Doctor feeding Jamie false information for Sontaran Stike to overhear in 'The Two Doctors' deceives without lying - then asks whether the Doctor can lie to himself, answering that incarnations can lie to later selves (the Eleventh's suspicious 'I have absolutely no idea' about the children on Gallifrey in 'The Day of the Doctor') but a current self cannot. The stakes are moral: against Kant's and Augustine's absolute prohibition of lying, Plato's Republic and Sidgwick's Methods of Ethics defend noble lies, and Robert C. Solomon's view of self-deception as coping with the unbearable suggests that if the Doctor did engineer himself to forget the Time War genocide - as Ten and Wilf did to Donna in 'Journey's End' - it might be a good man's forgivable way of going on.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 18 "8. Plato’s Chicago" — Littmann systematically maps Roth's Chicago onto Plato's Republic: like Marcus, Plato rejects democracy after Athens executed Socrates; both dissolve the family ('faction before blood' versus children raised in common and bred by state schedule); Erudite's IQ-selected leadership mirrors the rigorously trained philosopher-rulers, Dauntless the warrior class whose purely physical training Plato warns turns 'savage and harsh,' Abnegation's poverty the guardians's communism of property, and the factionless the powerless producers - with Plato's noble lie about the metals matching the Erudite's propaganda and serums as instruments of control. The shared flaw, he argues, is concentrated power without external checks, which corrupted Abnegation, corrupts every Dauntless leadership change, and would corrupt Plato's guardians too. The lesson is not to hand power to the least vicious but for democratic voters to confront their own ignorance - or end like Roth's America, in apocalyptic war.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 27 "15. The Serious Monk’s Guide to Re-writing History" — Framed as a monkey monk-to-be telling four bored children the 'history' of four Discworld novels, the chapter argues that history is not a record of what happened but a constructed narrative: in Wyrd Sisters the Duchess commissions Hwel's play to rewrite the murder of the king, since 'the past is what people remember, and memories are words.' In Small Gods, Brutha's photographic memory of Ephebe's burning library shows that even perfect recollection is lost unless written down, while in Thief of Time the History Monks openly rebuild time as a patchwork after the Big Crash, and Susan watches historians 'rebuilt the image of the past to suit the eyesight of today.' Drawing on W. H. Walsh's idea of history as intelligible narrative, it concludes that history is performative—what people are told it is—and that we ourselves are the crowbar that opens the box of history from the inside.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 19 "9. Pierce’s Republic" — Randall Jensen maps the Society onto Plato's Republic (Brown has said he drew on it): the Color hierarchy parallels the Myth of the Metals' gold, silver, and bronze souls, the Golds' scorn for Demokracy echoes Book VIII's account of degeneration into tyranny, and Leto's 'We are Plato's philosopher kings' claims a mantle Plato himself doubted anyone could ever fill. Darrow's story is the Allegory of the Cave run from below—a Helldiver literally raised in a mine, blinded by surface light, whose return to a shrunken, grayer garden mirrors the philosopher's homecoming—except Plato never imagined the prisoner carved into a Gold. The Noble Lie survives as the terraforming myth fed to lowReds while the surface has been habitable for centuries, and the chapter weighs Darrow's gospel ('we choose who we are') against Plato's caveats: you can choose who to be only within limits, if you are lucky and greatly helped.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 20 "10. Virtue Rising" — Darci Doll argues the Rising exposes the Society's intellectual oppression—each Color denied education and fed 'noble lies' about its role—and that lifting it sparks an 'Intellectual Reformation' proving Color does not dictate potential: Darrow out-performing Golds, Orion the un-carved Blue, Ragnar and Sefi exceeding their station. She uses Plato's Republic (producers, auxiliaries, guardians, the lower orders kept obedient by Noble Lies like the Reds' terraforming myth) as the Society's blueprint, then turns to Aristotle: potential is realized only through the right environment, instruction, and habituated character, and Darrow's practical wisdom—testing himself, reassessing after Titus and Cassius, doing what makes him his best self—lets him flourish and lead. Aristotle's critique of utility-only relations explains why the Society's alliances expire (Antonia executed once useless) while Darrow and Mustang's virtue friendships and just rule endure, opening a society where everyone, including women and lowColors denied opportunity rather than ability, can maximize potential.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 15 "5. Ministry of Truth Handbook Excerpt on the Strategic Use of Fallacious Reasoning for Thoughtcrime Prevention" — Rard's satirical Party handbook explains how to keep a population from thinking: keep the proles too poor and exhausted to reason, and deploy fallacies strategically, from ad hominem goat-caricatures of Goldstein at the Two Minutes Hate and straw man versions of his arguments, to destroying contrary evidence, appealing to fear of the old capitalist world, and Room 101's appeal to force, so false beliefs can be manufactured as easily as true ones. It presents Plato's noble lie as the Ministry's founding inspiration, calling the reader's mission 'a continuation of Plato's dream'. It also cites Aristotle's view that emotion must be disciplined for reason to work, which the Party inverts by deliberately triggering fear and hatred to disable rational thought.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 25 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Fallis uses Sheldon — a lousy liar with an elaborate theory of lying — to probe the philosophy of lying: Kant's absolute prohibition (even 'out of frivolity'), Bok's presumption against deceit, Plato's noble lies reserved for philosopher kings, and Nietzsche's self-deceiving overmen, whose counsel explains the 'un-unravelable webs' of fake Facebook and blog evidence for the imaginary cousin Leopold Houston. Ryle's knowing-how versus knowing-that split explains how Sheldon can state the rules ('casually, no rapid breathing') yet botch the performance, while the Bazinga! pranks and the insincere courtroom apology break the Augustinian definition that lying requires intent to deceive. Grice's norms of conversation then ground the author's own definition — lying as intending to violate the norm against saying what you believe false — until a hypothetical, convention-oblivious liar like Kripke forces him to concede a counterexample and admit he was wrong.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 15 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Cooke defends his three-year campaign of a lawful evil wizard (Oraximon, who magic-missiled an innkeeper and hid the bodies in a rope trick) against religious and secular critics. The epistemic charge fails because rulebooks are invitations to imagine, not assertions, and the Smurfs-as-Krishna example shows an 'attitude for export' needs authorial evidence D&D lacks; Hume's twin claims about the impropriety of imaginatively endorsing flawed sentiments are dismantled by splitting Can'tians from Won'tians over Gendler's stories and defending a 'Hardian' view on which resistance is just difficulty, making imaginative resistance a chimera. The causal charge fails on the evidence (the Werther effect and its video-game and jazz cousins are post hoc plus confirmation bias), the character-warping charge risks the unfalsifiability of the repressed-desire diagnosis, and Plato's ban on the arts — enforced via the noble lie — would be the price if imagining were as bad as doing.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 7 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Cam Cobb pits Socratic critical inquiry and Plato's Republic-style vocational streaming (classes sorted by the 'myth of the metals,' sold through a noble lie) against the Battle School curriculum, which is almost purely vocational and lacks the music, poetry, and liberal paideia that harmonize the soul. Testing Socrates' dialogic method, Dewey's aptitude-tracking education, and Freire's problem-posing alternative against the battleroom, the Giant's Drink, and Graff's secretly rewritten game rules, Cobb concludes Ender's schooling mixes conflicting pedagogies and ends in the teacher domination Freire feared, crystallized in Ender's lament 'I've spent my life as someone's pawn.'
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 30 "NOTES" — First defines lying — distinguishing it from mere error (Angela believing Peter dead), from the Haitian's non-verbal memory-wipe deception, and from Hiro's silent staging of Ando's fake death — then tests moral theories against the show's liars. Kant's categorical imperative bans all lying but is abandoned when Sylar demands a friend's hiding place; utilitarianism vindicates Victoria Pratt's lie about the virus vial yet also licenses Linderman's .07% explosion and Plato's noble lie of the earthborn metals, which the chapter rejects. Machiavelli's advice that princes may lie to keep power is played out by 'President Sylar' in 'Five Years Gone,' and the chapter finally endorses Sissela Bok's presumption against lying — a public-reasoning procedure modeled by Bob Bishop and Mohinder before Monica's virus injection.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 18 "Over Four Thousand Words to Say No" — Spanakos asks whether Stark's assembling, disassembling, and reassembling of the Avengers and his unseen-hand management of Civil War make him the Republic's philosopher guardian, and answers no. Tony fits the surface profile — the gold-souled ruler of Socrates' noble lie, the elite training, indifference to money, the technê of an MIT engineer who envisions the future — but he lacks epistêmê: he never climbs from the cave's shadows to grasp the forms of justice and the good, and his appetites (womanizing in The Ultimates, 'Demon in a Bottle') show a soul where passion is not ruled by reason. His puppet mastery is reactive problem-solving guided by each situation, not philosophy, and reading him as a philosopher king is our failure to read The Republic meditatively, as Ortega y Gasset urged.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 17 "The Office and Philosophy" — Tests the deceptions swirling around Dwight: Kant's two arguments against lying (universalizing the maxim 'lie whenever it saves face', and treating the deceived as a mere means) are set against Plato's noble lie from the Republic - Michael's empty 'Assistant Regional Manager' title may be a morally tolerable verbal lie because after 'The Fight' it restores their friendship, though it does not medicate the office as Plato's lie does the city. Epicurus' claim that only what is experienced can harm you ('what you don't know can't hurt you') is refuted by the thought of Angela's hypothetical fake love for Dwight: undetected deception is itself a harm. Finally Dwight's self-deception (believing the false promotion, Jim's telekinesis prank, the fax from his future self) is modeled by dividing the self - Plato's tripartite soul versus Descartes' simple, indivisible mind - suggesting cognitive science's modular brain as the better picture, and asking whether one can even wrong oneself.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 8 "Notes" — MacMullan argues Darth Plagueis is a paradox for Plato: wisdom as reason ruling spirit and appetite should be impossible for a Sith who feeds on passion, yet Plagueis stays patient, restrained, and rational for over a century. He reads Sidious's 'I will make it legal' and the Sith Code as Thrasymachus's 'justice is the advantage of the stronger,' and notes Plagueis even shares Plato's noble lie and eugenic breeding programs. Finding that Plato's prediction of self-destruction fails for Plagueis, the chapter turns to Nietzsche: master morality, the will to power, and life beyond good and evil better explain a Sith who cherishes bodily life and seeks to conquer death where Yoda and Socrates calmly disdain 'crude matter.'
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 22 "Notes" — Barkman and Alkema map Plato's Republic onto the fall of the Old Republic: the bickering Senate and Anakin's 'someone wise' exchange with Padme enact democracy's degeneration into tyranny, with Palpatine as Plato's werewolf-like protector-tyrant and Dooku's Sith name 'Tyranus' marking Thrasymachus's justice-as-strength as Sith doctrine. The Jedi approximate Plato's philosopher-guardians - courageous, temperate, reluctant to rule, surrendering their children to the Temple much like the Republic's breeding deceptions and noble lies. Justice as each part doing its own work applies to the tripartite soul as much as the state, and the chapter closes that democracy survives Endor but only if truth stays a beacon of the light side.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 27 "Nietzsche’s Overman as Posthuman Star Child in 2001 A Space Odyssey Jerold J. Abrams" — Abrams reads 2001 as a cinematic staging of Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, mapping the film's ape-to-human-to-Star-Child arc onto Zarathustra's evolutionary vision of the overman. He casts the discovery of the buried moon monolith as Kubrick's death of God (proving aliens, not God, seeded us) maintained by a Platonic noble lie, the astronauts as Nietzsche's higher men, and Bowman's decadent hotel-room decline plus Poole's fall as the last man and the dying tightrope walker. He then argues the prophecy may come true not via aliens but through Kurzweil's Singularity and Moravec's posthuman 'mind children'.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 9 "2. Socrates’s City and Seldon’s Galaxy" — Goldberg maps Plato's Republic onto Asimov's Foundation Trilogy: Socrates's three-class city (Guardians, Auxiliaries, Producers ruling by knowledge of the Forms) parallels Seldon's galaxy (Second Foundationers, First Foundationers, and everyone else, ruling by the abstract mathematics of psychohistory), with the tyrannical Thrasymachus paralleling the Mule. He shows the Prime Radiant functions as Plato's Allegory of the Cave, and that both Guardians and Second Foundationers govern through 'noble lies' (the metals myth; the Encyclopedia sham and the Second Foundation's fake destruction), then questions whether those lies are truly noble given doubts about objective truth.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 28 "17. Psychohistory’s Noble Lie" — Silcox explains why readers forgive Seldon's confessed lie that the Encyclopedia Galactica 'is a fraud, and always has been' by comparing it to Socrates's noble lie in Plato's Republic, which Popper and I.F. Stone condemn as antidemocratic. He contrasts the two—Socrates's lie preserves an existing kallipolis while Seldon's brings about a distant political goal that requires trusting psychohistory—and weighs them against modern transparency doctrines: Bentham's consequentialist case for publicity and Rawls's publicity condition grounding autonomy, plus Nguyen's worry that transparency distorts expert 'cognitive islands.' He concludes that a genuinely predictive science of history might rationally lead us to treat political transparency as negotiable, which is why Hari Seldon remains a noble hero despite 'engineering the narrative.'
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 16 "7. Anthony Bourdain’s Extremely Objectionable Stories" — Holmes examines Bourdain's horror graphic novel Hungry Ghosts as cautionary folklore in the tradition of Aesop and EC Comics. He stages a debate between Aristotle, who in the Rhetoric endorses fables as accessible moral tools, and Plato, who in the Republic wants to censor frightening tales for children — yet Holmes shows Plato himself (Euthyphro, Laws) praised fear as 'modesty,' and notes Bourdain used cautionary tales (Ronald McDonald 'has cooties') to steer his own daughter from fast food.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 25 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Johnson argues that the Santa Claus lie is immoral and should be abandoned, giving three reasons: it is deceptive lying (Kant's absolute prohibition is too strong, but the lie lacks life-saving justification and functions as a Platonic 'noble lie' no more noble than a cult leader's); Santa robs parents of credit and warps children's moral development and trust, illustrated by anguished 'finding out' stories and Virginia O'Hanlon's letter; and it damages credulity, invoking Clifford's 'Ethics of Belief' against belief on insufficient evidence while James's 'Will to Believe' cannot rescue Santa since evidence against him is overwhelming. He recommends revealing the truth early, even via a Socratic-Method questioning game.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 31 "29. Frank Herbert’s Dune as Philosophy The Need to Think for Yourself" — Reading the Sci Fi Channel miniseries Frank Herbert's Dune and Children of Dune, Littmann argues the saga warns against letting leaders or religions think for us: Paul Atreides fakes being the Fremen Mahdi, wages a holy war, and founds a theocratic tyranny that Alia and Leto II carry to worse extremes. He sets Plato's Republic (the guardian class, the noble lie, rule by the wise) and Hobbes against pro-democracy thinkers—Locke's consent and natural rights, Mill's harm principle, Dewey's democracy—then cites Locke, Paine and Russell on religion's dangers, closing with W.K. Clifford's 'ethics of belief' that one must not accept religious claims without sufficient evidence. The chapter reads Paul's dictatorship and the Bene Gesserit's engineered messiah as dramatizations of the historical abuses of concentrated and religious power.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 50 "47. Snowpiercer as Philosophy The Danger to Humanity" — Marquez 'pierces the veils' of Snowpiercer to argue the greatest danger to humanity is humanity itself. He reads Wilford's authoritarian, precisely population-controlled train through Plato's noble lie / myth of the metals (Mason's 'know your place'), Hobbes's social contract against a cannibalistic state of nature, and Machiavellian ends-justify-means to weigh whether Gilliam's secret compromise with Wilford is morally acceptable. He tests the orchestrated revolution against utilitarianism's greatest-happiness principle (Bentham, Mill's taxation-of-the-wealthy, Singer's impartiality) and against Rawls's veil of ignorance and difference principle versus Nozick's entitlement objection and Aquinas's just-war criteria, concluding each character's actions can be read as 'just,' which exposes anthropocentrism as the real veil.

### Perspectivism

Perspectivism is Nietzsche's view that there is no purely objective, view-from-nowhere knowledge; all seeing and knowing occurs from some particular standpoint shaped by interests, drives, and circumstances. Rather than concluding that anything goes, he suggests that understanding grows by drawing on many perspectives, since the more angles we bring to bear on a matter, the more complete our grasp of it becomes. The idea challenges the notion of a single absolute truth and treats our concepts and values as interpretations rather than neutral mirrors of reality.

- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 22 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Irwin takes Pilate's Quid est veritas as a guided tour of theories of truth applied to the film: Gibson's sympathetic Pilate embodies relativism, met with Nietzsche's 'truth is a woman' perspectivism and Baudrillard's postmodern laughter and rejected; Caiaphas and the bad thief demanding Jesus come down from the cross put the correspondence theory to work ('the proof is out there'), though beliefs hang on other beliefs ad infinitum; Simon of Cyrene's growing conviction models the coherence theory, exposed as necessary but not sufficient by Swinburne's case for versus Wells's case against the divinity of Jesus; and Pilate's Barabbas gambit parodies James's pragmatic theory, where working is not enough if there is no corresponding reality. He then retrieves Heidegger's reading of aletheia as uncovering, helped by the Quid est veritas anagram ('Est qui vir adest': it is the man before you) and Gadamer on truth seizing us like beauty, so that Jesus's 'I am the truth' and Claudia's dream-guided warnings point to truth as disclosure. Since disclosure alone cannot decide between inconsistent revealed claims, Irwin ends by leaving the viewer with a leap of faith and a first instinct as final answer.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 27 "“Trust Your Feelings”" — Fader tackles the paradox that Jedi lie while Sith tell the truth: Obi-Wan's 'Darth Vader betrayed and murdered your father,' Yoda's trickster masquerade on Dagobah, the Council's cover-up of its waning powers, against Vader's brutal truth at Cloud City and Palpatine's technically honest 'I love democracy.' Kant's absolute prohibition of lying is set against the utilitarian's greatest-good lie and Nietzsche's claim that truth is the accepted set of social lies; Obi-Wan's deception is then defended through Plato's noble lie and the Buddha's Parable of the House on Fire, where 'expedients' to save the oblivious are no falsehood, while Vader and Dooku wield literal truths as weapons without compassion. Luke's answer is to stop accepting anyone's version and build his own green lightsaber: truth as perspective, intention, and finally the heart's understanding that redeems Anakin.
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 20 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Bamford argues that Atkins's insistence that dieters evaluate the plan for their individual needs parallels Nietzsche's cultural therapy: as the death of God left modern culture nihilistic, so a processed-food culture suffers 'nutritional nihilism,' and the 'mega-orthodox' doctors who worship medical consensus with 'religious fervor' treat science as a replacement religion. Reading Ecce Homo's 'question of nutriment' alongside Twilight of the Idols, she shows that Nietzsche's perspectivism — no uninterpreted facts, only interpretations from physiological perspectives — makes each dieter fully responsible for interpretation, which is why Atkins must ask us to think for ourselves. The limit: where Atkins keeps an 'absolute faith in empirical science' (and Atkins Nutritionals mass-markets processed low-carb products), a properly Nietzschean therapy would question that faith too.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 24 "Tarantula’s End" — Goldblatt and Necarsulmer pair Dylan's Tarantula with Nietzsche's "The Tarantulas" from Zarathustra: both are books of advice, renaming, and stream-of-consciousness flow whose sections cohere through signature and attitude rather than narrative (the same Foucauldian author function). Both embody the intuitive artist of Plato's Ion and Nietzsche's Ecce Homo - the poet as medium whose language arrives as inspiration, all language being fresh or stale metaphor. Tarantula's vengeful vignettes and "Idiot Wind" dramatize the ressentiment Zarathustra warns against, its impenetrable juxtapositions ("harmonica battalions," "funeral landlord") work as Derridean catachresis - metaphor whose transfer fails yet exerts aesthetic force - and the book's dream of the burning tenement leaves Dylan unable, and absolved, to look back.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 98 "Rhetoric and Bullshit" — Following Jeremy Campbell's The Liar's Tale, the chapter argues that the truth/lies binary is oversimplified: even 'the sky is blue' depends on contested definitions and 'God is good' on the speaker's concepts, so we must separate capital-T Truth — the immutable, incorruptible kind Plato located beyond the flawed physical realm of perfect Forms, which made him scorn rhetoric and the Sophists as teachers of disguise — from lower-case, situated, perspectival truths. It then recruits Nietzsche, for whom humans have no 'organ' for Truth but a natural instinct for falsehood (shared with camouflaging animals), and Ken Gemes's reading of doctrinal Truth as a ritualized fiction manufactured to maintain institutional and religious power. On this view postmodernism studies truth within the shifting domain of language rather than denying objective reality.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 25 "Like Caine in Kung Fu" — Bence Nanay and Ian Schnee argue Pulp Fiction is genuinely Nietzschean, but not by celebrating violence: the film stages the crisis of meaning after God's death through two reactions to chance. Vincent is the passive nihilist—dogmatically insisting the six bullets mean nothing, inheriting gangster values unquestioned, modeling himself on Elvis—while Jules's 'moment of clarity' makes him a Nietzschean free spirit who creates perspective-relative meaning and breaks the cycle of violence by buying Ringo and Honey Bunny's lives. His plan to 'walk the earth, like Caine in Kung Fu' reworks Zarathustra's wandering, and the running toilets gag marks Vincent's blindness to the significance of events, which is why only one of them survives.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 26 "The Final Word That’s Right, I Said Preliminary Thoughts" — Patton starts from wildly disputed Springsteen interpretations — Reagan's 1984 campaign use of 'Born in the U.S.A.,' Flint protesters playing 'My Hometown' as civic pride, Kerry's 'No Surrender' — and asks whether any reading is better than another. He frames the issue as Socratic dialectic versus Gorgias-style rhetoric, passes through Augustine's polysemy (multiple intended levels of meaning, as in 'I'm on fire') to Nietzsche's claim that the text disappears beneath its interpretation, extended by Foucault (truth as an instrument of power) and Derridean deconstruction. His conclusion: authorial intent cannot settle meaning, but some readings ('Born in the U.S.A.' as pro-Reagan anthem) are non-starters, otherwise it is rhetoric all the way down and the sophists win.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 24 "The Prophet" — Presents Muad'Dib as Nietzsche's Zarathustra in the Dune universe: the sardonic self-mockery that keeps a great man from believing his own myth, the valuation of life-enhancing 'truths' over correspondence-truth (behind all logic stand 'value judgments,' as Beyond Good and Evil has it), and monumental, mythologized history against Mentat-accurate history that kills religion. Paul's Fremen, first hard and vital, go 'water-fat' under the paradise his jihad built, becoming Nietzsche's 'Ultimate Man'—the last man who has left the places where living was hard and demands 'a little poison now and then'—so Muad'Dib must become the Preacher to destroy the rigid code he created, as Zarathustra came to undo Zoroaster's morality; both prophets preach self-overcoming toward the Superman.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 33 "Deeply Dissecting Dexter" — Deborah Mellamphy uses Nietzsche's masks - 'every profound spirit needs a mask,' the will to power that requires deception for self-preservation - to explain both why Dexter's crafted normalcy works and why only the characters conscious of their own masks (Doakes, Lila, Brian, Trinity) see through his. Nietzsche's perspectivism and 'Truth and Lie in the Extra-Moral Sense' then dissolve any true self beneath the mask: if truths are 'worn out metaphors,' Dexter's question 'If you play a role long enough... does it ever become real?' has no stable answer. Following Sarah Kofman's reading, the chapter asks whether we are all 'but this veil itself' and concludes that Dexter goes a step beyond Nietzsche by locating the truth of identity in the many layered masks themselves.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 19 "Leap of Faith" — Dionne argues Cobb's 'most resilient parasite' works only as an idea embedded in a coherent story - 'my father doesn't want me to be him' - and that since ideas define who we are, each person is less a host than a collection of well-planted narratives. Using Bergson on embodied, memory-and-desire-mediated perception (Cobb's fear of the bridge triggering Mal's projection) and Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil on perspectival appearance as the price of life, she claims dreams differ from reality in degree, not kind: we are beings-in-the-world who stabilize contingency through story-making and 'strive for positive logic'. Hence knowledge always demands the leap of faith that Saito and Mal demand of Cobb, the film becomes a meta-narrative with Fischer as its audience, and the wobbling top offers only an interpretation of a fact, never the fact itself.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 49 "Dandelions on My Cloud" — Uses 'Dandelion'—truth as a bright yellow flower that blows away—to mark the withering of Enlightenment confidence in plain, visible truth under deconstruction. Kierkegaard's 'truth is subjectivity' explains why truth on 'Get Off of My Cloud' cannot be shared directly ('Don't hang around 'cause two's a crowd'), and Nietzsche goes further: there is no truth to find, only wills to power making truths—'you can't always get what you want... you just might find you get what you need.'
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 32 "19. The Alchemy of Flat Worlds" — Staged as Professor Moby Dickens Melville's 'Philosophy of Worlds' course uniting Discworld wizards with the geometric Flatlanders of Abbott's novella, the chapter contrasts a storytelling, narrative-causality philosophy of Discworld with Flatland's mathematical, hierarchy-obsessed rationalism, and extends the contrast to physics (wizards favor loop quantum gravity, Flatlanders string theory) and theology (Hex's self-designed universe and words of power versus Flatland's circle-priests who rule women declared 'deficient in Reason'). When a Flatlander woman, Ms. Transversal, protests that calling the new softer approach 'feminine' repeats Abbott's sexism, the class closes with the narrator's suggestion, from a chalk-nub's-eye view, that everything we know may reflect the direction from which we see rather than the truth itself.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 34 "22. The Irrelevance of Truth" — Jan Kyrre Berg Friis argues, with Nietzsche, that truth is a 'mobile army of metaphors', a relational event between people rather than an objective correspondence, and that the will to truth is subordinate to the will to power — the difference being that Trump-style 'alternative truth' is dishonest domination while Nietzsche's askesis is self-transformation. He layers in the Buddhist and Zen (Dogen) diagnosis of perception as conceptual distortion, Descartes' ego cogito as the fatal Western turn, and Heidegger's warning that calculative, technological thinking covers over our tacit lived background, producing exactly the one-dimensional minds a Ministry of Truth can feed. Rorty's advice to drop the truth-talk, Kant's insight that reality is sifted through the perceiver, and the cognitive-science of confirmation bias explain why facts no longer bite in the post-truth newsfeed.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 22 "11. Lip Sync for Your Life" — Guilel Treiber reads the Season Ten reunion blow-up - Asia O'Hara blaming the show for letting The Vixen walk out, RuPaul insisting people must 'want to meet halfway' - as an unresolvable conflict between two value systems. The show's official 'C.U.N.T.' virtues (charisma, uniqueness, nerve, talent) are individualistic, market-driven values that professionalize drag, while the implicit 'A.S.S.E.' values (acceptance, solidarity, support, empowerment) descend from LGBTQ+ history from Stonewall and Marsha P. Johnson to ACT-UP. Using Nietzsche's On the Genealogy of Morals and its project of the 'revaluation of all values,' he argues values gain worth through conflict rather than progress, so there is no view from nowhere that settles the dispute. Miss Congeniality, the queens' revolt over Valentina's title, and Tammie Brown's clash with RuPaul show the show's magic lies in never deciding between the two - even though market pressure keeps devaluing solidarity.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 21 "Dull Reality The Tragic View of Life" — A Nietzschean interpretation: Alice's unastonished pursuit of the White Rabbit exemplifies the 'will to ignorance' hidden within the will to truth, since every perspective is created by selecting and simplifying while we convince ourselves we have discovered rather than invented. Rick Mayock reads the Caterpillar's 'Who are YOU?' and the mushroom as lessons in perspectivism and in the self as a grammatical fiction (no doer behind the deed, no lightning behind the flash), the Queen's beheadings and ruleless croquet as a flux of competing wills to power, and the Hatter's madness as Dionysian against Alice's Apollonian calm, with Greek tragedy supplying the metaphysical comfort that makes 'dull reality' livable.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 22 "Can You Face the Bat" — Sarah Donovan and Nicholas Richardson use Nietzsche and Foucault to present Batman as a self-constructed identity: across Batman: Year One, Arkham Asylum, and The Dark Knight Returns, Bruce consciously builds the persona ('Yes, Father, I shall become a bat') rather than revealing a deeper true self. Foucault's constructed categories of normal and abnormal surface in Arkham Asylum's 'super-sane' Joker and the Alice in Wonderland parallels that put Batman's own sanity in question alongside Amadeus Arkham's madness. Nietzsche's will to power and eternal recurrence, via the shepherd biting the snake in Zarathustra, explain why Bruce can face the bat that others flee, becoming heroic where Arkham and Dr. Cavendish go insane.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 24 "The Prophet" — Reads Paul-Muad'Dib as a Nietzschean prophet: his sardonic greatness mirrors Zarathustra the laughing prophet, the Fremen's implanted legends illustrate Nietzsche's point that value matters more than truth (logic being only one perspective on the world), and the Untimely Meditations account of monumental myth explains why Muad'Dib must become the Preacher to destroy his own petrified religion. It likens the water-fat new Fremen of Children of Dune to Nietzsche's soft, risk-averse last men, and presents both Zarathustra and Muad'Dib as all-too-human founders who create a religion, recognize it as 'the most fateful of errors', and turn against it, with self-discipline rather than divine intervention as the true virtue.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 19 "Leap of Faith" — Dionne reads Cobb's 'idea is the most resilient parasite' as a claim about narrative: what gets incepted in Fischer is a story ('my father doesn't want me to follow in his footsteps'), and by the same token each of us is a collection of incepted stories rather than a stable self. Drawing on Bergson's account of perception mediated by memory and desire (Cobb's bridge triggering Mal's projection), Nietzsche's perspectivism — truth is a 'moral prejudice' and 'we must mistake ourselves' — and the embodiment of the being-in-the-world, she argues dreams differ from reality only in degree, since both are interested story-making under time pressure. The payoff is meta-filmic: Fischer is the spectator and Cobb the director, and the final spinning top becomes the audience's own totem — there is no fact of the matter, only interpretation, so watching the ending is itself the leap of faith.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 11 "Notes" — Adams pairs Anakin with Achilles to show how Palpatine's lesson that 'good is a point of view' - Nietzsche's claim that there are no moral facts, only interpretations - nearly destroys both heroes before a father's love pulls them back: Priam's tears before Achilles, Luke unmasking Vader. Against nihilism the chapter defends moral realism through Apollo's lion simile (compassion and respect are objective facts about what persons require) and Kant's self-critical inquiry, with the Jedi Council's twelve-way deliberation illustrating that some interpretations are better than others, beyond Hume's problem of induction. Both epics settle on a 'Pagan Golden Rule' - help your friends and harm your enemies, but never lose compassion for either.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 24 "Nietzschean Themes in the Films of Charlie Kaufman" — Shaw argues Kaufman's films embody a Nietzschean 'Dionysian pessimism' organized around the will to power, eternal recurrence, perspectivism, and a bundle-theory of the self. He reads Being John Malkovich through the bundle self: personal identity is the dominant drive that acts, so Malkovich 'becomes' Lester/Mertin, the will that controls the vessel. Adaptation's Laroche voices Nietzsche's plastic power of forgetting, and Eternal Sunshine dramatizes eternal recurrence and amor fati as Joel and Clementine choose to repeat their doomed love. Synecdoche, New York, by contrast, Shaw judges a failure of passive nihilism—Caden as the fly who never leaves the bottle—deadening rather than life-affirming.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 21 "From “Impassioned Morality” to “Bloodless Agnosticism” A Philosophy of David Cronenberg through the Burroughs" — Jones Irwin analyzes Cronenberg's adaptations of Burroughs's Naked Lunch and Ballard's Crash, arguing that while all three share an aesthetic of body horror and a Nietzschean perspectivist experimentalism, Burroughs and Ballard hold an 'impassioned moralism' (Crash as cautionary tale, Marcuse's one-dimensional man, an ethics of complicity and responsibility) that Cronenberg replaces with 'bloodless agnosticism.' Cronenberg aestheticizes Burroughs's wife-killing and reads Crash literally, using Plato's appearance/reality (cave) distinction to show he strips out the sociopolitical and moral frame the writers intended.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 22 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Sanders coins 'sunshine noir' for Miami Vice as postmodern neo-noir, defining postmodernism via antirealism, skepticism about knowledge, and enigmas of personal identity, anticipated by Nietzsche's perspectivism. He analyzes three episodes: 'Heart of Darkness', where undercover agent Artie Rollins is consumed by his fantasy self (mirroring Crockett's Sonny Burnett) and hangs himself; 'Shadow in the Dark', where Crockett adopts the burglar's mind-set (Dilthey's Verstehen) in a dreamlike, glass-imagery structure that undermines the realist camera; and 'Lend Me an Ear', where the surveillance expert Duddy, echoing The Conversation, collapses into paranoid moral solipsism.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 15 "From Dollars to Iron The Currency of Clint Eastwood's Westerns" — McNaron traces Clint Eastwood's evolving western hero from the amoral 'Man with No Name' to The Outlaw Josey Wales, using Will Wright's plot typology plus Nietzsche, Aristotle, and Kierkegaard. He reads the Eastwood antihero's 'manly nihilism' and prizing of strength and style through Nietzsche's master/slave morality and perspectivism, his virtues (self-control, phronesis) through Aristotle, and his elevation of the aesthetic over the ethical/religious against Kierkegaard's stages. The film's central claim—that only words with 'iron' behind them (Josey and Ten Bears's pact) can found genuine community, unlike government's 'double tongues'—grounds a transcendental argument about the conditions for authentic community and justified vengeance.
- **The Philosophy of Werner Herzog**, ch. 13 "Fake News and Ecstatic Truths" — Kyle Novak uses Herzog's fabricated Pascal epigraph in Lessons of Darkness to distinguish 'ecstatic truth' from Trump-era 'alternative facts,' arguing that unlike Kellyanne Conway's deception, Herzog openly reveals his inventions to deepen an artistic experience. Rejecting Russell's correspondence theory of truth, Novak turns to Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation and The Gulf War Did Not Take Place to show how media create norms and a hyperreality independent of facts, then to Nietzsche's 'On Truth and Lies' (truth as agreed-upon metaphor) and Deleuze's affirmation of life as a non-relativist standard, concluding that Lessons of Darkness is 'sparse on facts but full of truths' that penetrate deeper than CNN footage.
- **The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute**, ch. 14 "2. Misinterpretation as the Author’s Responsibility (Nietzsche’s fascism, for instance)" — Berel Lang asks whether an author is responsible for being misinterpreted, defining a 'Fascist Minimum' (priority of the state over the individual, plus natural inequality asserted through war) and testing Nietzsche against it. He finds Nietzsche flatly rejects the first condition—his 'coldest of all cold monsters' attacks on the state and nationalism—and accepts the second only with heavy qualification. Lang locates Nietzsche's partial culpability in a 'Fallacy of Composition' by which readers like Bäumler transposed individual will to power onto the collective state, arguing that Nietzsche, foreseeing this abuse, chose not to 'build a fence' around his meaning and so bears responsibility 'up to a point.'
- **The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute**, ch. 26 "13. A Godfather Too Nazism as a Nietzschean “Experiment”" — Fischer contends that the 'historically effective' (not the 'real') Nietzsche could be read from opposite perspectives, and that Nazism is best understood as a post-Nietzschean 'experiment' licensed by the death of God and the collapse of accepted values ('wir machen einen Versuch mit der Wahrheit'). Invoking Nietzsche's own perspectivism from the Genealogy, and citing calls to 'push what is falling,' the coming 'fight for dominion of the earth' and the Cesare-Borgia-over-Parsifal remark, he argues Nietzsche was 'half a Nazi and half an anti-Nazi'—a genuine part-time godfather, against Kaufmann's overly 'gentle' de-Nazified reading.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 25 "23. The X-Files as Philosophy Navigating the “Truth Out There”" — The chapter argues that Darin Morgan's X-Files episodes philosophize by critiquing the show's own 'the truth is out there' mantra from within. Through the conflicting hypnosis testimonies and identical camera blocking in 'Jose Chung's From Outer Space,' Morgan cinematically stages Nietzsche's perspectivism and the claim that 'truth is as subjective as reality'; through Clyde Bruckman and the doomed Ansel of 'Quagmire,' he mounts an anti-Socratic case that relentlessly pursuing truth (as Mulder does) is not worth the ruin it brings. Kowalski then rebuts Morgan using Descartes's cogito and inference-to-the-best-explanation to defend objective truth against radical skepticism, arguing subjectivism about truth is self-refuting.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 95 "89. The Joker as Philosopher Killing Jokes" — Brake reads Moore and Bolland's The Killing Joke as staging Camus's absurd: the Joker tortures Commissioner Gordon to prove the world is random and unjust ('one bad day') and that reason, tied to continuous memory, should be abandoned for a fragmented 'multiple choice' self. Drawing on Nietzsche's wave-like unstable self (via Morrison's 'super-sane' Joker) and Foucault on how madness haunts modern reason, the chapter argues Batman and Gordon also flirt with madness, while questioning whether the Joker, seeking revenge, has really embraced the absurd or is more rational than he admits.

### The Problem of Evil

The problem of evil is the challenge of reconciling the existence of a God who is all-powerful, all-knowing, and wholly good with the reality of suffering and wrongdoing in the world. In its logical form it alleges an outright contradiction between such a God and any evil at all, while its evidential form argues that the sheer amount and distribution of suffering makes God's existence unlikely. Responses, known as theodicies, appeal to free will, soul-making, or the limits of human understanding to explain why a good God might permit evil.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 26 "Against Fascism" — Neal King argues the Buffyverse is proto-fascist: Buffy kills demons and vampires on sight within a race-like hierarchy, tempered only by an Augustinian split between natural and moral evil (soulless vampires cannot choose otherwise; soul-bearing humans like Faith, Willow, and Warren can repent), she derives authority from an ancient calling rather than democracy, and the graduation battle of 'Graduation Day, Part Two' stages citizenship forged in mass combat. He imagines a fascist Buffyverse of 'brownskirt' death squads and concludes only the show's secrecy prevents full fascism, finally recommending that the racism be dropped but the ritual sacrifice of evildoers kept — with Willow's flaying of Warren as the model.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 29 "No Big Win" — Reads sacrifice, salvation, and redemption in the Buffyverse as secular myth: vampires manifest the shadow-side of the human (Liam's resentment becomes Angelus, William's repressed romanticism becomes Spike's rebellion), and the contrast between soulless Spike's genuine moral growth through love of Buffy and human Xander's arrested development shows redemption is measured by 'what have you done with what you've been given.' The Purpose of Evil section argues good and evil must stay in balance because without evil there is no free choice and hence no redemption, and Angel's 'no big win' epiphany — no grand plan, only lessening suffering one kindness at a time — locates life's meaning in the journey of becoming rather than final victory.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 21 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Scott Davison asks whether Tolkien's world is Manichean - two equal forces of Good and Evil - and answers no: the Ring is not 'altogether evil' in itself but animated by Sauron's infused will, and nothing, not even Sauron, is totally evil, since 'nothing is evil in the beginning'. Developing Augustine's account, he shows evil as parasitic privation - Ringwraiths wear robes 'to give shape to their nothingness', the Eye is 'a window into nothing' - and traces evil to inordinate desire: Sam stays content with his garden while Boromir, Saruman, Denethor, and Sauron reach for more than their place allows. Evil unmakes itself (Saruman dies by Wormtongue's knife), and because goodness is the world's default, there is always hope of overcoming it.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 28 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Thomas Hibbs reads the Quest's ending as providential: the Ring is destroyed against Frodo's own will at the Cracks of Doom, through Gollum, exactly as Gandalf hinted when he said Bilbo was 'meant' to find the Ring, 'and not by its maker'. Providence first appears as chance - Bilbo's arrival, Aragorn's landing at the Pelennor, Gandalf 'sent back' until his task is done - and is discerned only in hindsight as the epic's dramatic unity. Against the worry that providence cancels freedom, he uses Kant on duty and dignity (Frodo's 'I will take the Ring', Sam's 'I must see it through', set against Denethor ruling his 'own end'), while noting Tolkien rejects Kant's autonomy/heteronomy split, and with Augustine he treats evil as parasitic, able only to mar itself ('Oft evil will shall evil mar').
- **The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am**, ch. 33 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" — Uses the show to argue the problem of evil is evidential rather than logical, and tests each theodicy against Sopranos cases: evil as natural-law by-product (Junior's and Jackie's cancers), punishment for sin (Carmela's cancer scare, Ralph telling Father Phil his hospitalized son is God's payback in 'Whoever Did This'), God's higher morality (rejected as meaningless as 'a triangle with four sides'), long-run goods (Artie's restaurant fire), and character-building (rejected with Melfi's 'How many people have to die for your personal growth?'). The free-will defense also fails - God could have given us Meadow-like dispositions - and Tony's 'You're born to this shit' versus Melfi's insistence on genuine choice dramatizes the debate. The chapter ends with Tony as the Old Testament Yahweh writ small: a jealous, vengeful, tribal ruler whose appeal is no more mysterious than His.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 12 "From Knowledge to Faith" — Lawler reads Crimes and Misdemeanors through Kant's problem of the Highest Good: Judah's unpunished murder of Dolores shows a world where the wicked prosper and the good (Cliff, the blind Ben) suffer, the scandal Job complains of, while Levy's suicide shows that a bare existentialist 'yes' to life fails without love. Kant's 'I had to deny knowledge to make room for faith' is applied to the film's two visions: the deterministic, dog-eat-dog world of science and Adam Smith's economic egoism (with Hobbes's war of all against all) is only appearance, not reality. Kant's gallows example shows Judah could have discovered authentic freedom by respecting Dolores's dignity rather than seeing 'the black eyes of an insect', and the postulates of freedom, God, and immortality ground Ben's not-really-blind faith — so it is Judah who is truly blind.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 24 "The End Is It All Darkness" — John Pappas reads Crimes and Misdemeanors through Glaucon's ring of Gyges in Plato's Republic: Judah Rosenthal's wealth and prestige are his invisibility ring, and when his mistress Dolores threatens exposure he 'pushes the button', has his gangster brother Jack murder her, and gets away with it. Against Socrates' claim that injustice corrodes the harmonious soul and that virtue is its own reward, the film, unlike Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment, lets the murderer and the 'yutz' Lester prosper while honest Clifford loses everything; Bergson's theory of the comic explains why Lester is invisible to himself, and Rousseau's reverie about what he would do with the ring marks Clifford as the one man who might use it decently. Aunt May's post-Holocaust atheism, 'might makes right' with nothing 'handed down in stone', supplies the argument from evil that releases Judah, leaving only the qualified hope that it is 'not all darkness'.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 26 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Dallas Willard defends the film's excess of violence as its whole point: it visualizes human evil as beyond the remedies of education, law, or counseling (the route Plato and Aristotle tried), with Satan — the androgynous figure carrying the smug dwarf through the scourging crowd — explaining why only Christ's non-resistant embrace of the cross can break evil's grip. Against the passive reading of 'the Passion,' he argues Jesus 'played' his judges, deliberately laying down his life to inaugurate the kingdom of God. The argument leans on the hidden God (deus absconditus): God stays hidden, contra Sartre's 'no nature' self-creation and closer to Pico della Mirandola, so that we can freely make ourselves, which is also why demanding 'more evidence' misses what belief in God requires.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 29 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Paul Moser answers the objection that an all-loving God could not plan His Son's torture by arguing the cross is God's scandalous self-giving love: Jesus is no mere moral guru but the unique atoning sacrifice (the mad/Satanic/Son-of-God trilemma, 'he who delivered me to you has the greater sin'), and the crucifixion is God's grand reversal where self-giving love defeats death. He attacks the 'nice god' of natural theology as domesticating idolatry — God hides His plans from 'the wise and the intelligent' — and holds that we know God not by philosophical evidence but through Gethsemane-style filial obedience ('not my will but yours'), noting that Gibson himself appears in the film driving a nail, casting all of us as the crucifiers whom God forgives.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 15 "The Fate of Evil after the Overthrow of the Empire" — Brown treats Luke's 'Is the Dark Side stronger?' as the problem of evil: distinguishing natural evils (the wampa, bigger fish) from moral evils (Tarkin destroying Alderaan), he surveys the Platonic craftsman working recalcitrant matter and the Manichean dualism of two gods - the Emperor as would-be 'evil incarnate' - before giving Augustine's answer. On Augustine's free-will defense, no creature is inherently evil; the origin of each moral evil is the creature's own pride and free choice, so Anakin, not the Emperor's seduction, is responsible for his turn ('I'm a Jedi. I know I'm better than this'). The chapter ends on whether evil can ever be finally defeated, arguing the Jedi prophecies of 'balance' fit a world where evil is a permanent possibility that heroism needs.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 32 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Frames the problem of pain with Hume's Dialogues (Demea and Philo) and reconstructs Lewis's answer as played out on Aslan: pain is God's megaphone that rouses Edmund on the Witch's frozen sledge and strips Eustace's dragon skin in the transforming embrace. Suffering also reveals hidden strengths, as when Aslan's pursuit goads Shasta into unexpected courage, modeled on Augustine's reading of the binding of Isaac as teaching Abraham, not God, what Abraham could endure. Aravis's claw wounds are treated as retributive punishment, tear for tear, exactly proportioned to the drugged slave's whipping, which the chapter defends via Lewis's retributivist theory against purely deterrent punishment. Because divine goodness aims at making creatures good rather than merely happy, Aslan can be both good and terrible, 'not a tame lion', since free will cannot be coerced into perfection.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 36 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Observes that only Talking Animals enter Aslan's country when Narnia ends in The Last Battle, then critically examines Lewis's case against wider animal salvation: derivative immortality through human love (Sarah Smith's train of beasts in The Great Divorce), compensation of animal pain in an afterlife, Lewis's follow-Descartes claim that most animals are sentient but not conscious enough to feel pain or have a surviving 'self'. The chapter argues each point fails: the physiological evidence shows animals suffer, resurrection or God-given souls remain possible (Strawberry's transformation into a winged Talking horse), and a compensatory hereafter is still the most promising answer to why a loving God permits the fawn's miserable death. Aquinas's rational-creature hierarchy frames the Talking/Dumb divide, and the Hindu-Buddhist rebirth theodicy is considered and rejected as unbiblical.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 17 "Prayer (A Euphemism for Butt-Kissing and Begging)" — Argues the Pythons' religious gags perform philosophy's preliminary job of challenging doctrine: the 'every sperm is sacred' family makes God a voyeur of contraception, the Life of Brian stoning (rocks flying each time anyone utters 'Jehovah') shows blasphemy law run absurd, and 'Christmas in Heaven' exposes heavenly reward as material compensation. Deploying Socrates and Plato — the Republic's ban on portraying pettiful gods, the Apology on why the virtuous need not fear death, and above all the Euthyphro — the chapter reads the witch-weighing and the Holy Hand Grenade as the ancient problem whether acts are just because God sanctions them, and the chaplain's toadying prayer against God's own 'don't grovel' as proof that sacrifice and prayer are bargaining a perfect being has no need of. The upshot is not atheism but the Socratic verdict that the mobs punishing blasphemy, not the mocked, are the real blasphemers.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 8 "U2 and Philosophy" — Wrathall's introduction argues U2 is philosophically interesting because its enormous popularity holds up a mirror to what 'we' care about (by Nietzsche's test of how a culture stands toward life) and because the band publicly wrestles with the contradictions of the technological-global economy: unprecedented freedom of choice paired with loss of rooted identity, and distant suffering ('Crumbs from Your Table') that we feel both powerless to fix and responsible for. Its showcase reading treats 'Miracle Drug' as a musical theodicy: Bono's plea 'God, I need your help tonight' is answered by the Edge's guitar and by the Matthew 25:35 refrain, so science and medicine count as works of Christian charity. The piece then frames the volume's essays: Plato's ascent of love in the early songs, Kierkegaardian despair after Achtung Baby, Bono's search for authentic identity, the simulacra of 'Even Better than the Real Thing', being-toward-death in the apocalyptic songs, and the Plato-versus-Aristotle quarrel over music's emotional power.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 17 "U2 and Philosophy" — Merrick sets XTC's 'Dear God' - being 'just struck' that no loving, all-powerful God rules this world - against U2's laments ('Wake Up Dead Man', 'Peace on Earth', '40') and Bono's reading of the Psalms as the blues shouted at God: both share outrage, but U2 adds yearning for the redemption promised in 'the story about eternity' plus Jubilee 2000-style action against debt and AIDS. He then argues the atheistic reaction to evil cannot be reason-producing, since neither divine design nor unguided evolution would give us a faculty that 'just sees' atheism from evil, any more than one that just sees there is no plant life on Mars. If God instead made us so that outrage at evil can trigger conviction that he will make all right, U2's reaction - 'Grace makes beauty out of ugly things' - can be as reasonable as visual perception.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 21 "Introduction" — Frames Part IV's philosophy of religion chapters. Johnson's chapter sets Cartman's million-dollar theme park against God's goodness, with South Park characters giving answers echoing Calvin, Hick, and Job; Gallagher's uses Rose's 'I just know' on Lost and Aquinas' distinctions between knowledge, opinion, and faith to argue that faith is not knowledge; and Eberl and Vines' uses Battlestar Galactica's Cylon monotheism versus Colonial religion and atheism to ask whether God can be proven, whether evil disproves him, and whether life is meaningful without God.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 22 "Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy" — Johnson turns 'Cartmanland' into a survey of answers to the problem of evil: Kyle's hemorrhoid-versus-Cartman's-wealth argument is the logical problem of moral evil; the story of Job fails because Job's continued belief does not rebut the evidence; Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' mirrors Calvin's and Edwards' God-glorifying answer; and Stan's 'Cartman is totally miserable' restores Kyle's faith via second-order goods. The free will defense (via Augustine) handles moral evil but not natural evil, so the chapter closes with John Hick's soul-making theodicy — mirrored by South Park's Jesus saying life is about overcoming problems and growing — before conceding the evidential problem of evil still stands.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 24 "“You Have to Believe in Something”" — Eberl and Vines use Battlestar Galactica to weigh theism against atheism: Baltar's scientific rationalism meets Aquinas' five ways (the universe's ordered structure demands an unmoved, uncaused cause), Six's faith faces the problem of evil answered through Augustine on the perverse will and John Hick's soul-making (Starbuck's mother, 'your life is a testament to pain'), while Hume's faulty-architect analogy presses the atheist case. The chapter concludes with Russell's 'A Free Man's Worship': even in a Godless universe the Colonials find meaning in comradeship and humanity's survival — 'the gods shall lift those who lift each other.'
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 12 "A Proper Answer" — Tallon takes Psycho as a case study in the problem of evil: after Hume's Epicurean challenge, Marion's shower murder and Norman's shattered psyche exemplify Marilyn McCord Adams's 'horrendous evils,' whose grotesque disproportion between any crime and its fate threatens to destroy the positive meaning of a life. The free will defense (Plantinga, Augustine) fails because Marion's death is bad luck rather than punished choice, and Hick's soul-making theodicy fails because evil here shatters character rather than building it. Carroll's definition of monsters is revised so that monsters are beings of severe disorder and disproportion, which Norman, Dracula, and Hitler all display, and Swinburne's Principle of Honesty offers the closest answer: God allows horrors because systematically preventing them would deceive us about the truth that evil is the privation of proper order, inherently grotesque and disordered.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 19 "Encore" — Randall Auxier adopts 'I trust Phil' — Phil Lesh the bass player who hears the whole sound — as his epistemic principle for asking whether death is to be dreaded, staging the essay around interview riffs with Deadheads Dale, Robbie, and Cory. Socrates in the Phaedo and the Buddha's Four Noble Truths converge on welcoming death — samsara is the 'Samsonite Scenario', bad luggage your own wishing keeps repacking — while Hume's Dialogues make God's power, goodness, and evil an inconsistent triad, so immortality is 'not that cool'. Kant's postulates (God, freedom, immortality) and categorical imperative prove too rule-bound for creative life; Whitehead's self-creativity and 'objective immortality of the past' supply the real bass line: even God cannot unmake what you have played, and the properly Grateful response is gratitude for the chance to add your riff to the Acid Test.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 6 "Introduction" — The editors' introduction opens with Socrates on trial for corrupting the youth of Athens and quips that on stage before the youth of Athens, Georgia, Cash could claim he was only asking "What is truth?" It frames Cash as Kris Kristofferson's "walking contradiction" whose paradoxes generate the book's questions: how evil fits a world rated by a benevolent God, where the enduring "I" hides while Cash insisted he was always changing, and what makes a law unjust. It also presents the Man in Black as social critic lobbying officials at San Quentin and Folsom for prison reform and raising money for reservation schools, before welcoming readers with the 1969 Arthur, Illinois concert where hippies and Amish rubbed shoulders.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 27 "Redemption" — Stephen Bilynskyj tests John Hick's soul-making theodicy—that God allows suffering because virtues like courage, temperance, and compassion need pain to form—against Cash's life and songs. Using Aristotle on habituation by pleasure and pain (Cash's first amphetamine euphoria and the ostrich-attack painkillers as missed occasions for temperance) and Aquinas on innate aptitude and divinely infused virtue, he argues virtue can form without suffering (by genes or miracle), so soul-making alone cannot justify evil, as Cash himself implies about his mother's grief after Jack's death. Cash instead locates redemption in Christ's suffering ('Redemption,' 'Why Me, Lord?'), while the intervention by his son John Carter shows pain still occasioning real growth in temperance.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 28 "“A Boy Named Sue” A Cashian Theodicy" — Jamie Carlin Watson reads Cash's Christian worldview as Augustinian: evil is not a positive substance but a privation or corruption of good (contra the monism Leibniz risks and the Manichean dualism Augustine rejected), so humans alone bear blame for moral evil through freely corrupting good things—'Cocaine Blues,' 'The Wall,' the Folsom prisoner who admits he 'had it coming,' and the divided self of 'The Beast in Me' echoing Romans 7. Natural evil, as in 'Guess Things Happen That Way' and the flood of 'Five Feet High and Rising' (Cash's mother's 'blessing' of rich river dirt), serves punishment or greater goods. 'A Boy Named Sue' dramatizes the residual tension: the father's get-tough-or-die theodicy convinces neither Sue nor us that the sheer amount of evil is justified.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 29 "Christmas in Jamaica" — David Werther frames Jack Cash's saw death—which Cash told Nick Tosches he considered murder—and the 1982 armed robbery at Cinnamon Hill as tests of Epicurus's old questions (quoted via Hume): could a good, powerful God have prevented these evils? Distinguishing the evidential from the logical problem, he answers the logical problem with Plantinga's libertarian free will: not even God could ensure Cash freely 'walked the line' with Vivian, since guaranteeing fidelity would eliminate freedom. He rebuts the compatibilist counterobjection by arguing, with Aquinas, that nothing can be the cause of its own nature, and argues heaven can still fulfill Johnny and June's hope of meeting 'on the far side banks of the Jordan' even if the redeemed can no longer act wrongly.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 23 "Moments of Redemption" — Ventimiglia sets Augustine's three answers to the problem of evil (free will, the toddler-at-the-doctor 'greater good,' evil as privation) against Nebraska's title track, where mass murderer Charlie Starkweather's 'I guess there's just a meanness in this world' makes Augustine's metaphysical gymnastics look like sophistry. 'Atlantic City' and 'Johnny 99' show free will compromised by debts, job loss and winners-and-losers, and Springsteen neither glorifies nor explains evil away. What Bruce and Augustine share is the yearning for redemption: Plato's Symposium pictures Eros — poor, barefoot, homeless, a hunger for the beautiful — and Springsteen answers that hunger with temporary moments of deliverance ('meet me tonight in Atlantic City') rather than guaranteed salvation.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 21 "Death on Veridian III" — Uses the holodeck to re-run the problem of evil: if a safe, painless simulated world like Barclay's fantasy life in 'Hollow Pursuits' is available, why is the painful real one better? Against Hume's Dialogues complaint that a benevolent God should have cut the pain, and Leibniz's best-of-all-possible-worlds optimism, the authors stack Whitehead's 'major beauty' of intensity, Aristotle's tragic magnitude, Swinburne's good of serious responsibility, and Hick's soul-making, reading Moriarty's imprisonment in 'Ship in a Bottle,' Q's humbling in 'Déjà Q,' and Kirk leaving the Nexus because 'nothing here matters' as evidence that intensity, responsibility, and character growth exist only in the real world. Kirk's death on Veridian III in Generations supplies the cautionary counterweight: the real world's goods cost real suffering.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 34 "Rescuing Princess Zelda" — Collins runs the problem of evil in Hyrule: Mackie's logical problem (an all-good, all-powerful God inconsistent with Ganondorf's evil) partially dissolves because nothing in the games says the three goddesses are omnipotent or omniscient, and Plantinga's free will defense, plus the best-of-all-possible-worlds idea, shows the Triforce is itself a free-will device, since a wish-granter that could grant any desire cannot limit evil without undoing itself. A 'game-making theodicy' modeled on Hick's soul-making theodicy explains why evil must be excessive and randomly distributed (else players would never strive to grow), and why the goddesses therefore provided a chosen hero: Link, unlike anyone on Earth, is the divine answer to excessive evil, divinely marked to reclaim the Triforce and rescue Zelda.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 19 "Roll Credits" — Dunn contrasts Baum's book, where evil is wonderfully 'small'—Dorothy melts the Witch in a fit of righteous anger at a stolen Silver Shoe, and personal plus social virtues (kindness repaid by the field-mice Queen) reliably conquer it—with the 1939 film, which smuggles back the 'heartaches and nightmares' Baum banished and resolves the Witch only by an accidental stroke of luck. He sorts Oz's harms into moral evils (the Witch's enslavements, the Wizard's frauds) and natural evils (the cyclone, the Deadly Poppy Field), cites Hume's catalogue of the world's ills, and observes that Baum needs neither Kant's postulate of God and a future life to join virtue with happiness nor John Hick's 'vale of soul-making' theodicy—Oz simply delivers the reward. Dorothy's abundant virtue at age five rebukes Aristotle (children, he says, cannot be virtuous or happy) and instead embodies Rousseau's Emile, natural goodness uncorrupted by civilization, while Chesterton's Doctrine of Conditional Joy and Tolkien's insistence on serious, non-technological magic frame the Old-World Christian outlook that Baum's demystified American fairy tale—and the movie's ending—quietly betray.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 24 "Thinking in Rainbows" — Jason Lee reads Hail to the Thief as a metaphysics of evil anchored in blurred boundaries between self and other: the "radiohead" conceit (Descartes' inert matter vs. thinking souls, Bowie's Thomas Newton) makes the sentient android of "Paranoid Android" the emblem of a self porous to signals and control, while "Where I End and You Begin" ("I will eat you alive") locates evil in the feared Other, glossed through Heidegger's das Nichts (evil as lack, not a thing) and Foucault's account of Enlightenment reason classing unreason as inhuman. He hears "Sit Down. Stand Up." as Auschwitz ("the raindrops could be gas") and "Go to Sleep" via The Wicker Man's human sacrifice, then argues The Most Gigantic Lying Mouth of All Time and Yorke's turn to Friends of the Earth and pay-what-you-want In Rainbows show philosophy is no longer sovereign: discourse with the Other is "responsibility, the call to respond ethically" — you have not been paying attention, so act before it's too late.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 12 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Robison measures Pullman's Authority against the three attributes that make the Christian God worthy of worship and finds it fails all three: the suffering of intercision victims like Tony Makarios and the Authority's delegation to the malevolent Metatron defeat omnibenevolence, because unlike with the real God we know no free-will theodicy applies, since the Authority simply does not care; his ignorance of Lyra's destiny (which witches and the Consistorial Court learn long before he does) defeats omniscience; and his demented weeping in the crystal litter before dissolving in open air defeats omnipotence. Since the Authority never created the universe and lied about being its creator, he is not God at all, so Pullman's plot never refutes the God of the philosophers. What the books do establish, she argues, is a powerful attack on organized religion: the Magisterium's suppression of Dust research and harming of children mirror real religious institutions' punishment of Galileo, resistance to evolution, and persecution of dissenters.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 25 "Red Sox Future" — Peter Kreeft argues that the classic pre-2004 Red Sox fan's philosophy is 'Primitive Mysticism' across all eight divisions of philosophy: certainty comes by mystical intuition (fans 'just know' Murphy's Law will strike, as with Dent in 1978 and Buckner in 1986), Parmenides's identity puzzles frame the post-championship identity crisis, free will only chooses among fated tortures, and the greatest good is humiliating the Yankees in Manichean fashion. He opposes Hegel's rational philosophy of history ('the real is the rational') with a history written by 'an insane, drunken, demon-possessed leprechaun,' and inverts the problem of evil: eighty-six years of systematically improbable suffering is probable evidence for a God whose design is a test of faith rather than a refutation of Him. The 2004 title's new rational-optimist 'Enlightenment' identity now threatens to erase the lovable old mysticism, leaving the fan unsure whether to mourn or rejoice.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 8 "Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New ‘Intelligent Falling’ Theory" — Ruiz uses Onion stories—'Jesus Answers Half The Prayers At Area Roulette Table,' 'God Answers Prayers Of Paralyzed Little Boy,' 'Christianity Celebrates One Billionth Unanswered Prayer'—to argue that belief in God lacks rational justification. Following Hume's empiricism (all ideas trace to sense perception), methodological naturalism, and Ockham's Razor, he shows that feelings of God's presence, scriptural circularity, and answered prayers (riddled with selection bias) all fail as evidence, and the prayer hypothesis is unfalsifiable—a theory that explains any outcome, like the brain tumor thanking God for its surviving surgery, is supported by no evidence. He closes by dismantling Paley's watchmaker design argument through the infinite regress ('who designed God?') and by treating 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' as the reductio of design reasoning.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 13 "Jesus Delays Second Coming Because Of Offensive Article" — Littmann runs Hume's Dialogues argument from evil through Onion headlines: 'God Answers Prayers Of Paralyzed Little Boy' (Timmy Yu's resounding no), 'God Outdoes Terrorists Yet Again,' 'God Wastes Miracle On Running Catch In Outfield,' and 'God Cites Moving In Mysterious Ways As Motive In Killing Of 3,000 Papua New Guineans.' He dispatches the theodicies one by one: limiting God's power or goodness (as Mill's lesser deity would) abandons the God of the tradition; the free will defense fails because police rightly restrain gunmen and no human freedom explains hurricanes; soul-building is pointless for a being who could implant compassion innately or stage fake evils; the 'no best possible world' dodge would excuse the reporter who watches a man burn; and the mystery defense makes reason useless. He concludes no all-knowing, all-good, all-powerful God exists, while insisting readers think it through for themselves.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 30 "Voltaire Lives" — Douglas Ficek traces The Onion's God stories — 'Lord Under Investigation For Failure To Provide,' God refusing to heal paralyzed little Timmy Yu, and 'God Cites Moving In Mysterious Ways' — back through Voltaire's Candide to Leibniz's theodicy, the 'best of all possible worlds' doctrine that Dr. Pangloss keeps reciting through hanging, slavery, and syphilis until Candide concludes we must cultivate our garden. The chapter's sharpest claim is that theodicy works by victim-blaming: Jerry Falwell's 9/11 rant earned the headline-only 'Jerry Falwell: Is That Guy A Dick Or What?' because he excused God by blaming secular Americans, just as Pastor Ellsworth blames heathen tsunami victims.
