When Eleanor, Chidi, Jason, and Tahani learn the point system and can no longer earn points, they form the 'Soul Squad' to be virtuous for virtue's sake, echoing Aristotle's telos and Kant's claim that acting from fear of hell is a heteronomous, non-moral motive. She reads the unfair points system (no human admitted in 521 years) through Rawls's Veil of Ignorance and shifts the show toward rehabilitative justice, and treats the Good Place residents' boredom via Bernard Williams's tedium-of-immortality argument, with Chidi's 'wave returns to the ocean' speech mapped onto Hindu atman/Brahman and moksha.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 10 "8. Breaking Bad as Philosophy The Moral Aesthetics of the Anti-hero’s Journey" — Koepsell reads Breaking Bad as a satirical epic whose antihero Walter White illustrates philosophy better than argument can. He casts Walt's pro/con list before killing Krazy-8 as an ad absurdum refutation of Bentham's hedonic calculus and a violation of Kant's categorical imperative (treating Krazy-8 as mere means), and shows Walt cultivating the Aristotelian vices — recklessness, intemperance, injustice — rather than virtues. Drawing on Sartre, he argues Walt lives in bad faith by becoming 'Heisenberg' for the look of the other (the 'say my name' scene), like Leone's Man with No Name, and that Camus's Sisyphus marks the happiness Walt refused. He concludes the show endorses Hume's emotivism: justice is an aesthetic felt experience, not a rule.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 46 "43. Ex Machina as Philosophy Mendacia Ex Machina (Lies from a Machine)" — Grinnell argues Ex Machina is fundamentally about lying, read through Kant's deontology. He frames Nathan's rigged Turing test on Ava against Glaucon's Ring of Gyges challenge and Kant's two formulations of the categorical imperative, deriving three 'wrinkles': lying is heteronomous programming rather than the autonomy Nathan seeks; the experiment is defensible only if Ava fails, since a genuine person may not be manipulated (Formula of Humanity); and the cascade of lies among Nathan, Caleb, and Ava vindicates Kant's absolute prohibition on lying. He uses Caleb's telling of Frank Jackson's Mary's Room and Searle's weak/strong AI distinction to question whether Ava's 'pleasure response' amounts to genuine consciousness or personhood.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 62 "59. Don’t Look Up as Philosophy Comets, Climate Change, and Why the Snacks Are Not Free" — The chapter argues Don't Look Up is less a film than a moral imperative: its comet is an allegory for climate change, and Randall Mindy's on-air breakdown presents Singer-style simple premises (the end of human life is bad; prevent bad things you can) that compel action. It uses Plato's knowledge-as-the-Good and 'blameworthy ignorance' to condemn the willfully ignorant (Kate's parents, the Orlean Bros) who act as if they know, and Kant's categorical imperative to condemn General Themes's 'free snacks' lie and to cast the moral as the rational. It defends the comet/climate analogy against critics and insists individual action is insufficient while collective government action is required.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 81 "76. The Last of Us as Moral Philosophy Teleological Particularism and Why Joel Is Not a Villain" — Horn takes The Last of Us as moral philosophy, arguing Joel is read as a villain only because players assume consequentialism or deontology. On Bentham/Mill's utilitarianism Joel fails to maximize utility by killing many to save Ellie; on Kant's categorical imperative his lying, stealing and killing are always impermissible. Horn instead defends 'teleological particularism' — an agent acts rightly when acting in conformity with a role, roles being socially constructed and variable — so Joel's role as Ellie's surrogate father (mirrored in his carrying her out as he carried Sarah, and the 'Future Days' lyric) obligates him to put her above humanity. On this view Joel's refusal to let the Fireflies kill Ellie, and his final lie, are morally permissible, not villainous.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 85 "80. Detroit Become Human as Philosophy Moral Reasoning Through Gameplay" — Engels and Evans argue that Detroit: Become Human stages moral reasoning through the interactive stories of the androids Connor, Kara, and Markus, whose 'deviant' awakening they read through Frankfurt's distinction between wantons and persons with second-order desires and through Kant's requirement of the ability to do otherwise. Scenes like Markus scavenging a pump regulator from a dying android, the blood-on-hands visualization after his speech, and Kara protecting Alice force players to weigh Kantian, utilitarian, virtue, and Gilligan-style care frameworks. Through Alice's reveal as an android and the grieving-widower scene, the game makes an implicit anti-speciesist argument (via Singer) that beings who can suffer are morally considerable, and that agency and responsibility emerge through suffering and struggle.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 93 "87. Frank Miller’s Batman as Philosophy “The World Only Makes Sense When You Force It To”" — Bein reads Frank Miller's Batman (chiefly The Dark Knight Returns and Year One) as rejecting the utilitarianism he ascribes to Superman—who would 'rightly' nuke a city to prevent two—in favor of a Nietzschean will to power, distinguished from mere force (Macht vs. Kraft), born of Miller's own mugging. The Joker problem is worked through Kant's categorical imperative, desert-based death penalty, and the slippery slope of denying moral standing to the insane. Bein then separates Miller's avowed libertarianism (Nozick's canteen/lifeguard thought experiments, the minimal state) from Bruce Wayne's coercive 'Bat-libertarianism,' and confronts the 'Frank Miller problem' of Holy Terror's Islamophobia against Miller's anti-corporate, anti-Reagan streak.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 100 "94. Yes, Roya and Philosophy The Art of Submission" — Goldberg, Gavaler, and Chavez use Trotman and Denich's Yes, Roya—where Roya dominates Joe and Wylie professionally (publishing under Joe's name) and sexually, all consensually—to ask how the three major Western ethical theories can accommodate consensual dominant/submissive relationships. They argue Aristotle's virtue ethics handles them via unequal friendships (submissives depending more, within a mean), Kant's Formula of Universal Law permits them once consent is built into the maxim (aligning with the Formula of Humanity), and Mill's utilitarianism sanctions them because justice and felt safety, grounded in consent, follow from the Greatest Happiness Principle.

### I–Thou Relation

The I–Thou relation is a central idea of the Austrian-born Jewish philosopher Martin Buber, set out in his 1923 work I and Thou. Buber distinguishes two basic ways of relating to the world: the I–It attitude, in which we treat others as objects to be used, analyzed, or experienced, and the I–Thou attitude, in which we meet another as a genuine presence in a direct, mutual encounter. Authentic existence, for Buber, is dialogical, arising in these moments of meeting, which he saw as ultimately pointing toward relation with the eternal Thou, or God.

- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 15 "Bad Faith" — Lee reads the 'Breakdown' episode of Alfred Hitchcock Presents existentially: when the executive Callou coldly fires Humka and hangs up on his despair, he treats a person as a thing, Buber's 'I-It' pseudo-listening where Humka sought an 'I-Thou' dialogue with the godlike source of authority in his world. Heidegger's account of inauthenticity explains the mask of rational control behind which Callou hides, and Sartre's bad faith names the self-deception by which he pretends his godlike management of others is justifiable. Paralyzed and taken for a corpse after a car crash, Callou can be saved only when rational strategy fails and he finally weeps: the single tear reveals his caring nature, Jessie addresses him person-to-person, and, vulnerable before God and others, he becomes an authentic self, Hitchcock's pointed moral for bosses who give an employee the sack.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 17 "There is No Dark Side of the Moon Really. Matter of Fact It’s All Dark" — Johnston reads The Dark Side of the Moon through Buber's I and Thou: modern life traps us in the I-It mode of experience, from 'Welcome to the Machine' to teachers who treat students as replaceable Its ('Hey, teacher, leave us kids alone!') and Horkheimer's instrumental reason that turns personnel into 'human resources,' while the album repeatedly calls us to the I-You encounter, from 'Echoes'' strangers whose glances meet ('I am you and what I see is me,' Waters's origin of empathy) to 'Breathe''s 'don't be afraid to care.' He links the opening heartbeat and the breath of 'Breathe' to Buber's eternal You, defends Buddhism against Buber's charge that enlightenment is worldless monologue (the Buddha becomes one with the world, a perfect reciprocity like the innate You of the womb), and accepts Nietzsche's point that the Enlightenment's abstract God is dead while insisting, with Buber, that encounter with the eternal You remains possible. The album itself, he concludes, resists degenerating into an It: even if 'the sun is eclipsed by the moon,' the light persists and Dark Side can be the antidote to the It-world.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 21 "A Better Way of Living Your Life" — Akers argues the Doctor follows neither rule deontology, utilitarian calculation, nor virtue ethics, but a relational ethics of care in Noddings's and Slote's sense, expressed as Buber's I-Thou stance — insisting an enslaved Ood is 'a "he," not an "it"' and addressing Donna, Jack, and Rose each as individuals in 'Journey's End'. Linking this to Nussbaum's claim that wonder widens moral concern and to Kant's dynamic and mathematical sublime, she argues the Doctor needs human companions like Rose, Martha, and Donna as a human-scale reference point that renews his wonder — and with it his ethics — while his wiping of Donna's memory shows the care tradition's dangers of power imbalance.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 182 "Chapter 34 - Beyond Lies the Wub" — Dick's first published story dramatizes the moral status of a rational nonhuman: Peterson's wub, a telepathic, philosophical Martian pig-creature, reads minds, discusses Odysseus and individuation, and pleads that it is 'a sensible being like yourselves', yet Captain Franco - obsessed with eating it - freezes it mid-sentence, shoots it looking him in the eye ('Back on the farm we had hogs'), and serves it for dinner, dismissing Peterson's grief with 'It is only organic matter, now.' The wub's personhood is established entirely through language and philosophy, but speech fails to protect it from being treated as meat, and the closing irony - Franco resuming the wub's own Odysseus meditation, as if the mind survived its meal - underscores how thin the line is between person and livestock. The story thus stages the problem of other minds and the ethics of killing sentient beings who demand to be addressed eye-to-eye rather than dined upon.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 19 "9. Are You Experienced" — Proposes an 'experientialism' — subjective conscious experience as fundamental reality, defended against eliminativists who would explain experience away as illusion — and finds its moral core in Martin Buber: the title song and 'May This Be Love' call the beloved out of an I-It world ('made out of gold and can't be sold') into reciprocal I-You relation ('take hold of my hand'), while 'The Wind Cries Mary,' 'Purple Haze,' and 'Manic Depression' lament love that is absent or unreciprocated. Experiences feel most intensely real, the chapter argues, when the Platonic order of love puts what matters most at stake — which is why kissing the sky, even without being kissed back, is worth recommending.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 27 "15. I, Thou, and the Neighborhood" — James McLachlan pairs Rogers's 'holy ground' between television set and viewer with Buber's turn from ecstatic religion to the everyday after failing the young visitor of 1914 who came to him in need: the I-You relation of full presence versus the I-It of use is what 'It's You I Like' sings. Against Sartre's 'Hell is other people' and Augustine's reading of the burning bush as the omnipotent God, Rogers and Buber (with Rosenzweig's translation of God's name as 'the One who will be present') make listening, presence, and everyday 'twinklings' the substance of neighborly love.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 18 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Edelheit, a rabbi, reads Stewart's Jewish persona as an echo of Martin Buber: both disclaim the titles (philosopher, journalist) yet 'point out the window' at what they have seen, and both practice engagement, 'You shall not withhold yourself', with genuine responsibility as real responding, epitomized for him by the face-to-face Crossfire confrontation. He walks through the 'Matzorian Candidate' segment on the Republican Jewish Coalition (the 'Yarmulkometer' ratings, Michele Bachmann's kibbutz years and mispronounced 'chutzpah'), the 'Faith/Off' Passover-versus-Easter segment pitting a chocolate egg against the Seder plate ('Jews! Camera 3'), and Earth (The Book)'s satirically rewritten Binding of Isaac and Reform-Judaism prayer jokes. All of this is read as Buberian dialogue, mocking religion from within rather than at it, and refusing silence in the lineage of Rabbi Joachim Prinz's warning that the most tragic problem is silence.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 16 "It Worked" — Lee reads Jack, Locke, and Desmond as studies in Sartrean bad faith and authenticity: Christian Shephard's Red Sox fatalism is determinism as an excuse for moral failure, Locke swings from a Kierkegaardian leap of faith (pushing the button as his Abraham-and-Isaac trial) into nihilism when the Pearl film suggests the button is a psychological experiment, and Desmond's Humean skepticism yields to sacrificial faith in the fail-safe. He argues Jacob is the show's greatest con man, so Jack's acceptance of destiny in 'The End' remains a free choice rather than predestination. The finale's sideways world then moves Lost from secular existentialism to religious existentialism, read through Buber's I-Thou relation in Sawyer and Juliet's 'It worked' reunion and the all-religions church, where as Gandhi held every path leads to the same place.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 28 "26_LaRocca_Chapter_025.html" — Bill Nichols writes an open letter to Errol Morris explaining his bodily 'revulsion' at Standard Operating Procedure, Morris's film on the Abu Ghraib torture photographs. Nichols gives three reasons: the painfully limited, remorseless perspective of the MP guards elevated to mythic screen scale; the morally impossible reenactment tracking shots that put the viewer in the torturers' point of view (compared to Schindler's List); and the total absence of the Iraqi detainees' voices. He faults Morris for decontextualizing and fetishizing the images and forfeiting a moral center, contrasting the film with Rithy Panh's S-21, and casts the missing ethical encounter in terms of Buber's I-Thou relation of mutual honesty while wishing he had Fanon's capacity to treat the perpetrators' suffering.
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 3 "Introduction" — The editors' introduction surveys Nolan's oeuvre chronologically to argue that a recurring theme of self-destruction and unstable self-identity runs through every film. It reads Following's needy Young Man through Buber's I/Thou (existing fully only when a Thou acknowledges you) and Hegel's master/slave dependence between Cobb and his mark, casts Inception's spinning top as a version of Descartes's dream argument about telling the real from the constructed, and invokes Hobbes when the Joker introduces 'a little anarchy' into Gotham. It frames Doodlebug as Nolan's most Freudian film and Interstellar as uniting personal identity, moral choice, and epistemology in Cooper's self-sacrifice.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 21 "A Better Way of Living Your Life" — Laura Geuy Akers argues the Doctor lives by a relational ethics of care rather than deontology, utilitarianism, or virtue ethics. Drawing on Noddings's care ethics and Buber's I-Thou versus I-It stance, she shows the Doctor responds to particular others (insisting the Ood is "a he, not an it," addressing each companion individually before surrender) and even ethically cares for the Master. She pairs this with Nussbaum's and Kant's accounts of wonder and the sublime, arguing the Doctor's human companions (Rose, Martha, Donna) restore his sense of wonder and give his immortal life meaning.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 16 "It Worked" — Sander Lee reads Jack, Locke, and Desmond through Sartre's bad faith and authenticity and the objectifying 'Look' (the keyhole example), casting Jack the man-of-science as a Humean skeptic who condemns his father's fatalist evasion of responsibility while Locke's devotion to pushing the button is a Kierkegaardian leap of faith modeled on Abraham and Isaac. Desmond David Hume embodies skepticism yet opens to omens and self-sacrifice; and Lee argues the finale's multi-faith 'church' moves Lost from Sartre's secular existentialism toward Kierkegaard and Buber's I-Thou relation, exemplified by Sawyer and Juliet's redemptive bond and Gandhi-like religious universalism.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 18 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Joseph Edelheit hears an echo of Martin Buber in Stewart's Jewish persona and satiric method, likening Buber's 'I am no philosopher… I go to the window and point to what I have seen' to Stewart pointing at media and political hypocrisy. Reading Buber's dialogical I-Thou, ideal of the character-forming teacher, and demand against silence, he interprets 'The Matzorian Candidate,' the Passover-vs-Easter 'Faith/Off' segment, the Earth (The Book) Binding-of-Isaac parody, and Stewart's 'Jews! Camera 3' address as face-to-face, responsible engagement—satire as a valid form of Buberian dialogue against the evil of silence.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 17 "From There to Here, from Here to There, Diversity Is Everywhere" — Tanya Jeffcoat builds a philosophy of diversity around 'normative hubris' and 'totalizing tendencies,' using the Sneetches, the butter-battling Yooks and Zooks, and Daisy-Head Mayzie as cases of in-group/out-group dehumanization. Encountering the Other is framed through Buber's I-It versus I-Thou (Yertle treating his subjects as a throne), Fanon on the psychic violence and alienation of the oppressed, McIntosh's invisible knapsack of privilege, and Freire's humanization. Horton and the Lorax model standing with the disenfranchised, and Jeffcoat rebuts moral relativism via universal human rights and Dewey's democracy as a personal way of life that condemns intolerance.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 25 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Mattern argues the heart of good fatherhood is mercy – 'faithful, compassionate love' – as an attitude of the heart, not a technique. Drawing on Aquinas's account of habitus and his ranking of mercy among the greatest virtues, plus Gabriel Marcel's 'creative fidelity,' Solovyov, Jean Vanier, and Karol Wojtyla on love as affirming another's value, he contrasts remote, justice-oriented fathers with empathic ones. He illustrates with overlapping Venn-diagram circles of father and child and with responding to his 7-year-old son's shoplifting through listening and repair rather than spanking.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 16 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Hernandez contrasts 'dark' existentialism — Sartre's café-bound claim that hell is other people and that the self is imprisoned in others' looks (illustrated by Starbucks' Pike Place backlash reshaping its identity), and Camus's absurd alienation — with an 'optimistic existentialism' that finds meaning in community. Drawing on Kierkegaard's Christian love, Jaspers's 'encounter,' Marcel's turn toward the other (her Sweet Eugene's pregnancy story), and above all Buber's I–Thou versus I–It, she argues the coffee community (neighborhood boards, fair-trade activism, the neighborly cup) is an existential ground where isolated bodies-toward-death create shared hope by treating each patron as a Thou rather than a discarded It.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 27 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Silber uses his own Match.com romance with Karin to argue that virtual 'meeting' differs phenomenologically from face-to-face meeting, which Buber's I-Thou (vs I-It) makes into a whole-being encounter that online traces and aspects cannot supply, invoking 'all real living is meeting.' He treats the dating market as a site of Kantian danger, contrasting price with the dignity of persons in the kingdom of ends, and warns that the market's efficiency threatens objectification and commodification. He then deploys Sartre's bad faith, facticity and transcendence, and 'existence precedes essence' to diagnose online self-misrepresentation (lying about height, age, photos) as inauthenticity, while briefly setting Derrida's 'nothing outside the text' against Plato's Phaedrus preference for speech over writing.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 21 "19. The Orville as Philosophy The Dangers of Religion" — The chapter argues that Seth MacFarlane's The Orville is a pointed critique of religion, especially when merged with political and military power. Through the warrior-god Avis worshipped by the Krill (read as stand-ins for militant evangelicals and Islamist jihadists) and the Moclans' patriarchal bigotry, it contends religion is portrayed as archaic and dangerous. It deploys Socrates's Euthyphro argument to reject divine command theory, contrasts the Krill's dogmatic certainty with the secular Union's self-correcting ethics, and invokes Buber's I–Thou to explain the 'de-souling' of outsiders, while defending Lockean separation of church and state against theocracy and theonomistic ethics.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 84 "79. Cyberpunk 2077 as Philosophy Balancing the (Mystical) Ghost in the (Transhuman) Machine" — Lay reads Cyberpunk 2077's transhuman Night City against the enhancement debate. Using the Ship of Theseus, Parfit's continuity plus fission/fusion (V and Johnny 'fusing,' the Delamain AIs) and Clark and Chalmers's extended mind, he argues enhancement neither destroys personal identity (which Parfit says doesn't matter) nor dehumanizes users — it may be the purest expression of Clark's cyborg humanity. The real danger is corporate exploitation of bodies, explained via Adorno's culture industry and Arendt's banality of evil. Buddhist nonattachment (Nagarjuna's emptiness, echoed by a Schopenhauer shard) grounds each ending's pacification-versus-attachment theme, but Lay corrects it with Weil's critique of power and Buber's I-Thou, concluding the game urges transcending the boundary between 'me' and 'you' through mystical interpersonal relation.

### Ren (benevolence/humaneness)

Ren, often translated as benevolence, humaneness, or co-humanity, is the central virtue of Confucian ethics. It names the disposition to care for others and to treat them with the consideration one would wish for oneself, expressed in Confucius's counsel not to do to others what you would not want done to you. For Confucius, ren is the inner moral quality that animates all the virtues and marks the fully realized human being, cultivated through self-discipline and relationships rather than merely followed as a rule.

- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 23 "One with the Team" — Chelsea Harry contends that Red Sox Nation embodies a Confucian rather than Cartesian self: against Descartes's cogito and the egocentric, endorsement-chasing player (A-Rod, the traded Manny), the Sox way treats selfhood as constituted by family, community and mutual sacrifice, from Mike Lowell's hometown discount to Yaz's hospital escape and Schilling's bloody sock. She maps Confucian benevolence (jen) onto Wakefield, Varitek and Ortiz describing how fan love powers their play, filial piety onto the retired numbers honoring franchise elders like Pesky, Doerr and Cronin, and Chung-ying Cheng's 'naturality' onto the fans' claim to be the team's twenty-sixth player, so Johnny Damon's defection reads as the treachery of an ungrateful villager. The 'je ne sais quoi' of team spirit is thus Confucian unity: becoming oneself by subordinating the I to the We.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 7 "Free Your Mind, and Your Roundhouse Will Follow" — Young argues that dojo courtesy is not the fantasy that good manners win fights (Napoleon and the Karate Kid's Johnny lost on skill, not rudeness) but the framing of a craft within a way of life. He maps Aristotle's techne/ethos distinction onto the Japanese jutsu/do pairing to show founders like Kano, Funakoshi and Ueshiba treated fighting as one part of a whole ethical character, reads his seiza apology to an injured yellow belt through Confucian ren, li, yi and shu, and traces Shinto purity into the sincerity (kime) of committed sparring. His black-belt humiliation by seniors becomes Zen's 'courtesy of brutal': ego-deflating violence that trains no-mindedness (muga, Takuan Soho's fudoshin).
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 13 "“Well, It Got Big Laughs”" — Barkman uses Confucius (ren, yi, li, and zheng ming, treating each person according to what he or she is) and Aristotle (eudaimonia, virtue as a habituated mean between extremes, practical wisdom) to indict 30 Rock for valorizing Jack's 'semi-virtuous path', the smug middle between best and worst announced in 'Do-Over'. He catalogues injustices the show laughs off: Liz's serial lies about her age, hobbies, and adoption; Jack's priority flu shots for the powerful in 'Flu Shot'; Tracy's insubordination about dogfighting in 'Rosemary's Baby'; and Kenneth's servility as everyone's punching bag. On liberality and piety, Jack's confession that 'capitalism is my religion' and Liz's 'I pretty well do whatever Oprah tells me' show the show settling for semi-virtue, which the chapter says even comedy must not endorse.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 30 "Every Soul Experiences the Battle Within" — Reads Zuko's arc as a war between Legalism and Confucianism: Ozai's agni kai scarring of his son, Azulon's death sentence, the Fire Nation Oath and school discipline ('The Headband') all enact Han Fei's principle that bad human nature needs terrifying sanctions, and Azula's 'trust is for fools' completes it. Against this stands Iroh's Confucian education in ren — teaching that honor cannot be separated from humaneness, that a mugger deserves tea and encouragement, and that wu-wei-like patience knows when to speak. Mencius's innate compassion explains why Zuko's 'amazing lie' realization could unfold, Katara, Sokka, and Hakoda embody Confucian filial bonds that adopt Aang, Toph, and finally Zuko, and Solzhenitsyn's gulag insight closes the chapter: the line between good and evil runs through every human heart.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 30 "Every Soul Experiences the Battle Within" — Reads the Fire Nation royal family as a philosophical battle between Legalism (Han Fei, taking Xunzi's dictum that human nature is evil, so order requires terrifying sanctions: Ozai burning Zuko in the agni kai so 'suffering will be your teacher', Azulon's death sentence on Zuko, the Fire Nation Oath recited in schools) and Confucianism (Iroh teaching ren, that true honor cannot be had apart from humaneness, preferring honorable begging over theft, and talking a would-be mugger into tea). Zuko's 'battle within' is the legacy of his two great-grandfathers, Sozin's Legalism versus Roku's line, and it is resolved when he disowns Ozai, calls Iroh his 'real father', and is adopted into Team Avatar, whose filial bonds (Katara's care, Hakoda's sacrifice) contrast with the scheming royal family. The chapter closes with Solzhenitsyn's image of the line between good and evil passing through every human heart to explain why Zuko's inner war resonates.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 11 "“Your Heart Knows”" — Argues that Disney's Mulan transplants a distinctly modern Western ideal of the authentic self ('true to your heart,' 'Reflection') into a Confucian honor culture where the self is constituted by roles and relationships, filial piety (xiao), and ren as the virtue that binds people into larger wholes — which is why the film flopped in China. The matchmaker debacle, Fa Zhou's 'I will die doing what's right,' and the family's shame show a culture where dishonor stains the whole family and even luck (the cricket Cri-Kee) fixes moral standing, conflicting with Western assumptions about individual responsibility. The chapter ends by noting Mulan now resonates with young Chinese viewers, asking whether the Western individualist self is a truth about humanity or a cultural export that, like the Huns, has scaled the Great Wall.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 32 "The Rhythm by Which We Live Our Lives" — Kowalski interprets Kuzco's arc through Mencius: the emperor's pampered upbringing (eight hands replacing a squeezed toy, Yzma's loveless regency) is the 'hatchets and frost' of the Ox Mountain parable blunting his innate moral sprouts. The gorge scene stages Mencius's child-at-the-well thought experiment — Kuzco's spontaneous snatch of falling Pacha is a 'give-away' action betraying compassion he denies having, which Pacha diagnoses just as Mencius did King Xuan sparing the ox — and Pacha's family, quasi-adopting Kuzco, supplies the loving soil Mencius says the sprouts of ren need to grow.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 12 "Notes" — Decker parallels the Republic's fall into Palpatine's Empire with the Zhou dynasty's collapse that birthed Chinese philosophy, reading three Jedi from the Dark Times comics through it. K'Kruhk, guided by the Zatoichi-like Master Zao, learns wu-wei - following the Force rather than forcing outcomes, with Laozi's Dao as the Force's Chinese analogue. Dass Jennir's struggle over what 'Jedi' means after killing a slaver becomes Confucian rectification of names and the cultivation of ren, while Kai Hudorra's loss of faith, withdrawal to a casino, and final sacrificial stand against Vader embody Mozi-style pragmatic minimalism redeemed by Jennir's virtuous example.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 31 "“Tell Your Sister, You Were Right”" — Yang argues that Luke's surrender to Vader on Endor is neither foolish nor irrational but an exercise of Confucian filial piety: Luke reveres the absent Anakin as an exemplar (picked out through admiration of Obi-Wan's stories and the lightsaber), insists 'I know there is good in you' against Vader's claim that the name means nothing, and is vindicated when Anakin turns and says 'You were right about me'. His imperfect training under Obi-Wan and Yoda functions like Confucian ritual (li), forming habits that respond with harmonious ease to surprises such as Palpatine's trap, and filial piety extends past death in the funeral pyre Luke builds on Endor, honoring his father as the Analects prescribes.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 31 "NOTES" — The Terjesens pit Kant's impersonal morality — Sam's contractual distance from the thieving Mickens is exactly how he would treat strangers — against Confucius and Mencius, for whom filial duties are the nursery of virtue: we learn benevolence by serving parents and revering elders, Lafayette's care for Lettie Mae and Tara shows family forming moral character, and the Upright Gong's covering for a father's sheep-stealing grounds Jason's 'sometimes the right thing to do is the wrong thing'. Mencius's King Shun, who abdicates and carries his criminal father into exile, models how Tommy and Jason should put family first while accepting the cost, while Mozi's universal love surfaces in Godric's 'forgiveness is love', and the chapter concludes that family counts only insofar as it develops our moral nature — the line between Tommy and Sam.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 12 "Third Hole Finding the (Fair)Way with Confucius and Ben Hogan" — Laumakis builds an analogy between pursuing excellence in golf and living a flourishing human life, then contrasts two models. Reading Confucius's Great Learning and Analects onto golf, he casts a repeating swing as a 'well-ordered kingdom' rooted in self-cultivation, and reinterprets ren, li, yi, and xiao so the 'authoritative player' masters the game through ritual practice, a teacher-parent (xiao), and doing what is appropriate in each lie. Against this social conception he sets Ben Hogan's Five Lessons as a 'rugged individualist' account stressing solitary practice and personal responsibility, and proposes a contextual pluralism as a mean between communitarian absolutism and individualist relativism.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 29 "Fourteenth Hole Plato and Confucius on the Form of Golf From the Real to the Ideal" — Stephen Laumakis stages a thought experiment pitting Plato the Idealist against Confucius the Realist/Pragmatist on how to think about and play golf. On Plato's theory of Forms, every club, ball and swing is an imperfect copy of a timeless, unchanging Form—there is a 'perfect' swing (Tiger Woods, Ernie Els) that par and the handicap system let us measure ourselves against, so golf is about striving toward the Ideal. Confucius, read through the 'Great Learning' and 'Analects' (li, ren, self-cultivation, unrelenting practice), instead prizes the situation-sensitive sage who negotiates each bad lie (Phil Mickelson's flop shots). Laumakis concludes the good golfer must integrate both: pursue perfection while wielding practical wisdom about when to go for it and when to lay up.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — The editors' introduction argues that the unifying theme of Lee's films is the struggle for authentic self-identity, framed through Charles Taylor's dialogical self and Kierkegaard's line that anxiety is the dizziness of freedom. It surveys how Confucian virtues (ren, li, xiao) and Daoist wu-wei play out across Pushing Hands, The Wedding Banquet, Eat Drink Man Woman, Crouching Tiger, Sense and Sensibility, Brokeback Mountain and others, treating each protagonist as caught between traditional obligation and personal desire. It invokes Nietzsche's claim that all philosophy is autobiography to justify reading Lee's films (he said 'it's all in my films') as a coherent authorial philosophy.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Kohler-Ryan and Palmer treat 'sense' and 'sensibility' as a spectrum Lee explores through sisterhood in Sense and Sensibility (Elinor/Marianne) and Crouching Tiger (Shu Lien/Jen). Elinor and Shu Lien embody sense, Shu Lien specifically the Confucian balance of li and ren that lets her soften ritual with humanity; Marianne embodies Burke's British-Romantic sublime while Jen embodies Daoist immersion in the dao. Reading door-frames, windows, hair-combing rituals and Shu Lien's hairpin as symbols, they argue only Sense and Sensibility achieves integration in time, whereas Li Mu Bai's confession that he lived sense and sensibility as separate spheres comes too late.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Bush argues that Brokeback Mountain transcends both the heterosexual western archetype and queer theory by presenting male sexuality through Mencius' philosophy and John Corvino's ethics of homosexuality. Using Mencius' four sprouts (ren, li, yi, zhi) and doctrine of natural goodness, he reads Ennis as the character in whom sexuality is contextual, cultivated and moral rather than merely physical, so the relationship between Ennis and Jack becomes an ethical friendship grounded in ren, the virtue Mencius says is most intense among friends. The bystanders Aguirre and Alma keeping the secret, and the final shirt-and-postcard scene, illustrate zhi as contextual moral judgment and homosexuality reframed as ethical rather than sexual.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 23 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Komasinski explains Confucius's advice to fathers through three ideas: ritual (li, glossed as 'cultural grammar' – engagement rings, saying 'I love you'), excellence/virtue as excelling at relating to others (ren, 'co-humanity'), and wisdom. Using the Analects' 'Upright Gong' passage (fathers and sons cover for each other) beside Plato's Euthyphro, he shows Confucius prizes the father-son bond over law, and reads the parable of the prodigal son and Tu Wei-ming's 'personality ideal' to argue fathers should lead by virtuous example rather than punishment.

### Li (ritual propriety)

Li refers to the rituals, manners, and forms of proper conduct that structure social and ceremonial life in Confucian thought. Ranging from religious rites to everyday etiquette, li provides the concrete patterns through which people express respect, mark relationships, and harmonize their communities. Confucius held that observing li was not empty formality but a means of cultivating inner virtue, so that outward propriety and genuine moral feeling reinforce one another.

- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 17 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — In an imaginary salon hosted by the baker 'la Brioche,' the goddess Eris drops a golden apple inscribed 'Atkins,' and three philosophers fight over the credit. Rousseau claims Atkins's war on refined flour and 'invented fake food' as his own back-to-nature, state-of-nature legacy; Confucius counters that Americans are 'grazers' without li, that culture is nature's flower, and that only ritual propriety can counteract the advertising that fills the void; Democritus claims the scientific core — 'hyperinsulism,' 'benign dietary ketosis' — as atomism's heir, deriding Rousseau's general will as democratic truth-concocting and Plato's otherworldly philosopher-king. The debate ranges over free will versus scientific prediction-and-control and ends unresolved over a refusal of brioche.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 29 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Jones narrates a day riding a customized Sportster around O'ahu as a lived Daoism that heals the Platonic-Cartesian mind-body split: the ride enacts Zhuangzi's 'rambling without destination' and Cook Ding's effortless wu-wei, rider li (the low hand-greeting among riders) is Confucian ritual propriety, and the island's dry and wet ranges embody yin and yang through whose flow the rider blends. Heraclitus's 'expect the unexpected' and 'the sun is new every day' are vindicated when a container truck stops short and only the disciplined, ego-less low-side, dropping the beloved bike while riding the skid, saves the rider's life, sealing the day's lesson that there is never freedom without discipline. Sartre's hell of other people appears in the cagers' compartmentalized inattention, and the chapter closes with Zhuangzi: 'The way is made by walking it.'
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 10 "I Still Miss Someone The Self and Its Travels Along the Way" — Geisz explains the Confucian social dao of ritual (li), humaneness (ren), filial piety and the junzi, the Daodejing's metaphysical Dao with its unity of opposites, and Zhuangzi's tales of free wandering, then maps all three onto Cash's songs. Zhuangzi's "Free and Easy Wandering" answers Cash's road songs ("I've Been Everywhere," "The Wanderer"), Cook Ding's effortless carving answers John Henry's hammering in "The Legend of John Henry's Hammer," and the scrambled countdown of "Twenty-Five Minutes to Go" echoes Zhuangzi's logic-bending humor. The payoff is Cash's own country Yin-Yang of interdependent opposites, freedom chained to imprisonment ("Folsom Prison Blues"), sin twinned with redemption ("I Hung My Head"), fidelity with betrayal ("Jackson," "Cocaine Blues"), and a self that, unlike Zhuangzi's self-forgetting sage, must travel a temporal path carrying its guilt, yet stays on what Geisz calls a very wide superhighway of a Dao.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 7 "Free Your Mind, and Your Roundhouse Will Follow" — Young argues that dojo courtesy is not the fantasy that good manners win fights (Napoleon and the Karate Kid's Johnny lost on skill, not rudeness) but the framing of a craft within a way of life. He maps Aristotle's techne/ethos distinction onto the Japanese jutsu/do pairing to show founders like Kano, Funakoshi and Ueshiba treated fighting as one part of a whole ethical character, reads his seiza apology to an injured yellow belt through Confucian ren, li, yi and shu, and traces Shinto purity into the sincerity (kime) of committed sparring. His black-belt humiliation by seniors becomes Zen's 'courtesy of brutal': ego-deflating violence that trains no-mindedness (muga, Takuan Soho's fudoshin).
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 8 "Of the Simple and Complex" — The book's introduction argues that Downton Abbey's genius is letting universal moral and social realities burst forth in particular incidents: the snuffbox affair makes Thomas a classic villain (stealing, defaming Bates) and Bates a Christ-, Socrates-, or Confucius-type innocent, showing that moral clarity is beautiful rather than superficial. It reads the Thomas-Bates-Grantham hierarchy as an invitation to think about 'greater and lesser,' tying propriety (Confucius), dharma, and justice (Aristotle) to paying attention to social difference, which Western viewers raised on equality find foreign yet intriguing. It closes by insisting the characters are more complex than their types - Thomas takes a beating to spare Jimmy, Bates may have killed outside the law - and previews the volume's themes of Humean 'small morals' (etiquette), women's rights, work, place, and war.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 34 "20. The Good and the Gracious" — Olson and Taliaferro read manners as the story's moral barometer: the genuine, effusive compliments exchanged by Westley and Inigo atop the Cliffs of Insanity, and Fezzik's sporting wrestling, express care and connection, while Humperdinck's and Rugen's courtly politeness is camouflage for torture, murder, and war. Against Machiavelli's instrumental use of courtesy in The Prince, they recruit Plato's sophrosyne as 'good form' inseparable from justice, wisdom, and courage, and Confucian li as etiquette that instructs and steadies us toward virtue, with Hobbes's 'small morals' marking the hollow version; they add that manners also police class, from Buttercup's 'Farm Boy' to reality TV and the financiers of the Great Recession who used the correct fork.
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 13 "“Well, It Got Big Laughs”" — Barkman uses Confucius (ren, yi, li, and zheng ming, treating each person according to what he or she is) and Aristotle (eudaimonia, virtue as a habituated mean between extremes, practical wisdom) to indict 30 Rock for valorizing Jack's 'semi-virtuous path', the smug middle between best and worst announced in 'Do-Over'. He catalogues injustices the show laughs off: Liz's serial lies about her age, hobbies, and adoption; Jack's priority flu shots for the powerful in 'Flu Shot'; Tracy's insubordination about dogfighting in 'Rosemary's Baby'; and Kenneth's servility as everyone's punching bag. On liberality and piety, Jack's confession that 'capitalism is my religion' and Liz's 'I pretty well do whatever Oprah tells me' show the show settling for semi-virtue, which the chapter says even comedy must not endorse.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 8 "Of the Simple and Complex" — The editors' introduction argues that Downton's quaint domestic plots burst with universal moral and social meaning beneath their surface. Using the season 1 snuffbox incident, in which Thomas frames the innocent Bates for theft, it shows how the episode stages archetypal villainy and innocence akin to the universal figures of Plato's Republic and world mythology, so the 'simple' plot is morally clear rather than superficial. It then reads the hierarchy of Thomas, Bates, and Lord Grantham through Confucian propriety and Aristotelian justice, suggesting that justice partly consists in attention to 'greater and lesser,' something Western viewers raised on equality find foreign yet intriguing. Finally it insists that as concrete persons all three are morally mixed (Thomas takes a beating to spare Jimmy, Bates may have killed outside the law, Grantham is generous to tenants but cold to his daughters), and that this complexity is what rewards philosophical reflection, along with Hume's 'small morals' of etiquette.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 31 "“Tell Your Sister, You Were Right”" — Yang argues that Luke's surrender to Vader on Endor is neither foolish nor irrational but an exercise of Confucian filial piety: Luke reveres the absent Anakin as an exemplar (picked out through admiration of Obi-Wan's stories and the lightsaber), insists 'I know there is good in you' against Vader's claim that the name means nothing, and is vindicated when Anakin turns and says 'You were right about me'. His imperfect training under Obi-Wan and Yoda functions like Confucian ritual (li), forming habits that respond with harmonious ease to surprises such as Palpatine's trap, and filial piety extends past death in the funeral pyre Luke builds on Endor, honoring his father as the Analects prescribes.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 12 "Third Hole Finding the (Fair)Way with Confucius and Ben Hogan" — Laumakis builds an analogy between pursuing excellence in golf and living a flourishing human life, then contrasts two models. Reading Confucius's Great Learning and Analects onto golf, he casts a repeating swing as a 'well-ordered kingdom' rooted in self-cultivation, and reinterprets ren, li, yi, and xiao so the 'authoritative player' masters the game through ritual practice, a teacher-parent (xiao), and doing what is appropriate in each lie. Against this social conception he sets Ben Hogan's Five Lessons as a 'rugged individualist' account stressing solitary practice and personal responsibility, and proposes a contextual pluralism as a mean between communitarian absolutism and individualist relativism.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 29 "Fourteenth Hole Plato and Confucius on the Form of Golf From the Real to the Ideal" — Stephen Laumakis stages a thought experiment pitting Plato the Idealist against Confucius the Realist/Pragmatist on how to think about and play golf. On Plato's theory of Forms, every club, ball and swing is an imperfect copy of a timeless, unchanging Form—there is a 'perfect' swing (Tiger Woods, Ernie Els) that par and the handicap system let us measure ourselves against, so golf is about striving toward the Ideal. Confucius, read through the 'Great Learning' and 'Analects' (li, ren, self-cultivation, unrelenting practice), instead prizes the situation-sensitive sage who negotiates each bad lie (Phil Mickelson's flop shots). Laumakis concludes the good golfer must integrate both: pursue perfection while wielding practical wisdom about when to go for it and when to lay up.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Kohler-Ryan and Palmer treat 'sense' and 'sensibility' as a spectrum Lee explores through sisterhood in Sense and Sensibility (Elinor/Marianne) and Crouching Tiger (Shu Lien/Jen). Elinor and Shu Lien embody sense, Shu Lien specifically the Confucian balance of li and ren that lets her soften ritual with humanity; Marianne embodies Burke's British-Romantic sublime while Jen embodies Daoist immersion in the dao. Reading door-frames, windows, hair-combing rituals and Shu Lien's hairpin as symbols, they argue only Sense and Sensibility achieves integration in time, whereas Li Mu Bai's confession that he lived sense and sensibility as separate spheres comes too late.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Thompson argues that Lee's 'cowboy aesthetic' of rugged isolation in Brokeback Mountain (Ennis and Jack) and Crouching Tiger (Li Mu Bai, Shu Lien, Jen) is only apparent: the characters are always already embedded in Confucius' five cardinal relationships, read through Xunzi's darker view that selfish desire must be curbed by ritual and social hierarchy. Ennis and Jack seem lone individuals but are defined by ties to Alma, family and each other, and Jen's redemption comes when she abandons self-serving desire to re-establish her Confucian relationships. Citing Nietzsche's gloss on Aristotle that only a beast or a god lives alone, it concludes there is no truly isolated cowboy.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Bush argues that Brokeback Mountain transcends both the heterosexual western archetype and queer theory by presenting male sexuality through Mencius' philosophy and John Corvino's ethics of homosexuality. Using Mencius' four sprouts (ren, li, yi, zhi) and doctrine of natural goodness, he reads Ennis as the character in whom sexuality is contextual, cultivated and moral rather than merely physical, so the relationship between Ennis and Jack becomes an ethical friendship grounded in ren, the virtue Mencius says is most intense among friends. The bystanders Aguirre and Alma keeping the secret, and the final shirt-and-postcard scene, illustrate zhi as contextual moral judgment and homosexuality reframed as ethical rather than sexual.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Dull reads Eat Drink Man Woman through a Hall-and-Ames 'focus-field' model of personhood, analyzing harmony via metaphors of a culinary dish, music and a sports team where each element keeps its integrity within a whole. He diagnoses the Chu family by pairing Mencius (morality as expression of the four sprouts) against Xunzi (desire must be structured by ritual): Chef Chu is 'repressed as a turtle', Jia-Jen hides behind ritual, Jia-Ning acts on impulse, and Jia-Chien lacks direction. Their romantic transformations restore harmony, answering Chu's question 'is there more than food and sex?' affirmatively, as expression, desire and ritual come into balance and his sense of taste returns.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 23 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Komasinski explains Confucius's advice to fathers through three ideas: ritual (li, glossed as 'cultural grammar' – engagement rings, saying 'I love you'), excellence/virtue as excelling at relating to others (ren, 'co-humanity'), and wisdom. Using the Analects' 'Upright Gong' passage (fathers and sons cover for each other) beside Plato's Euthyphro, he shows Confucius prizes the father-son bond over law, and reads the parable of the prodigal son and Tu Wei-ming's 'personality ideal' to argue fathers should lead by virtuous example rather than punishment.

### Tripartite Soul

The tripartite soul is Plato's account, chiefly in the Republic, of the human psyche as composed of three parts: reason, which seeks truth and can grasp what is best; spirit, the seat of anger, ambition, and the love of honor; and appetite, the desires for food, drink, sex, and material goods. He argues for the division by noting inner conflict, as when a person is thirsty yet refuses to drink, showing that one part can oppose another. Justice in the individual consists in these parts fulfilling their roles under the rule of reason, mirroring the ordering of classes in the just city. The model grounds Plato's psychology, ethics, and political theory alike.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 9 "The Buffyverse’s Moral Compass" — Greg Forster argues the Buffyverse's moral structure is neither Christian nor Nietzschean vampire fiction but Platonic eudaimonism: the just person is always happier than the unjust. Faith is the test case — her pleasure-seeking turn to evil with Mayor Wilkins, her body-swap theft of Buffy's life in 'Who Are You?', her self-disgust ('You're nothing! Disgusting, murderous bitch!'), and her begging Angel to kill her in 'Five by Five' enact Plato's Republic examples of the Ring of Gyges and the unjust person mistakenly honored while the just one is punished. Buffy's invisible crime spree in 'Gone' and her 'the work that I have to do' sacrifice in 'The Gift' display the same eudaimonist pattern, with the caveat that the Buffyverse follows a Rousseau-like moral psychology in which compassion, not reason, does the moral work.
- **The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am**, ch. 15 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" — Argues ancient ethics explains why Tony, who has 'the world by the balls', still feels like a loser. Plato's Republic diagnoses him as a 'civil war' of unintegrated motivations (loving father and murderer at once, as in 'College'), a condition power over others only worsens; Aristotle teaches that happiness is activity with self-sufficient, integrated desires rather than a list of possessions, and Epicurus's 'sober reasoning' is the therapy Tony never gets. The Hawthorne quotation Tony reads in 'College' and his Gary Cooper ideal from 'The Happy Wanderer' frame the point: Cooper in High Noon is unmesswithable because he does not need vengeance, whereas Tony's compulsive revenge shows the world has the grip on him.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 11 "Why Not to Buy the Porsche" — Skoble uses Manhattan's confrontation scene — Isaac telling Yale 'you're too easy on yourself... you'd rather buy the Porsche' over the hominid skeleton — to build an account of integrity as fidelity to correct moral principles, requiring an integrated character in which reason and desire agree. He distinguishes integrity from mere consistency (the 'consistent Nazi') and from stubbornness, and models it on Plato's just person who 'harmonizes the three parts of himself'. Aristotle's account of habituation defends Isaac's slippery slope: Yale's repeated lies for expediency are forming the kind of character who would inform on friends, so integrity is an objective yardstick of a well-lived life, as Isaac's amends to Tracy at the end confirms.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 146 "The Common Good versus the Greater Good" — Maps Voldemort onto the Sophists - Thrasymachus's claim that the unjust always come out ahead - through his pattern of exploiting followers' trust for power and pleasure, while Plato's two-pronged reply runs: cosmic justice in the afterlife (the flayed child beneath the bench as Voldemort's just fate, sealing it by refusing remorse) and the intrinsic goodness of justice via the tripartite soul with reason ruling spirit and appetite, the four cardinal virtues, and the health analogy. Harry, seeking Dumbledore's wisdom, showing courage in facing death, and devoted to justice for wizards and Muggles, embodies the moral life as the rational choice, while Voldemort's snakelike appearance externalizes his disordered, sick soul.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 81 "Superheroes and the Ring of Gyges" — The chapter's heart: Glaucon's Ring of Gyges and 'harsh view' of human nature — justice as the weak's compact against the strong, a lineage running from Hobbes to Nietzsche — are powerfully denied by superheroes and by Frodo, who resist the power of the ring. Socrates' tripartite soul and justice-as-psychic-harmony are read as preparation for the Republic's real answer, the ascent to the eternal Form of the Good, which the chapter extends through Aristotle's teleology and virtue ethics: super-powered people, denied any standard social role, must wrestle with what their potential is for — from Kingdom Come's retired Superman and Spider-Man 2's Peter Parker to Astro City's Samaritan, with Uncle Ben's 'With great power comes great responsibility' as the upshot.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 99 "Reasons to Be Moral" — Extracts two candidate answers from Spider-Man — Reason One, that immorality rebounds on you (Uncle Ben's death), tested and weakened by the Ms. Poore poverty-theft case, and Spider-Man's agonized "Because it is right" to the Green Goblin, the Kant-and-Bradley motive of duty — and finds both insufficient to show morality is rational. It then tests Plato's answer that only the moral have harmony of soul (reason governing appetite and spirit) against Flash Thompson and self-forgiving sinners, and Aristotle's "virtue is its own reward" against the thought experiment of virtuous Arachnid-Girl rotting in prison while the fraudulent Norm Osborne flourishes.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 29 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Reads Eustace, Uncle Andrew, Experiment House, and Miraz's censored Narnia as Lewis's portraits of modern secularism, which treats the world as mere resource and dismisses the transcendent regardless of evidence. It argues that denying intrinsic value collapses into a Nietzschean master morality of power, visible in Uncle Andrew's use of the children as guinea pigs and the Lone Islands' slave trade, and exposes the secular 'conditioner's' self-exemption as a violation of the Principle of Relevant Difference. Against the Green Witch's debunking of Puddleglum's sun and Aslan as copies of a lamp and a cat, it deploys the Platonic-Cartesian copy/original model of ideas to argue transcendent ideas (eternity, perfection, necessary being) cannot be derived from lower material causes, suggesting instead that the material world is the 'shadowland' copy of a divine original.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 11 "Poker and Philosophy" — Ventimiglia mines No-Limit Hold'em for seven lessons philosophers also teach: we lack certain knowledge (Descartes' cogito is the famous quest for certainty, but philosophy's own history of disagreement proves uncertainty is the human condition), and like William James against Clifford we must still believe and act without the nuts — waiting for pocket aces while the blinds eat you alive is no strategy. Risking everything echoes Thoreau's escape from lives of quiet desperation, trusting hunches over arithmetic follows Thoreau and Peirce's sentimentalism, and the Darwin-and-Spencer competition of tournament poker hides a deeper cooperative social contract: get caught cheating and you are out of the game. It closes with Plato's four classic virtues from the Republic — wisdom, courage, moderation, and the justice of a balanced soul — as the perfection of a poker player.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 25 "U2 and Philosophy" — Tollefsen revives Plato's ancient quarrel between philosophy and poetry: artistic imitations, three removes from the Forms and aimed at the soul's emotional part, stir 'imitative emotions' - purer, shorter-lived, effort-free surrogates for the real labors of love, faith and community - and he builds a four-stage account of the U2 formula (idealized transcendent love in the lyrics, religious imagery fusing lover and God, the Edge's Big Music crescendo, and the concert 'you' extended to the crowd, as in the Elevation-tour 'I Will Follow' with its 'Amazing Grace' bells) to show U2 are masters of exactly this seduction. The healing fans felt after September 11th may therefore be an image of redemption rather than the reality. Where Aristotle and Aquinas would educate the emotions rather than suppress them, Tollefsen's quarrel is with imitation itself; his verdict is that U2 suffer from Misplaced Artistic Pretension - high imagery where honest trash (or genuine complexity) would do.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 12 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Getachew maps Plato's Republic archetypes onto the Bond universe: the appetite-ruled Tyrant is Goldfinger, Zorin, Stromberg and the SPECTRE megalomaniacs; the spirit-ruled Guardian is 007, compared to Alcibiades and to Medea's vengeful fury (Bond letting Trevelyan fall 'For me'); and the reason-ruled Philosopher-King is M, whose ideal republic of common children and expendable numbers mirrors MI6's recruitment of orphans and its treatment of Bond as '007', never a person. She then challenges Plato's preference for the eternal Forms and immortality, using Freud on transience and Heidegger's being-toward-death (via Tolstoy's Ivan Ilych) to argue that mortality and risk are what make life worth living. Bond's stylish risk-taking, like the cello-case downhill escape, shows we need a balance between the Guardian and the man of thought.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 25 "Introduction" — Frames Part V's ethics chapters. Adams' chapter updates Plato's ring of Gyges for Heroes — with Claire's and Sylar's powers, why be moral? — answered by the properly ordered tripartite soul; McAleer's uses The Office to illustrate Aristotle's wit as a mean between buffoonery and boorishness; White's uses the Batman/Joker problem and a Bat-trolley version of Foot's case to argue deontologically that Batman need not kill the Joker; and Loftis' reads Watchmen's Ozymandias and Rorschach as a failed utilitarian and a failed deontologist, pointing to 'who watches the watchmen.'
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 26 "But Isn’t It Only Natural" — Adams answers Plato's ring-of-Gyges challenge with Heroes: even when invisible, wrongdoing corrupts the wrongdoer, because justice is to the soul what health is to the body. Claire's refusal to claim credit for the fire rescue shows thumos (spirit) responsive to logistikos (reason), Sylar's uncontrollable hunger for powers is epithumetikon (appetite) ruling the soul, and Hiro's Vegas cheating shows how injustice makes life spin out of control; Claire's apology to Brody illustrates the Pagan Golden Rule — help your friends, harm your enemies — tempered by Plato's caution that enemies may become friends.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 9 "Evaluating Zelda" — Frome tackles the paradox of fiction through Wind Waker: why do we fear Gohma, feel sad when Link leaves his grandmother on Outset Island, or care when Tetra's identity is revealed, though we know none of it is real? He rejects the illusion theory (we never suspend disbelief enough to call the police), Carroll's thought theory (fear is too fast and too vivid for mere thoughts), and Walton's pretend theory (involuntary pretending and the uniform way all players see the sail break it). Instead he argues for a multi-level mind, modeled on Plato's divided soul in the Republic and Fodor's mental modules: local unconscious appraisals react to the fire as if real, while a global appraisal of reality-status keeps us in our chairs.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 14 "How Beckenbauer and Zidane Practiced the Four Cardinal Virtues" — Coumoundouros explains soccer greatness through three Platonic ideas: the Form of the footballer, which Pelé (1,281 goals, three World Cups, the save by Banks his header 'infected' with greatness and the infamous miss against Uruguay) and Maradona (the Hand of God and the Goal of the Century past five English defenders) approximate as near-perfect imitations, with position-specific Forms like forward Form for Pelé and attacking-midfielder Form for Maradona. Excellence as performing a proper function well (Republic 353a) then accounts for modern players—Ronaldo's evolved winger role, Henry converted by Wenger into a striker, Marta averaging a goal per game proving women's soccer equals the men's. Finally the Republic's four cardinal virtues grounded in the tripartite soul apply off and on the pitch: Beckenbauer playing the 1970 'Game of the Century' with a fractured clavicle and marshaling the 1974 final shows courage, wisdom, and moderation in just balance, while Zidane's 2006 head-butt on Materazzi shows the spirited part overwhelming reason, and with it greatness itself.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 10 "And the Winner Is" — Lynch pits Plato against the Shaolin monks on the nature of the self that martial training is supposed to master. Plato's Republic makes the athlete-warrior Guardian a harmonious, rationally ruled tripartite soul whose bravery is 'remembering what ought and ought not to be feared', trained so reason governs aggression; Buddhism instead dissolves the self into five impermanent aggregates (illustrated by the chariot analogy) and reads mushin as a direct taste of no-self. He awards the practical decision to the Buddhist fighting monks, since no-self explains martial spontaneity and naturally arising compassion, while admitting Plato's substantive rational soul is not strictly refuted.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 39 "You Don’t Always Get Along" — The chapter animates Hume's bundle as a 'little republic' of mental citizens without a universal citizen, staging a dialogue between Person-Hume, who cannot believe there is no self, and Philosopher-Hume, who counsels beer and billiards. It traces the view back to Plato's Republic: the tripartite soul (with Freud's id-ego-superego as a modern rerun), the example of desiring and refusing the same cold beer when you must collect your mother from the airport, and Leontius raging at his own eyes before the corpses, cross-chatter as civil strife among inner citizens, exactly what the doctors diagnose as Fred's symptom.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 143 "A Palace Revolution" — The fantasy election brings in Plato's Republic: Richards's defense attorney Bill Carter functions as his Ring of Gyges, letting him vanish from legal consequences and raising Plato's question of whether we act justly only from fear of punishment. The tripartite soul is mapped onto Keef — appetites (drugs, sex, Jagger's 'Bitch'), spirit (the Glimmer Twins' rivalry), rationality (busting his head reaching for a library book) — and justice becomes the harmony under rationality's rule. In the ideal city of philosopher kings, auxiliaries, and workers, the sign at the gate reads 'NO POETS, NO ROCK'N'ROLLERS': Richards is exactly the corrupting poet Plato bars.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 144 "Shout and Scream and Kill the King" — The election plays out: Richards blows away the auxiliaries with 'Play with Fire' and whips the working-class appetites into a frenzy (put on Exile on Main Street after a few rounds to test Plato's fear of the poets). Young Keef's soul is appetite-led — the 'Blue Lena' Bentley with its hidden drug compartment embodies a spirit in service of drugs and artistic hunger, with rationality demoted to scoring the fix. The resulting Republic of Keef, driven fast on the edge of a cliff, vindicates Plato's warning that wherever the appetites lead, tyranny soon follows — as the author concedes through his own pipe-smoking.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 9 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Auxier argues that Klosterman's signature lists always carry an 'immanent order' of value, illustrated by the twenty-two teenagers' simultaneous classroom thoughts in Downtown Owl and his own contested ranking of the five greatest rock bands. He reads the seventeen-page sober conversation between Julia and Vance, printed with 'what she meant' and 'what he meant' under each remark, through Kant's extensive versus intensive magnitudes: the spoken words are an extensive whole, but the multiple unshared perspectives form an intensive whole no list can exhaust, which is why philosophers crave the 'tug of necessity' that intensive relations never deliver. Plato's Leontius, who rubbernecked at corpses despite his disgust, explains both Klosterman's TMI confessions in Killing Yourself to Live and the 'recoil of the shit-canon' by which we learn to order our desires, while Julia's carbon-monoxide death in the blizzard shows the world converting intensive possibilities into extensive necessity.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 10 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Greg Littmann stages Plato's hypothetical review of American Gods under the Republic's charges against poetry: the novel is full of 'greatest of all lies' about gods behaving badly, from Odin and Loki's sacrificial plot to Czernobog's head-smashing, gods degrading themselves into lesser forms like Horus the road-kill-eating hawk and Media as Lucille Ball, and characters ruled by passion rather than reason, from Mad Sweeney drinking himself to death to Thor's suicide, corrupting a soul that should be governed by rationality. Against this he sets Aristotle's Poetics: listening to music and intellectual leisure are valuable in themselves, fiction is more philosophic than history because it shows what could happen, the impossible is justified when it astounds, and catharsis through pity for figures like the weeping Mad Sweeney purges rather than corrupts. Because American Gods' absurd premise unfolds with internally probable, character-consistent events (loyal Shadow, loving Laura, grifter Odin), it satisfies Aristotle's requirement that fantasy make artistic sense.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 24 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Greg Littmann maps Ape City onto Plato's Republic class by class: orangutan rulers who legislate, censor, and propagandize; gorilla warriors who enforce; chimpanzee producers who do all the work - including, pointedly, the science Plato made no provision for; and humans as the 'barbarians' Plato says may be enslaved or exterminated. The overlaps are detailed: the Sacred Scrolls' first article of faith functions as the noble lie's myth of the metals, orangutan funerals promise heaven to keep gorillas unafraid of death, and Zaius's erasing of Taylor's dust-writing and blowing up of the archaeological cave enact the rulers' duty to supervise stories. But the films also refute Plato: hereditary orangutans show that power corrupts philosopher kings, Dr. Honorius's 'reason' is dogma serving the faith, the gelding threat that finally breaks Taylor cracks the tripartite-soul analogy of justice, and democracy's rough virtue is that it lets us remove rulers 'without sticking anybody with iron spears.'
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 14 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Hirschbein has Freud analyze the audience first: like Van Alden, the repressed hypocrite whose true self erupts in drowning Sebso and burning his workplace tormentor, we watch Nucky and Jimmy as avatars of our own repressed aggression and lust. Freud's contest of Eros and Thanatos - his reframing of Plato's tripartite soul as id, ego, and superego - explains why civilization demands renunciation while spectacle like Boardwalk supplies vicarious gratification, with Milgram's and Zimbardo's experiments showing how thin the civilized veneer is. Jimmy's seduction by his mother and killing of the Commodore enact the Oedipus complex writ large, Freud's primal-horde story of the sons' parridical revolt against the father, and the show's catharsis is what lets us live with the sin.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 9 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Jeff Ewing argues the moral fabric of Ender's Game is virtue-ethical, first testing Ender's leadership against Plato's cardinal virtues, tripartite soul, and rigid class hierarchy of the Republic, then finding Aristotle a far better fit. Ender's trademark use of the minimum force necessary against Stilson, Bonzo, and the buggers sits at Aristotle's mean between cowardice and excess, while his adaptability and disregard for rules and hierarchy only count as virtues in Aristotle's framework - though his ignorance of crucial facts explains why xenocide, like his beatings, fell outside the mean.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 22 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Jennifer Baker asks whether the Devil does ethics any good and answers no. Against the tempter hypothesis she sets the traditional virtue ethics of Plato, Aristotle, the Stoics, and the Epicureans, where bad behavior traces to habituated vice rather than demons, and the cure is consciously cultivating virtues by hitting the mean between excess and deficiency - Johnny's practiced honesty, the Evangelical cousin's marital vows. She faults the Devil as a one-size-fits-all explanation of evil, a glamour machine (via Postrel and the Romantic Satan of Blake, Byron, and Milton), and a scare tactic the Epicureans warned corrupts character, closing with Plato's divided-soul counsel to aim at long-term goods and a dismissal of Luther's spite-drinking stratagem.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 26 "15. Death Begets Death" — The Bocks trace Darrow's education out of vengeance: in Plato's tripartite soul the spirited part (anger) must obey reason, and Aristotle's virtue of mildness—anger at the right things, toward the right people, for the right length of time—is the golden mean between slavish and irascible that Darrow has not yet reached. Darrow learns the difference when he hands Titus over to Cassius's vendetta and admits 'That wasn't justice': retribution in Kant's lex talionis tradition must be dispassionate and proportional, while vengeance is past-oriented and insatiable, and Darrow's own bombing of the Ganymede docks shows how troubling even his 'justice' remains. Against Darrow's violent justice-in-love the chapter sets Martin Luther King Jr.'s agape and loving-forgiveness—Sevro hanging and then forgiving Cassius, Darrow forgiving Tactus, Mustang pulling her brother's legs for a merciful death—closing with King's warning that constructive ends can never justify destructive means, and Darrow's own admission that 'the war is not over.'
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 21 "11. The Unruly Woman" — Sets Plato's Republic case against the poets, with its censored storytellers, heroes who bear misfortune quietly, and worry that comedy feeds the soul's appetitive part, against Schumer's program of celebrating flaws. Young Amy raiding her roommate's hidden Twinkies and lasagna illustrates the appetitive soul overruling reason, and memoir chapters like 'Secret Bad Habits' do exactly what Plato feared by licensing readers to enjoy what they would be ashamed to confess. Li argues that the unruly women of Schumer, Dunham, Broad City, and Kaling legitimately answer Plato's ancient quarrel by representing messy, complicated female experience rather than modeling virtue.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 15 "5. Another Day in the Neighborhood" — Sydney Ball and Eric Mohr interleave a college student's Tuesday with her six-year-old self watching the show: Plato's Republic (439c) on the rational part overruling the appetitive frames procrastination and lost youthful energy, Kant's autonomy frames doing what you should without being told, and Heidegger's 'They' frames her supermarket jealousy, dissolved by complimenting a stranger's shoes just as Henrietta Pussycat overcame jealousy of Grandpere's fancy granddaughter Collette (episodes 1176-1180). The lesson, learned from Mister Rogers's words about stopping, is authenticity: 'I like you just the way you are.'
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 18 "Death" — Reads Alien3's Fury 161 through impurity and contagion: Mary Douglas's 'matter out of place,' Foucault's confinement of the mad (the YY-chromosome inmates quarantined as social infection; Golic's fixation on the 'dragon' as Schopenhauer's madness of a fixed idea), Hegel and Schelling's philosophies of biology in which disease, decline, and death are necessary moments of life, and Plato's virtue-as-health of the soul. Ripley's fall into the molten lead embraces Schelling's 'indifference' of freedom and its enemy - she refuses Bishop's quack offer to 'deal with the malignancy' so Weyland-Yutani can never harvest the queen inside her.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 9 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Jeff Ewing asks which moral theory governs the novel, finding deontology absent and a contest between Graff's utilitarian recruiting pitch and a virtue-ethical focus on character: the I.F. allowed a 'Third' because it wanted Ender's traits rather than his acts. Mapping Plato's cardinal virtues and tripartite-soul politics against Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, he argues Ender's minimum-force self-defense, adaptability, and disregard for hierarchy are Aristotelian virtues, while his killings of Stilson, Bonzo, and the buggers fall outside the mean only because he lacked the intellectual virtue of grasping his full situation.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 16 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Eric Silverman argues Game of Thrones explodes the storybook link between virtue and worldly happiness: Ned, 'one man in ten thousand,' is betrayed and executed, so Plato's claim that the just person is happy must mean psychic order rather than material flourishing - reason ruling spirit and appetite - as with Bran, who flourishes as a greenseer though he will never walk again. Cersei is Plato's tyrant, her soul ruled by insatiable appetite and paranoia, so no external goods can ever satisfy her, while Aristotle's correction - virtue necessary but not sufficient for eudaimonia, which also needs health, friends, and good fortune - explains why both Ned (virtue without external goods) and Cersei (goods without virtue) end up unhappy.
