Finally he inverts Pascal's Wager: since playing the game of thrones risks total loss (torture, humiliation, death) for limited gain, and even winning hollows you out - Robert confesses he was 'never so alive as when I was winning this throne or so dead as now that I've won it' - only a fool would play.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 9 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Southworth uses the War of Light to ask what role emotion should play in moral reasoning: Sinestro rules Korugar through fear, the Star Sapphires kidnap Sinestro Corps prisoners to convert them to love, Atrocitus's rage was forged by the Manhunters' massacre, Larfleeze hoards, and the Blue Lanterns merely hope that hope matters. On Aristotle's account every corps errs by excess: Atrocitus's rage makes him miss chances to kill Sinestro, Fatality's love benches John Stewart from saving his friends, and even the Green Lanterns' will-only ideal fails, since total fearlessness is itself vicious and Plato's picture has reason directing emotion like a general directing soldiers. He ends by defending Mill's utilitarianism: the Guardians' real failure was not detachment but pretending to be detached, and reading them as flawed 'benevolent, disinterested spectators' vindicates the Corps while explaining their moral growth after Scar and the Blackest Night.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 25 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Barkman retells Glaucon's Ring of Gyges, a shepherd's invisibility ring used to seduce the queen and murder the king, as Lord Acton's claim that absolute power corrupts, and answers with Plato: injustice disorders the tripartite soul, so the unjust sacrifice the happiness that matters most. The Guardians of the Universe are Plato's guardians writ cosmic, wise enough to rule themselves; Yalan Gur fell only when the yellow weakness was removed from his ring, Sinestro never had the wisdom ('You have never understood us'), and Hal's lapses, resigning for Carol Ferris and the Emerald Twilight rampage, are ignorance of the proper value of things rather than evil, since 'Hal's not evil... He believes he's acting for the right reasons.' The power ring is a modern Ring of Gyges, and Plato's test explains both who passes it and who fails.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 146 "The Common Good versus the Greater Good" — Casts the Harry-Voldemort conflict as Socrates versus the Sophists: Thrasymachus's Republic claim that the unjust always come out ahead describes Voldemort's exploitation of his followers' trust exactly. The flayed child under the chair at King's Cross enacts Plato's afterlife justice, and the Republic's tripartite soul and cardinal virtues explain why Harry's reason-ruled courage, wisdom, and justice make the moral life the rational choice, as rational as choosing bodily health over chronic illness.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 16 "NOTES" — Adams uses Plato's Ring of Gyges to ask whether superpowered people have reason to be moral, answering through the tripartite soul: Claire declining credit for the fire rescue shows well-governed thumos, her calculated revenge on Brody shows logistics ruling spirit, while Sylar's uncontrollable hunger for powers is textbook epithumetikon and intemperance that makes his life spin 'super' out of control. Cases like Micah's ATM thefts and Hiro's Vegas cheating (punished by a desert beating) illustrate that vice harms the agent's own soul, since justice is the soul's health. Claire's hospital apology to Brody is read through the Pagan Golden Rule and Sophocles' Ajax: enemies can become friends, so virtue, not mere conformity, is 'only natural' for heroes and ordinary people alike.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Argues the Underwoods' success is not far-fetched fiction but the structural outcome four critics of democracy predict. Plato's Republic supplies the spine: the kallipolis of philosopher-guardians decays through timocracy and oligarchy into democracy, whose love of freedom invites the tyrant — Peter Russo with his random desires is the democratic soul, Frank the tyrannical soul ruled by one illicit appetite, doomed to the fear and friendlessness Book 9 describes (which Season 3 delivers). Hobbes and Hegel then explain why monarchy may beat popular rule (the monarch's private interest aligns with the public's; the monarch lets a people will as one), and Marx reframes the whole show economically — SanCorp, Tusk and Feng as capitalists, the laid-off shipyard workers as proletariat, and AmWorks as self-interested politicians flirting with expropriation. Against all four, Mill's Considerations on Representative Government gives the democratic reply — elections force responsiveness, participation educates citizens — so the burden falls on viewers to keep elections fair, the press free, and checks on unscrupulous politicians effective.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 18 "Over Four Thousand Words to Say No" — Spanakos asks whether Stark's assembling, disassembling, and reassembling of the Avengers and his unseen-hand management of Civil War make him the Republic's philosopher guardian, and answers no. Tony fits the surface profile — the gold-souled ruler of Socrates' noble lie, the elite training, indifference to money, the technê of an MIT engineer who envisions the future — but he lacks epistêmê: he never climbs from the cave's shadows to grasp the forms of justice and the good, and his appetites (womanizing in The Ultimates, 'Demon in a Bottle') show a soul where passion is not ruled by reason. His puppet mastery is reactive problem-solving guided by each situation, not philosophy, and reading him as a philosopher king is our failure to read The Republic meditatively, as Ortega y Gasset urged.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 9 "Evaluating Zelda" — Jonathan Frome tackles the paradox of fiction through Wind Waker: why do we fear Gohma, feel sad when Link leaves his grandmother on Outset Island, and feel touched when Aryll gives him her telescope, given that none of it is real? He rejects the illusion theory (we never call the police when Aryll is kidnapped), Carroll's thought theory (on-screen monsters act too fast for conscious thought), and Walton's pretend theory (we cannot voluntarily stop seeing the sail as a sail). Instead he proposes a multi-level mind — drawing on Plato's Republic (the thirsty non-drinker and Leontius and the corpses) plus Fodor's modules and Grodal's local/global appraisals — on which lower-level processes react to Hyrule as real while the global appraisal knows it is only a game.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 24 "Notes" — Writing as a mechanic, Gordon argues Max embodies Plato's Republic: like the ship-of-state navigator, only someone who knows justice may rule, and the Myth of the Charioteer — reason holding the reins over spirit and appetite — explains why the Nightrider's unchecked spirit crashes while the cool-headed, deliberative Max endures. On punishment, Plato's rejection of retaliation (the unjust should be made just, not harmed) interrogates Max's execution of Johnny the Boy, while Polemarchus's 'render to each his due' frames the just-deserts debate. Mill's harm principle then justifies Max's force against the gangs once the state and its courts have vanished, leaving Max an administrator of street justice.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 10 "“All That Is Solid Melts into Air”" — Dunn reads Mad Men through Plato's Republic: the passions are the 'mad masters' Cephalus describes, embodied in Pete Campbell's au pair indiscretion and remorse, and because passions cannot tell staged appearance from reality, the mimetic perfection of Don's 'You're a whore' scene with Betty grips viewers exactly as Plato feared televised drama would, watering the parts of the soul that should be ruled. He extends the point to advertising: Don's 'I make pictures where people appear to be in love' and 'love was invented by guys like me to sell nylons' work because mimesis bypasses reason and attaches feeling to images, while Aristotle's account of imitation shows drama can also train virtue by making us delight in what we should. Marx and Engels' 'all that is solid melts into air' frames the title sequence, where Don's office dissolves past advertising images revealed as empty simulacra, until the final shot restores the convincing façade of his confidence.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 27 "“I’m Enjoying the Story So Far, but I Have a Feeling It’s Not Going to End Well”" — South uses 'New Amsterdam' to examine how social convention, not personal authority, constrains agency: Bert Cooper's 'New York City is a marvelous machine' and 'There are other rules... His mother is Dorothy Dyckman Campbell' reveal that Pete's value lies in a name he doesn't understand, just as Don's authority dissolves before forces neither he nor Pete consented to. Reading through Plato's Republic city-soul analogy and Adeimantus's warning that changes in music insinuate themselves 'little by little' into character and laws, the chapter shows Pete missing the worth of his old-family name, the Bethlehem Steel man missing that steel cannot be advertised like flour, and Don, despite seizing a fresh identity, quietly conforming to the suburban corporate script he claims never to have envisioned. The Kennedy-assassination pitch to Peggy ('The way that they saw themselves is gone') and Conrad Hilton's 'It's business' close on Plato's caution: the city's gears keep turning, and 'people don't change' may be the show's last word.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 17 "The Office and Philosophy" — Tests the deceptions swirling around Dwight: Kant's two arguments against lying (universalizing the maxim 'lie whenever it saves face', and treating the deceived as a mere means) are set against Plato's noble lie from the Republic - Michael's empty 'Assistant Regional Manager' title may be a morally tolerable verbal lie because after 'The Fight' it restores their friendship, though it does not medicate the office as Plato's lie does the city. Epicurus' claim that only what is experienced can harm you ('what you don't know can't hurt you') is refuted by the thought of Angela's hypothetical fake love for Dwight: undetected deception is itself a harm. Finally Dwight's self-deception (believing the false promotion, Jim's telekinesis prank, the fax from his future self) is modeled by dividing the self - Plato's tripartite soul versus Descartes' simple, indivisible mind - suggesting cognitive science's modular brain as the better picture, and asking whether one can even wrong oneself.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 31 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Reads South Park's music through the Greek doctrine of ethos: Sextus Empiricus' story of Pythagoras sobering drunk youths with slow aulos tunes and Plato's banishment of the soft Ionian and Lydian modes anticipate episodes where music directly changes behavior — Slayer's 'Raining Blood' scattering the hippie horde in 'Die Hippie Die', Cher blasted at the ATF standoff, and the Brown Noise in 'World Wide Recorder Concert'. Plato's tripartite soul maps how the Succubus's 'Morning After' spell enchants Chef's appetitive soul until the boys reverse the melody, while the Sirens' cosmic harmony in the Republic's Myth of Er links back to pitch-planet correspondences. Against Plato's view of music as inferior imitation, Schopenhauer's claim that music copies the Will itself explains why Grandpa's Enya torture in 'Death' communicates despair better than argument; authenticity judgments (Phil Collins appreciated only on Ritalin, Cartman's cynically reworded Faith + 1 hits) echo Plato's demand that music imitate the good.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 10 "Notes" — Tim Challans treats Kirk, Picard, Archer, and Janeway as case studies in moral psychology, with the captain as Plato's charioteer balancing the horses of Spock's logic and McCoy's feeling. He reads Picard's 'there are four lights' coercion in 'Chain of Command' and his Locutus guilt in 'Family' through Rawls's shame/guilt distinction and Nancy Sherman's 'moral injury', while Kirk's 'I need my pain' refusal of Sybok and Archer's Xindi-era regrets show commanders owning guilt, regret, and remorse. Drawing on Nussbaum's 'upheavals of thought' and Hume's passions, he argues that a rare, well-integrated moral psychology—pride tempered by humility, as Q's lesson in 'Tapestry' demonstrates—is what qualifies the one-in-a-million starship captain.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 8 "Notes" — MacMullan argues Darth Plagueis is a paradox for Plato: wisdom as reason ruling spirit and appetite should be impossible for a Sith who feeds on passion, yet Plagueis stays patient, restrained, and rational for over a century. He reads Sidious's 'I will make it legal' and the Sith Code as Thrasymachus's 'justice is the advantage of the stronger,' and notes Plagueis even shares Plato's noble lie and eugenic breeding programs. Finding that Plato's prediction of self-destruction fails for Plagueis, the chapter turns to Nietzsche: master morality, the will to power, and life beyond good and evil better explain a Sith who cherishes bodily life and seeks to conquer death where Yoda and Socrates calmly disdain 'crude matter.'
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 22 "Notes" — Barkman and Alkema map Plato's Republic onto the fall of the Old Republic: the bickering Senate and Anakin's 'someone wise' exchange with Padme enact democracy's degeneration into tyranny, with Palpatine as Plato's werewolf-like protector-tyrant and Dooku's Sith name 'Tyranus' marking Thrasymachus's justice-as-strength as Sith doctrine. The Jedi approximate Plato's philosopher-guardians - courageous, temperate, reluctant to rule, surrendering their children to the Temple much like the Republic's breeding deceptions and noble lies. Justice as each part doing its own work applies to the tripartite soul as much as the state, and the chapter closes that democracy survives Endor but only if truth stays a beacon of the light side.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 24 "Notes" — Compares the noir detective's relation to Vinci with Socrates' gadfly role in Athens from the Apology, arguing both operate at the city's center and its margins as instruments of collective self-examination. Via Deleuze's 'Philosophy of Crime Novels' it contrasts the classic detective as an agent of truth (Poe, Christie) with the hard-boiled detective as an agent of action who stirs the system — Ani's undercover infiltration of the businessmen's party — forcing what Deleuze calls the 'power of falsehood' to reveal and conceal. Plato's Republic city–soul analogy then frames Velcoro, Bezzerides, and Woodrugh as disordered souls mirroring Vinci's corrupt class structure, whose cases restore equilibrium without achieving Platonic justice.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 31 "Plato and Aristotle on the Role of Soul in Taking the Rock to the Hole" — Daniel Gallagher reads Patrick Sparks's 2005 Elite Eight free-throw clank and miracle buzzer-beater through Plato's tripartite soul: the rational part failed at the line but the spirited part carried the off-balance game-tying three, while the Republic's three classes map onto basketball's workers (Steve Nash's passes), warriors (Dennis Rodman's rebounding), and rulers (John Stockton's leadership). Aristotle's four character types structure learning a jump shot - vicious, weak, self-controlled, and finally virtuous, as reason and inclination harmonize through repetition ('we are what we repeatedly do') - and the golden mean governs shot selection between the ball hog and the compulsive passer, with Michael Jordan as the player whose habituated instincts find the mean. Against Kantian armchair ethics, the jump shot and Kareem's sky hook were discovered by trial and error: virtuous performers set the standard, and we become good shooters by watching and imitating them.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 12 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Paul Cantor and Peter Hufnagel use Nietzsche's essay 'Homer's Contest' to argue that the competitive spirit the Greeks called thumos links philosophy and athletics, presenting Plato's dialogues as 'the Olympics of philosophy' in which Socrates is the last man standing. They trace thumos as the spirited third part of the soul in Plato's Republic, the guardians' quality that reason must tame through gymnastics and music, and as the force Socrates enlists to win the thumotic youths Glaucon and Adeimantus to philosophy. They then read Achilles in the Iliad and its funeral games in Book XXIII as a build-up/discharge/calm cycle of thumos, offering athletics as Homer's alternative channel for the same warlike energy.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 14 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Heather Reid interprets the Olympic Charter's first Fundamental Principle through the ancient ideal of aretE, arguing the metaphysical structure of sport, contests that create purposeless obstacles, exists to cultivate and celebrate human excellence rather than to beat opponents or make money. Citing Plato the wrestler, Suits's definition of game-playing, and Homer's funeral games, she maps five virtues onto sport: eusEbeia (reverence for ideals beyond oneself), andreia (courageous endurance in agOn), sOphrosynE (harmonious power and control), dikaiosynE (justice as rule-order and proper function), and sophia (the athlete's pursuit of truth about human capacity, akin to 'flow'). The goal she proposes is the 'Olympian soul.'
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 21 "Spartacus and the Second Part of the Soul Gordon Braden" — Braden argues that Kubrick's Spartacus, despite its chaotic production, coheres around Plato's tripartite soul as mediated by Plutarch's analysis of Roman politics. He maps the film's rivalries onto to thymoeides, the soul's 'second' spirited part governed by philotimia (love of honor): Crassus's obsessive hamilla with Gracchus, and his skewed contest with Spartacus over Varinia and Antoninus. Reading Draba's trident-throw and Crassus's closing 'now I fear him' as the spirited part's competitiveness overrunning reason, Braden shows the gladiatorial paired combat mirroring republican politics on its way to the Principate.
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — Kowalski likens Goodfellas' Henry Hill to Plato's Gyges: both act immorally with near-total impunity, posing Glaucon's challenge in the Republic of why one should be just when one can escape all consequences. He applies Plato's tripartite soul (appetitive, spirited, rational) to Henry (runaway appetite/cocaine), Tommy (overstretched spirit, killing Billy Batts and Spider out of wounded pride) and cool, untroubled Paulie, treating them as the disharmonious 'unbalanced self.' Against the objection that these gangsters seem happy, he deploys Plato's health/happiness analogy and the feeling-happy vs being-happy distinction to argue they suffer 'cancer of the soul' and cannot be truly happy.
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — Conard uses Mean Streets' guilt-ridden Charlie to survey conceptions of unhappiness against three definitions of happiness: beatitude (Aquinas), pleasure (Mill's hedonism), and flourishing (Aristotle's eudaimonia). He reads Charlie as damned in his own Catholic eyes, then invokes Nietzsche's Genealogy that religion manufactures guilt from internalized instinct, Plato's disordered soul and akrasia to explain Charlie's conflicting desires, and Schopenhauer's and Freud's pessimism that suffering is our natural state. He argues Charlie reaches dysdaimonia by acquiring vices and pursuing an ignoble (gangster) life, closing with Plato's Symposium and Sartre's facticity/transcendence to cast unhappiness as an ontological lack at the heart of human desire.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Skoble argues that A Simple Plan dramatizes Plato's Republic almost exactly: justice as psychological harmony among the parts of the soul, and injustice as self-destructive disharmony. When Hank, Jacob, and Lou keep found money, they enact Thrasymachus's and the Ring of Gyges challenge (would you be unjust if you'd never be caught?). Hank miscalculates his own self-interest, mistaking wealth for happiness; the deception, distrust, and murders that follow (including Hank killing Jacob) show that even the criminal who evades capture is ruined by his corrupted character, exactly as Plato predicts.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Braden argues that Kubrick's Spartacus, despite its chaotic production, coheres around Plato's tripartite soul as mediated by Plutarch's analysis of Roman politics. He maps the film's gladiatorial paria and the Crassus–Gracchus rivalry onto to thymoeides, the spirited/competitive middle part of the soul that Plutarch renders as philotimia (love of honor) driving the alpha males of classical history. The central thesis is that Crassus (Laurence Olivier) is ruled by this competitive second part: his skewed hamilla with Spartacus plays out not just on the battlefield but through the erotic triangle over Varinia and Antoninus ('he steals my boy, I steal his girl'), so the Republic falls to a coup driven by the restless, honor-seeking part of the soul.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 28 "17. Is Morality for Suckers" — The chapter reads Jimmy through Plato's Republic, likening his resolve to stop letting conscience stop him to Glaucon's Ring of Gyges thesis that people act immorally whenever they can escape detection, as when Jimmy dodges 'bullets' in his Matrix-like winning speech. Using Plato's tripartite soul, it diagnoses Jimmy as ruled by his appetitive and spirited parts rather than reason, hence lacking self-control and unable to find morality pleasant in itself. It then tests and finds wanting Plato's arguments (contemplative pleasure, connectedness, the immortality of the rational part) that a healthy, reason-ruled soul is both moral and happiest, granting Jimmy's intense scamming pleasures their pull.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 8 "1. Is Rationality an Illusion" — Litman and Zelcer argue that Foundation dramatizes Hume's thesis that reason is the slave of the passions: the robot Demerzel (Daneel Olivaw) and the mutant Mule accomplish history by directly amplifying emotions like Seldon's pride, after which their victims' reason confabulates rational justifications (motivated reasoning). They trace the emotion-versus-reason debate from Plato's tripartite charioteer soul through Aristotle's rational animal and Christian moral psychology to Hume's secularized version, and use the Wye rebellion and Pritcher's converted loyalty to show emotional manipulation works like an optical illusion, persisting even once the victim knows about it.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 26 "But Isn’t It Only Natural" — Adams uses the superpowered characters of Heroes to teach Plato's Republic. The Ring of Gyges question, whether one with the power to escape consequences has reason to be just, is posed by Sylar, Daphne, and Hiro cheating in Vegas. Adams maps Plato's tripartite soul, thumos, logistikon, and epithumetikon, onto Claire's courage and wisdom and Sylar's ruinous intemperance, arguing justice is psychic health so vices grow worse the more power one has. He adds the 'Pagan Golden Rule' (help friends, harm enemies) to read Claire's apology to Brody, concluding virtue is natural to a well-ordered human soul and is its own reward.
- **Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low**, ch. 9 "BLUES" — The editors' introduction argues blues and philosophy are close kin in confronting the struggling soul. It reads Lightnin' Hopkins's 'Lonesome Dog' through Plato's tripartite soul from Republic IX — the howling 'dog' is the appetitive part — but claims the blues achieves a 'blues harmony' rather than Plato's reason-ruled harmony. It casts Socrates, calm before execution in the Phaedo, as having a 'bluesy sensibility' that rises above worry through philosophizing, invokes Bentham's claim that the capacity to suffer is what matters morally to gloss the blues as knowledge of suffering, and likens the blues' triumphant affirmation to Nietzsche's positivity.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 26 "But Isn’t It Only Natural" — Don Adams uses Heroes' superpowered characters (who could commit perfect crimes like Gyges with his invisibility ring) to argue Plato's case that virtue is its own reward. He maps Plato's tripartite soul onto the characters: Claire's thumos (spirit/honor) tempered by logistikos (reason) yields courage and wisdom, while Sylar's ruling appetite (his hunger for powers) is intemperance and injustice that makes his life spin out of control. Reading justice as psychic health, and glossing the 'Pagan Golden Rule' (help friends, harm enemies, but enemies may become friends), Adams argues it is 'only natural' for even the powerful to be virtuous rather than exploit others.

### The Philosopher King

The philosopher king is Plato's proposal, argued in the Republic, that political power should be held by those who have genuine knowledge of the Good rather than by the wealthy, the popular, or the ambitious. Because rulers guided by true understanding rather than self-interest would govern for the benefit of the whole community, Plato concludes that a just city requires that philosophers become kings or kings become philosophers. The idea reflects his distrust of democracy, which he thought vulnerable to demagogues and the untutored desires of the many. It ties legitimate authority to wisdom and to a rigorous education aimed at grasping the Forms.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 73 "Unknown" — The chapter contrasts two theories of liberation: the Platonic one, where an exceptional external liberator - a philosopher-king, or the traditional God-man savior the film's characters initially expect - leads humanity out of illusion, and Kant's Enlightenment alternative that 'the slaves can only be truly free if they free themselves', with Jesus recast as the model of our own inner potential rather than a miracle-working savior. The film's arc, it argues, moves from Choi's 'my own personal Jesus Christ' (a caricature of liberation) to a finale that overturns all expectations of an external savior.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 82 "Unknown" — The chapter concludes that the One is a universal Teacher rather than an exceptional Superman-Savior: liberation cannot come from a Philosopher King or an all-powerful benefactor, since sleeping humanity already rejected the unearned happiness the AI's first Matrix offered. Neo's closing promise of 'a world without rules and controls, without borders or boundaries, a world where anything is possible' echoes Jesus's 'the works that I do, shall he do also' - he shows others how to be like him, so 'the One may be the first superhuman being, but he is not the last'.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 71 "Plato and Dumbledore Separated at Birth" — David Lay Williams and Alan J. Kellner open their essay with paired epigraphs from Dumbledore ('Those who are best suited to power are those who have never sought it') and Plato ('A city in which those who are going to rule are least eager to rule is necessarily best'). Against Lord Acton's dictum that power corrupts, they present Plato's ingeniously simple solution - power must never reside with those who lust for it, since disinterest paradoxically makes the best rulers - and announce that this lesson is central to the climax of the entire Harry Potter series.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 72 "Fudge and Umbridge The Lessons of Obviously Unfit Power-Brokers" — The section draws a biography-by-biography parallel between Plato and Dumbledore: each lived through upheaval (the Peloponnesian War, the Thirty, and Socrates' execution; Grindelwald and Voldemort), each renounced a political career after disillusion, and each turned from politics to education, founding the Academy and leading Hogwarts. It explains the Republic's philosopher-rulers and their four cardinal virtues, argues that intelligence alone (Lex Luthor, Hannibal Lecter) plus excessive self-love disqualifies a ruler, and introduces Glaucon's Ring of Gyges as Plato's test of incorruptibility - a legend it says Rowling revives in Harry's invisibility cloak.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 73 "Voldemort and Dumbledore Two Tempted by Power" — The authors run Plato's criteria on the wizarding world's obviously unfit power-brokers. Umbridge fails as a ruler: her 'I must not tell lies' blood-quill detentions and multiplying Educational Decrees expose a lust for power that grows with her authority, and she lacks all the cardinal virtues, especially self-control. Fudge's insecurity proves equally corrupting - his denial of Voldemort's return, smearing Harry in the press, and tilting Harry's Wizengamot hearing (moving its time to exclude Dumbledore) all serve only to keep him in office, so both, like Plato's tyrants, lose the power they clutch at.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 74 "Harry’s Cloak, the Ring of Gyges, and the Temptations of Power" — This section contrasts Voldemort and Dumbledore as two figures tempted by power. Tom Riddle's egocentrism - frightening and controlling other children at the orphanage, treating his 'friends' as mere followers, killing Lily, and splintering his soul for Horcruxes - violates Kant's dictum never to use persons merely as means and fits Plato's category of the least trustworthy rulers. Dumbledore, though tempted in youth by Grindelwald's 'for the greater good' schemes and later by Marvolo Gaunt's ring, is venerable for Socratic self-knowledge: knowing 'I was not to be trusted with power,' he repeatedly refused the Ministry and so promoted justice by teaching.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 75 "NOTES" — The concluding section argues that Harry passes Plato's Ring of Gyges test, which Rowling rebuilds around the Invisibility Cloak: unlike Gyges, Harry never uses invisibility for selfish gain, refuses Scrimgeour's offer of his dream job, hunts Horcruxes rather than making them, and at eleven pulls the Sorcerer's Stone from his pocket precisely because Dumbledore's enchantment lets only someone who wants to find but not use it do so. This indifference to the lure of power, joined to courage, justice, and self-restraint, is the Platonic quality that makes Harry fit to rule.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 25 "Palpatine’s Legacy" — Decker reconstructs Palpatine's career as a case study in how democracies die: using Aristotle's definition of tyranny and the precedent of Pisistratus and Julius Caesar, he shows Palpatine manufacturing the Separatist threat so the Senate grants him emergency powers - a twist on Machiavelli's loved-versus-feared dictum in which playing the reluctant democrat is itself the means to absolute rule. The Attack of the Clones debate between Anakin ('Someone wise' should make people agree) and Padme becomes a clash between Leo Strauss's philosopher-king ideal of rule by the virtuous few and John Dewey's conception of democracy as a way of life trusting the intelligence of common people, with Rousseau's social contract framing the stakes. The chapter concludes that democratic ends require democratic means and that unaccountable 'watchers' - Straussian statesmen or Anakins - are exactly the path to Empire.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 9 "From Rhyme to Reason This Shit Ain’t Easy" — The editors' introduction argues that hip hop and philosophy are both street-born examinations of life in pursuit of wisdom: Socrates's elenchus is likened to MC lyrical battles and call-and-response (his interrogations compared to Rakim's technique, his execution for corrupting the youth to the fate of a controversial rapper), while Plato's philosopher-king parallels Kurtis Blow and Run-D.M.C. claiming thrones. After a Bronx hip-hop history sketch (Kool Herc, BDP's "The Bridge is Over"), they frame the volume around hip hop's suppressed fifth element of knowledge and preview its pairings: Aquinas and Rakim on God, Plato and Lauryn Hill on love, Sartre and Lil' Kim's gaze, Kant and Ice Cube on punishment, Hegel and Nas, Hobbes and Dead Prez, Mill and Chappelle on epithets. Record companies don't own hip hop and universities don't own philosophy, they conclude - both belong to whoever understands, loves, and respects them.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 19 "U2 and Philosophy" — Delancey asks why anyone should take moral and political cues from a rock band and answers via Heidegger: in a mediascape where a few corporations orchestrate what everyone hears, the mass tune is das Man ('Numb'), and adopting it is inauthenticity - so U2, who believe what they sing for their own reasons ('Mothers of the Disappeared' against the official line on Latin America), may be among the most authentic voices available. Plato's tripartite soul and Aristotle's golden mean supply the thesis that reason needs rightly trained passion: the righteous anger of 'Sunday Bloody Sunday' and 'Silver and Gold' and the resolve of 'Walk On' are practical wisdom in song, the emotions democracy requires. Against Plato's philosopher-king and his noble lies, Delancey argues utopia can only be fostered, not enforced - so in a democracy, if you want to change the world, you may have to sing to people.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 12 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Getachew maps Plato's Republic archetypes onto the Bond universe: the appetite-ruled Tyrant is Goldfinger, Zorin, Stromberg and the SPECTRE megalomaniacs; the spirit-ruled Guardian is 007, compared to Alcibiades and to Medea's vengeful fury (Bond letting Trevelyan fall 'For me'); and the reason-ruled Philosopher-King is M, whose ideal republic of common children and expendable numbers mirrors MI6's recruitment of orphans and its treatment of Bond as '007', never a person. She then challenges Plato's preference for the eternal Forms and immortality, using Freud on transience and Heidegger's being-toward-death (via Tolstoy's Ivan Ilych) to argue that mortality and risk are what make life worth living. Bond's stylish risk-taking, like the cello-case downhill escape, shows we need a balance between the Guardian and the man of thought.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 14 "You Can’t Tell the Players Without a Program" — Auxier revives Plato's ancient quarrel with the poets — the Republic's banishment of imitators whose pretty words are copies that stir the masses' feelings, the philosopher-king's city, the Ion's contempt for rhapsodes, Socrates' wisdom as Delphic acknowledgment of ignorance — while branding Plato an elitist and 'Poetry NIMBY.' He then stages a fantasy dithyramb contest at the Meadowlands where Dylan ('Subterranean Homesick Blues') and Springsteen ('Blinded by the Light') trade internal rhymes and alliteration before Weird Al's palindromes deflate Bob's seriousness. The virtuous poet wins all nine Muses by wooing their mother Mnemosyne — tapping the collective memory of the race with gratitude and discipline — which explains why Springsteen, unlike the prideful Dylan who lost the Muses, retains moral authority; the philosophers, needless to say, are just jealous of the bar.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 10 "And the Winner Is" — Lynch pits Plato against the Shaolin monks on the nature of the self that martial training is supposed to master. Plato's Republic makes the athlete-warrior Guardian a harmonious, rationally ruled tripartite soul whose bravery is 'remembering what ought and ought not to be feared', trained so reason governs aggression; Buddhism instead dissolves the self into five impermanent aggregates (illustrated by the chariot analogy) and reads mushin as a direct taste of no-self. He awards the practical decision to the Buddhist fighting monks, since no-self explains martial spontaneity and naturally arising compassion, while admitting Plato's substantive rational soul is not strictly refuted.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 19 "The Ideal Candidate" — Nathan Zook uses the 'Royal Krabby' election from Vote for SpongeBob and the global-warming plot of SpongeBob Goes Green to weigh democracy. Mr. Krabs's rigged election, run only to sell patties, exemplifies C. Wright Mills's power elite manipulating the appearance of popular rule; Plato would bar Producer-class SpongeBob and Squidward from ruling and prefers educated Guardians, while Mill defends each citizen's liberty to choose and democracy's alliance with education (SpongeBob learns about global warming from Sandy). Aristotle's polity — citizens administering the state for the common interest — makes SpongeBob the ideal candidate because he saves Bikini Bottom without claiming power.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 69 "Rule of the Wise" — Updates Plato's rule of the wise to the pre-cogs of 'Minority Report,' noting that Socrates' 'divine sign' made him a kind of pre-cog. It then argues expertise cannot be operationalized — self-proclaimed authorities from Sarah Palin to Barack Obama disagree, and there is no accepted test of who the experts are — closing with Plato's own comparison of voters to children choosing between the doctor's medicine and the confectioner's candy, which explains why the Founders added the Electoral College.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 143 "A Palace Revolution" — The fantasy election brings in Plato's Republic: Richards's defense attorney Bill Carter functions as his Ring of Gyges, letting him vanish from legal consequences and raising Plato's question of whether we act justly only from fear of punishment. The tripartite soul is mapped onto Keef — appetites (drugs, sex, Jagger's 'Bitch'), spirit (the Glimmer Twins' rivalry), rationality (busting his head reaching for a library book) — and justice becomes the harmony under rationality's rule. In the ideal city of philosopher kings, auxiliaries, and workers, the sign at the gate reads 'NO POETS, NO ROCK'N'ROLLERS': Richards is exactly the corrupting poet Plato bars.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 144 "Shout and Scream and Kill the King" — The election plays out: Richards blows away the auxiliaries with 'Play with Fire' and whips the working-class appetites into a frenzy (put on Exile on Main Street after a few rounds to test Plato's fear of the poets). Young Keef's soul is appetite-led — the 'Blue Lena' Bentley with its hidden drug compartment embodies a spirit in service of drugs and artistic hunger, with rationality demoted to scoring the fix. The resulting Republic of Keef, driven fast on the edge of a cliff, vindicates Plato's warning that wherever the appetites lead, tyranny soon follows — as the author concedes through his own pipe-smoking.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 24 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Greg Littmann maps Ape City onto Plato's Republic class by class: orangutan rulers who legislate, censor, and propagandize; gorilla warriors who enforce; chimpanzee producers who do all the work - including, pointedly, the science Plato made no provision for; and humans as the 'barbarians' Plato says may be enslaved or exterminated. The overlaps are detailed: the Sacred Scrolls' first article of faith functions as the noble lie's myth of the metals, orangutan funerals promise heaven to keep gorillas unafraid of death, and Zaius's erasing of Taylor's dust-writing and blowing up of the archaeological cave enact the rulers' duty to supervise stories. But the films also refute Plato: hereditary orangutans show that power corrupts philosopher kings, Dr. Honorius's 'reason' is dogma serving the faith, the gelding threat that finally breaks Taylor cracks the tripartite-soul analogy of justice, and democracy's rough virtue is that it lets us remove rulers 'without sticking anybody with iron spears.'
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 26 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter reads season two's families through Engels's Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State: Mags performs the patriarch's role of accumulating and bequeathing wealth (the Black Pike payout 'sufficient to provide for my kin for generations'), Arlo fails it by hoarding nothing for Raylan, and Ava joins Boyd's crime precisely when he hands her the mine money for her mortgage - a moment the author calls borderline prostitution, as Engels predicts. Hegel's Philosophy of Right, where the family exists for love and for forming free moral beings who must leave it, exposes the Bennetts' failure on both counts, while Aristotle's Politics (the polis is prior to the family) and Plato's Republic (rulers without private families, children raised in common) ground the claim that feuding clans need the state. The Kentucky-fried twist: when government and coal companies treat mountain families as spoil, family is sometimes all you've got.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 18 "8. Plato’s Chicago" — Littmann systematically maps Roth's Chicago onto Plato's Republic: like Marcus, Plato rejects democracy after Athens executed Socrates; both dissolve the family ('faction before blood' versus children raised in common and bred by state schedule); Erudite's IQ-selected leadership mirrors the rigorously trained philosopher-rulers, Dauntless the warrior class whose purely physical training Plato warns turns 'savage and harsh,' Abnegation's poverty the guardians's communism of property, and the factionless the powerless producers - with Plato's noble lie about the metals matching the Erudite's propaganda and serums as instruments of control. The shared flaw, he argues, is concentrated power without external checks, which corrupted Abnegation, corrupts every Dauntless leadership change, and would corrupt Plato's guardians too. The lesson is not to hand power to the least vicious but for democratic voters to confront their own ignorance - or end like Roth's America, in apocalyptic war.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 25 "14. You Have to Be Good before You Can Be Smart" — The Bocks argue that the Erudite pairing of ignorance with knowledge is morally loaded: with Linda Zagzebski's and James Montmarquet's virtue epistemology, high-end knowledge requires intellectual virtues like the courage to test your beliefs publicly, so you really do have to be good before you can be smart. The Erudite manifesto's curriculum omits the humanities that open the mind, and its IQ-only leadership test fails Plato's requirement that philosopher kings love wisdom itself and, like the freed cave-prisoner, return to benefit society - which is why Jeanine, driven by lust for power and concealment of the truth beyond the fence, is 'a poor example of a philosopher king.' Both the Erudite and the Bureau reason as consequentialists ('Knowledge is power... power to do good') to justify slaughtering Abnegation and experimenting on unconsenting Chicagoans, when the pursuit of knowledge must be constrained by informed consent and human dignity.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 17 "7. Pratchett’s Republic" — Kempner maps Plato's Republic onto Ankh-Morpork: Vetinari is the Philosopher King, the Watch of Guards! Guards! are the Guardians who devote themselves to the good of the whole community, and Platonic justice as keeping everything in its right place is Vetinari's guild-licensing, topiary-tending rule - including the jail cell whose locks are all on the inside. Against Plato's banishment of poets, The Truth shows words serving the just city: William de Worde's pursuit of 'the big truth' exposes the frame-up of Vetinari and extends the circle of Guardians to the free press. The chapter concludes that Pratchett keeps Plato's ideal only by bending it to observable reality - Vetinari rules for the city rather than remaking its people.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 19 "9. Pierce’s Republic" — Randall Jensen maps the Society onto Plato's Republic (Brown has said he drew on it): the Color hierarchy parallels the Myth of the Metals' gold, silver, and bronze souls, the Golds' scorn for Demokracy echoes Book VIII's account of degeneration into tyranny, and Leto's 'We are Plato's philosopher kings' claims a mantle Plato himself doubted anyone could ever fill. Darrow's story is the Allegory of the Cave run from below—a Helldiver literally raised in a mine, blinded by surface light, whose return to a shrunken, grayer garden mirrors the philosopher's homecoming—except Plato never imagined the prisoner carved into a Gold. The Noble Lie survives as the terraforming myth fed to lowReds while the surface has been habitable for centuries, and the chapter weighs Darrow's gospel ('we choose who we are') against Plato's caveats: you can choose who to be only within limits, if you are lucky and greatly helped.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 15 "6. The Self-Willed and Ignorant Law" — Marc Cole argues the Reich's and Japan's governments have the structure of Plato's Republic: supreme power in a political expert who is above the law and manages citizens' work, breeding, education, and music from cradle to grave — in some ways more controlling than the Nazis, since Plato abolishes the family outright. John Smith's son Thomas, condemned to death by a law blind to particular circumstances, embodies the Statesman's 'self-willed and ignorant' law, and after weighing the doctor/patient defense of rule by expertise, the chapter sides with democratic republics and warns that multiplying laws and state management inches us toward Plato's republic or the Reich.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 27 "16. Would You Buy a Used Car from This Avenger" — Ericson uses the used-car litmus test to examine trust in the MCU: through McLeod's three criteria and Peperzak's contrast of the objectifying and interactive approaches, Tony's control-seeking distance (the lone-gun-slinger act of Iron Man 2) fails trust while Steve's soldier-style trust anchors the Winter Soldier thriller against Fury's 'This isn't freedom, this is fear' and HYDRA's coercion-eliminating project. Plato's rule that power should go only to those who do not want it explains why Cap can be entrusted with superpowers, Nietzsche's megalomaniac late letters frame Tony's drive to 'cleave history in two' by building Ultron and then the messianic Vision, and Banner's Hulk illustrates the Freudian road from repression to sublimation as the condition of self-trust. It ends with Cap's concealment of Bucky's killing of Tony's parents as the betrayal of trust that only a decision to forgive might repair.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 20 "10. Intelligence and Duh-mocracy" — Saunders uses Adams's induhviduals and a hundred-voter dilution example in which smart people's votes are swamped to stage the classic case against democracy: Plato's physician analogy against Athenian rule by the ignorant and his philosopher-kings, Jason Brennan's hobbits, hooligans, and Vulcans with voter licensing, Mill's plural votes for the demonstrably wise, and Nussbaum's claim that humanities education breeds empathetic democratic citizens. Each fix fails on Dilbert's own terms, since competence tests demean the labeled, the Pointy-Haired Boss would amass extra votes while Dilbert-grade engineers lack political judgment, Asok's degree would not help, and the more educated are demographically skewed toward men. He concludes that equal votes win as a pragmatic default and muses that workplaces, not polities, might be the truer target of democratization.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 17 "7 Should Wakanda Take Over the World The Ethics of International Power" — Littmann asks whether Wakanda should take over the world, staging N'Jobu's and Killmonger's 'Wakanda could rule them all... the right way' plan against the history of benevolently justified empire: Roman civilization of barbarians, Kipling's white man's burden, and Mill's trusteeship argument for educating non-Europeans toward democracy. Plato's Republic case for rule by the wisest initially favors Wakandan conquest, but Kant's Perpetual Peace condemnation of conquering 'European savages,' Mill's own four reasons imperial rule goes wrong (ignorance of local conditions, lack of sympathy, partiality, exploitation), and Diderot's claim that distance from home erodes moral restraint convince him domination breeds abuse; he endorses Nakia's aid-and-refuge outreach and Mill's hope that the 'aristocracy of nationality' will one day look as wrong as racism.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 32 "The Burden of the End of the World" — Reads Naomi's escape from collapsing Ganymede — sedating Amos to leave the freighter, then stepping out before a crowd of more than a hundred stranded Belters to propose saving only the youngest — as Arendt's 'doing' politics, action justified by the seeing-and-being-seen of shared speech rather than by the strategic 'making' calculus Melissa and Amos use to justify abandoning the crowd. Naomi must alternate between the two — Champa's measured violence organizes the crowd — without letting making become the ethical metric, because, as she says, 'every shitty thing we do makes the next one that much easier.' Marco embodies politics reduced to pure making (abandoning six million on Ceres), Holden stays trapped in righteous strategizing that never defeats the protomolecule's uncertainty, and the chapter closes on Arendt's story of Plato's philosopher-king: trying to eliminate uncertainty by preemptive rule only multiplies risk, so resilience comes from doing politics together.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 22 "Notes" — Dal Barco maps Lucy's arc in the Amazon series onto Plato's cave stage by stage: Vault 33's fake sky, curated history lessons, and Vault-Tec-managed information are the shadow-puppet show, her first step into the sun after Hank's abduction by Moldaver is the freed prisoner's blinding ascent, the hidden hospital vault tempts her (and Maximus, who wants to stay) like the return to the cave, and the truth - her father helped orchestrate the nuclear war, her mother is now a ghoul - plays the role the sun and the Good play in the Republic. Plato's claim that only the educated philosopher who has seen beyond the cave should govern (Republic 496a, 519a-d) explains why Lucy, unlike the frightened Norm or the tempted Maximus, goes back out into the wastes: she is becoming the philosopher-ruler whose hard-won knowledge enables Moldaver to restore power to the surface and begin a civilization no longer built on shadows. The chapter answers its own question - yes, it was worth leaving the vault for the truth.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 25 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Barkman retells Glaucon's Ring of Gyges, a shepherd's invisibility ring used to seduce the queen and murder the king, as Lord Acton's claim that absolute power corrupts, and answers with Plato: injustice disorders the tripartite soul, so the unjust sacrifice the happiness that matters most. The Guardians of the Universe are Plato's guardians writ cosmic, wise enough to rule themselves; Yalan Gur fell only when the yellow weakness was removed from his ring, Sinestro never had the wisdom ('You have never understood us'), and Hal's lapses, resigning for Carol Ferris and the Emerald Twilight rampage, are ignorance of the proper value of things rather than evil, since 'Hal's not evil... He believes he's acting for the right reasons.' The power ring is a modern Ring of Gyges, and Plato's test explains both who passes it and who fails.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 71 "Plato and Dumbledore Separated at Birth" — Opening 'Dumbledore, Plato, and the Lust for Power,' the chapter pairs Dumbledore's 'those who are best suited to power are those who have never sought it' with Plato's 'a city in which those who are going to rule are least eager to rule is necessarily best.' Against Lord Acton's resigned 'power corrupts,' it presents Plato's remedy, reserving power for the reluctant rather than the power-hungry, as the lesson of the entire series' climax.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 72 "Fudge and Umbridge The Lessons of Obviously Unfit Power-Brokers" — The chapter draws tight parallels between Plato's political life and Dumbledore's: both watched gifted, power-hungry pupils betray their cities (Alcibiades and Tom Riddle), both recoiled from tyrannical regimes (the Thirty under Critias; the duel with Grindelwald that killed his sister), and both turned from politics to education, founding the Academy and leading Hogwarts. It explains the Republic's philosopher-rulers, their four cardinal virtues, and the decades of training meant to 'distinguish the Potters from the Malfoys,' then introduces Glaucon's Ring of Gyges as Plato's test of who can resist invisible power, the legend Rowling mirrors in the Deathly Hallows and Harry's invisibility cloak, with Voldemort's unicorn-blood survival showing how the tyrant's life burns short.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 73 "Voldemort and Dumbledore Two Tempted by Power" — The chapter grades would-be Ministers of Magic on Plato's ruler criteria: Dolores Umbridge fails utterly, her 'I must not tell lies' blood-quill detentions and multiplying Educational Decrees exposing a lust for power that grows with her authority and a total lack of courage, wisdom, justice, and self-control. Cornelius Fudge's insecurity breeds dictatorial damage control, trashing Harry in the press and rigging his hearing over the dementor attack on Dudley, so that craving power, he loses it; both are Platonic object lessons in how not to rule.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 74 "Harry’s Cloak, the Ring of Gyges, and the Temptations of Power" — The chapter reads Tom Riddle as Plato's unfit ruler: from the orphanage ('I can make them hurt if I want to') he violates Kant's dictum never to use persons merely as means, treating even his 'friends' as followers, killing Lily despite Snape's devotion, and splitting his soul for Horcruxes. Dumbledore, offered the Ministry repeatedly yet refusing because 'power was my weakness and my temptation,' has the Socratic self-knowledge that he cannot be trusted with power, and that self-awareness, not flawless virtue, is what keeps him from Grindelwald's and Voldemort's path and makes him the series' nearest philosopher-ruler.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 75 "NOTES" — The chapter argues Harry passes the Ring of Gyges test that Voldemort fails: despite years of invisible freedom under the Cloak he never exploits it, refuses Scrimgeour's offer of his dream job to serve the whole wizarding community, hunts Horcruxes instead of making them, and at eleven alone retrieves the Sorcerer's Stone from the Mirror of Erised precisely because he does not want to use it. This indifference to the lure of power is exactly the Platonic qualification Dumbledore and Plato both demand of those fit to rule.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Argues the Underwoods' success is not far-fetched fiction but the structural outcome four critics of democracy predict. Plato's Republic supplies the spine: the kallipolis of philosopher-guardians decays through timocracy and oligarchy into democracy, whose love of freedom invites the tyrant — Peter Russo with his random desires is the democratic soul, Frank the tyrannical soul ruled by one illicit appetite, doomed to the fear and friendlessness Book 9 describes (which Season 3 delivers). Hobbes and Hegel then explain why monarchy may beat popular rule (the monarch's private interest aligns with the public's; the monarch lets a people will as one), and Marx reframes the whole show economically — SanCorp, Tusk and Feng as capitalists, the laid-off shipyard workers as proletariat, and AmWorks as self-interested politicians flirting with expropriation. Against all four, Mill's Considerations on Representative Government gives the democratic reply — elections force responsiveness, participation educates citizens — so the burden falls on viewers to keep elections fair, the press free, and checks on unscrupulous politicians effective.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Shea argues the Underwoods' rise is structurally guaranteed rather than far-fetched, surveying democracy's critics: Plato's Republic Books 8-9 has the kallipolis of philosopher-guardians decay through timocracy and oligarchy into democracy, where a 'protector'-tyrant like Frank exploits the drones and the people's love of freedom (Russo as the prototypical democratic soul, Tusk as the oligarch-in-fact), while the tyrant ends fear-ridden and friendless — precisely Frank's Season 3. Hobbes and Hegel then reverse the verdict, arguing monarchy aligns the ruler's private interest with the public good and lets a people will as one instead of a formless mass — the insight Tom Yates has about voters identifying with the Underwoods as people — and Marx reframes it economically: SanCorp, Tusk, and Feng are the capitalist structure, and Frank's AmWorks, entitlement cuts, and nationalization threats show self-interested politicians siding with a growing proletariat. Against all four, Mill's Considerations on Representative Government supplies the democratic reply — responsiveness, better information, and citizen participation mean an Underwood cannot last if we keep fair elections, a free press, and real checks.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 10 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Anne Torkelson reads Panem through the Republic and the Laws: because mousike imitates states of soul and slowly molds character, Socrates polices music and poetry in the just city and fears innovation in musical modes, and the Capitol's own outlawing of songs quietly confirms music's power. She shows 'The Meadow Song' replacing Katniss's grief with hope and inspiring the flowers for Rue, the forbidden 'Hanging Tree' planting the Socratic question of whether an unjust life is a fate worse than death (paralleling Socrates's own unjust execution, the hemlock, and the nightlock pact Katniss, Gale, and Peeta make), and Rue's four notes mutating from an orchard work-signal into a salute of defiance when the District 11 man whistles them on the Victory Tour, at the cost of his life. Music, which Katniss dismisses as 'somewhere between hair ribbons and rainbows,' turns out to be the force that shapes her character and carries the revolution.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 18 "Over Four Thousand Words to Say No" — Spanakos asks whether Stark's assembling, disassembling, and reassembling of the Avengers and his unseen-hand management of Civil War make him the Republic's philosopher guardian, and answers no. Tony fits the surface profile — the gold-souled ruler of Socrates' noble lie, the elite training, indifference to money, the technê of an MIT engineer who envisions the future — but he lacks epistêmê: he never climbs from the cave's shadows to grasp the forms of justice and the good, and his appetites (womanizing in The Ultimates, 'Demon in a Bottle') show a soul where passion is not ruled by reason. His puppet mastery is reactive problem-solving guided by each situation, not philosophy, and reading him as a philosopher king is our failure to read The Republic meditatively, as Ortega y Gasset urged.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 22 "Notes" — Barkman and Alkema map Plato's Republic onto the fall of the Old Republic: the bickering Senate and Anakin's 'someone wise' exchange with Padme enact democracy's degeneration into tyranny, with Palpatine as Plato's werewolf-like protector-tyrant and Dooku's Sith name 'Tyranus' marking Thrasymachus's justice-as-strength as Sith doctrine. The Jedi approximate Plato's philosopher-guardians - courageous, temperate, reluctant to rule, surrendering their children to the Temple much like the Republic's breeding deceptions and noble lies. Justice as each part doing its own work applies to the tripartite soul as much as the state, and the chapter closes that democracy survives Endor but only if truth stays a beacon of the light side.
- **The Philosophy of Tim Burton**, ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" — Steve Benton reads Burton's Sleepy Hollow as a meditation on rationality and anti-intellectualism, contrasting it with Washington Irving's original where brainy Ichabod is run out of town. Burton's Ichabod, a rationalist constable, prevails only after tempering his faith in science with emotion, intuition, and the spirit world associated with his mother and Katrina—the paper-disk toy (bird/cage) symbolizing how head and heart must spin together. Benton maps the film's models of rationality onto Plato's philosopher-king and distrust of the mob and Hobbes's war of all against all (Burton's corrupt New York and Sleepy Hollow) versus the collaborative, democratic reason of Locke, Mill's On Liberty, and Dewey, invoking Aristotle and Nussbaum on emotion's role in practical wisdom; he leaves open whether the film is transgressive or a conventional 'woman heals cold rational man' Hollywood tale.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 28 "17. Psychohistory’s Noble Lie" — Silcox explains why readers forgive Seldon's confessed lie that the Encyclopedia Galactica 'is a fraud, and always has been' by comparing it to Socrates's noble lie in Plato's Republic, which Popper and I.F. Stone condemn as antidemocratic. He contrasts the two—Socrates's lie preserves an existing kallipolis while Seldon's brings about a distant political goal that requires trusting psychohistory—and weighs them against modern transparency doctrines: Bentham's consequentialist case for publicity and Rawls's publicity condition grounding autonomy, plus Nguyen's worry that transparency distorts expert 'cognitive islands.' He concludes that a genuinely predictive science of history might rationally lead us to treat political transparency as negotiable, which is why Hari Seldon remains a noble hero despite 'engineering the narrative.'
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 14 "5. Friendship, Fun, Freedom, Food, and the Future" — Le Gall and Taliaferro read Bourdain's Libya and Iran episodes of Parts Unknown through Pierre Hadot's 'philosophy as a way of life,' arguing that Gaddafi and Khomeini were failed Platonic philosopher-kings. They interpret ordinary Libyans and Iranians eating Uncle Kentucky chicken, playing pinball, or hosting feasts as popular 'spiritual exercises' — tatonnement — showing how the personal becomes political and how friendship, fun, freedom, and food nourish the Socratic care of the soul.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 29 "GARDENING" — Evans presents Texcotzingo, the hilltop garden-retreat of the fifteenth-century Texcocan king Nezahualcoyotl, as the achievement of an Aztec philosopher-king who was landscape designer, hydraulic engineer and statesman. She argues the botanical garden as a genre—a 'green encyclopedia' cataloguing a realm's flora—was pioneered by Aztec kings, and that within an animist cosmos where mountains and water pulse with sacred spirit, Nezahualcoyotl's aqueduct, pools and terraced gardens made the hill a living embodiment of the altepetl (the 'water-hill' city-state). The garden thus symbolically enacts his political domain, dynastic history (three pools for three ancestral capitals) and cosmic order, even as she cautions his reputation as poet and monotheist was inflated by later Spanish and Christian chroniclers.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 31 "29. Frank Herbert’s Dune as Philosophy The Need to Think for Yourself" — Reading the Sci Fi Channel miniseries Frank Herbert's Dune and Children of Dune, Littmann argues the saga warns against letting leaders or religions think for us: Paul Atreides fakes being the Fremen Mahdi, wages a holy war, and founds a theocratic tyranny that Alia and Leto II carry to worse extremes. He sets Plato's Republic (the guardian class, the noble lie, rule by the wise) and Hobbes against pro-democracy thinkers—Locke's consent and natural rights, Mill's harm principle, Dewey's democracy—then cites Locke, Paine and Russell on religion's dangers, closing with W.K. Clifford's 'ethics of belief' that one must not accept religious claims without sufficient evidence. The chapter reads Paul's dictatorship and the Bene Gesserit's engineered messiah as dramatizations of the historical abuses of concentrated and religious power.

### Possible Worlds

Possible worlds are complete alternative ways things might have been, used in logic and metaphysics to analyze claims about necessity and possibility: a statement is necessary if it holds in all possible worlds and possible if it holds in at least one. David Lewis defended the striking doctrine of modal realism, on which these worlds are not mere abstractions or fictions but concrete realities as fully existent as our own, spatiotemporally isolated from us. Though few accept Lewis's full realism, possible-worlds talk has become an indispensable tool across philosophy of language, modality, and counterfactual reasoning.

- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 79 "So, Is Dumbledore Gay" — Gendler tests whether fictional truth works like historical truth and finds it fails: whereas a biographer discovers facts about the one actual world, a storyteller chooses among infinitely many imaginary worlds - David Lewis's point that 'every way that a world could possibly be is a way that some world is' - so storytelling mixes creation with discovery. She distinguishes the 'primary truths' stated on the Potter novels' 4,100 pages (discounting trivial inconsistencies like Percy's badge color and Moaning Myrtle's S-bend versus U-bend) from unstated 'secondary truths' like Hermione having ten fingers, rejects a maximal inclusiveness principle that would import every actual-world fact into the story, and closes with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics advice to seek only the exactness a subject allows.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 119 "The DC Comics Multiverse" — Recounts how DC resolved its Silver Age continuity mess: rather than treat Jay Garrick's adventures as a fiction-within-a-fiction, Flash #123 has Barry Allen cross into Earth-2 and meet Garrick — and one cannot meet a merely fictional character — so the multiverse is born. As alternative histories multiplied and heroes routinely world-hopped, the only correction strategy left was postulating yet another world, setting up 1985's Crisis.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 120 "Crisis on Infinite Earths The Story Unfolds" — Summarizes Crisis: Krona's forbidden experiment splits one universe into a multiverse plus an antimatter universe whose Anti-Monitor devours worlds; the Monitor self-sacrifices to pocket five Earths; heroes and villains travel to the dawn of time, where the Spectre's intervention leaves a single positive-matter universe. The aftermath — Superman of Earth-2 mourning a Lois who "never existed," three Supermen on one Earth — sets up the two metaphysical conjectures, time travel and multiverse, to be examined.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 122 "More Things in Heaven and Earth" — Surveys real multiverse arguments: the Everett-Wheeler many-worlds reading of quantum mechanics, fine-tuning explained by every possible initial condition existing somewhere rather than by God, and David Lewis's modal realism, on which every way the world could have been is a causally isolated world — it was possible to write a shorter chapter because in some world Hanley did. Tegmark's physics multiverses round out the menu before the question: does any of this fit Crisis?
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 123 "A Multiversity" — Rules out Lewis's modal realism for the DC multiverse (DC worlds interact; Lewis's are causally isolated) and standard branching many-worlds too, then proposes "hypertime," a second time dimension that makes sense of a traveler arriving in another timeline's "1984." Since Crisis speaks of the multiverse becoming one "at the dawn of time" — something that cannot happen in plain time or hypertime — Hanley posits a six-dimensional cosmos with "supertime" and superhistories.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 125 "Identity in Crisis" — Poses the persistence problem through Superman-1 and Superman-2: are they strictly identical? Perdurantism — persons as four-dimensional space-time worms made of temporal parts — makes them distinct worms with no parts in common, so Superman meeting his counterpart is no stranger than you meeting a friend; endurantism, with wholly present strict identity, could identify them across timelines but balks at the impossibility of Superman meeting himself.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 20 "Poker and Philosophy" — Northcott loses his first casino tournament to a fluky inside straight and mines the bad beat for philosophy of science: objective odds collapse into knowledge-relative probabilities (a card-tracking magician would assign different numbers to the very same draw), Laplacean determinism versus quantum chance bears on whether decision theory presupposes free will, and bad-beat counterfactuals — 'I'd have won the tournament but for that hand' — get David Lewis's possible-worlds closeness analysis and Hume's counterfactual account of causation, with no settled verdict. Even game theory cannot deliver a perfect system: a Nash-equilibrium strategy is only optimal against other optimal players, so the mindless all-in 'Stupidus' beats it. Conclusion: no can't-lose system exists, and poker will never be a game for robots.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 19 "Putting Together the Triforce" — Duncan and Gee study the Nintendo NSider forum threads where fans build Zelda timelines, showing that their marshaling of evidence (Ganon's trident, whether the Master Sword is 'legendary' because of an earlier hero or its sage creators, Hyrule's geography as a marker of time) mirrors scientific argumentation. Using Latour and Woolgar's Laboratory Life, they argue that what 'counts' as evidence, even down to excluding the BS Zelda and CD-i games as non-canon, is socially constructed within a community of practice, not value-free data. David Lewis's plurality of worlds supplies the metaphysics for the split-timeline debate after Ocarina of Time, and the chapter concludes that knowledge in general, in labs and in fandoms alike, is constructed through tools, discourse, and interaction.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 17 "The Loneliest Witch" — Auxier gives three theories of why water melts the Wicked Witch, one for each register of Oz: as dream (Bergson's account of dreams as memory explains the fire/water effect-swap), as Baum's fairytale (Susanne Langer's presentational symbols make dryness-wickedness versus water-as-life the tale's moral physics), and as Gregory Maguire's possible world, where the philosophy of language takes over. He narrates Frege's sense/reference distinction—mayor of the Munchkins—to explain how fiction can support truth and falsity ('Dorothy melts the Witch' true, 'Dorothy tried to melt her' false), then deploys Putnam's Twin Earth thought experiment: 'water' in Oz is XYZ while Kansas water is H2O, so Elphaba's word 'water' does not mean what Dorothy's does, and meanings just aren't in the head. Elphaba—the unique being straddling two worlds, killed by H2O she cannot name and terrified by dreams of oceans—is offered as an even stronger argument for Putnam's semantic externalism than Twin Earth's molecule-for-molecule doppelgangers.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 20 "Getting to Oz" — Auxier uses the Wizard's demand that Dorothy kill the Witch to split 'ought' from 'can'—ethics from the metaphysics and logic of possibility—and then asks whether Oz is a genuinely possible world. He explains David Lewis's modal realism (every genuine possibility actual in its own causally isolated world) through counterfactuals about which network aired the film, dissolves the silver-versus-ruby slippers conflict by assigning book-Oz and film-Oz to different possible worlds, and argues that since no flat contradiction can be eked out of the Oz stories, Lewis is committed to Oz's being real—though Maguire's inter-world travel and Elphaba's hybrid, soul-less trans-world identity (her counterpart in our world being, playfully, Dorothy) stretch Lewis's 'counterparts' doctrine to its limit. Peirce supplies the closing caution, with Boole, that logic is a set of norms for how we can and ought to think rather than a proven mirror of other worlds, so believing in Oz's full reality remains permissible fun rather than an obligation.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 20 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Auxier tests Pullman's many-worlds premise, setting Asriel's coin-toss explanation and the Barnard-Stokes hypothesis against Book III's claim that unchosen possibilities are 'snuffed out like candles,' then measures the trilogy against David Lewis's causally independent possible worlds, which forbid the subtle knife's transworld travel and leave the chill Lyra feels at the thought of 'another Lyra' in Will's Oxford as an unresolved transworld-identity puzzle. Compiling fourteen kinds of conscious beings from humans and dæmons to specters and the Abyss itself, he argues Pullman's cosmology is panpsychist and aesthetic rather than moral or epistemic, ordered by what the alethiometer, the knife, and the spyglass can and cannot do, with the alethiometer submitting to the knife and love alone able to break it, as Will's love for his mother and for Lyra does twice. Peirce's agapicism, evolution by creative love alongside chance and mechanical necessity, supplies the closest philosophical analogue to Pullman's 'Matter loved Dust.'
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 24 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Finley puts Pullman's parallel worlds beside philosophers' possible worlds: the twin Oxfords sharing Simon Parslow's scratched initials invite the inference that Lyra's world has its own Madagascar, while modal realists like Lewis ('out there going on') take possible worlds to really exist and more skeptical theorists treat them as convenient fictions like 'in the story.' She contrasts their origins, quantum splitting at the level of elementary particles versus eternal logical possibility, explains why the indexical 'actual world' is one we can never leave, and argues that Lewis's underdetermination of fiction means the books describe not one possible world but vast numbers differing in unmentioned details like the population of alternate Madagascar. Lewis's counterpart theory then resolves Lyra's chill at 'perhaps there was a Lyra': the counterpart in Will's Oxford could never be her, only someone remarkably like her.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 13 "Which World Am I In" — Juan Ferret tells the story from inside the game: Admetus the Human Mage, chased through Alterac Valley by an Undead Rogue, works through Zeno's paradox of motion, the convergence of infinite series, and whether space and time are discrete, coached by a bodiless voice that turns out to be his player. The voice's revelations — 'You are my creation,' autorun, polymorph, Blink — force the free-will-versus-determinism question from the character's side, since every action is controlled from above. Reference frames, Heisenberg's uncertainty, EPR entanglement, and hidden nods to David Lewis ('Siwel Divad' on possible worlds) and many-worlds theory leave the mage wondering which world, server, or parallel universe he really inhabits.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 32 "Too Big a Byte to Chew" — Kylie Prymus uses a slain Orc to stage the metaphysics of Azeroth: whether the 'dead' Orc is anything more than electrons obeying code (Democritus's atomism), and why explaining Ironforge's empty Tuesday mornings forces us to 'go meta' just as Aristotle's Metaphysics went beyond his Physics. The problem of other minds gets a WoW twist: without nameplates we would sort NPC from PC by the argument from analogy, the same imperfect tool we use offline for pain, coma patients, and animal minds. David Lewis's plurality of worlds becomes concrete through servers — 'the gates could be open' is true for the Uther player because on Medivh they opened on January 23rd — and she concludes that the real world is no better defined than Azeroth.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 41 "Where in the World(s) Are We" — Ablondi asks whether fans' 'if only' claims—'If Bob Stanley had struck out Mookie Wilson, the Sox would have won in 1986,' 'if Pesky had hurried his relay in 1946'—can be true when they lack truthmakers in the actual world. He presents David Lewis's modal realism and counterpart theory as the standard solution, then objects: a Fisk counterpart with a different body, birthday and nickname, or a Red Sox made of 1986 Mets counterparts, is not recognizably Fisk or the Red Sox, and nobody cares about a Lonborg counterpart who won Game Seven.
