- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 5 "Sherlock Holmes as Epistemologist" — Baggett reconstructs Holmes's detective practice as an expansive epistemology built on observation, background knowledge, and abductive inference-to-the-best-explanation, using cases like 'The Blue Carbuncle' hat and the 'eliminate the impossible' maxim. He argues Holmes's boldness in drawing inferences is intellectual courage rather than hubris, invoking William James on the risk of losing truth by excessive caution. He then tests Holmes against feminist epistemologists who fault his cult of cold objectivity and mistrust of women (the Mary Morstan and Irene Adler episodes), concluding Holmes is partly vindicated by his imagination, intuition, and passion but still too fragmented between reason and emotion.
- **The Philosophy of Spike Lee**, ch. 15 "(Still) Fighting the Power Public Space and the Unspeakable Privacy of the Other in Do the Right Thing" — Finnegan reads Do the Right Thing as a dramatization of philosophical skepticism and the 'problem of other minds,' using Wittgenstein's private-language argument, Austin's speech acts, and Cavell to argue that racism is not an epistemic failure to 'know' the Other but an ethical refusal to acknowledge. She shows Lee's split cinematic style (naturalistic interiority for the Italian Americans, alienating canted wide-angle shots for Radio Raheem and the black characters) enacts what being 'othered' looks like, while the Racial Slur Montage stages words as perlocutionary acts and Arendt's 'space of appearances' explains the black characters' exclusion. Mookie's thrown trash can and Sal's Wall of Fame register powerlessness rather than resolution.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 17 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Murray and Schuler argue that Kubrick's unifying vision is a dogmatic skepticism - the 'banality of the good' - in which good characters (Dax, Alice, Alex's parents) are flat and helpless while the wicked have sass, and irony rules. Drawing on Hume's essay 'The Sceptic' and Marx's dissertation on Epicurus's swerving atom, they read Kubrick as a 'rebel without a cause' whose skeptical tropes of cosmic insignificance, present pleasure, and the veneer over the ape (Dr. Strangelove, The Killing, 2001, A Clockwork Orange, Eyes Wide Shut) accommodate rather than comprehend capitalist modernity. They contend Kubrick's Sartrean 'make your own meaning' answer is a false door, since projecting value either really transforms the world (refuting the claim it is indifferent) or projects nothing at all.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — The editors' introduction surveys the volume and frames Soderbergh as a maker of 'philosophical cinema' whose films engage epistemology, metaphysics, and ethics. It previews the essays' claims: that sex, lies, and videotape and Schizopolis stage epistemological questions of truth, evidence, and skepticism; that The Underneath and The Limey use Bergson's durée to explore time and self-understanding; that Traffic tests Kant's ethics against Sartrean individual decision; and that Solaris recasts memory and authenticity via Augustine and Baudrillard's simulacra. It positions Soderbergh within Indiewood filmmaking after Welles as a self-reflexive artist.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Rodriguez-Ruiz argues that Schizopolis and sex, lies, and videotape function as everyday 'thought experiments' about knowledge, contrasting them with Descartes's evil-genius and dream arguments and Dretske's disguised-zebra case. Fletcher must literally become his wife's lover's double to know she is cheating, and Ann pieces together John's affair from a stray earring, dramatizing how high the bar for knowledge of others is and how much depends on lucky accident. The trashcan-music scene stages the problem of induction and Lehrer's Mr. Truetemp. Soderbergh's boss's 'confirm nor deny' speech and Lester's preventable death show the films endorse a moderate skepticism that still affirms nature and power as real, rejecting full relativism and dogmatism.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 23 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Sanders reads Soderbergh's HBO series K Street as a paranoid meditation on appearance and reality set in a Washington lobbying firm, where James Carville and Mary Matalin play fictionalized versions of themselves and the reclusive owner Richard Bergstrom manipulates everyone from afar while endlessly rewatching Mildred Pierce. Through three unresolved mysteries and a 'house of mirrors' structure, the show dramatizes the characters' skepticism about their capacity to know reality and Bergstrom's moral solipsism. Sanders argues Soderbergh's run-and-gun docudrama form itself enacts the epistemic uncertainty, leaving the text radically underdetermined about whether Bergstrom is a con man, a pawn, or a phantom-chasing paranoid.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 16 "“All in War with Time” Medium as Meditation in Sherman’s March" — Rhu reads Ross McElwee's Sherman's March—ostensibly a documentary about Sherman's Civil War campaign but really about a heartbroken filmmaker's search for love amid Cold War nuclear dread—through Walker Percy's The Last Gentleman and Stanley Cavell's The World Viewed. He shows how the film enacts Cavell's ontology of film (viewing the world "from behind the self," movies as reliefs from private fantasy) and the dialogue between perfectionism and skepticism Cavell draws from Emerson's "Experience" and Nietzsche and Kierkegaard. McElwee's deliberately unpolished, self-conscious "personal documentary"—stumbling on the riverbank, leaving in his own second thoughts—turns the war film into a meditation on consciousness, mediation, and being "all in war with Time."
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 4 "02_LaRocca_Chapter_001.html" — Cavell argues that photography's power expresses the mind's fall into skepticism about the external world, reading film as 'a moving image of skepticism' since we see things present to us that are not actually before us. Interpreting Capra's Mr. Deeds Goes to Town, he treats Gary Cooper's Deeds defending his 'fidgetiness' as thinking as a popular-cinema reenactment of Descartes's cogito: after Emerson, who says we can no longer say 'I think, I am' for ourselves, the proof of existence shifts from the mind's self-certainty to the live body's visible restlessness caught by the camera. He links the fidgeting body to Heidegger's das Man and Nietzsche's last man, and invokes Wittgenstein and Emerson on our being 'away' from the world.
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 6 "Spinning Tops and Brains in Vats" — This bundle of essays reads Memento and Inception as epistemology. Knepp uses Peirce's icon/index/symbol triad and Plato's Phaedrus critique of writing to show Leonard Shelby's tattoos and Polaroids give a false illusion of permanent truth (he tattoos Teddy as 'John G.' on purpose). Hoffman uses Kierkegaard's subjective truth to contrast Leonard, who lies to himself while pretending to gather objective 'facts', with Cobb, who takes a Kierkegaardian leap of faith and walks away from the spinning totem to embrace his children. Watson runs the Cartesian/Pyrrhonist dream argument against Inception's totems, arguing beliefs can be valuable via intellectual virtue even if unverifiable, and Lindenmuth pits Nozick's experience machine against Cobb's choice of real children over the dream-shade of Mal to argue reality matters more than pleasure.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 17 "Doomed to Be Perceived" — Paula Smithka uses the Vashta Nerada and Weeping Angels to examine perception and the reality of unobservables. She sets Berkeley's "to be is to be perceived" against Locke's hidden substance and Hume's empiricist skepticism (and Paley's design argument), then distinguishes direct from indirect perceptual evidence, using the shadows, skeletal remains, and Neptune's discovery to frame scientific realism versus van Fraassen's antirealism. The Weeping Angels invert Berkeley, existing only when unperceived and turning to stone when observed, so for them to be is NOT to be perceived.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 11 "How to do Philosophy" — Johnson uses Stephen Colbert's coinages to refute relativism and gut-thinking. 'My Truth' represents individual relativism and 'Wikiality' cultural relativism, both of which Johnson rejects via the correspondence theory of truth and counterexamples like slavery and Nazi Germany. 'Truthiness' is intuitionism, which Johnson attacks using Locke's critique of 'enthusiasts' who reason in a circle, and he argues that appeals to 'a right to my opinion' reveal indifference to truth. Following Socrates, he concludes we should defend beliefs with argument and admit ignorance rather than trust the gut.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 13 "Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress" — Jacoby uses Stan Marsh as the embodiment of W. K. Clifford's ethics of belief, that it is always wrong to believe on insufficient evidence. Stan debunks TV psychic John Edward, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the one making extraordinary claims. Jacoby distinguishes evidential from prudential reasons, presents and criticizes Pascal's Wager (using 'Cartmanland' and the problem of undeserved suffering), and argues via Clifford that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken the mind and, as Stan tells Edward, slow 'the progress of all mankind.'
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 14 "Skepticism Outside the Matrix" — Lawrence uses The Matrix to raise Cartesian skepticism: Neo's deception dramatizes Descartes's dream argument and evil demon, the computer-run Matrix being a technological version of the demon. He argues even Morpheus cannot be certain he has truly awakened ('the Matrix within the Matrix'), so the only certainty is Descartes's cogito. Drawing on Russell's 'Appearance and Reality,' he then argues that even setting aside Matrix scenarios, naive realism fails, since a chair's color, texture, solidity and shape are all perception-relative, leaving the external world's nature deeply uncertain.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 20 "10. Memories Are Made of This" — Nisley reads two episodes through Hume's skepticism about the continued existence of objects and selves, which rests on memory, resemblance, and imagination rather than proof. In 'And When the Sky Was Opened,' three spacemen (Forbes, Harrington, Gart) progressively vanish as memory and corroborating testimony fail, dramatizing Hume's point that belief in continued existence needs more than force and vivacity of ideas. In 'The Trouble with Templeton,' Booth's dead wife Laura reappears but behaves unlike his memories, showing the imagination 'feigns' continuity; both episodes undermine memory as the foundation of rational belief.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 14 "Neither Here, nor There, nor Anywhere" — Randall Auxier reads Green Eggs and Ham as a primer in Peircean pragmatism. The contrarian 'C' illustrates how thinking only begins when a problem interrupts action, and Peirce's distinction between 'genuine doubt' and settled belief-as-habit explains why C clings to 'I do not like them' without ever trying them. Auxier runs C's stubbornness through Peirce's four methods of fixing belief (Authority, A Priori, Tenacity, Science), arguing C relies on tenacity, and likens Sam-I-Am to Saint Monica pestering Augustine into genuine doubt, so that even after C eats the eggs he only knows they settled belief in one context.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 15 "McElligot’s Pool Epistemology (with Fish!)" — Ron Novy uses Marco's faith that unseen fish swim in McElligot's Pool to survey theories of knowledge as justified true belief. The farmer's empiricism and Marco's inference from a book frame a tour through Descartes's evil-genius doubt and skepticism, Locke's primary/secondary qualities (indirect realism), Berkeley's idealism ('to be is to be perceived'), and rationalist a priori knowledge, before turning to feminist epistemology (Schott, Kant's 'intuitions without concepts are blind,' Nietzsche on perspectival seeing) and Quine's naturalized epistemology to argue knowers are situated and the pool may indeed be 'bigger than you or I know.'
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 22 "Chapter 10 Mark Twain’s Serious Humor and That Peculiar Institution" — Kramer argues, against Davenport, that Twain can be simultaneously serious and funny, using humor to attack the 'spirit of seriousness'—the dogmatic certitude and epistemic closure Sartre and Beauvoir describe—rather than sincerity itself. Drawing on Schopenhauer's account of seriousness and Beauvoir's remark that the mystified slave takes his condition as natural, Kramer shows Twain's satire of Christianity ('Little Bessie,' 'Letters from the Earth,' the anti-adultery commandment, the Philippines massacre) exposing the incongruity between professed omnibenevolence and real suffering. Like Democritus the 'laughing philosopher' and a Socratic ironist, Twain undermines complacent certainty without offering dogmatic Truth in its place.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 23 "Chapter 11 Socratic Irony in Twain’s Skeptical Religious Jeremiads" — Jacquette demands a precise definition of Twain's much-invoked irony, adopting Vlastos's/Quintilian's formula that irony says the contrary of what is meant while letting the real meaning be recovered. He classifies Twain's irony as local vs. global and comic vs. sober (tragic/historical): 'Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc' is globally ironic (falsely presented as de Conte's eyewitness manuscript), while the relic-mocking passages of 'The Innocents Abroad' (St. Luke's Madonna, kegs of true-cross nails, three skulls of John the Baptist) are local comic irony. Jacquette concludes Twain's irony is distinctively Socratic: like Socrates interpreting the Delphic oracle, Twain makes a moral and epistemic virtue of ridiculing experts who claim to know what no one can know about God, sin, and the afterlife.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 11 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Jurgensen and Southworth apply Hume's argument against miracles to the virgin birth, treating it as a claimed violation of the natural law that virgins do not conceive. They attack the credibility of the only witnesses, Matthew and Luke, noting their third-hand sources (Mark, Q, L/M), their contradiction over whether Mary and Joseph were married, and the mistranslation of Isaiah's ambiguous 'almah' as the Greek 'parthenos' (literal virgin). Invoking Hume's four defects of miracle testimony and his maxim that no testimony suffices unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the event, they conclude a rational person must reject the Christmas miracle.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 27 "GARDENING" — O'Brien reads Voltaire's closing injunction in Candide, 'we must cultivate our garden,' through David Hume to argue that gardening is therapy—a retreat from metaphysics and religion into the tranquility of common life. Hume rejects belief in miracles and religious 'enthusiasm' not by logic but by recalling everyday reasoning (a melon seed, not a miracle, explains melons in the greenhouse), and the gardener is the sophisticated artisan-reasoner attuned to nature's regularities. Gardening inculcates Humean virtues (industry, patience, balancing action, pleasure and indolence) and Haybron's attunement/engagement/endorsement, yielding Epicurean ataraxia; the Sisyphean gardener (Camus) fighting slugs, and Wittgenstein taking up gardening as a cure, illustrate the point.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 14 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Roche's 'Seeing Snakes' attacks the psychedelicist claim (William James on nitrous oxide, Huxley's 'reducing valve,' Leary) that drugs including cannabis reveal reality-as-it-is. He deploys Russell's line that we 'can make no distinction between the man who eats little and sees heaven and the man who drinks much and sees snakes,' and a reliabilist demand that knowledge have a source proven reliable over independently verifiable cases, to argue drug 'revelations' are indistinguishable from delusion. Foucault is cited that drugs have 'nothing to do with truth and falsity,' and Nietzsche's Dionysian veil-of-Maya passage is used as an example of the mystical rhetoric he debunks.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 21 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Kakko's 'Hallucinatory Terror' uses Fitz Hugh Ludlow's 1857 The Hasheesh Eater to ask 'How can these things be?' — the ontological status of hallucinations that neither exist nor fail to exist. He traces Ludlow's own reading from Locke's empiricism through Hume's skeptical worry that all perception may be hallucinatory with no verifiable external object, to Kant's Copernican turn: the phenomenal/noumenal distinction, synthetic a priori judgments, and space and time as pure forms of intuition. Kant's framework lets Kakko recast Ludlow's 'virtual change of worlds' as a literal, non-metaphorical restructuring of the intuitions conditioning experience.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 27 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Penrose subjects the 'soft drug / hard drug' distinction to conceptual analysis, arguing that—unlike genuinely graded soft-vs-hard eggs—it tracks no single real spectrum. He tests three candidate bases: phenomenological intensity of the high (incoherent, since 'comparable amounts' and interpersonal 'highness' can't be measured), addictiveness (fails, since the traditional distinction counts non-addictive LSD as 'hard'), and dangerousness (Nutt's Lancet study ranks cannabis as more dangerous than some 'hard' drugs, and the distinction trades on illicitly excluding legal alcohol and nicotine). He concludes drugs vary along many distinct property-lines, so the traditional binary is simply false.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 29 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Downes argues, against a Cartesian confidence in self-knowledge, that climbers do not have reliable access to their own internal states while climbing. Drawing on Nisbett and Wilson's sock experiment and dual-process 'new unconscious' psychology, he shows self-reports are often post-hoc confabulations: climbers who declare a wobbler 'felt easy,' claim to be 'not strong enough' on moves they later top-rope easily, or unknowingly dab or stand on the rope. He recommends leaning on external 'scaffolding' (partners, chalk marks, guidebooks) and the 'you're only as good as your last problem' rule to temper dangerous self-assessments, since overrating ability sits in a deceptively close possible world.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 14 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — David Robles's 'The Seeker' argues that declining trust in Western absolutist religion drives people toward yoga as an experiential, self-directed spirituality. His central move is that Patanjali's Yoga Sutras rank direct perception above testimony and scripture — mirroring the scientific method — so yoga functions as a 'spiritual science' harmonious with empiricism, whereas established religion rests on second-hand revelation. He distinguishes 'spiritual' (personal, inspiration-based) from 'religious' (culturally binding dogma) and casts the American 'seeker' as building a better, results-oriented, pragmatic spirituality.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 16 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Steve Jacobson's 'Standing on Your Head' asks whether an educated Westerner can reasonably believe 'yoga theory' (chakras, prana, kundalini, koshas) given that science has superseded ancient theories. He raises a 'standard objection' from the superior predictive power of science (invoking Hume's problem of induction), rejects weak replies, but argues via the epistemology of testimony that people with weak scientific grounds and strong critical testimony can rationally accept yoga theory. He concludes that even if no part of it is credible, abandoning it would leave yoga intact — 'yoga with fewer illusions.'
- **Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low**, ch. 23 "BLUES" — Jesse Steinberg argues that doubt — a pervasive blues theme (B. B. King's 'nobody loves me but my momma,' Otis Spann's 'another mule kickin' in my stall,' Buddy Guy's 'I Smell a Rat') — supports Descartes's external-world skepticism, since knowledge would require ruling out the dreaming hypothesis. Against the 'I don't care' hedonistic reply he deploys Nozick's experience machine to show we value authentic reality over mere pleasant appearance, and he rejects contextualism as a solution. Endorsing Socrates' examined life, he settles for strong justification rather than certainty, reading Charley Patton's 'can't tell my future, can't tell my past' as the blues' honest coping with irreducible doubt.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 8 "Horror and the Idea of Everyday Life On Skeptical Threats in Psycho and The Birds" — Philip J. Nickel argues horror has an epistemological value structurally parallel to philosophical skepticism: it maliciously rips away the tacit 'cognitive trust' backing our everyday actions. In The Birds, the diner 'symposium' where Mrs. Bundy's confident science that birds cannot coordinate an attack is refuted moments later dramatizes a paranoid scenario we cannot rationally rule out. In Psycho, Marion Crane's isolation and misplaced trust in the seemingly normal Norman Bates enacts the skeptical premise that the ordinary person you rely on could murder you. Like Hume returning to backgammon, viewers can only resume everyday life, which Nickel says horror exposes as a necessary but insecure construction.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 8 "2. The Matrix" — Rowlands reads The Matrix as a vivid staging of Cartesian skepticism: Neo's pod-world is Descartes's dream and evil-demon conjectures (AI plays the demon) plus the modern brain-in-a-vat, showing we cannot be certain the external world exists. He uses the 'there is no air/muscles' and 'twin buildings' variant of Putnam's Twin Earth to argue we cannot even be certain which thoughts we think. The Hume-Nietzsche bundle critique undermines even the cogito, and the spoon-bending boy ('there is no spoon') illustrates Berkeley's idealism as the endpoint of skepticism about the physical world.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 14 "Skepticism Outside the Matrix" — Matt Lawrence uses The Matrix to stage the skeptical problem, running Descartes's dream argument and evil-demon method of doubt (the Matrix as a technological demon) and even a 'Matrix within the Matrix' to show Morpheus cannot know he is awake. Descartes's cogito supplies the one certainty that survives radical deception. Lawrence then draws on Russell's analysis of the red chair to argue against naive realism: color, texture, solidity, and shape are appearances, so even setting aside the Matrix we cannot know the world in itself.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 25 "23. The X-Files as Philosophy Navigating the “Truth Out There”" — The chapter argues that Darin Morgan's X-Files episodes philosophize by critiquing the show's own 'the truth is out there' mantra from within. Through the conflicting hypnosis testimonies and identical camera blocking in 'Jose Chung's From Outer Space,' Morgan cinematically stages Nietzsche's perspectivism and the claim that 'truth is as subjective as reality'; through Clyde Bruckman and the doomed Ansel of 'Quagmire,' he mounts an anti-Socratic case that relentlessly pursuing truth (as Mulder does) is not worth the ruin it brings. Kowalski then rebuts Morgan using Descartes's cogito and inference-to-the-best-explanation to defend objective truth against radical skepticism, arguing subjectivism about truth is self-refuting.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 52 "49. A Serious Man as Philosophy The Elusiveness of Moral Knowledge" — Biderman reads the Coens' A Serious Man through Beauvoir's figure of the 'serious man' (from The Ethics of Ambiguity), the man who craves a single absolute value and blinds himself to moral complexity: physics professor Larry Gopnik, beset by divorce, a bribing student Clive, and Sy Ableman's death, seeks moral knowledge that would let him be such a man. The chapter argues Larry's quest fails across cognitivist, noncognitivist, and pluralist accounts of moral knowledge, showing moral knowledge to be elusive if not impossible. The film's Kafkaesque fables (the Dibbuk, the Goy's Teeth, Rabbi Nachtner's 'L'olam ha-ba', Schrodinger's cat, and the Binding of Isaac in Caravaggio's painting) all stage the absurd collapse of interpretation, echoing the Book of Job, which Maimonides read as a parable rather than history.

### The Shadow

The shadow, in Carl Jung's psychology, is the part of the personality that a person refuses to recognize in themselves—the impulses, weaknesses, and desires judged unacceptable and therefore repressed or projected onto others. Because it is disowned rather than absent, the shadow retains its energy and can erupt unbidden or be seen distorted in the people one despises. Jung argued that psychological maturity requires confronting and integrating the shadow rather than denying it, since owning one's darker side is a precondition for wholeness and self-knowledge.

- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 48 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Liz Stillwaggon Swan explains why crime dramas like Criminal Minds, CSI, and Bones are so watchable: Jung's shadow archetype and collective unconscious mean the Devil in human form on screen taps humanity's shared dark layer, while Aristotle's catharsis lets viewers experience pity and fear safely from the couch, identifying with characters like repulsed Garcia or intellectualizing Dr. Brennan. She adds the CSI effect - jurors with warped expectations of DNA and fingerprint work - and argues the shows satisfy a deep need to see devils like Bundy and Dahmer caught within a tidy forty-three minutes.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 61 "The Devil and Philosophy" — John Thompson argues Mara, who unleashes armies and seductive daughters on the Buddha-to-be under the bodhi tree, is not 'the Buddhist Satan': he has not fallen, wages no cosmic war against a supreme God, and merely personifies trsna (grasping) as overlord of samsara. He finds textbook glosses like Huston Smith's misleading, and praises Bertolucci's Little Buddha, where Mara rises from a pool as Siddhartha's mirror twin - 'Oh Lord of my own Ego, you are pure illusion. You do not exist' - a portrayal he reads through Karen Armstrong's Jungian shadow self and Campbell's Freudian eros-and-thanatos frame, concluding that we are Mara/Satan.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 29 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Tim Jones uses Jung's Shadow to argue Dracula is the British Empire's Shadow Self: everything the Count does in Britain - draining resources, reshaping native identities - mirrors what Britain does abroad, minus the benevolent veneer, while Ego-projection explains why Harker's crew must annihilate him rather than admit what he reflects. The chapter adds that colonial stereotypes became self-fulfilling, with colonized peoples made to live the imposed identities, and reads the era's reverse-invasion fiction (mummies, The War of the Worlds) as a collective staking of the Shadow. It closes by recommending Jungian ownership of the Shadow instead of projection.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 31 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Callis reads the 1931 Lugosi film through Jung: Dracula is Mina's Shadow archetype and animus, embodying her repressed fear of sexuality and of the married life she claims to want, while the vampire's presence in every culture places him in the collective unconscious. Mina's arc - the Call to Adventure, crossing the threshold into Dracula's embrace, and 'resurrection' after his staking - becomes a Shero's Journey of confronting the shadow, with Dracula also playing the Shapeshifter archetype. The chapter ends doubting the happy ending, asking whether Mina defeated her shadow or merely surrendered her dreams of freedom.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 21 "11. Meeting the Monstrous Self" — Piven reads 'The Width of a Circle''s monster sitting by the tree through the doppelgänger tradition (Rank's The Double, Dostoevsky, Kirk's 'Enemy Within,' Luke finding his own face in Vader's mask): the monstrous double is the self, and social identity is the mask that hides it, so 'we have met Sauron and he is us.' Deploying Jungian archetype against mere stereotype, Nietzsche's dictum that truth kills, and the Freudian superego - the devil as its alter ego, perversely enjoying the condemnation it inflicts - the chapter argues Bowie's erotic devil scene shows how moralistic societies brand innocent desire monstrous, and that an agonizing encounter with the inner monster, not clichéd self-mythology, is the dire necessity of self-knowledge.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 12 "2. Know Thyself, Agent Cooper!" — Reads the Season Two Black Lodge finale as Cooper's failed journey of self-knowledge, framed by Socrates' Delphic "know thyself" and the unexamined life. Against Hume's bundle theory — when Hume looks inward he only ever finds particular perceptions, never a self — the chapter sets the Vedanta/Tibetan Buddhist ideal of knowing the true Self beyond thought (the ocean versus its waves), with the Black Lodge as the place Hawk calls a passage "every soul must pass on its way to perfection." Cooper's screaming white-eyed Laura, the flickering Caroline/Annie corpse, and his grinning doppelgänger are Jungian shadow-projections paralleled scene-by-scene with the wrathful visions of the Tibetan Book of the Dead; entering with imperfect courage, he flees his fears instead of integrating them, splitting into trapped good Dale and the rampaging Mr. C of The Return.
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 23 "10. Stranger Shadows" — Cornell reads the Upside Down as an externalized Jungian Shadow: the faceless Demogorgon, 'almost human but it wasn't,' embodies the archetypal shadow of the collective unconscious intruding into Hawkins, and the moral task is integrating it with the conscious ego. Will's possession by the Shadow Monster shows what Jung calls the ego identifying with an unintegrated shadow (his timidity leaving him overpowered), while El is the contrast: after her symbolic rebirth from the fleshy wall she faces absolute evil, acknowledges her own monstrous capacity to kill, and turns the shadow into heroism, ending at Nietzsche's 'becoming who she is.'

### The World as Will

In Arthur Schopenhauer's metaphysics, the world we perceive is mere representation, appearance ordered by the mind, while its inner reality is Will—a blind, purposeless striving that underlies all of nature and every living thing. Adapting Kant's distinction between appearance and thing-in-itself, Schopenhauer identified the thing-in-itself with this restless Will, manifest in the drives of animals, the growth of plants, and even the forces of inanimate matter. Because the Will is a ceaseless craving without ultimate aim, existence driven by it is marked by perpetual want and dissatisfaction. He set out this vision in The World as Will and Representation, where art and, more fully, the denial of the will offer relief from its demands.

- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 22 "U2 and Philosophy" — Han-Pile tests three traditional philosophies of music against U2's own talk about music: the rationalist (Descartes and Leibniz's 'unconscious exercise of arithmetic', satirized by Hit Song Science finding U2 mathematically close to Beethoven), the subjectivist (Hegel and Wackenroder on music as the expression of inner feeling, mirrored in Bono's method of articulating in words the feeling the band first found in improvisation), and the metaphysical (the Pythagorean-Boethian musica mundana whose harmony with our music 'Gloria' and 'Wake Up Dead Man' both invoke, consummated in Schopenhauer's music as direct copy of the will, which Nietzsche's critique of Wagner undermines). Against all three she sets Heidegger's Stimmung: music discloses shared moods - atmospheres that color how a whole world shows up, as 'Beautiful Day' or 'Bullet the Blue Sky' demonstrate. U2's vocation is thus to shift the numbed basic disposition of the age ('Zooropa', 'Numb') toward joy and compassion - rock 'n' roll as an alarm clock for 'dreaming up the world we want to live in'.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 11 "The End of the Leash" — Travis Anderson unleashes Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy on Reservoir Dogs, reading the color-coded aliases as an Apollonian dismemberment of a primordial unity and the pop soundtrack ('Little Green Bag', 'Stuck in the Middle with You') as the Dionysian music structuring the film from within. He defends the ear-cutting scene's excess as creative Dionysian expression rather than gratuity, answering Ella Taylor's charge of 'frighteningly pure art'. Mr. Pink's survival—professional, anonymous, untouched by compassion—marks the reconstituted Dionysus: all but one color must die for the gang to be rejoined in the redemptive orgy of Greek tragedy.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 28 "A Link to the Present" — Compagno argues that the word 'I' in Zelda simultaneously names Link, the virtual body, and the player, the invisible will, and builds this into a 'Schopenhauerian Console': as Schopenhauer held, we have freedom of action but not freedom of will, since the decisions of the unknowable will never appear in consciousness (against Descartes' free mind and Dennett's Cartesian theater critique). Kant's transcendental subject, standing at the border of experience, becomes the player's perspective from which Hyrule exists, what Foucault would call an empirical-transcendental doublet. The payoff: Link's quest is fated and scripted, yet the player wills it in a perpetual present, enacting Schopenhauer's lesson that a determined life is still lived as one's own free act.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 19 "When the Levee Breaks Excess as Truth" — Flynn reads the Swan Song logo (Rimmer's falling Apollo) and songs like 'Kashmir,' 'Whole Lotta Love,' and 'When the Levee Breaks' through Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy: individuals are temporary manifestations of a chaotic primordial unity (Schopenhauer's will), and Dionysian art redeems that suffering by celebrating the very excess that undoes us. The sandstorm of 'Kashmir,' the relentless sexual longing of the traveling blues, Plant's death-moan-as-ecstasy in 'In My Time of Dying,' and Bonham's levee-crushing drums all enact 'excess revealed as truth' — joyous laments in which words bleed into music. This is not hedonism, Flynn argues, but ecstatic awareness that the self's boundaries are artificial and its dissolution is a kind of reunion.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 28 "A (Bronx) Cheer to the Red Sox “Without Whom, Not as Much”" — Writing as a Yankees fan, Konig asks what makes a championship worth wanting: after Schopenhauer's picture of endless striving as suffering, he brings in Richard Taylor (meaning lies in the activity itself, never its completion) and then Nietzsche's will to power, which seeks worthy resistance to overcome. Thought experiments—a childhood 'big game' that turns out to be tee-ball, and the 2004 Sox trouncing the minor-league Atlantic League—show a title without worthy opposition is hollow. Hence the Yankees' twentieth-century dominance would mean nothing without the Red Sox as the sustained, worthy enemy (Bucky Dent, the Pedro-Zimmer melee, the 2004 ALCS collapse included).
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 30 "Are These World Series Champions Really Our Red Sox" — Lee casts pre-2004 fandom as a Kierkegaardian leap of faith ('We Believe') and the Curse of the Bambino as Schopenhauer's irrational deterministic will, with the 1918–2004 cycle of spring hope and October collapse as Camus's Sisyphus. But he argues fans are really existentialists: blaming losses on fate or the Curse is Sartrean bad faith that evades responsibility, since fans did hold Bill Buckner (1986 error) and Grady Little (leaving a spent Pedro in during 2003 ALCS Game 7) individually accountable. The 2004 and 2007 champions remain 'our' Red Sox because we freely choose to care about the team's journey, not because it has a fixed essence; a coda borrows Russell's point about ambiguous reference for the word 'Yankee,' and Andy Wasif's appendix runs Yankees-as-evil through relativism, objectivism and subjectivism.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 32 "Escape to Doctor Who" — Reads the Master as the personification of Schopenhauer's blind, pointless Will: the Doctor's line 'In many ways we have the same mind' is taken literally, so the Master is the dark noumenal side in everyone, seen in the hypnotized Farrel whose ambition the Master acts out and Colonel Trenchard whose patriotism becomes the Master's weapon in 'The Sea Devils'. Building from Kant's phenomena/noumena distinction, he explains the Will as the inaccessible force we glimpse through inner bodily awareness, evil because purposeless. Watching the Doctor's serial victories is then offered as a light, Schopenhauerian escape through art from the terror of the Will.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 13 "I Listen to Public Radio" — Natasha Liebig reads Squidward as Schopenhauer made flesh: his endless craving for musical fame and revenge on Squilliam exemplifies the blind, irrational will-to-live whose frustration just is suffering, so even success could never satisfy him and others' joys (SpongeBob and Patrick playing) become his bellum omnium. Yet Squidward's clarinet, self-portraits and dance are Schopenhauer's aesthetic escape — will-less contemplation of universal Ideas, with music the most metaphysical art — granting fleeting moments of peace until his neighbors interrupt. The chapter closes on the irony that Schopenhauer's genius is childlike, so SpongeBob and Patrick's effortless wonder may make them the truer artists.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 27 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Liane Heller pairs Cohen and Schopenhauer - born and died on September 21st, the autumnal equinox - as two explorers of the world's irrational negativity who both retreat to 'a room' to create. Schopenhauer's directionless Will, his pessimism about a life of constant suffering, his notorious misogyny in 'On Women,' and his ascetic denial of the will-to-live (with his contempt for Judaism and preference for the Upanishads and Buddhist compassion) are set against Cohen's affirmation that love is 'the only engine of survival,' his five-year Zen retreat that could not hold him, and his return to the Judaism of the 'little Jew who wrote the Bible.' A closing imagined dialogue has a humbled Schopenhauer confronted with Cohen's self-compassion and ordinary joys, admitting the limits of his own field of vision.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 27 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter reads Harlan's family bonds through Freud's Oedipus Complex - Raylan bails Arlo out only at stepmother Helen's request, and Coover whimpers 'I'm sorry, Mamma' while cradled in Mags's arms after she hammers his hand, the submissive son destroyed by his need for his mother's approval. It then applies Schopenhauer's pessimism to Winona's pregnancy: if life is suffering, as On the Vanity of Existence argues, bringing a child into Harlan is selfish vanity, and Mags's dynasty-building - grooming Loretta, bequeathing the weed business - is the will-to-live seeking immortality through the family name. Only Boyd and Ava's unsentimental care for the demented Arlo, the chapter suggests, escapes both the Oedipal trap and the vanity of lineage.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 13 "2. Sex Has Something Behind It" — John Heaney pairs Louis with Schopenhauer: both see human existence as error-shaped misery, but more importantly both treat sex as the will-to-live tricking the intellect into serving the species while we mistake the species' good for our own. He reads the 'Come on, God' stand-up (every beautiful thought about a woman followed by a disgusting one) and Louie's 'So Old/Playdate' speech that 'sex is really trying to have a family' as comedic versions of Schopenhauer's metaphysics of love, with episodes like 'Bummer/Blueberries' (a decapitation killing Louie's lust mid-non-date), 'Elevator Part 4' (the civil divorce flashback ending in a possible pregnancy), and 'Eddie' (a man losing the will-to-live along with the will-to-love) enacting the oscillation between sexual arousal and suicidal despair. Even Louis's devotion to his daughters fits Schopenhauer's claim that the sexual delusion transfers to offspring, which is why 'Eddie' ends with Louie refusing to name his reasons to live - he has to pick up his kids in the morning.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 14 "5. Jimi, Janis, and Jim" — Traces 'genius' from the indwelling genie of an art to Goethe as the first person the public called a genius, then applies Kant's doctrine — the genius gives the rule to future art, produces what no determinate rule can govern, and cannot explain or teach what he does — to Jimi (having the Experience learn 'Sgt. Pepper' on one hearing to play it back to the Beatles three days after its release), Janis ('a victim of my own insides'), and Jim. Schopenhauer's dark side of genius — more mind than character, a will that 'affirms its own life by denying the life of others' — explains why the 27 Club burned out, and why we say 'Jimi lives' but 'Jim is still alive.'
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 30 "17. Through Plastic Our Secrets Seen" — Uses Schopenhauer's World as Will to explain why the citizens of Twin Peaks keep living lives they despise: all willing arises from deficiency and suffering, so Shelly cannot leave Leo, Ben cannot face his children, and Ed is consumed oscillating between Norma and Nadine, while the blind will — not reflection — determines who we become. Since only pain is known directly and its absence slides into boredom and banality (Ed's restless drama-making), the town's double lives — Jacoby's coconut tapes hiding Laura's confession, Bobby's dealing, Ben's brothel — are the will's concealed kernels. Laura's wrapped corpse then functions as the reveal: death shows each character's truth, and the chapter closes by turning Socrates' unexamined life against itself, asking what happens when self-examination only uncovers what we wished hidden, as Cooper's daily-present advice offers the lone consolation.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 15 "6. You Don’t Need to Be Human to Have a Human Hand" — Sue Zemka contrasts the film's opening eye — reason and consciousness, in a tradition Arendt summarizes as thinking figured as seeing — with its closing image of Deckard's hand reaching toward Ana's through glass, the sense of touch leading out toward others. Schopenhauer explains K's wondering gaze at his own hands in the snow as the human predicament of being both will and representation, subject and object at once, while Condillac's and Maine de Biran's statue thought experiments ('I feel, therefore I am' against Descartes's cogito) are charged with imagining humanness in isolated figures. The film's answer is relational and political: humanness is made in relationships and resistance, from the Joi-Mariette hand-synced sex scene to the final father-daughter touch.
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 31 "19. Beauty of The Elder" — Courtland Lewis uses KISS's reviled concept album Music from 'The Elder' as a case study in aesthetics. He contrasts objective theories of beauty (Plato and the Golden Ratio, tested against the 4/4 stomp of 'Rock and Roll All Nite') with Hume's taste and Kant's immediacy thesis that beauty is judged without inference, adds the disinterestedness of aesthetic pleasure, and applies Noel Carroll's moderate actual intentionalism (with Jerrold Levinson on what a musical work is) to argue that fans and band co-create the album's meaning. Peter French's collective memory explains why 'The Elder sucks' hardened into fan identity after Casablanca reordered the track listing and wrecked the boy-hero story, and Schopenhauer's claim that music expresses the in-itself of the world redeems the fans who find the album beautiful.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 36 "Free to Be You and Me" — Barker reconciles Cylon programming with freedom through compatibilism and Schopenhauer's 'intelligible character': Boomer's sabotage and shooting of Adama and her betrayal of the Cylons to save Tyrol both flow from one innate, conflicted character, just as Baltar's cowardly 'conversion' to the Cylon god expresses his opportunism. Tigh's decision to keep serving after learning he is a Cylon ('My name is Saul Tigh; I am an officer in the colonial fleet') shows character unchanged by revelation. Starbuck's 'special destiny' in 'Maelstrom' is reread not as fate but as her own character - mother-induced self-doubt at war with pilot confidence - which she finally accepts in the vortex; freedom is not freedom from programming but the necessity of manifesting who one already is.
- **Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality**, ch. 14 "Black sabbath & philosophy" — James Heathers asks why the most improbable band became the one true originator of heavy metal and answers with Schopenhauer: industrial Aston, Birmingham was a monument to the ceaseless, unsatisfied striving of the Will, and music, which maps directly onto the Will itself, gave that world its voice. The tritone's numerically hideous ratios, a point traced through Rameau back to Pythagoras, make it the natural interval of morbidity, which is why "Black Sabbath" and everything from Liszt's Dante Sonata to death metal is marinated in it, and why doom was not a predictable development like Deep Purple or Led Zeppelin. He closes on the irony that Schopenhauer, who preached ascetic denial of the Will, would have loathed a band that answered factory-town despair by smothering the Will in lager, hash, cocaine, and women, only to breed more want in the worst of all possible worlds.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 35 "21 Listening to the Music of Indiana Jones John Williams and Aesthetic Appreciation" — Argues that John Williams's score, more than the stunts or cinematography, drives aesthetic appreciation of the films, walking cue by cue through 'In the Idol's Temple,' 'Marion's Theme,' the 'Desert Chase,' 'Scherzo for Motorcycle and Orchestra,' and 'The Miracle of the Ark.' Applying Jenefer Robinson's philosophy of music, our responses split into culturally coded associations (marches with patriotism, chorales with reverence, Eastern-inflected themes with calm), 'emotions of appreciation' aroused by the sheer beauty of the writing, and emotion-guided grasp of complex structures like the scherzo's shifting keys. Schopenhauer's claim that music fitted to a scene 'discloses its most secret meaning' explains how the villain chords reveal Toht and the Ark cue makes the divine wrath felt.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 28 "Franken-Stark" — Curtis argues Iron Man dramatizes the problem of progress: Schopenhauer's insatiable will explains why every technological fix — the chest plate, the armor, the artificial nervous system — spawns new suffering and dependency, and his pessimism, with Kierkegaard's freedom within insecurity, Nietzsche's flawed Übermensch going out 'in a blaze of glory,' and Sartre's 'cautiously optimistic' existentialism, recasts Iron Man as a tragic antihero rather than a perfected Superman or Batman. Stark's wounded heart, alcoholism as self-medication ('the demon is not in the bottle but in the addict'), and doomed romances with Bethany Cabe and Rumiko Fujikawa make him the flawed hero who has simply learned to live with imperfection. Like Mary Shelley's monster, his extensions have become him — we are all 'Franken-Starks' facing the consequences of our own inventions.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 28 "A Link to the Present" — Dario Compagno uses Schopenhauer's distinction between freedom of action and freedom of will — consciousness never witnesses the moment of decision, only hears the will's outcomes — to model the player-Link relation in Zelda. He proposes a 'Schopenhauerian Console' against Dennett's Cartesian theater: Link is the immanent virtual body in Hyrule, the player's will is the transcendent force outside it, and Kant's transcendental subject is the perspective on the border of experience that connects the two when the gamer becomes 'Link's player'. Foucault's 'empirical-transcendental doublet' explains why 'I am Link' is ambiguous exactly the way 'I' is ambiguous in real life, pointing at once to a body and to an invisible ruling will.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 31 "Notes" — Belluomini analyzes how Junkie XL's score drives Fury Road aesthetically. Aristotle's Politics Book 8 and his theory of catharsis explain why the 'Bloodbag' cue's war-drum rhythms imitate the War Boys' anger and fear while purging ours, and 'emotions of appreciation' at the beauty of 'Brothers in Arms' and 'Storm Is Coming' deepen our admiration of the film. Max's cello motif — one, two, or three repeated notes — telegraphs his panic, safety, or menace and advances the plot with almost no dialogue, and Schopenhauer's claim that the right music is a scene's 'most accurate and distinct commentary' fits the hopeful 'Claw Trucks' cue as Max chooses redemption.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 31 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Reads South Park's music through the Greek doctrine of ethos: Sextus Empiricus' story of Pythagoras sobering drunk youths with slow aulos tunes and Plato's banishment of the soft Ionian and Lydian modes anticipate episodes where music directly changes behavior — Slayer's 'Raining Blood' scattering the hippie horde in 'Die Hippie Die', Cher blasted at the ATF standoff, and the Brown Noise in 'World Wide Recorder Concert'. Plato's tripartite soul maps how the Succubus's 'Morning After' spell enchants Chef's appetitive soul until the boys reverse the melody, while the Sirens' cosmic harmony in the Republic's Myth of Er links back to pitch-planet correspondences. Against Plato's view of music as inferior imitation, Schopenhauer's claim that music copies the Will itself explains why Grandpa's Enya torture in 'Death' communicates despair better than argument; authenticity judgments (Phil Collins appreciated only on Ritalin, Cartman's cynically reworded Faith + 1 hits) echo Plato's demand that music imitate the good.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 7 "Notes" — Argues Rust Cohle's stated pessimism and in-principle embrace of suicide closely track Schopenhauer's view that suffering is built into the world with no providential redemption, yet the two diverge because Schopenhauer condemned suicide as an affirmation of the will-to-live rather than its denial. The chapter traces Rust's three-stage arc — jaded wannabe-suicidal pessimist who nonetheless energetically investigates the Dora Lange case, resigned drinker, and finally cautious affirmer of life after the Yellow King confrontation — and contends his detective work is really motivated by a Schopenhauerian morality of compassion and justice, not mere 'programming.' Rust's finale conversion is read as an evidence-based judgment that thoroughgoing pessimism is intellectually dishonest, since compassion and justice do score nontrivial victories.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 8 "Notes" — Reads Carcosa, the Yellow King, and Ledoux's 'time is a flat circle' as cosmic horror in the lineage of Lovecraft and Ligotti, arguing that the genre's dread — that monsters exist and the fixed laws of nature may fail — is a metaphor for realizing Schopenhauer's blind will, with Rust's car monologues in 'The Long Bright Dark' presented as a beginner's guide to Schopenhauer. It notes Rust inverts the usual Lovecraft protagonist by starting the story already horrified, and that eternal recurrence framed through Schopenhauer's sphere-of-time makes even the rescued children's torment maddeningly endless. The chapter closes by complaining that the finale 'Form and Void' betrays both genres: the occult becomes ordinary crime and Rust's 'light is winning' star-field reverses Schopenhauer's pessimistic cosmology.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Traces Cohle's opening monologue directly to Schopenhauer — reality as a purposeless will whose satisfied desires breed only boredom, answered by ascetic denial of the will-to-live rather than suicide. It then explains Nietzsche's eternal recurrence as the true test of life-affirmation, via the Gay Science demon and Zarathustra's ordeal with the Small Man, and interprets will to power as finding meaning in overcoming resisting conditions, so that affirmation does not mean approving everything that happens. Hatab argues the show's horrified version of the flat circle is Schopenhauerian rather than Nietzschean, and that Cohle's 'light is winning' ending is ambiguous — if it rests on a supernatural reunion with Sophia, it would betray Nietzsche's this-worldly affirmation.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 28 "Notes" — Argues 'time is a flat circle' means neither a metaphysical cosmology nor M-theory physics nor reincarnation, but is Nietzsche's eternal recurrence as a thought experiment about how to live. Tracing Rust's pessimism and his lack of the 'constitution for suicide' (echoing Schopenhauer's claim that suicide affirms the will-to-live, with starvation as its only true denial), it shows the flat circle operating as both trap and cure: obsessing over it keeps Rust on the Yellow King case until his near-death experience becomes the 'tremendous moment' of amor fati. Heidegger's view in Being and Time that anxiety before death can empower meaningful existence frames Rust's final affirmation — escaping the flat circle by faithfully acknowledging it, through sacrifice.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 30 "17. Through Plastic Our Secrets Seen" — Winters uses Schopenhauer's World as Will and Idea to argue that the townsfolk (Shelly, Leo, Ben, Josie, Ed, and Laura) do not freely choose the lives they despise but are driven by the blind will, and so live double lives whose secrets a single death exposes. Laura, unlike the others who mismanage their passions, was denied the chance to develop her own values, so she pursued danger, drugs, and prostitution to see herself through her own eyes; death, he argues, reveals true character (the townsfolk's rush to bury her, their guilt), turning Socrates' unexamined-life dictum uneasy—sometimes what examination reveals is a monster we would rather not see.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 23 "Ride the Pink Horse Money, Mischance, Murder, and the Monads of Film Noir" — Silver reads Robert Montgomery's Ride the Pink Horse as a prototypically noir embodiment of Schopenhauer's The World as Will and Representation. The revenge-driven Gagin, like Hugo, is enslaved to money and will—'a man can do what he wants, but not want what he wants'—and takes the limits of his own field of vision for the limits of the world, blind to the monads and Platonic-cave shadows of fate around him. Against him stand Pancho's suffering kindness and the Indian girl Pila's selfless compassion, which Silver aligns with Schopenhauer's dictum that 'compassion is the basis of all morality' and his prizing of aesthetic transcendence. The carousel (tío vivo) and the burning of Zozobra, the god of bad luck, become symbols of will's pointless circular striving from which only sacrifice and art offer escape.
- **The Philosophy of Werner Herzog**, ch. 11 "Nature and Natural Meaning in Grizzly Man" — Marc Furstenau reads Grizzly Man as Herzog's philosophy of nature, arguing that Herzog's vision of nature as chaos, hostility, and murder mirrors Schopenhauer's terrifying Will and the fact/value split, and that Herzog blames Timothy Treadwell's sentimental faith in natural harmony for his and Amie Huguenard's deaths while secretly sharing Treadwell's amor fati. Using Iris Murdoch's Metaphysics as a Guide to Morals and Mary Midgley's Beast and Man, Furstenau contends that both Herzog and Schopenhauer succumb to an 'outrageous simplicity' that denies animal agency; against them he argues, via Midgley, that culture is natural and interspecies sympathy is real, reading Treadwell's extreme close-up of the bear (where Herzog sees 'only the overwhelming indifference of nature') as evidence of imaginative continuity between human and animal.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 32 "Escape to Doctor Who" — Ken Curry reads the Master as Schopenhauer's Will personified. After sketching Kant's phenomena/noumena and Schopenhauer's identification of the noumenal thing-in-itself as a blind, pointless (and thus evil) Will known indirectly through the body, he argues the Master ('in many ways we have the same mind,' 'Logopolis') is the dark Will present in everyone. Through 'Terror of the Autons' and 'The Sea Devils' he shows the Master exploiting the fatal vanity of Farrel and Colonel Trenchard as their own evil counterpart, with good (the Doctor) narrowly triumphing so the Will's cruelty entertains rather than oppresses us.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 28 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Howe distinguishes fine art, erotica, and pornography by the 'aesthetic distance' or disinterestedness the viewer can sustain, drawing on Schopenhauer's account of aesthetic contemplation (the perceiver dissolving individual will to become a 'pure subject' mirroring the object) and Bullough's 'psychical distance'. He argues pornography merely provokes vulgar genital arousal by exaggerating body parts out of gestalt balance (contra Feinberg, who allowed a painting to be both fine art and porn), so it forfeits disinterest entirely, while erotica provokes affection tied to romantic love and can approach fine art. Using Degas' Nude Study he concedes erotica and fine art differ only by degree, whereas pornography differs in kind because it permits no aesthetic attitude.
- **Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low**, ch. 18 "BLUES" — David C. Drake argues that the blues' distinctive achievement is presenting 'sadness as beauty,' which lets performers and listeners find their own sorrow beautiful and thus therapeutic. He surveys theories of beauty — Plato's proportion/harmony/unity and Aristotle's order/symmetry (a beautiful life needs some sorrow), Kant's claim that beauty is a subjective-yet-universal judgment requiring reflection, Lyotard's sublime that 'pleases only by causing pain,' and Schopenhauer's view that aesthetic contemplation temporarily frees us from the striving Will — and links beauty to truth and goodness (Keats, Nietzsche's 'whoever despises himself respects himself as one who despises') to explain why blues sorrow feels good.

### Philosophical Pessimism

Philosophical pessimism, as developed by Arthur Schopenhauer, is the view that existence is fundamentally characterized by suffering and that, on balance, it would be better not to strive after the endless demands of the will to life. Because life is driven by insatiable craving, satisfaction is fleeting and quickly gives way to new want or to boredom, so that pain outweighs pleasure over the whole of existence. Schopenhauer drew partly on Buddhist and Hindu themes in concluding that liberation lies in quieting the will rather than gratifying it. His pessimism deeply influenced later thinkers and artists, including Nietzsche, who wrestled with it, and Freud, who echoed its picture of the psyche as governed by relentless drives.

- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 12 "Death Knight as Overman" — Luke Cuddy asks whether playing WoW can answer nihilism, using Schopenhauer's bleak remark on our sudden existence and Nietzsche's death of God to set up the problem — King Bangalash dies and WoW goes on, just as humans die and the universe continues. Entering Huizinga's Magic Circle gives Azeroth its meanings, but the player must then dissolve the circle, recognize that the game itself is meaningless, and keep playing anyway — creating the toon as a work of art in the Dionysian spirit. A maxed Death Knight still is not Nietzsche's Overman, because the player affirms only her in-game existence; the fifth step is carrying that self-creation back into real life.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 28 "A (Bronx) Cheer to the Red Sox “Without Whom, Not as Much”" — Writing as a Yankees fan, Konig asks what makes a championship worth wanting: after Schopenhauer's picture of endless striving as suffering, he brings in Richard Taylor (meaning lies in the activity itself, never its completion) and then Nietzsche's will to power, which seeks worthy resistance to overcome. Thought experiments—a childhood 'big game' that turns out to be tee-ball, and the 2004 Sox trouncing the minor-league Atlantic League—show a title without worthy opposition is hollow. Hence the Yankees' twentieth-century dominance would mean nothing without the Red Sox as the sustained, worthy enemy (Bucky Dent, the Pedro-Zimmer melee, the 2004 ALCS collapse included).
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 32 "Escape to Doctor Who" — Reads the Master as the personification of Schopenhauer's blind, pointless Will: the Doctor's line 'In many ways we have the same mind' is taken literally, so the Master is the dark noumenal side in everyone, seen in the hypnotized Farrel whose ambition the Master acts out and Colonel Trenchard whose patriotism becomes the Master's weapon in 'The Sea Devils'. Building from Kant's phenomena/noumena distinction, he explains the Will as the inaccessible force we glimpse through inner bodily awareness, evil because purposeless. Watching the Doctor's serial victories is then offered as a light, Schopenhauerian escape through art from the terror of the Will.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 13 "I Listen to Public Radio" — Natasha Liebig reads Squidward as Schopenhauer made flesh: his endless craving for musical fame and revenge on Squilliam exemplifies the blind, irrational will-to-live whose frustration just is suffering, so even success could never satisfy him and others' joys (SpongeBob and Patrick playing) become his bellum omnium. Yet Squidward's clarinet, self-portraits and dance are Schopenhauer's aesthetic escape — will-less contemplation of universal Ideas, with music the most metaphysical art — granting fleeting moments of peace until his neighbors interrupt. The chapter closes on the irony that Schopenhauer's genius is childlike, so SpongeBob and Patrick's effortless wonder may make them the truer artists.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 27 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Liane Heller pairs Cohen and Schopenhauer - born and died on September 21st, the autumnal equinox - as two explorers of the world's irrational negativity who both retreat to 'a room' to create. Schopenhauer's directionless Will, his pessimism about a life of constant suffering, his notorious misogyny in 'On Women,' and his ascetic denial of the will-to-live (with his contempt for Judaism and preference for the Upanishads and Buddhist compassion) are set against Cohen's affirmation that love is 'the only engine of survival,' his five-year Zen retreat that could not hold him, and his return to the Judaism of the 'little Jew who wrote the Bible.' A closing imagined dialogue has a humbled Schopenhauer confronted with Cohen's self-compassion and ordinary joys, admitting the limits of his own field of vision.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 27 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter reads Harlan's family bonds through Freud's Oedipus Complex - Raylan bails Arlo out only at stepmother Helen's request, and Coover whimpers 'I'm sorry, Mamma' while cradled in Mags's arms after she hammers his hand, the submissive son destroyed by his need for his mother's approval. It then applies Schopenhauer's pessimism to Winona's pregnancy: if life is suffering, as On the Vanity of Existence argues, bringing a child into Harlan is selfish vanity, and Mags's dynasty-building - grooming Loretta, bequeathing the weed business - is the will-to-live seeking immortality through the family name. Only Boyd and Ava's unsentimental care for the demented Arlo, the chapter suggests, escapes both the Oedipal trap and the vanity of lineage.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 13 "2. Sex Has Something Behind It" — John Heaney pairs Louis with Schopenhauer: both see human existence as error-shaped misery, but more importantly both treat sex as the will-to-live tricking the intellect into serving the species while we mistake the species' good for our own. He reads the 'Come on, God' stand-up (every beautiful thought about a woman followed by a disgusting one) and Louie's 'So Old/Playdate' speech that 'sex is really trying to have a family' as comedic versions of Schopenhauer's metaphysics of love, with episodes like 'Bummer/Blueberries' (a decapitation killing Louie's lust mid-non-date), 'Elevator Part 4' (the civil divorce flashback ending in a possible pregnancy), and 'Eddie' (a man losing the will-to-live along with the will-to-love) enacting the oscillation between sexual arousal and suicidal despair. Even Louis's devotion to his daughters fits Schopenhauer's claim that the sexual delusion transfers to offspring, which is why 'Eddie' ends with Louie refusing to name his reasons to live - he has to pick up his kids in the morning.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 11 "3. Mermen and Dismemberment" — Contends that Hendrix's discord is philosophy-as-discord: 'I Don't Live Today' (the Native American dead-in-life), the Woodstock 'Star-Spangled Banner' with its bombs and sirens against sporting-event sentimentality, 'Machine Gun,' and 'House Burning Down' lacerate listeners so they actually feel war's atrocities instead of parroting patriotic clichés. Against this the chapter sets the oceanic, womb-like escape fantasies of '1983 (A Merman I Should Turn to Be)' and 'Valleys of Neptune,' treating them through Schopenhauer as metaphysical consolation, Marx's opiate, and Nietzsche's 'hangman's metaphysics,' and concludes that Hendrix finally refuses such world-denying illusions — and Heideggerian inauthentic withdrawal — in favor of existential engagement with suffering here and now.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 18 "Death" — Reads Alien3's Fury 161 through impurity and contagion: Mary Douglas's 'matter out of place,' Foucault's confinement of the mad (the YY-chromosome inmates quarantined as social infection; Golic's fixation on the 'dragon' as Schopenhauer's madness of a fixed idea), Hegel and Schelling's philosophies of biology in which disease, decline, and death are necessary moments of life, and Plato's virtue-as-health of the soul. Ripley's fall into the molten lead embraces Schelling's 'indifference' of freedom and its enemy - she refuses Bishop's quack offer to 'deal with the malignancy' so Weyland-Yutani can never harvest the queen inside her.
- **Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality**, ch. 14 "Black sabbath & philosophy" — James Heathers asks why the most improbable band became the one true originator of heavy metal and answers with Schopenhauer: industrial Aston, Birmingham was a monument to the ceaseless, unsatisfied striving of the Will, and music, which maps directly onto the Will itself, gave that world its voice. The tritone's numerically hideous ratios, a point traced through Rameau back to Pythagoras, make it the natural interval of morbidity, which is why "Black Sabbath" and everything from Liszt's Dante Sonata to death metal is marinated in it, and why doom was not a predictable development like Deep Purple or Led Zeppelin. He closes on the irony that Schopenhauer, who preached ascetic denial of the Will, would have loathed a band that answered factory-town despair by smothering the Will in lager, hash, cocaine, and women, only to breed more want in the worst of all possible worlds.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 28 "Franken-Stark" — Curtis argues Iron Man dramatizes the problem of progress: Schopenhauer's insatiable will explains why every technological fix — the chest plate, the armor, the artificial nervous system — spawns new suffering and dependency, and his pessimism, with Kierkegaard's freedom within insecurity, Nietzsche's flawed Übermensch going out 'in a blaze of glory,' and Sartre's 'cautiously optimistic' existentialism, recasts Iron Man as a tragic antihero rather than a perfected Superman or Batman. Stark's wounded heart, alcoholism as self-medication ('the demon is not in the bottle but in the addict'), and doomed romances with Bethany Cabe and Rumiko Fujikawa make him the flawed hero who has simply learned to live with imperfection. Like Mary Shelley's monster, his extensions have become him — we are all 'Franken-Starks' facing the consequences of our own inventions.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 7 "Notes" — Argues Rust Cohle's stated pessimism and in-principle embrace of suicide closely track Schopenhauer's view that suffering is built into the world with no providential redemption, yet the two diverge because Schopenhauer condemned suicide as an affirmation of the will-to-live rather than its denial. The chapter traces Rust's three-stage arc — jaded wannabe-suicidal pessimist who nonetheless energetically investigates the Dora Lange case, resigned drinker, and finally cautious affirmer of life after the Yellow King confrontation — and contends his detective work is really motivated by a Schopenhauerian morality of compassion and justice, not mere 'programming.' Rust's finale conversion is read as an evidence-based judgment that thoroughgoing pessimism is intellectually dishonest, since compassion and justice do score nontrivial victories.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 8 "Notes" — Reads Carcosa, the Yellow King, and Ledoux's 'time is a flat circle' as cosmic horror in the lineage of Lovecraft and Ligotti, arguing that the genre's dread — that monsters exist and the fixed laws of nature may fail — is a metaphor for realizing Schopenhauer's blind will, with Rust's car monologues in 'The Long Bright Dark' presented as a beginner's guide to Schopenhauer. It notes Rust inverts the usual Lovecraft protagonist by starting the story already horrified, and that eternal recurrence framed through Schopenhauer's sphere-of-time makes even the rescued children's torment maddeningly endless. The chapter closes by complaining that the finale 'Form and Void' betrays both genres: the occult becomes ordinary crime and Rust's 'light is winning' star-field reverses Schopenhauer's pessimistic cosmology.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 9 "Notes" — Distinguishes philosophical pessimism (Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Camus, Unamuno) — the denial that the universe is an ordered place whose laws human reason can grasp — from mere gloominess, and reads Rust's 'time is a flat circle' as Nietzschean anti-metaphysics of a world going nowhere. It argues pessimism makes Rust the better detective because, expecting no rational order, he sees what is actually there, while optimist Marty's illusions about family and career multiply his losses and end with him losing both. Against conflating pessimism with despair, the chapter splits ideas (pessimism) from attitudes (hope), showing how Hart's heart and Cohle's clear sight combine into the show's ideal of hopeful pessimism.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 12 "Notes" — Reconstructs Rust's scattered remarks — the world as 'one giant gutter,' procreation as the hubris of yanking a soul out of nonexistence into the thresher — into an explicit anti-natalist argument, testing each premise and conceding procreation is selfish while questioning whether every life nets more harm than good. It presents David Benatar's asymmetry between the absence of pain (always good) and the absence of pleasure (bad only for someone deprived), illustrating it with the show: contraception as procreative duty, the wrongness of conceiving in Tuttle's Louisiana, and the emptiness of Childress' temple as a good in itself. The chapter concludes that Rust's 'opt out of a raw deal' is philosophically defensible, with Schopenhauer's desire-pendulum and Hobbes' 'nasty, brutish, and short' backing the claim that most lives are bad.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Traces Cohle's opening monologue directly to Schopenhauer — reality as a purposeless will whose satisfied desires breed only boredom, answered by ascetic denial of the will-to-live rather than suicide. It then explains Nietzsche's eternal recurrence as the true test of life-affirmation, via the Gay Science demon and Zarathustra's ordeal with the Small Man, and interprets will to power as finding meaning in overcoming resisting conditions, so that affirmation does not mean approving everything that happens. Hatab argues the show's horrified version of the flat circle is Schopenhauerian rather than Nietzschean, and that Cohle's 'light is winning' ending is ambiguous — if it rests on a supernatural reunion with Sophia, it would betray Nietzsche's this-worldly affirmation.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 9 "Acknowledgment" — William Irwin diagnoses Neptune, from the 09-ers down to the PCH-ers, with status anxiety (via Alain de Botton's Status Anxiety) and prescribes the Stoic remedy: Epictetus on the insult lying in our judgment rather than the insulter, and Marcus Aurelius, the emperor who chose serenity over vengeance, show how Keith and Veronica ground self-worth in virtue no one can take away. Sartre's 'hell is other people' and the look explain how Veronica is reduced to a dumb blonde and Duncan to a murderer until he flees to Cuba, while Schopenhauer's choice between loneliness and vulgarity frames Mac's switched-at-birth longing, Wallace's basketball-bought status, and Weevil's self-made standing as PCH leader. Irwin closes by offering the show itself as Aristotelian catharsis-through-comedy, art as therapy for the viewer's own status anxiety.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 32 "Sixteenth Hole Golf and the Meaning of Life" — Randy Lunsford uses Annika Sorenstam's early retirement to ask what makes golf—and life—meaningful, surveying religious versus scientific accounts of purpose and E. J. Bond's claim that meaning comes from pursuing objectively valuable ends, not just satisfying desire. He tests Epicurean hedonism and Nozick's experience machine (we want to really shoot the course record, not merely feel we did), Taylor's reworking of the Sisyphus myth (meaning via injected desire), and Schopenhauer's pessimism that satisfied desire only yields boredom. He argues golf's very finitude—eighteen holes, like a mortal life—gives it meaning, so excellence, relationships, playing by the rules, and taking responsibility for each shot are what make both golf and life worthwhile.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 15 "Film Noir and the Meaning of Life" — Steven Sanders uses film noir to motivate philosophical reflection on the meaning of life, reading its pessimistic sensibility (Touch of Evil, Detour, Out of the Past, D.O.A., Vertigo) as the presupposition that life is meaningless per se. He runs through Schopenhauer's pessimistic arguments from the vanity and transience of existence, Nagel's rebuttal that our not mattering in a million years does not stop things mattering now, and the tension between Sartrean existentialist freedom and noir's Freudian fatalism of the inescapable past. He then lays out three models of meaninglessness (Baier's worthlessness and purposelessness, Camus/Nagel's absurdity met with irony), reading noir protagonists as ironists, before rejecting the noir view that life must be meaningless and arguing that meaning is a matter of degree, requiring realizable projects of positive value.
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — Conard uses Mean Streets' guilt-ridden Charlie to survey conceptions of unhappiness against three definitions of happiness: beatitude (Aquinas), pleasure (Mill's hedonism), and flourishing (Aristotle's eudaimonia). He reads Charlie as damned in his own Catholic eyes, then invokes Nietzsche's Genealogy that religion manufactures guilt from internalized instinct, Plato's disordered soul and akrasia to explain Charlie's conflicting desires, and Schopenhauer's and Freud's pessimism that suffering is our natural state. He argues Charlie reaches dysdaimonia by acquiring vices and pursuing an ignoble (gangster) life, closing with Plato's Symposium and Sartre's facticity/transcendence to cast unhappiness as an ontological lack at the heart of human desire.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 11 "My Troubles Are Going to Have Troubles with Me Schopenhauer, Pessimism, and Nietzsche" — Jacob Held pits Schopenhauer's pessimism against Nietzschean affirmation using I Had Trouble in Getting to Solla Sollew. He reads Schopenhauer's will-to-life and 'pendulum between pain and boredom' into Seuss's endlessly striving characters, and treats the mirage-towns Solla Sollew and Boola Boo Ball as proof there is no escape from suffering.
