The protagonist's final line, 'I've bought a big bat... now my troubles are going to have troubles with me,' becomes Nietzsche's yes-saying: instead of the ascetic renunciation Schopenhauer prescribes, Seuss's child-hero affirms life, redeeming its accidents the way Nietzsche's eternal-recurrence thought experiment and 'become a child' passage in Zarathustra demand.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 20 "From Desperation to Haven" — Held reads The Tommyknockers, Desperation, and The Regulators through Arthur Schopenhauer's pessimism, arguing King's worlds are 'always already sunk in evil' and that the will to live swings life between pain and boredom even before the supernatural arrives. He identifies egoism as the root of King's cruelty (Hilly banishing David Brown to Altair-4, Bobbi turning her dog into a battery) and offers Schopenhauer's compassion-based virtue ethic, 'injure no one; help everyone,' as the answer, supported by MacIntyre on the degradation of happiness and set against Nietzsche's 'last man' and nihilism. Gard's rescue of David Brown ('the kid matters or nothing matters') and Johnny Marinville's self-sacrifice in Desperation exemplify the heroic, compassionate life that defies the dark.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 19 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Clack's 'Cannabis and the Human Condition' reads intoxication through Freud's Civilization and its Discontents, where drugs are the 'crudest but most effective' palliative against a life 'too hard for us,' tied to the pleasure principle and the Nirvana/death-instinct drive to discharge stimulus. He supplements Freud with Schopenhauer's pessimism — life oscillating between suffering and boredom — to add 'stimulus hunger' Freud ignored, arguing cannabis both dampens and stokes the 'fire in the brain' depending on THC potency (high vs. stoned). He concludes that, like religion, art and love, cannabis augments a bleak existence, so 'all cannabis use is medicinal.'

### Ethics of Compassion

Schopenhauer grounded morality not in reason or duty but in compassion, the immediate participation in another's suffering that moves us to relieve it. He argued that ethical action arises when the ordinary boundary between self and other is momentarily overcome, so that we recognize in another being the same will that constitutes our own inner nature. This metaphysical insight—that at the deepest level all beings are one—explains why genuine kindness is possible and why cruelty and egoism rest on the illusion of separateness. His ethics of compassion, set out in On the Basis of Morality, offered a pointed alternative to Kant's rule-based account of moral obligation.

- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 27 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Liane Heller pairs Cohen and Schopenhauer - born and died on September 21st, the autumnal equinox - as two explorers of the world's irrational negativity who both retreat to 'a room' to create. A closing imagined dialogue has a humbled Schopenhauer confronted with Cohen's self-compassion and ordinary joys, admitting the limits of his own field of vision.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 7 "Notes" — Argues Rust Cohle's stated pessimism and in-principle embrace of suicide closely track Schopenhauer's view that suffering is built into the world with no providential redemption, yet the two diverge because Schopenhauer condemned suicide as an affirmation of the will-to-live rather than its denial. Rust's finale conversion is read as an evidence-based judgment that thoroughgoing pessimism is intellectually dishonest, since compassion and justice do score nontrivial victories.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 23 "Ride the Pink Horse Money, Mischance, Murder, and the Monads of Film Noir" — Silver reads Robert Montgomery's Ride the Pink Horse as a prototypically noir embodiment of Schopenhauer's The World as Will and Representation. The revenge-driven Gagin, like Hugo, is enslaved to money and will—'a man can do what he wants, but not want what he wants'—and takes the limits of his own field of vision for the limits of the world, blind to the monads and Platonic-cave shadows of fate around him. Against him stand Pancho's suffering kindness and the Indian girl Pila's selfless compassion, which Silver aligns with Schopenhauer's dictum that 'compassion is the basis of all morality' and his prizing of aesthetic transcendence. The carousel (tío vivo) and the burning of Zozobra, the god of bad luck, become symbols of will's pointless circular striving from which only sacrifice and art offer escape.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 20 "From Desperation to Haven" — Held reads The Tommyknockers, Desperation, and The Regulators through Arthur Schopenhauer's pessimism, arguing King's worlds are 'always already sunk in evil' and that the will to live swings life between pain and boredom even before the supernatural arrives. He identifies egoism as the root of King's cruelty (Hilly banishing David Brown to Altair-4, Bobbi turning her dog into a battery) and offers Schopenhauer's compassion-based virtue ethic, 'injure no one; help everyone,' as the answer, supported by MacIntyre on the degradation of happiness and set against Nietzsche's 'last man' and nihilism. ### Death Is Nothing to Us

The maxim that "death is nothing to us" is the core of Epicurus's argument against the fear of dying. Since Epicurus held that good and evil consist in sensation, and death is the total absence of sensation, he reasoned that death can neither be experienced nor harm the one who dies: where death is, we are not, and where we are, death is not. The teaching was meant not as cold consolation but as therapy, freeing people from an anxiety Epicurus considered the chief obstacle to a tranquil life.

- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 24 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Bill Davis asks why Arwen would 'choose a mortal life' with Aragorn and why wise elves and men call death a gift. The Ringwraiths show that existence can be worse than death - undead kings whose frustrated nature is perpetual torment - while Socrates in the Apology, Lucretius, Sartre, and Camus supply reasons not to fear annihilation, and the elves' endless life raises Boethius's and Bernard Williams's problem of boring immortality (Camus's Sisyphus, Wowbagger the Infinitely Prolonged). He concludes that Arwen and Aragorn, uncommonly wise and loving, accept death as Ilúvatar's gift: she prefers a finite life of deep love, and they trust the old stories of a world 'remade' beyond the circles of Arda.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 139 "The Approaching Battle" — Introduces the chapter's Heideggerian frame: authenticity comes from facing mortality rather than evading it, against the Epicurean advice to be unconcerned since death is merely the end of experience and so happens to no one; death's imminence forces us to define ourselves and not live half-asleep. Harry, death-marked since infancy, lives authentically where Voldemort lives inauthentically, with Plato's dictum that true philosophers make dying their profession as ancient corroboration.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 7 "Not to Put Too Fine a Point on It" — Richard Greene asks why becoming Undead is bad for the one who becomes Undead and why we rank it worse than death, restricting himself to unfriendly vampires and zombies (setting aside soulful exceptions like Angel, Spike, Louis, and Ed from Shaun of the Dead). He tests Nagel's deprivation view (vampires gain infinite experiences, so nothing is deprived) and Williams's desire-frustration view (undeath replaces rather than frustrates desires: scotch for blood, pork roast for raw flesh), then Mill's better-Socrates-dissatisfied comparison and the thought that the Undead's evil nature makes undeath objectively bad. Each fails, so he concludes undeath is not objectively bad, only comparatively bad, and one might as well make the best of it.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 21 "Deserving to Be a Vampire" — Ted Preston asks whether becoming a vampire would be morally good or desirable, working through Forever Knight's Nick draining his lover, Blade feeding on stored blood, and The Lost Boys' promise that Michael will 'never grow old'. He argues vampires are not evil by nature: if they cannot control their hunger they are pitied rather than blamed (though we remain Aristotle-responsible for choosing to become addicted), and consensual, non-lethal feeding is no worse than mortals eating animals, since the bite only becomes murder by choice. Against Epicurus's claim that death is nothing to us, he uses Furley and Nussbaum's deprivation view - death vindictively empties our long-term projects like marriage or a career - so vampiric immortality genuinely preserves value, while the standard boredom objection fails because there are repeatable pleasures in a changing world. The thought experiment ends as moral psychology for mortals: since neither of us will become a vampire, live a life that would be worthy of eternity.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 31 "I’ll Get Up and Fly Away" — Ian Duckles and Eric Rubenstein use the community's losses of Pigpen and Jerry Garcia to ask whether death is bad, running Epicurus's argument that being dead is no experience and hence no harm, the tedium-of-immortality argument that eternal life would eventually exhaust every fundamental desire, and Socrates's Phaedo claim that death frees the soul to philosophize — which disturbingly implies Pigpen's early 'burn out' was the better fate. Their resolution is Heidegger: authentically confronting death as the end of all possibilities strips socially imposed values (consumerist 'keeping up with the Joneses') and frees us to create our own projects, so mortality itself is something to be grateful for. On this reading the Deadhead counterculture — rejecting 1950s suburban scripts for free love, psychedelics, and life on tour — lived Heideggerian authenticity, and it is better to fade away (like Garcia) than to burn out (like Pigpen).
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 26 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Greene applies the philosophy of death to Pullman's worlds, starting from the Epicurean puzzle that death is bad only if experienced, so it cannot be bad, plus the asymmetry puzzle about prenatal non-existence, then testing the Deprivation View (Father Gomez's bullet would rob Lyra of Oxford, the alethiometer, and love) and the Desire-Frustration View (Iorek's frustrated desires) against a universe whose dead do persist as ghosts. The world of the dead, with its harpies, eternal boredom, and the pain of leaving Pan with the Boatman, seems to refute Epicurus by making death a miserable experience after all. But the twist reframes everything: the dead who stream through Will's knife-hole to dissolve into Dust are choosing death over the afterlife, and since for them the good things of life are already off the table, death is not bad at all, which is exactly why they choose it.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 7 "Not to Put Too Fine a Point on It" — Richard Greene asks why becoming Undead is bad for the one who becomes Undead, and why it seems worse than death, testing vampire and zombie cases against the standard accounts of death's badness. Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' sets the experiential-blank frame, but Nagel's deprivation view fails because immortal vampires lose far fewer goods than they gain, and Williams's desire-frustration view fails because zombification replaces desires (scotch for blood) rather than frustrating cancelled ones. Mill's 'better Socrates dissatisfied than a pig satisfied' comparison also falls short since it yields only comparative, not objective, badness; Greene concludes Undeath is dreaded because the Undead do evil things, but no argument shows it is objectively bad, so one might as well make the best of it.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 21 "Deserving to Be a Vampire" — Ted Preston asks whether becoming a vampire would be morally good or desirable, working through The Lost Boys, Underworld, Blade, Forever Knight, and Interview with the Vampire. He argues vampirism is not intrinsically immoral: if vampires cannot restrain their feeding we pity rather than blame them, though with Aristotle we still hold people responsible for choosing to become the kind of being that cannot; and feeding need be no worse than mortal carnivory, since consensual feeding (Blade's stored blood, Karen Jenson's donation, Madeleine's offer to Louis) makes the bite more like dentistry with consent than assault. On desirability he weighs Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' against the Furley-Nussbaum claim that death deprives a life of its long-term projects and relationships, concluding immortality's appeal is rational and that boredom is not inevitable in a changing world. The thought experiment ends in ethics: vampire or mortal, a life's worth depends on choices, so live a life worthy of eternity.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 17 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Salazar takes Professor Farnsworth's cry that the crew's age regression in 'Teenage Mutant Leela's Hurdles' will end in 'a fate worse than death: pre-life! Then death' as a test of whether death is bad. Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' says death cannot be experienced, so the deprivation account of Nagel's 'Death' is needed to explain how death is bad for the one deprived of a valuable future - a dispute staged by Bender's suicide-booth despair in 'Space Pilot 3000' after learning his bending built the booths. The chapter then argues losing one's identity and values can be worse than death (Bender's and Fry's flight from career-chip assignments, the Professor's love of being 161, Leela's frustrated teen redo), closing with Frankl's Man's Search for Meaning and Leela's sacrifice of her regained youth: inner integrity, not erasing the past, makes life worth living.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 10 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Hauskeller argues Shelley's Victor was sane and benevolently motivated, and reads the 'playing God' warning (Whale's 'now I know what it feels to be God!', the Genesis tree of life, the sorcerer's apprentice) as a claim that crossing nature's lines is dangerous rather than sinful. He then flips the story: like the creature, we are children abandoned by a creator who withholds eternal life, so the real wrong is a creator's failure of duty and love - while Epicurus's death-is-nothing-to-us argument and the picture of a childless, static immortal world undermine the transhumanist case that death is the greatest evil. The chapter ends with Aristotle's mean: obsessive pursuit of knowledge and immortality wrecks happiness, which lies in discovering that our native town is the world and living in the present.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 67 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Clint Jones argues LaVey's Satanic Bible rests on a misreading of Epicurus: genuine Epicurean hedonism is not limitless indulgence but the ordered life of the Tetrapharmakon - don't fear gods or death, the good is easy to get, pain is endurable - together with the threefold division of desires, which reserves constant gratification for natural and necessary things like water, bread, and friendship. By licensing gluttony and every whim so long as no one else is hurt, LaVeyan Satanism fails as the pleasure-as-virtue philosophy it claims to revive, leaving its followers with base, unfulfilling pleasures that are, well, Hellish.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 73 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Magus Peter Gilmore closes the exchange: LaVeyan Satanism honestly embraces the selfishness most people already live by (sharing Ayn Rand's enshrined self-interest), and Epicurus's own letters to Menoeceus - on not fearing death, choosing the most pleasant over the longest life, pragmatic justice, and the need for natural science - show deep congruence with LaVey. Against Pitkänen on Eastern religions, whose reincarnation and karmic debt he reads as denigration of carnal existence, and against Jones's shaky-foundation charge (Christianity itself was a Hebraic/Hellenic mash-up), he concludes Satanists are proud 'Hell-raisers' celebrating the only life there is.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 11 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Brendan Shea reads Cohen through the three Hellenistic schools. Socrates's trial in the Apology mirrors the persecuted singer of 'A Singer Must Die,' with 'Everybody Knows' and 'Democracy' voicing a Socratic mix of empathy and pessimism about whether democracy can deal rationally with its critics. Stoics such as Epictetus ground the present-focused, resigned acceptance of loss in 'Hey, That's No Way to Say Goodbye' and 'If It Be Your Will'; the Pyrrhonian skepticism of Sextus Empiricus illuminates the narrator's calming, unresolvable ignorance in 'Famous Blue Raincoat'; and the Epicurean atomism of Epicurus and Lucretius - death is nothing to us, empty desires are unsatisfiable - underlies 'A Thousand Kisses Deep.' Hypatia's murder and Cohen's 'Joan of Arc' close the chapter: the examined life is an all-consuming, sometimes fatal commitment that is nonetheless worthwhile.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 12 "1. Reading the Signs" — Di Bernardo reads the religious language of The Walking Dead as sustained irony - a 'doubleness of sense' - arguing that the walkers, churches, and signs comment critically on faith rather than endorse it. He tracks the church scenes (the Southern Baptist church of 2.1 'What Lies Ahead' with its timed bells and sitting-dead congregation, Gabriel's Saint Sarah's where Maggie answers that it is 'just four walls and a roof'), the ambiguous 'sanctuary' and Terminus signs, and the comic-book Jesus (Paul Monroe) as a machine-gun savior, concluding that the scriptural promise of eternal life through consuming flesh and blood yields only undead life. Against Epicurus's consolation that death is nothing to us, and in the shadow of Nietzsche's madman announcing the death of God, the chapter warns against investing absolute trust in any signs - religious or secular - a warning capped by Rick biting out Joe's throat as his own 'day of reckoning.'
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 34 "15. My Zombie, My Self" — Greene asks what Walking Dead-type walkers are and answers with the Platonic method of definition learned from Socrates: place them in the genus undead (died but not at rest, neither alive nor dead) and differentiate them by differentia - corporeal, mindless, lacking superhuman or magical powers, still decomposing. Aristotle's hierarchy of life functions (nutrition, locomotion, reason) explains why walkers are not alive despite ambulating, and the standards of death (putrefaction, heart-lung, whole-brain, higher-brain) all certify that walkers are dead yet active. The chapter closes on personal identity - whether you survive becoming a zombie, as Carol's face at the barn and Carl's "she'll turn" about Lori presuppose - and admits the author chooses the self-interested reading that he could become his own zombie, for the sake of the scare.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 18 "6. You’re Gonna Die" — Ethan Mills uses the Buddha and Epicurus to show that Louis meets death with laughter instead of fear. The Buddha's diagnosis of dukkha ('dissatisfactoriness') explains the Blu-Ray player and cellphone bits - consumer desire just restarts the craving cycle - and impermanence frames both the Amia heartbreak that Dr. Bigelow reframes as 'misery is wasted on the miserable' and Louie's 'life isn't that long... it's happy math' reflection, while rebirth would only make things worse since you would have to repeat junior high forever. Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us (where death is, you are not) grounds Louie's 'lots of things happen after you die, just none of them include you,' backed by atomism - at death our atoms scatter - and by gods who, like Louie's maybe-God with no heaven, guarantee no immortality. The USO duckling episode models the payoff: comedy defuses our deepest anxiety about annihilation the way it defuses the soldiers' tension in Afghanistan.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 34 "21. After Death It Can Get Worse" — Sam Director asks whether Amazon's unauthorized changes to Dick's novel posthumously harmed him, and against Epicurus's Letter to Menoeceus claim that the dead no longer exist to be harmed, he defends harm as desire-frustration that need not be experienced (Childan's unknown counterfeit antiques, Juliana's deception by Joe) and can involve desires reaching past death (Baynes's Operation Dandelion warning dying with Tedeki). Since Dick delighted in the Blade Runner footage and wanted science fiction to thrive, the chapter concludes the TV adaptation fulfilled rather than thwarted his desires — he is no worse off, maybe better off.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 25 "13. Rick, Morty, and the Cure for Unhappiness" — The chapter diagnoses Rick's 'Wubba Lubba dub-dub' ('I am in great pain, please help me') as chronic Epicurean suffering and prescribes the tetrapharmakos, the four-part cure. Don't fear the gods: Epicurus's indifferent atomist gods versus Rick's atheism, his panic prayer in 'A Rickle in Time', and Toxic Rick's 'If god exists, it's me' as ego rather than argument. Don't fear death, since 'where death is, I am not', though infinite replacements make Rick and Morty fear each other's death rather than their own. The good is easy to get, so booze, Eyeholes, and Szechuan sauce must yield to water, friends, and family; and the terrible is easy to endure, as when Rick stops resenting Birdperson's wedding and finally turns himself in for his family.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 28 "16. Death Becomes Her" — Hendrik Kempt reads Drag Race's pervasive death imagery - death-drops, the 'lip sync for your life,' mirror messages, the 'Death Becomes Her' runway - through the philosophy of death. Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' and Stoic self-possession (Ru's 'pay them bitches no mind,' Violet Chachki enduring a tiny corset) explain why elimination, like death, gives no ground for worry once it arrives, while Socrates' 'philosophy is training for death' makes the show a workout video for dying - Socrates even dying fussing over a rooster like a drag mother to Miss Fame. Heidegger's thrownness and being-toward-death set up Sartre's radically free, future-oriented self - so voluntary exits like BenDeLaCreme's self-elimination and Charlie Hides's listless lip-sync betray one's own plans - and Camus's Sisyphus makes Chi Chi DeVayne and Roxxxy Andrews's doomed All Stars returns models of 'acceptance without resignation.' The closing weighs transhumanism's promise of conquered death against a DragCon-forever thought experiment, concluding with Ru's roast eulogy for Lady Bunny that love and irreverence, not immortal life, are the point.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 18 "Batman Forever" — Randall Jensen examines the boyhood promise Bruce made after his parents' murder ('I swear by the spirits of my parents... to avenge their deaths by spending the rest of my life warring on all criminals') and argues it is a backward-looking, deontological moral reason that consequentialism cannot accommodate. He then asks whether a promise to the dead can bind at all, weighing Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us against Aristotle's and Thomas Nagel's postmortem and unexperienced harms, concluding Bruce wrongs the living people Thomas and Martha Wayne were if he breaks it. From The Dark Knight Returns to Kingdom Come, Batman emerges as a man who can never fully keep the promise yet cannot live without it.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 13 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — O'Loughlin reads Walter biting off a nihilist's ear and the Dude refusing to walk out on league play as concrete realizations of ancient friendship: Aristotle's eudaimonia requires friends as 'second selves' whose shared activity (bowling in the friends' company) structures the excellent life, while Epicurus's Garden ordered life around simple pleasures and ataraxia, with friendship supplying pleasant memory and a kind of immortality after death. Because we moderns claim friendship's value without practicing its costs, the Dude's priorities look comic yet pierce us — and Donny's death, the Ralph's coffee can, and 'let's go bowling' become Epicurean commemoration rather than irreverence.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 25 "The Value of Finitude" — The chapter tests each motive for uploading to San Junipero and finds it wanting: Kantian cosmic justice fails because the resort neither rewards the good nor can punish the wicked; Tolstoy's cosmic-insignificance dread fails because a finite life can still be meaningful, and even Epicurus and Lucretius deflate the fear of death (while Nagel notes death's evil lies in foreclosed possibilities, and Williams's Makropulos case warns eternal life breeds boredom). Nozick's experience machine is the closest analogy, but the chapter argues San Junipero differs — residents know it is digital and share it with other conscious people — before Nussbaum's argument lands: without finitude there is no risk, so no courage, sacrifice, or deep love, which is why Kelly's forty-nine real years with Richard outweigh forever with Yorkie.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 44 "The Death of Death" — Reading Black Mirror's deaths through Bandersnatch's train ending, Be Right Back's AshBot, and San Junipero, the chapter uses Heidegger's presence-at-hand (Stefan's absent mother and rabbit remain present as possibilities he can act on) and Derrida's différance (the meaning of life and death is endlessly deferred as technology scrambles the presence/absence binary - Martha's simulated Ash, Liam's Grain deletions, Chris's guilt-haunted fiancée). A central section frames the whole debate as transhumanism - Kurzweil's three bridges to the posthuman against Fukuyama's warning that self-directed evolution replaces God - before Camus resolves the question of meaning: Kelly and Yorkie, like Sisyphus, create meaning by choosing their fate in a VR heaven that objectively matters nothing. Freud's Eros/Thanatos drives and Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' close the chapter's question of whether to extend, hasten, or simply accept mortality.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 40 "I think we've all arrived at a very special place, eh Spiritually Ecumenically Grammatically —Captain Jack Spa" — Miller uses Disney deaths to stage the philosophy of death: Plato's immortal soul and Phaedo's affinity argument illuminate Frollo's lust-driven plunge into hellfire, while Epicurus's atomism, his 'death is nothing to us' argument applied to Marlin's terror in Finding Nemo, and Lucretius's symmetry argument are tested against Coco, where Ernesto's forgotten 'final death' versus Hector's restored place on the ofrenda makes posthumous harm plausible. Aquinas's 'my soul is not me' grounds embodiment, Confucius makes Mulan's risking death for father, ancestors, and country a virtuous Confucian death, and Deloria's indigenous web of relations reads Mufasa's Circle of Life, Moana's grandmother, and Brother Bear's ancestral spirits.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 9 "Notes" — Mackenzie Graham uses Fallout 3's Project Purity - James's sacrificial death and the Lone Wanderer's choice among feeding the purifier with their own life, poisoning the water for the Enclave, or destroying it - to ask whether death and posthumous events can be bad for the one who dies. Against Epicurus's claim that death is nothing to us, the chapter defends deprivationism with the Megaton quest (the Lone Wanderer's desire to save the town is thwarted even if the rearmed bomb destroys it unbeknownst to them) and weighs Feinberg and Pitcher's ante-mortem person against the problem of the subject, using the Great War's redefinition of October 22, 2077 to block backward causation. The 'Blood Ties' quest with the Family's cannibals then raises posthumous wrongs: since no existing subject is harmed or wronged, the chapter ends by asking whether cannibalism is an impersonal wrong against personhood itself, on the model of respecting nature.
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 24 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — Kevin Fitzpatrick uses Vivi Orunitia and the self-aware Black Mages of Final Fantasy IX, who call death 'stopping,' to ask whether the fear of death is justified, answering that death harms only insofar as it frustrates a person's values, such as Vivi's morality, his thirst for knowledge, and his care for others' happiness. He brings in Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us because the dead feel no pain, casts Necron, who wants to return all life to a painless 'zero world' because fear of death has corrupted it, as a darker Epicurean, and weighs the deprivation objection, death cheats us of future goods like Chocobo Hot and Cold, against the puzzle of when death's harm could even occur.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 139 "The Approaching Battle" — Frames death as philosophy's ultimate question and contrasts the Epicurean advice to be unconcerned since death is simply the end of us with Heidegger's authenticity: boldly facing that death may come at any moment keeps us from living half-asleep, a view Plato anticipated by teaching that true philosophers make dying their profession. Harry, confronted with death from infancy, lives authentically, while Voldemort's flight from death marks him as the inauthentic case the essay traces through the Deathly Hallows death march.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 17 "The Office and Philosophy" — Tests the deceptions swirling around Dwight: Kant's two arguments against lying (universalizing the maxim 'lie whenever it saves face', and treating the deceived as a mere means) are set against Plato's noble lie from the Republic - Michael's empty 'Assistant Regional Manager' title may be a morally tolerable verbal lie because after 'The Fight' it restores their friendship, though it does not medicate the office as Plato's lie does the city. Epicurus' claim that only what is experienced can harm you ('what you don't know can't hurt you') is refuted by the thought of Angela's hypothetical fake love for Dwight: undetected deception is itself a harm. Finally Dwight's self-deception (believing the false promotion, Jim's telekinesis prank, the fax from his future self) is modeled by dividing the self - Plato's tripartite soul versus Descartes' simple, indivisible mind - suggesting cognitive science's modular brain as the better picture, and asking whether one can even wrong oneself.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 25 "NOTES" — Jason Eberl answers John's 'you just can't go around killing people' by asking what exactly is bad about death, weighing Aquinas's claim that life is a fundamental good against Epicurus and Lucretius's arguments that death is nothing to us — applied to Sarah's 'you're already dead' and to the victim shot on August 28, 1997, who loses only one more day of a doomed life. Feldman's ante-mortem harm and McMahan's deprivation account explain how Judgment Day harms people before it arrives, while Nagel replies that experience itself is positive however bad its contents, which is why the survivors keep fighting Skynet. Utilitarian ripple-effects, Kantian dignity (the H-K crushing skulls), and Marquis's loss-of-future argument all condemn the Terminators' indiscriminate killing, and the chapter ends with the T-101's 'I know now why you cry' as recognition that death is an evil because it strips us of our emotional attachments.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 18 "The Grim Reaper on Baker Street" — Glass-Turner examines death across the Holmes canon, opening with Kierkegaard's claim that death's explanation discloses the explainer's own inner being and pairing Holmes with TV's Dr. House as materialist puzzle-solvers who rule out the supernatural ('no ghosts need apply'). She weighs Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' against the wrongness of murder, then argues Holmes's pig- and cadaver-experiments coexist with reverence for the dead and hints of belief in an afterlife ('compensation hereafter' in 'The Veiled Lodger'), reading him via William James as open to more than the physical. She closes on Holmes's calm acceptance of his own Reichenbach death and Conan Doyle's later turn to spiritualism after his wife's death.
- **The Philosophy of Werner Herzog**, ch. 12 "Reflections from the Abyss Herzog’s Philosophy of Death" — M. Blake Wilson traces Herzog's philosophy of death and the 'abyss' across Grizzly Man and Into the Abyss, examining how Herzog frames human, animal, and self-killings and refuses the retributive impulse. Against Kant's demand that murderers must die and Matthew Kramer's purgative rationale for capital punishment, Wilson enlists Nietzsche's warnings about the drive to punish and Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us,' while contrasting Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' with the 'accountant's truth' via journalistic and bear-attack literature (Jans, Herrero) that accuses Herzog of a 'Hollywoodized' portrait of Treadwell. He coins 'vivicide' for the killing of a human by a non-human animal and questions whether Bear 141 committed murder or was merely a scavenger.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 21 "11. The One Truly Serious Philosophical Problem" — Doll surveys philosophical views on suicide to make sense of Bourdain's death, opening with Camus's claim that suicide is the one serious philosophical problem. She weighs Plato's Phaedo prohibition (we are the gods' possessions) against his allowance for extreme misfortune, Aristotle's view that suicide violates one's duty to self and community, and Seneca's Stoic position that a wise man 'lives as long as he ought, not as long as he can' — framing Bourdain's death as an autonomous choice.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 25 "Chapter 12 The American Diogenes" — Johnson argues Twain is best understood not as a religious skeptic but as an 'American Diogenes'—a Cynic of Christianity-as-practiced. As Diogenes 'defaced the coinage' to remove counterfeit customs, Twain uses 'sacred profanity' (honest, even profane speech that exposes phony piety, e.g. the swearing butcher, Satanic narrators in 'The Mysterious Stranger' and 'Letters from the Earth') to strike four counterfeit coins: superstition/special providence, hypocrisy, artificial 'Moral Sense'/conscience, and heavenly rewards. On death Twain matches Diogenes and Epicurus (annihilation is nothing to fear), and his self-description as 'Member at Large for the Human Race' mirrors Diogenes the cosmopolitan; Diogenes carries a lantern to find a real human, Twain a mirror to show we are worse than we think.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 26 "Chapter 13 An Epicurean Consideration of Superstitions in Mark Twain and in the Good Life" — Baker reads Twain's ghost stories and superstition through Epicurean virtue ethics, which holds that false beliefs—above all the terror of death—breed empty desires that block eudaimonia. Citing Twain's Autobiography passage that 'annihilation has no terrors for me' as a near-verbatim Epicurean line, and using Lucretius and Nussbaum's 'Therapy of Desire,' she aligns Huck's disdain for a useless conscience and his rejection of wealth ('being rich ain't what it's cracked up to be') with the Epicurean pursuit of simple natural pleasures. She notes a tension: by making tall-tale-telling and Sunday-school-shirking so enjoyable, Twain the satirist spreads the very superstitions the Epicureans would eradicate, seeming to work at cross-purposes with them.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 28 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Kover argues that anti-hunting animal-liberation thought (Singer, Regan) objects to hunting not because it alienates us from nature but because it connects us too intimately to it—to the cycle of eating and being eaten and thus to our own mortality. Using Ernest Becker's 'denial of death' and Paul Rozin on disgust at our animality, he reads vegetarianism from Pythagoras's flesh-renouncing purification to modern ethical veganism as an ascetic refusal of edibility, and cites Val Plumwood's critique of humans placing themselves outside the food chain, concluding with Petersen and Shepard that the hunter's acceptance of death affirms life.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 30 "GARDENING" — Campbell explains why Epicurus set his school in a walled garden on the edge of Athens ('Live unnoticed'), contrasting it with the Stoics' public Stoa: the Garden was a self-sufficient community of friends pursuing ataraxia through natural, necessary pleasures and philosophy as therapy for the soul. Drawing on Lucretius's account of prehistory in On the Nature of Things, he shows the Epicureans saw cities as a decadent fall—driven by the fear of death and the gods—from a near-paradise of proto-Epicurean friendship pacts, and read the garden and the locus amoenus of pastoral picnics as a recovered golden age. Diogenes of Oinoanda's inscription imagines a future in which all become gardening philosophers and city walls become redundant.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 15 "9. Blade Runner" — Using Blade Runner's replicants ('I want more life, fucker!') and Roy's dying soliloquy, Rowlands asks how death can harm the one who dies. He states the Epicurean argument (while we live death is not yet; when dead there is no one to harm) and answers via harms of deprivation, illustrated by Tyrell's imagined brain damage. Drawing on Wittgenstein (death as the limit of life) and Heidegger's being-towards-death/being-towards-a-future, he distinguishes weak (non-conceptual) from strong (conceptual) possession of a future, arguing death harms more those with more invested. Linear time and the ultimate horizon of death are what let a life have meaning at all.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 24 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Bill Davis explains why Arwen relinquishes elvish immortality and why Aragorn and Frodo accept death as a 'gift,' contrasting the Ringwraiths' cursed undeath (an Aristotelian frustration of their mortal nature) with genuine mortality. He surveys real-world responses to death: Socrates' calm confidence in the soul, Lucretius's and the existentialists' liberation through annihilation, and worries from Bernard Williams and others about the tedium of immortality, which Boethius answers with a timeless heaven. Davis argues Arwen chooses a finite life of deep love over deathless boredom, and that all three accept death trusting Iluvatar's love promises a world remade beyond the circles of the world.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 57 "54. The Man from Earth as Philosophy The Desirability of Immortality" — Berk brings The Man from Earth—about John Oldman, a 14,000-year-old non-aging man—into dialogue with Bernard Williams's 'The Makropulos Case,' which argues immortality must become boring and identity-destroying (the dilemma of exhausted versus radically changed categorical desires). Against these 'immortality curmudgeons,' the chapter argues John's mild boredom, enduring loves, friendships, and pursuit of knowledge show an immortal life can stay worth living, invoking Fischer's 'repeatable pleasures.' It also engages Nussbaum's 'Mortal Immortals' and Beauvoir's All Men Are Mortal (the miserable Fosca), which tie courage and love to finitude and sacrifice, noting John is only 'medically' rather than 'genuinely' immortal and so can still make sacrifices.

### Atomism

Ancient atomism, developed by Leucippus and especially Democritus in the fifth century BCE, holds that reality consists of countless indivisible particles, atoms, moving through empty space, or void. All apparent qualities and changes are explained by the arrangement, motion, and combination of these unchanging bodies, so that nothing exists but atoms and the void. This thoroughly materialist and mechanistic picture offered an early way to reconcile the reality of change with a stable underlying substance, and it profoundly influenced later thinkers such as Epicurus.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 52 "Unknown" — This section lays out causal determinism through Laplace's demon: an intelligence that knew every force and every position could compute the entire future, leaving no one free or responsible, so people in the Matrix would be no worse off than we are. It notes that both sides of the nature-nurture debate (including B.F. Skinner) agree behavior is caused by forces beyond our control, and turns to Epicurus, who posited random atomic 'swerves' to make room for free will. Modern quantum indeterminacy, it concludes, likewise expels determinism from physics and at least makes free will possible, though randomness alone cannot ground responsibility.
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 17 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — In an imaginary salon hosted by the baker 'la Brioche,' the goddess Eris drops a golden apple inscribed 'Atkins,' and three philosophers fight over the credit. Rousseau claims Atkins's war on refined flour and 'invented fake food' as his own back-to-nature, state-of-nature legacy; Confucius counters that Americans are 'grazers' without li, that culture is nature's flower, and that only ritual propriety can counteract the advertising that fills the void; Democritus claims the scientific core — 'hyperinsulism,' 'benign dietary ketosis' — as atomism's heir, deriding Rousseau's general will as democratic truth-concocting and Plato's otherworldly philosopher-king. The debate ranges over free will versus scientific prediction-and-control and ends unresolved over a refusal of brioche.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 32 "Too Big a Byte to Chew" — Kylie Prymus uses a slain Orc to stage the metaphysics of Azeroth: whether the 'dead' Orc is anything more than electrons obeying code (Democritus's atomism), and why explaining Ironforge's empty Tuesday mornings forces us to 'go meta' just as Aristotle's Metaphysics went beyond his Physics. The problem of other minds gets a WoW twist: without nameplates we would sort NPC from PC by the argument from analogy, the same imperfect tool we use offline for pain, coma patients, and animal minds. David Lewis's plurality of worlds becomes concrete through servers — 'the gates could be open' is true for the Uther player because on Medivh they opened on January 23rd — and she concludes that the real world is no better defined than Azeroth.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 16 "Hope" — Beck reads Snakes & Arrows as popular Epicureanism delivered by Lucretius' method: just as De Rerum Natura puts honey on the rim of the cup so Romans swallow philosophical medicine disguised as poetry, Rush's melodies smuggle reflection on pain, luck, and religion past listeners who think they are just rocking, with repeated choruses doing the work of Epicurean prolepsis. The random swerve of atoms explains 'The Larger Bowl''s unequal fortunes ('Some are blessed and some are cursed'), while the shore-watcher's relief at another's shipwreck and the concertgoer's pleasure exemplify Epicurean ataraxia. 'Faithless' and 'Armor and Sword' ('Pray and pass the ammunition') echo Lucretius' trampling of superstitious religio, and the chapter closes with Philodemus' Herculaneum scroll: don't fear god, don't worry about death.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 24 "Architecture and the Dream Machine" — Botz-Bornstein argues Inception presents dreams neither as separate worlds nor as Freudian symbols but as hackable programs, making the film itself a 'thinking machine' in Jean Epstein's sense: it synchronizes kicks, safe codes and the Piaf countdown like a computer coordinating contradictory layers of time. He links inception to Dawkins's meme theory, with the planted idea growing 'like a cancer' in Mal, and to the projections of Solaris, showing how the film unusually combines cognitive and psychoanalytic models in one vertical dream structure. Democritus's atomism frames Epstein's 'grains of reality' and the film's atomized media-images of the real world, while Benjamin and Baudrillard let him read Cobb's Limbo dystopia, Mombasa and Dubai's empty skyscrapers as an allegory of a globalized world of hackable neoliberal dream machines.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 22 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Levi Bryant argues the D&D universe models a 'flat ontology' of active substances whose powers (affects) actualize differently under local conditions, asking Democritus-style individuation questions about whether a band of ogres at a tavern is one entity or many. Characters and their gear form alliances that generate genuinely new beings, so the blind man with his cane, or Moorcock's Elric fed by the soul-drinking sword Stormbringer, is a different entity than without it, and he borrows Clark and Chalmers' extended mind hypothesis to deny that thinking happens only inside the head. The dice then supply chance that generates necessity: the Dungeon Master's throws conjure traps, wraiths and saving throws that form 'regimes of attraction' to which every player and monster must respond.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 18 "6. You’re Gonna Die" — Ethan Mills uses the Buddha and Epicurus to show that Louis meets death with laughter instead of fear. The Buddha's diagnosis of dukkha ('dissatisfactoriness') explains the Blu-Ray player and cellphone bits - consumer desire just restarts the craving cycle - and impermanence frames both the Amia heartbreak that Dr. Bigelow reframes as 'misery is wasted on the miserable' and Louie's 'life isn't that long... it's happy math' reflection, while rebirth would only make things worse since you would have to repeat junior high forever. Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us (where death is, you are not) grounds Louie's 'lots of things happen after you die, just none of them include you,' backed by atomism - at death our atoms scatter - and by gods who, like Louie's maybe-God with no heaven, guarantee no immortality. The USO duckling episode models the payoff: comedy defuses our deepest anxiety about annihilation the way it defuses the soldiers' tension in Afghanistan.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 31 "18. Fate on the Discworld and Roundworld" — Written as a dialogue in which Death visits the sweeper Lu-Tze, the chapter distinguishes Discworld fate—narrativium and narrative causality, where million-to-one chances come off and Mort's attempt to save a princess bounced back into an alternative timeline—from the Roundworld debates about determinism. Epicurus's swerving atom, the Stoic compatibilism of Chrysippus (choices flowing from one's own beliefs and desires, which Death admits he prefers), Carneades's 'voluntary motion of the mind' and his truth-without-necessity solution to future contingents, and Augustine and Boethius on desire-based choice and God's atemporal foreknowledge are all worked through. The Disc's changeable past—Dios traveling back to found Djelibeybi, Rincewind's sandwich seeding life, Vimes in his own past—is what motivates Carneades's distinction between truth and necessity, and the Stoic line that fate can work through the witches' own free choices.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 22 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Levi Bryant uses the D&D universe to expound a 'flat ontology' of active substances: every entity, from enchanted swords to white dragons, has a virtual proper being (powers or 'affects') that actualizes variable 'local manifestations' depending on circumstances like lighting or armor. Adopting Andy Clark and David Chalmers's extended mind hypothesis, he argues a blind man with a cane, a smartphone owner, or Elric wielding Stormbringer is a literally different mind or entity, and that alliances (Raistlin's Staff of Magius, a warrior's plate armor) generate genuinely new powers rather than mere tool-use. Against Democritus's atomism, he holds aggregates can be individuals, and the game's dice embody his claim that chance produces necessity: throws generate 'regimes of attraction' no DM or player controls. D&D thus mirrors our own world of hidden powers, aleatory encounters and collectives of humans and nonhumans.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 24 "Architecture and the Dream Machine" — Thorsten Botz-Bornstein argues that Inception presents dreams neither as divine messages nor as stylized fantasy but as hackable programs, making the film itself a 'thinking machine' in Jean Epstein's sense — a 'robot brain' whose synchronized kicks, Piaf countdown, and phone-number safes 'think' the different layers of time instead of reproducing a reality, with slow motion as cognition rather than dream-sign (against Bazin). He reads inception as Dawkins's meme theory given a psychoanalytic vertical dimension: the idea is implanted deep in the subconscious (Fischer's relation to his father), can grow autonomously 'like a cancer' as Mal's did, and subconscious projections converge 'like white blood cells' as in Solaris. The chapter then traces how the computer era — hypertext, Second Life, media-absorbed realities like Baudrillard's 9/11 — reshaped cinematic dreams and architecture, so that Ariadne's 'pure creation,' Cobb's Limbo dystopia, and Dubai's empty speculative towers all become the 'gilded dreamworlds' of an ephemeralized, hacker-ready built world — the dream machine as allegory of the globalized world, with atomized grains of reality echoing Democritus via Epstein and Benjamin's account of cinema bursting the prison of the everyday.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 9 "Notes" — Shores opens with Sophie's World comparing LEGO bricks to Democritus' indivisible, endlessly recombinable atoms, and argues LEGO is a system of play and an 'object to think with' that models how ideas and worldviews are assembled, disassembled, and rebuilt. He contrasts Plato's Republic-era suspicion that children's play must be regulated with the Socratic playfulness that treats philosophy itself as serious play, and enlists Locke and Rousseau on play-based learning and Freud on the child at play as a creative writer rearranging its world. Lord Business' Kragle shows play taken too seriously becoming inert, while Caillois' ludus/paidia distinction frames the difference between themed narrative sets, free building, and the goal-directed rigidity of the LEGO video games.

### The Death Drive (Thanatos)

The death drive, sometimes called Thanatos, is the concept Sigmund Freud introduced in Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920) to name a fundamental urge toward dissolution, aggression, and a return to an inanimate state. He proposed it to explain phenomena the pleasure principle could not, such as the compulsion to repeat traumatic experiences and the persistence of self-destructive behavior. Set against Eros, the life drive that binds and preserves, the death drive expresses a countervailing tendency toward discharge, destruction, and the undoing of tension. The idea remains among Freud's most speculative and disputed, yet influential in later psychoanalytic and cultural theory.

- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 25 "The Possibility of a Non-Repressive Civilization" — Simon Clark reads Romero's four Dead films through Freud's Civilization and Its Discontents: the zombie is the return of the repressed, the ripped-out instinctual life of a civilization that demands work, and it multiplies exactly as humans (Stephen defending the mall, Ben fighting Mr. Cooper) lapse into unlawful self-gratification. The bite unites Eros and Thanatos - an erotic, engorged cannibalism that also regresses victims to rotting matter, which Clark glosses with Creed's vagina dentata. He then argues Day of the Dead's beach ending (John fishing, Sarah at peace) stages Marcuse's non-repressive civilization where work becomes play and liberated sexuality rejoins Eros, while Land of the Dead goes further: the evolved, tool-using zombies led by Big Daddy are the martyrs who actually found Marcuse's impossible pleasurable community, leaving living humans still fenced inside repression.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 29 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Christopher Ketcham narrates a night listening to Dear Heather during a café blackout, in which darkness becomes Eugene Minkowski's 'lived space' - more personal than light, with auditory space as its own dark space - and Cohen's voice leads him down into a shared funk of loss and depression. Through Heidegger he diagnoses his own shrunken, past-bound, thrown existence and reinterprets being-toward-death not as a downward spiral but as being toward his own remaining possibilities, and through Freud's death drive he names the 'unobtrusive death wish' he had let dwell unchallenged in him. The essay closes with a Heideggerian resolve toward resoluteness and future possibility, glimpsing a street-worn 'Suzanne' in the dark as hope rather than absence.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 30 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Pötzsch reads Dracula through Freud's Civilization and Its Discontents: the Count fascinates because he lives out the aggression and sexual freedom civilization forces us to renounce, embodying the innate hostility in Freud's 'man is the wolf to man.' Freud's account - group power replacing individual might, 'love thy neighbor' as an impossible demand, the super-ego as an inner Van Helsing breeding guilt over forbidden impulses, with the id and ego mediating - is mapped onto Jonathan's 'wicked, burning desire' for the vampire women. The upshot: we resent culture because we traded happiness for security, yet living like Dracula would get our throats cut.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 25 "14. David Bowie’s Sadness" — Ketcham argues Bowie's sadness is ours: via Deleuze and Guattari's Anti-Oedipus he casts consumer capitalism as a machine producing schizophrenic fad-following (the stuck high-school footballer, the Benetton self), of which Bowie's serial personas are both symptom and escape - 'always crashing in the same car' yet never repeating. Minkowski's lived time and the Buddha's anatman ground the dance as pure becoming without a dancer, while Heidegger's das Man and being-toward-death explain why authentic self-creation - which, unlike Sellers or Williams, Bowie survived - exacts the price Freud's beyond-the-pleasure-principle names as compulsive repetition, turned by Bowie into a life wish.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 21 "10. Change of Heart" — Auxier names Petty the master of "liminal moments" when something is finally seen for what it is (the betrayed lover's realization behind "You Got Lucky," the unknown pain of "American Girl"), then stages the 1929 Davos debate between Cassirer's humane, Goethe-reading phenomenology and Heidegger's Angst before the abyss, being-toward-death, and the "moment of vision." He indicts Heidegger's Nazism and betrayal of Husserl as what "Petty-ness," the asshole-beast crouching in everyone's darkdeepdown, becomes when it wins, contrasting Petty's public apology for the Confederate flag and his cease-and-desist to George W. Bush. The chapter ends with the unguarded Petty smile as "Here Comes My Girl" made philosophy, an instance of authentic being-with-others that Heidegger declared impossible.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 29 "18. Iron Man’s Choice to Die" — Argues Tony's death in Endgame is best explained three ways: via Freud's Eros/Thanatos drives (Tony oscillates between the cabin family-life drive and the risk-seeking death drive that takes him aboard the donut ship in Infinity War and has him lay down to die with Nebula), via Camus's absurd (like Sisyphus, Tony creates subjective meaning by choosing — Pepper, Morgan, and finally the snap itself, 'Part of the journey is the end'), and via consequentialism (the snap as a desirable consequence, contrasting Infinity War's deontological 'We don't trade lives' with Endgame's 'whatever it takes'). It contends that because the time heist rewrites history, deaths in both films — Vision's, Natasha's, Tony's — risk becoming meaningless, so Tony dies on his terms to make his death meaningful.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 39 "27. I Am Inevitable" — Reads Thanos's 'I am inevitable' (his name echoing thanatos) as death personified, then asks 'whose death?' through Heidegger — 'people die' is the evasive 'one dies,' and Tony's final snap and 'I am Iron Man' figure an authentic appropriation of being-toward-death that redeems his guilt — before Blanchot's reversal and Lacan's symbolic death dissolve that authenticity into impersonal, language-borne dying (Loki's 'No resurrections this time' as the meta-textual murder of comic-book death). It ends with Deleuze's Nietzschean eternal return as the empty form of time that the time heist and quantum multiverse enact, concluding the real inevitability 'engraved in the very fabric of reality' belongs to Steve Rogers and Peggy Carter's dance, not to Thanos or Iron Man.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 37 "Taking in the View from the Paranoid Position" — Christian reads the fleet through Freud's death instinct and Melanie Klein's paranoid position: Starbuck's self-destruction, Tigh and Ellen's sadomasochism, and Baltar's relationship with Six fuse Eros and Thanatos, and 'Maelstrom' returns Starbuck to the abusive mother whose rejection of her love taught her that love itself is poisonous. Humans project all aggression and badness onto the Cylons they created - 'toaster' talk, Cain's torture of Gina - to keep a split between good self and evil other. The price is permanent vigilance in the watchtower: since anyone might be a Cylon (the Chief's fear, Baltar's test), the crew can never be sure the projected badness is not their own, which is why the machines must keep 'coming back.'
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 24 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Hunt treats the film as a direct view of a single subject's unconscious, Freud-style: the Dude is the pre-Oedipal narcissist, the Big Lebowski the father toppled from his wheelchair-throne after the confrontation, Maude the mother, with a scattered superego distributed across the Stranger's moralizing and the Malibu sheriff's 'Stay out of Malibu!'. Donny and Walter figure oral and anal fixations, Jesus the threatening playground peer, and Bunny and the nihilists Freud's life and death drives — so Donny's death in the parking-lot melee lets the ego fuse death-drive energy into life, and the Dude's walk-away from the little Lebowski back to bowling and White Russians reads as repression into comfortable pre-Oedipal phantasy.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 44 "The Death of Death" — Reading Black Mirror's deaths through Bandersnatch's train ending, Be Right Back's AshBot, and San Junipero, the chapter uses Heidegger's presence-at-hand (Stefan's absent mother and rabbit remain present as possibilities he can act on) and Derrida's différance (the meaning of life and death is endlessly deferred as technology scrambles the presence/absence binary - Martha's simulated Ash, Liam's Grain deletions, Chris's guilt-haunted fiancée). A central section frames the whole debate as transhumanism - Kurzweil's three bridges to the posthuman against Fukuyama's warning that self-directed evolution replaces God - before Camus resolves the question of meaning: Kelly and Yorkie, like Sisyphus, create meaning by choosing their fate in a VR heaven that objectively matters nothing. Freud's Eros/Thanatos drives and Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' close the chapter's question of whether to extend, hasten, or simply accept mortality.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 24 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Sets up Sons of Anarchy as a Hamlet retelling — Jax the prince, Clay the Claudius who murdered John Teller and married Gemma, Tara a gutsier Ophelia — and reads it through Freud and Ernest Jones's Hamlet and Oedipus: Jax's protest that he 'untwisted my mommy thing a long time ago,' his toleration of Gemma's meddling, and the Season 4/5 finale tableaux where Gemma displaces Tara at his side betray an unresolved Oedipus complex. Freud's three agencies get bodies: Clay as pure Id (beating Gemma in 'Hands'), Tara as Superego, Jax as the mediating Ego, with SAMCRO itself a collective Id worshipped in its 'chapel.' Oral and anal-stage fixations explain the Sons' chain-smoking, recklessness, and defiance of authority, while the Id's civil war between libido and the death drive plays out in Gemma's post-beating sex binge and Jax's unconscious pleasure in killing.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 19 "NOTES" — Hirschbein presents True Blood as a Freudian fable: vampires live the unrepressed id's Eros and Thanatos that civilization forces the rest of us to renounce, which is why they defeat all three sources of suffering (mortal bodies, nature, hostile neighbors) and why the show's convulsive sex and violence thrill us. Glamouring reproduces the posthypnotic suggestion that proved the unconscious to Freud, Sookie's mind-reading confirms his dark discoveries about our sexualized aggression, vampire myths work as projection screens for desires we disown, and Marcuse's complaint about 'genital tyranny' and sublimation frames Sookie's love as a near-realization of Freud's St. Francis ideal.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 21 "Moral Man in the Dark City Film Noir, the Postwar Religious Revival, and The Accused" — Palmer nuances the 'dark mirror' theory of noir by recovering a redemptive subgroup, reading Dieterle's The Accused through the postwar religious revival and the writings of Reinhold Niebuhr and Erich Fromm. Where Lang's The Woman in the Window only chastens its professor via a dream, The Accused stages a genuinely penitential arc: repressed psychology professor Wilma Tuttle kills the aggressive student Bill in panic, then is therapeutically forced to relive the crime (at the prizefight and in the reenactment) until love with lawyer Warren Ford delivers her from 'separateness.' Palmer argues this patriarchal, therapeutic 'conversion'—glamorizing Loretta Young out of her mannish disguise—reconfigures Niebuhr's taming of passion and Fromm's account of love as a decision, heralding a coming 'culture of narcissism.'
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 6 "Introduction War Films and the Ineffability of War" — LaRocca argues that a war film can never be war itself but only a mediated, post-facto fabrication, and reads the camera and the gun as twinned instruments ('point and shoot' becoming digital 'point and click' in Skyfall). He mobilizes Baudrillard's claim that the Gulf War 'did not take place' to describe war video games and CGI spectacle (Avatar, Call of Duty) as hyperreal simulacra, and Freud's 'Why War?' letter and death instinct to explain the compulsive proliferation of war representation. Foucault ('peace is a coded war'), Heraclitus ('war is father of all'), and Isaiah Berlin's plurality of incompatible values frame war's ineffability and perpetuity, while Cavell's ontology of film grounds the viewer's 'mechanically assured' helplessness before on-screen dying bodies.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 24 "War and Its Fictional Recovery On-Screen Narrative Management of Death in The Big Red One and The Thin Red Lin" — Bronfen takes Freud's 'Thoughts for the Times on War and Death' (life 'recovers its full content' when war forces us to believe in death) and his theory of the death drive and the uncanny double as a template for how war films manage mortality through fiction. In Fuller's The Big Red One, the nameless Sergeant's guilt-driven distinction between killing and murder, his Nazi double Schroeder, and the compulsively repeated stabbing scene at the crucifix let the hero convert contingent slaughter into a restitutive story where survival is 'the only glory,' echoing Freud's Eros–Thanatos struggle. In Malick's The Thin Red Line, Private Witt splits not into warlike and peacetime selves but into bodily and spiritual presence, embracing death as transcendence into 'shining light' that doubles the light of cinema itself. Both films strike a pact with the viewer, who dies with the heroes yet safely survives them.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 20 "10. Some Dark Genie" — Calef asks whether Bourdain's choice to become a heroin addict could be rational and responsible, using Mill's On Liberty and Harm Principle (including the voluntary-slavery exception) to argue addiction is reversible and can minimize suffering when alternatives are bleak. He then reads Bourdain's self-destructive drives — the drunk cliff-driving 'death trip' — through Freud's death drive (Thanatos) and Schopenhauer's pessimism, concluding the 'dark genie' was partly disease-like and thus not wholly blameworthy.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 17 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Casey McKittrick accounts for gay 'bareback' pornography — the erotic celebration of condomless anal sex and visible semen exchange (the reinsertion shot, gangbang formats like Dawson's 50-Load Weekend). He situates it against the pathologizing of homosexuality, citing Foucault's History of Sexuality on the Victorian 'invention' of the homosexual and Lee Edelman on queer sexuality as outside reproductive futurity. Drawing on Freud's account of loss and the death drive (eros and thanatos), he reads semen as the 'lost object' — 'brothers' milk' — and bareback video as a fantasy screen restoring intimacy severed by AIDS, animating the struggle between the erotic and the lethal.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 19 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Clack's 'Cannabis and the Human Condition' reads intoxication through Freud's Civilization and its Discontents, where drugs are the 'crudest but most effective' palliative against a life 'too hard for us,' tied to the pleasure principle and the Nirvana/death-instinct drive to discharge stimulus. He supplements Freud with Schopenhauer's pessimism — life oscillating between suffering and boredom — to add 'stimulus hunger' Freud ignored, arguing cannabis both dampens and stokes the 'fire in the brain' depending on THC potency (high vs. stoned). He concludes that, like religion, art and love, cannabis augments a bleak existence, so 'all cannabis use is medicinal.'
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 31 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Piven mounts an 'epistemology of murder,' invoking Hume and Nietzsche to argue that most of what we 'know' about serial killers and terrorists is projected fantasy and prejudice, amplified by fear (Terror Management Theory). Rereading Lord of the Flies and the Milgram studies, he claims violence follows from shame, humiliation, and abuse (Athens's 'violentization') rather than innate evil, and uses Freud's fort-da game and repetition compulsion to argue killers displace their own woundedness and 'soul murder' onto surrogate victims. He controversially links serial killers, who sexualize death and merge with victims, to terrorists who sanctify displaced sexual rage as God's will — a 'serial killer in sheik's clothing.'

### The They-Self (das Man)

The they-self, or das Man, is Heidegger's name for the anonymous "one" that governs much of everyday life—as in what "one" does, says, or thinks—into which individuals typically dissolve. In this mode people conform to averaged expectations, letting public opinion decide their choices and thereby covering over their own responsibility for existence. Heidegger regards this as the ordinary, largely inauthentic condition of Dasein, from which authentic selfhood must be won back rather than presupposed.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 7 "Monologue" — Editor William Irwin's introduction explains why Seinfeld is philosophical: 'Seinfeld' sounds like German for 'field of being,' echoing Heidegger's Sein und Zeit, and he tells students to picture the four at Monk's coffee shop when Heidegger describes the 'idle chatter' of the inauthentic mode of being, while George's 'what is the opposite of what I would normally do?' shows the courage of changing one's way of seeing. He frames the whole book with Socrates' claim that the unexamined life is not worth living - the Seinfeld characters examine their lives constantly, though Socrates would approve of neither their lives nor their examinations - and with Nietzsche's 'A Book for None and All' subtitle, then lays out the volume's four-act structure.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 23 "Inauthenticity and Fascism" — David Detmer treats Zelig, the mock-documentary 'chameleon man' who turns black, Chinese, fat, or a Nazi depending on his company, as a stark dramatization of personal identity and the existentialist critique of inauthenticity. After rejecting the memory, bodily-continuity, and immaterial-soul criteria of identity, the chapter takes the existentialist line, quoting Heidegger on Dasein's selfhood, that a self is its choices, projects, and commitments, so Zelig's chameleonism is self-estrangement motivated by fear and the craving to be liked. Politically, the chapter draws Allen's lesson that genocides happen not because millions go mad but because millions passively conform, made literal by Zelig appearing at a Hitler rally, and supports it with Asch's conformity experiments and Milgram's obedience studies.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 14 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Auxier uses the question 'Would Bruce Springsteen ride a Honda?' as an ontological probe: Honda embodies defensible middle-class values while a Harley is not primarily a machine but 'a decision about life and what makes it valuable', a suicide machine Jesus could have ridden into Jerusalem and whose absence would render Easy Rider meaningless even if Fonda rode some other Harley. His own boyhood purchase of a Honda XL 70 over the Harley Z90 becomes a lesson in Heideggerian honesty, since he knew he belonged on a Honda, while buyers who choose for appearances are consumed by das Man, the they-self that lives inauthentically through images and slogans. Using Husserl's method of imaginative variation on the question, he concludes that the Harley as cultural icon represents an existential decision and the life that follows from it.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 19 "U2 and Philosophy" — Delancey asks why anyone should take moral and political cues from a rock band and answers via Heidegger: in a mediascape where a few corporations orchestrate what everyone hears, the mass tune is das Man ('Numb'), and adopting it is inauthenticity - so U2, who believe what they sing for their own reasons ('Mothers of the Disappeared' against the official line on Latin America), may be among the most authentic voices available. Plato's tripartite soul and Aristotle's golden mean supply the thesis that reason needs rightly trained passion: the righteous anger of 'Sunday Bloody Sunday' and 'Silver and Gold' and the resolve of 'Walk On' are practical wisdom in song, the emotions democracy requires. Against Plato's philosopher-king and his noble lies, Delancey argues utopia can only be fostered, not enforced - so in a democracy, if you want to change the world, you may have to sing to people.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 20 "U2 and Philosophy" — Benfell reads U2's apocalyptic songs through Heidegger rather than through eschatological doctrine: 'The Playboy Mansion' depicts fallenness in the 'they', a consumerist paradise with 'no time for sorrow' that lets us flee our own death, while the angel's fall in Wenders' films evoked by 'Stay' and the day-to-day constraints of 'Some Days Are Better than Others' illustrate thrownness, and 'Gone' existential guilt as an unpayable debt. A verse-by-verse reading of 'Until the End of the World' - the Judas-at-the-last-supper reading as one register - shows the speaker moving from 'passing time' and playing roles in the 'they' to anxious guiltiness and the call of conscience, reaching for the one whose resolute waiting models anticipatory resoluteness. The 'end of the world', he concludes, is the end of the speaker's own world: U2's apocalyptic imagery calls listeners to authentic, finite existence, not to prediction of last things.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 13 "Heil Heidegger Dracula’s Willing Executioners" — Adam Barrows reads Stoker's Dracula through Being and Time: the staking of Lucy is the liberation of a true humanity trapped in a deathless shell, and Dracula's endless, mirror-less, selfless existence is Heideggerian inauthenticity - the 'they' that tranquilizes the dying, Renfield's seduction repeating the neighbors' comforting, the refusal of being-toward-death - so vampire-hunting becomes a philosophical task of enforcing authentic, death-claiming being. The chapter then turns the critique on Heidegger himself: his Nazi membership and fundamental ontology's contempt for the everyday leave a gap for racial purity thinking, making Van Helsing's 'butcher work' look like the ritual expulsion of the inauthentic from ontological purity, and asking whether, in adaptation after adaptation, we are Dracula's willing executioners.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 29 "Epilogue" — Auxier's epilogue teaches readers to build playful 'ontologies' from the book's list of Springsteen's proper names — imagining Elvis's .44 Magnum ('Betsy') traveling from a Vegas evidence room into 'Johnny 99' and '57 Channels,' and asking 'Would Bruce ride a Honda?' He borrows Heidegger's idea that the answer already lives in the question, and uses das Man — the inauthentic 'they-self' that chooses by appearances — to contrast Harley riders who confront an existential decision with Honda's self-conserving middle-class pragmatism. The Harley as 'suicide machine' (like Captain America in Easy Rider, like Jesus's passion) embodies freedom and authenticity; Foucault's Borgesian Chinese encyclopedia reminds us that orders of things are conventional, so the ontology itself is one imaginative path among many.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 27 "If You Think that You’re Strong Enough . ." — Matthew Lampert argues that Radiohead's stock theme of "alienation" is exactly Heideggerian inauthenticity: das Man's platitudes made audible in "Fitter Happier," the falling into the world's "uninhibited hustle" of "Ripcord" and "Let Down," and the tranquility that hides both the problem and any exit. He traces the band's arc from the punk-romantic fix of "Anyone Can Play Guitar" (choose and win yourself, form a band) to a deeper diagnosis on The Bends and OK Computer, where Heidegger's Ge-stell and standing-reserve show that in a technological framework only further technological solutions to technological alienation are available. Following "Why Poets?" and Holderlin's question, he concludes that Kid A makes Radiohead the poets in a desolate time: by risking disappearance itself ("How to Disappear Completely," "Idioteque") and singing alienation in its fullness rather than offering false hope, they stare into the abyss where "the more brightly do the ways into the saving power begin to shine."
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 20 "The Fruitcake as Performative Exemplar" — John Kaag pairs Buffett's 'Fruitcakes' with Judith Butler's constructivism: institutions 'girl' infants through interpellation (the sonogram naming), the heterosexual imperative abjects gay, lesbian, and transgender 'nobodies,' and these excluded fruitcakes are the cosmic baker's half-baked people. The movie-theater stanza ('a twelve pound Nestle Crunch for twenty-five dollars') becomes Heidegger's das Man, others thinking and choosing for us, while Buffett's 'mea culpa' refrain and 'Religion's in the hands of some crazy-ass people' attack the guilt constitutive of Christian subjecthood, with Dewey's broad, doctrine-free religious experience offered as common ground. Buffett concerts themselves are read as performative exemplars — drag-show-like borderland communities where four generations act out the 'little bit of fruitcake' in everyone as a quiet political protest against enforced normalcy.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 34 "One Last Anguished Existential Scream" — Argues Neon Genesis Evangelion and Akira dramatize a justified anxiety about humanity's evolutionary future: SEELE's Human Instrumentality Project — dissolving everyone into the Sea of LCL because separate, mutually harming individuals have 'run the course' of their evolution — is Heideggerian anxiety (the objectless unease that breaks us out of 'the They') curdled, via Mary Midgley's 'fatalism,' into the belief that genes, Moore's Law, or 'the Market' leave no room for human choice. Akira's Numbered Children, who sacrifice themselves to remove Tetsuo and save Kaneda, model the responsible alternative: accepting that the power is coming, screaming about it, and still choosing how humanity faces it rather than abdicating to fate.
