- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 23 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Robison-Greene reads the returning soldiers through Camus and Sartre. War reveals the absurd - Jimmy's Argonne story of the German soldier who would not die even in a hopeless situation strips life of inherent value - and Van Alden's fervent Christianity is the escapist response to absurdity, bad faith that denies his own desires. Jimmy and Richard are trapped in bad faith over facticity and transcendence, Richard pinned by 'the look' of a community that only sees his ruined face ('Hell is other people'); neither fully becomes an absurd hero like Meursault, since Richard still craves meaningful ties, but Jimmy finally embraces the absurd at the War Memorial, arranging his own death with the calm of a man who 'died in the trenches, years back.'
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 16 "The Devil and Philosophy" — James McLachlan splits the Satans of history into 'the Rebel' of Romanticism (Blake, Shelley's turn to Prometheus, the sexy vampires of film) and 'the Asshole' who wants to be God. Using Sartre's 'hell is other people' and the desire to be a complete being, he reads Dracula, Scarface's Tony Montana, and Bond villains as figures who cannot endure the otherness of real persons. With Bohme and especially Schelling's two wills - self-assertion and love of others - he argues evil is a positive, perverted order of pure egoism, and that not even Satan can achieve the total asshole-ness he wants, because selfhood exists only in relation to others.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 21 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Lisa Warenski reads 'Suzanne' as staging a phenomenological account of self-awareness: with Husserl and Merleau-Ponty the body is not an object but the lived first-person perspective - so 'touch a perfect body with a mind' is literal - and with Sartre's keyhole example from Being and Nothingness we become aware of ourselves through the gaze of the other. Developmental psychology's mother as 'magical mirror,' who reflects the child's emerging mind, is connected to Hegel's paradox of recognition, and to Aristotle's and Neera Badhwar's friends as mirrors of the soul. On this basis Suzanne's mind-touch has epistemic value: love reflects you truly and shows you what you might become, whether as Jesus's agape or Suzanne's appreciative philia.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 18 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Neal reads Litchfield through Sartre's No Exit: Alex, the ex who both agonizes and galvanizes Piper, makes the other inmates, not the walls, the hell of prison, just as Piper shouts 'I love you and I fucking hate you.' The 'Scared Straight' episode ('Bora Bora Bora') drives the deeper point when Piper tells Dina that the real punishment is coming face to face with who you are: 'I'm scared that I'm not myself in here and I'm scared that I am.' Stripped of distractions, Piper undergoes an existential crisis that forces the self-awareness authenticity requires, though prison's limits keep a fully authentic life out of reach.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 27 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Felder stages Sartre against Merleau-Ponty on the mind-body problem and other minds, opening with the shower scene where Taystee's 'you got them TV titties' makes Piper an object under a gaze, as Pornstache's look converts being caught into shame. But Piper pulling her towel back to appraise her own breasts 'sees-with' Taystee, and the audience's access to Piper's feelings shows perception is shared, not solipsistic. Merleau-Ponty's incarnated subjectivity, the flesh of the opening credits' real inmates' eyes, and actors' embodied performances dissolve the problem of other minds that Sartre's alienated subject-object model leaves open.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 25 "11. Louis C.K.’s No-Bullshit Philosophy" — Marie Snyder uses Sartre's existentialism to unpack Louis's Conan monologue about the 'forever empty': with God gone we are condemned to be free, thrown into a world with no ready-made purpose and alone with our choices - which explains both the cellphone distraction economy and the Live in Portland bit that 'even if you're with someone, you're alone.' Authenticity means ruthlessly honest self-awareness and owning every choice with no excuses - Sartre's waiter example, the claim that there is no cowardly temperament, and Louis's refusal to let 'a flaw in the human male' excuse the tits bit or porn masturbation. Since in choosing for ourselves we choose for all humanity, Snyder pairs Sartre's universalized responsibility with Louis's 'act in a way that, if everybody acted that way, things would work out,' and reads intimate others, as in the Sartre-Beauvoir open relationship, as mirrors that reflect us back to ourselves against the connectionless 'we're just cummers' porn culture. Bad faith - self-deception, distraction, blame - is the fallenness Louis keeps diagnosing in his audiences and confessing in himself.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 16 "7. Being for Red" — Courtland Lewis asks who Darrow is—Red, Gold, hybrid, savior—and surveys theories of the self: Plato's immortal soul ruling the body, Descartes's cogito as thinking thing, and Hume's denial that introspection ever reveals more than a stream of perceptions (we never experience a soul, only thinking). Freud's id-ego-superego offers a secular soul, but Sartre carries the chapter: Darrow is being-for-itself, perpetually projecting what he is not, tortured by the Look of others—Eo seeing a savior, Mustang holding him at gunpoint, Roque's betrayed friendship—and prone to bad faith through 'guardrails' like the Vale, excuses about Eo and Uncle Narol, and pining for Mustang instead of owning his choice. Since existence precedes essence, Darrow is nothing but the sum of his free choices, and to live otherwise is to choose slavery.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 12 "4. Faces from Another Dimension" — Hooke frames the volume through Levinas's claim that the face presents itself from a dimension of transcendence, with Kierkegaard's Abraham, Sartre's existential look, and Beauvoir's faces of the elderly and the second sex in the background, plus Lingis on trust. He shows how TZ masks its deadliest figures with trusted faces — Robert Redford as Death in 'Nothing in the Dark,' Sebastian Cabot's avuncular Pip revealing 'This is the other place!' in 'A Nice Place to Visit,' the witch of 'Jess-Belle,' the gentle Kanamits whose book turns out to be a cookbook — so that proof of trust is nearly impossible and the show has us laughing with the Devil. The Turing test is applied to Alicia's tear in 'The Lonely' (clearly in love 'regardless of the organs or hardware beneath'), the slot machine of 'The Fever,' and the aged couple of 'The Trade-Ins,' whose faces silently recognize a lost shared life.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 19 "8. Tom Petty Didn’t Really Need to Know" — Zelinski and Fallis chart Petty's epistemic arc. His early songs ("I Need to Know," "Fooled Again," "Shadow of a Doubt") crave certainty about lovers' fidelity, a Desmond-free obsession closest to Descartes' quest for certainty beyond doubt, except Petty's problem is other minds, not the external world, and his trust that eyes directly reveal feeling sides with Moore's common-sense perception; Sartre's "hell is other people" names why another free person's future love can never be certain. From Full Moon Fever onward ("Into the Great Wide Open," "Time to Move On," "Learning to Fly") Petty instead embodies Pyrrhonian suspension of judgment and the Buddha's "don't know mind" and Daoist farmer's "we'll see," finding tranquility in uncertainty, craving nothing, flying with eyes open.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 20 "9. Another Wig Underneath" — Cooper argues that the 'vulnerability' Drag Race demands is really a marketable persona, not truth. Working through Butler's Gender Trouble (built on Beauvoir's 'one is not born, but rather becomes a woman'), she concedes drag reveals gender's imitative structure, but shows it also confirms identity: Latrice Royale's padded 'Natural Woman' lip sync reads as authentic, and trans queens like Peppermint and Gia Gunn use drag to articulate womanhood, with Husserl's intersubjectivity invoked to insist that constructed gender is no less real for not being empirical. Willam's edit-spliced 'I'm not acting' breakdown and Shannel's deliberate wig-doff show honesty becoming inconsequential next to spectacle, while Untucked's Interior Illusions Lounge is framed as Sartre's No Exit hell of unending observation. Against RuPaul's 'born naked' self-help nihilism ('identity is a joke'), she ends warning that the show no longer lets Katya take off the chicken suit.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 30 "16. Is Hell Other People" — Berk compares the show to Sartre's No Exit, where Garcin, Inez, and Estelle are locked in a drawing room as each other's torturers, and notes that Michael's experiment 'in the spirit of Sartre' fails because the four humans befriend and improve each other instead. She then corrects the standard reading: Sartre himself insisted 'Hell is other people' is conditional on twisted, bad-faith relationships of over-dependence on others' judgment, as with Tahani's craving for her parents' approval, and the footnote in Being and Nothingness about a 'radical conversion' to authenticity leaves room for healthy relations. Read this way, the show's message that flawed people can find salvation through each other is compatible with, not a refutation of, Sartre.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 14 "The Grain Can Lead Us to Know Too Much" — The chapter argues that the Grain in The Entire History of You ruins Liam and Ffion's marriage not because the truth is bad but because total transparency destroys trust (via Luhmann), feeds a paranoid cycle where any deleted footage looks like guilt, and strips Fi of authority over her own life story. Goffman, Plessner, and Simmel ground the claim that social masks, tact, and privacy are preconditions of selfhood, while Sartre's 'look' explains Fi's shame when Liam forces her to replay her infidelity and Rousseau explains how dependence on others' gaze makes us unfree. Framed by Foucault's reading of Oedipus as a victim of his own knowledge, it concludes that Liam should have let the past lie — and ends with Byung-Chul Han's transparency society as our own already-arrived trajectory.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 22 "A Black Mirror of Our Anxieties" — Nosedive's star ratings are read as a digital panopticon — Bentham's prison design generalized by Foucault's Discipline and Punish — with China's Zhima Credit and Social Credit Systems showing the 'future is already here.' Rousseau's general will and Plato's ship-of-state frame the tyranny-of-the-majority worry (Chester destroyed by an office mob, Lacie jailed for a wedding toast, post-truth tribalism), which Mill's harm principle rebuts: Lacie's rant harms no one and should not be punished. Sartre's 'look' and No Exit explain Lacie's staged cookie photo ('Heaven!') and her final liberating exchange of insults with her cellmate, while Goffman's masks ground the epistemological worry that digital profiles are performances we nonetheless trust, and Bourdieu's symbolic capital names what the scores actually measure.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 10 "A Hope for the Future" — Reads The Little Mermaid as a step forward from the man-requiring damsels of Snow White and Sleeping Beauty: Ariel reverses the rescue by saving Eric, and Aristotle's 'all men by nature desire to know' is stretched to cover her curiosity about the human world. But Ursula's bargain trading Ariel's voice for legs dramatizes the long history of silenced women (Eve, Pandora, Cassandra, the scold's bridle), and the film's sexy, silent Ariel is exactly what Mulvey's male gaze, built on Sartre's 'the look,' criticizes. Applying Beauvoir's 'one is not born but becomes a woman,' the chapter argues Ariel shows biology is not destiny yet still regresses into needing a man, concluding she is a flawed but real advance toward better heroines.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 30 "16. Is Hell Other People" — Puts the show beside Sartre's No Exit, its acknowledged inspiration: Michael's neighborhood, like Garcin, Inez, and Estelle's drawing room, locks flawed people together to torture each other, but the four humans keep helping each other instead ('we improved each other, and the four of us became a team'). Against the standard reading, it uses Sartre's 1964 preface ('if relations with someone else are twisted... that other person can only be Hell'), the Being and Nothingness footnote about a 'radical conversion' from bad faith to authenticity, and his late remark that 'Heaven is each other' to argue the two works are compatible: other people are Hell only under dependence on their judgment — Season One Tahani's condition — while authentic relationships can succeed.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 15 "Notes" — Chelstrom uses the progression from guided DUPLO builds to free design to argue that autonomy develops in degrees and is relational rather than purely individualist. Kant's self-thinking agent — for whom precepts and formulas are the 'ball and chain' of immaturity — explains Emmet's dependence on Octan's instruction booklets and Lord Business's profit from deference, and Korsgaard's definition frames the individualist autonomy the Master Builders embody. Yet their lone-wolf autonomy fails, and Sartre's look plus Beauvoir's account of woman forced to assume herself as Other explain Wyldstyle/Lucy's deference to others' expectations; Catriona Mackenzie's relational autonomy recasts 'Everything is Awesome' as peers supporting each other's self-development, with Emmet's friendship letting Lucy accept herself.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 22 "The Office and Philosophy" — Applies Sartre's Being and Nothingness to the mockumentary: Pam's bad faith consists in pretending she has no choice between Jim and Roy (her garbled 'I'm not into Jim' conversation with Karen in 'Ben Franklin'), while the camera's Look - Sartre's keyhole peeper caught in the hallway - turns her into an object not of her making when she is caught watching Jim and Karen in 'The Merger', and her shame finally lets her own her feelings. David Brent's pride (posing with his Inside Paper magazine cover) tries to control the Other's look and fails, since the freely respected gaze he craves cannot be extracted; and the ever-possible camera functions as Foucault's panopticon (Bentham's prison design), visible and unverifiable, silencing Jan on speakerphone in 'Cocktails' and forcing Dwight and Angela's 'Don't linger. Break left' choreography, which makes the viewer a complicit co-worker.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 10 "Responsibility" — Christiansen reads SNL's first head writer Michael O'Donoghue ('Mr. Mike') through Sartre: the Least-Loved Bedtime Tales (Brer Rabbit skinned alive, 'there's no moral... just random acts of meaningless violence') dramatize a world where existence precedes essence and narratives lie; 'Sartresky and Hutch' stages the absurd via a Vietnam veteran with PTSD; and the needles-in-the-eyes impressions embody Sartre's vulnerability to the Other, which Mr. Mike's dark glasses shut out. The chapter ends with Sartre's Marxist turn in the Critique of Dialectical Reason, arguing O'Donoghue's angry 'Police State' sketch shows that scarcity, alienation, and organized state violence are contingent and can be fought, which is where his nihilism leaves room for hope.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 12 "4. Faces from Another Dimension" — Hooke uses Levinas's account of the face (and Lingis on trust) to read the Zone's faces: the bandaged woman and pig-faced surgeons of 'The Eye of the Beholder' unseat our standards of the normal, while trusted faces are weaponized by Robert Redford's Grim Reaper in 'Nothing in the Dark,' Sebastian Cabot's Satan in 'A Nice Place to Visit,' and the gentle Kanamit of 'To Serve Man.' Alicia's tear in 'The Lonely' and John and Marie Holt's wordless recognition in 'The Trade-Ins' show trust and love exceeding proof or evidence. Sartre's existential look, with Kierkegaard's Abraham and Beauvoir's second sex, frames how a face puts our freedom and trust in question.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 9 "Acknowledgment" — William Irwin diagnoses Neptune, from the 09-ers down to the PCH-ers, with status anxiety (via Alain de Botton's Status Anxiety) and prescribes the Stoic remedy: Epictetus on the insult lying in our judgment rather than the insulter, and Marcus Aurelius, the emperor who chose serenity over vengeance, show how Keith and Veronica ground self-worth in virtue no one can take away. Sartre's 'hell is other people' and the look explain how Veronica is reduced to a dumb blonde and Duncan to a murderer until he flees to Cuba, while Schopenhauer's choice between loneliness and vulgarity frames Mac's switched-at-birth longing, Wallace's basketball-bought status, and Weevil's self-made standing as PCH leader. Irwin closes by offering the show itself as Aristotelian catharsis-through-comedy, art as therapy for the viewer's own status anxiety.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 21 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Schmetkamp reads The Ice Storm through the philosophy of love and Hegelian recognition theory, defending a dialogical model of love (Krebs, Scheler's shared feeling) against union (Plato, Nozick, Solomon) and care (Aristotle, Frankfurt) models. She shows the Hood and Carver families lack autonomy-granting mutual recognition: Ben and Janey's affair is mere egoistic gratification, Elena would surrender her 'I' for a 'we', and Mikey seeks stilled 'molecules' and the Fantastic Four's negative zone. Invoking Sartre's the-look as objectification and shame, she argues Mikey's death finally breaks the ice through empathy and sympathy (Scheler, Stein), as Jim weeps and Elena speaks Ben's name.
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — McMahon argues After Hours uses dark comedy to reveal the existential truth that anyone, at any moment, is vulnerable to absurdity. She sets Sartre's account (absurdity as the contingency of existence, fled via bad faith) beside Camus' (absurdity as a feeling born of the clash between human need for order and the world's silence), then maps Paul Hackett's nightmarish SoHo night onto Sartre's Nausea (the ordinary Roquentin overwhelmed by objects and people) and No Exit ('hell is other people'), where others become the mechanism that discloses the absurd. She contends comedy, like horror, exploits our fascination with grim spectacle, and that laughing at absurdity—rather than horrific spectacle—lets audiences acknowledge and manage existential anxiety and still live well.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 12 "4. A Muscle Car and a Mythic Quest" — Huntingford reads Sam and Dean as the Cowboy incarnation of Jung's universal Mythic Hero archetype, their Impala road-trip an odyssey of Campbell's monomyth and Jungian individuation confronting the 'shadow' (Amara as the Darkness). She uses Hegel to cast the brothers' alienation as the start of self-discovery toward absolute knowledge, Kierkegaard to praise their nonconformity over the crowd, and Sartre's 'hell is other people' and freedom-as-otherness to argue the Quest requires killing the false narrative self—Chuck the Trickster—to become free.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 17 "8. Self-Hatred as Identity" — Cash argues that Jimmy and Mike become their Breaking Bad selves through a 'negative self-relation' (a term from Martin Hägglund) rather than Walt's outward resentment. Mike's 'I broke my boy' speech in 'Five-O' shows him internalizing guilt for making Matty 'debase' himself, leaving nothing to live for but stashing money for Kaylee; Jimmy internalizes Chuck's verdict that he is 'Slippin' Jimmy with a law degree, a chimp with a machine gun,' so each success as Saul only confirms the worst image of himself. Cash uses Sartre's Being and Nothingness—that one cannot truly be evil 'for myself' without judging oneself as an other—to argue Jimmy's self-hatred must become unconscious for the Saul mask to become his face.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 33 "The Viewer and the Look" — Meyer and Schneider use The Office's mockumentary camera to dramatize Sartre's 'the Look' and bad faith. Pam pretends she cannot choose between Roy and Jim (bad faith as being-in-itself), and is shamed when the camera catches her watching Jim and Karen; David Brent's prideful self-promotion tries and fails to control the Other's gaze. They tie the ever-present camera to the Foucault/Bentham panopticon: Jan, Dwight, and Angela police themselves because they might be watched, making the viewer complicit in the workers' existential crises.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 16 "It Worked" — Sander Lee reads Jack, Locke, and Desmond through Sartre's bad faith and authenticity and the objectifying 'Look' (the keyhole example), casting Jack the man-of-science as a Humean skeptic who condemns his father's fatalist evasion of responsibility while Locke's devotion to pushing the button is a Kierkegaardian leap of faith modeled on Abraham and Isaac. Desmond David Hume embodies skepticism yet opens to omens and self-sacrifice; and Lee argues the finale's multi-faith 'church' moves Lost from Sartre's secular existentialism toward Kierkegaard and Buber's I-Thou relation, exemplified by Sawyer and Juliet's redemptive bond and Gandhi-like religious universalism.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 16 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Hernandez contrasts 'dark' existentialism — Sartre's café-bound claim that hell is other people and that the self is imprisoned in others' looks (illustrated by Starbucks' Pike Place backlash reshaping its identity), and Camus's absurd alienation — with an 'optimistic existentialism' that finds meaning in community. Drawing on Kierkegaard's Christian love, Jaspers's 'encounter,' Marcel's turn toward the other (her Sweet Eugene's pregnancy story), and above all Buber's I–Thou versus I–It, she argues the coffee community (neighborhood boards, fair-trade activism, the neighborly cup) is an existential ground where isolated bodies-toward-death create shared hope by treating each patron as a Thou rather than a discarded It.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 11 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Winters reads the Zodiac Killer's taunting letters through Sartre's account of 'the look' from Being and Nothingness. He argues Zodiac's letters function like a snapped twig or a lit window: they make Northern Californians experience themselves as seen objects, hunted 'slaves' and pawns in Zodiac's game rather than free subjects. A phenomenological (first-person) analysis of the fear Zodiac induces, and of how his letters restrict the choices available within our facticity, is offered as superior to psychological or analytic accounts for explaining our fascination with the macabre.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 11 "Who is Who" — Focused on the 'Monstrous Other' and the 'base under siege' story, the chapter uses Hegel's master-slave struggle for recognition and Sartre's 'the look' to read Cybermen, the Flood ('Waters of Mars') and the Silurians as Others through which humans define themselves, with Levinas on the face and history. Its final section frames the Doctor and the Master as Gothic doubles of love and strife, using Spinoza's monism, principle of sufficient reason and conatus to argue the power-hungry Master paradoxically fits Spinoza's system better than the order-imposing 'Dark Doctor.'
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 33 "The Viewer and the Look" — Meyer and Schneider read The Office through Sartre's "the Look" and bad faith: the mockumentary camera catches characters as objects, as when Pam is caught gazing at Jim and freezes in shame, or pretends she has no choice about Roy (bad faith). David Brent's prideful posing tries to control the Other's look and fails. They add Foucault's panopticon — Dwight, Angela, and Jan police themselves because the camera might be watching — making the viewer complicit in exposing the employees' existential crises.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 49 "46. The Shawshank Redemption as Philosophy Freedom and Panopticism" — Hooke reads The Shawshank Redemption through two lenses. From Sartre he takes 'hell is other people' and the objectifying look from No Exit and Being and Nothingness — Shawshank's warden and 'sisters' embody a worldly hell of 'never' and 'always' — but argues Andy and Red's friendship, Andy's Mozart broadcast, and the hopeful ending invert Sartre, making freedom the shared warmth of friendship rather than the devouring gaze. From Foucault's Discipline and Punish he reads the prison's shift from spectacle to disciplinary surveillance and solitary confinement as panopticism, extending Foucault's insight that prisons, schools, and hospitals mirror one another (illustrated by his COVID-era campus). He closes with Nietzschean genealogy and redemption through laughter, joy, and giving.

### Virtues, Practices and Traditions

Alasdair MacIntyre sought to revive an Aristotelian account of the virtues by embedding them in the concepts of a practice, the narrative unity of a human life, and a moral tradition. A practice is a cooperative human activity with internal goods, such as medicine or chess, and the virtues are the qualities that enable us to achieve those goods and to sustain the practices and communities that transmit them. On his view, a single life is intelligible as a quest for the good, and that quest is always carried out from within a historically extended tradition of inquiry rather than from a neutral standpoint. MacIntyre argued that modern moral discourse is fragmented precisely because it has lost this teleological and traditional framework.

- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 23 "America’s Game" — William Morgan answers Richard Rorty's charge that American pop culture breeds only militaristic chauvinism by pointing to baseball's moral self-story: played for love of the game (Whitman) rather than market value. Using MacIntyre's notion of a practice's internal goods, he argues baseball's excellences and fair play are shared, socially constructed goods that resist commodification; through Annette Baier's ethics of trust and Bernard Williams's 'one thought too many' (saving your wife because she is your wife), the home team extends familial trust into a public moral community. Hence the moral outrage of 'Say it ain't so, Joe' after the 1919 Black Sox scandal and 'Say It Ain't So Sammy' after Sosa's corked bat: fans demand that players justify themselves to the community whose common good the game embodies.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 38 "20b" — A paired political-philosophy debate over Alex Rodriguez's $252 million contract. Albert Duncan defends the salary as the just outcome of market forces: stars like Bonds, McGwire, and Sosa maximize fan satisfaction, pack stadiums (600,000 extra Cardinals tickets in 1998), and generate hundreds of millions for local economies. Joel Shuman, a self-described socialist, replies with Alasdair MacIntyre's notion of baseball as a 'practice' whose intrinsic goods belong to a traditioned community of players, coaches, and fans: when market ideology alienates fans, unbalances competition, and prices out small markets, money has stopped serving the human activity it was meant to be part of.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 26 "Goals for All Ages and All Occasions" — Opening with Camus's line that crushing truths perish from being acknowledged (and his Sisyphus, invoked to show the intrinsically interested player always wins), the authors force football to face its ugly side—divers, Pepe kicking Casquero on the ground, Catania's mooning free-kick screen, referee Pérez Burrull's robbery of Osasuna, the Heysel disaster, Bilardo pinning opponents and drugging Branco, FIFA's resistance to technology—analyzing it all with MacIntyre's account of social practices: football's constitutive rules and internal goods generate standards of excellence that cheating betrays for extrinsic rewards. Their positive ideal is the Greek Kalon, the noble-and-beautiful they field for Plato and Aristotle, exemplified when De Rossi confesses his handball goal against Messina or opponents return the ball after an injury stoppage—the beau geste uniting aesthetic grace and moral honor, as in the 4–4 Arsenal–Liverpool classic where 'neither side deserved to lose'. The ugly, they conclude, is exactly what lets the beautiful shine, as Eto'o floats over Scholes's tackle to assist a Messi goal.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 15 "An Eye for an Eye" — Mihaela Frunza and Anatolia Bessemer use MacIntyre's Whose Justice? Which Rationality? to frame Holmes's casual felonies, the disguised-clergyman trick on Irene Adler, freeing Captain Croker after staging a mock courtroom in 'The Abbey Grange', and compounding a felony with Isadora Klein in 'The Three Gables', as one tradition of justice among several with no neutral court of appeal. Against the police's letter-of-the-law tradition stand the criminals' own codes of retribution, above all Jefferson Hope in A Study in Scarlet letting 'the high God judge' between the poisoned and harmless pills, making Holmes and his prey mirror-image vigilantes who prefer restitution or chivalric acquittal to statutory punishment.
- **Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within**, ch. 17 "Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy" — Mudde and Piercey argue Curb depicts Nietzschean nihilism made humdrum: in Larry's world 'the highest values devalue themselves,' so Ted Danson's 'anonymous' donation is leaked for glory, a terrorist warning becomes leverage in a tiff with Mindy Reiser, and strangers judge everyone constantly because no one is a moral authority. The Platonic and Aristotelian answers to what 'the good' is have no purchase here; moral language survives only as a hollow shell, which is MacIntyre's 'simulacra of morality,' and his own remedy—rebuilding communities that give moral rules a point—fails because on Curb community is hell ('I'd rather have the thieves than the neighbors'). Since ought no longer implies can, the show is tragic, though the Tourettic chef's opening night in 'The Grand Opening,' where Larry leads a communal torrent of obscenities in solidarity, offers a fragile glimpse of doing a little good.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 18 "8. How Shitty Can a Hero Be" — Corey Horn maps the Deadpool movie onto Joseph Campbell's monomyth—ordinary world, call to adventure (the cancer diagnosis), refusal of the recruiter's offer, acceptance, and the ordeal of hunting Ajax—then asks whether a mercenary chasing reward can be a hero at all. MacIntyre's chess example distinguishes instrumental from intrinsic rewards of a practice, and Kant splits motivation into duty versus self-interested motives; since Wade hunts Ajax to recover his face and Vanessa, both thinkers would deny his journey is moral. Still, MacIntyre's allowance for migrating from instrumental to intrinsic motivation leaves Deadpool a hero-in-progress, already promising Colossus he will consider joining the X-Men.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 17 "7. How Captain America and Iron Man Embody America" — Altmann contrasts Tony's individualist cosmopolitanism - privatizing world peace, building Ultron alone - with Steve's community-rooted patriotism, the team player from war bonds through the Howling Commandos to Winter Soldier. Using Scruton's definition of patriotism as standing or falling together, MacIntyre's claim that morality grows only within a particular community, and Nussbaum's suggestion to be a patriot first and grow into a cosmopolitan, he concludes Cap's thoughtful patriotism is morally preferable while Tony's globe-saving individualism keeps backfiring. The best American would combine Tony's concern for the whole Earth with Steve's love of neighbor, so no civil war is needed.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 25 "14. After the Blackout" — Martin Muchall treats the offscreen Blackout as an emblem of the moral catastrophe diagnosed in MacIntyre's After Virtue: our moral vocabulary has shattered into emotivist hissing and clapping, with Roy's murder of Tyrell, his 'God of biomechanics', staging the death of God and the 'everything is permitted' that follows. Utilitarian pleasure and Kantian cold reason (Spock, who must tell the truth to the murderer at the door) have both failed, leaving neoliberal hypercapitalism — corporate psychopathy, the orphanage sweatshop, the Baseline as workplace performance review — as the real villain. Against this, K's ending models the Buddha: everything is impermanent, there is no self to defend, and his selfless, empathetic death points to a morality grounded in evolved and cultivable altruism.
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 20 "Too Big to Function" — Terjesen argues Jack's combined title, Vice President of East Coast Television and Microwave Oven Programming, exhibits the corporate mentality: following Robert Jackall's Moral Mazes, credit flows up (Jack's Trivection oven) and blame flows down (Greenzo, the fireworks fiasco), so managers learn to avoid decisive action. Peter French's thesis that corporations are moral persons explains why GE runs fine with Don Geiss in a coma and Kathy Geiss playing with unicorns, so no one at the top needs to understand the businesses they oversee. MacIntyre's distinction between practices with internal goods and external rewards shows profit-thinking erasing comedy's internal good, turning TGS into 'pos-mens' and product integration, and Adam Smith's attack on distant, ignorant regulators is turned against conglomerate central management itself.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 28 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Interrogates Gob's catchphrase 'I've made a huge mistake': on Aristotle's account of hexis, the mean of truthfulness and proper pride, and justice as proportional distribution, Gob's prison-escape key stunt and 'Hermano' jealousy make him wicked rather than merely error-prone, since he lacks grasp of his own injustices. Hume's sentimentalist reply is that immorality is a nonrational moral sense refined only through experience, so mistakes could educate Gob, except he roofies away his one growth moment with Steve Holt (!). MacIntyre's practices (the Magician's Alliance versus non-practitioner Gob) and the narrative unity of character explain why a man who tells no coherent story of himself ends up with no wisdom.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 20 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Nicholas argues the film's supposed nihilists, Walter, and the Big Lebowski are all failed Nietzschean value-creators: Walter's arbitrary givings of value ('Donny was a good man... he was one of us') just enact nihilism, and the disabled achiever's money-and-plaques world mistakes symbols for value. He then uses Charles Taylor's three malaises of modernity — disenchantment, disengagement, atomism — to explain the Dude's world (even bowling stops mattering: 'Fuck the tournament'), and finds the way out in MacIntyre's notion of a practice: bowling's internal goods, standards of excellence, and community of giving and receiving tie the three friends to meanings outside themselves, resisting nihilism.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 30 "It’s Life in the Solar System, Jim, But Not as We Know It" — Uses MacIntyre's demand for self-knowledge — awareness of the social and political currents that shape one's beliefs — to diagnose the Martian Congressional Republic's exceptionalism (Lopez berating 'short-sighted and selfish' Earthers from the Donnager) and to chart Bobbie Draper's redemption arc: refusing to fire first on Ganymede, refusing to bear false witness after the hearings, protecting Holden at the Ring Station, defecting to Avasarala, and finally rescuing Naomi. It maps MCR culture onto American space culture — Kennedy's Rice speech, the Mars Society and National Space Society founding statements, Zubrin's Case for Mars, and Patricia Limerick's and Linda Billings's critique of the 'conquering the space frontier' metaphor, with Carnap's frameworks and Kuhn's incommensurability explaining how metaphors hide alternatives — and argues the MCR never acquires self-knowledge, a failure that ends in its alliance with Marco Inaros and the move to Laconia, while Draper's willingness to update her beliefs shows what philosophy asks of real spaceflight advocates.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Kuzma uses MacIntyre's After Virtue to argue the Wasteland is modern morality itself: a fragmentary rubble where, like Bartertown's cobbled-together vehicles, utilitarian and deontological fragments survive without the shared telos that gave them meaning. Immortan Joe's V8 cult imposes a false telos and embodies Nietzsche's will-to-power Übermensch, while Bartertown's rules express mere individualism without any vision of the good life. Max — 'haunted by those I could not protect' — can seek the good life only by joining Furiosa's community and embracing its telos, and the Green Place turns out to be not a place but a way of life, confirming MacIntyre's Aristotle over Nietzsche.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 22 "Reconciliation Doesn’t Come in a Bottle" — Elia reads Don through Camus's Clamence in The Fall, an establishment success shadowed by guilt and self-medication, while insisting Don is no existential hero: unlike Sisyphus or Meursault, Dick Whitman never lucidly chose his freedom, he merely fled his past by stealing dog tags in Korea. Using MacIntyre's After Virtue opposition between Nietzschean value-creation and Aristotelian tradition-embeddedness, the chapter argues Don lacks integrity, the virtue that justifies breaks in one's narrative by deeper commitments, which is why peace appears only when past and present reconcile: phoning Anna as 'Dick Whitman,' the ocean immersion, and the confession to Betty ('I can explain' / 'You're a very, very gifted story-teller'). His justice is real but thin, a merit-based accounting that works at the office (promoting Peggy on talent) yet fails Betty, the children, and Adam, and reconciliation, the title insists, doesn't come in a bottle.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 30 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Sanford argues, through the arc of the Raimi trilogy, that Peter becomes good by becoming the narrator of his own life. On Aristotle's Poetics — a story has a beginning, middle, and end, and art imitates life — and MacIntyre's claim that man is a 'story-telling animal' whose life is 'the unity of a narrative quest,' Peter's involuntary obligations (orphanhood, Uncle Ben's death, the spider bite, love for MJ) ground the voluntary ones, and his quest is to use his great powers responsibly. Tracking Aristotle's categories, Peter moves from incontinence (vengeance on Flint Marko, the jazz-club strut in Spider-Man 3) through continence to genuine virtue, and his practice of telling his own story — 'it's the choices that make us who we are' — models how we must get our own stories straight to flourish.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 4 "Allure of the West" — Nicholas Moll reads the Westworld park as a tabletop-style sandbox and LARP role-play experience with Ford as Game Master mediating guests' mediated 'illusion of choice.' Drawing on MacIntyre's narrative unity of a life and Bernard Williams's critique about the constraints of coherence, he argues guests author competing self-narratives to reach greater self-knowledge, as William discovers his capacity for ruthlessness and becomes the Man in Black. He contends violence functions as the rule-mediated engine of this 'gameful,' educative experience, and that Ford's transformative insight is aimed less at the guests than at the hosts who are engaged in the park's production.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 12 "Basketball Purists" — Kretchmar defends a 'modified purist' view that team-oriented, fundamentals-based basketball is generally better than the individualist modernist game, offering three arguments. The functionalist argument borrows Searle's account of constitutive rules to say ten-person interactive complexity makes a richer, more durable 'test' (like chess vs. tic-tac-toe); the variety argument uses Mill's On Liberty to warn that market pressures homogenize basketball toward football; and the communitarian argument uses MacIntyre's notion of a 'practice' with internal goods to show ESPN Streetball's isolated one-on-one feats erode basketball as a cooperative practice.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 17 "Love–Love A Fresh Start at Finding Value and Virtue in Tennis" — Tommy Valentini argues that because winning lies outside a player's control (he could never beat Nadal by simply choosing to), success in tennis should be redefined around what is controllable. Using Alasdair MacIntyre's After Virtue, he treats tennis as a MacIntyrean practice and distinguishes external goods (trophies, prize money, ranking—zero-sum, tied to winning) from internal goods (full effort, positive attitude, sportsmanship) that require the virtues of justice, honesty, and courage and are available to winner and loser alike. Drawing on Aristotelian justice ('giving each their due') and Randolph Feezell on the opponent as competitor-and-friend, he holds up Arthur Ashe's Stoic response to AIDS in Days of Grace as the exemplar of carrying tennis's internal goods into life in the face of an uncontrollable outcome, death.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 19 "Stabbing Seles Fans and Fair Play" — Opening with Gunther Parche's stabbing of Monica Seles to injure Steffi Graf's rival, the chapter argues that a win-at-all-costs mentality misunderstands sport's value. Using Suits's account of games (lusory goals, means, rules, attitude) and rejecting bare formalism for Simon's broad internalism, it grounds tennis's intrinsic worth in the difficulty of achievement, the level of the opponent, and MacIntyre's notion of a practice with internal goods. It reframes fair play as 'respect for the game,' classifies fans as partisan, purist, or ideally moderate partisan, and concludes that by eliminating Seles, Parche damaged not just her but Graf's legacy and tennis itself because he loved the game too little.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 10 "Charlie Kaufman, Screenwriter" — Evans reads Adaptation as a creation story: the character Charlie Kaufman must make a script 'out of nothing' rather than transcribe Susan Orlean's Orchid Thief, so the film enacts Deleuze's idea of the writer as fabulator who confronts the audience with the text as invention. She sets Charlie's Genesis-like 'beginning without end' against Donald and Robert McKee's Aristotelian, plot-driven Story where the ending justifies the means (glossing MacIntyre's 'stories are lived before they are told'). Naming the character after himself, she argues, marks the distance between imaginative making (poesis) and Orlean's realist journalism (mimesis).
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — The editors' introduction argues that Eastwood, though no academic, does 'practical philosophy' through his films as a craftsman who inherits and then revises genres (revising the Western in Unforgiven, rethinking rugged individualism in Million Dollar Baby and Gran Torino). Invoking MacIntyre's claim that we are only co-authors of interlocking narratives, it reads Eastwood's focus on decisive moral choices (Francesca's refusal to leave in Bridges of Madison County, Butch Haynes in A Perfect World) as a 'laboratory of moral psychology' echoing Aristotle's 'choice discriminates character.' It ties his concern with loss, justice, and Aristotelian friendship and flourishing (Grinnell on Million Dollar Baby) to a Socratic 'know thyself,' arguing his philosophizing is implicit and nonverbal rather than argued in words.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 22 "“A Homespun Murder Story” Film Noir and the Problem of Modernity in Fargo" — Abrams reads Fargo as a noir study of modernity via MacIntyre's After Virtue: humans are 'story-telling animals,' and the Enlightenment project (Descartes, Sartre) shredded the shared myth, leaving Cartesian monadic selves who float in a void as 'unscripted, anxious stutterers.' The whiteout blizzard becomes an ontological tabula rasa of Heraclitean flux where every conversation collapses (Jerry, Carl, Mike Yanagita, even Marge at the drive-thru). Abrams reads Marge as morally good but intellectually shallow—wrong to call the sublime, Kantian 'dynamically sublime' day 'beautiful'—and Grimsrud as the one who dimly 'sees' the modern abyss, so the film hands the deeper mystery of modernity's crime to the viewer.
- **The Philosophy of Spike Lee**, ch. 11 "Aristotle and MacIntyre on Justice in 25th Hour" — Conard uses Lee's 25th Hour to test Aristotle's claim that justice is inseparable from community and necessary for eudaimonia, and MacIntyre's charge that liberal individualist society lacks any common good. Comparing the greedy Wall Street broker Frank (an Aristotelian overreacher driven by pleonexia) with the drug dealer Monty (fairer, though convicted under unjust Rockefeller laws), he argues Monty is not unjust yet still cannot flourish in a fragmented New York. Monty's profane bathroom 'fuck you' soliloquy dramatizes the city's incommensurable values, while the post-9/11 fellow-feeling offers a fleeting glimpse of the shared good MacIntyre says modern society lacks.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 36 "One More Thing, Don’t Blink!" — Michelle Saint and Peter French explain why 'Blink' is horrifying despite the Weeping Angels being beautiful, not disgusting. Using Noël Carroll's fear-plus-disgust theory of art-horror as a foil, they draw on Frankfurt's account of caring and MacIntyre's narrative identity to argue the Angels destroy personhood: by hurling Kathy Nightingale out of her time and place they strip away everything she cares about and the narrative that constitutes her self. They then revise Carroll, proposing horror is fear plus impotence: the Angels weaponize the impossible task of not blinking, exposing our powerlessness to protect our own identity.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 17 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — LaRocca unpacks MacIntyre's After Virtue claim that Austen is 'the last great representative of the classical tradition of the virtues.' He traces MacIntyre's argument that Austen synthesizes Homeric social roles, Aristotelian practical wisdom (phronesis), and Christian humility, making constancy her master virtue (analogous to phronesis) and distinguishing genuine amiability from mere agreeableness (Knightley on Frank Churchill: 'amiable only in French'). He contrasts Austen's internal, teleological virtue with Franklin's utilitarian ledger, cites Ryle's 'gradal' Aristotelian reading of Austen's character vocabulary and C.S. Lewis on her Christian 'undeception,' and reads Fanny Price's charmless constancy as exemplary of virtue over charm.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 28 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Scott reads Dickens's A Christmas Carol through virtue theory, treating Scrooge's transformation as a lesson in the virtues of generosity and gratitude that constitute eudaimonia (human flourishing). Drawing on Niebuhr, he explains Scrooge's greed as an anxious, insecurity-driven quest for security through wealth that fails because flourishing depends on relationships, not money (the poor-but-happy Cratchits). He invokes MacIntyre's 'just generosity' and Aristotelian habituation to show virtues are cultivated through practice, and uses Charles Taylor's weak/strong evaluations to warn that Christmas consumerism threatens 'keeping Christmas' by reducing moral worth to preferences and purchases.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 25 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Joe Kraus argues Tolkien wrote The Lord of the Rings as a protest against modernism, the mood that 'all that is solid melts into air' and that the past no longer matters, voiced by Marx, Freud, and Nietzsche's 'God is dead.' Tolkien's heroes survive because they remember lore and tradition (Gandalf watching the Shire, Sam's book-learning at Cirith Ungol), while Saruman and Denethor embody modern despair: they misuse the palantir, lose faith in tradition, and can only try to destroy the present. Against Berman's claim that there is no escape from modernism, Kraus reads Middle-earth as a fantasy where clinging to tradition still yields real, tangible power and certainty.

### Stoicism

Stoicism is a school of Hellenistic philosophy founded by Zeno of Citium around 300 BCE and later developed by figures such as Epictetus, Seneca, and Marcus Aurelius. It teaches that virtue—living in accordance with reason and nature—is the only true good, and that a flourishing life comes from mastering one's judgments rather than external circumstances. Because emotions like fear and anger arise from mistaken beliefs about what is good or bad, the Stoics sought to cultivate reason and equanimity in the face of whatever fortune brings.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 68 "Unknown" — The chapter proposes three theses: happiness is centrally tranquillity (ataraxia), whose enemy is anxiety - the 'splinter in your mind' that things are out of kilter; the rival Aristotelian view treats happiness as activity (energeia) of soul in accordance with excellence (arete), an objectivism that explains how a contented 'human battery' or happy slave is mistaken about being happy; and neither view suffices alone, since a passionless apatheia is barren and dry. Lived happiness is instead equipoise - settledness in one's basic stance that is compatible with turbulent passions and commitments, more like Neo's active decision-making and discovery than a lazy virtual tryst with the woman in red.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 22 "Emotions and Aesthetic Response" — Carolyn Korsmeyer uses BtVS to stage philosophy's ambivalence about emotion — dangerous passion versus intuitive sagacity — through three cases: anger as beast within and practical power (Xander's love spell in 'Bewitched, Bothered and Bewildered,' Willow's wish-spells in 'Something Blue,' 'My emotions give me power' to Kendra), grief as the one emotion no magic can undo (Epictetus's jug-and-child counsel set against 'The Body' and Dawn trying to resurrect Joyce), and love's non-fungibility (Anya's vengeance-demon past leaves her without the wider affection that makes singular love credible, while Spike's messy human history makes his obsession believable). She draws on Plato's wild-beast appetites and spirited element of the Republic, Aristotle on anger and emotional disposition as character, Kant's reason-above-nature picture, and Martha Nussbaum on art's particular cases. Finally she turns to aesthetic response: the show's comedy ('She saved the world a lot') regulates audience emotion, keeping the serial's catharsis from tipping into manipulation.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 14 "Kierkegaard Lays It Down" — Willie Young uses the sacrifice bunt (Derek Jeter's perfect one versus Placido Polanco's failed one) to test philosophical accounts of sacrifice. Aristotle treats bunting for teammates as friendship and civic virtue in the polis, while Seneca's Stoic sacrifices only to exercise virtue itself, detached from particular friends and refusing retaliation for hit batters. Hegel's modern ideal of self-renunciation makes the player a cog in the team machine (the Big Red Machine), obeying the manager's calculations; against this, Kierkegaard's Abraham, whose absolute duty to God is 'higher than the universal' through infinite resignation, exposes baseball's mechanical, manager-ordered sacrifice and asks whether the game trains obedient citizens who sacrifice as they are told.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 10 "“Control, Control, You Must Learn Control”" — Stephens reads Yoda as a Stoic sage: Luke's first impressions are blinded by appearance, but Yoda exhibits the Stoic virtues of patience, timeliness, focus on the present, apatheia (freedom from fear, anger, and hate), and ascetic discipline (askesis), living by the dichotomy of control. He reconstructs the contrasting 'logic of the Dark Side' - anger to hatred to aggression to the mastery of others - showing the Emperor as a tyrant who, unlike the self-mastering Stoic (Marcus Aurelius being the counterexample among rulers), seeks to control what is not up to him, so Vader's 'I must obey my master' is servitude to vice. The chapter also marks Stoic limits: the Emperor rightly rejects felt compassion but wrongly refuses beneficence and Stoic cosmopolitanism, and Stoic physicalism cannot accommodate Yoda's 'luminous beings' afterlife.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 41 "A Doomed Pursuit of Power and Glory" — Doom, declaring 'Power has ever been my God', steals the Silver Surfer's cosmic power, and the authors correct Lord Acton: power itself does not corrupt - only the flawed vessel it is poured into, while the uncorrupted are not destroyed by its loss ('Though bereft of my power - I do not crawl!'). The imprisoned Surfer's tranquil equanimity, they argue, is the voice of a Stoic philosopher, and Marvel shares with the best ancient philosophers a faith in a built-in cosmic justice whereby wrongly gotten power destroys its holder - fulfilled when Galactus strips Doom of what was never his.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 74 "What Wisdom Requires" — Explains what wisdom demands: subordinating the loud, here-and-now deliverances of the senses and emotions to reason and the larger picture — as in Plato's wise person contemplating the eternal Forms and the Republic's long course of training, the Bhagavad-Gita's detachment, and Stoic meditative practice. It argues experience is nonetheless central (a sixteen-year-old Captain Marvel could not have it), cites Stick's parting from Matt Murdock in Daredevil over uncontrolled emotion, and uses Casablanca to mark the cultural shift that makes us doubt the larger picture's claims.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 15 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Over an evening at the Iron Post biker bar, Auxier maps four habitues onto the Hellenistic schools: Cowboy, the Vietnam chopper pilot whose bar is a Garden of modest pleasures, loyalty, and withdrawal from power games, is an Epicurean; the laconic Bear, who doubts that even possessing knowledge would make us better off and suspends judgment, is a Pyrrhonian (unlike the coffee-house Carneadean); Happy Jack, the 'true nature's child' of 'Born to Be Wild' who defies convention and keeps nothing six months, is Diogenes's Cynic; and Gary, the Vietnam-damaged recovering alcoholic, is a damaged Stoic who has not reached apatheia. He concludes that bikers are postmodern pagans whose philosophy is enacted rather than propounded, a Biker Platonism that refuses the Christian-Platonic divorce of body and spirit and lives by honor, freedom, and a pagan fatalism that accepts the consequences of one's choices.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 10 "“All Good Things Must Come to an End”" — Thorsrud casts Spock and Data's exchange in 'Unification, Part II' — Spock dispassionate by choice, Data longing for emotion — as a replay of the ancient debate between Stoics and Peripatetics over whether to eliminate or moderate the passions. The Aristotelian side is built from Data's emotion-chip rage while killing a Borg ('Descent'), his unfelt breakup with Jenna ('In Theory'), and Riker's defense of trust after Ishara's betrayal ('Legacy'): emotions are judgments with pleasure or pain, there is a right amount to feel, and invulnerability costs the 'emotional bonds that make us who we are.' The Stoic reply uses Epictetus's distinction between involuntary impressions and assent (Picard's fear on the Borg ship vs. the holodeck), Cicero's refusal to 'moderate' what is simply a fault, and Seneca on anger, exemplified by Spock's 'quite logical relief' in 'Amok Time', his calculated desperation in 'The Galileo Seven', and his saving the bigot Stiles in 'Balance of Terror' — leaving the Peripatetic conclusion that fortune's goods are not mere indifferents and we may rightly 'smile with so little provocation.'
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 15 "“Here, Here, What’s All This Jabber-wapping When There’s Work to Be Done ”" — Tschaepe reads Professor Marvel and the Wizard as skilled givers of 'folk explanations'—stories about desires, beliefs, and feelings that work where logical, scientific, or mechanistic explanations fail—because each explanation is fitted to the pragmatic considerations of its audience and problem. With the companions the Wizard works through a failed dualist argument (a brain is not a mind) for the Scarecrow, an abbreviated Stoic ataraxy pitch for the Tin Man, and Aristotle's discretion-is-valor point for the Lion, settling in each case on folk psychology plus a token (Th.D. diploma, heart-shaped clock, Legion of Courage medal) that supplies the recognition actually needed. Dorothy, whose desire for home is real rather than mistaken, gets no folk explanation from anybody: she must combine the heel-tapping instruction with her own articulated desire—'there's no place like home'—which the chapter treats as pragmatically, not logically, effective.
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 8 "Too Much Tequila, Or Not Quite Enough" — Doug Anderson reads Buffett as an 'American Stoic' — unlike his friend the Cynic Hunter S. Thompson, who dropped out and died, Buffett accepts his fated world of competitive capitalism and controls the one thing Stoics say we can: his own attitudes, 'changes in latitudes, changes in attitudes.' He leans on Seneca's advice to Serenus that wine and dreaming liberate the mind ('drink washes cares away') to interpret the dialectic of dreaming and drinking in 'Margaritaville,' 'Five o'Clock Somewhere,' and 'License to Chill' as Stoic self-renewal — the margarita even frees the singer to admit his own fault — with Emerson's intoxication-speaking poet as the American model. Excess is the failure mode: the expatriates of 'Banana Republics' who mistake the dream for an end state and Buffett's late-thirties hangover reckoning mark the Stoic middle path between deadening routine and 'too much tequila.'
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 13 "It’s Time for the Other Walkie-Talkie" — Dodge puts Monk on the case of friendship's nature, structured by Aristotle's three kinds from the Nicomachean Ethics: Hal Tucker's fake buddy act in 'Mr. Monk Makes a Friend' is pure utility, while Natalie's is virtue-friendship — she is his friend 'in spite of' the job since 'he doesn't pay her that much.' The friend as mirror and 'second self' grounds the claim that Stottlemeyer, Sharona, Natalie and Randy reflect Monk's excellence back to him, and Bacon's point that a friend redoubles joys and cuts griefs in half is shown when they stay up all night during his suicide watch. Seneca's Stoic counsel — judge a person long before admitting him, then hold nothing back — is exemplified by Natalie's fish-over-moon-rock test of Monk's character, while Montaigne's once-in-centuries friendship in which two selves blur fits only Trudy, whose dying words 'bread and butter' tell Monk they belong together. Plato's Lysis (the 'great cosmic swirly' Monk cites in 'Mr. Monk and the Bully') opens the puzzle Socrates could not solve, and the single walkie-talkie his father gave him shows why the chapter's verdict — Monk now has friends — matters.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 12 "Red Sox Fandom and Internal Harmony" — John McHugh uses his urge to confront Grady Little, who left a spent Pedro Martinez in during Game Seven of the 2003 ALCS, to ask how fans should govern the primal emotions fandom generates. Stoic self-command fails because Epictetus's advice (avoid caring about games entirely, focus only on what you control) would extinguish fandom itself, so McHugh adapts Adam Smith's impartial spectator: the virtuous fan imagines being watched by a sympathetic but emotionally distant fellow fan, settling on a Chicago Cubs fan who gets Bartman the way a Sox fan gets Buckner and Grady. He concludes that we each harbor a team of role-specific inner consciences, and the practical task is harmonizing the Red Sox-fan identity with our other identities rather than suppressing it or being consumed by it.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 5 "Fighting Talk" — The editors' introduction argues that philosophy and fighting have been companions since Socrates the soldier and Plato the wrestler (whose name means 'broad shouldered' from the gym), and that each can illuminate the other. It tours the volume through concrete cases: budo courtesy drawn from Shinto, Confucianism and Zen; the Shaolin monks' exercises as a route to Buddhahood; Western chivalry and Gordon Marino's boxing as educations in Aristotelian courage; fencing's egoism and value; and the Stoicism of karate and utilitarianism of Kano's judo. Philosophy clarifies fighting traditions, while fights supply puzzles for ethics, aesthetics, and the philosophy of mind.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 13 "An Enemy Lying in Ambush" — Fuller reads his teenage collapse while holding shiko dachi at his Eighth Kyu grading as a weakness of will, and argues that karate is Stoic discipline embodied. He explains the dichotomy of control through Epictetus's barbecue etiquette and the Kill Bill II buried-alive scene (only the Bride's years of disciplined training, not magic, break the coffin), then lays out living according to nature, Zeno's apatheia, Marcus Aurelius's Meditations, and Seneca's nightly self-examination as the model of askesis. Kata becomes 'a defiant stand against irrational emotion-chasing', and since only virtue is up to us, the enemy 'lying in ambush' is always internal: ourselves.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 30 "Time Enough to Drink the Poison" — Domino reads 'The Veiled Lodger' as a drama about hope in a world after God: Holmes's 'Your life is not your own; keep your hands off it' revives Plato's Phaedo argument that we are the gods' possessions, but deist-or-atheist Mrs. Ronder is unmoved, so Holmes falls back on the Leibnizian alternative to the Stoic and Cartesian 'patience without hope' — the example of patient suffering as 'the most precious of all lessons,' grounded in Leibniz's hope that the world is no 'cruel jest.' Jefferson Hope's two pill boxes in A Study in Scarlet literalize the Leibnizian link between hope and divine justice by letting God choose who dies, while Trelawney Hope's gullibility makes the surname ironic. Mrs. Ronder's true hope was reunion with Leonardo, which his death destroyed; what saves her is a new hope founded on Watson's text, since only a writer ('I have made a slight change of name and place') can change the past.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 13 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Curko and Greguric read Klosterman's glam-rock fandom as a problem of identity and masks: Nietzsche's Apollonian-Dionysian split casts Chuck as a self-controlled Apollonian writing about Dionysian excess in Guns N' Roses, Motley Crue, and Whitesnake, while Descartes's remark that actors wear masks to hide their shame introduces the tribute band Paradise City, a 'real copy' whose members would have no personalities left if they fully succeeded. The authors extend the mask question to Facebook and online avatars, where media saturation makes us 'copies without the original' and identity stops being self-same. They end by crowning Klosterman a modern Socrates of 'Know thyself' and a Stoic exemplar: admire your heroes like Satriani but do not steal their identities, control what you can (never your reputation or your time of death), and keep daring the endless search for self-knowledge.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 20 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Ashley Barkman argues that feminism is unrealistic and inefficient in the apocalypse: citing sex-difference research such as Bandura's Bobo doll experiments, she claims masculine aggression and strength are what leadership requires when authority must be asserted physically, as when Rick pipes Merle and shoves Daryl, or Shane tackles Ed and Jim. The quarry laundry scenes stage the debate - Jacqui's protest at 'all the Hattie McDaniel work' versus Lori's 'this isn't about women's rights... doing what needs to be done' - and Barkman sides with Lori, treating the division of labor as survival logistics under a natural-law premise that it is moral to act according to nature. Andrea the sharpshooter and Michonne the swordswoman show women can excel as heroic exceptions without leading, and the chapter concludes leadership should stay with good men like Rick.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 22 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Schwanebeck reads Nucky's fastidious grooming and Prohibition's purity crusade through the body politic metaphor: from Cicero and Seneca's De Clementia, where head and body of the state depend on each other, through Hobbes's bearded Leviathan frontispiece, to temperance propaganda that framed alcohol as poison entering the national bloodstream and wartime posters demanding 'a clean America.' The show exposes the purity ideal as illusion - the true purists are the Klan massacring Chalky's men and the hand-washing Van Alden shouting 'Let these waters wash you clean!' over Sebso's drowning body. Nucky rules less like Seneca's genuinely clement emperor than like Machiavelli's prince who merely appears virtuous, and the gangster genre's kingly tropes ('Et tu, Eli?') crown him head of Atlantic City's body politic.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 28 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Laderoute reads 'The Late Philip J. Fry' - the forward-only time machine overshooting past the year one billion and the last protons to a second Big Bang and an identical universe (ten feet lower, conveniently crushing its duplicates) - as a tour of cosmology from Aristotle's static, eternal, Earth-centered heavens through the Stoics' providential determinism and fiery ekpyrosis to Big Bang cosmology and heat death, which is why the Professor is so shocked. Nietzsche's Gay Science 341 supplies the existential payoff: faced with living identically forever, one can react with horror or delight, and eternal recurrence becomes a challenge to become the person you want to be. Fry, a billion years late for his Cavern on the Green dinner, reads Leela's message carved in stone, and in the repeated universe finally arrives on time - 'That was the old Fry... he's dead now' - amor fati enacted.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 16 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Billard concedes the Stoic point that we control neither our passions nor nature ('life will always find a way', Sattler's 'you never had control'), as the bucardo cloning failure shows, but argues this proves the park rushed, not that de-extinction is impossible. Dangerousness is subjective, raptor intelligence is a logistics problem rather than a metaphysical objection, and since humans have already caused the sixth mass extinction we may have a duty to bring species back. Because revived animals would be 'neo-dinosaurs' built from fragmentary DNA, de-extinction is creation rather than resurrection, less like playing God than like the transhumanist enhancement humans already practice.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 11 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Brendan Shea reads Cohen through the three Hellenistic schools. Socrates's trial in the Apology mirrors the persecuted singer of 'A Singer Must Die,' with 'Everybody Knows' and 'Democracy' voicing a Socratic mix of empathy and pessimism about whether democracy can deal rationally with its critics. Stoics such as Epictetus ground the present-focused, resigned acceptance of loss in 'Hey, That's No Way to Say Goodbye' and 'If It Be Your Will'; the Pyrrhonian skepticism of Sextus Empiricus illuminates the narrator's calming, unresolvable ignorance in 'Famous Blue Raincoat'; and the Epicurean atomism of Epicurus and Lucretius - death is nothing to us, empty desires are unsatisfiable - underlies 'A Thousand Kisses Deep.' Hypatia's murder and Cohen's 'Joan of Arc' close the chapter: the examined life is an all-consuming, sometimes fatal commitment that is nonetheless worthwhile.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 13 "Homeland and Philosophy" — John Karavitis evaluates four suicide events: Afsal Hamid's suicide in CIA custody, Aileen Morgan's cutting her throat with a lens, Brody's aborted suicide bombing, and Carrie's ECT as a 'suicide' of her old self. Kant's absolute ban on suicide (it denies your humanity) clashes with Seneca's Stoic counsel that a life of miserable captivity need not be continued, and with Singer's utilitarian permission of euthanasia that reduces suffering - under both, Hamid's and Aileen's suicides are defensible while Brody's emotionally driven bombing is not. Dana's plea that her father is needed recasts Aristotle's point that suicide wrongs the community, and Sloterdijk's analysis of rage turned on oneself frames Carrie's amoral self-destruction.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 34 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Re-examining 'The Enchiridion!' trial by trial - the gnome illusions, the ogre whose dollar Finn steals and then returns, the dark mage's brain world, the wallop given the Key-per in devil pajamas - the chapter argues Finn wins the hero's handbook without being righteous: he is brave, tender and ingenious, but gullible, hasty and violent, slaying whatever he is told is evil and running from the gnome test. Epictetus's Stoic Enchiridion supplies the standard the show's book lacks: only virtue matters, wealth, fame and comfort are indifferents, and a real handbook teaches how to lose, age and admit mistakes, not just how to win, which is exactly what Billy's quit-heroism shows Ooo's greatest hero never learned. Because bravery without good judgment could as easily serve a Nazi, a terrorist or the Lich, Finn's lack of practical wisdom means the 'most righteous hero' in Ooo is an impetuous boy - proof of how morally broken the Land of Ooo is.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 16 "4. On Being a Dead Person Who Hasn’t Died Yet" — Mark Ralkowski argues that Louis's 'dead people who haven't died yet' bit sounds like Marcus Aurelius, and that Dr. Bigelow's Season Four advice about back pain, the three-legged dog, and heartbreak works as the Stoic spiritual exercises Pierre Hadot described - above all the 'view from above' that re-describes things to strip them to their true value. Epictetus's dichotomy of control explains Bigelow's core advice: pain is not 'up to us' but our judgments about it are, so Louie should adjust his expectations to nature ('every second without back pain is a lucky second') instead of demanding a pain-free life. The apparently un-Stoic counsel to savor heartbreak ('misery is wasted on the miserable') is defended as genuinely Stoic: viewing his lost love from the perspective of a dead-person-who-hasn't-died-yet, Louie can accept sadness as precious and impermanent rather than being crushed by it. The chapter concedes Louis is no philosopher, but suggests his bits - contrasted with Seinfeld's 'polished' version on Talking Funny - can be read as newly discovered Meditations for comedy audiences.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 17 "5. Just Want a Shitty Body" — Bekka Williams argues that Louis's 'just want a shitty body' bit restates Epictetus's central Stoic teaching - want events to happen as they do happen, because only judgments, efforts, and desires are 'up to us' while bodies, reputations, and outcomes are not. She reads the Late Show arc (Tardigan's non-offer of the job, then Louie's triumphant 'Hey Letterman, I did it!' when Letterman stays) as Epictetus's cardplayer ideal: total effort on what is controllable, calm acceptance of what is not, alongside the bits about disgusting bodies, 'do the shit out of your job,' Jane and the mango pop, and Louis's self-trained habit of intercepting impulsive desires like the motorcycle urge. Like Epictetus, Louis is presented as a truth-teller who corrects mistaken impressions even when it is unpleasant, and the chapter uses him to rebut the charge that Stoicism means not caring.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 22 "10. How to Be Free" — O'Connell and Sirvent argue Seneca's Stoic freedom - release from fear of death and from every attachment - illuminates the two most enslaved groups in the story. The Unsullied's training strips them of possessions, names, lust, and fear, with Grey Worm's shame at fearing death for Missandei's sake showing exactly what attachment does to this freedom, while the Faceless Men's 'valar morghulis' mantra works like Seneca's recommended contemplation of death, letting Arya drink blindly from the cup at the House of Black and White. The chapter concludes that a fearlessness built by slaves and assassins really is a kind of freedom beyond their servitude, though Seneca would recoil at the brutal methods that produce it.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 14 "3. Can Charlie Brown Be Happy" — The chapter asks why Charlie Brown is unhappy despite being kind, active, and engaged, and answers with ancient virtue ethics: happiness is not winning or approval but ethical self-transformation, so his dependence on others' regard ('How did the other team feel?') is the real problem. It diagnoses him with Daniel Haybron's three dimensions of happiness - strong on engagement but lacking attunement (nervous, self-conscious) and endorsement (cheerlessness) - and asks why his shyness so irritates the gang. Epictetus's image of Socrates playing ball at his trial and Cicero's dancing analogy supply the Stoic remedy: losing costs no virtue, what he controls is being ethical, and how you play the game is everything.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 20 "10. Defying Fate" — Benjamin Evans reads Frank as fate's plaything, Tagomi's hydrogen-bomb gambit as an attempt to steer an uncontrollable web of events, and Hitler's claim that destiny belongs only to 'some men' as political exploitation of fate-talk. Stoicism (Zeno through Marcus Aurelius) explains Ed's serenity-prayer acceptance and the sinister Nazi version in which the 'natural order' means wolves eating sheep, but the chapter's verdict follows Adorno's studies of astrology and the occult: believing in fate seeds authoritarian submission, so Juliana letting Joe sail to Mexico — trusting her own judgment over the prophetic film — is the show's Adornian heroism.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 27 "15. Bias Is Rational!" — Percival, whose Myth of the Closed Mind Adams cites, rebuts the Moist Robot Hypothesis that visual, emotional, repetitive anchors make us ninety-percent irrational. Against Kahneman's fast-and-dumb System 1 he sets Gigerenzer's ecological rationality (the gaze-angle heuristic that catches fly balls, the recognition heuristic that lets ignorant German students beat Americans on Detroit versus Milwaukee), then goes further with Popper's critical rationalism: babies as little scientists conjecturing and refuting, experience always theory-laden (the duck-rabbit), and Newton's boy on the seashore facing an infinite but navigable ocean of error elimination. The Stoic insight that all emotion is thoughtful and all thought emotional (the falling-tiles misperception that flips anger to relief) shows feelings track beliefs, so a free battle of the biases, not fact-free affirmation in the lineage of Le Bon and Pavlovian conditioning, is how rationality actually works.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 28 "15. June the Stoic" — Lequien asks how June might endure Gilead and answers with Epictetus: like the slave-philosopher, she can locate freedom in what is 'up to her'—detaching from her body during the Ceremony ('What he is fucking is the lower part of my body'), relinquishing property, and learning not to call husband or daughter her own. He tests alternatives—Camus's question of suicide (the shatterproof glass), utilitarianism (the coerced 'We are very happy'), Tronto's care ethics (Gilead smothers the sorority that could make care meaningful), and the Particicution as a licensed Two Minutes Hate—before concluding that 'Nolite te bastardes carborundorum' functions as June's Stoic mantra: mastery of her own responses is the one victory the Sons of Jacob cannot take.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 33 "20.
