Getting Your Shit Together Stoic Style" — The chapter argues Rick is at his best an Epictetus-style Stoic: in 'A Rickle in Time' his total certainty keeps the split timelines perfectly synced, enacting 'choice alone is vice, choice alone is virtue'; his 'love is a chemical reaction... focus on science' speech in 'Rick Potion #9' treats passion as an impression outside the sphere of control; and his 'don't think about it' dismissal of the Hitler-cured-cancer reality applies the dichotomy of control to an unmasterable multiverse. Epictetus's model of hardship as training is vindicated by Cronenberged Jerry, whose struggle preserves his dignity in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption', and the chapter closes with the Stoic promise Rick's life shows: not pleasure but contentment.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 14 "5. A Replicant’s Guide to Becoming Human" — Justin Kitchen uses the Stoic 'cradle argument' — Chrysippus on self-preservation, echoed in Wallace's 'the first thought tends to fear, to preserve the clay' — to deny that replicant slavery is natural, noting Seneca's point that rage like Batty's derails reason. Mapping the Stoic process of oikeiosis through Hierocles's concentric circles onto the films, he traces four stages: the Nexus-6's fight for survival, Rachael identifying with Deckard in love, the Nexus-8s' revolutionary community under Freysa, and finally K, who disobeys Freysa's order and sacrifices himself for Deckard as a Stoic cosmopolitan, a fellow citizen of the world. Replicants can become human because they develop through the same expanding circles of concern.
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 30 "18. What Does It Mean if the Band Plays Forever" — Robert Grant Price treats KISS's repeated farewell tours — the 2000 Farewell Tour followed by twelve more tours, then the End of the Road Tour — as false endings that keep reshaping the band's story, running two counterfactuals: folding in 1982 would have made a tragedy of celebrity, quitting after the 2001 Farewell Tour a comedy of graceful closure, while the actual open-ended career risks farce. He then asks whether an aging rock star can be wise, contrasting Stoic virtue — Marcus Aurelius's Meditations on self-control and humility, the cardinal virtues of Prudence, Fortitude, Justice, and Temperance — with the hedonism and libertinism of rock's party ethos, from 'Uh! All Night' to Bernini's Ecstasy of St. Teresa. Knowing when to place an ending, he concludes, is ultimately the philosophical question of what one's life is for.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 34 "Sometimes We Can Let Go" — Sets P.F. Strawson's blame-as-moral-anger picture against the Seneca/Buddhist case that anger is revenge-hungry poison, then reads ATLA as modeling ways to hold people responsible without toxic anger. Katara may stay angry at Yon Rha after 'The Southern Raiders' yet forgo revenge because he is incorrigible and not worth it, while forgiving Zuko on Lucy Allais's 'wiping the slate clean' logic since his villainy no longer reflects his character. Iroh's 'I was never angry; I was afraid that you had lost your way' and his tea with the mugger Tycho show blame being skipped entirely in favor of compassion, and Zuko's shift from hypocritical self-blame to self-compassion after confronting Ozai lets him take responsibility without self-destructive rage.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 34 "Sometimes We Can Let Go" — Sets the intuition that angry blame is how we hold people responsible (Strawson; Katara's useful fury at Pakku's sexism, Iroh's 'whatever you do to that spirit, I will unleash on you tenfold') against the Senecan and Buddhist verdict that anger is greedy for revenge, and reads ATLA as modeling ways to hold people responsible without toxic anger. In 'The Southern Raiders' Katara neither forgives Yon Rha nor kills him, showing that blame can be set down when expressing it is pointless, while she forgives Zuko in Lucy Allais's 'wiping the slate clean' sense because his past betrayal no longer speaks to his present character. Iroh's handling of the mugger in Ba Sing Se ('I was never angry; I was afraid that you had lost your way') models responding to the suffering behind wrongdoing with compassion instead of blame, and Zuko's self-anger is diagnosed as hypocritical self-blame whose antidote is self-compassion: acknowledging how he himself was hurt is what finally lets him take ownership of his wrongs.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 16 "6. Keeping It under Control" — Mills reads Mr. Bates, the lame, twice-imprisoned, uncomplaining valet, as Downton's Epictetus, using him and the household to teach the Stoic dichotomy of control: only our judgments, desires, and actions are up to us, while jobs, reputations, and inheritances (Thomas's coveted valet post, Mary's scandal, Molesley's flower cup) are 'preferred indifferents' to be pursued without enslavement. Death figures as the great rejected indifferent, handled through Pamuk's demise and Mrs. Hughes's calm 'One day, I will die' upon finding a lump, as well as the grief of Isobel and Mary over Matthew. The closing section turns to Hierocles's concentric circles, with Sybil helping Gwen and Carson comforting Mary as drawing outsiders into the inner circle, a Stoic cosmopolitanism that Thomas, who sees the Crawleys as mere employers, fails entirely. The Dowager's 'I hope we're in control of something, if only ourselves' serves as the chapter's Stoic motto.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 13 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — George Dunn tests Katniss's luck-saturated life against Kant's claim that the good will shines 'like a jewel' regardless of fortune, with Peeta's vow to 'die as myself' as the stronghold the Gamemakers cannot touch, and with Seneca's dictum that what Fortune has not given she cannot take away. He then runs Nagel's four kinds of moral luck through the trilogy: Haymitch's reaping-made alcoholism as constitutive luck, Rue's death sparing Katniss an impossible final choice as circumstantial luck, Peeta's rooftop words echoing unconsciously behind the flowers for Rue as causal luck, and the revolution's success as resultant luck without which Katniss would have been the destroyer of District 12 rather than its torchbearer. Framing the Gamemakers as Fortuna on her wheel, he ends with the berries: since Katniss can never untangle whether she held them out from love, defiance, or self-protection, even moral worth proves hostage to luck and to the opacity of our own motives.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 20 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Abigail Myers runs Stoic doctrine against Katniss's biography: Zeno's thesis that only moral goodness is good (with Plutarch Heavensbee's renunciation of Capitol privilege as indifference to wealth and status), Seneca's 'On the Shortness of Life' against deferring living, Epictetus's dichotomy of control including the uncomfortable advice to kiss wife and child as mortals, and Marcus Aurelius's practical Meditations as the gentler 'Stoic for beginners' who would be president of Panem. Katniss comes out Stoic in her frugality, her mortality-shadowed appreciation of small joys, and her firm moral code, but decidedly un-Stoic in her fierce attachments to Rue, Peeta, and Prim. Yet her final choice of Peeta over Gale is itself Stoic, Myers argues: she forgives what Peeta's hijacking made him do since it was never in his control, refuses a noble friendship that would endorse Gale and Coin's slaughter of innocents, and chooses in accordance with nature and reason so as to survive as herself with her values intact.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 32 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Barkman reads the trilogy's Roman texture — panem et circenses, gladiatorial Games, tyrants named Coriolanus and Caesar — through the Stoic Seneca, who lived under Nero just as Katniss lives under Snow. Seneca's distinction between the good (virtue alone), the merely preferable (wealth, fame, power), and the bad (vice) explains the Capitol: Snow and Coin traded virtue for preferables and so became vicious, while the citizens' binge-and-purge luxury mirrors the Roman decadence Seneca condemned. The Hunger Games are the gladiatorial 'pure murder' that corrupts emperors, crowds, and tributes alike, and the districts are slaves whose liberation — like Katniss declaring 'I'm done killing their slaves' — is Seneca's freedom from slavery to fear and vice. Katniss and Peeta's self-sacrificial love and refusal to be changed exemplify the Stoic virtue the Capitol cannot take away.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 10 "1 Acting Without Thinking The Sagacity of Indiana Jones" — Justin Kitchen rebuts the consequentialist charge (voiced by Big Bang Theory's Amy Farrah Fowler) that Indy plays no role in Raiders' outcome — the Nazis would have opened the Ark and died anyway — by shifting to virtue ethics: Indy's goodness lies in his character, not his consequences. His spontaneous 'I'm making this up as I go' decisions are read as Stoic sage-like action flowing from the two-stage moral education depicted in The Young Indiana Jones Chronicles, from Krishnamurti's lesson on death to Epictetus's 'winter training' in practice. The cardinal virtues as knowledge explain his instinctive courage (lifeboat, lead-lined refrigerator) and temperance (running past treasure), while his snake panic, his flash of greed at the Grail in Crusade, and his strained bonds with Marion and his father show he is a hero approaching but not yet attaining sagehood.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 9 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Mussett asks whether Peter Parker's painful life counts as a good life by testing five philosophers' answers against the comics and films. Kurtz's secular humanism finds Peter wanting in pleasure and acclaim (Uncle Ben dead by his inaction, J. Jonah Jameson's smear campaigns), while Rand's Objectivism condemns Spider-Man as the embodiment of the 'morality of sacrifice' she rejected, noting Steve Ditko's Objectivist devotion. Epictetus scores Peter highly on duty but fails him on self-mastery, since his happiness hinges on attachments to Aunt May and MJ he cannot control; Frankl would see Peter's meaning in his irreplaceable responsibility, evidenced by his refusal of Dr. Judas Traveller's offer of a peaceful life at the cost of innocents (Amazing Spider-Man #402); and Aquinas vindicates Peter's suffering as good pain in a virtuous, charitable life.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 9 "Notes" — Hummel maps the Jedi Order onto Epictetus's Stoicism: philosophy as a way of life, virtue through wisdom, the dichotomy of control ('some things are up to us'), and treating outcomes like flying or other people's fates as preferred indifferents within the will of the Force. Anakin falls because he misconceives power as the ability to do amazing things - stopping people from dying - instead of mastery of his own judgments, and he refuses Stoic indifference toward Shmi and Padme. The chapter also indicts the Jedi's own un-Stoic lapses: mind tricks on Watto, entering the Clone Wars, and Mace Windu's attempt to execute a subdued Sidious.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 19 "Notes" — Taliaferro and Beck trace a philosophy of love through Anakin: fatherless, he attaches compulsively to Shmi and then Padme, refusing the Stoic limits on control that Yoda and Epictetus teach, so that love curdles into the vow to 'stop people from dying.' Vader's fatherhood is the caricature of love - offering Luke power instead of care - until Luke's compassion and Vader's final self-sacrifice redeem it. The lesson: love must be tempered by humility about what Zeno and the Stoics placed outside our control, and broken family bonds can be partly repaired through costly self-sacrifice.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 30 "Notes" — Quinn argues Rebecca is the show's Stoic: Marcus Aurelius's maxims about judgments, obstacles, and morning meetings with the ungrateful map onto her recovery from Rupert - accepting reality, forgiving as a choice within her control, the lion power pose, 'every disadvantage has its advantage' - with the dichotomy of control as her operating principle. Framed by Gen X self-reliance and second-wave feminism (Friedan's problem with no name, Beauvoir's woman as Other under Rupert), the chapter follows her from vengeful boss to mentor of Keeley and Nora, Bantr-era 'bossgirl' dater of Sam, and finally the Richmond family's matriarch.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 9 "Acknowledgment" — William Irwin diagnoses Neptune, from the 09-ers down to the PCH-ers, with status anxiety (via Alain de Botton's Status Anxiety) and prescribes the Stoic remedy: Epictetus on the insult lying in our judgment rather than the insulter, and Marcus Aurelius, the emperor who chose serenity over vengeance, show how Keith and Veronica ground self-worth in virtue no one can take away. Sartre's 'hell is other people' and the look explain how Veronica is reduced to a dumb blonde and Duncan to a murderer until he flees to Cuba, while Schopenhauer's choice between loneliness and vulgarity frames Mac's switched-at-birth longing, Wallace's basketball-bought status, and Weevil's self-made standing as PCH leader. Irwin closes by offering the show itself as Aristotelian catharsis-through-comedy, art as therapy for the viewer's own status anxiety.
- **Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test**, ch. 9 "H E N R I B E R G S O N" — Three Part Three essays on Dr. Manhattan's strange relation to time and fate. Christopher Drohan reads Manhattan's simultaneous 'intricately structured jewel' of time through Bergson's Matter and Memory — perception interlaced with memory, the pure past persisting in every act, time as lived duration — so that 'Nothing ever ends, Adrian' becomes a Bergsonian insight and the thermodynamic-miracle speech an intuition of life's creative improbability. Arthur Ward argues theological fatalism (Boethius and Aquinas placing a timeless God outside time, Paley's watchmaker behind Jon the watchmaker's son with his clock-shaped Martian palace) does not doom Laurie's free will, because Jon's own claims are inconsistent — he is surprised by the cancer rumors, misses Veidt's tachyon-shielded plan, and acts drugged — so either his foresight or his fatalism must be false. Andrew Terjesen reads Manhattan as a Stoic sage: Seneca and Epictetus on emotions as false judgments explain his 'a live body and a dead body contain the same number of particles,' his Mars epiphany is the sage's 'good emotion' of joy at the thermodynamic miracle, and his impersonal 'clock without a craftsman' completes a Neo-Stoic line running through Descartes to Spinoza's God-who-is-Nature.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 13 "Hardwood Dojos" — Bassham and Hamilton distill six success principles from coaches Smith, Pitino, Summitt, and Krzyzewski and show each echoes great philosophers, treating the court as a 'dojo' or place of enlightenment. Setting goals and pursuing excellence through habit map to Aristotle's eudaimonia and doctrine of habituation (Shaq the 'Big Aristotle' given the Nicomachean Ethics by Phil Jackson); the emphasis on outworking adversity and controlling only one's own effort maps to Stoics like Seneca, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius, as when Summitt and Dean Smith tell players to control what they can and accept the rest.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 18 "“They Don't Pay Nobody to Be Humble!” Football's Ego Problem" — Holowchak diagnoses football's ego problem—Keyshawn Johnson's deactivation, Terrell Owens's self-promotion, Deion Sanders's showboating—as fed by sensationalism (via Dewey) and statistical obsession that pull players out of the team framework. He proposes 'Aretism,' a modern progressivist ethics built on Stoic oikeiosis (Chrysippus, Cicero, Seneca, Epictetus and Hierokles's concentric circles) balancing self- and other-concern, and on Kant's injunction to treat others as ends. The virtuous athlete competes fully while respecting opponents, sport, and the 'moral zone' of Stoic sagacity.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 21 "Heroes of the Coliseum" — Reid draws an extended analogy between big-time college football players and Roman gladiators—both socially marginalized entertainers, controlled by coaches/editors and crowds, risking their bodies for others' entertainment. Through Roman Stoicism (Seneca, Epictetus, Cicero) she argues virtus does not depend on external wealth, status, or freedom but on accepting fate and excelling within one's role, so exploited athletes can still be genuine heroes of virtue. Following Marcus Aurelius's distaste for the games, she concludes those with power over players' unjust conditions are morally obliged to improve them.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 14 "Excuses, Excuses Inside the Mind of a Complainer" — Kevin Kinghorn, drawing on interviews with coach Brad Gilbert, dissects why tennis players and their parents complain and make excuses. He catalogs cognitive biases and the vividness effect (why a bad call, like McEnroe's 'You cannot be serious!' outburst, sticks and feels like persecution) as forms of irrationality, and notes Stoicism (which he attributes to Zeno) as a philosophy that would suppress the complaining temperament. His central mechanism is Freudian self-deception: citing Freud's hypnotized-umbrella subject who invents a reason for his own behavior, he argues tennis parents pretend their child is destined for greatness and then genuinely come to believe the lie, so excuse-making becomes a self-destructive sign a player will never be a champion. He also reads Andrea Jaeger's ambivalence about winning as evidence of mixed, partly unconscious motivations.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 17 "Love–Love A Fresh Start at Finding Value and Virtue in Tennis" — Tommy Valentini argues that because winning lies outside a player's control (he could never beat Nadal by simply choosing to), success in tennis should be redefined around what is controllable. Using Alasdair MacIntyre's After Virtue, he treats tennis as a MacIntyrean practice and distinguishes external goods (trophies, prize money, ranking—zero-sum, tied to winning) from internal goods (full effort, positive attitude, sportsmanship) that require the virtues of justice, honesty, and courage and are available to winner and loser alike. Drawing on Aristotelian justice ('giving each their due') and Randolph Feezell on the opponent as competitor-and-friend, he holds up Arthur Ashe's Stoic response to AIDS in Days of Grace as the exemplar of carrying tennis's internal goods into life in the face of an uncontrollable outcome, death.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 7 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Calhoun argues Eastwood's films move from solitary violent individualism (the Man with No Name, Dirty Harry) to what he calls 'post-Christian Stoic existentialism.' Using Epictetus's actor-in-a-play image and Marcus Aurelius on doing one's duty, he reads Butch Haynes in A Perfect World and William Munny in Unforgiven as figures 'dragged by the cart' of fate who nonetheless play their assigned role with dignity, while God is absent — Nietzsche's 'death of God.' Francesca's Stoic governance of impulse in Bridges of Madison County, Frankie's Kierkegaardian choice in Million Dollar Baby, and Walt's sacrificial community-building in Gran Torino show autonomous moral agency amid cultural collapse, with faint intimations of transcendence.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 19 "The Big Score Fate, Morality, and Meaningful Life in The Killing Steven M. Sanders" — Sanders reads Kubrick's heist film The Killing through Stoic and Aristotelian ethics, casting Johnny Clay (Sterling Hayden) as a 'stoical cool' figure whose surrender line 'What's the difference?' embodies apatheia, acceptance of fate. He argues Clay's doom (the burst suitcase, Nikki's fatal horseshoe) works as Kubrick's fate-driven moral verdict but strains Aristotle's principle that a truly prudent agent would not suddenly go to pieces. Weighing Aristotelian character-evaluation against Mill's outcome-based ethics, Sanders questions why Clay 'must' fail and treats his lack of self-critical rationality as the real obstacle to a meaningful life.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 17 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Murray and Schuler argue that Kubrick's unifying vision is a dogmatic skepticism - the 'banality of the good' - in which good characters (Dax, Alice, Alex's parents) are flat and helpless while the wicked have sass, and irony rules. Drawing on Hume's essay 'The Sceptic' and Marx's dissertation on Epicurus's swerving atom, they read Kubrick as a 'rebel without a cause' whose skeptical tropes of cosmic insignificance, present pleasure, and the veneer over the ape (Dr. Strangelove, The Killing, 2001, A Clockwork Orange, Eyes Wide Shut) accommodate rather than comprehend capitalist modernity. They contend Kubrick's Sartrean 'make your own meaning' answer is a false door, since projecting value either really transforms the world (refuting the claim it is indifferent) or projects nothing at all.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Sanders reads Kubrick's heist film The Killing through Stoic ethics, casting Johnny Clay (Sterling Hayden) as a member of the 'cult of the cool' whose reticence and final resigned 'What's the difference?' surrender embody apatheia and acceptance of fate/logos. He tests Spencer Selby's claim that Clay and the sharpshooter Nikki must fail because their motives are immoral, arguing instead via an Aristotelian principle (virtues are stable dispositions) that their sudden lapses—the flimsy suitcase, Nikki's racial slur that loses him the lucky horseshoe—are Kubrick stacking the deck rather than genuine character. He closes by weighing Clay's life against models of a meaningful life (exuberance/romanticism vs. rationalism/self-fulfillment), faulting Clay for never subjecting his chosen ends to self-critical reason.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 7 "“Do Not Forsake Me, Oh, My Darling” Loneliness and Solitude in Westerns" — Biderman argues that the western hero's solitude carries philosophical benefits, distinguishing being alone from feeling lonely (McCauley in Heat: 'I'm alone, I'm not lonely'). Epistemically he likens the silent, self-reliant hero (Kane in High Noon, Shane, Munny in Unforgiven, Blondie) to Descartes retreating into methodological doubt and solipsistic solitude to secure knowledge. Ethically he sets Aristotle's claim that man is a social animal (so the friendless hero cannot flourish) against Stoic detachment and Sartrean/existentialist authenticity, concluding the hero must be 'lone' because his heroism is inseparable from his chosen solitude.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 14 "6. The Morality of Mike’s Manifesto" — The Gibsons analyze Mike Ehrmantraut's code—'if you make a deal with somebody, you keep your word'—through virtue ethics and Stoicism. Aristotle's function argument and Golden Mean partly vindicate Mike's counsel toward temperance and restraint (not carrying a gun, sparing the Salamanca driver), yet Aristotle's claim that 'bad people are full of regrets' marks him as a flawed 'wicked' man given his inner turmoil over breaking his son. They read his calm as Stoic (Marcus Aurelius's Meditations on controlling the mind, Spartan simplicity), and weigh Kant's intent-based defense of his killing the dirty cops Hoffman and Fensky against Mill's social-rule view of sanctionable wrongs.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 14 "5. Friendship, Fun, Freedom, Food, and the Future" — Le Gall and Taliaferro read Bourdain's Libya and Iran episodes of Parts Unknown through Pierre Hadot's 'philosophy as a way of life,' arguing that Gaddafi and Khomeini were failed Platonic philosopher-kings. They interpret ordinary Libyans and Iranians eating Uncle Kentucky chicken, playing pinball, or hosting feasts as popular 'spiritual exercises' — tatonnement — showing how the personal becomes political and how friendship, fun, freedom, and food nourish the Socratic care of the soul.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 21 "11. The One Truly Serious Philosophical Problem" — Doll surveys philosophical views on suicide to make sense of Bourdain's death, opening with Camus's claim that suicide is the one serious philosophical problem. She weighs Plato's Phaedo prohibition (we are the gods' possessions) against his allowance for extreme misfortune, Aristotle's view that suicide violates one's duty to self and community, and Seneca's Stoic position that a wise man 'lives as long as he ought, not as long as he can' — framing Bourdain's death as an autonomous choice.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 25 "MOTHERHOOD" — Jen Baker interrogates why unmedicated 'natural' childbirth is treated as morally superior, dissecting five senses of 'natural' and rejecting each, including a social-Darwinist appeal to evolution she deems dangerous. She engages Montaigne (via Cicero) on philosophizing as learning to die and cites Dylan Thomas and Neil Young on facing pain soberly, then turns to the Stoics' claim that pain 'is nothing to us' – arguing from a neo-Aristotelian/Stoic virtue ethics that pain has no moral value and that keeping one's wits with an epidural can preserve moral agency, so natural birth is an 'optional and amoral' thrill, not a virtue; she frames it with Bill Cosby's and Carol Burnett's labor jokes.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 16 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Gregory and Tod Bassham argue Stoicism is the seaman's philosophy of agency, teaching a clear-eyed grasp of what we can control, influence, or not control at all. Using Epictetus's play metaphor and 'you will fetter my leg but not my will,' Seneca and Marcus Aurelius on fear, they map three techniques onto sailing: cheerful resignation (Gerry Spiess righting Yankee Girl, Shackleton's James Caird crew laughing amid the Southern Ocean), self-sufficiency (splicing lines, emotional independence on a cramped boat), and negative visualization / premeditatio malorum (practicing docking under sail, imagining lost rudders). Skip Allen scuttling Wildflower and Dinelli's endurance illustrate the trichotomy of control and freedom of mind.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 18 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Taliaferro and Le Gall's 'The Great Escape' weighs four philosophical objections to cannabis-induced altered states — falsehood (Plato's ban on poetry/theatre in the Republic), distortion of reason (Euripides' Bacchae, James on nitrous oxide), undermining of agency (the Sirens, De Quincey's opium), and loss of self-determination (the Stoic Epictetus on freedom) — then surveys Jewish, Christian and Islamic treatments of wine, coffee and hashish. They rebut the objections using Aristotle's cathartic defense of theatre and Locke's imagination-based account of freedom, concluding that if cannabis is no worse than wine the philosophical and religious case against it is not decisive.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 12 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Kevin Krein argues that the freedom climbers report feeling is not freedom of movement, political freedom, or free will—on those measures a roped climber pinned on a ledge is less free—but the Stoic freedom of aligning one's will with what nature allows. Using Chrysippus' tethered-dog image and the Stoic identification of human logos with cosmic reason, he claims the climber who understands and accepts the mountain's conditions and wills only what it permits becomes free, which is why experienced climbers feel freest when their options are fewest. He adds Epictetus' dichotomy of control: the mountain (storms, avalanches, one's own failing body) is largely outside our power, so limiting desire to what we control—composure, choices, effort—is how a climber stays free in any conditions.
- **Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low**, ch. 22 "BLUES" — Brian Domino frames a choice between the reasoned Stoic life and the emotional life through the Rolling Stones and the blues. He presents Epictetus's Stoicism — apatheia, the dichotomy of control, and the Enchiridion's 'it was given back' — applied to blues themes of floods, death, and cheating women ('When the Levee Breaks,' Robert Johnson's 'Terraplane Blues'), arguing emotions stem from false beliefs and akrasia. Against this he sets 'Jumping Jack Flash,' 'Monkey Man,' and '(I Can't Get No) Satisfaction' as celebrations of raw emotional existence, invoking Plato's tension of reason and passion and Nietzsche's image of the 'music-making Socrates' to leave the choice deliberately unresolved.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 5 "3. Star Trek as Philosophy Spock as Stoic Sage" — Pigliucci argues that Gene Roddenberry built an implicit argument for Stoicism into Star Trek's Spock, contra both the 'suppressed emotion / stiff upper lip' caricature and Farren's claim that Kirk is the truer Stoic. Reading Spock's talk of 'emotion' as the disruptive pathe and his 'logic' as the broad Stoic study of reason, he shows Spock embodying the dichotomy of control ('my legs, they're broken'), the four cardinal virtues, and Stoic cosmopolitanism aboard the Enterprise. Drawing on Brouwer's account of the sage, he tracks Spock's development from prokopton toward sagehood, cultivating eupatheiai like love and friendship (the Wrath of Khan sacrifice) and declaring 'logic is the beginning of wisdom, not the end.'
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 27 "25. The Mandalorian as Philosophy “This Is the Way”" — The chapter argues that The Mandalorian defends virtue ethics with care as the primary virtue. It maps Mando's creed and 'Canons of Honor' (strength, honor, loyalty, death) onto Stoicism's discipline of desire and cardinal virtues, quoting Marcus Aurelius and Seneca, and reads his transformation after adopting Grogu as Aristotelian moral development toward eudaimonia and flourishing. Using Stocker's critique of impartialist ethics and Noddings's and Slote's ethics of care, Belluomini argues Mando's caring relation with Grogu, his engrossment and motivational displacement, and his removing his helmet at the end show that care ranks highest among the virtues and should guide our own 'Way.'
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 38 "35. Star Wars as Philosophy A Genealogy of the Force" — Eberl builds a genealogy of the Force across the Skywalker saga, using Augustine to reject the Manichaean light/dark dualism Yoda voices ('Luminous beings are we') in favor of evil as a privation of good and as 'inordinate desire' for temporal goods, which explains Anakin's fall through his refusal to let Padme die. He casts Palpatine as a Nietzschean who declares 'good is a point of view' and pursues will to power and the ubermensch, contrasting this with the Stoicism of Seneca and Yoda ('train yourself to let go of everything you fear to lose'). The sequel trilogy's disenchanted galaxy is read through Charles Taylor, and Rey and Ben's redemption shows evil defeated not by hatred but by rightly-ordered love ('Saving what we love').
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 66 "62. Hannah Gadsby as Philosopher Is Comedy Really Such a Good Thing" — The chapter treats Hannah Gadsby's Nanette as philosophical comedy, weighing her four reasons for quitting: self-deprecation is humiliation for the marginalized, jokes' setup-punchline structure cannot heal trauma, comic relief lets audiences off the hook, and anger only spreads hatred. It distinguishes self-lacerating from ethical, existential, and ironic self-deprecation, and contrasts Critchley's Freudian neo-Stoic humor (super-ego viewing the ego as trivial, akin to Epictetus and cognitive therapy) with the Willetts' feminist 'collective catharsis.' Against Gadsby's claim that anger cannot be constructive, it sets Nussbaum's Anger and Forgiveness alongside Lorde and Srinivasan to argue anger can recover agency and register injustice, and defends Nanette as genuine comedy and 'stand-up catharsis.'

### Walden (deliberate living)

Walden records Henry David Thoreau's experiment in deliberate living, undertaken during his two years in a cabin by Walden Pond, where he sought to strip life to its essentials and confront what it had to teach. His aim was to live simply and consciously—reducing needs, observing nature closely, and resisting the distractions of a commercial society—so as to discover what is truly necessary for a meaningful existence. The book blends memoir, natural observation, and social criticism into a sustained argument for self-examined, intentional life.

- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 16 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Gregory Bassham distills six keys to happiness from Tolkien's hobbits and elves: delight in simple pleasures (Epicurus on natural pleasures, Thoreau's Walden simplicity), making light of troubles (Sam's star above Mordor, with Marcus Aurelius and Augustine on courage and hope), friendship (Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics read against Sam, Merry, and Pippin refusing to let Frodo go alone), good character, beauty and creativity (Lothlórien versus Mordor, 'flow'), and wonder (Tom Bombadil, Frodo's 'recovery' of fresh vision at Cerin Amroth). He argues Tolkien thereby becomes a philosophical guide, pointing from the Shire and Rivendell to a richer, more joy-filled life.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 11 "Poker and Philosophy" — Ventimiglia mines No-Limit Hold'em for seven lessons philosophers also teach: we lack certain knowledge (Descartes' cogito is the famous quest for certainty, but philosophy's own history of disagreement proves uncertainty is the human condition), and like William James against Clifford we must still believe and act without the nuts — waiting for pocket aces while the blinds eat you alive is no strategy. Risking everything echoes Thoreau's escape from lives of quiet desperation, trusting hunches over arithmetic follows Thoreau and Peirce's sentimentalism, and the Darwin-and-Spencer competition of tournament poker hides a deeper cooperative social contract: get caught cheating and you are out of the game. It closes with Plato's four classic virtues from the Republic — wisdom, courage, moderation, and the justice of a balanced soul — as the perfection of a poker player.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 15 "Let Your Heart Be the Anchor and the Beat of Your Own Song" — Berti reads Neil Peart's 1997-98 catastrophes (his daughter's car accident, his wife's cancer death) and the 55,000-mile Ghost Rider motorcycle exile through Sartrean existentialism: existence precedes essence, so with no God-given script Peart must author his own reactions, exactly as Sartre's student had to choose between mother and Resistance. The chapter tracks alienation ('I do not know who I am'), the duty to choose rather than lean on outside voices, and 'The Pass' as the voice telling a suicidal teenager to walk back from the razor's edge. Thoreau's Walden retreat supplies the model for the healing road, and Peart's own directives ('keep moving; kick your own ass, gently') enact 'Freewill' and 'Something for Nothing': we are the ones who choose, and the choice to live made all that followed (re-marriage, Vapor Trails, five more tours) possible.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 6 "UNSC Briefing" — Fred Van Lente's introduction argues that Master Chief is deliberately an empty shell—faceless, ageless, mostly silent—so the player's identity grafted onto him brings both to life at once in Halo: Combat Evolved's opening cryo-wakeup tutorial. He frames the book with Thoreau's Walden claim that philosophy is living simplicity, mapping it onto the Chief's ascetic soldier existence, and on Socrates: a game worth playing is worth examining, since the unexamined game is not worth playing. He closes with Aristotle's potentiality and actuality: the game actualizes the Chief as a kicker of alien ass, and the book actualizes the series' social and philosophical potential.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 22 "Friends—Don’t Leave Home without ’Em" — Greg Ahrenhoerster places SpongeBob in literary history between Transcendentalism and naturalism: 'Nature Pants' is a failed Walden — SpongeBob gives away his possessions for Jellyfish Fields but his 'jellyfish instincts' fail as badly as self-reliance in London's 'To Build a Fire' — while 'Squidville' shows the industrial city's cold indifference as in Crane's Maggie. 'Jellyfish Hunter' warns that trying to exploit nature (Krabs's jelly factory) invites nature's reprisal, since civilized beings without instinct are at nature's mercy. The naturalist moral, against Transcendentalist solitude, is that we survive only through each other: visit Jellyfish Fields, but bring a friend.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 178 "Chapter 31 - “Piper in the Woods”" — David Svolba hunts the 'distinct new idea' of 'Piper in the Woods': able-bodied garrison men on Asteroid Y-3 claim to have become plants so they can abandon jobs in a machine where 'the men are parts, and each has his job' - a radical but understandable response to lives devoted to meaningless, alienated labor whose ends they no longer identify with. Reading the story with Thoreau's warning that in a technological world we become 'tools of our tools', and likening the defectors to Timothy Leary's drop-outs, it presents Dick's tacit approval of the sun-basking plant-people as social criticism of a dehumanizing techno-industrial order that sees resistance only as laziness. The darker suggestion is that such a form of life is strangely hard to resist: escape collapses into self-imposed dehumanization, making the story perhaps a parable of drug-like escapism.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 12 "a4.xhtml" — Bronson argues that walking is a philosophical practice against modern placelessness (Giddens' 'phantasmagoric' locality): Thorin survived Smaug's attack because as a youth he 'was a good adventurous lad, always on the move', and Tolkien's wise figures - slow, flower-stopping Tolkien himself, Gandalf who 'went to look ahead' and was brought back 'by looking behind', Bilbo's silent walking, Beorn's bear-travels - all practice attentive movement through place. He backs this with Montaigne's retirement to his tower and bringing thoughts back to the orchard, Thoreau's woods-walking that must be spiritual as well as physical, the Tao Te Ching's 'good travelers leave no tracks' and Zhuangzi's wandering virtues, and Buddhist walking meditation from the Buddha's wandering monks to Thich Nhat Hanh's peace steps.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 15 "The Industrious Sherlock Holmes" — Bassham diagnoses Holmes as a workaholic against clinical criteria (obsessive work, few relationships, perfectionism, health neglect through fasting and cocaine), then traces the rise of the Protestant work ethic (Calvin, Weber, Carlyle) and its modern decline. Drawing on Thoreau's Walden critique of 'lives of quiet desperation,' Pieper on leisure, and the 'affluenza' literature, he distinguishes pathological from benign workaholism by warning signs and by motivation. He concludes Holmes is a pathological workaholic in his symptoms but redeemed by his noble, non-materialistic motive of fighting crime and achieving justice.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 14 "5 Neil Young Lover of Sun, Moon and Cars" — Anderson traces Young's environmentalism from the hippie-romantic nature worship of "After the Gold Rush" and Greendale toward a pragmatic "middle way" that reconciles his love of nature with his love of cars and recording technology (the Lincvolt project, Storytone). Drawing on Thoreau, Muir and Leopold's land ethic while rejecting the fixed prescriptions of Singer and Regan, he presents Young as an experimentalist "meliorist" who owns his own complicity in CO2 abuse and urges informed, practical, self-aware action rather than utopian or deontological solutions.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 18 "9 Neil Young’s Search for the Simple Life" — Watson and Riches reinterpret "A Man Needs a Maid" not as simple misogyny but as Young's ambivalent inner conflict between craving companionship and fearing the pain of intimacy. They read his pursuit of the "simple life" ("Heart of Gold," avoidance of reading) through Epicurean simplicity, Aristotle's eudaimonia, Bowlby/Freudian avoidant attachment and cognitive dissonance, and Sartre's "bad faith" as self-deception, set against Thoreau's chosen solitude and Aristotle's claim that the non-social being is "beast or god."

### The Unconscious

The unconscious is the cornerstone of Sigmund Freud's psychoanalysis: a region of the mind holding thoughts, memories, and desires that are hidden from awareness yet powerfully shape feeling and behavior. Freud held that many such contents are actively repressed because they are threatening or unacceptable, and that they resurface in disguised form through dreams, slips of the tongue, symptoms, and jokes. Interpreting these expressions was, for him, the route to understanding neurosis and the self. The claim that we are not transparent to ourselves—that much mental life is inaccessible to introspection—has been enormously influential and much contested.

- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 15 "Fast Zombies" — K. Silem Mohammad explains the horror of zombie slowness through Freud's uncanny - the return of the repressed, from White Zombie's hypnotized slaves (a figure for alienated industrial labor) to Romero's shuffling radioactive ghouls - then rebuilds undeath on Spinoza's Ethics: death as a body's parts acquiring a different proportion of motion and rest, the mind as a 'spiritual automaton,' and (via Deleuze's ethology of composition, decomposition, and bad encounters) zombies as bodies that decompose living bodies and recompose them as zombie bodies, replacing moral good and evil with good and bad. The fast zombies of 28 Days Later and the Dawn remake abandon hunger and the uncanny for pure rage and 'the Real,' signaling a late-capitalist permanent crisis in which the living have had their chance and blown it.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 28 "The Meta-Fear of Fear" — Noel Carroll traces Halloween's Undead imagery to the Celtic Samhain and its Catholic absorption into All Hallows' Eve, then asks the paradox: why do we take pleasure in images of the death that, as Heidegger says, is the deep source of Angst we spend our lives denying? He examines Ernest Jones's Freudian analysis - the vampire as wish-fulfillment disguising an incestuous desire, horror as the price the super-ego exacts - and rejects it as theoretically expensive, invoking the demand for simpler, more economical explanation. His own hypothesis is the 'meta-fear of fear': adolescent viewers (and aging ones) use horror films and the holiday's zombie costumes to test and master fear itself, with parody and Bergson's laughter as companion devices of emotional control - a folk remedy that needs no unconscious to work.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 35 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Cynthia Coe argues the novel's horror lies in the creature's liminality: he is neither human nor inhuman, and Victor's instant labeling of him as 'monster,' 'demon,' and 'fiend' shields Victor from his own responsibility, since the word 'monster' descends from a sign or omen we mistake for the evil itself. Freud's uncanny - the heimlich turning unheimlich, the repressed coming to light - explains why a being 'more horrid from its very resemblance' to us terrifies more than an obvious alien, a mechanism the chapter parallels with European anti-Semitism as hatred of an internal enemy. Shelley's moral point is that failures of empathy are moral failures: Victor holds the creature responsible as a free-willed demon while denying him personhood, and the tragedy grows from that contradictory projection until the neat categories of victim, monster, and evil collapse.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 26 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Paweł Dobrosielski and Marcin Napiórkowski read Flowers for Hitler as Cohen's answer to Adorno's dictum that to write poetry after Auschwitz is barbaric - Cohen writes poetry that self-consciously knows it comes after the end of poetry. Using Freud's distinction between the vocabulary and grammar of dreams, they show the collection is assembled from a small repertoire of recurring images (ovens, ashes, telephones, radios, green grass, Nazi names) whose awkward normality expresses repression: life goes on as if nothing had happened. Arendt's banality of evil, born of the Eichmann trial, is directly alluded to in 'All There Is to Know about Adolf Eichmann,' and the book ends by universalizing Holocaust memory - the poet waking with a number on his forearm, feeling like victim and perpetrator alike - until the grass itself is grown on ashes and every flower is a flower for Hitler.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 27 "Girls and Philosophy" — Fisher explains the show's cycle - the girls want someone only while that person rejects them - through psychoanalytic theories of desire. Freud supplies the id/ego/superego machinery (cocaine-era Hannah dancing to 'I Don't Care (I Love It)' as pure id; Dunham's body-critical audience as the superego), while Lacan's desire - the 'untold' that must be named (Hannah's bedroom kink questions to Eric), drive, and jouissance beyond the pleasure principle - shows desire circling its object and never being satisfied, as when Hannah's e-book deal collapses into her worst OCD episode. Žižek's objet a as the object-cause of desire reads Marnie loving Charlie only once he is over her: desire reproduces itself rather than reaching its goal.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 26 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Framing the 'Frost & Fire' episode as an imagined storyboard meeting, the chapter asks whether Finn's erotic dream of Flame Princess is a Freudian wish-fulfillment rising from his subconscious after he deliberately lies to provoke the Ice King-Flame Princess fight so the dream will return. Via Foucault's Care of the Self, it introduces Artemidorus's method of reading dreams for the real and moral consequences they portend, suggesting Finn's dream already warns him that his deception will cost him the relationship, with the Cosmic Owl whispering that he 'screwed up'. The writers conclude that sleeping and waking lives bleed into each other, and that Finn's refusal to read the warning leaves him burned: broken hearts, a torched Ice Kingdom, and the princess gone.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 30 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Pötzsch reads Dracula through Freud's Civilization and Its Discontents: the Count fascinates because he lives out the aggression and sexual freedom civilization forces us to renounce, embodying the innate hostility in Freud's 'man is the wolf to man.' Freud's account - group power replacing individual might, 'love thy neighbor' as an impossible demand, the super-ego as an inner Van Helsing breeding guilt over forbidden impulses, with the id and ego mediating - is mapped onto Jonathan's 'wicked, burning desire' for the vampire women. The upshot: we resent culture because we traded happiness for security, yet living like Dracula would get our throats cut.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 14 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Daniel Leonard takes CharDee MacDennis, the Gang's three-level drinking game, as an unconscious confession read through Freud's structural model. The 'Mind' level - grudge trivia like 'Denis is asshole. Why Charlie hate?' and drawing-guessing 'based solely on feel' - runs on the id and the pleasure principle; the 'Body' level of darts, kennels, and the no-cursing rule is restraint, properly the ego's job of deferring gratification (which only Dennis's manipulative D.E.N.N.I.S. System grotesquely exercises); and the 'Spirit' level of Emotional Battery and Public Humiliation externalizes the superego's guilt and ego-ideal, with Frank as the all-seeing punishing father. The Gang's psychology is backwards - their 'Mind' level tests exactly what is not conscious - and their over-strong superegos surface in rationalization and the Black Card's coin flip, while smashing the losers' idealized game pieces enacts a wishful symbolic patricide.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 13 "4. How Possible Is the Impossible Girl" — Smith asks how one Clara can exist as Oswin the converted Dalek, a Victorian governess, and a present-day nanny, and answers with philosophy of mind: after the real Clara steps into the Doctor's timeline on Trenzalore, the 'echoes' are best understood as manifestations within the Doctor's own subconscious, read through Freud's dream interpretation and id-ego-superego (the echoes act as his conscience) and Jung's archetypes, collective unconscious, individuation, and synchronicity—her name meaning clarity, her red wardrobe marking the copies, and the leaf of 'The Rings of Akhaten' as the meaningful coincidence that produced her. Aristotle's Categories frames what Oswin still shares with humanity after Dalek conversion, and the soufflé-is-the-recipe line together with social-cognition research on multiple selves supports the conclusion that the Claras are metaphysically the same person despite different bodies and roles—making the 'Impossible Girl' possible.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 36 "21. Forgetting Is the Human Superpower" — Seymour reads the War-through-Eleventh Doctors through Freud's notion of Afterwardness (Nachtraeglichkeit) from Studies on Hysteria - memory is continually reforged as new information recontextualizes the past - so that learning Gallifrey was saved in 'The Day of the Doctor' changes not the Doctor but his memories of himself, turning penance into hope. She traces each Self constructed from Time War memory: Nine's guilt exploited by the Gelth and voiced in 'Boom Town' ('Only a killer would know that'), Ten's hubris once he forgets what he is capable of ('Time Lord Victorious' in 'The Waters of Mars'), and Eleven's danger when the memory fades and companions must remind him who he is ('A Town Called Mercy'). The chapter concludes the Doctor must keep the memory of his regret to keep being the Doctor - Clara's 'What you've always done. Be a doctor.'
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 25 "13. Topophilia; or, How We Got Hooked on Downton" — Elvis reads the show's opening credits shot by shot - Isis on the lawn, the opening shutter, the servant bell, the letter rack, the watched pot, the measured table setting, the falling rose petal, the lamplight, the feather duster - to explain our addiction to Downton through Bachelard's The Poetics of Space. Topophilia (love of place), daydream, and the unconscious mind's bank of unnoticed experience make the intimate small spaces of the credits invitations to feel at home in the Abbey, while Deleuze's 'haptic' explains how vision and sound trigger touch-like immersion. The show's improbable global appeal, she concludes, lies not in pompous grandeur but in small intimate moments that bring viewers home.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 32 "18. Doctor, Heal Thyself" — McClelland argues Lecter is a flawed healer: reading Starling's FBI disgrace as social exclusion, he shows how Lecter's hypnotic drugs and deep-hypnosis 'treatment' let her revisit and metabolize her repressed rage at her dead father — the parental imago he named back in Silence of the Lambs — producing a chrysalis-like metamorphosis completed when she defies Krendler at the dinner and asks for more of his brains. The healing is symmetric, since Starling's insight into Lecter's own Mischa fixation releases him too, and the chapter closes with an Aristotelian verdict — choice reveals character, and whether the couple's Buenos Aires partnership counts as good depends on long-term flourishing we have not yet seen.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 35 "16. The Truth about the Walkers" — Kempner reads the show's serial bait-and-switch over the walkers' origin - Jenner's failed CDC, Eugene's exposed lie on the road to Washington - as an enactment of Deleuze and Guattari's multiplicity against "the reduction to the ONE." Their anti-Oedipal attack on Freud, who fixed the Wolfman's dream to a single castrating father, mirrors how characters who hunt one knowable cause (Rick's hope of CDC rescue, Hershel's barn of curable walkers, Abraham's mission) are punished with death, while Michonne survives precisely by accepting walkers as an irreducible pack rather than something to be understood. The chapter concludes the series should never explain the walkers: multiple causes and small-t truths replace any single Truth, which is why relief never arrives and survival means living with unknowability.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 41 "23. Louis C.K. Meets the Unconscious" — Reads the 'of course, but maybe' bit as a wrestling match between Lacan's big Other—society's unwritten rule book of queues, taboos, and approval—and the Freudian unconscious that betrays itself in the therapist's 'the climax results in the death of the woman' slip and other parapraxes. Jokes then work as sublimation and a release valve: Louis's nut-allergy and slavery bits ('you all clapped for dead kids... you don't get to cherry-pick') let audiences laugh at their disavowed 'I know very well, but...' contradictions, though comedy remains confession without absolution.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 28 "15. Joffrey on the Couch" — Wills asks why audiences so relish hating Joffrey and answers with Freud's Totem and Taboo: the incest taboo was instituted precisely because the desire persists in the unconscious, and Joffrey - the product of 'accumulative incest' with cousin-grandparents and sibling parents - embodies the broken taboo. Reading the furious fan reactions (his death 'wasn't horrible enough,' the meticulous lists of his worst acts) as projection and successful repression, the chapter argues that vilifying Joffrey channels our own repressed taboo-breaking urges, while Westeros's distanced past setting lets us dissociate from the savagery exactly as Freud's staging of primitive peoples did.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 41 "26. Why We Love to Watch Deadpool . . . Play with Himself" — Using the Deadpool video game, the chapter argues Wade is a god who is all-powerful (rewriting the game world with his crayon-scrawled script and manufacturing fake credits), all-knowing (reading the player's mind through the fourth wall and literally entering Rogue's), and plainly not all-good (slapping an unconscious Wolverine, ogling dead Vertigo, ignoring Apocalypse three times for a billion dollars), so that dystheism - belief in a god with serious issues - dissolves the problem of evil. The free-will defense collapses because Deadpool wrote the script the villains obey, giving players only the illusion of choice. The voices in Wade's head are explicitly cast as Freud's structural model, with his Ego and SuperEgo talking while WadePrime, the Id, does most of the voice-work.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 27 "16. Would You Buy a Used Car from This Avenger" — Ericson uses the used-car litmus test to examine trust in the MCU: through McLeod's three criteria and Peperzak's contrast of the objectifying and interactive approaches, Tony's control-seeking distance (the lone-gun-slinger act of Iron Man 2) fails trust while Steve's soldier-style trust anchors the Winter Soldier thriller against Fury's 'This isn't freedom, this is fear' and HYDRA's coercion-eliminating project. Plato's rule that power should go only to those who do not want it explains why Cap can be entrusted with superpowers, Nietzsche's megalomaniac late letters frame Tony's drive to 'cleave history in two' by building Ultron and then the messianic Vision, and Banner's Hulk illustrates the Freudian road from repression to sublimation as the condition of self-trust. It ends with Cap's concealment of Bucky's killing of Tony's parents as the betrayal of trust that only a decision to forgive might repair.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 20 "9. 24 7 Newsleep" — Buchanan argues the Party 'sleep-hacks' its citizens because sleep is an active state of thought, a lineage he traces from Aristotle's theory of dreaming through Freud's Interpretation of Dreams, and is therefore a site of potential resistance that must be colonized. Between the Physical Jerks, telescreen trumpet-calls, a Thought Police able to inspect anyone 'asleep or awake' without warning, and O'Brien's manipulation of Winston's sleep schedule during torture, Winston is trapped in 'Newsleep', a derealized blur of dream and reality that makes doublethink the only available way of thinking. He extends the diagnosis to our own 24/7 economy of phones and Trump's all-hours tweets, concluding that Orwell's warning is that we must guard our sleep.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 16 "7. Amy Schumer or the Incongruities" — Pits Freud's psychoanalytic theory of wit, where harmless nonsense smuggles tendentious sexual content past the superego's censor, against the incongruity theory of comic amusement, using 'Boner Doctor' as the test case. Carroll argues the psychoanalytic account makes the superego absurdly gullible, citing Foucault on how thoroughly sexuality is now discussed, and cannot capture what is specific to Schumer. Incongruity theory can: sketches like 'Sexting' and Trainwreck's doll analogy for infidelity generate laughter from violated norms of ladylike decorum, exposing her feminism as a sustained subversion of the modest, uninterested stereotype of womanhood.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 10 "2. Where Is the Twilight Zone" — Scalambrino argues the Twilight Zone is a televised expression of Breton's surrealism, starting from Descartes: the cogito and the mind–body problem made reason the measure of the 'clear and distinct,' and surrealism seeks to unbind the imagination from exactly that rational leash. He reads 'A World of His Own' as surrealist automatic writing, 'The Mirror' as Dalí's paranoiac-critical method, and Freud's psychoanalysis as both allied with and (following Adorno's diagnosis of the movement's death) too restrictive for surrealism's project. Episodes like 'Shadow Play' (a man who dreams the world), 'The Shelter,' 'The Lonely,' and 'A Stop at Willoughby' provoke the uncanny — the strangely familiar — in viewers, which is where the Zone is located.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 11 "2. Echoes of Past and Present" — Crippen and Dixon treat the album Echo, written during Petty's divorce, heroin use and severe depression, as organized by crisis and reversion: its lyrics and productions compulsively echo earlier eras of his life, from 1950s TV westerns and his abusive father in "About to Give Out" to the Jeff Lynne years and Wildflowers in "Accused of Love" and "Echo." They invoke Freud and Lacan's psychoanalytic account of trauma repetition, where the past is relived in hope of a different outcome and sublimated into art. The album's sparse, energy-conserving repetition is then read through Nietzsche's will-to-power cycle, in which merely holding on is symptomatic of illness, yet the closing "One More Day, One More Night" and the album's very creation exemplify Nietzschean health as strength to expand against obstacles, since we possess art lest we perish of the truth.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 11 "2. Mesmeric Mister Rogers" — Marlene Clark argues Fred Rogers was a mesmerist in the lineage of Franz Mesmer's animal magnetism, a hypnotic appeal that survived mesmerism's debunking by passing into Freud and Breuer's psychoanalytic transference and into the primitive, unconscious sex appeal of screen idols like Brad Pitt. She details episode 1588, where Rogers defuses bathtub-drain fears with 'You Can Never Go Down the Drain' and scuba-suited Neighbor Aber frightens Henrietta Pussycat, and the 1969 Senate hearing where reciting 'What Do You Do with the Mad That You Feel?' visibly entranced Senator Pastore into awarding PBS 20 million dollars.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 26 "15. Life Is a Laugh and Death Is a Joke" — Jarno Hietalahti applies the three classic theories of humor to Endgame: incongruity theory explains trickster Loki, 'an epitome or embodiment of humor' who cheats death and escapes with the Tesseract; Hobbes's superiority theory from Leviathan, laughter as 'sudden glory' at others' weakness (extended by Gruner's game of humor with winners and losers), explains Thanos's self-satisfied smirks as he shrugs off the heroes' combined assault and snaps half of life away; and Freud's relief theory, in which jokes express the unconscious and release inner tension, explains fat Thor's terror-ridden laughter as escape from his failure, grief, and lost control. The chapter concludes that humor is neither good nor bad in itself but part of a worldview, and that death as the horizon giving life meaning is precisely what makes laughter possible for beings like us and like the superheroes.
- **Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney**, ch. 21 "11. When Is a Lawyer Not a Lawyer" — Karavitis argues Mason is secretly two other professionals: a historian and a psychoanalyst. Following Plato's Theaetetus definition of knowledge as justified true belief and the correspondence and coherence theories of truth, he shows Mason iteratively reconstructing the recent past from facts to theory to revised theory, refusing Hamilton Burger's circumstantial first stories and hunting the motive that is history's 'why' (H. Stuart Hughes's psychohistorical method), exactly what historians do; then, via Freud's defense mechanisms, he reads the recurring courtroom confession as an 'abreaction' in which the murderer, confronted with lie and truth at once, breaks down on the stand, and Mason's own total absorption in murder cases (no private life in 271 episodes) as sublimation of something repressed.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 11 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Runs the Bluths through Freudian psychoanalysis: George Sr. hiding in the attic ('Sad Sack', 'Good Grief!') illustrates the unconscious, preconscious, and repression; Michael acts as ego mediating the family's id demands (the unfrozen stock spree) against George Michael's super-ego; Tobias dressing as a pirate among homosexuals and Michael's 'brother...bother' and 'Egg' slips are parapraxes betraying repressed desire; Buster's Motherboy dates and 'Why I Want to Marry My Mother' enact a failed Oedipus complex; and the brothers' scheme against George Sr. in 'Making a Stand' reenacts the primal horde of Totem and Taboo, origin of the incest taboo that haunts George Michael and Maeby.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 11 "The Avatar Unparalleled Opportunities" — Cuddy argues the gamer's bond with the avatar is an extension of the ego: Freud's id/ego/superego model explains why playing a Cylon Raider or flying the 'Bastille Day' mission lets gamers reconcile unconscious desires with the superego's demands in ways reality forbids. But when we lose we disconnect from the avatar and blame the game or 'cheating' opponents, which Sartre diagnoses as bad faith, a denial of freedom, contrasted with Adama's 'a man takes responsibility for his actions' in '33' and Baltar's vacillation over the vice-presidency. Through facticity (the unforgiving no-save 2003 game) and existence preceding essence, the chapter concludes that videogames offer unparalleled opportunities to practice Sartrean responsibility and achieve Freudian reconciliation through the right avatar.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 24 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Hunt treats the film as a direct view of a single subject's unconscious, Freud-style: the Dude is the pre-Oedipal narcissist, the Big Lebowski the father toppled from his wheelchair-throne after the confrontation, Maude the mother, with a scattered superego distributed across the Stranger's moralizing and the Malibu sheriff's 'Stay out of Malibu!'. Donny and Walter figure oral and anal fixations, Jesus the threatening playground peer, and Bunny and the nihilists Freud's life and death drives — so Donny's death in the parking-lot melee lets the ego fuse death-drive energy into life, and the Dude's walk-away from the little Lebowski back to bowling and White Russians reads as repression into comfortable pre-Oedipal phantasy.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 33 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Griffioen distinguishes two kinds of truthiness: believing what one prefers to be true (motivated epistemic irrationality) and justifying beliefs by gut feeling, using Colbert's premiere clips about Bush knowing Harriet Miers's heart and feeling that taking out Saddam was right. She models the first as wishful thinking and self-deception via a Samantha Bee/Jason Jones marital-fidelity example, works through the static and dynamic paradoxes of self-deception, rejects the Freudian divided-mind solution (imagined as Colbert debating himself in 'Formidable Opponent'), and defends an attention-directing account instead. Gut feelings justify only when they implicitly track facts, yielding her proposed fallacy argumentum Colberti ad ventrem.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 8 "Legal and Not So Legal Forms of Inception" — Brogaard argues the film's inception method is more science than fiction, starting from the neuroscience of dreaming: against Hobson's activation-synthesis model (and Dennett's related wake-up narrative theory, both heirs to Freud's symbol-based dream interpretation), she cites evidence that dreams arise from dopamine-driven cortical motivation areas rather than the brain stem, so streamlined, plot-driven shared dreams cannot be ruled out. Savants like Tammet and Padgett show the brain can compute super-fast below awareness, which makes sense of the film's dream-time compression. She then speculates real mechanisms for the heist — LaBerge's lucid-dream masks, transcranial magnetic stimulation plus an artificial corpus callosum to tap a subject's right hemisphere — and treats Cobb's planting of 'my father doesn't want me to be him' in Fischer as achievable today by cruder means like mind control and fear conditioning.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 17 "Do We Give Shakespeare the Last Word" — Kapper treats Inception as a hip epistemological puzzle — unlike The Matrix, the question is not what is real but how we could know — and follows Ariadne's thread (her mythological clue-giving names the chapter) through the tradition: Plato's Theaetetus and Descartes's supremely cunning deceiver pose 'Am I dreaming now?', Wittgenstein shows the doubt is senseless since 'if I am dreaming, this remark is being dreamed as well', Freud makes dreams the royal road to the unconscious, and Heraclitus says only the waking share a common cosmos. The payoff is Eastern: Zhuangzi's butterfly, Indra's net of mutually reflected jewels, and Schopenhauer's single-dreamer universe turn waking up into an endless regress, so the Buddhist ideal of the awakened one — nirvana, where the ideas of real and dream cease to pertain — becomes the reading of Cobb turning away from the top.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 18 "Day Residue" — Auxier reverse-engineers how Nolan's dream-sharing could work — sedatives aligning brainwaves like a laser, the electrical dream machine, nested electromagnetic fields — and argues each deeper level buys time at the cost of lucidity, with Limbo as 'psychosis of forgetting.' He explains the film through Susanne Langer's theory of mythic consciousness: dreams become communicable only when forced into narrative order, so dream architecture is the insertion of images that survive transformation into the subject's dispositions — hence Eames plants the pinwheel in the safe so Fischer believes he placed it himself, and the Mombasa elders represent a collective, pre-modern consciousness modern individuals have lost. The resolution of the baggage-claim puzzle (Fischer's calm) is that the inception removed a doubt rather than planting one: doubt spreads easily in modern minds, and Fischer touched the ancestral place where 'our fathers desire our happiness.'
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 27 "Epilog" — Nicolas Floury reads the entire film as the single dream of a neurotic subject — Cobb asleep on the plane, every character assembled from fellow passengers and airport figures — in which he works through the Lacanian conflict where the neurotic 'does not desire what he wants and does not want what he actually desires': Cobb wants to keep living with Mal ('In my dreams we are still together') while wishing to complete her mourning. The dream levels are reinterpreted as stages of Freudian dream-work: level 1 ruled by desire, level 2 where the counter-desire and Ariadne-as-double intervene, the snow fortress war as the internal battle climaxing when Cobb shoots Mal, and the limbos as melancholic self-enclosure — 'a life without desire, a life under the seal of death.' Cobb's final choice of a 'steady desire' completes the mourning: Piaf's 'Non, je ne regrette rien' marks his renunciation and serves as the wake-up signal, father-figure Miles embodies the life instinct telling him to 'come back to reality,' and the still-spinning top is Mal's expelled beloved object, set where it can no longer block his return to life.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 30 "Dreams and Nightmares" — Valentin Husson reads Inception through Heidegger's account of poetic dwelling: to dwell is to build, and because the dream 'creates and perceives the world simultaneously,' every dreamer is a poet whose dwelling springs from an ungrounded origin — Freud's unconscious producing dreams as 'the (concealed) fulfillment of a (repressed) desire,' Lacan's unconscious 'marked by a blank,' and the Mystery from which, per Heidegger's essays on art and dwelling and Mallarmé's poetics, all creation comes. The dream's twofold building — Ariadne's durable architecture plus the subject's ceaseless populating of it — explains why extractors stay safe only while the dreamer unknowingly keeps creating, and why Cobb forbids building dreams from memory rather than 'out of nothing.' Cobb's guilt turns his dreams into nightmares, 'the reign of the uninhabitable,' until Ariadne, like her mythic thread leading Theseus from the labyrinth, guides him out of Limbo so dwelling becomes possible again — the film as a modern Odyssey in which 'man dwells poetically,' with the viewer suspended over the top already taken in by the Mystery.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 24 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Sets up Sons of Anarchy as a Hamlet retelling — Jax the prince, Clay the Claudius who murdered John Teller and married Gemma, Tara a gutsier Ophelia — and reads it through Freud and Ernest Jones's Hamlet and Oedipus: Jax's protest that he 'untwisted my mommy thing a long time ago,' his toleration of Gemma's meddling, and the Season 4/5 finale tableaux where Gemma displaces Tara at his side betray an unresolved Oedipus complex. Freud's three agencies get bodies: Clay as pure Id (beating Gemma in 'Hands'), Tara as Superego, Jax as the mediating Ego, with SAMCRO itself a collective Id worshipped in its 'chapel.' Oral and anal-stage fixations explain the Sons' chain-smoking, recklessness, and defiance of authority, while the Id's civil war between libido and the death drive plays out in Gemma's post-beating sex binge and Jax's unconscious pleasure in killing.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 7 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Young argues that South Park is perceived as dangerous for exactly the reasons Socrates was tried and executed in Plato's Apology: both 'corrupt the youth' by mocking religion, questioning authority, and exposing that the supposed teachers (Mr. Garrison's flip-flopping creationism, Mrs. Broflovski's moral panics, the 'Death' boycott of Terrance and Phillip) do not know what they think they know. He diagnoses Cartman as an Eichmann figure whose banal, thoughtless evil—feeding Scott Tenorman his parents, torturing Muslims with farts—consists in the inability to think from another's standpoint, while Kyle and Stan's friendship embodies Arendt's dialogic thinking and Aristotle's mean between ideological extremes, as when they see both the merit and the smugness of hybrid drivers in 'Smug Alert'. Freud's theory that jokes break through repression explains why the show's vulgarity is essential rather than gratuitous: it verbalizes what culture silences so that it can be thought through, making South Park a Socratic gadfly rather than a corrupter.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 28 "“An Energy Field Created by All Living Things”" — Baur argues that the Jedi metaphysics is non-dualistic rather than a simple good-versus-evil opposition, reading the Force through Spinoza: ideas become more or less true as they cohere with other ideas (so 'Luke loves Leia', 'Han is a mercenary', and 'Vader is evil' all need qualification), and everything seeks power by the conatus that Yoda and Obi-Wan attribute to the Force. The light side seeks power in balance with other things while the dark side, per the Sith Rule of Two, plays a zero-sum game. Luke's arc mirrors Oedipus: denying his inherited psychological likeness to Vader only enacts it, and only by acknowledging and owning the anger he inherited from his father can he gain power over it and enable Vader's redemption and his own.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 19 "NOTES" — Hirschbein presents True Blood as a Freudian fable: vampires live the unrepressed id's Eros and Thanatos that civilization forces the rest of us to renounce, which is why they defeat all three sources of suffering (mortal bodies, nature, hostile neighbors) and why the show's convulsive sex and violence thrill us. Glamouring reproduces the posthypnotic suggestion that proved the unconscious to Freud, Sookie's mind-reading confirms his dark discoveries about our sexualized aggression, vampire myths work as projection screens for desires we disown, and Marcuse's complaint about 'genital tyranny' and sublimation frames Sookie's love as a near-realization of Freud's St. Francis ideal.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 25 "Notes" — Reads the Cohle–Hart pairing through Lacan: Cohle is at peace with the constitutive lack introduced after the mirror stage, and his hysteric's fixation on the Other's desire is what makes him the superior interrogator, while Hart exhibits obsessional neurosis and 'interpassivity,' letting the preacher's congregation do his believing for him. Following Deleuze's Oedipal structure of detective fiction and Hegel's point that heroes are denied guilt, the chapter compares Rust to Oedipus — both men who, after a child's death, renounce the father function through anti-natalism — while arguing Cohle surpasses Oedipus by philosophically mastering the knowledge that Oedipus lacked. Rust's tying off of his 'circle of violence' is read as the Lacanian sinthome: putting his symptom to work in the service of the case rather than being destroyed by it.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 10 "2. Where Is the Twilight Zone" — Scalambrino reads the Zone as a televised expression of surrealist philosophy: Breton's sought 'point of the mind' where life and death, real and imagined cease to be contradictions, realized in episodes like 'A World of His Own' (automatic writing) and 'The Mirror' (Dali's paranoiac-critical method). Descartes's cogito and the mind-body dualism supply the rational 'leash' that surrealism unbinds, questioned by 'Shadow Play,' where a man insists the world is his dream. Following Adorno's verdict that psychoanalytic interpretation killed official surrealism, he argues the show endures by provoking the uncanny ('The Shelter,' 'The Lonely,' 'A Stop at Willoughby') without being pinned to Freudian readings.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 14 "Excuses, Excuses Inside the Mind of a Complainer" — Kevin Kinghorn, drawing on interviews with coach Brad Gilbert, dissects why tennis players and their parents complain and make excuses. He catalogs cognitive biases and the vividness effect (why a bad call, like McEnroe's 'You cannot be serious!' outburst, sticks and feels like persecution) as forms of irrationality, and notes Stoicism (which he attributes to Zeno) as a philosophy that would suppress the complaining temperament. His central mechanism is Freudian self-deception: citing Freud's hypnotized-umbrella subject who invents a reason for his own behavior, he argues tennis parents pretend their child is destined for greatness and then genuinely come to believe the lie, so excuse-making becomes a self-destructive sign a player will never be a champion. He also reads Andrea Jaeger's ambivalence about winning as evidence of mixed, partly unconscious motivations.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Gilmore reads Unforgiven as Socratic wisdom done in images — the recognition that we do not know what we really want.
