- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 23 "The Loneliness of the Goalkeeper (Again)" — Winters celebrates the goalkeeper's fingertip save—Gordon Banks denying Pelé's header in 1970—as football's aesthetic summit, reading the keeper as the lonely, 'stark mad' outsider of existentialist fiction, a lineage he anchors in Camus, the goalkeeper of Algiers who said all he knew of morality he learnt from football. Kant supplies both the dove of the first Critique—needing the air's resistance, just as the tango's strict steps enable the dancer's personality—and the target of critique: against Kantian disinterested contemplation, he adopts Graham's Nietzschean, Dionysiac aesthetics of participation, so spectators proprioceptively feel the keeper twisting in mid-air, as Wittgenstein's question about the galloping horse picture suggests the movement enters our muscles and joints. Understanding a save or a back-heel means seeing it under a general type ('that' free kick, 'that' volley, from Beckham at Wembley back to Garrincha), and Bloch's ruminations in Handke's The Goalie's Anxiety at the Penalty Kick show the keeper alone at the liminal limit where concession and prevention meet.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 23 "Living Beauty" — Saltzman explains why a flowing Shaolin Kenpo form is beautiful by way of Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy: the Apollonian geometry of square, triangle and circle fuses with Dionysian power and intention, just as yang hardness needs yin softness. She grounds the body's fitness for this in the Golden Ratio known to Pythagoras, answers 'beauty is in the eye of the beholder' with Clive Bell's 'significant form' as an objective structure that trained judges can recognize, and locates 'living beauty' in the practitioner's own breakthrough, the moment when, as Nietzsche and Yeats agree, the dancer and the dance dissolve into pure mindless movement.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 20 "A Single, Perfect Sphere" — Reads Rush's 'Hemispheres' as a correction to Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness: Apollo's gifts of reason leave the people joyless, Dionysus's release into passion leaves them starving in winter, and Cygnus is made god of Balance because human nature thinks and feels at once. Against Descartes's two substances and the 'Robots Plus' picture, the author argues feeling is not supernatural icing on a machine but how survival-minded organisms stay in phenomenal contact with the world, so physicalism needs deepening rather than a nonphysical mind.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 174 "Chapter 22 - Frenzy" — Opens Randall Auxier's chapter with the 2011 Vancouver Stanley Cup riot and its viral kissing-couple photograph to pose the driving question: why do built-up group emotion, sex and violence fuse so explosively, and why does that fusion in public still "get yourself in trouble with the Man"? The contrast is pointed: the laid-back West Coast crowd "right across the Bay from hippie central" couldn't get through a 1969 Stones concert without violence and death — "It's just a shot away, you know?"
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 175 "Please Allow Me to Introduce Myself" — Confesses that Brian Jones — violent and cruel even in Keith Richards's autobiography, with no kind words from Mick and Charlie on the fortieth anniversary of his death — is for Auxier the face of the Sixties' negative energy and the figure "laughing with delight" in Don McLean's "American Pie" verse on Altamont. The section sets up the whole chapter as a meditation on "what gets sacrificed on the altar of rock'n'roll, when the Dionysian frenzy turns ugly."
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 176 "The Nature of My Game" — Distinguishes the individual craziness of a Brian Jones (and perhaps Meredith Hunter waving his pistol at Altamont) from the crowd frenzy that takes over when the Stones play, quoting Richards's Life memories of girls who "lost themselves" — "beyond what they wanted to be... You stood as much chance in a fucking river full of piranhas." Richards says "the music might be the trigger, but the bullet, nobody knows what that is"; Auxier argues the Stones deliberately crafted personae and performances that tap a deep human susceptibility to frenzy, and goes hunting for the bullet.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 177 "Reading the Riot Act" — Reads Stones-concert riots — the Wisbech Corn Exchange brawl Richards recounts in Life — against the British Riot Act of 1714 and the purely aesthetic riot at the pagan ballet The Rite of Spring in 1913, noting conventional crowds forgive a sports brawl more readily than a Stones tragedy. In every such release of mass emotion there is a moment when "all order has disappeared and we come face to face with... whatever it is 'we' are without that imposed order," leaving nothing for memory to hang on — and the chapter insists the scary tone of violence formed around the Stones in a way it never did around Beatlemania.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 179 "Gimme that Old Time Religion" — Carries the frenzy back to the Eleusinian Mysteries and the Dionysian festivals that were falling into ill repute by Plato's day: Socrates himself was an initiate, and Plato wrote on how eros makes humans "mad with passion," whitewashed his teacher in the Symposium, and claimed Socrates never got drunk. Plato also held that certain kinds of music ignite desire and lead to weakness and "effeminacy," associating manliness with rational self-restraint and advocating banning such modes — in short, "no Stones concert allowed in Plato's city."
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 183 "Use All Your Well-learned Politesse" — Sets Johann Jakob Bachofen's ruined-reputation matriarchy hypothesis (and Marija Gimbutas's "civilization of the goddess") against patriarchal control, finding the division alive in the male insecurity displayed whenever men prance for girls — Elvis, the Beatles and the Stones alike. Bachofen's young friend Friedrich Nietzsche named the two energies: Apollonian regimentation and order versus Dionysian overflow, "the accursed share," and the chapter reads the 1960s as one more Dionysian break-out that the "heavy-handed, patriarchal Cold War" could not bottle up.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 184 "Mother’s Little Helpers" — Introduces the Cambridge scholar Jane Ellen Harrison, whose books trace Greek religion from a swampy matriarchy to the Olympian age, with Dionysus as the holy child of the Mother — flayed and divided among the faithful — the very pattern Christianity retold in the Jesus story. Auxier credits Jagger's "keen intellect" and wide sense of history, then endorses Nietzsche's complaint that Christianity is "a puny, slave morality" that renders humanity effeminate: "That's exactly what I like about Christianity," since over-weaning masculinity needs opposing.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 185 "Won’t You Guess My Name" — Riffs on Harrison's Themis to cast Mick as Kouros, the golden boy served by the Kouretes — "the original name of the Rolling Stones" — until he surfaces as Dionysus among the Olympians, "sort of like the irony of Mick Jagger becoming a Knight of the Realm." It splits the males into orgy-tolerant girly-men and woman-hating "manly men" of the Sour Grapes Clubs, warns not to underestimate the girly-men, and contrasts Elvis, who went into the army and became acceptable, with Mick, who kept the Kouretes under his thumb — deliberately feminine, dangerous, and cooler than the Beatles.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 186 "“They’re So Ugly It’s Appealing”" — Takes the screaming fan's verdict ("They're so ugly it's appealing") and Ian Stewart's sidelining for looking "like a man" as evidence the Stones deliberately cultivated an androgynous ugliness to violate gendered expectations — "they weren't just a bunch of guys who bent the rules, they were off-sides." The blatant misogyny of the lyrics is read as compensation for that effeminacy among the Dionysian libation bearers in a patriarchal age, keeping the manly men at arm's length — while noting only Brian Jones actually abused women.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 187 "Pleased to Meet You" — Blames "the Father of All Pissing Contests" — the Cold War — for forcing English boys who love women into songs hostile to them ("Under My Thumb," "Stupid Girl," "Yesterday's Papers"), and argues two theses: the Stones don't hate women, this culture hates women; and the men who call the goddess's servants "fags" are the ones who built and maintain that misogynistic culture. The Dionysian frenzy of the 1960s took a dark turn as 1968's death toll (Vietnam, MLK, RFK) exposed the world the manly men had built: the Beatles quit, "but the Stones looked the demon square in the eye and guessed its name."
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 188 "From Woodstock to Altamont" — Crowns the Stones' prophetic 1969 tour, ending at Altamont, as "the genuine Dionysian frenzy" that ended the Sixties — Woodstock being merely "a glorious and well-deserved vacation from the bullshit" — and reads Brian Jones's death as his own choosing, empires falling "for about the same reasons." Auxier recalls his father taking him to Gimme Shelter in Memphis, the movie that permanently formed his refusal of the patriarchy, and advises parents to make a friend of Mick Jagger, since "Dionysus will have his day" and will take his accursed share of your kids sooner or later.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 13 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Curko and Greguric read Klosterman's glam-rock fandom as a problem of identity and masks: Nietzsche's Apollonian-Dionysian split casts Chuck as a self-controlled Apollonian writing about Dionysian excess in Guns N' Roses, Motley Crue, and Whitesnake, while Descartes's remark that actors wear masks to hide their shame introduces the tribute band Paradise City, a 'real copy' whose members would have no personalities left if they fully succeeded. The authors extend the mask question to Facebook and online avatars, where media saturation makes us 'copies without the original' and identity stops being self-same. They end by crowning Klosterman a modern Socrates of 'Know thyself' and a Stoic exemplar: admire your heroes like Satriani but do not steal their identities, control what you can (never your reputation or your time of death), and keep daring the endless search for self-knowledge.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 30 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Brittingham argues The Wire is a Nietzschean rather than merely Aristotelian tragedy, a wrestling between the Apollonian orientation of order, statistics, and illusion (Rawls's clearance rates, Burrell's bureaucracy, Stringer's business plans) and the Dionysian reveling in the Game's chaos and suffering (Avon accepting that 'you only gotta fuck up once', McNulty's intoxicated self-destruction). Stringer is Nietzsche's 'theoretical man' whose faith that thought can correct existence, embodied in the New Day Co-Op, cannot save him from Omar's 'It ain't about money', while McNulty is the Dionysiac man inside the Apollonian institution until Freamon's 'the job will not save you' forces his resignation. The chapter closes by reading the characters' resigned embrace of their fates as Nietzschean affirmation: since neither the job, intelligence, violence, nor the gods will save you, the only response is to say yes to life anyway.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 18 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Edward Winters answers his sister's question - why listen to such depressing music - through Lorca's duende, the 'black sounds' of deep song that, as Nick Cave says, every true love song must contain. He argues duende resists definition yet is recognizable in Cohen, and connects it to Nietzsche's Dionysian art of participation (war dances, anthems, 'Dance Me to the End of Love') as against Kant's disinterested aesthetic distance, so music can re-enchant a disenchanted world. Via Kant's account of artistic genius and Cohen's testimony that Lorca and six flamenco chords gave him his voice, Winters concludes Cohen's dark, honest beauty has duende - which is why it lifts and tears at the heart rather than depressing.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 27 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Martyn Jones stages a fictional Nietzsche telling Mac, Dennis, and Charlie the plot of 'The Gang Solves the Gas Crisis' as a parable of metaphysics gone wrong. Mac and Dennis's scheming is Apollonian - imposing logical order and 'paradigms' on a recalcitrant world - while Charlie is Dionysian, the designated wildcard whose uncontainable energy (sabotaging the van and ripping out the brakes) dooms every plan that tries to harness him, since Apollonian schemes fatally imagine they can contain Dionysian force. Reason is a gloss, not a truth-tracker: like every theology and philosophy it is an expression of will, a survival tool serving selfish ends, so the delusional gas scheme needs no truth to serve its purpose. Charlie alone is praised as a proto-Übermensch - innocent, creative, founding his own values without resentment - and the tale closes musing that even an eternal recurrence of their botched schemes might be willed all over again.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 9 "1. Where Have All the Supermen Gone" — Holdier argues that neither hero is Nietzsche's Übermensch: Superman's servile mild-mannered Clark Kent guise would strike Nietzsche as slave morality, while Batman's self-loathing (his Hush confession that deep down he is not a good person) and breakable human body disqualify him too. Instead, reading them through The Birth of Tragedy and Grant Morrison's Supergods, Superman embodies the Apollonian force of order, sunlight, and rationality and Batman the Dionysian force of chaos and passion, so their battles (The Dark Knight Returns, Batman v Superman) are the inevitable but never-final friction of art's twin poles. The fight's real winner is the reader, who gets both deities at once.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 33 "21. Batman Is Superman" — The chapter argues that Bale's Batman, not the alien Superman, is Nietzsche's Übermensch: a mortal whose identity is forged in the unreconciled struggle between Dionysian emotion and Apollonian reason - vengeance against justice in Batman Begins - and who relives his traumas as Nietzschean eternal recurrence, from the bat-filled well to the prison leap of The Dark Knight Rises. The Joker is his dark double, whose will to power and ferry-boat experiment nearly extinguish Gotham's hope, but Batman absorbs the chaos and sacrifices his heroic name, whereas Superman in Injustice, losing Lois, falls into a vengeful Dionysian abyss he cannot master. Only a mortal who extends his limits without succumbing to the herd's 'gravity of madness' can be Nietzsche's superman, so the mortal, conflicted, imitable Batman is the true superman.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 17 "5. Rhapsody on a Theme by Schroeder" — The chapter argues Schroeder's monomaniacal devotion to his toy piano and Beethoven is a Nietzschean way of life: he refuses the herd's path and the self-denying 'priestly' values of ordinary childhood, and treats music as the highest creative force, as The Birth of Tragedy claims. Nietzsche's demon of eternal recurrence becomes a test Schroeder passes - he lives for this life and could will its exact repetition - while Schopenhauer backs the claim that music discloses the world's inner nature as language cannot, and the Christmas-dance scene shows the communal fusion Nietzsche heard in song and dance. Strips about Lucy on the piano, his 'grown accustomed to that face' shock when she moves away, and the Beethoven's-birthday holiday cast Lucy as his unsuspecting muse; but as a would-be Ubermensch he must go beyond playing Beethoven and create his own compositions.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 9 "1. I Stand Up Next to a Mountain" — Reads Hendrix as Joseph Campbell's hero on the monomyth of separation, initiation, and return: the mother's death and gypsy prophecy of 'Voodoo Chile' stage the separation, the Venus witch's ring the initiation, and the transcending guitar solo the return, with Prometheus as the type of the fire-bringer punished by promoters, Little Richard, and audiences demanding the hits. Through Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy it casts the Monterey guitar-burning and the Dionysian intensity of the Experience as tragic art whose hero 'shoulders the whole Dionysiac world for us,' and closes with Aristotle's Politics on catharsis — 'Machine Gun''s sonic battle imagery as purgation that transforms violence into a cry for peace.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 13 "4. Tom Petty and the Meaning of Life" — Innes reads Petty through The Birth of Tragedy: Petty fuses Dionysian frenzy (the Oakland Coliseum "Makin' Some Noise" crowd as communal creation) with Apollonian form, and his refusal of genres, synthesizers and the hit-factory gives life the creative meaning Nietzsche demands. Jeff Lynne and ELO are cast as the contemporary Wagner, Socratic and Apollonian producers of pleasant ditties like "Don't Bring Me Down" that lack access to tragedy. Petty's "Trailer" models Greek tragedy (impulse as hamartia foreclosing freedom), while his lawsuits against MCA and The Last DJ dramatize the tragic bind that free musical expression needs the very industry that restrains it.
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 25 "14. The Joyful Relativity of Kondoms and Kaskets" — Casey Rentmeester reads KISS through Nietzsche and Mikhail Bakhtin. The music — 'Rock and Roll All Nite,' 'Love Gun,' and the Alive! spectacle of blood-spitting, fire-breathing personas — embodies Nietzsche's Dionysian, the raw instinctual side that Socratic rationalism suppressed, with concerts supplying the Dionysian fusion of the crowd. The band's transformations into the Demon and Starchild (which Gene and Paul describe as real, not acted), the face-painted audiences, and the taboo-breaking merchandise — KISS Kondoms that helped destigmatize condoms, the KISS Kasket that turned death into celebration as at Dimebag Darrell Abbott's funeral — enact Bakhtin's carnival, whose 'joyful relativity' decrowns the serious, with Zarathustra's 'free death' framing the Kasket as festival rather than mourning.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 21 "Dull Reality The Tragic View of Life" — A Nietzschean interpretation: Alice's unastonished pursuit of the White Rabbit exemplifies the 'will to ignorance' hidden within the will to truth, since every perspective is created by selecting and simplifying while we convince ourselves we have discovered rather than invented. Rick Mayock reads the Caterpillar's 'Who are YOU?' and the mushroom as lessons in perspectivism and in the self as a grammatical fiction (no doer behind the deed, no lightning behind the flash), the Queen's beheadings and ruleless croquet as a flux of competing wills to power, and the Hatter's madness as Dionysian against Alice's Apollonian calm, with Greek tragedy supplying the metaphysical comfort that makes 'dull reality' livable.
- **Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality**, ch. 20 "Black sabbath & philosophy" — Dennis Knepp finds Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy gods at the birth of heavy metal: the Dionysian is the intoxication Nietzsche says makes art possible, realized in Sabbath's Hamburg residencies, Bill Ward's banana peels, the cough that opens "Sweet Leaf", and the mosh-pit loss of self that cures loneliness through communal revel, while the Apollonian is the god of terrifying dreams and visions seen in Geezer Butler's black apparition at the foot of his bed, the origin of "Black Sabbath", and Iommi's ghosts and angels. He argues Sabbath only looks Satanic because Christianity turned the satyrs and old gods into devils, and he rewrites Nietzsche's aphorisms Sabbath-style ("Iron Man is dead, and we have killed him") to drive the identification home.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 23 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Torosyan argues The Daily Show models the critical thinking and good-faith civic discourse that real politics and TV news lack, reading John Oliver's 'Civil Disservice' interview with Froma Harrop and Stewart's clips of Rumsfeld contradicting himself on WMDs as exposing bullshit in Frankfurt's sense: assertion indifferent to truth. Stewart's reframing of William Bennett's gay-marriage talking points (is the debate about marriage or about who counts as human?) and his self-effacing interviews with Ramesh Ponnuru enact Rousseau's social-contract ideal of what news owes the public against Machiavellian ends-justify-means manipulation. Gadamer supplies the demand that Bennett question his own horizons, Nietzsche's Apollonian-Dionysian account of tragedy frames the show's satire, and the Tao Te Ching's 'let yourself be partial' governs the whole chapter.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 19 "Each of Us Would See Ourselves" — The Teschners cast Don as a Nietzschean creator of value in technological culture: his nihilism ('There is no big lie. There is no system. The universe is indifferent') and 'What you call love was invented by guys like me to sell nylons' embody anti-foundationalism, while the beatnik Roy plays the resentful slave mentality whose passion lives only off what it despises. Don's creative process (sleep on it, 'forget it, and an idea will jump in your face') mirrors the camel-lion-child metamorphoses of Zarathustra, and the collapse of the principium individuationis explains his fluid identities from Dick Whitman to the 'Adam and Eve' fantasy with Rachel. Heidegger's techné frames the Kodak Carousel as genuine art, a revealing that transfigures 'a hell of a gadget' into 'a place where we know we are loved,' at the tragic price of a man outside community, and the falling figure of the credits is one 'we would each see ourselves' in.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 39 "Notes" — Reads "The City on the Edge of Forever" through Romanticism: the Guardian of Forever strands Kirk and Spock without historical reference points - a nihilist moment of pure meaninglessness - and Kirk's Romantic response is to rebuild the narrative of the past even at the cost of letting Edith Keeler die. Hegel's philosophy of history explains the compulsion to record (Spock's anguished "I've missed taping centuries of living history"), why Edith's unwitting world-historical role is to die under a truck rather than lead a pacifist America to Nazi conquest, and Novalis's call to "make the world Romantic" frames Spock's self-rescue as young Selek in "Yesteryear". Kirk, Spock, and McCoy become Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy archetypes - Tragic Hero, Apollonian, Dionysian - converging in the street scene where McCoy lunges to save Edith, Spock waits on logic, and Kirk, seizing McCoy's arms, finds a tragic beauty in her death.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 9 "1. Where Have All the Supermen Gone" — Holdier tests each hero against Nietzsche: Superman looks like the Übermensch but his mild-mannered Clark Kent pose is slave morality that would turn Nietzsche's stomach, while Batman's will-forged heroism (his Year One vow, 'what does not kill me makes me stronger') seems more overman-like until his self-loathing in Hush ('deep down, I'm not [a good person]') disqualifies him too. Neither qualifies; instead Superman embodies the Apollonian sun-god force of The Birth of Tragedy and Batman the Dionysian, so their Dark Knight Returns clash is the inevitable but never-final friction of art's twin poles — and the readers are the ones who win the fight.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 33 "21. Batman Is Superman" — Argues that Christian Bale's Batman, not the alien Superman, embodies Nietzsche's Übermensch: a mortal, flawed, lonely hero whose identity is forged in the unreconciled struggle between Dionysian vengeance and Apollonian reason across Nolan's trilogy. Batman Begins enacts eternal recurrence as Bruce repeatedly relives and integrates the well, the opera, and his parents' murder; The Dark Knight's Joker is Batman's Janus-faced shadow whose ferry experiment nearly proves the herd's 'gravity of madness,' and Dent's fall shows what Batman resists becoming. Superman II's temporarily mortal Superman is beaten by a truck driver and retreats to invincibility, proving the immortal alien can never overreach mortal limits as the Übermensch must.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 21 "NOTES" — Corn and Dunn read Maryann's takeover of Bon Temps through René Girard's scapegoat theory: mimetic desire breeds the resentments Sookie hears all day, the crowd's 'wild energy' dissolves the Apollonian individual into Dionysian self-forgetfulness (Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy, Plato's assembly that echoes blame until judgment drowns), and the town and the Fellowship of the Sun alike restore solidarity by uniting against vampires — or against Sam on the sacrificial oak. Godric's self-delivery to the Newlins is a failed Christlike sacrifice, so the chapter ends with Sookie's 'God doesn't punish, God forgives' as Girard's alternative to founding community on sacrificial violence.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 13 "Notes" — Takes Nietzsche's 'man is the cruelest animal' and argues the show's real exploration of cruelty lies not in the cult's crimes, which stay mysterious, but in the Cohle–Hart relationship, whose private cruelties are closer to the human condition. It explains human cruelty through theory of mind — knowing we make others suffer — and through the moral vocabulary of desert, karma, and Schadenfreude (Nietzsche's slave morality inventing hell) that hides our pleasure in suffering, which Nietzsche sees as the key to life-affirmation against Buddhist and Christian world-denial. The chapter maps Hart as Dionysian energy and Cohle as Apollonian form, and reads Rust's 2012 talk of eternal recurrence as a ruse concealing his search for a Nietzschean moment of ecstatic affirmation of all the cruelty he has caused and endured.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 23 "Notes" — Uses Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy and Lacan's ethics of psychoanalysis to argue season two failed as tragedy because feminist morality became the inflated 'Good' that blocks the transgression of limits through which Dionysian wisdom is won. Season one works because Rust's philosophy filters the Carcosa horrors without moralizing, whereas season two — failing Aristotle's catharsis model and repeating Euripides' mistake — represses the sexual knowledge troubling Velcoro, Bezzerides, and Woodrugh, so Dionysus returns only as money and violence, as in The Bacchae. Ani's arc is read through Nietzschean ressentiment toward her father and Freud's return of the repressed, with Kantian sexual dignity ('maybe you were put on earth for more than fucking') and the male gaze as the contemporary Good the show never crosses.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 12 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Paul Cantor and Peter Hufnagel use Nietzsche's essay 'Homer's Contest' to argue that the competitive spirit the Greeks called thumos links philosophy and athletics, presenting Plato's dialogues as 'the Olympics of philosophy' in which Socrates is the last man standing. They trace thumos as the spirited third part of the soul in Plato's Republic, the guardians' quality that reason must tame through gymnastics and music, and as the force Socrates enlists to win the thumotic youths Glaucon and Adeimantus to philosophy. They then read Achilles in the Iliad and its funeral games in Book XXIII as a build-up/discharge/calm cycle of thumos, offering athletics as Homer's alternative channel for the same warlike energy.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 11 "Federer as Religious Experience" — David Foster Wallace argues that watching Roger Federer live at Wimbledon delivers a near-religious experience because top sport is a prime venue for 'kinetic beauty'—a beauty rooted in human beings' reconciliation with the fact of having a body. He reads the 2006 Federer-Nadal final as a clash of the Apollonian (Federer's clinical northern artistry) against the Dionysian (Nadal's martial southern machismo), and dwells on specific Federer Moments (the reverse-thrust forehand winner against Agassi at the 2005 US Open) as instances where an athlete seems exempt from physical law. He treats Federer's grace as ineffable, defining it by what it is not, and juxtaposes the transcendent beauty of the body against the suffering body of cancer-survivor coin-tosser William Caines.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 11 "No Country for Old Men The Coens’ Tragic Western" — Gilmore reads No Country for Old Men as the Coens' tragic Western, casting Llewelyn Moss as an Oedipus-like hero whose competence-plus-hubris (wounding the antelope, going back to the dying man) triggers his ruin, per Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and the Delphic 'know thyself.' Anton Chigurh is a Nietzschean force beyond good and evil whose coin-toss rule preserves invulnerability by subordinating desire to chance, an amoral Dionysian wildness the essay ties to Thoreau's 'in Wildness is the preservation of the world' and Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian balance from The Birth of Tragedy. Heraclitus's 'geometrical mean' models the hunter-to-prey structure (Chigurh:humans::Moss:antelope), and Bell's fatalism and closing dream of carrying fire voice a Greek-tragic 'you reap what you sow.'
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 24 "12. It’s Not About BOB—It Never Was" — Huntingford argues Lynch reveres madness as the true source of insight, casting Cooper as the Romantic 'mad poet' and Socratic divinely-inspired Oracle (Phaedrus) whose dream-forays reveal Twin Peaks' buried truths while 'normal' is the real evil. She frames BOB—born from the atomic blast—and garmonbozia through Kant's Sublime as the fearful, irregular power behind nature that exceeds reason, and reads Cooper's tragic ka (via Stephen King's Dark Tower) and shadow-self confrontation, plus Rousseau's ethics of truth-seeking, as the show's message: some mysteries are not meant to be solved, and to embrace that madness is freedom.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Arnett reads Mann's 'modern crime films' through Nietzsche and Marc Augé's 'nonplace,' arguing Mann is a director-architect who exerts a will to power over institutional space (Atlanta's High Museum becomes Lecktor's prison in Manhunter; Neil's glass beach house in Heat). Mann's heroes are Nietzsche's 'godless' who refuse the herd, becoming Dionysian figures who redefine space—Neil and Vincent as Dionysian/Apollonian artists whose LAX showdown is a 'frenzy' of convergence. The endless recurrence of place-versus-nonplace, and Vincent killing Neil only to be trapped in supermodernity himself, dramatizes Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and Dionysian pessimism.
- **The Philosophy of Werner Herzog**, ch. 8 "Herzog’s Sublime and Ecstatic Truth" — Patricia Castello Branco argues that Herzog's sublime is Burkean and physiological rather than Kantian and transcendental: in Aguirre, Fitzcarraldo, and Grizzly Man the protagonists' encounter with overwhelming nature defeats reason and works through the body (Kinski's distorted performance, Treadwell's death) rather than confirming reason's supremacy as in Kant's Critique of Judgment. She maps Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' onto Nietzsche's Dionysian from The Birth of Tragedy, where the principium individuationis dissolves and the hero merges with nature's creating-and-destroying flux, and glosses ecstatic truth via Heidegger's aletheia as unconcealment reached through fabrication and stylization.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 10 "1 Primal and Spontaneous Neil Young’s Aesthetics of Authenticity" — Forest argues that Neil Young's habit of keeping early, flawed takes with Crazy Horse ("audio verite") embodies an aesthetic of authenticity as primal spontaneity. He reads Young through Emerson's self-reliance and trust in first impressions, Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian split (Harvest vs. Tonight's the Night, Young's onstage abandon on "Like a Hurricane"), Benjamin's loss of aura in mechanical reproduction, and Collingwood's art/craft distinction, contending that the "garage band" imperfections of jams like "Down by the River" let fans identify with the band's expressive, un-repeatable moment.
- **The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute**, ch. 15 "3. Experiences with Nietzsche" — Müller-Lauter interweaves memoir—hearing 'Praised be what makes hard!' and 'What does not kill me makes me stronger' torn from context in Nazi Weimar—with a systematic account of Nietzsche's nihilism as the devaluation of the highest values following the death of God. He traces the move from 'incomplete' to 'perfect' nihilism and the revaluation of values through the free spirit and the legislating Dionysian philosopher, insisting (against Bäumler's and Lukács's systematizations of the unauthorized Will to Power) that Nietzsche's experimental, fragmentary thought resists both fascist and Marxist appropriation.
- **The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute**, ch. 18 "6. Nietzsche contra Wagner on the Jews" — Yovel reads Nietzsche's break with Wagner as a self-overcoming that freed him to hand Wagner's redemptive role—catalyst of a new Dionysian Europe—to the modern secular Jews Wagner despised. He maps a structured ambivalence: fierce anti-anti-Semitism (grounded philosophically in Nietzsche's rejection of nationalism, racism, the state-cult, and ressentiment) coexisting with a fierce critique of ancient 'priestly' Judaism as the genealogical root of Christian slave morality. Contrasting Nietzsche with Wagner's Judaism in Music, he shows Wagner legitimized public hate-speech (dramatized in Siegfried's gratuitous loathing of Mime) while Nietzsche prized self-mastery, so the two men's later Nazi abuse—by Elisabeth and Winifred, the two 'women-priests'—rests on opposite relations to what each actually held.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 17 "8. Why Do We Care Who Bourdain Really Was" — Finn asks why fans cared about Bourdain's 'authenticity,' arguing his persona of freedom from bourgeois convention embodied Sartre's rejection of 'bad faith' while his meticulous control made him, per Keefe, 'Apollo in drag as Dionysus.' Reading the Hanoi/Obama episode as proof that even the President wanted to be Bourdain, she suggests his freedom (Kierkegaard's 'dizziness') may have become a trap, and proposes 'integrity' rather than authenticity as the word for his consistency.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 23 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Torosyan argues that The Daily Show models critical thinking and postmodern self-awareness, using Stewart's interviews to show how to reframe debate and act in good faith. He reads Stewart's demand that news media serve the public through Rousseau's social contract, casts scaremongering politicians as following Machiavelli's advice to 'learn how not to be good,' invokes Gadamer's hermeneutics to argue that guests like William Bennett fail to question their own prejudices, and uses Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian tension to explain the show's tragicomic satire (e.g., the 'Smallpox Blankets' joke and Bush reading Camus's The Stranger).
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 3 "Introduction" — Jacob Held defends the philosophy-and-popular-culture project against snobbery and argues that King's horror is genuine philosophy because it forces readers to confront finitude, meaning, and their deepest values. He reads King's own account of 'existential horror' through Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian pairing, casting the horror tale as a Dionysian crack in an Apollonian order that ends by restoring equilibrium, and frames doing this fun, relatable work as its own eudaimonia poised between nihilism and Aristotelian flourishing. Using Lovecraft's Cthulhu and King's Desperation/The Regulators (Tak), he claims horror shakes us into reaffirming the values that orient us and so bridges abstract academic philosophy and lived experience.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 25 "GARDENING" — Neuman decodes the Bosquet de la Colonnade at Versailles as a symbolic Temple of Apollo that glorifies Louis XIV as overseer of cosmic harmony. He argues Hardouin-Mansart fused the circular peripteral temple with Hadrian's Maritime Theatre, and used simple ratios (1:2 bays) drawn from the Pythagorean-Platonic system of universal proportion—the harmony of the spheres tied to Apollo's seven-stringed lyre and seven planets—to align architecture, the seven planets, and monarchical order. The spandrel pairing of lyre and panpipe evokes the Apollo–Marsyas/Pan contests, read as the reason-versus-passion, Apollonian-versus-Dionysian dichotomy; the whole garden is also linked to Descartes's geometrization of boundless axial space.
- **Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low**, ch. 22 "BLUES" — Brian Domino frames a choice between the reasoned Stoic life and the emotional life through the Rolling Stones and the blues. He presents Epictetus's Stoicism — apatheia, the dichotomy of control, and the Enchiridion's 'it was given back' — applied to blues themes of floods, death, and cheating women ('When the Levee Breaks,' Robert Johnson's 'Terraplane Blues'), arguing emotions stem from false beliefs and akrasia. Against this he sets 'Jumping Jack Flash,' 'Monkey Man,' and '(I Can't Get No) Satisfaction' as celebrations of raw emotional existence, invoking Plato's tension of reason and passion and Nietzsche's image of the 'music-making Socrates' to leave the choice deliberately unresolved.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 14 "8. Star Wars" — Rowlands reads Star Wars as Manichaean (light vs dark side of the Force) and contrasts it with Plato, for whom evil is merely absence of good and the form of the good is most real, an idea Augustine (via Plotinus) folded into Christianity. Siding with Lucas that Darth Vader's evil is palpably real, he then uses Nietzsche's 'Dionysus against the Crucified': the Christian strategy represses drives (Freudian repression), the 'hippy' strategy merely expresses them, but greatness requires sublimation into higher forms. Vader taps his dark side but fails to sublimate, so he is a flawed unbalanced megalomaniac (like Nietzsche's Borgia/Napoleon), not a true Ubermensch living life as art.

### Master and Slave Morality

In On the Genealogy of Morality, Nietzsche distinguishes two contrasting sources of moral valuation. Master morality arises among the strong and self-affirming, who call their own qualities "good" and see weakness as merely "bad"; slave morality arises among the oppressed and resentful, who first brand the powerful as "evil" and then define themselves as "good" by contrast. Nietzsche argues that much of modern Western morality, especially values like humility and pity, descends from this reactive slave revolt in ethics, and he uses the distinction to question the origins and worth of our inherited moral concepts.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 10 "Persuasion As Drama" — Karl Schudt contends that Nietzsche's genealogy of slave morality cannot be refuted by reason (Nietzsche denies reason itself), so drama must persuade where dialectic cannot: a believable story of a Nietzschean life acts as an empathic experiment. Faith is constructed as the Nietzschean ideal — strong, healthy, ruthless ('Find a couple of studs, use them, and discard them'), dismissive of reflection ('You think too much') — serving Mayor Wilkins, whom Schudt reads as a genuine Übermensch sacrificing mankind's mass for his ascension. Watching her world collapse (the accidental killing in 'Bad Girls', her mirror scene in 'Who Are You?', the torture of Wesley and confession on Angel) gives viewers an Aristotelian pity-and-fear warning that the unjust life ends badly, completing her 'leap from Nietzsche to Socrates.'
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 87 "Why Are the X-Men Good" — Systematically rejects candidate explanations of the X-Men's goodness: not self-interested calculation (the world's hostility undercuts it, blunting Magneto's argument), not innate constitution (Magneto chose otherwise, and the Cyclops–Wolverine–Jean Grey triangle shows ordinary desires), not fear of punishment, and not Nietzschean pity or herd resentment — the X-Men are the strong and healthy ones. The chapter's positive account: love of the good is learned through relationships with those who are good to us, from Xavier's loving school that gradually transforms Wolverine and Magneto's Nazi-scarred past to Peter Parker's formative upbringing by Uncle Ben and Aunt May.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 22 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Janice Daurio sets Plato's Thrasymachus and Callicles and Nietzsche's immoralism against three Narnian immoralists: Uncle Andrew, who exempts 'profound students and great thinkers' from rules meant for little boys, servants, and women; Queen Jadis, whose Deplorable Word and 'What else were they there for but to do my will?' embody might-makes-right; and the Green Witch, who extends going beyond good and evil to going beyond truth itself. Following Lewis's moral realism (the Golden Rule and Natural Law as facts like gravity, with Hobbes's lesson that someone always turns up with more power), she shows the immoralists cannot live by their own creed, since Uncle Andrew resents being treated as Jadis's slave, and since Lewis ties real authority to service, as when humble Frank the Cabby is made king.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 29 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Reads Eustace, Uncle Andrew, Experiment House, and Miraz's censored Narnia as Lewis's portraits of modern secularism, which treats the world as mere resource and dismisses the transcendent regardless of evidence. It argues that denying intrinsic value collapses into a Nietzschean master morality of power, visible in Uncle Andrew's use of the children as guinea pigs and the Lone Islands' slave trade, and exposes the secular 'conditioner's' self-exemption as a violation of the Principle of Relevant Difference. Against the Green Witch's debunking of Puddleglum's sun and Aslan as copies of a lamp and a cat, it deploys the Platonic-Cartesian copy/original model of ideas to argue transcendent ideas (eternity, perfection, necessary being) cannot be derived from lower material causes, suggesting instead that the material world is the 'shadowland' copy of a divine original.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 16 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Matheson examines the 'master animal' imagery saturating Fleming's novels - Donovan Grant's reptilian physique in From Russia with Love, Blofeld's animal magnetism, villains feeding victims to sharks and crocodiles - as an exercise in Social Darwinism where, as Mr. Big puts it, wolves live by wolf's laws and sheep call them criminals. Using Nietzsche's Übermensch, the blond beast of the Genealogy, and Zarathustra's self-overcoming, she distinguishes Apollonian eaters like M (who curb appetite) from doomed Dionysian gluttons like Giuseppe Petacchi, arguing that Fleming makes dining and will power the test of who counts as an Overman. Bond differs from his megalomaniac foes only in keeping his own will to power and stomach under control, and the chapter closes by warning that Hollywood's romanticizing of the master animal keeps us valuing a brutally primitive masculinity Fleming himself mocked as a 'cardboard booby'.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 17 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Landa argues that Bond's apparent defense of democracy against Übermensch villains is itself profoundly Nietzschean: Bond's exquisite, disciplined hedonism (the Minton-china breakfast, disgust at Mr. Du Pont's 'eating like a pig'), his obsessive competitiveness at baccarat and golf, and his contempt for mass democracy mark him as an aristocratic bourgeois hero in Nietzsche's mold. The gambling scenes enact a Calvinist logic of predestination in which losing at Casino Royale devastates Bond because his very worth depends on winning, and the 'human muck' he defends at Blades turns out to be the exclusive elite. Dr. No, Mr. Big, Drax, and Blofeld are cast as evil, explicit Nietzscheans while Bond serves a good, unspoken Western Nietzscheanism - so the Cold War showdown with Blofeld, who invokes Nietzsche by name, is elitism fighting counterfeit elitism, making Bond 'a secret agent in the service of Nietzscheanism'.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 31 "Metallica, Nihilism, and Nostalgia" — Peter Fosl reads Metallica's lyrics ("Leper Messiah," "The God That Failed," "One," "To Live Is to Die," "Escape") as extending Nietzsche's and Marx's critiques of Christianity: religion as slave morality born of ressentiment and as opium deadening the oppressed, illustrated by the landmine veteran of "One" pleading with a silent God and Hetfield's abandoned-childhood grief. He argues the band often falls into the "incomplete nihilism" Nietzsche predicted, lamenting God's failure and longing nostalgically for the Christian meaning it can no longer believe in rather than transvaluating values. Yet the defiance of "The Four Horsemen" and "Escape" and the band's creative power show it also working toward an overcoming of Christian nihilism, confirmed for Fosl by Hetfield's post-rehab health.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 32 "“They Have a Plan”" — Robert Sharp reads the Cylon uprising in Battlestar Galactica as Nietzsche's slave revolt in morality: enslaved by humans, the Cylons react with resentment and overturn their masters' values, just as early Christians did under Rome. The humans keep a master morality (Colonial polytheism, warrior elites, call signs like Apollo and Athena), while Cylon monotheism, doctrines of the soul (Leoben's sermons to Starbuck, Gina's suicidal faith), equality, and consensus government reproduce slave morality's move from bodily weakness to spiritual superiority. The New Caprica occupation debate among the Cavils, Six, and Boomer, and D'Anna's boxing, show the former slaves seeking not just destruction but conversion of their masters to a religion that makes Cylons equal.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 19 "The Doors Are Never Locked" — Held reads Cash's Walk the Line retort "Well, they're not Christians then" as a thesis about redemption: since, with Augustine, we rejoice most at the sinner saved, and since the Sermon on the Mount forbids judging what we cannot know (anyone's deep character), humility demands withholding condemnation and hoping even the worst can change. He contrasts Christian redemption, a revaluation of the person that needs outside grace (Cash needed June and the Carters; nobody is self-made), with Nietzsche's attack on redemption as slave-morality self-hatred, granting that Nietzsche's eternal recurrence also revalues the past but objecting that self-revaluation collapses into rationalization, as Cash's Saul in Man in White shows. Forgiveness proper requires repentance and a solvent character, like paying off a debt; the shame of the "Long Black Veil" woman shows why; and because we see "through a glass darkly," nobody, not the Reno murderer, not Joe Bean, is beyond hope, which is why the doors are never locked and why execution or life without parole claims a judgment of moral worth that is not ours to make.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 11 "Meaning The Final Frontier" — Biderman and Devlin read The Wrath of Khan as a Nietzschean test of whether revenge can ground a meaningful life after the death of God: Kirk, stuck 'flying a goddamn computer console' as an admiral, and the Genesis project seek meaning through creation without God, while Khan, broken by exile on Ceti Alpha V, chooses vengeance. Using Nozick's contrast between impartial retribution and personally satisfying revenge, and Nietzsche's will to power, master-slave morality, and ressentiment, they argue Khan had the superhuman gifts and independence from herd morality of a candidate Overman, but let revenge enslave him — culminating in Genesis turned weapon and his dying 'For hate's sake . . . I spit my last breath at thee,' a resounding No to life. Spock's mirror-image self-sacrifice, which affirms life, is offered as the better Nietzschean Overman.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 16 "Can We Play Beyond Good and Evil" — Drzaic and Rauch argue Link is 'good by default' because ludus play (rule-bound, goal-directed, winning the designed story) locks the player into the designers' morality, while paidia play, player-invented goals like the Ocarina of Time flying glitch or the Fierce Deity rampage in Majora's Mask, escapes the story's moral frame entirely. They then map this onto Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil: protagonist Link embodies slave morality (reactive, fear-avoiding, pity, patience, restoring the old Hyrule Ganon disturbed), while the elite paidia player is value-creating like the master, honoring power and secrecy (Huizinga) rather than the protagonist's virtue. The chapter concludes that in videogames the good/evil opposition is welded to ludus, and Zelda fans' naughtiness shows play can go beyond good and evil.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 24 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Barkman takes the 1986 movie poster's 'Beyond Good. Beyond Evil.' as a Nietzsche allusion and argues the cartoon refutes it: Skyfire's 'It is wrong,' Orion Pax's repudiation of admired power in 'War Dawn,' and Optimus's humble 'Thrones are for Decepticons' make Megatron a would-be superman and villain while Optimus is a Platonic guardian of a universal moral law binding even Unicron and the Quintessons. A reductio against cultural relativism (the Decepticon invasion of Earth, First Aid's failed pacifism in 'The Ultimate Weapon') plus C.S. Lewis-style archetypes explain why Optimus - a Christ-type who died saving the world - endures while GoBots do not.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 23 "What Mr. Colbert Has Taught Us (Besides Everything)" — In full truthiness voice, Michaud explains Colbert's failed 2008 presidential run — the South Carolina Democratic Executive Council's 13-3 vote keeping him off the ballot — as exactly what Nietzsche predicted: the resentful weak, the 'sheep,' hold the super-man down by redefining meekness as strength. He walks through will-to-power as self-overcoming, the lambs-and-birds-of-prey parable from the Genealogy, and Christianity as slave morality, then 'corrects' Nietzsche by relocating slave morality in the liberal media rather than God, ending with Colbert as the man of the future who 'affirms life without resentment.'
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 27 "The Will to Nothingness, or What Happens when the Red Sox Win" — Nolen Gertz runs the Sox-Yankees rivalry through Nietzsche's On the Genealogy of Morals: the Steinbrenner Yankees are masters whose 'good' simply means strong and winning, while Sox fans are slaves whose 'Yankees suck!' is ressentiment's imaginary revenge, intensified into the most spiritual and poisonous hatred by eighty-six years of impotence. The priestly slaves defeated the masters by cleverness rather than force, mirrored when Epstein's sabermetric 'religion' of prospects and projections terrified the Yankees into converting, building a farm system and embracing the slavish virtues they had scorned. The final twist is Nietzsche's will to nothingness: once the masters fell in 2004 the fans' suffering lost its meaning, breeding bandwagon guilt, pink-hat resentment and nihilistic exhaustion, so freedom requires a transvaluation that lets fans simply enjoy watching baseball.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 19 "Does Life Imitate Soccer" — Minister condemns 'negative soccer'—Sunderland at 28% possession and zero shots at Old Trafford, Stoke's goalless stalemate at Anfield, Bolton's two shots at the Emirates—through Nietzsche's genealogy of morality: teams that recognize superior opponents redefine the game's goal in slave-like resentment, replacing the pursuit of excellence, creativity, courage, and honor with a safety-first legalism of not losing, just as individual diving (Ronaldo's 'superman' dive, Drogba's histrionics) betrays the strong character, while Di Canio catching the ball for the injured keeper and Arshavin protesting his own penalty display honor. Marx then explains why the tactic is structural rather than a personal failing: Premier League revenue gaps, Champions League money, Abramovich's Chelsea billions, and the $55 million cost of relegation economically compel small clubs into what Minister reads as Marxian alienation—players unable to express themselves or flourish because economic forces dictate their play. He ends asking whether life imitates soccer: whether our own financial pressures likewise price excellence, honor, and self-expression out of ordinary lives.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 31 "Life A Celebration" — Reads John Simm's Master as Nietzsche's most advanced nihilist: having seen the universe die at Utopia, he judges life valueless and converts ressentiment into a joyful will to nothingness, dancing to the Scissor Sisters over his victims. The Ninth Doctor's arc in 'Dalek' mirrors this danger ('What are you changing into?') until he refuses to destroy the last Dalek, beginning his yes-saying to finite life. Following Deleuze's reading, the Doctor defeats the Master not with Martha's gun but with forgiveness ('I forgive you') and her storytelling network, embodying the Übermensch who carries his affirmation into the abyss of the end of the universe.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 16 "That Naive Cube! How Long Must I Suffer This" — Nicholas Michaud inverts the show's morality through Nietzsche: Plankton's tenacity, ambition and self-overcoming make him a super-organism driven by the will to power (traced to Schopenhauer's will to live), while Bikini Bottom's lionizing of SpongeBob's mediocrity is slave morality that judges by intentions to keep the strong down. Quoting the lambs and birds of prey from On the Genealogy of Morals and the 'incurably mediocre' passage from Beyond Good and Evil, he argues Plankton is the unsung hero who treats SpongeBob as an equal, Krabs a mere exploiter — and SpongeBob, who makes mediocrity contagious, the true villain.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 46 "Flowers" — Reads the Flowers album's blooms as dark—'Ruby Tuesday' can't be chained to a life where nothing's gained, and the heliotrope becomes Derrida's figure for philosophy forever turning toward its conceptual sun of truth, knowledge, or the good. That heliotropic bias, the metaphysics of presence, is illustrated by Augustine's treatment of evil as mere privation of good, which Nietzsche's genealogy of slave morality overturns by deriving good and evil from the same source, 'beyond good and evil.'
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 184 "Mother’s Little Helpers" — Introduces the Cambridge scholar Jane Ellen Harrison, whose books trace Greek religion from a swampy matriarchy to the Olympian age, with Dionysus as the holy child of the Mother — flayed and divided among the faithful — the very pattern Christianity retold in the Jesus story. Auxier credits Jagger's "keen intellect" and wide sense of history, then endorses Nietzsche's complaint that Christianity is "a puny, slave morality" that renders humanity effeminate: "That's exactly what I like about Christianity," since over-weaning masculinity needs opposing.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 28 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Framed by Dick's wait in a Klosterman signing line, the chapter asks how a critic acquires rock-star power. Plato's Ion supplies the magnet chain of inspiration (muse, poet, rhapsode, spectator), which puts Klosterman near the spectator end — he 'only got to second base' with the muse Thalia until Downtown Owl. Nietzsche's master and slave moralities then explain the critic's ascent: Klosterman is the cunning slave-priest who seizes power from warrior-artists through wit and articulate opinion, exactly as priestly values overthrew warrior values. Dick half-endorses the diagnosis, admits he prefers the slave's world of safety, and concludes that power — even the power to sell books and pay rent — is how we stay alive.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 32 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Rard tests whether objective morality survives the apocalypse by running four theories against Season Two: Plato's Forms explain universal truths about walkers ('walkers survive so long as their brains are relatively undamaged') but cannot handle white lies or changed circumstances, and Aristotle's virtue ethics reads Rick's rush from the shot Carl as rashness and Shane's supply run as courage, yet virtues prove relative and luck-dependent in a collapsed world. Natural law founders on clashing intuitions — Merle's racism and Hershel's barn of walkers each claim self-evidence. The chapter's center is Nietzschean: Hershel's barn is slave morality that pities the 'sick,' Maggie breaks from it, and Shane's sacrifice of Otis and opening of the barn enact a will-to-power master morality without joy, while Rick alone moves toward amor fati — embracing the world as it is, refusing guilt over Lori's affair, and insisting the baby be born into the Walk Age.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 21 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Clifton measures Omar against four Nietzschean criteria for the overman: as a free spirit he is 'in the wind, so to speak,' detached from home, money, and eventually even lovers like Brandon and Butchie; as a non-dogmatist about truth he uses it as a tool, lying under oath at Bird's trial yet sparing Brother Mouzone when the lie no longer holds; and as a noble of the Genealogy he is an active hunter who embraces the will to power, telling Wee-Bey 'you come at the king, you best not miss.' But Omar fails the fourth test, value-creation: his code keeps the good/evil scale intact rather than overturning it, so in the Three Metamorphoses he remains the lion who slays 'Thou Shalt' but never becomes the value-creating child. The verdict, in Nietzsche's own phrase, is that Omar is noble but 'human, all too human.'
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 18 "Psych and Philosophy" — Ruiz casts Lassiter as Nietzsche's slave - his worth defined reactively against Shawn, his advice that 'all romance ends in despair or death' reproducing the Judeo-Christian slave revolt in morality that turned weakness into virtue - and Shawn as the master, a self-propelled wheel who bakes a pineapple cake in an Easy Bake oven for nineteen hours whether or not anyone is watching. Shawn's generosity (helping the wrongly accused, the ghost-struck, and the deluded, once even crediting a cat with solving murders in '9 Lives') is read as the noble overflow of superabundant power rather than pity, and his hostage-saving risk-taking as will to power understood as self-mastery. Even the central lie gets a dialectical reading - like art, pretending to be psychic reveals the truth hidden behind appearances - though the chapter concedes Shawn's slavish moments, from daddy issues to his obsession with one-upping Declan in 'Shawn 2.0.'
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 22 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — King weighs whether Victor or his creation bears the blame, opening with a thought experiment in which a neighbor's self-aware android burns your town and asking 'does he deserve to share that fate?' Maslow's hierarchy of needs explains the monster's fixation on a mate as a starved 'love need' created by Victor's abandonment, and Piaget's cognitive stages test whether the monster had matured enough to 'could have done otherwise' - while Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil attack on morality as tyrannical herd-style slave morality threatens to dissolve blame entirely, and Sartre's existentialism leaves each agent choosing without objective moral foundations. Refusing both the absolutist's unconditional verdict and dogmatic relativism, the chapter applies the criminal law's mens rea ('guilty mind') test to monster, android, and creator alike, and leaves the final verdict of guilt deliberately open.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 35 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Comparing Finn with Gilgamesh, Achilles, Cuchulainn and Beowulf, the chapter shows how deeply he belongs to the archaic heroic code: a warrior who loves combat, seeks glory in tough-guy contests, fights dirty like Odysseus, and is fiercely loyal to Jake, his friends and his community. Against this tradition, Finn's unprecedented willingness to help any stranger who cries for help and his refusal to kill the 'unaligned' ant mark the post-heroic morality that began when Socrates told Athenians to care for their souls rather than status and Plato designed a city serving the common good - the author explicitly frames this through Nietzsche's complaint that Greek philosophy derailed the healthy, competitive heroic values. The chapter sides with Finn and the self-sacrificing Lemonjohn over Achilles, concluding that the secret of the Enchiridion is doing whatever the common good requires, warrior or not.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 13 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Noel measures Jobs against the four cardinal virtues from Plato's Republic and finds him wanting: imprudent (NeXT, the Lisa), unjust (taking the GUI from Xerox PARC, 'more fun to be a pirate'), intemperate (cruel outbursts like the 'dogshit for icing' cake), with only a brash, mind-changing courage. Drawing on Aristotle's golden mean from the Nicomachean Ethics, Nietzsche's master-slave morality and his Will to Power line about the man who 'determines values' for millennia, and Joseph Campbell's hero's journey, he argues entrepreneurs are a breed apart whose real virtues are independence of mind, vision, and audacity—and that Jobs, the anti-social creator who would not fit in, changed the world precisely because the cardinal virtues were 'prison walls' to him.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 19 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Michaud reads the novel through Nietzsche: the Crew of Light are resentful sheep banding together to kill a lion, damning Dracula not for wrongdoing but for his will-to-power, his hunting, and his reproduction - things humans do daily to animals - while the tale's enduring popularity over Nietzsche's heresy proves the death of God never happened, since we still use religion to console ourselves about dying. Following Ernest Becker's Denial of Death, he argues Dracula stories are humanity's immortality project: we must narrate the destruction of physical immortality to persuade ourselves it is a curse ('it would suck to be immortal') and that heroic, spiritual salvation in heaven is the better eternity.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 12 "4. Nietzsche’s Faction Test" — Mallalieu uses Nietzsche's slave morality, will to power, and Ubermensch to read Roth's social experiment: Abnegation's foot-washing, guilt-driven selflessness is slave morality, Amity's drugged peace makes them willing slaves, and Peter - cruel, self-promoting, guilt-ridden - is the most Nietzschean character, whose memory wipe is an attempt to forget his way out of slave morality. Even the heroes turn out Nietzschean when Tris and Tobias dose the Bureau with memory serum, since Nietzsche holds that the old values must be forgotten before new ones can be created. But the chapter concludes the price is too high: losing your values along with your memories means losing your identity ('I would rather be dead than empty'), so Nietzsche's imagined experiment, played out through the Bureau's tools, would be a world good only for the strong and cruel.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 17 "7. How Batman Cowed a God" — Reider reads the two heroes through Nietzsche's genealogy of morals: Superman's humility, guilt, empathy, and farmer-parent values (he is Clark Kent at heart, keeping the alter ego to unload the burden of his power) are textbook slave morality, making him the unwitting pawn of the weak rather than Nietzsche's Übermensch, while Batman's pride, wrath, and vow of vengeance - he refuses to kill the Joker or Robin's attacker not from respect for life but from aristocratic pride - revive the pagan "good" of Achilles dragging Hector's body. From this he builds a deliberately provocative strategic claim: because slave morality leaves Superman secretly craving to be bested and made ordinary again, the merely human Batman can stare down and "cow" the god in their showdowns, winning the psychological war Wonder Woman's and Lois's preferences supposedly confirm.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 29 "15. The C-Word" — Works through the ethics of cloning and genetic selection, starting with the objection that such technologies are "unnatural": that reasoning commits the naturalistic fallacy, since following Hume you can't get an ought from an is, and human ingenuity (roads, eyeglasses, IVF) is itself part of nature. Using Nietzsche's Genealogy account of master morality — good as the noble traits of intelligence, beauty, and strength — the chapter asks whether parents would then be obliged to engineer better children, while warning where trait-selection slides: Nazi eugenics, racist trait-lists (both Leda and Castor are white and conventionally attractive), and "abilism" against the deaf. It concludes that cloning itself is not evil: Projects Leda and Castor are immoral not because they clone but because they treat clones as mere means to an end, in Kant's sense, and trample their autonomy.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 31 "18. Thus Slaughtered Deadpool" — The chapter argues Deadpool is neither hero nor anti-hero but Nietzsche's Ubermensch beyond good and evil: perceiving the writers as the 'man at the typewriter' who keeps the Marvel cast as unwitting sheep under a slave morality, he kills the Marvel Universe in Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe to free them from their creators. In Deadpool Killustrated he murders the literary archetypes (Moby-Dick, the Little Mermaid, Tom Sawyer) so the heroes they inspired can never be written, compared to the Overman demolishing inherited values before they corrupt the next generation, and in Deadpool Kills Deadpool he slaughters every version of himself to force the creator-god into the open. Since 'good' and 'bad' are categories of the herd whose very source is corrupt, the author declines to judge the slaughter at all.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 25 "11. The Gods Are Dead and Elliot Has Killed Them" — Robison-Greene reads Elliot's chapel monologue - 'If I don't listen to my imaginary friend, why the fuck should I listen to yours?' - as a Problem of Evil argument: an omniscient, omnipotent, omnibenevolent God is incompatible with the unnecessary suffering of his father's death and of massive income inequality. The 'gods' Elliot kills are also Mr. Robot ('like all gods their madness takes you prisoner') and the religion of materialism, and Nietzsche supplies the blueprint for what follows: the Genealogy's slave revolt in values as the model for fsociety's uprising, and the Parable of the Madman plus the Ubermensch to cast Elliot-as-Mr. Robot as the creator of new values - though unlike Nietzsche's slaves, the oppressed here are complicit in their own subordination.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 13 "4. He’s a Hero in a Bottle, Baby" — Insooks deploys Nietzsche to argue Iron Man is the better hero: Cap's prized humility and relatability are sheep morality, the resentful herd value that drags the excellent down to average (as when society savored the Olympic swimmer's fall), while Tony honestly owns his superiority and keeps self-overcoming, building ever-better suits rather than resting on a serum gifted in a bottle. On this view Cap's manufactured modesty insults people who genuinely struggle, and the true super hero inspires from the mountaintop - build yourself a suit and get up here - instead of pretending to be just like us.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 19 "8. Neither the Hero You Deserve Nor the Hero You Need" — Reading 'Vindicators 3' through Nietzsche, the chapter argues the superhero team are slave-morality charlatans whose duty to protect the weak is the herd's imaginary revenge, while Rick, who defeated Worldender drunk, embodies master morality and honest will to power, against Jerry's dishonest version in the Pluto-not-a-planet fight of 'Something Ricked This Way Comes'. Rick's casual destruction of Worldender becomes Nietzsche's death of God, the collapse of the value-source that gave the Vindicators' lives meaning, which Vance Maximus denies at the cost of his life. The chapter then tests Rick against the Ubermensch via the camel-lion-child metaphor and concludes he is at best Nietzsche's lion, tainted by resentment over his lost family rather than the value-creating child, leaving Morty and Simple Rick as long-shot candidates.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 38 "26. Thanos’s Mistake" — Argues Thanos embodies Nietzschean master morality — his will as its own justification, 'the hardest choices require the strongest wills,' echoing the Melian dialogue's 'the strong do what they will, the weak suffer what they must,' with Doctor Strange answering in kind ('you'll find our will equal to yours') — while the Avengers speak from slave morality, judging by intentions and branding genocide evil. Thanos's real error, though, is a categorical one: imposing a technical quantity fix (a one-time 50 percent cull) on a social relationship problem, since Hardin's carrying-capacity logic and the St. Matthew Island reindeer show populations must self-limit like apex predators, making his correction a mere stopgap that confuses quantity with relationship.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 29 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Reads Bluth contradiction through Kant's categorical imperative: Lindsay's lie about her shopgirl job, Gob's jealousy bred by comparative parenting, and George Michael's conformist drift show both the imperative's force and the danger of its empty formalism, while the 'Afternoon Delight' double entendres test whether good intentions suffice for Kantian worth. Nietzsche then answers that morality itself is the contradiction: virtue manufactured from ressentiment ('weakness is being lied into something meritorious'), the will to power turned inward as nihilism, with self-overcoming and value creation as the exit; Mary Douglas's joke theory closes the chapter by explaining why all this contradiction is comic and why the joke is on Gob.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 20 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Nicholas argues the film's supposed nihilists, Walter, and the Big Lebowski are all failed Nietzschean value-creators: Walter's arbitrary givings of value ('Donny was a good man... he was one of us') just enact nihilism, and the disabled achiever's money-and-plaques world mistakes symbols for value. He then uses Charles Taylor's three malaises of modernity — disenchantment, disengagement, atomism — to explain the Dude's world (even bowling stops mattering: 'Fuck the tournament'), and finds the way out in MacIntyre's notion of a practice: bowling's internal goods, standards of excellence, and community of giving and receiving tie the three friends to meanings outside themselves, resisting nihilism.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 38 "“Exit Game”" — Reading 'Striking Vipers' through its closed- and open-door imagery, the chapter asks whether Danny and Karl's virtual sex as Lance and Roxette is adultery, testing the question with Plato's Ring of Gyges (what people do when no one can see them), Locke's memory theory (if Danny remembers Roxette's sex acts, is Roxette Danny?), and behaviorist replies that only physical penetration counts. Nietzsche supplies the chapter's frame: his master/slave morality and his view of life as self-created representational art explain how the characters' hidden, mind-only moral inversion creates real existential meaning in virtual sex. The episode's fusion of bodily and mental pleasure is said to break down Mill's higher/lower pleasures distinction - 'lower' physical virtual pleasures yield a 'higher' sense of wholeness - and Schopenhauer's insatiable striving plus Husserl's meaning-conferring perception underwrite the conclusion that virtual love can be real, with Danny and Theo's once-a-year open marriage endorsed as an act-consequentialist balance between monotonous fidelity and escapist fantasy.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 5 "A Shared Higher Thirst" — Cleary reads Strange as a would-be Nietzschean Übermensch — brilliant, striving, and flirting with nihilism via the 'tiny momentary speck' line — whose narcissism, not his ideals, blocks both self-overcoming and love. Strange's rage at Christine Palmer's wine and cheese ('don't pity me') is explained through Nietzsche's attack on pity as herd morality, and his fixation on restoring his old surgeon-self as refusing Zarathustra's call to burn oneself to ashes. The Ancient One leaving him to die on Everest, Mordo's hard training, and Wong refusing to laugh at his jokes exemplify Nietzschean friendship as challenge and 'war,' culminating in the 'shared higher thirst for an ideal above them' that lets Strange overcome himself.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 29 "17. Downton Abbey as Eternal Recurrence" — Christopher Ketcham provocatively equates primogeniture and entail - the legal machinery that returns Downton intact to each generation - with Nietzsche's 'greatest weight,' the eternal recurrence. Working through Lawrence Hatab's five interpretations of the doctrine, he asks whether the Abbey's continuity is cosmological (it is not, since estate taxes and squandering heirs keep chipping away), a Zarathustra-style life-affirming yes to the agrarian world against the 'nihilism' of capitalist fashion, or merely symbolic like a listing in Burke's Peerage beside fossilized dinosaur bones. His answer comes via Violet, the family, and the servants, who have 'become one with the property': the Abbey recurs only anthropomorphically, and even that stickiness is dissolving under industrialization, the death tax, and the war that killed off three royal cousins' empires.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 18 "Amos Is No Superman" — Pankaj Singh reads Amos through Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals: Amos' division of people into 'bad ones, ones you follow, and ones you need to protect', his outsourcing of moral judgment to Naomi and Holden ('Naomi wouldn't like it'), his fearlessness, and his violent spontaneity make him 'evil' by slave morality yet good by master morality. Unlike Prax, who has to be stopped from shooting Strickland out of ressentiment, Amos kills without revenge ('I am that guy'), and his fistfights with Miller and Alex discharge hostility immediately so it never poisons — the strong natures Nietzsche praises that 'form, mold, recuperate and forget.' His 'crew comes first' and 'better to go down swinging' express the will to power as discharge of strength rather than mere self-preservation, but because he never sublimates or overcomes his drives, the chapter concludes Amos is no Übermensch — 'but then again, who is?'
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 9 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — Kylie Prymus asks whether Kefka is truly mad, using Foucault's Madness and Civilization to argue that madness is a label society applies to dismiss what it cannot control, so players and heroes refute Kefka with the ad hominem 'you're crazy' rather than answering him. She then reads Kefka's 'monument to non-existence' through Nietzsche: his godlike discovery that existence has no justification echoes the death of God, our horror at him reflects slave morality's relabeling of noble strength as evil, and the heroes' appeal to purposes he lacks fails because existence is only a hypothetical imperative. Kefka ends up a failed Ubermensch who overthrows the gods but cannot overcome nihilism, leaving the World of Ruin heroes the genuinely Nietzschean task of creating meaning where none is given.
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 21 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — David Hahn argues that Spira's Yevon religion is exactly what Machiavelli and Nietzsche warned against: hope for the Calm and a Sin-free future makes Spirans otherworldly and passive, forbidding machina, revering self-sacrificing Summoner martyrs, and blaming themselves for Sin, just as just-war Christianity left Machiavelli's princes passive and dependent on mercenaries, paralleled by Seymour and Kinoc standing idle at Operation Mi'ihen. Nietzsche's slave revolt in morality explains Yevon's sanctification of meekness and death, while Machiavelli's account of religion as a political instrument, from Numa to Scipio's oath, explains why the lie of Yevon held Spira together, and why its collapse may bring either Nietzschean rebirth or Machiavellian chaos.
