Against Descartes's mind-body split and Plato's distrust of appearance, Bond's gun is an organic extension of his body rather than a symbol, and his sensual immersion in the world is what lets him see what others cannot.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 36 "The Price of Existence" — Bonnie Mann reads Twilight through Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex: Bella is the "relative being" whose existence has meaning only in orbit around Edward, clumsy, self-sacrificing, carried and watched, living the myth of the eternal feminine in which the masculine gaze confers being on a girl otherwise taught the world is defined without reference to her. She locates the fantasy's pull in the contradictory messages of twenty-first-century girlhood (Pipher, Phillips, Bordo), where being attractive to boys remains the first avenue to existing at all. Yet she also finds a feminist subtext: the vampire transformation returns Bella to the "I can" body, faster and stronger than Edward and saving the day herself, though Meyer ultimately re-sells the old promise that a woman wins existence through self-annihilation for others.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 6 "“I Got this Guitar and I Learned How to Make It Talk”" — The editors unpack Springsteen's 1988 speech inducting Bob Dylan: Elvis freed America's body from Cold War-era repression (duck-and-cover fear, Calvinist stiffness), Dylan freed the mind by bringing ambiguity ('Mr. Tambourine Man,' 'Maggie's Farm'), and Springsteen's own project was to free heart and soul — 'heartwork' in the early songs, 'soulwork' from Nebraska on. Their key philosophical move is embodied: you are not under the school desk because you are afraid, you are afraid because your body is under the desk, so intellectual freedom grows out of bodily freedom, and the guitar — flesh stretched over wood — literally talks for and with the audience. The revolution still fails, they concede, since hearts stay broken and the soul finds only hope in hard work, decency, family, and conversation.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 18 "Stable Bodies" — Heinricy argues the human/Cylon line is drawn on the body: following Mary Douglas, bodies function as cultural boundaries, so Cylons figure as contamination to be hunted (Boomer in the fleet) and marked as other by violence (Gina's torture), though Athena's loyal service and Tigh's exposure show the fear is socially constructed rather than natural. Cylon insides are known only through technology (Caprica Six's glowing spine, Athena's blood interface in 'Flight of the Phoenix'), and their bodies' stability — no scars, aging, or change — is paid for in unstable minds (Tigh killing Ellen, Boomer strangling Hera), whereas messy human bodies carry potential, hope, and change, as Apollo's weight fluctuation shows. Since we are all already cyborgs (vaccines, pills, GMOs), the Numbers are a further human-machine integration, and Hera and Nicky's blending is the ultimate 'contamination' and a new hope.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 10 "Game versus Place" — Wilson argues that Wind Waker's Ballad of Gales warp sacrifices environmental presence for goal-oriented play: the long, uneventful sails where waves, cloud patterns, and quiet soundscapes dominate are precisely when Hyrule feels like a place, and teleporting turns it into a disposable grid of destinations. Drawing on Castells' spaces of flows versus places, Schivelbusch's 'annihilation of space and time' by the railway (the player becomes a 'human parcel'), and de Certeau's opposition between the panoptic map view and the embodied everyday view, he contends the very existence of the warp option colors all distance traveled. Even panoramic pleasures like hang-gliding over Outset Island, he notes, must be balanced against pure map-grid travel.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 23 "Nightmares" — Auxier asks why the flying monkeys and the shriveling feet of the Wicked Witch of the East give children lifelong nightmares, and answers with a phenomenology of three frightening sequences in escalating duration: the instant shriveling shot, the five-minute cyclone (paired with 'The Great Gig in the Sky' in the Dark Side of the Rainbow sync), and the monkey air-raid. Kierkegaard's Concept of Anxiety supplies the depth psychology: innocence is ignorance, and the child's dreaming spirit projects its own nothing outward, fastening fear onto figures like the monkeys (who are, he notes, played by the Munchkin actors themselves). Merleau-Ponty's lived body versus habit body explains the mechanics: cinema seizes the body's usual 'tour of inspection,' Fleming manipulates active and passive synthesis (the scoreless build-up to the window blow, the barely noticed arsenal of weapons in the Haunted Forest, the dimming lights), and children construct a rigid, inescapable habit body within a single viewing, so the nightmare is the monkey inside our own projected world.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 28 "Knives Out" — Michael Thompson argues that the much-debated rhythm of "Pyramid Song" — 4/4 with syncopation, 3/3/4/3/3 groupings, or shifting signatures; Yorke says it is only "felt" — is philosophically pointed: by violating ordinary temporal expectations it forces an awareness of time itself, just as Chopin's nocturnes used time-signature changes to voice the nostalgia and melancholy of his Polish exile. Drawing on Gadamer's historically affected consciousness and the embodied, rhythmic daily life described by Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty, he reads the lyrics' row-boat to heaven ("all my past and futures") as a synoptic flash in which one sees past, present, and future as one organic whole. Because Yorke's heaven echoes Talking Heads' "Heaven" as a place where nothing happens, the song's consolation is that nothing lies outside our temporal embedding — with past and future united "there was nothing to fear and nothing to doubt."
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 12 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Using the hidden sides of Transformers - a robot inside a Camaro, a tank inside a robot - the authors stage the philosophy of perception: Descartes's innate geometrical rules and Berkeley's bodily cross-referencing both fail to explain how Sam Witwicky can know the steelyard robot is his Camaro, while Merleau-Ponty's embodied account of focus, background, and 'indeterminate vision' explains it through the perceiver's lived body. They extend this to the 'Autobot Spike' mind-transfer episode and to CGI: virtual Transformers on screen feel hollow because light-created images have no hidden surfaces for our bodies to investigate and grasp.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 11 "19" — Four 'Phase Five' puzzle essays. Lindahl-Urben and Taliaferro use Secret Wars to test omnipotence: the Beyonder, Doom, and Galactus cannot do the logically impossible (no spherical cubes, no stone too heavy to lift), two omnipotent beings collide, and a truly omnipotent being has no desires - so villains can never climb to the top they crave. Matthewson and Wall use Frankfurt cases and reasons-responsive source compatibilism to explain why Eddie Brock is responsible for Venom's villainy (he voluntarily bonded and endorses the symbiote's adjusted psychology) while Anne Weying, horrified by what the symbiote made her do, bears only minimal blame. Pickavance reconstructs the Ship of Theseus with Sandman's 'mansand': combining part exchange with materialism lets Norman Osborn reassemble a duplicate Sandman from his scattered remains, and since neither principle nor soul-dualism comes free, personal identity through material change remains unsolved. Loader argues Brainiac's reinvention as a 'facts and logic' computer embodies disembodied Cartesian AI, so the frame problem (Dennett's exploding robots) and embodied cognition (Clark's Tetris, Dreyfus) suggest his detachment from body and world would make him less, not more, intelligent than the humans he scorns.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 9 "Wave Goodbye from the Catbus" — Heinricy argues anime is the richest medium for posthuman theory because it shows bodies 'in a state of becoming' rather than as grotesque boundary violations: Miyazaki's Catbus and Totoro, Haku's dragon transformation and Chihiro's pig parents in Spirited Away, and the cursed pig-headed aviator of Porco Rosso all treat morphing bodies as possibility, not horror. She sorts anime posthumanism into two valences: a 'Ghost in the Machine' dream of consciousness leaving the body altogether (Motoko merging with the net in Ghost in the Shell), which she rebuts via N. Katherine Hayles's point that consciousness is embodied and would change with any new body, and hybrid configurations like mecha (Gundam, Robotech) where body and machine drive each other. Following Donna Haraway, she contends we are all already cyborgs — vaccines, engineered food, treated water — and credits Japan's nuclear history (via Susan Napier) and its shape-shifting folklore for why anime embraces rather than fears the transformed body.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 11 "The Transforming Body" — McBlane reads Oshii's Ghost in the Shell as staging the collision between a humanist framework — Cartesian ghost-in-shell dualism where consciousness is the seat of identity — and a posthuman 'mindbody' of distributed cognition in which the body is an informational circuit extending into the net, so a data body is still a body. Motoko's crisis (is the real me the organic brain, the ghost, or nothing?) deepens through the hacked garbage-truck man ('There's nothing sadder than a puppet without a ghost') and resolves only in her fusion with the Puppet Master, whose line 'Your effort to remain what you are is what limits you' enacts the shift from one ghost to multiple, distributed subjectivities ending in a little girl's body with 'The net is vast.' Heidegger's Dasein and being-in-the-world supply the claim that access to Being expands beyond the human into technological and informational modes, while the film's angelic transcendence imagery shows how residual humanist mind-body splits persist even in a posthuman story.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 23 "The Loneliness of the Goalkeeper (Again)" — Winters celebrates the goalkeeper's fingertip save—Gordon Banks denying Pelé's header in 1970—as football's aesthetic summit, reading the keeper as the lonely, 'stark mad' outsider of existentialist fiction, a lineage he anchors in Camus, the goalkeeper of Algiers who said all he knew of morality he learnt from football. Kant supplies both the dove of the first Critique—needing the air's resistance, just as the tango's strict steps enable the dancer's personality—and the target of critique: against Kantian disinterested contemplation, he adopts Graham's Nietzschean, Dionysiac aesthetics of participation, so spectators proprioceptively feel the keeper twisting in mid-air, as Wittgenstein's question about the galloping horse picture suggests the movement enters our muscles and joints. Understanding a save or a back-heel means seeing it under a general type ('that' free kick, 'that' volley, from Beckham at Wembley back to Garrincha), and Bloch's ruminations in Handke's The Goalie's Anxiety at the Penalty Kick show the keeper alone at the liminal limit where concession and prevention meet.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 21 "The Moving Shadow of Truth" — Haffner and Vogel define martial arts by a Wittgensteinian family resemblance to combat and organize the promise of self-improvement as paired opposites, working them Hegelian dialectic style, granting some truth to each side. They ask whether training brings peace or violence (Hobbes's shield for a war of all against all and Freudian catharsis versus Aristotle's worry that habituated violence breeds violence), strength fantasies or Socratic humility about weakness (with Sun Tzu's know-your-enemy and Foucault on the teacher's gaze and dojo power games), Cartesian dualism versus embodiment, and appreciation of tradition versus its distortion. The lesson is that the martial path holds both light and shadow, and separating enlightenment from self-deception takes eternal vigilance.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 19 "Leap of Faith" — Dionne argues Cobb's 'most resilient parasite' works only as an idea embedded in a coherent story - 'my father doesn't want me to be him' - and that since ideas define who we are, each person is less a host than a collection of well-planted narratives. Using Bergson on embodied, memory-and-desire-mediated perception (Cobb's fear of the bridge triggering Mal's projection) and Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil on perspectival appearance as the price of life, she claims dreams differ from reality in degree, not kind: we are beings-in-the-world who stabilize contingency through story-making and 'strive for positive logic'. Hence knowledge always demands the leap of faith that Saito and Mal demand of Cobb, the film becomes a meta-narrative with Fischer as its audience, and the wobbling top offers only an interpretation of a fact, never the fact itself.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 21 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Lisa Warenski reads 'Suzanne' as staging a phenomenological account of self-awareness: with Husserl and Merleau-Ponty the body is not an object but the lived first-person perspective - so 'touch a perfect body with a mind' is literal - and with Sartre's keyhole example from Being and Nothingness we become aware of ourselves through the gaze of the other. Developmental psychology's mother as 'magical mirror,' who reflects the child's emerging mind, is connected to Hegel's paradox of recognition, and to Aristotle's and Neera Badhwar's friends as mirrors of the soul. On this basis Suzanne's mind-touch has epistemic value: love reflects you truly and shows you what you might become, whether as Jesus's agape or Suzanne's appreciative philia.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 27 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Felder stages Sartre against Merleau-Ponty on the mind-body problem and other minds, opening with the shower scene where Taystee's 'you got them TV titties' makes Piper an object under a gaze, as Pornstache's look converts being caught into shame. But Piper pulling her towel back to appraise her own breasts 'sees-with' Taystee, and the audience's access to Piper's feelings shows perception is shared, not solipsistic. Merleau-Ponty's incarnated subjectivity, the flesh of the opening credits' real inmates' eyes, and actors' embodied performances dissolve the problem of other minds that Sartre's alienated subject-object model leaves open.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 41 "26. Time Lords Are Us" — Elder argues the 'back to front' love story of the Doctor and River Song - her past is his future, as at Lake Silencio - refutes both the objective 'river' model of time and the subjective 'song' model on which the mind assembles moments like notes into a flow. Following Merleau-Ponty, he grounds the experience of flow in pre-reflective embodied perception: Clara's walk around the TARDIS and her 'it's smaller on the outside' show a finite body gripping a multifaceted world, so that 'time is the subject and the subject is time.' Because temporalities, unlike private consciousnesses, can intertwine in a shared present, the Doctor and River can build a relationship out of each other's pasts and futures - and in this sense we are all Time Lords.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 22 "11. Of Bats and Supermen" — Springett argues Superman, not Batman, is the proper goal of transhumanism - Batman's training and gadgets are only a stage toward transcending the human condition - and that the eugenics and Social Darwinism objection fails because Superman directs his superior fitness at saving the less fit. Through Merleau-Ponty's embodied cognition (Lois's churning stomach over a deadline, Alfred retracing his steps and posture to recall a thought, the "Subway Superman" Wesley Autrey's instinctive track rescue) he shows that radically different bodies mean radically different minds and moral perception. That turns Nagel's "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" into "what is it like to be Superman?" - a problem of other minds for our transhuman future, with Watchmen's Doctor Manhattan as the warning of a transcendent being who simply stops caring about humans.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 34 "21. Welcome to My World" — Built on Jakob von Uexküll's Umwelt—the 'island of the senses' that enfolds each creature, illustrated by a moth that smells only a mate's pheromone and hears only the bat's echolocation—the chapter argues that every Discworld being likewise inhabits a sliced-down life world rather than the world as a whole. The ambiguous puzuma running near light speed, dream-spinning dromes that starve victims inside stolen Umwelten, the two-dimensional Shadowing Lemma, Gaspode's pathogen-warring skin, the hermit elephant's hut, and the re-annual plant that flowers a year before its seeds each show a life world carved out by what an organism can sense and use, whether its world runs on science or magic—prompting the suggestion that the Umwelt is more fundamental than either.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 18 "7. I Am and Am Not You" — Reads the opening scene phenomenologically: when Sarah sees her face on Beth, her identity does not merely change genetically but unravels generatively, since her birth, ancestry, and place in world-history are all thrown into question. Using Husserl's lived-body (the absolute "here" of experience), his static/genetic/generative levels of analysis, the homeworld/alienworld distinction (Clone Club solidifies its identity against the Castor "brothers," until Helena cradles the dying Rudy), and Husserl's co-originality of I and world, the chapter presents identity as intersubjective, constituted by shared projects like Sarah's fight for Kira and the Clone Club's tribe-rituals. Kierkegaard's "life must be lived forwards but understood backwards" is broadened: to understand identity we must look before our own birth and beyond our death, into the lifeworld we inherit and pass on.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 15 "5. Other People’s Body Parts" — Explains Kyle Spencer's horror at the body Madison and Zoe assembled from other people's parts through the history of soul-body theories: Aristotle's De Anima account of the soul as the faculties of a living body (plus the Physiognomonics claim that small people have small minds - poor Ma Petite), Plato's Timaeus on body parts designed for philosophy and reincarnation into bodies fitted to one's vices, Avicenna's soul as a faculty-binding nexus that chooses its bodily vehicle like a vehicle serves its owner, and Merleau-Ponty's habitual body (the Axeman's axe as part of his body, phantom limbs), which best explains why walking around on someone else's legs 'has got to mess with you a little'.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 15 "6. You Don’t Need to Be Human to Have a Human Hand" — Sue Zemka contrasts the film's opening eye — reason and consciousness, in a tradition Arendt summarizes as thinking figured as seeing — with its closing image of Deckard's hand reaching toward Ana's through glass, the sense of touch leading out toward others. Schopenhauer explains K's wondering gaze at his own hands in the snow as the human predicament of being both will and representation, subject and object at once, while Condillac's and Maine de Biran's statue thought experiments ('I feel, therefore I am' against Descartes's cogito) are charged with imagining humanness in isolated figures. The film's answer is relational and political: humanness is made in relationships and resistance, from the Joi-Mariette hand-synced sex scene to the final father-daughter touch.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 26 "15. The Phenomenology of Replicant Life and Death" — Zachary Sheldon analyzes 2049's style of violence through Merleau-Ponty's account of film as perceived conduct that shows consciousness thrown into the world, plus the defamiliarizing power of camera choices. In the killings of Sapper and Joshi and the underwater K-Luv fight, the fatal blows are elided, glimpsed only in reaction shots, or distanced through high angles and blurred bodies, so the audience's embodied, empathetic response makes a replicant's death feel exactly as real as a human's. If we feel Sapper die as we would feel a man die, the film's stylistic answer goes, the divide between kinds was never really there; K dies on the stairs because he has truly lived.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 38 "22. Professor Stomachache Needs Neuroscience" — Zebrowski brings Antonio Damasio's Somatic Marker Hypothesis to bear on Chidi's stomachaches: gut feelings built from a lifetime of social experience are essential decision-making shortcuts, not noise corrupting pure reason, as the tirelessly deliberating frontal-lobe patient shows. Chidi's failure is not brain damage but a refusal to trust his own somatic alarms while insisting ethics can be computed, exactly the mind-body split that Scanlon's contractualism, where morality is negotiated with other people, and Dewey's 'morals is education' both reject. Combined with Mark Johnson's moral imagination, this explains how the dead humans keep growing morally after death: bodies, relationships, and culture continue tuning their ethical instincts.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 20 "I’m an Alien. And That’s OK" — Reads Ripley's arc through Alison Stone's maternal subjectivity: her mothering of Jonesy and Newt shows the maternal is relational as much as bodily (neither ever gestated in her), Mother (MU/TH/UR) and the Queen stage the 'malevolent mother' against her ('Get away from her, you BITCH!'), and Alien3's unwanted pregnancy forces a violent separation in which only death asserts her selfhood. In Resurrection, Ripley-8 relives Helene Deutsch's quasi-infantile emotional fusion with her hybrid child before killing it, illustrating why Stone demands nonviolent differentiation rather than a complete break from the maternal body - 'I'm a stranger here myself.'
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 19 "Is a Man Not Entitled to the Sweat of His Brow" — Schevelier uses the Andrew Ryan assassination to teach phenomenology: the moment the controller stops responding, the 'mineness' of the experience collapses and the story stops being yours, revealing that Jack's (and the player's) freedom depended on a thin self-narrative the mind 'desperately struggles to create', per Lutece's epigraph. Nagel's bat shows why no brain scan captures what it is like to play, while Husserl, Heidegger, and Merleau-Ponty supply the toolkit; Heidegger's hammer, which shows itself in use or in breakdown, explains both immersive scenes like the Kashmir restaurant and what breaks them (bugs, wrong display, a talking protagonist). Following Merleau-Ponty's claim that art records subjective experience, the chapter treats Levine's team as artistic phenomenologists whose design question 'What is this experience we are trying to make?' turned Columbia and Elizabeth into phenomenological analyses to be read.
- **Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality**, ch. 15 "Black sabbath & philosophy" — Ken Pepper uses Merleau-Ponty's Phenomenology of Perception to explain how Tony Iommi's homemade plastic fingertips work: like the blind man's cane, they are incorporated into his body schema so that he perceives the fretboard through them, refuting the Cartesian "objective body" picture on which playing would be inner plans causing finger movements. On creative freedom, the chapter stages Merleau-Ponty against Sartre's radical freedom, Iommi did choose to relearn guitar after hearing two-fingered Django Reinhardt, and his restricted two-finger chords, lighter strings, and drop tunings birthed heavy metal, but Sartre is wrong that attitude alone transcends disability, since some possibilities (playing at all without the tips) were simply not live. Only Iommi, taking up the possibilities his body-in-his-situation afforded, could have invented metal.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 24 "Inside the Lived Body" — Pits Merleau-Ponty's embodied self against Descartes' representationalism and mind-over-matter dualism to read Inside Out: Riley's five personified emotions look like homunculi inviting an infinite regress, but the film actually shows a holistic body-subject whose emotions arise in situations and with others. Joy's campaign to keep Riley 'okay' dramatizes the futility of constant happiness and the necessity of Sadness, while Riley's hockey stick becoming an extension of her body illustrates Merleau-Ponty's claim that skillful coping lives in the body rather than in Sadness's 'mind manuals.' The chapter ends on childhood's lived present and the film's power to hold loss before us instead of pushing past it.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 11 "Notes" — David Lawrence opens with Fallout 4's 'Blind Betrayal', where Elder Maxson orders the player to execute Paladin Danse once his synth origin is revealed, and argues that moral status is a matter of capacities - sense of self, notion of past and future, values, life-plans, moral agency - drawing on Charles Taylor's concept of a person and narrative identity, not on biological substrate. Nick Valentine's hunt for Eddie Winter in 'Long Time Coming' and Curie's chosen embodiment in 'Emergent Behavior' show machines weaving reconstructed pasts into new life-plans, while ghouls like Hancock and Raul ('Old School Ghoul') and super mutants like Fawkes (who refuses to enter the lethal radiation chamber: 'I would not rob you of that') and the community-builder Marcus prove branded monsters can be more human than human. The factions embody warring philosophies of moral status: the Institute's property-slavery of its creations, the Brotherhood's 'wisdom of repugnance' (Leon Kass), and the Railroad's capacity-based abolitionism, with DiMA's Far Harbor question - how do you know you are not a synth? - turning the issue on the player.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 38 "22. Professor Stomachache Needs Neuroscience" — Brings Antonio Damasio's Somatic Marker Hypothesis to Chidi's stomachaches: gut feelings are evolved, body-based shortcuts built from a lifetime of social interaction that prune options in real-time moral choice, so Chidi's classroom mastery paired with real-world collapse mirrors Damasio's ventromedial patients — except Chidi has the alarms and refuses to trust them, insisting ethics is pure calculation. Mark Johnson's moral imagination (his own draft-number dilemma) and Scanlon's contractualism (morality is other people) reinforce that we are not disembodied reasoners. Combining Dewey's 'morals is education' with Damasio's claim that somatic learning never stops, the chapter explains how Eleanor and friends keep growing morally even after death — bodies, social bonds and all.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 27 "NOTES" — The section rejects the 'captain of a ship' picture of mind directing body, quoting Descartes himself on being so 'compounded and intermingled' with the body as to form 'a single whole,' and reads the Polyjuice episodes as proof: Harry in Runcorn's body naturally 'thunders' with a powerful voice and punches with an enormous fist, while Luna recognizes Harry through 'Barny's' face, impossible if mind and body were separable. The conclusion is that transformed people are unified man-dog wholes, and that even Muggle changes such as weight loss, learning to ride a bike, or Crouch-as-Moody show that changing our bodies changes who we are.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 19 "Leap of Faith" — Dionne reads Cobb's 'idea is the most resilient parasite' as a claim about narrative: what gets incepted in Fischer is a story ('my father doesn't want me to follow in his footsteps'), and by the same token each of us is a collection of incepted stories rather than a stable self. Drawing on Bergson's account of perception mediated by memory and desire (Cobb's bridge triggering Mal's projection), Nietzsche's perspectivism — truth is a 'moral prejudice' and 'we must mistake ourselves' — and the embodiment of the being-in-the-world, she argues dreams differ from reality only in degree, since both are interested story-making under time pressure. The payoff is meta-filmic: Fischer is the spectator and Cobb the director, and the final spinning top becomes the audience's own totem — there is no fact of the matter, only interpretation, so watching the ending is itself the leap of faith.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 21 "Putting One’s Mind into a Body" — Seng reads the 2008 film's crash-and-stabilizer flying lessons as philosophy of mind: at first the armor seems to confirm Descartes' dualism, with Stark the thinking substance piloting a mechanical body and Jarvis playing the pineal gland. But Stark smashing into the ceiling while learning to fly shows the embodied mind of Dewey and Merleau-Ponty — habits, spatial existence, and the imported home preferences that make the suit feel like his own skin, so that the repulsors whir closed when he stands down before the village gunmen. Dewey's view of intelligence as acting on estimates of a situation then explains Stark's growth from selfish playboy to sharable goods (beating the merely self-interested Stane), and Jarvis counts as Stark's mind made manifest in the suit.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 10 "Game versus Place" — Douglas Wilson argues that Wind Waker's Ballad of Gales warping degrades 'environmental presence' — the feeling of being in a virtual place — by privileging destination over journey, just as Wolfgang Schivelbusch said railway travel annihilated space and time for nineteenth-century passengers. Using Castells's contrast between spaces of flows and spaces of places and Michel de Certeau's opposition of the panoptic map view to embodied everyday experience, he shows how the map-grid teleport interface turns Hyrule's ocean into abstract, disposable space. He concedes warping is a defensible design compromise, but insists that goal-oriented play crowds out the sense of place that makes virtual worlds valuable as more than games.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 32 "Notes" — Di Summa reads Jenny Beavan's costume design as philosophy of technology: Immortan Joe's oxygen-fed carapace and the chrome-spraying War Boys visualize Heidegger's warning that technology converts nature and bodies into resources, while Max's blood-drip tether to Nux literalizes our co-dependence on machines — and on each other's flesh and blood. Through Rosemarie Garland-Thomson's staring, Sherri Irvin's body aesthetics, and Tobin Siebers's disability aesthetics, Furiosa's uncovered stump becomes an act of aesthetic exploration that defeats ableism: in this film, disability is a thing for heroes, and vulnerability is itself a human strength.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 19 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Spencer gives a phenomenological account of bodily transformation in the films: with Merleau-Ponty, Peter's new body changes his world — walls become surfaces to climb — and grants motor knowledge that needs no calculation, while Norman Osborn's deliberately seized powers feed pride and Doc Ock's grief shows how transformation can sweep a weak will into vice. Virtue, on Aquinas's definition as the perfection of a power, develops only through choices and habits worked out across a whole life, so ethics is deeper than rule-following. With Levinas, the call to goodness is experienced bodily: sympathy with others' suffering draws Peter out of himself — he rushes into a burning building even when powerless in Spider-Man 2 — and the Green Goblin lives a self-contradiction by feigning deafness to it, while eros for Mary Jane both distracts from and ennobles the quest.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 19 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Uses SAMCRO's ink—Jax's full Reaper backpiece and John Teller memorial, Opie's portrait of Donna, Tig's marine 'Death Before Dishonor,' Juice's head tattoos—to argue that personal identity lives in the body, not just the mind. Descartes's cogito opens the 'I ink, therefore I am' framing but proves too thin to connect the thinking Jax to the tattooed body, so the chapter turns to Merleau-Ponty's claim that 'it is the body which points out, and which speaks': the tattoo makes the body itself the expression, and its meaning stays inexhaustible as the wearer changes. The Kyle Hobart episode—burned and cut for failing to black out his Reaper after expulsion—shows tattoos as identity claims the community can veto, making 'fire or knife' an enforced correction of a false statement about who he is.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 22 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Reads Jax's '92 miles an hour' monologue in 'Sovereign' through Heidegger and Hubert Dreyfus: expert riding, Chibs's pub brawling, and Tara's surgery are pre-reflective embodied skills that conscious rule-following would only ruin. Tig fixing bikes in the Teller-Morrow garage illustrates readiness-to-hand, Bobby's smoke-spewing Fat Boy the breakdown of un-readiness-to-hand, and browsing the Harley parts catalogue the detached present-at-hand. Against the alienation of calculative, instrumental thinking (Marx, Heidegger's standing-reserve — Clay selling the club to the Galindo Cartel, Cara Cara's porn bodies), the chapter follows Pirsig: maintenance is a form of care, so Opie rebuilding a '65 Panhead after Donna's death reconciles the biker with technology instead of enslaving him to it.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 26 "Notes" — Argues Star Trek functions like the Greek myths Nussbaum describes: modern tales of transformation (Gary Mitchell in "Where No Man Has Gone Before", Charlie X, Roger Korby) that let audiences judge what makes someone human. It rejects the Cartesian reading (Richard Hanley's Is Data Human?) in which Data's humanity is just a matter of being a rational mind, and develops instead a feminist, developmental account of personhood drawn from Annette Baier: persons are "second persons" who learn the arts of personhood from caretakers. Data, Seven of Nine, and Voyager's Doctor, all lacking real childhoods and families, must learn play, touch, love, and interdependence from their crews, with Janeway modeling family for Seven and Kes socializing the Doctor. Picard's farewell to Shinzon in Nemesis and to Data's B-4 caps the claim that humanity is an achievement of self-improvement in relationship, not a fixed essence.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Applies Husserl's phenomenology - noesis (the act of meaning-giving), noema (the meaning arrived at), and the life-world - to Voyager's Doctor and Seven of Nine as they build selves from conscious experience. Reads "Latent Image" (the Doctor's deleted memories of choosing Harry Kim's life over another ensign's) and "Infinite Regress" (Seven's channeling of assimilated personalities) as parallel guilt experiences whose noemata teach each that past choices remain part of identity without governing it. Their forced isolation in "One", the Doctor's unrequited love in "Someone to Watch over Me", and "Body and Soul", where the Doctor savors food and sensation through Seven's body, generate a shared noema: social interaction and embodied experience are what make a life-world, even for photons and drones.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 29 "Notes" — Reads Jedi training through Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology and the enactivism of Varela, Thompson, and Rosch: Obi-Wan's blast-shield remote drill and Yoda's Dagobah obstacle course work because perception, thought, and action are one embodied flow rather than a perception-cognition-action 'sandwich.' Luke fails to lift the X-wing because his habits do not yet present the ship as liftable, while for Yoda 'size matters not'; and Jedi need no special Force-organ (so midi-chlorians are redundant) because skilled interaction, like Bach-y-Rita's tactile-vision subjects, determines what experience is like.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 22 "11. Of Bats and Supermen" — Springett argues Superman, not Batman, is the right goal for a transhumanist future: through Merleau-Ponty's embodied cognition (Lois's deadline nausea, Alfred recovering a thought by redoing his posture, real-life 'Subway Superman' Wesley Autrey's gut-level rescue) he shows bodies shape thought and morality, so a super-body means a super-mind. Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' becomes 'what is it like to be Superman' — a problem of superhero minds, with Doctor Manhattan's indifference as the cautionary case — while Superman's rescues of the less fit show transcendence need not slide into eugenics or Social Darwinism.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 11 "Federer as Religious Experience" — David Foster Wallace argues that watching Roger Federer live at Wimbledon delivers a near-religious experience because top sport is a prime venue for 'kinetic beauty'—a beauty rooted in human beings' reconciliation with the fact of having a body. He reads the 2006 Federer-Nadal final as a clash of the Apollonian (Federer's clinical northern artistry) against the Dionysian (Nadal's martial southern machismo), and dwells on specific Federer Moments (the reverse-thrust forehand winner against Agassi at the 2005 US Open) as instances where an athlete seems exempt from physical law. He treats Federer's grace as ineffable, defining it by what it is not, and juxtaposes the transcendent beauty of the body against the suffering body of cancer-survivor coin-tosser William Caines.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Kroustallis reads Lust, Caution through perception rather than hidden emotion, arguing Wong Chia Chi abandons the disengaged, sight-only aesthetic of Mrs. Mak and comes to perceive Mr. Yee's world with her whole engaged body. He uses Merleau-Ponty's Phenomenology of Perception to justify the three graphic sex scenes as bodily, essentially ambiguous cognition (the lipstick-marked cup, the flat key as motor intentionality) that links perception directly to action without unconscious representations. He frames Wong's development toward harmony via Fang Dongmei's neo-Confucian 'creative creativity' and a yin-yang polarity of meek and strong, with rain and jasmine flowers as an engaged natural environment.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 14 "“I am not an I” Performative (Self)Identity in the Poetry of Bob Kaufman" — Pynn reads Bob Kaufman's poems ('Forget To Not,' 'Would You Wear My Eyes?,' 'Benediction,' 'Jail Poems') as enacting a performative, intersubjective selfhood: against Beauvoir's 'flavor of death' in American conformity and Sartre's dictum that existence precedes essence, Kaufman replaces the drive to invincibility with 'nakedness' and vulnerability. Merleau-Ponty's embodied intercorporeity and Buddhist ontology—impermanence, non-self, compassion, and ahimsa—let the poet's 'I am not an I' burn the isolated ego into a communal 'thousand me's,' with slavery's trauma inscribed on the body and Kaufman's 1963 Buddhist vow of silence as liberating practice.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 20 "High Off the Page Representing the Drug Experience in the Work of Jack Kerouac and Allen Ginsberg" — Erik Mortenson argues that Kerouac's and Ginsberg's drug writing works 'through the body' to transmit the altered temporality of intoxication to the reader, using Merleau-Ponty's account of original speech and the lived body as gesture, and Deleuze and Guattari's 'Body Without Organs' and speeds. Marijuana expands the present into Kerouac's long exfoliating sentences and empathetic 'digging' (Visions of Cody, On the Road), while Benzedrine contracts it into the accelerated confessional rush of The Subterraneans; Ginsberg's LSD poems ('Lysergic Acid,' 'Wales Visitation') hit the limit of representing timelessness. The chapter concludes the writing lets the nonuser get 'high off the page' without the dependency Deleuze and Guattari warn of.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 11 "On Being John Malkovich and Not Being Yourself" — Falzon argues that Being John Malkovich stages the Cartesian self as a nonbodily homunculus — Craig 'riding' behind Malkovich's eyes via the vision-limiting cutout and muffled audio — only to expose its absurdity when Malkovich enters his own portal and finds a world reduced to 'Malkovich, Malkovich.' As Craig learns to fully inhabit and puppeteer the body, the film shifts to Merleau-Ponty's and Dewey's embodied 'lived body' organized by habit. Reading Craig's takeover as Foucauldian subjectification through training, Falzon contrasts Craig's self-entrapping mastery with Lotte's genuine self-transcendence, her openness to being other than herself.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 15 "Knockout! Killer’s Kiss, the Somatic, and Kubrick Kevin S. Decker" — Decker reads Killer's Kiss (and later 2001, A Clockwork Orange, Eyes Wide Shut) through Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology of the lived body ('I am my body'), recovering the somatic that Socrates and Plato's Phaedo denigrated. In Killer's Kiss the boxing match, the mannequin-warehouse fight where bodies become weapons, spatial camera work, and the theme of contingency foreground embodiment; 2001 makes viewers feel their own bodies in space, and A Clockwork Orange's Ludovico 'cure' rewires the body-mind. Drawing on pragmatists Shusterman and Sullivan and on Foucault's biopower, he argues the anonymous masked bodies of Eyes Wide Shut turn Merleau-Ponty's projective intentionality into domination rather than communication.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 16 "2001 A Philosophical Odyssey" — Stoehr interprets Kubrick's 2001 as inducing a feeling of disembodied presence through unrooted camerawork (contrasted with Ford's The Searchers), matching its theme of technology severing us from the natural world and our bodies. Drawing on Heidegger's Dasein and Hubert Dreyfus's On the Internet, he argues there are no context-free Archimedean standpoints and stages the Plato-versus-Nietzsche debate over the body: Plato's Phaedo prizes the soul's escape from the body, while Nietzsche's Zarathustra affirms embodied, situated existence. HAL's seeming humanity underscores that machines lacking bodies cannot fully replicate human intelligence.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Decker reads Killer's Kiss (with 2001, A Clockwork Orange, and Eyes Wide Shut) to recover the philosophy of the body against the Socratic-Platonic-Cartesian denigration of the somatic. Using Merleau-Ponty's existential phenomenology ('I am my body') and pragmatists like Shusterman and Sullivan, he shows Kubrick's obsessive use of space, contingency, and the visceral - Davy's boxing match, the mannequin-warehouse fight, the weightless bodies of 2001, the Ludovico brainwashing of Alex, and the anonymous masked bodies of Eyes Wide Shut - to argue that subjectivity is corporeal and that anonymity of bodies can fund Foucauldian domination rather than liberation.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 15 "The Violated Body Affective Experience and Somatic Intensity in Zero Dark Thirty" — Burgoyne argues that Kathryn Bigelow's Zero Dark Thirty places the violated body at the center of its rendering of the War on Terror, using somatic intensity and affective experience against Steven Shaviro's reading of the film as pure, affect-draining proceduralism. He traces Maya's arc from witness to coercive agent through the torture of Ammar, the Goya-like montage of interrogation videos, and the suicide-bomb killing of her friend Jessica, mapping the film onto Sarah Cole's poles of disenchanted violence (the raw, exposed flesh of the interrogations) and enchanted violence (the technologically choreographed, almost magical SEAL raid on Abbottabad, likened to Baudrillardian simulated combat). The closing unzipping of bin Laden's body bag deflates any triumph into embodied ambiguity.
- **The Philosophy of Werner Herzog**, ch. 16 "Werner Herzog and the Documentary as a Revelatory Practice" — Antony Fredriksson argues that Herzog's documentaries are not veridical fact-representations but a 'revelatory practice,' aligning Herzog's ecstatic-versus-accountant's-truth distinction with phenomenology (Merleau-Ponty, Husserl, Waldenfels). Using Merleau-Ponty's reading of Fabrice at Waterloo, he claims lived experience is contingent and pre-narrative, and that films like La Soufriere (a catastrophe that never happens), White Diamond (swifts behind the waterfall), and Echoes from a Somber Empire (the nicotine-addicted monkey) reveal the alien, attention-grabbing world beyond habitual seeing — a 'pathos' that reads the viewer rather than neutrally recording facts.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 8 "06_LaRocca_Chapter_005.html" — Sobchack offers a semiotic phenomenology of how real death is represented in documentary, arguing that death itself always exceeds and confounds indexical representation—we never see death, only dying and the corpse. Using Aries on the modern taboo-ing of natural death, Barthes on the traumatic photograph, and the Zapruder assassination footage whose frame-by-frame scrutiny yields only mystification, she shows why violent, abrupt mortification of the lived body is the most effective cinematic sign of death. Drawing on Heidegger's Being-toward-death and its deferral, Beauvoir's 'no such thing as a natural death,' and Merleau-Ponty's lived body, she classifies documentary's ethical 'gazes' at death (accidental, helpless, endangered, interventional, humane, professional) as inscriptions of the filmmaker's moral stance in an embodied ethical space.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 29 "27_LaRocca_Chapter_026.html" — Michael Fried reads Douglas Gordon and Philippe Parreno's Zidane: A Twenty-First Century Portrait, seventeen synchronized cameras trained on Zinedine Zidane through one Real Madrid match, as a portrait that lays bare a new relation between absorption and being-beheld. Set within Fried's own absorption/theatricality tradition, the film shows Zidane wholly absorbed yet acutely conscious of eighty thousand spectators ('you are never alone'), which Fried reads via Heidegger's notion that even this 'bare' absorbed consciousness discloses a shared world (underscored by the halftime global news montage). He then stages the film as evidence in the McDowell-Dreyfus dispute over whether perception is conceptual, arguing that Zidane's 'expert coping' looks 'permeated by mindedness' (McDowell) rather than the non-conceptual absorbed coping Dreyfus, following Merleau-Ponty's embodied phenomenology, describes.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 20 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Acton draws on her anthropological fieldwork riding to hounds in English foxhound packs to explore the human/equine partnership with the 'made hunter' horse. Using Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology of the body-in-movement and Tim Ingold's notion of 'dwelling,' she argues the rider experiences the hunt through 'muscular consciousness' and 'centaur hours,' taking on the horse's senses and physicality. Trusting the sharp horse to 'work it out' — as when her hunter checked pace to avoid a collision at a jump — becomes an embodied, timeless collaboration binding rider, horse, hounds, and landscape.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 35 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Through the narrative of 'Aisha', a feminist who is aroused by SM imagery she has been taught to disown, Khan attacks the censorship of SM pornography and its 'monkey see, monkey do' harm hypothesis (citing declining rape rates). She names three state-inflicted harms: physical violence (prison sentences in Guglielmi and R. v. Brown), phenomenological violence—using Husserl and Merleau-Ponty's embodied phenomenology to argue courts dismiss submissives' lived reality as 'worthless'—and epistemic violence, using Foucault's power/knowledge to show how the Supreme Court of Canada in Little Sisters overrode expert and practitioner testimony about coded SM meaning. She argues SM consent and pleasure are real knowledge that censorship, aligned with MacKinnon/Dworkin anti-porn feminism, coercively erases.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 18 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Brunstein surveys emerging wearable technology — solar-charging jackets, the M-Dress cell-phone dress, invisibility cloaks, the Hug Shirt, Diana Eng's Heartbeat Hoodie — framed by superhero costumes (Wonder Woman's lasso, Iron Man's exoskeleton) and Haraway's 'Cyborg Manifesto.' She argues that as garments start to *do* things and integrate aesthetically, the grotesque cyborg becomes the glamorous 'supermodel' cyborg, and that this reshapes how we construct the self. Her central philosophical lens is Clark and Chalmers's 'extended mind' / active externalism (with the Tetris example): if clothing becomes a functional extension of cognition, our garments' capabilities become part of a reconstructed self.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 17 "GARDENING" — Michael Moss examines how the British grew Brussels sprouts and other 'English' vegetables across the Empire to recreate home and 'put down roots,' reading gardens as tropes of Britishness and imperial identity. He draws on David Cooper's claim—rooted in Heidegger's and Merleau-Ponty's notions of dynamic, embodied engagement—that 'certain garden practices necessarily induce virtues,' which colonial writers invoked to justify gardening's moral and civilizing purpose. He exposes the irony that most 'British' vegetables were themselves appropriated introductions, mirroring Kew's plant-hunting empire.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 31 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Karlsen argues that climbing routes are genuine aesthetic objects and that judging a route beautiful is a real aesthetic judgment, not mere pleasure. Against Kant's demand that beauty require detachment (which would confine climbing to the 'merely agreeable') and against Aristotle's exclusion of the bodily senses, he distinguishes a 'line' (seen from the ground, like The Nose) from a 'route' (actually climbed) and contends that proprioception, the felt sense of bodily movement, yields information about the route itself, not just the body. Invoking the phenomenological 'transparency of experience' (Moore's diaphanousness), he concludes proprioception is an aesthetic sense that lets widely-agreed classics emerge.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 21 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Rachel Falkenstern argues that although tattoos seem permanent, the embodied self is changing and finite, so tattoos are 'illusions of permanence.' Using Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology she dissolves the mind/body and self/tattoo boundary (we are our bodies, the world shapes us and we shape it); using the German aesthetic tradition from Kant to Hegel she reads a tattoo as a sensuous 'appearance of freedom' and links the Romantic notion of Bildung (self-formation) to choosing ink. She adds Foucault's aesthetic self-transformation and Shusterman's somaesthetics/Deweyan pragmatism to cast tattooing as reciprocal self-expression and self-creation that offers a glimpse of infinity within finitude.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 27 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Lee argues that tattooing is a performative 'practice of writing' whose meaning always exceeds its origin, comparing Holocaust survivor Tova Friedman's Auschwitz number 'A27633' with the Suicide Girl Jaylin's chosen feminist ink. Drawing on Judith Butler's account of the body as a site of inscription and counter-inscription, and Walter Benjamin's 'Critique of Violence' distinguishing law-making from law-preserving force, she claims Friedman's tattoo resists the Nazi law itself while Jaylin's only satirizes heteropatriarchy. She then invokes Baudrillard's 'ecstasy of communication' and the obscene to show tattooing can desubjectify by dissolving the embodied self into pornographic information.

### Amor Fati (love of fate)

Amor fati, Latin for "love of fate," is Nietzsche's formula for the highest affirmation of life: not merely to endure what happens but to love it, wanting nothing to be different in the past, present, or future. It stands opposed to resentment and to the wish that reality were other than it is, treating even suffering and necessity as things to be embraced rather than merely tolerated. Nietzsche presents this loving acceptance of one's whole existence as a sign of psychological greatness and a companion to his idea of eternal recurrence.

- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 18 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Eric Bronson places Tolkien among the 'sometimes merry' existentialists: Nietzsche's artist who says Yes amid catastrophe and needs 'the power to forget', Jaspers on machines estranging us from our past, and Arendt on Eichmann's obedient inhumanity and the few who create joy in dark times. The elves' songs in Rivendell and Lórien are joy born of sorrow and dispossession - Galadriel suffers because she remembers too much, trying to 'embalm time', while Arwen forgoes immortality for Aragorn. Her refusal of the Ring ('I will diminish, and go into the West, and remain Galadriel') embodies the existentialist affirmation: trust your own light, know what to remember and what to forget.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 30 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Lenore Wright reads Sam and Frodo's Quest through the two journey motifs of Western philosophy: the journey out (Plato's cave, structuring Augustine's Confessions and Descartes' escape from the senses' deceptions) and the journey inward (the cogito, self-transformation, with Nussbaum's claim that literature gives philosophy a body). Frodo's steps out of the Shire-cave - selling Bag End, 'I will take the Ring, though I do not know the way' - create the Fellowship and its freedoms, while Boromir attains self-knowledge only at death's door and Gandalf, Aragorn, and Sam are remade by the road. Against classical heroes like Theseus and Odysseus, Sam and Frodo are modern pilgrims - Nietzschean Yea-sayers becoming who they are, with Heideggerian 'potentiality-for-Being' - whereas Sméagol and Saruman live inauthentically, defined by their pasts.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 24 "Tarantula’s End" — Goldblatt and Necarsulmer pair Dylan's Tarantula with Nietzsche's "The Tarantulas" from Zarathustra: both are books of advice, renaming, and stream-of-consciousness flow whose sections cohere through signature and attitude rather than narrative (the same Foucauldian author function). Both embody the intuitive artist of Plato's Ion and Nietzsche's Ecce Homo - the poet as medium whose language arrives as inspiration, all language being fresh or stale metaphor. Tarantula's vengeful vignettes and "Idiot Wind" dramatize the ressentiment Zarathustra warns against, its impenetrable juxtapositions ("harmonica battalions," "funeral landlord") work as Derridean catachresis - metaphor whose transfer fails yet exerts aesthetic force - and the book's dream of the burning tenement leaves Dylan unable, and absolved, to look back.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 29 "Will You Say Yes" — Bruce finds Nietzsche's eternal return in the NES Zelda's clockless, endlessly restartable structure: the same game recurs every time you press start, yet since the player changes, each playthrough manifests the forces anew, and the demon's question 'do you desire this once more?' becomes 'do you will to play once more?'. Link's growth through eight dungeons to face Ganon is read as will-to-power, personal strength and self-overcoming rather than mere domination, and saying yes to the struggle is amor fati. Against Plato's two-worlds doctrine of Forms and the Christian after-worldly (both Nietzsche's targets), the original Zelda offers no guide, no Bible, and no linear time to a final judgment: this looped world is the only one, so it must be affirmed.
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 16 "How We Still Might Manage a Smile Being Pirates and Making Meaning" — Adam Glover reads 'A Pirate Looks at Forty' through Kristeva's intertextuality: since every text and self is a 'mosaic of quotations' pirated from pre-existing sources, Buffett's confession that he was born 'two hundred years too late' makes him an ironic pirate who can no longer believe or plunder unselfconsciously, unlike the oblivious common-sense pirate. Invoking Barthes's death of the author, he argues the pirate's life is a hard freedom to improvise multiple meanings (the ever-changing 'head uptown' variations in the song) with full responsibility for one's choices. The chapter ends weighing Camus's worry that meaninglessness makes life not worth living against the Nietzsche of The Birth of Tragedy, who answers that the meaning of life is life itself, and it sides with Buffett against Socrates's 'unexamined life' while admitting it cannot settle the question.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 10 "15" — Three 'Phase Four' essays. Moseley reads the Joker across Batman #1, The Killing Joke, The Dark Knight, A Death in the Family, and Dark Knight Returns as a 'moral monster' who knowingly does evil - and, following Anscombe and Scanlon's guise-of-the-good analysis, pursues aesthetic 'higher values' in a Camus-like affirmation of the absurd, embracing the irrationality Batman's rational moral order cannot fathom. Levin uses X-gene biology (Beast's explanation in Astonishing X-Men, genotype vs phenotype, M-Day) to strip Magneto's Homo sapiens superior claim of any genetic or phenotypic basis, then argues via the moral community of rational persons (Kant's criterion) that mutants and humans share one moral community, condemning both the Registration Act and mutant separatism. O'Neil's prose piece traces Harvey Dent from Calvinist certainty through the acid that scars him to cosmic doubt - quantum randomness, many worlds, Sartre's condemnation to freedom - until Nietzsche's amor fati lets him embrace duality and let the scarred two-headed coin decide good and evil.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 11 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Auxier argues the trilogy is narrated on a Nietzschean lattice rather than being a mere inverted Milton: after tracing the Paradise Lost, Genesis 6, and Pseudepigrapha sources (Azazel as the model for Asriel, Metatron from Third Enoch, Dust from Milton's warring particles), he reads Mrs. Coulter's speech to Father MacPhail about seeking God out and giving him 'the gift of death' as Nietzsche's death of God fused with a description of Nietzsche's own final dementia. Will and Lyra become overman and overwoman beyond good and evil: Will rises by his will and his willingness to kill (the alethiometer's verdict 'He is a murderer' makes him a worthy companion), while Lyra commands both truth and lies, the alethiometer embodying truth as 'a mobile army of metaphors.' But the chapter's payoff is critical: Pullman does not endorse Nietzsche, since in a world where the will to power dominates, the overwoman Mrs. Coulter has no place and falls with Asriel and Metatron into the Abyss, while Xaphania's teaching offers a disciplined, workful imagination as an alternative.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 161 "Chapter 25 - Untimely Speculations" — Heath Massey's introduction to Chapter 25 opens with Nietzsche's Gay Science passage on intellects that might experience time backward, then stages the demon of eternal recurrence: every pain and joy returning in the same sequence in a world without aim, which either crushes you or becomes 'the highest formula of affirmation', amor fati. Eternal recurrence is a test of the will separating 'man' from 'overman', since one could not celebrate it while believing the world needs a divine purpose. The chapter then maps Dick's imaginative variations of temporality onto two Nietzschean tendencies - disruptions of time-sense that render characters powerless, and extraordinary temporalities that liberate them beyond finite human time, culminating in Dick's theory of supertemporality.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 23 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Brandon Kempner reads Gaiman's Batman: Whatever Happened to the Caped Crusader? as Nietzschean eternal recurrence: Batman dies and is reborn as the infant Bruce Wayne to repeat his life exactly, because Gaiman first strips away every teleological ending, Catwoman kills Batman, Alfred reveals he invented the Joker, and the Moore-style domestic bliss of the Superman farewell is denied. With God dead there is no Heaven, telos, or external reward, so, like Nietzsche's Overman who creates values above the city's conventional morality, Batman's meaning can lie only in the lived repetition itself: 'the only reward you get for being Batman? You get to be Batman,' the highest formula of life-affirmation. Kempner extends the pattern to the funeral-framed rebirth of a new Dream in Sandman: The Wake, showing Gaiman's recurring obsession with cycles that have 'no endings' across his work.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 32 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Rard tests whether objective morality survives the apocalypse by running four theories against Season Two: Plato's Forms explain universal truths about walkers ('walkers survive so long as their brains are relatively undamaged') but cannot handle white lies or changed circumstances, and Aristotle's virtue ethics reads Rick's rush from the shot Carl as rashness and Shane's supply run as courage, yet virtues prove relative and luck-dependent in a collapsed world. Natural law founders on clashing intuitions — Merle's racism and Hershel's barn of walkers each claim self-evidence. The chapter's center is Nietzschean: Hershel's barn is slave morality that pities the 'sick,' Maggie breaks from it, and Shane's sacrifice of Otis and opening of the barn enact a will-to-power master morality without joy, while Rick alone moves toward amor fati — embracing the world as it is, refusing guilt over Lori's affair, and insisting the baby be born into the Walk Age.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 21 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Clifton measures Omar against four Nietzschean criteria for the overman: as a free spirit he is 'in the wind, so to speak,' detached from home, money, and eventually even lovers like Brandon and Butchie; as a non-dogmatist about truth he uses it as a tool, lying under oath at Bird's trial yet sparing Brother Mouzone when the lie no longer holds; and as a noble of the Genealogy he is an active hunter who embraces the will to power, telling Wee-Bey 'you come at the king, you best not miss.' But Omar fails the fourth test, value-creation: his code keeps the good/evil scale intact rather than overturning it, so in the Three Metamorphoses he remains the lion who slays 'Thou Shalt' but never becomes the value-creating child. The verdict, in Nietzsche's own phrase, is that Omar is noble but 'human, all too human.'
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 30 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Brittingham argues The Wire is a Nietzschean rather than merely Aristotelian tragedy, a wrestling between the Apollonian orientation of order, statistics, and illusion (Rawls's clearance rates, Burrell's bureaucracy, Stringer's business plans) and the Dionysian reveling in the Game's chaos and suffering (Avon accepting that 'you only gotta fuck up once', McNulty's intoxicated self-destruction). Stringer is Nietzsche's 'theoretical man' whose faith that thought can correct existence, embodied in the New Day Co-Op, cannot save him from Omar's 'It ain't about money', while McNulty is the Dionysiac man inside the Apollonian institution until Freamon's 'the job will not save you' forces his resignation. The chapter closes by reading the characters' resigned embrace of their fates as Nietzschean affirmation: since neither the job, intelligence, violence, nor the gods will save you, the only response is to say yes to life anyway.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 28 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Laderoute reads 'The Late Philip J. Fry' - the forward-only time machine overshooting past the year one billion and the last protons to a second Big Bang and an identical universe (ten feet lower, conveniently crushing its duplicates) - as a tour of cosmology from Aristotle's static, eternal, Earth-centered heavens through the Stoics' providential determinism and fiery ekpyrosis to Big Bang cosmology and heat death, which is why the Professor is so shocked. Nietzsche's Gay Science 341 supplies the existential payoff: faced with living identically forever, one can react with horror or delight, and eternal recurrence becomes a challenge to become the person you want to be. Fry, a billion years late for his Cavern on the Green dinner, reads Leela's message carved in stone, and in the repeated universe finally arrives on time - 'That was the old Fry... he's dead now' - amor fati enacted.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 45 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Steven Neumann reads the sold-my-soul legends around Led Zeppelin ('here's to my sweet Satan' backwards on 'Stairway to Heaven'), Black Sabbath, and bluesman Robert Johnson at the Clarksdale crossroads as a parable of Nietzsche's amor fati: every joy comes bundled with suffering, so greatness means affirming the whole package. He deploys the eternal recurrence thought experiment - would you will your life, Plant's dead son and Bonham's fatal bender included, to repeat eternally? - and contrasts the ascetic denial of pleasure with Nietzsche's claim in Ecce Homo that his own sickness and obscurity made him love fate all the more.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 27 "14. The Doctor’s Desire for Human Suffering" — Cooper reads 'Rise of the Cybermen' and 'The Age of Steel' as staging Nietzsche against Mill's pain-eradicating utilitarianism: John Lumic, who builds the Cybermen to abolish his sickness, exemplifies the life-denying herd—losing his creativity, craving 'unity and uniformity,' becoming 'a living brain with a heart of steel'—while the Doctor, answering that a life without pain would be 'you might as well kill me,' affirms suffering as the source of creativity, striving, and strength. She extends the Nietzschean reading to the Doctor's character: his guilt over the Time War double-genocide and his loneliness ('the only certainty left is that you'll end up alone') become the pain that makes him merciful, from offering Dalek Caan compassion after 'Evolution of the Daleks' to forgiving the Master in 'Last of the Time Lords,' so that mercy is, as the Genealogy of Morals says, 'the privilege of the most powerful man.'
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 12 "1. Everything’s Amazing and Nobody’s Happy" — Max Elder reads Louis through Nietzsche's Gay Science claim that all philosophy is unconscious memoir, arguing Louis's confession-like comedy reveals dark truths we would rather flee - the Conan 'everything's amazing and nobody's happy' bit, the 'I know the darkness' exchange with the Christian woman, and the Subway/Pamela scene where a homeless man bathes behind a subway violinist. Using Nietzsche's line that man alone laughs because he suffers so deeply, and The Birth of Tragedy's comic as the artistic discharge of the nausea of absurdity, the chapter argues Louis's laughter performs a gestalt switch that ties the ugly to the beautiful and so redeems it. It reads the religions-supply-meaning argument - God's mockery-laughter versus Nietzsche's holy laughter - as the reason redemption now happens in comedy clubs rather than churches, and closes with Louie's 'Country Drive' scolding of Jane ('you don't get to be bored') as Nietzschean embrace of the amazing fact of being alive.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 21 "9. My Dharma Is the Road that Never Ends" — Reads Twin Peaks: The Return as a commitment to Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and amor fati: Cooper is trapped in an existential time loop (Dougie's relearning, Wally's Part 4 Dharma speech, the final-episode Cooper/Richard do-over) and must learn to love every horrific repetition, quoting the Gay Science demon passage and Nietzsche's Will to Power on enduring recurrence. The chapter frames Lynch and Frost as Romantics — Novalis on wonder, Isaiah Berlin's Roots of Romanticism on the artist's inner vision — who break three storytelling rules (authors create stories, protagonists solve problems, stories have endings), so that Laura's mystery stays a living Jack-the-Ripper-style mystery and the story becomes a meta-narrative co-created with viewers, echoing Buddhist pratityasamutpada and Russell's beginningless world. Cooper's finale is a Sisyphean task he accepts, making his integrity the audience's own test.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 14 "5. The Funny Thing about Being Yourself" — Reads Schumer's comedy as Nietzschean self-creation: like the tightrope walker over the abyss she confronts who she is, says 'Yes' to life in the spirit of the eternal recurrence and amor fati, and 'gives style' to her character by wearing mistakes as badges of honor, notably reclaiming her paparazzi photos in the Leather Special. Balke then casts her as Rorty's ironist, whose continual burning of old material keeps her free of a 'final vocabulary' in a contingent world, with 'Amy Goes Deep' doing the Rortian work of testing herself against others. He closes with George Herbert Mead's account of a self formed through social interaction with significant others.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 3 "A Strange Realization" — Dunn argues that Strange begins as a foot soldier of the Baconian project (Bacon and Descartes' program of conquering nature and treating death as an enemy to be subdued, embodied in his surgical God-complex and neurogenesis research), and that its shipwreck drives him to Kamar-Taj. Using Nietzsche, he reads both Strange and Kaecilius as sick with the 'spirit of revenge against time' — Kaecilius fleeing into Dormammu's timeless Dark Dimension as Nietzsche's Hinterweltler, Strange clinging to his unrecoverable past. The climactic 'Dormammu, I've come to bargain' time loop is interpreted as Nietzsche's eternal return weaponized, and Strange's 'Pain's an old friend' as his achievement of amor fati, echoing the Ancient One's dying claim that death is what gives life meaning.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 29 "17. Downton Abbey as Eternal Recurrence" — Christopher Ketcham provocatively equates primogeniture and entail - the legal machinery that returns Downton intact to each generation - with Nietzsche's 'greatest weight,' the eternal recurrence. Working through Lawrence Hatab's five interpretations of the doctrine, he asks whether the Abbey's continuity is cosmological (it is not, since estate taxes and squandering heirs keep chipping away), a Zarathustra-style life-affirming yes to the agrarian world against the 'nihilism' of capitalist fashion, or merely symbolic like a listing in Burke's Peerage beside fossilized dinosaur bones. His answer comes via Violet, the family, and the servants, who have 'become one with the property': the Abbey recurs only anthropomorphically, and even that stickiness is dissolving under industrialization, the death tax, and the war that killed off three royal cousins' empires.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 14 "NOTES" — Shores reads Volume 1 through Nietzsche's eternal recurrence as a self-test of life-affirmation: Adam sealed in a coffin embodies recurrence in its 'most terrible form,' Future Hiro's string map dramatizes Nietzsche's claim that every action is indissolubly tied to all others, and Linderman's speech divorcing happiness from meaning is answered by Nietzsche's demand to crave nothing more fervently than the eternal return. The chapter stresses where the show diverges: Claire insists 'the future is not written in stone' and the heroes rewrite destiny, while Arthur Petrelli ironically holds a copy of Thus Spoke Zarathustra while contradicting it. Hiro's failed attempts to save Charlie and his father (Kaito's 'we cannot play God') frame the amor fati question of whether free will means changing events or willing them eternally.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 14 "Notes" — Argues against the title claim of the previous chapter: Frank is a Nietzschean master type — he defines good as good-for-him, embraces pain as strength, and keeps no allegiances once Walker and Vasquez break their promise — while Peter Russo is the paradigmatic reactive slave who cannot command himself and blames others, exactly Nietzsche's 'he who cannot command himself is commanded'. But the overman requires self-overcoming, the sublimation of drives into creation, and amor fati, and Frank only dominates others for vengeful ends: his whole scheme grows from ressentiment over the Secretary of State snub, he affirms other wills merely as investments, and in Season 3 he becomes a slave to his own position. The chapter uses the Cesare Borgia misreading (better a Borgia than a Parsifal as raw material, but Borgia was no overman), Napoleon's corruption, and Goethe's creative wholeness to conclude that Frank remains 'all-too-human' — destruction without creation.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 14 "Notes" — Meyer mounts the counter-case: Frank exemplifies Nietzsche's master type (good as good-for-him, 'no longer are we bound by allegiances') and Russo the slave type ('he who cannot command himself is commanded'), but the overman is a synthesis of neither. He corrects the Leopold-and-Loeb 'above the law' reading and the Cesare Borgia identification: the genuine overman sublimates strong drives into creation — Goethe's self-discipline, Beethoven's new norms — and affirms other wills in themselves rather than as instruments, which Frank never does with Zoe, Peter, or Claire. Frank's revenge-driven scheming is slave-like psychological warfare, ruling others is the 'pettiest' form of power, and by Season 3 he is the slave of his own presidency — destructive without creating, and lacking even amor fati.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 17 "7 Indiana Jones and Existential Self-Affirmation" — Daniel Tilsley reads The Last Crusade as an excavation of identity: the fedora Fedora bestows after young Indy's defeat, the twenty-six-year quest for the Cross of Coronado ('All my life'), and the chosen name 'Indiana' (taken from the family dog) are acts of Nietzschean self-affirmation — amor fati and the willingness to will the Eternal Recurrence of one's life. The villains fail because they seek external artifacts to patch deficient lives, whereas the Grail Knight, like Camus's Sisyphus, authentically affirms his endless task of guarding the cup. The arc completes when Henry Sr. finally calls his son 'Indiana' while hanging from the abyss, recognizing the man he chose to become, and Crystal Skull repeats the pattern with Mutt and the fedora's eventual inheritance.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 29 "Will You Say Yes" — Michael Bruce ('Zeldathustra') reads the original Legend of Zelda through Nietzsche's thought of eternal recurrence: with no game clock, the ability to save, and looped enemy patterns, every playthrough repeats the same structure, and the player faces the demon's question — do you will to play once more and innumerable times more? The Triforce's split between Wisdom and Power becomes Nietzsche's opposition of the will-to-truth and the will-to-power, with Link's dungeon-by-dungeon self-overcoming enacting amor fati. Against Plato's two-world doctrine of Forms and the Christian after-worldly, the chapter insists the game (like life) gets its meaning from this world only — experimentation, repetition as training, and saying yes.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 26 "Notes" — Conway reads Fury Road as a homecoming (nostos) story that overturns Homer's patriarchal template of Odysseus: Furiosa's trusted Green Place proves as idealistic as the War Boys' Valhalla, and both are diagnosed by Nietzsche's critique of idealism as 'mendaciousness in the face of what is necessary.' The cure is amor fati joined to Max's flinty realism — turn around and make a home by retaking the Citadel — while Hegel's master-slave dialectic explains Immortan Joe's unacknowledged dependency on the women he enslaves for milk, heirs, and recognition. The film ends with Furiosa raised up as a matriarchal ruler and Max departing as the self-exiled wounded healer, barred by his own guilt from the green place he helped make.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 40 "Notes" — Argues Q embodies Nietzsche's revaluation of values: contemptuous of herd-like safety, Q subjects Picard and the crew to trials ("Encounter at Farpoint", "Hide and Q", "All Good Things"'s "the trial never ends") meant to force growth beyond conventional morality, seek out other "supermen", and embrace risk - Q's "bloody nose" defense after eighteen crewmen die at the Borg in "Q Who?". The Borg figure as everything Nietzschean individualism despises, a mindless collectivism that robs drones of the passion the strong need to individuate, and Q's offer to join Picard as guide pictures a friendship between Nietzsche's self-mastered few.
