- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 21 "Buffy As a Watcher (of Sorts)" — Jason Kawal tests virtue ethics's 'act as the virtuous person would act' (Hursthouse's criterion) against Xander's 'What would Buffy do?': Buffy qualifies as a moral exemplar with heroic actions (nightly patrols, the 'Gift' plunge) and saintly sacrifices (the 'Doublemeat Palace' McJob for Dawn), but imitation fails — Xander lacks her abilities, tastes, relationships, and pure bravery, and stripping those away one by one turns Buffy into a copy of Xander. Worse, much of what Buffy does is supererogatory (Giles: 'She's a hero... She's not like us' in 'The Gift,' before killing Ben himself), so ordinary people are not morally required to do what she would do. His fix: ask what a fully informed, unimpaired virtuous observer — an 'angelic Buffy looking over our shoulders,' never drugged into 'Beer Bad' cave-Buffy — would deem right for us, given our own abilities and commitments.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 85 "Abilities" — Bassham tests each sense of choice against the novels: internal-choices are uninformative (Dudley resolving to give up sweets), act-choices mislead since character is settled habit - Hermione's occasional rule-breaking for Dumbledore's Army doesn't make her a rebel - and overt acts cannot reveal motives, as Snape's apparent Death Eater loyalty conceals devotion to Dumbledore and Lily. Motive-choices like Harry's decision to enter the Chamber to save Ginny are most revealing, but self-deception (Vernon Dursley's rationalizations) and wizarding complications - Harry's vision of attacking Arthur Weasley, Voldemort's implanted false memory in Morfin Gaunt, the Imperius Curse, Polyjuice Potion, and a Priori Incantatem thought experiment - show that in Rowling's world choices may be unknowable even to their maker.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 32 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Anna Lännström runs a full moral-responsibility audit on Gibson's tormented, remorseful Judas: Aristotle's analysis of excusing conditions (insanity, Satanic possession, ignorance) partly alleviates his guilt as it does Peter's denial; Boethius's timelessly eternal God is deployed against the foreknowledge problem and then criticized as self-defeating; and the Edwards/Frankfurt compatibilist solution is applied — Judas could not have done otherwise because God would not have permitted it, yet acted freely since he did what he wanted. Consequentialism (Mill) oddly makes the betrayal nearly harmless or even salvific, Kantian intention-analysis turns on whether Judas was a greedy embezzler or a Zealot trying to force a revolt, and virtue ethics weighs his immediate remorse and attempt to return the silver against the habitual greed John and Matthew attribute to him.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 15 "Defining a Hero and a Superhero" — Loeb and Morris take on the argument that 'superhero' is an oxymoron - the more super (and invulnerable) a being, the less it risks, so the less heroic it can be, which would disqualify Superman except under Kryptonite. They rebut it by insisting heroism is a moral category: a hero is a person of noble character whose worthy achievements are guided by the good, so a superhero is a person of noble character with superhuman powers or superhumanly developed abilities, which gets Batman and Green Arrow into the fray. They extend heroism to everyday firefighters, nurses, and stay-at-home mothers, and use J. Jonah Jameson's resentment of Spider-Man to show how the hero's sacrifice stands as a standing rebuke to spectators' inertia.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 16 "How to Be a Hero" — Using Superman for All Seasons, the authors argue that Clark's heroic choice required real sacrifice - leaving his family, Smallville, and Lana Lang to serve more people - and that sacrifice and the self-discipline behind it are underappreciated virtues, down payments on great goods attainable no other way, as with Peter Parker and Matt Murdock too. The hero, they say, is a normative concept with a claim on us, and since Plato held that the good is inherently attractive and draws us toward it, well-told superhero stories have genuine moral force, keeping self-discipline, self-sacrifice, and aspiration alive while entertaining us.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 18 "The Example of the Superhero" — Quoting Seneca's advice to 'choose for yourself a moral hero' as an ethical pattern and to 'live as if he were watching you', the chapter argues that superheroes can function for us exactly as the Stoic recommended: Superman inspires us, Batman keeps us going when the going is tough, Spider-Man teaches that conscience outranks the crowd's voices, and Daredevil shows that limitations need not hold us back. It closes practically: ask 'What would Superman do?' and go do your version of it.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 23 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Gayne Anacker defines moral imagination, the capacity to see one's values and life from fresh moral perspectives, and argues the Chronicles exercise it through three character types readers live through: flawed repenters (Edmund, Eustace, Bree, Aravis), the essentially good under trial (Lucy believing her Aslan sighting in Prince Caspian, Caspian's greed on Goldwater Island), and the fatally self-absorbed (Uncle Andrew, Shift), together with portrayals of worship and of true versus usurped nobility (Peter versus Miraz). Philosophically he contends the stories' effectiveness supports virtue ethics over action-centered modern theories, and that disagreement among ethical theorists is no ground for relativism: no one needs theoretical consensus to know Miraz is evil.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 23 "A Call to Unchanging Truths" — Francis Beckwith argues the 1979-81 Christian albums are no aberration: Dylan's whole career presupposes moral realism, an objective moral law built into the universe - "Dignity never been photographed" names an irreducible moral property, and the judgments in "With God on Our Side" and "Blowin' in the Wind" only make sense if right and wrong are unchanging across eras. The six-month sentence William Zanzinger receives in "The Lonesome Death of Hattie Carroll" is condemned on retributive, lex talionis grounds rather than any utilitarian calculus of consequences, and "Forever Young" and "What Good Am I?" urge virtue practiced for its own sake. The chapter thus reads Dylan's conversion as the surfacing of commitments - against relativism, for virtue and unchanging truths - always latent in songs like "The Times They Are A-Changin'."
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 41 "It’s Not That Simple" — Donal O'Mathuna uses 24 to run the torture debate: the ticking bomb scenario (Syed Ali's nuclear bomb, Miles pressing to torture Audrey) dramatizes the utilitarian case for forward-looking interrogational torture, while Jack slicing off the Russian consul's finger and Morris's broken guilt show torture as a deontological violation that destroys character on both sides and usually fails to extract truth. Against the show's sanitized, banal presentation (Agent Burke as the "kindly torturer"), he sets Abu Ghraib, the systematic training of torturers, and the metastatic spread of torture programs once permitted. Fiction can open the ethical question, he concludes, but must not be mistaken for the reality of torture.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 12 "Lessons Learned" — Curry argues that The Wiz, the all-Black 1978 remake, dramatizes the acquisition of a distinctively Black 'racial virtue'—a habitual excellence defined in quasi-Aristotelian terms and grounded in W.E.B. Du Bois's picture of races as 'vast families' bound by common history and a divinely rooted race feeling (with Alexander Crummell and William H. Ferris as supporting race theorists). Dorothy, a Harlem kindergarten teacher who has never been south of 125th Street, lacks knowledge of self, and each companion personifies a virtue she must claim: the newspaper-stuffed Scarecrow, whose crows' 'crow commandments' and song 'You Can't Win' embody internalized racist miseducation; the Tin Man's capacity for feeling; and Fleetwood Coupe de Ville's courage outside the New York Public Library, glossed through Ferris's call for 'lion-like men.' Evillene's sweatshop creed that 'suffering is food for the soul' personifies the redemptive-suffering myth and failed-integrationism the chapter rejects, while Glinda's 'believe in yourself' and 'A Brand New Day' make honest admittance of racial reality the precondition of 'co-authoring' the world.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 25 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Neil maps Optimus Prime onto Joseph Campbell's hero's journey: the naive dock worker Orion Pax is deceived and nearly killed by Megatron, rebuilt by the ancient Primus as the first Autobot, and raised to leadership through the four stages of separation, trials, supernatural aid, and return. Evolutionary 'group-fitness' psychology explains why children wept at his 1986 death, and his cooperative coaching-style leadership is cataloged episode by episode - honoring the duel he lost to Megatron's cheating in 'Heavy Metal War,' refusing to condemn Mirage without evidence, exposing the evil clone by insisting on rescuing Spike, and turning Omega Supreme from revenge to save San Francisco before his sacrificial passing of the Matrix.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 22 "Why More Beautiful Means Morally Better" — Durà-Vilà distinguishes narrow on-pitch morality (condemning dives, feigned fouls, and simulation, which no cultural permissiveness justifies) from a broader ethics of how one conducts a fulfilling life, and argues football should be appreciated two-dimensionally—result and aesthetic pleasure together—as shown by Barcelona and Real Madrid fans who grow angry at ugly play even in victory. His positive thesis is that playing beautifully is morally better: the aesthetic tradition of the Brazilian and Dutch schools, Michels and Cruyff's total football flowing into Guardiola's Barcelona, Wenger's Arsenal, and the Spain of Xavi and Iniesta promotes life-enhancing values of creativity, skill, and vision, while results-only football invites the tricks of technically limited players and managers. He concedes a dull team could be narrowly moral and a beautiful team could still dive, but maintains that beauty makes unethical play less sensible and more perverse, and that aesthetic football carries values worth exporting beyond the pitch.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 7 "Ridicule Is a Survival Strategy" — Kaye argues that the highest form of ridicule, which The Onion has mastered, targets not stupidity but cheating—specifically 'asscheating,' believing what you want to be true. She reads 'I Believe In Evolution, Except For The Whole Triassic Period' as skewering people who understand Darwin perfectly but exempt humans from evolution because admitting we are just another animal means admitting we die like everything else, the move behind Aquinas-style teleological add-ons that only invite a regress of gods supplying 'extras.' Articles on breast implants, the 'New Nietzschean Diet,' and Tour de France doping all show asscheats artificially inflating their evolutionary fitness; since natural selection stamps every organism with the purpose of survival and reproduction, asscheating is a vice, and ridiculing the asscheats who pollute the gene pool is itself a survival strategy.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 13 "Cobol’s Backyard" — Malloy argues the real protagonists of Inception are corporations: Cobol Engineering, Proclus Global and Fischer-Morrow move Cobb, Saito and Fischer like chess pieces, making the film a case study in corporate moral personhood. He builds personhood from the capacity to contract and hold rights (Saito buying the airline as Proclus's representative), to bear responsibility for what is done in its name, and to decide through corporate procedures, and he rebuts the objections that corporations lack moral emotions and virtues or vices by distinguishing personhood from personality - psychopaths are still moral persons. He ends with Fischer-Morrow's dilemma between Friedman's shareholder-primacy view and the duties of a member of a moral community, concluding that a monopoly on half the world's energy supply would wrong that community.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 31 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Barkman takes Andrea's mermaid-necklace question ('I don't think those rules apply any more') as a test of natural law: self-evident principles — general beneficence (Glenn's 'shit creek' rescue, Morgan's warning that it 'takes away a piece of your soul'), special beneficence toward family (Lori's 'Don't be so trusting,' Morales's 'best for my family'), and piety (Guillermo staying with the abandoned elders) — still bind after the state's collapse, while 'do not steal' is merely derived, so the unowned necklace is fair game and Rick could take some but not most of Andrea's food. Aristotle's practical wisdom resolves the cannibal hunters' collision between preserving their lives and not killing innocents — starving is the morally preferable choice — since virtue weighs principles 'all things considered.' Against Carol's 'we can make new rules' relativism the natural law outlives governments, and Father Gabriel errs by calling walkers 'abominations,' conflating bad (dysfunctional) with evil (willful) — whereas the Governor, who knowingly ignores the moral law, reduces himself to walker level.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 15 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Bzdak uses Wee-Bey's 'you askin' too much' - and his ultimate yes to letting Bunny take Namond out of the Game - to pose the Puzzle of Impartiality: morality seems to require equal consideration (Plato's Socrates rejecting justice as helping friends and harming enemies; the impartialism built into Bentham's, Mill's, and Singer's utilitarianism), yet the show's most admirable moment is a father's partiality, and its worst parents, De'Londa and Raylene, fail exactly by not being partial to their own children. He tests a Greater Good Principle against cops protecting cops, Kima choosing honesty over loyalty to McNulty and Freamon, and Bunk's disgusted speech to Omar about the code that splits the community into victims who matter and victims who don't. The principle handles Carver reporting Colicchio but not the burning-building cases, and the show's verdict is that both too much and too little partiality destroy lives, with no single criterion deciding.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 16 "The Wire and Philosophy" — McAleer ranks three Season-long deceptions - Sobotka's smuggling least wrong, McNulty's fake serial killer worse, Templeton's fabricated Sun stories worst - and argues that only the agents' motives and character explain the degrees of wrongness, against Mill's claim that motive has nothing to do with an action's morality and Kant's distinction between acting in accordance with and from duty. Aristotle's virtue ethics and his difference between practical wisdom and mere cleverness vindicate these verdicts: Sobotka lies to save a dying union, McNulty's cleverness is corrupted by his need to be the smartest boy in the room while Lester's additions lack all wisdom, and Templeton lies from naked careerism with no redemption arc. The chapter closes with the 'Haynes Principle' - 'you need a lot of context to seriously examine anything' - as the case for a messier, character-based moral philosophy.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 22 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Jennifer Baker asks whether the Devil does ethics any good and answers no. Against the tempter hypothesis she sets the traditional virtue ethics of Plato, Aristotle, the Stoics, and the Epicureans, where bad behavior traces to habituated vice rather than demons, and the cure is consciously cultivating virtues by hitting the mean between excess and deficiency - Johnny's practiced honesty, the Evangelical cousin's marital vows. She faults the Devil as a one-size-fits-all explanation of evil, a glamour machine (via Postrel and the Romantic Satan of Blake, Byron, and Milton), and a scare tactic the Epicureans warned corrupts character, closing with Plato's divided-soul counsel to aim at long-term goods and a dismissal of Luther's spite-drinking stratagem.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 31 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Robert Arp uses Saul's interrogation of Afsal Hamid (sleep-deprivation via cold, strobe lights, heavy metal) and the good cop/bad cop dynamics of Brody's 'Q&A' interrogation to examine deception in interrogations, including the nine-step Reid technique and its role in false confessions documented by the Innocence Project. He then tests the routine practice of lying to sources against three frameworks: Kant's absolute duty not to lie, Mill-inspired rule utilitarianism, which permits lies when telling truth regularly harms but lets interrogation exceptions serve the greater good, and Aristotle's virtue theory, on which habitual lying makes the agent vicious. Saul's lie about Hamid's family shows why the utilitarian exception dominates in the war on terror.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 22 "Girls and Philosophy" — Sirvent and Avery take Shoshanna's Listen, Ladies! advice book to ask whether rules can govern romance, contrasting Kantian rule-duty ethics (Ray's dating rules that are 'not commandments') with Bentham-Mill utilitarian calculation (Jessa's 'depends on the virgin'). Kierkegaard and Nietzsche - extended through Žižek's Lacanian 'Big Other' of God, Duty, or Utility - show such impersonal systems let us dodge responsibility: Jessa plays Kierkegaard's aesthete escaping boredom, while Hannah's 'just to be an asshole' boss seduction and the Marnie-Elijah hookup express ressentiment and self-hatred. Their positive proposal is Aristotelian virtue ethics - becoming a certain kind of person - completed by Butler's Undoing Gender: to be ethical you must risk being 'undone by each other,' as Adam demands of Hannah ('You don't wanna know me').
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 23 "Girls and Philosophy" — Mahon and Walker rebrand the seven deadly sins for Girls: Self-Absorption as Augustine's 'love of one's own excellence' (Hannah pitching her e-book at her editor's funeral, calling her grandmother 'the old Flo Job... sluttin' around'), Entitlement for Hannah's 'voice of my generation' demands and Marnie's rage at Charlie's success, and Sleeping Around as the John Paul II point about reducing a person to an object of gratification - Adam's fantasy sex with Hannah and his degradation of Natalia. Envy (Hannah on Tally's tragedy), gluttony in drug-fueled relapses (Aquinas's five ways), flakiness as Kant's indolent free-rider who needs others but never helps (Jessa missing her own abortion), and Senecan irritability (Jessa spitting at the Bushwick party, Ray's hatreds, Shoshanna's 'whiny nothings' outburst) complete the survey - redeemed by the girls' stubborn friendship.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 31 "Girls and Philosophy" — LaRocca asks what the liberal arts (Dunham's Oberlin, the girls' rural-college degrees) are for, reading Girls through the Greek notion of paideia: Plato's discussions of whether virtue can be taught (Protagoras), rhetoric as a mere 'knack' versus care of the soul (Gorgias), and education as becoming human (Republic), joined to Isocrates's 'development of judgment' as the father of liberal education. Against contemporary self-expression-and-selfie culture, he holds that the self is constituted outer-directed - Hannah's mentorship of her traumatized cousin Rebecca being the show's clinic in empathy - and he uses the agon (Honig, Mouffe) to recast the Beach House blowup as contest over whether the others are 'worthy' opponents. Dunham-as-doppelganger (like Plato's Socrates, like Kaufman in Adaptation) makes the show itself a work of paideia and a criticism of modern academic humanism, with Aristotle's Poetics invoked for drama's basis in conflict.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 38 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Reading Finn's first season as a three-stage hero's journey - winning the Enchiridion on Mount Cragdor, being tested in 'Business Time', 'City of Thieves', 'Ocean of Fear' and 'Henchman', then doubly confirmed when Billy recognizes him - the chapter extracts a working handbook of heroism from his stumbles. Its lessons: heroism needs reason as much as courage (thinking through the gnome 'illusions', knocking himself unconscious to beat the Fear Feaster), plain luck plays a real and uneven part in saving Jake from the ogre, retribution should be temporary (the ogre's returned dollar), and heroes must check their sources (Penny's con). The deepest tension is that justice and compassion, instinct and reason, violence and non-violence must be perpetually balanced - Billy's nonviolent way becomes its own injustice when Finn medicates villagers without consent - so a real hero is simply someone who never stops trying to hold the balance.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 16 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Hicks starts from young Jobs the 'little terror' expelled from third grade and asks whether he failed the school system or the system failed him, answering that America's entrepreneurs are produced by culture outside school—garage workshops, Heathkits, dirt-bike ramps, and parents who back initiative—rather than rows, rote learning, and standardized tests. He catalogues the entrepreneurial character traits Jobs displayed (informed creative judgment, ambition and integrity like the carpenter's hidden plywood, initiative calling Bill Hewlett at home, courage, perseverance through the Lisa, NeXT, and Pixar losses, win-win trade, leadership) and proposes risk-exercise curricula, Montessori methods, and programs like NFTE so schooling can deliberately cultivate the virtues of a flourishing entrepreneurial life.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 24 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Meyer reads Jobs through 'individualistic perfectionism'—the Aristotelian tradition (via Rasmussen and Den Uyl, and Veatch) on which flourishing is objective to human nature yet agent-relative, an endless striving unique to each person's talents rather than Kant's by-the-book categorical imperative applied impersonally to all. Jobs embodied this: the 'bicycle of the mind' faith that reason and tools extend human efficiency, practical wisdom weighing goods like friendship, health, and art through Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, experimental self-discovery (Zen, calligraphy, fruitarian diets), and the exile-to-NeXT-to-Pixar-to-iMac arc of constant re-evaluation—so the right question is not whether Jobs 'was' a moral perfectionist but whether each of us keeps striving in our own key.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 9 "Magnetic North" — Siler answers the Twelfth Doctor's question 'Am I a good man?' from 'Into the Dalek' by arguing that goodness is the Doctor's 'magnetic north'—the stable moral orientation his regenerations bend back toward, the force that drove him from Gallifrey's corrupt Time Lords. He concedes a dark side, from the would-be caveman killing of 'An Unearthly Child' to the 'Time Lord Victorious' arrogance of 'The Waters of Mars,' but insists character must be judged over a whole life, including the Doctor's effect on companions like Jo Grant, Leela, Ace, and Rose, whom he teaches 'a better way of livin' your life.' Clara's closing verdict—that he tries to be good and 'that's probably the point'—caps the claim that a settled direction of character, not perfection, makes him a good man.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 10 "1. A Good Man Goes to War" — Pless argues the Doctor's shift from the Ninth's self-avowed 'coward, any day' to the Eleventh's gun-toting action hero tracks real-world politics and markets rather than internal story logic: after the 7/7 London bombings and amid the War on Terror, and as the show's global export grew, a war-weary British ideal gave way to the decisive 'Oncoming Storm.' She traces the arc through the Tenth's gleeful xenocide of the Racnoss in 'The Runaway Bride,' the eternal punishment of the Family of Blood, the Eleventh brainwashing humanity to exterminate the Silence in 'Day of the Moon,' and the assault of 'A Good Man Goes to War,' before 'The Day of the Doctor' retcons the Time War so the Doctor never destroyed the Time Lords, validating the action-hero persona. Her conclusion: in a crisis culture demanding proactive heroes, cowardice—once the Doctor's honest self-assessment—was rebranded as vice.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 14 "5. Overcoming Evil with Love" — Bogosian argues the film locates evil not in human nature itself, as Jeanine claims when she calls human nature 'the enemy,' but in cultivable vices - Al's jealousy and fear of failure leading to attempted murder and suicide, Eric's and Jeanine's lust for power - and that only altruistic, self-sacrificial love can counteract them. With Aristotle's point that friendship is essential to developing virtue and to the good life, he shows the faction system fails on its own terms: a single virtue in isolation corrupts (Candor's truth without kindness), and a system that removes real moral and political freedom destroys the flourishing it promises. Tris's parents' sacrifices and the Tris-Four relationship - honest training advice, protection of her Divergence, and the gun-to-her-own-forehead scene where love breaks the simulation's grip - model the love that overcomes the corrupt system.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 23 "12. The Courage of Selflessness" — Pless argues that courage and selflessness are not the opposed traits of Dauntless and Abnegation but one and the same virtue: any properly selfless act requires moral courage, any truly courageous act requires sacrifice so that others may prosper, and both depend on an outside party in need and on overriding the instinct of self-preservation. Because a rewarded sacrifice becomes social capital - the lunch-giving and bullet-catching examples - neither virtue can be institutionalized: Abnegation's legalistic rules and Marcus's publicly displayed selflessness destroy selflessness by removing choice, and Eric's fear-eradicating initiation produces glory and cruelty instead of courage, since fear connotes responsibility. Natalie and Andrew Prior's shared, gender-subverting sacrifices, and Tris stepping in to take Al's knives, show the single virtue of selfless courage chosen in the moment, culminating in a death that is an extension of her character rather than a surprise.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 25 "14. You Have to Be Good before You Can Be Smart" — The Bocks argue that the Erudite pairing of ignorance with knowledge is morally loaded: with Linda Zagzebski's and James Montmarquet's virtue epistemology, high-end knowledge requires intellectual virtues like the courage to test your beliefs publicly, so you really do have to be good before you can be smart. The Erudite manifesto's curriculum omits the humanities that open the mind, and its IQ-only leadership test fails Plato's requirement that philosopher kings love wisdom itself and, like the freed cave-prisoner, return to benefit society - which is why Jeanine, driven by lust for power and concealment of the truth beyond the fence, is 'a poor example of a philosopher king.' Both the Erudite and the Bureau reason as consequentialists ('Knowledge is power... power to do good') to justify slaughtering Abnegation and experimenting on unconsenting Chicagoans, when the pursuit of knowledge must be constrained by informed consent and human dignity.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 26 "15. Tell the Truth at All Costs" — Bowman argues Candor is the most philosophically important faction because its absolute honesty is Kant's ethics: truthfulness as a perfect duty grounded in free will, making even politeness 'deception in pretty packaging,' and forbidding a lie even when the Erudite come to Merciless Mart hunting Tris - which mirrors Kant's reply to Benjamin Constant that one must not lie even to the murderer at the door. Against this he sets Aristotle's virtue ethics, where truth bows to wisdom, justice, and fortitude when the choice is handing hidden Jews to the SS, and Bentham's utilitarianism, which Amity enacts when it lies at the gates to keep the peace and save lives. The Candor Manifesto's 'web of individual-to-individual relationships' and Kant's kingdom of ends explain why universal honesty alone could make truth safe - and why Christina, the Candor, is the one left standing when the city's deception finally destroys it.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 31 "19. Why Divergent are Actually Convergent" — Schenkewitz argues Chicago's downfall is built into its ideal: each faction drills a single virtue through total lifestyle discipline - Abnegation's mirror rules and gray houses, Candor's black and white dress - until 'you become what you do,' but a solitary virtue inverts into its own vice once it is cut off from the others: Erudite's knowledge becomes a lust for power, Dauntless bravery cruelty, Candor honesty callousness, Amity peace passivity, Abnegation selflessness stifling. The Divergent, who naturally hold all the virtues together in one unified character, are therefore the city's apex rather than its disease: Tris never stops being Abnegation while being Dauntless, and her worth lies in negotiating among virtues and making real choices from real alternatives, unlike the faction archetypes. Justice, the chapter concludes, requires the convergence of all the virtues within each person - the Divergent are actually convergent.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 12 "3. What’s So Bad about Eating People" — McCraw imagines Lecter defending each class of victim with a different ethical theory: the Momund and Dortlich kills through Natural Law Theory plus lex talionis retribution (Dortlich ate Mischa, so he is eaten; Momund treated the aunt as meat, so he is treated as meat), the 'Sorbet' Rolodex dinner-party victims through a perverted Kantianism that swaps politeness for rationality so the rude forfeit humanity and corpses have no moral standing, and Krendler, Raspail, and Chilton through consequentialist accounting of worlds improved by their deaths. He concludes that only virtue ethics resists such distortion: Lecter's cold, callous, manipulative character and his isolated, paranoid, friendless life show that no possessor of good character could eat people, so cannibalism really is bad even when the murders are bracketed.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 13 "4. A Cape and a Code" — Farrell traces the heroes' knightly nicknames (Dark Knight, Caped Crusader, Man of Steel) to medieval chivalry as C.S. Lewis defines it in "The Necessity of Chivalry": the knight's double demand to be both stern and meek, each "to the nth degree," with knightly character a work of art achieved rather than a gift of nature. Both heroes show the split (playboy Bruce versus Spartan Batman in Batman Begins, meek Clark versus bold Superman), and both go to extremes - Batman's interrogation-room brutality in The Dark Knight, Superman turning back time for Lois in Superman: The Movie - but Lewis's hardest test is the mighty man who restrains himself. Superman's lifelong self-restraint, contrasted with uninhibited red-kryptonite Clark in Smallville's "Red," makes him the truer modern knight.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 11 "3. Hero or Villain" — Kevin McCain asks whether Darrow the hero and Nero au Augustus the villain can really be told apart, noting both hold noble goals (Eo's dream versus preserving humanity) and share brutal means. Consequentialism fails to separate them: Darrow's sacrifice of dockworkers and Sons of Ares to Romulus mirrors Nero's 'I do what I need to do to protect the greater good,' and Harmony's sacrificing Evey shows the same ends-justify-means reasoning. Kantian ethics condemns both, since each lies to people and sacrifices them without consent, treating them as mere means to an end. Virtue ethics finally offers grounds: Aristotle's requirement of proper motivation, developed through Michael Slote, distinguishes Darrow, who acts from love for Eo, his friends, and the Colors and is wracked by guilt, from Nero, who is fueled by inhuman pride and feels nothing at Eo's hanging—so motivation may be what makes one forgivable and the other a villain, though the chapter ends wondering if good intentions pave the road to Hell.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 16 "4. Is it God or the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown" — Using It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown (1966), the chapter asks whether belief without evidence can be rational, contrasting the classic evidentialist view (rational beliefs must be basic or derived from basics, in the tradition of Locke and Hume) with Alvin Plantinga's properly basic beliefs and a virtue theory of rational belief built on Aristotle-style intellectual virtues like humility, courage, and charity. Linus fails on every account - he insulates himself from counterevidence ('If you really are a fake, don't tell me'), lets the belief cost him friends and trick-or-treating, and never updates after the Pumpkin's no-show - while Sally's pumpkin-patch vigil shows rationality as a balance of evidence, value, and risk. The upshot: God-belief formed responsibly within a trusting community can be rational in a way Linus's solitary, evidence-dodging Pumpkin faith cannot.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 10 "1. Breaking Sixteen Walls" — Rhiannon Grant argues Deadpool's fourth-wall breaks make him a great philosopher and sociologist because they enact the examined life: like Socrates's unexamined-life dictum, Deadpool steps outside his world to ask new questions about it ('Stewart or McAvoy?'), and even examines his own habit of examining—the 'sixteen walls' break inside a break. Wittgenstein's fly-bottle becomes the trap of circular philosophical argument that Deadpool escapes by seeing the bottle from outside, while Berkeley's solipsism is the failed attempt to live as if the world existed only in one's mind. A closing dialogue has Professor X coach Deadpool through insider/outsider research ethics and objectivity (the sperm-and-egg microscope example), showing how fourth-wall skill lets a researcher view a community from both inside and outside.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 32 "19. Deadpool Can’t Know Fear" — Borrowing Socrates' definition of courage as remaining steadfast in the face of danger and choosing death above dishonor, the chapter argues that Deadpool's healing factor removes his risk of death, so he cannot experience the fear of helpless annihilation, cannot display courage, and is not an anti-hero but 'post-heroic.' Worse, mapping Luttwak's post-heroic warfare of drones and ballistic missiles onto his invulnerability, the chapter shows how fighting Deadpool drags opponents like the ULTIMATUM contract army and Crossbones into a trap where they can never test his courage and are stripped of their role as defenders, becoming mere targets. It closes that having a little fear and the chance to overcome it might be better than being unable to die.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 24 "14. The Gods of Marvel" — Gerald Browning argues that Marvel's heroes reprise ancient mythic archetypes: Tony Stark is Hephaestus, the smith-god who forges wonders in darkness (mirrored in the cave scene where Stark builds the arc reactor and later the Thorbuster armor), while Steve Rogers is a Heracles-like demigod who stays rooted in humanity yet battles Death itself (Thanos as Captain America's Thanatos). He frames the Civil War split as the old brains-versus-brawn, realist-versus-idealist divide, with Cap seeing registration as a repeat of Hitler registering the Jews and Stark seeing cold logic in it. Judged as characters stripped of their powers, the round goes to Captain America because selflessness is a virtue Stark's ego cannot match.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 28 "15. Clueless Rebels" — Luft reads Petty's apology for flying the Confederate flag as the awakening of justice, the Platonic cardinal virtue and Aristotle's common-good virtue, and asks what is worth defending. Socrates refusing escape in the Crito, Jesus, Njal's saga and Harry Potter exemplify self-sacrificial refusal to defend oneself for a higher ideal, the model Petty aspires to in "I Won't Back Down." Through Royce, Fletcher and Keller on loyalty, the Confederate "clueless rebels" are diagnosed with misplaced loyalty: regional pride is ethical only when we hold something as ours because it is right, never as right because it is ours.
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 28 "14. Friends Don’t Lie" — Bowman tests Hawkins friendships against Aristotle's three kinds in the Nicomachean Ethics: Dustin and Lucas's shared-comics pleasure collapses into rivalry over Max, Nancy and Jonathan's utility ends once Will and Barb are found, and Barb's fatal poolside loyalty to Nancy, though one-directional, is a friendship of virtue. Nietzsche's ideal of friends who strengthen us through conflict recasts those very fights (Lucas confronting Eleven's power misuse) as the best friendship, care ethics (Gilligan and Noddings) makes the mutual one-caring Party the real answer to who teaches Eleven friendship, and Derrida's Politics of Friendship grounds democracy and society itself in such everyday reciprocity, which is why Eleven's 'friends don't lie' compass pulls her back from Kali's violence to close the gate.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 33 "20. What Would Mister Rogers Say" — Jennifer Shaw Fischer and Bob Fischer apply Rogers's ideal of 'making goodness attractive' to the 2018 family-separation crisis: knowing his own son's abrupt, unexplained surgical separation caused lifelong trauma, and that his King Friday bomb-scare arc rejects trigger-happy generals for 'Generals of peace,' they argue any policy requiring border agents to lie that children are 'going to a shower' is too ugly to balance our values rightly. Rogers's unpushy vegetarianism ('I don't want to eat anything that has a mother') shows the difference between having a reason and being virtuous: making goodness lovely rather than argumentative.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 11 "3. Confronting Grief in the Post-Snap World" — Benjamin Carpenter applies Judith Butler's idea of grievability from Precarious Life and Frames of War to Endgame: lives matter insofar as they can be mourned, and Thanos renders his billions of victims ungrievable by scale, turning deaths into statistics beside white stone monuments Scott finds his own name on. Most Avengers turn away (Tony retreats, Thor kills Thanos and sinks into depression, Clint goes on a murderous rampage), but Natasha stays at her post, keeping agency and hope alive, which is what lets Scott find her and the team reassemble. Her willing self-sacrifice on Vormir makes her the moral opposite of Thanos, 'the ultimate egoist' who wraps genocide in the language of balance and kills only others, and the chapter asks why Tony's funeral gets a long communal mourning while Natasha is mostly forgotten.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 8 "Ethicists Assemble!" — White casts the 'Avengers Prime' as three living ethical systems: Tony Stark is the utilitarian who, during Civil War and the registration crisis, bets on outcomes he alone claims to foresee (stopping the Crimson Dynamo's heart, enlisting the Thunderbolts, exiling the Hulk); Captain America is the deontologist who refuses registration on principle ('we maintained the principles we swore to defend... you sold your principles') and rejects the Punisher and the Negative Zone prison regardless of consequences; Thor is the virtue ethicist who condemns Iron Man not by utility or duty but for violating loyalty, trust, and friendship in cloning him, and who refuses the Twilight Sword because using it would make him 'the same demon'. The chapter argues all three frameworks still demand judgment and conviction, which the heroes share.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 11 "Sometimes Heroes Fail" — James DiGiovanna asks whether it was right for Batman to turn street kids Dick Grayson and Jason Todd into Robin. He tests the training against Kant's universalizability (including the Joker-demanding-to-know-where-Robin-is lie example), against Bentham and Mill's utilitarian appeal to Gotham's general good, and finally reads it through the virtue ethics of Plato, Aristotle, and MacIntyre's After Virtue, where Robin is trained into a role-specific character rather than taught rules. Jason's rashness and death at the Joker's hands show Batman failed to moderate his ward's courage, and the chapter concludes Batman is 'a lousy deontologist, a decent consequentialist, and some kind of virtue ethicist.'
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 20 "Batman Is a Moral Exemplar" — Ryan Indy Rhodes and David Kyle Johnson defend Batman as a genuine moral exemplar whose justice, beneficence, generosity, and courage (from reprinting No Man's Land land deeds to sacrificing his reputation in Batman Begins) are worth emulating even though no one can copy his feats. They rebut the unrealistic objection, the language objection that 'Batman is virtuous' lacks a truthmaker (likening it to 'dragons breathe fire'), and the exaggeration objection by noting that exemplars like Buddha, Jesus, and Socrates reach us through embellished, partly fictional depictions anyway. Fiction even helps, since we can read Batman's thought balloons, and his growth into an 'icon' supplies the stable true character that emulation requires.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 31 "To Be Continued . ." — Galen Foresman arms Bat-fans with value theory: most evaluative comparisons of Batman and Superman beg the question, since Super-fans load pros-and-cons lists with superpowers and Bat-fans with intelligence without independently justifying why those traits count. He then argues that bravery is essential to superhero greatness, because the brave person knowingly confronts danger, so the powerless, bulletable Batman is systematically braver than the nearly invulnerable Superman. The conclusion inverts the fans' debate: the very superpowers Super-fans celebrate are what disqualify Superman from being the better hero.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 27 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Michaud asks whether the Dude's sloth is a vice and answers no: from Russell's 'In Praise of Idleness' he argues that overwork chiefly serves the rich — exactly how the Big Lebowski exploits the Dude as unpaid courier while sneering 'The bums will always lose' — and from Aristotle's and Cicero's moderatio he argues the Dude practices a mean between frantic work and paralysis, working hard when it matters (the drop, the rug). The fable of the ant and the grasshopper, retold, shows both die anyway, while the Dude 'works at being unemployed' and enjoys the time he has — sloth, ironically, does a kind of work.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 12 "Our First Gaze into the Black Mirror" — Collins and Boesch use Prime Minister Callow's coerced live sex act with a pig in The National Anthem to weigh conflicting moral obligations: the public's initial 72% Kantian refusal flips to an 86% utilitarian capitulation after the kidnapper's finger video, and the withheld revelation that Susannah was released half an hour early undermines any consequentialist justification of the act. A virtue-theory reading faults Callow's character for faking the rescue video and putting self-interest first, and the UKN media's Kantian compliance collapses once ratings are at stake. The closing section applies Martha Nussbaum's theory of disgust (contamination transferring disgust from blood and vomit to the spectacle-watchers themselves) to argue the episode's graphic imagery functions as a moral emotion condemning the audience's own obsession with spectacle.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 29 "“King of space, right here!”" — The chapter asks whether Robert Daly wrongs the USS Callister NPCs even if they are 'merely' sentient code: his theft of co-workers' DNA violates a fundamental right to privacy, and Kant's focus on the will shows his in-game intentions aim at real people — he logs in solely to strangle James's NPC and make him confess to being pathetic, wanting to harm the actual James. Aristotle's virtue ethics supplies the second indictment: because hyperrealistic VR blurs game and life, Daly's daily practice of cruelty habituates vice and makes cruelty part of who he is, unlike clearly fictional violence such as Mortal Kombat. Merleau-Ponty's intentionality links avatar actions to the self, so the chapter ends by asking what our own intentions in games like The Sims or Grand Theft Auto reveal about our character.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 31 "Learning from Mia’s Mistakes" — The chapter grades each of Mia's escalations in Crocodile — helping Rob hide the cyclist's body, killing Rob fifteen years later, then killing Shazia, her husband, and baby Ali to keep the secret — under Kant's categorical imperative (the cover-up cannot be universalized and treats persons as means), the utilitarian calculus (which also condemns every killing once the widow's suffering and Mia's guilt are counted), and feminist care ethics, which rejects her defense that she killed to protect her family because care obligations never cancel proportionality and others' rights. Aristotle's virtue ethics supplies the diagnosis: Mia's undoing is lack of practical wisdom — every split-second choice (which she never had time to deliberate) went wrong because she lacked virtuous habits. The chapter urges practicing everyday virtue so we never take the first step down her path.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 10 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Merli argues from alignment role-play against Aristotelian virtue ethics: a morally decent player convincingly runs a vicious treacherous thief who frames others for murder, and a 'moral mediocrity' runs a genuinely good paladin, so the ability to judge what the virtuous agent would do is one thing and being virtuous another. This undermines the McDowell/Hursthouse/Jacobson line that only the virtuous, with habituated emotional responses, can 'see what to do' — the role-playing skill works off-line, without feeling the character's fear or sharing its motives, so right-action judgment does not require trained emotion. He adds that if the virtue ethicist retorts that non-virtuous players never really get it right, the contrast between guessing dice in a fist (verifiable success) and claiming to read auras (unverifiable) shows the retort makes virtue look fraudulent, and that role-playing, unlike reading Austen, demands active deliberation from another's point of view, exposing abilities literary examples miss.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 9 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Henry Jacoby's introduction frames the volume around mortality: winter is coming, all men must die (valar morghulis), yet through honor, duty, and philosophy 'first we'll live' meaningful lives. Playing on Arya's mantra 'fear cuts deeper than swords,' he claims logic cuts deeper still - swords defend bodies, but logic defends our ideas, beliefs, and values - leaning on Socrates' claim that no evil can befall a good person, since the virtuous soul stands in harmony against desire and influence. He previews the essays: Hobbes as a maester, the dark side of chivalry, Robb's questionable war, Arya and Zen, and Ned's need of Machiavelli.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 73 "Voldemort and Dumbledore Two Tempted by Power" — The chapter grades would-be Ministers of Magic on Plato's ruler criteria: Dolores Umbridge fails utterly, her 'I must not tell lies' blood-quill detentions and multiplying Educational Decrees exposing a lust for power that grows with her authority and a total lack of courage, wisdom, justice, and self-control. Cornelius Fudge's insecurity breeds dictatorial damage control, trashing Harry in the press and rigging his hearing over the dementor attack on Dudley, so that craving power, he loses it; both are Platonic object lessons in how not to rule.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 87 "Beyond Choices Toward a Deeper Self-Understanding" — The chapter concedes Dumbledore's claim with qualifications: trivial, universal, unconscious, innate, or unrecognized abilities (Harry's Parseltongue before Sorcerer's Stone) reveal nothing, and the qualities Slytherin prized in Harry, resourcefulness, determination, and a certain disregard for rules, are morally neutral, since Voldemort's resourcefulness serves domination and immortality while Harry's saves his friends and fights tyranny. Yet abilities won only through hard work and self-sacrifice, and ethical capacities like empathy, prudence, and resilience do disclose character, so honest self-reflection about abilities matters too.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 92 "The Ultimate Measure of a Person" — Quoting Lucretius, that in danger and peril 'the mask is torn off, the reality remains,' the chapter argues that ordinary behavior is stereotypical and only situations of challenge and adversity reveal what kind of person someone truly is. Harry and his friends pass repeated tests of courage, loyalty, intelligence, and resourcefulness and emerge humble but battle-tested heroes like Frodo's fellowship, with Ron's temporary abandonment in Deathly Hallows the instructive exception.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 102 "NOTES" — The essay's conclusion shows reality correcting every character's prejudgments: Dumbledore's wizard-supremacy dreams die with his sister, Merope's with the end of the love potion, Ron's with distance from the Horcrux, the Malfoys' when Voldemort threatens Draco, and Harry matures from naive boy to cocky teen to discerning young man. Garver draws the thesis that epistemology is inseparable from ethics, bravery and loyalty require true belief about danger and about Dumbledore's real faults, and Rowling's narrative misdirection makes readers undergo the same correction, so that following Harry's transformation we become better people, with even Dudley's change giving hope to the most resistant reader.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 25 "Relax, Tony—You’re Safe!" — Nielsen uses the unity-of-virtue thesis (UVT) to ask how morally flawed Tony can be a virtuous Iron Man. Plato's Meno and Laches — Nicias' 'thoughtful courage' versus mere rashness — explain why apparently brave villains like Doctor Doom, Iron Monger, and the Mandarin are actually fearless rather than courageous, while Aristotle's distinction between natural virtue and full virtue plus prudence explains how Tony can be courageous yet intemperate with alcohol and women. Susan Wolf's argument that practical knowledge is essentially unified justifies UVT while making perfect virtue an unreachable ideal, so flawed, striving Stark — unlike Doom — is about as virtuous as a human being gets.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 26 "Here Lies an Avenger" — The Pattersons read 'The Mask in the Iron Man' as moral education: Tony's repeated 'I have a good life' litany maps onto Aristotle's eudaimonia — friends like Rhodey, Pepper, and Happy, wealth, health, sobriety, and life itself as goods chosen for the sake of happiness — while Niebuhr's community of value makes the Avengers the community of trust and loyalty that grounds those ideals. Tony fails as teacher when the sentient armor kills Whiplash, cannot grieve with him, and fails Aristotle's friendship test of willing good for the friend for his own sake, its identity dangerously conflated with Tony's. The reversal comes when Tony lives the virtue of self-sacrifice — dying 'because I'm an Avenger' — and the armor, finally grasping nobility, rips out its own mechanical heart to save him, earning the grave marker 'Here lies Iron Man, Avenger.'
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Kuzma uses MacIntyre's After Virtue to argue the Wasteland is modern morality itself: a fragmentary rubble where, like Bartertown's cobbled-together vehicles, utilitarian and deontological fragments survive without the shared telos that gave them meaning. Immortan Joe's V8 cult imposes a false telos and embodies Nietzsche's will-to-power Übermensch, while Bartertown's rules express mere individualism without any vision of the good life. Max — 'haunted by those I could not protect' — can seek the good life only by joining Furiosa's community and embracing its telos, and the Green Place turns out to be not a place but a way of life, confirming MacIntyre's Aristotle over Nietzsche.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 15 "The Universe Is Not Indifferent" — White takes Bert Cooper's shelf display of Atlas Shrugged seriously and argues, against Cooper's claim that Don is 'completely self-interested,' that Don is the conventional image of the egoist rather than a Randian one: he is a second-hander whose stolen identity makes his life a lie, so Betty is married to a man who does not exist and only Anna Draper, who sees Dick Whitman, gives him psychological visibility. Objectivism's primacy of existence explains why every lie collides with facts (the train recognition, Adam's newspaper photo, the misplaced dog-tag parcel) and why Don's 'ruthlessness' and the 'indifferent universe' he complains of are products of his own vices, since what is, is. The chapter walks through Rand's virtues (rationality, independence, honesty, productiveness, pride, self-esteem grounded in objective self-appraisal, not the 'whore-child' label) to show Don sought spiritual gain through deceit and so placed his self-esteem against reality.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 21 "Nonetheless, Don Can Be a Real Heel" — Terjesen asks whether Don is a good man, testing his mixed record (egalitarian instincts, loyalty to Mohawk Airlines, protecting Horace Jr., against habitual adultery and the stolen identity) through Aristotle's habituation, Plato's Protagoras unity-of-virtues theses, Hume's sensible knave, and John Doris's situationist attack on global character traits. The unity theses imply Don's vices undermine his virtues (affairs make him unavailable when Betty crashes; evasions about his past block honesty), and Doris's dime-in-the-payphone literature suggests even Don's reliability may be circumstance-bound, as with Pete's weddings-and-vacations-only philandering. Against full situationism, Don's consistent rules (never forcing women, valuing women he genuinely finds interesting) point to 'regional' traits, yet Roger's verdict stands: 'You're no good with relationships because you don't value them,' since Don runs family on a business code, from Adam's bribe to 'that's what people do' consolation for Pete.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 22 "Reconciliation Doesn’t Come in a Bottle" — Elia reads Don through Camus's Clamence in The Fall, an establishment success shadowed by guilt and self-medication, while insisting Don is no existential hero: unlike Sisyphus or Meursault, Dick Whitman never lucidly chose his freedom, he merely fled his past by stealing dog tags in Korea. Using MacIntyre's After Virtue opposition between Nietzschean value-creation and Aristotelian tradition-embeddedness, the chapter argues Don lacks integrity, the virtue that justifies breaks in one's narrative by deeper commitments, which is why peace appears only when past and present reconcile: phoning Anna as 'Dick Whitman,' the ocean immersion, and the confession to Betty ('I can explain' / 'You're a very, very gifted story-teller'). His justice is real but thin, a merit-based accounting that works at the office (promoting Peggy on talent) yet fails Betty, the children, and Adam, and reconciliation, the title insists, doesn't come in a bottle.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 29 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — White examines the fan fury over 'One More Day,' in which Peter and MJ trade their marriage to Mephisto to save Aunt May's life. Virtue ethics evaluates people by stable character traits, but situationist psychology (the pay-phone coin experiments, Doris's Lack of Character) argues behavior tracks trivial situational details, not traits — while fictional characters like Captain America and Peter Parker are written with simpler, firmer traits, so making a deal with the devil reads as glaringly out of character and betrays the audience's trust. Since the true agents were editor Joe Quesada and the writers, White asks whether creators owe fans fidelity to a character's established identity, and closes by arguing that even if real character is situational, integrity — being the same person across situations — remains a virtue worth aspiring to, including toward ourselves.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 10 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Takes Tig's misplaced revenge on Laroy—which kills Veronica Pope and triggers Damon Pope's burning of Tig's daughter and Opie's prison murder—together with the club's unconditional convoy rescue in 'To Be, Act 1' to ask whether loyalty is a virtue. It tests three accounts: the Aristotelian view (via Ladd's 'loyal Nazi is a contradiction') that only the virtuous can be loyal, which would deny that SAMCRO members can be loyal at all; the Humean view that loyalty is bigoted partiality; and the Kantian point that only the good will is unconditionally good, so loyalty can serve any wrongdoing. The chapter defends Ewin's line that loyalty is good in itself but issues in right action only joined with virtue, while the Stahl frame-up of Opie and Donna's death show the dark enforcement side—'rats deserve to die, end of story.'
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 13 "4. A Cape and a Code" — Farrell traces the heroes to medieval knighthood and evaluates them by C.S. Lewis's 'The Necessity of Chivalry': both live the double demand of fierceness and meekness (Batman brutalizing the Joker in The Dark Knight yet gifting a boy his surveillance gear; Superman turning back time for Lois yet rescuing a girl's cat), and both must achieve knightly character 'by art, not nature'. The decisive difference is restraint: Superman's Pa Kent lessons and the Smallville 'Red' red-kryptonite episode show the mighty man choosing self-control, making Kal-El the truer chivalric knight, where Lewis's examples (Achilles, triumphant generals) show power without meekness is no heroism.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 14 "5. How Heroes Argue" — LaBauve opens with an imagined Justice League showdown over a Joker hostage where Batman sways the crowd with pathos (fear of failing the innocent) and Superman wins them back through ethos — years of trusted character — to stage the chapter's claim from Aristotle's On Rhetoric. Superman alone balances all three appeals: Batman's pathos is all too human (Nolan's tormented Bruce) and his logos is master-detective method, but pure pathos risks Hitler-style demagoguery and pure logos is inhuman, while Superman's surpassing ethos — reinforced by the Kill Bill Vol. 2 monologue that Clark Kent is the costume — makes him the virtuous exemplar who 'must win'.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 16 "Notes" — Loftin argues the Diamond Dogs enact Aristotle's complete friendship: Jamie and Rebecca fail at friendship because they misconceive the good as self-gratification, and following Philippa Foot's natural-kind account of human good (plus Cicero on goodwill and C. S. Lewis's Four Loves) he shows friendship is an intrinsic good of human beings as such. Ted's vulnerability before Beard, Nate, and Higgins invites them into virtuous activity, Higgins's defection from Rebecca's sabotage scheme displays friendship against a relationship fueled by hurt, and Nate's status-hunger explains why he mistakes Ted's laughter and Rupert's patronage for friendship.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 22 "Notes" — Austin weighs Lombardi's 'winning is the only thing' (embodied in Beard's protest when Ted refuses to bench Roy against Man City) against the sportsmanship tradition and Robert Simon's view of sport as a mutual quest for excellence through challenge. He argues the 'New Lasso Way' vindicates both: Ted's locker-room speech after relegation, his note to Jamie ('Way to make the extra pass') after Jamie's assist beats Richmond, Pep's cameo, and the retitling of Trent's book to The Richmond Way show that people matter more than winning while winning still matters, with Ted's humility ('It's not about me') as the ground of the balance.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 31 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Barkman distinguishes the self-evident natural law (general beneficence, special preference for family, piety to parents as Confucius taught, duties to the weak) from derivative rules like 'do not steal' and from positive law, concluding that Andrea's mermaid necklace looting question in 'Guts' is really about whether natural law still binds when the state has collapsed. He argues it does: Andrea's necklace is unowned and free to take, Rick taking surplus food from Andrea would be justified by equal claims to survival, and Carol's 'we can make new rules' polygamy proposal fails because the natural law is prior to any government. The cannibal hunters of Issues #61-66 show what happens without virtue and Aristotle's practical wisdom for weighing conflicting principles, and walkers are bad but not evil, while a Governor-like human who ignores the natural law 'reduces himself to the level of a walker.'
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 21 "Notes" — White reconstructs the 'Sacrifice' storyline - Maxwell Lord mind-controlling Superman, telling lasso-bound Wonder Woman 'Kill me,' and her snapping his neck - and asks whether it was right. He argues Wonder Woman reasons as a threshold deontologist: her usual respect for life holds until the certain cost of letting Lord live (he would wield Superman to kill again) crosses the threshold where the consequentialist body-count argument takes over, and she was justified, so she would do it again. The contrast with Batman's refusal to kill the Joker shows his refusal is virtue-ethical self-definition ('I won't become them'), while Diana, regretting the necessity but feeling no remorse, is an Amazon warrior for whom lethal protection of lives is sometimes exactly the job.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 21 "The Wizard versus the General" — Walls argues Bob Knight ('the General') is a greater coach than John Wooden ('the Wizard') on two criteria. First, drawing on Aristotle's remark that a good general makes the most of the troops at his disposal and Mortimer Adler's proportional standard of achievement, he says Knight won three titles with far less NBA talent while Wooden always had all-stars like Alcindor and Walton. Second, on integrity (Sophocles' 'fail with honor' over 'win by cheating'), he contrasts Knight's clean, high-graduation-rate program against widely alleged NCAA violations by UCLA booster Sam Gilbert, concluding Knight's temper flaws damage his legacy less than cheating damages Wooden's.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 13 "Fourth Hole “Quiet…Please!” Reflections on Golf and Civility" — McNaron argues that golf promotes civility both empirically and normatively through its rules (self-scoring, self-called penalties) and its etiquette (silence during a swing, care for the course). Using an Aristotelian virtue-ethics frame plus Kekes's 'conduct according to custom' and Calhoun's expressivist account of civility as communicating respect, he treats civility as a mean acquired by habituation and opposes it to skloka, the petty hostility of win-at-all-costs sport. He defends golf's quiet against charges of classism, reads Tiger Woods's outburst at a shutter-clicking photographer as justified anger at an etiquette breach, and names the Ryder Cup's jingoism, boorish spectators, and intrusive media as threats to golf's civil, contemplative character.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 14 "Fifth Hole How Golf Builds and Shapes Moral Character" — Beller and Stoll ask why empirical moral-reasoning research finds that sport generally does not build character, yet golfers score highest of all athletes. Using Aristotle's account of right conduct and Lickona's triad of moral knowing, feeling, and acting, they argue character forms through role models, social environment, and cognitive dissonance, supported by neuroplasticity research on the brain's capacity for moral growth. They contrast golf's self-policing tradition (Bobby Jones, Meg Mallon, Greg Norman, the film Bagger Vance) with the gamesmanship coached in team sports, and address Gilligan's 'different voice' by reporting that female golfers reason at least as highly as males, concluding that golf's honor-bound moral community sets it apart.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 15 "Sixth Hole Virtue Ethics From Caddyshack to Better Golf" — McElreath tests three ethical theories against golf intuitions and argues virtue ethics wins. Consequentialism rightly judges a postal carrier's choice to work over golf but wrongly permits Judge Smails in Caddyshack to kick his ball when no bad consequences follow; Kantian ethics correctly condemns Smails's deceptive maxim as non-universalizable but mishandles the play-versus-work case. Virtue ethics, judging acts by what an ideally virtuous person would characteristically do, gets both right via the relevant virtues of justice and honesty, and he then applies benevolence, justice, and tolerance to argue golf should better treat women, minorities, disabled players (Casey Martin's cart), and homosexuals.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 8 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Michael Austin argues that a truly Olympic greatness requires moral, not merely athletic, excellence, reading Aristotle's magnanimity (megalopsychia, 'greatness of soul') as the crowning virtue that unifies all others. He tests this against three Olympians: bobsledder Eugenio Monti, who lent a rival team a part and lost gold; sprinter Wilma Rudolph, who forced her homecoming parade to be integrated; and runner Emil Zatopek, who gave away his gold medal and defied the Soviet invasion of Prague. Using Robert Adams's idea of 'modules of virtue,' he explains why some champions show self-control in sport but not in life, whereas the magnanimous person holds every virtue across every domain.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 18 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Jeffrey Fry imagines adding 'Virtuous' to the Olympic motto and awarding medals for moral excellence, then argues the reform faces near-insuperable hurdles. Drawing on Kant, he objects that rewarding virtue corrupts motive, since a morally worthy act must be done from duty, not for a prize (illustrated by a hypothetical rule giving basketball teams a point for helping up fallen opponents), and notes Kant reserves the just apportioning of happiness to God's omniscience, which human judges lack. He adds epistemological problems (cross-cultural disagreement about virtues, echoing Plato's Euthyphro; the opacity of motives and courage) and political ones (biased judges, nations losing face), proposing instead rare, formal recognition of extraordinary acts like Dorando Pietri's and coach Haakensmoen's.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 17 "Love–Love A Fresh Start at Finding Value and Virtue in Tennis" — Tommy Valentini argues that because winning lies outside a player's control (he could never beat Nadal by simply choosing to), success in tennis should be redefined around what is controllable. Using Alasdair MacIntyre's After Virtue, he treats tennis as a MacIntyrean practice and distinguishes external goods (trophies, prize money, ranking—zero-sum, tied to winning) from internal goods (full effort, positive attitude, sportsmanship) that require the virtues of justice, honesty, and courage and are available to winner and loser alike. Drawing on Aristotelian justice ('giving each their due') and Randolph Feezell on the opponent as competitor-and-friend, he holds up Arthur Ashe's Stoic response to AIDS in Days of Grace as the exemplar of carrying tennis's internal goods into life in the face of an uncontrollable outcome, death.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 19 "Stabbing Seles Fans and Fair Play" — Opening with Gunther Parche's stabbing of Monica Seles to injure Steffi Graf's rival, the chapter argues that a win-at-all-costs mentality misunderstands sport's value. Using Suits's account of games (lusory goals, means, rules, attitude) and rejecting bare formalism for Simon's broad internalism, it grounds tennis's intrinsic worth in the difficulty of achievement, the level of the opponent, and MacIntyre's notion of a practice with internal goods. It reframes fair play as 'respect for the game,' classifies fans as partisan, purist, or ideally moderate partisan, and concludes that by eliminating Seles, Parche damaged not just her but Graf's legacy and tennis itself because he loved the game too little.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Roberts argues that across Lee's 'Father Knows Best' trilogy (Pushing Hands, The Wedding Banquet, Eat Drink Man Woman) the clash between traditional Confucian values and Western modernity is best resolved by the virtue ethics of Confucius and Aristotle rather than by deontology or utilitarianism. Master Chu literally refusing to be pushed, the Gaos accepting Winston's homosexual relationship, and Chef Chu adapting to his daughters all require Aristotle's golden mean and habituated virtue, which accommodate special relationships and situations. Kant's categorical imperative (rejecting paternalism as treating persons as means) and Mill's harm principle are shown to be too rule-bound to reconcile tradition with modern individualism.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 14 "“And It’s Such a Beautiful Day!” shame and Fargo" — Hanrahan and Stearns read Fargo through Aristotle's theory of shame and its link to friendship, sorting the characters into his moral hierarchy: Gaear is the shameless self-indulgent man, Jerry is the morally incontinent one whose flickers of shame (before Scotty, before the swindled customer) stay inert against his greed, and Marge is the exemplar of excellence. They argue that a capacity for shame requires valuing others non-instrumentally, which the co-conspirators cannot do because they relate only through friendships of utility (Carl and the prostitute, Jerry using his son). Marge's friendship-of-the-good with Norm grounds both her decency and her ability to mediate others' shame, and her 'it's such a beautiful day' expresses the same noninstrumental valuing that makes moral concern possible.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 28 "15. The Evil in These Woods" — Rose-Barry surveys how Twin Peaks conceives evil—as Augustine's privation of good, as the Manichean clash of White and Black Lodges, and as Ricoeur's defilement (the sooty Woodsmen, BOB entering hosts)—then uses Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics distinction of vice, incontinence, and bestiality to argue Windom Earle is a better example of an evil person than BOB. Because BOB is all appetite ('I don't need—I want'), a beast lacking reason, he is like Aristotle's bestial man whose best part is merely absent; the vicious, rational Earle, who relishes wickedness and invents ever-crueler torments, has the worse condition of character—and evil, being human, can be fought.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 11 "Moral Clarity and Practical Reason in Film Noir" — Aeon Skoble argues against the common view that noir depicts a world without ethics, contending that noirs are actually exercises in moral clarity. He reads Frank Chambers's deliberations in Postman and Walter Neff's in Double Indemnity as Aristotelian practical reasoning gone wrong (they fail eudaimonia and are punished), while Sam Spade's decision to turn in Brigid shows objective good reasons at work. Using Touch of Evil, he shows that a corrupt cop like Quinlan being pursued affirms moral realism and refutes subjectivism, and he sides with Aristotelian virtue and Platonic objective justice over Kant's rigid categorical imperative (which would forbid the detective's useful lies or lying to Nazis). He concludes that because bad noir characters do not flourish, even films about immoral acts are morally edifying rather than corrupting role models.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 19 "The Big Score Fate, Morality, and Meaningful Life in The Killing Steven M. Sanders" — Sanders reads Kubrick's heist film The Killing through Stoic and Aristotelian ethics, casting Johnny Clay (Sterling Hayden) as a 'stoical cool' figure whose surrender line 'What's the difference?' embodies apatheia, acceptance of fate. He argues Clay's doom (the burst suitcase, Nikki's fatal horseshoe) works as Kubrick's fate-driven moral verdict but strains Aristotle's principle that a truly prudent agent would not suddenly go to pieces. Weighing Aristotelian character-evaluation against Mill's outcome-based ethics, Sanders questions why Clay 'must' fail and treats his lack of self-critical rationality as the real obstacle to a meaningful life.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 6 "Not the Crime, but the Man Sherlock Holmes and Charles Augustus Milverton" — Rozema examines 'The Adventure of Charles Augustus Milverton,' in which Holmes burgles a blackmailer's house, feigns an engagement to the maid, and watches Milverton's murder without intervening. He argues that Kantian deontology (too abstract to judge rectification) and consequentialism (paralyzed by unpredictable outcomes) both fail to assess Holmes's acts, whereas Plato and Aristotle's virtue ethics fits: judging the man's character over the isolated act. Citing Plato's 'true falsehood' vs. 'falsehood in words' and Aristotle on voluntary acts and the storm-tossed captain jettisoning cargo, he concludes a virtuous person may rightly do what is normally forbidden against a vicious foe like Milverton.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 9 "Watsons, Adlers, Lestrades, and Moriarties On the Nature of Friends and Enemies" — Tallon applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics taxonomy of friendship—of use, of pleasure, and of virtue—to Holmes's relationships, plus Aquinas on friends helping each other flourish. The Baker Street Irregulars and Mrs. Hudson are friends of use; Holmes has few friends of pleasure; Watson is the friend of virtue, an 'other self' sharing virtue, support, and activity (getting Holmes off cocaine, taking a bullet). Inverting the account, he classifies Holmes's enemies as competitor (Irene Adler), rival/'frenemy' (Lestrade and Gregson), and foe (Moriarty), arguing a foe—an anti-self—can never become a friend.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 13 "Sherlock Holmes and the Ethics of Hyperspecialization" — Costello and Bassham critique Holmes's 'brain-attic' theory from 'A Study in Scarlet'—that the mind has fixed capacity and should hold only vocationally useful knowledge. Cognitive science (interference and schema theory) and the sociology of social/cultural capital show useless knowledge is often useful, as when Holmes trades boxing lore or reads cultural cues. They then argue for a duty of self-improvement grounded in consequentialism, Kantian and Rossian deontology, and virtue ethics (Aristotle, Aquinas, MacIntyre) plus Socratic care of the soul, concluding that Holmes—an omnivorous reader who quotes Goethe and Hafiz—doesn't practice what he preaches and took specialization too far.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 16 "The Dog that did not Bark Learning how to Read “The Book of Life”" — Biondi uses the silent dog of 'Silver Blaze' to teach reasoning from absence, arguing Holmes's 'imagination' is a cultivable art—Peircean abduction combining observation, background knowledge, and the virtues of independence, courage, patience, and impartiality. She traces how Holmes finds Silver Blaze at Mapleton and unmasks Straker as the horse's would-be nobbler by consulting 'the book of life.' Framed by Emerson's 'study nature' and 'know thyself' (and Aristotle on what holds 'for the most part'), she uses the Irene Adler and 'Norbury'/Yellow Face failures to show how prejudice and overconfidence blind even Holmes to alternative hypotheses.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 17 "Aristotle on Detective Fiction" — Sayers's 1935 essay reads Aristotle's Poetics as the finest guide to writing detective fiction, mapping tragedy onto the mystery: primacy of plot over character, unity of action, appropriate length, catharsis, and the parts of Peripety, Discovery, and Suffering with the criminal's hamartia. Its centerpiece is 'paralogismos'—the art of framing lies rightly by stating true consequents (B) so the reader infers a false antecedent (A) himself, illustrated by the Jones/Smith gramophone bluff, Knox's Viaduct Murder double bluff, and the 'Watsonity' fallacy behind Roger Ackroyd. She invokes 'The Hound of the Baskervilles,' 'The Speckled Band,' and 'The Copper Beeches' as Aristotelian exemplars.
