- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 20 "No Country for Old Men The Decline of Ethics and the West(ern)" — William J. Devlin argues that No Country for Old Men deconstructs the western's three ingredients (moral hero, comprehensible villain, redemptive showdown) and collapses the genre into Nietzschean nihilism. Where Shane's courage is legible through Aristotelian virtue-ethics and Kantian deontology, Sheriff Bell grows old and afraid, walking away rather than confronting evil. Anton Chigurh perverts deontology—killing on 'principle' and because he 'gave his word'—while his coin flips invoke Nagel's moral luck to disclaim responsibility, so the good/bad polarity dissolves and, as Ellis says, 'you can't stop what's comin'.'
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 17 "A Spielbergian Ethics of the Family in Saving Private Ryan and The Color Purple" — Clewis defines a 'Spielbergian ethics of the family,' a care-based virtue ethics holding that we owe unique obligations to family and close friends grounded in personal identity, and contrasts it with utilitarian and Kantian approaches. In Saving Private Ryan the squad-as-family and the Ryan brotherhood explain why Miller says Ryan must 'earn this' and why living an ordinary good life suffices; in The Color Purple sisterhood (Nettie/Celie), fatherhood, and motherhood ground obligations of care, forgiveness, and reconciliation. He evaluates the view's feasibility while warning it neglects wider social influences and the is/ought gap.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 25 "Why the Doctor Is So Special" — Sarah Honeychurch and Niall Barr argue Daleks and Cybermen will never beat humanity because they are speciesist, judging worth solely by logic and resemblance. Using Peter Singer's animal-liberation account of speciesism (and Ryder's coinage), they claim the capacity to feel pain and empathy grounds moral consideration, and that Martha Nussbaum's and Aristotle's view of emotions as trainable judgments makes feeling essential to good moral reasoning. The humanized Daleks (the "Dalek" who absorbs Rose's DNA, Dalek Sec) show emotion's transformative power, and the Doctor's empathy, unlike other Time Lords, is why he succeeds.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 10 "3. Can It Be Right to Defend the Guilty" — Cook tests whether lawyers may defend the legally and morally guilty against several ethical theories, anchored by Saul's contemplated lie at Lalo Salamanca's bail hearing (knowing Lalo murdered Fred Whalen). Kant's contradiction-in-conception makes lying to the court a perfect duty to refrain from, but Cook shows this looks too rigid via the invented 'Jemma' surgeon case; act and rule consequentialism (Bentham, Mill, Hooker) permit honest defenses while diverging on lies and mitigation. He argues Hume's sentimentalist virtue ethics best fits intuition: Saul's bail lie is wrong because motivated by self-interest rather than the procedural justice a virtuous advocate should feel.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 30 "19. Can We Blame Jimmy for Being Jimmy" — The chapter runs Thomas Nagel's 'Moral Luck' argument on Jimmy, cataloguing his constitutive, circumstantial, causal-deterministic, and outcome luck (the con-man 'wolves and sheep' encounter, the Chicago sunroof children, the missed 1.6 million) to suggest we cannot fairly blame him. It then rebuts Nagel with a poker-and-wager analogy: since 'wagering on freedom weakly dominates' wagering on fatalism, we should treat character as cultivable through virtue theory's habits. It concludes that because nobody prevented Jimmy from changing and he has the resourcefulness to do so, his moral decline was unnecessary and blameworthy.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 22 "12. Bourdain’s Taste for Freedom" — Porot and Simon argue Bourdain's goodness is best captured by virtue ethics rather than deontology or consequentialism, and read his life through Isaiah Berlin's positive/negative liberty (via MacCallum and Carter). They contend Bourdain's indulgence of his 'lower self' through addiction and excess was paradoxically the path by which his 'higher self' of empathy and compassion grew — echoing Hesse's Siddhartha, the Buddhist Middle Way, and Aristotle's mean — recasting his suicide in mystical rather than cynical terms.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 13 "NOTES" — Charles Taliaferro and Dan Kastrul argue, following Aristotle's dispositional account of character, that who the castaways are is a matter of what they would do under different conditions, illustrated by Mr. Eko's circumstance-driven violence and Ben Linus's shifting good-guy/bad-guy conduct. They deploy Plato's Myth of Gyges (the ring of invisibility) to test whether characters like Sun would act justly only when watched, and, against a completely reversed morality ('an island where skinning babies is good'), they argue via Chesterton that some overriding values are non-relative, so the show never fully reverses good and evil even amid its mysteries.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 25 "Real World Island" — Patricia Brace and Rob Arp argue that Lost characters move from blameworthy to praiseworthy by ceasing to objectify others and instead objectifying themselves for a greater good. Using Kant's formula to treat persons as ends and never mere means, they condemn Ben Linus's lifelong manipulation while crediting his tearful mea culpa over Alex and his flash-sideways sacrifice for his student. Mill's utilitarianism justifies Sayid's assassinations and Kate's shooting of Un-Locke as trades for the greater number, and Aristotle's virtue ethics of cultivated respect and courage explains Charlie's Looking Glass suicide mission and Jack's Christlike self-sacrifice at the Heart of the Island, framing self-objectification as redemption.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 14 "Stephen King and the Art of Horror" — Littmann stages a mock trial of King's horror using classical aesthetics: Plato prosecutes, condemning fiction as lies that misrepresent gods, afterlife, and paternal authority (Carrie's mother, Jack Torrance, the Loser's Club disobeying elders) and corrupt morals through spectacle. Aristotle counters that Poetics-style poetry is 'more philosophical than history' and that tragedy's catharsis purges pity and fear, which King echoes in Danse Macabre's claim that horror lances real terrors via Danny Torrance, Paul Sheldon, and Louis Creed. Hume's 'Of Tragedy' explains why we enjoy fictional suffering (Pennywise, Annie Wilkes) we would hate in life; Littmann finally revises Hume, arguing horror's pleasure is the spur to imagination rather than mere appreciation of artistic skill.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 20 "From Desperation to Haven" — Held reads The Tommyknockers, Desperation, and The Regulators through Arthur Schopenhauer's pessimism, arguing King's worlds are 'always already sunk in evil' and that the will to live swings life between pain and boredom even before the supernatural arrives. He identifies egoism as the root of King's cruelty (Hilly banishing David Brown to Altair-4, Bobbi turning her dog into a battery) and offers Schopenhauer's compassion-based virtue ethic, 'injure no one; help everyone,' as the answer, supported by MacIntyre on the degradation of happiness and set against Nietzsche's 'last man' and nihilism. Gard's rescue of David Brown ('the kid matters or nothing matters') and Johnny Marinville's self-sacrifice in Desperation exemplify the heroic, compassionate life that defies the dark.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 17 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — LaRocca unpacks MacIntyre's After Virtue claim that Austen is 'the last great representative of the classical tradition of the virtues.' He traces MacIntyre's argument that Austen synthesizes Homeric social roles, Aristotelian practical wisdom (phronesis), and Christian humility, making constancy her master virtue (analogous to phronesis) and distinguishing genuine amiability from mere agreeableness (Knightley on Frank Churchill: 'amiable only in French'). He contrasts Austen's internal, teleological virtue with Franklin's utilitarian ledger, cites Ryle's 'gradal' Aristotelian reading of Austen's character vocabulary and C.S. Lewis on her Christian 'undeception,' and reads Fanny Price's charmless constancy as exemplary of virtue over charm.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 22 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Cantwell reads Emma through 'perfectionism' and parody, arguing that Cassandra and later readers turned Jane Austen into a 'picture of perfection' while Emma herself is a flawed paragon. Drawing on Andrew Miller's Burdens of Perfection, she treats moral improvement as socially constructed and responsive to exemplars, set against Highbury's upward mobility (the Westons, Coles, Martins destabilizing class lines). Emma's attempt to remake Harriet Smith in her own image is a parody of the gentlewoman (Bakhtin on parody) that exposes Emma's own vanity; the crisis of imagining Harriet marrying Knightley forces the self-knowledge that lets Emma finally pursue genuine, socially situated perfection.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 26 "Chapter 13 An Epicurean Consideration of Superstitions in Mark Twain and in the Good Life" — Baker reads Twain's ghost stories and superstition through Epicurean virtue ethics, which holds that false beliefs—above all the terror of death—breed empty desires that block eudaimonia. Citing Twain's Autobiography passage that 'annihilation has no terrors for me' as a near-verbatim Epicurean line, and using Lucretius and Nussbaum's 'Therapy of Desire,' she aligns Huck's disdain for a useless conscience and his rejection of wealth ('being rich ain't what it's cracked up to be') with the Epicurean pursuit of simple natural pleasures. She notes a tension: by making tall-tale-telling and Sunday-school-shirking so enjoyable, Twain the satirist spreads the very superstitions the Epicureans would eradicate, seeming to work at cross-purposes with them.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 23 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Komasinski explains Confucius's advice to fathers through three ideas: ritual (li, glossed as 'cultural grammar' – engagement rings, saying 'I love you'), excellence/virtue as excelling at relating to others (ren, 'co-humanity'), and wisdom. Using the Analects' 'Upright Gong' passage (fathers and sons cover for each other) beside Plato's Euthyphro, he shows Confucius prizes the father-son bond over law, and reads the parable of the prodigal son and Tu Wei-ming's 'personality ideal' to argue fathers should lead by virtuous example rather than punishment.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 24 "MOTHERHOOD" — Kevin and Janet Elliott argue that letting infants 'cry it out' (as advocated by Ferber and Weissbluth) is ethically problematic because all three major ethical theories – utilitarianism, deontology, and virtue ethics – condemn causing a child extended distress absent overriding reasons, with virtue ethics' compassion making the strongest case. They rebut claims that the crying causes little suffering and that co-sleeping is unsafe or ruins parental sleep, concluding that co-sleeping (historically near-universal) is often the ethically preferable alternative while stressing that the right choice varies by family and child.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 25 "MOTHERHOOD" — Jen Baker interrogates why unmedicated 'natural' childbirth is treated as morally superior, dissecting five senses of 'natural' and rejecting each, including a social-Darwinist appeal to evolution she deems dangerous. She engages Montaigne (via Cicero) on philosophizing as learning to die and cites Dylan Thomas and Neil Young on facing pain soberly, then turns to the Stoics' claim that pain 'is nothing to us' – arguing from a neo-Aristotelian/Stoic virtue ethics that pain has no moral value and that keeping one's wits with an epidural can preserve moral agency, so natural birth is an 'optional and amoral' thrill, not a virtue; she frames it with Bill Cosby's and Carol Burnett's labor jokes.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 28 "MOTHERHOOD" — Nin Kirkham applies neo-Aristotelian virtue ethics to define the 'virtues of motherhood' as character dispositions that let a mother flourish (achieve eudaimonia) qua mother. She elaborates three virtues – endurance (commitment, selflessness, and long-view 'vision,' likened to endurance running), liberality (knowing when to let a child go), and moral exemplarity – each analyzed as an Aristotelian mean between vices of excess and deficit, and argues good mothering is learned by example and does not license judging other mothers against one's own ideal.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 13 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Ilundáin-Agurruza stages his essay as a 'philosophical hunt,' first conceding Peter Singer's utilitarian case that sport hunting is wrong because it causes animal suffering for trivial ends, then arguing hunting can be non-trivial. Drawing on Aristotelian virtue ethics and Ortega y Gasset, he defends the 'Virtuous Hunter' who follows 'Diana's Code,' handicaps himself for a one-shot kill, and feels for the prey — citing De Niro's Michael in The Deer Hunter and Woody Allen's Love & Death — while condemning canned hunts and demeaning language ('varmint,' 'harvesting') as vicious extremes on a continuum.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 14 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Opening with his intimate encounter with a wolf, Vitali argues that 'fair chase' cannot mean fairness to the animal — since a right to fair chase would imply a more basic right not to be hunted, conceding the anti-hunting case. Instead, invoking Aristotelian human flourishing and Leopold's land ethic, he relocates fair chase to the hunter: hunting is moral only if it serves the biotic community through conservation and lets the hunter enter the predator-prey life-death continuum. He illustrates self-handicapping through master hunter Milo Burcham stalking a distant muley with a recurve bow.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 22 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Marvin, a social anthropologist, argues that for 'nature hunters' (Kellert's typology) a taxidermy trophy is not a dead animal but a living souvenir — un recuerdo — that enshrines the memory of a fair-chase hunt. Using Susan Stewart on the souvenir's part/whole incompleteness and Appadurai on value as 'difficulty of acquisition,' he shows how the lethal shot, the pose-reversed photograph, and the taxidermist's craft convert a wild animal into a personal memento that only lives through the hunter's narrative. How the animal was killed (ethically, authentically) matters more than that it was killed; the trophy is the hunter's self-awarded token of ethical excellence.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 32 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Brophy warns of a coming 'pornographic singularity' when veridical, immersive, interactive, unbounded virtual reality (extrapolated from Second Life, Rapelay, and Sony's brain-stimulation patent) makes hypersex and hyper-romance supplant real intimacy. He uses Baudrillard's hyperreal/simulacra to explain how airbrushed models and 'pornbots' render real women 'just bad porn', invokes Nozick's experience machine as literally realized, and argues that utilitarianism and Kant's humanity formula fail to condemn using pornbots, so only Aristotelian virtue theory locates the wrong—the user malfunctions and cannot flourish as escalating deviance (furries, age-play, rape games) conditions vice. His bleak prophecy is that unbounded virtual desire will corrode families and community.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 14 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Russell argues that being 'cool' is an aesthetic virtue distinct from being fashionable: the fashionable but anxious tryhard 'Allegra' fails to be cool precisely because her studied effort to win social approval is visible, whereas figures like James Dean or Marlene Dietrich seem effortlessly cool. Drawing an analogy to happiness and to moral virtues like compassion, he treats cool as a *self-effacing* goal — achieved only by caring about aesthetic matters for their own sake rather than for status, the way a genuinely virtuous person is moved directly by others' welfare rather than by a desire to be seen as good. He uses a Simpsons exchange (Homer, Marge, Bart, Lisa on what makes someone cool) to show that not-caring alone is insufficient.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 27 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — La Caze rehabilitates fashion against Kant's own dismissal of it (in the *Anthropology*) as vanity and imitation, arguing that Kant's aesthetics actually supply the tools to value it. She applies his account of the disinterested judgment of taste, free vs. adherent beauty, and 'genius' (originality that provides an exemplary model — Chanel's freer dressing, Dior's New Look, punk DIY, the Sartorialist's street style) to both the making and the wearing of clothes. Drawing on Kant's claim that the beautiful is a symbol of the morally good and the 'virtues of social intercourse,' and on Iris Marion Young's pleasures of touch, bonding, and fantasy, she argues fashion can be a proto-moral, cosmopolitan force, countering Plato's, Beauvoir's, and Svendsen's denigration.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 18 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Haire and Nelson read the film A Christmas Story as evidence that consumerism has replaced religion as America's faith: the Parker family shows no religious markers, and Ralphie's single-minded quest for the Red Ryder BB gun mirrors the identity-defining, transformative role religion once played. Using Aristotle's virtue ethics, they name consumerism a Christmas vice opposed to candidate Christmas virtues of being religious, traditional and family-centered. When the BB gun nearly blinds Ralphie and the hounds ruin the turkey, the consumerist ideal fails; the family's makeshift Chinese-restaurant dinner shows the family-centered virtue overcoming the vice, so 'all was right with the world'.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 26 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Gavrielides argues that going along with the Santa custom (leaving cookies, filling stockings, providing 'evidence') genuinely is lying, but that it is not wrong. She tests three ethical frameworks: a Kantian deontological analysis (with the 'murderer at the door' case) makes the lie at best 'wrong but permissible,' failing to capture parents' intuition of innocence; a Millian utilitarian analysis reduces character to a mere tool for good action; only virtue ethics, grounded in Plato's Republic account of edifying storytelling and Aristotelian character formation, captures why Santa stories are good — they cultivate kindness, charity, and self-reflection, and the myth is self-destructing as children's critical thought naturally dismantles it.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 28 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Scott reads Dickens's A Christmas Carol through virtue theory, treating Scrooge's transformation as a lesson in the virtues of generosity and gratitude that constitute eudaimonia (human flourishing). Drawing on Niebuhr, he explains Scrooge's greed as an anxious, insecurity-driven quest for security through wealth that fails because flourishing depends on relationships, not money (the poor-but-happy Cratchits). He invokes MacIntyre's 'just generosity' and Aristotelian habituation to show virtues are cultivated through practice, and uses Charles Taylor's weak/strong evaluations to warn that Christmas consumerism threatens 'keeping Christmas' by reducing moral worth to preferences and purchases.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 9 "CYCLING" — O'Brien's editorial introduction frames gardening as engaging core philosophical questions and previews the volume. It argues that gardening promotes a good life not through hedonistic pleasure but through virtuous traits like patience and a Stoic-tinged tranquility that ancient philosophers from Epicurus to Hume prized, and it invokes Kant to cast the gardener as a visual artist. It also sketches gardens as cosmic symbols (Pythagorean ratios at Versailles) and closes on Plato's Phaedrus image of educating the soul as tending plants.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 11 "GARDENING" — Isis Brook argues that gardening objectively improves both the land (through composting, nurturing plants, and Warwick Fox's 'responsive cohesion' with wider contexts) and the gardener's moral character. Taking a virtue-ethics approach and drawing on David Cooper, she holds that gardening practices incidentally cultivate patience, humility, recognition of reality, care for others, and open-heartedness. She uses concrete cases—Sackville-West's white garden at Sissinghurst, her own failed Cerinthe and thriving ferns—to show how collaborating with nature nurtures these flourishing-related virtues.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 12 "GARDENING" — Meghan Ray reads classical agrarian texts to show that Greeks and Romans invested cultivating the soil with civic, moral, and religious meaning. Through Hesiod's Works and Days and Xenophon's Oeconomicus (with its Gardener/King Cyrus), and the Roman Scriptores Rei Rusticae (Cato, Varro, Columella) plus Virgil's Georgics, she argues farming was portrayed as the only honorable, pious profession that builds character—diligence, endurance, justice—and sustains the state. The chapter connects horticulture to a virtue-centered vision of the good and righteous life.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 17 "GARDENING" — Michael Moss examines how the British grew Brussels sprouts and other 'English' vegetables across the Empire to recreate home and 'put down roots,' reading gardens as tropes of Britishness and imperial identity. He draws on David Cooper's claim—rooted in Heidegger's and Merleau-Ponty's notions of dynamic, embodied engagement—that 'certain garden practices necessarily induce virtues,' which colonial writers invoked to justify gardening's moral and civilizing purpose. He exposes the irony that most 'British' vegetables were themselves appropriated introductions, mirroring Kew's plant-hunting empire.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 18 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Pam Sailors distinguishes two kinds of high-altitude climber: the goal-oriented 'summiteer,' who pursues the summit at all costs for self-affirmation and may neglect others, and the process-oriented 'mountaineer,' who seeks relationship with the mountain, attains self-transcendence, and feels moral responsibility for comrades. Drawing on J. S. Russell and Jonathan Simon, and on cases like the 2006 abandonment of David Sharp versus Dan Mazur giving up his summit to save Lincoln Hall, she argues both types find value in dangerous sport but that the mountaineer—exhibiting courage, compassion, and care—is the morally better person. She backs this with Reinhold Messner, Ed Viesturs, and Sherpa judgment that mountains are not conquered but simply allow, or do not allow, us to climb them.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 25 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Agnafors asks whether free soloing is morally permissible, opening with soloists dropping ice chips into his coffee cup to show soloing is not purely private. He tests Locke's natural rights to life and liberty (concluding no act is truly private since rescues, taxpayers, and grieving families are affected), Aristotle's virtue ethics (worrying that habitual risk-taking forms a reckless character), and Bentham and Mill's consequentialism (Bill's confidence-boosting solo of Nutcracker versus Derek Hersey's fatal fall). He concludes no universal answer exists, offering one rule: the soloist must carefully weigh all these considerations beforehand.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 30 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Baker dismisses common objections to tattoos (shallow individuality, permanence, ugliness) as aesthetic rather than moral, then uses Greco-Roman virtue ethics—quoting Seneca's Moral Epistles on the soul, the balanced psyche, and matching one's norms to one's motivations—to isolate her real target: the 'tough tattoo.' She argues that a badass or tough-guy tattoo appropriates an outlaw subculture's imagery and, per Seneca's warning that approving a little violence approves it all, cultivates a vicious rather than virtuous psyche. Recalling friends who bragged about beatings, she invokes Socratic self-examination ('know thyself') to test whether looking tough is an accurate or worthy self-representation.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 17 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Brophy puts Showtime's Dexter Morgan on 'ethical trial' before the reader-as-jury, applying four tests. Utilitarianism approves because killing killers maximizes happiness (the Ticking Time Bomb analogy); Kant's categorical imperative and even Kant's own endorsement of executing murderers cast Dexter as a 'just executioner' applying a dark golden rule; virtue theory finds Dexter progressing toward moderation and flourishing as a 'warrior' in his social role; and Rawls's veil of ignorance suggests one would consent to Dexter patrolling one's neighborhood. Brophy concludes Dexter is morally excusable, perhaps praiseworthy.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 29 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Iyengar-tradition teacher Jeff Logan argues that yoga philosophy — mythology such as the warrior Virabhadra behind virabhadrasana and Hanuman behind hanumanasana — must be taught alongside asana, or practice becomes 'mere acrobatics.' Using the parking-lot and door-cutting anecdotes to show yamas like non-harm and selflessness ignored, and citing a childhood-diet study, he contends teachers should not preach the eight limbs but embed subliminal precepts in physical cues ('extend your legs straight and true'), so students come to live rather than merely know yoga's virtue ethics.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 30 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Julinna Oxley argues that yoga ethics is best understood as an Aristotelian virtue ethic rather than a rule-set: the yamas and niyamas name character traits to cultivate, not commands (citing Iyengar that 'violence is a state of mind, not a diet'). Laying out virtue ethics' elements — habituation, the mean, practical reason, community — she derives two paramount 'yogic virtues,' mindfulness and self-discipline/self-improvement, that are relative to each practitioner and community, so no single diet or lifestyle (e.g., vegetarianism, teetotaling) is universally required for the virtuous yogi off the mat.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 32 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Ethics professor Paul MacNeill argues ethics is intrinsic to yoga and knowable only through practice, not by mining texts — a Western reason-first bias that trivializes it. He shows the yamas and niyamas are counter-measures aimed at samadhi (paralleling how Aristotle's virtues aim at eudaimonia, though yoga subordinates reason), and that Vedanta's transcendent and Kashmir Shaivism's immanent metaphysics both function as instruments toward expanded awareness. From that dissolution of the separate self, he claims, compassion flows naturally, so Hatha yoga's asana and pranayama dissolve the ingrained bodily/mental habits that block ethical, equilibrium-born action.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 14 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — John Rowan and Patricia Hallen build an extended elevator metaphor for dating (Ann and Bob riding floors, pushing buttons to raise or lower intimacy, gravity pulling toward breakup) to capture Heraclitus's insight that a relationship is a reality in constant change, while invoking Plato to insist the conceptual reality of a relationship is as real as physical objects. They define dating as gauging the possibility of eventual commitment, cite Hume's canoe image for implicit communication of shared destination, and ground their strategies—be yourself, go slowly, communicate, befriend—in Aristotle's virtue ethics, treating honesty, courage, and loyalty as habits lying in the golden mean between deficiency and excess (e.g., the Look Who's Talking date who overshares is 'excessively honest').
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 21 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Joshua Heter mounts a virtue-theoretic case against being set up on blind dates, using Aristotle's notion of telos and the distinction between fleeting 'hot-fudge happiness' and eudaimonia, the flourishing of a well-lived life (illustrated by long-married Bill and Fran). He argues a 'guy's' function is achieved by exercising his whole nature, and dramatizes this with Zoo-bear versus Wild-bear: the zoo-fed bear has its hunger and safety met but cannot flourish because it never hunts or roams, just as matchmaking meets the romantic need while letting a man's 'social muscles' atrophy. Invoking Aristotle's philia (and Nussbaum on Aristotelian virtue), he concedes friends mean well but recommends they merely introduce people and let things progress naturally rather than force an 'unnatural' match.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 22 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Aeon Skoble uses the characters to argue for Aristotelian virtue ethics over Kantian duty and utilitarian consequence, since right action flows from developed character and practical reason rather than rule-following. He reads Sam's loyalty and Aragorn's temperance as genuine virtue, Boromir as flawed-but-decent (undone by resentment and pride), and Smeagol's swift murder of Deagol as proof the Ring's corrupting power depends partly on prior character. Skoble contends Kant's rules would make Sam's loyalty no better than a Ringwraith's, and utilitarianism's demand for foreknowledge suits only Galadriel, so virtue ethics best fits Tolkien's flawed, developing heroes.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 41 "It’s Not That Simple" — O'Mathuna uses 24's Jack Bauer to stage the ethics of torture through the "ticking bomb" argument. He frames it with deontology (torture treats persons as mere means), utilitarianism (Shue's ticking-bomb calculus, Mike Novick's "a few may die to save millions"), and virtue ethics (what torture does to Jack and Agent Burke). Marshalling the UN Convention, evidence that torture usually fails (Jack endures Chinese torture; Fayed is tricked, not broken), and its spread to innocents like Audrey Raines, he concludes the sanitized fictional case misrepresents torture's real degradation.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 5 "3. Star Trek as Philosophy Spock as Stoic Sage" — Pigliucci argues that Gene Roddenberry built an implicit argument for Stoicism into Star Trek's Spock, contra both the 'suppressed emotion / stiff upper lip' caricature and Farren's claim that Kirk is the truer Stoic. Reading Spock's talk of 'emotion' as the disruptive pathe and his 'logic' as the broad Stoic study of reason, he shows Spock embodying the dichotomy of control ('my legs, they're broken'), the four cardinal virtues, and Stoic cosmopolitanism aboard the Enterprise. Drawing on Brouwer's account of the sage, he tracks Spock's development from prokopton toward sagehood, cultivating eupatheiai like love and friendship (the Wrath of Khan sacrifice) and declaring 'logic is the beginning of wisdom, not the end.'
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 29 "27. Squid Game as Philosophy The Myths of Democracy" — The chapter argues that Squid Game exposes five 'myths' of democracy by showing how its trappings mask control by the wealthy few. Using Aristotle's Politics and Nicomachean Ethics it attacks the myth of free choice (the players' consent is coerced by debt) and the failure to cultivate virtue and transparency (Gi-hun deceives Il-nam in the marble game); it uses Sen and Nussbaum's capability approach to deny genuine empowerment; and it applies Plato's Phaedo two-worlds doctrine to argue the game instantiates no true form of truth, beauty, goodness, or justice. Il-nam's tie-breaking vote and Player 111's advantages illustrate that equality is only superficial, leaving a Hobbesian war of all against all inside a democratic shell.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 42 "39. Harry Potter as Philosophy Five Types of Friendship" — Okapal uses the Harry Potter films to expand Aristotle's theory of philia (friendship/love), which recognizes friendships for virtue, pleasure, and utility grounded in other-regarding concern, intimacy, choice, and a surrounding community. He argues the films show that friendships for pleasure and utility each come in beneficent and maleficent forms distinguished by whether motivations are other-regarding or purely self-regarding: the Quidditch team and the Harry-Ginny romance are beneficent pleasure-friendships (Ginny hides the Prince's book out of concern for Harry), while the Hermione-McLaggen date and Ron-Lavender fling are maleficent and short-lived. Slughorn's Slug Club is a beneficent utility-friendship of mutual advantage one may freely leave, whereas Voldemort's Death Eaters are maleficent, with all benefit flowing one way and no exit, yielding five types of friendship and locating Gryffindor's courage, inclusiveness, and loyalty as the ground of virtuous friendship.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 69 "65. Louis CK as Philosopher The King and His Fall" — Marra Henrigillis first shows CK as 'philosopher king of comedy'—his cell-phone/'forever empty' bit echoing Buddhist and Stoic teaching on sitting with suffering, his 'why?' bit echoing Quine on not ontologizing, his 'So Did The Fat Lady' episode exposing how society denies fat women full humanity—then uses his 2017 misconduct scandal to stage competing verdicts: the feminist case for banning him (rape culture, power dynamics), Plato on censoring vicious art, Mill's four-part defense of free expression and Nozick's free-market/entitlement view against cancellation, and Aristotle's virtue ethics (character judged over a whole life) plus Pompa's prison-education view that no one is only their worst act.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 87 "82. Planescape Torment as Philosophy Regret Can Change the Nature of a Man" — Gubka argues that Planescape: Torment answers Ravel's riddle 'What can change the nature of a man?' with 'regret,' read through Aristotle's claim that virtues are developed by habitually practicing virtuous action. The Nameless One's regret over betraying Deionarra and over the innocents killed to sustain his immortality motivates redemptive acts—apologizing to Deionarra, surrendering his immortality—shifting his alignment toward Good. The chapter rebuts Hobbes's Psychological Egoism (TNO's genuinely altruistic self-sacrifice) and Spinoza's warning that regret only doubles misery, arguing instead that apt regret is a golden-mean virtue between remorselessness and self-condemnation whose very painfulness makes it motivating.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 100 "94. Yes, Roya and Philosophy The Art of Submission" — Goldberg, Gavaler, and Chavez use Trotman and Denich's Yes, Roya—where Roya dominates Joe and Wylie professionally (publishing under Joe's name) and sexually, all consensually—to ask how the three major Western ethical theories can accommodate consensual dominant/submissive relationships. They argue Aristotle's virtue ethics handles them via unequal friendships (submissives depending more, within a mean), Kant's Formula of Universal Law permits them once consent is built into the maxim (aligning with the Formula of Humanity), and Mill's utilitarianism sanctions them because justice and felt safety, grounded in consent, follow from the Greatest Happiness Principle.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 13 "4. The Good of the Doctor" — The chapter distinguishes aesthetic 'good' (taste, beauty of the Daleks) from ethical 'good,' then tests the Doctor against the major moral theories: utilitarianism (rejected when Sarah Jane urges exterminating the Daleks in 'Genesis of the Daleks'), Kantian duty ethics (the Doctor's 'never met anyone who wasn't important' and attempts to save Davros and the Master), virtue ethics (the Eleventh Doctor guarding Christmas in 'The Time of the Doctor'), and feminist care ethics. Concluding that none quite fits because the Doctor values non-rational beings and feels compassion, the author proposes the Doctor follows Wolterstorff's 'ethic of need'—justice as meeting the needs of all—consistent with 'getting in the thick of things' as a flâneur.

### Two Concepts of Liberty

In his 1958 lecture Two Concepts of Liberty, Isaiah Berlin distinguishes negative liberty, the absence of interference by others, from positive liberty, the capacity for self-mastery or self-rule. Negative liberty asks how wide the area is within which a person may act unobstructed; positive liberty asks who or what governs one's choices. Berlin warned that the ideal of positive liberty, however attractive, can be twisted into justifications for coercion when authorities claim to know a person's 'real' self or true interests better than the person does, and he defended the priority of leaving individuals a protected sphere of noninterference.

- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 16 "Synthesis" — Elizabeth Brake asks what freedom Dylan's outlaw persona - refusing Maggie's Farm, possessive love, and conformity - actually wins, framing the answer with Berlin's two concepts of liberty. Dylan's negations look like Berlin's negative freedom, but Hegel's critique of the "freedom of the void" shows mere refusal ends in emptiness, so she reconstructs a Millian and Emersonian ideal of self-realization for which negative liberty is only the condition. "To live outside the law, you must be honest" supplies the synthesis: outside social law the free person answers to the Emersonian law of his own nature and to undistorted honesty with others, a more severe morality Dylan shares with Emerson and Nietzsche.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 24 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Rollin opposes mandatory helmet laws by contrasting two conceptions of freedom: the Hobbesian absence-of-constraint view ('go to hell in my own way', from Pinocchio's 'no strings on me' to the trapped coyote) and the rational-order view running from Plato (ranked classes, noble lies, censorship, contempt for democracy) through Rousseau's 'forced to be free', which Popper already identified as the enemy of the open society. Since, as the obesity-as-disease example and Robert Paul Wolff's expert-government argument show, we cannot claim certainty about value judgments the way we can about fractures, paternalism fails: if danger justified coercion we would have to ban motorcycles, skiing, parachuting, and bull-riding alike. Helmet laws in effect claim society knows what you ought to want better than you do, and Rollin's answer to his British colleague's 'what will you do if you injure your brain?' is to join the Department of Food Science and Nutrition.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 14 "3. Click Bait for Black Fish" — Porot reads Elliot through Berlin's positive liberty: people are enslaved to their lower selves - the 'daemons' of addiction and primal urge Elliot describes in 'eps1.3_da3m0ns.mp4' - and freedom requires a contract in which an external force holds you to your higher self. Elliot writes such contracts with Shayla over his drugs and imagines Mr. Robot as the paternalistic enforcer who pushes him off the pier when he breaks his word, while corporations run the reverse contract, 'hacking' people from within through addictive sugar, clickbait, and advertising. The black fish dream crystallizes this: everyone at the office devours the confined fish of reverse-contract slavery while Elliot alone eats Pop's pie - freedom through the father figure of Mr. Robot.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 14 "4. Non-State Enemies of Freedom" — Nash argues 1984 has been misread as a critique of state power alone; through Newspeak's silencing of thought (in the tradition Austin, MacKinnon, and Langton developed) it shows how any concentration of power oppresses via control of words, data, and information. Drawing on Goldstein's manual's debt to James Burnham's managerial revolution and Sheldon Wolin's 'inverted totalitarianism', she reads the non-centralized Oceania as a warning about non-state enemies: corporations, think tanks running the 'Tobacco Strategy', and global institutions peddling misleading poverty statistics. Popper, Arendt, and Berlin exemplify the state-focused liberalism she thinks blinded us to these horizontal threats, while the Newspeak appendix's past tense shows Orwell expected totalitarianism to be beatable through evidence and democracy.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 38 "24. A Modern utopia" — Robin Bunce reads 2049 as a libertarian utopia realized: a Los Angeles without welfare, planning, or federal power, where Hayek's market knowledge and Nozick's minimal state have won and everything from water to children to replicants is voluntarily bought and sold. Yet the result is a slave state, and Nozick's freedom-as-non-coercion — the negative liberty Berlin also held — cannot explain Luv, the film's most privileged character, who is nonetheless a slave because her existence hangs wholly on Wallace's will. Quentin Skinner's and Algernon Sidney's neo-Roman liberty, independence from another's will, explains her fear, and the Baseline, like Orwell's 'Thou Art', reveals an ambition to enslave not actions but souls; Freysa's 'we are our own masters' is a republican declaration of independence.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 24 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Lowe stages a 'Tolerance Bowl' between Sheldon's scientism and Mary's fundamentalism, opened with Berlin's liberal answer to pluralism — everyone entitled to their opinion, yet Sheldon insists 'evolution isn't an opinion, it's fact' and Mary's tolerance becomes its own tyranny. Davidson's argument that there is no very idea of a radically different conceptual scheme shows mother and son argue from shared concepts (DNA, intelligent design), but both remain metaphysical realists who cannot brook disagreement, while Rorty's 'the world does not speak' antirealism encourages fallibilist tolerance only to congeal into a 'what-we-have' dogma of its own that cannot account for genuine plurality. Nobody wins the bowl: each worldview makes tolerance hard in its own way.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 24 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Goguen reads the Winchesters through two masculine ideals: the warrior (Dean and Michael, chivalric protection culminating in Dean's 'protecting Sam... it's who I am') and the sovereign (Sam and Lucifer, whose freedom is analyzed with Isaiah Berlin's negative and positive liberty, with nods to Hobbes's absolute sovereign and Nietzsche's Übermensch). The show's stoic culture, where 'baring my soul like a freaking girl' is an insult, keeps the L-word unspoken, making Ellen's dying 'I will always love you, baby' to Jo a foil the brothers cannot match. Plato's Symposium, via Aristophanes' myth of split soulmates, and Aristotle's claim that the purest love is between virtuous male friends make sense of the 'psychotically, irrationally, erotically codependent' bond, and the chapter concludes that true masculinity requires embracing the seemingly supernatural: love.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 36 "23. Why Does Jimmy Get to Determine Chuck’s Healthcare" — The chapter uses Chuck's EHS to probe when paternalistic intervention against a competent person's will is justified. It argues Chuck is epistemically irrational (the hidden battery and electrified bed disprove his causal beliefs) yet notes, via Sharon Street and Nietzsche, that we all act on 'illogical' but coherent evaluative attitudes, so absurdity alone cannot license Dr. Cruz's push to commit him. Invoking Isaiah Berlin's warning against oppression in the name of someone's 'real self' and Mill-style concern for self-regarding choices, it finally uses Simone de Beauvoir to distinguish Jimmy's genuine devotion to Chuck from Chuck's controlling 'tyranny,' which shaped Jimmy's turn into Saul.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 22 "12. Bourdain’s Taste for Freedom" — Porot and Simon argue Bourdain's goodness is best captured by virtue ethics rather than deontology or consequentialism, and read his life through Isaiah Berlin's positive/negative liberty (via MacCallum and Carter). They contend Bourdain's indulgence of his 'lower self' through addiction and excess was paradoxically the path by which his 'higher self' of empathy and compassion grew — echoing Hesse's Siddhartha, the Buddhist Middle Way, and Aristotle's mean — recasting his suicide in mystical rather than cynical terms.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 34 "21. That Unnamed Zone We Call Freedom" — Hooke reads Serling's ambivalence toward the State through the liberal–libertarian debate between Rawls's A Theory of Justice (equal rights and the difference principle) and Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia (the minimal state, wary of a central authority regulating personal life). 'The Obsolete Man' (the condemned librarian Wordsworth laughing before the Chancellor), 'Eye of the Beholder' ('The State is not God'), and 'The Shelter' dramatize the shepherd-paradox (via Foucault) and the danger of any state that crushes human dignity; freedom, like the Nietzschean laughter Wordsworth aims at power, cannot be defined but is known in experience.

### Faith and Reason

The relationship between faith and reason concerns how religious belief stands in relation to rational argument and evidence. Positions range from rationalism, which holds that belief must be justified by reason, to fideism, which maintains that faith is independent of or even opposed to rational proof, with many thinkers seeking a middle path in which faith and reason are complementary. The debate runs throughout the history of philosophy and theology, from medieval attempts to demonstrate God's existence to modern discussions of whether religious commitment can be reasonable without conclusive proof.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 62 "Unknown" — Taking the film's cafeteria religion seriously as 'Neo-pluralism', the chapter distinguishes four varieties of religious pluralism and finds each wanting: extreme pluralism dies by simple logic since of 100,000 religions many contradict one another; fundamental-teachings pluralism fails because the great religions differ on genuinely fundamental doctrines (Islam's personal God versus Theravada's non-theism versus the Trinity); cafeteria pluralism produces incoherent transplantings (reincarnation fits Hinduism but not Buddhism or Christianity) and lacks any rational justification short of wishful thinking; and Hick's Kantian transcendental pluralism posits an unintelligible, wholly unknowable Real while demanding the doublethink - highlighted by Alvin Plantinga - of continuing to hold beliefs one recognizes as literally false.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 63 "Unknown" — The chapter rebuts three pluralist objections to religious exclusivism: the 'equal fruits' argument confuses hard exclusivism with the common soft (inclusivist) form that freely admits salvation and authentic experience outside one tradition; the arrogance charge rests on a principle that would condemn every political and moral conviction held in the face of reasonable disagreement, and is self-refuting - Plantinga's 'philosophical tar baby'; and the arbitrariness charge begs the question, since pluralists assume rather than argue that no religion could have better evidence, which is precisely the point at issue between exclusivism and pluralism.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 77 "Unknown" — This section explains why the moral quest needs faith: because the ideal Matrix of morality seems powerless against the hard world built on separation and egotism, Kant postulates freedom, God, and immortality as what we must believe to remain faithful to our basic moral choice. It develops the first postulate - freedom: the essence of moral experience is anti-deterministic, scientific knowledge consists in deterministic explanation and so cannot know free will without reducing it to its opposite, therefore we must have faith in our power to choose - the creed of liberators on the way to 'the promised land of Zion, the kingdom of heaven on earth'.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 13 "Who Should Be Committed" — Thomas Senor argues that rooting for the perennially losing Cubs is rationally and morally on a par with religious commitment: genuine fandom, like faith, is loyalty that survives repeated disappointment (distinguished from the zealot's 'my team right or wrong' via the Portland Trailblazers' 'Jailblazers' era). Since beliefs and fan loyalties are not under direct voluntary control, he rereads Pascal's wager not as choosing to believe but as cultivating belief indirectly: attending Mass the way moving to Chicago and following the Cubs daily can make you a fan. The believer's epistemic optimism toward religious experience and the devout's second-order hope in dark times mirror the Cubs fan's springtime optimism, so neither Cubs fans nor the religious should be committed.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 12 "From Knowledge to Faith" — Lawler reads Crimes and Misdemeanors through Kant's problem of the Highest Good: Judah's unpunished murder of Dolores shows a world where the wicked prosper and the good (Cliff, the blind Ben) suffer, the scandal Job complains of, while Levy's suicide shows that a bare existentialist 'yes' to life fails without love. Kant's 'I had to deny knowledge to make room for faith' is applied to the film's two visions: the deterministic, dog-eat-dog world of science and Adam Smith's economic egoism (with Hobbes's war of all against all) is only appearance, not reality. Kant's gallows example shows Judah could have discovered authentic freedom by respecting Dolores's dignity rather than seeing 'the black eyes of an insect', and the postulates of freedom, God, and immortality ground Ben's not-really-blind faith — so it is Judah who is truly blind.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 7 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Editor Jorge Gracia's preface frames The Passion as a phenomenon that stirs people too deeply for indifference (a minister's fatal heart attack in a Brazilian cinema, reviews ranging from zero to five stars) and argues its religious stakes give its questions more bite than those of The Matrix or The Lord of the Rings. It lays out the book's five controversies: whether Christ had to suffer violently and what atonement means, whether the film is anti-Semitic, how faith relates to truth and to reading the Gospels as God's word, why Christ was killed, and whether Judas can be morally responsible for a betrayal God foreknew and redemption required. Gracia insists the collection takes no side and offers only a point of departure.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 9 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — McInerny argues Gibson's film works like Kierkegaard's indirect communication: its shocking graphic realism, against the tamed stations of the cross and serene crucifixes of Catholic churches, targets nominal Christians and forces each viewer to hear Jesus's 'I want you' and confront the scandal of the Incarnation rather than domesticate it. He reads the film alongside Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions as embroidery with no meaning apart from the Gospels, and invokes Aquinas on the Eucharist as the continuing memorial of the passion in which Christ is hidden under bread and wine. The film is 'a sign of contradiction' that, like Nietzsche's self-declared Antichrist, divides humanity into acceptance or rejection, so that efforts to keep religion within the bounds of reason alone must distort it.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 12 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Walls argues the controversy lies not in the gore but in who died on the cross and why, and shows Gibson weaving the three classic atonement theories: Christ crushing the serpent in Gethsemane as the Christus-Victor ransom (with Augustine's mousetrap image), the Isaiah 53 scourging and Gibson's own hand driving the nail as Anselm-style penal substitution in which the innocent dies so the guilty Barabbas in each of us goes free, and the transformed characters (Mary Magdalene, Simon of Cyrene, the good thief, the kneeling soldier) as Abelard's moral influence. Against Kant's charge that atonement is a superstitious substitute for moral transformation, he cites Swinburne and Quinn: pleading the atonement requires repentance, and the tens of thousands of reported conversions and confessions show it transforms lives. He concludes that any adequate account needs all three theories, objective payment and subjective transformation alike, and that atonement aims at mercy and reconciliation rather than retribution.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 18 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Kurtz, the secular humanist, argues the film is a political weapon of the Religious Right (O'Reilly, Dobson, Gingrich) that presents fantasy as fact: Gibson claims fidelity to the Gospels while borrowing torture scenes such as the bridge plunge and the savage flogging from Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions, whitewashing the historical Pilate, and erasing that Jesus, Mary, and the disciples were themselves Jews. Applying historical criticism, he contends the Gospels are anonymous, second- and third-hand missionary propaganda written forty to seventy years after Jesus, shaped by the rivalry between rabbinic Judaism and Gentile-seeking Jewish Christianity and canonized politically at Nicaea under Constantine. He concludes by defending the freedom of inquiry, skeptical scrutiny of all sacred texts, and the First Amendment's separation of church and state against the film's power to inflame anti-Semitism and the American culture war.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 20 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Bronson argues Gibson's fixation on Jesus's suffering is not a Christian oddity but a deeply Jewish mystical one: using William James's four marks of mystical experience (ineffability, noetic quality, transiency, passivity), he reads the Gethsemane opening, where Jesus crushes Satan's serpent and receives a vision of the Father, as a classic mystical trial in the line of Moses at Sinai, Daniel's chariot-throne vision, Elijah's fiery ascent, John the Baptist, Paul's blinding light, and later the Kabbalah and Hasidic masters whose path to God runs through anguish. The Platonic Socrates of the Symposium and Phaedrus (wisdom arriving through the madness of love) and the medieval agreement of al-Ghazali, Maimonides, and Aquinas that reason cannot reach God frame his philosophy-versus-mysticism contrast, including the film's mother-son floorboard scene as love but not full mystical contact. The added scene where Pilate's wife tells him 'If you will not hear the truth, no one can tell you' shows Gibson siding with the mystical path to truth over Pilate's pragmatic one.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 23 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Jorge Gracia reframes the fidelity controversy as a problem in the theory of interpretation: Gibson had to make countless choices the Gospels leave silent (Christ's worn clothing, the Italian landscape, Jesus staring into the camera at the Last Supper, added scenes like Satan raging and demon children haunting Judas), so the film is unavoidably an interpretation. He surveys five criteria interpreters of Scripture have used — personal intuition (illustrated by Augustine's 'take and read' in the Confessions), ecclesial authority and the visions of nuns Emmerich and Agreda, sola scriptura, historical scholarship, and tradition (Aquinas's camp; Veronica's veil, the Shroud, the virgin Mary's prominence) — and argues each is inadequate alone because every one rests on prior theology. Hence disputes about the film are really disputes between theologies, and the film makes sense only within Gibson's Catholic view of Jesus as the Messiah announced by Isaiah 53.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 26 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Dallas Willard defends the film's excess of violence as its whole point: it visualizes human evil as beyond the remedies of education, law, or counseling (the route Plato and Aristotle tried), with Satan — the androgynous figure carrying the smug dwarf through the scourging crowd — explaining why only Christ's non-resistant embrace of the cross can break evil's grip. Against the passive reading of 'the Passion,' he argues Jesus 'played' his judges, deliberately laying down his life to inaugurate the kingdom of God. The argument leans on the hidden God (deus absconditus): God stays hidden, contra Sartre's 'no nature' self-creation and closer to Pico della Mirandola, so that we can freely make ourselves, which is also why demanding 'more evidence' misses what belief in God requires.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 29 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Paul Moser answers the objection that an all-loving God could not plan His Son's torture by arguing the cross is God's scandalous self-giving love: Jesus is no mere moral guru but the unique atoning sacrifice (the mad/Satanic/Son-of-God trilemma, 'he who delivered me to you has the greater sin'), and the crucifixion is God's grand reversal where self-giving love defeats death. He attacks the 'nice god' of natural theology as domesticating idolatry — God hides His plans from 'the wise and the intelligent' — and holds that we know God not by philosophical evidence but through Gethsemane-style filial obedience ('not my will but yours'), noting that Gibson himself appears in the film driving a nail, casting all of us as the crucifiers whom God forgives.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 33 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Bassham and Bagget observe that amid the film's unscriptural brutality Jesus never resists — he stops Peter's sword, heals Malchus's ear, and climbs back up for a second scourging — and ask whether this nonviolence can be rationally grounded without theological premises. They reject four classic readings of 'resist not evil' (Catholic counels-of-perfection, Schweitzer's interim ethics, Luther's penitential ethic, Tolstoy's absolute pacifism, noting Jesus himself used force against the money-changers) in favor of a hyperbole-plus-implicit-qualifier reading; then they show act utilitarianism licenses atrocities, rule utilitarianism at best yields an unpalatable absolute pacifism, and Kantian single-principle deontology preserves a right of self-defense Jesus's ethic calls us to lay aside — closing with a 'character model' of the Passion (duty vs freedom vs character) on which nonviolence is becoming the kind of person for whom violence is no longer an option, justified ultimately only by the cross.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 34 "The Man and His Faith" — Morris argues Daredevil is the rare mainstream hero with a religious interior life: raised nominally Catholic in Hell's Kitchen, his absent mother a nun who calls him 'a servant of God', he prays, thinks in religious categories, and complains to God like King David in the Psalms ('Why do the wicked prosper?'). Distinguishing mere outward religiosity from authentic faith, he proposes his 'Double Power Principle' - whatever has power for ill has equal power for good, religion included - and asks whether faith is blind like Matt Murdock or perceptive like his radar sense: a source of strength or of weakness for a costumed vigilante.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 35 "Faith and Fear" — Against Quentin Beck's claim that 'a man without fear is a man without faith', Morris argues the fear-based account of religion (Freud's) mistakes superstition for faith: authentic faith is a commitment of the heart rather than intellectual certitude, so the truly fearless are likely people of strong faith, as the martyrs show. He then distinguishes paralyzing self-referential 'fear of' from motivating 'fear that' (better called concern), concluding Daredevil genuinely is the Man Without Fear precisely because his deep-down faithfulness sustains him - he lives 'by faith and not by sight'.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 106 "Gloom, Doom, and Morality" — Works out naturalism's moral cost: no purpose behind our existence, no blueprint for life, Russell's hope that sensitive souls can love the tragic beauty of it anyway, and the Wilson-Ruse claim that ethics is "an illusion fobbed off on us by our genes," which loses its grip once seen through — like Macbeth's dagger. Against this it sets Kant's moral faith: morality makes rational sense only if we postulate God and immortality so virtue is finally rewarded, and the chapter concludes naturalism offers no deep basis for the life-risking duties a hero like Superman faces.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 108 "A Theological Basis for Super-Heroics" — Proposes that Christian theism's doctrines of heaven, hell and Christ's return resolve the truth/justice tension by grounding moral obligation in God's perfectly moral nature and guaranteeing that justice prevails. It rebuts Maggin's claim that faith in a power greater than ours breeds inaction: God works through human co-creators, so Superman still has a duty to do what he can, and the objective hope of ultimate justice is exactly the corrective that despairing Superman and tyrannical, fear-ruling Batman in Kingdom Come both lack.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 109 "Hope and the Human Challenge" — Reads Superman's return — "Up in the sky!", the crowd hailing "the second coming of Superman" at the UN — as the enacted theology of Kingdom Come: hope in a greater power revives a world "hungry for hope" and draws the other heroes back to the fray. The Spectre's charge to the preacher Norman McCay, "you exist to give hope," voices the chapter's conclusion that a supernatural eschatology holds hope, truth, and individual responsibility together in a way naturalism's unyielding despair cannot.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 15 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Steven Lovell reads the Green Witch's enchantment in The Silver Chair (the sun is only a copy of the lamp, Aslan only a bigger cat, Narnia a children's tale) as Lewis's staging of the Freudian critique of religion, and answers that similarity cannot tell copy from original, that the genetic fallacy vitiates arguing from a belief's origin, and that Aslan is 'not safe,' so Christianity is hardly wish-fulfillment (Augustine's restless heart and Pascal's God-shaped hole point the other way). Puddleglum's stamping out the fire and vow to live 'as like a Narnian as I can even if there isn't any Narnia' is defended through Pascal's Wager and James's 'The Will to Believe': the reality of Narnia is a live, forced, and momentous option that may legitimately be decided on passional grounds.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 35 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Debunks the 'Anscombe legend' that Lewis abandoned rational apologetics for children's stories after his 1948 Socratic Club defeat by Elizabeth Anscombe over the argument that naturalism is self-refuting. It shows Lewis revised and expanded the argument in the 1960 Miracles, incorporating Anscombe's reasons/causes distinction, and kept writing apologetic essays, while the Professor's trilemma about Lucy (liar, lunatic, or truthful) mirrors the Trilemma of Mere Christianity and shows Narnia using logic, not fleeing it. It rejects A.N. Wilson's identification of the Green Witch with Anscombe and argues the Chronicles teach that prudence and faith are compatible virtues: Edmund's rationalizing, Trumpkin's honest skepticism, and Puzzle's blind trust in Shift all show that fideistic faith is a vice, not what Lewis asks of children.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 17 "Prayer (A Euphemism for Butt-Kissing and Begging)" — Argues the Pythons' religious gags perform philosophy's preliminary job of challenging doctrine: the 'every sperm is sacred' family makes God a voyeur of contraception, the Life of Brian stoning (rocks flying each time anyone utters 'Jehovah') shows blasphemy law run absurd, and 'Christmas in Heaven' exposes heavenly reward as material compensation. Deploying Socrates and Plato — the Republic's ban on portraying pettiful gods, the Apology on why the virtuous need not fear death, and above all the Euthyphro — the chapter reads the witch-weighing and the Holy Hand Grenade as the ancient problem whether acts are just because God sanctions them, and the chaplain's toadying prayer against God's own 'don't grovel' as proof that sacrifice and prayer are bargaining a perfect being has no need of. The upshot is not atheism but the Socratic verdict that the mobs punishing blasphemy, not the mocked, are the real blasphemers.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 17 "U2 and Philosophy" — Merrick sets XTC's 'Dear God' - being 'just struck' that no loving, all-powerful God rules this world - against U2's laments ('Wake Up Dead Man', 'Peace on Earth', '40') and Bono's reading of the Psalms as the blues shouted at God: both share outrage, but U2 adds yearning for the redemption promised in 'the story about eternity' plus Jubilee 2000-style action against debt and AIDS. He then argues the atheistic reaction to evil cannot be reason-producing, since neither divine design nor unguided evolution would give us a faculty that 'just sees' atheism from evil, any more than one that just sees there is no plant life on Mars. If God instead made us so that outrage at evil can trigger conviction that he will make all right, U2's reaction - 'Grace makes beauty out of ugly things' - can be as reasonable as visual perception.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 24 "U2 and Philosophy" — Cleveland sorts the knowing and feeling of U2's lyrics ('Vertigo', 'Beautiful Day', 'Staring at the Sun', 'Daddy's Gonna Pay for Your Crash Car') into Russell's varieties of knowledge - propositional, acquaintance, know-how - and argues that the feeling U2 champions against thought is knowledge by acquaintance: direct, concept-free awareness that, in religious cases, just is Jamesian mystical revelation as against revelation as a set of propositional truths, which is why Bono tells his father he 'hears something back from the silence' rather than holding doctrines. James supplies both the view that feeling is the deeper source of religion and the pragmatist answer to the problem of origins - 'by their fruits ye shall know them', so religious feeling is vindicated by moral transformation. Hume's slave-of-the-passions thesis explains why such feeling, not inert moral knowledge, moves Bono's social justice work: 'God is love, and as much as I respond... in acting in that love, that's my religion'.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 13 "Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress" — Jacoby reads Stan Marsh as W.K. Clifford's ethics of belief in action: from 'All About the Mormons' ('you better have something to back it up') to 'The Biggest Douche in the Universe,' Stan insists the burden of proof lies with claimants and that faith used as a fallback is no evidence at all. 'Cartmanland' and the story of Job serve to criticize Pascal's Wager — a good God would not eternally torment the virtuous nonbeliever, and the Wager simply assumes its afterlife payoff — while the harms of Miss Information's holistic healers, David Blaine's cult suicide, and Scientology show Clifford was right that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken minds and, as Stan tells John Edward, slow down the progress of all mankind.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 21 "Introduction" — Frames Part IV's philosophy of religion chapters. Johnson's chapter sets Cartman's million-dollar theme park against God's goodness, with South Park characters giving answers echoing Calvin, Hick, and Job; Gallagher's uses Rose's 'I just know' on Lost and Aquinas' distinctions between knowledge, opinion, and faith to argue that faith is not knowledge; and Eberl and Vines' uses Battlestar Galactica's Cylon monotheism versus Colonial religion and atheism to ask whether God can be proven, whether evil disproves him, and whether life is meaningful without God.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 23 "To Know … and Believe" — Gallagher reads Lost's Rose through Aquinas: faith is 'mid-way between knowledge and opinion,' sharing the certainty of episteme and the imperfection of doxa, so Rose's 'I just know' about Bernard's survival and her island cure confuses what she believes with what she knows. Aquinas' five ways ground natural knowledge that God exists, and the castaways' failures are diagnosed as sins against faith — Charlie's despair is acedia while Rose's certainty is the presumption (praesumptio) of elevating faith to demonstrated knowledge; the lesson is that faith perfects reason without replacing it.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 31 "Damned If You Do, and Damned If You Don’t" — Bryan McHenry asks whether manipulating religious belief for political ends is ever moral, using Adama's motivational lie about Earth, Roslin's Pythia-driven 'dying leader' campaign (compared with George W. Bush's faith-based politics), and the Cylons' evangelical monotheism aimed at scaring Baltar into conversion. Machiavelli's Prince licenses rulers who use a religion they do not share, and the chapter judges Adama's hope-based use of the Earth myth and Roslin's uniting religiosity as essentially moral while the Cylons wield faith as a coercive weapon. Madison's Enlightenment demand that religion be directed by reason and conviction rather than force supplies the standard the fear-based Cylon conversion of Baltar fails.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 41 "So Say We All" — Richard Berger reads the 're-imagined' series through Bakhtin's dialogism: Moore's show is not a GINO remake but a polyphonic dialogue with the 1978 series and its own sources, including the Book of Mormon, von Daniken's Chariots of the Gods, Greek myth and fan fiction. That polyphony appears on screen as a spectrum of belief, from Baltar's militant atheism argued over with Number Six's fundamentalism, a staging of the Dawkins-Hitchens debate in which the two extremes prove close enough for conversion, to Roslin's prophetic politics. The chapter argues the reboot is 'more Battlestar Galactica' because it makes the original's latent religious debates explicit.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 14 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Yuen reads the silver guillotine of intercision against infant circumcision: both cut unconsenting children as acts of faith, Mrs. Coulter's belief that severing dæmons prevents original sin mirroring the Abrahamic covenant of Genesis 17. Deploying W.K. Clifford's shipowner ('It is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone to believe anything upon insufficient evidence') and Hume's claim that belief is an involuntary feeling no will can command, he argues that the real moral fault lies in acting on uninvestigated beliefs in ways that harm others, while Mrs. Coulter's non-consensual experiments on kidnapped children are wrong independently of what she believes. He concludes that if cutting Pantalaimon from Lyra is wrong, circumcision is wrong for the same reasons though less severely, at worst as irresponsible as exposing a child to chicken pox.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 21 "Do You Believe It" — Patrick Tiernan argues that Fenway fandom is a genuine religion: William James's four marks of mystical experience (ineffability, noetic quality, transiency, passivity) map onto memories of Buckner's error and Dave Roberts's steal, and Peter Berger's 'signals of transcendence' structure the rituals of Truck Day, the hopes of spring training, the damnation of Bucky Dent and Johnny Damon, and the humor of 'Cowboy Up.' He roots the Curse of the Bambino in New England's Puritan-Calvinist legacy of persecution and original sin (Frazee's sale of Ruth), then deploys Hume's account of superstition from 'Of Superstition and Enthusiasm' to deflate the exorcism rituals fans actually performed, from a Sox hat on Everest to dredging for Ruth's piano, as post hoc fallacies. Even so, the rituals reveal the human need for religious practice, and Maslow's peak experience renders the 2004 comeback a brush with the sacred, so the Faithful believe because they have to.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 24 "Breaking the Eighth Commandment" — Joel Cade maps baseball's traditionalist-versus-sabermetric war onto the faith-and-reason debate: Joe Morgan's refusal to even read Moneyball repeats Tertullian's fideism, Ted Williams's Science of Hitting exemplifies Augustine's 'faith seeking understanding,' and Wade Boggs's game-day chicken ritual completes his rational hitting exactly as Aquinas says faith completes reason. Theo Epstein's 2004 front office fused the models under the motto 'understanding justifies faith,' using statistics to discover when supposedly obsolete traditional weapons like the stolen base actually work, which is why the seemingly anti-Moneyball Dave Roberts trade paid off in The Steal against Mariano Rivera in Game Four of the ALCS. The chapter closes with the joke that Augustine, who stole pears, would bless stealing second: reconciling faith and reason is how the Sox reversed the Curse, and maybe how faith- and reason-guided people might reconcile.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 28 "Get Serious" — David Kyle Johnson takes Nietzsche's suggestion that God is slowly dying and reads The Onion's religion stories — the faith healer who loses a patient during a routine miracle, Kansas fundamentalists lobbying to overturn the Second Law of Thermodynamics, and 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' — as evidence of secularization. He splits blind faith (irrational belief despite evidence, as with Bush's 'Blind-Faith-Based Initiatives') from genuine faith as belief without sufficient evidence, arguing religion does science badly whenever it shields creationism from falsification. But science rests on unproven assumptions too, he shows via Hume's problem of induction, Descartes' skeptical problem, and Wittgenstein's charge that naming a 'strong nuclear force' explains no more than God pushing things down. Ockham's razor then decides for atheism — an unexplained universe is simpler than God plus a universe — though William James's will to believe leaves a door open for faith where evidence is impossible, qualified by Clifford's warning that beliefs likely to harm others are never permissible.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 16 "Hope" — Beck reads Snakes & Arrows as popular Epicureanism delivered by Lucretius' method: just as De Rerum Natura puts honey on the rim of the cup so Romans swallow philosophical medicine disguised as poetry, Rush's melodies smuggle reflection on pain, luck, and religion past listeners who think they are just rocking, with repeated choruses doing the work of Epicurean prolepsis. The random swerve of atoms explains 'The Larger Bowl''s unequal fortunes ('Some are blessed and some are cursed'), while the shore-watcher's relief at another's shipwreck and the concertgoer's pleasure exemplify Epicurean ataraxia. 'Faithless' and 'Armor and Sword' ('Pray and pass the ammunition') echo Lucretius' trampling of superstitious religio, and the chapter closes with Philodemus' Herculaneum scroll: don't fear god, don't worry about death.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 18 "Sweet Miracles of (Secular) Faith, Hope, and Love" — Florek reconstructs Peart's ethics as Aristotelian virtue ethics: aiming at eudaimonia rather than feeling good, 'Freewill' chooses autonomy and responsibility as virtues, and 'Vital Signs' adds persistence and courage ('courageous convictions will drag the dream into existence'), with a compassionate expansion toward ordinary sufferers in 'Distant Early Warning', 'Red Sector A' ('I must help my mother stand up straight'), and 'Everyday Glory'. Peart's existential consciousness then confronts finitude ('Time Stand Still', the fading memory of 'Vapor Trail'), contingency ('Roll the Bones' — 'Why does it happen? Because it happens'), and the absurd of Sartre and Camus ('The Stars Look Down' — an indifferent universe that answers nothing).
