He argues Charlie reaches dysdaimonia by acquiring vices and pursuing an ignoble (gangster) life, closing with Plato's Symposium and Sartre's facticity/transcendence to cast unhappiness as an ontological lack at the heart of human desire.
- **The Philosophy of Spike Lee**, ch. 11 "Aristotle and MacIntyre on Justice in 25th Hour" — Conard uses Lee's 25th Hour to test Aristotle's claim that justice is inseparable from community and necessary for eudaimonia, and MacIntyre's charge that liberal individualist society lacks any common good. Comparing the greedy Wall Street broker Frank (an Aristotelian overreacher driven by pleonexia) with the drug dealer Monty (fairer, though convicted under unjust Rockefeller laws), he argues Monty is not unjust yet still cannot flourish in a fragmented New York. Monty's profane bathroom 'fuck you' soliloquy dramatizes the city's incommensurable values, while the post-9/11 fellow-feeling offers a fleeting glimpse of the shared good MacIntyre says modern society lacks.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 8 "Civilization and Its Discontents The Self-Sufficient Western Hero" — Den Uyl builds a composite philosophic picture of self-sufficiency from Aristotle's autarkeia (reason-guided virtuous activity, requiring external goods and civilization) and Spinoza's freedom as acting from one's own nature guided by adequate ideas, then tests it on John Ford's heroes. In The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance, Tom Doniphon is 'procedurally' self-sufficient in the precivilized West while Ransom Stoddard embodies civilized reason, and neither can inhabit the other's world. He argues the western's deepest value is Emersonian self-reliance—fidelity to one's own unique nature (the 'cactus rose')—which civilization threatens even as it enables Aristotelian flourishing.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 18 "9 Neil Young’s Search for the Simple Life" — Watson and Riches reinterpret "A Man Needs a Maid" not as simple misogyny but as Young's ambivalent inner conflict between craving companionship and fearing the pain of intimacy. They read his pursuit of the "simple life" ("Heart of Gold," avoidance of reading) through Epicurean simplicity, Aristotle's eudaimonia, Bowlby/Freudian avoidant attachment and cognitive dissonance, and Sartre's "bad faith" as self-deception, set against Thoreau's chosen solitude and Aristotle's claim that the non-social being is "beast or god."
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 4 "Love, Value, and the Human Destiny in Interstellar" — Belluomini and Dunn use Interstellar's clash between Cooper's partial parental love and Professor Brand's species-level 'Plan B' to ask why the survival of humanity matters and what 'saving humanity' means. Drawing on Aristotle, they treat Cooper's daughter Murph as 'another self' loved as an end in itself and tie the good to individual happiness (eudaimonia), so 5,000 faceless embryos could never be the intrinsic good a real family is. They then turn to Kant to argue humans have unconditional value (dignity) as rational beings, which both grounds a reason to preserve the species AND condemns Brand's 'monstrous lie' as treating people merely as means to an end they do not share.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 20 "10. Cas Is Family" — Doll traces Castiel's arc from a cold Divine-Command/utilitarian 'hammer of the Lord' to a member of the Winchester family through Aristotle's ethics. She argues Cas learns to contemplate and act on the chief good under Dean's tutelage, pursuing eudaimonia by habituation despite repeated failures (becoming a false god, the Leviathans), and that his bond with Sam and Dean grows through Aristotle's three friendships—utility, pleasure, and finally the rare true friendship of virtuous character—culminating in his self-sacrificing declaration of love that defeats Billie.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 14 "5. Friendship, Fun, Freedom, Food, and the Future" — Le Gall and Taliaferro read Bourdain's Libya and Iran episodes of Parts Unknown through Pierre Hadot's 'philosophy as a way of life,' arguing that Gaddafi and Khomeini were failed Platonic philosopher-kings. They interpret ordinary Libyans and Iranians eating Uncle Kentucky chicken, playing pinball, or hosting feasts as popular 'spiritual exercises' — tatonnement — showing how the personal becomes political and how friendship, fun, freedom, and food nourish the Socratic care of the soul.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 27 "Lessons Learned" — McAleer uses the British Office to teach Aristotle's virtue ethics, treating wit as a character virtue that is a mean between the vices of buffoonery (excess) and boorishness (deficiency). David Brent is the buffoon, slave to his need to be thought funny; Gareth Keenan the literalist boor who cannot take or get a joke; and Tim Canterbury the ready-wit whose ironic humor is appropriate to circumstance. McAleer argues wit shows Aristotle's morality is broader than duty or outcome, aiming at eudaimonia, and that humor's uncodifiability, like Wittgenstein's remarks, mirrors how virtue requires practical wisdom rather than rules.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 49 "House and the Life of Reason" — Henry Jacoby argues that despite House's line that we are 'selfish, base animals crawling across the Earth,' House lives a meaningful life. Rejecting God-, soul-, and afterlife-based meaning (House's Euthyphro-style objections and his '97 Seconds' near-death experiment), Jacoby locates meaning in the Socratic examined life and Aristotle's life of reason as humanity's proper function. House's relentless curiosity and puzzle-solving, tied to action and to saving lives, exemplify reason governing desire and yield eudaimonia - so 'doing things changes things,' and House, however miserable he seems, leads the examined, meaningful life.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 10 "Oh, the Places You’ll Go! The Examined, Happy Life" — Benjamin Rider reads Oh, the Places You'll Go! through Socrates' claim that the unexamined life is not worth living. He argues the Sneetches' star-obsession, Yertle's tower, Gertrude McFuzz's feathers, and the Once-ler's 'biggering' are the false, unexamined beliefs about wealth and status that Socrates said wreck the soul, while Bartholomew Cubbins and Horton model the wise, courageous endurance Socrates seeks but fails to define with the generals Laches and Nicias in Plato's Laches. The 'Waiting Place' becomes the life of someone who never questions what really makes him happy, and Seuss's call to use 'the brains in your head' echoes Socrates' insistence in the Crito and Phaedo on living by rational reflection.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 25 "It’s Not Personal . . . It’s Just Bizzyneuss Business Ethics, the Company, and Its Stakeholders" — Pierlott frames the shareholder-versus-stakeholder debate (Friedman versus Freeman) using Aristotle's function argument to ask what makes a 'good' company, then judges business relationships by Kant's humanity formula. McBean's manipulation of the Sneetches and the digital-TV cases show consumers used merely as means; McGurk's cavalier overworking of Sneelock in If I Ran the Circus and Maitland's sweatshop defense are answered with Marx's account of labor exploitation and Aristotle's voluntary-versus-mixed actions; the Once-ler's Lorax devastation shows firms externalizing environmental costs when profit is maximized at any value unprotected by law.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 3 "Introduction" — Jacob Held defends the philosophy-and-popular-culture project against snobbery and argues that King's horror is genuine philosophy because it forces readers to confront finitude, meaning, and their deepest values. He reads King's own account of 'existential horror' through Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian pairing, casting the horror tale as a Dionysian crack in an Apollonian order that ends by restoring equilibrium, and frames doing this fun, relatable work as its own eudaimonia poised between nihilism and Aristotelian flourishing. Using Lovecraft's Cthulhu and King's Desperation/The Regulators (Tak), he claims horror shakes us into reaffirming the values that orient us and so bridges abstract academic philosophy and lived experience.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 10 "Stephen King and Aristotelian Friendship" — Bertha Alvarez Manninen reads The Body (Stand by Me) and Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption through Aristotle's Nicomachean and Eudemian Ethics on the three friendships. Andy and Norton/the guards exemplify friendships of utility (the tax help, the Rita Hayworth poster), the boys' tree-house camaraderie and Vern/Teddy exemplify pleasure friendships that dissolve as characters change, while Gordie-and-Chris and Andy-and-Red model enduring friendships of virtue rooted in mutual good will, shared confidences, and cultivating each other's excellence. Manninen then presses Aristotle: his strict 'only good men' criterion and his debt-bound, property-like view of the parent-child bond fail the flawed-but-loyal Andy/Red and the abusive fathers in The Body, showing human friendship is more complex than his taxonomy allows.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 8 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Marinucci's editorial introduction surveys the volume, framing Austen's six novels as a body of work with philosophical value across love/marriage, morality/virtue, wealth/class, concepts, and zombie mashups. It previews each contributor's thesis: Bufacchi reading Anne Elliot and the Bennets through Fricker's epistemic injustice, Dougherty aligning Austen's ideal marriage with Aristotelian complete friendship, Lindenmuth pairing Austen with Nietzsche on marital happiness, and Bane's Marxist reading of the 1940 Pride and Prejudice film. It argues Austen is an 'accidental philosopher' whose insight into social relations, especially women's vulnerability, carries philosophical weight.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 13 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Lindenmuth pairs Austen with Nietzsche on what makes a happy marriage, reading Pride and Prejudice's clashes over Lizzy's refusals of Mr. Collins and Darcy, and Lady Catherine's and Sir Thomas Bertram's aristocratic insistence that superiors should choose for inferiors. He uses Nietzsche's 'philosophizing with a hammer' to cast Austen as smashing the dead traditions of entailment and arranged marriage, and Nietzsche's aphorisms (a good marriage rests on a talent for friendship and good conversation; sensuality makes love grow too fast) to judge the couples, concluding Austen holds an Aristotelian, objective view of happiness as a reward for getting life right rather than mere desire-satisfaction.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 16 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Potzsch reads Emma as an Aristotelian study of eudaimonia, arguing Emma's self-deception and the flattery of those around her block her from true happiness, which for Aristotle is activity of the soul in accordance with reason and virtue. She diagnoses Emma's cruelty to Miss Bates at Box Hill as Aristotelian akrasia (moral weakness): Emma knows better but is overpowered by the desire to shine, showing virtue has not yet become her second nature. She contrasts Emma and Mrs. Elton's pursuit of honor (which Aristotle deems superficial, illustrated via Plato's Euthyphro) with Knightley's genuine virtue, and closes on Aristotle's ranking of the contemplative over the political life.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 26 "Chapter 13 An Epicurean Consideration of Superstitions in Mark Twain and in the Good Life" — Baker reads Twain's ghost stories and superstition through Epicurean virtue ethics, which holds that false beliefs—above all the terror of death—breed empty desires that block eudaimonia. Citing Twain's Autobiography passage that 'annihilation has no terrors for me' as a near-verbatim Epicurean line, and using Lucretius and Nussbaum's 'Therapy of Desire,' she aligns Huck's disdain for a useless conscience and his rejection of wealth ('being rich ain't what it's cracked up to be') with the Epicurean pursuit of simple natural pleasures. She notes a tension: by making tall-tale-telling and Sunday-school-shirking so enjoyable, Twain the satirist spreads the very superstitions the Epicureans would eradicate, seeming to work at cross-purposes with them.
- **Food & Philosophy - Eat, Think, and Be Merry**, ch. 8 "Chapter 2" — Verene interprets Plutarch's Dinner of the Seven Wise Men, in which Thales, Solon, Bias and the others gather at Corinth under Periander and turn a plain dinner into a symposium on good government, household economics, and the soul. He reads their exchanges through Aristotle: Thales' claim that a ruler's happiness is to die naturally in old age is glossed by Aristotle's eudaimonia (no one is called happy until life is complete), the assigned-seating companions exemplify Aristotle's friendship of utility, and the pivot from politics to home management mirrors Aristotle linking Politics to Economics. Solon's Stoic argument that dependence on food enslaves the soul, and Thales' correction of the Ethiopian king's riddle-answers (virtue not God as most helpful), show the Seven speaking as philosophers rather than gourmets, with Epicurus invoked on death being nothing to the living.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 28 "MOTHERHOOD" — Nin Kirkham applies neo-Aristotelian virtue ethics to define the 'virtues of motherhood' as character dispositions that let a mother flourish (achieve eudaimonia) qua mother. She elaborates three virtues – endurance (commitment, selflessness, and long-view 'vision,' likened to endurance running), liberality (knowing when to let a child go), and moral exemplarity – each analyzed as an Aristotelian mean between vices of excess and deficit, and argues good mothering is learned by example and does not license judging other mothers against one's own ideal.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 7 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Patrick Goold's introduction frames the whole volume by applying Socrates' 'ti esti?' question to sailing — asking what sailing essentially is — and concludes there is no timeless essence (counterexamples like iceboating and windsurfing defeat every definition), so the reflective sailor, like the philosopher, must proceed without certainty. He then invokes Aristotle's notion of telos/final cause to ask what draws people to sailing's danger and discomfort, previewing the essays: Part I finds self-knowledge and virtue in facing peril (Stillwaggon, Jobson, Lebens on eudaimonia, Hutch), while later parts treat sailing as a path to flourishing through Zen, Stoicism, Spinoza, aesthetics, and physics.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 12 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Crista Lebens narrates a C-Scow sail on an inland lake — preparing the boat, casting off, coming about, capsizing, returning to the pier — as a journey toward Aristotelian eudaimonia (human flourishing). She argues sailing demands phronesis (practical wisdom) as body-knowledge, that coming about requires the Greek 'middle path' between being 'in irons' and capsizing, and that competence 'cannot be faked' so sailing forces one to live 'in truth' (via Werth's and Kierkegaard's account of the crowd 'in untruth'). Using Borgmann's device/thing distinction, she casts the sailboat as a 'thing' that calls forth skilled engagement, unlike the powerboat as a 'device' of consumption, and links truth to the beauty of a well-trimmed sail.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 22 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Jesse Steinberg and Michael Stuckart distinguish instrumental from intrinsic value (using Frankena's list) across sailing's gear, knowledge, and aesthetics, then argue via Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics that sailing is a route to eudaimonia through the cultivation of virtue. They show sailing exemplifies courage as the golden mean between cowardice and foolhardiness (deciding whether to go out in twenty-knot winds, judging teen solo circumnavigators), being hard-working (the mean between laziness and workaholism), and cleverness (jury-rigging, navigation). They contend sailing demands a broader, deeper range of virtues than golf, bowling, or power-boating, making it an especially rich — though not the only — path to a flourishing, happy life.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 20 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Sadler argues black coffee, unlike ceremonial tea, is the realist emblem of our anxious, isolated postmodern condition, and that the chain coffeehouse is a 'non-place' of public anonymity that only simulates the sociality we crave. Against Aristotle's confident view of humans as social animals whose eudaimonia presupposes a settled social order, she sets Nietzsche's alienated individual free to create values — then argues Nietzsche errs: using the trivial cappuccino-vs-latte choice, she shows (via Wittgenstein's private-language argument and Korsgaard) that even solitary choices need reasons intelligible to others, so individual choice cannot be self-justifying and our search for meaningful, non-arbitrary lives is irreducibly social.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 32 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Keleher applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics to coffee, arguing that eudaimonia (flourishing, not mere pleasant feeling) is rational activity in accordance with virtue, that the human ergon is reason, and that money, pleasure, and honor are only instrumental to it. She illustrates the golden mean and phronêsis with coffee choices—the temperate drinker like Katherine or Samantha calibrates cups to her own tolerance and circumstances rather than a fixed number—and distinguishes the truly virtuous drinker from the merely continent one who still craves the forbidden 750-calorie frappuccino. She coins the minor virtue of 'javavity,' the habit of drinking good coffee the right way for the right reasons with the right feeling, and suggests that were Aristotle alive, coffee would join his 'external goods,' the proper equipment for doing noble acts.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 14 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Opening with his intimate encounter with a wolf, Vitali argues that 'fair chase' cannot mean fairness to the animal — since a right to fair chase would imply a more basic right not to be hunted, conceding the anti-hunting case. Instead, invoking Aristotelian human flourishing and Leopold's land ethic, he relocates fair chase to the hunter: hunting is moral only if it serves the biotic community through conservation and lets the hunter enter the predator-prey life-death continuum. He illustrates self-handicapping through master hunter Milo Burcham stalking a distant muley with a recurve bow.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 12 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Dylan Ryder (a working porn star) and Dave Monroe argue that being a porn performer does not necessarily lower the prudential quality of one's life, against the common-sense view (fed by films like Boogie Nights) that porn stars are damaged, coerced, or degraded. They reject Aristotle's claim that virtue is necessary for eudaimonia and, citing Kant's deontology and utilitarianism as theories that sever welfare from morality, distinguish moral value from subjective wellbeing. Deploying the 'Happy Slave' thought experiment and Ron Amundson's disability-welfare research, they contend outsiders' pity reflects social stigma, not the performer's own first-personal welfare judgment.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 18 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Haire and Nelson read the film A Christmas Story as evidence that consumerism has replaced religion as America's faith: the Parker family shows no religious markers, and Ralphie's single-minded quest for the Red Ryder BB gun mirrors the identity-defining, transformative role religion once played. Using Aristotle's virtue ethics, they name consumerism a Christmas vice opposed to candidate Christmas virtues of being religious, traditional and family-centered. When the BB gun nearly blinds Ralphie and the hounds ruin the turkey, the consumerist ideal fails; the family's makeshift Chinese-restaurant dinner shows the family-centered virtue overcoming the vice, so 'all was right with the world'.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 28 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Scott reads Dickens's A Christmas Carol through virtue theory, treating Scrooge's transformation as a lesson in the virtues of generosity and gratitude that constitute eudaimonia (human flourishing). Drawing on Niebuhr, he explains Scrooge's greed as an anxious, insecurity-driven quest for security through wealth that fails because flourishing depends on relationships, not money (the poor-but-happy Cratchits). He invokes MacIntyre's 'just generosity' and Aristotelian habituation to show virtues are cultivated through practice, and uses Charles Taylor's weak/strong evaluations to warn that Christmas consumerism threatens 'keeping Christmas' by reducing moral worth to preferences and purchases.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 9 "CYCLING" — O'Brien's editorial introduction frames gardening as engaging core philosophical questions and previews the volume. It argues that gardening promotes a good life not through hedonistic pleasure but through virtuous traits like patience and a Stoic-tinged tranquility that ancient philosophers from Epicurus to Hume prized, and it invokes Kant to cast the gardener as a visual artist. It also sketches gardens as cosmic symbols (Pythagorean ratios at Versailles) and closes on Plato's Phaedrus image of educating the soul as tending plants.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 11 "GARDENING" — Isis Brook argues that gardening objectively improves both the land (through composting, nurturing plants, and Warwick Fox's 'responsive cohesion' with wider contexts) and the gardener's moral character. Taking a virtue-ethics approach and drawing on David Cooper, she holds that gardening practices incidentally cultivate patience, humility, recognition of reality, care for others, and open-heartedness. She uses concrete cases—Sackville-West's white garden at Sissinghurst, her own failed Cerinthe and thriving ferns—to show how collaborating with nature nurtures these flourishing-related virtues.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 31 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Schick asks whether humans need to alter consciousness (Weil, Maslow's hierarchy, Siegel's animal examples of reindeer, elephants, and rats seeking intoxicants) and concludes we have no such need, though we can flourish from it. He applies Sen and Nussbaum's capabilities approach, arguing cannabis enhances Nussbaum's second (bodily health, via endocannabinoids and medical uses) and fourth (senses, imagination, thought, via enriched music perception and possible creativity) capabilities. Citing Aristotle's and the Buddha's golden mean against abuse, and evidence of no lasting brain harm, he judges paternalistic prohibition an unjustified deprivation of the capabilities needed for a good life.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 17 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Brian Treanor argues from Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics that climbing is a crucible for cultivating virtues (arete) that contribute to flourishing (eudaimonia), stressing that virtue is acquired by habituation and lies in a mean 'relative to us'—so casting off on the Bachar-Yerian is courage for a 5.11 leader but rashness for a 5.9 climber. He shows how climbing's self-imposed 'rules' (Tejada-Flores' games) forge courage (feeling the right balance of fear and confidence, as in John Sherman's Fisher Towers epic and Steve House's judicious retreats on K7), humility (honestly measuring oneself against pioneers who used inferior gear, per Chouinard and Messner's 'murder of the impossible'), and reverence for nature (Thoreau, Muir, Brower). His thesis is that in a coddled, technological world climbing is uncommonly well suited to building these excellences of character.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 32 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Ethics professor Paul MacNeill argues ethics is intrinsic to yoga and knowable only through practice, not by mining texts — a Western reason-first bias that trivializes it. He shows the yamas and niyamas are counter-measures aimed at samadhi (paralleling how Aristotle's virtues aim at eudaimonia, though yoga subordinates reason), and that Vedanta's transcendent and Kashmir Shaivism's immanent metaphysics both function as instruments toward expanded awareness. From that dissolution of the separate self, he claims, compassion flows naturally, so Hatha yoga's asana and pranayama dissolve the ingrained bodily/mental habits that block ethical, equilibrium-born action.
- **Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low**, ch. 20 "BLUES" — Roopen Majithia asks why a music born of African-American suffering became universally beloved and answers with Aristotle's account of musical catharsis in the Politics. Drawing on the Nicomachean Ethics link between habituated action, emotion, and disposition (as courage is built by acting courageously), he argues music images real emotions and thereby purges excess feeling. Modern electric urban blues (T-Bone Walker's 'Stormy Monday,' Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf), with its danceable, sexually charged rhythm, recreates the emotional landscape of repetitive urban work and, aided by dancing, effects a broad catharsis — which also explains why non-black communal performers can play it and why intimate bars beat arenas.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 21 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Joshua Heter mounts a virtue-theoretic case against being set up on blind dates, using Aristotle's notion of telos and the distinction between fleeting 'hot-fudge happiness' and eudaimonia, the flourishing of a well-lived life (illustrated by long-married Bill and Fran). He argues a 'guy's' function is achieved by exercising his whole nature, and dramatizes this with Zoo-bear versus Wild-bear: the zoo-fed bear has its hunger and safety met but cannot flourish because it never hunts or roams, just as matchmaking meets the romantic need while letting a man's 'social muscles' atrophy. Invoking Aristotle's philia (and Nussbaum on Aristotelian virtue), he concedes friends mean well but recommends they merely introduce people and let things progress naturally rather than force an 'unnatural' match.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 29 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Naar and Masala defend the 'Secret Underground Internet Seduction Community' by grounding it in Darwinian sexual selection (the peacock's tail, mate value, women prioritizing status and men prioritizing youth/beauty) and an Aristotelian ideal of happiness as excellence: they read the community's aim of becoming a well-rounded seducer as cultivating virtue and social/emotional 'mating intelligence' that yields eudaimonic fulfillment. Against the Kantian objection that seduction training uses women merely as means, they offer a consequentialist and 'deflationist' reply that deception and manipulation already pervade ordinary courtship (makeup, lying about age), so raising one's mate value is morally neutral, and they extend the point to women's active and passive seduction strategies (Cleopatra, groupies).
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 16 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Gregory Bassham mines the happy communities of the Shire, Rivendell, and Lothlorien for six keys to happiness: delight in simple things (linked to Epicurus's natural pleasures and Thoreau's Walden simplicity), making light of troubles, close friendship (grounded in Aristotle's claim that friendship is the greatest external good), good character, cherishing beauty and creativity, and recovering wonder. He argues Tolkien's hobbits and elves illustrate what modern happiness research confirms, so Tolkien functions as a philosophical guide to a more joy-filled life.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 17 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Jorge Gracia contrasts Sam and Gollum, two hobbits of shared nature and culture who both pursue happiness but reach opposite ends. Gollum's happiness is possession of the Precious, a thing, sought in isolation and won by murdering Deagol, which destroys him; Sam's happiness is fellowship in the Shire with Frodo and Rosie, and his love for Frodo lets him surrender the Ring where Gollum cannot. Drawing on Aristotle's tie between happiness, one's nature, and friendship, Gracia concludes that for ordinary beings happiness is achievable only in a social context whose key is love expressed as loyalty and sharing.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 27 "Lessons Learned" — Sean McAleer uses the British Office to teach Aristotle's virtue ethics, treating wit as a virtue that is a mean between the vices of buffoonery (excess) and boorishness (deficiency). David Brent is the buffoon, 'the slave of his sense of humor,' who jests inappropriately; Gareth is the boorish literalist who cannot take or get a joke; Tim is the ready-wit whose ironic humor is appropriate to the situation, exercising practical wisdom (phronesis). McAleer argues virtue is about acting and feeling appropriately (not mere moderation), that Aristotle's morality is broad enough to include humor as part of flourishing (eudaimonia), and that, like humor, virtue is noncodifiable.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 49 "House and the Life of Reason" — Jacoby argues that despite House calling us "selfish, base animals," House lives Socrates' examined life and Aristotle's life of reason. He dismisses God-given meaning using the Euthyphro dilemma and rejects the soul and afterlife (the "97 Seconds" self-experiment), insisting "our actions here are all that matters." Meaning must be both subjective and objective; House's puzzle-solving realizes humanity's rational function, tied to action and virtue, and — per Aristotle — yields eudaimonia, so his life is meaningful even when it doesn't feel that way to him.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 27 "25. The Mandalorian as Philosophy “This Is the Way”" — The chapter argues that The Mandalorian defends virtue ethics with care as the primary virtue. It maps Mando's creed and 'Canons of Honor' (strength, honor, loyalty, death) onto Stoicism's discipline of desire and cardinal virtues, quoting Marcus Aurelius and Seneca, and reads his transformation after adopting Grogu as Aristotelian moral development toward eudaimonia and flourishing. Using Stocker's critique of impartialist ethics and Noddings's and Slote's ethics of care, Belluomini argues Mando's caring relation with Grogu, his engrossment and motivational displacement, and his removing his helmet at the end show that care ranks highest among the virtues and should guide our own 'Way.'
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 89 "84. The Legend of Zelda Breath of the Wild as Philosophy Teaching the Player to Be Comfortable Being Alone" — Lay argues that Breath of the Wild teaches, chiefly through design rather than plot, that solitude is good for the player. He tests eternal return (the recurring Ganon-Zelda-Link cycle across the series), Sartrean absolute freedom and Kierkegaardian anxiety of choice (BotW's Korok-dung 'reward' and refusal to attach external meaning push players to make their own meaning), and Kierkegaard's inward 'repetition.' He lands on Mill's and Schopenhauer's defense of solitude-in-nature as self-actualizing rather than isolating, and reads sequence-breaking exploits as Marx-style spontaneous creative activity, concluding the game frames solitude as a path to eudaimonia and human flourishing.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 101 "95. The Walking Dead as Philosophy Rick Grimes and Community Building in an Apocalypse" — Jones argues that Kirkman's The Walking Dead uses Rick Grimes's community-building to probe utopia and dystopia, reading the prison, Alexandria, Woodbury, the Saviors, and the Commonwealth through Aristotle's six constitutional forms—with the polity (rule by many for the common good enabling eudaimonia) as the standard for a good society and tyranny/oligarchy/corrupt forms marking dystopias like Negan's compound and the class-tyrannical Commonwealth. Invoking More's and Mill's coinages of utopia and dystopia, the chapter asks why Rick's final society, despite his moral evolution, ends up rebuilding the hierarchical pre-apocalyptic order rather than the more egalitarian, flourishing alliance he had forged.

### Socratic Method (elenchus)

The Socratic method, or elenchus, is a form of cooperative inquiry in which a claim is tested through a disciplined series of questions rather than asserted or refuted directly. Socrates would draw out a person's definition of some notion such as justice or courage, then expose contradictions among the beliefs they held alongside it, leading them to abandon or refine the original view. Its aim is less to win an argument than to clear away false confidence and move both parties closer to a defensible understanding. The method treats knowledge as something arrived at through examination, not received ready-made.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 9 "Unknown" — Irwin parallels Neo's mission with Socrates' divine commission from the Oracle at Delphi to 'wake up' Athens: both are driven by a single question ('What is the Matrix?' versus 'What is the good life?'), both are charged by the authorities, and both sting a complacent public. He explains the Socratic method through the Euthyphro exchange on holiness, where a follow-up question ('Is the holy holy because the gods approve it, or do they approve it because it is holy?') exposes Euthyphro's ignorance, and introduces Socrates' mantra 'I know nothing' as the humility that launches his quest just as Neo's lack of self-knowledge launches his.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 10 "Unknown" — Irwin compares the film's kitchen-table Oracle with the Pythia at Delphi: both utter cryptic prophecies that seekers misread, from Croesus's doomed war to Morpheus's certainty that Neo is the One, and both make self-knowledge the real key to interpretation. He reads the 'Temet Nosce' sign and the cookie scene through the Delphic maxims 'Know thyself' and 'Nothing in excess', arguing Neo fulfills the prophecy only when he comes to know and believe in himself, and closes by linking Socrates' gadfly mission and 'the unexamined life is not worth living' to Fight Club, Boys Don't Cry, and Memento.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 19 "Kant, Aristotle, and the Cheater" — Answering Cal Ripken's Socratic question 'What is cheating?' (raised by Sammy Sosa's corked bat and Gaylord Perry's spitball), Randolph Feezell stages a dialogue between Abbey's Kantian absolutism, Trev's traditionalism, and Ron's win-at-all-costs realism. Kant's categorical imperative grounds the absolutist: intending to break a rule to gain an edge is making yourself an arbitrary exception to rules that bind all players equally. Aristotle's virtue ethics then lets the traditionalist say that some strategic rule-breaking belongs to a sport's 'prescriptive atmosphere' (stealing signs, the balk pickoff, catching framing), since honesty and courage are means between excess and defect guided by judgment rather than exceptionless rules, while corking a bat stays cheating because it defies the tradition and hides from umpires.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 35 "Last Pitch" — Reid argues that baseball and Socratic elenchus are both constructed to cultivate aretē, excellence. She maps four parallels onto concrete moments: both live off uncertainty (pre-game jitters, the 2001 Rivera–Gonzalez Series finish), both require risking failure (Ted Williams playing a doubleheader to protect his .400, Kirk Gibson's hobbling 1988 homer off Dennis Eckersley, Billy Beane's fear beside Lenny Dykstra), both demand active self-testing (Lou Gehrig retiring when complimented on a routine play), and both impose an obligation to return and challenge others — Plato's cave allegory, Socrates the gadfly, the aging champion who applauds the record-breaker. The Delphic oracle's riddle, that Socrates is wisest in knowing his ignorance, is the batter's-box humility every at-bat demands.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 27 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Takes Digory's dying remark 'It's all in Plato' as the key to the Chronicles. It compares the Professor's guided questioning of Peter and Susan about Lucy's wardrobe testimony to the Socratic method, though noting he supplies evidential maxims rather than eliciting a virtue-definition as Socrates does with Cephalus on justice. It maps Underland in The Silver Chair onto the Allegory of the Cave (Rilian bound in his silver chair like the chained prisoners, the Green Witch's enchantment that denies any world beyond), observing that the Witch 'plays Aristotle' by ridiculing Aslan as an invented perfect Form, while Puddleglum's 'stand by the play-world' speech echoes Socrates's reply to Glaucon that the ideal pattern is none the worse for being unrealizable. Finally it reads the 'real Narnia' of The Last Battle ('world within world, Narnia within Narnia') as Christian Platonism, with the nested heavens even raising Plato's Third Man problem.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 9 "From Rhyme to Reason This Shit Ain’t Easy" — The editors' introduction argues that hip hop and philosophy are both street-born examinations of life in pursuit of wisdom: Socrates's elenchus is likened to MC lyrical battles and call-and-response (his interrogations compared to Rakim's technique, his execution for corrupting the youth to the fate of a controversial rapper), while Plato's philosopher-king parallels Kurtis Blow and Run-D.M.C. claiming thrones. After a Bronx hip-hop history sketch (Kool Herc, BDP's "The Bridge is Over"), they frame the volume around hip hop's suppressed fifth element of knowledge and preview its pairings: Aquinas and Rakim on God, Plato and Lauryn Hill on love, Sartre and Lil' Kim's gaze, Kant and Ice Cube on punishment, Hegel and Nas, Hobbes and Dead Prez, Mill and Chappelle on epithets. Record companies don't own hip hop and universities don't own philosophy, they conclude - both belong to whoever understands, loves, and respects them.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 87 "Chapter 13 - Political Bullshit and the Stoic Story of Self" — Evans concludes that the antidote to political bullshit is a discursive culture trained in Socratic skills of self-examination — citizens taught to recognize how their own views may be imperfect and how to refine them — together with the analytic-philosophical style his Oxford tutor called 'a very good bullshit detector'. Experts may lead debates by their greater factual knowledge and critical acumen, but the debates must stay democratically inclusive rather than become an elite monopoly. Citing G.A. Cohen, he warns that too much fashionable philosophy disparages truth and so itself produces bullshit, and that using the ubiquity of bullshit to justify the cynicism thesis's crippling inertia would be potentially catastrophic.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 8 "Introduction" — Introduces Part I by casting South Park, The Daily Show, and The Colbert Report as modern Socratic gadflies. It previews Young's comparison of the show's 'corruption of the youth' controversies to Socrates' trial, Arp's use of Johnnie Cochran's Chewbacca Defense to teach logic and fallacies, and Johnson's use of Colbert's 'wikiality' and 'truthiness' to attack relativism and the myth that everyone has a right to their opinion.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 12 "Springsteen’s Revolution" — Anderson and Anderson open with the Che Guevara t-shirt problem and Marcuse's one-dimensional man: the system assimilates protest, so internal critique (Springsteen on the cover of Rolling Stone, its Chevrolet calendar, the Eagles sold at Wal-Mart, Adorno's verdict on co-opted popular music) is a sop to Cerberus. Against this they set Springsteen's own account of his music as 'a very long conversation with my audience' — a transactional public service — and argue he survives the co-optation charge as a 'Socratic revolutionary' who, like Socrates refusing to leave Athens, works from within: listening without obeying ('I liked the old Bruce better'), refusing to ride the Born to Run wave, turning to Guthrie and Seeger, and drawing no hard conclusions, only opening spaces of reflection ('Born in the U.S.A.', 'Radio Nowhere', 'Long Walk Home'). Revolution is just another form of work — practice, sweat, and the personal job of 'growin' up.'
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 26 "The Final Word That’s Right, I Said Preliminary Thoughts" — Patton starts from wildly disputed Springsteen interpretations — Reagan's 1984 campaign use of 'Born in the U.S.A.,' Flint protesters playing 'My Hometown' as civic pride, Kerry's 'No Surrender' — and asks whether any reading is better than another. He frames the issue as Socratic dialectic versus Gorgias-style rhetoric, passes through Augustine's polysemy (multiple intended levels of meaning, as in 'I'm on fire') to Nietzsche's claim that the text disappears beneath its interpretation, extended by Foucault (truth as an instrument of power) and Derridean deconstruction. His conclusion: authorial intent cannot settle meaning, but some readings ('Born in the U.S.A.' as pro-Reagan anthem) are non-starters, otherwise it is rhetoric all the way down and the sophists win.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 28 "Springsteen’s Martyrdom" — The Bells parallel Socrates' forcible 'abduction' to the house of the arms merchant Cephalus in Republic Book I with Springsteen's 1984 political abduction, when Reagan and Mondale both pretended he had endorsed them and George Will invited him to be laureate of 'joyous overconsumption.' They read the Republic's luxurious city — its Ring of Gyges parasites, censorship of poets, and wars born of appetite — as an elenchus run against the control (epoche) of the healthy working city of Book II, so readers who take the 'ideal' city at face value err exactly like fans who hear patriotism in 'Born in the U.S.A.' Songs like 'Youngstown,' 'The Angel' and 'Galveston Bay' likewise critique overconsumption, imperialism and the censorship of artists, and both artist-critics risk the martyrdom Socrates suffered for speaking truth to the powerful.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 14 "Democratization of Media—Philosophy for All!" — Parker recounts training for the Seoul Marathon on a treadmill with philosophy podcasts (Philosophy Talk, Philosophy Bites, LibriVox) to argue the iPod works as a 'next-generation book' that can democratize philosophy -- yet, like the book, it cannot supply the two-way dialogue that Socrates practiced in the agora and that Plato's Academy, Aristotle's Lyceum, and Epicurus's Garden were built to sustain. He distinguishes studying philosophy -- compiling, say, Kant's claim that one cannot act except in ways one could will all others to act -- from doing it, and argues that credentials and canon cannot displace each person's inescapable role as 'the arbiters of our own thoughts.' The Nazis' misconstrual of Nietzsche is his example of interpretation without critical guardianship, and he concludes that the academy's stronghold on teaching philosophy is loosening even if wikis and virtual forums never fully replace professional expertise.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 15 "After Forgetting" — Sturgis argues that iPods plus the collaborative Web 2.0 will end education's age of memorization: the school 'cheaters' storing test answers in lyrics files are early adopters of a world where, as Plato's Meno already allowed, knowledge can be retrieved rather than remembered, and a remote server is no more crash-prone than a brain ('the server could crash, but so could I'). His own podcasted environmental-ethics course shows Socratic, question-driven lecturing and radio's 'theater of the mind' reaching distance learners, while MIT OpenCourseWare and Berkeley webcasts (a trucker listening to Hubert Dreyfus) globalize elite content. Following Dewey on reflection and artistry, he predicts a post-factual pedagogy of assessing sources -- he catches Wikipedia misreading an iPod '90 percent market share' claim -- collaborative creation, and candid acceptance that we are already integrated with technological devices.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 30 "19 - The Rhodesian Stranger" — A comic Socratic dialogue, a pastiche of Plato's Phaedrus, in which a time-lost 'Rhodesian Stranger' wanders in mid-conversation to defend reading against Socrates' retelling of the Thamus-and-Thoth myth — writing as inert painting that gives 'the semblance of truth', summed up in the Stranger's quoting his 'fellow Rhodish' philosopher Schopenhauer: thoughts on paper are footprints in the sand, the path seen but not what was seen along the way. Socrates' elenchus (the ship ticket versus the journey, walking beside a friend and turning back to check on him rather than posting signposts) drives the Stranger into inventing a myth in which gods replace abused speech with pea-pods whose planted seeds become pod-casts gathered by pod-catchers — podcasting imagined as friends dialoguing together toward the true and the good. Socrates closes skeptically, doubting that disconnected pod-communication escapes trivia and universal broadcast, but concedes 'surely beauty is as faithful a guide towards the good as is truth.'
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 7 "Setting Up the Game" — Editor Luke Cuddy's introduction: he argues videogames, and the Zelda franchise in particular, deserve philosophical attention, then frames the book's spirit with Plato's Meno. Just as Socrates' questioning leads the slave boy from thinking he knows to actually knowing that a double-sized square has area sixteen, the gamer's struggle through dungeons is rewarded with the item-room fanfare (the ladder, the silver arrow) as an 'AHA!' feeling of insight. The chapter lists the franchise's games and the book's guiding questions, stressing that the gamer guides Link rather than passively watching.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 20 "Colbert Is (the Tragedy and Comedy of) America, and So Are We" — Ralkowski asks whether Colbert is America's Socrates, comparing Colbert's ironic interviews (Caitlin Flanagan on feminism, Harvey Mansfield on manliness, Howard Dean's superdelegates, the ABC Stephanopoulos-Gibson debate) to Socrates' definitional refutations of Euthyphro and the Athenian elite. Like Socrates in Plato's cave allegory, Colbert is a shadow on the wall undermining truthiness from within, yet both fail: audiences laugh, guests collect the campaign-donation 'Colbert Bump,' and nothing changes, making America the self-satisfied one who is ignorant of its ignorance. Through Nehamas's contrast of Socratic and Platonic irony and the Symposium's demand that the greatest work read as both tragedy and comedy, the chapter concludes Colbert may be America's Plato — condemning and laughing at us like a Sisyphean liberator who knows we will not leave the cave.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 43 "Ah, Doctor. We Know You by Reputation" — Argues Doctor Who is philosophy's ally by way of Plato's Gorgias distinction between teaching, which produces justified true belief, and rhetoric, which wins by persuasion: the Master is the master rhetorician whose hypnotic manipulation manufactures unreliable beliefs, while the Doctor is the Socratic teacher who gives information and lets companions decide. Socrates's descriptions of philosophy (the good life, sense of wonder, love of real knowledge) are matched to the show's career as an educational program that teaches viewers to reflect on how they reason, how they treat 'others' like Daleks and Silurians, and to revise their views, that is, to live the examined life.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 10 "A Toolbox for Your Holmes" — Sami Paavola and Lauri Jaervilehto reconstruct the textbook on detection Holmes never wrote: following Jaakko Hintikka's interrogative (Socratic) model, where the right question cracks the case, as with the dog that did nothing in the night-time in 'Silver Blaze', and Peirce's triad of deduction, induction and abduction, the backward reasoning from effects to causes exemplified by the Watson-just-from-Afghanistan chain in A Study in Scarlet. They add Peirce's categories of Firstness, Secondness and Thirdness to show Holmes succeeds because he fuses imagination and reverie with fieldwork, experiment and exact inference. The chapter closes with a twelve-point practical toolbox distilled from the canon.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 25 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Carl Ehrett and Sarah Worth ask whether D&D is really a game (imagining Bill and Ted challenging Death to a campaign) and model the search for a definition of 'game' on Socrates dismantling Euthyphro's attempted definitions of piety, only for Wittgenstein's family resemblance to dissolve the project. On that view D&D still counts as a game despite lacking winning and losing, because its rule-governedness survives 'rule 0' license to bend rules whenever bending them crafts a better story. To explain why players who know the world is not real are nonetheless engrossed, they present Radford's paradox of fiction and adopt Walton's make-believe theory: the miniature on the table is a prop prescribing the imagining of an owlbear, so genuine quasi-emotions respond to truths in the fiction, making D&D an unusually gripping interactive story.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 19 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Timothy Sexton traces Jeopardy!'s format to the fallout from the 1950s quiz show scandals, when Charles Van Doren's rigged run on Twenty-One destroyed the elitist model of expert knowledge and television pivoted to anti-elitist game shows like The Price Is Right. He reads that pivot as parallel to the Cold-War abandonment of Dewey's progressive education for a utilitarian, worker-training curriculum, as documented by Diane Ravitch and Olaf Hoerschelmann. Jeopardy! endures as the 'Gnostic' compromise between quiz show and game show: it keeps elitist knowledge but demands that it be displayed in the Socratic ritual of answering in the form of a question, which lets a trivia show rise above the dumbed-down Millionaire era.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 23 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Rick Mayock stops a fictional Jeopardy! clock to apply Plato's divided line: most contestants, like the cave prisoners rewarded for predicting shadow sequences, trade in doxa - conjecture (eikasia) and belief (pistis) - while the Meno's slave boy shows how Socratic questioning ties true opinions down into knowledge. Winning requires only dianoia, hypothetical reasoning from hypotheses and definitions, never noesis, the dialectic that ascends to the eternal Forms; the Phaedo's example of perfect 'equality' shows why the 'Aha!' of recognition is re-cognition by an immortal soul already acquainted with the Forms. Watson, lacking such a soul, can clear a buzz threshold but never have an Aha! moment - it is Daedalus's statue, lifelike but sure to run away from the truth unless tied down.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 26 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Daniel Wanless reads Jeopardy! through the Meno: contestants can formulate the right question only because the answer is already given, just as Socrates answers Meno's paradox by claiming that all inquiry is recollection of truths the immortal soul already holds - latent knowledge that explains how Ken Jennings buzzes in before he consciously knows the response. A priori logical ability (the slave boy's doubled square, the law of non-contradiction applied to which of three cities is southernmost) guides the search for answers, while Final Jeopardy!'s blind wagering embodies Kierkegaard's 'life is only understood backwards, but it must be lived forwards.' Socrates would bet it all, Wanless concludes, because the unexamined life is not worth living: his whole life was preparation for the ultimate Final Jeopardy!, lived in the form of a question.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 22 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Fisher argues The Wire makes homosexuality a source of excellence: Omar and Kima blend masculine and feminine traits in something like Butler's gender-performative terms, build Aristotelian friendships of virtue (Kima and Cheryl pushing each other's careers), and can make the sacrifices - solitude, giving up family - that excellence in the drug war demands, while the homophobia of the streets and the precinct forces them to keep proving themselves. Omar's crossword comfort with 'them myths' frames him as a contemporary Socrates: a mentor-lover of boys, accused of amorality by Levy much as Socrates was charged with corrupting Athens's youth, answering with a Socratic reversal ('I got the shotgun, you got the briefcase'), and dying for his code in the city he would not leave. The chapter reads the show's refusal of coming-out storylines - Rawls's silent gay-bar cameo, Snoop's never-confirmed sexuality - as its most radical statement about sexuality in America.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 31 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — John Huss asks whether Andy Serkis deserved an Oscar nomination for playing Caesar through performance capture, and argues that 'What is acting?' is a Socratic-style definitional question (like stumping Euthyphro on piety) of the sort Wittgenstein diagnosed as a language confusion, since the definition of movie acting is in flux. Using the seeing-as debate, Kuhnian theory-ladenness of observation versus Fodor's Muller-Lyer point that belief does not dictate sight, he explains why animators and fans see such different things in the identical raw footage. He concludes, with James Franco, that acting is an emergent ensemble property of actors reacting to one another on a shared stage, which performance capture enables rather than threatens, and a coda notes PETA's hope that CG performers will end the use of animal actors.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 9 "Psych and Philosophy" — Michaud argues that Shawn's whole psychic career runs on fallacies of relevance - the red herring of claiming to be psychic to dodge arrest, plus ad hominem mockery that deflects Lassiter's fraud accusations - so the show's comedy turns on bad logic being used to lead people to true conclusions. Socrates supplies the opposing voice: like the Sophists who argued any side for money, Shawn reasons for convenience and amusement, and his deception is an inconsistency of the kind Socrates refused in Plato's Crito, where he would not bribe his way out of a death sentence. An invented Platonic-style dialogue has Socrates question Shawn until he concedes that lying breeds more lying and harm - 'her name is Truth!' - before Shawn escapes the elenchus by spotting lipstick on Socrates's collar. The chapter leaves the verdict open: Shawn saves lives and raises the world's happiness, but his trickery also trains Santa Barbara to reason badly and trust con artists.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 30 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Cobb treats the show's storytellers as narrative pedagogues. Nucky's wharf-rat speech is story truth rather than happening truth - Plato's Republic question of true and false tales - and because it allows no dialogue or questioning it fails as full pedagogy; Chalky's story of his father's lynching ties past to present in the interrogation of the Klansman; Rothstein's billiard-ball anecdote for Frankie Yale is episodic memory shaped into identity and threat, a coerced but genuine reasoning exchange ('Do you know what the moral is of this tale, Mr. Yale?'). Measured against Socrates' question-posing inquiry in the Euthyphro, Kant's On Education, and Freire's dialogical 'critical co-investigators,' Nucky, Chalky, and Rothstein all emerge as reflective but deficient pedagogues at large.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 30 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Mills-Knutsen reads the Brain Spawn - floating brains whose pain at others' thoughts drives them to dumb life down and finally to hoard all knowledge in the Infosphere ('The Day the Earth Stood Stupid,' 'The Why of Fry') - as Futurama's funhouse mirror of the West's distrust of intellectuals, from Pandora and Eve to Frankenstein and comic-book evil geniuses. Fry, the delta-brainwave-lacking hero made stupid by doing 'the nasty in the pasty,' stabs the Big Brain with Bonfire of the Vanities and later banishes the Brains to another dimension, just as Athens executed Socrates. A close reading of Plato's Apology - Socrates's feigned ignorance exposing everyone else's, his demand of free meals in lieu of exile, and his prophecy of even more annoying successors - maps onto the Big Brain's snobbery and onto universities (Wernstrom's tenure scam in 'A Big Piece of Garbage,' Amy's doctorate in 'That Darn Katz!') as society's way of paying intellectuals to stay out of the way.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 7 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Cam Cobb weighs Battle School against competing philosophies of education: Plato's Republic supplies vocational sorting by natural aptitude (complete with the myth of the metals as a 'noble lie'), while Socratic dialogue and Paulo Freire's problem-posing pedagogy demand the shared critical inquiry Ender never gets. He argues Graff's curriculum is almost purely vocational - military history, tactics, the Giant's Drink, battleroom drills - leaving no liberal paideia, and that the teachers' constant rule-changing leaves Ender feeling like 'someone's pawn,' exactly the banking-style teacher domination Freire warned against.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 51 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Roger Hunt reads Bill Hicks's stand-up as a Socratic comedy exposing Satan's three-point plan: suppress knowledge, breed ignorance, and profit from hypocrisy - from the Waffle House 'readah' scene to Bush-era Gulf War spin ('we looked at the receipts'), JFK-assassination distraction via American Gladiators, and pop stars and marketers who 'suck Satan's cock' (Rick Astley, corporate rock, advertising). Where the Genesis serpent offered knowledge, Hicks's Devil is the force that suppresses it, and Hicks paid a Socratic price - an early death for 'corrupting' his audience - for pointing this out.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 20 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Christopher Lauer argues Cohen's lyrics seduce through Socratic irony as Kierkegaard analyzes it in The Concept of Irony: ostentatious self-concealment that makes hearers aware of the gap between words and intentions, building 'personality' and promising intimacy. Songs like 'Closing Time,' 'Everybody Knows,' and 'Democracy' oscillate between cynical third-person verdicts and sudden second-person address, offering a hidden sincerity only to withdraw it - an erotic improvement on Plato's Socrates that dissolves its own ironic distance. 'Hallelujah' and 'Anthem' make the program explicit, treating brokenness as the space in which love develops, while 'Tower of Song' shows the bleak side: irony collapsing into pure cynicism, the singer speaking sweetly from the Tower long after all promises of genuine intimacy have been disavowed.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 19 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Roger Hunt answers 'what do philosophers do?' through Dennis's seduction methodology. Frank embodies empiricism, leaving the comfort of principle for the messiness of the world as Hume did when he found no impression of causation, space, or time; Mac embodies rationalism, reasoning with total confidence from a principle he cannot doubt, as Descartes did from the cogito; and the dialectic of Socrates and Plato, questioning beliefs in dialogue to see what survives scrutiny, describes philosophy as it is actually practiced. Boethius's Consolation - the imprisoned author consoled by dialogues with Lady Philosophy - supplies the frame of philosophy as an encounter with a woman one pursues, and each D.E.N.N.I.S. step maps onto the craft: Demonstrating value to the problem, Engaging physically in its awkward grind, Nurturing dependence through thesis panic, Neglect and Inspiring hope on the road to the defense, then Separating entirely - 'be a sociopath about it.'
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 21 "8. Should Jane Get to Be Bored" — Daniel Addison defends Louie's 'you don't get to be bored' admonishment of Jane in 'Country Drive' against Mathew Remski's charge that it transfers adult anxiety, pointing to Louis's Conan 'forever empty' monologue and reddit advice as proof that Louis insists on facing despair rather than fleeing it. The real aim, he argues, is Socratic: Louis wants Jane and the plane-complaining generation brought to aporia, the perplexity Plato's Socrates induces in the Meno's slave boy so that, no longer thinking he knows, he 'would be glad to find out.' Aristotle grounds the optimism - every human by nature desires to know, philosophy begins in wonder, and our deepest happiness lies in contemplating - so Louis's 'everything's amazing' tirade is a demand that we become philosophical rather than 'kinda satisfied' consumers. Boredom, on this reading, is failed wonder, and Louie is playing Socrates to his daughter.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 13 "4. Scoundrels, the Lot of Us" — Karavitis finds a Hegelian dialectic in the three-panel Dilbert strip (thesis, antithesis, synthesis) delivered through irony, then tests that irony against philosophy: Socrates' feigned-ignorance questioning that leaves interlocutors in aporia, Hegel's complaint that irony is vanity withdrawing from objective reality, and Kierkegaard's dissertation on the concept of irony plus Either/Or, where irony is the bridge from the aesthetic to the ethical life. The punchline is that after nearly three decades of Dilbert the white-collar workplace has not changed, so readers who feel superior to their bosses and co-workers have taken the vain, narcissistic, aesthetic reading Hegel warned against, making the joke a scoundrelly way of avoiding responsibility. A Leo Strauss aside casts Adams as an esoteric writer whose irony preserves him from the powerful.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 29 "17. Sweeping Up God’s Debris" — Robison-Greene reads God's Debris as a Socratic dialogue on speed: the Avatar, like Socrates after the Delphic oracle, guts the Postman's confidence so he can unlearn, and the whole book functions as a Cartesian skeptical hypothesis in the dream-and-evil-demon lineage, here that we are the dust of a self-destructed God and perception is illusion, with gravity re-described as probability. Her counterattack is that the cosmology commits category mistakes, since probability cannot cause dust to reappear any more than Joe can consist of tallness, and that God made of probability is incoherent even for an omnipotent being. The five levels of awareness collapse too: level-four skeptics are just people who trust reliable methods, and the Avatar's claim that the mind is an illusion generator is self-defeating, since his own omniscience presupposes objective truth.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 15 "6. No Wisdom to Offer You" — Distinguishes public intellectuals like Chomsky, who deliver their own conclusions, from public philosophers who get audiences thinking for themselves, and argues Schumer is the latter. Her memoir claim that she has 'no wisdom to offer' is set beside the Socratic ignorance of Plato's Apology, where wisdom is worth nothing. Sketches like 'Football Town Nights', whose coach condemns rape only to praise violent domination, and 'The Trial of Bill Cosby' withhold conclusions and force viewers to work out for themselves the links between football and rape culture, or between un-conflicted entertainment and justice.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 18 "7. Rick and Morty as Socratic Television" — The chapter argues Harmon and Roiland write the show as Socratic dialogue: in 'Mortynight Run' Morty's confident moral position (saving Fart from Krombopulos Michael is right) is dismantled until Morty himself pulls the trigger, leaving him in aporia; in 'Auto Erotic Assimilation' Summer's faith in freedom is razed by Unity's happy paternalist hive and the nipple-shaped race war it unleashes; and 'Look Who's Purging Now' refuses to choose between liberalism and conservatism when the post-purge town instantly re-founds the Festival. Like Socrates in Plato's Meno, the show's goal is not to teach lessons but to reduce viewers to confusion, because doing philosophy begins there.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 32 "19. The Citadel of Ricks Is Untruth" — The chapter reads Rick C-137's war on the Citadel through Kierkegaard's claim that the crowd is untruth: the Council of Ricks is the leveling public, envying and punishing the passionate individual ('You're a rogue Rick, irrational, passionate'), as Rick J-22's breakdown over Simple Rick's wafers in 'The Ricklantis Mixup' dramatizes, while our Rick stays himself by refusing consensus. From Philosophical Fragments, via Socrates's maieutic midwifery, it draws Kierkegaard's ethics of selfhood: one person can only be the occasion for another's self-knowledge and must then push them away to become individuals. That is exactly Rick's advice to Beth in 'The ABCs of Beth', to leave Jerry, saddle her universe, and become herself, since only Beth can make Beth.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 13 "4. The Gently Socratic Inquiry of Fred Rogers" — Ben Lukey and Steve Bein, veterans of p4c Hawai'i, argue Rogers ran a 'gently Socratic' community of inquiry on television: unlike Socrates the public gadfly who made asses of interlocutors, Rogers created intellectual safety, treating Daniel Striped Tiger's 'What does assassination mean?' (after MLK's murder) and the Officer Clemmons kiddie-pool scene as philosophy with children. Using Dr. Tom Jackson's Good Thinker's Toolkit to show children are philosophers, they defend 'little p philosophy' as activity over 'Big P Philosophy' as content, casting Rogers and Socrates as midwives rather than lecturers.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 43 "30. Socratic Superheroism" — Stages a dialogue between Socrates and Nebula to build a four-part scorecard of 'Socratic Heroism' — question all assumptions, intellectual humility (Socrates before the Delphic oracle: 'I am very conscious that I am not wise at all'), improve society without ever doing injustice, and courage unto death (the gadfly of the Apology) — then scores Thanos 0 for 4: 'I am incapable of error' and 'reality can be whatever I want' are the very opposites of humility and of objective, heavenly truth. It nominates Doctor Strange as the MCU's Socratic hero, whose humbling at Kamar-Taj, willingness to hand over the Time Stone against the obvious choice, and trust in the one winning future among 14,000,605 pass the tests.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 14 "“Consider Your Verdict!”" — Splits Wonderland's nonsense into the tolerable kind (strange but lawful regularities, like mushroom side-effects and walking the opposite way to reach the Red Queen, which Alice masters by experiment) and the intolerable kind (the creatures' eristic logic). Using Hume's fork of relations of ideas versus matters of fact, George Dunn and Brian McDonald argue Alice rightly concludes the pig-baby is merely an out-of-the-way matter of fact, while the White Queen's 'jam every other day: to-day isn't any other day' and the King's beheading of the bodiless Cheshire Cat repeat the Sophists' tricks from Plato's Euthydemus, which Socrates deflates from the standpoint of common sense and the examined life. The Knave's trial ('sentence first, verdict afterwards') lands on cable-news pundits who, like the show trials of Stalin, argue from predetermined conclusions.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 24 "A Nonsense Too Far" — Places Carroll's nonsense in a Greco-Roman tradition of philosophically useful absurdity: Socrates exposing Euthyphro's definitions of piety as nonsense, Plato's tongue-in-cheek Republic calculation that the tyrant's life is 729 times worse, and Diogenes ridiculing slavery even while sold on the auction block. Charles Taliaferro and Elizabeth Olson argue the jokes land only because Alice stays sane, curious, polite, and self-controlled, the stable foil who keeps the death threats and cruelty of Wonderland and the Looking-Glass on the amusing side of the ledger, and that nonsense goes 'too far' in Kafka's The Trial, where losing the sane, good center turns absurdity into meaninglessness.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 14 "Hoist by his Own Petard" — Powell reads Norman Osborn's Dark Reign as a living lesson from Plato's Gorgias and Alcibiades: Osborn's media-staged killing of the Skrull Queen and his hollow rebranding of S.H.I.E.L.D. into H.A.M.M.E.R. are the sophistic 'knack' of persuasion substituting for the genuine craft of statecraft, just as Polus's ideal Sophist imagines power without self-control. Like Alcibiades, Osborn lacks the Socratic self-knowledge that comes only through critical self-reflection with honest friends, and instead surrounds himself with flatterers and villains while his own Goblin persona—mirrored in the Sentry's Void—grows stronger. Loki's goading of the unsanctioned Siege of Asgard completes the cautionary tale: the sophist who created fake institutions is destroyed by them, hoist by his own petard.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 16 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Barad maps fifth-century Athens onto contemporary America to cast Stewart as a Socratic reformer confronting modern sophists, advertisers, pundits and media figures who make weaker arguments appear stronger without caring about truth, exemplified by Ed Helms admitting network stories are pre-written from 'conventional wisdom' and Ann Coulter's conformity-peddling. She details the shared method: flattering the 'expert', feigned ignorance, and layer-by-layer questioning that traps targets like Rumsfeld ('It may not seem like much, but for this administration it's a huge policy shift') in contradiction, with Socratic irony doing the work of Stewart's awestruck deadpan and mute astonished reactions to Bush clips. Against Bill O'Reilly's 'stoned slacker' charge she cites the Annenberg finding that the show's young audience is better informed, and weighs Ken Tucker's 'monkey' question through the Crossfire 'I'm not going to be your monkey' exchange, concluding that, like Socrates facing trial and execution, Stewart uses irony as means and truth as end.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 20 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Blessing and Marren mine Stewart's two interviews with Harry Frankfurt to work out the lie/bullshit distinction: liars like Edwards, Weiner and Clinton know and care about the truth they distort, while bullshitters, from Travelodge PR stunts to subprime lenders, are indifferent to truth in service of selling, which is why Frankfurt calls bullshit the more corrosive force. They take up Stewart's Socratic questioning of whether political spin is a subset of bullshit, and answer that spinners, unlike bullshitters, must know the truth in order to color it, making spin closer to lying in attitude, tolerated because Spin Alley agrees not to call bullshit on it. Documenting the PR-ization of media (the Cardiff University study behind Flat Earth News, the Wall Street Journal press-release finding), they close with Frankfurt's On Truth sequel, that a society cannot survive without truth, with ridicule of the kind The Daily Show practices as the best defense.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 10 "The Sorcerer Socratic" — Timm argues Strange follows Socrates' path from arrogance to Socratic heroism: the hand injury forces intellectual humility (the Oracle-at-Delphi moment), the Ancient One's keyhole metaphor and astral-form lesson ('to show you just how much you don't know') enact the Socratic method of questioning the supposedly wise, and the astral projection is literally the examined life — Socrates' unexamined life not worth living. Strange's commitment to protecting humanity from interdimensional evil parallels the gadfly who risks death to improve Athens, his refusal to do injustice even under pressure echoes the Crito, and his repeated willingness to die for others (facing Dormammu, holding the Shambler back) completes the Socratic Hero profile.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 25 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Ehrett and Worth ask whether D&D is really a game and why we invest so much in it. Against the Socratic model (the Euthyphro dialogue's search for a common thread defining piety, here applied to 'game'), they deploy Wittgenstein's family-resemblance account from the Philosophical Investigations, concluding D&D lacks clear winning and losing but is rule-governed, with the twist that rule-breaking is legitimate exactly when it serves the game's primary purpose of group storytelling. They then take up the paradox of fiction: since players know the world is not real, Radford's puzzle arises, and Kendall Walton's make-believe theory of props and fictional truths supplies their answer, making D&D an especially gripping fiction because players are participants rather than observers.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 7 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Cam Cobb pits Socratic critical inquiry and Plato's Republic-style vocational streaming (classes sorted by the 'myth of the metals,' sold through a noble lie) against the Battle School curriculum, which is almost purely vocational and lacks the music, poetry, and liberal paideia that harmonize the soul. Testing Socrates' dialogic method, Dewey's aptitude-tracking education, and Freire's problem-posing alternative against the battleroom, the Giant's Drink, and Graff's secretly rewritten game rules, Cobb concludes Ender's schooling mixes conflicting pedagogies and ends in the teacher domination Freire feared, crystallized in Ender's lament 'I've spent my life as someone's pawn.'
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 7 "Setting Up the Game" — Editor Luke Cuddy's introduction argues that videogames, and Zelda in particular, deserve philosophy because the gamer actively guides Link instead of passively watching, which raises questions about Link's will, Hyrule's space and time, the Triforce, timeline theories, and death. It surveys the franchise from the 1986 NES original through Phantom Hourglass and the fandom culture around it. Its central move is reading Plato's Meno — Socrates questioning the slave boy until the boy truly knows the doubled square — as the model of the 'AHA!' feeling, which it parallels to Link triumphantly hoisting a dungeon item like the ladder while the four rising notes play.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 12 "And Now, Deep Thoughts…" — Reynolds places comedy on a spectrum from philosophy to satire to smart-assery and argues SNL mostly sits at the silly end: Gumby, Mr. Robinson, Hermione's cleavage, and Hobbit Office are parody with an absurd twist but no constructive target, unlike genuine satire such as Mr. Bill. He develops the comparison through Aristophanes' Clouds, whose caricature of Socrates at the Thinkery helped send him to his death, and through the 'Playboy Philosophy' sketch with Belushi as Socrates. Socrates himself emerges as a satirist: the oracle of Delphi, his claim to know only that he knows nothing, and his elenchus that unmasks the supposedly wise are read as comedy in the service of seriousness, before the chapter concedes SNL's absurdism is philosophical mainly in mocking an absurd world.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 33 "31_LaRocca_Chapter_030.html" — Hoffman reads Sarah Polley's Stories We Tell and Joshua Oppenheimer's The Act of Killing through Kierkegaard's account of indirect communication and 'deceiving into the truth.' Like the Socratic maieutic teacher who removes his authority and lets pupils reach their own conclusions, both directors withhold voice-of-God assertion and instead present multiple, conflicting, sometimes ethically monstrous storytellers, indulging their delusions to expose them. Polley stages fake Super-8 home movies and rival accounts of her mother and paternity so that truth becomes subjective appropriation rather than objective fact; Oppenheimer lets Indonesian genocide perpetrators reenact their killings as Hollywood fantasies until Anwar Congo is 'deceived' into his own broken self-awareness, indicting the regime that still celebrates him.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 43 "Ah, Doctor.
