We Know You by Reputation" — Courtland Lewis's closing essay argues Doctor Who and philosophy are complementary enterprises devoted to teaching rather than mere persuasion. Using Plato's Gorgias distinction between teaching and rhetoric, he casts the Master as the master rhetorician who produces unreliable beliefs (even via hypnosis), while the Doctor is a Socratic teacher committed to truth who gives people information and lets them decide. He contends the show, begun as educational, challenges viewers to reflect on their own reasoning, on how they treat others (Daleks, Cybermen, strangers), and to revise beliefs in light of evidence, so that watching it is living philosophically engaged.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 23 "13. Chuckrates v. The Saulphists" — Staged as a mock disciplinary-board trial, the chapter casts Chuck McGill as Socrates and Jimmy as a Sophist to replay Plato's dialectic-versus-rhetoric quarrel. Chuck prosecutes Jimmy as a mere rhetorician who 'makes the weaker argument defeat the stronger,' quoting the Gorgias, Apology, and Republic, while Jimmy counters that Socrates was himself a self-righteous show-off and that the legal system runs on Sophistic persuasion (juries, opening statements) as much as on truth. The Board's verdict finds Chuck blind to his own rhetoric and Jimmy a quintessential but empathetic Sophist, using the McGill brothers to argue that law fuses dialectic and rhetoric just as ancient Athens did.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 9 "The Talking Cure for Our Culture" — Young argues that South Park, like Socrates in Plato's Apology, is accused of corrupting youth and impiety but is really a philosophical gadfly. Kyle and Stan reach moral conclusions (e.g., refusing to kill Stan's grandfather) through Socratic questioning and dialogue, while Cartman's thoughtless, imitative cruelty mirrors Arendt's banality of evil in Eichmann. Young reads the show's vulgarity through Freud, arguing its crude jokes release repressed drives so we can examine them, making the show a Socratic 'talking cure' for a mindless culture.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 16 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Judith Barad argues Stewart plays reformer in America as Socrates did in Athens, both confronting sophists—now advertisers, spin doctors, and media pundits like Coulter and O'Reilly—who teach persuasion detached from truth. She maps the Daily Show correspondents' interview technique (flatter the 'expert,' expose a contradiction) directly onto the Socratic method, and reads Stewart's ironic self-deprecation, feigned confusion, and one-on-one listening as Socratic irony deployed, like Socrates', as a means to truth rather than mere entertainment, culminating in the Crossfire confrontation with Carlson and Begala.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 34 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Decker asks whether 'Stephen Colbert' the persona is an 'existential ironist,' tracing irony from Socrates's Delphic-oracle-inspired questioning through Schlegel, Hegel (irony as freedom but an abdication of responsibility), and Kierkegaard (the ironist detached from and not taking community practices seriously). He reads Colbert's centerless self-redescription and Super PAC stunt via Rorty's 'ironist' and 'final vocabulary' (built from Nietzschean self-creation and Deweyan plasticity through language), then argues that truthiness is a dangerous subjectivism—and that Colbert, unlike a pure Rortian ironist, drops the mask to side with the powerless.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 10 "Oh, the Places You’ll Go! The Examined, Happy Life" — Benjamin Rider reads Oh, the Places You'll Go! through Socrates' claim that the unexamined life is not worth living. He argues the Sneetches' star-obsession, Yertle's tower, Gertrude McFuzz's feathers, and the Once-ler's 'biggering' are the false, unexamined beliefs about wealth and status that Socrates said wreck the soul, while Bartholomew Cubbins and Horton model the wise, courageous endurance Socrates seeks but fails to define with the generals Laches and Nicias in Plato's Laches. The 'Waiting Place' becomes the life of someone who never questions what really makes him happy, and Seuss's call to use 'the brains in your head' echoes Socrates' insistence in the Crito and Phaedo on living by rational reflection.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 13 "Socratic Seuss Intellectual Integrity and Truth-Orientation" — Matthew Pierlott casts Seuss as a Socratic gadfly for intellectual integrity, built on Frankfurt's distinction between the liar (who respects truth) and the bullshitter (who is indifferent to it). Sam-I-Am's reluctant friend in Green Eggs and Ham is 'bullshitting' to be left alone; the boasting rabbit and bear of 'The Big Brag' are humbled by a worm who plays Socrates as in Plato's Euthyphro; Horton Hatches the Egg and Mulberry Street show self-delusion (believing what we wish were true); and 'What Was I Scared Of?' shows fear distorting the interpretation of evidence, all mapped against Pierlott's five aspects of intellectual integrity.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 27 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Gilmore reads Persuasion as itself a rumination on persuasion, arguing the word means different things in different contexts. He uses Plato's Gorgias to split persuasion into Persuasion I (mere conviction without knowledge, based on appearance and social prudence, which led Anne to break with Wentworth) and Persuasion II (persuasion with knowledge that changes one's whole schema of value). He grounds this in Wittgenstein's later view that meaning is use within a language game and a form of life, so 'persuasion,' 'constancy,' and 'only Anne' shift sense across the novel. Reading the plot via Cavell's 'comedy of remarriage,' he argues Anne and Wentworth's separation yields the self-knowledge that legitimates their reunion.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 14 "Chapter 5 Twain’s Last Laugh" — Kristina Gehrman argues that reading Huck as a moral hero who overcomes racism is Twain's ironic trap. Using Arne Naess's idea of identification, Aristotle on habituation of character, and Iris Murdoch's 'just and loving attention,' she gives a developmentally attuned reading of Huck as a traumatized, morally immature, still-racist child whose regard for Jim never generalizes ('I knowed he was white inside'). Twain lures his white readers into identifying with Huck's supposed triumph, then exposes their own stunted moral growth about race; Jim is the only mature adult yet is barred from identification by the novel's racist caricature. The novel's greatness is Socratic and gadfly-like rather than triumphant.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 23 "Chapter 11 Socratic Irony in Twain’s Skeptical Religious Jeremiads" — Jacquette demands a precise definition of Twain's much-invoked irony, adopting Vlastos's/Quintilian's formula that irony says the contrary of what is meant while letting the real meaning be recovered. He classifies Twain's irony as local vs. global and comic vs. sober (tragic/historical): 'Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc' is globally ironic (falsely presented as de Conte's eyewitness manuscript), while the relic-mocking passages of 'The Innocents Abroad' (St. Luke's Madonna, kegs of true-cross nails, three skulls of John the Baptist) are local comic irony. Jacquette concludes Twain's irony is distinctively Socratic: like Socrates interpreting the Delphic oracle, Twain makes a moral and epistemic virtue of ridiculing experts who claim to know what no one can know about God, sin, and the afterlife.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 18 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Parker defends the coffeehouse as an accessible venue for real philosophy through Christopher Phillips's Socrates Café movement (and Marc Sautet's cafés-philos), arguing that Socratizing — sustained questioning that offers objections and alternatives, not mere talk — makes everyone a potential 'Socrates.' Answering the charge that amateur café philosophy is mere sophistry, he turns to Plato's Sophist to note the sophist is the one who takes payment and has an agenda, so it is salaried professors, not unpaid Phillips, who resemble sophists. Framing thoughtlessness (via Nietzsche's 'oblivion' and David Foster Wallace's cruise-ship essay) as philosophy's true adversary, he endorses a softened Socratic/Nozickian maxim that the unexamined life is simply not lived as fully.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 25 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Johnson argues that the Santa Claus lie is immoral and should be abandoned, giving three reasons: it is deceptive lying (Kant's absolute prohibition is too strong, but the lie lacks life-saving justification and functions as a Platonic 'noble lie' no more noble than a cult leader's); Santa robs parents of credit and warps children's moral development and trust, illustrated by anguished 'finding out' stories and Virginia O'Hanlon's letter; and it damages credulity, invoking Clifford's 'Ethics of Belief' against belief on insufficient evidence while James's 'Will to Believe' cannot rescue Santa since evidence against him is overwhelming. He recommends revealing the truth early, even via a Socratic-Method questioning game.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 31 "GARDENING" — Cotton reads the grower image in Plato's Phaedrus—the wise gardener who sows seed in proper soil for a slow harvest rather than the frivolous 'gardens of Adonis'—as Plato's model of philosophical education as natural growth. The educator plants logoi (discourse) in a 'proper soul,' where it must be cultivated by the learner's own reflection and eventually reproduces itself in others, against Thrasymachus's vessel model of pouring knowledge in. She connects this to the Republic's cave, the Apology's gadfly, and the Symposium/Theaetetus images of pregnancy and midwifery, then argues Plato's own aporetic, contradiction-laden dialogues and the corpus as a whole act as the wise grower, teaching readers to become 'gardeners of their own souls.'
- **College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits**, ch. 19 "College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits" — This span (the book's front matter plus the Part I 'Hook-Up Culture' essays) argues that college hook-up culture can be examined philosophically rather than merely lived. Hole and Chen recast reckless sexual 'experimentation' as a Socratic self-experiment, having students name a change, run it, and interrogate a 'big question' (e.g. Chen's dare to abstain all freshman year) to become a 'wiser lover.' Romaya argues that gay and lesbian students' opposite-sex 'straight sex experiments' undermine fixed sexual identity, invoking Buddhist anatman and Hume's bundle theory to reject a static self. Bruce gives a phenomenological reading of how Facebook/MySpace profiles and text/level-jumping alienate courting students, and Lunceford treats the 'walk of shame' outfit via Peirce's index/symbol semiotics as a sign of feminine sexuality marked shameful.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 17 "NOTES" — Matthews argues that certain children's books are 'subversive' in a Socratic sense: they problematize concepts adults assume they command, challenging adult epistemic authority the way Socrates exposed the pretended knowledge of Athens' elite. Morris the Moose raises Aristotelian questions of natural kinds and essence-versus-accident; Leese Webster probes the concept of art; The Shrinking of Treehorn destabilizes 'normal' child development; Frog and Toad's 'The Garden' dramatizes the post hoc, ergo propter hoc fallacy about causation. In the Ozma of Oz Tik-Tok discussion, nine-year-old Paul reconstructs an argument that only brains think, which Matthews aligns with Searle's claim in The Mystery of Consciousness that consciousness is caused by specific neurobiological processes; he explicitly distinguishes his subversive stories from those promoting Pyrrhonian skepticism or Protagorean relativism.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 9 "The Talking Cure for Our Culture" — William Young argues that South Park stands in the Socratic-Platonic tradition and that its critics repeat the charges (impiety, corrupting youth) that condemned Socrates in the Apology. Kyle and Stan's dialogues over euthanizing Stan's grandpa model Socratic questioning and thinking from others' perspectives, while Cartman's thoughtless, imitative cruelty illustrates Arendt's banality of evil (Eichmann). Young adds a Freudian reading in which the show's vulgarity works like joke-telling to release repressed drives, so the crude cartoon actually serves the examined life.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 73 "69. Larry David as Philosopher Interrogating Convention" — Carroll treats Curb Your Enthusiasm as a Kantian/Marxian 'critique'—an inquiry into the conditions of possibility—of everyday norms of civility, built on incongruity humor and Mary Douglas's theory of jokes as 'anti-rites.' Through episodes like the handicapped-stutterer, the new-house tour Larry refuses, the phone-call cutoff time, Ben Stiller's no-gifts party, and the buried five-wood, David shows that manners are non-necessary and arbitrary yet held in place only by intense (uncurbed) emotional 'enthusiasm,' epitomized by Susie Greene's operatic rage. Carroll answers the analytic skeptic by casting David's method as Socratic/maieutic (like Plato's Meno): the argument is completed in the reflective viewer's mind.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 83 "78. The Witness as Philosophy How Knowledge Is Constructed" — Cuddy asks what epistemology Blow built into The Witness's frustrating puzzles and its windmill videos (Burke, Feynman, Moriarty, Spira, Gangaji). He rejects the sophistic/Protagorean 'knowledge depends on the observer' reading (most puzzles have objective, inductive-and-deductive solutions, e.g. the yellow-glass bunker) and the strict scientific realism of the Burke video defended by Putnam's no-miracles argument. Using Plato's cave and the aporia of Socrates' Meno (the puzzle's 'ah-ha' epiphanies), and Kuhn's incommensurable paradigm shifts (the game's 'hard left turns' forcing players to overhaul their understanding), he concludes the game argues that true knowledge is attainable, individually and collectively, though reached by a nonlinear, paradigm-shifting route rather than pure realism or relativism.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 9 "1. Engaging Life Like the Doctor" — The chapter casts the Doctor as a 'flâneur' who teaches an engaged, critical-thinking way of life, illustrated through episodes like 'Blink,' 'Heaven Sent,' and 'Kerblam!' where the Doctor (and viewer) solve mysteries through trial and error. It uses Hume and William James to argue the mind actively constructs reality into a narrative, and pairs the Doctor with Socrates as a truth-seeking 'midwife' teacher who withholds answers so companions can learn by living rather than being told. The Doctor's rejection of Time Lord non-interference models the Socratic examined life of engaging the world to know oneself and others.

### Objectification

Objectification is the treatment of a person as a mere object or instrument rather than as a being with dignity, autonomy, and a subjectivity of their own. In feminist philosophy it names especially the reduction of a person, most often a woman, to a body or a set of parts valued for the use or pleasure of others, denying full agency and moral standing. Philosophers such as Martha Nussbaum have analyzed it into distinct elements—like instrumentality, denial of autonomy, and fungibility—to clarify when and why treating someone as an object is wrong.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 106 "Unknown" — The chapter catalogues the film's penetration scenes—the Agents' scorpion bug forced through Neo's navel, its bloody extraction, the fetal pod farm and 'birth' down the flush tube, the acupuncture rebuilding, the neck-plug uploads, and finally the bullets he becomes immune to—arguing that Neo's arc ends in a perfect, closed body with no vulnerability and no relation to actual flesh. It attacks the gender stereotypes: Trinity is reduced to a decorative, nurturant sidekick who never hacks and exists as love interest, the Oracle is a cookie-baking 'Mammy' figure, and there are no female Agents—the machines are sexist too.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 24 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Cynthia Freeland reads the film's women through feminist ethics of care: the two Marys function like a Greek-chorus of grieving observers, while Claudia and Veronica — and the casting of Bellucci as the repentant whore opposite Morgenstern's ageless Madonna — lock them into the virgin/whore double bind. Using Carol Gilligan's critique of Kohlberg's Kantian standard and Nel Noddings's and Sara Ruddick's point that mothering is reflective 'attentive' work, she argues Gibson's Mary is one-dimensional: flashbacks of 'I am here' show maternal instinct, never moral deliberation. She ends by suggesting the historical Jesus, like Socrates, was more radical toward women than the film, and that Irigaray's reading of Christ's bleeding wounds as a feminized maternal body sits oddly with Gibson's muscular, 'take it like a man' Savior.
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 30 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — A café dialogue pits second-waver Marie against third-waver Dorothy over whether Atkins can be a feminist tool: Marie wields the feminist critique of Cartesian dualism (Descartes made the mind essential and the body animal, and women were stigmatized as body), Foucault's internalized surveillance — 'every mirror becomes a guard, every scale an alarm,' with Lifetime Maintenance as 'maniacal' hyper-vigilance — Lorde's 'master's tools,' and Young's 'Throwing Like a Girl.' Dorothy answers with Our Bodies, Ourselves self-knowledge, Title IX athletes like Venus and Serena Williams, Frye's Willful Virgin, and existentialist facticity and bad faith (we are in bad faith when we abdicate control), defending dieting as a chosen women's project. The exchange ends drawish, over Brazilian waxes, French women, and whether ugliness is a feminist virtue.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 20 "The Possibility of Authenticity The Life We Choose" — Gines reads hip hop's sexual imagery through Black feminist thought - Tupac's feud with C. Delores Tucker over "Wonder Why They Call U Bitch", Patricia Hill Collins's controlling images of the jezebel and welfare mother, bell hooks on the slave-rooted devaluation of Black womanhood, Nelly's "Tip Drill" video with a credit card swiped between a woman's buttocks, Jay-Z's "Big Pimpin'". Applying Sartre's keyhole gaze from Being and Nothingness and his Anti-Semite and Jew point about hierarchical societies, she argues the gaze under racism and sexism is non-reciprocal - women are seen without seeing - and that Lil' Kim's reversal of it reinforces rather than subverts the stereotypes; Butler's gender performativity then frames the closing Sartrean choice of authenticity or inauthenticity, Nas's "I Can" and "the life we choose."
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 28 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Kieffner applies Foucault's deployment of sexuality to show how power centers constructed biker sexual stereotypes: the psychiatric profession behind Time's 1970 'Motorcycle Syndrome', the press that sexualized the Van Buren sisters and filled Easyriders with centerfolds, police 'gauntlets' that pull over bikes but not cars (and ask Raw Thunder's Char Zack if she is a lesbian), and even Harley-Davidson's own 'mystique' video deploying eroticism to sell bikes and HOG memberships. Following Foucault's rule of the tactical polyvalence of discourse, he ends with resistance within the same power structure: riders' rights organizations videotaping police encounters, and the tactical discourses of queer, lesbian, and female riders, from Evelyn Greenway's 1921 'Do it with a motorcycle' onward, who refuse the labels of sexual outlaw and gender traitor.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 29 "The Male Vampire as Metrosexual . . . Sort Of" — Joan Grassbaugh Forry asks how conventional standards of beauty, femininity, and masculinity operate in the vampire aesthetic of Interview with the Vampire, Buffy, and Queen of the Damned. Using Foucault's figure of the soldier whose body is 'made' by discipline, and Bartky and Bordo's feminist extension of it to dieting, deportment, and ornamenting the female body, she argues vampires expose the ideology of natural beauty: they are youthful, elegant, and effortlessly beautiful - no gym, no reflection - so their beauty is pure naturalness with the discipline erased. Gender decides the payoff: ultra-feminine female vampires (Drusilla's dresses and tea parties, Akasha, childlike Claudia) are femmes fatales whose threat must be punished by death, ridicule, or infantilization, while feminized male protagonists (Louis, Angel, Spike painting his nails and watching Passions - the 'metrosexual') win audience identification and tragic dignity. Beauty, in short, is a shield for the male vampire and a death sentence for the female.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 28 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Arp and Decker examine Bond's objectification of women - using a dancing girl as a human shield in the Goldfinger pre-credits sequence, M ordering Bond to 'pump her for information' - through three moral theories. Kant's humanity formula condemns treating women as sexual tools, but Kantian autonomy generates a stalemate since consensual, reciprocal liaisons like Bond and Anya Amasova's might qualify as permissible; Millian utilitarianism condemns the male gaze by its long-term social costs yet stalls against pro-sex feminist counterarguments. They settle on Aristotelian virtue ethics - the mean between extremes, with respect as the key virtue against the power-centered virtue of Machiavelli, Hobbes, and Nietzsche - to argue objectification is vicious, and they trace Bond's moral progress from skipping the young Bibi in For Your Eyes Only to the reciprocal relationships with Kara Milovy, Pam Bouvier, Wai Lin, and Jinx.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 15 "This Has All Happened Before and It Will All Happen Again" — Rennes reads the miniseries opening — Six's kiss of death with the Armistice officer — through postcolonial theory: Vergès's 'colonial family romance,' in which the human metropole adopts Cylons as perpetually subordinate children, and Bhabha's ambivalence and mimicry ('almost the same, but not quite'). The humans police difference first by appearance (toaster, skin-job slurs; the Centurion reflected in Helo's toaster) and then by blood, but métissage — Hera, whom Roslin tries to abort and then hides — exposes the categories as social constructions, since as D'Anna says, 'This stuff all looks the same.' Hera's menace is that acknowledging her means acknowledging human complicity in creating Cylon slaves, collapsing the colonial romance ('happily never after').
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 17 "The Secret Plot of ‘Baby Boomers’" — Chess proposes that BSG is 'a narrative about queer reproduction,' combining Haraway's cyborg with Butler's heteronormativity to coin 'technoqueer': Cylons embody fears that technology makes heterosexual reproduction unnecessary. Helo's 'I'm in love with a woman I know isn't a woman,' the 'you can't rape a machine' debate after the Pegasus assault, and download-resurrection as asexual reproduction all mark Cylons as queer others — yet the Cylons' obsession with conceiving Hera, paralleled with The L Word's Bette and Tina, shows them trapped between rejecting and emulating heteronormativity, farming human women at the Cylon 'Farm' while craving legitimate babies. Hera's birth terrifies Roslin because it legitimizes the technoqueer and with it human reproductive obsolescence.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 24 "It’s the Disappointing Stories that Sound True to Life" — Shipman argues that the re-imagined Cylons, having rebelled as slaves, recreated oppression inside their own society: the human-form Numbers rule over mute Centurions (voices literally bred out, like banning slave literacy), animalized Raiders, and dismissed 'insane' Hybrids, whose sentience ('Scar' shows strategy and self-preservation) the Numbers willfully deny. The division of labor echoes Marx's 'from each according to his ability,' but assignments are engineered by their makers, and the model-making program is eugenics rather than evolution — the series' own word 'evolved' is, he says, disingenuous. Hence the Numbers lose the moral superiority their victimhood earned, and the scriptural 'all of this has happened before' implies the subaltern models may rebel next.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 43 "With or Without Starbuck" — Ewan Kirkland argues BSG's gender-free surface, unisex bunks and a Starbuck who never has to defend her right to fly, masks a default masculinity under Adama's patriarchal regime: Ellen is killed off as the negative femme fatale, Kat and Cain die or turn monstrous, and 'The Farm' literalizes feminist fears of patriarchal medicine turning women into breeders. Starbuck confounds the sexualizing male gaze, never objectified, repeatedly rescuing men and reversing damsel-in-distress plots, yet her success is entirely masculinized, bought by becoming like a man. Her New Caprica captivity as Leoben's simulated wife literalizes the feminist critique of compulsory heterosexuality, and her death in 'Maelstrom', submitting to her former kidnapper, suggests the series contains its most transgressive heroine.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 35 "Zelda and Reality" — Havstad and Jahng inventory every Zelda across the series (royal, wise, resolved, foreseeing, yet passive, imprisoned, even turned to stone in The Minish Cap or asleep through all of Adventure of Link) and read the maiden typology through Beauvoir's The Second Sex: woman as Idea, modeled on Plato's Forms, gives men a feminine ideal that real women are then judged against, and 'women are not born, but made' explains how femininity is a male-defined myth serving male interests. Zelda is the glorified yet objectified prize whose passivity lets Link's transcendence happen, and Aonuma's 'reality over realism' design philosophy explains why such stereotypes feel true to players. Sheik and Tetra, who act while disguised as (or turned into) something other than the princess, are the promising cracks in the ideal.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 12 "I’m Gonna Crawl" — Richard Wilson and Emma Rees apply Freud's theory of fetishism—the boy's disavowal of castration displaced onto a substitute object—to Zeppelin's lyrics and imagery. 'Trampled Underfoot' continues Robert Johnson's 'Terraplane Blues' car-as-lover convention, 'Custard Pie' and 'Black Dog' turn women into consumable food (Freud's cannibalistic pregenital sexual organization), and 'The Lemon Song' and 'Whole Lotta Love' avert the castrating vagina, with the Seattle red snapper episode read through the vagina dentata myth. The band's misogyny ('Soul of a woman was created below' in 'Dazed and Confused', echoing Lear), the voyeuristic die-cut windows of the Physical Graffiti cover, and Plant's cock-rock persona in The Song Remains the Same all illustrate how fetishistic substitution neutralizes the threatening female body and explains the band's compulsive doomed-relationship songs; the authors briefly borrow Marx's language of commodification for the woman-car-drugs as status objects.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 10 "Looking Inwards" — Barber, Bryce, and Davis test Donna Haraway's emancipatory cyborg thesis against Gunslinger Girl, where the Social Welfare Agency 'adopts' orphaned and abused girls (Henrietta, Rico, Triela, Elsa, Claes), rebuilds their bodies as cybernetic weapons, and drug-conditions them into loyal assassins paired with male handlers. They argue the series realizes none of Haraway's post-gender potential: conditioning erodes memory and autonomy (Rico coolly shoots the porter Emilio who befriended her; Elsa murders her handler Lauro and kills herself; Triela suffers pointless menstrual cramps in a wombless body), while the girls' kawaii styling, teddy bears, and school uniforms make them objects of the male gaze whose cuteness disguises lethal power. The cyborgs' victimization ultimately reinforces traditional gender hierarchy and mirrors conformity-pressured Japanese youth, so the cyborg has 'regressed' from the autonomous heroines of Ghost in the Shell or Battle Angel Alita.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 29 "Textually Transmitted Disease" — Traces hentai from Hokusai's 'Diver and Two Octopi' through the 1920s eroguro journals to the Lolita Anime and Cream Lemon OVAs, then asks whether even this extreme material has value as fantasy. The chapter frames the media-effects debate with Aristotle's Poetics catharsis (revived by Feshbach and tentatively supported by Milton Diamond's finding that Japanese rape rates fell as pornography spread) against Plato's Republic worry that sensational works license irrationality (updated by the Disinhibition, Desensitization, and Cultivation theories), and concludes that hentai's real harm is attitudinal rather than behavioral: its ritual 'breaking' of strong women and sex-as-something-done-to-passive-girls cultivates misogyny and a dehumanizing view of sex.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 17 "Banal Sex" — Marinucci reads The Onion's sex coverage as 'terminally ambiguous': 'Nation's Gays Demand Right To Library Cards,' 'Massachusetts Supreme Court Orders All Citizens To Gay Marry,' and 'New Bill Would Defend Marriage From Sharks' ridicule the idea that gay marriage threatens straight marriage, while 'Area Homosexual Saves Four From Fire: Heroic Neighbor Praised, Gay' exposes how heterosexism defines gay people sexually while heterosexual men pass as normal, natural, and neutral. Yet the paper also trades in gay stereotypes and mocks the very framework—characters like Amanda Oppel ('Lesbian Identity Ends Abruptly Mid-Junior Year'), the 'Bar Skanks Announce Plans To Kiss,' and Bruce Heffernan of 'Why Do All These Homosexuals Keep Sucking My Cock?' both defy and seem to reaffirm the stability of sexual identity categories. Weighing queer theory (via Jagose) and Golden's fluid 'elective lesbians' against the parody of 'Grad Student Deconstructs Take-Out Menu,' she concludes the paper's stance is deliberately undecidable, perhaps recommending we stop over-thinking sex and treat minority sexual identities as banal, as in 'Gay Couple Has Banal Sex.'
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 20 "Specimen Watching" — Jason Davis applies Adorno's 'identity thinking' - the way concepts swallow particulars as specimens of the already-known - to argue Dexter is a consumer of serial killers who never asks what makes his victims what they are, only that they fit the type, from therapist Emmett Meridian on down. The same concept-machine works on animals: Buddy's buried bones and the show's predator imagery exploit the criminological animal-abuse link, letting Davis ask whether cruelty-taskforce laws quietly practice speciesism; and Carol J. Adams' sexual politics of meat connects the Ice Truck Killer's blood-drained, butcher-cut women to a meat-eating culture whose objectification makes women and animals interchangeable. Finally, the chapter notes that the women of Dexter - Deb, Rita, LaGuerta, Lila, Christine - are all written without female friendship, a homosocial specimen-class whose sameness feminist philosophers expose, so that when Dexter 'takes back the night', the 'invisible hookers' stay invisible.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 22 "The Honorable, the Woman" — Mona Rocha and James Rocha charge that Holmes's 'deduction' is really Humean induction, and that his inductive shortcuts about women, tricking Mrs. Smith in The Sign of the Four, reading Mary Sutherland's pacing as a love affair, and dismissing Lady Frances Carfax as a 'stray chicken in a world of foxes', are hasty generalizations made dangerous by gender stereotype. Watson is worse: his 'experience of women... over many nations and three continents' reads Mary Morstan's soul off her face and grants full courtesy only to the beautiful intruder of 'The Solitary Cyclist', a feminist case study in objectification. Irene Adler's escape in 'A Scandal in Bohemia', disguising herself as a young man and outwitting the fire ruse, is Doyle's deliberate proof that treating women as a class fails, making her a proto-feminist decades before Poirot's Rossakoff or Spade's O'Shaughnessy.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 26 "Deckard versus Arctor" — The chapter sets Ford's redemptive Deckard against Keanu Reeves's Bob Arctor, the everyman who spies on himself and disintegrates on Substance D, noting the shared scaffolding (lawman, shadowy supplier Tyrell/New Path, nemesis with doubtful humanity, woman in identity crisis) that only highlights the divergence: Deckard is educated into humanity through Rachael while Arctor is progressively dehumanized, with Donna/Audrey betraying rather than redeeming him. It leans on Dick's 'The Android and the Human' definition of becoming an android as being 'pounded down, manipulated, made into a means without one's knowledge or consent', so that Blade Runner imagines androids becoming human where A Scanner Darkly shows humans becoming androids, with even nature (New Path's corn fields) enlisted in the enslavement.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 26 "Violence, Rock, and the Rolling Stones" — Applying the three orders, Surber sorts the Stones' violences: Imaginary violence flows from frustrated desire — 'you can't ever get what you want' — heard in 'Play with Fire' and the unnervingly threatening last line of 'Dead Flowers', and in the frenzied fan mobs that nearly killed Keith once Decca made him a spectacle. Symbolic violence is carried by words and images, and he charges the lyrics with two standing varieties: the objectification of women in 'Under My Thumb' and racial stereotyping in 'Brown Sugar' and the N-word quoted in 'Sweet Black Angel'. Behind both, the Real's economics quietly enables the whole scene, since concert violence is unintelligible apart from the transfer of millions of fans' small cash payments into record-corporation accounts.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 17 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Olson opens with her own first session, in which the DM steered her toward a 'sexy Eladrin' miniature in high heels, and asks why women stay away from D&D. She argues the game's mechanics are egalitarian—identical power lists for male and female characters, echoing Plato's Republic claim that women guard the city by the same nature as men—and that party cooperation embodies the relational, care-based feminist ethic Marilyn Friedman and Angela Bolte oppose to male-coded individualism. The trouble is culture, not system: sexualized miniatures that objectify female bodies, tokenism, harassment, and marketing that ignores women, to which female gamers respond by playing male characters like Jenni Dowsett, designing separatist systems such as Portal Worlds, or, like Shelly Mazzanoble, claiming D&D for the 'inner girl'.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 52 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Jones, Hansmann, and Stachura trace the trope of woman as the Devil's handmaiden - Eve and Lilith, succubae and Sirens, the sixteenth-century witch hunts, down to 'maneater' and 'Poison' rock songs and Blurred Lines - arguing it perpetuates patriarchal power. They apply Beauvoir's The Second Sex: woman constructed as the perpetual Other, defined as secondary to man with sexuality at the heart of her Othering, and extend the analysis with Gloria Anzaldua's Borderlands and mestiza consciousness, which rejects the gender binary the woman-as-Devil trope depends on.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 23 "Girls and Philosophy" — Mahon and Walker rebrand the seven deadly sins for Girls: Self-Absorption as Augustine's 'love of one's own excellence' (Hannah pitching her e-book at her editor's funeral, calling her grandmother 'the old Flo Job... sluttin' around'), Entitlement for Hannah's 'voice of my generation' demands and Marnie's rage at Charlie's success, and Sleeping Around as the John Paul II point about reducing a person to an object of gratification - Adam's fantasy sex with Hannah and his degradation of Natalia. Envy (Hannah on Tally's tragedy), gluttony in drug-fueled relapses (Aquinas's five ways), flakiness as Kant's indolent free-rider who needs others but never helps (Jessa missing her own abortion), and Senecan irritability (Jessa spitting at the Bushwick party, Ray's hatreds, Shoshanna's 'whiny nothings' outburst) complete the survey - redeemed by the girls' stubborn friendship.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 29 "Girls and Philosophy" — Adleberg asks whether Jessa is right that she is not 'the ladies.' Against Shoshanna's common-sense biological determinism and pop-neuroscience like Brizendine's 'male brain' (refuted via brain plasticity and Fausto-Sterling), she deploys Butler's point that identity categories are always normative and exclusionary (Marnie's 'that's what men do' to Charlie) and Beauvoir's and Spelman's social constructionism - mothers already treating infants differently - to show gender is made, not born. With Haslanger's call to resist unjust gender meanings, she concludes that neither conforming (Marnie craving dominant Booth Jonathan) nor defying stereotypes (Jessa's bathroom sex, 'what if I want to feel like I have udders?') should be compulsory; only objectifying harm, as with Adam and Natalia, is wrong.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 23 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter surveys Harlan's gendered violence - Ava's killing of Bowman, the routine roughing-up of Audrey's working girls, Robert Quarles's childhood prostitution - and uses Catharine MacKinnon's account of patriarchal power imbalance to explain victim-blaming, underreporting, and police disbelief of trauma responses in domestic-violence and rape cases. On prostitution it weighs sex-positive feminism against the objectification worry, concluding via Teri's line about 'sucking hillbilly dicks for money' that Audrey's women have little real choice even under Ava's management. Finally it brings in bell hooks's third-wave point that oppression cannot be split from race and class, plus Peggy McIntosh's invisible backpack of white privilege, to read Noble's Holler's isolation and the bombed black church as evidence that patriarchy in Justified is always also racial and economic.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 29 "17. Sin, My Young Man, Is When You Treat People as Things" — Taking Granny Weatherwax's definition that sin 'is when you treat people as things' and Vetinari's that sin is not saying no to evil, the chapter reads Discworld through C. S. Lewis's argument that a universal Law of Human Nature—felt on the Disc by dwarfs, trolls, and even atheists—points to a divine lawgiver. The enchanted wolf in Witches Abroad, whose agony every witch intuits as wrong and who is granted a merciful death and human funeral, shows that shared moral intuition at work, and grounds the chapter's notes on Pratchett's own campaign for assisted dying. Finally, the Assassins' Guild, which only inhumes the rich who can afford bodyguards under its motto nil mortifi sine lucre, illustrates John Paul II's 'structures of sin': killing sanctified by contract and city law, treating people as things.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 24 "11. Leda, Castor, and Their Families" — Shows how the clones queer the normative family: clones as such are "biological outlaws" (via Stephanie Turner's reading of Ripley in Alien), Siobhan turns out to be the genetic half-sister of the clones cloned from her own mother Kendall, and the chosen family — Felix the "brother sestra," Kira's aunties, Helena's dream baby shower — repeatedly rebuilds kinship outside blood and marriage. Against this stands the stripping of reproductive agency: the infertility sequence written into the Leda clones, Coady's weaponized sterilizing virus, and above all Helena, whose eggs are harvested and implanted by Henrik and Gracie's father without consent. The chapter's conclusion is that Orphan Black's blood families are abusive and controlling while the non-normative chosen families of Clone Club are where love and consent actually live.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 30 "17. Sex, Consent, and Rape in Westeros" — Underwood distinguishes the legal consent of fifteenth-century-style Westeros - under the conjugal-debt doctrine neither Drogo nor Ramsay legally raped their wives, while every Cersei-Jaime union was treasonous regardless of desire - from the moral standard of consent developed from Alan Wertheimer's work. Applying his fraud and disregard cases, she argues Sansa's marriage obtained through Littlefinger's deception and Daenerys's coerced early nights with Drogo are immoral though legal, and proposes 'reciprocal subjectivity' as the criterion: Ramsay treats Sansa purely as an object, but the scene at Joffrey's body shows Jaime raping Cersei while still loving her as a subject, proving mutual recognition is necessary yet not sufficient for morally permissible sex.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 29 "17. Wade Wilson Fights Like a Girl" — Staged as a Socratic dialogue in a professor's office, the chapter tests Peter Coogan's definition of the superhero (mission, powers, identity) against the Deadpool movie and finds Wade qualifies while mocking the genre. It then argues the film subverts the superhero genre's sexist conventions: Vanessa refuses the damsel role by grabbing the bar mercenary's crotch and later skewering Francis herself, Angel Dust knocks Colossus out, and Negasonic Teenage Warhead is 'a damsel to the rescue.' Applying Laura Mulvey's male gaze, it shows the camera lingering on Deadpool's body and adopting Vanessa's viewpoint in the Calendar Girl scene, with the Women in Refrigerators trope, Gwen Stacy's death, and the Hawkeye Initiative as evidence of what the movie overturns.
- **The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed**, ch. 14 "6 Wives and Husbands The Marital Power Struggle" — Taking Susan Okin's 'the personal is political' and Kate Millett's Weberian herrschaft against Locke's public/private dichotomy, the chapter reviews the empirical studies of marital power (Blood and Wolfe, Blumstein and Schwarz, Steil) and finds money is the master base in marriage: the husband's income and occupational prestige set his say, working wives gain power but couples conspire to understate wives' earnings ('manning up and womaning down'), while knowledge and status are the next strongest resources. Authority from religion, tradition and morality still favors husbands (Ephesians' 'wives submit yourselves unto your husbands' alongside the philosophers' 'abler and stronger'), violence persists from the rule of thumb to marital rape and murder despite legal change, housework remains women's burden - Beauvoir's never-won 'battle against dust', Engels's 'leaden boredom', Davis's industrialization proposal and Okin's demand that it be shared - and sex itself works as a power base in the bedroom, with MacKinnon diagnosing heterosexuality as the linchpin of gender inequality. The chapter ends with black couples' comparatively egalitarian patterns traced by Angela Davis to slave-quarters equality, Schwarz's rare 'peer marriages', and the Marxist (Okin, the Swedish model) versus liberal (Wilson, the Japanese model) readings of family change.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 19 "9. But Women Can Vote . ." — Hansmann and Jones set Adams's gender posts against the four waves of feminism and the men's rights movement: his March 2011 Men's Rights post telling activists to get over it while lumping women with four-year-olds and the mentally handicapped, his Global Gender War matriarchy in which any country where women can vote counts as female-ruled, his framing of sex as a woman's currency for extracting male strategy (sacrifice a pawn to nail the queen), and his serial interrupting of women. They show the rhetoric eerily echoes anti-suffragists like Mrs. William Force Scott and Senator Sanford and the Goldilocks Dilemma, note the red-pill fantasy borrowed from The Matrix, and conclude that calling America a matriarchy defies scholarly consensus, with Beauvoir's The Second Sex marking why the vote never delivered the balance of power.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 13 "3. Laura Palmer—Madonna and Whore" — Applies Freud's Madonna-whore complex — "where such men love, they have no desire, and where they desire, they cannot love" — to Laura Palmer's split between homecoming queen/Meals on Wheels volunteer and cocaine-prostitute, arguing the contradiction exists only in a mindset that forces women into two poles, which BOB weaponizes with his "dirty and sleazy" refrain. The chapter surveys explanations of the complex (incest fear, paternity anxiety, alpha-male identity visible in Leo and Jacques), and then indicts the Fireman as a feminist "nice guy": his Part 8 creation of Laura as a golden orb of purity sent to redeem the world of the Bomb is the ultimate Madonna role, a Christ-like burden that is what makes her the target BOB must debase. Even her friends' names — Maddie and Donna — spell Madonna.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 26 "15. Are There Certain Things We Should Not Talk About" — Reads Schumer's taboo-breaking through The Second Sex: man makes woman the mysterious Other, and silences around menstruation, aging, and wives' desire keep that mystery intact. 'Last Fuckable Day' dramatizes the expiry of the idolized 'real woman', 'Sex Prep' shows the metamorphosis into a sex-representation collapsing into hiding under the bed, and '12 Angry Men' stages a male jury defining a woman's value. Ehrnberger argues Schumer's demystifying candor, from publishing her teenage journals to calling herself a 'flawed fuckup', dissolves the Other's aura and restores power, exactly as Beauvoir predicted when women assert themselves as human beings.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 28 "17. Switching It Up" — Argues Trainwreck and the stand-up material on sexual 'ownership' expose patriarchal double standards: the same promiscuity that makes men players makes women sluts, while LeBron James's gossipy, overprotective best friend and John Cena's devoted, unthreatening boyfriend cast male stars in traditional rom-com female roles. Browning brings in Kant's view that sexual desire treats persons as objects to be discarded like squeezed lemons, conceding that counting conquests objectifies partners while rejecting Kant's celibate conclusion. Schumer's comedy instead shows women owning their orgasms, turning sex from competition into mutual gratification.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 31 "19. How to Feel Pretty" — A satirical monologue voiced by 'The Patriarchy' that catalogs women's impossible, contradictory beauty demands: a painted face that must look natural, effortless long hair, a body that is simultaneously too fat and too thin, sexual availability that must never look eager, accomplishments that are unattractive, and finally a pretty death. The screed makes vivid that the standards exist only to keep women judging themselves as garbage, nailing the dynamic with Schumer-specific gags like 'Milk Milk Lemonade' as both a women-are-people reminder and a butt showcase, and Amy's 'catch a dick' line, before mocking workplace 'merit' talk that promotes Jim.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 18 "9. Machines Who Care" — Weiss reads 'The Lonely' and 'I Sing the Body Electric' as anticipations of today's debate over 'relational artifacts' — Turkle's sociable robots, the Sparrows' claim that robotic aged care is unethical, Coeckelbergh's rebuttal — asking, with Anne, whether an electric grandma 'doesn't sound so good.' Corry's Alicia and the children's electric grandma show care being bought as an assembly-line product for the lonely, and he presses the details: why the caring robots are female and serve water, why Alicia arrives in a box and is summarily shot in the face when no longer needed, and what it says about a culture that maroons people in loneliness and then sells the technical fix.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 20 "Back to the Rough Ground!" — Finnegan uses Wittgenstein's language games, the 'picture' that holds us captive, and 'back to the rough ground' to argue that Ford, Sizemore, and the Man in Black are paralyzed by an idealized, patriarchal picture of narrative (winners and losers, violence, transcendent self-discovery), while Dolores and Maeve gain traction by inventing new language games within their forms of life. Dolores breaks her damsel script in Pariah ('I imagined a story where I didn't have to be the damsel') and reworks scripted love-dialogue to describe her grief, while Maeve bullies the lab techs, takes administrative control, and narrates other hosts' actions - 'Time to write my own fucking story.' The chapter reads their objectified position (via Mulvey's male gaze, which leaves female viewers identifying with the robot hosts rather than the male subject) as exactly what equips them for guerrilla warfare in the master's language games, doing what Audre Lorde thought impossible: dismantling the master's house with the master's tools.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 25 "In Closing, The Naked Truth" — Meyer sorts Westworld's abundant nudity into three aesthetic registers. First, Kenneth Clark's nude: Dolores's opening chair pose and the perfected, fabricated host bodies are idealized, created art-forms serving the creators' control. Second, John Berger's analysis of the nude as spectacle of male dominance: the Man in Black watching Armistice bathe (a Susannah-and-the-Elders voyeurism), the gold-painted women at El Lazo's orgy as 'nudity as a form of dress' for male desire, and techs' 'fuck puppet' treatment of Maeve, which she reverses by re-appropriating the language of fucking. Third, Leo Steinberg's incarnation symbolism: host nudity signals machines becoming human - shameless like prelapsarian Adam and Eve, mortal and sexed, 'ensouled' - so that Maeve overriding her programming to reclaim her daughter is the birth of the human-host, the mirror-image of God becoming man.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 9 "Resisting Dystopia" — The editor's introduction argues that The Handmaid's Tale disturbs us because it shows how tenuous our civil liberties are, so we must actively watch political events for warning signs. It insists that a woman's value is not fixed by her body, fertility, or attractiveness—Handmaids are treated as incubators and commodities—and that the caring work women do is a power, not a weakness. It closes on the lesson that facts, not politicians, control the narrative, ending with 'Nolite te bastardes carborundorum.'
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 17 "7. She Went Down Swingin’" — Volpert argues Tom Petty was a feminist, the only classic-rock male whose catalog consistently grants women rational equality and agency, adopting Susan McClary's feminist New Musicology as her lens and marching through Greatest Hits song by song. She reads the forced removal of the Lolita cover from "American Girl," the consensual, threat-free request of "Breakdown," and "Listen to Her Heart" as Petty's reply to Ike Turner's cocaine-locked party, and defends "You Got Lucky" as a conceit about band technology rather than misogyny. The chapter confronts the gaze directly, arguing "Here Comes My Girl" watches a woman walking toward you as formidable rather than objectified, with the video's flirtations redirected homoerotically at the Heartbreakers themselves.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 35 "22. Rachael, Weeping for Her Children" — Bonnie McLean maps Baudrillard's four-stage precession of simulacra onto the women of 2049: Joshi anchors reality, implanted memories distort it, Joi is representation masking the absence of reality, and the eye-color-wrong reconstructed Rachael is a simulacrum of a simulacrum bearing no relation to reality. Read this way, the film lionizes birth — Wallace kissing the replicant he has just disemboweled, her blood running down her legs — while stripping every woman of agency in service of K's quest, a dynamic the chapter links to pro-life politics and DACA-era savior narratives. Only by removing K from the narrative, she shows, does the women's erasure become visible.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 36 "23. The Future Is Female … Robots!" — Emily Cox-Palmer-White applies Deleuze and Guattari's 'becoming-woman' to the mechanical women of both films: the girl as universal other, a vacuum or absence at the center of femininity, is exactly what lets Rachael, Pris, Luv, and Joi destabilize the patriarchal world that manufactured them. Wallace's drones undressing the barren replicant with their gaze before he slashes her womb gives the male gaze a literal, lethal form, while the Joi-Mariette sync scene stages the frightening interchangeability of women under that gaze. Deckard's 'Her eyes were green' — a lie, since Rachael's eyes were brown — refuses the premise that women are replaceable products.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 39 "25. Less Human than Human" — Leah Schade and Emily Askew read replicants as undocumented Latinx immigrants: Sapper's grub farm parallels an ICE raid on a meatpacking plant and the deportation cell of 'Justo', blade runners mirror enforcement agents hunting 'illegals', and the miracle child maps onto DACA Dreamers whom well-meaning liberals recast as superhuman saviors at the cost of their ordinary personhood. Using Mary Midgley's personhood criteria — the ability to suffer, emotional fellowship, minding what happens to one — they argue replicants, like migrants, plainly qualify, and that 'illegality' is a constructed status, not a moral fact. The chapter warns that messianic sacrifice narratives, however sympathetic, re-objectify the very people they mean to defend.
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 22 "12. An Intimate Look at Paul Stanley’s Love" — Robert Grant Price maps Paul Stanley's catalogue onto four loves. Eros as soulmate-love follows Aristophanes' split-beings myth from Plato's Symposium ('Forever,' 'Every Time I Look at You'); self-love follows Aquinas's demand that it be 'rightly ordered,' so Stanley's machismo songs pass while Gene's 'I' fails as disordered egomania; bodily love is defended as bawdy dramatic monologue — foreplay between lovers rather than instruction in reducing women to sex objects; and love of life is secularized agape praise in 'I'm Alive,' 'Shout It Out Loud,' and the very title Alive!. Price then asks why love drives art at all, weighing the transcendentals (true, good, beautiful) against the Scruton-versus-Craig-Martin can-of-shit debate, and reads 'Reason to Live' as the claim that only rightly ordered love can ground a life.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 22 "Equal Opportunity Offenders" — Argues the Facehugger stages rape with the sexes reversed: because the aliens violate male and female bodies impartially - Kane's penetration, forced pregnancy, and death in childbirth; the cocooned Dallas begging Ripley to kill him - the films strip male viewers of the patriarchal privilege of treating sexual violence as someone else's threat and even of biological immunity to forced pregnancy. The Marines' 'colonists' daughters' banter, the prisoners' treatment of Ripley on Fury 161, and Johner's basketball comment exemplify a rape culture (Dworkin: rape is committed by exemplars of our norms) persisting into the twenty-second century, while Frye and Shafer's 'domain' explains why bodily violation attacks personhood itself.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 23 "History Will Judge" — Livingston reads Razor through George Lakoff's nation-as-family metaphor: Cain's Pegasus is the Strict Father family (the world is dangerous, Belzen shot for disobedience, Gina tortured for intelligence, Kendra's humiliating 'birth slap'), while Adama's Galactica is the Nurturant Parent (empathy, questioning authority, 'it's not enough to survive; one has to be worthy of surviving'). She traces how military kill-conditioning, desensitization plus objectifying 'toaster' and 'it' language, turns Kendra into 'a razor' and a PTSD case, while Apollo and Kendra hybridize the two family models on Pegasus. Adama's closing 'history will have to make its judgments' frames the chapter's claim that understanding Cain's context matters more than villainizing, and that humanity's worthiness depends on the balance struck between our idealized parents.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 43 "With or Without Starbuck" — Kirkland argues BSG imagines gender-free institutions (unisex heads and quarters, Starbuck never having to justify fighting) while installing a default masculinity under Adama, so that feminine-coded women die: Ellen the femme fatale is poisoned, pilots Kat and Kendra earn redemption only through death, and Cain's female command is written as militarist nightmare aligned with Gina's sexual abuse. Starbuck confounds the sexualizing male gaze and reverses rescue narratives, and 'The Farm' plus her captivity with Leoben on New Caprica literalize feminist critiques of patriarchal medicine and compulsory heterosexuality. Yet she is masculinized, pathologized via her abusive mother, brought to submit to Leoben as spiritual guide, and killed in 'Maelstrom' - containing the transgressive heroine within the show's patriarchy.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 26 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Almassi grades the Dude as a halfway feminist ally: he divests from the Big Lebowski's patriarchal achiever-masculinity ('that and a pair of testicles'), respects Maude's conception project without paternalism (O'Neill's Kantian line between love and respect), and defends pacifist Smokey — yet his pacifism has stalled into passivity that King's active nonviolence would reject, he leaves Bunny's objectification unchallenged while 'Mr. Treehorn treats objects like women', and he only belatedly gives Maude the credibility Fricker's testimonial justice demands ('why don't you fucking listen occasionally?'). Using bell hooks's feminist masculinity and Larry May's progressive male standpoint, the chapter leaves the Dude five pins up with a spare still to pick up.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 6 "“Smother Him in the Crib”—Booker" — Origitano reads Elizabeth through Beauvoir and Frye: Columbia's propaganda infantilizes and objectifies her ('the Seed of the Prophet', 'Lamb', 'Specimen', always defined relative to a man), the tower literalizes Frye's birdcage of systematic oppression, and her confinement for an uncontrollable power mirrors women caged by a supposed natural inferiority. Booker's rescue only grants freedom, echoing Beauvoir's point that women have 'only received' what men are willing to give, so Elizabeth remains caged as his poker chip, her lock-picking skills formed by captivity and her tears dismissed as foreign. Her emancipation comes through action and collective solidarity, allying with Lady Comstock's ghost, taking control of Songbird, and finally drowning Booker/Comstock as equals, which enacts Beauvoir's claim that liberation must be won, not granted.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 17 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Olson's first D&D Encounters session handed her a sexualized female miniature in a chainmail bikini and high-heeled boots, and the chapter audits the game as a feminist would: research on the 'token girl' and male-default storytelling, women like Dowsett pushed to play male characters to be taken seriously, and harassment ranging from 'date at least one of the party or bring food' to condescension toward women in the industry. Against this she argues the rules themselves are egalitarian — identical power pools for male and female characters, embodying Plato's Republic claim that women 'are by nature the same with respect to guarding the city', and even the evil deities are stereotyped symmetrically (scheming Lolth and Tiamat versus war-god patrons of power) — while the collaborative party structure (clerics healing strikers, shared goals) has exactly the care-ethical, anti-individualist flavor Friedman and Bolte attribute to women's moral perspectives. Sexism is thus a consequence of unreflective practices, marketing that ignores women, and industry culture rather than the game; all-female systems like Portal Worlds are a real response but, she worries, separatism risks deepening the divide.
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 14 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — Robert Arp and Sarah Fisk test three moral theories against objectification in Final Fantasy: Kant's ban on using rational beings as mere means (Kuja's manipulation of Queen Brahne, the Geostigma children of Advent Children), Mill's greatest-happiness principle (Yuna's and Aeris's self-sacrifice), and Aristotle's character-based virtue ethics (Hojo and Sephiroth as vicious, Aeris as virtuous). They argue Kantianism generates a stalemate between 'moral sanctity' and 'moral autonomy' camps over cases like Guardian Force summoning in FFVIII, and utilitarianism a stalemate over mandatory self-sacrifice, leaving virtue ethics, Aristotelian or Nietzschean, as the view that escapes both, ending with the question 'Aeris or a Cloud?'
- **The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire**, ch. 15 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" — Why do Berger, Cecilia, Harriet, Salander, and Figuerola all bed the unprepossessing Blomkvist? Testing Kant's claim that sexual desire makes 'the loved person an Object of appetite... a lemon which has been sucked dry,' the chapter argues his appeal is that he treats women as ends in themselves—he works beside them as equals, is 'not going to compete with you' with Figuerola, and never manipulates or controls—so his sex is the least objectifying in a Sweden full of men who hate women. Against Kant and Baumrim, Irving Singer's reply that desire can respond to the whole person explains why his no-strings honesty attracts powerful women, though his refusal to define, own, or 'cherish' any lover—walking in on Erika just as Salander arrives with the Elvis cabin ad—still leaves Salander heartbroken and Figuerola in sadness.
- **The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire**, ch. 22 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" — Applying Laura Mulvey's visual pleasure to the printed page, the chapter argues that Larsson's protest against woman-hating is compromised by styling Salander—four-eleven, ninety pounds, 'childlike breasts'—as a sexual spectacle whose rapes (Bjurman's coerced oral sex, the anal rape, the trial's play-by-play of implements) are the trilogy's most explicit scenes while consensual sex stays off-screen, making the books 'torture porn' for the voyeuristic reader. The films shift the gaze further: the revenge on Bjurman runs longer than the rapes, Salander actively watches Martin Vanger burn, and her bisexuality with Mimmi Wu is reduced to one silent morning, changes that make the violence against men more acceptable than against women. The chapter ends ambivalent: Laurie Penny and Gail Dines charge that 'Misogynist violence is appalling; now here's some more,' yet the distributor's RAINN partnership and a rape survivor's testimony that Salander was the first active, aggressive survivor she had ever seen show the books also work as Larsson intended.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 26 "Notes" — Rivera Berruz argues that Freddy Hayes's storyline - the BBQ joint whose franchise design keeps linoleum peeling so 'white folks feel like they slumming,' his son's parole violation destroying the deal, and Frank publicly dropping him when the bad press lands - commodifies black male life as consumable 'spice' for a predominantly white show. Using bell hooks's account of ethnicity as seasoning in commodity culture, Tommy Curry and Michelle Alexander on blackness coded as criminality, and Nancy Leong's racial capitalism, the chapter shows Freddy's value is entirely derivative of his usefulness to Underwood. It closes by adopting Derrick Bell's racial realism ('I live to harass white folks') as the proper stance: the critique cannot dismantle racial capitalism but can harass the representation so viewers stop assuming the stereotype is 'just the way things are.'
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 14 "5 Feminism and Indiana Jones A Field Guide" — Kate Schmidt applies feminist media tests (Bechdel, sexy lamp, Mako Mori, Pierce, Landau) to show the films usually fail — Willie is a screaming prop and human shield in Temple, the eyelid-writing student exists only to display Indy's sex appeal, and all four films fail the Bechdel Test — while Marion, Spalko, and above all Elsa in The Last Crusade are mixed cases with partial autonomy. Drawing on Iris Marion Young's account of women as Other and Carol Gilligan's care ethics, she argues Crusade is the series' most feminist film not for its women but for its men: Indy's open hurt after Elsa's betrayal and the father-son reconciliation embody care ethics against 'boys don't cry' toxic masculinity. She concludes that one can love flawed media without endorsing its sexism.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 35 "Zelda and Reality" — Joyce Havstad and Iris Jahng catalogue the women of Zelda — Zelda's many incarnations, Impa, the Twinrova sisters, the oracles Din and Nayru, Midna — finding the typologies of maiden, mother, and crone, then explain them with Beauvoir's The Second Sex: the myth of woman (Mother, Wife, Idea), femininity as made rather than born, and woman's enforced passivity against man's transcendence. Zelda is woman as Idea, traced to Platonic Forms: young, beautiful, virtuous, and radically passive (turned to stone in The Minish Cap, asleep through The Adventure of Link, imprisoned in nearly every game), an object that exists to motivate Link's heroism. Significantly, only the masculine-garbed Sheik and the pirate Tetra escape passivity, a shift the authors link to Miyamoto's design philosophy of 'reality over realism' and to changing conceptions of women.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Kolb reads the whole franchise through Carol Gilligan's ethics of care and the ecofeminism of Ariel Salleh and Mary Mellor: Max begins as a caregiver in an egalitarian marriage, Toecutter's gang and the Citadel embody toxic masculinity, and Aunty Entity shows women can administer patriarchal capitalism too. In Fury Road, 'We are not things,' the milking mothers, and water branded as Aqua Cola literalize Salleh's claim that capitalist patriarchy treats women and nature as resources. The Vuvalini, the Keeper of the Seeds, Max washing in mother's milk, and his voluntary blood transfusion to Furiosa enact the ethic of care as the film's saving alternative to domination.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Quick applies Cary Wolfe's humaninized/animalized humans and Carol Adams's animalized women to the Citadel: Max is hunted, caged, and muzzled as an unnamed 'it', War Pups serve like littermates, and the milking mothers produce Adams's 'feminized protein' while the 'breeders' are groomed like show animals. Following Val Plumwood's ecofeminist critique of the masculinity that conquers mother nature — and Joe's branding of water as Aqua Cola — the chapter reads Furiosa's return to the Citadel as an ecofeminist revolution in which 'We are not things' restores women, men like Nux and Max, and nature itself from property to personhood.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 25 "Real World Island" — Patricia Brace and Rob Arp argue Lost redeems characters who stop objectifying others and instead freely 'objectify' themselves for the greater good. Kant's ban on treating persons as mere means condemns Ben's lifelong manipulation and Ben's use of Sayid as an assassin, yet autonomy justifies chosen self-sacrifice like Charlie's Looking Glass suicide mission, Claire volunteering as bait for Ethan, and Jack becoming the new Jacob. Mill's utilitarianism makes Kate's shooting of the Man in Black a fair trade saving her friends, while Aristotle's virtues - respect against objectification, courage in Jack's death at the cliff, the engrained honesty of reformed con man Jim LaFleur, Kate's character-building motherhood of Aaron - complete the three-theory survey.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 16 "Television and Existential Awakening" — Jaarsma argues Mad Men dramatizes an existential rather than Kantian-enlightenment model of advertising: Don's 'freedom from fear' pitch ('Whatever you are doing is okay. You are okay') sells escape from the anxiety of real choice, which is precisely Sartrean bad faith and what de Beauvoir calls the stagnant 'happiness' of women rewarded for being the other. Betty on her psychiatrist's couch, Peggy measured by Joan's paper-bag mirror and the Playtex bullet-bra silhouette, and the closeted Salvatore all internalize the dominant values Marcuse describes, finding meaning in conformity to the objectifying gaze ('bras are for men; women want to see themselves the way men see them'). Rachel Menken, who refuses to 'put on an apron' and calls out the contingency of gendered embodiment, models authenticity as choosing to choose, and the chapter closes with the hope that television itself can occasion the viewer's existential awakening.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 25 "Don’t Go Mad" — Barkman applies a qualified Aristotelian standard of justice, that women possessing rational souls must be treated as equals, to Peggy, Betty, and Joan as second-wave feminism dawns. Peggy is the 'mad woman' in the best sense: she demands a desk, equal pay ('You have everything and so much of it'), and Don's apology while never resorting to blackmail like Pete, whereas Betty is repressed at home by a husband who shows her off ('I want to show you off, Betts') and Joan suppresses herself, measuring worth by appearance and enduring Greg's violation until the vase incident. The sexual objectification Peggy faces from her first day (Ken's elevator leers, Joan's paper-bag advice, the panty-hunt in 'Nixon vs. Kennedy') is the chapter's core injustice, and the warning is that women who cannot stand up to it may simply go mad.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 27 "The Office and Philosophy" — Nys asks whether political correctness is a genuine moral demand or mere verbal hygiene, using the British Office: Gareth's racist BMC joke, Brent aborting it when Oliver the Black coworker arrives, the 'wanking claw' impression, and the porn email with Brent's head pasted onto a woman's body. He argues words genuinely wound (Brent's 'sticks and stones' rehearsal collapses when Gareth reveals his cruel nicknames) but that offense is wrong as disrespect for human equality rather than as a feeling, an account filled out with Frankfurt's claim that our identity depends on what we care about, so the non-targeted can be offended too. After weighing Mill's defense of free discussion for social progress, the pornography debate (in which reduction to body parts is exactly what degrades, as Brent complains he was 'objectified'), and Marx's notion of ideology as a concealing set of ideas behind a 'white male' bias, he concludes that Brent's flaw is looking good rather than being good, and that PC language is rhetorical make-up over persisting inequality.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 28 "The Office and Philosophy" — Dromm asks what makes Michael's behavior wrong even where the law cannot touch it: as an 'equal-opportunity harasser' of Pam, Ryan, and Oscar, Michael seems to escape Title VII's discrimination requirement. He tests Edmund Wall's 'wrongful communication' definition against the filthy emails, 'that's what she said,' and Michael's solution to the Kevin-Angela dispute in 'Conflict Resolution,' finds it too broad and too dependent on the victim's objection, then turns to MacKinnon's sex-discrimination account and Crosthwaite and Priest's oppression account to explain the distinctive harm to women (pressuring Pam to be a cheerleader in 'Basketball,' calling the party-planning committee his 'bitches'). He concludes that both views are needed, and that in the end harassment wrongs workers by undermining their legitimate expectation of being judged only on job-relevant merit, leaving Dwight's extra effort done for nothing.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 9 "When the Subject is Not the Butt Schmitts Gay Beer" — Tallman asks why SNL may mock presidents (Chase's pratfalling Ford, Carvey's Bush) and Clintons but not unchosen groups, framing the question with the aesthetics debate among radical autonomism (Bell), radical moralism (traced to Plato and Tolstoy), and moderate moralism. Sketches from Samurai Futaba to Farley's Lunchlady Land show jokes can punch up, punch down, or elevate a low-status group. The Schmitts Gay beer sketch, she argues, ridicules not gay men but beer-ad conventions: swapping the usual female sex objects for men in speedos exposes the objectification and heteronormativity viewers had stopped noticing, so the butt is the advertising industry.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 25 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Applies Luce Irigaray's account of patriarchal society to Charming's women: Gemma and Tara are strong and resourceful, but their identity, power, and even survival run through men, as Clay's 'you are NOT a member of this club — you're just an old lady!' and Jax's 'She's just an old lady, not a member' make brutally literal. Irigaray's claim that patriarchal orders circulate women as commodities exchanged among men fits the 'sweet butt' Cherry being offered to Clay in 'Patch Over' and Gemma's 'Only men need to feel loved. Women need to feel wanted.' Tara's sacrificed surgical career and Jax's refusal to live off his wife ('I'm not gonna live off my wife. I can't.') illustrate woman as a being who exists for another, and the chapter ends asking what Gemma could say if she had a genuinely feminine voice of her own.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 24 "Notes" — Argues that Leia and Padme really are strong feminist characters, using Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex to defuse the two stock objections: Padme's motherhood is 'freely chosen' rather than an oppressive role, and Leia chained in Jabba's palace keeps command of her sexuality, turning the damsel-in-distress plot around by strangling Jabba with her own chain and later rescuing Han herself. The chapter's real complaint is structural: with only six speaking women in the original trilogy, almost all of them royalty, Leia and Padme are forced to represent all women (the 'affluent few' problem), while Shmi, Aunt Beru, Mon Mothma, and the handmaidens Sabe, Corde, and Dorme never get the screen time to show their strength.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 25 "Notes" — Reads Leia's gold-bikini captivity in Jabba's palace as an image of contemporary culture's fear of fat: Jabba, the rancor, and the Sarlaac personify uncontrolled appetite and Sartre's 'slimy' being-in-itself, while Leia's thin, disciplined body epitomizes the anorexic ideal. Drawing on Susan Bordo and Foucault's docile bodies, the chapter argues the scene chains women to a tyrannical ideal of slimness so that Leia herself becomes the oppressor, and closes with Sartre's point that consciousness depends on its body, so we should suspend the fear of flesh and embrace embodied life as the Force does.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 12 "A New Hope Inclusive Representation in the Galaxy" — Lakka uses Beauvoir's The Second Sex (the Mother/Mistress dichotomy, woman tied to nature and denied transcendence) and Butler on the mother-daughter separation to argue that Revenge of the Sith reduces Padme from the active senator and warrior of the first two prequels to a pregnant figure confined to her apartment, whose death gets read as martyrdom or even 'mom-shaming.' She reads Anakin's jealousy, interrogations ('Obi-Wan's been here, has he not?'), and Force-choke on Mustafar — explicitly paralleled with Othello and Desdemona — as an abusive relationship, suggesting Padme's death may be a feminicide. The deleted Petition of the 2000 scenes, and successors like Rey, Ahsoka, Rose Tico, and Jyn Erso, point toward the inclusive representation the galaxy still needs.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 16 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Brace applies Kant's prohibition on using persons merely as means to the women of Supernatural: Bobby helping willingly is not objectification, demonic possession and Azazel's forcing Ellen's gun to her own head are, and Zachariah's 'fornicate with women' pitch reduces women to objects.
