- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 7 "Free Your Mind, and Your Roundhouse Will Follow" — Young argues that dojo courtesy is not the fantasy that good manners win fights (Napoleon and the Karate Kid's Johnny lost on skill, not rudeness) but the framing of a craft within a way of life. He maps Aristotle's techne/ethos distinction onto the Japanese jutsu/do pairing to show founders like Kano, Funakoshi and Ueshiba treated fighting as one part of a whole ethical character, reads his seiza apology to an injured yellow belt through Confucian ren, li, yi and shu, and traces Shinto purity into the sincerity (kime) of committed sparring. His black-belt humiliation by seniors becomes Zen's 'courtesy of brutal': ego-deflating violence that trains no-mindedness (muga, Takuan Soho's fudoshin).
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 13 "“Well, It Got Big Laughs”" — Barkman uses Confucius (ren, yi, li, and zheng ming, treating each person according to what he or she is) and Aristotle (eudaimonia, virtue as a habituated mean between extremes, practical wisdom) to indict 30 Rock for valorizing Jack's 'semi-virtuous path', the smug middle between best and worst announced in 'Do-Over'. He catalogues injustices the show laughs off: Liz's serial lies about her age, hobbies, and adoption; Jack's priority flu shots for the powerful in 'Flu Shot'; Tracy's insubordination about dogfighting in 'Rosemary's Baby'; and Kenneth's servility as everyone's punching bag. On liberality and piety, Jack's confession that 'capitalism is my religion' and Liz's 'I pretty well do whatever Oprah tells me' show the show settling for semi-virtue, which the chapter says even comedy must not endorse.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 30 "Every Soul Experiences the Battle Within" — Reads Zuko's arc as a war between Legalism and Confucianism: Ozai's agni kai scarring of his son, Azulon's death sentence, the Fire Nation Oath and school discipline ('The Headband') all enact Han Fei's principle that bad human nature needs terrifying sanctions, and Azula's 'trust is for fools' completes it. Against this stands Iroh's Confucian education in ren — teaching that honor cannot be separated from humaneness, that a mugger deserves tea and encouragement, and that wu-wei-like patience knows when to speak. Mencius's innate compassion explains why Zuko's 'amazing lie' realization could unfold, Katara, Sokka, and Hakoda embody Confucian filial bonds that adopt Aang, Toph, and finally Zuko, and Solzhenitsyn's gulag insight closes the chapter: the line between good and evil runs through every human heart.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 30 "Every Soul Experiences the Battle Within" — Reads the Fire Nation royal family as a philosophical battle between Legalism (Han Fei, taking Xunzi's dictum that human nature is evil, so order requires terrifying sanctions: Ozai burning Zuko in the agni kai so 'suffering will be your teacher', Azulon's death sentence on Zuko, the Fire Nation Oath recited in schools) and Confucianism (Iroh teaching ren, that true honor cannot be had apart from humaneness, preferring honorable begging over theft, and talking a would-be mugger into tea). Zuko's 'battle within' is the legacy of his two great-grandfathers, Sozin's Legalism versus Roku's line, and it is resolved when he disowns Ozai, calls Iroh his 'real father', and is adopted into Team Avatar, whose filial bonds (Katara's care, Hakoda's sacrifice) contrast with the scheming royal family. The chapter closes with Solzhenitsyn's image of the line between good and evil passing through every human heart to explain why Zuko's inner war resonates.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 11 "“Your Heart Knows”" — Argues that Disney's Mulan transplants a distinctly modern Western ideal of the authentic self ('true to your heart,' 'Reflection') into a Confucian honor culture where the self is constituted by roles and relationships, filial piety (xiao), and ren as the virtue that binds people into larger wholes — which is why the film flopped in China. The matchmaker debacle, Fa Zhou's 'I will die doing what's right,' and the family's shame show a culture where dishonor stains the whole family and even luck (the cricket Cri-Kee) fixes moral standing, conflicting with Western assumptions about individual responsibility. The chapter ends by noting Mulan now resonates with young Chinese viewers, asking whether the Western individualist self is a truth about humanity or a cultural export that, like the Huns, has scaled the Great Wall.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 32 "The Rhythm by Which We Live Our Lives" — Kowalski interprets Kuzco's arc through Mencius: the emperor's pampered upbringing (eight hands replacing a squeezed toy, Yzma's loveless regency) is the 'hatchets and frost' of the Ox Mountain parable blunting his innate moral sprouts. The gorge scene stages Mencius's child-at-the-well thought experiment — Kuzco's spontaneous snatch of falling Pacha is a 'give-away' action betraying compassion he denies having, which Pacha diagnoses just as Mencius did King Xuan sparing the ox — and Pacha's family, quasi-adopting Kuzco, supplies the loving soil Mencius says the sprouts of ren need to grow.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 12 "Notes" — Decker parallels the Republic's fall into Palpatine's Empire with the Zhou dynasty's collapse that birthed Chinese philosophy, reading three Jedi from the Dark Times comics through it. K'Kruhk, guided by the Zatoichi-like Master Zao, learns wu-wei - following the Force rather than forcing outcomes, with Laozi's Dao as the Force's Chinese analogue. Dass Jennir's struggle over what 'Jedi' means after killing a slaver becomes Confucian rectification of names and the cultivation of ren, while Kai Hudorra's loss of faith, withdrawal to a casino, and final sacrificial stand against Vader embody Mozi-style pragmatic minimalism redeemed by Jennir's virtuous example.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 31 "“Tell Your Sister, You Were Right”" — Yang argues that Luke's surrender to Vader on Endor is neither foolish nor irrational but an exercise of Confucian filial piety: Luke reveres the absent Anakin as an exemplar (picked out through admiration of Obi-Wan's stories and the lightsaber), insists 'I know there is good in you' against Vader's claim that the name means nothing, and is vindicated when Anakin turns and says 'You were right about me'. His imperfect training under Obi-Wan and Yoda functions like Confucian ritual (li), forming habits that respond with harmonious ease to surprises such as Palpatine's trap, and filial piety extends past death in the funeral pyre Luke builds on Endor, honoring his father as the Analects prescribes.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 31 "NOTES" — The Terjesens pit Kant's impersonal morality — Sam's contractual distance from the thieving Mickens is exactly how he would treat strangers — against Confucius and Mencius, for whom filial duties are the nursery of virtue: we learn benevolence by serving parents and revering elders, Lafayette's care for Lettie Mae and Tara shows family forming moral character, and the Upright Gong's covering for a father's sheep-stealing grounds Jason's 'sometimes the right thing to do is the wrong thing'. Mencius's King Shun, who abdicates and carries his criminal father into exile, models how Tommy and Jason should put family first while accepting the cost, while Mozi's universal love surfaces in Godric's 'forgiveness is love', and the chapter concludes that family counts only insofar as it develops our moral nature — the line between Tommy and Sam.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 12 "Third Hole Finding the (Fair)Way with Confucius and Ben Hogan" — Laumakis builds an analogy between pursuing excellence in golf and living a flourishing human life, then contrasts two models. Reading Confucius's Great Learning and Analects onto golf, he casts a repeating swing as a 'well-ordered kingdom' rooted in self-cultivation, and reinterprets ren, li, yi, and xiao so the 'authoritative player' masters the game through ritual practice, a teacher-parent (xiao), and doing what is appropriate in each lie. Against this social conception he sets Ben Hogan's Five Lessons as a 'rugged individualist' account stressing solitary practice and personal responsibility, and proposes a contextual pluralism as a mean between communitarian absolutism and individualist relativism.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 29 "Fourteenth Hole Plato and Confucius on the Form of Golf From the Real to the Ideal" — Stephen Laumakis stages a thought experiment pitting Plato the Idealist against Confucius the Realist/Pragmatist on how to think about and play golf. On Plato's theory of Forms, every club, ball and swing is an imperfect copy of a timeless, unchanging Form—there is a 'perfect' swing (Tiger Woods, Ernie Els) that par and the handicap system let us measure ourselves against, so golf is about striving toward the Ideal. Confucius, read through the 'Great Learning' and 'Analects' (li, ren, self-cultivation, unrelenting practice), instead prizes the situation-sensitive sage who negotiates each bad lie (Phil Mickelson's flop shots). Laumakis concludes the good golfer must integrate both: pursue perfection while wielding practical wisdom about when to go for it and when to lay up.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — The editors' introduction argues that the unifying theme of Lee's films is the struggle for authentic self-identity, framed through Charles Taylor's dialogical self and Kierkegaard's line that anxiety is the dizziness of freedom. It surveys how Confucian virtues (ren, li, xiao) and Daoist wu-wei play out across Pushing Hands, The Wedding Banquet, Eat Drink Man Woman, Crouching Tiger, Sense and Sensibility, Brokeback Mountain and others, treating each protagonist as caught between traditional obligation and personal desire. It invokes Nietzsche's claim that all philosophy is autobiography to justify reading Lee's films (he said 'it's all in my films') as a coherent authorial philosophy.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Kohler-Ryan and Palmer treat 'sense' and 'sensibility' as a spectrum Lee explores through sisterhood in Sense and Sensibility (Elinor/Marianne) and Crouching Tiger (Shu Lien/Jen). Elinor and Shu Lien embody sense, Shu Lien specifically the Confucian balance of li and ren that lets her soften ritual with humanity; Marianne embodies Burke's British-Romantic sublime while Jen embodies Daoist immersion in the dao. Reading door-frames, windows, hair-combing rituals and Shu Lien's hairpin as symbols, they argue only Sense and Sensibility achieves integration in time, whereas Li Mu Bai's confession that he lived sense and sensibility as separate spheres comes too late.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Bush argues that Brokeback Mountain transcends both the heterosexual western archetype and queer theory by presenting male sexuality through Mencius' philosophy and John Corvino's ethics of homosexuality. Using Mencius' four sprouts (ren, li, yi, zhi) and doctrine of natural goodness, he reads Ennis as the character in whom sexuality is contextual, cultivated and moral rather than merely physical, so the relationship between Ennis and Jack becomes an ethical friendship grounded in ren, the virtue Mencius says is most intense among friends. The bystanders Aguirre and Alma keeping the secret, and the final shirt-and-postcard scene, illustrate zhi as contextual moral judgment and homosexuality reframed as ethical rather than sexual.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 23 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Komasinski explains Confucius's advice to fathers through three ideas: ritual (li, glossed as 'cultural grammar' – engagement rings, saying 'I love you'), excellence/virtue as excelling at relating to others (ren, 'co-humanity'), and wisdom. Using the Analects' 'Upright Gong' passage (fathers and sons cover for each other) beside Plato's Euthyphro, he shows Confucius prizes the father-son bond over law, and reads the parable of the prodigal son and Tu Wei-ming's 'personality ideal' to argue fathers should lead by virtuous example rather than punishment.

### Natural Law

Natural law, as systematized by Thomas Aquinas, is the theory that there is an objective moral order accessible to human reason and grounded in the rational nature that all persons share. Aquinas holds that natural law is the rational creature's participation in the eternal law by which God governs creation, and that its first precept is to do good and avoid evil, from which more specific duties follow by reflecting on natural human goods such as life, knowledge, and society. Because it rests on reason rather than revelation, it is meant to bind all people regardless of faith or culture. The theory has profoundly shaped Western ethics, jurisprudence, and ideas of human rights.

- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 20 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Tim Mosteller identifies Lewis's Tao from The Abolition of Man with Aquinas's Natural Law, an objective moral order knowable by all rational beings, and maps three responses onto Narnian characters: wholehearted acceptance (Peter, Lucy, Tirian, Reepicheep), selective 'Innovators' who pick and choose (Shift and Miraz, with Nietzsche's invented master-values as the philosophical extreme), and total rejection by 'Conditioners' (Ginger the Cat, who reverts to dumb beast, and Uncle Andrew, who loses the animals' speech). Individual laws are illustrated by Mr. Tumnus freeing Lucy, Aslan scratching Aravis for her gladness at the slave girl's beating, Nikabrik's treacherous Realpolitik, Lucy's eavesdropping spell in the Magician's book, and Jill's showing-off at the cliff.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 31 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Barkman takes Andrea's mermaid-necklace question ('I don't think those rules apply any more') as a test of natural law: self-evident principles — general beneficence (Glenn's 'shit creek' rescue, Morgan's warning that it 'takes away a piece of your soul'), special beneficence toward family (Lori's 'Don't be so trusting,' Morales's 'best for my family'), and piety (Guillermo staying with the abandoned elders) — still bind after the state's collapse, while 'do not steal' is merely derived, so the unowned necklace is fair game and Rick could take some but not most of Andrea's food. Aristotle's practical wisdom resolves the cannibal hunters' collision between preserving their lives and not killing innocents — starving is the morally preferable choice — since virtue weighs principles 'all things considered.' Against Carol's 'we can make new rules' relativism the natural law outlives governments, and Father Gabriel errs by calling walkers 'abominations,' conflating bad (dysfunctional) with evil (willful) — whereas the Governor, who knowingly ignores the moral law, reduces himself to walker level.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 24 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Kody Cooper runs Ender's life through classical just war theory: Augustine's axiom that peace is the end of all war explains why even his playground battles aim at a just peace, while the I.F.'s deliberate refusal to protect him from Bonzo's gang throws Ender into the Hobbesian state of nature where each person holds personal authority to use deadly force in self-defense. Sunzi's insistence that a commander must know the enemy grounds Ender's empathic preparation, and Cooper concludes the Third Invasion fails right intention, last resort, discrimination, and proportionality - so the guilt Ender carries is really the I.F.'s and humanity's.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 39 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Michael Stark and A.G. Holdier diagnose the park's collapse as vice rather than accident, using Aquinas's virtue ethics grounded in natural law: Hammond's imprudence (never weighing whether resurrection is right, shrugging off Malcolm's lunch-table warning, still planning 'corrections' over melted ice cream) and Gennaro's intemperance (admissions up to ten thousand dollars a day, 'coupon day', money tunnel-vision), both flowering from pride, the worst vice. Malcolm, despite the flirting and leather, is the only consistently virtuous character: prudence in situational judgment (waving a flare to lure the T. rex away from the kids), temperance about wealth and about Sattler, plus fortitude and justice - even lying to comfort Lex and Tim in the tree reflects character, not rule-breaking. Aquinas's point that virtues are lifelong course corrections, never a finished state, frames the closing Kierkegaard quote about never being finished with life's task.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 12 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Jordan asks what makes Dracula obey his rules (no entry without an invitation, native soil, garlic, the crucifix) when he obeys no morality: self-imposed Kantian moral rules and a vampire-cabal enforcing Hohfeldian duties both fail because the Count's self-interest is too strong, so the rules must be natural law set by God or nature. He then uses Wesley Hohfeld's jural relations (duty, claim, liberty, power, immunity, liability, disability) to analyze Dracula's rule over his brides, servants, and victims - Lucy's lost consent shifting power and letting the Count through her door - concluding that only this legal-relations analysis plus natural law explains both Dracula's restraints and his apparent violations of physics like defying gravity and commanding the weather.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 12 "3. What’s So Bad about Eating People" — McCraw imagines Lecter defending each class of victim with a different ethical theory: the Momund and Dortlich kills through Natural Law Theory plus lex talionis retribution (Dortlich ate Mischa, so he is eaten; Momund treated the aunt as meat, so he is treated as meat), the 'Sorbet' Rolodex dinner-party victims through a perverted Kantianism that swaps politeness for rationality so the rude forfeit humanity and corpses have no moral standing, and Krendler, Raspail, and Chilton through consequentialist accounting of worlds improved by their deaths. He concludes that only virtue ethics resists such distortion: Lecter's cold, callous, manipulative character and his isolated, paranoid, friendless life show that no possessor of good character could eat people, so cannibalism really is bad even when the murders are bracketed.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 30 "13. Carol’s Transformation" — Delfino and Lesinski trace Carol's arc from abused wife (Ed's beatings, Sophia's death, "I didn't think I could be strong") to the judge-jury-executioner she once refused to be, reading the transformation through Aristotle's claim in the Nicomachean Ethics that repeated actions forge moral character. They then evaluate her killings: the murder of Karen and David fails on both act- and rule-utilitarian grounds (it did not stop the flu, and Glenn and Sasha survived while the group was shattered), whereas killing the delusional Lizzie is defensible both utilitarianly and by Aquinas's natural-law exception that an evildoer may be killed for the welfare of the whole community when no public authority remains. Her confession to Tyreese and Tyreese's forgiveness complete the phoenix rebirth symbolized by the burning walkers in "Consumed."
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 29 "17. Sin, My Young Man, Is When You Treat People as Things" — Taking Granny Weatherwax's definition that sin 'is when you treat people as things' and Vetinari's that sin is not saying no to evil, the chapter reads Discworld through C. S. Lewis's argument that a universal Law of Human Nature—felt on the Disc by dwarfs, trolls, and even atheists—points to a divine lawgiver. The enchanted wolf in Witches Abroad, whose agony every witch intuits as wrong and who is granted a merciful death and human funeral, shows that shared moral intuition at work, and grounds the chapter's notes on Pratchett's own campaign for assisted dying. Finally, the Assassins' Guild, which only inhumes the rich who can afford bodyguards under its motto nil mortifi sine lucre, illustrates John Paul II's 'structures of sin': killing sanctified by contract and city law, treating people as things.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 22 "12. The Law of Red Rising" — Christopher Ketcham frames the Society through jurisprudence's debate between natural and positive law, opening with Gramsci's hegemony: Reds have internalized the Golds' message that their slave toil is heroic terraforming service, becoming 'enabled martyrs' who hate rival clans rather than their rulers. He deploys Hobbes's state of nature versus state of laws (Reds live in a state of war against Mars while Golds legislate in a state of law), Locke's suggestion that a sovereign can leave some people in the state of nature, Aquinas-style higher law, and H.L.A. Hart's positivism with Bentham and Austin—a law need not be moral to be law—to argue the Golds' caste statutes are valid yet ungrounded. His coda casts Darrow as Homer Plessy: Goldness, like whiteness in Plessy v. Ferguson, is inheritable property Reds cannot claim, and because Reds who speak are hanged, the law excludes the very voices Hart himself said keep laws from becoming terrible.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 27 "14. The Gods Hate Incest" — Barkman defends the near-universal Westerosi condemnation of incest. Against Freud's Oedipal account - which Jaime and Cersei's childhood romance seems to fit - he deploys Edward Westermarck's aversion hypothesis, primate evidence, and the Taiwanese simpua-marriage studies to argue that co-raised siblings should feel natural sexual aversion, so the twins are either instinctually malformed or unconvincingly written, while cases like Black Walder and Littlefinger with Sansa fit the effect fine. He then grounds the taboo in Natural Law - deduced from 'do no harm,' care of the weak, and natural family roles, plus the harms of inbreeding and endogamy - and concludes that children of incest like Joffrey are abominations by choice, not by birth.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 23 "12. Are We Really Sure They’re Wrong" — Timothy Hsiao argues we cannot condemn the burning of the disabled or Smith's son's mandated euthanasia by appealing to Nazi values, since cultural relativism would make the Resistance the real wrongdoers; the horror we feel presupposes an objective natural law known to reason, the violation of which grounded the Nuremberg trials. From Augustine's 'an unjust law is no law at all,' the chapter then tests the Resistance's armed rebellion against the five just-war conditions — proper authority (the Resistance as agent of the moral law), just cause, reasonable chance of success (the newsreels as grounds for hope), proportionality, and last resort — and finds it justified.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 25 "13. Burn the Witch!" — Argues Coven is a feminist counterpoint to Aquinas's Natural Law - the reason-grounded doctrine of universal human nature historically wielded against 'unnatural' women, from Zoe's vagina-dentata power to Misty burned in the bayou - and, drawing on Augustine's Confessions ('Things that exist are good', so corruptibility implies goodness to lose) and Lady Macbeth's 'unsex me here', shows that women who are both witch and woman break any single natural moral code; Myrtle Snow, who embraces her double nature and goes 'proudly to the flame', proves Natural Law works only as Cupp-style discernment, not as commandments.
- **Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney**, ch. 11 "3. Perry Mason v. Saul Goodman" — Scalambrino compares Mason and Better Call Saul's Saul Goodman, who pull the same shady moves (Perry's evidence switching in 'The Case of the Crimson Kiss' and 'The Case of the Restless Redhead', Saul's fabricated 'pie sitting' videos) yet receive opposite moral verdicts. He frames this through natural law (Aquinas, Kant) versus legal positivism (Hobbes's command theory, Nietzsche's law as power), the audience's 'God's-eye' perspective, and the means/ends distinction, concluding provocatively that Perry's tampering is actually easier to justify from the positivist side, since he gambles on hunches without knowing his client is innocent, while the show's premises (he is already rich and famous, his clients always innocent) make the material conditions of Saul's lawyering moot for him.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 12 "I Control It by Surrendering Control" — Pérez stages the film's natural-law debate through Ayn Rand's Objectivism (Steve Ditko's avowed influence): Mordo's absolutism — 'there is no other way,' 'the bill comes due' — mirrors the axioms of existence, consciousness, and identity (A is A), with Cicero and Aquinas' divinely eternal natural law as the older backdrop. Rand's system is strained by the film's events: Wong dies and is un-died when Strange rolls back time in Hong Kong, and the Eye of Agamotto's time loop creates three simultaneous realities, so 'A' is no longer self-evidently one thing. The chapter concludes that Strange, exercising exactly the Objectivist freedom to think and choose, violates natural law in order to uphold it — sacrificing himself Prometheus- or Sisyphus-like in the Dormammu bargain — while Mordo's departure is wounded pride rather than principle.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 29 "Magic and Deep Magic" — The chapter argues that Strange's universe implicitly contains the Creator God of theism rather than just Marvel's gods: Aristotle's impersonal prime mover will not do because Strange needs a relatable source of an objective moral order, so Aquinas's all-good author of eternal, natural, and divine law supplies the framework. It reads three comics as evidence: Strange defeating Dracula by invoking the Tetragrammaton, the Sise-Neg saga where a sorcerer who attains godhood at the dawn of time learns to recreate the universe exactly as the first cause made it, and the World War Hulk story where summoning Zom shows the hubris of violating the moral order—closing with C.S. Lewis's 'deep magic' as cooperation with the created order versus dark magic's will to control it.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 24 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Kody Cooper argues Ender's tortured conscience demonstrates the classical just war framework: from Augustine's axiom that peace is the end of war and the five jus ad bellum requirements, to the verdict that the Third Invasion fails right intention, last resort, discrimination, and proportionality because the rational hive-queens were never given a real chance at coexistence. He reads the I.F.'s withholding of protection as throwing Ender into a Hobbesian state of nature where his fights with bullies count as private just wars, and concludes Ender carries the sins of the I.F. and humanity rather than his own guilt.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 27 "Notes" — The chapter maps four schools of ethics onto Fallout 4's Commonwealth: Aristotle's virtue ethics reads Preston Garvey's settlement defense as the mean between recklessness and cowardice and temperance as moderate chem use; Kant's Categorical Imperative is tested on stealing ammo in Concord and on the Battle of Bunker Hill choice to warn the Railroad, where loyal silence to Father fails universalization and treats synths merely as means. Aquinas's natural law ethics, keyed to the telos of power armor, workbenches, and Pip-Boys, condemns the Institute's creation of synths by analogy to the IVF debate while still demanding dignity for synths who already exist. Finally, Bentham's utilitarianism is the one framework under which Father's Institute — adaptive labor force, scientific progress, stability and order — can sincerely believe itself morally justified.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 11 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Puts Aquinas's Murder Principle—the private, intentional killing of an innocent is always murder—to the Men of Mayhem, arguing the Sons lack the public authority Aquinas requires to kill even the guilty. The show itself erodes the state/private line Aquinas needs: corrupt agents Kohn and Stahl, and the CIA's Romeo Parada running the Galindo Cartel, make the badge look like no moral credential at all. The Doctrine of Double Effect sorts the rest: Jax shooting first in self-defense, Tara's morphine for the dying Unser, and Juice's hypothetical land-mine sacrifice are merely foreseen deaths, while Jax syringing Clay or Juice's intentional hanging would be murder. The chapter concludes that even if Aquinas condemns the Sons, his questions about authority, innocence, and intention are exactly the ones the show forces on viewers.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 11 "Jedi and Sith Ethics “Similar in Almost Every Way”" — Shea, Archer, and Banning argue that Star Wars' moral framework is natural law ethics in the tradition of Aristotle and Aquinas: the light side humanizes (Force healing, Qui-Gon's spirit surviving death, Grogu curing Greef Karga) while the dark side dehumanizes (Maul's bisection, Palpatine's deformation, Anakin's disfigurement), and apparent counterexamples like Luke's lost hand always trace back to prior vice. Aquinas's claim that the most general principles of natural law can never be blotted out explains why 'there is still good in' Vader and why redemption is always possible. The Jedi and Sith codes embody opposed views of human nature — relational, altruistic, and accepting of mortality versus atomistic, egoistic, and obsessed with cheating death through midi-chlorian manipulation.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 17 "NOTES" — Brace and Arp systematically map the coffin-to-closet analogy: 'God hates fangs' echoes Fred Phelps, Eddie's leap from closeted family man to vampire lover parallels coming out, and vampire media normalization (Fang magazine, teen soaps) mirrors Ellen and Dawson's Creek. They distinguish orientation from action, rebut the natural-law argument that nonprocreative sex is unnatural (it would condemn infertile and contracepting heterosexuals too), and fix the moral line at consent — Bill asking before fang and penis penetrate is healthy, while Lorena's forced turning of Bill and the Rattrays' draining of him, 'objectified and crucified' for his blood, are violations; on that basis they argue vampires deserve equal rights under the VRA.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 31 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Barkman distinguishes the self-evident natural law (general beneficence, special preference for family, piety to parents as Confucius taught, duties to the weak) from derivative rules like 'do not steal' and from positive law, concluding that Andrea's mermaid necklace looting question in 'Guts' is really about whether natural law still binds when the state has collapsed. He argues it does: Andrea's necklace is unowned and free to take, Rick taking surplus food from Andrea would be justified by equal claims to survival, and Carol's 'we can make new rules' polygamy proposal fails because the natural law is prior to any government. The cannibal hunters of Issues #61-66 show what happens without virtue and Aristotle's practical wisdom for weighing conflicting principles, and walkers are bad but not evil, while a Governor-like human who ignores the natural law 'reduces himself to the level of a walker.'
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 23 "Notes" — Barkman and Tokbergenova defend 'just torture': Wonder Woman's lasso interrogations of Captain Nazi, the double agent Marcia in the 1970s pilot (saving the Brooklyn Navy Yard's 70,000 workers), and the terrorist Nikos Aegeus are ticking-bomb cases of the sort Henry Shue concedes, and the authors answer Luban's slippery-slope objection with absolute limits (never the innocent or the family) and Dershowitz-style torture warrants. Citing Aristotle's Rhetoric that coerced testimony is often false, they propose trained professional torturers, and conclude that since the right thing is not always the ideal thing, torture should be legalized, rare, and conducted openly - as Wonder Woman models.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Flynn contends certain Westerns depict a 'law that stands behind the law' — a moral/natural law transcending and grounding the weak civil order — using High Noon, where Hadleyville proves unworthy of Kane's rectitude. High Plains Drifter evolves this into divine, supernatural retribution: the nameless Stranger, a pale-horse agent of apocalyptic justice, precisely punishes Lago for abetting the marshal Duncan's murder (whipping the whippers, renaming the town Hell). Flynn argues this vision is dangerous: by insulating justice from deliberation and depicting it as revelatory and divine, it derides the discursive, civil processes (Habermas-style communicative action) actually needed to make justice 'ours,' risking mere private vengeance — 'deserve's got nothin' to do with it.'
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 15 "What Is Wrong with Cloning a Dinosaur Jurassic Park and Nature as a Source of Moral Authority" — Spence uses the Hammond-Malcolm debate in Jurassic Park to ask whether nature can ground moral authority. He distinguishes prudential risk arguments (Grant, Sattler) from Malcolm's distinctly moral charge that cloning dinosaurs is 'anti-nature,' then deploys Hume's is/ought problem and Hume's essay 'On Suicide' to argue there is no principled natural/unnatural line and no valid inference from natural facts to moral oughts. Examining natural-law theory (Aquinas, Cicero, 'perverted faculty' arguments), he concludes tampering with nature may be unwise but is not inherently immoral.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 18 "Human Rights, Human Nature, and Amistad" — Baggett and Foreman use Amistad to reconstruct Locke's theory of natural rights: Cinque's mutiny and John Quincy Adams's Supreme Court plea that man's natural state is freedom illustrate Locke's claim that God's workmanship makes us his property and therefore un-ownable by other men. They contrast Locke's voluntarist natural law with Aquinas's, note Adams rebutting the Hobbesian 'war of all against all' quoted in the pro-slavery Executive Review, and invoke Mill's perfect/imperfect duty distinction (Baldwin's obligation to his clients) plus Bentham's rights-denying utilitarianism, which they map onto Calhoun's warning about the cost of abolition.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 16 "They May Not Be Human, but Could Daleks Be People Too" — Bonnie Green and Chris Willmott use the Daleks' human-factor experiments ("The Evil of the Daleks," "Dalek," "Daleks in Manhattan") to lay out the philosophy-of-biology "species problem": are species natural kinds, individuals, or sets? They trace essentialism from an Aristotelian God-given essence through Darwin's overthrow of it to modern genetic essentialism (the humanizing Dalek DNA), then use the Dalek/Thal split to survey biological species concepts and monism versus pluralism. They close with personhood and Peter Singer's speciesism, asking whether human-Dalek Sec would deserve rights.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 26 "24. Game of Thrones as Philosophy Cynical Realpolitiks" — The chapter argues that Game of Thrones advances a thoroughgoing cynicism about political legitimacy, captured by Varys's riddle that 'power resides where men believe it resides.' It documents the dubious claims of Robert 'the Usurper' and the pyromaniacal Daenerys, the barbaric Lockean 'state of nature' among the Wildlings, and the false ideals of chivalry and religion, with Littlefinger and Varys voicing Machiavellian realpolitik. Silverman and Riordan then offer two views the show never considers: Locke's social-contract theory of natural rights (which would justify deposing Aerys or Daenerys) and Aquinas's four-part test for genuine law (reason, common good, proper authority, promulgation), arguing a legitimate state remains possible against the show's cynicism.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 35 "32. Okja as Philosophy Why Animals Matter" — Jensen frames Okja around three views of the super-pig Okja's moral status: Mirando treats her as mere property, the Animal Liberation Front as a symbol to be sacrificed for the cause, and the girl Mija as a friend and person. He dismantles Mirando's 'human exceptionalism'—amoralism, Aquinas's natural-law teleology, the Kantian persons-only view, and Descartes' claim that animals are unfeeling automata—then develops the ALF's liberation through Singer's equal consideration of interests, Bentham's 'can they suffer?', and speciesism as prejudice, weighing consequentialist (utilitarian) against deontological (rights, Regan) foundations. He closes with hierarchical moral status and Bernard Williams's 'one thought too many,' arguing Mija's love for Okja shows that at some point relationship matters more than moral calculation.

### Practical Wisdom (phronesis)

Phronesis, usually rendered as practical wisdom or prudence, is for Aristotle the intellectual virtue that governs good action in particular circumstances. Unlike theoretical knowledge, which concerns unchanging truths, practical wisdom is the capacity to perceive what the situation requires and to deliberate well about how to achieve worthwhile ends. In the Nicomachean Ethics it is the master virtue of conduct, since without it the moral virtues lack direction, and it cannot be reduced to rules but is acquired through experience and habituation.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 24 "Elaine, Kramer, and Newman Not Wise" — Aeon Skoble argues Seinfeld explicates Aristotelian virtue ethics against utilitarian and Kantian rivals: Jerry's 'I don't want to be an orgy guy' and George's fear of becoming 'one of those guys' ask what sort of person to be, not which rule to follow. George's 'do the opposite' in 'The Opposite' is an update of the Delphic oracle - only he who recognizes his own idiocy (Socratic ignorance) can act well, with Jerry deducing the logic and serving as his phronemos, alongside Superman. Elaine's rule-worship and Jujyfruits utilitarianism backfire, Kramer lacks the social dialectic virtue needs, and the ironic appeals to Newman as arbiter expose the paradox that choosing a role model wisely already requires the wisdom one lacks.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 22 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Aeon Skoble uses Tolkien's characters to defend Aristotelian virtue ethics against Kantian and utilitarian rivals. Sam's loyalty is a virtue because critically directed at a worthy friend while Wormtongue's loyalty to Saruman is not; Sméagol's instant murder of Déagol reveals prior vice that let the Ring corrupt him quickly, whereas Bilbo resists it for sixty years; Aragorn's temperance and teachableness contrast Boromir's resentment and pride. Working through Aristotle's doctrine of the mean (courage between cowardice and rashness), practical wisdom, and the phronemos as role model, he argues that rule-following cannot capture moral perception (do we owe truth to Black Riders?) and that utilitarianism absurdly requires Galadriel's foresight.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 31 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Jonathan Sanford distinguishes necessity of the end, of compulsion, and of nature to argue Christ's passion was both necessary and free: justice requires reparation for the harmony Adam and Eve broke, God cannot simply waive it without making a mockery of sin, yet no compulsion operates on Christ — unlike the blind inner drives Nietzsche's will to power or Schopenhauer's will would represent. Using Aristotle, he argues Christ's fully virtuous character (practical wisdom plus courage and temperance become a 'second nature') makes disobedience nearly unimaginable, and his divinity makes it impossible, so his choice 'could not have been different' precisely because it was perfectly free; the Gethsemane agony shows not division in the God-man but the difficulty of holding his human and divine wills in unity.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 36 "Daredevil’s Faith as a Source of Strength" — Testing whether Daredevil's fearlessness is really the vice of rashness, Morris invokes Aristotle's doctrine that every virtue is a mean between two vices, with courage between cowardice and foolhardiness - but since fear is not the only brake on recklessness, prudence can do that work instead, as when Matt calmly backs down from Iron Man's federal authority in Born Again. He concludes that the religious values Matt absorbed - love of neighbor, respect for truth, concern for justice - supply exactly the guidance prudence needs, making faith a distinct form of spiritual strength.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 7 "Foreword" — Cornel West argues that Plato's dialogues invented philosophy as a Socratic genre of cross-examination and bold frank speech (parrhesia) about ordinary life, and that hip-hop music - like the spirituals, blues, and jazz - enacts that same parrhesia against conventional morality and entrenched power. He claims reading hip hop philosophically demands metaphilosophical subtlety, showing how paideia, phronesis, and parrhesia operate in the work of cultural producers under free-market fundamentalism and authoritarianism. Because the racial dimension of hip hop is inescapable, he says philosophers must break their discipline's silence on race and music (neglected figures like Du Bois and Alain Locke alongside Aristotle, Kant, and Rorty), closing with Cicero's Socrates who turned philosophy from the heavens to earth and William James's pragmatism that took it from the academy to the streets.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 13 "Poker and Philosophy" — Young reads David Sklansky's fundamental theorem of poker — play as if you could see all the cards — through Aristotle and Husserl. Aristotle's phronesis and virtue-as-habituation explain how excellent players come to perceive the particulars (pot odds, opponent tendencies, the best possible hand) and stay unharmed even when losing with the best play, while Husserl's Cartesian Meditations, translated hand-by-hand into poker terms, supply analogical appresentation for knowing the other minds seated across the table. Chris Moneymaker's 2003 'Bluff of the Century' all-in with nothing against Sammy Farha shows how bluffing randomizes play and lets you shape the truth you seek, until a slow-played quad aces ends the night in Socratic humility about the limits of knowledge.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 14 "“Hey, Let’s Get the Stuff We Need!” Putting the Mall in Its Place" — Matthew Walker reads Dawn of the Dead through Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and Politics: the survivors' mall orgy curdles into boredom ('What have we done to ourselves?'), illustrating pleonexia, the graspingness for more than one's share of the goods of fortune that Aristotle roots in an unlimited desire for mere living - which may even explain why Romero's dead return, grasping from beyond the grave for more un-death. Aristotle's dismissal of the life of enjoyment as fit for cattle, his account of eudaimonia as the life in which our rational capacities flourish, and his defense of acquisition bounded by the good life explain why unlimited consumption zombifies the living, and why Peter and Fran must finally leave the mall empty-handed.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 19 "Cold Clammy Consistency" — Wayne Yuen argues vampires are moral agents - rational by Aristotle's standard of practical wisdom (Lestat's investments and his judgments about evildoers tasting better) and free despite their blood-craving, since craving is a strong preference, not the compulsion of the heroin addict or the castaway drinking seawater. Since animal blood is a viable alternative (Louis's rats, Angel and Spike's butcher's blood), the justifications for drinking human blood - taste, reaching full potential, spiritual peace - all fail against the principle that a world with less unnecessary suffering is better. Then the consistency argument turns on us: factory-farmed meat inflicts unnecessary suffering for the sake of taste while vegetarianism is fully viable, so condemning vampires while eating chicken is inconsistent - we as human beings are vampiric.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 18 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Taliaferro and Le Gall rebut Paul Johnson's 1958 charge that Doctor No combines 'the sadism of a schoolboy bully', adolescent sex longings, and suburban snobbery. They show Bond kills for justice rather than spite (his reluctant assignment against von Hammerstein in 'For Your Eyes Only'), that Colonel Sun repudiates de Sadean torture before dying, and that the disturbing 'semi-rape' passage of The Spy Who Loved Me reflects Vivienne Michel's voice, not Bond's conduct. They read Bond's eros as an ironic use of the medieval courtly-love and Mariology tradition in which sex redeems 'lost women' like Pussy Galore, defend his dress and manners through the ancient heroic tradition (Theseus's fatal neglect of the white sails, Leonidas combing his beard at Thermopylae), and conclude Bond is a chivalric, comic hero - a 'delightful impossibility' in Aristotle's Poetics' sense who embodies Socratic soldierly virtue and Platonic optimism.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 27 "Lessons Learned" — McAleer maps The Office onto Aristotle's ethics: David Brent is the buffoon who is 'the slave of his sense of humor,' Gareth the literalist boor who cannot take a joke, and Tim the ready wit whose irony responds to the situation — together illustrating that a virtue is a qualitative mean of acting and feeling appropriately, fixed by practical wisdom rather than rules. That humor cannot be codified mirrors the uncodifiability of Aristotelian ethics, and wit's very status as a virtue shows Aristotle's morality is broader than modern duty-and-outcome ethics: it aims at the flourishing (eudaimonia) of the whole person.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 9 "Dorothy Growing Up in the Land of Oz" — McCall and Auxier use Aristotle's virtue ethics to unpack the Wizard's claim to be 'a good man but a bad wizard' and to argue that no external token—the diploma, heart watch, or medal—can confer virtue, which is cultivated only through practice and experience. Each companion lacks something specific: the Scarecrow the intellectual virtues and phronesis, the Tin Man the feelings and stable states of character that regulate emotion, the Lion the sophrosyne that balances thinking and feeling into courage as the mean between recklessness and cowardice. Aristotle's three grades of friendship (utility, pleasure, virtue) frame the companions' bond with Dorothy, and MacIntyre's account of virtues internal to practices explains why the Wizard's public recognition still matters. Dorothy herself begins as the child Aristotle says cannot yet be virtuous—fleeing Miss Gulch in Kansas—but by defending Toto against the Lion and leading the quest she grows into a responsible moral agent, which is what her delayed homecoming requires.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 29 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Plauche grounds Optimus Prime's line 'Freedom is the right of all sentient beings' in 'Aristotelian liberalism': since Energon, like our food, is scarce and requires labor and creativity, any volitional artificial life needs a moral code whose standard is flourishing (following Foot's natural goodness), cultivating intellectual and moral virtues from prudence, independence, and honesty to benevolence and courage. Ricardo and Mises's law of association - illustrated by Ratchet and a human mechanic both profiting from specialization despite Ratchet's absolute superiority - plus the ruinous cost of war give even superior aliens reason to respect our rights to life, liberty, and property rather than enslave or exterminate us, as Megatron would.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 33 "Tie Goes to the Runner" — St. Martin runs the Fenway 'pink hat' controversy through Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: the virtuous fan is the mean between the deficient bandwagoner who waves at NESN cameras mid-pitch and the excessive diehard who memorizes Dice-K's ERA to belittle others. Terry Francona's courage in sending Dave Roberts in the 2004 ALCS (versus a reckless Ortiz steal attempt) illustrates virtue as the mean between cowardice and foolhardiness, and Aristotle's contrast between the love of honor and the love of contemplation shows both pink hatters and stats-obsessed diehards err by making fandom about themselves. She concludes that accepting fans in any color hat is the truly virtuous mean.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 19 "Cold Clammy Consistency" — Wayne Yuen argues vampires are moral agents because they meet Aristotle's test of practical wisdom (Lestat's investments and his judgment that 'evildoers... taste better') and retain free will, since their blood-lust is a craving not a compulsion and Louis's rat diet in Interview with the Vampire, like Angel's in Buffy, proves an alternative exists. TASTE, full potential, and spiritual peace all fail to justify human blood, because killing a person brings more unnecessary suffering than killing a rat, the same suffering-based principle that condemns factory farming. The 'cold clammy consistency' punchline: since humans need not eat meat, condemning vampire blood-drinkers while dining on chicken, pork, and beef is hypocrisy, because we are vampiric too and only our choice of which life to ingest separates the monstrous from the virtuous.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 29 "The Final Whistle" — Andrew Lambert defends the rationality of being a football fan by updating Aristotle: living well in a liberal consumer democracy demands an accessible source of beauty, catharsis, belonging, public discourse, and altruism, and fandom trains exactly these sensibilities — from his childhood prayers for Everton to the 1914 Christmas Truce match and supporters' trusts that own clubs like Exeter City. The mature 'fan of football' takes an ironic view of the 'loyal fan's' tribal passions, gaining the practical wisdom that keeps rivalry (the Liverpool–Everton derby, the 1969 'Football War') from curdling into violence. Fandom thus answers critics who dismiss it as consumerist escapism or bad faith.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 25 "Jousting for Virtue" — Farrell argues that the medieval code of chivalry is a living case study for Aristotle's virtue ethics: Lancelot, 'mekest in hall and sternest to his foe', embodies the paradox C.S. Lewis names as meek and fierce 'to the nth', which Farrell reads as Aristotle's courage, the golden mean between cowardice and rashness, exercised 'to the right extent, at the right time, with the right motive'. The joust, meanwhile, was a proving ground where knightly virtues became second nature through habituated practice, since as Aristotle says 'it is no easy task to be good'. Western martial arts, he concludes, are 'moral kung fu': a fencing match with one's own standards of virtue.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 22 "World Death Rate Holding Steady At 100 Percent" — Dan Miori, a palliative-care physician assistant, uses Onion medical stories — 'Loved Ones Recall Local Man's Cowardly Battle With Cancer,' the 'Vehicular Manslaughter Doctor,' animal hoarder Tricia McCory's 'I'm A Diseased And Deformed Animal Lover,' and the Terry Schiavo American Voices — to survey how end-of-life decisions actually get made. He runs each dilemma through Mill's consequentialism, Kant's deontology, and Aristotle's virtue ethics (with Monty Python's Philosopher's Song as running gag), then through Beauchamp and Childress's four principles of medical ethics, showing that McCory's kindness to dying animals fails autonomy and nonmaleficence because kindness can be cruel. The chapter closes by restoring 'euthanasia' to its Greek meaning of 'good death,' arguing that accepting the 100 percent death rate means planning ahead with living wills and honest bad-news delivery rather than dying tube-filled in an ICU.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 7 "The End of the Story" — Reads the Gom Jabbar test as Herbert's definition of humanity: Paul endures Mohiam's pain box because a human stays in the trap to turn it on the trapper and protect the species, while an animal only chews off its own leg. The Butlerian Jihad's ban on 'a machine in the likeness of a man's mind' is applied to our own iPod-and-PDA dependence, with Mentat Thufir Hawat showing that losing the machine-crutch 'forced human minds to develop,' in line with Aristotle's phronesis and the politics of the common good (and Plato's contemplation as the core of happiness). The chapter closes by turning the human/animal test on the modern West—Baron Harkonnen-like consumers whose water-hungry beef habit makes us the trap of our own environmental collapse.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 16 "The Spice of Meaning" — Mines Dune for an account of the meaningful life by contrasting the Harkonnens, who amass power for its own sake and grind Yueh's very identity to dust, with the Fremen, whose rigid rituals give meaning but suffocate anyone who lives entirely inside them—with Duke Leto's abolition of the beggars' water-towel custom as the failure case in between. Following Aristotle's method of starting from 'the views of the wise,' the chapter argues virtue is an open-ended, formulaless skill: rising above inherited identities while repairing the social bonds they sustain, as Paul and Jessica do by breaking selected Fremen rules and leaving the sietch stronger. The worm-rider, feet shifting on sand above a creature that can never be fully controlled, is the closing image of a struggle that never finally resolves.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 20 "Yours Is Superior, therefore I Concede to You" — Adam Barkman evaluates King Neptune's kingship through Dante's De Monarchia: kingship is God-ordained, justice means treating each being according to its nature, and a true king is a servant-leader who must possess the four cardinal virtues and three theological ones. Neptune ('I'm the king. That's what I do', before executing a crown polisher and smiting at every problem) has courage but lacks prudence and temperance; Triton has prudence without courage; and levelheaded Mindy would be the best ruler, though Dante's tradition would disqualify her because she is female. The chapter concludes neither Neptune nor Triton has enough virtue or political knowledge to be a good king, and reform rather than deposition is the Dantean answer.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 60 "A Rolling Stone Gathers . . . Happiness" — Brings in Epicurus, speaking through Cicero, to correct the Cyrenaics: pursue pleasure rationally, declining pleasures that purchase greater later pains—Keith's drug-related legal bills, 'Sister Morphine's' desperation—and sometimes enduring pain for greater pleasure later, like kicking junk to enjoy raising children. Advocating simple living, a hierarchy of pleasures ranked by sober reasoning, and prudence (phronesis) as the chief virtue, it pictures modern Epicureans at a rock festival passing out condoms and running the needle exchange.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 15 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Jonas-Sebastien Beaudry reads Neverwhere's magic invisibility as a model of real social invisibility: after Richard helps the injured Door he loses his job, his fiancee Jessica, and even the ability to be perceived, joining the homeless, slaves, and Jews under Nazism as people excluded from the moral community whose needs no longer register. Using Arendt's banality of evil to explain everyday indifference and Richard Rorty on torturers who fail to see a 'real' human, he distinguishes radical from partial invisibility, shown in Jessica stepping over the bleeding Door and misreading her need as 'sleep it off.' The remedy is Iris Murdoch's 'loving gaze' of just and careful attention, which seizes Richard before he can rationalize, backed by a practical wisdom about whose needs matter, so that acknowledging the invisible, down to apologizing to a rat in London Below, is what makes both them and us better.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 31 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Barkman takes Andrea's mermaid-necklace question ('I don't think those rules apply any more') as a test of natural law: self-evident principles — general beneficence (Glenn's 'shit creek' rescue, Morgan's warning that it 'takes away a piece of your soul'), special beneficence toward family (Lori's 'Don't be so trusting,' Morales's 'best for my family'), and piety (Guillermo staying with the abandoned elders) — still bind after the state's collapse, while 'do not steal' is merely derived, so the unowned necklace is fair game and Rick could take some but not most of Andrea's food. Aristotle's practical wisdom resolves the cannibal hunters' collision between preserving their lives and not killing innocents — starving is the morally preferable choice — since virtue weighs principles 'all things considered.' Against Carol's 'we can make new rules' relativism the natural law outlives governments, and Father Gabriel errs by calling walkers 'abominations,' conflating bad (dysfunctional) with evil (willful) — whereas the Governor, who knowingly ignores the moral law, reduces himself to walker level.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 10 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Merli argues that good role-playing refutes Aristotelian virtue ethics: decent players convincingly play genuinely evil thieves and morally mediocre players play truly virtuous paladins, so the skill of judging what the virtuous agent would do cannot require being virtuous or having the habituated emotions McDowell, Hursthouse, and Jacobson say are necessary to 'see what to do'. Using a dice-guessing versus unverifiable aura-reading analogy, he shows that the virtue ethicist's escape—denying non-virtuous players can get it right—makes virtuous judgment look fraudulent and untestable. Because role-playing demands active first-person deliberation rather than the passive reception of literary fiction, it exposes that judging rightly and being virtuous are distinct skills, with implications for how habituation and moral education work.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 16 "The Wire and Philosophy" — McAleer ranks three Season-long deceptions - Sobotka's smuggling least wrong, McNulty's fake serial killer worse, Templeton's fabricated Sun stories worst - and argues that only the agents' motives and character explain the degrees of wrongness, against Mill's claim that motive has nothing to do with an action's morality and Kant's distinction between acting in accordance with and from duty. Aristotle's virtue ethics and his difference between practical wisdom and mere cleverness vindicate these verdicts: Sobotka lies to save a dying union, McNulty's cleverness is corrupted by his need to be the smartest boy in the room while Lester's additions lack all wisdom, and Templeton lies from naked careerism with no redemption arc. The chapter closes with the 'Haynes Principle' - 'you need a lot of context to seriously examine anything' - as the case for a messier, character-based moral philosophy.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 17 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Grinnell reads Rawls's dotted case lists, Marimow's rip-and-run, Burrell's 'dope on the table,' and Prez being told he teaches the test rather than math as Aristotle's function argument gone wrong: professionals who reduce their purpose to stats and pleasing bosses are 'doing well' instead of 'doing good,' which is just what Plato says badly governed cities reward with honor. The characters who grasp their real function - Daniels refusing cheap felony stats, Bunk refusing to turn cases black without the true murderer, Freamon hunting bodies in vacants despite Landsman's fury - defy the Game at career cost, while Colvin's Hamsterdam and McNulty's fake killer show the opposite failure of zealous judgment without humility or rule of law. The chapter ends on the paradox that trusting professional judgment risks messes, but defining professions by numbers eliminates excellence altogether.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 34 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Re-examining 'The Enchiridion!' trial by trial - the gnome illusions, the ogre whose dollar Finn steals and then returns, the dark mage's brain world, the wallop given the Key-per in devil pajamas - the chapter argues Finn wins the hero's handbook without being righteous: he is brave, tender and ingenious, but gullible, hasty and violent, slaying whatever he is told is evil and running from the gnome test. Epictetus's Stoic Enchiridion supplies the standard the show's book lacks: only virtue matters, wealth, fame and comfort are indifferents, and a real handbook teaches how to lose, age and admit mistakes, not just how to win, which is exactly what Billy's quit-heroism shows Ooo's greatest hero never learned. Because bravery without good judgment could as easily serve a Nazi, a terrorist or the Lich, Finn's lack of practical wisdom means the 'most righteous hero' in Ooo is an impetuous boy - proof of how morally broken the Land of Ooo is.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 37 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — The chapter argues Finn is not yet a true hero but is on a quest to become one: against rule systems like Mill's greatest-happiness utilitarianism and Kantian respect for persons, virtue ethics asks not 'what should I do' but 'who should I be', and Aristotle's point that children lack fully developed practical reason explains why Finn's good intentions misfire - removing Donny exposes the house people to Why-wolves, and Penny's trick humiliates him in the City of Thieves. Martha Nussbaum's ideal of every person as free and of equal dignity grounds heroism in the common good, and her work on literature and popular culture explains how watching Finn's exaggerated choices trains our own moral judgment. Citing Franco and Zimbardo's psychology of real heroes - empathy, risk tolerance, persistence - and closing with Seneca's 'how nobly you live', it concludes that since Aristotelian virtue is a habit, anyone can start by admitting they suck at heroism and practicing, as Jake's advice puts it.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 38 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Reading Finn's first season as a three-stage hero's journey - winning the Enchiridion on Mount Cragdor, being tested in 'Business Time', 'City of Thieves', 'Ocean of Fear' and 'Henchman', then doubly confirmed when Billy recognizes him - the chapter extracts a working handbook of heroism from his stumbles. Its lessons: heroism needs reason as much as courage (thinking through the gnome 'illusions', knocking himself unconscious to beat the Fear Feaster), plain luck plays a real and uneven part in saving Jake from the ogre, retribution should be temporary (the ogre's returned dollar), and heroes must check their sources (Penny's con). The deepest tension is that justice and compassion, instinct and reason, violence and non-violence must be perpetually balanced - Billy's nonviolent way becomes its own injustice when Finn medicates villagers without consent - so a real hero is simply someone who never stops trying to hold the balance.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 24 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Meyer reads Jobs through 'individualistic perfectionism'—the Aristotelian tradition (via Rasmussen and Den Uyl, and Veatch) on which flourishing is objective to human nature yet agent-relative, an endless striving unique to each person's talents rather than Kant's by-the-book categorical imperative applied impersonally to all. Jobs embodied this: the 'bicycle of the mind' faith that reason and tools extend human efficiency, practical wisdom weighing goods like friendship, health, and art through Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, experimental self-discovery (Zen, calligraphy, fruitarian diets), and the exile-to-NeXT-to-Pixar-to-iMac arc of constant re-evaluation—so the right question is not whether Jobs 'was' a moral perfectionist but whether each of us keeps striving in our own key.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 18 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Adam Henschke argues that Frank Reynolds, of all people, is a role model - not a virtuous man overall, but virtuous in one structural sense. Using Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, each Gang member's project is diagnosed as the vice of excessive self-delusion: Charlie's Waitress obsession he cannot see through even at her musical rejection, Dee's acting stardom she will not work for and that ends in suicide-adjacent despair, Mac's muscle-bound self-image despite 'diabitis', and Dennis's Golden God delusion culminating in 'the implication' and his car stash of 'fetish shit'. Rickety Cricket embodies the opposite vice, total loss of the capacity to imagine oneself otherwise (via Catriona Mackenzie's relational autonomy), and Frank charts the Aristotelian mean between the two - he rejected his delusive country-club life, knows exactly what he chose with Roxy, and his plans succeed where the Gang's fail - making 'What would Frank do?' a genuine exercise of practical wisdom.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 27 "14. Re Production" — Framed as leaked Project memoranda, the chapter argues Projects Leda and Castor embody philosophy's male-rational/female-reproductive dichotomy: Aristotle's function argument defined the human good (eudaimonia) through rationality while relegating women to reproduction, and the clones' engineered diseases literalize the split — fatal illness of the reproductive organs in the Leda clones, of the brain in the Castor. Simone de Beauvoir's Second Sex supplies the critique: "woman" treated as synonymous with womb, the Other denied the rich self-definition granted men, visible in Leda's passive unmonitored clones versus Castor's self-aware, active brothers. Combining a redeemed Aristotle (practical wisdom shows virtuous potential is not set by biological sex) with Beauvoir's free, independent woman, the chapter concludes both reproductive and rational autonomy must be restored to the clones of both sexes.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 20 "10. Virtue Rising" — Darci Doll argues the Rising exposes the Society's intellectual oppression—each Color denied education and fed 'noble lies' about its role—and that lifting it sparks an 'Intellectual Reformation' proving Color does not dictate potential: Darrow out-performing Golds, Orion the un-carved Blue, Ragnar and Sefi exceeding their station. She uses Plato's Republic (producers, auxiliaries, guardians, the lower orders kept obedient by Noble Lies like the Reds' terraforming myth) as the Society's blueprint, then turns to Aristotle: potential is realized only through the right environment, instruction, and habituated character, and Darrow's practical wisdom—testing himself, reassessing after Titus and Cassius, doing what makes him his best self—lets him flourish and lead. Aristotle's critique of utility-only relations explains why the Society's alliances expire (Antonia executed once useless) while Darrow and Mustang's virtue friendships and just rule endure, opening a society where everyone, including women and lowColors denied opportunity rather than ability, can maximize potential.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 46 "30. Trying to Do Good with Arya, Tyrion, and the Hound" — Thomas sets Aristotle's practical wisdom against Bentham's utility calculus and Kant's consequence-proof rules, then watches all three struggle in season six. Arya's merciful refusal to poison Lady Crane backfires when the Waif kills her more painfully anyway; Tyrion's compromise with the Masters - phasing out slavery gradually, 'I trust their self-interest' - nearly loses Meereen when they attack by sea; and the resurrected Hound, after Brother Ray's massacre, concludes that 'lots of horrible shit in this world gets done for something larger than ourselves,' so being good in Westeros, as everywhere, means choosing without being able to know the consequences in advance.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 30 "15. Reset Virtues" — Doll argues Elliot approximates Aristotelian virtue despite his vices: he craves eudaimonia, uses practical wisdom to recognize the harm the 5/9 hack caused innocent people ('I'll own it all'), and habituates himself against vice by confessing, exposing Ray's website, and restraining Mr. Robot even at the cost of Adderall binges and prison. Leon's 'existence could be beautiful, or it could be ugly, but that's on you' frames the choice of a life to fight for, and Krista's counsel leads Elliot to the golden mean of a 'handshake' with Mr. Robot - integrating the two identities rather than annihilating one - while the viewer serves as the if/then programming keeping him virtuous.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 14 "5. Why the Good Man Is a Great Leader" — Nisley reads Civil War through Aristotle's good man and good leader: Cap shows courage but lacks temperance and practical wisdom - his rash Lagos operation, his rage-borne beating of Tony, his choice of Bucky over the Avengers' common end - and his ceaseless struggle between passion and reason falls short of virtue. Applying Aristotle's account of philia, she argues the Avengers are a friendship of the virtuous that requires deliberation toward justice, which Cap dissolves by tearing the team apart, while Tony's reasoned acceptance of UN oversight, moderation after Ultron, and concern for the whole team make him the good man fit to lead.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 36 "21. A Response to Professor Pieixoto" — Doll writes a fictional keynote by 'Professor Anadicrad' answering Pieixoto's 'our job is not to censure but to understand': the fact that we view the past through an anachronistic lens does not forbid normative judgment, since Aristotle's practical wisdom—honed by hindsight, aiming at the golden mean and eudaimonia—gives historians a standard for judging whether a society cultivated virtue or vice. Gilead fails that standard spectacularly: it banned the reading that shapes values, reduced women to reproductive function, and required heteronormative forced procreation, blocking the relationships and habits flourishing needs. Beauvoir corrects even Aristotle's own biology-based view of women, and the chapter closes that a purely descriptive history would doom us to repeat Gilead's atrocities.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 8 "On Philosophers and Drag Queens" — The editors' introduction argues that Drag Race is an unexplored philosophical playground because it builds on marginalized black and Latinx queer herstory and because RuPaul, whose creed of love and self-improvement makes her a philosopher in her own right, has made the show her magnum opus. It invokes Plato's cave to explain why philosophers crave the 'untucked' version of everything RuPaul shows on stage. Its central move is a virtue-ethics reading of the show's judging: Ru's demand that a queen first be fierce, and through fierceness achieve charisma, uniqueness, nerve and talent, mirrors Aristotle's question of what makes a good person, with fierceness playing the role phronesis plays in securing the other virtues. Comparing queens like Silky Nutmeg Ganache, Jinkx Monsoon, Yara Sofia and Sharon Needles, it poses 'what makes a good drag queen?' as a live philosophical problem.
- **Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney**, ch. 22 "12. What about Della Street" — Birondo evaluates Della Street through moral psychology and Aristotelian virtue ethics: she is an excellent secretary in the role-specific sense (the Gregg shorthand that traps Robert Caddo's contradiction outside The Lonely Heiress crime scene) and supplies the 'woman's angle' the office needs, while Perry displays Aristotle's practical wisdom in court but a failure of recognition toward her, under-crediting her and kissing her for her 'feminine charms' upon her skullduggery in ways that today would be sexual harassment. The chapter also applies Aristotle on habituation through Mrs. Caddo's 'wildcat' tantrums hardening into character, and asks whether Della's team-playing beyond her duties is admirable, sad, or itself the product of mid-century sexism.
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 10 "Olympic Tetherball A Final Lesson on Moral Frailty" — The chapter asks whether Kenneth the page is a Kantian rule absolutist who never makes exceptions, or an Aristotelian 'contextual absolutist' who sees that the right act depends on circumstances, as when he runs the Hill Witch ruse to scare Tracy into eating well. Jack's lifeboat hypothetical and rigged-elevator test bounce off Kenneth's refusal to believe in hypothetical situations, but Jack's gift of illegal cable exposes Kenneth's moral frailty when he enjoys the stolen channels. It concludes that Kenneth's gullibility, trust, and loyalty make his simple moral vision both admirable and easily corrupted, and that the real lesson is facing our failures with resolve rather than shame.
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 13 "“Well, It Got Big Laughs”" — Barkman uses Confucius (ren, yi, li, and zheng ming, treating each person according to what he or she is) and Aristotle (eudaimonia, virtue as a habituated mean between extremes, practical wisdom) to indict 30 Rock for valorizing Jack's 'semi-virtuous path', the smug middle between best and worst announced in 'Do-Over'. He catalogues injustices the show laughs off: Liz's serial lies about her age, hobbies, and adoption; Jack's priority flu shots for the powerful in 'Flu Shot'; Tracy's insubordination about dogfighting in 'Rosemary's Baby'; and Kenneth's servility as everyone's punching bag. On liberality and piety, Jack's confession that 'capitalism is my religion' and Liz's 'I pretty well do whatever Oprah tells me' show the show settling for semi-virtue, which the chapter says even comedy must not endorse.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 15 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — The Bocks test three answers to the good life against the show: Howard as hedonist (laser-obstacle-strip-chess, the 'whore of Omaha') read through Bentham, Mill's higher and lower pleasures, and Aristippus; ethical egoism via Glaucon's ring of Gyges and Howard's offer to Skype rather than visit the deported Raj; and Hobbes's state of nature and social contract read into Sheldon's roommate agreement, whose lack of a Hobbesian sovereign leaves 'I settle all ties' arbitrary and rule-following too thin for ethics. Aristotle's virtue and practical wisdom crown Leonard — the nucleus of the social group, as Amy says — as the closest thing to the phronimos. The gang's sabotage of Dennis Kim with a manufactured girlfriend closes the chapter by asking who really ruined whose life.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 9 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Zeccardi and Ma deconstruct the film's hierarchical dichotomy between Walter's rule-obsessed ethical generalism (Shabbas rules, 'MARK IT ZERO!') and the nihilists' particularist 'Zere ARE no ROOLZ', using Derrida and Culler's method of undermining the opposition the text privileges. Each extreme fails: Walter's principles collide in the beeper dilemma, and active Nietzschean nihilism makes the nihilists unpredictable cowards. The Dude emerges as an Aristotelian agent of virtue whose phronesis perceptively weighs contextual facts (Smokey's disputed toe, the carpet-pissers' false assumption) against principles, making 'What would the Dude do?' a question about character rather than rules.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 31 "Learning from Mia’s Mistakes" — The chapter grades each of Mia's escalations in Crocodile — helping Rob hide the cyclist's body, killing Rob fifteen years later, then killing Shazia, her husband, and baby Ali to keep the secret — under Kant's categorical imperative (the cover-up cannot be universalized and treats persons as means), the utilitarian calculus (which also condemns every killing once the widow's suffering and Mia's guilt are counted), and feminist care ethics, which rejects her defense that she killed to protect her family because care obligations never cancel proportionality and others' rights. Aristotle's virtue ethics supplies the diagnosis: Mia's undoing is lack of practical wisdom — every split-second choice (which she never had time to deliberate) went wrong because she lacked virtuous habits. The chapter urges practicing everyday virtue so we never take the first step down her path.
