Following Aristotle against Plato that poetic skill is a teachable craft, plus psychology of jazz-improvisation studies, flow states, and Zhuangzi's butcher Cook Ding, she argues creativity is the joyful mastery of a process, so following instructions is the etude-stage that builds the database of moves from which free creation grows.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 26 "Paradise Found" — Paul Brown maps The Minish Cap's Hyrule onto utopian theory: Plato's Republic classes reappear as royal family (guardians), castle guards (auxiliaries), and market traders (producers), but Hyrule improves on Plato with no slavery, fluid social boundaries (Princess Zelda wandering the festival unrecognized), and Mayor Hagen's local democracy. Aristotle's polis supplies the town's design — small enough for community, walled for defense, river-powered — while Kant's disinterested appreciation of the beautiful fits Miyamoto's 'miniature garden' of pastoral idyll. The spiritual dimension completes the utopia: the benevolent Picori/Minish are a God walking unseen among people, a fuzzy religion without prophet or persecution, so no leap of faith is even necessary.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 24 "Indiscernibles and Autonomous Viewers “Time to Write my Own Fucking Story”" — Forest and Beckley-Forest ask whether Westworld is self-referential 'high art' or 'meta-kitsch,' tracing aesthetic modernism from Kant's subjective turn through Greenberg's avant-garde/kitsch split and Adorno's autonomous versus heteronomous art. They read Sizemore's clichéd Western narratives and the park's stock characters as commodified kitsch that mirrors the show's own corporate constraints under HBO, and use Danto's Brillo Box problem of indiscernibles to argue that host/guest and entertainment/art distinctions lie in the viewer's reflection. Dolores's line 'when I discover who I am, I'll be free' models the Adorno-style liberation available to an alert viewer.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 17 "The Beauty of the Game" — The Brands stage a broadcast-booth debate about whether a championship game was 'beautiful,' with Dickie V defending Hume's subjectivism ('beauty is in the eye of the beholder' and the expert's delicacy of taste) and Billy defending Plato's objective Form of Beauty. Jim exposes each side's flaw (Hume's circular appeal to experts, Plato's third-man regress from the Parmenides/Aristotle) and proposes a synthesis: games have 'outer beauty' (universally observable fluid motion, like improvised jazz or dance) and 'inner beauty' (the strategy and reason the knowledgeable fan grasps), reconciling the objective and subjective.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 14 "The Beauty of Football" — Parker asks what pleases football fans and argues the answer is beauty, framed around a Michael Vick scramble against the Ravens. He applies Kant's Critique of Judgment—beauty as disinterested, an end in itself, and its judgments nonconceptual yet universal ('you should too')—to explain why fans watch games rather than read box scores, and why skilled offensive play by Barry Sanders or Joe Montana strikes us as beautiful. Using Ted Cohen's 'circles of taste' and an informal survey, he concludes beauty admits of degree and depends on the viewer's grasp of context.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 10 "Second Hole On the Beauty and Sublimity of Golf" — Fudge and Ulatowski argue that golf's aesthetic appeal has two sources: the course as a designed landscape best appreciated (via Walton's 'Categories of Art') under the category of gardens, and the sublimity of players' character. They apply Kant's 'Observations on the Feeling of the Beautiful and Sublime' to distinguish beautiful courses (Augusta) from sublime ones (Pebble Beach, St. Andrews) and to explain Bobby Jones's self-imposed penalty at the 1925 U.S. Open as the noble sublime, since 'subduing one's passions through principles is sublime.' They link the consistent rule-following golf demands to Kant's categorical imperative and read human dignity as 'beyond price' against Hobbes's price-based account, while Schopenhauer's critique of the French garden frames the environmental objection to courses.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 30 "Fifteenth Hole The “Ideal” Swing, the “Ideal” Body Myths of Optimization" — Jason and Laurence Holt attack two 'optimization' myths in golf culture via a philosophy of kinesiology: the averaging model (that the ideal swing is the statistical mean of elite swings) and the athlete model (that more general fitness makes a better golfer). Against the first they invoke multiple realizability from philosophy of mind—there is no single perfect swing, since Bobby Jones's over-parallel backswing, Hagen's short fast swing, and the quirky swings of Trevino and Furyk all succeed on different bodies. Against the second they note golf's modest physical demands and argue Tiger Woods's heavy conditioning caused injury without improving results. They diagnose the false ideal as an aesthetic bias favoring 'beautiful' swings and athletic-looking bodies, using Suits's definition of games to defend golf as a genuine sport of gross physical skill.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 30 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Sharpe analyzes the Olympics as an aestheticized 'spectacle' (Debord, after Marx's commodity analysis) whose real product is the shareable 'Olympic moment.' Reading Kant's Critique of Judgment through Terry Eagleton, he argues the games trade on the sensus communis Kant finds in the judgment 'this is beautiful', an intimated universal harmony among humans that mirrors the ancient Olympic ekecheiria (truce). He links Beijing 2008's simulated fireworks and lip-synced girl to Baudrillard's simulacra, and uses Benjamin's 'Work of Art' essay, Riefenstahl's Olympia and Hegel's account of Greek sculpture to show how the Nazis' 1936 Games weaponized this aesthetic power, warning the spectacle serves both good and evil.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 11 "Federer as Religious Experience" — David Foster Wallace argues that watching Roger Federer live at Wimbledon delivers a near-religious experience because top sport is a prime venue for 'kinetic beauty'—a beauty rooted in human beings' reconciliation with the fact of having a body. He reads the 2006 Federer-Nadal final as a clash of the Apollonian (Federer's clinical northern artistry) against the Dionysian (Nadal's martial southern machismo), and dwells on specific Federer Moments (the reverse-thrust forehand winner against Agassi at the 2005 US Open) as instances where an athlete seems exempt from physical law. He treats Federer's grace as ineffable, defining it by what it is not, and juxtaposes the transcendent beauty of the body against the suffering body of cancer-survivor coin-tosser William Caines.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 13 "Why Are All Tennis Films Bad" — Mark Huston argues no truly great tennis film—a 'Raging Bull of tennis'—will ever be made, and builds his case through genre theory. He contrasts an Aristotelian essentialist approach to defining a genre (necessary and sufficient conditions, as in Noel Carroll's Poetics-derived definition of horror) with a Wittgensteinian 'family resemblance' account, adopting the latter to identify overlapping-but-nonessential core features of the sports film (representing a real sport, literal not merely metaphorical emphasis, a culminating sporting moment, an athlete protagonist). Reading Nobody's Perfect, Wimbledon, and Tennis, Anyone...?, and citing David Foster Wallace on how tennis's speed is essentially untelevisable, he concludes tennis's un-representability on screen plus the genre's uplift bar it from the aesthetic seriousness that wins critical greatness.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 18 "A Court Conversation" — Cast as a dialogue with an updated Kant at a tournament, the chapter applies Kant's aesthetics to spectating tennis: it distinguishes free from dependent beauty (a McEnroe drop volley or a Federer stroke judged against the game's history and rules), locates the sublime in a booming ace, a broken record, and the fan's disinterested enthusiasm, and defends aesthetic judgments as disinterested yet subjectively universal. It then turns Kant's ethics onto the court, arguing that calling a line honestly against your own interest has moral worth only when done autonomously, for its own sake, and that gamesmanship like faked injury timeouts seeks an unfair advantage and so is wrong even when within the rules.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Kohler-Ryan and Palmer treat 'sense' and 'sensibility' as a spectrum Lee explores through sisterhood in Sense and Sensibility (Elinor/Marianne) and Crouching Tiger (Shu Lien/Jen). Elinor and Shu Lien embody sense, Shu Lien specifically the Confucian balance of li and ren that lets her soften ritual with humanity; Marianne embodies Burke's British-Romantic sublime while Jen embodies Daoist immersion in the dao. Reading door-frames, windows, hair-combing rituals and Shu Lien's hairpin as symbols, they argue only Sense and Sensibility achieves integration in time, whereas Li Mu Bai's confession that he lived sense and sensibility as separate spheres comes too late.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 12 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Jameson and Brace read Sense and Sensibility and Brokeback Mountain through Burke's and Gilpin's aesthetics of the sublime, the beautiful and the picturesque, mapped onto the Chinese yin/yang and qi of landscape. In Sense and Sensibility, manicured French/Brownian gardens (beautiful, sanctioned) versus wild picturesque nature (sublime, passionate) mirror Elinor's controlled sense and Marianne's storm-caught sensibility, with Willoughby's rescue and Brandon's steadiness keyed to landscape. In Brokeback Mountain the masculine sublime wilderness (yang) versus feminine confining civilization (yin) is built through tightly framed interiors, sweeping exteriors and an 'aesthetics of isolation' that exposes American freedom as a costly illusion for Ennis and Jack.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 22 "“A Homespun Murder Story” Film Noir and the Problem of Modernity in Fargo" — Abrams reads Fargo as a noir study of modernity via MacIntyre's After Virtue: humans are 'story-telling animals,' and the Enlightenment project (Descartes, Sartre) shredded the shared myth, leaving Cartesian monadic selves who float in a void as 'unscripted, anxious stutterers.' The whiteout blizzard becomes an ontological tabula rasa of Heraclitean flux where every conversation collapses (Jerry, Carl, Mike Yanagita, even Marge at the drive-thru). Abrams reads Marge as morally good but intellectually shallow—wrong to call the sublime, Kantian 'dynamically sublime' day 'beautiful'—and Grimsrud as the one who dimly 'sees' the modern abyss, so the film hands the deeper mystery of modernity's crime to the viewer.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 17 "6. But What Does It Mean" — Kreider argues Twin Peaks is less about determinate meaning than about handing viewers incomplete, underdetermined content to complete themselves. He reads the opening sequence's waterfalls and trees through Kant's aesthetic 'purposiveness without purpose,' the swaying traffic light and 'the full blossom of the evening' as Russell's incomplete symbols, and the range of legitimate interpretations through Quine's underdetermination of theory by evidence; Susanne Langer's Feeling and Form adds that film creates a dreamlike virtual present, so the Part 8 atomic-bomb sequence works exactly as a dream we must interpret.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 24 "12. It’s Not About BOB—It Never Was" — Huntingford argues Lynch reveres madness as the true source of insight, casting Cooper as the Romantic 'mad poet' and Socratic divinely-inspired Oracle (Phaedrus) whose dream-forays reveal Twin Peaks' buried truths while 'normal' is the real evil. She frames BOB—born from the atomic blast—and garmonbozia through Kant's Sublime as the fearful, irregular power behind nature that exceeds reason, and reads Cooper's tragic ka (via Stephen King's Dark Tower) and shadow-self confrontation, plus Rousseau's ethics of truth-seeking, as the show's message: some mysteries are not meant to be solved, and to embrace that madness is freedom.
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — Richard Gilmore reads After Hours as a nocturnal katabasis in which office worker Paul Hackett is repeatedly offered, and repeatedly fails at, authentic encounter with the SoHo women and their artworks (Kiki's papier-mache man, the plaster-of-paris bagel). Using Levinas's totality-versus-infinity and the ethics of conversation, Kant's two worlds of interest and disinterested aesthetic judgment, and Dewey's Art as Experience, Gilmore argues that art and sex alike (per Picasso and Nagel's 'double reciprocal incarnation') demand abandoning one's 'logic of the same' to perceive the other. Foucault's disciplinary kronos-time versus kairos, and Zizek's anamorphic spot, frame Paul's entrapment in solipsism until, encased as a literal artwork and reborn at the office gates, he finally offers himself to June.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Ritzer argues Mann's aesthetics of horror in The Keep and Manhunter is an aestheticization of horror—the frightening transformed into the beautiful through mise-en-scène, color, and montage. Against Hegel's Lectures on Fine Art, which bans the purely negative and horrific from aesthetics, Ritzer marshals Schiller, De Quincey, and Auden to split the ethical from the aesthetic: Dollarhyde stages corpses as artworks and Graham reads crime scenes as an art critic. The Keep pushes further into Barthes's 'obtuse meaning' and Deleuze and Guattari's 'planes of immanence,' its stylized images referring to nothing but themselves—horror filmed solely for horror's sake.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Gilmore reads Chinatown as neo-noir that is itself a kind of philosophy, engaging the hermeneutics of suspicion (Nietzsche, Freud, Marx) and existentialist alienation. Curly eating the venetian blinds signals a desire to recover a less painful blindness; Jake Gittes's 'conceptual scotomas' (Dennett) and hubris make him miss counternarratives, paralleling Oedipus as detective. Using Freud on the uncanny and doppelgangers (Jake doubled with Hollis Mulwray and Noah Cross) and Aristotle's Poetics on catharsis and the sublime, Gilmore argues 'Chinatown' names the abyss where every narrative is undone, and that facing this dark sublimity is the way of wisdom.
- **The Philosophy of Spike Lee**, ch. 22 "Transcendence and Sublimity in Spike Lee’s Signature Shot" — Abrams analyzes Lee's 'signature shot'—a character silently gliding forward toward the viewer—as a phenomenological device that ejects the immersed viewer back into self-aware spectatorship, drawing on Heidegger's account of anticipation and being futural in Being and Time and Danto's claim that a self-conscious camera makes the film about being viewed. He tracks the shot in Malcolm X (levitating before his assassination), 25th Hour (Mary floating on Ecstasy), and Inside Man (Frazier's superhuman, robotic rush after the staged execution). He then argues the shot is aesthetically sublime in Longinus's and Kant's sense: it renders characters superhuman and elevated off the ground, an objective image of subjective transcendence that signs Lee as both filmmaker and philosopher.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 25 "“Profoundly Unreconciled to Nature” Ecstatic Truth and the Humanistic Sublime in Werner Herzog’s War Films" — LaRocca argues against Thomas Weiskel that the 'humanistic sublime' is not an oxymoron, using Herzog's war films (Lessons of Darkness, Little Dieter Needs to Fly, Rescue Dawn) to show a sublime that returns us to the human at the limit of existence rather than transcending it. Building on Kant's link between the sublime and human dignity—and Kant's claim that sublimity lies in our ideas, not in nature—he reads Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' (fabrication that exceeds the 'accountant's truth') as the vehicle: staged monologues, borrowed music, and recontextualized documentary footage disclose an inner reality. Herzog's Heideggerian gloss on aletheia as un-concealment aligns cinema itself with truth, and Dengler's bear ('the only friend I had was death') exemplifies war as the space of radical mortality where the humanistic sublime dawns for the safe spectator, contrasted with Malick's more Darwinian, nature-indifferent vision.
- **The Philosophy of Werner Herzog**, ch. 8 "Herzog’s Sublime and Ecstatic Truth" — Patricia Castello Branco argues that Herzog's sublime is Burkean and physiological rather than Kantian and transcendental: in Aguirre, Fitzcarraldo, and Grizzly Man the protagonists' encounter with overwhelming nature defeats reason and works through the body (Kinski's distorted performance, Treadwell's death) rather than confirming reason's supremacy as in Kant's Critique of Judgment. She maps Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' onto Nietzsche's Dionysian from The Birth of Tragedy, where the principium individuationis dissolves and the hero merges with nature's creating-and-destroying flux, and glosses ecstatic truth via Heidegger's aletheia as unconcealment reached through fabrication and stylization.
- **The Philosophy of Werner Herzog**, ch. 14 "The Great Ecstasy of Werner Herzog Truth, Heidegger, Apocalypse" — Ian Alexander Moore reads Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' through Heidegger's account of truth as aletheia (unconcealment) and 'The Origin of the Work of Art,' arguing that Herzog's fabricated Pascal epigraph and Wagner Prelude in Lessons of Darkness and Lo and Behold elevate viewers into a sublime, ecstatic state that discloses a truth beyond the 'accountant's' factual. He connects the slow-motion ski-jumps of The Great Ecstasy of Woodcarver Steiner to Heidegger's ecstatic standing-outside-oneself, and treats Lessons of Darkness's burning Kuwaiti oil fields as an apocalyptic un-covering. He also warns that planetary information technology (echoing Heidegger's Question Concerning Technology) threatens the very oblivion of ecstatic truth.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 37 "A Beautiful Destiny" — Clive Cazeaux asks whether the Daleks can be beautiful, canvassing theories of beauty to resolve the puzzle of a monster being beautiful. He distinguishes Kant's higher natural beauty (and his suspicion of 'dependent,' purpose-designed beauty like the Dalek casing) from Hegel's view that beauty in art, perceiving thought in matter, is higher, and finds Plato most helpful: to call the Daleks beautiful is Platonic love, being drawn to engage with them as a wholly-other form of life whose design succeeds. He surveys Alexander of Hales, Rosenkranz's aesthetic inferno, and formalism (the Krutikov design parallel) without a final verdict, showing the dispute turns on metaphysics.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 11 "3. The Nasty Bits" — Calef asks how Bourdain could find disgusting foods (cobra heart, blood soup, warthog anus) delicious, using Korsmeyer's taxonomy of disgust and the 'paradox of aversion.' He argues their appeal comes from Aristotelian learning-through-representation, Burke's and Bullough's sublime experienced at psychical distance, and Kristeva's 'abject' — foods that remind us of death and mortality let Bourdain transcend and disarm it by eating them appreciatively.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 21 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Ilundáin-Agurruza, Gagliardini Graça, and Jáuregui-Olaiz chart sailing's aesthetic facets — sublime, tempestuous, graceful, existential. They deploy Kant's analysis of the sublime as the balance between the imagination's failure before the ocean's immensity/power and the pleasure of meeting it through skill and reason (Ilundáin sailing in thirty-knot gusts on the point of balance between fear and joy). Dewey's notion of 'an experience' anchors sailing's transformative, self-revealing potential, terrifying storms included (Jáuregui's Snowgoose ordeal mistaking a bordello's red light for a harbor). Closing with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, they argue freedom is 'relative' and earned: we cannot change the wind but adjust the sails, gaining restrained autonomy by cultivating skill within constraint.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 25 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Wear traces the espresso aesthetic from the idealized, egalitarian Italian caffè—which he reads as an 'aestheticized Marxist' image of identical shots for businessman and street sweeper—to its dilution under neoliberal consumer choice, epitomized by the endless-customization L.A. Story 'half-caf twist of lemon' scene. He invokes Kant's Critique of Judgement and the sublime to argue that flavor and taste-judgment are neglected aesthetic faculties, and enlists the Frankfurt School (Adorno, Benjamin, Marcuse) and Bourdieu's cultural capital to explain how the market absorbs the espresso's beauty. He concludes that a single humble shot, as a memorial to the vast exploited labor chain behind it, is a truer aesthetic object than a branded frappuccino.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 17 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Clark analyzes Disney's Bambi as anti-hunting art, showing how the animators used music and the Kantian sublime — keeping Man and Death offscreen, 'felt rather than seen' — to make viewers feel hunting is cosmic murder, while the cute cartoon animals stay merely 'seen.' He then critiques Matt Cartmill, who dissolves hunting by using science and utilitarianism to erase the Man/Nature split (making hunting indistinguishable from murder), faulting Cartmill for flattening life and rejecting the sublime. He resolves the tension via Richard Nelson's The Island Within and Koyukon hunting, which honors continuity and the sublime without a Man/Nature dichotomy.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 27 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — La Caze rehabilitates fashion against Kant's own dismissal of it (in the *Anthropology*) as vanity and imitation, arguing that Kant's aesthetics actually supply the tools to value it. She applies his account of the disinterested judgment of taste, free vs. adherent beauty, and 'genius' (originality that provides an exemplary model — Chanel's freer dressing, Dior's New Look, punk DIY, the Sartorialist's street style) to both the making and the wearing of clothes. Drawing on Kant's claim that the beautiful is a symbol of the morally good and the 'virtues of social intercourse,' and on Iris Marion Young's pleasures of touch, bonding, and fantasy, she argues fashion can be a proto-moral, cosmopolitan force, countering Plato's, Beauvoir's, and Svendsen's denigration.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 22 "GARDENING" — Barwell and Powell challenge Kant's classification of landscape gardening as a subcategory of painting ('for the eye only') by arguing that gardens, unlike static paintings or sculpture, essentially present the passing of time visually. Because gardens are made of living organisms that grow, flower, senesce and decay at different rates—an oak, a drift of crocuses, a managed lawn—they generate visual rhythms analogous to musical rhythm, with diurnal and seasonal cycles supplying a 'rhythmus firmus' (pulse and meter) that nature, not the designer, provides. Using Susanne Langer's claim that 'music makes the passage of time audible,' they conclude gardens make time visible and so deserve status as a distinctive art form.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 23 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Jacquette argues that cannabis opens a 'creative inner space' of loosened associations but is skeptical it yields genuine, lasting insight, using Ginsberg's claim to have newly 'apprehended the structure' of jazz and classical music and the conjecture that Shakespeare's Sonnet 76 'invention in a noted weed' hints he wrote high. He treats the aesthetic case as a phenomenology problem: separating cannabis's real contribution to appreciation from mere buzz-glow. He then defends a right to get high by invoking the Declaration's 'pursuit of happiness' and a Mill-style principle that private, non-harming pleasure should not be criminalized.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 31 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Karlsen argues that climbing routes are genuine aesthetic objects and that judging a route beautiful is a real aesthetic judgment, not mere pleasure. Against Kant's demand that beauty require detachment (which would confine climbing to the 'merely agreeable') and against Aristotle's exclusion of the bodily senses, he distinguishes a 'line' (seen from the ground, like The Nose) from a 'route' (actually climbed) and contends that proprioception, the felt sense of bodily movement, yields information about the route itself, not just the body. Invoking the phenomenological 'transparency of experience' (Moore's diaphanousness), he concludes proprioception is an aesthetic sense that lets widely-agreed classics emerge.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 21 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Rachel Falkenstern argues that although tattoos seem permanent, the embodied self is changing and finite, so tattoos are 'illusions of permanence.' Using Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology she dissolves the mind/body and self/tattoo boundary (we are our bodies, the world shapes us and we shape it); using the German aesthetic tradition from Kant to Hegel she reads a tattoo as a sensuous 'appearance of freedom' and links the Romantic notion of Bildung (self-formation) to choosing ink. She adds Foucault's aesthetic self-transformation and Shusterman's somaesthetics/Deweyan pragmatism to cast tattooing as reciprocal self-expression and self-creation that offers a glimpse of infinity within finitude.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 21 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Nicole Dunas's 'The Feeling of Beauty' recounts founding the Real Beauty Yoga Project after a teacher-training 'modeling day' where consultants photographed only the five thinnest students, enacting division rather than yogic union. Framing the beauty question against Kant's claim that beauty is objective, and drawing on David Abram's participatory perception and Susan Bordo on airbrushed bodies, she argues that objectifying beauty into an image to be gazed at (the male gaze, the isolated cosmetic-surgery gaze) severs us from it, whereas Hatha yoga's tantric, present-moment embodiment lets beauty be lived rather than consumed.
- **Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low**, ch. 18 "BLUES" — David C. Drake argues that the blues' distinctive achievement is presenting 'sadness as beauty,' which lets performers and listeners find their own sorrow beautiful and thus therapeutic. He surveys theories of beauty — Plato's proportion/harmony/unity and Aristotle's order/symmetry (a beautiful life needs some sorrow), Kant's claim that beauty is a subjective-yet-universal judgment requiring reflection, Lyotard's sublime that 'pleases only by causing pain,' and Schopenhauer's view that aesthetic contemplation temporarily frees us from the striving Will — and links beauty to truth and goodness (Keats, Nietzsche's 'whoever despises himself respects himself as one who despises') to explain why blues sorrow feels good.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 18 "“Hot with Rapture and Cold with Fear” Grotesque, Sublime, and Postmodern Transformations in Patrick Süskind's" — Cokal reads Suskind's Perfume and Tykwer's film through the intertwined categories of the grotesque and the sublime. The odorless murderer Grenouille is a Bakhtinian grotesque body who nonetheless has Kantian sublime experiences of the plum girl's and Laure's scents, and Cokal uses Kant's and Lyotard's accounts of the sublime (the soul 'immobilized, as good as dead') to explain the awe that Grenouille both feels and, via his 'angel's scent,' induces in the orgy at his execution. Grenouille's uncanny encounter with his own lack of smell in the cave is read through Freud's uncanny, and his final cannibalistic dismemberment collapses the sublime back into the grotesque.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 12 "NOTES" — Ted Cohen denies there is any sound argument from 'X is better than Y' to 'it is better to like X,' using Bach vs. Elvis vs. Milton Babbitt on complexity to show the criterion collapses. He reframes art around 'communities of appreciation'—citing Augustine's claim that a people is defined by what it loves in common—and reports (via a blues club in Memphis and the Marriage of Figaro) that what all appreciators of a work share is 'nothing' but their love of it, a Goodman-style nominalism. He challenges Kant's insistence that genuine aesthetic judgments claim universality, arguing real appreciative communities are less-than-universal overlapping circles.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 13 "NOTES" — Richard Shusterman defends the entertainment value of popular art from a pragmatist ('meliorist') stance, tracing entertainment's genealogy through Plato, Aristotle, Montaigne, Kant, Hegel, Nietzsche, Heidegger and Adorno—whose 'culture industry' opposes pleasure to cognition. Using rap (KRS-One's 'Edutainment', Public Enemy, Ice-T) and T.S. Eliot's 'superior amusement,' he argues knowledge and enjoyment are compatible. He rejects Hannah Arendt's contrast of imperishable art vs. life-serving entertainment, and critiques G.E. Moore's Principia Ethica 'method of absolute isolation' for intrinsic value, replacing it with a Deweyan transactional account in which even intrinsic values are relational and temporal.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 82 "77. Journey as Philosophy Meaning, Connection, and the Sublime" — Hamer argues Journey works through the interplay of connection, the sublime and meaning. The wordless multiplayer bond with an unnameable stranger before vast vistas dramatizes emotional connection where the ancestors' greed failed. The looming mountain and immense dunes evoke the sublime, read through Burke's pleasurable terror and Kant's mathematical and dynamical sublime (imagination overwhelmed while reason comprehends; feeling power over a nature that cannot harm the deathless player, then rebirth surpassing the sublime into joy). The cyclical return to the start recasts the game as Camus's Myth of Sisyphus: a meaningless repeated ascent that players nonetheless replay, so we must imagine the Traveler — and ourselves — happy to make the beautiful repetition our own.

### Human Nature Is Bad (and needs ritual)

Xunzi took the opposing Confucian view that human nature is bad, or at least unruly, since people are born with self-interested desires that, left unchecked, lead to conflict and disorder. For Xunzi goodness is not innate but a deliberate achievement, produced by ritual, education, and the accumulated wisdom of the sages, which reshape raw impulses into virtuous conduct. His emphasis on ritual (li) and conscious effort as the source of morality directly answered Mencius's claim that virtue grows from natural sprouts.

- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 30 "Every Soul Experiences the Battle Within" — Reads Zuko's arc as a war between Legalism and Confucianism: Ozai's agni kai scarring of his son, Azulon's death sentence, the Fire Nation Oath and school discipline ('The Headband') all enact Han Fei's principle that bad human nature needs terrifying sanctions, and Azula's 'trust is for fools' completes it. Against this stands Iroh's Confucian education in ren — teaching that honor cannot be separated from humaneness, that a mugger deserves tea and encouragement, and that wu-wei-like patience knows when to speak. Mencius's innate compassion explains why Zuko's 'amazing lie' realization could unfold, Katara, Sokka, and Hakoda embody Confucian filial bonds that adopt Aang, Toph, and finally Zuko, and Solzhenitsyn's gulag insight closes the chapter: the line between good and evil runs through every human heart.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 30 "Every Soul Experiences the Battle Within" — Reads the Fire Nation royal family as a philosophical battle between Legalism (Han Fei, taking Xunzi's dictum that human nature is evil, so order requires terrifying sanctions: Ozai burning Zuko in the agni kai so 'suffering will be your teacher', Azulon's death sentence on Zuko, the Fire Nation Oath recited in schools) and Confucianism (Iroh teaching ren, that true honor cannot be had apart from humaneness, preferring honorable begging over theft, and talking a would-be mugger into tea). Zuko's 'battle within' is the legacy of his two great-grandfathers, Sozin's Legalism versus Roku's line, and it is resolved when he disowns Ozai, calls Iroh his 'real father', and is adopted into Team Avatar, whose filial bonds (Katara's care, Hakoda's sacrifice) contrast with the scheming royal family. The chapter closes with Solzhenitsyn's image of the line between good and evil passing through every human heart to explain why Zuko's inner war resonates.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Curry and Lang test 'War never changes' through Hobbes and Xunzi: the wasteland - where the Ghoul asks who ever elected the 'President' in 'The Trap' and Cooper Howard decays outside all political order - is Hobbes's state of nature of restless power-seeking, while Xunzi's claim that bad human nature needs ritual (li) and righteousness (yi) explains a world with no moral education, where Elder Cleric Quintus pairs noble talk with 'power is taken, not given'. Fallout's Great War then fails every just-war test: China's invasion of Alaska stretches just cause, the corporatist US lacks right authority, propaganda undid last resort, mutually assured destruction explodes proportionality, and Vault-Tec shelters plus battlefield mini-nukes breach discrimination and proportionality in bello - with Operation Anchorage's propaganda simulation illustrating the revisionist point that fighting cleanly cannot redeem an unjust war. China's 'righteous army' (yi bing) tradition - Sunzi's strategic restraint, Mohist defensive war, Mengzi's true king, Xunzi's punitive righteous war - leaves no trace beyond Captain Zao, so the war's constancy marks the failure of every philosophical attempt to bind war to justice.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Thompson argues that Lee's 'cowboy aesthetic' of rugged isolation in Brokeback Mountain (Ennis and Jack) and Crouching Tiger (Li Mu Bai, Shu Lien, Jen) is only apparent: the characters are always already embedded in Confucius' five cardinal relationships, read through Xunzi's darker view that selfish desire must be curbed by ritual and social hierarchy. Ennis and Jack seem lone individuals but are defined by ties to Alma, family and each other, and Jen's redemption comes when she abandons self-serving desire to re-establish her Confucian relationships. Citing Nietzsche's gloss on Aristotle that only a beast or a god lives alone, it concludes there is no truly isolated cowboy.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Dull reads Eat Drink Man Woman through a Hall-and-Ames 'focus-field' model of personhood, analyzing harmony via metaphors of a culinary dish, music and a sports team where each element keeps its integrity within a whole. He diagnoses the Chu family by pairing Mencius (morality as expression of the four sprouts) against Xunzi (desire must be structured by ritual): Chef Chu is 'repressed as a turtle', Jia-Jen hides behind ritual, Jia-Ning acts on impulse, and Jia-Chien lacks direction. Their romantic transformations restore harmony, answering Chu's question 'is there more than food and sex?' affirmatively, as expression, desire and ritual come into balance and his sense of taste returns.

### Human Nature Is Good

Mencius held that human nature is fundamentally good, arguing that everyone is born with incipient moral tendencies he called the four sprouts—compassion, shame, courtesy, and a sense of right and wrong. On this view wrongdoing arises not from an evil nature but from neglect, bad circumstances, or failure to nurture these innate beginnings, much as a plant withers without care. The task of ethics is therefore to cultivate and extend these natural feelings so they mature into the full virtues, a position that shaped later Confucian debates about moral education.

- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 30 "Every Soul Experiences the Battle Within" — Reads Zuko's arc as a war between Legalism and Confucianism: Ozai's agni kai scarring of his son, Azulon's death sentence, the Fire Nation Oath and school discipline ('The Headband') all enact Han Fei's principle that bad human nature needs terrifying sanctions, and Azula's 'trust is for fools' completes it. Against this stands Iroh's Confucian education in ren — teaching that honor cannot be separated from humaneness, that a mugger deserves tea and encouragement, and that wu-wei-like patience knows when to speak. Mencius's innate compassion explains why Zuko's 'amazing lie' realization could unfold, Katara, Sokka, and Hakoda embody Confucian filial bonds that adopt Aang, Toph, and finally Zuko, and Solzhenitsyn's gulag insight closes the chapter: the line between good and evil runs through every human heart.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 30 "Every Soul Experiences the Battle Within" — Reads the Fire Nation royal family as a philosophical battle between Legalism (Han Fei, taking Xunzi's dictum that human nature is evil, so order requires terrifying sanctions: Ozai burning Zuko in the agni kai so 'suffering will be your teacher', Azulon's death sentence on Zuko, the Fire Nation Oath recited in schools) and Confucianism (Iroh teaching ren, that true honor cannot be had apart from humaneness, preferring honorable begging over theft, and talking a would-be mugger into tea). Zuko's 'battle within' is the legacy of his two great-grandfathers, Sozin's Legalism versus Roku's line, and it is resolved when he disowns Ozai, calls Iroh his 'real father', and is adopted into Team Avatar, whose filial bonds (Katara's care, Hakoda's sacrifice) contrast with the scheming royal family. The chapter closes with Solzhenitsyn's image of the line between good and evil passing through every human heart to explain why Zuko's inner war resonates.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 32 "The Rhythm by Which We Live Our Lives" — Kowalski interprets Kuzco's arc through Mencius: the emperor's pampered upbringing (eight hands replacing a squeezed toy, Yzma's loveless regency) is the 'hatchets and frost' of the Ox Mountain parable blunting his innate moral sprouts. The gorge scene stages Mencius's child-at-the-well thought experiment — Kuzco's spontaneous snatch of falling Pacha is a 'give-away' action betraying compassion he denies having, which Pacha diagnoses just as Mencius did King Xuan sparing the ox — and Pacha's family, quasi-adopting Kuzco, supplies the loving soil Mencius says the sprouts of ren need to grow.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 31 "NOTES" — The Terjesens pit Kant's impersonal morality — Sam's contractual distance from the thieving Mickens is exactly how he would treat strangers — against Confucius and Mencius, for whom filial duties are the nursery of virtue: we learn benevolence by serving parents and revering elders, Lafayette's care for Lettie Mae and Tara shows family forming moral character, and the Upright Gong's covering for a father's sheep-stealing grounds Jason's 'sometimes the right thing to do is the wrong thing'. Mencius's King Shun, who abdicates and carries his criminal father into exile, models how Tommy and Jason should put family first while accepting the cost, while Mozi's universal love surfaces in Godric's 'forgiveness is love', and the chapter concludes that family counts only insofar as it develops our moral nature — the line between Tommy and Sam.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Bush argues that Brokeback Mountain transcends both the heterosexual western archetype and queer theory by presenting male sexuality through Mencius' philosophy and John Corvino's ethics of homosexuality. Using Mencius' four sprouts (ren, li, yi, zhi) and doctrine of natural goodness, he reads Ennis as the character in whom sexuality is contextual, cultivated and moral rather than merely physical, so the relationship between Ennis and Jack becomes an ethical friendship grounded in ren, the virtue Mencius says is most intense among friends. The bystanders Aguirre and Alma keeping the secret, and the final shirt-and-postcard scene, illustrate zhi as contextual moral judgment and homosexuality reframed as ethical rather than sexual.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Dull reads Eat Drink Man Woman through a Hall-and-Ames 'focus-field' model of personhood, analyzing harmony via metaphors of a culinary dish, music and a sports team where each element keeps its integrity within a whole. He diagnoses the Chu family by pairing Mencius (morality as expression of the four sprouts) against Xunzi (desire must be structured by ritual): Chef Chu is 'repressed as a turtle', Jia-Jen hides behind ritual, Jia-Ning acts on impulse, and Jia-Chien lacks direction. Their romantic transformations restore harmony, answering Chu's question 'is there more than food and sex?' affirmatively, as expression, desire and ritual come into balance and his sense of taste returns.

### Binary Oppositions

Binary oppositions are the paired, contrasting terms—such as speech and writing, presence and absence, nature and culture, or reason and emotion—through which Western thought has often organized meaning. Jacques Derrida observed that such pairs are rarely equal: one term is typically privileged as primary or natural while the other is treated as derivative or deficient. Deconstruction targets this hierarchy, showing that the favored term secretly depends on the one it subordinates, so the opposition cannot hold as cleanly as it claims. Exposing this instability was central to Derrida's critique of how philosophy establishes and enforces value.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 18 "Possibilities of Postmodern Education Beyond Control" — Toby Daspit reads Season Four as a drama of postmodern education: the Initiative's will to master and dissect — Walsh's Frankenstein-project Adam, who murders a boy to see how he works, fulfilling Wordsworth's 'we murder to dissect' — embodies the Cartesian split and the Hegelian drive to negate the other, while Buffy's world deconstructs fixed identity (Darla reversing the horror-movie opening, the Faith/Buffy body swap in 'Who Are You?', Jonathan's 'Superstar') and thwarts prophecy's metanarrative in 'Prophecy Girl.' Against modernist schooling's 'controlled circumstances' and Freire's banking model (Professor Riegert ejecting Buffy from class, Walsh's transmission lectures), the show models knowledge as collective work — the Scoobies' research sessions in Giles's library, Giles's fluid mentorship versus Kendra's by-the-book training, and the relational magic of 'Primeval' — offering education beyond control in an emergent, postmodern world.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 24 "A Political Philosophy of Vampires" — Phillip Cole takes Rousseau's remark that the eighteenth-century vampire epidemics had complete legal proof - the Arnold Paole exhumations - and argues Rousseau's real point was political: authorities manufacture imaginary monsters, as in the witch craze, to exploit fear and hold power over their own populations. Freud's account of the uncanny explains why the horror is not death itself but the returning dead (the watching eyes of Scratchy in Itchy and Scratchy, versus the serene corpses of Six Feet Under, whose absurdity the show meets with wry amusement), and Julia Kristeva's abjection explains the corpse as the ultimate boundary-breaker. The vampire then resurfaces as the demonized outsider - Stoker's Dracula coded as the unassimilated Jewish immigrant, today's terrorist - exposing political borders as arbitrary fabrications. Buffy completes the collapse of the us/them binary: Angel and Spike join the slayer, and the most shocking killings (Faith's accidental human kill, Warren's stray bullet hitting Tara) are all too human, so the real subject of border policing is the community's own members.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 22 "The Verdict" — Turner runs an ethical audit of iPod use through Levinas's face-to-face: sharing one iPod with his wife forces 'musical justice' negotiations (veto power over a Motörhead cut, gnashing through Bette Midler), his toddler son's listening requires vigilance, and illegal downloading fails Levinas's test that morality begins by ceding 'my place in the sun' to the Other — hence Radiohead's pay-what-you-want release as the Levinasian move, and iPod cafés where strangers DJ for each other while language preserves alterity. Heidegger supplies the counterweight: the shuffle's 'openness to mystery' versus calculative mastery that reduces The Who's Tommy to the 'Pinball Wizard' riff and silences all non-digital media, just as Kant's conditions of possible experience (space, time) would silence things outside them. Derrida's point that categories contain traces of what they exclude illuminates unclassifiable marginal works — bluegrass Pink Floyd, San Francisco Symphony plays Metallica — and the verdict closes with Hölderlin's 'where danger is, grows the saving power also', exiting Plato's cave by thinking the iPod's ethics at all.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 13 "The Postmodern Condition" — Rafe McGregor claims The Hound of the Baskervilles is not a detective story at all: the hound that never bites anyone and Holmes's failure to foresee fog on Dartmoor are, via Derrida's Of Grammatology, the aporia and re-mark where the mystery-horror hierarchy of the text deconstructs. He then applies Noel Carroll's philosophy of horror, the phosphorus-painted hound as a category-crossing monster producing fear plus disgust and Grimpen Mire as horror geography, to reclassify the novel as gothic horror alongside Frankenstein, Jekyll and Hyde and Dracula. The final section ties the book's enduring mass appeal to the postmodern condition, tracing the collapse of certainty from Nietzsche's prophecies about the end of Christian values to Derrida's claim that truth is never finally available, leaving anxiety as the novel's real engine.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 46 "Flowers" — Reads the Flowers album's blooms as dark—'Ruby Tuesday' can't be chained to a life where nothing's gained, and the heliotrope becomes Derrida's figure for philosophy forever turning toward its conceptual sun of truth, knowledge, or the good. That heliotropic bias, the metaphysics of presence, is illustrated by Augustine's treatment of evil as mere privation of good, which Nietzsche's genealogy of slave morality overturns by deriving good and evil from the same source, 'beyond good and evil.'
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 48 "Out of the Cave" — Traces the light-versus-darkness metaphor tradition from Plato's cave and Socrates' unexamined life through medieval 'illumination' and the Enlightenment to St. Paul's glass darkly, then lets Nietzsche ('shadow is as needful as light') and Derrida's deconstruction of presence/absence oppositions overturn it. The Stones do the same work in song: 'Just as every cop is a criminal, and all the sinners saints' in 'Sympathy for the Devil,' with 'Here Comes the Sun' overturned by 'Paint It Black' and 'Let It Be' by 'Let It Bleed.'
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 33 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — William McGinney argues Jerry Goldsmith's modernist score, with its twelve-tone themes, ostinati, cuica, slide whistle, and ram's horn, carries no inherent meaning but acquires it through learned associations: its dissonance recalls Cold War modernist concert music promoted as the high art of Western freedom, while its Stravinsky-like rhythms and 'primitive' timbres mark the apes as other and feed the film's deconstruction of the human-ape, advanced-primitive, civilized-barbaric oppositions. Because Taylor is given no heroic music, the score undercuts identification with him as an anti-hero, and its modernist associations implicate the technocratic, militarized West he represents in Earth's self-destruction. The chapter's machinery is the semiotic view of Kant, Adorno, Cage, Peirce, and Saussure: music modifies a film's images the way adjectives modify nouns.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 30 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Caroline Mosser treats the creature's tragedy as humanist prejudice rather than necessity: the blind De Lacey accepts the eloquent creature sight unseen, so he passes Alan Turing's test, and only the sighted family's terror at his body rejects him - bias against the artificial, not reason. She reads the creature's development through fire, language, and revolution as Rousseau's progression from natural innocence to corruption by society, and Donna Haraway's cyborg as the figure he prefigures: an unfaithful illegitimate offspring who rebels against his father and undermines patriarchal Western self/other dualisms. The chapter concludes that society cannot accept enhanced or posthuman beings until it finds a middle ground beyond its binary grids of good/bad and Self/Other, since otherwise any new life we create will be Othered, hated, and oppressed like Frankenstein's.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 32 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Michael Mendelson rereads James Whale's 1931 Frankenstein as a metaphysics of appearance versus reality: the seemingly monstrous creature killed Fritz only after Fritz tormented him with fire and the whip, killed Dr. Waldman while Waldman was trying to dissect him alive, and drowned Maria in innocent play, expecting her to float like the flowers they had been throwing. The 'criminal brain' was Fritz's accident and explains less than we assume, since the creature spares Henry's fiancée when she screams and faints. The real point is alterity: otherness is a relation, not a property, and individual and social identity are built by excluding an outside where monsters reside - so the horror was inside the well-ordered village all along, the monster is us, and we are its creators.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 36 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Jessie Dern uses Derrida's Rogues and The Animal that Therefore I Am to show that naming is power: Victor cries 'Devil!' before the creature has done anything, and labels like 'monster,' 'rogue,' and 'animal' are performative verdicts that reveal the labeler, who secures his own goodness by negating the Other, more than the labeled. The novel multiplies the pattern, from Justine's confessor making her 'think that I was the monster that he said I was' to Elizabeth's 'men appear to me as monsters thirsting for each other's blood,' while Victor, guarding his self-image, becomes the monster himself. Against the Nietzsche epigraph about fighting monsters, the chapter closes with Derrida's playful self-application ('the animal that therefore I am') as the move the creature never gets to make: contesting the label and claiming a name and a self.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 19 "Walker Bite. Differentiating the Dead" — Di Bernardo argues that the swarm of names for the undead - walkers, roamers, lurkers, biters, empties, geeks - shows the world does not carve itself into pre-existing essences: communities construct their own classifications, as when Alice mocks Rick's group's roamers/lurkers taxonomy ('They all bite. Biters makes a ton more sense') and titles like 'Governor,' 'The Kingdom,' and 'Jesus' are disavowed by their bearers. Naming is a conferral of power that reveals the namers, since without absolute authority every name is a self-authorized exercise of power. Finally the living dead destabilize the strict living/dead opposition, and Rick's dogmatic 'us against them' slips into his own admission 'We are the Walking Dead!', with painful ethical consequences for how we police inclusion and exclusion in our world.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 11 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Donovan and Richardson read the Maltusian split, with the male Guardians banning emotion through the Book of Oa on Oa and the female Zamarons leaving to found the violet light of love on Zamaron, as the Western association of men with reason and women with emotion. They deploy Gilligan's different-voice reply to Kohlberg, the Pythagorean table of opposites via Genevieve Lloyd, Hegel's exclusion of women from the public sphere, and Jaggar's liberal-feminist critique of 'ahistorical' reason, whose comic-book analogue is the third law banning relationships between Lanterns. The chapter ends by arguing the standoff is a false dichotomy the comics themselves begin to dissolve: Kyle's 'Lanterns with heart' speech to the Guardians, the repeal of the third law, and the Indigo Tribe's plan to recombine the seven corps into the white light of creation.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 30 "Keep the Needle on the Record" — Donavan Muir argues Lost's narrative world, unlike Jane Eyre's, requires its own metaphysics, and that this metaphysics is an order of balanced binary oppositions: Jacob and the Man in Black as twins diverged at birth, the cave scale's light and dark stones that Locke knocks out of balance in 'The Substitute,' science/faith, with characters like Jack converting from one pole into its opposite. The proper model is the yin-yang in motion - the Tao as a balanced ontological flow in which interdependent opposites wax and wane - so that treating the poles as independent is the delusion that threatens the island's order. The finale, where both Jacob and the Man in Black cease to exist and the castaways are freed, enacts the Mahayana Buddhist Middle Way: enlightenment as letting go of rigid oppositions that interdependence double-negates.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 32 "Notes" — Pits Donna Haraway's Cyborg Manifesto against Star Trek's horror of the Borg, reading Locutus/Picard, Hugh, and Seven of Nine as tests of the Federation values of autonomy, individuality, and authenticity against the rival Borg values of heteronomy, collectivity, and simulation. Picard's "My culture is based on freedom and self-determination" exchange with the Borg, Hugh's discovery of his name and first-person "I", and Seven's tug-of-war with the Borg Queen in "Dark Frontier" dramatize what assimilation threatens. The chapter then defends a Haraway-inspired feminist reboot: women and minorities were long denied autonomy, individuality, and authenticity by prejudice and stereotype (Seven still must look "warp-core hot" in her catsuit), the human/machine and man/woman binaries were always false, and since we already live as cyborgs of apps, implants, and networks, resistance was negligible - the real Borg problem is their violent means, not their values.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 11 "Mea culpa" — Correcting her own initial dismissal of the show as Nancy Drew redux, the author argues Neptune is structured by a white/Hispanic racial binary laid over the millionaire/work-for-millionaires class binary, enforced through Logan's 'spic and span' jab at Weevil, Mr. Daniels's 'pumping his gas' insult, and the 'coconut' label for Latinos who cross over. Borrowing Saussure's binary oppositions and de Beauvoir's account of how a dominant group constructs a stigmatized Other, she shows the 09-ers defining themselves against everyone else, with teacher Daniels quietly siding with wealth against both boys. Bourdieu's cultural capital then explains why Wallace (basketball, scholarship, colorblind friendships) can cross boundaries that leave Weevil working as a janitor, and she concludes the show keeps race admirably visible in a supposedly postracial era.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Nelson argues that critics forget Soderbergh directed Erin Brockovich because they file his career under the art/commerce binary, and he uses Nietzsche's attack on the 'faith in antithetical values' and Derrida's deconstruction to expose such binaries (art/entertainment, independent/mainstream, activity/passivity) as gendered, hierarchical, and unstable. He then shows the film's real signature is a 'self-centered narration' totally focalized through Julia Roberts's Erin, so that a tension between the movie's altruistic content and its Erin-fixated form never resolves. The chapter treats the binary as a rhetorically useful but collapsing tool rather than a real opposition.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 21 "The Northwestern McCabe and Mrs. Miller" — Deborah Knight and George McKnight read Altman's McCabe and Mrs. Miller as an 'end-of-genre' western in the ironic mode, using Frye's Aristotle-derived mythos to map the classic western's binary oppositions (hero/villain, community/wilderness, virgin/whore) and then show the film collapsing them. Against Nussbaum's and Booth's ethical criticism, which extols works that make us 'finely aware and richly responsible,' they argue irony is itself a moral stance of detached scrutiny: McCabe is no hero but a vulgar, unimaginative businessman crushed by the Harrison Shaughnessy company and shot in the back in the snow while the town obliviously saves its burning church, dramatizing the implosion of the western's moral vision.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 30 "Keep the Needle on the Record" — Donavan S. Muir argues that Lost deliberately withholds its metanarrative so viewers must construct its metaphysics, which he identifies as an order of balanced binary oppositions. Drawing on the spinning Taoist yin-yang, he reads the interdependent, mutually converting poles—Jack from man of science to man of faith, Sawyer from con man to protector—and the light/dark scales in Widmore's painting and the cave (Locke throwing out the white rock) as figures for a Tao whose balance sustains existence. Invoking Derrida's traces and Mahayana Buddhism's Middle Way and emptiness, he reads Jacob and the Man in Black as twins whose oppositions must be annihilated, so that only when both cease to exist in 'The End' are the castaways set free.

### Emptiness (sunyata)

Emptiness, or sunyata, is the teaching that all things lack any fixed, independent essence and exist only in dependence on causes, conditions, and conceptual designation. It was developed most rigorously by the Indian philosopher Nagarjuna, founder of the Madhyamaka school, who used relentless dialectical arguments to show that positing self-existent entities leads to contradiction. Rather than a claim that nothing exists, emptiness holds that things are real precisely because they are dependently arisen and thus without inherent nature. For Nagarjuna this insight dissolves the grasping and metaphysical confusion that bind beings to suffering.

- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 21 "Analyzing Emptiness" — Paul Gass reads the Dead's hippie milieu (the Beats, the Acid Tests, Buddhist-monk lyricist Peter Monk) as a conduit for Buddhist doctrine, taking the 'Eyes of the World' chorus as an invitation to awaken to Buddha-nature. He explains the Four Noble Truths, karma, and the five aggregates to argue the self is an illusion, using the image of a flame passed between lighters at a Dead show to picture rebirth without a persisting soul. The chapter then presents Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka middle way — emptiness itself must not be clutched as an absolute truth — and reads the 'redeemer... wagon loaded with clay' verse of 'Eyes of the World' as the Mahayana bodhisattva liberating all beings, with emptiness finally discarded like the boat after crossing the river.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 26 "Sudden Enlightenment" — Luke Cuddy and Michael Bruce ask whether Beatrix Kiddo could reach enlightenment, reading Kill Bill's nonlinear plotting as a Buddhist interconnected web of causes: Pai Mei's Five Point Palm technique causes both the coffin escape and Bill's death, and Budd's degraded trailer life is karma catching up. Beatrix grasps the structure of suffering and its cause—she locates it in Bill and the squad and eliminates them—but mistakes that for ending suffering itself, and her declared lack of 'mercy, compassion, and forgiveness' blocks the compassion enlightenment requires, while Bill's 'natural born killer' story contradicts impermanence and no-self. The chapter closes on her bathroom-floor ecstasy as a candidate case of Zen sudden enlightenment, left to the reader to judge by how she would one day treat a vengeful Nikki.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 26 "Mr. Monk Murdered Trudy" — Green argues Monk is an unintentional Bodhisattva whose OCD enacts the Four Bodhisattva Vows: the compulsion to touch lampposts is the first vow's blind desires, his monastic minimalism the Dharma gate, and his crime-solving compassion for a disordered world the third vow, with the Dhammapada's teaching that the untamed mind produces suffering exemplified by Monk and by Harold Krenshaw's rival ordering. Like Vimalakirti feigning illness, or Shawn Spencer in Psych, and like the father in the Lotus Sutra's burning-house parable, Monk and his writers use skillful deception to awaken viewers to suffering and loving kindness. The title thesis is that Monk cannot solve Trudy's murder because he accepts responsibility for it: by Thich Nhat Hanh's Interbeing there is no absolute self and other, so solving the case requires the Zen 'kill the Buddha' eradication of the self, Monk's nirvana-as-extinction and the end of the series.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 8 "2 - An Interview with Bodhidharma" — Priest stages a spoof radio interview with Bodhidharma at the Shaolin Temple to argue that the monks' fighting exercises are really meditation: a fist passing an inch from your nose focuses the mind, and repeatedly practicing violent techniques makes practitioners less violent. Bodhidharma explains that a liter of goat's milk, a marauding thug, and even the reporter's self are only conceptual labels over 'thusness' (tathata), that attachment and the desire to strike cause suffering to the striker, and that the Buddha's compassion permits self-defense without aggression. The punchline is the reporter's unanswered last question: 'They're not really about fighting, are they?'
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 34 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Bernard Wills takes the reference to The Cloud of Unknowing in 'The Window' as the key to Cohen's lifelong fascination with apophatic, negative mysticism - God sought beyond every image in a 'naked intent of love,' as in the medieval Cloud, Dionysius, Maimonides, and Kabbalah - against the kataphatic way of affirmation. He reads Recent Songs as an album of exile and the play of union and separation ('Un Canadien Errant,' 'Ballad of the Absent Mare'), where the incarnate Word is 'stuttered' and 'frozen,' a passion without resurrection. Cohen's later Zen turn is thus prefigured: the emptiness of sunyata and the Neo-Platonic descent from and return to the One are positive nothingness - self-overcoming in the service of compassion rather than the black-romantic nihilism of self-annihilation.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 36 "22. The Many-Faced God and Indian Philosophy" — Van Eyghen maps the Faceless Men onto Indian philosophy: their one God of many faces parallels Vedanta's Brahman in personal form as Ishvara, and Arya's training to become 'no one' parallels shedding the ego toward identity with Brahman - with Jaqen as guru and the stick-beating ritual as an example of identity fusion in Harvey Whitehouse's cognitive science of religion. But the Faceless Men may go further than Vedanta toward Buddhism, since they worship a god with no face of his own and aim at no-self rather than union, while Arya's pragmatic adoption of the shellfish-merchant disguise echoes the Bhagavad Gita's Krishna: perform your duty without attachment to any self.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 17 "8. Ode to Joi" — Steve Bein first tests Joi against Mary Anne Warren's five functionalist personhood criteria — consciousness, reason, self-motivated activity, communication, self-awareness — and finds she passes, which makes Luv's stomping of the emanator a murder. The Buddha's no-self doctrine then denies that anyone, Joi included, is an enduring person: we are bundles of fleeting psychophysical processes, 'like tears in rain', which threatens to let Luv plead that the Luv who killed Joi no longer exists. Nagarjuna's two truths resolve the courtroom problem: ultimately there are no persons, but conventionally 'Luv killed Joi' is perfectly true, and the karma ripples through the whole network.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 8 "Introduction" — De Cruz and De Smedt argue that ATLA subverts the Chosen One trope: Aang's training is slow and non-linear, he needs dedicated teachers, and saving the world is a team effort in which Katara leads and Sokka plans. The show's central theme is oneness, voiced by Guru Pathik's 'illusion of separation' ('The Guru') and Huu's banyan-grove tree ('The Swamp'), which the editors trace to Daoist, Huayan Buddhist (Fazang's golden lion), and Indigenous traditions of interdependence. They frame the volume's engagement with genocide, imperialism, ecological destruction, and Ba Sing Se's authoritarian denial as proof that philosophy is needed for human flourishing.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 30 "Keep the Needle on the Record" — Donavan Muir argues Lost's narrative world, unlike Jane Eyre's, requires its own metaphysics, and that this metaphysics is an order of balanced binary oppositions: Jacob and the Man in Black as twins diverged at birth, the cave scale's light and dark stones that Locke knocks out of balance in 'The Substitute,' science/faith, with characters like Jack converting from one pole into its opposite. The proper model is the yin-yang in motion - the Tao as a balanced ontological flow in which interdependent opposites wax and wane - so that treating the poles as independent is the delusion that threatens the island's order. The finale, where both Jacob and the Man in Black cease to exist and the castaways are freed, enacts the Mahayana Buddhist Middle Way: enlightenment as letting go of rigid oppositions that interdependence double-negates.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 21 "Genius All the Time The Beats, Spontaneous Presence, and Primordial Ground" — Marc Olmsted reads Beat spontaneity through Tantric (Vajrayana) Buddhism, arguing that 'first thought, best thought' and Kerouac's 'Mind is shapely, art is shapely' rest on the view that enlightenment/awareness is already present and need only be recognized. He maps Ginsberg's poetics onto the Tantric terms Ground, Path, and Fruition, tying shamatha-vipashyana practice and the doctrine of anatta (no-self) to the poet catching the first pre-conceptual thought. Ginsberg's Blake visions, his study under Trungpa and Gelek Rinpoche, and Burroughs's cut-up 'homemade yankee tantra' are offered as evidence that Beat composition enacts a Buddhist recognition of primordial, empty, self-existing awareness.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 26 "Between Social Ecology and Deep Ecology Gary Snyder’s Ecological Philosophy" — Paul Messersmith-Glavin positions Snyder as a bridge between deep ecology and social ecology. He shows how Sessions and Devall enlist Snyder's Mahayana Buddhism (emptiness/sunyata, Dogen's 'Mind means trees, fence posts, tiles, and grasses') and Spinoza's monism for a biocentric, consciousness-changing deep ecology descended from Naess and Leopold's land ethic. Against this, he sets Bookchin's social ecology, which roots the ecological crisis in human hierarchy and attacks deep ecology's ahistorical 'cosmic oneness' and misanthropic Earth First! statements. Snyder's threefold nature/wild/wilderness distinction, bioregionalism, and reading of Marx and anarchism let him hold both, insisting environmental and social justice are 'all one front.'
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 30 "Keep the Needle on the Record" — Donavan S. Muir argues that Lost deliberately withholds its metanarrative so viewers must construct its metaphysics, which he identifies as an order of balanced binary oppositions. Drawing on the spinning Taoist yin-yang, he reads the interdependent, mutually converting poles—Jack from man of science to man of faith, Sawyer from con man to protector—and the light/dark scales in Widmore's painting and the cave (Locke throwing out the white rock) as figures for a Tao whose balance sustains existence. Invoking Derrida's traces and Mahayana Buddhism's Middle Way and emptiness, he reads Jacob and the Man in Black as twins whose oppositions must be annihilated, so that only when both cease to exist in 'The End' are the castaways set free.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 84 "79. Cyberpunk 2077 as Philosophy Balancing the (Mystical) Ghost in the (Transhuman) Machine" — Lay reads Cyberpunk 2077's transhuman Night City against the enhancement debate. Using the Ship of Theseus, Parfit's continuity plus fission/fusion (V and Johnny 'fusing,' the Delamain AIs) and Clark and Chalmers's extended mind, he argues enhancement neither destroys personal identity (which Parfit says doesn't matter) nor dehumanizes users — it may be the purest expression of Clark's cyborg humanity. The real danger is corporate exploitation of bodies, explained via Adorno's culture industry and Arendt's banality of evil. Buddhist nonattachment (Nagarjuna's emptiness, echoed by a Schopenhauer shard) grounds each ending's pacification-versus-attachment theme, but Lay corrects it with Weil's critique of power and Buber's I-Thou, concluding the game urges transcending the boundary between 'me' and 'you' through mystical interpersonal relation.

### The Meaning of Life

The question of the meaning of life asks whether human existence has a point, purpose, or significance, and if so, what makes a life meaningful. Answers divide between those who locate meaning in something beyond us, such as God or an objective moral order, and those who hold that meaning is created by human beings through their projects, relationships, and values. The question gained special urgency in modern thought as traditional religious frameworks were questioned, prompting responses ranging from nihilism to existentialist affirmations of self-created purpose.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 65 "Happiness and Cypher’s Choice Is Ignorance Bliss" — Opening Griswold's essay (with Locke's line on happiness disturbed by new uneasiness as epigraph), the chapter asks why happiness - the question of existential urgency that Aristotle treated as the ultimate end of our activities - has received so little philosophical treatment (no Platonic dialogue is devoted to it) while non-philosophers assume there is an answer to be found. It presents The Matrix as a rare clever movie that genuinely presses the question of what happiness is, whether the film's answer is tenable, and how we would construct a better one of our own, with Cypher's choice as the test case.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 67 "Unknown" — Through Cypher's steak deal the chapter separates contentment - the subjective tranquility of satisfied desire, as in the contented slave, the happy tyrant, or a dog - from happiness, which must be answerable to an objective arrangement of one's life. Four thought experiments (a painless Ataraxy drug, an impostor posing as Keanu Reeves, the heating-vent fantasist imagining he is Mr. Onassis, the drunk's morning-after mirror) and Othello show self-deluded 'happiness' is unstable, truncated, and not the real thing. Happiness therefore requires reflective second-order endorsement of one's desires - wanting the desires one has - as when Neo takes the hard path of saving Morpheus, and this links happiness to a conception of the life worth living.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 29 "No Big Win" — Reads sacrifice, salvation, and redemption in the Buffyverse as secular myth: vampires manifest the shadow-side of the human (Liam's resentment becomes Angelus, William's repressed romanticism becomes Spike's rebellion), and the contrast between soulless Spike's genuine moral growth through love of Buffy and human Xander's arrested development shows redemption is measured by 'what have you done with what you've been given.' The Purpose of Evil section argues good and evil must stay in balance because without evil there is no free choice and hence no redemption, and Angel's 'no big win' epiphany — no grand plan, only lessening suffering one kindness at a time — locates life's meaning in the journey of becoming rather than final victory.
- **The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am**, ch. 12 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" — Argues The Sopranos is a morality play and existential drama, an X-rated Waiting for Godot about despair and man's search for meaning. Tony's crew are Gabbard's 'band of lost boys' fleeing Christopher's 'regularness of life' through violence: on Sartre's account they assert Being over Nothingness by acting, and on Ernest Becker's they deny death and insignificance through heroic crime. The chapter contrasts Tony's professed code of honor and family with his actual motive (the thrill of the hunt, unlike Vito Corleone's necessity) and frames the series' tension as his Janus-faced attempt to be a Machiavellian boss by day and a loving family man by night, a dichotomy he cannot sustain.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 10 "The Failure of Our Attempts at Meaning" — Conard argues that Allen's films converge on one position: life is inherently meaningless because nothing in the universe is permanent, so only something eternal (God) could ground value — and God is a self-deception ('tradition is the illusion of permanence' in Deconstructing Harry; Rabbi Ben's 'blind faith' in Crimes and Misdemeanors). He traces the impermanence argument from Mickey Sachs's mortality panic in Hannah and Her Sisters and young Alvy's dread of the expanding universe in Annie Hall, to Lloyd's 'temporary convulsion' speech in September, Sandy Bates's 'Ozymandias Melancholia' in Stardust Memories, and Louis Levy's suicide. Since real value would require permanence, Conard concludes, Allen's characters' attempts at meaning through romance (Peter's 'I have to sleep alone tonight' in September) and art (Renata's failed faith in posterity in Interiors) are merely distractions and self-deceptions we need 'like we need the air'.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 13 "Hope and Despair" — Jarvie argues Allen is a 'pragmatic optimist': since dramatizing is not arguing, no character's philosophy (not Sol's 'choose God over truth', not Levy's) can be imputed to Allen, but the ongoing act of filmmaking itself affirms that life is worth continuing. He maps optimism and despair across four films — Mickey's gun and Duck Soup epiphany in Hannah and Her Sisters, the reconstituted couples' self-deceiving rationalizations in Husbands and Wives, Harry's writer's block, and Crimes and Misdemeanors, where Judah literally gets away with murder and Ben's moral-structure faith is shown as naive. Against Sander Lee's hopeful reading of the ending, he develops criteria for interpretation: avoid the biographical fallacy and 'eisegesis', respect authorial statements unless there is overwhelming argument against them.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 28 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Bruce Reichenbach reads the film's choreographed pas de deux as three distinct theories of atonement: the conquest dance with Satan in Gethsemane (crushing the serpent of Genesis 3:15, Satan's final scream) enacts the Christus victor view of the Church Fathers; Simon of Cyrene's reluctant co-bearing of the cross illustrates Abelard's moral-influence view, though Gibson shows resilient fortitude rather than the love Abelard's theory requires to transform Simon; and Mary's mirrored 'parallel dance' makes her a co-redemptrix sharing her son's agony. Against this he sets Heidegger — Jesus grasps his death with anticipatory resolve, thrownness, and the 'moment of vision' with Mary, but dies for the Other rather than to authenticate his own life — and faults the film for omitting Anselm's (and Swinburne's) substitutionary atonement entirely: no sin, repentance, reparation, or penance appears, unlike Maximilian Kolbe's real substitution at Auschwitz.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 105 "Hope, Obligation, and the Big Picture" — Argues whether Wonder Woman's "must" really binds Superman — whether he is obliged to leave the Fortress and fight again — depends on one's eschatology or big-picture worldview. It contrasts Christian theism's purposeful culmination with naturalism, whose outlook is fixed by Bertrand Russell's "unyielding despair" passage: accidental collocations of atoms, no preservation beyond the grave, and all human achievement buried beneath the debris of a ruined universe, heroism included.
