Using the Analects' 'Upright Gong' passage (fathers and sons cover for each other) beside Plato's Euthyphro, he shows Confucius prizes the father-son bond over law, and reads the parable of the prodigal son and Tu Wei-ming's 'personality ideal' to argue fathers should lead by virtuous example rather than punishment.

### Ren (benevolence/humaneness)

Ren, often translated as benevolence, humaneness, or co-humanity, is the central virtue of Confucian ethics. It names the disposition to care for others and to treat them with the consideration one would wish for oneself, expressed in Confucius's counsel not to do to others what you would not want done to you. For Confucius, ren is the inner moral quality that animates all the virtues and marks the fully realized human being, cultivated through self-discipline and relationships rather than merely followed as a rule.

- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 30 "Every Soul Experiences the Battle Within" — Reads Zuko's arc as a war between Legalism and Confucianism: Ozai's agni kai scarring of his son, Azulon's death sentence, the Fire Nation Oath and school discipline ('The Headband') all enact Han Fei's principle that bad human nature needs terrifying sanctions, and Azula's 'trust is for fools' completes it. Against this stands Iroh's Confucian education in ren — teaching that honor cannot be separated from humaneness, that a mugger deserves tea and encouragement, and that wu-wei-like patience knows when to speak. Mencius's innate compassion explains why Zuko's 'amazing lie' realization could unfold, Katara, Sokka, and Hakoda embody Confucian filial bonds that adopt Aang, Toph, and finally Zuko, and Solzhenitsyn's gulag insight closes the chapter: the line between good and evil runs through every human heart.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 30 "Every Soul Experiences the Battle Within" — Reads the Fire Nation royal family as a philosophical battle between Legalism (Han Fei, taking Xunzi's dictum that human nature is evil, so order requires terrifying sanctions: Ozai burning Zuko in the agni kai so 'suffering will be your teacher', Azulon's death sentence on Zuko, the Fire Nation Oath recited in schools) and Confucianism (Iroh teaching ren, that true honor cannot be had apart from humaneness, preferring honorable begging over theft, and talking a would-be mugger into tea). Zuko's 'battle within' is the legacy of his two great-grandfathers, Sozin's Legalism versus Roku's line, and it is resolved when he disowns Ozai, calls Iroh his 'real father', and is adopted into Team Avatar, whose filial bonds (Katara's care, Hakoda's sacrifice) contrast with the scheming royal family. The chapter closes with Solzhenitsyn's image of the line between good and evil passing through every human heart to explain why Zuko's inner war resonates.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 11 "“Your Heart Knows”" — Argues that Disney's Mulan transplants a distinctly modern Western ideal of the authentic self ('true to your heart,' 'Reflection') into a Confucian honor culture where the self is constituted by roles and relationships, filial piety (xiao), and ren as the virtue that binds people into larger wholes — which is why the film flopped in China. The matchmaker debacle, Fa Zhou's 'I will die doing what's right,' and the family's shame show a culture where dishonor stains the whole family and even luck (the cricket Cri-Kee) fixes moral standing, conflicting with Western assumptions about individual responsibility. The chapter ends by noting Mulan now resonates with young Chinese viewers, asking whether the Western individualist self is a truth about humanity or a cultural export that, like the Huns, has scaled the Great Wall.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 32 "The Rhythm by Which We Live Our Lives" — Kowalski interprets Kuzco's arc through Mencius: the emperor's pampered upbringing (eight hands replacing a squeezed toy, Yzma's loveless regency) is the 'hatchets and frost' of the Ox Mountain parable blunting his innate moral sprouts. The gorge scene stages Mencius's child-at-the-well thought experiment — Kuzco's spontaneous snatch of falling Pacha is a 'give-away' action betraying compassion he denies having, which Pacha diagnoses just as Mencius did King Xuan sparing the ox — and Pacha's family, quasi-adopting Kuzco, supplies the loving soil Mencius says the sprouts of ren need to grow.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 12 "Notes" — Decker parallels the Republic's fall into Palpatine's Empire with the Zhou dynasty's collapse that birthed Chinese philosophy, reading three Jedi from the Dark Times comics through it. K'Kruhk, guided by the Zatoichi-like Master Zao, learns wu-wei - following the Force rather than forcing outcomes, with Laozi's Dao as the Force's Chinese analogue. Dass Jennir's struggle over what 'Jedi' means after killing a slaver becomes Confucian rectification of names and the cultivation of ren, while Kai Hudorra's loss of faith, withdrawal to a casino, and final sacrificial stand against Vader embody Mozi-style pragmatic minimalism redeemed by Jennir's virtuous example.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 31 "“Tell Your Sister, You Were Right”" — Yang argues that Luke's surrender to Vader on Endor is neither foolish nor irrational but an exercise of Confucian filial piety: Luke reveres the absent Anakin as an exemplar (picked out through admiration of Obi-Wan's stories and the lightsaber), insists 'I know there is good in you' against Vader's claim that the name means nothing, and is vindicated when Anakin turns and says 'You were right about me'. His imperfect training under Obi-Wan and Yoda functions like Confucian ritual (li), forming habits that respond with harmonious ease to surprises such as Palpatine's trap, and filial piety extends past death in the funeral pyre Luke builds on Endor, honoring his father as the Analects prescribes.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 31 "NOTES" — The Terjesens pit Kant's impersonal morality — Sam's contractual distance from the thieving Mickens is exactly how he would treat strangers — against Confucius and Mencius, for whom filial duties are the nursery of virtue: we learn benevolence by serving parents and revering elders, Lafayette's care for Lettie Mae and Tara shows family forming moral character, and the Upright Gong's covering for a father's sheep-stealing grounds Jason's 'sometimes the right thing to do is the wrong thing'. Mencius's King Shun, who abdicates and carries his criminal father into exile, models how Tommy and Jason should put family first while accepting the cost, while Mozi's universal love surfaces in Godric's 'forgiveness is love', and the chapter concludes that family counts only insofar as it develops our moral nature — the line between Tommy and Sam.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 12 "Third Hole Finding the (Fair)Way with Confucius and Ben Hogan" — Laumakis builds an analogy between pursuing excellence in golf and living a flourishing human life, then contrasts two models. Reading Confucius's Great Learning and Analects onto golf, he casts a repeating swing as a 'well-ordered kingdom' rooted in self-cultivation, and reinterprets ren, li, yi, and xiao so the 'authoritative player' masters the game through ritual practice, a teacher-parent (xiao), and doing what is appropriate in each lie. Against this social conception he sets Ben Hogan's Five Lessons as a 'rugged individualist' account stressing solitary practice and personal responsibility, and proposes a contextual pluralism as a mean between communitarian absolutism and individualist relativism.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 29 "Fourteenth Hole Plato and Confucius on the Form of Golf From the Real to the Ideal" — Stephen Laumakis stages a thought experiment pitting Plato the Idealist against Confucius the Realist/Pragmatist on how to think about and play golf. On Plato's theory of Forms, every club, ball and swing is an imperfect copy of a timeless, unchanging Form—there is a 'perfect' swing (Tiger Woods, Ernie Els) that par and the handicap system let us measure ourselves against, so golf is about striving toward the Ideal. Confucius, read through the 'Great Learning' and 'Analects' (li, ren, self-cultivation, unrelenting practice), instead prizes the situation-sensitive sage who negotiates each bad lie (Phil Mickelson's flop shots). Laumakis concludes the good golfer must integrate both: pursue perfection while wielding practical wisdom about when to go for it and when to lay up.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — The editors' introduction argues that the unifying theme of Lee's films is the struggle for authentic self-identity, framed through Charles Taylor's dialogical self and Kierkegaard's line that anxiety is the dizziness of freedom. It surveys how Confucian virtues (ren, li, xiao) and Daoist wu-wei play out across Pushing Hands, The Wedding Banquet, Eat Drink Man Woman, Crouching Tiger, Sense and Sensibility, Brokeback Mountain and others, treating each protagonist as caught between traditional obligation and personal desire. It invokes Nietzsche's claim that all philosophy is autobiography to justify reading Lee's films (he said 'it's all in my films') as a coherent authorial philosophy.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Kohler-Ryan and Palmer treat 'sense' and 'sensibility' as a spectrum Lee explores through sisterhood in Sense and Sensibility (Elinor/Marianne) and Crouching Tiger (Shu Lien/Jen). Elinor and Shu Lien embody sense, Shu Lien specifically the Confucian balance of li and ren that lets her soften ritual with humanity; Marianne embodies Burke's British-Romantic sublime while Jen embodies Daoist immersion in the dao. Reading door-frames, windows, hair-combing rituals and Shu Lien's hairpin as symbols, they argue only Sense and Sensibility achieves integration in time, whereas Li Mu Bai's confession that he lived sense and sensibility as separate spheres comes too late.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Bush argues that Brokeback Mountain transcends both the heterosexual western archetype and queer theory by presenting male sexuality through Mencius' philosophy and John Corvino's ethics of homosexuality. Using Mencius' four sprouts (ren, li, yi, zhi) and doctrine of natural goodness, he reads Ennis as the character in whom sexuality is contextual, cultivated and moral rather than merely physical, so the relationship between Ennis and Jack becomes an ethical friendship grounded in ren, the virtue Mencius says is most intense among friends. The bystanders Aguirre and Alma keeping the secret, and the final shirt-and-postcard scene, illustrate zhi as contextual moral judgment and homosexuality reframed as ethical rather than sexual.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 23 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Komasinski explains Confucius's advice to fathers through three ideas: ritual (li, glossed as 'cultural grammar' – engagement rings, saying 'I love you'), excellence/virtue as excelling at relating to others (ren, 'co-humanity'), and wisdom. Using the Analects' 'Upright Gong' passage (fathers and sons cover for each other) beside Plato's Euthyphro, he shows Confucius prizes the father-son bond over law, and reads the parable of the prodigal son and Tu Wei-ming's 'personality ideal' to argue fathers should lead by virtuous example rather than punishment.

### The Tao (the Way)

The Tao, or the Way, is the central notion of Daoism: the nameless, formless source and ordering principle from which all things arise and to which they return. In the Daodejing, associated with Laozi, the Tao is said to be beyond full description or definition—"the Tao that can be spoken is not the eternal Tao"—yet it can be sensed and followed by those who cultivate stillness and simplicity. Living well means aligning oneself with this natural course rather than resisting it through force, ambition, or excessive contrivance.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 14 "Was it a Show about Nothing" — Eric Bronson takes George's NBC pitch for 'a show about nothing' as a live philosophical problem: Parmenides argued we cannot meaningfully speak of what-is-not (so Art Vandelay is unsayable), but Plato's Sophist answers that nothing is 'otherness' with real power - the puffy shirt is something other than beautiful, and 'The Parking Garage' is doing something other than what is interesting or useful. Lao Tzu's Tao Te Ching goes further: the nameless Tao begets the ten thousand things, and wei wu wei (action through non-action) conquers, as in 'The Chinese Restaurant', where a whole episode of standing in line doing nothing is itself something happening.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 29 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Jennifer McMahon and Steve Csaki compare Tolkien with Zen Buddhism and Taoism on four themes while insisting on the real differences. Tolkien's talking trees (Old Man Willow, Treebeard's 'half awake' forest) invite comparison with Buddhist universal sentience and Dogen's walking mountains, but Tolkien anthropomorphizes where Buddhism grants non-human modes of sentience; the hobbits' ties to the Shire echo dependent origination, though Tolkien's stewardship and preference for the domesticated Shire over sinister wild nature remain Western. Frodo's succession of mentors (Bilbo, Gandalf, Aragorn, and the unlikely 'Master Samwise') parallels the Zen master-student relation, while Tolkien's war of light against darkness - nine Walkers against nine Riders - is decisively not the Taoist balance of yin and yang, for Taoists destroying either cosmic force would itself produce evil.
- **The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am**, ch. 14 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" — Argues Tony misappropriates Sun Tzu's Art of War: he applies tactical precepts like deception, formlessness and 'Balk the enemy's power' (citing the book in 'He Is Risen' after Melfi's jab in 'Big Girls Don't Cry'), but ignores the philosophical core. The chapter contrasts Sun Tzu's monistic one-world view of yin-yang interdependence, harmony and winning without fighting with the Greek two-world dualism of Plato and with the Christianity that lets Tony tell Melfi 'soldiers don't go to hell' in 'From Where to Eternity'. Tony's sausage panic attacks in 'Fortunate Son' show his failure to see how his crimes ripple through his family, and because he lacks the commander's exemplary character and harmony, Tony is 'just a soldier', not a ruler.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 29 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Jones narrates a day riding a customized Sportster around O'ahu as a lived Daoism that heals the Platonic-Cartesian mind-body split: the ride enacts Zhuangzi's 'rambling without destination' and Cook Ding's effortless wu-wei, rider li (the low hand-greeting among riders) is Confucian ritual propriety, and the island's dry and wet ranges embody yin and yang through whose flow the rider blends. Heraclitus's 'expect the unexpected' and 'the sun is new every day' are vindicated when a container truck stops short and only the disciplined, ego-less low-side, dropping the beloved bike while riding the skid, saves the rider's life, sealing the day's lesson that there is never freedom without discipline. Sartre's hell of other people appears in the cagers' compartmentalized inattention, and the chapter closes with Zhuangzi: 'The way is made by walking it.'
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 46 "Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat" — In a fictional interview with the Taoist sage "Bat-Tzu," Mark White explains Taoism through Batman's circle: Bruce's yang-dominated life of vengeance and paranoia needs the yin that Dick and Tim supply, shown by his forgiveness of Zatanna and tenderness toward Helena's baby, while Jason Todd illustrates the fate of the unbalanced who cannot accept death. Alfred emerges as the Taoist sage practicing wei-wu-wei, effortless service like Chuang Tzu's butcher, balancing right and wrong in Bruce, and the Batman-Joker duality shows yin and yang defining each other. Lao Tzu's sayings on balance, complementary opposites, and water-like yielding organize the whole reading.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 10 "I Still Miss Someone The Self and Its Travels Along the Way" — Geisz explains the Confucian social dao of ritual (li), humaneness (ren), filial piety and the junzi, the Daodejing's metaphysical Dao with its unity of opposites, and Zhuangzi's tales of free wandering, then maps all three onto Cash's songs. Zhuangzi's "Free and Easy Wandering" answers Cash's road songs ("I've Been Everywhere," "The Wanderer"), Cook Ding's effortless carving answers John Henry's hammering in "The Legend of John Henry's Hammer," and the scrambled countdown of "Twenty-Five Minutes to Go" echoes Zhuangzi's logic-bending humor. The payoff is Cash's own country Yin-Yang of interdependent opposites, freedom chained to imprisonment ("Folsom Prison Blues"), sin twinned with redemption ("I Hung My Head"), fidelity with betrayal ("Jackson," "Cocaine Blues"), and a self that, unlike Zhuangzi's self-forgetting sage, must travel a temporal path carrying its guilt, yet stays on what Geisz calls a very wide superhighway of a Dao.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 38 "Teddy Baseball" — Lee reads Ted Williams's The Science of Hitting as a Daoist skill story from the Zhuangzi: 'get a good ball to hit' matches the cicada-catcher's total absorption in the cicada's wings, hitting 'by feel' like the carpenter's hammer matches Cook Ding carving without looking, and Williams's midnight batting practice after Korea matches the wheelwright grown old at his craft—effortless spontaneity produced by disciplined practice and unified attention, not mere mechanics. Williams's 'proper thinking' is Daoist sorting of objective conditions rather than abstract disputation. The closing tale of the old woman who cannot teach the Way to someone lacking the stuff explains why Williams failed as Senators manager: his players did not have the native talent to receive it.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 20 "The End" — Chan contrasts Zhuangzi's butterfly dream, where dream and reality form one transformable whole and the self is forgotten, with Inception's dreams, which are rigidly structured and must be kept strictly separate from reality for Cobb to function. She shows that the film's motifs (the dream machine, the spinning top, the faceless children) work as narrative codes marking each dream layer, making Inception an example of 'dream explaining' rather than Tarkovsky-style 'dream worshipping'. The chapter concludes that Inception's 'dreams' are really a meta-space narrative device, as in Nolan's short Doodlebug, and that the film lacks the Daoist sense of the whole, so Cobb can never transform into the butterfly.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 36 "Psych and Philosophy" — John Thompson argues Psych embodies the Daoist Way of reversal from the Daodejing and Zhuangzi: every episode begins with a death that triggers Shawn and Gus's irreverent, backwards-tracing investigation, their untrained spontaneous 'gifts' exemplify wu wei like Cook Ding carving an ox, and their bickering partnership is yin-yang interplay (as when Gus leads the joking in 'An Evening with Mr. Yang'). Zhuangzi singing at his wife's funeral parallels the Shabby the Sea Lion and 'Dust in the Wind' funeral parodies, the show's blurred TV-versus-fandom reality echoes the butterfly dream, Lassiter succeeds when he relaxes into wu wei ('Feet Don't Kill Me Now'), and the closing bloopers enact Dao's endless reversal - though the chapter ends by conceding Dao defies the very label 'Daoist show.'
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 36 "22. The Dao of Master Westley" — Doll tests each character against the Dao: Confucius's identification of the Dao with tradition and ritual fails because Florinese tradition is exactly what enables Humperdinck's murder and war plans, so she turns to Laozi's De and wu-wei, diagnosing Vizzini's fatal overconfidence (he lacked Socratic knowledge of his own ignorance), Humperdinck's paranoia, and Buttercup's passivity as failures to sense when to act and when to refrain. Westley emerges as Zhuangzi's ideal - like Cook Ting the butcher, mastering skills until instinct suffices: adapting through the Fire Swamp, treating Vizzini's death as 'an appropriate death', yet sparing Inigo and Fezzik because killing them would be against nature, which is why the giant and the Spaniard accept him as their sage.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 42 "27. The Mystic with the Mouth" — In a lecture Deadpool keeps interrupting, the chapter reads the Merc's violence through Bataille's Theory of Religion: sacrifice as the search for lost intimacy, killing as the moment sacrificer and victim escape the profane world of mere things into sacred immanence, and sovereignty as the freedom glimpsed in destruction, with Rudolf Otto's mysterium tremendum et fascinans naming the awe Deadpool's massacres (the Circle Chase nunchuks, the Ultimate cartoon, the movie's highway slaughter) provoke. His 'dark Dao' of unhappy wandering is then set against the playful ways of the Zhuangzi - Cook Ding's ox-butchering, the Peng bird, the maimed teacher Wang Tai - as a Daoist path of inner-worldly transcendence that is amoral and gore-soaked. The payoff is the human tension of being both animal and angel: Deadpool is 'a savage god of mystical mayhem.'
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 27 "15. Farts, Butterflies, and Inner Truth" — Franklin Perkins reads Frank's fear that his jewelry business might start World War III — 'you can't fart without changing the balance in the universe' — as the butterfly-effect problem of acting inside a complexity we cannot grasp, from the Roosevelt assassination down to Tagomi's Colt .44. Against the Germans' fatal flight into abstraction (Volk, Blut, Ehre), the chapter presents the I Ching, read through Chinese correlative cosmology of the Tao and yin-yang, as a manual for mole-like, concrete, adaptive interpretation in which each casting (hexagram 11's 'wall falls back into the moat,' the purple knee bands) means only through creative engagement, ending with hexagram 61: our world arose as contingently as a throw of the yarrow stalks.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 27 "The Way of the Archer" — White reads Clint Barton through the Tao Te Ching and Chuang Tzu: Hawkeye's instinctive archery—'use your bow gently, naturally, instinctively'—is wei wu wei, while his bragging, his glory-chasing failure against Iron Man, and his attempt to become Goliath all violate it by striving against his own nature, until the Kree-Skrull War teaches him the bow is his way. Chuang Tzu's butcher carves the lesson that the effortless path (the straightforward shot) is the skilled one, and Lao Tzu's sage-leadership—lowering oneself, deflecting praise—is exactly how Captain America handles Clint's insurrections. Lao Tzu on sages putting themselves last illuminates Hawkeye's sacrificial death and his legacy passed to Kate Bishop, while the butterfly dream frames his resurrection and the House of M's rewritten reality: with no way to compare the states, life and death are both to be welcomed as parts of the Way.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 34 "NOTES" — The book's final chapter is a mock interview in which 'Bat-Tzu' applies Taoism to Bruce Wayne's life: his yang (hard, retributive crime-fighting) has dominated his yin (his tenderness toward Dick, Tim, and Helena), and Robin has always been the yin balancing the Dark Knight. Quoting Lao-Tzu's Tao Te Ching and Chuang-Tzu on duality, acceptance of death (Jason Todd's resurrection), and effortlessness, the piece casts Alfred as the Taoist sage whose help exemplifies wu-wei, like Chuang-Tzu's butcher who cuts without dulling his blade. It even reads Batman's most intimidating feature, his absent shadow, as proof that nothingness can matter more than substance.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 15 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Lynch tests the fan claims that the Dude is 'the Duddha' or a practicing Daoist: the Dude has wu wei in his effortless arts of bowling and abiding and shares Zhuangzi's withdrawal from society (the Nixon bowling poster, learning from drunks, Donny's ashes scattered with naturalistic acceptance), but lacks Daoist metaphysics, the Dao's inexpressibility, and any articulated views. The Buddha parallels are real — nonattachment, practice over theory (the poisoned-arrow parable), compassion for Bunny — yet Gautama's radical discipline and middle path are the opposite of the Dude's laziness, so Dudeism emerges as an undisciplined American cousin, and the Dude follows 'just his way and his alone'.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 14 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Morgan Deane reads Ender's tactics as Sunzi's Art of War in action: winning all future fights by terror, exploiting Bonzo's hot anger, 'fatal terrain' when Graff stacks hopeless odds, formlessness that hides intent, and fluid toon formations that move like water — all grounded in Daoist harmony with the Way and the Confucian role-duty of the general-as-father who throws soldiers into hopeless positions to win their devotion. He also finds Legalist rewards-and-punishments in Ender's command of Dragon Army, concluding Ender qualifies as a Sunzi-style military genius whose empathy is the steep moral price of victory.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 10 "a3.xhtml" — Brannigan reads Bilbo's tug-of-war between Baggins security and Took adventure through Taoism: the two desires are not contradictory but the interplay of yin and yang, and true dwelling is found in the journey itself, as the 'Roads go ever on' song says. Greed is the great weight - Thorin enslaved by the treasure he 'never forgot', Smaug hoarding for hoarding's sake, even the orc-loving of machines - and the cure is the mirror-mind of Empty Mind that reflects without grasping, illustrated by the Taoist masters tale of 'Gold-Is-Heavy' and 'Empty-Mind'. Beorn, who lives on honey indifferent to gold, and Bilbo, who in the spirit of wu-wei sheds his desire for the Arkenstone and finally lets go of the Ring, embody life in harmony with the Tao.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 20 "The End" — Hiu M. Chan contrasts Zhuangzi's butterfly dream with Inception's plot: Zhuangzi forgets his self, dreams without planning, and ends in the 'transformation and unity' of dreamer and butterfly, whereas Cobb's self is constantly highlighted — he plans missions, codes his dreams with motifs (the spinning top, the dream machine, the faceless children, distinct locations, weather, crosscutting), and can never fuse dream and reality. The chapter maps the film's four-layer 'meta-space' narrative structure (exposition through resolution distributed across dream layers) and argues the 'dreams' are really programmed, coded narrative devices, the opposite of the Daoist 'whole' in which reality itself is the biggest dream and a true person no longer dreams. Against semiotic 'dream explaining' (the top means dreaming), she holds that in Daoism the top would mean nothing beyond a spinning top, and contrasts Nolan with Tarkovsky's 'dream worshipping' films like The Mirror. The ending's reunion is thus only apparent: Inception lacks the Daoist harmony that would let Cobb 'become the butterfly.'
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 28 "Notes" — Bein reads the LEGO brick as the Daodejing's 'uncarved block': a single brick is an invitation rather than a toy, and precisely because it is empty of meaning (and mostly empty of plastic — the stud-and-tube marriage of yin and yang) it can become anything, whereas printed, specialized pieces 'are diminished by being added to'. Against the Greek obsession with definition — Socrates refusing sophistry while insisting one cannot rule justly without defining justice, Plato's definition dialogues, Aristotle's inheritance of the precision ideal, and William James's 'think clearly' — Daoist imprecision is defended as a philosophical stance: dao is a way, an activity, not a thing. Wei wu wei ('doing without doing') explains Emmet's winning plan of building the utterly ordinary Octan spaceship, why Lord Business's penny-throw is genius without sagacity (coercive, not water-like), and why governing should be like cooking a small fish — minimal, attentive intervention.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 29 "NOTE" — Shai Biderman and William Devlin argue the character John Locke begins as an empiricist in the mold of his philosophical namesake - his boar hunting, tracking, and trebuchet-building against the hatch all follow the scientific method befitting a tabula rasa mind furnished by experience - but the miracle of his healed legs poses a 'why' that empirical explanation of 'how' cannot answer. He therefore converts to the Taoism of the Tao Te Ching: the moth-cocoon lesson to Charlie, 'I stopped looking' for Sun's ring, reading dreams and signs from the island, and finally his self-sacrifice to stop the time flashes all enact following the Way. The chapter reads the black-and-white backgammon stones, Locke's one-black-one-white eyes in Claire's dream, and Jacob versus the Man in Black as yin-yang complementarity, with empiricism and Taoism finally interdependent like the dots in each half.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 30 "Keep the Needle on the Record" — Donavan Muir argues Lost's narrative world, unlike Jane Eyre's, requires its own metaphysics, and that this metaphysics is an order of balanced binary oppositions: Jacob and the Man in Black as twins diverged at birth, the cave scale's light and dark stones that Locke knocks out of balance in 'The Substitute,' science/faith, with characters like Jack converting from one pole into its opposite. The proper model is the yin-yang in motion - the Tao as a balanced ontological flow in which interdependent opposites wax and wane - so that treating the poles as independent is the delusion that threatens the island's order. The finale, where both Jacob and the Man in Black cease to exist and the castaways are freed, enacts the Mahayana Buddhist Middle Way: enlightenment as letting go of rigid oppositions that interdependence double-negates.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 12 "Notes" — Decker parallels the Republic's fall into Palpatine's Empire with the Zhou dynasty's collapse that birthed Chinese philosophy, reading three Jedi from the Dark Times comics through it. K'Kruhk, guided by the Zatoichi-like Master Zao, learns wu-wei - following the Force rather than forcing outcomes, with Laozi's Dao as the Force's Chinese analogue. Dass Jennir's struggle over what 'Jedi' means after killing a slaver becomes Confucian rectification of names and the cultivation of ren, while Kai Hudorra's loss of faith, withdrawal to a casino, and final sacrificial stand against Vader embody Mozi-style pragmatic minimalism redeemed by Jennir's virtuous example.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 10 "Notes" — Schiltz reads Isaac McAdoo as a Zhuangzian sage: his virtuoso haircut scene in 'Man City' parallels Zhuangzi's butcher who carves oxen by following the natural seams of the dao, and his candid, simple, guileless character mirrors the Daoist mistrust of complexity and language. Isaac's slump in 'Rainbow' is diagnosed as lost wu-wei ('all up in his head'), cured by Roy's no-stakes pickup games that restore effortless action, and Laozi's 'ruling a great state is like cooking a small fish' explains Isaac's wordless leadership during Sam's Dubai Air protest and the suit-wearing gesture at Rebecca's father's funeral.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 23 "The Dao of Hoops" — Dirk Dunbar, a former professional player, argues that Daoist concepts illuminate basketball excellence and that the sport can be a path to the Dao. Balancing yin and yang means blending competition with surrender and strategy with spontaneity; Zhuangzi's archer shows how craving victory drains power. Wuwei explains the 'zone' of effortless play Dunbar experienced while scoring sixty-five points in a high school game and seventy-four in Iceland, while qi grounds free-throw breathing and visualization and ziran the discipline of releasing a shot without willing it in. Drawing on Daode jing verses and Phil Jackson's Sacred Hoops, he claims basketball teaches a life of disciplined surrender beyond the ego.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 27 "Thirteenth Hole Free and Easy Wandering on the Golf Course Swing Like a Taoist" — Scott F. Parker reads golf's paradox—that you play your best shot when you stop trying so hard—through the Taoism of the 'Tao Te Ching' and the 'Chuang Tzu.' Using the parable of the archer (skill is constant but attachment to the prize ruins the shot), Cook Ting carving the ox by spirit not force, and Master Yu accepting his deformity, he draws out nonattachment to results, 'doing without doing' (wei wu wei), and self-knowledge/self-acceptance, illustrated by Zach Johnson never going for a par 5 in two at the 2007 Masters and Tiger Woods rarely swinging all-out. The essay embodies the Taoist point that the Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao: to try to not-try is self-defeating, so one must simply not try.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — McRae reads Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon as a dramatization of the tension between Confucian humanism and Daoist naturalism over how to cultivate an authentic 'focus-field' self. Li Mu Bai and Yu Shu Lien are exemplary persons (junzi) bound by the wuxia code and li, unable to voice their love, while Jen rebels into criminal freedom under Jade Fox; Li's use of the green bamboo forest against Jen embodies wu-wei and rou (yielding suppleness). It argues that authentic self-cultivation, and Jen's final leap, require balancing Daoist natural freedom against Confucian roles, since freedom without relationships exacts a fatal price.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Kohler-Ryan and Palmer treat 'sense' and 'sensibility' as a spectrum Lee explores through sisterhood in Sense and Sensibility (Elinor/Marianne) and Crouching Tiger (Shu Lien/Jen). Elinor and Shu Lien embody sense, Shu Lien specifically the Confucian balance of li and ren that lets her soften ritual with humanity; Marianne embodies Burke's British-Romantic sublime while Jen embodies Daoist immersion in the dao. Reading door-frames, windows, hair-combing rituals and Shu Lien's hairpin as symbols, they argue only Sense and Sensibility achieves integration in time, whereas Li Mu Bai's confession that he lived sense and sensibility as separate spheres comes too late.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 23 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Hole reads The Ice Storm's prophetic opening as a meditation on 'what is impending', weaving existentialism with Zen Buddhism and Daoism. He uses the Four Noble Truths and the Zen story of the monk 'still carrying the woman' to show the families suffer through attachment to rigid self-images, and Jung's synchronicity and the Daoist dao/wu-wei to read the ice storm's formation and Mikey's chance electrocution as an interdependent flow the characters resist. Centrally he applies Heidegger's being-toward-death—death as ownmost, non-relational, not-to-be-outstripped—arguing that fleeing one's death is fleeing one's authentic being, alongside Kierkegaard's leap of faith and Nietzsche's living dangerously; he closes by applying the argument to his own mortality.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 19 "10. The Dao of Psychohistory" — Fried reframes Asimov's binary (do individual choices matter to history?) through four Chinese theories of non-action (wu wei). Confucian non-action, ruling by moral example and retiring under an unjust ruler, illuminates Onum Barr's dignified private life; the Dao De Jing's mystical libertarianism, where people self-transform when the ruler stops intervening, resembles Gaia's ruler-less holism; Legalist impersonal non-action (Han Fei's ruler who hides his desires and lets harsh law act) has no clear Foundation analogue; and Zhuangzi's useless tree models Gaal Dornick's TV arc, in which she reclaims agency precisely by choosing private non-action over a scripted role in galactic history.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 46 "Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat" — In a mock interview with 'Bat-Tzu' (a disguised Alfred), Mark White explains Taoism through Batman. Bruce is dangerously dominated by yang after his parents' deaths and needs the yin balance that Robin (Dick as the lighthearted 'Batman with a feminine side') and his spiritual quest restore; Batman's fear-inducing shadow illustrates Lao-Tzu's usefulness of nothingness. Alfred is the Taoist sage embodying wei-wu-wei - 'action without action' - quietly serving like Chuang-Tzu's effortless butcher and like water that wears down stone, harmonizing Bruce's warring opposites toward the Way.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 29 "NOTE" — Shai Biderman and William J. Devlin trace John Locke the character's shift from the empiricism of his philosophical namesake to Taoism. Early Locke is the tabula-rasa empiricist and scientific-method hunter and hatch-engineer, but his miraculous restored ability to walk, Jacob's touch, and his visions push him to ask 'why' rather than 'how.' They argue Locke comes to follow the Tao—the unnamable Way symbolized by the black-and-white yin-yang seen in backgammon pieces and Claire's dream—advising Charlie via the struggling moth, teaching Walt to visualize the knife's path, and finding Sun's ring by not looking, ultimately reading his sacrificial death as effortless surrender to the island's flow.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 30 "Keep the Needle on the Record" — Donavan S. Muir argues that Lost deliberately withholds its metanarrative so viewers must construct its metaphysics, which he identifies as an order of balanced binary oppositions. Drawing on the spinning Taoist yin-yang, he reads the interdependent, mutually converting poles—Jack from man of science to man of faith, Sawyer from con man to protector—and the light/dark scales in Widmore's painting and the cave (Locke throwing out the white rock) as figures for a Tao whose balance sustains existence. Invoking Derrida's traces and Mahayana Buddhism's Middle Way and emptiness, he reads Jacob and the Man in Black as twins whose oppositions must be annihilated, so that only when both cease to exist in 'The End' are the castaways set free.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 15 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Hathaway and Sharpley analyze the cannabis experience of medical-'compassion club' users through Csikszentmihalyi's concept of 'flow.' They ground flow in William James's 'stream of consciousness' and in Taoism, reading Tao as 'a patterned flow of the universe' and wu wei as the effortless equilibrium users describe ('it just centers me,' 'I take an inventory on my soul'). Against Western monophasic medicine, they defend users' 'anecdotal' testimony as legitimate knowledge of a body–mind–spirit balance that cannabis restores.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 8 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — John Friend's foreword surveys yoga's three classical philosophical systems and connects them to how modern Hatha yoga is practiced: Classical (Patanjali) yoga as separating purusha (spirit) from prakriti (matter) to reach kaivalya; Vedanta as neutralizing maya to realize the unity of atman with the supreme; and non-dual Tantra, from which Hatha yoga derives, treating body and mind as frequencies of one divine Shiva-Shakti energy. It argues yoga's enduring claim is that the essential self is free, and that direct lived experience of that freedom outranks merely intellectual knowledge of the texts.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 46 "Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat" — White stages a mock interview with "Bat-Tzu" (revealed to be Alfred) to read Batman through Taoism. Lao-Tzu and Chuang-Tzu supply the ideal of balancing yin and yang: Bruce lets his hard, vengeful yang dominate and needs Robin's yin, while Dick keeps balance and Tim risks losing his. Bruce's intimidating shadow illustrates the usefulness of nothingness, and Chuang-Tzu's teaching on accepting death frames Jason Todd's fate. Alfred embodies the Taoist sage — wei-wu-wei, water-like flexibility, and effortless, unspoken guidance.

### Wu Wei (effortless action)

Wu wei, often translated as effortless action or non-forcing, is the Daoist ideal of acting in accordance with the natural flow of things rather than against it. It does not mean doing nothing, but acting without strain, coercion, or self-assertive striving, so that one's conduct arises spontaneously and fits the situation, as water finds its own path around obstacles. Associated with Laozi and the Daodejing, wu wei holds that the most effective and harmonious results come from restraint and responsiveness rather than aggressive control.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 14 "Was it a Show about Nothing" — Eric Bronson takes George's NBC pitch for 'a show about nothing' as a live philosophical problem: Parmenides argued we cannot meaningfully speak of what-is-not (so Art Vandelay is unsayable), but Plato's Sophist answers that nothing is 'otherness' with real power - the puffy shirt is something other than beautiful, and 'The Parking Garage' is doing something other than what is interesting or useful. Lao Tzu's Tao Te Ching goes further: the nameless Tao begets the ten thousand things, and wei wu wei (action through non-action) conquers, as in 'The Chinese Restaurant', where a whole episode of standing in line doing nothing is itself something happening.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 11 "“Great Warrior Wars Not Make One Great”" — Robinson (a Zen monk) argues the Force is best understood as ch'i and the Jedi path as philosophical Taoism and Zen: the Light and Dark Sides are the yin-yang polarity whose 'balance' Anakin's prophecy restores, and Anakin's fall is the Buddhist three poisons - clinging attachment to his mother and Padme breeding fear, anger, and hate. Yoda's teaching is Zen practice: 'You must unlearn what you have learned' is wu-wei (effortless action), 'Do or do not' rejects the divided mind of trying, and the Dagobah cave parallels the sword master Tesshu's koan insight that the real enemy is one's own mind ('no-enemy'). The chapter also traces Jedi genealogy to Bodhidharma's Shaolin kung-fu, the Korean Hwa Rang and Japanese Sohei warrior monks, and Bushido's samurai code, noting 'Jedi' derives from 'jidai geki'.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 13 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Priest argues that Pirsig's Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance is far more genuinely Zen than its disclaimer admits: once riding becomes effortless, the dissolution of the subject-object distinction that Dogen calls genjokoan arrives on the open road ('you ARE the driving and the road and the elements'), and the Harley's relaxed posture and low-revving thug-thug-thug rhythm make it a better vehicle for suchness than cars or whinier bikes. Even maintenance done as an end in itself is genjokoan, and because ultimate reality erases every conceptual distinction, care of self, others, and the bike amount to the same thing, the Mahayana ground of compassion; the mountain-and-water Zen saying resolves the paradox that the unconceptualized and the conceptualized are one. Suffering, on the Buddhist diagnosis Priest applies, comes from imposing conceptual grids that see the world wrong, and seeing it aright dissolves it.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 29 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Jones narrates a day riding a customized Sportster around O'ahu as a lived Daoism that heals the Platonic-Cartesian mind-body split: the ride enacts Zhuangzi's 'rambling without destination' and Cook Ding's effortless wu-wei, rider li (the low hand-greeting among riders) is Confucian ritual propriety, and the island's dry and wet ranges embody yin and yang through whose flow the rider blends. Heraclitus's 'expect the unexpected' and 'the sun is new every day' are vindicated when a container truck stops short and only the disciplined, ego-less low-side, dropping the beloved bike while riding the skid, saves the rider's life, sealing the day's lesson that there is never freedom without discipline. Sartre's hell of other people appears in the cagers' compartmentalized inattention, and the chapter closes with Zhuangzi: 'The way is made by walking it.'
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 46 "Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat" — In a fictional interview with the Taoist sage "Bat-Tzu," Mark White explains Taoism through Batman's circle: Bruce's yang-dominated life of vengeance and paranoia needs the yin that Dick and Tim supply, shown by his forgiveness of Zatanna and tenderness toward Helena's baby, while Jason Todd illustrates the fate of the unbalanced who cannot accept death. Alfred emerges as the Taoist sage practicing wei-wu-wei, effortless service like Chuang Tzu's butcher, balancing right and wrong in Bruce, and the Batman-Joker duality shows yin and yang defining each other. Lao Tzu's sayings on balance, complementary opposites, and water-like yielding organize the whole reading.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 30 "Sometimes We Live No Particular Way but Our Own" — Matthew Turner argues that a 'Playin' in the Band' jam — the band drifting from the tune into long collective improvisation and back — models a Stoic solution to free will shared by Epictetus, Spinoza, and Chuang Tzu: freedom is not uncaused choosing but responding well within constraints, so by the dichotomy of control there is no point resenting the band when it flubs a climax. Spinoza's definition of the free thing as one determined by its own nature, and Chuang Tzu's butcher who cuts oxen by spirit beyond skill, show the band letting the music 'play them' — Jerry's 'Tennessee Jed' riff never played the same way twice — as learned skill becomes second nature. Because the Dead jam within banks (keys, mutual listening, ability) yet generate something genuinely new and transcended every genre of 1960s music where the Monkees merely copied the Beatles, the Stoic attitude proves creative rather than quietist, an analogue for living freely within our own constraints.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 28 "The Bronze Dragonflight Invisible Leadership" — Moses Wolfenstein applies The Prince to guild leadership: the infamous Dives Onyxia wipe ('50 DKP minus!') shows why being feared beats being loved — players flooded to join and even requested his abusive raid calls — so long as fear never curdles into hatred, while PUGs and battlegrounds replay Machiavelli's warning that mercenary troops are 'disunited, ambitious, without discipline, disloyal.' Against this he sets Laozi's Daodejing verse 17, where the best rulers are scarcely known by their subjects and the people credit themselves — embodied by the hidden bronze dragonflight and Chromie, and by the back-channel guild officer who invisibly paves the road to victory.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 38 "Teddy Baseball" — Lee reads Ted Williams's The Science of Hitting as a Daoist skill story from the Zhuangzi: 'get a good ball to hit' matches the cicada-catcher's total absorption in the cicada's wings, hitting 'by feel' like the carpenter's hammer matches Cook Ding carving without looking, and Williams's midnight batting practice after Korea matches the wheelwright grown old at his craft—effortless spontaneity produced by disciplined practice and unified attention, not mere mechanics. Williams's 'proper thinking' is Daoist sorting of objective conditions rather than abstract disputation. The closing tale of the old woman who cannot teach the Way to someone lacking the stuff explains why Williams failed as Senators manager: his players did not have the native talent to receive it.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 36 "Psych and Philosophy" — John Thompson argues Psych embodies the Daoist Way of reversal from the Daodejing and Zhuangzi: every episode begins with a death that triggers Shawn and Gus's irreverent, backwards-tracing investigation, their untrained spontaneous 'gifts' exemplify wu wei like Cook Ding carving an ox, and their bickering partnership is yin-yang interplay (as when Gus leads the joking in 'An Evening with Mr. Yang'). Zhuangzi singing at his wife's funeral parallels the Shabby the Sea Lion and 'Dust in the Wind' funeral parodies, the show's blurred TV-versus-fandom reality echoes the butterfly dream, Lassiter succeeds when he relaxes into wu wei ('Feet Don't Kill Me Now'), and the closing bloopers enact Dao's endless reversal - though the chapter ends by conceding Dao defies the very label 'Daoist show.'
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 32 "Girls and Philosophy" — Carleo and D'Ambrosio read Hannah's 'busy trying to become who I am' through the classical Chinese debate over names: her self-claimed title 'writer' preceding any conduct is the Confucian nightmare of names divorced from actuality, diagnosed by the Analects's rectification of names ('rulers should rule, fathers should father') and the sheep-stealing passage warning against over-identifying with a single role. Adam, by contrast, lives the Daoist ideal - the empty vessel of the Daodejing acting by wu wei, and Zhuangzi's butterfly dream fluidity in his role-play sex and absorbed woodworking, unattached to titles. Mencius and Xunzi frame the resolution: by Season Three Hannah finally rectifies names at GQ while Adam's non-identity turns delusional, vindicating the ideal of being an 'internal sage and external king' - Daoist in private, responsible to roles in public.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 36 "22. The Dao of Master Westley" — Doll tests each character against the Dao: Confucius's identification of the Dao with tradition and ritual fails because Florinese tradition is exactly what enables Humperdinck's murder and war plans, so she turns to Laozi's De and wu-wei, diagnosing Vizzini's fatal overconfidence (he lacked Socratic knowledge of his own ignorance), Humperdinck's paranoia, and Buttercup's passivity as failures to sense when to act and when to refrain. Westley emerges as Zhuangzi's ideal - like Cook Ting the butcher, mastering skills until instinct suffices: adapting through the Fire Swamp, treating Vizzini's death as 'an appropriate death', yet sparing Inigo and Fezzik because killing them would be against nature, which is why the giant and the Spaniard accept him as their sage.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 30 "18. Lessons from Fred Rogers’s Dao" — John Thompson reads Rogers as a Zhuangzian sage without claiming he was a Daoist: the show's spare sets and simple cast embody the uncarved block and Zhuangzi's Dao present 'in the piss and shit' of the everyday; its refusal of 'bombardment' pace is Cook Ding slowly carving the ox and xiaoyaoyou, free and easy wandering, as when X the Owl must wait for Cousin Mary's visit. The post-9/11 'look for the helpers' PSAs, the Burger King parody he publicly rebuffed, and the Emmys ten seconds of silence mark Rogers as a zhenren, a genuine person at home in ziran.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 12 "The Wisdom of Combination" — Isrow maps each bending art to its real martial art and source philosophy: Katara's Taiji waterbending embodies Daoist wu-wei when she forgoes revenge on Yon Rha ('The Southern Raiders'); Toph's Hong Jia earthbending expresses the Buddhist eightfold path's Right Speech through her insistence on truth; Zuko's Northern Shaolin firebending enacts the Four Noble Truths, his desire-driven suffering ending only when he abandons chasing the Avatar; and Aang's Daoist Baguazhang airbending makes freedom openness to change, shown in his receptivity to Iroh's advice. The Avatar's true power is combining these character strengths, not merely wielding four elements.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 32 "A Zhuangzian Sage All Along" — Argues Iroh's Book One laziness and foolishness is a pose implementing Zhuangzi's advice for handling a misguided ruler: do not pressure him, empty yourself of doctrines and credit, and stay deliberately useless (tea, Pai Sho, naps) so you are neither noxious nor a tool. Zhuangzi's fictional dialogue between Confucius and Yan Hui about reforming the young lord of Wei maps onto Iroh beside Zuko, and the episode where Iroh finally gives explicit advice about Ozai ('Avatar Day') proves the point — Zuko rejects both the advice and Iroh the moment the sage stops playing the fool. The authors add an empirical study on Prolific participants showing even first-time, unfamiliar viewers already rate Iroh as wise, supporting the reading that Iroh was a Zhuangzian sage all along.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 12 "The Wisdom of Combination" — A martial artist maps each bending style onto the real art it animates and its parent philosophy: Katara's Taiji waterbending embodies wu-wei, shown when she spares Yon Rha in 'The Southern Raiders' as strength rather than weakness; Toph's Hong Jia earthbending grounds her insistence on truth, an example of the Buddhist eightfold path's Right Speech; Zuko's driven Northern Shaolin temperament walks through the first three Noble Truths, from suffering caused by desire for his honor to its cessation when he joins Team Avatar; and Aang's Baguazhang airbending expresses freedom as openness to change and to Iroh's counsel. The Avatar's power is therefore not four bendings but the combination of the four character strengths.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 32 "A Zhuangzian Sage All Along" — Argues that Iroh's Book One laziness and foolishness is a Zhuangzian pose rather than genuine folly: like Zhuangzi's fictional Confucius counseling Yan Hui not to lecture the young, willful lord of Wei, Iroh never pressures Zuko directly, keeps himself unthreatening by playing the fool over tea and Pai Sho, and practices the 'use of uselessness' so he is never a tool of the prince's quest, 'singing' his wisdom only when Zuko is ready to hear it. The couple's falling out in 'Avatar Day', triggered precisely when Iroh offers explicit moral advice, confirms the strategy, since Zuko rejects both the advice and the uncle. The authors add an empirical study (Prolific participants rating clips): even viewers totally unfamiliar with the series rate Book One Iroh as wise and suspect his foolishness is strategic, supporting the interpretation that he is a Zhuangzian sage all along, and that ATLA in turn illuminates Zhuangzi's cryptic political advice.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 27 "The Way of the Archer" — White reads Clint Barton through the Tao Te Ching and Chuang Tzu: Hawkeye's instinctive archery—'use your bow gently, naturally, instinctively'—is wei wu wei, while his bragging, his glory-chasing failure against Iron Man, and his attempt to become Goliath all violate it by striving against his own nature, until the Kree-Skrull War teaches him the bow is his way. Chuang Tzu's butcher carves the lesson that the effortless path (the straightforward shot) is the skilled one, and Lao Tzu's sage-leadership—lowering oneself, deflecting praise—is exactly how Captain America handles Clint's insurrections. Lao Tzu on sages putting themselves last illuminates Hawkeye's sacrificial death and his legacy passed to Kate Bishop, while the butterfly dream frames his resurrection and the House of M's rewritten reality: with no way to compare the states, life and death are both to be welcomed as parts of the Way.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 34 "NOTES" — The book's final chapter is a mock interview in which 'Bat-Tzu' applies Taoism to Bruce Wayne's life: his yang (hard, retributive crime-fighting) has dominated his yin (his tenderness toward Dick, Tim, and Helena), and Robin has always been the yin balancing the Dark Knight. Quoting Lao-Tzu's Tao Te Ching and Chuang-Tzu on duality, acceptance of death (Jason Todd's resurrection), and effortlessness, the piece casts Alfred as the Taoist sage whose help exemplifies wu-wei, like Chuang-Tzu's butcher who cuts without dulling his blade. It even reads Batman's most intimidating feature, his absent shadow, as proof that nothingness can matter more than substance.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 15 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Lynch tests the fan claims that the Dude is 'the Duddha' or a practicing Daoist: the Dude has wu wei in his effortless arts of bowling and abiding and shares Zhuangzi's withdrawal from society (the Nixon bowling poster, learning from drunks, Donny's ashes scattered with naturalistic acceptance), but lacks Daoist metaphysics, the Dao's inexpressibility, and any articulated views. The Buddha parallels are real — nonattachment, practice over theory (the poisoned-arrow parable), compassion for Bunny — yet Gautama's radical discipline and middle path are the opposite of the Dude's laziness, so Dudeism emerges as an undisciplined American cousin, and the Dude follows 'just his way and his alone'.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 29 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Timothy Christopher opens with the Zen archer who 'lets the arrow fall' rather than releasing it: once the arrow is in the air it goes where it will, which he offers as a model of Dungeon Mastering, since a DM plans a campaign but cannot control where players take it once play begins. He maps DM mindsets onto two axes (control over the world, control over the characters) yielding four archetypes: the balanced guide, the minimal host, the rule-enforcing arbiter, and the railroad-imposing puppet master, each with its own measure of success. Like a Zen archer who could subtly bend wind and gravity, a crafty DM invisibly influences the arrow in flight, and groups should agree on the preferred style up front to avoid friction.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 32 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Arya's arc from Needle to answering 'No one' is read as Aristotelian virtue ethics fused with East Asian philosophy: virtues are habits acquired only through practice, so the Water Dance's endless drills and martial-arts blocks that must become automatic mirror the honest person who tells the truth without deliberating. Syrio's lessons - 'looking is not seeing,' the story of the ordinary tomcat the other bravos mistook for a fabulous beast, being fully present with your trouble - teach Zen seeing and mindfulness, while 'be like water' and the steel that must be part of your arm embody Laozi's effortless wu wei. The Faceless Men's initiation, from discarding her possessions to the literal removal of Arya's face, becomes the Zen slaying of the ego, making her a 'Zen-Ninja-Aristotelian' on the path to eudaimonia.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 10 "a3.xhtml" — Brannigan reads Bilbo's tug-of-war between Baggins security and Took adventure through Taoism: the two desires are not contradictory but the interplay of yin and yang, and true dwelling is found in the journey itself, as the 'Roads go ever on' song says. Greed is the great weight - Thorin enslaved by the treasure he 'never forgot', Smaug hoarding for hoarding's sake, even the orc-loving of machines - and the cure is the mirror-mind of Empty Mind that reflects without grasping, illustrated by the Taoist masters tale of 'Gold-Is-Heavy' and 'Empty-Mind'. Beorn, who lives on honey indifferent to gold, and Bilbo, who in the spirit of wu-wei sheds his desire for the Arkenstone and finally lets go of the Ring, embody life in harmony with the Tao.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 8 "Notes" — Willard poses the paradox of creativity: how can a toy that promises creativity come with rigid instructions and a purist fan culture that polices what counts as legitimate building? She reads The LEGO Movie as staging three rival models — the Master Builders' unfettered recombination (Plato's Ion on poetic madness and Kant's mysterious free-playing genius), Emmet's 'thinking outside the box' that yields the mocked double-decker couch, and Finn's father's meticulous vision. Following Aristotle against Plato that poetic skill is a teachable craft, plus psychology of jazz-improvisation studies, flow states, and Zhuangzi's butcher Cook Ding, she argues creativity is the joyful mastery of a process, so following instructions is the etude-stage that builds the database of moves from which free creation grows.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 28 "Notes" — Bein reads the LEGO brick as the Daodejing's 'uncarved block': a single brick is an invitation rather than a toy, and precisely because it is empty of meaning (and mostly empty of plastic — the stud-and-tube marriage of yin and yang) it can become anything, whereas printed, specialized pieces 'are diminished by being added to'. Against the Greek obsession with definition — Socrates refusing sophistry while insisting one cannot rule justly without defining justice, Plato's definition dialogues, Aristotle's inheritance of the precision ideal, and William James's 'think clearly' — Daoist imprecision is defended as a philosophical stance: dao is a way, an activity, not a thing. Wei wu wei ('doing without doing') explains Emmet's winning plan of building the utterly ordinary Octan spaceship, why Lord Business's penny-throw is genius without sagacity (coercive, not water-like), and why governing should be like cooking a small fish — minimal, attentive intervention.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 12 "Notes" — Decker parallels the Republic's fall into Palpatine's Empire with the Zhou dynasty's collapse that birthed Chinese philosophy, reading three Jedi from the Dark Times comics through it. K'Kruhk, guided by the Zatoichi-like Master Zao, learns wu-wei - following the Force rather than forcing outcomes, with Laozi's Dao as the Force's Chinese analogue. Dass Jennir's struggle over what 'Jedi' means after killing a slaver becomes Confucian rectification of names and the cultivation of ren, while Kai Hudorra's loss of faith, withdrawal to a casino, and final sacrificial stand against Vader embody Mozi-style pragmatic minimalism redeemed by Jennir's virtuous example.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 9 "“Now This Is Podracing!”" — Johnson reads The Phantom Menace as having distinctly Daoist flavors: Shmi's 'you cannot stop the change any more than you can stop the suns from setting,' the Naboo-Gungan 'symbiont circle,' and midi-chlorian symbiosis all express the Daoist unity of opposites and the constant flow of change. He argues Qui-Gon Jinn acts as a Daoist sage practicing wu wei — 'concentrate on the moment,' 'another solution will present itself' — while nearly everyone else in the film makes wrong predictions and grasps at outcomes. Even Anakin's accidental 'Oops!' victory over the Droid Control Ship is presented as success without trying, the practical meaning of 'Do or do not. There is no try.'
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 10 "Notes" — Schiltz reads Isaac McAdoo as a Zhuangzian sage: his virtuoso haircut scene in 'Man City' parallels Zhuangzi's butcher who carves oxen by following the natural seams of the dao, and his candid, simple, guileless character mirrors the Daoist mistrust of complexity and language. Isaac's slump in 'Rainbow' is diagnosed as lost wu-wei ('all up in his head'), cured by Roy's no-stakes pickup games that restore effortless action, and Laozi's 'ruling a great state is like cooking a small fish' explains Isaac's wordless leadership during Sam's Dubai Air protest and the suit-wearing gesture at Rebecca's father's funeral.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 23 "The Dao of Hoops" — Dirk Dunbar, a former professional player, argues that Daoist concepts illuminate basketball excellence and that the sport can be a path to the Dao. Balancing yin and yang means blending competition with surrender and strategy with spontaneity; Zhuangzi's archer shows how craving victory drains power. Wuwei explains the 'zone' of effortless play Dunbar experienced while scoring sixty-five points in a high school game and seventy-four in Iceland, while qi grounds free-throw breathing and visualization and ziran the discipline of releasing a shot without willing it in. Drawing on Daode jing verses and Phil Jackson's Sacred Hoops, he claims basketball teaches a life of disciplined surrender beyond the ego.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 23 "Tenth Hole Life Lessons" — Tom Regan narrates his return to golf, playing hallowed Pebble Beach and then a humble nine-hole course at Pismo Beach, dogged throughout by a perfectionist inner 'doppelganger' who demands he hit his best shot every time and berates him when he fails. The lesson comes from Jason, an ex-convict at Pismo, who tells him it doesn't matter how good you are 'as long as you're there when you play' and to 'just let it go' rather than think about golfing. Regan then plays nine holes without a word from his doppelganger, dramatizing an effortless, present, ego-quieting acceptance close to wu wei and Zen letting-go rather than any doctrine he names.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 27 "Thirteenth Hole Free and Easy Wandering on the Golf Course Swing Like a Taoist" — Scott F. Parker reads golf's paradox—that you play your best shot when you stop trying so hard—through the Taoism of the 'Tao Te Ching' and the 'Chuang Tzu.' Using the parable of the archer (skill is constant but attachment to the prize ruins the shot), Cook Ting carving the ox by spirit not force, and Master Yu accepting his deformity, he draws out nonattachment to results, 'doing without doing' (wei wu wei), and self-knowledge/self-acceptance, illustrated by Zach Johnson never going for a par 5 in two at the 2007 Masters and Tiger Woods rarely swinging all-out. The essay embodies the Taoist point that the Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao: to try to not-try is self-defeating, so one must simply not try.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — The editors' introduction argues that the unifying theme of Lee's films is the struggle for authentic self-identity, framed through Charles Taylor's dialogical self and Kierkegaard's line that anxiety is the dizziness of freedom. It surveys how Confucian virtues (ren, li, xiao) and Daoist wu-wei play out across Pushing Hands, The Wedding Banquet, Eat Drink Man Woman, Crouching Tiger, Sense and Sensibility, Brokeback Mountain and others, treating each protagonist as caught between traditional obligation and personal desire. It invokes Nietzsche's claim that all philosophy is autobiography to justify reading Lee's films (he said 'it's all in my films') as a coherent authorial philosophy.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — McRae reads Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon as a dramatization of the tension between Confucian humanism and Daoist naturalism over how to cultivate an authentic 'focus-field' self. Li Mu Bai and Yu Shu Lien are exemplary persons (junzi) bound by the wuxia code and li, unable to voice their love, while Jen rebels into criminal freedom under Jade Fox; Li's use of the green bamboo forest against Jen embodies wu-wei and rou (yielding suppleness). It argues that authentic self-cultivation, and Jen's final leap, require balancing Daoist natural freedom against Confucian roles, since freedom without relationships exacts a fatal price.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Kroustallis reads Lust, Caution through perception rather than hidden emotion, arguing Wong Chia Chi abandons the disengaged, sight-only aesthetic of Mrs. Mak and comes to perceive Mr. Yee's world with her whole engaged body. He uses Merleau-Ponty's Phenomenology of Perception to justify the three graphic sex scenes as bodily, essentially ambiguous cognition (the lipstick-marked cup, the flat key as motor intentionality) that links perception directly to action without unconscious representations. He frames Wong's development toward harmony via Fang Dongmei's neo-Confucian 'creative creativity' and a yin-yang polarity of meek and strong, with rain and jasmine flowers as an engaged natural environment.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 19 "10. The Dao of Psychohistory" — Fried reframes Asimov's binary (do individual choices matter to history?) through four Chinese theories of non-action (wu wei). Confucian non-action, ruling by moral example and retiring under an unjust ruler, illuminates Onum Barr's dignified private life; the Dao De Jing's mystical libertarianism, where people self-transform when the ruler stops intervening, resembles Gaia's ruler-less holism; Legalist impersonal non-action (Han Fei's ruler who hides his desires and lets harsh law act) has no clear Foundation analogue; and Zhuangzi's useless tree models Gaal Dornick's TV arc, in which she reclaims agency precisely by choosing private non-action over a scripted role in galactic history.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 46 "Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat" — In a mock interview with 'Bat-Tzu' (a disguised Alfred), Mark White explains Taoism through Batman. Bruce is dangerously dominated by yang after his parents' deaths and needs the yin balance that Robin (Dick as the lighthearted 'Batman with a feminine side') and his spiritual quest restore; Batman's fear-inducing shadow illustrates Lao-Tzu's usefulness of nothingness. Alfred is the Taoist sage embodying wei-wu-wei - 'action without action' - quietly serving like Chuang-Tzu's effortless butcher and like water that wears down stone, harmonizing Bruce's warring opposites toward the Way.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 29 "NOTE" — Shai Biderman and William J. Devlin trace John Locke the character's shift from the empiricism of his philosophical namesake to Taoism. Early Locke is the tabula-rasa empiricist and scientific-method hunter and hatch-engineer, but his miraculous restored ability to walk, Jacob's touch, and his visions push him to ask 'why' rather than 'how.' They argue Locke comes to follow the Tao—the unnamable Way symbolized by the black-and-white yin-yang seen in backgammon pieces and Claire's dream—advising Charlie via the struggling moth, teaching Walt to visualize the knife's path, and finding Sun's ring by not looking, ultimately reading his sacrificial death as effortless surrender to the island's flow.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 13 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Richard Hutch develops a phenomenology of 'moral presence' — an assertion of human integrity in the face of despair when nothing else can be done — from the autobiographies of solo ocean sailors. He identifies three pathways: technical finesse (Robin Knox-Johnston, whose 'God helps those who help themselves' pragmatism Hutch reads as the Taoist wu-wei, action through non-action), cosmic quest (Bernard Moitessier's mystical communion, slingshot instead of radio), and personal test (Kay Cottee's epiphany near Cape Horn, transforming terror into fascination via Otto's mysterium tremendum et fascinans). He frames sailing as tragic-comic drama with technology as a deus ex machina, arguing that doing nothing is often the zenith of value.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 15 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Hathaway and Sharpley analyze the cannabis experience of medical-'compassion club' users through Csikszentmihalyi's concept of 'flow.' They ground flow in William James's 'stream of consciousness' and in Taoism, reading Tao as 'a patterned flow of the universe' and wu wei as the effortless equilibrium users describe ('it just centers me,' 'I take an inventory on my soul'). Against Western monophasic medicine, they defend users' 'anecdotal' testimony as legitimate knowledge of a body–mind–spirit balance that cannabis restores.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 24 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Brown and Tien build a 'Kantian Gate' from Kant's Formula of Universal Law: you should date only if you wouldn't mind your dates acting on your own dating maxim, which bars the manipulative, deceptive, or coercive dater while permitting many ends. For those who pass the gate, they recommend pursuing Csikszentmihalyi's 'flow' and the Zhuangzi's cultivated spontaneity, describing a two-part self-cultivation (purging debilitating social programming via 'forgetting' and xinzhai, then training to act in accord with the Dao) so one can 'be in the moment' and get truly lucky on a first date. They apply the seven elements of flow directly to dating conversation, eye contact, and feedback.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 46 "Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat" — White stages a mock interview with "Bat-Tzu" (revealed to be Alfred) to read Batman through Taoism. Lao-Tzu and Chuang-Tzu supply the ideal of balancing yin and yang: Bruce lets his hard, vengeful yang dominate and needs Robin's yin, while Dick keeps balance and Tim risks losing his. Bruce's intimidating shadow illustrates the usefulness of nothingness, and Chuang-Tzu's teaching on accepting death frames Jason Todd's fate. Alfred embodies the Taoist sage — wei-wu-wei, water-like flexibility, and effortless, unspoken guidance.

### Taoism (Daoism)

Taoism (Daoism) is a Chinese philosophical and religious tradition centered on living in harmony with the Tao, the underlying pattern and source of all things. Associated with the Daodejing attributed to Laozi and the writings of Zhuangzi, it prizes spontaneity, simplicity, and naturalness over rigid convention, striving, and artificial control. As a philosophy it counsels yielding to the natural course of events rather than forcing outcomes, and it later developed into organized religious forms with their own practices and pursuit of longevity.

- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 11 "“Great Warrior Wars Not Make One Great”" — Robinson (a Zen monk) argues the Force is best understood as ch'i and the Jedi path as philosophical Taoism and Zen: the Light and Dark Sides are the yin-yang polarity whose 'balance' Anakin's prophecy restores, and Anakin's fall is the Buddhist three poisons - clinging attachment to his mother and Padme breeding fear, anger, and hate. Yoda's teaching is Zen practice: 'You must unlearn what you have learned' is wu-wei (effortless action), 'Do or do not' rejects the divided mind of trying, and the Dagobah cave parallels the sword master Tesshu's koan insight that the real enemy is one's own mind ('no-enemy'). The chapter also traces Jedi genealogy to Bodhidharma's Shaolin kung-fu, the Korean Hwa Rang and Japanese Sohei warrior monks, and Bushido's samurai code, noting 'Jedi' derives from 'jidai geki'.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 46 "Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat" — In a fictional interview with the Taoist sage "Bat-Tzu," Mark White explains Taoism through Batman's circle: Bruce's yang-dominated life of vengeance and paranoia needs the yin that Dick and Tim supply, shown by his forgiveness of Zatanna and tenderness toward Helena's baby, while Jason Todd illustrates the fate of the unbalanced who cannot accept death. Alfred emerges as the Taoist sage practicing wei-wu-wei, effortless service like Chuang Tzu's butcher, balancing right and wrong in Bruce, and the Batman-Joker duality shows yin and yang defining each other. Lao Tzu's sayings on balance, complementary opposites, and water-like yielding organize the whole reading.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 25 "You Legend, You Martyr" — Erin Kealey reads Syd Barrett's 1967–68 collapse through Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy: Barrett 'surrendered his subjectivity in the Dionysian process' to make Piper's songs — 'Astronomy Domine', the wordless 'Interstellar Overdrive', 'Matilda Mother' where 'the words had different meaning' — and 'Chapter 24', written from an I Ching divination on change and return. 'Bike' teeters on psychosis as the room of musical tunes swallows the singer, and 'Jugband Blues' ('much obliged to you for making it clear that I'm not here') with the motionless Scarecrow foretells the catatonia that ended his tenure, after which the band pivoted from anarchic spontaneity to the meticulous Apollonian constructions of Dark Side through The Wall. Following Nietzsche, Kealey argues that the fall of this tragic hero — mourned in 'Shine on You Crazy Diamond' and mirrored in Pink's exploits in The Wall — affirms life, since art alone transfigures the horror of existence into something worth living.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 10 "I Still Miss Someone The Self and Its Travels Along the Way" — Geisz explains the Confucian social dao of ritual (li), humaneness (ren), filial piety and the junzi, the Daodejing's metaphysical Dao with its unity of opposites, and Zhuangzi's tales of free wandering, then maps all three onto Cash's songs.
