- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 9 "Plato’s Cave Again" — Curran uses Shadow of a Doubt to teach epistemology: Charlie's claim to 'know' her uncle distinguishes knowledge by acquaintance from propositional knowledge as justified true belief, with the permanently stuck 'Til Two clock showing a true belief that is not knowledge because its warrant is unreliable. Coherence (Hegel, Blanshard), pragmatist (James, Dewey), and correspondence theories of truth are tested against the townspeople's false but convenient beliefs about Uncle Charlie, and only correspondence survives. Kant's absolute duty not to lie is weighed against Mill's act and rule utilitarianism for the detectives' deceptions, and a feminist care-ethics perspective assesses Charlie's shielding her mother from the truth. Plato's cave frames the cinema itself: film can deceive like shadows on a wall, yet the detectives' unused photograph shows the camera can also reveal truth, so movies help us face facts, at the price, as Charlie pays, of lost innocence.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 20 "Turning the Tables" — Wartenberg argues that North by Northwest pits two defective ethical stances against each other: the Professor's 'zealous patriotism,' exposed as callous in the USIA scene where he lets the innocent Thornhill be killed as the Kaplan decoy and spends Eve in the line of danger ('War is hell, Mr. Thornhill, even when it's a cold one'), and Thornhill's 'ethical particularism,' akin to the feminist ethics of care, exposed as headstrong when love-driven rashness leaves both lovers dangling on Mount Rushmore and only the Professor's intervention saves them. Yet the ending's match cut from Rushmore to the train berth reveals Hitchcock's real McGuffin: the Professor fails less as a moralist than as a bad director whose staged deceptions misfire, and the film's true philosophical claim is self-reflexive, that only film has the power to reconcile patriotism and romantic love, an optimistic world existing only in the artifice of the camera.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 10 "You May Wonder How Come I Love You Care and Ethics" — Gimbel asks what the E Street Band's marathon multiple encores mean, starting from social contract theory: Hobbes's state of nature ('no home, no job, no peace, no rest') and Locke's contract explain the ticket as a financial IOU — so a drunk, short Hendrix show wrongs you financially but not morally — while the contractual view of moral duty (the 'Hungry Heart' narrator who abandoned his wife and kids in Baltimore) cannot explain why a missing encore feels like personal betrayal. The gift theory fails too, since encores are expected, and expected things are not gifts. Care ethics (Ruddick, Noddings) fits instead: devoted fans make the band part of their identity, Springsteen sings 'to you about you,' and the No Nukes 90-minute set became permanent because he would not give his people less — while 'Pink Cadillac' shows the limit case, since you cannot love someone for her Cadillac.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 23 "History Will Judge" — Livingston reads the Razor movie through George Lakoff's Strict Father and Nurturant Parent models: Cain's Pegasus assumes a dangerous world and enforces obedience (shooting Belzen for refusing orders, the torture of Gina), while Adama's Galactica assumes empathy and open questioning (asking Boomer 'Why do you hate us so much?', sparing Starbuck). Kendra Shaw is the 'child' conditioned by desensitization and objectifying language into a killing razor and a PTSD victim, whose recovery under Apollo shows the two family models being blended — boldness with communication. Adama's verdict that 'history will have to make its judgments' frames the chapter's claim that understanding Cain requires seeing the family culture that produced her.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 22 "Toward Caring" — Sylvia models the Doctor on feminist care ethics: Gilligan's response to Kohlberg's justice-tinged scales and Noddings's distinction between natural caring (for Rose, Martha, Peri in 'The Caves of Androzani') and ethical caring, which explains his forgiveness of the Master and compassion for Dalek Caan after genocides. Against utilitarian impartiality — which cannot say why he should save his companion over a stranger — the relationship itself grounds the obligation, while his vengeful moment facing the lone Dalek in 'Dalek' shows what caring burnout looks like.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 119 "Beyond Lies the Other" — The section reads Dick's first published story, 'Beyond Lies the Wub,' as the origin of his career-defining theme: the jovial, philosophic wub survives the captain who sees only fresh meat because its empathy is so total it can exchange minds with the man about to slaughter it. Defining empathy as seeing the world from another's viewpoint plus sympathizing (which the cornering cat, predicting the rat's moves, lacks), it ends with Dick's Exegesis: an evil magician-deity occludes our minds until a savior in trash form restores them, and without such a revelation you, the reader, are 'nothing but a robot.'
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 121 "Can a Blade Runner Love a Robot" — The section contrasts Dick's bleaker novel, where J.R. Isadore's love for the androids dies when they cut the legs off his rare spider and Deckard's union with Rachael is the 'summa of falsity and mechanical motions' that fuels his resolve to destroy them, with the film's redemptive romance built on Rachael being 'more human than human.' It argues the movie preserves Dick's thesis anyway: Roy Batty's final act of saving the enemy who hunted him shows the empathy that makes the replicants persons, perhaps more than human.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 122 "How to Build a Moral Robot" — This section draws design morals from Dick's warnings: machines built as ersatz humans deny the value of being human, robotic sexual partners are doomed deceptions (the novel's Deckard-Rachael encounter is the case study), and a genuine artificial moral agent needs empathy 'logically equivalent to agape,' though a machine reasoning on sound moral principles could still count as a limited moral agent with proportionate rights and responsibilities. The Three Stigmata's Palmer Eldritch, returned from deep space as a machine treating humans as resources, shows that the netherward pull toward machinehood threatens humans themselves.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 133 "He Ain’t Heavy, He’s My Other" — This section stages Levinas's infinite responsibility for the Other against Heidegger's tendency to treat others as tools for warding off death: J.R. Isidore's one-way care for androids who vivisect a spider, Dick's 'The Android and the Human' warning that androidization means becoming predictable means, and the treatment of animals as the litmus test of humanity. The self becomes real through selfless action (Tagomi saving a stranger, Sweetscent returning to his wife), and because the height separating self and Other descends from Descartes's idea of infinity, meeting the face of the poor stranger, from Radio Free Albemuth's beggar to The Adjustment Bureau's Chairman, is an encounter with God.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 134 "Fifty Ways to Love Your Other" — The section reads Levinas's demand to experience the Other's suffering in the Other's place as Dick's empathy made literal: the shifting points of view that blur heroes and villains, Felix Buckman's tears, Molinari developing his people's symptoms, and the empathy boxes bonding users to Mercer's endless stoning, a fraud whose falsity is beside the point because the concern is the real thing. Villains are precisely those who refuse the transfer, and the ordinary one-way gift, buying a stranger a drink with no return, enacts the Golden Rule: even if the universe isn't real, Melina is right, kiss each other anyway.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 15 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Jonas-Sebastien Beaudry reads Neverwhere's magic invisibility as a model of real social invisibility: after Richard helps the injured Door he loses his job, his fiancee Jessica, and even the ability to be perceived, joining the homeless, slaves, and Jews under Nazism as people excluded from the moral community whose needs no longer register. Using Arendt's banality of evil to explain everyday indifference and Richard Rorty on torturers who fail to see a 'real' human, he distinguishes radical from partial invisibility, shown in Jessica stepping over the bleeding Door and misreading her need as 'sleep it off.' The remedy is Iris Murdoch's 'loving gaze' of just and careful attention, which seizes Richard before he can rationalize, backed by a practical wisdom about whose needs matter, so that acknowledging the invisible, down to apologizing to a rat in London Below, is what makes both them and us better.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 17 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Olson opens with her own first session, in which the DM steered her toward a 'sexy Eladrin' miniature in high heels, and asks why women stay away from D&D. She argues the game's mechanics are egalitarian—identical power lists for male and female characters, echoing Plato's Republic claim that women guard the city by the same nature as men—and that party cooperation embodies the relational, care-based feminist ethic Marilyn Friedman and Angela Bolte oppose to male-coded individualism. The trouble is culture, not system: sexualized miniatures that objectify female bodies, tokenism, harassment, and marketing that ignores women, to which female gamers respond by playing male characters like Jenni Dowsett, designing separatist systems such as Portal Worlds, or, like Shelly Mazzanoble, claiming D&D for the 'inner girl'.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 25 "The Wire and Philosophy" — The Rochas argue that the only two women in the Game, Snoop on the street side and Kima on the police side, embody a 'militant feminism' in the lineage of the Black Panthers' Kathleen Cleaver and the Weather Underground's Bernardine Dohrn: women can excel at anything men can, including violence (Snoop as Marlo's natural soldier, repurposing a Hardware Barn nail gun, wearing womanhood only as a costume), and violence is justified when used for just ends (Kima overcoming fear to police). They then use Gilligan and Noddings's care ethics to explain the finale: Kima's dedication to relationships and care for the overlooked homeless victims lets her discern that McNulty and Freamon's fake-serial-killer scheme is an immoral masculinized rationalization, so she turns in her friends and becomes the show's moral conscience.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 19 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Jonas-Sebastien Beaudry defends a 'moderate speciesism' built on relationships rather than individual capacities: Taylor's trial strips him of clothes, name, and speech - the symbols of ethical community - showing how institutional speciesism rationalizes domination behind the Sacred Scrolls' Declaration-of-Independence-style self-evidence. Against Singer's anti-speciesist challenge that any distinctively human capacity is shared by some animals or missing from some humans, he argues both camps wrongly pedestal intrinsic traits, and reads Taylor's love for the mute Nova together with the failed Project Nim as showing that within-species bonds of love, care, and family are genuinely and justifiably valuable without licensing mistreatment. Bernard Williams's 'The Human Prejudice' - should we surrender to superior invading aliens? - marks where impartial anti-speciesism leads, while Zaius's 'Man is evil' and the doomsday-bomb ending show extreme speciesism as self-fulfilling prophecy.
- **The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia**, ch. 15 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" — Kathleen Poorman Dougherty sets Kant's universal, emotion-free morality (echoed in Kohlberg's justice stages and Judge Abernathy's 'blind court' claim in 'Infamy') against Carol Gilligan's care ethic, which she says fits Saint Alicia far better: Alicia's practical advice to Jennifer Lewis in the pilot, driving Kenny home in 'Home', and telling Kenny's father 'I care a lot more about your son than he does' show connection producing both better morality and better lawyering. Feminist theorists like Nel Noddings and Sara Ruddick treat this care orientation as morally superior, not merely different, but the chapter's later sections weigh the cost: Kalinda's burnout warning, Alicia's resentment at always hand-holding clients, and the double bind by which women absorb society's unpaid caring labor. The verdict is that care is genuinely moral, but it must become a shared burden.
- **How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness**, ch. 20 "How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy" — The chapter argues HIMYM offers two complementary feminist icons: Robin embodies personal autonomy and independence - fighting from 'but, um' early-morning shifts to lead anchor, and grieving infertility as stolen autonomy rather than lost motherhood - while Lily, and even more Marshall, exemplify Carol Gilligan's feminist care ethics with its emphasis on emotion over impartiality, cooperation over competition, and partiality toward loved ones. Aristotle's golden mean supplies the test Robin passes by balancing career and love instead of pushing one to an extreme. The twist that a male character best exemplifies care ethics, with Lily bridging the two moral outlooks, is offered as the show's progressive complexity about gender.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 23 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Robison-Greene argues Rawlsian ideal theory breaks down at Litchfield: Soso's hunger strike gets only cosmetic concessions from Caputo, Sophia's WAC human-rights platform loses to Taystee's realism, and Piper learns the council 'is basically bullshit,' showing how idealization made by the powerful ignores the lived facts of Mendoza's abusive marriage, Jimmy's 'compassionate' death sentence, and Sophia's denied hormones. Against taking a 'moral holiday' in prison, she proposes care ethics, with role-based duties sensitive to actual circumstances, as the morality that fits life inside, and suggests non-ideal theory may fit the outside world too.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 14 "5. Every Lonely Monster Needs a Companion" — Gadsden asks why a near-omnipotent Time Lord needs companions at all and tests four hypotheses against his solo meltdowns—executing Solomon in 'Dinosaurs on a Spaceship,' nearly murdering Jex in 'A Town Called Mercy,' and declaring himself 'Time Lord Victorious' in 'The Waters of Mars.' He rejects the Lord Acton power-corrupts hypothesis via Glaucon's ring story in Plato's Republic, since powerless companions offer no threat of reprisal or dishonor, and qualifies J.J. Sylvia's care-ethics 'empathetic link' because the Doctor cares for non-human species like the Star Whale too. He favors two answers: Hume's fact/value gap as a millennium-long moral myopia ('I can't see it anymore,' the deleted 'Flesh and Stone' confession), and Aristotle's point in the Nicomachean Ethics that only virtuous friends—moral peers who mirror us—can expose the Doctor's blind spots, like his 'God Complex.'
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 24 "12. Should We Really Care about the Crawleys" — Jones takes up the charge that loving Downton seduces viewers into admiring inequality, and answers that the Crawleys deserve our care because birth, not choice, gave them their position, so they should be judged only by what they do with it: Grantham paying for Mrs. Patmore's eye surgery, Violet throwing the flower contest after Isobel's challenge, the family gradually embracing Branson. He reads the show as a manifesto for social change through sympathetic contact between classes rather than Irish-style revolt - befriend the rich and their good nature will start to level the playing field. His own objection is that this makes change partly the responsibility of the less privileged, from Thomas being asked to soften Carson's homophobia to the poor being asked to be nice to the rich today.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 28 "11. I Ain’t No Hollaback Girl!" — Callens explains Carol's killing of Lizzie in "The Grove" through Kohlberg's stages of moral development, arguing Carol reasons at the post-conventional level (pre-apocalypse law and punishment no longer bind) while Rick, Hershel, and Daryl stay conventional, and then layers Maslow's hierarchy of needs on top: because survival needs are perpetually threatened, characters regress between stages, and only self-actualized Carol accepts reality and makes group-preserving choices like executing Lizzie and mercy-killing Karen and David. Gilligan's justice-versus-care critique supplies the gendered frame - Carol moves to the middle of the justice-care continuum, her diminished care (unlike Season Two's grief over Sophia) is what makes her post-conventional, and her non-lethal Terminus rescue contrasts with Rick's summary execution of Gareth.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 29 "12. They Just Want Me to Be Like Them" — Castro and Beisecker diagnose Lizzie's walker fixation as prolonged grief disorder: she displaces grief for her father onto the walker "Nick," denies final death ("They're just different"), and treats reanimation as a viable form of life she might join ("Maybe I should change"). They argue Carol's suppressive guardianship - the "look at the flowers" distraction and calling Lizzie weak and confused - aggravated the avoidance at the root of the disorder, so Lizzie's "transformation" of Mika was a misguided moral experiment rather than murder by a monster. The chapter contrasts Tyreese's affirming care ("You each do things your own way") as the guardianship that might have saved the girls, and notes Carol's refusal to let Lizzie reanimate denies her the dying-wish courtesy the group once granted Jim.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 18 "7. And the Most Despicable Jessica Lange Character Is . ." — Ranks Jessica Lange's characters from least to most despicable using moral philosophy: Sister Jude earns credit for acting from duty (reporting the Nazi Dr. Arden at personal risk, Kant-style) and for genuinely feeling remorse; Elsa Mars partly honors the matriarchal obligations of care ethics but lacks Aristotle's habitual virtue and moderation, selling Bette and Dot to Dandy for fame; Constance Langdon abuses and effectively murders her disabled children; and Fiona Goode, motivated exclusively by youth, beauty, and power, murders her Supreme and torments Cordelia - never once acting out of concern for others.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 23 "11. The Mother of All Bombs" — Uses Hannah Arendt's On Violence — violence begets a more violent world, and WWII birthed the cold war rather than peace — to read Part 8, where the Trinity test, via the entity Judy/Mother, births BOB, whose garmonbozia-hunger is nuclear-age destruction feeding on female pain. Carol Gilligan's account of patriarchal silencing of women's voices (Naido's shut eyes, Laura's violated diary, the Persephone pattern of girls who must "die") and Gilbert and Gubar's dying "Angel in the House" frame Laura as both born from the Fireman and Señorita Dido as an antidote to the Bomb and destroyed by the mother wound Sarah Palmer carries. Against the toxic masculinity of Mr. C, Richard, and Chad, the show's good men — Cooper, the Trumans, Hawk, Bobby — embody Gilligan's ethic of care, and the chapter ends by demanding America put down its weapons and listen to women.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 18 "9. Machines Who Care" — Weiss reads 'The Lonely' and 'I Sing the Body Electric' as anticipations of today's debate over 'relational artifacts' — Turkle's sociable robots, the Sparrows' claim that robotic aged care is unethical, Coeckelbergh's rebuttal — asking, with Anne, whether an electric grandma 'doesn't sound so good.' Corry's Alicia and the children's electric grandma show care being bought as an assembly-line product for the lonely, and he presses the details: why the caring robots are female and serve water, why Alicia arrives in a box and is summarily shot in the face when no longer needed, and what it says about a culture that maroons people in loneliness and then sells the technical fix.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 28 "15. June the Stoic" — Lequien asks how June might endure Gilead and answers with Epictetus: like the slave-philosopher, she can locate freedom in what is 'up to her'—detaching from her body during the Ceremony ('What he is fucking is the lower part of my body'), relinquishing property, and learning not to call husband or daughter her own. He tests alternatives—Camus's question of suicide (the shatterproof glass), utilitarianism (the coerced 'We are very happy'), Tronto's care ethics (Gilead smothers the sorority that could make care meaningful), and the Particicution as a licensed Two Minutes Hate—before concluding that 'Nolite te bastardes carborundorum' functions as June's Stoic mantra: mastery of her own responses is the one victory the Sons of Jacob cannot take.
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 28 "14. Friends Don’t Lie" — Bowman tests Hawkins friendships against Aristotle's three kinds in the Nicomachean Ethics: Dustin and Lucas's shared-comics pleasure collapses into rivalry over Max, Nancy and Jonathan's utility ends once Will and Barb are found, and Barb's fatal poolside loyalty to Nancy, though one-directional, is a friendship of virtue. Nietzsche's ideal of friends who strengthen us through conflict recasts those very fights (Lucas confronting Eleven's power misuse) as the best friendship, care ethics (Gilligan and Noddings) makes the mutual one-caring Party the real answer to who teaches Eleven friendship, and Derrida's Politics of Friendship grounds democracy and society itself in such everyday reciprocity, which is why Eleven's 'friends don't lie' compass pulls her back from Kali's violence to close the gate.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 37 "24. Fred Rogers and the Ethics of Care" — A.G. Holdier places Rogers squarely in the care ethics of Gilligan and Noddings: against Kohlberg's justice stages (the Heinz dilemma recast with Henrietta Pussycat and X the Owl), care means Joan Tronto's four elements of attentiveness, responsibility, competence, and responsiveness, shown in the Clemmons kiddie pool, the Soviet guest understood through an interpreter, and 'just the way you are.' Extending care to animals via Rogers's vegetarianism and Carol Adams's 'absent referent,' and to the self via the closing benediction, he argues Rogers embodied care as particular, embodied practice rather than formula.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 28 "15. Chidi’s Indecision" — Vannatta argues Chidi's indecision exposes the shared flaw of the Big Three theories, Kantian deontology, Bentham and Mill's consequentialism, and Aristotle's virtue ethics of the golden mean: their rationalism pretends moral conflict can be eliminated by applying the correct rule, when Chidi's trolley terror shows moral situations are experienced as genuinely uncertain. Dewey's 'Three Independent Factors in Morals', the Good of desire, the Right of duty, and the Virtuous of communal praise, legitimizes that felt uncertainty and explains Eleanor's talent for finding option C between binary dilemmas. The chapter concludes that the show's real, unspoken moral theory is care ethics: partiality, relationship maintenance, and moral growth through the experience of being cared for, as Eleanor learns from Chidi's friendship rather than his lectures.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 1 "Introduction" — Book introduction: recounts how the 1979 cast were the first casualties of the Chestburster scene (real butcher-shop organs, Veronica Cartwright fainting), then previews the volume's payload - personhood questions about Ash, Bishop, David and the Ripley clone; Marx on why Weyland-Yutani sacrifices crews for profit; Plato's Republic on children in warfare via Newt; Lovecraftian cosmic horror; feminist readings of Ripley as care ethicist and mother; and continental takes - Xenomorphs as Nietzsche's Ubermensch, Camus on Ripley-8's refusal to commit suicide, and Sartre on a Xenomorph's right to resist us.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 10 "Not Bad, for a [Wo]man" — Argues Ripley's crossed-heart promise to Newt shows partialist care rightly overriding impartial justice: Kant, Mill, and Rachels demand everyone count for one, but Gilligan's critique of Kohlberg and Noddings's carer-cared-for relation - completed in Newt's 'I knew you'd come' - explain why Ripley duct-tapes two guns together and descends into the hive. Her flexible, relational problem-solving (the lighter-sprinkler trick against the Facehuggers, learning the pulse rifle) beats Gorman's mission-first command, and the trolley-style arithmetic she rejects when the one on the tracks is her little girl is not a moral failing; even nuking the Queen's eggs raises Singer-style speciesism questions.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 21 "A Professional, a Mother, and Someone Who Cares" — Asks whether Ripley is a feminist and answers 'only sometimes': her quarantine refusal ('Yes, I read you. The answer is negative') and her reasons for killing the Alien3 specimen ('a lot of innocent people will die') invoke rules, chain of command, and anonymous future victims - Kohlberg's post-conventional reasoning, not Gilligan's care voice - whereas the hot-chocolate scene with Newt and the unhesitating hive rescue exhibit the care-focused feminism of Gilligan and Noddings. Against the status-oriented reading of Vasquez's 'have you ever been mistaken for a man?' exchange, Ripley emerges as atypical of either stereotype: a professional, a mother, and someone who cares.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 21 "Repairing Our Worlds" — Fice reads ATLA through the feminist ethics of care, using Joan Tronto's phases of caring-about, taking care of, and care-giving to analyze Katara: freeing Aang from the iceberg, offering to heal Zuko's scar in the Crystal Catacombs, and her full arc as the Painted Lady feeding, healing, and freeing a polluted village. Care also misfires ('Imprisoned') and is devalued as feminine 'women's work' when Toph calls Katara motherly ('The Runaway'), a myth the chapter rejects. Care scales politically too: the Gaang's defeat of Fire Nation imperialism is care repairing the world, while Azula's indifference to Ty Lee and Mai marks her villainy.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 21 "Repairing Our Worlds" — Fice reads Katara through Joan Tronto's care ethics, tracking the phases in episodes: 'caring about' the refugees on 'The Serpent's Pass' and Zuko's scar in the Crystal Catacombs, 'taking care of' in freeing Aang from the iceberg, and 'care-giving' in 'The Painted Lady,' where she feeds, heals, and cleans up a polluted factory town. Care misfires are part of the theory, as when she pushes Haru to earthbend in 'Imprisoned' and gets him arrested, and Toph's 'motherly' jab lets the chapter reject the myth that care is essentially feminine, citing bell hooks. The larger claim is political: the Gaang's war against Fire Nation imperialism is care at world scale, repairing the world so its people can live well.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 30 "What Not to Do as a Parent" — The chapter pinpoints Marie's failure in Arkangel using Feinberg's parental-rights framework: by filtering out every fright (the neighbor's dog, her father's stroke) she violated Sara's right to an open future, misconstrued her welfare and protection rights, and stunted the empathy that makes a child a fully functioning human being. Aristotle's golden mean frames over-parenting as a vice of excess — as damaging as neglect — and Ruddick's maternal ethics of care also convicts Marie, since mothering requires fostering growth and social acceptability, not just preserving life. The Philip K. Dick comparison lands the conclusion: an android is distinguished from a human only by lacking empathy, so Marie has manufactured a partial android rather than raised a child.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 31 "Learning from Mia’s Mistakes" — The chapter grades each of Mia's escalations in Crocodile — helping Rob hide the cyclist's body, killing Rob fifteen years later, then killing Shazia, her husband, and baby Ali to keep the secret — under Kant's categorical imperative (the cover-up cannot be universalized and treats persons as means), the utilitarian calculus (which also condemns every killing once the widow's suffering and Mia's guilt are counted), and feminist care ethics, which rejects her defense that she killed to protect her family because care obligations never cancel proportionality and others' rights. Aristotle's virtue ethics supplies the diagnosis: Mia's undoing is lack of practical wisdom — every split-second choice (which she never had time to deliberate) went wrong because she lacked virtuous habits. The chapter urges practicing everyday virtue so we never take the first step down her path.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 17 "How Far I'll Go" — Maps the four waves of feminism onto Disney princess history: Snow White, Cinderella, and Aurora as chattel passed from parents to fairies to princes, betraying even first-wave rights; Beauvoir's 'one is not born but becomes a woman' and Friedan's feminine mystique explaining why the original trio's happiness is measured by marriage. Third-wave princesses are read with Wolf's beauty myth (Ariel and Jasmine as iron maidens), Butler's gender performativity, and Gilligan's care ethics (Ariel's and Belle's contextual, caring moral reasoning versus their fathers' principles). The fourth-wave princesses from Tiana to Moana need no man at all while male leads (Naveen, Flynn, Kristoff, Maui) become vulnerable sidekicks, ending with #GiveElsaAGirlfriend and the thought that equality is balance rather than sameness.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 17 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Olson's first D&D Encounters session handed her a sexualized female miniature in a chainmail bikini and high-heeled boots, and the chapter audits the game as a feminist would: research on the 'token girl' and male-default storytelling, women like Dowsett pushed to play male characters to be taken seriously, and harassment ranging from 'date at least one of the party or bring food' to condescension toward women in the industry. Against this she argues the rules themselves are egalitarian — identical power pools for male and female characters, embodying Plato's Republic claim that women 'are by nature the same with respect to guarding the city', and even the evil deities are stereotyped symmetrically (scheming Lolth and Tiamat versus war-god patrons of power) — while the collaborative party structure (clerics healing strikers, shared goals) has exactly the care-ethical, anti-individualist flavor Friedman and Bolte attribute to women's moral perspectives. Sexism is thus a consequence of unreflective practices, marketing that ignores women, and industry culture rather than the game; all-female systems like Portal Worlds are a real response but, she worries, separatism risks deepening the divide.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 37 "Notes" — Opening from the author's own grief — she nearly stopped playing Fallout 4 because its murdered spouse and kidnapped son echoed the loss of her real infant son — the chapter applies the ethics of care of Gilligan, Noddings, and Tronto to Fallout's wasteland. Care relationships structure the games: the Fallout 3 father whose flight from Vault 101 propels the plot, Dogmeat's loyal responsiveness as relational reciprocity, and the Fallout 4 son Shaun, where caring for your child collides with caring for a Commonwealth his Institute endangers. Settlement-building, faction choice (Lyons's Brotherhood handing out clean water versus the Railroad's liberation of synths), and even the Black Widow perk path that saves Megaton all become care-laden moral acts — care as protest against the wasteland's ethos of bare survival.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 28 "15. Chidi’s Indecision" — Surveys the 'Big Three' through the show: Kantian deontology (Chidi's boots lie, Tahani's mere-means charity), Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism (Jason's alligator frame-up, the trolley simulation), and Aristotle's golden mean (courage between Jason's rashness and Chidi's paralyzed deficiency), arguing their shared rationalism cannot accommodate the real uncertainty Chidi feels. John Dewey's 'Three Independent Factors in Morals' — the Good, the Right, and the Virtuous as irreducible — explains why Chidi sees only binaries while Eleanor finds 'option C' and imagines the Medium Place. The chapter concludes the show's unstated moral theory is care ethics: relational selves, justified partiality toward friends, and moral growth through the experience of being cared for, as when Chidi models care rather than lecturing it.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 11 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Donovan and Richardson read the Maltusian split, with the male Guardians banning emotion through the Book of Oa on Oa and the female Zamarons leaving to found the violet light of love on Zamaron, as the Western association of men with reason and women with emotion. They deploy Gilligan's different-voice reply to Kohlberg, the Pythagorean table of opposites via Genevieve Lloyd, Hegel's exclusion of women from the public sphere, and Jaggar's liberal-feminist critique of 'ahistorical' reason, whose comic-book analogue is the third law banning relationships between Lanterns. The chapter ends by arguing the standoff is a false dichotomy the comics themselves begin to dissolve: Kyle's 'Lanterns with heart' speech to the Guardians, the repeal of the third law, and the Indigo Tribe's plan to recombine the seven corps into the white light of creation.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 28 "NOTES" — Reads the show's eclipse icon against Plato's sun of the good — goodness has become hard to discern — and tests four theories of evil on the characters: Socrates' claim that no one errs knowingly is half-confirmed since villains like Angela and Nathan always take themselves to be doing right; Aristotle's akrasia and vice as an excess or deficiency of disposition fit Sylar's blood-scrawled 'Forgive me' apartment and his uncontrolled hunger; and Nietzsche's Übermensch and pre-Christian master morality raise the uncomfortable question of why Sylar preying on inferiors is not heroic like Achilles. The chapter's endorsed answer is Gilligan's ethics of care: the heroes are good because they care — Matt for Molly and Daphne, Bennet for Claire — while evil is the absence of care, though Bennet's authoritarian, family-only care shows that care itself must be both widened and restrained.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 29 "NOTES" — Explains the seemingly incomprehensible things Heroes characters do for family by sorting their motives into three theories of family obligation: universal justice (framed by Socrates confronting Euthyphro for prosecuting his own father), care ethics' partiality to loved ones, and Confucian role-based duty with its asymmetrical parent–child, husband–wife, and sibling obligations. Noah Bennet turns out to be Confucian in practice ('I'm your father, Claire Bear') despite his universalist Company rhetoric, Hiro defies Kaito's Confucianism for the greater good while Kaito still teaches him the sword because that is a father's role, Niki and Janice act from care while D.L. and Micah act from roles, Mohinder's duty is Confucian sonship to his dead father, and the Haitian kills his own brother Baron precisely because stopping him is his brotherly role.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 22 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Averill argues that Katniss's morality is built on care for particular people rather than impartial principle: she volunteers for Prim, protects Rue because the girl resembles her sister, and spares a wounded District 2 soldier at the Nut because he recalls her father and the Seam. Measured against Kant's impartial justice perspective (embodied by Thresh sparing Katniss to repay a debt to Rue), she falls short — but Gilligan's care perspective and Noddings's distinction between natural and ethical caring recast this as a valid, even heroic, moral development. Using Noddings, the chapter traces Katniss's arc from natural care for Prim toward ethical care for strangers and even enemies, and reads her assassination of Coin as care for all of Panem's future children rather than revenge. Care, the chapter concludes, can even justify violence when it protects the vulnerable.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 14 "5 Feminism and Indiana Jones A Field Guide" — Kate Schmidt applies feminist media tests (Bechdel, sexy lamp, Mako Mori, Pierce, Landau) to show the films usually fail — Willie is a screaming prop and human shield in Temple, the eyelid-writing student exists only to display Indy's sex appeal, and all four films fail the Bechdel Test — while Marion, Spalko, and above all Elsa in The Last Crusade are mixed cases with partial autonomy. Drawing on Iris Marion Young's account of women as Other and Carol Gilligan's care ethics, she argues Crusade is the series' most feminist film not for its women but for its men: Indy's open hurt after Elsa's betrayal and the father-son reconciliation embody care ethics against 'boys don't cry' toxic masculinity. She concludes that one can love flawed media without endorsing its sexism.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Kolb reads the whole franchise through Carol Gilligan's ethics of care and the ecofeminism of Ariel Salleh and Mary Mellor: Max begins as a caregiver in an egalitarian marriage, Toecutter's gang and the Citadel embody toxic masculinity, and Aunty Entity shows women can administer patriarchal capitalism too. In Fury Road, 'We are not things,' the milking mothers, and water branded as Aqua Cola literalize Salleh's claim that capitalist patriarchy treats women and nature as resources. The Vuvalini, the Keeper of the Seeds, Max washing in mother's milk, and his voluntary blood transfusion to Furiosa enact the ethic of care as the film's saving alternative to domination.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 24 "“To a Place Where We Know We Are Loved”" — Myers grades the moral development of the Sterling Cooper cast with Kohlberg's justice stages and Gilligan's ethics of care in order to find Aristotelian friendships, which require equals in moral development who wish each other good for the other's sake. Don and Peggy emerge as moral equivalents, each hiding a dark secret (the stolen identity; the baby given away) and each having done for the other what no one else could, from the hospital visit ('Move forward') to Don's 'nobody understands that, but you do' recruitment pitch; Joan and Roger form a second pair whose mutual esteem survives his marriage to Jane and her departure, shown when he trusts her to build Sterling Cooper Draper Pryce. Closing with Aristotle's claim that friendship holds states together, the chapter gives the new agency a better-than-average chance because these friendships are 'not for sale.'
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 26 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Frames the show's tension between the masculine public sphere (the chapel table, guns, club politics) and the feminine domestic sphere that actually sustains life, using Aristotle's oikos/polis division and Arendt's The Human Condition on the public/private realms. Gemma, dismissed as 'just an old lady,' proves the private sphere's power: she brought the club to Charming, orchestrates Jax's rise to the presidency, and converts her rape by Weston's LOAN goons into family solidarity that puts Jax's VP patch back on. Gilligan's and Baier's ethics of care then reads Lyla's abortion as a caring choice about family size, Tara's 'my job as your old lady is to be strong when and where you can't be' as care turned to strength, and Gemma's care curdling into retributive justice against Clay.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 26 "Notes" — Argues Star Trek functions like the Greek myths Nussbaum describes: modern tales of transformation (Gary Mitchell in "Where No Man Has Gone Before", Charlie X, Roger Korby) that let audiences judge what makes someone human. It rejects the Cartesian reading (Richard Hanley's Is Data Human?) in which Data's humanity is just a matter of being a rational mind, and develops instead a feminist, developmental account of personhood drawn from Annette Baier: persons are "second persons" who learn the arts of personhood from caretakers. Data, Seven of Nine, and Voyager's Doctor, all lacking real childhoods and families, must learn play, touch, love, and interdependence from their crews, with Janeway modeling family for Seven and Kes socializing the Doctor. Picard's farewell to Shinzon in Nemesis and to Data's B-4 caps the claim that humanity is an achievement of self-improvement in relationship, not a fixed essence.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 35 "“So, What Happens If You Take That Thing Off ”" — Ebner charts Din Djarin's moral development from a rights-based frame - hierarchy, Guild rules, 'I can bring you in warm, or I can bring you in cold' - to Carol Gilligan's ethics of care, a shift catalyzed by Kuiil's lessons ('You can trade', 'I have spoken') and completed by the Child. He re-reads Gilligan's pharmacy dilemma through 'The Sin', where Mando hijacks a speeder droid at gunpoint, and 'The Marshal', where trading with Cobb Vanth recasts the armor dispute as responsibility toward a threatened town rather than a contest of rights. Djarin's helmet decisions - refusing Omera, unmasking for Mayfeld's facial scan, and finally removing the helmet to say goodbye to Grogu - track his metamorphosis from rules and entitlements to responsibilities and relationships.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Young uses bell hooks's patriarchal masculinity (with Kate Manne on misogyny as enforcement) to read the show: Jamie is patriarchal terror's product, Rupert's promiscuity and Rebecca's subjection are two sides of male control, and Roy Kent's 'hard man' persona inherits the hardness Nietzsche praised and philosophy's traditional suspicion of emotion. Against this, hooks's definition of love as the will to nurture spiritual growth explains Ted's coaching, the training-room exorcism's shared vulnerability, Sam's openness, and Nate's status-hunger as the struggle to invert the gender pyramid, ending with Nate refusing Rupert's poisoned patriarchal gifts.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 13 "NOTES" — Chotiner tests Sarah Connor's plan to shoot Miles Dyson (one innocent life for three billion) against Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism and against Kant's deontology, showing both stall: utilitarianism licenses harvesting the author's organs for transplant patients, while Kant forbids using Dyson as a mere means and even condemns the mall kid's protective lie to the T-1000. Through Kohlberg's Heinz dilemma and Carol Gilligan's discovery that girls reason to preserve relationships rather than from abstract principles, he argues T2 stages the film's own answer: John and the reprogrammed T-101 care for Dyson's wounds and enlist him in destroying his research instead of using or sparing him on principle. 'I know now why you cry' caps the claim that morality needs the emotional capacity to care, not just rational maxims, with Sarah's gender-role reversal (she blasts through the elevator roof while the Terminator is the 'perfect mother') framing the whole argument.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 32 "Notes" — This multi-author epilogue collects short 'cutting-room-floor' reflections on poignant WoT quotes. Cooke reads Ingtar's confession as the existential fear of historical oblivion (historia as both history and story) driving a patriot into Darkfriendship. DeVan uses Covril's oak-and-wind metaphor to argue arguments strengthen through opposition, marshaling Confucius, Proverbs, al-Kindi, Milton, and Socrates's unexamined life. Held reads Min's arranged-marriage counsel with Nietzsche's amor fati and Epictetus's Heracles to reject resentment of unchosen fate. Pike reads Nynaeve sentencing the sul'dam through Carol Gilligan's and Annette Baier's ethics of care versus obligation (care can judge more harshly, per C.S. Lewis). Xhignesse reads the oak-and-willow line as Aesop woven into Randland's background.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Johnson-Moxley tests Perez's lasso of truth - which makes people face truths about themselves, like being dragged from Plato's cave - against four ethical touchstones: Kantian duty (truth-telling as a perfect duty, respect for autonomy), utilitarianism, virtue ethics, and care ethics. Cases drive the argument: binding Ares so he sees his apocalypse annihilates what he rules, freeing Vanessa from Dr. Psycho's false memories only with her permission, and lashing two warlords into 'twins of pain' to end bloodshed. She concludes via Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity that compelling truth is justified only to restore someone's rational self-direction, never paternalistically, with Gandhi's satyagraha ('truth-force') as the model of active, compassionate truth-telling.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 22 "Notes" — Bein argues Wonder Woman uniquely fuses two supposedly incompatible moralities: bushido - Nitobe's eight samurai virtues, Sun Tzu's benevolence of ending war swiftly, worthy-opponent rituals mirrored in superhero costumes - and the feminist ethics of care Gilligan and Noddings built against a Western canon (Aristotle, Kant) that called women too emotional for morality. Wonder Woman's killing of Maxwell Lord to free Superman is re-read as the care-ethical beach case: saving your own child over a stranger's is not a failure of impartiality, and in his Gotham-versus-Themyscira invasion thought experiment she would defend Gotham because its people are vulnerable non-combatants, not because a utilitarian ledger favors it.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 31 "Notes" — Chavez, Gavaler, and Goldberg trace Marston's 'Love Leader' kink - bracelets of submission, Venus girdles, Paradise Island bondage games, Earth One's collaring of Steve Trevor - to nineteenth-century maternalist feminism, then map the care ethics of Gilligan, Noddings, and Tronto onto both the comic and real-world BDSM. Reform (later Transformation) Island embodies a care-based alternative to punishment: rather than retribution, von Gunther and Irene are transformed by loving authority into people who save their captors, and Wonder Woman rescues the drowning villain Eviless because 'Aphrodite's Law commands us to save lives always - enemies or not.' The BDSM community's 4Cs (consent, communication, caring, caution) turn out to be Tronto's four elements of care, so the good dominant just is the good care-giver.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 14 "Fifth Hole How Golf Builds and Shapes Moral Character" — Beller and Stoll ask why empirical moral-reasoning research finds that sport generally does not build character, yet golfers score highest of all athletes. Using Aristotle's account of right conduct and Lickona's triad of moral knowing, feeling, and acting, they argue character forms through role models, social environment, and cognitive dissonance, supported by neuroplasticity research on the brain's capacity for moral growth. They contrast golf's self-policing tradition (Bobby Jones, Meg Mallon, Greg Norman, the film Bagger Vance) with the gamesmanship coached in team sports, and address Gilligan's 'different voice' by reporting that female golfers reason at least as highly as males, concluding that golf's honor-bound moral community sets it apart.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 23 "11. The Mother of All Bombs" — Kolb argues Laura Palmer embodies the 'Angel in the House' ideal (Gilbert and Gubar) whose perfection is a beautiful dead girl, and reads The Return's linkage of the Trinity bomb to BOB/Judy through Arendt's On Violence—violence begets a more violent, hostile world that especially victimizes women. Using Gilligan's In a Different Voice, she shows how women's voices (Naido/Diane, the Log Lady, Laura's diary) are silenced by toxic masculinity (Mr. C, Richard, Chad), while the 'good men' embody an ethic of care; the manufactured post-war social order names its bombs after mothers and treats women as perfect-yet-fallen others.
- **The Philosophy of Joss Whedon**, ch. 8 "Conclusion" — The concluding chapter argues that Joss Whedon 'does philosophy' on television, not merely illustrates it, by ranking degrees of filmic philosophizing (via Wartenberg, Shaw, Mulhall) and showing the Whedenverse meets them. It reads Angel/Angelus and Fred/Illyria as cinematic thought experiments that generate 'metaphysical complexity' about personal identity, playing memory- and continuity-of-consciousness theories (Locke, Parfit) against a soul theory, and reads Connor's origin as exemplifying Kane's libertarian free will. It contends Whedon endorses a Noddings-style ethics of care and an existentialist yet God-independent morality, epitomized by Angel's 'Epiphany' speech ('the smallest act of kindness is the greatest thing') and 'Deep Down,' plus the 'Man on the Street' Academic monologue, staging a negative project against the claim that ethics is incoherent without God through the self-sacrifices of Simon, Cordelia, and Buffy.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 17 "A Spielbergian Ethics of the Family in Saving Private Ryan and The Color Purple" — Clewis defines a 'Spielbergian ethics of the family,' a care-based virtue ethics holding that we owe unique obligations to family and close friends grounded in personal identity, and contrasts it with utilitarian and Kantian approaches. In Saving Private Ryan the squad-as-family and the Ryan brotherhood explain why Miller says Ryan must 'earn this' and why living an ordinary good life suffices; in The Color Purple sisterhood (Nettie/Celie), fatherhood, and motherhood ground obligations of care, forgiveness, and reconciliation. He evaluates the view's feasibility while warning it neglects wider social influences and the is/ought gap.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 19 "10 Listening with Neil’s Vulnerable Voice and the Ethics of Care" — Jostedt argues that Young's raw, high "dental" singing voice (contrasted with Dylan's nasal sneer) invites empathetic "listening-with" rather than the detached individualism of Kant's deontology or Mill's utilitarianism. Drawing on Gilligan's In a Different Voice, Jane Addams and the ethics of care's emphasis on relatedness, he shows how songs like "Ohio," "Stringman," "Cortez the Killer" and the album Trans (evoking his son's cerebral palsy) make listeners feel with the downtrodden and disabled.
- **Joss Whedon as Philosopher**, ch. 7 "Angel, Angelus, and Personal Identity" — This file gathers Part II, arguing Whedon actually philosophizes through film. It works through the film-as-philosophy debate (Mulhall's 'bold thesis' and its critics Baggini, Smith, Livingston, Russell, and Wartenberg), using 'Hush' as a Zen-like case that resists linguistic paraphrase and The Cabin in the Woods to pit Mill's utilitarianism against Noddings's ethics of care (Dana refusing to kill Marty to save the world). Its capstone treats the Angel/Angelus problem as a personal-identity thought experiment, staging the soul theory (Plato), body theory (Hobbes/Holtz), and Locke's and Parfit's memory/psychological-continuity theories, and arguing Whedon's eight-season Angel-Angelus and Fred-Illyria cases serve as a cinematic counterexample to Neo-Lockean continuity, ultimately endorsing a care-based view of what matters in identity.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 21 "A Better Way of Living Your Life" — Laura Geuy Akers argues the Doctor lives by a relational ethics of care rather than deontology, utilitarianism, or virtue ethics. Drawing on Noddings's care ethics and Buber's I-Thou versus I-It stance, she shows the Doctor responds to particular others (insisting the Ood is "a he, not an it," addressing each companion individually before surrender) and even ethically cares for the Master. She pairs this with Nussbaum's and Kant's accounts of wonder and the sublime, arguing the Doctor's human companions (Rose, Martha, Donna) restore his sense of wonder and give his immortal life meaning.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 22 "Toward Caring" — J.J. Sylvia argues the Doctor, though male, is an ideal exemplar of the feminist ethics of care developed by Carol Gilligan (against Kohlberg's justice-only scale) and Nel Noddings. Contrasting the caring "Doctor" with the dominating "Master," he uses Rita Manning's account of caring as responsiveness and obligation to argue that an ethics of care, unlike impartial utilitarianism, explains why the Doctor should save his companion over a stranger. Noddings's natural-versus-ethical caring explains the Doctor forgiving the Master and offering compassion to Dalek Caan, and companions supply reciprocal care that guards against burnout.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 35 "You’re Basically “a Stuffed Animal Made by Grandma”" — Renee Kyle contrasts Dr. House's detached 'doctor knows best' justice ethic with Dr. Cameron's feminist ethic of care drawn from Carol Gilligan's In a Different Voice. Cameron builds trusting relationships, sees patients as embedded in social networks, and refuses to deceive or bully (as with Ezra and the newborns in 'Maternity'), whereas House treats patients as abstract puzzle-pieces. Kyle also voices the feminist worry that valorizing care can lead women to care at personal cost, as when Cameron's own grief over her dead husband derails her professional judgment.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 17 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Nease lays out a game plan for raising ethical children, using Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics – eudaimonia as a flourishing life, virtue as the mean between extremes, and the master-skills of practical wisdom and self-control – as the core, mocking 'character counts' posters as no substitute for early habit-formation. He folds in Kant's motive of duty, Nietzsche's will-to-power (glossed via Janet Jackson's Control) as the drive to master oneself, and argues empathy (Theodor Lipps' inner imitation), self-awareness, concentration (Husserl's foreground/background), and a respect for justice must be cultivated to 'stack the deck' toward a good adult.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 18 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Terjesen defends a distinctively paternal form of caring against care ethics' maternal bias. Reviewing Kohlberg's moral-development scale, Gilligan's justice-vs-care orientations, and Noddings' 'engrossment' model of caring, he argues these frameworks make it seem fathers like his own undemonstrative Norwegian dad don't care. He reconceives 'paternalism' (via Gerald Dworkin's soft paternalism and examples like Darth Vader and Bambi's father) as tough-love caring focused on the child's future self, complementary to maternal caring and distinct from the impersonal justice orientation.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 25 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Mattern argues the heart of good fatherhood is mercy – 'faithful, compassionate love' – as an attitude of the heart, not a technique. Drawing on Aquinas's account of habitus and his ranking of mercy among the greatest virtues, plus Gabriel Marcel's 'creative fidelity,' Solovyov, Jean Vanier, and Karol Wojtyla on love as affirming another's value, he contrasts remote, justice-oriented fathers with empathic ones. He illustrates with overlapping Venn-diagram circles of father and child and with responding to his 7-year-old son's shoplifting through listening and repair rather than spanking.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 22 "MOTHERHOOD" — Chris Mulford, a nurse and lactation consultant, analyzes infant feeding as an ethical question of rights, duties, and responsibilities, drawing on a feminist ethic of care and the claim that women learn empathy through caregiving (linked to oxytocin's role in birth and nursing). She argues that the right at stake is the mother-child dyad's 'protection from interference' with breastfeeding, that no mother is saddled with a solitary duty to breastfeed, and that the duty toward breastfeeding falls on the whole community; she frames the mother's dependency on 'the kindness of strangers' via A Streetcar Named Desire and the innate 'breast crawl.'
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 23 "MOTHERHOOD" — Maureen Sander-Staudt uses a feminist ethic of care – especially Carol Gilligan's mole-and-porcupine fable of reciprocal accommodation – to argue that pressuring women to nurse privately or covered imposes 'lactational burkas.' She runs public breastfeeding through the Miller obscenity test to show it is not obscene, opening with Gloria Steinem's 'If men could menstruate' to imagine 'milkmen,' and cites the Emily Gillette Freedom-flight ejection, Facebook's photo removal, the Janet Jackson Superbowl scandal, and PETA's human-milk proposal to expose hypocritical, biologically reductive double standards about the female breast.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 35 "You’re Basically “a Stuffed Animal Made by Grandma”" — Kyle contrasts House's detached, impartial "ethic of justice" with Dr. Cameron's feminist ethic of care, drawn from Carol Gilligan's In a Different Voice. Cameron builds trusting relationships, refuses to deceive patients, and attends to their social networks — letting parents hold their dying baby in "Maternity," defending Ezra's autonomy in "Informed Consent." But Kyle also presses the standard critique that valorizing care can cost the carer: Cameron's own grief over her dead husband derails her professional judgment in "Acceptance" and pushes her toward Houselike tactics.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 16 "14. The Doctor as Philosopher The Collectivist-Realist Pacifism of the Doctor and the Quest for Social Justice" — Smithka argues the Doctor is a 'collectivist-realist pacifist': morally opposed to war yet willing, as a last resort, to use lethal force for social justice. She places the Doctor on Cady's warism-to-pacifism continuum (past absolute and collectivist pacifism), augmenting it with Martin Luther King Jr.'s realist pacifism — ethical appeals 'undergirded by constructive coercive power' — and Gandhi's ahimsa and belief that no one is beyond redemption (the Doctor sparing Davros, offering enemies a choice). She tests Kant's duty ethics and respect for persons (Rule 1: the Doctor lies), Ross's prima facie duties, Mill's utilitarianism ('The Fires of Pompeii,' 'The Beast Below'), Gilligan/Noddings care ethics, and Wolterstorff's 'life of needs,' and reads 'The Day of the Doctor' as a Rawlsian veil of ignorance brokering Zygon-human peace.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 27 "25. The Mandalorian as Philosophy “This Is the Way”" — The chapter argues that The Mandalorian defends virtue ethics with care as the primary virtue. It maps Mando's creed and 'Canons of Honor' (strength, honor, loyalty, death) onto Stoicism's discipline of desire and cardinal virtues, quoting Marcus Aurelius and Seneca, and reads his transformation after adopting Grogu as Aristotelian moral development toward eudaimonia and flourishing. Using Stocker's critique of impartialist ethics and Noddings's and Slote's ethics of care, Belluomini argues Mando's caring relation with Grogu, his engrossment and motivational displacement, and his removing his helmet at the end show that care ranks highest among the virtues and should guide our own 'Way.'
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 13 "4. The Good of the Doctor" — The chapter distinguishes aesthetic 'good' (taste, beauty of the Daleks) from ethical 'good,' then tests the Doctor against the major moral theories: utilitarianism (rejected when Sarah Jane urges exterminating the Daleks in 'Genesis of the Daleks'), Kantian duty ethics (the Doctor's 'never met anyone who wasn't important' and attempts to save Davros and the Master), virtue ethics (the Eleventh Doctor guarding Christmas in 'The Time of the Doctor'), and feminist care ethics. Concluding that none quite fits because the Doctor values non-rational beings and feels compassion, the author proposes the Doctor follows Wolterstorff's 'ethic of need'—justice as meeting the needs of all—consistent with 'getting in the thick of things' as a flâneur.

### Buddhism

Buddhism is a family of traditions arising from the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, in ancient India, aimed at understanding and ending suffering. It diagnoses ordinary existence as marked by dissatisfaction rooted in craving and ignorance, and it offers a path of ethical conduct, mental discipline, and insight leading toward liberation, often described as nirvana. Rejecting reliance on a creator deity for salvation, Buddhism emphasizes practices such as meditation and the cultivation of wisdom and compassion, and it has developed into diverse schools across Asia and beyond.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 56 "Unknown" — Brannigan reads the film's mirror imagery through the Buddha's mirror instruction to his son Rahula: Neo touching the dripping mirror and becoming the mirror marks his awakening to the naked truth (aletheia as nakedness) that his world is a programmed illusion, Smith's dark sunglasses distort while Morpheus's mirrored glasses clarify, and Neo's reflection in the spoon-bending boy's spoon signals clarity. 'There is no spoon' parallels the Zen mondo where neither flag nor wind moves but only mind, and shows that reflected images are not reality - the world is maya. The deepest lesson is anatman: just as there is no spoon there is no Neo, no fixed self, and Rahula's lesson grounds the interdependence (pratityasamutpada) of all actions on others.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 58 "Unknown" — Brannigan tests whether The Matrix is a Buddhist film and finds four incongruities: its Zoroastrian good-versus-evil dualism (the system and those in it as 'enemies') against karuna and metta, its glorified gun violence ('guns, lots of guns') against ahimsa, its crass language against right speech, and its human-centeredness against the Buddha-nature of all sentient beings, including 'sentient programs'. He concedes the slaughter might be read symbolically as slaying the mind's three poisons, as Manjusri's sword does, but rejects calling the result 'American Buddhism'. He concludes the film is a deliberate syncretism of Christianity, Platonism, and Buddhism that still conveys the Buddhist message of liberation from the mind.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 61 "Unknown" — The chapter argues the film is by no means a Christian movie: Neo is a violent, far-from-sinless mere human savior; the fundamental human problem is ignorance and illusion (Gnostic and Eastern) rather than sin and alienation from God; the rebels' belief that Neo is the reincarnation of the earlier liberator mirrors the Dalai Lama search the Wachowskis cite, though reincarnation is rejected by all major Christian sects; and 'there is no spoon' asserts the illusoriness of empirical reality that Christianity denies. The film's malleable, cyclical time and the Wachowskis' answer that faith is 'in oneself' complete a syncretistic tapestry the essay goes on to examine as religious pluralism.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 29 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Jennifer McMahon and Steve Csaki compare Tolkien with Zen Buddhism and Taoism on four themes while insisting on the real differences. Tolkien's talking trees (Old Man Willow, Treebeard's 'half awake' forest) invite comparison with Buddhist universal sentience and Dogen's walking mountains, but Tolkien anthropomorphizes where Buddhism grants non-human modes of sentience; the hobbits' ties to the Shire echo dependent origination, though Tolkien's stewardship and preference for the domesticated Shire over sinister wild nature remain Western. Frodo's succession of mentors (Bilbo, Gandalf, Aragorn, and the unlikely 'Master Samwise') parallels the Zen master-student relation, while Tolkien's war of light against darkness - nine Walkers against nine Riders - is decisively not the Taoist balance of yin and yang, for Taoists destroying either cosmic force would itself produce evil.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 28 "Ballparks, Dojos, and Other Places of Enlightenment" — Bassham argues that the core advice of hitting instructors like Ted Williams ('get a good ball to hit') and Charley Lau ('tension is the enemy') echoes Zen Buddhist principles, walking through patience, relaxation, self-knowledge, visualization (Reggie Jackson, Willie Stargell, Barry Bonds's on-deck imagery), practice, Bruce Lee-style kime concentration, and mushin or no-mind. Mickey Mantle going 0-for-30 after over-thinking Ted Williams's hitting tips, and Tony Gwynn's 'see the ball and react,' show how conscious analysis interferes with the muscle memory a half-second fastball demands. If kendo is practiced in a dojo — a 'place of enlightenment' — he concludes, ballparks and batting cages may be dojos too, with the caveat that Cobb, Ruth, and Mantle hardly model egoless humility.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 29 "What’s Wrong with Generalization" — Brannigan uses Japanese baseball to ask what is wrong with cultural generalization. He presents the Bushido case — samurai-style self-denial, absolute loyalty (Kawakami's Yomiuri Giants), Suisha Tobita's 'training of death,' resolve (konjo), team harmony (wa), and a relational self grounded in Buddhism's no-self and Confucian identity-through-relationships — then tests it against counter-evidence: Sadaharu Oh's flamingo swing owed as much to individual talent and Hiroshi Arakawa's unconventional kendo-and-aikido coaching as to sensei imitation, the 'new breed' (Ochiai, Egawa) flouts the old ways, and William Kelly's 'Whiting problem' warns against polarizing Japanese and American baseball. The chapter's 'three strikes' against the label 'Japanese baseball' conclude that generalizations become dangerous when treated as monolithic nets cast over an entire culture.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 8 "“A New Broom Sweeps Clean, but an Old Broom Knows Every Corner”" — Callis interweaves a memoir of the teenage boyfriend who played her Dark Side and later killed himself with an account of Easy Star Records' 2003 reggae remake, Dub Side of the Moon, arguing that the album's themes of time, money, materialism, and madness translate naturally into Rasta reasoning. Nyabinghi drumming, singjay toasting, and bong-bubble effects re-read 'Money' (the cash register replaced by a lighter firing the chalice) and 'Time' (Ranking Joe's 'Time is the master') through Rasta rejection of Babylon, anti-capitalist subsistence, and 'soon come' patience, which she glosses with the Buddhist principle that things happen in their own time. The reggae setting, she concludes, weaves all this pain and madness, from Barrett's collapse to her own ghosts, into something more optimistic than the original ever sounded.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 17 "There is No Dark Side of the Moon Really. Matter of Fact It’s All Dark" — Johnston reads The Dark Side of the Moon through Buber's I and Thou: modern life traps us in the I-It mode of experience, from 'Welcome to the Machine' to teachers who treat students as replaceable Its ('Hey, teacher, leave us kids alone!') and Horkheimer's instrumental reason that turns personnel into 'human resources,' while the album repeatedly calls us to the I-You encounter, from 'Echoes'' strangers whose glances meet ('I am you and what I see is me,' Waters's origin of empathy) to 'Breathe''s 'don't be afraid to care.' He links the opening heartbeat and the breath of 'Breathe' to Buber's eternal You, defends Buddhism against Buber's charge that enlightenment is worldless monologue (the Buddha becomes one with the world, a perfect reciprocity like the innate You of the womb), and accepts Nietzsche's point that the Enlightenment's abstract God is dead while insisting, with Buber, that encounter with the eternal You remains possible. The album itself, he concludes, resists degenerating into an It: even if 'the sun is eclipsed by the moon,' the light persists and Dark Side can be the antidote to the It-world.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 24 "Alchemic Heroism" — Reads Edward and Alphonse Elric as a single composite 'alchemic hero' who fuses Japanese heroic archetypes: the dual-hero rooted in the Izanami-Izanagi creation myth and yin-yang complementarity (brash yang Ed, calm yin Al whose armored body actually fights better), the student hero forged by Izumi Curtis's brutal island training, and the wandering redemption seeker atoning for the forbidden attempt to resurrect their mother. It argues that the sacrifice built into this fusion — Al's lost senses, puberty, and body — mirrors Japan's own cultural alchemy of absorbing Buddhism, Confucianism, and yin-yang thought while retaining a coherent national identity.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 5 "Fighting Talk" — The editors' introduction argues that philosophy and fighting have been companions since Socrates the soldier and Plato the wrestler (whose name means 'broad shouldered' from the gym), and that each can illuminate the other. It tours the volume through concrete cases: budo courtesy drawn from Shinto, Confucianism and Zen; the Shaolin monks' exercises as a route to Buddhahood; Western chivalry and Gordon Marino's boxing as educations in Aristotelian courage; fencing's egoism and value; and the Stoicism of karate and utilitarianism of Kano's judo. Philosophy clarifies fighting traditions, while fights supply puzzles for ethics, aesthetics, and the philosophy of mind.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 22 "What Monkey Should Have Known" — Mortensen opens with Monkey from Journey to the West beating six robbers to death despite Tripitaka's protest, and asks whether a practitioner of budo can be a Buddhist. He defends three principles, Take No Life, No First Strike and Stop Before Harm, qualifying them via the Upaya-kausalya Sutra's sea captain, Funakoshi's 'there is no first strike in karate', Ueshiba's purely defensive aikido, the initiator's bad karma, and the exception of multiple attackers; then he applies them to weapons, arguing that wooden weapons (the jo, Musashi's bokken, above all the humble walking stick, the 'last legal weapon') fit the precepts where the katana does not. Monkey, in short, should have carried a stick.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 17 "All for Love" — Jerry Piven argues Dexter's void is not genetic sociopathy but trauma: witnessing his mother's chainsaw murder and lying in her blood deadened his feelings, and each ritualized kill restages that catastrophe with the roles reversed, Dexter mastering death as the angel of it, reducing the murderer to a drop of blood he imprisons on a slide. Reading Harry's ghost as a Hamlet-father super-ego, he contends Dexter kills not only to master trauma but to please the father who channels his rage - murder 'for love' - and then generalizes: Arendt's banality of evil, Pascal on the void and faith, Kierkegaard and Heidegger on fleeing despair into conformity, Buddhist emptiness, and Becker-style terror-management findings explain how ordinary people, frightened of death and hungry for a leader's approval, can be manipulated into sanctioned slaughter, from Abu Ghraib to jihadism.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 18 "Halo as a Catalyst for a Buddhism Videogame" — Luke Cuddy uses Halo 3 checkpoints and emulator save states—two mutually exclusive Flood-fight outcomes both in some sense true—to make David Lewis's possible worlds and modal truth concrete, with Leibniz as the doctrine's ancestor. Halo's infinite lives make players genuinely angry, and the chapter argues this is upaya territory: like the father in the Lotus Sutra's parable of the burning house, the game promises mastery (the goat-, deer-, and ox-carts) to lure players toward something greater outside it. Master Chief becomes a Bodhisattva whose avatar slides between extension of self and other, provoking the 'who am I?' crisis that reveals the ego as empty at the ultimate level of the Two-Fold Truth, while the Dalai Lama's enemies-as-teachers turns the seven-year-old who pwns you into practice in the first two Noble Truths' suffering and anger.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 37 "The Awakened One" — Callis reads Holmes as a Buddhist practitioner despite the cocaine and the cigars in the coalscuttle: 'You see, but you do not observe' and 'The emotional qualities are antagonistic to clear reasoning' match Vipassana bare attention and the Theravada ideal of the cool, rational, emotionally distant sage, and his improvised violin scraping works like Thich Nhat Hanh's walking meditation — a witness without commentary. The picture is completed by Doyle's Buddhism of Ceylon in The Sign of Four, Holmes's two years 'spending some days with the head lama' in Tibet ('The Empty House'), and his sitting 'like some strange Buddha' in 'The Veiled Lodger.' She maps his method onto the Yoga Sutras' dharana, dhyana, and samadhi — patient attention to the blood-scratched plaster, sustained fixation on the crime scene, ego-surrendering contemplation — making Holmes an 'awakened one' who loves truth for its own sake while Watson lives on autopilot.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 17 "Do We Give Shakespeare the Last Word" — Kapper reads Inception as epistemology rather than metaphysics - not what is real but how we could know - running from Plato's Theaetetus (the first dream-recognition question) through Descartes's deceptive demon and Freud's royal road to the unconscious, to Wittgenstein's point that 'I may be dreaming' is senseless because the remark itself would be dreamed, and Heraclitus's line that only the waking share a common world. The Ariadne thread is the clue: as in the Theseus myth, dream architecture gives the labyrinth a shareable narrative place, but only a hint, never a way to wake. He then goes east - Zhuangzi's butterfly, Indra's net of mutually reflecting jewels, Schopenhauer's universe dreamed by a single dreamer, William James's many consciousnesses - to ask how many times we must die before waking, ending with Buddhism: 'Buddha means awakened one', and Cobb's turning from the top enacts Nirvana, where the real-versus-dream question stops pertaining.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 27 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Liane Heller pairs Cohen and Schopenhauer - born and died on September 21st, the autumnal equinox - as two explorers of the world's irrational negativity who both retreat to 'a room' to create. Schopenhauer's directionless Will, his pessimism about a life of constant suffering, his notorious misogyny in 'On Women,' and his ascetic denial of the will-to-live (with his contempt for Judaism and preference for the Upanishads and Buddhist compassion) are set against Cohen's affirmation that love is 'the only engine of survival,' his five-year Zen retreat that could not hold him, and his return to the Judaism of the 'little Jew who wrote the Bible.' A closing imagined dialogue has a humbled Schopenhauer confronted with Cohen's self-compassion and ordinary joys, admitting the limits of his own field of vision.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 11 "3. Tris Finds Enlightenment" — Rhine argues that Tris's heroism rests on Buddhist practice: her breath-counting on the Ferris wheel and inside Four's fear landscape, her emotional intelligence, and her awareness of the parental 'voices in her head' are classic meditative disciplines for calming the ego whose clinging, on the Buddhist account, is the cause of suffering (dukkha). She reads Abnegation's gray houses, plain food, and four-times-a-year mirror as ritual ego-diminishment - a middle way between indulgence and the extreme asceticism the Buddha rejected - that explains why most Divergent arise from Abnegation. Contemporary neuroscience is then recruited: the amygdala-versus-prefrontal-cortex struggle Will describes, and monks' heightened gamma waves, explain how Tris can see the simulation as a simulation, like Neo in The Matrix, and act while others are paralyzed by fear.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 15 "6. Bowie the Buddhist" — Muchall reads 'Quicksand' and 'Where Are We Now?' as suffused with Tibetan Buddhism: 'Don't believe in yourself' voices the anatta teaching Bowie absorbed studying with Chime Rinpoche and from Chogyam Trungpa, whose 'spiritual materialism' warns that ego converts even spirituality and ideologies to its own use.
