- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 19 "This Is Our World" — Miguel Sicart reads the 'Gnome Tea Party' — dozens of nearly nude gnome warriors parading in Ironforge to protest Warrior-class nerfs until Blizzard banned their accounts — as non-violent protest in the tradition of Thoreau and Gandhi. Against Blizzard's models of players-as-consumers and players-as-troublemakers, which he traces to Huizinga's Homo Ludens, he argues that players are Homo poieticus: creative beings who make the values they play by and act on them. Using the 'Flourishing Ethics' framework built from Aristotle's virtue ethics and Wiener's information ethics, he concludes that WoW's architectures of control and account-banning are an unethical design that damages players' capacity to flourish — Azeroth is our world too.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 12 "You Don’t Have to Be Like Him to Like Him" — Levitt reads Monk through Aristotle's virtue ethics: a man of character whose police virtues survive Trudy's murder but whose phobias produce akrasia — in the pilot he knows he must descend the germ-filled sewer to save Sharona and freezes anyway, doing the right thing only at agonizing cost. Virtue as habit and the golden mean (friendliness as the mean between obsequiousness and standoffishness) frame his slow progress toward acting rightly without thinking, which is also why Stottlemeyer cannot recommend his reinstatement — he doubts the illness, not the man. Aristotle's three friendships sort Monk's relationships: utility (the department, employer Sharona), pleasure, and virtue — Natalie, who after watching Monk save Julie's fish over the priceless moon rock saw her late husband's goodness in him. Ethos, pathos, logos and catharsis then explain viewer identification: watching Monk move from akrasia toward balance (Dr. Kroger's 'N. Hope' note that turns out to mean New Hope) lets audiences identify with, and be ennobled by, a character we would never want to be.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 21 "Redemption and Hope for the Future" — Peters applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics account of courage — the mean between confidence and fear, shown only in facing an honorable death in war for a noble motive — to Colin MacLeod's two-thousand-year hunt for Marcus Octavius, the Immortal Roman who killed his wife Moya, in Highlander: The Search for Vengeance. Because MacLeod fights from pain and rage, 'like wild beasts,' and secretly seeks death as refuge from grief ('to seek death as a refuge from poverty, or love... is not the act of a brave man'), Aristotle would judge him a coward despite his fearlessness — Amergan the spirit guide diagnoses him the same way. Redemption comes only when Dahlia and the villagers threatened by Marcus's new Rome give him a noble cause and hopefulness: he becomes their general, fights with discipline instead of rage, and turns Marcus's own quickening to destroying the virus, illustrating the chapter's closing thought that for an Immortal dying is easy and living courageously is hard.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 19 "Forgiveness and the Fenway Faithful" — Rory Kraft uses Aristotle's virtue ethics to explain why Red Sox Nation forgave Tim Wakefield (whose mistake Aaron Boone turned into the 2003 ALCS-ending homer) and Ted Williams, but scapegoated Bill Buckner for 'the error' and eventually cast off Manny Ramirez. Because Aristotle judges a complete life, one swallow does not make a summer, Buckner's .991 fielding percentage and 2,715 hits should contextualize his lapse, yet some acts are bad without degrees like Aristotle's adultery, theft and murder, and a World Series-deciding error crossed that line. Kraft distinguishes Aristotle's categories, Wakefield's mistake (ignorance of Boone's changed plan) versus Buckner's misadventure (contrary to reasonable expectation) versus Manny's voluntary injustices, concluding that learning when to forgive players who are family taught the Nation what forgiveness itself means, sealed by Buckner's 2008 standing ovation.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 33 "Tie Goes to the Runner" — St. Martin runs the Fenway 'pink hat' controversy through Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: the virtuous fan is the mean between the deficient bandwagoner who waves at NESN cameras mid-pitch and the excessive diehard who memorizes Dice-K's ERA to belittle others. Terry Francona's courage in sending Dave Roberts in the 2004 ALCS (versus a reckless Ortiz steal attempt) illustrates virtue as the mean between cowardice and foolhardiness, and Aristotle's contrast between the love of honor and the love of contemplation shows both pink hatters and stats-obsessed diehards err by making fandom about themselves. She concludes that accepting fans in any color hat is the truly virtuous mean.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 14 "“Hey, Let’s Get the Stuff We Need!” Putting the Mall in Its Place" — Matthew Walker reads Dawn of the Dead's survivors, who loot the mall, gorge, grow bored, and degenerate into glitzy despair beside the zombies clawing to get back in, through Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and Politics. Peter's 'They're us' is glossed by pleonexia, the grasping disposition to want more, which Aristotle roots in being serious about mere living rather than living well, and the quartet's hedonistic 'sweet life' is the life of enjoyment Aristotle dismisses as fit for cattle because it atrophies the rational capacities that make us human. Romero is no Puritan scold: material goods remain instrumentally useful and the mall a sanctuary, but like Aristotle he shows a life of unlimited acquisition is a kind of living death, which is why Peter and Fran must leave empty-handed.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 19 "Cold Clammy Consistency" — Wayne Yuen argues vampires are moral agents because they meet Aristotle's test of practical wisdom (Lestat's investments and his judgment that 'evildoers... taste better') and retain free will, since their blood-lust is a craving not a compulsion and Louis's rat diet in Interview with the Vampire, like Angel's in Buffy, proves an alternative exists. TASTE, full potential, and spiritual peace all fail to justify human blood, because killing a person brings more unnecessary suffering than killing a rat, the same suffering-based principle that condemns factory farming. The 'cold clammy consistency' punchline: since humans need not eat meat, condemning vampire blood-drinkers while dining on chicken, pork, and beef is hypocrisy, because we are vampiric too and only our choice of which life to ingest separates the monstrous from the virtuous.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 13 "Extra Time" — Kent argues soccer is Aristotle's favorite sport because everything in both is organized around the goal: the four causes explain shinguards (plastic, curved shape, Mitre's workers, protection) and the game itself, with the final cause—scoring—defining a thing's identity and goodness, so two differently made balls are both soccerballs if kicked toward a net. Soccer best fulfills sport's three purposes (physical and moral discipline, theatrical imitation with catharsis, recreation): its ninety minutes of uninterrupted continuity force hundreds of renewed acts of self-mastery in Aristotle's sense of courage and the right amount, its single referee with limited powers embodies Aristotle's preferred limited monarchy, and Argentina's sportsmanlike throw-in returning the ball after Cameroon kicks it out for an injured player exemplifies equity—making a rightful exception to the letter of the law. Own goals, where a defender's error harms his own side, supply the hamartia of Aristotelian tragedy, giving fans a healthy catharsis of pity and fear.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 29 "The Final Whistle" — Andrew Lambert defends the rationality of being a football fan by updating Aristotle: living well in a liberal consumer democracy demands an accessible source of beauty, catharsis, belonging, public discourse, and altruism, and fandom trains exactly these sensibilities — from his childhood prayers for Everton to the 1914 Christmas Truce match and supporters' trusts that own clubs like Exeter City. The mature 'fan of football' takes an ironic view of the 'loyal fan's' tribal passions, gaining the practical wisdom that keeps rivalry (the Liverpool–Everton derby, the 1969 'Football War') from curdling into violence. Fandom thus answers critics who dismiss it as consumerist escapism or bad faith.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 5 "Fighting Talk" — The editors' introduction argues that philosophy and fighting have been companions since Socrates the soldier and Plato the wrestler (whose name means 'broad shouldered' from the gym), and that each can illuminate the other. It tours the volume through concrete cases: budo courtesy drawn from Shinto, Confucianism and Zen; the Shaolin monks' exercises as a route to Buddhahood; Western chivalry and Gordon Marino's boxing as educations in Aristotelian courage; fencing's egoism and value; and the Stoicism of karate and utilitarianism of Kano's judo. Philosophy clarifies fighting traditions, while fights supply puzzles for ethics, aesthetics, and the philosophy of mind.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 7 "Free Your Mind, and Your Roundhouse Will Follow" — Young argues that dojo courtesy is not the fantasy that good manners win fights (Napoleon and the Karate Kid's Johnny lost on skill, not rudeness) but the framing of a craft within a way of life. He maps Aristotle's techne/ethos distinction onto the Japanese jutsu/do pairing to show founders like Kano, Funakoshi and Ueshiba treated fighting as one part of a whole ethical character, reads his seiza apology to an injured yellow belt through Confucian ren, li, yi and shu, and traces Shinto purity into the sincerity (kime) of committed sparring. His black-belt humiliation by seniors becomes Zen's 'courtesy of brutal': ego-deflating violence that trains no-mindedness (muga, Takuan Soho's fudoshin).
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 17 "The Way of the Place" — Beattie uses Henri Lefebvre's account of the production of space to read the dojo as a 'differential space' practitioners actively create against abstract, conformist space. He shows how bow-ins, founder portraits, Japanese counting, mats, dogi and belt hierarchies mark ownership, bind the school to a lineage, separate 'dojo' from 'street', and shape bodies and safety (with Kendo's door-side seating and MMA's display of physique as hierarchy written into space). Play matters too: Aristotle's point that virtues are built by habit explains how playing at combat in a safe place breeds real courage, and the whole exercise teaches a moving balance between inside and outside.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 25 "Jousting for Virtue" — Farrell argues that the medieval code of chivalry is a living case study for Aristotle's virtue ethics: Lancelot, 'mekest in hall and sternest to his foe', embodies the paradox C.S. Lewis names as meek and fierce 'to the nth', which Farrell reads as Aristotle's courage, the golden mean between cowardice and rashness, exercised 'to the right extent, at the right time, with the right motive'. The joust, meanwhile, was a proving ground where knightly virtues became second nature through habituated practice, since as Aristotle says 'it is no easy task to be good'. Western martial arts, he concludes, are 'moral kung fu': a fencing match with one's own standards of virtue.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 26 "Boxing, a School for Virtues" — Marino answers colleagues who call college boxing 'teaching violence' with an Aristotelian defense: courage is the mean between fearlessness and excessive fear, and the ring is one of the few workshops where fear is actually practiced. He cites Wacquant's boxing gym as 'a school of morality' in Durkheim's sense, Rotella's 'education at the fights', and boxers like Maja Cavlovic and George Foreman on how training takes over when fear hits, to argue boxing forges emotional self-command. His challenge to his own students: 'How can you be consistently honest or just if you don't have the mettle to take a hit?'
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 11 "In All Fucking Seriousness" — Arp asks why well-placed 'fucks' in Onion headlines like 'Guy In Philosophy Class Needs To Shut The Fuck Up' are funny, and answers with the golden mean traced to Aristotle and Confucius, who both prized self-control and being a good role model to children: swearing is virtuous when it hits the mean between the vice of too much (gangsta rap's every-other-word profanity, the cemetery gardener's rant, Glengarry Glen Ross) and the vice of too little. He sorts Onion stories into vice tables—'Loved Ones Recall Local Man's Cowardly Battle With Cancer' illustrates the vice of cowardice, with courage as the hitting-the-mark mean—and concludes that a well-placed fuck is both funny and virtuous precisely because so many people treat the word as taboo.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 22 "World Death Rate Holding Steady At 100 Percent" — Dan Miori, a palliative-care physician assistant, uses Onion medical stories — 'Loved Ones Recall Local Man's Cowardly Battle With Cancer,' the 'Vehicular Manslaughter Doctor,' animal hoarder Tricia McCory's 'I'm A Diseased And Deformed Animal Lover,' and the Terry Schiavo American Voices — to survey how end-of-life decisions actually get made. He runs each dilemma through Mill's consequentialism, Kant's deontology, and Aristotle's virtue ethics (with Monty Python's Philosopher's Song as running gag), then through Beauchamp and Childress's four principles of medical ethics, showing that McCory's kindness to dying animals fails autonomy and nonmaleficence because kindness can be cruel. The chapter closes by restoring 'euthanasia' to its Greek meaning of 'good death,' arguing that accepting the 100 percent death rate means planning ahead with living wills and honest bad-news delivery rather than dying tube-filled in an ICU.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 23 "Allons-y into the Starry Heavens" — Smith reads the Doctor–Rose tragedy through Kantian deontology: shaped by Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's virtue ethics into a good will, both must still choose duty over inclination, so in 'Parting of the Ways' and the Battle of Canary Wharf in 'Doomsday' they each act from the categorical imperative — sacrificing their love to save humanity — because love, as Kant warns, impels partiality. Even in 'Journey's End' the Doctor sends Rose to Pete's World with the meta-crisis Doctor for the greater good, ending alone under Kant's starry heavens and the moral law within.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 25 "Why the Doctor Is So Special" — Applying Singer's animal-liberation concept of speciesism — judging moral worth by capacity to feel pain rather than by intelligence or likeness — the authors argue the Daleks are 'super-speciesist' and that Lumic's emotional inhibitors make the Cybermen the same failure, unable to share a universe with unlike beings. Since emotions are judgments that can be educated into fitting responses (Nussbaum, Aristotle), and since Daleks infused with Rose's or Diagoras's DNA collapse into empathetic beings, the chapter concludes that emotion and empathy are why the Daleks will never win and why the Doctor, marked by his companions, is special among Time Lords.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 34 "I Am the Bad Wolf" — Answers Davros's charge that the Doctor fashions companions into weapons by examining his character through virtue ethics: his unifying virtue is Heideggerian 'authentic concern', always offering aggressors like the Nestene or the Sycorax a choice so they become genuinely responsible, as in the fly-swatting thought experiment. Companions instead act from compassion, which lacks impartiality and produces the 'Bad Wolf Syndrome' (Rose's Dalek genocide, Martha's Osterhagen Key, Jack's warp star). Since for Aristotle a friend is 'another himself', the companions' actions are in a sense the Doctor's own yet founded on a distorted disposition, which is why he runs from his past.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 16 "The Spice of Meaning" — Mines Dune for an account of the meaningful life by contrasting the Harkonnens, who amass power for its own sake and grind Yueh's very identity to dust, with the Fremen, whose rigid rituals give meaning but suffocate anyone who lives entirely inside them—with Duke Leto's abolition of the beggars' water-towel custom as the failure case in between. Following Aristotle's method of starting from 'the views of the wise,' the chapter argues virtue is an open-ended, formulaless skill: rising above inherited identities while repairing the social bonds they sustain, as Paul and Jessica do by breaking selected Fremen rules and leaving the sietch stronger. The worm-rider, feet shifting on sand above a creature that can never be fully controlled, is the closing image of a struggle that never finally resolves.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 17 "Alone into the Desert" — Audits Duniverse lives by Socrates's standard—the condition of the soul over wealth and power, with justice, courage, temperance, and wisdom—finding Baron Harkonnen utterly wanting, 'Leto the Just' compromised by forgery and concubinage, Paul unjust in his myth-making holy war (though Plato's Republic would smile on ruling myths), and the Fremen admirable in temperance and courage but fatally sure of themselves where Socrates prized knowing that you do not know. Aristotle's function argument and golden mean follow: Paul's first worm-ride is courage between rashness and cowardice, but Paul's and Leto II's extreme, humanity-saving selflessness has no excess to moderate and so breaks the doctrine of the mean. The author concludes Socrates is too harsh and Aristotle closer, yet even he fails: sometimes the best life requires extreme virtue and even injustice, as with the two Atreides emperors.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 18 "Sweet Miracles of (Secular) Faith, Hope, and Love" — Florek reconstructs Peart's ethics as Aristotelian virtue ethics: aiming at eudaimonia rather than feeling good, 'Freewill' chooses autonomy and responsibility as virtues, and 'Vital Signs' adds persistence and courage ('courageous convictions will drag the dream into existence'), with a compassionate expansion toward ordinary sufferers in 'Distant Early Warning', 'Red Sector A' ('I must help my mother stand up straight'), and 'Everyday Glory'. Peart's existential consciousness then confronts finitude ('Time Stand Still', the fading memory of 'Vapor Trail'), contingency ('Roll the Bones' — 'Why does it happen? Because it happens'), and the absurd of Sartre and Camus ('The Stars Look Down' — an indifferent universe that answers nothing). The 1997-98 tragedies turn this existential consciousness tragic, and the post-tragic resolution of Vapor Trails and 'Faithless' is a secular faith in hope and love — Peart's answer to 1 Corinthians 13 without God — grounded in being loved by Carrie Nuttall.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 23 "You Control Your Urges—They Do Not Control You" — Waller and McAlear first rebut the amoral reading: Dexter does feel (he sobs over Rita, loves Deb, misses Harry) and does control his urges through the Code, so morality applies to him, and the Dark Passenger is merely everyone's socially unacceptable desires - the very thing that gives rise to moral codes. They then test the three theories: Aristotelian virtue ethics mostly fails because murder admits no mean and Harry's Code teaches killer's skills rather than virtues (though its 'don't kill innocents' dispositions are genuine virtues); utilitarianism fails even in rule-utilitarian form - via the organ-harvesting doctor and Harry's own utilitarian guilt over Laura Moser's death - because Dexter kills because the Code requires it, not because it maximizes happiness. What fits is dark deontology: like Kant's argument that murderers consent to their own execution out of respect for their rationality, Dexter kills only killers, acts from duty rather than enjoyment, and treats 'don't get caught' as a condition for the possibility of his true imperative.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 34 "Becoming a Real Boy" — Phillip Deen places Dexter on the scale of character types from Book VII of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics - temperate, morally strong (Angel Batista), morally weak (Deb), self-indulgent (Masuka), and the beast - rejecting the Socratic view that vice is mere ignorance, and argues Dexter is neither self-indulgent nor simply beastly but a 'morally strong beast.' The decisive test is Kant's tribunal of conscience and the morality-versus-prudence question: Dexter gathers proof before killing, feels remorse for Jonathan Farrow, and tells Trinity 'No, but I want to be' morally superior - yet his delight at Doakes's death exposes mere prudence. Deen closes with Brian's Heideggerian offer of authenticity ('you could be yourself around me') refused: Dexter hopes that by pretending the feelings are there he may one day 'turn into a real boy.'
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 11 "Why Is It the Best Day Ever" — Nicole Pramik argues SpongeBob is Aristotle's self-mastered man: his daily cheerfulness is eudaimonia, a happiness earned by practicing virtue as the mean between vices of excess and deficiency. The chapter tests each mean with episodes — courage between cowardly isolation ('I Had an Accident') and recklessness ('A Life in a Day'), honor between Patrick's under-the-rock humility and Squidward's Easter-Island vanity, honesty in 'Hooky' and 'Wet Painters', and good temper mended with Patrick in 'New Student Starfish' and 'The Fry Cook Games'. His moderation in pleasure and wealth, contrasted with Mr. Krabs's stinginess, and his F.U.N. Song friendship (Aristotle's greatest external good) show the golden mean served up on a sesame seed bun.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 20 "The Best Kind of Friend" — Ruth Tallman tests Holmes and Watson against Aristotle's requirement in the Nicomachean Ethics that perfect friendship exists only between the 'alike in excellence': since the two live by irreconcilable moral codes (Holmes's cocaine and burglaries versus Watson's clean living and law-abidingness), Aristotelian moral naturalism denies they can be true friends at all, despite the raw panic in 'The Three Garridebs' proving mutual devotion. Recasting the pair as moral pluralists with different 'good for me's, she argues Holmes is actually the better friend, an 'integrity-promoting' friend who urges Watson to stay home from the Milverton burglary to honor Watson's own code, while the proselytizing Watson, who nags about cocaine yet tags along anyway, repeatedly violates his own integrity.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 36 "The Game’s Afoot" — Littmann poses Holmes's cocaine habit as philosophy's classic akrasia puzzle: Socrates denies weakness of will, treating it as mis-measured pleasure in which nearer pleasures loom larger — the King of Bohemia risking scandal for Irene Adler's company, Sir George Burnwell's gambling, Holmes's immediate relief of boredom — while Aristotle objects in the Nicomachean Ethics that reason really is clouded by passion, the way 'Black Peter' Carey's murderous violence is clouded by rum, so the cure is habituated practice rather than a science of measuring pleasures. Aristotle's account fits our sense that Holmes, 'the most perfect reasoning and observing machine,' knowingly chooses the lesser good. The verdict is that this is the one case Holmes failed to solve: it was Watson, not Holmes's own reason and will, who 'weaned him from that drug mania.'
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 18 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Flanders reads Killing Yourself to Live as asking whether dying can be good for the person who dies: Jeff Buckley's 'Hallelujah' and Kurt Cobain's myth became deeper and more successful only after the fact, as if death were a career move. He answers with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, where the fortunes of descendants can affect the happiness of the dead: our life-stories outlive their authors, so fans' posthumous devotion can really benefit Buckley, though no posthumous fame can add virtue that was never lived (Michael Jackson's rehabilitation cannot touch how he actually lived). Klosterman's road trip ultimately undercuts the question: the earnest Great White concert mourners remember what truly was there, while Cobain's fans retroactively invent meaning to gain 'credibility by mourning retrospectively', so worshipping the rock dead manufactures an inauthentic afterlife, and Klosterman must kill the unserious fan in himself to live.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 21 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Wayne Yuen uses The Graveyard Book to teach the good life: Bod's family's murder, like students owing their existence to the Holocaust, is an unalloyed moral evil that still enables a better life, and Saul Smilansky's distinction between being 'sorry for' and 'sorry that' lets Bod benefit without endorsing the tragedy. His graveyard education is Aristotelian, virtues acquired through practice and models, from the Owenses' duty and Silas's wisdom to 'righteous indignation' against school bullies and friendship with Scarlett as intrinsically valuable, all building toward eudaimonia. The existentialist virtue of authenticity (attributed to Sartre and Kierkegaard) explains why Bod must be 'nobody but himself' rather than a copy of the vampire Silas, why the scavenged identities of the ghouls mark inauthenticity, and why wiping Scarlett's memory threatens her authenticity, resolving the apparent conflict between virtue and being oneself because bravery or wisdom is relative to the individual.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 25 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Answers Walt's claim that drug laws are arbitrary by separating legality from morality and defending objective moral principles, chief among them do-no-harm and a 'clear-headedness principle' obligating us to shun mind-clouding substances - a principle it attributes to thinkers from the Buddha to Kant while borrowing Aristotle's ideal of becoming brave, temperate, just, and wise. It sorts drugs by whether they cloud the mind rather than medical-versus-recreational, weighing coffee, Hank's cigars and homebrew, Skyler's cigarettes, and meth's 1200-percent dopamine spike (Spooge's neglected kid in 'Peekaboo'). Verdict: meth use is straightforwardly immoral, and therefore so are selling and cooking it - meeting Douglas Husak's challenge to actually give reasons for condemnation.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 32 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Stages the standard three-way ethics debate on Walt: deontology's universalizability (Kant) absurdly forbids killing Krazy-8 even to save Walt's family, utilitarianism (Mill) licenses both cooking meth and murdering dealers - a outright contradiction - while Aristotle's virtue ethics judges character rather than acts and convicts Walt of vice: he endangers his family, misses Holly's birth, habituates himself into Heisenberg, and defrauds his school. Because acts and consequences alone cannot see character, virtue ethics is offered as the needed complement. The closing move widens the lens to America itself, arguing the capitalist success ethos and our appetite for anti-heroes like Tony Soprano and Dexter reveal a society that praises viciousness - 'we are what we repeatedly do.'
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 27 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Greeley argues the zombie crystallizes specifically modern fears: with Aristotle and Aquinas he reads walkers as humans stripped of their essential nature and potential, which Rick's uncustomary eulogies ('I'm sorry this happened to you') acknowledge. Following Philippe Aries, he ties modern death anxiety to urbanization, hidden cemeteries, and the loss of religious consolation, citing the CDC arc where Jenner's science offers only a self-destruct and Jacqui falls back on 'the wrath of God.' Rousseau's thesis that society corrupts explains why the survivors in the woods seem more alive — warlord Guillermo turns out to be protecting nursing-home patients and pizza-deliverer Glenn becomes a hero — while the 'Bradbury's Storewide Sale' sign, the Walmart trampling, and Fromm's shift from utopias to dystopias suggest the shuffling horde is an image of our own consumerist, distracted, dehumanized modernity.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 9 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Littmann answers the charge that D&D is a waste of time with Aristotle: pleasure is good as an end in itself, humanity's function is thinking, so even munchkin power-gaming and 4E combat roles are worthwhile intellectual activity under the function argument. He then treats D&D as participatory art—improvisational storytelling offering catharsis (smacking goblins to purge aggression) and the Poetics' license to explore what could be, like the dwarf chieftain grieving a disintegrated son or deciding what a friend owes the thief in the scorpion nest. A good DM, on this Aristotelian view, makes plots unfold with internal probability and characters act from consistent personality, yet 'just playing my character' never excuses ruining another player's fun, since artistic value never suspends the virtues governing how we treat people.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 10 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Merli argues that good role-playing refutes Aristotelian virtue ethics: decent players convincingly play genuinely evil thieves and morally mediocre players play truly virtuous paladins, so the skill of judging what the virtuous agent would do cannot require being virtuous or having the habituated emotions McDowell, Hursthouse, and Jacobson say are necessary to 'see what to do'. Using a dice-guessing versus unverifiable aura-reading analogy, he shows that the virtue ethicist's escape—denying non-virtuous players can get it right—makes virtuous judgment look fraudulent and untestable. Because role-playing demands active first-person deliberation rather than the passive reception of literary fiction, it exposes that judging rightly and being virtuous are distinct skills, with implications for how habituation and moral education work.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 15 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Cooke defends his three-year lawful-evil wizard campaign against religious and secular critics by dismantling each style of argument. The propaganda charge fails because D&D rulebooks present no 'attitudes for export' about the real world; the puzzle of imaginative resistance dissolves once Can'tian and Won'tian readings are rejected for a 'Hardian' view that some things are merely hard to imagine, undercutting Dadlez's explanation of the Romulan spy's angry opponents; and the Werther-effect-style empirical case against D&D collapses on the data like parallel panics over jazz, video games, and pornography. The remaining character-warping objection—the Platonic and Aristotelian habituation worry that enjoying evil play mistrains the sentiments Hume warned about—turns unfalsifiable in the way repressed-desire claims do, leaving a firm moral gap between imagining evil and doing it.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 17 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Grinnell reads Rawls's dotted case lists, Marimow's rip-and-run, Burrell's 'dope on the table,' and Prez being told he teaches the test rather than math as Aristotle's function argument gone wrong: professionals who reduce their purpose to stats and pleasing bosses are 'doing well' instead of 'doing good,' which is just what Plato says badly governed cities reward with honor. The characters who grasp their real function - Daniels refusing cheap felony stats, Bunk refusing to turn cases black without the true murderer, Freamon hunting bodies in vacants despite Landsman's fury - defy the Game at career cost, while Colvin's Hamsterdam and McNulty's fake killer show the opposite failure of zealous judgment without humility or rule of law. The chapter ends on the paradox that trusting professional judgment risks messes, but defining professions by numbers eliminates excellence altogether.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 23 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Trerise argues Omar is virtuous in Aristotle's full sense: honest on the stand ('I robs drug dealers... I got the shotgun, you got the briefcase'), courageous, consistent, and generous, with even his vengefulness a mean between extremes given a world where no one else will check Avon or Marlo - unlike Marlo he never guns on citizens and even pays Prop Joe for clock repairs. Virtue theory's attention to context separates his killings of Stinkum, Savino, and Stringer from Marlo's power-consolidating murders and shows him achieving whatever eudaimonia his world allows, though his obsession after Stringer's setup, which got Tosha killed, marks his one real excess. The catch is exemplification - Omar is disturbed that children play at being Omar, and Michael becomes the new him - yet the chapter concludes that some vigilantism is a social necessity on the streets and that Omar's swapped body tag names the injustice done to the street's truly virtuous.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 34 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Cooper argues The Wire stages two rival pictures of power: Hobbes's New School, where power is 'present means to some future apparent good', the good is only the apparently good relative to each desire, and honor is reputation indifferent to whether it is earned through love or fear (Clay Davis's graft, Ziggy's leather jacket, Avon displaying Brandon's mutilated body to 'send a message', Marlo spending exorbitant sums and torturing Butchie so his name keeps ringing out), and the Old School of Aristotle and Aquinas, where power is oriented to perfection and objective goods like family, friendship, and truth. Against the fear-based honor of the kingpins he sets McNulty's failed redemption and the successful reforms of Cutty's boxing gym, Walon's sobriety, and Bubs, whose prudence in taking the Sun job, temperance, justice at the Viva House, and fortitude in facing Sherrod's death embody the cardinal virtues, showing that even in the 'dark corner of the American experiment' virtue has the power to move.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 16 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Massimo Pigliucci reads Rise as a Greek tragedy of hubris and asks whether Will Rodman dosing his father with ALZ-112 was wrong, first dissolving the 'it's unnatural' objection and probing the cure/enhancement border with Daniels's Peter-and-Johnny growth-hormone case, vaccination-as-enhancement, and Eubulides's bald-man paradox. He then runs the decision through three ethical theories: Millian consequentialism condemns it by its results (his father dies and humanity goes extinct, though chimp happiness might outweigh that), Kant's humanity formula condemns using his father as an unconsenting experimental subject, and Aristotelian virtue ethics vindicates Will's compassion and courage - Pigliucci's own view, since sometimes our best is just not enough. He closes by rejecting Baylis and Robert's technological-inevitability thesis (we abandoned the Concorde, CFCs, and nuclear weapons before) and lets Jacobs's plunge into San Francisco Bay stand as the penalty for market hubris.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 37 "Psych and Philosophy" — Patricia Brace maps Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics categories of friendship onto Psych: Shawn's first-season ties to the SBPD are friendships of utility, the shared hobbies and bar nights (tap dancing in 'Feet Don't Kill Me Now,' 'Neil Simon's Lover's Retreat') build friendships of pleasure, and Shawn-Juliet matures from utilitarian boundaries into erotic friendship. Lassiter's lie-detector threat to protect Juliet in 'Shawn Rescues Darth Vader' and the lifelong Shawn-Gus bond ('Gus Walks into a Bank') approach complete friendship grounded in virtue, while the Henry-Shawn paternal friendship heals as Shawn develops the golden mean, and the vicious Mr. Yin and Yang - full of regret, incapable of complete friendship - show the life without it.
- **The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia**, ch. 24 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" — Jennifer Swanson asks whether Alicia can 'have it all', starting from Aristotle: Peter fails the moral virtues (faithfulness, honesty, courage), Jackie's intrusive moments undermine her kindness since Aristotle's unity of the virtues ties them together, and Eli Gold's perfect frankness leaves no room for perfect tact. Following Michael Slote's partial values and impossibility of perfection, she argues career and family are paired values in which gaining one loses the other, as Alicia discovers being pulled between Molly the nanny, Cary's 'she'll have something to fall back on', Diane's partner-track warning, and dumping Will after Grace's twelve butt-dials in 'Parenting Made Easy'. Since perfection is impossible in principle, the answer is balance across all the values of a good life, not Caitlin's retreat into 'I just want to be a mom'.
- **The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia**, ch. 27 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" — John Fitzpatrick asks whether voters should care that Alicia stands beside Peter, from the Season One resignation press conference to the finale's withheld hand. After a rapid tour of right-action theories grounded in the show - Eli Gold's egoism, Peter's 'pitted' evidence tip as consequentialism, Alicia keeping Jonas Stern's dementia secret as deontology, the Florrick-Childs no-children pact as social contract - he turns to Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: eudaimonia as a life weaving pleasure, friendship, and practical activity, in which mentors like Will and Diane let us contemplate virtue in others and improve our own character. His conclusion: Alicia's endorsement matters not because she is a good wife but because she is a good person whose judgment reveals Peter's character.
- **The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia**, ch. 28 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" — The Azevedos read Plato's Republic Book I as a manual for professionalism: Socrates argues the practitioner - doctor, ruler, lawyer - serves the patient, citizen, and client rather than himself, while Thrasymachus's cynicism that injustice pays and people only seem just is embodied by Eli Gold ('I lie for a living') and by stunt lawyers Nancy Crozier, Patti Nyholm, Louis Canning, and the secretive Jonas Stern. Alicia answers with Aristotle's virtue ethics: professionalism as a cluster virtue cultivated through habituated action, hitting the mean and doing the right thing at the right time for the right reasons. Saint Alicia shows how costly being good all the time is, yet the chapter sides with her striving for virtue over Thrasymachus's goldbrick glory.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 15 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Brace and Kingsbury use the Nicomachean Ethics to argue that Nucky, Chalky, and Margaret mistake pleasure and the mere instruments of happiness - tailored suits, money, useful connections, the appearance of virtue - for Aristotle's stable, self-sustaining virtuous activity, so their lives stay unstable and empty. Nucky 'buys' even Jimmy and Margaret, Chalky's jail-cell staging with David Copperfield shows how fragile his facade of cultivation is, and Margaret's acquisitions end in blackmail and in bribing God over Emily's polio. Only Richard Harrow, the Tin Man whose collage-clippings represent a happiness he believes he can never have, moves toward real Aristotelian friendship through Jimmy's 'Of course I would; right down to the last bullet' - the philia Aristotle calls most necessary for a happy life.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 9 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Jeff Ewing argues the moral fabric of Ender's Game is virtue-ethical, first testing Ender's leadership against Plato's cardinal virtues, tripartite soul, and rigid class hierarchy of the Republic, then finding Aristotle a far better fit. Ender's trademark use of the minimum force necessary against Stilson, Bonzo, and the buggers sits at Aristotle's mean between cowardice and excess, while his adaptability and disregard for rules and hierarchy only count as virtues in Aristotle's framework - though his ignorance of crucial facts explains why xenocide, like his beatings, fell outside the mean.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 23 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Danielle Wylie uses Aristotle's conditions for voluntary action - control and knowledge - to argue Ender's planetary strike is one of his 'mixed cases' made under coercion and factual ignorance, so praise and blame attach elsewhere: Graff and Rackham, who foresaw the attack and could easily have stopped it, meet both conditions through culpable omission. Borrowing Rachels' Smith-and-Jones drowning case to show moral responsibility can exist without causal responsibility, she ends with Ender's non-blameworthy 'taking responsibility' as Speaker for the Dead.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 31 "The Devil and Philosophy" — George Dunn asks whether the Joker's 'some men just want to watch the world burn' motivelessness even makes sense. Against Baumeister's 'Myth of Pure Evil' and the Socratic-Aristotelian thesis that all wrongdoing aims at some apparent good, he tests Kant's claim that no human can be a diabolical being, Claudia Card's definition of diabolical evil as engineering others' moral corruption, and the Satan of Job as prosecuting accuser - which fits the Joker's ferry 'social experiment' and his breaking of Harvey Dent. The upshot is that the Joker's evil, fed by pride and the wish for credit for the conflagration, is instrumental, pathological, and banal after all, its best answer being the convict who throws the detonator out the window.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 17 "Homeland and Philosophy" — April Marratto and Adam Barkman use Foucault's appropriation of Bentham's panopticon - surveillance whose mere threat disciplines - to read Carrie's illegal watches on the Brody house, the family's stay in the safe house, and Dana's discovery that speech about her father's Islam is policed. Against Foucault's claim that freedom is an illusion maintained by power, the chapter sets Aristotle's view that freedom is a self-directed will choosing rightly (Dana making amends for the hit-and-run) and Rousseau's social contract, under which citizens trade equal freedoms for equal protection. Both would endorse Saul forcing Brody's detox for the country's sake, concluding absolute freedom is neither possible nor desirable.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 37 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — The chapter argues Finn is not yet a true hero but is on a quest to become one: against rule systems like Mill's greatest-happiness utilitarianism and Kantian respect for persons, virtue ethics asks not 'what should I do' but 'who should I be', and Aristotle's point that children lack fully developed practical reason explains why Finn's good intentions misfire - removing Donny exposes the house people to Why-wolves, and Penny's trick humiliates him in the City of Thieves. Martha Nussbaum's ideal of every person as free and of equal dignity grounds heroism in the common good, and her work on literature and popular culture explains how watching Finn's exaggerated choices trains our own moral judgment. Citing Franco and Zimbardo's psychology of real heroes - empathy, risk tolerance, persistence - and closing with Seneca's 'how nobly you live', it concludes that since Aristotelian virtue is a habit, anyone can start by admitting they suck at heroism and practicing, as Jake's advice puts it.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 9 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter argues Boyd Crowder personifies coolness - composure, wily cleverness, unconventionality, intelligence, likability - as shown in the 'Cottonmouth' payroll-robbery scene where he turns his flip phone into a room bug, overhears Kyle planning to blow him up in the mine, and lets the plotters kill themselves. Jon Cotton borrows Wittgenstein's family-resemblance model to define coolness as an indefinable cluster of traits (with Dewey Crowe as the agreed uncool case), and reaches back to Socrates' defining of ethical virtues and the Republic's just, well-ordered soul to argue that coolness is a genuine ethical virtue - the excellence of a properly functioning person - in a scientific, post-religious ethics.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 31 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter diagnoses Raylan with Aristotle's akrasia (lack of self-restraint): Art's 'lost cause' lecture, Arlo's boast that he has never shot anyone, and Boyd's 'you wake up in the morning pretending that you are not the bad guy' all charge him with acting on passion against his own calculations - sleeping with witness Ava, resuming adultery with Winona when her ring comes off. Because Raylan feels regret, the Aristotelian mark of the unselfrestrained person who knows his condition, he is curable and lacks self-restraint by habit rather than nature (Nicky Augustine's limo verdict: 'it's not who you are'). The chapter reads Raylan's signature move - forcing men to draw first so their deaths count as justified - as a perversion of justice by an akratic who is not wicked, and the series arc as his slow acquisition of self-restraint.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 13 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Noel measures Jobs against the four cardinal virtues from Plato's Republic and finds him wanting: imprudent (NeXT, the Lisa), unjust (taking the GUI from Xerox PARC, 'more fun to be a pirate'), intemperate (cruel outbursts like the 'dogshit for icing' cake), with only a brash, mind-changing courage. Drawing on Aristotle's golden mean from the Nicomachean Ethics, Nietzsche's master-slave morality and his Will to Power line about the man who 'determines values' for millennia, and Joseph Campbell's hero's journey, he argues entrepreneurs are a breed apart whose real virtues are independence of mind, vision, and audacity—and that Jobs, the anti-social creator who would not fit in, changed the world precisely because the cardinal virtues were 'prison walls' to him.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 17 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Kyle Alkema and Adam Barkman ask what would make the Gang happy and answer with Aristotle's virtue ethics: happiness is long-run flourishing built on virtuous habits, with the golden mean (courage between cowardice and recklessness) as the rule for choice. The Gang instead lives a 'Reverse Virtue Ethic' - trying extremes first by crude trial and error, like sniffing gasoline to check that it is gasoline - along three roads: quick money (welfare crack scams, robbing their own parents' house), lust (the D.E.N.N.I.S. System's seduce-and-abandon script, where Dennis cheerfully accepts the charge of sociopathy), and validation ('You're not gay, you're just really, really vain'). Their residual Catholicism supplies consciences and limits - Mac's talk of God smiting them, confession, fears of Hell - but no reasoned morality, leaving them trapped in 'one day at a time' gratification as reverse role models.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 18 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Adam Henschke argues that Frank Reynolds, of all people, is a role model - not a virtuous man overall, but virtuous in one structural sense. Using Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, each Gang member's project is diagnosed as the vice of excessive self-delusion: Charlie's Waitress obsession he cannot see through even at her musical rejection, Dee's acting stardom she will not work for and that ends in suicide-adjacent despair, Mac's muscle-bound self-image despite 'diabitis', and Dennis's Golden God delusion culminating in 'the implication' and his car stash of 'fetish shit'. Rickety Cricket embodies the opposite vice, total loss of the capacity to imagine oneself otherwise (via Catriona Mackenzie's relational autonomy), and Frank charts the Aristotelian mean between the two - he rejected his delusive country-club life, knows exactly what he chose with Roxy, and his plans succeed where the Gang's fail - making 'What would Frank do?' a genuine exercise of practical wisdom.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 30 "17. The Friends of a Time Lord" — Littmann applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics taxonomy of friendship - pleasure, usefulness, and mutual goodness - to fifty years of Doctor-companion pairings, from the Hartnell Doctor's glee touring Vortis with Ian to New Series companions chosen as friends who routinely save the day, from Barbara's Dalek revolt to Clara saving every incarnation of the Doctor. He argues Aristotle would still judge the Doctor's friendships defective: they are short-lived, unequal in station, intellect, and morality, and the companions cannot know him well enough (not even his name) for the perfect friendship of the good. Littmann then corrects Aristotle on two counts: friends need not be moral experts to serve as moral critics (Rose in 'Dalek,' Amy in 'A Town Called Mercy'), and the Doctor's favoritism toward his companions - risking worlds to save them, as when Rory weighs Amy's life against the universe in 'The Big Bang' - shows that preferring friends over strangers is itself his most frequent moral failing.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 24 "13. Dauntless Courage" — The Bocks test whether the Dauntless are brave or merely reckless using Plato's Laches and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics. Socrates refutes Eric's definition of courage as never surrendering - the Scythian cavalry fights while fleeing, and endurance without wisdom is foolhardiness - while Aristotle locates courage as the mean between rashness and cowardice, acquired by habituation ('we become brave by doing brave acts'), which redeems much Dauntless training: Tris jumps onto the roof a second time without hesitation because practice has shaped her. Fearlessness is neither necessary nor sufficient - Four ignores his four fears rather than lacking them, and only madmen feel none - so the brave person fears the right things, at the right time, for noble ends: Eric is ruthless rather than courageous, while Tris's mother's sacrifice and Tris's taking Caleb's place at the death-serum lab show courage aimed at the good of others, with Four's grieving perseverance showing it can even serve self-preservation out of love.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 30 "18. The Virtues of Choosing Your Faction" — Pascoe contrasts Aristotle's and Kant's theories of virtue through the Choosing Ceremony. On Aristotle's account virtues are taught (intellectual) and then habituated into character (moral), tied to one's function, so Susan flourishes because aptitude, upbringing, and choice align while the transfer Al withers - but Tris, Divergent with multiple aptitudes, needs Kant instead: natural virtues are mere 'gifts of nature' that become good only through good will, and her perfect duties to herself and imperfect duties regarding family and faction can justify choosing Dauntless over staying in Abnegation. Kant wins the day: because a corrupted community like Eric's Dauntless redefines bravery into obedience, Tris must think for herself - 'maybe I am wired like the Divergent' - choosing her virtues out of duty and self-respect rather than inheriting them.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 31 "19. Why Divergent are Actually Convergent" — Schenkewitz argues Chicago's downfall is built into its ideal: each faction drills a single virtue through total lifestyle discipline - Abnegation's mirror rules and gray houses, Candor's black and white dress - until 'you become what you do,' but a solitary virtue inverts into its own vice once it is cut off from the others: Erudite's knowledge becomes a lust for power, Dauntless bravery cruelty, Candor honesty callousness, Amity peace passivity, Abnegation selflessness stifling. The Divergent, who naturally hold all the virtues together in one unified character, are therefore the city's apex rather than its disease: Tris never stops being Abnegation while being Dauntless, and her worth lies in negotiating among virtues and making real choices from real alternatives, unlike the faction archetypes. Justice, the chapter concludes, requires the convergence of all the virtues within each person - the Divergent are actually convergent.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 15 "5. The Morality of Manners" — Dougherty argues that at Downton manners are not incidental etiquette but a central means of demonstrating moral character and respect. Matthew's shift from calling valeting 'a very silly occupation for a grown man' to valuing Molesley's role shows decorum tracking his growing respect; Branson's tweed suit at white-tie dinners and 'uniforms of oppression' display disrespect even where his politics are sound; Sir Richard's parting boorishness betrays a lack of moral character; and the Dowager Countess's polished barbs prove manners can serve as a mask for self-interest rather than virtue. The framework combines Nancy Sherman's 'aesthetic of character,' Aristotle's person of extraordinary virtue whose goodness must appear in particular ways, and Sarah Buss's idea that good manners constantly remind us that others are worthy of respect.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 18 "5. Back from the Dead" — Devlin and Cooper trace Rick's moral arc as a struggle between Mill-style consequentialism - twisted by the apocalypse into a 'Greatest Survival Principle' of mere survival (Dawn Lerner's Grady, Enid's 'JSS') - and Aristotelian virtue ethics. Shane's murder of Otis, the Governor's rule over Woodbury and killing of Martinez and Pete, and Terminus's cannibalism all show survival-only reasoning dissolving humanity, a decline the show underlines with literal mirror reflections of Shane as a walker. Rick falls after killing Shane and nearly trades Michonne to the Governor, is brought back by Lori's judging vision and the sight of Carl going cold, and reclaims virtues as habits grown like Hershel's seeds - 'We get to come back' (4.8 'Too Far Gone') - though Seasons 4 and 5 leave him balancing a harder character, down to 'We didn't want to waste the bullets,' with the drive to survive.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 30 "13. Carol’s Transformation" — Delfino and Lesinski trace Carol's arc from abused wife (Ed's beatings, Sophia's death, "I didn't think I could be strong") to the judge-jury-executioner she once refused to be, reading the transformation through Aristotle's claim in the Nicomachean Ethics that repeated actions forge moral character. They then evaluate her killings: the murder of Karen and David fails on both act- and rule-utilitarian grounds (it did not stop the flu, and Glenn and Sasha survived while the group was shattered), whereas killing the delusional Lizzie is defensible both utilitarianly and by Aquinas's natural-law exception that an evildoer may be killed for the welfare of the whole community when no public authority remains. Her confession to Tyreese and Tyreese's forgiveness complete the phoenix rebirth symbolized by the burning walkers in "Consumed."
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 24 "12. Should I Really Stop That Rhyming" — Yuen uses the rhyming scene to analyze annoyance - rhyme hijacks Vizzini's attention, the Goldman/Morgenstern interruptions betray invested expectations, and fans' endless quotation is annoying through sheer repetition - concluding that annoyance is irreducibly relative and contextual. Aristotle's virtue theory supplies the moral frame: friendliness and wittiness, golden means between obsequiousness and surliness, buffoonery and boorishness, make being annoying a character flaw that damages the communal eudaimonia Aristotle takes the good life to require. Since these virtues may be supererogatory ideals rather than obligations, Yuen borrows Kant's imperfect duty to develop one's talents to explain why Inigo had to become a master swordsman - failing to hone the skill his one great goal demands would be a failure of self-respect.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 14 "3. When to Hate and When to Be Irate" — Daniel Alloy opens with Aristotle's demand that one be angry 'as and when and for as long as one ought' and builds a theory distinguishing anger (a response to a specific offense, seeking proportional payback) from hatred (a response to a thing's very existence, seeking its destruction). He tests the theory on Louis's bits - hating deer as a class and fantasizing about giving them AIDS, the six-year-old 'Jizzanthapuss,' the Pig Newtons fight with a three-year-old, the Cinnabon clerk, the 'Awesome Possum' hipster, and the justified driver who yells 'suck a sack of dicks.' He argues justified hatred is impossible, since it would require a pure-malevolence being that could not be an autonomous person, so hatred is always wrong while properly proportioned anger remains a necessary part of the moral life. Kant supplies the self-respect dimension ('one who makes himself a worm cannot complain if people step on him'): failing to get angry at real wrongs done to you or your children signals a character deficiency, not virtue.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 14 "5. How Heroes Argue" — LaBauve opens with a staged Justice League debate over rescuing the Joker's hostages, where Batman's emotional, vengeance-tinged appeal loses to Superman's trust-based plea, and reads it through Aristotle's On Rhetoric: Batman persuades almost entirely by pathos (the relatable brokenness of Nolan's trilogy) with detective's logos, while Superman balances pathos, logos, and above all ethos, since Aristotle calls the speaker's character the strongest appeal. Against Max Landis's claim that Superman is irrelevant, he pairs the Death of Superman with Nietzsche's "God is dead" parable and the Kill Bill monologue to argue that Superman is a mythology of virtue - alongside real moral heroes like Gandhi, King, and Jesus - showing humans the ideal they ought to become, so Superman not only wins but must win.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 19 "9. Masks, Hearts, and Superheroes" — Dupree and Fuš build an independent definition of the "true superhero" from identity statements (Batman = Bruce Wayne, Clark Kent = Superman): only an essentially human character who forges near-superhuman excellence through cultivated virtue can count, and Aristotle's virtue ethics supplies the standard. Batman qualifies - his refusal to kill the Joker shows the struggle for the golden mean between foolhardiness and cowardice, and Gotham Knights #31 shows how far he plans to avoid killing - whereas powers merely given, Superman's Kryptonian biology or the Green Lantern ring (their update of Gyges's Ring), bestow no virtue, as Kyle Rayner's and Guy Gardner's early careers show. Since Clark Kent is "in his heart" the alien Superman while Bruce Wayne is merely Batman's mask, Batman is a true superhero and Superman is not.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 22 "11. Can a Leopard Change Its Shorts" — Alloy asks whether Rincewind - the wizard who runs from Twoflower, the Dungeon Dimensions, and the Agatean Empire alike - is really a coward. Aristotle's doctrine of the mean frames cowardice as the deficiency of fear-regulation between foolhardy Cohen the Barbarian and true courage, with character traits describing, explaining, and predicting Rincewind's flight. But the situationist challenge - Harman's reading of the cookie, hurry, and obedience experiments - denies that character traits exist, and the replies available to the virtue ethicist (Miller's continence/incontinence distinction, Alfano's 'dodge') leave almost nobody with virtues or vices, so the chapter concludes Rincewind cannot be a coward: cowardice, like the leopard's shorts, was never there to begin with.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 20 "10. Virtue Rising" — Darci Doll argues the Rising exposes the Society's intellectual oppression—each Color denied education and fed 'noble lies' about its role—and that lifting it sparks an 'Intellectual Reformation' proving Color does not dictate potential: Darrow out-performing Golds, Orion the un-carved Blue, Ragnar and Sefi exceeding their station. She uses Plato's Republic (producers, auxiliaries, guardians, the lower orders kept obedient by Noble Lies like the Reds' terraforming myth) as the Society's blueprint, then turns to Aristotle: potential is realized only through the right environment, instruction, and habituated character, and Darrow's practical wisdom—testing himself, reassessing after Titus and Cassius, doing what makes him his best self—lets him flourish and lead. Aristotle's critique of utility-only relations explains why the Society's alliances expire (Antonia executed once useless) while Darrow and Mustang's virtue friendships and just rule endure, opening a society where everyone, including women and lowColors denied opportunity rather than ability, can maximize potential.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 18 "7. Jon Snow, a Misshapen Christ Figure" — Rosa argues Westeros is a moral wasteland stripped of exemplars - heroes die, and vice spreads by imitation, as with Joffrey, Ramsay, and the Mountain - so Jon Snow functions as the series' Christ figure: the humble hidden king revealed in Bran's vision, the reformer uniting wildlings and Watch against death, killed by his brothers in 'Mother's Mercy' and risen in 'Home.' Using Aristotle's virtue ethics - Bran's archery lesson as the image of eudaimonia, hamartia as missing the mark, character formed by watching and imitating exemplars like Ned at the deserter's execution - the chapter claims the world is redeemable only through 'minority moral reform' embodied in a complete life, as with Jesus, Gandhi, and Martin Luther King Jr.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 47 "31. Paying the Iron Price" — Hansberger reads Theon's return to the Iron Islands as an Aristotelian failure of virtue: excess lust toward Yara on the road, the 'small soul' of gold-bought jewelry where Balon demands iron-price honor, and the rashness rather than courage of trying to hold Winterfell with twenty men. But Balon's virtues are the vices of a piratical society that rewards reaving and rape, and through Charles Taylor's ethics of authenticity the chapter argues Theon's deeper failure is not knowing who he is - Stark or Greyjoy - so Ramsay's breaking of him into Reek completes a collapse of self that began at home; authenticity, it concludes, depends on virtue and social relations, which is why Theon can only begin to recover by choosing to serve Yara.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 14 "3. Can Charlie Brown Be Happy" — The chapter asks why Charlie Brown is unhappy despite being kind, active, and engaged, and answers with ancient virtue ethics: happiness is not winning or approval but ethical self-transformation, so his dependence on others' regard ('How did the other team feel?') is the real problem. It diagnoses him with Daniel Haybron's three dimensions of happiness - strong on engagement but lacking attunement (nervous, self-conscious) and endorsement (cheerlessness) - and asks why his shyness so irritates the gang. Epictetus's image of Socrates playing ball at his trial and Cicero's dancing analogy supply the Stoic remedy: losing costs no virtue, what he controls is being ethical, and how you play the game is everything.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 26 "12. Aaugh! Why Is Being Moral So Hard" — The chapter claims Schulz's humor is built on moral failure and illustrates the three main moral theories with specific strips: utilitarianism via Bentham's 'sovereign masters' of pain and pleasure and Charlie's 'to make others happy' (with Lucy noting nobody is making her happy), Kantian deontology via Sally's crayon lie and Snoopy's 'I haven't bitten anyone on the leg recently' as fulfilling a negative duty, and Aristotle's virtue ethics via the failed steal of home (foolhardy rather than courageous), the unmailed Valentine (cowardly), the golden mean, and Joe Shlabotnik as a hopeless role model. Charlie gritting his teeth shows mistaking a virtue's external markers for the virtue itself. It concludes we fit none of the theories well, yet Peanuts keeps a spirit of hope - happiness is a warm puppy, and Charlie's grit is genuine even if he cannot see it.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 27 "15. Good Citizen Deadpool" — Using Aristotle's Politics, the chapter splits the good man from the good citizen and argues that the Marvel Universe's 'city' needs mercenaries to keep its balance between heroes and villains, as in Deadpool vs Thanos where the In-Betweener steps in when Death is imprisoned and the balance tips toward Chaos. Deadpool's contract killing - hitting Hydra and AIM targets heroes won't touch - fulfills his role in that city, so he can be a good citizen without being a good man, a standard of all-around virtue that Colossus, the 'boy scout' produced by CGI, better fits. The thought experiment of an assassin for 'Deadpooltopia' shows how a dreadful man can still be a good citizen by serving his city's own idea of the good.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 13 "2. If I Don’t Listen to My Imaginary Friend, Why the Fuck Should I Listen to Yours" — Kreider stages a chat between Plato and Aristotle about the show. On Plato's account, mimesis is an imitation of an imitation of the Forms, so Elliot's imaginary friend, his fake persona with Krista, and the Mr. Robot personality are intellectually and morally dangerous deceptions that let him commit terrorism without his rational self's consent; yet the Republic's censored poetry for the auxiliaries explains how fsociety's masked videos teach true beliefs, and how Elliot uses the fictional Mr. Robot to educate himself toward ideas he already knew were right. Aristotle's Poetics then defends imitation as natural and instructive - the show is a cautionary tragedy, and the Mr. Robot crutch is how Elliot eventually steps up to claim responsibility.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 30 "15. Reset Virtues" — Doll argues Elliot approximates Aristotelian virtue despite his vices: he craves eudaimonia, uses practical wisdom to recognize the harm the 5/9 hack caused innocent people ('I'll own it all'), and habituates himself against vice by confessing, exposing Ray's website, and restraining Mr. Robot even at the cost of Adderall binges and prison. Leon's 'existence could be beautiful, or it could be ugly, but that's on you' frames the choice of a life to fight for, and Krista's counsel leads Elliot to the golden mean of a 'handshake' with Mr. Robot - integrating the two identities rather than annihilating one - while the viewer serves as the if/then programming keeping him virtuous.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 17 "6. Horror Can Be Great Drama" — Applies Aristotle's Poetics wholesale - mimesis of possible actions, the six elements of tragedy, complete plots of proper magnitude, reversal and recognition, hamartia, and catharsis as the perfecting of fear and pity - to argue that Murder House (Ben's lust as tragic flaw and his double reversal to redemption in death) and Asylum (Sister Jude's irascibility and pride punished then reformed) are genuine high tragedies, and then uses the Nicomachean Ethics (virtue as a mean between extremes; justice as both retributive and rehabilitative) to show the seasons teach virtue, while Coven, Freak Show, and Hotel fall short because their characters' fates are undeserved and the moral message goes murky.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 10 "1. How to Fail at Almost Everything and Still Be a Hero" — Malloy argues Iron Man is the better hero precisely because he fails constantly - Armor Wars, the Registration Act, alcoholism, a string of collapsed Stark companies - while Steve Rogers was born heroic and never stumbles. Using Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, he treats perseverance as a virtue between cowardly quitting and Cap's stubborn excess (his doomed stand against Thanos in Infinity Gauntlet), and separates Tony's virtuous perseverance from Dr. Doom's identical behavior by its motives: Tony honestly examines his failures to help people, while Doom only looks for someone to blame.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 14 "5. Why the Good Man Is a Great Leader" — Nisley reads Civil War through Aristotle's good man and good leader: Cap shows courage but lacks temperance and practical wisdom - his rash Lagos operation, his rage-borne beating of Tony, his choice of Bucky over the Avengers' common end - and his ceaseless struggle between passion and reason falls short of virtue. Applying Aristotle's account of philia, she argues the Avengers are a friendship of the virtuous that requires deliberation toward justice, which Cap dissolves by tearing the team apart, while Tony's reasoned acceptance of UN oversight, moderation after Ultron, and concern for the whole team make him the good man fit to lead.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 14 "5. The Serious Point of Scott’s Humor" — Guerra and Barkman argue that Dilbert's humor is doing serious philosophical work: strips like the Pointy-Haired Boss's scheme to strip app users of free will, rebranded by Dilbert as marketing, distill manipulative corporate practice to its absurd essential core, and humor serves as a logical tool that, when it preserves the target's integrity rather than straw-manning it, exposes the equivocation in earnest arguments about getting something from nothing. They ground the practice in Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, where wittiness is the virtuous mean between the vices of buffoonery and boorishness, read Adams's catalogue of failures and his luck-first, passion-is-bullshit account of success as a Socratic acknowledgment of ignorance that deflates the American Dream, and treat Win Bigly's persuasion lessons (visuals, repetition, intentional mistakes, the Hitler counterexample) as further proof that Adams has the virtue of wit.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 28 "15. The Evil in These Woods" — Tests three accounts of evil against the show. Augustine's privation theory — evil as nothingness, forged against Manichean dualism — fails to capture a Twin Peaks that is genuinely Manichean, with the Experiment vomiting BOB out of the Trinity blast and the Black and White Lodges in eternal conflict; Ricoeur's symbolism of defilement fits the filthy-haired BOB, the sooty Woodsmen, and the frog-moth contaminating the sleeping girl. The decisive framework is Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics triad of vice, incontinence, and bestiality: Ben Horne's and Laura's weakness of will, the town's ordinary vices, and BOB's appetite-only bestiality ("I don't need anything. I want") versus Windom Earle, whose intact but corrupted reason — the macabre chess game, murdering Catherine beside Cooper, hunting Cooper's soul — makes him, per Aristotle's claim that vice is worse than bestiality, the show's truly evil person and proof that evil is human and fightable.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 7 "Buddha ex Machina" — Lyons applies Masahiro Mori's uncanny valley to the hosts, whose near-human faces and movements turn initial revulsion into empathy — doubling it because the hosts suffer under programming humans would resist. She then argues, through Aristotle's virtue and vice and Nietzsche's discipline of great suffering, that hosts like Maeve (returning for her daughter) and Dolores ('I choose to see the beauty') display more 'human excellence' than the guests: Logan's hand-stabbing cruelty is mere vice and the Man in Black's scalping sadism falls under Aristotle's bestial. Humanity, she concludes, is a way of behaving rather than a way of being, and Mori's hope that robots may carry buddha-nature completes the title's reversal of machine and god.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 8 "“I Always Felt this Place was Missing a Real Villain. Hence, My Humble Contribution.”" — Eberl asks whether living out Sizemore-style fantasies can reveal or only corrode character: applying Aristotle's account of virtues and vices as habituated dispositions, he argues William's three decades in the park habituated the vices that made him the Man in Black — the park reveals rather than suspends the self — while cruelty toward humanlike hosts hardens us toward people, as Aquinas and Kant warn about kindness to animals. Against Ford's claim that humans are wantons in tight loops, Maeve's editing of her own code after learning her escape was scripted makes her a Frankfurtian person who aligns first-order desires with second-order volitions, grounding her narrative identity and personhood. William too attains personhood by actualizing a second-order desire for a different life, with the hosts' free fight back evoking Nietzsche's will to power and Nozick's point that we want to actually do things, not merely experience them.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 20 "9. Wherever the Road Leads" — Watkins takes the recurring road image ("Runnin' Down a Dream," "Kings Highway," "Learning to Fly") as a probe of whether the future is open. Against determinism and Aristotle-style fatalism she argues from lived experience: we cannot feel our choices as unfree, and even a determined world would remain unpredictable, so Petty's open road wins. His optimism in "It'll All Work Out" needs no faith in a good outcome, only the passing of time under our feet, and persistence then becomes an Aristotelian virtue required for eudaimonia, a duty owed to the kind of beings we are, and Sartrean authenticity in which Petty made himself through his project of rock'n'roll.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 31 "19. If Everyone’s Special, … Is Anyone Special" — Grace Wehniainen defends 'you are special' against the Fox & Friends 'evil man' charge by separating intrinsic from extrinsic value: on Rogers's 1 Corinthians 12 and Genesis 1:27 reading, worth is God-given and unearned, like the family dog whose napping life has intrinsic value (with Tom Regan's agreement) regardless of tricks. Specialness as 'belonging specifically to a particular person' needs no trophies, only Socratic self-examination before the mirror, Aristotle's true versus vulgar self-love from the Nicomachean Ethics, and Albert Ellis's self-acceptance over performance-based self-esteem.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 8 "On Philosophers and Drag Queens" — The editors' introduction argues that Drag Race is an unexplored philosophical playground because it builds on marginalized black and Latinx queer herstory and because RuPaul, whose creed of love and self-improvement makes her a philosopher in her own right, has made the show her magnum opus. It invokes Plato's cave to explain why philosophers crave the 'untucked' version of everything RuPaul shows on stage. Its central move is a virtue-ethics reading of the show's judging: Ru's demand that a queen first be fierce, and through fierceness achieve charisma, uniqueness, nerve and talent, mirrors Aristotle's question of what makes a good person, with fierceness playing the role phronesis plays in securing the other virtues. Comparing queens like Silky Nutmeg Ganache, Jinkx Monsoon, Yara Sofia and Sharon Needles, it poses 'what makes a good drag queen?' as a live philosophical problem.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 13 "4. Is It Immoral to Read Someone to Filth" — Birnie stages Alexis Michelle's hurt at the Season 9 body-shaming reads against Bianca Del Rio's 'rolodex of hate' to ask whether reading is immoral. He surveys the philosophical ethics of humor — Plato's Philebus on laughter as malicious delight in others' self-ignorance, Hobbes's 'sudden glory', Schopenhauer on why ridicule hurts, the Stoics' ideal of never laughing, Aristotle's eutrapelia as the golden mean between vulgar buffoon and boor, the Spencer–Freud relief theory, and Bergson's laughter as society's corrective — before endorsing the play theory: reads are consensual mock-aggression, verbal sport honed by marginalized black and Latinx ball culture. From this he derives three guidelines (play signals and consent, timing and audience given the show's younger mainstream viewers, openness to challenge) and concludes Katya's bus-stop read of Roxxxy was acceptable while stereotype reads need care.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 27 "14. Is Kant the Reason Everyone Hates Moral Philosophy Professors" — Duindam defends Kant against the charge that he makes moral philosophy professors insufferable, walking through maxims and the two-question Categorical Imperative test with frozen-yogurt and stealing examples, and arguing that Kant's notorious 'you cannot lie to the murderer' essay is an obscure legal point whose actual test permits lying to demons. On the trolley, the bridge, and Michael's forced organ-harvesting scenario, Kant's humanity formula, never treat persons merely as means, explains both Chidi's refusal to kill Eleanor and the difference between switching tracks and pushing a man.
