Witnessing his parents' murder confronts Bruce with Angst and being-toward-death, and in Miller's Year One the bat crashing through the window lets him authentically choose 'I shall become a bat.' Hart argues this dissolves the free-will/determinism binary - Bruce's choice is neither causally compelled by trauma nor wholly unconditioned, but an authentic self-determination amid thrown possibilities.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 11 "3. The Short-Sightedness of Henry Bemis" — Pichanick reads 'Time Enough at Last' as a meditation on our ambivalent dependence on technology and other people. Henry Bemis experiences the bank, his marriage, and finally the post-nuclear wasteland as successive 'cages' where time belongs to others; his misanthropic wish for a timeless world to himself is granted only for his glasses to shatter, revealing his short-sighted fantasy of exempting himself from the technological system on which even his vision depends. Pichanick concludes the episode demands not another pair of glasses but a philosophical clarity about our limits and interdependence.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 24 "13. No Place like a Non-Place" — Pagnoni Berns, Juvé, and Aguilar apply Marc Augé's concept of the 'non-place'—transit spaces (roads, airports, ships, hotels, malls) of anonymity and 'supermodernity' that confer no identity—to the show's empty landscapes. Postwar gender and identity crises play out in 'Passage on the Lady Anne' (slowness versus speed), 'The Hitch-Hiker' and 'The Passersby' (the road as a non-place where dead women refuse their fate), 'Will the Real Martian Please Step Up?', 'Nightmare at 20,000 Feet,' 'The Parallel,' 'The After Hours,' and 'The Four of Us Are Dying,' where identification briefly pierces anonymity, often fatally.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 22 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Collins-Cavanaugh asks what makes a 'real' father, framing it as authenticity. He pairs Sartre's existentialist authenticity – free choice, anxiety, and the bad faith of adopting others' ready-made plans, with 'real cookie' and Derek Jeter examples – against Charles Taylor's dialogical authenticity, in which choices are made within a 'horizon of meaning' set by others. He argues authentic fatherhood combines both: a father must freely own his choices (provider dad vs nurturer dad) while grounding them in his child's needs, concluding he'll go bake cookies with his son Connor.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 24 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Balogun presents a traditional Yoruba-African conception of 'authentic' fatherhood as a holistic role – spiritual, moral, metaphysical, physical, and material – within an extended, collective family where paternal uncles and grandparents share fathering. He stresses moral education through alo apamo riddles, moonlight folktales (the tortoise, his wife Yonibo, and the priest), and proverbs, and argues contemporary fathers everywhere should learn from this model: total rather than piecemeal responsibility, storytelling over mere cartoon-watching, and treating children as 'ours' rather than 'mine.'
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 19 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Seitz gives an existential-phenomenological meditation on hunting's essence, leaning on Ortega y Gasset's Meditations on Hunting: 'one does not hunt in order to kill; on the contrary, one kills in order to have hunted.' Using his daughter Sabina's squirrel-versus-grouse reasoning and his own pronghorn stalks, he argues meat is the 'sign' but not the essence, and (via Heidegger) that hunting is 'a mode of revealing.' Contrasting Marx and Heidegger on technology with Ortega's claim that hunting 'cannot progress,' he frames the hunter as 'natural/prehistoric man' annihilating historical time — a vanishing figure in a climate-changed, thirsty future.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 31 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Koppedrayer analyzes the modern North American 'traditional' and 'primitive' bowhunting movement—the Traditional Bowyer's Bible, magazines like Primitive Archer, and gatherings like ETAR—where crafting a selfbow from a single wood stave and hunting under a 'fair chase' ethic promise an authentic, unencumbered, 'really real' experience against high-tech compound bows. Drawing on Arjun Appadurai's 'synchronic warehouse of cultural scenarios,' she argues the past functions as a reproducible resource yielding a hyperreal authenticity, and that bowmakers describe the self-made bow as an embodiment of the maker's own substance and a spiritual link to earlier hunters.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 20 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Yim argues that clothing is a primary vehicle for autonomy, authenticity, and moral solidarity. Drawing on Mill's *On Liberty* and 'experiments in living,' he treats a teenager testing modest-vs-expressive dress against her mother, and 'Fashion Freaks' patterns for wheelchair users, as cases where wardrobe choice actualizes self-determination. He then reads dress as an emblem of communal solidarity and critique — the 1968 Smith/Carlos Olympic salute, the Israeli Kibbutz and Amish plain dress (with Rumspringa as a test of authenticity), gang colors, hippie androgyny, vegan 'cruelty-free' clothing, gay Levi's 501s, and Lubna Hussein's trouser trial in Sudan — concluding 'we are what we wear.'
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 20 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Ben Levey uses the fast-food (sport) versus haute-cuisine (trad) analogy and then Hegel's Phenomenology to argue that trad climbing offers a more authentic experience than sport climbing. Applying the master–slave dialectic, he casts the trad climber (like his mentor Martin risking a groundfall on 'Resurrection' placing natural protection) as the slave: through genuine fear, the setting aside of desire, and work that leaves the rock in its independent, unaltered state, the climber comes to identify with the world rather than dominate it. Sport climbing, where bolts subordinate the rock's natural features to the climber's chosen safe line, corresponds to the master who never overcomes the world's independence, yielding only the limited satisfaction of having played the game ethically.
- **College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits**, ch. 21 "College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits" — This span turns to the ethics and epistemology of college sex. Kania argues there is no clear line between close friendship and a sexual relationship, so condemning student-professor sex logically forces condemning student-professor friendship—rejecting Golash's split and defending carefully-conducted consensual relationships. Layne narrates Socrates/Alcibiades, Abelard/Heloise, and Heidegger/Arendt to contrast Socratic eros (Plato's Symposium, love as a friend of wisdom directed at the soul) and Heideggerian authentic love ('I want you to be what you are') against Abelard's exploitative lust. McDowell mines epistemology (justification, taking beliefs 'to heart,' reflective equilibrium) to argue better thinking yields better, more autonomous sex. Pinku weighs 'plain sex' against Nagel's interpersonal-arousal account of embodiment to ask whether sex needs love, and Brophy uses Kantian dignity (treating the body as a mere means, not an end) to argue that prostitution and webcam porn undertaken to pay tuition violate the student's autonomy.
- **Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low**, ch. 24 "BLUES" — Robert and Benjamin Stolorow argue the blues is musical therapy that lets us face universally traumatizing dimensions of existence. Drawing on Robert Stolorow's Trauma and Human Existence, they hold that emotional pain becomes traumatic only when it finds no 'relational home,' and that trauma shatters the 'absolutisms of everyday life,' exposing the existential vulnerability of finite, mortal beings — an explicitly Heideggerian being-toward-death and authenticity of owning rather than evading vulnerability. Blues lyrics (Louisiana Red's 'Too Poor to Die,' Willie Dixon's 'One More Mile to Go') voice tragic-ironic mortality, while pitch-bending and major/minor ambiguity viscerally hold the pain in a shared, therapeutic conversation.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 34 "Determinism and the Dark Knight" — Hart uses Heidegger's Being and Time to explain Batman beyond the free-will/determinism binary. Dasein is a "thrown-project" always being-toward-death; Alfred's world of trays and clocks illustrates the interpretive horizon of a chosen life. Witnessing his parents' murder confronts Bruce Wayne with Angst and his own finitude, and — as in Miller's Year One, where a bat crashes through the window and he decides "I shall become a bat" — he authentically chooses his crime-fighting mission rather than being mechanically driven by trauma or vengeance.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 48 "Reap a Destiny" — The Walls brothers read Harry Potter's confrontation with death through Heidegger's authenticity and being-toward-death: Harry's calm march to the Forbidden Forest and Colin Creevey's sacrifice exemplify accepting mortality, while Voldemort's terror of death makes him inauthentic. The King's Cross scene lets Dumbledore be Harry's Heideggerian hero from the past; via William James's "sow a thought … reap a destiny," Aristotle, Locke on memory-identity, and Kant on the afterlife, they argue our choices forge a character — and Voldemort's refusal of remorse seals his ruin.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 55 "52. Fight Club as Philosophy I Am Jack’s Existential Struggle" — Oya reads Fincher's Fight Club in existentialist, nonethical terms as the story of the unnamed narrator 'Jack' and his struggle for an authentic, self-governed life. Consumerism (the 'Ikea nesting instinct'), the masculinity of underwear ads, religion, and finally Tyler Durden's hunter-gatherer creed are all rejected as externally imposed answers that deny authenticity; Fight Club and Project Mayhem merely swap one alienation for another. Jack's shooting himself to purge Tyler dramatizes self-affirmation. The chapter grounds this in Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity ('the genuine man will not agree to recognize any foreign absolute'), contrasts Nietzsche and Unamuno on self-affirmation, cites Hobbes on the brutish state of nature to condemn Tyler's utopia, and invokes Plato's cave to argue a comfortable but externally governed life is still not authentic.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 59 "56. Pulp Fiction as Philosophy Bad Faith, Authenticity, and the Path of the Righteous Man" — The chapter argues that in Pulp Fiction the authentic characters get 'saved' and the inauthentic do not. Using Sartre's bad faith, it reads Vincent as fleeing into his facticity (his gangster role and social obligations) and Pumpkin as evading responsibility, while Butch acknowledges both his past (the father's watch) and his freedom. Heidegger's 'falling' and das Man explain Vincent's unmoved everyday mode after the miracle. Kierkegaard's three forms of despair from The Sickness unto Death rank the characters, with Jules alone transcending despair by accepting God's grace after 'divine intervention' stopped the bullets, making his Ezekiel monologue the film's key to a deeper authenticity.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 77 "73. Hasan Minhaj as Philosopher Navigating the Struggles of Identity" — Singh reads Minhaj's comedy of identity through existentialism, arguing his call for 'authenticity' over the first generation's 'assimilation' (the 'American dream tax' and 'biryani' arguments about choosing one's life) enacts Sartre's existence-precedes-essence and rejection of bad faith. He frames Minhaj's Indian-American-Muslim conflict via Heidegger's thrownness and facticity and the move from the they-self (das Man) to authentic self, contrasting it with Sartre's facticity as a limit on freedom. Minhaj's 'global citizen' anti-nationalism, his 'love is bigger than fear,' and 'may the best argument win' are presented as prescriptions for navigating national, ethnic, religious and personal identity while flagging fallacies like hasty generalization behind Islamophobia.

### Eudaimonia (flourishing)

Eudaimonia is the central aim of Aristotle's ethics, often rendered as happiness but better understood as flourishing or living well over the course of a whole life. It is not a passing feeling of pleasure but the condition of a human being who fully realizes their nature by acting excellently in accordance with reason and virtue. Aristotle argues that eudaimonia is the final end sought for its own sake, to which all other goods are ultimately directed, and that it depends chiefly on the exercise of the virtues, supported by adequate external goods and good fortune. Achieving it is thus a matter of lifelong activity and character, not of momentary satisfaction.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 10 "George and Virtue—Like Oil and Water" — Daniel Barwick runs George through Aristotle's function argument and finds him wanting: a paradigm of 'the many' who thinks happiness is fortune and momentary victories over others (free parking, perfect airport pickups) rather than activity of the soul in accordance with virtue. His 'do the opposite' epiphany in 'The Opposite' embraces the more extreme vice rather than steering toward the rationally chosen mean, and his self-hatred, laziness, and pleasure-seeking fail all three of Aristotle's tips for hitting the mean. Since George will never practice virtuous action until it becomes habit, Barwick concludes George is doomed to his miserable existence - which is, conveniently for us, why he is funny.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 65 "Happiness and Cypher’s Choice Is Ignorance Bliss" — Opening Griswold's essay (with Locke's line on happiness disturbed by new uneasiness as epigraph), the chapter asks why happiness - the question of existential urgency that Aristotle treated as the ultimate end of our activities - has received so little philosophical treatment (no Platonic dialogue is devoted to it) while non-philosophers assume there is an answer to be found. It presents The Matrix as a rare clever movie that genuinely presses the question of what happiness is, whether the film's answer is tenable, and how we would construct a better one of our own, with Cypher's choice as the test case.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 68 "Unknown" — The chapter proposes three theses: happiness is centrally tranquillity (ataraxia), whose enemy is anxiety - the 'splinter in your mind' that things are out of kilter; the rival Aristotelian view treats happiness as activity (energeia) of soul in accordance with excellence (arete), an objectivism that explains how a contented 'human battery' or happy slave is mistaken about being happy; and neither view suffices alone, since a passionless apatheia is barren and dry. Lived happiness is instead equipoise - settledness in one's basic stance that is compatible with turbulent passions and commitments, more like Neo's active decision-making and discovery than a lazy virtual tryst with the woman in red.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 9 "The Buffyverse’s Moral Compass" — Greg Forster argues the Buffyverse's moral structure is neither Christian nor Nietzschean vampire fiction but Platonic eudaimonism: the just person is always happier than the unjust. Faith is the test case — her pleasure-seeking turn to evil with Mayor Wilkins, her body-swap theft of Buffy's life in 'Who Are You?', her self-disgust ('You're nothing! Disgusting, murderous bitch!'), and her begging Angel to kill her in 'Five by Five' enact Plato's Republic examples of the Ring of Gyges and the unjust person mistakenly honored while the just one is punished. Buffy's invisible crime spree in 'Gone' and her 'the work that I have to do' sacrifice in 'The Gift' display the same eudaimonist pattern, with the caveat that the Buffyverse follows a Rousseau-like moral psychology in which compassion, not reason, does the moral work.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 16 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Gregory Bassham distills six keys to happiness from Tolkien's hobbits and elves: delight in simple pleasures (Epicurus on natural pleasures, Thoreau's Walden simplicity), making light of troubles (Sam's star above Mordor, with Marcus Aurelius and Augustine on courage and hope), friendship (Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics read against Sam, Merry, and Pippin refusing to let Frodo go alone), good character, beauty and creativity (Lothlórien versus Mordor, 'flow'), and wonder (Tom Bombadil, Frodo's 'recovery' of fresh vision at Cerin Amroth). He argues Tolkien thereby becomes a philosophical guide, pointing from the Shire and Rivendell to a richer, more joy-filled life.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 17 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Jorge Gracia contrasts Sam and Gollum as two hobbits of the same nature and culture seeking the same happy life, so their success and failure are instructive for ordinary people like us. Gollum's happiness is solitary possession of the Ring - he murders Déagol for it and ends 'into the dust' - while Sam's is fellowship in the Shire with Rosie and Frodo, pursued through loyalty and giving (spending Galadriel's seed-box to restore the Shire). The pivotal episode is Gollum's trembling caress of Frodo's knee, 'the most tragic moment in the Tale', squandered when Sam's jealous rebuke drives him back to treachery. With Aristotle on friendship and self-love, the chapter concludes that happiness is achievable only in a social context and its key is love.
- **The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am**, ch. 15 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" — Argues ancient ethics explains why Tony, who has 'the world by the balls', still feels like a loser. Plato's Republic diagnoses him as a 'civil war' of unintegrated motivations (loving father and murderer at once, as in 'College'), a condition power over others only worsens; Aristotle teaches that happiness is activity with self-sufficient, integrated desires rather than a list of possessions, and Epicurus's 'sober reasoning' is the therapy Tony never gets. The Hawthorne quotation Tony reads in 'College' and his Gary Cooper ideal from 'The Happy Wanderer' frame the point: Cooper in High Noon is unmesswithable because he does not need vengeance, whereas Tony's compulsive revenge shows the world has the grip on him.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 11 "Why Not to Buy the Porsche" — Skoble uses Manhattan's confrontation scene — Isaac telling Yale 'you're too easy on yourself... you'd rather buy the Porsche' over the hominid skeleton — to build an account of integrity as fidelity to correct moral principles, requiring an integrated character in which reason and desire agree. He distinguishes integrity from mere consistency (the 'consistent Nazi') and from stubbornness, and models it on Plato's just person who 'harmonizes the three parts of himself'. Aristotle's account of habituation defends Isaac's slippery slope: Yale's repeated lies for expediency are forming the kind of character who would inform on friends, so integrity is an objective yardstick of a well-lived life, as Isaac's amends to Tracy at the end confirms.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 126 "The Ugly" — Argues Hogwarts' purely vocational curriculum gives students the tools of power without the wisdom to use them: measured against Adler's three aims of schooling, it surveys the classic accounts of education's purpose - Plato's wisdom and well-ordered society, Aristotle's eudaimonia as excellent activity, Locke's 'virtue and wisdom', Rousseau's natural child-centered education, Kant's character formation, Dewey's growth - and concludes Hogwarts fails to form lifelong learners equipped for wizarding society's problems, including, as Hermione says, wizards' sense of superiority to other creatures.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 148 "The End of the Story" — Argues Socrates and Dumbledore both die for virtue and the common good: Socrates refuses exile because the examined life matters more than wealth or reputation, his martyrdom an exemplar that could benefit Athens, and Dumbledore's arranged death protects Snape's spying for the anti-Voldemort cause. Two Muggle lessons follow - live devoted to something larger than yourself (Lily's sacrifice, with King, Gandhi, Jesus, and Socrates as real-world parallels) and find mentors, as Dumbledore's humility, honesty, and praise in the Order of the Phoenix prophecy conversation enable Harry to fulfill his destiny, with dead mentors like Aristotle, Confucius, and Jesus still able to teach us through their books.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 12 "The Need to Belong" — Working out Birthright's answer, Waid argues that even the solar-powered Kal-El shares the human need to belong, so he can connect with humanity not by hiding his alien side but by embracing it. Echoing a Marianne Williamson passage about our fear of being 'powerful beyond measure', Waid has Superman wear the S-shield - the banner of his Kryptonian 'tribe' - and use his powers openly, because only by living authentically in service of others does he truly belong. He links this to Aristotle's discovery that happiness is rooted in living with excellence, which Superman 'in his own way' found too.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 13 "The Great Paradox" — Waid closes by drawing out the paradox that Superman's shining selflessness is achieved through acting in his own self-interest: in saving others he exercises his distinctive powers and fulfills his authentic destiny, which fulfills him, while embracing his own nature and history puts him in the one activity that most helps others. There is no blanket choice between self and community, he argues - properly fulfilling one's own nature redounds to everyone's benefit - and Superman thereby becomes a mirror for examining the balance of selflessness and self-interest in the reader's own life.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 63 "The Elusiveness of a Complete Friendship" — Argues that Batman himself is chiefly responsible for the elusiveness of complete friendship: the promise to his murdered parents consumes the personal investment such friendship needs, so everyone — Gordon, Dent, the Robins, Batgirl, Alfred — must fit into the mission, as his Hush confession to Catwoman ('I am not very good at this. Having friends.') shows. Aristotle's remark that the good man is a friend to himself lets the chapter cast Bruce and Batman as 'one soul in two personae,' the only virtue friendship left to him. It closes as a cautionary tale: a life of mission can cost the balance — and the friendship — that a good and happy life requires.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 18 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Laura Garcia assembles Narnian heroes: Jill, Eustace, and Puddleglum untying Rilian at likely lethal cost, Eustace hacking at the Sea Serpent, unarmed Shasta charging the lion to save Aravis, and Digory refusing the Witch's offer of the apple that could heal his dying mother. She asks whether egoist theories can explain such deeds and argues they cannot: Hobbes's disguised self-interest, Butler's and Paley's reward schemes, Hume's sympathy, and MacIntyre's identity-based interests all fall short. Only love of others for their own sake, and (for Jill and Digory) trust in Aslan's proven goodness, explains both the heroic choices and our admiration of them as supererogatory acts beyond the call of duty.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 19 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Devin Brown uses Eustace, who dodges work on Dragon Island until he wakes as a dragon and discovers he would rather be hungry among human friends than comfortable alone, to contrast Epicurean hedonism and Tom Sawyer's work-avoidance with Mill's higher pleasures and the 'Sherlock Holmes philosophy of work.' Weighing Aristotle's contemplative life against Lewis's love of quests, he reads Father Christmas's tailored gifts and 'everyone must do what he can do best' as an Acorn Philosophy of Vocation with a Marxian 'from each according to his ability' echo, condemns wrong livelihoods like Governor Gumpas's slave trade, and closes on leisure and Aristotle's golden mean, which Lewis turns into 'golden extremes.'
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 14 "“Hey, Let’s Get the Stuff We Need!” Putting the Mall in Its Place" — Matthew Walker reads Dawn of the Dead through Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and Politics: the survivors' mall orgy curdles into boredom ('What have we done to ourselves?'), illustrating pleonexia, the graspingness for more than one's share of the goods of fortune that Aristotle roots in an unlimited desire for mere living - which may even explain why Romero's dead return, grasping from beyond the grave for more un-death. Aristotle's dismissal of the life of enjoyment as fit for cattle, his account of eudaimonia as the life in which our rational capacities flourish, and his defense of acquisition bounded by the good life explain why unlimited consumption zombifies the living, and why Peter and Fran must finally leave the mall empty-handed.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 90 "Bullshit Around the Globe" — Building on Peter Goldie's account of how life-narratives shape emotion, and Martha Nussbaum's view of emotions as judgments of value and importance (which the chapter identifies with the Greek Stoic view), it explains where bullshit gets its power over us. Because an episode's place in a narrative determines what we feel — Oedipus could be delighted to have married Jocasta but not his mother — bullshit works by 'educating' our emotions, telling us what should make us proud, patriotic, angry or frightened, and what belongs in a eudaimonistic life. It closes by warning that bullshit appeals to the base and non-rational part of us and so degrades us, before turning to examples from international politics.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 27 "Lessons Learned" — McAleer maps The Office onto Aristotle's ethics: David Brent is the buffoon who is 'the slave of his sense of humor,' Gareth the literalist boor who cannot take a joke, and Tim the ready wit whose irony responds to the situation — together illustrating that a virtue is a qualitative mean of acting and feeling appropriately, fixed by practical wisdom rather than rules. That humor cannot be codified mirrors the uncodifiability of Aristotelian ethics, and wit's very status as a virtue shows Aristotle's morality is broader than modern duty-and-outcome ethics: it aims at the flourishing (eudaimonia) of the whole person.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 49 "House and the Life of Reason" — Henry Jacoby takes seriously House's nihilist sound bites ("selfish, base animals," his baiting of Sister Augustine and Foreman's chapel prayer, his clinically dead experiment in "97 Seconds") but argues House actually lives the Socratic examined life and Aristotle's life of reason: his puzzle-solving saves lives, exercises humanity's distinctive function, and issues in eudaimonia. The Euthyphro dilemma shows meaning cannot be grounded in God's plan, and House's refusal of afterlife comfort leaves "our actions here" as all that matters. Against the unexamined life, House's "What's the point in living without curiosity?" makes him a Socratic figure who chooses meaning through reason rather than faith.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 23 "Why Be Moral" — Sanders uses Bruno Anthony's 'criss-cross' murder-swap proposal to Guy Haines in Strangers on a Train to pose the classic question 'Why be moral?' to the charming amoralist. He tests three answers: Kant's categorical imperative fails because Bruno's egoist maxim ('remove obstacles to your happiness') can apparently be universalized; Hobbesian contractarian 'morality pays' fails because Bruno free-rides on others' restraint; and the Rachels/Nelson/Thomas psychological-health answer assumes rather than proves that Bruno should care about comparable suffering. A thought experiment comparing the moral life with the Bruno-state from an impartial standpoint leads to Aristotle's eudaimonia: morality is constitutive of human flourishing, so Bruno enjoys only a counterfeit happiness.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 15 "Tough and Tender, The Dead Keep Truckin’" — Gary Ciocco traces a line from Emerson and James through Kerouac, Ginsberg, and Neal Cassady to the Grateful Dead: Emerson's nonconformist 'infinitude of man' and James's 'live options' and religious appetite for being 'more fully alive' become, in the Beats, the project of living life itself as art ('the only people for me are the mad ones'). He argues the Beats splintered because each chased an atomistic, individual epiphany — Kerouac swinging wholesale from tender- to tough-minded temperament — while the Dead turned the same Jamesian hunger into a shared communal religious experience, a 'kindler, gentler' scene that better achieves Aristotle's eudaimonia. Cassady, muse of On the Road and driver of the Pranksters' bus, literally connects the two movements, but the Dead's unity-in-diversity made them the evolution, not the echo, of the Beats.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 27 "A Happy Ending" — Bickham asks why Dorothy is so eager to leave heroic, Technicolor Oz for the gray, childless, Gulch-dominated farm, and whether, like Hamlet's delay, her rash choice can be evaluated as hers rather than her author's. Aristotle's account of the good life as the exercise of our highest capacities, requiring friends and material goods, makes Oz look like the better home for the competent twelve- or thirteen-year-old he takes Dorothy to be, against the hedonisms of Aristippus, Epicurus, and Bentham and Plato's body-denying dualism. But caring about Dorothy first needs defending from the paradox of fiction, which he works through Currie's simulation theory and Walton's make-believe emotions before dissolving the puzzle: storytelling suspends the reign of logic, so wishing Dorothy well is natural. Finally Heidegger's being-toward-death shows 'happily ever after' is impossible anywhere, and he throws the problem to the reader: write a happy ending for Dorothy in Kansas.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 13 "Where Tragedy Ends and Community Begins" — Lott takes up Augustine's puzzle about why we enjoy watching sufferings we would flee, and answers for Radiohead with Aristotle's theory of tragedy: songs like 'Karma Police', 'Exit Music', and 'Fake Plastic Trees' sketch fragmentary characters in breakdown whose undeserved yet partly self-inflicted sufferings — 'Just'''s 'you do it to yourself' is hamartia — evoke pity and fear and then catharsis. Singing along makes identification uniquely intense in pop ('for a minute there, I lost myself' blurs the listener into the character), while music's 'natural sweetness' and its dynamics of build, climax, and release carry the purgation, from the terror of 'Climbing Up the Walls' to the slow ache of 'Videotape'. Because tragedy, unlike history, deals in universals, songs like 'The Bends' and 'High and Dry' open onto reflection on happiness, vulnerability, and the culture that fosters isolation, ending in the thin but real community of listeners who recognize their shared fragility.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 29 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Plauche grounds Optimus Prime's line 'Freedom is the right of all sentient beings' in 'Aristotelian liberalism': since Energon, like our food, is scarce and requires labor and creativity, any volitional artificial life needs a moral code whose standard is flourishing (following Foot's natural goodness), cultivating intellectual and moral virtues from prudence, independence, and honesty to benevolence and courage. Ricardo and Mises's law of association - illustrated by Ratchet and a human mechanic both profiting from specialization despite Ratchet's absolute superiority - plus the ruinous cost of war give even superior aliens reason to respect our rights to life, liberty, and property rather than enslave or exterminate us, as Megatron would.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 26 "The Aftermath of Tragedy" — Argues that Grave of the Fireflies works as a critique of anime's child-hero convention: Seita acts exactly like a plucky anime protagonist when he defies his not-actually-evil aunt, strikes out on his own with Setsuko, ignores the farmer's advice to apologize and return, and demands a quick fix from the doctor — but these 'heroic' choices kill them both, because he lacks the developed capacity to reason. Against the medieval 'child as little adult' picture that most anime (Dragon Ball, Pokémon, Yu-Gi-Oh!) romanticizes, the chapter deploys Aristotle's view of children as unfinished beings who cannot yet reason or achieve happiness, concluding the film is a cautionary tale about the years of nurture and guidance real children need.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 28 "Equivalent Exchange" — Reads alchemy's law of equivalent exchange as a parable of capitalism: Locke's labor-mixing argument explains how hours of a life become property and why money is 'distilled life'; Aristotle's attack on limitless wealth-getting (the Midas problem) and Aquinas's capital vices explain how pursuing money for its own sake brings the homunculi — Greed, Pride, and the Sloth the Elric brothers' forbidden act produced — into the world. Marx's 1844 Manuscripts supply the punchline that money performs 'human alchemy' on people, buying their time, esteem, and bodies the way red stones are made from sacrificed humans, so the chapter concludes that capital, like the Philosopher's Stone, profits only by consuming lives and that markets must be held to a promise of fairness and care beyond mere exchange.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 19 "Forgiveness and the Fenway Faithful" — Rory Kraft uses Aristotle's virtue ethics to explain why Red Sox Nation forgave Tim Wakefield (whose mistake Aaron Boone turned into the 2003 ALCS-ending homer) and Ted Williams, but scapegoated Bill Buckner for 'the error' and eventually cast off Manny Ramirez. Because Aristotle judges a complete life, one swallow does not make a summer, Buckner's .991 fielding percentage and 2,715 hits should contextualize his lapse, yet some acts are bad without degrees like Aristotle's adultery, theft and murder, and a World Series-deciding error crossed that line. Kraft distinguishes Aristotle's categories, Wakefield's mistake (ignorance of Boone's changed plan) versus Buckner's misadventure (contrary to reasonable expectation) versus Manny's voluntary injustices, concluding that learning when to forgive players who are family taught the Nation what forgiveness itself means, sealed by Buckner's 2008 standing ovation.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 14 "“Hey, Let’s Get the Stuff We Need!” Putting the Mall in Its Place" — Matthew Walker reads Dawn of the Dead's survivors, who loot the mall, gorge, grow bored, and degenerate into glitzy despair beside the zombies clawing to get back in, through Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and Politics. Peter's 'They're us' is glossed by pleonexia, the grasping disposition to want more, which Aristotle roots in being serious about mere living rather than living well, and the quartet's hedonistic 'sweet life' is the life of enjoyment Aristotle dismisses as fit for cattle because it atrophies the rational capacities that make us human. Romero is no Puritan scold: material goods remain instrumentally useful and the mall a sanctuary, but like Aristotle he shows a life of unlimited acquisition is a kind of living death, which is why Peter and Fran must leave empty-handed.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 29 "The Final Whistle" — Andrew Lambert defends the rationality of being a football fan by updating Aristotle: living well in a liberal consumer democracy demands an accessible source of beauty, catharsis, belonging, public discourse, and altruism, and fandom trains exactly these sensibilities — from his childhood prayers for Everton to the 1914 Christmas Truce match and supporters' trusts that own clubs like Exeter City. The mature 'fan of football' takes an ironic view of the 'loyal fan's' tribal passions, gaining the practical wisdom that keeps rivalry (the Liverpool–Everton derby, the 1969 'Football War') from curdling into violence. Fandom thus answers critics who dismiss it as consumerist escapism or bad faith.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 7 "The End of the Story" — Reads the Gom Jabbar test as Herbert's definition of humanity: Paul endures Mohiam's pain box because a human stays in the trap to turn it on the trapper and protect the species, while an animal only chews off its own leg. The Butlerian Jihad's ban on 'a machine in the likeness of a man's mind' is applied to our own iPod-and-PDA dependence, with Mentat Thufir Hawat showing that losing the machine-crutch 'forced human minds to develop,' in line with Aristotle's phronesis and the politics of the common good (and Plato's contemplation as the core of happiness). The chapter closes by turning the human/animal test on the modern West—Baron Harkonnen-like consumers whose water-hungry beef habit makes us the trap of our own environmental collapse.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 18 "Sweet Miracles of (Secular) Faith, Hope, and Love" — Florek reconstructs Peart's ethics as Aristotelian virtue ethics: aiming at eudaimonia rather than feeling good, 'Freewill' chooses autonomy and responsibility as virtues, and 'Vital Signs' adds persistence and courage ('courageous convictions will drag the dream into existence'), with a compassionate expansion toward ordinary sufferers in 'Distant Early Warning', 'Red Sector A' ('I must help my mother stand up straight'), and 'Everyday Glory'. Peart's existential consciousness then confronts finitude ('Time Stand Still', the fading memory of 'Vapor Trail'), contingency ('Roll the Bones' — 'Why does it happen? Because it happens'), and the absurd of Sartre and Camus ('The Stars Look Down' — an indifferent universe that answers nothing). The 1997-98 tragedies turn this existential consciousness tragic, and the post-tragic resolution of Vapor Trails and 'Faithless' is a secular faith in hope and love — Peart's answer to 1 Corinthians 13 without God — grounded in being loved by Carrie Nuttall.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 11 "Why Is It the Best Day Ever" — Nicole Pramik argues SpongeBob is Aristotle's self-mastered man: his daily cheerfulness is eudaimonia, a happiness earned by practicing virtue as the mean between vices of excess and deficiency. The chapter tests each mean with episodes — courage between cowardly isolation ('I Had an Accident') and recklessness ('A Life in a Day'), honor between Patrick's under-the-rock humility and Squidward's Easter-Island vanity, honesty in 'Hooky' and 'Wet Painters', and good temper mended with Patrick in 'New Student Starfish' and 'The Fry Cook Games'. His moderation in pleasure and wealth, contrasted with Mr. Krabs's stinginess, and his F.U.N. Song friendship (Aristotle's greatest external good) show the golden mean served up on a sesame seed bun.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 14 "So, You Tried to Kill Me Over a Little New Age Management, Eh" — Joseph Foy weighs Mr. Krabs against Ayn Rand's celebration of money-making, Marx's charge that Krabs commodifies his employees — wagering SpongeBob to Plankton in 'Welcome to the Chum Bucket' and working him 43 days without a break in 'Fear of a Krabby Patty' — and Aristotle's and Adam Smith's insistence that wealth is merely instrumental to flourishing. The verdict: Krabs inverts means and ends, fetishizing money until he sells SpongeBob's soul for 62 cents ('Born Again Krabs') and trades his own body for his millionth dollar ('Clams'). His real failing is the unexamined life — he never asks what would actually make him happy — which makes him tragically human rather than simply villainous.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 18 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Flanders reads Killing Yourself to Live as asking whether dying can be good for the person who dies: Jeff Buckley's 'Hallelujah' and Kurt Cobain's myth became deeper and more successful only after the fact, as if death were a career move. He answers with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, where the fortunes of descendants can affect the happiness of the dead: our life-stories outlive their authors, so fans' posthumous devotion can really benefit Buckley, though no posthumous fame can add virtue that was never lived (Michael Jackson's rehabilitation cannot touch how he actually lived). Klosterman's road trip ultimately undercuts the question: the earnest Great White concert mourners remember what truly was there, while Cobain's fans retroactively invent meaning to gain 'credibility by mourning retrospectively', so worshipping the rock dead manufactures an inauthentic afterlife, and Klosterman must kill the unserious fan in himself to live.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 29 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Fitzpatrick asks whether Klosterman's low-culture project (tribute bands, Toby Keith, the McNuggets diet) is mere titillation or genuinely valuable. Bentham's pushpin-versus-poetry hedonism matches Klosterman's rejection of 'guilty pleasures,' while Aristotle's eudaimonia — and Plato's forms, on which a tribute band is a copy of a copy of a copy — condemns a life of amusement. Mill resolves the question twice over: higher and lower pleasures justify ranking Klosterman's contemplative criticism above mere sensation, and On Liberty's free market of ideas shows that even false or partial low-culture claims (about Garth Brooks, Spurlock's Super Size Me) keep high culture's truths from decaying into unexamined dogma.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 10 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Greg Littmann stages Plato's hypothetical review of American Gods under the Republic's charges against poetry: the novel is full of 'greatest of all lies' about gods behaving badly, from Odin and Loki's sacrificial plot to Czernobog's head-smashing, gods degrading themselves into lesser forms like Horus the road-kill-eating hawk and Media as Lucille Ball, and characters ruled by passion rather than reason, from Mad Sweeney drinking himself to death to Thor's suicide, corrupting a soul that should be governed by rationality. Against this he sets Aristotle's Poetics: listening to music and intellectual leisure are valuable in themselves, fiction is more philosophic than history because it shows what could happen, the impossible is justified when it astounds, and catharsis through pity for figures like the weeping Mad Sweeney purges rather than corrupts. Because American Gods' absurd premise unfolds with internally probable, character-consistent events (loyal Shadow, loving Laura, grifter Odin), it satisfies Aristotle's requirement that fantasy make artistic sense.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 21 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Wayne Yuen uses The Graveyard Book to teach the good life: Bod's family's murder, like students owing their existence to the Holocaust, is an unalloyed moral evil that still enables a better life, and Saul Smilansky's distinction between being 'sorry for' and 'sorry that' lets Bod benefit without endorsing the tragedy. His graveyard education is Aristotelian, virtues acquired through practice and models, from the Owenses' duty and Silas's wisdom to 'righteous indignation' against school bullies and friendship with Scarlett as intrinsically valuable, all building toward eudaimonia. The existentialist virtue of authenticity (attributed to Sartre and Kierkegaard) explains why Bod must be 'nobody but himself' rather than a copy of the vampire Silas, why the scavenged identities of the ghouls mark inauthenticity, and why wiping Scarlett's memory threatens her authenticity, resolving the apparent conflict between virtue and being oneself because bravery or wisdom is relative to the individual.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 9 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Littmann answers the charge that D&D is a waste of time with Aristotle: pleasure is good as an end in itself, humanity's function is thinking, so even munchkin power-gaming and 4E combat roles are worthwhile intellectual activity under the function argument. He then treats D&D as participatory art—improvisational storytelling offering catharsis (smacking goblins to purge aggression) and the Poetics' license to explore what could be, like the dwarf chieftain grieving a disintegrated son or deciding what a friend owes the thief in the scorpion nest. A good DM, on this Aristotelian view, makes plots unfold with internal probability and characters act from consistent personality, yet 'just playing my character' never excuses ruining another player's fun, since artistic value never suspends the virtues governing how we treat people.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 13 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Classicist and Jeopardy! champion Daniel Melia reads the show as a mirror of American exceptionalism, contrasting it with European hits like Big Brother: Jeopardy! is pure individual contest rewarding a faith in classless meritocracy, its Daily Doubles and come-from-behind Final Jeopardy! wagers enact the American belief in redemption and self-reinvention, and its buzzer timing and Before-and-After clues test frontier virtues of physical reflex and improvisation. He argues that its middlebrow categories (Magritte, Sibelius, Paul Revere) preserve shared American cultural capital, and that the show's free-flowing, low-context, information-sharing format answers the question 'What does it mean to be an American, Alex?' and indexes what Americans count as living the good life.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 27 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Five-time champion Matt Kohlstedt argues that winning Jeopardy! reflects gamesmanship and a love of learning rather than education itself, and warns against the 'Jeopardy!-ization' of schooling: high-stakes testing makes teachers assembly-line trainers and students regurgitators, and produces the on-air 'Jeopardy! effect' of choking under pressure that made him flub the number of articles in the Constitution. Drawing on his late grandfather's book on teacher education and Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs and peak experiences, he defends a philosophy of education aimed at self-actualized teachers who, like Alex Trebek's mid-round contestant interviews, treat students as whole human beings rather than test statistics.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 9 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Prof Joe's introduction casts The Wire, like Socrates, as a gadfly that refuses to let any viewer rest comfortably: tough-on-crime conservatives, Hamsterdam-friendly libertarians, hopeful liberals watching Royce and Carcetti, techno-optimists watching Freamon's wire, and capitalists watching the docks and the Baltimore Sun all get their beliefs challenged with no easy answers. It retells Socrates's refusal to escape Athens as valuing the quality of life over its quantity, and sets that against the Puritan work-ethic myth that blames the corner boys and fiends for their own fate while Aristotle's flourishing is rebranded as the American pursuit of happiness. The essay closes by previewing the book's six 'Cases' (the Game, tactics, Omar, boundaries, tragedy, sentencing) around Socrates's own question: how ought we to live?
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 23 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Trerise argues Omar is virtuous in Aristotle's full sense: honest on the stand ('I robs drug dealers... I got the shotgun, you got the briefcase'), courageous, consistent, and generous, with even his vengefulness a mean between extremes given a world where no one else will check Avon or Marlo - unlike Marlo he never guns on citizens and even pays Prop Joe for clock repairs. Virtue theory's attention to context separates his killings of Stinkum, Savino, and Stringer from Marlo's power-consolidating murders and shows him achieving whatever eudaimonia his world allows, though his obsession after Stringer's setup, which got Tosha killed, marks his one real excess. The catch is exemplification - Omar is disturbed that children play at being Omar, and Michael becomes the new him - yet the chapter concludes that some vigilantism is a social necessity on the streets and that Omar's swapped body tag names the injustice done to the street's truly virtuous.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 37 "Psych and Philosophy" — Patricia Brace maps Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics categories of friendship onto Psych: Shawn's first-season ties to the SBPD are friendships of utility, the shared hobbies and bar nights (tap dancing in 'Feet Don't Kill Me Now,' 'Neil Simon's Lover's Retreat') build friendships of pleasure, and Shawn-Juliet matures from utilitarian boundaries into erotic friendship. Lassiter's lie-detector threat to protect Juliet in 'Shawn Rescues Darth Vader' and the lifelong Shawn-Gus bond ('Gus Walks into a Bank') approach complete friendship grounded in virtue, while the Henry-Shawn paternal friendship heals as Shawn develops the golden mean, and the vicious Mr. Yin and Yang - full of regret, incapable of complete friendship - show the life without it.
- **The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia**, ch. 24 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" — Jennifer Swanson asks whether Alicia can 'have it all', starting from Aristotle: Peter fails the moral virtues (faithfulness, honesty, courage), Jackie's intrusive moments undermine her kindness since Aristotle's unity of the virtues ties them together, and Eli Gold's perfect frankness leaves no room for perfect tact. Following Michael Slote's partial values and impossibility of perfection, she argues career and family are paired values in which gaining one loses the other, as Alicia discovers being pulled between Molly the nanny, Cary's 'she'll have something to fall back on', Diane's partner-track warning, and dumping Will after Grace's twelve butt-dials in 'Parenting Made Easy'. Since perfection is impossible in principle, the answer is balance across all the values of a good life, not Caitlin's retreat into 'I just want to be a mom'.
- **The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia**, ch. 27 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" — John Fitzpatrick asks whether voters should care that Alicia stands beside Peter, from the Season One resignation press conference to the finale's withheld hand. After a rapid tour of right-action theories grounded in the show - Eli Gold's egoism, Peter's 'pitted' evidence tip as consequentialism, Alicia keeping Jonas Stern's dementia secret as deontology, the Florrick-Childs no-children pact as social contract - he turns to Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: eudaimonia as a life weaving pleasure, friendship, and practical activity, in which mentors like Will and Diane let us contemplate virtue in others and improve our own character. His conclusion: Alicia's endorsement matters not because she is a good wife but because she is a good person whose judgment reveals Peter's character.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 15 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Brace and Kingsbury use the Nicomachean Ethics to argue that Nucky, Chalky, and Margaret mistake pleasure and the mere instruments of happiness - tailored suits, money, useful connections, the appearance of virtue - for Aristotle's stable, self-sustaining virtuous activity, so their lives stay unstable and empty. Nucky 'buys' even Jimmy and Margaret, Chalky's jail-cell staging with David Copperfield shows how fragile his facade of cultivation is, and Margaret's acquisitions end in blackmail and in bribing God over Emily's polio. Only Richard Harrow, the Tin Man whose collage-clippings represent a happiness he believes he can never have, moves toward real Aristotelian friendship through Jimmy's 'Of course I would; right down to the last bullet' - the philia Aristotle calls most necessary for a happy life.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 10 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Hauskeller argues Shelley's Victor was sane and benevolently motivated, and reads the 'playing God' warning (Whale's 'now I know what it feels to be God!', the Genesis tree of life, the sorcerer's apprentice) as a claim that crossing nature's lines is dangerous rather than sinful. He then flips the story: like the creature, we are children abandoned by a creator who withholds eternal life, so the real wrong is a creator's failure of duty and love - while Epicurus's death-is-nothing-to-us argument and the picture of a childless, static immortal world undermine the transhumanist case that death is the greatest evil. The chapter ends with Aristotle's mean: obsessive pursuit of knowledge and immortality wrecks happiness, which lies in discovering that our native town is the world and living in the present.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 9 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Jeff Ewing argues the moral fabric of Ender's Game is virtue-ethical, first testing Ender's leadership against Plato's cardinal virtues, tripartite soul, and rigid class hierarchy of the Republic, then finding Aristotle a far better fit. Ender's trademark use of the minimum force necessary against Stilson, Bonzo, and the buggers sits at Aristotle's mean between cowardice and excess, while his adaptability and disregard for rules and hierarchy only count as virtues in Aristotle's framework - though his ignorance of crucial facts explains why xenocide, like his beatings, fell outside the mean.
- **How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness**, ch. 20 "How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy" — The chapter argues HIMYM offers two complementary feminist icons: Robin embodies personal autonomy and independence - fighting from 'but, um' early-morning shifts to lead anchor, and grieving infertility as stolen autonomy rather than lost motherhood - while Lily, and even more Marshall, exemplify Carol Gilligan's feminist care ethics with its emphasis on emotion over impartiality, cooperation over competition, and partiality toward loved ones. Aristotle's golden mean supplies the test Robin passes by balancing career and love instead of pushing one to an extreme. The twist that a male character best exemplifies care ethics, with Lily bridging the two moral outlooks, is offered as the show's progressive complexity about gender.
- **How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness**, ch. 25 "How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy" — Framed as a sports broadcast with Aristotle as commentator, the chapter tests an evolutionary ethics ('BEES': the good is the naturally desirable, so the Pleistocene Stinson strategy of spreading genes grounds Barney's womanizing) against its classic critics. Hume's is-ought gap and Moore's open question argument are deployed against deriving Barney's right to pursue tail from human nature, while William Casebeer's evolutionary ethics replies that 'good' can be defined by present reproductive success - under which lying and eternal bachelorhood fail, since commitment is what reproduces genomes in urban New York ('BIRDS'). The chapter concludes that evolutionary ethics can support the Bro Code only by contestable redefinition, and the lying objection stands.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 37 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — The chapter argues Finn is not yet a true hero but is on a quest to become one: against rule systems like Mill's greatest-happiness utilitarianism and Kantian respect for persons, virtue ethics asks not 'what should I do' but 'who should I be', and Aristotle's point that children lack fully developed practical reason explains why Finn's good intentions misfire - removing Donny exposes the house people to Why-wolves, and Penny's trick humiliates him in the City of Thieves. Martha Nussbaum's ideal of every person as free and of equal dignity grounds heroism in the common good, and her work on literature and popular culture explains how watching Finn's exaggerated choices trains our own moral judgment. Citing Franco and Zimbardo's psychology of real heroes - empathy, risk tolerance, persistence - and closing with Seneca's 'how nobly you live', it concludes that since Aristotelian virtue is a habit, anyone can start by admitting they suck at heroism and practicing, as Jake's advice puts it.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 16 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Hicks starts from young Jobs the 'little terror' expelled from third grade and asks whether he failed the school system or the system failed him, answering that America's entrepreneurs are produced by culture outside school—garage workshops, Heathkits, dirt-bike ramps, and parents who back initiative—rather than rows, rote learning, and standardized tests. He catalogues the entrepreneurial character traits Jobs displayed (informed creative judgment, ambition and integrity like the carpenter's hidden plywood, initiative calling Bill Hewlett at home, courage, perseverance through the Lisa, NeXT, and Pixar losses, win-win trade, leadership) and proposes risk-exercise curricula, Montessori methods, and programs like NFTE so schooling can deliberately cultivate the virtues of a flourishing entrepreneurial life.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 19 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Thomas asks whether the Apple II, Macintosh, and iPod were great products regardless of sales or great because they sold, and answers that market success is real evidence of value: each sale is a buyer's revealed preference in a voluntary trade, a stronger test than critics or focus groups, which is why Jobs's flops (NeXT, the G4 Cube) were overdesigned, overpriced failures of utility rather than quality. Against Hume's quoted doctrine that reason is and ought only to be the slave of the passions (hunger strikers and Jobs's own vegan fanaticism defeat any basic-desire theory), he follows Rand and Philippa Foot in grounding value in objective human needs and capacities, so products designed for those needs—like the iPhone the Apple team built for themselves—could be expected to succeed.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 24 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Meyer reads Jobs through 'individualistic perfectionism'—the Aristotelian tradition (via Rasmussen and Den Uyl, and Veatch) on which flourishing is objective to human nature yet agent-relative, an endless striving unique to each person's talents rather than Kant's by-the-book categorical imperative applied impersonally to all. Jobs embodied this: the 'bicycle of the mind' faith that reason and tools extend human efficiency, practical wisdom weighing goods like friendship, health, and art through Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, experimental self-discovery (Zen, calligraphy, fruitarian diets), and the exile-to-NeXT-to-Pixar-to-iMac arc of constant re-evaluation—so the right question is not whether Jobs 'was' a moral perfectionist but whether each of us keeps striving in our own key.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 16 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Altmann stages a moral (not legal) trial of Dracula with three expert witnesses: Kant testifies that Dracula universalizes murder only for himself while fleeing Harker's kukri, and that he reduced Harker to a mere meal, violating the categorical imperative and deserving execution; Mill weighs consequences, tallying the misery done to Lucy, her mother, and the Bloofer Lady's child victims, and argues the greatest happiness lies in imprisoning the Count for medical study instead; Aristotle argues the child-brained vampire lacks the reason and self-control needed for eudaimonia and so merits imprisonment rather than death. The chapter hands the verdict to the reader, showing guilt is agreed but punishment diverges across the three frameworks.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 17 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Kyle Alkema and Adam Barkman ask what would make the Gang happy and answer with Aristotle's virtue ethics: happiness is long-run flourishing built on virtuous habits, with the golden mean (courage between cowardice and recklessness) as the rule for choice. The Gang instead lives a 'Reverse Virtue Ethic' - trying extremes first by crude trial and error, like sniffing gasoline to check that it is gasoline - along three roads: quick money (welfare crack scams, robbing their own parents' house), lust (the D.E.N.N.I.S. System's seduce-and-abandon script, where Dennis cheerfully accepts the charge of sociopathy), and validation ('You're not gay, you're just really, really vain'). Their residual Catholicism supplies consciences and limits - Mac's talk of God smiting them, confession, fears of Hell - but no reasoned morality, leaving them trapped in 'one day at a time' gratification as reverse role models.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 12 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Robison-Greene asks whether there are principled standards for 'shipping' TV couples and applies Platonic-Aristotelian flourishing criteria (long-term safety, emotional needs, trust, and mutual growth toward virtue) to Piper's options: Alex fails on safety and trust (selling Piper out, the perjury advice), Larry fails on empathy and growth, so by real-life standards we should ship none of them. She concludes shipping is mostly aesthetic, then proposes minimal moral rules for our attitudes toward fictional relationships: never ship Pornstache, respect consent, and never let race, gender, or orientation decide.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 30 "17. The Friends of a Time Lord" — Littmann applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics taxonomy of friendship - pleasure, usefulness, and mutual goodness - to fifty years of Doctor-companion pairings, from the Hartnell Doctor's glee touring Vortis with Ian to New Series companions chosen as friends who routinely save the day, from Barbara's Dalek revolt to Clara saving every incarnation of the Doctor. He argues Aristotle would still judge the Doctor's friendships defective: they are short-lived, unequal in station, intellect, and morality, and the companions cannot know him well enough (not even his name) for the perfect friendship of the good. Littmann then corrects Aristotle on two counts: friends need not be moral experts to serve as moral critics (Rose in 'Dalek,' Amy in 'A Town Called Mercy'), and the Doctor's favoritism toward his companions - risking worlds to save them, as when Rory weighs Amy's life against the universe in 'The Big Bang' - shows that preferring friends over strangers is itself his most frequent moral failing.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 14 "5. Overcoming Evil with Love" — Bogosian argues the film locates evil not in human nature itself, as Jeanine claims when she calls human nature 'the enemy,' but in cultivable vices - Al's jealousy and fear of failure leading to attempted murder and suicide, Eric's and Jeanine's lust for power - and that only altruistic, self-sacrificial love can counteract them. With Aristotle's point that friendship is essential to developing virtue and to the good life, he shows the faction system fails on its own terms: a single virtue in isolation corrupts (Candor's truth without kindness), and a system that removes real moral and political freedom destroys the flourishing it promises. Tris's parents' sacrifices and the Tris-Four relationship - honest training advice, protection of her Divergence, and the gun-to-her-own-forehead scene where love breaks the simulation's grip - model the love that overcomes the corrupt system.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 30 "18. The Virtues of Choosing Your Faction" — Pascoe contrasts Aristotle's and Kant's theories of virtue through the Choosing Ceremony. On Aristotle's account virtues are taught (intellectual) and then habituated into character (moral), tied to one's function, so Susan flourishes because aptitude, upbringing, and choice align while the transfer Al withers - but Tris, Divergent with multiple aptitudes, needs Kant instead: natural virtues are mere 'gifts of nature' that become good only through good will, and her perfect duties to herself and imperfect duties regarding family and faction can justify choosing Dauntless over staying in Abnegation. Kant wins the day: because a corrupted community like Eric's Dauntless redefines bravery into obedience, Tris must think for herself - 'maybe I am wired like the Divergent' - choosing her virtues out of duty and self-respect rather than inheriting them.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 13 "4. Finding One’s Place and Being Useful" — Karavitis argues that work, not social class, is Downton's real theme, sorting characters in a two-by-two matrix of class membership against acceptance or rejection of the existing social order. Those who accept their place stagnate - Violet ('We don't work,' 'What is a weekend?'), Robert the mismanaging custodian, the perpetually jobless Molesley - while those who reject it flourish: Isobel's drive to be 'useful,' Sybil's nursing ('I feel useful for the first time in my life'), Gwen's hidden typewriter, Alfred's Ritz training. He surveys Rousseau on work's role in inequality, Smith on the division of labor, and Marx on labor and ideology on the negative side, and Aristotle, Russell's 'In Praise of Idleness,' and Pieper on leisure and personal projects on the positive side, ending with the prediction that automation will soon give everyone the Crawley daughters' problem of what to do with a life without work.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 32 "18. Doctor, Heal Thyself" — McClelland argues Lecter is a flawed healer: reading Starling's FBI disgrace as social exclusion, he shows how Lecter's hypnotic drugs and deep-hypnosis 'treatment' let her revisit and metabolize her repressed rage at her dead father — the parental imago he named back in Silence of the Lambs — producing a chrysalis-like metamorphosis completed when she defies Krendler at the dinner and asks for more of his brains. The healing is symmetric, since Starling's insight into Lecter's own Mischa fixation releases him too, and the chapter closes with an Aristotelian verdict — choice reveals character, and whether the couple's Buenos Aires partnership counts as good depends on long-term flourishing we have not yet seen.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 18 "5. Back from the Dead" — Devlin and Cooper trace Rick's moral arc as a struggle between Mill-style consequentialism - twisted by the apocalypse into a 'Greatest Survival Principle' of mere survival (Dawn Lerner's Grady, Enid's 'JSS') - and Aristotelian virtue ethics. Shane's murder of Otis, the Governor's rule over Woodbury and killing of Martinez and Pete, and Terminus's cannibalism all show survival-only reasoning dissolving humanity, a decline the show underlines with literal mirror reflections of Shane as a walker. Rick falls after killing Shane and nearly trades Michonne to the Governor, is brought back by Lori's judging vision and the sight of Carl going cold, and reclaims virtues as habits grown like Hershel's seeds - 'We get to come back' (4.8 'Too Far Gone') - though Seasons 4 and 5 leave him balancing a harder character, down to 'We didn't want to waste the bullets,' with the drive to survive.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 24 "12. Should I Really Stop That Rhyming" — Yuen uses the rhyming scene to analyze annoyance - rhyme hijacks Vizzini's attention, the Goldman/Morgenstern interruptions betray invested expectations, and fans' endless quotation is annoying through sheer repetition - concluding that annoyance is irreducibly relative and contextual. Aristotle's virtue theory supplies the moral frame: friendliness and wittiness, golden means between obsequiousness and surliness, buffoonery and boorishness, make being annoying a character flaw that damages the communal eudaimonia Aristotle takes the good life to require. Since these virtues may be supererogatory ideals rather than obligations, Yuen borrows Kant's imperfect duty to develop one's talents to explain why Inigo had to become a master swordsman - failing to hone the skill his one great goal demands would be a failure of self-respect.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 27 "14. The End of Inigo Montoya" — Elsby and Luzecky read Inigo through Aristotle's doctrine of the four causes: his life is organized by a final cause, revenge on the Six-Fingered Man as the thing that is 'just good', which explains every action from fencing drills to eating breakfast. The famous mantra works because habit embodies the final cause - repeating 'My name is Inigo Montoya' lets trained movement carry him through wounds that should end the fight. When revenge is achieved the chain of ends terminates and 'Inigo Montoya' ends with it, which is why his rebirth as the Dread Pirate Roberts is needed; the chapter generalizes that our habits, not grand outside purposes, are how final causes give lives their ends.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 21 "8. Should Jane Get to Be Bored" — Daniel Addison defends Louie's 'you don't get to be bored' admonishment of Jane in 'Country Drive' against Mathew Remski's charge that it transfers adult anxiety, pointing to Louis's Conan 'forever empty' monologue and reddit advice as proof that Louis insists on facing despair rather than fleeing it. The real aim, he argues, is Socratic: Louis wants Jane and the plane-complaining generation brought to aporia, the perplexity Plato's Socrates induces in the Meno's slave boy so that, no longer thinking he knows, he 'would be glad to find out.' Aristotle grounds the optimism - every human by nature desires to know, philosophy begins in wonder, and our deepest happiness lies in contemplating - so Louis's 'everything's amazing' tirade is a demand that we become philosophical rather than 'kinda satisfied' consumers. Boredom, on this reading, is failed wonder, and Louie is playing Socrates to his daughter.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 13 "3. When Clone Club Looks for Answers" — Maps two ancient accounts of happiness onto the two clones we meet first. Cosima is the Aristotelian: like her fellow biologist Aristotle she holds that knowing truth for its own sake is essential to human flourishing, so she demands Sarah's briefcase ("the answers are in the briefcase"), studies a murdered sister's autopsy, and accepts Leekie's offer of unfettered research even inside Dyad. Alison is the Epicurean: happiness is the removal of pain and protection from threat, so she wants nothing to do with the C-word, hunts her monitor only to restore her safety, and signs Leekie's contract for the promise that her family will be left alone.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 27 "14. Re Production" — Framed as leaked Project memoranda, the chapter argues Projects Leda and Castor embody philosophy's male-rational/female-reproductive dichotomy: Aristotle's function argument defined the human good (eudaimonia) through rationality while relegating women to reproduction, and the clones' engineered diseases literalize the split — fatal illness of the reproductive organs in the Leda clones, of the brain in the Castor. Simone de Beauvoir's Second Sex supplies the critique: "woman" treated as synonymous with womb, the Other denied the rich self-definition granted men, visible in Leda's passive unmonitored clones versus Castor's self-aware, active brothers. Combining a redeemed Aristotle (practical wisdom shows virtuous potential is not set by biological sex) with Beauvoir's free, independent woman, the chapter concludes both reproductive and rational autonomy must be restored to the clones of both sexes.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 18 "7. Jon Snow, a Misshapen Christ Figure" — Rosa argues Westeros is a moral wasteland stripped of exemplars - heroes die, and vice spreads by imitation, as with Joffrey, Ramsay, and the Mountain - so Jon Snow functions as the series' Christ figure: the humble hidden king revealed in Bran's vision, the reformer uniting wildlings and Watch against death, killed by his brothers in 'Mother's Mercy' and risen in 'Home.' Using Aristotle's virtue ethics - Bran's archery lesson as the image of eudaimonia, hamartia as missing the mark, character formed by watching and imitating exemplars like Ned at the deserter's execution - the chapter claims the world is redeemable only through 'minority moral reform' embodied in a complete life, as with Jesus, Gandhi, and Martin Luther King Jr.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 45 "29. The Best of Friends" — Geyer sorts Game of Thrones friendships by Aristotle's three kinds in the Nicomachean Ethics. Robert and Ned's bond, formed in Jon Arryn's fosterage and shared war, is friendship of pleasure, which frays over Rhaegar's 'dragonspawn'; Tyrion and Bronn is friendship of utility, dissolving exactly as Aristotle predicts when Lollys's marriage pays better than a trial by combat in 'Mockingbird'; and Jon and Sam, each valuing the other's character for its own sake at the Wall, approach the only true friendship - the virtue friendship - supporting the claim that eudaimonia needs such relationships alongside external goods.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 14 "3. Can Charlie Brown Be Happy" — The chapter asks why Charlie Brown is unhappy despite being kind, active, and engaged, and answers with ancient virtue ethics: happiness is not winning or approval but ethical self-transformation, so his dependence on others' regard ('How did the other team feel?') is the real problem. It diagnoses him with Daniel Haybron's three dimensions of happiness - strong on engagement but lacking attunement (nervous, self-conscious) and endorsement (cheerlessness) - and asks why his shyness so irritates the gang. Epictetus's image of Socrates playing ball at his trial and Cicero's dancing analogy supply the Stoic remedy: losing costs no virtue, what he controls is being ethical, and how you play the game is everything.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 30 "15. Reset Virtues" — Doll argues Elliot approximates Aristotelian virtue despite his vices: he craves eudaimonia, uses practical wisdom to recognize the harm the 5/9 hack caused innocent people ('I'll own it all'), and habituates himself against vice by confessing, exposing Ray's website, and restraining Mr. Robot even at the cost of Adderall binges and prison. Leon's 'existence could be beautiful, or it could be ugly, but that's on you' frames the choice of a life to fight for, and Krista's counsel leads Elliot to the golden mean of a 'handshake' with Mr. Robot - integrating the two identities rather than annihilating one - while the viewer serves as the if/then programming keeping him virtuous.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 25 "13. Burn the Witch!" — Argues Coven is a feminist counterpoint to Aquinas's Natural Law - the reason-grounded doctrine of universal human nature historically wielded against 'unnatural' women, from Zoe's vagina-dentata power to Misty burned in the bayou - and, drawing on Augustine's Confessions ('Things that exist are good', so corruptibility implies goodness to lose) and Lady Macbeth's 'unsex me here', shows that women who are both witch and woman break any single natural moral code; Myrtle Snow, who embraces her double nature and goes 'proudly to the flame', proves Natural Law works only as Cupp-style discernment, not as commandments.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 12 "2. Physical Jerks Ungood" — Di Nucci compares the Party's mandatory morning Physical Jerks to the modern middle-class ritual of pre-work exercise, asking who needs an oppressor when we oppress ourselves. He argues exercise carries a hidden political price: the time, energy, and solitude it consumes (Orwell shows exercise making it harder for Winston to think and remember) leave citizens too exhausted for the political engagement Aristotle considered necessary to the good life. Like Juvenal's bread and circuses, now 'panem et iphones', and like private schooling, fitness culture also deepens class inequality because working-class people lack the time and energy to access it.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 19 "8. Human Enhancement for Freedom" — Koï asks whether biomedical enhancement could make humans resistant to the totalitarian subjugation shown in 1984, where the Party keeps proles too poor and distracted to think and dims Outer Party minds with Newspeak, erased history, and propaganda. Testing Persson and Savulescu's program of enhancing intelligence and moral empathy, she finds intelligence enhancement an educated gamble, since the gifted are also the most likely to embrace extremism and to start totalitarian movements, and empathy politically selective: Nazis directed it only at the in-group and even invoked it to justify the 'euthanasia' murders, while Party propaganda exploits citizens' empathy for horror stories of pre-revolution child labor. Her conclusion is that whatever capacity we enhance, the oligarchy could turn it to its own use: none of us will ever be immune to the love of Big Brother.
