Mimi Marinucci pairs Glaucon's Ring of Gyges with Suler's online disinhibition effect to argue that Facebook's forced integration of audiences (students, colleagues, Mom all reading one profile) suppresses 'fronting' and so can foster authentic self-expression; Mariam Thalos answers with Sartre's analysis of the gaze and Beauvoir's woman-as-Other that the elective, endlessly plastic profile cannot anchor the bonding only face-to-face encounter provides - hence 'Why I Am Not a Friend' - while Wandel and Beavers use Groundhog Day's Phil Connors and Goffman's presentation of self to defend identity play as real self-discovery, and Vejby and Wittkower ask whether Facebook is Debord's Spectacle 2.0 or a platform for Situationist detournement. Finally, Craig Condella measures 'friending' against Aristotle's three friendships and Cicero's 'handmaid of virtue' (via the Seinfeld episode where Keith Hernandez asks Jerry to help him move), and Matthew Tedesco sets 322 Facebook friends against Godwin's burning archbishop to press the utilitarian impartiality challenge, deploying Williams's 'one thought too many' shipwreck case and criticizing Frank Jackson's sector-plan defense of partiality.
- **Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_**, ch. 4 "index" — Six essays on friendship in the Facebook age. Tedesco asks whether the low-demand 'Facebook friendship' can reconcile the utilitarian demand for impartiality (Mill, Railton, Kagan) with the partiality of real friends, and concludes Facebook ties are only supplementary to relationships built elsewhere. Hamington surveys a hundred users and argues in Noddings's care-ethics terms that Facebook's information transfer makes caring possible (knowledge of the concrete other is necessary for care), though it also makes dropping a student over one racist comment effortless. Bloor reads Facebook through Heidegger's technological nihilism and the anonymous 'one', warning that speed of exchange erodes Aristotle's few deep, morally formative friendships, while Briggle's farewell letter to Facebook judges the site by Ivan Illich's convivial-tool criteria and Cuonzo recasts pokes and virtual gifts as efficient successors to primate grooming; Lattimore applies Bakhtin's 'excess of seeing' to how viewers 'consummate' other users' self-presentations.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 34 "I Am the Bad Wolf" — Answers Davros's charge that the Doctor fashions companions into weapons by examining his character through virtue ethics: his unifying virtue is Heideggerian 'authentic concern', always offering aggressors like the Nestene or the Sycorax a choice so they become genuinely responsible, as in the fly-swatting thought experiment. Companions instead act from compassion, which lacks impartiality and produces the 'Bad Wolf Syndrome' (Rose's Dalek genocide, Martha's Osterhagen Key, Jack's warp star). Since for Aristotle a friend is 'another himself', the companions' actions are in a sense the Doctor's own yet founded on a distorted disposition, which is why he runs from his past.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 11 "Why Is It the Best Day Ever" — Nicole Pramik argues SpongeBob is Aristotle's self-mastered man: his daily cheerfulness is eudaimonia, a happiness earned by practicing virtue as the mean between vices of excess and deficiency. The chapter tests each mean with episodes — courage between cowardly isolation ('I Had an Accident') and recklessness ('A Life in a Day'), honor between Patrick's under-the-rock humility and Squidward's Easter-Island vanity, honesty in 'Hooky' and 'Wet Painters', and good temper mended with Patrick in 'New Student Starfish' and 'The Fry Cook Games'. His moderation in pleasure and wealth, contrasted with Mr. Krabs's stinginess, and his F.U.N. Song friendship (Aristotle's greatest external good) show the golden mean served up on a sesame seed bun.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 20 "The Best Kind of Friend" — Ruth Tallman tests Holmes and Watson against Aristotle's requirement in the Nicomachean Ethics that perfect friendship exists only between the 'alike in excellence': since the two live by irreconcilable moral codes (Holmes's cocaine and burglaries versus Watson's clean living and law-abidingness), Aristotelian moral naturalism denies they can be true friends at all, despite the raw panic in 'The Three Garridebs' proving mutual devotion. Recasting the pair as moral pluralists with different 'good for me's, she argues Holmes is actually the better friend, an 'integrity-promoting' friend who urges Watson to stay home from the Milverton burglary to honor Watson's own code, while the proselytizing Watson, who nags about cocaine yet tags along anyway, repeatedly violates his own integrity.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 21 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Wayne Yuen uses The Graveyard Book to teach the good life: Bod's family's murder, like students owing their existence to the Holocaust, is an unalloyed moral evil that still enables a better life, and Saul Smilansky's distinction between being 'sorry for' and 'sorry that' lets Bod benefit without endorsing the tragedy. His graveyard education is Aristotelian, virtues acquired through practice and models, from the Owenses' duty and Silas's wisdom to 'righteous indignation' against school bullies and friendship with Scarlett as intrinsically valuable, all building toward eudaimonia. The existentialist virtue of authenticity (attributed to Sartre and Kierkegaard) explains why Bod must be 'nobody but himself' rather than a copy of the vampire Silas, why the scavenged identities of the ghouls mark inauthenticity, and why wiping Scarlett's memory threatens her authenticity, resolving the apparent conflict between virtue and being oneself because bravery or wisdom is relative to the individual.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 22 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Fisher argues The Wire makes homosexuality a source of excellence: Omar and Kima blend masculine and feminine traits in something like Butler's gender-performative terms, build Aristotelian friendships of virtue (Kima and Cheryl pushing each other's careers), and can make the sacrifices - solitude, giving up family - that excellence in the drug war demands, while the homophobia of the streets and the precinct forces them to keep proving themselves. Omar's crossword comfort with 'them myths' frames him as a contemporary Socrates: a mentor-lover of boys, accused of amorality by Levy much as Socrates was charged with corrupting Athens's youth, answering with a Socratic reversal ('I got the shotgun, you got the briefcase'), and dying for his code in the city he would not leave. The chapter reads the show's refusal of coming-out storylines - Rawls's silent gay-bar cameo, Snoop's never-confirmed sexuality - as its most radical statement about sexuality in America.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 37 "Psych and Philosophy" — Patricia Brace maps Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics categories of friendship onto Psych: Shawn's first-season ties to the SBPD are friendships of utility, the shared hobbies and bar nights (tap dancing in 'Feet Don't Kill Me Now,' 'Neil Simon's Lover's Retreat') build friendships of pleasure, and Shawn-Juliet matures from utilitarian boundaries into erotic friendship. Lassiter's lie-detector threat to protect Juliet in 'Shawn Rescues Darth Vader' and the lifelong Shawn-Gus bond ('Gus Walks into a Bank') approach complete friendship grounded in virtue, while the Henry-Shawn paternal friendship heals as Shawn develops the golden mean, and the vicious Mr. Yin and Yang - full of regret, incapable of complete friendship - show the life without it.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 38 "Psych and Philosophy" — C. Scott Sevier argues Henry deliberately recreated Shawn as Aristotle's 'another self' - Lassiter's 'which one?' joke in the kidnapping episode makes the identity explicit - and reads this through Plato's Symposium: via Diotima's ladder of love and the doctrine of forms, Henry achieves immortality by reproducing beauty in his son's educated soul, not just his body. The chapter then frames Shawn's fierce independence against his constant recourse to Henry's voice as the collision between medieval deference to authority and the modern ideal of autonomy in Descartes and Kant, showing that both thinkers quietly borrowed from Augustine (the causal adequacy principle, the good will), so Shawn's 'autonomy' is itself the product of his father's training - an internalized authority indistinguishable from his own.
- **The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia**, ch. 27 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" — John Fitzpatrick asks whether voters should care that Alicia stands beside Peter, from the Season One resignation press conference to the finale's withheld hand. After a rapid tour of right-action theories grounded in the show - Eli Gold's egoism, Peter's 'pitted' evidence tip as consequentialism, Alicia keeping Jonas Stern's dementia secret as deontology, the Florrick-Childs no-children pact as social contract - he turns to Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: eudaimonia as a life weaving pleasure, friendship, and practical activity, in which mentors like Will and Diane let us contemplate virtue in others and improve our own character. His conclusion: Alicia's endorsement matters not because she is a good wife but because she is a good person whose judgment reveals Peter's character.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 15 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Brace and Kingsbury use the Nicomachean Ethics to argue that Nucky, Chalky, and Margaret mistake pleasure and the mere instruments of happiness - tailored suits, money, useful connections, the appearance of virtue - for Aristotle's stable, self-sustaining virtuous activity, so their lives stay unstable and empty. Nucky 'buys' even Jimmy and Margaret, Chalky's jail-cell staging with David Copperfield shows how fragile his facade of cultivation is, and Margaret's acquisitions end in blackmail and in bribing God over Emily's polio. Only Richard Harrow, the Tin Man whose collage-clippings represent a happiness he believes he can never have, moves toward real Aristotelian friendship through Jimmy's 'Of course I would; right down to the last bullet' - the philia Aristotle calls most necessary for a happy life.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 19 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Jeffery Nicholas argues Card tries to write Ender as Nietzsche's self-sufficient superman - Graff's isolation program, the will to power, and Rackham's 'humanity does not ask us to be happy' - but the novel actually vindicates Aristotle's claim in the Politics that man is a political animal who cannot flourish without friends. Ender's difference from the beast-like Peter and the hive-minded buggers, his longing for Valentine, Alai, and Petra, and his despair in isolation show that friendship, not domination, is what makes him human.
- **How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness**, ch. 10 "How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy" — The chapter argues Barney is best understood as a committed ethical egoist, distinguishing egoism from egotism, immoralism, and moral skepticism through the Playbook's Scuba Diver scam. Ainsworth rejects psychological egoism (Joey's view in Friends) using evolution and apparent counterexamples like Marshall's Christmas Eve deliveries, then uses Glaucon's ring of Gyges from the Republic to ask whether anyone would resist injustice with guaranteed impunity. The friendship objection is dissolved via Aristotle's 'a friend is another self': once friends are included in the ego, saving Marshall's relationship or rushing to Ted's hospital bed counts as self-interest, constrained like chess by absolute rules such as the Bro Code's Article 150.
- **How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness**, ch. 14 "How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy" — The chapter argues the Bro Code's real value lies not in getting laid but in structuring homosocial bonds, listing its best articles (loyalty, equality, generosity) alongside its most sexist ones (the Hot/Crazy Scale, Article 101). Karioris explains men's competitive relations through hegemonic masculinity - the school-bully dominance that forces all masculinities to compete and pushes women out - and invokes Foucault's 'Friendship as a Way of Life' for how bonds between men can escape taboo and emotional distance. Robin as wingwoman ('a better Ted than Ted') and the gang's gender transgressions show the Code can be amended toward equality, with Aristotle's friendship of mutual cooperation and benefit, 'quid pro bro', as the standard.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 14 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Brittany Lorenz and Adam Barkman apply the Greek four-loves framework (storge, eros, philia, agape) to Homeland's relationships. Terrorism breaks storge by destroying comfort in familiar places; broken eros appears in the Brody-Jessica-Mike-Carrie square and Mira's lover who loves 'making love' rather than her; philia falters because Brody hides his Islam from Jessica, and Abu Nazir's bond with Brody is Aristotle's friendship of utility, dissolving when the advantage ceases. Brody's agape for country is broken because fighting abroad violates his prior duties as husband and father, so the show offers only glimpses of loves that might be redeemed.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 12 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Robison-Greene asks whether there are principled standards for 'shipping' TV couples and applies Platonic-Aristotelian flourishing criteria (long-term safety, emotional needs, trust, and mutual growth toward virtue) to Piper's options: Alex fails on safety and trust (selling Piper out, the perjury advice), Larry fails on empathy and growth, so by real-life standards we should ship none of them. She concludes shipping is mostly aesthetic, then proposes minimal moral rules for our attitudes toward fictional relationships: never ship Pornstache, respect consent, and never let race, gender, or orientation decide.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 30 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Elsby and Luzecky use Nicomachean Ethics VIII to sort Litchfield's bonds: Red's kitchen empire runs on friendships of utility that dissolve when her pipeline closes, race pre-assigns everyone's default friends, and Vee, who sleeps with RJ before having him killed, is incapable of friendship in any sense. The chapter locates genuine Aristotelian friendship only in Red's concern that Nicky stay off heroin (wishing her good for her own sake) and reads Red's sparing of Vee, held by a plastic bag, as respect without care, the recognition of a kindred quality that distinguishes Red from her evil counterpart.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 14 "5. Every Lonely Monster Needs a Companion" — Gadsden asks why a near-omnipotent Time Lord needs companions at all and tests four hypotheses against his solo meltdowns—executing Solomon in 'Dinosaurs on a Spaceship,' nearly murdering Jex in 'A Town Called Mercy,' and declaring himself 'Time Lord Victorious' in 'The Waters of Mars.' He rejects the Lord Acton power-corrupts hypothesis via Glaucon's ring story in Plato's Republic, since powerless companions offer no threat of reprisal or dishonor, and qualifies J.J. Sylvia's care-ethics 'empathetic link' because the Doctor cares for non-human species like the Star Whale too. He favors two answers: Hume's fact/value gap as a millennium-long moral myopia ('I can't see it anymore,' the deleted 'Flesh and Stone' confession), and Aristotle's point in the Nicomachean Ethics that only virtuous friends—moral peers who mirror us—can expose the Doctor's blind spots, like his 'God Complex.'
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 30 "17. The Friends of a Time Lord" — Littmann applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics taxonomy of friendship - pleasure, usefulness, and mutual goodness - to fifty years of Doctor-companion pairings, from the Hartnell Doctor's glee touring Vortis with Ian to New Series companions chosen as friends who routinely save the day, from Barbara's Dalek revolt to Clara saving every incarnation of the Doctor. He argues Aristotle would still judge the Doctor's friendships defective: they are short-lived, unequal in station, intellect, and morality, and the companions cannot know him well enough (not even his name) for the perfect friendship of the good. Littmann then corrects Aristotle on two counts: friends need not be moral experts to serve as moral critics (Rose in 'Dalek,' Amy in 'A Town Called Mercy'), and the Doctor's favoritism toward his companions - risking worlds to save them, as when Rory weighs Amy's life against the universe in 'The Big Bang' - shows that preferring friends over strangers is itself his most frequent moral failing.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 14 "5. Overcoming Evil with Love" — Bogosian argues the film locates evil not in human nature itself, as Jeanine claims when she calls human nature 'the enemy,' but in cultivable vices - Al's jealousy and fear of failure leading to attempted murder and suicide, Eric's and Jeanine's lust for power - and that only altruistic, self-sacrificial love can counteract them. With Aristotle's point that friendship is essential to developing virtue and to the good life, he shows the faction system fails on its own terms: a single virtue in isolation corrupts (Candor's truth without kindness), and a system that removes real moral and political freedom destroys the flourishing it promises. Tris's parents' sacrifices and the Tris-Four relationship - honest training advice, protection of her Divergence, and the gun-to-her-own-forehead scene where love breaks the simulation's grip - model the love that overcomes the corrupt system.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 28 "16. What Do We Really Owe Our Parents" — Karavitis uses Tris and Tobias to stage the filial-piety debate: Tris, who loves her parents and learns to see them with adult eyes after discovering their hidden pasts, remains 'allegiant' to the end, while the abused Tobias owes Marcus and Evelyn nothing and reaches only a cautious adult reconciliation with his mother. After surveying Confucian xiao (with Mencius, and Buddhism's forced accommodation of it) and the Abrahamic commandments on one side, and Norman Daniels's and Jane English's autonomy-based arguments that children never consented to be born and so owe nothing on the other, he concludes no rational argument mandates filial duties from adult children. Aristotle's three types of friendship supply the one defensible model: only when adult children and parents meet as virtuous equals can a chosen, consensual relationship carrying care, gratitude, and love arise - so 'as adults, we owe our parents nothing,' though love may freely flow.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 16 "6. The Psychiatrist as Sociopathic God" — Hassert takes Lecter's 'First principles, Clarice' at its Aristotelian word - nature is revealed through capacities and action, as an acorn's telos is not pumpkins and a kitten will never be a Great Dane - to explain Lecter's psychiatry: he reads each patient's essence and potential, prescribing Mason Verger's face-peeling so appearance finally matches essence, and force-raising Will toward equality so that Aristotelian perfect friendship between the alike-in-virtue (which Franklyn's flattery can never reach) might become possible. Reading God through Augustine's account of evil as the destruction of a preexisting good and Mischa's murder, the chapter argues that Lecter emulates a capricious deity - 'Typhoid and swans - it all comes from the same place' - and, unlike Nietzsche, does not pronounce God dead but merely misconceptualized, while his friendships fail because he must corrupt the other into his own image rather than love an equal.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 22 "10. The Light from Friendship" — Pavelich sets Aristotle's account of friendship - recognized and reciprocated goodwill between equals, perfected in the friendship of the good who 'share our souls', a standard met only by Jack and Bella Crawford - against Nietzsche's friendship as striving between overmen, who honor 'one's best enemy' in the friend and grow through conflict. He reads Hannibal's treatment of Will (hiding the encephalitis, framing him, serving the Nietzschean trout) as Nietzschean friend-making - Lies that are supposed to spur Will's growth, consistent with an Übermensch who tells Will 'Killing must feel good to God' and says 'I don't hide from God' - while Will's masquerade of friendship is betrayal in both senses, since Will seeks an Aristotelian soulmate and finds a killer he must stop. Because each betrays the other, neither Aristotelian nor Nietzschean friendship survives, though the moments before the Mizumono bloodbath - Hannibal inviting Will to just walk away - glimpse a real friendship already made impossible.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 25 "Walker Bite. If I Don’t Save the World, I Have No Value" — This Walker Bite uses Eugene Porter's exposed lie about being the scientist who can cure the outbreak (5.5 "Self Help") to ask what makes a person valuable once their usefulness collapses. Eugene himself sums up an instrumental view of his own worth - "If I don't cure the disease, if I don't save the world, I have no value" - and admits he sabotaged the bus to stall the DC mission. Against this, Tara's "We're friends. We have each other's backs... You're stuck with us. No matter what" argues that persons are valued for themselves within a community rather than as means, and the chapter lands on Abraham's "people need people" as the real ground of Eugene's place in the group.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 12 "2. Why Men of Action Don’t Lie" — Mahon maps the film's non-romantic relationships onto Aristotle's philia: the loyal friendship of Inigo and Fezzik under Vizzini's abuse, expanded into a four-person 'family' once Westley, who defeated and spared them with respect, joins them to storm the castle. He argues deception in the film tracks the absence of philia - bad men incapable of friendship (Vizzini, Humperdinck, Rugen) lie to anyone, while friends never lie to each other and the early duels are sportsmanlike. Westley's line 'We are men of action. Lies do not become us' encodes an honor code that real men do not lie to real men even when enemies (hence Westley cheats Vizzini in the Battle of Wits with both goblets poisoned, and the chapter analyzes the resulting triple- and quadruple-bluff regress), while the one exception - Westley letting Buttercup stay deceived about Humperdinck - exposes the code's chauvinism, matching Aristotle's view that philia in its purest form exists only between male equals.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 20 "10. Virtue Rising" — Darci Doll argues the Rising exposes the Society's intellectual oppression—each Color denied education and fed 'noble lies' about its role—and that lifting it sparks an 'Intellectual Reformation' proving Color does not dictate potential: Darrow out-performing Golds, Orion the un-carved Blue, Ragnar and Sefi exceeding their station. She uses Plato's Republic (producers, auxiliaries, guardians, the lower orders kept obedient by Noble Lies like the Reds' terraforming myth) as the Society's blueprint, then turns to Aristotle: potential is realized only through the right environment, instruction, and habituated character, and Darrow's practical wisdom—testing himself, reassessing after Titus and Cassius, doing what makes him his best self—lets him flourish and lead. Aristotle's critique of utility-only relations explains why the Society's alliances expire (Antonia executed once useless) while Darrow and Mustang's virtue friendships and just rule endure, opening a society where everyone, including women and lowColors denied opportunity rather than ability, can maximize potential.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 45 "29. The Best of Friends" — Geyer sorts Game of Thrones friendships by Aristotle's three kinds in the Nicomachean Ethics. Robert and Ned's bond, formed in Jon Arryn's fosterage and shared war, is friendship of pleasure, which frays over Rhaegar's 'dragonspawn'; Tyrion and Bronn is friendship of utility, dissolving exactly as Aristotle predicts when Lollys's marriage pays better than a trial by combat in 'Mockingbird'; and Jon and Sam, each valuing the other's character for its own sake at the Wall, approach the only true friendship - the virtue friendship - supporting the claim that eudaimonia needs such relationships alongside external goods.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 30 "15. We’re on Your Side, Charlie Brown" — The chapter asks why Charlie Brown never abandons the friends who torment him and answers with friendship philosophy: Aristotle's three kinds of friendship fit the gang (pleasure-based childhood play - baseball, trick-or-treating, Christmas plays - as the nursery for later perfect friendships of good will), while Marilyn Friedman's 'moral growth' and 'moral empiricism' explain how even Lucy's blunt 'snap out of it' gives Charlie perspectives from 'reliable moral witnesses.' Annette Baier's account of trust as accepted vulnerability redeems his 'gullibility': better to risk the pulled football than live in an atmosphere of suspicion. The 'Our Manager' uniform of Charlie Brown's All-Stars and the decorated tiny Christmas tree show that on the things that matter his friends can always be trusted to take his side - and Charlie is always first to forgive.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 26 "14. I’m an X-Man!" — Daniel Alloy argues Deadpool keeps insisting 'I'm an X-Man!' because being a hero is not a private choice but a social standing: with Aristotle's beast-or-god line about those who cannot live in society and Hegel's account of mutual recognition in the Phenomenology of Spirit, he contends Wade needs heroes he recognizes to recognize him as one in return. The Thunderbolts ('the selfish Avengers') and X-Force recruited him as a merc and so could not grant that recognition, and Cable offers approval from superiority rather than recognition between equals—a friendship of utility where Wade wants one of virtue. Only Captain America's Avengers card treats him as an equal, and even that recognition must be completed by the whole hero community before Wade can accept himself as the hero he already is.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 14 "5. Why the Good Man Is a Great Leader" — Nisley reads Civil War through Aristotle's good man and good leader: Cap shows courage but lacks temperance and practical wisdom - his rash Lagos operation, his rage-borne beating of Tony, his choice of Bucky over the Avengers' common end - and his ceaseless struggle between passion and reason falls short of virtue. Applying Aristotle's account of philia, she argues the Avengers are a friendship of the virtuous that requires deliberation toward justice, which Cap dissolves by tearing the team apart, while Tony's reasoned acceptance of UN oversight, moderation after Ultron, and concern for the whole team make him the good man fit to lead.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 15 "6. Who’s the Better Friend" — Bowman sorts Marvel relationships through Aristotle's three friendships: Ant-Man's starstruck alliance is friendship of pleasure, Obadiah Stane's partnership with Tony a toxic friendship of utility, and Steve's bond with Bucky a friendship of virtue that loves without reciprocity - making Cap better TO his friends, though saving Bucky endangers everyone else. Turning to Derrida's Politics of Friendship, where fraternity grounds democratic equality among all persons, he argues Tony's refusal to privilege any individual over mankind makes him better FOR his friends. The Civil War split thus replays the old tension between personal autonomy and responsibility to humanity, at the destructive scale only super-powered friends can achieve.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 31 "18. War Means Fighting and Fighting Includes Philosophizing" — Vuckovich reads 'Still Valley' as a moral battlefield: Confederate scout Sgt. Paradine finds a witchcraft handbook that has frozen a Union patrol before Gettysburg, and Glaucon's Ring of Gyges account from the Republic — the really unjust person winning without scruple while seeming just — frames the temptation of an invisible, effortless victory. Aristotle's friendships of shared wickedness illuminate his bond with the witchman Teague, who exploits Paradine's desperation to pass on his own curse, until Paradine casts the handbook into the campfire, choosing a principle of fairness over a Devil-guaranteed win and accepting the shame of a 'Pyrrhic loss.'
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 28 "14. Friends Don’t Lie" — Bowman tests Hawkins friendships against Aristotle's three kinds in the Nicomachean Ethics: Dustin and Lucas's shared-comics pleasure collapses into rivalry over Max, Nancy and Jonathan's utility ends once Will and Barb are found, and Barb's fatal poolside loyalty to Nancy, though one-directional, is a friendship of virtue. Nietzsche's ideal of friends who strengthen us through conflict recasts those very fights (Lucas confronting Eleven's power misuse) as the best friendship, care ethics (Gilligan and Noddings) makes the mutual one-caring Party the real answer to who teaches Eleven friendship, and Derrida's Politics of Friendship grounds democracy and society itself in such everyday reciprocity, which is why Eleven's 'friends don't lie' compass pulls her back from Kali's violence to close the gate.
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 12 "Aristotle to the Rescue" — Yim applies Aristotle's three kinds of friendship from the Nicomachean Ethics to the show: Tracy with Grizz and Dot Com in 'Hardball', and Tracy with Jenna in 'Flu Shot', are friendships of utility that dissolve when the benefit ends, while Liz and Jenna's long shared history looks deep but remains mutual usefulness between ambitious colleagues. Liz and Jack, by contrast, evolve from David-versus-Goliath adversaries in the pilot into something like virtuous friendship, culminating in 'Retreat to Move Forward' when Liz humbles herself with a terrible improv routine and a shirt-ripping dance to save Jack's standing before the Six Sigma crowd. The chapter argues the show thereby dramatizes that self-sacrificial goodwill is what makes a friendship worth the risk.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 17 "Neither Gods nor Beasts But Political Animals" — Spanakos denies the official line that the Avengers assemble from necessity—Thor beats Loki alone—arguing instead through Aristotle that the team is a polis: heroes join for safety but stay for the good life, since outside the polis one is either a god or a beast. Ms. Marvel's miserable solo run (unrecognized by Stilt-Man, a 'Where Are They Now?' has-been) ends only when she returns to lead the Mighty Avengers among friends who share her arete; the self-loathing Jessica Jones finds eudaimonia through philia with Carol, Luke Cage, and the team that delivers her baby; even the arrogant Hank Pym regains excellence by defending Tony and leading a new team. Even gods like Thor and near-beasts like the Hulk, the chapter concludes, need the Avengers to flourish.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 32 "BSFs Best Superfriends Forever" — Daniel Malloy argues Batman and Superman are friends who disagree about friendship itself: Superman practices Aristotle's highest philia between good men who are 'another self' and true equals, symbolized by the kryptonite ring he trusts Batman to use on him should he go rogue, while Batman's friendship is Nietzschean, loving in his friend the overman 'as your cause' in the one equal he respects as a rival. Stories like Tower of Babel, Bruce Wayne: Fugitive, and the Brother Eye satellite show Batman manipulates everyone except this one peer, and that he never fights Superman fairly because he does not need to. Their fundamental, unresolvable differences, Malloy concludes, are exactly what strengthen the World's Finest friendship.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 10 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Kowalski maps Aristotle's three kinds of friendship onto the gang: pleasure-friendships (Halo and paintball nights, and Raj's fury when Howard abandons their kite fight for a jogger), utility-friendships (Sheldon's failed Friendship Algorithm bid on Kripke for lab access, and the roommate agreement's Friendship Rider invoked over the CERN trip). Complete friendship — mutual care for the other's own sake between moral equals — looks closest in Leonard and Sheldon, yet Sheldon's pancake-breakfast apology collapses the moment Leonard refuses to take him to Switzerland ('Drat. No Frodo for you'), exposing contractual utility where genuine care should be. The chapter concludes no pairing in the show achieves Aristotle's rare complete friendship, and asks whether similarity is really required for true 'besties.'
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 27 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Barkman diagnoses four mama's boys: Raj's selective mutism under his parents' webcam meddling, Sheldon's comfort-seeking from a fundamentalist mother ('Soft Kitty,' mandatory grace), Howard's learned helplessness with his foghorn mother, and Leonard raised as Beverly's lab subject, his hugging machine echoing the wire-mother monkey experiment. Plato and Aristotle ground the charge of injustice — receiving less than one's station deserves, and wrongs against intimates are 'more terrible' — so parents bear special obligations their neglect breaches, a contemporary point pressed in the care-ethics tradition of Noddings. Cognitive-dissonance theory and Putman's Aristotelian 'psychological courage' prescribe honest self-reckoning for mothers and sons alike, with Leonard furthest along after confronting Beverly in 'The Maternal Congruence.'
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 28 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Evans defends the Penny–Sheldon friendship as genuine by three universal marks — mutual care (two Saturnalia-miracle hugs), intimacy (keeping Penny's community-college secret; friends who direct and interpret each other's conduct), and shared activity (singing 'Soft Kitty' in the round) — and then argues its deep differences are not an obstacle but the engine of moral growth. Against Aristotle's similarity-based complete friendship, oriented to a shared eudaimonia, he offers a modern pluralist account: Sheldon's self-aware jokes, dancing, and social awareness and Penny's physics lessons show each growing toward the other's way of flourishing without becoming alike, which a friend as similar as Amy could never force.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 13 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — O'Loughlin reads Walter biting off a nihilist's ear and the Dude refusing to walk out on league play as concrete realizations of ancient friendship: Aristotle's eudaimonia requires friends as 'second selves' whose shared activity (bowling in the friends' company) structures the excellent life, while Epicurus's Garden ordered life around simple pleasures and ataraxia, with friendship supplying pleasant memory and a kind of immortality after death. Because we moderns claim friendship's value without practicing its costs, the Dude's priorities look comic yet pierce us — and Donny's death, the Ralph's coffee can, and 'let's go bowling' become Epicurean commemoration rather than irreverence.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 40 "“Oh, honey, I’ll do anything for you”" — Using Rachel's Ashley Too doll, the chapter distinguishes robots as instruments (Kevin's MAUZR mouse) from social robots designed to be perceived 'as being present in the way a person is,' and invokes Heidegger's 'Question Concerning Technology' to argue that social robots break the instrumentalist picture: it is our empathy - triggered even by the insubstantial hologram Ashley Eternal - that they exploit. The Aristotelian test of friendship (we emulate those we admire, and friendship forms virtuous character) shows Ashley Too fails: her flattery installs false confidence, and because she never requires Rachel to attend to another's needs, she models no real friendship. Girard's mimetic desire explains Rachel's borrowed aspiration to become Ashley O and Jack's emulation of their dead mother, so the chapter concludes robot 'friends' are poor friends - not because they are machines, but because a real friendship is 'an education in the social virtues.'
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 22 "The Sorcerer So Human" — The chapter argues Strange fails Aristotle's golden mean at both stages of his life: as a surgeon he chose cases for money and fame (greed and gluttony rather than generosity and temperance), and as Sorcerer Supreme he swings to the opposite extreme of total self-denial, refusing sleep, love, and friendship with Clea, Wong, and the Ancient One, since relationships between unequals cannot be the reciprocal philia Aristotle demands. It reads his hardest choices—the Dark Dimension left to Dormammu to save Earth, the Illuminati destroying parallel Earths during the incursions, and spending the last drop of the panacea on Wong rather than the world—as tragic dilemmas that show both the virtue ethicist's need for judgment and a defensible-but-excessive partiality toward friends.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 19 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Jeffery Nicholas contrasts the superman Card seems to write — Graff's isolated Ender conditioned to impose his will like Nietzsche's overman, for whom happiness is only the feeling of overcoming resistance — with Aristotle's claim that man is a political animal who cannot flourish without friends. Peter is Aristotle's 'tribeless, lawless, hearthless' beast, the speechless buggers lack a common good until the queen communicates with Ender, and Ender's despair lifts only through friendship with Valentine, Alai, and Petra, proving the novel a meditation on 'without friends no one would choose to live.'
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 41 "Snape’s Choice" — The section reads Snape's double life through the definition of love shared by writers from Aristotle to Aquinas, willing the good of the other for the other's own sake: he protects people he dislikes because his love for Lily wills their good. As an Occlumens he empties himself of feeling to lie to Voldemort's face, concealing rather than renouncing his love for Lily, and only while dying from Nagini's bite does he freely offer Harry the memories revealing that Harry is a Horcrux.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 91 "Unknown" — Because we each view life from our own 'personal mini-cam,' we can be too close to ourselves to see truly, so friends serve as honest mirrors in which we see ourselves as we really are. Hermione shows Harry his insensitivity to Cho, the trio helps Neville overcome his painful shyness, and Hagrid teaches Ron that friendship should not be wrecked by petty jealousy, while the friendless Dursleys, Lockhart, and Slughorn never progress in self-understanding.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Jackson reads the show through Rousseau's contrast between the general will and a pathological 'corporate will': Frank discards Freddy the moment his criminal past goes viral, Tusk and Walker's old friendship curdles into mutual blackmail, and Remy and Jackie trade intimacy for career protection - all reducing Aristotle's true friendship to friendships of utility and pleasure subordinated to institutions that treat persons as means. Rousseau's account of civilization degrading natural self-love (amour de soi) into vanity (amour-propre) explains why Washington's corporate ethos leaves no friends, only 'loose ends' to be eliminated, from Zoe pushed onto the platform to Doug hunting Rachel. The chapter ends with 'Man is born free, but is everywhere in chains' as the verdict on corporate personhood's conquest of human bonds.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 36 "Notes" — Johnson sorts Frank's six friendships through Aristotle's three kinds: Freddy and Meechum are friendships of pleasure (ribs and candor; loyalty and sex), while Doug, Cathy Durant, Tusk, and Jackie Sharp are friendships of utility that dissolve when usefulness ends - Jackie endorsing Dunbar being the proof. Even Frank's marriage fails the test of true friendship, since Aristotle holds that only good people can mirror each other's character, and badness corrupts the self-knowledge friendship provides. Because Aristotle deems friendship 'most indispensable for life' and eudaimonia requires virtuous activity joined to good fortune, the chapter ends hoping Frank can still choose the good for its own sake - a hope Claire's walkout after Iowa badly dents.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Reads the show through Rousseau's contrast between the general will and a pathological 'corporate will': governments and corporations are sociopathic artificial persons that depersonalize their agents, degrading natural self-love (amour de soi) into status-hungry amour-propre. On this account Frank's break with Freddy ('just a good customer'), the Tusk-Walker alliance, and Remy and Jackie's bought loyalties are Aristotelian friendships of utility or pleasure crushed under the corporate will, never true friendship, leaving Washington with 'honor without virtue' and men 'everywhere in chains'.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 36 "Notes" — Sorts Frank's six friendships using Aristotle's three types: Freddy and Meechum are friendships of pleasure, Doug, Durant, Tusk, and Jackie friendships of utility, while Claire-despite 'I love that woman more than sharks love blood'-cannot be a true friend of the good because true friendship requires two people of good character seeing themselves in each other. Since Aristotle ties friendship to flourishing, the chapter ends hoping that Frank, who has good fortune but neither good character nor true friends, may yet choose virtue and the good life.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 26 "Here Lies an Avenger" — The Pattersons read 'The Mask in the Iron Man' as moral education: Tony's repeated 'I have a good life' litany maps onto Aristotle's eudaimonia — friends like Rhodey, Pepper, and Happy, wealth, health, sobriety, and life itself as goods chosen for the sake of happiness — while Niebuhr's community of value makes the Avengers the community of trust and loyalty that grounds those ideals. Tony fails as teacher when the sentient armor kills Whiplash, cannot grieve with him, and fails Aristotle's friendship test of willing good for the friend for his own sake, its identity dangerously conflated with Tony's. The reversal comes when Tony lives the virtue of self-sacrifice — dying 'because I'm an Avenger' — and the armor, finally grasping nobility, rips out its own mechanical heart to save him, earning the grave marker 'Here lies Iron Man, Avenger.'
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 19 "NOTES" — Fosl argues that although the survivors' internal order looks Lockean - Jack's uncoerced leadership, natural rights, minimal government - and is bonded by Rousseauan pity and Humean sympathy (Kate staying in the cage with Sawyer, 'live together, die alone'), the show's deepest political logic follows Carl Schmitt's friend-enemy distinction: the survivors cohere only in opposition to the Others, torture is excused in liberal terms, and conflicts end in redemptive violence, with Jack both killing the enemy and dying a Christlike sacrifice. Hobbes's absence from the character names signals the show's rejection of a war of all against all among the survivors, yet the finale's divine manipulation of the castaways, with Jacob treating people as means against Kantian autonomy, repudiates the liberal hope of a rational peace altogether.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 23 "NOTES" — Michael Austin asks what adult children owe their fathers through Jack and Christian Shephard (the drunken-surgery cover-up, 'You don't have what it takes') and Locke and Anthony Cooper (the kidney con, the defenestration). He weighs Jane English's view that parental sacrifice creates friendship rather than debt - so Locke owed Cooper nothing, and true friends like Hurley and the crib-building Locke never keep accounts - against Sidgwick's three possible sources of filial obligation (relationship quality, biological tie, gratitude for services) and David Mellow's debt-of-gratitude argument. Austin concludes that the mutual needs of parents and children - Miles reaching for Pierre Chang in 1974, Jack and Christian's reconciliation in the church - best explain what they owe each other.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 24 "“To a Place Where We Know We Are Loved”" — Myers grades the moral development of the Sterling Cooper cast with Kohlberg's justice stages and Gilligan's ethics of care in order to find Aristotelian friendships, which require equals in moral development who wish each other good for the other's sake. Don and Peggy emerge as moral equivalents, each hiding a dark secret (the stolen identity; the baby given away) and each having done for the other what no one else could, from the hospital visit ('Move forward') to Don's 'nobody understands that, but you do' recruitment pitch; Joan and Roger form a second pair whose mutual esteem survives his marriage to Jane and her departure, shown when he trusts her to build Sterling Cooper Draper Pryce. Closing with Aristotle's claim that friendship holds states together, the chapter gives the new agency a better-than-average chance because these friendships are 'not for sale.'
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 31 "The Office and Philosophy" — Arp and Watson sort Dunder Mifflin's relationships into five conceptions of love: Roy's erotic 'best sex of your life' Valentine's offer to Pam as blind eros; Angela and Dwight's pursuit of an idealized mate read through Plato's Forms and the Symposium's ascent to Beauty; Aristotle's three friendships, under which the office's alliances are mere utility while Jim and Pam's teapot sacrifice in 'Christmas Party' approaches virtue friendship; the Stoic-Kantian 'equal loving' of universal respect, laughed at when Michael ranks himself with Bono and Lincoln; and agape-style family loyalty that leads Dwight to supply Michael his urine in 'Drug Testing'. The chapter concludes that Michael exemplifies a selfishness Western philosophy has no name for, failing at every form of love.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 25 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Spanakos asks why Spider-Man is called 'friendly' by testing Peter's relationships against Aristotle's three philias (pleasure, utility, virtue) and the proportionality principle that the morally inferior friend should love the superior more — a principle that breaks down for a superhero as godlike as Spider-Man. Peter's secrecy and self-sacrifice block true Aristotelian fellowship with MJ, whose crush on Spidey is mere fantasy-love, and Harry's friendship rests on pleasure and utility, failing every Aristotelian test. Yet against philia the chapter sets Christian agape (St. Basil, John 15, C.S. Lewis's Four Loves): unconditional, self-sacrificial love for the unlovable, which Peter practices toward his betrayers and which Harry finally enacts when he dies saving Peter in Spider-Man 3 — an agape that makes him Peter's equal.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 8 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Eberl reads Jax's Season 5 dilemma (Tara's ultimatum to leave SAMCRO or lose his family) through Aristotle's account of virtue as character cultivated by habituation in a polis. SAMCRO nurtures genuine virtues—Opie's selfless loyalty, courage under fire, the club's communal generosity toward Donna and Lyla—alongside vices like Clay's greed and Tig's lust, with the golden mean distinguishing Bobby's critical loyalty from Chuckie's obsequiousness and Juice's rash minefield charge. Fr. Ashby's fight to keep Abel in Belfast away from Jax's cycle of violence, and the contrast between Deputy Chief Hale's law-abiding ideals and Mayor Hale's self-serving development, illustrate Aristotle's claim that legislators and environments make citizens good or bad. The chapter concludes that Jax's very mix of virtue and vice—the 'savage' needed to head the table—may be what reform requires, at moral cost.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 10 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Takes Tig's misplaced revenge on Laroy—which kills Veronica Pope and triggers Damon Pope's burning of Tig's daughter and Opie's prison murder—together with the club's unconditional convoy rescue in 'To Be, Act 1' to ask whether loyalty is a virtue. It tests three accounts: the Aristotelian view (via Ladd's 'loyal Nazi is a contradiction') that only the virtuous can be loyal, which would deny that SAMCRO members can be loyal at all; the Humean view that loyalty is bigoted partiality; and the Kantian point that only the good will is unconditionally good, so loyalty can serve any wrongdoing. The chapter defends Ewin's line that loyalty is good in itself but issues in right action only joined with virtue, while the Stahl frame-up of Opie and Donna's death show the dark enforcement side—'rats deserve to die, end of story.'
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 31 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Presents three ancient alternatives to SAMCRO's warrior ethic. Diogenes the Cynic, 'the earliest of all the fathers of anarchy,' matches J.T.'s Harley-commune ideal — reject greed, convention, and wage slavery like Tig punching the clock at Teller-Morrow — but the chapter argues pure anarchy regenerates hierarchy: with no authority, revenge becomes the only justice and 'a big guy like Clay' mugs 'a small guy like Chuckie.' Plato's Republic supplies the reformist pole — impartial justice for all citizens rather than loyalty circles, rulers picked from proven warriors for wisdom (Tara belongs healing, not scheming), family curbed where it breeds Gemma-style favoritism — yet proves too authoritarian, so Aristotle's function argument (reason as the human ergon), virtue, and the three kinds of friendship (SAMCRO's pleasure-friendships, Clay–Unser's usefulness) sketch a livable middle way with duties even to strangers.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 9 "Notes" — Jerold Abrams reads J. J. Abrams's Kirk as Aristotle's megalopsychos and 'god among men' from the Politics: too excellent to be a mere crewmember, disdainful of rank, speaking openly from love and hate, and a law unto himself. The four-on-one bar fight, reprogramming the unwinnable Kobayashi Maru, declaring 'Some should be' above the Prime Directive to Pike, and his exile to frozen Delta Vega (like the Argonauts stranding Heracles) all enact Aristotle's dilemma that a society must either exile such a man or submit to his monarchy. Spock, a great-souled man himself, becomes Kirk's 'second self' in Aristotle's truest friendship once Kirk takes the captain's chair.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 31 "Notes" — Applies Aristotle's three friendships to Trek: Ferengi Rules of Acquisition dealings and treaties as utility friendships, Bashir and O'Brien's darts and racquetball as friendship of pleasure, and virtuous friendship as requiring emotion, mutual goodwill, and irreplaceable intrinsic valuing - which emotionless Data fails at with Jenna D'Sora in "In Theory". The core argument, following Badhwar, is that consequentialism is logically and psychologically incompatible with virtuous friendship: Spock's "needs of the many" maxim and Data's "for the greater good" experimentation on Geordi in "Descent, Part II" show friends being treated as sacrificeable instruments, while the Kobayashi Maru cheat shows consequentialist reasoning blessing outcomes over means. Kirk's reversal - "the needs of the one outweigh the needs of the many" in The Search for Spock - and T'Pol's years caring for the amnesiac Archer in "Twilight" exemplify acting out of friendship rather than for any further goal.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Littmann shows Luke, Leia, and Han repeatedly put friends and family above the galaxy's freedom - Luke abandoning Dagobah for Bespin, the Jabba rescue, refusing to kill Vader - in the tradition of Homer's heroes, then submits them to Athenian scrutiny. Socrates's refusal to escape his Athens prison and his implicit just agreement with the city set civic duty over friendship; Plato would abolish the guardians' family and censor the Zeus-Kronos patricide myth yet approves of Luke sparing Vader; Aristotle prizes philia but holds citizens belong to the state. He concludes the philosophers mostly win: heroic loyalty is often moral failure, and good moral reasoning asks how many people an action affects, not just whom you love.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 25 "Humanoids and Droids Having Sex" — Munn and Weijers argue that Lando and L3-37 in Solo display all the hallmarks of friendship and one-sided romantic love: Lando abandons self-preservation to carry the injured L3 to the Falcon and endorses her droid-emancipation crusade, while L3 tells Qi'ra she has considered a relationship with him but finds them 'not compatible'. Testing Bennet Helm's four accounts of love (union, deep mutual caring, valuing, emotional state) against the film, they conclude humanoid-droid love is genuinely possible, and that L3's claim that sex with Lando 'works' is plausible once sex is defined broadly as any activity yielding sexual reward. They ground droid friendship in Aristotle's incomplete versus complete friendships, contrasting the rewarding partnerships of R2-D2 with Anakin and BB-8 with Poe against the merely strategic Han-Lando Sabacc rivalry.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 43 "“And I, I'm All the Jedi!”" — Okapal uses Aristotle's three friendships to frame the saga as a story of desert children seeking community: utility friendships like Hondo Ohnaka's and the Sith Rule of Two, where Darth Bane's apprentice is a mere instrument and Sidious calls Maul, Tyranus, and Vader 'easy to replace', stand against the other-regarding virtuous friendships of Obi-Wan, Kanan, and the Rey-Finn-Poe triad, where friends sacrifice for each other's sake as Ezra learns about Kanan in 'A World Between Worlds'. Luke's premature departure for Cloud City fails the 'for the other's sake' test Yoda poses. Rey can only choose the Jedi community knowingly once she learns she is Palpatine's granddaughter, and her closing claim 'I'm Rey Skywalker' is a choice between two value systems - the plural, other-regarding Jedi Code versus the self-regarding 'I' of the Sith Code - making friendship and community, not blood, the root of identity.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 24 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Goguen reads the Winchesters through two masculine ideals: the warrior (Dean and Michael, chivalric protection culminating in Dean's 'protecting Sam... it's who I am') and the sovereign (Sam and Lucifer, whose freedom is analyzed with Isaiah Berlin's negative and positive liberty, with nods to Hobbes's absolute sovereign and Nietzsche's Übermensch). The show's stoic culture, where 'baring my soul like a freaking girl' is an insult, keeps the L-word unspoken, making Ellen's dying 'I will always love you, baby' to Jo a foil the brothers cannot match. Plato's Symposium, via Aristophanes' myth of split soulmates, and Aristotle's claim that the purest love is between virtuous male friends make sense of the 'psychotically, irrationally, erotically codependent' bond, and the chapter concludes that true masculinity requires embracing the seemingly supernatural: love.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 12 "Notes" — Begley and Biondi argue Ted is an ethical egoist in the Aristotelian-Randian sense: like Howard Roark of The Fountainhead (Ted's favorite book), he is a self-loving creator who loves his work, has a 'self-sufficient ego' immune to others' approval, and pursues long-range values, so his kindness and biscuits are rational self-interest, not selflessness. Against Hobbesian psychological egoism they distinguish genuine egoists from narcissists like Rupert and hedonists like Season 1 Jamie, defend Ted's divorce and the curse-reverse ceremony as only apparent sacrifices, and read his panic-attack therapy arc as the egoist's project of achieving inner wholeness.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 15 "Notes" — Forte maps the Richmond cast onto Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: Rebecca, Nate, Roy, and Jamie begin incontinent or near-vicious; courage is the mean between Nate's cowardice and Roy's rashness; and their friendless misery illustrates why friendship (utility, pleasure, complete) is necessary for eudaimonia. Ted's coaching works as a modern strengths-based complement to Aristotelian habituation - Phoebe's Princess-and-Dragon play tempers Roy, Jamie's competitiveness is redirected into team play, Nate misses the mean and becomes mean - and the finale's 'progress over perfection' framing shows all of them as works in progress toward teloi.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 16 "Notes" — Loftin argues the Diamond Dogs enact Aristotle's complete friendship: Jamie and Rebecca fail at friendship because they misconceive the good as self-gratification, and following Philippa Foot's natural-kind account of human good (plus Cicero on goodwill and C. S. Lewis's Four Loves) he shows friendship is an intrinsic good of human beings as such. Ted's vulnerability before Beard, Nate, and Higgins invites them into virtuous activity, Higgins's defection from Rebecca's sabotage scheme displays friendship against a relationship fueled by hurt, and Nate's status-hunger explains why he mistakes Ted's laughter and Rupert's patronage for friendship.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 17 "Notes" — Wible asks whether Ted's friendliness with players and staff constitutes moral friendship, testing it against Aristotle's three friendship types, Hume on solitude, and Bennett Helm's conditions (shared activity, intimacy, mutual care) plus a power-imbalance requirement Kant's respect for persons underwrites. This condemns Rebecca and Sam's relationship as a conflict of interest too risky to permit, questions Led Tasso and benching decisions, yet concludes that Aristotle's virtue friendship between coach and player is possible and preferable to Drewe's limited utility-friendship, since Ted's virtuous friendships make players better people while still knowing when to prioritize team over individual.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 31 "18. War Means Fighting and Fighting Includes Philosophizing" — Vuckovich reads 'Still Valley' through Glaucon's Ring of Gyges: Sgt. Paradine, handed a witchcraft handbook that freezes the Union army before Gettysburg, confronts the temptation of costless, unearned victory, and his burning of the handbook rather than renounce God preserves a principle worth more than winning. Aristotle's claim that bad men can be friends through shared wickedness explains the witchman Teague's bond with Paradine, an 'alliance' that recruits the desperate soldier to do the Devil's dirty work. The chapter ends on the shameful secret legacy: even burying the episode leaves Paradine with a private war in his conscience, a pyrrhic loss for a fighting man who almost surrendered what he holds sacred.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 18 "“See, This Dame Walks In”" — Catlyn Origitano sorts Veronica's relationships through Aristotle's three kinds of friendship in the Nicomachean Ethics: Keith and Cliff McCormack's referral exchange is a friendship of utility, Logan and Dick's partying a friendship of pleasure, and Wallace's bond with Veronica utility fraying into his complaint 'How about you do me a favor for once?' when reciprocity turns one-sided. Perfect friendship of virtue requires mutual trust between genuinely good people, and the chapter's audit finds no one qualifies — Wallace lies and cheats, Logan supplied the GHB and ran from the Tijuana fire, and Veronica's snooping and 'I'm not built that way' refusal to trust disqualify her too. She concludes that noir Neptune itself, where 'the people you love let you down,' may block perfect friendship, though the movie-era Veronica, retired from detection, might at last be ready for one.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 18 "Notes" — Hoffman and Kolmes use Aristotle's friendship as 'another self' and Kant's 'exchange of welfare' to value the pre-New 52 Superman-Wonder Woman friendship (Rucka's heart-to-hearts, Superman choosing to save Wonder Woman over Lois's father), then argue DC's 2011 reboot of the pair into a romance exemplifies Brake's amatonormativity and the heteronormative 'When Harry Met Sally' assumption that cross-gender closeness must be sexual. Diana's answer to Lois - 'We're just good friends' - becomes a refusal to rank friendship below romance. The erasure matters beyond comics: it denies role models for cross-gender friendship and stigmatizes bi and pansexual people as incapable of friendship at all.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 24 "Notes" — Tobienne reads Wonder Woman as sophia personified and a rhetorician in Aristotle's sense, whose real weapon is persuasion: he dissects the Rucka 'Lies' dialogue where she talks the feral Cheetah back to her humanity ('You are a WOMAN... You are my FRIEND!') and her verbal disarmament of a mind-sick Power Girl while holding her in a headlock. Nicomachean Ethics VI grounds the claim that practical wisdom recognizes the need for friends - each woman needs the other - and Wonder Woman's own submission to Athena and Aphrodite explains how the lasso of loving authority, not brute force, disarms Man's World.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 10 "Building Communities One Gym at a Time" — Webb uses Indiana high school basketball to argue the communitarian case against liberal individualism: drawing on MacIntyre, Sandel, and Walzer, he contends communities (not rights-bearing individuals) are the source of meaning, and that small-town gyms like the New Castle Fieldhouse were public spaces that built genuine community. He reads Rick Mount's choice of hometown fame over the pros, the Milan miracle, and the abolition of Indiana's single-class tournament as evidence that mass media and national sport replace real 'face-to-face' communities with 'virtual' ones, using Conseco Fieldhouse's nostalgic theming as his prime example of that loss.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 17 "The Beauty of the Game" — The Brands stage a broadcast-booth debate about whether a championship game was 'beautiful,' with Dickie V defending Hume's subjectivism ('beauty is in the eye of the beholder' and the expert's delicacy of taste) and Billy defending Plato's objective Form of Beauty. Jim exposes each side's flaw (Hume's circular appeal to experts, Plato's third-man regress from the Parmenides/Aristotle) and proposes a synthesis: games have 'outer beauty' (universally observable fluid motion, like improvised jazz or dance) and 'inner beauty' (the strategy and reason the knowledgeable fan grasps), reconciling the objective and subjective.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 11 "Football and Aristotle'S Philosophy of Friendship" — Gallagher maps Aristotle's three kinds of philia onto football: friendship of utility (the quarterback needing his offensive linemen), of pleasure (Friday-night high school and college ball), and of shared goodness (Bo Schembechler's bond with Anthony Carter, who deflected reporters to teammates). He reads the Steelers dynasty and Paterno's locker-room 'love' through Aristotle's 'concord' and 'a single soul in two bodies,' and answers Bertrand Russell's worry about violent competition by insisting football is grounded in philia, not enmity.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 33 "Seventeenth Hole More Than a Playing Partner Golf and Friendship" — Andy Wible argues that although golf looks like the ultimate solitary sport, it is unusually good at fostering friendship, and analyzes friendship through Aristotle's three kinds (utility, pleasure, and the highest, based on the friend's good character), supplemented by Laurence Thomas (choice, equality, mutual trust) and Blum on care as a moral phenomenon. Golf's long unhurried rounds, self-called penalties, handicap system, shared memorable shots, and retirement communities build the intimacy, trust and equality Aristotle prizes, and Robert Simon's 'mutual quest for excellence' reconciles competition with goodwill. Wible then confronts friendship's partiality—exclusionary country clubs and the sex-segregated LPGA—using Marilyn Friedman's voluntary friendship communities to argue clubs should drop discrimination on race, sex, religion and orientation while keeping friendship's care and loyalty.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 24 "Friendship, Rivalry, and Excellence" — The chapter uses Aristotle's three friendships (pleasure, usefulness, virtue) to ask how tennis rivals competing for one prize can be friends, illustrating pleasure with Borg and Gerulaitis, usefulness with the tense but genuine Ashe-McEnroe Davis Cup bond, and virtue with the Evert-Navratilova rivalry that grew into deep mutual care despite a competitive women's tour. It adds C. S. Lewis's view that friends stand side by side absorbed in a shared thing, then reads Jimmy Connors as a Nietzschean Ubermensch whose master-morality drive to dominate makes him, paradoxically, the best 'star friend' by pushing rivals to their limits. It closes unresolved on whether the tension between friendship and rivalry can ever be eliminated.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 15 "Me and You Identity, Love, and Friendship in the Films of Charlie Kaufman" — Den Uyl argues that Kaufman's films are really about friendship rather than romance, reading them through Aristotle's character friendship (the friend as 'other self' and mirror of self-knowledge) and Montaigne's ideal of a free, voluntary friendship that also engages the body. Charlie's fictional twin Donald in Adaptation externalizes the integrity Charlie lacks, and only after internalizing Donald can he say 'I love her'; Caden in Synecdoche fails because he looks only at himself. Love succeeds, on this reading, only when grounded in the self-sufficiency and self-respect that make one capable of an 'other self,' as Eternal Sunshine's Joel and Clementine haltingly discover.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 17 "Charlie Kaufman, Philosophy, and the Small Screen" — Chambers reads Kaufman's TV sitcom Ned and Stacey through queer theory, arguing its marriage-of-convenience premise stages a critique of 'the normal.' Because Ned and Stacey only play at being husband and wife and never desire the romantic telos, the show troubles heteronormativity more than the openly gay Will & Grace, whose characters chase marriage and family. Chambers uses Butler's Lacanian notion of masquerade to claim there is no 'real' husband or wife beneath the role, only role-playing, and ties this to the philia (not eros) bond of the leads and to the masquerade running through Kaufman's films.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — The editors' introduction argues that Eastwood, though no academic, does 'practical philosophy' through his films as a craftsman who inherits and then revises genres (revising the Western in Unforgiven, rethinking rugged individualism in Million Dollar Baby and Gran Torino). Invoking MacIntyre's claim that we are only co-authors of interlocking narratives, it reads Eastwood's focus on decisive moral choices (Francesca's refusal to leave in Bridges of Madison County, Butch Haynes in A Perfect World) as a 'laboratory of moral psychology' echoing Aristotle's 'choice discriminates character.' It ties his concern with loss, justice, and Aristotelian friendship and flourishing (Grinnell on Million Dollar Baby) to a Socratic 'know thyself,' arguing his philosophizing is implicit and nonverbal rather than argued in words.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 12 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Grinnell applies Aristotle's classification of friendship (utility, pleasure, and complete character-friendship between equals in excellence) to Million Dollar Baby and Gran Torino. Frankie/Maggie and Walt/Thao begin as incomplete, utility relationships across barriers of age, sex, and culture, then ripen into character-friendships of 'other selves' who pursue each other's good. He resolves the apparent paradox that friendship demands bringing about a death: Frankie euthanizes Maggie against his own wishes to honor her autonomy and whole-life excellence, while Walt engineers his own death and deceives Thao to spare him a vengeance that would destroy his character — each an Aristotelian sacrifice of self-interest for the friend that preserves the friendship's excellence.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 14 "“And It’s Such a Beautiful Day!” shame and Fargo" — Hanrahan and Stearns read Fargo through Aristotle's theory of shame and its link to friendship, sorting the characters into his moral hierarchy: Gaear is the shameless self-indulgent man, Jerry is the morally incontinent one whose flickers of shame (before Scotty, before the swindled customer) stay inert against his greed, and Marge is the exemplar of excellence. They argue that a capacity for shame requires valuing others non-instrumentally, which the co-conspirators cannot do because they relate only through friendships of utility (Carl and the prostitute, Jerry using his son). Marge's friendship-of-the-good with Norm grounds both her decency and her ability to mediate others' shame, and her 'it's such a beautiful day' expresses the same noninstrumental valuing that makes moral concern possible.
- **The Philosophy of Joss Whedon**, ch. 6 "The Peculiarities of Free Will" — This file collects Part I chapters 1-5. It argues Whedon's heroes (Angel, Buffy, Spike, Simon, Echo, Captain America) achieve authentic selfhood by resisting depersonalizing forces, reading their 'angst' through Heidegger and Sartre while insisting Whedon is more Socratic than existentialist because he affirms objective goods, synthesized via a Rawlsian just society. It then adds Aristotle on friendship and community (Toy Story, Jayne, Angel's team) and defends an atheistic ethics grounding natural rights in Locke and Kant plus Aristotelian virtue (Spike's re-ensoulment), using the Euthyphro to reject divine-command theory. The title chapter argues Whedon's paradoxical portrayal of free will in The Shepherd's Tale, Dollhouse and Cabin fits neither hard determinism nor compatibilism but Robert Kane's libertarian self-forming actions.
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — Sanders reads Casino as a dramatization of ethical egoism, using the parasitic bond between Nicky Santoro and Ace Rothstein to ask whether an egoist who treats a friend as a mere instrument can have real friendship. He distinguishes 'maximizing' egoism (Nicky's ruinous take-everything drive, ending in his beating death) from a 'satisficing' egoism that restricts its own dispositions, arguing against Blum, Wilcox and an Aristotelian objection that only the maximizing version is truly incompatible with friendship. Aristotle's account of virtue and friendship supplies the standard the film's egoists fall short of.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 9 "Watsons, Adlers, Lestrades, and Moriarties On the Nature of Friends and Enemies" — Tallon applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics taxonomy of friendship—of use, of pleasure, and of virtue—to Holmes's relationships, plus Aquinas on friends helping each other flourish. The Baker Street Irregulars and Mrs. Hudson are friends of use; Holmes has few friends of pleasure; Watson is the friend of virtue, an 'other self' sharing virtue, support, and activity (getting Holmes off cocaine, taking a bullet). Inverting the account, he classifies Holmes's enemies as competitor (Irene Adler), rival/'frenemy' (Lestrade and Gregson), and foe (Moriarty), arguing a foe—an anti-self—can never become a friend.
- **Joss Whedon as Philosopher**, ch. 6 "The Peculiarities of Free Will" — This file collects Part I's chapters, arguing the Whedonverse embodies serious philosophy. It reads Angel, Buffy, Simon Tam, Echo, and the Avengers through Heidegger's inauthenticity/angst and Sartre's existentialism (Dr. Horrible and the Operative as inauthentic 'monsters'), then adds Rawls and Aristotle to claim some authentic lives are better led, using Gyges's ring (in 'Gone' and 'In the Dark') and Aristotelian friendship (Team Angel, Serenity's crew) as touchstones. It defends an atheistic moral realism via Kant on personhood and Locke's natural rights (Mal insisting Saffron is 'no one's property'), and closes on free will: reading The Shepherd's Tale, Dollhouse, and The Cabin in the Woods against d'Holbach's hard determinism, Flamson's compatibilism, and Robert Kane's libertarian self-forming actions (Connor's choice in 'Inside Out').
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 4 "Love, Value, and the Human Destiny in Interstellar" — Belluomini and Dunn use Interstellar's clash between Cooper's partial parental love and Professor Brand's species-level 'Plan B' to ask why the survival of humanity matters and what 'saving humanity' means. Drawing on Aristotle, they treat Cooper's daughter Murph as 'another self' loved as an end in itself and tie the good to individual happiness (eudaimonia), so 5,000 faceless embryos could never be the intrinsic good a real family is. They then turn to Kant to argue humans have unconditional value (dignity) as rational beings, which both grounds a reason to preserve the species AND condemns Brand's 'monstrous lie' as treating people merely as means to an end they do not share.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 34 "I Am the Bad Wolf" — Roman Altshuler answers Davros's charge that the Doctor is a 'destroyer of worlds' using Aristotelian virtue ethics. He argues the Doctor's chief virtue is not compassion but Heideggerian 'authentic concern': offering aggressors (the Nestene, Sontarans, the Master) a genuine choice so they become responsible for escalating, illustrated by the fly-swatter thought experiment. Companions, being 'another self' (Aristotle on friendship), make their acts partly the Doctor's own, yet their human 'Bad Wolf Syndrome' lets compassion override the impartial concern that requires respecting choice, which is why the Doctor runs from what his companions do in his name.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 20 "10. Cas Is Family" — Doll traces Castiel's arc from a cold Divine-Command/utilitarian 'hammer of the Lord' to a member of the Winchester family through Aristotle's ethics. She argues Cas learns to contemplate and act on the chief good under Dean's tutelage, pursuing eudaimonia by habituation despite repeated failures (becoming a false god, the Leviathans), and that his bond with Sam and Dean grows through Aristotle's three friendships—utility, pleasure, and finally the rare true friendship of virtuous character—culminating in his self-sacrificing declaration of love that defeats Billie.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 23 "NOTES" — Michael W. Austin applies Jane English's claim that adult children owe their parents 'nothing' to the fraught father-son relationships of Lost. He works through Jack and Christian Shephard's operating-room cover-up, Locke being conned out of a kidney and paralyzed by Anthony Cooper, and Sawyer's murder-suicide father to argue that parental sacrifices create debts only on the commonsense view English rejects. English's alternative is that such sacrifices ideally generate friendship rather than obligation, which Austin illustrates with the unbookkept mutual aid among Sawyer, Kate, Hurley, and Locke, contrasting Jack's line 'I'm not one of his friends' about retrieving his dead father.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 31 "18. War Means Fighting and Fighting Includes Philosophizing" — Vuckovich analyzes 'Still Valley,' where Confederate Sergeant Paradine can win the Civil War using a witchcraft handbook that freezes Union troops but only by renouncing God. He reads Paradine's temptation through Glaucon's Ring of Gyges myth in Plato's Republic (the committed unjust man who outdoes enemies without scruple) and Aristotle's friendships of shared pleasure (Paradine and the witchman Teague bonded by hatred of the enemy). Paradine burns the handbook rather than damn the Confederacy, preserving a core principle of fairness even at the cost of an easy victory—winning isn't everything.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 10 "Stephen King and Aristotelian Friendship" — Bertha Alvarez Manninen reads The Body (Stand by Me) and Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption through Aristotle's Nicomachean and Eudemian Ethics on the three friendships. Andy and Norton/the guards exemplify friendships of utility (the tax help, the Rita Hayworth poster), the boys' tree-house camaraderie and Vern/Teddy exemplify pleasure friendships that dissolve as characters change, while Gordie-and-Chris and Andy-and-Red model enduring friendships of virtue rooted in mutual good will, shared confidences, and cultivating each other's excellence.
