- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 20 "“The Wrong Direction”" — Barkman builds a definition of lying (communicating what one believes false while hiding that fact, with intent to hurt or disrespect, which distinguishes mere deception and parts ways with Aquinas's blanket ban) and applies it to five advertising worries, from bags of chips designed to invite false inference to the Belle Jolie 'promise' no one actually believes and the Israeli Tourism ad that omits danger. Persuasion is legitimate because rational souls are equals to be treated as ends (Aristotle's justice), but manipulation (ads aimed at preschoolers that use children to pressure parents) and fear-preying coercion (Clearasil on insecure teenagers, nylons to unmarried women like Rachel Menken) treat people as means, while government must regulate factually (FDA 'smoking kills' labels) without overriding adult choice. Responsibility is then distributed across producer, agency, media, public, and state, and Don was indeed 'looking in the wrong direction' in this sense: being able to talk anyone into anything does not mean he should.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 11 "The Office and Philosophy" — Weighs the morality of Jim and Pam's workplace flirting (while Pam is engaged to Roy) using three ethical frameworks: act utilitarianism has them tot up their own happiness against effects on co-workers' morale and Dunder-Mifflin's bottom line; rule utilitarianism models HR's blanket anti-dating policies and asks whether Jim and Pam could justify an exception without destroying the rule (the Hawaiian shirt day analogy); deontology searches for duties against office romance (favoritism in evaluation, distraction from duties) and finds none once harassment is set aside, concluding that in the absence of a deontological prohibition, Jim and Pam may keep flirting until 5 p.m.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 11 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — White analyzes Spider-Man's public unmasking in Civil War as a familiar ethical choice between the right and the good. Peter's promise to Tony Stark and obedience to the Superhuman Registration Act are deontological duties, explicated through Kant's test of universalizing the maxim of promise-breaking, while his worry for Aunt May and MJ pulls him toward consequentialist reasoning whose uncertainty, complexity, and incommensurability the chapter details. Aunt May's 'some things are worth the risk' speech tips Peter toward principle, but the Kingpin's sniper shoots her anyway, and Peter's hellish aftermath — ending in the Mephisto deal of 'One More Day' — shows both the tragedy of doing the right thing and the argument that when consequences are unknowable one should simply do what is right.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 10 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Takes Tig's misplaced revenge on Laroy—which kills Veronica Pope and triggers Damon Pope's burning of Tig's daughter and Opie's prison murder—together with the club's unconditional convoy rescue in 'To Be, Act 1' to ask whether loyalty is a virtue. It tests three accounts: the Aristotelian view (via Ladd's 'loyal Nazi is a contradiction') that only the virtuous can be loyal, which would deny that SAMCRO members can be loyal at all; the Humean view that loyalty is bigoted partiality; and the Kantian point that only the good will is unconditionally good, so loyalty can serve any wrongdoing. The chapter defends Ewin's line that loyalty is good in itself but issues in right action only joined with virtue, while the Stahl frame-up of Opie and Donna's death show the dark enforcement side—'rats deserve to die, end of story.'
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 27 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Defends South Park's anti-paternalism on both consequentialist and deontological grounds. 'Major Boobage' shows the futility of Gerald's cat ban meant to stop kids 'cheesing' — Kenny still gets high and Gerald himself relapses — while 'Medicinal Fried Chicken' shows how the KFC prohibition births a violent black market, with Cartman's $85 snack pushing him into the Colonel's Scarface-style drug war. On the deontological side, Mill's 'over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign', Locke's self-ownership, and Kantian respect for rational agents (via Nozick's inviolability, and the authors' autarchy-versus-autonomy distinction) ground the claim that coercion is wrong even when benevolent: 'Butt Out' has Kyle and Stan tell Rob Reiner that forcing others to quit smoking is fascism, while Big Tobacco's Kevin Harris wins their approval simply by informing and letting people choose.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 22 "“Rebellions Are Built on Hope!”" — Eberl asks whether Galen Erso, who knowingly resumed work on the Death Star while planting its exhaust-port flaw, is culpable for the deaths on Jedha, Scarif, and Alderaan. A utilitarian defense (his flaw net-saved the galaxy, per the negative-responsibility principle applied to the Death Star II 'Clerks' debate) founders on moral luck — everything depended on Luke's impossible shot — while Bernard Williams's integrity objection, via the chemist 'George' case, condemns his betrayal of conscience. The chapter finally deploys Thomistic tools for cooperation with evil: because Galen's contribution was mediate and remote (Tarkin ordered the firing, the gunners pulled the triggers, Leia's defiance provoked Alderaan's destruction) and the weapon would have been built without him, his collusion is justified by the reasonable hope — the 'new hope' — of the Death Star's destruction.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 18 "8. Saints and Superheroes" — Alloy uses supererogation — Urmson's saints-and-heroes puzzle — to separate the heroes: utilitarianism (via Singer's Famine, Affluence, and Morality, where even Clark's novelty glasses are stolen from charity) and deontology both erase acts that are good but not required, and Susan Wolf's moral saints show where that lands — a Bruce Wayne with no hobbies, friends, or life, like Astro City's Samaritan. Alloy's own Raz-style fix (requirements overridden by moral permitting reasons) yields the verdict: Batman risks his life by choice and so is a true hero, while Superman, facing no real danger, merely does what his powers make morally required — 'a good person with the powers of a living god'.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 24 "13. Time to Choose" — Goldberg and Gavaler read Superman's first-year Action Comics adventures (reforming the Blakely Mine owner, demolishing slums, buying back swindled stock) as consequentialism on Millian lines, and Batman's Detective Comics year (letting the Joker's victims die while 'the time isn't ripe', the batarang deflected by invisible glass) as a dark, vengeance-based cousin of Kant's duty ethics. Moral luck is the pivot — deontology ignores it, consequentialism is hostage to it — but Superman's powers cancel luck, and in the opening Luthor/Joker two-bomb scenario Superman defuses while Batman chases the villain, so the chapter rules Superman's 'super consequentialism' the superior code.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 17 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Browning shows that 'Jus in Bello' is built from Romero's Night of the Living Dead: the besieged police station is a 'survival space' (a form he traces to Matheson's I Am Legend), Henricksen takes Ben's role and Nancy Barbra's, and the massed possessed townspeople mirror the shuffling zombie horde. Inside that space the show stages a clash of values, Ruby's utilitarian spell requiring Nancy's heart against Dean's absolute refusal to kill an innocent ('your choice is not a choice'), resolved by the rock-salt-and-exorcism plan that kills no one. The survival space works as a proving ground for its occupants' values, and the ending, where Lilith slaughters Nancy anyway, indicts the heroes' scruples and asks what the body count says about the viewers who enjoyed it.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 34 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Yuen argues cannibalism is not automatically wrong: both utilitarian and Kantian frameworks permit eating the already-dead in a genuine survival situation like the Andes crash of Alive, since corpses lose no happiness and lack the rational nature owed dignity. But Chris's hunters in 'Fear the Hunters' become moral monsters because they kill to eat (murdering their own children, amputating and eating the still-living Dale to prolong his terror), which neither maximizes utility nor treats persons as ends, and Chris's 'we had no choice' excuse fails because starving is not a license to murder when one could befriend other survivors, eat walkers, or starve. Rick's execution of the hunters is then defended on Kantian grounds of deserved punishment: applying Chris's own maxim ('if Dale was good as a steak, so is Chris') as a universal law.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 24 "Notes" — Kowalski applies Kant's ethics to the Aes Sedai Three Oaths in the Amazon series, arguing that because the Oath Rod makes sisters physically unable to lie, 'ought implies can' means they get no moral credit for truth-telling, like praising water for freezing. He examines acting from duty versus according to duty (few Aes Sedai accept the Oaths for the right reason; Moiraine may be the exception), and the universal-law formulation against lying promises. He then presses Kant's absolutism through Moiraine's careful literal truths to the Whitecloak Valda ('I have a sister in Whitebridge'), arguing that Kant's own 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' and Schopenhauer's self-defense objection show WoT can talk back to Kant about conflicting duties.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 25 "Notes" — Bein uses the 'kill baby Hitler' time-machine puzzle and the question of whether Moiraine and Lan should still the Dragon Reborn to probe the Aes Sedai's mysterious ethics. He argues they are not Kantian deontologists (the Three Oaths are loose plot-device rules Moiraine games with ambiguous innuendo, and Kant forbids treating the ferryman as mere means) and are bad consequentialists at best (they cannot lightning-bolt Valda or Hitler who are not Darkfriends). He proposes they are closest to Buddhist ethics: wise compassion good in itself (Tam sitting with dying Tigraine regardless of outcome), and reads the flexible Oaths through upaya (skillful means) and a WoT-adapted Eightfold Path, making them less pacifist nuns than violence-reducing Shaolin nuns.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 21 "Notes" — White reconstructs the 'Sacrifice' storyline - Maxwell Lord mind-controlling Superman, telling lasso-bound Wonder Woman 'Kill me,' and her snapping his neck - and asks whether it was right. He argues Wonder Woman reasons as a threshold deontologist: her usual respect for life holds until the certain cost of letting Lord live (he would wield Superman to kill again) crosses the threshold where the consequentialist body-count argument takes over, and she was justified, so she would do it again. The contrast with Batman's refusal to kill the Joker shows his refusal is virtue-ethical self-definition ('I won't become them'), while Diana, regretting the necessity but feeling no remorse, is an Amazon warrior for whom lethal protection of lives is sometimes exactly the job.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 23 "Notes" — Barkman and Tokbergenova defend 'just torture': Wonder Woman's lasso interrogations of Captain Nazi, the double agent Marcia in the 1970s pilot (saving the Brooklyn Navy Yard's 70,000 workers), and the terrorist Nikos Aegeus are ticking-bomb cases of the sort Henry Shue concedes, and the authors answer Luban's slippery-slope objection with absolute limits (never the innocent or the family) and Dershowitz-style torture warrants. Citing Aristotle's Rhetoric that coerced testimony is often false, they propose trained professional torturers, and conclude that since the right thing is not always the ideal thing, torture should be legalized, rare, and conducted openly - as Wonder Woman models.
- **X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse**, ch. 6 "X-Men and Philosophy" — Four-plus essays. White defends Jean Grey's altruistic suicide in the Dark Phoenix Saga through Kant's categorical imperative (both formulas) and the confl icting-duty case of the rabid-dog letter, ranking deontology over utilitarian and virtue readings. Kavadlo reads the X-Men as existential literature, tying Sartre's bad faith and anti-Semitism and Camus's Sisyphus to the mutants' Jewish/Holocaust roots and never-ending serial struggle. Burnett uses Mister Sinister, Sentinels, and eugenics to trace bioethics through Spencer's evolutionary ethics and Galton. Dunn casts Layla Miller as Bacon's 'knowledge is power' against Aristotle's contemplative ideal. The Davis 'Magneto, Mutation, and Morality' essay begins here, opening the evolutionary-ethics question of Xavier vs. Magneto.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 11 "To Hack or Not to Hack" — Kennedy asks how a great player like Kareem (the NBA's career foul leader) can be excellent while fouling so much, and answers that deontology (Kant's categorical imperative) and utilitarianism (Mill's greatest-happiness principle) can condemn dangerous 'goon' fouling but cannot explain why the legal Hack-a-Shaq strategy still feels 'clownish.' Invoking Shaq's self-nickname 'the Big Aristotle,' he argues Aristotelian virtue ethics fits better: the excellent player, like the person of good character, perceives the situation rightly and fouls (or risks a foul) at the right time in the right way, so excellence is a habit of seeing well rather than rule-following.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 15 "5. Albert Among the Chowder-Head Yokels and Blithering Hayseeds" — The Phillipses argue that abrasive forensic agent Albert Rosenfield is a model Kantian: his refusal to lie to spare Truman's feelings follows the formula of universal law, and his insistence that Truman be punished for the assault treats Truman as an autonomous end. They run Gordon Cole's manipulative lying through the universalizability test (it fails, unlike wanting pie), distinguish hypothetical from categorical imperatives via Cooper's rebuff of Audrey, and read Albert's 'I love you, Sheriff Truman' and Gandhi/King nonviolence as respect for persons as ends in themselves—duty done for the right reason.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Berger uses Harold Becker's The Onion Field to challenge Kant's moral idealism. Kant held that any rational being can deduce categorical imperatives and that conscience necessarily convicts the guilty and vindicates the innocent. Yet the killers Powell and Smith feel no guilt for murdering Kant-admiring cop Ian Campbell (Smith calls guilt a trick 'rich white guys dreamed up'), while the innocent, blameless Hettinger is destroyed by shame, thievery, and near-suicide. Berger weighs Schopenhauer's 'evil genius' objection and the sociopathy explanation, concluding Hettinger's guilt is a doomed attempt to preserve moral meaning.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 13 "Sherlock Holmes and the Ethics of Hyperspecialization" — Costello and Bassham critique Holmes's 'brain-attic' theory from 'A Study in Scarlet'—that the mind has fixed capacity and should hold only vocationally useful knowledge. Cognitive science (interference and schema theory) and the sociology of social/cultural capital show useless knowledge is often useful, as when Holmes trades boxing lore or reads cultural cues. They then argue for a duty of self-improvement grounded in consequentialism, Kantian and Rossian deontology, and virtue ethics (Aristotle, Aquinas, MacIntyre) plus Socratic care of the soul, concluding that Holmes—an omnivorous reader who quotes Goethe and Hafiz—doesn't practice what he preaches and took specialization too far.
- **The Philosophy of Spike Lee**, ch. 18 "The Dialectic of King and X in Do the Right Thing" — Silberstein reads Do the Right Thing as staging the ideological dialectic between Martin Luther King Jr.'s absolute nonviolence and Malcolm X's defense of retaliatory self-defense, both grounded in a theologically informed natural-law view of rights (King's Christian imago dei, X's Islamic tradition). He argues King mixes a deontological ethic (violence is always wrong) with a Gandhian consequentialist claim that violence begets violence, while X frames a race war as a just holy war. The film's Radio Raheem (LOVE/HATE knuckles), Buggin' Out's boycott of Sal's Wall of Fame, the Racial Slur Montage, and Mookie throwing the trash can dramatize whether ends justify means; the closing Sal-Mookie money exchange reframes racism as symptom of a deeper capitalist greed both King and X came to critique.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 26 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Biderman and Devlin use Traffic's four intertwined characters to test Kantian moral absolutism, applying the three formulations of the categorical imperative: Helena's decision to have witness Eduardo Ruiz murdered fails universalization, while Javier's whistleblowing on General Salazar (motivated only by duty, refusing reward) passes the autonomy formula. They argue Kant handles these cleanly but strains on DEA agent Montel's revenge (treating Carlos as a means) and outright fails on drug-czar Robert Wakefield's conflict between two absolute duties, to nation and to his addicted daughter. Following Sartre's critique that the categorical imperative is too abstract for concrete dilemmas, they show Soderbergh siding with existentialist choice as Robert invents his own law and quits to save his daughter.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 16 "The Duty of Reason Kantian Ethics in High Noon" — Evans argues that Marshal Will Kane in High Noon is Kant's ideal moral agent, acting from duty and a good will rather than from consequences. He shows the townsfolk, Kane's friends, Harvey Pell, Helen Ramirez, and Amy all reasoning consequentially or heteronomously (the mayor privileging the town's finances, Mildred lying about Sam per Kant's essay on the supposed right to lie), while Frank Miller's revenge is a maxim that cannot be universalized. Kane's maxim of standing against lawlessness regardless of cost satisfies all three formulations of the categorical imperative—universal law, humanity as an end, and autonomy—making him a member of the kingdom of ends and contrasting Kant with Mill's utilitarianism.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 18 "The Cost of the Code Ethical Consequences in High Noon and The Ox-Bow Incident" — Ken Hada reads High Noon and The Ox-Bow Incident through Nussbaum's neo-Aristotelian critique of Kantian duty. Will Kane's absolute, self-sacrificing return to face Frank Miller and Major Tetley's honor-bound insistence on hanging the accused both exemplify the Kantian categorical imperative applied without regard to consequences. The essay argues that the films themselves undermine this code: Kane's triumph brings no joy and Tetley's rigid 'reason' masks self-interest and produces the lynching of three innocent men. Following Nussbaum, it holds that attention to particulars, emotion, and social context—embodied by Davies in Ox-Bow—yields more just moral perception than blind allegiance to an absolute rule.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 20 "No Country for Old Men The Decline of Ethics and the West(ern)" — William J. Devlin argues that No Country for Old Men deconstructs the western's three ingredients (moral hero, comprehensible villain, redemptive showdown) and collapses the genre into Nietzschean nihilism. Where Shane's courage is legible through Aristotelian virtue-ethics and Kantian deontology, Sheriff Bell grows old and afraid, walking away rather than confronting evil. Anton Chigurh perverts deontology—killing on 'principle' and because he 'gave his word'—while his coin flips invoke Nagel's moral luck to disclaim responsibility, so the good/bad polarity dissolves and, as Ellis says, 'you can't stop what's comin'.'
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 21 "The Northwestern McCabe and Mrs. Miller" — Deborah Knight and George McKnight read Altman's McCabe and Mrs. Miller as an 'end-of-genre' western in the ironic mode, using Frye's Aristotle-derived mythos to map the classic western's binary oppositions (hero/villain, community/wilderness, virgin/whore) and then show the film collapsing them. Against Nussbaum's and Booth's ethical criticism, which extols works that make us 'finely aware and richly responsible,' they argue irony is itself a moral stance of detached scrutiny: McCabe is no hero but a vulgar, unimaginative businessman crushed by the Harrison Shaughnessy company and shot in the back in the snow while the town obliviously saves its burning church, dramatizing the implosion of the western's moral vision.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 19 "10 Listening with Neil’s Vulnerable Voice and the Ethics of Care" — Jostedt argues that Young's raw, high "dental" singing voice (contrasted with Dylan's nasal sneer) invites empathetic "listening-with" rather than the detached individualism of Kant's deontology or Mill's utilitarianism. Drawing on Gilligan's In a Different Voice, Jane Addams and the ethics of care's emphasis on relatedness, he shows how songs like "Ohio," "Stringman," "Cortez the Killer" and the album Trans (evoking his son's cerebral palsy) make listeners feel with the downtrodden and disabled.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 23 "Allons-y into the Starry Heavens" — Donna Marie Smith uses the Doctor and Rose's separation in "Doomsday" and "Journey's End" to explicate Kantian deontology. After framing the Doctor's virtues via Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and distinguishing eros, philia, and agape (with Reinette illustrating chivalrous self-sacrifice), she argues that Kant's categorical imperative and the duty-versus-inclination conflict explain why the Doctor and Rose Kant be together: their love pulls toward partiality while duty to save humanity is what they ought to do, so acting for the greater good is precisely what forces their parting.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 26 "Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign" — Courtland Lewis argues the Cybermen are not evil but altruistic, distinguishing utilitarianism (right equals good consequences) from Kantian duty-ethics (right can diverge from good), using the Doctor's "Genesis of the Daleks" dilemma about killing a future dictator. He reads the Cybermen as "Cybertarians" who genuinely aim to cure human pain and death, and attacks the Doctor's "Age of Steel" argument that it is good to strive for but bad to achieve a pain-free deathless life. He proposes that Cybermen's real fault is violating autonomy through forced upgrades, and that respecting informed consent (a medical-ethics ad campaign) would make upgrading morally acceptable.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 18 "8. Which Brother Is the Good One" — Browning contrasts the brothers' ethics: Dean is a consequentialist who judges hunts by outcomes ('the ends justify the means,' killing werewolf Madison or faith-healer Roy for the greater good), while Sam is a deontologist who treats lying, stealing, and killing as wrong in themselves. Tracking episodes like 'Bloodlust,' 'Croatoan,' and 'Fresh Blood,' he argues the murder-versus-kill distinction and the blurring line between human and monster show Dean's darker consequentialism is better suited to the Hunter's war, though both are driven to do good.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 19 "9. God the Programmer Is Dead" — De Vries defines a 'monster' in Supernatural as one who breaks the social contract, then argues Sam and Dean are deontologists loyal to a rigid duty—but a 'social contract of two' (family) that produces double standards toward Cas and Jack. She contrasts the angels' box-checking utilitarianism and Hobbesian collapse without God, Hell's contractual capitalist democracy, and Chuck as a controlling 'programmer God' whose perfection cannot tolerate imperfection; Jack's hands-off deity and Chuck's Nietzschean death-of-God let humanity write its own moral code.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 8 "1. Scamming for Fun" — Clipsham distinguishes Jimmy and Kim's 'scamming for fun' (deceiving Ken over rare tequila in 'Switch', or a montage of pointless cons in 'Marco') from the 'scheming for benefits' of Mike, Gus, and Chuck, who lie only to secure a specific end. Using Kant's prohibition on treating people merely as means, he argues that scheming for a benefit is more disrespectful than scamming for its own sake, because the latter treats a mark as an unwitting player in a game rather than a tool. He also rejects the worry that fun-scamming corrupts character, noting Jimmy was already dishonest and that Gus and Lalo's worst vices have no root in playful deception.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 31 "20. Why Is Breaking Skateboarders’ Legs Wrong" — The chapter uses three characters to test three single-value moral theories: Chuck as a Kantian deontologist whose rigid loyalty to the categorical imperative and the 'sacred' law destroys his bond with Jimmy; Jimmy as a Mill-style consequentialist whose ends-justify-means scams (Sandpiper, the squat-cobbler film) let him decide what counts as good outcomes and cost him integrity, invoking Bernard Williams; and Mike as a Scanlonian contractualist who honors even immoral agreements like the Tuco hit. Through cases like the 'murderer at the door,' it argues each theory alone leads people to do wrong, so a moral life must combine outcomes, rules, and contracts.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 33 "21. Finding the Good in Nacho" — The chapter uses Kant to argue that Nacho Varga, though a genuinely bad drug dealer, can perform morally worthy acts in isolated moments. Because Kant locates morality in the rational will and intention rather than accomplishment, it treats Nacho's attempts on the Salamancas and his desire to leave the game as evidence of active moral reasoning, while conceding his motives are muddied by self-interest and love for his father (the shopkeeper example warns against acts done for loved ones). Its clean case is the phone call in 'Something Unforgivable,' where Nacho risks everything to plead for Lalo's near-innocent staff, doing the right thing purely because it is right.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 26 "15. Morality and Manipulation" — Kahn frames the Foundation series around personal autonomy, using Mill's image of humans as a growing tree rather than a machine 'built after a model' to condemn both coercion and manipulation. He shows Hari Seldon as a paradoxical champion of autonomy who nonetheless deceives his own followers about the fraudulent Encyclopedia Galactica and secretly forecloses their freedom of action via the Seldon Plan and Second Foundation—echoing the Mule's mind-control of Han Pritcher. He reads Salvor Hardin's maxim ('never let your sense of morals prevent you from doing what is right') as consequentialism that maximizes galaxy-wide autonomy, contrasts it with the deontology exemplified by Gaia/Bliss (who refuse to manipulate Trevize) and critics like Toran Darell and Branno, and leaves the reader to judge as Bliss urges Pelorat to think for himself.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 27 "16. Psycho-historian or Psycho Historian" — Bellantoni asks what Seldon owes future generations, pitting moral presentism against his 'mystical' identification with humanity (echoing Scheffler's Why Worry about Future Generations?). She tests the Seldon Plan under Bentham's hedonic calculus—finding time-discounting and uncertainty about what follows the thirty-thousand-year interregnum undercut it—and under Kantian deontology, arguing Seldon's mass manipulation of Gaal Dornick, his inquisitors, and the Encyclopedists treats people merely as means and violates their autonomy. Weighing longtermism against Whitehead's claim (in Adventures of Ideas) that civilizations must die to seed new ones, she suggests Seldon's engineered revival of a spent civilization may itself be a barbaric imposition on future people who would not choose it.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 28 "So, Case Closed – Right" — White asks why Batman won't kill the Joker, framing it through utilitarianism (killing one to save the Joker's many future victims) versus deontology (killing is wrong regardless of consequences). Using Foot and Thomson's trolley and transplant cases, plus agent-neutral versus agent-relative rules, he notes key disanalogies: the Joker is not a moral innocent but the very cause of the danger, which pushes toward killing him. But because future killings are only probable, doing so would be 'prepunishment,' and White, a self-described deontologist, concludes it is genuinely hard to say Batman is right, though he admires the restraint.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 29 "“Who watches the watchmen ”" — Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as a would-be consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) whose plan to kill millions to end the Cold War exposes utilitarianism's neglect of rights and, via Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ends,' its dependence on an unknowable infinite future. Rorschach poses as a Kantian deontologist ('I shall not compromise') but Loftis shows his hypocrisy, black-and-white dichotomous thinking, and failure to respect persons betray Kant's categorical imperative. Loftis argues neither theory is truly held by either character; both are rationalizations of power, and the comic's real target, captured by 'Who watches the watchmen?', is authoritarianism itself.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 41 "It’s Not That Simple" — Donal O'Mathuna uses 24's Jack Bauer to dissect the ethics of torture, centering on Henry Shue's utilitarian 'ticking bomb' argument that torturing the bomber to save thousands is justified. He weighs deontology (torture treats persons as mere means) and virtue ethics (it degrades torturers like Agent Burke) against the utilitarian case, and shows the show itself refutes the argument: torture didn't get Fayed's bombs, innocents like Audrey Raines get caught, torturers are ruined, and Shue himself recanted - so the sanitized ticking-bomb fantasy misrepresents real, degrading torture.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 24 "NOTES" — Becky Vartabedian uses W. D. Ross's agent-specific ethics of prima facie duties to evaluate Michael's betrayal at the dock. She lays out Ross's six duties—fidelity, gratitude, justice, beneficence, self-improvement, noninjury—and argues Michael's role as Walt's father makes beneficence his 'actual duty,' overriding fidelity and noninjury to Jack, Kate, and Sawyer. Because overridden duties do not vanish, Michael incurs guilt and owes amends (he is also implicated in the deaths of Libby and Ana Lucia), which Ross calls the 'moral risk' of choosing between competing prima facie duties; Locke's refusal to push the button is read as a duty of self-improvement whose rightness still depends on the intervening facts.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 20 "Pragmatist Ethics with John Dewey, Horton, and the Lorax" — Alexander contrasts Dewey's reflective, character-centered ethics with utilitarianism and Kantian deontology using the Lorax and Horton. The Once-ler is cast as the shortsighted 'utilitarian' maximizing Thneed happiness while the Lorax, urging us to 'stop and think' about the whole ecosystem, is really a Deweyan practicing reflective morality and deliberation as 'dramatic rehearsal.' Horton's conscientious care for the Whos illustrates Dewey's 'Who Factor' and growth of character rather than cold rule-following, showing morality as the ongoing education of desire toward inclusive, shared ends.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 24 "MOTHERHOOD" — Kevin and Janet Elliott argue that letting infants 'cry it out' (as advocated by Ferber and Weissbluth) is ethically problematic because all three major ethical theories – utilitarianism, deontology, and virtue ethics – condemn causing a child extended distress absent overriding reasons, with virtue ethics' compassion making the strongest case. They rebut claims that the crying causes little suffering and that co-sleeping is unsafe or ruins parental sleep, concluding that co-sleeping (historically near-universal) is often the ethically preferable alternative while stressing that the right choice varies by family and child.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 12 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Dylan Ryder (a working porn star) and Dave Monroe argue that being a porn performer does not necessarily lower the prudential quality of one's life, against the common-sense view (fed by films like Boogie Nights) that porn stars are damaged, coerced, or degraded. They reject Aristotle's claim that virtue is necessary for eudaimonia and, citing Kant's deontology and utilitarianism as theories that sever welfare from morality, distinguish moral value from subjective wellbeing. Deploying the 'Happy Slave' thought experiment and Ron Amundson's disability-welfare research, they contend outsiders' pity reflects social stigma, not the performer's own first-personal welfare judgment.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 26 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Gavrielides argues that going along with the Santa custom (leaving cookies, filling stockings, providing 'evidence') genuinely is lying, but that it is not wrong. She tests three ethical frameworks: a Kantian deontological analysis (with the 'murderer at the door' case) makes the lie at best 'wrong but permissible,' failing to capture parents' intuition of innocence; a Millian utilitarian analysis reduces character to a mere tool for good action; only virtue ethics, grounded in Plato's Republic account of edifying storytelling and Aristotelian character formation, captures why Santa stories are good — they cultivate kindness, charity, and self-reflection, and the myth is self-destructing as children's critical thought naturally dismantles it.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 12 "Who is Who" — This chapter tests the Doctor's ethics against consequentialism and Kantian/Nagelian deontology, arguing both fail because his alien longevity and time-travelling relation to consequences resist algorithmic moral judgment ('School Reunion,' 'Attack of the Cybermen'). It proposes instead de Beauvoir's 'ethics of ambiguity' rooted in Romanticism and Sartrean radical freedom and bad faith (the student anecdote; Turlough refusing the Enlightenment diamond), casting the Doctor as a Promethean figure who liberates companions into risky self-perfection.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 28 "So, Case Closed – Right" — Mark White asks why Batman doesn't kill the Joker, using the question to contrast utilitarianism (kill one to save the Joker's future victims) with deontology (killing is wrong regardless of consequences), and Batman's own agent-centered refusal. He runs Foot and Thomson's trolley problem and the transplant surgeon case, then modifies them: the Joker is the guilty one who created the danger, his future victims are uncertain, and killing him would be 'prepunishment' for crimes not yet committed. White, a self-described deontologist, concludes the case is genuinely hard and admits great good might have come from killing the Joker, using comics as thought experiments about killing to prevent future killing.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 29 "“Who watches the watchmen ”" — J. Robert Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as an apparent consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) who sacrifices millions of New Yorkers for the greater good, and Rorschach as an apparent deontologist ('I shall not compromise'), then argues neither is true to his stated theory. Utilitarianism is critiqued through Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ever ends' (the infinite future defeats the calculus) and its trouble grounding rights, while Rorschach's hypocritical, dichotomous, disrespect-for-persons stance is shown to be fascism, not Kant's categorical imperative (universalization and treating persons as ends). Loftis contends the deeper target is authoritarianism itself: the corrupt superheroes show that ethical theories are rationalizations of power, so no one should be entrusted with too much of it.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 41 "It’s Not That Simple" — O'Mathuna uses 24's Jack Bauer to stage the ethics of torture through the "ticking bomb" argument. He frames it with deontology (torture treats persons as mere means), utilitarianism (Shue's ticking-bomb calculus, Mike Novick's "a few may die to save millions"), and virtue ethics (what torture does to Jack and Agent Burke). Marshalling the UN Convention, evidence that torture usually fails (Jack endures Chinese torture; Fayed is tricked, not broken), and its spread to innocents like Audrey Raines, he concludes the sanitized fictional case misrepresents torture's real degradation.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 11 "9. The Handmaid’s Tale as Philosophy Autonomy and Reproductive Freedom" — Robison-Greene argues that Gilead's core wrong is denying women autonomy, reducing them from Kantian moral agents to moral patients — walking incubators. She uses Frankfurt's theory of personhood (second-order desires and volitions about what we care about) to show how Gilead dismantles a woman's will by restricting first-order options, language, and critical thinking, so Offred's Scrabble tiles and forbidden reading become acts of reclaimed autonomy. She situates the Sons of Jacob's 'feminine function' ideology in Plato's Republic classes, Aristotle's natural slaves and History of Animals, Aquinas's natural-law subordination of women, and Malebranche's brain-fiber claims, contrasting Beauvoir's complicity of women and framing forced reproduction as the deontology-versus-consequentialism clash over whether species survival could ever justify treating women as mere means.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 81 "76. The Last of Us as Moral Philosophy Teleological Particularism and Why Joel Is Not a Villain" — Horn takes The Last of Us as moral philosophy, arguing Joel is read as a villain only because players assume consequentialism or deontology. On Bentham/Mill's utilitarianism Joel fails to maximize utility by killing many to save Ellie; on Kant's categorical imperative his lying, stealing and killing are always impermissible. Horn instead defends 'teleological particularism' — an agent acts rightly when acting in conformity with a role, roles being socially constructed and variable — so Joel's role as Ellie's surrogate father (mirrored in his carrying her out as he carried Sarah, and the 'Future Days' lyric) obligates him to put her above humanity. On this view Joel's refusal to let the Fireflies kill Ellie, and his final lie, are morally permissible, not villainous.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 13 "4. The Good of the Doctor" — The chapter distinguishes aesthetic 'good' (taste, beauty of the Daleks) from ethical 'good,' then tests the Doctor against the major moral theories: utilitarianism (rejected when Sarah Jane urges exterminating the Daleks in 'Genesis of the Daleks'), Kantian duty ethics (the Doctor's 'never met anyone who wasn't important' and attempts to save Davros and the Master), virtue ethics (the Eleventh Doctor guarding Christmas in 'The Time of the Doctor'), and feminist care ethics. Concluding that none quite fits because the Doctor values non-rational beings and feels compassion, the author proposes the Doctor follows Wolterstorff's 'ethic of need'—justice as meeting the needs of all—consistent with 'getting in the thick of things' as a flâneur.

### Justice as Fairness

Justice as fairness is the name John Rawls gave to his theory of a just society, developed most fully in A Theory of Justice. Its core is that principles of justice are those that free and equal persons would agree to under fair conditions, modeled by the original position and the veil of ignorance. Rawls proposed two main principles: each person is guaranteed an extensive scheme of equal basic liberties, and social and economic inequalities are permissible only if they attach to positions open to all and work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged. The theory offered a systematic liberal alternative to utilitarianism and reshaped political philosophy in the late twentieth century.

- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 17 "Mr. Rawls and the Decision Procedure" — Joseph Ulatowski uses Mr. Blonde's torture of Marvin to test theories of punishment. He argues Blonde is not a mere psychopath but a retributivist within his social code—punishing clerks who 'touched the alarm' and cops who violated Mill's harm principle—while distinguishing acting on a principle from merely acting in accordance with one, since Blonde acts from sadistic urges. After reviewing Kant's lex talionis and the utilitarian theory's flaws, he asks whether Hart and Sterba's Rawlsian 'retributivism as fairness', whose principles are chosen behind a veil of ignorance, could justify Blonde's actions, concluding Blonde could not by his own lights have done otherwise than punish.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 24 "What Is Justice" — Johnny Huss extracts multiple theories of justice from 'Jacob Green'—desert (traced to Plato's Republic), equal treatment, conventionalism, and systemic injustice—and argues that desert collapses once responsibility is pushed back to factors beyond our control (Cash's God-given voice, the 'victim of the times'). Rawls's veil of ignorance supplies the standard for judging institutions: since anyone could be Jacob Green, we could not accept principles that let anyone 'get done like Jacob Green got done.' The chapter extends this to social justice for Native Americans via 'The Ballad of Ira Hayes' and 'As Long as the Grass Shall Grow,' including the flooded Cornplanter Tract, and closes insisting justice requires action, not just principles.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 18 "Go Slowly" — Wittkower frames In Rainbows' pay-what-you-want release with Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry: music is expressive communication awkwardly trapped in commodity form — even 'Happy Birthday' has an owner until 2030 — and digital distribution is finally tearing that frame down. He then applies Rawls's justice as fairness to music distribution: the first principle now supports everyone's liberty to listen, rip, and share, because viable alternative models mean restricting listeners can no longer be justified as necessary to artists; and the difference principle, with the sadists-objection to utilitarian aggregation, shows that how benefits are distributed among persons matters, which he extends to racial wealth gaps and the affirmative-action dilemma. His conclusion is that we must 'go slowly': listeners' rights to their culture outweigh labels' legitimate profit expectations, the way emancipation outweighed plantation business models, and labels must adapt into service providers rather than gatekeepers.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 23 "The Politics of Difference" — Debra Jackson argues that despite its ethnic and gender stereotypes the Warcraft universe is structurally a Rawlsian liberal utopia: designers choose class balance behind a veil of ignorance, racial traits are symmetric, professions are open to all, and a difference principle guarantees even the most disadvantaged player a decent experience. Plato's Republic supplies the gender argument — as Plato made the soul rather than reproductive function the criterion for guardians, WoW makes gender irrelevant to gameplay. Yet players import real-world prejudice (anti-Gnome hate speech, female toons shunted into healer roles, mocked male Blood Elves), so structural equality never yields substantial equality: WoW is sexist and racist because we are.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 35 "Tearing Down Fenway Now That Would Be Offensive" — Mathis argues fans' contempt for ticket resellers is not about being overcharged, since resellers only charge what Fenway's scarcity market will bear. Following Rawls's A Theory of Justice, he treats access to Red Sox tickets as a public good deliberately sheltered from the free market by the random online waiting room, the five-year season-ticket list, baseball's antitrust exemption, and the 1924 Massachusetts anti-scalping law—all of which promote egalitarian access and a sense of community. Reselling offends because it exploits for private profit a good we collectively protect from market forces, as tearing down Fenway itself would.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 14 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Shaun Young tests Jeopardy! against equality as an 'essentially contested concept': Aristotle's proportional equality (treat like cases as like) seems to justify the winner-take-all payout as deserved, Locke's reward for the industrious explains why equal outcomes would kill incentive, and Rawls's two principles - fair equality of opportunity plus the difference principle - capture the show's identical rules and level playing field. He then raises harder challenges: Dworkin's equality of resources, Kymlicka's charge that the Americo-centric clue bank shortchanges minority cultures (with Quebec's Bill 101 as legitimate differentiated rights), and the capabilities approach of Sen and Nussbaum applied to would-be contestants who cannot operate the signaling device. Citing Isaiah Berlin's pluralism, he concludes that no final verdict on Jeopardy!'s equality is possible - and that spectators would not want one, since Jennings's seventy-four-game streak thrills precisely because of inequality between players.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 25 "Girls and Philosophy" — Ketcham sets Hannah B (Brooklyn) beside an imagined Hannah D (a Darfur village terrorized by the Janjaweed) to ask whether personal fulfillment depends on culture or on the individual. Rejecting relativism (which, per Alford, cannot even condemn suppression of belief), he turns to Rawls's Law of Peoples - five minimal human rights any well-ordered society must grant - and builds a thought experiment, 'Blandland,' a minimally compliant country where both Hannahs relocate. His conclusion: even Rawlsian minimum rights, under which life can remain Hobbes's 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short,' plus personal drive and the attitudes of others, jointly and indeterminately decide what either Hannah can become.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 23 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Robison-Greene argues Rawlsian ideal theory breaks down at Litchfield: Soso's hunger strike gets only cosmetic concessions from Caputo, Sophia's WAC human-rights platform loses to Taystee's realism, and Piper learns the council 'is basically bullshit,' showing how idealization made by the powerful ignores the lived facts of Mendoza's abusive marriage, Jimmy's 'compassionate' death sentence, and Sophia's denied hormones. Against taking a 'moral holiday' in prison, she proposes care ethics, with role-based duties sensitive to actual circumstances, as the morality that fits life inside, and suggests non-ideal theory may fit the outside world too.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 13 "3. The Magic of a Promise" — Alloy reads the whole story as being about promises - Westley's 'I will always come for you,' Humperdinck's insincerely made and casually broken vows to Buttercup, and Inigo's vow of vengeance to his murdered father. He tests conventionalism, using Rawls's idea that breaking a promise cheats on a fair rule-bound practice (illustrated by Inigo's rule-governed duel and the Battle of Wits where both parties cheat), against expectationalism, on which obligation comes from the trust and expectations created, as when Humperdinck manipulates Buttercup through her trust. Both theories struggle with Inigo's promise to a dead man, so Alloy argues with Searle that it is responsibility for intent that makes a promise, and defends his own view - against the Hobbesian consensus - that every promise is also a self-promise whose binding force is the promisor's self-respect: promises 'make us people.'
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 24 "13. Mustang’s Future Generations" — Courtland Lewis asks what Mustang owes future generations when rebuilding the Society, first showing that standard moral theories stall: nonexistent people lack rationality, cannot contract, cannot be treated virtuously, and utilitarian forecasting fails since we cannot know whether the Jackal's nuking of Luna might have led, in the deep future, to prosperity. Derek Parfit's Reasons and Persons then strikes: any policy choice creates a different future generation, total utility drives the Repugnant Conclusion (a maximally populous world of barely-worth-living lives, uncomfortably like the Society's Reds), and average utility yields the mere addition paradox (Mustang's Society is both no worse off and worse off when Andromeda's low-pleasure civilization is added). The chapter's solution is Rawls: the original position behind the veil of ignorance—where the Sovereign would not know she is a Gold—yields justice as fairness and maximin reasoning for the just savings problem, choosing to save more than is consumed; against Tim Mulgan's objection that this loops back to the Repugnant Conclusion, Lewis answers that real carrying capacities make the repugnant world impossible.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 30 "18. Oppression Pretty Much Sucks" — Reads I Feel Pretty through feminist critiques of oppression: Bartky's Fashion-Beauty Complex turns the desire to feel pretty into a parasitic scheme of creams and credit-card debt, Du Bois's double consciousness captures Renee post-head-injury seeing herself as beautiful against the world's verdict, and Freud's account of hating those most like us explains the Highlander-style rivalry between women. The chapter then dismantles Rawls's distributive justice via Iris Marion Young, arguing rights are not goods to hand out and that 'imagine everyone is the same' thinking entrenches privilege. The alternative is celebrating difference, which is exactly what Schumer's prettiness-as-self-celebration performs.
- **Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney**, ch. 10 "2. A Paragon of Righteous Virtue" — Allinson reads Gardner's novels, especially The Case of the Blonde Bonanza, as philosophy disguised as pulp: Mason acts from curiosity, compassion, and justice rather than utility, a 'pure Kantian or ancient Confucian' deontologist whose loyalty to clients ('erase ATTORNEY AT LAW from the door') functions as his own Categorical Imperative. The chapter's crux is the perjury dilemma of the Blonde Bonanza: Mrs. Winlock's offered false testimony would free Dianne Alder, which Mason twice refuses yet curses ('To hell with it'), showing that the plot's deus ex machina dissolves but never solves the ethical dilemma, while George Winlock's truth-telling-at-any-cost mirrors Kant's prohibition on lying even to the Gestapo. Socrates's better-to-suffer-evil, Plato's Meno reversal, Aristotle's rhetoric, Confucian and Hebrew filial piety in Dianne's character, and Rawls's justice as fairness all serve as lenses on Mason's virtues.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 27 "#WithGreatPowerComesGreatResponsibility" — The chapter weighs the #dangers of trial by Twitter — Tess's suicide attempt after a mob turned on her, Clara Meades killed over a war-memorial photo, the fundamental attribution error and echo chambers convicting the innocent, and Rawls's point that unpredictable, lawless punishment destroys liberty — against the #benefits, above all #MeToo as 'the beautiful flip side of #DeathTo' that finally held powerful abusers accountable when courts would not. Arendt's banality of evil explains both Garrett Scholes's bee-drone scheme and the ordinariness of the shamers: Parke's 'He's ordinary. That is the type,' and Liza Bahar's crowdsourced 'Fucking Bitch' cake show diffused responsibility enabling cruelty. The moral drawn is that anonymous power over others' lives demands conscious, individual responsibility for every click.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 12 "3 Sins of the Fathers Historical Injustice and Its Repair in lack Panther" — Almassi contrasts Rawlsian ideal theory (the veil of ignorance, justice as fairness) with Charles Mills's critique that idealization marginalizes actual historic oppression, arguing the film's characters seek Aristotle's corrective justice in a world already steeped in wrongdoing: the 1991 deaths of W'Kabi's parents at Klaue's hands and of N'Jobu at T'Chaka's. He works through the Museum of Great Britain axe scene as restitution, W'Kabi's 'you kill him where he stands' and Killmonger's 'I'mma make sure we're even' as retribution (tested against Walen's proportionality principles, with vengeance untethered from legitimate punishment), and Nakia's and T'Challa's outreach centers as Margaret Urban Walker-style relational repair, reading T'Chaka's concealment of N'Jobu's death as actively constructed ignorance in service of isolationism.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 10 "Notes" — Argues that Rawls' ideal theory rests on a 'strict compliance' assumption — citizens and politicians who pursue justice rather than self-interest — which makes his ideal society look like The West Wing, while House of Cards depicts the real one: teachers' unions fighting performance standards, Senator Haas blocking the omnibus bill for electoral fear, Jackie Sharp trading favors, and SanCorp's Remy Danton buying votes against Russo's watershed bill. The chapter traces the competing 'every man a knave' tradition — Smith's invisible hand converting the butcher's self-love into our dinner, Hume's maxim for constitution-designers, Madison's 'ambition counteract ambition', and Buchanan's public choice revival — and uses the theory of the second best to argue we must design institutions (publicly financed elections, balanced-budget and inflation amendments, a generality constraint) that assume Underwoods run for Congress.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 10 "Notes" — Kogelmann argues that political philosophers' ideal theory rests on Rawls's 'strict compliance' assumption — the West Wing picture where citizens and politicians pursue the public good — while House of Cards depicts the reality: Russo's zoning constituent, the teachers' union fighting performance standards, Senator Haas and Sharp's colleagues trading votes for self-interest. By the theory of the second best, ideals designed for selfless politicians misfire in a world with Frank and Remy Danton in it, so he recruits the older 'every man a knave' tradition — Adam Smith's self-love turned to public benefit, Hume's maxim, Madison's ambition-countering-ambition, Buchanan's 'politics without romance' — to redesign institutions against rent-seeking (SanCorp's purchase of votes on Russo's watershed bill) and politicians' short election-cycle horizons (Claire courting Senator Mendoza), via public financing and balanced-budget and inflation rules.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 13 "NOTES" — Foy reads the Great Revelation and the Vampire Rights Amendment as a test of social contract theory: Nan Flanagan's 'we pay taxes, we deserve civil rights' invokes the Lockean bargain of obedience for protection, but Locke's God-given natural rights falter when the Fellowship denies vampires souls, and Locke excludes atheists and never imagined vampires. The chapter's resolution is Rawls: behind a veil of ignorance where deliberators might wake up vampire or human, anti-vampire bigots like the Newlins and supremacist nests alike would choose equal basic liberties plus distributive justice — including limits on vampires' centuries of accumulated wealth — so Sookie's 'let the law do it' to Rene marks a pluralist peace no theistic contract could deliver.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 16 "What's so Bad about Performance-Enhancing Drugs" — Ryan evaluates three arguments that using performance-enhancing drugs is wrong, drawing on cases like Barry Bonds, Lyle Alzado, and Ben Johnson. The Against-the-Rules argument shows only that PED use breaks current rules, not that it should be banned; the Unfairness argument overgeneralizes, since sport is full of tolerated unfairness (better coaching, nutrition, natural gifts); and the Harm-and-Pressure argument turns on empirical facts and a paternalism-versus-autonomy debate about whether adults may choose the risk. She concludes no argument yet establishes that PEDs ought to be banned as inherently wrong.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 17 "The True Nature of Cheating" — Swain and Brand build a definition of cheating by successive counterexamples set in a fictional State-versus-Central championship. They move from breaking a formal rule for unfair advantage, to including informal conventions (the hypothetical pre-rule Bonds steroid case), to 'enhancing one's chances of winning' (a coach fielding ineligible players to level the field), and finally add a defeasibility clause so that convention-sanctioned tactics like running out the play clock are not cheating. Trash-talking within the rules is classed as gamesmanship, not cheating.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 20 "Crowning a True Champion The Case for a College Football Playoff" — Austin argues the BCS is unjust and that a sixteen-team college football playoff should decide the champion on the field, using the undefeated 2006 Boise State Broncos as his key case. He applies a merit-based principle of distributive justice, taking 'victory on the field' rather than economic contribution as the appropriate basis of desert, and invokes Robert Simon's ideal of athletic competition as 'a mutual quest for excellence through challenge.' He answers BCS defenders and academic-integrity worries (Gordon Gee) by proposing reforms that let sport enhance the university's mission.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 23 "Upon Further Review Instant Replay Is an All-or-Nothing Affair" — Smith argues that consistency in applying rules and their motivations forces instant replay to be all-or-nothing: either every play is reviewable or none is. He shows the two rationales—'get the calls right' and 'preserve the flow of the game'—each apply to all plays, then dismantles the reviewable/nonreviewable line by arguing neither the 'judgment call' distinction (goal-line and fumble calls are judgment-laden, field goals are not) nor the 'correctable call' distinction (every play is correctable, e.g. via replaying the down) can hold, using the Roethlisberger Super Bowl XL touchdown as a case.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 24 "Does the Salary Cap Make the NFL a Fairer League" — Collins-Cavanaugh presents the NFL salary cap as a model of utilitarian distributive justice via Mill's greatest happiness principle: owners and fans gain (guaranteed revenue and a fairer, more competitive league) while players lose relatively little. He then tests empirically—competitive-balance scores, playoff berths, championship distribution, and comparison to MLB and the NBA—and finds little evidence the cap actually increases fairness. Because the claimed fan happiness is not genuinely caused by the cap, the utilitarian justification collapses, leaving only the players' net loss against the owners' gain.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 29 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Hardman and Iorwerth argue that Olympic 'nation-swapping' should be judged by Coubertin's 'sincere internationalism' and Stephen Nathanson's 'moderate patriotism' (grounded, they note, in Rawls's justice as fairness), which permits a special but non-aggressive concern for one's country. They contrast the 'reflective national', whose national attachment evolves genuinely over time (the runner Wilson Kipketer settling in Denmark), with 'enlightened' and 'nomadic' cosmopolitans (Kenyan-born Qatari Saif Saaeed Shaheen bought for money, Jamaican-born Slovenian Merlene Ottey), whose transfers are economic and thin. They propose using Olympic Solidarity funding to offset the poverty that drives talent transfers rather than merely tightening Rule 42.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 15 "Justice, Power, and Love The Political Philosophy of Intolerable Cruelty" — Biderman and Devlin trace Intolerable Cruelty through three theories of justice enacted by divorce attorney Miles Massey and femme fatale Marylin. 'Justice as power' is Thrasymachus's 'advantage of the stronger' and Machiavelli's might-makes-right, seen in Miles's courtroom war-room rhetoric and teeth imagery and in Marylin's plan to 'nail his ass' via marriage. 'Justice as compromise' is Hobbes's social contract escaping the state of nature, but the film shows the Massey pre-nup's signing and tearing to be merely a mask for power. When Miles and Marylin genuinely fall in love, their indifference to each other's wealth becomes a Rawlsian veil of ignorance and difference principle—justice as fairness—though the cynical Funniest Divorce Videos ending leaves that victory unguaranteed.
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 5 "“Are You Watching Closely ”" — Foy and Dale argue that Nolan's Dark Knight trilogy stages a conservative critique of liberal political theory. They set Locke's pre-political natural rights and Rawls's priority-of-rights ('each person possesses an inviolability... that even the welfare of society cannot override') against a Batman who wiretaps all of Gotham, tortures, and kidnaps Lau, treating social order as the thing that overrides individual rights. Batman is cast as a Humean conservative who grounds authority in habit and custom rather than an imaginary social contract, invoking Carl Schmitt's 'state of exception' (the Roman dictator Dent describes) and Burke's non-elected natural aristocracy to justify the billionaire elite Wayne saving a liberal order from the Joker's nihilism and Bane's Marxist-Leninist revolution.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 11 "NOTES" — Deborah R. Barnbaum reads season 6's flash-sideways as a set of counterfactual conditionals ('if Sawyer weren't a con man, then he would have been a cop') and uses David Lewis's possible-worlds semantics and his ordered similarity priorities to judge which are plausible. She argues Sawyer-as-cop is a 'closest world' change of one fact while Jack-and-Juliet-with-a-son changes too much to be true, and she pairs this with Rawls's veil of ignorance and A Theory of Justice as a parallel counterfactual thought experiment governing how the castaways should ration scarce water and medicine.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 34 "21. That Unnamed Zone We Call Freedom" — Hooke reads Serling's ambivalence toward the State through the liberal–libertarian debate between Rawls's A Theory of Justice (equal rights and the difference principle) and Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia (the minimal state, wary of a central authority regulating personal life). 'The Obsolete Man' (the condemned librarian Wordsworth laughing before the Chancellor), 'Eye of the Beholder' ('The State is not God'), and 'The Shelter' dramatize the shepherd-paradox (via Foucault) and the danger of any state that crushes human dignity; freedom, like the Nietzschean laughter Wordsworth aims at power, cannot be defined but is known in experience.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 23 "Rebellion in Sala-ma-Sond The Social Contract and a Turtle Named Mack" — Novy uses King Yertle's tyranny and Mack's revolt to survey social-contract theory. Hobbes explains why turtles leave the war-of-all state of nature for an absolute sovereign, but Yertle, ruling only for himself, becomes 'no king at all'; Locke then justifies overthrowing him because a ruler who destroys his subjects' property and lives dissolves the contract. Kant grounds the contract in innate freedom, while Rawls's original position and veil of ignorance test Sala-ma-Sond for justice as fairness, and King's civil disobedience frames Mack's rights-claiming burp as demanding the contract be honored for all.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 47 "44. Gattaca as Philosophy Genoism and Justice" — Grinnell argues Gattaca depicts a society built on 'intrinsic genoism' and diagnoses it with Rawls's justice as fairness. He adapts Appiah's distinction between racialism and intrinsic vs. extrinsic racism to genoism, showing that Valids like Josef, Anton, and Eugene treat In-valids like Vincent as inferior simply for being In-valid, discounting all counterevidence. Using Janet Radcliffe Richards's 'separate spheres' argument he shows the caste system is either superfluous or unjust, and via Kitcher's 'life theme' he argues nearly everyone — Vincent, Irene, Anton, Eugene — suffers a low quality of life from having their theme thrust upon them. He concludes that Rawls's veil of ignorance and difference principle would dismantle the separate spheres and give everyone a fair, autonomy-respecting shot at their chosen life.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 50 "47. Snowpiercer as Philosophy The Danger to Humanity" — Marquez 'pierces the veils' of Snowpiercer to argue the greatest danger to humanity is humanity itself. He reads Wilford's authoritarian, precisely population-controlled train through Plato's noble lie / myth of the metals (Mason's 'know your place'), Hobbes's social contract against a cannibalistic state of nature, and Machiavellian ends-justify-means to weigh whether Gilliam's secret compromise with Wilford is morally acceptable. He tests the orchestrated revolution against utilitarianism's greatest-happiness principle (Bentham, Mill's taxation-of-the-wealthy, Singer's impartiality) and against Rawls's veil of ignorance and difference principle versus Nozick's entitlement objection and Aquinas's just-war criteria, concluding each character's actions can be read as 'just,' which exposes anthropocentrism as the real veil.

### Moral Luck

Moral luck is the puzzle that arises when factors beyond an agent's control seem to affect how much moral praise or blame they deserve, even though a widely held principle says people should be judged only for what is within their control. Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel independently drew attention to it: a reckless driver who happens to kill a child is blamed far more than an equally reckless driver who happens to hit no one, though the difference is sheer chance. Nagel distinguished several varieties, including luck in outcomes, in circumstances, and in the constitution one is born with. The problem is troubling because it suggests that ordinary moral judgment cannot be reconciled with the intuition that responsibility should track only voluntary choice.

- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 12 "The Mystery Solved" — Avery Kolers uses "Only a Pawn in Their Game" and its companion "Who Killed Davey Moore?" to argue that Dylan treats Byron de la Beckwith as a pawn: a poor white duped by divide-and-rule tactics, the psychological wage of whiteness, shame, and lynch-mob indoctrination into fearing a Hobbesian war of all against all. Against Aristotle's account of acting in ignorance, the chapter asks whether Beckwith's ignorance of his real enemies was culpable, concluding his bad moral luck (in Bernard Williams's sense) was manufactured by white supremacy and so reflects back on all white people. Dylan's refusal to name or voice Beckwith adopts Strawson-style objective attitudes, making blaming itself a political act aimed at the system rather than the shooter.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 21 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Michaud asks whether a prophesied savior can be a hero: since Lyra can succeed only in ignorance of the witches' prophecy (Dr. Lanselius's condition), either others keep her ignorant and she saves the world or someone tells her and she fails, so the outcome never depends on her any more than Iorek's eating of Iofur's heart depends on bear choice. Frankfurt's counterexample, recast with the Magisterium's Fra Pavel standing by to force your choice, shows one can be blameworthy despite being unable to do otherwise, and Fischer's guidance control, a reasons-responsive decision-making mechanism that is your own, checked across possible worlds, explains why responsibility survives absent alternatives. But Lyra's case exposes a flaw in that account: her success hinges on things she cannot control, so responsibility is shared among all who kept the prophecy secret, and heroism lies in character and self-sacrifice rather than sole control of the outcome.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 16 "If Only . ." — Bryan Pilkington applies Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel's analysis of moral luck, where factors outside an agent's control change how we evaluate the very same act, to Bill Buckner's Game Six error of 1986, alongside constructed cases of Jon Lester skipping the last page of his scouting sheet and a Fenway Franks truck driver who skips his brake check. Drawing on Nagel on negligence, Williams's notion of agent-regret (only Buckner, not Bob Stanley or Rich Gedman, can feel it), and a standard of reasonable expectation for a veteran first baseman, he concludes Buckner can rightly be blamed for the error and even for losing Game Six, though not for the World Series or for the cruel vilification he received. The chapter thus disciplines the fan's 'if only' blame game: a curse is never a satisfying target of blame, but neither is the situation instead of the person.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 18 "Luck as Anathema" — Eylon and Horowitz defend the maligned manager's excuse 'we outplayed them and were plain unlucky' by distinguishing genuine football luck from fluke-luck: unlike sprinting, where outrunning your opponent and finishing fourth is incoherent, football's rules constitute rather than merely measure the skill, and 'almosts'—Roritania City hitting the woodwork eight times while United's one sloppy shot goes in—show ability and success genuinely coming apart. The accusation that football rewards the undeserving then exposes the control condition of moral desert, illustrated by two assassins whose shots differ only by an intervening swallow and by a never-bribed referee who would have taken the money, so that the luck football manifestly displays infects morality and politics generally. Football is anathema to some fans precisely because, unlike life where luck also rules, it displays luck inside an activity explicitly designed to reward merit—yet the authors conclude that 'almosts' and the all-or-nothing scoring are also the source of the game's beauty, and nobody who loves it would have luck removed.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 11 "You Can’t Help What Happened to You. But You Can Make the Best of It" — Daniel Haas asks whether we can blame Dexter at all if his Dark Passenger is a compulsion formed by the shipping-container trauma he did not choose, and whether consistency then forces us to excuse the Trinity Killer and Ice Truck Killer too. Distinguishing attributive responsibility from accountability, he argues psychopaths cannot be motivated by moral reasons because they lack the moral emotions, and that it was sheer luck whether a traumatized boy landed in Harry's loving home and Code (Dexter) or a mental institution (Brian). Yet Dexter's critical reflection on and revision of Harry's Code, and his willingness to forgo turning himself in to spare Deb, Rita and the kids, paradoxically make him more accountable than ordinary psychopaths and even praiseworthy for his quest to become 'a little wooden boy' who is more human, even if he still deserves to be locked up.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 24 "Where the Bodies Lie" — Daniel P. Malloy uses Dexter to lay out the three kinds of moral luck introduced by Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel: constitutive luck (witnessing his mother's murder and being adopted by Harry, who taught him the Code instead of getting treatment, made Dexter a controlled killer while his brother Brian became 'an unchecked version' of the same child), situational luck (the choice between Brian and Debra in 'Born Free,' the forced kidnapping of Doakes), and resultant luck (Lila burning the shack with Doakes inside, and Dexter's mistaken kill of the innocent photographer Jonathan Farrow in 'Slack Tide,' which he meets with remorse and agent-regret). Against the thought that luck erases responsibility, Malloy argues that intentions remain fully ours, borrowing David Lewis's claim that attempted and successful murderers deserve identical punishment - so Dexter is answerable for every kill.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 16 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Dan Burkett defends Brody against blame for flipping the suicide-vest switch in 'Marine One' by arguing he was not free. On the desire-satisfaction view Brody freely avenge Issa, but via Locke's locked-room thought experiment (Carrie contentedly 'freely' staying in a house she cannot leave) the chapter motivates the libertarian requirement that one could have done otherwise, which Nazir's years of torture and brainwashing may have removed. The malfunctioning vest then raises moral luck - Brody is no better a person because the bomb failed - and since Dana's plea restricts his options just as coercively, the best defense grants Brody freedom throughout, making the switch blameworthy and his free choice to come home genuinely redemptive.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 14 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — McCrossin asks why Finn and Jake forgive Marceline although she tries to kill Jake, evicts them twice, drains Princess Bubblegum, and never shows remorse. Jake's change of heart ('my fear was based on ignorance') comes from witnessing her father Hunson Abadeer's cruelty and her abandoned childhood, so her bad acts flow from causes outside her control rather than pure choice. The chapter presses the remaining problem: we normally forgive the penitent offender, not the unrepentant one, and Marceline—unlike the moping vampires of Twilight, Underworld, and True Blood—never regrets, leaving readers to decide whether understanding without remorse can ground trust and friendship.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 38 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Reading Finn's first season as a three-stage hero's journey - winning the Enchiridion on Mount Cragdor, being tested in 'Business Time', 'City of Thieves', 'Ocean of Fear' and 'Henchman', then doubly confirmed when Billy recognizes him - the chapter extracts a working handbook of heroism from his stumbles. Its lessons: heroism needs reason as much as courage (thinking through the gnome 'illusions', knocking himself unconscious to beat the Fear Feaster), plain luck plays a real and uneven part in saving Jake from the ogre, retribution should be temporary (the ogre's returned dollar), and heroes must check their sources (Penny's con). The deepest tension is that justice and compassion, instinct and reason, violence and non-violence must be perpetually balanced - Billy's nonviolent way becomes its own injustice when Finn medicates villagers without consent - so a real hero is simply someone who never stops trying to hold the balance.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 18 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Altmann asks whether Dracula is blameworthy for his killings: John Martin Fischer's guidance control, Kant's reason-centered morality, and Hume's 'yay/boo' approval-and-disapproval theory (the heroes' anguish over Mina) all seem to condemn him, since the Count coolly plans feedings and uses his intellect for evil. But Nagel-style luck undermines all three accounts, because Dracula never consented to his transformation, lacks the conscience needed to even recognize right and wrong, and, like the holy-wafer-branded Mina, is fixed by God's rejection with no hope of redemption - so the chapter concludes Dracula is evil yet a victim of circumstance deserving no full blame.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 24 "12. Should We Really Care about the Crawleys" — Jones takes up the charge that loving Downton seduces viewers into admiring inequality, and answers that the Crawleys deserve our care because birth, not choice, gave them their position, so they should be judged only by what they do with it: Grantham paying for Mrs. Patmore's eye surgery, Violet throwing the flower contest after Isobel's challenge, the family gradually embracing Branson. He reads the show as a manifesto for social change through sympathetic contact between classes rather than Irish-style revolt - befriend the rich and their good nature will start to level the playing field. His own objection is that this makes change partly the responsibility of the less privileged, from Thomas being asked to soften Carson's homophobia to the poor being asked to be nice to the rich today.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 24 "13.
