Time to Choose" — Goldberg and Gavaler read the heroes' first-year comics (The Superman Chronicles, The Batman Chronicles) as rival moral codes: Superman is a "super consequentialist" out to benefit mankind - reforming the Blakely Mine owner, demolishing slums, buying back swindled stock - while Batman is a "dark deontologist" whose vengeance oath makes consequences irrelevant, waiting out the Joker's murders of Claridge, Wilde, and Judge Drake because catching the villain, not saving victims, is his duty. Mill's utilitarianism frames Superman's consequentialism and Kant's Groundwork - intentions over outcomes, the batarang blocked by invisible glass leaving Batman's morality untouched - frames Batman's, with moral luck the battleground: deontology shrugs it off, but Superman's powers let him smooth luck over too. On the opening dilemma, Superman defuses the bomb while Batman chases the villain, so the authors judge Superman's code superior because Batman's can let hundreds die without moral failure.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 37 "24. The Fifty-Third Card" — Writing as the Joker playing 'the fifty-third card,' the chapter trashes both heroes at once: Superman is an attention-starved show-off who could save people invisibly but wants worship, and Batman is a billionaire who pours his fortune into toys and beatings while thousands of children die for want of the charity he could give. The real punchline is our hypocrisy: we are only as moral as our circumstances allow (born in the ghetto we would steal too), we mourn pets while eating smarter pigs and buying chocolate picked by child slaves, and in The Dark Knight's ferry scene everyone would really have pushed the button - since choosing not to help kills as surely as detonating, 'we kill every day.' The only honest hero would drop moral pretense, do what he genuinely thinks right, and remind us that under the skin we are all clowns laughing as the world burns.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 24 "13. But Why Is Our World Better" — Tim Jones asks why Juliana and Tagomi are right to call the Allies-win world 'better' when our world also holds the Red Army's mass rapes in Berlin, Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and the Czech expulsions — a German widow or hibakusha who found Axis-victory reels could call them 'a better world' without being evil. His answer is a numbers-of-victims argument: Juliana's world duplicates our atrocities (the Heisenberg Device on Washington mirrors Hiroshima) and adds unique ones like the Nazi genocide in Africa, so our world is better for the most people — though its victims deserve the empathy and remembrance Obama showed at Hiroshima.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 25 "14. Reel Lucky" — Elizabeth Rard uses Thomas Nagel's moral luck to show that Juliana's heroism and John Smith's Nazi career are largely products of circumstances beyond their control — Trudy's death in front of her, being born German twenty years before the war — while Frank's interrupted assassination of the Crown Prince shows luck intervening mid-action. The twist is that the Grasshopper newsreels would give High Castle characters what we lack: evidence of how the same people act under different luck, so their characters could be ranked across timelines in a way largely immune to luck, where we must judge from actual conduct alone.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 20 "10. Multiple Murderer Emily Middleton" — Treats Snatched as a series of case studies in personal responsibility: who originated an action, who created the situation, and what was intended. Emily's non-refundable tickets and drunken night out are hers, but she did not kidnap herself, and the film's title card ('The kidnappers did bad stuff, too') lures viewers out of victim-blaming. Her shovel killing of Morgado's nephew and accidental spear-gun killing of his son are judged through Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics III.2 on acts done in ignorance of circumstances, excusing the 'multiple murderer' while showing how perspective and intent shift blame.
- **Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney**, ch. 9 "1. Is Perry Mason a Good Guy" — Muyskens asks whether Mason is genuinely good, noting his spotless record may be pure resultant luck: he never knows when he takes a case whether the client is innocent, as 'The Case of the Velvet Claws' shows when Eva Belter lies, tampers with the will, and even confesses to murder yet turns out to have missed. Using Kant's good will and Nagel's four types of moral luck (circumstantial, constitutive, resultant, causal), she argues outcomes alone cannot make Mason praiseworthy, then reads 'The Case of the Deadly Verdict' (his only loss, where he keeps investigating out of faith in Janice Barton) and 'The Case of the Terrified Typist' (where he engineers a mistrial for a guilty client) as proof that his commitment to justice, not his win record, is what makes him a good guy.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 11 "“Your Heart Knows”" — Argues that Disney's Mulan transplants a distinctly modern Western ideal of the authentic self ('true to your heart,' 'Reflection') into a Confucian honor culture where the self is constituted by roles and relationships, filial piety (xiao), and ren as the virtue that binds people into larger wholes — which is why the film flopped in China. The matchmaker debacle, Fa Zhou's 'I will die doing what's right,' and the family's shame show a culture where dishonor stains the whole family and even luck (the cricket Cri-Kee) fixes moral standing, conflicting with Western assumptions about individual responsibility. The chapter ends by noting Mulan now resonates with young Chinese viewers, asking whether the Western individualist self is a truth about humanity or a cultural export that, like the Huns, has scaled the Great Wall.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 27 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Tyrion - born a reviled dwarf who killed his mother, yet heir to Lannister wealth, wits, and Jaime's knightly example - frames Nagel's paradox of moral luck: his compassion toward Jon Snow and Sansa is constitutive luck, and his carefully run wildfire defense of King's Landing shows resultant luck, since the same prudent act deserves praise in one outcome and blame had it burned the city. Kant's good will, applied to Tyrion's protection of Shae as treating her as an end and never merely as a means against Cersei, is offered as a rescue but only neutralizes resultant luck, leaving constitutive and circumstantial luck untouched. The chapter ends with Nagel's shrinking 'extensionless point' of genuine agency, concluding we cannot keep both moral responsibility and the principle that we are blamed only for what we control.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 37 "a18.xhtml" — Jensen dissects Bilbo's run of luck - the fish that leaps to his feet mid-riddle, the drunken elf-guards, above all his hand falling on the Ring in the dark - using Aristotle's account of luck as the rare, uncontrolled coincidence of ordinary causes (an orc leaving the back door ajar plus a hobbit's six-meals-a-day girth). He then deploys Nagel's kinds of moral luck: Bilbo's constitutive luck (born a Baggins with Took blood, Rawls' 'natural lottery'), circumstantial luck, and resultant luck (finding the Ring, which he could not control but which dooms Sauron). Against Kant's good will that is 'like a jewel' beyond luck and Plato's 'no harm can befall a good man', the chapter argues that Thorin's dragon-sickness, the orcs' unlucky birth, and Bilbo's outcome-dependent standing show that praise and blame do - and should - reach beyond the agent's control.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 13 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — George Dunn tests Katniss's luck-saturated life against Kant's claim that the good will shines 'like a jewel' regardless of fortune, with Peeta's vow to 'die as myself' as the stronghold the Gamemakers cannot touch, and with Seneca's dictum that what Fortune has not given she cannot take away. He then runs Nagel's four kinds of moral luck through the trilogy: Haymitch's reaping-made alcoholism as constitutive luck, Rue's death sparing Katniss an impossible final choice as circumstantial luck, Peeta's rooftop words echoing unconsciously behind the flowers for Rue as causal luck, and the revolution's success as resultant luck without which Katniss would have been the destroyer of District 12 rather than its torchbearer. Framing the Gamemakers as Fortuna on her wheel, he ends with the berries: since Katniss can never untangle whether she held them out from love, defiance, or self-protection, even moral worth proves hostage to luck and to the opacity of our own motives.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 13 "The Hero’s Responsibility" — White defends Tony against blame for Captain America's assassination: spearheading registration in Civil War was a tragic dilemma, and Tony took the least bad option because 'if not me, who?' — telling Cap's corpse he sacrificed their friendship to save lives. Cap's death traces through Crossbones, the mind-controlled Sharon Carter, Dr. Faustus, and the Red Skull, not any direct act of Tony's; without foreseeability or wrongdoing, the chain of 'might haves' does not add up to responsibility, just as pushing someone out of a truck's path does not make you liable for the manhole they fall into. The motivation-centered lens of Kantian deontology and Aristotelian virtue ethics supports Tony (he gave up status, friends, and Cap himself), and living with tragic choices, as he does facing the Hulk, is itself heroic.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 22 "Notes" — Kitchen asks who is to blame in a Wasteland where Nux's 'We're not to blame!' is the standing excuse. Blaster's death in Thunderdome illustrates the problem of many hands — no one, from Max to Ironbar, was sufficient and maybe no one necessary — while Nagel's resultant, circumstantial, and constitutive luck seem to excuse War Boys indoctrinated from puphood. Applying Frankfurt's freedom of action and freedom of the will together with Susan Wolf's Real Self view through three hypothetical War Boys (Maniac, Fanatic, Addict), he argues Nux becomes praiseworthy when Capable prompts him to reflect on and revise his desires, while Immortan Joe, Slit, and the other leaders are fully responsible.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 33 "Where Do We Go from Here – Buh‐Bye!" — Southworth asks whether SNL's dumb characters, the Ladies Man, Celebrity Jeopardy's Burt Reynolds, Ferrell's Bush, can be too stupid for moral responsibility. Aristotle's capacity for decision grounds moral agency; the Merit View, sharpened by Williams's constitutive moral luck and the Control Principle, blames Ferrell's deliberately nasty Connery but not the hapless Reynolds; and Mill's consequentialist view of praise and blame as nudges for 'progressive beings' explains Stuart Smalley's affirmations and Gilly's scoldings. Strawson's reactive attitudes finally resolve the puzzle: pitiable Bush is no proper target of blame, which is why we love him, though making him so lovable may have helped the real Bush escape accountability.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 15 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Tallon uses the problem of moral luck (Williams and Nagel) to ask how blameworthy Peter really is for Uncle Ben's death: the Peter who let the thief go and the counterfactual Peter whose thief was caught at the elevator act identically, yet outcome luck makes the first feel like a murderer, clashing with Kant's Control Principle that only the good will has moral worth. Drawing on Williams's 'agent regret' and Susan Wolf's 'nameless virtue' of taking responsibility for consequences, the chapter separates culpability — Peter is guilty only of letting a thief go, with the intervening agency of the criminal breaking the causal chain — from responsibility for damage. Aunt May's own misguided confession that she caused Ben's death by arguing with him (Amazing Spider-Man #479) shows how virtuous people confuse involvement in a causal chain with guilt.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 16 "Notes" — Michaud puts Jar Jar Binks on trial for proposing the emergency powers that let Palpatine become Emperor and doom the galaxy. He weighs Nagel's resultant moral luck through a two-Lukes landspeeder case, Susan Wolf's virtue-based reply that equal fault can deserve different feelings, Kant's 'ought implies can' and the categorical imperative, and a Frankfurt-style scenario in which Palpatine's hypothetical mind-trick removes Jar Jar's ability to choose otherwise. The verdict: as a deceived, politically limited character trying to do good, Jar Jar is not guilty of the Empire's crimes - only of being obnoxious.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 22 "“Rebellions Are Built on Hope!”" — Eberl asks whether Galen Erso, who knowingly resumed work on the Death Star while planting its exhaust-port flaw, is culpable for the deaths on Jedha, Scarif, and Alderaan. A utilitarian defense (his flaw net-saved the galaxy, per the negative-responsibility principle applied to the Death Star II 'Clerks' debate) founders on moral luck — everything depended on Luke's impossible shot — while Bernard Williams's integrity objection, via the chemist 'George' case, condemns his betrayal of conscience. The chapter finally deploys Thomistic tools for cooperation with evil: because Galen's contribution was mediate and remote (Tarkin ordered the firing, the gunners pulled the triggers, Leia's defiance provoked Alderaan's destruction) and the weapon would have been built without him, his collusion is justified by the reasonable hope — the 'new hope' — of the Death Star's destruction.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 24 "13. Time to Choose" — Goldberg and Gavaler read Superman's first-year Action Comics adventures (reforming the Blakely Mine owner, demolishing slums, buying back swindled stock) as consequentialism on Millian lines, and Batman's Detective Comics year (letting the Joker's victims die while 'the time isn't ripe', the batarang deflected by invisible glass) as a dark, vengeance-based cousin of Kant's duty ethics. Moral luck is the pivot — deontology ignores it, consequentialism is hostage to it — but Superman's powers cancel luck, and in the opening Luthor/Joker two-bomb scenario Superman defuses while Batman chases the villain, so the chapter rules Superman's 'super consequentialism' the superior code.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 16 "The Breaks of the Game" — Davison analyzes luck and fairness in basketball, using Dennett's claim that the more skill (control) a player has, the less luck is involved, so luckiness is relative to persons and times (a fan's half-court shot versus Meadowlark Lemon's). Distinguishing fairness as equality from fairness as desert, and invoking Bernard Williams's 'constitutive luck,' he argues that the game's mechanisms (spherical ball, jump ball, many possessions, referees) minimize luck, and that famous lucky plays like Robert Horry's shot, NC State over Houston, and the phantom foul on Scottie Pippen do not make outcomes unfair, since fallible human refs are a necessary part of the game.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 10 "On Fumbling the Ball" — Fry uses fumbles—Tony Romo's botched hold, Jerome Bettis's near-disaster saved by Roethlisberger, Leon Lett's showboating—as psychodramas illustrating the fragility of the good life. He invokes Aristotle's worry that one cannot call a life happy until it is complete, and Thomas Nagel's 'moral luck' (the negligent truck driver) to argue our culpability for fumbling, on the field and in life, is shaped by contingency, so responses should be discriminating. He draws on Frankfurt on caring and closes on redemption through effort, luck, and grace.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 14 "Where the Rainbow Ends Eyes Wide Shut Karen D. Hoffman" — Hoffman reads Eyes Wide Shut as Kubrick's most optimistic film, tracing how Bill and Alice Harford are 'awakened' to the uncontrollable power of sexual desire and thereby strengthen their marriage. Bill's Kantian confidence—that principled duty guarantees fidelity—is shattered by Alice's confession of overwhelming desire for the naval officer, which exposes their fidelity as mere moral luck. Through the models, Marion, Domino, and the anonymous masked orgy at Somerton (where sex is impersonal 'bodies touching bodies'), Bill seeks but fails to feel Eros; the couple finally choose a consciously chosen fidelity, and Alice's closing 'fuck' insists raw desire belongs inside marriage, which Hoffman links to Kierkegaard's view of marital love living and winning in time.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Hoffman reads Eyes Wide Shut as Kubrick's most optimistic film, about whether marital fidelity can be chosen rather than accidental. Bill's confidence in his own and Alice's fidelity is a Kantian appeal - duty and rational principle over inclination - which Alice's confession of overwhelming desire for the naval officer, and Bill's night among the masked orgy, expose as vulnerable to uncontrollable desire and moral luck. Hoffman argues that by unmasking and honestly acknowledging these desires (and drawing on Kierkegaard on marriage existing 'in time') the Harfords consciously rechoose their marriage, so their fidelity is no longer merely accidental.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 20 "No Country for Old Men The Decline of Ethics and the West(ern)" — William J. Devlin argues that No Country for Old Men deconstructs the western's three ingredients (moral hero, comprehensible villain, redemptive showdown) and collapses the genre into Nietzschean nihilism. Where Shane's courage is legible through Aristotelian virtue-ethics and Kantian deontology, Sheriff Bell grows old and afraid, walking away rather than confronting evil. Anton Chigurh perverts deontology—killing on 'principle' and because he 'gave his word'—while his coin flips invoke Nagel's moral luck to disclaim responsibility, so the good/bad polarity dissolves and, as Ellis says, 'you can't stop what's comin'.'
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 30 "19. Can We Blame Jimmy for Being Jimmy" — The chapter runs Thomas Nagel's 'Moral Luck' argument on Jimmy, cataloguing his constitutive, circumstantial, causal-deterministic, and outcome luck (the con-man 'wolves and sheep' encounter, the Chicago sunroof children, the missed 1.6 million) to suggest we cannot fairly blame him. It then rebuts Nagel with a poker-and-wager analogy: since 'wagering on freedom weakly dominates' wagering on fatalism, we should treat character as cultivable through virtue theory's habits. It concludes that because nobody prevented Jimmy from changing and he has the resourcefulness to do so, his moral decline was unnecessary and blameworthy.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 18 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Dadlez argues Austen gives a formative account of circumstantial moral luck (Nagel and Williams) via counterfactual character pairs. In Mansfield Park, the indolent sisters Lady Bertram and Mrs. Price share a character but differ only in fortune: wealth lets Lady Bertram appear respectable while poverty exposes Mrs. Price as a slattern, suggesting Hume's 'virtue in rags' has a counterpart, 'vice in dishabille.' In Sense and Sensibility, Marianne and Colonel Brandon's Eliza share a warm, unguarded nature, but a forced marriage ruins Eliza while family support saves Marianne. Austen deploys counterfactuals in both directions, showing respectability can hinge on luck and thereby mitigating blame as well as assigning it.

### Death Is Nothing to Us

The maxim that "death is nothing to us" is the core of Epicurus's argument against the fear of dying. Since Epicurus held that good and evil consist in sensation, and death is the total absence of sensation, he reasoned that death can neither be experienced nor harm the one who dies: where death is, we are not, and where we are, death is not. The teaching was meant not as cold consolation but as therapy, freeing people from an anxiety Epicurus considered the chief obstacle to a tranquil life.

- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 24 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Bill Davis asks why Arwen would 'choose a mortal life' with Aragorn and why wise elves and men call death a gift. The Ringwraiths show that existence can be worse than death - undead kings whose frustrated nature is perpetual torment - while Socrates in the Apology, Lucretius, Sartre, and Camus supply reasons not to fear annihilation, and the elves' endless life raises Boethius's and Bernard Williams's problem of boring immortality (Camus's Sisyphus, Wowbagger the Infinitely Prolonged). He concludes that Arwen and Aragorn, uncommonly wise and loving, accept death as Ilúvatar's gift: she prefers a finite life of deep love, and they trust the old stories of a world 'remade' beyond the circles of Arda.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 139 "The Approaching Battle" — Introduces the chapter's Heideggerian frame: authenticity comes from facing mortality rather than evading it, against the Epicurean advice to be unconcerned since death is merely the end of experience and so happens to no one; death's imminence forces us to define ourselves and not live half-asleep. Harry, death-marked since infancy, lives authentically where Voldemort lives inauthentically, with Plato's dictum that true philosophers make dying their profession as ancient corroboration.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 7 "Not to Put Too Fine a Point on It" — Richard Greene asks why becoming Undead is bad for the one who becomes Undead and why we rank it worse than death, restricting himself to unfriendly vampires and zombies (setting aside soulful exceptions like Angel, Spike, Louis, and Ed from Shaun of the Dead). He tests Nagel's deprivation view (vampires gain infinite experiences, so nothing is deprived) and Williams's desire-frustration view (undeath replaces rather than frustrates desires: scotch for blood, pork roast for raw flesh), then Mill's better-Socrates-dissatisfied comparison and the thought that the Undead's evil nature makes undeath objectively bad. Each fails, so he concludes undeath is not objectively bad, only comparatively bad, and one might as well make the best of it.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 21 "Deserving to Be a Vampire" — Ted Preston asks whether becoming a vampire would be morally good or desirable, working through Forever Knight's Nick draining his lover, Blade feeding on stored blood, and The Lost Boys' promise that Michael will 'never grow old'. He argues vampires are not evil by nature: if they cannot control their hunger they are pitied rather than blamed (though we remain Aristotle-responsible for choosing to become addicted), and consensual, non-lethal feeding is no worse than mortals eating animals, since the bite only becomes murder by choice. Against Epicurus's claim that death is nothing to us, he uses Furley and Nussbaum's deprivation view - death vindictively empties our long-term projects like marriage or a career - so vampiric immortality genuinely preserves value, while the standard boredom objection fails because there are repeatable pleasures in a changing world. The thought experiment ends as moral psychology for mortals: since neither of us will become a vampire, live a life that would be worthy of eternity.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 31 "I’ll Get Up and Fly Away" — Ian Duckles and Eric Rubenstein use the community's losses of Pigpen and Jerry Garcia to ask whether death is bad, running Epicurus's argument that being dead is no experience and hence no harm, the tedium-of-immortality argument that eternal life would eventually exhaust every fundamental desire, and Socrates's Phaedo claim that death frees the soul to philosophize — which disturbingly implies Pigpen's early 'burn out' was the better fate. Their resolution is Heidegger: authentically confronting death as the end of all possibilities strips socially imposed values (consumerist 'keeping up with the Joneses') and frees us to create our own projects, so mortality itself is something to be grateful for. On this reading the Deadhead counterculture — rejecting 1950s suburban scripts for free love, psychedelics, and life on tour — lived Heideggerian authenticity, and it is better to fade away (like Garcia) than to burn out (like Pigpen).
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 26 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Greene applies the philosophy of death to Pullman's worlds, starting from the Epicurean puzzle that death is bad only if experienced, so it cannot be bad, plus the asymmetry puzzle about prenatal non-existence, then testing the Deprivation View (Father Gomez's bullet would rob Lyra of Oxford, the alethiometer, and love) and the Desire-Frustration View (Iorek's frustrated desires) against a universe whose dead do persist as ghosts. The world of the dead, with its harpies, eternal boredom, and the pain of leaving Pan with the Boatman, seems to refute Epicurus by making death a miserable experience after all. But the twist reframes everything: the dead who stream through Will's knife-hole to dissolve into Dust are choosing death over the afterlife, and since for them the good things of life are already off the table, death is not bad at all, which is exactly why they choose it.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 7 "Not to Put Too Fine a Point on It" — Richard Greene asks why becoming Undead is bad for the one who becomes Undead, and why it seems worse than death, testing vampire and zombie cases against the standard accounts of death's badness. Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' sets the experiential-blank frame, but Nagel's deprivation view fails because immortal vampires lose far fewer goods than they gain, and Williams's desire-frustration view fails because zombification replaces desires (scotch for blood) rather than frustrating cancelled ones. Mill's 'better Socrates dissatisfied than a pig satisfied' comparison also falls short since it yields only comparative, not objective, badness; Greene concludes Undeath is dreaded because the Undead do evil things, but no argument shows it is objectively bad, so one might as well make the best of it.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 21 "Deserving to Be a Vampire" — Ted Preston asks whether becoming a vampire would be morally good or desirable, working through The Lost Boys, Underworld, Blade, Forever Knight, and Interview with the Vampire. He argues vampirism is not intrinsically immoral: if vampires cannot restrain their feeding we pity rather than blame them, though with Aristotle we still hold people responsible for choosing to become the kind of being that cannot; and feeding need be no worse than mortal carnivory, since consensual feeding (Blade's stored blood, Karen Jenson's donation, Madeleine's offer to Louis) makes the bite more like dentistry with consent than assault. On desirability he weighs Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' against the Furley-Nussbaum claim that death deprives a life of its long-term projects and relationships, concluding immortality's appeal is rational and that boredom is not inevitable in a changing world. The thought experiment ends in ethics: vampire or mortal, a life's worth depends on choices, so live a life worthy of eternity.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 17 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Salazar takes Professor Farnsworth's cry that the crew's age regression in 'Teenage Mutant Leela's Hurdles' will end in 'a fate worse than death: pre-life! Then death' as a test of whether death is bad. Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' says death cannot be experienced, so the deprivation account of Nagel's 'Death' is needed to explain how death is bad for the one deprived of a valuable future - a dispute staged by Bender's suicide-booth despair in 'Space Pilot 3000' after learning his bending built the booths. The chapter then argues losing one's identity and values can be worse than death (Bender's and Fry's flight from career-chip assignments, the Professor's love of being 161, Leela's frustrated teen redo), closing with Frankl's Man's Search for Meaning and Leela's sacrifice of her regained youth: inner integrity, not erasing the past, makes life worth living.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 10 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Hauskeller argues Shelley's Victor was sane and benevolently motivated, and reads the 'playing God' warning (Whale's 'now I know what it feels to be God!', the Genesis tree of life, the sorcerer's apprentice) as a claim that crossing nature's lines is dangerous rather than sinful. He then flips the story: like the creature, we are children abandoned by a creator who withholds eternal life, so the real wrong is a creator's failure of duty and love - while Epicurus's death-is-nothing-to-us argument and the picture of a childless, static immortal world undermine the transhumanist case that death is the greatest evil. The chapter ends with Aristotle's mean: obsessive pursuit of knowledge and immortality wrecks happiness, which lies in discovering that our native town is the world and living in the present.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 67 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Clint Jones argues LaVey's Satanic Bible rests on a misreading of Epicurus: genuine Epicurean hedonism is not limitless indulgence but the ordered life of the Tetrapharmakon - don't fear gods or death, the good is easy to get, pain is endurable - together with the threefold division of desires, which reserves constant gratification for natural and necessary things like water, bread, and friendship. By licensing gluttony and every whim so long as no one else is hurt, LaVeyan Satanism fails as the pleasure-as-virtue philosophy it claims to revive, leaving its followers with base, unfulfilling pleasures that are, well, Hellish.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 73 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Magus Peter Gilmore closes the exchange: LaVeyan Satanism honestly embraces the selfishness most people already live by (sharing Ayn Rand's enshrined self-interest), and Epicurus's own letters to Menoeceus - on not fearing death, choosing the most pleasant over the longest life, pragmatic justice, and the need for natural science - show deep congruence with LaVey. Against Pitkänen on Eastern religions, whose reincarnation and karmic debt he reads as denigration of carnal existence, and against Jones's shaky-foundation charge (Christianity itself was a Hebraic/Hellenic mash-up), he concludes Satanists are proud 'Hell-raisers' celebrating the only life there is.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 11 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Brendan Shea reads Cohen through the three Hellenistic schools. Socrates's trial in the Apology mirrors the persecuted singer of 'A Singer Must Die,' with 'Everybody Knows' and 'Democracy' voicing a Socratic mix of empathy and pessimism about whether democracy can deal rationally with its critics. Stoics such as Epictetus ground the present-focused, resigned acceptance of loss in 'Hey, That's No Way to Say Goodbye' and 'If It Be Your Will'; the Pyrrhonian skepticism of Sextus Empiricus illuminates the narrator's calming, unresolvable ignorance in 'Famous Blue Raincoat'; and the Epicurean atomism of Epicurus and Lucretius - death is nothing to us, empty desires are unsatisfiable - underlies 'A Thousand Kisses Deep.' Hypatia's murder and Cohen's 'Joan of Arc' close the chapter: the examined life is an all-consuming, sometimes fatal commitment that is nonetheless worthwhile.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 12 "1. Reading the Signs" — Di Bernardo reads the religious language of The Walking Dead as sustained irony - a 'doubleness of sense' - arguing that the walkers, churches, and signs comment critically on faith rather than endorse it. He tracks the church scenes (the Southern Baptist church of 2.1 'What Lies Ahead' with its timed bells and sitting-dead congregation, Gabriel's Saint Sarah's where Maggie answers that it is 'just four walls and a roof'), the ambiguous 'sanctuary' and Terminus signs, and the comic-book Jesus (Paul Monroe) as a machine-gun savior, concluding that the scriptural promise of eternal life through consuming flesh and blood yields only undead life. Against Epicurus's consolation that death is nothing to us, and in the shadow of Nietzsche's madman announcing the death of God, the chapter warns against investing absolute trust in any signs - religious or secular - a warning capped by Rick biting out Joe's throat as his own 'day of reckoning.'
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 34 "15. My Zombie, My Self" — Greene asks what Walking Dead-type walkers are and answers with the Platonic method of definition learned from Socrates: place them in the genus undead (died but not at rest, neither alive nor dead) and differentiate them by differentia - corporeal, mindless, lacking superhuman or magical powers, still decomposing. Aristotle's hierarchy of life functions (nutrition, locomotion, reason) explains why walkers are not alive despite ambulating, and the standards of death (putrefaction, heart-lung, whole-brain, higher-brain) all certify that walkers are dead yet active. The chapter closes on personal identity - whether you survive becoming a zombie, as Carol's face at the barn and Carl's "she'll turn" about Lori presuppose - and admits the author chooses the self-interested reading that he could become his own zombie, for the sake of the scare.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 18 "6. You’re Gonna Die" — Ethan Mills uses the Buddha and Epicurus to show that Louis meets death with laughter instead of fear. The Buddha's diagnosis of dukkha ('dissatisfactoriness') explains the Blu-Ray player and cellphone bits - consumer desire just restarts the craving cycle - and impermanence frames both the Amia heartbreak that Dr. Bigelow reframes as 'misery is wasted on the miserable' and Louie's 'life isn't that long... it's happy math' reflection, while rebirth would only make things worse since you would have to repeat junior high forever. Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us (where death is, you are not) grounds Louie's 'lots of things happen after you die, just none of them include you,' backed by atomism - at death our atoms scatter - and by gods who, like Louie's maybe-God with no heaven, guarantee no immortality. The USO duckling episode models the payoff: comedy defuses our deepest anxiety about annihilation the way it defuses the soldiers' tension in Afghanistan.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 34 "21. After Death It Can Get Worse" — Sam Director asks whether Amazon's unauthorized changes to Dick's novel posthumously harmed him, and against Epicurus's Letter to Menoeceus claim that the dead no longer exist to be harmed, he defends harm as desire-frustration that need not be experienced (Childan's unknown counterfeit antiques, Juliana's deception by Joe) and can involve desires reaching past death (Baynes's Operation Dandelion warning dying with Tedeki). Since Dick delighted in the Blade Runner footage and wanted science fiction to thrive, the chapter concludes the TV adaptation fulfilled rather than thwarted his desires — he is no worse off, maybe better off.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 25 "13. Rick, Morty, and the Cure for Unhappiness" — The chapter diagnoses Rick's 'Wubba Lubba dub-dub' ('I am in great pain, please help me') as chronic Epicurean suffering and prescribes the tetrapharmakos, the four-part cure. Don't fear the gods: Epicurus's indifferent atomist gods versus Rick's atheism, his panic prayer in 'A Rickle in Time', and Toxic Rick's 'If god exists, it's me' as ego rather than argument. Don't fear death, since 'where death is, I am not', though infinite replacements make Rick and Morty fear each other's death rather than their own. The good is easy to get, so booze, Eyeholes, and Szechuan sauce must yield to water, friends, and family; and the terrible is easy to endure, as when Rick stops resenting Birdperson's wedding and finally turns himself in for his family.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 28 "16. Death Becomes Her" — Hendrik Kempt reads Drag Race's pervasive death imagery - death-drops, the 'lip sync for your life,' mirror messages, the 'Death Becomes Her' runway - through the philosophy of death. Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' and Stoic self-possession (Ru's 'pay them bitches no mind,' Violet Chachki enduring a tiny corset) explain why elimination, like death, gives no ground for worry once it arrives, while Socrates' 'philosophy is training for death' makes the show a workout video for dying - Socrates even dying fussing over a rooster like a drag mother to Miss Fame. Heidegger's thrownness and being-toward-death set up Sartre's radically free, future-oriented self - so voluntary exits like BenDeLaCreme's self-elimination and Charlie Hides's listless lip-sync betray one's own plans - and Camus's Sisyphus makes Chi Chi DeVayne and Roxxxy Andrews's doomed All Stars returns models of 'acceptance without resignation.' The closing weighs transhumanism's promise of conquered death against a DragCon-forever thought experiment, concluding with Ru's roast eulogy for Lady Bunny that love and irreverence, not immortal life, are the point.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 18 "Batman Forever" — Randall Jensen examines the boyhood promise Bruce made after his parents' murder ('I swear by the spirits of my parents... to avenge their deaths by spending the rest of my life warring on all criminals') and argues it is a backward-looking, deontological moral reason that consequentialism cannot accommodate. He then asks whether a promise to the dead can bind at all, weighing Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us against Aristotle's and Thomas Nagel's postmortem and unexperienced harms, concluding Bruce wrongs the living people Thomas and Martha Wayne were if he breaks it. From The Dark Knight Returns to Kingdom Come, Batman emerges as a man who can never fully keep the promise yet cannot live without it.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 13 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — O'Loughlin reads Walter biting off a nihilist's ear and the Dude refusing to walk out on league play as concrete realizations of ancient friendship: Aristotle's eudaimonia requires friends as 'second selves' whose shared activity (bowling in the friends' company) structures the excellent life, while Epicurus's Garden ordered life around simple pleasures and ataraxia, with friendship supplying pleasant memory and a kind of immortality after death. Because we moderns claim friendship's value without practicing its costs, the Dude's priorities look comic yet pierce us — and Donny's death, the Ralph's coffee can, and 'let's go bowling' become Epicurean commemoration rather than irreverence.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 25 "The Value of Finitude" — The chapter tests each motive for uploading to San Junipero and finds it wanting: Kantian cosmic justice fails because the resort neither rewards the good nor can punish the wicked; Tolstoy's cosmic-insignificance dread fails because a finite life can still be meaningful, and even Epicurus and Lucretius deflate the fear of death (while Nagel notes death's evil lies in foreclosed possibilities, and Williams's Makropulos case warns eternal life breeds boredom). Nozick's experience machine is the closest analogy, but the chapter argues San Junipero differs — residents know it is digital and share it with other conscious people — before Nussbaum's argument lands: without finitude there is no risk, so no courage, sacrifice, or deep love, which is why Kelly's forty-nine real years with Richard outweigh forever with Yorkie.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 44 "The Death of Death" — Reading Black Mirror's deaths through Bandersnatch's train ending, Be Right Back's AshBot, and San Junipero, the chapter uses Heidegger's presence-at-hand (Stefan's absent mother and rabbit remain present as possibilities he can act on) and Derrida's différance (the meaning of life and death is endlessly deferred as technology scrambles the presence/absence binary - Martha's simulated Ash, Liam's Grain deletions, Chris's guilt-haunted fiancée). A central section frames the whole debate as transhumanism - Kurzweil's three bridges to the posthuman against Fukuyama's warning that self-directed evolution replaces God - before Camus resolves the question of meaning: Kelly and Yorkie, like Sisyphus, create meaning by choosing their fate in a VR heaven that objectively matters nothing. Freud's Eros/Thanatos drives and Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' close the chapter's question of whether to extend, hasten, or simply accept mortality.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 40 "I think we've all arrived at a very special place, eh Spiritually Ecumenically Grammatically —Captain Jack Spa" — Miller uses Disney deaths to stage the philosophy of death: Plato's immortal soul and Phaedo's affinity argument illuminate Frollo's lust-driven plunge into hellfire, while Epicurus's atomism, his 'death is nothing to us' argument applied to Marlin's terror in Finding Nemo, and Lucretius's symmetry argument are tested against Coco, where Ernesto's forgotten 'final death' versus Hector's restored place on the ofrenda makes posthumous harm plausible. Aquinas's 'my soul is not me' grounds embodiment, Confucius makes Mulan's risking death for father, ancestors, and country a virtuous Confucian death, and Deloria's indigenous web of relations reads Mufasa's Circle of Life, Moana's grandmother, and Brother Bear's ancestral spirits.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 9 "Notes" — Mackenzie Graham uses Fallout 3's Project Purity - James's sacrificial death and the Lone Wanderer's choice among feeding the purifier with their own life, poisoning the water for the Enclave, or destroying it - to ask whether death and posthumous events can be bad for the one who dies. Against Epicurus's claim that death is nothing to us, the chapter defends deprivationism with the Megaton quest (the Lone Wanderer's desire to save the town is thwarted even if the rearmed bomb destroys it unbeknownst to them) and weighs Feinberg and Pitcher's ante-mortem person against the problem of the subject, using the Great War's redefinition of October 22, 2077 to block backward causation. The 'Blood Ties' quest with the Family's cannibals then raises posthumous wrongs: since no existing subject is harmed or wronged, the chapter ends by asking whether cannibalism is an impersonal wrong against personhood itself, on the model of respecting nature.
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 24 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — Kevin Fitzpatrick uses Vivi Orunitia and the self-aware Black Mages of Final Fantasy IX, who call death 'stopping,' to ask whether the fear of death is justified, answering that death harms only insofar as it frustrates a person's values, such as Vivi's morality, his thirst for knowledge, and his care for others' happiness. He brings in Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us because the dead feel no pain, casts Necron, who wants to return all life to a painless 'zero world' because fear of death has corrupted it, as a darker Epicurean, and weighs the deprivation objection, death cheats us of future goods like Chocobo Hot and Cold, against the puzzle of when death's harm could even occur.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 139 "The Approaching Battle" — Frames death as philosophy's ultimate question and contrasts the Epicurean advice to be unconcerned since death is simply the end of us with Heidegger's authenticity: boldly facing that death may come at any moment keeps us from living half-asleep, a view Plato anticipated by teaching that true philosophers make dying their profession. Harry, confronted with death from infancy, lives authentically, while Voldemort's flight from death marks him as the inauthentic case the essay traces through the Deathly Hallows death march.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 17 "The Office and Philosophy" — Tests the deceptions swirling around Dwight: Kant's two arguments against lying (universalizing the maxim 'lie whenever it saves face', and treating the deceived as a mere means) are set against Plato's noble lie from the Republic - Michael's empty 'Assistant Regional Manager' title may be a morally tolerable verbal lie because after 'The Fight' it restores their friendship, though it does not medicate the office as Plato's lie does the city. Epicurus' claim that only what is experienced can harm you ('what you don't know can't hurt you') is refuted by the thought of Angela's hypothetical fake love for Dwight: undetected deception is itself a harm. Finally Dwight's self-deception (believing the false promotion, Jim's telekinesis prank, the fax from his future self) is modeled by dividing the self - Plato's tripartite soul versus Descartes' simple, indivisible mind - suggesting cognitive science's modular brain as the better picture, and asking whether one can even wrong oneself.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 25 "NOTES" — Jason Eberl answers John's 'you just can't go around killing people' by asking what exactly is bad about death, weighing Aquinas's claim that life is a fundamental good against Epicurus and Lucretius's arguments that death is nothing to us — applied to Sarah's 'you're already dead' and to the victim shot on August 28, 1997, who loses only one more day of a doomed life. Feldman's ante-mortem harm and McMahan's deprivation account explain how Judgment Day harms people before it arrives, while Nagel replies that experience itself is positive however bad its contents, which is why the survivors keep fighting Skynet. Utilitarian ripple-effects, Kantian dignity (the H-K crushing skulls), and Marquis's loss-of-future argument all condemn the Terminators' indiscriminate killing, and the chapter ends with the T-101's 'I know now why you cry' as recognition that death is an evil because it strips us of our emotional attachments.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 18 "The Grim Reaper on Baker Street" — Glass-Turner examines death across the Holmes canon, opening with Kierkegaard's claim that death's explanation discloses the explainer's own inner being and pairing Holmes with TV's Dr. House as materialist puzzle-solvers who rule out the supernatural ('no ghosts need apply'). She weighs Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' against the wrongness of murder, then argues Holmes's pig- and cadaver-experiments coexist with reverence for the dead and hints of belief in an afterlife ('compensation hereafter' in 'The Veiled Lodger'), reading him via William James as open to more than the physical. She closes on Holmes's calm acceptance of his own Reichenbach death and Conan Doyle's later turn to spiritualism after his wife's death.
- **The Philosophy of Werner Herzog**, ch. 12 "Reflections from the Abyss Herzog’s Philosophy of Death" — M. Blake Wilson traces Herzog's philosophy of death and the 'abyss' across Grizzly Man and Into the Abyss, examining how Herzog frames human, animal, and self-killings and refuses the retributive impulse. Against Kant's demand that murderers must die and Matthew Kramer's purgative rationale for capital punishment, Wilson enlists Nietzsche's warnings about the drive to punish and Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us,' while contrasting Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' with the 'accountant's truth' via journalistic and bear-attack literature (Jans, Herrero) that accuses Herzog of a 'Hollywoodized' portrait of Treadwell. He coins 'vivicide' for the killing of a human by a non-human animal and questions whether Bear 141 committed murder or was merely a scavenger.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 21 "11. The One Truly Serious Philosophical Problem" — Doll surveys philosophical views on suicide to make sense of Bourdain's death, opening with Camus's claim that suicide is the one serious philosophical problem. She weighs Plato's Phaedo prohibition (we are the gods' possessions) against his allowance for extreme misfortune, Aristotle's view that suicide violates one's duty to self and community, and Seneca's Stoic position that a wise man 'lives as long as he ought, not as long as he can' — framing Bourdain's death as an autonomous choice.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 25 "Chapter 12 The American Diogenes" — Johnson argues Twain is best understood not as a religious skeptic but as an 'American Diogenes'—a Cynic of Christianity-as-practiced. As Diogenes 'defaced the coinage' to remove counterfeit customs, Twain uses 'sacred profanity' (honest, even profane speech that exposes phony piety, e.g. the swearing butcher, Satanic narrators in 'The Mysterious Stranger' and 'Letters from the Earth') to strike four counterfeit coins: superstition/special providence, hypocrisy, artificial 'Moral Sense'/conscience, and heavenly rewards. On death Twain matches Diogenes and Epicurus (annihilation is nothing to fear), and his self-description as 'Member at Large for the Human Race' mirrors Diogenes the cosmopolitan; Diogenes carries a lantern to find a real human, Twain a mirror to show we are worse than we think.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 26 "Chapter 13 An Epicurean Consideration of Superstitions in Mark Twain and in the Good Life" — Baker reads Twain's ghost stories and superstition through Epicurean virtue ethics, which holds that false beliefs—above all the terror of death—breed empty desires that block eudaimonia. Citing Twain's Autobiography passage that 'annihilation has no terrors for me' as a near-verbatim Epicurean line, and using Lucretius and Nussbaum's 'Therapy of Desire,' she aligns Huck's disdain for a useless conscience and his rejection of wealth ('being rich ain't what it's cracked up to be') with the Epicurean pursuit of simple natural pleasures. She notes a tension: by making tall-tale-telling and Sunday-school-shirking so enjoyable, Twain the satirist spreads the very superstitions the Epicureans would eradicate, seeming to work at cross-purposes with them.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 28 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Kover argues that anti-hunting animal-liberation thought (Singer, Regan) objects to hunting not because it alienates us from nature but because it connects us too intimately to it—to the cycle of eating and being eaten and thus to our own mortality. Using Ernest Becker's 'denial of death' and Paul Rozin on disgust at our animality, he reads vegetarianism from Pythagoras's flesh-renouncing purification to modern ethical veganism as an ascetic refusal of edibility, and cites Val Plumwood's critique of humans placing themselves outside the food chain, concluding with Petersen and Shepard that the hunter's acceptance of death affirms life.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 30 "GARDENING" — Campbell explains why Epicurus set his school in a walled garden on the edge of Athens ('Live unnoticed'), contrasting it with the Stoics' public Stoa: the Garden was a self-sufficient community of friends pursuing ataraxia through natural, necessary pleasures and philosophy as therapy for the soul. Drawing on Lucretius's account of prehistory in On the Nature of Things, he shows the Epicureans saw cities as a decadent fall—driven by the fear of death and the gods—from a near-paradise of proto-Epicurean friendship pacts, and read the garden and the locus amoenus of pastoral picnics as a recovered golden age. Diogenes of Oinoanda's inscription imagines a future in which all become gardening philosophers and city walls become redundant.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 15 "9. Blade Runner" — Using Blade Runner's replicants ('I want more life, fucker!') and Roy's dying soliloquy, Rowlands asks how death can harm the one who dies. He states the Epicurean argument (while we live death is not yet; when dead there is no one to harm) and answers via harms of deprivation, illustrated by Tyrell's imagined brain damage. Drawing on Wittgenstein (death as the limit of life) and Heidegger's being-towards-death/being-towards-a-future, he distinguishes weak (non-conceptual) from strong (conceptual) possession of a future, arguing death harms more those with more invested. Linear time and the ultimate horizon of death are what let a life have meaning at all.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 24 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Bill Davis explains why Arwen relinquishes elvish immortality and why Aragorn and Frodo accept death as a 'gift,' contrasting the Ringwraiths' cursed undeath (an Aristotelian frustration of their mortal nature) with genuine mortality. He surveys real-world responses to death: Socrates' calm confidence in the soul, Lucretius's and the existentialists' liberation through annihilation, and worries from Bernard Williams and others about the tedium of immortality, which Boethius answers with a timeless heaven. Davis argues Arwen chooses a finite life of deep love over deathless boredom, and that all three accept death trusting Iluvatar's love promises a world remade beyond the circles of the world.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 57 "54. The Man from Earth as Philosophy The Desirability of Immortality" — Berk brings The Man from Earth—about John Oldman, a 14,000-year-old non-aging man—into dialogue with Bernard Williams's 'The Makropulos Case,' which argues immortality must become boring and identity-destroying (the dilemma of exhausted versus radically changed categorical desires). Against these 'immortality curmudgeons,' the chapter argues John's mild boredom, enduring loves, friendships, and pursuit of knowledge show an immortal life can stay worth living, invoking Fischer's 'repeatable pleasures.' It also engages Nussbaum's 'Mortal Immortals' and Beauvoir's All Men Are Mortal (the miserable Fosca), which tie courage and love to finitude and sacrifice, noting John is only 'medically' rather than 'genuinely' immortal and so can still make sacrifices.

### Immortality and the Soul

Questions of immortality and the soul concern whether some part of a person, often called the soul or mind, survives bodily death, and what such survival would consist in. Dualist traditions, from Plato onward, treat the soul as a distinct immaterial substance capable of existing apart from the body, while materialists deny any such separable entity and tie personal existence to the living organism. The topic bears on religious hopes for an afterlife, on debates about personal identity over time, and on what it would even mean for the same person to persist beyond death.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 60 "Unknown" — This section catalogues the film's Christian typology, noting it was released on Easter weekend: Neo is the messianic 'One' (an anagram, and Greek for 'new'), Choi calls him 'my own personal Jesus Christ', Thomas Anderson means doubting Thomas and 'Son of man', his pod escape is a virgin birth, his hosing-down rescue a baptism, the Agents' temptation parallels the desert, and Trinity's kiss raises the genuinely dead Neo to a glorified body that flies - transfiguration and ascension included. Cypher is Judas/Lucifer, Zion the heavenly city, and the Nebuchadnezzar's plate cites Mark 3:11's 'You are the Son of God'.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 80 "Unknown" — The chapter presents the subway confrontation as the film's turning point: defying the crew's iron rule that one runs from Agents, and Cypher's 'realistic' sneering, Neo freely accepts death to save Morpheus, overcoming the fundamental fear that grounds the Matrix's power in both worlds. The Oracle's 'next life' prophecy is then fulfilled to the letter when Trinity - 'I'm not afraid anymore... you can't be dead. Because I love you' - refuses to believe in death, and Neo returns in his next life as the One.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 81 "Unknown" — The chapter argues the third postulate must be a this-worldly immortality: since no single lifetime suffices to realize the Highest Good, Kant himself (in Universal Natural History) imagined the soul reborn over and over as it climbs the ladder of human perfection, and Mahayana Buddhism's bodhisattva - who chooses to remain on the wheel of rebirth to enlighten all beings - matches the monkish boy 'Potential' and the Oracle's hints. The One accordingly appears in three incarnations: the earlier liberator who freed the first rebels, Neo's second life, and the third life glimpsed at the film's end.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 24 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Bill Davis asks why Arwen would 'choose a mortal life' with Aragorn and why wise elves and men call death a gift. The Ringwraiths show that existence can be worse than death - undead kings whose frustrated nature is perpetual torment - while Socrates in the Apology, Lucretius, Sartre, and Camus supply reasons not to fear annihilation, and the elves' endless life raises Boethius's and Bernard Williams's problem of boring immortality (Camus's Sisyphus, Wowbagger the Infinitely Prolonged). He concludes that Arwen and Aragorn, uncommonly wise and loving, accept death as Ilúvatar's gift: she prefers a finite life of deep love, and they trust the old stories of a world 'remade' beyond the circles of Arda.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 10 "The Failure of Our Attempts at Meaning" — Conard argues that Allen's films converge on one position: life is inherently meaningless because nothing in the universe is permanent, so only something eternal (God) could ground value — and God is a self-deception ('tradition is the illusion of permanence' in Deconstructing Harry; Rabbi Ben's 'blind faith' in Crimes and Misdemeanors). He traces the impermanence argument from Mickey Sachs's mortality panic in Hannah and Her Sisters and young Alvy's dread of the expanding universe in Annie Hall, to Lloyd's 'temporary convulsion' speech in September, Sandy Bates's 'Ozymandias Melancholia' in Stardust Memories, and Louis Levy's suicide. Since real value would require permanence, Conard concludes, Allen's characters' attempts at meaning through romance (Peter's 'I have to sleep alone tonight' in September) and art (Renata's failed faith in posterity in Interiors) are merely distractions and self-deceptions we need 'like we need the air'.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 12 "From Knowledge to Faith" — Lawler reads Crimes and Misdemeanors through Kant's problem of the Highest Good: Judah's unpunished murder of Dolores shows a world where the wicked prosper and the good (Cliff, the blind Ben) suffer, the scandal Job complains of, while Levy's suicide shows that a bare existentialist 'yes' to life fails without love. Kant's 'I had to deny knowledge to make room for faith' is applied to the film's two visions: the deterministic, dog-eat-dog world of science and Adam Smith's economic egoism (with Hobbes's war of all against all) is only appearance, not reality. Kant's gallows example shows Judah could have discovered authentic freedom by respecting Dolores's dignity rather than seeing 'the black eyes of an insect', and the postulates of freedom, God, and immortality ground Ben's not-really-blind faith — so it is Judah who is truly blind.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 11 "Philosophical Conceptions of the Soul" — Scott Sehon opens his chapter by cataloguing how central souls are to the plot: Harry, Sirius, and Dudley narrowly escape dementors while Barty Crouch Jr. does not, and Voldemort's Horcruxes split his soul into eight parts that must all be destroyed before he can die. He sets up the guiding question of what the soul is in Rowling's world, where souls generally survive bodily death, and announces a survey of philosophical accounts to test whether her picture is plausible.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 18 "The Dementor’s Kiss" — Argues materialism is straightforwardly false within the Potter universe, using Hermione's claim that a sword through the body leaves the soul untouched, and then taxonomizes the forms surviving souls take: Nearly Headless Nick's explanation that ghosts are imprints of wizards who refused to 'go on', Voldemort's bodiless state as 'less than the meanest ghost' after his curse rebounded on baby Harry, the graveyard echo in Goblet of Fire where Cedric and Harry's parents emerge 'more solid' than ghosts, and the Resurrection Stone in Deathly Hallows returning Sirius, Lupin, and his parents as 'neither ghost nor truly flesh'.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 20 "A Plausible View" — Reconstructs Slughorn's lesson to young Tom Riddle, that murder rips the soul and the torn piece can be hidden in a Horcrux, an act 'against nature', and argues that because Voldemort's intellect and magical powers remain intact while his capacity to charm gives way to rule by fear and his body becomes snake-like, Rowling's soul must be the sentimental one: our humanity, love, and moral conscience. On this view the soul is damaged by supreme evil and can be repaired only through remorse, which is exactly what Harry urges on Voldemort ('be a man... try for some remorse') before the final killing curse rebounds.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 21 "NOTES" — Steps outside the fiction to ask whether Rowling's hybrid soul theory is actually plausible, answering probably not: neuroscience shows no brain events lacking physical cause, mind-body interaction remains the classic obstacle for any dualism, and it is doubly implausible that an immaterial substance would be responsible only for our deepest emotions and conscience. The differing physical powers of ghosts, Resurrection Stone shades, and Horcrux-souls make the metaphysics even harder, though the chapter concedes that a fictional soul picture that vividly dramatizes what we care about needs no truth to make a terrific story.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 133 "The Integrity Objection" — Draws Voldemort's inversion in full: each Horcrux rips and destabilizes his soul (Hermione notes only excruciating remorse could reunite it, a pain that could destroy him), his attempt on baby Harry leaves him disembodied vapor parasitic on others' blood and limbs, in stark contrast to the feasting, affection, and romance of Harry's circle. The Godric's Hollow inscription 'the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death' and Hermione's claim that the soul survives whatever happens to the body ground the contrast between Voldemort's unmourned, mundane death and the honored, grieved dead - Dobby, Fred, Lupin, Tonks, Colin Creevey.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 141 "Reap a Destiny" — Reads the King's Cross limbo through Heidegger's counsel to choose a hero from the past and gain insight through dialogue with them: Dumbledore appears not as a king of that place but as the humble penitent, confessing his youthful hunger for glory, and the way-station evokes purgatory. The flayed child beneath the bench shows Voldemort's soul beyond repair - his fear of death drove the very choices that now give him reason to fear it - and Tolkien's remark that The Lord of the Rings is really about 'death and the desire for deathlessness' (Sauron pouring his life-force into the One Ring) frames the motif.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 142 "NOTES" — Argues via William James's 'sow a thought... reap a destiny' and Aristotle's account of how repeated action incrementally shapes the soul that Voldemort's flayed remnant is a character fully forged by choices, stuck with itself forever - a postmortem fate Heidegger's atheism cannot frame but Rowling's afterlife can. The section weighs Locke's memory-and-character account of identity, Kant's postulate that harmony of virtue and happiness requires an afterlife, and Pascal on why the immortality question must govern how we live, and ends asking whether Voldemort's evil is ignorance, as Plato held, or a cultivated appetite that only vice can satisfy.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 27 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Gareth Matthews contrasts Plato's serene Phaedo — Socrates conducting a seminar on immortality, death as the cure for life's ills, 'we owe a cock to Asclepius' — with Gibson's prolonged torture, while noting deep parallels: both men were condemned by large courts on religious charges (impiety, blasphemy) with political subtexts. Socrates in the Apology models facing death through Socratic ignorance ('to fear death is to think oneself wise when one is not'), and Matthews argues Gibson's magnified suffering makes Christ an icon of an atonement nobody could imitate rather than a model for our own deaths; only the Gethsemane prayer and 'why hast thou forsaken me' (read via Cullmann) can actually help a believer face dying.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 100 "In It for the Long Run" — Adds Reason Five — being moral always pays in the long run, where the long run includes life after death — arguing that a perfectly good and all-powerful God would not set up a moral order that penalizes virtue, so Peter Parker's virtue is guaranteed its reward beyond this life. It notes that Eastern reincarnation-plus-karma makes the same promise (the more virtuous this life, the better the next), and that since Peter, Uncle Ben and Aunt May would never water morality down, the morally serious are pushed toward these metaphysical guarantees.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 103 "Chapter 16 - Superman and Kingdom Come The Surprise of Philosophical Theology" — Opens the philosophical-theology chapter by mapping Superman onto Christ: Kal-El sent by his father Jor-El from dying Krypton in a rocket parallels Jesus sent by the Father to Bethlehem, both alien saviors raised as small-town boys. It announces eschatology — final things, ultimate outcomes, whether the hope for justice is an empty utopian dream — as the lens through which the graphic novel Kingdom Come will be read.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 105 "Hope, Obligation, and the Big Picture" — Argues whether Wonder Woman's "must" really binds Superman — whether he is obliged to leave the Fortress and fight again — depends on one's eschatology or big-picture worldview. It contrasts Christian theism's purposeful culmination with naturalism, whose outlook is fixed by Bertrand Russell's "unyielding despair" passage: accidental collocations of atoms, no preservation beyond the grave, and all human achievement buried beneath the debris of a ruined universe, heroism included.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 106 "Gloom, Doom, and Morality" — Works out naturalism's moral cost: no purpose behind our existence, no blueprint for life, Russell's hope that sensitive souls can love the tragic beauty of it anyway, and the Wilson-Ruse claim that ethics is "an illusion fobbed off on us by our genes," which loses its grip once seen through — like Macbeth's dagger. Against this it sets Kant's moral faith: morality makes rational sense only if we postulate God and immortality so virtue is finally rewarded, and the chapter concludes naturalism offers no deep basis for the life-risking duties a hero like Superman faces.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 108 "A Theological Basis for Super-Heroics" — Proposes that Christian theism's doctrines of heaven, hell and Christ's return resolve the truth/justice tension by grounding moral obligation in God's perfectly moral nature and guaranteeing that justice prevails. It rebuts Maggin's claim that faith in a power greater than ours breeds inaction: God works through human co-creators, so Superman still has a duty to do what he can, and the objective hope of ultimate justice is exactly the corrective that despairing Superman and tyrannical, fear-ruling Batman in Kingdom Come both lack.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 109 "Hope and the Human Challenge" — Reads Superman's return — "Up in the sky!", the crowd hailing "the second coming of Superman" at the UN — as the enacted theology of Kingdom Come: hope in a greater power revives a world "hungry for hope" and draws the other heroes back to the fray. The Spectre's charge to the preacher Norman McCay, "you exist to give hope," voices the chapter's conclusion that a supernatural eschatology holds hope, truth, and individual responsibility together in a way naturalism's unyielding despair cannot.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 36 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Observes that only Talking Animals enter Aslan's country when Narnia ends in The Last Battle, then critically examines Lewis's case against wider animal salvation: derivative immortality through human love (Sarah Smith's train of beasts in The Great Divorce), compensation of animal pain in an afterlife, Lewis's follow-Descartes claim that most animals are sentient but not conscious enough to feel pain or have a surviving 'self'. The chapter argues each point fails: the physiological evidence shows animals suffer, resurrection or God-given souls remain possible (Strawberry's transformation into a winged Talking horse), and a compensatory hereafter is still the most promising answer to why a loving God permits the fawn's miserable death. Aquinas's rational-creature hierarchy frames the Talking/Dumb divide, and the Hindu-Buddhist rebirth theodicy is considered and rejected as unbiblical.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 22 "Look Up, Look Up" — James Spiegel reads Dylan's God-haunted songwriting through philosophy of religion, sorting strong Augustinian-Aquinian providence ("Every Grain of Sand," "When He Returns") from the weak, risk-taking God of "Highway 61 Revisited" and "Joey." Dylan's moral judgmentalism combined with theological determinism makes him a compatibilist in Augustine's mold, while "Disease of Conceit" and "Pressing On" ("it run in my vein") press the compatibilist puzzle that Plantinga's libertarian power of contrary choice is meant to solve. Original sin becomes the "disease of conceit," and Socrates' Phaedo plus Kant's three postulates - God, freedom, immortality - ground Dylan's hope that "death is not the end," closing with Love and Theft's "Look up, look up."
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 21 "Deserving to Be a Vampire" — Ted Preston asks whether becoming a vampire would be morally good or desirable, working through Forever Knight's Nick draining his lover, Blade feeding on stored blood, and The Lost Boys' promise that Michael will 'never grow old'. He argues vampires are not evil by nature: if they cannot control their hunger they are pitied rather than blamed (though we remain Aristotle-responsible for choosing to become addicted), and consensual, non-lethal feeding is no worse than mortals eating animals, since the bite only becomes murder by choice. Against Epicurus's claim that death is nothing to us, he uses Furley and Nussbaum's deprivation view - death vindictively empties our long-term projects like marriage or a career - so vampiric immortality genuinely preserves value, while the standard boredom objection fails because there are repeatable pleasures in a changing world. The thought experiment ends as moral psychology for mortals: since neither of us will become a vampire, live a life that would be worthy of eternity.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 30 "Oh Yes, There Will Be Blood" — Rachel Robison asks why blood, of all substances, carries metaphysical powers in vampire lore - Elizabeth Bathory's youth-giving baths, Dracula's control over Mina once she drinks his blood, Sookie's bond with Bill in True Blood. Her explanation is historical: the ancient cardiocentric view (Aristotle, Empedocles, Chrysippus placing the rational center in the heart and making blood its product) plus Galenic humorism and bloodletting made blood the carrier of the self, so drinking someone's blood plausibly transmits bits of their personal identity, knowledge, and even domination over one's free will. She then tests the show's synthetic 'True Blood': either some essential property of blood (or of the act of drinking it) carries the power, or the legend is parasitic on our lingering habit of locating emotion and character in the heart ('hot blooded') - either way the myth stays credible because our metaphors of blood never died.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 32 "“They Have a Plan”" — Robert Sharp reads the Cylon uprising in Battlestar Galactica as Nietzsche's slave revolt in morality: enslaved by humans, the Cylons react with resentment and overturn their masters' values, just as early Christians did under Rome. The humans keep a master morality (Colonial polytheism, warrior elites, call signs like Apollo and Athena), while Cylon monotheism, doctrines of the soul (Leoben's sermons to Starbuck, Gina's suicidal faith), equality, and consensus government reproduce slave morality's move from bodily weakness to spiritual superiority. The New Caprica occupation debate among the Cavils, Six, and Boomer, and D'Anna's boxing, show the former slaves seeking not just destruction but conversion of their masters to a religion that makes Cylons equal.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 48 "Reap a Destiny" — Jonathan and Jerry Walls read Deathly Hallows philosophically: Harry's willing march into the Forbidden Forest is Heideggerian authenticity, confronting being-toward-death, while Voldemort's horcruxes and the maimed King's Cross stowaway are the inauthentic flight from mortality that ruins the soul. The afterlife scene raises the stakes of this life: by James's "sow a thought... reap a destiny," Aristotle's habituation, and Locke's memory-based identity, Voldemort's lifelong refusal of remorse fixes his character beyond repair, and Kant and Pascal supply reasons why belief in an afterlife transforms morality. Dumbledore's purgatory-like repentance, contrasted with Voldemort's fate, shows that our choices reap a destiny we must live with forever.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 19 "Encore" — Randall Auxier adopts 'I trust Phil' — Phil Lesh the bass player who hears the whole sound — as his epistemic principle for asking whether death is to be dreaded, staging the essay around interview riffs with Deadheads Dale, Robbie, and Cory. Socrates in the Phaedo and the Buddha's Four Noble Truths converge on welcoming death — samsara is the 'Samsonite Scenario', bad luggage your own wishing keeps repacking — while Hume's Dialogues make God's power, goodness, and evil an inconsistent triad, so immortality is 'not that cool'. Kant's postulates (God, freedom, immortality) and categorical imperative prove too rule-bound for creative life; Whitehead's self-creativity and 'objective immortality of the past' supply the real bass line: even God cannot unmake what you have played, and the properly Grateful response is gratitude for the chance to add your riff to the Acid Test.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 31 "I’ll Get Up and Fly Away" — Ian Duckles and Eric Rubenstein use the community's losses of Pigpen and Jerry Garcia to ask whether death is bad, running Epicurus's argument that being dead is no experience and hence no harm, the tedium-of-immortality argument that eternal life would eventually exhaust every fundamental desire, and Socrates's Phaedo claim that death frees the soul to philosophize — which disturbingly implies Pigpen's early 'burn out' was the better fate. Their resolution is Heidegger: authentically confronting death as the end of all possibilities strips socially imposed values (consumerist 'keeping up with the Joneses') and frees us to create our own projects, so mortality itself is something to be grateful for. On this reading the Deadhead counterculture — rejecting 1950s suburban scripts for free love, psychedelics, and life on tour — lived Heideggerian authenticity, and it is better to fade away (like Garcia) than to burn out (like Pigpen).
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 26 "Memories Are Made of This" — Randall Jensen asks whether Cash's hope of reunion with the dead ('Meet Me in Heaven,' 'If We Never Meet Again This Side of Heaven') is even coherent, using the 'One Piece at a Time' Cadillac and a hypothetical 1954 Plymouth to retell the Ship of Theseus puzzle about identity through part replacement. He canvasses Platonic dualism from the Phaedo (Cash is his soul, the body a rusty cage), the materialist hope that God can reassemble a resurrected body despite dispersed matter, and the psychological-continuity view that persons are 'made of memories,' ending on the duplication problem: if God made two heavenly bodies both carrying Cash's memories, which one would be Cash?
