On a Nietzschean reading the narrator becomes an Overman revaluing values, seeing conscience as the internalized lie of slave morality; on a Humean reading conscience is moral feeling (not reason), so once it is destroyed the narrator can still reason about right yet has no motive to act morally, illustrating the oak-tree and willful-murder arguments that vice lies in sentiment, not relations or facts. Boardman concludes both interpretations fit yet neither settles whether Twain endorses or lampoons the result—our horror at the crimes is what makes the story funny.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 19 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Florell and Wilson, psychologists, survey parenting through the nature–nurture debate, casting Locke's tabula rasa against Rousseau's noble-savage view of children, alongside Piaget and Kohlberg on moral development and Walter Mischel's marshmallow experiment on impulse control. They map the four parenting styles (authoritarian, permissive, uninvolved, authoritative) on responsiveness and control, argue authoritative parenting is optimal, and advise fathers to adjust discipline to each child's innate temperament rather than enforce rigid gender roles.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 11 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Gary Jobson, writing from a long racing career with no philosophical vocabulary, offers practical wisdom on generating the inner strength and courage to win: focus on the task at hand rather than the outcome, visualize the race, stay calm under adversity, and 'have fun.' Through stories of Buddy Melges, Ted Turner's Fastnet, and Dennis Conner's America's Cup comeback, plus his own collegiate turnaround under coach Graham Hall, he argues resolve (not luck) drives comebacks, and he treats leadership, mentorship, patience, and consistency as cultivated traits of character — an implicit account of the virtues a competitive sailor must build.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 24 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Geist, a conservation biologist, argues from physiology (elastin-digesting enzymes, B12 need), athletics (one-legged balancing for stalking, precision throwing), and the herbivore-like pattern of human speciation that humans evolved as hunters — a 'carnivorous herbivore.' He contends morality itself was born from hunting: because tools-as-weapons (clubs, spears) let an aggressor kill without retaliation, escaping natural selection's check, early humans had to invent social taboos distinguishing right from wrong. He contrasts Neanderthal 'rodeo' close-quarters spearing with Cro-Magnon distance throwing, linking spear-tracking to endurance running, language, and art — concluding that questioning hunting's morality questions our humanity.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 20 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Deal and Waller use Lakoff and Johnson's conceptual-metaphor theory to explain how we grasp Santa's God-like moral omniscience through human metaphors. Santa 'sees from above' (North Pole, flight), judges with 'cool' reason yet remains jolly, and – echoing Plato's Phaedrus charioteer and Descartes' solitary reasoner – masters his appetites and decides free of bias. His gift-giving runs on a 'moral accounting' metaphor where good deeds are commodities exchanged for presents and 'moral authority is parental authority'; they read A Christmas Story's BB-gun lesson through this frame and finally liken Santa's impartial, dispassionate sorting of naughty and nice to the impersonal law of karma.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 32 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Funke examines how the 'gateway' argument is supposed to work by treating it as a claim about weakness of will, split into two mechanisms. Motivational externalism—illustrated by Milgram's obedience experiments and Doris's situationism—holds that the illicit-market situation, not the drug, pushes users toward hard drugs, which implies legalization, not prohibition. Motivational internalism, using Michael Smith's contest between normative and motivational reasons and second-order desires, locates the risk in cannabis's creative 'analysis paralysis' and idealizing imagination; Funke argues that this imaginative value, like religion, is worth its risk and that neuropharmacology (THC's distinct cannabinoid mechanism) undercuts the internalist gateway claim.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 13 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Alfano uses the trial of 'Sunset Strip Killer' Doug Clark to argue that situational forces and attribution biases may have swayed his jury regardless of the actual evidence. Drawing on Milgram's obedience study, Zimbardo's prison simulation, Knobe's intentionality vignettes, and Haidt's disgust experiments, he shows how gender bias, pretrial media, and revulsion at Clark's necrophilia could distort judgments of guilt. He closes with Nozick's truth-tracking account of knowledge to press whether a juror who would have convicted anyway can be said to know Clark is guilty.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 15 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Howard surveys serial killers from Liu Pengli and Locusta through Gilles de Rais, Bathory, Bichel, Panzram, and modern killers she interviewed (Bobby Joe Long, Shawcross, Milat, Birnie) to illustrate 'practical moral skepticism': the thesis that one can know right from wrong yet feel no motivation to be good. She distinguishes this from epistemic moral skepticism and argues that many killers, often privileged or unconstrained, understood moral codes but were driven instead by power, sadism, fatigue, or anger, showing that a failure of moral motivation is ancient rather than modern.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 16 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Vargas argues that a psychopathic serial killer can be profoundly evil yet not morally responsible. Reviewing the clinical literature (Hare, the moral/conventional rule distinction, the 'mrah'/harm thought experiment), he holds that psychopaths are blind to moral rules and so, since blame requires understanding wrongdoing, cannot be blamed — the appropriate response is quarantine rather than resentment. He then separates evil from responsibility: to be evil is to desire others' harm for its own sake, and such evil, like being a jerk, need not be something one is responsible for, which is why psychopathic killers can be genuinely evil though not blameworthy.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 19 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Dietrich and Hall explain why fictional serial killers (Hannibal, the Joker, Dexter, Grendel) allure us. Curiosity drives us to seek explanations for the mysterious, but the deeper pull comes from 'co-activation' of fear and pleasure inside a 'protective frame' (the screen or page) that strips away empathy for victims. They argue humans are rule-following creatures who must assert selfhood through rule-breaking to secure freedom, so the serial killer becomes an alluring avatar of ultimate freedom — the idea of the killer, safely framed, lets us test how thin the veneer of morality really is, as the Joker taunts.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 22 "SERIAL KILLERS" — The Schechters contrast John Wayne Gacy with Jane Toppan and other female killers (Lydia Sherman, Carol Bundy) to ask what female serial murder reveals about human nature and the nativism/empiricism (nature/nurture) debate. They argue women tend to kill through poisoning and 'lethal nurturing' of intimates rather than phallic-aggressive stranger-murder, so female killers form a 'natural kind' that both violates and grotesquely exaggerates stereotypes of femininity. They conclude that serial killers, male and female, are also a single kind whose ruthlessness and egotism are a monstrous but recognizably human — and partly innate — reflection of our common nature.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 23 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Keegan analyzes Buffalo Bill's line from Silence of the Lambs ('It puts the lotion in the basket') to ask why it repulses us. He argues clinical labels like antisocial personality disorder smuggle in unexamined norms and focus only on behaviors, missing the deep-seated traits behind them, so psychopathy should be distinguished from ASPD. Using Habermas's communicative rationality — grounded in perspective-taking and reciprocity and, via de Waal, in our evolved primate sociality — he contends that psychopaths like Buffalo Bill, Ramirez, and Kemper have lost the communicative capacity underlying empathy, and our revulsion is our own communicative rationality registering that violation.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 24 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Terjesen critiques the 'lack of empathy' explanation of serial killing by disentangling empathy into understanding, vicarious feeling, and connection, and showing each either is possessed by killers or leads to circular reasoning (citing Deigh's 'mature empathy' and autism as a counterexample). Real killers like Dahmer, Rader, and 'Angels of Death' such as Cullen and Harvey act from sexual desire, rage, or even excessive empathy, so empathy shapes how they kill (intimate vs. distancing methods, echoing Greene's trolley/footbridge study) rather than whether they kill. He favors Kennett's lack-of-impulse-control and poor risk-assessment account instead.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 29 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Iyengar-tradition teacher Jeff Logan argues that yoga philosophy — mythology such as the warrior Virabhadra behind virabhadrasana and Hanuman behind hanumanasana — must be taught alongside asana, or practice becomes 'mere acrobatics.' Using the parking-lot and door-cutting anecdotes to show yamas like non-harm and selflessness ignored, and citing a childhood-diet study, he contends teachers should not preach the eight limbs but embed subliminal precepts in physical cues ('extend your legs straight and true'), so students come to live rather than merely know yoga's virtue ethics.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 17 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Kristie Miller asks whether any dating behavior—dating a sibling, a gorilla, or a blow-up doll—is genuinely 'taboo' in the prudential (self-interested, utility-maximizing) rather than ethical sense, using decision theory's notion of maximizing expected utility. She sorts behaviors labeled 'pathological' into merely conventionally pathological, pseudo-pathological (e.g., polyandry explained by resource scarcity and childrearing), and genuinely pathological (arising from malfunctioning evolved mate-selection modules like symmetry or MHC-odor detection). Because inclusive fitness and utility diverge, and using future-selves discounting and weakness of will (the stable partner vs. the bad-boy biker), she concludes that in some circumstances even dating a sibling or a gorilla can be the utility-maximizing, and thus rational, choice.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 7 "Introduction" — Thomas Fahy's editorial introduction frames the volume by comparing horror to his skydiving experience: both offer the thrill of confronting danger within a promise of safety. He organizes the collection's essays around morality, identity, cultural history, and aesthetics, previewing how each contributor yokes a pop-culture horror text to a philosopher (Nickel's skeptical reading of Psycho/The Birds, Morris on Kant and torture-horror, his own Hobbes reading of In Cold Blood, Lutz's Marx and Land of the Dead). He argues horror's 'play,' hybridity, and repetition let it raise questions about fear, suffering, justice, and the human capacity for violence.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 39 "36. The Godfather as Philosophy Honor, Power, Family, and Evil" — Belliotti reads The Godfather as a study of the irresolvable conflict between a nineteenth-century Sicilian value system, l'ordine della famiglia, grounded in honor and the accumulation of power within a fixed family order, and a twentieth-century American ethic of individualism and commercial success, arguing the Sicilian vision must wither in the US for lack of its sustaining conditions. He offers a four-part philosophical analysis of honor (a binding code, group affiliation, internalization, and disproportionate redress) that explains Don Vito's contempt for the assimilationist undertaker Bonasera and his willingness to risk everything (the severed horse head sent to Woltz) on a matter of principle, insisting through Michael that 'it's all personal.' He supplements this with a taxonomy of power-over as oppression, paternalism, and empowerment, and argues Don Vito's evils are morally sanitized so viewers cheer his revenge.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 85 "80. Detroit Become Human as Philosophy Moral Reasoning Through Gameplay" — Engels and Evans argue that Detroit: Become Human stages moral reasoning through the interactive stories of the androids Connor, Kara, and Markus, whose 'deviant' awakening they read through Frankfurt's distinction between wantons and persons with second-order desires and through Kant's requirement of the ability to do otherwise. Scenes like Markus scavenging a pump regulator from a dying android, the blood-on-hands visualization after his speech, and Kara protecting Alice force players to weigh Kantian, utilitarian, virtue, and Gilligan-style care frameworks. Through Alice's reveal as an android and the grieving-widower scene, the game makes an implicit anti-speciesist argument (via Singer) that beings who can suffer are morally considerable, and that agency and responsibility emerge through suffering and struggle.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 14 "5. Monsters and Evil in Doctor Who" — The chapter defines a 'moral monster' as one who delights in evil acts, arguing (via Jonathan Glover and Laurence Thomas) that Hitler-style evil is all-too-human, not alien. Using Hume's claim that action springs from passion, it contends the emotionless Cybermen are a mere force of nature (bad but not evil), whereas the Daleks, driven by hatred, tribalism, and a closed belief system, are genuinely evil monsters; the manipulating Master mirrors our everyday lying. It then examines retributive justice through Solomon's execution in 'Dinosaurs on a Spaceship' and 'A Town Called Mercy,' rejecting purely backward- or forward-looking punishment (citing Rawls on utilitarianism's injustice) in favor of the Doctor's needs-based, 'reprobative' punishment, mercy, and self-forgiveness over the Time War.

### Philosophy of Love

The philosophy of love examines the nature, varieties, and value of love, asking what it is to love another person and why love matters to a good life. Drawing on distinctions inherited from the Greeks — eros as desire, philia as friendship, agape as selfless care — it explores whether love is a response to a beloved's qualities or a commitment that bestows value, and how it relates to reason, autonomy, and morality. Central puzzles include whether love can be justified, whether it is under our control, and what it means to love someone for who they are.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 12 "The Noir Consequences of Sex Eros, Death, and the Possibility of Love" — Thomas Hibbs reads BtVS as feminist noir: like classic noir it traps characters in labyrinths where the past bears down on the present (Buffy torn from heaven in 'After Life,' Angel's gypsy curse in 'Innocence,' the psych-ward ending of 'Normal Again'), and it rejects both Enlightenment optimism and the Nietzschean beyond-good-and-evil self-creation Hibbs finds in neo-noir like Body Heat and Thelma and Louise. Sex in Sunnydale always carries noir consequences — Angel losing his soul at the moment of 'true happiness,' Buffy's self-lacerating Spike affair ending in his attempted rape — so the show is skeptical of sexual liberation while recovering a classical eros as longing for wholeness. The Season Six finale locates the 'true essence of magic' in sacrificial love: Xander's yellow-crayon plea in 'Grave' reaches the 'spark of humanity' in Willow where all force fails.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 22 "Emotions and Aesthetic Response" — Carolyn Korsmeyer uses BtVS to stage philosophy's ambivalence about emotion — dangerous passion versus intuitive sagacity — through three cases: anger as beast within and practical power (Xander's love spell in 'Bewitched, Bothered and Bewildered,' Willow's wish-spells in 'Something Blue,' 'My emotions give me power' to Kendra), grief as the one emotion no magic can undo (Epictetus's jug-and-child counsel set against 'The Body' and Dawn trying to resurrect Joyce), and love's non-fungibility (Anya's vengeance-demon past leaves her without the wider affection that makes singular love credible, while Spike's messy human history makes his obsession believable). She draws on Plato's wild-beast appetites and spirited element of the Republic, Aristotle on anger and emotional disposition as character, Kant's reason-above-nature picture, and Martha Nussbaum on art's particular cases. Finally she turns to aesthetic response: the show's comedy ('She saved the world a lot') regulates audience emotion, keeping the serial's catharsis from tipping into manipulation.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 23 "Erotic Love and Friendship" — Maps Aristotle's three levels of friendship onto Buffy's three boyfriends: Riley is a utility friendship chosen for the rational goal of a 'normal' boyfriend (echoed by Warren's robot April and the Buffybot, which prove programmed perfection cannot be loved), Spike is a pleasure friendship driven by passion and danger that Buffy ends in 'As You Were,' and Angel is a complete friendship where each values the other for his own sake despite the gypsy curse. This lets the authors solve Aristotle's love paradox (is erotic love chosen or does it choose us?) by adding Augustine's and William of Ockham's third power of the soul, the will: an arational faculty that values the other as an end in himself, neither rationally chosen nor irrationally caused.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 34 "Psychical Dynamics of Love and Lust" — Levine and Schneider apply Freud's 1912 essay on the debasement in love — 'where they love they do not desire and where they desire they cannot love' — to argue that BtVS succeeds not through innovation or moral seriousness but through the conventional 'girl next door': Angel's forbidden-vampire sex is the show's best because forbiddenness heightens desire, Xander's pedestal-placing of Buffy forecloses satisfaction, and Drusilla and Cordelia are already 'debased' sexual objects. Along the way they polemicize against Buffy scholars for projecting their own fantasies onto a show that reinforces, rather than subverts, gender stereotypes and the forbiddenness of sex for young women.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 17 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Jorge Gracia contrasts Sam and Gollum as two hobbits of the same nature and culture seeking the same happy life, so their success and failure are instructive for ordinary people like us. Gollum's happiness is solitary possession of the Ring - he murders Déagol for it and ends 'into the dust' - while Sam's is fellowship in the Shire with Rosie and Frodo, pursued through loyalty and giving (spending Galadriel's seed-box to restore the Shire). The pivotal episode is Gollum's trembling caress of Frodo's knee, 'the most tragic moment in the Tale', squandered when Sam's jealous rebuke drives him back to treachery. With Aristotle on friendship and self-love, the chapter concludes that happiness is achievable only in a social context and its key is love.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 18 "“Just What They Say It for I Never Knew”" — South argues Allen's signature old recordings from the American songbook are a philosophical device grounded in Aristotle: the Rhetoric's view that emotions carry cognitive orientations that reshape judgment, and the Politics' claim that music forms character, explain why songs comment on the plots they score. He reads Hannah and Her Sisters through 'You Made Me Love You', 'Bewitched, Bothered and Bewildered', and 'I'm in Love Again' — scoring Elliot's inconstancy, Mickey's 'You don't deserve Cole Porter' judgment of Holly, and her growth into someone whose new musical taste signals ethical maturity — and Everyone Says I Love You as a darker cycle where fantasy and finitude ('It's Later Than You Think') drive the compulsion to love again. The happy ending is precisely why Allen called the film a 'cop out': its music says love fades and is out of our control, while the plot pretends otherwise.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 19 "Humor and Philosophy" — Ascione deploys Schopenhauer's theory of laughter — the sudden, paradoxical subsumption of an object under a heterogeneous concept — as the framework for showing how Annie Hall's gags do philosophical work. The subtitled balcony conversation exposes the self-monitoring deception of new romance, the street-interview 'love fades' scene smuggles in the unpopular thesis that lasting romantic love is mythical (culminating in the dead-shark line), the grammar-school reunion raises questions about what shapes adult character, and the 'dynamite ham' dinner, the pastrami-on-white-with-mayo, and the California scenes diagnose Alvy's own New York provincialism. Because humor suspends judgment and deflects resistance, Allen can deliver social and cultural analysis that audiences would reject if stated straight.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 26 "Love and Self-Discovery" — Mary Nichols argues The Curse of the Jade Scorpion answers The Maltese Falcon: where Sam Spade's cynicism leaves society no reason to trust its lone hero, C.W. Briggs, unknowingly stealing for the magician Polgar while hypnotized, is saved by love, friendship, and the office community of North Coast Casualty. The jade scorpion's trance, meant to cover crime, uncovers truth, as C.W. and Betty Ann admit under hypnosis the love and fear their waking selves hide, so that 'crystal clear' memory and self-knowledge, rather than Spade's rejection of dreams, free them from both the curse and crime. Against the noir world and Lester's 'comedy is tragedy plus time', the chapter holds that everyone has 'a little bit of larceny' in them and that experiences of love, friendship, and community are what form the character that keeps it in check.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 38 "Snape and the Many-Splendored Thing" — Catherine Jack Deavel and David Paul Deavel open with the puzzle of Dumbledore's 'ironclad' certainty about Snape, maintained even after Snape kills him and attested by McGonagall's report that his repentance was 'absolutely genuine'. Their answer is Snape's unrequited love for Lily Potter, and they set the chapter's task: to examine, against the suspicion that redemptive love-talk is mere sentimentality, what philosophers have said about love's nature and its power to transform and to mislead judgment.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 39 "The Abandoned Boys" — Surveys the classical triad of eros, philia, and agape from Plato's Symposium onward and maps it onto the series: the Weasleys, Ron and Hermione, and Harry and Ginny exemplify romantic love, Dumbledore's remark that Voldemort never had a friend dramatizes the absence of philia, and Lily's self-giving love that repels Quirrell and Voldemort is agape. Because traditional accounts treat love as an act of the will rather than a feeling, Snape's persistent dislikes cannot disprove that his love for Lily has transformed him.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 41 "Snape’s Choice" — Defines love, with Aristotle, Aquinas, and M. Scott Peck, as willing the good of the other for the other's own sake, and reads Snape's double-agent life as love expressed in action despite real hatred: he protects Harry's enemies at constant risk while disliking most of them. His Occlumency, the skill to lie to Voldemort's face, reveals both strength and weakness, for rather than renouncing love as Voldemort did he only conceals it, and his dying gift of memories to Harry, revealing that Harry is a Horcrux, must be freely offered because his thoughts can never be taken.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 42 "A Work in Progress" — Reads Snape's love for Lily through Plato's Symposium: his childhood watching of Lily with 'undisguised greed', his failure to ask Voldemort to spare her husband and child, 'You disgust me', shows a love that desires Lily's good only as it relates to him, falling short of Aristotle's beloved as 'second self'. Diotima's 'possession of the good forever' and 'giving birth in beauty' describe how his love matures into genuine virtue, a deepening Pope Benedict XVI's picture of love as 'ecstasy', an exodus out of the closed self toward self-giving, completes.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 43 "NOTES" — Argues Snape's redemption is gradual virtue-building rather than instant transformation, since vice and virtue are habits built up over time and his resentments persist even as his actions serve the good. His doe Patronus, matching Lily's, manifests Aristotle's beloved as a second self, his remorse, an emotion he shares with Harry but Voldemort cannot feel, begins to knit his damaged soul whole, and Harry's forgiveness, naming his son Albus Severus for 'the bravest man I ever knew', completes the arc love began.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 45 "Violently Pink Products" — Gregory Bassham opens by contrasting Muggle spending on attractiveness with the wizarding world's far more reliable magical love potions, and poses the ethical problem of their nonconsensual use. The chapter's test cases are the two key episodes: Merope Gaunt's use of a love potion to ensnare Tom Riddle Sr., Voldemort's father, and her eventual choice to stop dosing him at great cost to herself and her unborn son.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 46 "Little Hangleton" — Catalogues what Half-Blood Prince establishes about love potions: Fred and George sell them legally at Weasleys' Wizard Wheezes, Hermione identifies Amortentia by its mother-of-pearl sheen and personal smell, and Slughorn warns it 'doesn't really create love... It is impossible to manufacture or imitate love', producing only obsessive infatuation, as Ron's Romilda Vane episode demonstrates. The section ends by introducing Voldemort's mother as the person who actually used one.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 47 "Real Love or Mere Infatuation" — Retells Dumbledore's reconstruction of Merope Gaunt's ensnarement of Tom Riddle Sr.: Harry correctly narrows the cause of the squire's son's behavior to the Imperius Curse or a love potion, and Dumbledore concludes she dosed him, then chose to stop, wrongly hoping he had come to love her or would stay for the baby. The section closes on Dumbledore's insistence that this backstory 'has everything to do with the prophecy' about Harry and Voldemort.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 48 "Not His Mother’s Son" — Argues Merope did not truly love Riddle because the potion robbed him of the freedom to do otherwise, invoking Harry Frankfurt's denial that alternative possibilities are necessary for freedom and noting that even compatibilists deny potion-induced affection is free, since Tom would not have wanted to love her under magical inducement. Real love respects the beloved's true interests and creates a relationship in which both grow, and even self-administered potions wrong the user by forfeiting the moral growth that only uncoerced commitment makes possible.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 49 "NOTES" — Contends that Voldemort was not his mother's son: what defines a person is the habitual pattern of choices, as in Aristotle's 'we are what we consistently do', and Merope, who freed Riddle at the cost of her own life and renounced magic entirely, is a genuine though partial redemption, whereas Voldemort followed Marvolo Gaunt and Salazar Slytherin instead. Quoting William Hasker on how love potions trap both parties because love must be freely bestowed, the section argues character is destiny only if forged by free choice, and that Harry, protected by his mother's sacrificial love, shows what Voldemort's rejection of love and vulnerability destroyed.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 54 "The Triumph of Love" — Tracks love's escalation across the series as a force that overwhelms evil without competing: Lily's skin-deep sacrificial love repels Quirrell in Sorcerer's Stone, Harry spares Pettigrew out of love for Lupin and Sirius, his love for Sirius expels Voldemort's possession at the Ministry, and Dumbledore names it 'a force that is at once more wonderful and more terrible than death'. In Deathly Hallows love extends to Kreacher, Griphook, and Dobby, and culminates in Harry's astonishing plea that Voldemort 'try for some remorse', his redefinition of manhood in 'be a man', and victory through willing sacrifice and a single defensive spell rather than a duel, vindicating traditionally feminine values over hypermasculine domination.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 18 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Laura Garcia assembles Narnian heroes: Jill, Eustace, and Puddleglum untying Rilian at likely lethal cost, Eustace hacking at the Sea Serpent, unarmed Shasta charging the lion to save Aravis, and Digory refusing the Witch's offer of the apple that could heal his dying mother. She asks whether egoist theories can explain such deeds and argues they cannot: Hobbes's disguised self-interest, Butler's and Paley's reward schemes, Hume's sympathy, and MacIntyre's identity-based interests all fall short. Only love of others for their own sake, and (for Jill and Digory) trust in Aslan's proven goodness, explains both the heroic choices and our admiration of them as supererogatory acts beyond the call of duty.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 12 "The Mysteries of Love Revealed" — Shelby stages Plato's Symposium as a cipher of raps on love to answer hip-hop "love haters" like Jay-Z ("I got ninety-nine problems but a bitch ain't one"): Pausanias's vulgar versus spiritual love, Aristophanes's myth of split halves read through Method Man and Mary J. Blige's "You're All I Need" and Biggie's "Me & My Bitch", and Socrates's ladder from beautiful bodies to Beauty itself, with Lauryn Hill's "Zion" as birth of beautiful offspring. He objects that Socrates makes the beloved a replaceable means to the good, and argues that Alcibiades's drunken confession supplies what is missing - love's possession, exclusivity, reciprocity, and drama (The Roots: "lies come in, that's where the drama begins") - concluding that love ain't just 'bout da booty but demands a vulnerability the love hater rightly fears.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 10 "Love Minus Zero, No Limit or Going, Going Gone" — Doug Anderson reads Dylan's Planet Waves as a modern Symposium: each song stages a rung on Diotima's ladder, from the puppy love of "You Angel You" through the physical eros of "Tough Mama" and "Hazel," the agape of "Forever Young," and the complementary true love of "Wedding Song." Like Socrates refusing Alcibiades in "Going, Going Gone," Dylan abandons finite beloveds because his highest eros is the creative act itself - poets achieve the immortality Diotima demands by giving birth to immortal works rather than children. The chapter argues both Plato and Dylan finally define love as desire for truth and beauty that outlasts any particular relationship.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 31 "A Meditation on the Word" — Randall Auxier and Eileen Townsend fictionalize the history of philosophy as vampire predation in letters, emails, and IMs (1983-2009) between the 800-year-old Etienne Lavec - a student of Siger de Brabant who drained Thomas Aquinas over the Summa's Treatise on Angels, which wrote vampires out of existence - and Paulie, a freshman turned at Memphis State. Lavec recounts tasting Pico, Spinoza, Hegel, and the willing Kierkegaard, sparing Nietzsche who 'stole some of my ideas about free death', and contrasts vampire self-knowledge (embracing desire) with the Socratic beginning in affirmed ignorance. The centerpiece is Foucault: Lavec summarizes his genealogies of how institutions create the sick, the mad, the prisoner, and the pervert, fails to drain him, and is then haunted for decades by posthumous publications, taunting 'nietzsche26' emails, and finally a catacombs trap - power/knowledge that refuses to die. Lavec's embedded 'Meditation on the Word' recasts the Logos of John's Gospel so that vampires are the uncreated darkness at the boundary of the divine Word, pure self-grounding desire 'beyond good and evil', while the closing Twilight-era chats satirize Stephenie Meyer's sparkling, abstinent Edward as Foucauldian 'sin by words'.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 18 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Taliaferro and Le Gall rebut Paul Johnson's 1958 charge that Doctor No combines 'the sadism of a schoolboy bully', adolescent sex longings, and suburban snobbery. They show Bond kills for justice rather than spite (his reluctant assignment against von Hammerstein in 'For Your Eyes Only'), that Colonel Sun repudiates de Sadean torture before dying, and that the disturbing 'semi-rape' passage of The Spy Who Loved Me reflects Vivienne Michel's voice, not Bond's conduct. They read Bond's eros as an ironic use of the medieval courtly-love and Mariology tradition in which sex redeems 'lost women' like Pussy Galore, defend his dress and manners through the ancient heroic tradition (Theseus's fatal neglect of the white sails, Leonidas combing his beard at Thermopylae), and conclude Bond is a chivalric, comic hero - a 'delightful impossibility' in Aristotle's Poetics' sense who embodies Socratic soldierly virtue and Platonic optimism.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 13 "To Nest or Not to Nest" — Halwani and Jones read The Birds as Hitchcock's warning about romantic love: love compromises autonomy through joint decision-making, emotional dependence, and exposure to contingencies like jealousy, betrayal, sickness, and death. Plato's Symposium stages the alternatives, Socrates's ladder of love culminating in the eternal Form of Beauty versus Alcibiades's speech for the painful, contingent love of a unique person, and Nussbaum's reading underscores that these two visions of romantic love are mutually exclusive. In the film, bird attacks strike whenever Melanie, Mitch, Annie, or Lydia treat love as a game or possession, while the caged lovebirds, the only birds that never attack, show that only love sealed in a 'gilded cage' could be cost-free; lovers must instead face love's price wisely, maturely, and courageously.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 17 "Knots" — Carroll argues that Vertigo rewards repeated viewing not because of its wildly improbable crime plot but because its double love story is a contribution to the philosophy of love: citing Aristotle's Poetics on drama as a 'concrete universal,' he treats Scottie and Judy as ideal character types, the projective fantasist and the enabler, whose sequential romances invite viewers to compare them and so discover love's inherent fault line, fantasy. Fantasy legitimately fuels infatuation, courtship, idealization, and the imagined future lovers share, but Scottie's remodeling of Judy (the grey suit, the hair, the necklace) becomes blinding projection that denies the beloved's irreplaceable particularity despite her plea to be loved 'just the way I am.' Judy's need to be loved makes her complicit in her own erasure, a Laingian 'knot' in which acting on her motive defeats it, while the film maieutically draws this analysis from the viewer, as Socrates drew geometry from the slave in the Meno.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 14 "Love Gone Good" — Johnson reads Cash as practicing "philosophy as a way of life" rather than theorizing: his love-gone-bad songs ("Cocaine Blues," "I shot a man in Reno," the addictions he chose) honor the descent into darkness, aligned with Socrates going down to Piraeus in the Republic, Nietzsche's Zarathustra descending into the depths, and biblical descents from Jacob at the Jabbok to Jonah to Christ, while his love-gone-good songs ("Daddy Sang Bass," "Man in Black") show the turn outward through which love interrupts darkness without erasing it. He frames this with Gabriel Marcel's "creative fidelity" (being at the disposal of others), Paul Tillich's courage to be, in which love is stronger than the nonbeing of death, and Sartre's Existentialism Is a Humanism, where wanting my freedom obligates me to want everyone's. The Man in Black thus carries "a little darkness" on his back while insisting "all God's children ain't free," a lived, political-ethical philosophy rather than a doctrine.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 17 "Conclusion June Love Beyond the Jordan" — Sennett builds "June Love" out of June Carter Cash's documented love, from the "Hurt" video's staircase glance to Rosanne Cash's eulogy that June saw your potential and "lifted them up" for you to see, and the love that steadied John through addictions and infidelity for thirty-five years. He stages the philosophy-of-love dilemma between appraisal theories (Velleman, grounding love in Kantian dignity that demands respect but cannot justify loving John rather than anyone) and bestowal theories (Irving Singer, on which love projects value and so cannot be justified at all), with Frankfurt's volitional account as a side note, and proposes June Love, loving the beloved's potentiality, as the hybrid that is both objective and active and can justify loving this person. He also distinguishes June Love from codependence: enabling entrenches the addict's destruction, whereas June's confronting-and-encouraging love, echoed in "Ring of Fire" and "Far Side Banks of Jordan," called Cash to transformation while leaving him himself.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 16 "The Kiss" — Auxier reads 'Born to Run' as Peter Pan's seduction of Wendy, drawing on Barrie's novel: Mrs. Darling's withheld kiss becomes Peter in Wendy's imagination, the narrator at the nursery window ('Wendy let me in') offers the everlasting kiss, and the glockenspiel is Tinkerbell. The philosophical war is imagination versus reason: Descartes — Captain Hook — wields the chiliagon and the cogito to convict imagination of unreliability, while Vico's imaginative universals (Wendy, Captain Hook, the city-as-altar with its downtown heart and necropolis, which is why Newark and Camden's decay strikes us as defilement) show that reason itself is a modification grown from myth, memory, and Darwin's crocodile of natural history. Since 'I imagine, therefore I am' grounds what 'I think' presupposes, the lonely rider can take Mrs. Darling's kiss 'quite easily' — the song's climax teaches Wendy to fly to a Neverland outside time where the kiss lasts forever.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 13 "It’s Time for the Other Walkie-Talkie" — Dodge puts Monk on the case of friendship's nature, structured by Aristotle's three kinds from the Nicomachean Ethics: Hal Tucker's fake buddy act in 'Mr. Monk Makes a Friend' is pure utility, while Natalie's is virtue-friendship — she is his friend 'in spite of' the job since 'he doesn't pay her that much.' The friend as mirror and 'second self' grounds the claim that Stottlemeyer, Sharona, Natalie and Randy reflect Monk's excellence back to him, and Bacon's point that a friend redoubles joys and cuts griefs in half is shown when they stay up all night during his suicide watch. Seneca's Stoic counsel — judge a person long before admitting him, then hold nothing back — is exemplified by Natalie's fish-over-moon-rock test of Monk's character, while Montaigne's once-in-centuries friendship in which two selves blur fits only Trudy, whose dying words 'bread and butter' tell Monk they belong together. Plato's Lysis (the 'great cosmic swirly' Monk cites in 'Mr. Monk and the Bully') opens the puzzle Socrates could not solve, and the single walkie-talkie his father gave him shows why the chapter's verdict — Monk now has friends — matters.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 29 "Love and Doctors" — Asks whether 'the Doctor' is a Kripkean rigid designator naming one individual or a non-rigid role filled by different people, using the Ninth Doctor's deathbed doubts and the Time Crash memory loop to settle on the rigid reading. He then deploys Locke's body/organism/person distinctions, Parfit's overlapping psychological-connectedness fix to Reid's transitivity objection (Sarah Jane across 1983-1996-2006), and the amnesia-prone regenerations and the Valeyard to show the organism survives regeneration while the person might not. Finally he argues that because DoctorTwo in 'Journey's End' shares all the Doctor's psychologically connected memories of Rose, fission makes them two persons with equal claim, so Rose gets the person she actually loved.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 19 "Surviving Fusion" — Amy Kind asks whether the Holmes who marries Laurie R. King's Mary Russell could still be Holmes, weighing Aristophanes' speech in Plato's Symposium (Zeus split the original spherical humans, and love seeks our lost half) against Derek Parfit's fusion case from Reasons and Persons, in which two people grow into one body, which we would all find horrifying. Against Nozick's account of love as becoming a 'we', Delaney's merger and Gaylin's 'fused identity', she deploys Marilyn Friedman's federation model, lovers as sovereign states forming a flexible third entity, to argue that Holmes and Russell's marriage survives because its fusion reshapes identity without obliterating it: his 'half a creature with two brains and four eyes' and her refusal of the nickname 'Zherlock Mary' show both lovers keeping separate selves.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 24 "Nagging Spouses and Robotic Home-Wreckers" — The chapter shows Hollywoodization reaching romance: the film gives us a bachelor Deckard and a shy, rescue-worthy Rachael in a classic love story that ends with the couple fleeing together, while the novel gives Deckard a badgering wife Iran and a Rachael Rosen who is a sociopath seducing him precisely so that killing androids like her becomes impossible. Knight-rescues-damsel becomes nebbish-manipulated-by-a-psychopathic-machine, and the chapter insists this wholesale rewriting of Dick's ideas about love and marriage carries philosophical implications that are easy to miss.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 120 "How to Tell if You Are Really Just a Robot" — Using Imposter's Spence Olham, Rachel in Blade Runner, and 'The Electric Ant,' the section asks how anyone could verify they are not a machine with implanted memories and drives, noting that Dick wrote himself into Garson Poole and re-enacted Poole's drastic self-experimentation in his decades of drug use. It then argues Dick's real criterion is agape, the spontaneous, unconditional love of ancient and Christian philosophy, which robots can simulate but never experience since they love only because programmed: 'You are a robot if you cannot experience empathy.'
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 121 "Can a Blade Runner Love a Robot" — The section contrasts Dick's bleaker novel, where J.R. Isadore's love for the androids dies when they cut the legs off his rare spider and Deckard's union with Rachael is the 'summa of falsity and mechanical motions' that fuels his resolve to destroy them, with the film's redemptive romance built on Rachael being 'more human than human.' It argues the movie preserves Dick's thesis anyway: Roy Batty's final act of saving the enemy who hunted him shows the empathy that makes the replicants persons, perhaps more than human.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 10 "Pretty Pairs" — Auxier ranks the Glimmer Twins against other songwriting pairs — Lennon-McCartney as a corporation rather than a cooperation, the Gershwins and John-Taupin as split lyricist-composer teams, Page-Plant and Waters-Gilmour as fellow full collaborations — and argues Mick and Keith matter most philosophically because they 'actually always loved each other', like twin sons of different mothers and a bickering married couple. Citing Christopher Andersen's love-triangle story of the Edith Grove flat, he claims the creative process is inseparable from eros in the ancient sense, with jealousy and envy as its close companions. Two huge personalities locked in one room without blowing up the house is what makes their collaboration so philosophically interesting.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 80 "The Rolling Stones and Philosophy" — Closing track-list of Chapter 9, pairing songs from Exile on Main St. with Liz Phair's song-for-song answer Exile in Guyville under the heading of romantic and sexual exile. 'Loving Cup' meets 'Mesmerizing' as unrequited lust from male and female sides, 'Happy' meets 'Fuck and Run' on whether lasting attachments are possible, and 'Ventilator Blues' meets 'Divorce Song' on the loaded-gun violence of failing relationships. The pairing argues Phair and Jagger/Richards map the same territory of oversexed dissatisfaction from opposite perspectives.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 114 "Chapter 13 - You Can’t Always Get What You Want" — Luke Dick opens Chapter 13 with Sartre's 1947 line about marriage taboos versus contraceptives in college back yards and sets Western monogamy — inherited through church and institutions, with divorce thanks to Henry VIII — against the Stones' womanizing image, 'Some Girls' included. A timeline frames the test: Sartre and Beauvoir's 1927 pact of open love, Jagger fashioning himself Don Juan incarnate ('Sexually, yes. Financially, no. Philosophically, trying'), Charlie Watts' steadfast 1964 marriage, and Keith stealing Anita from Brian Jones. The chapter asks whether humans are cut out for monogamy at all.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 115 "Saw Her Today at the Reception" — Dick reads 'You Can't Always Get What You Want' as an anatomy of wanting to keep something and let it go at once, locating the revelation not in Mr. Jimmy or the demonstration but in the reception scene, where Mick confronts that love will never fulfill his expectations. He generalizes to ordinary life: domestic routine can blissfully stabilize a meaningful life or leave the heart 'looking bored behind the drum set,' and rock stardom's surfeit of mates only multiplies the strain. This raises the chapter's governing question — what is a tradition, and should it dictate anything?
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 117 "Practiced at the Art of Deception" — Dick diagnoses Jagger's contradiction: he wants to be both knight and sorcerer, accepted by the aristocratic tradition while living out 'Some Girls,' but you cannot be establishment and counterculture at once. The pendulum swings from sleeping with Keith's girlfriend Anita — passion fulfilled, tradition left a vacuous hole — back home to Marianne while he craves the next mistress. This incongruous moral bearings problem guarantees Mick's unfulfillment, the very tension 'You Can't Always Get What You Want' sings of.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 118 "Glass of Wine in Her Hand" — Dick portraits Keith as Bacchus incarnate, guided by camaraderie and a will for collective hedonistic comfort rather than any defined moral impulse, with romantic and platonic lines blurred — everyone nearby drinks the vapors from his cauldron. The chaos works inside the circle but turns deadly on contact with a world that needs yellow lines: Marlon running amok on the '76 tour, partners straying while Keith passes out. His verdict: Keith would be dead if he hadn't been a Rolling Stone.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 119 "If You Try Sometimes . ." — Dick closes with Charlie Watts near seventy, married to Shirley Ann Shepherd since 1964, whose only indulgence at Hugh Hefner's Playboy mansion in 1972 was the billiard room. He weighs explanations — little impulse for sexual diversity, indifference to passion's initial stages, or resilience compelled by promises and tradition — while admitting marriages are tense, burning things where fatigue is common. Watts endures as he drums: he doesn't drop the beat when his arms get tired.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 179 "Gimme that Old Time Religion" — Carries the frenzy back to the Eleusinian Mysteries and the Dionysian festivals that were falling into ill repute by Plato's day: Socrates himself was an initiate, and Plato wrote on how eros makes humans "mad with passion," whitewashed his teacher in the Symposium, and claimed Socrates never got drunk. Plato also held that certain kinds of music ignite desire and lead to weakness and "effeminacy," associating manliness with rational self-restraint and advocating banning such modes — in short, "no Stones concert allowed in Plato's city."
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 30 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Mistich and McCullough read Klosterman's desire essays through the psychoanalytic-philosophical tradition. 'This Is Emo' — 'No woman will ever satisfy me' — is glossed with Žižek, Lacan, and Butler: desire is not meant to be fulfilled, and satisfaction would only kill it, so Klosterman's failed Waldorf Astoria romance is structurally inevitable. Kojève's Hegelian thesis that all desire is desire for the other's recognition explains Billy Joel's tragic craving for rock-critic canonization, the cereal-box hunger to be 'cool,' and Klosterman's three-week ultimatum to Diane, while Freud's theory of fantasy shows how pop culture (Lloyd Dobler, internet porn) scripts the romantic and sexual desires it then frustrates.
- **The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia**, ch. 14 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" — Celine Morin reads Alicia's love life through the Greek triad agape, eros, and philia as laid out in Plato's Symposium: her unconditional agape for Peter is eroded by his demands for forgiveness ('Stripped', 'Boom'), while the Socratic myth of Eros born from Penia's lack explains why she tells Will their affair is 'romantic because it didn't happen'. She argues Alicia abandons the romantic soul-mate model of her pearl-necklace marriage for Giddens's egalitarian 'pure relationship' with Will, but stays moored to the old family structure, hesitating on the doorstep in the Season Three cliffhanger 'The Dream Time'. Her discovery of feminism through Diane Lockhart is what lets Alicia weigh leaving that structure without destroying her family.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 16 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Lewis argues that Futurama's answer to the fear of being forgotten - Zoidberg thriving on negative attention, Bender's billion-cubit statue and the Shrimpkins' forced worship both failing - is to become existentially intertwined with others through friendship, love, and family. Bender's arc in 'A Pharaoh to Remember' is read through Camus's Sisyphus: life itself is meaningless, but our freedom lets us fill it with meaning, which Bender finds not in monuments or worship but in seeing others remember him. Fry's devotion in 'Godfellas' and 'Jurassic Bark' (Seymour waiting outside Panucci's forever), Bender's Big Score, the holophonor opera of 'The Devil's Hands Are Idle Playthings,' and Yancey naming his son after Fry in 'The Luck of the Fryish' show remembrance surviving inside the people we have shaped, including the viewers.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 33 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Taft pairs Fry with Don Quixote: both are media-saturated characters who live as if inside fiction, break the fourth wall, and are dismissed as madmen - Fry scripting a finale for Single Female Lawyer to placate the Omicronians in 'When Aliens Attack,' Quixote blaming enchanters whenever his fantasies misfire. The chapter asks where reality ends and fiction begins, contrasting the Canon's charge that novels merely delight with the Priest's reply that stories display the beauty of a mind - dramatized when Fry's holophoner music, not worm-given strength or the Robot Devil's hands, is what moves Leela in 'Parasites Lost' and 'The Devil's Hands Are Idle Playthings.' Ending with the opera that spills into its own audience until Hermes sings 'Is this really happening or just being staged?,' the chapter argues a life of enchantment can bend reality toward fantasy - Fry authors his own story just as Quixote's neighbors finally beg him to ride again.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 28 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Mirko Garasic reads Victor as the Modern Prometheus of the myth Plato tells in the Protagoras: like the Titan punished for stealing fire, Victor's purely technical gift of life fails because, as Zeus tells Hermes, justice and reverence must be shared by all or cities cannot exist. The chapter's real subject is love - Prometheus suffers for loving the humans he made, and the creature asks for a female companion while Victor's hate-filled destruction of her unleashes the second wave of revenge. Tim Burton's Frankenweenie splits this love/hate dualism: young Victor's tear over Sparky makes the experiment work, the classmates' prize-greed and the xenophobic mayor produce the real monsters, and Mr. Rzykruski teaches that science severed from emotion is empty. Via Zygmunt Bauman's liquid modernity, Garasic concludes that our own detached, networked isolation is the danger: scientific progress alone never makes a better society, love and community do.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 33 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Mike Kugler argues Shelley's novel tests the radical idealism of her father William Godwin, her mother Mary Wollstonecraft, and her husband Percy: Victor's Promethean project of perfecting humanity in isolation, away from the 'intimate circle' of family and friends, produces a creature whose natural benevolence is destroyed only by repeated exclusion, first by the De Laceys. Drawing on Rousseau's and Wollstonecraft's view that children raised by benevolent parents develop their innate sympathy, the chapter reads the creature as an abandoned child - a new Adam who becomes a Satanic rebel when every community rejects him - and Victor's attempt at reproduction without women and mothers as the novel's deepest violation. The redemptive counterfactual is adoption: what if Victor had raised the creature in his home, as his father did Elizabeth?
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 12 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Andrew Zimmerman Jones argues Ender's genius is empathy cashed out through game theory: from Plato's Laches on courage to Hume's account of sympathy, sizing up the enemy's thinking is the winning strategy, and Ender's love ('in that very moment I also love him') reframes conflicts with Peter and the buggers so they can end rather than merely be won. His one failure is never extending this empathy to Graff and Rackham, so he cannot see that his final battleroom rule-breaking - 'the enemy's gate is down' - is exactly the move the adults' larger game was designed to produce.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 20 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Christopher Lauer argues Cohen's lyrics seduce through Socratic irony as Kierkegaard analyzes it in The Concept of Irony: ostentatious self-concealment that makes hearers aware of the gap between words and intentions, building 'personality' and promising intimacy. Songs like 'Closing Time,' 'Everybody Knows,' and 'Democracy' oscillate between cynical third-person verdicts and sudden second-person address, offering a hidden sincerity only to withdraw it - an erotic improvement on Plato's Socrates that dissolves its own ironic distance. 'Hallelujah' and 'Anthem' make the program explicit, treating brokenness as the space in which love develops, while 'Tower of Song' shows the bleak side: irony collapsing into pure cynicism, the singer speaking sweetly from the Tower long after all promises of genuine intimacy have been disavowed.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 22 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Simon Riches argues that Cohen fuses the erotic with the spiritual - worshipping female beauty as religious experience in 'Light as the Breeze' and 'Night Comes On' - and that this produces conflicted, self-deceiving relationships in songs like 'Famous Blue Raincoat' and 'Chelsea Hotel #2.' Against the classical theory of concepts embodied in Socrates' demand for essences, he deploys Wittgenstein's language games and family resemblance, Wittgensteinian views of religious belief, and Davidson's divided mind to deny that love has a rationally coherent essence. Following Richard Rorty, Cohen emerges as an ironist who rejects any 'final vocabulary' of love, and this very contingency and irony ground his authenticity as a singer of romantic love.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 14 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Brittany Lorenz and Adam Barkman apply the Greek four-loves framework (storge, eros, philia, agape) to Homeland's relationships. Terrorism breaks storge by destroying comfort in familiar places; broken eros appears in the Brody-Jessica-Mike-Carrie square and Mira's lover who loves 'making love' rather than her; philia falters because Brody hides his Islam from Jessica, and Abu Nazir's bond with Brody is Aristotle's friendship of utility, dissolving when the advantage ceases. Brody's agape for country is broken because fighting abroad violates his prior duties as husband and father, so the show offers only glimpses of loves that might be redeemed.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 13 "Girls and Philosophy" — McCrossin asks whether Adam's Season Two finale run across Brooklyn to break down the door of a dangerously unraveling Hannah ('I was always here') is heroic, set against Hannah's 'You don't need to be like a hero' chair-and-mattress scene and Adam's 'I don't want to help... I was doing it because I love you' quarrel. He argues an act is heroic - being an 'Extraordinary Samaritan' like Wesley Autrey, the Subway Samaritan, unlike the trained Sullenberger - only when done on purpose to help, not from obligation, training, or love's compulsion, testing the point with Batman's motives. Since Adam insists no one ever does anything from a want to help, his rescue's heroic status is left genuinely open.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 27 "Girls and Philosophy" — Fisher explains the show's cycle - the girls want someone only while that person rejects them - through psychoanalytic theories of desire. Freud supplies the id/ego/superego machinery (cocaine-era Hannah dancing to 'I Don't Care (I Love It)' as pure id; Dunham's body-critical audience as the superego), while Lacan's desire - the 'untold' that must be named (Hannah's bedroom kink questions to Eric), drive, and jouissance beyond the pleasure principle - shows desire circling its object and never being satisfied, as when Hannah's e-book deal collapses into her worst OCD episode. Žižek's objet a as the object-cause of desire reads Marnie loving Charlie only once he is over her: desire reproduces itself rather than reaching its goal.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 30 "Girls and Philosophy" — Zurba reads all four girls through Julia Kristeva's adolescent malady: the faith that 'there certainly can not not be an absolutely satisfying other,' which curdles into a 'kamikaze syndrome' of nihilism and self-destruction when the ideal love object disappoints. Hannah's idealized Adam ('too absent, too present or too weird') fails her, producing self-deprecating sex, compulsive counting, and the q-tip collapse; Marnie's disappointment becomes boredom and cruelty toward Hannah; Jessa's absent father leaves her 'swimming without a life vest' on heroin; Shoshanna invests hers in Sex and the City pastiche yet alone learns to love Ray as he is. Following Kristeva (and Freud) the cure is not the perfect partner but love as psychic openness, imagination, and treating the self as 'a work in progress.'
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 12 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Robison-Greene asks whether there are principled standards for 'shipping' TV couples and applies Platonic-Aristotelian flourishing criteria (long-term safety, emotional needs, trust, and mutual growth toward virtue) to Piper's options: Alex fails on safety and trust (selling Piper out, the perjury advice), Larry fails on empathy and growth, so by real-life standards we should ship none of them. She concludes shipping is mostly aesthetic, then proposes minimal moral rules for our attitudes toward fictional relationships: never ship Pornstache, respect consent, and never let race, gender, or orientation decide.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 14 "5. Overcoming Evil with Love" — Bogosian argues the film locates evil not in human nature itself, as Jeanine claims when she calls human nature 'the enemy,' but in cultivable vices - Al's jealousy and fear of failure leading to attempted murder and suicide, Eric's and Jeanine's lust for power - and that only altruistic, self-sacrificial love can counteract them. With Aristotle's point that friendship is essential to developing virtue and to the good life, he shows the faction system fails on its own terms: a single virtue in isolation corrupts (Candor's truth without kindness), and a system that removes real moral and political freedom destroys the flourishing it promises. Tris's parents' sacrifices and the Tris-Four relationship - honest training advice, protection of her Divergence, and the gun-to-her-own-forehead scene where love breaks the simulation's grip - model the love that overcomes the corrupt system.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 12 "3. Matthew’s Dark Side" — Wills uses Georg Simmel's The Philosophy of Money to argue Matthew's two-season arc is a corruption story rather than a romance: the principled middle-class lawyer who vows Downton will not change him, calls valeting 'a very silly occupation,' and wants to dress himself gradually lets wealth enchant him, dodges reviewing the entail, and returns for Mary. He reads the Mary-Matthew match as an economic transaction that neatly solves the succession problem - money as the aristocracy's toy, Mary becoming part of the deal - against Anna and Bates's money-free courtship as the show's only genuinely loving relationship. The chapter ends by turning Simmel's warning on the audience: we root for the couple because we are as powerless before wealth's charm, and as greedy for it, as Matthew is.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 37 "23. Justice in Love" — Adam Barkman and Noah van Brenk read Downton through C. S. Lewis's four loves (storge, eros, philia, agape) and Plato's Republic definition of justice as each thing performing its role, arguing that agape satisfies justice and then transcends it by loving the naturally unlovable. Their examples are Anna and Bates's forged thirty-pound note for the jobless Molesley, Bates and Lord Grantham sparing Thomas prison after the Jimmy incident by introducing 'a little kindness into the equation,' and Lavinia refusing Matthew's justice-only dismissal of her after his paralyzing injury. False agape appears in Thomas's manipulation of the nanny and in Vera Bates's possessive 'love,' which ends in her suicide staged as Bates's crime.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 38 "24. Climbing the Ladder of Love" — Brendan Shea matches each speech of Plato's Symposium to a Downton plot: Phaedrus's love-inspired heroism to Thomas defending Jimmy from the robbers, Pausanias's legally shaped 'heavenly love' to Mary's path from the Pamuk scandal to wholehearted commitment with Matthew, Eryximachus's love as order to Carson and Mrs. Hughes, Aristophanes's split halves to Anna and Bates, and Agathon's tongue-in-cheek praise of love to Edith's missteps. Socrates's ladder of love then structures Sybil and Tom's romance as physical attraction ascending into love of moral beauty and wisdom - her nursing, his estate stewardship - making love the engine that gives the characters' lives meaning and, as the final rung hints, makes philosophers of them all.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 30 "17. The Miracle of True Love" — Elsby and Luzecky use the Phaedo to make sense of Westley being 'mostly dead': Socrates's cyclical argument that opposites generate each other, Aristotle's distinctions between contradictories and contraries, and the observation that life and death here come in degrees together recast life and death as spectrum concepts rather than strict opposites. True love emerges as a second opposite of death: answering Simmias's objection that a soul, like a lyre's harmony, perishes with its instrument, they argue true love is a harmony binding persons and actions that persists beyond the particular lovers - which is how the film's miracle of true love conquers death.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 15 "6. Driven by Love to Go to War" — John Karavitis deploys Alain Badiou's account of love as a contingent encounter founding the 'Two scene'—seeing the world from the perspective of difference—to argue that Darrow and Eo were never truly in love: their glade conversation, his 'nobility of obedience' against her 'live for more,' was two monologues, and you cannot love a memory. He then diagnoses Darrow as a narcissist in Rousseau's sense of amour-propre—self-love turned vanity that lies to itself—whose quest serves to manage his shame at failing to protect Eo, citing Erich Fromm on narcissism's path to fascism and Aristotle on habituation into Gold ways. Only the Jackal's stone-table imprisonment shatters the narcissism ('Man is no island'), letting Darrow embrace agape, with Ovid's Echo and Narcissus and the haemanthus framing the trilogy as a warning against self-love.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 12 "1. Charlie’s Eternal Quest for the Little Red-Haired Girl" — The chapter reads Charlie Brown's lifelong, unconsummated longing for the never-seen Little Red-Haired Girl as a quest narrative without closure: like Beckett's Vladimir and Estragon he cannot act, and like Camus's Sisyphus he is an absurd hero whose dignity lies in persisting (the 2,120 lunch hours, the losing team, the pulled football) without reward. Using Lacan's account of desire - the wish for the Other's recognition, suspended between the demand for need and the demand for love - it argues Schulz keeps her invisible (except one 1998 silhouette) precisely so Charlie's desire stays in permanent suspension, like a Hitchcock MacGuffin. The closing section attacks The Peanuts Movie (2015) for betraying this existential vision: by showing the girl, rewarding Charlie with a kiss, and swapping Sisyphean defiance for 'believe in yourself' truisms, it delivers Sisyphus from his rock and so kills what made him admirable.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 12 "4. Hendrix—Freedom and Love" — The editor asks where Hendrix's 'bestness' lies by testing whether he was ever free: his songs demand freedom ('If 6 Was 9,' 'Stone Free,' 'Freedom,' 'Ezy Ryder') but never assert that the human condition is free, and his caffeine-style appetites, exploitative contracts, and management suggest determination rather than liberty. A detour through 'Hey Joe' as premeditated murder — compared with Othello and the Ice-T 'Cop Killer' affair — argues that fabricated narrators make it impossible to glean an artist's own moral sense from songs. He concludes that Hendrix's deepest mastery was the treatment of love, from 'The Wind Cries Mary' to 'Little Wing,' making him the sixties' most powerful spokesman for love rather than freedom, per the quoted 'when the power of love overcomes the love of power.'
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 19 "9. Are You Experienced" — Proposes an 'experientialism' — subjective conscious experience as fundamental reality, defended against eliminativists who would explain experience away as illusion — and finds its moral core in Martin Buber: the title song and 'May This Be Love' call the beloved out of an I-It world ('made out of gold and can't be sold') into reciprocal I-You relation ('take hold of my hand'), while 'The Wind Cries Mary,' 'Purple Haze,' and 'Manic Depression' lament love that is absent or unreciprocated. Experiences feel most intensely real, the chapter argues, when the Platonic order of love puts what matters most at stake — which is why kissing the sky, even without being kissed back, is worth recommending.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 21 "10. Love, Truluv" — Sandefur argues that what makes totalitarianism unique is its demand that subjects love their ruler, and that this project is doomed because love is selective, unequal, internal, and inalienable, invoking Aristotle's critique of Plato's community of wives and children, Machiavelli on whether rulers should be loved or feared, and Arendt on conscience as internal dialogue and totalitarianism as total rule. Winston and Julia's sex is a political act asserting the individual against the collective, while the Two Minutes Hate channels repressed erotic energy into sanctioned ecstasy directed at Big Brother, as at Khomeini's funeral. What finally breaks Winston in Room 101 is not torture as such but his surrender of Julia, the one thing that was truly his, which collapses the distinction between love and rape.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 14 "5. True Love or Artificial Love" — Clayman uses 'The Lonely' as a case study for whether Corry's love for the robot Alicia is true love, classifying it through C.S. Lewis's four loves (charity, affection, friendship, Eros) and their gift-, need-, and appreciative-love qualities. He deploys Peirce's pragmatic maxim to read the meaning of 'truly loving' off its practical effects, answers the objection that a machine beloved involves prejudice with Singer's speciesism, and borrows Kendall Walton's 'Fearing Fictions' to explain how Corry, knowing Alicia is a machine, 'becomes fictional' and role-plays a believer — concluding he showed affection and friendship born of loneliness, not Eros, since he would not sacrifice his place on the ship for her.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 10 "1. Do You Long for Having Your Heart Interlinked" — Timothy Shanahan asks whether K and Joi's relationship counts as romance, sex, and love, using Locke's definition of a person as a thinking, reflective being to ask whether a programmed AI can love, and weighing Joi's programming against the determinism that may bind human lovers too. He reads the Joi-Mariette-K sex scene through Plato's Symposium myth of severed halves seeking union, substance dualism, and a Kant-inspired 'controlled hallucination' view of perception, concluding all sex is a person-to-person conscious connection through bodily intermediaries. Deckard's rejection of Wallace's replica Rachael is explained with a Mona Lisa forgery analogy: an indistinguishable copy still lacks the irreplaceable original person. The baseline question 'Do you long for having your heart interlinked?' frames love as the longing of lonely cells of awareness to connect.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 27 "15. I, Thou, and the Neighborhood" — James McLachlan pairs Rogers's 'holy ground' between television set and viewer with Buber's turn from ecstatic religion to the everyday after failing the young visitor of 1914 who came to him in need: the I-You relation of full presence versus the I-It of use is what 'It's You I Like' sings. Against Sartre's 'Hell is other people' and Augustine's reading of the burning bush as the omnipotent God, Rogers and Buber (with Rosenzweig's translation of God's name as 'the One who will be present') make listening, presence, and everyday 'twinklings' the substance of neighborly love.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 42 "29. I Am Iron Man" — Reads Tony Stark's fifteen-year transformation — from Yinsen's 'Is this the last act of defiance of the great Tony Stark?' in the cave to the final snap — through Maurice Blondel's philosophy of action, where meaning comes from what we will and do rather than what we know, each willed action building toward an ultimate end. It frames the journey as taking on an infinite responsibility for the other (Levinas's register): the wormhole flight in The Avengers, the armor-around-the-world obsession after the Scarlet Witch's vision, Ultron, Civil War, and finally the snap as the pure act of radical love that answers Yinsen's 'Don't waste your life.'
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 20 "10. KISS Was Made for Lovin’ You" — Courtland Lewis categorizes virtually the entire KISS catalogue by kind of love. Using Nicholas Wolterstorff's distinctions, he sorts erotic-activity songs ('Uh! All Night,' 'Deuce'), erotic-attachment songs ('I Still Love You,' 'Calling Dr. Love'), and erotic-attraction songs ('I Was Made for Lovin' You,' 'Hotter than Hell'), flags the disturbing near-statutory trio ('Christine Sixteen,' 'Goin' Blind,' 'Domino'), and adds non-erotic attachment, philia ('Childhood's End'), agape ('I Will Be There'), and the thirty-three percent of songs advocating a way of life ('Lick It Up' as an anti-suicide anthem of self-reclamation). He concludes with Aristotle and Plato on flourishing and Wolterstorff's claim that lives are 'shot through with love,' inviting readers to re-sort the lists with better reasons.
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 21 "11. Excess (I Love It)" — Robert Vuckovich reads KISS's sex songs through Aristippus of Cyrene's hedonism: immediate bodily pleasure is the highest good, so the 'urge to merge' of 'Fits Like a Glove,' the whips of 'Sweet Pain,' the persuasion of 'Nothin' to Lose,' and the stewardess encounter of 'Room Service' are candid validations of pleasure — morally acceptable where desire and consent are mutual. Aristippus's cautions (the prostitute visit, the three courtesans he declined, his non-exclusive arrangement with Lais) ground the chapter's limits on excess, mirrored in Gene passing girls to Point Blank's guitarist and Paul's shift to quality over quantity. The Cyrenaic alternation of work and play matches KISS's 'God Gave Rock'n'Roll to You II' ethic — sweat first, then indulge — and Cicero's report that the body is 'nature's canon and rule' closes the case.
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 22 "12. An Intimate Look at Paul Stanley’s Love" — Robert Grant Price maps Paul Stanley's catalogue onto four loves. Eros as soulmate-love follows Aristophanes' split-beings myth from Plato's Symposium ('Forever,' 'Every Time I Look at You'); self-love follows Aquinas's demand that it be 'rightly ordered,' so Stanley's machismo songs pass while Gene's 'I' fails as disordered egomania; bodily love is defended as bawdy dramatic monologue — foreplay between lovers rather than instruction in reducing women to sex objects; and love of life is secularized agape praise in 'I'm Alive,' 'Shout It Out Loud,' and the very title Alive!. Price then asks why love drives art at all, weighing the transcendentals (true, good, beautiful) against the Scruton-versus-Craig-Martin can-of-shit debate, and reads 'Reason to Live' as the claim that only rightly ordered love can ground a life.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 26 "Love American Style" — Klayman asks whether the android Vision can love the human Scarlet Witch, working through C.S. Lewis's four loves to show affection, friendship, Eros, and charity are all open to human-android pairs, with their marriage best read as Eros—preoccupation with one irreplaceable self rather than sexual desire. Peter Singer's attack on speciesism is extended into 'organicism', the prejudice that dismisses synthetic beings: the Vision suffers, has interests, and laments that 'we artificial life-forms are still the least accepted', so denying androids love is arbitrary bias. Peirce's pragmatic maxim settles the question by practical effects—the Vision's care, kindness, attentiveness, and intimacy with Wanda just are loving—whether the lover is flesh or machine.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 16 "Taking the Leap (It’s Not Fair)" — Against the natural reading that Be Right Back fails because AshBot is a poor copy, the chapter argues that even a perfect duplicate, AshBot+, would not be Ash: like a perfect forgery of a twenty-dollar bill, it would share all intrinsic but none of Ash's relational properties (being Martha's beloved, the coming father of her child), which also exposes a fission paradox for psychological-continuity theories. Nozick's account of love as a 'we' — shared memory, autonomy, and well-being — explains why Martha cannot trade up or replace a dead partner without destroying the self constituted by the relationship. Parfit's view that only psychological continuity matters is then rejected: because Martha's relationship survives only if Ash does, survival itself matters, and Martha must mourn rather than cling to a specter.
