- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 45 "Anti‐love Shows What Love Is" — The chapter takes Irma Thomas's 'Anyone Who Knows What Love Is (Will Understand)?' - the song Brooker plants across five episodes - as the key to the series, defining love with Aquinas (to love is to wish the good by which the beloved flourishes, rooted in proper self-love, on an Aristotelian base) and evil as the void left where that good is withheld. Each episode that plays the song features characters who mishear it: Hot Shot's judges take Abi's sacrificial love song as an audition for submission to WraithBabes, Joe misreads Beth's song as meant for him and kills Beth's father in the resulting void, and Mia in Crocodile refuses the self-sacrificing loving act of confessing, murdering to fill the gap. Callow's pig-for-a-princess self-sacrifice, Theo's speech about commitment, and digital Walton dying to protect a copy of his son Tommy are the exceptions that know what love is, so the chapter concludes Black Mirror is as much about a world emptied of love as about dangerous technology.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 18 "Robots and Romance" — Contrasts Disney's 'Irrational Matriarchy and Patriarchy' families (Triton destroying Ariel's grotto, Mother Gothel exploiting Rapunzel, Frollo imprisoning Quasimodo) with its Family Unity Model, using the Filmer–Locke debate: parents are stewards, not owners, and children have Locke's liberty to leave and choose marriage. The positive model is built on John Paul II's theology of the body — Quasimodo's 'Heaven's Light' versus Frollo's 'Hellfire' as gift-love versus using Esmeralda as an object of lust — with the Beast transformed into virtue by Belle's self-sacrificing love. It then answers Beauvoir's charge that housewifery is immanent drudgery with Elastigirl and Edna Mode's 'Done properly, parenting is heroic,' closing with WALL-E and EVE's hand-hold waking screen-addled humans back to family life.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 30 "We Can Fix this Hand in Hand" — Heit reads Frozen through Marion's claim that 'I love you' usually certifies the speaker's ego: Anna's knocking ('Do you want to build a snowman?') is love as the risky question 'Does anyone out there love me?' asked despite years of rejection, while Hans's whirlwind engagement is Marion's 'vanity' masquerading as love. Against the prince-saves-princess script, the act of true love that thaws Anna's frozen heart turns out to be her own self-giving gesture toward Elsa, showing that true love overcomes fear rather than fulfilling one's own needs.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 12 "3. Matthew’s Dark Side" — Wills deploys Georg Simmel's The Philosophy of Money, with its thesis that growing wealth corrodes individuality, to reread Matthew Crawley's courtship of Mary as corruption rather than romance: the man who vows Downton won't change him soon accepts Molesley's valeting, savors finding no grounds to challenge the entail, and returns to the fortune he claimed to renounce. He contrasts their 'relationship of convenience,' which conveniently solves the succession problem, with the penniless Anna and Bates courtship as the show's picture of love uncontaminated by money. The darker claim is that viewers are corrupted alongside Matthew, rooting for a marriage that serves the estate's economic structure, so the show indicts our own captivity to wealth.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 37 "23. Justice in Love" — Adam Barkman and Noah van Brenk apply C.S. Lewis's four loves to Downton, arguing that every love requires Platonic justice - each thing treated according to its role, as in the servants' 'My Lord' hierarchy and Bates's equal right to a fair trial - but that agape, sacrificial love, satisfies justice and then transcends it by loving the unlovable. Anna and Bates's forged thirty-pound note for the destitute Molesley, Bates sparing his hated enemy Thomas from prison, and Lavinia refusing Matthew's 'think of me as dead' dismissal are true agape, while Vera Bates's possessive blackmail and Thomas's scheme against the nanny merely ape it. The upshot is Lord Grantham's line to Alfred: do not abandon your beliefs, 'just introduce a little kindness into the equation' - justice tempered by mercy in both directions.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 38 "24. Climbing the Ladder of Love" — Brendan Shea reads Downton's romances through each speech of Plato's Symposium in turn. Phaedrus's love-inspired heroism explains Thomas taking a beating to save Jimmy; Pausanias's contrast of common and heavenly love maps onto Mary learning to work within social rules rather than around them (Pamuk versus Matthew); Eryximachus's orderly love is Carson and Mrs. Hughes's skilled, harmonious running of the house; Aristophanes's severed halves fit Anna and Bates merging their lives through prison and rape; and Agathon's naive praise diagnoses Edith's misdirected pursuit of love. Finally Socrates's ladder of love - desire for immortality ascending from one beautiful beloved to moral beauty itself - is played out by Tom and Sybil, whose romance leads him from chauffeur to estate manager and her from fashionable life to nursing, exactly as the ladder predicts.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 12 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Andrew Zimmerman Jones treats Ender's conflicts as games analyzable by von Neumann's minimax theorem and the theory of zero-sum, imperfect-information games, arguing Ender wins by redefining the game itself ('the enemy's gate is down') while his empathy fails only with Graff, whose larger game Ender never suspects because he never treats the adults as the enemy. He unpacks Ender's claim that to understand an enemy is to love him through Socrates' words in Plato's Laches on courage, Hume's account of sympathy, and the Christian agape of 'love your enemies,' mapping a continuum from sympathy through empathy to love.
- **The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire**, ch. 15 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" — Why do Berger, Cecilia, Harriet, Salander, and Figuerola all bed the unprepossessing Blomkvist? Testing Kant's claim that sexual desire makes 'the loved person an Object of appetite... a lemon which has been sucked dry,' the chapter argues his appeal is that he treats women as ends in themselves—he works beside them as equals, is 'not going to compete with you' with Figuerola, and never manipulates or controls—so his sex is the least objectifying in a Sweden full of men who hate women. Against Kant and Baumrim, Irving Singer's reply that desire can respond to the whole person explains why his no-strings honesty attracts powerful women, though his refusal to define, own, or 'cherish' any lover—walking in on Erika just as Salander arrives with the Elvis cabin ad—still leaves Salander heartbroken and Figuerola in sadness.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 9 "Introduction" — The introduction argues, citing Plato's saying that philosophy begins in wonder, that children's fantasy like Rowling's is a natural home for philosophy, since young readers can be nourished by ideas they cannot fully digest, like Fang gnawing a dragon bone. It canvasses the volume's guiding questions: whether love is the most powerful magic, whether souls exist and can be split by Horcruxes, what Animagi and boggarts teach about personal identity, whether choices reveal more than abilities, and whether Snape can be redeemed. It closes by framing the book in the Blackwell series tradition of using pop culture to teach philosophy, updating the 2004 Open Court volume now that all seven novels are out.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 38 "Snape and the Many-Splendored Thing" — The section opens the Deavels' chapter with the puzzle of Dumbledore's 'ironclad reason' for trusting Snape even after Snape kills him, recalling McGonagall's 'he trusted... always,' and names the answer: Snape's unrequited love for Lily, which leads circuitously to his redemption. It previews the philosophical questions about the nature and varieties of love and its power to blind judgment that the chapter will bring to Snape's story.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 39 "The Abandoned Boys" — Surveying eros, philia, and agape, from the Weasleys' romantic love to Voldemort's never having wanted a friend to 'God is love,' the section draws on Plato's Symposium, where crude physical desire is progressively refined toward the beautiful and divine, to argue that love is primarily a choice of the will rather than a feeling. Hence Snape's continuing dislike of Harry is no evidence against his transformation by love; acting for others' good despite his emotions is precisely the testimony to it.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 40 "Snape the Occlumens" — The section positions Snape as the third 'abandoned boy' beside Harry and Voldemort, a half-blood from an unhappy home for whom Hogwarts, as Harry observes, is where all three 'found home.' Voldemort chose power, selfishness, and a fragmented psyche while Harry opened his heart to friends and grew into integrity, and the section asks what makes this 'complicated amalgam of darkness and light,' Dumbledore's double agent and killer, tick.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 41 "Snape’s Choice" — The section reads Snape's double life through the definition of love shared by writers from Aristotle to Aquinas, willing the good of the other for the other's own sake: he protects people he dislikes because his love for Lily wills their good. As an Occlumens he empties himself of feeling to lie to Voldemort's face, concealing rather than renouncing his love for Lily, and only while dying from Nagini's bite does he freely offer Harry the memories revealing that Harry is a Horcrux.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 42 "A Work in Progress" — Tracing Snape's love from the greedy boyhood watching of Lily and the Mudblood rupture through his plea to save Lily alone, which draws Dumbledore's 'You disgust me,' the section judges it short of Aristotle's beloved as a 'second self,' since he wanted Lily's good only as it related to him. Diotima's teaching in the Symposium that 'love is wanting to possess the good forever' and Benedict XVI's love as 'an ongoing exodus out of the closed inward-looking self' frame how Snape's unrequited love gradually 'gives birth in beauty' to virtue in him.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 43 "NOTES" — The section argues that vice and virtue are habits built up over time: Snape still rages at Harry-as-James and sneers at Tonks's wolf Patronus as 'weak,' yet his own doe Patronus, matching Lily's, is the magical emblem of his transformation by love. Contrasting friends, who strengthen the soul's integrity by sharing joys and sorrows, with Voldemort, whose Horcruxes give him eight 'selves' while making him less human, it reads remorse as what knits a damaged soul back together, sealed by Harry's forgiveness and the name 'Albus Severus.'
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 46 "Little Hangleton" — The section collects the love-potion material of Half-Blood Prince: Fred and George's 'violently pink products' at Weasleys' Wizard Wheezes, Amortentia's mother-of-pearl sheen and the smell of freshly mown grass that Hermione dare not finish naming, Slughorn's warning that it causes 'a powerful infatuation or obsession' rather than love, and Ron's Romilda Vane episode from spiked Chocolate Cauldrons. This sets up the chapter's question of what kind of person would actually use one, answered by Voldemort's mother.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 47 "Real Love or Mere Infatuation" — Retelling Dumbledore's reconstruction for Harry, the section sets Merope Gaunt's love potion beside the Imperius Curse, one of the three unforgivable curses that robs victims of their will, as the two ways she might have won Tom Riddle Sr., noting that Harry immediately pairs them as will-robbing magic. Dumbledore's guess that Merope 'could not bear to continue enslaving him' and stopped dosing him, only to be abandoned and left to die, raises the chapter's question of what this loveless origin has to do with the prophecy.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 48 "Not His Mother’s Son" — The section argues Merope did not truly love Riddle Sr. because the potion stole his freedom: doing what you want is necessary but not sufficient for freedom, which also requires the ability to do otherwise, the 'libertarian' freedom Tom lacked. It canvasses Harry Frankfurt and the compatibilists who deny that doing-otherwise is necessary yet concedes even they would deny Tom freely loved Merope, and extends the argument to potions taken on oneself, which cheat us of becoming better persons through the hard work of real relationships.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 49 "NOTES" — Against the obvious reading of Voldemort's loveless begetting, the section argues he is 'not his mother's son': he imitates Marvolo and Salazar Slytherin, while Merope, on Aristotle's principle that we are what we consistently do, redeemed herself by stopping the potion, renouncing magic entirely, and choosing love over hate at the cost of her life. Character is destiny only if forged by genuinely free choices rather than blood or fate, so Merope shows not even the most tragic beginnings are destined for darkness, while Voldemort, who never loved and never wanted a friend, chose otherwise, leaving Harry as the true mother's son, shielded by 'a more ancient and powerful magic than any potion.'
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 54 "The Triumph of Love" — Reading the series' set pieces as the triumph of traditionally feminine values over masculine aggression, the section moves from Lily's sacrificial love burning Quirrell, through Harry sparing Pettigrew for Lupin's and Sirius's sake, to love expelling Voldemort during the Ministry possession, where 'it was your heart that saved you' and Dumbledore names a force 'more wonderful and more terrible than death.' Harry's kindness to Kreacher, Griphook, and Dobby pays off in the Horcrux hunt, his plea that Voldemort 'try for some remorse' redefines true manhood as incorporating the feminine, and the Forest sacrifice wins the war with a defensive Expelliarmus rather than a duel, showing love more important than aggression.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 25 "Notes" — Southworth and Tallman defend the Underwood marriage by way of Richard Wasserstrom's three grounds for condemning adultery (promise breaking, deception, pain): Frank and Claire's openly negotiated nonmonogamy - Frank disclosing the Zoe affair over breakfast, the Meechum threesome, Claire's nights with Adam Galloway - breaks no promise and involves minimal deception, so it is morally permissible. They reject Vincent Punzo's dualist claim that sex must merge souls, arguing that view rests on unverifiable theology and sets people up for guilt. The marriage's real strength is its egalitarian mutuality - Claire's sabotage of the watershed bill works as tit-for-tat strategy that restores the partnership - and agreed nonmonogamy suits Frank's bisexuality better than monogamy, which would force him to give up part of what it means to be Frank.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 25 "Notes" — Defends the Underwoods' open marriage by applying Wasserstrom's account of adultery (wrong via promise-breaking, deception, and pain): Frank and Claire's mutually negotiated nonmonogamy-frank transparency with Claire about Zoe, Claire rushing home to Frank from Adam's-apartment avoids all three wrongs, and Punzo's dualist claim that sex merges souls is rejected as unverifiable and damaging. It reads the marriage as an egalitarian partnership whose tit-for-tat renegotiation after Claire's watershed-bill sabotage and their agreed childlessness ('I promise you freedom from that') show that nonmonogamy strengthens rather than corrodes their bond.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 31 "The Office and Philosophy" — Arp and Watson sort Dunder Mifflin's relationships into five conceptions of love: Roy's erotic 'best sex of your life' Valentine's offer to Pam as blind eros; Angela and Dwight's pursuit of an idealized mate read through Plato's Forms and the Symposium's ascent to Beauty; Aristotle's three friendships, under which the office's alliances are mere utility while Jim and Pam's teapot sacrifice in 'Christmas Party' approaches virtue friendship; the Stoic-Kantian 'equal loving' of universal respect, laughed at when Michael ranks himself with Bono and Lincoln; and agape-style family loyalty that leads Dwight to supply Michael his urine in 'Drug Testing'. The chapter concludes that Michael exemplifies a selfishness Western philosophy has no name for, failing at every form of love.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 29 "Dysfunctional Family Feud The No Special Obligations View" — Southworth and Tallman use David Spade's 'falling star' joke about Eddie Murphy, and Murphy's twenty-year SNL boycott, to test three theories of familial obligation against the show's self-described 'family.' The role-based Just Because View, identified with Confucian filial piety, condemns Spade's disrespect toward an SNL elder but also forbids Murphy's divorce from the family; the contractarian Reciprocity View says Spade owes Dennis Miller but not Murphy, unless Murphy's saving the early show counts; and Jane English's No Special Obligations View, on which family should work like friendship, love rather than debt, clears Spade entirely. Sketches from the Vogelchecks' kissing family to Dysfunctional Family Feud supply the counterexamples.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 24 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Taliaferro and Little ask whether Spider-Man can champion justice and love Mary Jane at the same time, framed by Mandela's tension between obligations to family and to community. Through paired scenarios — rescuing an endangered coworker at possible mortal cost versus a lover's plea to become a surgeon rather than join a deadly crime-fighting unit — they conclude that justice trumps romance in unforeseen emergencies, while romance can rightly govern the choice of a vocation. For Spider-Man the two fuse rather than conflict, since MJ loves him partly for his commitment to justice, though Gwen Stacy's death on the bridge — where his webbing snapped her neck — shows a hero can lose both at once.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 25 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Spanakos asks why Spider-Man is called 'friendly' by testing Peter's relationships against Aristotle's three philias (pleasure, utility, virtue) and the proportionality principle that the morally inferior friend should love the superior more — a principle that breaks down for a superhero as godlike as Spider-Man. Peter's secrecy and self-sacrifice block true Aristotelian fellowship with MJ, whose crush on Spidey is mere fantasy-love, and Harry's friendship rests on pleasure and utility, failing every Aristotelian test. Yet against philia the chapter sets Christian agape (St. Basil, John 15, C.S. Lewis's Four Loves): unconditional, self-sacrificial love for the unlovable, which Peter practices toward his betrayers and which Harry finally enacts when he dies saving Peter in Spider-Man 3 — an agape that makes him Peter's equal.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 19 "Notes" — Taliaferro and Beck trace a philosophy of love through Anakin: fatherless, he attaches compulsively to Shmi and then Padme, refusing the Stoic limits on control that Yoda and Epictetus teach, so that love curdles into the vow to 'stop people from dying.' Vader's fatherhood is the caricature of love - offering Luke power instead of care - until Luke's compassion and Vader's final self-sacrifice redeem it. The lesson: love must be tempered by humility about what Zeno and the Stoics placed outside our control, and broken family bonds can be partly repaired through costly self-sacrifice.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 25 "Humanoids and Droids Having Sex" — Munn and Weijers argue that Lando and L3-37 in Solo display all the hallmarks of friendship and one-sided romantic love: Lando abandons self-preservation to carry the injured L3 to the Falcon and endorses her droid-emancipation crusade, while L3 tells Qi'ra she has considered a relationship with him but finds them 'not compatible'. Testing Bennet Helm's four accounts of love (union, deep mutual caring, valuing, emotional state) against the film, they conclude humanoid-droid love is genuinely possible, and that L3's claim that sex with Lando 'works' is plausible once sex is defined broadly as any activity yielding sexual reward. They ground droid friendship in Aristotle's incomplete versus complete friendships, contrasting the rewarding partnerships of R2-D2 with Anakin and BB-8 with Poe against the merely strategic Han-Lando Sabacc rivalry.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 34 "“Wherever I Go, He Goes”" — Bishop and Bishop map The Mandalorian's Outer Rim onto a taxonomy of power: Nevarro's lawlessness is Hobbes's state of nature out of which sovereigns like Palpatine ('a safe and secure society') carve order by social contract, the Guild's codes and Djarin's creed exemplify Foucault's disciplinary power, and the Client's and Dr. Pershing's harvesting of Grogu's biology - like the Kaminoans' cloning of Jango Fett - is biopower. Against this 'binds of power' ontology they set Grogu's helpless generation of love, a 'little way' that converts Djarin, Omera, Cara Dune, and Greef Karga, and culminates in Djarin twice unhelmeting for Grogu's sake, proposing an ontology of love rather than power as the galaxy's alternative.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 42 "Overcoming Death through the Force of Love" — Lawler reads the nine-film saga as a love story in three acts structured by Plato: Anakin and Padme's passionate love - which Diotima's ladder in the Symposium treats as the necessary first rung the Jedi wrongly condemn - drives his fall, in a Phaedrus-style conflict between the upward rational horse and the downward sensuous one. The original trilogy centers the detached Platonic love of Luke and Leia, while the Rey-Kylo 'dyad in the Force' fulfills Aristophanes' halfling myth of reunited other halves and brings balance, just as Alcibiades' failure to climb beyond the first rung parallels Anakin's fixation on one person. When Ren revives the dead Rey in a Romeo-and-Juliet inversion, the chapter concludes Yoda was wrong: the Force transforms into the dead rather than them into it.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 24 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Goguen reads the Winchesters through two masculine ideals: the warrior (Dean and Michael, chivalric protection culminating in Dean's 'protecting Sam... it's who I am') and the sovereign (Sam and Lucifer, whose freedom is analyzed with Isaiah Berlin's negative and positive liberty, with nods to Hobbes's absolute sovereign and Nietzsche's Übermensch). The show's stoic culture, where 'baring my soul like a freaking girl' is an insult, keeps the L-word unspoken, making Ellen's dying 'I will always love you, baby' to Jo a foil the brothers cannot match. Plato's Symposium, via Aristophanes' myth of split soulmates, and Aristotle's claim that the purest love is between virtuous male friends make sense of the 'psychotically, irrationally, erotically codependent' bond, and the chapter concludes that true masculinity requires embracing the seemingly supernatural: love.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 32 "Notes" — Baggett asks whether Rupert is beyond the grace the show extends to everyone else. She surveys theories of forgiveness - Butler's change of emotion, treatment and performative accounts, and Stump's Aquinas-based framework grounding forgiveness in the love that desires another's good and union, separable from reconciliation - then applies Aristotle's corrupted bad person whose vice 'makes moral truths invisible' as Rupert's limit case. Ted's darts-based tough love is contrasted with Sassy's vengeful certainty and Deborah's cheap grace, and the chapter leaves Rupert's turnaround possible but entirely his choice, while his choices have already been making him.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 14 "5. True Love or Artificial Love" — Klayman treats 'The Lonely' as a case study on whether Corry's love for the robot Alicia is true love. Using C.S. Lewis's four loves plus Peirce's pragmatic maxim (a concept's meaning is its practical effects), he argues Corry showed affection and appreciation but not Eros: he gave Alicia nothing, needed her merely against loneliness, and boarded the ship without sacrificing anything for her. Denying that a machine could be loved, he adds, would be a prejudice akin to Singer's speciesism, and Kendall Walton's 'Fearing Fictions' explains how Corry becomes fictional alongside a make-believe person.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 29 "Notes" — DeVan uses Rand's marriage to Aviendha, Elayne, and Min (and Jordan's own two-girlfriend anecdote) to survey ethical frameworks on polyamory, arguing the answer depends on which lens one uses. Sorting love into the Greek types (ludus, eros, mania, pragma, storge, philia, agape), he runs romantic, sexual, and marital polyamory through emotivism (Ayer), ethical egoism (Ayn Rand, the Forsaken), cultural relativism and social contract (Hobbes, the Aiel), natural law and Kantian duty (the Mahabharata's Draupadi, Genesis), divine command and religion (Judaism, Christianity, Islam), and consequentialism/utilitarianism, rights, and Aristotelian/virtue ethics, invoking Cadsuane's cattle analogy and Brad Wilcox's data favoring monogamy.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 30 "Notes" — Mahon debunks three myths about the original magic lasso: it is not a magic lie detector (Diana already runs a real polygraph on the spy Elva Dove), it is not an enslavement device (slavery is domination, and even the chained Amazons never submitted), and its truth-compulsion is no coincidence. Reading Marston's four-emotion psychology, he shows the lasso and the bracelets of submission are metaphors for love's asymmetric inducement/submission bond - Aphrodite captivates, the Amazons submit - and since lying is precisely an attempt to impose one's will and dominate the hearer (Rotenstreich), a perfectly lassoed person lacks all dominance emotion and so can only submit, and therefore cannot lie. The lasso's later depowering into a mere 'lasso of truth' becomes evidence of the comic industry's discomfort with feminine power.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 33 "Seventeenth Hole More Than a Playing Partner Golf and Friendship" — Andy Wible argues that although golf looks like the ultimate solitary sport, it is unusually good at fostering friendship, and analyzes friendship through Aristotle's three kinds (utility, pleasure, and the highest, based on the friend's good character), supplemented by Laurence Thomas (choice, equality, mutual trust) and Blum on care as a moral phenomenon. Golf's long unhurried rounds, self-called penalties, handicap system, shared memorable shots, and retirement communities build the intimacy, trust and equality Aristotle prizes, and Robert Simon's 'mutual quest for excellence' reconciles competition with goodwill. Wible then confronts friendship's partiality—exclusionary country clubs and the sex-segregated LPGA—using Marilyn Friedman's voluntary friendship communities to argue clubs should drop discrimination on race, sex, religion and orientation while keeping friendship's care and loyalty.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 21 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Schmetkamp reads The Ice Storm through the philosophy of love and Hegelian recognition theory, defending a dialogical model of love (Krebs, Scheler's shared feeling) against union (Plato, Nozick, Solomon) and care (Aristotle, Frankfurt) models. She shows the Hood and Carver families lack autonomy-granting mutual recognition: Ben and Janey's affair is mere egoistic gratification, Elena would surrender her 'I' for a 'we', and Mikey seeks stilled 'molecules' and the Fantastic Four's negative zone. Invoking Sartre's the-look as objectification and shame, she argues Mikey's death finally breaks the ice through empathy and sympathy (Scheler, Stein), as Jim weeps and Elena speaks Ben's name.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 24 "Two Ways of Enduring the Flames The Existential Dialectics of Love in Kierkegaard and Bukowski" — Andreas Seland argues that Kierkegaard and Bukowski offer opposed responses to a Romantic 'paradox of love': the beloved is a dialectical object, part inner imago (Shelley's veiled maid in 'Alastor,' Stendhal's crystallization, Lacan/Zizek) and part uncontrollable external person, and this gap breeds despair. Kierkegaard's Knight of Faith in Fear and Trembling resolves it by infinite resignation and the absurd leap, internalizing the gap and severing the tie to the real to love the princess only interiorly. Bukowski's Chinaski in Women does the opposite, deliberately choosing unstable 'Lydia-object' women who embody the gap, seeking the insecurity itself as a line of flight beyond bourgeois love and even beyond himself.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 15 "Me and You Identity, Love, and Friendship in the Films of Charlie Kaufman" — Den Uyl argues that Kaufman's films are really about friendship rather than romance, reading them through Aristotle's character friendship (the friend as 'other self' and mirror of self-knowledge) and Montaigne's ideal of a free, voluntary friendship that also engages the body. Charlie's fictional twin Donald in Adaptation externalizes the integrity Charlie lacks, and only after internalizing Donald can he say 'I love her'; Caden in Synecdoche fails because he looks only at himself. Love succeeds, on this reading, only when grounded in the self-sufficiency and self-respect that make one capable of an 'other self,' as Eternal Sunshine's Joel and Clementine haltingly discover.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 16 "I Don’t Know, Just Wait Remembering Remarriage in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind" — Day reads Eternal Sunshine as Cavell's Hollywood comedy of remarriage: the kaleidoscopic middle in 'Joel's head' is the couple's remarriage conversation, a 'green world' where they invent a shared childhood and learn what it means to have memories together. Against a tape-recorder model of memory, he invokes the later Wittgenstein's private-language argument to argue there is no private memory — what Joel remembers he can return to Clementine in conversation. He rereads Mary's Nietzsche, the eternal recurrence, not as the end of regret but as affirming it (Joel's 'I wish I'd stayed. I do.'), and claims viewers themselves remember the erased past for the pair across the hallway's ten seconds of waiting.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 14 "Where the Rainbow Ends Eyes Wide Shut Karen D. Hoffman" — Hoffman reads Eyes Wide Shut as Kubrick's most optimistic film, tracing how Bill and Alice Harford are 'awakened' to the uncontrollable power of sexual desire and thereby strengthen their marriage. Bill's Kantian confidence—that principled duty guarantees fidelity—is shattered by Alice's confession of overwhelming desire for the naval officer, which exposes their fidelity as mere moral luck. Through the models, Marion, Domino, and the anonymous masked orgy at Somerton (where sex is impersonal 'bodies touching bodies'), Bill seeks but fails to feel Eros; the couple finally choose a consciously chosen fidelity, and Alice's closing 'fuck' insists raw desire belongs inside marriage, which Hoffman links to Kierkegaard's view of marital love living and winning in time.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Hoffman reads Eyes Wide Shut as Kubrick's most optimistic film, about whether marital fidelity can be chosen rather than accidental. Bill's confidence in his own and Alice's fidelity is a Kantian appeal - duty and rational principle over inclination - which Alice's confession of overwhelming desire for the naval officer, and Bill's night among the masked orgy, expose as vulnerable to uncontrollable desire and moral luck. Hoffman argues that by unmasking and honestly acknowledging these desires (and drawing on Kierkegaard on marriage existing 'in time') the Harfords consciously rechoose their marriage, so their fidelity is no longer merely accidental.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 10 "The Recovery of Childhood and the Search for the Absent Father" — Le Gall and Taliaferro read E.T., Hook, and the Indiana Jones trilogy through a Socratic-Platonic ideal in which the true 'adventure' ends not in glory (kleos) but in homecoming, beauty, and restored parent-child love. Indiana abandons the grail to grab his father's hand and hears 'Indiana' instead of 'Junior'; Elliott becomes a father to E.T. while E.T. teaches him loss; Peter Banning must recover his Pan-childhood to save his kids. They tie this to the Republic's Myth of Er, the Symposium's ladder of love, and xenia (hospitality) as the setting for wisdom.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 23 "Allons-y into the Starry Heavens" — Donna Marie Smith uses the Doctor and Rose's separation in "Doomsday" and "Journey's End" to explicate Kantian deontology. After framing the Doctor's virtues via Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and distinguishing eros, philia, and agape (with Reinette illustrating chivalrous self-sacrifice), she argues that Kant's categorical imperative and the duty-versus-inclination conflict explain why the Doctor and Rose Kant be together: their love pulls toward partiality while duty to save humanity is what they ought to do, so acting for the greater good is precisely what forces their parting.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 11 "3. Why Do I Have to Be Some Kind of Hero" — Zanin reads the Winchesters' sense of moral responsibility through Dostoevsky's The Karamazov Brothers, mapping Dean onto the sensualist/atheist Dmitri-Ivan and Sam onto the faithful Alyosha. Via Father Zossima's dictum that we are 'responsible to all for all,' she argues Sam and Dean's brotherhood is Christian self-sacrificial 'love in action'—shown in Dean choosing Sam over a normal life in 'Bad Boys' and the djinn world—which grounds why they keep saving strangers even after rejecting God's plan.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 14 "5. True Love or Artificial Love" — Klayman analyzes whether James Corry's love for the robot Alicia in 'The Lonely' is true love, using C.S. Lewis's four loves (charity, affection, friendship, Eros) and their three qualities (gift-, need-, appreciative-love), plus Peirce's pragmatic maxim to define 'truly loving' by its practical effects. He argues true love falls within Eros and requires a reciprocating individual, invoking Peter Singer's speciesism to reject a human-only requirement; concluding Corry showed only appreciative-love (not gift- or need-love) and that his bond was really companionship—Corry became fictional (Walton) to have something to believe in.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 11 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Winkle reads Sense and Sensibility as steering a 'middle road' between cold rational calculation and sentimental self-indulgence, and casts Austen as proto-feminist. She uses Wollstonecraft's Vindication to explain why Austen's silly wives (Mrs. Bennet, Lucy Steele) are products of a deficient female education that trains women to please rather than reason. She then reads Elinor Dashwood's measured love for Edward, and Marianne's near-fatal collapse over Willoughby, through bell hooks's claim that 'falling in love' surrenders agency, arguing Elinor chooses love as an act of will while Marianne must learn sense before finding lasting love with Colonel Brandon.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 12 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Gibson argues Austen's novels are propelled by dialectical forces (signaled by titles like Pride and Prejudice and Sense and Sensibility) that are reconciled through the marriage bond, invoking the Platonic origin of dialectic and drawing on Harold Bloom's reading of Darcy and Elizabeth as sharing a common will. Love functions as the transcendent principle that resolves opposition, but Gibson stresses (citing Derrida on the gift) that in Austen love never fully escapes the economic and social 'prisons' of marriage: Charlotte Lucas's loveless match, Fanny Price's poverty, and Anne Elliot's coerced broken engagement all show love succeeding only alongside wealth and status.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 13 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Lindenmuth pairs Austen with Nietzsche on what makes a happy marriage, reading Pride and Prejudice's clashes over Lizzy's refusals of Mr. Collins and Darcy, and Lady Catherine's and Sir Thomas Bertram's aristocratic insistence that superiors should choose for inferiors. He uses Nietzsche's 'philosophizing with a hammer' to cast Austen as smashing the dead traditions of entailment and arranged marriage, and Nietzsche's aphorisms (a good marriage rests on a talent for friendship and good conversation; sensuality makes love grow too fast) to judge the couples, concluding Austen holds an Aristotelian, objective view of happiness as a reward for getting life right rather than mere desire-satisfaction.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 20 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Fiona Woollard asks whether Zach's solo use of pornography (while partner Kelly is out) counts as cheating on their monogamous relationship. Drawing on her account of monogamy as restricting sexual intercourse to loving relationships, she argues that masturbation to porn is not sexual intercourse — there is no interaction with 'Jenna' — and that fantasizing about loveless sex is not the same as having it, so it need not undermine the significance of lovemaking; indeed masturbation aids healthy sexual self-exploration. She concedes, however, that porn which eroticizes the degradation of women (per Dworkin and MacKinnon, and Alice Walker's story 'Porn') can betray a loving relationship by revealing objectifying attitudes.
- **College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits**, ch. 20 "College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits" — This span closes the walk-of-shame semiotics and then applies ancient ethics to college relationships. Puka defends long-distance college relationships through Aristotle's account of philia—arguing (provocatively, per Aristotle) that love is an activity, so being apart 'murders' love unless couples make Skype, sexting, and texting into the relationship's real medium rather than a substitute. Stephens brings Epicurus and Lucretius to 'friends with benefits': since sexual passion is a natural-but-unnecessary desire that breeds anxiety and love is a wound to the mind, while friendship is necessary for ataraxia, he concludes students should skip the sex and keep the friend—'friends are the real benefits,' echoing Tina Turner's 'What's Love Got to Do with It?' Levine/Mongeau and Smith/Morrison supply communication-research data on how FWB relationships form, are negotiated (usually not), and often end when one partner 'catches feelings.'
- **College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits**, ch. 21 "College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits" — This span turns to the ethics and epistemology of college sex. Kania argues there is no clear line between close friendship and a sexual relationship, so condemning student-professor sex logically forces condemning student-professor friendship—rejecting Golash's split and defending carefully-conducted consensual relationships. Layne narrates Socrates/Alcibiades, Abelard/Heloise, and Heidegger/Arendt to contrast Socratic eros (Plato's Symposium, love as a friend of wisdom directed at the soul) and Heideggerian authentic love ('I want you to be what you are') against Abelard's exploitative lust. McDowell mines epistemology (justification, taking beliefs 'to heart,' reflective equilibrium) to argue better thinking yields better, more autonomous sex. Pinku weighs 'plain sex' against Nagel's interpersonal-arousal account of embodiment to ask whether sex needs love, and Brophy uses Kantian dignity (treating the body as a mere means, not an end) to argue that prostitution and webcam porn undertaken to pay tuition violate the student's autonomy.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 7 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — In this foreword Joshua Wolf Shenk recounts an intoxicating blind date with 'Rachael' to argue that dating exposes the core existential dilemma of social creatures: we crave ecstasy (ekstasis, 'standing outside oneself') yet can only connect by holding on to a discrete identity. He blames the modern isolation of the self on Descartes' claim that the self inhabits its own subjective realm and Hobbes' picture of natural man as solitary, and cites Camus that once you choose to live, the real question is how to relate to others. His unresolved paradox—needing the mantra 'I was complete before I met you' while knowing it is false—frames love as the tension between self-sufficiency and merger.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 9 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Editors Kristie Miller and Marlene Clark introduce the volume by opening with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics claim that the human drive to couple is even stronger than the drive to live as a political being and that fulfillment rests in loving relationships. They frame dating as a rule-governed 'game' with aims and strategies and preview each contributor's essay—Jenkins on flirting, Langan on conservative men, Samp and Cohen against unconditional love, the elevator metaphor, cyberdating, evolutionary seduction, and Colyvan's game-theoretic mate search—tying age-old ethical questions about treating partners well to new work in evolutionary psychology, decision theory, and the ethics of online romance.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 11 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Carrie Jenkins does analytic conceptual analysis of flirting, rejecting the Oxford English Dictionary's claim that flirting requires having no serious intentions. She distinguishes 'flirting' from merely 'behaving flirtatiously' (Joe who over-holds eye contact, the tourist touching her earlobe in Italy are flirtatious without flirting) and argues flirting requires an intention to act in ways disposed to raise flirter-flirtee romance to salience, done in a 'knowing yet playful' way. Borrowing Kripke's 'killer yellow' to imagine 'killer-flirts' who die on contact, and citing chatbot studies, she concludes one can flirt with an imagined or non-human target only if one believes it can respond significantly.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 12 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Emily Langan uses focus-group data from 75 self-described ideologically conservative, mostly Christian young men to argue that flirting is a site of moral decision-making, opening with Hitch's 'right broom' line to show these men reject its libido-driven premise. She reports three shared themes—flirting is not about sex but about honesty of motive, timing within a relationship's stages, and reciprocity ('it has to be a two-way street')—and three tensions (healthy vs. harmful, superficial vs. serious, overt vs. covert), drawing on courtship-stage and flirting-style research to show that, contrary to the stereotype that only women agonize over relationships, conservative men wrestle with being 'risqué yet respectable.'
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 13 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Jennifer Samp and Andrew Cohen argue against the Notebook-style romantic ideal of unconditional love, casting dating as a 'calculated exchange' explained by social-exchange and interdependence theory (comparison level and comparison level of alternatives). Adopting Aristotle's distinction between friendships of utility/pleasure and 'complete friendships' in which one values the friend as 'another self' and as an end in itself, they hold the best romances are complete friendships—yet insist even these must be conditioned. Their key thought experiment: a genuinely boundless love would survive discovering one's partner is a child-molesting murderer; since it should not, 'true love knows bounds' and remains part of a good life only because it can be defeated by such reasons.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 16 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Mary Beth Yount asks whether being 'crazy in love' really resembles mental illness, noting lovesickness was a diagnosis for nearly two millennia and that love's mood swings mimic bipolar or schizophrenic symptoms. She organizes the analysis around the four Greek loves—eros (with Plato's ladder from physical beauty to the Forms, i.e., 'Platonic love'), philia (Aristotle's Nicomachean friendship of good character), storge (familial affection), and agape (C.S. Lewis's unconditional charity)—arguing a full romance blends all four. She then surveys Fisher, Aron, and Brown's fMRI work showing romantic love as a dopamine-driven mammalian mate-choice drive stronger than the sex drive, and the 'protest'/'resignation' stages of rejection, to reassure daters their craziness is normal biology, not disorder.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 42 "39. Harry Potter as Philosophy Five Types of Friendship" — Okapal uses the Harry Potter films to expand Aristotle's theory of philia (friendship/love), which recognizes friendships for virtue, pleasure, and utility grounded in other-regarding concern, intimacy, choice, and a surrounding community. He argues the films show that friendships for pleasure and utility each come in beneficent and maleficent forms distinguished by whether motivations are other-regarding or purely self-regarding: the Quidditch team and the Harry-Ginny romance are beneficent pleasure-friendships (Ginny hides the Prince's book out of concern for Harry), while the Hermione-McLaggen date and Ron-Lavender fling are maleficent and short-lived. Slughorn's Slug Club is a beneficent utility-friendship of mutual advantage one may freely leave, whereas Voldemort's Death Eaters are maleficent, with all benefit flowing one way and no exit, yielding five types of friendship and locating Gryffindor's courage, inclusiveness, and loyalty as the ground of virtuous friendship.

### Humanity as an End in Itself

The humanity formula is one of Immanuel Kant's expressions of the categorical imperative, requiring that we treat humanity, whether in ourselves or in others, always as an end and never merely as a means. Because rational beings possess an intrinsic worth, or dignity, that is not exchangeable for any price, they must never be used simply as instruments for someone else's purposes. The principle grounds duties such as honesty and respect and has become a touchstone for arguments about human dignity and the wrongness of manipulation and coercion.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 17 "Conquering the Inner Demon" — James Lawler casts Buffy as a contemporary allegory of Plato's cave-escaped philosopher and reads the show through Kant: the Slayer moves between a hellish lower world of instrumental appetite and an intelligible higher world of the soul, and Kant's Copernican revolution ('objects must conform to our knowledge') explains Marcie's invisibility in 'Out of Mind, Out of Sight' and the fear-made-flesh Master of 'Nightmares.' Kant's formula that every rational being exists as an end in himself grounds Buffy's duty in 'Anne' ('I am Buffy, the Vampire Slayer'), her rejection of Spike's chip as no substitute for a soul in 'Crush,' and her 'As You Were' admission that using Spike treats him as a mere means. Season Six explores 'too much heaven': Buffy's blissful death in 'The Gift' makes earthly life hell, and only conquering the inner demon — Willow's fear-driven dark magic defeated by Xander's yellow-crayon love in 'Grave' — restores the balance between heavens and hells.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 24 "Following the Moral Law" — Applies Kant's Formula of Universal Law and Formula of Humanity on two levels. Individually, Buffy's sacrifice in Dawn's place in 'The Gift' and her post-resurrection return to duty in 'Once More, with Feeling' show her will determined by duty rather than the inclination to a normal life, while Oz's werewolf episodes show inclination swamping reason. Systemically, the Slayer's coercion of demons is justified only because their actions destroy a Kantian state of right in Sunnydale, and Kant's account of radical evil — subordinating the moral law to the maxim of self-love — explains why demons and human villains like Warren's Trio are evil; the chapter closes worrying that the Slayer, like the Initiative's Adam, answers to no one.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 32 "The Moral Sophistication of Buffy the Vampire Slayer" — Greene and Yuen reconstruct seven moral principles from Buffy's conduct — slay those who typically harm humans, never harm humans (Faith's accidental killing of the Mayor's henchman), spare the defenseless and the controllable (chip'd Spike, caged Oz) — and note that blackmailing Spike and roughing up demons would violate Kant's Formula of Humanity if the patients were rational persons, exposing the show's human/non-human moral hierarchy and its animal-rights parallel. 'The Gift' dramatizes deontology (Buffy refuses to kill Ben) against consequentialism (Giles strangles him), and the chapter ranks BtVS above after-school-special, culpable-clown, and faux-realist TV morality because it supports its stands by appeal to general moral principles while keeping Aristotelian habituation and real-life moral complexity in view.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 12 "From Knowledge to Faith" — Lawler reads Crimes and Misdemeanors through Kant's problem of the Highest Good: Judah's unpunished murder of Dolores shows a world where the wicked prosper and the good (Cliff, the blind Ben) suffer, the scandal Job complains of, while Levy's suicide shows that a bare existentialist 'yes' to life fails without love. Kant's 'I had to deny knowledge to make room for faith' is applied to the film's two visions: the deterministic, dog-eat-dog world of science and Adam Smith's economic egoism (with Hobbes's war of all against all) is only appearance, not reality. Kant's gallows example shows Judah could have discovered authentic freedom by respecting Dolores's dignity rather than seeing 'the black eyes of an insect', and the postulates of freedom, God, and immortality ground Ben's not-really-blind faith — so it is Judah who is truly blind.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 60 "The Sorting Hat Speaks Division and Divisiveness" — This section argues that patriotism violates the principle of equal moral worth shared by utilitarians and Kantians alike: Bentham's 'each to count for one, and none for more than one' means the Minister of Magic's pain counts no more than a house-elf's, while Kant's formula forbids treating anyone (Muggle or wizard) merely as a means. It reads Death Eater pureblood ideology as ordinary racism and sexism, cites Potterwatch's 'every human life is worth the same, and worth saving' and Hermione's S.P.E.W. campaign against 'slave labor,' and asks how preferring countrymen over foreigners differs from preferring people of one's race or gender, since neither is something a person controls.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 74 "Harry’s Cloak, the Ring of Gyges, and the Temptations of Power" — This section contrasts Voldemort and Dumbledore as two figures tempted by power. Tom Riddle's egocentrism - frightening and controlling other children at the orphanage, treating his 'friends' as mere followers, killing Lily, and splintering his soul for Horcruxes - violates Kant's dictum never to use persons merely as means and fits Plato's category of the least trustworthy rulers. Dumbledore, though tempted in youth by Grindelwald's 'for the greater good' schemes and later by Marvolo Gaunt's ring, is venerable for Socratic self-knowledge: knowing 'I was not to be trusted with power,' he repeatedly refused the Ministry and so promoted justice by teaching.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 13 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Taliaferro, writing as a personalist, worries that Gibson's relentless focus on torture eclipses the whole person of Christ: like torture victims losing peripheral vision, viewers lose sight of his teaching, healings, nonviolence, and resurrection, and the satisfaction-theology framing risks relishing redemptive suffering itself. His reconciliation thought-experiment (Patricia's betrayal of Kris and the God-man who resurrects the murdered child) argues that the resurrection, not the passion alone, completes at-one-ment, since no amount of suffering can undo past wrong. He contrasts Gandalf's laughing return in The Return of the King with a Gibson Jesus who could not plausibly laugh after rising, and invokes Scheler's St. Francis, who loves the wholeness behind sickness rather than the sickness, to urge that the film's intensity edges out a life-affirming view of persons as irreducibly valuable in themselves.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 12 "“You Know . . . What They’re Up Against”" — Dees finds moral ambiguity lurking in Star Wars' black-and-white universe: Han Solo's Hobbesian ethical egoism ('I take orders from just one person - me') is shown to be coherent and gradually transformed by friendship with Luke and Leia into commitment to a cause. Lando's betrayal of Han on Bespin is defended as a straightforward Mill-Bentham utilitarian choice by a responsible official, weighed against Bernard Williams's Jim-and-the-commandant integrity objection, which the author rejects as moral vanity. Count Dooku's apparent idealism is exposed as evil's tool, and Anakin's massacre of the Sand People is condemned as non-ambiguous barbarity via Kant's formula of humanity (and Hume on reason's role with the passions), leaving only late Vader as genuinely morally ambiguous.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 17 "Send in the Clones!" — Hanley defends a provocative 'yes' to cloning, genetic engineering, and clone armies. He dismisses the 'yuck factor' as showing nothing inherently bad, argues via non-identity-style cases (a genetically corrected or maimed Luke is a different child who is not thereby harmed) that early genetic manipulation harms no one, and distinguishes brainwashing, coercion, and inducement (Obi-Wan's death-stick mind trick, Vader's threats to Lando, Jar Jar's exploitation) to ask when bending another's will is permissible. Turning to warfare, he applies Just War theory's conditions - judging Anakin's slaughter of the Sand People guilty on nearly every count - and concludes that troops with deliberately diminished autonomy may be the least objectionable solution to the ethics of recruitment, training, and deployment: send in the clones.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 43 "Power and Glory Tests of Virtue" — The chapter's thesis is that superhero ethics is not utilitarianism (whose perverse 'evil twin' governs Marvel villains) but personalism - the tradition from Borden Parker Bowne to Martin Buber, rooted in Kant's insistence that every person be treated as an end and never merely as a means, and aiming at his 'kingdom of ends'. Heroes who refuse to weigh one innocent against the many enact personalism, and it redeems even Galactus: lying defeated, he is saved by Captain America's and Reed Richards' insistence that 'We had no choice, Galactus', which wins the devourer into a moral community. The authors read the whole arc as the ancient warning against hubris retold in contemporary storytelling.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 93 "I’m a Lover, Not a Fighter!" — Turns to Kantian nonconsequentialism: persons must be treated as ends in themselves and never merely as means, from duty rather than consequences, with negative duties (not harming) stronger than positive duties (aiding) — so Reed Richards may not kill a pedestrian for organs to heal Doctor Doom's victims, though a utilitarian would require it. Since neither becoming Spider-Man nor refusing to violates any negative duty, being a superhero is supererogatory: 'with great power comes great responsibility' is at most a duty not to misuse power, and precisely because heroes don't have to do what they do — as Clark Kent's Superman II choice shows — their choosing it is what makes them praiseworthy.
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 13 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Dennis uses Kant to sort eaters into the fundamentally unfree (Herbert, raised on Atkins and thieving, who merely ploughs on), the fundamentally random (Rita, whose synapses and muscles would fire in chaos), and the autonomous, arguing that only an autonomous person can genuinely decide whether to follow Atkins — by weighing friends' testimonials against the medical establishment rather than habit, whim, or advertising. The categorical imperative grounds the autonomous life: 'lie when you can gain' fails universalization, and treating humanity as an end means offering a vegetarian guest food she is comfortable with instead of pressing Atkins meat on her. His own 'Dan Dennis Diet,' built by experiment and reasoning, illustrates autonomy in practice, and the case of Kitty shows that observing someone's diet never reveals whether its holder is unfree or autonomous.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 26 "James Bond and Philosophy" — McKinney argues that '007' is a technological construction distinct from the human James Bond: drawing on Dewey's broad view of technology as technique (the shaken martini as technological artifact), Heidegger's account of naming as revealing and enframing, and Don Ihde's technological embodiment (the party-game hand axe that is art, paperweight, or tool depending on perception). Film dialogue shows the naming at work: Moneypenny calls him 'James' but announces '007 is here' to M; Goldfinger greets '007' and is corrected with 'My name is James Bond'; M threatens '008 can replace you' and, in Die Another Day, declares 'You are no use to anyone now' while rescinding his status. The chapter closes with the Kantian point that persons must be treated as ends in themselves, yet the designation '007' constitutes Bond as precisely a replaceable means to MI6's ends.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 28 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Arp and Decker examine Bond's objectification of women - using a dancing girl as a human shield in the Goldfinger pre-credits sequence, M ordering Bond to 'pump her for information' - through three moral theories. Kant's humanity formula condemns treating women as sexual tools, but Kantian autonomy generates a stalemate since consensual, reciprocal liaisons like Bond and Anya Amasova's might qualify as permissible; Millian utilitarianism condemns the male gaze by its long-term social costs yet stalls against pro-sex feminist counterarguments. They settle on Aristotelian virtue ethics - the mean between extremes, with respect as the key virtue against the power-centered virtue of Machiavelli, Hobbes, and Nietzsche - to argue objectification is vicious, and they trace Bond's moral progress from skipping the young Bibi in For Your Eyes Only to the reciprocal relationships with Kara Milovy, Pam Bouvier, Wai Lin, and Jinx.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 29 "“Who watches the watchmen ”" — Loftis argues Watchmen's real target is authoritarianism, with Ozymandias and Rorschach as corrupted rationalizers. Ozymandias calls himself a consequentialist, but his Bentham-Mill utilitarianism cannot survive Dr. Manhattan's 'Nothing ever ends' — an infinite future makes utility sums impossible — and it ignores the rights of the New Yorkers he slaughters as mere means. Rorschach's deontology is hypocrisy (he admires Truman's Hiroshima trade-off and says 'can't make an omelet without breaking eggs'), mistaking Kant's categorical imperative — universalize your maxim, treat humanity never merely as a means — for black-and-white thinking in service of fascist thuggery, while the nonideological Nite Owls embody the lesson that no one should be trusted with such power.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 15 "The Virtues of Superhumans" — Rachel Robison tests the Deadly Viper Assassination Squad against three ethical theories. Act and rule utilitarianism condemn killing Vernita in front of Nikki and revenge in general; Kant's categorical imperative condemns Elle's black-mamba betrayal of Budd (contradiction in conception), O-Ren's beheading of a dissenter (contradiction in will), and Buck's selling of comatose women (treating persons as mere means). She concludes the Squad instead follows a bastardized Aristotelian virtue ethics—Bill's Superman speech, contempt for Budd's shotgun bushwhack and Elle's poisoning of Pai Mei define courage as the mean between cowardice and rashness—so Beatrix would be cowardly not to seek revenge.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 17 "Conclusion June Love Beyond the Jordan" — Sennett builds "June Love" out of June Carter Cash's documented love, from the "Hurt" video's staircase glance to Rosanne Cash's eulogy that June saw your potential and "lifted them up" for you to see, and the love that steadied John through addictions and infidelity for thirty-five years. He stages the philosophy-of-love dilemma between appraisal theories (Velleman, grounding love in Kantian dignity that demands respect but cannot justify loving John rather than anyone) and bestowal theories (Irving Singer, on which love projects value and so cannot be justified at all), with Frankfurt's volitional account as a side note, and proposes June Love, loving the beloved's potentiality, as the hybrid that is both objective and active and can justify loving this person. He also distinguishes June Love from codependence: enabling entrenches the addict's destruction, whereas June's confronting-and-encouraging love, echoed in "Ring of Fire" and "Far Side Banks of Jordan," called Cash to transformation while leaving him himself.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 20 "From Cash to Kant—and Back Again" — Yolanda Estes pairs Cash with Kant as two duty-based moralists: Cash's Golden Rule in 'The Preacher Said, Jesus Said' parallels Kant's formula of humanity (never treating persons merely as means), and Cash's 'good heart' matches Kant's good will, since songs like 'Sam Hall,' 'Folsom Prison Blues' (the man shot in Reno 'just to watch him die'), and 'I Hung My Head' weigh inner motives over outcomes. Because earthly law never balances the moral scale, she reads Kant's kingdom of ends and Cash's apocalyptic kingdom of God in 'When the Man Comes Around' and 'God's Gonna Cut You Down' as parallel objects of faith: we must live as if perfect justice already prevails, working to improve this world rather than waiting for the next.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 25 "Seeing Ourselves Reflected Back" — Gray asks whether Cylons deserve moral consideration, starting from Kant's demand to treat humanity never merely as a means: the New Caprica suicide bombings and Adama's plan to weaponize a Cylon virus treat captives merely as means, while Helo's sabotage of 'A Measure of Salvation' acknowledges their intrinsic value. D'Anna's dissent before being boxed and Athena's defection for Helo show the rational autonomy Kant's personhood requires; if that is dismissed as programming, Singer's sentience criterion (Leoben tortured, Gina catatonic) and Warren's multi-criterial personhood — including Boomer's 'I have a conscience' in 'Downloaded' — still open personhood to Cylons. The chapter ends on the humans' double standard (Athena accepted, guns drawn on Caprica Six) as a mirror for our own treatment of uncertain others.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 16 "“I’ve Never Been Good at Good-byes”" — Lee treats DS9's Cardassian Occupation as a case of transitional justice like post-Holocaust and post-apartheid reckonings, asking whether Odo, security chief on Terok Nor, was a collaborator. Applying Kant's deontology — the good will, both formulations of the categorical imperative, illustrated by Kai Opaka's Kendra Valley betrayal, Quark's smuggling in 'Little Green Men', and Sisko's fraud in 'In the Pale Moonlight' — he judges Odo's letting three innocent Bajorans die in 'Things Past' as negligence, but his years-long cover-up as using the victims merely as means to protect his reputation, and hence genuine collaboration, as was his neglect of duty under the Link's pull in 'Behind the Lines.' Kant's imperfect duty of beneficence then redeems Odo's final departure from Kira: returning to cure and educate the Founders in 'What You Leave Behind' is a moral duty owed to rational beings.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 8 "There’s No Place Like Home" — Luke Dick stages Immanuel Kant as the 'Supreme Critical Chancellor of Munchkinland' and runs the film through Kantian ethics: against hedonism, utilitarianism, and command-based religion, the formula of universalizability condemns the Wizard's lies and his use of the companions as mere means, while the ends-in-themselves principle raises the awkward case of Glinda and Dorothy keeping the dead Witch of the East's ruby slippers. Judging the characters, the Lion's rescue of Dorothy is morally praiseworthy (duty against strong inclination), the brainless Scarecrow falls outside Kant's jurisdiction, and the sentimental Tin Man is pre-emptively condemned. The chapter finally rebels against its Chancellor: cases like returning the slippers, or Toto versus Almira Gulch, show that a world of absolute morality lies only 'somewhere over the rainbow,' and real moral life in Kansas needs Baum's Tin Man heart reconciled with Kantian duty.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 23 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Michaud reads the Autobot-Decepticon war as a contest of ethical systems: Optimus's fair fighting, his refusal to ignore human casualties, and Bumblebee's friendship with the inferior Spike instantiate Kant's categorical imperative and the treatment of rational beings as ends in themselves. The Decepticons run through the egoist tradition - Hobbes's psychological egoism from Leviathan, Starscream's self-defeating normative egoism, and Megatron as Ayn Rand's rational egoist taunting 'You still fight for the weak; that is why you lose' - leaving the reader to choose between Kant's world of peaceful obligation and Rand's world of power where, like Starscream, you die alone.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 8 "8" — Four 'Phase Two' essays on the nature of evil. Arp argues that in V for Vendetta V is a utilitarian user of persons just like the fascist Norsefire state - using Dascombe as a shield and torturing Evey 'for her own good' - so Kant's demand to treat humanity never merely as a means condemns the hero-as-villain, though 'moral autonomy' Kantians complicate the verdict. Poon stages the Aquinas-Ockham debate over will and intellect as Magneto reprograms Sentinels against New York (Ultimate X-Men #05), arguing the will cannot choose against the intellect's judgment, so supervillains like Magneto, Ra's al Ghul, and Apocalypse act for what seems good to them with a deeply flawed conception of the good. Robichaud uses Superman Returns, Civil War, and Captain America vs the Red Skull to test Mackie's error theory, prescriptivism, expressivism, and moral relativism, defending moral objectivism against the Modern Age's gray morality. Sylvia IV and Walters use Bentham, Mill's higher and lower pleasures with competent judges, and Railton's ideal-advisor moral realism to dismantle Mojo's defense that his Spineless Ones' ratings-driven bloodsports are just desire-satisfaction, indicting our own reality TV.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 17 "Close the Door, Put Out the Lights" — Scott Calef tests three ethical theories against Led Zeppelin's off-stage destruction: TV-tossing, samurai-slashed hotel rooms, food fights, sharks hung in closets at the Edgewater Inn, the red snapper incident, and Jimmy Page's relationship with fourteen-year-old Lori Maddox. Classical utilitarianism weighs Bonzo's glee against the traumatized chambermaid, displaced guests, and unpaid-for sleep loss, generally condemning the pranks while leaving the supposedly consensual snapper episode uncomfortably open. Kant condemns across the board: Plant's fake tour itineraries and the stolen 'Black Beauty' Les Paul fail the universalizability test, trashing hotel rooms is self-defeating when universalized, and treating the Portland woman as a mere means violates her dignity as a rational agent; Aristotle's golden mean finds the band's excess nowhere near virtue, whatever Caligula would say. The chapter closes by separating moral judgment of the men from appreciation of the music.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 18 "The Legend Has Come True. The Wind Has Come Back" — Haas opposes two princesses of Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind: Kushana of Tolmekia, whose 'whatever it takes' survivalism (invading Pejite, resurrecting a God-Warrior) is consequentialism pursued to its limit, and Nausicaa, whose attention to each act — befriending the biting fox-squirrel, staying her sword over her father's killer because vengeance would doom the Valley — restricts means, not just ends. The reductio comes from Pejite, whose torture of a baby Ohmu to bait a stampede on the Valley is exactly what strict outcome-maximization requires; against this, Kant's demand to treat beings as ends in themselves explains Nausicaa's 'mysterious power' of empathy. Because she respects the jungle and the sentient Ohmu rather than viewing nature anthropocentrically as a plague to burn, she discovers the plants are purifying the war-poisoned earth — the knowledge that saves everyone and proves Kushana's conquering approach self-defeating even on its own terms.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 40 "Lester’s Duties and Capabilities" — Maguire asks whether the Royals did wrong by trying to hit in the late innings of Jon Lester's May 2008 no-hitter, working through Kant's distinction between perfect duties (always binding—playing hard, honoring the codified rules) and imperfect duties (praiseworthy obligations that admit exceptions—respecting the unwritten convention against bunting for a hit in a blowout). Sympathy for Lester's cancer recovery must not enter the calculation, since Jim Abbott's 1993 no-hitter shows the duty must universalize; bunting would be 'bush league' rather than wrong, a lapse in imperfect duty. He extends the analysis to Francona's pitch counts and warns that wanting Ellsbury to bunt against a Yankees no-hitter would treat the pitcher as a mere means to fan pride.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 34 "Kind of, Sort of a Lie, But neither Immoral nor Illegal" — Cynthia McWilliams imagines a reader beating her neighbor after taking 'Pedophile Nervous For First Day Of School' literally, and asks whether The Onion lied to her and whether that lie was wrong. She defines a lie as asserting what you believe false (intent to deceive is not required), then tests the satire on both classic accounts: on Kant's categorical imperative, a lie without intent to deceive does not use readers merely as means, while on Mill's utilitarianism the entertainment benefit outweighs harm unless serious harm is reasonably foreseeable — the limit case being the 1938 and Quito 1949 War of the Worlds broadcasts, the second of which killed six people in a riot. Her verdict: The Onion is 'kind of, sort of a lie' but neither immoral nor illegal, passing even the Brandenburg 'imminent lawless action' standard for free speech.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 15 "I’ve Got No Strings . ." — Richard Greene asks whether it was practically rational for Dexter to trust Lumen rather than kill her, to help her revenge-kill the Fowler ring, and to train her as a killer. The good outcomes do not help - Masuka's strip-club windfall shows luck is not rationality, and Socrates' Apology argument that corrupters risk harm from those they corrupt, together with Dexter's prior disaster in training Miguel, means the consequences were not foreseeably good. Kantian tests fail too - no one could will a universal law of killing, and killing violates the victim's autonomy and humanity as an end in itself - as do decision theory and instrumentality theories, so no account of practical rationality vindicates Dexter's choices, suggesting instead that the emotionless 'wooden boy' is beginning to become a real one.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 14 "Invisibility or Honesty" — Schulzke argues inception's fundamental wrongness is a violation of autonomy read through Kant: the Fischer team treats him merely as a means, and even Cobb's benevolently intended inception on Mal disrespects humanity by stripping her self-determination, leaving her - like someone acting under coercion - no longer a responsible moral agent. Extraction he judges the lesser evil, though a world of dream espionage would end private mental life, since even the most guarded secrets surface in dreams. The payoff is a new twist on the Ring of Gyges from Plato's Republic: an invisibility ring could no longer shield injustice because a dreamer's deeds remain recorded and extractable, so Kant's absolute ban on lying could make extraction an engine of honesty - as when Ariadne's extraction on Cobb exposes the danger Mal poses and ultimately saves Cobb himself.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 42 "The Valuable Self" — The chapter turns from metaphysics to morals: for Kant the self is the most valuable thing in the world, a subject that must never be used as a mere means, since turning a subject into an object is the ultimate immorality. The authorities' plan to hollow Arctor into an unwitting infiltrator, and Donna's lament that he 'didn't volunteer', make the point concrete: what is valuable in us is the self's fuzziness, including its mystery of free will, and to remake a person into a scanner, 'a mere thing that just watches and never chooses', is the ultimate crime.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 75 "Chapter 11 - We Can Manipulate You Wholesale" — Reads Total Recall's opening scenes — Harry's shifty eyes, then the reveal that his friendship, Lori's marriage, and even Benny's cab-driving are all sanctioned deceptions directed at Quaid — as manipulation commissioned by an outside element that sets the agenda of each relationship. Using people this way already troubles Kantian ethics, the chapter concludes, and an outside element directing individuals to do it is 'potentially enough to have Immanuel Kant spin in his grave.'
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 77 "Finding a Lever for Manipulation" — Explains the spy tradecraft acronym MISE (Money, Ideology, Sex, Ego) and walks through 'Fred's' recruitment method in A Scanner Darkly — building trust through drug purchases under false pretenses until the mark must betray another confidant for Fred's benefit. The same template covers Lori, Harry, and Hauser in Total Recall, for whom Quaid 'becomes nothing more than a means': monitoring his return to Mars, or locating the rebel leadership.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 78 "Categorically, We Have an Imperative Problem" — Measures the spying in A Scanner Darkly and Total Recall against Kant's second formulation of the categorical imperative: Benny merely tracks Quaid, while the federal agents sacrifice 'Fred's' entire psyche, devaluing his humanity as a mere means. It then stages the real-world debate the fiction mirrors — the Pike and Church Committees, Godfrey's preference for technological collection, and Langan's utilitarian defense that devaluing a few is justified when society's safety requires it.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 79 "Utilitarian Doesn’t Necessarily Mean Coveralls" — Lays out the utilitarian case for the spying in A Scanner Darkly: with New Path immune to inspection and Substance D addiction spreading, sacrificing Bob Arctor — secretly addicted to breakdown point and implanted with the little-flowers trigger — maximizes outcomes for the many. Against this stands the Kantian rebuttal that he should never have been made 'just another means,' likely never again to be 'an able-minded and self-determining person,' and the chapter adds the overlooked victim: the manipulator who violates the categorical imperative.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 20 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Solves the 'riddle' of Gus by showing his empire runs on corporate instrumental rationality: the careful, emotion-disciplined Los Pollos CEO launders meth through legitimate business, treats chemists as replaceable parts (the Gale plan), and exacts revenge on the cartel in 'Salud' by drinking his own poisoned tequila.
