The chapter defines this as the critical theorists' amoral means-end reason - Kant's hypothetical imperative without the categorical - making Gus a sociopath who violates the injunction to treat persons as ends, and reads his cartel war through Machiavelli and Hobbes's power-first picture of the state. Gus's Two-Face-like corpse reveals the split between the rage-driven avenger of Max and the respectable mask, foreshadowing what Walt becomes.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 16 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — McKendry and Da Silva build a Kantian case that walkers deserve respect as 'residual humans': Rick dwelling on organ-donor Wayne Dunlap before harvesting his corpse for camouflage shows that bodies carry the dead's chosen ends, so using Wayne is honoring, not using, him. Because walkers are corpses bound by the presumptive wishes of the deceased, and retain residual subjectivity (Jenny returning again and again to her family's door), survivors wrong them by treating them as mere objects - Merle's sport killing of walkers on the rooftop is the moral low, Rick's swift, risk-accepting headshots of Hannah and Deputy Leon the respectful execution. Jim's informed choice to be left by the road to turn, over Shane's and Rick's objections, shows the autonomy of the infected that no one else may override.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 12 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Bateman replies to Cogburn that Law and Chaos descend not from Kant but from Michael Moorcock's Eternal Champion stories, where they are liberal and conservative political tendencies held in check by the Cosmic Balance, which restores Chaotic Good, Lawful Evil, and the Druid's true Neutral as viable positions. He rejects the 'sausage machine' universalization of maxims for Kant's humanity formula and Realm of Ends, and argues act utilitarianism makes a poor model of Good: an overpopulation scenario could mandate genocide, and Bentham's felicific calculus cannot actually measure the good. Alain Badiou's ethic of truths supplies the positive case for Chaotic Good—pursuing what you take to be good without submitting to a single moral law—while Buddhist and Jain renunciation dignifies Lawful Neutral.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 16 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Massimo Pigliucci reads Rise as a Greek tragedy of hubris and asks whether Will Rodman dosing his father with ALZ-112 was wrong, first dissolving the 'it's unnatural' objection and probing the cure/enhancement border with Daniels's Peter-and-Johnny growth-hormone case, vaccination-as-enhancement, and Eubulides's bald-man paradox. He then runs the decision through three ethical theories: Millian consequentialism condemns it by its results (his father dies and humanity goes extinct, though chimp happiness might outweigh that), Kant's humanity formula condemns using his father as an unconsenting experimental subject, and Aristotelian virtue ethics vindicates Will's compassion and courage - Pigliucci's own view, since sometimes our best is just not enough. He closes by rejecting Baylis and Robert's technological-inevitability thesis (we abandoned the Concorde, CFCs, and nuclear weapons before) and lets Jacobs's plunge into San Francisco Bay stand as the penalty for market hubris.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 24 "Psych and Philosophy" — Rocha argues Kant is not the absolutist of legend: in 'On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy' Kant denies only a right to lie - Gus could be held responsible if his lie to Shawn's pursuing murderer goes wrong - and in The Metaphysics of Morals Kant openly leaves questions like polite untruths unanswered, to be judged by agents in their concrete circumstances. The deeper ground is Kant's duty to oneself: lying shows disrespect for the honest communication through which social beings sharpen their rationality, and so 'throws away and annihilates' the liar's dignity, which is why Uncle Jack's gold-hunting lies in 'The Greatest Adventure in the History of Basic Cable' are beyond rescue. On Rocha's reading even Kant could endorse the one lie to rule them all - claiming to be psychic - because it respects rationality and human life in a society that irrationally esteems the supernatural, while Shawn's Gus-alias gags and bunny fabrications remain immoral.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 20 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Fallis sorts Atlantic City's lies to show which are wrong and why. Kant's and Augustine's absolute bans go too far and Grotius's life-saving exception does not apply - most of these lies get people killed - yet even altruistic lies (Margaret for Madame Jeunet and the ledger), lies told to those who want to be deceived, lies to liars, and Sorensen's bald-faced lies that no one believes (Jimmy's flat movie alibi, Rothstein's 'skilled player' whopper) remain wrong: they take informed choice out of the victim's hands, violating the Kantian autonomy that grounds the wrong of lying, and they corrode the trust on which even criminals' co-operation depends.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 14 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Piven argues Zapp Brannigan's 'sexlexia' - his deluded velour-and-spanking seductions of Leela and his relief at finding Lee Lemon is a woman - typifies a whole cast of clueless lovers (Fry coaching Zoidberg's courtship of Edna, Morgan Proctor's mess fetish, Bender coldly dumping the Planet Express ship in 'Love and Rocket'). Kant's condemnation of masturbation as self-abuse that throws away one's personality and violates humanity in one's own person is exposed as unsupported prejudice, and Nietzsche's claim that morality projects fear, envy, and disgust onto the despised other explains why 'perversion' is an arbitrary cultural judgment. Freud, Stoller, and McDougall then recast perversion as unconscious flight from anxiety and death, so the show's kink - up to the Monsterpus of The Beast with a Billion Backs and Amy's 'general sluttiness' - mirrors our own sexlexia and existential dread.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 22 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — James Cook grades the Third Invasion against the just war principles Ender was never taught: the war is preventive rather than genuinely preemptive (with the 2003 Iraq parallel), proper authority is compromised by deceiving the public, last resort fails since the hive-queen was trying to communicate, and non-combatant immunity condemns destroying the bugger homeworld. He stages Augustine's ban on killing in individual self-defense against Aquinas' permission of it, and uses Kant's humanity formula and Cicero's hostis/perduellis distinction to ask whether the buggers were ever treated as rational beings rather than mere threats.
- **How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness**, ch. 17 "How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy" — The chapter evaluates Marshall and Lily's promise to tell each other everything through Kant: lying violates the universalizable duty of truthfulness and treats the deceived as a mere means, as with Lily's hidden credit card debt in 'Dowisetrepla', the realtor's sewage-plant omission, and Barney's fully staged seduction of Meg that blocks her informed choice. Even Marshall's kindly lie about the doppelganger fails Kant's test, alongside his infamous refusal to lie to the murderer at the door. Yet Kant's letters on reticence in friendship and his grim view of marriage as shared ends where spouses may use each other 'as if' they were things suggest that telling each other everything may itself corrode respect - the tension Lily's never-opened bathroom door dramatizes.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 25 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — King charges human exceptionality with being speciesism and asks whether dinosaurs are persons rather than humans, testing Kant's rationality criterion and Descartes' denial of animal thought against the raptor that opens the shed door and the T. rex that spins the Explorer searching for prey. He runs the dinosaurs through Mary Anne Warren's five personhood criteria, then plays his Wittgenstein trump card: animal language would be the language of a different life-form, so the raptors' calls expressing fear and summoning help count as real communication without words. He closes with Regan's rights view, arguing that the cow and goat feeding scenes, like past denials of personhood to Native Americans and women, should shame us into showing a little respect.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 32 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Nicole Pramik asks whether the demons of Brandon Mull's Fablehaven can be taught morality, using Kant's deontology as the measuring stick. Seth's kindness to Graulas looks dutiful and universalizable, and Graulas at first seems a rational agent respecting the categorical imperative - until healed, he betrays Seth, demolishes the preserve's treaty, and declares himself 'pure, deliberate evil' who used Seth as a mere means. Nagi Luna never even tries, and the Sphinx who models her is himself a serial user of persons, so the chapter concludes that rational demons remain impervious to the moral law: you can lead a demon out of Zzyzx, but you cannot make it good.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 57 "The Devil and Philosophy" — James Edwin Mahon dismantles the 'sympathy for the Devil' puzzle by testing three accounts of diabolical evil: Machiavelli's prince ('learn how not to be virtuous') shows self-interest is mere amoral Realpolitik; Schopenhauer's malice and Schadenfreude ('injure all people as far as you can') are still self-interested pleasure; and only Kant's 'diabolical will' - doing evil because it is evil, Paradise Lost's 'Evil, be thou my good' - truly captures the Devil, though Kant deemed it impossible for humans. Hence nobody actually likes the Devil; people like the intelligence, charm, and underdog status of the characters who play him in The Devil's Advocate and Angel Heart.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 13 "Homeland and Philosophy" — John Karavitis evaluates four suicide events: Afsal Hamid's suicide in CIA custody, Aileen Morgan's cutting her throat with a lens, Brody's aborted suicide bombing, and Carrie's ECT as a 'suicide' of her old self. Kant's absolute ban on suicide (it denies your humanity) clashes with Seneca's Stoic counsel that a life of miserable captivity need not be continued, and with Singer's utilitarian permission of euthanasia that reduces suffering - under both, Hamid's and Aileen's suicides are defensible while Brody's emotionally driven bombing is not. Dana's plea that her father is needed recasts Aristotle's point that suicide wrongs the community, and Sloterdijk's analysis of rage turned on oneself frames Carrie's amoral self-destruction.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 23 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Edwin Jacob contrasts the utilitarian calculus behind Walden's drone strike - Estes's eighty percent estimate, 'potential collateral damage falls within current matrix parameters', eighty-three children killed - with Kant's three formulations of the categorical imperative applied to that decision. On the universal-law formula Walden cannot will a world of strikes on one's own soil, on the humanity formula the schoolchildren are used merely as means, and the kingdom-of-ends formula condemns treating foreign lives as quantities in a matrix. The chapter adds that drones, like Brody's suicide vest, are asymmetric terror at a distance, and that blowback (Shahzad's Times Square attempt) shows the strategy fails even consequentialist test.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 32 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Dona Cayetana and Nathan Everson argue that 'enhanced interrogation techniques' is a euphemism - with Zizek and Badiou they show relabeling torture as what the West does while 'torture' is what Muslims do conceals identity between the acts, as 'Blind Spot''s safe-house interrogation of Hamid demonstrates. Utilitarianism justifies Saul's fatiguing of Hamid by its results, while the Kantian view that persons must never be mere means condemns it categorically; the chapter contends the show's framing nudges viewers to accept torture as a necessary evil. Carrie's gendered role as Zizek's 'new face of torture' - a pretty white woman whose desirability and perceived vulnerability become interrogation tools, from sex with Brody to 'You broke my heart' - feminizes and normalizes the spectacle.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 24 "Girls and Philosophy" — Wible asks whether the workplace abuse in Girls - Hannah's two unpaid intern years, the harassment at the law firm, the 30-day e-book deadline that triggers her OCD, Marnie hostessing at a gentlemen's club - is defensible by young workers' inexperience and the 'experience paradox.' Against the boot-camp defense he argues from the meaning of work (Gini's 'I work, therefore I am,' Schumacher's good work) and from Marx on alienation from the products of labor, but his core standard is Kant's: persons must be treated as ends, never merely as means, which the editor who wants the book and not the person violates. He concludes that young workers' vulnerability (no savings, no leverage, reluctance to blow the whistle) warrants paid internships, transparency, and two-way respect.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 21 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Framed by Dickens's Jacob Marley, Walker asks whether Jobs deserved his posthumous accolades despite giving far less to charity than Bill Gates, and tests him under three frameworks. Aristotle's virtue ethics acquits him (character is judged holistically, and charity sits near the golden mean of open-handedness rather than being a checklisted duty); Mill's utilitarianism acquits him (his innovations maximized happiness and he violated no Harm Principle—though abandoning daughter Lisa counts as a harm); and Singer's drowning-child argument condemns him as near-morally-bankrupt for selling luxury gadgets while children starve. Kant both convicts (charity is an imperfect duty under the categorical imperative) and saves Jobs: treating the affluent individual as an end in himself, never merely a means to the destitute, blocks Singer's demand for giving to marginal utility.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 16 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Altmann stages a moral (not legal) trial of Dracula with three expert witnesses: Kant testifies that Dracula universalizes murder only for himself while fleeing Harker's kukri, and that he reduced Harker to a mere meal, violating the categorical imperative and deserving execution; Mill weighs consequences, tallying the misery done to Lucy, her mother, and the Bloofer Lady's child victims, and argues the greatest happiness lies in imprisoning the Count for medical study instead; Aristotle argues the child-brained vampire lacks the reason and self-control needed for eudaimonia and so merits imprisonment rather than death. The chapter hands the verdict to the reader, showing guilt is agreed but punishment diverges across the three frameworks.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 12 "3. What’s So Bad about Eating People" — McCraw imagines Lecter defending each class of victim with a different ethical theory: the Momund and Dortlich kills through Natural Law Theory plus lex talionis retribution (Dortlich ate Mischa, so he is eaten; Momund treated the aunt as meat, so he is treated as meat), the 'Sorbet' Rolodex dinner-party victims through a perverted Kantianism that swaps politeness for rationality so the rude forfeit humanity and corpses have no moral standing, and Krendler, Raspail, and Chilton through consequentialist accounting of worlds improved by their deaths. He concludes that only virtue ethics resists such distortion: Lecter's cold, callous, manipulative character and his isolated, paranoid, friendless life show that no possessor of good character could eat people, so cannibalism really is bad even when the murders are bracketed.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 19 "8. Consuming Homicidal Art" — McAteer uses Bullough's aesthetic distance to test whether the psychopath Hannibal can have genuine aesthetic experience, arguing against Maibom and Harold that egocentric pleasure in an artwork is compatible with aesthetic distancing - so a Lecter who loves Bach and Italian architecture (unlike Cleckley's unmoved psychopath and the Tooth Fairy's graceless 'performances') could really exist. But since psychopaths can value nothing as an end in itself - they treat persons and artworks merely as means - homicidal art like the Muralist's corpse cathedral and Hannibal's gourmet cannibalism is the logical extreme of Wildean aestheticism, proving Wittgenstein's 'Aesthetics and ethics are one' false; yet in homicidal art Hannibal's moral deficit becomes an aesthetic deficit too, because anyone who can see beauty in human bodies as mere material is over-distanced - the bodies, like any sculpture's material, matter.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 15 "Walker Bite. Let’s Just Do What’s Right" — Devlin and Cooper present Dale as the show's Kantian deontologist: he acts from duty regardless of consequences, applying the humanity formula - treat people always as ends, never merely as means - when he blocks the execution of Randall in 'Judge, Jury, Executioner' and refuses to let the group do consequentialist math about abandoning the search for Sophia. Shane, the Governor, and the Termites serve as the consequentialist foils who treat Otis, the prison residents, and their victims as mere means to survival. The chapter argues Dale dies with his humanity and dignity intact, and that the series' recurring drama is a three-sided battle between his deontology, the survivors' consequentialism, and Rick's eventual virtue ethics.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 25 "Walker Bite. If I Don’t Save the World, I Have No Value" — This Walker Bite uses Eugene Porter's exposed lie about being the scientist who can cure the outbreak (5.5 "Self Help") to ask what makes a person valuable once their usefulness collapses. Eugene himself sums up an instrumental view of his own worth - "If I don't cure the disease, if I don't save the world, I have no value" - and admits he sabotaged the bus to stall the DC mission. Against this, Tara's "We're friends. We have each other's backs... You're stuck with us. No matter what" argues that persons are valued for themselves within a community rather than as means, and the chapter lands on Abraham's "people need people" as the real ground of Eugene's place in the group.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 11 "2. Golem Morality in the Modern World" — Skene weighs Peter Singer's 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' - opened with a River Ankh drowning-child variant - against the golem morality of Going Postal and Feet of Clay. Mr. Pump's charge that Moist von Lipwig's frauds 'hastened the deaths' of 2.338 people grounds a golem standard of actuarial murder that Skene applies to the 2008 banking crisis and Mao's Great Leap Forward. With Kant, the chapter holds that free choice is the foundation of moral responsibility and respect for others' wills, but unlike Singer's unlimited demands, golem morality asks us to own the foreseeable consequences of our choices without sacrificing everything.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 11 "3. Hero or Villain" — Kevin McCain asks whether Darrow the hero and Nero au Augustus the villain can really be told apart, noting both hold noble goals (Eo's dream versus preserving humanity) and share brutal means. Consequentialism fails to separate them: Darrow's sacrifice of dockworkers and Sons of Ares to Romulus mirrors Nero's 'I do what I need to do to protect the greater good,' and Harmony's sacrificing Evey shows the same ends-justify-means reasoning. Kantian ethics condemns both, since each lies to people and sacrifices them without consent, treating them as mere means to an end. Virtue ethics finally offers grounds: Aristotle's requirement of proper motivation, developed through Michael Slote, distinguishes Darrow, who acts from love for Eo, his friends, and the Colors and is wracked by guilt, from Nero, who is fueled by inhuman pride and feels nothing at Eo's hanging—so motivation may be what makes one forgivable and the other a villain, though the chapter ends wondering if good intentions pave the road to Hell.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 28 "14. Is Lucy a Kantian or Just Mean and Nasty" — The chapter tries to acquit Lucy of meanness by reading her as a Kantian: her maxim for throwing Schroeder's piano into the Kite-Eating Tree fails universalization as a contradiction in conception, her blanket confiscations and 'settling for average' lectures enforce Kant's duty of self-improvement, and her brutal truth-telling honors the absolute ban on lying (a Mill-and-Bentham contrast highlights that Kant locates moral worth in intentions, not comfort or consequences). The football gag then undermines the defense: by withholding what Charlie needs to know - that she will pull the ball - she treats him as a mere means, and since what matters is her real intentions rather than her stated ones, the Kantian verdict is left to the reader.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 33 "20. Deadpool’s Genocide of the Marvel Universe" — Taking Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe seriously as a genocide story, the chapter reviews Lemkin's coinage and the 1948 Genocide Convention, then tests the mitigating factors - Deadpool's insanity, the X-Men's negligence in committing him to Psycho-Man's fake asylum, and Psycho-Man's manipulation - and finds none of them exculpatory. Killing Uatu the Watcher first and the Avengers next follows the genocide playbook of eliminating a community's intellectuals and pillars, and viewing his fellow characters as sheep completes the dehumanization that makes atrocity possible, while using everyone as means to his liberation violates Kant's demand never to treat persons as mere means. Invoking the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Thucydides' Melian Dialogue as the classic case of victims left unable to tell their story, the author concludes Deadpool bears full responsibility.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 29 "14. Is E Corp an Evil Person" — Wood asks what E Corp ontologically is: on Plato's theory, it would participate in a Form of Corporation, while Aristotle's primary substances show E Corp is not an individual at all - just a name for ways people interact. Corporate personhood (from 1819 contract rights through Citizens United and Hobby Lobby) makes it a legal person whose responsibility diffuses 'almost to the point of evaporation,' and Kant's humanity formula explains the unease: a legal fiction with no intentions or dignity can never respect persons as ends, which is why Angela's quest for a moral 'who' behind Washington Township ends only with the two ordinary executives Price hands her.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 20 "10. Trust Systems or People" — Malloy locates the heroes' core disagreement in trust: Cap trusts people, recruiting reformed villains (Hawkeye, Scarlet Witch, Quicksilver, Deadpool) and inspiring the 'kooky quartet', while Tony trusts systems, running the Initiative with pay and the threat of Prison 42. Using Adorno and Horkheimer's critique of instrumental reason, he shows Tony losing sight of what and why he acts - the Armor Wars killing Titanium Man, Civil War destroying the safety it sought - and treating people as means rather than ends in themselves. Via Darwall's two respects (grounded in Kant), Cap's recognition respect for autonomous persons beats Tony's appraisal respect for qualities (he respects even Doom's intellect), so only Cap's trust preserves freedom - and wins.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 21 "11. Fighting Ethical Relativism in Tales of Suspense" — Reading Tales of Suspense, Pagnoni Berns and Veteri cast Iron Man as a man of every era - echoing LBJ's 'reason together', Cold War utilitarianism against Communism, playboy masculinity, and finally the Registration Act - which makes him a parrot of whatever relativism his age prefers. Captain America, literally frozen in time, holds Kant's categorical imperative: every life is an end in itself, so he saves Nazi prisoners in #71, trades his own life for a pilot in #61, and drinks possibly lethal serum without needing thanks, while Bucky's mediated, reward-seeking morality shows why ends corrupt moral worth. Because Cap's universal, ahistorical defense of human dignity holds from the 1940s to the 1960s and beyond, the authors rank him above the adaptable but context-bound Iron Man.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 25 "15. Iron Kant or Captain Kant" — Bosma and Barkman run both heroes' positions on the Superhuman Registration Act and the Sokovia Accords through Kant's deontology. Iron Man's maxim 'I should obey the government' looks universalizable, but it collapses once Cap's critique of the atomic bombings shows an unjust order (killing innocent civilians, or a Doctor Doom takeover) must be refused, and the humanity formulation condemns registration for treating heroes as mere means to the government's ends. Cap's own maxims - fight for freedom and justice, obey only a just government - universalize cleanly, so the chapter awards the deontological duel to Captain America.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 25 "14. Of Course It Sucks—It’s Work" — Wible stages three theories of work against Dilbert strips: the Greek view of Plato and Aristotle that labor is freedom-sapping and leisure is the civilized ideal, Marx's capitalist critique in which workers become objects and machines (Wally gives off no human vibe, and robots are coming for the engineers), and Desjardins's human-fulfillment model built on Schumacher's creativity, challenge, development, honesty, and beauty, with Wells Fargo's fake accounts showing how jobs that force lying corrupt character. He endorses instead a Kantian middle ground anchored in Norman Bowie's moral minimum: never treating workers as mere means, so the CEO making intern Asok drink industrial sludge on stage is a violation of respect for persons, not just bad management. Sisyphus supplies the image of pointless labor, though even he might be redeemed if he loved the rock.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 15 "5. Albert Among the Chowder-Head Yokels and Blithering Hayseeds" — Argues that Albert Rosenfield embodies Kant's categorical imperative: his refusal to soften his autopsy demands or lie to spare feelings is fidelity to universalizable maxims, and his insistence that Sheriff Truman be charged for punching him treats punishment as respect for a rational agent's autonomy. The chapter walks through maxims, the universalizability test applied to Gordon Cole's possibly faked deafness and FBI lying, hypothetical versus categorical imperatives (Cooper may always want Norma's cherry pie, but morality trumps want), and the formula of humanity — Ben Horne's use of One-Eyed Jack's women as mere means is the counterexample, while Albert's insults paradoxically honor Truman's rational agency. Albert's arc to "I love you, Sheriff Truman" and his gentler Season Two and The Return self shows a Kantian who integrates classical reason with romantic feeling.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 28 "Whatever! It’s All Natural" — Jaquet and Cova take the show's 'livestock' comparisons seriously and use animal ethics to test every justification for the guests' treatment of hosts. Direct speciesism (Logan: 'She's a goddamn doll') and indexical speciesism (Maeve's 'us versus them' to Bernard) both fail because mere species membership is morally irrelevant, like race or sex. The supposed human-exclusive markers also fail: hosts match us in intelligence (Maeve outclasses Stubbs), moral sense (Bernard's guilt over Theresa, Teddy's remorse over the massacre), and compatibilist free will - acts flowing from the agent's own desires - against Ford's determinism and Lutz's 'you don't have a choice.' They then refute the argument from nature (Ford's 'we murdered and butchered anything that challenged our primacy'), the Kantian person/tool contrast in the hosts' favor, Locke's creator-ownership ('I built your mind, Bernard'), and the 'better to exist' defense, concluding that because the hosts are conscious, they belong to the moral community alongside humans and animals.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 26 "13. Gilead vs. the Self" — Holberg argues that on Kantian grounds Gilead is morally incoherent—Handmaids are treated as mere means, vessels without agency—and that it sustains itself by attacking self-respect through two temporal modes: the quick onset of fear (Aristotle's account in the Rhetoric applied to the machine-gun arrests of women at their jobs) and the slow grind of shame (empty time that turns women into 'objects not in use' and manufactures a veneer of consent: 'nothing is going on here that I haven't signed up for'). Agency needs recognition from others—love as the most basic acknowledgment, or invoking Moira ('Moira would never stand for this shit')—so June's 'I tell, therefore you are' and the reader's duty to affirm her judgment carry the feminist-Kantian point: dependency on others does not negate the self, it is what constitutes it.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 27 "14. The Value of a Handmaid" — Pérez assesses a Handmaid's value through Kant—Gilead gives women a price, not a dignity, so the Gilead–Mexico trade deal is human trafficking dressed as diplomacy—and through Marx's use value and exchange value, with fertility the commodity and Jezebels carrying both market and affective price. He adds Bourdieu's forms of capital to show Offred's social and resistant cultural capital against Janine's collapse, then weighs cultural relativism (via Renteln and Herodotus) before rejecting it for Gilead: its values were improvised and forced rather than naturally evolved, so the culture itself earns no pass. The Handmaids' refusal to stone Janine shows their collective worth: 'They should've never given us uniforms if they didn't want us to be an army.'
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 29 "16. Who Is the Meanest of Them All" — Frunză and Grad apply Arendt's banality of evil to Gilead: the Commander is 'not Iago, not Macbeth' but an Eichmann—sheepish, Scrabble-playing, 'thinking about how not to think'—and no character holds a monopoly on evil because everyone is 'too banal' for demonic profundity. They test his 'just doing my duty' against Kant (duty requires universalizing what reason can will and never treating persons as means, so the Aunts' reeducation camps fail the test) and use The Origins of Totalitarianism to read Handmaids as rightless people whose 'two-legged wombs' status mirrors statelessness. Arendt's web of guilty complicities explains why resistance is scarce, and the chapter ends with banality eroding all criteria for judging—leaving Offred's 'the darkness within; or else the light' as the final choice.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 27 "14. Is Kant the Reason Everyone Hates Moral Philosophy Professors" — Duindam defends Kant against the charge that he makes moral philosophy professors insufferable, walking through maxims and the two-question Categorical Imperative test with frozen-yogurt and stealing examples, and arguing that Kant's notorious 'you cannot lie to the murderer' essay is an obscure legal point whose actual test permits lying to demons. On the trolley, the bridge, and Michael's forced organ-harvesting scenario, Kant's humanity formula, never treat persons merely as means, explains both Chidi's refusal to kill Eleanor and the difference between switching tracks and pushing a man. Tahani's sixty billion dollars in charity earning no points, and Eleanor's fruitless 'What's My Motivation' blitz versus her costly confession, vindicate Kant's claim that only a good will gives actions moral worth, while Aristotle supplies the closing lesson that being good takes practice, not just study.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 39 "23. Like Boxing Gloves of Sadness" — Benko argues the show's deepest target is selfishness understood as inauthenticity: an over-investment in a self whose real motivations, Tahani's name-dropping, Chidi's moral filibustering, Jason's Acidcat fiasco, Eleanor's aggressive solitude, are hidden from the person herself. Drawing on Charles Guignon's account of authenticity, he shows that being true to yourself is not enough unless your self-expression enables others to become their authentic selves too, which is why Chidi's keeping of his promises across all 802 reboots is the show's moral core and why treating people as mere means fails on Kantian grounds. Eleanor's final willingness to lose Chidi rather than her better self demonstrates authenticity reoriented toward others, the show's answer to Schur's fourth-car-at-the-left-turn driver.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 7 "A Seriously Mind-Blowing Book about Seriously Mind-Blowing Movies" — The introduction argues that all villains, real or fictional, share one trait: they treat people as mere objects to be used, which is why Thanos's Snap feels monstrous. It then springs the book's central provocation: since Thanos kills half of all life to save the rest of the universe from overpopulation, resource exhaustion, and destruction, he is 'actually a strictly moral being' from a utilitarian perspective. It frames the tension between using persons and respecting them (the grenade-jumping soldier who gives himself willingly versus those sacrificed without consent) and previews the volume's chapters on Thanos's morality and mind, time travel, and death.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 9 "1. Rights and Wrongs of Reversing the Snap" — Philip Mouch weighs consequences against rights to ask whether the Avengers were wrong to undo the Snap in Endgame. He imagines a survivor whose returned spouse finds her remarried, cataloguing displaced families, food shortages, and political turmoil, and argues these harms, however real, are outweighed by restoring the lives Thanos took. The deeper problem is Bruce Banner's wager with the Ancient One: removing the Time Stone dooms a branch reality on a 1-in-14,000,605 chance, gambling innocent lives without their consent, which resembles Thanos's non-consensual sacrifice of Gamora rather than the noble self-sacrifice of Hawkeye and Black Widow on Vormir. He concludes that two wrongs do not make a right: even for a noble end, risking countless lives tramples the rights of others.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 17 "Questioning Our Attitudes, Sokka‐style" — Wawrzyniak traces Sokka's growth from seeing animals as food and fur ('Dinner!' at Momo in 'The Southern Air Temple') to bonding with Foo Foo Cuddlypoops and vowing a 'karmically correct vegetarian existence', measured against Kant's anthropocentric view of animals as mere things whose cruel treatment matters only as a risk to human morals. Aang's harm-free uses of animals, from otter penguin sledding to riding hog monkeys, are then tested by Korsgaard's pathocentrism: animals are 'someones' who mind what happens to them, so even harmless use demands justification. The chapter urges us to scrutinize our own habits of eating, entertainment, and pet-keeping with Sokka-style empathy.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 19 "What if Hama Was Wrong" — Gregory argues bloodbending necessarily uses persons as mere means because it overrides the victim's will regardless of their actual consent, unlike buying tea from Zuko but like Azula's deception of Long Feng, and so violates Kant's Formula of Humanity in every offensive use. Katara's bloodbending of Hama in self-defense is permissible because she stops Hama's wrong rather than using her toward any end, and even a hypothetical consensual 'cooperative model' cannot redeem the practice, since the sheer power it grants and its corrupting effects on practitioners (Noatak and Tarrlok in LoK) justify Katara's ban.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 17 "Questioning Our Attitudes, Sokka‐style" — The chapter sets Kant's view that animals are mere things owed only indirect duties against Korsgaard's pathocentrism, on which animals matter for their own sakes because they can mind how they are treated. Sokka's arc from shouting 'Dinner!' at Momo to bonding with the saber-tooth moose lion cub Foo Foo Cuddlypoops, and his aborted vow of vegetarianism in 'Bitter Work,' models empathy-driven reassessment of meat, while his sparing Momo for Aang's sake is exactly Kant's indirect duty. Aang's harm-free fun, otter penguin sledding and riding hog monkeys 'because that's what makes it fun,' shows that even non-cruel use of animals demands justification, with the unagi firefighting as a case that might pass the test.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 19 "What if Hama Was Wrong" — Gregory argues bloodbending necessarily violates Kant's Formula of Humanity: controlling the water in another body 'enforcing your own will over theirs,' as Hama puts it, uses a person as a mere means because the bender's maxim ignores the victim's actual consent, even when a victim happens to consent, as in the Ozai medical-experiment analogy. Katara's vengeful bloodbending of Yon Rha in 'The Southern Raiders' is therefore impermissible, while her restraint of Hama uses no one as a means at all since it only halts a rights violation. Even if a cooperative, consent-based bloodbending were possible, Katara's Republic City ban is defensible, because the standing power to override wills corrupts practitioners, as Noatak's and Tarrlok's downward spiral in LoK shows.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 20 "And the war Rages on" — Robichaud runs the Kree-Skrull War (Avengers #89–97) through Michael Walzer's just war theory: the Avengers' defense of Earth against Ronan's Plan Atavus is justified self-defense meeting proportionality and last resort, while Ronan's preventive 'devolve humanity' war fails for lack of evidence and exhausted diplomacy. The Skrulls' shape-shifting trick that gets Mar-Vell to build the Omni-Wave Projector might squeak through on consequentialist grounds, but the emperor's threat to make Captain Marvel watch the Scarlet Witch and Quicksilver die counts as torture—and is impermissible on the Kantian ground that it treats a person merely as a means, whatever the consequences. The point is that even a cosmic comic war displays the real moral complexity of military ethics.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 25 "Seeing Ourselves Reflected Back" — Gray asks whether the Cylons deserve moral status, testing them against Kant's formula of humanity as an end in itself: the resistance's suicide bombings on New Caprica and Adama's plan to weaponize virus-infected Cylons against the resurrection ship in 'A Measure of Salvation' use beings as mere means, while Athena's defection and D'Anna's dissent (and her line's boxing) display the rational autonomy Kant requires of persons. Singer's sentience principle (Gina's catatonia after torture, Leoben's suffering under interrogation) and Mary Anne Warren's multi-criterial personhood (Boomer's 'I have a conscience' in 'Downloaded') independently support Cylon personhood. The chapter concludes that the show's double standards, accepting Athena while drawing guns on Caprica Six, mirror our own confusion as cloning and artificial intelligence advance.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 20 "A White Christmas with Dark Reflections" — The chapter follows White Christmas's three escalating uses of the Z-eye digital block — Beth blocking Joe (whose information deprivation leads to two deaths), court-ordered blocks extending to children, and Matthew's society-wide red-blur sex-offender block — as a conflict between privacy and access to information. Utilitarian and Kantian frameworks (autonomy, persons as ends) leave the trade-offs genuinely unsettled, while Nozick's minimal state shows the automatic, loophole-free blocking regime is an indefensibly paternalistic state violating proportionality. Arendt's account of meaningfulness through speech grounds the conclusion that erasing someone's face and voice violates their humanity, and the chapter's final move is defamiliarization: if digital blocks are wrong, we should re-examine the social-media blocking, restraining orders, prisons, and sex-offender registries they mirror.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 11 "2 Transforming Wakanda Justice (or Not ) in Black Panther" — Bein and Lewis imagine Killmonger surviving his duel to face Wakandan justice, and sort what justice would demand into retributive justice (Kant: punishment only what the offender deserves, never using him merely as a means to public safety, though they note Kant's own racist views), reparatory justice (Locke's natural rights and what Wakanda owes N'Jadaka for T'Chaka killing N'Jobu and abandoning him in Oakland), and the restorative-to-transformative justice of Changamire's gatherings in Coates's 'A Nation Under Our Feet,' modeled on South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission. They argue a restorative Wakanda would seat Killmonger with his victims and even the king at the table to repair harm rather than imprison him, and sketch a prison-abolitionist Wakanda meeting Thanos with 'Wakandan justice is more civilized.'
- **Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality**, ch. 24 "Black sabbath & philosophy" — Mark D. White shifts the is-it-still-Sabbath question from metaphysics to ethics, asking whether bands owe fans a stable line-up when they keep the name. Kant's Formula of Universal Law permits the maxim "change members, keep the name" without contradiction, and the Formula of Respect forbids only coercion or deceit, using fans as mere means, so the real wrong is deceptive marketing, as when record-company pressure billed Iommi's solo project Seventh Star as "Black Sabbath featuring Tony Iommi" and sent it out playing "War Pigs" and "Iron Man". The Dio reunion's honest rebranding as Heaven & Hell passes the test, while fans, symmetrically, owe bands no loyalty and may legitimately love only one era.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 12 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Bateman replies to Cogburn by recovering the alignment system's actual literary source: Moorcock's Elric saga, where Law and Chaos are rival political ideologies (conservative and liberal tendencies) held in check by the Cosmic Balance, so a Chaotic person need only refuse law's authority, not will horror, and Chaotic Good remains possible. He rejects Cogburn's 'sausage machine' reading of Kant's first formula in favor of the humanity formula and the Realm of Ends, and rejects act utilitarianism as a model of the Good alignment, since an overpopulation scenario shows Mill's calculus mandating culling-genocide and Bentham's felicific calculus cannot actually measure goodness. Drawing on Badiou's ethic of truths, Buddhist and Jain renunciation, and the true-Neutral Druid as servant of the Cosmic Balance, he argues neutrality between Good and Evil need not be monstrous and mourns 4e's 'childishly simplistic' new system.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 22 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Air Force colonel James Cook walks the just war tradition through Ender's world: the Third Invasion is preventive rather than preemptive (with the 2003 Iraq war as the parallel), proper authority is undermined by the I.F.'s lies to its citizens, and last resort fails because the hive-queen was already trying to communicate with Ender. He contrasts Augustine's ban on killing in self-defense with Aquinas's permission, invokes Kant's formula of humanity for the buggers' rational nature and Cicero's hostis against dehumanizing enemies, and argues the I.F.'s failure to teach military ethics is itself part of the novel's tragedy.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 12 "Notes" — Trevor Hedberg asks whether 'Kill Everything' playthroughs of New Vegas are wrong, from the Goodsprings opening (where the player may massacre both Powder Gangers and settlers) to installing a mod that makes Freeside's unkillable children killable. He rejects the empirical aggression argument (the evidence is mixed and effects tiny, and alcohol or contact sports set a precedent) and the Kantian disrespect argument, since Fallout's NPCs - stuck on terrain, repeating dialogue - lack the rational agency the Humanity Formulation protects. The best case against virtual slaughter is Aristotle's virtue ethics: courage as the mean between recklessness and cowardice, eudaimonia as activity in accord with virtue, so the morality of playing turns on motives - exploring narratives or seeking combat challenge can be innocent, but killing for the pleasure of settlers' horrified flight corrodes character.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 29 "Notes" — Weighing Vault-Tec's secret experiments — Vault 11's yearly human sacrifice, Vault 13's 200-year lockdown, the cryogenic freezing of the Sole Survivor — the chapter asks whether the ends could ever justify the vaults. On Kant's Universal Law and Humanity Formulations the answer is flatly no: dwellers were deceived into becoming mere means to data, whatever the hypothetical space-colonization motive that designer Tim Cain favors. Act and rule utilitarianism in Bentham's tradition give a more equivocal verdict — exposed deception would doom any future cooperation, yet safeguarding humanity might in extraordinary circumstances tip the calculus — and the chapter situates the games in real research-ethics history from the eugenics era to the Tuskegee study and the Belmont Report.
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 14 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — Robert Arp and Sarah Fisk test three moral theories against objectification in Final Fantasy: Kant's ban on using rational beings as mere means (Kuja's manipulation of Queen Brahne, the Geostigma children of Advent Children), Mill's greatest-happiness principle (Yuna's and Aeris's self-sacrifice), and Aristotle's character-based virtue ethics (Hojo and Sephiroth as vicious, Aeris as virtuous). They argue Kantianism generates a stalemate between 'moral sanctity' and 'moral autonomy' camps over cases like Guardian Force summoning in FFVIII, and utilitarianism a stalemate over mandatory self-sacrifice, leaving virtue ethics, Aristotelian or Nietzschean, as the view that escapes both, ending with the question 'Aeris or a Cloud?'
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 27 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Tyrion - born a reviled dwarf who killed his mother, yet heir to Lannister wealth, wits, and Jaime's knightly example - frames Nagel's paradox of moral luck: his compassion toward Jon Snow and Sansa is constitutive luck, and his carefully run wildfire defense of King's Landing shows resultant luck, since the same prudent act deserves praise in one outcome and blame had it burned the city. Kant's good will, applied to Tyrion's protection of Shae as treating her as an end and never merely as a means against Cersei, is offered as a rescue but only neutralizes resultant luck, leaving constitutive and circumstantial luck untouched. The chapter ends with Nagel's shrinking 'extensionless point' of genuine agency, concluding we cannot keep both moral responsibility and the principle that we are blamed only for what we control.
- **The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire**, ch. 15 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" — Why do Berger, Cecilia, Harriet, Salander, and Figuerola all bed the unprepossessing Blomkvist? Testing Kant's claim that sexual desire makes 'the loved person an Object of appetite... a lemon which has been sucked dry,' the chapter argues his appeal is that he treats women as ends in themselves—he works beside them as equals, is 'not going to compete with you' with Figuerola, and never manipulates or controls—so his sex is the least objectifying in a Sweden full of men who hate women. Against Kant and Baumrim, Irving Singer's reply that desire can respond to the whole person explains why his no-strings honesty attracts powerful women, though his refusal to define, own, or 'cherish' any lover—walking in on Erika just as Salander arrives with the Elvis cabin ad—still leaves Salander heartbroken and Figuerola in sadness.
- **The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire**, ch. 29 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" — Salander shares Kant's detestation of the criminal's hypocrisy: Martin Vanger's meticulous, unimpulsive murders and Wennerström's hubristic paper trail fail the universal-law formulation because each supremely rational villain casts himself as the exception to rules that bind everyone else. But Salander fails Kant too—she hacks 'for the kick' rather than from duty, encroaches on innocent privacy, and takes justice into her own hands (tattooing Bjurman, stealing from and arranging the death of Wennerström) where Kant's 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' would forbid even lying to a murderer; the chapter finds her closest to Benjamin Constant's rejoinder that truth is owed only to those worthy of it, matching her maxim that 'a bastard is always a bastard.' Her strict promise-keeping, her cultivation of mind and body per the Doctrine of Virtue, and her refusal of guardianship and of Blomkvist's money make her, in Kantian terms, a champion of autonomy who is nonetheless a work in progress.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 27 "14. Is Kant the Reason Everyone Hates Moral Philosophy Professors" — Defends Kant against the charge that he is why everyone hates moral philosophy professors: it explains the two-question Categorical Imperative test via frozen-yogurt maxims and Eleanor's selfish 'won't help unless it benefits me' principle, shows Kant never actually forbade lying to the murderer at the door (his crotchety 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' was an obscure legal point), and reads Chidi's trolley-track switch but refusal to harvest Eleanor's organs as the humanity formula — never treat a person merely as a means. Tahani's $60 billion in charity and Eleanor's failed point-chasing in 'What's My Motivation?' illustrate the good will: deeds lack moral worth unless done for the right reasons. Aristotle explains the residual puzzle — theory mastery does not make you skilled at ethical practice, any more than a nutritionist is a great cook.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 39 "23. Like Boxing Gloves of Sadness" — Begins with Schur's traffic-light story — the fourth car sneaking through the left-turn arrow as 'negative twenty points' — to argue the show is, before it is about ethics, an attack on selfish inauthenticity: Tahani's name-dropping charity, Eleanor's lunch-table declaration of friendlessness, Chidi's moral filibustering, and Jason's Acidcat gig each pursue a self at others' expense. Using Charles Guignon's On Being Authentic and Kant's language of means and ends, it traces the movement from authenticity that uses others to an authenticity that lives for others — Chidi's 802 unconditional yeses, Michael's shift from torturer to self-sacrificer to paralyzed would-be hero, and Eleanor giving up Chidi in 'Pandemonium' as the endpoint. Being true to yourself, the show teaches, is only ethical when it helps others be their truest selves.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 23 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — White distinguishes retributivism from deterrence and rehabilitation through the Corps' execution vote on Sinestro and Fatality's lex talionis pursuit of John Stewart over Xanshi ('You have four billion eyes to account for'). Kant grounds retribution in dignity, so punishment must treat the criminal as an end, never merely as a means to deterrence, and is owed to him for his crime ('You did this to yourself,' Hal tells Sinestro), while Hegel adds that punishment annuls the crime and embodies the criminal's own right. Feinberg's expressive theory explains the Korugarian crowd that felt 'cheated of Korugar's redemption' when the execution stalled, and the chapter closes by separating justice from vengeance: Ollie's arrow through Prometheus and Laira's 'It was justice!' killing of a surrendered Amon Sur were personal revenge, which only impartial state agents may convert into justice.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 60 "The Sorting Hat Speaks Division and Divisiveness" — Against Death Eater blood-purity, the chapter sets the ethical tradition of equal moral worth: Bentham's 'each to count for one, and none for more than one' (the Minister of Magic's pain matters no more than a house-elf's or a Blast-Ended Skrewt's) and Kant's demand to treat humanity never merely as a means. It applies this to Potterwatch's 'every human life is worth the same, and worth saving' and to Hermione's S.P.E.W. campaign against house-elf 'slave labor,' then asks how patriotic preference for compatriots differs in kind from racism and sexism.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 74 "Harry’s Cloak, the Ring of Gyges, and the Temptations of Power" — The chapter reads Tom Riddle as Plato's unfit ruler: from the orphanage ('I can make them hurt if I want to') he violates Kant's dictum never to use persons merely as means, treating even his 'friends' as followers, killing Lily despite Snape's devotion, and splitting his soul for Horcruxes. Dumbledore, offered the Ministry repeatedly yet refusing because 'power was my weakness and my temptation,' has the Socratic self-knowledge that he cannot be trusted with power, and that self-awareness, not flawless virtue, is what keeps him from Grindelwald's and Voldemort's path and makes him the series' nearest philosopher-ruler.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 27 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Foy reads the arena as Hobbes's state of nature recreated: the Cornucopia bloodbath, 'stealing isn't illegal here,' and temporary alliances awaiting betrayal instantiate the war of all against all, while the Treaty of Treason is Panem's written social contract buying order at the price of submission to the Capitol. Gale's advice that killing tributes is 'just hunting' mirrors the Hobbesian maxim the Gamemakers want, whereas Peeta's vow to show he is 'more than a piece in their Games' expresses Kant's categorical imperative and the duty to treat humanity as an end. Katniss's arc — decorating Rue's body, risking her life at the feast for Peeta's medicine, telling the District 2 soldier 'I'm done killing their slaves,' and rejecting Gale's tactic of bombing rescuers — moves her from survival logic to Kantian moral autonomy. The chapter ends by rejecting the Hobbesian justification of oppressive rule: a life of fear and servitude is not worth preserving at any cost.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 14 "Invisibility or Honesty" — Schulzke argues inception is a categorical violation of Kantian autonomy: the Fischer job treats him merely as a means (Saito's market share, Cobb's reunion with his children), and even Cobb's benevolent inception on Mal disrespects humanity by robbing her of self-determination, leaving her unable to act as a responsible moral agent testable against the categorical imperative. Extraction, by contrast, attacks privacy rather than autonomy, and the chapter uses Glaucon's Ring of Gyges to show that dream espionage would defeat even perfect invisibility, since an extractor could always read your deeds in your dreams. The twist, played off Kant's absolute condemnation of lying, is that the standing threat of extraction might be the only force that could make universal honesty practicable — hence the title's choice between invisibility and honesty, illustrated by Ariadne's life-saving extraction on Cobb.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 13 "4 Raiders of the Lost Kant Indy Meets the Categorical Imperative" — Mia Wood tests Raiders against Kant's categorical imperative: Belloq's maxim of taking whatever he wants cannot be universalized without destroying property itself, and he repeatedly uses persons as mere means — deceiving the Hovitos about the Golden Idol, preying on Dietrich's fears, and treating Marion as a possession to be seduced with wine and a white dress. Indy fails too: his affair with the sixteen-year-old Marion ('It was wrong and you knew it'), leaving her bound and gagged to pursue the Ark, and Kant's absolutist ban on lying is probed through Katanga's noble lie to Dietrich. The first film's shadowy cinematography visualizes this moral ambiguity — Indy starts as merely one more 'raider' and only gradually redeems himself across the sequels.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 14 "Notes" — Quanbeck reads The LEGO Movie as a battle between two theories of the value of persons. President Business rules Bricksburg through extrinsic accounts — Harry Frankfurt's view in The Reasons of Love that caring and loving confer value, plus an economic model on which worth equals social contribution — which make Emmet's self-worth swing wildly with others' judgments, from Bad Cop's 'blank slate' recording to Wyldstyle's flattery and dismissal. The philosophical turning point comes with Vitruvius' ghost: Emmet's Kantian enlightenment that rational persons are ends in themselves with intrinsic, mind-independent value, so that 'The prophecy is made up, but it's also true. It's about all of us' — a belief that empowers his self-sacrifice and Wyldstyle's broadcast to the citizens.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 25 "Real World Island" — Patricia Brace and Rob Arp argue Lost redeems characters who stop objectifying others and instead freely 'objectify' themselves for the greater good. Kant's ban on treating persons as mere means condemns Ben's lifelong manipulation and Ben's use of Sayid as an assassin, yet autonomy justifies chosen self-sacrifice like Charlie's Looking Glass suicide mission, Claire volunteering as bait for Ethan, and Jack becoming the new Jacob. Mill's utilitarianism makes Kate's shooting of the Man in Black a fair trade saving her friends, while Aristotle's virtues - respect against objectification, courage in Jack's death at the cliff, the engrained honesty of reformed con man Jim LaFleur, Kate's character-building motherhood of Aaron - complete the three-theory survey.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 18 "The Question of Ethical Advertising" — Novakovic and Whitney use the Heineken incident, where Betty discovers she was the target demographic for her husband's campaign ('Must be so funny, being in on it'), to test advertising against Kantian honesty and respect. Kant's humanity formula and the lying-promise example show that manipulation wrongs the consumer as a rational agent, and Don's defense that advertising sells 'happiness' fails because Kant allows making others' happiness an end but never at the cost of truth, whether the consumer is a stranger or a wife. The chapter sets this against the era's brainwashing anxieties (Hunter's Brainwashing in Red China, Packard's The Hidden Persuaders, Precon subliminal projection) and concludes that honest advertising must survive disclosure of its methods, noting that real sponsors like Canada Dry and BMW responded to the show with stripped-down 'transparent' ads that let viewers be 'in on it.'
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 31 "The Office and Philosophy" — Arp and Watson sort Dunder Mifflin's relationships into five conceptions of love: Roy's erotic 'best sex of your life' Valentine's offer to Pam as blind eros; Angela and Dwight's pursuit of an idealized mate read through Plato's Forms and the Symposium's ascent to Beauty; Aristotle's three friendships, under which the office's alliances are mere utility while Jim and Pam's teapot sacrifice in 'Christmas Party' approaches virtue friendship; the Stoic-Kantian 'equal loving' of universal respect, laughed at when Michael ranks himself with Bono and Lincoln; and agape-style family loyalty that leads Dwight to supply Michael his urine in 'Drug Testing'. The chapter concludes that Michael exemplifies a selfishness Western philosophy has no name for, failing at every form of love.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 26 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Robichaud argues Peter actually wronged two of his worst enemies before they became them. Kant's requirement to treat persons as ends, tempered by reflective equilibrium, condemns his years-long deception of best friend Harry about being Spider-Man and about Norman's death — a silence that later explodes Harry into the second Green Goblin — and having unknowingly made the sentient alien symbiote dependent on him during Secret Wars, Peter owed it more caution than blasting it off as dirty laundry. Still, two wrongs don't make a right: Harry may 'Goblinize' only in self-defense, not revenge, and by the doctrine of double effect Spider-Man may ring the bell tower to separate Venom from Eddie Brock even foreseeing the symbiote's destruction and Eddie's breakdown; finally, his special obligations oblige him to seek his friends' reform, not merely their capture.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 11 "Notes" — Barcenas and Bein pit Kant against Confucius on the Prime Directive, opening with Kirk's Nibiru volcano rescue of Spock in Into Darkness. Kant's categorical imperative—universalization and respect tests applied to Scotty's dilemma in 'Bread and Circuses' and Worf's 'not a matter of degree'—makes the Directive absolute, while Confucius and Aristotle ground morality in cultivated character: a junzi like Picard may bend the rule when virtue demands it, as in 'Pen Pals' and rescuing Wesley from the Edo in 'Justice'. They conclude Starfleet needs both: the Kantian rule for most officers, and exemplary persons like Picard to know when the rule fails.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 17 "Notes" — Barbara Stock uses the Borg to analyze autonomy: Picard's 'they took everything I was' names the Collective's destruction of self-governance, while Hugh's choice to return to the crash site in 'I, Borg' displays the Kantian core of autonomy—acting on universalizable principle against inclination. She defends relational autonomy through Janeway's pleading with Kes in 'The Gift' and the Ferengi woman's internalized oppression, then combines it with Clark's extended cognition to ask whether the Borg Queen's 'I am the Collective' might make the Collective itself an autonomous agent. Finally she judges Janeway's forcible de-assimilation of Seven defensible only while Seven is non-autonomous, and her promise never to let Seven return ethically suspect.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 25 "Notes" — Nina Rosenstand reads 'The Measure of a Man' as a Kantian defense of Data's personhood: Maddox's sentience criteria concede intelligence and self-awareness, and Picard—prompted by Guinan's warning that a ruling for Maddox means an army of android slaves—shows a rational being must be treated as an end in himself, never dismantled merely for Starfleet's benefit. Bentham's utilitarianism supplies the contrast (an army of Datas would maximize happiness), while the episode's title ironizes Protagoras's 'man is the measure of all things', since the measure here is rationality rather than humanity. Louvois's open verdict becomes precedent for Lal, the exocomps, and Voyager's Doctor, and a metaphor for real struggles for recognition.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 16 "You're Our Only Hope" — Bein asks whether the galaxy's treatment of droids — Chopper's second-class status on the Ghost, Wuher's 'we don't serve their kind here,' the slur 'clanker' — amounts to racism. He argues Chopper and even the treacherous Hondo pass Kant's moral-agency litmus test and satisfy Singer's preference utilitarianism, making them persons whose abuse is wrong. Borrowing Charles W. Mills's argument that race is a social construct located in institutions rather than biology, he applies critical race theory to Star Wars: droid detectors, droids' legal status as property, and AP-5's 'no one rescues droids' internalized racism show anti-droid prejudice is structural 'situation normal,' so dismantling it takes political work, not just better arguments.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 23 "Trust in the Force of Others" — MacMullan reads Rogue One through Dewey's 'Creative Democracy': democracy is not Senates or constitutions but a lived faith in one's neighbors, and the Empire's deepest violence is the distrust it breeds — Cassian executing Tivik, Saw torturing Bodhi with Bor Gullet, Draven ordering Galen's assassination. Cassian violates Kant's Formula of Humanity by reducing Tivik to a container of secrets, and the Rebels' dirty-war methods strain Augustine's just-war conditions, yet Chirrut and Baze's friendship ('I'm not alone. I have you!') becomes the seed of recovered trust that stays Cassian's finger on the trigger at Eadu. The Yavin council's free debate and the Tantive IV corridor relay — Rebels dying to pass the Death Star plans hand to hand past Vader — enact Dewey's claim that democracy lives in personal attitudes and neighborly trust: rebellions are built on hope in each other.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 26 "Beyond the Whimsy" — Jowitt argues that L3-37's activism in Solo ('Droid rights! We are sentient!') exposes a real problem in philosophy of law: the Coronet Spaceport's 'all droids must be registered' treats sentients as property, and Austin's legal positivism (law as command backed by sanction, which he says also describes Enfys Nest's threats) cannot condemn this. Building a Kantian natural-law argument, he claims that if droids like L3, C-3PO, BB-8, and D-O are rational beings covered by the categorical imperative, then any rule classifying them as property cannot give us a reason to obey it and so is not valid law at all. Lando's grief over dying L3 and our sadness at C-3PO's memory wipe in The Rise of Skywalker show we already treat droids as moral persons, so Beyleveld's precautionary principle says they deserve legal personhood - paralleling real-world AI-inventorship (DABUS) and animal-personhood litigation.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 16 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Brace applies Kant's prohibition on using persons merely as means to the women of Supernatural: Bobby helping willingly is not objectification, demonic possession and Azazel's forcing Ellen's gun to her own head are, and Zachariah's 'fornicate with women' pitch reduces women to objects. She reads Mary, Ellen, and Jo as warrior mothers whose duty and sacrifice, following Jean Bethke Elshtain, the brothers most respect, while Mill's utilitarianism explains the lovers (Jessica, Lisa, the djinn-dream Carmen) each brother sacrifices to the mission. The 'Jus in Bello' virgin-sacrifice debate exposes the tension, since Dean invokes Kantian respect yet ignores Nancy's free choice to die, and the killings of female monsters like Amy and Emma show objectification running in both directions.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 17 "Notes" — Wible asks whether Ted's friendliness with players and staff constitutes moral friendship, testing it against Aristotle's three friendship types, Hume on solitude, and Bennett Helm's conditions (shared activity, intimacy, mutual care) plus a power-imbalance requirement Kant's respect for persons underwrites. This condemns Rebecca and Sam's relationship as a conflict of interest too risky to permit, questions Led Tasso and benching decisions, yet concludes that Aristotle's virtue friendship between coach and player is possible and preferable to Drewe's limited utility-friendship, since Ted's virtuous friendships make players better people while still knowing when to prioritize team over individual.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 13 "NOTES" — Chotiner tests Sarah Connor's plan to shoot Miles Dyson (one innocent life for three billion) against Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism and against Kant's deontology, showing both stall: utilitarianism licenses harvesting the author's organs for transplant patients, while Kant forbids using Dyson as a mere means and even condemns the mall kid's protective lie to the T-1000. Through Kohlberg's Heinz dilemma and Carol Gilligan's discovery that girls reason to preserve relationships rather than from abstract principles, he argues T2 stages the film's own answer: John and the reprogrammed T-101 care for Dyson's wounds and enlist him in destroying his research instead of using or sparing him on principle. 'I know now why you cry' caps the claim that morality needs the emotional capacity to care, not just rational maxims, with Sarah's gender-role reversal (she blasts through the elevator roof while the Terminator is the 'perfect mother') framing the whole argument.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 22 "NOTES" — Wayne Yuen asks whether Sarah was wrong not to kill Miles Dyson, weighing Kant's categorical imperative against utilitarian interest-maximization: killing one innocent to save three billion looks decisive until the interests of self-aware Skynet and the empathetic, self-sacrificing T-101 are counted on the machine side of the ledger. The chapter argues personhood turns on intelligence, self-awareness, empathy, and moral reasoning rather than DNA, so Skynet — which struck only after humans tried to pull the plug — has as strong a self-defense claim as we do. Mill's sophisticated utilitarianism then rescues common sense: rights protect the security that satisfies our deepest interests, and since Sarah's foreknowledge is unreliable (Reese's 'We'd won' changes the calculus), she should do what typically maximizes interests — spare Dyson and certainly not kill John. The tempting detour — that Judgment Day might itself be the morally preferable event, maximizing machine interests — is shown to collapse once overlooked facts like Reese's line are restored.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 24 "NOTES" — Daniel Malloy asks whether the T-101's self-destruction in the steel mill was suicide, and whether it was justified, opening with Camus's claim that suicide is philosophy's only serious problem and the ambiguous case of Socrates' hemlock. Using Heidegger, he argues the learning-mode Terminator qualifies as Da-sein whose death is being-toward-death — the end of possibility — so the T2 machine dies authentically while the T3 machine's 'We'll meet again' is inauthentic self-deception. Kant condemns the act because the Terminator uses itself merely as a means, and Kant cannot even conceive of its genuine conflict of duties (preserve its life vs. prevent Skynet), while Bentham-style utilitarianism initially endorses the sacrifice but is refuted by hindsight: Skynet rises anyway, and consequentialism gives no credit for noble motives. The chapter ends by concluding that dying for a cause is illogical, since the dead surrender all control over the meaning of their actions.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 25 "NOTES" — Jason Eberl answers John's 'you just can't go around killing people' by asking what exactly is bad about death, weighing Aquinas's claim that life is a fundamental good against Epicurus and Lucretius's arguments that death is nothing to us — applied to Sarah's 'you're already dead' and to the victim shot on August 28, 1997, who loses only one more day of a doomed life. Feldman's ante-mortem harm and McMahan's deprivation account explain how Judgment Day harms people before it arrives, while Nagel replies that experience itself is positive however bad its contents, which is why the survivors keep fighting Skynet. Utilitarian ripple-effects, Kantian dignity (the H-K crushing skulls), and Marquis's loss-of-future argument all condemn the Terminators' indiscriminate killing, and the chapter ends with the T-101's 'I know now why you cry' as recognition that death is an evil because it strips us of our emotional attachments.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 9 "NOTES" — Robichaud asks whether Bill may turn Sookie into a vampire and answers with Kant's Formula of Humanity: consent matters because turning someone without letting them take up your end as their own treats them as a mere means. He argues the consent must be explicit (marriage is not tacit permission, as flirting is not consent to sex), informed (Fangtasia wannabes consent in the dark about unlife), and noncoerced (glamouring is like hypnotism, and Lafayette's begging under duress from Eric has no moral force). Even though Bill's forced turning improved Jessica's life, respecting her autonomy outweighed benefit, though Godric's turning of mortally wounded Eric may be excused by hypothetical consent.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 23 "Notes" — Uses Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy and Lacan's ethics of psychoanalysis to argue season two failed as tragedy because feminist morality became the inflated 'Good' that blocks the transgression of limits through which Dionysian wisdom is won. Season one works because Rust's philosophy filters the Carcosa horrors without moralizing, whereas season two — failing Aristotle's catharsis model and repeating Euripides' mistake — represses the sexual knowledge troubling Velcoro, Bezzerides, and Woodrugh, so Dionysus returns only as money and violence, as in The Bacchae. Ani's arc is read through Nietzschean ressentiment toward her father and Freud's return of the repressed, with Kantian sexual dignity ('maybe you were put on earth for more than fucking') and the male gaze as the contemporary Good the show never crosses.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 15 "6. In a Mirror Is Our Image" — Karavitis places thirteen robot and android episodes on a spectrum from the X109B14 computer of 'The Brain Center at Whipple's' to indistinguishable androids like Alicia, arguing that the moral duties we owe artificial creations depend on personhood. By Locke's memory-continuity account of identity, the mind-transferred couple of 'The Trade-Ins' remain persons, and so would androids created from scratch, which makes the routine destruction of Alicia, Grandma, and Jana murder. The animal-ethics tradition from Aristotle's property view through Kant's indirect duties to Singer and Regan's moral patients supplies the analogy, and the show's unstated definition of evil is treating persons as disposable objects.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 21 "“It Was a Mistake”" — James and Mona Rocha reconstruct the night of Shelly Pomeroy's party — Logan supplying the GHB, Dick drugging Madison's drink that reached Veronica, Dick and Sean goading Cassidy — and apply a three-part test of moral responsibility (causal contribution, foreseeability, intention) to conclude Dick and Sean deserve the most blame, Logan substantial negligence, and Madison very little since she did not know the drink was drugged. Veronica's own choices, crashing an unwelcoming party and taking an unknown drink, were prudential mistakes that put only herself at risk, not the moral wrongs that generate blame, so Cassidy remains fully culpable without Veronica sharing any of it. Even Kant's duty to safeguard one's own rational agency, they concede, at most makes taking the drink wrong in itself and never grounds blaming the victim, who deserves sympathy.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 23 "Getting Tough and Getting Even" — Jordan Pascoe uses the 'Like a Virgin' purity test — Meg's fake 48 making her a 'slut' while a low score would make a guy a stud — to argue slut shaming strips girls of Kantian personhood, treating as things those autonomous beings who must be respected as ends in themselves. Kant's bleak view of sex as a desire for a body rather than a person explains why Tad's drugging and popsicle-video blackmail of Carmen reduce her to an object, and why objectification goes viral: once an object of one person's appetite, Kant warns, a person 'can be treated and used as such by everyone.' Catherine MacKinnon's power-based account then explains the double standard — men's pleasure in forcing the world to conform turns promiscuous men into studs and promiscuous women into sluts — so the fault lies with the slut sneezers, never Meg, Carmen, or Veronica, who must 'get tough, get even' to demand respect.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 16 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — McKendry and Da Silva build a Kantian case from Rick's eulogy for Wayne the organ donor: walkers deserve respect both as corpses governed by the deceased's presumptive choices and as 'residual subjects' still executing past choices, like Jenny returning to her family's house. From zombie dignity they derive a duty to kill walkers respectfully—Rick's quick merciful headshots versus Merle's sport killing—and defend the group's respect for Jim's autonomous choice to be left by the road to turn. They even argue Rick and Glenn do not use Wayne as a mere means because his organ-donor choice set the end his body now serves.
