- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 11 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Auxier argues the trilogy is narrated on a Nietzschean lattice rather than being a mere inverted Milton: after tracing the Paradise Lost, Genesis 6, and Pseudepigrapha sources (Azazel as the model for Asriel, Metatron from Third Enoch, Dust from Milton's warring particles), he reads Mrs. Coulter's speech to Father MacPhail about seeking God out and giving him 'the gift of death' as Nietzsche's death of God fused with a description of Nietzsche's own final dementia. Will and Lyra become overman and overwoman beyond good and evil: Will rises by his will and his willingness to kill (the alethiometer's verdict 'He is a murderer' makes him a worthy companion), while Lyra commands both truth and lies, the alethiometer embodying truth as 'a mobile army of metaphors.' But the chapter's payoff is critical: Pullman does not endorse Nietzsche, since in a world where the will to power dominates, the overwoman Mrs. Coulter has no place and falls with Asriel and Metatron into the Abyss, while Xaphania's teaching offers a disciplined, workful imagination as an alternative.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 161 "Chapter 25 - Untimely Speculations" — Heath Massey's introduction to Chapter 25 opens with Nietzsche's Gay Science passage on intellects that might experience time backward, then stages the demon of eternal recurrence: every pain and joy returning in the same sequence in a world without aim, which either crushes you or becomes 'the highest formula of affirmation', amor fati. Eternal recurrence is a test of the will separating 'man' from 'overman', since one could not celebrate it while believing the world needs a divine purpose. The chapter then maps Dick's imaginative variations of temporality onto two Nietzschean tendencies - disruptions of time-sense that render characters powerless, and extraordinary temporalities that liberate them beyond finite human time, culminating in Dick's theory of supertemporality.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 23 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Brandon Kempner reads Gaiman's Batman: Whatever Happened to the Caped Crusader? as Nietzschean eternal recurrence: Batman dies and is reborn as the infant Bruce Wayne to repeat his life exactly, because Gaiman first strips away every teleological ending, Catwoman kills Batman, Alfred reveals he invented the Joker, and the Moore-style domestic bliss of the Superman farewell is denied. With God dead there is no Heaven, telos, or external reward, so, like Nietzsche's Overman who creates values above the city's conventional morality, Batman's meaning can lie only in the lived repetition itself: 'the only reward you get for being Batman? You get to be Batman,' the highest formula of life-affirmation. Kempner extends the pattern to the funeral-framed rebirth of a new Dream in Sandman: The Wake, showing Gaiman's recurring obsession with cycles that have 'no endings' across his work.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 32 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Rard tests whether objective morality survives the apocalypse by running four theories against Season Two: Plato's Forms explain universal truths about walkers ('walkers survive so long as their brains are relatively undamaged') but cannot handle white lies or changed circumstances, and Aristotle's virtue ethics reads Rick's rush from the shot Carl as rashness and Shane's supply run as courage, yet virtues prove relative and luck-dependent in a collapsed world. Natural law founders on clashing intuitions — Merle's racism and Hershel's barn of walkers each claim self-evidence. The chapter's center is Nietzschean: Hershel's barn is slave morality that pities the 'sick,' Maggie breaks from it, and Shane's sacrifice of Otis and opening of the barn enact a will-to-power master morality without joy, while Rick alone moves toward amor fati — embracing the world as it is, refusing guilt over Lori's affair, and insisting the baby be born into the Walk Age.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 21 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Clifton measures Omar against four Nietzschean criteria for the overman: as a free spirit he is 'in the wind, so to speak,' detached from home, money, and eventually even lovers like Brandon and Butchie; as a non-dogmatist about truth he uses it as a tool, lying under oath at Bird's trial yet sparing Brother Mouzone when the lie no longer holds; and as a noble of the Genealogy he is an active hunter who embraces the will to power, telling Wee-Bey 'you come at the king, you best not miss.' But Omar fails the fourth test, value-creation: his code keeps the good/evil scale intact rather than overturning it, so in the Three Metamorphoses he remains the lion who slays 'Thou Shalt' but never becomes the value-creating child. The verdict, in Nietzsche's own phrase, is that Omar is noble but 'human, all too human.'
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 30 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Brittingham argues The Wire is a Nietzschean rather than merely Aristotelian tragedy, a wrestling between the Apollonian orientation of order, statistics, and illusion (Rawls's clearance rates, Burrell's bureaucracy, Stringer's business plans) and the Dionysian reveling in the Game's chaos and suffering (Avon accepting that 'you only gotta fuck up once', McNulty's intoxicated self-destruction). Stringer is Nietzsche's 'theoretical man' whose faith that thought can correct existence, embodied in the New Day Co-Op, cannot save him from Omar's 'It ain't about money', while McNulty is the Dionysiac man inside the Apollonian institution until Freamon's 'the job will not save you' forces his resignation. The chapter closes by reading the characters' resigned embrace of their fates as Nietzschean affirmation: since neither the job, intelligence, violence, nor the gods will save you, the only response is to say yes to life anyway.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 28 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Laderoute reads 'The Late Philip J. Fry' - the forward-only time machine overshooting past the year one billion and the last protons to a second Big Bang and an identical universe (ten feet lower, conveniently crushing its duplicates) - as a tour of cosmology from Aristotle's static, eternal, Earth-centered heavens through the Stoics' providential determinism and fiery ekpyrosis to Big Bang cosmology and heat death, which is why the Professor is so shocked. Nietzsche's Gay Science 341 supplies the existential payoff: faced with living identically forever, one can react with horror or delight, and eternal recurrence becomes a challenge to become the person you want to be. Fry, a billion years late for his Cavern on the Green dinner, reads Leela's message carved in stone, and in the repeated universe finally arrives on time - 'That was the old Fry... he's dead now' - amor fati enacted.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 45 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Steven Neumann reads the sold-my-soul legends around Led Zeppelin ('here's to my sweet Satan' backwards on 'Stairway to Heaven'), Black Sabbath, and bluesman Robert Johnson at the Clarksdale crossroads as a parable of Nietzsche's amor fati: every joy comes bundled with suffering, so greatness means affirming the whole package. He deploys the eternal recurrence thought experiment - would you will your life, Plant's dead son and Bonham's fatal bender included, to repeat eternally? - and contrasts the ascetic denial of pleasure with Nietzsche's claim in Ecce Homo that his own sickness and obscurity made him love fate all the more.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 27 "14. The Doctor’s Desire for Human Suffering" — Cooper reads 'Rise of the Cybermen' and 'The Age of Steel' as staging Nietzsche against Mill's pain-eradicating utilitarianism: John Lumic, who builds the Cybermen to abolish his sickness, exemplifies the life-denying herd—losing his creativity, craving 'unity and uniformity,' becoming 'a living brain with a heart of steel'—while the Doctor, answering that a life without pain would be 'you might as well kill me,' affirms suffering as the source of creativity, striving, and strength. She extends the Nietzschean reading to the Doctor's character: his guilt over the Time War double-genocide and his loneliness ('the only certainty left is that you'll end up alone') become the pain that makes him merciful, from offering Dalek Caan compassion after 'Evolution of the Daleks' to forgiving the Master in 'Last of the Time Lords,' so that mercy is, as the Genealogy of Morals says, 'the privilege of the most powerful man.'
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 12 "1. Everything’s Amazing and Nobody’s Happy" — Max Elder reads Louis through Nietzsche's Gay Science claim that all philosophy is unconscious memoir, arguing Louis's confession-like comedy reveals dark truths we would rather flee - the Conan 'everything's amazing and nobody's happy' bit, the 'I know the darkness' exchange with the Christian woman, and the Subway/Pamela scene where a homeless man bathes behind a subway violinist. Using Nietzsche's line that man alone laughs because he suffers so deeply, and The Birth of Tragedy's comic as the artistic discharge of the nausea of absurdity, the chapter argues Louis's laughter performs a gestalt switch that ties the ugly to the beautiful and so redeems it. It reads the religions-supply-meaning argument - God's mockery-laughter versus Nietzsche's holy laughter - as the reason redemption now happens in comedy clubs rather than churches, and closes with Louie's 'Country Drive' scolding of Jane ('you don't get to be bored') as Nietzschean embrace of the amazing fact of being alive.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 21 "9. My Dharma Is the Road that Never Ends" — Reads Twin Peaks: The Return as a commitment to Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and amor fati: Cooper is trapped in an existential time loop (Dougie's relearning, Wally's Part 4 Dharma speech, the final-episode Cooper/Richard do-over) and must learn to love every horrific repetition, quoting the Gay Science demon passage and Nietzsche's Will to Power on enduring recurrence. The chapter frames Lynch and Frost as Romantics — Novalis on wonder, Isaiah Berlin's Roots of Romanticism on the artist's inner vision — who break three storytelling rules (authors create stories, protagonists solve problems, stories have endings), so that Laura's mystery stays a living Jack-the-Ripper-style mystery and the story becomes a meta-narrative co-created with viewers, echoing Buddhist pratityasamutpada and Russell's beginningless world. Cooper's finale is a Sisyphean task he accepts, making his integrity the audience's own test.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 14 "5. The Funny Thing about Being Yourself" — Reads Schumer's comedy as Nietzschean self-creation: like the tightrope walker over the abyss she confronts who she is, says 'Yes' to life in the spirit of the eternal recurrence and amor fati, and 'gives style' to her character by wearing mistakes as badges of honor, notably reclaiming her paparazzi photos in the Leather Special. Balke then casts her as Rorty's ironist, whose continual burning of old material keeps her free of a 'final vocabulary' in a contingent world, with 'Amy Goes Deep' doing the Rortian work of testing herself against others. He closes with George Herbert Mead's account of a self formed through social interaction with significant others.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 3 "A Strange Realization" — Dunn argues that Strange begins as a foot soldier of the Baconian project (Bacon and Descartes' program of conquering nature and treating death as an enemy to be subdued, embodied in his surgical God-complex and neurogenesis research), and that its shipwreck drives him to Kamar-Taj. Using Nietzsche, he reads both Strange and Kaecilius as sick with the 'spirit of revenge against time' — Kaecilius fleeing into Dormammu's timeless Dark Dimension as Nietzsche's Hinterweltler, Strange clinging to his unrecoverable past. The climactic 'Dormammu, I've come to bargain' time loop is interpreted as Nietzsche's eternal return weaponized, and Strange's 'Pain's an old friend' as his achievement of amor fati, echoing the Ancient One's dying claim that death is what gives life meaning.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 29 "17. Downton Abbey as Eternal Recurrence" — Christopher Ketcham provocatively equates primogeniture and entail - the legal machinery that returns Downton intact to each generation - with Nietzsche's 'greatest weight,' the eternal recurrence. Working through Lawrence Hatab's five interpretations of the doctrine, he asks whether the Abbey's continuity is cosmological (it is not, since estate taxes and squandering heirs keep chipping away), a Zarathustra-style life-affirming yes to the agrarian world against the 'nihilism' of capitalist fashion, or merely symbolic like a listing in Burke's Peerage beside fossilized dinosaur bones. His answer comes via Violet, the family, and the servants, who have 'become one with the property': the Abbey recurs only anthropomorphically, and even that stickiness is dissolving under industrialization, the death tax, and the war that killed off three royal cousins' empires.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 14 "NOTES" — Shores reads Volume 1 through Nietzsche's eternal recurrence as a self-test of life-affirmation: Adam sealed in a coffin embodies recurrence in its 'most terrible form,' Future Hiro's string map dramatizes Nietzsche's claim that every action is indissolubly tied to all others, and Linderman's speech divorcing happiness from meaning is answered by Nietzsche's demand to crave nothing more fervently than the eternal return. The chapter stresses where the show diverges: Claire insists 'the future is not written in stone' and the heroes rewrite destiny, while Arthur Petrelli ironically holds a copy of Thus Spoke Zarathustra while contradicting it. Hiro's failed attempts to save Charlie and his father (Kaito's 'we cannot play God') frame the amor fati question of whether free will means changing events or willing them eternally.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 14 "Notes" — Argues against the title claim of the previous chapter: Frank is a Nietzschean master type — he defines good as good-for-him, embraces pain as strength, and keeps no allegiances once Walker and Vasquez break their promise — while Peter Russo is the paradigmatic reactive slave who cannot command himself and blames others, exactly Nietzsche's 'he who cannot command himself is commanded'. But the overman requires self-overcoming, the sublimation of drives into creation, and amor fati, and Frank only dominates others for vengeful ends: his whole scheme grows from ressentiment over the Secretary of State snub, he affirms other wills merely as investments, and in Season 3 he becomes a slave to his own position. The chapter uses the Cesare Borgia misreading (better a Borgia than a Parsifal as raw material, but Borgia was no overman), Napoleon's corruption, and Goethe's creative wholeness to conclude that Frank remains 'all-too-human' — destruction without creation.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 14 "Notes" — Meyer mounts the counter-case: Frank exemplifies Nietzsche's master type (good as good-for-him, 'no longer are we bound by allegiances') and Russo the slave type ('he who cannot command himself is commanded'), but the overman is a synthesis of neither. He corrects the Leopold-and-Loeb 'above the law' reading and the Cesare Borgia identification: the genuine overman sublimates strong drives into creation — Goethe's self-discipline, Beethoven's new norms — and affirms other wills in themselves rather than as instruments, which Frank never does with Zoe, Peter, or Claire. Frank's revenge-driven scheming is slave-like psychological warfare, ruling others is the 'pettiest' form of power, and by Season 3 he is the slave of his own presidency — destructive without creating, and lacking even amor fati.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 17 "7 Indiana Jones and Existential Self-Affirmation" — Daniel Tilsley reads The Last Crusade as an excavation of identity: the fedora Fedora bestows after young Indy's defeat, the twenty-six-year quest for the Cross of Coronado ('All my life'), and the chosen name 'Indiana' (taken from the family dog) are acts of Nietzschean self-affirmation — amor fati and the willingness to will the Eternal Recurrence of one's life. The villains fail because they seek external artifacts to patch deficient lives, whereas the Grail Knight, like Camus's Sisyphus, authentically affirms his endless task of guarding the cup. The arc completes when Henry Sr. finally calls his son 'Indiana' while hanging from the abyss, recognizing the man he chose to become, and Crystal Skull repeats the pattern with Mutt and the fedora's eventual inheritance.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 29 "Will You Say Yes" — Michael Bruce ('Zeldathustra') reads the original Legend of Zelda through Nietzsche's thought of eternal recurrence: with no game clock, the ability to save, and looped enemy patterns, every playthrough repeats the same structure, and the player faces the demon's question — do you will to play once more and innumerable times more? The Triforce's split between Wisdom and Power becomes Nietzsche's opposition of the will-to-truth and the will-to-power, with Link's dungeon-by-dungeon self-overcoming enacting amor fati. Against Plato's two-world doctrine of Forms and the Christian after-worldly, the chapter insists the game (like life) gets its meaning from this world only — experimentation, repetition as training, and saying yes.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 26 "Notes" — Conway reads Fury Road as a homecoming (nostos) story that overturns Homer's patriarchal template of Odysseus: Furiosa's trusted Green Place proves as idealistic as the War Boys' Valhalla, and both are diagnosed by Nietzsche's critique of idealism as 'mendaciousness in the face of what is necessary.' The cure is amor fati joined to Max's flinty realism — turn around and make a home by retaking the Citadel — while Hegel's master-slave dialectic explains Immortan Joe's unacknowledged dependency on the women he enslaves for milk, heirs, and recognition. The film ends with Furiosa raised up as a matriarchal ruler and Max departing as the self-exiled wounded healer, barred by his own guilt from the green place he helped make.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 40 "Notes" — Argues Q embodies Nietzsche's revaluation of values: contemptuous of herd-like safety, Q subjects Picard and the crew to trials ("Encounter at Farpoint", "Hide and Q", "All Good Things"'s "the trial never ends") meant to force growth beyond conventional morality, seek out other "supermen", and embrace risk - Q's "bloody nose" defense after eighteen crewmen die at the Borg in "Q Who?". The Borg figure as everything Nietzschean individualism despises, a mindless collectivism that robs drones of the passion the strong need to individuate, and Q's offer to join Picard as guide pictures a friendship between Nietzsche's self-mastered few. The lesson of "Tapestry" is amor fati: Picard must embrace the Nausicaan knife fight that nearly killed him, since undoing it makes a safe, unnoticed man - though the authors finally refuse Nietzsche's harsher dictum that the weak should perish, siding with healing over Q's education-by-death.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 28 "Notes" — Argues 'time is a flat circle' means neither a metaphysical cosmology nor M-theory physics nor reincarnation, but is Nietzsche's eternal recurrence as a thought experiment about how to live. Tracing Rust's pessimism and his lack of the 'constitution for suicide' (echoing Schopenhauer's claim that suicide affirms the will-to-live, with starvation as its only true denial), it shows the flat circle operating as both trap and cure: obsessing over it keeps Rust on the Yellow King case until his near-death experience becomes the 'tremendous moment' of amor fati. Heidegger's view in Being and Time that anxiety before death can empower meaningful existence frames Rust's final affirmation — escaping the flat circle by faithfully acknowledging it, through sacrifice.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 15 "Notes" — Michels reads the Amazon series' first two seasons as a Nietzschean tale organized around eternal recurrence, treating the turning Wheel as Nietzsche's 'existential imperative' and greatest weight: the ferryman who dies vainly saving his son fails the test, while Loial urges the heroes to make themselves unforgettable. He maps Nietzsche's monumental, antiquarian, and critical uses of history onto Moiraine's lesson about the song of Manetheren, contrasts the Ubermensch with the 'last man,' and reads Moiraine's will to power against the ascetic, life-denying Way of the Leaf of the Tuatha'an. Lanfear and Ishamael embody nihilism and resentment, while amor fati names the life-affirming embrace of fate Nietzsche prized.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 32 "Notes" — This multi-author epilogue collects short 'cutting-room-floor' reflections on poignant WoT quotes. Cooke reads Ingtar's confession as the existential fear of historical oblivion (historia as both history and story) driving a patriot into Darkfriendship. DeVan uses Covril's oak-and-wind metaphor to argue arguments strengthen through opposition, marshaling Confucius, Proverbs, al-Kindi, Milton, and Socrates's unexamined life. Held reads Min's arranged-marriage counsel with Nietzsche's amor fati and Epictetus's Heracles to reject resentment of unchosen fate. Pike reads Nynaeve sentencing the sul'dam through Carol Gilligan's and Annette Baier's ethics of care versus obligation (care can judge more harshly, per C.S. Lewis). Xhignesse reads the oak-and-willow line as Aesop woven into Randland's background.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 10 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Scott Parker argues that distance runner Steve Prefontaine, who finished a medal-less fourth at Munich 1972, embodied the true essence of the Olympics better than any champion, an essence he identifies with Nietzsche's 'higher man' and Emerson's self-reliance rather than winning. He aligns Pre's front-running, effort, confidence, and will with Nietzschean self-overcoming and life-affirmation and Emersonian self-valuation, arguing value is what the valuer assigns himself through hard work. Reading Pre's exhausted stumble to the finish as a possible enactment of amor fati, love of fate, Parker holds that if Pre did his best he should love rather than merely accept his defeat.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 19 "Wholly Communion Poetry, Philosophy, and Spontaneous Bop Cinema" — Sterritt reads Peter Whitehead's 1965 film 'Wholly Communion,' shot at London's International Poetry Incarnation, as 'spontaneous bop cinema' embodying Beat poetics through Bakhtin's dialogic/carnivalesque and the schizoanalysis of Deleuze and Guattari. Ginsberg's drunken recitation of 'The Change' becomes a 'body without organs' entering the 'chaosmos' on the plane of immanence; Jandl's sound poetry is pure Deleuzian sensation. Adrian Mitchell's anti-Vietnam 'To Whom It May Concern' is read through Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and amor fati and Deleuze's 'difference in repetition,' its incantatory counter-words a materialist line of flight against the order-words of war.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 23 "Synecdoche, in Part" — Smith reads every Kaufman film as a farce about the self-defeating quest to 'become who you are,' with Synecdoche, New York as its culmination: Caden's MacArthur-funded attempt to represent all of life in a warehouse collapses into infinite regress because a representation of everything must contain itself. He frames Kaufman's films as Montaignean/Emersonian essays—fragmentary self-portraits—and argues the film's limits are death and language, since language always puts us at one remove from the life we already are. The transcendence it evokes is naturalistic, akin to Nietzsche's amor fati and Emerson's 'we are born to a whole': wholeness is not achieved but already possessed, and the hidden knowledge of it turns tragedy into farce.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 24 "Nietzschean Themes in the Films of Charlie Kaufman" — Shaw argues Kaufman's films embody a Nietzschean 'Dionysian pessimism' organized around the will to power, eternal recurrence, perspectivism, and a bundle-theory of the self. He reads Being John Malkovich through the bundle self: personal identity is the dominant drive that acts, so Malkovich 'becomes' Lester/Mertin, the will that controls the vessel. Adaptation's Laroche voices Nietzsche's plastic power of forgetting, and Eternal Sunshine dramatizes eternal recurrence and amor fati as Joel and Clementine choose to repeat their doomed love. Synecdoche, New York, by contrast, Shaw judges a failure of passive nihilism—Caden as the fly who never leaves the bottle—deadening rather than life-affirming.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 21 "9. My Dharma Is the Road that Never Ends" — Potter and Cobb argue that Twin Peaks is a Romantic refusal of resolution: mysteries live by not being solved, so Lynch and Frost break the rules that stories need authors, protagonists who solve problems, and endings. They read Cooper's entrapment in a time loop through Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and amor fati (quoting The Gay Science and The Will to Power), tie Wally Brando's Dharma speech and Isaiah Berlin's Roots of Romanticism to the theme, and argue the real 'story' is the endless meta-narrative co-created between the show and each viewer—Life itself as process without endpoint.
- **The Philosophy of Werner Herzog**, ch. 11 "Nature and Natural Meaning in Grizzly Man" — Marc Furstenau reads Grizzly Man as Herzog's philosophy of nature, arguing that Herzog's vision of nature as chaos, hostility, and murder mirrors Schopenhauer's terrifying Will and the fact/value split, and that Herzog blames Timothy Treadwell's sentimental faith in natural harmony for his and Amie Huguenard's deaths while secretly sharing Treadwell's amor fati. Using Iris Murdoch's Metaphysics as a Guide to Morals and Mary Midgley's Beast and Man, Furstenau contends that both Herzog and Schopenhauer succumb to an 'outrageous simplicity' that denies animal agency; against them he argues, via Midgley, that culture is natural and interspecies sympathy is real, reading Treadwell's extreme close-up of the bear (where Herzog sees 'only the overwhelming indifference of nature') as evidence of imaginative continuity between human and animal.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 31 "Life A Celebration" — Adam Riggio uses Deleuze's reading of Nietzsche to cast the Simm Master as a nihilist who, having seen the valueless dying universe at Utopia, wills nothingness and universal destruction out of ressentiment. The Doctor is Nietzsche's Overman who overcomes the reactive forces of revenge: in 'Dalek' he recognizes his own vengefulness and turns from it, and in 'Last of the Time Lords' he defeats the Master not with Martha's fake gun but by saying 'I forgive you,' affirming finite life with a 'beneficent Yes-saying' rather than surrendering to enmity.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 9 "1. Human, All Too Human" — Holdier reads Supernatural's finale through Nietzsche, arguing that Chuck's exposure as a cruel author-God and his defeat by the Winchesters dramatizes the 'death of God' as the freedom to invent one's own meaning. Dean and Sam's stubborn refusal to 'stay down' on the lakeshore against Chuck embodies amor fati—saying yes to circumstance—while Jack, birthed and taught by ordinary humans, becomes the Ubermensch who replaces God, showing humanity as a bridge to something greater than itself.
- **The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute**, ch. 25 "12. Nietzsche and the Fascist Dimension The Case of Ernst Jünger" — Ohana locates fascism's 'nihilistic-totalitarian syndrome' in the Janus-faced combination of Nietzschean nihilism and the Overman's will to power, whereby ethics is replaced by aesthetics and the self-creating 'new man' shapes reality ex nihilo. He reads Ernst Jünger's Stahlgewittern, Der Arbeiter and 'Total Mobilization' as the aestheticization of war and technology into a work-state, and traces Heidegger's fascination with Jünger's 'will to will' back to Nietzsche and Hölderlin—arguing that, following Camus, one cannot ignore the directionless dynamism leading from Nietzschean perspectivism toward Rosenberg's marching-column politics.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 11 "My Troubles Are Going to Have Troubles with Me Schopenhauer, Pessimism, and Nietzsche" — Jacob Held pits Schopenhauer's pessimism against Nietzschean affirmation using I Had Trouble in Getting to Solla Sollew. He reads Schopenhauer's will-to-life and 'pendulum between pain and boredom' into Seuss's endlessly striving characters, and treats the mirage-towns Solla Sollew and Boola Boo Ball as proof there is no escape from suffering. The protagonist's final line, 'I've bought a big bat... now my troubles are going to have troubles with me,' becomes Nietzsche's yes-saying: instead of the ascetic renunciation Schopenhauer prescribes, Seuss's child-hero affirms life, redeeming its accidents the way Nietzsche's eternal-recurrence thought experiment and 'become a child' passage in Zarathustra demand.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 7 "“Gan Is Dead”" — Garret Merriam reads the ending of The Dark Tower—Roland scaling the Tower only to be flung back to the Mohaine Desert to repeat his quest—as a literal enactment of Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and its demon's test. Roland fails the test ('Please, not again!') because he treats his life as a teleological quest ('all things serve the beam') rather than embracing that 'ka is a wheel'; the Horn of Eld and Furth's hope of 'escaping the trap' miss the point. Merriam argues that once Roland accepts 'Gan is dead'—that meaning must be self-made, not bestowed from the Tower—he could achieve amor fati, and closes with Camus's Sisyphus: we must imagine Roland happy.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 19 "Shock Value A Deleuzean Encounter with James Purdy's Narrow Rooms" — Gross stages a Deleuze-and-Guattari 'encounter' with Purdy's Narrow Rooms, refusing Freudian or Marxist 'interpretosis' in favor of asking what the novel does. He reads Roy Sturtevant the 'renderer' as a multiplicity and traces the characters' becomings-animal (Sid's 'becoming-shark' in the locker-room sex act, becoming-horse, becoming-insect) and the crucifixion of Roy on the barn door as horror that dissolves the boundaries between master and slave, lover and torturer. Invoking Deleuze's debt to Spinoza, Nietzsche, and the Stoics, Gross argues that the joyful amor fati of art embraces horror as an expansion of life rather than something to be vanquished.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 18 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Eric Bronson reads the elves of Rivendell and especially Lothlorien through the 'merrier' existentialists, arguing that lasting joy requires facing the abyss and still affirming life, and knowing, as Nietzsche urged, what to remember and what to forget. Galadriel sings in dark times yet is burdened by remembering too much, unable to let go of her cursed past, so her regret shows the danger Jaspers and Arendt also diagnosed of losing oneself. When she refuses Frodo's Ring and chooses to 'diminish and remain Galadriel,' she embodies the existentialist's affirmation and trust in one's own inner light.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 18 "Epilogue" — The closing essay exhorts readers to 'approach life as the Doctor'—engaged, compassionate, and critically thinking—insisting each person is important and that fandom passion, even when fractious, expresses the Doctor's engaged life (invoking Voltaire on free expression). Using 'Father's Day' and 'The Day of the Doctor,' it argues we cannot change the past but must seize the present, and ties 'truth' and 'trust' to a shared root to claim a meaningful life requires trusting oneself and others rather than merely proving oneself right. It affirms that wisdom is lived truth, that being wrong is how we mature, and that courage is doing what must be done while afraid.

### Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation

The philosophy of punishment asks what, if anything, justifies the state in deliberately imposing hardship on those who break the law. Retributive theories hold that punishment is deserved as a response to wrongdoing, repaying guilt in proportion to the offense regardless of future benefit, whereas rehabilitative and other consequentialist theories justify punishment by its results, chiefly reforming the offender and reducing future crime. The debate turns on whether we punish because a wrong was done or in order to bring about better outcomes, and many modern accounts try to combine both aims.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 25 "Crime and Character" — Theodore Schick uses the Latham Good Samaritan law to argue that doing nothing can be something: against Jackie Chiles' bystander defense he sets the French bad-Samaritan statute, Thomson's Henry Fonda cases (distinguishing supererogatory aid from the duty of the 'minimally decent Samaritan'), and Rachels' Smith/Jones pair - Jones lets the child drown and is exactly as culpable as killer Smith - to show a duty of easy rescue exists, so the gang's failure to dial 911 on Jerry's cell phone deserved punishment. But in the 'Crime and Character' section he argues the trial itself was rigged: character evidence was inadmissible, and the four are not bad people, just people who failed their duty once.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 28 "Buffy Should’ve Killed Ben" — Jacob Held pits retributivism against utilitarian theories of punishment using three Buffyverse cases: vengeance demons Anya and Halfrek show that 'just desert' is arbitrary, relative, and subjective; Angel's gypsy curse (punishment as desert) secures society less reliably than Spike's Initiative chip (pure deterrence), while Oz's preventive caging raises the problem of punishing the innocent. The hard case is 'The Gift': Buffy refuses to kill the innocent Ben, but Held sides with Giles, who strangles him — arguing that since the state's end is security and freedom, one life may rightly be traded for six billion.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 37 "19b" — A paired debate on whether Pete Rose belongs in the Hall of Fame despite his lifetime ban for betting on the Reds, framed by retributive versus utilitarian theories of punishment. Aeon Skoble argues yes: betting on one's own team to win commits no fraud like throwing games, and Cooperstown honors baseball excellence, not moral perfection — the Hall already enshrines racists, adulterers, and cheats. Mark Hamilton answers no with the Dowd Report's evidence, Rule 21(d), and Giamatti's banishment statement: a managing gambler may sacrifice the season to settle tonight's debt, and reinstatement without remorse would declare the game's rules toothless.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 19 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Corlett applies the ethics of racism, due process, responsibility, and punishment to the film: he argues The Passion is not racist because it depicts dissenting Sanhedrin members, the supportive Simon of Cyrene, and the Jewish Mary and Jesus, so blame falls on individual wrongdoers like Caiaphas rather than on Jews as a group, and audiences' misreadings are not the artist's fault. He catalogs the violations of due process (guilty-until-proven-innocent before the Sanhedrin, beatings en route to the hearing, the swap for the convicted killer Barabbas) and the failure to separate religious from civil authority. On punishment he defends a principle of proportionality and desert: Jesus's innocence made his torture and execution unjust, but abuse does not negate proper use, so the film gives no argument against capital punishment per se while giving evildoers who escape earthly justice their deserts only if God is just.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 32 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Frames the problem of pain with Hume's Dialogues (Demea and Philo) and reconstructs Lewis's answer as played out on Aslan: pain is God's megaphone that rouses Edmund on the Witch's frozen sledge and strips Eustace's dragon skin in the transforming embrace. Suffering also reveals hidden strengths, as when Aslan's pursuit goads Shasta into unexpected courage, modeled on Augustine's reading of the binding of Isaac as teaching Abraham, not God, what Abraham could endure. Aravis's claw wounds are treated as retributive punishment, tear for tear, exactly proportioned to the drugged slave's whipping, which the chapter defends via Lewis's retributivist theory against purely deterrent punishment. Because divine goodness aims at making creatures good rather than merely happy, Aslan can be both good and terrible, 'not a tame lion', since free will cannot be coerced into perfection.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 29 "Prison Ghetto" — Kelly takes gangsta rap's payback attitude (50 Cent, Nas, Dr. Dre, OutKast) as the starting point for the philosophy of punishment: rappers doubt retribution because police, courts, and prisons lack legitimate authority over them - Public Enemy's "Black Steel in the Hour of Chaos" rejects the government's letter. Weighing Kantian and Nozickian retributivism against Bentham's consequentialist rationales, she argues desert, proportionality, and authority all fail in a racist system - racial profiling, the crack-versus-powder sentencing disparity, Wacquant's prison-ghetto thesis, Goodie Mob's "Cell Therapy", Dead Prez's "Behind Enemy Lines", KRS-One's officer-overseer analogy - leaving incapacitation as racialized social control rather than justice.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 23 "A Call to Unchanging Truths" — Francis Beckwith argues the 1979-81 Christian albums are no aberration: Dylan's whole career presupposes moral realism, an objective moral law built into the universe - "Dignity never been photographed" names an irreducible moral property, and the judgments in "With God on Our Side" and "Blowin' in the Wind" only make sense if right and wrong are unchanging across eras. The six-month sentence William Zanzinger receives in "The Lonesome Death of Hattie Carroll" is condemned on retributive, lex talionis grounds rather than any utilitarian calculus of consequences, and "Forever Young" and "What Good Am I?" urge virtue practiced for its own sake. The chapter thus reads Dylan's conversion as the surfacing of commitments - against relativism, for virtue and unchanging truths - always latent in songs like "The Times They Are A-Changin'."
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 9 "Just Desserts" — Asks how the exploding-glutton Mr. Creosote sequence in 'The Autumn Years' of The Meaning of Life can provoke laughter rather than horror, given that Creosote shares the monster's marks of physiological impossibility and disgusting category-violation (like Frankenstein's monster or the Alien). The answer: horror requires disgust plus fear, and Creosote, like the slapstick clown, is marked as neither able to harm nor be harmed, so the audience's fear-condition for horror is never met. A second layer of the laughter is vindictive: the maitre d''s wafer-thin mint is retributive justice, a morality-play punishment for gluttony in the lineage of Spenser's Gluttony and Dante's Inferno, so black comedy trades on our sense that the victim deserves what he gets.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 18 "Universal Rights Vampires, Space Aliens, Robots, and Humans" — John Draeger asks which Undead can be held accountable for bloodthirsty behavior: Romero's zombies are amoral, like a poisonous plant or Cleckley's empathy-free psychopath Milt, while Dracula meticulously plans his move to London and so passes the cognitive test. Stoker's narcissistic Count stays amoral, but Coppola's Dracula (who warns Mina of her curse), Rice's guilt-torn Louis, and the self-deceiving, cruelty-enjoying Lestat show empathy, self-control, and moral reflection, making them immoral and responsible - which entitles vampires to due process rather than Van Helsing's vigilantism, to punishment aimed at rehabilitation, and to equal rights including civic participation and marriage, since the same standard would govern space aliens, robots, and humans.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 22 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Held argues that our pleasure in Bond's kill-then-quip routine - 'Shocking' after electrocuting a henchman in Goldfinger, tossing Killifer to the sharks that ate Felix with 'You earned it, you keep it' - reveals tacit retributive and deterrent theories of punishment that place villains outside the moral community. Using the distinction between mere humiliation (deflating Dr. No's pretense: 'Minnows pretending they're whales') and Humiliation that denies common humanity, he shows Bond dehumanizes disfigured, 'othered' villains, even as the novels present them as disenfranchised figures - Dr. No rejecting his father's name, Mr. Big demanding recognition as the first great black criminal - whose rage is a warped demand for Hegelian mutual recognition. He proposes instead Jean Hampton's moral education theory, which treats criminals as moral agents capable of reform, concluding with Jaws's redemption in Moonraker as proof that no one is beyond it.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 28 "So, Case Closed – Right" — White asks why Batman never simply kills the Joker despite the graveyard he keeps filling, framing the question with Foot's and Thomson's trolley problem and the transplant-surgeon variant. Utilitarianism says kill one to save many; deontology says the agent-relative 'do not kill' — but the Batman case differs from the classic dilemmas because the Joker himself endangers his victims, Batman cannot be certain he will kill again (the foggy-track variant), and killing him would amount to the Minority Report-style prepunishment of a crime not yet committed. White, a self-described strict deontologist, concedes the case is genuinely hard and leaves the means-versus-ends debate open.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 39 "Gaining Trust from the Past" — Richard Davies treats the Oceanic 815 survivors' beach as a "framed" state of nature: the stolen water is a tragedy of the commons, Sawyer's "finders keepers" defense of Shannon's inhalers stages Hobbes's war of all against all against Locke's natural rights, and Jack and Sayid's torture of Sawyer marks the first step toward civil society, a claim to punish on another's behalf. He argues no theory of human nature (Rousseau's "Innocence" versus a "Trust No. 1" attitude) is needed to understand the castaways: cooperation grows through iterated prisoner's-dilemma tit-for-tat strategies, which also recasts the real difference between Hobbesian and Lockean states of nature.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 14 "Are We Going Too Far" — David Kyle Johnson distinguishes revenge (personal, emotional, unlimited) from retribution and argues that 'Tarantino's view'—mercy should be common practice yet revenge can be justified—is consistent: Jules buys Pumpkin and Honey Bunny's lives but never waives a right of vengeance, since they never wronged him. He tests the view against Bushido, showing Beatrix's revolt against her lord Bill violates the samurai code, and against karma, which makes revenge unnecessary. After finding that Hobbes, Locke, Nietzsche and Socrates all leave revenge's justification open, he defends it—citing Budd's 'that woman deserves her revenge'—so long as the punishment fits the crime and spares innocents, as when Beatrix refuses to make herself even by killing Vernita's daughter Nikki.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 17 "Mr. Rawls and the Decision Procedure" — Joseph Ulatowski uses Mr. Blonde's torture of Marvin to test theories of punishment. He argues Blonde is not a mere psychopath but a retributivist within his social code—punishing clerks who 'touched the alarm' and cops who violated Mill's harm principle—while distinguishing acting on a principle from merely acting in accordance with one, since Blonde acts from sadistic urges. After reviewing Kant's lex talionis and the utilitarian theory's flaws, he asks whether Hart and Sterba's Rawlsian 'retributivism as fairness', whose principles are chosen behind a veil of ignorance, could justify Blonde's actions, concluding Blonde could not by his own lights have done otherwise than punish.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 15 "John Henry, the Steam-Engine, and Folsom Prisoners" — Mulnix pairs Cash with John Stuart Mill on the priority of quality of life over mere life: Mill's 1868 Parliament speech defends capital punishment as more humane than the "living tomb" of life imprisonment, and Cash agrees in the Folsom liner notes (the prisoner envying the cockroach that can leave) and in "The Mercy Seat," where the electric chair becomes both mercy and the throne of God. Mill's higher and lower pleasures, competent judges, and On Liberty's individuality illuminate Cash's gallery of fools, the "Folsom Prison Blues" narrator who shot a man just to watch him die, the mother-defying Billy Joe of "Don't Take Your Guns to Town," characters whose unreflective rebellion squanders rational freedom. John Henry, by contrast, exercised his higher faculties against the steam-engine and so died happy, proving the chapter's Millian thesis that freedom matters as a means to self-directed, deliberated happiness.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 22 "The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly" — Johnson and Schmitz argue that Cash, through songs like 'San Quentin,' 'Jacob Green,' and his cover of 'The Mercy Seat,' championed reforming prisons from a retributive to a rehabilitative model and abolishing capital punishment (songs like 'Joe Bean' and 'Long Black Veil' center executed innocents). They defend Cash with Mill: Socrates shows vengeful retributive sentiment is immoral, Mill's harm principle says government may coerce only to prevent harm, so punishment should be justified only by future deterrence and rehabilitation. Since the death penalty's deterrent effect is empirically weak (California, Missouri-vs-Iowa murder rates) and wrongful convictions are common, Mill today would join Cash in calling for abolition.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 18 "Universal Rights Vampires, Space Aliens, Robots, and Humans" — John Draeger argues Romero's catatonic zombies, like plants, lack the cognition and empathy to be blamed, while vampires split: Stoker's narcissistic Dracula resembles Cleckley's amoral psychopath Milt, but Coppola's remorseful Dracula, Anne Rice's guilt-tormented Louis, and the self-deceiving Lestat ('the trick is not to think about it') all grasp consequences, feel others' pain, and can exercise self-control, so they are immoral rather than amoral and accountable for their killings. Accountability brings rights: Van Helsing's summary staking is vigilantism that denies Dracula a fair trial, rehabilitable vampires like Louis might earn civic participation, and a nonviolent, honest vampire suitor cannot be rejected merely for being Undead. The principle generalizes to aliens and robots: whatever can reflect morally must be held responsible and treated with equal dignity.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 11 "You Can’t Help What Happened to You. But You Can Make the Best of It" — Daniel Haas asks whether we can blame Dexter at all if his Dark Passenger is a compulsion formed by the shipping-container trauma he did not choose, and whether consistency then forces us to excuse the Trinity Killer and Ice Truck Killer too. Distinguishing attributive responsibility from accountability, he argues psychopaths cannot be motivated by moral reasons because they lack the moral emotions, and that it was sheer luck whether a traumatized boy landed in Harry's loving home and Code (Dexter) or a mental institution (Brian). Yet Dexter's critical reflection on and revision of Harry's Code, and his willingness to forgo turning himself in to spare Deb, Rita and the kids, paradoxically make him more accountable than ordinary psychopaths and even praiseworthy for his quest to become 'a little wooden boy' who is more human, even if he still deserves to be locked up.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 27 "The Final Thrust to the Abdomen" — Eric Holmes argues that what we enjoy in Dexter is not killing but punishing, and reads the show through Michel Foucault's Discipline and Punish (with Hobbes and Locke on the right to punish): since the eighteenth century punishment has moved from public torture to the abstract, painless deprivation of liberty, and Dexter is a deliberate throwback to the older Sovereign. Every detail of the ritual is analyzed as torture designed to make the victim recognize he deserves it - displaying photos or the corpses of their victims (Mike Donovan), forced nudity and harsh light, and letting the punishment fit the crime (Trinity's own claw hammer, telling Miguel he killed Oscar). Dexter is 'the Sovereign we've been waiting for,' an unemotional agent of deserved pain that modern incarceration no longer provides.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 15 "An Eye for an Eye" — Mihaela Frunza and Anatolia Bessemer use MacIntyre's Whose Justice? Which Rationality? to frame Holmes's casual felonies, the disguised-clergyman trick on Irene Adler, freeing Captain Croker after staging a mock courtroom in 'The Abbey Grange', and compounding a felony with Isadora Klein in 'The Three Gables', as one tradition of justice among several with no neutral court of appeal. Against the police's letter-of-the-law tradition stand the criminals' own codes of retribution, above all Jefferson Hope in A Study in Scarlet letting 'the high God judge' between the poisoned and harmless pills, making Holmes and his prey mirror-image vigilantes who prefer restitution or chivalric acquittal to statutory punishment.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 66 "Pre-Crime and Pre-Punishment" — Frames 'Minority Report' with Nietzsche's charge that men were considered 'free' only so they could be judged and punished, and with Anselm's De Concordia, where God, outside time, foreknows our choices without determining them. Pre-Crime can punish Anderton and the pre-criminals now only because their not-yet-made choices are treated as absolutely free, and the 1954 context — HUAC, Hoover's anonymous accusations, the Communist Control Act — shows people punished for the present guilt of a future crime.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 124 "01. Don’t We Arrest Innocent People" — Writing as a Precrime PR manual, the section answers the charge that arresting people who have broken no law punishes the innocent: pre-criminals genuinely lack mens rea, so punitive blame would be inappropriate, but their detention is justified as prophylactic quarantine, like isolating an infant with a dangerous contagious disease, under a non-punitive containing attitude. It cites Dick's own 'Minority Report' language of 'neutralizing' Anderton and 'the prophylactic pre-detection of criminals,' plus the film's Hall of Containment, as evidence the system is preventive rather than punitive.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 125 "02. But Is It Really Inappropriate to Punish Pre-criminals" — The section defends punitive attitudes toward pre-criminals through a 'pre-punishment' thought experiment: if Walter Wrath credibly announces tomorrow's wrongful harm and will escape all future blame, punishing him now is better than never blaming him at all. Precrime cases are analogous, it argues, because being stopped by others is no credit to the offender and not the right kind of fact to exculpate him; the person who would have done it 'remains on the hook.'
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 130 "04. What about Leaks" — The section weighs leaking predictions to pre-criminals so they can reroute (the I-future), and rejects it for three reasons: the precogs' predictions are accurate only for people who never learn of them, standing by to catch a forewarned killer is costly, and would-be murderers have no right to know, since unlike a citizen facing contaminated water they could have avoided their path by not choosing it. It closes the guide's case that Precrime arrests people who deserve arrest, with appropriate attitudes and compelling evidence, without violating rights.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 20 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Najwa Al-Tabaa reads Sandman: Season of Mists through Derrida's paradox that only the unforgivable can truly be forgiven: Morpheus's freeing of Nada works as forgiveness precisely because condemning his lover to Hell was unforgivable, while Lucifer, who was never wronged by the damned, can give them only a devalued semblance of pardon, and they cling to punishment they feel they deserve. She then brings in Foucault's Discipline and Punish and Bentham's Panopticon to read the angels' rebuilt Hell of redemption as the modern rehabilitative prison, where watched souls are expected to reform themselves. The experiment fails, she argues, because redemption is imposed without hearing the prisoners, violating Derrida's condition that forgiveness needs a shared language, so the inmates prefer Lucifer's honest eternity of despair to a salvation they never asked for, a lesson about real prisons that seek rehabilitation through punishment.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 34 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Yuen distinguishes heroic survival cannibalism, as in the Andes crash of Alive, from the 'Fear the Hunters' cannibals: both utilitarianism and Kantianism permit eating those who already died out of necessity, since the dead lose no utility and corpses lack the rationality that grounds Kantian dignity. But Chris's band killed children to eat them and kept the living Dale as a food store, which fails both theories and cannot be excused by 'we don't do this because we want to,' since alternatives existed — joining other survivors, eating walkers ('zombitarianism'), or starving, because survival is never a moral obligation. Rick's execution of the hunters is then defended as Kantian retributive punishment: if Chris universalized his maxim that people may be hunted for food, then, as Rick suggests while biting Chris's neck, 'if Dale was good as a steak, so is Chris.'
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 27 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Hoskins and Wikoff use Cutty's release after fourteen years in Jessup to ask what it means to have 'paid your debt to society' when ex-offenders still face bans on housing, jobs, welfare, student loans, and voting. They test the standard defenses: the consequentialist safety argument fails because these bans push men like Cutty back into the Game ('This game is rigged, man'); the competence argument collapses since McNulty, who did not even know the Democratic candidate, is no more competent a voter; and Judge Friendly's Locke-inspired social-contract claim that criminals forfeit their voice in lawmaking cannot explain why Prez's pistol-whipping or Clay Davis's corruption would not equally forfeit theirs. They conclude that continuing to punish after the sentence ends is unjust, and that Cutty's boxing gym shows former prisoners can reform.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 12 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Littmann argues that stripped of religious scruple, Shelley's own supreme virtue - kindness, embodied in Victor's family, Elizabeth, Clerval, and the cottagers - actually supports creating artificial life: the monster is benevolent until mistreated, and superior corpse-people would be a race of geniuses rather than a threat we may preemptively suppress. The monster himself invents utilitarianism ('relative as they were, as I applied them, to pleasure and pain alone'), De Lacey nearly lives it by promising the stranger rehabilitation over punishment, but Victor's case against building a mate is exposed as speciesism - he tallies unborn humans' futures while ignoring the joys of unborn cadaver folk, though utilitarians were the first to speak for animal rights. Since intelligent otherness is humanity's only chance at non-human friendship and the risks of Prometheus's fire paid off, the chapter rewrites the modern Prometheus as a blessing and ends with a re-imagined creation scene where the monster says 'I love you' to a Victor who finally names him Nigel.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 23 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Galliott treats Frankenstein as the template for blaming lethal autonomous robots: Victor alone created his creature, but today's 'frankennovation' - Ronald Arkin's 'ethical governor' algorithms, DARPA funding, degree programs in robot warfare, and the South African robotic cannon that killed nine spectators - distributes responsibility across engineers, educators (Victor's father and Professors Krempe and Waldman, who never properly warned him about Agrippa's 'sad trash'), universities, and the military-industrial complex. Yet Shelley's articulate, Paradise Lost-quoting monster is a rational, intentional killer who can be held morally responsible and even punished, as Rob Sparrow demands of machines. Because responsibility does not dilute with numbers - two murderers do not get half a life sentence each - the chapter concludes that everyone in the chain, and all of us who do nothing to stop it, shares the blame for monstrous creations.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 17 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Littmann uses Adventure Time as a stockpile of thought experiments against free will: Finn excuses Billy (possessed by the Lich), hug-wolf Finn, amulet-Marceline, red-starved Marceline, the magically animated hat Little Dude, and crown-cursed Simon, yet punishes the Lich and Lemongrab, whose destructive desires are exactly as unchosen—Lemongrab even protests 'you made me like this.' Since deterministic causation and randomness exhaust the options, we are 'machines made of meat' wearing ice crowns inside our skulls, so deserved suffering makes no sense. The chapter concludes that just-deserts retribution (Princess Cookie's life sentence, America's prisons) should give way to deterrence, protection, and rehabilitation—freeing the Simon Petrikovs underneath.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 18 "Justified and Philosophy" — Cast as a pub dialogue between philosopher Christian Cotton and therapist Anthony Palazzo over Ava Crowder's killing of her abusive husband Bowman at supper, the chapter asks when extra-legal violence is morally justified. It explains her entrapment through systems theory - homeostasis, learned helplessness, self-esteem destruction, false hope - and takes up Kant's debt metaphor for punishment, on which wrongdoers owe a penalty and retribution restores balance, to ask who may collect when the legal system treats domestic violence as a 'family matter'. They conclude Bowman did not strictly deserve death, but Ava's 'I did what I had to do' is best understood as acting from anger in pursuit of justice and self-reclamation rather than on anger for vengeance.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 17 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Ketcham greets Piper Kerman at the prison door with Bentham's ghost: the state's utility calculation of her drug money laundering, the rat's discounted sentence, and the design of the panopticon, whose one-way inspection tower was meant to make surveillance cheap, obedience automatic, and prisoners productive and even saved. He contrasts that reform vision with the reality reconstructed from the book, where punishment falls on everyone, including families paying commissary prices and denied visits, and Danbury's 'vocational training' amounts to changing light bulbs. Bentham's own principle that 'punishment is an evil' is turned against a system that warehouses rather than rehabilitates.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 29 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Duffy applies Susan Wolf's formula (subjective attraction meeting objective attractiveness) to Red's cooking, Poussey's friendship, and Taystee's library work, arguing these women meet the conditions yet still cannot live meaningful lives because Litchfield hands out 'chickens': WAC, the mock job fair, and the yard chicken are illusions of meaning designed to keep inmates quiet, as Healy admits with his bath-before-dinner analogy. Only projects that change the prison's conditions themselves, Piper's newsletter sting and Soso's hunger strike, are genuinely meaningful, and the yogic dharma of non-attachment (Yoga Jones's mandala advice) is a survival tool, not a substitute. She closes that guards too can find meaning, and have an obligation, in rehabilitating rather than punishing.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 16 "7. Give Peace a Chance" — Lewis argues the Dauntless Manifesto's claim that 'justice is more important than peace' rests on a mistake: following Nicholas Wolterstorff's account of shalom, real peace just is justice - each person receiving what Ulpian called their due and enjoying their rights - so the two cannot come apart. He shows each faction works with a different, deficient conception of peace (Amity's drug-induced calm, Erudite's negotiated order, Abnegation's self-erasure), then uses Aristotle's three types of justice to dismantle Jeanine's best defense, that her slaughter of Abnegation and the Divergents is retributive justice: the accused are innocent and her 'peace' is coercion, propaganda, and fear. The chapter ends with concrete reforms - welcome the factionless as a sixth service faction, let factions teach each other their virtues - so that Roth's Chicago could actually achieve the ethical community of peace-through-justice.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 20 "6. Punishing Negan" — Yuen asks why Rick imprisons Negan after the Saviors' war instead of executing the man who beats people to death with 'Lucille' and runs a mafia-like protection racket. He surveys retributivism (fair play and eye-for-an-eye equality) and deterrence, including Glenn's lawless Challenger driving, then defends Rick's refusal to kill via 'we're better than him,' the weakness of execution as a deterrent for Negan's followers, and the brutalization effect that would poison the character of the fledgling civilization. But he argues Negan's basement isolation - no exercise, no decency, his victim as judge and warden - fails Rick's own civilizing vision, and proposes restorative justice with apology, forgiveness, and mediated reparations as the punishment a civilization that claims human life is precious ought to build.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 21 "9. Why Revenge Is So Sweet" — Haas asks why we cheer Inigo's vendetta against Rugen when moral philosophy condemns vengeance as emotionally driven injustice. Distinguishing impartial, proportional punishment from personal revenge, he then uses the honor-culture literature (Nisbett and Cohen, Tamler Sommers) to argue that in lawless Florin - where the 'justice system' is run by the villain who ordered the murder - Inigo's personal retribution is a justified duty of honor, since no institutional avenue exists. The deeper pull of revenge stories, he concludes, is that victims have a special moral standing to punish - which is why Rugen dying by anyone's hand but Inigo's would be unsatisfying - while a variant story (Westley as the killer) would call instead for atonement and forgiveness, showing that revenge is made admirable by how stories are told.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 22 "10. Making the Punishment Fit the Crime" — Heter defends Inigo's killing of Rugen as pure retribution - not deterrence or prevention, since Rugen 'deserves' to die for a murder long past. Locke's state of nature grounds the right to punish in victims, who merely transfer it to the state for prudential reasons, so in tyrannical Florin, where no reasonable expectation of justice exists, Montoya is within his rights to execute punishment himself. Kant's retributivism (the island whose inhabitants become accomplices if they spare convicted murderers, from the Metaphysics of Morals) supports the claim that murderers deserve death, and against the objection that proportionality need not mean identity of kind (following M.A. Moore, using Fezzik's hypothetical house-burning), the chapter argues death is the only punishment weighty enough to fit murder.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 26 "15. Death Begets Death" — The Bocks trace Darrow's education out of vengeance: in Plato's tripartite soul the spirited part (anger) must obey reason, and Aristotle's virtue of mildness—anger at the right things, toward the right people, for the right length of time—is the golden mean between slavish and irascible that Darrow has not yet reached. Darrow learns the difference when he hands Titus over to Cassius's vendetta and admits 'That wasn't justice': retribution in Kant's lex talionis tradition must be dispassionate and proportional, while vengeance is past-oriented and insatiable, and Darrow's own bombing of the Ganymede docks shows how troubling even his 'justice' remains. Against Darrow's violent justice-in-love the chapter sets Martin Luther King Jr.'s agape and loving-forgiveness—Sevro hanging and then forgiving Cassius, Darrow forgiving Tactus, Mustang pulling her brother's legs for a merciful death—closing with King's warning that constructive ends can never justify destructive means, and Darrow's own admission that 'the war is not over.'
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 27 "16. Can We All Get Along" — Courtland Lewis tackles transitional justice after atrocity: with the Rising won, what is to be done with millions of Golds complicit in slavery, rape, and torture? He tests Peter French's virtuous vengeance—punishment that fits the wrong, grounded in Locke's natural rights—and finds Darrow's destruction of Gold society fails it (disproportionate, unsober, punishing young Julian for his ancestors' crimes), then turns to Jessica Wolfendale's argument that declaring anyone unforgivable adopts the wrongdoer's own devaluing outlook, exactly as Darrow becomes what he despises. The working model is South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission—confession, conditional amnesty, truth-telling, reparations, Tutu, Mandela, Beth Savage hoping to meet her bomber—applied to Mars through Mustang-style dignified engagement on Adam Michnik's model and Slavenka Drakulic's lesson that every Color inherits responsibility for rejecting the Society's past.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 11 "1. What’s So Scary about Demonic Possession" — Using the Asylum possession arc - the boy who rips open the pig's heart, the demon exposing Sister Jude's hit-and-run secret and whispering 'You're Bloody Face' to Thredson, and Sister Mary Eunice's corruption - the chapter argues that possession stories terrify because they break our identity judgments through time, the same judgments on which moral responsibility, criminal punishment (the Manson family parole cases, Phineas Gage), trust, and personal safety depend. Descartes's mind-body union and psychological-continuity theories of identity explain why sameness of body can no longer guarantee sameness of person, and why we fear our own identity being erased next.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 15 "5. One of Us Is a Manipulative Demon" — Malloy tests compatibilism, libertarian free will, and determinism against Michael's predicament: he must be able to predict the humans whose unchosen torture he is administering, using Jason's death locked in the safe to show how free motives and external causes combine. Eleanor's confession and Chidi's boat-and-French-poetry paradise fantasy, read through Sartre, complicate the internal/external divide compatibilism needs, while the humans' eerie constancy across 802 reboots suggests determinism. The conclusion is that a system distributing eternal reward and punishment on desert is doubly unjust if determinism is true, since punishment could only ever be justified as forward-looking encouragement, never as what anyone deserves.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 17 "6. A Better Bad Place" — Grosz asks whether Judge Gen could justly condemn Team Cockroach to eternal torment, testing the classic 'sins against an infinite being deserve infinite punishment' defense built on Anselm's God as that than which nothing greater can be conceived, and finding that no such being exists on the show. He rejects the continuing-sin model of Hell because the Bad Place's physical torture precludes both further sinning and moral reform, and argues purely retributive eternal punishment fails the utilitarian test. His proposal, a non-torturous 'Bad Place 3.0' modeled on C.S. Lewis's The Great Divorce where people face the natural consequences of their vice until they reform, could be justified as what is best for the person.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 16 "Avengers, Forgive!" — Malloy builds an account of forgiveness around the Avengers' habit of recruiting ex-villains: Arendt's 'predicament of irreversibility' explains why we cannot undo Wonder Man's revenge scheme against Stark, so resentment must be overcome; Derrida's claim that only the unforgivable is truly forgivable frames the House of M question, whether Quicksilver's manipulation of Wanda's reality-warping is a crime beyond forgiveness. Forgiveness means relinquishing resentment without excusing responsibility or condoning the wrong, so Iron Man has the 'moral power' to forgive Hawkeye, while the team's charter-based standing lets the Avengers forgive Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch on the community's behalf. The chapter closes by separating avenging (justice) from revenge, and punishment (retribution that repays debts) from forgiveness, which is why expelled members like Iron Man and Hank Pym could be readmitted.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 18 "Avengers Rehabilitate!" — Terjesen asks whether Cap's Kooky Quartet-style rehabilitation really works, pitting Aristotle's fixed-character virtue ethics against John Doris's situationist 'local traits' (backed by Milgram's experiments): Hawkeye succeeded because his regional traits—hotheadedness and a need for approval—were redirected to heroism, not erased, as when he cheats the Grandmaster to save the universe. Aristotle's continence-versus-virtue and vice-versus-incontinence distinctions explain why Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch keep backsliding, why Moonstone's true viciousness defeats rehabilitation while Songbird and MACH-1 reform. Against deterrence and retributivist theories of punishment, rehabilitation is defensible when applied early and to the unhardened—the Avengers Academy children and Young Avenger Patriot—so the Avengers can rehabilitate as well as avenge.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 17 "“Don’t forget, she’s a dangerous individual”" — The chapter tests the White Bear Justice Park's daily torture of Victoria Skillane against every major theory of punishment: Kant and Hegel's retributivism makes her deserve punishment (her crime could not be universalized and annulled justice) but cannot justify a punishment disproportionate to the crime. Locke's memory criterion suggests Punished Victoria is not the person who did the crime, though Parfit's psychological continuity and Thomson's bodily continuity restore the identity. Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism partially vindicates the park as deterrence and incapacitation, but cannot explain the laughing crowds — which Machiavelli's civic spectacle and Nietzsche's genealogy of punishment (Schadenfreude as moralized creditor-debtor pleasure) explain: the crowd is gleefully reenacting Victoria's own crime and calling it justice.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 20 "A White Christmas with Dark Reflections" — The chapter follows White Christmas's three escalating uses of the Z-eye digital block — Beth blocking Joe (whose information deprivation leads to two deaths), court-ordered blocks extending to children, and Matthew's society-wide red-blur sex-offender block — as a conflict between privacy and access to information. Utilitarian and Kantian frameworks (autonomy, persons as ends) leave the trade-offs genuinely unsettled, while Nozick's minimal state shows the automatic, loophole-free blocking regime is an indefensibly paternalistic state violating proportionality. Arendt's account of meaningfulness through speech grounds the conclusion that erasing someone's face and voice violates their humanity, and the chapter's final move is defamiliarization: if digital blocks are wrong, we should re-examine the social-media blocking, restraining orders, prisons, and sex-offender registries they mirror.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 24 "Do We Attain Justice by Punishment" — Kenny's blackmail arc in Shut Up and Dance — the twist that reclassifies the sympathetic protagonist as a child-pornography offender — anchors an argument that the hackers' vigilantism cannot attain justice: their punishments are unannounced, disproportionate, aimed at merely moral wrongs (infidelity, racist emails), and exempt from the presumption of innocence and nulla poena sine lege that states replaced vendetta with. A distinction between natural-law and legal-positivist conceptions of justice shows why punishment belongs to the state alone. Against retribution ('a mere prison sentence is too good for Kenny'), Bentham's and Mill's utilitarianism — deterrence, incapacitation, and above all rehabilitation, capped by the harm principle — shows punishment should be no more than deterrence requires, making the hackers sadists rather than agents of justice.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 11 "2 Transforming Wakanda Justice (or Not ) in Black Panther" — Bein and Lewis imagine Killmonger surviving his duel to face Wakandan justice, and sort what justice would demand into retributive justice (Kant: punishment only what the offender deserves, never using him merely as a means to public safety, though they note Kant's own racist views), reparatory justice (Locke's natural rights and what Wakanda owes N'Jadaka for T'Chaka killing N'Jobu and abandoning him in Oakland), and the restorative-to-transformative justice of Changamire's gatherings in Coates's 'A Nation Under Our Feet,' modeled on South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission. They argue a restorative Wakanda would seat Killmonger with his victims and even the king at the table to repair harm rather than imprison him, and sketch a prison-abolitionist Wakanda meeting Thanos with 'Wakandan justice is more civilized.'
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 12 "3 Sins of the Fathers Historical Injustice and Its Repair in lack Panther" — Almassi contrasts Rawlsian ideal theory (the veil of ignorance, justice as fairness) with Charles Mills's critique that idealization marginalizes actual historic oppression, arguing the film's characters seek Aristotle's corrective justice in a world already steeped in wrongdoing: the 1991 deaths of W'Kabi's parents at Klaue's hands and of N'Jobu at T'Chaka's. He works through the Museum of Great Britain axe scene as restitution, W'Kabi's 'you kill him where he stands' and Killmonger's 'I'mma make sure we're even' as retribution (tested against Walen's proportionality principles, with vengeance untethered from legitimate punishment), and Nakia's and T'Challa's outreach centers as Margaret Urban Walker-style relational repair, reading T'Chaka's concealment of N'Jobu's death as actively constructed ignorance in service of isolationism.
- **The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire**, ch. 28 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" — Using the Nicomachean Ethics and the Rhetoric, the chapter vindicates the pleasure readers take in Salander's Taser-and-tattoo revenge on Bjurman: Aristotle distinguishes revenge, done for the satisfaction of the one wronged, from punishment, and requires that the wrongdoer know who avenges and why—which is why Lisbeth waits until Bjurman wakes before inking i am a sadistic pig, a pervert and a rapist across his torso. Proper anger on the right grounds is a virtue (hatred alone is corrosive), Larsson is cast as the rhetorician who must keep our trust to 'put the judge into a certain frame of mind,' and the revenge emerges as the deliberated, rational means toward the end Aristotle calls eudaimonia: independence from a bogus guardianship and a life worth living, since under 'proportionate reciprocity' those who cannot requite evil with evil are slaves.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 11 "1. The Good, the Bad, and the Bureaucratic" — Reads the show's automatic, unquestionable point system as Hannah Arendt's bureaucracy — 'rule by Nobody' in which no one, not Michael, not Shawn, not even Judge Gen, has authority over the system ('He's not God, he's a bureaucrat').
