News to me') he argues that belief attribution requires concept possession, and concept possession requires a background of true beliefs, so total falsehood is unintelligible - a meaning-holist point he credits to Quine, Davidson and Sellars - though he concedes the machines could still make most of our beliefs false, so the Matrix Possibility survives.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 25 "Unknown" — Korsmeyer reads the film through classic problems of perception: Descartes's dreaming argument (Neo's sweaty awakenings), the evil deceiver updated as the evil computer, and the pod scene as her 'scariest philosophical problem', the brain-in-a-vat thought experiment, with Berkeley's esse est percipi as the Matrix's governing premise. She also notes the film's structural constraint - like all dreaming plots from Calderon to The X-Files its viewpoint must stand outside the Matrix - and uses Mouse's Tasty Wheat puzzle to show how reference to a never-experienced world breaks down.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 98 "Real Genre and Virtual Philosophy" — Knight and McKnight argue The Matrix must be read as a mixed-genre film: pure genres are 'a theorist's fiction', and the film's genre inheritance supplies the narrative roots of its philosophical thematics - Plato's cave from the Republic, Descartes's Dream Hypothesis from the Meditations, Nietzsche's Ubermensch, Zen Buddhism, and apocalyptic Christianity. Recognizing the genre mix explains both why the film raises questions about justified true belief in a virtual world, free will versus deterministic control, and appearance versus reality, and why it offers no philosophical answers, only genre ones.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 115 "Unknown" — Developing thesis one, the chapter shows Morpheus's question—'How would you know the difference between the dream world and the real world?'—restates Plato's cave dwellers mistaking shadows for things and Descartes's First Meditation progression from unreliable senses to dreaming to the malicious demon that makes every belief false. What is genuinely new is that computer simulation and brain science have made the once-outlandish demon scenario thinkable, so the film has made philosophy teachers' job easier: global skepticism no longer seems ridiculous, and maybe you are lying in a tub of goo right now.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 15 "Smelly Knowledge" — Andrew Aberdein sorts the Buffyverse's science-supernatural encounters into three grades — reduction to present science, reduction to a future science, and the irreducibly supernatural — illustrated by Sunnydale's rationalizers and Giles's inner skeptic in 'Tabula Rasa,' the Initiative's DNA testing of Oz in 'New Moon Rising,' and the show's characteristic 'creepy mix of magic and science' (Jenny Calendar's 'the divine exists in cyberspace'). He reads 'Normal Again' through Descartes's deceiving-demon skepticism, links Spike's chip and Walsh's Adam to the Phineas Gage case (emotion is needed for rational decision), and maps the grades onto the ancients-versus-moderns quarrel and Feyerabend's methodological anarchism. Giles's 'smelly knowledge' speech about books versus computers anticipates a pluralist, socially sensitive epistemology that enriches rather than rejects science.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 18 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Kurtz, the secular humanist, argues the film is a political weapon of the Religious Right (O'Reilly, Dobson, Gingrich) that presents fantasy as fact: Gibson claims fidelity to the Gospels while borrowing torture scenes such as the bridge plunge and the savage flogging from Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions, whitewashing the historical Pilate, and erasing that Jesus, Mary, and the disciples were themselves Jews. Applying historical criticism, he contends the Gospels are anonymous, second- and third-hand missionary propaganda written forty to seventy years after Jesus, shaped by the rivalry between rabbinic Judaism and Gentile-seeking Jewish Christianity and canonized politically at Nicaea under Constantine. He concludes by defending the freedom of inquiry, skeptical scrutiny of all sacred texts, and the First Amendment's separation of church and state against the film's power to inflame anti-Semitism and the American culture war.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 21 "“May The Force Be with You”" — Jones uses the Force's telekinesis (Luke's lightsaber flying to his hand, Yoda raising the X-wing) to probe the metaphysics of causation. Hume shows we never observe the necessary connection between cause and effect - only constant conjunction and habit - so Jedi mind-power is no more mysterious than gravity or magnetism; Leibniz's Monadology argues one substance cannot transfer properties to another, so 'how' any cause works is unintelligible; and Hume's problem of induction (will Tatooine's twin suns rise tomorrow? will Vader's officers always choke?) shows law-governed expectations cannot be non-circularly justified. Concurring with Russell that 'cause' is a relic, the chapter concludes the Force qualifies as a kind of cause precisely because our causal concept is too vague to exclude it - and plugs science fiction as a laboratory for sharpening concepts.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 14 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Thomas Senor turns the Professor's trilemma about Lucy (lying, mad, or telling the truth) into a general account of when to believe incredible testimony: weigh the testifier's reliability against how well the claim fits your background beliefs. He shows why Lucy's siblings should have believed her second report of Aslan in Prince Caspian, since by then talking animals and a resurrected Lion no longer clashed with what they knew, and then applies the framework to 'Julia's' report of hearing God, arguing that believing, disbelieving, or withholding rationally depends on the hearer's own background commitments. A footnote explains why Hume on miracles does not fit Lucy's case, since she claims no violation of natural law.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 19 "The Blessings of Tranquility" — Michael Chiariello takes Dylan's "the truth is true whether you wanna believe it or not" as a correspondence theory of truth, then rejects both the gospel-era absolutism of "Precious Angel" and the relativism (from Protagoras' man-the-measure to modern subjectivism) that would make Dylan's changes of course harmless. The alternative he defends is Pyrrhonian skepticism in Sextus Empiricus's sense: truth is objective but never fully assured, so suspending judgment yields tranquility. Dylan's career - from the ambiguous "Blowin' in the Wind" through "Watching the River Flow" and "Things Have Changed" to the two versions of "Every Grain of Sand" ("the reality of man" vs "a perfect finished plan") - embodies this balanced, non-dogmatic search the way of God designed it.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 18 "The Epilogue A Question of Belief" — Systematically pairs Hume's philosophy of religion with Python parodies: Anselm's ontological argument fails because existence cannot be defined into a concept (the Yeti-spotter who never spotted one), with Arthur 'Two Sheds' Jackson, Ron Obvious, and Confuse-A-Cat illustrating the gap between conceivability and possibility; the Galaxy Song's cosmic order and the mock hymn 'All Things Dull and Ugly' stage the design argument and Hume's reply that creation shows moral indifference as readily as benevolence; and Brian's 'miracles' — being 'taken up' then spotted sprinting, curing Simon the hermit by landing on his foot — illustrate Hume's 'Of Miracles' on the unreliability of testimony. Hume's Natural History claim that the cause of religion is fear surfaces in the 'O Father, please don't boil us' hymn and in Arthur's groveling before a God who hates it. Both Hume and the Pythons end in suspended judgment about God — settled, if at all, only by the wrestling match in which 'God exists by two falls to a submission.'
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 50 "The Problem with Bullshitting" — Against the bullshitter the chapter recruits Peirce: genuine inquiry is defined not by method or results but by the attitude of truly wanting true answers, so homicide detectives, philologists, and car mechanics all count as scientists in this sense. Bullshitting is a free-rider riding the bus of real inquiry - even the bullshitter wants his doctor not to bullshit - and the chapter formulates an epistemic imperative: proceed on the hope that there is a true answer and act from the desire to find it, with fallibilism, not skepticism, the viable stance (the passenger who can occupy any vacant seat cannot occupy them all).
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 12 "Introduction" — Frames Part II's epistemology chapters. Jacoby's chapter uses Stan Marsh debunking TV psychic John Edward, holistic healers, and Mormon belief to teach the ethics of belief against Pascal's wager; Lawrence's uses The Matrix to pose the skeptical problem and Descartes' response; Silverman's uses Adama's lie about Earth in Battlestar Galactica to raise the Gettier problem and the Clifford–James dispute over believing without sufficient evidence.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 13 "Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress" — Jacoby reads Stan Marsh as W.K. Clifford's ethics of belief in action: from 'All About the Mormons' ('you better have something to back it up') to 'The Biggest Douche in the Universe,' Stan insists the burden of proof lies with claimants and that faith used as a fallback is no evidence at all. 'Cartmanland' and the story of Job serve to criticize Pascal's Wager — a good God would not eternally torment the virtuous nonbeliever, and the Wager simply assumes its afterlife payoff — while the harms of Miss Information's holistic healers, David Blaine's cult suicide, and Scientology show Clifford was right that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken minds and, as Stan tells John Edward, slow down the progress of all mankind.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 14 "Skepticism Outside the Matrix" — Lawrence uses The Matrix to walk through Descartes' method of doubt: the dream argument, the evil demon reborn as a machine-run simulation, and invented worse cases ('Neo's Worst Nightmare,' a Matrix-within-the-Matrix that deceives even Morpheus' awakened rebels). The cogito is the only certainty that survives and Descartes' proof of God falls short, so certainty about the external world is unavailable; the chapter then borrows Russell's red-chair analysis of color, texture, and solidity to argue that even outside any Matrix, naive realism is false and we know only appearances.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 18 "Vertigo and Epistemological Vertigo" — Flory reads Vertigo as an epistemological parable: Scottie's 'hardheaded Scot' method, collecting facts and deducing from universal principles, fails three times (the step-stool 'cure' for his acrophobia, explaining away Madeleine's 'possession' with the horse statue, forcing Judy up the bell tower for confirmation), delivering an implicit critique of Vienna Circle positivism in the manner of Carnap and Ayer. Against Scottie, the chapter mobilizes Kuhn's theory-laden facts, Aristotle's point that human conduct resists codification by exceptionless laws, and Hume's 'slave of the passions,' with Descartes's automata and Chalmers's philosophical zombies framing the problem of other minds. Midge, who knows people emotionally as well as factually, models the alternative: philosophers who fear 'epistemological vertigo' should give up epistemological training wheels and accept that minds, especially emotions, escape law-like rules.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 30 "Marnie An Enigma to Herself" — Yanal sets Descartes's two claims about mind - certainty about one's own thoughts (via the method of doubt and the deceiving-evil-genius possibility) and skepticism about other minds (hats and coats that may cover automata) - against Wittgenstein's counters, then reads Shadow of a Doubt and Marnie as Hitchcock's counterexamples. In Shadow of a Doubt the two Charlies, twins in blood and in the film's doubling motifs, are 'transparent' to each other - Young Charlie alone knows her uncle is the Merry Widow Murderer - refuting other-minds skepticism; in Marnie, repressed memory of killing her mother's sailor client leaves Marnie ignorant of her own mind until Mark's amateur therapy recovers it, refuting Cartesian self-certainty. Both films thus side with Wittgenstein: one person can know another's mind, and one can be an enigma to oneself.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 21 "Wondering and Dreaming. The Words Have Different Meanings" — Scott Calef argues that the causal theory of perception — the inflatable pig over Battersea reaches you only as an internal representation — breeds Cartesian skepticism: the dreaming argument, asylum inmates who don't know they're mad ('the lunatic is in my head'), the evil demon, and the modern brain-in-a-vat version behind The Matrix. Locke's unknowable substratum behind the Dark Side jacket's qualities and Berkeley's idealism deepen the veil of perception, with 'Julia Dream', Waters's 'If I go insane, please don't stick your wires in my brain', and Syd's 'Jugband Blues' self-diagnosis as Floyd illustrations. Against skepticism he deploys mutual corroboration ('It takes two to know'), J.L. Austin's point that waking experience is qualitatively unlike dreams ('A Pillow of Winds': 'the dream is gone'), and Wittgenstein's beetle-in-a-box private language argument (rebranded as Lucifer Sam's cat) — a purely private language is impossible, so skepticism expressed in language defeats itself, leaving the Barrett-era enigma to keep philosophy's original wonder alive.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 13 "No Reason to Get Excited" — After 'Crossroads, Part 2' revealed Anders, Foster, Tigh, and Tyrol as Cylons, the chapter argues we can know that we exist (Descartes' cogito) without knowing what we are, since even Boomer's Cylon-detection result — Baltar's lie about the green light — could itself be a dream, returning us to Descartes' whirlpool. Moore's common-sense realism fails against the skeptic's special standards, and contextualism / relevant alternatives (Dretske) lets Starbuck dismiss dreaming-hypotheses about a Viper but cannot dismiss the possibility that you are a sleeper Cylon in a world where anyone might be one. Following Hume, who escaped skeptical paralysis by dining and playing backgammon, Tigh's 'report to your stations' shows the only live option: carry on being the person you want to be.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 14 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Steiff reads the 2007 movie as a sustained lesson in perceptual error: Sam's Porsche disappointment at the dealership, the parents' 'earthquake' misperception, and the Camaro that no one at Bobby B's lot suspects show that we see what context, expectation, and conditioning (the kitten experiments) lead us to see. She distinguishes illusion - misperceiving an object really present, as Sam misperceives Bumblebee as just a car - from hallucination, and weighs direct realism against representative realism's 'veil of perception' using film tricks from Melies's jammed camera to the Lumiere brothers' panic-inducing train, leaving Sam's knowledge resting on fallible but indispensable sense experience.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 16 "It-Getting The Truth about Truthiness" — Ethan Mills runs a 'Better Know a Skeptic' four-parter applied to the show: Pyrrhonian skepticism (Sextus Empiricus's suspension of judgment and living by appearances, played out in the Jon-says-worst-versus-Stephen-says-greatest Bush debate), Modern skepticism (Montaigne's fideist custom-worship and Hume's dream argument for why knowledge of couches, Doritos, and presidents is impossible), and Indian skepticism (Nagarjuna's circle that means of knowledge cannot be established without things known, illustrated with Stephen Sr. and Stephen Jr. as both father and son, plus Jayarasi's destruction of epistemology). He adds 'political skepticism' - the American sense that political knowledge is impossible - which breeds wikiality, an internet relativism ('reality we just agreed on') that the WØRD's own bullet points ('Wikipedia can tell a lie') undermine. Truthiness, he concludes, is Stephen's false cure for political skepticism: commitment without facts, a 'truthiness of the appearances'; but Sextus shows skeptics can still act on appearances without dogmatism, so we can vote and argue on the best evidence, as in Sagan's science-as-democracy, without certainty.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 22 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Michaud wonders whether the Magisterium's censorship of Dust research could be epistemically justified, building the answer from Descartes's dreaming and deceiving-demon doubts (imagine waking to find your dæmon was only a dream), Moore's common-sense 'I know I have two hands' reply, and Dretske's relevant alternatives, arriving at Lewis's 'Elusive Knowledge': inquiry itself ratchets up the standards for knowledge until certainty dissolves, which is exactly what happens to Lyra, and to readers, once they start asking questions about Dust and other worlds. On this view the Magisterium had a Lewisian motive to suppress inquiry, since unquestioning belief preserves the certainty on which its power and promise of salvation rest. But because philosophical questions like 'Is God good?' can never meet the raised standards anyway, the chapter concludes that a little doubt is preferable to the dogmatism and bigotry certainty breeds.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 9 "Area Philosopher (Me!) Is Sick Of The Stupid Debate About Stupid" — Cuddy stages the generational-decline debate between Mark Bauerlein's The Dumbest Generation and Stephen Johnson's Everything Bad Is Good for You, showing that Onion stories can be marshaled for both sides: Aristophanes complaining that today's audiences 'just don't get me' vindicates the perennial declinist, while 'US Students Lead World in Detention' wryly supports Johnson's sleeper curve. Comparing Bauerlein to Aristophanes and the 'Our Dumb World' entry on Aristotle and Plato's schools closing, he concludes every era teems with idiots, so The Onion could have existed in any century. Because induction from earlier generations' failed predictions cannot settle whether Millennials really are dumber, he suspends judgment and toasts The Onion as the smartest perspective around.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 32 "Point-Counterpoint Funny versus Really, Really Funny" — Andrew Terjesen starts from real cases of Onion satire taken literally — a Michigan sheriff warning about al-Qaida telemarketing, the Beijing Evening News plagiarizing 'Congress Threatens To Leave D.C.', Deborah Norville reporting that 58 percent of American exercise is televised — and explains them through the Problem of Other Minds. Descartes' hats-and-cloaks worry and Russell's analogy solution show how we infer that a straight-faced writer is 'just kidding,' but the analogy fails when cultural context, prejudice (Fred Phelps citing the gay-recruitment story, Christians forwarding the Harry Potter Satanism piece), or wishful thinking breaks the comparison with our own joking behavior. The upshot is that humor is engineered misunderstanding — the Onion works by analogy to real news, and could never warn readers off without destroying the joke.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 17 "Doomed to Be Perceived" — Smithka tests Berkeley's 'to be is to be perceived' against two monsters: the Vashta Nerada, whose existence is inferred from indirect evidence (counting shadows, the 'ghosting' of Miss Evangelista) much like Neptune was inferred from Uranus's orbit, and the Weeping Angels, which act only when unperceived and so falsify Berkeley's principle. Working through Locke on substance, Hume's skepticism about unperceivable causes like God, Paley's watchmaker design argument, and scientific realism (Sellars, Churchland) versus van Fraassen's empirically adequate anti-realism, she concludes the Doctor is a realist about unobservables — for whom the Angels are real but 'doomed to be perceived'.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 7 "Know Thyself" — George Reisch's introduction frames the volume with Martha Stout's claim that one in twenty-five people is a conscience-free sociopath who hides in plain sight, arguing that we viewers do the hiding work for them just as Deb, LaGuerta and Batista's assumptions shield Dexter. It presents Dexter's incessant inner questioning as the show's philosophical hook and previews the book's competing verdicts on Harry's Code: monster, Kantian-style model actor, utilitarian good, aesthete, or superhero. It ends by inverting Socrates: normally we point 'know thyself' inward, but the real epistemic danger is the sociopath next door, so our skepticism should aim at the guy in forensics - unless we are ourselves among the one-in-twenty-five, in which case Socrates' injunction to self-examination was spot on.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 13 "More than a Feeling" — Rachel Robison-Greene asks whether Dexter's rule to 'be sure' actually gives him knowledge of his victims' guilt. Distinguishing Cartesian certainty - skeptical hypotheses about deceiving senses, dreams and evil demons, echoing The Matrix - from mere felt certainty, she tests the belief-truth-justification analysis of knowledge traced to Plato against the show: LaGuerta's witness theory fails on belief, Deb's conviction that Neil Perry is the Ice Truck Killer fails on truth, and Astor's accusation of Dexter fails on justification. Neither strong internalism (Dexter straps down Jamie Jaworski without knowing how the murder was done), weak internalism, coherence theory (his false but coherent case against Jonathan Farrow), nor reliabilism (his spidey-sense is explicitly not sufficient by his own admission) captures his practice, so his 'certainty' is just a feeling - and the people on his table may include ones he does not know to be guilty.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 24 "Do I Even Care if I’m Dreaming" — Kate Elson Anderson reads 'Sleepy Time' — SpongeBob's tour of his neighbors' dream clouds, from Gary's library to Patrick's quarter-fed kiddie ride to Krabs's Moby Dollar — through Descartes's First Meditation dream argument that no sure mark distinguishes waking from dreaming. Norman Malcolm's claim that one cannot even ask 'Am I dreaming?' while asleep is contradicted by SpongeBob's lucid wandering, and Patrick's mundane dream (he would not even conjure another quarter) proves Descartes's point that dreams can be indistinguishable from reality. SpongeBob's final move — asking the question but never waiting for an answer — leaves Descartes baffled by a truth-seeker immune to skepticism.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 7 "Happy Ending" — Wenmackers uses Inception's dream levels and its ambiguous spinning-top ending as a guided tour of skeptical philosophy, diagramming how dreams-within-dreams, kicks, Limbo and exponentially dilated dream time work. She tests the totem against Zhuangzi's butterfly and lucid-dreaming reality checks, then runs Plato's Cave and the eternal Forms, Descartes's cogito and evil demon, Putnam's brain-in-a-vat, and Nozick's experience machine to ask whether Cobb's world - or ours - is real. Her conclusion is Socratic ('know that you know nothing'): subjective reality feels equally real on every level and the top level can never be known. She even argues that dream-time dilation means Cobb should not kill himself while in doubt, since real time barely passes, so a little philosophy rescues the happy ending.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 9 "Does the Top Fall Does It Matter in the End" — Andersen contends Inception goes one deeper than Descartes: where the dream argument threatened only the external world, inception threatens the autonomy of thought itself, since the 'core conception' that defines identity - Fischer's reading of his father's dying word 'disappointed' - can be implanted. Tracing Nolan's obsession with thought-manipulation through his earlier films (the manipulator Cobb of Following, Leonard's self-deception in Memento, the Joker's schemes), he shows inception as co-opting subjectivity. Against the Cartesian answer of doubting everything, the fates of Mal and Cobb in Limbo - where doubt, once planted, grows devastatingly, and where a totem cannot guard against self-deception - teach that the way back to reality is the leap of trust in others: only by opening himself to Ariadne, Miles and his children can Cobb turn away from the top and go home.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 17 "Do We Give Shakespeare the Last Word" — Kapper reads Inception as epistemology rather than metaphysics - not what is real but how we could know - running from Plato's Theaetetus (the first dream-recognition question) through Descartes's deceptive demon and Freud's royal road to the unconscious, to Wittgenstein's point that 'I may be dreaming' is senseless because the remark itself would be dreamed, and Heraclitus's line that only the waking share a common world. The Ariadne thread is the clue: as in the Theseus myth, dream architecture gives the labyrinth a shareable narrative place, but only a hint, never a way to wake. He then goes east - Zhuangzi's butterfly, Indra's net of mutually reflecting jewels, Schopenhauer's universe dreamed by a single dreamer, William James's many consciousnesses - to ask how many times we must die before waking, ending with Buddhism: 'Buddha means awakened one', and Cobb's turning from the top enacts Nirvana, where the real-versus-dream question stops pertaining.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 23 "An Old Man, Filled with Regret . ." — Brophy argues Cobb's shared dreams are best modeled on MMORPG virtual worlds like Second Life and World of Warcraft: Ariadne is a world-building architect in the mold of Second Life's Escher Relativity House, dreamers are avatars, and the film's looping architectures mirror the toroidal grids of game worlds. Reading the film as an addict's 'long con', he claims the real inception was planting in Cobb's own head the idea that his game-world is real: Mal is a 'gamer's widow' whose in-game suicide deleted her character, and Cobb is the avatar of an unseen addicted player who has forgotten the game. Borges's map that covers the empire, Baudrillard's claim that the simulacrum becomes the preferred reality, Bostrom's simulation argument, and Homer's lotus-eaters all support the warning that we already prefer simulated worlds, so the last shot means the real Cobb will one day wake as an old man filled with regret.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 7 "Chapter 01 - Hollywood Doesn’t Know Dick" — Ethan Mills opens his 'investigation' of Hollywood's Dick adaptations (Blade Runner, Total Recall, Minority Report, The Adjustment Bureau) by insisting that fan complaints signal something essential lost in translation from print to film, not mere infidelity. He frames the issue as a clash between two philosophical worldviews about free will and knowledge, adopting a bounty-hunter persona to hunt down what Hollywood changed.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 8 "We Can Conceive It for Ourselves Wholesale" — Mills defines the 'Holly-worldview' (good defeats evil, free will secures the triumph of the human spirit, heroes discover truth before the credits roll) and opposes it to the Dickian worldview of paranoia, ignorance and accepted unfreedom, where a 'happy ending' means accepting some inevitable, possibly depressing fact about our place in the universe. He announces the chapter's plan: to test whether the Holly-worldview survives Dick's challenges to its two tenets, free will and knowledge.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 11 "Skepticism for Fun and Profit" — Mills uses the Blade Runner cuts to stage skepticism: the theatrical happy ending hides the question, the Director's Cut unicorn hints Scott wants Deckard to be a replicant, but Dick's novel has Luba Luft tell Deckard 'You must be an android' and presses him on whether his Voigt-Kampff memories are false, leaving the question unresolved for the reader and for Deckard himself. Since any evidence (empathy, the test's own accuracy) can itself be doubted, the novel is more radically skeptical than the films, because it makes both hypotheses compatible with all the evidence. He then shows Ubik pushing this to the limit, where characters cannot tell what year it is, whether their money is real, or even whether they are alive or dead.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 13 "What’s So Bad about Skepticism" — Mills argues that for the ancient skeptics skepticism was the cure, not the disease: Sextus Empiricus prescribes setting equally strong arguments against each other until judgment is suspended and tranquility follows. He reads Nagarjuna and Jayarashi as more radical, using contradictions to uproot the very impulse to hold philosophical views at all, weaning themselves from attachment even to Buddhist views. Applied to Dick, both approaches would have us stop agonizing over whether Deckard is an android or the Ubik characters are dead: the best way to stop worrying is to stop wanting the answers.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 48 "Selfless" — The chapter concedes that no rule, psyche, body, soul, or combined, accommodates all of Dick's transformations, and refuses to blame Dick for incoherence: his stories force our own conflicting intuitions about wubs, Quaids and downloaded minds into the open. Pessimist, optimist and skeptic each get a verdict, the skeptic's being the chapter's cliffhanger: if we are none of these things, maybe there are no enduring persons at all.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 51 "How Do You Know You’re Not an Android" — The chapter weaponizes the cogito for Deckard's predicament: the fact that 'the lights are on' for you seems to prove you are human, but Descartes' leap from thinking to an immaterial soul is unjustified, since introspection cannot show whether your thoughts run on a soul, a bundle of neurons, or a silicon chip. Hume's 'I never can catch myself at any time without a perception' supplies the precedent, and the conclusion is that no amount of inner experience rules out being an android, so you will have to go take the V-K test after all.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 52 "The Art of Knowing Arctor" — The chapter takes Fred's surveillance of Arctor as a literal solution to the eye-cannot-see-itself problem: split in two, Bob finally observes himself from a detached, evaluative outside, hoping the scanner sees 'clearly' where he sees 'only murk'. Real self-scanning follows, since an fMRI revealing synthetic parts behind your eye sockets would settle the android question and neural correlates might someday sort enduring love from lust, before Alva Noe's Out of Our Heads objection that mental states must be sought in whole organisms interacting with their environments, which would give Arctor's whole-habitat self-scanning the edge over the constrained brain scan.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 89 "How Are Things in Glocca Morra—or Anywhere Else, for That Matter" — Opens Gerard Casey's part by asking whether David Norris is really free or governed by an external agency, then argues from perception itself: the stick that looks bent in the fish tank and the rainbow that exists only for an observer positioned between sunlight and raindrops show that ordinary experience is already a construct of sensory limits, expectations, and language. This prepares the radical question of whether everything in our experience is in some way an illusion.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 99 "Chapter 15 - Lies, Incorporated" — Opens Don Fallis's part with an inventory of Dickian deception: Quaid's implanted memories, replicants deceived into believing they are human in Blade Runner and Impostor, the framed Anderton, Ragle Gumm's manufactured town, and the Bureau's constant adjustments. Unlike Descartes' malicious demon or The Matrix, these are not skeptical hypotheticals but the kinds of deception that corporations, parties, and governments actually perpetrate — with us often complicit in our own deception.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 102 "Who Deceives Us" — Defines the conspiracy through Cohaagen's team — Lori, Harry, Benny, and the turncoat Hauser — with the Adjustment Bureau as 'the quintessential conspiracy' claiming good consequences for humanity. Popper's argument that belief in efficient grand conspiracies is irrational (his 'cock-up theory of society') is tested against the Bureau's own bungled coffee spill that lets David meet Elise, while Keeley's Hume-style critique and the specter of unbridled skepticism about spouses, friends, and memories frame what it would cost to believe in such conspiracies.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 131 "Chapter 20 - If the Universe Isn’t Real, How Should We Treat Other People" — Andrew M. Butler's introduction opens with the ambiguous endings of Total Recall, Minority Report, and Blade Runner (the fade to white, the too-neat reunion, the improbable sunset) to pose skeptical doubt about whether any of Dick's realities are real, surveying Eye in the Sky, Flow My Tears, Time Out of Joint, and Next. Against the thought that if nothing is real nothing matters, it sets Eric Sweetscent returning to his failing wife, and introduces Dick's aim to fuse Hebrew monotheism with Heidegger's philosophy of thrownness, noting that Levinas made the attempt first and that for Dick the authentic human is the one who cares for others.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 132 "To Be or Not To Be—Is That the Question" — The section introduces Levinas (Heidegger's student, Nazi internment camp survivor, Talmudic scholar) for whom ethics outranks ontology ('To be or not to be? Is that the question?'), and illustrates his strange distinction between existents and existing through Dick's existing-without-existents: the hallucinated town of The Cosmic Puppets, the aura of fake American relics in The Man in the High Castle, Freck's nonexistent aphids. Working through phenomenology, the idios kosmos / koinos kosmos split of A Maze of Death and Eye in the Sky, and the eerie 'There is' of the void, it reworks Descartes's cogito into Levinas's question ('I think, therefore what should I do?') because out there is the Other.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 9 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Elizabeth Swanstrom reads Mr. Wednesday's recruitment of Shadow in American Gods as a two-man con that exploits Hume's account of causation: because the mind projects causal links from constant conjunction, Odin and Loki stage a chain of 'coincidences' (Laura's death, rerouted flights, the first-class seat) and use classic misdirection, from Sweeney's warning at Jack's Crocodile Bar to the Herodotus tale of Croesus, so that the mark never looks at the hand with the coin in it. Setting Hume's billiard-ball analysis against Seneca and the Stoic idea of derivative causality, she argues Wednesday manipulates association rather than chance itself. Shadow's counter-training in coin sleights, especially the Sucker Vanish, and Sweeney's gift of the resurrection coin that revives Laura introduce genuine chance, letting Shadow see the set-up, stop the sacrificial battle, and demonstrate that a causally saturated world still leaves room to break the game.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 32 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Tom McBride reads the film through Wittgenstein's On Certainty: Dr. Zaius's certainties (flight is impossible, humans come from the forests) are hinge or riverbed propositions that cannot be doubted within the ape form of life, so Taylor's true story sounds not false but insane, like claiming to have slept on the moon. Speaking and able to prompt empirical investigation, Taylor fractures a foundational principle where G.E. Moore, facing a 'wild tribe' playing a different language game, could only confess that things 'stand fast' with him; and Zaius's explicit origin myth, a parallel to Plato's Myth of the Metals, is flimsy precisely because rulers who must insist on rules are not potent and are reduced to destroying the cave evidence. The genre's appeal is Margaret Atwood's 'controlled hallucination': crazy doors that swing on safe hinges, rivers that still have stable beds.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 20 "Psych and Philosophy" — McCraw turns the question 'should we trust Shawn?' into the philosophy of testimony: Lassiter's policy of never believing without independent evidence embodies Hume's demand that testimony be backed by evidence of the speaker's reliability, while Buzz McNab's instant faith embodies Reid's innate principles of veracity and credulity, and both extremes fail the department - Lassiter solves too late, McNab chases every early false lead. Juliet's developing, flexible trust - suspicious at first, convinced by results, never naive - models the circumstantial middle path that no hard-and-fast Humean or Reidian rule can capture. The verdict: treat Shawn's testimony as both psychic and psychotic, trusting the track record in some cases and discounting the wilder 'visions' in others, because when to trust is unavoidably vague and case-by-case.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 33 "Psych and Philosophy" — Courtney Neal explains that Santa Barbara believes Shawn is psychic because pseudoscience offers easier, more appealing explanations than the truth: in the pilot, 'he's psychic' beats 'he's the killer' as a narrative that fits the facts, and psychic claims are worded so they cannot be disproved. She shows how Shawn's real observational deductions are packaged through cold reading (the comic-convention scene in 'Shawn vs. the Red Phantom'), Robert Cialdini's social-influence principles of liking, social proof, and commitment/consistency, and the self-fulfilling prophecy of his reputation - so even Lassiter's skepticism cannot dislodge a belief the city keeps confirming.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 40 "Psych and Philosophy" — This chapter is a skeptical debunking tour of real-life 'psycho psychics' - Babylonian astrologers, the Delphi oracle that set Socrates testing the claim he was wisest, Nostradamus's hindsight-friendly quatrains, Blavatsky, Cayce, spoon-bender Uri Geller, and Sylvia Browne's failed Shawn Hornbeck prediction - arguing that no repeatable, peer-reviewed evidence of ESP has ever existed and that figures like cold-reading psychic detective Peter Hurkos thrive on gullibility. It ties to Psych through Gus's credulity about UFOs and werewolves and the real police practice of consulting psychic detectives that Shawn's con parodies, while Houdini's congressional testimony and James Randi's Million Dollar Challenge model the evidence-demanding skepticism the show's fake psychic gets away from.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 24 "The Devil and Philosophy" — John Karavitis (with tongue-in-cheek co-author 'Lucifer') treats The Ninth Gate as an epistemology case study, sorting the characters' beliefs about the Devil - true-believer Balkan, skeptic book-dealer Corso, the occult-tourist Order of the Silver Serpent - and testing them against Plato's Theaetetus definitions of knowledge as perception, true belief, and justified true belief. Balkan's justification is only an internally coherent web of book-learned beliefs, while Corso's external evidence (engravings signed 'LCF,' his journey's experiences) is weighed by the general reliability of his sources. Descartes' dreaming and the deceiving demon then leave the viewer skeptical that the Devil ever appeared at all.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 26 "The Devil and Philosophy" — The Bocks use the courtroom frame of The Exorcism of Emily Rose to ask whether anyone could be justified in believing in demon possession, since the same seizures, polyglot voices, and levitations read differently under naturalism and supernaturalism. Kuhn's paradigms explain why neither worldview abandons ship at anomalies, and they weigh Wiebe's 'finite spirits as theoretical entities,' Hume's miracles argument (with Levine's Red Sea thought experiment as rebuttal), and the Cartesian ghost-in-the-machine premise that possession would require. Testing even a Men in Black alien hypothesis against the religiously specific phenomena, they conclude that a witnessed case like Emily's could rationally justify belief in possession.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 25 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Don Fallis frames Homeland as a world of real epistemic warfare - unlike Descartes' hypothetical malicious demon, terrorists and the CIA actively engineer false appearances (Brody the war hero, Carrie the support-group veteran, Saul's memory-card trick). He analyzes lying versus true-but-misleading statements, uses Russell's barber paradox to define double agents without contradiction, and shows how Carrie, Dana, and Lauder each detect an inconsistency (Yorkshire Gold tea, the locked bedroom, Walker's three missed shots). Following Hume on testimony and Peirce's abduction - inference to the best explanation - Dana concludes her father is a terrorist, and Coady's defense of conspiracy theories vindicates Lauder's Brody-Walker hypothesis.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 16 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Michaud plays the 'David Hume' Card Wars deck against Princess Bubblegum's confidence in science: following Hume's problem of induction, every scientific law rests on observation and is only probabilistic—we never observe the necessary connection between cause and effect, whether in magnetism, Jake's hunger-induced jerkiness, or the first law of thermodynamics. Humans are pattern-makers who project causal order onto the world (seeing Gunter in clouds, blaming one bubblegum incident), while quantum physics reveals genuine randomness that Einstein hated. Ooo's residents, who watch Tree Trunks explode and simply move on, may grasp reality better than we do, because they never smuggle in stable, lawlike expectations that the show—and the universe—keep violating.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 24 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Arp uses King Worm's dream-within-dreams to pose the perception-reality problem: distinguishing perceiver, perceptions, and perceived, he maps the triad onto Plato's allegory of the cave, then contrasts epistemological and metaphysical realism (the fallen tree fort still makes sound waves unheard; Pythagoras discovered rather than invented his theorem) with idealism and antirealism, whose dead end is solipsism—Lumpy Space Princess locked in a private movie theater of perceptions. Hume's picture of the mind as a theater of successive perceptions and Berkeley's Hylas-and-Philonous worry that we are trapped inside perceptual reality give the skeptical threat its force. The chapter sides with Jake—'You gotta focus on what's real, man'—while conceding that after 'King Worm' Finn and Jake can never be certain they escaped the hypnotism.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 13 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter turns Raylan's claim that shooting Tommy Bucks was 'justified' into a question of epistemic justification, expounding Plato's Meno definition of knowledge as justified true belief, Gettier's 1963 counterexamples (rebuilt with Boyd truly but luckily predicting that a marshal will be arrested), and the repairs of Goldman's no-false-causal-link condition and Harman's inference to the best explanation. It then grades the show's reasoners: Raylan knows the Crowes rather than Boyd killed Wade Messer, Boyd knows Cassie milks the revival snakes' venom, Art Mullen does not yet know Raylan helped Winona return the evidence-room money, and gut-feeling victims like Ellen May do not know what they saw. Against Humean skepticism about cause and effect it defends inductive, detective-style knowledge - Raylan can know who done it without courtroom proof.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 7 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Using 'Flowers for Charlie', where a placebo pill convinces two scientists and even the Waitress that Charlie has become a genius, the chapter asks what actually makes something philosophy. Sounding smart is not philosophy: big words, the Sokal-style hoax paper submitted to a leading journal, and the 'Guru Effect' of credulous admirers all fail, yet Charlie's pronouncements turn out true by sheer luck - which is exactly Edmund Gettier's problem of epistemic luck illustrated with the broken-clock example. Since we can never verify our premises or our reasoning, the chapter sides with Aristotle's response to Plato's theory of forms that we can never determine what a thing is, only what it is not, and concludes the show is philosophical precisely because the Gang is the exact antithesis of reality, truth, and right action.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 25 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Fenner Tanswell uses 'Reynolds vs. Reynolds: The Cereal Defense' - the Gang's in-bar trial over Frank's blind driving versus Dennis's cereal-at-the-wheel - as a catalogue of crooked thinking. We get valid forms distinguished from soundness (modus ponens with 'if poop is funny, then Frank pooped in the bed'; Charlie's modus tollens from Frank's no-donkey-brains certificate), then the fallacies: the argument from ignorance by which Dennis's lacking a certificate proves him donkey-brained, Dee's ad hominem against Mac, Dennis's appeal to authority, and Mac's 'Science Is a Liar Sometimes' poster, which equivocates between mere skeptical doubt (even Descartes's) and reasonable doubt by straw-manning science as claiming infallibility. True to form, the Gang convicts Dee 'for comedy rather than on any logical basis.'
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 26 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Archibald casts Crazy Eyes as the show's Don Quixote, read through Descartes's Meditations: like Descartes ridding himself of conditioned false beliefs, Suzanne slaps her head to 'reset' and question everything, and like Quixote she blames an inner evil enchanter when her noble illusions collapse. Her rationalist imagination (chivalry, poetry, Piper as her Dulcinea) produces false beliefs that hurt, above all her devoted service to the manipulative Vee, yet the same faculty creates the beauty, coping, and nobility that make an ugly prison survivable, so truth may not be all that matters.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 22 "11. What Mary Didn’t Know" — Demeter reconstructs five rival explanations of Mary's hesitation to accept Matthew - emotional uncertainty, greed, fear of social exclusion over Pamuk, bad conscience, and conflicting family pressures - and argues none can be singled out as true. Via Frayn's Copenhagen, Dennett's 'Real Patterns,' and Henry James's The Golden Bowl as read by Robert Pippin, he defends the indeterminacy of psychological interpretation: motives are accessed only through behavior filtered through the interpreter's own psychological apparatus, and on the stronger view there are no motivation-facts prior to interpretation at all. What Mary did not know about her own hesitation may therefore not be knowable in principle, by her or by us.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 36 "17. What if Our Reality Is One Big Hallucination" — Arp starts from Rick's hallucinations of Lori - the disconnected phone in "Hounded," the touch and kiss in "Home" - and Michonne's confessed visions, showing how Rick distinguishes them through coherence with causal law and through third-person verification (Michonne watching him stroke empty air; Morgan's isolation in "Clear" showing why social checks matter). He then widens this into the theory of knowledge: the perceiver-perception-perceived triangle, epistemological and metaphysical realism versus idealism and antirealism, Berkeley's picture of the mind as a movie theater we cannot exit, and the Walking Dead twist on the falling tree in the forest, concluding that even if reality were one big hallucination we would still live - and refuse to walk off cliffs - as realists.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 38 "18. Gruesome Walkers" — Yuen turns the walkers into a lesson on Hume's problem of induction: the pre-apocalyptic belief that the dead do not rise was justified by all past experience until Rick wakes to a world where they do, and Rick's distrust of Alexandria repeats the same inductive move from Woodbury, Terminus, and Grady - useful, Hume says, since custom compels us, but never knowledge. Russell's chicken illustrates the fatal surprise, and Goodman's grue (the pun of the title) shows the outbreak could be a future-swinging regularity like the seventeen-year cicadas, undermining even Jenner's experimental science. Popper's falsificationism is offered as the rescue - Shane's reanimation falsifies the "walkers make walkers" theory, leaving the "everyone is infected" theory corroborated but never known.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 28 "15. It Would Take a Miracle!" — Barkman and Käärid ask whether Miracle Max's revival of 'mostly dead' Westley is a miracle, staging David Hume - for whom a violation of natural law is never more credible than mistaken or lying testimony, so Hume in Florin would call Max a deceiver and Inigo and Fezzik barbarous dupes - against C.S. Lewis, for whom a miracle is a new, unpredictable element introduced into nature rather than a violation of it. They add puzzles neither philosopher addresses: whether Westley was truly dead, whether a 'rotten miracle' would still count, and why Max's miracles seem to require 'unshattered' confidence, concluding that Florin's miracles are person-dependent in a way Hume's skepticism and Lewis's supernaturalism both miss.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 18 "8. Honesty Trumps Cleverness Sam Vimes and Commonsense Philosophy" — Skene argues Sam Vimes embodies Thomas Reid's common sense philosophy across Feet of Clay, Thud!, Night Watch, and Jingo: he refuses speculation (his hatred of Holmes-style clue-deduction and the Summoning Dark), is irreverent toward false authorities from Sergeant Colon's 'School of My Dad Always Said' to Lord Rust's glorious wars, and checks every theory against reality. Moore's here-is-one-hand reply to Humean skepticism and Socrates' unmasking of pompous authorities illustrate the method, and Huemer's political realism - taxation as demanded money with menaces, social systems judged by how they work for real people - echoes Vimes's verdicts on Reg Shoe's utopian barricade and Swing's phrenology. The lesson is Vimes's own: 'Common sense and facts! That's what works.'
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 28 "16. Getting at the Truth" — The chapter sets out the Platonic justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge with Discworld examples—Archchancellor Ridcully as a fallible authority, the physics of thaum particles as coherentist justification—before constructing a Discworld Gettier case in which a young wizard sees a fake level-seven wizard killed and truly but accidentally reports that 'a level seven wizard was killed.' It then tests the standard repairs, applying Nozick's truth-tracking function and Goldman's causation function to a case where a man blames the notorious Reacher Gilt for a theft actually committed by the dwarf he bumped into, and argues that neither truth-tracking nor specificity makes the problem go away. The upshot is that Discworlders, used to expecting to be wrong, may let go of false 'knowledge' more easily than our confidently wrong Roundworld.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 38 "23. How Can We Know Anything in a World of Magic and Miracles" — Baldwin asks whether Westerosi characters can know anything inductive in a world without lawlike nature: seasons of unpredictable length, wargs in animal minds, Faceless Men changing faces, and resurrections by Thoros, Melisandre, and Qyburn. After laying out the Platonic justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge (those who saw the pyre are justified in believing Dany is the mother of dragons; those relying on rumor are not), he runs Hume's problem of induction - we never perceive causal connection, so no jar of wildfire must explode - against Reid's common-sense reply that reason and induction stand or fall together, concluding that Westeros gives its people special reasons for skepticism while we, lacking evidence of magical irregularity, are rational to trust everyday inductive belief.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 21 "8. For Hume the Ball Tolls!" — The chapter argues Charlie Brown's repeated falls for Lucy's football gag are failures of induction: given the history of the gag since 1951 (first with Violet, then Lucy's fake reasons each fall - a handshake, a contract, a hundred million dollars), he should draw the meta-level conclusion that she will always pull the ball away. It then tries Hume's problem of induction as his defense, but since that would cost him all knowledge of the external world (that Snoopy is a beagle, that Lucy is mean) and end in skepticism, Charlie - a student of his world, not a doubter of it - cannot take it. The verdict: he is not a blockhead but determined and committed, willing to lose every fall because kicking that ball would be worth it, as in the 1979 hospital strip where he finally gets his kick and still ends up on his back.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 10 "Real, This Book" — The volume's introduction is written in Elliot's paranoid voice, doubting whether the book, the reader, or reality itself exist. It lays out the questions the essays will tackle: fsociety's hack of the Evil Corporation, whether it was political ideology or revenge for the corporation killing Elliot's and Darlene's father, whether either motive (or hacking in general) can be justified, and what order could survive after the financial system falls.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 22 "9. What Elliot Doesn’t Know Won’t Hurt You (Or Will It )" — Greene argues Elliot is in the worst possible position for a knower: Descartes's skeptical scenarios of madness, dreams, and the evil demon apply to everyone, but hit Elliot harder through morphine and ecstasy hallucinations, lucid dreams indistinguishable from waking (as Whiterose suggests), and a dissociative disorder so severe he spends months in prison believing he lives at his mother's house - with Mr. Robot even hiding facts from him, blocking the Socratic 'know thyself.' Yet by the Meno's knowledge problem he may be no worse off: he still catches the pedophile ring and brings down E Corp, so the hero of the show succeeds without knowledge.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 33 "17. Our Lying Eyes" — Wood asks how Elliot - and we, who see only what he sees - can know anything, and contrasts two empiricisms: Locke's white-paper mind furnished by ideas copied from mind-independent objects, which explains Mr. Robot as perceptual error, and Berkeley's idealism, on which only ideas and their divine cause exist, which makes Elliot's unshared hallucination of Mr. Robot dangerously hard to distinguish from reality. Consistency of perception is the only test left, and it fails Elliot until the pier video proves no one pushed him - and fails us again when his cozy Season Two routine turns out to be prison.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 31 "18. How to Deal with Reality when We’re not Built To" — The Zawadzkis and Cisowski argue Dick's deliberate confusion enacts what psychology and radical skepticism say about cognition: our 'cognitive miser' brains build simplified models, and the films shatter them, producing Leon Festinger's cognitive dissonance — Frank's chain of external justifications for his rebellion, Joe and John facing excuses they cannot so easily make, Tagomi's overload after killing the two Nazi agents. Following Karl Jaspers, such limit situations can force a leap into a new mode of thinking (Tagomi's transport to a world where the killings never happened), with radical skepticism — Bertrand Russell's five-minute hypothesis — and the I Ching as vehicles for dealing with a reality we are not built to handle.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 10 "2. Persuade Me Once, Shame on You . ." — Greene dismantles both phases of Adams's case that Trump is a Master Persuader. The trait-list phase (opening with big demands, the Intentional Wrongness Persuasion Play, never apologizing, exuding confidence, recruiting the reciprocity instinct, and the talent stack) fails because doing what master persuaders do is not being one, by the Tom Brady versus Archie Manning point that we never define good quarterbacks by wins alone and by the Kantian thought that an act must be done for the right reason. The reality phase borrows Plato, Hume, and Kant to deny us access to an objective world, but the chapter replies that the experts' predictive failures illustrate Hume's problem of induction rather than proving there are no facts, notes Adams even misreads Plato, and observes that nothing links the Persuasion Filter's one success to Trump's skills rather than to a one-off political climate.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 29 "17. Sweeping Up God’s Debris" — Robison-Greene reads God's Debris as a Socratic dialogue on speed: the Avatar, like Socrates after the Delphic oracle, guts the Postman's confidence so he can unlearn, and the whole book functions as a Cartesian skeptical hypothesis in the dream-and-evil-demon lineage, here that we are the dust of a self-destructed God and perception is illusion, with gravity re-described as probability. Her counterattack is that the cosmology commits category mistakes, since probability cannot cause dust to reappear any more than Joe can consist of tallness, and that God made of probability is incoherent even for an omnipotent being. The five levels of awareness collapse too: level-four skeptics are just people who trust reliable methods, and the Avatar's claim that the mind is an illusion generator is self-defeating, since his own omniscience presupposes objective truth.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 17 "8. What Are You Hearing" — Wissner reads TZ's musical scores through Plato's account of music as manufactured, mimetic signs and Aristotle's doctrine of ethos — that melodies represent character and emotion and can change minds without words. She shows how in 'Perchance to Dream' and 'A Stop at Willoughby' reverberation, Theremin-like electronics, and recurring five-note motifs mark dream states against the acoustic French horn of waking reality, how shared cues in 'Twenty-Two' and 'Shadow Play' trap Liz and Adam in circular nightmares that may also be premonitions, and how the piano ostinato of 'The Midnight Sun' reveals Norma's heat-death dream — music answering whether we, or the characters, can ever be sure we are awake rather than dreaming or imagining.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 20 "10. Memories Are Made of This" — Nisley applies Hume's skeptical account of belief in continued existence — built from resemblance, constancy, 'force and vivacity,' and testimony — to 'And When the Sky Was Opened,' where Colonel Harrington, then Clegg Forbes, then Major Gart each cease to exist as memory and corroboration (bartender, girlfriend, general, headlines) collapse layer by layer. 'The Trouble with Templeton' gives the complementary case: Booth's speakeasy reunion with his dead wife Laura shows the imagination feigning the uninterrupted existence of a person whose constancy and vivacity no longer match his memories, so the senses and memory are exposed as no foundation for rational belief in continued existence.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 13 "3. The M. Night Sh-imulation Hypothesis" — The chapter runs Bostrom's simulation argument against 'M. Night Shaym-Aliens!', where the Zigerions trap Rick in simulations-within-simulations to steal his concentrated dark matter formula, and reads their cheap shortcuts ('My man!' NPCs, human music, Jerry's Appley award) as the glitches and shadow-people Bostrom predicts. It presses the epistemological problem that any evidence for the simulation equally supports its denial, an underdetermination that devastates the theory, and traces the lineage of 'the real world isn't real' through Plato's summoners and allegory of the cave, Descartes's dream doubt, and Paley's design analogy (Morty as the beautiful machine), ending with the microverse battery of 'The Ricks Must Be Crazy': this is the universe we live in, so get used to it.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 20 "9. The Fallacy of the Many Heads" — The chapter uses Headism in 'Get Schwifty' as a case study in illusory correlation: Principal Vagina walks out to pray just as the Cromulons approve of Rick and Morty's song, so the town builds a false cause-and-effect religion from coincidence, compounding false positives until Beth and Jerry are nearly sacrificed to the Giant Heads. Drawing on Daniel Kahneman's System 1/System 2 model and Peter Wason's confirmation-bias studies, it argues the characters reason rationally on the information available but never check whether their information is sufficient, the same lazy thinking that sustains religious faith, ghost photos, and the Loch Ness Monster. The cure is effortful skepticism, stopping to ask whether we might be wrong, lest we end up shooting Mr. Poopybutthole.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 22 "11. Are You Imagining That Poopybutthole" — Reading 'Total Rickall' as an evil-genius scenario, the chapter treats the memory parasites (Uncle Steve, Sleepy Gary, Reverse Giraffe) as Descartes's deceiving demon lodged in the Smiths' reconstructive memories, with Rick's written headcount an empirical defense that methodical doubt undermines. Morty's formula that parasites implant only good memories is shown to be merely inductive rather than certain like the cogito, so Beth's shooting of Mr. Poopybutthole becomes the test case: applying Aquinas's three kinds of ignorance, the chapter argues she remains morally responsible despite genuine remorse because she neglected the chance to reconsider Morty's probabilistic rule. The upshot is Descartes's advice to restrain the will beyond what the intellect certifies: shoot for the arm, not the head.
- **Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney**, ch. 15 "6. The Facts Don’t Speak for Themselves" — Muyskens asks why Burger and Tragg's evidence keeps pointing at innocent people, answering with Hume's distinction between relations of ideas and matters of fact and the problem of induction: inferences from past experience are never guaranteed. In 'The Case of the Shapely Shadow' the prosecution's seven pieces of testimony against Janice Wainwright are reasonable but false, and only Mason, because he believes his client, presses to the water-records discovery that exposes Cole Troy; 'The Case of the Runaway Corpse' then shows Burger and Tragg settling on Myrna Davenport on flimsy, self-contradictory evidence and simply failing to investigate, while Mason withholds judgment, checks her account against documents and witnesses, and digs until justified true belief is achieved.
- **Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney**, ch. 16 "7. Beyond a Reasonable Doubt" — Jordan argues Mason's real superpower is logic rather than client selection or legal brilliance: since conviction requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt before a unanimous jury, and since by the problem of induction (traced from Sextus Empiricus's regression arguments through Hume) no accumulation of probabilities yields deductive certainty, the prosecution can never conclusively prove guilt while Mason need only exploit that structural gap, as in The Case of the Howling Dog's cab-driver and document evidence and the TV movie Perry Mason Returns where Della is the accused. He illustrates with modus ponens examples about Della and Hamilton Burger, contrasting sound deductive arguments with merely strong inductive ones like predicting Mason's next win.
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 26 "15. The Rashomon Effect in KISS’s Autobiographies" — Michael Forest and Matthew Mitchell read the four original members' autobiographies as a Rashomon effect, focused on the conflicting accounts of recording Destroyer and of who really wrote 'Beth.' Bernard Lonergan's 'scotosis' — the intellectual blind spot that censors evidence against our preferred view — explains how each memoirist constructs memories protecting his self-image, while Sartre's bad faith from Being and Nothingness (distinguished from lying via the woman-on-a-date example) explains how they may have deceived themselves rather than lied. Comparing Gene's, Ace's, Peter's, Paul's, and Lydia Criss's five accounts, the chapter concludes that no one is a reliable narrator and no one a sheer fabricator — and that fans reading the memoirs must guard against their own blind spots and bad faith.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 19 "Perceptions Are Fine, but Dull Reality Is Still Better" — Distinguishes perceiver, perceptions, and perceived external objects to ask whether Alice, or anyone, can get beyond her perceptions to a mind-independent world, entering through Robert Arp's own painkiller hallucination of stones that were really Jell-O. The chapter sets epistemological idealism and metaphysical antirealism (the movie-theater-in-the-mind picture, traced to Plato's cave and Berkeley's suggestion that we are trapped inside perceptual reality) against the epistemological and metaphysical realism it finds in Alice and Carroll: fossilized ferns, dodo birds, and the Pythagorean theorem are discovered rather than invented, and at story's end everything rightly changes 'to dull reality'.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 20 "The Real Is Fake and the Fake Is Real" — Takes Morpheus's red-pill speech at face value to ask whether Alice is a drug story, then argues the deeper point: the distinction between normal and distorted experience is exaggerated or specious because all perception is conditioned by expectation, mood, and chemistry, whether on caffeine or psilocybin. Scott F. Parker reads the Red King's dream alongside Plato's Theaetetus dream argument and Zhuangzi's butterfly dream to show we can never prove we are awake, then weighs William James's nitrous-oxide revelations and Aldous Huxley's mescaline 'Mind at Large' as reasons altered states might sometimes show reality more truly, concluding that the real is fake, the fake is real, and Wonderland's syndrome is now a recognized medical condition.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 13 "No Reason to Get Excited" — The chapter turns the Final Five reveal (Tigh, Tyrol, Anders, Foster) and Boomer's sleeper activation into a skeptical problem about self-knowledge: Descartes's dreaming doubt (Roslin's Opera House dream) and the cogito show we can know that we exist but not what we are, and Baltar's rigged 'bright green' Cylon test destroys testimonial assurance. G.E. Moore's common-sense realism fails to engage the skeptic's special standards, and contextualism and Dretske's relevant-alternatives theory cannot help because in a world of sleeper Cylons the possibility 'I might be one' is always relevant. The answer is Hume's: like Tigh declaring 'I am an officer in the Colonial Fleet' and Anders repeating 'I am Samuel T. Anders' before his first combat mission, we banish skeptical paralysis by carrying on with life, dining and playing backgammon.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 46 "Heaven is a Place on Earth" — The chapter argues Black Mirror's perception tech works because the brain constructs experience top-down (predictive coding), so implants like Playtest's mushroom, Arkangel's filter, and Men Against Fire's MASS can inject perceptions and suppress error signals - and Cooper's total VR illusion defeats every one of Descartes's strategies (memory continuity, cross-checking the senses, reason) for telling dream from reality, killing him seconds after implantation. Nozick's experience machine illuminates Danny's preference for Striking Vipers X over his marriage and Arkangel's lesson that filtering Sara's childhood perceptions left her unable to read danger or emotion. Foucault's panopticon (via Bentham) frames White Christmas's cookie interrogation modeled on real police deception (Frazier v. Cupp), the MASS implant's manufacture of 'roach' targets for killing, and Nosedive's self-imposed social ratings as modern perceptual discipline - with only trusted others (Catarina, Susan, Kelly) punching through the manipulation.
- **Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality**, ch. 27 "Black sabbath & philosophy" — Kevin McCain turns Ozzy's "Am I Going Insane?" into a lived version of Descartes' skeptical scenarios, the madman who cannot trust his senses, the dream argument, the deceiving demon, and asks whether Ozzy can know anything at all. Using inference to the best explanation, he argues the commonsense external-world view beats skeptical scenarios because it predicts experiences (drop the book on your toe) and raises fewer unanswerable questions, so Ozzy keeps knowledge in the no-answer and "no" cases, but if he has reason to think he is insane and everyone tells him "yes", his reasons are defeated and he cannot even know their answers, leaving him, like the rest of us, one testimonial crisis from the void.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 28 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Pigliucci reads the 'Evolution, Schmevolution' series (Helms's Dayton, Tennessee reenactment-town piece, Stewart's panel with ID proponent Dembski and the scrotum question) as one of the best media treatments of the creation-evolution controversy. Popper's falsificationism marks intelligent design as non-science, since Dembski's designer works outside testable law and miracles are, as Larson says, unrepeatable and unfalsifiable, while Stewart's bad-design jokes about the scrotum and Mayr's 99.99% extinction figure replay the problem of evil. A compressed tour of rationalism (Plato to Descartes's radical doubt) versus Hume's empiricism explains why science yields tentative conclusions, and the chapter ends that resolving the controversy, like Aristotle's eudaimonia, is a lifelong personal project.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 20 "Happily Ever After" — Runs Descartes' dreaming argument and evil-genius doubt on Aurora, for whom the scenario is literal: Maleficent is an actually existing deceiver who could have enchanted her whole life in a dungeon. G. E. Moore's common-sense proof — 'here is a hand,' dubbed the Pinocchio test after the real boy — and the Moorean shift answer the skeptic, illustrated by Maleficent deploying Zeno's paradox to stop Prince Phillip's sword, where Phillip rightly clings to the more certain premise that motion is possible. Nozick's experience machine explains why Aurora should care: we want to actually be good and live real lives rather than merely experience them, so authentic 'happily ever after' requires knowing our experiences are backed by reality.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 8 "Out of the Orb" — Boudreaux maps Strange's comic-book journey into the Orb of Agamotto (dragged in by the Silver Dagger, greeted by a hookah-smoking caterpillar, tempted by counterfeit heroes like the Silver Surfer and Hulk) onto Descartes's Meditations. Empiricism (Locke's tabula rasa, Hume's sense-data) collapses when the senses are so thoroughly deceived inside the Orb, and innate ideas plus the Law of Non-Contradiction are not enough, so Strange reasons his way to the cogito — 'Nothing merits belief here — except oneself!' — just as Descartes doubts the evil demon. The caterpillar is revealed as Agamotto, playing the role of Descartes's non-deceiving God whose guidance lets Strange escape, and Strange's astral projections are offered as dramatic proof of mind-body dualism.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 23 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Abraham Schwab turns Ygritte's 'You know nothing, Jon Snow' into a theory of epistemic humility: Jon misreads wildling courtship norms, Sam's dragonglass shatters on wight Small Paul, Lord Mormont assumes Mance fights like a southern king and pays for it at the Fist of First Men, while Arya's accurate self-knowledge keeps her alive. Formalizing with justified true belief - Sam's lucky dagger thrust is not knowledge, and the Watch's warranted belief that the dead Othor was harmless justifies falsity - he uses Lysa's letter, which sent Ned to King's Landing on a lie, to ask what justification is: Descartes's absolute certainty is too strict, reliabilism vindicates testimony ('dark wings, dark words'), so that only Sansa need witness Ned's beheading for the Starks to know it, and between Melisandre's circular dogma about Azor Ahai and total skepticism, moderate skepticism best governs belief - a humility the south lacked about the Horn of Winter.
- **The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire**, ch. 19 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" — Philosopher Sven Ove Hansson's memoir shows the trilogy's realism came from Larsson's decades of unpaid extremism-watching: patiently archiving Nazi and racist networks, exposing the Sweden Democrats as Per Engdahl's 1979 repackaging of fascism in anti-immigrant dress (the same strategy as Britain's National Front), and forcing Skeptics' scrutiny onto the publisher of David Irving's Holocaust-denying Göring biography. It presents Larsson's anti-pseudoscience skepticism—astrology, faith healing, pyramidology, racist biology—his rejection of the postmodern idea that knowledge is mere social construction ('The Holocaust was not a social construction'), and his philosophically interesting argument that astrology's deterministic worldview is a stifling, self-fulfilling spiritual posture. The honor-killing analysis pairing Fadime Sahindal with Melissa Nordell demonstrates his method of using philosophical case-comparison to expose moral prejudice in taken-for-granted categories—habits of mind that resurface in the novels' hidden power structures and rationalist heroine.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 109 "NOTES" — Surveys near-death-experience research from Moody's Life after Life to Susan Blackmore's debunking explanations (oxygen starvation, cultural variation) and argues the skeptical conclusion does not follow: a child's vision of her living dog Sparky on the other side could still be a genuine divinely created revelation happening wholly inside her head. It reads Harry's King's Cross way-station the same way, since wizards can channel themselves through portraits, ghosts, and Legilimency, and closes with Emerson's Over-Soul claim that moments of faith deserve to be ascribed more reality than ordinary experience.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 7 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — The editors' introduction frames the trilogy as Katniss's quest to peel away Panem's layers of lies, likening her self-examination and self-control to the Delphic 'Know Thyself' and 'Nothing in Excess' and calling her skeptical spirit the engine of her wisdom. It poses the book's driving questions: why we enjoy watching others suffer, whether ordinary morality survives the arena, and how easily our own reality-TV-shaped world could slide into Panem's, noting that Collins modeled the Games on the Roman Colosseum. It presents dystopian exaggeration (children slaughtered for entertainment, tyrants, starving workers) as a cautionary mirror of trends already present in our society, and casts the contributors' chapters as a therapeutic game of 'Real or Not Real' played with the reader.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 5 "Who’s Putting Ideas in Your Head" — The book's introduction frames Inception as the newest chapter in the dream-skepticism tradition: Plato's question about how we explain our perceptions of reality and Descartes's point that we can never be sure we are not dreaming, with the twist that Descartes never doubted our thoughts are our own while the film contests exactly that. It previews the volume's rival readings — the single-dream theory of the airline flight, Brophy's claim that the shared dreams are server-based electronic worlds like Second Life, and neuroscience suggesting we act on thoughts before we are aware of them. It also stakes out the ethics: inception as a violation of autonomy akin to propaganda, advertising or brainwashing, and the diagnosis that Inception is fundamentally a tale from the business world of corporations.
