- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 7 "Happy Ending" — Wenmackers uses the spinning-top ending — Cobb reuniting with his children while the top wobbles off-screen — to run a guided tour of skeptical philosophy through the film's dream mechanics (totems, kicks, Limbo, exponential dream-time). She diagrams and compares Zhuangzi's butterfly, Plato's Cave and theory of Forms, Socratic know-that-you-know-nothing, Descartes's cogito and evil demon, Putnam's brain-in-a-vat, and Nozick's experience machine, arguing that Inception does to its viewers what Plato's Cave was meant to do: make us doubt our own level of reality, so that Nolan himself performs inception on the audience. Her resolution is subjectivist — from inside, every level feels equally real, so like Cobb you should turn away from the top and make the best of wherever you are, which even rescues the happy ending since dream-time runs faster than real time.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 10 "The Power of Choice" — Rennett stages Ariadne's 'who would want to be stuck in a dream for ten years?' against Nozick's experience machine: Nozick's three reasons for staying unplugged (doing rather than merely experiencing, being a determinate person, contact with a reality deeper than human construction) map onto Cobb's reasons for leaving Limbo — he wants to actually raise his children, be a good father, and love children who can love him back rather than projections. Against Nozick, the chapter enlists Berkeley's esse est percipi to explain Mal's choice: a perceived world is real, and Inception's shared dreams pass Berkeley's intersubjective test in ways private dreams cannot (Cobb apologizes to Arthur for being shot; dream acts carry waking consequences). It concludes that reality becomes what we choose to believe — Cobb's final refusal to watch the top, like the cave prisoners rejecting release, is the power of choice.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 22 "The Kick—Back to ‘Reality’" — Richardson and McWilliams read Inception as an 'existential heist film' by diving through four layers of meaning. At the layer of reality they use Descartes's dream skepticism and wax argument, Hume on belief as custom and cause-effect, and Goffman on being shocked between frames to argue the film makes touch — the fall that wakes, pain ('pain is in the mind'), Saito's wrong-textured polyester carpet, the broken totems (Cobb's top, Arthur's loaded die, Ariadne's holed chess piece) — the only semi-trustworthy sense, while Mal, who locks her totem in the dollhouse safe and picks the dream, replays the cave prisoner who chooses the shadows. The car-chase layer ('downwards is the only way forwards'), Saito's 'old man filled with regrets' limbo, and the pharmacy dreamers who 'come to be woken up' are read through existentialism (Beckett's Waiting for Godot, Jaspers on loneliness and nothingness) and Peirce on the continuity of consciousness, with Cobb cast as the ideological existentialist who chooses action and reality where Cypher in The Matrix and Vanilla Sky's David face the same choice. The chapter then treats the film's reflexivity — the team as screenwriter/producer/director, the Escher-esque Penrose stairs, cross-cut dream time à la Peckinpah — as a lesson in film theory, and finally reaches phenomenology: Cobb's angry projection of Mal shows the dream world displaying his subjective meanings, against Arthur's calm, orderly hotel mindscape.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 23 "12 The Shadow Realities of Indiana Jones" — Matthew Crippen and Matthew Dixon read the franchise's caves through Plato's allegory: in Crusade, stand-ins for God (the Cross of Coronado, the Grail, with the decoy chalices as shadows of a representation) appear underground, while Indy's self-realizations with his father occur at sunlit cave mouths, inching from shadow toward the Good. They fuse this with newer, active accounts of truth — James's 'truth happens to an idea' realized in the leap from the lion's head, Dewey on poetry as revelation, and Heidegger's aletheia as unconcealment — while Nietzsche's critique shows Platonic fictions can still be life-enhancing. The father and son 'shadow' one another (with Oedipal overtones through Elsa) until Henry Sr. relinquishes the Grail to save 'Indiana,' his path out of the cave.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 18 "Over Four Thousand Words to Say No" — Spanakos asks whether Stark's assembling, disassembling, and reassembling of the Avengers and his unseen-hand management of Civil War make him the Republic's philosopher guardian, and answers no. Tony fits the surface profile — the gold-souled ruler of Socrates' noble lie, the elite training, indifference to money, the technê of an MIT engineer who envisions the future — but he lacks epistêmê: he never climbs from the cave's shadows to grasp the forms of justice and the good, and his appetites (womanizing in The Ultimates, 'Demon in a Bottle') show a soul where passion is not ruled by reason. His puppet mastery is reactive problem-solving guided by each situation, not philosophy, and reading him as a philosopher king is our failure to read The Republic meditatively, as Ortega y Gasset urged.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 31 "Live From New York" — Perez sorts SNL's realities using Plato's cave and Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation: Kate McKinnon's Bieber Calvin Klein ad is a first-phase reflection, Natalie Portman's raps a masking second phase, Ferrell's commodified Bush a second-order copy, and Maya Rudolph's Donatella Versace a third-phase simulacrum with no reality behind it that Versace herself protested. The Church Lady's 2016 Update appearance and the Palin-meets-Palin and Hillary-at-the-bar sketches show characters substituting for the real, while the May 2018 cold open where the real Stormy Daniels tells Baldwin's Trump 'a storm's a-comin',' live-tweeted by @nbcsnl, achieves Baudrillard's hyperreality where fiction and reality are abolished as distinct. Studio 8H becomes a Plato's cave viewers willingly re-enter each Saturday to glimpse the real through simulation.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 37 "Notes" — Uses the holodeck as a working model for the ancient claim that everyday reality is appearance: Plato's cave shadows, maya in Hindu and Buddhist thought, and Bostrom's simulation argument (his ancestor simulations mirrored in Data and Geordi's endless Holmes holoprograms) converge with quantum "holographic universe" speculation to suggest our universe may be a cosmic holoprogram with limit conditions like light speed as processing boundaries. Moriarty seizing the Enterprise in "Ship in a Bottle", Vic Fontaine, and the EMH dramatize self-aware programs confronting their code, and the chapter argues our "free will" may be similarly bounded - Data-as-Holmes must stay in character, and Picard "can't transcend the script" any more than his NPCs can. Picard's closing admission that our reality may be "an elaborate simulation running inside a little device" delivers the skeptical upshot, alongside the ethical question of whether self-aware holograms deserve rights.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 35 "22. Unmasking the World and Its Heroes" — Claims the Superman-vs-Batman debate misses the point: both heroes are cave-escapers who must first see beyond appearances—Bruce renouncing vengeance on Joe Chill and then shaking Gotham from apathy (the ferries refusing the Joker's detonators), Clark learning from Jonathan and Jor-El that his powers are not for touchdowns but to lead humanity out by example. Masks serve the Socratic warning of the Apology that the just man must act privately to survive—Jonathan Kent dies keeping Clark's secret—yet risk becoming their own trap, from Smallville's Red Kryptonite ring to Batman's sonar surveillance that Lucius Fox calls too much power for one person. The chapter closes on Socratic ignorance and Man of Steel's genesis chambers: a hero, like Socrates, knows his wisdom is worth nothing, and anyone who chooses can be one.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Johnson-Moxley tests Perez's lasso of truth - which makes people face truths about themselves, like being dragged from Plato's cave - against four ethical touchstones: Kantian duty (truth-telling as a perfect duty, respect for autonomy), utilitarianism, virtue ethics, and care ethics. Cases drive the argument: binding Ares so he sees his apocalypse annihilates what he rules, freeing Vanessa from Dr. Psycho's false memories only with her permission, and lashing two warlords into 'twins of pain' to end bloodshed. She concludes via Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity that compelling truth is justified only to restore someone's rational self-direction, never paternalistically, with Gandhi's satyagraha ('truth-force') as the model of active, compassionate truth-telling.
- **X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse**, ch. 7 "X-Men and Philosophy" — This block finishes Davis's essay (Xavier's 'good nonsense' rules vs. Magneto/Dennett/Hobbes evolutionary morality) then runs several more. Robichaud's 'Professor X Wants You' weighs whether Storm should join the X-Men or Brotherhood using Nozick's experience machine (Rogue vs. 'Eugor') for well-being and Dworkin's civil-disobedience tiers for when violent resistance is permissible. Housel's 'X-Women' reads Jean Grey, Rachel Summers, Scarlet Witch, Storm, Mystique, Rogue, and Kitty through Sartre's 'existence precedes essence,' bad faith, Ortega's project, and Baudrillard. McWilliams uses Singer's speciesism and human-rights declarations to ask if mutants deserve moral consideration and whether torture/experimentation on them can be justified. Darowski reads Deadpool's fourth-wall breaks as postmodern metafiction raising Plato's-cave ontological questions.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 24 "Hoop Dreams, Blacktop Realities" — Bernard Jackson Jr. argues that basketball is an institution where black manhood is socially constructed (leaning on Naomi Zack's feminist point that gender identity is imposed by social designation), and that love among black players is essential to that construction while toughness is equivocal - the 'soft' label stuck to the gentlemanly David Robinson even as the Pistons walked off without congratulating the Bulls. Reading the documentary Hoop Dreams, he shows Arthur Agee and William Gates being used as commodities by recruiters, Coach Pingatore, and family expectations, invoking Marx on exploitation and 'use value' (Spike Lee's Nike-camp speech) and Kant's demand that persons be treated as ends, never merely as means. He likens William Gates's return to Chicago's Cabrini-Green as a minister to Plato's enlightened prisoner going back down into the cave.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy and Non-Philosophy of Potato Salad" — Scribner uses Ginsberg's 'Howl for Carl Solomon'—and Solomon's throwing potato salad at a Dada lecture—to ask whether the Beats' performative acts count as philosophy at all. He argues philosophy is constituted by self-contestation, its relation to a 'non-philosophy' of madness and raw experience, reading Solomon's silence and Ginsberg's poetic mediation through Foucault's 'Madness and Civilization' and Derrida's rebuttal in 'Cogito and the History of Madness.' Ginsberg-to-Solomon is made analogous to philosophy-to-the-Beats: a betraying translator who nonetheless must give the mute event voice, grounded in Plato's failure to banish the poets from the Republic.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 8 "Raising Arizona as an American Comedy" — Gilmore reads Raising Arizona as a classical comedy (bad-beginning-to-good-ending) about the American 'optative mood' of self-creation, using Hi McDunnough's outlaw-to-family arc and his name-as-height-metaphor to figure Emerson's aspirational American self. He deploys Plato's two kinds of cave-laughter to distinguish the film's 'tender,' welcoming comedy (Hi and Ed, Gale and Evelle) from mocking ridicule, and frames Hi's need to abandon outlaw identity via Heidegger's Augenblick and Badiou's 'event' sparked in Ed's mug-shot flash. Nietzsche on dreams-as-origin-of-metaphysics grounds the film's dream/reality tension, and Hi's over-identification with the outlaw universal is glossed as Sartrean bad faith.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 21 "From “Impassioned Morality” to “Bloodless Agnosticism” A Philosophy of David Cronenberg through the Burroughs" — Jones Irwin analyzes Cronenberg's adaptations of Burroughs's Naked Lunch and Ballard's Crash, arguing that while all three share an aesthetic of body horror and a Nietzschean perspectivist experimentalism, Burroughs and Ballard hold an 'impassioned moralism' (Crash as cautionary tale, Marcuse's one-dimensional man, an ethics of complicity and responsibility) that Cronenberg replaces with 'bloodless agnosticism.' Cronenberg aestheticizes Burroughs's wife-killing and reads Crash literally, using Plato's appearance/reality (cave) distinction to show he strips out the sociopolitical and moral frame the writers intended.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 18 "7. The Art of Playing Along with Dancing Little People" — Luzecky and Elsby argue that Twin Peaks is genuine art because, against Plato's condemnation of mimetic art as confusing copies to be exiled, it fulfills Aristotle's Poetics: art's essential function is dramatic reversal, surprising and transfixing us (Dougie's absurd casino win, the dancing Man from Another Place). Drawing on Gadamer's 'Spiel' (play/game) and Ingarden's schematized, incomplete artworks, they contend the work of art exists only as an ongoing rhythmic 'to and fro' between image and viewer—so we complete the Red Room scene by participating in it, moving it from potentiality to actuality.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 22 "The Matrix, the Cave, and the Cogito" — Conard argues that The Matrix alludes to Plato's cave (the pod-bound humans mistaking the program for reality, Neo's painful ascent) and to Descartes' dream argument and evil-genius doubt (the singular consciousness generating the Matrix), but betrays their spirit by rejecting transcendence and the a priori. Because the film is 'Christianity without God'—Neo can only remake the shadow-world of the Matrix, not touch ultimate reality—it grounds knowledge in a subjective gut feeling ('being the One is just like being in love') rather than Descartes' intellectual intuition of God or Plato's rational grasp of the Forms, leaving no answer to whether life outside the Matrix is itself another illusion.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 28 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — McFarland reads Soderbergh's Solaris as a meditation on recollection, recognition, and repetition, grounding it in Platonic recollection (the Phaedo, the cave, and the Symposium's love as desire) and Augustine's Confessions, where memory strains toward an elusive beloved-as-God, the 'cruel miracle' of present absence. When Solaris materializes Rheya, Chris Kelvin first jettisons the 'bad copy' but then, tempted by Snow, embraces Deleuze's endless degraded repetition of copies to erase his guilt over her suicide. Against this, Gibarian voices a Kierkegaardian call (Repetition, Either/Or) that there are 'only choices'; McFarland faults Chris, like Odysseus choosing Kalypso's island, for choosing the deathless eternal present over the human world of forward-moving choice.
- **The Philosophy of Tim Burton**, ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" — LaRocca argues Burton's 'Ed Wood' (1994) is a metafilm that, via Baudrillard's simulacra and Plato's cave/dialectic, transforms how we watch Wood's 'bad' films. He casts Wood as a cave-dweller and naive literalist who conflates representation with reality ('film equals life,' 'that was perfect'), while Burton is the Platonic dialectician who posits two worlds and provokes thought. He distinguishes two interacting metafilm types—biographical simulacrum (a hyperreal Ed Wood with no original, per Baudrillard's 'artificial resurrection') and mimetic reenactment (loyal remakes of Wood's films)—so that Martin Landau's Lugosi and Parker-as-Fuller's non-acting reveal the emotional 'affect without illusion' latent in Wood's work.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 21 "The Work of Art in the Age of Embedded Journalism Fiction versus Depiction in Zero Dark Thirty" — Evans argues that Kathryn Bigelow's Zero Dark Thirty fails morally and epistemically because its immersive 'boots-on-the-ground' realism traps the viewer inside Maya's single point of view, so we can never see the CIA torture program's lunacy the way an outside witness would. Drawing on Wittgenstein's Tractatus claim that the subject is a limit of the world (the eye that cannot see itself), she shows how the film effaces its own privileged viewpoint to pass off a partial view as impartial reality. Against this she sets a Platonic point that genuine reality is glimpsed only through fiction that ironically juxtaposes contrasting viewpoints, citing scenes like the SEALs' banter and Maya's final weeping where the film briefly becomes true art. The 'depiction is not endorsement' defense collapses because the narrative logic still credits torture with finding bin Laden.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 18 "16_LaRocca_Chapter_015.html" — Dan Geva re-reads Dziga Vertov's The Man with the Movie Camera as a coherent philosophy of documentary he calls 'praxis' or 'cine-seeing the invisible,' distilling ten 'diktats' (Unplayed Cinema, Life-Caught-Unawares, the interval theory of montage, etc.). He argues Vertov, like Plato, Marx, Nietzsche and Freud, privileges hidden depths over surface appearance, and reads the dialectical move from 'film fact' to 'film thing' as a Hegelian synthesis rather than a paradox. Crucially he aligns Vertov's Kino-Eye truth with Heidegger's notion of truth as aletheia (a partial unconcealment) rather than correspondence, tying the camera's revelation of the invisible to Heidegger's meditation on technology and seeing.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 22 "12. A Cave of His Own Making" — Golden reinterprets Plato's Allegory of the Cave to argue Chuck enslaves himself in a 'cave of his own making'—his hypochondriacal electromagnetic hypersensitivity—to keep Jimmy accountable and to exact vengeance for Jimmy's unpunished childhood thefts. Using Aristotle's De Anima psychology and the function argument, he places Chuck's imagination (phantasia) below reason: Chuck retains the rationality to serve clients like Mesa Verde and to detect Jimmy's document fraud, but sinks below the Golden Mean into the vices of meanness (short of kindness) and cowardice (short of courage) toward his brother. He adds Kierkegaard's Repetition: Chuck is stuck in backward-looking 'recollection' of vengeance and cannot make the forward, committed 'repetition' of simply being Jimmy's brother.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 9 "2. Socrates’s City and Seldon’s Galaxy" — Goldberg maps Plato's Republic onto Asimov's Foundation Trilogy: Socrates's three-class city (Guardians, Auxiliaries, Producers ruling by knowledge of the Forms) parallels Seldon's galaxy (Second Foundationers, First Foundationers, and everyone else, ruling by the abstract mathematics of psychohistory), with the tyrannical Thrasymachus paralleling the Mule. He shows the Prime Radiant functions as Plato's Allegory of the Cave, and that both Guardians and Second Foundationers govern through 'noble lies' (the metals myth; the Encyclopedia sham and the Second Foundation's fake destruction), then questions whether those lies are truly noble given doubts about objective truth.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 9 "1. A Man for All Seasonings" — Shaffer uses Brillat-Savarin's distinction between direct and reflective taste and Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' to argue gastronomic expertise is only the acquired ability to describe tastes richly, not a superior sense. He then casts Bourdain as a culinary Socrates who, like the freed prisoner in Plato's allegory of the cave, returns to lead provincial eaters out of the darkness of narrow experience toward cultural tolerance.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 14 "Stephen King and the Art of Horror" — Littmann stages a mock trial of King's horror using classical aesthetics: Plato prosecutes, condemning fiction as lies that misrepresent gods, afterlife, and paternal authority (Carrie's mother, Jack Torrance, the Loser's Club disobeying elders) and corrupt morals through spectacle. Aristotle counters that Poetics-style poetry is 'more philosophical than history' and that tragedy's catharsis purges pity and fear, which King echoes in Danse Macabre's claim that horror lances real terrors via Danny Torrance, Paul Sheldon, and Louis Creed. Hume's 'Of Tragedy' explains why we enjoy fictional suffering (Pennywise, Annie Wilkes) we would hate in life; Littmann finally revises Hume, arguing horror's pleasure is the spur to imagination rather than mere appreciation of artistic skill.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 27 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Baron, a new father, weighs whether to let his son Maxwell consume violent popular media (from Halloween to SpongeBob, Grand Theft Auto, and Schindler's List) by testing three hypotheses. He uses Plato's Republic warning against exposing the young to stories they can't interpret for the 'causal hypothesis'; Aristotle's Poetics on learning pleasure from painful images for the 'edification hypothesis'; and Aristotle's account of tragic catharsis (homeopathic vs allopathic purging) for the 'catharsis hypothesis,' concluding that context matters more than ratings and that fathers watching alongside their children are the decisive influence.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 8 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Porn journalist Gram Ponante's foreword riffs on Plato's Allegory of the Cave, casting porn as the shadows on the cave wall and the viewer as both prisoner and fire. He argues that unlike the manipulated prisoners, the porn viewer actively projects meaning onto a deliberately thin surface — forgiving porn its fake 'MILF' and 'schoolgirl' labels because the images 'become what we want them to be.' Porn is 'a cave to be filled in,' and adding plot or realism only breaks the fantasy by making the images less available for projection.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 31 "GARDENING" — Cotton reads the grower image in Plato's Phaedrus—the wise gardener who sows seed in proper soil for a slow harvest rather than the frivolous 'gardens of Adonis'—as Plato's model of philosophical education as natural growth. The educator plants logoi (discourse) in a 'proper soul,' where it must be cultivated by the learner's own reflection and eventually reproduces itself in others, against Thrasymachus's vessel model of pouring knowledge in. She connects this to the Republic's cave, the Apology's gadfly, and the Symposium/Theaetetus images of pregnancy and midwifery, then argues Plato's own aporetic, contradiction-laden dialogues and the corpus as a whole act as the wise grower, teaching readers to become 'gardeners of their own souls.'
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 25 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Thorsby reads 'getting high' as a rupture of ordinary, unreflective consciousness and asks why cannabis use grows fastest in the affluent capitalist West. He pairs Plato's allegory of the cave—ordinary consciousness as prisoners mistaking shadows for reality—with Marx's account of alienation and commodity fetishism, in which workers are estranged from the products of their labor and see value as inhering in things rather than in human labor. Drawing on Fromm's 'having vs. being,' he argues that cannabis offers a momentary escape from and critique of this alienated consciousness, though it cannot cure it.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 18 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Ken Burak describes teaching yoga in his philosophy class — a 'three wheels' exercise moving from the true self behind our masks to the Upanishadic identity of Atman and Brahman ('Thou Art That') — to give students embodied access to the universal/particular problem. He reads Western philosophy from Plato's Phaedo (Socrates seeking death as liberation of soul from body) through Descartes' doubt as a 2500-year practice of pratyahara (sense-withdrawal), one limb mistaken for the whole journey, and asks what asana and this long retreat could each bring the other.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 30 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — J. Lenore Wright reads the Quest through the Western journey-narrative, both outward (Plato's climb out of the cave, Augustine's conversion) and inward (Descartes's methodological doubt turning toward the cogito). Frodo's leaving the Shire and freely accepting the Ring dramatizes the outward journey and the limits of freedom, while the wounding-and-healing of Sam, Merry, and Pippin marks an existential journey toward the Nietzschean charge to 'become who you are.' Wright contrasts the Yea-saying hobbits, transformed into resilient masters, with Nay-sayers Smeagol and Saruman locked in inauthentic self-pity, and argues Tolkien's ordinary pilgrims show that binding oneself to the good makes ordinary life extraordinary.
- **Comics as Philosophy**, ch. 6 "index" — This composite chapter argues philosophy through several comics. Jeremy Barris pairs Plato's dialogues with Amazing Spider-Man, using the allegory of the cave, the Forms, and Platonic love/eros to show that Spider-Man's bodily beauty, awkwardness, and self-trivializing irony draw readers toward goodness the way Plato says lust for beautiful bodies leads the soul upward to truth. Iain Thomson reads Moore and Gibbons's Watchmen as a 'deconstruction of the hero,' running Rorschach, Ozymandias and Dr. Manhattan through Nietzsche's Ubermensch and 'do not throw away the hero in your soul,' Heidegger's authentic 'choosing one's hero' and the uncanny, Kierkegaard's knight of faith, and Baudrillard's idea that an extreme realization destroys its own idea. Laura and Paul Canis read Daniel Clowes's Ghost World through Sartre's existentialism: Enid's post-high-school 'three o'clock' limbo enacts thrownness, abandonment, radical freedom and the flight from it into bad faith, contrasting Enid's authentic self-creation with Rebecca's settled conformity. Aldo Regalado's essay treats Tarzan, Superman, Captain America and the Black Panther as responses to modernity and race.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 6 "NOTES" — William Irwin's introduction argues philosophy must engage popular culture rather than fear it as Plato feared Homer and the poets. He invokes Plato's allegory of the cave to make the case that the philosopher who has left the cave must return and 'learn to see the shadows again'—use The Simpsons, The Matrix and Seinfeld as the vernacular through which prisoners can be led out—and answers Adorno-style culture-industry worries that mass entertainment is mere opiate. He closes by echoing Aristotle's serious treatment of the popular art (tragedy) of his day as warrant for treating today's pop culture philosophically.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 9 "NOTES" — Irwin asks 'what is popular culture?', rejecting Noel Carroll's 'mass art' accessibility criterion (using the Sex Pistols, Slipknot and the Beatles as counterexamples of inaccessible-yet-popular art) and Walter Benjamin's aura/mechanical-reproduction account, settling on popular culture as 'artifacts and subjects of mass interest and appreciation.' He rebuts Adorno's and Zizek's culture-industry charge that pop culture (e.g. The Matrix, The X-Files) ideologically ensnares audiences, and again deploys Plato's cave and the returning prisoner—citing Socrates meeting interlocutors where they are—to justify using pop culture as a bridge to philosophy while warning against 'abuse' (studying pop culture as philosophy).
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 4 "2. Twilight Zone as Philosophy 101" — Marinucci uses The Twilight Zone as a triple introduction to philosophy, the show, and the handbook, arguing that philosophy is defined not by necessary-and-sufficient conditions but by Wittgensteinian family resemblance and salient features (curiosity, depth, abstraction, controversy) learned through MacIntyre-style immersion in a practice. She reads episodes as thought experiments: the amnesiac astronaut in 'Where Is Everybody?' and living-doll/robot episodes echo Plato's cave and Descartes's Method of Doubt about appearance versus reality, Nagel's 'what is it like to be a bat?' frames the problem of other minds, and episodes like 'The Shelter' and 'It's a Good Life' dramatize the tension between egoism and altruism and social conformity, including feminist gaslighting in 'Twenty Two.'
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 44 "41. Blade Runner as Philosophy What Does It Mean to Be Human" — Shanahan argues Blade Runner is philosophical despite Ridley Scott's denial, using the replicants (Roy Batty, Rachael, Leon) as defamiliarizing 'mirrors' for the human condition. He shows the Nexus-6 replicants satisfy Descartes' two criteria for a thinking soul (linguistic flexibility, novel problem-solving) while human characters like Deckard prove as cold and empathy-deficient as the machines, collapsing the human/replicant distinction the Voight-Kampff test presumes. He then reads Rachael's implanted memories through Locke's memory theory of personal identity, Roy's 'tears in rain' death through Epicurean worries about finitude, and frames the whole via Plato's Cave line 'they are like us' — the replicants model our own concerns with memory, death, and the meaning of a temporally bounded life.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 51 "48. The Matrix as Philosophy Understanding Knowledge, Belief, Choice, and Reality" — Perez reads the Matrix trilogy as a sustained argument about how choosing what to believe and 'know' shapes the reality we live in. He opens with Descartes' dream problem and cogito, contrasting Descartes' foundationalism with Rorty's anti-foundationalism to explain Cypher's choice to reject reality for the Matrix's certitude, and uses Searle's brute vs. institutional facts (the cookies, the steak, 'there is no spoon') to show social reality is constructed. Against the fatalism of the Oracle, Architect, and Merovingian, he argues nearly every character makes free choices, and resolves the tension via Hume's compatibilism — liberty requires necessity, and choices gain meaning only in response to causality — while noting agent-causation objections (Reid, O'Connor, Rowe) that make Neo's 'Because I choose to' significant. Gettier's justified-true-belief critique and Plato's Cave frame the knowledge and enlightenment themes.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 68 "64. George Carlin as Philosopher It’s All Bullshit. Is It Bad for Ya" — Engels reads Carlin's insistence that 'it's all bullshit, and it's bad for ya' as a defense of truth over comforting illusion, mapping his bits onto Plato's Allegory of the Cave (Carlin dragging audiences up from shadows like 'prostitution is immoral' or 'the American Dream' to expose deeper essences), Nozick's Experience Machine (Carlin's sun-worship chosen because it is real, not a pleasing fiction), and Clifford/Beauvoir on the ethics of belief and the 'serious world.' Bits on rights, the sanctity of life, homelessness/'houselessness,' and 'proud to be an American' show Carlin arguing that false beliefs breed complacency and harm, so there are moral reasons to prefer truth.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 83 "78. The Witness as Philosophy How Knowledge Is Constructed" — Cuddy asks what epistemology Blow built into The Witness's frustrating puzzles and its windmill videos (Burke, Feynman, Moriarty, Spira, Gangaji). He rejects the sophistic/Protagorean 'knowledge depends on the observer' reading (most puzzles have objective, inductive-and-deductive solutions, e.g. the yellow-glass bunker) and the strict scientific realism of the Burke video defended by Putnam's no-miracles argument. Using Plato's cave and the aporia of Socrates' Meno (the puzzle's 'ah-ha' epiphanies), and Kuhn's incommensurable paradigm shifts (the game's 'hard left turns' forcing players to overhaul their understanding), he concludes the game argues that true knowledge is attainable, individually and collectively, though reached by a nonlinear, paradigm-shifting route rather than pure realism or relativism.

### Brain in a Vat

The brain-in-a-vat scenario imagines that your brain has been removed and kept alive in a vat, fed electrical signals by a computer so that your entire experience of an external world is an elaborate illusion. It is a modern version of Descartes's skeptical doubt, raising the worry that you could never rule out such a predicament from the inside and so cannot be certain anything you perceive is real. Hilary Putnam gave the puzzle a notable twist, arguing on grounds of the theory of reference that the sentence "I am a brain in a vat" is self-refuting and cannot be true if uttered by an envatted brain.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 16 "Unknown" — The authors carry the skeptical scenario into the twentieth century: Peter Unger's evil scientist uses computer-driven electrodes to fabricate our belief in rocks and chairs, and Hilary Putnam's brain-in-a-vat story from Reason, Truth, and History deceives us about everything we seem to perceive, with the computer supplying feedback for our attempted actions. Noting how closely this matches the pod-bound humans of The Matrix, they pose Putnam's question - 'How do you know you aren't in this predicament?' - as a sword of Damocles hanging over everyday knowledge.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 25 "Unknown" — Korsmeyer reads the film through classic problems of perception: Descartes's dreaming argument (Neo's sweaty awakenings), the evil deceiver updated as the evil computer, and the pod scene as her 'scariest philosophical problem', the brain-in-a-vat thought experiment, with Berkeley's esse est percipi as the Matrix's governing premise. She also notes the film's structural constraint - like all dreaming plots from Calderon to The X-Files its viewpoint must stand outside the Matrix - and uses Mouse's Tasty Wheat puzzle to show how reference to a never-experienced world breaks down.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 23 "Does Rush Offer a Way Out" — Uses Rush's 1980s lyrics about facades and trust — 'Limelight''s strangers, 'Show Don't Tell''s refusal to take things on faith, 'War Paint''s lying mirror, and the synthesizer as an instrument that can fake any other sound — to stage skepticism about other minds, running from Descartes's cogito through solipsism and behaviorism. Wittgenstein's beetle-in-a-box and private-language argument dissolve the inner/outer confusion as a grammatical one, and 'Turn the Page' supplies the way out of the fly-bottle: nothing survives a vacuum, and with other people all we can do is be reminded.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 40 "The Evil Genius that Turns Moriarty into a Brain in a Vat" — Samardzija reads Star Trek's holodeck Moriarty as Descartes updated: Data plays Holmes on the holodeck while Dr. Pulaski's Nietzschean jibe (from 'The Illogical Necessary' in Human, All Too Human) denies that computation can be human, and the holographic Moriarty proves his sentience not by deduction but by feelingCrowded intuitions first and then invoking Descartes' cogito ergo sum to Picard. In 'Ship in a Bottle' he nests a simulation of the Enterprise inside the Holmes holodeck to trick the crew into believing he has escaped — an evil-genius, brain-in-a-vat scenario that ends with Picard admitting our own reality 'might be nothing more than an elaborate simulation.' The paradox is that only the unemotional android Data can detect the deception, so rationality bars him from humanity while Moriarty stays eternally deceived into thinking he has become human — and Doyle's own 'hereditary tendencies' account of Moriarty's evil, the chapter notes, is a Victorian biological determinism the hologram rebels against.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 7 "Happy Ending" — Wenmackers uses Inception's dream levels and its ambiguous spinning-top ending as a guided tour of skeptical philosophy, diagramming how dreams-within-dreams, kicks, Limbo and exponentially dilated dream time work. She tests the totem against Zhuangzi's butterfly and lucid-dreaming reality checks, then runs Plato's Cave and the eternal Forms, Descartes's cogito and evil demon, Putnam's brain-in-a-vat, and Nozick's experience machine to ask whether Cobb's world - or ours - is real. Her conclusion is Socratic ('know that you know nothing'): subjective reality feels equally real on every level and the top level can never be known. She even argues that dream-time dilation means Cobb should not kill himself while in doubt, since real time barely passes, so a little philosophy rescues the happy ending.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 20 "9. How the Doctor Knows" — Smithka argues the Doctor is a reliabilist about knowledge rather than a Cartesian strong foundationalist: using 'Amy's Choice,' 'The Beast Below' (the glass of water, the engine room, Amy's inference that the Star Whale came willingly), 'Silence in the Library' (the chicken-leg experiment implicating the Vashta Nerada), and Davros's Dalek trials in 'Genesis of the Daleks,' she shows him trusting perception in the right causal chain and reasoning inductively and abductively—Peirce's inference to the best explanation—instead of demanding Cartesian certainty. Against Descartes's dream and evil-genius skepticism, updated as Putnam-style brain-in-a-vat scenarios via the Dream Crabs of 'Last Christmas' and the Dream Lord's two-worlds game, she deploys Goldman's three criteria for perceptual knowledge: justification is packed into reliable belief-forming processes, and doubt is warranted only in known abnormal contexts like funhouses or Dream Lord games.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 22 "11. What the Soufflé Girl Could Teach Descartes" — Becker-Lindenthal uses 'Amy's Choice' to revise Descartes's dream skepticism: the Dream Lord is not an external evil demon but the Doctor's own repressed alter ego fed by psychic pollen, so the self-delusion Descartes dismissed becomes the real deceiver, read through Freud's Interpretation of Dreams (Rory's death as the Doctor's wish, Amy's choice as Thanatos). She then reads Oswin in 'Asylum of the Daleks' as a brain-in-a-vat variant (Putnam's Reason, Truth and History) with a crucial difference—Oswin hacks the Dalek program and follows her own agenda—so her self-deceptive soufflé-baking fantasy is a self-formation that preserves her 'I' inside Dalek hardware, complicating Ryle's rejection of the ghost in the machine. Finally, the Doctor judges Oswin by a Turing test plus Putnam's test of reference (the impossible milk and eggs), but her self-deception is vindicated when it lets her save the Doctor and the universe.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 7 "Happy Ending" — Wenmackers uses the spinning-top ending — Cobb reuniting with his children while the top wobbles off-screen — to run a guided tour of skeptical philosophy through the film's dream mechanics (totems, kicks, Limbo, exponential dream-time). She diagrams and compares Zhuangzi's butterfly, Plato's Cave and theory of Forms, Socratic know-that-you-know-nothing, Descartes's cogito and evil demon, Putnam's brain-in-a-vat, and Nozick's experience machine, arguing that Inception does to its viewers what Plato's Cave was meant to do: make us doubt our own level of reality, so that Nolan himself performs inception on the audience. Her resolution is subjectivist — from inside, every level feels equally real, so like Cobb you should turn away from the top and make the best of wherever you are, which even rescues the happy ending since dream-time runs faster than real time.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 12 "Inside the Helmet What Do Football Players Know" — Geivett uses football to illustrate epistemology, distinguishing factual (propositional) from competence (skill) knowledge through what running backs and quarterbacks must know and enact under split-second pressure, including 'football physics' vectors on a rollout pass. He treats the athlete's need to be mindful of knowledge amid stadium noise as a lesson in reliable belief, then critiques classroom skeptics who deploy Descartes's evil-demon and the brain-in-a-vat thought experiment, arguing mere logical possibility is no evidence for skepticism.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 12 "eXistenZial Angst" — Duncan Pritchard reads eXistenZ as staging radical skepticism with existential force: unlike the standard brain-in-a-vat scenario, the game 'creeps up' on Ted and Allegra so they feel the transition from reality to doubt, producing angst. Invoking Wittgenstein's On Certainty (doubt radicalized is madness), he argues sanity requires belief but not true belief, so the pair achieve a new doxastic equilibrium. He also reads the spinal 'bioport' pod as a case of Clark and Chalmers's extended cognition, where technology becomes part of and subverts the agents' cognitive processes.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 14 "Skepticism Outside the Matrix" — Lawrence uses The Matrix to raise Cartesian skepticism: Neo's deception dramatizes Descartes's dream argument and evil demon, the computer-run Matrix being a technological version of the demon. He argues even Morpheus cannot be certain he has truly awakened ('the Matrix within the Matrix'), so the only certainty is Descartes's cogito. Drawing on Russell's 'Appearance and Reality,' he then argues that even setting aside Matrix scenarios, naive realism fails, since a chair's color, texture, solidity and shape are all perception-relative, leaving the external world's nature deeply uncertain.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 27 "MOTHERHOOD" — Sara Goering uses the fantasy of a child 'off button' as a thought experiment, situating it alongside Plato's Ring of Gyges, the brain-in-a-vat, and personal-identity puzzles to argue that such control would be overused and would treat children as objects rather than developing subjects. She then turns reflexive, critiquing thought experiments themselves – including Rawls's veil of ignorance (via Okin and Benhabib) and Susan Brison's critique of personal-identity cases – for diverting from the messy real world, arguing that the off-button fantasy really signals the need for 'distributed mothering' and structural support; she illustrates with The Matrix, Multiplicity, Harry Potter, and Woolf's 'room of one's own.'
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 8 "Horror and the Idea of Everyday Life On Skeptical Threats in Psycho and The Birds" — Philip J. Nickel argues horror has an epistemological value structurally parallel to philosophical skepticism: it maliciously rips away the tacit 'cognitive trust' backing our everyday actions. In The Birds, the diner 'symposium' where Mrs. Bundy's confident science that birds cannot coordinate an attack is refuted moments later dramatizes a paranoid scenario we cannot rationally rule out. In Psycho, Marion Crane's isolation and misplaced trust in the seemingly normal Norman Bates enacts the skeptical premise that the ordinary person you rely on could murder you. Like Hume returning to backgammon, viewers can only resume everyday life, which Nickel says horror exposes as a necessary but insecure construction.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 8 "2. The Matrix" — Rowlands reads The Matrix as a vivid staging of Cartesian skepticism: Neo's pod-world is Descartes's dream and evil-demon conjectures (AI plays the demon) plus the modern brain-in-a-vat, showing we cannot be certain the external world exists. He uses the 'there is no air/muscles' and 'twin buildings' variant of Putnam's Twin Earth to argue we cannot even be certain which thoughts we think. The Hume-Nietzsche bundle critique undermines even the cogito, and the spoon-bending boy ('there is no spoon') illustrates Berkeley's idealism as the endpoint of skepticism about the physical world.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 14 "Skepticism Outside the Matrix" — Matt Lawrence uses The Matrix to stage the skeptical problem, running Descartes's dream argument and evil-demon method of doubt (the Matrix as a technological demon) and even a 'Matrix within the Matrix' to show Morpheus cannot know he is awake. Descartes's cogito supplies the one certainty that survives radical deception. Lawrence then draws on Russell's analysis of the red chair to argue against naive realism: color, texture, solidity, and shape are appearances, so even setting aside the Matrix we cannot know the world in itself.

### The Dichotomy of Control

The dichotomy of control, most sharply stated by the Stoic Epictetus, divides everything into what is "up to us" and what is not. Our judgments, desires, and choices lie within our power, while our bodies, reputations, possessions, and outcomes ultimately do not. The practical counsel that follows is to invest our concern only in what we control and to accept the rest with equanimity, since misery arises from trying to command things that were never ours to command.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 22 "Emotions and Aesthetic Response" — Carolyn Korsmeyer uses BtVS to stage philosophy's ambivalence about emotion — dangerous passion versus intuitive sagacity — through three cases: anger as beast within and practical power (Xander's love spell in 'Bewitched, Bothered and Bewildered,' Willow's wish-spells in 'Something Blue,' 'My emotions give me power' to Kendra), grief as the one emotion no magic can undo (Epictetus's jug-and-child counsel set against 'The Body' and Dawn trying to resurrect Joyce), and love's non-fungibility (Anya's vengeance-demon past leaves her without the wider affection that makes singular love credible, while Spike's messy human history makes his obsession believable). She draws on Plato's wild-beast appetites and spirited element of the Republic, Aristotle on anger and emotional disposition as character, Kant's reason-above-nature picture, and Martha Nussbaum on art's particular cases. Finally she turns to aesthetic response: the show's comedy ('She saved the world a lot') regulates audience emotion, keeping the serial's catharsis from tipping into manipulation.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 10 "“Control, Control, You Must Learn Control”" — Stephens reads Yoda as a Stoic sage: Luke's first impressions are blinded by appearance, but Yoda exhibits the Stoic virtues of patience, timeliness, focus on the present, apatheia (freedom from fear, anger, and hate), and ascetic discipline (askesis), living by the dichotomy of control. He reconstructs the contrasting 'logic of the Dark Side' - anger to hatred to aggression to the mastery of others - showing the Emperor as a tyrant who, unlike the self-mastering Stoic (Marcus Aurelius being the counterexample among rulers), seeks to control what is not up to him, so Vader's 'I must obey my master' is servitude to vice. The chapter also marks Stoic limits: the Emperor rightly rejects felt compassion but wrongly refuses beneficence and Stoic cosmopolitanism, and Stoic physicalism cannot accommodate Yoda's 'luminous beings' afterlife.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 31 "Poker and Philosophy" — Housel surveys a century of poker on screen — from the Tombstone Birdcage Theater's 'bird in a gilded cage' through Maverick, The Gambler, Rounders, and ESPN's Tilt with its brothel-break 'Matador' — to show women cast as eye-candy, damsels, or flukes (Joanne Woodward winning a high-stakes game without knowing how to play). Against the myth stands Annie Duke, who beat her brother Howard on the way to the 2004 Tournament of Champions title. The argument: poker rewards reading and projecting emotion, so women socialized into emotional intelligence hold an edge over macho men who suppress it — a retooled Stoicism fusing Epictetus's 'make the best use of what is in your power' with Gilligan's care ethics, backed by Nietzsche's trust in the senses and Sun Tzu's 'pretend inferiority and encourage his arrogance.'
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 30 "Sometimes We Live No Particular Way but Our Own" — Matthew Turner argues that a 'Playin' in the Band' jam — the band drifting from the tune into long collective improvisation and back — models a Stoic solution to free will shared by Epictetus, Spinoza, and Chuang Tzu: freedom is not uncaused choosing but responding well within constraints, so by the dichotomy of control there is no point resenting the band when it flubs a climax. Spinoza's definition of the free thing as one determined by its own nature, and Chuang Tzu's butcher who cuts oxen by spirit beyond skill, show the band letting the music 'play them' — Jerry's 'Tennessee Jed' riff never played the same way twice — as learned skill becomes second nature. Because the Dead jam within banks (keys, mutual listening, ability) yet generate something genuinely new and transcended every genre of 1960s music where the Monkees merely copied the Beatles, the Stoic attitude proves creative rather than quietist, an analogue for living freely within our own constraints.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 10 "“All Good Things Must Come to an End”" — Thorsrud casts Spock and Data's exchange in 'Unification, Part II' — Spock dispassionate by choice, Data longing for emotion — as a replay of the ancient debate between Stoics and Peripatetics over whether to eliminate or moderate the passions. The Aristotelian side is built from Data's emotion-chip rage while killing a Borg ('Descent'), his unfelt breakup with Jenna ('In Theory'), and Riker's defense of trust after Ishara's betrayal ('Legacy'): emotions are judgments with pleasure or pain, there is a right amount to feel, and invulnerability costs the 'emotional bonds that make us who we are.' The Stoic reply uses Epictetus's distinction between involuntary impressions and assent (Picard's fear on the Borg ship vs. the holodeck), Cicero's refusal to 'moderate' what is simply a fault, and Seneca on anger, exemplified by Spock's 'quite logical relief' in 'Amok Time', his calculated desperation in 'The Galileo Seven', and his saving the bigot Stiles in 'Balance of Terror' — leaving the Peripatetic conclusion that fortune's goods are not mere indifferents and we may rightly 'smile with so little provocation.'
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 8 "Too Much Tequila, Or Not Quite Enough" — Doug Anderson reads Buffett as an 'American Stoic' — unlike his friend the Cynic Hunter S. Thompson, who dropped out and died, Buffett accepts his fated world of competitive capitalism and controls the one thing Stoics say we can: his own attitudes, 'changes in latitudes, changes in attitudes.' He leans on Seneca's advice to Serenus that wine and dreaming liberate the mind ('drink washes cares away') to interpret the dialectic of dreaming and drinking in 'Margaritaville,' 'Five o'Clock Somewhere,' and 'License to Chill' as Stoic self-renewal — the margarita even frees the singer to admit his own fault — with Emerson's intoxication-speaking poet as the American model. Excess is the failure mode: the expatriates of 'Banana Republics' who mistake the dream for an end state and Buffett's late-thirties hangover reckoning mark the Stoic middle path between deadening routine and 'too much tequila.'
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 12 "Red Sox Fandom and Internal Harmony" — John McHugh uses his urge to confront Grady Little, who left a spent Pedro Martinez in during Game Seven of the 2003 ALCS, to ask how fans should govern the primal emotions fandom generates. Stoic self-command fails because Epictetus's advice (avoid caring about games entirely, focus only on what you control) would extinguish fandom itself, so McHugh adapts Adam Smith's impartial spectator: the virtuous fan imagines being watched by a sympathetic but emotionally distant fellow fan, settling on a Chicago Cubs fan who gets Bartman the way a Sox fan gets Buckner and Grady. He concludes that we each harbor a team of role-specific inner consciences, and the practical task is harmonizing the Red Sox-fan identity with our other identities rather than suppressing it or being consumed by it.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 13 "An Enemy Lying in Ambush" — Fuller reads his teenage collapse while holding shiko dachi at his Eighth Kyu grading as a weakness of will, and argues that karate is Stoic discipline embodied. He explains the dichotomy of control through Epictetus's barbecue etiquette and the Kill Bill II buried-alive scene (only the Bride's years of disciplined training, not magic, break the coffin), then lays out living according to nature, Zeno's apatheia, Marcus Aurelius's Meditations, and Seneca's nightly self-examination as the model of askesis. Kata becomes 'a defiant stand against irrational emotion-chasing', and since only virtue is up to us, the enemy 'lying in ambush' is always internal: ourselves.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 13 "Enjoy These Moments" — Earleywine argues that Rush's lyrics trained a generation in the core moves of cognitive-behavioral therapy, an idea he traces back to Epictetus before Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck rediscovered it against Freudian orthodoxy. He maps specific distortions onto specific songs: 'Witch Hunt' on dichotomous labeling, 'Distant Early Warning' ('black and whites of youth') on all-or-nothing thinking, 'Emotion Detector' on emotional reasoning, 'Vital Signs' and 'Totem' on thoughts altering perception, and 'Subdivisions' ('Conform or be cast out') as realistic critique rather than maladaptive thought. The final step, acting on examined values and savoring the present ('Time Stand Still', 'The Camera Eye', 'Chain Lightning'), makes the songs the incarnation of their own advice: just listen.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 11 "The Stoic Warrior" — Jeff Sharpless imagines a Spartan mourning Kurt-051 and asking what his abduction, augmentation, and endless war mean, concluding his life is absurd in Camus's sense: bred as an instrument by the very humanity he is celebrated for saving. Camus's Sisyphus supplies one answer—meaning in the defiant moment of turning back down the hill, which recasts Master Chief's 'I need a weapon' as either hollow absurdity or quiet revolt. Epictetus supplies the alternative: distinguish what is up to us from what is not, withhold assent from impressions like 'we are all going to die,' and the Chief's silence becomes Stoic tranquility—though the chapter concedes Stoicism risks minimizing the injustice done to the Spartan children.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 30 "Time Enough to Drink the Poison" — Domino reads 'The Veiled Lodger' as a drama about hope in a world after God: Holmes's 'Your life is not your own; keep your hands off it' revives Plato's Phaedo argument that we are the gods' possessions, but deist-or-atheist Mrs. Ronder is unmoved, so Holmes falls back on the Leibnizian alternative to the Stoic and Cartesian 'patience without hope' — the example of patient suffering as 'the most precious of all lessons,' grounded in Leibniz's hope that the world is no 'cruel jest.' Jefferson Hope's two pill boxes in A Study in Scarlet literalize the Leibnizian link between hope and divine justice by letting God choose who dies, while Trelawney Hope's gullibility makes the surname ironic. Mrs. Ronder's true hope was reunion with Leonardo, which his death destroyed; what saves her is a new hope founded on Watson's text, since only a writer ('I have made a slight change of name and place') can change the past.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 13 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Curko and Greguric read Klosterman's glam-rock fandom as a problem of identity and masks: Nietzsche's Apollonian-Dionysian split casts Chuck as a self-controlled Apollonian writing about Dionysian excess in Guns N' Roses, Motley Crue, and Whitesnake, while Descartes's remark that actors wear masks to hide their shame introduces the tribute band Paradise City, a 'real copy' whose members would have no personalities left if they fully succeeded. The authors extend the mask question to Facebook and online avatars, where media saturation makes us 'copies without the original' and identity stops being self-same. They end by crowning Klosterman a modern Socrates of 'Know thyself' and a Stoic exemplar: admire your heroes like Satriani but do not steal their identities, control what you can (never your reputation or your time of death), and keep daring the endless search for self-knowledge.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 16 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Billard concedes the Stoic point that we control neither our passions nor nature ('life will always find a way', Sattler's 'you never had control'), as the bucardo cloning failure shows, but argues this proves the park rushed, not that de-extinction is impossible. Dangerousness is subjective, raptor intelligence is a logistics problem rather than a metaphysical objection, and since humans have already caused the sixth mass extinction we may have a duty to bring species back. Because revived animals would be 'neo-dinosaurs' built from fragmentary DNA, de-extinction is creation rather than resurrection, less like playing God than like the transhumanist enhancement humans already practice.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 36 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — The chapter assembles real-life versions of Finn's Enchiridion, starting with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: the Golden Mean locates each virtue between two vices, so true courage is knowing when to fight and when to run - cowardice and 'stupidteous' recklessness as deficiency and excess - a balance Finn's all-out bravery lacks. Epictetus's Stoic Handbook (which inspired the emperor Marcus Aurelius) teaches that happiness depends only on one's own reactions and that events are good or bad by how we take them, making it a manual even the chronically disappointed Ice King could use, while Christine de Pizan's book of chivalry prepares heroes for defeat and Erasmus's Handbook of the Christian Knight with Praise of Folly makes Finn and Jake's 'foolish' mercy look righteous. Finally Kant's Groundwork supplies duty for duty's sake: by the categorical imperative, Finn was entitled to steal the ogre's dollar only if, as an ogre who had swallowed Jake, he would accept the same theft from a hero.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 16 "6. Keeping It under Control" — Mills presents Bates - lame leg, repeated prison spells, the public fall when O'Brien kicks his cane - as an Epictetan Stoic who 'manages' misfortune by confining his concern to what he controls, echoing the Dowager's 'I hope we're in control of something, if only ourselves.' The chapter explains the dichotomy of control and preferred indifferents through Thomas's enslaved pursuit of the valet post, O'Brien's soap-on-the-floor scheme, Mary's panicked engagement to Richard Carlisle, and Mrs. Hughes's proportioning of her cancer scare, and treats death as the great rejected indifferent via Pamuk, Sybil, and Matthew. It closes with Hierocles' concentric circles: the household's best moments (Sybil helping Gwen, the staff rallying to free Bates) collapse upstairs and downstairs into one family, while Thomas's closed inner circle marks his failure of Stoic virtue.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 16 "4. On Being a Dead Person Who Hasn’t Died Yet" — Mark Ralkowski argues that Louis's 'dead people who haven't died yet' bit sounds like Marcus Aurelius, and that Dr. Bigelow's Season Four advice about back pain, the three-legged dog, and heartbreak works as the Stoic spiritual exercises Pierre Hadot described - above all the 'view from above' that re-describes things to strip them to their true value. Epictetus's dichotomy of control explains Bigelow's core advice: pain is not 'up to us' but our judgments about it are, so Louie should adjust his expectations to nature ('every second without back pain is a lucky second') instead of demanding a pain-free life. The apparently un-Stoic counsel to savor heartbreak ('misery is wasted on the miserable') is defended as genuinely Stoic: viewing his lost love from the perspective of a dead-person-who-hasn't-died-yet, Louie can accept sadness as precious and impermanent rather than being crushed by it. The chapter concedes Louis is no philosopher, but suggests his bits - contrasted with Seinfeld's 'polished' version on Talking Funny - can be read as newly discovered Meditations for comedy audiences.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 17 "5. Just Want a Shitty Body" — Bekka Williams argues that Louis's 'just want a shitty body' bit restates Epictetus's central Stoic teaching - want events to happen as they do happen, because only judgments, efforts, and desires are 'up to us' while bodies, reputations, and outcomes are not. She reads the Late Show arc (Tardigan's non-offer of the job, then Louie's triumphant 'Hey Letterman, I did it!' when Letterman stays) as Epictetus's cardplayer ideal: total effort on what is controllable, calm acceptance of what is not, alongside the bits about disgusting bodies, 'do the shit out of your job,' Jane and the mango pop, and Louis's self-trained habit of intercepting impulsive desires like the motorcycle urge. Like Epictetus, Louis is presented as a truth-teller who corrects mistaken impressions even when it is unpleasant, and the chapter uses him to rebut the charge that Stoicism means not caring.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 14 "3. Can Charlie Brown Be Happy" — The chapter asks why Charlie Brown is unhappy despite being kind, active, and engaged, and answers with ancient virtue ethics: happiness is not winning or approval but ethical self-transformation, so his dependence on others' regard ('How did the other team feel?') is the real problem. It diagnoses him with Daniel Haybron's three dimensions of happiness - strong on engagement but lacking attunement (nervous, self-conscious) and endorsement (cheerlessness) - and asks why his shyness so irritates the gang. Epictetus's image of Socrates playing ball at his trial and Cicero's dancing analogy supply the Stoic remedy: losing costs no virtue, what he controls is being ethical, and how you play the game is everything.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 13 "4. How Much Deadpool Is Too Much Deadpool" — The chapter argues Deadpool is entertaining because of, not despite, his excesses: his gratuitous violence and rapid-fire wisecracks breach the disciplined hero ideal, measured against Zeno of Citium's stoic dichotomy of control (accept the torture you cannot change, master your response) and Aristotle's golden mean between deficient and excessive force, which Wade flouts when he savors punishing Ajax instead of finishing quickly. Bakhtin's carnival excess explains the grotesque, orifice-obsessed humor that mocks 'normal' decency, and Derrida's 'internal drifting' (via Poe's Purloined Letter) frames Deadpool's first appearance being FedExed back to sender and his threshold position, where gags spill across comic, game, and film frames—making vigilante justice 'a supplement to the supplement' of law and exposing how each medium works.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 20 "10. Defying Fate" — Benjamin Evans reads Frank as fate's plaything, Tagomi's hydrogen-bomb gambit as an attempt to steer an uncontrollable web of events, and Hitler's claim that destiny belongs only to 'some men' as political exploitation of fate-talk. Stoicism (Zeno through Marcus Aurelius) explains Ed's serenity-prayer acceptance and the sinister Nazi version in which the 'natural order' means wolves eating sheep, but the chapter's verdict follows Adorno's studies of astrology and the occult: believing in fate seeds authoritarian submission, so Juliana letting Joe sail to Mexico — trusting her own judgment over the prophetic film — is the show's Adornian heroism.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 28 "15. June the Stoic" — Lequien asks how June might endure Gilead and answers with Epictetus: like the slave-philosopher, she can locate freedom in what is 'up to her'—detaching from her body during the Ceremony ('What he is fucking is the lower part of my body'), relinquishing property, and learning not to call husband or daughter her own. He tests alternatives—Camus's question of suicide (the shatterproof glass), utilitarianism (the coerced 'We are very happy'), Tronto's care ethics (Gilead smothers the sorority that could make care meaningful), and the Particicution as a licensed Two Minutes Hate—before concluding that 'Nolite te bastardes carborundorum' functions as June's Stoic mantra: mastery of her own responses is the one victory the Sons of Jacob cannot take.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 33 "20. Getting Your Shit Together Stoic Style" — The chapter argues Rick is at his best an Epictetus-style Stoic: in 'A Rickle in Time' his total certainty keeps the split timelines perfectly synced, enacting 'choice alone is vice, choice alone is virtue'; his 'love is a chemical reaction... focus on science' speech in 'Rick Potion #9' treats passion as an impression outside the sphere of control; and his 'don't think about it' dismissal of the Hitler-cured-cancer reality applies the dichotomy of control to an unmasterable multiverse. Epictetus's model of hardship as training is vindicated by Cronenberged Jerry, whose struggle preserves his dignity in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption', and the chapter closes with the Stoic promise Rick's life shows: not pleasure but contentment.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 32 "Two Philosophies, Two Compasses to Navigate Life" — Against 'Hang the DJ,' where Frank and Amy's coaching system assigns partners and expiration dates inside a simulated dating park, the chapter argues a Stoic would refuse to sign up: delegating judgments to the coach violates Epictetus's dichotomy of control, and the endless date-cycle fails all four virtues, treating dates (like Amy's bored lovemaking) as means rather than inherently worthy persons. An existentialist reading via Sartre says nearly every system-arranged relationship is bad faith - couples act as if compatible against the expiry they were given, as Frank and Nicola do - and only Frank and Amy's open-ended, freely chosen relationship escapes it, so their 'fuck off' to the system is a leap of faith that 998 of 1000 simulated couples make, which is how the app computes its 99.8% match. The authors close with Camus's absurd, doubting that the real Frank and Amy, who cannot rebel against an app that tells them they belong together, will fare as well as their simulations.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 16 "6. Keeping It under Control" — Mills reads Mr. Bates, the lame, twice-imprisoned, uncomplaining valet, as Downton's Epictetus, using him and the household to teach the Stoic dichotomy of control: only our judgments, desires, and actions are up to us, while jobs, reputations, and inheritances (Thomas's coveted valet post, Mary's scandal, Molesley's flower cup) are 'preferred indifferents' to be pursued without enslavement. Death figures as the great rejected indifferent, handled through Pamuk's demise and Mrs. Hughes's calm 'One day, I will die' upon finding a lump, as well as the grief of Isobel and Mary over Matthew. The closing section turns to Hierocles's concentric circles, with Sybil helping Gwen and Carson comforting Mary as drawing outsiders into the inner circle, a Stoic cosmopolitanism that Thomas, who sees the Crawleys as mere employers, fails entirely. The Dowager's 'I hope we're in control of something, if only ourselves' serves as the chapter's Stoic motto.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 20 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Dryden asks whether the Lanterns' relationships are weaknesses or strengths. Epictetus's dichotomy of control would have recruits greet the Sinestro Corps' display of their families' eyeballs with Stoic indifference, and Kant brands fear for loved ones heteronomous; yet Donna Parker refuses the ring for her children, Amnee and Matoo Pree surrender their rings rather than stop loving, and Kilowog dines with energy constructs of his dead family, showing attachments partly constitute who people are. Feminist relational autonomy resolves the tension: Kyle escapes Parallax only by grasping Hal's hand ('we don't have to do it alone'), and Soranik Natu cannot excise Sinestro's crest or parentage any more than Donchin's Huntington's-disease daughter can sever family ties, so autonomy competency means negotiating unchosen relationships rather than escaping them.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 20 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Abigail Myers runs Stoic doctrine against Katniss's biography: Zeno's thesis that only moral goodness is good (with Plutarch Heavensbee's renunciation of Capitol privilege as indifference to wealth and status), Seneca's 'On the Shortness of Life' against deferring living, Epictetus's dichotomy of control including the uncomfortable advice to kiss wife and child as mortals, and Marcus Aurelius's practical Meditations as the gentler 'Stoic for beginners' who would be president of Panem. Katniss comes out Stoic in her frugality, her mortality-shadowed appreciation of small joys, and her firm moral code, but decidedly un-Stoic in her fierce attachments to Rue, Peeta, and Prim. Yet her final choice of Peeta over Gale is itself Stoic, Myers argues: she forgives what Peeta's hijacking made him do since it was never in his control, refuses a noble friendship that would endorse Gale and Coin's slaughter of innocents, and chooses in accordance with nature and reason so as to survive as herself with her values intact.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 9 "Notes" — Hummel maps the Jedi Order onto Epictetus's Stoicism: philosophy as a way of life, virtue through wisdom, the dichotomy of control ('some things are up to us'), and treating outcomes like flying or other people's fates as preferred indifferents within the will of the Force. Anakin falls because he misconceives power as the ability to do amazing things - stopping people from dying - instead of mastery of his own judgments, and he refuses Stoic indifference toward Shmi and Padme. The chapter also indicts the Jedi's own un-Stoic lapses: mind tricks on Watto, entering the Clone Wars, and Mace Windu's attempt to execute a subdued Sidious.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 19 "Notes" — Taliaferro and Beck trace a philosophy of love through Anakin: fatherless, he attaches compulsively to Shmi and then Padme, refusing the Stoic limits on control that Yoda and Epictetus teach, so that love curdles into the vow to 'stop people from dying.' Vader's fatherhood is the caricature of love - offering Luke power instead of care - until Luke's compassion and Vader's final self-sacrifice redeem it. The lesson: love must be tempered by humility about what Zeno and the Stoics placed outside our control, and broken family bonds can be partly repaired through costly self-sacrifice.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 30 "Notes" — Quinn argues Rebecca is the show's Stoic: Marcus Aurelius's maxims about judgments, obstacles, and morning meetings with the ungrateful map onto her recovery from Rupert - accepting reality, forgiving as a choice within her control, the lion power pose, 'every disadvantage has its advantage' - with the dichotomy of control as her operating principle. Framed by Gen X self-reliance and second-wave feminism (Friedan's problem with no name, Beauvoir's woman as Other under Rupert), the chapter follows her from vengeful boss to mentor of Keeley and Nora, Bantr-era 'bossgirl' dater of Sam, and finally the Richmond family's matriarch.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 9 "Acknowledgment" — William Irwin diagnoses Neptune, from the 09-ers down to the PCH-ers, with status anxiety (via Alain de Botton's Status Anxiety) and prescribes the Stoic remedy: Epictetus on the insult lying in our judgment rather than the insulter, and Marcus Aurelius, the emperor who chose serenity over vengeance, show how Keith and Veronica ground self-worth in virtue no one can take away. Sartre's 'hell is other people' and the look explain how Veronica is reduced to a dumb blonde and Duncan to a murderer until he flees to Cuba, while Schopenhauer's choice between loneliness and vulgarity frames Mac's switched-at-birth longing, Wallace's basketball-bought status, and Weevil's self-made standing as PCH leader. Irwin closes by offering the show itself as Aristotelian catharsis-through-comedy, art as therapy for the viewer's own status anxiety.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 13 "Hardwood Dojos" — Bassham and Hamilton distill six success principles from coaches Smith, Pitino, Summitt, and Krzyzewski and show each echoes great philosophers, treating the court as a 'dojo' or place of enlightenment. Setting goals and pursuing excellence through habit map to Aristotle's eudaimonia and doctrine of habituation (Shaq the 'Big Aristotle' given the Nicomachean Ethics by Phil Jackson); the emphasis on outworking adversity and controlling only one's own effort maps to Stoics like Seneca, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius, as when Summitt and Dean Smith tell players to control what they can and accept the rest.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 18 "“They Don't Pay Nobody to Be Humble!” Football's Ego Problem" — Holowchak diagnoses football's ego problem—Keyshawn Johnson's deactivation, Terrell Owens's self-promotion, Deion Sanders's showboating—as fed by sensationalism (via Dewey) and statistical obsession that pull players out of the team framework. He proposes 'Aretism,' a modern progressivist ethics built on Stoic oikeiosis (Chrysippus, Cicero, Seneca, Epictetus and Hierokles's concentric circles) balancing self- and other-concern, and on Kant's injunction to treat others as ends. The virtuous athlete competes fully while respecting opponents, sport, and the 'moral zone' of Stoic sagacity.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 21 "Heroes of the Coliseum" — Reid draws an extended analogy between big-time college football players and Roman gladiators—both socially marginalized entertainers, controlled by coaches/editors and crowds, risking their bodies for others' entertainment. Through Roman Stoicism (Seneca, Epictetus, Cicero) she argues virtus does not depend on external wealth, status, or freedom but on accepting fate and excelling within one's role, so exploited athletes can still be genuine heroes of virtue. Following Marcus Aurelius's distaste for the games, she concludes those with power over players' unjust conditions are morally obliged to improve them.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 7 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Calhoun argues Eastwood's films move from solitary violent individualism (the Man with No Name, Dirty Harry) to what he calls 'post-Christian Stoic existentialism.' Using Epictetus's actor-in-a-play image and Marcus Aurelius on doing one's duty, he reads Butch Haynes in A Perfect World and William Munny in Unforgiven as figures 'dragged by the cart' of fate who nonetheless play their assigned role with dignity, while God is absent — Nietzsche's 'death of God.' Francesca's Stoic governance of impulse in Bridges of Madison County, Frankie's Kierkegaardian choice in Million Dollar Baby, and Walt's sacrificial community-building in Gran Torino show autonomous moral agency amid cultural collapse, with faint intimations of transcendence.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 16 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Gregory and Tod Bassham argue Stoicism is the seaman's philosophy of agency, teaching a clear-eyed grasp of what we can control, influence, or not control at all. Using Epictetus's play metaphor and 'you will fetter my leg but not my will,' Seneca and Marcus Aurelius on fear, they map three techniques onto sailing: cheerful resignation (Gerry Spiess righting Yankee Girl, Shackleton's James Caird crew laughing amid the Southern Ocean), self-sufficiency (splicing lines, emotional independence on a cramped boat), and negative visualization / premeditatio malorum (practicing docking under sail, imagining lost rudders). Skip Allen scuttling Wildflower and Dinelli's endurance illustrate the trichotomy of control and freedom of mind.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 12 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Kevin Krein argues that the freedom climbers report feeling is not freedom of movement, political freedom, or free will—on those measures a roped climber pinned on a ledge is less free—but the Stoic freedom of aligning one's will with what nature allows. Using Chrysippus' tethered-dog image and the Stoic identification of human logos with cosmic reason, he claims the climber who understands and accepts the mountain's conditions and wills only what it permits becomes free, which is why experienced climbers feel freest when their options are fewest.
