- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 44 "31. Does the Hulk Have a Soul" — Weighs whether the Hulk has a soul by running philosophy of mind's three positions: substance dualism (qualia and the hard problem, Plantinga's modal argument via Leibniz's Law — Peter Parker really is Spider-Man — but an unresolved mind–body interaction problem), physicalism (causal closure and conservation of energy, rebutted through objective truths and Einstein's dynamic spacetime), and idealism (Berkeley's master argument plus the holographic principle and quantum observation). It concludes idealism best explains Banner: Hulk and Banner share one mind/soul whose information is projected as two different 3D bodies, with the Ancient One's 'source code that shapes reality' speech in Doctor Strange as idealism's on-screen statement.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 19 "Perceptions Are Fine, but Dull Reality Is Still Better" — Distinguishes perceiver, perceptions, and perceived external objects to ask whether Alice, or anyone, can get beyond her perceptions to a mind-independent world, entering through Robert Arp's own painkiller hallucination of stones that were really Jell-O. The chapter sets epistemological idealism and metaphysical antirealism (the movie-theater-in-the-mind picture, traced to Plato's cave and Berkeley's suggestion that we are trapped inside perceptual reality) against the epistemological and metaphysical realism it finds in Alice and Carroll: fossilized ferns, dodo birds, and the Pythagorean theorem are discovered rather than invented, and at story's end everything rightly changes 'to dull reality'.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 107 "Rowling as an Inkling" — Argues Dumbledore's remark dissolves a false dilemma: the Hermione-as-idea versus Emma Watson contrast shows that existing in the head need not mean unreal. It then surveys thinkers who agree that mind and reality overlap: Plato's forms (the many broomsticks as imperfect copies of the ideal broomstick), Descartes on knowing essences by reason, Kant's mind-constructed objects, Berkeley's esse est percipi, Mill's phenomenalism, and Yogacara Buddhism's consciousness-fabricated emptiness, concluding that what is in the head can be genuinely real.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 10 "The Power of Choice" — Rennett stages Ariadne's 'who would want to be stuck in a dream for ten years?' against Nozick's experience machine: Nozick's three reasons for staying unplugged (doing rather than merely experiencing, being a determinate person, contact with a reality deeper than human construction) map onto Cobb's reasons for leaving Limbo — he wants to actually raise his children, be a good father, and love children who can love him back rather than projections. Against Nozick, the chapter enlists Berkeley's esse est percipi to explain Mal's choice: a perceived world is real, and Inception's shared dreams pass Berkeley's intersubjective test in ways private dreams cannot (Cobb apologizes to Arthur for being shot; dream acts carry waking consequences). It concludes that reality becomes what we choose to believe — Cobb's final refusal to watch the top, like the cave prisoners rejecting release, is the power of choice.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 17 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Terjesen uses spider-sense to tour early-modern philosophy of perception: against direct realism, Locke's indirect realism and its primary/secondary quality distinction suggest 'dangerousness' is a perceiver-relative secondary quality — bombs threaten Spider-Man but not the Hulk, and Mysterio manufactures danger-experiences — while Berkeley's idealism and Hume's phenomenalism radicalize the resulting skepticism about ever verifying sense data. The decisive clue is that spider-sense fails when Aunt May conks Peter with a vase (Amazing Spider-Man #114) and when his mentor Miles Warren becomes the Jackal: Peter does not fear those he loves. This supports Hume's sentimentalist account of moral judgment, on which vice is found not in the act but in the disapproving sentiment, moderated by Reid's common-sense reply that perception always already contains judgment — so spider-sense is a moralized judgment about what to avoid, not a Geiger counter.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 21 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Chaib takes Ruby's line that Hell is 'forgetting what you are' and reads God's character through early modern philosophy: Descartes' supremely real being and deceiving demon frame Castiel's delusion of godhood and Ruby's manipulation of Sam, Spinoza's denial that evil exists (it is 'inadequate knowledge') explains the comprehensible motives of Crowley and Lucifer, Berkeley's claim that things persist only because God perceives them makes a dead God an existential threat, and Kant's 'moral theism' rebuts dogmatic atheism. With Hegel and Fromm, Hell becomes self-forgetting and communion with God becomes self-knowledge achieved through knowing others, the opposite of Ruby's Hell. The chapter concludes via Locke that closing Hell's gates would deny once-human demons the redemption tied to our very idea of God, so the brothers' forgiving love, unlike Michael and Lucifer's rigidity, reflects God's nature.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 35 "Eighteenth Hole Swing Thoughts Tough Questions for a Tough Game" — Andy Wible closes the volume with fourteen open-ended 'swing thoughts'—short provocations applying philosophy to golf rather than arguing a thesis. He asks whether golf's subdued, rational fans make it morally superior (Plato and Aristotle on reason ruling emotion), whether Tiger Woods effectively wielded Plato's Ring of Gyges by sinning while invisible, whether Berkeley's idealism means your clubs and playing partners are mere perceptions (and whether that would matter), and invokes Augustine's 'an unjust law is no law at all' to license civil disobedience against unfair rules like spike marks. Further questions probe environmental harm, prayer as cheating, Casey Martin's cart, and whether perfect virtual golf would count as 'real' golf.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 16 "14_LaRocca_Chapter_013.html" — Mieke Bal frames her documentaries Mille et un jours and the installation Nothing is Missing around the ethical tension between 'modesty' and 'intimacy' in filming trauma. She reads Descartes's Passions of the Soul against the vulgate dualist cogito—arguing the isolating 'I think, I am' enacts his own abandonment trauma—and sets it beside Spinoza's socially constituted subject, while using Berkeley's 'esse est percipi' (reversed via the empowering close-up of a mother's face) and Deleuze's affection-image and rhizome. The multiplied, dispersed 'voice' of the Tunisian wedding film and Elena's silences become tools of a 'migratory aesthetics.'
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 30 "28_LaRocca_Chapter_027.html" — Hagberg argues that Grant Gee's documentary Patience (After Sebald) achieves a truthful portrait of W. G. Sebald not by static correspondence but by enacting his shifting, connection-making sensibility, as displayed in The Rings of Saturn. He deploys Wittgenstein's remarks on aspect-perception and 'seeing-as' (the duck-rabbit, the 'lighting up of an aspect') to show that perception is always already inflected by imagination, memory and language-games, dismantling the empiricist picture of Locke, Hume and Berkeley in which brute sensation precedes reflection. Borges's 'The Garden of Forking Paths' and 'Tlon, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius' supply the model of a Heraclitean flux of forking, mind-dependent connections, and the film's darkroom-like fading images and layered soundtrack are read as mimetically faithful to how a human sensibility perceives and remembers.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 17 "Doomed to Be Perceived" — Paula Smithka uses the Vashta Nerada and Weeping Angels to examine perception and the reality of unobservables. She sets Berkeley's "to be is to be perceived" against Locke's hidden substance and Hume's empiricist skepticism (and Paley's design argument), then distinguishes direct from indirect perceptual evidence, using the shadows, skeletal remains, and Neptune's discovery to frame scientific realism versus van Fraassen's antirealism. The Weeping Angels invert Berkeley, existing only when unperceived and turning to stone when observed, so for them to be is NOT to be perceived.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 15 "McElligot’s Pool Epistemology (with Fish!)" — Ron Novy uses Marco's faith that unseen fish swim in McElligot's Pool to survey theories of knowledge as justified true belief. The farmer's empiricism and Marco's inference from a book frame a tour through Descartes's evil-genius doubt and skepticism, Locke's primary/secondary qualities (indirect realism), Berkeley's idealism ('to be is to be perceived'), and rationalist a priori knowledge, before turning to feminist epistemology (Schott, Kant's 'intuitions without concepts are blind,' Nietzsche on perspectival seeing) and Quine's naturalized epistemology to argue knowers are situated and the pool may indeed be 'bigger than you or I know.'
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 8 "2. The Matrix" — Rowlands reads The Matrix as a vivid staging of Cartesian skepticism: Neo's pod-world is Descartes's dream and evil-demon conjectures (AI plays the demon) plus the modern brain-in-a-vat, showing we cannot be certain the external world exists. He uses the 'there is no air/muscles' and 'twin buildings' variant of Putnam's Twin Earth to argue we cannot even be certain which thoughts we think. The Hume-Nietzsche bundle critique undermines even the cogito, and the spoon-bending boy ('there is no spoon') illustrates Berkeley's idealism as the endpoint of skepticism about the physical world.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 88 "83. Disco Elysium as Philosophy Solipsism, Existentialism, and Simulacra" — Khamis reads Disco Elysium's 'Pale'—a property-less substance said to be decaying human thought that consumes reality—through three idealisms. The phasmid's warning that the world might vanish if humans stop thinking it evokes Berkeley's subjective idealism (esse est percipi) but without God as guarantor, leaving Harry in existential dread. The Pale as human-produced 'second nature' laid over 'first nature' evokes Kant's and Schelling's transcendental idealism, while the Pale as decaying signs without signification—like the vacuous dockworker 'sheriffs'—matches Baudrillard's hyperreality and simulacra, where information proliferates as meaning collapses, paralleling the amnesiac Harry's own loss and remaking of self.

### Philosophical Zombies

A philosophical zombie is an imagined being physically and behaviorally identical to a normal human but wholly lacking conscious experience—there is nothing it is like to be it, even as it walks, talks, and reacts exactly as we do. David Chalmers uses the apparent conceivability of such creatures to argue that consciousness cannot be fully explained by physical facts alone, since a complete account of brain and behavior would leave the presence of subjective experience unexplained. The thought experiment sharpens the so-called hard problem of consciousness and remains a central weapon in debates between physicalists and their critics.

- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 10 "Resting in Peace" — Manuel Vargas argues the Undead are not a natural kind but a nominal kind - vampires, zombies, and composite creatures like Frankenstein's monster share nothing except our classificatory practice - and that most actual Undead would probably be of natural origin (viruses, viroids, seeds, cryonics cases) rather than supernatural. He distinguishes philosophical zombies (Chalmers's conscious-less duplicates) from genuinely Undead beings, then defines malevolent evil as acting on a non-instrumental desire to harm others. On that definition zombies (mere appetite, like a deadly virus) and even vampires (whose damnation, contrary to early Buffy, need not add malicious motives) probably lack it, so if we ever meet the Undead they would be less likely to be evil than any random living person.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 11 "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep" — Larry Hauser stages the philosophy-of-mind zombie debate through Blade Runner's Replicants: Descartes's animal automata and his hats-and-coats worry about other minds, Turing's universal machines grounding functionalism, Kripke's necessity of scientific identifications (water is necessarily H2O), and Searle's silicon-chip replacement scenario show how zombies 'eat' behaviorist, functionalist, and identity-theoretic accounts of mind. He then deploys his own 'good zombies' - the beloved who might be a zombie, super-smart NEXUS 9s, venerable zombie thinkers - to block the dualist retreat on the cognitive side of the mind. The essay closes by doubting, with Chalmers's phenomenal zombies in view, that such zombies are coherently conceivable after all, and asks whether Deckard has been 'retiring' persons like Rachel all along.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 17 "Postmodern Postmortem" — Dale Jacquette distinguishes Hollywood zombies from Chalmers-style philosophical zombies, imagines a smiley-face birthmark that makes the latter visible, and argues that since zombies lack consciousness, pain, and intention, they are amoral - so zombie gladiatorial games would wrong no one, an improvement on the Roman munera Seneca condemned as pure murder. The thought experiment then turns on itself: even with zombie-only upbringing, screened audiences, and everything short of actual suffering on the zombies' side, the games would still be wrong for what they symbolically enact - the social condoning of slaughter of genetically human beings for entertainment. The conclusion is that consciousness and personhood do not exhaust morality: zombies get a moral pass, while the entire moral burden falls on the conscios who organize and watch.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 28 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Koepsell accepts that Autobots are virtuous and Decepticons vicious, then asks whether ethical war-bots are even possible, using the military's autonomous-weapons program, Asimov's Three Laws, and a kitten-sensing washing machine to argue that designed-in 'ethics' is only the designer's morality, like A Clockwork Orange's conditioned Alex, because it involves no real choice. Searle's Chinese Room and Turing's test then cast doubt on whether any mind, even our own, makes genuinely free choices, so he concludes that the appearance of virtue - behavior that reliably works - is all we ever have for humans or Autobots alike, and we should build machines as well as Optimus Prime and Bumblebee.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 11 "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep" — Larry Hauser reads Blade Runner's replicants alongside the philosophical-zombie thought experiment: like Rachel, who passes as human until a Voigt-Kampff test, zombies are outwardly perfect replicas with 'nobody home' inside. He traces the problem from Descartes's beast-automata and hats-and-coats worry about other minds, through Turing's universal machines and Kripke's necessary identifications (water is H2O), to the way zombie scenarios devour behaviorism, functionalism, and mind-brain identity theory, using Searle's silicon-chip replacement to imagine consciousness shrinking while behavior continues. His own 'familiar' and 'super-smart' zombies (a beloved with no qualia, NEXUS-9 geniuses) argue thought without felt experience is conceivable, before he concludes the phenomenal-zombie conception may self-destruct because a first-person point of view requires the very qualia it strips away.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 17 "Postmodern Postmortem" — Dale Jacquette distinguishes Hollywood zombies from Chalmers's philosophical zombies, imagining birthmarked beings whose behavior is run entirely by the brain stem so they speak, run corporations, and bleed like conscios while feeling nothing. He then proposes zombie gladiators: since amoral automata cannot suffer or anticipate death, arena blood sport between them seems morally permissible where Roman games condemned by Seneca were not. The thought experiment turns on itself: shielding conscios from attachments and vicarious suffering cannot cure the institution's symbolic statement that killing human-shaped beings for entertainment is fine, so even if consciousness grounds moral responsibility, how we treat the unconscious still reflects on us, and zombies can be wronged in the only sense left, through what we make ourselves.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 14 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — T. Bradley Richards takes The Sandman's Dreamworld seriously as a hypothesis: could our nightly dreams be travels to a mind-independent place like Morpheus's realm? Starting from Zhuangzi's butterfly dream and Descartes's dream argument, he uses Berkeley's God-sustained idealism as a model for how Morpheus's mind could uphold the Dreamworld's order, and a thought experiment about glitchy dream-travel defuses Descartes's appeal to the discontinuity of dreams. Against the objection that dreams are blatantly contradictory ('it was Dave, but it also wasn't Dave'), he deploys Russell's theory of descriptions against Meinongian subsistence, Chalmers-style conceivability-implies-possibility reasoning from philosophical zombies, and Graham Priest's dialetheism, concluding that dreams could be experiences of an objective world, with waking and dreaming on a par.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 10 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Editor Wayne Yuen's introduction argues that zombies are worth doing philosophy over: an apocalyptic world without government, law enforcement, or private property raises live questions about how survivors should treat one another, whether life becomes 'nasty, brutish, and short', and whether it is wrong to kill a walker. He frames walkers philosophically through Descartes's mindless human-looking automatons and David Chalmers's P-zombies, creatures functionally like us with no inner life. Morgan keeping photo albums instead of supplies in 'Days Gone Bye' shows that what we leave behind after the apocalypse is how we lived - our philosophy.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 12 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Gordon Hawkes uses the P-zombie debate to ask whether there is something in a person no walker can eat. Rick telling Morgan over zombified Duane that 'that's just his body' voices Cartesian dualism, while Dr. Jenner's TS-19 scan - the neocortex 'you part' that never comes back - voices materialism, as does Dr. Stevens's dying claim that he is 'just evolving into a different, worse life form'. The chapter stages Chalmers's zombie argument (a molecule-identical twin with no inner experience) against Dennett's zimbo objection, with Ryle's 'ghost in the machine' marking the interaction problem for dualism, and closes on the intuition that no brain scan of Test Subject 19 reveals what the zombie fever feels like.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 13 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Greg Littmann asks whether 'you' survive a walker bite, testing bodily identity, behaviorism, and functionalism as theories of personal survival against Jenner's verdict that after death 'everything you ever were... gone'. His centerpiece adapts Daniel Dennett: survivors yoke walkers to plows and tanks, dangle meat to move them between positions labeled 1 and 0, and gradually build a rope-and-corpse computer functionally identical to a human brain - which behaviorism and functionalism must call conscious, yet which we can conceive as utterly dark inside. The lesson is that we cannot know whether any system, walker, animal, or AI, is conscious, so treatment of non-human systems may need to err on the side of caution.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 12 "Violent Ends" — Richards asks what it is like to be a host, combining three lenses: Searle's biological naturalism (thinking machines must be built from materials with the right causal powers, and the hosts' synthetic flesh may qualify), Nagel's bat (even if hosts are conscious, their perfectly relived memories, curated pain, and blind spots like 'it doesn't look like anything to me' may make their experience as inconceivable to us as echolocation), and Chalmers's philosophical zombies (hosts behave exactly like us, yet beings identical to them with no inner light are conceivable). He reads Ford's contradictory testimony — praising Bernard's guilt as 'a thing of beauty' while denying consciousness exists — as a shift to a deflationary view with no threshold for being alive, and argues the show's choice to film human and host experience in the same style keeps the question deliberately open while fostering empathy.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 8 "The Last Bit" — Cook asks whether Rapture's Plasmids and ghosts refute physicalism and answers no: Plasmid powers are genetically engineered via ADAM and thus describable in physical vocabulary, while contractor Bill McDonagh's audio diary explains the ghosts of Rapture as leaked memories passed through gene-swapping, so all their facts supervene on physical facts in Chalmers's sense. The classic anti-physicalist pressures, Chalmers's zombie argument and the Nagel-style gap between objective physical description and subjective qualia ('the smell of poo'), do not apply because Rapture's phenomena carry no extra subjective residue. Invoking Clarke's third law that advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic, he concludes Andrew Ryan did not choose the impossible.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 42 "Ethical Issues" — Focusing on White Christmas's cookies and Ashley Too's synaptic snapshot, the chapter argues behavior can never settle whether an artificial system is conscious: the Turing test fails against Geminoid-robot-style cases where recorded signals produce human-like behavior, and philosophical-zombie possibilities plus the point that computations and information patterns are subjective interpretations (not objective physical properties) mean only discovering the physical neural correlates of consciousness could tell us whether a cookie feels pain. It then separates copying from transferring: with souls and substance dualism rejected, Black Museum's 'transfers' are really copies, and San Junipero's upload would house a copy whose future experiences are as alien to Yorkie as a plaster cast of her feet. Ethically, if cookies are conscious, then Matt's breaking of Cookie-Greta, Daly's captives, and Clayton's keychain are torture of persons, and it is the very uncertainty about cookie consciousness that lets characters rationalize the abuse - which is why the in-world legislation granting cookies human rights matters.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 21 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Henry Jacoby wields Westeros's strange beings against the mind-body problem: Nagel's 'what it is like' question becomes 'What is it like to be a direwolf?', and wargs like Bran-in-Summer and Orell's eagle ask whether one point of view can literally inhabit another. Against Descartes's denial of animal consciousness (only language users have souls; Mormont's raven crying 'Corn!' is a machine), he argues Ghost's pain behavior and direwolf physiology ground animal consciousness exactly as our brothers' behavior grounds theirs. Wargs do not refute materialism - in Westeros magic violates physical law without invoking nonphysical stuff - and 'Zombie Sansa', the philosophers' phenomenal zombie, together with the reanimated wights, is impossible in our world (with Russell, experiences are brain events known directly) and conceivable beyond the Wall only because the supernatural breaks the laws of nature.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 25 "NOTES" — Distinguishes Matt Parkman's supernatural telepathy from the 'mundane mind reading' everyone performs, then argues even Matt's power cannot solve the problem of other minds: the suicidal woman's thoughts he hears in the bar ('One Giant Leap') could be part of a Maury-Parkman-style illusion, and a brain-to-brain link could never rule out that others are Chalmers-style philosophical zombies. After grounding the skepticism in Descartes' cogito and method of doubt, it defends our everyday attribution of minds by analogy (Audrey Hanson reading Claire's insincerity) on pragmatic grounds, and maps Matt's progression from hearing thoughts to nightmare manipulation and compulsion onto the four adaptive functions philosophers assign to mind reading: interpretation, prediction, coordination, and influence. It closes by showing why neuroimaging-based technological mind reading remains a pipe dream, since brain recordings are quantitative syntax without semantics.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 30 "NOTES" — Antti Kuusela argues from Wittgenstein that behavior is the touchstone — indeed constitutive — of mental life, so the question is whether Terminators behave like beings with minds. Searle's Chinese room and Ned Block's blockhead explain the read-only T-101's head-up-display of canned responses as symbol-shuffling without understanding, and the T-1000's 'I know this hurts' seems empty from a machine that cannot feel pain. The pivot is the learning-mode switch John and Sarah flip: the T-101 acquires slang, keeps promises, and acts for reasons Skynet cannot predict, passing the Lovelace test, and the Wittgensteinian dismissal of Chalmers's philosophical zombie removes the last reason to deny it a mental life — making the steel-mill sacrifice the destruction of a rights-bearing someone rather than something.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Interrogates the tension in Cohle's 'deny our programming' line: if we are programmed biological puppets, how could we deny the program? It contrasts Sartre's radical free will and its crushing responsibility with Frankfurt cases and second-order desires — Marty as the 'wanton' who never acts on his desire not to desire affairs — and with Schopenhauer's will and Spinoza's causal determinism, both of which locate a kind of freedom in increased consciousness of our causes. The chapter concludes that self-consciousness, Rust's 'tragic misstep,' is in fact the only tool for reprogramming ourselves, imagined through a world of philosophical zombies who could neither suffer nor choose.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 10 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Wayne Yuen's introduction argues that a serialized zombie apocalypse, unlike a zombie movie, lets us explore life among the dead: how survivors like Rick, Lori, and Glenn should treat one another and divide labor, whether private property and equality survive without government, invoking Morgan weighing photo albums against supplies and the question of whether the new world is 'nasty, brutish, and short'. It frames zombies philosophically through Descartes's mindless automatons and Chalmers's P-zombies, and asks whether killing a walker could be wrong if walkers have inner lives, like dolphins or pandas, just less cute.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 12 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Gordon Hawkes uses Rick's words to Morgan over zombified Duane ('that's just his body—there's nothing of your son left in there') to set up Cartesian dualism against the materialism of Drs. Jenner and Stevens ('just tasty meat all the way down'), with Ryle's 'ghost in the machine' as the standard objection. He then explains Chalmers's zombie argument that a physically identical unconscious twin is conceivable, so consciousness is non-physical, and Dennett's 'zimbo' rebuttal that a creature endlessly reflecting on its own states would believe itself conscious. The chapter closes by asking whether there is 'something it is like' to be a walker shuffling through Atlanta, and sides with Rick's anti-materialism.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 12 "Violent Ends" — Bradley Richards asks what it is like to be a host, using Nagel's 'what is it like to be a bat?' to argue that whether we can conceive host experience depends on how similar it is to ours, and Searle's biological view to ask whether hosts are made of the right stuff. He catalogs how host perception, emotion, and especially memory differ from human (Maeve's perfect reliving of memories versus our hazy constructive recall, 'is this now?'), and weighs Chalmers's philosophical zombies against the hosts. He notes the show depicts host and human experience in the identical cinematic style to preserve ambiguity, and links memory, self-consciousness, and freedom via Dolores's maze, suggesting hosts may be phenomenally conscious before becoming self-aware.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 22 "A.I. Artificial Intelligence Artistic Indulgence or Advanced Inquiry" — White argues A.I. dramatizes the mind-body problem through the mecha child David, proposing a 'Strengthened Turing Test' (STT) in which the audience knows he is a machine yet must judge whether he truly loves Monica. He runs Searle's Chinese Room (David as mere rule-follower with no qualia) against Nagel's 'what is it like' and Chalmers's zombie argument and property-dualist multiple realizability, which would let a sufficiently complex David be genuinely conscious. White contends the imprinting device—David's built-in need for one other being—is what lets him pass the STT, sidestepping Cartesian dualism's interaction problem.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 30 "18. Foundation and Consciousness" — Lang and Haun use Foundation to explore consciousness, noting Asimov's robots (Daneel, Andrew Martin) are simply granted minds and that a system giving all the right signs could still be a Chalmers-style philosophical zombie. Their central case is Golan Trevize merging with the starship Far Star, which they read through Clark and Chalmers's Extended Mind Thesis and the Otto-and-Inga notebook example, arguing Trevize goes beyond Otto because he gains qualitatively new experiences (feeling magnetic fields, 360-degree sight). They then test extension against Integrated Information Theory and split-brain evidence, and read the planetary group mind Gaia as panpsychism (invoking Spinoza's God-as-nature, Leibniz's monads, and Fechner's world-mind) that faces the Combination Problem, partly eased by telepathic links that relax the privacy of minds.

### Rectification of Names

The rectification of names is the Confucian idea that social and moral order depends on making words match reality, so that a ruler truly rules, a father truly acts as a father, and each role is filled according to its proper meaning. Confucius argued that when names and actualities drift apart, language loses its force, obligations become unclear, and society falls into disorder. The remedy is to align conduct with the standards implied by one's titles and relationships, treating accurate naming as the foundation of good government and ethics.

- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 13 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Nicolas Michaud catalogues the demonic hierarchy - de Spina's goblins, incubi, and familiars, Dante's Malebranche, Binsfeld's seven princes of Hell - through Dungeon Keeper's Dark Mistress, World of Warcraft succubi, Se7en, Hellraiser's Pinhead, Hellboy, and Spawn. His real argument is ontological: names are power, and what we call the Devil fixes how we treat him. Recovering the Hebrew sense of 'satan' as an appointed adversary and 'Lucifer' as light-bringer (compared to Prometheus), he argues the same being could be reframed from tempter to giver of knowledge, much as naming Columbus's invasion a 'discovery' launders atrocity.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 32 "Girls and Philosophy" — Carleo and D'Ambrosio read Hannah's 'busy trying to become who I am' through the classical Chinese debate over names: her self-claimed title 'writer' preceding any conduct is the Confucian nightmare of names divorced from actuality, diagnosed by the Analects's rectification of names ('rulers should rule, fathers should father') and the sheep-stealing passage warning against over-identifying with a single role. Adam, by contrast, lives the Daoist ideal - the empty vessel of the Daodejing acting by wu wei, and Zhuangzi's butterfly dream fluidity in his role-play sex and absorbed woodworking, unattached to titles. Mencius and Xunzi frame the resolution: by Season Three Hannah finally rectifies names at GQ while Adam's non-identity turns delusional, vindicating the ideal of being an 'internal sage and external king' - Daoist in private, responsible to roles in public.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 14 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Morgan Deane reads Ender's tactics as Sunzi's Art of War in action: winning all future fights by terror, exploiting Bonzo's hot anger, 'fatal terrain' when Graff stacks hopeless odds, formlessness that hides intent, and fluid toon formations that move like water — all grounded in Daoist harmony with the Way and the Confucian role-duty of the general-as-father who throws soldiers into hopeless positions to win their devotion. He also finds Legalist rewards-and-punishments in Ender's command of Dragon Army, concluding Ender qualifies as a Sunzi-style military genius whose empathy is the steep moral price of victory.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 12 "Notes" — Decker parallels the Republic's fall into Palpatine's Empire with the Zhou dynasty's collapse that birthed Chinese philosophy, reading three Jedi from the Dark Times comics through it. K'Kruhk, guided by the Zatoichi-like Master Zao, learns wu-wei - following the Force rather than forcing outcomes, with Laozi's Dao as the Force's Chinese analogue. Dass Jennir's struggle over what 'Jedi' means after killing a slaver becomes Confucian rectification of names and the cultivation of ren, while Kai Hudorra's loss of faith, withdrawal to a casino, and final sacrificial stand against Vader embody Mozi-style pragmatic minimalism redeemed by Jennir's virtuous example.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 31 "NOTES" — The Terjesens pit Kant's impersonal morality — Sam's contractual distance from the thieving Mickens is exactly how he would treat strangers — against Confucius and Mencius, for whom filial duties are the nursery of virtue: we learn benevolence by serving parents and revering elders, Lafayette's care for Lettie Mae and Tara shows family forming moral character, and the Upright Gong's covering for a father's sheep-stealing grounds Jason's 'sometimes the right thing to do is the wrong thing'. Mencius's King Shun, who abdicates and carries his criminal father into exile, models how Tommy and Jason should put family first while accepting the cost, while Mozi's universal love surfaces in Godric's 'forgiveness is love', and the chapter concludes that family counts only insofar as it develops our moral nature — the line between Tommy and Sam.

### Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know)

Socratic ignorance is the recognition that one does not possess the wisdom one might be tempted to claim, captured in the idea that Socrates was wisest because he alone knew that he knew nothing of real importance. Rather than a pose of false modesty, it names an honest awareness of the limits of one's understanding, which Socrates took to be the necessary starting point for genuine inquiry. Those who mistakenly believe they already know cannot learn, whereas acknowledging ignorance opens the way to seeking truth. This stance underlies his relentless questioning of experts who claimed authority they could not justify.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 9 "The Fates of Socrates and Seinfeld" — William Irwin compares Jerry and Socrates: the 'Jerry problem' of whether the fictional Jerry is the real Jerry (complicated by Seinlanguage) mirrors the Socratic problem of separating Socrates from Plato's dialogues. Jerry, like Socrates the gadfly, provokes his circle with questions that hunt for essences - the black-and-white cookie, 'is soup a meal?' - and shares Socrates' irony (the 'War: What Is It Good For?' gag in 'The Marine Biologist' works exactly like Socratic shamming ignorance). But where Socrates died serenely per the Apology and Phaedo, Jerry is self-absorbed and ends the series convicted under the Good Samaritan law, doing his stand-up 'gadfly' routine for prison inmates - an examined life, but not an exemplary one.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 9 "Unknown" — Irwin parallels Neo's mission with Socrates' divine commission from the Oracle at Delphi to 'wake up' Athens: both are driven by a single question ('What is the Matrix?' versus 'What is the good life?'), both are charged by the authorities, and both sting a complacent public. He explains the Socratic method through the Euthyphro exchange on holiness, where a follow-up question ('Is the holy holy because the gods approve it, or do they approve it because it is holy?') exposes Euthyphro's ignorance, and introduces Socrates' mantra 'I know nothing' as the humility that launches his quest just as Neo's lack of self-knowledge launches his.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 10 "Unknown" — Irwin compares the film's kitchen-table Oracle with the Pythia at Delphi: both utter cryptic prophecies that seekers misread, from Croesus's doomed war to Morpheus's certainty that Neo is the One, and both make self-knowledge the real key to interpretation. He reads the 'Temet Nosce' sign and the cookie scene through the Delphic maxims 'Know thyself' and 'Nothing in excess', arguing Neo fulfills the prophecy only when he comes to know and believe in himself, and closes by linking Socrates' gadfly mission and 'the unexamined life is not worth living' to Fight Club, Boys Don't Cry, and Memento.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 35 "Last Pitch" — Reid argues that baseball and Socratic elenchus are both constructed to cultivate aretē, excellence. She maps four parallels onto concrete moments: both live off uncertainty (pre-game jitters, the 2001 Rivera–Gonzalez Series finish), both require risking failure (Ted Williams playing a doubleheader to protect his .400, Kirk Gibson's hobbling 1988 homer off Dennis Eckersley, Billy Beane's fear beside Lenny Dykstra), both demand active self-testing (Lou Gehrig retiring when complimented on a routine play), and both impose an obligation to return and challenge others — Plato's cave allegory, Socrates the gadfly, the aging champion who applauds the record-breaker. The Delphic oracle's riddle, that Socrates is wisest in knowing his ignorance, is the batter's-box humility every at-bat demands.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 27 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Gareth Matthews contrasts Plato's serene Phaedo — Socrates conducting a seminar on immortality, death as the cure for life's ills, 'we owe a cock to Asclepius' — with Gibson's prolonged torture, while noting deep parallels: both men were condemned by large courts on religious charges (impiety, blasphemy) with political subtexts. Socrates in the Apology models facing death through Socratic ignorance ('to fear death is to think oneself wise when one is not'), and Matthews argues Gibson's magnified suffering makes Christ an icon of an atonement nobody could imitate rather than a model for our own deaths; only the Gethsemane prayer and 'why hast thou forsaken me' (read via Cullmann) can actually help a believer face dying.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 11 "The One Question I Could Not Answer" — Comic writer Mark Waid, hired by DC editor Dan DiDio to re-imagine Superman in Superman: Birthright, is stumped by the question 'Why does he do what he does?' He argues that post-9/11 kids see the Big Blue Boy Scout as an ultraconservative protector of a corrupt status quo, making him irrelevant to a generation that knows heroes from metal detectors and assassinated visionaries. Invoking Socrates' claim that the genuine search for wisdom begins with admitting we do not know, Waid resolves to unlearn a lifetime of Superman lore, and locates the key to the character's motivation in Kal-El's utter aloneness: he is the sole survivor of Krypton and 'doesn't belong here'.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 13 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Kevin Kinghorn uses virtue epistemology (Sosa, Code) to solve the puzzle of why Uncle Andrew alone hears only roaring when Aslan sings Narnia into being: he fails all four intellectual virtues. He does not value truth for its own sake (unlike Frank the Cabby), indulges wishful thinking (like Edmund defending the Witch for Turkish Delight, or imagining Jadis fancies him), lets fear dictate belief (terror of the animals he has vivisected), and lacks Socratic self-knowledge, which the dragonized Eustace painfully acquires. A closing reading of Prince Caspian has each character's ability to see Aslan track their earlier trust in Lucy's testimony: sin blinds, and faith produces its own authenticating evidence.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 13 "Poker and Philosophy" — Young reads David Sklansky's fundamental theorem of poker — play as if you could see all the cards — through Aristotle and Husserl. Aristotle's phronesis and virtue-as-habituation explain how excellent players come to perceive the particulars (pot odds, opponent tendencies, the best possible hand) and stay unharmed even when losing with the best play, while Husserl's Cartesian Meditations, translated hand-by-hand into poker terms, supply analogical appresentation for knowing the other minds seated across the table. Chris Moneymaker's 2003 'Bluff of the Century' all-in with nothing against Sammy Farha shows how bluffing randomizes play and lets you shape the truth you seek, until a slow-played quad aces ends the night in Socratic humility about the limits of knowledge.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 8 "Bullshit and Philosophy" — 'The Dream of a Bullshit-Free Culture' argues Frankfurt revives a centuries-old philosophical tradition: Socrates searching for genuinely wise people rather than purveyors of hearsay, Descartes' Meditations discarding every belief short of certainty, and Hume's forkcondemning divinity-school metaphysics that contains neither abstract nor experimental reasoning to the flames. The twentieth-century apotheosis is the Vienna Circle, whose Rudolf Carnap dissected Heidegger's 'Das Nichts selbst nichtet' as mere appearance of meaning, calling metaphysicians 'musicians without musical ability'. The editors cast Frankfurt as the latest carrier of this Enlightenment anti-bullshit torch, with the book's popularity reconnecting seminar-room philosophy to the marketplace and voting booth.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 9 "The Talking Cure for Our Culture" — Young argues South Park is perceived as dangerous for the very reasons Socrates was executed — corrupting the youth and impiety — and that like Socrates it is really a gadfly promoting the examined life. Cartman is read through Arendt's Eichmann: evil as thoughtlessness, the inability to think from another's standpoint or ask if one can live with oneself, while Kyle and Stan's dialogues (such as deliberating Stan's grandfather's euthanasia request in 'Death') model the perspective-taking Arendt calls thinking. A final Freudian section explains the show's vulgarity as essential: jokes work like dreams, releasing repressed drives so the culture can talk through what it forbids.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 11 "How to do Philosophy" — Johnson argues through Colbert's satire that truth is neither individual ('My Truth') nor cultural ('wikiality' — a Wikipedia entry does not become true by consensus), since relativism is self-contradictory and implies slavery was not wrong before abolition. He deploys Locke's attack on 'enthusiasm' to show 'truthiness' is circular reasoning — sure because one is sure — and dismantles the 'right to my opinion' as a bid to shield beliefs from evidence, closing with Socrates' model: when evidence runs out, admit ignorance and keep doing philosophy.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 19 "“You Rationalize” Jackie Brown’s Pragmatism" — K. Silem Mohammad argues Jackie Brown is a study in aporia and Wittgensteinian aspect perception: Ray Nicolette's purple/white bag paralysis, Ordell's 'Is that Rutger Hauer?' mistake, Jackie on the LAX moving walkway, and 'Across 110th Street' turning diegetic all force a re-description of experience within particular language games. The thrice-repeated Del Amo money switch-off adds no information but displays the characters' differing aspects of one event. Against Ordell's mind-fucking 'logical chains', Jackie's 'that's what you do to go through with the shit you start, you rationalize' embodies a pragmatist view of reason as context-bound use, matched by Max's calmly uncertain 'I think I do. Good enough?'
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 14 "You Can’t Tell the Players Without a Program" — Auxier revives Plato's ancient quarrel with the poets — the Republic's banishment of imitators whose pretty words are copies that stir the masses' feelings, the philosopher-king's city, the Ion's contempt for rhapsodes, Socrates' wisdom as Delphic acknowledgment of ignorance — while branding Plato an elitist and 'Poetry NIMBY.' He then stages a fantasy dithyramb contest at the Meadowlands where Dylan ('Subterranean Homesick Blues') and Springsteen ('Blinded by the Light') trade internal rhymes and alliteration before Weird Al's palindromes deflate Bob's seriousness. The virtuous poet wins all nine Muses by wooing their mother Mnemosyne — tapping the collective memory of the race with gratitude and discipline — which explains why Springsteen, unlike the prideful Dylan who lost the Muses, retains moral authority; the philosophers, needless to say, are just jealous of the bar.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 9 "Where Do We Go from Here" — David Kyle Johnson argues that Colbert's gut-thinking persona (the Harriet Miers 'I know her heart' bit, 'that's my right' on the Panama Canal) satirizes a real and widespread vice, and he refutes the philosophies behind it. Individual and moral relativism collapse into self-contradiction and absurdity ('Lincoln was not assassinated' would be 'true for' someone; Hitler could not be condemned), while gut-justification is what Locke called 'enthusiasm' - a belief that is 'its own proof,' circular like the prophet whose revelation needs no burning bush. Following Jamie Whyte, he dismantles the 'right to my opinion' (running example: the friend who insists on a grassy-knoll shooter despite the melon-head evidence): there is no epistemic or moral right to undefended belief, and no right to intellectual comfort. Against this he holds up Socrates, wisest because he alone admitted ignorance, and insists philosophy and politics progress only through argument, so truthiness is never an acceptable substitute.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 20 "Colbert Is (the Tragedy and Comedy of) America, and So Are We" — Ralkowski asks whether Colbert is America's Socrates, comparing Colbert's ironic interviews (Caitlin Flanagan on feminism, Harvey Mansfield on manliness, Howard Dean's superdelegates, the ABC Stephanopoulos-Gibson debate) to Socrates' definitional refutations of Euthyphro and the Athenian elite. Like Socrates in Plato's cave allegory, Colbert is a shadow on the wall undermining truthiness from within, yet both fail: audiences laugh, guests collect the campaign-donation 'Colbert Bump,' and nothing changes, making America the self-satisfied one who is ignorant of its ignorance. Through Nehamas's contrast of Socratic and Platonic irony and the Symposium's demand that the greatest work read as both tragedy and comedy, the chapter concludes Colbert may be America's Plato — condemning and laughing at us like a Sisyphean liberator who knows we will not leave the cave.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 7 "World of Warcraft and Philosophy" — The editors' introduction, framed as an in-game quest log ('Read a Philosophy Book,' reward: +21 Intellect), argues that WoW is a profound cultural phenomenon that deserves philosophy because the world is virtual but the people, guilds, and Blizzard developers behind it are real. It models philosophizing on Socrates' claim that he knew he did not know, inviting readers to honestly examine the guiding principles they already rely on when playing and living. Chapters can be tackled in any order like a quest log, and the goal is a more open mind about gamer life rather than final answers.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 17 "Alone into the Desert" — Audits Duniverse lives by Socrates's standard—the condition of the soul over wealth and power, with justice, courage, temperance, and wisdom—finding Baron Harkonnen utterly wanting, 'Leto the Just' compromised by forgery and concubinage, Paul unjust in his myth-making holy war (though Plato's Republic would smile on ruling myths), and the Fremen admirable in temperance and courage but fatally sure of themselves where Socrates prized knowing that you do not know. Aristotle's function argument and golden mean follow: Paul's first worm-ride is courage between rashness and cowardice, but Paul's and Leto II's extreme, humanity-saving selflessness has no excess to moderate and so breaks the doctrine of the mean. The author concludes Socrates is too harsh and Aristotle closer, yet even he fails: sometimes the best life requires extreme virtue and even injustice, as with the two Atreides emperors.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 7 "Know Thyself" — George Reisch's introduction frames the volume with Martha Stout's claim that one in twenty-five people is a conscience-free sociopath who hides in plain sight, arguing that we viewers do the hiding work for them just as Deb, LaGuerta and Batista's assumptions shield Dexter. It presents Dexter's incessant inner questioning as the show's philosophical hook and previews the book's competing verdicts on Harry's Code: monster, Kantian-style model actor, utilitarian good, aesthete, or superhero. It ends by inverting Socrates: normally we point 'know thyself' inward, but the real epistemic danger is the sociopath next door, so our skepticism should aim at the guy in forensics - unless we are ourselves among the one-in-twenty-five, in which case Socrates' injunction to self-examination was spot on.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 27 "Secret Revealed . . . I Wonder" — Robert Vuckovich reads 'The Secret Box' through Plato's Theaetetus — wonder as the birth of philosophy, with Patrick playing Socratic midwife to SpongeBob's desire to know — and Hobbes's diagnosis of curiosity as 'a lust of the mind' that obsesses and torments until satisfied. SpongeBob's masked break-in turns epistemic desire into what Cicero condemns as 'knavery that wears the mask of wisdom', nearly destroying the friendship, while the Charmides ideal of self-knowledge as temperance is exactly what he lacks. The episode ends like a Platonic dialogue in aporia: SpongeBob peeks but does not search, learns nothing, and Patrick still guards the secret.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 179 "Chapter 32 - “The Exit Door Leads In”" — Eric Beck reads 'The Exit Door Leads In' as a modernized Platonic dialogue: like Oedipus before the Sphinx, the average salesman Bob Bibleman wins mandatory university admission by answering a computerized waiter's riddle, staging the Delphic 'Know Thyself' against Plato's Gorgias ideal of self-mastery, while Plato's Socrates in Charmides disclaims healthy self-knowledge. When Bibleman's terminal spills classified engine schematics, he decides not on universal principle but on what he thinks the authorities want; his honest answer that he would have handed them over anyway gets him expelled for failing a test he could not read, a double bind showing self-knowledge is contingent and situational. Dick thus revises knowing oneself as negotiation of the state's expectations rather than discovery of an essence, though the ending - Bibleman paying the computer after deciding not to - leaves open that he may one day rebel and need re-education.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 10 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Vannatta explains why Seinfeld reruns now fall flat through Klosterman's neologism 'unironically': since about 1991 irony has become the invisible background of American comedy, a pervasive detachment that David Foster Wallace named and that Jedediah Purdy's For Common Things attacks as the gap between phenomenon and essence. Against Purdy's ironist (Seinfeld's Jerry, mastered by irony, believing in nothing but his own interests), the chapter sets Kierkegaard's Socrates, whose 'infinite absolute negativity' and confessing ignorance serve a truth he cannot define, and asks whether Klosterman, probing the gap between Bono's rehearsed car-ride persona and his inner self, is master of irony or mastered by it. The answer places Chuck midway between the two jailed ironists, Socrates and the Seinfeld finale: like Socrates he knows his own ignorance and serves the undefined idea of self-understanding, but only through pop-culture resemblance (KISS where Jerry used Superman), unable to master irony any more than he can bite his own teeth.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 13 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Curko and Greguric read Klosterman's glam-rock fandom as a problem of identity and masks: Nietzsche's Apollonian-Dionysian split casts Chuck as a self-controlled Apollonian writing about Dionysian excess in Guns N' Roses, Motley Crue, and Whitesnake, while Descartes's remark that actors wear masks to hide their shame introduces the tribute band Paradise City, a 'real copy' whose members would have no personalities left if they fully succeeded. The authors extend the mask question to Facebook and online avatars, where media saturation makes us 'copies without the original' and identity stops being self-same. They end by crowning Klosterman a modern Socrates of 'Know thyself' and a Stoic exemplar: admire your heroes like Satriani but do not steal their identities, control what you can (never your reputation or your time of death), and keep daring the endless search for self-knowledge.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 26 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Daniel Wanless reads Jeopardy! through the Meno: contestants can formulate the right question only because the answer is already given, just as Socrates answers Meno's paradox by claiming that all inquiry is recollection of truths the immortal soul already holds - latent knowledge that explains how Ken Jennings buzzes in before he consciously knows the response. A priori logical ability (the slave boy's doubled square, the law of non-contradiction applied to which of three cities is southernmost) guides the search for answers, while Final Jeopardy!'s blind wagering embodies Kierkegaard's 'life is only understood backwards, but it must be lived forwards.' Socrates would bet it all, Wanless concludes, because the unexamined life is not worth living: his whole life was preparation for the ultimate Final Jeopardy!, lived in the form of a question.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 30 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Mills-Knutsen reads the Brain Spawn - floating brains whose pain at others' thoughts drives them to dumb life down and finally to hoard all knowledge in the Infosphere ('The Day the Earth Stood Stupid,' 'The Why of Fry') - as Futurama's funhouse mirror of the West's distrust of intellectuals, from Pandora and Eve to Frankenstein and comic-book evil geniuses. Fry, the delta-brainwave-lacking hero made stupid by doing 'the nasty in the pasty,' stabs the Big Brain with Bonfire of the Vanities and later banishes the Brains to another dimension, just as Athens executed Socrates. A close reading of Plato's Apology - Socrates's feigned ignorance exposing everyone else's, his demand of free meals in lieu of exile, and his prophecy of even more annoying successors - maps onto the Big Brain's snobbery and onto universities (Wernstrom's tenure scam in 'A Big Piece of Garbage,' Amy's doctorate in 'That Darn Katz!') as society's way of paying intellectuals to stay out of the way.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 20 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Christopher Lauer argues Cohen's lyrics seduce through Socratic irony as Kierkegaard analyzes it in The Concept of Irony: ostentatious self-concealment that makes hearers aware of the gap between words and intentions, building 'personality' and promising intimacy. Songs like 'Closing Time,' 'Everybody Knows,' and 'Democracy' oscillate between cynical third-person verdicts and sudden second-person address, offering a hidden sincerity only to withdraw it - an erotic improvement on Plato's Socrates that dissolves its own ironic distance. 'Hallelujah' and 'Anthem' make the program explicit, treating brokenness as the space in which love develops, while 'Tower of Song' shows the bleak side: irony collapsing into pure cynicism, the singer speaking sweetly from the Tower long after all promises of genuine intimacy have been disavowed.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 36 "22. The Dao of Master Westley" — Doll tests each character against the Dao: Confucius's identification of the Dao with tradition and ritual fails because Florinese tradition is exactly what enables Humperdinck's murder and war plans, so she turns to Laozi's De and wu-wei, diagnosing Vizzini's fatal overconfidence (he lacked Socratic knowledge of his own ignorance), Humperdinck's paranoia, and Buttercup's passivity as failures to sense when to act and when to refrain. Westley emerges as Zhuangzi's ideal - like Cook Ting the butcher, mastering skills until instinct suffices: adapting through the Fire Swamp, treating Vizzini's death as 'an appropriate death', yet sparing Inigo and Fezzik because killing them would be against nature, which is why the giant and the Spaniard accept him as their sage.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 21 "8. Should Jane Get to Be Bored" — Daniel Addison defends Louie's 'you don't get to be bored' admonishment of Jane in 'Country Drive' against Mathew Remski's charge that it transfers adult anxiety, pointing to Louis's Conan 'forever empty' monologue and reddit advice as proof that Louis insists on facing despair rather than fleeing it. The real aim, he argues, is Socratic: Louis wants Jane and the plane-complaining generation brought to aporia, the perplexity Plato's Socrates induces in the Meno's slave boy so that, no longer thinking he knows, he 'would be glad to find out.' Aristotle grounds the optimism - every human by nature desires to know, philosophy begins in wonder, and our deepest happiness lies in contemplating - so Louis's 'everything's amazing' tirade is a demand that we become philosophical rather than 'kinda satisfied' consumers. Boredom, on this reading, is failed wonder, and Louie is playing Socrates to his daughter.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 35 "22. Unmasking the World and Its Heroes" — Mapping both heroes onto Plato's cave, the chapter argues each must first see past shadows: Bruce abandons revenge on Joe Chill to change Gotham's whole idea of justice, its citizens climb out of apathy when the Dark Knight ferries refuse the Joker's detonators, and Clark needs Jonathan Kent ('It's not to score touchdowns') and Jor-El to learn what his powers are for. Socrates' Apology supplies the mask's rationale - the just man must lead a private life to survive, so secret identities protect loved ones from Luthor's kryptonite stabbing and FBI kidnapping - and Plato's warning that the returned cave-escapee would be killed explains why the heroes must lead by hope rather than force. The oracle story's lesson that wisdom is knowing that you know nothing grounds the close: anyone can be a hero, as Batman tells Gordon about the coat around a boy's shoulders.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 12 "3. The Only Chapter in This Book You Need to Read!" — Writing as two bickering versions of himself from different universes, Karavitis reads Deadpool Kills Deadpool as showing that the multiverse of Deadpools is the delusion of a single narcissist: the alternate 'Pools' are mirror-image projections of himself (Lacan's mirror stage), his self-love is Rousseau's pathological amour propre rather than healthy amour de soi, and his claim to be the progenitor of all reality is solipsism—hence there is no fourth wall. Freud, Fromm, and Marcuse supply rival diagnoses of that narcissism, from arrested development to proto-fascist willfulness to authentic rebellion against social control through unconscious conformity. A closing twist argues philosophers who claim sole access to truth are the same solipsistic narcissists, which would make Socrates, who never claimed a final answer, the only true philosopher.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 32 "19. Deadpool Can’t Know Fear" — Borrowing Socrates' definition of courage as remaining steadfast in the face of danger and choosing death above dishonor, the chapter argues that Deadpool's healing factor removes his risk of death, so he cannot experience the fear of helpless annihilation, cannot display courage, and is not an anti-hero but 'post-heroic.' Worse, mapping Luttwak's post-heroic warfare of drones and ballistic missiles onto his invulnerability, the chapter shows how fighting Deadpool drags opponents like the ULTIMATUM contract army and Crossbones into a trap where they can never test his courage and are stripped of their role as defenders, becoming mere targets. It closes that having a little fear and the chance to overcome it might be better than being unable to die.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 13 "4. Scoundrels, the Lot of Us" — Karavitis finds a Hegelian dialectic in the three-panel Dilbert strip (thesis, antithesis, synthesis) delivered through irony, then tests that irony against philosophy: Socrates' feigned-ignorance questioning that leaves interlocutors in aporia, Hegel's complaint that irony is vanity withdrawing from objective reality, and Kierkegaard's dissertation on the concept of irony plus Either/Or, where irony is the bridge from the aesthetic to the ethical life. The punchline is that after nearly three decades of Dilbert the white-collar workplace has not changed, so readers who feel superior to their bosses and co-workers have taken the vain, narcissistic, aesthetic reading Hegel warned against, making the joke a scoundrelly way of avoiding responsibility. A Leo Strauss aside casts Adams as an esoteric writer whose irony preserves him from the powerful.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 14 "5. The Serious Point of Scott’s Humor" — Guerra and Barkman argue that Dilbert's humor is doing serious philosophical work: strips like the Pointy-Haired Boss's scheme to strip app users of free will, rebranded by Dilbert as marketing, distill manipulative corporate practice to its absurd essential core, and humor serves as a logical tool that, when it preserves the target's integrity rather than straw-manning it, exposes the equivocation in earnest arguments about getting something from nothing. They ground the practice in Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, where wittiness is the virtuous mean between the vices of buffoonery and boorishness, read Adams's catalogue of failures and his luck-first, passion-is-bullshit account of success as a Socratic acknowledgment of ignorance that deflates the American Dream, and treat Win Bigly's persuasion lessons (visuals, repetition, intentional mistakes, the Hitler counterexample) as further proof that Adams has the virtue of wit.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 15 "6. No Wisdom to Offer You" — Distinguishes public intellectuals like Chomsky, who deliver their own conclusions, from public philosophers who get audiences thinking for themselves, and argues Schumer is the latter. Her memoir claim that she has 'no wisdom to offer' is set beside the Socratic ignorance of Plato's Apology, where wisdom is worth nothing. Sketches like 'Football Town Nights', whose coach condemns rape only to praise violent domination, and 'The Trial of Bill Cosby' withhold conclusions and force viewers to work out for themselves the links between football and rape culture, or between un-conflicted entertainment and justice.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 21 "9. A Rose by Any Other Brand" — Callis treats Gilead's rise as a marketing campaign, reading it through Thom Braun's philosophy of branding built on Heraclitus (brands as false stability amid flux, the 'hidden connection' of the 'Balm in Gilead' hymn), Socratic questioning that Gilead forbids its citizens, Plato's brand-as-becoming, and Aristotle's four causes (the Sons of Jacob as efficient cause, the subjugation of women as the brand's function). She argues the brand was doomed because its core premise—that women exist to breed—is false, so Waterford's quip that love is 'lust with a good marketing campaign' foreshadows its Shakespearean collapse. The resistance works the other way: handmaids reclaiming their real names ('My name is June—and I will survive') is what breaks the brand.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 18 "7. Rick and Morty as Socratic Television" — The chapter argues Harmon and Roiland write the show as Socratic dialogue: in 'Mortynight Run' Morty's confident moral position (saving Fart from Krombopulos Michael is right) is dismantled until Morty himself pulls the trigger, leaving him in aporia; in 'Auto Erotic Assimilation' Summer's faith in freedom is razed by Unity's happy paternalist hive and the nipple-shaped race war it unleashes; and 'Look Who's Purging Now' refuses to choose between liberalism and conservatism when the post-purge town instantly re-founds the Festival. Like Socrates in Plato's Meno, the show's goal is not to teach lessons but to reduce viewers to confusion, because doing philosophy begins there.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 12 "3. Wonder and Philosophy as a Way Home" — Nathan and Leilani Mueller argue the theme song's 'neighborly day in this beautywood' makes beauty a transcendental leading to wisdom, as in Plato's Symposium ascent to loving the beautiful itself and Aquinas's convertibility of truth, goodness, and beauty. Reading Rogers's questioning of batteries and boxes (episode 1655) through the Meno's genuine curiosity and Pierre Hadot's account of philosophy as a way of life, they tour the show's three philosophical spaces: the domestic living room, the community visit (blind saxophonist Eric Kloss), and Make-Believe as thought experiment.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 13 "4. The Gently Socratic Inquiry of Fred Rogers" — Ben Lukey and Steve Bein, veterans of p4c Hawai'i, argue Rogers ran a 'gently Socratic' community of inquiry on television: unlike Socrates the public gadfly who made asses of interlocutors, Rogers created intellectual safety, treating Daniel Striped Tiger's 'What does assassination mean?' (after MLK's murder) and the Officer Clemmons kiddie-pool scene as philosophy with children. Using Dr. Tom Jackson's Good Thinker's Toolkit to show children are philosophers, they defend 'little p philosophy' as activity over 'Big P Philosophy' as content, casting Rogers and Socrates as midwives rather than lecturers.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 37 "21. You Gotta Be Bad if You Wanna Be Good" — Shearer argues the show dismantles ethical dualism, the good/evil binary that sorts people wholly into the Good Place or the Bad Place and that underwrites real-world 'us versus them' thinking. Following Aristotle, being good is a learnable skill like reading or an instrument, acquired by practice and unlearning, not a fixed nature. Following Socrates in the Apology, progress begins with admitting you do not know, and the chapter shows that the characters who self-generate that admission, Eleanor confessing and Michael realizing he loves the humans, grow the most, while Jason's moral neutrality exposes a case the Good Place/Bad Place binary cannot classify at all.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 43 "30. Socratic Superheroism" — Stages a dialogue between Socrates and Nebula to build a four-part scorecard of 'Socratic Heroism' — question all assumptions, intellectual humility (Socrates before the Delphic oracle: 'I am very conscious that I am not wise at all'), improve society without ever doing injustice, and courage unto death (the gadfly of the Apology) — then scores Thanos 0 for 4: 'I am incapable of error' and 'reality can be whatever I want' are the very opposites of humility and of objective, heavenly truth. It nominates Doctor Strange as the MCU's Socratic hero, whose humbling at Kamar-Taj, willingness to hand over the Time Stone against the obvious choice, and trust in the one winning future among 14,000,605 pass the tests.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 16 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Barad maps fifth-century Athens onto contemporary America to cast Stewart as a Socratic reformer confronting modern sophists, advertisers, pundits and media figures who make weaker arguments appear stronger without caring about truth, exemplified by Ed Helms admitting network stories are pre-written from 'conventional wisdom' and Ann Coulter's conformity-peddling. She details the shared method: flattering the 'expert', feigned ignorance, and layer-by-layer questioning that traps targets like Rumsfeld ('It may not seem like much, but for this administration it's a huge policy shift') in contradiction, with Socratic irony doing the work of Stewart's awestruck deadpan and mute astonished reactions to Bush clips. Against Bill O'Reilly's 'stoned slacker' charge she cites the Annenberg finding that the show's young audience is better informed, and weighs Ken Tucker's 'monkey' question through the Crossfire 'I'm not going to be your monkey' exchange, concluding that, like Socrates facing trial and execution, Stewart uses irony as means and truth as end.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 34 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Decker asks whether the 'Stephen Colbert' persona is the ironist of the Romantics and Rorty: the precise inverse of Socrates, who was declared wisest by the Delphic oracle precisely because he knew he knew nothing. Through Schlegel's Romantic irony, Hegel's complaint that the ironist abdicates responsibility, Kierkegaard's reading of Socrates as standing ironically above every relationship, and Rorty's ironist with her radically doubtable 'final vocabulary', he reads Colbert's self-redescription, Rally to Restore Sanity and/or Fear, and Super PAC stunt as exposing the contingency of political selves. Yet truthiness at its worst is dangerous subjectivism, and the chapter ends with Colbert breaking persona before Congress ('I like talking about people who have no power') as the non-ironic face that keeps the irony honest.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 10 "The Sorcerer Socratic" — Timm argues Strange follows Socrates' path from arrogance to Socratic heroism: the hand injury forces intellectual humility (the Oracle-at-Delphi moment), the Ancient One's keyhole metaphor and astral-form lesson ('to show you just how much you don't know') enact the Socratic method of questioning the supposedly wise, and the astral projection is literally the examined life — Socrates' unexamined life not worth living. Strange's commitment to protecting humanity from interdimensional evil parallels the gadfly who risks death to improve Athens, his refusal to do injustice even under pressure echoes the Crito, and his repeated willingness to die for others (facing Dormammu, holding the Shambler back) completes the Socratic Hero profile.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 11 "We Can All Be Socratics Supreme" — Pape uses the Ancient One's keyhole metaphor to argue that all knowledge is partial and biased: Bacon's confident scientific method ('human knowledge and human power meet in one') is itself just a useful belief, while Socratic awareness of one's ignorance — knowing that you have blind spots, even if you cannot see them — is the real wisdom. She reads the film's running gags as bias lessons (the 'Mister Doctor' exchange, Strange mistaking the wifi password 'Shamballa' for a mantra, the noble-savage prejudice) and feminist critiques of impartiality as itself partial. The whitewashing controversy around Tilda Swinton's Ancient One — weighed against the Fu Manchu stereotype of the 1963 comics and Iron Man 3's Mandarin-as-Trevor-Slattery subversion — shows how filmmakers can confront the biases they cannot simply remove.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 20 "Knock and the Door Will Be Opened… Eventually" — The chapter reads Strange pounding on Kamar-Taj's door as Kierkegaard's passionate collision with 'that which thought cannot think': the materialist surgeon hits the unknown as a frontier, takes offense at the Ancient One's talk of healing through belief, and can only proceed by surrendering intellectual control ('I control it by surrendering control?'). It applies Kierkegaard's two teachers from Philosophical Fragments: Pangborn is healed the Socratic way, recollecting a power already within him, while the Ancient One's astral knock-out and eviction of Strange acts like the god as teacher, forcing him to discover that he is untruth, until faith becomes 'controlling magic by surrendering to it.'
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 17 "Alone into the Desert" — Has Socrates and Aristotle rate the good life in the Duniverse: the Baron fails every Socratic virtue (breaking his promise to Yueh, intemperance, betrayal), Duke Leto is 'Leto the Just' yet forges certificates and plans adultery, Paul's theocratic myth-making is unjust despite his temperance and courage, and the Fremen are brave and temperate but fatally unquestioning, lacking the Socratic awareness of ignorance that would have saved them from manipulation. Aristotle's function argument, his doctrine of the mean (Paul's worm-riding as courage between rashness and cowardice), and his external goods are then applied, but the author finally breaks with both philosophers: Paul's and Leto II's extreme selflessness admits no mean, their unjust oppression can still be right, and such extreme self-sacrifice may be the best life of all.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 23 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Abraham Schwab turns Ygritte's 'You know nothing, Jon Snow' into a theory of epistemic humility: Jon misreads wildling courtship norms, Sam's dragonglass shatters on wight Small Paul, Lord Mormont assumes Mance fights like a southern king and pays for it at the Fist of First Men, while Arya's accurate self-knowledge keeps her alive. Formalizing with justified true belief - Sam's lucky dagger thrust is not knowledge, and the Watch's warranted belief that the dead Othor was harmless justifies falsity - he uses Lysa's letter, which sent Ned to King's Landing on a lie, to ask what justification is: Descartes's absolute certainty is too strict, reliabilism vindicates testimony ('dark wings, dark words'), so that only Sansa need witness Ned's beheading for the Starks to know it, and between Melisandre's circular dogma about Azor Ahai and total skepticism, moderate skepticism best governs belief - a humility the south lacked about the Horn of Winter.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 37 "21. You Gotta Be Bad if You Wanna Be Good" — Argues that no one can improve without first admitting they are bad: the rigid Good Place/Bad Place binary is ethical dualism whose cracks show in Mindy St. Claire's Medium Place and Jason, a naive moral neutral who fits neither side. Socrates' Apology supplies the method — wisdom is knowing what you do not know, so self-aware fault-finding precedes growth — while Aristotle's account of virtue as learned by practice, like an instrument, grounds the claim that goodness can be acquired even in the afterlife, though unlearning old habits is harder. Eleanor's trash storm, Tahani's failed party, and Chidi's theory-practice gap mark each character's admissions of error, and the worst offenders, Eleanor and Michael, improve most because they confess unprompted.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 74 "Harry’s Cloak, the Ring of Gyges, and the Temptations of Power" — The chapter reads Tom Riddle as Plato's unfit ruler: from the orphanage ('I can make them hurt if I want to') he violates Kant's dictum never to use persons merely as means, treating even his 'friends' as followers, killing Lily despite Snape's devotion, and splitting his soul for Horcruxes.
