- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 24 "Inside the Lived Body" — Pits Merleau-Ponty's embodied self against Descartes' representationalism and mind-over-matter dualism to read Inside Out: Riley's five personified emotions look like homunculi inviting an infinite regress, but the film actually shows a holistic body-subject whose emotions arise in situations and with others. Joy's campaign to keep Riley 'okay' dramatizes the futility of constant happiness and the necessity of Sadness, while Riley's hockey stick becoming an extension of her body illustrates Merleau-Ponty's claim that skillful coping lives in the body rather than in Sadness's 'mind manuals.' The chapter ends on childhood's lived present and the film's power to hold loss before us instead of pushing past it.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 8 "Out of the Orb" — Boudreaux maps Strange's comic-book journey into the Orb of Agamotto (dragged in by the Silver Dagger, greeted by a hookah-smoking caterpillar, tempted by counterfeit heroes like the Silver Surfer and Hulk) onto Descartes's Meditations. Empiricism (Locke's tabula rasa, Hume's sense-data) collapses when the senses are so thoroughly deceived inside the Orb, and innate ideas plus the Law of Non-Contradiction are not enough, so Strange reasons his way to the cogito — 'Nothing merits belief here — except oneself!' — just as Descartes doubts the evil demon. The caterpillar is revealed as Agamotto, playing the role of Descartes's non-deceiving God whose guidance lets Strange escape, and Strange's astral projections are offered as dramatic proof of mind-body dualism.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 14 "“Strange Magic,” Electric Light Orchestra, 1975" — Kowalski reads the film's astral-form scenes as a dramatization of Cartesian substance dualism against Strange's opening physicalism ('There is no such thing as spirit! We are made of matter and nothing more'): the Ancient One pushing his astral body out refutes physicalism, his soul reads books while his body sleeps, and he fights Kaecilius's acolyte as a visible astral form in Christine Palmer's ER. The chapter then confronts the classic interaction problem — Descartes' pineal gland and 'animal spirits,' Elisabeth of Bohemia's and Garrett Thomson's objections — asking how an immaterial astral form can turn pages or knock over vending machines, joking that it would take 'a very strange form of interactionism.' The Ancient One's account of magic as energy drawn from other dimensions of the multiverse is offered as the film's own dualist reply, with a closing plea for the epistemic humility Strange had to learn.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 21 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Henry Jacoby wields Westeros's strange beings against the mind-body problem: Nagel's 'what it is like' question becomes 'What is it like to be a direwolf?', and wargs like Bran-in-Summer and Orell's eagle ask whether one point of view can literally inhabit another. Against Descartes's denial of animal consciousness (only language users have souls; Mormont's raven crying 'Corn!' is a machine), he argues Ghost's pain behavior and direwolf physiology ground animal consciousness exactly as our brothers' behavior grounds theirs. Wargs do not refute materialism - in Westeros magic violates physical law without invoking nonphysical stuff - and 'Zombie Sansa', the philosophers' phenomenal zombie, together with the reanimated wights, is impossible in our world (with Russell, experiences are brain events known directly) and conceivable beyond the Wall only because the supernatural breaks the laws of nature.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 15 "Unknown" — This section of the soul chapter lays out the Cartesian view: the immaterial soul explains only language and higher-level cognition, while material causes suffice for sensation, which consigns nonhuman animals to soullessness. It applies the view to Rowling's borderline creatures, such as owls that understand human speech and Crookshanks's suspicious intelligence, before introducing materialism as the fourth conception of the soul.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 19 "Horcruxes" — Using Lupin's account of the Dementor's Kiss, in which the victim goes on existing as an empty shell with no sense of self or memory, the section rules out the life-source and sentience views of the soul and probably the Cartesian view too, since a soulless Barty Crouch Jr. might still perceive the room. The author proposes the soulless state is like severe dementia or Lockhart after his backfired memory charm, raising the question of what, if anything, makes the shell still a person.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 20 "A Plausible View" — Reconstructing Slughorn's lesson to young Riddle, the section argues that because Voldemort's brain, senses, and magical powers survive his soul being ripped into seven, the Cartesian and sentience views are excluded and Rowling must hold the sentimental view: the soul is our capacity to love and our moral conscience. Voldemort's snake-faced transformation and his followers' fear-based loyalty, where even Bellatrix worships his power rather than being charmed, dramatize his lost humanity, and only remorse, which Harry begs him to 'try for' before the rebounding curse kills him, could have repaired the damage.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 21 "NOTES" — The concluding section of the soul essay asks whether Rowling's combined theory is likely true and answers probably not: there is no evidence of immaterial causes of brain events, the centuries-old mind-body interaction problem looms, and it is especially implausible that a separate substance handles only our deepest emotions and moral traits, with the added wrinkle that souls in the story display different physical powers depending on which spell conjures them. Yet it concedes that implausible metaphysics is no flaw in fiction that makes vivid what we care about and 'makes for a terrific story.'
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 24 "Whose Reasons" — The section applies the Cartesian division of persons into mind plus body, generating four possible descriptions of Padfoot such as Sirius's mind in a dog's body, and shows each fails: McGonagall's 'non-being' quip cannot house Sirius's vanished body, and neither pairing explains why Padfoot both chases his tail and stands on his hind legs to see Harry off at King's Cross. So the mind-body distinction cannot say what the transformed Sirius is.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 26 "A Unified Self" — The section tries a division of labor in which Sirius's mind explains his human gestures while his dog's body explains the tail-chasing, tested by the thought experiment of Sirius having become a bear instead, who would have done bear things rather than chase a tail he never had. But the price is absurdity: pleasure must reside in the body, giving Padfoot's body reasons of its own that could clash with Sirius's mind, as in 'I didn't want to chase my tail, but my body wanted to,' so the mind/body split buckles.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 27 "NOTES" — The section rejects the 'captain of a ship' picture of mind directing body, quoting Descartes himself on being so 'compounded and intermingled' with the body as to form 'a single whole,' and reads the Polyjuice episodes as proof: Harry in Runcorn's body naturally 'thunders' with a powerful voice and punches with an enormous fist, while Luna recognizes Harry through 'Barny's' face, impossible if mind and body were separable. The conclusion is that transformed people are unified man-dog wholes, and that even Muggle changes such as weight loss, learning to ride a bike, or Crouch-as-Moody show that changing our bodies changes who we are.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 112 "The Hallows of the Mind" — Uses Rowling's light-made-liquid description of the Pensieve's silvery contents to stage the materialism versus dualism debate: Hobbes-style materialists can treat ghosts like Nearly Headless Nick and the strands of thought clinging to wands or leaking from dying wizards as matter, while Cartesian dualists find support in Harry's fear at King's Cross that he might exist only as disembodied thought. Snape's remark that the mind is a complex and many-layered thing frames how little is settled about the mind-brain relation.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 21 "Putting One’s Mind into a Body" — Seng reads the 2008 film's crash-and-stabilizer flying lessons as philosophy of mind: at first the armor seems to confirm Descartes' dualism, with Stark the thinking substance piloting a mechanical body and Jarvis playing the pineal gland. But Stark smashing into the ceiling while learning to fly shows the embodied mind of Dewey and Merleau-Ponty — habits, spatial existence, and the imported home preferences that make the suit feel like his own skin, so that the repulsors whir closed when he stands down before the village gunmen. Dewey's view of intelligence as acting on estimates of a situation then explains Stark's growth from selfish playboy to sharable goods (beating the merely self-interested Stane), and Jarvis counts as Stark's mind made manifest in the suit.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 16 "Notes" — Dan Dinello reads the Borg as the nightmare double of Data: where Data embodies Asimov's Laws of Robotics and Federation humanism, the Borg realize Jacques Ellul's and Langdon Winner's thesis that technology is an autonomous, totalitarian force assimilating its makers rather than a neutral tool. He traces the Collective's shared mind and quest for 'perfection' to transhumanism (Max More, James Hughes), whose philosophical roots lie in Descartes's mechanical body and mind-as-information—the very premise of Ira Graves's consciousness upload in 'The Schizoid Man'. Picard's tear as Locutus and Hugh's acquired individuality in 'I, Borg' show that creativity and liberal humanist values, not technology, defeat the ultimate techno-totalitarian dystopia.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 23 "Notes" — William Jaworski argues, opening with Breaking Bad's Skinny Pete and Badger, that you should never enter a transporter: after showing the MEM converter violates Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, he asks whether the reassembled pattern is you or a replica. He tests three escape routes—Vulcan katra substance dualism (The Wrath of Khan, The Search for Spock) in the tradition of Plato and Descartes; constitutionalism, on which you survive total replacement by robotic parts as Picard nearly does under Borg assimilation; and Parfit's survival-without-identity answer to Riker's fission in 'Second Chances'. Each fails or costs too much: dualism wrecks moral intuitions about killing, constitutionalism faces the two-Riker indeterminacy, and mere 'survival' cannot sustain the particularity of love.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 26 "Notes" — Argues Star Trek functions like the Greek myths Nussbaum describes: modern tales of transformation (Gary Mitchell in "Where No Man Has Gone Before", Charlie X, Roger Korby) that let audiences judge what makes someone human. It rejects the Cartesian reading (Richard Hanley's Is Data Human?) in which Data's humanity is just a matter of being a rational mind, and develops instead a feminist, developmental account of personhood drawn from Annette Baier: persons are "second persons" who learn the arts of personhood from caretakers. Data, Seven of Nine, and Voyager's Doctor, all lacking real childhoods and families, must learn play, touch, love, and interdependence from their crews, with Janeway modeling family for Seven and Kes socializing the Doctor. Picard's farewell to Shinzon in Nemesis and to Data's B-4 caps the claim that humanity is an achievement of self-improvement in relationship, not a fixed essence.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 30 "Notes" — Argues through Alfred North Whitehead's philosophy of organism - reality as momentary actual occasions with mental and physical poles, nested societies, and canalization - that Star Trek's advanced beings are not, and could not be, purely incorporeal. Mindless feeders like the dikironium cloud creature and the Drella show bodilessness is not sufficient for advancement, while parasitic Zetars and Ronin show it can be a liability; the Douwd, the Companion, and Amanda Rogers's Q parents voluntarily tether to bodies for love and new experience. The Q's stagnation and civil war ("Death Wish", "The Q and the Grey") illustrate Whitehead's balance of survival against creative advance: what looks like "freedom from physical form" is really "freedom of physical form", since a purely mental entity would be an unsustainable organism.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 38 "Notes" — Uses a vintage Blue Snaggletooth action figure to illustrate Dennett's three stances - physical (AFA wear-grading of dented boots), design (why the Sears-exclusive mispack is valuable), and intentional (predicting whether Han would shoot first at a pedant correcting his parsec gaffe) - arguing that play trains a third-person science of mind that Descartes' first-person introspection and dualism could never verify. Dennett's account of religion as a misapplied intentional stance then explains begging the Falcon to 'hold together' and Zeus's lightning as projected intention, with the twist that children playing with figures know they are pretending while the superstitious mind does not.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 23 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Blackmon and Foresman ask what makes ghosts, spells, and holy water supernatural, rejecting definitions based on fiction, disbelief, or weirdness, and using Quine's point about the circularity of dictionary definitions to show lexicography cannot settle the question. Definitions keyed to current science or to the causal nexus fail because ghosts in Supernatural and in Hamlet causally interact, Bobby's ghost talks, moves objects, and possesses a maid, so the authors define the supernatural as what can on occasion transcend the world of material interaction. Descartes' interactionist substance dualism supplies the model: the cogito (even a djinn cannot make you falsely believe you exist), the pineal gland as the soul's point of causal contact, and a testable hypothesis that makes the supernatural scientifically investigable and implies that we, as spirits, are supernatural too.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 9 "NOTES" — Dunn reads Descartes' bete-machine doctrine (animals as soulless automata explicable by 'billiard ball' mechanics) against the Terminator universe, since Descartes' two tests for true men - genuine language and versatile reason - are in fact passed by the machines: the T-101 deploys 'Hasta la vista, baby' hours after learning not to sound like a dork and marshals skills far beyond a clock. Sarah Connor instead locates the soul in the heart, and via Spinoza's conatus - the instinctual valuation of one's own existence that Terminators lack ('no emotion about it one way or another') - she judges even linguistically brilliant machines soulless and irrational, as Mary Midgley says of computers that do not know what matters. Kyle's line about 'dreaming about dogs' closes the chapter: by the Sarah Connor criterion dogs are ensouled sentinels, the very thing Descartes denied.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 25 "NOTES" — Peppers-Bates and Rust stage Weber's disenchantment of the world in Sookie's relationship with Bill: her scientific-naturalist demand to know what animates him meets his 'magic', and although Searle and Nagel show consciousness resists scientific reduction (so 'miracle' is not absurd for the mind), Bill's vitalist, quasi-Cartesian dodge is a bait-and-switch about digestion. Sookie's real question is Sartrean — whether vampires, seemingly driven by blood bonds, hierarchy, and appetite, can freely choose their projects — and the chapter answers yes: Malcolm's cruelty presupposes he could do otherwise, Sookie's 'blood tie thing' excuse is bad faith in Eric's eyes, and Eric's wooing of her after regaining his memory is a freely chosen project that re-enchants her world.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 10 "2. Where Is the Twilight Zone" — Scalambrino reads the Zone as a televised expression of surrealist philosophy: Breton's sought 'point of the mind' where life and death, real and imagined cease to be contradictions, realized in episodes like 'A World of His Own' (automatic writing) and 'The Mirror' (Dali's paranoiac-critical method). Descartes's cogito and the mind-body dualism supply the rational 'leash' that surrealism unbinds, questioned by 'Shadow Play,' where a man insists the world is his dream. Following Adorno's verdict that psychoanalytic interpretation killed official surrealism, he argues the show endures by provoking the uncanny ('The Shelter,' 'The Lonely,' 'A Stop at Willoughby') without being pinned to Freudian readings.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 12 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Gordon Hawkes uses Rick's words to Morgan over zombified Duane ('that's just his body—there's nothing of your son left in there') to set up Cartesian dualism against the materialism of Drs. Jenner and Stevens ('just tasty meat all the way down'), with Ryle's 'ghost in the machine' as the standard objection. He then explains Chalmers's zombie argument that a physically identical unconscious twin is conceivable, so consciousness is non-physical, and Dennett's 'zimbo' rebuttal that a creature endlessly reflecting on its own states would believe itself conscious. The chapter closes by asking whether there is 'something it is like' to be a walker shuffling through Atlanta, and sides with Rick's anti-materialism.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 13 "Does the Piano Play Itself" — Michael Versteeg and Adam Barkman use the player piano to introduce Ford's eliminative materialism, aligning his 'consciousness does not exist' speech with Churchland and Dennett against the common-sense view of a self distinct from the body. They present Descartes' res cogitans/res extensa dualism and the pineal-gland 'magical transaction' as the target, then Churchland's claim that Folk-Psychology's beliefs and desires will be eliminated by neuroscience, and Dennett's Multiple Drafts model rejecting the Cartesian Theater and the manifest self. They note Ford's self-contradiction in speaking of a 'who' who makes choices while denying selves exist, concluding that if eliminativism holds, humans are complex machines like the piano and the hosts, everything being 'what it isn't.'
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 31 "Notes" — Swanstrom and Fletcher analyze the saidin/saidar gender distinction through Aristotelian gender essentialism (men hot/active dominating saidin, women cool/passive surrendering to saidar) and hylomorphism. Using Balthamel's soul placed in a woman's body (Halima/Aran'gar) who still channels saidin, plus Avicenna's floating man and Descartes' dualism elevating soul to essence, they argue the soul, not the body, determines which half of the Power one touches, while Aquinas's soul-body union (needed by Birgitte and shown by the soulless Gray Men) preserves 'balance.' They then use hylomorphism to let showrunner Rafe Judkins strip gender essentialism yet keep saidin/saidar via 'Jain Doe': an ungendered soul leaning one way, correlated to sex only by biological population balance.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 16 "Joanne Kyger “Descartes and the Splendor Of” Bridging Dualisms through Collaboration and Experimentation" — Falk analyzes Joanne Kyger's 1968 experimental video 'Descartes' and its script 'Descartes and the Splendor Of,' a condensed rewrite of the 'Discourse on Method' that subverts Descartes's mind-body dualism and privileging of reason. Kyger deflates the cogito with slang ('to doubt is a drag'), substitutes Buddhist, Taoist (Zhuangzi's butterfly dream), and Confucian terms, and—voicing and performing Descartes as a woman doing housework and as 'Mother God'—feminizes the most masculine of professions. Reading this through Judith Butler's 'Gender Trouble' and gender performativity, Falk shows the parody destabilizes the mind/body, male/female hierarchy Cartesian dualism underwrites.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 8 "Introduction" — LaRocca frames the whole volume around Kaufman's recurring 'who-what-why' of selfhood, arguing that his films literalize an inner alterity in which we are others to ourselves. He runs through Being John Malkovich (a homunculus inside another's head), Adaptation (a genetic twin), and Eternal Sunshine (memory as the very definition of who one is) to show doubling as Kaufman's method, and lists eternal recurrence among the philosophical conundra Kaufman embeds in flawed characters. The essay reads Kaufman's pseudonymity and self-naming as intensifying, not closing, the gap between the self and its double.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 11 "On Being John Malkovich and Not Being Yourself" — Falzon argues that Being John Malkovich stages the Cartesian self as a nonbodily homunculus — Craig 'riding' behind Malkovich's eyes via the vision-limiting cutout and muffled audio — only to expose its absurdity when Malkovich enters his own portal and finds a world reduced to 'Malkovich, Malkovich.' As Craig learns to fully inhabit and puppeteer the body, the film shifts to Merleau-Ponty's and Dewey's embodied 'lived body' organized by habit. Reading Craig's takeover as Foucauldian subjectification through training, Falzon contrasts Craig's self-entrapping mastery with Lotte's genuine self-transcendence, her openness to being other than herself.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 20 "Heidegger and the Problem of Interpretation in Barton Fink" — Conard uses Barton Fink as a springboard into Heidegger's theory of interpretation, contrasting it with Cartesian dualism. Barton, the 'life of the mind' artist whose skull-like hotel room symbolizes his isolation, is a Cartesian subject cut off from the practical, meaning-giving contexts (Heidegger's workshop, the ready-to-hand versus present-at-hand typewriter) in which equipment is understood and interpreted. Conard argues the film's uninterpretable elements—the box, the wall photo, the mosquitoes—resist meaning precisely because Barton is severed from the web of relations that would let anything show up as meaningful, illustrating Dasein's temporal, potentiality-driven being.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 5 "Introduction" — Simon Riches's introduction frames the whole volume around Cronenberg's obsession with the Cartesian mind-body split, quoting the director that horror comes from being unable to reconcile a sharp mind with a dying body. It surveys the three parts of the book, showing how films like The Fly stage bodily transformation and personal identity, eXistenZ stages skepticism about the external world, and A History of Violence stages the nature of the self, arguing Cronenberg wears his philosophical interests 'on his sleeve.'
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 7 "The Fly and the Human Ironies of Disgust" — Colin McGinn reads Cronenberg's The Fly as a meditation on human disgust and self-disgust: Seth Brundle's metamorphosis into Brundlefly does not cross an ontological boundary but dramatizes that the human being was already a loathsome organic monster, a 'god who shits.' McGinn ties this to a Cartesian mind-body duality (a fine mind trapped in a decaying insect shell mirrors our own embodiment) and, via Nussbaum, to how projected self-disgust stigmatizes despised groups; the cinematic image itself is an 'antidisgust medium' that lets us feel only quasi-disgust.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 33 "19. A Pataphysical Cherry Pie" — Pagnoni Berns, Aguilar, and Veteri argue Twin Peaks stages metaphysics—a dual reality of a physical world and an unknowable superimposed one—drawing on Descartes' dualism and Gustav Fechner's animistic day/night double aspect (souls of plants, the Log Lady's log). They then claim its real philosophy is Alfred Jarry's pataphysics, the science of imaginary solutions to real problems: Cooper solves crimes not by deduction but by absurd means—smelling trees, throwing rocks at a bottle while naming suspects, reading dreams—superimposing another plane on ours (echoing Baudrillard), so Twin Peaks is 'metaphysics with humor.'
- **The Philosophy of Horror**, ch. 10 "Brave new worlds cyborg futures and female subjectivity" — Examining 'reproductive technohorror' from Shelley's Frankenstein through Splice, The Unborn and The Machine, the chapter argues these films code science as masculine domination of feminised nature (via Bordo's Cartesian masculinisation and Merchant's Bacon) and eliminate the female body altogether so man can create life without woman. It contrasts this with Haraway's post-gender cyborg and Braidotti's Deleuzean metal-morphoses, using becoming-woman and the rhizome to imagine reproductive difference as productive rather than as the erasable 'female problem'.
- **The Philosophy of Joss Whedon**, ch. 7 "Angel, Angelus, and Personal Identity" — This file collects Part II chapters 6-9. It defends Stephen Mulhall's 'bold thesis' against Baggini, Murray Smith and Livingston, using Whedon's dialogue-free episode 'Hush' as film that 'shows' a Zen-like epistemic point resisting paraphrase, and works through the Russell-Wartenberg debate over whether narrative film can convey arguments (via The Matrix and Eternal Sunshine). It reads The Cabin in the Woods as a counterargument to utilitarianism grounded in Nel Noddings's ethics of care ('people are more important than humanity') and an Aristotelian theory of worthwhile horror. The Angel/Angelus chapter stages the Wes-Holtz dispute as competing theories of personal identity, testing Locke's memory theory and Parfit's psychological-continuity view against Whedon's soul-based metaphysics to argue what ultimately matters is one's care-based relations with others.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 14 "Apocalypse Within The War Epic as Crisis of Self-Identity" — Hagberg reads Coppola's Apocalypse Now as a sustained dismantling of the "privileged access" / perceptual model of self-knowledge, in which the self inspects private inner objects insulated from the outer world. Captain Willard's voyage upriver shows the opposite: he comes to know himself only relationally, by studying Kurtz's file and measuring himself against Kilgore, Chef, Lance, and Colby, and through self-defining acts like shooting the wounded woman in the sampan and finally machete-killing Kurtz. Willard's clarifying self-composition marks Socrates' examined life, whereas Kurtz—self-deceived, an "imitator of an actor" in Nietzsche's phrase, exhibiting Freudian derealization and depersonalization—is the tragedy of the unexamined life, the true Oedipus blinded by a false self-image.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 22 "A.I. Artificial Intelligence Artistic Indulgence or Advanced Inquiry" — White argues A.I. dramatizes the mind-body problem through the mecha child David, proposing a 'Strengthened Turing Test' (STT) in which the audience knows he is a machine yet must judge whether he truly loves Monica. He runs Searle's Chinese Room (David as mere rule-follower with no qualia) against Nagel's 'what is it like' and Chalmers's zombie argument and property-dualist multiple realizability, which would let a sufficiently complex David be genuinely conscious. White contends the imprinting device—David's built-in need for one other being—is what lets him pass the STT, sidestepping Cartesian dualism's interaction problem.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 16 "14_LaRocca_Chapter_013.html" — Mieke Bal frames her documentaries Mille et un jours and the installation Nothing is Missing around the ethical tension between 'modesty' and 'intimacy' in filming trauma. She reads Descartes's Passions of the Soul against the vulgate dualist cogito—arguing the isolating 'I think, I am' enacts his own abandonment trauma—and sets it beside Spinoza's socially constituted subject, while using Berkeley's 'esse est percipi' (reversed via the empowering close-up of a mother's face) and Deleuze's affection-image and rhizome. The multiplied, dispersed 'voice' of the Tunisian wedding film and Elena's silences become tools of a 'migratory aesthetics.'
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 10 "I Think, Therefore I Exist . . . I Think" — David Kyle Johnson uses regeneration and the DoctorDonna to ask what makes the First and Tenth Doctor the same person. He debunks the Platonic/Cartesian soul via Phineas Gage and brain science, refutes Locke's memory criterion with Reid's transitivity and the amnesia/John Smith cases, questions Parfit's causal-chain view via the "Journey's End" meta-crisis, then argues persons are four-dimensional "time worms" (sets of stages) before pushing to the deflationary conclusion that, like a "heap," a person may not exist as a discrete entity at all.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 26 "16. Better Call Saul Because Chuck’s Condition Is Real" — The chapter treats Chuck McGill's electromagnetic hypersensitivity as a case study in the metaphysics and phenomenology of medicine, asking whether an unmeasurable condition is 'real.' It contrasts a realist demand for a biomarker with an anti-realist, phenomenological stance that privileges Chuck's first-person lived experience, and blames Cartesian mind-body dualism for medicine's split between neurology and psychiatry that leaves Chuck uncared for. Reading his blackouts, space blanket, and nocebo-driven coma as psychosomatic, it argues that stigmatizing 'crazy' media portrayals of Chuck worsened his isolation and that a whole-person, first-person-narrative approach was needed.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 17 "The Role of Matter Biology or Function" — Lawrence uses The Matrix to survey theories of mind. Neo's apparent mind-body separation fits Descartes's dualism, but Lawrence argues dualism fails on the interaction problem and lack of evidence, so the Matrix scenario supports materialism. He explains reductive (identity) and eliminative materialism (via Churchland and the Tastee Wheat question), then frames the biology-versus-function debate: Searle's emergent-property view (the beer-can thirst model) holds brain biochemistry is essential to consciousness, while functionalism (Lewis's Martian pain) holds any system with the right input-output relations has mental states, and Lawrence argues functionalism underlies the very idea of sentient machines like Agent Smith.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 20 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Steve Matthews uses windsurfing to analyze Csikszentmihalyi's 'flow' — the loss of self-awareness in skilled action between boredom and anxiety — and argues its intensity comes from 'integration,' where footstraps and harness bind sailor to kit so the equipment becomes 'an extension of oneself.' Invoking Descartes' own admission that mind and body form a unity (not merely pilot in a vessel), he applies Clark and Chalmers's extended-mind thesis: the windsurfer's kit and body form a coupled cognitive system, so 'I' extends to include the gear. He distinguishes true flow from mere goal-satisfaction (rejecting the ocean-cruiser's landfall as flow) and, via Velleman, locates flow's value in intrinsically motivated action that is its own end.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 8 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Robert Arp's introduction takes Descartes' 'I think, therefore I am' and its mind–body dualism (the conceivability argument that mind is distinct from body) and inverts it into the book's motto 'I am, therefore I ink': the tattooed person insists identity is bodily-based self-expression, challenging the Cartesian idea that the essential self is a non-bodily thinking thing. Arp flags Descartes' possible question-begging, then previews each chapter, framing tattoos as fertile ground for the philosophy of the person, personal identity over time, and self-expression.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 9 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Editor Liz Stillwaggon Swan uses her rejection of Descartes' mind–body dualism to reinterpret yoga's promise of 'union.' Drawing on Spinoza's view that mind and matter are two aspects of a single reality, she argues 'mind' is just a placeholder for embodied abilities, so a yogi who denies a separate spirit cannot literally 'unite' mind and body — they are already one. She reframes yogic union (via Megan Burke's essay) as uniting self with nature, and defends practicing yoga for physical and psychological benefit without any spiritual claim, likening secularized yoga to secular Christmas.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 18 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Ken Burak describes teaching yoga in his philosophy class — a 'three wheels' exercise moving from the true self behind our masks to the Upanishadic identity of Atman and Brahman ('Thou Art That') — to give students embodied access to the universal/particular problem. He reads Western philosophy from Plato's Phaedo (Socrates seeking death as liberation of soul from body) through Descartes' doubt as a 2500-year practice of pratyahara (sense-withdrawal), one limb mistaken for the whole journey, and asks what asana and this long retreat could each bring the other.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 19 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — J. Neil Otte contrasts Patanjali's 'weak' dualism — in which prakriti and purusha are revealed as united in samadhi — with Descartes' 'deep' dualism of irreconcilable mind and body, whose interaction problem (Princess Elisabeth's objection, the pineal gland) it never solved. He traces La Mettrie's materialist 'Man a Machine,' Wittgenstein on public meaning, and neuroscience (Penfield, out-of-body proprioception experiments) to argue mind depends on brain, and that yoga's 'interdependence' of mind and body fits modern science better than either Cartesian dualism or eliminative materialism — so yoga's critics will come around.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 22 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Debra Merskin content-analyzes 52 Yoga Journal covers (2000–2008) and finds every model white and 96% shown full-body, mostly looking away — posed as unaware of a scopophilic, hierarchical gaze that puts them in vulnerability. She uses Goffman's gender-display coding and the male-gaze framework to argue that a publication about a mind–body practice (which, contra Descartes' mind/body divide, neuroscience shows are intertwined) bears a special responsibility to present racially inclusive, non-objectifying images rather than reproducing the 'sex sells' formula of Cosmopolitan or Maxim.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 9 "3. Terminator I & II" — Rowlands uses the Terminator cyborg to pose the mind-body problem: how the inside view (consciousness, intentionality) meshes with the outside view (neurons firing). He rejects dualism because it only says what mind is not and cannot explain mind-body interaction (no mass, so no momentum/energy transfer), and because it would make intelligent-machine sci-fi impossible. He argues for materialism, then distinguishes 'nerd' symbol-crunching AI (Schank's restaurant scripts, Deep Blue) from 'jock' neural-network, embodied designs as the route to building an intelligent Terminator that can flexibly respond like Arnie mugging the biker.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 11 "5. Minority Report" — Rowlands uses Minority Report's precogs (a truncated Laplace's demon) to argue the film is about determinism: to certainly foresee a murder the future must be fixed by the past, distinct from predestination. He runs the dilemma of determinism, using Cruise's choice not to shoot Leo Crow: if actions are caused they are inevitable and unfree; if uncaused (indeterminism) they are merely random, citing Libet/Kornhuber experiments and the involuntary-arm-twitch example. He rejects Hume's compatibilism (freedom is doing as you please) because genuine freedom requires 'pleasing as you please,' and rejects agent-causation theory as reviving dualism's problems.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 17 "The Role of Matter Biology or Function" — Matt Lawrence uses The Matrix to survey theories of mind, arguing the 'brain-stimulation' premise favors materialism over Descartes's dualism (which alone easily explains Neo's mind-body separation at the Train Station but lacks empirical support and an interaction mechanism). He explains reductive versus eliminative materialism (Churchland's denial of folk-psychological 'beliefs' via Tastee Wheat) and then Searle's biological emergentism (the beer-can thirst machine) against functionalism (Lewis's Martian pain; Agent Smith's seamless transfer into Bane). He concludes the films are best read functionally, making sentient machines genuine minds.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 44 "41. Blade Runner as Philosophy What Does It Mean to Be Human" — Shanahan argues Blade Runner is philosophical despite Ridley Scott's denial, using the replicants (Roy Batty, Rachael, Leon) as defamiliarizing 'mirrors' for the human condition. He shows the Nexus-6 replicants satisfy Descartes' two criteria for a thinking soul (linguistic flexibility, novel problem-solving) while human characters like Deckard prove as cold and empathy-deficient as the machines, collapsing the human/replicant distinction the Voight-Kampff test presumes. He then reads Rachael's implanted memories through Locke's memory theory of personal identity, Roy's 'tears in rain' death through Epicurean worries about finitude, and frames the whole via Plato's Cave line 'they are like us' — the replicants model our own concerns with memory, death, and the meaning of a temporally bounded life.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 58 "55. Avatar as Philosophy The Metaphysics of Switching Bodies" — Tepley asks whether Jake Sully's final body-switch with his avatar in Cameron's Avatar is metaphysically possible without brain transplant or souls. Using Locke's definition of a person and the transitivity of numerical identity, he shows animalism forbids body-switching, substance dualism (Descartes/Plato) is unavailable in the film's materialist world, and merely copying a brain pattern creates a duplicate, not the same person. His positive solution uses the constitution view (Aristotelian in origin) plus Clark's extended-mind idea to argue Jake literally extends into his avatar, then—via an analogy with split-brain corpus-callosum cases discussed by Nagel, Parfit, and van Inwagen—shrinks back so long as no second stream of consciousness forms, a model he extends to secular survival of death by mind-uploading.

### Gender Performativity

Gender performativity is Judith Butler's thesis that gender is not the expression of a stable inner essence but is constituted through repeated acts, gestures, and stylizations of the body that produce the illusion of a natural, fixed identity. On this view there is no 'doer behind the deed': the appearance of an underlying gendered self is an effect of the very performances it seems to cause. Developed in Gender Trouble (1990), the idea challenges the assumption that sex grounds gender and opens space for understanding how norms can be subverted through their own repetition.

- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 20 "The Possibility of Authenticity The Life We Choose" — Gines reads hip hop's sexual imagery through Black feminist thought - Tupac's feud with C. Delores Tucker over "Wonder Why They Call U Bitch", Patricia Hill Collins's controlling images of the jezebel and welfare mother, bell hooks on the slave-rooted devaluation of Black womanhood, Nelly's "Tip Drill" video with a credit card swiped between a woman's buttocks, Jay-Z's "Big Pimpin'". Applying Sartre's keyhole gaze from Being and Nothingness and his Anti-Semite and Jew point about hierarchical societies, she argues the gaze under racism and sexism is non-reciprocal - women are seen without seeing - and that Lil' Kim's reversal of it reinforces rather than subverts the stereotypes; Butler's gender performativity then frames the closing Sartrean choice of authenticity or inauthenticity, Nas's "I Can" and "the life we choose."
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 13 "Yes, but What About the Killer Rabbit" — Argues the Pythons invert Arthurian legend's traditional patriarchal function, using Holy Grail — made amid 1970s women's liberation and legal abortion — to expose the absurdity of patriarchy rather than endorse it. The Black Knight's 'None shall pass' embodies an abstract, relationship-blind masculine ethics that the chapter sets against care ethics, while the witch-weighing scene shows Arthur and Bedevere's male bonding eclipsing the mob's victim. Castle Anthrax's 'perilous bed' and the Prince Herbert rescue — Launcelot's heterosexual-matrix heroics collapsing when the damsel in the tower is a prince who enjoys musicals — turn courtly love and gender roles into farce, making the film as much a document of 1970s gender politics as a medieval satire.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 16 "Who They Are or Who They Want to Be" — Harwood-Smith argues via Judith Butler's performativity that Cylons have no pre-cultural 'I': Six is female because she performs femininity, and performing humanity increasingly makes it real — sex being the catalyst that destabilized Athena, who switches sides, while Boomer never takes responsibility for shooting Adama and so remains a slave to her programming. The performance runs backward too: humans who sleep with Cylons (Baltar, Tyrol, Helo treated as a 'toaster lover') absorb self-doubt about their own humanity, against the Cartesian inner 'I' that Baltar, who remade himself from farm-boy Aerelon, clings to. Butler's thesis is vindicated: if preprogrammed machines can be changed by the roles they play, anybody could.
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 20 "The Fruitcake as Performative Exemplar" — John Kaag pairs Buffett's 'Fruitcakes' with Judith Butler's constructivism: institutions 'girl' infants through interpellation (the sonogram naming), the heterosexual imperative abjects gay, lesbian, and transgender 'nobodies,' and these excluded fruitcakes are the cosmic baker's half-baked people. The movie-theater stanza ('a twelve pound Nestle Crunch for twenty-five dollars') becomes Heidegger's das Man, others thinking and choosing for us, while Buffett's 'mea culpa' refrain and 'Religion's in the hands of some crazy-ass people' attack the guilt constitutive of Christian subjecthood, with Dewey's broad, doctrine-free religious experience offered as common ground. Buffett concerts themselves are read as performative exemplars — drag-show-like borderland communities where four generations act out the 'little bit of fruitcake' in everyone as a quiet political protest against enforced normalcy.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 29 "The Male Vampire as Metrosexual . . . Sort Of" — Joan Grassbaugh Forry argues the 'vampire aesthetic' both enforces and destabilizes constructed norms of beauty and gender, reading vampire representation through Foucault's made soldier (the body produced by discipline rather than nature) and the Bartky-Bordo feminist analysis of disciplinary beauty practices. Vampires are effortlessly, youthfully beautiful — exempt from the dieting, grooming, and ornamentation that produce femininity — yet their beauty must appear natural, which is exactly the demand beauty culture makes of women; Queen Akasha, Drusilla, and child-vampire Claudia are ultra-feminine femmes fatale whose threat is neutralized by childlike femininity and punished by death or ridicule (Claudia ashes in the sunlight, Drusilla is made to look foolish), while the feminized male protagonists — Louis and Armand in Interview with the Vampire, Angel and nail-polishing, Passions-watching Spike in Buffy, Langella's elegant Dracula — turn beauty, taste, and expressed emotion into audience identification and beautiful martyrdom. The payoff: in the realm of the Undead the male vampire becomes a beautiful martyr while the female vampire becomes a disastrous woman we love to hate.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 21 "Defiant Male Behavior" — Julia Round traces Holmes from Baden-Powell's Scouting for Boys, which told scoutmasters to teach 'Sherlock-Holmesism', through Victorian essentialist masculinity, 'true, cold reason', stoicism under the poison darts of The Sign of the Four, yet violin, moods and the feminized domesticity of Baker Street, to argue Doyle's stories already unsettle gender essentialism. Gregory House of House, built from the same blueprint (221B, a shooter named Moriarty, a lost love named Adler, Wilson as Watson), embodies and mocks both the 1980s 'new man' and the 1990s 'new lad', cooking, soap operas, manipulation, Segways and the 'Rubik's complex', landing in Judith Butler's world where gendered behavior is a performance and masculinity is fallible, immature, and constructed.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 185 "Won’t You Guess My Name" — Riffs on Harrison's Themis to cast Mick as Kouros, the golden boy served by the Kouretes — "the original name of the Rolling Stones" — until he surfaces as Dionysus among the Olympians, "sort of like the irony of Mick Jagger becoming a Knight of the Realm." It splits the males into orgy-tolerant girly-men and woman-hating "manly men" of the Sour Grapes Clubs, warns not to underestimate the girly-men, and contrasts Elvis, who went into the army and became acceptable, with Mick, who kept the Kouretes under his thumb — deliberately feminine, dangerous, and cooler than the Beatles.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 186 "“They’re So Ugly It’s Appealing”" — Takes the screaming fan's verdict ("They're so ugly it's appealing") and Ian Stewart's sidelining for looking "like a man" as evidence the Stones deliberately cultivated an androgynous ugliness to violate gendered expectations — "they weren't just a bunch of guys who bent the rules, they were off-sides." The blatant misogyny of the lyrics is read as compensation for that effeminacy among the Dionysian libation bearers in a patriarchal age, keeping the manly men at arm's length — while noting only Brian Jones actually abused women.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 15 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Rood unpacks Klosterman's 'This Is Emo' thesis that no woman will ever satisfy him: women love Lloyd Dobler rather than John Cusack, and everyone measures real relationships against Hollywood fake love (Coldplay songs, the Woody Allen Personality Type) until, as Klosterman puts it, real people actively trying to live like fake people are no less fake. He reads this through Sartre's cafe waiter and Butler's gender performativity to argue identity is learned performance, and through Plato's cave updated to a reclining-seat movie theater where we mistake projected shadows for real love. The deepest diagnosis is Baudrillard's hyperreal, glossed as a social-constructionist rerun of Kant's Copernican revolution, against which Rood's own objection lands: Klosterman covertly assumes a pure unmediated self that cannot exist, so the answer to fake love is not escape from mediation but self-control within it.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 20 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Ashley Barkman argues that feminism is unrealistic and inefficient in the apocalypse: citing sex-difference research such as Bandura's Bobo doll experiments, she claims masculine aggression and strength are what leadership requires when authority must be asserted physically, as when Rick pipes Merle and shoves Daryl, or Shane tackles Ed and Jim. The quarry laundry scenes stage the debate - Jacqui's protest at 'all the Hattie McDaniel work' versus Lori's 'this isn't about women's rights... doing what needs to be done' - and Barkman sides with Lori, treating the division of labor as survival logistics under a natural-law premise that it is moral to act according to nature. Andrea the sharpshooter and Michonne the swordswoman show women can excel as heroic exceptions without leading, and the chapter concludes leadership should stay with good men like Rick.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 21 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Pye and O'Sullivan use Judith Butler's claim that gender is performative to read the walkers as genderless: they keep the trappings of biological sex but perform no gender, and like drag queens they 'trouble gender' when the little girl walker turns to face Rick. The survivors, by contrast, drag patriarchy along as cultural baggage - Lori telling Carl 'I'm a girl, you talk to him' while Shane teaches frogs, Ed bullying the laundry line, the men confiscating Andrea's gun while Daryl keeps his crossbow - though counter-examples (Andrea and Amy fishing for the camp, Guillermo's camp of caretaking 'vatos' led by a former custodian and a nurse, Rick teaching Andrea the safety) show gender can be learned differently. Invoking Rorty's thought that assumptions become visible only when their contradictories sound plausible, they argue survival itself demands shedding these roles, since the genderless dead threaten everyone equally.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 22 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Fisher argues The Wire makes homosexuality a source of excellence: Omar and Kima blend masculine and feminine traits in something like Butler's gender-performative terms, build Aristotelian friendships of virtue (Kima and Cheryl pushing each other's careers), and can make the sacrifices - solitude, giving up family - that excellence in the drug war demands, while the homophobia of the streets and the precinct forces them to keep proving themselves. Omar's crossword comfort with 'them myths' frames him as a contemporary Socrates: a mentor-lover of boys, accused of amorality by Levy much as Socrates was charged with corrupting Athens's youth, answering with a Socratic reversal ('I got the shotgun, you got the briefcase'), and dying for his code in the city he would not leave. The chapter reads the show's refusal of coming-out storylines - Rawls's silent gay-bar cameo, Snoop's never-confirmed sexuality - as its most radical statement about sexuality in America.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 13 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Wieland Schwanebeck surveys the many masculinities in Cohen's songs - spies, soldiers, cowboys, rabbis, captains - and argues they mostly appear broken, mocked, or failing (the losing partisan, the captain whose ship leaks or crew deserts), which puts the 'real man' ideal in doubt. He shows how Cohen's Jewishness plays against stereotypes of the bookish, unathletic Jewish man, usually embraced and then inverted with Socratic irony, as in 'Is This What You Wanted' and 'Lover Lover Lover.' Following Judith Butler's Gender Trouble, he reads Cohen's stage persona - the tailored suit, kneeling, clowning, and erotic ambiguity - as a repeated performance demonstrating that masculinity is 'an imitation without an origin.'
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 29 "Girls and Philosophy" — Adleberg asks whether Jessa is right that she is not 'the ladies.' Against Shoshanna's common-sense biological determinism and pop-neuroscience like Brizendine's 'male brain' (refuted via brain plasticity and Fausto-Sterling), she deploys Butler's point that identity categories are always normative and exclusionary (Marnie's 'that's what men do' to Charlie) and Beauvoir's and Spelman's social constructionism - mothers already treating infants differently - to show gender is made, not born. With Haslanger's call to resist unjust gender meanings, she concludes that neither conforming (Marnie craving dominant Booth Jonathan) nor defying stereotypes (Jessa's bathroom sex, 'what if I want to feel like I have udders?') should be compulsory; only objectifying harm, as with Adam and Natalia, is wrong.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 31 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — The chapter uses Adventure Time's gender play - Fionna and Cake, princesses holding nearly all political power in Ooo, Jake as terrified helicopter dad, Mannish Man's parody of manliness - to ask what being a man or woman really means. Following Judith Butler's Gender Trouble, it argues sex does not fix gender: the Lumpy Space King and Queen share one body, Flame King is a flame in a suit, and Butler's critique of the MIT 'master gene' experiment shows how the assumption that men and women are opposites smuggles cultural convention into science. Finn is read as performing masculinity - Billy worship, dungeon codes, the endless 'Dungeon Train' - caught in a crisis of masculinity between what society says a man is and who he is, with the ghost of Shoko in 'The Vault' and the accepted grass sword as steps toward a heroism that is his own.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 28 "Dracula and Philosophy" — De Waal reads Dracula through Judith Butler's gender performativity: the Count terrifies because he 'does' gender wrong - a captor who cooks and mothers Jonathan like an 'angel in the house,' feeds Mina from his breast, and turns Lucy from Victorian maiden into wanton vamp. Harker as a 'dude in distress,' Van Helsing's hysteria, and the Dracula-Mina scene that 'opens new orifices' become parodies exposing gender as an incessant citation of copies. The hunters' 'sterilizing' of Dracula's boxes of earth is read against the eugenics movement and society's police function against gender-nonconforming people.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 32 "19. The Doctor is a (Wo)Man!" — Kellen asks whether the Doctor could regenerate as a woman, marshaling the canon evidence (the Corsair's lives as both sexes, the Sisterhood of Karn offering 'man or woman,' Missy) to show biology poses no obstacle - clownfish and rare human sex changes make the point mundane. Against Peter Davison's claim that a female Doctor 'doesn't work,' he deploys Simone de Beauvoir's 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' and Judith Butler's account in Gender Trouble of gender as a stylized repetition of acts performed over time, arguing the Doctor already performs care-ethicist, 'feminine' roles and could just as well perform female ones. Since regeneration routinely transforms personality without ending the Doctor, the only remaining objection is bias toward a supposedly male core identity.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 24 "13. How to Be a Dwarf" — Using Carrot (a human raised in a dwarf mine who is accepted as a dwarf), Cheery Littlebottom (an openly female dwarf), and Gladys the golem, the chapter argues that social identity is neither biology nor a one-time choice but an ongoing performance that must also be recognized by insiders and outsiders. It applies de Beauvoir's 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' to Cheery's creation of a female dwarf gender against the deep-downers' equality that treats every dwarf as male, and reads the black ribboners versus the Magpyrs as assimilation versus doubling down on identity. Essentialist outsiders like Fred Colon and the Campaign for Equal Heights fail because they cling to stereotypes when individuals like Cheery or Carrot do not fit the mold, while Vetinari's indifference and Mrs. Cake's accommodations leave identity to those who must choose and perform it.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 24 "13. The Madness of the Musician" — Lampert explains why Bowie is called the first postmodern pop star - he ironically shows that 'acting like' a rock star just is being one, refusing the genius myth by cobbling influences and confessing 'I lie an awful lot' - and grounds this in Sloterdijk's cynical reason and Diderot's Rameau's Nephew, whose honest liar Lui owns the mask-wearing vices everyone else hides. Hegel's Phenomenology supplies the title: the musician's universal deception is 'the madness of the musician,' the 'I' hollowed into pure ironic distance from all its masks (Descartes's separable self become image-manipulation), yet Hegel's hint that the cynic's vain talk can rise into 'a spiritual self of truly universal worth' points beyond Bowie's hyper-real self-referentiality to punk's DIY injunction to be your own hero - and to reading all sexuality, like Bowie's, as performance.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 10 "1. Free Falling into Postmodernism" — Sewell reads Petty's 1976 debut through Jameson's postmodernism: Petty's music is a cut-and-paste amalgam of 1960s jangle, 1970s heartland rock and punk attitude whose pastiche dissolves the high/low art distinction as aesthetic production merges with commodity production, which is exactly why it feels timeless. He then applies Butler's performativity to Petty's "cool," arguing the persona was learned and performed so incessantly that Petty and his audience came to experience it as innate. Finally Baudrillard's hyperreal and simulacra frame the conclusion that there never was a "real" Petty, only copies of copies, yet if the perceived sincerity feels real and empowering, it is real enough.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 34 "21. The Trouble with Joi" — M.J. Ryder uses Judith Butler's Gender Trouble to argue that Joi's womanhood is a performance, and so is her humanity: an 'it' playing a woman playing a human, in nested layers from Ana de Armas through the hologram to the 1950s housewife act. The chapter situates this in the real economy of female-voiced assistants (Siri, Cortana) scripted by human writers to seem real and trustworthy, and rereads the awkward Mariette threesome as Joi acting out what she believes human sex is, the two bodies never quite coinciding. Joi's final choice of mortal peril — 'like a real girl' — completes the performance, which is why the film leaves us unsure whether performing humanity differs from having it.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 7 "Foreword" — Kate Bornstein's foreword argues that Drag Race is the first pop phenomenon to present drag life and performance as a continuum rather than a one-night bar show, letting viewers watch queens learn their gender 'at the level of values' rather than rules. She frames drag as 'the proudly flamboyant performance of a broken binary' at the heart of postmodern gender theory, pointing to the casual pronoun shifts among contestants as theory in action. Quoting Season 11 winner Yvie Oddly on how different aesthetics show the possibilities of human experience, she casts both RuPaul and the show's contestants as gender royalty who embody values no one grew up with rules for.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 20 "9. Another Wig Underneath" — Cooper argues that the 'vulnerability' Drag Race demands is really a marketable persona, not truth. Working through Butler's Gender Trouble (built on Beauvoir's 'one is not born, but rather becomes a woman'), she concedes drag reveals gender's imitative structure, but shows it also confirms identity: Latrice Royale's padded 'Natural Woman' lip sync reads as authentic, and trans queens like Peppermint and Gia Gunn use drag to articulate womanhood, with Husserl's intersubjectivity invoked to insist that constructed gender is no less real for not being empirical. Willam's edit-spliced 'I'm not acting' breakdown and Shannel's deliberate wig-doff show honesty becoming inconsequential next to spectacle, while Untucked's Interior Illusions Lounge is framed as Sartre's No Exit hell of unending observation. Against RuPaul's 'born naked' self-help nihilism ('identity is a joke'), she ends warning that the show no longer lets Katya take off the chicken suit.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 21 "10. And the Rest Is Drag" — Oliver Norman takes RuPaul's lyric 'we're all born naked and the rest is drag' from 'Born Naked' and asks whether its claim that everyone does drag all the time contradicts a show that crowns one drag superstar. Through Judith Butler's Gender Trouble and 'Gender is Burning' he reads drag as a play on gender that can either parody the male/female binary or reinforce it (the Mary Cheney misogyny charge, Michelle Visage's 'show woman not boy' critique, fishy queens like Courtney Act and trans queens like Gia Gunn). He then deploys Erving Goffman's Presentation of Self in Everyday Life: everyday social roles - the doctor's white coat, Alaska's Mae West on Snatch Game, the ideal pageant queen - are scripted performances with 'ideal types,' so the muscle-car seducer in the song is doing unwitting drag. The resolution: 'drag as ontology' is the low everyday form everyone performs, while Drag Race stages the high-art form that consciously fucks with the social script.
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 28 "Final Act" — Shaw argues everyone at 30 Rock performs a role that shields them from Sartrean radical freedom: Kenneth is Sartre's cafe waiter in bad faith, believing television is America's true art form and willing to 'die at my post' for NBC, while Jack psyches himself up with corporate slogans and Jenna's 'Black Tie' candor about marrying the last Hapsburg to be taken care of is the rare moment of good faith. Butler's gender performativity explains Jack's masculinity as a repeated script, from his Glengarry Glen Ross 'always be talking' allusion to Baldwin's brass-balls speech to his homosocial man-crushes on Don Geiss and Dick Cheney. Plato's wariness of imitation, Nietzsche on hypocrisy hardening into character, and Santayana's tragic mask frame the closing thought: the actors know they are performing, but the characters, like us, do not.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 20 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Uses the sex/gender distinction drawn since Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex to read Tobias: biologically male but performing femininity (knitting, Mrs. Featherbottom, crying in the shower in cutoffs), he exposes our false conflations of sex, gender, and sexual orientation behind the running 'Tobias is gay' gag. His interchangeable pronoun use (Steve Holt (!) is a 'she' when cast as Beatrice) and 'buy-curious' double entendres embody the claim that gender is something we do rather than are, and the chapter proposes him as an androgynous, possibly pansexual ideal whose real 'problem' is society's gender biases, not his.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 16 "Who They Are or Who They Want to Be" — Harwood-Smith argues, against Descartes's pre-given 'I think therefore I am,' that Judith Butler's performativity explains the Cylons: Six is female because she performs femininity, no copy performs identically, and Cylon society fractures into hybrid identities with an 'embarrassed etc.' Sexual contact with humans is the catalyst that makes performance constitute reality, producing Athena's defection, Caprica Six's celebrity status, and D'Anna's religious fervor, while Cylons who never slept with humans stay apart. The same dynamic destabilizes humans who sleep with Cylons: Baltar's 'I must be a Cylon because I slept with one,' Tyrol's fear, and Helo's 'toaster lover' stigma, with Tigh's chosen stability ('that's the man I want to be') as the counterexample of performing who you want to be.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 29 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — White and Fisher run the show's women (and men) through feminist philosophy: the sex/gender distinction from Plato's Republic Book V and Mill's Subjection of Women through Beauvoir's 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' and Butler's antiessentialist performativity. Penny's hyper-femininity reads as Butlerian parody that satirizes the script, the Penny–Bernadette–Amy lineup exposes the custom that smarts and beauty must trade off, and Elizabeth Plimpton and Leslie Winkle ('come for the breasts, stay for the brains') break it — while the four guys fail every 'real man' stereotype beside Penny's muscle-bound exes like Zack. Gender emerges as an artificial label that limits everyone, and seeing that would be the show's ultimate change through parody.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 23 "12 Panther Mystique Wakandan Feminism Demystified" — Wright and Pérez ask whether Wakanda's powerful women are feminists, arguing M'Baku's dismissal of Shuri as a child trades on Friedan's feminine mystique while Wakandan women escape Beauvoir's woman as the Other because their society, lacking any history of female oppression, never inscribed the second sex. Drawing on Lorde, Davis, Collins, and Walker's womanism, they read Shuri's rejection of romance, Okoye's throne-loyalty, and Nakia's stubbornness as self-definition and interdependency across difference, then use Butler's gender performativity to explain why Okoye squirms in a wig while Nakia breezes through Seoul: womanhood performed in womanist (community-centered) versus feminist (individual-transcendence) modes, with Wakanda modeling the collective call for solidarity the authors hope the future inherits.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 17 "How Far I'll Go" — Maps the four waves of feminism onto Disney princess history: Snow White, Cinderella, and Aurora as chattel passed from parents to fairies to princes, betraying even first-wave rights; Beauvoir's 'one is not born but becomes a woman' and Friedan's feminine mystique explaining why the original trio's happiness is measured by marriage. Third-wave princesses are read with Wolf's beauty myth (Ariel and Jasmine as iron maidens), Butler's gender performativity, and Gilligan's care ethics (Ariel's and Belle's contextual, caring moral reasoning versus their fathers' principles). The fourth-wave princesses from Tiana to Moana need no man at all while male leads (Naveen, Flynn, Kristoff, Maui) become vulnerable sidekicks, ending with #GiveElsaAGirlfriend and the thought that equality is balance rather than sameness.
- **The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire**, ch. 13 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" — Reading Salander as genderqueer rather than simply a woman, the chapter argues her feminism lies in swift retaliation against those who abuse women and in economic and sexual independence from men, while her refusal of every identity label ('I don't know what I am') aligns her with queer theory's anti-identity politics. Judith Butler's performativity grounds the reading: Salander's body modifications and wardrobe 'undo' conventional gendering, and her drag-like aliases—the big-busted heiress Monica Sholes and the quiet Irene Nesser—succeed at fraud and flight only through absolute adherence to heteronormative femininity, proving gender is continuously constructed. Foucault's History of Sexuality frames her pathologization, institutionalization, and regulated sexuality as the medicalization of the sexually peculiar, a disciplinary script she reverses by hacking, surveilling, and exposing the authorities who pathologized her, tattooing i am a sadistic pig, a pervert and a rapist onto Bjurman.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 21 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Jessica Miller shows Katniss coded masculine, since Collins built her from Theseus and Spartacus and her breadwinning, hunting, and defiance fit masculine norms, while Prim embodies everything Beauvoir says civilization 'produces' as feminine, and Panem itself proves oddly gender-neutral: women work the mines, Finnick is the sex symbol sold by Snow, and Coin is as ruthless as any man. She then reads Katniss's romance performance through Judith Butler: the kisses, caresses, and televised wedding gowns do not express a preexisting femininity but constitute one, down to Butler's radical claim that sex itself is a cultural norm, which reframes even the Games' reaping of one boy and one girl as a gendered ritual rather than a presocial biological fact. Cinna's burning bridal gown that transforms Katniss into the mockingjay makes the political payoff explicit: gender performed strategically becomes the rebellion's power, and the hunter-and-baker partnership offers an alternative to the dominant romance script.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 29 "Iron Man The End" — The Housels read Iron Man through Butler's gender performativity and Arendt's 'right to have rights': the male-voiced Jarvis replacing the female AI Jocasta, Tony's womanizing, and the evolving corporeal styles of Black Widow, Bethany Cabe, Madame Masque, and Sunset Bain all enact society's gender script across the waves of feminism, with the black leather suit arriving only in 1970 amid Second Wave Feminism. Arendt's Eichmann reporting and the 'banality of evil' — coined the same year, 1963, that Lee, Lieber, Heck, and Kirby, all children of Jewish immigrants, launched Iron Man — supply the justice frame: Tony's transformation of conscience after Afghanistan and his vigilante justice against his own oppressors refuse silent conformity and insist, ignoring political boundaries, that all oppressed people have rights.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 22 "“A Pamphlet’s Not Going to Cover It”" — Kasey Butcher and Megan Peters argue Veronica embodies a third-wave, sex-positive feminism: as jury foreman in 'One Angry Veronica' she refuses the 'Barbie' role the captain of industry assigns her; her over-the-top masquerades (flirting with store clerk Duane Anders, the temptation scenario at Patrick Nevin's door, mimicking Logan's manspreading) expose gender as a performance; and her defense of Carmen Ruiz against Tad's blackmail shows her grasp of how race, class, and gender intersect, per Kimberlé Crenshaw. Against the show's caricature of Lilith House as humorless 'feminist killjoys' picketing the Hearst rapes, they contend Veronica models a feminism that keeps femininity, sexuality, and play — refusing slut shaming while fighting for rape victims, an incest survivor, and blackmailed girls.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 21 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Pye and O'Sullivan use Judith Butler's performativity to read walkers as genderless proof that gender is done, not born: the little-girl walker 'troubles' gender like drag, while survivors regressively re-perform patriarchy—Lori's 'I'm a girl, you talk to him', Carol at the washboard, the men confiscating Andrea's gun while Daryl keeps his crossbow. They invoke Butler's primitive clan and incest taboo to explain how Shane's camp, Lori and Carl's haircuts, and Ed's threats reproduce protector/protected roles, yet point to counterexamples—Andrea and Amy fishing, Felipe the nurse, Carl asking to be taught—that show roles can be learned differently. Via Rorty's remark that assumptions become visible when their contradictories sound plausible, they argue clinging to gender baggage endangers everyone against an enemy stripped of ego and social contract that does not discriminate.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Jones examines Renna breaking Egwene into a damane in the Amazon series to argue that identity is a social performance policed by power, drawing on Erving Goffman's dramaturgical self and Judith Butler's gender performativity (scripts, props, and 'gender trouble' exemplified by Min's dress). He argues the a'dam enforces Renna's directing so completely that a damane cannot even pretend to be subjugated while holding a true self in reserve, taking performativity to its extreme. Using Dahl and Lukes on power, Becker on labeling, and Giddens's structuration, he shows how Seanchan institutional power makes labels like damane and marath'damane stick, and asks bleakly whether any agency (even suicide) remains.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 12 "Notes" — Donovan uses the New 52 Azzarello run's gods as a catalogue of gender stereotypes - jealous Hera hunting Zola, woman-incinerating Apollo, hyper-masculine First Born, self-sacrificing Demeter - then tracks Hera's transformation after Apollo makes her mortal as a Beauvoirian passage from immanence (being Zeus's Other, defined by his desire) to transcendence (charting an independent identity, aiding baby Zeke). Foucault's Panopticon explains how gender norms are internalized without an enforcer, and Butler's drag example grounds the claim that Wonder Woman accepting the god of war mantle - leading a female Amazon army 'not as your princess but as the god of war' - is a subversive performance of gender.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 25 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Jonsson argues that modern sport enforces masculine norms and that the East German 'wonder girls' (Koch, Ender, Krabbe), along with Stella Walsh, Jarmila Kratochvilova and Caster Semenya, were 'gender radical' Amazons who challenged the link between masculinity and maleness by winning with 'masculine' bodies. Drawing on Judith Butler's claim that gender ideals are not static and women's sport can rearticulate them, he treats the doping-built Eastern Bloc athletes as progressive because they contradicted how female athletes are 'supposed' to look. He critiques Jane English's appeal to 'permanent biological differences' and laments that after 1989 commercialized sport (symbolized by Flo Jo's marketed femininity) hardened conservative gender norms again.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 16 "Joanne Kyger “Descartes and the Splendor Of” Bridging Dualisms through Collaboration and Experimentation" — Falk analyzes Joanne Kyger's 1968 experimental video 'Descartes' and its script 'Descartes and the Splendor Of,' a condensed rewrite of the 'Discourse on Method' that subverts Descartes's mind-body dualism and privileging of reason. Kyger deflates the cogito with slang ('to doubt is a drag'), substitutes Buddhist, Taoist (Zhuangzi's butterfly dream), and Confucian terms, and—voicing and performing Descartes as a woman doing housework and as 'Mother God'—feminizes the most masculine of professions. Reading this through Judith Butler's 'Gender Trouble' and gender performativity, Falk shows the parody destabilizes the mind/body, male/female hierarchy Cartesian dualism underwrites.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 17 "Charlie Kaufman, Philosophy, and the Small Screen" — Chambers reads Kaufman's TV sitcom Ned and Stacey through queer theory, arguing its marriage-of-convenience premise stages a critique of 'the normal.' Because Ned and Stacey only play at being husband and wife and never desire the romantic telos, the show troubles heteronormativity more than the openly gay Will & Grace, whose characters chase marriage and family. Chambers uses Butler's Lacanian notion of masquerade to claim there is no 'real' husband or wife beneath the role, only role-playing, and ties this to the philia (not eros) bond of the leads and to the masquerade running through Kaufman's films.
- **The Philosophy of Horror**, ch. 8 "Heteronormative horrors" — Reading virgins and the vagina dentata as the dyad through which horror polices female sexuality, the chapter uses Irigaray's account of the virgin as prop to male subjectivity and Creed's femme castratrice to analyse Halloween's 'Final Girl', Teeth's toothed-vagina revenge on abstinence-only purity culture, Jennifer's Body and Haute Tension. It closes with Rich's 'compulsory heterosexuality' and Wittig's 'heterosexual contract' to argue horror naturalises heteronormativity by casting female sexuality as either contained (virgin) or monstrously open (vagina dentata).
- **The Philosophy of Spike Lee**, ch. 17 "Feminists and “Freaks” She’s Gotta Have It and Girl 6" — Hoffman assesses whether Lee's She's Gotta Have It and Girl 6 offer liberated female sexuality, drawing on second- and third-wave feminism and bell hooks. She argues Nola Darling only appears empowered before the rape scene and her submission ('Yours') reveal her as an underdeveloped object of the male gaze, whereas Girl 6, as a phone-sex worker consciously performing gender for callers, better exposes gender as socially constructed in a Butler-like sense. Even so, Girl 6's real feminist force lies not in its heroine but in its exposure of oppressive industries, especially the opening Tarantino audition where only the director's gaze counts.
- **The Philosophy of Werner Herzog**, ch. 18 "Herzog’s Philosophy of Masculinism" — Will Lehman argues that beneath Herzog's rejection of any guiding philosophy lies a 'masculinism' that exalts traditionally manly traits (courage, strength, independence, emotional control) as the heroic. Drawing on gender theory (Dozier on beards and the performance of gender), he shows Herzog fetishizing 'manly men,' reading illiteracy and calloused hands as authentic manhood (Jared Talbert in Into the Abyss), and coding even his female subject Juliane Koepcke (Wings of Hope) in masculine terms. Lehman reads Herzog's reenactment 'therapy' with Dengler and Dorrington as an assertion of dominance, while noting Herzog avoids overt misogyny or homophobia.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 30 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Zanin reads Pride and Prejudice and Zombies through Freud, Aristotle, and Levinas.
