- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 20 "Forwards Win Matches but Defences Win Trophies" — Wall asks when the professional foul—the defender who 'had to bring him down'—could be a genuinely moral act, testing it against Kantian universalizability and the good will and against Bentham-and-Mill utilitarianism, and settling on psychologically altruistic motivation as what could override the foul's default wrongness. Against the psychological egoists (La Rochefoucauld, Slote, Hobbes) who would dissolve even Di Canio's caught ball into self-interest, he deploys Nagel's argument from The Possibility of Altruism and the soldier-on-the-grenade case, then derives tight conditions: a deliberate, minimally harmful foul, in a game it can decide, in a semifinal whose red card the fouler will certainly miss. Ballack's 2002 tactical foul on Lee Chun-Soo comes closest but fails (he stayed on the pitch), as do Schumacher's assault on Battiston, Fletcher's pointless foul at 4–0 up, and Abidal's accidental clip—so genuinely moral professional fouls are rare, but defenders get the most shots at being the team's saints.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 19 "Back at the Bins, or Loving Your Enemy Like Your Neighbor" — Kohn begins with her own response to a serial bin-tipper: practicing iaido sword draws in full view of the neighbours to intimidate an imagined Other. Contrasting iaido's virtual opponent (a mere tool for the self) with aikido's real partners, she deploys Levinas's face of the Other, responsibility without waiting for reciprocity and philosophy as 'the Wisdom of Love', alongside Arendt's shared responsibility for the world's conflicts, to argue that care for even one's attacker comes first, with Kant's categorical imperative as the generalizable counterpart to Levinas's ethics. Her confession: she treated the imagined culprit as an object of hate, when meeting 'the Face' would have demanded an apology and maybe a hug.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 34 "Kind of, Sort of a Lie, But neither Immoral nor Illegal" — Cynthia McWilliams imagines a reader beating her neighbor after taking 'Pedophile Nervous For First Day Of School' literally, and asks whether The Onion lied to her and whether that lie was wrong. She defines a lie as asserting what you believe false (intent to deceive is not required), then tests the satire on both classic accounts: on Kant's categorical imperative, a lie without intent to deceive does not use readers merely as means, while on Mill's utilitarianism the entertainment benefit outweighs harm unless serious harm is reasonably foreseeable — the limit case being the 1938 and Quito 1949 War of the Worlds broadcasts, the second of which killed six people in a riot. Her verdict: The Onion is 'kind of, sort of a lie' but neither immoral nor illegal, passing even the Brandenburg 'imminent lawless action' standard for free speech.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 23 "Allons-y into the Starry Heavens" — Smith reads the Doctor–Rose tragedy through Kantian deontology: shaped by Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's virtue ethics into a good will, both must still choose duty over inclination, so in 'Parting of the Ways' and the Battle of Canary Wharf in 'Doomsday' they each act from the categorical imperative — sacrificing their love to save humanity — because love, as Kant warns, impels partiality. Even in 'Journey's End' the Doctor sends Rose to Pete's World with the meta-crisis Doctor for the greater good, ending alone under Kant's starry heavens and the moral law within.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 8 "The (Single) Garden Path" — Compares Herbert's three eugenics programs: the Bene Gesserit's centuries-long Kwisatz Haderach breeding scheme (explicitly modeled on the communal breeding of the guardians in Plato's Republic, undone when Jessica bears Paul a generation early and he escapes their control), Leto II's Golden Path breeding for Siona's invisibility to prescience, and the Tleilaxu axolotl-tank immortality that collapses when their Face Dancers out-mimic them. Each program is weighed ethically—Leto as the 'ultimate consequentialist' whose species-saving tyranny invokes Mill's utilitarianism and Machiavelli's ends-justify-the-means, the Sisterhood as shifting toward Kantian duties against using persons as mere means. Herbert's lesson: 'the most dangerous of all creations is a rigid code of ethics,' whether aimed at a single person, a single result, or a single agenda.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 15 "I’ve Got No Strings . ." — Richard Greene asks whether it was practically rational for Dexter to trust Lumen rather than kill her, to help her revenge-kill the Fowler ring, and to train her as a killer. The good outcomes do not help - Masuka's strip-club windfall shows luck is not rationality, and Socrates' Apology argument that corrupters risk harm from those they corrupt, together with Dexter's prior disaster in training Miguel, means the consequences were not foreseeably good. Kantian tests fail too - no one could will a universal law of killing, and killing violates the victim's autonomy and humanity as an end in itself - as do decision theory and instrumentality theories, so no account of practical rationality vindicates Dexter's choices, suggesting instead that the emotionless 'wooden boy' is beginning to become a real one.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 22 "Vigilante Hero" — Epright and Worth argue that rule-following - the Ten Commandments, the Golden Rule, Kant's categorical imperative (whose consistent Kantian never lies even to Nazis), or the Bentham-Mill principle of utility (whose consistent utilitarian must torture if stakes are high) - never made anyone moral, and Dexter's Code is the case in point: it gives the appearance of morality while licensing murder, and its source (Harry, 'God', the texts) cannot vindicate it. Drawing on Jonah Lehrer's neuroscience that moral judgment is emotional first with reason as post-hoc lawyer, they argue the emotionless Dexter is the madman who has lost everything except his reason, and Kohlberg's moral-development stages find him stuck at the pre-conventional level, below a fifth-grader - punishment-avoidance and you-scratch-my-back reasoning, never universal principles or respect for persons. Real Dexter-inspired killers (Mark Twitchell, Andrew Conley) clinch the verdict: he is neither vigilante hero nor moral agent, just a selfish addict whose rule-governed kills justify nothing.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 23 "You Control Your Urges—They Do Not Control You" — Waller and McAlear first rebut the amoral reading: Dexter does feel (he sobs over Rita, loves Deb, misses Harry) and does control his urges through the Code, so morality applies to him, and the Dark Passenger is merely everyone's socially unacceptable desires - the very thing that gives rise to moral codes. They then test the three theories: Aristotelian virtue ethics mostly fails because murder admits no mean and Harry's Code teaches killer's skills rather than virtues (though its 'don't kill innocents' dispositions are genuine virtues); utilitarianism fails even in rule-utilitarian form - via the organ-harvesting doctor and Harry's own utilitarian guilt over Laura Moser's death - because Dexter kills because the Code requires it, not because it maximizes happiness. What fits is dark deontology: like Kant's argument that murderers consent to their own execution out of respect for their rationality, Dexter kills only killers, acts from duty rather than enjoyment, and treats 'don't get caught' as a condition for the possibility of his true imperative.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 14 "Invisibility or Honesty" — Schulzke argues inception's fundamental wrongness is a violation of autonomy read through Kant: the Fischer team treats him merely as a means, and even Cobb's benevolently intended inception on Mal disrespects humanity by stripping her self-determination, leaving her - like someone acting under coercion - no longer a responsible moral agent. Extraction he judges the lesser evil, though a world of dream espionage would end private mental life, since even the most guarded secrets surface in dreams. The payoff is a new twist on the Ring of Gyges from Plato's Republic: an invisibility ring could no longer shield injustice because a dreamer's deeds remain recorded and extractable, so Kant's absolute ban on lying could make extraction an engine of honesty - as when Ariadne's extraction on Cobb exposes the danger Mal poses and ultimately saves Cobb himself.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 78 "Categorically, We Have an Imperative Problem" — Measures the spying in A Scanner Darkly and Total Recall against Kant's second formulation of the categorical imperative: Benny merely tracks Quaid, while the federal agents sacrifice 'Fred's' entire psyche, devaluing his humanity as a mere means. It then stages the real-world debate the fiction mirrors — the Pike and Church Committees, Godfrey's preference for technological collection, and Langan's utilitarian defense that devaluing a few is justified when society's safety requires it.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 20 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Solves the 'riddle' of Gus by showing his empire runs on corporate instrumental rationality: the careful, emotion-disciplined Los Pollos CEO launders meth through legitimate business, treats chemists as replaceable parts (the Gale plan), and exacts revenge on the cartel in 'Salud' by drinking his own poisoned tequila. The chapter defines this as the critical theorists' amoral means-end reason - Kant's hypothetical imperative without the categorical - making Gus a sociopath who violates the injunction to treat persons as ends, and reads his cartel war through Machiavelli and Hobbes's power-first picture of the state. Gus's Two-Face-like corpse reveals the split between the rage-driven avenger of Max and the respectable mask, foreshadowing what Walt becomes.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 32 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Stages the standard three-way ethics debate on Walt: deontology's universalizability (Kant) absurdly forbids killing Krazy-8 even to save Walt's family, utilitarianism (Mill) licenses both cooking meth and murdering dealers - a outright contradiction - while Aristotle's virtue ethics judges character rather than acts and convicts Walt of vice: he endangers his family, misses Holly's birth, habituates himself into Heisenberg, and defrauds his school. Because acts and consequences alone cannot see character, virtue ethics is offered as the needed complement. The closing move widens the lens to America itself, arguing the capitalist success ethos and our appetite for anti-heroes like Tony Soprano and Dexter reveal a society that praises viciousness - 'we are what we repeatedly do.'
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 34 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Yuen distinguishes heroic survival cannibalism, as in the Andes crash of Alive, from the 'Fear the Hunters' cannibals: both utilitarianism and Kantianism permit eating those who already died out of necessity, since the dead lose no utility and corpses lack the rationality that grounds Kantian dignity. But Chris's band killed children to eat them and kept the living Dale as a food store, which fails both theories and cannot be excused by 'we don't do this because we want to,' since alternatives existed — joining other survivors, eating walkers ('zombitarianism'), or starving, because survival is never a moral obligation. Rick's execution of the hunters is then defended as Kantian retributive punishment: if Chris universalized his maxim that people may be hunted for food, then, as Rick suggests while biting Chris's neck, 'if Dale was good as a steak, so is Chris.'
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 11 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Cogburn protests Fourth Edition's contraction of the nine alignments and rebuilds the system philosophically: Lawful means willing universalizable law in Kant's categorical-imperative sense (the liar and murderer treating themselves as exceptions), Good means willing the greatest happiness in Mill's utilitarian sense, yielding a nine-box grid of moral psychologies. He populates it with fantasy archetypes—Haomane Firstborn as pathological Lawful Neutral, Karsa Orlong as Chaotic Neutral, Abercrombie's torturer Glotka as Neutral Neutral in Hannah Arendt's 'banality of evil' mold, hierarchic vampires and cynical politicians as Lawful Evil, Conan's raiders as Chaotic Evil. On this scheme Chaotic Good is genuinely empty, Drizzt and Robin Hood types are really Lawful or Neutral Good, and a Neutral Good versus Lawful Good dispute over killing one innocent to save thousands shows how gameplay can stage classic ethics thought experiments.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 19 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Fallis tests Kant's claim that a universal 'lie whenever it is to your advantage' would necessarily destroy itself, and David Lewis's stricter thesis that communication requires mostly truth-tellers, against a West Baltimore where Avon, Omar, the cops, the lawyers, and Templeton all lie constantly. Parfit's rejoinder - that as long as some people sometimes tell the truth, deception stays possible - explains how Bubbles's lies keep working, while the heroin market shows Kant's mechanism at full scale: Stringer cutting product and rebranding 'pandemic' until 'every dope fiend in the city knows that Avon been putting out piss, calling it shit' and Westside dope collapses. Since Gant's and Greggs's costly truths still anchor the practice, the chapter concludes The Wire cannot quite refute Kant: it is not possible for nobody to walk the straight and narrow track.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 29 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — John Wilkins treats Caesar, who spares the neighbor he has beaten, as a Kantian exemplar whose reason lets him adopt the Categorical Imperative, contrasting him with the rational egoism of the film's human keepers and executives. He argues the film trades on the outdated Great Chain of Being, which Darwinian tree thinking dissolves: with no higher or lower species, only branching homologies, human nature must be continuous with ape nature, and talk of innate species essences must allow for statistical variation and dispositions rather than determination. Caesar's morality also needs more than reason, namely the primate dispositions of deference and empathy scaffolded by his human family, though Buck's instant moral conversion after enhancement shows the film is ambivalent about whether scaffolding alone explains it.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 25 "Psych and Philosophy" — Stephenson tests Shawn's ruse against the major theories of justified deceit and finds it wanting: Plato's Myth of the Metals excuses paternalistic noble lies for social harmony that Shawn's self-aggrandizing motives cannot claim, utilitarianism collapses on the long-term costs of exposure (Gus, Juliet, Henry, and the SBPD condemned by association; clients betrayed; trust in law enforcement eroded), Kant's universalizability test sinks maxims like 'lie whenever a career opportunity is at stake,' and Popper's open society condemns just the deceit on which the psychic brand runs. Even the mutual-deceit analogy to poker and Sissela Bok's reasonable-person publicity test fail, since no public forum of reasonable people would bless duping paying private clients. The escape is extra-moral: Shawn's mischievous hokum is the socially necessary boundary-pusher, whose lesson against unreflective occult belief lands best when delivered with a laugh.
- **The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia**, ch. 15 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" — Kathleen Poorman Dougherty sets Kant's universal, emotion-free morality (echoed in Kohlberg's justice stages and Judge Abernathy's 'blind court' claim in 'Infamy') against Carol Gilligan's care ethic, which she says fits Saint Alicia far better: Alicia's practical advice to Jennifer Lewis in the pilot, driving Kenny home in 'Home', and telling Kenny's father 'I care a lot more about your son than he does' show connection producing both better morality and better lawyering. Feminist theorists like Nel Noddings and Sara Ruddick treat this care orientation as morally superior, not merely different, but the chapter's later sections weigh the cost: Kalinda's burnout warning, Alicia's resentment at always hand-holding clients, and the double bind by which women absorb society's unpaid caring labor. The verdict is that care is genuinely moral, but it must become a shared burden.
- **The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia**, ch. 18 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" — Lisa McNulty asks what could oblige us to believe someone: Peter's lying fails Kant's Categorical Imperative (a world of universal liars makes lying impossible), while friendship explains Alicia's readiness to believe client Kenny Chatham even before the evidence does. The 'Death Zone' libel trial over an Everest death shows that one's position of power fixes whom one owes presumptive belief - a reader should side with Cardiff, a judge must presume Lambrose innocent - and Pascal's Wager supplies the method of 'behaving like a believer': withholding rumors, withholding conviction, and Alicia publicly playing the wife and sleeping with Peter in a bid to believe in her marriage again. She concludes Peter forfeited any right to be believed, so Alicia has no moral obligation to behave like a good wife.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 20 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Fallis sorts Atlantic City's lies to show which are wrong and why. Kant's and Augustine's absolute bans go too far and Grotius's life-saving exception does not apply - most of these lies get people killed - yet even altruistic lies (Margaret for Madame Jeunet and the ledger), lies told to those who want to be deceived, lies to liars, and Sorensen's bald-faced lies that no one believes (Jimmy's flat movie alibi, Rothstein's 'skilled player' whopper) remain wrong: they take informed choice out of the victim's hands, violating the Kantian autonomy that grounds the wrong of lying, and they corrode the trust on which even criminals' co-operation depends.
- **How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness**, ch. 17 "How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy" — The chapter evaluates Marshall and Lily's promise to tell each other everything through Kant: lying violates the universalizable duty of truthfulness and treats the deceived as a mere means, as with Lily's hidden credit card debt in 'Dowisetrepla', the realtor's sewage-plant omission, and Barney's fully staged seduction of Meg that blocks her informed choice. Even Marshall's kindly lie about the doppelganger fails Kant's test, alongside his infamous refusal to lie to the murderer at the door. Yet Kant's letters on reticence in friendship and his grim view of marriage as shared ends where spouses may use each other 'as if' they were things suggest that telling each other everything may itself corrode respect - the tension Lily's never-opened bathroom door dramatizes.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 30 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Danny Smith applies Kant's three grades of evil from Religion within the Limits of Reason Alone to The Dark Knight. Batman's saving Harvey over Rachel out of love is normal evil (pathological inclination trumping duty, his 'never kill' rule hardened into moral self-satisfaction), Two-Face's coin is radical evil (outsourcing his freedom and responsibility to chance), and the Joker - burning his own money, making his scarred face the true mask, wanting only chaos - is diabolical evil done for its own sake. Smith then presses Kant's embarrassing problem that evil pursued purely on principle, with no pathological motive, is indistinguishable from the highest good, and half-sympathetically re-reads the Joker as the honest rebel in a corrupt Gotham.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 31 "The Devil and Philosophy" — George Dunn asks whether the Joker's 'some men just want to watch the world burn' motivelessness even makes sense. Against Baumeister's 'Myth of Pure Evil' and the Socratic-Aristotelian thesis that all wrongdoing aims at some apparent good, he tests Kant's claim that no human can be a diabolical being, Claudia Card's definition of diabolical evil as engineering others' moral corruption, and the Satan of Job as prosecuting accuser - which fits the Joker's ferry 'social experiment' and his breaking of Harvey Dent. The upshot is that the Joker's evil, fed by pride and the wish for credit for the conflagration, is instrumental, pathological, and banal after all, its best answer being the convict who throws the detonator out the window.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 32 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Nicole Pramik asks whether the demons of Brandon Mull's Fablehaven can be taught morality, using Kant's deontology as the measuring stick. Seth's kindness to Graulas looks dutiful and universalizable, and Graulas at first seems a rational agent respecting the categorical imperative - until healed, he betrays Seth, demolishes the preserve's treaty, and declares himself 'pure, deliberate evil' who used Seth as a mere means. Nagi Luna never even tries, and the Sphinx who models her is himself a serial user of persons, so the chapter concludes that rational demons remain impervious to the moral law: you can lead a demon out of Zzyzx, but you cannot make it good.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 62 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Robert Arp treats Voltaire's 'If God did not exist, then it would be necessary to invent Him' as a conditional claim and argues it is false: Kant's categorical imperative (universalize the action, as with lying and the collapsing practice of borrowing) and Mill's utilitarian cost-benefit calculus secure social order with no god and no Devil required. He then concedes that since most people are driven by guilt and fear rather than reason, inventing the Devil as an archetype of evil to be avoided at all costs may after all be a useful fiction.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 23 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Edwin Jacob contrasts the utilitarian calculus behind Walden's drone strike - Estes's eighty percent estimate, 'potential collateral damage falls within current matrix parameters', eighty-three children killed - with Kant's three formulations of the categorical imperative applied to that decision. On the universal-law formula Walden cannot will a world of strikes on one's own soil, on the humanity formula the schoolchildren are used merely as means, and the kingdom-of-ends formula condemns treating foreign lives as quantities in a matrix. The chapter adds that drones, like Brody's suicide vest, are asymmetric terror at a distance, and that blowback (Shahzad's Times Square attempt) shows the strategy fails even consequentialist test.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 13 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Montoya tests Simon's choice to sacrifice his sanity by wearing the crown to save child Marceline against three ethical theories. Aquinas's doctrine of double effect clears him because the intended good (saving her life) outweighs the merely foreseen side effect (her tears, his possible future evils); Kant's categorical imperative rules out universalizing 'let children die to save myself,' since a world of universal using destroys the rule itself; and a fountain case where Finn must choose between world-saving plans and a drowning candy child separates act from rule utilitarianism, with rule utilitarianism preserving the duty to rescue. All three converge on the verdict that Simon, not Finn, is Ooo's greatest hero.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 36 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — The chapter assembles real-life versions of Finn's Enchiridion, starting with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: the Golden Mean locates each virtue between two vices, so true courage is knowing when to fight and when to run - cowardice and 'stupidteous' recklessness as deficiency and excess - a balance Finn's all-out bravery lacks. Epictetus's Stoic Handbook (which inspired the emperor Marcus Aurelius) teaches that happiness depends only on one's own reactions and that events are good or bad by how we take them, making it a manual even the chronically disappointed Ice King could use, while Christine de Pizan's book of chivalry prepares heroes for defeat and Erasmus's Handbook of the Christian Knight with Praise of Folly makes Finn and Jake's 'foolish' mercy look righteous. Finally Kant's Groundwork supplies duty for duty's sake: by the categorical imperative, Finn was entitled to steal the ogre's dollar only if, as an ogre who had swallowed Jake, he would accept the same theft from a hero.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 21 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Framed by Dickens's Jacob Marley, Walker asks whether Jobs deserved his posthumous accolades despite giving far less to charity than Bill Gates, and tests him under three frameworks. Aristotle's virtue ethics acquits him (character is judged holistically, and charity sits near the golden mean of open-handedness rather than being a checklisted duty); Mill's utilitarianism acquits him (his innovations maximized happiness and he violated no Harm Principle—though abandoning daughter Lisa counts as a harm); and Singer's drowning-child argument condemns him as near-morally-bankrupt for selling luxury gadgets while children starve. Kant both convicts (charity is an imperfect duty under the categorical imperative) and saves Jobs: treating the affluent individual as an end in himself, never merely a means to the destitute, blocks Singer's demand for giving to marginal utility.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 16 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Altmann stages a moral (not legal) trial of Dracula with three expert witnesses: Kant testifies that Dracula universalizes murder only for himself while fleeing Harker's kukri, and that he reduced Harker to a mere meal, violating the categorical imperative and deserving execution; Mill weighs consequences, tallying the misery done to Lucy, her mother, and the Bloofer Lady's child victims, and argues the greatest happiness lies in imprisoning the Count for medical study instead; Aristotle argues the child-brained vampire lacks the reason and self-control needed for eudaimonia and so merits imprisonment rather than death. The chapter hands the verdict to the reader, showing guilt is agreed but punishment diverges across the three frameworks.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 28 "15. The Way of the Doctor Is Deception" — Dodge takes Rule #1 - the Doctor lies - through the major theories of lying: Bernard Williams's definition (asserting what you believe false with intent to deceive), Aristotle's claim that all lies are base, Kant's categorical imperative and respect for persons (even the Vinvocci's shimmer disguises in 'The End of Time' abuse trust), and Bentham's pleasure-pain calculus, which condemns the faked death at Lake Silencio ('The Impossible Astronaut') for the grief it caused Amy and Rory yet rewards the greater happiness it made possible. Against the absolutists he sets Plato's Noble Lie from the Republic - the elite falsehood that keeps society functioning - as what the Doctor emulates by deceiving the universe into thinking him dead ('The Wedding of River Song'), and Nietzsche's point in Human, All Too Human that lying is ethically neutral when the pretense is sustainable, as when the Doctor hides the ganger-Amy switch from Rory ('The Almost People'). The upshot: the Doctor's lies are wrong in themselves but routinely justified by the good they do, which is why sometimes the hero lies.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 35 "20. The Doctor Lies" — McCain distinguishes lying (directly asserting what you believe false to make another believe it) from mere deception - the Sixth Doctor feeding Jamie false information for Sontaran Stike to overhear in 'The Two Doctors' deceives without lying - then asks whether the Doctor can lie to himself, answering that incarnations can lie to later selves (the Eleventh's suspicious 'I have absolutely no idea' about the children on Gallifrey in 'The Day of the Doctor') but a current self cannot. The stakes are moral: against Kant's and Augustine's absolute prohibition of lying, Plato's Republic and Sidgwick's Methods of Ethics defend noble lies, and Robert C. Solomon's view of self-deception as coping with the unbearable suggests that if the Doctor did engineer himself to forget the Time War genocide - as Ten and Wilf did to Donna in 'Journey's End' - it might be a good man's forgivable way of going on.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 39 "24. Who’s Duty to Whom" — Dawson asks why the Doctor sides with humans and humanoids against rational non-humanoids, testing Kant first: a logic-grounded categorical morality can count the Daleks as immoral rather than amoral (universalized slavery is incoherent), but pure reason cannot motivate Daleks or the Master, and Kant's theory absurdly condemns the Doctor's lies and his theft of the TARDIS. Hobbesian psychological egoism and the social contract fare worse - the Daleks are no co-signatories, and self-sacrifices from Katarina to the Doctor's seemingly final years on Trenzalore resist the egoist's retelling - so the chapter lands with Hume: sympathy and benevolence found morality on feeling, which explains and partly excuses the Doctor's parochial partiality for beings who resemble him, making him 'at least half-Humean.'
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 26 "15. Tell the Truth at All Costs" — Bowman argues Candor is the most philosophically important faction because its absolute honesty is Kant's ethics: truthfulness as a perfect duty grounded in free will, making even politeness 'deception in pretty packaging,' and forbidding a lie even when the Erudite come to Merciless Mart hunting Tris - which mirrors Kant's reply to Benjamin Constant that one must not lie even to the murderer at the door. Against this he sets Aristotle's virtue ethics, where truth bows to wisdom, justice, and fortitude when the choice is handing hidden Jews to the SS, and Bentham's utilitarianism, which Amity enacts when it lies at the gates to keep the peace and save lives. The Candor Manifesto's 'web of individual-to-individual relationships' and Kant's kingdom of ends explain why universal honesty alone could make truth safe - and why Christina, the Candor, is the one left standing when the city's deception finally destroys it.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 10 "1. Finding the Meaning of Life in Downton Abbey" — Blessing tests the Steve Jobs/Oprah 'do what you love' creed against Downton, where rigid class structure assigns nearly everyone a role they did not choose. She distinguishes happiness from meaningfulness (Matthew's war wounds, Mary's grief after his death) and purposefulness (Grantham's custodian speech), then weighs subjectivist theories of meaning, including Nietzsche's idea that meaning arises from the passionate process itself, against Nozick's permanence view and Susan Wolf's hybrid 'subjective attraction meets objective attractiveness,' adding Kant's duty to develop one's talents against a world of idle pleasure. She concludes that the Abbey's ethos - Grantham as custodian not owner, Carson's pride in service, Patmore's kitchen, 'I have no right to be unhappy' - shows that socially necessary work one does not love can still make a meaningful life, while DWYL is elitist and narcissistic.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 19 "8. Lie Is So Unmusical a Word" — Neal pits Kant's absolute prohibition on lying against Violet's scheme after Sybil's death: the Dowager pressures Dr. Clarkson to 'review the evidence' until he tells Cora and Robert that surgery could not have saved their daughter, reuniting the marriage his honest second opinion had broken. Working through the Categorical Imperative, the murderer-at-the-door case, and Kant's essay 'On a Supposed Right to Lie Because of Philanthropic Concerns,' the chapter asks whether Clarkson actually lied ('Lie is so unmusical a word'). It concludes that his rational, carefully planned, dignity-respecting lie to save the family meets the criteria for a Kantian exception, so the rule against lying still holds while this particular lie is morally permitted.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 29 "17. Downton Abbey as Eternal Recurrence" — Christopher Ketcham asks whether primogeniture and entail make Downton Abbey a social embodiment of Nietzsche's eternal recurrence - the same estate, without revision, turned over generation after generation like the eternal hourglass of existence. Working through Lawrence Hatab's five interpretations of the doctrine, he tests royal continuity against death duties, the nihilism of industrial capitalism, and the Great War that killed heirs and empires, and borrows Kant's categorical imperative as an analogy for Britain's uniquely preserved 'royal categorical imperative' of continuity. The Abbey's recurrence survives only anthropomorphically - Violet, the family, the servants, and the tenants as its living organs - and the chapter wonders whether such ossified continuity, like dinosaur bones, is really eternal.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 15 "Walker Bite. Let’s Just Do What’s Right" — Devlin and Cooper present Dale as the show's Kantian deontologist: he acts from duty regardless of consequences, applying the humanity formula - treat people always as ends, never merely as means - when he blocks the execution of Randall in 'Judge, Jury, Executioner' and refuses to let the group do consequentialist math about abandoning the search for Sophia. Shane, the Governor, and the Termites serve as the consequentialist foils who treat Otis, the prison residents, and their victims as mere means to survival. The chapter argues Dale dies with his humanity and dignity intact, and that the series' recurring drama is a three-sided battle between his deontology, the survivors' consequentialism, and Rick's eventual virtue ethics.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 11 "1. True Love and False Fronts" — Fallis argues the movie is really about lying and duplicity, not true love: Humperdinck frames Guilder for Buttercup's abduction, the Dread Pirate Roberts is a serial persona, and even the heroes bluff their way into the castle. He treats this as 'adversarial epistemology,' showing that Descartes's malicious demon and Kant's argument that universalized lying is impossible only rule out extreme scenarios and cannot unmask mundane deceivers like Vizzini and Humperdinck (a point he sharpens with Parfit's objection that liars sometimes profitably tell the truth). What does real work are Hume's tools for evaluating testimony: Valerie catches Miracle Max lying about 'to blave' by asking what he has to gain, and Buttercup catches Humperdinck when his claim that every ship in the armada will accompany the honeymoon contradicts his promise of the four fastest ships.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 24 "13. Time to Choose" — Goldberg and Gavaler read the heroes' first-year comics (The Superman Chronicles, The Batman Chronicles) as rival moral codes: Superman is a "super consequentialist" out to benefit mankind - reforming the Blakely Mine owner, demolishing slums, buying back swindled stock - while Batman is a "dark deontologist" whose vengeance oath makes consequences irrelevant, waiting out the Joker's murders of Claridge, Wilde, and Judge Drake because catching the villain, not saving victims, is his duty. Mill's utilitarianism frames Superman's consequentialism and Kant's Groundwork - intentions over outcomes, the batarang blocked by invisible glass leaving Batman's morality untouched - frames Batman's, with moral luck the battleground: deontology shrugs it off, but Superman's powers let him smooth luck over too. On the opening dilemma, Superman defuses the bomb while Batman chases the villain, so the authors judge Superman's code superior because Batman's can let hundreds die without moral failure.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 21 "9. Variation under Ethics" — Weighs the clones' bodily autonomy against the special obligations they owe one another, since genetic sisters can harm each other as no strangers can: Helena's murder of Katja nearly pins a killing on Sarah, and Vic's drug-world drags danger into Alison's suburb. The chapter builds a clone-specific cousin of Kant's categorical imperative — "act only and always in a way that you would want your clone to act" — to argue that the clones' liberty may be legitimately more restricted than ours: Alison's public drunkenness endangers sisters who can be mistaken for her, clones arguably must stay in Clone Club and share medical information like Cosima's illness, and hard cases (Beth's suicide leaving cases dangling, the brain-cut-open Castor clone begging Helena to kill him) all turn on balancing autonomy against what we owe others.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 46 "30. Trying to Do Good with Arya, Tyrion, and the Hound" — Thomas sets Aristotle's practical wisdom against Bentham's utility calculus and Kant's consequence-proof rules, then watches all three struggle in season six. Arya's merciful refusal to poison Lady Crane backfires when the Waif kills her more painfully anyway; Tyrion's compromise with the Masters - phasing out slavery gradually, 'I trust their self-interest' - nearly loses Meereen when they attack by sea; and the resurrected Hound, after Brother Ray's massacre, concludes that 'lots of horrible shit in this world gets done for something larger than ourselves,' so being good in Westeros, as everywhere, means choosing without being able to know the consequences in advance.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 26 "12. Aaugh! Why Is Being Moral So Hard" — The chapter claims Schulz's humor is built on moral failure and illustrates the three main moral theories with specific strips: utilitarianism via Bentham's 'sovereign masters' of pain and pleasure and Charlie's 'to make others happy' (with Lucy noting nobody is making her happy), Kantian deontology via Sally's crayon lie and Snoopy's 'I haven't bitten anyone on the leg recently' as fulfilling a negative duty, and Aristotle's virtue ethics via the failed steal of home (foolhardy rather than courageous), the unmailed Valentine (cowardly), the golden mean, and Joe Shlabotnik as a hopeless role model. Charlie gritting his teeth shows mistaking a virtue's external markers for the virtue itself. It concludes we fit none of the theories well, yet Peanuts keeps a spirit of hope - happiness is a warm puppy, and Charlie's grit is genuine even if he cannot see it.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 28 "14. Is Lucy a Kantian or Just Mean and Nasty" — The chapter tries to acquit Lucy of meanness by reading her as a Kantian: her maxim for throwing Schroeder's piano into the Kite-Eating Tree fails universalization as a contradiction in conception, her blanket confiscations and 'settling for average' lectures enforce Kant's duty of self-improvement, and her brutal truth-telling honors the absolute ban on lying (a Mill-and-Bentham contrast highlights that Kant locates moral worth in intentions, not comfort or consequences). The football gag then undermines the defense: by withholding what Charlie needs to know - that she will pull the ball - she treats him as a mere means, and since what matters is her real intentions rather than her stated ones, the Kantian verdict is left to the reader.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 18 "7. And the Most Despicable Jessica Lange Character Is . ." — Ranks Jessica Lange's characters from least to most despicable using moral philosophy: Sister Jude earns credit for acting from duty (reporting the Nazi Dr. Arden at personal risk, Kant-style) and for genuinely feeling remorse; Elsa Mars partly honors the matriarchal obligations of care ethics but lacks Aristotle's habitual virtue and moderation, selling Bette and Dot to Dandy for fame; Constance Langdon abuses and effectively murders her disabled children; and Fiona Goode, motivated exclusively by youth, beauty, and power, murders her Supreme and torments Cordelia - never once acting out of concern for others.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 21 "11. Fighting Ethical Relativism in Tales of Suspense" — Reading Tales of Suspense, Pagnoni Berns and Veteri cast Iron Man as a man of every era - echoing LBJ's 'reason together', Cold War utilitarianism against Communism, playboy masculinity, and finally the Registration Act - which makes him a parrot of whatever relativism his age prefers. Captain America, literally frozen in time, holds Kant's categorical imperative: every life is an end in itself, so he saves Nazi prisoners in #71, trades his own life for a pilot in #61, and drinks possibly lethal serum without needing thanks, while Bucky's mediated, reward-seeking morality shows why ends corrupt moral worth. Because Cap's universal, ahistorical defense of human dignity holds from the 1940s to the 1960s and beyond, the authors rank him above the adaptable but context-bound Iron Man.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 25 "15. Iron Kant or Captain Kant" — Bosma and Barkman run both heroes' positions on the Superhuman Registration Act and the Sokovia Accords through Kant's deontology. Iron Man's maxim 'I should obey the government' looks universalizable, but it collapses once Cap's critique of the atomic bombings shows an unjust order (killing innocent civilians, or a Doctor Doom takeover) must be refused, and the humanity formulation condemns registration for treating heroes as mere means to the government's ends. Cap's own maxims - fight for freedom and justice, obey only a just government - universalize cleanly, so the chapter awards the deontological duel to Captain America.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 15 "5. Albert Among the Chowder-Head Yokels and Blithering Hayseeds" — Argues that Albert Rosenfield embodies Kant's categorical imperative: his refusal to soften his autopsy demands or lie to spare feelings is fidelity to universalizable maxims, and his insistence that Sheriff Truman be charged for punching him treats punishment as respect for a rational agent's autonomy. The chapter walks through maxims, the universalizability test applied to Gordon Cole's possibly faked deafness and FBI lying, hypothetical versus categorical imperatives (Cooper may always want Norma's cherry pie, but morality trumps want), and the formula of humanity — Ben Horne's use of One-Eyed Jack's women as mere means is the counterexample, while Albert's insults paradoxically honor Truman's rational agency. Albert's arc to "I love you, Sheriff Truman" and his gentler Season Two and The Return self shows a Kantian who integrates classical reason with romantic feeling.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 27 "16. Who Am I to You" — James Okapal sets up the Kantian view — moral agency, shown by passing the contradiction-in-conception test (which Wallace's 'all should be masters of slaves' fails), is the precondition of moral status, so non-agents like replicants, on Tibor Machan's extension of Kant to animals, matter no more than toasters — against the ethics of care of Nel Noddings and Carol Gilligan. On the care reading, K's and Batty's final acts of ethical caring, like Joi's risky choices for K, confer moral status on another and thereby constitute moral agency, reversing the Kantian order. Empathy, not universalizable reason, is what removes bricks from Joshi's wall.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 21 "9. Send The Good Place to the Bad Place" — Sheldon argues the Season One twist makes the show itself a moral paradox: a series about ethics that lies to its audience for thirteen episodes, breaking the informal contract it built through 'truth in fiction'. Through Chidi's red-cowboy-boots lie and Eleanor's plot to murder Janet, 'The Eternal Shriek' stages Kant's absolute prohibition on lying against Eleanor's Machiavellian ends-justify-means reasoning, with confession portrayed as the only release from escalating deception. The chapter ends with Eleanor citing Jonathan Dancy's moral particularism to get Chidi to lie his way through the Bad Place, leaving viewers to decide whether the show's own deception is justified by the ethical conversation it forces.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 22 "10. A Love Story between Theory and Praxis" — Altmann allegorizes Chidi as Theory and Eleanor as Praxis, whose 'love story' shows each completing the other: Chidi's lessons in utilitarianism and Kant's Categorical Imperative give Eleanor reasons, and eventually a lived example in Michael's feigned self-sacrifice, to confess her lie, while Eleanor's pragmatism in the Bad Place teaches Chidi that principles useless in the world must be revised. Michael's arc from designing psychological torture to giving Eleanor his portal pin demonstrates a theory of human nature, that people cannot change, being falsified by praxis. The chapter closes with Eleanor re-entering the cycle by finding Chidi's lectures online, recommending the union of theory and praxis as how anyone becomes a better person.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 23 "11. Those Agonizing Choices" — Romanowski traces Chidi's indecision from the cowboy-boots lie through the rock-paper-scissors panic attack, arguing the show treats the agony of deciding as the universal human moral condition rather than a professor joke. 'The Trolley Problem' makes Foot's dilemma literal torture, and the show pointedly never gives the right answer, confirming Chidi's claim that there are no clean solutions to hard moral questions. Eleanor's Dancy-inspired particularism pitch in 'Rhonda, Diana, Jake, and Trent' and Michael's 'I solved the Trolley Problem: you sacrifice yourself' moment, together with Chidi finally kissing Eleanor, show that acknowledging uncertainty is no excuse for inaction.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 27 "14. Is Kant the Reason Everyone Hates Moral Philosophy Professors" — Duindam defends Kant against the charge that he makes moral philosophy professors insufferable, walking through maxims and the two-question Categorical Imperative test with frozen-yogurt and stealing examples, and arguing that Kant's notorious 'you cannot lie to the murderer' essay is an obscure legal point whose actual test permits lying to demons. On the trolley, the bridge, and Michael's forced organ-harvesting scenario, Kant's humanity formula, never treat persons merely as means, explains both Chidi's refusal to kill Eleanor and the difference between switching tracks and pushing a man. Tahani's sixty billion dollars in charity earning no points, and Eleanor's fruitless 'What's My Motivation' blitz versus her costly confession, vindicate Kant's claim that only a good will gives actions moral worth, while Aristotle supplies the closing lesson that being good takes practice, not just study.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 36 "20. Moral Health Warning" — The moral philosopher Jonathan Dancy issues a warning against the show's premise that studying moral philosophy can make you a better person, the assumption behind Chidi's entire tutelage of Eleanor. What makes someone good is their motivation, and reading Kant and Scanlon is at best self-indulgent study that never redirects the will toward the right; indeed anyone genuinely motivated by the good would stop reading moral philosophy and go do good instead. He also contests the Kantian thought that only action done from a sense of duty earns moral credit: Douglas Wynegar's roses for his grandmother, given out of love, should count without any thought of obligation.
- **Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney**, ch. 10 "2. A Paragon of Righteous Virtue" — Allinson reads Gardner's novels, especially The Case of the Blonde Bonanza, as philosophy disguised as pulp: Mason acts from curiosity, compassion, and justice rather than utility, a 'pure Kantian or ancient Confucian' deontologist whose loyalty to clients ('erase ATTORNEY AT LAW from the door') functions as his own Categorical Imperative. The chapter's crux is the perjury dilemma of the Blonde Bonanza: Mrs. Winlock's offered false testimony would free Dianne Alder, which Mason twice refuses yet curses ('To hell with it'), showing that the plot's deus ex machina dissolves but never solves the ethical dilemma, while George Winlock's truth-telling-at-any-cost mirrors Kant's prohibition on lying even to the Gestapo. Socrates's better-to-suffer-evil, Plato's Meno reversal, Aristotle's rhetoric, Confucian and Hebrew filial piety in Dianne's character, and Rawls's justice as fairness all serve as lenses on Mason's virtues.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 29 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Reads Bluth contradiction through Kant's categorical imperative: Lindsay's lie about her shopgirl job, Gob's jealousy bred by comparative parenting, and George Michael's conformist drift show both the imperative's force and the danger of its empty formalism, while the 'Afternoon Delight' double entendres test whether good intentions suffice for Kantian worth. Nietzsche then answers that morality itself is the contradiction: virtue manufactured from ressentiment ('weakness is being lied into something meritorious'), the will to power turned inward as nihilism, with self-overcoming and value creation as the exit; Mary Douglas's joke theory closes the chapter by explaining why all this contradiction is comic and why the joke is on Gob.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 19 "What if Hama Was Wrong" — Gregory argues bloodbending necessarily uses persons as mere means because it overrides the victim's will regardless of their actual consent, unlike buying tea from Zuko but like Azula's deception of Long Feng, and so violates Kant's Formula of Humanity in every offensive use. Katara's bloodbending of Hama in self-defense is permissible because she stops Hama's wrong rather than using her toward any end, and even a hypothetical consensual 'cooperative model' cannot redeem the practice, since the sheer power it grants and its corrupting effects on practitioners (Noatak and Tarrlok in LoK) justify Katara's ban.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 11 "Sometimes Heroes Fail" — James DiGiovanna asks whether it was right for Batman to turn street kids Dick Grayson and Jason Todd into Robin. He tests the training against Kant's universalizability (including the Joker-demanding-to-know-where-Robin-is lie example), against Bentham and Mill's utilitarian appeal to Gotham's general good, and finally reads it through the virtue ethics of Plato, Aristotle, and MacIntyre's After Virtue, where Robin is trained into a role-specific character rather than taught rules. Jason's rashness and death at the Joker's hands show Batman failed to moderate his ward's courage, and the chapter concludes Batman is 'a lousy deontologist, a decent consequentialist, and some kind of virtue ethicist.'
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 25 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Fallis uses Sheldon — a lousy liar with an elaborate theory of lying — to probe the philosophy of lying: Kant's absolute prohibition (even 'out of frivolity'), Bok's presumption against deceit, Plato's noble lies reserved for philosopher kings, and Nietzsche's self-deceiving overmen, whose counsel explains the 'un-unravelable webs' of fake Facebook and blog evidence for the imaginary cousin Leopold Houston. Ryle's knowing-how versus knowing-that split explains how Sheldon can state the rules ('casually, no rapid breathing') yet botch the performance, while the Bazinga! pranks and the insincere courtroom apology break the Augustinian definition that lying requires intent to deceive. Grice's norms of conversation then ground the author's own definition — lying as intending to violate the norm against saying what you believe false — until a hypothetical, convention-oblivious liar like Kripke forces him to concede a counterexample and admit he was wrong.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 18 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Jollimore and Jones diagnose three 'very unDude' vices: Walter's rule rigidity, which confuses Kant's hypothetical rules of games (don't cross the foul line) with categorical moral ones and needs 'rules all the way down' to ward off nihilism; the Big Lebowski's hypocritical inauthenticity, a fake achiever living on his daughter's allowance who collapses facedown before his own rug; and the exclusionism with which everyone shuts Donny out of the conversation. Against these the Dude exhibits Aristotelian virtue as good judgment (knowing when rules don't apply), the Golden Mean between Walter and the nihilists, and Singer-style inclusion — 'he's in bed with everybody' — making him an authentic man of humor and perspective.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 12 "Our First Gaze into the Black Mirror" — Collins and Boesch use Prime Minister Callow's coerced live sex act with a pig in The National Anthem to weigh conflicting moral obligations: the public's initial 72% Kantian refusal flips to an 86% utilitarian capitulation after the kidnapper's finger video, and the withheld revelation that Susannah was released half an hour early undermines any consequentialist justification of the act. A virtue-theory reading faults Callow's character for faking the rescue video and putting self-interest first, and the UKN media's Kantian compliance collapses once ratings are at stake. The closing section applies Martha Nussbaum's theory of disgust (contamination transferring disgust from blood and vomit to the spectacle-watchers themselves) to argue the episode's graphic imagery functions as a moral emotion condemning the audience's own obsession with spectacle.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 17 "“Don’t forget, she’s a dangerous individual”" — The chapter tests the White Bear Justice Park's daily torture of Victoria Skillane against every major theory of punishment: Kant and Hegel's retributivism makes her deserve punishment (her crime could not be universalized and annulled justice) but cannot justify a punishment disproportionate to the crime. Locke's memory criterion suggests Punished Victoria is not the person who did the crime, though Parfit's psychological continuity and Thomson's bodily continuity restore the identity. Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism partially vindicates the park as deterrence and incapacitation, but cannot explain the laughing crowds — which Machiavelli's civic spectacle and Nietzsche's genealogy of punishment (Schadenfreude as moralized creditor-debtor pleasure) explain: the crowd is gleefully reenacting Victoria's own crime and calling it justice.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 31 "Learning from Mia’s Mistakes" — The chapter grades each of Mia's escalations in Crocodile — helping Rob hide the cyclist's body, killing Rob fifteen years later, then killing Shazia, her husband, and baby Ali to keep the secret — under Kant's categorical imperative (the cover-up cannot be universalized and treats persons as means), the utilitarian calculus (which also condemns every killing once the widow's suffering and Mia's guilt are counted), and feminist care ethics, which rejects her defense that she killed to protect her family because care obligations never cancel proportionality and others' rights. Aristotle's virtue ethics supplies the diagnosis: Mia's undoing is lack of practical wisdom — every split-second choice (which she never had time to deliberate) went wrong because she lacked virtuous habits. The chapter urges practicing everyday virtue so we never take the first step down her path.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 32 "20 The Value of Vibranium" — Edwardo Pérez asks what makes vibranium 'the most valuable metal known to man' through Marx's distinction between use value and exchange value: Klaue prizes exchange value (money, power, a black-market arm), while Wakandans structure their whole society around use value and never trade the metal. The museum scene raises cultural property - does vibranium belong to Wakanda, as the cultural nationalist holds, or to humanity, as the cultural internationalist holds? - and T'Challa's shift on sharing it is analyzed through Kant's categorical imperative versus Bentham's utilitarian calculus, with his saving of Agent Ross and sparing of M'Baku vindicated by their consequences. Vibranium's greatest value, the chapter concludes, is atonement: redeeming T'Chaka's crime and uniting humanity as 'one single tribe.'
- **Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality**, ch. 24 "Black sabbath & philosophy" — Mark D. White shifts the is-it-still-Sabbath question from metaphysics to ethics, asking whether bands owe fans a stable line-up when they keep the name. Kant's Formula of Universal Law permits the maxim "change members, keep the name" without contradiction, and the Formula of Respect forbids only coercion or deceit, using fans as mere means, so the real wrong is deceptive marketing, as when record-company pressure billed Iommi's solo project Seventh Star as "Black Sabbath featuring Tony Iommi" and sent it out playing "War Pigs" and "Iron Man". The Dio reunion's honest rebranding as Heaven & Hell passes the test, while fans, symmetrically, owe bands no loyalty and may legitimately love only one era.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 33 "“It's Been Handed Down from Goof to Goof to Goof, and Now, It's Yours, Son”" — Mentyka uses Goofy to test theories of the good life: Socratic intellectualism stumbles on uneducated-but-good Goofy, Kant's categorical imperative absurdly forbids handing Max the 'goof to goof' fishing pole (Goofy can't will it universal law), Mill's utilitarianism fails when Max's lukewarm reception makes the gift happiness-reducing, and Singer's extension to animals muddies Pluto the dog against Goofy the dog treated as a person. The chapter resolves with Scheler's claim that we first encounter values through moral exemplars — earnest, bumbling Goofy — not through rules or consequences, and a closing plea that philosophers narrate less like the smug 'How to...' narrator.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 10 "1. Finding the Meaning of Life in Downton Abbey" — Blessing pits Steve Jobs's 'Do What You Love' creed (and Oprah's 'follow your bliss') against Downton's world of inherited roles, where nobody from Anna to Lady Mary chooses their work. She distinguishes happiness from meaningfulness, since Matthew's war wounds and Mary's grief over his death are painful yet deeply meaningful, and tests subjectivist theories such as Nietzsche's meaning-as-passionate-process against Nozick's demand that a meaningful life leave permanent traces and Susan Wolf's hybrid 'loving objects that are worthy of love.' Kant's duty to develop one's talents rather than idle for pleasure, and Lord Grantham's self-description as 'a custodian, not an owner,' anchor the show's counter-ethos of duty over desire, embodied in Carson, Mrs. Hughes, and Mrs. Patmore's pride in unloved, socially necessary work. The chapter concludes that Downton validates hard honest work as an end in itself, challenging the narcissism of the 'holy You' and expressive individualism.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 19 "8. Lie Is So Unmusical a Word" — Neal weighs Dr. Clarkson's coached retraction, that surgery would not have saved Sybil after all, engineered by Violet with 'Lie is so unmusical a word' to end Cora's blame of Robert and reunite the grieving couple, against Kant's absolute prohibition on lying in his moral works and in 'On a Supposed Right to Lie.' She lays out Kant's reasoning that lying destroys the trust, dignity, and rights that make rules binding, with the murderer-at-the-door case as the classic objection, then argues Clarkson's lie approaches an exception because it is rational, carefully deliberated, and aimed at preserving the Crawleys' dignity and the household itself rather than personal gain. The chapter concludes that the Kantian rule still holds generally, but this particular lie, for this particular moral reason, can be excused.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 8 "The (Single) Garden Path" — Argues Herbert populates Dune with three long-running eugenics programs, each with a different ethical stance: the Bene Gesserit's Kwisatz Haderach breeding scheme (whose communal guardian-breeding deliberately recalls Socrates' Kallipolis in the Republic), Leto II's Golden Path, and the Bene Tleilax's axolotl-tank genetic design for immortality. It reads the chastened Sisterhood of the later novels as moving from consequentialist to Kantian, deontological ground ('never seek to create a human being in any one image'), frames Leto II as the ultimate utilitarian whose species-saving end allegedly justifies Machiavellian means (with Siona's objection that he had no right), and shows the Tleilaxu destroyed by their own monomaniacal religious code. Conclusion: 'the most dangerous of all creations is a rigid code of ethics.'
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 11 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Cogburn attacks Fourth Edition's contraction of the nine alignments to five: it deletes archetypes that fantasy literature needs, since Karsa Orlong (who wills the destruction of all civilization without sadism) and Jacqueline Carey's Haomane Firstborn (who loves cold mathematical order while his laws lead to genocide) fit nowhere in the new scheme. He rebuilds alignment by taking it to describe what a character wills in Kant's sense, mapping the law-chaos axis onto the categorical imperative (the liar and murderer must take themselves to be exceptions to universal laws) and the good-evil axis onto Mill's greatest happiness principle, which yields a Lawful Good of Gandhi and King, a Neutral Good modeled on Jesus breaking Sabbath law out of love, and Lawful Evil exemplified by vampire hierarchies and politicians whose policies create hell abroad. Joe Abercrombie's torturer San Dan Glotka becomes the archetypal Neutral Neutral, 'banality of evil' in Arendt's sense, and the chapter concludes Chaotic Good is empty because willing the destruction of universalizability cannot consistently will less pain.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 10 "Notes" — Eric Silverman asks whether the Amazon series' Lucy and Maximus should have children, framing the wasteland through Hobbes's state of nature where life is 'nasty, brutish, and short' and even vaults are limiting experiments. He lays out Benatar's Harm Argument (pain outweighs pleasure, so procreation is procreational Russian roulette) and Shiffrin's Consent Argument (no one consents to being born, as Sartre's 'I did not ask to be born' concedes), then rebuts them: Socrates, the Stoics, and Aristotle make virtue and meaning rather than pleasure the goal of life, so a harsh wasteland full of people needing help suits a virtuous, sacrificial life like the hero's exile at the end of the original Fallout. Parental proxy consent legitimizes procreation as it does children's medical decisions, and Kant's universalization test defeats the demand for pre-natal consent, since universalizing it would eliminate the very rational beings whose consent it protects - so Lucy's 'Okey dokey!' optimism wins.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 27 "Notes" — The chapter maps four schools of ethics onto Fallout 4's Commonwealth: Aristotle's virtue ethics reads Preston Garvey's settlement defense as the mean between recklessness and cowardice and temperance as moderate chem use; Kant's Categorical Imperative is tested on stealing ammo in Concord and on the Battle of Bunker Hill choice to warn the Railroad, where loyal silence to Father fails universalization and treats synths merely as means. Aquinas's natural law ethics, keyed to the telos of power armor, workbenches, and Pip-Boys, condemns the Institute's creation of synths by analogy to the IVF debate while still demanding dignity for synths who already exist. Finally, Bentham's utilitarianism is the one framework under which Father's Institute — adaptive labor force, scientific progress, stability and order — can sincerely believe itself morally justified.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 29 "Notes" — Weighing Vault-Tec's secret experiments — Vault 11's yearly human sacrifice, Vault 13's 200-year lockdown, the cryogenic freezing of the Sole Survivor — the chapter asks whether the ends could ever justify the vaults. On Kant's Universal Law and Humanity Formulations the answer is flatly no: dwellers were deceived into becoming mere means to data, whatever the hypothetical space-colonization motive that designer Tim Cain favors. Act and rule utilitarianism in Bentham's tradition give a more equivocal verdict — exposed deception would doom any future cooperation, yet safeguarding humanity might in extraordinary circumstances tip the calculus — and the chapter situates the games in real research-ethics history from the eugenics era to the Tuskegee study and the Belmont Report.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 27 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Tyrion - born a reviled dwarf who killed his mother, yet heir to Lannister wealth, wits, and Jaime's knightly example - frames Nagel's paradox of moral luck: his compassion toward Jon Snow and Sansa is constitutive luck, and his carefully run wildfire defense of King's Landing shows resultant luck, since the same prudent act deserves praise in one outcome and blame had it burned the city. Kant's good will, applied to Tyrion's protection of Shae as treating her as an end and never merely as a means against Cersei, is offered as a rescue but only neutralizes resultant luck, leaving constitutive and circumstantial luck untouched. The chapter ends with Nagel's shrinking 'extensionless point' of genuine agency, concluding we cannot keep both moral responsibility and the principle that we are blamed only for what we control.
- **The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire**, ch. 29 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" — Salander shares Kant's detestation of the criminal's hypocrisy: Martin Vanger's meticulous, unimpulsive murders and Wennerström's hubristic paper trail fail the universal-law formulation because each supremely rational villain casts himself as the exception to rules that bind everyone else. But Salander fails Kant too—she hacks 'for the kick' rather than from duty, encroaches on innocent privacy, and takes justice into her own hands (tattooing Bjurman, stealing from and arranging the death of Wennerström) where Kant's 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' would forbid even lying to a murderer; the chapter finds her closest to Benjamin Constant's rejoinder that truth is owed only to those worthy of it, matching her maxim that 'a bastard is always a bastard.' Her strict promise-keeping, her cultivation of mind and body per the Doctrine of Virtue, and her refusal of guardianship and of Blomkvist's money make her, in Kantian terms, a champion of autonomy who is nonetheless a work in progress.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 21 "9. Send The Good Place to the Bad Place" — Asks whether a show about ethics may lie to its audience for a whole season: the Season One twist breaks the viewer's implicit contract even though the show keeps its internal 'truth in fiction'. Through 'The Eternal Shriek' it stages the debate — Chidi's Kantian ban on lying (the red cowboy boots saga with Henry, ending in a confession that defeats Henry) against Eleanor's Machiavellian ends-justify-means plot to 'kill' Janet — and reads the show's cascade of confessions as its answer that truth-telling absolves. Eleanor citing Jonathan Dancy's moral particularism in 'Rhonda, Diana, Jake, and Trent' lets Chidi lie his way through Hell, leaving viewers to decide whether the twist's ethical education justifies the deception.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 22 "10. A Love Story between Theory and Praxis" — Casts Chidi as Theory and Eleanor as Praxis in an allegorical love story: Chidi's Kantian universalizability about lying and his utilitarian lesson (confess, because the neighborhood's welfare outweighs you) only move Eleanor when she sees Theory enacted — Michael's willingness to absorb eternal torture in her place convinces her the theory 'has legs'. Praxis repays the debt when Eleanor's moral particularism pushes Chidi to lie to demons and play his part in the Bad Place party, and Michael's conversion from torturer to someone who sacrifices his portal pin for Eleanor ('Rhonda, Diana, Jake, and Trent') completes the union. The moral: theory is born in the world, but only practice lets it thrive there.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 23 "11. Those Agonizing Choices" — Treats Chidi's indecision (rock-paper-scissors panic, the soul-mate dilemma, the boots lie) as the show's authentic portrait of how hard moral life is, not just a professor joke. Michael's live-action Trolley Problem — Foot's thought experiment made literal, with Henry's bloody boots flying at Chidi — is read as torture precisely because it weaponizes Chidi's defining trait, and the show pointedly never hands the audience a right answer. Eleanor's Dancy-inspired movies-vs-er argument ('Your boy Kant would say never break a promise') finally lets Chidi act, and Scanlon's What We Owe to Each Other frames his arc's resolution: we choose to be good because of our bonds with others, as when he kisses Eleanor in 'Somewhere Else' and Michael 'solves' the trolley by sacrificing himself.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 27 "14. Is Kant the Reason Everyone Hates Moral Philosophy Professors" — Defends Kant against the charge that he is why everyone hates moral philosophy professors: it explains the two-question Categorical Imperative test via frozen-yogurt maxims and Eleanor's selfish 'won't help unless it benefits me' principle, shows Kant never actually forbade lying to the murderer at the door (his crotchety 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' was an obscure legal point), and reads Chidi's trolley-track switch but refusal to harvest Eleanor's organs as the humanity formula — never treat a person merely as a means. Tahani's $60 billion in charity and Eleanor's failed point-chasing in 'What's My Motivation?' illustrate the good will: deeds lack moral worth unless done for the right reasons. Aristotle explains the residual puzzle — theory mastery does not make you skilled at ethical practice, any more than a nutritionist is a great cook.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 36 "20. Moral Health Warning" — A health warning from Jonathan Dancy himself: the show's premise that Chidi's lessons in Kant, Scanlon, and the Trolley Problem can make Eleanor better is false, because becoming good requires a change in motivation and intellectual study shapes motivation at most indirectly — and might attach to the wrong as easily as the right, since moral philosophy studies both. Worse, studying ethics looks like self-indulgence, time spent on Kant that could have gone to doing actual good. Against the Kantian thought that only acting from a sense of duty earns moral credit, Dancy argues that sympathetic love — Doug Wynegar bringing his grandmother roses simply for her sake — is enough, which undermines both Kant and Chidi's entire teaching project.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 30 "NOTES" — First defines lying — distinguishing it from mere error (Angela believing Peter dead), from the Haitian's non-verbal memory-wipe deception, and from Hiro's silent staging of Ando's fake death — then tests moral theories against the show's liars. Kant's categorical imperative bans all lying but is abandoned when Sylar demands a friend's hiding place; utilitarianism vindicates Victoria Pratt's lie about the virus vial yet also licenses Linderman's .07% explosion and Plato's noble lie of the earthborn metals, which the chapter rejects. Machiavelli's advice that princes may lie to keep power is played out by 'President Sylar' in 'Five Years Gone,' and the chapter finally endorses Sissela Bok's presumption against lying — a public-reasoning procedure modeled by Bob Bishop and Mohinder before Monica's virus injection.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 27 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Foy reads the arena as Hobbes's state of nature recreated: the Cornucopia bloodbath, 'stealing isn't illegal here,' and temporary alliances awaiting betrayal instantiate the war of all against all, while the Treaty of Treason is Panem's written social contract buying order at the price of submission to the Capitol. Gale's advice that killing tributes is 'just hunting' mirrors the Hobbesian maxim the Gamemakers want, whereas Peeta's vow to show he is 'more than a piece in their Games' expresses Kant's categorical imperative and the duty to treat humanity as an end. Katniss's arc — decorating Rue's body, risking her life at the feast for Peeta's medicine, telling the District 2 soldier 'I'm done killing their slaves,' and rejecting Gale's tactic of bombing rescuers — moves her from survival logic to Kantian moral autonomy. The chapter ends by rejecting the Hobbesian justification of oppressive rule: a life of fear and servitude is not worth preserving at any cost.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 14 "Invisibility or Honesty" — Schulzke argues inception is a categorical violation of Kantian autonomy: the Fischer job treats him merely as a means (Saito's market share, Cobb's reunion with his children), and even Cobb's benevolent inception on Mal disrespects humanity by robbing her of self-determination, leaving her unable to act as a responsible moral agent testable against the categorical imperative. Extraction, by contrast, attacks privacy rather than autonomy, and the chapter uses Glaucon's Ring of Gyges to show that dream espionage would defeat even perfect invisibility, since an extractor could always read your deeds in your dreams. The twist, played off Kant's absolute condemnation of lying, is that the standing threat of extraction might be the only force that could make universal honesty practicable — hence the title's choice between invisibility and honesty, illustrated by Ariadne's life-saving extraction on Cobb.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 13 "4 Raiders of the Lost Kant Indy Meets the Categorical Imperative" — Mia Wood tests Raiders against Kant's categorical imperative: Belloq's maxim of taking whatever he wants cannot be universalized without destroying property itself, and he repeatedly uses persons as mere means — deceiving the Hovitos about the Golden Idol, preying on Dietrich's fears, and treating Marion as a possession to be seduced with wine and a white dress. Indy fails too: his affair with the sixteen-year-old Marion ('It was wrong and you knew it'), leaving her bound and gagged to pursue the Ark, and Kant's absolutist ban on lying is probed through Katanga's noble lie to Dietrich. The first film's shadowy cinematography visualizes this moral ambiguity — Indy starts as merely one more 'raider' and only gradually redeems himself across the sequels.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 24 "Can You Find Your Moral Compass" — Donovan and Richardson test Tony's moral compass in 'Armor Wars' and 'Extremis' against the three major schools. Utilitarianism fails because Tony will not sacrifice even one innocent for the greater good — he changes tactics to save a single pilot from the Raiders and rages when the Controller's human zombie dies — and Kantian deontology fails because Tony bends rules ('lives to mean more than rules') and is driven by emotion rather than pure reason. Aristotle fits: Tony is obsessed not just with doing good but with being good, snarling at his own reflection, asking filmmaker Pillinger 'Have you changed anything? Me neither,' until Extremis lets him 'be the Iron Man inside and out,' uniting agent and deed as Aristotelian character requires.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 13 "Notes" — Robson argues that The Man Upstairs' real moral flaw is neither stinginess toward Finn nor mere instruction-following, both of which he defends, but 'rule worship': treating LEGO construction instructions — rules with at best conventional status like chess or etiquette rules — as sacrosanct commandments to be followed for their own sake. The contrast is with Kant, who does claim absolute status for central moral rules such as the prohibition on lying, and with the moral/conventional distinction from psychologists like Kelly and Stich that The Man cannot grasp. Emmet's rule-following differs because it serves goals like fitting in, and the flaw scales from office Micromanagers and Velma Staplebot to Inspector Javert and the mafioso, showing how misdirected rule worship becomes genuinely vicious.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 18 "The Question of Ethical Advertising" — Novakovic and Whitney use the Heineken incident, where Betty discovers she was the target demographic for her husband's campaign ('Must be so funny, being in on it'), to test advertising against Kantian honesty and respect.
