Wondering What It’s All For" — Trip McCrossin reads Lord Grantham's 'we've dreamed a dream' as an echo of Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 2 and follows the war story line - Matthew and William missing before Amiens, William's slow death, Mr. Lang's shell shock, Mrs. Patmore's nephew Archie shot for cowardice - to show how obscure war's causes and realities remain to those who have not lived them. The Dowager Countess's 'we don't always get our just deserts' as Matthew dies under his car, and the stretcher-bearer's 'it comes down to luck,' raise the problem of evil from the Book of Job: good and bad fortune fall without premonition or meaning. Against complacency about war's inevitability, the chapter argues that since class and traffic harms can be reduced, warfare's can be too - we should 'band together as Daniel,' interpret the wars a few dream up, and not allow them to come to be.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 32 "19. Of Downton and Drones" — Jai Galliott contrasts the roughly level killing field of WWI, in which William dies and Matthew is paralyzed in the trenches alongside aristocrats who suffered proportionally the heaviest losses, with today's drone age, in which remote pilots drawn largely from the lower and middle classes bear the burden of fighting. Tracing unmanned weapons from WWI tele-operated motorboats and the Sperry and Kettering aerial torpedoes to Reaper drones flown by a 'PlayStation generation,' he argues that radical technological asymmetry breaks Just War Theory - undermining last resort and proportionality and the mutual imposition of risk that Kahn and Sparrow make the basis of combatants' rights. He proposes that highly asymmetric force be restrained into something like international policing, while conceding, like Mrs. Patmore with her electric mixer, that nothing will stop us being dragged into the drone age.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 23 "8. The Warring Dead" — Morris applies just war theory's distinction between justice of war and justice in war to Season 3's Woodbury-prison conflict, staging Walzer's moral symmetry of combatants - soldiers on both sides may permissibly kill each other regardless of their cause - against McMahan's critique, illustrated by the bank robber who kills a cop in 'self-defense.' McMahan's distinction between objective justification and excuses like coercion and ignorance is worked through Maggie giving up the prison's location under threat to Glenn in 'When the Dead Come Knocking' and the Woodbury militia's ignorance of the Governor's raids. He concludes the prison group fights a justified defensive war, the ignorant Woodbury fighters are excused but not justified, and real culpability lies with the Governor and his henchmen.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 23 "11. Have Fun Overthrowing This Evil Government!" — Gibson reads Humperdinck's fabricated-pretext war against Guilder (framing Guilder for Buttercup's murder, with Vizzini's crew as private military contractors) through Just War Theory: it fails the jus ad bellum just-cause requirement built on Augustine and Aquinas, since the war would be retribution sparked by staged wrongdoing, and contractor motives of profit compound the violation. Michael Davis's critique of the ticking-time-bomb defense then shows that Rugen's torture of Westley is exactly the 'institution of torture' whose moral cost forbids ever licensing torture, since the torturer must be trained on victims first. Finally, even Hobbes's Leviathan - the most absolutist of social contract views - requires the sovereign to protect the people's safety and administer equal justice, so Humperdinck's record makes his rule illegitimate and the storming of the castle a justified insurrection.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 42 "26. Horrifying Violence, Gratuitous Sex, and the Truth" — Silverman concedes Game of Thrones can be watched viciously - sadistically relishing Theon's flaying or using it as soft pornography - but denies the show is inherently immoral. From Plato's Republic he takes the test of whether a narrative serves or obscures reality (Socrates was executed partly on the slander of Aristophanes' Clouds) and argues the show is honest where epics lie: war is ugly and kills innocents, measured against the Augustinian just-war criteria that even the Brotherhood Without Banners decays past; humans really are as sexually preoccupied as Plato's appetitive soul, Freud's id, or Augustine's original sin; and honor without practical wisdom - Ned versus Tyrion on Aristotle's ideal - is a recipe for ruin.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 12 "1. The Deed of F’ing Society" — Rocha reads fsociety's 5/9 logic-bomb attack on E Corp as anarchist 'propaganda of the deed' - a shocking act meant to wake people from their comfortable slumber inside hierarchy - and positions it between Alexander Berkman's violent anarchism (mirroring Phillip Price's 'bullet in the right place') and Gandhi's nonviolent self-suffering, quoting satyagraha and the older Goldman's rejection of violence. He then runs the hack through just war theory's four questions (necessity, proportionality, justification, effectiveness), noting that wiping the debt records also destroyed savings and indirectly got people like Gideon killed, and that fsociety, as Trenton says, never paints the alternative society - so the reader is left to answer whether the deed was justified.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 23 "12. Are We Really Sure They’re Wrong" — Timothy Hsiao argues we cannot condemn the burning of the disabled or Smith's son's mandated euthanasia by appealing to Nazi values, since cultural relativism would make the Resistance the real wrongdoers; the horror we feel presupposes an objective natural law known to reason, the violation of which grounded the Nuremberg trials. From Augustine's 'an unjust law is no law at all,' the chapter then tests the Resistance's armed rebellion against the five just-war conditions — proper authority (the Resistance as agent of the moral law), just cause, reasonable chance of success (the newsreels as grounds for hope), proportionality, and last resort — and finds it justified.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 28 "17. Please Hold for a Call from God" — In a satirical dialogue, God phones Aquinas in heaven and orders a Summa-style investigation of which superhero should lift the world out of an economic crisis and which should stop a looming war. Aquinas rules that the Lazarus-like Captain America, teamed with a Nobel economist, should handle the depression, then returns to his own treatise On War - sovereign authority, just cause, right intention, with Augustine's definition of just war quoted from the Summa - to ask whether a loyal subject may choose the good over the sovereign in an unjust war. He concludes that billionaire Iron Man is the only figure with sovereign-like standing to countermand an unjust war, while worrying about billionaire power, superhero bandwagons, and Satan getting wind of the reasoning.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 16 "5. Inside Gilead’s Misogynist Parlors" — Hirschbein unravels the Genesis story of Abraham, Sarah, and Hagar as the script Gilead rereads to rationalize its 'misogynist parlors,' arguing that Gilead's exegesis is propaganda rather than scholarship—cherry-picking scripture that Nietzsche joked would appall the actual Jesus. He then spins the reader's moral compass: with Rorty's ironist he asks whether anyone initiated into Abraham's tribe or raised in Gilead can be blamed—are even Hitler and Commander Waterford products of their time?—and weighs Ofglen's suicide bombing of the Rachel and Leah Center against just war criteria of proportion, innocence, and chance of success. Finally, with Freud and Niebuhr, he suggests the Sons of Jacob built their surveillance state on a depraved view of human nature, so utopian schemes—Gilead included—are doomed from the founding.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 1 "Introduction" — Book introduction: recounts how the 1979 cast were the first casualties of the Chestburster scene (real butcher-shop organs, Veronica Cartwright fainting), then previews the volume's payload - personhood questions about Ash, Bishop, David and the Ripley clone; Marx on why Weyland-Yutani sacrifices crews for profit; Plato's Republic on children in warfare via Newt; Lovecraftian cosmic horror; feminist readings of Ripley as care ethicist and mother; and continental takes - Xenomorphs as Nietzsche's Ubermensch, Camus on Ripley-8's refusal to commit suicide, and Sartre on a Xenomorph's right to resist us.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 12 "Easing Back on the APC’s Throttle" — Treats Engineers, Xenomorphs, and humans as states and reads the APC debate through Thucydides' Melian dialogue ('the strong do what they will') and the jus in bello criteria of discrimination, military necessity, and proportionality. It concludes that Ripley's 'nuke the site from orbit' and Vasquez's nerve gas are vengeance masquerading as realism - the Xeno threat is no longer imminent, so Walzer's 'supreme emergency' is unavailable - while Hudson's withdrawal (even Burke's species-preservation plea) fits both realism and just war restraint; the Ben Tre 'we destroyed the town to save it' fiasco in Vietnam is the cautionary parallel.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 20 "And the war Rages on" — Robichaud runs the Kree-Skrull War (Avengers #89–97) through Michael Walzer's just war theory: the Avengers' defense of Earth against Ronan's Plan Atavus is justified self-defense meeting proportionality and last resort, while Ronan's preventive 'devolve humanity' war fails for lack of evidence and exhausted diplomacy. The Skrulls' shape-shifting trick that gets Mar-Vell to build the Omni-Wave Projector might squeak through on consequentialist grounds, but the emperor's threat to make Captain Marvel watch the Scarlet Witch and Quicksilver die counts as torture—and is impermissible on the Kantian ground that it treats a person merely as a means, whatever the consequences. The point is that even a cosmic comic war displays the real moral complexity of military ethics.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 21 "“This is the Kind of Thing that is Going to Bite US in the Butt”" — Melançon pictures Avengers ethics as Hawkeye's arrow sliding along a line from deontological duty toward consequentialist results, focusing on secrets and lies: Doctor Strange's deception—disguising his Sanctum Sanctorum as a coffee shop to shelter the underground New Avengers after Civil War—is tested against Michael Walzer's 'supreme emergency', the wartime exception (Allied bombing of Germany, the ticking time bomb) that permits violating your own values so they can survive. Strange keeps sliding—possessed by a demon against the Hulk—until the Eye of Agamotto strips him of his title, showing emergencies must stay rare and the agent 'worthy of surviving'. Steve Rogers's secret black-ops Secret Avengers repeat the danger: unlike democratic intelligence agencies, they have zero oversight or accountability, so the WikiLeaks-style leak of their informant dealings threatens the reputation of the whole Avengers enterprise.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 17 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Taking the film's opening 'This will not stand' seriously, Svolba and Betz read the Dude and Walter's rug campaign alongside the 1991 Gulf War through just war theory: just cause exists (soiled rug, invaded Kuwait), but Walter's gun at Smokey's foul line violates last resort and proportionality ('You're not wrong, Walter, you're just an asshole'), Aquinas's right intention is compromised when the ransom errand is motivated by the twenty grand, and Locke's case for right authority explains why justice cannot be left to 'fucking amateurs' like Walter, who overestimates injuries and retaliates disproportionately. Jus in bello discrimination fails everywhere — the neighbor's Corvette, the goons' mistaken Lebowski — and the escalation kills the innocent Donny.
- **Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality**, ch. 28 "Black sabbath & philosophy" — Jacob Held uses "War Pigs", "Electric Funeral", and "Children of the Grave" to teach just war theory's two halves, jus ad bellum (just cause, last resort, proportion) and jus in bello (proportion and discrimination toward non-combatants), reading Sabbath as condemning unjust wars like Vietnam and atomic overkill rather than all force, with Ozzy's "Thank God for the Bomb" voicing deterrence. Citing Walzer on "even in hell, it is possible to be more or less humane", he argues pacifism functions as a vital moral check, and that the war on terror fails just war standards outright: it cannot be won, so any means, assassination, torture, reclassifying terrorists outside both soldier and criminal law, are disproportionate and morally bankrupt, exactly the war-pig behavior the song's judgment day condemns.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 31 "18. Wondering What It’s All For" — Trip McCrossin follows Lord Grantham's 'We've dreamed a dream' - an allusion to Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 2 - through the warfare story line of seasons 2 and 3, from Matthew and William missing in action to Matthew's death under a truck. Mr. Lang's shell-shocked confrontations with the eager volunteer William and with Mrs. Patmore over her executed nephew Archie dramatize the gulf between those who know what war is like and those who can only imagine it, while the meaningless deaths of Matthew and the stretcher-bearer who is shot mid-sentence raise the Job-like problem of evil in the Dowager's words, 'we don't always get our just deserts.' The chapter argues against complacency about warfare's inevitability: because total war is dreamed up by the few, the rest of us should 'band together as Daniel,' interpret those dreams in advance, and refuse to let them come to be.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 32 "19. Of Downton and Drones" — Jai Galliott contrasts Downton's WWI, where aristocrats like Matthew died in the trenches alongside footmen like William on a roughly level playing field, with today's drone age, in which the fighting burden falls on the lower and middle classes (future Reaper pilots recruited from the 'PlayStation generation') while risk to our own side approaches zero. He traces unmanned weapons from WWI tele-operated motorboats, the Land Torpedo, and the Kettering Bug back through Agincourt's longbows and Omdurman's machine guns to the Gulf War and Kosovo, and argues that when technological asymmetry becomes extreme, Just War Theory breaks down: such war can hardly be a last resort, strains the proportionality calculus, and violates the chivalric justice of treating an equal as an equal (via Paul Kahn's paradox of riskless warfare and Robert Sparrow's threat-based immunity). His proposal is that highly asymmetric force be applied with restraint, more like international policing than war.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 22 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Air Force colonel James Cook walks the just war tradition through Ender's world: the Third Invasion is preventive rather than preemptive (with the 2003 Iraq war as the parallel), proper authority is undermined by the I.F.'s lies to its citizens, and last resort fails because the hive-queen was already trying to communicate with Ender. He contrasts Augustine's ban on killing in self-defense with Aquinas's permission, invokes Kant's formula of humanity for the buggers' rational nature and Cicero's hostis against dehumanizing enemies, and argues the I.F.'s failure to teach military ethics is itself part of the novel's tragedy.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 24 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Kody Cooper argues Ender's tortured conscience demonstrates the classical just war framework: from Augustine's axiom that peace is the end of war and the five jus ad bellum requirements, to the verdict that the Third Invasion fails right intention, last resort, discrimination, and proportionality because the rational hive-queens were never given a real chance at coexistence. He reads the I.F.'s withholding of protection as throwing Ender into a Hobbesian state of nature where his fights with bullies count as private just wars, and concludes Ender carries the sins of the I.F. and humanity rather than his own guilt.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 20 "What Promotes Moral Behavior" — Matthew D. Atkinson and Darin DeWitt use the Canterbury's ignored mayday in 'Dulcinea' — Captain McDowell's 'let the good God Darwin sort it out' versus Ade Nygaard's appeal to law, karma, and obligation — to ask what binds people when no central authority enforces rules. Through Michael Walzer's just war theory they read the Earth-Mars war: moral language is not 'cheap talk' (even Errinwright must dress aggression as peace and manipulates Reverend Volovodov's words), aggression and imminence govern when to fight, and five 'how to fight' principles — noncombatant immunity on Eros and Ganymede, POW rights for the Martian marines on the Kittur Chennamma, leaders' rather than soldiers' responsibility (Fred Johnson's defection after Anderson Station), proportionality in Errinwright's 'a base for a base' Deimos strike, and the rejection of ends-justify-means utilitarianism — discipline even Holden and Amos as they reflect on free will and culpability. The chapter concludes The Expanse is optimistic: human decency survives even in the anarchic Belt because characters keep reflecting on what their obligations to one another are.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Curry and Lang test 'War never changes' through Hobbes and Xunzi: the wasteland - where the Ghoul asks who ever elected the 'President' in 'The Trap' and Cooper Howard decays outside all political order - is Hobbes's state of nature of restless power-seeking, while Xunzi's claim that bad human nature needs ritual (li) and righteousness (yi) explains a world with no moral education, where Elder Cleric Quintus pairs noble talk with 'power is taken, not given'. Fallout's Great War then fails every just-war test: China's invasion of Alaska stretches just cause, the corporatist US lacks right authority, propaganda undid last resort, mutually assured destruction explodes proportionality, and Vault-Tec shelters plus battlefield mini-nukes breach discrimination and proportionality in bello - with Operation Anchorage's propaganda simulation illustrating the revisionist point that fighting cleanly cannot redeem an unjust war. China's 'righteous army' (yi bing) tradition - Sunzi's strategic restraint, Mohist defensive war, Mengzi's true king, Xunzi's punitive righteous war - leaves no trace beyond Captain Zao, so the war's constancy marks the failure of every philosophical attempt to bind war to justice.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 14 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Richard H. Corrigan tests Robb Stark's war against Joffrey with just war theory, criteria for resorting to war (legitimate authority, just cause, right intention, last resort, probability of success, proportionality) and for conduct (discrimination, treatment of prisoners, no reprisals). Robb is a legitimate authority acclaimed King in the North, offers rejected peace terms, and fights cleanly - Jaime is humanely held at Riverrun while Sansa is beaten by Joffrey, and Gregor Clegane's murders, rapes, and the Dothraki sack of the Lhazareen mark the other side's atrocities. Yet Corrigan concludes Robb fails right intention: his dominant motive is vengeance for his father, not the free North he professes, so although we root for him, his war cannot strictly be called just.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 23 "a10.xhtml" — Johnson tests the Battle of Five Armies against just war theory as developed from Augustine through Aquinas: the men under Bard satisfy legitimate authority, just cause and last resort (they bargained, even using the Arkenstone as leverage and trying economic pressure), the Elvenking explicitly waits rather than start 'this war for gold', while the dwarves fail the criteria because greed and pride are not just causes and a thirteenth-share was a cheap price for peace. The war that actually happens - the three armies uniting against Bolg's orc-host - is justified self- and other-defense, whereas the orcs' motives (revenge, plunder, conquest) are unjust. Against apparent pacifist evidence (Tom Bombadil, Frodo at the Shire 'scouring', Gandalf's 'pity' for Gollum), Johnson reads Tolkien's letters as endorsing war as sometimes necessary and sometimes 'in the right', though Tolkien rejects the theory's reasonable-chance-of-success condition given the hopeless stands at Helm's Deep and the Morannon.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 17 "Notes" — Perry frames Frank through Walzer's problem of dirty hands, taking its name from Sartre's play ('I have dirty hands right up to the elbows... Do you think you can govern innocently?') and Machiavelli's advice to 'enter into evil when forced by necessity' — the pilot's mercy killing of the dog and 'just shy of treason, which is politics' being the show's emblems. He maps the field onto the show: utilitarians for whom breaking rules can be right, absolutists like the bishop ('Love God, and love each other. Period.'), and Walzer's later 'supreme emergency' threshold deontology applied to Frank's child-killing drone strike and his desperate deal with Petrov in the Jordan Valley. The verdict: Frank's only edge over Heather Dunbar is a proven capacity to dirty his hands when needed, but he lacks the scruples that keep that capacity from becoming routine wrongdoing, so he is probably still the wrong man for the job.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 28 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Melançon tests the Mockingjay revolution against the just-war tradition's three parts: jus ad bellum, jus in bello, and jus post bellum. The districts satisfy just cause, right intention, last resort, and proportionality against the Capitol, but stumble on competent authority — no legitimate state authorizes their rebellion — a problem the chapter says forces the tradition to admit popular self-determination. Both sides then violate jus in bello: the rebels' avalanche on the Nut fails military necessity and proportionality, and the bombing of the Capitol's child shields plus the medics treating them breaches distinction twice, making the rebels as bad as the Capitol. The contemplated final Hunger Games with Capitol children would violate jus post bellum, so the revolution was not a just war and only stumbles into peace.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 36 "22 “Germany Has Declared War on the Jones Boys!” Asymmetric Strategy and Honor among Raiders" — Reads Indy through Clausewitz's On War: as one man against a nation-state ('Germany has declared war on the Jones boys!'), he must fight asymmetrically — shooting the scimitar duelist in Cairo, letting the plane's propeller finish the chivalrous German strongman, ambushing convoys one or two foes at a time, and cutting the Temple's rope bridge to nullify Mola Ram's numbers. Because symmetric combat carries the honor code of chivalry and its absence shades into terrorism, the chapter asks whether fighting dirty for a good cause is permissible, contrasting Star Wars, whose rebels always win through decisive symmetric battles. Indy never lands the decisive blow — God and the British do — so he remains a beloved but 'unheroic' raider rather than a soldier.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 16 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Asks whether SAMCRO's gun suppliers, the Real IRA, are terrorists or freedom fighters, using Walzer's definition of terrorism as random killing of innocents to spread fear and his combatant/non-combatant distinction. The Irish Kings pass as freedom fighters—Kutz's three criteria of internal ordering (the hierarchy that has Sean Casey strangle the turncoat Cameron Hayes), just aims (a united Ireland), and target discrimination fit them—whereas Jimmy O, recruiting children as young as ten and attacking anyone with Loyalist sympathies, fails; his real motive being profit, Fr. Ashby concludes 'he's not a soldier anymore, just a gangster,' prompting the chapter's new category: thug. Fr. Ashby's own complicity in a church execution, redeemed by becoming a hostage so Abel can return to Jax, closes the moral ledger.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 17 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Runs SAMCRO's conflicts with the Mayans, the Lobos Sonora, and the ATF through just war theory's jus ad bellum, focusing on right authority: Clay's dismissal of Salazar ('I don't recognize your bullshit MC') is exactly how Walzer would treat Clay's own war declarations. Walzer's analogy of the sovereign state to Tara shooting her home-invader Kohn grounds the right of self-defense in sovereignty, and the chapter tests SAMCRO against four features of statehood and six of nationhood—brothers as compatriots, the club's founding history obligating Jax, church votes, Charming turf, the Reaper tattoo, and self-determination—to crown it a 'mini-nation-state on wheels.' The catch is Clay's own admission that Sons are US citizens: the United States remains sovereign over them, leaving open whether sub-state nations like SAMCRO (or the Palestinians) can ever legitimately declare war.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 13 "Notes" — David Boersema reads Star Trek as a survey of peace studies, distinguishing negative peace from positive peace via 'The Cloud Minders', where Troglyte Vanna demands her people's 'right to the clouds' in Stratos. Against Anan 7's 'we're a killer species' in 'A Taste of Armageddon'—explicitly mirrored in post-9/11 drone war and 'shock and awe'—he enlists Hobbes, Freud, and McCoy's defense of the dark Kirk in 'The Enemy Within' to question whether violence is natural, and treats Kodos's 'some had to die that others might live' in 'The Conscience of the King' as the utilitarian justification for atrocity. Gem's compassion in 'The Empath', Kirk sparing the Gorn in 'Arena', and the Horta's misread attack in 'The Devil in the Dark' display nonviolence, deterrence, and corrected perception as alternatives to war.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 14 "Notes" — Camosy takes up Randal's charge in Clerks that destroying Death Star II killed innocent independent contractors. Against utilitarian reasoning he deploys just war theory: terrorism is intentionally targeting innocents as a means, so Tarkin's destruction of Alderaan (and, he argues, Hiroshima) qualifies, while the Rebels, who would have been 'pleased' if the workers took the day off, do not. Since the crew was mostly conscripted clones and programmed droids with no moral responsibility, and destroying the station saved billions, the attack passes the proportionality test - an exercise in double-effect reasoning that asks fans to question the 'good guys lens.'
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 15 "Notes" — LaRocca argues Boba Fett is best understood as an amoralist - neither a moral relativist nor an ethical egoist, but someone who has withdrawn from moral judgment altogether - reading his terse 'As you wish' to Vader and his insuring of Han's survival purely for payment as evidence. Through Michael Walzer's account of the soldier's constrained choice and the 'good mercenary' debate, he asks whether mercenary violence (Blackwater, private military contractors) really differs morally from a conscript's or clone's. The upshot is that Fett's grayness between Empire and Rebellion exposes amoralism as a surprisingly central part of political and military life.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 23 "Trust in the Force of Others" — MacMullan reads Rogue One through Dewey's 'Creative Democracy': democracy is not Senates or constitutions but a lived faith in one's neighbors, and the Empire's deepest violence is the distrust it breeds — Cassian executing Tivik, Saw torturing Bodhi with Bor Gullet, Draven ordering Galen's assassination. Cassian violates Kant's Formula of Humanity by reducing Tivik to a container of secrets, and the Rebels' dirty-war methods strain Augustine's just-war conditions, yet Chirrut and Baze's friendship ('I'm not alone. I have you!') becomes the seed of recovered trust that stays Cassian's finger on the trigger at Eadu. The Yavin council's free debate and the Tantive IV corridor relay — Rebels dying to pass the Death Star plans hand to hand past Vader — enact Dewey's claim that democracy lives in personal attitudes and neighborly trust: rebellions are built on hope in each other.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 10 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Shannon Ford reconstructs the Winchesters' ethics of killing: self-defense and defense of others justify lethal force, as when Sam kills Jeremy in 'Dream a Little Dream of Me' and Andy shoots Ansem to save Dean in 'Simon Said,' while Dean's refusal of Ruby's virgin-sacrifice spell in 'Jus in Bello' and sparing the disarmed Pa Bender mark lines they will not cross even when the math favors killing. Killing possessed innocents like Meg is treated as permissible only under necessity and with regret. The chapter then argues that once the brothers hunt to banish all demons from the world, their conflict is war rather than hunting, so just war theory (jus ad bellum and jus in bello) might license killings ordinary morality forbids, a slippage dramatized by Gordon's enjoyment of killing and Dean's unjustifiable killing of Amy.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 17 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Browning shows that 'Jus in Bello' is built from Romero's Night of the Living Dead: the besieged police station is a 'survival space' (a form he traces to Matheson's I Am Legend), Henricksen takes Ben's role and Nancy Barbra's, and the massed possessed townspeople mirror the shuffling zombie horde. Inside that space the show stages a clash of values, Ruby's utilitarian spell requiring Nancy's heart against Dean's absolute refusal to kill an innocent ('your choice is not a choice'), resolved by the rock-salt-and-exorcism plan that kills no one. The survival space works as a proving ground for its occupants' values, and the ending, where Lilith slaughters Nancy anyway, indicts the heroes' scruples and asks what the body count says about the viewers who enjoyed it.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 23 "NOTES" — Phillip Seng runs the human-Skynet war through the three parts of just-war theory and finds the moral ground shakier than it looks: T2's briefing reveals Skynet launched its strike only after humans tried to pull the plug, so the machines claim the same self-defense 'just cause' humans do, while Skynet flunks last resort (it decides 'in a microsecond' with no negotiation), legitimate authority, proportionality (killing everyone to avoid being switched off), and discrimination. He then shows Sarah becoming a Terminator herself when she locks her laser sight on the innocent Miles Dyson, violating the same just-conduct rules she judges the machines by, and stopping only at his crying family. The chapter closes by doubting the war could ever have a just resolution, since the films point toward genocide rather than a peace treaty with Skynet.
- **Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test**, ch. 5 "P A R T O N E" — Christopher Robichaud's essay asks what morality can demand of Dr. Manhattan after the accident strips him of the moral emotions (in Jesse Prinz's Humean vein) needed to value persons, which is why he can tell Laurie 'I read atoms' and rank human life beside rubble. It then asks what grounds morality's authority over a being no one can punish, rejecting divine command theory (Manhattan's 'clock without a craftsman') and doubting Kant's rational grounding applies to someone lacking moral concepts, so 'no one is above the moral law' may rest on a brute fact. It closes on political morality: a United States made a hyperpower by Manhattan's service (as in his Vietnam intervention) may not claim a double standard, since sovereignty blocks preventive war even when the US would win at little cost.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 26 "Notes" — Gibson argues Rand's creation of the Asha'man and the Black Tower is a 'dirty hands' problem (Michael Walzer, tracing to Machiavelli): even in the just war against the Dark One, Rand does something morally objectionable by building men trained to be weapons and then, distrusting Mazrim Taim, abdicating oversight so Taim (a Forsaken) corrupts them. He reframes the Asha'man as lethal autonomous weapons, using the ICRC's Ingvild Bode on algorithmic bias in data, design, and use to argue Rand and Taim's biases were 'trained' into these walking weapons, and connects the speed and loss of control of autonomous war to WoT's theme of balance and the real-world ethics of emerging military AI.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Held examines the Tuatha'an Way of the Leaf as universal pacifism grounded not in religion, utility, or rights but in the metaphysical care of the self, echoing Gandhi's idea that violence taints the soul of the doer (shown by Adan exiling Lewin for rescuing raped girls and by Aram's tragic fall). He argues the Tinkers' pacifism, while idyllic, is untenable in a broken world: through Augustine's two cities, Aquinas's natural self-preservation and doctrine of double effect, and just war theory's jus ad bellum and jus in bello, he contends intentions matter and that no hero of WoT could be a pacifist, concluding the Tinkers free-ride parasitically on those who fight the Shadow and that their peace is not real peace but self-serving order-less quiet.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 28 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Taliaferro and Le Gall examine when a nation or athlete may justifiably boycott the Olympics, distinguishing 'material' from 'formal' contribution and weighing available alternatives and the stringency of values (e.g., Gandhi's boycott of British goods, apartheid boycotts, the Lysistrata sex strike). They argue attending is not itself endorsement of the host regime, so the heavy, often irrecoverable cost to individual athletes places a strong burden of proof on any boycott. Surveying the 1956, 1980 and 1984 boycotts (which changed little) and the 1936 Berlin Games (where Jesse Owens's participation did real good), they conclude only a credible threat of serious bodily harm clearly justifies boycotting.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 24 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Mahon asks whether Ride with the Devil endorses the proverb that all's fair in love and war, locating the film's moral core in its outsiders—the German immigrant Jake, the freed slave Holt, and the young widow Sue Lee. Against Sunzi's undiscriminating claim that warfare is the art of deceit, he argues the film sides with Machiavelli's Discourses distinction between honorable ruses of war and dishonorable perfidy: the bushwhackers' wearing of Union blue and Jake's lies are ruses, but the Lawrence massacre and refusing to ambush women under a truce mark limits Jake will not cross. In love, Sue Lee's shift from romantic lying to 'now is the truth' shows honesty is finally required, so all is not fair.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 14 "Technology and Ethics in The Day the Earth Stood Still" — Skoble reads The Day the Earth Stood Still as an allegory about the ethics of force and technology. He argues Klaatu's ultimatum extends Mill's harm principle to the interplanetary level: societies may fight among themselves but not threaten others, so Gort's robot police enforce a right to peace that no one has a right to violate. He distinguishes the robots' narrow, non-paternalistic authority from Hobbes's absolute sovereign, defends the ultimatum as preemptive self-defense rather than a rights violation, and contrasts the film's trust in machines with the later technophobia of Colossus and The Terminator.
- **The Philosophy of Spike Lee**, ch. 18 "The Dialectic of King and X in Do the Right Thing" — Silberstein reads Do the Right Thing as staging the ideological dialectic between Martin Luther King Jr.'s absolute nonviolence and Malcolm X's defense of retaliatory self-defense, both grounded in a theologically informed natural-law view of rights (King's Christian imago dei, X's Islamic tradition). He argues King mixes a deontological ethic (violence is always wrong) with a Gandhian consequentialist claim that violence begets violence, while X frames a race war as a just holy war. The film's Radio Raheem (LOVE/HATE knuckles), Buggin' Out's boycott of Sal's Wall of Fame, the Racial Slur Montage, and Mookie throwing the trash can dramatize whether ends justify means; the closing Sal-Mookie money exchange reframes racism as symptom of a deeper capitalist greed both King and X came to critique.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 20 "General Patton and Private Ryan The Conflicting Reality of War and Films about War" — Fiala uses Patton's opening speech ("an army is a team… this individuality stuff is a bunch of crap") against Saving Private Ryan's mission to rescue one soldier to frame war's basic conflict between the collective and the individual, and to expose the problem of "realism" in representing war. He aligns the collectivist realist ethics of war against the just-war tradition's deontological respect for individuals as Kantian ends-in-themselves, and contrasts Patton's aerial, above-the-battle viewpoint with Private Ryan's first-person D-Day realism. Drawing on Tim O'Brien's claim that a true war story is never moral, and on Nussbaum's and Glover's moral imagination, he concludes that no film can synthesize war's public and private perspectives—mirroring the failure of moral imagination that produces war itself.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 21 "The Work of Art in the Age of Embedded Journalism Fiction versus Depiction in Zero Dark Thirty" — Evans argues that Kathryn Bigelow's Zero Dark Thirty fails morally and epistemically because its immersive 'boots-on-the-ground' realism traps the viewer inside Maya's single point of view, so we can never see the CIA torture program's lunacy the way an outside witness would. Drawing on Wittgenstein's Tractatus claim that the subject is a limit of the world (the eye that cannot see itself), she shows how the film effaces its own privileged viewpoint to pass off a partial view as impartial reality. Against this she sets a Platonic point that genuine reality is glimpsed only through fiction that ironically juxtaposes contrasting viewpoints, citing scenes like the SEALs' banter and Maya's final weeping where the film briefly becomes true art. The 'depiction is not endorsement' defense collapses because the narrative logic still credits torture with finding bin Laden.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 19 "Terrorism, Counterterrorism, and “The Story of What Happens Next” in Munich" — Foy reads Munich's Operation Wrath of God as Spielberg's argument for retribution over vengeance in state counterterrorism. Yvonne's Marcuse/Hegel relativism and the agents' 'think of yourself as a soldier' language-games are dismissed as Avner's psychological breakdown shows morality is objective. Foy deploys Nozick's five procedural differences between retribution and revenge and Kant's view of retribution as impersonal and rational, echoes Socrates in the Crito (retaliation harms one's own soul) via Avner's decay, and cites Aristotle's 'war for the sake of peace' and jus in bello discrimination/proportionality in the Hamshari and Jeanette assassinations.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 30 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Scruton reads the literature and music of hunting—Homer's Odyssey and Argos, Wagner's Parsifal, Tristan and the Ring, Melville's Moby Dick, Cooper's Last of the Mohicans, and English foxhunting from Sir Gawain to Surtees and Masefield's Reynard the Fox—as recovering the hunter-gatherer's sacred, totemic bond with animals and the theme of ritual sacrifice. He grounds the distinction between virtuous and 'lawless' hunting in Plato's Laws, where 'sacred hunting' of quadrupeds run down by men, horses, and dogs is defended as piety, and aligns it with Ortega's insistence on self-imposed limits that keep the hunt from becoming mere butchery.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 16 "14. The Doctor as Philosopher The Collectivist-Realist Pacifism of the Doctor and the Quest for Social Justice" — Smithka argues the Doctor is a 'collectivist-realist pacifist': morally opposed to war yet willing, as a last resort, to use lethal force for social justice. She places the Doctor on Cady's warism-to-pacifism continuum (past absolute and collectivist pacifism), augmenting it with Martin Luther King Jr.'s realist pacifism — ethical appeals 'undergirded by constructive coercive power' — and Gandhi's ahimsa and belief that no one is beyond redemption (the Doctor sparing Davros, offering enemies a choice). She tests Kant's duty ethics and respect for persons (Rule 1: the Doctor lies), Ross's prima facie duties, Mill's utilitarianism ('The Fires of Pompeii,' 'The Beast Below'), Gilligan/Noddings care ethics, and Wolterstorff's 'life of needs,' and reads 'The Day of the Doctor' as a Rawlsian veil of ignorance brokering Zygon-human peace.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 50 "47. Snowpiercer as Philosophy The Danger to Humanity" — Marquez 'pierces the veils' of Snowpiercer to argue the greatest danger to humanity is humanity itself. He reads Wilford's authoritarian, precisely population-controlled train through Plato's noble lie / myth of the metals (Mason's 'know your place'), Hobbes's social contract against a cannibalistic state of nature, and Machiavellian ends-justify-means to weigh whether Gilliam's secret compromise with Wilford is morally acceptable. He tests the orchestrated revolution against utilitarianism's greatest-happiness principle (Bentham, Mill's taxation-of-the-wealthy, Singer's impartiality) and against Rawls's veil of ignorance and difference principle versus Nozick's entitlement objection and Aquinas's just-war criteria, concluding each character's actions can be read as 'just,' which exposes anthropocentrism as the real veil.

### Non-Self (anatman)

Non-self, or anatman, is the Buddhist claim that there is no permanent, unchanging self or soul underlying our experience. What we take to be a fixed "I" is, on this view, a shifting bundle of physical and mental processes that continually arise and dissolve, held together only by habit and craving. Understanding non-self is intended to undercut the self-centered grasping that drives suffering, and it distinguishes Buddhism from traditions that posit an enduring soul.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 56 "Unknown" — Brannigan reads the film's mirror imagery through the Buddha's mirror instruction to his son Rahula: Neo touching the dripping mirror and becoming the mirror marks his awakening to the naked truth (aletheia as nakedness) that his world is a programmed illusion, Smith's dark sunglasses distort while Morpheus's mirrored glasses clarify, and Neo's reflection in the spoon-bending boy's spoon signals clarity. 'There is no spoon' parallels the Zen mondo where neither flag nor wind moves but only mind, and shows that reflected images are not reality - the world is maya. The deepest lesson is anatman: just as there is no spoon there is no Neo, no fixed self, and Rahula's lesson grounds the interdependence (pratityasamutpada) of all actions on others.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 124 "Unknown" — The chapter reads 'the One' through the concentration-camp survivor who, by sheer presence, retained others' dignity and will to live—a place in the social link filled by transference rather than real qualities—and opposes this to the film's One, who merely learns the virtualized reality's rules can be suspended, a paranoid notion that reduces the resistance of the Real to weak will. The spoon-bending child's 'there is no spoon' should have pushed the film to the Buddhist proposition that I myself do not exist, while Agent Smith's speech that humans 'define their reality through suffering and misery' makes him the analyst-figure whose lesson is that reality is that which resists.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 21 "“Nobody’s Bob Dylan”" — Vernezze and Lulewicz take Dylan's 1964 Halloween quip "I got my Bob Dylan mask on" as an entry into personal identity, testing each theory against his life: the bodily view (Zimmerman to Dylan) survives cell turnover but stumbles on brain-transplant cases; Locke's memory theory handles them but faces Reid's brave-officer regress and Alzheimer's cases, and Dylan's reincarnation lyrics ("Shelter from the Storm," "I and I") ignore memory altogether. The Christian soul view of the gospel albums ("When He Returns," "Gotta Serve Somebody") follows Descartes and Plato but cannot justify the swirl-to-filling inference that souls exist. The chapter ends sympathetic to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist no-self: Dylan's "I is another," his name as fabrication, and the cover album Self Portrait all deny a fixed self-created essence.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 13 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Priest argues that Pirsig's Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance is far more genuinely Zen than its disclaimer admits: once riding becomes effortless, the dissolution of the subject-object distinction that Dogen calls genjokoan arrives on the open road ('you ARE the driving and the road and the elements'), and the Harley's relaxed posture and low-revving thug-thug-thug rhythm make it a better vehicle for suchness than cars or whinier bikes. Even maintenance done as an end in itself is genjokoan, and because ultimate reality erases every conceptual distinction, care of self, others, and the bike amount to the same thing, the Mahayana ground of compassion; the mountain-and-water Zen saying resolves the paradox that the unconceptualized and the conceptualized are one. Suffering, on the Buddhist diagnosis Priest applies, comes from imposing conceptual grids that see the world wrong, and seeing it aright dissolves it.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 14 "Mind the Mindfulness" — Reads The Meaning of Life as a sustained reductio of transcendentalism — the two-world metaphysics shared by Plato, Augustine, and Vedanta's Brahman/atman — arguing that the film's dehumanizing sketches (the machine that goes 'ping,' the 'every sperm is sacred' father selling his children, the Vegas-style Christmas in Heaven) show how otherworldly belief overrides this-worldly compassion. It parallels the Buddha's scriptural critiques: the Agganna sutta against caste, the no-self (anatta) doctrine against the Bhagavad Gita's soul that licenses Krishna to tell Arjuna killing is a favor, and impermanence (anicca) against the fantasy of eternal bliss. Python's grotesque — Creosote's explosion, the organ-donor lady's 'Galaxy Song' despair — matches Buddhist corpse meditations, while the film steers between hedonism (Creosote) and nihilism (the housewife who surrenders her liver) toward the Buddha's Middle Way and, against everyday distraction (the boardroom's 'people are not wearing enough hats,' the couple who think Schopenhauer begins with an S), toward mindfulness (sati).
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 44 "“How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons" — James McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism: the fleet's sleepless FTL jumps in "33" and Roslin's dwindling survivor counts enact the four noble truths, Leoben's interrogation scenes teach that suffering comes from ignorant attachment, and Dogen's no-self and impermanence frame the show's interdependent characters. Cylon resurrection, D'Anna's serial deaths, and the prophecy that "all of this has happened before" model karma and samsara, while Nishida's kenotic God of Absolute Nothingness makes sense of Six and Leoben's God of love. Because Cylons feel pain, fear death away from a resurrection ship, and act volitionally, McRae concludes they are persons in the Buddhist sense, owed the compassion of the Eightfold Path.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 21 "Analyzing Emptiness" — Paul Gass reads the Dead's hippie milieu (the Beats, the Acid Tests, Buddhist-monk lyricist Peter Monk) as a conduit for Buddhist doctrine, taking the 'Eyes of the World' chorus as an invitation to awaken to Buddha-nature. He explains the Four Noble Truths, karma, and the five aggregates to argue the self is an illusion, using the image of a flame passed between lighters at a Dead show to picture rebirth without a persisting soul. The chapter then presents Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka middle way — emptiness itself must not be clutched as an absolute truth — and reads the 'redeemer... wagon loaded with clay' verse of 'Eyes of the World' as the Mahayana bodhisattva liberating all beings, with emptiness finally discarded like the boat after crossing the river.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 9 "“Logic Without Need Is Sterile”" — Writing as a Vulcan philosophy professor and student of Spock, the chapter reconstructs Vulcan civilization from Surak's Awakening as three interlocking modes of logic — formal logic (whose first law, Kiri-kin-tha's 'nothing unreal exists', parallels Parmenides), ethical logic (the axiom 'the needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few'), and meditative discipline — and maps them onto Patanjali's Yoga: the yamas, meditation, and samadhi's cosmic oneness, with ahimsa linking Surak to Gandhi and King. It then rereads Star Trek: The Motion Picture, where V'Ger's pure logic leaves both it and Spock asking 'Is this all that I am?', and Spock's mind meld with V'Ger becomes a tantric union that integrates feeling with logic after the failure of Kolinahr. The chapter's thesis is that 'logic without need is sterile': logic is 'the beginning of wisdom . . . not the end', and Spock's rebirth culminates in choosing the human thing precisely when it is not the logical thing.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 26 "Mr. Monk Murdered Trudy" — Green argues Monk is an unintentional Bodhisattva whose OCD enacts the Four Bodhisattva Vows: the compulsion to touch lampposts is the first vow's blind desires, his monastic minimalism the Dharma gate, and his crime-solving compassion for a disordered world the third vow, with the Dhammapada's teaching that the untamed mind produces suffering exemplified by Monk and by Harold Krenshaw's rival ordering. Like Vimalakirti feigning illness, or Shawn Spencer in Psych, and like the father in the Lotus Sutra's burning-house parable, Monk and his writers use skillful deception to awaken viewers to suffering and loving kindness. The title thesis is that Monk cannot solve Trudy's murder because he accepts responsibility for it: by Thich Nhat Hanh's Interbeing there is no absolute self and other, so solving the case requires the Zen 'kill the Buddha' eradication of the self, Monk's nirvana-as-extinction and the end of the series.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 8 "2 - An Interview with Bodhidharma" — Priest stages a spoof radio interview with Bodhidharma at the Shaolin Temple to argue that the monks' fighting exercises are really meditation: a fist passing an inch from your nose focuses the mind, and repeatedly practicing violent techniques makes practitioners less violent. Bodhidharma explains that a liter of goat's milk, a marauding thug, and even the reporter's self are only conceptual labels over 'thusness' (tathata), that attachment and the desire to strike cause suffering to the striker, and that the Buddha's compassion permits self-defense without aggression. The punchline is the reporter's unanswered last question: 'They're not really about fighting, are they?'
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 10 "And the Winner Is" — Lynch pits Plato against the Shaolin monks on the nature of the self that martial training is supposed to master. Plato's Republic makes the athlete-warrior Guardian a harmonious, rationally ruled tripartite soul whose bravery is 'remembering what ought and ought not to be feared', trained so reason governs aggression; Buddhism instead dissolves the self into five impermanent aggregates (illustrated by the chariot analogy) and reads mushin as a direct taste of no-self. He awards the practical decision to the Buddhist fighting monks, since no-self explains martial spontaneity and naturally arising compassion, while admitting Plato's substantive rational soul is not strictly refuted.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 18 "Halo as a Catalyst for a Buddhism Videogame" — Luke Cuddy uses Halo 3 checkpoints and emulator save states—two mutually exclusive Flood-fight outcomes both in some sense true—to make David Lewis's possible worlds and modal truth concrete, with Leibniz as the doctrine's ancestor. Halo's infinite lives make players genuinely angry, and the chapter argues this is upaya territory: like the father in the Lotus Sutra's parable of the burning house, the game promises mastery (the goat-, deer-, and ox-carts) to lure players toward something greater outside it. Master Chief becomes a Bodhisattva whose avatar slides between extension of self and other, provoking the 'who am I?' crisis that reveals the ego as empty at the ultimate level of the Two-Fold Truth, while the Dalai Lama's enemies-as-teachers turns the seven-year-old who pwns you into practice in the first two Noble Truths' suffering and anger.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 50 "Chapter 07 - Scan Thyself" — Butler frames Dick as the latest in philosophy's self-knowledge line: the Delphic 'know thyself' that Socrates made essential to the good life at the cost of his own, the Buddha who sought himself and found only an illusion at the root of suffering, Descartes whose entire philosophy rests on confidence in knowledge of himself as an immaterial being, and Dick's own 8,000-page Exegesis. The chapter's hook is the stakes of self-ignorance (what if you turned out to be something horrible?) and its Dickian version: how do you know you are not an android?
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 61 "The Devil and Philosophy" — John Thompson argues Mara, who unleashes armies and seductive daughters on the Buddha-to-be under the bodhi tree, is not 'the Buddhist Satan': he has not fallen, wages no cosmic war against a supreme God, and merely personifies trsna (grasping) as overlord of samsara. He finds textbook glosses like Huston Smith's misleading, and praises Bertolucci's Little Buddha, where Mara rises from a pool as Siddhartha's mirror twin - 'Oh Lord of my own Ego, you are pure illusion. You do not exist' - a portrayal he reads through Karen Armstrong's Jungian shadow self and Campbell's Freudian eros-and-thanatos frame, concluding that we are Mara/Satan.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 22 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Klein and Fundora trace Jobs's Buddhism from Reed College meditation and the seven-month India pilgrimage (reading Yogananda's Autobiography of a Yogi yearly) to the Zen minimalism of Apple design, arguing his temper tantrums, harsh speech, and reality distortion field do not disqualify him from being 'on the path' since Buddhism is a practice, not a creed test. They expound the Four Noble Truths (dukkha in its three kinds, via Thich Nhat Hanh), the Eightfold Path's Middle Way, and anatta—the non-self they compare to Hume's bundle theory of the self against Descartes's thinking thing—and read Jobs's strip-away-the-essence aesthetics, the three-click intuitive iPod interface that keeps users in the moment, the non-dualist marriage of art and technology, and his Think Different self-reliance as deeply Buddhist authenticity.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 11 "3. Tris Finds Enlightenment" — Rhine argues that Tris's heroism rests on Buddhist practice: her breath-counting on the Ferris wheel and inside Four's fear landscape, her emotional intelligence, and her awareness of the parental 'voices in her head' are classic meditative disciplines for calming the ego whose clinging, on the Buddhist account, is the cause of suffering (dukkha). She reads Abnegation's gray houses, plain food, and four-times-a-year mirror as ritual ego-diminishment - a middle way between indulgence and the extreme asceticism the Buddha rejected - that explains why most Divergent arise from Abnegation. Contemporary neuroscience is then recruited: the amygdala-versus-prefrontal-cortex struggle Will describes, and monks' heightened gamma waves, explain how Tris can see the simulation as a simulation, like Neo in The Matrix, and act while others are paralyzed by fear.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 36 "23. I Fight Crime in My Sleep" — Staged as a Fight Club parody in which a Buddhist psychiatrist, Dr. Quinzel, evaluates a costumed narrator sent to Arkham, the chapter argues neither hero is close to awakening: Batman's crime-fighting is craving that perpetuates dukkha, his secret identities a twice-constructed self that the Buddha's no-self teaching dissolves, and his violence fails the test that 'hostility is never appeased by hostility.' Superman fares no better - his super-intellect imposes illusory order on impermanence, his flight and X-ray vision are distractions beside the Buddha-eye and tapas, and as one of the titans of the six realms he is further from Buddhahood than a human - while the doctor defines justice as karma rather than retaliation and finds Batman one step from American Psycho's Bateman. Only conquering Mara, one's own inner deceiver, is 'the only superpower worth having,' and the closing reveal that the doctor has a plan of her own for 'Mr. Kent' caps the diagnosis.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 17 "6. One Clone from Another" — Asks what metaphysically individuates one Leda clone from another, surveying the tradition: Aristotelian substances bearing properties, Plato's and Descartes's non-repeatable individual essences, Berkeley's and Hegel's soul-substances, Aquinas's matter-based view, Locke's memory-based personal identity (with its sleeping-copy and consciousness-download objections), and Hume's argument that substance is a meaningless idea. It then turns to the Buddhist framework — the Four Noble Truths, anatman (no eternal self), the five skandhas, and dependent origination, illustrated by Alison's soap-and-drug crates — before closing with Nishida Kitaro's logic of contradictory self-identity. Read through that lens, the clone dance party in Felix's loft shows each clone's moves are truly her own precisely because they incorporate and mirror her sisters': identity is relational, not intrinsic.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 31 "17. Dialog with the Buddha" — A Platonic-style fictional dialogue in which a newly enlightened "Canadian Buddha" walks out of the northern Ontario bush to the Prolethean farm and debates Tomas, Henry, and Bonnie over whether clones are abominations. Using karma, rebirth, the gandhabba that carries consciousness-flux to a new embryo, the no-soul doctrine, and the eightfold path, the Buddha argues clones are ordinary beings of the karmic flux — like the split bacterium, nothing unnatural — but that cloning multiplies clinging: hosts crave immortality through copies, each clone inherits the host's whole accumulated karma, and Henry's dream of training an army of Helena-clones would only deepen the unsatisfactoriness the Buddha's mustard-seed lesson says clinging to the dead always brings. Only ending the cycle through enlightenment releases anyone; the clone, like the lost child, is not the one you lost.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 15 "6. Bowie the Buddhist" — Muchall reads 'Quicksand' and 'Where Are We Now?' as suffused with Tibetan Buddhism: 'Don't believe in yourself' voices the anatta teaching Bowie absorbed studying with Chime Rinpoche and from Chogyam Trungpa, whose 'spiritual materialism' warns that ego converts even spirituality and ideologies to its own use. After retelling the Buddha's life, the Four Noble Truths' three kinds of dukkha, and the five aggregates that reveal no permanent self, the chapter maps the song's 'ragged hole' and bardos onto the Tibetan Book of the Dead's after-death journey, and reads Bowie's morphing personas as lived acknowledgment that there is no fixed self - 'there's nothing in here.'
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 25 "14. David Bowie’s Sadness" — Ketcham argues Bowie's sadness is ours: via Deleuze and Guattari's Anti-Oedipus he casts consumer capitalism as a machine producing schizophrenic fad-following (the stuck high-school footballer, the Benetton self), of which Bowie's serial personas are both symptom and escape - 'always crashing in the same car' yet never repeating. Minkowski's lived time and the Buddha's anatman ground the dance as pure becoming without a dancer, while Heidegger's das Man and being-toward-death explain why authentic self-creation - which, unlike Sellers or Williams, Bowie survived - exacts the price Freud's beyond-the-pleasure-principle names as compulsive repetition, turned by Bowie into a life wish.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 36 "22. The Many-Faced God and Indian Philosophy" — Van Eyghen maps the Faceless Men onto Indian philosophy: their one God of many faces parallels Vedanta's Brahman in personal form as Ishvara, and Arya's training to become 'no one' parallels shedding the ego toward identity with Brahman - with Jaqen as guru and the stick-beating ritual as an example of identity fusion in Harvey Whitehouse's cognitive science of religion. But the Faceless Men may go further than Vedanta toward Buddhism, since they worship a god with no face of his own and aim at no-self rather than union, while Arya's pragmatic adoption of the shellfish-merchant disguise echoes the Bhagavad Gita's Krishna: perform your duty without attachment to any self.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 24 "12. A Month from Now, I’ll Be a Balding, Toothless Skeleton" — Reads Fiona Goode's war against fading - the experimental RM47 serum, rejecting the Axeman's escape because he would watch her decay, the Papa Legba bargain that collapses because she has no soul - alongside Delphine LaLaurie's blood facials and Marie Laveau's child sacrifices, as illustrations of Buddhist dukkha and the three thirsts (kama for sense pleasure, bhava for existence, vibhava for annihilation). Legba's 'you don't have a soul' becomes an accidentally liberating glimpse of anatta, and Cordelia's dying advice - 'feel the fear... let it all go' - is the mindfulness, echoing Buddhaghosa's corpse meditations, that might have freed Fiona.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 17 "8. Ode to Joi" — Steve Bein first tests Joi against Mary Anne Warren's five functionalist personhood criteria — consciousness, reason, self-motivated activity, communication, self-awareness — and finds she passes, which makes Luv's stomping of the emanator a murder. The Buddha's no-self doctrine then denies that anyone, Joi included, is an enduring person: we are bundles of fleeting psychophysical processes, 'like tears in rain', which threatens to let Luv plead that the Luv who killed Joi no longer exists. Nagarjuna's two truths resolve the courtroom problem: ultimately there are no persons, but conventionally 'Luv killed Joi' is perfectly true, and the karma ripples through the whole network.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 25 "14. After the Blackout" — Martin Muchall treats the offscreen Blackout as an emblem of the moral catastrophe diagnosed in MacIntyre's After Virtue: our moral vocabulary has shattered into emotivist hissing and clapping, with Roy's murder of Tyrell, his 'God of biomechanics', staging the death of God and the 'everything is permitted' that follows. Utilitarian pleasure and Kantian cold reason (Spock, who must tell the truth to the murderer at the door) have both failed, leaving neoliberal hypercapitalism — corporate psychopathy, the orphanage sweatshop, the Baseline as workplace performance review — as the real villain. Against this, K's ending models the Buddha: everything is impermanent, there is no self to defend, and his selfless, empathetic death points to a morality grounded in evolved and cultivable altruism.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 14 "4. Can We Do Enough Good" — Fetterman argues no one can do enough good to earn The Good Place because the real question is who defines good. Moving from Hobbes's state of nature and Rousseau's innate compassion to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist doctrine of non-self, he shows the four humans' characters were assembled by their formative communities, which is Michael's whole defense before Judge Gen. But Nietzsche's account of how communities christen their own customs 'good' exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife accountants impose their in-group preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's life of point-maximization fails, and why Michael should be asking the Frozen Yogurt Problem instead of blaming demon tampering.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 38 "Fearlessness and Power" — Rebuts Ozai's taunt 'you are still weak' with a Buddhist reading of energybending: Aang wins not by domination but because his unbendable spirit is total vulnerability, a true heart that has abandoned the five hindrances (sensory desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness, doubt — each traced through the chakras, the Serpent's Pass, and 'Nightmares and Daydreams') and a true mind freed from the fundamental delusion of a separate self that 'The Swamp' and 'The Guru' dissolve. The spirit-merging with Ozai is read through Indra's net, and Aang's merciful halt mirrors Indra's Jataka victory where compassion for eagle hatchlings — not force — defeats the demons. Fearlessness, on Sylvia Boorstein's Zen story, is the natural corollary of compassion, so Aang's weakness by Ozai's standard is precisely his power.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 38 "Fearlessness and Power" — Argues that Aang's energybending victory over Ozai vindicates a Buddhist conception of power against Ozai's equation of power with domination: the Lion Turtle's 'unbendable spirit' is not resistance but thorough vulnerability, achieved through the true heart (overcoming the five hindrances mapped onto Aang's sensory desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness, and doubt across the series) and the true mind (overcoming the fundamental delusion of a self separate from others, learned from Huu in 'The Swamp' and Guru Pathik). The merging of Aang's and Ozai's spirits is pictured by the metaphor of Indra's net, and Indra's own Jataka victory, halting his assault to protect eagle hatchlings and disorienting the demons, parallels Aang's refusal to win by killing. Drawing on a Zen story of the abbot who could 'be run through by a sword without batting an eye', the chapter concludes that Aang's fearlessness flows from compassion, so that weakness by Ozai's standard is precisely the power that defeats him.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 40 "Journey’s End and a Vision of a New Community" — Reads Aang's quest through the Karmapa Ogyen Trinley Dorje's book Interconnected: like the seventeenth Karmapa, identified at age seven and taken from his family, Aang learns that an exalted title complicates friendship and that freedom is self-control rather than the rugged individualism of the American hero's quest. Training episodes (Katara's jealous competition in 'The Waterbending Scroll', Jeong Jeong's warnings, the Toph-versus-Katara sifu debate in 'Bitter Work') show moral training as communal, widening from Team Avatar as adoptive family toward universal compassion, with Aang's refusal to open the seventh chakra illustrating how local attachment can obstruct universal love. Zuko's counter-arc from competition, isolation, and betrayal to humility, forgiveness, and contentment shows compassion turning an enemy into a friend, and the finale's simultaneous battles (White Lotus liberating Ba Sing Se, Sokka and Toph destroying the fleet) affirm that Aang wins as an 'interdependent individual', never alone.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 26 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — LoPresti uses 'This Week in God' segments (Ed Helms refereeing a Hindu-versus-Mayan 'faith-off', Colbert's roast line that all religions are infinite paths to accepting Jesus, Rob Corddry's purification rituals and God Exchange stock ticker) to lay out exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism as responses to religious diversity. Inclusivism like Colbert's 'anonymous Christian' logic is exposed as intellectual imperialism that erases genuinely distinct teachings such as the Buddhist non-self and impermanence, while the chapter defends a deep pluralism against the relativism that makes 'all religions equally true' meaningless. Its eulogy for the God Machine borrows Marx's view of religion as an instrument of mass control to explain why religious humor now survives only through a political lens.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 12 "Hakuna Matata, Bodhisattva" — Sets up Disney's maxim 'Hey kid, you can be a hero' as the direct opposite of Zen's 'Hey kid, you can be a buddha': escapism versus liberation, told through the life of Dogen, whose monastic choice parallels Disney hero narratives. Mickey in Steamboat Willie — a bundle of still frames with no sound and no real 'he' — illustrates the Buddha's three marks of existence (emptiness, impermanence, frustration), and the chapter argues Disney products are calibrated distractions from these marks while Dogen counsels facing them, with Ariel's Andersen fate as the price of fantasy. It closes on Disney's merchandising machine (Yoda, Star Wars sequels, direct-to-video cash grabs) as everything the countercultural minimalist Yoda or Baloo's bare necessities stand against, concluding that real hakuna matata is accepting impermanence rather than escaping it.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 14 "4. Can We Do Enough Good" — Interrogates Chidi's question 'why do we choose to be good?' through Hobbes's selfish state of nature, Rousseau's hardwired compassion (Michael's 'little voice' in Eleanor's head), and Hume's bundle theory extended Buddhist-style to a non-self, which grounds Michael's plea to Judge Gen that bad communities made the four humans bad and a better community (Team Cockroach, the Brainy Bunch) can make them good. Nietzsche's account of how communities define their own customs as 'good' then exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife's accountants impose their in-group's preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's point-maximizing life cannot clear the bar. The chapter ends by asking Michael's real question: who gets to decide what's good?
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 21 "a9.xhtml" — The chapter argues Tolkien's clearest moral in The Hobbit is against possessiveness, starting from Aquinas' definition of greed as 'immoderate love of riches': dragon-sickness ruins Thorin and drowns the Master of Lake-town starving in the wilderness with his gold, and Gollum shows the isolating end of a life organized around a 'precious'. Buddhism reframes the diagnosis - Gollum's craving (tanha) is rooted in ignorance (avidya) of the self's illusoriness, since grasping enriches a self that does not exist, per the Four Noble Truths - while Laozi's 'he who knows he has enough is rich' and Thoreau's 'a man is rich in proportion to the things he can afford to let alone' are embodied by Beorn and the gift-giving, nearly government-less hobbits. Bilbo's generosity - giving away the Arkenstone worth 'more than a river of gold', taking only two small chests, later giving Sting and the mithril coat to Frodo - is the book's counter-example to greed.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 29 "Notes" — Kahn argues LEGO play embodies the Buddhist teaching of impermanence that the Buddha states in the Digha Nikaya ('Impermanent are all component things...'): his childhood urge to superglue creations and Finn's father's Kragle dramatize the clinging that produces anxiety when things change, from brick formulations to discontinued sets and even funerals' wilting flowers. The LEGO Star Wars Death Star illustrates non-self — no Death Star exists apart from its 3,803 pieces, and no self apart from shifting aggregates — and the five aggregates (form, sensation, perception, formations, consciousness) are unpacked through building experiences like discovering a daughter has opened the mint Taj Mahal set. Tibetan sand mandalas, painstakingly built then ritually dissolved, model the ceremonial demolition of LEGO creations, teaching acceptance of change without sliding into a nihilistic 'why bother building at all'.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 18 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Godwin reads Spider-Man 3's black-suit episode as a question about the self: with the symbiote amplifying his anger, is Peter still Peter? Against Hume's and the Buddha's bundle theories, on which the self is only an imagined aggregate of thoughts and feelings, and Reid's common-sense simple self, she advances the pragmatist 'social self' of Peirce, James, Dewey, and Mead, updated as Engel's biopsychosocial model: Peter's identity is a shifting web of biology, psyche, and relationships (Aunt May, MJ, Harry) expressed in actions and character. Eddie succumbs to the symbiote because, as Dewey says of the slave to his own blind desires, hatred constitutes who he is, while Peter's thicker web of good relations lets him shed the suit at the church bell.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 36 "23. I Fight Crime in My Sleep" — A Fight Club-style Arkham case study: a patient's hallucinated Superman companion is diagnosed by a Buddhist psychiatrist who explains the three marks of existence—impermanence, non-self, and dissatisfaction—arguing superheroes impose order and a fabricated second self on a world that resists both, so Superman's super-intellect and even flight are distractions (levitation should be ignored; the Buddha-eye beats x-ray vision) while Batman's violence and psychosis, compared to American Psycho's Patrick Bateman, make awakening impossible—both are victims of Mara. A robber literally named David Hume objects that the heroes' law and order is grounded on what ought to be rather than what is, and a Gandhi quote on preferring one's own bad government explains why Batman finally kryptonites his alien 'friend.' The verdict inverts the book's debate: conquering the deceiver within is the only superpower worth having.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 18 "Notes" — Reads Rust's 'dream inside a locked room' and 'everybody is nobody' monologues through the dream-argument and illusion-of-self traditions: the Upanishads and Advaita's atman/brahman, Vasubandhu's Buddhist non-self, Zhuangzi's butterfly dream, Plato's Theaetetus, and Descartes' dream doubt, plus Metzinger's self-model neuroscience. It diagnoses Rust as a neuro-nihilist in Metzinger's sense and defines his predicament with Nietzsche's nihilist, who judges the world as it is that it ought not to be, while noting Schopenhauer misread India's religions as pessimistic. Thompson argues nihilism is a deep insight gone awry — the self is not a thing but an enacted process like dancing — and reads Rust's final near-death experience of love as proof that transcendence of the dream of being a person is possible.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 19 "The Zen Master and the Big Aristotle" — Allhoff and Vaidya argue against the skeptic that philosophy is useless 'bullshit' (nodding to Frankfurt's book) by showing how Phil Jackson's coaching applies it. Jackson's Zen Buddhism, especially zazen meditation and selfless 'triangle offense' play, teaches players to empty the ego and stay in the present, transforming Jordan from point-maker to play-maker; and Jackson's gift of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics to Shaquille O'Neal, who then dubbed himself 'the Big Aristotle,' illustrates Aristotle's doctrine that excellence (his improved free-throw shooting, his generosity) is a habit built by repetition.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 26 "Twelfth Hole Midround and Midlife Defining Moments" — Andy Wible uses defining mid-round shots (the water ball on Augusta's twelfth, the shank that ruins a round) as a way into theories of personal identity, asking why some events make us who we are. He runs through body theory, Descartes's soul theory ('I think, therefore I am'), and Locke's memory theory (the prince-and-cobbler case), refining it with Shoemaker's quasi-memories, to argue that memory is central to identity and explains why a golfer cannot shake a bad shot. He then weighs the Buddhist/Humean/Heraclitean denial of a permanent self as a coping tool ('someone else hit the shank') and debates whether the beta-blocker Propranolol, which dulls adrenaline-fixed memories, could ethically erase the yips much as it treats PTSD.
