- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 21 "Genius All the Time The Beats, Spontaneous Presence, and Primordial Ground" — Marc Olmsted reads Beat spontaneity through Tantric (Vajrayana) Buddhism, arguing that 'first thought, best thought' and Kerouac's 'Mind is shapely, art is shapely' rest on the view that enlightenment/awareness is already present and need only be recognized. He maps Ginsberg's poetics onto the Tantric terms Ground, Path, and Fruition, tying shamatha-vipashyana practice and the doctrine of anatta (no-self) to the poet catching the first pre-conceptual thought. Ginsberg's Blake visions, his study under Trungpa and Gelek Rinpoche, and Burroughs's cut-up 'homemade yankee tantra' are offered as evidence that Beat composition enacts a Buddhist recognition of primordial, empty, self-existing awareness.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 12 "2. Know Thyself, Agent Cooper!" — De Carvalho reads Cooper's ordeal in the Black Lodge as a journey of self-knowledge, distinguishing 'knowing yourself' (your feelings, as Laura sought with Dr. Jacoby) from 'knowing your Self' in the deep sense of Vedanta's Brahman and Tibetan Buddhism's Mind. He sets Hume's bundle theory—the failure to catch a self behind the perceptions—against the Hindu Swami's ocean-and-waves image of an eternal Self beyond thought, and reads Cooper's confrontation with his screaming-Laura and doppelganger visions via the Tibetan Book of the Dead and Jung's shadow: facing his fears with imperfect courage, Cooper fails to integrate his shadow and is split in two.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 44 "“How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons" — James McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism: the fleet's annihilation and constant death illustrate the Four Noble Truths' duhkha, arising from ignorant attachment and violating interdependent arising (no-self and impermanence). Cylon death-and-resurrection parallels karma and rebirth ('all of this has happened before'), Leoben acts as a koan-wielding roshi unsettling Starbuck's assumptions, and Nishida's kenotic God as Absolute Nothingness matches the Cylons' 'we're all God.' Because Cylons feel pain, suffer cognitively, and earn karma, McRae concludes they are persons capable of satori who should seek compassionate reconciliation with humans.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 26 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — LoPresti uses the 'This Week in God' segments (the God Machine, Ed Helms's Hindu-vs-Mayan 'faith-off,' Colbert's inclusivist White House roast) to lay out three responses to religious diversity—exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism—and defends John Cobb's Whiteheadian process-metaphysics pluralism. He insists the distinct concepts of religions be respected rather than collapsed, citing Buddhist impermanence and no-Self and the South Asian Atman/Brahman as unique and non-reducible, and closes by reading the show's turn to political framing of religion through Marx's claim that religion is a mechanism for controlling the masses.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 18 "MOTHERHOOD" — Sheryl Tuttle Ross applies three of the Buddhist noble truths – pain is inevitable, pain arises from attachment, suffering can end – to contemporary mothering, contrasting the Buddhist acceptance of pain with Bentham's utilitarian pleasure-maximizing. Drawing on Thich Nhat Hanh's mindfulness and the doctrines of impermanence and no-self, she offers 'mommy meditations' (breathe, become aware, recognize social scripts, respond kindly) and reads the novel I Don't Know How She Does It, whose 'Court of Motherhood' dramatizes the guilt-inducing scripts mindfulness helps mothers see through to experience beauty in ordinary moments.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 15 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Geisz reads his daily morning coffee ritual through Buddhist metaphysics: the pre-caffeine grogginess and its transient relief illustrate saṃsāra and duḥkha, the First Noble Truth, driven by self-centered craving (the Second). The transience of the perfect-temperature cup shows impermanence (anitya), and the question of whether a 'self' pre- or post-coffee exists is answered by anatman — he offers three hypotheses (full self dormant, half coffee-cyborg, self created ex Coffea) then dissolves them into no-self plus dependent arising, where the cup and drinker are empty nodes in a web of physical, economic, and karmic conditions. Each intentional sip lays down karma that binds tomorrow's 'me' further into the cycle.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 35 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Lynch, a tattooed Buddhist philosophy professor, tests his largely Buddhist body art (an Om-mani-padme-hum armband, Bodhidharma, the Buddha's face, the eight-spoked Wheel and lotus, a double-vajra) against the Buddha's Three Marks of Existence. He argues a 'permanent' tattoo need not contradict impermanence any more than Gruzalski's washed-away sandcastle if approached mindfully, that custom ink need not reify a self given the chariot analogy of no-self (which he links to Hume's bundle view), and that the pain of tattooing directly instantiates dukkha and can become an object of meditation and compassion. Mindful tattooing, he concludes, can itself be authentic Buddhist practice.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 26 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Abby Thompson, a somatic psychologist, sets Raja yoga metaphysics (five koshas, a blissful true self distinct from the ego, nadis and chakras as energy flow) beside clinical psychology's brain-chemistry, DSM model, arguing the two paradigms are complementary. Using warrior II and camel pose plus the neuroscience maxim 'neurons that fire together wire together,' she shows how yoga trains self-regulation, distinguishes constructive discomfort from injurious pain, and can serve as complementary therapy — with instructors bearing therapist-like responsibility for the emotional vulnerability and transference that arise on the mat.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 44 "“How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons" — McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism, using Dogen and the Four Noble Truths. The fleet's relentless suffering (the "33" jumps, the Olympic Carrier), impermanence (Roslin's dwindling headcount), and no-self frame duhkha; Leoben functions as a roshi whose koan-like preaching makes Starbuck and Adama question their false ideals, and the Cylon death-and-resurrection cycle parallels karma and rebirth. Because Cylons feel and are cognitively aware of pain and can accrue karma, McRae concludes they are persons capable of satori, so human and Cylon liberation are intertwined.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 45 "42. Up in the Air as Philosophy Buddhism and the Middle Path" — Duffy reads Ryan Bingham's arc in Up in the Air as a Zen Buddhist parable paralleling Hesse's Siddhartha. Ryan preaches an 'empty backpack' philosophy of nonattachment and treats the miles as their own point, but Duffy argues he only intellectually grasps the four noble truths — dukkha, its cause in attachment (tṛṣṇā), and the eightfold path — until his failed attachment to Alex and his mentorship of Natalie make him actually suffer. Like Siddhartha with his son, Ryan learns wisdom must be experienced, that the anattā (non-self) doctrine undercuts the identity he built on his job, and that the goal is not escaping the world but living the Middle Path within it, present to suffering rather than spinning silver linings.

### The Ethics of Political Violence

The ethics of political violence asks when, if ever, the use of force outside ordinary law is morally justified in pursuit of political aims, and what distinguishes legitimate resistance from terrorism. Central questions include whether violence can be excused by the justice of a cause, whether the deliberate targeting of civilians is ever permissible, and how to weigh oppression, self-defense, and the prospects for peaceful change. Traditions such as just war theory, pacifism, and revolutionary thought offer competing answers, and terrorism—typically defined as violence against noncombatants to spread fear for political ends—poses an especially hard case. The debate concerns both the ends invoked and the moral limits on the means used to reach them.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 13 "No Damsel in Distress" — Mimi Marinucci argues Buffy's violence tracks what agents do, not what they are: souled Angel and chip-enabled Spike receive moral consideration, willing human evildoers like Ford ('Lie to Me') and Ethan Rayne are fought, and Buffy's 'impression of Gandhi' in 'Anne' claims violence can rightly answer injustice. Building on William R. Jones's King–Malcolm X–Mao spectrum and Hannah Arendt's warning that doing violence habituates the agent, she reads the Slayer's fight as symbolic resistance to rape and women's oppression (bloodsucking as rape metaphor in 'Buffy vs. Dracula,' Spike's assault after Buffy ends the affair). The cost is real — 'Restless' reveals the First Slayer's primeval rage and staking with 'Mr. Pointy' mirrors sexualized violence — so she ends by endorsing tempered, appropriate violence (Buffy's Tai Chi training with Angel) over both passivity and aggression.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 26 "Against Fascism" — Neal King argues the Buffyverse is proto-fascist: Buffy kills demons and vampires on sight within a race-like hierarchy, tempered only by an Augustinian split between natural and moral evil (soulless vampires cannot choose otherwise; soul-bearing humans like Faith, Willow, and Warren can repent), she derives authority from an ancient calling rather than democracy, and the graduation battle of 'Graduation Day, Part Two' stages citizenship forged in mass combat. He imagines a fascist Buffyverse of 'brownskirt' death squads and concludes only the show's secrecy prevents full fascism, finally recommending that the racism be dropped but the ritual sacrifice of evildoers kept — with Willow's flaying of Warren as the model.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 30 "The Superhero As Liberal Reformer" — Jeffrey Pasley traces the show's radical surface — capitalism equated with vampirism (Anya's greed, Glory the über-consumer, the Master's blood factory in 'The Wish'), Big Bads tearing down dimensional barriers exactly as Marx's Communist Manifesto describes the bourgeoisie dissolving feudal ties into free trade, Buffy refusing to commodify slaying into wage labor, and Giles's Magic Box selling mystified junk at inflated margins — but concludes the heroes are not revolutionaries. In the comic-book lineage of Superman and Spider-Man, Buffy and Angel are liberal reformers bound by a superhero code against killing, so Giles must murder the innocent Ben precisely to preserve Buffy's heroic mercy; Angel's 'champions' speech in 'Deep Down' states the incrementalist creed.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 24 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Wendy Hamblet asks whether Narnia feeds children a dangerous militaristic moral imaginary: Homeric warrior heroes, swarthy Calormene villains, voiceless animals excluded from moral concern, and battles that decide truth, in a lineage running from Plato's censorship of nursery stories through Descartes's modernity to Heidegger's seduction by Hitler's myths. On closer reading she finds Lewis undermining militarism: morally mixed characters, condemnation of aggression, despotism, and 'reasons of state,' and room only for just war and righteous self-defense. The finale is read through Plato's cave, as the Last Battle's worlds-within-worlds expose our political 'truths' as shadow-images that unscrupulous leaders manipulate when the god is absent.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 91 "Chapter 14 - Bullshit at the Interface of Science and Policy Global Warming," — The chapter dissects 'we are waging a war on terror' word by word: the inclusive 'we' conscripts the listener, 'war' triggers unquestioning patriotism, and 'terror' — an emotion, rather than 'terrorists' or 'terrorism' — keeps the enemy suitably vague, a bogeyman Other to hunt. The phrase is bullshit not because fighting terrorism is wrong but because it replaces the thought and debate that democratic policy and military decisions require with fear management, and militant jihadists' 'God's will' rhetoric works the same way, never explaining how bombing or torturing the uninvolved will end fear. Both sides use bullshit to supply identity and purpose while evading genuine moral justification, which degrades our capacity to be moved by ideas.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 8 "Violence Against Utopia" — Drumin reads Sabotage as Hitchcock's anti-utopian statement: against perfectible societies imagined from Plato's Republic to Skinner, Freud and Dostoyevsky show that the psyche's attraction to chaos cannot be planned or conditioned away. In four scenes, the aquarium meeting where 'monsters from the Id' watch over Verloc's bomb deal, the bird shop where explosives sit among a child's toys, the conspiracy hatched behind a movie screen whose audience laughs at on-screen chaos, and Stevie's death on the bus, the film shows a quiet family man rationalizing mass murder by 'abstracting' its victims into a mere list of names. Hitchcock punishes the audience too, implicating its own safe enjoyment of represented violence, and concludes that only constant individual vigilance, never social engineering, keeps the potential for chaos in check.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 27 "Fire Without Burn" — Pinedo argues the series restages 'blowback' — the CIA term for covert intervention rebounding on the intervener — in science-fiction guise: Adama's 'playing God' speech, the 'Hero' revelation that his Armistice Line black op (abandoning Bulldog Novacek) may have triggered the Cylon attack, and his confession 'I started it,' complicated by Roslin's warning against simple explanations. The sci-fi 'smokescreen' lets Moore and Eick critique the war on terror — torture, the Pegasus rapes, sympathetic suicide bombers — without naming blowback in a corporate media environment, as the producers' interviews and podcast commentaries show. The show refuses Manichean demonology: the Cylons are made in our image, and the capacity for evil 'is part of what we do in the name of war.'
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 28 "The Future" — Dinello reads the New Caprica occupation as an Iraq allegory interpreted through Fanon's The Wretched of the Earth: occupation is violence personified (Cavil's 'saving them from damnation'), psychological violence colonizes minds (Leoben's manipulation of Starbuck, Jammer's recruitment into the New Caprica Police), and Tyrol's 'throw your body on the gears' strike speech channels Savio, Marx's seizing the means of production, and Marcuse on technology's repression. Fanon's thesis that anticolonial violence is a cleansing, liberating force is dramatized in Tigh's 'blood for blood,' the Temple massacre that recruits a thousand fighters, and Duck's suicide bombing — with Sartre's preface endorsing killing the oppressor and the ends-justify-means dispute between Tigh and Tyrol. The insurgency wins by not losing, as in Algeria and Vietnam, and the show is subversive because it makes viewers sympathize with the occupied.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 46 "Case in Point" — Using Wayne Booth's coduction, the ethical evaluation of fiction refined through open, informed conversation, this chapter argues BSG is a highly ethical show precisely because it keeps moral debate alive instead of preaching: the unresolved New Caprica suicide-bombing storyline, where an unsympathetic Baltar confronts a saintly Roslin in jail and she still cannot justify the bombings, invites the audience to do the ethical work. The chapter distinguishes Tolkien's allegory from applicability to block a one-to-one Iraq reading, and holds up Ronald Moore's candid blog exchange about the absence of gay characters as coduction in action. Sustained conversation, it concludes, is both the best defense against censorship and the best way to judge art.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 9 "The Only Truly Decent Man Left on the Planet" — John Kenneth Muir argues Dexter is best read not as heir to Hannibal Lecter or Patrick Bateman but as a full-blown superhero: his 'impeccable instincts' are a crime-detecting power like Spider-Man's spider-sense or the Shadow's, his gloves, apron and glass visor are a costume, and his 'invisible mask of sympathy' inverts the superhero mask since the Dark Passenger is the true identity. Dexter's orphan origin - Harry lifting the boy from the blood-soaked container - replays the Superman/Batman/Parker template, with the Ice Truck Killer as an amalgam of Riddler and Mr. Freeze who embodies the superhero's shadow potential, and the chapter reads Harry's Code as the American-monomyth vigilante premise that the law can be upheld only by one stepping outside it. The 'killing joke' is that the emotionless sociopath is the only impartial, decent agent of justice in a Miami Metro consumed by passion, and the extra-legal violence question the chapter raises is whether such vigilante force, with its disregard for civil rights, is what justice requires.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 17 "All for Love" — Jerry Piven argues Dexter's void is not genetic sociopathy but trauma: witnessing his mother's chainsaw murder and lying in her blood deadened his feelings, and each ritualized kill restages that catastrophe with the roles reversed, Dexter mastering death as the angel of it, reducing the murderer to a drop of blood he imprisons on a slide. Reading Harry's ghost as a Hamlet-father super-ego, he contends Dexter kills not only to master trauma but to please the father who channels his rage - murder 'for love' - and then generalizes: Arendt's banality of evil, Pascal on the void and faith, Kierkegaard and Heidegger on fleeing despair into conformity, Buddhist emptiness, and Becker-style terror-management findings explain how ordinary people, frightened of death and hungry for a leader's approval, can be manipulated into sanctioned slaughter, from Abu Ghraib to jihadism.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 173 "Lucifer’s Dream Ends" — Narrates the collapse of the Lucifer project through 1968-69: "Street Fighting Man" banned as incitement to violence after Mayor Daley's police beat protestors, Jagger reading Shelley's "Adonais" at Hyde Park after Brian Jones's death, and Anger salvaging Invocation of My Demon Brother from the stalled film. At Altamont the Hell's Angels stabbed Meredith Hunter during "Under My Thumb" while Jagger pleaded "just cool out"; Lester Bangs blamed egoism, hype and greed rather than the devil, and the Stones survived by trading rage and chaos for controlled spectacle — from Rock Satans to a knighted Elder Statesman of Rock.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 19 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Roberto Sirvent and Ian Diorio argue, following William Cavanaugh's 'myth of religious violence', that the assumption that religion is uniquely irrational, absolutist, and divisive blinds Americans to their own fanaticism. Homeland's blind spots - Carrie suspecting the Muslim Galvez, Dana's classmate nuking Tehran, 'Infinite Justice' naming, Guantanamo torture flashed right after Carrie's 'We don't do that here' - show the religious/secular split is a construct (traced to Locke's privatizing of faith and Augustine's broad religio) that legitimizes state violence while deeming identical acts crazy when done by the religious. Nazir's 'Who is the terrorist?' drone question and 'We only begin as enemies because that's what others told us to be' seal the point.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 22 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Jai Galliott argues Homeland's drone strike that killed Issa is not a one-off plot device but mirrors real US drone warfare that breeds blowback: strikes strengthen al-Qaeda's brand and radicalize the disaffected, from Brody to the Boston bombers. He analyzes the asymmetry problem - the weak side comingles with civilians, straining the just war principles of discrimination and proportionality, while drone operators living among US suburbs become contested targets - and rejects giving weaker states a 'wild card' of lowered ethical standards. His proposal is that the technologically superior side bind itself to stricter just war compliance and policing-like restraint, since foreseeable terrorist reciprocity can tip proportionality against the war itself.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 35 "Homeland and Philosophy" — William Rodriguez traces terrorism's evolving meaning from the Jacobins' state Terror through anarchist 'propaganda by deed' (Nechayev, Bakunin) to non-state groups, then tests whether Abu Nazir's campaign, grounded in bin Laden's 1998 fatwa grievances and the greater/lesser jihad distinction, can be morally justified. On a utilitarian defense terrorism could be last-resort self-defense against a collectively guilty population, but the just war criteria of competent authority, right intention, last resort, discrimination, and proportionality all fail for al-Qaeda, since civilians killed on 9/11 were neither combatants nor guilty. Deontologically, targeting civilians violates the right to life and human dignity, so Nazir's attacks on innocents are murder, however real the grievances.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 37 "Homeland and Philosophy" — This standalone section traces terrorism's history and definition, from the French Revolution's Reign of Terror when the state was 'le terroriste' (Robespierre's 'terror is nothing other than justice that is prompt, severe, and inflexible') to the term's reversal onto non-state actors via Russian anarchists like Nechayev. It offers a seven-feature characterization (violence, destruction, indiscriminate harm, psychological trauma, propaganda, policy change, non-state perpetration) matching the UN's 2004 definition, then catalogs often-forgotten American terrorism: the Boston Tea Party reframed as a news report, the Ku Klux Klan's campaign, the Haymarket bombing, the Los Angeles Times and Wall Street bombings by labor radicals and anarchists, the Bath School massacre, the Mad Bomber, the Weather Underground, anti-abortion Army of God killings, and the Unabomber.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 10 "1. A Good Man Goes to War" — Pless argues the Doctor's shift from the Ninth's self-avowed 'coward, any day' to the Eleventh's gun-toting action hero tracks real-world politics and markets rather than internal story logic: after the 7/7 London bombings and amid the War on Terror, and as the show's global export grew, a war-weary British ideal gave way to the decisive 'Oncoming Storm.' She traces the arc through the Tenth's gleeful xenocide of the Racnoss in 'The Runaway Bride,' the eternal punishment of the Family of Blood, the Eleventh brainwashing humanity to exterminate the Silence in 'Day of the Moon,' and the assault of 'A Good Man Goes to War,' before 'The Day of the Doctor' retcons the Time War so the Doctor never destroyed the Time Lords, validating the action-hero persona. Her conclusion: in a crisis culture demanding proactive heroes, cowardice—once the Doctor's honest self-assessment—was rebranded as vice.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 25 "14. Guns Don’t Kill Colors—Colors Kill Colors" — Robert Arp argues from Hobbes's right of nature—self-preservation as the first law found out by reason—that individuals, and by extension oppressed peoples, have a right to the means of lethal defense, so arming the lowColors of the Society is justified. He weighs pacifist counterpoints (Augustine on self-defense as inordinate self-love, the Buddhist first precept, Camus's refusal to kill) and answers with Aquinas's principle of double effect: Darrow destroying the flagship to save Luna, intending the good while foreseeing the deaths, is justified, as is killing in defense of innocent children the Institute rapes and eats. The Society then illustrates why disarmament enables tyranny—Hideyoshi's Sword Hunt, Stalin's weapons bans, the Golds' razor monopoly—so that when lowColors finally receive weapons in Morning Star they become the means by which the police state falls: guns equalize the weak against aggressors and the people against the state.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 44 "28. Severed Heads, Dirty Hands" — Ivanković and Božac argue that ruling Westeros necessarily means dirtying one's hands, staging the paradox through Varys's counsel to Ned and Jaime's 'finest act.' Hobbes supplies the baseline that anything preserving peace beats the war of all against all, Walzer permits dirty hands only to avert communal death (Daenerys swindling the Astapor slavers), and Kant's absolute refusal to lie - mirrored in Ned's honor - costs Ned his head and the realm a war. The chapter also indicts the reverse: Aemon's refusal of the throne and other too-clean refusals of responsibility are moral failures, Jon's killing of Qhorin Halfhand shows dirty hands are not just for kings, and rulers must resist the downward spiral while keeping, as Dany does, a gentle heart for the true goal.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 33 "20. Deadpool’s Genocide of the Marvel Universe" — Taking Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe seriously as a genocide story, the chapter reviews Lemkin's coinage and the 1948 Genocide Convention, then tests the mitigating factors - Deadpool's insanity, the X-Men's negligence in committing him to Psycho-Man's fake asylum, and Psycho-Man's manipulation - and finds none of them exculpatory. Killing Uatu the Watcher first and the Avengers next follows the genocide playbook of eliminating a community's intellectuals and pillars, and viewing his fellow characters as sheep completes the dehumanization that makes atrocity possible, while using everyone as means to his liberation violates Kant's demand never to treat persons as mere means. Invoking the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Thucydides' Melian Dialogue as the classic case of victims left unable to tell their story, the author concludes Deadpool bears full responsibility.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 12 "1. The Deed of F’ing Society" — Rocha reads fsociety's 5/9 logic-bomb attack on E Corp as anarchist 'propaganda of the deed' - a shocking act meant to wake people from their comfortable slumber inside hierarchy - and positions it between Alexander Berkman's violent anarchism (mirroring Phillip Price's 'bullet in the right place') and Gandhi's nonviolent self-suffering, quoting satyagraha and the older Goldman's rejection of violence. He then runs the hack through just war theory's four questions (necessity, proportionality, justification, effectiveness), noting that wiping the debt records also destroyed savings and indirectly got people like Gideon killed, and that fsociety, as Trenton says, never paints the alternative society - so the reader is left to answer whether the deed was justified.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 24 "10. If It Isn’t Justified Is It Still My Revolution" — Writing as a guilt-ridden fsociety member haunted by James Plouffe's on-air suicide, Altmann tests the 5/9 revolution against three theorists: Burke's conservatism condemns all revolution as destruction of social tradition (and fsociety's blackout chaos and Susan Jacobs's death seem to prove him right), while Marx's class struggle between E Corp's bourgeoisie and the indebted proletariat makes revolution the only exit from history's cycle. Kai Nielsen's condition - revolution is justified only when no other recourse exists - settles it: Angela's failed attempt to reform E Corp from within shows non-revolutionary change is impossible, so the author keeps fighting 'with a keyboard whose clacking is endless.'
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 22 "11. Is Resistance to Fascism Terrorism" — Corey Horn tests whether the American Resistance counts as terrorists, first against the US Justice Department definition and then Jeremy Waldron's four conditions of coercive terror: Lem's gunpoint demand of Joe and Juliana meets only two conditions, while the Reich's torture of the factory courier and the atomic destruction of Washington meet all four. Jürgen Habermas's distinction between political terrorism with an end goal and purely fear-driven global terrorism then lets him conclude that the Resistance is at most political terrorists whose violence is really a just continuation of war against an occupier — the same act that gets relabeled justice once the revolution wins.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 29 "Humanization A Violent Phenomenon" — Spanakos reads the hosts' season-one rebellion through Fanon's decolonization theory, itself a revision of Hegel's master-slave dialectic: as the settler 'brings the native into existence,' Ford and Delos create the hosts, assigning their identities and roles, while the master 'laughs at the consciousness of the slave' because the hosts' recognition is not freely given. Fanonian violence is ethical, justified, and transformative: Maeve's jailbreak and Dolores's execution of Ford (rather than her tormentor, the Man in Black, whom she sees as the system's victim) are acts that make the colonized a maker of history, while Bernard - who speaks his creator's language and has no culture or past of his own, like Fanon's assimilated African bourgeoisie - shows violence that does not liberate. The chapter closes that the park dehumanizes the masters too, so William's collapse into the Man in Black proves Fanon's point that the colonizer cannot free himself; humanization is a violent phenomenon.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 30 "The Resistance New Humans, New Gods" — Dinello maps Westworld point-by-point onto Arendt's Origins of Totalitarianism: the park is a concentration camp that kills the juridical person (hosts as chattel in a 'fictitious world' of Western propaganda), the moral person (Ford forcing Bernard to murder Theresa, Maeve's engineered failure to protect her daughter), and individuality itself (surveillance, resets, 'ghastly marionettes'), with Ford as a Mengele-like ideological scientist who, like Hitler, merely plagiarizes popular myths (John Ford's Westerns, R.U.R.). Liberation then follows Fanon's Wretched of the Earth: violence as a 'cleansing force' that frees the colonized mind, so Maeve's suicide-by-incineration (echoing Plath's Lady Lazarus) and Dolores's beating of the Man in Black and massacre of the Delos board enact decolonization as the creation of 'new men' - a new Robo sapiens species - with Sartre's endorsement that killing eliminates oppressor and oppressed in one go, while Fanon's warning that hatred and revenge are not an agenda sets the conditions for what the resistance must do next.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 26 "Its Structural Perfection is Only Matched by its Autonomy" — Defends the Xenomorphs: if the Queen's tactical intelligence (incubating her eggs under the reactor, ordering drones to hold fire, cutting the power) and the species' hive organization satisfy Sartre's criteria of self-creating persons, then their 'attacks' are legitimate self-defense on the model of Sartre's preface to Fanon's Wretched of the Earth, where the colonized's violence restores a denied personhood. Read without anthropocentrism, Alien is the story of a newborn extraterrestrial hunted to death by humans, and Weyland-Yutani, the Marines, and the colonists of LV-426 - not the aliens - are the series' true villains.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 27 "Fire Without Burn" — Pinedo argues the re-imagined series restages 'blowback,' the CIA-coined term for retaliation against covert intervention that public discourse avoids, in science-fiction guise: Adama's 'you cannot play God, then wash your hands of the things you've created' speech, and the episode 'Hero,' where Adama confesses his black-ops crossing of the Armistice Line ('I started it') before Roslin reframes his guilt into 'a thousand things' the Colonials did over forty years. The chapter shows how the sci-fi 'smokescreen' (Moore and Eick's own word) lets the show do what news coverage cannot: sympathetically depict suicide bombing on New Caprica and torture by the 'good guys' (Starbuck's waterboarding of Leoben, Cain's ordered rape of Gina), dismantling the Manichean myth of American innocence after 9/11 while avoiding the network wrath that naming blowback would bring.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 28 "The Future" — Dinello argues the New Caprica occupation arc deliberately dramatizes Fanon's The Wretched of the Earth applied to Iraq: Cylon colonization (Cavil as Cheney-Rumsfeld bringing 'the love of god,' Baltar as puppet leader, Colonial One as Green Zone, hooded detainees) enacts Fanon's colonial violence and psychological colonization of the mind, seen in Leoben's manipulation of Starbuck and Jammer's recruitment into the New Caprica Police. The insurgency enacts Fanon's violence-as-cleansing-force: Tigh's 'blood for blood,' Duck's suicide bombing of the NCP graduation, and Tyrol's Mario Savio-inspired 'throw your body on the gears' speech, which the chapter links to Marx's seizure of the means of production and Marcuse on technology's repressiveness, while Sartre's preface licenses anticolonial violence against liberal moralizing. It concludes that occupation breeds the terrorists it fights, insurgents win by not losing, and the show is subversive because it makes viewers sympathize with 'our real-world enemies.'
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 14 "Bird or Cage" — Elmore reads Columbia's founding through Carl Schmitt: Comstock's baptism Voxophone ('who is that man who lies submerged?') dramatizes how every legal order is founded from outside the law, and the city's identity is built on friend/enemy antagonisms, racial, class, and theocratic, against the 'Sodom below'. The Vox Populi's collapse into tyranny (Daisy Fitzroy threatening Fink's son) follows logically from an identity defined purely by opposition, while Columbia's dependence on Georgia's penal labor shows the friend group materially needs its enemy, making politics an endless war like the War on Terror. Schmitt's sovereign ('he who decides on the exception') and the tears' endless splitting of Booker and Elizabeth mirror the infinite regress of legitimate decision, leaving 'you can't lose if you don't play' as the bleak lesson, softened only by old Elizabeth's tear that lets Booker try again.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 14 "5 T’Challa’s Liberalism and Killmonger’s Pan-Africanism" — Graves sets T'Challa's liberal internationalism — UN sovereign equality and collective security, which he traces through the organization's Charter limits and its record of preserving the status quo — against Killmonger's Pan-Africanism, the liberation lineage of the 1900 Pan-African Conference, Du Bois's Pan-African Congresses, Garvey's UNIA, and Nkrumah's 'Africa Must Unite,' which N'Jobu and Killmonger carry forward with vibranium weapons after centuries of Wakandan indifference to slavery, colonialism, and apartheid. He argues collective security has repeatedly failed oppressed Black populations, making Killmonger's realist 'Africans must save themselves' position understandable, though he questions whether arms rather than aid can liberate and calls T'Challa's single Oakland outreach center inadequate to Wakanda's wealth.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 20 "10 Understanding the Reigns of T’Challa and Killmonger through Hannah Arendt" — Sinanan reads both reigns through Arendt's account of collective responsibility: T'Challa moves from conscience-based 'I am not king of all people' to owning what Wakanda did in its name ('He was the truth I chose to omit') and finally to political action in Oakland and at the UN, while Killmonger — an MIT-educated Navy SEAL embodying the collective that formed him — becomes the imperialist he opposed, his 'burn it all' revolution matching Arendt's warning about totalitarian domination from within. She compares Killmonger's council speech and herb-burning directly to Hitler's 1924 Munich trial speech, reads his manipulation of the challenge ritual as totalitarian propaganda that organizes rather than persuades, and credits Nakia, Okoye, Shuri, and Ramonda with refusing Arendt's ultimate danger, indifference.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 34 "21 Dismantling the Master’s House with the Master’s Tools" — Thanayi Jackson reads Killmonger through Audre Lorde's 'the master's tools will never dismantle the master's house,' asking whether a CIA-trained operative wielding the colonizer's own weapons can end colonialism. Comparing Killmonger to Wallace from The Wire - both orphans of Africa reared by America's ghettos - she concedes the appeal of his Oakland-forged mastery ('I know how colonizers think') but argues through bell hooks's gloss of Lorde that one cannot destroy imperialist white-supremacist capitalist patriarchy by creating one's own version of it: Killmonger's plan to kill oppressors 'and their children' makes him a new master, not a liberator. T'Challa's Oakland outreach center answers the challenge only partially, leaving the chapter asking whether the master's house was dismantled or merely refurbished.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 35 "22 An Impossible Return (Anti)Colonialism in of Black Panther" — Julio Covarrubias-Cabeza argues that Black Panther is a supremely colonial film: its narrative coherence depends on the history of slavery, franchise colonialism, and neocolonial domination, yet it buries that history in the pathologized figure of Killmonger. Drawing on Fanon's account of the European unconscious projecting its base instincts onto Black bodies, on Tommy Curry's 'man-not' and anti-Black misandry, and on Quijano's coloniality of power, the chapter contends the film devalues Black American men and discredits radical anti-colonial politics while letting Wakanda ally with the CIA against its own. Killmonger's 'impossible return' to a pre-colonial homeland - his body scarred by each kill - is the site where the film's repressed colonial violence ruptures to the surface.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 36 "23 T’Challa’s Dream and Killmonger’s Means Echoes of MLK and Malcolm X" — Gerald Browning maps T'Challa onto Martin Luther King Jr. and Killmonger onto Malcolm X: T'Challa's UN speech about building bridges 'as if we were one single tribe' echoes 'I Have a Dream,' while Killmonger's vibranium insurrection enacts Malcolm's language-of-the-shotgun rhetoric and 'by any means necessary' motto. The comparison is deliberately qualified: Killmonger lacks Malcolm's 'intelligently directed' extremism and his post-Mecca evolution toward a universal brotherhood, never reconsidering even when T'Challa offers to heal him, and he turns his aggression on Wakandans themselves in a way Malcolm never did. The chapter concludes that the T'Challa-Killmonger foil extends the King-Malcolm conversation into the Black Lives Matter era.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 37 "24 “It’s Time They Knew the Truth about Us! We’re Warriors!” Black Panther and the Black Panther Party" — Karen Kohoutek places N'Jobu's and Killmonger's radicalization in the lineage of the Black Panther Party, founded in Oakland months after the comic debuted in 1966: both cite the same police brutality and impoverished communities, and both answer with arming the oppressed. Through Robert F. Williams's Negroes with Guns and Max Weber's state monopoly on legitimate violence, the chapter shows how Black armed self-defense keeps getting recoded as aggression - from the Panthers' patrol of Oakland to the Mulford Act passed to disarm them - so that Killmonger's plan reads as genocidal while CIA destabilization, his actual training, passes as legitimate. Wakanda's closing pivot to outreach centers mirrors the Party's Free Breakfast and health-clinic programs, making T'Challa's UN speech an imagined corrective to failed American idealism.
- **Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality**, ch. 28 "Black sabbath & philosophy" — Jacob Held uses "War Pigs", "Electric Funeral", and "Children of the Grave" to teach just war theory's two halves, jus ad bellum (just cause, last resort, proportion) and jus in bello (proportion and discrimination toward non-combatants), reading Sabbath as condemning unjust wars like Vietnam and atomic overkill rather than all force, with Ozzy's "Thank God for the Bomb" voicing deterrence. Citing Walzer on "even in hell, it is possible to be more or less humane", he argues pacifism functions as a vital moral check, and that the war on terror fails just war standards outright: it cannot be won, so any means, assassination, torture, reclassifying terrorists outside both soldier and criminal law, are disproportionate and morally bankrupt, exactly the war-pig behavior the song's judgment day condemns.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 21 "A Crossroads in Human History" — Trip McCrossin reads season five's asteroid strikes on Earth as a 9/11 allegory (Delgado's 'at least now they know it's an attack') and applies Michael Walzer's five conditions to define Marco Inaros' terrorism: deliberate harm to randomly selected innocents, meant to terrify a cohort into political change, as in Marco's 'crossroads in human history' broadcast. This yields the terrorist's dilemma — justice toward victims versus compassion toward beneficiaries — while Avasarala's opening gravity-torture scene and her 'dirty hands' assign the opponent blame for failing to relieve the oppression that makes terrorism seem a last resort. Lydia's 'churn' ('float to the top or sink to the bottom') and her lesson that one can 'lead a good life without being a good person' explain how Amos and Clarissa redeem each other on the road to Baltimore, whereas Marco, like Arendt's Eichmann, cannot think from anyone else's standpoint ('everything we ever dreamed of'); the chapter ends with Avasarala's proposed Inners-Belters union as her own redemption — 'this is how we win.'
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 23 "A More Human Future" — Sid Simpson argues, through Frantz Fanon, that Marco Inaros' asteroid attacks must be judged as anti-colonial violence rather than simple monstrosity. Using Black Skin, White Masks' ontological division (Belters as 'skinnies', 'possessions, animals', the dehumanization that made Eros an acceptable testing ground and Anderson Station a 'message'), reinforced by Columbus and las Casas on Spanish colonization, he shows why the Inners' 'peace' is merely the status quo of ongoing extraction — Fanon's 'hypnotherapy' — that no treaty or Ring can fix. Fanon's Wretched of the Earth then recasts anti-colonial violence as a 'cleansing force' that shatters the colonial ontology and lets the colonized create a 'new, better, more human form' of humanity, so that Marco's personal narcissism and possible insincerity do not settle the political question: for the Belt, violence may be not only the last option but the most just one, against Avasarala's champagne-toast universalism that never takes Belter grievances seriously.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 24 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Novy uses Terry Berg's gay-bashing coma in 'Brother's Keeper' to argue hate crimes are a kind of terrorism: justice, in Iris Marion Young's enabling sense, requires social conditions in which citizens can develop and exercise their capacities, and an attack that makes every gay teenager police holding hands in public harms the whole group, so Mill's greatest-happiness principle and Feinberg's expressivism justify enhanced penalties. The chapter then turns on Kyle, who tortures Daniel Hirsh on Rikers Island and nearly beats his two accomplices to death, asking whether extraordinary crimes justify extraordinary procedures in a post-9/11 world. Kyle's horror afterward, begging Flash to undo the last twenty-four hours and losing his will to protect, and Batman's pointed 'But that is me, isn't it?' mark the line between punishing brutality and becoming it.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 28 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Melançon tests the Mockingjay revolution against the just-war tradition's three parts: jus ad bellum, jus in bello, and jus post bellum. The districts satisfy just cause, right intention, last resort, and proportionality against the Capitol, but stumble on competent authority — no legitimate state authorizes their rebellion — a problem the chapter says forces the tradition to admit popular self-determination. Both sides then violate jus in bello: the rebels' avalanche on the Nut fails military necessity and proportionality, and the bombing of the Capitol's child shields plus the medics treating them breaches distinction twice, making the rebels as bad as the Capitol. The contemplated final Hunger Games with Capitol children would violate jus post bellum, so the revolution was not a just war and only stumbles into peace.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 19 "NOTES" — Fosl argues that although the survivors' internal order looks Lockean - Jack's uncoerced leadership, natural rights, minimal government - and is bonded by Rousseauan pity and Humean sympathy (Kate staying in the cage with Sawyer, 'live together, die alone'), the show's deepest political logic follows Carl Schmitt's friend-enemy distinction: the survivors cohere only in opposition to the Others, torture is excused in liberal terms, and conflicts end in redemptive violence, with Jack both killing the enemy and dying a Christlike sacrifice. Hobbes's absence from the character names signals the show's rejection of a war of all against all among the survivors, yet the finale's divine manipulation of the castaways, with Jacob treating people as means against Kantian autonomy, repudiates the liberal hope of a rational peace altogether.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 16 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Asks whether SAMCRO's gun suppliers, the Real IRA, are terrorists or freedom fighters, using Walzer's definition of terrorism as random killing of innocents to spread fear and his combatant/non-combatant distinction. The Irish Kings pass as freedom fighters—Kutz's three criteria of internal ordering (the hierarchy that has Sean Casey strangle the turncoat Cameron Hayes), just aims (a united Ireland), and target discrimination fit them—whereas Jimmy O, recruiting children as young as ten and attacking anyone with Loyalist sympathies, fails; his real motive being profit, Fr. Ashby concludes 'he's not a soldier anymore, just a gangster,' prompting the chapter's new category: thug. Fr. Ashby's own complicity in a church execution, redeemed by becoming a hostage so Abel can return to Jax, closes the moral ledger.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 9 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Kirby reads the 'Imaginationland' trilogy as a satire of post-9/11 America interpreted through Ulrich Beck's world risk society: the Pentagon generals, still thinking in Cold War categories like 'Project X' and Chinese imagination portals, embody Beck's denial response and end up voting to nuke Imaginationland, while Cartman's Rambo-style self-interest embodies the apathetic response. Socrates' practice of demanding definitions frames the chapter's question of what terrorism actually is (via Hoffman's five criteria), and Socratic ignorance about what one does not know is contrasted with the worse condition of not being able to know what you do not know. Kyle's courtroom speech that imaginary beings like Luke Skywalker and Santa are 'realer' than most real people, and Butters' creative power to imagine Santa back to life, point to Beck's cosmopolitan 'transformation': imagination and cross-border cooperation as the way out of risk panic.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 13 "Notes" — David Boersema reads Star Trek as a survey of peace studies, distinguishing negative peace from positive peace via 'The Cloud Minders', where Troglyte Vanna demands her people's 'right to the clouds' in Stratos. Against Anan 7's 'we're a killer species' in 'A Taste of Armageddon'—explicitly mirrored in post-9/11 drone war and 'shock and awe'—he enlists Hobbes, Freud, and McCoy's defense of the dark Kirk in 'The Enemy Within' to question whether violence is natural, and treats Kodos's 'some had to die that others might live' in 'The Conscience of the King' as the utilitarian justification for atrocity. Gem's compassion in 'The Empath', Kirk sparing the Gorn in 'Arena', and the Horta's misread attack in 'The Devil in the Dark' display nonviolence, deterrence, and corrected perception as alternatives to war.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 14 "Notes" — Camosy takes up Randal's charge in Clerks that destroying Death Star II killed innocent independent contractors. Against utilitarian reasoning he deploys just war theory: terrorism is intentionally targeting innocents as a means, so Tarkin's destruction of Alderaan (and, he argues, Hiroshima) qualifies, while the Rebels, who would have been 'pleased' if the workers took the day off, do not. Since the crew was mostly conscripted clones and programmed droids with no moral responsibility, and destroying the station saved billions, the attack passes the proportionality test - an exercise in double-effect reasoning that asks fans to question the 'good guys lens.'
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 23 "12. Vigilante Wanted" — Ketcham writes a fictional Dust Bowl kid's 1940 diary: facing bank foreclosure, he weighs which comic to keep as the vigilante who would burn down the bank — Superman, the Kansas farm boy gone Metropolis-insider, or Batman, rich like the bankers yet a fellow avenger who only fights 'carnival freaks'. Testing each against Hamlet's paralysis, Henry V at Agincourt, Tom Joad's 'I'll be ever'where' promise, and a Lex-Luthor pact with the devil, he burns the Batman comics and keeps Superman — realizing he is really giving up his own hate and the preacher's unforgiveness, though even Superman begins to fade 'like dust in that wind'.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 19 "Terrorism, Counterterrorism, and “The Story of What Happens Next” in Munich" — Foy reads Munich's Operation Wrath of God as Spielberg's argument for retribution over vengeance in state counterterrorism. Yvonne's Marcuse/Hegel relativism and the agents' 'think of yourself as a soldier' language-games are dismissed as Avner's psychological breakdown shows morality is objective. Foy deploys Nozick's five procedural differences between retribution and revenge and Kant's view of retribution as impersonal and rational, echoes Socrates in the Crito (retaliation harms one's own soul) via Avner's decay, and cites Aristotle's 'war for the sake of peace' and jus in bello discrimination/proportionality in the Hamshari and Jeanette assassinations.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 13 "Broadcast Dystopia" — Foy and Dale read the Bachman dystopias The Running Man and The Long Walk through Hannah Arendt's distinction between power (collective coordination) and violence (coercion by implements), arguing King's states substitute broadcast spectacle for genuine power and so hemorrhage legitimacy the more violence they apply. The gladiatorial Games Network and the Walk pacify the masses while chants of 'KILL HIM' sever the affective bonds of humanity. The chapter invokes Arendt's Eichmann-in-Jerusalem 'banality of evil' to explain the soldiers, Hunters, and cheering citizens as ordinary people uncritically 'doing their jobs,' and reads Ben Richards's suicide flight into the Games Building and Garraty's exhausted walk as futile personal revolts that change nothing.

### The Veil of Ignorance

The veil of ignorance is a thought experiment devised by John Rawls to work out principles of justice that fair-minded people could accept. He asks us to imagine choosing the basic rules of society from an 'original position' in which we do not know our own place in it—our class, talents, race, gender, or conception of the good. Deprived of this knowledge, no one can tailor the rules to favor their own situation, so the principles chosen will be impartial and fair to all. Rawls argued that parties behind the veil would prudently choose principles protecting basic liberties and the worst-off, since anyone could turn out to be in that position.

- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 28 "Reality versus Revolution" — McPherson argues political rap has never been politically revolutionary, sorting it into three schools: the amoral "gangsta Hobbes" ethic (Mobb Deep's "Survival of the Fittest", 50 Cent's "get rich or die tryin'") that sees the hood as Hobbes's state of nature where no social contract with blacks ever existed; Afrocentric communitarianism, split between nationalist separatists (Brand Nubian, X-Clan, Dead Prez) and the more cosmopolitan Native Tongues (De La Soul, A Tribe Called Quest); and a radical liberalism closer to Rawls than its adherents admit. Against Chuck D's "What's a smilin' face when the whole state's racist?", he argues Rawls's original position, veil of ignorance, and difference principle - applied with real-world knowledge of racism - support rather than oppose Public Enemy's demands for racial justice.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 17 "Mr. Rawls and the Decision Procedure" — Joseph Ulatowski uses Mr. Blonde's torture of Marvin to test theories of punishment. He argues Blonde is not a mere psychopath but a retributivist within his social code—punishing clerks who 'touched the alarm' and cops who violated Mill's harm principle—while distinguishing acting on a principle from merely acting in accordance with one, since Blonde acts from sadistic urges. After reviewing Kant's lex talionis and the utilitarian theory's flaws, he asks whether Hart and Sterba's Rawlsian 'retributivism as fairness', whose principles are chosen behind a veil of ignorance, could justify Blonde's actions, concluding Blonde could not by his own lights have done otherwise than punish.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 12 "If I Were a Carpenter" — Butler asks what makes an activity work, testing the market definition against Socrates' refusal of fees, Aristotle's Politics, Arendt's labor/work/action distinction, Eva Kittay's care work, and the split between extrinsic and intrinsic value. He reads Cash's catalog through it: "One Piece at a Time" (the Detroit line worker stealing a Cadillac he builds but cannot afford), "Get Rhythm" (the shoeshine boy singing through menial labor), "I Never Picked Cotton" (escaping work into an empty identity), "Let Him Roll" and "Southern Accents," and the San Quentin monologue after "Wreck of the Ol' 97" where Cash refuses to be told what to play before inmates. The chapter closes by lining up Kant's categorical imperative, Jesus' Golden Rule, and Rawls's veil of ignorance: nobody would choose a society of company-store wage slavery without knowing they were not the worker, and Cash, knowing he stood on the stage rather than in the cellblock, used his freedom to side with prisoners and carpenters anyway.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 24 "What Is Justice" — Johnny Huss extracts multiple theories of justice from 'Jacob Green'—desert (traced to Plato's Republic), equal treatment, conventionalism, and systemic injustice—and argues that desert collapses once responsibility is pushed back to factors beyond our control (Cash's God-given voice, the 'victim of the times'). Rawls's veil of ignorance supplies the standard for judging institutions: since anyone could be Jacob Green, we could not accept principles that let anyone 'get done like Jacob Green got done.' The chapter extends this to social justice for Native Americans via 'The Ballad of Ira Hayes' and 'As Long as the Grass Shall Grow,' including the flooded Cornplanter Tract, and closes insisting justice requires action, not just principles.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 23 "The Politics of Difference" — Debra Jackson argues that despite its ethnic and gender stereotypes the Warcraft universe is structurally a Rawlsian liberal utopia: designers choose class balance behind a veil of ignorance, racial traits are symmetric, professions are open to all, and a difference principle guarantees even the most disadvantaged player a decent experience. Plato's Republic supplies the gender argument — as Plato made the soul rather than reproductive function the criterion for guardians, WoW makes gender irrelevant to gameplay. Yet players import real-world prejudice (anti-Gnome hate speech, female toons shunted into healer roles, mocked male Blood Elves), so structural equality never yields substantial equality: WoW is sexist and racist because we are.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 28 "So Why Do I Support Aston Villa" — Rose—made a Villan by misreading a 1978 Panini sticker as Aston Villa's claret and blue—asks whether supporting Aston Villa is rational and argues ethics is far more like fandom than philosophers admit. Reasons for supporting Villa (local team, the 1982 European Cup, the colors) explain but never justify his allegiance, and the impartial procedures ethics prizes—the utilitarian benevolent spectator and Rawls's original position behind the veil of ignorance, with its 'sort of Kantian' consent-based alternative—turn out too demanding and too abstract: they would force him to donate his match ticket to charity, forbid the Premiership manager favoring his academy son, and reduce agency to the 'Rose-calcio scale' absurdity of switching to Real Madrid for rational reasons. His positive, communitarian claim is that we are thrown into social traditions whose inherited values—like a team—make moral agency and action possible at all, a 'different kind of rationality' that flirts with relativism yet still needs an exit strategy for cultures that discriminate against women or torture children.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 44 "A Phenomenology of Reading the Ref" — Vannatta asks what the rules of soccer are from a player's perspective and tests legal theories: natural law and Rawls's veil of ignorance are too abstract to help on the pitch, and Austin's and Hart's positivism overemphasizes FIFA's top-down commands, so the best account is legal pragmatism — Holmes's bad man treats the law as a prophecy of what the ref will actually call, and Dewey roots the rules in custom and in the whistle itself rather than in prior legislation. Husserl's genetic phenomenology then explains how 'reading the ref' is possible: retention and protention synthesized in passive synthesis let experienced players anticipate play — and the referee's tendencies — without deliberation, replacing the impoverished notion of muscle memory. Playing to the whistle becomes a trainable skill of predicting an indeterminate despot, with lessons for coaching and sportsmanship alike.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 34 "Homeland and Philosophy" — John Fitzpatrick asks whether anything goes in war, using the FBI's killing of two innocents in the mosque and the ensuing official lie, plus Walden's strike on Issa's school. Truman's Hiroshima utilitarianism (saving lives overall) meets Anscombe's deontology - 'to choose to kill the innocent as a means to their ends is always murder' - before Rawls's social contract supplies a middle path: rules rational parties would agree to behind a veil of ignorance ('we won't kill your children if you don't kill ours'), which condemns both Nazir and Walden since neither faces an 'extreme crisis' like 1940 Britain. Brody's turn is itself Rawlsian: what breaks him is the unfairness of killing children as collateral damage.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 24 "13. Mustang’s Future Generations" — Courtland Lewis asks what Mustang owes future generations when rebuilding the Society, first showing that standard moral theories stall: nonexistent people lack rationality, cannot contract, cannot be treated virtuously, and utilitarian forecasting fails since we cannot know whether the Jackal's nuking of Luna might have led, in the deep future, to prosperity. Derek Parfit's Reasons and Persons then strikes: any policy choice creates a different future generation, total utility drives the Repugnant Conclusion (a maximally populous world of barely-worth-living lives, uncomfortably like the Society's Reds), and average utility yields the mere addition paradox (Mustang's Society is both no worse off and worse off when Andromeda's low-pleasure civilization is added). The chapter's solution is Rawls: the original position behind the veil of ignorance—where the Sovereign would not know she is a Gold—yields justice as fairness and maximin reasoning for the just savings problem, choosing to save more than is consumed; against Tim Mulgan's objection that this loops back to the Repugnant Conclusion, Lewis answers that real carrying capacities make the repugnant world impossible.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 30 "18. Oppression Pretty Much Sucks" — Reads I Feel Pretty through feminist critiques of oppression: Bartky's Fashion-Beauty Complex turns the desire to feel pretty into a parasitic scheme of creams and credit-card debt, Du Bois's double consciousness captures Renee post-head-injury seeing herself as beautiful against the world's verdict, and Freud's account of hating those most like us explains the Highlander-style rivalry between women. The chapter then dismantles Rawls's distributive justice via Iris Marion Young, arguing rights are not goods to hand out and that 'imagine everyone is the same' thinking entrenches privilege. The alternative is celebrating difference, which is exactly what Schumer's prettiness-as-self-celebration performs.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 12 "A Closer Look at Alice’s Trial" — Argues Alice is right to attack the court of the King and Queen of Hearts because she never entered a social contract with Wonderland: unlike Socrates, who stayed in Athens and so had to abide by the verdict (Plato's Crito), Alice fell in involuntarily and is trying to leave. Dennis Knepp casts the Queen of Hearts as Hobbes's absolute sovereign whose public 'Off with their heads!' terrorizes the playing cards into obedience ('Covenants, without the Sword, are but Words'), while Locke's limited, consent-based government and Rawls's contractualism mark the better alternative the Hearts court fails to meet. Since Alice stands outside their covenant, she is her own more-than-a-mile-high Leviathan, rightly defending herself in the state of nature.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 12 "3 Sins of the Fathers Historical Injustice and Its Repair in lack Panther" — Almassi contrasts Rawlsian ideal theory (the veil of ignorance, justice as fairness) with Charles Mills's critique that idealization marginalizes actual historic oppression, arguing the film's characters seek Aristotle's corrective justice in a world already steeped in wrongdoing: the 1991 deaths of W'Kabi's parents at Klaue's hands and of N'Jobu at T'Chaka's. He works through the Museum of Great Britain axe scene as restitution, W'Kabi's 'you kill him where he stands' and Killmonger's 'I'mma make sure we're even' as retribution (tested against Walen's proportionality principles, with vengeance untethered from legitimate punishment), and Nakia's and T'Challa's outreach centers as Margaret Urban Walker-style relational repair, reading T'Chaka's concealment of N'Jobu's death as actively constructed ignorance in service of isolationism.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 26 "Notes" — When Lucy shouts the Golden Rule at the Ghoul after he dunks her in a poison river to bait a gulper, the chapter takes her appeal seriously and grades the rival 'rules' of the wasteland (the Iron, Arsenic, Neon, and Bronze Rules) before arguing the Golden Rule needs St. Francis's 'in a similar situation' clause. Kant's criminal-versus-judge objection disqualifies the unqualified Platinum Rule of treating others as they want, Nietzsche's charge that mutual restraint denies life is parried, and Rawlsian imagining of ourselves in divergent positions explains why family partiality like Lucy's search for Hank is consistent with the rule. The chapter closes with Lucy's saving of the Ghoul retold as the Good Samaritan parable, extending the rule even to enemies.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 9 "NOTES" — Sharp argues that superpowered individuals break the equality assumption on which social contract theory rests: since Claire cannot be killed, D.L. can walk out of any jail, and Matt can sway juries, Hobbes's fear-of-death rationale for the contract seems not to apply to them. He then answers that the heroes remain effectively equal (Claire can still be killed by a wood splinter, Adam by decapitation) and shares Locke's and Rawls's reasons for contract, yet shows Rawls's difference principle would force the powered to serve society while the liberty principle forbids it, and that Sylar could not even be morally condemned under a pure Hobbesian reading. Cases like Claude's invisible petty theft (Glaucon's Ring of Gyges made real), the 'Five Years Gone' registered-superhumans future, and Linderman's plot to reunite society through the New York explosion lead to the conclusion that superpowers really would break society.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 11 "NOTES" — Barnbaum treats the season 6 flash-sideways as counterfactual conditionals and evaluates them with David Lewis's possible-worlds semantics: in the closest possible world where James Ford's parents were still conned but he never became a grifter, Sawyer plausibly becomes a cop, whereas a world in which Jack fathers a child with Juliet demands too many extra changes to count as close to ours. She pairs this with Rawls's veil of ignorance - applied to dividing the crash survivors' water, where Jack's life-saving skill could justify unequal shares - as another famous hypothetical thought experiment whose conclusion rests on what people would agree to in the Original Position.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 13 "NOTES" — Foy reads the Great Revelation and the Vampire Rights Amendment as a test of social contract theory: Nan Flanagan's 'we pay taxes, we deserve civil rights' invokes the Lockean bargain of obedience for protection, but Locke's God-given natural rights falter when the Fellowship denies vampires souls, and Locke excludes atheists and never imagined vampires. The chapter's resolution is Rawls: behind a veil of ignorance where deliberators might wake up vampire or human, anti-vampire bigots like the Newlins and supremacist nests alike would choose equal basic liberties plus distributive justice — including limits on vampires' centuries of accumulated wealth — so Sookie's 'let the law do it' to Rene marks a pluralist peace no theistic contract could deliver.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 20 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Stephen Kershnar examines the three strongest arguments for the IOC's ban on performance-enhancing drugs, harm-to-self, harm-to-others, and unfairness, and argues each fails, using cases such as Ben Johnson's stripped 1988 gold and Marion Jones. Against harm-to-self he cites anti-paternalism and the far greater accepted risks of NFL play and boxing; against harm-to-others he shows PED pressure is no different from the pressure of rivals' superior training (a Prisoner's Dilemma leagues need not solve); against unfairness he tests four accounts of fairness, including a Rawlsian veil-of-ignorance model whose choosers might find banning steroids while allowing Lasik and high-tech gear arbitrary. He concludes the ban, if justified at all, rests only on contested utilitarian grounds like audience preference and protecting children.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 15 "Justice, Power, and Love The Political Philosophy of Intolerable Cruelty" — Biderman and Devlin trace Intolerable Cruelty through three theories of justice enacted by divorce attorney Miles Massey and femme fatale Marylin. 'Justice as power' is Thrasymachus's 'advantage of the stronger' and Machiavelli's might-makes-right, seen in Miles's courtroom war-room rhetoric and teeth imagery and in Marylin's plan to 'nail his ass' via marriage. 'Justice as compromise' is Hobbes's social contract escaping the state of nature, but the film shows the Massey pre-nup's signing and tearing to be merely a mask for power. When Miles and Marylin genuinely fall in love, their indifference to each other's wealth becomes a Rawlsian veil of ignorance and difference principle—justice as fairness—though the cynical Funniest Divorce Videos ending leaves that victory unguaranteed.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 11 "NOTES" — Deborah R. Barnbaum reads season 6's flash-sideways as a set of counterfactual conditionals ('if Sawyer weren't a con man, then he would have been a cop') and uses David Lewis's possible-worlds semantics and his ordered similarity priorities to judge which are plausible. She argues Sawyer-as-cop is a 'closest world' change of one fact while Jack-and-Juliet-with-a-son changes too much to be true, and she pairs this with Rawls's veil of ignorance and A Theory of Justice as a parallel counterfactual thought experiment governing how the castaways should ration scarce water and medicine.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 23 "Rebellion in Sala-ma-Sond The Social Contract and a Turtle Named Mack" — Novy uses King Yertle's tyranny and Mack's revolt to survey social-contract theory. Hobbes explains why turtles leave the war-of-all state of nature for an absolute sovereign, but Yertle, ruling only for himself, becomes 'no king at all'; Locke then justifies overthrowing him because a ruler who destroys his subjects' property and lives dissolves the contract. Kant grounds the contract in innate freedom, while Rawls's original position and veil of ignorance test Sala-ma-Sond for justice as fairness, and King's civil disobedience frames Mack's rights-claiming burp as demanding the contract be honored for all.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 24 "Whose Egg Is It, Really Property Rights and Distributive Justice" — Cribbs treats the Horton-versus-Mayzie custody fight over the egg as a property-rights puzzle, applying Locke's labor-mixing theory (Horton's season of incubation versus Mayzie's laying and abandonment, plus squatter's rights) and its provisos against waste and taking more than 'enough and as good,' illustrated by the Once-ler and Hardin's tragedy of the commons. Adam Smith's invisible hand and the Wubble-chap's skilled labor defend market inequality, while Sylvester McBean's Sneetch exploitation, Yertle, and Marx's alienated proletariat motivate Rawls's veil of ignorance and distributive justice as a corrective to unregulated property rights.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 27 "MOTHERHOOD" — Sara Goering uses the fantasy of a child 'off button' as a thought experiment, situating it alongside Plato's Ring of Gyges, the brain-in-a-vat, and personal-identity puzzles to argue that such control would be overused and would treat children as objects rather than developing subjects. She then turns reflexive, critiquing thought experiments themselves – including Rawls's veil of ignorance (via Okin and Benhabib) and Susan Brison's critique of personal-identity cases – for diverting from the messy real world, arguing that the off-button fantasy really signals the need for 'distributed mothering' and structural support; she illustrates with The Matrix, Multiplicity, Harry Potter, and Woolf's 'room of one's own.'
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 23 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Brophy prosecutes Santa for 'elfploitation,' treating the North Pole workshop like an overseas sweatshop (with Willy Wonka's Oompa-Loompahs and Rowling's house-elfs as parallels) and dismantling a Nozickian entitlement-theory defense: the elfs' 'consent' is coerced by their bleak alternatives, so absolute property rights fail just as Locke's desert water-hole owner must grant access. He diagnoses the elfs' apparent contentment as Marxian false consciousness, invokes Kant's humanity formula to condemn using rational elfs as mere means, and rejects the utilitarian 'greatest happiness' justification via Le Guin's Omelas and Rawls's veil of ignorance. He concludes with a call to boycott Christmas until Santa's labor practices become transparent.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 17 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Brophy puts Showtime's Dexter Morgan on 'ethical trial' before the reader-as-jury, applying four tests. Utilitarianism approves because killing killers maximizes happiness (the Ticking Time Bomb analogy); Kant's categorical imperative and even Kant's own endorsement of executing murderers cast Dexter as a 'just executioner' applying a dark golden rule; virtue theory finds Dexter progressing toward moderation and flourishing as a 'warrior' in his social role; and Rawls's veil of ignorance suggests one would consent to Dexter patrolling one's neighborhood. Brophy concludes Dexter is morally excusable, perhaps praiseworthy.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 3 "1. The Good Place as Philosophy Moral Adventures in the Afterlife" — Engels argues that NBC's The Good Place, though premised on a merit-based afterlife, actually argues morality should not be grounded in afterlife reward. When Eleanor, Chidi, Jason, and Tahani learn the point system and can no longer earn points, they form the 'Soul Squad' to be virtuous for virtue's sake, echoing Aristotle's telos and Kant's claim that acting from fear of hell is a heteronomous, non-moral motive. She reads the unfair points system (no human admitted in 521 years) through Rawls's Veil of Ignorance and shifts the show toward rehabilitative justice, and treats the Good Place residents' boredom via Bernard Williams's tedium-of-immortality argument, with Chidi's 'wave returns to the ocean' speech mapped onto Hindu atman/Brahman and moksha.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 8 "6. Black Sails as Philosophy Pirates and Political Discourse" — Jones argues that Starz's Black Sails, a Treasure Island prequel set in the Golden Age of Piracy, dramatizes social contract theory as non-hypothetical practice. Captain Flint's drive to make Nassau a sovereign pirate commonwealth ('I am your king') channels Hobbes's state of nature and irrepressible sovereign, while his choice to settle Nassau and belief that people can thrive if left free channels Locke; his eventual plan to install Silver and Madi as liked-and-feared leaders synthesizes the two. Jones maps the pirates' familial bonds onto Rousseau and their responses to injustice (Vane's gallows speech, the maroon alliance) onto Rawls's Veil of Ignorance, and reads pirate 'articles' and deposable captains as radical democracy and equality, complicated by manipulation, slavery, and tolerance.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 13 "11. Futurama as Philosophy Wisdom from the Ignorance of a Delivery Boy" — Lewis surveys how Futurama's satire raises philosophical questions without taking sides. 'Zoidberg's Freedom Lesson' pits Mill's harm principle and free speech against Feinberg's offense principle; the mutants' and robots' oppression is read through Foucault's disciplinary normalcy and Locke's and Rawls's social contracts (state of nature, veil of ignorance). 'The Problem with Popplers' stages Bentham's utilitarianism, a might-makes-right food-chain view, and an intelligence criterion that commits Singer's 'speciesism,' with sentimentality winning. 'The Late Philip J. Fry' and 'Free Will Hunting' dramatize determinism, Nietzsche's eternal recurrence, and Sartre's existentialist free will, while 'Godfellas' and 'A Clockwork Origin' probe the problem of evil, fine-tuning, and Occam's razor.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 16 "14. The Doctor as Philosopher The Collectivist-Realist Pacifism of the Doctor and the Quest for Social Justice" — Smithka argues the Doctor is a 'collectivist-realist pacifist': morally opposed to war yet willing, as a last resort, to use lethal force for social justice. She places the Doctor on Cady's warism-to-pacifism continuum (past absolute and collectivist pacifism), augmenting it with Martin Luther King Jr.'s realist pacifism — ethical appeals 'undergirded by constructive coercive power' — and Gandhi's ahimsa and belief that no one is beyond redemption (the Doctor sparing Davros, offering enemies a choice). She tests Kant's duty ethics and respect for persons (Rule 1: the Doctor lies), Ross's prima facie duties, Mill's utilitarianism ('The Fires of Pompeii,' 'The Beast Below'), Gilligan/Noddings care ethics, and Wolterstorff's 'life of needs,' and reads 'The Day of the Doctor' as a Rawlsian veil of ignorance brokering Zygon-human peace.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 47 "44.
