- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 24 "Notes" — Writing as a mechanic, Gordon argues Max embodies Plato's Republic: like the ship-of-state navigator, only someone who knows justice may rule, and the Myth of the Charioteer — reason holding the reins over spirit and appetite — explains why the Nightrider's unchecked spirit crashes while the cool-headed, deliberative Max endures. On punishment, Plato's rejection of retaliation (the unjust should be made just, not harmed) interrogates Max's execution of Johnny the Boy, while Polemarchus's 'render to each his due' frames the just-deserts debate. Mill's harm principle then justifies Max's force against the gangs once the state and its courts have vanished, leaving Max an administrator of street justice.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 18 "NOTES" — Davies treats the beach camp as an actual state of nature: the stolen drinking water is a tragedy of the commons, Shannon's inhalers show how the crash scrubs pre-existing property rights (Hobbes: two men desiring the same thing become enemies), and Jack and Sayid's torture of Sawyer marks the first step toward Locke's civil society by enforcing others' rights through punishment rather than self-defense. He rejects theories of human nature - Rousseauan 'Innocence' versus a 'Trust No One' outlook - in favor of the repeated prisoner's dilemma, arguing the survivors stabilize cooperation through tit-for-tat: beginning cooperative with strangers and retaliating against the Others. On this reading the real difference between Hobbes and Locke is which round of the repeated dilemma each takes as the starting point.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 11 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Puts Aquinas's Murder Principle—the private, intentional killing of an innocent is always murder—to the Men of Mayhem, arguing the Sons lack the public authority Aquinas requires to kill even the guilty. The show itself erodes the state/private line Aquinas needs: corrupt agents Kohn and Stahl, and the CIA's Romeo Parada running the Galindo Cartel, make the badge look like no moral credential at all. The Doctrine of Double Effect sorts the rest: Jax shooting first in self-defense, Tara's morphine for the dying Unser, and Juice's hypothetical land-mine sacrifice are merely foreseen deaths, while Jax syringing Clay or Juice's intentional hanging would be murder. The chapter concludes that even if Aquinas condemns the Sons, his questions about authority, innocence, and intention are exactly the ones the show forces on viewers.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 13 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Foresman asks what would make Hell a justified punishment for the souls claimed by crossroads deals, like Mary, John, and Dean trading damnation to bring a loved one back to life. Using Joel Feinberg's expressive account of punishment, he argues that souls in Hell through stupid deals suffer mere bad consequences rather than punishment, because no message of moral condemnation reaches someone who never knew the rule. Bentham's utilitarian test fails to justify Hell, since a Hell nobody takes seriously deters nobody and nothing there is rehabilitated, and Kantian retributivism fails too because no finite wrong can deserve eternal torment, leaving Crowley's endless-queue Hell as at least better proportioned to desert.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 16 "Notes" — Uses Hans Kelsen's legal positivism — law as amoral coercive order sustained by sanction, validated by authority rather than morality — to interpret season two's competing normative systems, from Vinci's city hall to the cartel's execution of the informant Irina. Against this background it separates revenge from Hegelian retributivism, reading Velcoro's shift from killing his wife's rapist to persuading Lenny Osterman to seek exposure instead, and Frank's communicative, confessing execution of the traitor Blake, as conflicted exercises of justice. The finale's bloodshed is read through Hegel's theory of tragedy as a collision of spheres of justice, each justified in its own eyes, whose transgression may precipitate change in Vinci.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 17 "“Do You Not Instinctively Fear Me ”" — George Dunn weighs Veronica's creed that 'someone's always supposed to pay' — Carrie Bishop destroying Mr. Rooks for her friend, Logan getting himself jailed to beat Mercer, Veronica forfeiting the Kane Scholarship to watch Aaron Echolls convicted — against the case against vengeance running from Socrates' 'one must never do wrong in return' through Seneca's claim that the angry are insane and Plato's subordination of thumos to reason, with the ultimatum game showing people pay to punish even at their own expense. Nietzsche's creditor-debtor account explains the payoff: punishing the offender restores the status and self-esteem that humiliation stole, turning passive grief into an active grievance like Madison's crushed-and-cubed Mercedes. Yet Machiavelli's 'much safer to be feared than loved' finally vindicates a measure of payback, since Veronica's threats are how a disgraced outsider demands the respect fickle Neptune withholds from Meg.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 34 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Yuen argues cannibalism is not automatically wrong: both utilitarian and Kantian frameworks permit eating the already-dead in a genuine survival situation like the Andes crash of Alive, since corpses lose no happiness and lack the rational nature owed dignity. But Chris's hunters in 'Fear the Hunters' become moral monsters because they kill to eat (murdering their own children, amputating and eating the still-living Dale to prolong his terror), which neither maximizes utility nor treats persons as ends, and Chris's 'we had no choice' excuse fails because starving is not a license to murder when one could befriend other survivors, eat walkers, or starve. Rick's execution of the hunters is then defended on Kantian grounds of deserved punishment: applying Chris's own maxim ('if Dale was good as a steak, so is Chris') as a universal law.
- **Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test**, ch. 6 "H O N O R" — This file gathers three Part One essays. Jacob Held reads Rorschach's 'evil must be punished' credo (drowning Big Figure, executing the multiple rapist) as Kantian retributivism: wrongdoers are punished because they deserve it, out of respect for their dignity and honor, punishment restoring the moral order (with Hegel) — and Rorschach's flaw is lacking the humility and checks that keep just deserts from degenerating into the Black Freighter's vengeance. Tony Spanakos applies Max Weber's definition of the state as the monopoly of legitimate violence to argue the Keene Act rightly criminalizes vigilantes like Rorschach and Veidt, and that even state-sanctioned heroes (the Comedian gunning down his pregnant Vietnamese lover, Dr. Manhattan's amoral ending of Vietnam) show a badge cannot make superhero coercion legitimate. J. Keeping reconstructs Nietzsche's Übermensch — confronting the death of God and nihilism, creating values by 'giving style' to one's character via the camel-lion-child metamorphoses — and tests each Watchman against it, concluding only self-created Ozymandias comes close, though his mass murder is mere utilitarianism rather than genuine value creation.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 32 "Notes" — This multi-author epilogue collects short 'cutting-room-floor' reflections on poignant WoT quotes. Cooke reads Ingtar's confession as the existential fear of historical oblivion (historia as both history and story) driving a patriot into Darkfriendship. DeVan uses Covril's oak-and-wind metaphor to argue arguments strengthen through opposition, marshaling Confucius, Proverbs, al-Kindi, Milton, and Socrates's unexamined life. Held reads Min's arranged-marriage counsel with Nietzsche's amor fati and Epictetus's Heracles to reject resentment of unchosen fate. Pike reads Nynaeve sentencing the sul'dam through Carol Gilligan's and Annette Baier's ethics of care versus obligation (care can judge more harshly, per C.S. Lewis). Xhignesse reads the oak-and-willow line as Aesop woven into Randland's background.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 31 "Notes" — Chavez, Gavaler, and Goldberg trace Marston's 'Love Leader' kink - bracelets of submission, Venus girdles, Paradise Island bondage games, Earth One's collaring of Steve Trevor - to nineteenth-century maternalist feminism, then map the care ethics of Gilligan, Noddings, and Tronto onto both the comic and real-world BDSM. Reform (later Transformation) Island embodies a care-based alternative to punishment: rather than retribution, von Gunther and Irene are transformed by loving authority into people who save their captors, and Wonder Woman rescues the drowning villain Eviless because 'Aphrodite's Law commands us to save lives always - enemies or not.' The BDSM community's 4Cs (consent, communication, caring, caution) turn out to be Tronto's four elements of care, so the good dominant just is the good care-giver.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Flynn contends certain Westerns depict a 'law that stands behind the law' — a moral/natural law transcending and grounding the weak civil order — using High Noon, where Hadleyville proves unworthy of Kane's rectitude. High Plains Drifter evolves this into divine, supernatural retribution: the nameless Stranger, a pale-horse agent of apocalyptic justice, precisely punishes Lago for abetting the marshal Duncan's murder (whipping the whippers, renaming the town Hell). Flynn argues this vision is dangerous: by insulating justice from deliberation and depicting it as revelatory and divine, it derides the discursive, civil processes (Habermas-style communicative action) actually needed to make justice 'ours,' risking mere private vengeance — 'deserve's got nothin' to do with it.'
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Knight and McKnight use Northrop Frye's master genres to chart Eastwood's move from romance (the superior hero who defends a community, as Jed Cooper in Hang 'Em High, the Stranger in High Plains Drifter, Harry Callahan in Dirty Harry) toward tragedy with Mystic River, where Jimmy Markum kills the innocent Dave as his daughter's murderer and, like Oedipus, recognizes his error too late. They read the law-versus-justice tension through Aristotle's point in the Nichomachean Ethics that the lawful and the just are not coterminous, and cite McClelland glossing Walt Kowalski's self-sacrifice in Gran Torino as a supreme instance of Aristotelian practical wisdom (phronesis) that solves multiple problems at once.
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — Skoble uses Taxi Driver's Travis Bickle to probe when vigilantism is justified, invoking Locke's claim that in civil society individuals delegate private vengeance to the state for objectivity. He argues Travis's rescue of the trapped child prostitute Iris is legitimate (the police won't help, she can't help herself) while his plan to assassinate Senator Palantine is madness, drawing the key line between correctly identifying a deserving target and mere perceived evil (contrasting Travis with Death Wish's Kersey, Batman, and Klan lynch mobs). He closes with Socrates' 'unexamined life' as the remedy: contemplating justice so we can confront real badness rather than turn away.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — D'Aries and Hirsch read Paul Thomas Anderson's Hard Eight as a neo-noir moral inversion: the aging criminal Sydney seeks atonement not through religious penance but through selfless love, rescuing John and Clementine while removing the loathsome Jimmy (who knows Sydney killed John's father). They contrast him with Melville's Bob le flambeur and Besson's The Professional, where convention demands the criminal be punished. Sydney escapes formal justice but is sentenced to a 'prison without bars' of self-loathing (the bloodstained cuff), and the authors warn that such sympathy-for-the-devil inversions verge on nihilistic moral relativism.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 19 "Terrorism, Counterterrorism, and “The Story of What Happens Next” in Munich" — Foy reads Munich's Operation Wrath of God as Spielberg's argument for retribution over vengeance in state counterterrorism. Yvonne's Marcuse/Hegel relativism and the agents' 'think of yourself as a soldier' language-games are dismissed as Avner's psychological breakdown shows morality is objective. Foy deploys Nozick's five procedural differences between retribution and revenge and Kant's view of retribution as impersonal and rational, echoes Socrates in the Crito (retaliation harms one's own soul) via Avner's decay, and cites Aristotle's 'war for the sake of peace' and jus in bello discrimination/proportionality in the Hamshari and Jeanette assassinations.
- **The Philosophy of Werner Herzog**, ch. 12 "Reflections from the Abyss Herzog’s Philosophy of Death" — M. Blake Wilson traces Herzog's philosophy of death and the 'abyss' across Grizzly Man and Into the Abyss, examining how Herzog frames human, animal, and self-killings and refuses the retributive impulse. Against Kant's demand that murderers must die and Matthew Kramer's purgative rationale for capital punishment, Wilson enlists Nietzsche's warnings about the drive to punish and Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us,' while contrasting Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' with the 'accountant's truth' via journalistic and bear-attack literature (Jans, Herrero) that accuses Herzog of a 'Hollywoodized' portrait of Treadwell. He coins 'vivicide' for the killing of a human by a non-human animal and questions whether Bear 141 committed murder or was merely a scavenger.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 25 "14. Did Bourdain Go #MeToo Far" — Finn tests Catharine MacKinnon's 'Rape Redefined' — rape as sex compelled by inequality rather than lack of consent — against Bourdain's #MeToo allyship and his payment to Asia Argento's teenage accuser Jimmy Bennett. She argues MacKinnon's power-based standard could recognize Argento's act as assault, and reframes Bourdain's hush-money payment, via the Wendat/Huron compensation practices in Graeber and Wengrow, as a compassionate vengeance-staying reparation consistent with his empathy.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 30 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Earleywine dissects the moral versus practical arguments over prohibition, attacking legal moralism—the drug-czar claim (Bennett, Wilson) that use is wrong simply because it is immoral—as circular, and noting that the law does not criminalize every immoral act (broken contracts, lying). He shows purported moral arguments collapse into utilitarian harm estimates that the data undercut, since use rates are essentially orthogonal to policy across Amsterdam, Australia, Portugal, and US states. He then weighs anti-prohibition rights arguments (religion, privacy in Ravin, property via Szasz, self-determination) and closes on proportionality: owning a harmless plant merits no punishment.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 10 "The Justification of Torture-Horror Retribution and Sadism in Saw, Hostel, and The Devil's Rejects" — Jeremy Morris analyzes torture-horror through two questions: is the torture justified, and is the audience's enjoyment justified? He reads Saw's Jigsaw traps, Seven, and Last House on the Left as explorations of Kantian retributivism and lex talionis, where punishing the autonomous wrongdoer respects his autonomy. For purely sadistic films like Hostel, The Devil's Rejects, and Texas Chainsaw Massacre, he argues (via Humean sentimentalism against Kantian rationalism) that Cook's or Otis and Baby's infectious glee makes the torturer's delight the source of horror. A fully empathetic viewer can share both the victim's suffering and the torturer's joy without endorsing torture, so the genre is not immoral 'torture-porn.'
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 28 "So, Case Closed – Right" — Mark White asks why Batman doesn't kill the Joker, using the question to contrast utilitarianism (kill one to save the Joker's future victims) with deontology (killing is wrong regardless of consequences), and Batman's own agent-centered refusal. He runs Foot and Thomson's trolley problem and the transplant surgeon case, then modifies them: the Joker is the guilty one who created the danger, his future victims are uncertain, and killing him would be 'prepunishment' for crimes not yet committed. White, a self-described deontologist, concludes the case is genuinely hard and admits great good might have come from killing the Joker, using comics as thought experiments about killing to prevent future killing.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 56 "53. Tarantino as Philosopher Vengeance – Unfettered, Uncensored, but Not Unjustified" — Johnson treats Tarantino's post-2000 filmography as an argument that vengeance is morally permissible when proportionate and directed at the genuinely guilty: Beatrix in Kill Bill, Shosanna in Inglourious Basterds, and Django all get celebrated revenge, while The Hateful Eight is used to distinguish vengeance from retribution and legal versus 'frontier' justice via Nozick's and Bacon's definitions. He rebuts common and historical objections—reading Plato's Gorgias as endorsing due punishment, arguing Spinoza's monism and Hobbes's and Locke's social-contract views do not forbid proportional revenge, and citing Nietzsche and Beauvoir's Eye for an Eye (her refusal to pardon the collaborator Brasillach) to conclude cost-free, proportional revenge can be justified though mercy remains praiseworthy.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 14 "5. Monsters and Evil in Doctor Who" — The chapter defines a 'moral monster' as one who delights in evil acts, arguing (via Jonathan Glover and Laurence Thomas) that Hitler-style evil is all-too-human, not alien. Using Hume's claim that action springs from passion, it contends the emotionless Cybermen are a mere force of nature (bad but not evil), whereas the Daleks, driven by hatred, tribalism, and a closed belief system, are genuinely evil monsters; the manipulating Master mirrors our everyday lying. It then examines retributive justice through Solomon's execution in 'Dinosaurs on a Spaceship' and 'A Town Called Mercy,' rejecting purely backward- or forward-looking punishment (citing Rawls on utilitarianism's injustice) in favor of the Doctor's needs-based, 'reprobative' punishment, mercy, and self-forgiveness over the Time War.

### Buddhism

Buddhism is a family of traditions arising from the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, in ancient India, aimed at understanding and ending suffering. It diagnoses ordinary existence as marked by dissatisfaction rooted in craving and ignorance, and it offers a path of ethical conduct, mental discipline, and insight leading toward liberation, often described as nirvana. Rejecting reliance on a creator deity for salvation, Buddhism emphasizes practices such as meditation and the cultivation of wisdom and compassion, and it has developed into diverse schools across Asia and beyond.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 56 "Unknown" — Brannigan reads the film's mirror imagery through the Buddha's mirror instruction to his son Rahula: Neo touching the dripping mirror and becoming the mirror marks his awakening to the naked truth (aletheia as nakedness) that his world is a programmed illusion, Smith's dark sunglasses distort while Morpheus's mirrored glasses clarify, and Neo's reflection in the spoon-bending boy's spoon signals clarity. 'There is no spoon' parallels the Zen mondo where neither flag nor wind moves but only mind, and shows that reflected images are not reality - the world is maya. The deepest lesson is anatman: just as there is no spoon there is no Neo, no fixed self, and Rahula's lesson grounds the interdependence (pratityasamutpada) of all actions on others.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 58 "Unknown" — Brannigan tests whether The Matrix is a Buddhist film and finds four incongruities: its Zoroastrian good-versus-evil dualism (the system and those in it as 'enemies') against karuna and metta, its glorified gun violence ('guns, lots of guns') against ahimsa, its crass language against right speech, and its human-centeredness against the Buddha-nature of all sentient beings, including 'sentient programs'. He concedes the slaughter might be read symbolically as slaying the mind's three poisons, as Manjusri's sword does, but rejects calling the result 'American Buddhism'. He concludes the film is a deliberate syncretism of Christianity, Platonism, and Buddhism that still conveys the Buddhist message of liberation from the mind.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 61 "Unknown" — The chapter argues the film is by no means a Christian movie: Neo is a violent, far-from-sinless mere human savior; the fundamental human problem is ignorance and illusion (Gnostic and Eastern) rather than sin and alienation from God; the rebels' belief that Neo is the reincarnation of the earlier liberator mirrors the Dalai Lama search the Wachowskis cite, though reincarnation is rejected by all major Christian sects; and 'there is no spoon' asserts the illusoriness of empirical reality that Christianity denies. The film's malleable, cyclical time and the Wachowskis' answer that faith is 'in oneself' complete a syncretistic tapestry the essay goes on to examine as religious pluralism.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 29 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Jennifer McMahon and Steve Csaki compare Tolkien with Zen Buddhism and Taoism on four themes while insisting on the real differences. Tolkien's talking trees (Old Man Willow, Treebeard's 'half awake' forest) invite comparison with Buddhist universal sentience and Dogen's walking mountains, but Tolkien anthropomorphizes where Buddhism grants non-human modes of sentience; the hobbits' ties to the Shire echo dependent origination, though Tolkien's stewardship and preference for the domesticated Shire over sinister wild nature remain Western. Frodo's succession of mentors (Bilbo, Gandalf, Aragorn, and the unlikely 'Master Samwise') parallels the Zen master-student relation, while Tolkien's war of light against darkness - nine Walkers against nine Riders - is decisively not the Taoist balance of yin and yang, for Taoists destroying either cosmic force would itself produce evil.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 28 "Ballparks, Dojos, and Other Places of Enlightenment" — Bassham argues that the core advice of hitting instructors like Ted Williams ('get a good ball to hit') and Charley Lau ('tension is the enemy') echoes Zen Buddhist principles, walking through patience, relaxation, self-knowledge, visualization (Reggie Jackson, Willie Stargell, Barry Bonds's on-deck imagery), practice, Bruce Lee-style kime concentration, and mushin or no-mind. Mickey Mantle going 0-for-30 after over-thinking Ted Williams's hitting tips, and Tony Gwynn's 'see the ball and react,' show how conscious analysis interferes with the muscle memory a half-second fastball demands. If kendo is practiced in a dojo — a 'place of enlightenment' — he concludes, ballparks and batting cages may be dojos too, with the caveat that Cobb, Ruth, and Mantle hardly model egoless humility.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 29 "What’s Wrong with Generalization" — Brannigan uses Japanese baseball to ask what is wrong with cultural generalization. He presents the Bushido case — samurai-style self-denial, absolute loyalty (Kawakami's Yomiuri Giants), Suisha Tobita's 'training of death,' resolve (konjo), team harmony (wa), and a relational self grounded in Buddhism's no-self and Confucian identity-through-relationships — then tests it against counter-evidence: Sadaharu Oh's flamingo swing owed as much to individual talent and Hiroshi Arakawa's unconventional kendo-and-aikido coaching as to sensei imitation, the 'new breed' (Ochiai, Egawa) flouts the old ways, and William Kelly's 'Whiting problem' warns against polarizing Japanese and American baseball. The chapter's 'three strikes' against the label 'Japanese baseball' conclude that generalizations become dangerous when treated as monolithic nets cast over an entire culture.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 8 "“A New Broom Sweeps Clean, but an Old Broom Knows Every Corner”" — Callis interweaves a memoir of the teenage boyfriend who played her Dark Side and later killed himself with an account of Easy Star Records' 2003 reggae remake, Dub Side of the Moon, arguing that the album's themes of time, money, materialism, and madness translate naturally into Rasta reasoning. Nyabinghi drumming, singjay toasting, and bong-bubble effects re-read 'Money' (the cash register replaced by a lighter firing the chalice) and 'Time' (Ranking Joe's 'Time is the master') through Rasta rejection of Babylon, anti-capitalist subsistence, and 'soon come' patience, which she glosses with the Buddhist principle that things happen in their own time. The reggae setting, she concludes, weaves all this pain and madness, from Barrett's collapse to her own ghosts, into something more optimistic than the original ever sounded.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 17 "There is No Dark Side of the Moon Really. Matter of Fact It’s All Dark" — Johnston reads The Dark Side of the Moon through Buber's I and Thou: modern life traps us in the I-It mode of experience, from 'Welcome to the Machine' to teachers who treat students as replaceable Its ('Hey, teacher, leave us kids alone!') and Horkheimer's instrumental reason that turns personnel into 'human resources,' while the album repeatedly calls us to the I-You encounter, from 'Echoes'' strangers whose glances meet ('I am you and what I see is me,' Waters's origin of empathy) to 'Breathe''s 'don't be afraid to care.' He links the opening heartbeat and the breath of 'Breathe' to Buber's eternal You, defends Buddhism against Buber's charge that enlightenment is worldless monologue (the Buddha becomes one with the world, a perfect reciprocity like the innate You of the womb), and accepts Nietzsche's point that the Enlightenment's abstract God is dead while insisting, with Buber, that encounter with the eternal You remains possible. The album itself, he concludes, resists degenerating into an It: even if 'the sun is eclipsed by the moon,' the light persists and Dark Side can be the antidote to the It-world.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 24 "Alchemic Heroism" — Reads Edward and Alphonse Elric as a single composite 'alchemic hero' who fuses Japanese heroic archetypes: the dual-hero rooted in the Izanami-Izanagi creation myth and yin-yang complementarity (brash yang Ed, calm yin Al whose armored body actually fights better), the student hero forged by Izumi Curtis's brutal island training, and the wandering redemption seeker atoning for the forbidden attempt to resurrect their mother. It argues that the sacrifice built into this fusion — Al's lost senses, puberty, and body — mirrors Japan's own cultural alchemy of absorbing Buddhism, Confucianism, and yin-yang thought while retaining a coherent national identity.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 5 "Fighting Talk" — The editors' introduction argues that philosophy and fighting have been companions since Socrates the soldier and Plato the wrestler (whose name means 'broad shouldered' from the gym), and that each can illuminate the other. It tours the volume through concrete cases: budo courtesy drawn from Shinto, Confucianism and Zen; the Shaolin monks' exercises as a route to Buddhahood; Western chivalry and Gordon Marino's boxing as educations in Aristotelian courage; fencing's egoism and value; and the Stoicism of karate and utilitarianism of Kano's judo. Philosophy clarifies fighting traditions, while fights supply puzzles for ethics, aesthetics, and the philosophy of mind.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 22 "What Monkey Should Have Known" — Mortensen opens with Monkey from Journey to the West beating six robbers to death despite Tripitaka's protest, and asks whether a practitioner of budo can be a Buddhist. He defends three principles, Take No Life, No First Strike and Stop Before Harm, qualifying them via the Upaya-kausalya Sutra's sea captain, Funakoshi's 'there is no first strike in karate', Ueshiba's purely defensive aikido, the initiator's bad karma, and the exception of multiple attackers; then he applies them to weapons, arguing that wooden weapons (the jo, Musashi's bokken, above all the humble walking stick, the 'last legal weapon') fit the precepts where the katana does not. Monkey, in short, should have carried a stick.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 17 "All for Love" — Jerry Piven argues Dexter's void is not genetic sociopathy but trauma: witnessing his mother's chainsaw murder and lying in her blood deadened his feelings, and each ritualized kill restages that catastrophe with the roles reversed, Dexter mastering death as the angel of it, reducing the murderer to a drop of blood he imprisons on a slide. Reading Harry's ghost as a Hamlet-father super-ego, he contends Dexter kills not only to master trauma but to please the father who channels his rage - murder 'for love' - and then generalizes: Arendt's banality of evil, Pascal on the void and faith, Kierkegaard and Heidegger on fleeing despair into conformity, Buddhist emptiness, and Becker-style terror-management findings explain how ordinary people, frightened of death and hungry for a leader's approval, can be manipulated into sanctioned slaughter, from Abu Ghraib to jihadism.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 18 "Halo as a Catalyst for a Buddhism Videogame" — Luke Cuddy uses Halo 3 checkpoints and emulator save states—two mutually exclusive Flood-fight outcomes both in some sense true—to make David Lewis's possible worlds and modal truth concrete, with Leibniz as the doctrine's ancestor. Halo's infinite lives make players genuinely angry, and the chapter argues this is upaya territory: like the father in the Lotus Sutra's parable of the burning house, the game promises mastery (the goat-, deer-, and ox-carts) to lure players toward something greater outside it. Master Chief becomes a Bodhisattva whose avatar slides between extension of self and other, provoking the 'who am I?' crisis that reveals the ego as empty at the ultimate level of the Two-Fold Truth, while the Dalai Lama's enemies-as-teachers turns the seven-year-old who pwns you into practice in the first two Noble Truths' suffering and anger.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 37 "The Awakened One" — Callis reads Holmes as a Buddhist practitioner despite the cocaine and the cigars in the coalscuttle: 'You see, but you do not observe' and 'The emotional qualities are antagonistic to clear reasoning' match Vipassana bare attention and the Theravada ideal of the cool, rational, emotionally distant sage, and his improvised violin scraping works like Thich Nhat Hanh's walking meditation — a witness without commentary. The picture is completed by Doyle's Buddhism of Ceylon in The Sign of Four, Holmes's two years 'spending some days with the head lama' in Tibet ('The Empty House'), and his sitting 'like some strange Buddha' in 'The Veiled Lodger.' She maps his method onto the Yoga Sutras' dharana, dhyana, and samadhi — patient attention to the blood-scratched plaster, sustained fixation on the crime scene, ego-surrendering contemplation — making Holmes an 'awakened one' who loves truth for its own sake while Watson lives on autopilot.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 17 "Do We Give Shakespeare the Last Word" — Kapper reads Inception as epistemology rather than metaphysics - not what is real but how we could know - running from Plato's Theaetetus (the first dream-recognition question) through Descartes's deceptive demon and Freud's royal road to the unconscious, to Wittgenstein's point that 'I may be dreaming' is senseless because the remark itself would be dreamed, and Heraclitus's line that only the waking share a common world. The Ariadne thread is the clue: as in the Theseus myth, dream architecture gives the labyrinth a shareable narrative place, but only a hint, never a way to wake. He then goes east - Zhuangzi's butterfly, Indra's net of mutually reflecting jewels, Schopenhauer's universe dreamed by a single dreamer, William James's many consciousnesses - to ask how many times we must die before waking, ending with Buddhism: 'Buddha means awakened one', and Cobb's turning from the top enacts Nirvana, where the real-versus-dream question stops pertaining.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 27 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Liane Heller pairs Cohen and Schopenhauer - born and died on September 21st, the autumnal equinox - as two explorers of the world's irrational negativity who both retreat to 'a room' to create. Schopenhauer's directionless Will, his pessimism about a life of constant suffering, his notorious misogyny in 'On Women,' and his ascetic denial of the will-to-live (with his contempt for Judaism and preference for the Upanishads and Buddhist compassion) are set against Cohen's affirmation that love is 'the only engine of survival,' his five-year Zen retreat that could not hold him, and his return to the Judaism of the 'little Jew who wrote the Bible.' A closing imagined dialogue has a humbled Schopenhauer confronted with Cohen's self-compassion and ordinary joys, admitting the limits of his own field of vision.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 11 "3. Tris Finds Enlightenment" — Rhine argues that Tris's heroism rests on Buddhist practice: her breath-counting on the Ferris wheel and inside Four's fear landscape, her emotional intelligence, and her awareness of the parental 'voices in her head' are classic meditative disciplines for calming the ego whose clinging, on the Buddhist account, is the cause of suffering (dukkha). She reads Abnegation's gray houses, plain food, and four-times-a-year mirror as ritual ego-diminishment - a middle way between indulgence and the extreme asceticism the Buddha rejected - that explains why most Divergent arise from Abnegation. Contemporary neuroscience is then recruited: the amygdala-versus-prefrontal-cortex struggle Will describes, and monks' heightened gamma waves, explain how Tris can see the simulation as a simulation, like Neo in The Matrix, and act while others are paralyzed by fear.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 15 "6. Bowie the Buddhist" — Muchall reads 'Quicksand' and 'Where Are We Now?' as suffused with Tibetan Buddhism: 'Don't believe in yourself' voices the anatta teaching Bowie absorbed studying with Chime Rinpoche and from Chogyam Trungpa, whose 'spiritual materialism' warns that ego converts even spirituality and ideologies to its own use. After retelling the Buddha's life, the Four Noble Truths' three kinds of dukkha, and the five aggregates that reveal no permanent self, the chapter maps the song's 'ragged hole' and bardos onto the Tibetan Book of the Dead's after-death journey, and reads Bowie's morphing personas as lived acknowledgment that there is no fixed self - 'there's nothing in here.'
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 25 "13. The Origins of Self-Love" — Anna Marie Fennell reads RuPaul's 'If you can't love yourself, how in the hell you gonna love somebody else?' through theories of self-love. Erich Fromm's four elements of love and Buddhist non-attachment (Jinkx Monsoon's 'water off a duck's back,' the Season Ten Inner Saboteur characters like Eureka's Eufilthior) ground the claim that self-love precedes healthy love for others. Against Aristophanes' myth in Plato's Symposium - the round beings split by Zeus, forever seeking their other half, retold in Hedwig and the Angry Inch - she sides with Ru: completion comes from within, not from a soulmate. Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity (the sub-man and nihilist archetypes seen in self-sabotaging queens like Nina Bo'Nina Brown) and bell hooks's All About Love with Branden's six pillars of self-esteem map onto winners like Jinkx, Sharon Needles, Violet Chachki, and Bianca Del Rio, whose drag personas show existence preceding essence.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 7 "Preface" — Aaron Ehasz, ATLA's head writer, reflects that the show tested its characters' belief systems against their humanity: Aang's attempt to comfort himself with Buddhist detachment fails when Appa is taken, and he cannot let go of his love for Katara to unblock his final chakra and enter the Avatar State. Yet Uncle Iroh shows the opposite lesson, since by studying Water Tribe ideas he invents lightning redirection, the technique that lets Zuko survive his father and lets Team Avatar save the world. The preface concludes that philosophy both limits and unlocks human potential, capped with a joke about Hegel and hard ice cream.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 8 "Introduction" — De Cruz and De Smedt argue that ATLA subverts the Chosen One trope: Aang's training is slow and non-linear, he needs dedicated teachers, and saving the world is a team effort in which Katara leads and Sokka plans. The show's central theme is oneness, voiced by Guru Pathik's 'illusion of separation' ('The Guru') and Huu's banyan-grove tree ('The Swamp'), which the editors trace to Daoist, Huayan Buddhist (Fazang's golden lion), and Indigenous traditions of interdependence. They frame the volume's engagement with genocide, imperialism, ecological destruction, and Ba Sing Se's authoritarian denial as proof that philosophy is needed for human flourishing.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 12 "The Wisdom of Combination" — Isrow maps each bending art to its real martial art and source philosophy: Katara's Taiji waterbending embodies Daoist wu-wei when she forgoes revenge on Yon Rha ('The Southern Raiders'); Toph's Hong Jia earthbending expresses the Buddhist eightfold path's Right Speech through her insistence on truth; Zuko's Northern Shaolin firebending enacts the Four Noble Truths, his desire-driven suffering ending only when he abandons chasing the Avatar; and Aang's Daoist Baguazhang airbending makes freedom openness to change, shown in his receptivity to Iroh's advice. The Avatar's true power is combining these character strengths, not merely wielding four elements.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 28 "What Can We Learn" — Argues ATLA repeatedly dissolves false alternatives rather than solving conflicts, modeling the Buddha's middle way from the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta: refuse the two extremes instead of picking one. Earth is the case study — Bumi is both crazy and wise, Toph both blind and the most powerful bender, and 'The Cave of Two Lovers' shows the first earthbenders using their art for love, with Oma ending the feud by declaring the war over rather than destroying both villages. Aang's energybending against Ozai dissolves the kill-or-be-killed framework, Bumi's 'neutral jing' rejects fight-or-flight, and Toph's life refutes the capable-vs-helpless and girl-vs-fighter dichotomies her parents impose.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 38 "Fearlessness and Power" — Rebuts Ozai's taunt 'you are still weak' with a Buddhist reading of energybending: Aang wins not by domination but because his unbendable spirit is total vulnerability, a true heart that has abandoned the five hindrances (sensory desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness, doubt — each traced through the chakras, the Serpent's Pass, and 'Nightmares and Daydreams') and a true mind freed from the fundamental delusion of a separate self that 'The Swamp' and 'The Guru' dissolve. The spirit-merging with Ozai is read through Indra's net, and Aang's merciful halt mirrors Indra's Jataka victory where compassion for eagle hatchlings — not force — defeats the demons. Fearlessness, on Sylvia Boorstein's Zen story, is the natural corollary of compassion, so Aang's weakness by Ozai's standard is precisely his power.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 40 "Journey’s End and a Vision of a New Community" — Reads Aang's journey alongside the Karmapa Ogyen Trinley Dorje's Interconnected: both bear exalted titles that isolate them from friendship (Aang forbidden to play with peers and taken from Gyatso; Dorje taken from his family at seven), and both learn that heroism is relational — the series replaces the rugged-individual hero's quest with a communal model in which Katara, Sokka, Toph, Pakku, Jeong Jeong, and Zuko co-author Aang's moral training. Aang's refusal to open the seventh chakra over his attachment to Katara illustrates the Karmapa's warning that local attachment can block universal compassion, and Zuko's path from betrayal to forgiveness shows enemies as people enslaved to their own disturbing emotions. Aang ends as the Karmapa's 'interdependent individual', victorious only alongside the White Lotus and his friends.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 7 "Preface" — Head writer Aaron Ehasz asks what philosophy is for in ATLA and answers with the writers' unconscious conclusion: characters' belief systems are always tested against their humanity, and Aang's Buddhist detachment fails him twice, once when he loses Appa and once when opening the final chakra demands he let go of Katara. The counterexample is Iroh, whose study of Water Tribe techniques lets a firebender invent lightning redirection, the skill that lets Zuko survive his father and lets the saga resolve. So philosophy is not crushed by human need but is the key that unlocks humanity's potential, provided we stay open to ideas from other cultures.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 8 "Introduction" — The editors argue ATLA subverts the Chosen One trope: Aang learns slowly and non-linearly, needs a teacher for each element, stays weaker than Katara or Toph in specific skills, and saving the world is a team effort in which he is neither leader nor brains. They identify the show's unifying theme as oneness, the 'illusion of separation' voiced by Guru Pathik and the swampbender Huu, and trace it to East and South Asian schools such as Huayan and Chan Buddhism and to Indigenous traditions. Philosophy is presented as the tool the show itself uses against genocide, imperialism, and ecological destruction, with Ba Sing Se's 'no war' denial as the cautionary case.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 34 "Sometimes We Can Let Go" — Sets the intuition that angry blame is how we hold people responsible (Strawson; Katara's useful fury at Pakku's sexism, Iroh's 'whatever you do to that spirit, I will unleash on you tenfold') against the Senecan and Buddhist verdict that anger is greedy for revenge, and reads ATLA as modeling ways to hold people responsible without toxic anger. In 'The Southern Raiders' Katara neither forgives Yon Rha nor kills him, showing that blame can be set down when expressing it is pointless, while she forgives Zuko in Lucy Allais's 'wiping the slate clean' sense because his past betrayal no longer speaks to his present character. Iroh's handling of the mugger in Ba Sing Se ('I was never angry; I was afraid that you had lost your way') models responding to the suffering behind wrongdoing with compassion instead of blame, and Zuko's self-anger is diagnosed as hypocritical self-blame whose antidote is self-compassion: acknowledging how he himself was hurt is what finally lets him take ownership of his wrongs.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 38 "Fearlessness and Power" — Argues that Aang's energybending victory over Ozai vindicates a Buddhist conception of power against Ozai's equation of power with domination: the Lion Turtle's 'unbendable spirit' is not resistance but thorough vulnerability, achieved through the true heart (overcoming the five hindrances mapped onto Aang's sensory desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness, and doubt across the series) and the true mind (overcoming the fundamental delusion of a self separate from others, learned from Huu in 'The Swamp' and Guru Pathik). The merging of Aang's and Ozai's spirits is pictured by the metaphor of Indra's net, and Indra's own Jataka victory, halting his assault to protect eagle hatchlings and disorienting the demons, parallels Aang's refusal to win by killing. Drawing on a Zen story of the abbot who could 'be run through by a sword without batting an eye', the chapter concludes that Aang's fearlessness flows from compassion, so that weakness by Ozai's standard is precisely the power that defeats him.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 39 "Overcoming Dilemmas" — Frames Aang's conflict between his Avataric duty to restore balance even by killing Ozai and his Air Nomad duty of ahimsa as a genuine dilemma only if both obligations are non-negotiable (Tessman's negotiable and non-negotiable duties), then argues the show resolves it because Sublime Ahimsic Practice, the Four Sublime States joined to non-harm, reshapes the very conditions the dilemma rests on. Aang's cultivation of loving-kindness and his grasp of dependent origination (Huu's banyan-grove insight that everything is interconnected) keep him open to the world, which is what leads him to the Lion Turtle; energybending then lets him stop Ozai without killing, dissolving the kill-or-be-killed framework rather than choosing a horn. The Avataric role itself is read as Daoist yin-yang balance-keeping, and the chapter links Aang's triumph to the lessons of Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr., and nonviolent movements: becoming different people changes which options the world affords.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 40 "Journey’s End and a Vision of a New Community" — Reads Aang's quest through the Karmapa Ogyen Trinley Dorje's book Interconnected: like the seventeenth Karmapa, identified at age seven and taken from his family, Aang learns that an exalted title complicates friendship and that freedom is self-control rather than the rugged individualism of the American hero's quest. Training episodes (Katara's jealous competition in 'The Waterbending Scroll', Jeong Jeong's warnings, the Toph-versus-Katara sifu debate in 'Bitter Work') show moral training as communal, widening from Team Avatar as adoptive family toward universal compassion, with Aang's refusal to open the seventh chakra illustrating how local attachment can obstruct universal love. Zuko's counter-arc from competition, isolation, and betrayal to humility, forgiveness, and contentment shows compassion turning an enemy into a friend, and the finale's simultaneous battles (White Lotus liberating Ba Sing Se, Sokka and Toph destroying the fleet) affirm that Aang wins as an 'interdependent individual', never alone.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 15 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Lynch tests the fan claims that the Dude is 'the Duddha' or a practicing Daoist: the Dude has wu wei in his effortless arts of bowling and abiding and shares Zhuangzi's withdrawal from society (the Nixon bowling poster, learning from drunks, Donny's ashes scattered with naturalistic acceptance), but lacks Daoist metaphysics, the Dao's inexpressibility, and any articulated views. The Buddha parallels are real — nonattachment, practice over theory (the poisoned-arrow parable), compassion for Bunny — yet Gautama's radical discipline and middle path are the opposite of the Dude's laziness, so Dudeism emerges as an undisciplined American cousin, and the Dude follows 'just his way and his alone'.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 12 "a4.xhtml" — Bronson argues that walking is a philosophical practice against modern placelessness (Giddens' 'phantasmagoric' locality): Thorin survived Smaug's attack because as a youth he 'was a good adventurous lad, always on the move', and Tolkien's wise figures - slow, flower-stopping Tolkien himself, Gandalf who 'went to look ahead' and was brought back 'by looking behind', Bilbo's silent walking, Beorn's bear-travels - all practice attentive movement through place. He backs this with Montaigne's retirement to his tower and bringing thoughts back to the orchard, Thoreau's woods-walking that must be spiritual as well as physical, the Tao Te Ching's 'good travelers leave no tracks' and Zhuangzi's wandering virtues, and Buddhist walking meditation from the Buddha's wandering monks to Thich Nhat Hanh's peace steps.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 17 "Do We Give Shakespeare the Last Word" — Kapper treats Inception as a hip epistemological puzzle — unlike The Matrix, the question is not what is real but how we could know — and follows Ariadne's thread (her mythological clue-giving names the chapter) through the tradition: Plato's Theaetetus and Descartes's supremely cunning deceiver pose 'Am I dreaming now?', Wittgenstein shows the doubt is senseless since 'if I am dreaming, this remark is being dreamed as well', Freud makes dreams the royal road to the unconscious, and Heraclitus says only the waking share a common cosmos. The payoff is Eastern: Zhuangzi's butterfly, Indra's net of mutually reflected jewels, and Schopenhauer's single-dreamer universe turn waking up into an endless regress, so the Buddhist ideal of the awakened one — nirvana, where the ideas of real and dream cease to pertain — becomes the reading of Cobb turning away from the top.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 29 "Notes" — Kahn argues LEGO play embodies the Buddhist teaching of impermanence that the Buddha states in the Digha Nikaya ('Impermanent are all component things...'): his childhood urge to superglue creations and Finn's father's Kragle dramatize the clinging that produces anxiety when things change, from brick formulations to discontinued sets and even funerals' wilting flowers. The LEGO Star Wars Death Star illustrates non-self — no Death Star exists apart from its 3,803 pieces, and no self apart from shifting aggregates — and the five aggregates (form, sensation, perception, formations, consciousness) are unpacked through building experiences like discovering a daughter has opened the mint Taj Mahal set. Tibetan sand mandalas, painstakingly built then ritually dissolved, model the ceremonial demolition of LEGO creations, teaching acceptance of change without sliding into a nihilistic 'why bother building at all'.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 7 "Buddha ex Machina" — Siobhan Lyons applies Mori's 'uncanny valley' to the hosts' physical and personality evolution (Ford's jerky old model versus seamless newer hosts, Maeve and Clementine), noting empathy grows as they near sentience. She argues via Aristotle's account of virtue, vice, and brutality that the guests and technicians (Logan's casual cruelty, the Man in Black's beastly sadism) fall short of human excellence while the suffering, consciousness-seeking hosts transcend it, treating humanity as a way of behaving rather than being, and casting the hosts as Derridean undecidables. Invoking Nietzsche on suffering as the cultivator of greatness and Mori's 'Buddha in the robot,' she claims the hosts earn a humanity the biological humans merely inherit.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 10 "Beat U-topos or Taking Utopia on the Road The Case of Jack Kerouac" — Adamo argues Kerouac's 'On the Road' is a new kind of utopian text: because classical collective utopias (Plato's Republic through More) were judged by Berlin, Popper, and Arendt to slide into totalitarianism and to conflict with political liberalism's individualism, Kerouac relocates utopia from place to the individual life lived 'on the road' (u-topos = no-place). He reads Sal Paradise's disillusion with Dean Moriarty—who uses people up—versus his admiration for Mississippi Gene and the hobos as dramatizing J. S. Mill's harm principle, fused with the Buddhist vow to harm no living thing, radicalizing personal liberty as perpetual movement without injury to others.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 15 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — James Whitehill treats sailing his Cape Cod catboat, named Garuda, as a Zen practice modeled on Zen archery (kyudo) and tea ceremony. He organizes it into 'outer work' (technique and ritualized performance) and 'inner work' (cultivating ki energy through breathing and belly-awareness, then 'self-forgetting'), quoting Dogen's dictum that studying the self is forgetting the self, and forgetting the self is being authenticated by all things. The goal is a boat-and-sailor unity in which the sailor 'sails without sailing' — reaching, through mundane repetitive discipline rather than a sought-after peak experience, a nirvana-like state where wind, wave, and self merge.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 21 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Eric Swan argues that climbing embodies the principles and spirit of Zen, the experience of 'ordinary mind' finding the extraordinary in the ordinary and living fully in the present. Tracing Zen from the Buddha's Flower Sermon and Bodhidharma through Suzuki's 'Beginner's Mind' and Huineng's finger-and-moon, he maps Zen's four training paths—physical work, zazen (sitting meditation), koans, and interviews with masters—onto climbing: routes are like koans solved by insight and action rather than logic, 'being in the zone' is meditative absorption, and breath-regulation at the crux is zazen in motion. He holds up free soloist Derek Hersey, grinning hundreds of feet up Eldorado Canyon, and Chris Sharma, who writes of flowing 'like water' on the rock, as modern Zen masters who dissolve the separation between self, climb, and world.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 29 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Jennifer McMahon and Steve Csaki test Buddhist and Taoist parallels in the novel and find many only apparent. Tolkien's talking trees and ents anthropomorphize nature and grant it human-like consciousness, whereas Buddhism attributes sentience to all beings without projecting human consciousness, and Tolkien privileges domesticated over wild nature and stewardship over membership in nature. His master-student chain (Bilbo, Gandalf, Aragorn, 'Master Samwise') genuinely echoes the Zen necessity of the right master, as in Dogen's mushroom-cook mentor; but his good-versus-evil war, with light privileged over a personified dark power to be defeated, contradicts Taoism's yin-yang balance in which evil is imbalance, not a force to destroy.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 45 "42. Up in the Air as Philosophy Buddhism and the Middle Path" — Duffy reads Ryan Bingham's arc in Up in the Air as a Zen Buddhist parable paralleling Hesse's Siddhartha. Ryan preaches an 'empty backpack' philosophy of nonattachment and treats the miles as their own point, but Duffy argues he only intellectually grasps the four noble truths — dukkha, its cause in attachment (tṛṣṇā), and the eightfold path — until his failed attachment to Alex and his mentorship of Natalie make him actually suffer. Like Siddhartha with his son, Ryan learns wisdom must be experienced, that the anattā (non-self) doctrine undercuts the identity he built on his job, and that the goal is not escaping the world but living the Middle Path within it, present to suffering rather than spinning silver linings.

### Class Struggle

Class struggle is Marx and Engels's claim, announced in the opening of The Communist Manifesto, that the history of society is a history of conflict between classes with opposing economic interests. In capitalism this conflict centers on the bourgeoisie, who own the means of production, and the proletariat, who must sell their labor to survive. Marx held that this antagonism is built into the structure of production itself and that it would ultimately drive revolutionary change, making class conflict the engine of historical development.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 109 "The Matrix , Marx, and the Coppertop’s Life" — Danahay and Rieder read the film as dramatizing Marx's account of the exploited worker, from UPS drivers with tracking devices to keystroke-counted data clerks, continuing the workplace surveillance Marx attacked. The pivotal scene is Morpheus's loading-program lesson: 'You've been living in a dream world' followed by 'Welcome to the desert of the real' and the definition of the Matrix as control that turns a human being into the Duracell battery he holds up—the 'coppertop' Switch earlier called Neo.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 110 "Unknown" — The chapter reads the pod power plant—naked humans stacked like workers in corporate cubicles—through the Communist Manifesto's enslaved factory masses and 'Wage-Labor and Capital's' claim that labor power is a commodity sold by the clock like sugar. Against readings of alienation as private feeling, it uses Morpheus's 'The Matrix is a system' speech to show Marx's point that alienation is produced by the system of social relations: workers see their own labor as a commodity and cannot recognize their connection to the capital they generate.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 30 "The Superhero As Liberal Reformer" — Jeffrey Pasley traces the show's radical surface — capitalism equated with vampirism (Anya's greed, Glory the über-consumer, the Master's blood factory in 'The Wish'), Big Bads tearing down dimensional barriers exactly as Marx's Communist Manifesto describes the bourgeoisie dissolving feudal ties into free trade, Buffy refusing to commodify slaying into wage labor, and Giles's Magic Box selling mystified junk at inflated margins — but concludes the heroes are not revolutionaries. In the comic-book lineage of Superman and Spider-Man, Buffy and Angel are liberal reformers bound by a superhero code against killing, so Giles must murder the innocent Ben precisely to preserve Buffy's heroic mercy; Angel's 'champions' speech in 'Deep Down' states the incrementalist creed.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 15 "Hip Hop and “This Makin’ Dollars Shit”" — Pittman argues the rap battle - UTFO's "Roxanne, Roxanne" answered by Roxanne Shanté's "Roxanne's Revenge", Run-D.M.C.'s "Sucker MC's", Jay-Z's "Takeover" versus Nas's "Ether" - is hip hop's enactment of Hegel's master-slave struggle for recognition, where self-consciousness proves itself only through an all-or-nothing contest ending in domination rather than destruction. Gangsta rap (N.W.A's "Gangsta Gangsta", Ice Cube's fantasy raid on the suburbs) radicalizes the battle into a collective demand that America recognize black urban conditions, and the chapter turns to Du Bois's race-centered and Marx's class-centered revisions of Hegel's history to read "this makin' dollars shit" - Wu-Tang's "C.R.E.A.M.", Talib Kweli on capitalism and crack, Mos Def's "The Rape Over" - as the dialectic's capture of the cipher by corporate beef.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 16 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Goldstein applies Hegel's thesis-antithesis-synthesis and Marx's more complex, multidimensional dialectic to the splits within biker culture: bar-room stare-downs as struggles for recognition, wrenchers versus trailers, RUBs versus working-class riders, helmet disputes, and one-percenters versus the rest. He traces the collapse of brotherhood (the clenched fist of solidarity giving way to the selective wave) to the commodification of the motorcycle during the Japanese invasion and to Harley's own yuppie-era Willie G. marketing, arguing via commodity fetishism that bikers misread economic forces between manufacturers as personal differences. His conclusion is that the seeds of unity lie within the divisions, and that Harley-Davidson Motor Co. will not save the culture, since its task is profit, not tradition.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 40 "Downsizing Dreams" — Michael Bray argues the American Office portrays the "salaried masses," a class that exists in denying class: Jim, Pam, and Michael's rationalized, meaningless paper work realizes Marx's account of surplus value and degraded labor (the "run-out-the-clock" truck unloading, Pam's tepid watercolors), while their self-image survives by distinguishing itself from warehouse and prison labor. Episodes like Michael's condo purchase and Pam's "dreams are just dreams" show characters secretly longing for downsizing to force a different life. Against the New Yorker's claim that the show ignores class, Bray reads its comedy as standing on the edge of naming its economic conditions, with Michael's failure to inhabit management-speak making him, via Walter Benjamin, a last glimpse of "authentic humanity."
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 9 "Quittin’ Time" — Michels surveys Marx (alienation, false consciousness, the Communist Manifesto's reduction of family to economics), Weber's Protestant work ethic, and Arendt's labor/work/action distinction, then reads Springsteen's whole career against them, from 'Factory' (the working life that 'takes his hearing' and leaves 'someone's gonna get hurt tonight') through 'Hungry Heart,' 'Mansion on the Hill,' and The Ghost of Tom Joad ('Youngstown,' 'Sinaloa Cowboys,' 'Straight Time'). The verdict: Springsteen is a man of the left but no Marxist — his characters struggle with their own restlessness and with each other rather than with class oppressors, the wealthy suffer their own bourgeois malaise, and work, however brutal, is no cause for revolution. Nor does he share Arendt's ideal: his realm of freedom is unapologetically middle-class — cruising in a cool car, hanging with friends, getting with your favorite girl, and always the radio.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 24 "It’s the Disappointing Stories that Sound True to Life" — Shipman argues that the re-imagined Cylons, having rebelled as slaves, recreated oppression inside their own society: the human-form Numbers rule over mute Centurions (voices literally bred out, like banning slave literacy), animalized Raiders, and dismissed 'insane' Hybrids, whose sentience ('Scar' shows strategy and self-preservation) the Numbers willfully deny. The division of labor echoes Marx's 'from each according to his ability,' but assignments are engineered by their makers, and the model-making program is eugenics rather than evolution — the series' own word 'evolved' is, he says, disingenuous. Hence the Numbers lose the moral superiority their victimhood earned, and the scriptural 'all of this has happened before' implies the subaltern models may rebel next.
- **Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_**, ch. 6 "index" — Scholz completes his 'playground and factory' argument: user translations, photos and profiles are unpaid digital labor locked inside a walled garden whose data trails are sold to marketers and governments, even as the same platform hosts a genuine power to act together. Morgan and Clulow frame activism with the Communist Manifesto's class struggle, staging fictional discussion-board posts from Engels, Luxemburg and Chomsky that update the proletariat into the internet-era 'iProles', then show Facebook's ease breeding slacktivism, from the '1,000,000 For Obama To Grow An Afro!' group dwarfing real causes to the platform itself banning a father's 'Justice for Francesca Bimpson' page. Muhr and Pedersen use Zizek's interpassivity to argue the Facebook profile is a surrogate self that enjoys, believes and mourns on our behalf, like canned laughter or a Tibetan prayer wheel, deferring the social duty to be authentic while the site quietly installs its own ideology of relentlessly interesting happiness.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 26 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Curry refuses to celebrate The Wire, arguing that Simon's class-based realism ('more about class than race') misrepresents Black urban life, and he contrasts it with Black film from New Jack City to Menace II Society where these issues were already explored. Reading scenes like Rawls's 'project nigger' murders no one cares about, Bunk shrugging at Stringer's unsolved killing, and McNulty telling Brianna that nobody will look into D'Angelo's death, he argues the show registers an indifference specific to Black life, not to the poor as such. Drawing on W.E.B. Du Bois's account of colonialism and the slave trade as the genesis of modern capital ('capital noir') and rejecting the intersectional race-class-gender frame as a 'discursive distraction', he demands a racial realism in Derrick Bell's sense: racism is permanent, the underclass is really an racialized undercaste, and the War on Drugs continues Jim Crow by other means.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 31 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Zizek reads The Wire as subject-realism, a city's collective self-staging (with Simon as its DJ-curator) of the class struggle between the two Americas, where postmodern institutions play the Olympian gods and the self-propelling abstraction of capital is the Lacanian Real running the show, a point he anchors in Marx's prosopopoeia of commodities and 'real abstraction'. Following Jameson he catalogues the show's utopian gestures woven into reality (Frank's dream of revitalizing the port, Colvin's Hamsterdam, Prezbo's dice-based math, Avon and Stringer's last drink, D'Angelo's family utopia), then argues the Major Crimes unit of McNulty, Freamon, Kima, and Omar is a proto-Communist conspiratorial collective whose honest individual resistance (from Snot Boogie to McNulty's firing) merely feeds the system's self-reproduction. Hence his provocation: the only radical step beyond Simon's social-democratic reformism is the strike of the 'inherent transgressors', withdrawing the resistance that keeps the system alive so that Fate itself, not just its victims, can be changed.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 34 "Psych and Philosophy" — Jeff Ewing applies Marx's critique of religion - the supernatural as ruling-class ideology, 'the opium of the people,' behind which priests and shamans hide real material processes and prop up hierarchy - to Shawn, who likewise masks his genuinely material observational talent as psychic gift to escape arrest in the pilot and keep access to SBPD cases. But the comparison inverts: unlike Marx's priests, Shawn serves ordinary people rather than the ruling class, and the chapter concludes he is better understood as an alienated worker - forced by a repressive state's threat of prosecution to sell a false product, defined by what he is not, and never credited for his true skill.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 18 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Fitzpatrick runs Marx's account of alienated labor from the 1844 Manuscripts through the novel: Victor's creature is the product of estranged labor, 'an alien object exercising power over him,' which he cannot name, comes to loathe, and which finally destroys him - the devaluation of the creator tracking the increasing value of the thing made, while workers become commodities producing commodities. The De Laceys' eviction in Branagh's Mary Shelley's Frankenstein and the Ingolstadt cholera riots stage class struggle at feudalism's end, and Victor's failure to self-actualize (to 'hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon... criticize after dinner') shows how capitalism turns science into 'a tool of our own destruction.' The chapter closes with 'Frankenstorm' climate change as the alienated externality par excellence - capitalists selling us the rope with which we hang ourselves.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 19 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Sexton reads the park as capitalist ideology in action, quoting Marx and Engels on the ruling class controlling the means of mental production: Hammond's flea circus is the illusion we agree not to see, and Nedry's sabotage shows what happens when workers are told their poverty is their own problem. He applies Veblen's leisure class to Gennaro, who judges the night-vision goggles valuable because they are expensive, and Marx's general law of capitalist accumulation to Hammond's squeezing of wages once every other cost is beyond his control. The dinosaurs themselves figure as the exploited working class, held not by ideology but by electric fences, and when the fence falls they seize the park.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 11 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter argues coal made Boyd Crowder possible: company scrip, Bloody Harlan's union-busting terror, black lung (Boyd's would-be assassin takes the bridge job because mining ruined his lungs), and Black Pike's mountaintop removal leave Harlan no viable work outside the mines, so crime is the rational alternative. It reads this through Hegel's 'rabble' from the Philosophy of Right - civil society is never wealthy enough to prevent an excess of poverty, and the rabble loses the honor of self-support - plus Marcuse's affluent-society critique of an existence that 'violently defends its own servitude'. Boyd's outlawry, which sets its own code above mere criminality, is a rebellion against being pushed into the rabble, and Hegel's remedy of emigration explains why leaving Harlan is the only escape, though the coal train hauls coal out while the people stay.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 33 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Karavitis fabricates a recovered 'Dracula's Journal' in which the Count retells Stoker's plot as rational self-interest: he owes no one anything, Lucy 'came to me of her own free will,' Van Helsing's crew are a 'craven collective' spouting 'from each according to his ability,' and only objective reality - not their subjective feelings - counts. He claims a fundamental right to pursue his own happiness, casting himself as the thinking individual crushed by proletarian herd morality. An editor's framing email makes the point explicit: Rand-style egoism could justify even Dracula, a 'manual for vampires' set against Marx's collectivism.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 36 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Sexton's mock FBI COMPIC file stages a Cold War reading of Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein: screenwriters Lees and Rinaldo remake Dracula as Marx's Das Kapital vampire - capital as dead labour sucking living labour - so blood-draining becomes profit-draining and 'This man belongs to me!' the capitalist's claim on his workers. A fictional Ayn Rand review for HUAC decodes the film as collectivist propaganda that slanders the businessman McDougal and dreams of a creature with 'no will of his own,' touching Marxian alienation along the way. A final note links screenwriter Robert Lees's blacklisting by Sterling Hayden and his real-life decapitation to Stoker's vampire-killing instructions.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 19 "9. Class Warfare in Chicago" — Canode reads the trilogy as a study in class warfare: the factionless are the invisible lower class kept poor as a warning, the factions the middle class distracted by initiation rankings and faction pride, and the Bureau the self-righteous upper class that created and manipulates the whole system. Marx's analysis structures the argument - the ruling class's specter now haunts the powerless, and 'from each according to his ability' shades into coerced harmony - while the American Dream rhetoric of Carter, Reagan, and Obama plays the aptitude test's role: an ideology of merit that converts structural limits into personal failure. The Bureau's genetic sorting of GP scientists above GD support staff mirrors how meritocracy blames the poor for their poverty, so Tris's verdict - the factions 'gave us the illusion of choice without actually giving us a choice' - indicts the US class system too.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 11 "2. I May Be a Socialist, But I’m Not a Lunatic" — Walderczak stages the Branson-Robert-Matthew triangle as socialism, aristocratic conservatism, and capitalism colliding over the estate's duty to its people. He tracks how Tom's Marx-flavored socialism - really closer to Owen's and Fourier's utopian cooperatism - evaporates once he marries Sybil and co-manages the land, the chauffeur 'Branson' becoming family-member 'Tom,' a case of David Harvey's capitalist pacification. Meanwhile Robert's noblesse oblige - secretly paying a tenant's overdue rent from private funds, ranting 'profits, profits, profits,' treating ownership as custodianship of the tenants - leaves the author asking who the real socialist is, and answering that Robert's conservatism has far more in common with socialist ideals than Tom's self-confessed politics ever did.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 13 "4. Finding One’s Place and Being Useful" — Karavitis argues that work, not social class, is Downton's real theme, sorting characters in a two-by-two matrix of class membership against acceptance or rejection of the existing social order. Those who accept their place stagnate - Violet ('We don't work,' 'What is a weekend?'), Robert the mismanaging custodian, the perpetually jobless Molesley - while those who reject it flourish: Isobel's drive to be 'useful,' Sybil's nursing ('I feel useful for the first time in my life'), Gwen's hidden typewriter, Alfred's Ritz training. He surveys Rousseau on work's role in inequality, Smith on the division of labor, and Marx on labor and ideology on the negative side, and Aristotle, Russell's 'In Praise of Idleness,' and Pieper on leisure and personal projects on the positive side, ending with the prediction that automation will soon give everyone the Crawley daughters' problem of what to do with a life without work.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 24 "12. Should We Really Care about the Crawleys" — Jones takes up the charge that loving Downton seduces viewers into admiring inequality, and answers that the Crawleys deserve our care because birth, not choice, gave them their position, so they should be judged only by what they do with it: Grantham paying for Mrs. Patmore's eye surgery, Violet throwing the flower contest after Isobel's challenge, the family gradually embracing Branson. He reads the show as a manifesto for social change through sympathetic contact between classes rather than Irish-style revolt - befriend the rich and their good nature will start to level the playing field. His own objection is that this makes change partly the responsibility of the less privileged, from Thomas being asked to soften Carson's homophobia to the poor being asked to be nice to the rich today.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 7 "Red Rising and Philosophy" — The editors' introduction argues that Red Rising grips because it mirrors our own world of class struggle, where a Gold-like elite lives in luxury on the backs of oppressed laborers kept distracted by games and propaganda. It traces Darrow's arc from resigning himself to death after Eo's execution, through his carving and campaign of destruction, to the discovery that friendship with Sevro, Mustang, Victra, and Ragnar—not revenge—is what actually pulls him out of life's mines. It closes by previewing the volume's questions: whether enhancement could doom humanity, whether Darrow is the same person after the carving, love versus vengeance, how society should be structured, and the meaning of life.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 9 "1. When Evolution Strikes Back" — Tim Jones argues the Golds misread Darwin: they take themselves to be the perfected endpoint of natural selection and use the Passage and Institute to 'help Nature along' by culling weaker Golds, justifying the subjugation of lower Colors—the same social-Darwinist logic Hitler and Stalin used to dress up atrocity. Using Darwin's own contrast between natural selection and man-made selective breeding, he shows the Institute is an artificial arena and the Golds' shaping of Reds and Pinks is self-serving husbandry, not nature's work. The twist is that the very traits the Golds bred into lowReds—Helldiver knuckles, miner's endurance, drill-floor courage—are what win Darrow the Institute, the Iron Rain, and the fight against the Jackal, so their manipulated evolution becomes the tool of their own extinction, just as Quicksilver's case against the static Color hierarchy implies.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 23 "11. The Iron Bank Will Have Its Due" — Ewing argues money is the real determinant of the Iron Throne: Lannister gold made Cersei queen, Tyrell grain and taxation bought Margaery's crown, Baelish's financing decided the Battle of the Bastards, and the Iron Bank disciplines kings. Reading Westeros as a late-feudal economy through Marx - smallfolk whose work and taxes support lords who 'reap where they never sowed,' a hierarchy held by coercion and fear as the High Sparrow tells Olenna ('You are the few, we are the many'), and money dissolving feudal bonds into a 'money aristocracy' - he predicts the throne will go not to dragons or White Walkers but to the capitalist-financier figure of Petyr Baelish.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 37 "23. A Chimichanga for the Mercenary Soul" — Through Gramsci's Prison Notebooks the chapter casts Deadpool as the 'Eternal Proletariat': the military superstructure (Weapon X) recruited him precisely because he was broke and class-positioned, and as a mercenary he has no capital, no upward mobility, and no exit from wage-killing.
