His hunger beyond money - the Bullseye payday that ends in him shooting himself, the dead shark's verdict 'what you are . . . is alone' - drives him toward the X-Men, read as a subaltern coalition of the marginalized like Gramsci's socialist parties. But as a non-mutant 'mutate' who cannot meet the hegemonic standard of heroism (the Hit-Monkey arc with Spider-Man, his bitter plea to Wolverine that 'at least they wanted you'), his only Gramscian options are coalition building or reshaping the X-Men's culture from inside.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 24 "10. If It Isn’t Justified Is It Still My Revolution" — Writing as a guilt-ridden fsociety member haunted by James Plouffe's on-air suicide, Altmann tests the 5/9 revolution against three theorists: Burke's conservatism condemns all revolution as destruction of social tradition (and fsociety's blackout chaos and Susan Jacobs's death seem to prove him right), while Marx's class struggle between E Corp's bourgeoisie and the indebted proletariat makes revolution the only exit from history's cycle. Kai Nielsen's condition - revolution is justified only when no other recourse exists - settles it: Angela's failed attempt to reform E Corp from within shows non-revolutionary change is impossible, so the author keeps fighting 'with a keyboard whose clacking is endless.'
- **The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed**, ch. 9 "1 Introduction" — Smith introduces his project of explaining the subordination of women and blacks philosophically and empirically by comparing the social contract liberalism of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau with Marxism, building on Carole Pateman's Sexual Contract and Charles Mills's Racial Contract/Contract and Domination, which show the classic contracts were male supremacist and white supremacist. He argues sexual and racial egalitarianism is about politics and power, cataloguing nine power bases women and blacks should acquire, and stresses that because family and state are historically connected (Aristotle's Politics, Hobbes's 'little kingdoms', Locke's conjugal society, Rousseau's family as the oldest society, Engels's 'first class oppression' of the female by the male), equality in marriage may be a precondition for equality in society. He defends Marxism against Mills's dismissal of it as moribund, endorses MacKinnon's linking of sexism and racism while arguing (with Linda LaRue and Du Bois) that the racial contract has been more tyrannical than the sexual contract, and closes with Walzer's definition of egalitarianism as a society free of domination.
- **The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed**, ch. 10 "2 Power and Politics" — The chapter traces politics from the classical ethics-fused view (Aristotle's Politics, where politics exists for the sake of the good life yet also supplies one of the first justifications of patriarchy and the public/private split) to the Machiavelli-Hobbes break where politics becomes simply the possession and exercise of power, adopting Bertrand Russell's claim that power is the fundamental concept of social science. It then builds the book's central instrument, a Weber-derived analysis of nine power bases (money, knowledge/technology/information, religion, morality, authority, charisma, size/solidarity, violence, status), contrasting the Marxian reading - money as ultimately determinative, the ruling ideas of each age as the ideas of the ruling class, religion as the opium of the people, the state as a committee for managing bourgeois affairs - with the liberal-Weberian reading in which no single base is decisive. It closes by showing that Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau and Marx divide over the morality of egalitarianism (Popper's Marx moved by moral impulse versus Locke's possessive individualism), and that power is domain-specific, inert until used, skill-dependent and always relative.
- **The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed**, ch. 15 "7 The Bourgeoisie and the Blacks" — The chapter sets business - the US bourgeoisie whose privileged position Charles Beard read into the Constitution and which survived the Jacksonian and New Deal challenges by breaking labor through Taft-Hartley, right-to-work laws and the PATCO lockout, its solidarity secured while worker solidarity was undercut by what Marx called the Achilles heel of racism - against blacks as the paradigmatic powerless, shut out of every power base since slavery, which the chapter treats with Baptist and Marx's 1846 letter as a totalitarian system of super-exploited, tortured labor that built American capitalism, its neo-slavery progeny (Blackmon) pauperizing the black community under Dred Scott's 'subordinate and inferior class of beings'. It then narrates black counter-power base by base: the abolitionist interracial coalition wielding charisma (Douglass, Nat Turner, John Brown), information, morality and religion; the NAACP era and King's fusion of charisma, church religion, Myrdal's An American Dilemma and televised nonviolent provocation against Bull Connor's violence, contested by Malcolm X, SNCC and the Black Panthers; and a post-civil-rights scorecard showing a wealth base 94.2 percent white, persistent education and media gaps, constrained black officials from mayors to the symbolic Obama presidency, and a captive but potentially leveraged black vote in a 'Sisyphean' struggle.
- **The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed**, ch. 16 "8 Conclusion" — The conclusion restates the book's method - centering political philosophy in a consciously normative, empirical study of power - around its two contrasts: the family as a natural, subordination-requiring institution in liberalism versus a property-rooted, historically determined one in Marxism, and the state as a freely agreed contract of all (Locke, hence no food stamps) versus what actually happened, a charter 'ordained and established by a small group of wealthy white men, meeting in secret' to protect their wealth, so that the state which created gender and racial inequality must now play an equally decisive role in undoing it. Reviewing the nine bases since the 1960s, it finds women have closed the knowledge gap and nearly completed Engels's liberation program except universal child-care and non-exploitative housework, against conservative marriage-movement scholars like the Lockean Yenor, while blacks still face a tripling wealth gap that only social democratic capitalism on the Danish model plus comprehensive reparations can close - the latter argued on the moral base of power, Congress's 2009 apology, and Bernard Boxill's Lockean inheritance argument for a decades-long 'Reparations Superfund' as the civil rights issue of the 21st century.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 13 "3. Why Don’t the Proles Just Take Over" — Littmann asks why Oceania's proles, 85 percent of the population who could 'blow the Party to pieces tomorrow morning', never revolt, answering with Winston's diagnosis: until they become conscious they will never rebel. The Party keeps them unconscious through its media monopoly, crimestop, doublethink, reality control, perpetual war hysteria, and a nationalist identity that cuts them off from the international proletariat. He maps each mechanism onto the modern US, where six corporations control about 90 percent of media, citizens tailor their own reality bubbles, opponents are assumed to argue in bad faith, and partisan 'nationalisms' block common cause, arguing that American political conflict is mostly over facts rather than values.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 23 "11. Forever the Wild One" — Anders grounds Petty's artistic freedom in Kant's Critique of Judgment: genius, the innate talent for original art freed from patron control, describes Petty's refusal to let commercial success measure his work. Singer's practical ethics supplies the frame for the $8.98 fight over Hard Promises, where Petty weighed outcomes for all affected, especially teenage fans, and threatened to withhold the masters or rename the album "Eight Ninety-Eight." Marx's worker-owner analysis maps the Shelter-to-MCA contract saga, in which Petty was sold like a piece of meat, countersued, hid the master tapes nightly, and filed for bankruptcy like a worker confronting the owners who pocket the value of the records he produced.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 42 "28. Replicants of California, Unite!" — Christopher Innes gives 2049 a Marxist class analysis: the replicants are an enslaved working class, the Wallace Corporation the ruling class owning the means of production, and the LAPD a state apparatus with 'relative autonomy' that really upholds the system — K is a slave who kills his own kind without seeing his class position. Applying the materialist (not idealist) dialectic and the Eighteenth Brumaire's lesson about conflicting ruling-class interests, he reads Wallace, Atari, and even Ana as factions with divergent interests. Freysa's 'we are our own masters' and 'we are building our own army' mark the replicants as class conscious, aware of their Marxian 'species being', with nothing to lose but their chains.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 35 "22. Won’t You Be My Comrade" — Christopher Innes runs Marx's critique of Hegel's idealism against Mister Rogers: the show treats problems (divorce, war, the Clemmons pool scene) ideally, as symbolic gestures rather than material change, much as Hegel's storybook individuals miss money's role. Measured against Capital's alienated worker, 'an appendage to the machine,' contrasted with the suitcase worker who 'knows her work,' and the Communist Manifesto's 'bourgeois socialist' who demands reform not liberation, Rogers emerges as a progressive bourgeois socialist whose make-believe may console children for, or subtly resist, their future exploitation.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 14 "Alien Nation" — Reads Alien as a film about alienation in Marx's fourfold sense from the 1844 Manuscripts: the crew is estranged from the product of its labor (the retrieved Xenomorph turns on them), from the labor process (Brett and Parker's bonus dispute, Dallas shilling for the Company that deems him disposable), from species-being (infantile dependence on Mother, whose Special Order 937 merely formalizes an expendability they already live), and from one another (they never unite against the Company or suspect Ash). In Aliens the Colonial Marines repeat the failure, while the coordinated alien 'nation' under its queen - possible victims of Engineer colonization - makes the humans look like the inferior species.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 14 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Applies Marx's fourfold alienation (from product, from labor, from species-being, from others) to Bluth capitalism: George Michael dips and sells bananas he cannot keep, Lupe cleans Lucille's home under duress, and classes divide the family from the people it exploits. George Sr.'s Boyfights tapes and Caged Wisdom show the capitalist commodifying his children and himself, Gob's figurehead presidency turns employees into resources, Lindsay is 'having without being', and Engels's property-based account of the nuclear family explains Tobias's repressed sexuality; the cure offered is democratic socialism, since within-system fixes only get more absurd.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 16 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Reads Bluth bourgeois identity through Marx's class vocabulary: consumption as status display (Lucille's furs, $6,300 suits), labor-as-leisure (Tobias's acting, Buster's cartography, Gob's illusions), and the observation that the family's real workers are children, women of color like Lupe, and a Roomba. Class is performed, as Tom Jane's homeless method acting and Lucille's 'poolside only' meltdown show, and the Bluths' narcissism (Lindsay's cause-shopping activism, the family's disgust at Buster's severed hand) is analyzed as a form of bourgeois privilege, while the family fails at the reinvestment that would make it a proper bourgeoisie.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 14 "A Specter Is Haunting the Bending World" — Lin argues the Bending World's supernatural inequality breaks Hobbes's condition that even the weakest can kill the strongest, the equality that motivates the social contract, so might-is-right is magnified: Ozai rules without bargaining while weak Earth Kings become Dai Li figureheads. Energybending's built-in 'moral self-destruct' needs no earthly accountability, resembling the divine right of kings rather than Arendt's insight that violence eradicates politics, and Aang wisely remains a passive guardian. The Avatar's reincarnation creates recurring power vacuums, and because bending is a non-redistributable endowment, the Equalist revolution haunts the Bending World like the specter of communism in the Communist Manifesto.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 14 "A Specter Is Haunting the Bending World" — Lin uses Hobbes's observation that in our world the weakest can kill the strongest, grounding the social contract, to show what breaks when supernatural power is wildly unequal: Fire Lord Ozai need not bargain with generals as Earth Kings must with the Dai Li, and the eclipse is the only equalizer. Energybending gets a 'moral self-destruct' that no real technology has, making Aang an unaccountable guardian closer to the divine right of kings than to naturalist politics, though his refusal of rule keeps politics alive in Arendt's sense. Like Marx and Engels's specter of communism, the 'specter of Equalism' outlives Amon, because bending is a non-redistributable, lethal endowment, so democracy in Republic City is structurally haunted.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 24 "It’s the Disappointing Stories that Sound True to Life" — Shipman argues the series first builds viewer sympathy for Cylons as rebel slaves (their monotheism and their New Caprica role as US-style occupiers make them 'more like the viewers than the humans'), then undercuts it: the Numbers rebuilt Cylon society as oppressors, breeding the voices out of Centurions, dismissing the Hybrids as mad, and breeding the sentient Raiders (Starbuck's discovery in 'Scar') into functional animals. The opening narration's claim that Cylons 'evolved' is disingenuous, since the model hierarchy was deliberately engineered, 'not evolution, but eugenics,' with Marx's 'from each according to his ability' division of labor as thin cover for literal class construction. The former slaves became slave-owners, fulfilling 'all of this has happened before': heroes of one story become villains of the next, inviting the muted models to rebel against the Numbers in turn.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 16 "Symbolism How We Create Meaning" — DeHaven and Hendrickson read Columbia through Marx's class struggle: Comstock and Fink form the bourgeoisie controlling the means of production (Finkton, Handyman conversions of injured workers), while religion as 'opiate of the masses', the deified Founders, kinetoscope propaganda, and the Raffle keep the Shantytown proletariat in check. The Vox Populi's revolt instantiates conflict theory's inevitable collapse, but the revolution loses its ideals, turns anarchistic, and becomes the new oppressor burning Columbia. Against Marx the chapter sets Spencer-style structural functionalism (Fink's lions-and-oxen ecology justifying the status quo) and Rawls's difference principle, asking whether Columbia's inequalities ever benefited the least advantaged; Booker's rejection of baptism-as-erasure of his past contrasts with Comstock's laundered sins.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 11 "2. I May Be a Socialist, But I’m Not a Lunatic" — Walderezak tracks Tom Branson's trajectory from Marxist-quoting socialist chauffeur to estate manager, arguing that the show quietly makes Robert, not Tom, the 'real socialist.' Robert's aristocratic conservatism is read as noblesse oblige (funding the hospital, the Downton Fair, and secretly paying a tenant's arrears), while Matthew's capitalist drive for 'investment, increasing productivity, and reducing waste' is presented as the profit-first ownership system that Marx and Fourier actually criticized. Tom's socialism, closer to the utopian visions of Robert Owen and Charles Fourier than to Marx's class struggle, dissolves as he assimilates into the family ('I haven't abandoned all of my socialism, although sometimes it feels like it'), a capitulation the chapter explains through David Harvey's 'capitalist pacification,' whereby capitalism absorbs all facets of society. The chapter concludes that Robert's treatment of ownership as a duty owed to tenants approaches the cooperative ideals of Fourier and Owen more than Tom's abandoned radicalism ever did.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 24 "12. Should We Really Care about the Crawleys" — Jones takes on the charge, voiced amid rising real-world inequality, that loving Downton seduces viewers into admiring hierarchy, and answers that the Crawleys deserve our care because they are human beings who share our bereavements (Mary's grief for Matthew, Cora's miscarriage, Edith's jilting) and because they use moments of cross-class contact well: Grantham paying for Mrs. Patmore's eye surgery, Violet throwing the flower contest at Isobel's urging, and the family's genuine embrace of Tom Branson. He reads the show as a manifesto for gradual social change through sympathetic contact rather than the Irish revolutionaries' arson, but ends with a serious objection: this philosophy makes ending oppression partly the duty of the oppressed, from Carson's 'foul' remark about Thomas's sexuality to today's super-rich, so more radical activism may still be required.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 33 "20. Masters and Servants and Soldiers" — Carl Sobocinski asks whether WWI caused Downton's social upheavals or merely accelerated trends already underway, using the philosopher of history's problem of separating change from continuity. The Boer War bond between Lord Grantham and his former army 'batman' Bates displays the constancy of noblesse oblige beneath the class system, while Thomas Barrow wielding authority over his social superiors at the convalescent home, Sybil's hands-on nursing, and the socialist chauffeur Branson marrying into the aristocracy show genuine change - though he argues most of it (mass recruiting, field commissions for commoners) enlarged pre-1914 trends. Closing with The Clash's 'Something about England,' he notes the same era that transformed the Crawleys' world left the servant class's life largely unchanged, with change ultimately coming out on top.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 25 "“I Want to Conquer the World”" — Uses Agamben's bios/zoē distinction (with Foucault on biopolitics and fragmented sovereignty, Hardt and Negri's 'Empire', Marx on surplus-value, and Rosa Luxemburg on unchecked capital) to read the Anderson Station massacre, Murtry shooting Coop on New Terra, and Protogen infecting 1.5 million Belters on Eros as reductions of Belter life to bare life that corporate sovereigns may kill without homicide. It then argues the instability capitalism creates births authoritarian sovereigns — Murtry's martial law, Inaros's Free Navy, Duarte's Laconia — whose followers (Chandra Wei, Cyn, Santiago Singh) display the 'total, unrestricted, unconditional loyalty' Arendt says totalitarian power demands, and closes with Foucault's warning that liberal government's security-for-freedom trade slides into the very corruption and oppression it was meant to prevent.
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 20 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — Michel Beaulieu reads the series through Marx's materialist conception of history: the 'Proletariat Patrons' Movement' sign in FFIX's Alexandria, the job system as a class system, and Shinra dropping the Sector 7 plate on its own laboring class all instantiate class struggle, while Vaan's life in Rabanastre shows social existence determining consciousness. But he argues the heroes are not Marxist revolutionaries, since Cecil ends up King of Baron and the Light Warriors leave feudal structures intact, and the Moogles, the series' true proletarian serfs, never revolt, because no Final Fantasy world has yet matured to the stage where the Marxian transformation becomes possible.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 22 "Notes" — Byron and Wood use Marx's claim that the modern state is 'a committee for managing the common affairs of the bourgeoisie' to read House of Cards: Raymond Tusk secretly dictates President Walker's policies, SanCorp buys influence over Frank through Claire's water-filters favor, and Frank's rise to the vice presidency is engineered by capitalists to protect their market interests. Even Frank's seemingly pro-worker America Works plan serves capital, since gutting Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid to subsidize $45,000 hiring costs boosts business profit, and the Dunbar-Walmart dispute shows the state arbitrating between conflicting capitalists rather than aiding workers. The chapter concludes that worker victories like a Dunbar minimum-wage win would only be the bourgeoisie losing a battle while winning the class war, confirming Frank's line that 'democracy is so overrated.'
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 22 "Notes" — Argues that Marx's claim that the modern state is 'a committee for managing the common affairs of the bourgeoisie' explains House of Cards better than Frank's own power-over-money creed: Raymond Tusk and SanCorp dictate President Walker's policies and cost Frank the Secretary of State post, and even Frank's signature America Works jobs bill functions as a capitalist subsidy (government-paid wages, gutted entitlements), while the Dunbar-versus-Walmart fight over Medicaid shows the state arbitrating among capitalists. The authors conclude that even a worker victory like a Dunbar minimum-wage raise would only be a concession in an ongoing class conflict, so 'democracy is so overrated' because capital, not Frank, is really in charge of the White House.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 13 "Notes" — Thomas reads Bartertown's economy as embedded in social and political relations rather than a free market: the Underworld laborers versus Bartertown's elite stage Marx's class struggle, and the Aunty Entity–Master Blaster conflict runs through Hegel's thesis-antithesis-synthesis of capital versus labor. He treats the franchise as a post-peak-oil world, applies the tragedy of the commons and lifeboat ethics to water rationing and the Citadel's hierarchy, and counterposes Gandhi's cooperation, Adam Smith's invisible hand, and open-source-style collaboration. The conclusion: the Wasteland shows the failure of self-interest-based capitalism and the need for cooperative alternatives like direct democracy.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 21 "The Office and Philosophy" — Answers The New Yorker's claim that the American Office 'doesn't care about class' by reading it through Marx: capital's growth logic and surplus value explain the degraded office labor the show depicts (Stanley's 'run-out-the-clock type of situation' truck unloading, Pam's tepid watercolors, Roy's 'unloading trucks without meaning', Ryan's rejected assembly line), while the salaried masses' class position survives precisely as unnamable and denied - Michael's botched condo purchase, his fury at Ryan's business-school ambition, and Prison Martin's observation that office and prison are both 'doing the same thing every day'. Drawing on Kracauer, the chapter argues the show's comedy walks between distraction and awakening, and ends with Walter Benjamin's 'authentic humanity' located in the gap between professional and private life: Michael's failures make him an unwitting critique of the system that produced him.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 21 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Uses 'The Last of the Meheecans' to argue that Marx's account of labor-power needs race built into it: once Butters is mistaken for a Mexican immigrant 'Mantequilla', the couple who hit him hand him Windex and a leaf blower and he sings 'Work, Mexican, work', showing how racialization assigns his labor a demeaned value. The episode's conflicting stereotypes (lazy shiftless 'Meheecans' versus the hard-working backbone of service labor) and the mass 'Orgullo de Mantequilla' migration home reveal a super-exploited population. The author then recovers Marx's own writings on Polish and Irish liberation, American slavery, and Lincoln's reelection ('labor in the white skin cannot emancipate itself where in the black skin it is branded') to show that for Marx, racial and national domination were always obstacles to working-class freedom.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 23 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Reads '1%' — where Cartman's failed fitness test makes him the scapegoated one percent, and the school's 99% splinter into warring 83%, 30%, and 5% factions occupying the Red Robin (and its restroom) — through Rousseau's Social Contract on freedom and equality and the dismembered social body, showing how popular solidarity shatters into meaningless percentage tribes. 'Night of the Living Homeless' (the poor as zombies who 'feed on our change', Kyle's $20 spawning the swarm, the shotgun as the only remedy) dramatizes the dehumanizing social-Darwinist picture of the economic undead, and the underpants gnomes' business plan (Phase 1: Collect Underpants, Phase 2: ?, Phase 3: Profit) mocks CEOs who cannot say why they amass wealth. The chapter's own verdict: corporations as such are good (cars, computers, canned soup), and blame falls on the greedy individuals inside them, since death — Tolstoy's two meters of burial land — levels all players.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 19 "Notes" — Jeff Ewing argues the Federation's moneyless, postscarcity economy is Marx's transitional stage on the way to classless communism: Picard's 'we've eliminated hunger, want, the need for possessions' and Troi's exchange with Samuel Clemens in 'Time's Arrow' mark Marx's shift from the realm of necessity to the realm of freedom. He reconstructs Marx and Engels on alienation, the division of labor, labor-tokens, and the withering state to dissolve the apparent anomalies—Federation credits, Quark's tab, the Chateau Picard vineyard—as survivals of transition rather than capitalism. Rom's 'workers of the world unite' in 'Bar Association' and the self-actualizing leisure of Enterprise crews complete the case.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 15 "“We Were Trained to Be Keepers of the Peace, not Soldiers”" — Shakibnia reads The Clone Wars through Cornel West's three dogmas threatening democracy — free-market fundamentalism, aggressive militarism, escalating authoritarianism — and Chomsky's critique of inequality: Senator Halle Burtoni is a deliberate Halliburton/Cheney nod, and the banking-deregulation vote in 'Heroes on Both Sides' mirrors the US military-industrial complex. He argues the Separatist people's movement ('Corporations do not rule us!') was justified in seeking self-determination, while 'Sabotage' shows the Jedi losing legitimacy by becoming 'military weapons' — underpaid Temple worker Jackar Bowmani's squalid housing indicts the Republic's class divide. Ahsoka's departure and her maxim that 'it's every citizen's duty to challenge their leaders' model the accountability movement (like Black Lives Matter) that the Jedi failed to be.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 15 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Canode reads 'It's a Terrible Life' as Marx's alienation of labor: Dean Smith's corporate existence at Sandover Bridge & Iron is Zachariah's ruse, and the American dream, like the promise that one more hunt will finally let the brothers quit, is the ideology that keeps workers laboring for owners who profit from them. Sam and Dean become the proletariat and the angels the owners of the means of production, and their refusal of Heaven's plan enacts the Communist Manifesto's line that the bourgeoisie has forged the weapons of its own destruction. The closing meta-turn applies the critique to the audience: fans who watch, buy DVDs, and attend conventions are the bourgeoisie whose demand keeps the Winchesters hunting.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 15 "NOTES" — Ewing reads Cameron as a Marxist: Cyberdyne's profit-driven reverse-engineering of the recovered Terminator arm, Dyson's alienated labor ('Don't ask'), and U.S. militarism absorbing Cyber Research Systems develop Skynet as capitalism's 'final contradiction,' in which the drive for destructive, labor-replacing technology converges with the profit motive to threaten humanity. Sarah and John are useful to the resistance only when they exit wage labor - waitress to warrior, ATM hacking instead of work - dramatizing Marx's claim that liberation requires transcending class positions. Yet technology itself is neutral and reclaimable: the reprogrammed T-101 learning 'I know now why you cry' shows even killing machines can be humanized for liberation, and the saga ends where Marx does - not interpreting the world but changing it.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 25 "Anarchism and the Beats" — Ed D'Angelo argues the Beats had a philosophy after all: a romantic bohemian anarchism that made poetry a means to a religious transformation of consciousness, with political change following consciousness rather than the reverse. He shows Ginsberg inverting Plato's rationalist hierarchy (grounding reason in imagination and the body) and reads Beat 'criminality' as a shamanic journey to the unconscious underworld, distinct from Mailer's macho 'White Negro' hipster. He traces their lineage through Greenwich Village bohemia, Proudhon/Bakunin/Kropotkin anarchism, and pacifist anarchists like Rexroth and Dellinger, arguing the Beats rejected Marxist materialism and class warfare, and that the movement was 'born' out of Rexroth's anarchist poetry circle at the 1955 Six Gallery reading of 'Howl.'
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 25 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Tait gives a Fredric Jameson-derived Marxist reading of Ocean's Eleven, treating Danny Ocean's heist crew as a utopian 'figure of collectivity' whose diverse, cross-class, pan-American membership recalls the WWII combat film and rallies against Terry Benedict as the polysemous 'monster' (Jameson's shark in Jaws) standing for globalized capital displacing nostalgic American Las Vegas. He argues the victimless heist allegorizes a competing value system in which love, solidarity, and friendship trump money, restaging class conflict from Asphalt Jungle, Rififi, and Big Deal on Madonna Street. The film's utopian happy ending imagines redistributing wealth and 'beating the house' within the very system of late capital it critiques.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 11 "Beyond Panopticism The Biopolitical Labor of Surveillance and War in Contemporary Film" — Gooch argues that the post-2005 surveillance film cycle moves 'beyond panopticism': Foucault's disciplinary gaze gives way to Deleuze's 'societies of control,' and the surveiling gaze becomes direct domination and a form of biopolitical labor (Hardt and Negri) rather than an impersonal structure. He reads the prestige dramas (Redacted, Stop-Loss, In the Valley of Elah, Lions for Lambs) as exposing the soldier's proletarianization and self-surveillance, and the thrillers/blockbusters (Déjà Vu, The Kingdom, Body of Lies, The Bourne Ultimatum, Eagle Eye, Burn after Reading) as staging a Marxist antagonism between living labor (the watching hero) and the fixed capital of surveillance technology. Using Deleuze's 'degraded time-image,' Kant's needed separation of subject and law, and Benjamin/Agamben's state of exception, he shows Eagle Eye inverting law and subject to justify preemptive war and turn biopolitical labor into the labor of subjection.
- **Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy**, ch. 8 "Screaming for Change" — The methods chapter, laying out ideological rhetorical criticism supplemented by Gramsci's theory of hegemony. It explains Gramsci's revision of Marx: society as a dynamic core/periphery equilibrium rather than a rigid base/superstructure, hegemony maintained by 'force plus consent,' and the 'organic intellectual' who pierces 'common sense' to offer 'good sense.' On this basis it justifies analyzing four albums (Sex Pistols' Never Mind the Bollocks, Bad Religion's Suffer, Refused's Shape of Punk to Come, NOFX's Wolves in Wolves' Clothing) as sites where the subaltern contest hegemonic culture.
- **Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy**, ch. 9 "Screaming for Change" — The core analysis, reading all four albums track by track through Gramsci and Marx. The Sex Pistols' 'God Save the Queen' and 'Anarchy in the UK' attack the monarchy and consumerism as false consciousness; Bad Religion's 'Suffer' and 'You Are (The Government)' cast the state as gatekeeper of 'common sense' and religion as social-Darwinist superstition; Refused's 'New Noise' and 'The Deadly Rhythm' explicitly ventriloquize Marx on the production line, alienation, and organized revolt; NOFX's 'USA-Holes' and 'The Man I Killed' target Bush-era imperialism. Kristiansen extracts a shared subaltern rhetoric of nonconformity, anti-authoritarianism, and breaking 'the chains of false consciousness.'
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 40 "Downsizing Dreams" — Michael Bray argues the American Office does register class - precisely as a 'salaried mass' whose identity lies in denying class difference. Through Marx's account of surplus value and the degradation of rationalized labor (Stanley's 'run-out-the-clock,' Pam's deadened art, Michael's condo as consumer coffin), the office workers are alienated and secretly long for downsizing that never frees them. Bray invokes Benjamin to suggest Michael Scott's gap-ridden failure to be professional or private embodies what little 'authentic humanity' capitalism leaves, standing on the edge of naming the class it never names.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 24 "Whose Egg Is It, Really Property Rights and Distributive Justice" — Cribbs treats the Horton-versus-Mayzie custody fight over the egg as a property-rights puzzle, applying Locke's labor-mixing theory (Horton's season of incubation versus Mayzie's laying and abandonment, plus squatter's rights) and its provisos against waste and taking more than 'enough and as good,' illustrated by the Once-ler and Hardin's tragedy of the commons. Adam Smith's invisible hand and the Wubble-chap's skilled labor defend market inequality, while Sylvester McBean's Sneetch exploitation, Yertle, and Marx's alienated proletariat motivate Rawls's veil of ignorance and distributive justice as a corrective to unregulated property rights.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 23 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Bane surveys fidelity criticism of film adaptation (McFarlane, and especially George Bluestone's Novels into Film) and applies a Marxist reading to the 1940 Pride and Prejudice. He shows how Bluestone praises the film as faithfully capturing Austen's 'aristocratic dance,' then argues a single altered line, Darcy's 'the middle classes at play,' injects a post-Marx notion of class struggle absent from Austen's Regency world of gentry versus nobility. Reading the Bennet-Lucas competition as proletarian striving and set against the 1940s Red Scare and HUAC blacklist, Bane concludes that adaptation lets Austen's ironic critique of class speak to new times, marking her a great author across eras.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 19 "GARDENING" — Elizabeth Scott argues that the wartime allotment gardens of East London's Poplar were engines of working-class political development. Through allotment associations, laboring men learned letter-writing, accounting, public speaking, and democratic self-governance, negotiating with borough councils and the Port of London Authority and building solidarity that fed movements like the Poplar Rates Rebellion. She reads the 10-rod plot as restoring self-sufficiency and citizenship to a disenfranchised class, making gardening a grassroots site of cooperation, socialist activism, and political enfranchisement.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 15 "Zombies of the World, Unite Class Struggle and Alienation in Land of the Dead" — John Lutz reads Romero's Land of the Dead as a sustained Marxist allegory: the walled Pittsburgh with Kaufman's luxury Fiddler's Green tower over the exploited poor stands for America and global capitalist imperialism. The zombies embody Marx's alienated, dehumanized workers and the exploited underdeveloped South, while cannibalism/consumption figures commodities as 'dead labor.' The Fiddler's Green ad and Cholo's doomed aspiration illustrate Althusserian ideology (false consciousness). Big Daddy leading the zombies to arm themselves and cross the river dramatizes the growth of revolutionary class consciousness, and the destruction of Kaufman and the Green stages a socialist revolution in which the exploited are the ruling class's 'grave-diggers.'
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 40 "Downsizing Dreams" — Bray argues the American Office does depict class — precisely as a "salaried mass" whose identity rests on denying class difference. Using Marx's account of surplus value and alienated, deskilled labor (Stanley's "run-out-the-clock" situation, Pam's deadened art), he shows the office as a site of exploitation Michael Scott cannot properly manage. Michael's condo, the ex-convict comparing prison to Dunder-Mifflin, and Ryan's ambitions expose the gap between self-image and reality; via Walter Benjamin, Bray locates "authentic humanity" in that very tension.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 72 "68. Richard Pryor as Philosopher Stand-Up Comedy and Gramsci’s Organic Intellectual" — Healy reads Pryor through Gramsci's Prison Notebooks concept of the 'organic intellectual'—someone who gains specialized knowledge through lived experience and uses it to challenge a capitalist/racist hegemony—arguing Pryor's mainstream white fame let him smuggle the Black experience to the dominant class. Analyzing his concert films (Live in Concert, Live on the Sunset Strip, Here and Now), Healy shows Pryor's chokehold and police-dog bits, the 'Yee Haw'/lynching bit, and the Mudbone and Motif characters using laughter as a 'Trojan Horse' to make white audiences absorb police brutality, the Great Migration, and heroin death—Pryor as philosophy in action.

### The Dialectic

The dialectic is G.W.F. Hegel's method for tracing how thought, and reality itself, develops through contradiction and its resolution. A concept or condition generates a tension or opposition within itself, and this conflict is overcome in a higher stage that both cancels and preserves what came before—a movement Hegel captured with the term Aufhebung, or sublation. Often popularized as a triad of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis, the dialectic for Hegel describes an immanent, self-driven unfolding rather than an external formula imposed on its subject matter. It underlies his account of logic, history, and spirit as processes that advance toward greater self-understanding and completeness.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 111 "Unknown" — Grounding dialectics in Hegel and Trotsky's analogy of motion picture versus still photograph, the chapter reads the film's reflections—Neo mirrored in Morpheus's sunglasses with the red and blue pills, the fragmenting mirror, the doorknob—as a 'motion picture within the picture' tracking his dialectical growth. Before the red pill the same Neo appears in both lenses, an undialectical still; afterwards his image splits and evolves, and becoming 'the One' means reconciling the opposition of his Matrix and real-world lives—though Marxism, unlike the film, sees every synthesis as only half of a never-ending evolution.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 15 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Lawler charges that Gibson's atonement theology, in which the more barbaric the torture the greater the redemption, imprisons Christianity at the stage of Hegel's 'Unhappy Consciousness', where an infinite God is sundered from abject sinful humanity and a priestly mediator is needed. Reading the film through the master-slave dialectic (impotent master Pilate versus the dignified slave Simon of Cyrene; the world of separate egos as Hobbes's war of all against all), he argues that what dies on the cross is the separate ego itself, and that what rises is Geist, the 'I' that is 'We' of the loving human community. Against Tertullian's credo quia absurdum, and using Pascal's 'heart has its reasons' alongside Hegel's dialectical reason, he reads 'you are gods' and the prodigal son as teaching every person's essential divinity, so the film's own art (the Mater Dolorosa, our identification with the flesh-and-blood Jesus) implicitly undermines the separatist theology Gibson intends.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 15 "Hip Hop and “This Makin’ Dollars Shit”" — Pittman argues the rap battle - UTFO's "Roxanne, Roxanne" answered by Roxanne Shanté's "Roxanne's Revenge", Run-D.M.C.'s "Sucker MC's", Jay-Z's "Takeover" versus Nas's "Ether" - is hip hop's enactment of Hegel's master-slave struggle for recognition, where self-consciousness proves itself only through an all-or-nothing contest ending in domination rather than destruction. Gangsta rap (N.W.A's "Gangsta Gangsta", Ice Cube's fantasy raid on the suburbs) radicalizes the battle into a collective demand that America recognize black urban conditions, and the chapter turns to Du Bois's race-centered and Marx's class-centered revisions of Hegel's history to read "this makin' dollars shit" - Wu-Tang's "C.R.E.A.M.", Talib Kweli on capitalism and crack, Mos Def's "The Rape Over" - as the dialectic's capture of the cipher by corporate beef.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 16 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Goldstein applies Hegel's thesis-antithesis-synthesis and Marx's more complex, multidimensional dialectic to the splits within biker culture: bar-room stare-downs as struggles for recognition, wrenchers versus trailers, RUBs versus working-class riders, helmet disputes, and one-percenters versus the rest. He traces the collapse of brotherhood (the clenched fist of solidarity giving way to the selective wave) to the commodification of the motorcycle during the Japanese invasion and to Harley's own yuppie-era Willie G. marketing, arguing via commodity fetishism that bikers misread economic forces between manufacturers as personal differences. His conclusion is that the seeds of unity lie within the divisions, and that Harley-Davidson Motor Co. will not save the culture, since its task is profit, not tradition.
- **The Beatles and Philosophy - Nothing You Can Think that Can't Be Thunk**, ch. 8 "CHAPTER 1 “LET’S GET REAL, REAL GONE FOR A CHANGE”" — The chapter argues that Elvis's Sun recordings — the staged rupture in 'Milkcow Blues Boogie' ('That don't move me. Let's get real, real gone for a change') and the accidental 'acting the fool' emergence of 'That's All Right' — enacted an epistemological revolution: a leap out of modernity's rationalized, disembodied mode into repressed bodily affect, defining American cool as affective authenticity against Bill Haley's affected performativity. Elvis's immersion in a Black Memphis neighborhood and his emulation of Black performers made him a catalyst for racial-musical integration and the 'visceral empathy' that prepared desegregation, while the panic of critics (Sinatra, the Times, Congressman Celler) is reread via Hegel's 'tarrying with the negative' as the resistance Geist needs for its self-overcoming. Creative novelty is described with Whitehead's and William James's metaphors — the 'lure of feeling,' sudden phase transition, radical empiricism in what Elvis kept or dropped onstage — with his 'did it make me feel good' studio criterion and a Zen-like mushin statesmanship of loosing egoic control in the band.
- **The Beatles and Philosophy - Nothing You Can Think that Can't Be Thunk**, ch. 9 "CHAPTER 2 “A CREATIVE TENSION”" — The chapter traces the Beatles' rise as a case study in how novelty enters culture: Lennon and McCartney polarize into transgressive truth and melodic beauty, their 'creative tension' producing an emergent whole greater than either (the 'holding a mirror' songwriting method, their fused harmonies, the Decca audition versus Hamburg swings between commerce and authenticity). Hamburg is the underworld initiation where 'Mach Schau!' humiliation, absurdist humor read as Freudian catharsis, and Preludin-fueled marathon sets broke them out of English propriety into ecstatic physicality, before Epstein's suits and George Martin's harsh Abbey Road critique dragged the pendulum back toward rational professionalism. Against the Cartesian thesis that humanity is defined by the thinking mind ('I think, therefore I am'), the chapter reads 'Please Please Me,' Beatlemania's screaming crowds (citing Ehrenreich on female assertiveness and solidarity), and Rubber Soul as successive dialectical phase transitions integrating affect with intellect — a rock-and-roll answer to rationalized modernity, in James's wave-crest image of novelty flung ahead of history.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 22 "Meet You on the Dark Side of the Moon" — Jere Surber frames Pink Floyd as musical heirs to Parmenides's 'path of Non-Being', then maps Marx's four alienations onto the catalog: self-alienation in 'Brain Damage' ('There's someone in my head, but it's not me'), alienation by things in 'Welcome to the Machine', alienation from other persons in 'Us and Them' and The Final Cut's war trauma, and alienation from species-being in Animals ('Dogs'). Existential absence follows: Sartre's café scene, where the whole ensemble arranges itself around the missing Pierre, parallels the absent Syd and the father killed in World War II behind The Wall ('Comfortably Numb': 'the child is grown, the dream is gone'), while Heidegger's withdrawal of Being accounts for the cosmic Angst of 'Eclipse' and Obscured by Clouds. A postmodern coda reads the band's mid-thought-breaking lyrics and Ummagumma sound experiments as Derridean différance woven through language and sound.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 27 "16 - Quantitative and Qualitative Change" — This edited LibriVox podcast transcript catches three volunteers debating free culture: Wittkower argues copyright is an artificial monopoly justified only when printing presses made reproducing texts capital-intensive — now that consumer gear has put industrial-scale production in everyone's basement ('the working man has wrested the means of production from the big man'), a thirteen-year-old should be free to strip vocals and remix her culture. McGaughey's title thesis — cheap technology means a quantitative change becomes a qualitative change, 'which is by the way from Hegel's Logic' — answers Mowatt's deflation that the Internet merely lowers the bar for things you could always have done locally. Connecting Putnam's Bowling Alone decline of social trust to narrow-casting as a way of rebuilding communities of common concern, they hold up LibriVox's 1,668 free public-domain audiobooks (327 days of audio, volunteers on six continents) as a gift-economy counter-model to a culture we only 'rent' as serfs on branded soil.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 10 "And Your Little Dog Too!" — Altamura and Fritzman argue the film has the tripartite structure of Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit: gray Kansas is a partial truth (thesis), 'somewhere over the rainbow' the antithesis, and the synthesis is Dorothy's discovery that the home she yearned for was Kansas all along—a truth that emerges only through misrecognition, which is why Glinda cannot simply tell her the slippers' power. They read 'Over the Rainbow' through Hegel's 'unhappy consciousness' and side with Hegel's one world against the Kantian two-worlds reading (Kansas as the knowable island, Oz as the unknowable beyond) that they put in the mouths of heckling 'bullies' and detect in Rushdie. Against Rushdie's line that the companions 'already possess what they seek,' they insist the trio really were hollow men who became brainy, tender, and brave through the journey, the Wizard's trinkets supplying Hegelian public recognition. From the Philosophy of History they cast Dorothy as a world-historical individual whose unintentional destruction of both Witches and exposure of the Wizard advances Oz's freedom—Toto's deliberate pulling of the curtain included.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 20 "Bring the Balance Back Led Zeppelin and the Hegelian Dialectic" — Macan argues Zeppelin's contradictions — 'cock rock' versus androgyny, blues versus avant-garde sound collages, acoustic versus electric, East versus West — are Hegelian dualities driven toward monist synthesis by a World-Spirit working through the band's generation. He reads the physical riff sections and shadowy middle collages of 'Dazed and Confused' and 'Whole Lotta Love' as interpenetrating Primitive/Modern, African-American/European, and Male/Female poles; 'Stairway to Heaven''s seamless growth from recorder-and-lute evocations of Elizabethan England into full hard rock reconciles past and present (via Tolkien, the Hermit gatefold, the Lady and the Piper); and 'Kashmir' versus 'In the Light' stage Jung's East/West problem, with Crowley's Schopenhauerian will supplying the turn from wisdom sought without to wisdom found within.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 21 "The Moving Shadow of Truth" — Haffner and Vogel define martial arts by a Wittgensteinian family resemblance to combat and organize the promise of self-improvement as paired opposites, working them Hegelian dialectic style, granting some truth to each side. They ask whether training brings peace or violence (Hobbes's shield for a war of all against all and Freudian catharsis versus Aristotle's worry that habituated violence breeds violence), strength fantasies or Socratic humility about weakness (with Sun Tzu's know-your-enemy and Foucault on the teacher's gaze and dojo power games), Cartesian dualism versus embodiment, and appreciation of tradition versus its distortion. The lesson is that the martial path holds both light and shadow, and separating enlightenment from self-deception takes eternal vigilance.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 9 "The Heart and Mind United" — Sheinbaum argues against the assumption that Rush's rhythmic complexity is 'thinking' music opposed to bodily groove, showing through close listening that 'Subdivisions' (7/8 in 2+2+3 groups), 'Limelight' (4/4 and 3/4 bars interleaved), 'Jacob's Ladder' (alternating 5/4 and 6/4), and the 7/8 passages of 'La Villa Strangiato' all groove while the band retains standard eight-bar phrase structures. He treats meter and hypermeter as Western cultural constructions, and reads Rush's metric deviations as a musical image of the individual resisting a 'conformist social order' (citing Chris McDonald on the individualism Rush shares with Ayn Rand's middle-class virtues). His resolution is dialectical: complex and conventional elements operate as simultaneous poles in synthesis, so mind and body, thought and groove, are united rather than opposed, a point he presses against the racialized mind-body binary in writing about rhythm.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 14 "Let It Bleed" — Reconstructing the twins' songwriting mechanics — Keith re-voicing Mick's 'Brown Sugar' in open-G tuning, the producer Don Was shuttling between them during Bridges to Babylon as Keith sang wordless fragments that Mick turned into lyrics — Auxier argues their genius lives outside either man alone, in sparks between two interdependent, mutually wounded subjectivities. He names their destructive-yet-creative bond a classic case of what philosophers call dialectic, citing Hegel's view that cultural history is made through strife and that a Zeitgeist moves history with or without the cooperation of individuals. The Stones surfed the 1960s Zeitgeist all the way into the twenty-first century, and their willingness to 'let it bleed' kept the collaboration generative after they stopped being good mates around 1968.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 15 "Fifteen Minutes of Fame" — Auxier argues the twins were serious artists with a sense of the history they were living — true students and initiates of the blues whose aesthetic and spiritual value they recognized before Americans did. He mobilizes Hegel's claim that art gives sensuous appearance to the movement of history: Keith's guitar sound and Mick's stage strut are the clothes history wears between its stages, with geniuses hitting targets no one else sees, ahead of the slower-moving innards of politics and religion. The Stones used their fame to hoist the blues, the bottom rung of the cultural ladder, toward the center just as pop art and the beat poets lowered the wall between high and low, leaving high culture itself begging at the banquet.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 21 "The Songs" — Auxier argues that amid the manufactured illusions the songs are what is real: they are the primary illusions symbolizing how it feels to live in our times, and the appearance of the Jagger-Richards credit from Aftermath onward made the Stones creative forces rather than mere personas. Using Keith's Life account of writing Exile on Main Street on the fly — make the bare bones of a riff, snap the drums in, see what happens — he locates the creative secret in the tension of the dialectic between Mick and Keith, which builds until Charlie Watts kicks in. The genius finally lies beyond the twins in the group: they are the left and right ventricles of the heart of rock'n'roll, but the body that dances is the band.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 29 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Gurland-Blaker reads The Wire as Simon intended it, a Greek tragedy with institutions (police, docks, schools, politics, press) in place of the gods. Using Hegel's Aesthetics, he argues art unveils truth in sensuous form and that we identify with Sobotka, Bubbles, and Marlo because their magnified struggles are recognizably our own; dramatic tragedy works by staging collisions between incompatible but equally justified codes, exactly as Antigone's loyalty to divine law against Creon's law of the polis maps onto Avon's street rep, Stringer's business rationality, Marlo's name, and McNulty's vanity, all of which go down together. Stringer is the paradigm: the American Dream destroyed by the very virtues that constituted it ('deserve got nuthin' to do with it'), while the show out-Hegels Hegel by locating the deepest tragedy not in the heroes' deaths but in the restoration of the status quo, where lieutenants become colonels and mayors become governors and nothing changes.
- **How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness**, ch. 27 "How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy" — The chapter defends Barney's 'possimpible' as real philosophy. Aristotle's three formulations of the law of non-contradiction (from the Metaphysics) and Duns Scotus's ex falso quodlibet explosion argument show why classical logic must ban the possible and impossible becoming one - from one true contradiction, 'bimbos love studying formal logic' follows. Hegel's Science of Logic (the limit of the beer, the finite that is itself only by passing into its not-being) and Graham Priest's dialetheism from In Contradiction then argue limits are inherently contradictory, so the possimpible names the real turning point where opposites become each other - lived, the chapter claims, in Barney's transformation from lame hippie into suited bro.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 23 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Babette Babich traces the shifting 'you' of 'Hallelujah' and 'Suzanne' through Hegelian thesis-antithesis-synthesis and Empedocles's cycle of Love and Strife, reading the songs' ambiguity (David, Samson, the bound champion) as Cohen's sovereign having-it-both-ways. Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity frames the human condition of being what one is not, while Nietzsche - on broken promises, on women and distance, on the Antichrist - supplies both the critique of Cohen's courtly projections onto the feminine Other and the model of singularizing solitude. 'Who by Fire' is read against the Rosh Hashanah prayer Unetanneh Tokef as a song of fate, judgment, and atonement whose closing 'who shall I say is calling?' is quasi-Augustinian and Heideggerian: death singularizes each 'who' at the moment of its claim.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 30 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Knepp asks why Jobs's 'simplicity is the ultimate sophistication' produced the friendly, MoMA-collected Macintosh (the face-like design, the inviting handle, the signed internals) but collapsed into the $6,500 NeXT Cube, answering with Žižek's reading of Hegel in Less than Nothing: the original idea is already self-contradictory, the failure of NeXT (the over-engineered perfect cube, the $100,000 Rand logo trying too hard to be friendly) is its symptom, and the iMac is the second attempt that only the failed first choice makes possible. He grounds this in Kant's Critique of Pure Reason—the antinomies and the phenomenon/noumenon distinction that Hegel radicalized into a world driven by oppositions—finding the dialectic everywhere in Jobs: two sets of parents, orchards and Silicon Valley, 'Apple' as both high-tech and organic, and a childish lowercase signature made with grand cursive flair.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 27 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Karavitis applies Walter Benjamin's 'Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction' to his own deflated re-reading of Dracula: mass reproduction stripped the novel of its ritual aura, and film (stage Lugosi versus screen Lugosi) made art analyzable, political, and economically driven. He reads Stoker's epistolary form and Mina's surviving transcription - the originals destroyed - as heralding a postmodern world where every viewpoint is equally valid, so each reader's gaze (feminist, Marxist, Blacula, Count Chocula) remakes the Count. A closing dialectic moves from passive contemplation (thesis) through critical reading (antithesis) to readers becoming authors themselves (synthesis).
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 26 "14. Things Can Happen that Nobody Could Imagine Only a Few Years Ago" — Donna Marie Smith reads the series as a Hegelian drama in which the opposing forces of tradition and progress - Lord Grantham, Carson, and Violet defending the old estate world against Matthew, Sybil, and Tom Branson embracing new ideas - drive history as 'the progress of the consciousness of freedom.' Using Hegel's Elements of the Philosophy of Right, she explains why Robert treats upholding the entail against the protests of Mary, Cora, and even Violet as his duty as custodian, while noting Hegel's own objection that such inheritance law gives family members like the Crawley women 'no right to recognition.' The war announced at the season 1 garden party is read through Hegel's experience of Napoleon at Jena and his view that war can advance Geist, and the chapter closes with telephones, electric mixers, Sybil's marriage, and Isobel Crawley concluding that tradition and change can finally coexist.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 13 "4. Scoundrels, the Lot of Us" — Karavitis finds a Hegelian dialectic in the three-panel Dilbert strip (thesis, antithesis, synthesis) delivered through irony, then tests that irony against philosophy: Socrates' feigned-ignorance questioning that leaves interlocutors in aporia, Hegel's complaint that irony is vanity withdrawing from objective reality, and Kierkegaard's dissertation on the concept of irony plus Either/Or, where irony is the bridge from the aesthetic to the ethical life. The punchline is that after nearly three decades of Dilbert the white-collar workplace has not changed, so readers who feel superior to their bosses and co-workers have taken the vain, narcissistic, aesthetic reading Hegel warned against, making the joke a scoundrelly way of avoiding responsibility. A Leo Strauss aside casts Adams as an esoteric writer whose irony preserves him from the powerful.
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 16 "7. Destroyer Unmasked" — L.A. Recoder's densely dialectical essay presents KISS as a 'philosophical toy' that taught him creativity through destruction, pivoting on Paul Stanley's line that 'we loved you until we strapped on our guitars, and then we were there to destroy you.' He reads the oral history of KISS upstaging Black Sabbath — the 'KISS! KISS! KISS!' chant that got them thrown off the tour — and Ted Nugent's challenged escalation as the destroyer's veneration-through-destruction, then reads Chuck Schuldiner's death-metal band Death covering 'God of Thunder' as Hegel's tarrying with the negative: the KISS of Death turns round upon itself to become the Death of KISS, through which KISS is reborn.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 26 "14. Things Can Happen that Nobody Could Imagine Only a Few Years Ago" — Donna Marie Smith reads the series through Hegel's philosophy of history: the Crawleys' world is a clash of opposing forces - Lord Grantham's traditionalism against Matthew's and Branson's modernization, Violet's fear of electricity against Sybil's and Rose's embrace of the new - and this very conflict drives progress toward greater freedom. She uses Hegel's Elements of the Philosophy of Right both to explain the entail and primogeniture that bar Mary from inheriting (the law preserves the 'house' over the immediate family, which Hegel calls an infringement of the freedom of property) and to frame Robert's refusal to challenge it as duty to his social standing outweighing personal wishes. WWI, which Hegel experienced through Napoleon's occupation of Jena, is presented as a 'march toward freedom' that breaks down class barriers and finally pushes Robert to accept change on the estate: 'Let's give it a go and see what the future brings.'
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 13 "Notes" — Thomas reads Bartertown's economy as embedded in social and political relations rather than a free market: the Underworld laborers versus Bartertown's elite stage Marx's class struggle, and the Aunty Entity–Master Blaster conflict runs through Hegel's thesis-antithesis-synthesis of capital versus labor. He treats the franchise as a post-peak-oil world, applies the tragedy of the commons and lifeboat ethics to water rationing and the Citadel's hierarchy, and counterposes Gandhi's cooperation, Adam Smith's invisible hand, and open-source-style collaboration. The conclusion: the Wasteland shows the failure of self-interest-based capitalism and the need for cooperative alternatives like direct democracy.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 28 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Treats SAMCRO as the 'Sons of History': Hesiod's ages of decline fit the fall from the First 9's 1967 golden-age founding to the 'Age of Clay,' and Vico's corsi e recorsi explains how Clay's rational greed — muling cocaine for the Galindo Cartel — is the 'barbarism of reflection' that follows the loss of J.T.'s founding imagination. Christian providential history is tried against the show itself (Jax sleeping at the 'Patmos' mausoleum, 'The Revelator') but set aside for Hegel: Jax is the dialectical synthesis of thesis J.T. and antithesis Clay, keeping his father's ideals while acquiring Clay's cold cunning, which is how he outplays June Stahl and Damon Pope. Piney's counsel that Jax must 'find' his father before moving on makes the Delphic 'know thyself' the engine of the club's progress.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 20 "NOTES" — Jason Blahuta reads the saga through Hegel's Philosophy of History: Sarah and John Connor are World Historical Individuals — mere 'tools' of Geist — whose attempts to rewrite history, Sarah's hit on Miles Dyson in T2 and John's second try through General Brewster in T3, can only postpone Judgment Day, never redirect it, as the T-101's line 'Judgment Day is inevitable' concedes. The cunning of reason explains why removing Dyson or Brewster is futile: historical forces merely recruit replacements, so the script gets acted out by other actors. Because the dialectic's thesis-antithesis pattern (even the young John versus his mother) yields syntheses that carry both sides forward, the chapter concludes neither species can stop the other's rise, and only full-scale battle in the moving present decides which becomes Geist's end.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 16 "Notes" — Uses Hans Kelsen's legal positivism — law as amoral coercive order sustained by sanction, validated by authority rather than morality — to interpret season two's competing normative systems, from Vinci's city hall to the cartel's execution of the informant Irina. Against this background it separates revenge from Hegelian retributivism, reading Velcoro's shift from killing his wife's rapist to persuading Lenny Osterman to seek exposure instead, and Frank's communicative, confessing execution of the traitor Blake, as conflicted exercises of justice. The finale's bloodshed is read through Hegel's theory of tragedy as a collision of spheres of justice, each justified in its own eyes, whose transgression may precipitate change in Vinci.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Knepp reads the Paul Dini/Alex Ross 'Origin of Wonder Woman' as Hegel's three-stage philosophy of history in miniature: the Amazons begin in a Hobbesian war of all against all, negate it by retreating to Themyscira where only some are free, and Diana's disguised contest win supplies the second negation that carries Amazon ideals to all people - celebrated by the splash of red, white, and blue. He then traces the WWII stakes: Hegel tied history's culmination to German unification, German-American Hegelians transplanted the classical-freedom story to America, and Marston - ex-assistant to the anti-feminist German psychologist Munsterberg - turned the lie detector into the lasso, reclaiming truth-telling from misogynist German science for a feminist America fighting Hitler.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 19 "The Dialectic of Enlightenment in Metropolis" — Abrams reads Fritz Lang's Metropolis as anticipating Adorno and Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment by two decades. He maps the film's arc—from the Christian mythology of the catacombs, through Joh's technototalitarian rational city and the human-machine fusion of Rotwang's false Maria, back into ancient myth (the M-Machine as Moloch, the whore of Babylon, the Tower of Babel)—onto their thesis that Enlightenment reason turns totalitarian and reverts to mythology and madness. He ties reason's self-destruction to Nietzsche's will to power and contrasts the descent into 'absolute madness' with Hegel's progress toward absolute mind.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 25 "Go West, Young Woman! Hegel's Dialectic and Women's Identities in Western Films" — Gary Heba and Robin Murphy map women's identities in westerns onto Hegel's three-stage dialectic (aufheben as maintain/negate/transform), grafting on Bakhtin's monoglossic/heteroglossic discourse and Mulvey's and de Beauvoir's feminist film theory. Settler women (Marian in Shane, the mothers of The Searchers) are monoglossic—silenced, family-bound bearers of meaning; town women (Mrs. French in Appaloosa, Lily in How the West Was Won) are heteroglossic, sexualized spectacles marked by costume; and post-1970s figures like Ellen in The Quick and the Dead and Sara in Two Mules for Sister Sara become 'x-glossic,' transformational identities that subvert the male-gaze code and exceed the settler/town binary.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 18 "16_LaRocca_Chapter_015.html" — Dan Geva re-reads Dziga Vertov's The Man with the Movie Camera as a coherent philosophy of documentary he calls 'praxis' or 'cine-seeing the invisible,' distilling ten 'diktats' (Unplayed Cinema, Life-Caught-Unawares, the interval theory of montage, etc.). He argues Vertov, like Plato, Marx, Nietzsche and Freud, privileges hidden depths over surface appearance, and reads the dialectical move from 'film fact' to 'film thing' as a Hegelian synthesis rather than a paradox. Crucially he aligns Vertov's Kino-Eye truth with Heidegger's notion of truth as aletheia (a partial unconcealment) rather than correspondence, tying the camera's revelation of the invisible to Heidegger's meditation on technology and seeing.
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 7 "We Are the Change That We Seek" — These essays treat time, selfhood and substance across Nolan's films. Fosl argues Nolan's selves (Leonard, Bill in Following, the Borden twins, Bruce Wayne) are unstable narratives signified through manipulable objects, invoking Locke on memory-based identity, Augustine on memoria, Nietzsche on forgetting and Sartre/Gadamer on the manipulable past. LaRocca applies Clark and Chalmers's Extended Mind Thesis to Memento, arguing Leonard's tattoos and Polaroids are literal external memories whose deliberate falsification ('Don't believe his lies') makes him morally culpable for murder. Willis uses Lacan's gaze and objet a to read Following's voyeur-becomes-viewed structure and 'the box' as a lure. McGowan reads Interstellar through Hegel: the mysterious 'they' who opened the wormhole are revealed as future humanity, dissolving substance into subject and licensing Cooper's retroactive causality as the 'ghost' who saves Murph.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 12 "4. A Muscle Car and a Mythic Quest" — Huntingford reads Sam and Dean as the Cowboy incarnation of Jung's universal Mythic Hero archetype, their Impala road-trip an odyssey of Campbell's monomyth and Jungian individuation confronting the 'shadow' (Amara as the Darkness). She uses Hegel to cast the brothers' alienation as the start of self-discovery toward absolute knowledge, Kierkegaard to praise their nonconformity over the crowd, and Sartre's 'hell is other people' and freedom-as-otherness to argue the Quest requires killing the false narrative self—Chuck the Trickster—to become free.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 20 "11. An Interstellar Leap of Faith" — Barta and Lee read Seldon's Plan as a providence narrative and stage a three-way debate over it. Hegel's dialectical, Spirit-driven history (thesis-antithesis-synthesis, even yielding 'psycho-history' as a synthesis) is mirrored in the Foundation's succession of ruling crises and its Encyclopedia Galactica as absolute knowledge. Kierkegaard's leap of faith describes how Foundationists obey a plan they cannot see and whose Vault confirms only in hindsight, an ignorance the Plan actually requires (an observer effect). Marx's materialist dialectic appears in Hober Mallow's 'historic forces' and the priesthood of the Galactic Spirit as ideological control, but the authors argue the Foundationists' sincere faith in Seldon nests all critiques back inside a Hegelian providence.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 12 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Gibson argues Austen's novels are propelled by dialectical forces (signaled by titles like Pride and Prejudice and Sense and Sensibility) that are reconciled through the marriage bond, invoking the Platonic origin of dialectic and drawing on Harold Bloom's reading of Darcy and Elizabeth as sharing a common will. Love functions as the transcendent principle that resolves opposition, but Gibson stresses (citing Derrida on the gift) that in Austen love never fully escapes the economic and social 'prisons' of marriage: Charlotte Lucas's loveless match, Fanny Price's poverty, and Anne Elliot's coerced broken engagement all show love succeeding only alongside wealth and status.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 7 "Welcome Aboard the TARDIS—It’s Bigger on the Inside" — The author argues that Doctor Who functions as a 'great educator' that shapes viewers' reality and their conception of the good life, framing our birth into the world as being 'thrown' into a new environment we must assimilate. He applies Hegel's historical dialectic to the Doctor-versus-Daleks conflict, treating the Doctor (wisdom, liberty, compassion) and the Daleks (obedience, hatred, conquest) as opposing theses whose ongoing struggle synthesizes the wider universe's fear of the Daleks. Drawing on Carroll and Danesi, he claims pop culture like Doctor Who validates experience and creates collective structures of meaning, and that our chosen first Doctor becomes the interpretive framework through which we judge every later one.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 9 "1. Engaging Life Like the Doctor" — The chapter casts the Doctor as a 'flâneur' who teaches an engaged, critical-thinking way of life, illustrated through episodes like 'Blink,' 'Heaven Sent,' and 'Kerblam!' where the Doctor (and viewer) solve mysteries through trial and error. It uses Hume and William James to argue the mind actively constructs reality into a narrative, and pairs the Doctor with Socrates as a truth-seeking 'midwife' teacher who withholds answers so companions can learn by living rather than being told. The Doctor's rejection of Time Lord non-interference models the Socratic examined life of engaging the world to know oneself and others.

### The Invisible Hand

The invisible hand is Adam Smith's metaphor for the way individuals pursuing their own interests in a market can unintentionally promote outcomes that benefit society as a whole. Introduced in The Wealth of Nations, it holds that when people specialize and trade to their own advantage, the resulting coordination of prices and production tends to allocate resources efficiently without any central direction. The idea responds to the question of how order and mutual benefit can arise from self-interested action rather than deliberate design, though Smith himself hedged it with concern for justice and the moral limits of commerce.

- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 22 "Our Big, Fat, Greek Democracy" — Eric Bronson reads the brawling 1977-78 'Bronx Zoo' Yankees (Steinbrenner firing Billy Martin five times, Martin dragging Reggie Jackson off the field in Fenway, Jackson's dugout charge and defiant bunt) as an argument that dissent is good for democracy. Through Alexis de Tocqueville's warnings about majority conformity and democratic leveling (Nietzsche's herd mentality), he argues America needs gadflies like Socrates condemned by Athens for 'creating tension' and MLK's nonviolent troublemakers, while Adam Smith's invisible hand shows the Yankees' internal self-interest and conflict still produced championships, unlike the harmonious 1979 'We Are Family' Pirates. Dysfunctional discord, like free speech, keeps teams and democracies from going stagnant.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 38 "20b" — A paired political-philosophy debate over Alex Rodriguez's $252 million contract. Albert Duncan defends the salary as the just outcome of market forces: stars like Bonds, McGwire, and Sosa maximize fan satisfaction, pack stadiums (600,000 extra Cardinals tickets in 1998), and generate hundreds of millions for local economies. Joel Shuman, a self-described socialist, replies with Alasdair MacIntyre's notion of baseball as a 'practice' whose intrinsic goods belong to a traditioned community of players, coaches, and fans: when market ideology alienates fans, unbalances competition, and prices out small markets, money has stopped serving the human activity it was meant to be part of.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 20 "Knowledge and Nihilism Science and Monty Python’s The Meaning of Life" — Croskery tours the social institutions that promise guidance for a good life, pairing each with a Python work: Adam Smith's invisible hand and Bentham's greatest-happiness utilitarianism fail in the 'Merchant Banker' sketch, where charity leaves the banker 'a pound down on the whole deal', while Marxist market ideology and alienation surface in the Communist Quiz and the accountant who longs to be a lion tamer. In The Holy Grail, Aristotle's doctrine of the mean sorts Brave Sir Robin's cowardly flight from Sir Lancelot's rash slaughter of a wedding party and Galahad's desire-distorted chastity at Castle Anthrax, with Bedevere's duck-weighing witch logic showing reasoning without judgment, and Arthur's quest collapses because 'strange women lying in ponds handing out swords is no basis for a system of government'. Life of Brian's 'blessed are the cheesemakers' and the 'You're all individuals!' crowd ground a Kantian demand for autonomy against blind obedience to religious rules. The Meaning of Life's 'Galaxy Song' and 'spiraling coils of self-replicating DNA' pose Nietzschean nihilism — science dissolving the highest values — which the film's closing advice to be nice to people and keep a sense of humor answers with a modest, livable meaning.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 9 "Need that Cash to Feed that Jones" — Steven Gimbel and Brendan Cushing-Daniels argue that the Dead's parking-lot economy — tie-dye shirts priced at ten, twelve, or fifteen dollars, veggie burritos, dueling bootlegs — realized Adam Smith's classical picture of capitalism, not the corporate capitalism Marx attacked.
