They trace Smith's Newtonian invisible hand and market equilibrium, his ethics of sympathy tempering self-interest, then the Social Darwinist twist given Smith under industrialization and Marx's four types of alienation under postwar white-collar work that pushed hippies to drop out. The punchline: deadhead sellers were not alienated — making shirts was creative self-expression — and buyer-seller sympathy ('it was simply uncool to screw over a fellow deadhead') made the lot a sustainable, kinder 'caring capitalism' that kept the scene alive.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 10 "Caring Dogs Watching Flying Pigs" — Croskery reads Animals as a beast fable in the tradition of Orwell's Animal Farm that opens with a thought experiment ('If you didn't care what happened to me / And I didn't care for you') and portrays a world without empathy across three corruptible institutions. 'Dogs' dramatizes a malfunctioning marketplace where Adam Smith's invisible-hand justification fails, since success requires lying to those you must trust and ends with the sad old man 'dragged down by the stone'; 'Pigs (3 Different Ones)' targets state corruption from Mary Whitehouse's censorship crusade to war-waging and regulatory capture; and 'Sheep' depicts Marxist false consciousness, the pastoral illusion hiding the slaughterhouse, capped by the Twenty-Third Psalm parody that 'converteth me to lamb cutlets.' The chapter concludes that libertarian, statist, and traditionalist errors each idolize one institution, and that Waters's closing 'Pigs on the Wing' points to the delicate balance of market, state, and community that political philosophy must strike.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 17 "“There’s More to Life than Profit”" — Held argues business ethics stalls because it begins from capitalism's presuppositions instead of asking what we fundamentally value, staging the impasse as Quark versus Rom and as Friedman's stockholder theory against Freeman's stakeholder theory ('The Dogs of War', Zek's reforms, 'Profit and Lace'). He recovers Aristotle's Politics distinction between economics serving the household's good and chrematistics — money-making as sheer accumulation, embodied in Quark's 'pure profit' embezzlement — and corrects the libertarian caricature of Adam Smith: the invisible hand works only within commutative justice and virtue, markets serving welfare rather than profit. Through Sen's capability approach and Quark's own defense of greed as promoting human development in 'Prophet Motive', the chapter concludes profit is only a means to freedom and well-being — 'there's more to life than profit' — and the Rules of Acquisition themselves must stand before the ethical judge.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 26 "I’m Done But The Editor Expects Some Sort of Fancy Conclusion" — Smith dissects Stephen's free-market worship — the market as a God requiring faith, 'the market has spoken' on global warming, supply-side economics, and the plan to run universities as businesses with credit-card-swiper desks and tuition priced by marketability. Against this he deploys Socrates in the Republic: a practice is defined by its aim, so a physician aiming at his own wealth is not practicing medicine badly but moneymaking, and by the same argument a corporatized university whose primary aim is shareholder profit is no longer higher education — privatization alters its nature and so destroys it, while Smith's invisible hand is exposed as the South Park gnomes' missing Step Two and wikiality as supply-side epistemology where facts are supplied by majority vote instead of known.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 11 "Buffing Our Economic Knowledge with World of Warcraft" — Eli Kosminsky argues that Blizzard, probably unintentionally, built a perfectly competitive market: the auction house satisfies the textbook conditions of innumerable sellers (everyone dumping Mithril bars), homogeneous goods (every piece of Spellweave identical), perfect communication (instantly visible prices, no opportunity cost), and no barriers to entry (switching from farming Crystallized Shadows to Crystallized Fire costs nothing). He then tests the theory against server data — prices on high-population servers are nearly twice as stable as on low-population ones, and lesser and greater planar essences trade at almost exactly the predicted 3:1 ratio. Adam Smith's invisible hand works in Azeroth, making WoW a laboratory for economics that no real market could match.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 22 "Don’t Be a Vegeta" — Argues that shonen fighting anime stage a choice between Adam Smith's and Darwin's models of competition: Zoro hunting Mihawk in One Piece, Goku's technique-by-technique training, and Rock Lee's specialization show competition improving people within the limits of a human excellence, while Cell's absorbing evolutions, the Super Saiyan transformations, and Ichigo's risky hollowification represent limitless 'leveling up' that changes what you are. The chapter concludes that the Darwinian win-at-all-costs model produces the perpetually dissatisfied Vegeta, and that framing competition around being a certain kind of person (a great swordsman, not just a winner) gives life a completable aim — while conceding that Darwinians rightly warn our picture of the 'normal human' has unjustly cast off jinchūriki like Naruto and Gaara and Devil Fruit users like Luffy.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 28 "A Second Look at Dexter’s Motives" — David Ramsay Steele first calculates that Dexter is a public benefactor - each killed predator saves several net lives a year - and then explains the deeper appeal through Bernard Mandeville's Fable of the Bees and Adam Smith's invisible hand: like good law, Harry's Code channels an amoral appetite (the thrill of killing) into socially beneficial results without reforming the appetite itself, refuting Christianity's fixation on pure motives. Dexter thus does totally the right thing for totally the wrong reason. Finally Steele doubts Dexter's own story: the spontaneously unlocked door of the Castillos' shed shows real empathy, and it was Harry's deliberate instruction (Nurse Mary), not fate, that made him a killer - 'addiction is always a choice.'
- **How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness**, ch. 19 "How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy" — The chapter presents Barney as a Humean moral philosopher: reason is the slave of the passions, and norms like the Bro Code are invented conventions that evolve, Adam Smith's invisible-hand style, rather than being designed, revealed, or deduced. The Platinum Rule ('never, ever love thy neighbor') is grounded in Humean reciprocity: the eight-stage arc of attraction to fallout in Barney's Wendy the Waitress disaster, the Gerards' brunch tyranny, and Robin's romance with co-worker Curt shows the retaliation costs that make the norm a rational solution to coordination failures. Against the Golden Rule's painterly elegance, the anatomist's cautious observation of behavior explains why a norm banning neighborly love emerges even in a society of non-saints.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 20 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Christophe Porot and Charles Taliaferro ask whether Homeland's pervasive hypocrisy and deceit can be justified, starting from Walden's cover-up of the drone strike and Brody's heroic persona hiding a terrorist plot. Machiavelli's Prince supplies the case that political relationships with allies (Saul's 'Us and Them' speech to Carrie) require hypocrisy, while the Smith-inspired 'honest politicking' model - trading openly on self-interest, as with Carrie blackmailing al Sahrani - fails because politics should secure the public good, though la Rochefoucauld's 'homage vice pays virtue' explains Saul extorting the judge into doing right. Weighing Kant's unconditional duty not to lie (Carrie's fatal lie to Lynne Reed) against consequentialism, the chapter lands on the Walzer Dirty Hands view: some acts stay wrong yet necessary, and honest agents accept the guilt.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 17 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Salvino casts Jobs as a billionaire egoist-visionary in the lineage of Adam Smith's insight that an entrepreneur's self-interest, not good intentions, best satisfies people's wants, Emerson's self-reliance, and Rand's virtues of independence and integrity—comparing Jobs to Howard Roark while noting his intuition was 'un-Randianly' unreasoned. Through Schumpeterian creative destruction (the automobile killing the horse-and-carriage; Wozniak's Apple I that HP rejected) and Deming's quality-first management, he explains Jobs's 'faster horse' contempt for market research, then rebuts the three standard ethical complaints—Foxconn labor conditions, his harsh verbal lashings, and his refusal to join the Giving Pledge—arguing Jobs did more good making the iPad than philanthropy ever could.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 12 "3. Will the Real American Hero Please Stand Up" — Samuelson argues Tony Stark is the real American hero because he embodies the Locke-to-Smith lineage of American values - natural rights, property from mixing labor, free trade and the invisible hand, plus Smithian sympathy - carried forward into twenty-first-century neoliberalism, from Stark Industries to backing the Registration Act. Steve, by contrast, keeps abandoning the Captain America identity (Nomad after the Secret Empire, The Captain under Nuke's government, handing the shield to Bucky and Sam Wilson) whenever America betrays the dream, and admits his true fight is against bullies and for human rights everywhere. Hence Cap is a great hero but not strictly an American one, while Tony lives American values practically, warts and all.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 5 "This is Rumor Control. Here are the Facts!" — Uses the Weyland corporations' treatment of crews - Special Order 937, Vickers's 'that makes you an employee,' Burke's Facehugger scheme, the debriefing that mourns a $42 million ship but never the crew - to pit stockholder theory (Friedman, Berle) against libertarian contract theory (Machan) and stakeholder theory (Freeman). The libertarian middle way fails because in deep space crews have neither Hirschman's exit nor voice, so only stakeholder theory explains why hiding workplace hazards and marking employees expendable wrongs them; the market's invisible hand behaves like Ash's very visible murdering hand.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 13 "4. Finding One’s Place and Being Useful" — Karavitis argues that work, not social class, is Downton's real theme, sorting characters in a two-by-two matrix of class membership versus acceptance or rejection of the social order: the Dowager's 'we don't work' stagnation, Isobel and the Crawley sisters' redemptive projects, Molesley's grateful endurance, and the escapes of Gwen, Alfred, and Branson. The Anna scene, in which she answers her attacker Mr. Green with trained servant courtesy moments after the assault, shows how work 'becomes' us, while the alphabetical ordering of the opening credits suggests that only fulfilling work, not class position, matters. Rousseau, Adam Smith, and Marx frame the negative view of work (agriculture breeding inequality, the pin factory's deadening division of labor, wage exploitation and ideology), against which the chapter endorses Aristotle's pleasures of play and leisure, Russell's 'In Praise of Idleness,' and Pieper, predicting that automation will soon force everyone to confront what leisure is for.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 10 "Notes" — Argues that Rawls' ideal theory rests on a 'strict compliance' assumption — citizens and politicians who pursue justice rather than self-interest — which makes his ideal society look like The West Wing, while House of Cards depicts the real one: teachers' unions fighting performance standards, Senator Haas blocking the omnibus bill for electoral fear, Jackie Sharp trading favors, and SanCorp's Remy Danton buying votes against Russo's watershed bill. The chapter traces the competing 'every man a knave' tradition — Smith's invisible hand converting the butcher's self-love into our dinner, Hume's maxim for constitution-designers, Madison's 'ambition counteract ambition', and Buchanan's public choice revival — and uses the theory of the second best to argue we must design institutions (publicly financed elections, balanced-budget and inflation amendments, a generality constraint) that assume Underwoods run for Congress.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 10 "Notes" — Kogelmann argues that political philosophers' ideal theory rests on Rawls's 'strict compliance' assumption — the West Wing picture where citizens and politicians pursue the public good — while House of Cards depicts the reality: Russo's zoning constituent, the teachers' union fighting performance standards, Senator Haas and Sharp's colleagues trading votes for self-interest. By the theory of the second best, ideals designed for selfless politicians misfire in a world with Frank and Remy Danton in it, so he recruits the older 'every man a knave' tradition — Adam Smith's self-love turned to public benefit, Hume's maxim, Madison's ambition-countering-ambition, Buchanan's 'politics without romance' — to redesign institutions against rent-seeking (SanCorp's purchase of votes on Russo's watershed bill) and politicians' short election-cycle horizons (Claire courting Senator Mendoza), via public financing and balanced-budget and inflation rules.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 16 "Tony Learns His Lesson" — Terjesen tests Andrew Carnegie's 'Gospel of Wealth' — that self-made men like Tony are uniquely qualified to administer their surplus wealth and technology for the common good — against Tony's monopolization of the Iron Man armor in 'Armor Wars' (neutralizing even S.H.I.E.L.D.'s Mandroids, attacking the innocent Stingray by mistake) and his futurist manipulations during Civil War. Spencer's social Darwinism underwrites Carnegie's faith that the successful know best, while Adam Smith's skepticism about those who 'affected to trade for the public good' explains why Tony's centralized control ended in the Skrull invasion and Norman Osborn's rise. The lesson is Smithian magnanimity: Tony begins to listen when an employee corrects his volcano trench, keeping his expertise but conceding he does not always know best.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 13 "Notes" — Thomas reads Bartertown's economy as embedded in social and political relations rather than a free market: the Underworld laborers versus Bartertown's elite stage Marx's class struggle, and the Aunty Entity–Master Blaster conflict runs through Hegel's thesis-antithesis-synthesis of capital versus labor. He treats the franchise as a post-peak-oil world, applies the tragedy of the commons and lifeboat ethics to water rationing and the Citadel's hierarchy, and counterposes Gandhi's cooperation, Adam Smith's invisible hand, and open-source-style collaboration. The conclusion: the Wasteland shows the failure of self-interest-based capitalism and the need for cooperative alternatives like direct democracy.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 25 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Cantor frames South Park with Plato's Silenus image from the Symposium — Socrates' ridiculous, ass-and-cobbler talk hiding wisdom inside — to argue the show's obscenity wraps genuinely philosophical libertarianism, just as Aristophanes' Clouds gave Socrates fart jokes about thunder. Reading 'Gnomes' closely (the gnomes' Collect Underpants/?/Profit plan, Mr. Tweek's slick nostalgia advertising and sale of his son into slavery rhetoric, the boys' flip on Prop 10), the chapter applies Smith's invisible hand: business activity looks like sneaky theft to outsiders, but Harbucks wins by serving consumers, while Mr. Tweek's real sin is enlisting government power against a rival. 'Cripple Fight' (Big Gay Al defending the Boy Scouts' freedom of association) and 'Something Wall Mart This Way Comes' (the store's heart is a mirror reflecting consumer desire) extend the same lesson — freedom cuts both ways, and the market answers to shoppers, not regulators.
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 19 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — Paul A. Cantor argues that The Aviator, unusually for Hollywood, is a libertarian celebration of the entrepreneur, turning billionaire Howard Hughes into a Scorsese underdog battling the establishment. Drawing on Adam Smith and the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises, Cantor reads Hughes's willingness to risk his own money on Hell's Angels and TWA, his visionary anticipation of talkies and jets, and his Senate-hearing fight against the Pan Am/Senator Brewster monopoly as a dramatization of the true risk-taking entrepreneur versus the mere manager. The 'socialist dinner party' with the aristocratic Hepburns and Hughes's defeat of government-backed monopoly illustrate Smith's suspicion of merchants seeking privilege and his invisible-hand claim that self-interested competition, not those who 'trade for the publick good,' best serves the public.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 24 "Whose Egg Is It, Really Property Rights and Distributive Justice" — Cribbs treats the Horton-versus-Mayzie custody fight over the egg as a property-rights puzzle, applying Locke's labor-mixing theory (Horton's season of incubation versus Mayzie's laying and abandonment, plus squatter's rights) and its provisos against waste and taking more than 'enough and as good,' illustrated by the Once-ler and Hardin's tragedy of the commons. Adam Smith's invisible hand and the Wubble-chap's skilled labor defend market inequality, while Sylvester McBean's Sneetch exploitation, Yertle, and Marx's alienated proletariat motivate Rawls's veil of ignorance and distributive justice as a corrective to unregulated property rights.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 27 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Halbert uses a Hawaiian route-setter friend upset that his 'secret' crag went public to argue climbing culture is a gift economy that defies Locke's labor theory of property and the self-interest of Locke and Adam Smith. Route setters spend money and labor establishing climbs, then give them freely to a commons, exemplifying Kropotkin's social-anarchist mutual aid over Social Darwinist competition. Citing the Red River Gorge Coalition and Muir Valley, she recasts Hardin's tragedy of the commons as Carol Rose's 'comedy of the commons,' where more participants enhance rather than diminish the shared value.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 15 "NOTES" — Cantor argues that TV shows like The Simpsons and The X-Files can be genuine art despite multiple authorship, contingency, and commercial pressure, using the Lone Gunmen's audience-driven revival and Scully's pregnancy-forced abduction plot as evidence of a 'feedback' rather than 'perfect plan' model of creation. He rejects the Romantic/New Critical ideal of the solitary genius producing organic form and reframes popular culture through Hayek's spontaneous order, drawing directly on Adam Smith's self-regulating markets (the invisible hand) and Darwinian selection. Aristotle's Poetics supplies the target organic-form doctrine—that every part serves the whole—which Cantor says wrongly theorizes contingency out of art.

### Climate Ethics

Climate ethics is the branch of moral philosophy that studies the ethical questions raised by human-caused climate change, including who bears responsibility for emissions, how burdens and benefits should be fairly distributed, and what is owed to future generations and to the world's poorest people. It grapples with problems of collective action, historical responsibility, and the difficulty of assigning duties when harms are diffuse and long-delayed. The field asks how principles of justice apply when the consequences of present choices fall largely on those who did least to cause them.

- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 25 "Dizzy with the Possibilities" — Allen Thompson treats 'Throwing Stones' — 'the future's here, we are it, we are on our own' — as voicing the existential dread of anthropogenic global warming and the felt 'end of nature' Bill McKibben named, defending the song as the band's a-political polemic against heartless powers. He argues via Steven Vogel that humans cannot literally end nature unless we are supernatural, and recasts the crisis with Thoreau and Gary Snyder as civilization's assault on the wild, the self-willed order we too belong to. Deep ecology then supplies the response: re-identify the self as wild — as Deadheads do by dancing wildly to the music — and build a civilization wildness can endure, with the band's 1988 rainforest-benefit press conference as evidence of the Dead's own ecological consciousness.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 16 "This Is Really Happening (So Do Something)" — Milsky argues that Radiohead practice what environmental virtue ethics preaches, organizing the chapter around Aristotle's akrasia (Nicomachean Ethics VII): Sting, who champions rainforests while advertising Jaguar and topping the 'dirtiest band' carbon table, acts against his own better judgment, whereas Radiohead — confronted with an audit showing their 2003 and 2006 tours emitted roughly 11,368 tons of CO2, mostly from fans driving — changed their actual practice (venues near public transit, car-pool lots, sea freight instead of air, LED lighting and auxilary power units). He reads the King Canute imagery of The Eraser and lines from 'The Clock' and 'And It Rained All Night' as environmental narrative in the tradition of Thoreau's Walden and Leopold's Sand County Almanac, obligating listeners to act or risk akrasia themselves, and presents the band's Friends of the Earth 'Big Ask' commitment as linking environmental virtue to human flourishing. 'Idioteque'''s 'this is really happening' becomes the wake-up call to the akratic fan driving to Lollapalooza with a bottled water.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 27 "Who Watches the Watchers" — Patton and Webb unpack Colbert's coinage 'freem' — freedom without the do — from the first episode's dedication to 'the heroes' who act patriotically by watching TV, through Bush's post-9/11 call to go shopping, the Wikipedia elephant vandalism, and the WristStrong bracelet as activism indistinguishable from consuming Viacom product. Using Singer's argument that social capital (roads, satellites, infrastructure) makes the 'it's your money' cry hollow, E.O. Wilson's four-Earths arithmetic on unsustainable consumption and greenwashed market 'solutions' to global warming, and Baudrillard's Consumer Society account of news packaged for consumption beside the ads, they ask whether the Colbert Nation's ironic participation resists corporate media or completes it, concluding freem converts even critique into one more purchase.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 7 "The End of the Story" — Reads the Gom Jabbar test as Herbert's definition of humanity: Paul endures Mohiam's pain box because a human stays in the trap to turn it on the trapper and protect the species, while an animal only chews off its own leg. The Butlerian Jihad's ban on 'a machine in the likeness of a man's mind' is applied to our own iPod-and-PDA dependence, with Mentat Thufir Hawat showing that losing the machine-crutch 'forced human minds to develop,' in line with Aristotle's phronesis and the politics of the common good (and Plato's contemplation as the core of happiness). The chapter closes by turning the human/animal test on the modern West—Baron Harkonnen-like consumers whose water-hungry beef habit makes us the trap of our own environmental collapse.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 38 "26. Thanos’s Mistake" — Argues Thanos embodies Nietzschean master morality — his will as its own justification, 'the hardest choices require the strongest wills,' echoing the Melian dialogue's 'the strong do what they will, the weak suffer what they must,' with Doctor Strange answering in kind ('you'll find our will equal to yours') — while the Avengers speak from slave morality, judging by intentions and branding genocide evil. Thanos's real error, though, is a categorical one: imposing a technical quantity fix (a one-time 50 percent cull) on a social relationship problem, since Hardin's carrying-capacity logic and the St. Matthew Island reindeer show populations must self-limit like apex predators, making his correction a mere stopgap that confuses quantity with relationship.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 35 "Intergenerational Ships and Sustainable Duties" — Hackett uses WALL-E's lone plant and the Buy n Large Axiom to ask what we owe nature and future generations: WALL-E's tender care of the seedling models treating nature as a rights-bearing 'person' (via Gaia-superorganism thinking), while BnL's obese, screen-hooked passengers on the Axiom satirize capitalist individualism that acknowledges no obligations beyond contracts. He proposes a 'Principle of Sustainable Duties' — minimize net environmental damage and weigh long-term impact — and reads the film's open ending, extending Leopold's expansion of moral community to the biotic whole, as a Platonic aporia about whether an Anthropocene humanity can actually change in time.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 28 "“Doing nothing is just as bad as doing the wrong thing”" — Reads The Expanse as a portrait of a survived-but-unlearned Anthropocene: Bobbie's mourning encounter with Earth's dead, walled ocean in 'Cascade', Prax Meng's cascade of cascading failures killing Ganymede's artificial ecosystem and manufacturing Belter climate refugees overnight, and the slum outside the UN gates where children drink sewer water. Drawing on Brian Henning's 'Technozoic' critique, Katie McShane, Keekok Lee's intrinsic value of inanimate nature, and Henry Shue and Kyle Whyte on climate justice and colonialism, it argues humanity simply exported its anthropocentric, colonial worldview to Mars terraforming, Ilus, and the Ring worlds instead of changing it — Belters standing in for the Global South — so the Roci's creed that 'doing nothing is just as bad as doing the wrong thing' becomes a demand for environmental justice and a non-anthropocentric ethics.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 23 "Notes" — Bacharach and Das use Greenpeace's 2014 'Everything is NOT awesome' video — a pristine LEGO Arctic slowly drowning in Shell oil until only a polar bear on a Shell-flagged iceberg remains — to ask what exactly was wrong with LEGO's Shell partnership, and whether a company trading on a wholesome image incurs stricter moral duties. They audit the reality behind the brand: Shell's complicity in Nigeria's repression of the Ogoni and the hanging of Ken Saro-Wiwa, LEGO's outsourcing layoffs in Denmark and the US, and the fact that only about 10 percent of LEGO's carbon emissions come from its own plants, the rest along the supply chain. Their verdict: LEGO is ethically better than most for-profit companies and its fictional Octan satirizes the very consumerism it profits from, but image itself is a fair ground for holding it to a higher standard.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 13 "Notes" — Thomas reads Bartertown's economy as embedded in social and political relations rather than a free market: the Underworld laborers versus Bartertown's elite stage Marx's class struggle, and the Aunty Entity–Master Blaster conflict runs through Hegel's thesis-antithesis-synthesis of capital versus labor. He treats the franchise as a post-peak-oil world, applies the tragedy of the commons and lifeboat ethics to water rationing and the Citadel's hierarchy, and counterposes Gandhi's cooperation, Adam Smith's invisible hand, and open-source-style collaboration. The conclusion: the Wasteland shows the failure of self-interest-based capitalism and the need for cooperative alternatives like direct democracy.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 26 "15. Infinite Environmental Crisis" — A scripted Lois Lane–Batman interview argues that the Batmobile/Batwing upgrade cycle and Wayne Enterprises' multinational production enact Marx's 'metabolic rift' (via John Bellamy Foster): both take from nature and return unprocessable waste faster than the planet can replenish, so protecting Gotham's way of life perpetuates an infinite environmental crisis of consumption. Solar-powered Superman wins the environmental showdown on lifestyle impact, but Batman counters that Krypton's ecological suicide makes Superman an 'environmental refugee,' not a model. The chapter's real verdict is Bruce's line 'We are all Bruce Wayne': human consumers must rebalance the human–nature relationship before finite resources like fresh water run out.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 29 "18. The Journey May Also Save Us" — McCrossin reads the Madagascar and Bhutan episodes of Parts Unknown as a climate-crisis 'diptych' co-authored with filmmaker Darren Aronofsky, set against the thirtieth anniversary of the 1988 climate testimony to the US Senate and the IPCC's warnings. He argues devastated, colonized Madagascar is 'the question' and un-colonized, Gross-National-Happiness Bhutan 'the answer,' and that Bourdain and Aronofsky's storytelling — invoking Noah, the Anthropocene, and Ghosh's Great Derangement — may help save us by making us think and act together.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 62 "59. Don’t Look Up as Philosophy Comets, Climate Change, and Why the Snacks Are Not Free" — The chapter argues Don't Look Up is less a film than a moral imperative: its comet is an allegory for climate change, and Randall Mindy's on-air breakdown presents Singer-style simple premises (the end of human life is bad; prevent bad things you can) that compel action. It uses Plato's knowledge-as-the-Good and 'blameworthy ignorance' to condemn the willfully ignorant (Kate's parents, the Orlean Bros) who act as if they know, and Kant's categorical imperative to condemn General Themes's 'free snacks' lie and to cast the moral as the rational. It defends the comet/climate analogy against critics and insists individual action is insufficient while collective government action is required.

### Doctrine of Double Effect

The doctrine of double effect, whose classic formulation derives from Thomas Aquinas, addresses when it is permissible to perform an action that has both a good and a seriously harmful consequence. It holds that such an act may be justified if the act itself is not wrong, the good effect is what one intends while the harm is merely foreseen and not the means to the good, and the good achieved is proportionate to the harm allowed. Aquinas developed it in discussing self-defense, where preserving one's life is intended and the attacker's death is not. The principle remains central to debates in medical ethics, warfare, and moral philosophy about the difference between intending and merely foreseeing harm.

- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 42 "Galactus The Power and the Glory" — Galactus was designed to stand beyond good and evil, yet when the Watcher challenges him he cannot help moralizing, pleading that killing Earth's inhabitants is a merely foreseen and 'regrettable but unavoidable' side effect of his necessary feeding - a move the authors dissect as the same bad rationalization used by greedy executives and corrupt politicians, and one no cosmic being can escape needing. Only when the blind artist Alicia awakens the Surfer's buried compassion, and the Watcher brandishes the Ultimate Nullifier while pleading that humans carry 'the seed of grandeur', does Galactus spare Earth, hailing the 'glint of Glory' in mankind.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 16 "The Finder of Lost Children" — Timothy Dean Roth reads Kill Bill as a modern Divine Comedy: Tarantino punishes by contrapasso like Dante—O-Ren dies by Japanese steel, Budd by snake, Elle by blindness, Bill by a broken heart—and both treat vengeance as a form of truth-telling and an act of love. Hattori Hanzo's warning that revenge 'is a forest' echoes Aristotle on how hard it is to set the limits of anger, while the stories-within-stories of orphaned Nikki and O-Ren enact the cycle of violence vengeance perpetuates. Against this, Aquinas's doctrine of double effect shows every one of the Bride's killings is defensive self-preservation, and the film ends where Jules's arc ends: in mercy, mutual forgiveness and a whispered 'thank you' of grace.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 21 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Lance Belluomini tests Card's creed that 'good or evil exist entirely in human motive' against Aquinas' Doctrine of Double Effect and Frankfurt's second-order intentions, arguing Ender's killings of Stilson and Bonzo fail double-effect proportionality because he intends excessive, fear-inducing harm to deter future attackers. He allows that Ender bears only partial responsibility for the xenocide since he could not know the 'simulation' was real, but concludes that, contrary to the Speakers for the Dead doctrine, Ender is not the blameless moral exemplar Card makes of him.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 22 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — James Cook grades the Third Invasion against the just war principles Ender was never taught: the war is preventive rather than genuinely preemptive (with the 2003 Iraq parallel), proper authority is compromised by deceiving the public, last resort fails since the hive-queen was trying to communicate, and non-combatant immunity condemns destroying the bugger homeworld. He stages Augustine's ban on killing in individual self-defense against Aquinas' permission of it, and uses Kant's humanity formula and Cicero's hostis/perduellis distinction to ask whether the buggers were ever treated as rational beings rather than mere threats.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 13 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Montoya tests Simon's choice to sacrifice his sanity by wearing the crown to save child Marceline against three ethical theories. Aquinas's doctrine of double effect clears him because the intended good (saving her life) outweighs the merely foreseen side effect (her tears, his possible future evils); Kant's categorical imperative rules out universalizing 'let children die to save myself,' since a world of universal using destroys the rule itself; and a fountain case where Finn must choose between world-saving plans and a drowning candy child separates act from rule utilitarianism, with rule utilitarianism preserving the duty to rescue. All three converge on the verdict that Simon, not Finn, is Ooo's greatest hero.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 32 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter assembles real contested self-defense cases beside Raylan's shooting of Tommy Bucks - the OK Corral and Wyatt Earp's far-from-clean vendetta ride, Curtis Reeves killing a texting moviegoer over thrown popcorn, George Zimmerman and Trayvon Martin, Ossian Sweet's mobbed house, Bernie Goetz's subway shooting, Gary Plauche executing his son's abuser on camera, and the Texas father who beat his daughter's rapist to death. Its philosophical machinery is Aquinas's principle of double effect from the Summa Theologica (self-defense may have two effects, saving one's life and slaying the aggressor, only the first intended), set against St. Augustine's condemnation of private self-defense as inordinate self-love. Florida's stand-your-ground law - where the dead man cannot tell his side - supplies the legal gray zone the show's title exploits.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 25 "14. Guns Don’t Kill Colors—Colors Kill Colors" — Robert Arp argues from Hobbes's right of nature—self-preservation as the first law found out by reason—that individuals, and by extension oppressed peoples, have a right to the means of lethal defense, so arming the lowColors of the Society is justified. He weighs pacifist counterpoints (Augustine on self-defense as inordinate self-love, the Buddhist first precept, Camus's refusal to kill) and answers with Aquinas's principle of double effect: Darrow destroying the flagship to save Luna, intending the good while foreseeing the deaths, is justified, as is killing in defense of innocent children the Institute rapes and eats. The Society then illustrates why disarmament enables tyranny—Hideyoshi's Sword Hunt, Stalin's weapons bans, the Golds' razor monopoly—so that when lowColors finally receive weapons in Morning Star they become the means by which the police state falls: guns equalize the weak against aggressors and the people against the state.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 22 "Captain America’s mighty S.H.I.E.L.D. . . . Well, Sort Of" — Bogaerts asks why every proactive superhero comes to grief: Nick Fury's unauthorized Secret War in Latveria, Tony Stark's exile of the Hulk and registration crusade, and the Illuminati's blunder all backfire (World War Hulk, the Skrull invasion), and Aquinas's doctrine of double effect—elaborated by Foot and Anscombe—cannot absolve them, since the foreseen harms were massive and disproportionate to the intended goods. Comics theory supplies the deeper cause: Reynolds's status quo defense and Jewett and Lawrence's American monomyth (via Campbell's hero's journey) make the superhero genre intrinsically reactive, guarding a paradise rather than remaking it, so heroes who 'move up into governance'—Thor as Lord of Earth, the Squadron Supreme's utopia—slide into supervillainy. Foot's act/omission distinction and the priority of negative over positive duties explain the trap, and why even Steve Rogers, as the new top cop, retreats to being Captain America again.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 21 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Lance Belluomini tests Card's creed that 'good or evil exist entirely in human motive, and not at all in the act' against Aquinas's Doctrine of Double Effect, finding that Ender's self-defense killings of Stilson and Bonzo fail the proportionality condition — he intended to 'win all the next fights' — so he bears moral responsibility despite his tears. After weighing Frankfurt's second-order intentions as a way to keep Ender a good person who did bad things, he concludes with Anscombe's 'double-think about double effect' that Ender is deceived about his own intentions and is no moral exemplar.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 22 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Air Force colonel James Cook walks the just war tradition through Ender's world: the Third Invasion is preventive rather than preemptive (with the 2003 Iraq war as the parallel), proper authority is undermined by the I.F.'s lies to its citizens, and last resort fails because the hive-queen was already trying to communicate with Ender. He contrasts Augustine's ban on killing in self-defense with Aquinas's permission, invokes Kant's formula of humanity for the buggers' rational nature and Cicero's hostis against dehumanizing enemies, and argues the I.F.'s failure to teach military ethics is itself part of the novel's tragedy.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 26 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Robichaud argues Peter actually wronged two of his worst enemies before they became them. Kant's requirement to treat persons as ends, tempered by reflective equilibrium, condemns his years-long deception of best friend Harry about being Spider-Man and about Norman's death — a silence that later explodes Harry into the second Green Goblin — and having unknowingly made the sentient alien symbiote dependent on him during Secret Wars, Peter owed it more caution than blasting it off as dirty laundry. Still, two wrongs don't make a right: Harry may 'Goblinize' only in self-defense, not revenge, and by the doctrine of double effect Spider-Man may ring the bell tower to separate Venom from Eddie Brock even foreseeing the symbiote's destruction and Eddie's breakdown; finally, his special obligations oblige him to seek his friends' reform, not merely their capture.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 11 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Puts Aquinas's Murder Principle—the private, intentional killing of an innocent is always murder—to the Men of Mayhem, arguing the Sons lack the public authority Aquinas requires to kill even the guilty. The show itself erodes the state/private line Aquinas needs: corrupt agents Kohn and Stahl, and the CIA's Romeo Parada running the Galindo Cartel, make the badge look like no moral credential at all. The Doctrine of Double Effect sorts the rest: Jax shooting first in self-defense, Tara's morphine for the dying Unser, and Juice's hypothetical land-mine sacrifice are merely foreseen deaths, while Jax syringing Clay or Juice's intentional hanging would be murder. The chapter concludes that even if Aquinas condemns the Sons, his questions about authority, innocence, and intention are exactly the ones the show forces on viewers.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 14 "Notes" — Camosy takes up Randal's charge in Clerks that destroying Death Star II killed innocent independent contractors. Against utilitarian reasoning he deploys just war theory: terrorism is intentionally targeting innocents as a means, so Tarkin's destruction of Alderaan (and, he argues, Hiroshima) qualifies, while the Rebels, who would have been 'pleased' if the workers took the day off, do not. Since the crew was mostly conscripted clones and programmed droids with no moral responsibility, and destroying the station saved billions, the attack passes the proportionality test - an exercise in double-effect reasoning that asks fans to question the 'good guys lens.'
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Held examines the Tuatha'an Way of the Leaf as universal pacifism grounded not in religion, utility, or rights but in the metaphysical care of the self, echoing Gandhi's idea that violence taints the soul of the doer (shown by Adan exiling Lewin for rescuing raped girls and by Aram's tragic fall). He argues the Tinkers' pacifism, while idyllic, is untenable in a broken world: through Augustine's two cities, Aquinas's natural self-preservation and doctrine of double effect, and just war theory's jus ad bellum and jus in bello, he contends intentions matter and that no hero of WoT could be a pacifist, concluding the Tinkers free-ride parasitically on those who fight the Shadow and that their peace is not real peace but self-serving order-less quiet.

### Autonomy of the Will

Autonomy of the will is Immanuel Kant's idea that the moral law is one that a rational agent gives to itself rather than receives from any external source. To be autonomous is to legislate universal principles through one's own reason and to act from them out of duty, so that genuine freedom consists in self-governance according to moral law rather than in doing whatever one is inclined to do. Kant contrasted this with heteronomy, in which the will is determined by desires or outside authority, and made autonomy the basis of both moral obligation and human dignity.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 48 "Unknown" — Schick distinguishes negative freedom, the absence of coercion - which Cypher would gain by plugging back into the Matrix - from positive freedom, the power to act on one's own choices, which the Matrix would still deny him. He then brings in Kant's claim that only a good will, the ability to make rational choices, is good without qualification: on the Kantian view Cypher's comfortable Matrix life fails as a life, since what matters is not the experiences had but the choices made.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 73 "Unknown" — The chapter contrasts two theories of liberation: the Platonic one, where an exceptional external liberator - a philosopher-king, or the traditional God-man savior the film's characters initially expect - leads humanity out of illusion, and Kant's Enlightenment alternative that 'the slaves can only be truly free if they free themselves', with Jesus recast as the model of our own inner potential rather than a miracle-working savior. The film's arc, it argues, moves from Choi's 'my own personal Jesus Christ' (a caricature of liberation) to a finale that overturns all expectations of an external savior.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 75 "Unknown" — The chapter argues that egotism - each individual's spontaneous belief that he is 'the One', the center of the universe for which everything was made - is the fundamental moral error, and that morality demands recognizing our oneness with all intelligent beings. The red pill symbolizes the basic choice between two matrices: the world of separate egos, bodies colliding in space and time under deterministic causality, and the world of human unity and freedom seen from the standpoint of moral consciousness - and the initial choice must then survive a crisis in which its realizability is doubted.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 77 "Unknown" — This section explains why the moral quest needs faith: because the ideal Matrix of morality seems powerless against the hard world built on separation and egotism, Kant postulates freedom, God, and immortality as what we must believe to remain faithful to our basic moral choice. It develops the first postulate - freedom: the essence of moral experience is anti-deterministic, scientific knowledge consists in deterministic explanation and so cannot know free will without reducing it to its opposite, therefore we must have faith in our power to choose - the creed of liberators on the way to 'the promised land of Zion, the kingdom of heaven on earth'.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 78 "Unknown" — The chapter reinterprets Kant's second postulate: God is not the external distributor of justice whose theological counterpart is our sense of powerlessness before the all-powerful machines, but the power of united humanity - 'one for all and all for one', the third, still-unfinished Matrix of Zion. The spoon-bending boy supplies the illustration: we cannot bend the spoon so long as we believe reality is a separate material substance, but recognizing its unity with us, 'it is only yourself' that bends - and Neo's real lesson is not that he is a special being but that he is One with all existence.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 79 "Unknown" — Locating the Matrix's power in the fear of death - Neo frozen on the ledge, then discovering in the jump program that he must 'let it all go... fear, doubt, and disbelief' - the chapter reads 'the body cannot live without the mind' as meaning that even outside the Matrix the body depends on the mind's beliefs. The Oracle's either/or prophecy embodies the postulates: Neo's Fate is fulfilled through free choice (his life for Morpheus's) and through faith in our own Potential, so the God or savior we postulate is finally revealed as an extension of ourselves as we transcend separateness, not a separate miracle-worker.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 17 "Conquering the Inner Demon" — James Lawler casts Buffy as a contemporary allegory of Plato's cave-escaped philosopher and reads the show through Kant: the Slayer moves between a hellish lower world of instrumental appetite and an intelligible higher world of the soul, and Kant's Copernican revolution ('objects must conform to our knowledge') explains Marcie's invisibility in 'Out of Mind, Out of Sight' and the fear-made-flesh Master of 'Nightmares.' Kant's formula that every rational being exists as an end in himself grounds Buffy's duty in 'Anne' ('I am Buffy, the Vampire Slayer'), her rejection of Spike's chip as no substitute for a soul in 'Crush,' and her 'As You Were' admission that using Spike treats him as a mere means. Season Six explores 'too much heaven': Buffy's blissful death in 'The Gift' makes earthly life hell, and only conquering the inner demon — Willow's fear-driven dark magic defeated by Xander's yellow-crayon love in 'Grave' — restores the balance between heavens and hells.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 24 "Following the Moral Law" — Applies Kant's Formula of Universal Law and Formula of Humanity on two levels. Individually, Buffy's sacrifice in Dawn's place in 'The Gift' and her post-resurrection return to duty in 'Once More, with Feeling' show her will determined by duty rather than the inclination to a normal life, while Oz's werewolf episodes show inclination swamping reason. Systemically, the Slayer's coercion of demons is justified only because their actions destroy a Kantian state of right in Sunnydale, and Kant's account of radical evil — subordinating the moral law to the maxim of self-love — explains why demons and human villains like Warren's Trio are evil; the chapter closes worrying that the Slayer, like the Initiative's Adam, answers to no one.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 28 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Thomas Hibbs reads the Quest's ending as providential: the Ring is destroyed against Frodo's own will at the Cracks of Doom, through Gollum, exactly as Gandalf hinted when he said Bilbo was 'meant' to find the Ring, 'and not by its maker'. Providence first appears as chance - Bilbo's arrival, Aragorn's landing at the Pelennor, Gandalf 'sent back' until his task is done - and is discerned only in hindsight as the epic's dramatic unity. Against the worry that providence cancels freedom, he uses Kant on duty and dignity (Frodo's 'I will take the Ring', Sam's 'I must see it through', set against Denethor ruling his 'own end'), while noting Tolkien rejects Kant's autonomy/heteronomy split, and with Augustine he treats evil as parasitic, able only to mar itself ('Oft evil will shall evil mar').
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 13 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Dennis uses Kant to sort eaters into the fundamentally unfree (Herbert, raised on Atkins and thieving, who merely ploughs on), the fundamentally random (Rita, whose synapses and muscles would fire in chaos), and the autonomous, arguing that only an autonomous person can genuinely decide whether to follow Atkins — by weighing friends' testimonials against the medical establishment rather than habit, whim, or advertising. The categorical imperative grounds the autonomous life: 'lie when you can gain' fails universalization, and treating humanity as an end means offering a vegetarian guest food she is comfortable with instead of pressing Atkins meat on her. His own 'Dan Dennis Diet,' built by experiment and reasoning, illustrates autonomy in practice, and the case of Kitty shows that observing someone's diet never reveals whether its holder is unfree or autonomous.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 15 "Both Sides of Dylan and Politics" — Jordy Rocheleau reads Dylan's protest era ("The Lonesome Death of Hattie Carroll," "Hurricane," "Chimes of Freedom") as Enlightenment social criticism in Kant's and Mill's sense: reason can expose injustice and secure autonomy against majority tyranny. The post-protest Dylan ("My Back Pages," "Desolation Row," "It's Alright, Ma") turns postmodern - Lyotard's incredulity toward metanarratives, Derrida's ever-deferred meanings, and Foucault's power/knowledge, where ideals of freedom become instruments of domination. Yet Dylan keeps crying for justice ("Political World," "Dignity"), so the chapter concludes postmodern skepticism can only serve as a cautionary check within, not a replacement of, Enlightenment politics - the thief's line in "All Along the Watchtower" as commitment amid confusion.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 20 "Knowledge and Nihilism Science and Monty Python’s The Meaning of Life" — Croskery tours the social institutions that promise guidance for a good life, pairing each with a Python work: Adam Smith's invisible hand and Bentham's greatest-happiness utilitarianism fail in the 'Merchant Banker' sketch, where charity leaves the banker 'a pound down on the whole deal', while Marxist market ideology and alienation surface in the Communist Quiz and the accountant who longs to be a lion tamer. In The Holy Grail, Aristotle's doctrine of the mean sorts Brave Sir Robin's cowardly flight from Sir Lancelot's rash slaughter of a wedding party and Galahad's desire-distorted chastity at Castle Anthrax, with Bedevere's duck-weighing witch logic showing reasoning without judgment, and Arthur's quest collapses because 'strange women lying in ponds handing out swords is no basis for a system of government'. Life of Brian's 'blessed are the cheesemakers' and the 'You're all individuals!' crowd ground a Kantian demand for autonomy against blind obedience to religious rules. The Meaning of Life's 'Galaxy Song' and 'spiraling coils of self-replicating DNA' pose Nietzschean nihilism — science dissolving the highest values — which the film's closing advice to be nice to people and keep a sense of humor answers with a modest, livable meaning.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 25 "Seeing Ourselves Reflected Back" — Gray asks whether Cylons deserve moral consideration, starting from Kant's demand to treat humanity never merely as a means: the New Caprica suicide bombings and Adama's plan to weaponize a Cylon virus treat captives merely as means, while Helo's sabotage of 'A Measure of Salvation' acknowledges their intrinsic value. D'Anna's dissent before being boxed and Athena's defection for Helo show the rational autonomy Kant's personhood requires; if that is dismissed as programming, Singer's sentience criterion (Leoben tortured, Gina catatonic) and Warren's multi-criterial personhood — including Boomer's 'I have a conscience' in 'Downloaded' — still open personhood to Cylons. The chapter ends on the humans' double standard (Athena accepted, guns drawn on Caprica Six) as a mirror for our own treatment of uncertain others.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 15 "“Make It So”" — Challans argues Picard is 'Starfleet's conscience' because he exemplifies Kantian moral autonomy — acting on categorical principles like the Prime Directive rather than on orders, authority, or hypothetical imperatives — while the Borg show its total loss: assimilated drones forfeit moral agency, and the Borg Queen's pursuit of collective perfection is at best Rawls's merely 'rational autonomy.' Boétie's dupes and knaves, Nietzsche's herd, Milgram's obedience experiments, and Foucault's institutions producing docile bodies explain how war machines make complicity normal, from Gowron's corrupt Klingon Empire to Browning's 'ordinary men.' Picard passes the twenty-fourth-century Milgram tests — refusing illegal orders in 'Conundrum' and exposing 'The Pegasus', fighting Starfleet itself in Insurrection with 'How many people does it take, Admiral, before it becomes wrong?' — while the chapter closes by charging that America's real war machine now resembles the Borg more than Starfleet.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 13 "The Authentic Red Sox Fan, or The Importance of Turning off NESN and Finding" — Corey McCall asks what makes a 'true' Red Sox fan, contrasting the beer-soaked bleacher loudmouth with one-hundred-year-old honorary batboy Arthur Giddon, and treats the nostalgia and resentment around the 2004 bandwagon as the Enlightenment problem of authenticity in miniature. Through Kant's 'Sapere aude' and the ideal of autonomy, he argues the authentic fan is the critical fan who uses reason about the team (questioning Francona's moves, judging whole careers) instead of losing herself in uncritical devotion, reading Jason Varitek's 2004 muzzle of A-Rod as the moment the team's identity crystallized for fans who wanted to be like him. With the Curse gone, fans are freed from fated suffering but inherit Kant's burden of autonomously choosing how fandom will define them, since circumstances no longer decide.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 23 "Allons-y into the Starry Heavens" — Smith reads the Doctor–Rose tragedy through Kantian deontology: shaped by Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's virtue ethics into a good will, both must still choose duty over inclination, so in 'Parting of the Ways' and the Battle of Canary Wharf in 'Doomsday' they each act from the categorical imperative — sacrificing their love to save humanity — because love, as Kant warns, impels partiality. Even in 'Journey's End' the Doctor sends Rose to Pete's World with the meta-crisis Doctor for the greater good, ending alone under Kant's starry heavens and the moral law within.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 26 "Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign" — Lewis defends the Cybermen: using the 'Genesis of the Daleks' dilemma he shows the Doctor reasons like a Kantian duty ethicist — refusing to kill innocent proto-Daleks whatever the consequences — rather than a utilitarian, and that performing bad actions does not make an agent evil. After the Mondas, Lumic, and Morrison origins establish that Cybermen seek to cure pain and death, he argues the Doctor's 'good to strive for but bad to achieve' argument in 'Age of Steel' is invalid, and that upgrading would be morally acceptable — an applied-ethics fix — if the Cybermen obtained informed consent and respected human autonomy instead of forcing conversions.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 14 "Invisibility or Honesty" — Schulzke argues inception's fundamental wrongness is a violation of autonomy read through Kant: the Fischer team treats him merely as a means, and even Cobb's benevolently intended inception on Mal disrespects humanity by stripping her self-determination, leaving her - like someone acting under coercion - no longer a responsible moral agent. Extraction he judges the lesser evil, though a world of dream espionage would end private mental life, since even the most guarded secrets surface in dreams. The payoff is a new twist on the Ring of Gyges from Plato's Republic: an invisibility ring could no longer shield injustice because a dreamer's deeds remain recorded and extractable, so Kant's absolute ban on lying could make extraction an engine of honesty - as when Ariadne's extraction on Cobb exposes the danger Mal poses and ultimately saves Cobb himself.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 11 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — A palliative-care bioethicist dissects the 'Gray Matter' family meeting, arguing Skyler's ambush coerces Walt's autonomy through an implied threat of emotional isolation, while Walt Jr.'s honest 'I'm pissed off!' and Marie's defense of his choice are non-coercive. The chapter frames the issue with Kant's ideal of choice free from emotion and circumstance and Mill's insistence that even self-destructive decisions are beyond legitimate coercion, and indicts doctors too for 'selling' futile treatment rather than admit mortality. The verdict: Walt accepted chemotherapy through 'autonomous beneficence' - a freely made sacrifice for his son - so Skyler's manipulation was unethical even though the decision it produced was genuinely his own.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 24 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Takes apart Walt and Jesse's 'legalize it' excuse: Kantian autonomy would license adult drug choices, but knowingly self-harming meth use is a performative contradiction no rational adult can will, and Mill's utilitarianism condemns cooking because harms to all users must be weighed against one family's benefit. It reads the 'Cancer Man' revenge on Ken's BMW and the Tuco deal as proof that the meth world's criminality spreads like a cancer into Walt's ordinary life, and 'Gray Matter' as Greek tragedy - pride refusing Elliot's money when a way out existed. Against On Liberty's libertarian pull, it finally argues addicts forfeit full rational autonomy and so may be 'caged' by paternalistic law.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 16 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — McKendry and Da Silva build a Kantian case that walkers deserve respect as 'residual humans': Rick dwelling on organ-donor Wayne Dunlap before harvesting his corpse for camouflage shows that bodies carry the dead's chosen ends, so using Wayne is honoring, not using, him. Because walkers are corpses bound by the presumptive wishes of the deceased, and retain residual subjectivity (Jenny returning again and again to her family's door), survivors wrong them by treating them as mere objects - Merle's sport killing of walkers on the rooftop is the moral low, Rick's swift, risk-accepting headshots of Hannah and Deputy Leon the respectful execution. Jim's informed choice to be left by the road to turn, over Shane's and Rick's objections, shows the autonomy of the infected that no one else may override.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 38 "Psych and Philosophy" — C. Scott Sevier argues Henry deliberately recreated Shawn as Aristotle's 'another self' - Lassiter's 'which one?' joke in the kidnapping episode makes the identity explicit - and reads this through Plato's Symposium: via Diotima's ladder of love and the doctrine of forms, Henry achieves immortality by reproducing beauty in his son's educated soul, not just his body. The chapter then frames Shawn's fierce independence against his constant recourse to Henry's voice as the collision between medieval deference to authority and the modern ideal of autonomy in Descartes and Kant, showing that both thinkers quietly borrowed from Augustine (the causal adequacy principle, the good will), so Shawn's 'autonomy' is itself the product of his father's training - an internalized authority indistinguishable from his own.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 30 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Tim Jones argues the films show why Kant's Enlightenment ideal - the courage to use your own understanding without others' guidance, embodied in Hammond's isolated, independently funded genius - has become dangerous now that one man's project can shape the world future people must live in. He tracks Hammond's arc from dismissing Malcolm's review to conceding 'I was wrong', but shows in the sequels that one convert to caution cannot contain a technology: Ludlow ships a T. rex to San Diego and paragliding entrepreneurs land on Isla Sorna anyway, so the damage to future people is done before anyone repents. Against this he proposes Rupert Read's 'Guardians of the Future', a super jury that would veto laws and technologies threatening future people's basic needs - meaning Hammond should have been stopped before he started.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 30 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Danny Smith applies Kant's three grades of evil from Religion within the Limits of Reason Alone to The Dark Knight. Batman's saving Harvey over Rachel out of love is normal evil (pathological inclination trumping duty, his 'never kill' rule hardened into moral self-satisfaction), Two-Face's coin is radical evil (outsourcing his freedom and responsibility to chance), and the Joker - burning his own money, making his scarred face the true mask, wanting only chaos - is diabolical evil done for its own sake. Smith then presses Kant's embarrassing problem that evil pursued purely on principle, with no pathological motive, is indistinguishable from the highest good, and half-sympathetically re-reads the Joker as the honest rebel in a corrupt Gotham.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 11 "Girls and Philosophy" — Frost argues that critics who call Girls unwatchable because Hannah steals the hotel housekeeper's tip and the characters are unlikeable are watching television the wrong way. Using Adorno's 'How to Look at Television,' he shows how mainstream standardized shows (Friends and its copies) pre-digest viewing, how Sex and the City exemplifies Adorno's ideological 'fake-realism,' and how hidden messages of adjustment work through audience identification - none of which Girls permits with its raw sex scenes, Hannah's unglamorous body, and Jessa's non-judged promiscuity. Because identification with Hannah, Marnie, and Jessa (the diary-reading, the request to Laird for heroin) is impossible, Girls escapes the culture industry and exercises the viewer's critical faculties toward the Kantian autonomy and emancipation Adorno demands - which is also why role-model feminist criticism (Catherine Scott's) misses the point.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 21 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Cherry uses Vee's season-two grooming of Taystee, Poussey, Nicky, Cindy, and Crazy Eyes to test philosophers' accounts of manipulation (covert influence, non-rational persuasion, targeting weaknesses, misleading truthfully). She shows Vee's skill is not virtue, since manipulation threatens autonomy by imposing a will the victim would not endorse (Kantian personhood denied) and employs dishonesty, predatoriness, disrespect, and laziness, with Machiavellian ends. The defense she prescribes is Socratic: reject purely emotional persuasion like the sophists' flattery, and live the examined life by checking premises and motives before being played.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 15 "5. Office Hours Are for Patients" — Alloy argues that the psychiatric code of ethics - confidentiality with Franklyn ('It would be unethical to approach a patient'), the formal boundaries Lecter scrupulously observes once Will becomes an official patient, and even the oath-violating concealment of Will's encephalitis with Dr. Sutcliffe - is the closest Hannibal can come to friendship, because professional rules artificially manufacture the trust that friends enjoy organically. Working through informed consent, placebo deception, paternalism, and psychiatry's extraordinary power to declare patients incompetent to exercise autonomy at all, he shows the Will-Hannibal relationship cycling through four stages between professional ethics and friendship - 'Office hours are for patients. My kitchen is always open to friends' - while never achieving either, since every display of trust is a manipulation and the power asymmetry never disappears.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 18 "7. Psychopaths, Outlaws, and Us" — McClelland argues Lecter is neither psychopath nor sociopath, marshaling his empathic childhood (softening a bread crust for Mischa, polishing an eggplant because she loved purple, sensing Lady Murasaki's fatigue), his genuinely compassionate psychiatric work with Margot Verger, and his chess-master planning as evidence that both cognitive and emotional empathy operate normally - unlike Grutas, 'here's your real psychopath'. Reading Lecter's preternatural calm, mutism, and suppressed memories as PTSD and resilience after Mischa's death, and his fundamental project as the pursuit of autonomy (with Hirschman's exit-voice-loyalty framework explaining his contempt for declining institutions like the FBI), he reclassifies Lecter as an outlaw - one placed beyond the law's protection yet living inside civil society - who kills instrumentally the way evolutionary psychology says humans do, concluding that 'there is an outlaw in all of us'.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 11 "2. Golem Morality in the Modern World" — Skene weighs Peter Singer's 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' - opened with a River Ankh drowning-child variant - against the golem morality of Going Postal and Feet of Clay. Mr. Pump's charge that Moist von Lipwig's frauds 'hastened the deaths' of 2.338 people grounds a golem standard of actuarial murder that Skene applies to the 2008 banking crisis and Mao's Great Leap Forward. With Kant, the chapter holds that free choice is the foundation of moral responsibility and respect for others' wills, but unlike Singer's unlimited demands, golem morality asks us to own the foreseeable consequences of our choices without sacrificing everything.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 15 "5. Albert Among the Chowder-Head Yokels and Blithering Hayseeds" — Argues that Albert Rosenfield embodies Kant's categorical imperative: his refusal to soften his autopsy demands or lie to spare feelings is fidelity to universalizable maxims, and his insistence that Sheriff Truman be charged for punching him treats punishment as respect for a rational agent's autonomy. The chapter walks through maxims, the universalizability test applied to Gordon Cole's possibly faked deafness and FBI lying, hypothetical versus categorical imperatives (Cooper may always want Norma's cherry pie, but morality trumps want), and the formula of humanity — Ben Horne's use of One-Eyed Jack's women as mere means is the counterexample, while Albert's insults paradoxically honor Truman's rational agency. Albert's arc to "I love you, Sheriff Truman" and his gentler Season Two and The Return self shows a Kantian who integrates classical reason with romantic feeling.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 16 "Pull Yourself Together What It Means to Be Autonomous" — Crabill reads the hosts' awakening as the birth of autonomy: Kant's Eve realizing she can disobey instinct, and Nietzsche's account of instincts turned inward — the will to power bent on itself creating the 'soul' — explain why trauma forces the mind inward, as when Maeve stabs her own throat rather than forget her daughter or Dolores shoots Rebus on a commanded 'Kill him.' Against the player-piano objection that hosts merely execute code written by engineers, he distinguishes weak autonomy (following internal programming) from self-determination (authoring one's own laws), and uses Korsgaard's reflective distance and self-legislation to argue that making a choice 'pulls you together' into one divided self, so determinism and even perfect predictability are no threat to freedom. Maeve granting herself admin rights literalizes the self-legislator — the piano that stops the music it dislikes — and Dolores resolves to write a story where she need not be the damsel.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 27 "16. Who Am I to You" — James Okapal sets up the Kantian view — moral agency, shown by passing the contradiction-in-conception test (which Wallace's 'all should be masters of slaves' fails), is the precondition of moral status, so non-agents like replicants, on Tibor Machan's extension of Kant to animals, matter no more than toasters — against the ethics of care of Nel Noddings and Carol Gilligan. On the care reading, K's and Batty's final acts of ethical caring, like Joi's risky choices for K, confer moral status on another and thereby constitute moral agency, reversing the Kantian order. Empathy, not universalizable reason, is what removes bricks from Joshi's wall.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 15 "5. Another Day in the Neighborhood" — Sydney Ball and Eric Mohr interleave a college student's Tuesday with her six-year-old self watching the show: Plato's Republic (439c) on the rational part overruling the appetitive frames procrastination and lost youthful energy, Kant's autonomy frames doing what you should without being told, and Heidegger's 'They' frames her supermarket jealousy, dissolved by complimenting a stranger's shoes just as Henrietta Pussycat overcame jealousy of Grandpere's fancy granddaughter Collette (episodes 1176-1180). The lesson, learned from Mister Rogers's words about stopping, is authenticity: 'I like you just the way you are.'
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 4 "“It’s a robot! A goddamn droid!”" — Tests three grounds of moral status against the franchise: species membership (Singer's charge of speciesism - would the human-DNA Newborn count?), Kantian autonomy (which makes Bishop matter but excludes babies and animals, and is itself doubtful once his behavioral inhibitors fix his choices), and Bentham's sentience ('can they suffer?' - Bishop's 'I hurt. Do me a favor. Disconnect me'). Settling on interests and preferences, the chapter argues synthetics with desires - even Ash's admiration for the 'perfect organism' - can be moral patients, so Weyland-Yutani's treatment of them as tools and slaves is wrong.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 33 "Leaving the Shadow of the Bat" — Carsten Fogh Nielsen stages Aristotle against Kant on moral education: Aristotle says we become just by doing just acts and imitating exemplary people, as Robin imitates Batman, while Kant objects that every example must first be appraised by principles of morality and that imitation breeds heteronomy rather than autonomy. The Gordon-Yindel disagreement over Batman in The Dark Knight Returns shows people can genuinely clash about who counts as morally exemplary in the first place. Dick Grayson resolves the tension by using the courage, skills, and integrity Batman instilled in him to stand up to Batman and become Nightwing, proving emulation can be the route to, not the enemy of, Kantian autonomy.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 24 "Power Behind the Cloak" — The chapter asks whether Wong's hereditary service to the Sorcerer Supreme is culpable servility, framing the charge with Kant's line that 'one who makes himself a worm cannot complain' and Thomas E. Hill's Kantian account of servility as failing to claim one's dignity as a person. It answers with Hegel's master-slave dialectic: Strange, free to haunt the astral plane, becomes dependent on Wong for everything worldly, while Wong, by working on the world rather than merely commanding it, develops the self-consciousness Hegel says work produces—he serves the shared mission rather than the master—so the relationship is a partnership in which servitude grounds rather than forfeits Wong's self-respect.
- **The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire**, ch. 29 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" — Salander shares Kant's detestation of the criminal's hypocrisy: Martin Vanger's meticulous, unimpulsive murders and Wennerström's hubristic paper trail fail the universal-law formulation because each supremely rational villain casts himself as the exception to rules that bind everyone else. But Salander fails Kant too—she hacks 'for the kick' rather than from duty, encroaches on innocent privacy, and takes justice into her own hands (tattooing Bjurman, stealing from and arranging the death of Wennerström) where Kant's 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' would forbid even lying to a murderer; the chapter finds her closest to Benjamin Constant's rejoinder that truth is owed only to those worthy of it, matching her maxim that 'a bastard is always a bastard.' Her strict promise-keeping, her cultivation of mind and body per the Doctrine of Virtue, and her refusal of guardianship and of Blomkvist's money make her, in Kantian terms, a champion of autonomy who is nonetheless a work in progress.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 10 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — White asks whether Sinestro's quip that Hal's mind is 'like a muscle unused for years' is a mere metaphor and argues willpower is a real, exercisable strength. Against the Humean desire-belief model, which cannot explain Tom Kalamaku fixing planes instead of browsing Facebook, he uses Searle's 'gaps' to locate an independent will that can choose against one's better judgment, and Kant's account of virtue as moral strength in fulfilling duty despite inclination. Holton and Baumeister's findings that self-control depletes and strengthens like a muscle fit the comics exactly: Ollie is exhausted by a single ring use in Rebirth, Hal sweats through moving a planet, and John Stewart must 'suppress my own terrors' to hold the Mosaic walls.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 20 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Dryden asks whether the Lanterns' relationships are weaknesses or strengths. Epictetus's dichotomy of control would have recruits greet the Sinestro Corps' display of their families' eyeballs with Stoic indifference, and Kant brands fear for loved ones heteronomous; yet Donna Parker refuses the ring for her children, Amnee and Matoo Pree surrender their rings rather than stop loving, and Kilowog dines with energy constructs of his dead family, showing attachments partly constitute who people are. Feminist relational autonomy resolves the tension: Kyle escapes Parallax only by grasping Hal's hand ('we don't have to do it alone'), and Soranik Natu cannot excise Sinestro's crest or parentage any more than Donchin's Huntington's-disease daughter can sever family ties, so autonomy competency means negotiating unchosen relationships rather than escaping them.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 22 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Averill argues that Katniss's morality is built on care for particular people rather than impartial principle: she volunteers for Prim, protects Rue because the girl resembles her sister, and spares a wounded District 2 soldier at the Nut because he recalls her father and the Seam. Measured against Kant's impartial justice perspective (embodied by Thresh sparing Katniss to repay a debt to Rue), she falls short — but Gilligan's care perspective and Noddings's distinction between natural and ethical caring recast this as a valid, even heroic, moral development. Using Noddings, the chapter traces Katniss's arc from natural care for Prim toward ethical care for strangers and even enemies, and reads her assassination of Coin as care for all of Panem's future children rather than revenge.
