Care, the chapter concludes, can even justify violence when it protects the vulnerable.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 5 "Who’s Putting Ideas in Your Head" — The book's introduction frames Inception as the newest chapter in the dream-skepticism tradition: Plato's question about how we explain our perceptions of reality and Descartes's point that we can never be sure we are not dreaming, with the twist that Descartes never doubted our thoughts are our own while the film contests exactly that. It previews the volume's rival readings — the single-dream theory of the airline flight, Brophy's claim that the shared dreams are server-based electronic worlds like Second Life, and neuroscience suggesting we act on thoughts before we are aware of them. It also stakes out the ethics: inception as a violation of autonomy akin to propaganda, advertising or brainwashing, and the diagnosis that Inception is fundamentally a tale from the business world of corporations.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 14 "Invisibility or Honesty" — Schulzke argues inception is a categorical violation of Kantian autonomy: the Fischer job treats him merely as a means (Saito's market share, Cobb's reunion with his children), and even Cobb's benevolent inception on Mal disrespects humanity by robbing her of self-determination, leaving her unable to act as a responsible moral agent testable against the categorical imperative. Extraction, by contrast, attacks privacy rather than autonomy, and the chapter uses Glaucon's Ring of Gyges to show that dream espionage would defeat even perfect invisibility, since an extractor could always read your deeds in your dreams. The twist, played off Kant's absolute condemnation of lying, is that the standing threat of extraction might be the only force that could make universal honesty practicable — hence the title's choice between invisibility and honesty, illustrated by Ariadne's life-saving extraction on Cobb.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 15 "Notes" — Chelstrom uses the progression from guided DUPLO builds to free design to argue that autonomy develops in degrees and is relational rather than purely individualist. Kant's self-thinking agent — for whom precepts and formulas are the 'ball and chain' of immaturity — explains Emmet's dependence on Octan's instruction booklets and Lord Business's profit from deference, and Korsgaard's definition frames the individualist autonomy the Master Builders embody. Yet their lone-wolf autonomy fails, and Sartre's look plus Beauvoir's account of woman forced to assume herself as Other explain Wyldstyle/Lucy's deference to others' expectations; Catriona Mackenzie's relational autonomy recasts 'Everything is Awesome' as peers supporting each other's self-development, with Emmet's friendship letting Lucy accept herself.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 13 "The Office and Philosophy" — Reads Tim Canterbury of the UK Wernham-Hogg as an autonomous moral agent who nonetheless cannot act on his own judgments: Kant's categorical imperative is applied to Tim's stapler-through-the-window prank (universalizing the maxim of disposing of disputed objects passes the test, so Tim is in the clear), before the chapter diagnoses the office's pointlessness with Durkheim, Fromm and Merton's notion of anomie - David Brent's management produces moral lawlessness and boredom. Tim's dice speech, his swallowed resignation and accepted promotion, and his last-second failed dash to Dawn in the finale show a weak-willed conscience: he knows what he should do but lacks the conviction, making him the moral conscience of the show without being its moral hero.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 27 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Defends South Park's anti-paternalism on both consequentialist and deontological grounds. 'Major Boobage' shows the futility of Gerald's cat ban meant to stop kids 'cheesing' — Kenny still gets high and Gerald himself relapses — while 'Medicinal Fried Chicken' shows how the KFC prohibition births a violent black market, with Cartman's $85 snack pushing him into the Colonel's Scarface-style drug war. On the deontological side, Mill's 'over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign', Locke's self-ownership, and Kantian respect for rational agents (via Nozick's inviolability, and the authors' autarchy-versus-autonomy distinction) ground the claim that coercion is wrong even when benevolent: 'Butt Out' has Kyle and Stan tell Rob Reiner that forcing others to quit smoking is fascism, while Big Tobacco's Kevin Harris wins their approval simply by informing and letting people choose.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 17 "Notes" — Barbara Stock uses the Borg to analyze autonomy: Picard's 'they took everything I was' names the Collective's destruction of self-governance, while Hugh's choice to return to the crash site in 'I, Borg' displays the Kantian core of autonomy—acting on universalizable principle against inclination. She defends relational autonomy through Janeway's pleading with Kes in 'The Gift' and the Ferengi woman's internalized oppression, then combines it with Clark's extended cognition to ask whether the Borg Queen's 'I am the Collective' might make the Collective itself an autonomous agent. Finally she judges Janeway's forcible de-assimilation of Seven defensible only while Seven is non-autonomous, and her promise never to let Seven return ethically suspect.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 26 "Notes" — Uses the Zillo Beast arc, battle droids, mynocks, and Han shooting Greedo to test theories of moral status: Schweitzer-style reverence for life would forbid a Jedi from eating anything, genetic views breed Palpatine-style human chauvinism, Singer's sentience view makes droid suffering and Luke dropping the rancor's door morally troubling, and Kantian autonomy excludes cognitively impaired beings too harshly. The chapter weighs Palpatine as merely a 'sociopathic' goal-pursuer rather than a Kantian moral agent, and leaves the droid question open via the novel Children of the Jedi, where the droid-converted Nichos lacks even mere agency because he cannot override his programming.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 18 "Do Not Ask Him to Be Rational" — The Rochas argue the Jedi Council's conduct across the Temple-bombing arc — letting Tarkin take jurisdiction, then expelling Ahsoka and handing her over for trial on flimsy evidence in 'The Wrong Jedi' — exposes a Jedi ethics corrupted by deference to hierarchy. Ahsoka's decision to walk away enacts Kantian moral autonomy (self-legislation) against the Council's heteronomy, while Anakin, despite sharing her doubts, seeks another master in Palpatine and falls into heteronomy instead. Using Baier's account of trust and Iris Marion Young on social roles, they contend the Jedi's repudiation of feeling was the real failure: emotions like Ahsoka's fear rightly guided her to distrust the Council and even to trust Ventress.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 16 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — McKendry and Da Silva build a Kantian case from Rick's eulogy for Wayne the organ donor: walkers deserve respect both as corpses governed by the deceased's presumptive choices and as 'residual subjects' still executing past choices, like Jenny returning to her family's house. From zombie dignity they derive a duty to kill walkers respectfully—Rick's quick merciful headshots versus Merle's sport killing—and defend the group's respect for Jim's autonomous choice to be left by the road to turn. They even argue Rick and Glenn do not use Wayne as a mere means because his organ-donor choice set the end his body now serves.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 3 "The Ethics of Pretending to Be a Cowboy" — Don Fallis uses Westworld to work out definitions of pretense and deception, testing successive accounts (acting-as-if, Austin's intend-to-deceive, Langland-Hassan's believe-P-is-false) against cases like guests playing cowboys, Ford passing off Bernard as human, and Maeve and Hector pretending to be deactivated. He adopts a Cartesian evil-demon model of deception but rejects the claim that deception must manipulate perceived evidence, arguing Ford's direct implanting of Teddy's Wyatt backstory still counts. He concludes, citing Kant on autonomy and Walzer on foreseen collateral harm, that staff who intend to deceive the hosts and even guests who foreseeably contribute to it act wrongly, since deceived hosts suffer real harm to their agency.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 16 "Pull Yourself Together What It Means to Be Autonomous" — Joshua Crabill reads the hosts' awakening through Kant's story of Eve grasping autonomy and the etymology of autonomy as self-legislation, with Dolores swatting the fly and 'these violent delights' as her forbidden fruit. He uses Nietzsche's will-to-power turned inward to explain how the hosts' caged suffering builds an inner 'soul,' and Jaynes's bicameral commanding voice becoming one's own (Dolores hearing Arnold's voice turn into hers). Drawing on Korsgaard's reflective distance and Plato's divided soul, he distinguishes weak autonomy (following internal programming) from self-determination (authoring one's own law), arguing that Korsgaard's 'determinism is no threat to freedom' lets Maeve, gaining admin access and choosing her daughter, genuinely 'write my own story.'
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Johnson-Moxley tests Perez's lasso of truth - which makes people face truths about themselves, like being dragged from Plato's cave - against four ethical touchstones: Kantian duty (truth-telling as a perfect duty, respect for autonomy), utilitarianism, virtue ethics, and care ethics. Cases drive the argument: binding Ares so he sees his apocalypse annihilates what he rules, freeing Vanessa from Dr. Psycho's false memories only with her permission, and lashing two warlords into 'twins of pain' to end bloodshed. She concludes via Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity that compelling truth is justified only to restore someone's rational self-direction, never paternalistically, with Gandhi's satyagraha ('truth-force') as the model of active, compassionate truth-telling.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 18 "A Court Conversation" — Cast as a dialogue with an updated Kant at a tournament, the chapter applies Kant's aesthetics to spectating tennis: it distinguishes free from dependent beauty (a McEnroe drop volley or a Federer stroke judged against the game's history and rules), locates the sublime in a booming ace, a broken record, and the fan's disinterested enthusiasm, and defends aesthetic judgments as disinterested yet subjectively universal. It then turns Kant's ethics onto the court, arguing that calling a line honestly against your own interest has moral worth only when done autonomously, for its own sake, and that gamesmanship like faked injury timeouts seeks an unfair advantage and so is wrong even when within the rules.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 16 "The Duty of Reason Kantian Ethics in High Noon" — Evans argues that Marshal Will Kane in High Noon is Kant's ideal moral agent, acting from duty and a good will rather than from consequences. He shows the townsfolk, Kane's friends, Harvey Pell, Helen Ramirez, and Amy all reasoning consequentially or heteronomously (the mayor privileging the town's finances, Mildred lying about Sam per Kant's essay on the supposed right to lie), while Frank Miller's revenge is a maxim that cannot be universalized. Kane's maxim of standing against lawlessness regardless of cost satisfies all three formulations of the categorical imperative—universal law, humanity as an end, and autonomy—making him a member of the kingdom of ends and contrasting Kant with Mill's utilitarianism.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 23 "Allons-y into the Starry Heavens" — Donna Marie Smith uses the Doctor and Rose's separation in "Doomsday" and "Journey's End" to explicate Kantian deontology. After framing the Doctor's virtues via Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and distinguishing eros, philia, and agape (with Reinette illustrating chivalrous self-sacrifice), she argues that Kant's categorical imperative and the duty-versus-inclination conflict explain why the Doctor and Rose Kant be together: their love pulls toward partiality while duty to save humanity is what they ought to do, so acting for the greater good is precisely what forces their parting.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 26 "Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign" — Courtland Lewis argues the Cybermen are not evil but altruistic, distinguishing utilitarianism (right equals good consequences) from Kantian duty-ethics (right can diverge from good), using the Doctor's "Genesis of the Daleks" dilemma about killing a future dictator. He reads the Cybermen as "Cybertarians" who genuinely aim to cure human pain and death, and attacks the Doctor's "Age of Steel" argument that it is good to strive for but bad to achieve a pain-free deathless life. He proposes that Cybermen's real fault is violating autonomy through forced upgrades, and that respecting informed consent (a medical-ethics ad campaign) would make upgrading morally acceptable.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 16 "7. More Mothers, Lovers, and Other Monsters" — Brace surveys the later-season mother figures—Mary, Kelly, Jody, Rowena, Mrs. Butters, Charlie—arguing they are repeatedly used as emotional tools against the Winchesters, which she reads through Kant's warning against treating persons merely as means. She stresses loss of free will and agency: Mary's British Men of Letters 'realignment' and Mrs. Butters's coercive programming strip their autonomy and reduce them to objects/killers, while their reclaimed agency and self-sacrifice restore their Kantian standing as ends in themselves.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 26 "15. Morality and Manipulation" — Kahn frames the Foundation series around personal autonomy, using Mill's image of humans as a growing tree rather than a machine 'built after a model' to condemn both coercion and manipulation. He shows Hari Seldon as a paradoxical champion of autonomy who nonetheless deceives his own followers about the fraudulent Encyclopedia Galactica and secretly forecloses their freedom of action via the Seldon Plan and Second Foundation—echoing the Mule's mind-control of Han Pritcher. He reads Salvor Hardin's maxim ('never let your sense of morals prevent you from doing what is right') as consequentialism that maximizes galaxy-wide autonomy, contrasts it with the deontology exemplified by Gaia/Bliss (who refuse to manipulate Trevize) and critics like Toran Darell and Branno, and leaves the reader to judge as Bliss urges Pelorat to think for himself.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 27 "16. Psycho-historian or Psycho Historian" — Bellantoni asks what Seldon owes future generations, pitting moral presentism against his 'mystical' identification with humanity (echoing Scheffler's Why Worry about Future Generations?). She tests the Seldon Plan under Bentham's hedonic calculus—finding time-discounting and uncertainty about what follows the thirty-thousand-year interregnum undercut it—and under Kantian deontology, arguing Seldon's mass manipulation of Gaal Dornick, his inquisitors, and the Encyclopedists treats people merely as means and violates their autonomy. Weighing longtermism against Whitehead's claim (in Adventures of Ideas) that civilizations must die to seed new ones, she suggests Seldon's engineered revival of a spent civilization may itself be a barbaric imposition on future people who would not choose it.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 28 "17. Chef of the Future" — Cheong convenes the 'documentary-ethics panel' invited by Roadrunner director Morgan Neville over the AI deepfake of Bourdain's voice reading lines he never spoke. Using Beauchamp and Childress's principle of autonomy, the Midler v. Ford voice-impersonation case, and worries from AI ethicists and epistemologists (Fallis, Muller) that deepfakes threaten knowledge and trust, he argues the synthesized voice denies Bourdain the 'right of reply' and deceives viewers — then reveals he had ChatGPT ghost-write parts of the chapter to make the point.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 19 "Horton Hears You, Too! Seuss and Kant on Respecting Persons" — Kowalski reads Horton Hatches the Egg and Horton Hears a Who! through Kant's two formulations of the categorical imperative. Mayzie's lying promise to Horton fails the universal-law test just like Kant's lying-loan and tax-shirking (Jo-Jo) cases, while Horton's insistence that 'a person's a person, no matter how small' embodies the ends-in-themselves formula treating the Whos as ends with dignity, not things. The essay argues Horton's fidelity is heroic rather than strictly required, revising Kant's moral absolutism (the inquiring-murderer case) so that when duties conflict one should act to disrespect persons least.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 20 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Swindler argues the ideal of fatherhood is to engender autonomy – a blend of independence and interdependence – in one's children. Treating fatherhood as an abstract social role (compared to a baseball pitcher) constituted by collective intentions, he uses Kant's 'ought implies can' to link accountability to autonomy and his constitutive-vs-regulative rules (the promise to take his son fishing) to show fathers must teach children to reflect on the concept of a rule, not merely follow it, modeling self-governance rather than authoritarian control.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 29 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Carreras, writing as a son, examines the ethical tension in the father-son relationship between using a father's inevitable influence and fostering the son's autonomy. Opening with Aristotle on parents loving children as 'something of himself,' he uses the case of Jerry (a lawyer) pressuring his son Jose (who loves 18th-century English literature) to argue for a 'foundational view' of autonomy – that the best life is one embraced 'from the inside,' likened to seeing without a value-blindfold – and advises fathers to ask 'Is this what he truly wants, or what I want?'
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 30 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Morgan asks when it is wrong for fathers to impose their ideals on children, arguing that forcing activities (like violin practice) risks alienation because meaningful pursuits must be embraced 'from the inside.' Using Robert Noggle's Rawls-derived hierarchy of goods (basic, pre-primary, primary, secondary, specialized), he grants fathers may guide toward universal goods but rejects Noggle's claim that parents may impose a full religious worldview, favoring David Archard's weaker right to 'guide family life' while respecting the child's growing capacity to choose – permitting compelled practice of talents only in light of the child's emerging identity.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 25 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Heaps uses the loaded question a stranger asks a tattooed person ('aren't you afraid of being stuck with it?') to raise the freedom-versus-determinism problem, then rejects Kant's Critique of Practical Reason solution of an 'alternate nature' of rational autonomy because it quarantines free choice from the physical act of being inked. He argues instead for an 'embodied freedom' that rests on but is not determined by biology, illustrated by deciding, saving for, sitting through, and healing a tattoo. He closes with Socrates' 'know thyself' and 'the unexamined life is not worth living,' making self-examination the way to develop the effective willingness that real freedom requires.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 10 "The Justification of Torture-Horror Retribution and Sadism in Saw, Hostel, and The Devil's Rejects" — Jeremy Morris analyzes torture-horror through two questions: is the torture justified, and is the audience's enjoyment justified? He reads Saw's Jigsaw traps, Seven, and Last House on the Left as explorations of Kantian retributivism and lex talionis, where punishing the autonomous wrongdoer respects his autonomy. For purely sadistic films like Hostel, The Devil's Rejects, and Texas Chainsaw Massacre, he argues (via Humean sentimentalism against Kantian rationalism) that Cook's or Otis and Baby's infectious glee makes the torturer's delight the source of horror. A fully empathetic viewer can share both the victim's suffering and the torturer's joy without endorsing torture, so the genre is not immoral 'torture-porn.'
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 11 "9. The Handmaid’s Tale as Philosophy Autonomy and Reproductive Freedom" — Robison-Greene argues that Gilead's core wrong is denying women autonomy, reducing them from Kantian moral agents to moral patients — walking incubators. She uses Frankfurt's theory of personhood (second-order desires and volitions about what we care about) to show how Gilead dismantles a woman's will by restricting first-order options, language, and critical thinking, so Offred's Scrabble tiles and forbidden reading become acts of reclaimed autonomy. She situates the Sons of Jacob's 'feminine function' ideology in Plato's Republic classes, Aristotle's natural slaves and History of Animals, Aquinas's natural-law subordination of women, and Malebranche's brain-fiber claims, contrasting Beauvoir's complicity of women and framing forced reproduction as the deontology-versus-consequentialism clash over whether species survival could ever justify treating women as mere means.

### The Ethics of Ambiguity

The Ethics of Ambiguity is Simone de Beauvoir's attempt to build a moral philosophy on existentialist foundations, taking seriously the claim that human beings have no fixed essence and must create meaning through their choices. She argues that freedom is the source of all value, but because we are always situated among others whose freedom matters as much as our own, genuine freedom requires willing the liberation of others rather than treating them as means. The ambiguity of the title names the human condition itself—we are at once free consciousness and bound flesh, subject and object—and ethics consists in embracing that tension rather than fleeing it into bad faith.

- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 20 "“Howzat!” Prometheus Is a Fast Bowler" — Decker argues the Doctor's morality resists formula — his motives are private, his timey-wimey perspective complicates consequentialist calculation, and the 'Genesis of the Daleks' child hypothetical breaks rule theories like Kant's and Mill's — so he reads it as an 'ethics of ambiguity' fusing Romanticism (Shelley's imagination, the infinite glimpsed in cups of tea and small beautiful events, Romantic-Gothic divided consciousness) with Sartrean existentialism. Via Sartre's WWII student, bad faith, and Beauvoir's 'adventurer' contrasted with the sub-man and the serious man, he casts the Doctor as a Gallifreyan Prometheus whose gifts of freedom are both dreadful and delightful.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 26 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Robison-Greene applies Beauvoir to the show's women. Powerful men are the One and women (like Chalky's community under the Klan) are made the inessential Other, and Beauvoir's apparatus - bad faith, the 'appeal' free beings must make to one another, and the happiness that lets women be complicit in their own oppression - frames Lucy, Gillian, and Margaret. Lucy happily performs the role her men write for her, Gillian is so consumed by the fact of her rape that even her apparent freedom keeps her the object of male desire ('just the loneliest person on earth'), while Margaret - Temperance Leaguer, advocate for women's reproductive health, and finally the woman who shuts the door on Nucky's cash - comes closest to making the appeal and to freedom.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 23 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Babette Babich traces the shifting 'you' of 'Hallelujah' and 'Suzanne' through Hegelian thesis-antithesis-synthesis and Empedocles's cycle of Love and Strife, reading the songs' ambiguity (David, Samson, the bound champion) as Cohen's sovereign having-it-both-ways. Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity frames the human condition of being what one is not, while Nietzsche - on broken promises, on women and distance, on the Antichrist - supplies both the critique of Cohen's courtly projections onto the feminine Other and the model of singularizing solitude. 'Who by Fire' is read against the Rosh Hashanah prayer Unetanneh Tokef as a song of fate, judgment, and atonement whose closing 'who shall I say is calling?' is quasi-Augustinian and Heideggerian: death singularizes each 'who' at the moment of its claim.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 24 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Walker contrasts Pennsatucky's Christian fundamentalism with Piper's secular humanism (Kurtz's six features) in their 'Fool Me Once' confrontation. With no God, Sartre's existence precedes essence makes Piper condemned to create her own meaning: owning her crime to her mother and confessing the Pennsatucky prank, while Red and Vee play Sartre's cafe waiter, reducing themselves to chef and dealer, and Pennsatucky's 'defender of the unborn' persona is de Beauvoir's sub-man sheltering behind ready-made values. Marx's opium-of-the-people analogy explains why comforting, unverifiable belief can block the authentic, responsible pursuit of a meaningful life.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 20 "8. Laughing in the Face of the Absurd" — Argues that watching Beth die on the platform is Sarah's existential awakening — the absurd realization that "it is no longer true that everyone has their own face" — analyzed through Camus's absurd (the impossible and the contradictory), Sartre's nausea at inhuman humans, and Beauvoir's "subman" who never wakes from the mechanical life. Sarah must repeatedly witness "her own" death (Beth, Katja, Jennifer, the Helsinki clones), which robs death and life of settled meaning, yet she refuses nihilism: exercising the radical freedom Sartre says grounds all values, she fights Dyad on behalf of everyone's freedom, implicitly choosing it for all humanity. Like Camus's Sisyphus, whose rock is his thing, her struggle is her thing — and the Season Two clone dance party is her laughing in the face of the absurd.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 19 "9. When Jumpin’ Jack Flash Met Ziggy Stardust" — Auxier reads the 1973 Jagger-Bowie intimacy and rivalry ethically: Keith Richards's portrait of Mick's envy frames Kierkegaard's Either/Or warning against the aesthetic life and the Kantian morality-duty wedding Bowie fled, against Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity, which demands that one own one's freely chosen hollowing-out without appeal to any authority. Beauvoir's bad faith and authenticity then explain the outcome - Bowie beat Jagger by killing Ziggy, firing the Spiders, and finally making his very death a persona ('authentically Bowie'), while Jagger, forever only the Stones' singer, can respond only in bad faith, because 'hell is other people': each glimpsed the faker in the other.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 23 "12. Dilbert Is an Asshole and That’s Why He’ll Never Be Happy and Nobody Loves Him" — Elsby and Luzecky argue Dilbert's unhappiness is chosen: from 400 rejections he concludes the women lack quality, he calls insult-bombing gentle kidding, and when Dogbert cites man's rational essence he chooses to watch all-star wrestling, each a textbook Sartrean bad faith where he glimpses the truth and flees it. Measured against Aristotle's eudaimonia he lacks every virtue of the Nicomachean mean (courage as the midpoint of fear, rightly scaled ambition, wit), and since one swallow does not make a summer his whole life, not a day of it, could earn the name happy. The December 2017 addictive-app strips complete the verdict: Dilbert monetizes a zombie-making app for a raise, making him Beauvoir's serious man from The Ethics of Ambiguity, the intelligent sell-out who subordinates human value to a hierarchy he knows is hollow.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 17 "6. Serena Joy, Miserable, Despicable" — Elsby refuses to see Serena Joy as a self-determined villain, arguing she annihilates her own freedom—negating her humanity in Beauvoir's sense—to become an empty vessel for Gilead's will. Working through Aristotle on coerced and 'mixed' actions and the bad-upbringing excuse, Sartre on freedom and responsibility in Being and Nothingness, and Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity, she asks how much blame an oppressed woman deserves who nonetheless helped build her own subjugation and holds June down during the Ceremony. The answer runs through bad faith: Serena deceives herself until raping June is no longer a necessary wrong but a good in itself, and the 'unwomen' logic echoes Boethius's claim that evildoers cease to be human—comprehensible, but still abhorrent.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 25 "13. The Origins of Self-Love" — Anna Marie Fennell reads RuPaul's 'If you can't love yourself, how in the hell you gonna love somebody else?' through theories of self-love. Erich Fromm's four elements of love and Buddhist non-attachment (Jinkx Monsoon's 'water off a duck's back,' the Season Ten Inner Saboteur characters like Eureka's Eufilthior) ground the claim that self-love precedes healthy love for others. Against Aristophanes' myth in Plato's Symposium - the round beings split by Zeus, forever seeking their other half, retold in Hedwig and the Angry Inch - she sides with Ru: completion comes from within, not from a soulmate. Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity (the sub-man and nihilist archetypes seen in self-sabotaging queens like Nina Bo'Nina Brown) and bell hooks's All About Love with Branden's six pillars of self-esteem map onto winners like Jinkx, Sharon Needles, Violet Chachki, and Bianca Del Rio, whose drag personas show existence preceding essence.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 25 "What It Is Like to Be Out of the Asylum" — Ron Novy argues nobody can know what it is like to be Batman: deploying Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and a Mary's-Room variant with a color-deprived Barbara Gordon, he shows subjective experience resists even complete physical knowledge. Simone de Beauvoir's situated freedom then explains how 'one bad day' (Bruce's parents' murder, the Joker's Red Hood plunge into chemicals) threw each man into the same terrifying glimpse of Kant's noumenal world behind appearances, yet into opposite narratives of order and chaos. Even while sharing the joke that ends The Killing Joke, Batman and the Joker remain mutually unknowable, each the only one who can 'keep up' with the other.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 30 "Notes" — Hackett contrasts Frank's ethical egoism - acting like an invisible Ring of Gyges wearer who pushes Zoe in front of a train and kills Peter once they cannot be controlled - with Beauvoir's existentialist ethics, in which consciousness is a 'nothing' whose freedom is real only when it wills and sustains the freedom of others. Peter's drunken enslavement and Zoe's freely chosen deal with Frank illustrate the ambiguity of a freedom that is still causally situated, and Frank's Season 3 miscalculations with Jackie, Remy, and Claire show egoism's inability to weigh others' self-interest. Claire's sympathy for Michael Corrigan and her final walkout dramatize her learning Beauvoir's lesson that promoting others' freedom is the condition of one's own, the difference between self-interest and existential freedom.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 30 "Notes" — Contrasts Frank's ethical egoism with Beauvoir's existential ethics: Frank moves like an invisible Ring-of-Gyges wearer-murdering Zoe, reading everyone's self-interest-yet because he treats others purely as instruments his freedom is never 'prolonged through the freedom of others', and it fails in Season 3 when he miscalculates Jackie, Remy, and Claire. Claire's awakening through Michael Corrigan and her final walkout dramatize the Beauvoirian lesson that consciousness is freedom-as-nothingness whose values we remain collectively responsible for, not a license to will anything.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 9 "Note" — Held's introduction frames Wonder Woman as an ambiguous figure - a sexy superhero, feminist icon, even a god - and borrows Simone de Beauvoir's term 'ambiguity' from The Second Sex to name women's bind: acquiesce to gender norms and lose yourself, or become yourself and lose your place. He runs through Diana's either/ors (Steve Trevor, Themyscira or Boston, mortal or god, American or cosmopolitan) and argues she creates an identity only by defining herself against each expectation. Because everyone is torn between what they are and what they want to become, he concludes we should embrace Wonder Woman's contradictions and stake our commitments while living in ambiguity.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 11 "Notes" — Wright reads Wonder Woman's 75-year history through Beauvoir's 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman,' arguing Diana's move from Paradise Island to Man's World - surrendering eternal life for Steve Trevor - enacts the hard-won transcendence of immanence that The Second Sex demands. She shows the comics alternating between empowerment (Marston's 'woman of tomorrow,' an unpatriotic George Washington scolding women war workers) and regression (Trevor persuading Wonder Woman to marry and type memos about women's place being the home, the 1990s hyper-sexualized art), evidence that woman remains the Other to man's Subject. Wonder Woman's durability, she says, lies in exactly this ambiguity, and like Beauvoir's woman of tomorrow she models forging identity through projects in the world.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 16 "Notes" — Zanin surveys 75 years of Wonder Woman - Marston's bondage-inflected feminism (the Ordeal of a Thousand Links, bracelets that forfeit power to any man who chains them), Kanigher's romance-era drift, the 1968 Diana Prince fashion-bouticless era that opened just as feminists protested Miss America, and the Taco Whiz years - to ask whether 'wonder woman' has become an unattainable ideal that belittles women. Reading through Beauvoir's analyses of woman as Other, imposed femininity as immanence, and the body as situation, she argues the superwoman 'have it all' standard is a feminist faux pas, yet closes with Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity: rather than resent her perfection, women should accept the challenge on their own terms instead of acquiescing in mediocrity.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Johnson-Moxley tests Perez's lasso of truth - which makes people face truths about themselves, like being dragged from Plato's cave - against four ethical touchstones: Kantian duty (truth-telling as a perfect duty, respect for autonomy), utilitarianism, virtue ethics, and care ethics. Cases drive the argument: binding Ares so he sees his apocalypse annihilates what he rules, freeing Vanessa from Dr. Psycho's false memories only with her permission, and lashing two warlords into 'twins of pain' to end bloodshed. She concludes via Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity that compelling truth is justified only to restore someone's rational self-direction, never paternalistically, with Gandhi's satyagraha ('truth-force') as the model of active, compassionate truth-telling.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 20 "“Howzat!” Prometheus Is a Fast Bowler" — Kevin S. Decker argues the Doctor's morality is an "ethics of ambiguity" poised between Romanticism and existentialism, not any formula. Rejecting positivism, deontology, and utilitarianism as fits for the Doctor, he reads the Doctor's freedom, wandering, and rejection of Time Lord values through Sartre's radical freedom and bad faith (the student torn between mother and Free French) and Beauvoir's "adventurer" who confers value by choosing. The Romantic search for the infinite in small things and the Prometheus myth frame the Doctor as a liberating, self-defining moral exemplar.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 17 "MOTHERHOOD" — Elizabeth Butterfield reads her exhausting early motherhood through Simone de Beauvoir's The Ethics of Ambiguity and The Second Sex, arguing that 'the ideal mother,' like 'true womanhood,' is a social construction and that a mother is 'freedom in situation,' never a mother 'the way a stone is a stone.' She recasts Beauvoir's 'serious man' as the 'serious mother' who flees her freedom into the Motherhood Religion, and invokes Sartre's 'condemned to be free' and 'Hell is other people' (No Exit) to advocate the honest, self-aware 'genuine mother' over inauthentic self-sacrifice.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 12 "Who is Who" — This chapter tests the Doctor's ethics against consequentialism and Kantian/Nagelian deontology, arguing both fail because his alien longevity and time-travelling relation to consequences resist algorithmic moral judgment ('School Reunion,' 'Attack of the Cybermen'). It proposes instead de Beauvoir's 'ethics of ambiguity' rooted in Romanticism and Sartrean radical freedom and bad faith (the student anecdote; Turlough refusing the Enlightenment diamond), casting the Doctor as a Promethean figure who liberates companions into risky self-perfection.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 8 "NOTES" — Carolyn Korsmeyer uses Aristotle's Poetics dictum that the 'probable impossible' beats the possible improbable to argue popular narrative can actually conduct philosophy, not merely illustrate it. Her central case is that the TV series Angel—the ensouled, guilt-cursed vampire who concludes 'if nothing we do matters, then all that matters is what we do'—independently arrives at the same existentialist position as Simone de Beauvoir's The Ethics of Ambiguity, with no textual borrowing. She contrasts The Matrix's dramatically sustained Cartesian dream-doubt against the 'improbable impossible' Dallas dream-season, showing why one is a philosophical vehicle and the other bankrupt.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 36 "The Price of Existence" — Mann reads Stephenie Meyer's Twilight through Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex: Bella is the "relative being" who orbits Edward like a satellite, valued only through the constant masculine gaze, embodying the adolescent girl's renunciation of her "I can" body. Mann finds a buried feminist subtext — Bella's desire, Edward's restraint, and her vampire transformation into a fierce, powerful equal — but ultimately faults Meyer for reinstating the old promise that a woman gains subjecthood through self-annihilation in a sovereign man's eyes.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 17 "15. Grey’s Anatomy as Philosophy Ethical Ambiguity in Shades of Grey" — The chapter argues that Meredith Grey embodies Simone de Beauvoir's existentialist ethics from The Ethics of Ambiguity, rejecting the childlike 'spirit of seriousness' that treats moral rules as absolute. Through episodes where Meredith stabilizes a bomb inside a patient's chest, coaches a death-row inmate to induce his own brain death, switches an Alzheimer's-trial placebo for Adele, and commits insurance fraud to treat an immigrant child, it shows her breaking institutional protocol to positively will the freedom of others while owning her choices. It contrasts her authentic embrace of moral ambiguity and risk against Shepherd's, Bailey's, and Webber's rule-bound seriousness or self-interest, framing medical dilemmas as an ambiguous moral realm where no single correct answer exists.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 52 "49. A Serious Man as Philosophy The Elusiveness of Moral Knowledge" — Biderman reads the Coens' A Serious Man through Beauvoir's figure of the 'serious man' (from The Ethics of Ambiguity), the man who craves a single absolute value and blinds himself to moral complexity: physics professor Larry Gopnik, beset by divorce, a bribing student Clive, and Sy Ableman's death, seeks moral knowledge that would let him be such a man. The chapter argues Larry's quest fails across cognitivist, noncognitivist, and pluralist accounts of moral knowledge, showing moral knowledge to be elusive if not impossible. The film's Kafkaesque fables (the Dibbuk, the Goy's Teeth, Rabbi Nachtner's 'L'olam ha-ba', Schrodinger's cat, and the Binding of Isaac in Caravaggio's painting) all stage the absurd collapse of interpretation, echoing the Book of Job, which Maimonides read as a parable rather than history.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 68 "64. George Carlin as Philosopher It’s All Bullshit. Is It Bad for Ya" — Engels reads Carlin's insistence that 'it's all bullshit, and it's bad for ya' as a defense of truth over comforting illusion, mapping his bits onto Plato's Allegory of the Cave (Carlin dragging audiences up from shadows like 'prostitution is immoral' or 'the American Dream' to expose deeper essences), Nozick's Experience Machine (Carlin's sun-worship chosen because it is real, not a pleasing fiction), and Clifford/Beauvoir on the ethics of belief and the 'serious world.' Bits on rights, the sanctity of life, homelessness/'houselessness,' and 'proud to be an American' show Carlin arguing that false beliefs breed complacency and harm, so there are moral reasons to prefer truth.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 79 "75. Phoebe Waller-Bridge as Philosopher Conscious Women Making Choices" — Pande and Engels argue that Fleabag and Lulu (Crashing) embody Sartrean authenticity: they own their choices, balance facticity and transcendence, and stay outside bad faith, while the men (Anthony, the Priest) fall back on pregiven roles and let 'the Look' or their fundamental project decide for them. Fleabag's addressing the camera and finally shutting it out is read as breaking the gaze of the Other; the Priest choosing priesthood over love exemplifies denial of transcendence. Through Beauvoir's Second Sex, woman-as-Other, and ethics of ambiguity, they show Waller-Bridge's transgressive, sexually frank women reclaim self-definition, arguing viewers 'could do better to be' the kind of free, choosing women her protagonists are.

### Allegory of the Cave

The allegory of the cave, from Plato's Republic, imagines prisoners chained since birth so they see only shadows cast on a wall, mistaking these projections for reality. One prisoner is freed, painfully ascends to the sunlit world outside, and comes to understand that the shadows were mere images of true things. The story dramatizes Plato's distinction between the world of appearances and the world of the Forms, and it pictures education as a turning of the soul toward truth rather than a filling of it with facts. It also suggests why the enlightened person, returning to explain what they have seen, may be met with hostility.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 9 "The Fates of Socrates and Seinfeld" — William Irwin compares Jerry and Socrates: the 'Jerry problem' of whether the fictional Jerry is the real Jerry (complicated by Seinlanguage) mirrors the Socratic problem of separating Socrates from Plato's dialogues. Jerry, like Socrates the gadfly, provokes his circle with questions that hunt for essences - the black-and-white cookie, 'is soup a meal?' - and shares Socrates' irony (the 'War: What Is It Good For?' gag in 'The Marine Biologist' works exactly like Socratic shamming ignorance). But where Socrates died serenely per the Apology and Phaedo, Jerry is self-absorbed and ends the series convicted under the Good Samaritan law, doing his stand-up 'gadfly' routine for prison inmates - an examined life, but not an exemplary one.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 11 "Unknown" — Irwin reads Neo's unplugging as Plato's cave allegory restaged: the pod farms are the cave, the cables feeding the illusion are the chains, and Morpheus (named for the god of dreams) plays the liberator who drags the prisoner painfully into the light of 'the desert of the real'. He frames the 'prison for your mind' theme through figures who kept their minds free under captivity, notes that 'education' etymologically means 'leading out' as the prisoner is led out of the cave, and contrasts Neo, who would endure anything rather than return to illusion, with Cypher, who goes back to the shadows.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 12 "Unknown" — Irwin argues the cave story's real point is Plato's Theory of Forms: life inside the Matrix, like ordinary sensory life, is a realm of copies - sunsets, just acts, really good noodles - imitating Beauty, Justice and Goodness themselves. He reads 'there is no spoon' and Morpheus's 'no one can be told what the Matrix is' as Plato's claim that the Forms are grasped by intellect rather than senses, and explains Neo's amnesia and the film's deja vu through Plato's doctrine of recollection (anamnesis), with the soul beholding the Forms between incarnations.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 27 "Unknown" — Korsmeyer traces how the film deploys each sense: vision is both the channel of illusion and, as from Plato's cave onward, the metaphor for understanding ('Why do my eyes hurt?' 'You've never used them'); hearing serves surveillance and bodily invasion, from the centipede-like bug to the screaming 'WAKE UP!' and whispers that nearly touch; and smell marks corporeality, from Trinity's affectionate sniffing of the sleeping Neo to Agent Smith's disgust at human 'stink', which drives him to break protocol and remove his earpiece.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 31 "The Metaphysics of The Matrix" — Gracia and Sanford open with Neo and Trinity in the club and the question that drives the film, 'What is the Matrix?', mapping Neo's path out of the pod onto Plato's cave ascent while stressing the twist: what Neo finds is not the shining realm of Forms but a war-scarred desert, preferred only because it is true, and like Plato's escaped prisoner he returns to free the others. They state their three questions - what are appearance and reality, what separates them, and what properties belong to each - as the paradigmatically metaphysical questions the film poses.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 34 "Unknown" — The authors distinguish the two worlds twice over: by source, since everything in the Matrix issues from the AI machines' program while the real world's ultimate causes lie elsewhere; and by ontological status, since the unreal world depends entirely for its existence on real machines, electrical signals, and minds. They add that recognizing the difference requires a teacher - Morpheus playing to Neo's 'splinter in your mind', just as Plato's cave needs a first freed prisoner - though they file how we come to know this under epistemology rather than metaphysics.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 66 "Unknown" — The chapter reads the pod farms as Plato's cave from Republic VII: prisoners chained from birth who mistake projected images for reality and 'do not know that they are prisoners', insisting on the truth of their world. Morpheus, named for the god of dreams, is the liberator-expert who can rouse sleepers in the right sequence, and Neo's sense of not being sure he is awake parallels the prisoner's primeval recollections. With Plato, it argues that happiness is objective like health - one can say 'I am happy' and be wrong, as the battery-humans are - so true happiness and freedom depend on knowledge of what is real.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 89 "Unknown" — The chapter sets Neo and Cypher as the two poles of authenticity: Neo's unplugging is agony, like the prisoner dragged from Plato's cave - atrophied limbs, eyes that hurt because 'never used them before', and the cognitive shock of the 'desert of the real' - while Cypher, freed young and worn down by years of fear and gag-inducing goop, sells out the crew for a steak he knows does not exist: 'ignorance is bliss'. McMahon asks us to sympathize with Cypher, since in his place, facing perpetual annihilation, 'we too might opt for the illusion'.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 98 "Real Genre and Virtual Philosophy" — Knight and McKnight argue The Matrix must be read as a mixed-genre film: pure genres are 'a theorist's fiction', and the film's genre inheritance supplies the narrative roots of its philosophical thematics - Plato's cave from the Republic, Descartes's Dream Hypothesis from the Meditations, Nietzsche's Ubermensch, Zen Buddhism, and apocalyptic Christianity. Recognizing the genre mix explains both why the film raises questions about justified true belief in a virtual world, free will versus deterministic control, and appearance versus reality, and why it offers no philosophical answers, only genre ones.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 102 "Unknown" — The chapter argues that the film's philosophical allusions—students comparing the pod-bound humans to Plato's cave prisoners and Neo's bewilderment to Descartes's First Meditation dream hypothesis—are designed to generate suspense, anxiety, and horror rather than philosophical reflection. Because genre texts are centrifugal, pointing viewers to outside connections, and their pacing never lingers on themes, The Matrix can use philosophy only to trigger audience interest and never to argue for answers. Its conclusion is that the film is unquestionably real genre but only virtual philosophy.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 115 "Unknown" — Developing thesis one, the chapter shows Morpheus's question—'How would you know the difference between the dream world and the real world?'—restates Plato's cave dwellers mistaking shadows for things and Descartes's First Meditation progression from unreliable senses to dreaming to the malicious demon that makes every belief false. What is genuinely new is that computer simulation and brain science have made the once-outlandish demon scenario thinkable, so the film has made philosophy teachers' job easier: global skepticism no longer seems ridiculous, and maybe you are lying in a tub of goo right now.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 119 "The Matrix Or, The Two Sides of Perversion" — Žižek opens with the 'ideal spectator' beside him exclaiming 'so there is no reality!' and notes the film works as a Rorschach test in which Lacanians, Frankfurt School partisans, and New Agers all recognize themselves. He reframes Plato's cave: when the prisoners escape The Matrix's version of the cave, what they find outside is not the sunlit realm of the Good but the desolate 'desert of the real', and he asks whether the choice between reading the film as Capital colonizing subjectivity or as the virtual symbolic order as such is itself a false alternative.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 17 "Conquering the Inner Demon" — James Lawler casts Buffy as a contemporary allegory of Plato's cave-escaped philosopher and reads the show through Kant: the Slayer moves between a hellish lower world of instrumental appetite and an intelligible higher world of the soul, and Kant's Copernican revolution ('objects must conform to our knowledge') explains Marcie's invisibility in 'Out of Mind, Out of Sight' and the fear-made-flesh Master of 'Nightmares.' Kant's formula that every rational being exists as an end in himself grounds Buffy's duty in 'Anne' ('I am Buffy, the Vampire Slayer'), her rejection of Spike's chip as no substitute for a soul in 'Crush,' and her 'As You Were' admission that using Spike treats him as a mere means. Season Six explores 'too much heaven': Buffy's blissful death in 'The Gift' makes earthly life hell, and only conquering the inner demon — Willow's fear-driven dark magic defeated by Xander's yellow-crayon love in 'Grave' — restores the balance between heavens and hells.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 30 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Lenore Wright reads Sam and Frodo's Quest through the two journey motifs of Western philosophy: the journey out (Plato's cave, structuring Augustine's Confessions and Descartes' escape from the senses' deceptions) and the journey inward (the cogito, self-transformation, with Nussbaum's claim that literature gives philosophy a body). Frodo's steps out of the Shire-cave - selling Bag End, 'I will take the Ring, though I do not know the way' - create the Fellowship and its freedoms, while Boromir attains self-knowledge only at death's door and Gandalf, Aragorn, and Sam are remade by the road. Against classical heroes like Theseus and Odysseus, Sam and Frodo are modern pilgrims - Nietzschean Yea-sayers becoming who they are, with Heideggerian 'potentiality-for-Being' - whereas Sméagol and Saruman live inauthentically, defined by their pasts.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 35 "Last Pitch" — Reid argues that baseball and Socratic elenchus are both constructed to cultivate aretē, excellence. She maps four parallels onto concrete moments: both live off uncertainty (pre-game jitters, the 2001 Rivera–Gonzalez Series finish), both require risking failure (Ted Williams playing a doubleheader to protect his .400, Kirk Gibson's hobbling 1988 homer off Dennis Eckersley, Billy Beane's fear beside Lenny Dykstra), both demand active self-testing (Lou Gehrig retiring when complimented on a routine play), and both impose an obligation to return and challenge others — Plato's cave allegory, Socrates the gadfly, the aging champion who applauds the record-breaker. The Delphic oracle's riddle, that Socrates is wisest in knowing his ignorance, is the batter's-box humility every at-bat demands.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 105 "What Is Real" — Presents the two lines Rowling said she waited seventeen years to write: dying Harry, in the King's Cross limbo, asks Dumbledore whether their conversation is real or only 'inside my head', and Dumbledore answers that of course it is in his head but that does not make it unreal. The section frames this as the philosophical question of separating appearance from reality, cites A. J. Ayer's dismissal of his own near-death experience as hallucination, and introduces Plato's cave as the classic image of mistaking shadows for reality.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 14 "The Jedi Model" — Barad presents a handbook of Jedi virtue modeled on Plato's Republic: the Jedi are Plato's Guardians, trained through physical exercise and Socratic questioning to guard peace and justice. Aristotle's golden mean explains courage as the balance between Chewbacca's cowardly fear and Anakin's rash rush at Dooku, with Luke's decision to leave Dagobah counting as courage because it has just cause. Luke's Dagobah cave vision (Vader's mask opening to reveal his own face) is read as Plato's Cave allegory turned inward - self-knowledge of one's fear of becoming evil - while compassion and forgiveness, not forbidden attachment, complete the Jedi character. The chapter even defends Jedi mind tricks via Plato's noble lie (the myth of the metals) as manipulation of the weak-minded for the common good.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 24 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Wendy Hamblet asks whether Narnia feeds children a dangerous militaristic moral imaginary: Homeric warrior heroes, swarthy Calormene villains, voiceless animals excluded from moral concern, and battles that decide truth, in a lineage running from Plato's censorship of nursery stories through Descartes's modernity to Heidegger's seduction by Hitler's myths. On closer reading she finds Lewis undermining militarism: morally mixed characters, condemnation of aggression, despotism, and 'reasons of state,' and room only for just war and righteous self-defense. The finale is read through Plato's cave, as the Last Battle's worlds-within-worlds expose our political 'truths' as shadow-images that unscrupulous leaders manipulate when the god is absent.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 27 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Takes Digory's dying remark 'It's all in Plato' as the key to the Chronicles. It compares the Professor's guided questioning of Peter and Susan about Lucy's wardrobe testimony to the Socratic method, though noting he supplies evidential maxims rather than eliciting a virtue-definition as Socrates does with Cephalus on justice. It maps Underland in The Silver Chair onto the Allegory of the Cave (Rilian bound in his silver chair like the chained prisoners, the Green Witch's enchantment that denies any world beyond), observing that the Witch 'plays Aristotle' by ridiculing Aslan as an invented perfect Form, while Puddleglum's 'stand by the play-world' speech echoes Socrates's reply to Glaucon that the ideal pattern is none the worse for being unrealizable. Finally it reads the 'real Narnia' of The Last Battle ('world within world, Narnia within Narnia') as Christian Platonism, with the nested heavens even raising Plato's Third Man problem.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 23 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Harman argues the real heroes of Easy Rider are the two Harley-Davidsons: the exploding Captain America bike that drowns out its rider's corpse, the cocaine hidden in the gas tank like a prosthetic organ, and the obscured helmets and muffled dialogue reduce Fonda, Hopper, and Nicholson to 'stowaways and parasites' of their machines. He uses this reversal to attack Kant's Copernican Revolution, on which we could know only how Harleys appear to us and never the things in themselves, and to champion the Whitehead-Deleuze-Latour current in which genes, pickup trucks, bridges, and Harleys are autonomous actors no less than humans, against Plato's two-world heir of appearances and unknowable things. Billy and Captain America's 1960s transgression, he concludes, quietly ends in submission to the power, rhythm, and demands of their bikes.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 11 "U2 and Philosophy" — Dreyfus and Wrathall read U2's head/heart split through Kierkegaard's Sickness unto Death: the Christian-Platonic strategy of escaping the earthly (the sun-blindness of 'Staring at the Sun', the ascent of 'Gone') collapses into despair once both sides of the self prove essential, while 'The Playboy Mansion' and 'Discotheque' depict Kierkegaardian leveling and spiritlessness in consumer culture and 'Last Night on Earth' the aesthetic-sphere despair of living pure possibility. Pascal's contradictory great-and-miserable self and Augustine's two cities supply the tradition U2 inherits, and Nietzsche's 'nihilism' names what U2 calls 'pop'. They close by arguing that Bono's pseudonymous stage characters (the Fly, MacPhisto) do phenomenology just as Kierkegaard's pseudonyms do, and that U2's songs about something missing bear out despair's 'dialectic of eternity'.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 9 "Plato’s Cave Again" — Curran uses Shadow of a Doubt to teach epistemology: Charlie's claim to 'know' her uncle distinguishes knowledge by acquaintance from propositional knowledge as justified true belief, with the permanently stuck 'Til Two clock showing a true belief that is not knowledge because its warrant is unreliable. Coherence (Hegel, Blanshard), pragmatist (James, Dewey), and correspondence theories of truth are tested against the townspeople's false but convenient beliefs about Uncle Charlie, and only correspondence survives. Kant's absolute duty not to lie is weighed against Mill's act and rule utilitarianism for the detectives' deceptions, and a feminist care-ethics perspective assesses Charlie's shielding her mother from the truth. Plato's cave frames the cinema itself: film can deceive like shadows on a wall, yet the detectives' unused photograph shows the camera can also reveal truth, so movies help us face facts, at the price, as Charlie pays, of lost innocence.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 24 "Curtain Down" — Silberstein reads Rear Window as a self-reflexive film about film-watching: the shades rise like a curtain, the courtyard apartments play like frames on a filmstrip, and wheelchair-bound Jeff with his binoculars is the movie spectator - the courtyard is Plato's cave and we are the chained prisoners watching shadows (copies of copies of the forms). The chapter stages the Plato-versus-Aristotle debate over imitative art from Republic Book X and the Poetics, then argues the film vindicates both: Jeff's voyeurism breeds detachment and misjudgment (he misreads Lisa, Miss Torso, the composer and the newlyweds), yet the same watching awakens - the song 'Lisa' saves Miss Lonelyhearts from suicide, Thorwald is brought to justice, and Jeff and the audience leave the theater wiser about fantasy, boredom and their own lives.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 15 "Would You Help Me to Carry the Stone" — Weinstein argues critics who call Waters a gloomy misanthrope misread him: he is an existentialist whose work maps point for point onto Camus's absurd, the human demand for unity endlessly frustrated. Waters's imagery tracks Camus's: the sun (Plato's cave symbol of the good, and the light Sisyphus loved on earth) against the eclipsed moon of death and madness; the stone we secrete through failed communication ('the bad blood slows and turns to stone' in 'Dogs,' 'would you help me to carry the stone' in The Wall) against Sisyphus's rock; and Pink's Trial, condemned for 'showing feelings of an almost human nature,' replaying Meursault's condemnation for failing to cry at his mother's funeral. Since the institutions of home, school, military, and the music industry's machine block every genuine encounter, Waters's persistence in making art that mostly fails to communicate is itself the absurd revolt, so with Camus one must imagine Sisyphus happy, and Weinstein imagines Waters happy too.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 16 "Thinking Inside the Pod" — Condella reads the opening of Saturday Night Fever -- Tony Manero strutting to 'Stayin' Alive' while delivering a can of paint -- as the iPod condition in miniature: music that alters rather than captures reality, now dial-up-able for workouts ('Eye of the Tiger'), bus rides, and grocery runs. Through Heidegger he argues the iPod is calculative thinking incarnate, annihilating the time, silence, and solitude meditative thinking requires (the shower as last refuge), and deepening technological homelessness by flattening every place into whatever soundtrack we choose -- the Rhine dammed into a 'gigantic gasoline station,' the iPod pushing us 'pretty far down' in Plato's Cave, its very possibility prepared by Descartes's thinking thing. Yet his wife's yoga instructor chanting on a Bronx bus shows the iPod can also open meditative space, so what Heidegger demands is not Luddism but Gelassenheit, a free relationship to technology.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 19 "Youth and the Image" — Hickey argues the iPod is the 'iCon of a generation' because it is a Baudrillardian simulacrum of youth: like the Gulf War consumed as CNN fireworks or reality TV's fabricated 'real,' Apple's silhouette ads sell faceless dancers whose entire identity is the white device -- a 'symbolic cyborgism' read through Donna Haraway. The vernacular of iPodding, podcasting, and downloading forms what he calls, with Wittgenstein, a language game woven into the actions of the 'now' that authorizes this youthful, tech-savvy identity as natural, while the ads' imagery works like Platonic shadows in the caves of our desire. Still, citing Giddens's structure-agency negotiation and DeCerteau's consumer tactic of re-appropriating everyday images, he insists we are not brainwashed: we can switch off, refuse, or remake the images that 'tell us who we are.'
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 6 "Ex Astris, Scientia GEORGE A REISCH" — The editors' introduction takes Starfleet Academy's motto 'Ex Astris, Scientia' as its frame: Picard handing cadet Wesley Crusher a book by William James shows officers need philosophy, not just ship operations, and the starry-heavens motif runs from Thales and Plato's cave through Kant's 'moral law within and starry heavens above.' It surveys the book's Trek dilemmas (Picard and Dathon's alien language, Data's emotion chip, Khan's vengeance, Riker's Q powers) as 2,500-year-old philosophical problems, and argues Trek's optimism — Picard's 'the acquisition of wealth is no longer the driving force' — restates Aristotle's claim that all humans by nature desire to know. Like philosophy from Socrates on, Trek is presented as 'an entertaining, edifying preparation' for living by one's ideals, a life-education primer sealed with Roddenberry's advice to 'slip in a heavy idea or two.'
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 26 "Must I Repeat Myself" — Seng maps Dorothy's journey onto Plato's cave allegory: Kansas is the cave of shadows, Oz the painful ascent into light, and the crucial shared point is Socrates' demand that the freed prisoner go back down into the cave, which explains why Dorothy, once enlightened, must return to gray Kansas bearing self-knowledge. He surveys the film adaptations (1910, Semon's 1925, Eshbaugh's 1933, Fleming's 1939, Return to Oz, and The Wiz) to show that each rewrites 'home' as self-knowledge rather than a place, culminating in Glinda's The Wiz speech, 'If we know ourselves, we're always home, anywhere.' Kierkegaard's contrast between recollection and repetition then sorts the homecomings: Baum's Dorothy wills recollection of what was lost, while Diana Ross's Dorothy wills repetition, holding to her self amid change, which Seng says Kierkegaard regards as the equivalent of faith.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 20 "Colbert Is (the Tragedy and Comedy of) America, and So Are We" — Ralkowski asks whether Colbert is America's Socrates, comparing Colbert's ironic interviews (Caitlin Flanagan on feminism, Harvey Mansfield on manliness, Howard Dean's superdelegates, the ABC Stephanopoulos-Gibson debate) to Socrates' definitional refutations of Euthyphro and the Athenian elite. Like Socrates in Plato's cave allegory, Colbert is a shadow on the wall undermining truthiness from within, yet both fail: audiences laugh, guests collect the campaign-donation 'Colbert Bump,' and nothing changes, making America the self-satisfied one who is ignorant of its ignorance. Through Nehamas's contrast of Socratic and Platonic irony and the Symposium's demand that the greatest work read as both tragedy and comedy, the chapter concludes Colbert may be America's Plato — condemning and laughing at us like a Sisyphean liberator who knows we will not leave the cave.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 7 "4" — Four 'Phase One' essays. Dyer reads Mark Millar's Wanted through Plato's cave: Wesley Gibson escapes a pathetic life like the freed prisoner, but like Adolf Eichmann (via Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem) he murders his conscience, so the Fraternity's consequence-free world leaves him numb and unable to value anything - a descent deeper into the cave, ending in the banality of evil. Novy explains why henchmen betray using Aristotle's utility/pleasure/complete friendship distinction (Big Cheese, Henchmen Muenster and Feta): supervillain gangs are Hobbesian pirate crews with no enforcer, so a modus vivendi of self-interest collapses under interrogation and only Machiavellian fear secures loyalty. Foresman applies Goodman and Rawls's reflective equilibrium as a 'cheat' to rank Apocalypse, Magneto, Luthor, the Joker, and Bizarro, concluding the 'best of the worst' is judged on evil ends (or evil means, as with Magneto) and even on glorious failure. Arinder and Milton, in a staged descent-into-madness frame, diagnose mad science in Victor Frankenstein and Dr. Doom as science that denies value-laden theory choice - impossible because data underdetermine theory - breeding the hubris that dehumanizes the scientist.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 26 "You Can Discover More about a Person in an Hour of Play than in a Year of" — Tim Christopher weighs pseudonymity — multiple persistent in-game identities — against responsibility for what those identities do, opening with his accidental first 'honorable kill' and the real-world extremes of a stabbing over loud WoW and a murder over a borrowed virtual sword. Using the Tae Kwon Do mat as a model of the sacred gamespace, he argues that WoW's persistent world and anonymity invite misbehavior, yet since no one is kind in WoW out of fear of punishment, any kindness there may be kindness for its own sake — an honest character may be a better person than an honest player. Plato's Allegory of the Cave is his master image: players see only shadows (avatars) of the real people behind them and must remember the world outside the cave.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 33 "Cyborg Goddess" — Reads Ghost in the Shell as Donna Haraway's 'Cyborg Manifesto' made flesh: Major Kusanagi is built not born, has no sexuality or romance, and relegates male partners to sidekicks, enacting Haraway's post-gender cyborg that breaks the dualisms binding women to body, nature, and reproduction. The chapter traces the 'ghost' back through Koestler to Ryle's mockery of Descartes's mind-body dualism, reads the genderless, net-born Puppet Master as the Singularity of transhumanist philosophy, and interprets the Major–Puppet Master fusion — urged to 'come out of the shadows and into the light' in an explicit Plato's-cave gesture — as a posthuman, techno-spiritual 'Cyborg Goddess' that renders both gender and humanity obsolete.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 11 "He’s Got to Make His Own Mistakes" — Cole pits Plato against Walter Benjamin to vindicate the imitation of Rush: Plato's cave makes art a shadow twice removed from the Forms, and on that view a perfect copy is impossible and every cover degraded, while Peart's 'Limelight' calls the stage a 'gilded cage' that is 'just a prettified cave' yet, with 'we are merely players' (via Shakespeare), makes performing the way out rather than deeper in. Benjamin's translator essay, with its 'language forest' echo and 'pure language', shows how Rush's cover of 'Summertime Blues' on Feedback layers Blue Cheer and the Who into one perception, and how live variations of 'Witch Hunt' and the premature chord of 'Turn the Page' let error overtake and become the new original. The chapter exceeds Aristotle's principle of non-contradiction in 'pure language', where original, copy, and fan covers (Rock Band failures, the South Park 'Lil' Rush' flub, Rick Mercer's drum lesson) are fragments of one greater vessel, so errors are portals of discovery.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 12 "Guardian Training" — Roger Travis argues Plato would welcome Halo as guardian training: mimesis is really 'playing epic pretend,' and Halo, like the Homeric epics that were Athens' textbooks, trains players in a way of life. Plato's Republic Book 10 critique—the painted bed as copy of a copy of the Form of Bed—warns that playing Master Chief could let appetite rule, yet the Laws' admission that the ideal city's politeia is itself a mimesis turns the tables: the Republic is its own training simulation of philosophic pretend. Re-imagining the cave as prisoners tied to couches playing Super Mario Bros, he argues Halo's dutiful NPCs and waking-to-duty player (literal cryo-wakeups in Combat Evolved and Halo 3) make it philosophy in Plato's own sense, with Aristotle's catharsis leavening the verdict.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 7 "Happy Ending" — Wenmackers uses Inception's dream levels and its ambiguous spinning-top ending as a guided tour of skeptical philosophy, diagramming how dreams-within-dreams, kicks, Limbo and exponentially dilated dream time work. She tests the totem against Zhuangzi's butterfly and lucid-dreaming reality checks, then runs Plato's Cave and the eternal Forms, Descartes's cogito and evil demon, Putnam's brain-in-a-vat, and Nozick's experience machine to ask whether Cobb's world - or ours - is real. Her conclusion is Socratic ('know that you know nothing'): subjective reality feels equally real on every level and the top level can never be known. She even argues that dream-time dilation means Cobb should not kill himself while in doubt, since real time barely passes, so a little philosophy rescues the happy ending.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 10 "The Power of Choice" — Rennett tests Cobb's choice to leave Limbo against Nozick's three reasons for refusing the experience machine: we want to actually do things (raise his real children, not loving projections), to be a certain kind of person (Yusuf's dream-den addicts are 'indeterminate blobs'), and to touch something deeper than a man-made world. He then recruits Berkeley's esse est percipi to explain Mal's sincerity - she perceives Limbo and remembers it, so for her it is real - and argues that shared dreams differ from private dreams and the experience machine because they leave waking traces, like Mal's bullet in Arthur's leg. The chapter ends by making reality a matter of choice: like the cave prisoners of Plato's allegory, each character believes a world, and Cobb's ignoring of the top is his choice to live in the world with his children.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 22 "The Kick—Back to ‘Reality’" — The authors read the film in descending layers: reality as an ideology of touch and unreliable sensory experience, framed by Descartes's wax thought experiment and dream argument, with the kick explained through Hume's account of belief as custom and the totems as broken game pieces marking broken people (Mal's choice of the dream echoing prisoners returning to Plato's cave). The heist is then read as an existentialist drama where Cobb's 'downwards is the only way forwards' rejects the passive waiting of Beckett's Waiting for Godot and the pharmacy dreamers, with Jaspers's analysis of solitude making Limbo a hell of lonely regret that only an encounter with another can end. The chapter then argues the film is reflexively about movies (the crew mirrors a film crew, the Penrose stairs expose cinema's flat illusions, crosscutting manufactures time) before ending on Descartes's unresolved doubt about whether the final reality deserves our trust.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 94 "Chapter 14 - Trauma of the Real" — Introduces Paul Livingston's part with Dick's confession that reading Plato in college convinced him the empirical world was not truly real, then retells the cave of Republic Book VII in detail: prisoners bound since birth watching shadows of puppets cast by a fire. The cave becomes the frame for Dick's fiction — the 'reality' our percept-systems report is a show of images, and the philosophical quest is the prisoner's turn toward the archetypal reality behind the scenes.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 95 "Breakthrough to the Real" — Details the disorienting breakthrough in which characters learn that they themselves are fakes: Rachael's distress at her implanted memories ('How can it not know what it is?'), Deckard's paper unicorn in the director's cut confirming his own replicant status, and Ragle Gumm's soft-drink stand dissolving into a slip of paper reading 'SOFT-DRINK STAND' in Time Out of Joint. Each case maps onto the freed cave prisoner's discovery, and the disorientation is pressed onto the viewer: how can I be sure my own life and memories are not a fabrication?
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 97 "Procession of Dummies" — Uses Dick's 1972 one-sentence definition ('Reality is that which, when you stop believing in it, doesn't go away') and his claim that absolute reality reveals itself only when our space-time categories collapse, arguing the definition fits Lacan's Real better than Plato's picture of looking away from the cave wall. Through Žižek's readings, Ragle Gumm's objects being literally replaced by their symbolic labels and Deckard's replicant recognition as a 'total loss of the hero's symbolic identity' show the traumatic Real first appearing precisely where symbolically constituted reality fails.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 48 "Out of the Cave" — Traces the light-versus-darkness metaphor tradition from Plato's cave and Socrates' unexamined life through medieval 'illumination' and the Enlightenment to St. Paul's glass darkly, then lets Nietzsche ('shadow is as needful as light') and Derrida's deconstruction of presence/absence oppositions overturn it. The Stones do the same work in song: 'Just as every cop is a criminal, and all the sinners saints' in 'Sympathy for the Devil,' with 'Here Comes the Sun' overturned by 'Paint It Black' and 'Let It Be' by 'Let It Bleed.'
