The Buddha parallels are real — nonattachment, practice over theory (the poisoned-arrow parable), compassion for Bunny — yet Gautama's radical discipline and middle path are the opposite of the Dude's laziness, so Dudeism emerges as an undisciplined American cousin, and the Dude follows 'just his way and his alone'.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 12 "a4.xhtml" — Bronson argues that walking is a philosophical practice against modern placelessness (Giddens' 'phantasmagoric' locality): Thorin survived Smaug's attack because as a youth he 'was a good adventurous lad, always on the move', and Tolkien's wise figures - slow, flower-stopping Tolkien himself, Gandalf who 'went to look ahead' and was brought back 'by looking behind', Bilbo's silent walking, Beorn's bear-travels - all practice attentive movement through place. He backs this with Montaigne's retirement to his tower and bringing thoughts back to the orchard, Thoreau's woods-walking that must be spiritual as well as physical, the Tao Te Ching's 'good travelers leave no tracks' and Zhuangzi's wandering virtues, and Buddhist walking meditation from the Buddha's wandering monks to Thich Nhat Hanh's peace steps.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 17 "Do We Give Shakespeare the Last Word" — Kapper treats Inception as a hip epistemological puzzle — unlike The Matrix, the question is not what is real but how we could know — and follows Ariadne's thread (her mythological clue-giving names the chapter) through the tradition: Plato's Theaetetus and Descartes's supremely cunning deceiver pose 'Am I dreaming now?', Wittgenstein shows the doubt is senseless since 'if I am dreaming, this remark is being dreamed as well', Freud makes dreams the royal road to the unconscious, and Heraclitus says only the waking share a common cosmos. The payoff is Eastern: Zhuangzi's butterfly, Indra's net of mutually reflected jewels, and Schopenhauer's single-dreamer universe turn waking up into an endless regress, so the Buddhist ideal of the awakened one — nirvana, where the ideas of real and dream cease to pertain — becomes the reading of Cobb turning away from the top.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 29 "Notes" — Kahn argues LEGO play embodies the Buddhist teaching of impermanence that the Buddha states in the Digha Nikaya ('Impermanent are all component things...'): his childhood urge to superglue creations and Finn's father's Kragle dramatize the clinging that produces anxiety when things change, from brick formulations to discontinued sets and even funerals' wilting flowers. The LEGO Star Wars Death Star illustrates non-self — no Death Star exists apart from its 3,803 pieces, and no self apart from shifting aggregates — and the five aggregates (form, sensation, perception, formations, consciousness) are unpacked through building experiences like discovering a daughter has opened the mint Taj Mahal set. Tibetan sand mandalas, painstakingly built then ritually dissolved, model the ceremonial demolition of LEGO creations, teaching acceptance of change without sliding into a nihilistic 'why bother building at all'.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 7 "Buddha ex Machina" — Siobhan Lyons applies Mori's 'uncanny valley' to the hosts' physical and personality evolution (Ford's jerky old model versus seamless newer hosts, Maeve and Clementine), noting empathy grows as they near sentience. She argues via Aristotle's account of virtue, vice, and brutality that the guests and technicians (Logan's casual cruelty, the Man in Black's beastly sadism) fall short of human excellence while the suffering, consciousness-seeking hosts transcend it, treating humanity as a way of behaving rather than being, and casting the hosts as Derridean undecidables. Invoking Nietzsche on suffering as the cultivator of greatness and Mori's 'Buddha in the robot,' she claims the hosts earn a humanity the biological humans merely inherit.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 10 "Beat U-topos or Taking Utopia on the Road The Case of Jack Kerouac" — Adamo argues Kerouac's 'On the Road' is a new kind of utopian text: because classical collective utopias (Plato's Republic through More) were judged by Berlin, Popper, and Arendt to slide into totalitarianism and to conflict with political liberalism's individualism, Kerouac relocates utopia from place to the individual life lived 'on the road' (u-topos = no-place). He reads Sal Paradise's disillusion with Dean Moriarty—who uses people up—versus his admiration for Mississippi Gene and the hobos as dramatizing J. S. Mill's harm principle, fused with the Buddhist vow to harm no living thing, radicalizing personal liberty as perpetual movement without injury to others.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 15 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — James Whitehill treats sailing his Cape Cod catboat, named Garuda, as a Zen practice modeled on Zen archery (kyudo) and tea ceremony. He organizes it into 'outer work' (technique and ritualized performance) and 'inner work' (cultivating ki energy through breathing and belly-awareness, then 'self-forgetting'), quoting Dogen's dictum that studying the self is forgetting the self, and forgetting the self is being authenticated by all things. The goal is a boat-and-sailor unity in which the sailor 'sails without sailing' — reaching, through mundane repetitive discipline rather than a sought-after peak experience, a nirvana-like state where wind, wave, and self merge.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 21 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Eric Swan argues that climbing embodies the principles and spirit of Zen, the experience of 'ordinary mind' finding the extraordinary in the ordinary and living fully in the present. Tracing Zen from the Buddha's Flower Sermon and Bodhidharma through Suzuki's 'Beginner's Mind' and Huineng's finger-and-moon, he maps Zen's four training paths—physical work, zazen (sitting meditation), koans, and interviews with masters—onto climbing: routes are like koans solved by insight and action rather than logic, 'being in the zone' is meditative absorption, and breath-regulation at the crux is zazen in motion. He holds up free soloist Derek Hersey, grinning hundreds of feet up Eldorado Canyon, and Chris Sharma, who writes of flowing 'like water' on the rock, as modern Zen masters who dissolve the separation between self, climb, and world.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 29 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Jennifer McMahon and Steve Csaki test Buddhist and Taoist parallels in the novel and find many only apparent. Tolkien's talking trees and ents anthropomorphize nature and grant it human-like consciousness, whereas Buddhism attributes sentience to all beings without projecting human consciousness, and Tolkien privileges domesticated over wild nature and stewardship over membership in nature. His master-student chain (Bilbo, Gandalf, Aragorn, 'Master Samwise') genuinely echoes the Zen necessity of the right master, as in Dogen's mushroom-cook mentor; but his good-versus-evil war, with light privileged over a personified dark power to be defeated, contradicts Taoism's yin-yang balance in which evil is imbalance, not a force to destroy.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 45 "42. Up in the Air as Philosophy Buddhism and the Middle Path" — Duffy reads Ryan Bingham's arc in Up in the Air as a Zen Buddhist parable paralleling Hesse's Siddhartha. Ryan preaches an 'empty backpack' philosophy of nonattachment and treats the miles as their own point, but Duffy argues he only intellectually grasps the four noble truths — dukkha, its cause in attachment (tṛṣṇā), and the eightfold path — until his failed attachment to Alex and his mentorship of Natalie make him actually suffer. Like Siddhartha with his son, Ryan learns wisdom must be experienced, that the anattā (non-self) doctrine undercuts the identity he built on his job, and that the goal is not escaping the world but living the Middle Path within it, present to suffering rather than spinning silver linings.

### The Four Noble Truths

The Four Noble Truths form the core framework of the Buddha's teaching about suffering and its resolution. They state that life is pervaded by suffering or unsatisfactoriness (dukkha), that this suffering arises from craving and attachment, that it can cease when craving is extinguished, and that there is a path—the Noble Eightfold Path—leading to that cessation. Presented like a physician's diagnosis and cure, they set out both the problem of human dissatisfaction and a practical program for overcoming it.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 57 "Unknown" — This section develops the other edge of the mirror: the mind must not only reflect but be freed from reflection. Neo loses the Construct kumite because his mind 'stops' - Takuan Soho's detained mind that fixes on the sword instead of acting with mushin, no-mind - and his doubts before the Oracle show a mind still detained, since she never says he is not the One. Trinity's letting-go of fear revives Neo and his letting-go makes him the One, an instance of pratityasamutpada; the chapter maps the arc onto the Four Noble Truths, with Morpheus's 'prison for the mind' (for, not of) as the Third Truth's promise that liberation is possible through freeing the mind.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 14 "Mind the Mindfulness" — Reads The Meaning of Life as a sustained reductio of transcendentalism — the two-world metaphysics shared by Plato, Augustine, and Vedanta's Brahman/atman — arguing that the film's dehumanizing sketches (the machine that goes 'ping,' the 'every sperm is sacred' father selling his children, the Vegas-style Christmas in Heaven) show how otherworldly belief overrides this-worldly compassion. It parallels the Buddha's scriptural critiques: the Agganna sutta against caste, the no-self (anatta) doctrine against the Bhagavad Gita's soul that licenses Krishna to tell Arjuna killing is a favor, and impermanence (anicca) against the fantasy of eternal bliss. Python's grotesque — Creosote's explosion, the organ-donor lady's 'Galaxy Song' despair — matches Buddhist corpse meditations, while the film steers between hedonism (Creosote) and nihilism (the housewife who surrenders her liver) toward the Buddha's Middle Way and, against everyday distraction (the boardroom's 'people are not wearing enough hats,' the couple who think Schopenhauer begins with an S), toward mindfulness (sati).
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 44 "“How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons" — James McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism: the fleet's sleepless FTL jumps in "33" and Roslin's dwindling survivor counts enact the four noble truths, Leoben's interrogation scenes teach that suffering comes from ignorant attachment, and Dogen's no-self and impermanence frame the show's interdependent characters. Cylon resurrection, D'Anna's serial deaths, and the prophecy that "all of this has happened before" model karma and samsara, while Nishida's kenotic God of Absolute Nothingness makes sense of Six and Leoben's God of love. Because Cylons feel pain, fear death away from a resurrection ship, and act volitionally, McRae concludes they are persons in the Buddhist sense, owed the compassion of the Eightfold Path.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 19 "Encore" — Randall Auxier adopts 'I trust Phil' — Phil Lesh the bass player who hears the whole sound — as his epistemic principle for asking whether death is to be dreaded, staging the essay around interview riffs with Deadheads Dale, Robbie, and Cory. Socrates in the Phaedo and the Buddha's Four Noble Truths converge on welcoming death — samsara is the 'Samsonite Scenario', bad luggage your own wishing keeps repacking — while Hume's Dialogues make God's power, goodness, and evil an inconsistent triad, so immortality is 'not that cool'. Kant's postulates (God, freedom, immortality) and categorical imperative prove too rule-bound for creative life; Whitehead's self-creativity and 'objective immortality of the past' supply the real bass line: even God cannot unmake what you have played, and the properly Grateful response is gratitude for the chance to add your riff to the Acid Test.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 21 "Analyzing Emptiness" — Paul Gass reads the Dead's hippie milieu (the Beats, the Acid Tests, Buddhist-monk lyricist Peter Monk) as a conduit for Buddhist doctrine, taking the 'Eyes of the World' chorus as an invitation to awaken to Buddha-nature. He explains the Four Noble Truths, karma, and the five aggregates to argue the self is an illusion, using the image of a flame passed between lighters at a Dead show to picture rebirth without a persisting soul. The chapter then presents Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka middle way — emptiness itself must not be clutched as an absolute truth — and reads the 'redeemer... wagon loaded with clay' verse of 'Eyes of the World' as the Mahayana bodhisattva liberating all beings, with emptiness finally discarded like the boat after crossing the river.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 26 "Sudden Enlightenment" — Luke Cuddy and Michael Bruce ask whether Beatrix Kiddo could reach enlightenment, reading Kill Bill's nonlinear plotting as a Buddhist interconnected web of causes: Pai Mei's Five Point Palm technique causes both the coffin escape and Bill's death, and Budd's degraded trailer life is karma catching up. Beatrix grasps the structure of suffering and its cause—she locates it in Bill and the squad and eliminates them—but mistakes that for ending suffering itself, and her declared lack of 'mercy, compassion, and forgiveness' blocks the compassion enlightenment requires, while Bill's 'natural born killer' story contradicts impermanence and no-self. The chapter closes on her bathroom-floor ecstasy as a candidate case of Zen sudden enlightenment, left to the reader to judge by how she would one day treat a vengeful Nikki.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 18 "Halo as a Catalyst for a Buddhism Videogame" — Luke Cuddy uses Halo 3 checkpoints and emulator save states—two mutually exclusive Flood-fight outcomes both in some sense true—to make David Lewis's possible worlds and modal truth concrete, with Leibniz as the doctrine's ancestor. Halo's infinite lives make players genuinely angry, and the chapter argues this is upaya territory: like the father in the Lotus Sutra's parable of the burning house, the game promises mastery (the goat-, deer-, and ox-carts) to lure players toward something greater outside it. Master Chief becomes a Bodhisattva whose avatar slides between extension of self and other, provoking the 'who am I?' crisis that reveals the ego as empty at the ultimate level of the Two-Fold Truth, while the Dalai Lama's enemies-as-teachers turns the seven-year-old who pwns you into practice in the first two Noble Truths' suffering and anger.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 22 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Klein and Fundora trace Jobs's Buddhism from Reed College meditation and the seven-month India pilgrimage (reading Yogananda's Autobiography of a Yogi yearly) to the Zen minimalism of Apple design, arguing his temper tantrums, harsh speech, and reality distortion field do not disqualify him from being 'on the path' since Buddhism is a practice, not a creed test. They expound the Four Noble Truths (dukkha in its three kinds, via Thich Nhat Hanh), the Eightfold Path's Middle Way, and anatta—the non-self they compare to Hume's bundle theory of the self against Descartes's thinking thing—and read Jobs's strip-away-the-essence aesthetics, the three-click intuitive iPod interface that keeps users in the moment, the non-dualist marriage of art and technology, and his Think Different self-reliance as deeply Buddhist authenticity.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 11 "3. Tris Finds Enlightenment" — Rhine argues that Tris's heroism rests on Buddhist practice: her breath-counting on the Ferris wheel and inside Four's fear landscape, her emotional intelligence, and her awareness of the parental 'voices in her head' are classic meditative disciplines for calming the ego whose clinging, on the Buddhist account, is the cause of suffering (dukkha). She reads Abnegation's gray houses, plain food, and four-times-a-year mirror as ritual ego-diminishment - a middle way between indulgence and the extreme asceticism the Buddha rejected - that explains why most Divergent arise from Abnegation. Contemporary neuroscience is then recruited: the amygdala-versus-prefrontal-cortex struggle Will describes, and monks' heightened gamma waves, explain how Tris can see the simulation as a simulation, like Neo in The Matrix, and act while others are paralyzed by fear.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 18 "6. You’re Gonna Die" — Ethan Mills uses the Buddha and Epicurus to show that Louis meets death with laughter instead of fear. The Buddha's diagnosis of dukkha ('dissatisfactoriness') explains the Blu-Ray player and cellphone bits - consumer desire just restarts the craving cycle - and impermanence frames both the Amia heartbreak that Dr. Bigelow reframes as 'misery is wasted on the miserable' and Louie's 'life isn't that long... it's happy math' reflection, while rebirth would only make things worse since you would have to repeat junior high forever. Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us (where death is, you are not) grounds Louie's 'lots of things happen after you die, just none of them include you,' backed by atomism - at death our atoms scatter - and by gods who, like Louie's maybe-God with no heaven, guarantee no immortality. The USO duckling episode models the payoff: comedy defuses our deepest anxiety about annihilation the way it defuses the soldiers' tension in Afghanistan.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 36 "23. I Fight Crime in My Sleep" — Staged as a Fight Club parody in which a Buddhist psychiatrist, Dr. Quinzel, evaluates a costumed narrator sent to Arkham, the chapter argues neither hero is close to awakening: Batman's crime-fighting is craving that perpetuates dukkha, his secret identities a twice-constructed self that the Buddha's no-self teaching dissolves, and his violence fails the test that 'hostility is never appeased by hostility.' Superman fares no better - his super-intellect imposes illusory order on impermanence, his flight and X-ray vision are distractions beside the Buddha-eye and tapas, and as one of the titans of the six realms he is further from Buddhahood than a human - while the doctor defines justice as karma rather than retaliation and finds Batman one step from American Psycho's Bateman. Only conquering Mara, one's own inner deceiver, is 'the only superpower worth having,' and the closing reveal that the doctor has a plan of her own for 'Mr. Kent' caps the diagnosis.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 31 "17. Dialog with the Buddha" — A Platonic-style fictional dialogue in which a newly enlightened "Canadian Buddha" walks out of the northern Ontario bush to the Prolethean farm and debates Tomas, Henry, and Bonnie over whether clones are abominations. Using karma, rebirth, the gandhabba that carries consciousness-flux to a new embryo, the no-soul doctrine, and the eightfold path, the Buddha argues clones are ordinary beings of the karmic flux — like the split bacterium, nothing unnatural — but that cloning multiplies clinging: hosts crave immortality through copies, each clone inherits the host's whole accumulated karma, and Henry's dream of training an army of Helena-clones would only deepen the unsatisfactoriness the Buddha's mustard-seed lesson says clinging to the dead always brings. Only ending the cycle through enlightenment releases anyone; the clone, like the lost child, is not the one you lost.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 15 "6. Bowie the Buddhist" — Muchall reads 'Quicksand' and 'Where Are We Now?' as suffused with Tibetan Buddhism: 'Don't believe in yourself' voices the anatta teaching Bowie absorbed studying with Chime Rinpoche and from Chogyam Trungpa, whose 'spiritual materialism' warns that ego converts even spirituality and ideologies to its own use. After retelling the Buddha's life, the Four Noble Truths' three kinds of dukkha, and the five aggregates that reveal no permanent self, the chapter maps the song's 'ragged hole' and bardos onto the Tibetan Book of the Dead's after-death journey, and reads Bowie's morphing personas as lived acknowledgment that there is no fixed self - 'there's nothing in here.'
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 43 "28. Zen and the Art of Deadpool" — The chapter argues Deadpool's unconventional style belies a Zen Buddhist disposition: created as a balance of Spider-Man's wit and Wolverine's lethality (against his disciplined template Deathstroke), he displays mushin, the no-mind calm of the trained martial artist under fire. His story is mapped onto the Four Noble Truths - dukkha in the suicidal depression over his incurable cancer scarring, samudaya in his attachment to belonging that he masks with jokes and loner behavior, nirodha in his ended relationships with Death and Siryn, and magga in shooting himself in the head at the end of Dark Reign as a perverse stilling of the mind. His fourth-wall awareness is read as piercing maya, the veil of illusion, an enlightenment no other Marvel character shares, though he remains 'not a good Buddhist' since he still wallows in ego and attachment.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 23 "11. 999 Fingers" — Voiced by a composite being shredded together from every AHS character, the chapter retells the Buddha's path - Siddhartha sheltered from suffering like a pampered prince, enlightenment as watching 'every episode of American Horror Story', Mara's temptations, and Angulimala with his garland of 999 fingers converted to monkhood - to read Briarcliff's cruelty, Sister Jude's devil, and Bloody Face's son Johnny as suffering born of clinging, in a contingent, moment-to-moment world of karma and rebirth, while Nietzsche's killed God, eternal recurrence, and ressentiment frame the question of who is to blame when there is no creator.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 24 "12. A Month from Now, I’ll Be a Balding, Toothless Skeleton" — Reads Fiona Goode's war against fading - the experimental RM47 serum, rejecting the Axeman's escape because he would watch her decay, the Papa Legba bargain that collapses because she has no soul - alongside Delphine LaLaurie's blood facials and Marie Laveau's child sacrifices, as illustrations of Buddhist dukkha and the three thirsts (kama for sense pleasure, bhava for existence, vibhava for annihilation). Legba's 'you don't have a soul' becomes an accidentally liberating glimpse of anatta, and Cordelia's dying advice - 'feel the fear... let it all go' - is the mindfulness, echoing Buddhaghosa's corpse meditations, that might have freed Fiona.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 26 "15. Happy in Oceania" — Ćirić and Ćurko ask what philosophy could have done for Winston, imagining a counterfactual Oceania where he reads Walpole's line that the world is 'a comedy to those that think, a tragedy to those that feel' and learns from Julia that another worldview is possible. They present philosophy as therapy: Kant's notion of worldview (Weltanschauung), Epicurean ataraxia, the Buddhist four noble truths, Frankl's logotherapy, and Stoic premeditation of the worst as resources for reworking the beliefs that made Winston live in fear. The Party's true target, they argue, is critical thinking — from Dewey's ideal of education as learning to think to Frankfurt's On Bullshit — and Kant's Enlightenment motto 'have the courage to use your own understanding' is the weapon that could still defeat Ingsoc.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 12 "The Wisdom of Combination" — Isrow maps each bending art to its real martial art and source philosophy: Katara's Taiji waterbending embodies Daoist wu-wei when she forgoes revenge on Yon Rha ('The Southern Raiders'); Toph's Hong Jia earthbending expresses the Buddhist eightfold path's Right Speech through her insistence on truth; Zuko's Northern Shaolin firebending enacts the Four Noble Truths, his desire-driven suffering ending only when he abandons chasing the Avatar; and Aang's Daoist Baguazhang airbending makes freedom openness to change, shown in his receptivity to Iroh's advice. The Avatar's true power is combining these character strengths, not merely wielding four elements.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 28 "What Can We Learn" — Argues ATLA repeatedly dissolves false alternatives rather than solving conflicts, modeling the Buddha's middle way from the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta: refuse the two extremes instead of picking one. Earth is the case study — Bumi is both crazy and wise, Toph both blind and the most powerful bender, and 'The Cave of Two Lovers' shows the first earthbenders using their art for love, with Oma ending the feud by declaring the war over rather than destroying both villages. Aang's energybending against Ozai dissolves the kill-or-be-killed framework, Bumi's 'neutral jing' rejects fight-or-flight, and Toph's life refutes the capable-vs-helpless and girl-vs-fighter dichotomies her parents impose.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 12 "The Wisdom of Combination" — A martial artist maps each bending style onto the real art it animates and its parent philosophy: Katara's Taiji waterbending embodies wu-wei, shown when she spares Yon Rha in 'The Southern Raiders' as strength rather than weakness; Toph's Hong Jia earthbending grounds her insistence on truth, an example of the Buddhist eightfold path's Right Speech; Zuko's driven Northern Shaolin temperament walks through the first three Noble Truths, from suffering caused by desire for his honor to its cessation when he joins Team Avatar; and Aang's Baguazhang airbending expresses freedom as openness to change and to Iroh's counsel. The Avatar's power is therefore not four bendings but the combination of the four character strengths.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 28 "What Can We Learn" — Argues that ATLA teaches the rejection of false alternatives by first setting up one-sided stereotypes of earth and then dissolving them: Bumi is both crazy and rational, Toph both tough and sensitive (enjoying the Fancy Lady Day Spa), and earthbending originates in love and secrecy, not rock-throwing, in the tale of Oma and Shu. The chapter explicitly imports the Buddha's first sermon's middle way between sensual indulgence and self-mortification, applying it to Aang's refusal of both killing Ozai and being killed: energybending dissolves the 'kill or be killed' framework rather than picking a side, just as Bumi's 'neutral jing' refuses both attack and retreat. Oma ending the war by building Omashu with both villages, and the compromise over Yu Dao in The Promise, are read as dissolutions of us-vs-them framing, while the duality of Sozin and Roku ('anyone's capable of great good and great evil') shows two-sidedness as the condition of Zuko's redemption.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 34 "Happily, Ever After" — The chapter asks whether Nish's revenge in 'Black Museum' - poisoning Rolo and downloading his digital self into her father Clayton's eternal-electrocution exhibit - is morally justified. Nussbaum's Anger and Forgiveness condemns payback as sadism plus 'magical thinking' and prescribes transition-anger, then unconditional forgiveness, then best of all unconditional love (the prodigal son); Christian agape commands loving enemies and leaving wrath to God; and the Buddhist analysis of dukkha, karma and non-self shows Nish's hateful revenge generates worse karma than Rolo's greed and deepens the very suffering it means to end. The verdict: revenge, however emotionally satisfying, is never justified - even the tourists zapping Clayton and Nish zapping Rolo fall into the same trap.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 21 "a9.xhtml" — The chapter argues Tolkien's clearest moral in The Hobbit is against possessiveness, starting from Aquinas' definition of greed as 'immoderate love of riches': dragon-sickness ruins Thorin and drowns the Master of Lake-town starving in the wilderness with his gold, and Gollum shows the isolating end of a life organized around a 'precious'. Buddhism reframes the diagnosis - Gollum's craving (tanha) is rooted in ignorance (avidya) of the self's illusoriness, since grasping enriches a self that does not exist, per the Four Noble Truths - while Laozi's 'he who knows he has enough is rich' and Thoreau's 'a man is rich in proportion to the things he can afford to let alone' are embodied by Beorn and the gift-giving, nearly government-less hobbits. Bilbo's generosity - giving away the Arkenstone worth 'more than a river of gold', taking only two small chests, later giving Sting and the mithril coat to Frodo - is the book's counter-example to greed.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 36 "23. I Fight Crime in My Sleep" — A Fight Club-style Arkham case study: a patient's hallucinated Superman companion is diagnosed by a Buddhist psychiatrist who explains the three marks of existence—impermanence, non-self, and dissatisfaction—arguing superheroes impose order and a fabricated second self on a world that resists both, so Superman's super-intellect and even flight are distractions (levitation should be ignored; the Buddha-eye beats x-ray vision) while Batman's violence and psychosis, compared to American Psycho's Patrick Bateman, make awakening impossible—both are victims of Mara. A robber literally named David Hume objects that the heroes' law and order is grounded on what ought to be rather than what is, and a Gandhi quote on preferring one's own bad government explains why Batman finally kryptonites his alien 'friend.' The verdict inverts the book's debate: conquering the deceiver within is the only superpower worth having.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 19 "The Zen Master and the Big Aristotle" — Allhoff and Vaidya argue against the skeptic that philosophy is useless 'bullshit' (nodding to Frankfurt's book) by showing how Phil Jackson's coaching applies it. Jackson's Zen Buddhism, especially zazen meditation and selfless 'triangle offense' play, teaches players to empty the ego and stay in the present, transforming Jordan from point-maker to play-maker; and Jackson's gift of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics to Shaquille O'Neal, who then dubbed himself 'the Big Aristotle,' illustrates Aristotle's doctrine that excellence (his improved free-throw shooting, his generosity) is a habit built by repetition.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — McClelland opens with the Buddha's claim that all life is suffering and reads Eastwood's aging-hero films (The Eiger Sanction, Firefox, Unforgiven, In the Line of Fire, Blood Work, Mystic River, Million Dollar Baby, Gran Torino) as grounding two opposed inductions on the meaning of loss. The 'pessimistic induction' holds that many losses—Maggie's paralysis, Dave Boyle's abuse, Munny's dead—are irremediable, supporting an Aristotelian view that death dissolves the person with the body. The 'optimistic induction' draws on the science of ecological resilience to argue losses can be navigated with others' help; Walt's autonomous, meaning-making death exemplifies resilience. Hereafter's agnosticism about survival leaves Eastwood's own verdict on surviving death as 'I don't know.'
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 21 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — Judith Barad explains the puzzling elements of Kundun—the compassion for enemies, the child taken from his parents, the swept-away sand mandala, the sky burial—through Tibetan Buddhist ethics, arguing it closely parallels Greek and Roman Stoicism. She reads the young Dalai Lama's growth into compassion and nonviolence toward Mao and the Chinese alongside Epictetus's teaching that only our own judgments, not others' acts, can harm us, and that we must restrain desire and attachment. The Four Noble Truths reframe the film: because all things (including the self) are impermanent and interconnected, the destruction of the mandala and the feeding of the father's corpse to vultures enact detachment, and true liberation via the Eightfold Path is self-won inner peace that China cannot seize.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 44 "“How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons" — James McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism: the fleet's annihilation and constant death illustrate the Four Noble Truths' duhkha, arising from ignorant attachment and violating interdependent arising (no-self and impermanence). Cylon death-and-resurrection parallels karma and rebirth ('all of this has happened before'), Leoben acts as a koan-wielding roshi unsettling Starbuck's assumptions, and Nishida's kenotic God as Absolute Nothingness matches the Cylons' 'we're all God.' Because Cylons feel pain, suffer cognitively, and earn karma, McRae concludes they are persons capable of satori who should seek compassionate reconciliation with humans.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 18 "MOTHERHOOD" — Sheryl Tuttle Ross applies three of the Buddhist noble truths – pain is inevitable, pain arises from attachment, suffering can end – to contemporary mothering, contrasting the Buddhist acceptance of pain with Bentham's utilitarian pleasure-maximizing. Drawing on Thich Nhat Hanh's mindfulness and the doctrines of impermanence and no-self, she offers 'mommy meditations' (breathe, become aware, recognize social scripts, respond kindly) and reads the novel I Don't Know How She Does It, whose 'Court of Motherhood' dramatizes the guilt-inducing scripts mindfulness helps mothers see through to experience beauty in ordinary moments.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 15 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Geisz reads his daily morning coffee ritual through Buddhist metaphysics: the pre-caffeine grogginess and its transient relief illustrate saṃsāra and duḥkha, the First Noble Truth, driven by self-centered craving (the Second). The transience of the perfect-temperature cup shows impermanence (anitya), and the question of whether a 'self' pre- or post-coffee exists is answered by anatman — he offers three hypotheses (full self dormant, half coffee-cyborg, self created ex Coffea) then dissolves them into no-self plus dependent arising, where the cup and drinker are empty nodes in a web of physical, economic, and karmic conditions. Each intentional sip lays down karma that binds tomorrow's 'me' further into the cycle.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 35 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Lynch, a tattooed Buddhist philosophy professor, tests his largely Buddhist body art (an Om-mani-padme-hum armband, Bodhidharma, the Buddha's face, the eight-spoked Wheel and lotus, a double-vajra) against the Buddha's Three Marks of Existence. He argues a 'permanent' tattoo need not contradict impermanence any more than Gruzalski's washed-away sandcastle if approached mindfully, that custom ink need not reify a self given the chariot analogy of no-self (which he links to Hume's bundle view), and that the pain of tattooing directly instantiates dukkha and can become an object of meditation and compassion. Mindful tattooing, he concludes, can itself be authentic Buddhist practice.
- **Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low**, ch. 25 "BLUES" — Joseph Lynch uses Son House's 'Preachin' the Blues' — a fallen preacher who preaches the blues, not the gospel — to explore the tension between blues sensuality and religion, arguing the expression of suffering is itself liberation from it. He reads Marx's 'religion is the sigh of the oppressed creature' as making the blues a heart of a heartless world that voices and eases alienated labor; the Buddha's Four Noble Truths and impermanence as embracing suffering to be freed from craving; and Kierkegaard's passionate leap of faith, born of doubt and despair and contrasted with Hume, as the model for how blues 'preachers' like Son House and Robert Johnson embrace the absurd contradiction of embodied spirituality.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 44 "“How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons" — McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism, using Dogen and the Four Noble Truths. The fleet's relentless suffering (the "33" jumps, the Olympic Carrier), impermanence (Roslin's dwindling headcount), and no-self frame duhkha; Leoben functions as a roshi whose koan-like preaching makes Starbuck and Adama question their false ideals, and the Cylon death-and-resurrection cycle parallels karma and rebirth. Because Cylons feel and are cognitively aware of pain and can accrue karma, McRae concludes they are persons capable of satori, so human and Cylon liberation are intertwined.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 45 "42. Up in the Air as Philosophy Buddhism and the Middle Path" — Duffy reads Ryan Bingham's arc in Up in the Air as a Zen Buddhist parable paralleling Hesse's Siddhartha. Ryan preaches an 'empty backpack' philosophy of nonattachment and treats the miles as their own point, but Duffy argues he only intellectually grasps the four noble truths — dukkha, its cause in attachment (tṛṣṇā), and the eightfold path — until his failed attachment to Alex and his mentorship of Natalie make him actually suffer. Like Siddhartha with his son, Ryan learns wisdom must be experienced, that the anattā (non-self) doctrine undercuts the identity he built on his job, and that the goal is not escaping the world but living the Middle Path within it, present to suffering rather than spinning silver linings.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 69 "65. Louis CK as Philosopher The King and His Fall" — Marra Henrigillis first shows CK as 'philosopher king of comedy'—his cell-phone/'forever empty' bit echoing Buddhist and Stoic teaching on sitting with suffering, his 'why?' bit echoing Quine on not ontologizing, his 'So Did The Fat Lady' episode exposing how society denies fat women full humanity—then uses his 2017 misconduct scandal to stage competing verdicts: the feminist case for banning him (rape culture, power dynamics), Plato on censoring vicious art, Mill's four-part defense of free expression and Nozick's free-market/entitlement view against cancellation, and Aristotle's virtue ethics (character judged over a whole life) plus Pompa's prison-education view that no one is only their worst act.

### Karma and Rebirth

In Buddhist thought, karma is the principle that intentional actions carry moral consequences that shape one's future experience and, across the cycle of rebirth, one's future existences. Wholesome intentions and deeds tend toward better outcomes while harmful ones lead to suffering, so character and circumstance are understood as the ripening of past choices rather than the decree of a judging deity. Bound up with rebirth, karma explains the continuity of moral cause and effect through successive lives, until liberation frees one from the cycle altogether.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 61 "Unknown" — The chapter argues the film is by no means a Christian movie: Neo is a violent, far-from-sinless mere human savior; the fundamental human problem is ignorance and illusion (Gnostic and Eastern) rather than sin and alienation from God; the rebels' belief that Neo is the reincarnation of the earlier liberator mirrors the Dalai Lama search the Wachowskis cite, though reincarnation is rejected by all major Christian sects; and 'there is no spoon' asserts the illusoriness of empirical reality that Christianity denies. The film's malleable, cyclical time and the Wachowskis' answer that faith is 'in oneself' complete a syncretistic tapestry the essay goes on to examine as religious pluralism.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 81 "Unknown" — The chapter argues the third postulate must be a this-worldly immortality: since no single lifetime suffices to realize the Highest Good, Kant himself (in Universal Natural History) imagined the soul reborn over and over as it climbs the ladder of human perfection, and Mahayana Buddhism's bodhisattva - who chooses to remain on the wheel of rebirth to enlighten all beings - matches the monkish boy 'Potential' and the Oracle's hints. The One accordingly appears in three incarnations: the earlier liberator who freed the first rebels, Neo's second life, and the third life glimpsed at the film's end.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 100 "In It for the Long Run" — Adds Reason Five — being moral always pays in the long run, where the long run includes life after death — arguing that a perfectly good and all-powerful God would not set up a moral order that penalizes virtue, so Peter Parker's virtue is guaranteed its reward beyond this life. It notes that Eastern reincarnation-plus-karma makes the same promise (the more virtuous this life, the better the next), and that since Peter, Uncle Ben and Aunt May would never water morality down, the morally serious are pushed toward these metaphysical guarantees.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 101 "Superheroes, Duty, and the Biggest of Big Pictures" — Argues that non-theistic karma undermines itself: the impersonal moral laws connecting each soul's deeds to its circumstances in the next life would be enormously complex and would serve the moral end of justice, and order that intricate serving a moral end demands an intelligent cause, so reincarnation becomes evidence for God. It closes the chapter by comparing the universe's moral order to a superhero's origin story — it would have to begin with something like a God.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 36 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Observes that only Talking Animals enter Aslan's country when Narnia ends in The Last Battle, then critically examines Lewis's case against wider animal salvation: derivative immortality through human love (Sarah Smith's train of beasts in The Great Divorce), compensation of animal pain in an afterlife, Lewis's follow-Descartes claim that most animals are sentient but not conscious enough to feel pain or have a surviving 'self'. The chapter argues each point fails: the physiological evidence shows animals suffer, resurrection or God-given souls remain possible (Strawberry's transformation into a winged Talking horse), and a compensatory hereafter is still the most promising answer to why a loving God permits the fawn's miserable death. Aquinas's rational-creature hierarchy frames the Talking/Dumb divide, and the Hindu-Buddhist rebirth theodicy is considered and rejected as unbiblical.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 44 "“How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons" — James McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism: the fleet's sleepless FTL jumps in "33" and Roslin's dwindling survivor counts enact the four noble truths, Leoben's interrogation scenes teach that suffering comes from ignorant attachment, and Dogen's no-self and impermanence frame the show's interdependent characters. Cylon resurrection, D'Anna's serial deaths, and the prophecy that "all of this has happened before" model karma and samsara, while Nishida's kenotic God of Absolute Nothingness makes sense of Six and Leoben's God of love. Because Cylons feel pain, fear death away from a resurrection ship, and act volitionally, McRae concludes they are persons in the Buddhist sense, owed the compassion of the Eightfold Path.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 14 "Are We Going Too Far" — David Kyle Johnson distinguishes revenge (personal, emotional, unlimited) from retribution and argues that 'Tarantino's view'—mercy should be common practice yet revenge can be justified—is consistent: Jules buys Pumpkin and Honey Bunny's lives but never waives a right of vengeance, since they never wronged him. He tests the view against Bushido, showing Beatrix's revolt against her lord Bill violates the samurai code, and against karma, which makes revenge unnecessary. After finding that Hobbes, Locke, Nietzsche and Socrates all leave revenge's justification open, he defends it—citing Budd's 'that woman deserves her revenge'—so long as the punishment fits the crime and spares innocents, as when Beatrix refuses to make herself even by killing Vernita's daughter Nikki.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 26 "Sudden Enlightenment" — Luke Cuddy and Michael Bruce ask whether Beatrix Kiddo could reach enlightenment, reading Kill Bill's nonlinear plotting as a Buddhist interconnected web of causes: Pai Mei's Five Point Palm technique causes both the coffin escape and Bill's death, and Budd's degraded trailer life is karma catching up. Beatrix grasps the structure of suffering and its cause—she locates it in Bill and the squad and eliminates them—but mistakes that for ending suffering itself, and her declared lack of 'mercy, compassion, and forgiveness' blocks the compassion enlightenment requires, while Bill's 'natural born killer' story contradicts impermanence and no-self. The chapter closes on her bathroom-floor ecstasy as a candidate case of Zen sudden enlightenment, left to the reader to judge by how she would one day treat a vengeful Nikki.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 19 "Into the Future" — Hanley dismantles the four claimed human/Cylon differences: artificial reproduction is in principle possible for us; prosthetics already blur what we are made of; model copies differ like identical twins (Boomer is not Athena); and resurrection has human analogues — he proposes an SDTR (scanning, death, transmission, replication) model and uses van Inwagen's replica-switch account of bodily resurrection while rejecting soul-based reincarnation on Lockean grounds, since consciousness rather than soul is the criterion of identity. He defends reproductive cloning as reproduction, not replication (a clone is your child, not your copy), and reads Athena's memories of Tyrol as evidence she is a replicated Boomer. The upshot: being a Cylon is nothing to fear — 'I am a Cylon, and so are you.'
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 22 "What Monkey Should Have Known" — Mortensen opens with Monkey from Journey to the West beating six robbers to death despite Tripitaka's protest, and asks whether a practitioner of budo can be a Buddhist. He defends three principles, Take No Life, No First Strike and Stop Before Harm, qualifying them via the Upaya-kausalya Sutra's sea captain, Funakoshi's 'there is no first strike in karate', Ueshiba's purely defensive aikido, the initiator's bad karma, and the exception of multiple attackers; then he applies them to weapons, arguing that wooden weapons (the jo, Musashi's bokken, above all the humble walking stick, the 'last legal weapon') fit the precepts where the katana does not. Monkey, in short, should have carried a stick.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 36 "23. I Fight Crime in My Sleep" — Staged as a Fight Club parody in which a Buddhist psychiatrist, Dr. Quinzel, evaluates a costumed narrator sent to Arkham, the chapter argues neither hero is close to awakening: Batman's crime-fighting is craving that perpetuates dukkha, his secret identities a twice-constructed self that the Buddha's no-self teaching dissolves, and his violence fails the test that 'hostility is never appeased by hostility.' Superman fares no better - his super-intellect imposes illusory order on impermanence, his flight and X-ray vision are distractions beside the Buddha-eye and tapas, and as one of the titans of the six realms he is further from Buddhahood than a human - while the doctor defines justice as karma rather than retaliation and finds Batman one step from American Psycho's Bateman. Only conquering Mara, one's own inner deceiver, is 'the only superpower worth having,' and the closing reveal that the doctor has a plan of her own for 'Mr. Kent' caps the diagnosis.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 31 "17. Dialog with the Buddha" — A Platonic-style fictional dialogue in which a newly enlightened "Canadian Buddha" walks out of the northern Ontario bush to the Prolethean farm and debates Tomas, Henry, and Bonnie over whether clones are abominations. Using karma, rebirth, the gandhabba that carries consciousness-flux to a new embryo, the no-soul doctrine, and the eightfold path, the Buddha argues clones are ordinary beings of the karmic flux — like the split bacterium, nothing unnatural — but that cloning multiplies clinging: hosts crave immortality through copies, each clone inherits the host's whole accumulated karma, and Henry's dream of training an army of Helena-clones would only deepen the unsatisfactoriness the Buddha's mustard-seed lesson says clinging to the dead always brings. Only ending the cycle through enlightenment releases anyone; the clone, like the lost child, is not the one you lost.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 16 "6. The Accidental Hero" — Darian Shump judges Deadpool by Buddhist lights, applying karma as intentional action and skillful means—the permissibility of compassionate killing, after Rupert Gethin—to his Marvel NOW! career: protecting Agent Preston, saving a child and Nightcrawler Kim mid-battle, and the Niagara Bride assisted suicide whose fee he donates to a home for kids with cancer. A hypothetical Hydra spy with a bomb on a S.H.I.E.L.D. helicarrier shows how killing one murderer-to-be can be the compassionate act that saves everyone. He concludes Deadpool is an 'accidental hero'—a mercenary first whose good intentions make him a karmic hero—while Zenpool's failed pacifism in AXIS shows that renouncing violence betrays what makes Deadpool Deadpool.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 23 "11. 999 Fingers" — Voiced by a composite being shredded together from every AHS character, the chapter retells the Buddha's path - Siddhartha sheltered from suffering like a pampered prince, enlightenment as watching 'every episode of American Horror Story', Mara's temptations, and Angulimala with his garland of 999 fingers converted to monkhood - to read Briarcliff's cruelty, Sister Jude's devil, and Bloody Face's son Johnny as suffering born of clinging, in a contingent, moment-to-moment world of karma and rebirth, while Nietzsche's killed God, eternal recurrence, and ressentiment frame the question of who is to blame when there is no creator.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 17 "8. Ode to Joi" — Steve Bein first tests Joi against Mary Anne Warren's five functionalist personhood criteria — consciousness, reason, self-motivated activity, communication, self-awareness — and finds she passes, which makes Luv's stomping of the emanator a murder. The Buddha's no-self doctrine then denies that anyone, Joi included, is an enduring person: we are bundles of fleeting psychophysical processes, 'like tears in rain', which threatens to let Luv plead that the Luv who killed Joi no longer exists. Nagarjuna's two truths resolve the courtroom problem: ultimately there are no persons, but conventionally 'Luv killed Joi' is perfectly true, and the karma ripples through the whole network.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 34 "19. Hinduism Gets More than Five Percent Right" — Kaur and Gupta argue Hinduism got far more than five percent right, mapping the show's points onto karmic theory and the Bhagavad Gita's three kinds of action: right action, inaction, and wrong action. Eleanor's fruitless point-grubbing and selfless departure exemplify nishkama karma, desire-less action, while the 802 reboots and Janet's memory-wiped revivals mirror the birth-death-rebirth cycle on the way to self-realization. Ranking the cast on the Gita's ladder of unfoldment, desire-driven Eleanor and Jason below Tahani and knowledgeable Chidi, with Michael straying from his dharma and detached, duty-bound Janet nearest to Brahman, they show the series dramatizes the Gita's teaching that motivation, not the deed itself, determines an act's worth.
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 24 "The Danger of Thinking “Science Is Whatever We Want It to Be”; or, the" — Barkman reads the 30 Rock cast as prisoners who prefer delusion, using Plato's allegory of the cave and the Upanishadic scheme of samsara, karma, maya, and moksha, in which Atman is realized as one with Brahman, as twin diagnoses. Drew's 'bubble' of good looks, Liz's false memory of being a harmless nerd in 'Reunion' and her belief she can have it all, Jack's pride about his terrible sketch ideas, Kenneth's unexamined dogma ('I can't handle the truth!'), Jenna's age-hiding, and Tracy's white myths about diabetes and Colorado all illustrate ignorance of reality that costs happiness. The Hindu-Platonic lesson is that knowledge of reality, not Dr. Spaceman's 'science is whatever we want it to be', is the route to happiness, because ignorance is not bliss.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 34 "Happily, Ever After" — The chapter asks whether Nish's revenge in 'Black Museum' - poisoning Rolo and downloading his digital self into her father Clayton's eternal-electrocution exhibit - is morally justified. Nussbaum's Anger and Forgiveness condemns payback as sadism plus 'magical thinking' and prescribes transition-anger, then unconditional forgiveness, then best of all unconditional love (the prodigal son); Christian agape commands loving enemies and leaving wrath to God; and the Buddhist analysis of dukkha, karma and non-self shows Nish's hateful revenge generates worse karma than Rolo's greed and deepens the very suffering it means to end. The verdict: revenge, however emotionally satisfying, is never justified - even the tourists zapping Clayton and Nish zapping Rolo fall into the same trap.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 36 "23. I Fight Crime in My Sleep" — A Fight Club-style Arkham case study: a patient's hallucinated Superman companion is diagnosed by a Buddhist psychiatrist who explains the three marks of existence—impermanence, non-self, and dissatisfaction—arguing superheroes impose order and a fabricated second self on a world that resists both, so Superman's super-intellect and even flight are distractions (levitation should be ignored; the Buddha-eye beats x-ray vision) while Batman's violence and psychosis, compared to American Psycho's Patrick Bateman, make awakening impossible—both are victims of Mara. A robber literally named David Hume objects that the heroes' law and order is grounded on what ought to be rather than what is, and a Gandhi quote on preferring one's own bad government explains why Batman finally kryptonites his alien 'friend.' The verdict inverts the book's debate: conquering the deceiver within is the only superpower worth having.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 44 "“How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons" — James McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism: the fleet's annihilation and constant death illustrate the Four Noble Truths' duhkha, arising from ignorant attachment and violating interdependent arising (no-self and impermanence). Cylon death-and-resurrection parallels karma and rebirth ('all of this has happened before'), Leoben acts as a koan-wielding roshi unsettling Starbuck's assumptions, and Nishida's kenotic God as Absolute Nothingness matches the Cylons' 'we're all God.' Because Cylons feel pain, suffer cognitively, and earn karma, McRae concludes they are persons capable of satori who should seek compassionate reconciliation with humans.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 8 "Rāma of Gilead" — Matthew Butkus reads Roland Deschain of The Dark Tower as a parallel to Rama of the Ramayana and Arjuna of the Bhagavad Gita, mapping his cyclical existence onto the Hindu concepts of karma (his coupling with the demon spawning Mordred, letting Jake fall), dharma (the gunslinger's duty to protect the Beams as an avatar restoring cosmic order), samskara (character shaped by all past lives) and samsara (the death-rebirth cycle the Horn of Eld may or may not break). Like Krishna instructing the reluctant Arjuna, the text tells Roland he must 'stand and be true' regardless of misgivings; Butkus concludes the moral for readers is not violence but fulfilling one's own svadharma—to stand and be true in one's own station.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 15 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Geisz reads his daily morning coffee ritual through Buddhist metaphysics: the pre-caffeine grogginess and its transient relief illustrate saṃsāra and duḥkha, the First Noble Truth, driven by self-centered craving (the Second). The transience of the perfect-temperature cup shows impermanence (anitya), and the question of whether a 'self' pre- or post-coffee exists is answered by anatman — he offers three hypotheses (full self dormant, half coffee-cyborg, self created ex Coffea) then dissolves them into no-self plus dependent arising, where the cup and drinker are empty nodes in a web of physical, economic, and karmic conditions. Each intentional sip lays down karma that binds tomorrow's 'me' further into the cycle.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 20 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Deal and Waller use Lakoff and Johnson's conceptual-metaphor theory to explain how we grasp Santa's God-like moral omniscience through human metaphors. Santa 'sees from above' (North Pole, flight), judges with 'cool' reason yet remains jolly, and – echoing Plato's Phaedrus charioteer and Descartes' solitary reasoner – masters his appetites and decides free of bias. His gift-giving runs on a 'moral accounting' metaphor where good deeds are commodities exchanged for presents and 'moral authority is parental authority'; they read A Christmas Story's BB-gun lesson through this frame and finally liken Santa's impartial, dispassionate sorting of naughty and nice to the impersonal law of karma.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 13 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Kieran McManus's travel memoir 'Will I Find My Guru in India?' recounts his search from Kathmandu to Rishikesh and the Agama Yoga School, where teacher Kushru's lectures on karma, breath, and diet finally make asana click for him. His reported insight — that every thought and act moves him toward or away from his sacred potential, and that the yogi transcends suffering by treating each experience as neutral and as an opportunity, remaining present — applies a karmic and present-moment ethic to his own practice rather than expounding doctrine abstractly.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 44 "“How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons" — McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism, using Dogen and the Four Noble Truths. The fleet's relentless suffering (the "33" jumps, the Olympic Carrier), impermanence (Roslin's dwindling headcount), and no-self frame duhkha; Leoben functions as a roshi whose koan-like preaching makes Starbuck and Adama question their false ideals, and the Cylon death-and-resurrection cycle parallels karma and rebirth. Because Cylons feel and are cognitively aware of pain and can accrue karma, McRae concludes they are persons capable of satori, so human and Cylon liberation are intertwined.

### Impermanence (anicca)

Impermanence, or anicca, is the Buddhist teaching that all conditioned things are in constant flux, arising and passing away without any stable, lasting essence. Nothing—no object, feeling, thought, or self—remains fixed, and clinging to what is inherently changing is a central source of suffering. Recognizing impermanence is meant to loosen attachment and foster acceptance, and it stands alongside suffering and non-self as one of the three marks of existence in Buddhist thought.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 56 "Unknown" — Brannigan reads the film's mirror imagery through the Buddha's mirror instruction to his son Rahula: Neo touching the dripping mirror and becoming the mirror marks his awakening to the naked truth (aletheia as nakedness) that his world is a programmed illusion, Smith's dark sunglasses distort while Morpheus's mirrored glasses clarify, and Neo's reflection in the spoon-bending boy's spoon signals clarity. 'There is no spoon' parallels the Zen mondo where neither flag nor wind moves but only mind, and shows that reflected images are not reality - the world is maya. The deepest lesson is anatman: just as there is no spoon there is no Neo, no fixed self, and Rahula's lesson grounds the interdependence (pratityasamutpada) of all actions on others.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 14 "Mind the Mindfulness" — Reads The Meaning of Life as a sustained reductio of transcendentalism — the two-world metaphysics shared by Plato, Augustine, and Vedanta's Brahman/atman — arguing that the film's dehumanizing sketches (the machine that goes 'ping,' the 'every sperm is sacred' father selling his children, the Vegas-style Christmas in Heaven) show how otherworldly belief overrides this-worldly compassion. It parallels the Buddha's scriptural critiques: the Agganna sutta against caste, the no-self (anatta) doctrine against the Bhagavad Gita's soul that licenses Krishna to tell Arjuna killing is a favor, and impermanence (anicca) against the fantasy of eternal bliss. Python's grotesque — Creosote's explosion, the organ-donor lady's 'Galaxy Song' despair — matches Buddhist corpse meditations, while the film steers between hedonism (Creosote) and nihilism (the housewife who surrenders her liver) toward the Buddha's Middle Way and, against everyday distraction (the boardroom's 'people are not wearing enough hats,' the couple who think Schopenhauer begins with an S), toward mindfulness (sati).
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 44 "“How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons" — James McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism: the fleet's sleepless FTL jumps in "33" and Roslin's dwindling survivor counts enact the four noble truths, Leoben's interrogation scenes teach that suffering comes from ignorant attachment, and Dogen's no-self and impermanence frame the show's interdependent characters. Cylon resurrection, D'Anna's serial deaths, and the prophecy that "all of this has happened before" model karma and samsara, while Nishida's kenotic God of Absolute Nothingness makes sense of Six and Leoben's God of love. Because Cylons feel pain, fear death away from a resurrection ship, and act volitionally, McRae concludes they are persons in the Buddhist sense, owed the compassion of the Eightfold Path.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 21 "Analyzing Emptiness" — Paul Gass reads the Dead's hippie milieu (the Beats, the Acid Tests, Buddhist-monk lyricist Peter Monk) as a conduit for Buddhist doctrine, taking the 'Eyes of the World' chorus as an invitation to awaken to Buddha-nature. He explains the Four Noble Truths, karma, and the five aggregates to argue the self is an illusion, using the image of a flame passed between lighters at a Dead show to picture rebirth without a persisting soul. The chapter then presents Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka middle way — emptiness itself must not be clutched as an absolute truth — and reads the 'redeemer... wagon loaded with clay' verse of 'Eyes of the World' as the Mahayana bodhisattva liberating all beings, with emptiness finally discarded like the boat after crossing the river.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 37 "The Awakened One" — Callis reads Holmes as a Buddhist practitioner despite the cocaine and the cigars in the coalscuttle: 'You see, but you do not observe' and 'The emotional qualities are antagonistic to clear reasoning' match Vipassana bare attention and the Theravada ideal of the cool, rational, emotionally distant sage, and his improvised violin scraping works like Thich Nhat Hanh's walking meditation — a witness without commentary. The picture is completed by Doyle's Buddhism of Ceylon in The Sign of Four, Holmes's two years 'spending some days with the head lama' in Tibet ('The Empty House'), and his sitting 'like some strange Buddha' in 'The Veiled Lodger.' She maps his method onto the Yoga Sutras' dharana, dhyana, and samadhi — patient attention to the blood-scratched plaster, sustained fixation on the crime scene, ego-surrendering contemplation — making Holmes an 'awakened one' who loves truth for its own sake while Watson lives on autopilot.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 18 "6. You’re Gonna Die" — Ethan Mills uses the Buddha and Epicurus to show that Louis meets death with laughter instead of fear. The Buddha's diagnosis of dukkha ('dissatisfactoriness') explains the Blu-Ray player and cellphone bits - consumer desire just restarts the craving cycle - and impermanence frames both the Amia heartbreak that Dr. Bigelow reframes as 'misery is wasted on the miserable' and Louie's 'life isn't that long... it's happy math' reflection, while rebirth would only make things worse since you would have to repeat junior high forever. Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us (where death is, you are not) grounds Louie's 'lots of things happen after you die, just none of them include you,' backed by atomism - at death our atoms scatter - and by gods who, like Louie's maybe-God with no heaven, guarantee no immortality. The USO duckling episode models the payoff: comedy defuses our deepest anxiety about annihilation the way it defuses the soldiers' tension in Afghanistan.

I Fight Crime in My Sleep" — Staged as a Fight Club parody in which a Buddhist psychiatrist, Dr. Quinzel, evaluates a costumed narrator sent to Arkham, the chapter argues neither hero is close to awakening: Batman's crime-fighting is craving that perpetuates dukkha, his secret identities a twice-constructed self that the Buddha's no-self teaching dissolves, and his violence fails the test that 'hostility is never appeased by hostility.' Using karma, rebirth, the gandhabba that carries consciousness-flux to a new embryo, the no-soul doctrine, and the eightfold path, the Buddha argues clones are ordinary beings of the karmic flux — like the split bacterium, nothing unnatural — but that cloning multiplies clinging: hosts crave immortality through copies, each clone inherits the host's whole accumulated karma, and Henry's dream of training an army of Helena-clones would only deepen the unsatisfactoriness the Buddha's mustard-seed lesson says clinging to the dead always brings. - **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 15 "6. Bowie the Buddhist" — Muchall reads 'Quicksand' and 'Where Are We Now?' as suffused with Tibetan Buddhism: 'Don't believe in yourself' voices the anatta teaching Bowie absorbed studying with Chime Rinpoche and from Chogyam Trungpa, whose 'spiritual materialism' warns that ego converts even spirituality and ideologies to its own use. After retelling the Buddha's life, the Four Noble Truths' three kinds of dukkha, and the five aggregates that reveal no permanent self, the chapter maps the song's 'ragged hole' and bardos onto the Tibetan Book of the Dead's after-death journey, and reads Bowie's morphing personas as lived acknowledgment that there is no fixed self - 'there's nothing in here.'
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 10 "2. Zen and the Art of Guitar Burning" — Argues Hendrix's art worked like a Zen transmission outside words and doctrine: Nansen's cat, the Buddha's silent flower sermon, Zeami's hidden flower in Noh, and Linji burning the sutras frame the guitar-burning, playing with his teeth, and the backwards tape of 'Are You Experienced?' as skillful means that shock listeners out of dualistic discrimination into pure suchness. The Woodstock sequence — the 'Star-Spangled Banner' followed seamlessly by 'Purple Haze' and the 'Instrumental Solo' — is read as an eschatological passage from the death-symbolism of the national anthem to a Zen-like experiential beginning, with Hendrix acting as a Bodhisattva whose Stratocaster is the master's stick of compassion.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 23 "11. 999 Fingers" — Voiced by a composite being shredded together from every AHS character, the chapter retells the Buddha's path - Siddhartha sheltered from suffering like a pampered prince, enlightenment as watching 'every episode of American Horror Story', Mara's temptations, and Angulimala with his garland of 999 fingers converted to monkhood - to read Briarcliff's cruelty, Sister Jude's devil, and Bloody Face's son Johnny as suffering born of clinging, in a contingent, moment-to-moment world of karma and rebirth, while Nietzsche's killed God, eternal recurrence, and ressentiment frame the question of who is to blame when there is no creator.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 24 "12. A Month from Now, I’ll Be a Balding, Toothless Skeleton" — Reads Fiona Goode's war against fading - the experimental RM47 serum, rejecting the Axeman's escape because he would watch her decay, the Papa Legba bargain that collapses because she has no soul - alongside Delphine LaLaurie's blood facials and Marie Laveau's child sacrifices, as illustrations of Buddhist dukkha and the three thirsts (kama for sense pleasure, bhava for existence, vibhava for annihilation). Legba's 'you don't have a soul' becomes an accidentally liberating glimpse of anatta, and Cordelia's dying advice - 'feel the fear... let it all go' - is the mindfulness, echoing Buddhaghosa's corpse meditations, that might have freed Fiona.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 25 "14. After the Blackout" — Martin Muchall treats the offscreen Blackout as an emblem of the moral catastrophe diagnosed in MacIntyre's After Virtue: our moral vocabulary has shattered into emotivist hissing and clapping, with Roy's murder of Tyrell, his 'God of biomechanics', staging the death of God and the 'everything is permitted' that follows. Utilitarian pleasure and Kantian cold reason (Spock, who must tell the truth to the murderer at the door) have both failed, leaving neoliberal hypercapitalism — corporate psychopathy, the orphanage sweatshop, the Baseline as workplace performance review — as the real villain. Against this, K's ending models the Buddha: everything is impermanent, there is no self to defend, and his selfless, empathetic death points to a morality grounded in evolved and cultivable altruism.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 12 "Hakuna Matata, Bodhisattva" — Sets up Disney's maxim 'Hey kid, you can be a hero' as the direct opposite of Zen's 'Hey kid, you can be a buddha': escapism versus liberation, told through the life of Dogen, whose monastic choice parallels Disney hero narratives. Mickey in Steamboat Willie — a bundle of still frames with no sound and no real 'he' — illustrates the Buddha's three marks of existence (emptiness, impermanence, frustration), and the chapter argues Disney products are calibrated distractions from these marks while Dogen counsels facing them, with Ariel's Andersen fate as the price of fantasy. It closes on Disney's merchandising machine (Yoda, Star Wars sequels, direct-to-video cash grabs) as everything the countercultural minimalist Yoda or Baloo's bare necessities stand against, concluding that real hakuna matata is accepting impermanence rather than escaping it.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 29 "Notes" — Kahn argues LEGO play embodies the Buddhist teaching of impermanence that the Buddha states in the Digha Nikaya ('Impermanent are all component things...'): his childhood urge to superglue creations and Finn's father's Kragle dramatize the clinging that produces anxiety when things change, from brick formulations to discontinued sets and even funerals' wilting flowers. The LEGO Star Wars Death Star illustrates non-self — no Death Star exists apart from its 3,803 pieces, and no self apart from shifting aggregates — and the five aggregates (form, sensation, perception, formations, consciousness) are unpacked through building experiences like discovering a daughter has opened the mint Taj Mahal set. Tibetan sand mandalas, painstakingly built then ritually dissolved, model the ceremonial demolition of LEGO creations, teaching acceptance of change without sliding into a nihilistic 'why bother building at all'.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 36 "23. I Fight Crime in My Sleep" — A Fight Club-style Arkham case study: a patient's hallucinated Superman companion is diagnosed by a Buddhist psychiatrist who explains the three marks of existence—impermanence, non-self, and dissatisfaction—arguing superheroes impose order and a fabricated second self on a world that resists both, so Superman's super-intellect and even flight are distractions (levitation should be ignored; the Buddha-eye beats x-ray vision) while Batman's violence and psychosis, compared to American Psycho's Patrick Bateman, make awakening impossible—both are victims of Mara. A robber literally named David Hume objects that the heroes' law and order is grounded on what ought to be rather than what is, and a Gandhi quote on preferring one's own bad government explains why Batman finally kryptonites his alien 'friend.' The verdict inverts the book's debate: conquering the deceiver within is the only superpower worth having.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Kang argues Lee's Taking Woodstock desexualizes and 'recloset[s]' Elliot Tiber's gay coming-out memoir, substituting a fluid 'queer' openness for Tiber's political gay identity and framing his homosexuality as an incidental, situationally-straight product of the festival (the woman-centered threesome, the chaste kiss with Paul). Drawing on Sedgwick, Butler and Foucault's history of sexuality, she critiques how the film neutralizes homophobia and omits the gay Buddhist mentor Georgette, whose teaching on karma, samsara and dukkha grounds Tiber's self-acceptance and unconditional love—reducing a gay everyman's struggle to one 'not-normal freak' among a hundred thousand.
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 21 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — Judith Barad explains the puzzling elements of Kundun—the compassion for enemies, the child taken from his parents, the swept-away sand mandala, the sky burial—through Tibetan Buddhist ethics, arguing it closely parallels Greek and Roman Stoicism. She reads the young Dalai Lama's growth into compassion and nonviolence toward Mao and the Chinese alongside Epictetus's teaching that only our own judgments, not others' acts, can harm us, and that we must restrain desire and attachment. The Four Noble Truths reframe the film: because all things (including the self) are impermanent and interconnected, the destruction of the mandala and the feeding of the father's corpse to vultures enact detachment, and true liberation via the Eightfold Path is self-won inner peace that China cannot seize.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 18 "MOTHERHOOD" — Sheryl Tuttle Ross applies three of the Buddhist noble truths – pain is inevitable, pain arises from attachment, suffering can end – to contemporary mothering, contrasting the Buddhist acceptance of pain with Bentham's utilitarian pleasure-maximizing. Drawing on Thich Nhat Hanh's mindfulness and the doctrines of impermanence and no-self, she offers 'mommy meditations' (breathe, become aware, recognize social scripts, respond kindly) and reads the novel I Don't Know How She Does It, whose 'Court of Motherhood' dramatizes the guilt-inducing scripts mindfulness helps mothers see through to experience beauty in ordinary moments.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 15 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Geisz reads his daily morning coffee ritual through Buddhist metaphysics: the pre-caffeine grogginess and its transient relief illustrate saṃsāra and duḥkha, the First Noble Truth, driven by self-centered craving (the Second). The transience of the perfect-temperature cup shows impermanence (anitya), and the question of whether a 'self' pre- or post-coffee exists is answered by anatman — he offers three hypotheses (full self dormant, half coffee-cyborg, self created ex Coffea) then dissolves them into no-self plus dependent arising, where the cup and drinker are empty nodes in a web of physical, economic, and karmic conditions. Each intentional sip lays down karma that binds tomorrow's 'me' further into the cycle.
- **Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom**, ch. 26 "GARDENING" — Mara Miller argues gardens do not merely sit inside time but actively structure six kinds of time (scientific, objective/shared, kairos, subjective, temporality, historical), opening with Augustine's puzzle that he knows what time is until asked to explain it. She contrasts Greek chronos with kairos (the right moment to plant after the last frost), shows how Versailles propagated a shared time (eternal, historic, recurring) and eighteenth-century English landscape gardens taught the long-range vision capitalism needed, and describes cyclical 'eternal recurrence' (Eliade).
