It then grades the show's reasoners: Raylan knows the Crowes rather than Boyd killed Wade Messer, Boyd knows Cassie milks the revival snakes' venom, Art Mullen does not yet know Raylan helped Winona return the evidence-room money, and gut-feeling victims like Ellen May do not know what they saw. Against Humean skepticism about cause and effect it defends inductive, detective-style knowledge - Raylan can know who done it without courtroom proof.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 19 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Roger Hunt answers 'what do philosophers do?' through Dennis's seduction methodology. Frank embodies empiricism, leaving the comfort of principle for the messiness of the world as Hume did when he found no impression of causation, space, or time; Mac embodies rationalism, reasoning with total confidence from a principle he cannot doubt, as Descartes did from the cogito; and the dialectic of Socrates and Plato, questioning beliefs in dialogue to see what survives scrutiny, describes philosophy as it is actually practiced. Boethius's Consolation - the imprisoned author consoled by dialogues with Lady Philosophy - supplies the frame of philosophy as an encounter with a woman one pursues, and each D.E.N.N.I.S. step maps onto the craft: Demonstrating value to the problem, Engaging physically in its awkward grind, Nurturing dependence through thesis panic, Neglect and Inspiring hope on the road to the defense, then Separating entirely - 'be a sociopath about it.'
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 38 "18. Gruesome Walkers" — Yuen turns the walkers into a lesson on Hume's problem of induction: the pre-apocalyptic belief that the dead do not rise was justified by all past experience until Rick wakes to a world where they do, and Rick's distrust of Alexandria repeats the same inductive move from Woodbury, Terminus, and Grady - useful, Hume says, since custom compels us, but never knowledge. Russell's chicken illustrates the fatal surprise, and Goodman's grue (the pun of the title) shows the outbreak could be a future-swinging regularity like the seventeen-year cicadas, undermining even Jenner's experimental science. Popper's falsificationism is offered as the rescue - Shane's reanimation falsifies the "walkers make walkers" theory, leaving the "everyone is infected" theory corroborated but never known.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 38 "23. How Can We Know Anything in a World of Magic and Miracles" — Baldwin asks whether Westerosi characters can know anything inductive in a world without lawlike nature: seasons of unpredictable length, wargs in animal minds, Faceless Men changing faces, and resurrections by Thoros, Melisandre, and Qyburn. After laying out the Platonic justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge (those who saw the pyre are justified in believing Dany is the mother of dragons; those relying on rumor are not), he runs Hume's problem of induction - we never perceive causal connection, so no jar of wildfire must explode - against Reid's common-sense reply that reason and induction stand or fall together, concluding that Westeros gives its people special reasons for skepticism while we, lacking evidence of magical irregularity, are rational to trust everyday inductive belief.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 21 "8. For Hume the Ball Tolls!" — The chapter argues Charlie Brown's repeated falls for Lucy's football gag are failures of induction: given the history of the gag since 1951 (first with Violet, then Lucy's fake reasons each fall - a handshake, a contract, a hundred million dollars), he should draw the meta-level conclusion that she will always pull the ball away. It then tries Hume's problem of induction as his defense, but since that would cost him all knowledge of the external world (that Snoopy is a beagle, that Lucy is mean) and end in skepticism, Charlie - a student of his world, not a doubter of it - cannot take it. The verdict: he is not a blockhead but determined and committed, willing to lose every fall because kicking that ball would be worth it, as in the 1979 hospital strip where he finally gets his kick and still ends up on his back.
- **Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality**, ch. 10 "2. Persuade Me Once, Shame on You . ." — Greene dismantles both phases of Adams's case that Trump is a Master Persuader. The trait-list phase (opening with big demands, the Intentional Wrongness Persuasion Play, never apologizing, exuding confidence, recruiting the reciprocity instinct, and the talent stack) fails because doing what master persuaders do is not being one, by the Tom Brady versus Archie Manning point that we never define good quarterbacks by wins alone and by the Kantian thought that an act must be done for the right reason. The reality phase borrows Plato, Hume, and Kant to deny us access to an objective world, but the chapter replies that the experts' predictive failures illustrate Hume's problem of induction rather than proving there are no facts, notes Adams even misreads Plato, and observes that nothing links the Persuasion Filter's one success to Trump's skills rather than to a one-off political climate.
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 30 "16. Gotta Have Faith" — Winters asks what faith is when the Party risks burning and becoming demodog chow so Eleven can close the gate: after arguing via George Michael and the talisman-free tunnels that faith need not be religious, he tests Bishop's models of faith against 'The Gate' (the affective and secular hope models fit; the belief and trust models fail because everyone has seen the Mind Flayer's work on Will). Hume's account that causation is never observed, only habituated, explains the Party's hope that heat will drive the Mind Flayer from Will and that Christmas lights will reach him, and Kierkegaard's teleological suspension of the ethical and knight of faith frame Eleven's willingness to die against the absurd, since aligning her life with friendship's higher purpose is what makes it meaningful.
- **Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney**, ch. 15 "6. The Facts Don’t Speak for Themselves" — Muyskens asks why Burger and Tragg's evidence keeps pointing at innocent people, answering with Hume's distinction between relations of ideas and matters of fact and the problem of induction: inferences from past experience are never guaranteed. In 'The Case of the Shapely Shadow' the prosecution's seven pieces of testimony against Janice Wainwright are reasonable but false, and only Mason, because he believes his client, presses to the water-records discovery that exposes Cole Troy; 'The Case of the Runaway Corpse' then shows Burger and Tragg settling on Myrna Davenport on flimsy, self-contradictory evidence and simply failing to investigate, while Mason withholds judgment, checks her account against documents and witnesses, and digs until justified true belief is achieved.
- **Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney**, ch. 16 "7. Beyond a Reasonable Doubt" — Jordan argues Mason's real superpower is logic rather than client selection or legal brilliance: since conviction requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt before a unanimous jury, and since by the problem of induction (traced from Sextus Empiricus's regression arguments through Hume) no accumulation of probabilities yields deductive certainty, the prosecution can never conclusively prove guilt while Mason need only exploit that structural gap, as in The Case of the Howling Dog's cab-driver and document evidence and the TV movie Perry Mason Returns where Della is the accused. He illustrates with modus ponens examples about Della and Hamilton Burger, contrasting sound deductive arguments with merely strong inductive ones like predicting Mason's next win.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 14 "“Consider Your Verdict!”" — Splits Wonderland's nonsense into the tolerable kind (strange but lawful regularities, like mushroom side-effects and walking the opposite way to reach the Red Queen, which Alice masters by experiment) and the intolerable kind (the creatures' eristic logic). Using Hume's fork of relations of ideas versus matters of fact, George Dunn and Brian McDonald argue Alice rightly concludes the pig-baby is merely an out-of-the-way matter of fact, while the White Queen's 'jam every other day: to-day isn't any other day' and the King's beheading of the bodiless Cheshire Cat repeat the Sophists' tricks from Plato's Euthydemus, which Socrates deflates from the standpoint of common sense and the examined life. The Knave's trial ('sentence first, verdict afterwards') lands on cable-news pundits who, like the show trials of Stalin, argue from predetermined conclusions.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 15 "The Lasting Legacy of Logic" — Treats Carroll the Oxford logician as a teacher hiding five lessons in Wonderland: watch your assumptions (the King infers the Knave's guilt from an unsigned letter), know what your words mean (Humpty Dumpty on 'glory'), don't confuse categories (the King's 'Nobody' and the Hatter's personified Time), don't switch subjects and predicates ('I mean what I say' versus 'I say what I mean'), and don't confuse necessary with sufficient conditions (Alice's Ada and Mabel arguments, with a hammer-and-egg illustration). David S. Brown grounds the lessons in Hume on causes discoverable only by experience, Aristotle's law of non-contradiction and categories, the Marx Brothers' 'Either he's dead or my watch has stopped', and Popper's point that a successful prediction cannot prove a hypothesis, only a failed one can refute it.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 16 "Wonderland and the Real World" — Extracts three problems of induction from Alice's misadventures: predicting the future (Hume's problem: nothing rationally compels Humpty Dumpty to agree the world will not turn into Wonderland at 6 a.m. tomorrow), proving whose dream it is (Quine's underdetermination of theory by evidence: Tweedledee can accommodate any evidence within the theory that Alice exists only in the Red King's dream), and translating Wonderese (Quine's indeterminacy: pointing at the White Rabbit cannot fix whether natives mean the rabbit, its parts, or its stages, nor what 'muchness' means). Brendan Shea shows Alice succeeding where the creatures fail by the criteria Hume and Quine endorse: experimentation, simplicity, conservatism of belief, and a principle of charity in translation.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 23 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Mackonis shows Sheldon is wrong about being wrong: Stuart's tomato counterexample ('it's very wrong to say it's a suspension bridge') refutes his claim that wrongness admits no gradation, and closeness to truth is cashed out with possible-worlds similarity — vegetable theory sits one small alteration from actuality, echoing Sheldon's own many-worlds refusal to dance in any of them. The Raj exchange ('So you were wrong' / 'I didn't say that') motivates many-valued logics in which degrees of truth let both be partly right, while the 'Cooper-Wrongness Paradox' argues that if Sheldon always knew when he was wrong, he could never know that he was wrong. Hume's problem of induction then shows his post-Toby confidence in his other beliefs can never be inductively verified, only sometimes falsified, and his French-sprinkled 'victory' over an exhausted Stuart is sheer logical fallacy.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 31 "APPENDIX - Who are Locke, Hume, and Rousseau The Losties’ Guide to Philosophers" — Scott Parker's appendix profiles the philosophers behind Lost's namesake characters: John Locke for the survivor (blank-slate empiricism, belief tempered by tolerance, The Reasonableness of Christianity), David Hume for Desmond (causation as habitual inference, with the button press as the image of induction, plus bundle-theory skepticism about the self), and Jean-Jacques Rousseau for Danielle ('man is naturally good, and only by institutions is he made bad,' private property as the root of inequality). It adds Jeremy Bentham (the alias on Locke's coffin), Kierkegaard via the Fear and Trembling Hurley finds under the Temple (Abraham's teleological suspension of the ethical and the leap of faith), Dogen on zazen, Edward Said for Sayid (Orientalism and the audience's own projected savagery onto the Others), and short lives of Kate Cooper Austin, Carlyle, Rutherford, Hugo Grotius, Bakunin, Ram Dass, Edmund Burke, Hawking, Minkowski, Faraday, C. S. Lewis, and Lennon.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 11 "Notes" — Adams pairs Anakin with Achilles to show how Palpatine's lesson that 'good is a point of view' - Nietzsche's claim that there are no moral facts, only interpretations - nearly destroys both heroes before a father's love pulls them back: Priam's tears before Achilles, Luke unmasking Vader. Against nihilism the chapter defends moral realism through Apollo's lion simile (compassion and respect are objective facts about what persons require) and Kant's self-critical inquiry, with the Jedi Council's twelve-way deliberation illustrating that some interpretations are better than others, beyond Hume's problem of induction. Both epics settle on a 'Pagan Golden Rule' - help your friends and harm your enemies, but never lose compassion for either.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 30 "Notes" — Asks whether Han Solo's 'hokey religions' dismissal of the Force is unreasonable given his evidence, answering no: Hume's argument against miracles explains why testimony of lightsaber tricks and mind tricks should not overturn Han's experience of consistent natural law, while Hume's problem of induction and custom/habit explain why both Han's 'luck' verdict and Obi-Wan's 'no such thing as luck' are habit-based generalizations. Peirce's fallibilism (backed by Putnam's 'fallibilism does not entail skepticism') lets Han and Obi-Wan each claim knowledge without certainty, echoing Obi-Wan's line that many truths depend greatly on our own point of view.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 27 "Kickstarting Inductive Inference" — Daniel Wilkenfeld analyzes Veronica's 'magic trick' in the 'One Angry Veronica' juryroom and her season-long bus-crash solution as Peter Lipton's inference to the best explanation: the hypothesis 'Beaver is a killer' wins by consilience (explaining the explosion, the dead rat, Curly Moran, even her chlamydia), simplicity, and completeness. But the criteria face Hume's problem of induction — why think the future will resemble the past, when yesterday's popular girl is today's pariah? — and Descartes's evil demon undermines even what Veronica 'sees,' since Curly Moran could fake a bus crash, leaving no non-circular justification for inferential habits none of us can live without. Following Nelson Goodman, Wilkenfeld concludes the demand for justification is misplaced: what matters is that Veronica reasons consistently, in the juryroom as at the cliff.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 28 "Feel the Big MO'" — Letson asks whether momentum in football is a real explanatory phenomenon, opening with the Bills' 1993 comeback over the Oilers. He notes momentum is invoked only for success and only for one team at a time, and struggles to separate it from the mere evidence of playing well, comparing it to 'talent.' Surveying psychological models (Taylor and Demick's momentum chain) and David Romer's fourth-down analysis denying momentum, he argues that even if a small momentum effect exists, its size relative to chance means appeals to it in any particular game are usually unjustified—like blaming one heart attack on smoking.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 8 "Sherlock's Reasoning Toolbox" — Pigliucci shows that Holmes's celebrated 'deduction' is really a mix of induction and abduction, contrasting Aristotelian syllogism and Cartesian rationalism (with its failed Cartesian circle) against the fallibility of real investigation. He walks through Hume's problem of induction (Russell's inductivist chicken), the Mill-Whewell 'great induction debate,' and Popper's falsificationism—qualified by the Neptune/Uranus episode where scientists shielded Newton. Using 'Thor Bridge' and 'The Three Students,' he concludes Holmes is a pragmatic scientist wielding a whole toolbox, since there is no single scientific method.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 12 "4. Demons, Game Shows, and Baguettes" — Wenmackers traces psychohistory's scientific lineage from Newtonian determinism through Laplace's demon, arguing Foundation stays within nineteenth-century limits by predicting only probabilities. She uses Newcomb's Paradox to capture the unease of living under a predicted Seldon Plan, Poincare's chaos and the three-body problem to show determinism need not mean predictability, and Poincare's baguette-fraud tale plus Quetelet's social physics and statistical mechanics to explain psychohistory's core assumption that mobs of billions behave lawfully even when individuals do not. She suggests Seldon's science was in some sense historically inevitable.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 22 "12. Raven Seldon Predicts Disaster" — Malloy argues psychohistory rests on induction and therefore inherits Hume's problem of induction: Seldon generalizes from Trantor's past to predict the Empire's fall, but nothing guarantees the future will resemble the past, and the Mule's unprecedented rise shows there is no deductive guarantee (the future-unlike-past idea is not self-contradictory). He tests Popper's falsificationism, under which psychohistory is science because it makes falsifiable predictions and can never be confirmed, then notes Popper leaves hypothesis-origin and post-failure revision inductive, and finally offers Reichenbach's pragmatic 'vindication' of induction, likening it to Hardin making do with the only tools at hand in a Seldon Crisis.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 11 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Jurgensen and Southworth apply Hume's argument against miracles to the virgin birth, treating it as a claimed violation of the natural law that virgins do not conceive. They attack the credibility of the only witnesses, Matthew and Luke, noting their third-hand sources (Mark, Q, L/M), their contradiction over whether Mary and Joseph were married, and the mistranslation of Isaiah's ambiguous 'almah' as the Greek 'parthenos' (literal virgin). Invoking Hume's four defects of miracle testimony and his maxim that no testimony suffices unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the event, they conclude a rational person must reject the Christmas miracle.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 21 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Kakko's 'Hallucinatory Terror' uses Fitz Hugh Ludlow's 1857 The Hasheesh Eater to ask 'How can these things be?' — the ontological status of hallucinations that neither exist nor fail to exist. He traces Ludlow's own reading from Locke's empiricism through Hume's skeptical worry that all perception may be hallucinatory with no verifiable external object, to Kant's Copernican turn: the phenomenal/noumenal distinction, synthetic a priori judgments, and space and time as pure forms of intuition. Kant's framework lets Kakko recast Ludlow's 'virtual change of worlds' as a literal, non-metaphorical restructuring of the intuitions conditioning experience.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 16 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Steve Jacobson's 'Standing on Your Head' asks whether an educated Westerner can reasonably believe 'yoga theory' (chakras, prana, kundalini, koshas) given that science has superseded ancient theories. He raises a 'standard objection' from the superior predictive power of science (invoking Hume's problem of induction), rejects weak replies, but argues via the epistemology of testimony that people with weak scientific grounds and strong critical testimony can rationally accept yoga theory. He concludes that even if no part of it is credible, abandoning it would leave yoga intact — 'yoga with fewer illusions.'
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 23 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Terjesen defines a 'real date' as a shared intention to try out romantic possibility, using Abelard's claim that intention (not behavior) determines the nature of an act to show that identical activities are or aren't dates depending on mutual intent. He then invokes Russell's argument-from-analogy account of knowing other minds to explain how daters 'mind-read' each other's intentions, and notes this yields only probable conclusions, generating an infinite regress ('I know that you know...') that only 'the Talk' resolves. He cites Hume's problem of induction as the deeper reason analogical inference can never be certain, and uses the Friends 'Mayor of the Friend Zone' gag and Ross and Rachel to argue the Friend Zone is a step toward, not a trap against, committed relationships.

### Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society

This is Rousseau's claim that human beings are naturally good, or at least innocent, and that vice, inequality, and misery arise not from our nature but from the development of society and its institutions. In the imagined state of nature people are self-sufficient and compassionate, but the growth of property, comparison, and dependence corrupts them, breeding pride, envy, and injustice. The thesis reverses the older view that civilization tames a naturally wicked animal, and it frames Rousseau's political and educational projects as attempts to recover or protect that original goodness. It shaped Romanticism and modern debates about whether social conditions or human nature is the deeper source of our ills.

- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 15 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Knight places Atkins's caveman utopia — Paleolithic abundance, hunter-gatherer vitality, downfall through agriculture — inside the primitivist tradition running from Ovid's Golden Age to Rousseau's Noble Savage, whose state of nature Rousseau himself admitted was 'mere conditional and hypothetical reasoning' aimed at European corruption. Using postcolonial critics (Spurr, Torgovnick, and Fanon's line that whites who feel 'too mechanized' turn to 'the men of color' for 'human sustenance'), she argues low-carb primitivism is self-reflexive nostalgia — South Beach cannot even date its own paradise — that also freezes living Inuit and Indigenous Australians as Stone Age remnants, hiding the colonial and economic causes of their diabetes and poverty.
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 17 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — In an imaginary salon hosted by the baker 'la Brioche,' the goddess Eris drops a golden apple inscribed 'Atkins,' and three philosophers fight over the credit. Rousseau claims Atkins's war on refined flour and 'invented fake food' as his own back-to-nature, state-of-nature legacy; Confucius counters that Americans are 'grazers' without li, that culture is nature's flower, and that only ritual propriety can counteract the advertising that fills the void; Democritus claims the scientific core — 'hyperinsulism,' 'benign dietary ketosis' — as atomism's heir, deriding Rousseau's general will as democratic truth-concocting and Plato's otherworldly philosopher-king. The debate ranges over free will versus scientific prediction-and-control and ends unresolved over a refusal of brioche.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 25 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Alford reads the biker image, born at Hollister in 1947 and fixed by The Wild One, through two opposed accounts of presocial man: the badass on his tricked-out Harley is Hobbes's natural man, all vanity, domination, and fear merely redirected to government, praising Chuck Zito's 'most primitive philosophy'; the club run with bonfire, brothers, old ladies, and Steppenwolf re-enacts Rousseau's golden age between the stupidity of brutes and the fatal enlightenment of civil man, before the first enclosed field ('this is mine') bred property, vanity, and misery. The paradox of a biker who is simultaneously threat and salvation dissolves once we see that 'primitive' and 'civilized' are mutually defining: suburbanites and bikers alike live both Hobbesian individualism and Rousseauvian community, each defining themselves against the other.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 19 "Roll Credits" — Dunn contrasts Baum's book, where evil is wonderfully 'small'—Dorothy melts the Witch in a fit of righteous anger at a stolen Silver Shoe, and personal plus social virtues (kindness repaid by the field-mice Queen) reliably conquer it—with the 1939 film, which smuggles back the 'heartaches and nightmares' Baum banished and resolves the Witch only by an accidental stroke of luck. He sorts Oz's harms into moral evils (the Witch's enslavements, the Wizard's frauds) and natural evils (the cyclone, the Deadly Poppy Field), cites Hume's catalogue of the world's ills, and observes that Baum needs neither Kant's postulate of God and a future life to join virtue with happiness nor John Hick's 'vale of soul-making' theodicy—Oz simply delivers the reward. Dorothy's abundant virtue at age five rebukes Aristotle (children, he says, cannot be virtuous or happy) and instead embodies Rousseau's Emile, natural goodness uncorrupted by civilization, while Chesterton's Doctrine of Conditional Joy and Tolkien's insistence on serious, non-technological magic frame the Old-World Christian outlook that Baum's demystified American fairy tale—and the movie's ending—quietly betray.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 13 "Singing of the Good Things" — Scott Calef asks whether Led Zeppelin's lives of wealth, groupies, and no-questions-asked liberty were genuinely free and therefore enviable. Locke's distinction between weak freedom (doing what you want, with Page happily locked in his suite at the Riot House) and strong freedom (being able to do otherwise, defended via beer-spilling concert excuses) is destabilized by the observation that no one ever does other than what they did. Rousseau then dominates: the state of nature versus LA, freedom as the capacity to resist natural impulse, which explains both Zep's libertine promiscuity and the paradox that heroin and alcohol enslave the very freedom that took them (the post-Physical Graffiti decline, Bonzo's death), while the band's violence—Bonham's assaults, the Oakland beating—shows society's suppression of natural pity, not natural aggression as Hobbes would have it. Socrates gets the last word: doing what we please is not doing what we truly want, so only the temperate person is free.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 27 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Greeley argues the zombie crystallizes specifically modern fears: with Aristotle and Aquinas he reads walkers as humans stripped of their essential nature and potential, which Rick's uncustomary eulogies ('I'm sorry this happened to you') acknowledge. Following Philippe Aries, he ties modern death anxiety to urbanization, hidden cemeteries, and the loss of religious consolation, citing the CDC arc where Jenner's science offers only a self-destruct and Jacqui falls back on 'the wrath of God.' Rousseau's thesis that society corrupts explains why the survivors in the woods seem more alive — warlord Guillermo turns out to be protecting nursing-home patients and pizza-deliverer Glenn becomes a hero — while the 'Bradbury's Storewide Sale' sign, the Walmart trampling, and Fromm's shift from utopias to dystopias suggest the shuffling horde is an image of our own consumerist, distracted, dehumanized modernity.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 24 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Fitzpatrick uses the social contract tradition to explain Prohibition-era Atlantic City. Hobbes's state of nature fits the gang warfare left where no Leviathan is strong enough to enforce federal law against Nucky; Locke's fits a night-watchman government overreaching into Prohibition and thereby breaking the contract, as with Nucky's illegitimate protection 'taxes'; Rousseau's noble savage corrupted by commercial society fits the Klan's pleasure in cruelty and innocent Tommy set against scheming adults. Ethical egoism frames Nucky's framing of Hans Schroeder, consequentialism the Temperance Union's cost-benefit failure, and deontology Margaret's lying campaign speech, while Marx's and Mill's view that human nature is malleable explains the season-spanning transformation of Nucky from half-gangster into 'a gangster and a half.'
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 11 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Chaib reads Craig Venter's 2010 synthetic bacterium 'Synthia' as a real-world Victor Frankenstein and tests it against Habermas's The Future of Human Nature, which condemns liberal eugenics because turning reproduction into manufacture undermines moral equality, rights, and autonomy - the same irresponsible isolation that made Victor abandon his creature and doom Justine. Rousseau and Thomas More supply the counter-program: hunger persists through unequal property ('This is mine'), not scarcity, so improving the human heart and social structures beats Venter's engineered fixes. Frankenweenie - where pets reanimated without love turn evil while Victor's beloved Sparky saves the town - lands the chapter's Arendtian moral that 'to live' is always plural (inter homines esse), so creators must care about their creations' relations with others.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 21 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Pötzsch explains the monster through Rousseau's Émile: innately good ('Everything is good as it comes from the hands of the Author of Nature'), the creature is corrupted because he experienced civilization 'too much and too soon' - the exact inverse of Rousseau's negative education, which shields the heart from vice instead of commanding, and lets the child learn 'through the mere force of things.' Victor knew his parents' model of paternal duty ('a deep consciousness of what they owed towards the being to which they had given life') yet abandoned his offspring and refused the female companion Rousseau deems essential to social development, so that wickedness born of weakness ('if I cannot inspire love, I will cause fear') murders William, Clerval, and Elizabeth. Shelley, a Rousseau admirer, makes Victor's science - an attempt to conquer rather than follow nature, fed by competitive professors at Ingolstadt - the very thing that dooms his parenting.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 30 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Caroline Mosser treats the creature's tragedy as humanist prejudice rather than necessity: the blind De Lacey accepts the eloquent creature sight unseen, so he passes Alan Turing's test, and only the sighted family's terror at his body rejects him - bias against the artificial, not reason. She reads the creature's development through fire, language, and revolution as Rousseau's progression from natural innocence to corruption by society, and Donna Haraway's cyborg as the figure he prefigures: an unfaithful illegitimate offspring who rebels against his father and undermines patriarchal Western self/other dualisms. The chapter concludes that society cannot accept enhanced or posthuman beings until it finds a middle ground beyond its binary grids of good/bad and Self/Other, since otherwise any new life we create will be Othered, hated, and oppressed like Frankenstein's.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 33 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Mike Kugler argues Shelley's novel tests the radical idealism of her father William Godwin, her mother Mary Wollstonecraft, and her husband Percy: Victor's Promethean project of perfecting humanity in isolation, away from the 'intimate circle' of family and friends, produces a creature whose natural benevolence is destroyed only by repeated exclusion, first by the De Laceys. Drawing on Rousseau's and Wollstonecraft's view that children raised by benevolent parents develop their innate sympathy, the chapter reads the creature as an abandoned child - a new Adam who becomes a Satanic rebel when every community rejects him - and Victor's attempt at reproduction without women and mothers as the novel's deepest violation. The redemptive counterfactual is adoption: what if Victor had raised the creature in his home, as his father did Elizabeth?
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 40 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Trip McCrossin casts the creature as a modern Job: repeatedly and unreasonably mistreated by the De Laceys, the rustic whose child he saved, and Victor despite his benevolence, he cries 'This was then the reward of my benevolence!' - but unlike Job he loses faith, because his problem of evil is secular, justifying not 'the Ways of God to Man' but 'the Ways of Man to monsters.' The chapter traces the problem from Job and Paradise Lost through Bayle's defense of faith over reason and the Optimists' 'best of all possible worlds,' whose credibility drowned with the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, setting Rousseau against Voltaire: Rousseau's Emile ('All is good leaving the hands of the author of things') demands that we make evil intelligible through self-knowledge, while Candide counsels tending our garden. The creature embodies Rousseau's line - 'I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend' - yet ends in self-abhorring remorse over Victor's death, leaving open whether self-knowledge can ever answer unreasonable suffering.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 28 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Trip McCrossin reads Carrie's 'I missed something once before... everyone's not me' as the modern, secular problem of evil: as Susan Neiman argues, unreasonable suffering threatens reason itself, and the Rousseau-Voltaire split defines the responses. Carrie takes Rousseau's side - 'All is good leaving the hands of the author of things' degenerates in human hands, so evil is intelligible and redemption possible, the chance at redemption she offers Brody and even Nazir - against Voltaire's Candide-style tending of the garden. The finale deepens this with Boethius's Consolation: Carrie's 'I believe one of the reasons I was put on this Earth was for our paths to cross' fuses fate with providence, and she accepts Brody's execution as a redemptive end 'more so if he dies'.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 12 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Gale and Barkman treat post-Mushroom-War Ooo as a state-of-nature laboratory for liberalism's three founders. The Forest Wizard who cages Finn in 'Storytelling' is Hobbes's Leviathan, kept in power by fear yet moderated by self-interest (Goblin King Xergiok's fall shows the leash); Princess Bubblegum's Candy Kingdom is Locke's civil society where citizens trade private revenge for impartial law—her lawful bow to Lemongrab shows she rules by contract, not fear; and 'City of Thieves' illustrates Rousseau's claim that property corrupts natural goodness, with Finn and Jake as his uncorrupted natural people. The chapter concludes that the rights language these thinkers forged is what keeps both Ooo and our world from sliding back into a war of all against all.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 15 "6. Tris’s Compassion and the Problem of Evil" — McCrossin reads Tris's whole arc as a struggle with the problem of evil, both the theological version from Job and the modern secular one Susan Neiman describes, in which unreasonable suffering threatens trust in human reason. He casts Tris as cut from Rousseau's mold - her insistence on making the evils of Jeanine, Marcus, and Evelyn intelligible - against Voltaire's Candide refusal to rationalize suffering, and treats the faction system as Rousseau's social-contract strategy for containing the inclination to evil while Tris herself plays a wartime Emile. The key is Tobias's lesson that selflessness and bravery are not that different: selflessness enables the courage that compassion motivates, from pressing her forehead to Jeanine's gun in the fear landscape to taking Caleb's place at the weapons lab, so that the trilogy ends with Tobias's 'we mend each other.'
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 14 "4. Acts of God" — McCrossin reads Lecter's parable of the church collapses - 'It must feel good to God - He does it all the time, and are we not made in His image?' - as Lecter's solution to the problem of evil in both its theological (Job) and secular (Neiman) forms: a malevolent deity of the kind de Sade's Saint-Fond describes, doing God's work becomes Lecter's justification, and killing feels good because 'if one does what God does enough times, one will become as God is'. Following Neiman, he sets Rousseau's tradition (evil must be made intelligible - 'All is well leaving the hands of the author of things') against Voltaire's Candide refusal of theodicy, showing that Will and Starling live in Rousseau's camp except when facing Lecter himself, and that the Hannibal/Hannibal Rising revelation that Mischa's murder 'happened' to him radically revises his earlier claim that 'we don't invent our natures', with Starling's reason finally making 'a place for Mischa' in Lecter and Starling together.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 12 "4. Raising Darrow" — Trip McCrossin reads Darrow's storyline as an engagement with the problem of evil in both its theological form (Harmony dubbing him Lazarus, the parables of John and Luke) and its secular form, which Susan Neiman traces to the Rousseau-Voltaire dispute: must evil be made intelligible or not? Darrow begins Voltairean—incredulous before the rigged Laurel and Eo's hanging ('She left me')—but his resurrection and political awakening on the surface remake him Rousseauian: evil is the misalignment of individual and general wills, and humans are corrupted by society, not born bad. The chapter reads Darrow's 'Man was born free' broadcast in Morning Star, his new social contract with Victra, and the education of Pax (with Lysander left to Cassius to 'raise him right') as Rousseau's Social Contract and Emile program—break the chains, then educate each generation so its contracts align ever closer with the general will.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 15 "6. Driven by Love to Go to War" — John Karavitis deploys Alain Badiou's account of love as a contingent encounter founding the 'Two scene'—seeing the world from the perspective of difference—to argue that Darrow and Eo were never truly in love: their glade conversation, his 'nobility of obedience' against her 'live for more,' was two monologues, and you cannot love a memory. He then diagnoses Darrow as a narcissist in Rousseau's sense of amour-propre—self-love turned vanity that lies to itself—whose quest serves to manage his shame at failing to protect Eo, citing Erich Fromm on narcissism's path to fascism and Aristotle on habituation into Gold ways. Only the Jackal's stone-table imprisonment shatters the narcissism ('Man is no island'), letting Darrow embrace agape, with Ovid's Echo and Narcissus and the haemanthus framing the trilogy as a warning against self-love.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 29 "16. Doppelgängers, Doubles, and Tulpas" — Reads the show's doubles through the danger of self-loss. La Rochefoucauld's amour-propre explains Josie Packard, whose courtier-like dissimulation ("she could survive by being what other people wanted to see") erodes her true self, while Norma refuses to feign virtue for critic M.T. Wentz or Walter Lawford's rebranding; Rousseau's account of esteem-seeking in modern society covers Sheriff Cable and Chad, who value Teresa Banks and the Log Lady only by others' judgment, against the Blue Rose agents whose values come from within. Jean Paul's doppelgänger, invented to satirize Fichte's I/not-I and intersubjective recognition, uncannies the Palmer home (Leland the abusing father), but the chapter concludes the show sides with Dostoyevsky rather than Jean Paul: Laura, like Mitya Karamazov, owns both her good and wicked halves, Leland splits, and Cooper's moral goodness is a wholeness — authenticity — that his doppelgänger lacks.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 19 "8. From the Handmaid’s Tale to the Handmaids’ Tale" — McCrossin reads Offred's silent prayers ('I want to know what I did to deserve this') as channeling the Book of Job, using Susan Neiman's distinction between the theological and secular problem of evil: even if we stop demanding explanations from God, we must still make evil intelligible, as Janine's Testifying cruelly refuses to do. He sets Rousseau against Voltaire on whether morality requires making evil intelligible, finding June Rousseauian for piecing together Gilead's hidden prehistory at the Boston Globe and for acting from compassion, as with the bread-truck driver's secret Quran. The Salvaging refusal—Ofglen first, then Offred, then sixty-five stones dropped with 'I'm sorry, Aunt Lydia'—shows compassion becoming solidarity and solidarity becoming a general will, transforming The Handmaid's Tale into The Handmaids' Tale.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 36 "23. The Neighborhood Is Us" — Trip McCrossin frames the show, via Susan Neiman, as Rousseau's answer to the problem of evil: bad things (including bad television) happen to good kids, but education can mitigate evil, which is why Rogers prefers Rousseau's demand to make evil intelligible to Voltaire's Candidean refusal and Pangloss's best-of-all-possible-worlds. Rogers pursued only Emile's second prong, making us as we ought to be by loving children 'just the way they are,' and the post-9/11 PSAs before King Friday's empty castle merge Make-Believe into reality, the last 'modulation' of his thirty-four-year ministry.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 14 "4. Can We Do Enough Good" — Fetterman argues no one can do enough good to earn The Good Place because the real question is who defines good. Moving from Hobbes's state of nature and Rousseau's innate compassion to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist doctrine of non-self, he shows the four humans' characters were assembled by their formative communities, which is Michael's whole defense before Judge Gen. But Nietzsche's account of how communities christen their own customs 'good' exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife accountants impose their in-group preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's life of point-maximization fails, and why Michael should be asking the Frozen Yogurt Problem instead of blaming demon tampering.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 33 "Reflections on Technophobia" — The chapter asks whether the technophobia of 'Metalhead' - robo-dogs hunting Bella and her friends across a wasteland - is justified, testing Daniel Dinello's list of fears (identity, values, emotion, freedom, life). Descartes's and Aquinas's human-uniqueness over the mechanical fails because the robo-dogs, like DeepMind, learn and problem-solve, while the episode's Rousseau-style romanticism (only the non-technological cliff, tree, sunlight and stream aid Bella) and the teddy-bear mission show technology amplifying compassion rather than threatening it. The real dangers are robots as Latourian 'black boxes': Asimov's Three Laws cannot be operationalized, and if we cannot know how robo-dogs decide, our frameworks for blame and punishment break down (who answers for a killing - robot, programmer, or, on Marx's analysis of capitalist technology as an instrument of oppression, the economic system behind it?). The chapter concludes that since we already share the world with robots, learning to live responsibly alongside them must replace simple fear.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 14 "4. Can We Do Enough Good" — Interrogates Chidi's question 'why do we choose to be good?' through Hobbes's selfish state of nature, Rousseau's hardwired compassion (Michael's 'little voice' in Eleanor's head), and Hume's bundle theory extended Buddhist-style to a non-self, which grounds Michael's plea to Judge Gen that bad communities made the four humans bad and a better community (Team Cockroach, the Brainy Bunch) can make them good. Nietzsche's account of how communities define their own customs as 'good' then exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife's accountants impose their in-group's preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's point-maximizing life cannot clear the bar. The chapter ends by asking Michael's real question: who gets to decide what's good?
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Jackson reads the show through Rousseau's contrast between the general will and a pathological 'corporate will': Frank discards Freddy the moment his criminal past goes viral, Tusk and Walker's old friendship curdles into mutual blackmail, and Remy and Jackie trade intimacy for career protection - all reducing Aristotle's true friendship to friendships of utility and pleasure subordinated to institutions that treat persons as means. Rousseau's account of civilization degrading natural self-love (amour de soi) into vanity (amour-propre) explains why Washington's corporate ethos leaves no friends, only 'loose ends' to be eliminated, from Zoe pushed onto the platform to Doug hunting Rachel. The chapter ends with 'Man is born free, but is everywhere in chains' as the verdict on corporate personhood's conquest of human bonds.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Reads the show through Rousseau's contrast between the general will and a pathological 'corporate will': governments and corporations are sociopathic artificial persons that depersonalize their agents, degrading natural self-love (amour de soi) into status-hungry amour-propre. On this account Frank's break with Freddy ('just a good customer'), the Tusk-Walker alliance, and Remy and Jackie's bought loyalties are Aristotelian friendships of utility or pleasure crushed under the corporate will, never true friendship, leaving Washington with 'honor without virtue' and men 'everywhere in chains'.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 24 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Coatney explains why Katniss fails at everything she fakes — the disastrous first propos ('that is how a revolution dies'), the studio Mockingjay shoots, the cover-story mission to kill Snow — through Rousseau's distinction between amour de soi (natural self-love) and amour-propre (vanity born of society): she is a natural person in a corrupt world of seeming. The chapter contrasts district self-preservation with Capitol vanity (Posy asking green-skinned Octavia 'Are you sick?'), and reads Haymitch's smooth deception as a costlier, self-destroying alternative to Katniss's inability to dissimulate. Since Rousseau doubts any return to the state of nature, Katniss's refusal to flee into the woods — 'I'm going to stay right here and cause all kinds of trouble' — shows her Nietzsche-noted fate of being punished for her virtue, still preferable to becoming like Effie.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 31 "APPENDIX - Who are Locke, Hume, and Rousseau The Losties’ Guide to Philosophers" — Scott Parker's appendix profiles the philosophers behind Lost's namesake characters: John Locke for the survivor (blank-slate empiricism, belief tempered by tolerance, The Reasonableness of Christianity), David Hume for Desmond (causation as habitual inference, with the button press as the image of induction, plus bundle-theory skepticism about the self), and Jean-Jacques Rousseau for Danielle ('man is naturally good, and only by institutions is he made bad,' private property as the root of inequality). It adds Jeremy Bentham (the alias on Locke's coffin), Kierkegaard via the Fear and Trembling Hurley finds under the Temple (Abraham's teleological suspension of the ethical and the leap of faith), Dogen on zazen, Edward Said for Sayid (Orientalism and the audience's own projected savagery onto the Others), and short lives of Kate Cooper Austin, Carlyle, Rutherford, Hugo Grotius, Bakunin, Ram Dass, Edmund Burke, Hawking, Minkowski, Faraday, C. S. Lewis, and Lennon.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 13 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Reads John Teller's failed 'off the social grid' experiment through the human-nature debate: Mencius's seed of sympathy (even Tig recoils at Dante's dogfights) and Rousseau's naturally good man corrupted by society inspired J.T.'s Goldman-fed anarchism, while Mill and Xunzi counter that virtue is a victory over instinct. Hobbes supplies the real diagnosis—not innate violence but the logic of anarchy among free and equal rivals: competition (the Mayans blowing up the warehouse), diffidence (first-strike temptations against Zobelle), and glory (Jax unable to let the bike-sitting insult pass). Clay's rule that 'retaliation must be harsh and immediate' and the escalating Tig–Veronica Pope–Damon Pope–Opie bloodbath show deterrence fueling cycles of violence, so the only escape from the 'nasty, brutish, and short' fringe is the Leviathan's social grid.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 15 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Explains what anarchism actually demands—rejection of external authority, voluntary association, and faith that people need no coercion to cooperate—and measures SAMCRO against it: the club's president, church votes, chain of command, and the impossibility of Jax negotiating an exit all betray Momma Anarchy. The individualist/collectivist debate inside anarchism maps onto J.T., who retreats to Nomad and Belfast when the collective disappoints his individualist ideal, versus Jax, whose commitment to family keeps him building the collective. Clay appears as the anti-anarchist 'stone-cold egoist' who rigs votes and kills suspected rats, and the chapter argues the experiment was doomed twice over: the founding Vietnam vets' military hierarchy, and the club's dependence on the capitalist society and state agencies (CIA RICO leverage) it rejects.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 28 "Notes" — Reads Star Trek's "final frontier" through the European encounter with American Indians: the Hobbesian war-of-all-against-all stereotype of the "bloodthirsty savage" and Rousseau's opposing noble savage frame "The Paradise Syndrome", whose wigwam-and-tepee set mixes tribes into a no-place utopia. The chapter uses Hegel-style staged histories to debunk Star Trek's warp/pre-warp developmental scale (Spock on the Organians in "Errand of Mercy") as metaphysical assumption rather than biology, and counterposes the Prime Directive's noninterference to indigenous self-sovereignty and the Haudenosaunee-style consent governance that inspired the Federation. Chakotay's vision quests, the medicine bundle, Wesley's habak experience with Lakanta the Traveler in "Journey's End", and the Medicine Wheel in "Cathexis" are then interpreted through Jung's archetypes and collective unconscious, with Kirk, Spock, McCoy, and Scotty as the four Jungian modes of consciousness.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 27 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Greeley argues the zombie embodies a specifically modern fear of losing our humanity: walkers are persons stripped of the potential Aristotle and Aquinas made the measure of human worth, which is why Rick uniquely eulogizes the walkers he puts down ('I'm sorry this happened to you'). Following Aries, he traces modern death anxiety to the split of faith from reason and reads the CDC arc ('TS-19') as science offering only a self-destruct quick death where Jacqui's 'wrath of God' guess at least offers meaning. Rousseau's claim that civilization corrupts explains the survivors' return to the woods, where pizza-deliverer Glenn's heroics and the 'kingpin' Guillermo protecting nursing-home patients show the apocalypse can bring out the best in us while the Bradbury's Sale storefront and trampled Walmart worker hint we were already the walking dead.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 12 "The Divided Self Kaufman, Kafka, Wittgenstein, and Human Nature" — Von der Ruhr reads Human Nature through Kafka's 'A Report to an Academy,' whose humanized ape frames the film's inverted arc (Puff raised as ape, civilized by Nathan, then reverted by Lila). Using Nietzsche's herd passage and Norman Malcolm on animal thought, he argues the human–animal difference is one of kind, so Lila's Rousseauian idealization of Puff as 'uncontaminated by civilization' and Puff's claim that 'words are evil' are confused. Invoking Wittgenstein's view that art should teach and that lying presupposes truth-telling, he faults the film's bleak, self-referential loves while crediting it as a mirror of the viewer's own thinking.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Woolfolk reads The Last of the Mohicans as staging a conflict between nature and civilization. The opening hunt is neither Hobbes's brutish state of nature nor quite Rousseau's amoral noble savage, since the Mohicans are full moral agents; Woolfolk uses Locke's Second Treatise to cast Hawkeye and the colonists as enforcing natural law and natural rights against English 'tyranny,' with Chingachgook's killing of Magua a justified execution. Rousseau's First and Second Discourses illuminate the hypocrisy and greed of Montcalm and the Europeans, and Camus's Meursault is invoked as a truer image of amoral natural man; Tocqueville frames Cora's democratic awakening as individualism.
- **The Philosophy of Tim Burton**, ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" — Mark Walling argues that the appeal of Burton-Depp characters lies in a recovered model of childhood consciousness. Against Freud's and Piaget's view that children perceive less and are locked in the here-and-now, Walling uses Alison Gopnik's cognitive science ('babies are more conscious than we are') and Rousseau's romantic ideal of the naturally good, untutored child to read Edward Scissorhands and Ed Wood. Edward is a naturally gifted, innocent artist destroyed by a corrupt suburban 'society'; Ed Wood, megaphone in hand, is 'an eight-year-old who wants to be a movie director,' whose inattentional, make-believe joy in filmmaking—not the finished product—embodies the wide, wondering child mind Burton celebrates.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 17 "The Power of Memory and the Memory of Power Wars and Graves in Westerns and Jidaigeki" — Brodey compares John Ford's Westerns (My Darling Clementine, She Wore a Yellow Ribbon, The Searchers, The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance) with Kurosawa's jidaigeki (Seven Samurai, Throne of Blood, Hidden Fortress, Yôjimbô) as postwar mythmaking that both buries and builds national identity after military defeat. She argues graves and gravestones are bivalent symbols—commemorating loss while risking perpetuating revenge—and that both directors oscillate between Rousseauean nostalgia for a nobler past and Hobbesian frontier brutality that must be tamed. Ford trusts that memory of past wrongs can spur a better future and enable forgiveness, while Kurosawa, more pessimistic and drawing on Buddhist cyclical detachment in Throne of Blood, warns of the dangers of both remembering and forgetting trauma.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 13 "“Order Out of the Mud” Deadwood and the State of Nature" — Cantor reads David Milch's Deadwood as a dramatization of 'order without law,' testing the mining camp against the state-of-nature theories of Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau. Deadwood is Hobbesian in its sources of violence (competition, diffidence, glory; Al Swearengen's alpha-male struggles), but Lockean in showing property rights and commerce arising spontaneously before the state—gold becomes a self-generated medium of exchange that even overrides prejudice (Hearst dealing with Odell). It is Rousseauian in its innate pity (Swearengen's mercy) and its skepticism that incorporation into the nation-state, symbolized by the telegraph and Hearst's abstract corporate power, counts as progress.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 23 "Savage Nations Native Americans and the Western" — Michael Valdez Moses uses Todorov's analysis of Columbus and Las Casas—the failure to grant the Other both equality and difference—to argue that Hollywood's Native Americans, whether demonized or idealized, are egocentric projections of white American concerns. He traces the 'noble savage' from Rousseau's Second Discourse and Ferguson's proto-republican warrior through Ford's Fort Apache (New Deal common man), the 1970s revisionist westerns (Little Big Man, A Man Called Horse) as countercultural Rousseauian dropouts and Vietnam allegory, and Dances with Wolves, culminating in Jarmusch's Dead Man, whose Nobody escapes the collective stereotype to stand as a genuinely individual, cosmopolitan character.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 39 "Gaining Trust from the Past" — Richard Davies treats the Oceanic 815 survivors of Lost as a real state of nature, playing on the characters named Locke, Rousseau, and Hume. The scarce-water and asthma-inhaler disputes are 'tragedies of the commons,' and Sawyer's 'finders keepers' embodies a Hobbesian 'Trust No. 1' while Hurley and Jack lean toward Rousseauian 'Innocence.' Using game theory's repeated prisoners' dilemma and 'tit-for-tat,' Davies argues a Lockean state of nature (opening with cooperation) rather than a doomed Hobbesian one lets the survivors build a commonwealth against the Others.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 19 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Florell and Wilson, psychologists, survey parenting through the nature–nurture debate, casting Locke's tabula rasa against Rousseau's noble-savage view of children, alongside Piaget and Kohlberg on moral development and Walter Mischel's marshmallow experiment on impulse control. They map the four parenting styles (authoritarian, permissive, uninvolved, authoritative) on responsiveness and control, argue authoritative parenting is optimal, and advise fathers to adjust discipline to each child's innate temperament rather than enforce rigid gender roles.

### Teleological Suspension of the Ethical

The teleological suspension of the ethical is Kierkegaard's provocative claim that faith can, in rare cases, require setting aside universal moral duty for the sake of a higher relation to the divine. His central example is Abraham, commanded to sacrifice Isaac, whose obedience makes no sense within ordinary ethics and can be justified only by a private, absolute duty to God. The idea dramatizes the gap between the ethical, which is universal and communicable, and faith, which is singular and cannot be fully explained to others.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 12 "Conclusion" — William Irwin argues Kramer is Kierkegaard's aesthete par excellence: his endless abandoned schemes (make-your-own-pizza, beach-smelling cologne, Kramerica Industries), his aliases (H.E. Pennypacker, Dr. Van Nostrand), and his 'Kavorka' revolving door of women enact Either/Or's 'crop rotation' method and the Diary of the Seducer, all flight from the despair hinted at in 'The Switch' ('All this time I'm trying not to be me'). His brief office job in 'The Bizarro Jerry' - 'structure... TCB, taking care of business' - is a flirtation with Judge William's ethical stage of commitment, and Irwin closes with a thought experiment: could Kramer ever make the leap of faith to the religious stage, performing his own teleological suspension of the ethical like Abraham?
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 14 "Kierkegaard Lays It Down" — Willie Young uses the sacrifice bunt (Derek Jeter's perfect one versus Placido Polanco's failed one) to test philosophical accounts of sacrifice. Aristotle treats bunting for teammates as friendship and civic virtue in the polis, while Seneca's Stoic sacrifices only to exercise virtue itself, detached from particular friends and refusing retaliation for hit batters. Hegel's modern ideal of self-renunciation makes the player a cog in the team machine (the Big Red Machine), obeying the manager's calculations; against this, Kierkegaard's Abraham, whose absolute duty to God is 'higher than the universal' through infinite resignation, exposes baseball's mechanical, manager-ordered sacrifice and asks whether the game trains obedient citizens who sacrifice as they are told.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 16 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter reads preacher Billy St. Cyr's snake-handling through Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling: like Abraham, Billy performs the absurd double movement - fully resigning himself to dying by rattlesnake while believing he will be spared - which is why Boyd Crowder, who abandoned faith for Hegel's objective rational certainty, can neither buy him out nor understand him. Kierkegaard's teleological suspension of the ethical explains why Billy and Abraham may set obedience to God above self-preservation and social morality, while Boyd's showdown in 'Truth and Consequences', where he hands Billy an un-milked rattlesnake, exposes that Billy's certainty has curdled into the hubris de Silentio warns against, so Billy is no Abraham. De Silentio's three marks - love, humility, no desire to instruct others - separate genuine faith from cult leaders and violent extremists.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 35 "21. Stannis—Knight of Faith or Tragic Hero" — Devlin asks whether Stannis, who burns Shireen to save his army, is Kierkegaard's knight of faith or merely a tragic hero. Stannis's duty-obsessed deontology - knighting Davos while cutting off his fingertips, striking 'beloved brother' from a letter as a lie - is Kantian, and the Shireen dilemma looks like Abraham's teleological suspension of the ethical; yet because Stannis always calculates and justifies ('Faith? In a real war, the side with the greater number wins nine times out of ten'), he never makes the leap on the strength of the absurd, and Davos ends up following Kant's own verdict on Abraham: 'If he commands you to burn children, your lord is evil.' He is therefore a tragic hero in the line of Agamemnon and Jephthah, rationally comprehensible and fittingly undone by Brienne's 'do your duty.'
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 18 "8. Believing the Impossible in a World of Compromise" — Brake maps Kierkegaard's spheres onto the rivals: Tony inhabits the ethical sphere of universal reason and compromise (Ross's 'that's how the world works', the tragic hero choosing lesser evils), while Steve lives the religious sphere of faith in the impossible - 'my faith's in people'. Through Fear and Trembling's Abraham, the comic Civil War (Tony manipulating Spider-Man, Steve's Japanese-internment warning), and Hickman's incursions where Steve alone tells the calculating Illuminati to believe, he argues a hero is judged by how he begins in faith, not by results. Steve's trust that the world can be saved 'by the absurd' is vindicated when Secret Wars restores the multiverse, and his simple 'I believe you' rescues Tony in Avengers Disassembled.
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 30 "16. Gotta Have Faith" — Winters asks what faith is when the Party risks burning and becoming demodog chow so Eleven can close the gate: after arguing via George Michael and the talisman-free tunnels that faith need not be religious, he tests Bishop's models of faith against 'The Gate' (the affective and secular hope models fit; the belief and trust models fail because everyone has seen the Mind Flayer's work on Will). Hume's account that causation is never observed, only habituated, explains the Party's hope that heat will drive the Mind Flayer from Will and that Christmas lights will reach him, and Kierkegaard's teleological suspension of the ethical and knight of faith frame Eleven's willingness to die against the absurd, since aligning her life with friendship's higher purpose is what makes it meaningful.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 30 "18. K’s Most Excellent Kierkegaardian Pilgrimage" — Ben Franz runs K and Luv through Kierkegaard's Either/Or and Fear and Trembling. Luv is the Knight of Faith, an Abraham whose total devotion to her god Wallace involves the teleological suspension of the ethical — killing the Rachael copy, torturing Joshi — and who dies, film-noir fashion, for failing her creator's command. K is the Knight of Infinite Resignation, repeatedly raised to believe he is special and repeatedly deflated — the wooden horse date, the nursemaid's denial, Joi's death — until he resigns himself to faking Deckard's death and reuniting father and daughter; in the noir inversion, the villain has perfect faith and the hero never attains it.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 22 "12. Why Blood Sacrifice" — Philip Wilson defines sacrifice as gift-giving with payback ('I give x in order to get y') and reads Thanos's murder of Gamora through Agamemnon's sacrifice of Iphigenia at Aulis, while Black Widow's willing leap from the same cliff parallels Christ's atoning self-sacrifice. The core is Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling: Abraham's binding of Isaac as the 'teleological suspension of the ethical,' where obeying God suspends universal morality, sharpened by Kant's argument that Abraham should have told the supposed divine voice he could never be certain it came from God. Wilson argues the films restore rather than suspend ethics, Gamora was murdered rather than sacrificed, Natasha died willingly with no collateral harm, and Tony's final 'I am Iron Man' self-sacrifice completes the tragic arc, leaving readers with Kierkegaard's sleepless questions about a moral order that demands blood.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 31 "19. Thanos Is No Abraham" — Uses Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling to compare Thanos's killing of Gamora on Mount Vormir with Abraham's binding of Isaac, laying out the aesthetic, ethical, and religious stages. It argues Thanos initially looks 'religious' — his sacrifice expresses a particular, personal encounter with the absolute balance of all things, neither an aesthetic whim nor an ethical calculation — but that his Endgame slip ('what I'm about to do to your stubborn, annoying little planet… I'm gonna enjoy it. Very, very much') exposes him as a mere aesthete dressing bloodlust in metaphysics. Hence Thanos is no Abraham, and the truly religious type remains a frightening but unrealized possibility.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 27 "15 Indiana Jones and the Leap of Faith" — Uses Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling to argue that Indy's step off the lion's head in Last Crusade is not a genuine leap of faith: Abraham's leap rests on absurd trust in God and the 'teleological suspension of the ethical,' whereas Indy acts to save his father and risks arming the Nazis — making him at most a tragic hero choosing between competing ethical duties. The chapter then sorts the film's believers into Kierkegaard's two knights, classifying Kazim of the Brotherhood as a Knight of Infinite Resignation, the Grail Knight as a near-miss Knight of Faith (he guards rather than lives in the ordinary world), and Henry and Marcus as devout but neither. Kierkegaard would complain that modern faith is 'dirt cheap' compared with Abraham's arduous biblical faith, and Indy's relief at not falling confirms he is no Knight of Faith.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 31 "APPENDIX - Who are Locke, Hume, and Rousseau The Losties’ Guide to Philosophers" — Scott Parker's appendix profiles the philosophers behind Lost's namesake characters: John Locke for the survivor (blank-slate empiricism, belief tempered by tolerance, The Reasonableness of Christianity), David Hume for Desmond (causation as habitual inference, with the button press as the image of induction, plus bundle-theory skepticism about the self), and Jean-Jacques Rousseau for Danielle ('man is naturally good, and only by institutions is he made bad,' private property as the root of inequality). It adds Jeremy Bentham (the alias on Locke's coffin), Kierkegaard via the Fear and Trembling Hurley finds under the Temple (Abraham's teleological suspension of the ethical and the leap of faith), Dogen on zazen, Edward Said for Sayid (Orientalism and the audience's own projected savagery onto the Others), and short lives of Kate Cooper Austin, Carlyle, Rutherford, Hugo Grotius, Bakunin, Ram Dass, Edmund Burke, Hawking, Minkowski, Faraday, C. S. Lewis, and Lennon.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 10 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Kukkonen reads Peter's never-extinguished guilt over Uncle Ben as an 'infinite debt' modeled on Anselm's atonement theology: no good deed repays the primal transgression, so even the heroic serum rescue for Aunt May in 'The Final Chapter' (Amazing Spider-Man #33) leaves the debt intact. Against the Nietzschean escape into self-sufficient magnanimity (Ben's ghostly blessing in 'Doom Service!'), he argues via Levinas and Derrida that Peter's responsibility extends to every stranger, as when a rescued policeman with Uncle Ben's face calls him back in 'Spider-Man No More!' (#50). Following Kierkegaard's Works of Love, the chapter concludes that Peter's heroics do not pay off but deepen his debt of love, since every choice heeds one call while unavoidably failing others.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 10 "Notes" — Lindenmuth reads Luke's endgame in Return of the Jedi as Kierkegaard's knight of faith, reversing Abraham's binding of Isaac: where Abraham raised the knife, Luke, pressed by Yoda and Obi-Wan to kill his father, throws his saber away. Jedi detachment ('train yourself to let go') is infinite resignation, and Han Solo's arc from self-interested smuggler to hero at Yavin traces Kierkegaard's aesthetic-to-ethical stages. Luke's double movement - resigning everything, his cause and his life, while trusting there is still good in Vader - suspends the ethical demand to kill and accomplishes what neither side thought possible: turning a Sith back to the light.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 36 "Purpose or Futility" — Tiernan reads Din Djarin as an Abraham figure from Fear and Trembling: like Kierkegaard's knight of faith, he teleologically suspends the ethical when he surrenders Grogu to the Jedi despite paternal attachment, just as Abraham consented to sacrifice Isaac. The chapter maps his journey onto Kierkegaard's three stages - the aesthetic temptation of settling down with Omera on Sorgan, the ethical duty of the Resol'nare and the Way, and the religious leap of faith in which purpose is regained by being given up. To become a true Mandalorian he must paradoxically abandon the creed that defines him, twice removing the helmet he swore never to remove - for the Morak facial scan and to bid Grogu farewell.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 26 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Round argues modern zombie fiction's real horror is humanity, reading The Walking Dead existentially: Rick builds meaning through self-imposed missions, revises his morals ('You kill, you die' then killing Dexter anyway), and demands in his 'We ARE the walking dead' speech (Issue #24) that the group admit their new nature instead of hiding in bad faith behind old rules. Kierkegaard's Abraham illuminates Rick's suspension of universal ethics, while Sergeant Abraham Ford's confession 'No. I did what I wanted to do' models owning one's choices, and his angst after Eugene's lie shows the cost of projected meaning collapsing. Camus supplies persistence against the absurd (suicides like Jim, Jacqui, and Carol exert the only control left), and Adorno's Marxist critique frames the Governor's Woodbury as an inauthentic hierarchy that denies its people authentic choice.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 18 "No Country for Old Men as Moral Philosophy" — McFarland reads the film as moral philosophy: Sheriff Bell faces a post-Kantian predicament, able to reconstruct how crimes happen but unable to 'measure' why, and dooms himself by tying duty to an outcome (his promise to make Llewelyn safe) rather than to Kant's unconditional imperative, so failure yields Bernard Williams-style shame. Llewelyn is cast against Kierkegaard's Abraham/Brutus distinction as a tragic hero who cannot suspend the ethical, while Chigurh functions as an ironic anti-philosopher who alternately grounds killing in self-interest ('what good is a rule if it got you here?') and in a perverse Kantian promise-keeping, until Carla Jean restores moral responsibility by refusing his coin toss.

### Transcendentalism

Transcendentalism was a nineteenth-century American intellectual and literary movement, centered in New England, that emphasized the primacy of intuition, the divinity of nature, and the inherent goodness and self-sufficiency of the individual. Drawing on Romanticism and German idealism, its figures—chiefly Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau—held that a deeper spiritual truth transcends the senses and is accessible directly through personal insight rather than through established institutions or received doctrine. The movement fed reform causes, from abolition to education, and reshaped American letters.

- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 22 "Friends—Don’t Leave Home without ’Em" — Greg Ahrenhoerster places SpongeBob in literary history between Transcendentalism and naturalism: 'Nature Pants' is a failed Walden — SpongeBob gives away his possessions for Jellyfish Fields but his 'jellyfish instincts' fail as badly as self-reliance in London's 'To Build a Fire' — while 'Squidville' shows the industrial city's cold indifference as in Crane's Maggie. 'Jellyfish Hunter' warns that trying to exploit nature (Krabs's jelly factory) invites nature's reprisal, since civilized beings without instinct are at nature's mercy. The naturalist moral, against Transcendentalist solitude, is that we survive only through each other: visit Jellyfish Fields, but bring a friend.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 43 "a21.xhtml" — Kraus argues The Hobbit is two different books depending on the reader's experience: read cold it is a fairy-tale of adventure, but reread after The Lord of the Rings - knowing what the Ring did to Bilbo and what 'precious' means - it becomes a song of innocence and experience like Blake's Songs and Wordsworth's 'emotion recollected in tranquillity', where Elrond's opening description points to the deep Silmarillion history a first-time reader cannot yet feel. Emerson's 'transparent eye-ball' from Nature - the self stripped bare and made original in the woods - becomes Bilbo's first use of the Ring, where invisibility lets him see Gollum's miserable humanity and choose pity; but the image darkens into Sauron's Lidless Eye, the totalizing knowledge that defines and devours selves. 'There and back again' thus echoes nostos turned nostalgia: Bilbo never truly gets back, having traded the child's innocence Thorin praises on his deathbed for an experience he cannot undo.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 11 "Being-at-Home Gary Snyder and the Poetics of Place" — Hayes reads Gary Snyder's poetry and prose on 'being-at-home' through Heidegger's claim that 'poetically man dwells' and his earth/world distinction, arguing Snyder's bioregionalism (renaming California the 'Shasta Bioregion,' America 'Turtle Island') roots identity in place while embracing Zen impermanence learned from Dōgen. Snyder's shamanic 'tawny grammar,' his pragmatic environmental program in 'Four Changes,' and his Transcendentalist lineage (Thoreau, Emerson) turn wildness into 'the state of complete awareness,' letting a place 'set free into its own presencing' and grounding a poetics of dwelling that is at once local, geological, and impermanent.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 23 "Synecdoche, in Part" — Smith reads every Kaufman film as a farce about the self-defeating quest to 'become who you are,' with Synecdoche, New York as its culmination: Caden's MacArthur-funded attempt to represent all of life in a warehouse collapses into infinite regress because a representation of everything must contain itself. He frames Kaufman's films as Montaignean/Emersonian essays—fragmentary self-portraits—and argues the film's limits are death and language, since language always puts us at one remove from the life we already are. The transcendence it evokes is naturalistic, akin to Nietzsche's amor fati and Emerson's 'we are born to a whole': wholeness is not achieved but already possessed, and the hidden knowledge of it turns tragedy into farce.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 5 "Foreword" — Robert Porfirio's foreword traces film noir's dark sensibility to a native strain in American culture rather than only to imported existentialism, running from Puritan gloom through Poe, Melville, and Hawthorne to the hard-boiled pulp of Hammett, Chandler, and Woolrich. He argues that William James's pragmatism sounded the death knell of the Emersonian/Thoreauvian transcendentalist faith in self-reliance and nature, leaving the way open for Darwinism, Freudianism, and Nietzschean pessimism to reduce the individual to a 'waif amidst forces.' He connects this to the Germanic emigres who brought expressionist style, suggesting they were drawn to an American darkness already present, and closes wondering what post-9/11 neo-noir will make of the same fear and paranoia.
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 22 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — R.
