- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 35 "Last Pitch" — Reid argues that baseball and Socratic elenchus are both constructed to cultivate aretē, excellence. She maps four parallels onto concrete moments: both live off uncertainty (pre-game jitters, the 2001 Rivera–Gonzalez Series finish), both require risking failure (Ted Williams playing a doubleheader to protect his .400, Kirk Gibson's hobbling 1988 homer off Dennis Eckersley, Billy Beane's fear beside Lenny Dykstra), both demand active self-testing (Lou Gehrig retiring when complimented on a routine play), and both impose an obligation to return and challenge others — Plato's cave allegory, Socrates the gadfly, the aging champion who applauds the record-breaker. The Delphic oracle's riddle, that Socrates is wisest in knowing his ignorance, is the batter's-box humility every at-bat demands.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 25 "Hope" — Jill Gordon reads Another Woman as a film about self-knowledge structured by Socrates' self-seeing eye from Plato's Alcibiades I: just as an eye sees itself only in another eye, the emotionally walled-off philosophy professor Marion Post finally sees her own repression by overhearing the 'other woman' Hope's therapy through a vent. Each of her relationships, with husband Ken, brother Paul, renounced lover Larry, stepdaughter Laura, and friend Claire, mirrors back truths ('she stands above people and evaluates them') that her self-deception refuses until her dream stages her own analysis and the final session describes her own life exactly. Counting the irrecoverable cost of her chances (Larry, the aborted child), the chapter closes with Rilke's 'Archaic Torso of Apollo', 'You must change your life', as the command Marion finally obeys, yielding a hard-won and still hopeful transformation.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 74 "Harry’s Cloak, the Ring of Gyges, and the Temptations of Power" — This section contrasts Voldemort and Dumbledore as two figures tempted by power. Tom Riddle's egocentrism - frightening and controlling other children at the orphanage, treating his 'friends' as mere followers, killing Lily, and splintering his soul for Horcruxes - violates Kant's dictum never to use persons merely as means and fits Plato's category of the least trustworthy rulers. Dumbledore, though tempted in youth by Grindelwald's 'for the greater good' schemes and later by Marvolo Gaunt's ring, is venerable for Socratic self-knowledge: knowing 'I was not to be trusted with power,' he repeatedly refused the Ministry and so promoted justice by teaching.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 89 "Unknown" — The section urges a Socratic habit of self-examination, with Dumbledore as its model: knowing his besetting weakness was the love of power, he repeatedly refused the post of Minister of Magic, and after his infatuation with Grindelwald made him 'lose his moral compass completely' he distrusted his own judgment in matters of the heart. The Pensieve, which lets Dumbledore siphon off excess memories and review them from a third-person perspective to 'spot patterns and links,' is presented as a literal device for living the examined life.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 148 "The End of the Story" — Argues Socrates and Dumbledore both die for virtue and the common good: Socrates refuses exile because the examined life matters more than wealth or reputation, his martyrdom an exemplar that could benefit Athens, and Dumbledore's arranged death protects Snape's spying for the anti-Voldemort cause. Two Muggle lessons follow - live devoted to something larger than yourself (Lily's sacrifice, with King, Gandhi, Jesus, and Socrates as real-world parallels) and find mentors, as Dumbledore's humility, honesty, and praise in the Order of the Phoenix prophecy conversation enable Harry to fulfill his destiny, with dead mentors like Aristotle, Confucius, and Jesus still able to teach us through their books.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 7 "Foreword" — Cornel West argues that Plato's dialogues invented philosophy as a Socratic genre of cross-examination and bold frank speech (parrhesia) about ordinary life, and that hip-hop music - like the spirituals, blues, and jazz - enacts that same parrhesia against conventional morality and entrenched power. He claims reading hip hop philosophically demands metaphilosophical subtlety, showing how paideia, phronesis, and parrhesia operate in the work of cultural producers under free-market fundamentalism and authoritarianism. Because the racial dimension of hip hop is inescapable, he says philosophers must break their discipline's silence on race and music (neglected figures like Du Bois and Alain Locke alongside Aristotle, Kant, and Rorty), closing with Cicero's Socrates who turned philosophy from the heavens to earth and William James's pragmatism that took it from the academy to the streets.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 9 "From Rhyme to Reason This Shit Ain’t Easy" — The editors' introduction argues that hip hop and philosophy are both street-born examinations of life in pursuit of wisdom: Socrates's elenchus is likened to MC lyrical battles and call-and-response (his interrogations compared to Rakim's technique, his execution for corrupting the youth to the fate of a controversial rapper), while Plato's philosopher-king parallels Kurtis Blow and Run-D.M.C. claiming thrones. After a Bronx hip-hop history sketch (Kool Herc, BDP's "The Bridge is Over"), they frame the volume around hip hop's suppressed fifth element of knowledge and preview its pairings: Aquinas and Rakim on God, Plato and Lauryn Hill on love, Sartre and Lil' Kim's gaze, Kant and Ice Cube on punishment, Hegel and Nas, Hobbes and Dead Prez, Mill and Chappelle on epithets. Record companies don't own hip hop and universities don't own philosophy, they conclude - both belong to whoever understands, loves, and respects them.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 15 "And Now for . . . Comedic Eliminativism" — Argues The Meaning of Life dismantles the 'axial' picture of life as a journey toward a salvific destination (Jaspers's Axial Age thinking), instanced in the headmaster who announces Jenkins's mother's death between Empire Day announcements, the tank fish who never connect Howard's being eaten to their own fate, and the restaurant couple ordering 'philosophy for two' with no appetite for wisdom. The classical answers all fail as delivered: Socrates's philosophy as learning how to die, Heidegger's claim that facing death reveals one's own unique possibilities, and Kant's three questions (What can I know? What should I do? For what may I hope?) collapse into the question of life's meaning, but religion has gone stale and philosophy has become detached trivia. The Pythons instead accomplish the user-friendly domestication of the death of God — the hearty laughter Nietzsche and Derrida counsel — and the chapter coins 'comedic eliminativism' on the model of eliminative materialism's dissolution of Descartes's mind-body problem: replace the yearning for the meaning of life with altered reactions, laughter itself as the solution to the riddle.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 9 "The Talking Cure for Our Culture" — Young argues South Park is perceived as dangerous for the very reasons Socrates was executed — corrupting the youth and impiety — and that like Socrates it is really a gadfly promoting the examined life. Cartman is read through Arendt's Eichmann: evil as thoughtlessness, the inability to think from another's standpoint or ask if one can live with oneself, while Kyle and Stan's dialogues (such as deliberating Stan's grandfather's euthanasia request in 'Death') model the perspective-taking Arendt calls thinking. A final Freudian section explains the show's vulgarity as essential: jokes work like dreams, releasing repressed drives so the culture can talk through what it forbids.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 49 "House and the Life of Reason" — Henry Jacoby takes seriously House's nihilist sound bites ("selfish, base animals," his baiting of Sister Augustine and Foreman's chapel prayer, his clinically dead experiment in "97 Seconds") but argues House actually lives the Socratic examined life and Aristotle's life of reason: his puzzle-solving saves lives, exercises humanity's distinctive function, and issues in eudaimonia. The Euthyphro dilemma shows meaning cannot be grounded in God's plan, and House's refusal of afterlife comfort leaves "our actions here" as all that matters. Against the unexamined life, House's "What's the point in living without curiosity?" makes him a Socratic figure who chooses meaning through reason rather than faith.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 28 "Resignation and Exploration—I’ll Climb the Hill in My Own Way" — Steven Gimbel asks how to live with the 'pink' malaise of Waters's lyrics and tests five options: capitulation (Marx's four alienations via 'In the Flesh?', 'Have a Cigar', and 'Dogs'), medication ('Comfortably Numb' and the Prozac-ad mother as one of the 'neuro-chemically well-adjusted sheep'), re-creation of childhood (Nietzsche's child playing 'between the fences of past and future' against memory's 'it was' in 'Remember a Day'), and emancipation through LSD or romanticized madness ('See Emily Play', 'Brain Damage'), with Syd Barrett's vacant eyes as the fatal counterexample. What survives is Camus's Sisyphus — fully conscious of his futility yet 'superior to his fate', imagined happy — joined to 'Fearless''s 'I'll climb that hill in my own way' and the mutual care of 'Pigs on the Wing', closing on Socrates' unexamined life: the answer lies in the searching itself, so living pink means living.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 6 "Ex Astris, Scientia GEORGE A REISCH" — The editors' introduction takes Starfleet Academy's motto 'Ex Astris, Scientia' as its frame: Picard handing cadet Wesley Crusher a book by William James shows officers need philosophy, not just ship operations, and the starry-heavens motif runs from Thales and Plato's cave through Kant's 'moral law within and starry heavens above.' It surveys the book's Trek dilemmas (Picard and Dathon's alien language, Data's emotion chip, Khan's vengeance, Riker's Q powers) as 2,500-year-old philosophical problems, and argues Trek's optimism — Picard's 'the acquisition of wealth is no longer the driving force' — restates Aristotle's claim that all humans by nature desire to know. Like philosophy from Socrates on, Trek is presented as 'an entertaining, edifying preparation' for living by one's ideals, a life-education primer sealed with Roddenberry's advice to 'slip in a heavy idea or two.'
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 26 "Must I Repeat Myself" — Seng maps Dorothy's journey onto Plato's cave allegory: Kansas is the cave of shadows, Oz the painful ascent into light, and the crucial shared point is Socrates' demand that the freed prisoner go back down into the cave, which explains why Dorothy, once enlightened, must return to gray Kansas bearing self-knowledge. He surveys the film adaptations (1910, Semon's 1925, Eshbaugh's 1933, Fleming's 1939, Return to Oz, and The Wiz) to show that each rewrites 'home' as self-knowledge rather than a place, culminating in Glinda's The Wiz speech, 'If we know ourselves, we're always home, anywhere.' Kierkegaard's contrast between recollection and repetition then sorts the homecomings: Baum's Dorothy wills recollection of what was lost, while Diana Ross's Dorothy wills repetition, holding to her self amid change, which Seng says Kierkegaard regards as the equivalent of faith.
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 16 "How We Still Might Manage a Smile Being Pirates and Making Meaning" — Adam Glover reads 'A Pirate Looks at Forty' through Kristeva's intertextuality: since every text and self is a 'mosaic of quotations' pirated from pre-existing sources, Buffett's confession that he was born 'two hundred years too late' makes him an ironic pirate who can no longer believe or plunder unselfconsciously, unlike the oblivious common-sense pirate. Invoking Barthes's death of the author, he argues the pirate's life is a hard freedom to improvise multiple meanings (the ever-changing 'head uptown' variations in the song) with full responsibility for one's choices. The chapter ends weighing Camus's worry that meaninglessness makes life not worth living against the Nietzsche of The Birth of Tragedy, who answers that the meaning of life is life itself, and it sides with Buffett against Socrates's 'unexamined life' while admitting it cannot settle the question.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 11 "Under-Confidence in Reason Once It’s Easier Said, then It’s Done" — Roben Torosyan turns Colbert into a negative textbook for critical thinking: the character embodies the exact opposite of the American Philosophical Association's seven critical-thinking dispositions (inquisitive, open-minded, truthseeking, systematic, analytical, judicious, confident in reason), from refusing to imagine Lisa Randall's extra dimensions, to 'the market doesn't lie' about the Bible, to placing himself above Maimonides, Socrates, and Aquinas in the stem-cell Formidable Opponent. Each section names the fallacies his shtick commits - appeal to popularity, appeal to ignorance, composition, circular reasoning, wishful thinking, appeal to consequences - using real WØRD bits like the Iraq 'no casualties' monologue and the cake-metaphor exchange about the war. The WØRD's self-undermining bullet points are read as Derridean deconstruction (différance): every assertion shot through with what differs from and defers it. Watching Colbert fail at the examined life Socrates recommended, the viewer learns to catch such abuses in pundits and in themselves.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 18 "Philosophy in the Age of Truthiness" — David Detmer explains how the twentieth century's scientific persuasion techniques plus electronic media, American anti-elitism ('science is elitist... Gravity Without Representation'), the conflation of a legal right to an opinion with its being right, and journalism's bankrupt objectivity doctrine produced the age of truthiness that Colbert satirizes (Britannica and the Panama Canal, Limbaugh, O'Reilly, and Coulter as the 'gasbags'). He then rebuts the book's implicit challenge that philosophers' appeals to intuition are themselves truthiness: self-evident truths like 'cruelty is wrong' or Euclid's axioms are needed to stop the infinite regress of justification, and they differ in kind from gut-feelings about historical or political claims whose denial is easily conceived. The Report's nightly ridicule of truthiness therefore serves Socrates' dictum that the unexamined life is not worth living, showing philosophy's value to a public that lets pundits decide by gut.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 25 "The Onion, Sarcasm, and the Good of Mankind" — Noah Levin recounts how the Onion article 'Area Man Committed To Being Spicy Food Guy' made him recognize his own obnoxious boasting about hot food and quietly change, presenting satire as continuing philosophy's self-help tradition back to Socrates' 'know thyself.' He distinguishes parody, satire, and sarcasm, then formalizes Onion jokes — the RIAA suing radio stations for giving away free music, and 'That Teen-Abstinence Rally Totally Rocked!' — as implicit reductio ad absurdum arguments whose absurd conclusions force rejection of a hidden premise. The sarcastic route beats a direct lecture, he argues, because the target must complete the three-step argument himself: identify the mocked trait, admit having it, and decide whether to change.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 43 "Ah, Doctor. We Know You by Reputation" — Argues Doctor Who is philosophy's ally by way of Plato's Gorgias distinction between teaching, which produces justified true belief, and rhetoric, which wins by persuasion: the Master is the master rhetorician whose hypnotic manipulation manufactures unreliable beliefs, while the Doctor is the Socratic teacher who gives information and lets companions decide. Socrates's descriptions of philosophy (the good life, sense of wonder, love of real knowledge) are matched to the show's career as an educational program that teaches viewers to reflect on how they reason, how they treat 'others' like Daleks and Silurians, and to revise their views, that is, to live the examined life.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 7 "Know Thyself" — George Reisch's introduction frames the volume with Martha Stout's claim that one in twenty-five people is a conscience-free sociopath who hides in plain sight, arguing that we viewers do the hiding work for them just as Deb, LaGuerta and Batista's assumptions shield Dexter. It presents Dexter's incessant inner questioning as the show's philosophical hook and previews the book's competing verdicts on Harry's Code: monster, Kantian-style model actor, utilitarian good, aesthete, or superhero. It ends by inverting Socrates: normally we point 'know thyself' inward, but the real epistemic danger is the sociopath next door, so our skepticism should aim at the guy in forensics - unless we are ourselves among the one-in-twenty-five, in which case Socrates' injunction to self-examination was spot on.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 6 "UNSC Briefing" — Fred Van Lente's introduction argues that Master Chief is deliberately an empty shell—faceless, ageless, mostly silent—so the player's identity grafted onto him brings both to life at once in Halo: Combat Evolved's opening cryo-wakeup tutorial. He frames the book with Thoreau's Walden claim that philosophy is living simplicity, mapping it onto the Chief's ascetic soldier existence, and on Socrates: a game worth playing is worth examining, since the unexamined game is not worth playing. He closes with Aristotle's potentiality and actuality: the game actualizes the Chief as a kicker of alien ass, and the book actualizes the series' social and philosophical potential.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 14 "So, You Tried to Kill Me Over a Little New Age Management, Eh" — Joseph Foy weighs Mr. Krabs against Ayn Rand's celebration of money-making, Marx's charge that Krabs commodifies his employees — wagering SpongeBob to Plankton in 'Welcome to the Chum Bucket' and working him 43 days without a break in 'Fear of a Krabby Patty' — and Aristotle's and Adam Smith's insistence that wealth is merely instrumental to flourishing. The verdict: Krabs inverts means and ends, fetishizing money until he sells SpongeBob's soul for 62 cents ('Born Again Krabs') and trades his own body for his millionth dollar ('Clams'). His real failing is the unexamined life — he never asks what would actually make him happy — which makes him tragically human rather than simply villainous.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 12 "Group Will" — Testerman turns inception against itself: Cobb and Saito believe they freely plan the Fischer job, but conscious will is a feeling, not a cause. From William James's effortful attention and Dewey's willpower she moves to Penfield's stimulated patients and Libet's readiness-potential experiments showing the brain prepares action before we feel we will it, so Fischer, Cobb and Saito are all equally 'incepted' by subconscious forces - 'freedom is ignorance of the causes of actions', as she glosses Spinoza, with Hume's point that causality is only inferred. Advertising, the foot-in-the-door effect and subliminal primes already do inception's work more cheaply, and the team's 'group will' flows from Saito's own unexamined drive for power, so against Socrates she concludes the unexamined life is perfectly suitable for living.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 50 "Chapter 07 - Scan Thyself" — Butler frames Dick as the latest in philosophy's self-knowledge line: the Delphic 'know thyself' that Socrates made essential to the good life at the cost of his own, the Buddha who sought himself and found only an illusion at the root of suffering, Descartes whose entire philosophy rests on confidence in knowledge of himself as an immaterial being, and Dick's own 8,000-page Exegesis. The chapter's hook is the stakes of self-ignorance (what if you turned out to be something horrible?) and its Dickian version: how do you know you are not an android?
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 179 "Chapter 32 - “The Exit Door Leads In”" — Eric Beck reads 'The Exit Door Leads In' as a modernized Platonic dialogue: like Oedipus before the Sphinx, the average salesman Bob Bibleman wins mandatory university admission by answering a computerized waiter's riddle, staging the Delphic 'Know Thyself' against Plato's Gorgias ideal of self-mastery, while Plato's Socrates in Charmides disclaims healthy self-knowledge. When Bibleman's terminal spills classified engine schematics, he decides not on universal principle but on what he thinks the authorities want; his honest answer that he would have handed them over anyway gets him expelled for failing a test he could not read, a double bind showing self-knowledge is contingent and situational. Dick thus revises knowing oneself as negotiation of the state's expectations rather than discovery of an essence, though the ending - Bibleman paying the computer after deciding not to - leaves open that he may one day rebel and need re-education.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 180 "Chapter 33 - “The Gun”" — Benjamin Stevens reads 'The Gun' - a mindless automated weapon still defending a dead community - as an early statement of Dick's fear that in the Cold War military-industrial complex our very capacities for thought, will and free action may have been objectified into products of a mechanized system that no longer serves us. He brings Dick into dialogue with Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry (we are industrially 'produced' as consumers, turned into the carbon-based equivalent of plastic), Walter Benjamin's loss of aura under mechanical reproduction, Hannah Arendt's worry that Sputnik signals an unwise desire to escape our earthliness, and Heidegger's broadened question concerning technology as social control. Like Plato, Dick insists the unexamined life is not worth living: the best life cannot be lived inside a culture that has, without our informed consent, made us artificial.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 48 "Out of the Cave" — Traces the light-versus-darkness metaphor tradition from Plato's cave and Socrates' unexamined life through medieval 'illumination' and the Enlightenment to St. Paul's glass darkly, then lets Nietzsche ('shadow is as needful as light') and Derrida's deconstruction of presence/absence oppositions overturn it. The Stones do the same work in song: 'Just as every cop is a criminal, and all the sinners saints' in 'Sympathy for the Devil,' with 'Here Comes the Sun' overturned by 'Paint It Black' and 'Let It Be' by 'Let It Bleed.'
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 10 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Vannatta explains why Seinfeld reruns now fall flat through Klosterman's neologism 'unironically': since about 1991 irony has become the invisible background of American comedy, a pervasive detachment that David Foster Wallace named and that Jedediah Purdy's For Common Things attacks as the gap between phenomenon and essence. Against Purdy's ironist (Seinfeld's Jerry, mastered by irony, believing in nothing but his own interests), the chapter sets Kierkegaard's Socrates, whose 'infinite absolute negativity' and confessing ignorance serve a truth he cannot define, and asks whether Klosterman, probing the gap between Bono's rehearsed car-ride persona and his inner self, is master of irony or mastered by it. The answer places Chuck midway between the two jailed ironists, Socrates and the Seinfeld finale: like Socrates he knows his own ignorance and serves the undefined idea of self-understanding, but only through pop-culture resemblance (KISS where Jerry used Superman), unable to master irony any more than he can bite his own teeth.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 8 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Jeopardy! champion Ken Jennings argues that the silly answer-in-the-form-of-a-question conceit is the engine of the show's appeal, because it turns every topic, even Belgium, into a fractal of surprising factual connections rather than a dull definition. He defends the old-school internalization of facts in a Google age - champions are congenitally curious 'sponges' whose stored knowledge makes them better citizens and thinkers - and speculates that what we call the Self is largely the accumulation of facts in one's head. His philosophy of the show in a nutshell: do not just answer in the form of a question, live your life in the form of a question.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 26 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Daniel Wanless reads Jeopardy! through the Meno: contestants can formulate the right question only because the answer is already given, just as Socrates answers Meno's paradox by claiming that all inquiry is recollection of truths the immortal soul already holds - latent knowledge that explains how Ken Jennings buzzes in before he consciously knows the response. A priori logical ability (the slave boy's doubled square, the law of non-contradiction applied to which of three cities is southernmost) guides the search for answers, while Final Jeopardy!'s blind wagering embodies Kierkegaard's 'life is only understood backwards, but it must be lived forwards.' Socrates would bet it all, Wanless concludes, because the unexamined life is not worth living: his whole life was preparation for the ultimate Final Jeopardy!, lived in the form of a question.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 9 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Prof Joe's introduction casts The Wire, like Socrates, as a gadfly that refuses to let any viewer rest comfortably: tough-on-crime conservatives, Hamsterdam-friendly libertarians, hopeful liberals watching Royce and Carcetti, techno-optimists watching Freamon's wire, and capitalists watching the docks and the Baltimore Sun all get their beliefs challenged with no easy answers. It retells Socrates's refusal to escape Athens as valuing the quality of life over its quantity, and sets that against the Puritan work-ethic myth that blames the corner boys and fiends for their own fate while Aristotle's flourishing is rebranded as the American pursuit of happiness. The essay closes by previewing the book's six 'Cases' (the Game, tactics, Omar, boundaries, tragedy, sentencing) around Socrates's own question: how ought we to live?
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 7 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Cam Cobb weighs Battle School against competing philosophies of education: Plato's Republic supplies vocational sorting by natural aptitude (complete with the myth of the metals as a 'noble lie'), while Socratic dialogue and Paulo Freire's problem-posing pedagogy demand the shared critical inquiry Ender never gets. He argues Graff's curriculum is almost purely vocational - military history, tactics, the Giant's Drink, battleroom drills - leaving no liberal paideia, and that the teachers' constant rule-changing leaves Ender feeling like 'someone's pawn,' exactly the banking-style teacher domination Freire warned against.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 51 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Roger Hunt reads Bill Hicks's stand-up as a Socratic comedy exposing Satan's three-point plan: suppress knowledge, breed ignorance, and profit from hypocrisy - from the Waffle House 'readah' scene to Bush-era Gulf War spin ('we looked at the receipts'), JFK-assassination distraction via American Gladiators, and pop stars and marketers who 'suck Satan's cock' (Rick Astley, corporate rock, advertising). Where the Genesis serpent offered knowledge, Hicks's Devil is the force that suppresses it, and Hicks paid a Socratic price - an early death for 'corrupting' his audience - for pointing this out.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 11 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Brendan Shea reads Cohen through the three Hellenistic schools. Socrates's trial in the Apology mirrors the persecuted singer of 'A Singer Must Die,' with 'Everybody Knows' and 'Democracy' voicing a Socratic mix of empathy and pessimism about whether democracy can deal rationally with its critics. Stoics such as Epictetus ground the present-focused, resigned acceptance of loss in 'Hey, That's No Way to Say Goodbye' and 'If It Be Your Will'; the Pyrrhonian skepticism of Sextus Empiricus illuminates the narrator's calming, unresolvable ignorance in 'Famous Blue Raincoat'; and the Epicurean atomism of Epicurus and Lucretius - death is nothing to us, empty desires are unsatisfiable - underlies 'A Thousand Kisses Deep.' Hypatia's murder and Cohen's 'Joan of Arc' close the chapter: the examined life is an all-consuming, sometimes fatal commitment that is nonetheless worthwhile.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 9 "Girls and Philosophy" — The editors' introduction argues that Girls is philosophical because it is stark, raw, and accurate about what is common to human existence: identity, friendship, expectations, and ultimately the meaning of life. It claims Hannah, for all her horribleness (the funeral pitch to her dying editor's widow, doing coke to write truthfully about drugs), follows Socrates's call to know thyself in a millennial register. It then surveys the volume's approaches - existentialism, business ethics, the seven deadly sins, Daoism and Confucianism, Freud, Kristeva - as ways of knowing Hannah, Marnie, Jessa, Shosh, Ray, and Adam, and thereby ourselves.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 16 "Girls and Philosophy" — Blessing and Wezowiczi test theories of life's meaning on the two narcissists of Girls: Hannah, whose purpose-driven pursuit of being a writer (manufacturing experiences, ignoring her father's medical procedure) shows that goal achievement alone collapses into Taylor's and Camus's Sisyphus problem, and Jessa, whose 'life addict' desire-satisfaction illustrates the Nietzschean live-in-the-moment view the authors find reckless and irresponsible. Using Wielenberg's excrement-eater and the subjectivist/objectivist debate, they land on Susan Wolf's 'loving objects that are worthy of love,' then argue via Socrates's examined life and Sartre's bad faith that neither Hannah's phony narrative nor Jessa's protective persona counts as authentic, examined living.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 35 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Comparing Finn with Gilgamesh, Achilles, Cuchulainn and Beowulf, the chapter shows how deeply he belongs to the archaic heroic code: a warrior who loves combat, seeks glory in tough-guy contests, fights dirty like Odysseus, and is fiercely loyal to Jake, his friends and his community. Against this tradition, Finn's unprecedented willingness to help any stranger who cries for help and his refusal to kill the 'unaligned' ant mark the post-heroic morality that began when Socrates told Athenians to care for their souls rather than status and Plato designed a city serving the common good - the author explicitly frames this through Nietzsche's complaint that Greek philosophy derailed the healthy, competitive heroic values. The chapter sides with Finn and the self-sacrificing Lemonjohn over Achilles, concluding that the secret of the Enchiridion is doing whatever the common good requires, warrior or not.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 21 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Cherry uses Vee's season-two grooming of Taystee, Poussey, Nicky, Cindy, and Crazy Eyes to test philosophers' accounts of manipulation (covert influence, non-rational persuasion, targeting weaknesses, misleading truthfully). She shows Vee's skill is not virtue, since manipulation threatens autonomy by imposing a will the victim would not endorse (Kantian personhood denied) and employs dishonesty, predatoriness, disrespect, and laziness, with Machiavellian ends. The defense she prescribes is Socratic: reject purely emotional persuasion like the sophists' flattery, and live the examined life by checking premises and motives before being played.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 7 "Choose!" — The editor's introduction argues that Roth's series does not just contain philosophy but actually does it, proposing hypotheses about virtue, social order, evil, and forgiveness and testing them for consistency. It casts Tris as a Socratic figure who retraces the Allegory of the Cave: she starts 'chained' inside the cave of Chicago's faction system, climbs out to discover the faction life is a lie, and is tortured and eventually killed for the truth she tries to bring back, just as the cave-dwellers would kill the returning prisoner. The introduction closes by insisting the series is really about choice - that wisdom, unlike knowledge, must be lived, that self-reflection and even self-doubt are the hallmark of the wise, and that when life offers no options, like Tris and the factionless, you have to create your own.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 8 "Hello, Dr. Lecter" — Westfall's introduction sorts Lecter's incarnations into four presentations: the psychopath (Brian Cox's 'Lecktor' in Manhunter, modeled on Harris's real-life Mexican prison doctor 'Dr. Salazar'), the anti-hero avenging Mischa in Hannibal Rising, the vampire (Hopkins's Silence of the Lambs Lecter as a Dracula figure who feeds from a sense of innate superiority), and the devil (Mikkelsen's fallen angel, Romula's 'Shaitan', wielder of the church-collapse argument that God enjoys killing). What unites them is a Nietzschean self-conception - Lecter as an Übermensch to whom ordinary law and morality do not apply - and a Socratic function: like Socrates in the Phaedrus, he goads Will, Clarice, and the audience into examining what we already are, posing questions he never resolves because each of us must take the 'rare gift' for ourselves.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 10 "1. Breaking Sixteen Walls" — Rhiannon Grant argues Deadpool's fourth-wall breaks make him a great philosopher and sociologist because they enact the examined life: like Socrates's unexamined-life dictum, Deadpool steps outside his world to ask new questions about it ('Stewart or McAvoy?'), and even examines his own habit of examining—the 'sixteen walls' break inside a break. Wittgenstein's fly-bottle becomes the trap of circular philosophical argument that Deadpool escapes by seeing the bottle from outside, while Berkeley's solipsism is the failed attempt to live as if the world existed only in one's mind. A closing dialogue has Professor X coach Deadpool through insider/outsider research ethics and objectivity (the sperm-and-egg microscope example), showing how fourth-wall skill lets a researcher view a community from both inside and outside.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 23 "12. Only Deadpool Is Sane" — Chad William Timm argues Deadpool is not really insane but was made 'insane' by power: via Foucault's genealogy of madness, experts like Dr. Brighton (a robotic shell for Psycho Man) at Ravenscroft and Dr. Whitby at Crossmore, along with the courts that institutionalize him after the Hulk trial, run a knowledge/power nexus that labels, sorts, and disciplines him until he internalizes the madman identity ('I think I might actually be crazy'). Nineteenth-century psychiatry's invented link between crime and madness secured the experts' authority, and disciplinary power plus technologies of the self made Deadpool discipline himself. Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe's 'I can see through the bull##$%' and his fourth-wall awareness become resistance to these regimes of truth, and the chapter closes by turning Socrates's examined life on the reader: be careful whom you tell.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 26 "15. Happy in Oceania" — Ćirić and Ćurko ask what philosophy could have done for Winston, imagining a counterfactual Oceania where he reads Walpole's line that the world is 'a comedy to those that think, a tragedy to those that feel' and learns from Julia that another worldview is possible. They present philosophy as therapy: Kant's notion of worldview (Weltanschauung), Epicurean ataraxia, the Buddhist four noble truths, Frankl's logotherapy, and Stoic premeditation of the worst as resources for reworking the beliefs that made Winston live in fear. The Party's true target, they argue, is critical thinking — from Dewey's ideal of education as learning to think to Frankfurt's On Bullshit — and Kant's Enlightenment motto 'have the courage to use your own understanding' is the weapon that could still defeat Ingsoc.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 12 "2. Know Thyself, Agent Cooper!" — Reads the Season Two Black Lodge finale as Cooper's failed journey of self-knowledge, framed by Socrates' Delphic "know thyself" and the unexamined life. Against Hume's bundle theory — when Hume looks inward he only ever finds particular perceptions, never a self — the chapter sets the Vedanta/Tibetan Buddhist ideal of knowing the true Self beyond thought (the ocean versus its waves), with the Black Lodge as the place Hawk calls a passage "every soul must pass on its way to perfection." Cooper's screaming white-eyed Laura, the flickering Caroline/Annie corpse, and his grinning doppelgänger are Jungian shadow-projections paralleled scene-by-scene with the wrathful visions of the Tibetan Book of the Dead; entering with imperfect courage, he flees his fears instead of integrating them, splitting into trapped good Dale and the rampaging Mr. C of The Return.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 30 "17. Through Plastic Our Secrets Seen" — Uses Schopenhauer's World as Will to explain why the citizens of Twin Peaks keep living lives they despise: all willing arises from deficiency and suffering, so Shelly cannot leave Leo, Ben cannot face his children, and Ed is consumed oscillating between Norma and Nadine, while the blind will — not reflection — determines who we become. Since only pain is known directly and its absence slides into boredom and banality (Ed's restless drama-making), the town's double lives — Jacoby's coconut tapes hiding Laura's confession, Bobby's dealing, Ben's brothel — are the will's concealed kernels. Laura's wrapped corpse then functions as the reveal: death shows each character's truth, and the chapter closes by turning Socrates' unexamined life against itself, asking what happens when self-examination only uncovers what we wished hidden, as Cooper's daily-present advice offers the lone consolation.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 7 "Dare to Enter the Zone" — The editors introduce the volume with Nietzsche's line about finding only 'apes of our ideal': TZ episodes dangle wishes (rejuvenated husbands, fallout shelters, Henry Bemis's time to read) that fate twists into cosmic jokes, so we laugh at what we fail to be. They cast Rod Serling as a reincarnation of Socrates, the gadfly of Athens, whose episodes work as thought experiments exposing expert promises as tricks, and set 'The Hunt' against this cynicism — the faithful dog Rip smells the Devil's gate so the old man reaches Heaven. The tension between our ideals and human frailty, they argue, is what made the show philosophical television.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 11 "3. The Short-Sightedness of Henry Bemis" — Pichanick reads 'Time Enough at Last' as a tragic dilemma: Henry Bemis's wish to own his time, away from the bank president's productivity, his wife's social demands, and the 'unrelenting clock,' is granted by a nuclear blast that turns solitude into a monotonous prison driving him to attempted suicide, until the library restores meaning, identity, and freedom. The shattered glasses then reveal his 'short-sightedness': his literal vision always depended on other people and on a piece of technology, so the possibility of meaning itself was socially and technologically manufactured. The episode's brilliance, he argues, is refusing to choose between accepting the social world's limits on our freedom and withdrawing from it — it only shows that misanthropic withdrawal is self-destruction.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 23 "12. The Twilight Zone on Our Doorstep" — Jones argues the Twilight Zone is not elsewhere: episodes like 'The Hitch-Hiker' and 'The Eye of the Beholder' never leave a recognizable America or an ordinary hospital, so the Zone is not a place on any map. Serling's border-crossing narrations plus the impossible catalysts (gremlins, aliens, Talky Tina) create a 'double distancing' — a metaphorical shelter that lets viewers handle mundane truths about selfishness, shakiness, and mortality as if they were strange. 'The Shelter' is the decisive exception: the one episode with no supernatural or futuristic catalyst, aired during the Berlin Crisis when Kennedy urged families to build fallout shelters, it collapses the shelter and forces viewers to see that the Zone is the room they are sitting in.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 9 "Scientifically, Introductions Are an Idiot Thing" — The introduction frames the whole book through the Rick/Jerry opposition: Rick is a Nietzschean artist-creator who insists the world is objectively meaningless and Godless yet keeps choosing his family, while Jerry is the herd-animal chasing socially approved values. It claims the show, like Nietzsche's deliberately difficult writing, sorts its audience into Jerrys who enjoy the dick jokes and Ricks who do the hard philosophical work of finding microscopic meaning in a meaningless cosmos. It closes with Socrates's 'unexamined life is not worth living' to justify submitting to philosophy's perplexity even if the Eyehole Man kicks the shit out of you.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 18 "7. Rick and Morty as Socratic Television" — The chapter argues Harmon and Roiland write the show as Socratic dialogue: in 'Mortynight Run' Morty's confident moral position (saving Fart from Krombopulos Michael is right) is dismantled until Morty himself pulls the trigger, leaving him in aporia; in 'Auto Erotic Assimilation' Summer's faith in freedom is razed by Unity's happy paternalist hive and the nipple-shaped race war it unleashes; and 'Look Who's Purging Now' refuses to choose between liberalism and conservatism when the post-purge town instantly re-founds the Festival. Like Socrates in Plato's Meno, the show's goal is not to teach lessons but to reduce viewers to confusion, because doing philosophy begins there.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 33 "20. Getting Your Shit Together Stoic Style" — The chapter argues Rick is at his best an Epictetus-style Stoic: in 'A Rickle in Time' his total certainty keeps the split timelines perfectly synced, enacting 'choice alone is vice, choice alone is virtue'; his 'love is a chemical reaction... focus on science' speech in 'Rick Potion #9' treats passion as an impression outside the sphere of control; and his 'don't think about it' dismissal of the Hitler-cured-cancer reality applies the dichotomy of control to an unmasterable multiverse. Epictetus's model of hardship as training is vindicated by Cronenberged Jerry, whose struggle preserves his dignity in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption', and the chapter closes with the Stoic promise Rick's life shows: not pleasure but contentment.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 31 "19. If Everyone’s Special, … Is Anyone Special" — Grace Wehniainen defends 'you are special' against the Fox & Friends 'evil man' charge by separating intrinsic from extrinsic value: on Rogers's 1 Corinthians 12 and Genesis 1:27 reading, worth is God-given and unearned, like the family dog whose napping life has intrinsic value (with Tom Regan's agreement) regardless of tricks. Specialness as 'belonging specifically to a particular person' needs no trophies, only Socratic self-examination before the mirror, Aristotle's true versus vulgar self-love from the Nicomachean Ethics, and Albert Ellis's self-acceptance over performance-based self-esteem.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 43 "30. Socratic Superheroism" — Stages a dialogue between Socrates and Nebula to build a four-part scorecard of 'Socratic Heroism' — question all assumptions, intellectual humility (Socrates before the Delphic oracle: 'I am very conscious that I am not wise at all'), improve society without ever doing injustice, and courage unto death (the gadfly of the Apology) — then scores Thanos 0 for 4: 'I am incapable of error' and 'reality can be whatever I want' are the very opposites of humility and of objective, heavenly truth. It nominates Doctor Strange as the MCU's Socratic hero, whose humbling at Kamar-Taj, willingness to hand over the Time Stone against the obvious choice, and trust in the one winning future among 14,000,605 pass the tests.
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 11 "3. Paul’s Lick It Up Philosophy" — Courtland Lewis reads Paul Stanley's autobiographies (Face the Music, Backstage Pass) and songs as a worked-out life philosophy. Stanley's turn from chasing approval to confronting his inner pain exemplifies Socrates' unexamined-life dictum; 'Reason to Live' is glossed through Camus's Sisyphus — ground your reason to live in something indestructible, your own self-chosen meaning — while Plato's Ion explains Stanley's mix of learned craft and divine-inspired performance. Aristotle's flourishing through moderation appears in the advice not to overplay 'Rock and Roll All Nite,' and Lewis adds Locke and Rousseau on how laws, boundaries, and education create rather than restrict freedom, closing with Stanley's 'questioning ourselves is not a weakness' as Socratic wisdom.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 14 "“Consider Your Verdict!”" — Splits Wonderland's nonsense into the tolerable kind (strange but lawful regularities, like mushroom side-effects and walking the opposite way to reach the Red Queen, which Alice masters by experiment) and the intolerable kind (the creatures' eristic logic). Using Hume's fork of relations of ideas versus matters of fact, George Dunn and Brian McDonald argue Alice rightly concludes the pig-baby is merely an out-of-the-way matter of fact, while the White Queen's 'jam every other day: to-day isn't any other day' and the King's beheading of the bodiless Cheshire Cat repeat the Sophists' tricks from Plato's Euthydemus, which Socrates deflates from the standpoint of common sense and the examined life. The Knave's trial ('sentence first, verdict afterwards') lands on cable-news pundits who, like the show trials of Stalin, argue from predetermined conclusions.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 9 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Tests Socrates' claim (via Plato's Apology and the Myth of the Cave) that the self-examined life is the happiest against the Bluths: Michael, the one who escapes the cave in the pilot (learning at the boat party that his father is a criminal and he was never getting partnership), turns out chronically miserable, while self-deceivers Gob, Lindsay, and Tobias are mostly content. The chapter concludes that Bertrand Russell's Conquest of Happiness fits better: reflection makes sinners (George Michael's self-loathing over Maeby), narcissists (Michael's need to be seen as good), and megalomaniacs (Kitty) unhappy, so the unexamined life is not a huge mistake, though moderate examination still pays.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 12 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Uses Sartre's cafe waiter, directly mirrored when Gob play-acts a waiter in 'S.O.B.s', to define bad faith as denying one's freedom by disappearing into roles: illusionist, Bluth Company president in George Sr.'s suit, 'any man' winning back Marta, Ward Cleaver father to Steve Holt (!). Distinguishing bad faith from impossible self-deception (beings-for-themselves have no pre-given essence), the chapter argues that even sincerity ('be yourself, Gob') is bad faith, and provocatively concludes Gob is happier and kinder to others in bad faith, reversing Socrates' 'know thyself'.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 22 "Let's Go Fly a Kite!" — Argues Mary Poppins is really the redemption story of George Banks, who leads what Socrates called the unexamined life: his six-minute paternal schedule, shredded nursery advertisement, and blindness to the bird woman show a man who has 'forgotten who he is' and lost the child's wonder. G. K. Chesterton supplies the diagnosis and cure — fairyland as the 'sunny country of common sense,' imagination that 'makes settled things strange,' and astonishment that there is something rather than nothing (with Leibniz's question and a Russell quote) — so that Banks is saved when the bank run strips his ambition. The mended kite, built by the whole family, closes the argument that one can keep the heart of a child while keeping the mind of an adult.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 10 "The Sorcerer Socratic" — Timm argues Strange follows Socrates' path from arrogance to Socratic heroism: the hand injury forces intellectual humility (the Oracle-at-Delphi moment), the Ancient One's keyhole metaphor and astral-form lesson ('to show you just how much you don't know') enact the Socratic method of questioning the supposedly wise, and the astral projection is literally the examined life — Socrates' unexamined life not worth living. Strange's commitment to protecting humanity from interdimensional evil parallels the gadfly who risks death to improve Athens, his refusal to do injustice even under pressure echoes the Crito, and his repeated willingness to die for others (facing Dormammu, holding the Shambler back) completes the Socratic Hero profile.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 7 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Cam Cobb pits Socratic critical inquiry and Plato's Republic-style vocational streaming (classes sorted by the 'myth of the metals,' sold through a noble lie) against the Battle School curriculum, which is almost purely vocational and lacks the music, poetry, and liberal paideia that harmonize the soul. Testing Socrates' dialogic method, Dewey's aptitude-tracking education, and Freire's problem-posing alternative against the battleroom, the Giant's Drink, and Graff's secretly rewritten game rules, Cobb concludes Ender's schooling mixes conflicting pedagogies and ends in the teacher domination Freire feared, crystallized in Ender's lament 'I've spent my life as someone's pawn.'
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 83 "Choices" — Opening 'Choices vs. Abilities: Dumbledore on Self-Understanding' with Socrates' 'know thyself,' Bassham frames the books as Harry's progress from appearance to reality: the boy under the stairs who thinks himself ordinary gradually learns who he is. The pivot is the end of Chamber of Secrets, where Harry, alarmed that he shares Parseltongue and Slytherin potential with Voldemort, receives Dumbledore's dictum 'It is our choices, Harry, that show us what we truly are, far more than our abilities,' which Bassham sets out to test.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 88 "Unknown" — The chapter uses Gilderoy Lockhart as the failure case of self-knowledge by introspection: convinced he is a great Defense teacher and duelist, he cannot manage a cage of Cornish pixies, is floored by Snape's Expelliarmus, and removes all the bones from Harry's arm, because his rose-colored 'cognitive blinders' mean he looks but does not see. Bassham then previews four remedies for self-knowledge, each illustrated in the books: cultivate habitual self-examination, stay alert to irrational tendencies, get help from friends, and challenge yourself.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 89 "Unknown" — The chapter urges the Socratic examined life as a standing habit rather than a crisis response, since, as Thomas Pangle observes, most of us reflect seriously only when in trouble. Dumbledore is the model: knowing his besetting weakness was love of power, he refused the Ministry repeatedly, and after losing his 'moral compass completely' over Grindelwald he chose a celibate scholarly life, using the Pensieve's third-person view of his own memories, which makes it 'easier to spot patterns and links,' as an instrument of self-examination.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 148 "The End of the Story" — Completes the parallel: Socrates died refusing to abandon the examined life, and his martyrdom, like Dumbledore's staged death that protected Snape's spying, served the common good, since there can be no common good without individual goodness. The chapter closes with two Muggle lessons, live devoted to something larger than yourself as Lily Potter, Dumbledore, Harry, King, Gandhi, Jesus, and Socrates did, and find mentors, as Harry found Dumbledore and as readers can find in Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics or Confucius.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 17 "a7.xhtml" — The chapter sets the bloody classical ideal of glory (Homer's kleos, Beowulf, Alexander modeling himself on Achilles) - which Augustine already condemned as libido dominandi - against Plato's alternative of a life aimed at the good, the true and the beautiful. Thorin's last charge at the Battle of Five Armies fits the heroic tradition, but Tolkien's real point is that Bilbo, the 'grocer' who feels the dwarves' treasure-lust yet walks away from it, and who ends by inviting the dwarves to four-o'clock tea instead of a victory feast, shows glory subordinated to domestic beauty and humility. Socrates' question in the Apology - why care so little for wisdom and the soul's improvement while chasing wealth, honor and reputation - is exactly the temptation Bilbo resists, and the Symposium's move from battle to a drinking-party of love-of-beauty mirrors Tolkien's placement of heroism in hobbits rather than warriors.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 8 "Notes" — Argues that Underwood's fourth-wall asides are the show's device for dramatizing the Platonic being-versus-seeming distinction: his public performances (reassuring Blythe over the leaked education bill, the confessional letter typed on the Underwood typewriter to destroy Walker, goading the President into appointing a special prosecutor) are contradicted point by point by what he tells the camera. The chapter reads Frank as a Ring of Gyges success story — the show so far teaches it is better to be the bad guy who seems good — while Socrates' examined life from the Apology and Crito shows Frank never asks why he wants power, and his cockiness is the opposite of Socratic ignorance. It closes with the Gorgias' contrast of Sophistic rhetoric (producing belief, not knowledge) and Machiavelli's advice to feign, casting Frank as the manipulator of opinion Socrates called a tyrant's politics.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 8 "Notes" — Gray argues Frank's fourth-wall asides dramatize Plato's being-versus-seeming distinction: the camera confidences reveal the true motive behind the public performance, as in the Blythe education-bill martyrdom gambit, the deliberately failed persuasion of Walker over the special prosecutor, and the seduction letter typed on the Underwood typewriter. The chapter reads Frank as winning the Ring of Gyges bet — enjoying adultery, corruption, and murder while seeming good — exactly the outcome the Republic sets out to refute. Against this it sets Socrates' examined life and Apology profession of ignorance: Frank pursues power without asking to what end, and his mastery of rhetoric over knowledge makes him the Sophist of the Gorgias rather than Plato's true politician, with Machiavelli's dissembling prince as his model.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 7 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — The editors' introduction frames the trilogy as Katniss's quest to peel away Panem's layers of lies, likening her self-examination and self-control to the Delphic 'Know Thyself' and 'Nothing in Excess' and calling her skeptical spirit the engine of her wisdom. It poses the book's driving questions: why we enjoy watching others suffer, whether ordinary morality survives the arena, and how easily our own reality-TV-shaped world could slide into Panem's, noting that Collins modeled the Games on the Roman Colosseum. It presents dystopian exaggeration (children slaughtered for entertainment, tyrants, starving workers) as a cautionary mirror of trends already present in our society, and casts the contributors' chapters as a therapeutic game of 'Real or Not Real' played with the reader.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 12 "Group Will" — Testerman argues the film's heist is ironic because nobody in it acts from conscious will: citing Libet's readiness-potential experiments and Penfield's stimulation cases, she claims the feeling of willing is a post-hoc 'epistemic illusion,' so Fischer's inception merely dramatizes what happens all the time — Cobb's 'all experience is inception' becomes a thesis about ordinary agency, with Spinoza's dictum that freedom is ignorance of the causes of our actions as its motto. She reads the plot through this lens: Saito's unexamined hunger for power silently drives the team's 'group will,' Cobb's 'positive emotion trumps negative emotion' tactic exploits the limbic system, and cheaper tricks (Arthur's elephant, foot-in-the-door, subliminal advertising) would have worked as well. Against Socrates she concludes the unexamined life is perfectly livable, since introspection can never reach the subconscious causes of behavior.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 24 "13 Pride and Prudence in the Pursuit of Knowledge Indiana Jones, René Belloq, and Irina Spalko" — Argues that the desire to know is natural and good (Aristotle's Metaphysics, Socrates via Plato's Meno) only when bounded by moral limits, using Gilbert Meilaender's warning that curiosity becomes a vice when driven by pride or the lust for power. René Belloq opens the Ark seeking a personal audience with God and is incinerated; Irina Spalko demands 'tell me everything you know' from the interdimensional beings at Akator and her eyes burn out; prudent Indy tells Marion 'Don't look, no matter what happens' and leaves before the beings' 'big gift' of knowledge. The chapter concludes that pride must give way to prudence when unlocking the secrets of the universe.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 18 "The Office and Philosophy" — Pits authenticity - understood both as self-discovery and as existentialist self-creation after Sartre and Heidegger, requiring self-knowledge and meaningful relationships - against happiness as subjective well-being, in a case study of Michael Scott. Michael's closest 'friendships' are relationships of convenience (Dwight's betrayal in 'The Coup', the fear-induced Packer bond, self-destructive Jan), his 'Packer norms' of locker-room humor are unshakeable, and Shelley Taylor-style positive illusions (his self-image as progressive on Diversity Day, 'The World's Best Boss' mug) keep his moods afloat while truth-tellers like Jan and the Chili's bar patrons knock them down. The conclusion challenges Socrates' dictum: since Michael is psychologically incapable of achieving authenticity, perhaps for some people the examined life is simply not available, and trying for it only produces misery.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 7 "Cold Open The Introduction" — The editors introduce the volume by arguing that SNL, like philosophy, trains viewers to regard the world with a critical, questioning eye: four and a half decades of parody and satire wired generations of fans to think philosophically before they could articulate why. Land Shark, Spartan Cheerleaders, and Trump-era Update bits are cited as the shared generational memory the book will now analyze.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 7 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — The editor's Introduction explains why Spider-Man merits a philosophy book: Peter Parker is a self-reflective underdog with a strong moral compass he sometimes fails to follow, so his stories raise lived ethical questions rather than abstract metaphysics. Citing Plato's definition of philosophy as the love of wisdom and a way of life, Sanford frames the whole volume around Socrates' question 'how are you going to live your life?' and lists the questions Peter's life poses: the good life, the obligations attached to talents, friendship, identity over time, the ethics of enhancement, and whether life has meaning.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 7 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Young argues that South Park is perceived as dangerous for exactly the reasons Socrates was tried and executed in Plato's Apology: both 'corrupt the youth' by mocking religion, questioning authority, and exposing that the supposed teachers (Mr. Garrison's flip-flopping creationism, Mrs. Broflovski's moral panics, the 'Death' boycott of Terrance and Phillip) do not know what they think they know. He diagnoses Cartman as an Eichmann figure whose banal, thoughtless evil—feeding Scott Tenorman his parents, torturing Muslims with farts—consists in the inability to think from another's standpoint, while Kyle and Stan's friendship embodies Arendt's dialogic thinking and Aristotle's mean between ideological extremes, as when they see both the merit and the smugness of hybrid drivers in 'Smug Alert'. Freud's theory that jokes break through repression explains why the show's vulgarity is essential rather than gratuitous: it verbalizes what culture silences so that it can be thought through, making South Park a Socratic gadfly rather than a corrupter.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 8 "Notes" — Jason Eberl uses the amusement park of 'Shore Leave', Omicron Ceti III's spore paradise in 'This Side of Paradise', Landru's hedonistic 'red hour', and the Borg's relentless efficiency to argue that edifying play and leisure are necessary for intellectual, moral, and spiritual flourishing. Following Josef Pieper's Leisure, with Nozick's experience machine (applied to 'The Thaw' and Barclay's holodiction), Aristotle's 'we work in order to be at leisure', and Aquinas on wonder, he contrasts mere utility (bonum utile) with the common good a drone-only Collective can never have. He concludes that thoughtfully watching Star Trek is itself worthwhile leisure: science-fiction thought experiments that serve Socrates's examined life.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 5 "Introduction Welcome to the Psychosphere" — The editors' introduction asks why viewers willingly linger in True Detective's bleak Louisiana bayou and season two's Vinci, suggesting we may recognize something of ourselves in those worlds. It argues detectives and philosophers share the pursuit of truth, framing Rust Cohle and Marty Hart (and Velcoro and Bezzerides) as morally compromised lawmen who open the door to philosophy, invoking Socrates' 'unexamined life is not worth living.' It previews the book's coverage of pessimism, good and evil, tragedy, personal identity, and time via Socrates, Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Lacan, and Zizek.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 24 "Notes" — Compares the noir detective's relation to Vinci with Socrates' gadfly role in Athens from the Apology, arguing both operate at the city's center and its margins as instruments of collective self-examination. Via Deleuze's 'Philosophy of Crime Novels' it contrasts the classic detective as an agent of truth (Poe, Christie) with the hard-boiled detective as an agent of action who stirs the system — Ani's undercover infiltration of the businessmen's party — forcing what Deleuze calls the 'power of falsehood' to reveal and conceal. Plato's Republic city–soul analogy then frames Velcoro, Bezzerides, and Woodrugh as disordered souls mirroring Vinci's corrupt class structure, whose cases restore equilibrium without achieving Platonic justice.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 6 "Introduction Warm-Up" — Andy Wible's introduction argues that if Plato and Aristotle were alive they would be avid golfers, because both golf and philosophy seduce great minds with problems that look easy yet prove endlessly difficult. It frames golf as 'a Sudoku that cannot be solved' and pairs it with the eternal questions (right and wrong, who am I, beauty, God, meaning) to preview the volume's chapters. Golf becomes a vehicle for the examined life, enlivening philosophy through the lived experience of the game.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 12 "2. Know Thyself, Agent Cooper!" — De Carvalho reads Cooper's ordeal in the Black Lodge as a journey of self-knowledge, distinguishing 'knowing yourself' (your feelings, as Laura sought with Dr. Jacoby) from 'knowing your Self' in the deep sense of Vedanta's Brahman and Tibetan Buddhism's Mind. He sets Hume's bundle theory—the failure to catch a self behind the perceptions—against the Hindu Swami's ocean-and-waves image of an eternal Self beyond thought, and reads Cooper's confrontation with his screaming-Laura and doppelganger visions via the Tibetan Book of the Dead and Jung's shadow: facing his fears with imperfect courage, Cooper fails to integrate his shadow and is split in two.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 30 "17. Through Plastic Our Secrets Seen" — Winters uses Schopenhauer's World as Will and Idea to argue that the townsfolk (Shelly, Leo, Ben, Josie, Ed, and Laura) do not freely choose the lives they despise but are driven by the blind will, and so live double lives whose secrets a single death exposes. Laura, unlike the others who mismanage their passions, was denied the chance to develop her own values, so she pursued danger, drugs, and prostitution to see herself through her own eyes; death, he argues, reveals true character (the townsfolk's rush to bury her, their guilt), turning Socrates' unexamined-life dictum uneasy—sometimes what examination reveals is a monster we would rather not see.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Conard's editor's introduction defines film noir and neo-noir, cataloguing noir themes (moral ambivalence, alienation, pessimism, disorientation) across films like Blue Velvet, Angel Heart, L.A. Confidential, and The Usual Suspects, and previews the volume's thirteen essays. It argues neo-noir better embodies the noir outlook because its makers work self-consciously and can let criminals succeed. It closes by invoking Socrates' claim that the unexamined life is not worth living to justify philosophical reflection on these films.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 13 "Sherlock Holmes and the Ethics of Hyperspecialization" — Costello and Bassham critique Holmes's 'brain-attic' theory from 'A Study in Scarlet'—that the mind has fixed capacity and should hold only vocationally useful knowledge. Cognitive science (interference and schema theory) and the sociology of social/cultural capital show useless knowledge is often useful, as when Holmes trades boxing lore or reads cultural cues. They then argue for a duty of self-improvement grounded in consequentialism, Kantian and Rossian deontology, and virtue ethics (Aristotle, Aquinas, MacIntyre) plus Socratic care of the soul, concluding that Holmes—an omnivorous reader who quotes Goethe and Hafiz—doesn't practice what he preaches and took specialization too far.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 24 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Sterritt 'schizoanalyzes' The Informant! by arguing that its lying protagonist Mark Whitacre, an ADM executive turned FBI informant, is a nut psychoanalysis cannot crack because he has no unconscious depth: his self is Deleuze and Guattari's rhizomatic, depthless flow of desire with 'nothing behind it' (echoing Warhol). He reads Mark's compulsive fabrication as deterritorialization against the corporation-as-psychopath, links the film to the Socratic unexamined life and to William James's open, flux-embracing empiricism (via Cassavetes), and interprets the climactic collision of Mark's voiceover and dialogue as the film itself intervening as the ultimate informant.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 14 "Apocalypse Within The War Epic as Crisis of Self-Identity" — Hagberg reads Coppola's Apocalypse Now as a sustained dismantling of the "privileged access" / perceptual model of self-knowledge, in which the self inspects private inner objects insulated from the outer world. Captain Willard's voyage upriver shows the opposite: he comes to know himself only relationally, by studying Kurtz's file and measuring himself against Kilgore, Chef, Lance, and Colby, and through self-defining acts like shooting the wounded woman in the sampan and finally machete-killing Kurtz. Willard's clarifying self-composition marks Socrates' examined life, whereas Kurtz—self-deceived, an "imitator of an actor" in Nietzsche's phrase, exhibiting Freudian derealization and depersonalization—is the tragedy of the unexamined life, the true Oedipus blinded by a false self-image.
- **The Philosophy of Werner Herzog**, ch. 20 "Werner Herzog on Circles, Chickens and Impotency" — Tyler Tritten argues that Even Dwarfs Started Small and Stroszek are not principally political but share an essence: the impotency of the powerless dramatized through cyclical, repetitive motion (circling trucks, ski lifts, and above all chickens). He defends Herzog's 'apoliticism' — citing Herzog's preference for the medieval melior pars over numerical voting (echoing Rousseau's general will versus the popular vote, and Socrates against the many) — as locating the human condition beneath contingent social conditions. The handless, cannibalistic, circumambulating chicken becomes the emblem of a self-consuming nature and a humanity too proportionate to the beast, provoking a pure, aching laughter as the only revolt.
- **Joss Whedon as Philosopher**, ch. 5 "Introduction" — The introduction sets the book's guiding question of whether a fictional-narrative filmmaker (specifically Joss Whedon) can 'do philosophy' the way traditional philosophers do, using Whedon's television and film corpus as its test case. It frames philosophy as an activity of removing contradictions through argument and pursuing the examined life, invoking Socrates on the unexamined life and Sartrean/Heideggerian existentialism to argue that Whedon's Buffy, Angel, Firefly, and Dollhouse dramatize authenticity and choice. It previews reading Whedon's characters (Angel, Mal, Buffy) against Rawls, Plato, Aristotle, Kant, and Parfit to establish that the Whedonverse is genuinely philosophical.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 43 "Ah, Doctor. We Know You by Reputation" — Courtland Lewis's closing essay argues Doctor Who and philosophy are complementary enterprises devoted to teaching rather than mere persuasion. Using Plato's Gorgias distinction between teaching and rhetoric, he casts the Master as the master rhetorician who produces unreliable beliefs (even via hypnosis), while the Doctor is a Socratic teacher committed to truth who gives people information and lets them decide. He contends the show, begun as educational, challenges viewers to reflect on their own reasoning, on how they treat others (Daleks, Cybermen, strangers), and to revise beliefs in light of evidence, so that watching it is living philosophically engaged.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 23 "13. Chuckrates v. The Saulphists" — Staged as a mock disciplinary-board trial, the chapter casts Chuck McGill as Socrates and Jimmy as a Sophist to replay Plato's dialectic-versus-rhetoric quarrel. Chuck prosecutes Jimmy as a mere rhetorician who 'makes the weaker argument defeat the stronger,' quoting the Gorgias, Apology, and Republic, while Jimmy counters that Socrates was himself a self-righteous show-off and that the legal system runs on Sophistic persuasion (juries, opening statements) as much as on truth. The Board's verdict finds Chuck blind to his own rhetoric and Jimmy a quintessential but empathetic Sophist, using the McGill brothers to argue that law fuses dialectic and rhetoric just as ancient Athens did.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 7 "The Last Supper Game" — This editor's introduction frames Bourdain as a modern philosopher by playing a variation on his 'Last Meal' game and choosing Bourdain as the ideal dinner companion. It argues that Bourdain's professed humility about how little he knows ('realizing how small I am, and unwise') echoes Socratic ignorance and the love of wisdom, and previews the volume's questions about happiness, authenticity, taste, and freedom.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 9 "The Talking Cure for Our Culture" — Young argues that South Park, like Socrates in Plato's Apology, is accused of corrupting youth and impiety but is really a philosophical gadfly. Kyle and Stan reach moral conclusions (e.g., refusing to kill Stan's grandfather) through Socratic questioning and dialogue, while Cartman's thoughtless, imitative cruelty mirrors Arendt's banality of evil in Eichmann. Young reads the show's vulgarity through Freud, arguing its crude jokes release repressed drives so we can examine them, making the show a Socratic 'talking cure' for a mindless culture.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 49 "House and the Life of Reason" — Henry Jacoby argues that despite House's line that we are 'selfish, base animals crawling across the Earth,' House lives a meaningful life. Rejecting God-, soul-, and afterlife-based meaning (House's Euthyphro-style objections and his '97 Seconds' near-death experiment), Jacoby locates meaning in the Socratic examined life and Aristotle's life of reason as humanity's proper function. House's relentless curiosity and puzzle-solving, tied to action and to saving lives, exemplify reason governing desire and yield eudaimonia - so 'doing things changes things,' and House, however miserable he seems, leads the examined, meaningful life.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 12 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Greg Littmann defends political mockery as an ancient tradition (Aristophanes, Juvenal, Twain) but warns, using J.S. Mill's On Liberty, that if viewers let The Daily Show's jokes substitute for reasoned judgment the effect is like censorship, silencing ideas that must be heard to be understood. He cites Mill's arguments against silencing discussion and Plato's Meno on shackling true opinion with reasons, arguing that Stewart's virtue over Limbaugh is that he bills himself as comedy ('the show that leads into me is puppets making crank phone calls') and never presents mockery as a replacement for informed citizenship.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 7 "Dare to Enter the Zone" — Hooke and Rivera's editors' introduction argues that The Twilight Zone dramatizes the Nietzschean disappointment of the epigraph from Twilight of the Idols—that we seek great human beings and find only 'the apes of their ideal.' They cast Rod Serling as a reincarnated Socrates, a gadfly whose episodes ('Time Enough at Last,' 'The Hunt,' the eternal-youth trade-in) stage the gap between our ideals of love, justice, and truth and the treacherous, self-deluding creatures we actually are, so that viewers laugh at absurd twist endings because we are the species most deserving to be laughed at.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 10 "Oh, the Places You’ll Go! The Examined, Happy Life" — Benjamin Rider reads Oh, the Places You'll Go! through Socrates' claim that the unexamined life is not worth living. He argues the Sneetches' star-obsession, Yertle's tower, Gertrude McFuzz's feathers, and the Once-ler's 'biggering' are the false, unexamined beliefs about wealth and status that Socrates said wreck the soul, while Bartholomew Cubbins and Horton model the wise, courageous endurance Socrates seeks but fails to define with the generals Laches and Nicias in Plato's Laches. The 'Waiting Place' becomes the life of someone who never questions what really makes him happy, and Seuss's call to use 'the brains in your head' echoes Socrates' insistence in the Crito and Phaedo on living by rational reflection.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 14 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Dougherty argues Austen's ideal marriage mirrors Aristotle's complete friendship, where the friend is loved for who they are and becomes a 'second self.' She sorts Austen's relationships into Aristotle's three kinds: utility (Emma and Mrs. Elton, Charlotte and Mr. Collins), pleasure (Lydia and Wickham, the fading Emma-Harriet bond), and complete friendship grounded in mutual good character (Jane and Bingley, Elizabeth and Darcy, Emma and Knightley). Central is the 'second self' as mirror: Darcy's letter and Knightley's rebukes let Elizabeth and Emma see themselves ('Till this moment I never knew myself'), so marriage-as-friendship improves self-knowledge and virtue and must not be left to chance as Charlotte urges.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 16 "Chapter 6 The Gospel According to Mark (Twain)" — Craig Vasey reads Twain's Letters from the Earth, narrated by a skeptical Satan, as a defense of critical thinking rather than the ranting of a bitter old man.
