The Attack of the Clones debate between Anakin ('Someone wise' should make people agree) and Padme becomes a clash between Leo Strauss's philosopher-king ideal of rule by the virtuous few and John Dewey's conception of democracy as a way of life trusting the intelligence of common people, with Rousseau's social contract framing the stakes. The chapter concludes that democratic ends require democratic means and that unaccountable 'watchers' - Straussian statesmen or Anakins - are exactly the path to Empire.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 29 "Look On My Works, Ye Mighty" — Ozymandias, Watchmen's smartest human vigilante, kills three million New Yorkers with a staged alien attack to avert nuclear war, and Skoble walks through the question the novel forces: can the end justify the means? The heroes' darkest hour is their acquiescence in his scheme - only Rorschach rejects the utilitarian reasoning ('Never compromise... Evil must be punished') and is killed by Dr. Manhattan to keep the secret. Skoble leaves us asking whether Ozymandias is a misunderstood savior or has 'become a monster', and whether our recoil at his act is moral clarity or weakness.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 26 "Poker and Philosophy" — Hahn reads Doyle Brunson's Super System — 'I go into a Poker game with the idea of completely destroying it' — as applied Machiavelli: The Prince's fox and lion become the bluffer and the bully chip leader, 'better to be feared than loved' justifies cutting even old friend Sailor Roberts's throat at the table, and swift decisive attack (Tex Barch stomped out of the 2005 WSOP) avoids sowing the seeds of vengeance. Fortune rules half our events — the river card that fills an opponent's inside straight — so virtù means building dikes against the flood, as Cesare Borgia failed to do when his papal patron died. Sun Tzu's 'when able, seem to be unable' supplies the same disguise of strength in poker and in war.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 25 "Doing Things in Private" — Skoble asks exactly what Jeff does wrong in Rear Window and whether his illicit snooping can generate genuine duties. Against a purely consequentialist verdict ('it all worked out okay'), he argues that knowledge creates conditional obligations - given what he has seen of Thorwald, Jeff's intervention is obligatory rather than supererogatory, by 'ought implies can' - and he weighs autonomy-respecting limits on intervening in Miss Lonelyhearts' despair. He then analyzes privacy as a moral right grounded in reciprocal legitimate expectations, concluding that Jeff violated no such right since everything he watched was on public display, so the ends-justify-the-means charge mostly dissolves.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 28 "The Future" — Dinello reads the New Caprica occupation as an Iraq allegory interpreted through Fanon's The Wretched of the Earth: occupation is violence personified (Cavil's 'saving them from damnation'), psychological violence colonizes minds (Leoben's manipulation of Starbuck, Jammer's recruitment into the New Caprica Police), and Tyrol's 'throw your body on the gears' strike speech channels Savio, Marx's seizing the means of production, and Marcuse on technology's repression. Fanon's thesis that anticolonial violence is a cleansing, liberating force is dramatized in Tigh's 'blood for blood,' the Temple massacre that recruits a thousand fighters, and Duck's suicide bombing — with Sartre's preface endorsing killing the oppressor and the ends-justify-means dispute between Tigh and Tyrol. The insurgency wins by not losing, as in Algeria and Vietnam, and the show is subversive because it makes viewers sympathize with the occupied.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 31 "Damned If You Do, and Damned If You Don’t" — Bryan McHenry asks whether manipulating religious belief for political ends is ever moral, using Adama's motivational lie about Earth, Roslin's Pythia-driven 'dying leader' campaign (compared with George W. Bush's faith-based politics), and the Cylons' evangelical monotheism aimed at scaring Baltar into conversion. Machiavelli's Prince licenses rulers who use a religion they do not share, and the chapter judges Adama's hope-based use of the Earth myth and Roslin's uniting religiosity as essentially moral while the Cylons wield faith as a coercive weapon. Madison's Enlightenment demand that religion be directed by reason and conviction rather than force supplies the standard the fear-based Cylon conversion of Baltar fails.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 28 "The Bronze Dragonflight Invisible Leadership" — Moses Wolfenstein applies The Prince to guild leadership: the infamous Dives Onyxia wipe ('50 DKP minus!') shows why being feared beats being loved — players flooded to join and even requested his abusive raid calls — so long as fear never curdles into hatred, while PUGs and battlegrounds replay Machiavelli's warning that mercenary troops are 'disunited, ambitious, without discipline, disloyal.' Against this he sets Laozi's Daodejing verse 17, where the best rulers are scarcely known by their subjects and the people credit themselves — embodied by the hidden bronze dragonflight and Chromie, and by the back-channel guild officer who invisibly paves the road to victory.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 8 "The (Single) Garden Path" — Compares Herbert's three eugenics programs: the Bene Gesserit's centuries-long Kwisatz Haderach breeding scheme (explicitly modeled on the communal breeding of the guardians in Plato's Republic, undone when Jessica bears Paul a generation early and he escapes their control), Leto II's Golden Path breeding for Siona's invisibility to prescience, and the Tleilaxu axolotl-tank immortality that collapses when their Face Dancers out-mimic them. Each program is weighed ethically—Leto as the 'ultimate consequentialist' whose species-saving tyranny invokes Mill's utilitarianism and Machiavelli's ends-justify-the-means, the Sisterhood as shifting toward Kantian duties against using persons as mere means. Herbert's lesson: 'the most dangerous of all creations is a rigid code of ethics,' whether aimed at a single person, a single result, or a single agenda.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 15 "I’ve Got No Strings . ." — Richard Greene asks whether it was practically rational for Dexter to trust Lumen rather than kill her, to help her revenge-kill the Fowler ring, and to train her as a killer. The good outcomes do not help - Masuka's strip-club windfall shows luck is not rationality, and Socrates' Apology argument that corrupters risk harm from those they corrupt, together with Dexter's prior disaster in training Miguel, means the consequences were not foreseeably good. Kantian tests fail too - no one could will a universal law of killing, and killing violates the victim's autonomy and humanity as an end in itself - as do decision theory and instrumentality theories, so no account of practical rationality vindicates Dexter's choices, suggesting instead that the emotionless 'wooden boy' is beginning to become a real one.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 20 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Solves the 'riddle' of Gus by showing his empire runs on corporate instrumental rationality: the careful, emotion-disciplined Los Pollos CEO launders meth through legitimate business, treats chemists as replaceable parts (the Gale plan), and exacts revenge on the cartel in 'Salud' by drinking his own poisoned tequila. The chapter defines this as the critical theorists' amoral means-end reason - Kant's hypothetical imperative without the categorical - making Gus a sociopath who violates the injunction to treat persons as ends, and reads his cartel war through Machiavelli and Hobbes's power-first picture of the state. Gus's Two-Face-like corpse reveals the split between the rage-driven avenger of Max and the respectable mask, foreshadowing what Walt becomes.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 24 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Si Sheppard grades The Walking Dead's three settlements by political Realism: the Governor's Woodbury - cohesive, feared rather than loved, feeding his people arena spectacle to keep them from turning on him - beats Rick's West Central Prison, which never becomes a state at all. Rick lets Tyreese's vigilante murder pass, ruling as a first-among-equals with no institutions, no constitution, and no monopoly of legitimate force in Weber's sense, then covertly guns down Thomas and Dexter while hiding behind his cop credibility - 'it's me or you' reasoning indistinguishable from Shane's. Realism cares about power, not morality, so Rick's flaw is not cruelty but the absence of institution-building: he was never a bad father, just a bad founding father, who only becomes a Realist after Alexandria falls.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 7 "Psych and Philosophy" — Robert Arp's introduction argues Psych is perfect for philosophy because Henry's games train observation and inference exactly as philosophers hone them, while Shawn's ruse shows how clever people abuse those powers to deceive - quoting Machiavelli's line that one who deceives will always find those who allow themselves to be deceived. It sets up the book's recurring ethical question about lying: lies for the liar's profit (Shawn avoiding jail in the pilot), paternalistic lies for the hearer's own good (Henry telling seven-year-old Shawn he 'blacked out' about his mother's death), and lies to benefit many (promising a terrorist freedom to find his bomb). Since Shawn's lies solve cases and save lives, the introduction suggests they may not be so bad in the end, though it admits wishing he would just come clean as a talented honest detective.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 26 "Psych and Philosophy" — The Bock brothers ask whether Shawn's fake-psychic lie is morally permissible, testing it against Augustine's and Kant's absolute prohibitions on lying, Nietzsche's claim that all language is metaphorical (the 'Lights, Camera . . . Homicidio' acting-as-lying scene), and Machiavelli's ends-justify-the-means deception from The Prince. Using Sissela Bok's three-question test they contrast justified police undercover work - Juliet infiltrating the sorority in 'Scary Sherry' and the roller derby team in 'Talk Derby to Me' - with Shawn's ruse, which fails because it protects Shawn's own interests rather than others. They end by weighing Sorensen's bald-faced lies (Shawn's 'I know you know I'm not telling the truth') and conclude Chief Vick's genuine belief shows these are real, indefensible lies.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 12 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Littmann tests The Prince against the real bosses behind the show - Nucky Johnson, Capone, Luciano, Rothstein, Torrio - and argues that Prohibition-era history bears out Machiavelli's rules of power. Seizing new opportunities pays (Nucky turning Atlantic City into the World's Playground, Colosimo gunned down for refusing bootlegging, Luciano eliminating Masseria and Maranzano to modernize the Mafia), and harming a rival without crushing him invites revenge (Nucky's fatal leniency toward Jimmy, Maranzano leaving the scarred Luciano alive). A ruler needs good arms, must tailor appearances to each audience (Capone's banquet murder of Anselmi and Scalise, Nucky's respectability and staged generosity), and above all must avoid hatred - the downfall of Nucky, Capone, and Luciano, and of the needlessly arrogant Rothstein, shot over a gambling debt he could easily have paid.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 57 "The Devil and Philosophy" — James Edwin Mahon dismantles the 'sympathy for the Devil' puzzle by testing three accounts of diabolical evil: Machiavelli's prince ('learn how not to be virtuous') shows self-interest is mere amoral Realpolitik; Schopenhauer's malice and Schadenfreude ('injure all people as far as you can') are still self-interested pleasure; and only Kant's 'diabolical will' - doing evil because it is evil, Paradise Lost's 'Evil, be thou my good' - truly captures the Devil, though Kant deemed it impossible for humans. Hence nobody actually likes the Devil; people like the intelligence, charm, and underdog status of the characters who play him in The Devil's Advocate and Angel Heart.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 20 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Christophe Porot and Charles Taliaferro ask whether Homeland's pervasive hypocrisy and deceit can be justified, starting from Walden's cover-up of the drone strike and Brody's heroic persona hiding a terrorist plot. Machiavelli's Prince supplies the case that political relationships with allies (Saul's 'Us and Them' speech to Carrie) require hypocrisy, while the Smith-inspired 'honest politicking' model - trading openly on self-interest, as with Carrie blackmailing al Sahrani - fails because politics should secure the public good, though la Rochefoucauld's 'homage vice pays virtue' explains Saul extorting the judge into doing right. Weighing Kant's unconditional duty not to lie (Carrie's fatal lie to Lynne Reed) against consequentialism, the chapter lands on the Walzer Dirty Hands view: some acts stay wrong yet necessary, and honest agents accept the guilt.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 21 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Cherry uses Vee's season-two grooming of Taystee, Poussey, Nicky, Cindy, and Crazy Eyes to test philosophers' accounts of manipulation (covert influence, non-rational persuasion, targeting weaknesses, misleading truthfully). She shows Vee's skill is not virtue, since manipulation threatens autonomy by imposing a will the victim would not endorse (Kantian personhood denied) and employs dishonesty, predatoriness, disrespect, and laziness, with Machiavellian ends. The defense she prescribes is Socratic: reject purely emotional persuasion like the sophists' flattery, and live the examined life by checking premises and motives before being played.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 22 "7. Machiavelli Advises the Governor" — Littmann reads The Prince as advice the Governor already follows: kidnapping Andrea and Michonne, butchering the National Guard survivors for supplies, murdering his way to leadership of Martinez's camp, and maintaining a benevolent image through Woodbury picnics and gladiatorial walker-fights while ruling through fear at the gates. Machiavelli's maxims - crush rather than lightly injure, be feared but not hated, be lion and fox, adapt to the times - explain both the Governor's successes and his failures, such as massacring his own army outside the prison or letting rage over Penny's death cost him his eye. The chapter ends by grading Machiavelli largely right about dirty hands and military power but blind to resources like medicine and fuel, and draws the real lesson: shape the political environment so Machiavellian strategies stop paying.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 34 "20. The Good and the Gracious" — Olson and Taliaferro read manners as the story's moral barometer: the genuine, effusive compliments exchanged by Westley and Inigo atop the Cliffs of Insanity, and Fezzik's sporting wrestling, express care and connection, while Humperdinck's and Rugen's courtly politeness is camouflage for torture, murder, and war. Against Machiavelli's instrumental use of courtesy in The Prince, they recruit Plato's sophrosyne as 'good form' inseparable from justice, wisdom, and courage, and Confucian li as etiquette that instructs and steadies us toward virtue, with Hobbes's 'small morals' marking the hollow version; they add that manners also police class, from Buttercup's 'Farm Boy' to reality TV and the financiers of the Great Recession who used the correct fork.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 43 "27. Was the Red Wedding Massacre a Good Thing" — Van der Deijl takes Tywin's line to Tyrion - 'explain to me why it is more noble to kill ten thousand men in battle than a dozen at dinner' - as a serious consequentialist challenge about the Red Wedding. Working through utilitarianism, prioritarianism, and dirty-hands cases like Hiroshima and shooting down a hijacked plane, he concedes the massacre could have been justified had breaking Guest Right and killing 3,500 brought peace at minimal cost; but the consequences fail - Joffrey and Roose Bolton keep power, the institution of guest right erodes, and Tywin's real motive was family power rather than the greater good - so the massacre fails even the consequentialist test, and Tywin is a power-hungry conspirator, not Machiavelli's prince.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 21 "9. Send The Good Place to the Bad Place" — Sheldon argues the Season One twist makes the show itself a moral paradox: a series about ethics that lies to its audience for thirteen episodes, breaking the informal contract it built through 'truth in fiction'. Through Chidi's red-cowboy-boots lie and Eleanor's plot to murder Janet, 'The Eternal Shriek' stages Kant's absolute prohibition on lying against Eleanor's Machiavellian ends-justify-means reasoning, with confession portrayed as the only release from escalating deception. The chapter ends with Eleanor citing Jonathan Dancy's moral particularism to get Chidi to lie his way through the Bad Place, leaving viewers to decide whether the show's own deception is justified by the ethical conversation it forces.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 34 "22. The Mad Titan and the Mother of Dragons" — Pairs Thanos with Game of Thrones' Daenerys as twin Machiavellian utopians acting on 'the ends justify the means' (quoting The Prince and the Discourses): Daenerys burns King's Landing to 'break the wheel,' Thanos snaps half of life away 'at random, dispassionate, fair to rich and poor alike' as 'a small price to pay for salvation.' It roots both villains in cruel childhoods and a nature-versus-nurture question (with historical analogies to Hitler and Stalin), and in messiah complexes built on improbable success — 'Dread it, run from it, destiny arrives all the same' — while noting the key inversion: Thanos refuses to rule and dies content watching the sunrise, whereas the breaker of chains claims a new throne.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 31 "Damned If You Do, and Damned If You Don’t" — McHenry reads the re-imagined series as a holy-war allegory in which both sides weaponize religion, then asks whether that manipulation is ever moral. Adama's lie about Earth is Machiavellian statecraft (with Foucault's point that privileged knowledge holds power), yet defended as serving the greater good, while Roslin's Pythia-based campaign contrasts with Bush's faith-based fear politics. The Cylons emerge as evangelical fundamentalists whose conversion of Baltar through inner Number Six runs on fear, exactly what Madison's case for religious liberty forbids. The chapter concludes the show's own gods have sided with the Colonials.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 19 "9 T’Challa’s Machiavellian Methods" — Drake and Lloyd argue the comic-book T'Challa of 'Panther's Rage' is classically Machiavellian in a way the film's earnest king is not: he rules through fear and strategic violence against Killmonger's uprising, cultivates the appearance of The Prince's five qualities (mercy, faith, honesty, humanity, religion), and exploits Wakandan religion — letting subjects believe the Black Panther is divine, never doffing the sacred garb even when swimming with Monica — as an instrument for preserving power. Advisers like Taku ask whether T'Challa differs from Killmonger, and the chapter concludes that, sharing Machiavelli's low view of human nature, T'Challa never considers democracy and keeps his people quiescent through a divinity he knows is performance.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 8 "The (Single) Garden Path" — Argues Herbert populates Dune with three long-running eugenics programs, each with a different ethical stance: the Bene Gesserit's Kwisatz Haderach breeding scheme (whose communal guardian-breeding deliberately recalls Socrates' Kallipolis in the Republic), Leto II's Golden Path, and the Bene Tleilax's axolotl-tank genetic design for immortality. It reads the chastened Sisterhood of the later novels as moving from consequentialist to Kantian, deontological ground ('never seek to create a human being in any one image'), frames Leto II as the ultimate utilitarian whose species-saving end allegedly justifies Machiavellian means (with Siona's objection that he had no right), and shows the Tleilaxu destroyed by their own monomaniacal religious code. Conclusion: 'the most dangerous of all creations is a rigid code of ethics.'
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 21 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — David Hahn argues that Spira's Yevon religion is exactly what Machiavelli and Nietzsche warned against: hope for the Calm and a Sin-free future makes Spirans otherworldly and passive, forbidding machina, revering self-sacrificing Summoner martyrs, and blaming themselves for Sin, just as just-war Christianity left Machiavelli's princes passive and dependent on mercenaries, paralleled by Seymour and Kinoc standing idle at Operation Mi'ihen. Nietzsche's slave revolt in morality explains Yevon's sanctification of meekness and death, while Machiavelli's account of religion as a political instrument, from Numa to Scipio's oath, explains why the lie of Yevon held Spira together, and why its collapse may bring either Nietzschean rebirth or Machiavellian chaos.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 13 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Marcus Schulzke reads the War of the Five Kings through The Prince: who wins the Iron Throne is decided by virtu - skill adapted to shifting circumstances - against fortuna, and morality is no guide, since actions are good or bad only as they gain or hold power. The failures illustrate the lessons: Viserys's arrogance binds him to the wrong allies, Robert's emotions make him capricious, Joffrey makes himself hated instead of feared, Ned's uncompromising honesty and trust in Littlefinger destroy him, and Robb's dependency on Walder Frey's auxiliary forces proves fatal. The true Machiavellians are the mask-wearers - Littlefinger, Arya, Jon as lion-and-fox - and above all Tyrion, who wins the Blackwater by planning, and Daenerys, who builds her own army from freed slaves and so makes her own luck.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 17 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — David Hahn contends Ned died because of his honor, not for it. Hobbes explains why: words bind no one without fear of enforcement - Cersei ripping up Robert's will ('Is this meant to be your shield, Lord Stark?') exposes Ned's belief that allegiance alone secures the King's Justice - and the Iron Throne itself is a Leviathan, forged by Aegon's dragons ending the state of nature, whose force rather than justice holds the peace. Machiavelli supplies the indictment of Ned's idealism: 'we who presume to rule must do vile things for the good of the realm,' so Ned's refusal to assassinate Daenerys, his merciful warning to Cersei, and backing the rightful but war-prone Stannis over Renly cost him his head and plunged the realm into civil war; the security of the state demanded exiling or killing the Lannisters and crowning Renly.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 21 "9. Send The Good Place to the Bad Place" — Asks whether a show about ethics may lie to its audience for a whole season: the Season One twist breaks the viewer's implicit contract even though the show keeps its internal 'truth in fiction'. Through 'The Eternal Shriek' it stages the debate — Chidi's Kantian ban on lying (the red cowboy boots saga with Henry, ending in a confession that defeats Henry) against Eleanor's Machiavellian ends-justify-means plot to 'kill' Janet — and reads the show's cascade of confessions as its answer that truth-telling absolves. Eleanor citing Jonathan Dancy's moral particularism in 'Rhonda, Diana, Jake, and Trent' lets Chidi lie his way through Hell, leaving viewers to decide whether the twist's ethical education justifies the deception.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 30 "NOTES" — First defines lying — distinguishing it from mere error (Angela believing Peter dead), from the Haitian's non-verbal memory-wipe deception, and from Hiro's silent staging of Ando's fake death — then tests moral theories against the show's liars. Kant's categorical imperative bans all lying but is abandoned when Sylar demands a friend's hiding place; utilitarianism vindicates Victoria Pratt's lie about the virus vial yet also licenses Linderman's .07% explosion and Plato's noble lie of the earthborn metals, which the chapter rejects. Machiavelli's advice that princes may lie to keep power is played out by 'President Sylar' in 'Five Years Gone,' and the chapter finally endorses Sissela Bok's presumption against lying — a public-reasoning procedure modeled by Bob Bishop and Mohinder before Monica's virus injection.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 15 "Notes" — Argues Frank's rise is a genuinely successful illustration of The Prince: Machiavelli's advice to be prepared not to be virtuous shows in his lying (feigning loyalty to Walker while engineering his impeachment, promising Russo the governorship), his strategic murders of Russo and Zoe, his audacity in making his own luck ('turn over the table'), and his cultivation of a pious family-man image while privately spitting on the crucifix. The chapter also lets Machiavelli criticize Frank — revenge on Tusk (better to pamper or crush), Claire's fruitless generosity at CWI, alliances with the stronger, and being feared to the point of being hated, which costs him Sharp, Remy and Claire. Finally it tests The Prince against modern democracy — party discipline, sex-scandal politics, Obama's donated Nobel money, birther smears — concluding that since Machiavellians will always adapt to whatever system exists, citizens must reward results and stop judging by image.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 16 "Notes" — Runs through everything Frank does for a single project — the education reform bill: leaking Blythe's draft, gutting collective bargaining after promising Spinella ('I revised the parameters of my promise'), the Rasmussen speakership coup he then 'exposes', the shipyard-for-base trade, and the staged brick incident and strike-breaking — to show he endorses being 'other than good'. It then argues Machiavelli would not be impressed: Frank fails to keep up the appearance of integrity (Blythe, Feng and Vasquez all stop trusting him), inspires hatred rather than fear alone, and seeks power purely for its own sake where Machiavelli wanted it for the state's stability and liberty — the BBC's Francis Urquhart, who read The Prince and serves England, is the better Machiavellian. The chapter closes by weighing ironic and exposé readings of The Prince (Benner's critique, Rousseau's view that Machiavelli was unmasking princes, Dietz's sabotaging-gift reading) and concludes Frank fails even on the technique, not just the morality.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 29 "Notes" — Cooper reads Frank's one prayer - kneeling to pray 'to myself, for myself' - as a self-love he calls autoeroticism, built on metaphysical atheism, ruthless pragmatism, and happiness as power. Like Glaucon's Ring of Gyges, Frank's atheism removes divine punishment from the moral equation, so the murders of Peter Russo and Zoe Barnes incur only human risk, while his feigned piety at the Peachoid girl's vigil, broken promises to Tusk, and 'cruelty well used' toward Russo exemplify Machiavellian virtu taming fortuna. Against this the chapter sets Augustine's critique of the libido dominandi: Frank's remorse after betraying Freddy ('Do you think I'm a hypocrite?') shows the lust for domination enslaves rather than liberates, the way of the City of Man against the Augustinian freedom of self-giving love.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 15 "Notes" — Littmann tests Frank against The Prince and largely confirms the 'Machiavellian' label: his lies (playing the loyal confidant while engineering Walker's fall), his strategic murders of Russo and Zoe, his preference for weaker allies, and his manufactured piety and father stories all enact Machiavelli's advice that a prince must learn 'not to be good' while seeming merciful, faithful, and religious. But the debts run both ways: Claire's vindictive 'let's make him suffer' offends Machiavelli's pamper-or-crush rule, and modern democratic image politics (Obama donating his Nobel money, the Obama-as-Muslim smear) outperforms The Prince where voters punish fear and reward a generosity Machiavelli thought ruinous. The moral is not despair but vigilance: since Underwoods will always rise, citizens must reward genuine results rather than respond to images.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 16 "Notes" — Fallis walks through the education-reform arc — leaking Blythe's draft, gutting collective bargaining ('I revised the parameters of my promise'), framing Rasmussen in the speakership coup, the staged brick incident, and goading Spinella into felony assault — to show Frank follows Machiavelli's counsel to be 'other than good.' Yet Frank fails at Machiavelli's how and why: he never cultivates the appearance of integrity (Blythe, Feng, and Vasquez refuse to deal with a known liar), he inspires hatred as well as fear, and he seeks power for its own sake rather than the stability of the state, which makes the BBC's Francis Urquhart the superior Machiavellian. Even the revisionist readings of The Prince — Benner's irony, Rousseau's claim that Machiavelli was exposing princes' methods like an investigative reporter, Dietz's deliberate-sabotage thesis — would not rescue Frank, since he bungles the techniques regardless of their intent.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 14 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Argues that a motorcycle club is a Machiavellian regime in miniature: Jax's Season 3 fake betrayal of the club to Stahl—actually a set-up that shortens the crew's prison time and delivers both Stahl and Jimmy O to death—shows the prince's union of lion and fox in service of the club rather than himself. J.T. figures as a founder overcome by fortuna ('each savage event was a catalyst for the next... blood was every color'), lacking the virtu to impose his vision, while Clay wields deceit and force for mere egoism that Machiavelli would refuse the name of glory. Zobelle's self-description as a 'Machiavellian fool' flooding Charming with drugs, and Jax's admission that 'you can't sit in this chair without being a savage,' frame the chapter's question of whether manipulation and violence can serve a genuine common good.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 24 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Si Sheppard reads the comic through Realist state-formation theory: Shane's leadership rests on borrowed prestige and dies with him, West Central Prison collapses into anarchy because Rick never establishes a monopoly on legitimate force—letting Tyreese's vigilante murder pass—nor any institution beyond his personal authority, while the Governor's Woodbury thrives on fear, arenas, and bread-and-circuses. Citing Machiavelli's prince who is feared rather than loved, Weber's definition of the state, and Bismarck's unifying wars, he argues the prison loses the 'second anarchy' rivalry with Woodbury for want of scouting, sabotage, coalition-building, or any command structure that survives Rick's absences. Rick's confession that he would kill everyone in the Alexandria Safe Zone to keep Lori safe is post-moral Realism, yet he was 'a bad founding father' who only finally learns to build an army instead of relying on himself.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 14 "What Would Machiavelli Do" — Reitsma treats the refereeless pickup game as a Lockean state of nature and asks how to beat the 'strategic ticky-tacker' who calls phantom fouls to win. He condemns first-strike cheating as wrong on Kantian grounds (the cheat 'makes an exception of himself') and by an ideal of Homeric athletic honor, then asks whether retaliatory ticky-tacking is justified. Reading Machiavelli's 'dirty hands' argument alongside Locke's claim that in a state of nature each person may punish transgressors, he concludes proportionate tit-for-tat cheating can make one a legitimate 'agent of justice' when no referee exists.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 9 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Raymond Belliotti reads the twenty-year Olympic career of Italian sprinter Pietro Mennea, 'The Southern Arrow,' through Machiavelli's concept of virtu, the excellence relevant to one's function that lets a person master Fortuna. He distinguishes Machiavelli's military, political, civic, moral, and artistic virtu (using the Agathocles passage and the Life of Castruccio Castracani) and argues Mennea's physical prowess, mental toughness, and turning of anti-southern prejudice into motivation exemplify athletic virtu. Machiavelli would scoff at Olympic ideals of peace and brotherhood but relish the fierce international competition and the discipline of sport that Mennea embodied through his 1980 Moscow gold and later political career.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 24 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Mahon asks whether Ride with the Devil endorses the proverb that all's fair in love and war, locating the film's moral core in its outsiders—the German immigrant Jake, the freed slave Holt, and the young widow Sue Lee. Against Sunzi's undiscriminating claim that warfare is the art of deceit, he argues the film sides with Machiavelli's Discourses distinction between honorable ruses of war and dishonorable perfidy: the bushwhackers' wearing of Union blue and Jake's lies are ruses, but the Lawrence massacre and refusing to ambush women under a truce mark limits Jake will not cross. In love, Sue Lee's shift from romantic lying to 'now is the truth' shows honesty is finally required, so all is not fair.

### The Ethics of Care

The ethics of care is a moral approach that treats responsiveness to the needs of particular others, and the relationships in which we are embedded, as central to ethical life, rather than treating morality primarily as a matter of impartial rules or abstract rights. It grew out of Carol Gilligan's psychological research, which suggested that many people, and women in particular, reason morally in a distinct voice oriented toward care, connection, and the concrete circumstances of relationships, alongside the more familiar ethic of justice and rights. Care ethicists argue that dependence and caregiving are basic features of human life that traditional theories have marginalized. The approach reframes moral maturity around sustaining relationships and meeting real needs rather than applying universal principles.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 11 "Elaine’s Moral Character" — Sarah Worth asks whether Elaine is a feminist icon or 'just one of the boys.' Elaine passes every liberal-feminist benchmark - a Tufts education, the only steady career (Pendant Publishing, then the J. Peterman catalogue), financial and emotional independence - but fails the ethic of care: her dating ethics run on pettiness (dumping men for not offering pie, for dirty bathrooms, over Puddy's high-fiving), the 'spongeworthy' episode commodifies her own relationships, she shows no maternal instinct toward the ugly baby, and she secretly resents George's engagement. The conclusion: being one of the boys does not a feminist make, though Elaine still models an independence the women of Friends and Frasier lack.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 11 "“The Graduation” Autonomy and the Relational Self" — Jessica Prata Miller reads Buffy through Carol Gilligan's care perspective: Buffy's self is relational (the Scooby Gang, 'Dawn is a part of me' in 'The Gift'), her moral reasoning contextual rather than rule-bound (caging Oz instead of killing the werewolf, rejecting Riley's Initiative 'demons bad' abstraction), and her emotions a moral resource ('My emotions give me power'). She also weighs the criticisms — Buffy's secret harboring of Angel exposed in 'Revelations,' and Faith's utilitarian 'plus column' defense of hiding a killing, which Buffy rejects ('I am' the one who cries over the bystander). Comparing the three Slayers, Miller argues only Buffy attains moral autonomy: Kendra's unquestioning obedience and Faith's hyper-individualistic action-hero isolation both fail, while Buffy's 'I like to think of it as graduation' break from the Watchers' Council shows autonomy achieved within, not against, relationships.
- **The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am**, ch. 22 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" — Answers the title with 'fugheddaboutit' - Carmela is no feminist - but argues she reasons as a Gilligan-style care ethicist. Her moral voice evolves from Church-based justice arguments against Angie's divorce ('Commendatori'), through the justice-tradition confrontation with Dr. Krakower's refusal of 'blood money' ('Second Opinion'), to mature care ethics that balances self with others when she throws Tony out after the Svetlana revelation ('Whitecaps'). Using Noddings on reciprocity and 'total engrossment', the chapter reads the marriage's failure as failed caring, and the Furio romance and the Georgetown ricotta-pie intimidation as care reasoning that defies the submissive female stereotype feminists fear care ethics valorizes.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 24 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Cynthia Freeland reads the film's women through feminist ethics of care: the two Marys function like a Greek-chorus of grieving observers, while Claudia and Veronica — and the casting of Bellucci as the repentant whore opposite Morgenstern's ageless Madonna — lock them into the virgin/whore double bind. Using Carol Gilligan's critique of Kohlberg's Kantian standard and Nel Noddings's and Sara Ruddick's point that mothering is reflective 'attentive' work, she argues Gibson's Mary is one-dimensional: flashbacks of 'I am here' show maternal instinct, never moral deliberation. She ends by suggesting the historical Jesus, like Socrates, was more radical toward women than the film, and that Irigaray's reading of Christ's bleeding wounds as a feminized maternal body sits oddly with Gibson's muscular, 'take it like a man' Savior.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 46 "The Perfect Storm" — Storm's journey from being worshipped as a weather goddess in Kenya to joining Xavier's school fits Campbell's heroic cycle, and her bond with the demonic-looking, rosary-carrying Nightcrawler shows strangeness as a bridge to growth - the duality transcended into singularity when she tells him 'I have faith in you'. Housel then grades Storm at Kohlberg's post-conventional level of justice ethics, yet shows her shifting into Gilligan's care ethics when she dashes off to save eight mutant children from a government lab, mastering both 'masculine' justice and 'feminine' care - hence the 'perfect hero'.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 48 "Phoenix Rising Jean Grey" — Jean Grey, the self-doubting original X-Man of the Cyclops-Wolverine love triangle, evolves across the films - the phoenix necklace, growing powers, growing confidence - through all three Kohlberg levels to her self-sacrifice that saves the X-Men at the end of X2. Housel rejects reading that act as utilitarian calculation or as the unbalanced self-sacrifice some feminist readings of care ethics would fault: Jean acts not out of duty but out of love and care, beyond the call of duty - what philosophers call supererogation - becoming a female Christ figure whose phoenix image foreshadows resurrection and Campbell's return as 'Master of the Two Worlds'.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 13 "Yes, but What About the Killer Rabbit" — Argues the Pythons invert Arthurian legend's traditional patriarchal function, using Holy Grail — made amid 1970s women's liberation and legal abortion — to expose the absurdity of patriarchy rather than endorse it. The Black Knight's 'None shall pass' embodies an abstract, relationship-blind masculine ethics that the chapter sets against care ethics, while the witch-weighing scene shows Arthur and Bedevere's male bonding eclipsing the mob's victim. Castle Anthrax's 'perilous bed' and the Prince Herbert rescue — Launcelot's heterosexual-matrix heroics collapsing when the damsel in the tower is a prince who enjoys musicals — turn courtly love and gender roles into farce, making the film as much a document of 1970s gender politics as a medieval satire.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 31 "Poker and Philosophy" — Housel surveys a century of poker on screen — from the Tombstone Birdcage Theater's 'bird in a gilded cage' through Maverick, The Gambler, Rounders, and ESPN's Tilt with its brothel-break 'Matador' — to show women cast as eye-candy, damsels, or flukes (Joanne Woodward winning a high-stakes game without knowing how to play). Against the myth stands Annie Duke, who beat her brother Howard on the way to the 2004 Tournament of Champions title. The argument: poker rewards reading and projecting emotion, so women socialized into emotional intelligence hold an edge over macho men who suppress it — a retooled Stoicism fusing Epictetus's 'make the best use of what is in your power' with Gilligan's care ethics, backed by Nietzsche's trust in the senses and Sun Tzu's 'pretend inferiority and encourage his arrogance.'
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 18 "U2 and Philosophy" — The authors apply Gilligan's and Noddings' ethics of care to U2: 'Bad' shows the speaker as Noddings' 'one-caring', and 'Sometimes You Can't Make It on Your Own' - Bono caring for his dying father through anger and resentment - exemplifies care's insistence on the particular relationship over universal rules, refusing abstraction even of the usual songwriting metaphors. 'Peace on Earth' names the Omagh bomb's dead (Sean, Julia, Gareth, Ann, Breda) and 'Van Diemen's Land' refuses both IRA and British sides, showing care ethics rejecting the utilitarian accounting and the Kantian universalizability arguments that could rationalize such violence. They conclude U2 are philosophical rather than political feminists: Gilligan's 'different voice' is not a woman's voice, and the band's connected knowing - debt relief sung as connection in 'Beautiful Day' - makes maternal thinking 'loud, rhythmic, catchy, even cool'.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 35 "You’re Basically “a Stuffed Animal Made by Grandma”" — Renee Kyle sets House's detached "doctor knows best" medicine against Cameron's practice to argue for Carol Gilligan's feminist ethic of care: Cameron builds trust, refuses to deceive or bully (defending Ezra's control over his body in "Informed Consent"), and sees patients as embedded in relationships, arranging for parents to hold their newborn in "Maternity," where House sees only abstract puzzles. The chapter also presses the standard feminist worry that valorizing care can backfire: Cameron's unresolved grief stops her from telling terminal patients the truth, and by "Que Sera Sera" she secretly injects a patient who wants to leave the hospital, so that caring too much turns her into House.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 9 "Plato’s Cave Again" — Curran uses Shadow of a Doubt to teach epistemology: Charlie's claim to 'know' her uncle distinguishes knowledge by acquaintance from propositional knowledge as justified true belief, with the permanently stuck 'Til Two clock showing a true belief that is not knowledge because its warrant is unreliable. Coherence (Hegel, Blanshard), pragmatist (James, Dewey), and correspondence theories of truth are tested against the townspeople's false but convenient beliefs about Uncle Charlie, and only correspondence survives. Kant's absolute duty not to lie is weighed against Mill's act and rule utilitarianism for the detectives' deceptions, and a feminist care-ethics perspective assesses Charlie's shielding her mother from the truth. Plato's cave frames the cinema itself: film can deceive like shadows on a wall, yet the detectives' unused photograph shows the camera can also reveal truth, so movies help us face facts, at the price, as Charlie pays, of lost innocence.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 20 "Turning the Tables" — Wartenberg argues that North by Northwest pits two defective ethical stances against each other: the Professor's 'zealous patriotism,' exposed as callous in the USIA scene where he lets the innocent Thornhill be killed as the Kaplan decoy and spends Eve in the line of danger ('War is hell, Mr. Thornhill, even when it's a cold one'), and Thornhill's 'ethical particularism,' akin to the feminist ethics of care, exposed as headstrong when love-driven rashness leaves both lovers dangling on Mount Rushmore and only the Professor's intervention saves them. Yet the ending's match cut from Rushmore to the train berth reveals Hitchcock's real McGuffin: the Professor fails less as a moralist than as a bad director whose staged deceptions misfire, and the film's true philosophical claim is self-reflexive, that only film has the power to reconcile patriotism and romantic love, an optimistic world existing only in the artifice of the camera.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 10 "You May Wonder How Come I Love You Care and Ethics" — Gimbel asks what the E Street Band's marathon multiple encores mean, starting from social contract theory: Hobbes's state of nature ('no home, no job, no peace, no rest') and Locke's contract explain the ticket as a financial IOU — so a drunk, short Hendrix show wrongs you financially but not morally — while the contractual view of moral duty (the 'Hungry Heart' narrator who abandoned his wife and kids in Baltimore) cannot explain why a missing encore feels like personal betrayal. The gift theory fails too, since encores are expected, and expected things are not gifts. Care ethics (Ruddick, Noddings) fits instead: devoted fans make the band part of their identity, Springsteen sings 'to you about you,' and the No Nukes 90-minute set became permanent because he would not give his people less — while 'Pink Cadillac' shows the limit case, since you cannot love someone for her Cadillac.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 23 "History Will Judge" — Livingston reads the Razor movie through George Lakoff's Strict Father and Nurturant Parent models: Cain's Pegasus assumes a dangerous world and enforces obedience (shooting Belzen for refusing orders, the torture of Gina), while Adama's Galactica assumes empathy and open questioning (asking Boomer 'Why do you hate us so much?', sparing Starbuck). Kendra Shaw is the 'child' conditioned by desensitization and objectifying language into a killing razor and a PTSD victim, whose recovery under Apollo shows the two family models being blended — boldness with communication. Adama's verdict that 'history will have to make its judgments' frames the chapter's claim that understanding Cain requires seeing the family culture that produced her.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 22 "Toward Caring" — Sylvia models the Doctor on feminist care ethics: Gilligan's response to Kohlberg's justice-tinged scales and Noddings's distinction between natural caring (for Rose, Martha, Peri in 'The Caves of Androzani') and ethical caring, which explains his forgiveness of the Master and compassion for Dalek Caan after genocides. Against utilitarian impartiality — which cannot say why he should save his companion over a stranger — the relationship itself grounds the obligation, while his vengeful moment facing the lone Dalek in 'Dalek' shows what caring burnout looks like.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 119 "Beyond Lies the Other" — The section reads Dick's first published story, 'Beyond Lies the Wub,' as the origin of his career-defining theme: the jovial, philosophic wub survives the captain who sees only fresh meat because its empathy is so total it can exchange minds with the man about to slaughter it. Defining empathy as seeing the world from another's viewpoint plus sympathizing (which the cornering cat, predicting the rat's moves, lacks), it ends with Dick's Exegesis: an evil magician-deity occludes our minds until a savior in trash form restores them, and without such a revelation you, the reader, are 'nothing but a robot.'
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 121 "Can a Blade Runner Love a Robot" — The section contrasts Dick's bleaker novel, where J.R. Isadore's love for the androids dies when they cut the legs off his rare spider and Deckard's union with Rachael is the 'summa of falsity and mechanical motions' that fuels his resolve to destroy them, with the film's redemptive romance built on Rachael being 'more human than human.' It argues the movie preserves Dick's thesis anyway: Roy Batty's final act of saving the enemy who hunted him shows the empathy that makes the replicants persons, perhaps more than human.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 122 "How to Build a Moral Robot" — This section draws design morals from Dick's warnings: machines built as ersatz humans deny the value of being human, robotic sexual partners are doomed deceptions (the novel's Deckard-Rachael encounter is the case study), and a genuine artificial moral agent needs empathy 'logically equivalent to agape,' though a machine reasoning on sound moral principles could still count as a limited moral agent with proportionate rights and responsibilities. The Three Stigmata's Palmer Eldritch, returned from deep space as a machine treating humans as resources, shows that the netherward pull toward machinehood threatens humans themselves.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 133 "He Ain’t Heavy, He’s My Other" — This section stages Levinas's infinite responsibility for the Other against Heidegger's tendency to treat others as tools for warding off death: J.R. Isidore's one-way care for androids who vivisect a spider, Dick's 'The Android and the Human' warning that androidization means becoming predictable means, and the treatment of animals as the litmus test of humanity. The self becomes real through selfless action (Tagomi saving a stranger, Sweetscent returning to his wife), and because the height separating self and Other descends from Descartes's idea of infinity, meeting the face of the poor stranger, from Radio Free Albemuth's beggar to The Adjustment Bureau's Chairman, is an encounter with God.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 134 "Fifty Ways to Love Your Other" — The section reads Levinas's demand to experience the Other's suffering in the Other's place as Dick's empathy made literal: the shifting points of view that blur heroes and villains, Felix Buckman's tears, Molinari developing his people's symptoms, and the empathy boxes bonding users to Mercer's endless stoning, a fraud whose falsity is beside the point because the concern is the real thing. Villains are precisely those who refuse the transfer, and the ordinary one-way gift, buying a stranger a drink with no return, enacts the Golden Rule: even if the universe isn't real, Melina is right, kiss each other anyway.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 15 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Jonas-Sebastien Beaudry reads Neverwhere's magic invisibility as a model of real social invisibility: after Richard helps the injured Door he loses his job, his fiancee Jessica, and even the ability to be perceived, joining the homeless, slaves, and Jews under Nazism as people excluded from the moral community whose needs no longer register. Using Arendt's banality of evil to explain everyday indifference and Richard Rorty on torturers who fail to see a 'real' human, he distinguishes radical from partial invisibility, shown in Jessica stepping over the bleeding Door and misreading her need as 'sleep it off.' The remedy is Iris Murdoch's 'loving gaze' of just and careful attention, which seizes Richard before he can rationalize, backed by a practical wisdom about whose needs matter, so that acknowledging the invisible, down to apologizing to a rat in London Below, is what makes both them and us better.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 17 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Olson opens with her own first session, in which the DM steered her toward a 'sexy Eladrin' miniature in high heels, and asks why women stay away from D&D. She argues the game's mechanics are egalitarian—identical power lists for male and female characters, echoing Plato's Republic claim that women guard the city by the same nature as men—and that party cooperation embodies the relational, care-based feminist ethic Marilyn Friedman and Angela Bolte oppose to male-coded individualism. The trouble is culture, not system: sexualized miniatures that objectify female bodies, tokenism, harassment, and marketing that ignores women, to which female gamers respond by playing male characters like Jenni Dowsett, designing separatist systems such as Portal Worlds, or, like Shelly Mazzanoble, claiming D&D for the 'inner girl'.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 25 "The Wire and Philosophy" — The Rochas argue that the only two women in the Game, Snoop on the street side and Kima on the police side, embody a 'militant feminism' in the lineage of the Black Panthers' Kathleen Cleaver and the Weather Underground's Bernardine Dohrn: women can excel at anything men can, including violence (Snoop as Marlo's natural soldier, repurposing a Hardware Barn nail gun, wearing womanhood only as a costume), and violence is justified when used for just ends (Kima overcoming fear to police). They then use Gilligan and Noddings's care ethics to explain the finale: Kima's dedication to relationships and care for the overlooked homeless victims lets her discern that McNulty and Freamon's fake-serial-killer scheme is an immoral masculinized rationalization, so she turns in her friends and becomes the show's moral conscience.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 19 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Jonas-Sebastien Beaudry defends a 'moderate speciesism' built on relationships rather than individual capacities: Taylor's trial strips him of clothes, name, and speech - the symbols of ethical community - showing how institutional speciesism rationalizes domination behind the Sacred Scrolls' Declaration-of-Independence-style self-evidence. Against Singer's anti-speciesist challenge that any distinctively human capacity is shared by some animals or missing from some humans, he argues both camps wrongly pedestal intrinsic traits, and reads Taylor's love for the mute Nova together with the failed Project Nim as showing that within-species bonds of love, care, and family are genuinely and justifiably valuable without licensing mistreatment. Bernard Williams's 'The Human Prejudice' - should we surrender to superior invading aliens? - marks where impartial anti-speciesism leads, while Zaius's 'Man is evil' and the doomsday-bomb ending show extreme speciesism as self-fulfilling prophecy.
- **The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia**, ch. 15 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" — Kathleen Poorman Dougherty sets Kant's universal, emotion-free morality (echoed in Kohlberg's justice stages and Judge Abernathy's 'blind court' claim in 'Infamy') against Carol Gilligan's care ethic, which she says fits Saint Alicia far better: Alicia's practical advice to Jennifer Lewis in the pilot, driving Kenny home in 'Home', and telling Kenny's father 'I care a lot more about your son than he does' show connection producing both better morality and better lawyering. Feminist theorists like Nel Noddings and Sara Ruddick treat this care orientation as morally superior, not merely different, but the chapter's later sections weigh the cost: Kalinda's burnout warning, Alicia's resentment at always hand-holding clients, and the double bind by which women absorb society's unpaid caring labor. The verdict is that care is genuinely moral, but it must become a shared burden.
- **How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness**, ch. 20 "How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy" — The chapter argues HIMYM offers two complementary feminist icons: Robin embodies personal autonomy and independence - fighting from 'but, um' early-morning shifts to lead anchor, and grieving infertility as stolen autonomy rather than lost motherhood - while Lily, and even more Marshall, exemplify Carol Gilligan's feminist care ethics with its emphasis on emotion over impartiality, cooperation over competition, and partiality toward loved ones. Aristotle's golden mean supplies the test Robin passes by balancing career and love instead of pushing one to an extreme. The twist that a male character best exemplifies care ethics, with Lily bridging the two moral outlooks, is offered as the show's progressive complexity about gender.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 23 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Robison-Greene argues Rawlsian ideal theory breaks down at Litchfield: Soso's hunger strike gets only cosmetic concessions from Caputo, Sophia's WAC human-rights platform loses to Taystee's realism, and Piper learns the council 'is basically bullshit,' showing how idealization made by the powerful ignores the lived facts of Mendoza's abusive marriage, Jimmy's 'compassionate' death sentence, and Sophia's denied hormones. Against taking a 'moral holiday' in prison, she proposes care ethics, with role-based duties sensitive to actual circumstances, as the morality that fits life inside, and suggests non-ideal theory may fit the outside world too.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 14 "5. Every Lonely Monster Needs a Companion" — Gadsden asks why a near-omnipotent Time Lord needs companions at all and tests four hypotheses against his solo meltdowns—executing Solomon in 'Dinosaurs on a Spaceship,' nearly murdering Jex in 'A Town Called Mercy,' and declaring himself 'Time Lord Victorious' in 'The Waters of Mars.' He rejects the Lord Acton power-corrupts hypothesis via Glaucon's ring story in Plato's Republic, since powerless companions offer no threat of reprisal or dishonor, and qualifies J.J. Sylvia's care-ethics 'empathetic link' because the Doctor cares for non-human species like the Star Whale too. He favors two answers: Hume's fact/value gap as a millennium-long moral myopia ('I can't see it anymore,' the deleted 'Flesh and Stone' confession), and Aristotle's point in the Nicomachean Ethics that only virtuous friends—moral peers who mirror us—can expose the Doctor's blind spots, like his 'God Complex.'
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 24 "12. Should We Really Care about the Crawleys" — Jones takes up the charge that loving Downton seduces viewers into admiring inequality, and answers that the Crawleys deserve our care because birth, not choice, gave them their position, so they should be judged only by what they do with it: Grantham paying for Mrs. Patmore's eye surgery, Violet throwing the flower contest after Isobel's challenge, the family gradually embracing Branson. He reads the show as a manifesto for social change through sympathetic contact between classes rather than Irish-style revolt - befriend the rich and their good nature will start to level the playing field. His own objection is that this makes change partly the responsibility of the less privileged, from Thomas being asked to soften Carson's homophobia to the poor being asked to be nice to the rich today.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 28 "11. I Ain’t No Hollaback Girl!" — Callens explains Carol's killing of Lizzie in "The Grove" through Kohlberg's stages of moral development, arguing Carol reasons at the post-conventional level (pre-apocalypse law and punishment no longer bind) while Rick, Hershel, and Daryl stay conventional, and then layers Maslow's hierarchy of needs on top: because survival needs are perpetually threatened, characters regress between stages, and only self-actualized Carol accepts reality and makes group-preserving choices like executing Lizzie and mercy-killing Karen and David. Gilligan's justice-versus-care critique supplies the gendered frame - Carol moves to the middle of the justice-care continuum, her diminished care (unlike Season Two's grief over Sophia) is what makes her post-conventional, and her non-lethal Terminus rescue contrasts with Rick's summary execution of Gareth.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 29 "12. They Just Want Me to Be Like Them" — Castro and Beisecker diagnose Lizzie's walker fixation as prolonged grief disorder: she displaces grief for her father onto the walker "Nick," denies final death ("They're just different"), and treats reanimation as a viable form of life she might join ("Maybe I should change"). They argue Carol's suppressive guardianship - the "look at the flowers" distraction and calling Lizzie weak and confused - aggravated the avoidance at the root of the disorder, so Lizzie's "transformation" of Mika was a misguided moral experiment rather than murder by a monster. The chapter contrasts Tyreese's affirming care ("You each do things your own way") as the guardianship that might have saved the girls, and notes Carol's refusal to let Lizzie reanimate denies her the dying-wish courtesy the group once granted Jim.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 18 "7. And the Most Despicable Jessica Lange Character Is . ." — Ranks Jessica Lange's characters from least to most despicable using moral philosophy: Sister Jude earns credit for acting from duty (reporting the Nazi Dr. Arden at personal risk, Kant-style) and for genuinely feeling remorse; Elsa Mars partly honors the matriarchal obligations of care ethics but lacks Aristotle's habitual virtue and moderation, selling Bette and Dot to Dandy for fame; Constance Langdon abuses and effectively murders her disabled children; and Fiona Goode, motivated exclusively by youth, beauty, and power, murders her Supreme and torments Cordelia - never once acting out of concern for others.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 23 "11. The Mother of All Bombs" — Uses Hannah Arendt's On Violence — violence begets a more violent world, and WWII birthed the cold war rather than peace — to read Part 8, where the Trinity test, via the entity Judy/Mother, births BOB, whose garmonbozia-hunger is nuclear-age destruction feeding on female pain. Carol Gilligan's account of patriarchal silencing of women's voices (Naido's shut eyes, Laura's violated diary, the Persephone pattern of girls who must "die") and Gilbert and Gubar's dying "Angel in the House" frame Laura as both born from the Fireman and Señorita Dido as an antidote to the Bomb and destroyed by the mother wound Sarah Palmer carries. Against the toxic masculinity of Mr. C, Richard, and Chad, the show's good men — Cooper, the Trumans, Hawk, Bobby — embody Gilligan's ethic of care, and the chapter ends by demanding America put down its weapons and listen to women.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 18 "9. Machines Who Care" — Weiss reads 'The Lonely' and 'I Sing the Body Electric' as anticipations of today's debate over 'relational artifacts' — Turkle's sociable robots, the Sparrows' claim that robotic aged care is unethical, Coeckelbergh's rebuttal — asking, with Anne, whether an electric grandma 'doesn't sound so good.' Corry's Alicia and the children's electric grandma show care being bought as an assembly-line product for the lonely, and he presses the details: why the caring robots are female and serve water, why Alicia arrives in a box and is summarily shot in the face when no longer needed, and what it says about a culture that maroons people in loneliness and then sells the technical fix.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 28 "15. June the Stoic" — Lequien asks how June might endure Gilead and answers with Epictetus: like the slave-philosopher, she can locate freedom in what is 'up to her'—detaching from her body during the Ceremony ('What he is fucking is the lower part of my body'), relinquishing property, and learning not to call husband or daughter her own. He tests alternatives—Camus's question of suicide (the shatterproof glass), utilitarianism (the coerced 'We are very happy'), Tronto's care ethics (Gilead smothers the sorority that could make care meaningful), and the Particicution as a licensed Two Minutes Hate—before concluding that 'Nolite te bastardes carborundorum' functions as June's Stoic mantra: mastery of her own responses is the one victory the Sons of Jacob cannot take.
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 28 "14. Friends Don’t Lie" — Bowman tests Hawkins friendships against Aristotle's three kinds in the Nicomachean Ethics: Dustin and Lucas's shared-comics pleasure collapses into rivalry over Max, Nancy and Jonathan's utility ends once Will and Barb are found, and Barb's fatal poolside loyalty to Nancy, though one-directional, is a friendship of virtue. Nietzsche's ideal of friends who strengthen us through conflict recasts those very fights (Lucas confronting Eleven's power misuse) as the best friendship, care ethics (Gilligan and Noddings) makes the mutual one-caring Party the real answer to who teaches Eleven friendship, and Derrida's Politics of Friendship grounds democracy and society itself in such everyday reciprocity, which is why Eleven's 'friends don't lie' compass pulls her back from Kali's violence to close the gate.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 37 "24. Fred Rogers and the Ethics of Care" — A.G. Holdier places Rogers squarely in the care ethics of Gilligan and Noddings: against Kohlberg's justice stages (the Heinz dilemma recast with Henrietta Pussycat and X the Owl), care means Joan Tronto's four elements of attentiveness, responsibility, competence, and responsiveness, shown in the Clemmons kiddie pool, the Soviet guest understood through an interpreter, and 'just the way you are.' Extending care to animals via Rogers's vegetarianism and Carol Adams's 'absent referent,' and to the self via the closing benediction, he argues Rogers embodied care as particular, embodied practice rather than formula.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 28 "15. Chidi’s Indecision" — Vannatta argues Chidi's indecision exposes the shared flaw of the Big Three theories, Kantian deontology, Bentham and Mill's consequentialism, and Aristotle's virtue ethics of the golden mean: their rationalism pretends moral conflict can be eliminated by applying the correct rule, when Chidi's trolley terror shows moral situations are experienced as genuinely uncertain. Dewey's 'Three Independent Factors in Morals', the Good of desire, the Right of duty, and the Virtuous of communal praise, legitimizes that felt uncertainty and explains Eleanor's talent for finding option C between binary dilemmas. The chapter concludes that the show's real, unspoken moral theory is care ethics: partiality, relationship maintenance, and moral growth through the experience of being cared for, as Eleanor learns from Chidi's friendship rather than his lectures.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 1 "Introduction" — Book introduction: recounts how the 1979 cast were the first casualties of the Chestburster scene (real butcher-shop organs, Veronica Cartwright fainting), then previews the volume's payload - personhood questions about Ash, Bishop, David and the Ripley clone; Marx on why Weyland-Yutani sacrifices crews for profit; Plato's Republic on children in warfare via Newt; Lovecraftian cosmic horror; feminist readings of Ripley as care ethicist and mother; and continental takes - Xenomorphs as Nietzsche's Ubermensch, Camus on Ripley-8's refusal to commit suicide, and Sartre on a Xenomorph's right to resist us.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 10 "Not Bad, for a [Wo]man" — Argues Ripley's crossed-heart promise to Newt shows partialist care rightly overriding impartial justice: Kant, Mill, and Rachels demand everyone count for one, but Gilligan's critique of Kohlberg and Noddings's carer-cared-for relation - completed in Newt's 'I knew you'd come' - explain why Ripley duct-tapes two guns together and descends into the hive. Her flexible, relational problem-solving (the lighter-sprinkler trick against the Facehuggers, learning the pulse rifle) beats Gorman's mission-first command, and the trolley-style arithmetic she rejects when the one on the tracks is her little girl is not a moral failing; even nuking the Queen's eggs raises Singer-style speciesism questions.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 21 "A Professional, a Mother, and Someone Who Cares" — Asks whether Ripley is a feminist and answers 'only sometimes': her quarantine refusal ('Yes, I read you. The answer is negative') and her reasons for killing the Alien3 specimen ('a lot of innocent people will die') invoke rules, chain of command, and anonymous future victims - Kohlberg's post-conventional reasoning, not Gilligan's care voice - whereas the hot-chocolate scene with Newt and the unhesitating hive rescue exhibit the care-focused feminism of Gilligan and Noddings. Against the status-oriented reading of Vasquez's 'have you ever been mistaken for a man?' exchange, Ripley emerges as atypical of either stereotype: a professional, a mother, and someone who cares.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 21 "Repairing Our Worlds" — Fice reads ATLA through the feminist ethics of care, using Joan Tronto's phases of caring-about, taking care of, and care-giving to analyze Katara: freeing Aang from the iceberg, offering to heal Zuko's scar in the Crystal Catacombs, and her full arc as the Painted Lady feeding, healing, and freeing a polluted village. Care also misfires ('Imprisoned') and is devalued as feminine 'women's work' when Toph calls Katara motherly ('The Runaway'), a myth the chapter rejects. Care scales politically too: the Gaang's defeat of Fire Nation imperialism is care repairing the world, while Azula's indifference to Ty Lee and Mai marks her villainy.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 21 "Repairing Our Worlds" — Fice reads Katara through Joan Tronto's care ethics, tracking the phases in episodes: 'caring about' the refugees on 'The Serpent's Pass' and Zuko's scar in the Crystal Catacombs, 'taking care of' in freeing Aang from the iceberg, and 'care-giving' in 'The Painted Lady,' where she feeds, heals, and cleans up a polluted factory town. Care misfires are part of the theory, as when she pushes Haru to earthbend in 'Imprisoned' and gets him arrested, and Toph's 'motherly' jab lets the chapter reject the myth that care is essentially feminine, citing bell hooks. The larger claim is political: the Gaang's war against Fire Nation imperialism is care at world scale, repairing the world so its people can live well.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 30 "What Not to Do as a Parent" — The chapter pinpoints Marie's failure in Arkangel using Feinberg's parental-rights framework: by filtering out every fright (the neighbor's dog, her father's stroke) she violated Sara's right to an open future, misconstrued her welfare and protection rights, and stunted the empathy that makes a child a fully functioning human being. Aristotle's golden mean frames over-parenting as a vice of excess — as damaging as neglect — and Ruddick's maternal ethics of care also convicts Marie, since mothering requires fostering growth and social acceptability, not just preserving life. The Philip K. Dick comparison lands the conclusion: an android is distinguished from a human only by lacking empathy, so Marie has manufactured a partial android rather than raised a child.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 31 "Learning from Mia’s Mistakes" — The chapter grades each of Mia's escalations in Crocodile — helping Rob hide the cyclist's body, killing Rob fifteen years later, then killing Shazia, her husband, and baby Ali to keep the secret — under Kant's categorical imperative (the cover-up cannot be universalized and treats persons as means), the utilitarian calculus (which also condemns every killing once the widow's suffering and Mia's guilt are counted), and feminist care ethics, which rejects her defense that she killed to protect her family because care obligations never cancel proportionality and others' rights. Aristotle's virtue ethics supplies the diagnosis: Mia's undoing is lack of practical wisdom — every split-second choice (which she never had time to deliberate) went wrong because she lacked virtuous habits. The chapter urges practicing everyday virtue so we never take the first step down her path.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 17 "How Far I'll Go" — Maps the four waves of feminism onto Disney princess history: Snow White, Cinderella, and Aurora as chattel passed from parents to fairies to princes, betraying even first-wave rights; Beauvoir's 'one is not born but becomes a woman' and Friedan's feminine mystique explaining why the original trio's happiness is measured by marriage. Third-wave princesses are read with Wolf's beauty myth (Ariel and Jasmine as iron maidens), Butler's gender performativity, and Gilligan's care ethics (Ariel's and Belle's contextual, caring moral reasoning versus their fathers' principles). The fourth-wave princesses from Tiana to Moana need no man at all while male leads (Naveen, Flynn, Kristoff, Maui) become vulnerable sidekicks, ending with #GiveElsaAGirlfriend and the thought that equality is balance rather than sameness.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 17 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Olson's first D&D Encounters session handed her a sexualized female miniature in a chainmail bikini and high-heeled boots, and the chapter audits the game as a feminist would: research on the 'token girl' and male-default storytelling, women like Dowsett pushed to play male characters to be taken seriously, and harassment ranging from 'date at least one of the party or bring food' to condescension toward women in the industry. Against this she argues the rules themselves are egalitarian — identical power pools for male and female characters, embodying Plato's Republic claim that women 'are by nature the same with respect to guarding the city', and even the evil deities are stereotyped symmetrically (scheming Lolth and Tiamat versus war-god patrons of power) — while the collaborative party structure (clerics healing strikers, shared goals) has exactly the care-ethical, anti-individualist flavor Friedman and Bolte attribute to women's moral perspectives. Sexism is thus a consequence of unreflective practices, marketing that ignores women, and industry culture rather than the game; all-female systems like Portal Worlds are a real response but, she worries, separatism risks deepening the divide.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 37 "Notes" — Opening from the author's own grief — she nearly stopped playing Fallout 4 because its murdered spouse and kidnapped son echoed the loss of her real infant son — the chapter applies the ethics of care of Gilligan, Noddings, and Tronto to Fallout's wasteland. Care relationships structure the games: the Fallout 3 father whose flight from Vault 101 propels the plot, Dogmeat's loyal responsiveness as relational reciprocity, and the Fallout 4 son Shaun, where caring for your child collides with caring for a Commonwealth his Institute endangers. Settlement-building, faction choice (Lyons's Brotherhood handing out clean water versus the Railroad's liberation of synths), and even the Black Widow perk path that saves Megaton all become care-laden moral acts — care as protest against the wasteland's ethos of bare survival.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 28 "15. Chidi’s Indecision" — Surveys the 'Big Three' through the show: Kantian deontology (Chidi's boots lie, Tahani's mere-means charity), Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism (Jason's alligator frame-up, the trolley simulation), and Aristotle's golden mean (courage between Jason's rashness and Chidi's paralyzed deficiency), arguing their shared rationalism cannot accommodate the real uncertainty Chidi feels. John Dewey's 'Three Independent Factors in Morals' — the Good, the Right, and the Virtuous as irreducible — explains why Chidi sees only binaries while Eleanor finds 'option C' and imagines the Medium Place. The chapter concludes the show's unstated moral theory is care ethics: relational selves, justified partiality toward friends, and moral growth through the experience of being cared for, as when Chidi models care rather than lecturing it.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 11 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Donovan and Richardson read the Maltusian split, with the male Guardians banning emotion through the Book of Oa on Oa and the female Zamarons leaving to found the violet light of love on Zamaron, as the Western association of men with reason and women with emotion. They deploy Gilligan's different-voice reply to Kohlberg, the Pythagorean table of opposites via Genevieve Lloyd, Hegel's exclusion of women from the public sphere, and Jaggar's liberal-feminist critique of 'ahistorical' reason, whose comic-book analogue is the third law banning relationships between Lanterns.
