The chapter ends by arguing the standoff is a false dichotomy the comics themselves begin to dissolve: Kyle's 'Lanterns with heart' speech to the Guardians, the repeal of the third law, and the Indigo Tribe's plan to recombine the seven corps into the white light of creation.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 28 "NOTES" — Reads the show's eclipse icon against Plato's sun of the good — goodness has become hard to discern — and tests four theories of evil on the characters: Socrates' claim that no one errs knowingly is half-confirmed since villains like Angela and Nathan always take themselves to be doing right; Aristotle's akrasia and vice as an excess or deficiency of disposition fit Sylar's blood-scrawled 'Forgive me' apartment and his uncontrolled hunger; and Nietzsche's Übermensch and pre-Christian master morality raise the uncomfortable question of why Sylar preying on inferiors is not heroic like Achilles. The chapter's endorsed answer is Gilligan's ethics of care: the heroes are good because they care — Matt for Molly and Daphne, Bennet for Claire — while evil is the absence of care, though Bennet's authoritarian, family-only care shows that care itself must be both widened and restrained.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 29 "NOTES" — Explains the seemingly incomprehensible things Heroes characters do for family by sorting their motives into three theories of family obligation: universal justice (framed by Socrates confronting Euthyphro for prosecuting his own father), care ethics' partiality to loved ones, and Confucian role-based duty with its asymmetrical parent–child, husband–wife, and sibling obligations. Noah Bennet turns out to be Confucian in practice ('I'm your father, Claire Bear') despite his universalist Company rhetoric, Hiro defies Kaito's Confucianism for the greater good while Kaito still teaches him the sword because that is a father's role, Niki and Janice act from care while D.L. and Micah act from roles, Mohinder's duty is Confucian sonship to his dead father, and the Haitian kills his own brother Baron precisely because stopping him is his brotherly role.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 22 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Averill argues that Katniss's morality is built on care for particular people rather than impartial principle: she volunteers for Prim, protects Rue because the girl resembles her sister, and spares a wounded District 2 soldier at the Nut because he recalls her father and the Seam. Measured against Kant's impartial justice perspective (embodied by Thresh sparing Katniss to repay a debt to Rue), she falls short — but Gilligan's care perspective and Noddings's distinction between natural and ethical caring recast this as a valid, even heroic, moral development. Using Noddings, the chapter traces Katniss's arc from natural care for Prim toward ethical care for strangers and even enemies, and reads her assassination of Coin as care for all of Panem's future children rather than revenge. Care, the chapter concludes, can even justify violence when it protects the vulnerable.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 14 "5 Feminism and Indiana Jones A Field Guide" — Kate Schmidt applies feminist media tests (Bechdel, sexy lamp, Mako Mori, Pierce, Landau) to show the films usually fail — Willie is a screaming prop and human shield in Temple, the eyelid-writing student exists only to display Indy's sex appeal, and all four films fail the Bechdel Test — while Marion, Spalko, and above all Elsa in The Last Crusade are mixed cases with partial autonomy. Drawing on Iris Marion Young's account of women as Other and Carol Gilligan's care ethics, she argues Crusade is the series' most feminist film not for its women but for its men: Indy's open hurt after Elsa's betrayal and the father-son reconciliation embody care ethics against 'boys don't cry' toxic masculinity. She concludes that one can love flawed media without endorsing its sexism.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Kolb reads the whole franchise through Carol Gilligan's ethics of care and the ecofeminism of Ariel Salleh and Mary Mellor: Max begins as a caregiver in an egalitarian marriage, Toecutter's gang and the Citadel embody toxic masculinity, and Aunty Entity shows women can administer patriarchal capitalism too. In Fury Road, 'We are not things,' the milking mothers, and water branded as Aqua Cola literalize Salleh's claim that capitalist patriarchy treats women and nature as resources. The Vuvalini, the Keeper of the Seeds, Max washing in mother's milk, and his voluntary blood transfusion to Furiosa enact the ethic of care as the film's saving alternative to domination.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 24 "“To a Place Where We Know We Are Loved”" — Myers grades the moral development of the Sterling Cooper cast with Kohlberg's justice stages and Gilligan's ethics of care in order to find Aristotelian friendships, which require equals in moral development who wish each other good for the other's sake. Don and Peggy emerge as moral equivalents, each hiding a dark secret (the stolen identity; the baby given away) and each having done for the other what no one else could, from the hospital visit ('Move forward') to Don's 'nobody understands that, but you do' recruitment pitch; Joan and Roger form a second pair whose mutual esteem survives his marriage to Jane and her departure, shown when he trusts her to build Sterling Cooper Draper Pryce. Closing with Aristotle's claim that friendship holds states together, the chapter gives the new agency a better-than-average chance because these friendships are 'not for sale.'
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 26 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Frames the show's tension between the masculine public sphere (the chapel table, guns, club politics) and the feminine domestic sphere that actually sustains life, using Aristotle's oikos/polis division and Arendt's The Human Condition on the public/private realms. Gemma, dismissed as 'just an old lady,' proves the private sphere's power: she brought the club to Charming, orchestrates Jax's rise to the presidency, and converts her rape by Weston's LOAN goons into family solidarity that puts Jax's VP patch back on. Gilligan's and Baier's ethics of care then reads Lyla's abortion as a caring choice about family size, Tara's 'my job as your old lady is to be strong when and where you can't be' as care turned to strength, and Gemma's care curdling into retributive justice against Clay.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 26 "Notes" — Argues Star Trek functions like the Greek myths Nussbaum describes: modern tales of transformation (Gary Mitchell in "Where No Man Has Gone Before", Charlie X, Roger Korby) that let audiences judge what makes someone human. It rejects the Cartesian reading (Richard Hanley's Is Data Human?) in which Data's humanity is just a matter of being a rational mind, and develops instead a feminist, developmental account of personhood drawn from Annette Baier: persons are "second persons" who learn the arts of personhood from caretakers. Data, Seven of Nine, and Voyager's Doctor, all lacking real childhoods and families, must learn play, touch, love, and interdependence from their crews, with Janeway modeling family for Seven and Kes socializing the Doctor. Picard's farewell to Shinzon in Nemesis and to Data's B-4 caps the claim that humanity is an achievement of self-improvement in relationship, not a fixed essence.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 35 "“So, What Happens If You Take That Thing Off ”" — Ebner charts Din Djarin's moral development from a rights-based frame - hierarchy, Guild rules, 'I can bring you in warm, or I can bring you in cold' - to Carol Gilligan's ethics of care, a shift catalyzed by Kuiil's lessons ('You can trade', 'I have spoken') and completed by the Child. He re-reads Gilligan's pharmacy dilemma through 'The Sin', where Mando hijacks a speeder droid at gunpoint, and 'The Marshal', where trading with Cobb Vanth recasts the armor dispute as responsibility toward a threatened town rather than a contest of rights. Djarin's helmet decisions - refusing Omera, unmasking for Mayfeld's facial scan, and finally removing the helmet to say goodbye to Grogu - track his metamorphosis from rules and entitlements to responsibilities and relationships.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Young uses bell hooks's patriarchal masculinity (with Kate Manne on misogyny as enforcement) to read the show: Jamie is patriarchal terror's product, Rupert's promiscuity and Rebecca's subjection are two sides of male control, and Roy Kent's 'hard man' persona inherits the hardness Nietzsche praised and philosophy's traditional suspicion of emotion. Against this, hooks's definition of love as the will to nurture spiritual growth explains Ted's coaching, the training-room exorcism's shared vulnerability, Sam's openness, and Nate's status-hunger as the struggle to invert the gender pyramid, ending with Nate refusing Rupert's poisoned patriarchal gifts.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 13 "NOTES" — Chotiner tests Sarah Connor's plan to shoot Miles Dyson (one innocent life for three billion) against Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism and against Kant's deontology, showing both stall: utilitarianism licenses harvesting the author's organs for transplant patients, while Kant forbids using Dyson as a mere means and even condemns the mall kid's protective lie to the T-1000. Through Kohlberg's Heinz dilemma and Carol Gilligan's discovery that girls reason to preserve relationships rather than from abstract principles, he argues T2 stages the film's own answer: John and the reprogrammed T-101 care for Dyson's wounds and enlist him in destroying his research instead of using or sparing him on principle. 'I know now why you cry' caps the claim that morality needs the emotional capacity to care, not just rational maxims, with Sarah's gender-role reversal (she blasts through the elevator roof while the Terminator is the 'perfect mother') framing the whole argument.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 32 "Notes" — This multi-author epilogue collects short 'cutting-room-floor' reflections on poignant WoT quotes. Cooke reads Ingtar's confession as the existential fear of historical oblivion (historia as both history and story) driving a patriot into Darkfriendship. DeVan uses Covril's oak-and-wind metaphor to argue arguments strengthen through opposition, marshaling Confucius, Proverbs, al-Kindi, Milton, and Socrates's unexamined life. Held reads Min's arranged-marriage counsel with Nietzsche's amor fati and Epictetus's Heracles to reject resentment of unchosen fate. Pike reads Nynaeve sentencing the sul'dam through Carol Gilligan's and Annette Baier's ethics of care versus obligation (care can judge more harshly, per C.S. Lewis). Xhignesse reads the oak-and-willow line as Aesop woven into Randland's background.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Johnson-Moxley tests Perez's lasso of truth - which makes people face truths about themselves, like being dragged from Plato's cave - against four ethical touchstones: Kantian duty (truth-telling as a perfect duty, respect for autonomy), utilitarianism, virtue ethics, and care ethics. Cases drive the argument: binding Ares so he sees his apocalypse annihilates what he rules, freeing Vanessa from Dr. Psycho's false memories only with her permission, and lashing two warlords into 'twins of pain' to end bloodshed. She concludes via Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity that compelling truth is justified only to restore someone's rational self-direction, never paternalistically, with Gandhi's satyagraha ('truth-force') as the model of active, compassionate truth-telling.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 22 "Notes" — Bein argues Wonder Woman uniquely fuses two supposedly incompatible moralities: bushido - Nitobe's eight samurai virtues, Sun Tzu's benevolence of ending war swiftly, worthy-opponent rituals mirrored in superhero costumes - and the feminist ethics of care Gilligan and Noddings built against a Western canon (Aristotle, Kant) that called women too emotional for morality. Wonder Woman's killing of Maxwell Lord to free Superman is re-read as the care-ethical beach case: saving your own child over a stranger's is not a failure of impartiality, and in his Gotham-versus-Themyscira invasion thought experiment she would defend Gotham because its people are vulnerable non-combatants, not because a utilitarian ledger favors it.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 31 "Notes" — Chavez, Gavaler, and Goldberg trace Marston's 'Love Leader' kink - bracelets of submission, Venus girdles, Paradise Island bondage games, Earth One's collaring of Steve Trevor - to nineteenth-century maternalist feminism, then map the care ethics of Gilligan, Noddings, and Tronto onto both the comic and real-world BDSM. Reform (later Transformation) Island embodies a care-based alternative to punishment: rather than retribution, von Gunther and Irene are transformed by loving authority into people who save their captors, and Wonder Woman rescues the drowning villain Eviless because 'Aphrodite's Law commands us to save lives always - enemies or not.' The BDSM community's 4Cs (consent, communication, caring, caution) turn out to be Tronto's four elements of care, so the good dominant just is the good care-giver.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 14 "Fifth Hole How Golf Builds and Shapes Moral Character" — Beller and Stoll ask why empirical moral-reasoning research finds that sport generally does not build character, yet golfers score highest of all athletes. Using Aristotle's account of right conduct and Lickona's triad of moral knowing, feeling, and acting, they argue character forms through role models, social environment, and cognitive dissonance, supported by neuroplasticity research on the brain's capacity for moral growth. They contrast golf's self-policing tradition (Bobby Jones, Meg Mallon, Greg Norman, the film Bagger Vance) with the gamesmanship coached in team sports, and address Gilligan's 'different voice' by reporting that female golfers reason at least as highly as males, concluding that golf's honor-bound moral community sets it apart.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 23 "11. The Mother of All Bombs" — Kolb argues Laura Palmer embodies the 'Angel in the House' ideal (Gilbert and Gubar) whose perfection is a beautiful dead girl, and reads The Return's linkage of the Trinity bomb to BOB/Judy through Arendt's On Violence—violence begets a more violent, hostile world that especially victimizes women. Using Gilligan's In a Different Voice, she shows how women's voices (Naido/Diane, the Log Lady, Laura's diary) are silenced by toxic masculinity (Mr. C, Richard, Chad), while the 'good men' embody an ethic of care; the manufactured post-war social order names its bombs after mothers and treats women as perfect-yet-fallen others.
- **The Philosophy of Joss Whedon**, ch. 8 "Conclusion" — The concluding chapter argues that Joss Whedon 'does philosophy' on television, not merely illustrates it, by ranking degrees of filmic philosophizing (via Wartenberg, Shaw, Mulhall) and showing the Whedenverse meets them. It reads Angel/Angelus and Fred/Illyria as cinematic thought experiments that generate 'metaphysical complexity' about personal identity, playing memory- and continuity-of-consciousness theories (Locke, Parfit) against a soul theory, and reads Connor's origin as exemplifying Kane's libertarian free will. It contends Whedon endorses a Noddings-style ethics of care and an existentialist yet God-independent morality, epitomized by Angel's 'Epiphany' speech ('the smallest act of kindness is the greatest thing') and 'Deep Down,' plus the 'Man on the Street' Academic monologue, staging a negative project against the claim that ethics is incoherent without God through the self-sacrifices of Simon, Cordelia, and Buffy.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 17 "A Spielbergian Ethics of the Family in Saving Private Ryan and The Color Purple" — Clewis defines a 'Spielbergian ethics of the family,' a care-based virtue ethics holding that we owe unique obligations to family and close friends grounded in personal identity, and contrasts it with utilitarian and Kantian approaches. In Saving Private Ryan the squad-as-family and the Ryan brotherhood explain why Miller says Ryan must 'earn this' and why living an ordinary good life suffices; in The Color Purple sisterhood (Nettie/Celie), fatherhood, and motherhood ground obligations of care, forgiveness, and reconciliation. He evaluates the view's feasibility while warning it neglects wider social influences and the is/ought gap.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 19 "10 Listening with Neil’s Vulnerable Voice and the Ethics of Care" — Jostedt argues that Young's raw, high "dental" singing voice (contrasted with Dylan's nasal sneer) invites empathetic "listening-with" rather than the detached individualism of Kant's deontology or Mill's utilitarianism. Drawing on Gilligan's In a Different Voice, Jane Addams and the ethics of care's emphasis on relatedness, he shows how songs like "Ohio," "Stringman," "Cortez the Killer" and the album Trans (evoking his son's cerebral palsy) make listeners feel with the downtrodden and disabled.
- **Joss Whedon as Philosopher**, ch. 7 "Angel, Angelus, and Personal Identity" — This file gathers Part II, arguing Whedon actually philosophizes through film. It works through the film-as-philosophy debate (Mulhall's 'bold thesis' and its critics Baggini, Smith, Livingston, Russell, and Wartenberg), using 'Hush' as a Zen-like case that resists linguistic paraphrase and The Cabin in the Woods to pit Mill's utilitarianism against Noddings's ethics of care (Dana refusing to kill Marty to save the world). Its capstone treats the Angel/Angelus problem as a personal-identity thought experiment, staging the soul theory (Plato), body theory (Hobbes/Holtz), and Locke's and Parfit's memory/psychological-continuity theories, and arguing Whedon's eight-season Angel-Angelus and Fred-Illyria cases serve as a cinematic counterexample to Neo-Lockean continuity, ultimately endorsing a care-based view of what matters in identity.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 21 "A Better Way of Living Your Life" — Laura Geuy Akers argues the Doctor lives by a relational ethics of care rather than deontology, utilitarianism, or virtue ethics. Drawing on Noddings's care ethics and Buber's I-Thou versus I-It stance, she shows the Doctor responds to particular others (insisting the Ood is "a he, not an it," addressing each companion individually before surrender) and even ethically cares for the Master. She pairs this with Nussbaum's and Kant's accounts of wonder and the sublime, arguing the Doctor's human companions (Rose, Martha, Donna) restore his sense of wonder and give his immortal life meaning.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 22 "Toward Caring" — J.J. Sylvia argues the Doctor, though male, is an ideal exemplar of the feminist ethics of care developed by Carol Gilligan (against Kohlberg's justice-only scale) and Nel Noddings. Contrasting the caring "Doctor" with the dominating "Master," he uses Rita Manning's account of caring as responsiveness and obligation to argue that an ethics of care, unlike impartial utilitarianism, explains why the Doctor should save his companion over a stranger. Noddings's natural-versus-ethical caring explains the Doctor forgiving the Master and offering compassion to Dalek Caan, and companions supply reciprocal care that guards against burnout.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 35 "You’re Basically “a Stuffed Animal Made by Grandma”" — Renee Kyle contrasts Dr. House's detached 'doctor knows best' justice ethic with Dr. Cameron's feminist ethic of care drawn from Carol Gilligan's In a Different Voice. Cameron builds trusting relationships, sees patients as embedded in social networks, and refuses to deceive or bully (as with Ezra and the newborns in 'Maternity'), whereas House treats patients as abstract puzzle-pieces. Kyle also voices the feminist worry that valorizing care can lead women to care at personal cost, as when Cameron's own grief over her dead husband derails her professional judgment.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 17 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Nease lays out a game plan for raising ethical children, using Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics – eudaimonia as a flourishing life, virtue as the mean between extremes, and the master-skills of practical wisdom and self-control – as the core, mocking 'character counts' posters as no substitute for early habit-formation. He folds in Kant's motive of duty, Nietzsche's will-to-power (glossed via Janet Jackson's Control) as the drive to master oneself, and argues empathy (Theodor Lipps' inner imitation), self-awareness, concentration (Husserl's foreground/background), and a respect for justice must be cultivated to 'stack the deck' toward a good adult.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 18 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Terjesen defends a distinctively paternal form of caring against care ethics' maternal bias. Reviewing Kohlberg's moral-development scale, Gilligan's justice-vs-care orientations, and Noddings' 'engrossment' model of caring, he argues these frameworks make it seem fathers like his own undemonstrative Norwegian dad don't care. He reconceives 'paternalism' (via Gerald Dworkin's soft paternalism and examples like Darth Vader and Bambi's father) as tough-love caring focused on the child's future self, complementary to maternal caring and distinct from the impersonal justice orientation.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 25 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Mattern argues the heart of good fatherhood is mercy – 'faithful, compassionate love' – as an attitude of the heart, not a technique. Drawing on Aquinas's account of habitus and his ranking of mercy among the greatest virtues, plus Gabriel Marcel's 'creative fidelity,' Solovyov, Jean Vanier, and Karol Wojtyla on love as affirming another's value, he contrasts remote, justice-oriented fathers with empathic ones. He illustrates with overlapping Venn-diagram circles of father and child and with responding to his 7-year-old son's shoplifting through listening and repair rather than spanking.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 22 "MOTHERHOOD" — Chris Mulford, a nurse and lactation consultant, analyzes infant feeding as an ethical question of rights, duties, and responsibilities, drawing on a feminist ethic of care and the claim that women learn empathy through caregiving (linked to oxytocin's role in birth and nursing). She argues that the right at stake is the mother-child dyad's 'protection from interference' with breastfeeding, that no mother is saddled with a solitary duty to breastfeed, and that the duty toward breastfeeding falls on the whole community; she frames the mother's dependency on 'the kindness of strangers' via A Streetcar Named Desire and the innate 'breast crawl.'
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 23 "MOTHERHOOD" — Maureen Sander-Staudt uses a feminist ethic of care – especially Carol Gilligan's mole-and-porcupine fable of reciprocal accommodation – to argue that pressuring women to nurse privately or covered imposes 'lactational burkas.' She runs public breastfeeding through the Miller obscenity test to show it is not obscene, opening with Gloria Steinem's 'If men could menstruate' to imagine 'milkmen,' and cites the Emily Gillette Freedom-flight ejection, Facebook's photo removal, the Janet Jackson Superbowl scandal, and PETA's human-milk proposal to expose hypocritical, biologically reductive double standards about the female breast.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 35 "You’re Basically “a Stuffed Animal Made by Grandma”" — Kyle contrasts House's detached, impartial "ethic of justice" with Dr. Cameron's feminist ethic of care, drawn from Carol Gilligan's In a Different Voice. Cameron builds trusting relationships, refuses to deceive patients, and attends to their social networks — letting parents hold their dying baby in "Maternity," defending Ezra's autonomy in "Informed Consent." But Kyle also presses the standard critique that valorizing care can cost the carer: Cameron's own grief over her dead husband derails her professional judgment in "Acceptance" and pushes her toward Houselike tactics.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 16 "14. The Doctor as Philosopher The Collectivist-Realist Pacifism of the Doctor and the Quest for Social Justice" — Smithka argues the Doctor is a 'collectivist-realist pacifist': morally opposed to war yet willing, as a last resort, to use lethal force for social justice. She places the Doctor on Cady's warism-to-pacifism continuum (past absolute and collectivist pacifism), augmenting it with Martin Luther King Jr.'s realist pacifism — ethical appeals 'undergirded by constructive coercive power' — and Gandhi's ahimsa and belief that no one is beyond redemption (the Doctor sparing Davros, offering enemies a choice). She tests Kant's duty ethics and respect for persons (Rule 1: the Doctor lies), Ross's prima facie duties, Mill's utilitarianism ('The Fires of Pompeii,' 'The Beast Below'), Gilligan/Noddings care ethics, and Wolterstorff's 'life of needs,' and reads 'The Day of the Doctor' as a Rawlsian veil of ignorance brokering Zygon-human peace.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 27 "25. The Mandalorian as Philosophy “This Is the Way”" — The chapter argues that The Mandalorian defends virtue ethics with care as the primary virtue. It maps Mando's creed and 'Canons of Honor' (strength, honor, loyalty, death) onto Stoicism's discipline of desire and cardinal virtues, quoting Marcus Aurelius and Seneca, and reads his transformation after adopting Grogu as Aristotelian moral development toward eudaimonia and flourishing. Using Stocker's critique of impartialist ethics and Noddings's and Slote's ethics of care, Belluomini argues Mando's caring relation with Grogu, his engrossment and motivational displacement, and his removing his helmet at the end show that care ranks highest among the virtues and should guide our own 'Way.'
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 13 "4. The Good of the Doctor" — The chapter distinguishes aesthetic 'good' (taste, beauty of the Daleks) from ethical 'good,' then tests the Doctor against the major moral theories: utilitarianism (rejected when Sarah Jane urges exterminating the Daleks in 'Genesis of the Daleks'), Kantian duty ethics (the Doctor's 'never met anyone who wasn't important' and attempts to save Davros and the Master), virtue ethics (the Eleventh Doctor guarding Christmas in 'The Time of the Doctor'), and feminist care ethics. Concluding that none quite fits because the Doctor values non-rational beings and feels compassion, the author proposes the Doctor follows Wolterstorff's 'ethic of need'—justice as meeting the needs of all—consistent with 'getting in the thick of things' as a flâneur.

### The Trolley Problem

The trolley problem is a thought experiment in which a runaway trolley will kill five people unless it is diverted onto a side track where it will kill one, forcing a choice about whether it is permissible to act so that one dies instead of five. Introduced by Philippa Foot and later elaborated by Judith Jarvis Thomson, it is designed to test intuitions about the difference between killing and letting die, and between harm caused as a means and harm caused as a side effect. Its power comes from contrasting cases that seem numerically identical yet elicit opposite moral judgments, such as diverting the trolley versus pushing a large man off a bridge to stop it. The problem has become a standard tool for examining the doctrine of double effect and the limits of consequentialist reasoning.

- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 23 "So, What Have Philosophers Ever Done for Us" — Taylor defends philosophy's bizarre examples against critics like Leon Kass by comparing them to Python's self-reflexive comedy: the 'Complaints' sketch's regress of complaints-about-complaints mirrors how thought experiments make us the audience of our own thinking, as with two coalmine trolley cases that pressure a simple 'minimize pain' utilitarianism toward rule utilitarianism. The 'Police Station' sketch, where it would be better if mad Angus's carnivorous-blancmange story were false, is itself a counterexample to 'always tell the police the truth', and 'The Visitors' stale three-year-old drink invitation undermines the claim that 'inviting in' a fetus creates duties, sharpening Thomson's violinist argument that a right to life does not include a right to another's body. Singer's drowning-child style example and Thomson's violinist show that far-fetched cases clarify practical issues like abortion and famine relief precisely by detaching them from clouding emotion, and the Life of Brian 'What have the Romans ever done for us?' scene supplies the answer: philosophers' examples clarify our views, test them, and are amusing.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 25 "Introduction" — Frames Part V's ethics chapters. Adams' chapter updates Plato's ring of Gyges for Heroes — with Claire's and Sylar's powers, why be moral? — answered by the properly ordered tripartite soul; McAleer's uses The Office to illustrate Aristotle's wit as a mean between buffoonery and boorishness; White's uses the Batman/Joker problem and a Bat-trolley version of Foot's case to argue deontologically that Batman need not kill the Joker; and Loftis' reads Watchmen's Ozymandias and Rorschach as a failed utilitarian and a failed deontologist, pointing to 'who watches the watchmen.'
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 28 "So, Case Closed – Right" — White asks why Batman never simply kills the Joker despite the graveyard he keeps filling, framing the question with Foot's and Thomson's trolley problem and the transplant-surgeon variant. Utilitarianism says kill one to save many; deontology says the agent-relative 'do not kill' — but the Batman case differs from the classic dilemmas because the Joker himself endangers his victims, Batman cannot be certain he will kill again (the foggy-track variant), and killing him would amount to the Minority Report-style prepunishment of a crime not yet committed. White, a self-described strict deontologist, concedes the case is genuinely hard and leaves the means-versus-ends debate open.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 13 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Matthew Brophy argues the I.F. could only get a compassionate child to commit xenocide by presenting war as a game, a framing that neutralizes moral agency just as Milgram's shock experiments and the fake game show The Game of Death did. Using Sunzi's 'know your enemy' to frame the empathy paradox, Walzer's problem of dirty hands for Graff's lesser-evil choices, and Foot's trolley problem alongside drone 'Nintendo warfare' to show how distance makes killing easier, he concludes Ender was likely a willing pawn who let himself be deceived because he endorsed the war's survivalist goal.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 12 "2. How Can Torture Be This Funny" — Pavelich asks how a sitcom about torture can be funny, answering with incongruity theory and Bergson's view of comedy as social punishment, seen in Tahani paired with a silent monk and Michael failing 802 reboots. The centerpiece is 'The Trolley Problem': Michael drops Chidi into Foot's thought experiment so Chidi becomes the instrument of his own agony, and by Bernard Williams's principle the real wrongdoer is Michael, who set up the situation. Eternal torture works as comedy only because everyday crappiness is watched on a twenty-two-minute scale, and Eleanor's forgiveness of Michael after seeing the tortures in Janet's VR makes her the show's real moral hero.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 23 "11. Those Agonizing Choices" — Romanowski traces Chidi's indecision from the cowboy-boots lie through the rock-paper-scissors panic attack, arguing the show treats the agony of deciding as the universal human moral condition rather than a professor joke. 'The Trolley Problem' makes Foot's dilemma literal torture, and the show pointedly never gives the right answer, confirming Chidi's claim that there are no clean solutions to hard moral questions. Eleanor's Dancy-inspired particularism pitch in 'Rhonda, Diana, Jake, and Trent' and Michael's 'I solved the Trolley Problem: you sacrifice yourself' moment, together with Chidi finally kissing Eleanor, show that acknowledging uncertainty is no excuse for inaction.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 27 "14. Is Kant the Reason Everyone Hates Moral Philosophy Professors" — Duindam defends Kant against the charge that he makes moral philosophy professors insufferable, walking through maxims and the two-question Categorical Imperative test with frozen-yogurt and stealing examples, and arguing that Kant's notorious 'you cannot lie to the murderer' essay is an obscure legal point whose actual test permits lying to demons. On the trolley, the bridge, and Michael's forced organ-harvesting scenario, Kant's humanity formula, never treat persons merely as means, explains both Chidi's refusal to kill Eleanor and the difference between switching tracks and pushing a man. Tahani's sixty billion dollars in charity earning no points, and Eleanor's fruitless 'What's My Motivation' blitz versus her costly confession, vindicate Kant's claim that only a good will gives actions moral worth, while Aristotle supplies the closing lesson that being good takes practice, not just study.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 20 "10. Natasha, Gamora, and the Soul Stone" — T.J. McSherry frames the two Vormir deaths as 'a futuristic, utilitarian trolley problem,' using Mill's greatest-happiness principle to argue Natasha's martyrdom was the more utilitarian choice (only the Avengers mourn her, while Clint's children need a father), even as Thanos's tossing of Gamora shows the same sacrifice-of-few arithmetic the Avengers rely on. Because the amoral Soul Stone rewards good and evil deaths identically, the chapter turns to Plato's Symposium, casting Red Skull as a Diotiman spirit-mediator of love and ranking each relationship on Diotima's ladder: Thanos is 'stuck at level one' in his stunted love for Gamora, kept alive only as a useful sacrifice, while Clint and Natasha's non-romantic love reaches level four through shared history, empathy, and their fight over who gets to die for the other.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 32 "20. Thanos and the (Un)grateful Universe" — Argues that Infinity War only has the structure of a superhero movie when told from Thanos's perspective, and that he passes a three-part 'superhero test' — beneficent goal (saving the universe from overpopulation), self-sacrifice (killing Gamora, destroying the stones, 'I lost more than you can know'), and willingness to make the tough decisions — while the Avengers fail it, staying split after Civil War and acting from selfish motives (Ant-Man wants Hope back, Black Widow says 'we owe it to everyone who's not in this room'). It then applies utilitarianism — Titan's collapse, Gamora's planet turned 'paradise,' the whales in the Hudson, the Snap as a trolley-problem lever Thanos alone will pull — to conclude Thanos is the true hero of the saga and the Avengers the unintended villains.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 10 "Not Bad, for a [Wo]man" — Argues Ripley's crossed-heart promise to Newt shows partialist care rightly overriding impartial justice: Kant, Mill, and Rachels demand everyone count for one, but Gilligan's critique of Kohlberg and Noddings's carer-cared-for relation - completed in Newt's 'I knew you'd come' - explain why Ripley duct-tapes two guns together and descends into the hive. Her flexible, relational problem-solving (the lighter-sprinkler trick against the Facehuggers, learning the pulse rifle) beats Gorman's mission-first command, and the trolley-style arithmetic she rejects when the one on the tracks is her little girl is not a moral failing; even nuking the Queen's eggs raises Singer-style speciesism questions.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 10 "So, Case Closed-Right" — Mark D. White asks why Batman refuses to kill the Joker even after the Joker murdered Jason Todd, paralyzed Barbara Gordon, and killed Sarah Essen. Framing the refusal as deontological rather than utilitarian, he runs the case through Foot and Thomson's trolley problem and transplant case, arguing the classics disanalogize because the Joker himself creates the danger and because 'do not kill' is an agent-specific rule rather than an agent-neutral one. He extends the analysis to prepunishment via Philip K. Dick's Minority Report, and concedes that even a self-described strict deontologist can conclude Batman maybe should have killed the Joker years ago.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 13 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Matthew Brophy argues the I.F. neutralizes Ender's moral agency by masquerading xenocide as child's play: Rackham's paradox that total empathy with the buggers forbids killing them (Sunzi's 'know your enemy') is solved by deception, Walzer's problem of dirty hands is shifted from the child to the politicians, and Milgram-style game framing plus Foot's trolley-problem 'moral distance' show how killing grows easier at a console. Against the innocent-pawn reading, Brophy ends by suggesting Ender was a willing pawn who let himself be deceived in order to save humanity.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 12 "2. How Can Torture Be This Funny" — Asks how a sitcom about torture can be funny and answers with incongruity theory (circus music under Michael's dejection; a comedy set in Hell) plus Bergson's view of comedy as social correction that deflates those who deserve it — Tahani's name-dropping, Michael failing 802 reboots. It centers on 'The Trolley Problem': Michael teleporting Chidi's ethics lesson into real runaway trolleys ('not real, but the pain is') is both incongruous humor and genuine torture, and invoking Bernard Williams shows the real wrongdoer is Michael, who rigged the situation, not Chidi who must choose. Eternal torture, it concludes, only works as endless low-grade everyday crappiness, which is comic in twenty-two-minute doses — and Eleanor's twice-given forgiveness of Michael, after seeing the centuries of torture in Janet's VR device, is the show's real moral marvel.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 23 "11. Those Agonizing Choices" — Treats Chidi's indecision (rock-paper-scissors panic, the soul-mate dilemma, the boots lie) as the show's authentic portrait of how hard moral life is, not just a professor joke. Michael's live-action Trolley Problem — Foot's thought experiment made literal, with Henry's bloody boots flying at Chidi — is read as torture precisely because it weaponizes Chidi's defining trait, and the show pointedly never hands the audience a right answer. Eleanor's Dancy-inspired movies-vs-er argument ('Your boy Kant would say never break a promise') finally lets Chidi act, and Scanlon's What We Owe to Each Other frames his arc's resolution: we choose to be good because of our bonds with others, as when he kisses Eleanor in 'Somewhere Else' and Michael 'solves' the trolley by sacrificing himself.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 27 "14. Is Kant the Reason Everyone Hates Moral Philosophy Professors" — Defends Kant against the charge that he is why everyone hates moral philosophy professors: it explains the two-question Categorical Imperative test via frozen-yogurt maxims and Eleanor's selfish 'won't help unless it benefits me' principle, shows Kant never actually forbade lying to the murderer at the door (his crotchety 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' was an obscure legal point), and reads Chidi's trolley-track switch but refusal to harvest Eleanor's organs as the humanity formula — never treat a person merely as a means. Tahani's $60 billion in charity and Eleanor's failed point-chasing in 'What's My Motivation?' illustrate the good will: deeds lack moral worth unless done for the right reasons. Aristotle explains the residual puzzle — theory mastery does not make you skilled at ethical practice, any more than a nutritionist is a great cook.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 28 "So, Case Closed – Right" — White asks why Batman won't kill the Joker, framing it through utilitarianism (killing one to save the Joker's many future victims) versus deontology (killing is wrong regardless of consequences). Using Foot and Thomson's trolley and transplant cases, plus agent-neutral versus agent-relative rules, he notes key disanalogies: the Joker is not a moral innocent but the very cause of the danger, which pushes toward killing him. But because future killings are only probable, doing so would be 'prepunishment,' and White, a self-described deontologist, concludes it is genuinely hard to say Batman is right, though he admires the restraint.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 24 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Terjesen critiques the 'lack of empathy' explanation of serial killing by disentangling empathy into understanding, vicarious feeling, and connection, and showing each either is possessed by killers or leads to circular reasoning (citing Deigh's 'mature empathy' and autism as a counterexample). Real killers like Dahmer, Rader, and 'Angels of Death' such as Cullen and Harvey act from sexual desire, rage, or even excessive empathy, so empathy shapes how they kill (intimate vs. distancing methods, echoing Greene's trolley/footbridge study) rather than whether they kill. He favors Kennett's lack-of-impulse-control and poor risk-assessment account instead.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 28 "So, Case Closed – Right" — Mark White asks why Batman doesn't kill the Joker, using the question to contrast utilitarianism (kill one to save the Joker's future victims) with deontology (killing is wrong regardless of consequences), and Batman's own agent-centered refusal. He runs Foot and Thomson's trolley problem and the transplant surgeon case, then modifies them: the Joker is the guilty one who created the danger, his future victims are uncertain, and killing him would be 'prepunishment' for crimes not yet committed. White, a self-described deontologist, concludes the case is genuinely hard and admits great good might have come from killing the Joker, using comics as thought experiments about killing to prevent future killing.

### Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will)

Moral psychology studies the mental features that underlie moral life — character and its virtues and vices, moral motivation, and the failures of self-control that the tradition calls weakness of will, or akrasia. A central puzzle, posed since Socrates and Aristotle, is how a person can judge one course of action best yet knowingly do otherwise, revealing tensions among reason, desire, and habit. The field asks how traits are formed, how far character is stable across situations, and what role emotion plays in perceiving and doing what is right.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 10 "George and Virtue—Like Oil and Water" — Daniel Barwick runs George through Aristotle's function argument and finds him wanting: a paradigm of 'the many' who thinks happiness is fortune and momentary victories over others (free parking, perfect airport pickups) rather than activity of the soul in accordance with virtue. His 'do the opposite' epiphany in 'The Opposite' embraces the more extreme vice rather than steering toward the rationally chosen mean, and his self-hatred, laziness, and pleasure-seeking fail all three of Aristotle's tips for hitting the mean. Since George will never practice virtuous action until it becomes habit, Barwick concludes George is doomed to his miserable existence - which is, conveniently for us, why he is funny.
- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 19 "[Cue Bass]" — Jason Holt asks whether it is rational for George to 'do the opposite' and answers no. Distinguishing minimal, medial, and maximal rationality, he argues the Costanza Maneuver is neither reliable (its .800 batting average in 'The Opposite' is dumb luck - insulting Steinbrenner into a job and cowing movie thugs should not work) nor feasible: George's akrasia and impulse problems betray him, and the opposite of an action is usually indeterminate (Jerry: 'chicken salad is not the opposite of tuna... salmon swim against the current'). Since George knows all this, betting on the Maneuver is irrational - its success is precisely the joke, 'not as good, works better.'
- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 23 "Conclusion" — Robert Epperson defends the show against the 'no hugging, no learning' charge by arguing Seinfeld is about the pursuit of the moral life: the four constantly consult each other on right conduct (gift-giving, break-up timing, obligations to friends and parents), distinguishing the moral life from mere integrity. He grades each character - Kramer is Plato's man of right opinion without knowledge whose one maxim is 'listen to your little man,' George means rightly but is the man of wrong opinion, Elaine is undone by indecisiveness, Jerry is the moral axis whose flaw is vanity - and argues with Aristotle that it is precisely their imperfect characters that make their concern with acting rightly possible.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 19 "Making the Pain Go “Poof”" — James B. South argues Willow's Season Six turn — magic addiction, torturing Warren with a 'bored now,' attempting to end the world in 'Grave' — is tragic precisely because it is unintelligible: against Aristotle's account of tragedy, where pity requires seeing an intelligible mistake, Willow's destruction flows from Freudian depths (via Plato's 'lawless' desires and Jonathan Lear's 'enigmatic signifiers') that cannot be explained, only pointed to. The chapter traces the available evidence — her sidekick insecurity ('I'm not your sidekick!' in 'Fear, Itself'), her 'spurty knowledge' slip, making pain go 'poof' in 'Something Blue' — while insisting these unconscious swerves never add up to a reason for the final break. Xander's yellow-crayon memory in 'Grave' works not as explanation but as a second kind of break that opens space for Willow to regroup.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 42 "24b" — A paired philosophy-of-education debate on whether baseball players were better role models then or now. Edward Sullivan answers 'then' from lived memory: Ted Williams's Korean War service and his 1966 Hall of Fame induction speech demanding Satchel Paige and Josh Gibson be enshrined, and Jackie Robinson enduring Jim Crow spring training under Branch Rickey's pact of 'guts enough not to fight back.' Graham Harman answers 'now,' turning Socrates's Apology complaint that his most dangerous accusers are those safely dead into a diagnosis of nostalgia: the past buried Ty Cobb's and Cap Anson's racism, the Black Sox, and Hal Chase, while today's game is more racially open, physically dedicated, and union-protected.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 26 "Love and Self-Discovery" — Mary Nichols argues The Curse of the Jade Scorpion answers The Maltese Falcon: where Sam Spade's cynicism leaves society no reason to trust its lone hero, C.W. Briggs, unknowingly stealing for the magician Polgar while hypnotized, is saved by love, friendship, and the office community of North Coast Casualty. The jade scorpion's trance, meant to cover crime, uncovers truth, as C.W. and Betty Ann admit under hypnosis the love and fear their waking selves hide, so that 'crystal clear' memory and self-knowledge, rather than Spade's rejection of dreams, free them from both the curse and crime. Against the noir world and Lester's 'comedy is tragedy plus time', the chapter holds that everyone has 'a little bit of larceny' in them and that experiences of love, friendship, and community are what form the character that keeps it in check.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 20 "A Plausible View" — Reconstructs Slughorn's lesson to young Tom Riddle, that murder rips the soul and the torn piece can be hidden in a Horcrux, an act 'against nature', and argues that because Voldemort's intellect and magical powers remain intact while his capacity to charm gives way to rule by fear and his body becomes snake-like, Rowling's soul must be the sentimental one: our humanity, love, and moral conscience. On this view the soul is damaged by supreme evil and can be repaired only through remorse, which is exactly what Harry urges on Voldemort ('be a man... try for some remorse') before the final killing curse rebounds.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 41 "Snape’s Choice" — Defines love, with Aristotle, Aquinas, and M. Scott Peck, as willing the good of the other for the other's own sake, and reads Snape's double-agent life as love expressed in action despite real hatred: he protects Harry's enemies at constant risk while disliking most of them. His Occlumency, the skill to lie to Voldemort's face, reveals both strength and weakness, for rather than renouncing love as Voldemort did he only conceals it, and his dying gift of memories to Harry, revealing that Harry is a Horcrux, must be freely offered because his thoughts can never be taken.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 49 "NOTES" — Contends that Voldemort was not his mother's son: what defines a person is the habitual pattern of choices, as in Aristotle's 'we are what we consistently do', and Merope, who freed Riddle at the cost of her own life and renounced magic entirely, is a genuine though partial redemption, whereas Voldemort followed Marvolo Gaunt and Salazar Slytherin instead. Quoting William Hasker on how love potions trap both parties because love must be freely bestowed, the section argues character is destiny only if forged by free choice, and that Harry, protected by his mother's sacrificial love, shows what Voldemort's rejection of love and vulnerability destroyed.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 85 "Abilities" — Bassham tests each sense of choice against the novels: internal-choices are uninformative (Dudley resolving to give up sweets), act-choices mislead since character is settled habit - Hermione's occasional rule-breaking for Dumbledore's Army doesn't make her a rebel - and overt acts cannot reveal motives, as Snape's apparent Death Eater loyalty conceals devotion to Dumbledore and Lily. Motive-choices like Harry's decision to enter the Chamber to save Ginny are most revealing, but self-deception (Vernon Dursley's rationalizations) and wizarding complications - Harry's vision of attacking Arthur Weasley, Voldemort's implanted false memory in Morfin Gaunt, the Imperius Curse, Polyjuice Potion, and a Priori Incantatem thought experiment - show that in Rowling's world choices may be unknowable even to their maker.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 87 "Beyond Choices Toward a Deeper Self-Understanding" — Bassham concedes that most abilities reveal little: trivial, widely shared, involuntary, innate, or unrecognized capacities (Harry's Parseltongue before Sorcerer's Stone) say nothing about character, and even impressive gifts are morally neutral - the resourcefulness, determination, and disregard for rules Dumbledore lists are shared by Harry and Voldemort and differ only in how they are used. But abilities won through hard work and ethical capacities like empathy, prudence, and resilience do disclose character, so Dumbledore is right that choices are generally more revealing, provided we are also honest about what our abilities say about us.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 90 "Unknown" — This section catalogues the novels' full range of irrational thinking - Percy Weasley's rule fetish, Malfoy's racism and classism, Ron's jealousy, Fudge's closed-mindedness, Luna Lovegood's credulity - before concentrating on wizards' ethical blindness toward house-elf slavery. Because elves like Winky have been conditioned to regard freedom as shameful, most wizards see nothing wrong; Hermione insists that internalized oppression doesn't justify servitude, and Harry's moral growth is marked by digging Dobby's grave with his own hands and writing 'Here lies Dobby, a Free Elf.'
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 132 "The Inversion of Voldemort" — Distinguishes remorse from mere regret through Voldemort's cold 'I regret it' after ordering Nagini to kill Snape: remorse requires owning one's act, and at the final duel Harry addresses him as 'Tom Riddle' and demands he 'try for some remorse' - the death-to-self Riddle cannot perform. Dumbledore's remorse over the cursed Resurrection Stone ring and his arranged death, and Harry's voluntary death that destroys the Horcrux within him and restores his whole soul, exemplify dying to the past self for renewal, while Harry's renunciation of his temper toward Ron and Hermione and his love for Ginny mark his continuous moral regeneration.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 133 "The Integrity Objection" — Draws Voldemort's inversion in full: each Horcrux rips and destabilizes his soul (Hermione notes only excruciating remorse could reunite it, a pain that could destroy him), his attempt on baby Harry leaves him disembodied vapor parasitic on others' blood and limbs, in stark contrast to the feasting, affection, and romance of Harry's circle. The Godric's Hollow inscription 'the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death' and Hermione's claim that the soul survives whatever happens to the body ground the contrast between Voldemort's unmourned, mundane death and the honored, grieved dead - Dobby, Fred, Lupin, Tonks, Colin Creevey.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 142 "NOTES" — Argues via William James's 'sow a thought... reap a destiny' and Aristotle's account of how repeated action incrementally shapes the soul that Voldemort's flayed remnant is a character fully forged by choices, stuck with itself forever - a postmortem fate Heidegger's atheism cannot frame but Rowling's afterlife can. The section weighs Locke's memory-and-character account of identity, Kant's postulate that harmony of virtue and happiness requires an afterlife, and Pascal on why the immortality question must govern how we live, and ends asking whether Voldemort's evil is ignorance, as Plato held, or a cultivated appetite that only vice can satisfy.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 17 "Fear and the Superhero Stories" — The authors argue superhero stories speak to our fears twice: first by dramatizing external dangers (mad scientists, terrorists, alien menaces), and second by confronting the subtler fear of what using violence will do to our own souls, since habit and a 'rising threshold' of expectations can make once-unthinkable force come to seem necessary. Superheroes like Batman, Spider-Man, Daredevil, and Superman model the answer: they exercise force within strict limits and draw lines they will not cross, fighting evil without becoming evil, and so show that courage, determination, and character can prevail against adversity.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 40 "From Olympus to Galactus" — Taliaferro and Lindahl-Urben open with the Greek lesson of Icarus, destroyed by his intoxicated pursuit of glory, and map it onto the Marvel Universe, where a scientific accident made the Fantastic Four 'use their power to help mankind' while their great foes embody a maniacal pursuit of more. The section sets up the two contrasts to come: Dr. Doom, Reed Richards' megalomaniacal classmate, and Galactus, the planet-devourer 'almost beyond good and evil', with the Silver Surfer as his scout.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 46 "The Perfect Storm" — Storm's journey from being worshipped as a weather goddess in Kenya to joining Xavier's school fits Campbell's heroic cycle, and her bond with the demonic-looking, rosary-carrying Nightcrawler shows strangeness as a bridge to growth - the duality transcended into singularity when she tells him 'I have faith in you'. Housel then grades Storm at Kohlberg's post-conventional level of justice ethics, yet shows her shifting into Gilligan's care ethics when she dashes off to save eight mutant children from a government lab, mastering both 'masculine' justice and 'feminine' care - hence the 'perfect hero'.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 47 "The Shape-Shifting Mystique" — Mystique, Nightcrawler's abandoned mother, embodies unstable duality - female and male, serpent symbolism, a name rooted in the mystery priesthood - but Housel argues she can never complete the hero cycle because she is a sociopath who abandons her newborn, comas Xavier, impersonates a senator, and joins terrorist attacks. She perverts Kohlberg's rule-governed justice into wicked principles - 'her deeds are rule-governed, but the rules are clearly her own' - and her blanket hatred of humanity ironically betrays the fear and insecurity of a repressed humanity beneath: Storm's perfect anti-hero.
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 11 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Auxier, an Atkins dieter, argues the diet works for the reason Dewey gives in Human Nature and Conduct: habits built in calm moments are the bulwark against desire in crisis, and Atkins succeeds by reshaping which gratifications are habitually available — 'a steak for the black eye of desire.' He then transfers Atkins's physiology to thinking: television and advertising serve 'conceptual carbs,' packaged bundles of doubt, emotion, and readiness to act that bypass inquiry and leave the public 'intellectually diabetic' and ideological. Peirce's pragmatic maxim is translated into an eight-step mental exercise (worked through a parent's tattoo-or-piercing doubt about a teenage daughter), while Descartes's hyperbolic doubt is discarded in favor of pragmatism's 'genuine doubt.'
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 21 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Bill Davis argues that Narnia works as a classical moral-education environment: against Experiment House's science-worship, Narnia supplies the three ingredients Aristotle and Aquinas require, namely instruction, virtuous exemplars to imitate (Reepicheep's courage, Puddleglum's temperance), and habituation through repeated right action, which together transform Peter's indecision, Edmund's treachery, Lucy's envy, and Jill's timidity. What finally lasts beyond Narnia, he contends, is a transforming encounter with Aslan: Eustace's dragon skin torn off by the Lion, Jill's drink at the stream where 'there is no other stream,' and Digory's tearful confession. He closes by arguing today's self-esteem-based character education cannot replicate this, since it pursues virtue from love of self rather than love of the good.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 12 "The Mystery Solved" — Avery Kolers uses "Only a Pawn in Their Game" and its companion "Who Killed Davey Moore?" to argue that Dylan treats Byron de la Beckwith as a pawn: a poor white duped by divide-and-rule tactics, the psychological wage of whiteness, shame, and lynch-mob indoctrination into fearing a Hobbesian war of all against all. Against Aristotle's account of acting in ignorance, the chapter asks whether Beckwith's ignorance of his real enemies was culpable, concluding his bad moral luck (in Bernard Williams's sense) was manufactured by white supremacy and so reflects back on all white people. Dylan's refusal to name or voice Beckwith adopts Strawson-style objective attitudes, making blaming itself a political act aimed at the system rather than the shooter.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 18 "Poker and Philosophy" — Bassham and Marchese catalogue seven critical-thinking traps that cost even good players money: self-serving bias (Rochester Ricky donating $10,000 to Brunson's Texas road gamblers), short-term thinking (aimed at Aristippus' live-for-today hedonism), the availability heuristic (Brunson's red eights on a four-flush board), the fundamental attribution error (crediting wins to skill and losses to luck), loss aversion (which breeds tight-passive 'rocks'), superstitious thinking (Alexander ripping the pockets off his shirt for luck), and the gambler's fallacy (Ken Warren's bogus 'rush' theory of streaky cards). The moral is psychological self-knowledge: great players must know their own cognitive frailties, because — as Clint Eastwood says — a man's got to know his limitations.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 26 "U2 and Philosophy" — Werther answers Tollefsen with Aristotle's Politics: musical images of character effect real 'change[s] of soul', so a three-premise argument concludes that repeated exposure to U2's images of fine character and good action can habituate delight in virtue - King's courage in 'Pride (In the Name of Love)' (whatever the botched time of day, and as proved when Adam Clayton stepped between Bono and an FBI-confirmed death threat), the indignation and shame at global poverty in 'Crumbs from Your Table', and the compassion of 'Miracle Drug' for the locked-in writer Christopher Nolan. 'Exit' purges the band's demons and 'Until the End of the World' offers purification through holy fear, matching the medical and religious readings of Aristotelian catharsis. C.S. Lewis's Abolition of Man closes the case: without the aid of trained emotions the intellect is powerless, so a culture raised on U2's feelings may be better prepared to act well than one raised on syllogisms alone.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 18 "Universal Rights Vampires, Space Aliens, Robots, and Humans" — John Draeger asks which Undead can be held accountable for bloodthirsty behavior: Romero's zombies are amoral, like a poisonous plant or Cleckley's empathy-free psychopath Milt, while Dracula meticulously plans his move to London and so passes the cognitive test. Stoker's narcissistic Count stays amoral, but Coppola's Dracula (who warns Mina of her curse), Rice's guilt-torn Louis, and the self-deceiving, cruelty-enjoying Lestat show empathy, self-control, and moral reflection, making them immoral and responsible - which entitles vampires to due process rather than Van Helsing's vigilantism, to punishment aimed at rehabilitation, and to equal rights including civic participation and marriage, since the same standard would govern space aliens, robots, and humans.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 13 "James Bond and Philosophy" — South reads the famous opening of Thunderball - life as 'a heap of six to four against' - as Fleming's challenge to Western philosophy's promise of a harmonious fit between reason, personal good, and social good. Bond's shame at his hangover and bad bridge (analyzed through Bernard Williams's account of shame as grounding identity) drives him to the Shrublands spa and a new healthy, patient self, but SPECTRE's atomic blackmail and an assassination attempt push him back to scrambled eggs, bacon, and bourbon: 'life's too short.' With Adorno's bleak view that modern societies are implicated in evil (SPECTRE's bureaucratically worded ransom memo, gas chambers built by the same ingenuity as medicine) and Williams's thick ethical concepts, South argues Fleming's Bond shows there is no universal pattern making life meaningful; the spy's work lies outside conventional morality, and the odds of a happy, philosophically vindicated life are six to four against.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 41 "Chapter 6 - Performing Bullshit and the Post-Sincere Condition" — Concluding an essay on personality disorders, this chapter argues that pathological personalities (the antisocial, borderline, dependent, paranoiac) are especially good bullshitters and that their bullshit and distorted perceptions are what wreck their social relationships, since good relationships thrive on truth as much as on truthfulness. Against Frankfurt's claim that bullshit is the greater enemy of truth because indulging it erodes attention to reality, the author counters that the bullshitter does track truth at some level; bullshit's distinctive danger is that, unlike lying, it can be unconscious, so the sting of conscience never checks the habit.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 13 "An Amoral Universe" — James Spence rejects the DVD's profile of the Dogs as amoral psychopaths, arguing instead that Reservoir Dogs is filled with morality of just the kind Hume describes: natural sympathies plus artificial virtues constructed to manage conflicts among self-interested people. The tipping debate shows Mr. Pink reasoning with desert and fairness; Mr. Blonde's excuse that the clerks 'touched the alarm', White's 'Just cops' dehumanization, and the professional code restricting violence all display exactly the moral identity-management human psychology predicts. The film thus indirectly supports a third view on which morality grows from human nature and social interaction—criminals cannot actually think outside it.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 20 "Le temps de me laver les mains, or Bathroom Loyalties" — Randall Auxier reads Pulp Fiction's scrambled sequence through Bergson's distinction between clock time and lived, experienced time and through Aristotle's Poetics: Tarantino toys with the three unities to make viewers attend to every character, and only when the film is re-sequenced does it become 'Vinnie's Very Bad Day'. Vincent's fatal flaw is Aristotle's incontinence—weakness of will—signaled by the running bathroom gag and his unwashed hands, while Jules and Butch pass the same moral test of loyalty, whether delivering the briefcase or saving Marsellus from Zed. The moral: be loyal, don't be weak-willed, and wash your hands thoroughly, since in Tarantino nothing lacks perceptible difference.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 18 "And Beware of the Beast in Me" — Barnes takes Cash's infidelity despite the pledged fidelity of "I Walk the Line" and refuses the easy diagnoses of hypocrisy or lying: "Guess Things Happen that Way" voices a good will overcome by weakness, a frail human nature anyone shares. He supports this with the situationist experiments, the dime in the pay-phone slot, the Princeton seminarians in a hurry, Milgram's obedient schoolteachers, and the Stanford prison simulation that turned a pacifist student into an abusive guard, showing situation outweighs character. From Cash's songs he draws two moral lessons: charity toward wrongdoers, since the man in "I Never Picked Cotton" or the drunkard of "Kneeling Drunkard's Plea" might be us under the same circumstances, and prudence about compromising situations, as when Billy Joe's fatal pride in "Don't Take Your Guns to Town" proves his mother right.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 19 "The Doors Are Never Locked" — Held reads Cash's Walk the Line retort "Well, they're not Christians then" as a thesis about redemption: since, with Augustine, we rejoice most at the sinner saved, and since the Sermon on the Mount forbids judging what we cannot know (anyone's deep character), humility demands withholding condemnation and hoping even the worst can change. He contrasts Christian redemption, a revaluation of the person that needs outside grace (Cash needed June and the Carters; nobody is self-made), with Nietzsche's attack on redemption as slave-morality self-hatred, granting that Nietzsche's eternal recurrence also revalues the past but objecting that self-revaluation collapses into rationalization, as Cash's Saul in Man in White shows. Forgiveness proper requires repentance and a solvent character, like paying off a debt; the shame of the "Long Black Veil" woman shows why; and because we see "through a glass darkly," nobody, not the Reno murderer, not Joe Bean, is beyond hope, which is why the doors are never locked and why execution or life without parole claims a judgment of moral worth that is not ours to make.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 23 "History Will Judge" — Livingston reads the Razor movie through George Lakoff's Strict Father and Nurturant Parent models: Cain's Pegasus assumes a dangerous world and enforces obedience (shooting Belzen for refusing orders, the torture of Gina), while Adama's Galactica assumes empathy and open questioning (asking Boomer 'Why do you hate us so much?', sparing Starbuck). Kendra Shaw is the 'child' conditioned by desensitization and objectifying language into a killing razor and a PTSD victim, whose recovery under Apollo shows the two family models being blended — boldness with communication. Adama's verdict that 'history will have to make its judgments' frames the chapter's claim that understanding Cain requires seeing the family culture that produced her.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 16 "This Is Really Happening (So Do Something)" — Milsky argues that Radiohead practice what environmental virtue ethics preaches, organizing the chapter around Aristotle's akrasia (Nicomachean Ethics VII): Sting, who champions rainforests while advertising Jaguar and topping the 'dirtiest band' carbon table, acts against his own better judgment, whereas Radiohead — confronted with an audit showing their 2003 and 2006 tours emitted roughly 11,368 tons of CO2, mostly from fans driving — changed their actual practice (venues near public transit, car-pool lots, sea freight instead of air, LED lighting and auxilary power units). He reads the King Canute imagery of The Eraser and lines from 'The Clock' and 'And It Rained All Night' as environmental narrative in the tradition of Thoreau's Walden and Leopold's Sand County Almanac, obligating listeners to act or risk akrasia themselves, and presents the band's Friends of the Earth 'Big Ask' commitment as linking environmental virtue to human flourishing. 'Idioteque'''s 'this is really happening' becomes the wake-up call to the akratic fan driving to Lollapalooza with a bottled water.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 18 "Transformers and Philosophy" — A fictional five-session counseling narrative in which a burned-out Optimus Prime - running out of gas, embarrassed by 'WASH ME' written in his own dirt - secretly sees therapist Dr. Sara Sawyer. Through the empty-chair technique he speaks to the dead Jazz, admitting the survivor guilt of a leader who was fighting Megatron when Jazz fell, and confesses the night he nearly smashed a human teenager's car mistaken for a Decepticon; the Miracle Question helps him imagine peace. The dialogue dramatizes an internal transformation: the machine learns to name grief, anger, and sadness, admit mistakes to his team, and take R and R - in the authors' phrase, becoming more human.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 10 "15" — Three 'Phase Four' essays. Moseley reads the Joker across Batman #1, The Killing Joke, The Dark Knight, A Death in the Family, and Dark Knight Returns as a 'moral monster' who knowingly does evil - and, following Anscombe and Scanlon's guise-of-the-good analysis, pursues aesthetic 'higher values' in a Camus-like affirmation of the absurd, embracing the irrationality Batman's rational moral order cannot fathom. Levin uses X-gene biology (Beast's explanation in Astonishing X-Men, genotype vs phenotype, M-Day) to strip Magneto's Homo sapiens superior claim of any genetic or phenotypic basis, then argues via the moral community of rational persons (Kant's criterion) that mutants and humans share one moral community, condemning both the Registration Act and mutant separatism. O'Neil's prose piece traces Harvey Dent from Calvinist certainty through the acid that scars him to cosmic doubt - quantum randomness, many worlds, Sartre's condemnation to freedom - until Nietzsche's amor fati lets him embrace duality and let the scarred two-headed coin decide good and evil.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 12 "You Don’t Have to Be Like Him to Like Him" — Levitt reads Monk through Aristotle's virtue ethics: a man of character whose police virtues survive Trudy's murder but whose phobias produce akrasia — in the pilot he knows he must descend the germ-filled sewer to save Sharona and freezes anyway, doing the right thing only at agonizing cost. Virtue as habit and the golden mean (friendliness as the mean between obsequiousness and standoffishness) frame his slow progress toward acting rightly without thinking, which is also why Stottlemeyer cannot recommend his reinstatement — he doubts the illness, not the man. Aristotle's three friendships sort Monk's relationships: utility (the department, employer Sharona), pleasure, and virtue — Natalie, who after watching Monk save Julie's fish over the priceless moon rock saw her late husband's goodness in him. Ethos, pathos, logos and catharsis then explain viewer identification: watching Monk move from akrasia toward balance (Dr. Kroger's 'N. Hope' note that turns out to mean New Hope) lets audiences identify with, and be ennobled by, a character we would never want to be.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 21 "The Emotion-Reason Dilemma, Part II" — Pribram places Monk and Dr. House in the tradition of the brilliantly rational but emotionally plagued detective (Dragnet's emotionless Joe Friday vs Cracker's Fitz), arguing both shows treat excessive emotion as the price of genius: Monk's OCD is tied to his pattern-spotting ('You're a freak of nature'), and when medication cures the OCD in 'Mr. Monk Takes His Medicine' his detective genius vanishes. She applies Foucault's Birth of the Clinic to House's subtracting of the patient, but shows both series critique that modernist rationality through Eve in 'One Day, One Room', who forces House to face the rationally inexplicable. Using feminist scholarship (Jaggar, Alberti, Battersby), she argues the opposition of male reason to female emotion is a historically specific construction, and offers the best friends Stottlemeyer and Wilson as integrated alternatives who pay for their balance with ordinariness: polarization equals greatness, integration signals the mundane.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 18 "Universal Rights Vampires, Space Aliens, Robots, and Humans" — John Draeger argues Romero's catatonic zombies, like plants, lack the cognition and empathy to be blamed, while vampires split: Stoker's narcissistic Dracula resembles Cleckley's amoral psychopath Milt, but Coppola's remorseful Dracula, Anne Rice's guilt-tormented Louis, and the self-deceiving Lestat ('the trick is not to think about it') all grasp consequences, feel others' pain, and can exercise self-control, so they are immoral rather than amoral and accountable for their killings. Accountability brings rights: Van Helsing's summary staking is vigilantism that denies Dracula a fair trial, rehabilitable vampires like Louis might earn civic participation, and a nonviolent, honest vampire suitor cannot be rejected merely for being Undead. The principle generalizes to aliens and robots: whatever can reflect morally must be held responsible and treated with equal dignity.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 20 "Forwards Win Matches but Defences Win Trophies" — Wall asks when the professional foul—the defender who 'had to bring him down'—could be a genuinely moral act, testing it against Kantian universalizability and the good will and against Bentham-and-Mill utilitarianism, and settling on psychologically altruistic motivation as what could override the foul's default wrongness. Against the psychological egoists (La Rochefoucauld, Slote, Hobbes) who would dissolve even Di Canio's caught ball into self-interest, he deploys Nagel's argument from The Possibility of Altruism and the soldier-on-the-grenade case, then derives tight conditions: a deliberate, minimally harmful foul, in a game it can decide, in a semifinal whose red card the fouler will certainly miss. Ballack's 2002 tactical foul on Lee Chun-Soo comes closest but fails (he stayed on the pitch), as do Schumacher's assault on Battiston, Fletcher's pointless foul at 4–0 up, and Abidal's accidental clip—so genuinely moral professional fouls are rare, but defenders get the most shots at being the team's saints.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 11 "You Can’t Help What Happened to You. But You Can Make the Best of It" — Daniel Haas asks whether we can blame Dexter at all if his Dark Passenger is a compulsion formed by the shipping-container trauma he did not choose, and whether consistency then forces us to excuse the Trinity Killer and Ice Truck Killer too. Distinguishing attributive responsibility from accountability, he argues psychopaths cannot be motivated by moral reasons because they lack the moral emotions, and that it was sheer luck whether a traumatized boy landed in Harry's loving home and Code (Dexter) or a mental institution (Brian).
