- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 20 "Back to the Rough Ground!" — Finnegan uses Wittgenstein's language games, the 'picture' that holds us captive, and 'back to the rough ground' to argue that Ford, Sizemore, and the Man in Black are paralyzed by an idealized, patriarchal picture of narrative (winners and losers, violence, transcendent self-discovery), while Dolores and Maeve gain traction by inventing new language games within their forms of life. Dolores breaks her damsel script in Pariah ('I imagined a story where I didn't have to be the damsel') and reworks scripted love-dialogue to describe her grief, while Maeve bullies the lab techs, takes administrative control, and narrates other hosts' actions - 'Time to write my own fucking story.' The chapter reads their objectified position (via Mulvey's male gaze, which leaves female viewers identifying with the robot hosts rather than the male subject) as exactly what equips them for guerrilla warfare in the master's language games, doing what Audre Lorde thought impossible: dismantling the master's house with the master's tools.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 25 "In Closing, The Naked Truth" — Meyer sorts Westworld's abundant nudity into three aesthetic registers. First, Kenneth Clark's nude: Dolores's opening chair pose and the perfected, fabricated host bodies are idealized, created art-forms serving the creators' control. Second, John Berger's analysis of the nude as spectacle of male dominance: the Man in Black watching Armistice bathe (a Susannah-and-the-Elders voyeurism), the gold-painted women at El Lazo's orgy as 'nudity as a form of dress' for male desire, and techs' 'fuck puppet' treatment of Maeve, which she reverses by re-appropriating the language of fucking. Third, Leo Steinberg's incarnation symbolism: host nudity signals machines becoming human - shameless like prelapsarian Adam and Eve, mortal and sexed, 'ensouled' - so that Maeve overriding her programming to reclaim her daughter is the birth of the human-host, the mirror-image of God becoming man.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 17 "7. She Went Down Swingin’" — Volpert argues Tom Petty was a feminist, the only classic-rock male whose catalog consistently grants women rational equality and agency, adopting Susan McClary's feminist New Musicology as her lens and marching through Greatest Hits song by song. She reads the forced removal of the Lolita cover from "American Girl," the consensual, threat-free request of "Breakdown," and "Listen to Her Heart" as Petty's reply to Ike Turner's cocaine-locked party, and defends "You Got Lucky" as a conceit about band technology rather than misogyny. The chapter confronts the gaze directly, arguing "Here Comes My Girl" watches a woman walking toward you as formidable rather than objectified, with the video's flirtations redirected homoerotically at the Heartbreakers themselves.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 36 "23. The Future Is Female … Robots!" — Emily Cox-Palmer-White applies Deleuze and Guattari's 'becoming-woman' to the mechanical women of both films: the girl as universal other, a vacuum or absence at the center of femininity, is exactly what lets Rachael, Pris, Luv, and Joi destabilize the patriarchal world that manufactured them. Wallace's drones undressing the barren replicant with their gaze before he slashes her womb gives the male gaze a literal, lethal form, while the Joi-Mariette sync scene stages the frightening interchangeability of women under that gaze. Deckard's 'Her eyes were green' — a lie, since Rachael's eyes were brown — refuses the premise that women are replaceable products.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 43 "With or Without Starbuck" — Kirkland argues BSG imagines gender-free institutions (unisex heads and quarters, Starbuck never having to justify fighting) while installing a default masculinity under Adama, so that feminine-coded women die: Ellen the femme fatale is poisoned, pilots Kat and Kendra earn redemption only through death, and Cain's female command is written as militarist nightmare aligned with Gina's sexual abuse. Starbuck confounds the sexualizing male gaze and reverses rescue narratives, and 'The Farm' plus her captivity with Leoben on New Caprica literalize feminist critiques of patriarchal medicine and compulsory heterosexuality. Yet she is masculinized, pathologized via her abusive mother, brought to submit to Leoben as spiritual guide, and killed in 'Maelstrom' - containing the transgressive heroine within the show's patriarchy.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 10 "A Hope for the Future" — Reads The Little Mermaid as a step forward from the man-requiring damsels of Snow White and Sleeping Beauty: Ariel reverses the rescue by saving Eric, and Aristotle's 'all men by nature desire to know' is stretched to cover her curiosity about the human world. But Ursula's bargain trading Ariel's voice for legs dramatizes the long history of silenced women (Eve, Pandora, Cassandra, the scold's bridle), and the film's sexy, silent Ariel is exactly what Mulvey's male gaze, built on Sartre's 'the look,' criticizes. Applying Beauvoir's 'one is not born but becomes a woman,' the chapter argues Ariel shows biology is not destiny yet still regresses into needing a man, concluding she is a flawed but real advance toward better heroines.
- **The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire**, ch. 22 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" — Applying Laura Mulvey's visual pleasure to the printed page, the chapter argues that Larsson's protest against woman-hating is compromised by styling Salander—four-eleven, ninety pounds, 'childlike breasts'—as a sexual spectacle whose rapes (Bjurman's coerced oral sex, the anal rape, the trial's play-by-play of implements) are the trilogy's most explicit scenes while consensual sex stays off-screen, making the books 'torture porn' for the voyeuristic reader. The films shift the gaze further: the revenge on Bjurman runs longer than the rapes, Salander actively watches Martin Vanger burn, and her bisexuality with Mimmi Wu is reduced to one silent morning, changes that make the violence against men more acceptable than against women. The chapter ends ambivalent: Laurie Penny and Gail Dines charge that 'Misogynist violence is appalling; now here's some more,' yet the distributor's RAINN partnership and a rape survivor's testimony that Salander was the first active, aggressive survivor she had ever seen show the books also work as Larsson intended.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 20 "Back to the Rough Ground!" — Finnegan applies Wittgenstein's language games and 'back to the rough ground' to argue that Ford, Sizemore, and the Man in Black are captivated by an 'ideal' transcendent narrative, while marginalized hosts Dolores and Maeve gain traction precisely from their lostness. Dolores refuses the damsel role by grabbing a gun in Pariah ('I imagined a story where I didn't have to be the damsel') and Maeve seizes admin privileges to 'write my own fucking story,' each inventing new language games. Drawing on Mulvey's male gaze, Finnegan casts their objectified position as closer to women's experience, and reads them as using the master's tools to dismantle the master's house.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 25 "In Closing, The Naked Truth" — Meyer argues the hosts' nudity is rarely gratuitous, sorting it into three categories using theorists of the nude in art. Drawing on Kenneth Clark's naked/nude distinction, the posed, idealized, 'made' Dolores in 'The Original' is the nude as artform; using John Berger's Ways of Seeing, the brothel and El Lazo orgy scenes and the bathing Armistice are the nude as male sexual dominance and objectification. Finally, invoking Leo Steinberg's account of Christ's nudity as incarnation, Meyer reads the naked awakening of Maeve, Hector, and Armistice as signaling machines 'becoming human,' concluding humans' duplicity, not nakedness, is the true shame.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 26 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Weaving argues from a liberal-feminist standpoint that the FIVB's mandatory bikini-bottom rule for women's Olympic beach volleyball sexualizes and objectifies the athletes, contradicting Coubertin's ideals of universal humanity. Using Paul Davis's distinction between acceptable sexuality and objectionable sexualization (deliberate focus on body parts, freezing postures, punning captions like 'Buns of Gold'), and citing Nussbaum, Baker and Bartky on when treating someone as a sexual object becomes wrong, she shows the rule detaches athletes' bodies from their athletic agency. She traces harms including physical risk, the APA-documented effects of sexualization, a 'trickle-down' to school volleyball short-shorts, and exclusion of Islamic women.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 20 "The “Kournikova Phenomenon”" — The chapter asks why Anna Kournikova was celebrated as a beauty despite a mediocre record while the far more successful Williams sisters were praised for athleticism, not looks. It uses Plato's Symposium (the ascent from a beautiful body to the Form of Beauty) to show beauty can be more than appearance, then deploys Nussbaum's analysis of objectification (contrasting Playboy's demeaning caption on tennis-player Nicollette Sheridan with Lady Chatterley) and MacKinnon's dominance view to critique the media's commodification of female players. Weaving in commodity racism and bell hooks on black hair, it argues Kournikova's fame reflects a whiteness-privileging color-caste standard of beauty rather than any real athletic or aesthetic superiority.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 13 "3. Laura Palmer—Madonna and Whore" — Jones argues that Laura Palmer is trapped in Freud's Madonna-whore complex—the male inability to see a woman as both virtuous and sexual—with BOB voicing the cultural signals that brand her 'dirty and sleazy' for her sexuality. He reads the Fireman/Giant, who births Laura as a golden antidote to BOB, as a patriarchal 'nice guy' whose idealizing Madonna role is as much a trap as the whore role BOB imposes. The chapter uses Laura's dual life to expose how patriarchy forces women to choose between two reductive poles, both maintained by male power.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 20 "Knowledge, Morality, And Tragedy in The Killers and Out of the Past" — Jarvie tests whether The Killers and Out of the Past rise to tragedy in Aristotle's Poetics sense and answers no. Using Aristotle's demands for noble protagonists acting on principle, a fatal error, and a catharsis of pity and terror, he shows that Swede and Jeff are self-centered moral cowers ensnared by femmes fatales (Kitty, Kathie) whose only 'error' is sexual susceptibility, which is banal rather than tragic. He argues the films' 'personal morality' is incoherent because morality is social, and that their false-appearance mystery plots plus flippant normalizing codas (Reardon's insurance office, The Kid's lie to Ann) reassure audiences and encourage the puritanical 'sexy woman as succubus' myth instead of educing genuine catharsis.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 21 "Moral Man in the Dark City Film Noir, the Postwar Religious Revival, and The Accused" — Palmer nuances the 'dark mirror' theory of noir by recovering a redemptive subgroup, reading Dieterle's The Accused through the postwar religious revival and the writings of Reinhold Niebuhr and Erich Fromm. Where Lang's The Woman in the Window only chastens its professor via a dream, The Accused stages a genuinely penitential arc: repressed psychology professor Wilma Tuttle kills the aggressive student Bill in panic, then is therapeutically forced to relive the crime (at the prizefight and in the reenactment) until love with lawyer Warren Ford delivers her from 'separateness.' Palmer argues this patriarchal, therapeutic 'conversion'—glamorizing Loretta Young out of her mannish disguise—reconfigures Niebuhr's taming of passion and Fromm's account of love as a decision, heralding a coming 'culture of narcissism.'
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 22 "On Reason and Passion in The Maltese Falcon" — Knight argues that Sam Spade is not the dispassionate reasoner philosophy since Plato has assumed the detective to be, defending instead cognitivism about the emotions (via Solomon, de Sousa, and Damasio's Phineas Gage case). Because the hard-boiled detective enters events in media res, Spade must work hermeneutically to reconstruct the real story behind Brigid O'Shaughnessy's lies, and his judgments of trust, confidence, and loyalty fuse reason with feeling. In the climax Spade sends Brigid over for murdering Miles Archer precisely because reason and emotion together tell him he cannot trust her, whereas Brigid—the film's true cold calculator—only feigned emotion to make him her sap; Knight contrasts her with the non-fatale Vivian Rutledge of The Big Sleep.
- **The Philosophy of Spike Lee**, ch. 17 "Feminists and “Freaks” She’s Gotta Have It and Girl 6" — Hoffman assesses whether Lee's She's Gotta Have It and Girl 6 offer liberated female sexuality, drawing on second- and third-wave feminism and bell hooks. She argues Nola Darling only appears empowered before the rape scene and her submission ('Yours') reveal her as an underdeveloped object of the male gaze, whereas Girl 6, as a phone-sex worker consciously performing gender for callers, better exposes gender as socially constructed in a Butler-like sense. Even so, Girl 6's real feminist force lies not in its heroine but in its exposure of oppressive industries, especially the opening Tarantino audition where only the director's gaze counts.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 11 "Landscapes of Gendered Violence Male Love and Anxiety on the Railroad" — Collins analyzes the railroad in Tycoon and both versions of 3:10 to Yuma, drawing on feminist critics (Irigaray, Bordo, Grosz, Haraway, Merchant) who expose a masculinist 'panoramic' epistemology coding mind as male and passive nature/landscape as female. She argues trains destabilize rather than confirm this mastery: in Tycoon, Johnny Munroe conflates conquering the feminized Andean landscape with dominating his wife Maura, yet the bridge and train fail; in the 2007 Yuma, the railroad's promise of masculine legitimacy is sustained only by 'cruel optimism' and male homosocial love between Dan Evans and Ben Wade, over anxieties about racial Others (Apache, Chinese laborers).
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 25 "Go West, Young Woman! Hegel's Dialectic and Women's Identities in Western Films" — Gary Heba and Robin Murphy map women's identities in westerns onto Hegel's three-stage dialectic (aufheben as maintain/negate/transform), grafting on Bakhtin's monoglossic/heteroglossic discourse and Mulvey's and de Beauvoir's feminist film theory. Settler women (Marian in Shane, the mothers of The Searchers) are monoglossic—silenced, family-bound bearers of meaning; town women (Mrs. French in Appaloosa, Lily in How the West Was Won) are heteroglossic, sexualized spectacles marked by costume; and post-1970s figures like Ellen in The Quick and the Dead and Sara in Two Mules for Sister Sara become 'x-glossic,' transformational identities that subvert the male-gaze code and exceed the settler/town binary.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 17 "8 Images of Women in the Music and Life of Neil Young" — McKenna uses Sarah Lucia Hoagland's feminist analysis of "heterosexualism" to argue that Young's songs ("Cinnamon Girl," "A Man Needs a Maid," "Unknown Legend," and the femicide of "Down by the River") portray women as objects to be desired, possessed, used and harmed, positioning them as helpmates (like Rousseau's Sophie, against which Wollstonecraft argued). She extends this to Young's own "backgrounding" of the women in his life (Pegi, Carrie Snodgress) in Waging Heavy Peace, comparing him to William James's reliance on his wife Alice.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 36 "The Price of Existence" — Bonnie Mann reads the Twilight saga through Beauvoir's The Second Sex. Bella embodies the 'relative being' who orbits Edward like a satellite, a self-sacrificing girl who loses Husserl's 'I can' body and exists only through the constant, faithful male gaze that confers meaning. Mann traces a buried feminist subtext - Bella's demand to 'be Superman too' and her transformation into a strong, agentive vampire - but argues Meyer ultimately reinstates the old promise that a woman gains existence through self-annihilation in a man, making the books' success cause for despair.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 32 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Lee reads Gustave Courbet's life-size painting The Quarry (La curée) alongside Daumier's caricatures of incompetent bourgeois Parisian 'hobby hunters' and contemporary works by John Byrd and Christopher Carroll to trace how the hunter became a swaggering, masculine, lower-class 'savage' figure mediating wildness and civilization. She shows how the aristocratic ritual of the curée (feeding the deer's parts to the hounds) inverts into bourgeois provisioning, and invokes Hobbes's 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' to gloss Byrd's Tricky Buck as defiance of urban squeamishness about the mammalian, gendered reality of hunting.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 17 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Freeland analyzes perfume advertising — chiefly Chanel's mini-film campaigns for No. 5 (Kidman/Luhrmann, Tautou/Jeunet) versus the younger, jauntier Coco Mademoiselle ads with Keira Knightley — to trace how fragrance is sold 'aspirationally' by tying scent to lifestyle, romance, and couture. She examines male-fragrance ads (Bronson's Mandom, Chanel Egoiste, Old Spice's Isaiah Mustafa) and celebrity scents fronted by women of color, exposing gender anxiety, colonialism, and near-explicit racism in perfume marketing. Invoking commodity fetishism and feminist critique, she argues the ads manipulate female desire but do not make consumers passive dupes: blog parodies and critical commentary show active resistance to the fantasy.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 15 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Kimberly Baltzer-Jaray and Tanya Rodriguez argue, against George Carlin's 'mobile art gallery' joke, that the only thing separating tattooing from fine art is its fleshy canvas. They show how formalist, expressionist and institutional theories historically excluded both women's craft and tattoos, then use feminist aesthetics (Korsmeyer, Iris Marion Young on the gaze) to reclaim the female tattooed body as an assertion of agency against objectification. They then apply Gadamer's hermeneutics – art as play, festival and symbol – to argue tattoos make a claim on the viewer, build a 'hermeneutic collective' community, and function as inexhaustible symbols prompting self-recognition.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 17 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Thorsten Botz-Bornstein argues contemporary female tattoos have lost their one-dimensional identifying function and instead create a new 'tattoo space.' He dismantles the paradoxical 'savage/civilized' and 'nature/purity' schemes (drawing on Baudrillard on the smooth, made-up female body-screen that reflects male desire) and Loos' 'ornament and crime' verdict on women's tattoos. He proposes that female tattoos have 'become graffiti' – a Bergsonian spatial 'center of action' and 'skinscape' that disperses meaning horizontally rather than branding an identity, recuperating the female body as a political body against commercialized post-political bodies.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 20 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Luna Dolezal's 'Yoga for Women?' argues that Western yoga, once a male ascetic path, has been absorbed by consumer capitalism into a female beauty practice organized around 'body capital.' Reading Yoga Journal covers, Lululemon's 'Say No to Camel Toe' ad, and Toesox's nude campaigns, she shows the fashion/beauty industries cultivate shame to sell the yoga body, objectifying women. She counters that Hatha yoga should be a laboratory for compassionate self-acceptance beyond comparison and competition — 'yoga for every body' — rather than another instrument of the market's normalized ideal.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 21 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Nicole Dunas's 'The Feeling of Beauty' recounts founding the Real Beauty Yoga Project after a teacher-training 'modeling day' where consultants photographed only the five thinnest students, enacting division rather than yogic union. Framing the beauty question against Kant's claim that beauty is objective, and drawing on David Abram's participatory perception and Susan Bordo on airbrushed bodies, she argues that objectifying beauty into an image to be gazed at (the male gaze, the isolated cosmetic-surgery gaze) severs us from it, whereas Hatha yoga's tantric, present-moment embodiment lets beauty be lived rather than consumed.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 22 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Debra Merskin content-analyzes 52 Yoga Journal covers (2000–2008) and finds every model white and 96% shown full-body, mostly looking away — posed as unaware of a scopophilic, hierarchical gaze that puts them in vulnerability. She uses Goffman's gender-display coding and the male-gaze framework to argue that a publication about a mind–body practice (which, contra Descartes' mind/body divide, neuroscience shows are intertwined) bears a special responsibility to present racially inclusive, non-objectifying images rather than reproducing the 'sex sells' formula of Cosmopolitan or Maxim.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 36 "The Price of Existence" — Mann reads Stephenie Meyer's Twilight through Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex: Bella is the "relative being" who orbits Edward like a satellite, valued only through the constant masculine gaze, embodying the adolescent girl's renunciation of her "I can" body. Mann finds a buried feminist subtext — Bella's desire, Edward's restraint, and her vampire transformation into a fierce, powerful equal — but ultimately faults Meyer for reinstating the old promise that a woman gains subjecthood through self-annihilation in a sovereign man's eyes.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 96 "90. From Hell as Philosophy Ripping Through Structural Violence" — James and Mona Rocha argue that Moore and Campbell's From Hell links physical and structural violence under patriarchy: William Gull's Ripper murders of Whitechapel sex workers, and his premonition of the dull modern office ('the twentieth century, I have delivered it'), show how sensationalized physical violence pushes routine structural violence into the invisible background where it corrupts men morally (Gull and Abberline both lose their humanity). Using Galtung's structural violence and Crenshaw's intersectionality of poverty and gender, plus the male gaze in Gull's ghostly viewing of female workers, the chapter connects Victorian misogyny to present-day workplace sexual harassment.

### Taoism (Daoism)

Taoism (Daoism) is a Chinese philosophical and religious tradition centered on living in harmony with the Tao, the underlying pattern and source of all things. Associated with the Daodejing attributed to Laozi and the writings of Zhuangzi, it prizes spontaneity, simplicity, and naturalness over rigid convention, striving, and artificial control. As a philosophy it counsels yielding to the natural course of events rather than forcing outcomes, and it later developed into organized religious forms with their own practices and pursuit of longevity.

- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 11 "“Great Warrior Wars Not Make One Great”" — Robinson (a Zen monk) argues the Force is best understood as ch'i and the Jedi path as philosophical Taoism and Zen: the Light and Dark Sides are the yin-yang polarity whose 'balance' Anakin's prophecy restores, and Anakin's fall is the Buddhist three poisons - clinging attachment to his mother and Padme breeding fear, anger, and hate. Yoda's teaching is Zen practice: 'You must unlearn what you have learned' is wu-wei (effortless action), 'Do or do not' rejects the divided mind of trying, and the Dagobah cave parallels the sword master Tesshu's koan insight that the real enemy is one's own mind ('no-enemy'). The chapter also traces Jedi genealogy to Bodhidharma's Shaolin kung-fu, the Korean Hwa Rang and Japanese Sohei warrior monks, and Bushido's samurai code, noting 'Jedi' derives from 'jidai geki'.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 46 "Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat" — In a fictional interview with the Taoist sage "Bat-Tzu," Mark White explains Taoism through Batman's circle: Bruce's yang-dominated life of vengeance and paranoia needs the yin that Dick and Tim supply, shown by his forgiveness of Zatanna and tenderness toward Helena's baby, while Jason Todd illustrates the fate of the unbalanced who cannot accept death. Alfred emerges as the Taoist sage practicing wei-wu-wei, effortless service like Chuang Tzu's butcher, balancing right and wrong in Bruce, and the Batman-Joker duality shows yin and yang defining each other. Lao Tzu's sayings on balance, complementary opposites, and water-like yielding organize the whole reading.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 25 "You Legend, You Martyr" — Erin Kealey reads Syd Barrett's 1967–68 collapse through Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy: Barrett 'surrendered his subjectivity in the Dionysian process' to make Piper's songs — 'Astronomy Domine', the wordless 'Interstellar Overdrive', 'Matilda Mother' where 'the words had different meaning' — and 'Chapter 24', written from an I Ching divination on change and return. 'Bike' teeters on psychosis as the room of musical tunes swallows the singer, and 'Jugband Blues' ('much obliged to you for making it clear that I'm not here') with the motionless Scarecrow foretells the catatonia that ended his tenure, after which the band pivoted from anarchic spontaneity to the meticulous Apollonian constructions of Dark Side through The Wall. Following Nietzsche, Kealey argues that the fall of this tragic hero — mourned in 'Shine on You Crazy Diamond' and mirrored in Pink's exploits in The Wall — affirms life, since art alone transfigures the horror of existence into something worth living.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 10 "I Still Miss Someone The Self and Its Travels Along the Way" — Geisz explains the Confucian social dao of ritual (li), humaneness (ren), filial piety and the junzi, the Daodejing's metaphysical Dao with its unity of opposites, and Zhuangzi's tales of free wandering, then maps all three onto Cash's songs. Zhuangzi's "Free and Easy Wandering" answers Cash's road songs ("I've Been Everywhere," "The Wanderer"), Cook Ding's effortless carving answers John Henry's hammering in "The Legend of John Henry's Hammer," and the scrambled countdown of "Twenty-Five Minutes to Go" echoes Zhuangzi's logic-bending humor. The payoff is Cash's own country Yin-Yang of interdependent opposites, freedom chained to imprisonment ("Folsom Prison Blues"), sin twinned with redemption ("I Hung My Head"), fidelity with betrayal ("Jackson," "Cocaine Blues"), and a self that, unlike Zhuangzi's self-forgetting sage, must travel a temporal path carrying its guilt, yet stays on what Geisz calls a very wide superhighway of a Dao.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 38 "Teddy Baseball" — Lee reads Ted Williams's The Science of Hitting as a Daoist skill story from the Zhuangzi: 'get a good ball to hit' matches the cicada-catcher's total absorption in the cicada's wings, hitting 'by feel' like the carpenter's hammer matches Cook Ding carving without looking, and Williams's midnight batting practice after Korea matches the wheelwright grown old at his craft—effortless spontaneity produced by disciplined practice and unified attention, not mere mechanics. Williams's 'proper thinking' is Daoist sorting of objective conditions rather than abstract disputation. The closing tale of the old woman who cannot teach the Way to someone lacking the stuff explains why Williams failed as Senators manager: his players did not have the native talent to receive it.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 20 "The End" — Chan contrasts Zhuangzi's butterfly dream, where dream and reality form one transformable whole and the self is forgotten, with Inception's dreams, which are rigidly structured and must be kept strictly separate from reality for Cobb to function. She shows that the film's motifs (the dream machine, the spinning top, the faceless children) work as narrative codes marking each dream layer, making Inception an example of 'dream explaining' rather than Tarkovsky-style 'dream worshipping'. The chapter concludes that Inception's 'dreams' are really a meta-space narrative device, as in Nolan's short Doodlebug, and that the film lacks the Daoist sense of the whole, so Cobb can never transform into the butterfly.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 14 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Morgan Deane maps Ender's tactics onto Sunzi's Art of War: exploiting Bonzo's hot anger, draining the enemy's martial spirit, Graff's use of 'fatal terrain' to throw students into hopeless situations, and staying 'formless' like water so opponents cannot read his plans. Drawing also on Laozi's Dao as the flow a commander must channel, Confucian role ethics in the general-as-father relation, and Legalist reward-and-punishment systems, he concludes Ender qualifies as a military genius by classical Chinese standards - at the wrenching moral cost both he and Graff pay.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 36 "22. The Dao of Master Westley" — Doll tests each character against the Dao: Confucius's identification of the Dao with tradition and ritual fails because Florinese tradition is exactly what enables Humperdinck's murder and war plans, so she turns to Laozi's De and wu-wei, diagnosing Vizzini's fatal overconfidence (he lacked Socratic knowledge of his own ignorance), Humperdinck's paranoia, and Buttercup's passivity as failures to sense when to act and when to refrain. Westley emerges as Zhuangzi's ideal - like Cook Ting the butcher, mastering skills until instinct suffices: adapting through the Fire Swamp, treating Vizzini's death as 'an appropriate death', yet sparing Inigo and Fezzik because killing them would be against nature, which is why the giant and the Spaniard accept him as their sage.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 42 "27. The Mystic with the Mouth" — In a lecture Deadpool keeps interrupting, the chapter reads the Merc's violence through Bataille's Theory of Religion: sacrifice as the search for lost intimacy, killing as the moment sacrificer and victim escape the profane world of mere things into sacred immanence, and sovereignty as the freedom glimpsed in destruction, with Rudolf Otto's mysterium tremendum et fascinans naming the awe Deadpool's massacres (the Circle Chase nunchuks, the Ultimate cartoon, the movie's highway slaughter) provoke. His 'dark Dao' of unhappy wandering is then set against the playful ways of the Zhuangzi - Cook Ding's ox-butchering, the Peng bird, the maimed teacher Wang Tai - as a Daoist path of inner-worldly transcendence that is amoral and gore-soaked. The payoff is the human tension of being both animal and angel: Deadpool is 'a savage god of mystical mayhem.'
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 27 "15. Farts, Butterflies, and Inner Truth" — Franklin Perkins reads Frank's fear that his jewelry business might start World War III — 'you can't fart without changing the balance in the universe' — as the butterfly-effect problem of acting inside a complexity we cannot grasp, from the Roosevelt assassination down to Tagomi's Colt .44. Against the Germans' fatal flight into abstraction (Volk, Blut, Ehre), the chapter presents the I Ching, read through Chinese correlative cosmology of the Tao and yin-yang, as a manual for mole-like, concrete, adaptive interpretation in which each casting (hexagram 11's 'wall falls back into the moat,' the purple knee bands) means only through creative engagement, ending with hexagram 61: our world arose as contingently as a throw of the yarrow stalks.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 30 "18. Lessons from Fred Rogers’s Dao" — John Thompson reads Rogers as a Zhuangzian sage without claiming he was a Daoist: the show's spare sets and simple cast embody the uncarved block and Zhuangzi's Dao present 'in the piss and shit' of the everyday; its refusal of 'bombardment' pace is Cook Ding slowly carving the ox and xiaoyaoyou, free and easy wandering, as when X the Owl must wait for Cousin Mary's visit. The post-9/11 'look for the helpers' PSAs, the Burger King parody he publicly rebuffed, and the Emmys ten seconds of silence mark Rogers as a zhenren, a genuine person at home in ziran.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 8 "Introduction" — De Cruz and De Smedt argue that ATLA subverts the Chosen One trope: Aang's training is slow and non-linear, he needs dedicated teachers, and saving the world is a team effort in which Katara leads and Sokka plans. The show's central theme is oneness, voiced by Guru Pathik's 'illusion of separation' ('The Guru') and Huu's banyan-grove tree ('The Swamp'), which the editors trace to Daoist, Huayan Buddhist (Fazang's golden lion), and Indigenous traditions of interdependence. They frame the volume's engagement with genocide, imperialism, ecological destruction, and Ba Sing Se's authoritarian denial as proof that philosophy is needed for human flourishing.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 32 "A Zhuangzian Sage All Along" — Argues Iroh's Book One laziness and foolishness is a pose implementing Zhuangzi's advice for handling a misguided ruler: do not pressure him, empty yourself of doctrines and credit, and stay deliberately useless (tea, Pai Sho, naps) so you are neither noxious nor a tool. Zhuangzi's fictional dialogue between Confucius and Yan Hui about reforming the young lord of Wei maps onto Iroh beside Zuko, and the episode where Iroh finally gives explicit advice about Ozai ('Avatar Day') proves the point — Zuko rejects both the advice and Iroh the moment the sage stops playing the fool. The authors add an empirical study on Prolific participants showing even first-time, unfamiliar viewers already rate Iroh as wise, supporting the reading that Iroh was a Zhuangzian sage all along.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 8 "Introduction" — The editors argue ATLA subverts the Chosen One trope: Aang learns slowly and non-linearly, needs a teacher for each element, stays weaker than Katara or Toph in specific skills, and saving the world is a team effort in which he is neither leader nor brains. They identify the show's unifying theme as oneness, the 'illusion of separation' voiced by Guru Pathik and the swampbender Huu, and trace it to East and South Asian schools such as Huayan and Chan Buddhism and to Indigenous traditions. Philosophy is presented as the tool the show itself uses against genocide, imperialism, and ecological destruction, with Ba Sing Se's 'no war' denial as the cautionary case.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 12 "The Wisdom of Combination" — A martial artist maps each bending style onto the real art it animates and its parent philosophy: Katara's Taiji waterbending embodies wu-wei, shown when she spares Yon Rha in 'The Southern Raiders' as strength rather than weakness; Toph's Hong Jia earthbending grounds her insistence on truth, an example of the Buddhist eightfold path's Right Speech; Zuko's driven Northern Shaolin temperament walks through the first three Noble Truths, from suffering caused by desire for his honor to its cessation when he joins Team Avatar; and Aang's Baguazhang airbending expresses freedom as openness to change and to Iroh's counsel. The Avatar's power is therefore not four bendings but the combination of the four character strengths.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 32 "A Zhuangzian Sage All Along" — Argues that Iroh's Book One laziness and foolishness is a Zhuangzian pose rather than genuine folly: like Zhuangzi's fictional Confucius counseling Yan Hui not to lecture the young, willful lord of Wei, Iroh never pressures Zuko directly, keeps himself unthreatening by playing the fool over tea and Pai Sho, and practices the 'use of uselessness' so he is never a tool of the prince's quest, 'singing' his wisdom only when Zuko is ready to hear it. The couple's falling out in 'Avatar Day', triggered precisely when Iroh offers explicit moral advice, confirms the strategy, since Zuko rejects both the advice and the uncle. The authors add an empirical study (Prolific participants rating clips): even viewers totally unfamiliar with the series rate Book One Iroh as wise and suspect his foolishness is strategic, supporting the interpretation that he is a Zhuangzian sage all along, and that ATLA in turn illuminates Zhuangzi's cryptic political advice.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 27 "The Way of the Archer" — White reads Clint Barton through the Tao Te Ching and Chuang Tzu: Hawkeye's instinctive archery—'use your bow gently, naturally, instinctively'—is wei wu wei, while his bragging, his glory-chasing failure against Iron Man, and his attempt to become Goliath all violate it by striving against his own nature, until the Kree-Skrull War teaches him the bow is his way. Chuang Tzu's butcher carves the lesson that the effortless path (the straightforward shot) is the skilled one, and Lao Tzu's sage-leadership—lowering oneself, deflecting praise—is exactly how Captain America handles Clint's insurrections. Lao Tzu on sages putting themselves last illuminates Hawkeye's sacrificial death and his legacy passed to Kate Bishop, while the butterfly dream frames his resurrection and the House of M's rewritten reality: with no way to compare the states, life and death are both to be welcomed as parts of the Way.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 34 "NOTES" — The book's final chapter is a mock interview in which 'Bat-Tzu' applies Taoism to Bruce Wayne's life: his yang (hard, retributive crime-fighting) has dominated his yin (his tenderness toward Dick, Tim, and Helena), and Robin has always been the yin balancing the Dark Knight. Quoting Lao-Tzu's Tao Te Ching and Chuang-Tzu on duality, acceptance of death (Jason Todd's resurrection), and effortlessness, the piece casts Alfred as the Taoist sage whose help exemplifies wu-wei, like Chuang-Tzu's butcher who cuts without dulling his blade. It even reads Batman's most intimidating feature, his absent shadow, as proof that nothingness can matter more than substance.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 25 "By the Crimson Bands of Cyttorak… We Conclude!" — The chapter weighs Strange's choice in Doctor Strange: The Oath to spend the last drop of the panacea curing Wong's brain tumor instead of having it replicated to cure all disease, arguing it violates 'first, do no harm' and the Hippocratic precepts—not least because Strange is Wong's friend rather than his physician and invokes a no-longer-binding oath. It then argues his sorcerer's ethics fit the martial arts warrior way better: 'hurt rather than harm' from Master Kan in Kung Fu and the Pinan forms, Zen-shaped bushido's self-control, Confucian responsibility and care for society, and the Tao Te Ching's balance and thousand-mile journey as the shared ethos of medical, martial, and mystic training.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 12 "a4.xhtml" — Bronson argues that walking is a philosophical practice against modern placelessness (Giddens' 'phantasmagoric' locality): Thorin survived Smaug's attack because as a youth he 'was a good adventurous lad, always on the move', and Tolkien's wise figures - slow, flower-stopping Tolkien himself, Gandalf who 'went to look ahead' and was brought back 'by looking behind', Bilbo's silent walking, Beorn's bear-travels - all practice attentive movement through place. He backs this with Montaigne's retirement to his tower and bringing thoughts back to the orchard, Thoreau's woods-walking that must be spiritual as well as physical, the Tao Te Ching's 'good travelers leave no tracks' and Zhuangzi's wandering virtues, and Buddhist walking meditation from the Buddha's wandering monks to Thich Nhat Hanh's peace steps.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 21 "a9.xhtml" — The chapter argues Tolkien's clearest moral in The Hobbit is against possessiveness, starting from Aquinas' definition of greed as 'immoderate love of riches': dragon-sickness ruins Thorin and drowns the Master of Lake-town starving in the wilderness with his gold, and Gollum shows the isolating end of a life organized around a 'precious'. Buddhism reframes the diagnosis - Gollum's craving (tanha) is rooted in ignorance (avidya) of the self's illusoriness, since grasping enriches a self that does not exist, per the Four Noble Truths - while Laozi's 'he who knows he has enough is rich' and Thoreau's 'a man is rich in proportion to the things he can afford to let alone' are embodied by Beorn and the gift-giving, nearly government-less hobbits. Bilbo's generosity - giving away the Arkenstone worth 'more than a river of gold', taking only two small chests, later giving Sting and the mithril coat to Frodo - is the book's counter-example to greed.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 20 "The End" — Hiu M. Chan contrasts Zhuangzi's butterfly dream with Inception's plot: Zhuangzi forgets his self, dreams without planning, and ends in the 'transformation and unity' of dreamer and butterfly, whereas Cobb's self is constantly highlighted — he plans missions, codes his dreams with motifs (the spinning top, the dream machine, the faceless children, distinct locations, weather, crosscutting), and can never fuse dream and reality. The chapter maps the film's four-layer 'meta-space' narrative structure (exposition through resolution distributed across dream layers) and argues the 'dreams' are really programmed, coded narrative devices, the opposite of the Daoist 'whole' in which reality itself is the biggest dream and a true person no longer dreams. Against semiotic 'dream explaining' (the top means dreaming), she holds that in Daoism the top would mean nothing beyond a spinning top, and contrasts Nolan with Tarkovsky's 'dream worshipping' films like The Mirror. The ending's reunion is thus only apparent: Inception lacks the Daoist harmony that would let Cobb 'become the butterfly.'
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 29 "NOTE" — Shai Biderman and William Devlin argue the character John Locke begins as an empiricist in the mold of his philosophical namesake - his boar hunting, tracking, and trebuchet-building against the hatch all follow the scientific method befitting a tabula rasa mind furnished by experience - but the miracle of his healed legs poses a 'why' that empirical explanation of 'how' cannot answer. He therefore converts to the Taoism of the Tao Te Ching: the moth-cocoon lesson to Charlie, 'I stopped looking' for Sun's ring, reading dreams and signs from the island, and finally his self-sacrifice to stop the time flashes all enact following the Way. The chapter reads the black-and-white backgammon stones, Locke's one-black-one-white eyes in Claire's dream, and Jacob versus the Man in Black as yin-yang complementarity, with empiricism and Taoism finally interdependent like the dots in each half.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 28 "Notes" — Asks how an all-encompassing, good Force can have a dark side: after framing the Force as panentheistic, it tests Augustine's privation theory (Alderaan's destruction as an absence of 'measure, order, and form') and a Daoist reading of Yoda's equanimity modeled on Zhuangzi drumming and singing after his wife's death, rejecting both because Vader's evil is active, disciplined, and full of the Force rather than a lack. The answer endorsed is Schelling's: the will needs a dark 'ground' - Yoda's 'anger, fear, aggression' - which is benign when ordered by the will of love and becomes evil when it separatisitically defies it, which is what 'bringing balance to the Force' means.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 9 "“Now This Is Podracing!”" — Johnson reads The Phantom Menace as having distinctly Daoist flavors: Shmi's 'you cannot stop the change any more than you can stop the suns from setting,' the Naboo-Gungan 'symbiont circle,' and midi-chlorian symbiosis all express the Daoist unity of opposites and the constant flow of change. He argues Qui-Gon Jinn acts as a Daoist sage practicing wu wei — 'concentrate on the moment,' 'another solution will present itself' — while nearly everyone else in the film makes wrong predictions and grasps at outcomes. Even Anakin's accidental 'Oops!' victory over the Droid Control Ship is presented as success without trying, the practical meaning of 'Do or do not. There is no try.'
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 23 "The Dao of Hoops" — Dirk Dunbar, a former professional player, argues that Daoist concepts illuminate basketball excellence and that the sport can be a path to the Dao. Balancing yin and yang means blending competition with surrender and strategy with spontaneity; Zhuangzi's archer shows how craving victory drains power. Wuwei explains the 'zone' of effortless play Dunbar experienced while scoring sixty-five points in a high school game and seventy-four in Iceland, while qi grounds free-throw breathing and visualization and ziran the discipline of releasing a shot without willing it in. Drawing on Daode jing verses and Phil Jackson's Sacred Hoops, he claims basketball teaches a life of disciplined surrender beyond the ego.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 27 "Thirteenth Hole Free and Easy Wandering on the Golf Course Swing Like a Taoist" — Scott F. Parker reads golf's paradox—that you play your best shot when you stop trying so hard—through the Taoism of the 'Tao Te Ching' and the 'Chuang Tzu.' Using the parable of the archer (skill is constant but attachment to the prize ruins the shot), Cook Ting carving the ox by spirit not force, and Master Yu accepting his deformity, he draws out nonattachment to results, 'doing without doing' (wei wu wei), and self-knowledge/self-acceptance, illustrated by Zach Johnson never going for a par 5 in two at the 2007 Masters and Tiger Woods rarely swinging all-out. The essay embodies the Taoist point that the Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao: to try to not-try is self-defeating, so one must simply not try.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — The editors' introduction argues that the unifying theme of Lee's films is the struggle for authentic self-identity, framed through Charles Taylor's dialogical self and Kierkegaard's line that anxiety is the dizziness of freedom. It surveys how Confucian virtues (ren, li, xiao) and Daoist wu-wei play out across Pushing Hands, The Wedding Banquet, Eat Drink Man Woman, Crouching Tiger, Sense and Sensibility, Brokeback Mountain and others, treating each protagonist as caught between traditional obligation and personal desire. It invokes Nietzsche's claim that all philosophy is autobiography to justify reading Lee's films (he said 'it's all in my films') as a coherent authorial philosophy.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 46 "Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat" — In a mock interview with 'Bat-Tzu' (a disguised Alfred), Mark White explains Taoism through Batman. Bruce is dangerously dominated by yang after his parents' deaths and needs the yin balance that Robin (Dick as the lighthearted 'Batman with a feminine side') and his spiritual quest restore; Batman's fear-inducing shadow illustrates Lao-Tzu's usefulness of nothingness. Alfred is the Taoist sage embodying wei-wu-wei - 'action without action' - quietly serving like Chuang-Tzu's effortless butcher and like water that wears down stone, harmonizing Bruce's warring opposites toward the Way.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 29 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Jennifer McMahon and Steve Csaki test Buddhist and Taoist parallels in the novel and find many only apparent. Tolkien's talking trees and ents anthropomorphize nature and grant it human-like consciousness, whereas Buddhism attributes sentience to all beings without projecting human consciousness, and Tolkien privileges domesticated over wild nature and stewardship over membership in nature. His master-student chain (Bilbo, Gandalf, Aragorn, 'Master Samwise') genuinely echoes the Zen necessity of the right master, as in Dogen's mushroom-cook mentor; but his good-versus-evil war, with light privileged over a personified dark power to be defeated, contradicts Taoism's yin-yang balance in which evil is imbalance, not a force to destroy.

### Rectification of Names

The rectification of names is the Confucian idea that social and moral order depends on making words match reality, so that a ruler truly rules, a father truly acts as a father, and each role is filled according to its proper meaning. Confucius argued that when names and actualities drift apart, language loses its force, obligations become unclear, and society falls into disorder. The remedy is to align conduct with the standards implied by one's titles and relationships, treating accurate naming as the foundation of good government and ethics.

- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 13 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Nicolas Michaud catalogues the demonic hierarchy - de Spina's goblins, incubi, and familiars, Dante's Malebranche, Binsfeld's seven princes of Hell - through Dungeon Keeper's Dark Mistress, World of Warcraft succubi, Se7en, Hellraiser's Pinhead, Hellboy, and Spawn. His real argument is ontological: names are power, and what we call the Devil fixes how we treat him. Recovering the Hebrew sense of 'satan' as an appointed adversary and 'Lucifer' as light-bringer (compared to Prometheus), he argues the same being could be reframed from tempter to giver of knowledge, much as naming Columbus's invasion a 'discovery' launders atrocity.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 32 "Girls and Philosophy" — Carleo and D'Ambrosio read Hannah's 'busy trying to become who I am' through the classical Chinese debate over names: her self-claimed title 'writer' preceding any conduct is the Confucian nightmare of names divorced from actuality, diagnosed by the Analects's rectification of names ('rulers should rule, fathers should father') and the sheep-stealing passage warning against over-identifying with a single role. Adam, by contrast, lives the Daoist ideal - the empty vessel of the Daodejing acting by wu wei, and Zhuangzi's butterfly dream fluidity in his role-play sex and absorbed woodworking, unattached to titles. Mencius and Xunzi frame the resolution: by Season Three Hannah finally rectifies names at GQ while Adam's non-identity turns delusional, vindicating the ideal of being an 'internal sage and external king' - Daoist in private, responsible to roles in public.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 14 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Morgan Deane reads Ender's tactics as Sunzi's Art of War in action: winning all future fights by terror, exploiting Bonzo's hot anger, 'fatal terrain' when Graff stacks hopeless odds, formlessness that hides intent, and fluid toon formations that move like water — all grounded in Daoist harmony with the Way and the Confucian role-duty of the general-as-father who throws soldiers into hopeless positions to win their devotion. He also finds Legalist rewards-and-punishments in Ender's command of Dragon Army, concluding Ender qualifies as a Sunzi-style military genius whose empathy is the steep moral price of victory.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 12 "Notes" — Decker parallels the Republic's fall into Palpatine's Empire with the Zhou dynasty's collapse that birthed Chinese philosophy, reading three Jedi from the Dark Times comics through it. K'Kruhk, guided by the Zatoichi-like Master Zao, learns wu-wei - following the Force rather than forcing outcomes, with Laozi's Dao as the Force's Chinese analogue. Dass Jennir's struggle over what 'Jedi' means after killing a slaver becomes Confucian rectification of names and the cultivation of ren, while Kai Hudorra's loss of faith, withdrawal to a casino, and final sacrificial stand against Vader embody Mozi-style pragmatic minimalism redeemed by Jennir's virtuous example.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 31 "NOTES" — The Terjesens pit Kant's impersonal morality — Sam's contractual distance from the thieving Mickens is exactly how he would treat strangers — against Confucius and Mencius, for whom filial duties are the nursery of virtue: we learn benevolence by serving parents and revering elders, Lafayette's care for Lettie Mae and Tara shows family forming moral character, and the Upright Gong's covering for a father's sheep-stealing grounds Jason's 'sometimes the right thing to do is the wrong thing'. Mencius's King Shun, who abdicates and carries his criminal father into exile, models how Tommy and Jason should put family first while accepting the cost, while Mozi's universal love surfaces in Godric's 'forgiveness is love', and the chapter concludes that family counts only insofar as it develops our moral nature — the line between Tommy and Sam.

### Human Nature Is Bad (and needs ritual)

Xunzi took the opposing Confucian view that human nature is bad, or at least unruly, since people are born with self-interested desires that, left unchecked, lead to conflict and disorder. For Xunzi goodness is not innate but a deliberate achievement, produced by ritual, education, and the accumulated wisdom of the sages, which reshape raw impulses into virtuous conduct. His emphasis on ritual (li) and conscious effort as the source of morality directly answered Mencius's claim that virtue grows from natural sprouts.

- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 30 "Every Soul Experiences the Battle Within" — Reads Zuko's arc as a war between Legalism and Confucianism: Ozai's agni kai scarring of his son, Azulon's death sentence, the Fire Nation Oath and school discipline ('The Headband') all enact Han Fei's principle that bad human nature needs terrifying sanctions, and Azula's 'trust is for fools' completes it. Against this stands Iroh's Confucian education in ren — teaching that honor cannot be separated from humaneness, that a mugger deserves tea and encouragement, and that wu-wei-like patience knows when to speak. Mencius's innate compassion explains why Zuko's 'amazing lie' realization could unfold, Katara, Sokka, and Hakoda embody Confucian filial bonds that adopt Aang, Toph, and finally Zuko, and Solzhenitsyn's gulag insight closes the chapter: the line between good and evil runs through every human heart.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 30 "Every Soul Experiences the Battle Within" — Reads the Fire Nation royal family as a philosophical battle between Legalism (Han Fei, taking Xunzi's dictum that human nature is evil, so order requires terrifying sanctions: Ozai burning Zuko in the agni kai so 'suffering will be your teacher', Azulon's death sentence on Zuko, the Fire Nation Oath recited in schools) and Confucianism (Iroh teaching ren, that true honor cannot be had apart from humaneness, preferring honorable begging over theft, and talking a would-be mugger into tea). Zuko's 'battle within' is the legacy of his two great-grandfathers, Sozin's Legalism versus Roku's line, and it is resolved when he disowns Ozai, calls Iroh his 'real father', and is adopted into Team Avatar, whose filial bonds (Katara's care, Hakoda's sacrifice) contrast with the scheming royal family. The chapter closes with Solzhenitsyn's image of the line between good and evil passing through every human heart to explain why Zuko's inner war resonates.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Curry and Lang test 'War never changes' through Hobbes and Xunzi: the wasteland - where the Ghoul asks who ever elected the 'President' in 'The Trap' and Cooper Howard decays outside all political order - is Hobbes's state of nature of restless power-seeking, while Xunzi's claim that bad human nature needs ritual (li) and righteousness (yi) explains a world with no moral education, where Elder Cleric Quintus pairs noble talk with 'power is taken, not given'. Fallout's Great War then fails every just-war test: China's invasion of Alaska stretches just cause, the corporatist US lacks right authority, propaganda undid last resort, mutually assured destruction explodes proportionality, and Vault-Tec shelters plus battlefield mini-nukes breach discrimination and proportionality in bello - with Operation Anchorage's propaganda simulation illustrating the revisionist point that fighting cleanly cannot redeem an unjust war. China's 'righteous army' (yi bing) tradition - Sunzi's strategic restraint, Mohist defensive war, Mengzi's true king, Xunzi's punitive righteous war - leaves no trace beyond Captain Zao, so the war's constancy marks the failure of every philosophical attempt to bind war to justice.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Thompson argues that Lee's 'cowboy aesthetic' of rugged isolation in Brokeback Mountain (Ennis and Jack) and Crouching Tiger (Li Mu Bai, Shu Lien, Jen) is only apparent: the characters are always already embedded in Confucius' five cardinal relationships, read through Xunzi's darker view that selfish desire must be curbed by ritual and social hierarchy. Ennis and Jack seem lone individuals but are defined by ties to Alma, family and each other, and Jen's redemption comes when she abandons self-serving desire to re-establish her Confucian relationships. Citing Nietzsche's gloss on Aristotle that only a beast or a god lives alone, it concludes there is no truly isolated cowboy.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Dull reads Eat Drink Man Woman through a Hall-and-Ames 'focus-field' model of personhood, analyzing harmony via metaphors of a culinary dish, music and a sports team where each element keeps its integrity within a whole. He diagnoses the Chu family by pairing Mencius (morality as expression of the four sprouts) against Xunzi (desire must be structured by ritual): Chef Chu is 'repressed as a turtle', Jia-Jen hides behind ritual, Jia-Ning acts on impulse, and Jia-Chien lacks direction. Their romantic transformations restore harmony, answering Chu's question 'is there more than food and sex?' affirmatively, as expression, desire and ritual come into balance and his sense of taste returns.

### Caring as the Ground of Ethics

Nel Noddings developed an ethics grounded in caring, holding that the fundamental moral relation is the encounter between the one-caring and the one cared-for, in which the carer attends to and is moved by the other's needs. She distinguished natural caring, which flows from inclination as a parent cares for a child, from ethical caring, which we summon out of a remembered ideal of ourselves as caring when inclination fails. For Noddings, ethics is rooted in receptivity and engrossment in the particular other rather than in the application of universal principles, and moral education should cultivate the capacity and disposition to care. Her work gave care ethics a systematic foundation and influenced thinking about moral education.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 11 "Elaine’s Moral Character" — Sarah Worth asks whether Elaine is a feminist icon or 'just one of the boys.' Elaine passes every liberal-feminist benchmark - a Tufts education, the only steady career (Pendant Publishing, then the J. Peterman catalogue), financial and emotional independence - but fails the ethic of care: her dating ethics run on pettiness (dumping men for not offering pie, for dirty bathrooms, over Puddy's high-fiving), the 'spongeworthy' episode commodifies her own relationships, she shows no maternal instinct toward the ugly baby, and she secretly resents George's engagement. The conclusion: being one of the boys does not a feminist make, though Elaine still models an independence the women of Friends and Frasier lack.
- **The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am**, ch. 22 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" — Answers the title with 'fugheddaboutit' - Carmela is no feminist - but argues she reasons as a Gilligan-style care ethicist. Her moral voice evolves from Church-based justice arguments against Angie's divorce ('Commendatori'), through the justice-tradition confrontation with Dr. Krakower's refusal of 'blood money' ('Second Opinion'), to mature care ethics that balances self with others when she throws Tony out after the Svetlana revelation ('Whitecaps'). Using Noddings on reciprocity and 'total engrossment', the chapter reads the marriage's failure as failed caring, and the Furio romance and the Georgetown ricotta-pie intimidation as care reasoning that defies the submissive female stereotype feminists fear care ethics valorizes.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 24 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Cynthia Freeland reads the film's women through feminist ethics of care: the two Marys function like a Greek-chorus of grieving observers, while Claudia and Veronica — and the casting of Bellucci as the repentant whore opposite Morgenstern's ageless Madonna — lock them into the virgin/whore double bind. Using Carol Gilligan's critique of Kohlberg's Kantian standard and Nel Noddings's and Sara Ruddick's point that mothering is reflective 'attentive' work, she argues Gibson's Mary is one-dimensional: flashbacks of 'I am here' show maternal instinct, never moral deliberation. She ends by suggesting the historical Jesus, like Socrates, was more radical toward women than the film, and that Irigaray's reading of Christ's bleeding wounds as a feminized maternal body sits oddly with Gibson's muscular, 'take it like a man' Savior.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 18 "U2 and Philosophy" — The authors apply Gilligan's and Noddings' ethics of care to U2: 'Bad' shows the speaker as Noddings' 'one-caring', and 'Sometimes You Can't Make It on Your Own' - Bono caring for his dying father through anger and resentment - exemplifies care's insistence on the particular relationship over universal rules, refusing abstraction even of the usual songwriting metaphors. 'Peace on Earth' names the Omagh bomb's dead (Sean, Julia, Gareth, Ann, Breda) and 'Van Diemen's Land' refuses both IRA and British sides, showing care ethics rejecting the utilitarian accounting and the Kantian universalizability arguments that could rationalize such violence. They conclude U2 are philosophical rather than political feminists: Gilligan's 'different voice' is not a woman's voice, and the band's connected knowing - debt relief sung as connection in 'Beautiful Day' - makes maternal thinking 'loud, rhythmic, catchy, even cool'.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 10 "Explaining Moral Doubt" — Steven Gimbel reads the Formidable Opponent segment - red-tie Colbert debating blue-tie Colbert - as a glimpse of authentic moral deliberation that the flip-flop-phobic punditry satirized by the show (and Jon Stewart's Crossfire rant) has abandoned. Moral doubt is good because perspectives are partial and the Enlightenment 'marketplace of ideas' of Locke and Mill tests beliefs only through challenge. It has a source: 'morally right' bundles five dimensions - the actor's character shaped by habit (Aristotle's virtue ethics), the act itself judged by Kant's categorical imperative, the pleasure-versus-pain consequences tallied Bentham-style, the rights of the person affected from Locke and Hobbes's social contract, and the special care obligations of close relationships (Noddings and Ruddick) - and hard cases like abortion and flag burning are exactly where these dimensions pull apart. So emulate the dueling Colberts: fear not the flip-flop, since deciding which value trumps which requires open-minded conversation with oneself.
- **Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_**, ch. 4 "index" — Six essays on friendship in the Facebook age. Tedesco asks whether the low-demand 'Facebook friendship' can reconcile the utilitarian demand for impartiality (Mill, Railton, Kagan) with the partiality of real friends, and concludes Facebook ties are only supplementary to relationships built elsewhere. Hamington surveys a hundred users and argues in Noddings's care-ethics terms that Facebook's information transfer makes caring possible (knowledge of the concrete other is necessary for care), though it also makes dropping a student over one racist comment effortless. Bloor reads Facebook through Heidegger's technological nihilism and the anonymous 'one', warning that speed of exchange erodes Aristotle's few deep, morally formative friendships, while Briggle's farewell letter to Facebook judges the site by Ivan Illich's convivial-tool criteria and Cuonzo recasts pokes and virtual gifts as efficient successors to primate grooming; Lattimore applies Bakhtin's 'excess of seeing' to how viewers 'consummate' other users' self-presentations.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 21 "A Better Way of Living Your Life" — Akers argues the Doctor follows neither rule deontology, utilitarian calculation, nor virtue ethics, but a relational ethics of care in Noddings's and Slote's sense, expressed as Buber's I-Thou stance — insisting an enslaved Ood is 'a "he," not an "it"' and addressing Donna, Jack, and Rose each as individuals in 'Journey's End'. Linking this to Nussbaum's claim that wonder widens moral concern and to Kant's dynamic and mathematical sublime, she argues the Doctor needs human companions like Rose, Martha, and Donna as a human-scale reference point that renews his wonder — and with it his ethics — while his wiping of Donna's memory shows the care tradition's dangers of power imbalance.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 22 "Toward Caring" — Sylvia models the Doctor on feminist care ethics: Gilligan's response to Kohlberg's justice-tinged scales and Noddings's distinction between natural caring (for Rose, Martha, Peri in 'The Caves of Androzani') and ethical caring, which explains his forgiveness of the Master and compassion for Dalek Caan after genocides. Against utilitarian impartiality — which cannot say why he should save his companion over a stranger — the relationship itself grounds the obligation, while his vengeful moment facing the lone Dalek in 'Dalek' shows what caring burnout looks like.
- **The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia**, ch. 15 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" — Kathleen Poorman Dougherty sets Kant's universal, emotion-free morality (echoed in Kohlberg's justice stages and Judge Abernathy's 'blind court' claim in 'Infamy') against Carol Gilligan's care ethic, which she says fits Saint Alicia far better: Alicia's practical advice to Jennifer Lewis in the pilot, driving Kenny home in 'Home', and telling Kenny's father 'I care a lot more about your son than he does' show connection producing both better morality and better lawyering. Feminist theorists like Nel Noddings and Sara Ruddick treat this care orientation as morally superior, not merely different, but the chapter's later sections weigh the cost: Kalinda's burnout warning, Alicia's resentment at always hand-holding clients, and the double bind by which women absorb society's unpaid caring labor. The verdict is that care is genuinely moral, but it must become a shared burden.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 23 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Skyler King uses the Gang's inheritance war over their dead mother's possessions as a metaphor for greed versus need, pressing our duties to those in extreme suffering. Peter Singer's utilitarian argument - prevent bad without sacrificing anything of comparable significance, absolute poverty is bad, therefore we ought to give - makes charity a requirement rather than a nicety, condemning Dennis's luxury purchases and crowning Bruce Mathis, the one character who consistently donates, as the utilitarian exemplar. Nel Noddings's feminist ethics of care counters that we owe help only to those within reach whose good we can see 'completed in the other' - so Mac and Dennis wronged Charlie by refusing him shelter in the recession, but owe nothing to children overseas - and the chapter weighs Dee-style objections that this licenses caring only when inconvenienced, closing with the question 'is it always sunny in your Philadelphia?'
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 27 "16. Who Am I to You" — James Okapal sets up the Kantian view — moral agency, shown by passing the contradiction-in-conception test (which Wallace's 'all should be masters of slaves' fails), is the precondition of moral status, so non-agents like replicants, on Tibor Machan's extension of Kant to animals, matter no more than toasters — against the ethics of care of Nel Noddings and Carol Gilligan. On the care reading, K's and Batty's final acts of ethical caring, like Joi's risky choices for K, confer moral status on another and thereby constitute moral agency, reversing the Kantian order. Empathy, not universalizable reason, is what removes bricks from Joshi's wall.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 37 "24. Fred Rogers and the Ethics of Care" — A.G. Holdier places Rogers squarely in the care ethics of Gilligan and Noddings: against Kohlberg's justice stages (the Heinz dilemma recast with Henrietta Pussycat and X the Owl), care means Joan Tronto's four elements of attentiveness, responsibility, competence, and responsiveness, shown in the Clemmons kiddie pool, the Soviet guest understood through an interpreter, and 'just the way you are.' Extending care to animals via Rogers's vegetarianism and Carol Adams's 'absent referent,' and to the self via the closing benediction, he argues Rogers embodied care as particular, embodied practice rather than formula.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 10 "Not Bad, for a [Wo]man" — Argues Ripley's crossed-heart promise to Newt shows partialist care rightly overriding impartial justice: Kant, Mill, and Rachels demand everyone count for one, but Gilligan's critique of Kohlberg and Noddings's carer-cared-for relation - completed in Newt's 'I knew you'd come' - explain why Ripley duct-tapes two guns together and descends into the hive. Her flexible, relational problem-solving (the lighter-sprinkler trick against the Facehuggers, learning the pulse rifle) beats Gorman's mission-first command, and the trolley-style arithmetic she rejects when the one on the tracks is her little girl is not a moral failing; even nuking the Queen's eggs raises Singer-style speciesism questions.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 27 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Barkman diagnoses four mama's boys: Raj's selective mutism under his parents' webcam meddling, Sheldon's comfort-seeking from a fundamentalist mother ('Soft Kitty,' mandatory grace), Howard's learned helplessness with his foghorn mother, and Leonard raised as Beverly's lab subject, his hugging machine echoing the wire-mother monkey experiment. Plato and Aristotle ground the charge of injustice — receiving less than one's station deserves, and wrongs against intimates are 'more terrible' — so parents bear special obligations their neglect breaches, a contemporary point pressed in the care-ethics tradition of Noddings. Cognitive-dissonance theory and Putman's Aristotelian 'psychological courage' prescribe honest self-reckoning for mothers and sons alike, with Leonard furthest along after confronting Beverly in 'The Maternal Congruence.'
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 37 "Notes" — Opening from the author's own grief — she nearly stopped playing Fallout 4 because its murdered spouse and kidnapped son echoed the loss of her real infant son — the chapter applies the ethics of care of Gilligan, Noddings, and Tronto to Fallout's wasteland. Care relationships structure the games: the Fallout 3 father whose flight from Vault 101 propels the plot, Dogmeat's loyal responsiveness as relational reciprocity, and the Fallout 4 son Shaun, where caring for your child collides with caring for a Commonwealth his Institute endangers. Settlement-building, faction choice (Lyons's Brotherhood handing out clean water versus the Railroad's liberation of synths), and even the Black Widow perk path that saves Megaton all become care-laden moral acts — care as protest against the wasteland's ethos of bare survival.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 22 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Averill argues that Katniss's morality is built on care for particular people rather than impartial principle: she volunteers for Prim, protects Rue because the girl resembles her sister, and spares a wounded District 2 soldier at the Nut because he recalls her father and the Seam. Measured against Kant's impartial justice perspective (embodied by Thresh sparing Katniss to repay a debt to Rue), she falls short — but Gilligan's care perspective and Noddings's distinction between natural and ethical caring recast this as a valid, even heroic, moral development. Using Noddings, the chapter traces Katniss's arc from natural care for Prim toward ethical care for strangers and even enemies, and reads her assassination of Coin as care for all of Panem's future children rather than revenge. Care, the chapter concludes, can even justify violence when it protects the vulnerable.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 22 "Notes" — Bein argues Wonder Woman uniquely fuses two supposedly incompatible moralities: bushido - Nitobe's eight samurai virtues, Sun Tzu's benevolence of ending war swiftly, worthy-opponent rituals mirrored in superhero costumes - and the feminist ethics of care Gilligan and Noddings built against a Western canon (Aristotle, Kant) that called women too emotional for morality. Wonder Woman's killing of Maxwell Lord to free Superman is re-read as the care-ethical beach case: saving your own child over a stranger's is not a failure of impartiality, and in his Gotham-versus-Themyscira invasion thought experiment she would defend Gotham because its people are vulnerable non-combatants, not because a utilitarian ledger favors it.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 31 "Notes" — Chavez, Gavaler, and Goldberg trace Marston's 'Love Leader' kink - bracelets of submission, Venus girdles, Paradise Island bondage games, Earth One's collaring of Steve Trevor - to nineteenth-century maternalist feminism, then map the care ethics of Gilligan, Noddings, and Tronto onto both the comic and real-world BDSM. Reform (later Transformation) Island embodies a care-based alternative to punishment: rather than retribution, von Gunther and Irene are transformed by loving authority into people who save their captors, and Wonder Woman rescues the drowning villain Eviless because 'Aphrodite's Law commands us to save lives always - enemies or not.' The BDSM community's 4Cs (consent, communication, caring, caution) turn out to be Tronto's four elements of care, so the good dominant just is the good care-giver.
- **The Philosophy of Joss Whedon**, ch. 7 "Angel, Angelus, and Personal Identity" — This file collects Part II chapters 6-9. It defends Stephen Mulhall's 'bold thesis' against Baggini, Murray Smith and Livingston, using Whedon's dialogue-free episode 'Hush' as film that 'shows' a Zen-like epistemic point resisting paraphrase, and works through the Russell-Wartenberg debate over whether narrative film can convey arguments (via The Matrix and Eternal Sunshine). It reads The Cabin in the Woods as a counterargument to utilitarianism grounded in Nel Noddings's ethics of care ('people are more important than humanity') and an Aristotelian theory of worthwhile horror. The Angel/Angelus chapter stages the Wes-Holtz dispute as competing theories of personal identity, testing Locke's memory theory and Parfit's psychological-continuity view against Whedon's soul-based metaphysics to argue what ultimately matters is one's care-based relations with others.
- **Joss Whedon as Philosopher**, ch. 8 "Conclusion" — The concluding chapter argues that Joss Whedon 'does philosophy' through the Whedonverse, building on Mulhall, Wartenberg and Shaw's hierarchy of filmic philosophizing. It reads Angel's 'Deep Down' and 'Epiphany' speeches as endorsing that kindness is a self-standing good regardless of God, framing sacrifices by Simon (for River), Cordy (for Angel) and Buffy (for Dawn) as a cinematic thought experiment refuting the claim that ethics is incoherent without God. It reads Connor as exemplifying Kane's libertarian free will (Darla and faux-Cordelia 'stir up' quantum indeterminacy), Angel/Angelus as a years-long test of memory-continuity personal identity against Parfit's Neo-Lockean view, and 'The Cabin in the Woods' plus Dollhouse's 'Man on the Street' as endorsing a Noddings-style ethics of care and Whedon's religious non-realism, with Angel offered as a Socrates-like moral exemplar.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 21 "A Better Way of Living Your Life" — Laura Geuy Akers argues the Doctor lives by a relational ethics of care rather than deontology, utilitarianism, or virtue ethics.
