Because Aristotle deems friendship 'most indispensable for life' and eudaimonia requires virtuous activity joined to good fortune, the chapter ends hoping Frank can still choose the good for its own sake - a hope Claire's walkout after Iowa badly dents.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Reads the show through Rousseau's contrast between the general will and a pathological 'corporate will': governments and corporations are sociopathic artificial persons that depersonalize their agents, degrading natural self-love (amour de soi) into status-hungry amour-propre. On this account Frank's break with Freddy ('just a good customer'), the Tusk-Walker alliance, and Remy and Jackie's bought loyalties are Aristotelian friendships of utility or pleasure crushed under the corporate will, never true friendship, leaving Washington with 'honor without virtue' and men 'everywhere in chains'.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 36 "Notes" — Sorts Frank's six friendships using Aristotle's three types: Freddy and Meechum are friendships of pleasure, Doug, Durant, Tusk, and Jackie friendships of utility, while Claire-despite 'I love that woman more than sharks love blood'-cannot be a true friend of the good because true friendship requires two people of good character seeing themselves in each other. Since Aristotle ties friendship to flourishing, the chapter ends hoping that Frank, who has good fortune but neither good character nor true friends, may yet choose virtue and the good life.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 26 "Here Lies an Avenger" — The Pattersons read 'The Mask in the Iron Man' as moral education: Tony's repeated 'I have a good life' litany maps onto Aristotle's eudaimonia — friends like Rhodey, Pepper, and Happy, wealth, health, sobriety, and life itself as goods chosen for the sake of happiness — while Niebuhr's community of value makes the Avengers the community of trust and loyalty that grounds those ideals. Tony fails as teacher when the sentient armor kills Whiplash, cannot grieve with him, and fails Aristotle's friendship test of willing good for the friend for his own sake, its identity dangerously conflated with Tony's. The reversal comes when Tony lives the virtue of self-sacrifice — dying 'because I'm an Avenger' — and the armor, finally grasping nobility, rips out its own mechanical heart to save him, earning the grave marker 'Here lies Iron Man, Avenger.'
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 19 "NOTES" — Fosl argues that although the survivors' internal order looks Lockean - Jack's uncoerced leadership, natural rights, minimal government - and is bonded by Rousseauan pity and Humean sympathy (Kate staying in the cage with Sawyer, 'live together, die alone'), the show's deepest political logic follows Carl Schmitt's friend-enemy distinction: the survivors cohere only in opposition to the Others, torture is excused in liberal terms, and conflicts end in redemptive violence, with Jack both killing the enemy and dying a Christlike sacrifice. Hobbes's absence from the character names signals the show's rejection of a war of all against all among the survivors, yet the finale's divine manipulation of the castaways, with Jacob treating people as means against Kantian autonomy, repudiates the liberal hope of a rational peace altogether.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 23 "NOTES" — Michael Austin asks what adult children owe their fathers through Jack and Christian Shephard (the drunken-surgery cover-up, 'You don't have what it takes') and Locke and Anthony Cooper (the kidney con, the defenestration). He weighs Jane English's view that parental sacrifice creates friendship rather than debt - so Locke owed Cooper nothing, and true friends like Hurley and the crib-building Locke never keep accounts - against Sidgwick's three possible sources of filial obligation (relationship quality, biological tie, gratitude for services) and David Mellow's debt-of-gratitude argument. Austin concludes that the mutual needs of parents and children - Miles reaching for Pierre Chang in 1974, Jack and Christian's reconciliation in the church - best explain what they owe each other.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 24 "“To a Place Where We Know We Are Loved”" — Myers grades the moral development of the Sterling Cooper cast with Kohlberg's justice stages and Gilligan's ethics of care in order to find Aristotelian friendships, which require equals in moral development who wish each other good for the other's sake. Don and Peggy emerge as moral equivalents, each hiding a dark secret (the stolen identity; the baby given away) and each having done for the other what no one else could, from the hospital visit ('Move forward') to Don's 'nobody understands that, but you do' recruitment pitch; Joan and Roger form a second pair whose mutual esteem survives his marriage to Jane and her departure, shown when he trusts her to build Sterling Cooper Draper Pryce. Closing with Aristotle's claim that friendship holds states together, the chapter gives the new agency a better-than-average chance because these friendships are 'not for sale.'
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 31 "The Office and Philosophy" — Arp and Watson sort Dunder Mifflin's relationships into five conceptions of love: Roy's erotic 'best sex of your life' Valentine's offer to Pam as blind eros; Angela and Dwight's pursuit of an idealized mate read through Plato's Forms and the Symposium's ascent to Beauty; Aristotle's three friendships, under which the office's alliances are mere utility while Jim and Pam's teapot sacrifice in 'Christmas Party' approaches virtue friendship; the Stoic-Kantian 'equal loving' of universal respect, laughed at when Michael ranks himself with Bono and Lincoln; and agape-style family loyalty that leads Dwight to supply Michael his urine in 'Drug Testing'. The chapter concludes that Michael exemplifies a selfishness Western philosophy has no name for, failing at every form of love.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 25 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Spanakos asks why Spider-Man is called 'friendly' by testing Peter's relationships against Aristotle's three philias (pleasure, utility, virtue) and the proportionality principle that the morally inferior friend should love the superior more — a principle that breaks down for a superhero as godlike as Spider-Man. Peter's secrecy and self-sacrifice block true Aristotelian fellowship with MJ, whose crush on Spidey is mere fantasy-love, and Harry's friendship rests on pleasure and utility, failing every Aristotelian test. Yet against philia the chapter sets Christian agape (St. Basil, John 15, C.S. Lewis's Four Loves): unconditional, self-sacrificial love for the unlovable, which Peter practices toward his betrayers and which Harry finally enacts when he dies saving Peter in Spider-Man 3 — an agape that makes him Peter's equal.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 8 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Eberl reads Jax's Season 5 dilemma (Tara's ultimatum to leave SAMCRO or lose his family) through Aristotle's account of virtue as character cultivated by habituation in a polis. SAMCRO nurtures genuine virtues—Opie's selfless loyalty, courage under fire, the club's communal generosity toward Donna and Lyla—alongside vices like Clay's greed and Tig's lust, with the golden mean distinguishing Bobby's critical loyalty from Chuckie's obsequiousness and Juice's rash minefield charge. Fr. Ashby's fight to keep Abel in Belfast away from Jax's cycle of violence, and the contrast between Deputy Chief Hale's law-abiding ideals and Mayor Hale's self-serving development, illustrate Aristotle's claim that legislators and environments make citizens good or bad. The chapter concludes that Jax's very mix of virtue and vice—the 'savage' needed to head the table—may be what reform requires, at moral cost.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 10 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Takes Tig's misplaced revenge on Laroy—which kills Veronica Pope and triggers Damon Pope's burning of Tig's daughter and Opie's prison murder—together with the club's unconditional convoy rescue in 'To Be, Act 1' to ask whether loyalty is a virtue. It tests three accounts: the Aristotelian view (via Ladd's 'loyal Nazi is a contradiction') that only the virtuous can be loyal, which would deny that SAMCRO members can be loyal at all; the Humean view that loyalty is bigoted partiality; and the Kantian point that only the good will is unconditionally good, so loyalty can serve any wrongdoing. The chapter defends Ewin's line that loyalty is good in itself but issues in right action only joined with virtue, while the Stahl frame-up of Opie and Donna's death show the dark enforcement side—'rats deserve to die, end of story.'
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 31 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Presents three ancient alternatives to SAMCRO's warrior ethic. Diogenes the Cynic, 'the earliest of all the fathers of anarchy,' matches J.T.'s Harley-commune ideal — reject greed, convention, and wage slavery like Tig punching the clock at Teller-Morrow — but the chapter argues pure anarchy regenerates hierarchy: with no authority, revenge becomes the only justice and 'a big guy like Clay' mugs 'a small guy like Chuckie.' Plato's Republic supplies the reformist pole — impartial justice for all citizens rather than loyalty circles, rulers picked from proven warriors for wisdom (Tara belongs healing, not scheming), family curbed where it breeds Gemma-style favoritism — yet proves too authoritarian, so Aristotle's function argument (reason as the human ergon), virtue, and the three kinds of friendship (SAMCRO's pleasure-friendships, Clay–Unser's usefulness) sketch a livable middle way with duties even to strangers.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 9 "Notes" — Jerold Abrams reads J. J. Abrams's Kirk as Aristotle's megalopsychos and 'god among men' from the Politics: too excellent to be a mere crewmember, disdainful of rank, speaking openly from love and hate, and a law unto himself. The four-on-one bar fight, reprogramming the unwinnable Kobayashi Maru, declaring 'Some should be' above the Prime Directive to Pike, and his exile to frozen Delta Vega (like the Argonauts stranding Heracles) all enact Aristotle's dilemma that a society must either exile such a man or submit to his monarchy. Spock, a great-souled man himself, becomes Kirk's 'second self' in Aristotle's truest friendship once Kirk takes the captain's chair.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 31 "Notes" — Applies Aristotle's three friendships to Trek: Ferengi Rules of Acquisition dealings and treaties as utility friendships, Bashir and O'Brien's darts and racquetball as friendship of pleasure, and virtuous friendship as requiring emotion, mutual goodwill, and irreplaceable intrinsic valuing - which emotionless Data fails at with Jenna D'Sora in "In Theory". The core argument, following Badhwar, is that consequentialism is logically and psychologically incompatible with virtuous friendship: Spock's "needs of the many" maxim and Data's "for the greater good" experimentation on Geordi in "Descent, Part II" show friends being treated as sacrificeable instruments, while the Kobayashi Maru cheat shows consequentialist reasoning blessing outcomes over means. Kirk's reversal - "the needs of the one outweigh the needs of the many" in The Search for Spock - and T'Pol's years caring for the amnesiac Archer in "Twilight" exemplify acting out of friendship rather than for any further goal.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Littmann shows Luke, Leia, and Han repeatedly put friends and family above the galaxy's freedom - Luke abandoning Dagobah for Bespin, the Jabba rescue, refusing to kill Vader - in the tradition of Homer's heroes, then submits them to Athenian scrutiny. Socrates's refusal to escape his Athens prison and his implicit just agreement with the city set civic duty over friendship; Plato would abolish the guardians' family and censor the Zeus-Kronos patricide myth yet approves of Luke sparing Vader; Aristotle prizes philia but holds citizens belong to the state. He concludes the philosophers mostly win: heroic loyalty is often moral failure, and good moral reasoning asks how many people an action affects, not just whom you love.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 25 "Humanoids and Droids Having Sex" — Munn and Weijers argue that Lando and L3-37 in Solo display all the hallmarks of friendship and one-sided romantic love: Lando abandons self-preservation to carry the injured L3 to the Falcon and endorses her droid-emancipation crusade, while L3 tells Qi'ra she has considered a relationship with him but finds them 'not compatible'. Testing Bennet Helm's four accounts of love (union, deep mutual caring, valuing, emotional state) against the film, they conclude humanoid-droid love is genuinely possible, and that L3's claim that sex with Lando 'works' is plausible once sex is defined broadly as any activity yielding sexual reward. They ground droid friendship in Aristotle's incomplete versus complete friendships, contrasting the rewarding partnerships of R2-D2 with Anakin and BB-8 with Poe against the merely strategic Han-Lando Sabacc rivalry.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 43 "“And I, I'm All the Jedi!”" — Okapal uses Aristotle's three friendships to frame the saga as a story of desert children seeking community: utility friendships like Hondo Ohnaka's and the Sith Rule of Two, where Darth Bane's apprentice is a mere instrument and Sidious calls Maul, Tyranus, and Vader 'easy to replace', stand against the other-regarding virtuous friendships of Obi-Wan, Kanan, and the Rey-Finn-Poe triad, where friends sacrifice for each other's sake as Ezra learns about Kanan in 'A World Between Worlds'. Luke's premature departure for Cloud City fails the 'for the other's sake' test Yoda poses. Rey can only choose the Jedi community knowingly once she learns she is Palpatine's granddaughter, and her closing claim 'I'm Rey Skywalker' is a choice between two value systems - the plural, other-regarding Jedi Code versus the self-regarding 'I' of the Sith Code - making friendship and community, not blood, the root of identity.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 24 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Goguen reads the Winchesters through two masculine ideals: the warrior (Dean and Michael, chivalric protection culminating in Dean's 'protecting Sam... it's who I am') and the sovereign (Sam and Lucifer, whose freedom is analyzed with Isaiah Berlin's negative and positive liberty, with nods to Hobbes's absolute sovereign and Nietzsche's Übermensch). The show's stoic culture, where 'baring my soul like a freaking girl' is an insult, keeps the L-word unspoken, making Ellen's dying 'I will always love you, baby' to Jo a foil the brothers cannot match. Plato's Symposium, via Aristophanes' myth of split soulmates, and Aristotle's claim that the purest love is between virtuous male friends make sense of the 'psychotically, irrationally, erotically codependent' bond, and the chapter concludes that true masculinity requires embracing the seemingly supernatural: love.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 12 "Notes" — Begley and Biondi argue Ted is an ethical egoist in the Aristotelian-Randian sense: like Howard Roark of The Fountainhead (Ted's favorite book), he is a self-loving creator who loves his work, has a 'self-sufficient ego' immune to others' approval, and pursues long-range values, so his kindness and biscuits are rational self-interest, not selflessness. Against Hobbesian psychological egoism they distinguish genuine egoists from narcissists like Rupert and hedonists like Season 1 Jamie, defend Ted's divorce and the curse-reverse ceremony as only apparent sacrifices, and read his panic-attack therapy arc as the egoist's project of achieving inner wholeness.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 15 "Notes" — Forte maps the Richmond cast onto Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: Rebecca, Nate, Roy, and Jamie begin incontinent or near-vicious; courage is the mean between Nate's cowardice and Roy's rashness; and their friendless misery illustrates why friendship (utility, pleasure, complete) is necessary for eudaimonia. Ted's coaching works as a modern strengths-based complement to Aristotelian habituation - Phoebe's Princess-and-Dragon play tempers Roy, Jamie's competitiveness is redirected into team play, Nate misses the mean and becomes mean - and the finale's 'progress over perfection' framing shows all of them as works in progress toward teloi.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 16 "Notes" — Loftin argues the Diamond Dogs enact Aristotle's complete friendship: Jamie and Rebecca fail at friendship because they misconceive the good as self-gratification, and following Philippa Foot's natural-kind account of human good (plus Cicero on goodwill and C. S. Lewis's Four Loves) he shows friendship is an intrinsic good of human beings as such. Ted's vulnerability before Beard, Nate, and Higgins invites them into virtuous activity, Higgins's defection from Rebecca's sabotage scheme displays friendship against a relationship fueled by hurt, and Nate's status-hunger explains why he mistakes Ted's laughter and Rupert's patronage for friendship.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 17 "Notes" — Wible asks whether Ted's friendliness with players and staff constitutes moral friendship, testing it against Aristotle's three friendship types, Hume on solitude, and Bennett Helm's conditions (shared activity, intimacy, mutual care) plus a power-imbalance requirement Kant's respect for persons underwrites. This condemns Rebecca and Sam's relationship as a conflict of interest too risky to permit, questions Led Tasso and benching decisions, yet concludes that Aristotle's virtue friendship between coach and player is possible and preferable to Drewe's limited utility-friendship, since Ted's virtuous friendships make players better people while still knowing when to prioritize team over individual.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 31 "18. War Means Fighting and Fighting Includes Philosophizing" — Vuckovich reads 'Still Valley' through Glaucon's Ring of Gyges: Sgt. Paradine, handed a witchcraft handbook that freezes the Union army before Gettysburg, confronts the temptation of costless, unearned victory, and his burning of the handbook rather than renounce God preserves a principle worth more than winning. Aristotle's claim that bad men can be friends through shared wickedness explains the witchman Teague's bond with Paradine, an 'alliance' that recruits the desperate soldier to do the Devil's dirty work. The chapter ends on the shameful secret legacy: even burying the episode leaves Paradine with a private war in his conscience, a pyrrhic loss for a fighting man who almost surrendered what he holds sacred.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 18 "“See, This Dame Walks In”" — Catlyn Origitano sorts Veronica's relationships through Aristotle's three kinds of friendship in the Nicomachean Ethics: Keith and Cliff McCormack's referral exchange is a friendship of utility, Logan and Dick's partying a friendship of pleasure, and Wallace's bond with Veronica utility fraying into his complaint 'How about you do me a favor for once?' when reciprocity turns one-sided. Perfect friendship of virtue requires mutual trust between genuinely good people, and the chapter's audit finds no one qualifies — Wallace lies and cheats, Logan supplied the GHB and ran from the Tijuana fire, and Veronica's snooping and 'I'm not built that way' refusal to trust disqualify her too. She concludes that noir Neptune itself, where 'the people you love let you down,' may block perfect friendship, though the movie-era Veronica, retired from detection, might at last be ready for one.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 18 "Notes" — Hoffman and Kolmes use Aristotle's friendship as 'another self' and Kant's 'exchange of welfare' to value the pre-New 52 Superman-Wonder Woman friendship (Rucka's heart-to-hearts, Superman choosing to save Wonder Woman over Lois's father), then argue DC's 2011 reboot of the pair into a romance exemplifies Brake's amatonormativity and the heteronormative 'When Harry Met Sally' assumption that cross-gender closeness must be sexual. Diana's answer to Lois - 'We're just good friends' - becomes a refusal to rank friendship below romance. The erasure matters beyond comics: it denies role models for cross-gender friendship and stigmatizes bi and pansexual people as incapable of friendship at all.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 24 "Notes" — Tobienne reads Wonder Woman as sophia personified and a rhetorician in Aristotle's sense, whose real weapon is persuasion: he dissects the Rucka 'Lies' dialogue where she talks the feral Cheetah back to her humanity ('You are a WOMAN... You are my FRIEND!') and her verbal disarmament of a mind-sick Power Girl while holding her in a headlock. Nicomachean Ethics VI grounds the claim that practical wisdom recognizes the need for friends - each woman needs the other - and Wonder Woman's own submission to Athena and Aphrodite explains how the lasso of loving authority, not brute force, disarms Man's World.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 10 "Building Communities One Gym at a Time" — Webb uses Indiana high school basketball to argue the communitarian case against liberal individualism: drawing on MacIntyre, Sandel, and Walzer, he contends communities (not rights-bearing individuals) are the source of meaning, and that small-town gyms like the New Castle Fieldhouse were public spaces that built genuine community. He reads Rick Mount's choice of hometown fame over the pros, the Milan miracle, and the abolition of Indiana's single-class tournament as evidence that mass media and national sport replace real 'face-to-face' communities with 'virtual' ones, using Conseco Fieldhouse's nostalgic theming as his prime example of that loss.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 17 "The Beauty of the Game" — The Brands stage a broadcast-booth debate about whether a championship game was 'beautiful,' with Dickie V defending Hume's subjectivism ('beauty is in the eye of the beholder' and the expert's delicacy of taste) and Billy defending Plato's objective Form of Beauty. Jim exposes each side's flaw (Hume's circular appeal to experts, Plato's third-man regress from the Parmenides/Aristotle) and proposes a synthesis: games have 'outer beauty' (universally observable fluid motion, like improvised jazz or dance) and 'inner beauty' (the strategy and reason the knowledgeable fan grasps), reconciling the objective and subjective.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 11 "Football and Aristotle'S Philosophy of Friendship" — Gallagher maps Aristotle's three kinds of philia onto football: friendship of utility (the quarterback needing his offensive linemen), of pleasure (Friday-night high school and college ball), and of shared goodness (Bo Schembechler's bond with Anthony Carter, who deflected reporters to teammates). He reads the Steelers dynasty and Paterno's locker-room 'love' through Aristotle's 'concord' and 'a single soul in two bodies,' and answers Bertrand Russell's worry about violent competition by insisting football is grounded in philia, not enmity.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 33 "Seventeenth Hole More Than a Playing Partner Golf and Friendship" — Andy Wible argues that although golf looks like the ultimate solitary sport, it is unusually good at fostering friendship, and analyzes friendship through Aristotle's three kinds (utility, pleasure, and the highest, based on the friend's good character), supplemented by Laurence Thomas (choice, equality, mutual trust) and Blum on care as a moral phenomenon. Golf's long unhurried rounds, self-called penalties, handicap system, shared memorable shots, and retirement communities build the intimacy, trust and equality Aristotle prizes, and Robert Simon's 'mutual quest for excellence' reconciles competition with goodwill. Wible then confronts friendship's partiality—exclusionary country clubs and the sex-segregated LPGA—using Marilyn Friedman's voluntary friendship communities to argue clubs should drop discrimination on race, sex, religion and orientation while keeping friendship's care and loyalty.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 24 "Friendship, Rivalry, and Excellence" — The chapter uses Aristotle's three friendships (pleasure, usefulness, virtue) to ask how tennis rivals competing for one prize can be friends, illustrating pleasure with Borg and Gerulaitis, usefulness with the tense but genuine Ashe-McEnroe Davis Cup bond, and virtue with the Evert-Navratilova rivalry that grew into deep mutual care despite a competitive women's tour. It adds C. S. Lewis's view that friends stand side by side absorbed in a shared thing, then reads Jimmy Connors as a Nietzschean Ubermensch whose master-morality drive to dominate makes him, paradoxically, the best 'star friend' by pushing rivals to their limits. It closes unresolved on whether the tension between friendship and rivalry can ever be eliminated.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 15 "Me and You Identity, Love, and Friendship in the Films of Charlie Kaufman" — Den Uyl argues that Kaufman's films are really about friendship rather than romance, reading them through Aristotle's character friendship (the friend as 'other self' and mirror of self-knowledge) and Montaigne's ideal of a free, voluntary friendship that also engages the body. Charlie's fictional twin Donald in Adaptation externalizes the integrity Charlie lacks, and only after internalizing Donald can he say 'I love her'; Caden in Synecdoche fails because he looks only at himself. Love succeeds, on this reading, only when grounded in the self-sufficiency and self-respect that make one capable of an 'other self,' as Eternal Sunshine's Joel and Clementine haltingly discover.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 17 "Charlie Kaufman, Philosophy, and the Small Screen" — Chambers reads Kaufman's TV sitcom Ned and Stacey through queer theory, arguing its marriage-of-convenience premise stages a critique of 'the normal.' Because Ned and Stacey only play at being husband and wife and never desire the romantic telos, the show troubles heteronormativity more than the openly gay Will & Grace, whose characters chase marriage and family. Chambers uses Butler's Lacanian notion of masquerade to claim there is no 'real' husband or wife beneath the role, only role-playing, and ties this to the philia (not eros) bond of the leads and to the masquerade running through Kaufman's films.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — The editors' introduction argues that Eastwood, though no academic, does 'practical philosophy' through his films as a craftsman who inherits and then revises genres (revising the Western in Unforgiven, rethinking rugged individualism in Million Dollar Baby and Gran Torino). Invoking MacIntyre's claim that we are only co-authors of interlocking narratives, it reads Eastwood's focus on decisive moral choices (Francesca's refusal to leave in Bridges of Madison County, Butch Haynes in A Perfect World) as a 'laboratory of moral psychology' echoing Aristotle's 'choice discriminates character.' It ties his concern with loss, justice, and Aristotelian friendship and flourishing (Grinnell on Million Dollar Baby) to a Socratic 'know thyself,' arguing his philosophizing is implicit and nonverbal rather than argued in words.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 12 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Grinnell applies Aristotle's classification of friendship (utility, pleasure, and complete character-friendship between equals in excellence) to Million Dollar Baby and Gran Torino. Frankie/Maggie and Walt/Thao begin as incomplete, utility relationships across barriers of age, sex, and culture, then ripen into character-friendships of 'other selves' who pursue each other's good. He resolves the apparent paradox that friendship demands bringing about a death: Frankie euthanizes Maggie against his own wishes to honor her autonomy and whole-life excellence, while Walt engineers his own death and deceives Thao to spare him a vengeance that would destroy his character — each an Aristotelian sacrifice of self-interest for the friend that preserves the friendship's excellence.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 14 "“And It’s Such a Beautiful Day!” shame and Fargo" — Hanrahan and Stearns read Fargo through Aristotle's theory of shame and its link to friendship, sorting the characters into his moral hierarchy: Gaear is the shameless self-indulgent man, Jerry is the morally incontinent one whose flickers of shame (before Scotty, before the swindled customer) stay inert against his greed, and Marge is the exemplar of excellence. They argue that a capacity for shame requires valuing others non-instrumentally, which the co-conspirators cannot do because they relate only through friendships of utility (Carl and the prostitute, Jerry using his son). Marge's friendship-of-the-good with Norm grounds both her decency and her ability to mediate others' shame, and her 'it's such a beautiful day' expresses the same noninstrumental valuing that makes moral concern possible.
- **The Philosophy of Joss Whedon**, ch. 6 "The Peculiarities of Free Will" — This file collects Part I chapters 1-5. It argues Whedon's heroes (Angel, Buffy, Spike, Simon, Echo, Captain America) achieve authentic selfhood by resisting depersonalizing forces, reading their 'angst' through Heidegger and Sartre while insisting Whedon is more Socratic than existentialist because he affirms objective goods, synthesized via a Rawlsian just society. It then adds Aristotle on friendship and community (Toy Story, Jayne, Angel's team) and defends an atheistic ethics grounding natural rights in Locke and Kant plus Aristotelian virtue (Spike's re-ensoulment), using the Euthyphro to reject divine-command theory. The title chapter argues Whedon's paradoxical portrayal of free will in The Shepherd's Tale, Dollhouse and Cabin fits neither hard determinism nor compatibilism but Robert Kane's libertarian self-forming actions.
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — Sanders reads Casino as a dramatization of ethical egoism, using the parasitic bond between Nicky Santoro and Ace Rothstein to ask whether an egoist who treats a friend as a mere instrument can have real friendship. He distinguishes 'maximizing' egoism (Nicky's ruinous take-everything drive, ending in his beating death) from a 'satisficing' egoism that restricts its own dispositions, arguing against Blum, Wilcox and an Aristotelian objection that only the maximizing version is truly incompatible with friendship. Aristotle's account of virtue and friendship supplies the standard the film's egoists fall short of.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 9 "Watsons, Adlers, Lestrades, and Moriarties On the Nature of Friends and Enemies" — Tallon applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics taxonomy of friendship—of use, of pleasure, and of virtue—to Holmes's relationships, plus Aquinas on friends helping each other flourish. The Baker Street Irregulars and Mrs. Hudson are friends of use; Holmes has few friends of pleasure; Watson is the friend of virtue, an 'other self' sharing virtue, support, and activity (getting Holmes off cocaine, taking a bullet). Inverting the account, he classifies Holmes's enemies as competitor (Irene Adler), rival/'frenemy' (Lestrade and Gregson), and foe (Moriarty), arguing a foe—an anti-self—can never become a friend.
- **Joss Whedon as Philosopher**, ch. 6 "The Peculiarities of Free Will" — This file collects Part I's chapters, arguing the Whedonverse embodies serious philosophy. It reads Angel, Buffy, Simon Tam, Echo, and the Avengers through Heidegger's inauthenticity/angst and Sartre's existentialism (Dr. Horrible and the Operative as inauthentic 'monsters'), then adds Rawls and Aristotle to claim some authentic lives are better led, using Gyges's ring (in 'Gone' and 'In the Dark') and Aristotelian friendship (Team Angel, Serenity's crew) as touchstones. It defends an atheistic moral realism via Kant on personhood and Locke's natural rights (Mal insisting Saffron is 'no one's property'), and closes on free will: reading The Shepherd's Tale, Dollhouse, and The Cabin in the Woods against d'Holbach's hard determinism, Flamson's compatibilism, and Robert Kane's libertarian self-forming actions (Connor's choice in 'Inside Out').
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 4 "Love, Value, and the Human Destiny in Interstellar" — Belluomini and Dunn use Interstellar's clash between Cooper's partial parental love and Professor Brand's species-level 'Plan B' to ask why the survival of humanity matters and what 'saving humanity' means. Drawing on Aristotle, they treat Cooper's daughter Murph as 'another self' loved as an end in itself and tie the good to individual happiness (eudaimonia), so 5,000 faceless embryos could never be the intrinsic good a real family is. They then turn to Kant to argue humans have unconditional value (dignity) as rational beings, which both grounds a reason to preserve the species AND condemns Brand's 'monstrous lie' as treating people merely as means to an end they do not share.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 34 "I Am the Bad Wolf" — Roman Altshuler answers Davros's charge that the Doctor is a 'destroyer of worlds' using Aristotelian virtue ethics. He argues the Doctor's chief virtue is not compassion but Heideggerian 'authentic concern': offering aggressors (the Nestene, Sontarans, the Master) a genuine choice so they become responsible for escalating, illustrated by the fly-swatter thought experiment. Companions, being 'another self' (Aristotle on friendship), make their acts partly the Doctor's own, yet their human 'Bad Wolf Syndrome' lets compassion override the impartial concern that requires respecting choice, which is why the Doctor runs from what his companions do in his name.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 20 "10. Cas Is Family" — Doll traces Castiel's arc from a cold Divine-Command/utilitarian 'hammer of the Lord' to a member of the Winchester family through Aristotle's ethics. She argues Cas learns to contemplate and act on the chief good under Dean's tutelage, pursuing eudaimonia by habituation despite repeated failures (becoming a false god, the Leviathans), and that his bond with Sam and Dean grows through Aristotle's three friendships—utility, pleasure, and finally the rare true friendship of virtuous character—culminating in his self-sacrificing declaration of love that defeats Billie.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 23 "NOTES" — Michael W. Austin applies Jane English's claim that adult children owe their parents 'nothing' to the fraught father-son relationships of Lost. He works through Jack and Christian Shephard's operating-room cover-up, Locke being conned out of a kidney and paralyzed by Anthony Cooper, and Sawyer's murder-suicide father to argue that parental sacrifices create debts only on the commonsense view English rejects. English's alternative is that such sacrifices ideally generate friendship rather than obligation, which Austin illustrates with the unbookkept mutual aid among Sawyer, Kate, Hurley, and Locke, contrasting Jack's line 'I'm not one of his friends' about retrieving his dead father.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 31 "18. War Means Fighting and Fighting Includes Philosophizing" — Vuckovich analyzes 'Still Valley,' where Confederate Sergeant Paradine can win the Civil War using a witchcraft handbook that freezes Union troops but only by renouncing God. He reads Paradine's temptation through Glaucon's Ring of Gyges myth in Plato's Republic (the committed unjust man who outdoes enemies without scruple) and Aristotle's friendships of shared pleasure (Paradine and the witchman Teague bonded by hatred of the enemy). Paradine burns the handbook rather than damn the Confederacy, preserving a core principle of fairness even at the cost of an easy victory—winning isn't everything.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 10 "Stephen King and Aristotelian Friendship" — Bertha Alvarez Manninen reads The Body (Stand by Me) and Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption through Aristotle's Nicomachean and Eudemian Ethics on the three friendships. Andy and Norton/the guards exemplify friendships of utility (the tax help, the Rita Hayworth poster), the boys' tree-house camaraderie and Vern/Teddy exemplify pleasure friendships that dissolve as characters change, while Gordie-and-Chris and Andy-and-Red model enduring friendships of virtue rooted in mutual good will, shared confidences, and cultivating each other's excellence. Manninen then presses Aristotle: his strict 'only good men' criterion and his debt-bound, property-like view of the parent-child bond fail the flawed-but-loyal Andy/Red and the abusive fathers in The Body, showing human friendship is more complex than his taxonomy allows.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 8 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Marinucci's editorial introduction surveys the volume, framing Austen's six novels as a body of work with philosophical value across love/marriage, morality/virtue, wealth/class, concepts, and zombie mashups. It previews each contributor's thesis: Bufacchi reading Anne Elliot and the Bennets through Fricker's epistemic injustice, Dougherty aligning Austen's ideal marriage with Aristotelian complete friendship, Lindenmuth pairing Austen with Nietzsche on marital happiness, and Bane's Marxist reading of the 1940 Pride and Prejudice film. It argues Austen is an 'accidental philosopher' whose insight into social relations, especially women's vulnerability, carries philosophical weight.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 14 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Dougherty argues Austen's ideal marriage mirrors Aristotle's complete friendship, where the friend is loved for who they are and becomes a 'second self.' She sorts Austen's relationships into Aristotle's three kinds: utility (Emma and Mrs. Elton, Charlotte and Mr. Collins), pleasure (Lydia and Wickham, the fading Emma-Harriet bond), and complete friendship grounded in mutual good character (Jane and Bingley, Elizabeth and Darcy, Emma and Knightley). Central is the 'second self' as mirror: Darcy's letter and Knightley's rebukes let Elizabeth and Emma see themselves ('Till this moment I never knew myself'), so marriage-as-friendship improves self-knowledge and virtue and must not be left to chance as Charlotte urges.
- **Food & Philosophy - Eat, Think, and Be Merry**, ch. 7 "Chapter 1" — Verene argues that cooking marks the transition from nature to culture, reading Plato's Protagoras myth of Prometheus (fire and the practical arts) and the Republic's claim that a city's first need is food as evidence that humans alone 'eat' rather than 'feed.' Tracing Greco-Roman banquets, Vico's account of Roman dining, and Brillat-Savarin's Physiology of Taste, he connects the ordered courses of a proper meal to Aristotle's view of imagination as rooted in memory and to friendship at table. He ends by mapping Brillat-Savarin's gourmandism onto Epicurus's distinction between kinetic pleasures (eating fine food) and catastematic pleasure (ataraxia, the settled well-being of good health and stored memories of shared meals).
- **Food & Philosophy - Eat, Think, and Be Merry**, ch. 8 "Chapter 2" — Verene interprets Plutarch's Dinner of the Seven Wise Men, in which Thales, Solon, Bias and the others gather at Corinth under Periander and turn a plain dinner into a symposium on good government, household economics, and the soul. He reads their exchanges through Aristotle: Thales' claim that a ruler's happiness is to die naturally in old age is glossed by Aristotle's eudaimonia (no one is called happy until life is complete), the assigned-seating companions exemplify Aristotle's friendship of utility, and the pivot from politics to home management mirrors Aristotle linking Politics to Economics. Solon's Stoic argument that dependence on food enslaves the soul, and Thales' correction of the Ethiopian king's riddle-answers (virtue not God as most helpful), show the Seven speaking as philosophers rather than gourmets, with Epicurus invoked on death being nothing to the living.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 29 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Carreras, writing as a son, examines the ethical tension in the father-son relationship between using a father's inevitable influence and fostering the son's autonomy. Opening with Aristotle on parents loving children as 'something of himself,' he uses the case of Jerry (a lawyer) pressuring his son Jose (who loves 18th-century English literature) to argue for a 'foundational view' of autonomy – that the best life is one embraced 'from the inside,' likened to seeing without a value-blindfold – and advises fathers to ask 'Is this what he truly wants, or what I want?'
- **College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits**, ch. 20 "College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits" — This span closes the walk-of-shame semiotics and then applies ancient ethics to college relationships. Puka defends long-distance college relationships through Aristotle's account of philia—arguing (provocatively, per Aristotle) that love is an activity, so being apart 'murders' love unless couples make Skype, sexting, and texting into the relationship's real medium rather than a substitute. Stephens brings Epicurus and Lucretius to 'friends with benefits': since sexual passion is a natural-but-unnecessary desire that breeds anxiety and love is a wound to the mind, while friendship is necessary for ataraxia, he concludes students should skip the sex and keep the friend—'friends are the real benefits,' echoing Tina Turner's 'What's Love Got to Do with It?' Levine/Mongeau and Smith/Morrison supply communication-research data on how FWB relationships form, are negotiated (usually not), and often end when one partner 'catches feelings.'
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 9 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Editors Kristie Miller and Marlene Clark introduce the volume by opening with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics claim that the human drive to couple is even stronger than the drive to live as a political being and that fulfillment rests in loving relationships. They frame dating as a rule-governed 'game' with aims and strategies and preview each contributor's essay—Jenkins on flirting, Langan on conservative men, Samp and Cohen against unconditional love, the elevator metaphor, cyberdating, evolutionary seduction, and Colyvan's game-theoretic mate search—tying age-old ethical questions about treating partners well to new work in evolutionary psychology, decision theory, and the ethics of online romance.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 13 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Jennifer Samp and Andrew Cohen argue against the Notebook-style romantic ideal of unconditional love, casting dating as a 'calculated exchange' explained by social-exchange and interdependence theory (comparison level and comparison level of alternatives). Adopting Aristotle's distinction between friendships of utility/pleasure and 'complete friendships' in which one values the friend as 'another self' and as an end in itself, they hold the best romances are complete friendships—yet insist even these must be conditioned. Their key thought experiment: a genuinely boundless love would survive discovering one's partner is a child-molesting murderer; since it should not, 'true love knows bounds' and remains part of a good life only because it can be defeated by such reasons.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 16 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Mary Beth Yount asks whether being 'crazy in love' really resembles mental illness, noting lovesickness was a diagnosis for nearly two millennia and that love's mood swings mimic bipolar or schizophrenic symptoms. She organizes the analysis around the four Greek loves—eros (with Plato's ladder from physical beauty to the Forms, i.e., 'Platonic love'), philia (Aristotle's Nicomachean friendship of good character), storge (familial affection), and agape (C.S. Lewis's unconditional charity)—arguing a full romance blends all four. She then surveys Fisher, Aron, and Brown's fMRI work showing romantic love as a dopamine-driven mammalian mate-choice drive stronger than the sex drive, and the 'protest'/'resignation' stages of rejection, to reassure daters their craziness is normal biology, not disorder.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 21 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Joshua Heter mounts a virtue-theoretic case against being set up on blind dates, using Aristotle's notion of telos and the distinction between fleeting 'hot-fudge happiness' and eudaimonia, the flourishing of a well-lived life (illustrated by long-married Bill and Fran). He argues a 'guy's' function is achieved by exercising his whole nature, and dramatizes this with Zoo-bear versus Wild-bear: the zoo-fed bear has its hunger and safety met but cannot flourish because it never hunts or roams, just as matchmaking meets the romantic need while letting a man's 'social muscles' atrophy. Invoking Aristotle's philia (and Nussbaum on Aristotelian virtue), he concedes friends mean well but recommends they merely introduce people and let things progress naturally rather than force an 'unnatural' match.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 22 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Hamilton reads the pick-up-artist 'Game' (Mystery, Style, negs, peacocking, the Alpha frame) against Aristotle's great-souled magnanimous man, arguing that the jerk and the PUA succeed because they inadvertently mimic the Megalopsuche's self-containment and indifference to others' approval. He contends the ethical route is to genuinely acquire that character through habituation ('we become brave by acting bravely') rather than fake it, so the nice guy's supplication fails while true magnanimity requires the full virtues. He then uses Aristotle's three grades of friendship (utility, pleasure, and the highest disinterested philia) to argue that erotic relationships can rise to real friendship only where partners are equals, citing When Harry Met Sally on whether men and women can be friends.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 16 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Gregory Bassham mines the happy communities of the Shire, Rivendell, and Lothlorien for six keys to happiness: delight in simple things (linked to Epicurus's natural pleasures and Thoreau's Walden simplicity), making light of troubles, close friendship (grounded in Aristotle's claim that friendship is the greatest external good), good character, cherishing beauty and creativity, and recovering wonder. He argues Tolkien's hobbits and elves illustrate what modern happiness research confirms, so Tolkien functions as a philosophical guide to a more joy-filled life.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 17 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Jorge Gracia contrasts Sam and Gollum, two hobbits of shared nature and culture who both pursue happiness but reach opposite ends. Gollum's happiness is possession of the Precious, a thing, sought in isolation and won by murdering Deagol, which destroys him; Sam's happiness is fellowship in the Shire with Frodo and Rosie, and his love for Frodo lets him surrender the Ring where Gollum cannot. Drawing on Aristotle's tie between happiness, one's nature, and friendship, Gracia concludes that for ordinary beings happiness is achievable only in a social context whose key is love expressed as loyalty and sharing.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 14 "12. Firefly as Philosophy Social Contracts, Political Dissent, and Virtuous Communities" — Kowalski argues that Firefly and Serenity embody a distinctive political theory he calls 'Since I Found Serenity' (SIFS). The mindless, savage Reavers represent Hobbes's state of nature, showing government is necessary; but the Alliance's torture of River, the Miranda/Pax atrocity, and the murderous blue-gloved agents and Operative make a Hobbesian reading untenable and vindicate Locke's natural rights and right of revolution — Mal's 'I aim to misbehave' broadcast of the Miranda file is Lockean civil disobedience. He then presses the tacit-consent problem (the Browncoats cannot leave the 'Verse) and supplements Locke with Aristotle's friendship and community: Serenity's crew becomes a virtuous mobile commonwealth where friendship (Simon forgiving Jayne, Mal's 'love keeps her in the air') turns a commonwealth into a good-life community.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 15 "13. Arrested Development as Philosophy Family First What We Owe Our Parents" — Phillips uses the dysfunctional Bluths to ask what, if anything, adult children owe their parents. Against Sidgwick's reluctance and various grounds for filial obligation, he argues negatively through the family: George Sr. and Lucille never meet the motivation and above-duty conditions for a debt of gratitude; adopted Lindsay's absentee mothering of Maeby shows biology alone grounds nothing; and Michael's dutiful-son and overbearing-father roles show the social role of 'parent' is not enough (Hardimon's 'reflectively acceptable' roles). Positively, deploying Aristotle's three friendships (utility, pleasure, virtue), he argues that only a voluntary friendship of virtue grounds special obligations — illustrated when a rock-bottom, 'useless' Gob and George Sr. finally bond as near-equals, the show's closest thing to genuine friendship.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 41 "38. The Big Lebowski Nihilism, Masculinity, and Abiding Virtue" — Fosl argues that The Big Lebowski critiques traditional masculine ideals (soldier, tycoon, detective, patriarch) and offers in The Dude an alternative 'abiding' virtue rooted in Epicurean contented poverty and ataraxia (his simple pleasures, White Russians, and indifference to property), Aristotelian civic friendship or philia with Walter and Donny that holds a divided polity together, and a Wittgenstein/Aristotle-informed flexibility about applying rules that positions The Dude at a mean between Walter's rigid absolutism and the nihilists' deficiency. Most centrally the film confronts Nietzschean European nihilism ('God is dead'); The Dude answers it as a halfway Ubermensch through comedy, friendship, and Kierkegaardian and Camusian existential repetition (bowling as rolling the rock, Sisyphus made meaningful), abiding and reproducing his form of life against despair, death, and disillusionment.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 42 "39. Harry Potter as Philosophy Five Types of Friendship" — Okapal uses the Harry Potter films to expand Aristotle's theory of philia (friendship/love), which recognizes friendships for virtue, pleasure, and utility grounded in other-regarding concern, intimacy, choice, and a surrounding community. He argues the films show that friendships for pleasure and utility each come in beneficent and maleficent forms distinguished by whether motivations are other-regarding or purely self-regarding: the Quidditch team and the Harry-Ginny romance are beneficent pleasure-friendships (Ginny hides the Prince's book out of concern for Harry), while the Hermione-McLaggen date and Ron-Lavender fling are maleficent and short-lived. Slughorn's Slug Club is a beneficent utility-friendship of mutual advantage one may freely leave, whereas Voldemort's Death Eaters are maleficent, with all benefit flowing one way and no exit, yielding five types of friendship and locating Gryffindor's courage, inclusiveness, and loyalty as the ground of virtuous friendship.

### The State of Nature

The state of nature is a philosophical thought experiment imagining human life before or without political authority, used to justify the origins and limits of government. In Thomas Hobbes's version, set out in Leviathan, the absence of a common power leaves people in a condition of insecurity and mutual fear — a "war of all against all" in which life is "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short" — which rational individuals escape by contracting to submit to a sovereign. Later thinkers such as Locke and Rousseau reimagined the state of nature quite differently, but each used it to argue what legitimate political power must secure.

- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 15 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Knight places Atkins's caveman utopia — Paleolithic abundance, hunter-gatherer vitality, downfall through agriculture — inside the primitivist tradition running from Ovid's Golden Age to Rousseau's Noble Savage, whose state of nature Rousseau himself admitted was 'mere conditional and hypothetical reasoning' aimed at European corruption. Using postcolonial critics (Spurr, Torgovnick, and Fanon's line that whites who feel 'too mechanized' turn to 'the men of color' for 'human sustenance'), she argues low-carb primitivism is self-reflexive nostalgia — South Beach cannot even date its own paradise — that also freezes living Inuit and Indigenous Australians as Stone Age remnants, hiding the colonial and economic causes of their diabetes and poverty.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 17 "Resistance Raps" — James reads hardcore and underground rap - N.W.A's "F*** Tha Police", Ice-T's "Cop Killer", Dead Prez's "Police State" sampling Omali Yeshitela, Tupac's "Dear Mama" with its Panther 21/Cointelpro footage, Michael Franti's "Crime to Be Broke in America" - through Hobbes's Leviathan to argue that for criminalized black communities the social contract never held, so policing is not aberrational protection but the foundation of a police state. She distinguishes rebellion from revolution, argues capital converts the underground's insurgence into marketable alienation, faults hardcore's misogyny and policing of women and queers as counter-revolutionary, and concludes that a Leviathan which is the law cannot cohabit with democracy.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 28 "Reality versus Revolution" — McPherson argues political rap has never been politically revolutionary, sorting it into three schools: the amoral "gangsta Hobbes" ethic (Mobb Deep's "Survival of the Fittest", 50 Cent's "get rich or die tryin'") that sees the hood as Hobbes's state of nature where no social contract with blacks ever existed; Afrocentric communitarianism, split between nationalist separatists (Brand Nubian, X-Clan, Dead Prez) and the more cosmopolitan Native Tongues (De La Soul, A Tribe Called Quest); and a radical liberalism closer to Rawls than its adherents admit. Against Chuck D's "What's a smilin' face when the whole state's racist?", he argues Rawls's original position, veil of ignorance, and difference principle - applied with real-world knowledge of racism - support rather than oppose Public Enemy's demands for racial justice.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 12 "The Mystery Solved" — Avery Kolers uses "Only a Pawn in Their Game" and its companion "Who Killed Davey Moore?" to argue that Dylan treats Byron de la Beckwith as a pawn: a poor white duped by divide-and-rule tactics, the psychological wage of whiteness, shame, and lynch-mob indoctrination into fearing a Hobbesian war of all against all. Against Aristotle's account of acting in ignorance, the chapter asks whether Beckwith's ignorance of his real enemies was culpable, concluding his bad moral luck (in Bernard Williams's sense) was manufactured by white supremacy and so reflects back on all white people. Dylan's refusal to name or voice Beckwith adopts Strawson-style objective attitudes, making blaming itself a political act aimed at the system rather than the shooter.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 25 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Alford reads the biker image, born at Hollister in 1947 and fixed by The Wild One, through two opposed accounts of presocial man: the badass on his tricked-out Harley is Hobbes's natural man, all vanity, domination, and fear merely redirected to government, praising Chuck Zito's 'most primitive philosophy'; the club run with bonfire, brothers, old ladies, and Steppenwolf re-enacts Rousseau's golden age between the stupidity of brutes and the fatal enlightenment of civil man, before the first enclosed field ('this is mine') bred property, vanity, and misery. The paradox of a biker who is simultaneously threat and salvation dissolves once we see that 'primitive' and 'civilized' are mutually defining: suburbanites and bikers alike live both Hobbesian individualism and Rousseauvian community, each defining themselves against the other.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 30 "Poker and Philosophy" — Stoehr finds Hobbes in the saloon: poker in classic Westerns — Hatfield's farewell game in Stagecoach, and the cheating scene where Wyatt Earp first crosses Doc Holliday in My Darling Clementine — dramatizes the tension between the lawless state of nature ('solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short') and the rule-governed community built by an implicit social contract, with caught cheaters (Chihuahua signaling hole cards) marking where play reverts to primal vengeance. Poker itself is a Hobbesian paradox: a communal social event built on winner-takes-all competition, exercising both logic and intuition within luck's hard limits. The morally ambiguous Fordian hero — Doc Holliday above all — lives at the same crossroads of civilization and wilderness as the card table.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 26 "No Way Out" — Leah Murray reads Romero's Dead series as an argument about the American social contract, individualism versus communitarianism. Night of the Living Dead's farmhouse is Hobbes: fear throws strangers Ben and Mr. Cooper into a makeshift commonwealth whose individualist half ('every man for himself' in the basement) fails, while Dawn shows the Hobbesian next step - martial law as Leviathan - after the state of nature returns. Land of the Dead's Fiddler's Green is a fear-born contract corrupting into Kaufman's hierarchy, and Big Daddy's zombies form the counter-model, a Rousseauian community of the general will based on mutual bonds rather than terror, as the priest in Dawn already urged ('we must stop the killing... or lose the war'). Following Tocqueville on civic association, she concludes Romero's survivors - Ben, Peter, Sarah, Riley - vindicate communitarian cooperation, even though Night's bureaucratic ending suggests there may be no way out.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 39 "Gaining Trust from the Past" — Richard Davies treats the Oceanic 815 survivors' beach as a "framed" state of nature: the stolen water is a tragedy of the commons, Sawyer's "finders keepers" defense of Shannon's inhalers stages Hobbes's war of all against all against Locke's natural rights, and Jack and Sayid's torture of Sawyer marks the first step toward civil society, a claim to punish on another's behalf. He argues no theory of human nature (Rousseau's "Innocence" versus a "Trust No. 1" attitude) is needed to understand the castaways: cooperation grows through iterated prisoner's-dilemma tit-for-tat strategies, which also recasts the real difference between Hobbesian and Lockean states of nature.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 14 "“Your Heavenly Father Feeds Them”" — Calef takes the Tides restaurant scene ('Who are you? What are you?') and Diogenes's plucked rooster versus Plato's 'featherless biped' as a springboard for testing every classic criterion of humanity against the film. Aristotle's rational soul fails because Mrs. Bundy's 'brain pans' reasoning is wrong and some humans cannot reason; Descartes's language test fails because the myna bird can learn to talk while horrified humans go mute; Rousseau's free will fails because the birds behave unpredictably and resist instinct while humans are trapped, caged, and herd-like; Aristotle's political animal and Hobbes's social contract fail because the town's hoods and lawbreakers contrast with birds that flock together across species. Even the appeal to God's favor turns dark, as the drunk quotes scripture while Revelation's birds gather for a supper of human flesh, leaving the film a mirror in which we must examine ourselves.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 22 "E Pluribus Unum" — Auxier frames Hitchcock's Lifeboat against Garrett Hardin's 'lifeboat ethics' essay, arguing the lifeboat converts political questions into ethical ones by stranding the survivors outside law and politics ('We're on our own here. We can make our own law'). The survivors are ethical pluralists - Rittenhouse lives for money, Kovac for equality, Constance for fame, Joe for God, MacKenzie for care - and their clinging to private versions of the Good lets Nazi captain Willy, whose only principle is survival, manipulate them all. Using Maslow's hierarchy of needs, Auxier shows the boat descending to bare survival, yet argues the mob killing of Willy when he hoards water is moral outrage rather than survival-driven, and that the final rescue scene replays the opening dispute with nobody having grown - a vindication of pluralistic democracy capable of unified action.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 20 "Once I Was the Student, Now I Am the Master" — Johannes Bulhof reads 'Me and My Uncle' — the Dead's most-performed song, though hardly a fan favorite — as a parable against rational self-interest. The nephew learned everything from his uncle: how to cheat at cards, steal, and shoot first, so he rationally guns down the cowboys, takes the gold, and leaves his uncle's 'dead ass there by the side of the road' — the student out-mastering the teacher. Framing the song with Thrasymachus's Republic I claim that the unjust always profit (and his own students' admission they would cheat if they could get away with it), then with Hobbes's state of nature where equality, contested goods, and anticipatory striking make everyone enemies — even family — Bulhof argues the song's drunken lesson is that rational self-interest is communally irrational.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 22 "Don’t Get Into One" — Richard Greene renames the Tarantino standoff the 'ex-convict's dilemma' and models it as a special case of the prisoner's dilemma, running from Ordell and Louis's separate interrogation rooms to the White–Pink, Joe–White–Eddie and True Romance shoot-outs. He argues the standard group-rationality solution fails because ECDS participants have conflicting goals—Eddie protecting his father, White protecting Orange, Joe wanting revenge—and his survey of Tarantino's six cases shows escapes come from luck (Mr. Blonde's entrance, Nikki coming home) or shared interests (Beatrix's pregnancy), never group rationality. Tracing the dilemma back to Glaucon's contract argument in Plato's Republic, he concludes the only reliable solution is: don't get into one.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 10 "You May Wonder How Come I Love You Care and Ethics" — Gimbel asks what the E Street Band's marathon multiple encores mean, starting from social contract theory: Hobbes's state of nature ('no home, no job, no peace, no rest') and Locke's contract explain the ticket as a financial IOU — so a drunk, short Hendrix show wrongs you financially but not morally — while the contractual view of moral duty (the 'Hungry Heart' narrator who abandoned his wife and kids in Baltimore) cannot explain why a missing encore feels like personal betrayal. The gift theory fails too, since encores are expected, and expected things are not gifts. Care ethics (Ruddick, Noddings) fits instead: devoted fans make the band part of their identity, Springsteen sings 'to you about you,' and the No Nukes 90-minute set became permanent because he would not give his people less — while 'Pink Cadillac' shows the limit case, since you cannot love someone for her Cadillac.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 7 "4" — Four 'Phase One' essays. Dyer reads Mark Millar's Wanted through Plato's cave: Wesley Gibson escapes a pathetic life like the freed prisoner, but like Adolf Eichmann (via Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem) he murders his conscience, so the Fraternity's consequence-free world leaves him numb and unable to value anything - a descent deeper into the cave, ending in the banality of evil. Novy explains why henchmen betray using Aristotle's utility/pleasure/complete friendship distinction (Big Cheese, Henchmen Muenster and Feta): supervillain gangs are Hobbesian pirate crews with no enforcer, so a modus vivendi of self-interest collapses under interrogation and only Machiavellian fear secures loyalty. Foresman applies Goodman and Rawls's reflective equilibrium as a 'cheat' to rank Apocalypse, Magneto, Luthor, the Joker, and Bizarro, concluding the 'best of the worst' is judged on evil ends (or evil means, as with Magneto) and even on glorious failure. Arinder and Milton, in a staged descent-into-madness frame, diagnose mad science in Victor Frankenstein and Dr. Doom as science that denies value-laden theory choice - impossible because data underdetermine theory - breeding the hubris that dehumanizes the scientist.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 9 "12" — Four 'Phase Three' essays on world conquest. Terjesen asks whether Doctor Doom's magnanimity (Aristotle's great-souledness, contra the unity-of-virtues thesis Aquinas held and Philippa Foot qualified) makes him less villainous than The Authority, whose purely consequentialist paternalism - like Doom's Emperor Doom or Ozymandias's plot - usurps a free choice no mere power can justify. Barringer reads Marvel's Civil War through Hobbes: the Stamford explosion and unrestrained superpowers recreate the state of nature, the Registration Act is the surrender of freedom to a sovereign, and Stark, Richards, and Pym repeat Hobbes's flawed faith in 'scientific' deductive politics, sealed by the clone-Thor killing of Goliath. Hillerbrand and Sandburg pit Rorschach's Kantian deontology (no compromise, not even to save the world) against Ozymandias's utilitarian murder of three million New Yorkers in Watchmen, arguing via Laplace's Demon that even Dr. Manhattan - nihilist or Schopenhauerian recluse - cannot verify the outcome, so watchmen can be trusted only by knowing their limits. Ostrander's fictional NSC interview has Amanda Waller's Suicide Squad defended with Benthamite utility, the rejection of natural rights as 'nonsense on stilts,' and the Augustinian just-war criteria of just cause, right intent, and proportionality, while the interviewer exposes how conveniently those limits bend.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 13 "Singing of the Good Things" — Scott Calef asks whether Led Zeppelin's lives of wealth, groupies, and no-questions-asked liberty were genuinely free and therefore enviable. Locke's distinction between weak freedom (doing what you want, with Page happily locked in his suite at the Riot House) and strong freedom (being able to do otherwise, defended via beer-spilling concert excuses) is destabilized by the observation that no one ever does other than what they did. Rousseau then dominates: the state of nature versus LA, freedom as the capacity to resist natural impulse, which explains both Zep's libertine promiscuity and the paradox that heroin and alcohol enslave the very freedom that took them (the post-Physical Graffiti decline, Bonzo's death), while the band's violence—Bonham's assaults, the Oakland beating—shows society's suppression of natural pity, not natural aggression as Hobbes would have it. Socrates gets the last word: doing what we please is not doing what we truly want, so only the temperate person is free.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 26 "No Way Out" — Leah Murray argues Romero's Dead films stage the American contest between individualism and communitarianism inside the social contract: in Night of the Living Dead, communitarian Ben barricading the farmhouse against every-man-for-himself Mr. Cooper hiding in the basement; in Dawn of the Dead, the Peter-Roger-Fran-Stephen mall commune collapsing when Stephen's 'it's ours, we took it' meets the bikers; in Day of the Dead, Sarah's compassion against the racist, harassing soldiers; in Land of the Dead, Kaufman's Fiddler's Green as a Hobbesian Leviathan born of fear, complete with bread-and-circuses for the poor. Against the Hobbesian fear-born contract (Dawn opens in a full state-of-nature collapse) she sets Rousseau's general will and Tocqueville's civic association, embodied in Riley's freely formed community and in Big Daddy's zombies, who organize, turn from eating humans, and bring down the Leviathan. The films' verdict: fear-based individualist contracts collapse under their own contradictions, while compassionate cooperation — even among the Undead — is the only way out, even if Romero doubts its ultimate viability.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 27 "Is Fencing a Dishonorable Art" — Michaud argues that fencing is the loneliest and most egoistic martial art: alone on the strip, you seek to understand your opponent only in order to deceive them through disengages and parry-feints. He maps the bout onto Hobbes: psychological egoism, the dueling ground as a state of nature of 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short', and the referee as the Leviathan whose rules keep the bloodshed out while licensing normative egoism inside them. Testing defenses from Rand, Friedman and Carr's business 'rules of the game', he concludes that fencing kept its soldier's anything-goes ethos after the lethal stakes vanished, making it a 'dishonorable' art: a Hobbesian feast of solitude, egoism and deception.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 24 "The Dalek Within" — Comparing the Doctor's hesitation at the Dalek hatchery in 'Genesis of the Daleks' with the half-human Doctor's instant genocide in 'Journey's End', the authors argue the Daleks are mirrors of us: their survival-driven wars enact Hobbes's state of nature, while their industrial 'extermination' embodies Arendt's banality of evil and Weber's iron cage of instrumental rationality. Drawing on Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry and Foucault's disciplinary institutions — modern techniques that mold the inner life as Davros's genetic engineering molds the Kaleds — they conclude the Dalek tendency is a human possibility, so we cannot exterminate the Daleks without indicting ourselves.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 14 "Spice as the Vehicle of Power" — Reads the Duniverse as Hobbes's state of nature at galactic scale: Emperor, Landsraad houses, Guild, Bene Gesserit, and Tleilaxu are rationally self-preserving factions in a war of all against all over scarce spice, where 'justice' names only what enforcement power backs and life for the losers is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.' Leto II is the Leviathan—a literal 'mortal God,' half sandworm—whose spice monopoly and fusion of political with spiritual authority impose a forced peace; his assassination then shows split authority re-igniting the conflict in the Scattering and the Honored Matres. Paul's threat to destroy the spice and Leto's hoarding both illustrate that the power to destroy a thing is absolute control over it.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 21 "No Matter How You Flip the Patty . ." — Michael Dodge asks whether Krabs may guard the Krabby Patty formula, sorting Bikini Bottom's property into collective, communal (Jellyfish Fields) and private, and deploying the tragedy of the commons — Krabs's jellyfish-squeezing factory in 'Jellyfish Hunter' — to show why shared resources get rationally overexploited. Hobbes grounds Krabs's right in sovereign enforcement (without the law, 'Pineapple Fever''s chalk-line household collapses into animals fighting over the fridge), Locke in labor-mixing, with Krabs's identity bound to his patties since 'Help Wanted', and Hume in conventions of justice born of selfishness and scarcity. All three support Krabs's legal and moral right to his secret recipe against Plankton.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 20 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Solves the 'riddle' of Gus by showing his empire runs on corporate instrumental rationality: the careful, emotion-disciplined Los Pollos CEO launders meth through legitimate business, treats chemists as replaceable parts (the Gale plan), and exacts revenge on the cartel in 'Salud' by drinking his own poisoned tequila. The chapter defines this as the critical theorists' amoral means-end reason - Kant's hypothetical imperative without the categorical - making Gus a sociopath who violates the injunction to treat persons as ends, and reads his cartel war through Machiavelli and Hobbes's power-first picture of the state. Gus's Two-Face-like corpse reveals the split between the rage-driven avenger of Max and the respectable mask, foreshadowing what Walt becomes.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 10 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Editor Wayne Yuen's introduction argues that zombies are worth doing philosophy over: an apocalyptic world without government, law enforcement, or private property raises live questions about how survivors should treat one another, whether life becomes 'nasty, brutish, and short', and whether it is wrong to kill a walker. He frames walkers philosophically through Descartes's mindless human-looking automatons and David Chalmers's P-zombies, creatures functionally like us with no inner life. Morgan keeping photo albums instead of supplies in 'Days Gone Bye' shows that what we leave behind after the apocalypse is how we lived - our philosophy.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 19 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Jason Walker argues the zombie apocalypse is a Lockean rather than Hobbesian state of nature: rights to life, liberty, and property persist without government. Rick's 'I don't think those rules apply anymore' to Andrea over the mermaid necklace is justified by Locke's spoilage and 'enough and as good' provisos - the owner is almost certainly dead and the necklace would otherwise lie forever wasted - while Morgan's house-squatting, which protects the Thompsons' home, and Rick voluntarily sharing guns with Guillermo's nursing-home defenders show self-ownership and norms at work. The counter-cases, Chris's cannibal band ('a man's gotta eat') and the Governor, who treat persons as mere means, live out Hobbes's war of all against all and are destroyed by the Lockean right to punish that victims retain.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 24 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Si Sheppard grades The Walking Dead's three settlements by political Realism: the Governor's Woodbury - cohesive, feared rather than loved, feeding his people arena spectacle to keep them from turning on him - beats Rick's West Central Prison, which never becomes a state at all. Rick lets Tyreese's vigilante murder pass, ruling as a first-among-equals with no institutions, no constitution, and no monopoly of legitimate force in Weber's sense, then covertly guns down Thomas and Dexter while hiding behind his cop credibility - 'it's me or you' reasoning indistinguishable from Shane's. Realism cares about power, not morality, so Rick's flaw is not cruelty but the absence of institution-building: he was never a bad father, just a bad founding father, who only becomes a Realist after Alexandria falls.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 33 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Moosa uses the apocalypse as a moral laboratory: since 'murder' is by definition wrongful killing, Carl's shooting of Shane must be judged by his reasoning (saving his father), and Hobbes's state of nature — 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' — fits Kirkman's world, yet the survivors import morality into it, as when parents mercy-kill their children just as one would turn up a dying child's morphine. Taking up Camus's claim that suicide is the one truly serious philosophical problem, he argues our world is nearly as bad as the zombie landscape, so consistency commits comfortable readers to the same duty of aid (helping sufferers rather than opting out) that justifies the survivors' fighting on. Finally he argues procreation is the worst thing survivors can do — nonexistent children cannot suffer, so Lori's pregnancy and Glenn and Maggie's crib plans are immoral, and adopting existing children as Andrea and Dale did is the consistent course, an obligation that transfers to our world right now.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 13 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Allen asks how a virtual war zone can exist inside the United States, starting from Hobbes: Marlo's cool killing of the security guard who just wants to be recognized as a man looks like the rights-free state of nature where 'nothing can be unjust.' But he argues Locke's sharper distinction fits better - the underclass are nominal citizens whose rights to life, policing, and education exist on paper while their substance is denied, which for Locke places an oppressed minority in a state of war within a state, and makes the drug game a rational choice for Michael, Dukie, and Randy. Marlo's 'you want it to be one way, but it's the other way' names that collapsed protection, and the chapter ends with Locke's warning that majority apathy lets oppression persist, reading The Wire as protest art meant to move viewers to political action.
