This is Rousseau's claim that human beings are naturally good, or at least innocent, and that vice, inequality, and misery arise not from our nature but from the development of society and its institutions. In the imagined state of nature people are self-sufficient and compassionate, but the growth of property, comparison, and dependence corrupts them, breeding pride, envy, and injustice. The thesis reverses the older view that civilization tames a naturally wicked animal, and it frames Rousseau's political and educational projects as attempts to recover or protect that original goodness. It shaped Romanticism and modern debates about whether social conditions or human nature is the deeper source of our ills.

- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 15 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Knight places Atkins's caveman utopia — Paleolithic abundance, hunter-gatherer vitality, downfall through agriculture — inside the primitivist tradition running from Ovid's Golden Age to Rousseau's Noble Savage, whose state of nature Rousseau himself admitted was 'mere conditional and hypothetical reasoning' aimed at European corruption. Using postcolonial critics (Spurr, Torgovnick, and Fanon's line that whites who feel 'too mechanized' turn to 'the men of color' for 'human sustenance'), she argues low-carb primitivism is self-reflexive nostalgia — South Beach cannot even date its own paradise — that also freezes living Inuit and Indigenous Australians as Stone Age remnants, hiding the colonial and economic causes of their diabetes and poverty.
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 17 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — In an imaginary salon hosted by the baker 'la Brioche,' the goddess Eris drops a golden apple inscribed 'Atkins,' and three philosophers fight over the credit. Rousseau claims Atkins's war on refined flour and 'invented fake food' as his own back-to-nature, state-of-nature legacy; Confucius counters that Americans are 'grazers' without li, that culture is nature's flower, and that only ritual propriety can counteract the advertising that fills the void; Democritus claims the scientific core — 'hyperinsulism,' 'benign dietary ketosis' — as atomism's heir, deriding Rousseau's general will as democratic truth-concocting and Plato's otherworldly philosopher-king. The debate ranges over free will versus scientific prediction-and-control and ends unresolved over a refusal of brioche.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 25 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Alford reads the biker image, born at Hollister in 1947 and fixed by The Wild One, through two opposed accounts of presocial man: the badass on his tricked-out Harley is Hobbes's natural man, all vanity, domination, and fear merely redirected to government, praising Chuck Zito's 'most primitive philosophy'; the club run with bonfire, brothers, old ladies, and Steppenwolf re-enacts Rousseau's golden age between the stupidity of brutes and the fatal enlightenment of civil man, before the first enclosed field ('this is mine') bred property, vanity, and misery. The paradox of a biker who is simultaneously threat and salvation dissolves once we see that 'primitive' and 'civilized' are mutually defining: suburbanites and bikers alike live both Hobbesian individualism and Rousseauvian community, each defining themselves against the other.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 19 "Roll Credits" — Dunn contrasts Baum's book, where evil is wonderfully 'small'—Dorothy melts the Witch in a fit of righteous anger at a stolen Silver Shoe, and personal plus social virtues (kindness repaid by the field-mice Queen) reliably conquer it—with the 1939 film, which smuggles back the 'heartaches and nightmares' Baum banished and resolves the Witch only by an accidental stroke of luck. He sorts Oz's harms into moral evils (the Witch's enslavements, the Wizard's frauds) and natural evils (the cyclone, the Deadly Poppy Field), cites Hume's catalogue of the world's ills, and observes that Baum needs neither Kant's postulate of God and a future life to join virtue with happiness nor John Hick's 'vale of soul-making' theodicy—Oz simply delivers the reward. Dorothy's abundant virtue at age five rebukes Aristotle (children, he says, cannot be virtuous or happy) and instead embodies Rousseau's Emile, natural goodness uncorrupted by civilization, while Chesterton's Doctrine of Conditional Joy and Tolkien's insistence on serious, non-technological magic frame the Old-World Christian outlook that Baum's demystified American fairy tale—and the movie's ending—quietly betray.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 13 "Singing of the Good Things" — Scott Calef asks whether Led Zeppelin's lives of wealth, groupies, and no-questions-asked liberty were genuinely free and therefore enviable. Locke's distinction between weak freedom (doing what you want, with Page happily locked in his suite at the Riot House) and strong freedom (being able to do otherwise, defended via beer-spilling concert excuses) is destabilized by the observation that no one ever does other than what they did. Rousseau then dominates: the state of nature versus LA, freedom as the capacity to resist natural impulse, which explains both Zep's libertine promiscuity and the paradox that heroin and alcohol enslave the very freedom that took them (the post-Physical Graffiti decline, Bonzo's death), while the band's violence—Bonham's assaults, the Oakland beating—shows society's suppression of natural pity, not natural aggression as Hobbes would have it. Socrates gets the last word: doing what we please is not doing what we truly want, so only the temperate person is free.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 27 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Greeley argues the zombie crystallizes specifically modern fears: with Aristotle and Aquinas he reads walkers as humans stripped of their essential nature and potential, which Rick's uncustomary eulogies ('I'm sorry this happened to you') acknowledge. Following Philippe Aries, he ties modern death anxiety to urbanization, hidden cemeteries, and the loss of religious consolation, citing the CDC arc where Jenner's science offers only a self-destruct and Jacqui falls back on 'the wrath of God.' Rousseau's thesis that society corrupts explains why the survivors in the woods seem more alive — warlord Guillermo turns out to be protecting nursing-home patients and pizza-deliverer Glenn becomes a hero — while the 'Bradbury's Storewide Sale' sign, the Walmart trampling, and Fromm's shift from utopias to dystopias suggest the shuffling horde is an image of our own consumerist, distracted, dehumanized modernity.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 24 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Fitzpatrick uses the social contract tradition to explain Prohibition-era Atlantic City. Hobbes's state of nature fits the gang warfare left where no Leviathan is strong enough to enforce federal law against Nucky; Locke's fits a night-watchman government overreaching into Prohibition and thereby breaking the contract, as with Nucky's illegitimate protection 'taxes'; Rousseau's noble savage corrupted by commercial society fits the Klan's pleasure in cruelty and innocent Tommy set against scheming adults. Ethical egoism frames Nucky's framing of Hans Schroeder, consequentialism the Temperance Union's cost-benefit failure, and deontology Margaret's lying campaign speech, while Marx's and Mill's view that human nature is malleable explains the season-spanning transformation of Nucky from half-gangster into 'a gangster and a half.'
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 11 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Chaib reads Craig Venter's 2010 synthetic bacterium 'Synthia' as a real-world Victor Frankenstein and tests it against Habermas's The Future of Human Nature, which condemns liberal eugenics because turning reproduction into manufacture undermines moral equality, rights, and autonomy - the same irresponsible isolation that made Victor abandon his creature and doom Justine. Rousseau and Thomas More supply the counter-program: hunger persists through unequal property ('This is mine'), not scarcity, so improving the human heart and social structures beats Venter's engineered fixes. Frankenweenie - where pets reanimated without love turn evil while Victor's beloved Sparky saves the town - lands the chapter's Arendtian moral that 'to live' is always plural (inter homines esse), so creators must care about their creations' relations with others.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 21 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Pötzsch explains the monster through Rousseau's Émile: innately good ('Everything is good as it comes from the hands of the Author of Nature'), the creature is corrupted because he experienced civilization 'too much and too soon' - the exact inverse of Rousseau's negative education, which shields the heart from vice instead of commanding, and lets the child learn 'through the mere force of things.' Victor knew his parents' model of paternal duty ('a deep consciousness of what they owed towards the being to which they had given life') yet abandoned his offspring and refused the female companion Rousseau deems essential to social development, so that wickedness born of weakness ('if I cannot inspire love, I will cause fear') murders William, Clerval, and Elizabeth. Shelley, a Rousseau admirer, makes Victor's science - an attempt to conquer rather than follow nature, fed by competitive professors at Ingolstadt - the very thing that dooms his parenting.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 30 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Caroline Mosser treats the creature's tragedy as humanist prejudice rather than necessity: the blind De Lacey accepts the eloquent creature sight unseen, so he passes Alan Turing's test, and only the sighted family's terror at his body rejects him - bias against the artificial, not reason. She reads the creature's development through fire, language, and revolution as Rousseau's progression from natural innocence to corruption by society, and Donna Haraway's cyborg as the figure he prefigures: an unfaithful illegitimate offspring who rebels against his father and undermines patriarchal Western self/other dualisms. The chapter concludes that society cannot accept enhanced or posthuman beings until it finds a middle ground beyond its binary grids of good/bad and Self/Other, since otherwise any new life we create will be Othered, hated, and oppressed like Frankenstein's.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 33 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Mike Kugler argues Shelley's novel tests the radical idealism of her father William Godwin, her mother Mary Wollstonecraft, and her husband Percy: Victor's Promethean project of perfecting humanity in isolation, away from the 'intimate circle' of family and friends, produces a creature whose natural benevolence is destroyed only by repeated exclusion, first by the De Laceys. Drawing on Rousseau's and Wollstonecraft's view that children raised by benevolent parents develop their innate sympathy, the chapter reads the creature as an abandoned child - a new Adam who becomes a Satanic rebel when every community rejects him - and Victor's attempt at reproduction without women and mothers as the novel's deepest violation. The redemptive counterfactual is adoption: what if Victor had raised the creature in his home, as his father did Elizabeth?
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 40 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Trip McCrossin casts the creature as a modern Job: repeatedly and unreasonably mistreated by the De Laceys, the rustic whose child he saved, and Victor despite his benevolence, he cries 'This was then the reward of my benevolence!' - but unlike Job he loses faith, because his problem of evil is secular, justifying not 'the Ways of God to Man' but 'the Ways of Man to monsters.' The chapter traces the problem from Job and Paradise Lost through Bayle's defense of faith over reason and the Optimists' 'best of all possible worlds,' whose credibility drowned with the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, setting Rousseau against Voltaire: Rousseau's Emile ('All is good leaving the hands of the author of things') demands that we make evil intelligible through self-knowledge, while Candide counsels tending our garden. The creature embodies Rousseau's line - 'I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend' - yet ends in self-abhorring remorse over Victor's death, leaving open whether self-knowledge can ever answer unreasonable suffering.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 28 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Trip McCrossin reads Carrie's 'I missed something once before... everyone's not me' as the modern, secular problem of evil: as Susan Neiman argues, unreasonable suffering threatens reason itself, and the Rousseau-Voltaire split defines the responses. Carrie takes Rousseau's side - 'All is good leaving the hands of the author of things' degenerates in human hands, so evil is intelligible and redemption possible, the chance at redemption she offers Brody and even Nazir - against Voltaire's Candide-style tending of the garden. The finale deepens this with Boethius's Consolation: Carrie's 'I believe one of the reasons I was put on this Earth was for our paths to cross' fuses fate with providence, and she accepts Brody's execution as a redemptive end 'more so if he dies'.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 12 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Gale and Barkman treat post-Mushroom-War Ooo as a state-of-nature laboratory for liberalism's three founders. The Forest Wizard who cages Finn in 'Storytelling' is Hobbes's Leviathan, kept in power by fear yet moderated by self-interest (Goblin King Xergiok's fall shows the leash); Princess Bubblegum's Candy Kingdom is Locke's civil society where citizens trade private revenge for impartial law—her lawful bow to Lemongrab shows she rules by contract, not fear; and 'City of Thieves' illustrates Rousseau's claim that property corrupts natural goodness, with Finn and Jake as his uncorrupted natural people. The chapter concludes that the rights language these thinkers forged is what keeps both Ooo and our world from sliding back into a war of all against all.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 15 "6. Tris’s Compassion and the Problem of Evil" — McCrossin reads Tris's whole arc as a struggle with the problem of evil, both the theological version from Job and the modern secular one Susan Neiman describes, in which unreasonable suffering threatens trust in human reason. He casts Tris as cut from Rousseau's mold - her insistence on making the evils of Jeanine, Marcus, and Evelyn intelligible - against Voltaire's Candide refusal to rationalize suffering, and treats the faction system as Rousseau's social-contract strategy for containing the inclination to evil while Tris herself plays a wartime Emile. The key is Tobias's lesson that selflessness and bravery are not that different: selflessness enables the courage that compassion motivates, from pressing her forehead to Jeanine's gun in the fear landscape to taking Caleb's place at the weapons lab, so that the trilogy ends with Tobias's 'we mend each other.'
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 14 "4. Acts of God" — McCrossin reads Lecter's parable of the church collapses - 'It must feel good to God - He does it all the time, and are we not made in His image?' - as Lecter's solution to the problem of evil in both its theological (Job) and secular (Neiman) forms: a malevolent deity of the kind de Sade's Saint-Fond describes, doing God's work becomes Lecter's justification, and killing feels good because 'if one does what God does enough times, one will become as God is'. Following Neiman, he sets Rousseau's tradition (evil must be made intelligible - 'All is well leaving the hands of the author of things') against Voltaire's Candide refusal of theodicy, showing that Will and Starling live in Rousseau's camp except when facing Lecter himself, and that the Hannibal/Hannibal Rising revelation that Mischa's murder 'happened' to him radically revises his earlier claim that 'we don't invent our natures', with Starling's reason finally making 'a place for Mischa' in Lecter and Starling together.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 12 "4. Raising Darrow" — Trip McCrossin reads Darrow's storyline as an engagement with the problem of evil in both its theological form (Harmony dubbing him Lazarus, the parables of John and Luke) and its secular form, which Susan Neiman traces to the Rousseau-Voltaire dispute: must evil be made intelligible or not? Darrow begins Voltairean—incredulous before the rigged Laurel and Eo's hanging ('She left me')—but his resurrection and political awakening on the surface remake him Rousseauian: evil is the misalignment of individual and general wills, and humans are corrupted by society, not born bad. The chapter reads Darrow's 'Man was born free' broadcast in Morning Star, his new social contract with Victra, and the education of Pax (with Lysander left to Cassius to 'raise him right') as Rousseau's Social Contract and Emile program—break the chains, then educate each generation so its contracts align ever closer with the general will.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 15 "6. Driven by Love to Go to War" — John Karavitis deploys Alain Badiou's account of love as a contingent encounter founding the 'Two scene'—seeing the world from the perspective of difference—to argue that Darrow and Eo were never truly in love: their glade conversation, his 'nobility of obedience' against her 'live for more,' was two monologues, and you cannot love a memory. He then diagnoses Darrow as a narcissist in Rousseau's sense of amour-propre—self-love turned vanity that lies to itself—whose quest serves to manage his shame at failing to protect Eo, citing Erich Fromm on narcissism's path to fascism and Aristotle on habituation into Gold ways. Only the Jackal's stone-table imprisonment shatters the narcissism ('Man is no island'), letting Darrow embrace agape, with Ovid's Echo and Narcissus and the haemanthus framing the trilogy as a warning against self-love.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 29 "16. Doppelgängers, Doubles, and Tulpas" — Reads the show's doubles through the danger of self-loss. La Rochefoucauld's amour-propre explains Josie Packard, whose courtier-like dissimulation ("she could survive by being what other people wanted to see") erodes her true self, while Norma refuses to feign virtue for critic M.T. Wentz or Walter Lawford's rebranding; Rousseau's account of esteem-seeking in modern society covers Sheriff Cable and Chad, who value Teresa Banks and the Log Lady only by others' judgment, against the Blue Rose agents whose values come from within. Jean Paul's doppelgänger, invented to satirize Fichte's I/not-I and intersubjective recognition, uncannies the Palmer home (Leland the abusing father), but the chapter concludes the show sides with Dostoyevsky rather than Jean Paul: Laura, like Mitya Karamazov, owns both her good and wicked halves, Leland splits, and Cooper's moral goodness is a wholeness — authenticity — that his doppelgänger lacks.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 19 "8. From the Handmaid’s Tale to the Handmaids’ Tale" — McCrossin reads Offred's silent prayers ('I want to know what I did to deserve this') as channeling the Book of Job, using Susan Neiman's distinction between the theological and secular problem of evil: even if we stop demanding explanations from God, we must still make evil intelligible, as Janine's Testifying cruelly refuses to do. He sets Rousseau against Voltaire on whether morality requires making evil intelligible, finding June Rousseauian for piecing together Gilead's hidden prehistory at the Boston Globe and for acting from compassion, as with the bread-truck driver's secret Quran. The Salvaging refusal—Ofglen first, then Offred, then sixty-five stones dropped with 'I'm sorry, Aunt Lydia'—shows compassion becoming solidarity and solidarity becoming a general will, transforming The Handmaid's Tale into The Handmaids' Tale.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 36 "23. The Neighborhood Is Us" — Trip McCrossin frames the show, via Susan Neiman, as Rousseau's answer to the problem of evil: bad things (including bad television) happen to good kids, but education can mitigate evil, which is why Rogers prefers Rousseau's demand to make evil intelligible to Voltaire's Candidean refusal and Pangloss's best-of-all-possible-worlds. Rogers pursued only Emile's second prong, making us as we ought to be by loving children 'just the way they are,' and the post-9/11 PSAs before King Friday's empty castle merge Make-Believe into reality, the last 'modulation' of his thirty-four-year ministry.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 14 "4. Can We Do Enough Good" — Fetterman argues no one can do enough good to earn The Good Place because the real question is who defines good. Moving from Hobbes's state of nature and Rousseau's innate compassion to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist doctrine of non-self, he shows the four humans' characters were assembled by their formative communities, which is Michael's whole defense before Judge Gen. But Nietzsche's account of how communities christen their own customs 'good' exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife accountants impose their in-group preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's life of point-maximization fails, and why Michael should be asking the Frozen Yogurt Problem instead of blaming demon tampering.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 33 "Reflections on Technophobia" — The chapter asks whether the technophobia of 'Metalhead' - robo-dogs hunting Bella and her friends across a wasteland - is justified, testing Daniel Dinello's list of fears (identity, values, emotion, freedom, life). Descartes's and Aquinas's human-uniqueness over the mechanical fails because the robo-dogs, like DeepMind, learn and problem-solve, while the episode's Rousseau-style romanticism (only the non-technological cliff, tree, sunlight and stream aid Bella) and the teddy-bear mission show technology amplifying compassion rather than threatening it. The real dangers are robots as Latourian 'black boxes': Asimov's Three Laws cannot be operationalized, and if we cannot know how robo-dogs decide, our frameworks for blame and punishment break down (who answers for a killing - robot, programmer, or, on Marx's analysis of capitalist technology as an instrument of oppression, the economic system behind it?). The chapter concludes that since we already share the world with robots, learning to live responsibly alongside them must replace simple fear.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 14 "4. Can We Do Enough Good" — Interrogates Chidi's question 'why do we choose to be good?' through Hobbes's selfish state of nature, Rousseau's hardwired compassion (Michael's 'little voice' in Eleanor's head), and Hume's bundle theory extended Buddhist-style to a non-self, which grounds Michael's plea to Judge Gen that bad communities made the four humans bad and a better community (Team Cockroach, the Brainy Bunch) can make them good. Nietzsche's account of how communities define their own customs as 'good' then exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife's accountants impose their in-group's preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's point-maximizing life cannot clear the bar. The chapter ends by asking Michael's real question: who gets to decide what's good?
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Jackson reads the show through Rousseau's contrast between the general will and a pathological 'corporate will': Frank discards Freddy the moment his criminal past goes viral, Tusk and Walker's old friendship curdles into mutual blackmail, and Remy and Jackie trade intimacy for career protection - all reducing Aristotle's true friendship to friendships of utility and pleasure subordinated to institutions that treat persons as means. Rousseau's account of civilization degrading natural self-love (amour de soi) into vanity (amour-propre) explains why Washington's corporate ethos leaves no friends, only 'loose ends' to be eliminated, from Zoe pushed onto the platform to Doug hunting Rachel. The chapter ends with 'Man is born free, but is everywhere in chains' as the verdict on corporate personhood's conquest of human bonds.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Reads the show through Rousseau's contrast between the general will and a pathological 'corporate will': governments and corporations are sociopathic artificial persons that depersonalize their agents, degrading natural self-love (amour de soi) into status-hungry amour-propre. On this account Frank's break with Freddy ('just a good customer'), the Tusk-Walker alliance, and Remy and Jackie's bought loyalties are Aristotelian friendships of utility or pleasure crushed under the corporate will, never true friendship, leaving Washington with 'honor without virtue' and men 'everywhere in chains'.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 24 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Coatney explains why Katniss fails at everything she fakes — the disastrous first propos ('that is how a revolution dies'), the studio Mockingjay shoots, the cover-story mission to kill Snow — through Rousseau's distinction between amour de soi (natural self-love) and amour-propre (vanity born of society): she is a natural person in a corrupt world of seeming. The chapter contrasts district self-preservation with Capitol vanity (Posy asking green-skinned Octavia 'Are you sick?'), and reads Haymitch's smooth deception as a costlier, self-destroying alternative to Katniss's inability to dissimulate. Since Rousseau doubts any return to the state of nature, Katniss's refusal to flee into the woods — 'I'm going to stay right here and cause all kinds of trouble' — shows her Nietzsche-noted fate of being punished for her virtue, still preferable to becoming like Effie.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 31 "APPENDIX - Who are Locke, Hume, and Rousseau The Losties’ Guide to Philosophers" — Scott Parker's appendix profiles the philosophers behind Lost's namesake characters: John Locke for the survivor (blank-slate empiricism, belief tempered by tolerance, The Reasonableness of Christianity), David Hume for Desmond (causation as habitual inference, with the button press as the image of induction, plus bundle-theory skepticism about the self), and Jean-Jacques Rousseau for Danielle ('man is naturally good, and only by institutions is he made bad,' private property as the root of inequality). It adds Jeremy Bentham (the alias on Locke's coffin), Kierkegaard via the Fear and Trembling Hurley finds under the Temple (Abraham's teleological suspension of the ethical and the leap of faith), Dogen on zazen, Edward Said for Sayid (Orientalism and the audience's own projected savagery onto the Others), and short lives of Kate Cooper Austin, Carlyle, Rutherford, Hugo Grotius, Bakunin, Ram Dass, Edmund Burke, Hawking, Minkowski, Faraday, C. S. Lewis, and Lennon.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 13 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Reads John Teller's failed 'off the social grid' experiment through the human-nature debate: Mencius's seed of sympathy (even Tig recoils at Dante's dogfights) and Rousseau's naturally good man corrupted by society inspired J.T.'s Goldman-fed anarchism, while Mill and Xunzi counter that virtue is a victory over instinct. Hobbes supplies the real diagnosis—not innate violence but the logic of anarchy among free and equal rivals: competition (the Mayans blowing up the warehouse), diffidence (first-strike temptations against Zobelle), and glory (Jax unable to let the bike-sitting insult pass). Clay's rule that 'retaliation must be harsh and immediate' and the escalating Tig–Veronica Pope–Damon Pope–Opie bloodbath show deterrence fueling cycles of violence, so the only escape from the 'nasty, brutish, and short' fringe is the Leviathan's social grid.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 15 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Explains what anarchism actually demands—rejection of external authority, voluntary association, and faith that people need no coercion to cooperate—and measures SAMCRO against it: the club's president, church votes, chain of command, and the impossibility of Jax negotiating an exit all betray Momma Anarchy. The individualist/collectivist debate inside anarchism maps onto J.T., who retreats to Nomad and Belfast when the collective disappoints his individualist ideal, versus Jax, whose commitment to family keeps him building the collective. Clay appears as the anti-anarchist 'stone-cold egoist' who rigs votes and kills suspected rats, and the chapter argues the experiment was doomed twice over: the founding Vietnam vets' military hierarchy, and the club's dependence on the capitalist society and state agencies (CIA RICO leverage) it rejects.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 28 "Notes" — Reads Star Trek's "final frontier" through the European encounter with American Indians: the Hobbesian war-of-all-against-all stereotype of the "bloodthirsty savage" and Rousseau's opposing noble savage frame "The Paradise Syndrome", whose wigwam-and-tepee set mixes tribes into a no-place utopia. The chapter uses Hegel-style staged histories to debunk Star Trek's warp/pre-warp developmental scale (Spock on the Organians in "Errand of Mercy") as metaphysical assumption rather than biology, and counterposes the Prime Directive's noninterference to indigenous self-sovereignty and the Haudenosaunee-style consent governance that inspired the Federation. Chakotay's vision quests, the medicine bundle, Wesley's habak experience with Lakanta the Traveler in "Journey's End", and the Medicine Wheel in "Cathexis" are then interpreted through Jung's archetypes and collective unconscious, with Kirk, Spock, McCoy, and Scotty as the four Jungian modes of consciousness.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 27 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Greeley argues the zombie embodies a specifically modern fear of losing our humanity: walkers are persons stripped of the potential Aristotle and Aquinas made the measure of human worth, which is why Rick uniquely eulogizes the walkers he puts down ('I'm sorry this happened to you'). Following Aries, he traces modern death anxiety to the split of faith from reason and reads the CDC arc ('TS-19') as science offering only a self-destruct quick death where Jacqui's 'wrath of God' guess at least offers meaning. Rousseau's claim that civilization corrupts explains the survivors' return to the woods, where pizza-deliverer Glenn's heroics and the 'kingpin' Guillermo protecting nursing-home patients show the apocalypse can bring out the best in us while the Bradbury's Sale storefront and trampled Walmart worker hint we were already the walking dead.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 12 "The Divided Self Kaufman, Kafka, Wittgenstein, and Human Nature" — Von der Ruhr reads Human Nature through Kafka's 'A Report to an Academy,' whose humanized ape frames the film's inverted arc (Puff raised as ape, civilized by Nathan, then reverted by Lila). Using Nietzsche's herd passage and Norman Malcolm on animal thought, he argues the human–animal difference is one of kind, so Lila's Rousseauian idealization of Puff as 'uncontaminated by civilization' and Puff's claim that 'words are evil' are confused. Invoking Wittgenstein's view that art should teach and that lying presupposes truth-telling, he faults the film's bleak, self-referential loves while crediting it as a mirror of the viewer's own thinking.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Woolfolk reads The Last of the Mohicans as staging a conflict between nature and civilization. The opening hunt is neither Hobbes's brutish state of nature nor quite Rousseau's amoral noble savage, since the Mohicans are full moral agents; Woolfolk uses Locke's Second Treatise to cast Hawkeye and the colonists as enforcing natural law and natural rights against English 'tyranny,' with Chingachgook's killing of Magua a justified execution. Rousseau's First and Second Discourses illuminate the hypocrisy and greed of Montcalm and the Europeans, and Camus's Meursault is invoked as a truer image of amoral natural man; Tocqueville frames Cora's democratic awakening as individualism.
- **The Philosophy of Tim Burton**, ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" — Mark Walling argues that the appeal of Burton-Depp characters lies in a recovered model of childhood consciousness. Against Freud's and Piaget's view that children perceive less and are locked in the here-and-now, Walling uses Alison Gopnik's cognitive science ('babies are more conscious than we are') and Rousseau's romantic ideal of the naturally good, untutored child to read Edward Scissorhands and Ed Wood. Edward is a naturally gifted, innocent artist destroyed by a corrupt suburban 'society'; Ed Wood, megaphone in hand, is 'an eight-year-old who wants to be a movie director,' whose inattentional, make-believe joy in filmmaking—not the finished product—embodies the wide, wondering child mind Burton celebrates.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 17 "The Power of Memory and the Memory of Power Wars and Graves in Westerns and Jidaigeki" — Brodey compares John Ford's Westerns (My Darling Clementine, She Wore a Yellow Ribbon, The Searchers, The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance) with Kurosawa's jidaigeki (Seven Samurai, Throne of Blood, Hidden Fortress, Yôjimbô) as postwar mythmaking that both buries and builds national identity after military defeat. She argues graves and gravestones are bivalent symbols—commemorating loss while risking perpetuating revenge—and that both directors oscillate between Rousseauean nostalgia for a nobler past and Hobbesian frontier brutality that must be tamed. Ford trusts that memory of past wrongs can spur a better future and enable forgiveness, while Kurosawa, more pessimistic and drawing on Buddhist cyclical detachment in Throne of Blood, warns of the dangers of both remembering and forgetting trauma.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 13 "“Order Out of the Mud” Deadwood and the State of Nature" — Cantor reads David Milch's Deadwood as a dramatization of 'order without law,' testing the mining camp against the state-of-nature theories of Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau. Deadwood is Hobbesian in its sources of violence (competition, diffidence, glory; Al Swearengen's alpha-male struggles), but Lockean in showing property rights and commerce arising spontaneously before the state—gold becomes a self-generated medium of exchange that even overrides prejudice (Hearst dealing with Odell). It is Rousseauian in its innate pity (Swearengen's mercy) and its skepticism that incorporation into the nation-state, symbolized by the telegraph and Hearst's abstract corporate power, counts as progress.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 23 "Savage Nations Native Americans and the Western" — Michael Valdez Moses uses Todorov's analysis of Columbus and Las Casas—the failure to grant the Other both equality and difference—to argue that Hollywood's Native Americans, whether demonized or idealized, are egocentric projections of white American concerns. He traces the 'noble savage' from Rousseau's Second Discourse and Ferguson's proto-republican warrior through Ford's Fort Apache (New Deal common man), the 1970s revisionist westerns (Little Big Man, A Man Called Horse) as countercultural Rousseauian dropouts and Vietnam allegory, and Dances with Wolves, culminating in Jarmusch's Dead Man, whose Nobody escapes the collective stereotype to stand as a genuinely individual, cosmopolitan character.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 39 "Gaining Trust from the Past" — Richard Davies treats the Oceanic 815 survivors of Lost as a real state of nature, playing on the characters named Locke, Rousseau, and Hume. The scarce-water and asthma-inhaler disputes are 'tragedies of the commons,' and Sawyer's 'finders keepers' embodies a Hobbesian 'Trust No. 1' while Hurley and Jack lean toward Rousseauian 'Innocence.' Using game theory's repeated prisoners' dilemma and 'tit-for-tat,' Davies argues a Lockean state of nature (opening with cooperation) rather than a doomed Hobbesian one lets the survivors build a commonwealth against the Others.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 19 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Florell and Wilson, psychologists, survey parenting through the nature–nurture debate, casting Locke's tabula rasa against Rousseau's noble-savage view of children, alongside Piaget and Kohlberg on moral development and Walter Mischel's marshmallow experiment on impulse control. They map the four parenting styles (authoritarian, permissive, uninvolved, authoritative) on responsiveness and control, argue authoritative parenting is optimal, and advise fathers to adjust discipline to each child's innate temperament rather than enforce rigid gender roles.

### The Social Contract

The social contract is the idea that political authority and the obligation to obey it rest on an agreement, real or hypothetical, among the people who are to be governed. It responds to the question of what could legitimately bind free individuals to a common power rather than leaving them in a lawless condition. Thomas Hobbes gave the theory its classic modern form, arguing that in a state of nature life would be one of perpetual insecurity, so rational individuals consent to surrender much of their freedom to a sovereign in exchange for peace and protection. Later thinkers such as Locke and Rousseau reworked the terms of the bargain, but the shared move is to ground the state in consent rather than in divine right or brute force.

- **The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am**, ch. 23 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" — Argues Tony's self is communitarian - constituted by his roles as father, husband, don and executioner - against the Liberal metaphysics of individualism descending from Descartes's cogito (Livia's 'in the end you die in your own arms') and Hobbes's state of nature and social contract, with the mob boss miscast as a Hobbesian sovereign ('a supreme commander at the top, not the fuckin' Dave Clark Five'). The Naples trip in 'Commendatori' (Paulie discovering he is not really 'Napoletan''), the Columbus Day violence of 'Christopher', and the endless Godfather and Goodfellas mimicry (Christopher's bakery foot-shooting, Tony's Se7en-like murder of Ralphie) show identity as narrative, performed with and through others, not possessed by an isolated self.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 24 "The End Is It All Darkness" — John Pappas reads Crimes and Misdemeanors through Glaucon's ring of Gyges in Plato's Republic: Judah Rosenthal's wealth and prestige are his invisibility ring, and when his mistress Dolores threatens exposure he 'pushes the button', has his gangster brother Jack murder her, and gets away with it. Against Socrates' claim that injustice corrodes the harmonious soul and that virtue is its own reward, the film, unlike Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment, lets the murderer and the 'yutz' Lester prosper while honest Clifford loses everything; Bergson's theory of the comic explains why Lester is invisible to himself, and Rousseau's reverie about what he would do with the ring marks Clifford as the one man who might use it decently. Aunt May's post-Holocaust atheism, 'might makes right' with nothing 'handed down in stone', supplies the argument from evil that releases Judah, leaving only the qualified hope that it is 'not all darkness'.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 26 "Crime-Fighters and Vigilantes" — Skoble frames costumed crime-fighters as vigilantes by definition and tests them against Locke's argument that civil society requires each of us to give up the private right of vengeance to the state - under which superheroes who go looking for trouble are Paul Kersey of Death Wish with a mask. He then reads Miller's The Dark Knight Returns as the first mainstream examination of vigilantism's moral status: Batman tells a congressional committee 'Sure we're criminals... We have to be criminals', breaks laws that shield real criminals, and faces an arrest warrant, TV pundits, and a satirized psychiatrist blaming him for the Joker's crimes.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 38 "The Vigilante Man of Faith Hero or Tragic Figure" — Morris answers his title question 'both': Daredevil refuses to kill even Doctor Octopus ('Then I'd be no better than you'), saves the cancer-stricken Bullseye, and tells Typhoid Mary 'You are who you are because of the choices you make', denying that accidents or heritage define a person. To Detective Manolis he gives a law-and-society argument against private killing - 'The moment one man takes another man's life in his own hands, he is rejecting the law... I'm not God - I'm not the law - and I'm not a murderer' - yet his repeated sparing of Bullseye makes him feel complicit in later murders, the tragic cost of his faith, which he nonetheless concludes is strength rather than weakness.
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 24 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Wilkerson borrows the social contract tradition — Hobbes's mutual-restraint founding, radicalized by Pateman's sexual contract and Mills's racial contract — to recast antifat bias as a systematic breach of the social contract enforced by medicine (hallway weigh-ins, weight lectures instead of care), employment, transit seating, and TV fat jokes. Against Atkins's medical discourse of the 'obesity epidemic' she assembles Health at Every Size evidence, trans-fat and high-fructose corn syrup data, and the documented health damage of stigma and dieting itself, concluding that Atkins profits from recasting social problems as individual failings. Atkins for Life's success stories (Kerry Feather's volleyball and new husband, Luann Lockhart's proud daughter) are read as testimony that dieting works as ritual self-abasement purchasing group membership — hence Fat Liberation's 'another world is possible.'
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 17 "Resistance Raps" — James reads hardcore and underground rap - N.W.A's "F*** Tha Police", Ice-T's "Cop Killer", Dead Prez's "Police State" sampling Omali Yeshitela, Tupac's "Dear Mama" with its Panther 21/Cointelpro footage, Michael Franti's "Crime to Be Broke in America" - through Hobbes's Leviathan to argue that for criminalized black communities the social contract never held, so policing is not aberrational protection but the foundation of a police state. She distinguishes rebellion from revolution, argues capital converts the underground's insurgence into marketable alienation, faults hardcore's misogyny and policing of women and queers as counter-revolutionary, and concludes that a Leviathan which is the law cannot cohabit with democracy.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 27 "Post-Civil Rights Music" — Lawson argues political rap - Grandmaster Flash's "The Message", Public Enemy's "911 Is a Joke", Tupac's "Trapped", Dead Prez's "They Schools", Naughty By Nature, Ice Cube's "I Wanna Kill Sam" - challenges liberal political philosophy by claiming the social contract between blacks and the United States is broken: using Locke's Second Treatise account of state protection of life and property, he contends the state's failure of economic and physical protection voids blacks' political obligations. Drawing on Cornel West's diagnosis of black nihilism and Charles Mills's racial contract - a contract constructed for white supremacy - he reads conscious hip hop as post-civil-rights music continuing the black freedom struggle in a new voice, with KRS-One asking "Who protects us from you?"
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 28 "Reality versus Revolution" — McPherson argues political rap has never been politically revolutionary, sorting it into three schools: the amoral "gangsta Hobbes" ethic (Mobb Deep's "Survival of the Fittest", 50 Cent's "get rich or die tryin'") that sees the hood as Hobbes's state of nature where no social contract with blacks ever existed; Afrocentric communitarianism, split between nationalist separatists (Brand Nubian, X-Clan, Dead Prez) and the more cosmopolitan Native Tongues (De La Soul, A Tribe Called Quest); and a radical liberalism closer to Rawls than its adherents admit. Against Chuck D's "What's a smilin' face when the whole state's racist?", he argues Rawls's original position, veil of ignorance, and difference principle - applied with real-world knowledge of racism - support rather than oppose Public Enemy's demands for racial justice.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 25 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Alford reads the biker image, born at Hollister in 1947 and fixed by The Wild One, through two opposed accounts of presocial man: the badass on his tricked-out Harley is Hobbes's natural man, all vanity, domination, and fear merely redirected to government, praising Chuck Zito's 'most primitive philosophy'; the club run with bonfire, brothers, old ladies, and Steppenwolf re-enacts Rousseau's golden age between the stupidity of brutes and the fatal enlightenment of civil man, before the first enclosed field ('this is mine') bred property, vanity, and misery. The paradox of a biker who is simultaneously threat and salvation dissolves once we see that 'primitive' and 'civilized' are mutually defining: suburbanites and bikers alike live both Hobbesian individualism and Rousseauvian community, each defining themselves against the other.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 30 "Poker and Philosophy" — Stoehr finds Hobbes in the saloon: poker in classic Westerns — Hatfield's farewell game in Stagecoach, and the cheating scene where Wyatt Earp first crosses Doc Holliday in My Darling Clementine — dramatizes the tension between the lawless state of nature ('solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short') and the rule-governed community built by an implicit social contract, with caught cheaters (Chihuahua signaling hole cards) marking where play reverts to primal vengeance. Poker itself is a Hobbesian paradox: a communal social event built on winner-takes-all competition, exercising both logic and intuition within luck's hard limits. The morally ambiguous Fordian hero — Doc Holliday above all — lives at the same crossroads of civilization and wilderness as the card table.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 26 "No Way Out" — Leah Murray reads Romero's Dead series as an argument about the American social contract, individualism versus communitarianism. Night of the Living Dead's farmhouse is Hobbes: fear throws strangers Ben and Mr. Cooper into a makeshift commonwealth whose individualist half ('every man for himself' in the basement) fails, while Dawn shows the Hobbesian next step - martial law as Leviathan - after the state of nature returns. Land of the Dead's Fiddler's Green is a fear-born contract corrupting into Kaufman's hierarchy, and Big Daddy's zombies form the counter-model, a Rousseauian community of the general will based on mutual bonds rather than terror, as the priest in Dawn already urged ('we must stop the killing... or lose the war'). Following Tocqueville on civic association, she concludes Romero's survivors - Ben, Peter, Sarah, Riley - vindicate communitarian cooperation, even though Night's bureaucratic ending suggests there may be no way out.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 21 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Forster stages the dispute between Dr. No ('just a stupid policeman') and Scaramanga ('we are the same') over whether Bond's license to kill betrays the liberal rule of law it protects, connecting it to post-9/11 debates about executive power. He gives the rule of law a substantive ground in Locke's Two Treatises - prerogative power may suspend particular laws for the public good of preserving the community ('salus populi suprema lex'), illustrated by Locke's own career conspiring with Lord Ashley's spy network - and a procedural check in the separation of powers, mirrored in MI6's real parliamentary and judicial oversight. Both elements together, he concludes, let Bond's extra-legal work remain consistent with the rule of law: power exercised for the public good under institutional supervision, without which M's vendetta in 'For Your Eyes Only' would be indistinguishable from Scaramanga's contracts.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 39 "Gaining Trust from the Past" — Richard Davies treats the Oceanic 815 survivors' beach as a "framed" state of nature: the stolen water is a tragedy of the commons, Sawyer's "finders keepers" defense of Shannon's inhalers stages Hobbes's war of all against all against Locke's natural rights, and Jack and Sayid's torture of Sawyer marks the first step toward civil society, a claim to punish on another's behalf. He argues no theory of human nature (Rousseau's "Innocence" versus a "Trust No. 1" attitude) is needed to understand the castaways: cooperation grows through iterated prisoner's-dilemma tit-for-tat strategies, which also recasts the real difference between Hobbesian and Lockean states of nature.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 23 "Why Be Moral" — Sanders uses Bruno Anthony's 'criss-cross' murder-swap proposal to Guy Haines in Strangers on a Train to pose the classic question 'Why be moral?' to the charming amoralist. He tests three answers: Kant's categorical imperative fails because Bruno's egoist maxim ('remove obstacles to your happiness') can apparently be universalized; Hobbesian contractarian 'morality pays' fails because Bruno free-rides on others' restraint; and the Rachels/Nelson/Thomas psychological-health answer assumes rather than proves that Bruno should care about comparable suffering. A thought experiment comparing the moral life with the Bruno-state from an impartial standpoint leads to Aristotle's eudaimonia: morality is constitutive of human flourishing, so Bruno enjoys only a counterfeit happiness.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 10 "The Gathering of the Tribe Ironic Sacramentalism" — Horace Fairlamb argues the Grateful Dead were the Sixties' real revolutionary success: where the New Left failed by keeping confrontational politics, the Dead changed consciousness first, extending Mill's liberal 'experiments in living' into a whole alternative culture. He reads the total improvisation learned at the Acid Tests ('the form that follows chaos'), the band's leaderless 'functional anarchy' — Lesh: if anyone tried to take charge 'it would just dissolve in their hands' — and its flat business hierarchy with roadies as corporate presidents as a spontaneous order lived at the edge of chaos. The Deadhead community's ritual communitas, analyzed through Victor Turner's separation-liminality-reincorporation model, amounts to an 'ironic sacramentalism' that achieves what social contract from Hobbes (force), Locke (property), and Rawls (self-interest) cannot: unity that transcends difference while leaving it in place.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 22 "Don’t Get Into One" — Richard Greene renames the Tarantino standoff the 'ex-convict's dilemma' and models it as a special case of the prisoner's dilemma, running from Ordell and Louis's separate interrogation rooms to the White–Pink, Joe–White–Eddie and True Romance shoot-outs. He argues the standard group-rationality solution fails because ECDS participants have conflicting goals—Eddie protecting his father, White protecting Orange, Joe wanting revenge—and his survey of Tarantino's six cases shows escapes come from luck (Mr. Blonde's entrance, Nikki coming home) or shared interests (Beatrix's pregnancy), never group rationality. Tracing the dilemma back to Glaucon's contract argument in Plato's Republic, he concludes the only reliable solution is: don't get into one.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 10 "You May Wonder How Come I Love You Care and Ethics" — Gimbel asks what the E Street Band's marathon multiple encores mean, starting from social contract theory: Hobbes's state of nature ('no home, no job, no peace, no rest') and Locke's contract explain the ticket as a financial IOU — so a drunk, short Hendrix show wrongs you financially but not morally — while the contractual view of moral duty (the 'Hungry Heart' narrator who abandoned his wife and kids in Baltimore) cannot explain why a missing encore feels like personal betrayal. The gift theory fails too, since encores are expected, and expected things are not gifts. Care ethics (Ruddick, Noddings) fits instead: devoted fans make the band part of their identity, Springsteen sings 'to you about you,' and the No Nukes 90-minute set became permanent because he would not give his people less — while 'Pink Cadillac' shows the limit case, since you cannot love someone for her Cadillac.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 30 "Walking the Tightrope" — Louis Melancon weighs the Fleet leadership's secrets and lies: Adama's 'blind squirrel' lie about Earth, classifying the fact that Cylons look human, Roslin's faked death of the baby Hera, and Tom Zarek's secret collaboration courts on New Caprica. Democratic duty is framed as a deontological obligation of transparency grounded in the governed's trust, while the leadership repeatedly defaults to consequentialist wartime exceptions. The chapter proposes a rule-of-thumb: secrecy is justified only to hide specific information from an external threat like the Cylons, never to protect the government from its own citizens, and each violation erodes the trust on which Colonial democracy's 'soul' depends.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 26 "No Way Out" — Leah Murray argues Romero's Dead films stage the American contest between individualism and communitarianism inside the social contract: in Night of the Living Dead, communitarian Ben barricading the farmhouse against every-man-for-himself Mr. Cooper hiding in the basement; in Dawn of the Dead, the Peter-Roger-Fran-Stephen mall commune collapsing when Stephen's 'it's ours, we took it' meets the bikers; in Day of the Dead, Sarah's compassion against the racist, harassing soldiers; in Land of the Dead, Kaufman's Fiddler's Green as a Hobbesian Leviathan born of fear, complete with bread-and-circuses for the poor. Against the Hobbesian fear-born contract (Dawn opens in a full state-of-nature collapse) she sets Rousseau's general will and Tocqueville's civic association, embodied in Riley's freely formed community and in Big Daddy's zombies, who organize, turn from eating humans, and bring down the Leviathan. The films' verdict: fear-based individualist contracts collapse under their own contradictions, while compassionate cooperation — even among the Undead — is the only way out, even if Romero doubts its ultimate viability.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 44 "A Phenomenology of Reading the Ref" — Vannatta asks what the rules of soccer are from a player's perspective and tests legal theories: natural law and Rawls's veil of ignorance are too abstract to help on the pitch, and Austin's and Hart's positivism overemphasizes FIFA's top-down commands, so the best account is legal pragmatism — Holmes's bad man treats the law as a prophecy of what the ref will actually call, and Dewey roots the rules in custom and in the whistle itself rather than in prior legislation. Husserl's genetic phenomenology then explains how 'reading the ref' is possible: retention and protention synthesized in passive synthesis let experienced players anticipate play — and the referee's tendencies — without deliberation, replacing the impoverished notion of muscle memory. Playing to the whistle becomes a trainable skill of predicting an indeterminate despot, with lessons for coaching and sportsmanship alike.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 27 "Is Fencing a Dishonorable Art" — Michaud argues that fencing is the loneliest and most egoistic martial art: alone on the strip, you seek to understand your opponent only in order to deceive them through disengages and parry-feints. He maps the bout onto Hobbes: psychological egoism, the dueling ground as a state of nature of 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short', and the referee as the Leviathan whose rules keep the bloodshed out while licensing normative egoism inside them. Testing defenses from Rand, Friedman and Carr's business 'rules of the game', he concludes that fencing kept its soldier's anything-goes ethos after the lethal stakes vanished, making it a 'dishonorable' art: a Hobbesian feast of solitude, egoism and deception.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 15 "This Is the Age of Steel" — Littmann asks what a genuinely logical creature would do and grades the Cybermen against three accounts of reason: Hobbes's self-preservation and social contract, which the survival-focused Cybermen of 'The Tenth Planet' roughly satisfy but their later wars of conquest betray; Mill's utilitarianism, whose greatest-happiness principle, higher pleasures, liberty, and individuality condemn emotion-stripping, forced 'upgrades', and uniformity; and Hume's claim that reason alone motivates nothing, under which perfectly logical but emotionless Cybermen would simply do nothing at all. The upshot is that Cyberman 'logic' is incoherent — no theory of reason makes them rational.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 14 "Spice as the Vehicle of Power" — Reads the Duniverse as Hobbes's state of nature at galactic scale: Emperor, Landsraad houses, Guild, Bene Gesserit, and Tleilaxu are rationally self-preserving factions in a war of all against all over scarce spice, where 'justice' names only what enforcement power backs and life for the losers is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.' Leto II is the Leviathan—a literal 'mortal God,' half sandworm—whose spice monopoly and fusion of political with spiritual authority impose a forced peace; his assassination then shows split authority re-igniting the conflict in the Scattering and the Honored Matres. Paul's threat to destroy the spice and Leto's hoarding both illustrate that the power to destroy a thing is absolute control over it.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 21 "No Matter How You Flip the Patty . ." — Michael Dodge asks whether Krabs may guard the Krabby Patty formula, sorting Bikini Bottom's property into collective, communal (Jellyfish Fields) and private, and deploying the tragedy of the commons — Krabs's jellyfish-squeezing factory in 'Jellyfish Hunter' — to show why shared resources get rationally overexploited. Hobbes grounds Krabs's right in sovereign enforcement (without the law, 'Pineapple Fever''s chalk-line household collapses into animals fighting over the fridge), Locke in labor-mixing, with Krabs's identity bound to his patties since 'Help Wanted', and Hume in conventions of justice born of selfishness and scarcity. All three support Krabs's legal and moral right to his secret recipe against Plankton.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 19 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Jason Walker argues the zombie apocalypse is a Lockean rather than Hobbesian state of nature: rights to life, liberty, and property persist without government. Rick's 'I don't think those rules apply anymore' to Andrea over the mermaid necklace is justified by Locke's spoilage and 'enough and as good' provisos - the owner is almost certainly dead and the necklace would otherwise lie forever wasted - while Morgan's house-squatting, which protects the Thompsons' home, and Rick voluntarily sharing guns with Guillermo's nursing-home defenders show self-ownership and norms at work. The counter-cases, Chris's cannibal band ('a man's gotta eat') and the Governor, who treat persons as mere means, live out Hobbes's war of all against all and are destroyed by the Lockean right to punish that victims retain.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 27 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Hoskins and Wikoff use Cutty's release after fourteen years in Jessup to ask what it means to have 'paid your debt to society' when ex-offenders still face bans on housing, jobs, welfare, student loans, and voting. They test the standard defenses: the consequentialist safety argument fails because these bans push men like Cutty back into the Game ('This game is rigged, man'); the competence argument collapses since McNulty, who did not even know the Democratic candidate, is no more competent a voter; and Judge Friendly's Locke-inspired social-contract claim that criminals forfeit their voice in lawmaking cannot explain why Prez's pistol-whipping or Clay Davis's corruption would not equally forfeit theirs. They conclude that continuing to punish after the sentence ends is unjust, and that Cutty's boxing gym shows former prisoners can reform.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 25 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Leslie Dale Feldman reads the 1968 film's blasted opening as Hobbes's state of nature - 'solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short' - with the Lawgiver's 'Beware the beast Man' scroll echoing Hobbes's three causes of war (competition, fear, glory) and Plato's Ring of Gyges explaining why even the 'just' man acts rightly only under compulsion, both grounding the social contract's origin story. She then casts Dr. Zaius as Alexis de Tocqueville's tyranny of the majority - erasing Taylor's writing, lobotomizing Landon, and sealing Cornelius's cave 'to spare them all the care of thinking' - with Rousseau's man 'born free; and everywhere he is in chains' behind it. The chapter also traces Rod Serling's Twilight Zone fingerprints (nuclear-war twist endings like 'Time Enough at Last,' the cave of 'The Old Man in the Cave,' Adam-and-Eve survivor pairs, the beauty reversals of 'Eye of the Beholder') and reads Taylor and Nova's westward ride through Turner's frontier thesis and Kennedy's New Frontier, holding Serling's Hobbesian pessimism and his hope in tension.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 24 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Fitzpatrick uses the social contract tradition to explain Prohibition-era Atlantic City. Hobbes's state of nature fits the gang warfare left where no Leviathan is strong enough to enforce federal law against Nucky; Locke's fits a night-watchman government overreaching into Prohibition and thereby breaking the contract, as with Nucky's illegitimate protection 'taxes'; Rousseau's noble savage corrupted by commercial society fits the Klan's pleasure in cruelty and innocent Tommy set against scheming adults. Ethical egoism frames Nucky's framing of Hans Schroeder, consequentialism the Temperance Union's cost-benefit failure, and deontology Margaret's lying campaign speech, while Marx's and Mill's view that human nature is malleable explains the season-spanning transformation of Nucky from half-gangster into 'a gangster and a half.'
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 36 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Roberto Sirvent and Ian Diorio ask what the state really asks soldiers to die for: not Hobbes-and-Locke's rational social contract, since we are Heideggerian thrown into the wreckage of democracy rather than a pure founding state, but a nation that makes itself sacred. MacIntyre's charge that killing for the nation-state is 'killing for the telephone company' frames the analysis of America's civil liturgies - oaths (semper fidelis), flag ritual mirrored eerily in Brody burying Jessica's thrown Quran, saints, martyrs, and Saul pitting belief in America against belief in Allah. Augustine's civitas dei names the result: America as chosen city of God, and Islam terrifies the West because its creed claims devotion above any national flag.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 11 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Caballeros argues that political legitimacy in Ooo runs through parenthood: Princess Bubblegum rules the citizens she created ('You made me... you are my Glob'), the Ice King is redeemed when we learn Simon protected child Marceline, and the Flame King and Hunson Abadeer forfeit standing as fathers. Using Hobbes's view that a ruler is legitimate insofar as he protects his subjects, the chapter asks whether Bubblegum's protection-cum-manipulation—sabotaging Finn to let James die, jailing Tree Trunks—still counts, and it contrasts justified rebellion (Flame Princess deposing her father, Marceline resisting Abadeer) with Lumpy Space Princess's disastrous one. Good parenting, like good government, earns obedience; bad parenting loses the crown.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 12 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Gale and Barkman treat post-Mushroom-War Ooo as a state-of-nature laboratory for liberalism's three founders. The Forest Wizard who cages Finn in 'Storytelling' is Hobbes's Leviathan, kept in power by fear yet moderated by self-interest (Goblin King Xergiok's fall shows the leash); Princess Bubblegum's Candy Kingdom is Locke's civil society where citizens trade private revenge for impartial law—her lawful bow to Lemongrab shows she rules by contract, not fear; and 'City of Thieves' illustrates Rousseau's claim that property corrupts natural goodness, with Finn and Jake as his uncorrupted natural people. The chapter concludes that the rights language these thinkers forged is what keeps both Ooo and our world from sliding back into a war of all against all.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 39 "24. Who’s Duty to Whom" — Dawson asks why the Doctor sides with humans and humanoids against rational non-humanoids, testing Kant first: a logic-grounded categorical morality can count the Daleks as immoral rather than amoral (universalized slavery is incoherent), but pure reason cannot motivate Daleks or the Master, and Kant's theory absurdly condemns the Doctor's lies and his theft of the TARDIS. Hobbesian psychological egoism and the social contract fare worse - the Daleks are no co-signatories, and self-sacrifices from Katarina to the Doctor's seemingly final years on Trenzalore resist the egoist's retelling - so the chapter lands with Hume: sympathy and benevolence found morality on feeling, which explains and partly excuses the Doctor's parochial partiality for beings who resemble him, making him 'at least half-Humean.'
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 24 "9. Anarchy, State, and Apocalypse" — Da Silva and McKendry test the political legitimacy of four post-apocalyptic governance types: the Claimers' anarchy that collapses into Joe adjudicating 'claims', the Governor's and Rick's dictatorships ('This is not a democracy anymore!'), the prison Council's representative democracy with the three questions as a quasi-constitution, and Terminus's quasi-theocratic cannibal creed ('You're the butcher or you're the cattle'). Using Hobbes's state of nature and war of all against all, hypothetical social contract, and the twin tests of power and morality, they judge even the benevolent Rick-tatorship unjust because concentrated power is fallible and unaccountable. They conclude, with Churchill, that the Council's imperfect democracy is the worst form of government except for all the others.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 23 "11. Have Fun Overthrowing This Evil Government!" — Gibson reads Humperdinck's fabricated-pretext war against Guilder (framing Guilder for Buttercup's murder, with Vizzini's crew as private military contractors) through Just War Theory: it fails the jus ad bellum just-cause requirement built on Augustine and Aquinas, since the war would be retribution sparked by staged wrongdoing, and contractor motives of profit compound the violation. Michael Davis's critique of the ticking-time-bomb defense then shows that Rugen's torture of Westley is exactly the 'institution of torture' whose moral cost forbids ever licensing torture, since the torturer must be trained on victims first. Finally, even Hobbes's Leviathan - the most absolutist of social contract views - requires the sovereign to protect the people's safety and administer equal justice, so Humperdinck's record makes his rule illegitimate and the storming of the castle a justified insurrection.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 11 "2. Sure We’re Criminals" — Malloy asks whether the two law-breaking vigilantes are criminals and whether any duty to obey the law survives scrutiny. He runs consent theory through Superman surrendering in handcuffs in Man of Steel and the Red Son Superman's residence in the USSR, uses Darkseid's Apokolips as Hobbes's security sovereign against Locke's natural-rights limits, deploys Hume against tacit consent (Batman would never leave Gotham even in No Man's Land), and dismantles gratitude theory (the Kents' adoption involved a sacrificial choice the law cannot make) and fair play (Nozick's Batman-lottery undercuts "I'm not wearing hockey pads"). He lands near Wolff-style philosophical anarchism: Superman's constrained lawbreaking endorses the law's legitimacy while Batman treats law as one more tool in his war, making him a force of chaos.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 20 "10. Lord Vetinari’s Friendly Guide to Tyranny" — Alloy stages the debate over Vetinari's legitimacy as letters to the Ankh-Morpork Times: a writer channeling Hobbes defends the contracted sovereign - a 'mortal god' who cannot commit crimes and secures freedom through security - while 'the late Jeremy Bentham' judges the Patrician by the greatest good of the greatest number yet would disenfranchise golems and the 'differently-alive' dead. The anarchist Wolff Paul Roberts rebuts both, denying any right to rule, rejecting tacit consent by residence, and holding up the free golems as models of uncoerced virtue, before a final letter defends Vetinari's limited, functional government. The frame - Vetinari quietly orchestrating the whole correspondence and planning Roberts's next letter - shows tyranny curating its own philosophical defense.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 22 "12. The Law of Red Rising" — Christopher Ketcham frames the Society through jurisprudence's debate between natural and positive law, opening with Gramsci's hegemony: Reds have internalized the Golds' message that their slave toil is heroic terraforming service, becoming 'enabled martyrs' who hate rival clans rather than their rulers. He deploys Hobbes's state of nature versus state of laws (Reds live in a state of war against Mars while Golds legislate in a state of law), Locke's suggestion that a sovereign can leave some people in the state of nature, Aquinas-style higher law, and H.L.A. Hart's positivism with Bentham and Austin—a law need not be moral to be law—to argue the Golds' caste statutes are valid yet ungrounded. His coda casts Darrow as Homer Plessy: Goldness, like whiteness in Plessy v. Ferguson, is inheritable property Reds cannot claim, and because Reds who speak are hanged, the law excludes the very voices Hart himself said keep laws from becoming terrible.
- **The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed**, ch. 9 "1 Introduction" — Smith introduces his project of explaining the subordination of women and blacks philosophically and empirically by comparing the social contract liberalism of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau with Marxism, building on Carole Pateman's Sexual Contract and Charles Mills's Racial Contract/Contract and Domination, which show the classic contracts were male supremacist and white supremacist. He argues sexual and racial egalitarianism is about politics and power, cataloguing nine power bases women and blacks should acquire, and stresses that because family and state are historically connected (Aristotle's Politics, Hobbes's 'little kingdoms', Locke's conjugal society, Rousseau's family as the oldest society, Engels's 'first class oppression' of the female by the male), equality in marriage may be a precondition for equality in society. He defends Marxism against Mills's dismissal of it as moribund, endorses MacKinnon's linking of sexism and racism while arguing (with Linda LaRue and Du Bois) that the racial contract has been more tyrannical than the sexual contract, and closes with Walzer's definition of egalitarianism as a society free of domination.
- **The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed**, ch. 11 "3 On the Origin of the Family" — The chapter compares the liberal contract theorists with Engels (building on Morgan's Ancient Society) on the origin of the patriarchal monogamous family: Hobbes derives sovereign-husbanded 'little monarchies' from a state of nature in which women are men's equals, a derivation Susan Okin shows is contradictory; Locke grounds conjugal society in a voluntary compact with the husband as 'abler and stronger' last determiner, yet leaves women excluded from the social contract; Rousseau pairs passionate economic equality with some of the most sexist writing in Western thought, including fear of wives' sexual power in Emile. Against these static philosophies Engels gives a historical-materialist account in which the overthrow of mother right - the 'world historical defeat of the female sex' - followed from private property and inheritance, turning the bourgeois wife into a proletarian or prostitute while opening 'sex love' to the propertyless, and prescribing women's return to the labor force, socialized child-care, industrialized housework and easy divorce. John Stuart Mill's Subjection of Women appears as liberalism's one exception to its sexism, and a footnote sets Firestone's biological account of patriarchy against Engels's property account.
- **The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed**, ch. 12 "4 On the Origin of the State" — Opening with Newt Gingrich's complaint that students 'don't read enough Locke' and the Chinese premier's appeal to Rousseau, the chapter compares the three contract theorists' states of nature and purposes of government: Hobbes's war of every man against every man yielding an absolute sovereign with no separation of powers, Locke's peaceful nature in which mixing labor with land creates property and money then creates inequality, so that government's 'great and chief end' is protecting property through limited, separated powers and no food stamps, and Rousseau's compassionate natural humans corrupted when the first man enclosed land, so the state was founded on fraud and a general will that should 'force him to be free' and give people food stamps. Smith then reads the actual US founding as a chaste Lockean contract 'bastardized' on race and sex - the Declaration plagiarized from Locke, Abigail Adams's 'remember the ladies' laughed off, Dred Scott, with the 14th Amendment as the de-bastardizing 'Charter of Universal Freedom' - while Engels derives the state historically from the Iroquois and Greek gens, private property and class conflict. A final section documents white supremacy inside the tradition (Kant inventing the scientific concept of race, Hegel and Hume on Black inferiority), John Stuart Mill's 'Negro Question' as the tradition's decisive anti-racist break, Locke's own entanglements with the slave trade, and Marx's condemnation of slavery as super-exploitation.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 29 "18. Red vs. Blue or Both Simply Leviathan Green" — Smith reads Marvel's Civil War through Hobbes's Leviathan: unregulated superheroes live in a state of nature where life is violent and brutish (the Stamford explosion and Scarlet Witch's Lagos miscalculation as tipping points), and the Superhuman Registration Act is the social contract - a literal signed contract on Team Iron Man - offered as the way out. He then argues both leaders act as absolute sovereigns who never sought consent: Iron Man rules through the Illuminati, enforcement squads and the Negative Zone prison, Cap through an unofficial army bound by his own rules, as Moon Knight's tirade about their ego grudge match makes plain. The war is thus two Leviathans colliding and subjugating everyone else, resolved only when Iron Man's Leviathan wins and enforces registration.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 30 "19. The Superhero Challenge to State Sovereignty" — Ewing argues the Sokovia Accords are at bottom about state sovereignty: via Bodin's absolute sovereign, Hobbes's war of all against all and the Leviathan's monopoly on coercion, and Habermas's account of the modern territorial state's monopoly on legitimate violence, he shows that Avengers who ignore borders and cannot be countered (Thor, Hulk, Doctor Strange, Scarlet Witch) render the state's claim to sovereignty effectively meaningless - the US can only police rogue heroes by enlisting other heroes. Since states cannot guarantee enforcement and state power itself can turn predatory (HYDRA's infiltration of SHIELD, Nazi Germany, Cap's 'agendas change' warning), he concludes that neither unchecked heroes nor unchecked states should rule, and floats democratizing superpowers to restore the sovereignty of the populace.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 34 "22. A New Civil War" — Horn reads Marvel's Civil War as an allegory of post-9/11 America's Patriot Act debate over security versus liberty: Iron Man takes Hobbes's side, treating unregulated superhumans as the state of nature - a 'war of every man against every man' - that the Registration Act's social contract and punishment-backed rules must end, while Captain America takes Mill's On Liberty side, insisting full freedom for human nature must not be ceded to a government that will overreach, with Spider-Man torn between the two like the American citizen.
