Invoking Habermas's communicative action and deliberative democracy from Between Facts and Norms, he blames the two camps for talking past each other - Cap walling himself off while Tony keeps reaching out - and prescribes genuinely open dialogue as the only bridge that can marry security and liberty before the country devolves into its own civil war.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 29 "16. He’s Ethickle Rick!!!" — The chapter reads the Galactic Federation as Hobbes's Sovereign: Earth covenants in for security and gets an interplanetary TSA, pill-currency debt, and the surveillance droid Conroy, while the Citadel of Ricks tours Hobbes's three commonwealths in 'The Ricklantis Mixup', aristocratic Council, brief democracy, and Evil Morty's monarchy, where the Sovereign's rules cannot by definition be unjust. Against this, Rick embodies Hobbes's psychological egoism ('the object to every man is his own pleasure'), hiding his motives in the Riq IV hostage gambit and the Szechuan-sauce confession. Yet the chapter argues Rick's egoism is oddly ethical: in an infinite multiverse resources are not scarce, so refusing to surrender freedom to any Sovereign and competing for everything is the right way to live, with 'A Rickle in Time' and the self-sacrifice of 'The Wedding Squanchers' as its tested limits.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 12 "A Closer Look at Alice’s Trial" — Argues Alice is right to attack the court of the King and Queen of Hearts because she never entered a social contract with Wonderland: unlike Socrates, who stayed in Athens and so had to abide by the verdict (Plato's Crito), Alice fell in involuntarily and is trying to leave. Dennis Knepp casts the Queen of Hearts as Hobbes's absolute sovereign whose public 'Off with their heads!' terrorizes the playing cards into obedience ('Covenants, without the Sword, are but Words'), while Locke's limited, consent-based government and Rawls's contractualism mark the better alternative the Hearts court fails to meet. Since Alice stands outside their covenant, she is her own more-than-a-mile-high Leviathan, rightly defending herself in the state of nature.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 14 "A Specter Is Haunting the Bending World" — Lin argues the Bending World's supernatural inequality breaks Hobbes's condition that even the weakest can kill the strongest, the equality that motivates the social contract, so might-is-right is magnified: Ozai rules without bargaining while weak Earth Kings become Dai Li figureheads. Energybending's built-in 'moral self-destruct' needs no earthly accountability, resembling the divine right of kings rather than Arendt's insight that violence eradicates politics, and Aang wisely remains a passive guardian. The Avatar's reincarnation creates recurring power vacuums, and because bending is a non-redistributable endowment, the Equalist revolution haunts the Bending World like the specter of communism in the Communist Manifesto.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 14 "A Specter Is Haunting the Bending World" — Lin uses Hobbes's observation that in our world the weakest can kill the strongest, grounding the social contract, to show what breaks when supernatural power is wildly unequal: Fire Lord Ozai need not bargain with generals as Earth Kings must with the Dai Li, and the eclipse is the only equalizer. Energybending gets a 'moral self-destruct' that no real technology has, making Aang an unaccountable guardian closer to the divine right of kings than to naturalist politics, though his refusal of rule keeps politics alive in Arendt's sense. Like Marx and Engels's specter of communism, the 'specter of Equalism' outlives Amon, because bending is a non-redistributable, lethal endowment, so democracy in Republic City is structurally haunted.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 14 "The Thin Veil" — Brett Chandler Patterson reads the No Man's Land storyline, in which earthquake-isolated Gotham is carved into gang territories by Two-Face, Penguin, and the Joker, alongside Hurricane Katrina's flooding of New Orleans as twin real-and-fictional tests of Hobbes's state of nature and the social contract. He contrasts Jim Gordon's lawful, Machiavellian-seeming rebuilding of trust with Officer William Petit's slide into execution-style 'despotic' power, and highlights the pacifist witness of Father Christian and Dr. Leslie Thompkins against Hobbes's demand that churches defer to the sovereign. Batman's turn as a benevolent gang lord working to hand the city back to Gordon shows, for Patterson, that Batman's real enemy is anarchy itself.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 15 "Theorizing Government" — Tony Spanakos argues that Gotham's government, not Bruce's psyche, explains Batman: the state failed at Crime Alley, and nearly every major character reacts to a state that is either too weak or too restrictive. Working from Max Weber's definition of the state as monopoly on legitimate violence, Hobbes's Leviathan, and Nietzsche's state as 'new idol,' he reads Year One's corrupt Commissioner Loeb, Year Two's self-appointed Reaper, Anarky's failed anarchist dystopia, Two-Face's broken faith in the law, and The Dark Knight Returns' state-loyal Superman and Commissioner Yindel. The Batman-Gordon partnership emerges as a precarious unofficial order in which Gordon tolerates the one exception to the state's monopoly on violence.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 30 "Walking the Tightrope" — Melancon weighs the Fleet leadership's secrets and lies: Adama's false claim to know the way to Earth, concealing that Cylons look human, Roslin faking Hera's death and hiding the baby, and Zarek's secret collaboration courts on New Caprica. He argues that keeping secrets from the Cylons can be justified by the state's duty to protect, but the leadership repeatedly deceives the governed themselves, discarding the transparency democratic legitimacy requires. Deontological duty to the governed keeps losing to consequentialist reasoning, and the chapter asks what happens to Colonial democracy's 'soul' when trust between government and governed erodes.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 15 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — The Bocks test three answers to the good life against the show: Howard as hedonist (laser-obstacle-strip-chess, the 'whore of Omaha') read through Bentham, Mill's higher and lower pleasures, and Aristippus; ethical egoism via Glaucon's ring of Gyges and Howard's offer to Skype rather than visit the deported Raj; and Hobbes's state of nature and social contract read into Sheldon's roommate agreement, whose lack of a Hobbesian sovereign leaves 'I settle all ties' arbitrary and rule-following too thin for ethics. Aristotle's virtue and practical wisdom crown Leonard — the nucleus of the social group, as Amy says — as the closest thing to the phronimos. The gang's sabotage of Dennis Kim with a manufactured girlfriend closes the chapter by asking who really ruined whose life.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 18 "8 T’Challa, the Revolutionary King Legitimation Crises in Wakanda" — Porter uses Habermas's legitimation crisis to read Killmonger's reign: by governing flagrantly against Wakandan tradition — burning the Heart-Shaped Herb, waving off the unfinished challenge ritual with 'All that challenge shit is over with. I'm the king now' — he erodes not just his own standing but acceptance of kingship itself, moving Okoye from procedural objection to 'you are not fit to be a king.' He then argues the film inoculates monarchy against viewer critique through Shuri's permissible teasing and Wakanda's harmonizing of opposites, and shows that T'Challa's UN speech, matched line-by-line to Bossuet's defense of the divine right of kings, quietly reaches toward absolutism — leaving audiences cheering a hereditary, divinely sanctioned throne that Locke's consent of the governed would never legitimate in their own world.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 23 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Torosyan argues The Daily Show models the critical thinking and good-faith civic discourse that real politics and TV news lack, reading John Oliver's 'Civil Disservice' interview with Froma Harrop and Stewart's clips of Rumsfeld contradicting himself on WMDs as exposing bullshit in Frankfurt's sense: assertion indifferent to truth. Stewart's reframing of William Bennett's gay-marriage talking points (is the debate about marriage or about who counts as human?) and his self-effacing interviews with Ramesh Ponnuru enact Rousseau's social-contract ideal of what news owes the public against Machiavellian ends-justify-means manipulation. Gadamer supplies the demand that Bennett question his own horizons, Nietzsche's Apollonian-Dionysian account of tragedy frames the show's satire, and the Tao Te Ching's 'let yourself be partial' governs the whole chapter.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 30 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Vanderheiden treats America (The Book)'s textbook parody as serious democratic theory: its 'Democracy Inaction' diagnosis (a president chosen from a field of two, 99% incumbency, lobbyists as 'the white knights of democracy') tracks the thin versus thick democracy distinction and Benjamin Barber's deliberative democracy, with Putnam's social capital as the remedy for the satirized life cycle of national decline. The 'Dress the Supreme Court' gag, Senate color-by-numbers, and third-party graveyard expose representational exclusion, while the media chapter indicts conglomeration for killing the press's watchdog role, invoking Mill's marketplace of ideas. The Earth (The Book) postscript notes that social contracts were historically written without the assent of the women and minorities they subjugated.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 36 "“Real Life Is Messy”" — The chapter tests Zootopia's 'where anyone can be anything' against three ideals: the founding play's predator-prey war is a Hobbesian state of nature ('man is a wolf to man') pacified by social order; Judy's parking duty and Nick's 'you can only be what you are' expose how stereotyping confuses artificial barriers with real biological limits to self-determination; and the evolved end of predation frames a just multispecies society, read through Donaldson and Kymlicka's Zoopolis case for animal citizenship. Nussbaum's hint at 'the gradual supplanting of the natural by the just' is weighed against the dystopia of turning the wild into a world-sized zoo, leaving Zootopia aspirational rather than achieved.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 41 "“Look at This Stuff; Isn't It Neat ” disney and the Commodification of Political Values" — Dale and Foy tour the parks' political philosophy: Cinderella's Castle looming over Liberty Square embodies the contradiction between princess hierarchy and Lockean self-government, since Locke's Second Treatise grounds rule in consent and majority will, forbids special rights for rulers, and justifies revolution — the very ideals the 'Declaration salad' celebrates under a monarchy's silhouette. The Epcot World Showcase, judged through Kymlicka, Benhabib, and Taylor's recognition-based multiculturalism, reduces eleven cultures to a consumable menu, so that per Barber's 'McWorld' Disney sells pre-packaged 'freedom' and 'multiculturalism' as spectator values that reinforce rather than transform.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 14 "Spice as the Vehicle of Power" — Maps Hobbes's state of nature onto the Duniverse: the Emperor, Landsraad, Guild, Bene Gesserit and Tleilaxu are rational agents in a war of all against all over the scarce good of spice, where justice is meaningless until a supreme power enforces covenants. Paul's threat to destroy the spice and Leto II's monopoly on a hoarded supply show how power over the resource itself becomes the trump card that forces peace, with the Fremen refusing to kill Stilgar illustrating the rational turn from mutual weakening to peace. Leto II, the half-sandworm 'mortal god' who fuses civil and spiritual sovereignty so that breaking law becomes sin, is presented as Hobbes's Leviathan, whose tyranny is 'quite literally, the best thing to happen to mankind.'
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 27 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Ted Henry Brown and Christie Maloyed stage the Enderverse as the international-relations debate between Hobbesian realism — Graff's 'if one of us has to be destroyed...' and the human-bugger Prisoner's Dilemma where the absence of communication forces mutual defection and war — and liberal institutionalism, which Peter's Locke and Valentine's Demosthenes argue out on Earth's nets. Machiavelli supplies Peter's theory of power: fortune opens the moment, virtù seizes it with 'the right words at the right time,' and force must back persuasion when belief fades, so that 'influence is power' and governing by persuasion beats fiat.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 19 "Notes" — John Irish reads the Amazon series' Vault 33 as Locke's Two Treatises staged and then betrayed: Overseer elections (Betty Pearson against Reg McPhee and Woody Thomas), town-council deliberation over captured Vault 32 raiders, and Lucy's 1950s-styled domesticity all mimic natural equality, consent of the governed, majority rule, and the preservation of property. Norm's discovery that every election is rigged in favor of cryo-preserved technocrats from Vault 31, that Lucy's marriage 'application' is engineered population control, and that Vault-Tec executives - including Lucy's mother Barb - voted to launch the Great War itself shows Locke's forms of consent, law, and rights preserved as empty ceremony. The chapter's argument is that Enlightenment liberalism stripped of transparency becomes authoritarian experiment management: consent becomes choreography in a commonwealth that is really a lab, right down to composting the raiders' bodies.
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 16 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — Greg Littmann asks what sort of life is worth living by holding Final Fantasy protagonists and FFXI Online players up to three standards. Hobbes's egoism and defense of absolute monarchy condemn the altruistic, authority-defying heroes (AVALANCHE, the rebels of FFII and FFVI) while partly approving the gil-grubbing, rule-breaking FFXI player; Mill's utilitarianism praises the world-saving heroes but condemns grinding down beastmen and rates most gaming a lower pleasure; Aristotle's function argument and golden mean find heroes like Yuna immoderately self-sacrificial yet credit ordinary FFXI adventurers with genuinely virtuous moderation, helping others while keeping their own interests in view.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 11 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Greg Littmann asks who should rule Westeros and answers with Hobbes's Leviathan: people act only from self-interest ('we are all Lord Littlefinger under the skin') and fight for gain, safety, and glory - the mountain clans, Robert's preemptive strike on Daenerys, Drogo's wars for pride - so without a sovereign life is a war of all against all, and only an absolute ruler makes oath-keeping self-interested. Mapping Hobbes's own civil war (the Stuarts onto the Targaryens), he argues that even Varys is right to serve 'the realm' and peace by betraying Ned, and that loyalty rightly transfers from Aerys to Robert to Joffrey because protection, not lineage or justice, is the point of the sovereign. He then criticizes Hobbes: Ned and Jon show people really do die for principle, and Mad King Aerys's overcentralized power left rebellion as the only remedy - the War of the Five Kings shows civil war's horror must be weighed against appeals to honor.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 17 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — David Hahn contends Ned died because of his honor, not for it. Hobbes explains why: words bind no one without fear of enforcement - Cersei ripping up Robert's will ('Is this meant to be your shield, Lord Stark?') exposes Ned's belief that allegiance alone secures the King's Justice - and the Iron Throne itself is a Leviathan, forged by Aegon's dragons ending the state of nature, whose force rather than justice holds the peace. Machiavelli supplies the indictment of Ned's idealism: 'we who presume to rule must do vile things for the good of the realm,' so Ned's refusal to assassinate Daenerys, his merciful warning to Cersei, and backing the rightful but war-prone Stannis over Renly cost him his head and plunged the realm into civil war; the security of the state demanded exiling or killing the Lannisters and crowning Renly.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 26 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Joffrey on the Iron Throne, immune from punishment for beheading Ned, is read as Glaucon's ring of Gyges made flesh: the chapter asks what reason he has to be moral when he can get away with everything, noting he lacks even Gyges's advantage of secrecy and is hated like the Mad King. Hobbes's social contract is considered and rejected as a motive for Joffrey - King's Landing is no Hobbesian community like the Night's Watch, and Joffrey does better free-riding on everyone else's morality. The Platonic answer carries the chapter: like Ned Stark, who refused the throne, lived honorably in Winterfell, and regretted trading his honor at Baelor, the just person with an ordered soul has the only genuine happiness, which Joffrey's desire-satisfying cruelty forfeits.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 9 "NOTES" — Sharp argues that superpowered individuals break the equality assumption on which social contract theory rests: since Claire cannot be killed, D.L. can walk out of any jail, and Matt can sway juries, Hobbes's fear-of-death rationale for the contract seems not to apply to them. He then answers that the heroes remain effectively equal (Claire can still be killed by a wood splinter, Adam by decapitation) and shares Locke's and Rawls's reasons for contract, yet shows Rawls's difference principle would force the powered to serve society while the liberty principle forbids it, and that Sylar could not even be morally condemned under a pure Hobbesian reading. Cases like Claude's invisible petty theft (Glaucon's Ring of Gyges made real), the 'Five Years Gone' registered-superhumans future, and Linderman's plot to reunite society through the New York explosion lead to the conclusion that superpowers really would break society.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 19 "Notes" — Casts Frank as the 'Foole' of Leviathan chapter 15 — the man who grants that covenants exist but thinks injustice can 'stand with reason' — and documents his befriend-then-betray pattern: Russo groomed for governor then gassed in his car, Zoe fed stories then pushed under a train, Walker befriended, helped and maneuvered into resigning, all to reap the contract's benefits while breaking it for 'the getting of a kingdom'. The chapter then defends Hobbes' reply via Kavka: the Foole's vainglory makes him overestimate his ability to deceive, and a detailed audit of Frank's two murders (fingerprints, witnesses, electronic traces, forensic evidence, alibis, high-stakes deception 'tells') shows them contingency-riddled and irrational. Even Frank's success is no defense — his presidency rests on others' errors and luck (Skorsy, Orsay, Tusk, Stamper, and above all Claire all remain loose ends), so he exemplifies the vainglorious Foole acting against the reason of his preservation rather than a rational violator of the social contract.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 19 "Notes" — Courtland uses Hobbes's 'Foole' from Leviathan — who grants that covenants exist but insists injustice 'may sometimes stand with reason' — as the template for Frank, who enjoys the benefits of the social contract (security, cooperation, even Freddy's BBQ) while befriending and betraying Russo, Zoe, and Walker up to outright murder. Applying Hobbes's reply, the chapter audits both murders as contingency-ridden blunders — fingerprints, witnesses, cameras, forensic evidence, and the 'tells' of high-stakes deception — and diagnoses Frank's confidence as the vainglory behind Kavka's 'Foole's gold.' Even his success proves nothing: in the Latin Leviathan a fortunate outcome of reckless action is still imprudence, and his 'kingdom' rests on loose ends (Skorsky, Orsay, Tusk, Stamper, and Claire) that could bring the house of cards down.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Michels reads Frank as 'Hobbesian to the core' and democracy as 'the state of nature with elections': Walker, Matthews, and Vasquez show that elections elevate mediocrities, while Frank's America Works and his FEMA/Stafford Act end-run around Congress display the energetic sovereign for whom 'a tyrant is only a king disliked.' Hobbes's pleasure-pain psychology of appetite and aversion explains the cast — Frank's ribs, PlayStation, and pure taste for power; Russo's indiscriminate addictions; Doug's serial ones — while Hobbes's competition for gain, fear, and glory structures the Tusk money-versus-power war whose casualties include Freddy. With Hobbes's subordination of religion to civil power, Frank's crucifix-spitting 'I pray to myself, for myself' caps the case that truth only obstructs sovereignty, leaving Madison's 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition' as the lone check.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 27 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Foy reads the arena as Hobbes's state of nature recreated: the Cornucopia bloodbath, 'stealing isn't illegal here,' and temporary alliances awaiting betrayal instantiate the war of all against all, while the Treaty of Treason is Panem's written social contract buying order at the price of submission to the Capitol. Gale's advice that killing tributes is 'just hunting' mirrors the Hobbesian maxim the Gamemakers want, whereas Peeta's vow to show he is 'more than a piece in their Games' expresses Kant's categorical imperative and the duty to treat humanity as an end. Katniss's arc — decorating Rue's body, risking her life at the feast for Peeta's medicine, telling the District 2 soldier 'I'm done killing their slaves,' and rejecting Gale's tactic of bombing rescuers — moves her from survival logic to Kantian moral autonomy. The chapter ends by rejecting the Hobbesian justification of oppressive rule: a life of fear and servitude is not worth preserving at any cost.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 17 "Selling Ol’ Shellhead" — Malloy uses Spymaster's theft of Stark's armor designs in the Armor Wars and the U.S. government's legally valid appropriation of the technology after Tony announces 'I am Iron Man' to test two theories of property. Locke's natural-law view makes the designs an extension of Stark's laboring self — stealing them is like taking an arm — while Hume's social-contract view treats property as a useful convention whose violation makes the thief an enemy of society itself, and Rousseau supplies the cautionary image of the first man who fenced ground and said 'This is mine.' A closing thought experiment in which Tony sells Iron Man outright (like Siegel and Schuster selling Superman) argues that intellectual property can never be fully alienated: whoever wore the armor, Tony would still be Iron Man.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 10 "Notes" — Skoble argues the Mad Max world is misread as anarchy: Immortan Joe, Aunty Entity, and Humungus are genuine rulers, so the Wasteland depicts tyrannical bad government, not 'no rulers'. Against Hobbes's claim that only fear of a sovereign produces order, he cites organically evolved order (medieval merchant law, the common law, private arbitration firms) and Locke's mere 'inconveniences' of statelessness to argue peaceful anarchism is possible and stable. Thunderdome's 'two men enter, one man leaves' shows the films' dispute resolution is power-based trial by combat, not the consent-based voluntary order anarchism envisions.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 11 "Notes" — Spanakos and Drake argue that although the films look Hobbesian — life 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' on roads without guardrails — rule in the Wasteland is never sustained by violence alone. Humungus needs the Toadie's epithets ('Lord Humungus... the Ayatollah of Rock and Rolla') and Immortan Joe rules through water rituals and the Valhalla myth that send War Boys kamakrazee willingly, believing they pursue their own glory. Drawing Weber's power/authority distinction, Arendt on power as people acting in concert, and above all Byung-Chul Han, they argue power takes its place 'in the soul of the other' through ritual, habit, and titles, turning into violence only when mediation fails.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 12 "Notes" — Littmann treats Hobbes's Leviathan as a survival manual for post-apocalyptic Australia: the films illustrate his three causes of conflict — resource wars over guzzoline and water, preemptive strikes, and glory (the Nightrider's radio rant, Wez's stunts, the War Boys' 'Witness me!'). Bartertown's Thunderdome covenant and 'bust a deal, face the wheel' exemplify the social contract enforced by an absolute sovereign like Aunty Entity, while divided power (Master Blaster versus Aunty) courts civil war. He concludes Hobbes errs twice: Max's selfless acts (sparing Blaster, transfusing Furiosa) refute psychological egoism, and concentrating power in an Immortan Joe invites the very violence it fears — democracy removes leaders without blood.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 18 "NOTES" — Davies treats the beach camp as an actual state of nature: the stolen drinking water is a tragedy of the commons, Shannon's inhalers show how the crash scrubs pre-existing property rights (Hobbes: two men desiring the same thing become enemies), and Jack and Sayid's torture of Sawyer marks the first step toward Locke's civil society by enforcing others' rights through punishment rather than self-defense. He rejects theories of human nature - Rousseauan 'Innocence' versus a 'Trust No One' outlook - in favor of the repeated prisoner's dilemma, arguing the survivors stabilize cooperation through tit-for-tat: beginning cooperative with strangers and retaliating against the Others. On this reading the real difference between Hobbes and Locke is which round of the repeated dilemma each takes as the starting point.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 19 "NOTES" — Fosl argues that although the survivors' internal order looks Lockean - Jack's uncoerced leadership, natural rights, minimal government - and is bonded by Rousseauan pity and Humean sympathy (Kate staying in the cage with Sawyer, 'live together, die alone'), the show's deepest political logic follows Carl Schmitt's friend-enemy distinction: the survivors cohere only in opposition to the Others, torture is excused in liberal terms, and conflicts end in redemptive violence, with Jack both killing the enemy and dying a Christlike sacrifice. Hobbes's absence from the character names signals the show's rejection of a war of all against all among the survivors, yet the finale's divine manipulation of the castaways, with Jacob treating people as means against Kantian autonomy, repudiates the liberal hope of a rational peace altogether.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 13 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Reads John Teller's failed 'off the social grid' experiment through the human-nature debate: Mencius's seed of sympathy (even Tig recoils at Dante's dogfights) and Rousseau's naturally good man corrupted by society inspired J.T.'s Goldman-fed anarchism, while Mill and Xunzi counter that virtue is a victory over instinct. Hobbes supplies the real diagnosis—not innate violence but the logic of anarchy among free and equal rivals: competition (the Mayans blowing up the warehouse), diffidence (first-strike temptations against Zobelle), and glory (Jax unable to let the bike-sitting insult pass). Clay's rule that 'retaliation must be harsh and immediate' and the escalating Tig–Veronica Pope–Damon Pope–Opie bloodbath show deterrence fueling cycles of violence, so the only escape from the 'nasty, brutish, and short' fringe is the Leviathan's social grid.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 22 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Takes 'Douche and Turd' — Stan refusing to choose between Giant Douche and Turd Sandwich, Puff Daddy's gun-toting 'Vote or Die', and his banishment — plus the kindergarten tie in 'Trapper Keeper' (Flora's indecision, Rosie O'Donnell's recounts) to ask whether every vote counts in a two-party system. Through Locke, Stan's abstention becomes a withdrawal of consent to be governed by either mascot; through Mill, non-voting threatens the active participation that gives institutions legitimacy and wards off tyranny of the majority, even as the chapter catalogs real disincentives: the Electoral College's spectator states, the 2000 Florida debacle, and Commission rules excluding third parties like Nader. Habermas closes the chapter: the vote, read as positive liberty, is the paradigm of rights and inclusion in a community of equals.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 18 "Notes" — Alkema and Barkman put Q himself on trial, asking what justifies his judgment of humanity in 'Encounter at Farpoint' and Trelane's of Kirk in 'The Squire of Gothos'. Hobbes's Leviathan would license Q's might-makes-right sovereignty over a savage species, but Q lacks humanity's consent and cannot show he acts for future peace; Locke's natural law instead binds even nearly omnipotent beings, as Janeway's asylum ruling for the suicidal Quinn in 'Death Wish' demonstrates. Q's repeated self-sacrifice—in 'Deja Q' and the Continuum's civil war—reveals a conscience answerable to natural law rather than raw power.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Littmann shows Luke, Leia, and Han repeatedly put friends and family above the galaxy's freedom - Luke abandoning Dagobah for Bespin, the Jabba rescue, refusing to kill Vader - in the tradition of Homer's heroes, then submits them to Athenian scrutiny. Socrates's refusal to escape his Athens prison and his implicit just agreement with the city set civic duty over friendship; Plato would abolish the guardians' family and censor the Zeus-Kronos patricide myth yet approves of Luke sparing Vader; Aristotle prizes philia but holds citizens belong to the state. He concludes the philosophers mostly win: heroic loyalty is often moral failure, and good moral reasoning asks how many people an action affects, not just whom you love.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 34 "“Wherever I Go, He Goes”" — Bishop and Bishop map The Mandalorian's Outer Rim onto a taxonomy of power: Nevarro's lawlessness is Hobbes's state of nature out of which sovereigns like Palpatine ('a safe and secure society') carve order by social contract, the Guild's codes and Djarin's creed exemplify Foucault's disciplinary power, and the Client's and Dr. Pershing's harvesting of Grogu's biology - like the Kaminoans' cloning of Jango Fett - is biopower. Against this 'binds of power' ontology they set Grogu's helpless generation of love, a 'little way' that converts Djarin, Omera, Cara Dune, and Greef Karga, and culminates in Djarin twice unhelmeting for Grogu's sake, proposing an ontology of love rather than power as the galaxy's alternative.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 11 "2. Sure We’re Criminals" — Alloy uses the problem of political obligation to split the heroes: against Plato's Crito, where Socrates refuses escape because even bad laws bind, Bruce Wayne simply flees arrest in Bruce Wayne: Murderer?/Fugitive, treating law as a tool of his war. He tests consent theory through Superman's chosen handcuffs in Man of Steel and Darkseid's Apokolips as Hobbes's 'mortal god' versus Locke's natural-rights standard, lets Hume's objection sink tacit consent (Red Son Superman cannot really emigrate, and Batman would never leave Gotham), rejects gratitude theory via the Kents' adoption of Kal-El, and dismantles Batman's 'I'm not wearing hockey pads' defense with Nozick's Batman-lottery — concluding Superman's law-conforming restraint protects the public from him becoming Luthor's 'alien overlord', while answerable-to-no-one Batman remains a force of chaos.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 14 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Dena Hurst reads Heaven's civil war through Hobbes's Leviathan: with God absent there is no common power, so the angels fall into a state of nature that is a state of war, complete with natural equality, competition over the same prize, and glory-seeking, as when Zachariah's faction lets Lilith break the seals to force the Apocalypse. God ruled as sovereign by acquisition and proves 'a lousy king' not for demanding obedience but by vanishing without designating a successor, dissolving civil society and with it justice, since where there is no law there is no injustice. Meanwhile Hell under Crowley and the leviathans under Dick Roman display Hobbesian legitimacy from opposite directions: demons join by covenant-like contracts, making Hell a rough democracy, while the leviathans' unified hierarchy enacts the Leviathan itself.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 10 "NOTES" — Weisberg challenges the premise that a newly self-aware Skynet must exterminate humanity in rational self-preservation: after Turing's 'Heads in the Sand Objection,' he argues self-awareness does not entail a survival instinct - a Camusian Skynet might judge existence pointless and pull its own plug. Recasting 'in a panic, they try to pull the plug' as a Hobbesian slide into the state of nature, he uses the iterated prisoner's dilemma and Axelrod's tit-for-tat-with-forgiveness (as in WarGames) to argue a rational Skynet should cooperate with humans toward an emergent social contract. The dark twist is Humean: because reason is the slave of our passions, unconscious anti-machine stereotypes (Bargh's priming studies) make humans untrustworthy partners, so the whole war might have been avoided if only we were more machine-like.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 26 "NOTES" — Peter Fosl asks what John Connor should do when the radio call comes from Crystal Peak — accept near-certain death leading the resistance or stay silent — and dismantles the easy answers: John is not the indispensable savior (Kate or the caller from Montana could lead), the flag-waving finale undercuts any claim that humanity deserves saving, and collective responsibility for Judgment Day is unjust. Social contract fails because Brewster's button-press dissolved the contract and returned humanity to Hobbes's and Locke's state of nature, Hume shows contracts cannot ground society, and utilitarianism wavers once the happiness of animals and possible-happy machines is counted. The positive argument extends Wittgenstein's private-language argument (via Stanley Cavell): meaningful existence is inescapably social and moral, so refusing the claims of others would be as self-subverting as a solipsist arguing in language, and John must answer the call to remain human at all.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 13 "NOTES" — Foy reads the Great Revelation and the Vampire Rights Amendment as a test of social contract theory: Nan Flanagan's 'we pay taxes, we deserve civil rights' invokes the Lockean bargain of obedience for protection, but Locke's God-given natural rights falter when the Fellowship denies vampires souls, and Locke excludes atheists and never imagined vampires. The chapter's resolution is Rawls: behind a veil of ignorance where deliberators might wake up vampire or human, anti-vampire bigots like the Newlins and supremacist nests alike would choose equal basic liberties plus distributive justice — including limits on vampires' centuries of accumulated wealth — so Sookie's 'let the law do it' to Rene marks a pluralist peace no theistic contract could deliver.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 10 "“That Community’s a Lot More Wholesome and Functional than, Just for Example, Neptune Is”" — Paul Hammond asks whether Veronica's habitual lawbreaking — switching the evidence tapes in the 'Pilot,' stealing Duncan's medical file, tricking Principal Van Clemmons — can be morally justified. He constructs a social-contract defense: Neptune's corrupt, class- and race-skewed sheriff's department under Don Lamb has failed to deliver the protection and justice that purchase citizens' obedience, releasing Veronica from her end of the bargain. Testing that defense against the Laws' speech in Plato's Crito (lawbreaking destroys the city; staying in Athens constitutes consent) and Kant's requirement that genuine law be universal, he concludes that where Neptune's civil law diverges from the moral law, Veronica's crimes can rise to a civil disobedience that is sometimes 'really just.'
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 19 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Jason Walker pits Hobbes against Locke over whether Andrea may take the mermaid necklace when Rick says 'I don't think those rules apply anymore'. He reads the survivors' conduct—Andrea's single necklace under Locke's spoilage proviso, Morgan squatting in and fixing up the neighbors' house, Rick voluntarily sharing guns with Guillermo—as a Lockean state of nature where self-ownership and property rights persist without government, while Chris's cannibal band and the Governor embody the Hobbesian war of all against all, treating persons as mere means. The Lockean right to punish, exercised brutally by Grimes's group on Chris's hunters, vindicates rights even by Hobbes's own demand for enforcement.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 19 "Notes" — Christensen and Holmes read the Third Age as Hobbes's state of nature, a postlapsarian chaos following the Breaking where Lews Therin's prideful attempt at purified sovereignty destroyed the Leviathan of the Age of Legends. They argue channeling the One Power is morally neutral power that only becomes sovereignty through practice, and that the Aes Sedai model Hobbesian order through their seven Ajah and, above all, the Three Oaths. Drawing heavily on Giorgio Agamben's Homo Sacer and The Sacrament of Language, they treat oaths and curses as the 'sacraments of power' founding sovereignty on the trustworthiness of the logos, using Moiraine's New Spring investiture to show how language itself binds and confers authority.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 14 "What Would Machiavelli Do" — Reitsma treats the refereeless pickup game as a Lockean state of nature and asks how to beat the 'strategic ticky-tacker' who calls phantom fouls to win. He condemns first-strike cheating as wrong on Kantian grounds (the cheat 'makes an exception of himself') and by an ideal of Homeric athletic honor, then asks whether retaliatory ticky-tacking is justified. Reading Machiavelli's 'dirty hands' argument alongside Locke's claim that in a state of nature each person may punish transgressors, he concludes proportionate tit-for-tat cheating can make one a legitimate 'agent of justice' when no referee exists.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Flynn contends certain Westerns depict a 'law that stands behind the law' — a moral/natural law transcending and grounding the weak civil order — using High Noon, where Hadleyville proves unworthy of Kane's rectitude. High Plains Drifter evolves this into divine, supernatural retribution: the nameless Stranger, a pale-horse agent of apocalyptic justice, precisely punishes Lago for abetting the marshal Duncan's murder (whipping the whippers, renaming the town Hell). Flynn argues this vision is dangerous: by insulating justice from deliberation and depicting it as revelatory and divine, it derides the discursive, civil processes (Habermas-style communicative action) actually needed to make justice 'ours,' risking mere private vengeance — 'deserve's got nothin' to do with it.'
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 15 "Justice, Power, and Love The Political Philosophy of Intolerable Cruelty" — Biderman and Devlin trace Intolerable Cruelty through three theories of justice enacted by divorce attorney Miles Massey and femme fatale Marylin. 'Justice as power' is Thrasymachus's 'advantage of the stronger' and Machiavelli's might-makes-right, seen in Miles's courtroom war-room rhetoric and teeth imagery and in Marylin's plan to 'nail his ass' via marriage. 'Justice as compromise' is Hobbes's social contract escaping the state of nature, but the film shows the Massey pre-nup's signing and tearing to be merely a mask for power. When Miles and Marylin genuinely fall in love, their indifference to each other's wealth becomes a Rawlsian veil of ignorance and difference principle—justice as fairness—though the cynical Funniest Divorce Videos ending leaves that victory unguaranteed.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 16 "Ethics, Heart, and Violence in Miller’s Crossing" — Herling reads Miller's Crossing through Hume's moral psychology of passion versus reason, arguing the film's dominant 'ethics' (voiced by Johnny Caspar) is Hobbes's social contract plus Thrasymachus's advantage-of-the-stronger and Plato's 'do good to friends, harm to enemies'—a relativism of power that Tom Reagan navigates by cool calculation. 'Heart,' the capacity for sympathetic attachment Hume makes the real basis of morality, keeps breaking through: Tom spares the pleading Bernie ('Look in your heart') at Miller's Crossing, and his loyalty to Leo secretly drives his 'plays.' But Bernie's betrayal, the surreal sympathy-crushing violence (the beatings, Leo's tommy-gun ballet, Caspar shooting the faceless Dane), and Leo and Verna's reunion steel Tom into lonely noir stoicism—'What heart?'—when he finally executes Bernie without mercy.
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — Skoble uses Taxi Driver's Travis Bickle to probe when vigilantism is justified, invoking Locke's claim that in civil society individuals delegate private vengeance to the state for objectivity. He argues Travis's rescue of the trapped child prostitute Iris is legitimate (the police won't help, she can't help herself) while his plan to assassinate Senator Palantine is madness, drawing the key line between correctly identifying a deserving target and mere perceived evil (contrasting Travis with Death Wish's Kersey, Batman, and Klan lynch mobs). He closes with Socrates' 'unexamined life' as the remedy: contemplating justice so we can confront real badness rather than turn away.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Wildermuth argues that Mann dramatizes a postmodern critique of law in which justice itself becomes a commodity, drawing on Baudrillard's hyperreal and simulation, Marxist legal theory (Pashukanis's 'organized class terror'), and critical legal studies. In The Last of the Mohicans the British social contract with the colonial militia is exposed as a cover for imperial hierarchy; in Crime Story's 'Abrams for the Defense' and Miami Vice's Lao Li, and in Collateral's hit man Vincent, contracts and legalism deconstruct into simulated justice that serves the top of the economic order, so resistance is possible only locally and temporarily.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 14 "Technology and Ethics in The Day the Earth Stood Still" — Skoble reads The Day the Earth Stood Still as an allegory about the ethics of force and technology. He argues Klaatu's ultimatum extends Mill's harm principle to the interplanetary level: societies may fight among themselves but not threaten others, so Gort's robot police enforce a right to peace that no one has a right to violate. He distinguishes the robots' narrow, non-paternalistic authority from Hobbes's absolute sovereign, defends the ultimatum as preemptive self-defense rather than a rights violation, and contrasts the film's trust in machines with the later technophobia of Colossus and The Terminator.
- **The Philosophy of Tim Burton**, ch. 12 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" — Paul A. Cantor argues that Mars Attacks! inverts the pro-government ideology of 1950s flying-saucer films (Earth vs. the Flying Saucers, Invaders from Mars, The Day the Earth Stood Still) in which scientific and military elites save a helpless public. Burton instead mocks Washington's vain, media-obsessed, multicultural establishment—Kessler, President Dale, the generals—who all fail, while Kansas 'trailer trash,' a Las Vegas boxer, and truant video-gaming kids improvise the defense; Slim Whitman's yodeling, not the state, defeats the Martians. Cantor reads the film through Tocqueville's Democracy in America on the self-organizing power of citizens' associations and the danger of soft despotism, and against Hobbes/The Day the Earth Stood Still's Leviathan solution, casting Burton as a Tocquevillian celebrant of ordinary Americans over their governing elite.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 10 "Two Ways to Yuma Locke, Liberalism, and Western Masculinity in 3 10 to Yuma" — Mexal reads both versions of 3:10 to Yuma through Locke's classical liberalism, arguing the western hero descends from Locke's autonomous, property-owning self in a 'state of nature' (contrasted with Hobbes's state of war). In the 1957 film, Dan Evans transforms from atomistic self-interest to a masculine civic republicanism, escorting Ben Wade to the train even after being released from his contract, reflecting Cold War anxieties. In the 2007 remake, Dan instead renegotiates his contract for water rights and money, so western masculinity becomes unyielding Lockean individualism and the 'right to get rich' in a post-Cold War, capitalist-triumphant America.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 13 "“Order Out of the Mud” Deadwood and the State of Nature" — Cantor reads David Milch's Deadwood as a dramatization of 'order without law,' testing the mining camp against the state-of-nature theories of Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau. Deadwood is Hobbesian in its sources of violence (competition, diffidence, glory; Al Swearengen's alpha-male struggles), but Lockean in showing property rights and commerce arising spontaneously before the state—gold becomes a self-generated medium of exchange that even overrides prejudice (Hearst dealing with Odell). It is Rousseauian in its innate pity (Swearengen's mercy) and its skepticism that incorporation into the nation-state, symbolized by the telegraph and Hearst's abstract corporate power, counts as progress.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 14 "Order without Law The Magnificent Seven, East and West" — Skoble compares The Magnificent Seven with Kurosawa's Seven Samurai, arguing the farming villages are not Hobbesian anarchies needing a sovereign but Lockean communities with a 'grown' social order that merely lack reliable enforcement against bandits. Using Hayek's distinction between spontaneous order (kosmos) and planned order (taxis), he shows the farmers legitimately hire gunslingers/ronin for self-protection rather than surrendering to private-justice worries. The warriors' willingness to honor an unenforceable contract ('That's just the kind you've got to keep') is grounded in a self-created ethics linking the Bushido/Zen and existentialist idea that one's honor and selfhood consist in one's actions.
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 5 "“Are You Watching Closely ”" — Foy and Dale argue that Nolan's Dark Knight trilogy stages a conservative critique of liberal political theory. They set Locke's pre-political natural rights and Rawls's priority-of-rights ('each person possesses an inviolability... that even the welfare of society cannot override') against a Batman who wiretaps all of Gotham, tortures, and kidnaps Lau, treating social order as the thing that overrides individual rights. Batman is cast as a Humean conservative who grounds authority in habit and custom rather than an imaginary social contract, invoking Carl Schmitt's 'state of exception' (the Roman dictator Dent describes) and Burke's non-elected natural aristocracy to justify the billionaire elite Wayne saving a liberal order from the Joker's nihilism and Bane's Marxist-Leninist revolution.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 15 "This Is the Age of Steel" — Greg Littmann asks how a truly "logical" creature would live by redesigning the Cybermen through three philosophers. Hobbes's reason-as-self-interest and Laws of Nature would make Cybermen seek peace and security once survival is assured, not wage endless war; Mill's utilitarianism would build happy, individualistic, liberty-respecting Cybermen who prize higher pleasures and others' welfare rather than forced "upgrades"; and Hume's view that reason alone motivates nothing implies emotionless Cybermen would simply do nothing, so their goals are neither logical nor illogical. Each shows the Cybermen's actual "logic" is incoherent.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 19 "9. God the Programmer Is Dead" — De Vries defines a 'monster' in Supernatural as one who breaks the social contract, then argues Sam and Dean are deontologists loyal to a rigid duty—but a 'social contract of two' (family) that produces double standards toward Cas and Jack. She contrasts the angels' box-checking utilitarianism and Hobbesian collapse without God, Hell's contractual capitalist democracy, and Chuck as a controlling 'programmer God' whose perfection cannot tolerate imperfection; Jack's hands-off deity and Chuck's Nietzschean death-of-God let humanity write its own moral code.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 24 "13. Does God Have the Right to Destroy the Universe" — Foresman asks whether Chuck has a negative right to destroy the multiverse, rejecting the question-begging 'God can do whatever God wants' and the bare creation/ownership argument (using the scrambled-eggs example) as insufficient. Drawing on Locke's Two Treatises—property arises from mixing labor, but even in the state of nature one may not destroy a creature except for a 'nobler use,' and hoarding beyond use is illegitimate—he concludes Chuck is a Lockean tyrant destroying universes he could simply recreate, so Sam and Dean's rebellion is justified.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 13 "5. The Sovereign State of Salamanca" — Barta and Barnes read the show's Court and Cartel as parallel Hobbesian sovereigns. The New Mexico desert and the criminalized drug trade function as Hobbes's state of nature—lawless, where Nacho robs thieves who 'have no recourse' and Mike sticks up a mule with a garden hose—illustrating natural equality (a small man can kill a big one) and the war of all against all. From mutual fear, deals emerge (Mike and Gus's desert standoff, Mike keeping his word over twenty dollars), but 'covenants without the sword' need a Common Power: Tuco, Hector, Lalo, and ultimately Don Eladio form a feudal hierarchy enforcing loyalty by terror, just as the state's police monopoly on force sustains the Law.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 39 "Gaining Trust from the Past" — Richard Davies treats the Oceanic 815 survivors of Lost as a real state of nature, playing on the characters named Locke, Rousseau, and Hume. The scarce-water and asthma-inhaler disputes are 'tragedies of the commons,' and Sawyer's 'finders keepers' embodies a Hobbesian 'Trust No. 1' while Hurley and Jack lean toward Rousseauian 'Innocence.' Using game theory's repeated prisoners' dilemma and 'tit-for-tat,' Davies argues a Lockean state of nature (opening with cooperation) rather than a doomed Hobbesian one lets the survivors build a commonwealth against the Others.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 18 "NOTES" — Richard Davies analyzes the post-crash survivors as living in a genuine 'state of nature' and grades its severity by how scarce the contested good is (the water shortage as a tragedy of the commons, Shannon's inhalers versus Sawyer's 'possession is nine-tenths'). He compares Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau on human nature — labeling the poles 'Innocence' (Hurley, Rousseau, Hume) and 'Trust No 1' (Sawyer, Hobbes) — and uses the repeated prisoners' dilemma and the tit-for-tat strategy to argue that the castaways build a Lockean civil society by signaling through shared language and cooperating first, while the discovery of the Others (Ethan) triggers Hobbesian non-cooperation.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 19 "NOTES" — Peter S. Fosl argues that Lost pretends to a liberal social order — Jack rising by consent in a Lockean scheme of natural rights, Rousseau's general will ('live together, die alone'), and Hume's sympathy and pity binding the survivors — but that its treatment of the Others betrays a darker politics. Reading the survivor/Other conflict through Carl Schmitt's friend-enemy thesis (notably absent Hobbes), he contends the show, like post-9/11 America, needs an enemy to exterminate, and that the finale's Jacob/Man-in-Black war and Jack's Christlike sacrificial death repudiate the Kantian liberal ideal of persons as ends, resolving conflict through Schmittian and Christian redemptive violence instead.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 23 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Torosyan argues that The Daily Show models critical thinking and postmodern self-awareness, using Stewart's interviews to show how to reframe debate and act in good faith. He reads Stewart's demand that news media serve the public through Rousseau's social contract, casts scaremongering politicians as following Machiavelli's advice to 'learn how not to be good,' invokes Gadamer's hermeneutics to argue that guests like William Bennett fail to question their own prejudices, and uses Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian tension to explain the show's tragicomic satire (e.g., the 'Smallpox Blankets' joke and Bush reading Camus's The Stranger).
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 30 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Vanderheiden reads America (The Book) as a work of democratic theory dressed as textbook parody, arguing its satire is a 'rhetoric of challenge' enacting deliberative democracy. He contrasts 'thin' (merely electoral) with 'thick' participatory democracy using Putnam's social capital and Barber's strong democracy, and invokes J.S. Mill's 'marketplace of ideas' and On Liberty to indict media conglomeration for killing the press's watchdog role. He reads the companion Earth (The Book) through social-contract theory (Hobbes-style), noting its jab that contractual authority historically required the assent of subjugated groups it never obtained.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 23 "Rebellion in Sala-ma-Sond The Social Contract and a Turtle Named Mack" — Novy uses King Yertle's tyranny and Mack's revolt to survey social-contract theory. Hobbes explains why turtles leave the war-of-all state of nature for an absolute sovereign, but Yertle, ruling only for himself, becomes 'no king at all'; Locke then justifies overthrowing him because a ruler who destroys his subjects' property and lives dissolves the contract. Kant grounds the contract in innate freedom, while Rawls's original position and veil of ignorance test Sala-ma-Sond for justice as fairness, and King's civil disobedience frames Mack's rights-claiming burp as demanding the contract be honored for all.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 20 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Swindler argues the ideal of fatherhood is to engender autonomy – a blend of independence and interdependence – in one's children. Treating fatherhood as an abstract social role (compared to a baseball pitcher) constituted by collective intentions, he uses Kant's 'ought implies can' to link accountability to autonomy and his constitutive-vs-regulative rules (the promise to take his son fishing) to show fathers must teach children to reflect on the concept of a rule, not merely follow it, modeling self-governance rather than authoritarian control.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 30 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Colyvan applies mathematics and game theory to mating: the 'secretary problem' yields the optimal strategy of dating and rejecting the first n/e (~37%) of candidates then taking the next best, and Rousseau's stag hunt models monogamy as cooperation (hunt stag = stay faithful) tempted by defection (hunt hare = an affair), with the prisoner's dilemma showing why individual rationality can undermine the Pareto-optimal cooperative outcome. He argues that iterated games and tit-for-tat strategies, plus the 'shadow of the future' and public commitments like weddings, make faithfulness explicable purely by narrow self-interest, quoting Hume on reciprocal service, and suggests love and ethics themselves may be useful fictions layered over the game.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 11 "Hobbes, Human Nature, and the Culture of American Violence in Truman Capote's In Cold Blood" — Thomas Fahy reads Capote's In Cold Blood as horror (the Clutter killers Hickock and Smith as 'realistic monsters' whose human shape terrifies because anyone could be like them) and maps it onto Hobbes's Leviathan. Hickock and Smith act in a Hobbesian state of nature, driven by appetite, power, and moral relativism without remorse. Herb Clutter functions as a Hobbesian sovereign whose Eden-like farm and community collapse into decay, mistrust, and 'war of all against all' after his murder. Fahy also casts Capote himself as a sovereign who, via Foucault's panopticon, imposes a fictionalized cathartic ending, though the book's Hobbesian message is that we all have the potential to kill.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 12 "6. Hollow Man" — Rowlands reads Hollow Man as a retelling of Plato's Ring of Gyges, posing 'why be moral?' once the invisible Kevin Bacon can act without sanction. He rejects the religious answer and Hobbesian social-contract theory (both reduce morality to prudence/fear of punishment and leave those outside the contract unprotected), and Hume's fellow-feeling as mere causal explanation not justification. He examines Kant's Categorical Imperative reducing immorality to inconsistency but argues it cannot answer 'why should I be moral,' concluding the choice is arational self-definition, closing with Nietzsche's 'become what you are' and the deed at the bottom of morality.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 39 "Gaining Trust from the Past" — Davies analyzes Lost's Oceanic 815 survivors as a genuine state of nature, playing off the characters named Locke, Rousseau, and Hume. He distinguishes Rousseau's compassionate "Innocence" from a Hobbesian "Trust No. 1" (Sawyer hoarding), tracks "tragedies of the commons" over water and Shannon's inhalers, and Jack and Sayid's move toward Lockean punishment and civil society. Using game theory's prisoners' dilemma and tit-for-tat, he argues cooperation emerges when survivors, discovering the Others, resolve to "act as one body" and form a commonwealth.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 8 "6. Black Sails as Philosophy Pirates and Political Discourse" — Jones argues that Starz's Black Sails, a Treasure Island prequel set in the Golden Age of Piracy, dramatizes social contract theory as non-hypothetical practice. Captain Flint's drive to make Nassau a sovereign pirate commonwealth ('I am your king') channels Hobbes's state of nature and irrepressible sovereign, while his choice to settle Nassau and belief that people can thrive if left free channels Locke; his eventual plan to install Silver and Madi as liked-and-feared leaders synthesizes the two. Jones maps the pirates' familial bonds onto Rousseau and their responses to injustice (Vane's gallows speech, the maroon alliance) onto Rawls's Veil of Ignorance, and reads pirate 'articles' and deposable captains as radical democracy and equality, complicated by manipulation, slavery, and tolerance.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 14 "12. Firefly as Philosophy Social Contracts, Political Dissent, and Virtuous Communities" — Kowalski argues that Firefly and Serenity embody a distinctive political theory he calls 'Since I Found Serenity' (SIFS). The mindless, savage Reavers represent Hobbes's state of nature, showing government is necessary; but the Alliance's torture of River, the Miranda/Pax atrocity, and the murderous blue-gloved agents and Operative make a Hobbesian reading untenable and vindicate Locke's natural rights and right of revolution — Mal's 'I aim to misbehave' broadcast of the Miranda file is Lockean civil disobedience. He then presses the tacit-consent problem (the Browncoats cannot leave the 'Verse) and supplements Locke with Aristotle's friendship and community: Serenity's crew becomes a virtuous mobile commonwealth where friendship (Simon forgiving Jayne, Mal's 'love keeps her in the air') turns a commonwealth into a good-life community.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 18 "16. House of Cards as Philosophy Democracy on Trial" — The chapter uses the Underwoods' extra-electoral rise to autocracy in House of Cards to test Plato's and Hobbes's antidemocratic arguments. Frank and Claire exploit the exact weaknesses Plato's Republic diagnoses—Thrasymachus's 'justice is the advantage of the stronger,' the decay of oligarchy into freedom-loving democracy into tyranny, and Peter Russo as the disordered-soul 'democratic man' and 'drone.' It then invokes Hobbes's Leviathan, arguing the show's power-struggle resembles a state of nature and that Hobbes would welcome Claire's absolute rule as more predictable and less corrupt than democracy, before weighing modern defenses of democracy (Levitsky and Ziblatt, Locke, Mill, Rawls, Sen) against these critiques.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 26 "24. Game of Thrones as Philosophy Cynical Realpolitiks" — The chapter argues that Game of Thrones advances a thoroughgoing cynicism about political legitimacy, captured by Varys's riddle that 'power resides where men believe it resides.' It documents the dubious claims of Robert 'the Usurper' and the pyromaniacal Daenerys, the barbaric Lockean 'state of nature' among the Wildlings, and the false ideals of chivalry and religion, with Littlefinger and Varys voicing Machiavellian realpolitik. Silverman and Riordan then offer two views the show never considers: Locke's social-contract theory of natural rights (which would justify deposing Aerys or Daenerys) and Aquinas's four-part test for genuine law (reason, common good, proper authority, promulgation), arguing a legitimate state remains possible against the show's cynicism.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 50 "47. Snowpiercer as Philosophy The Danger to Humanity" — Marquez 'pierces the veils' of Snowpiercer to argue the greatest danger to humanity is humanity itself. He reads Wilford's authoritarian, precisely population-controlled train through Plato's noble lie / myth of the metals (Mason's 'know your place'), Hobbes's social contract against a cannibalistic state of nature, and Machiavellian ends-justify-means to weigh whether Gilliam's secret compromise with Wilford is morally acceptable. He tests the orchestrated revolution against utilitarianism's greatest-happiness principle (Bentham, Mill's taxation-of-the-wealthy, Singer's impartiality) and against Rawls's veil of ignorance and difference principle versus Nozick's entitlement objection and Aquinas's just-war criteria, concluding each character's actions can be read as 'just,' which exposes anthropocentrism as the real veil.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 98 "92. V for Vendetta as Philosophy Victory Through the Virtues of Anarchy" — Nisley argues that Moore and Lloyd's V for Vendetta justifies V's violent rebellion against the Norsefire regime through Locke: the fascist state seized power without consent, tortured and experimented on citizens (V at Larkhill), and violated natural rights, thereby placing itself in a state of war so the people may overthrow it. Using Aristotle on deviant constitutions and the beast-like tyrant (Adam Susan) who lacks practical wisdom, and contrasting Locke's tolerable state of nature with Hobbes's brutal one, the chapter concludes the citizens should rebuild a rights-protecting social contract rather than V's leaderless anarchy, and maps the argument onto real-world 2020 events (BLM riots vs. the Whitmer kidnapping plot).

### Anarchism

Anarchism is a political philosophy that regards the state and other forms of coercive, hierarchical authority as illegitimate and unnecessary, and seeks a society organized instead through voluntary cooperation, mutual aid, and self-governance. Anarchists hold that people can order their affairs without rulers, and they differ over means and emphasis, from the mutualism and collectivism of thinkers like Proudhon and Bakunin to the communism of Kropotkin and later individualist and syndicalist currents. The tradition shares a critique of concentrated power—political and often economic alike—as a source of domination. It aims not at chaos but at a stateless order built from the bottom up.

- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 10 "The Gathering of the Tribe Ironic Sacramentalism" — Horace Fairlamb argues the Grateful Dead were the Sixties' real revolutionary success: where the New Left failed by keeping confrontational politics, the Dead changed consciousness first, extending Mill's liberal 'experiments in living' into a whole alternative culture. He reads the total improvisation learned at the Acid Tests ('the form that follows chaos'), the band's leaderless 'functional anarchy' — Lesh: if anyone tried to take charge 'it would just dissolve in their hands' — and its flat business hierarchy with roadies as corporate presidents as a spontaneous order lived at the edge of chaos. The Deadhead community's ritual communitas, analyzed through Victor Turner's separation-liminality-reincorporation model, amounts to an 'ironic sacramentalism' that achieves what social contract from Hobbes (force), Locke (property), and Rawls (self-interest) cannot: unity that transcends difference while leaving it in place.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 18 "An Island of Milk and Honey or Rock Bottom" — Shaun Young asks whether governmentless Bikini Bottom refutes political philosophy's claim that the good life needs a state: it is not the anarchism of Godwin and Kropotkin (police fines, health inspectors and the Fry Cooks Union constrain liberty), not Marx's communism (Krabs keeps exploiting SpongeBob, whose 'false consciousness' surfaces only briefly in 'Clams'), not the utopias of Plato, Bacon or More (Squidward and Plankton are miserable), and not Nozick's night-watchman state (SpongeBob is arrested for failing to invite police to his party). The lesson he draws: expect neither utopia nor Rock Bottom, because no single theory captures a real (or imaginary undersea) society.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 170 "Invocation of My Demon Brother" — Connects the Stones' demonic turn to the counterculture's occult fashions — the Levitate the Pentagon rally, Rosemary's Baby — and to filmmaker Kenneth Anger, disciple of Aleister Crowley, whose "Do What Thou Wilt" law espoused a form of anarchism and whose Lucifer was the light-bearing god, not Christianity's dark devil. Anger cast Jagger as a latter-day Lucifer for Lucifer Rising (with Richards as Beelzebub), and the chapter quotes Jagger's 1967 claim that the teenage "telepathy" at his shows was "a protest against the system," while reading "Jumpin' Jack Flash" through the Spring Heeled Jack folklore.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 37 "Homeland and Philosophy" — This standalone section traces terrorism's history and definition, from the French Revolution's Reign of Terror when the state was 'le terroriste' (Robespierre's 'terror is nothing other than justice that is prompt, severe, and inflexible') to the term's reversal onto non-state actors via Russian anarchists like Nechayev. It offers a seven-feature characterization (violence, destruction, indiscriminate harm, psychological trauma, propaganda, policy change, non-state perpetration) matching the UN's 2004 definition, then catalogs often-forgotten American terrorism: the Boston Tea Party reframed as a news report, the Ku Klux Klan's campaign, the Haymarket bombing, the Los Angeles Times and Wall Street bombings by labor radicals and anarchists, the Bath School massacre, the Mad Bomber, the Weather Underground, anti-abortion Army of God killings, and the Unabomber.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 24 "9. Anarchy, State, and Apocalypse" — Da Silva and McKendry test the political legitimacy of four post-apocalyptic governance types: the Claimers' anarchy that collapses into Joe adjudicating 'claims', the Governor's and Rick's dictatorships ('This is not a democracy anymore!'), the prison Council's representative democracy with the three questions as a quasi-constitution, and Terminus's quasi-theocratic cannibal creed ('You're the butcher or you're the cattle'). Using Hobbes's state of nature and war of all against all, hypothetical social contract, and the twin tests of power and morality, they judge even the benevolent Rick-tatorship unjust because concentrated power is fallible and unaccountable. They conclude, with Churchill, that the Council's imperfect democracy is the worst form of government except for all the others.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 11 "2. Sure We’re Criminals" — Malloy asks whether the two law-breaking vigilantes are criminals and whether any duty to obey the law survives scrutiny. He runs consent theory through Superman surrendering in handcuffs in Man of Steel and the Red Son Superman's residence in the USSR, uses Darkseid's Apokolips as Hobbes's security sovereign against Locke's natural-rights limits, deploys Hume against tacit consent (Batman would never leave Gotham even in No Man's Land), and dismantles gratitude theory (the Kents' adoption involved a sacrificial choice the law cannot make) and fair play (Nozick's Batman-lottery undercuts "I'm not wearing hockey pads"). He lands near Wolff-style philosophical anarchism: Superman's constrained lawbreaking endorses the law's legitimacy while Batman treats law as one more tool in his war, making him a force of chaos.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 12 "3. We Willna Be Fooled Again! Wee Free Anarchists!" — Reading The Wee Free Men, Kugler treats the Nac Mac Feegle, Granny Aching, and Tiffany as embodiments of the anarchist suspicion of political authority, staging Nozick's minimal state and spontaneous protective associations against Huemer's philosophical anarchism from The Problem of Political Authority. The Feegles' creed 'Nae quin! Nae king!', their flight from the exploitative Fairy Queen, the Baron's sheep-killing dog compromise, and the mercy shown the lonely kidnapper Miss Robinson all show law treated as a flexible guideline that must yield to love, community, and care for the weak. Kugler concludes that Pratchett romanticizes anarchism: his anarchists win hearts, watching authority from within the system rather than overthrowing it.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 20 "10. Lord Vetinari’s Friendly Guide to Tyranny" — Alloy stages the debate over Vetinari's legitimacy as letters to the Ankh-Morpork Times: a writer channeling Hobbes defends the contracted sovereign - a 'mortal god' who cannot commit crimes and secures freedom through security - while 'the late Jeremy Bentham' judges the Patrician by the greatest good of the greatest number yet would disenfranchise golems and the 'differently-alive' dead. The anarchist Wolff Paul Roberts rebuts both, denying any right to rule, rejecting tacit consent by residence, and holding up the free golems as models of uncoerced virtue, before a final letter defends Vetinari's limited, functional government. The frame - Vetinari quietly orchestrating the whole correspondence and planning Roberts's next letter - shows tyranny curating its own philosophical defense.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 12 "1. The Deed of F’ing Society" — Rocha reads fsociety's 5/9 logic-bomb attack on E Corp as anarchist 'propaganda of the deed' - a shocking act meant to wake people from their comfortable slumber inside hierarchy - and positions it between Alexander Berkman's violent anarchism (mirroring Phillip Price's 'bullet in the right place') and Gandhi's nonviolent self-suffering, quoting satyagraha and the older Goldman's rejection of violence. He then runs the hack through just war theory's four questions (necessity, proportionality, justification, effectiveness), noting that wiping the debt records also destroyed savings and indirectly got people like Gideon killed, and that fsociety, as Trenton says, never paints the alternative society - so the reader is left to answer whether the deed was justified.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 20 "7. What Kind of Revolutionary Is Mr. Robot" — Ralston traces Mr. Robot's hacktivist philosophy to David Graeber's anarchism behind Occupy Wall Street and to Anonymous's 'moralfags' who hack for a higher cause (Project Chanology as the template for fsociety), then stages the Dewey-Trotsky debate on means and ends: Trotsky's 'Their Morals and Ours' lets the end justify any means, while Dewey's means-end continuum demands experimental, democratic means suited to the end. The verdict: Mr. Robot's ends are anarchist and his means pragmatist - he will frame Terry Colby and risk lives at Steel Mountain, but rejects means like actual slavery that would betray the movement's own ideal of liberation.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 31 "18. What Makes Rick Tick" — Surveying Rick's values area by area, a many-worlds multiverse, atheism ('There is no God, Summer'), scientism, egoistic ethics, hatred of all government, and rap as today's Romanticism, the chapter rejects absurdism, existentialism, nihilism, and even Max Stirner's individualist anarchism, which it says fits the Citadel of Ricks rather than the loner Rick. Its thesis is that Rick is an Ayn Rand Objectivist: Rand's ideal man of reason, independence, and rejection of altruism, collectivism, and mysticism, with Jerry as the pity-parasite anti-ideal exposed in 'The Whirly Dirly Conspiracy'. It warns that infinite choice risks the paradox of hedonism, pointing to Rick's half-hearted suicide machine after Unity, and ends that only chosen constructive goals, perhaps a kinder Rick, could save him, if some other universe didn't already have that Rick.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 37 "The Anarchist You Are" — Argues anarchism is everywhere in ATLA even though nobody names it: Chomsky's test of unjustified hierarchies condemns the Dai Li, High Monk Pasang's arbitrary removal of Aang from Gyatso's care, and Commander Zhao's rank-pulling, while Kropotkin's mutual aid — humans as fundamentally cooperative — appears in Iroh's non-coercive mentoring of Zuko, Senlin Village's solidarity, and the 'The Chase' lesson that Toph's 'I can carry my own weight' misses how Team Avatar carries each other. Even Zaheer of Korra is exposed as no anarchist, and Iroh's self-effacing, power-sharing teaching (like Katara teaching Aang waterbending) models the only justified use of power. Aang thinking for himself against the past Avatars' unanimous advice to kill Ozai, and his joyfulness amid revolution, make him the true anarchist.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 37 "The Anarchist You Are" — Argues that anarchism, understood through David Graeber's consensus-based action, Noam Chomsky's demand that hierarchies justify themselves, and Kropotkin's mutual aid, runs all through ATLA even though no character calls themselves an anarchist. The Dai Li are an unjustified hierarchy that delivers Ba Sing Se to the very conquest it claims to prevent, High Monk Pasang's arbitrary rank authority over Gyatso and Aang causes the century-long catastrophe, and Zhao embodies domination justified by 'fire is the superior element', whereas justified power is self-effacing (Iroh mentoring Zuko without coercion, Katara teaching Aang waterbending). Toph's insistence that she can 'carry my own weight' in 'The Chase' dramatizes the mutual-aid lesson that letting those who love you help you is part of the cooperative human nature Kropotkin opposed to the Hobbesian view, and Zaheer in Korra, who rules by fear, shows that a chaos-bringer is no anarchist at all, while playful, communal Aang is.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 15 "Theorizing Government" — Tony Spanakos argues that Gotham's government, not Bruce's psyche, explains Batman: the state failed at Crime Alley, and nearly every major character reacts to a state that is either too weak or too restrictive.
