Luke's double movement - resigning everything, his cause and his life, while trusting there is still good in Vader - suspends the ethical demand to kill and accomplishes what neither side thought possible: turning a Sith back to the light.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 40 "The Last Jedi A New Hope" — Johnson defends The Last Jedi's Luke against the 'you ruined Luke' charge: his pacifism was set up when he threw away his lightsaber before Palpatine in Return of the Jedi, and his call to end the Jedi follows the lesson Hobbes and Locke drew from the English civil wars - since religious matters cannot be settled by reason, only by violence, Jedi and Sith factions fighting for political power yield only bloodshed like the Clone Wars and two Death Stars. Luke also seeks to destroy the Jedi texts out of guilt by association for the Order's failures, and to the end he remains a consequentialist pacifist, defeating Kylo on Crait through a nonviolent Force projection rather than a real duel. Far from betraying the character, this growth into proactive nonviolence - capped by Rey's yellow-bladed, mainly defensive style - makes Luke 'the ultimate Jedi' and the Resistance's new hope.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 11 "Notes" — Baggett sets W. K. Clifford's evidentialism (the negligent shipowner; believing on insufficient evidence is a 'sin against mankind') against William James's precursive faith, which permits believing ahead of the evidence when an option is forced, live, momentous, and evidentially undecided. He applies this to Sam's taping over the Dubai Air logo as social-coordination faith, Richmond's belief that it can finally beat Everton, romantic risk-taking like Roy and Keeley's, and the marriage of belief with hard work (Ted's practice tirade, Nate's False Nine), ending with James and Pascal on how evidential ambiguity about God makes a passional step of faith rational.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 27 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Greeley argues the zombie embodies a specifically modern fear of losing our humanity: walkers are persons stripped of the potential Aristotle and Aquinas made the measure of human worth, which is why Rick uniquely eulogizes the walkers he puts down ('I'm sorry this happened to you'). Following Aries, he traces modern death anxiety to the split of faith from reason and reads the CDC arc ('TS-19') as science offering only a self-destruct quick death where Jacqui's 'wrath of God' guess at least offers meaning. Rousseau's claim that civilization corrupts explains the survivors' return to the woods, where pizza-deliverer Glenn's heroics and the 'kingpin' Guillermo protecting nursing-home patients show the apocalypse can bring out the best in us while the Bradbury's Sale storefront and trampled Walmart worker hint we were already the walking dead.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 26 "Notes" — Held asks what a god is and which gods deserve worship, using Rachels's definition (all-powerful, perfectly good, perfectly wise) to show no DC deity - dying Zeus, cruel Darkseid, creation-unmaking Parallax - qualifies, and that mere power generates fear, not the moral authority that could ground worship-worthiness or a parent-like right to command. Against the Christian campaigner Darrel Keyes, who calls Wonder Woman's cults idolatrous, he notes her gods visibly exist while his God is both unprovable and, per the Anselmian concept problem, indescribable without ceasing to be supreme. The chapter ends by relocating worship on earth: since we need orienting values whether or not gods exist, 'we could do worse than submit to the loving authority' of the justice, care, and integrity Diana embodies - pray to 'yourself, your own strength and character.'
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 26 "Is the Gridiron Holy Ground" — Hamilton analyzes the fusion of football, patriotism, and religion (Friday Night Lights' Odessa, Super Bowl rituals) as Rousseau's 'civil religion' from the Social Contract—socially unifying but content-empty and anti-intellectual, keeping faith bifurcated from real life. Drawing on Augustine's account of virtue as 'rightly ordered love' and vice as disordered love, he argues football has been wrongly elevated above higher goods. He rejects Higgs's incompatibility thesis for a Christian worldview approach—exemplified by Tony Dungy, Lovie Smith, and Joe Ehrman's 'men for others'—that makes the gridiron holy ground.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Clayton distinguishes the philosophical problem of evil (Aquinas's deductive argument, its inductive/evidential successors, and Plantinga's free-will defense) from what Plantinga calls the pastoral problem — the personal crisis suffering brings. He argues Eastwood, as 'practical philosopher,' registers the philosophical problem visually in Mystic River (camera panning heavenward at Katie's murder, the intercut Communion) but pointedly refuses to resolve it. In Hereafter the tsunami, deaths, and the twins' loss are met not with theodicy but with a recurring pastoral pattern of listening, being present, and acting compassionately (Dr. Rousseau with Marie, George's reading of Marcus), religion offering no answers.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 26 "15. God Is Good (Chuck Not So Much)" — Graves contrasts the Judeo-Christian God of scripture with Chuck, arguing Chuck fails theodicy: he neither shares human suffering (as Jesus does) nor pursues justice for the oppressed (as Yahweh does in Psalm 82), and using evolution to create sapient life guarantees disease, war, and injustice that Paley's Natural Theology design argument cannot excuse. He reads Amara's wish to unwind creation as arguably 'good,' rejects the Winchesters' fallacy that Nephilim Jack must inherit Lucifer's evil (nature versus nurture), and diagnoses Chuck as a pathological narcissist paralleling despotic real-world leaders.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 13 "Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress" — Jacoby uses Stan Marsh as the embodiment of W. K. Clifford's ethics of belief, that it is always wrong to believe on insufficient evidence. Stan debunks TV psychic John Edward, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the one making extraordinary claims. Jacoby distinguishes evidential from prudential reasons, presents and criticizes Pascal's Wager (using 'Cartmanland' and the problem of undeserved suffering), and argues via Clifford that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken the mind and, as Stan tells Edward, slow 'the progress of all mankind.'
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 22 "Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy" — Johnson uses 'Cartmanland' to lay out the problem of evil: Kyle loses his faith when the wicked Cartman gains perfect happiness, giving a logical problem-of-moral-evil argument against God. Johnson shows why the story of Job and Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' fail, then explains the greater-good and free-will defenses (invoking Augustine that only free acts are good) and the residual problem of natural evils like Kyle's hemorrhoid. He presents John Hick's soul-making theodicy, echoed by South Park's Jesus, that God permits both moral and natural evil so we develop character, while noting the surviving evidential problem of evil's sheer amount.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 23 "To Know … and Believe" — Gallagher uses Lost's Rose Henderson, who says 'I just know,' to expound Aquinas on faith and reason. Aquinas places faith midway between Plato's knowledge (epistêmê) and opinion (doxa) and distinguishes its material object (God) from its formal object (first truth). Gallagher explains that all knowledge begins in the senses, so God's existence is known only by demonstration (the five ways), while faith's fuller content requires grace. Rose's sins bracket the argument: Charlie's despair is acedia, while Rose's insistence that she 'knows' the island cured her is presumption, mistaking faith for scientific knowledge.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 25 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Sirvent and Baker use Stewart's mockery of politicians who claim a divine endorsement (Bachmann's certainty of a 'miracle,' Wyatt Cenac reporting from a Las Vegas-style heaven) to apply John Locke's critique of religious 'enthusiasm'—the arrogance of taking one's own intuitions for divine direction without weighing them against reason. They then deploy Gadamer's philosophical hermeneutics against the 'objectivism' of Glenn Beck and Pat Robertson, arguing that treating scripture as an unambiguous rulebook ignores how every reading is conditioned by culture and history.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 26 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — LoPresti uses the 'This Week in God' segments (the God Machine, Ed Helms's Hindu-vs-Mayan 'faith-off,' Colbert's inclusivist White House roast) to lay out three responses to religious diversity—exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism—and defends John Cobb's Whiteheadian process-metaphysics pluralism. He insists the distinct concepts of religions be respected rather than collapsed, citing Buddhist impermanence and no-Self and the South Asian Atman/Brahman as unique and non-reducible, and closes by reading the show's turn to political framing of religion through Marx's claim that religion is a mechanism for controlling the masses.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 27 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Johnson argues that Fox News's 'war on Christmas' is fabricated and that the real conflict is a centuries-long Christian war FOR Christmas—Constantine tacking Jesus's birth onto pagan late-December Saturnalia and solstice celebrations. Using Stewart's and Colbert's segments plus Kevin Bleyer-style history, he defends the separation of church and state (courthouse nativities and school Nativity plays as unconstitutional endorsements of Christianity), debunks David Barton's claims that Jefferson was a conservative Christian, and shows Jefferson the deist coining 'a wall of separation between church and state.'
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 4 "There Is No God in Desperation" — Sutton and Held use King's Desperation and its God-speaking boy David Carver to stage the problem of evil, opening with Hume's Epicurean dilemma and Rowe's and Draper's evidential arguments from superfluous suffering (Brian's coma, Pie's murder). They survey theistic replies as defenses (Augustine's evil-as-privation, skeptical-theism humility) and theodicies (Hick's soul-making 'God is refining,' the free-will theodicy, Aquinas on natural law preserving the whole), concluding with van Inwagen that we lack epistemic warrant to judge God. Held reframes evil as a human problem of suffering, and reads Marinville's arc through Kierkegaard's despair and Anselm's 'faith seeking understanding,' arguing the antidote to 'desperation' (unbelief) is a non-cognitive, affective faith that keeps investigating.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 16 "Chapter 6 The Gospel According to Mark (Twain)" — Craig Vasey reads Twain's Letters from the Earth, narrated by a skeptical Satan, as a defense of critical thinking rather than the ranting of a bitter old man. He unpacks Satan's mockery of a self-understanding in which God obsesses over and demands worship from humans, a sexless harp-playing Heaven, and the punishment of curious, ignorant Adam and Eve, echoing Hume's catalogue of suffering (the fly as 'divine ambassador'). Invoking Nietzsche on life-after-death as vengeance dressed as love, and Socrates' 'unexamined life,' Vasey argues Twain's real target is human gullibility and willful childishness, calling humanity to grow up, think, and take responsibility instead of scapegoating a celestial fantasy.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 30 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Morgan asks when it is wrong for fathers to impose their ideals on children, arguing that forcing activities (like violin practice) risks alienation because meaningful pursuits must be embraced 'from the inside.' Using Robert Noggle's Rawls-derived hierarchy of goods (basic, pre-primary, primary, secondary, specialized), he grants fathers may guide toward universal goods but rejects Noggle's claim that parents may impose a full religious worldview, favoring David Archard's weaker right to 'guide family life' while respecting the child's growing capacity to choose – permitting compelled practice of talents only in light of the child's emerging identity.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 13 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Austin uses the everyday sense that 'we need the bean' to introduce a metaphysical debate about whether we need God to ground ethics, framed through the fair-trade coffee case. He contrasts Erik Wielenberg, who treats necessary ethical truths (e.g., that unfair trade is wrong, that suffering is intrinsically evil) as brute 'furniture of the universe' and follows Kant in holding that we ought to be moral simply because it is our duty, with J. P. Moreland, who argues such objective moral values, our knowledge of them, and the normative pull of obligation fit a theistic worldview better than naturalism. The chapter presents God as the 'Necessary Ground of Being' behind moral reality without settling the dispute.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 8 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — In this foreword, historian Stephen Nissenbaum frames the book's central puzzle by asking the reader to picture Santa Claus kneeling in the Bethlehem manger and feeling why the image jars. He argues Christmas began as a fourth-century compromise: the Church Fathers fixed Jesus' birthday on December 25 to co-opt Saturnalia and the solstice and to refute Docetism (the claim Christ only 'seemed' to have a body) by giving him a human birthday. He traces how the resulting tension between piety and revelry led the Puritans to ban Christmas and how the secular, commercial Santa of Moore's 1823 poem came to dominate the American holiday, leaving the manger and the sleigh perpetually unreconciled.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 9 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Editor Scott Lowe's introduction surveys the volume, using the disputed origins of Christmas – the December date borrowed from Sol Invictus and Yule, the Christmas tree from Germanic custom, and a Santa descended from Odin, Thor and Krampus rather than any Christian saint – to show how little about the holiday is settled. It previews each contributor's argument, from Hume-based attacks on the virgin birth and Aiken's denial of a 'War on Christmas' to Foucauldian readings of Santa's surveillance, the ethics of the Santa lie, and atheist or Festivus alternatives, positioning the book as a set of philosophical debates over what Christmas actually means.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 12 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Theologian Victor Lyons defends the virgin birth against the Humean empiricist objection voiced by Dawkins, Hitchens and Harris. He marshals the creeds and Church Fathers (Ignatius, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Origen's reply to Celsus) and argues Matthew's and Luke's independent nativity narratives point to a pre-gospel tradition of the virginal conception. Against Hume's claim that a wise man proportions belief to evidence, Lyons contends experience is not an infallible guide and that ruling out the miraculous a priori is a circular limit on inquiry, casting Mary and Joseph as the first skeptics who nonetheless accepted an event outside natural experience.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 13 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Medievalist Todd Preston argues that 'Put Christ Back in Christmas' misreads the holiday, which in the English tradition was always a balance of Christian and non-Christian elements. He shows Augustine (in On Christian Doctrine) and Boethius (in the Consolation of Philosophy, guided by Lady Philosophy) licensed Christians to absorb useful pagan philosophy, and that this apologetic openness let King Alfred, Pope Gregory and St. Boniface repurpose rather than erase heathen practice – turning Thor's oak into the Christmas fir. Tracing the Old English 'Cristesmæsse', Yule/Jol and Modraniht, and the secular revelry of Sir Gawain that Wyclif condemned, he concludes an authentic Christmas keeps its pagan half.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 15 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Scott Aiken argues the conservative 'War on Christmas' pushed by Gibson and O'Reilly is illusory on both fronts: cultural Christianity has already won, and keeping nativity scenes out of public schools protects minority rights under the Establishment Clause rather than persecuting the majority. He then mounts a separate attack, claiming both Christmas myths are bad on their merits – the nativity (star that leads wise men, vanishing Magi, Joseph's pointless genealogy) promotes mere credulity rather than tested faith, while the Santa myth glorifies a slave-owning surveiller who makes goodness merely instrumental. He adds that teaching the false Santa story undercuts parents' testimonial authority to teach the gospel as true.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 16 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Guy Bennett-Hunter treats both the Santa story and the virginal conception as mythologies whose value lies in meaning, not literal fact, drawing on Barthes and Gadamer's dictum that a myth needs no verification outside itself. He deploys Hume on miracles and Russell's Teapot to argue it is no more rational to believe the sacred myth literally than the Santa one, then turns to Tillich's religious case: taking the virgin birth literally is idolatry that drags the ultimate God into the chain of cause and effect. He urges 'breaking' the myth – keeping its significance while dropping its literal truth – a ladder to be kicked away like Edmund Gosse's childhood test of idolatry.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 22 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Will Williams recounts the legend that St. Nicholas of Myra, the historical basis of Santa Claus, attended the Council of Nicaea (325) and punched the heretic Arius, who taught that the Son was created and not fully God ('there was a time when the Son was not'). Setting the fight to a parody of 'The Night Before Christmas', Williams explains via Athanasius why the divinity of Christ mattered – only if Jesus is truly God can his death secure salvation. He contrasts this fiercely theological bishop with the de-Christianized modern Santa, using the syncretism of 'Here Comes Santa Claus' to argue Nicholas would deplore what consumerist Christmas has become.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 30 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Tallman offers a naturalistic (atheist) justification for celebrating Christmas, arguing first that the holiday's date and rituals (December 25 solstice, Christmas trees, Odin-derived Santa) predate and are not exclusively Christian, so non-believers may find their own meaning in them. Drawing on George Santayana's and Steven Cahn's 'religious naturalism,' she argues rituals and moral communities give meaning without supernatural belief, so atheists engaging even overtly religious rites (like Westerners doing Hindu-rooted yoga) are not being disingenuous. She locates a secular 'spirit of Christmas' — giving, love, community — in It's a Wonderful Life, where humans, not God, save George Bailey, and closes on a Venn-diagram overlap of Christian and naturalist Christmases.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 31 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Mason, a developmental psychologist writing as a Pagan, narrates her decades-long religious journey through James Fowler's Stages of Faith model, using each stage to reinterpret Christmas. She recounts childhood confusion over carols and chimney-invading strangers, fundamentalist-Christian zeal (stage 3 group belonging, then stage-4 doubt as she 'crusaded' against pagan Christmas trees), Unitarian Universalist questioning, and finally Wiccan/Pagan practice centered on Hecate and the winter-solstice Wheel of the Year (rediscovering Christmas's pagan roots in holly, mistletoe, and Yule). Reaching Fowler's stage 5 'Conjunctive Faith,' she concludes Christmas is neither hers nor anyone's to own but a self-perpetuating commercial 'Hallmark' phenomenon she can now greet with equanimity.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 18 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Taliaferro and Le Gall's 'The Great Escape' weighs four philosophical objections to cannabis-induced altered states — falsehood (Plato's ban on poetry/theatre in the Republic), distortion of reason (Euripides' Bacchae, James on nitrous oxide), undermining of agency (the Sirens, De Quincey's opium), and loss of self-determination (the Stoic Epictetus on freedom) — then surveys Jewish, Christian and Islamic treatments of wine, coffee and hashish. They rebut the objections using Aristotle's cathartic defense of theatre and Locke's imagination-based account of freedom, concluding that if cannabis is no worse than wine the philosophical and religious case against it is not decisive.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 34 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Barkman, prompted by his wedding guests' shared discomfort with his best man's tattooed arms, sets out to dispel a 'Christian Confucian confusion' that reads piety as requiring a tattoo-free body. He shows Leviticus 19:28 and 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 condemn tattooing only where it signals allegiance to impure cults or misuse of the body, not tattooing in itself, and that Confucius's Hsiao King injunction against wounding the body one receives from one's parents was linked to tattoos only by Han Chinese racism against tattooed minorities. Citing General Yue Fei's mother inking loyalty on his back, he concludes ink can even be pious, though a child under a parent's legitimate authority owes obedience if forbidden it.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 13 "Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress" — Henry Jacoby channels W.K. Clifford's 'ethics of belief' through South Park's Stan Marsh, who debunks John Edward, holistic healers, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the believer and that faith is belief without evidence. The chapter distinguishes prudential from evidential reasons and dismantles Pascal's Wager using episodes like 'Cartmanland' (why would a good God torment nonbelievers?) and 'Do the Handicapped Go to Hell?' (which religion?). Stan's speech to Edward's audience frames uncritical belief as mental laziness that slows the progress of mankind.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 23 "To Know … and Believe" — Daniel Gallagher uses Lost's Rose, who insists 'I just know' her husband lives and the island cured her, to apply Aquinas's account of faith as 'mid-way between knowledge and opinion.' Drawing on Plato's episteme/doxa distinction and Aquinas's God/'first truth' conceptual distinction plus the five ways, he argues reason can demonstrate that God exists while faith (a grace) grasps what reason cannot. Rose exemplifies both the sin of presumption (mistaking faith for knowledge, treating the island as God's certain instrument) and, by contrast to Charlie's acedia, robust faith, so the chapter urges keeping faith and reason harmonized rather than conflated.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 21 "19. The Orville as Philosophy The Dangers of Religion" — The chapter argues that Seth MacFarlane's The Orville is a pointed critique of religion, especially when merged with political and military power. Through the warrior-god Avis worshipped by the Krill (read as stand-ins for militant evangelicals and Islamist jihadists) and the Moclans' patriarchal bigotry, it contends religion is portrayed as archaic and dangerous. It deploys Socrates's Euthyphro argument to reject divine command theory, contrasts the Krill's dogmatic certainty with the secular Union's self-correcting ethics, and invokes Buber's I–Thou to explain the 'de-souling' of outsiders, while defending Lockean separation of church and state against theocracy and theonomistic ethics.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 28 "26. Midnight Mass as Philosophy The Problems with Religion" — The chapter argues that Mike Flanagan's Midnight Mass, through its atheist surrogate Riley, mounts a cumulative case for atheism. Riley's 'campfire' theory naturalistically explains religion's origins; Riley and Dr. Gunning's refusal to call Leeza's healing a miracle enacts Hume's argument against testimony for miracles; Dr. Gunning's EPP explanation of the 'vampires' rebuts methodological naturalism. Sheriff Hassan's grief over his wife voices the problem of evil (Mackie) against the free-will defense (Plantinga), while Erin's dying monologue endorses a Humean/Buddhist no-self bundle theory over the soul. Johnson argues the series treats faith as an epistemic and moral vice and holy books as dangerously interpretable.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 31 "29. Frank Herbert’s Dune as Philosophy The Need to Think for Yourself" — Reading the Sci Fi Channel miniseries Frank Herbert's Dune and Children of Dune, Littmann argues the saga warns against letting leaders or religions think for us: Paul Atreides fakes being the Fremen Mahdi, wages a holy war, and founds a theocratic tyranny that Alia and Leto II carry to worse extremes. He sets Plato's Republic (the guardian class, the noble lie, rule by the wise) and Hobbes against pro-democracy thinkers—Locke's consent and natural rights, Mill's harm principle, Dewey's democracy—then cites Locke, Paine and Russell on religion's dangers, closing with W.K. Clifford's 'ethics of belief' that one must not accept religious claims without sufficient evidence. The chapter reads Paul's dictatorship and the Bene Gesserit's engineered messiah as dramatizations of the historical abuses of concentrated and religious power.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 64 "61. God’s Not Dead as Philosophy Trying to Prove God Exists" — The chapter evaluates the arguments college freshman Josh delivers in God's Not Dead and finds them to fail while the film demonizes atheists via caricature and the Christian persecution complex. It rebuts the Kalam cosmological argument (traced to al-Ghazali) with vacuum fluctuations and a quantum-foam explanation, shows the Big Bang refutes rather than confirms Genesis, and uses Russell's teapot and Hume's evidence proportioning on the burden of proof. Against Josh's 'without God everything is permissible' it applies Plato's Euthyphro to sink divine command theory, answers the free-will defense to the problem of evil, and closes that the film's fideism makes knowledge impossible.

## Nagarjuna

*c. 150–250 AD · 7 chapters in the corpus.*

Nagarjuna was an Indian Buddhist philosopher and founder of the Madhyamaka, or Middle Way, school of Mahayana thought. He is best known for the doctrine of emptiness, the claim that all phenomena lack any independent, intrinsic nature because they arise only in dependence on other things. Through rigorous dialectical arguments, developed most famously in his Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way, he sought to dissolve metaphysical extremes and fixed views while avoiding nihilism, an approach that profoundly shaped later Buddhist philosophy across Asia.

### Emptiness (sunyata)

Emptiness, or sunyata, is the teaching that all things lack any fixed, independent essence and exist only in dependence on causes, conditions, and conceptual designation. It was developed most rigorously by the Indian philosopher Nagarjuna, founder of the Madhyamaka school, who used relentless dialectical arguments to show that positing self-existent entities leads to contradiction. Rather than a claim that nothing exists, emptiness holds that things are real precisely because they are dependently arisen and thus without inherent nature. For Nagarjuna this insight dissolves the grasping and metaphysical confusion that bind beings to suffering.

- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 21 "Analyzing Emptiness" — Paul Gass reads the Dead's hippie milieu (the Beats, the Acid Tests, Buddhist-monk lyricist Peter Monk) as a conduit for Buddhist doctrine, taking the 'Eyes of the World' chorus as an invitation to awaken to Buddha-nature. He explains the Four Noble Truths, karma, and the five aggregates to argue the self is an illusion, using the image of a flame passed between lighters at a Dead show to picture rebirth without a persisting soul. The chapter then presents Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka middle way — emptiness itself must not be clutched as an absolute truth — and reads the 'redeemer... wagon loaded with clay' verse of 'Eyes of the World' as the Mahayana bodhisattva liberating all beings, with emptiness finally discarded like the boat after crossing the river.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 26 "Sudden Enlightenment" — Luke Cuddy and Michael Bruce ask whether Beatrix Kiddo could reach enlightenment, reading Kill Bill's nonlinear plotting as a Buddhist interconnected web of causes: Pai Mei's Five Point Palm technique causes both the coffin escape and Bill's death, and Budd's degraded trailer life is karma catching up. Beatrix grasps the structure of suffering and its cause—she locates it in Bill and the squad and eliminates them—but mistakes that for ending suffering itself, and her declared lack of 'mercy, compassion, and forgiveness' blocks the compassion enlightenment requires, while Bill's 'natural born killer' story contradicts impermanence and no-self. The chapter closes on her bathroom-floor ecstasy as a candidate case of Zen sudden enlightenment, left to the reader to judge by how she would one day treat a vengeful Nikki.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 26 "Mr. Monk Murdered Trudy" — Green argues Monk is an unintentional Bodhisattva whose OCD enacts the Four Bodhisattva Vows: the compulsion to touch lampposts is the first vow's blind desires, his monastic minimalism the Dharma gate, and his crime-solving compassion for a disordered world the third vow, with the Dhammapada's teaching that the untamed mind produces suffering exemplified by Monk and by Harold Krenshaw's rival ordering. Like Vimalakirti feigning illness, or Shawn Spencer in Psych, and like the father in the Lotus Sutra's burning-house parable, Monk and his writers use skillful deception to awaken viewers to suffering and loving kindness. The title thesis is that Monk cannot solve Trudy's murder because he accepts responsibility for it: by Thich Nhat Hanh's Interbeing there is no absolute self and other, so solving the case requires the Zen 'kill the Buddha' eradication of the self, Monk's nirvana-as-extinction and the end of the series.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 8 "2 - An Interview with Bodhidharma" — Priest stages a spoof radio interview with Bodhidharma at the Shaolin Temple to argue that the monks' fighting exercises are really meditation: a fist passing an inch from your nose focuses the mind, and repeatedly practicing violent techniques makes practitioners less violent. Bodhidharma explains that a liter of goat's milk, a marauding thug, and even the reporter's self are only conceptual labels over 'thusness' (tathata), that attachment and the desire to strike cause suffering to the striker, and that the Buddha's compassion permits self-defense without aggression. The punchline is the reporter's unanswered last question: 'They're not really about fighting, are they?'
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 34 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Bernard Wills takes the reference to The Cloud of Unknowing in 'The Window' as the key to Cohen's lifelong fascination with apophatic, negative mysticism - God sought beyond every image in a 'naked intent of love,' as in the medieval Cloud, Dionysius, Maimonides, and Kabbalah - against the kataphatic way of affirmation. He reads Recent Songs as an album of exile and the play of union and separation ('Un Canadien Errant,' 'Ballad of the Absent Mare'), where the incarnate Word is 'stuttered' and 'frozen,' a passion without resurrection. Cohen's later Zen turn is thus prefigured: the emptiness of sunyata and the Neo-Platonic descent from and return to the One are positive nothingness - self-overcoming in the service of compassion rather than the black-romantic nihilism of self-annihilation.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 36 "22. The Many-Faced God and Indian Philosophy" — Van Eyghen maps the Faceless Men onto Indian philosophy: their one God of many faces parallels Vedanta's Brahman in personal form as Ishvara, and Arya's training to become 'no one' parallels shedding the ego toward identity with Brahman - with Jaqen as guru and the stick-beating ritual as an example of identity fusion in Harvey Whitehouse's cognitive science of religion. But the Faceless Men may go further than Vedanta toward Buddhism, since they worship a god with no face of his own and aim at no-self rather than union, while Arya's pragmatic adoption of the shellfish-merchant disguise echoes the Bhagavad Gita's Krishna: perform your duty without attachment to any self.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 17 "8. Ode to Joi" — Steve Bein first tests Joi against Mary Anne Warren's five functionalist personhood criteria — consciousness, reason, self-motivated activity, communication, self-awareness — and finds she passes, which makes Luv's stomping of the emanator a murder. The Buddha's no-self doctrine then denies that anyone, Joi included, is an enduring person: we are bundles of fleeting psychophysical processes, 'like tears in rain', which threatens to let Luv plead that the Luv who killed Joi no longer exists. Nagarjuna's two truths resolve the courtroom problem: ultimately there are no persons, but conventionally 'Luv killed Joi' is perfectly true, and the karma ripples through the whole network.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 8 "Introduction" — De Cruz and De Smedt argue that ATLA subverts the Chosen One trope: Aang's training is slow and non-linear, he needs dedicated teachers, and saving the world is a team effort in which Katara leads and Sokka plans. The show's central theme is oneness, voiced by Guru Pathik's 'illusion of separation' ('The Guru') and Huu's banyan-grove tree ('The Swamp'), which the editors trace to Daoist, Huayan Buddhist (Fazang's golden lion), and Indigenous traditions of interdependence. They frame the volume's engagement with genocide, imperialism, ecological destruction, and Ba Sing Se's authoritarian denial as proof that philosophy is needed for human flourishing.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 30 "Keep the Needle on the Record" — Donavan Muir argues Lost's narrative world, unlike Jane Eyre's, requires its own metaphysics, and that this metaphysics is an order of balanced binary oppositions: Jacob and the Man in Black as twins diverged at birth, the cave scale's light and dark stones that Locke knocks out of balance in 'The Substitute,' science/faith, with characters like Jack converting from one pole into its opposite. The proper model is the yin-yang in motion - the Tao as a balanced ontological flow in which interdependent opposites wax and wane - so that treating the poles as independent is the delusion that threatens the island's order. The finale, where both Jacob and the Man in Black cease to exist and the castaways are freed, enacts the Mahayana Buddhist Middle Way: enlightenment as letting go of rigid oppositions that interdependence double-negates.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 21 "Genius All the Time The Beats, Spontaneous Presence, and Primordial Ground" — Marc Olmsted reads Beat spontaneity through Tantric (Vajrayana) Buddhism, arguing that 'first thought, best thought' and Kerouac's 'Mind is shapely, art is shapely' rest on the view that enlightenment/awareness is already present and need only be recognized. He maps Ginsberg's poetics onto the Tantric terms Ground, Path, and Fruition, tying shamatha-vipashyana practice and the doctrine of anatta (no-self) to the poet catching the first pre-conceptual thought. Ginsberg's Blake visions, his study under Trungpa and Gelek Rinpoche, and Burroughs's cut-up 'homemade yankee tantra' are offered as evidence that Beat composition enacts a Buddhist recognition of primordial, empty, self-existing awareness.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 26 "Between Social Ecology and Deep Ecology Gary Snyder’s Ecological Philosophy" — Paul Messersmith-Glavin positions Snyder as a bridge between deep ecology and social ecology. He shows how Sessions and Devall enlist Snyder's Mahayana Buddhism (emptiness/sunyata, Dogen's 'Mind means trees, fence posts, tiles, and grasses') and Spinoza's monism for a biocentric, consciousness-changing deep ecology descended from Naess and Leopold's land ethic. Against this, he sets Bookchin's social ecology, which roots the ecological crisis in human hierarchy and attacks deep ecology's ahistorical 'cosmic oneness' and misanthropic Earth First! statements. Snyder's threefold nature/wild/wilderness distinction, bioregionalism, and reading of Marx and anarchism let him hold both, insisting environmental and social justice are 'all one front.'
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 30 "Keep the Needle on the Record" — Donavan S. Muir argues that Lost deliberately withholds its metanarrative so viewers must construct its metaphysics, which he identifies as an order of balanced binary oppositions. Drawing on the spinning Taoist yin-yang, he reads the interdependent, mutually converting poles—Jack from man of science to man of faith, Sawyer from con man to protector—and the light/dark scales in Widmore's painting and the cave (Locke throwing out the white rock) as figures for a Tao whose balance sustains existence. Invoking Derrida's traces and Mahayana Buddhism's Middle Way and emptiness, he reads Jacob and the Man in Black as twins whose oppositions must be annihilated, so that only when both cease to exist in 'The End' are the castaways set free.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 84 "79. Cyberpunk 2077 as Philosophy Balancing the (Mystical) Ghost in the (Transhuman) Machine" — Lay reads Cyberpunk 2077's transhuman Night City against the enhancement debate. Using the Ship of Theseus, Parfit's continuity plus fission/fusion (V and Johnny 'fusing,' the Delamain AIs) and Clark and Chalmers's extended mind, he argues enhancement neither destroys personal identity (which Parfit says doesn't matter) nor dehumanizes users — it may be the purest expression of Clark's cyborg humanity. The real danger is corporate exploitation of bodies, explained via Adorno's culture industry and Arendt's banality of evil. Buddhist nonattachment (Nagarjuna's emptiness, echoed by a Schopenhauer shard) grounds each ending's pacification-versus-attachment theme, but Lay corrects it with Weil's critique of power and Buber's I-Thou, concluding the game urges transcending the boundary between 'me' and 'you' through mystical interpersonal relation.

### Non-Self (anatman)

Non-self, or anatman, is the Buddhist claim that there is no permanent, unchanging self or soul underlying our experience. What we take to be a fixed "I" is, on this view, a shifting bundle of physical and mental processes that continually arise and dissolve, held together only by habit and craving. Understanding non-self is intended to undercut the self-centered grasping that drives suffering, and it distinguishes Buddhism from traditions that posit an enduring soul.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 56 "Unknown" — Brannigan reads the film's mirror imagery through the Buddha's mirror instruction to his son Rahula: Neo touching the dripping mirror and becoming the mirror marks his awakening to the naked truth (aletheia as nakedness) that his world is a programmed illusion, Smith's dark sunglasses distort while Morpheus's mirrored glasses clarify, and Neo's reflection in the spoon-bending boy's spoon signals clarity. 'There is no spoon' parallels the Zen mondo where neither flag nor wind moves but only mind, and shows that reflected images are not reality - the world is maya. The deepest lesson is anatman: just as there is no spoon there is no Neo, no fixed self, and Rahula's lesson grounds the interdependence (pratityasamutpada) of all actions on others.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 124 "Unknown" — The chapter reads 'the One' through the concentration-camp survivor who, by sheer presence, retained others' dignity and will to live—a place in the social link filled by transference rather than real qualities—and opposes this to the film's One, who merely learns the virtualized reality's rules can be suspended, a paranoid notion that reduces the resistance of the Real to weak will. The spoon-bending child's 'there is no spoon' should have pushed the film to the Buddhist proposition that I myself do not exist, while Agent Smith's speech that humans 'define their reality through suffering and misery' makes him the analyst-figure whose lesson is that reality is that which resists.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 21 "“Nobody’s Bob Dylan”" — Vernezze and Lulewicz take Dylan's 1964 Halloween quip "I got my Bob Dylan mask on" as an entry into personal identity, testing each theory against his life: the bodily view (Zimmerman to Dylan) survives cell turnover but stumbles on brain-transplant cases; Locke's memory theory handles them but faces Reid's brave-officer regress and Alzheimer's cases, and Dylan's reincarnation lyrics ("Shelter from the Storm," "I and I") ignore memory altogether. The Christian soul view of the gospel albums ("When He Returns," "Gotta Serve Somebody") follows Descartes and Plato but cannot justify the swirl-to-filling inference that souls exist. The chapter ends sympathetic to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist no-self: Dylan's "I is another," his name as fabrication, and the cover album Self Portrait all deny a fixed self-created essence.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 13 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Priest argues that Pirsig's Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance is far more genuinely Zen than its disclaimer admits: once riding becomes effortless, the dissolution of the subject-object distinction that Dogen calls genjokoan arrives on the open road ('you ARE the driving and the road and the elements'), and the Harley's relaxed posture and low-revving thug-thug-thug rhythm make it a better vehicle for suchness than cars or whinier bikes. Even maintenance done as an end in itself is genjokoan, and because ultimate reality erases every conceptual distinction, care of self, others, and the bike amount to the same thing, the Mahayana ground of compassion; the mountain-and-water Zen saying resolves the paradox that the unconceptualized and the conceptualized are one. Suffering, on the Buddhist diagnosis Priest applies, comes from imposing conceptual grids that see the world wrong, and seeing it aright dissolves it.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 14 "Mind the Mindfulness" — Reads The Meaning of Life as a sustained reductio of transcendentalism — the two-world metaphysics shared by Plato, Augustine, and Vedanta's Brahman/atman — arguing that the film's dehumanizing sketches (the machine that goes 'ping,' the 'every sperm is sacred' father selling his children, the Vegas-style Christmas in Heaven) show how otherworldly belief overrides this-worldly compassion. It parallels the Buddha's scriptural critiques: the Agganna sutta against caste, the no-self (anatta) doctrine against the Bhagavad Gita's soul that licenses Krishna to tell Arjuna killing is a favor, and impermanence (anicca) against the fantasy of eternal bliss. Python's grotesque — Creosote's explosion, the organ-donor lady's 'Galaxy Song' despair — matches Buddhist corpse meditations, while the film steers between hedonism (Creosote) and nihilism (the housewife who surrenders her liver) toward the Buddha's Middle Way and, against everyday distraction (the boardroom's 'people are not wearing enough hats,' the couple who think Schopenhauer begins with an S), toward mindfulness (sati).
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 44 "“How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons" — James McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism: the fleet's sleepless FTL jumps in "33" and Roslin's dwindling survivor counts enact the four noble truths, Leoben's interrogation scenes teach that suffering comes from ignorant attachment, and Dogen's no-self and impermanence frame the show's interdependent characters. Cylon resurrection, D'Anna's serial deaths, and the prophecy that "all of this has happened before" model karma and samsara, while Nishida's kenotic God of Absolute Nothingness makes sense of Six and Leoben's God of love. Because Cylons feel pain, fear death away from a resurrection ship, and act volitionally, McRae concludes they are persons in the Buddhist sense, owed the compassion of the Eightfold Path.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 21 "Analyzing Emptiness" — Paul Gass reads the Dead's hippie milieu (the Beats, the Acid Tests, Buddhist-monk lyricist Peter Monk) as a conduit for Buddhist doctrine, taking the 'Eyes of the World' chorus as an invitation to awaken to Buddha-nature. He explains the Four Noble Truths, karma, and the five aggregates to argue the self is an illusion, using the image of a flame passed between lighters at a Dead show to picture rebirth without a persisting soul. The chapter then presents Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka middle way — emptiness itself must not be clutched as an absolute truth — and reads the 'redeemer... wagon loaded with clay' verse of 'Eyes of the World' as the Mahayana bodhisattva liberating all beings, with emptiness finally discarded like the boat after crossing the river.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 9 "“Logic Without Need Is Sterile”" — Writing as a Vulcan philosophy professor and student of Spock, the chapter reconstructs Vulcan civilization from Surak's Awakening as three interlocking modes of logic — formal logic (whose first law, Kiri-kin-tha's 'nothing unreal exists', parallels Parmenides), ethical logic (the axiom 'the needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few'), and meditative discipline — and maps them onto Patanjali's Yoga: the yamas, meditation, and samadhi's cosmic oneness, with ahimsa linking Surak to Gandhi and King. It then rereads Star Trek: The Motion Picture, where V'Ger's pure logic leaves both it and Spock asking 'Is this all that I am?', and Spock's mind meld with V'Ger becomes a tantric union that integrates feeling with logic after the failure of Kolinahr. The chapter's thesis is that 'logic without need is sterile': logic is 'the beginning of wisdom . . . not the end', and Spock's rebirth culminates in choosing the human thing precisely when it is not the logical thing.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 26 "Mr. Monk Murdered Trudy" — Green argues Monk is an unintentional Bodhisattva whose OCD enacts the Four Bodhisattva Vows: the compulsion to touch lampposts is the first vow's blind desires, his monastic minimalism the Dharma gate, and his crime-solving compassion for a disordered world the third vow, with the Dhammapada's teaching that the untamed mind produces suffering exemplified by Monk and by Harold Krenshaw's rival ordering. Like Vimalakirti feigning illness, or Shawn Spencer in Psych, and like the father in the Lotus Sutra's burning-house parable, Monk and his writers use skillful deception to awaken viewers to suffering and loving kindness. The title thesis is that Monk cannot solve Trudy's murder because he accepts responsibility for it: by Thich Nhat Hanh's Interbeing there is no absolute self and other, so solving the case requires the Zen 'kill the Buddha' eradication of the self, Monk's nirvana-as-extinction and the end of the series.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 8 "2 - An Interview with Bodhidharma" — Priest stages a spoof radio interview with Bodhidharma at the Shaolin Temple to argue that the monks' fighting exercises are really meditation: a fist passing an inch from your nose focuses the mind, and repeatedly practicing violent techniques makes practitioners less violent. Bodhidharma explains that a liter of goat's milk, a marauding thug, and even the reporter's self are only conceptual labels over 'thusness' (tathata), that attachment and the desire to strike cause suffering to the striker, and that the Buddha's compassion permits self-defense without aggression. The punchline is the reporter's unanswered last question: 'They're not really about fighting, are they?'
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 10 "And the Winner Is" — Lynch pits Plato against the Shaolin monks on the nature of the self that martial training is supposed to master. Plato's Republic makes the athlete-warrior Guardian a harmonious, rationally ruled tripartite soul whose bravery is 'remembering what ought and ought not to be feared', trained so reason governs aggression; Buddhism instead dissolves the self into five impermanent aggregates (illustrated by the chariot analogy) and reads mushin as a direct taste of no-self. He awards the practical decision to the Buddhist fighting monks, since no-self explains martial spontaneity and naturally arising compassion, while admitting Plato's substantive rational soul is not strictly refuted.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 18 "Halo as a Catalyst for a Buddhism Videogame" — Luke Cuddy uses Halo 3 checkpoints and emulator save states—two mutually exclusive Flood-fight outcomes both in some sense true—to make David Lewis's possible worlds and modal truth concrete, with Leibniz as the doctrine's ancestor. Halo's infinite lives make players genuinely angry, and the chapter argues this is upaya territory: like the father in the Lotus Sutra's parable of the burning house, the game promises mastery (the goat-, deer-, and ox-carts) to lure players toward something greater outside it. Master Chief becomes a Bodhisattva whose avatar slides between extension of self and other, provoking the 'who am I?' crisis that reveals the ego as empty at the ultimate level of the Two-Fold Truth, while the Dalai Lama's enemies-as-teachers turns the seven-year-old who pwns you into practice in the first two Noble Truths' suffering and anger.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 50 "Chapter 07 - Scan Thyself" — Butler frames Dick as the latest in philosophy's self-knowledge line: the Delphic 'know thyself' that Socrates made essential to the good life at the cost of his own, the Buddha who sought himself and found only an illusion at the root of suffering, Descartes whose entire philosophy rests on confidence in knowledge of himself as an immaterial being, and Dick's own 8,000-page Exegesis. The chapter's hook is the stakes of self-ignorance (what if you turned out to be something horrible?) and its Dickian version: how do you know you are not an android?
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 61 "The Devil and Philosophy" — John Thompson argues Mara, who unleashes armies and seductive daughters on the Buddha-to-be under the bodhi tree, is not 'the Buddhist Satan': he has not fallen, wages no cosmic war against a supreme God, and merely personifies trsna (grasping) as overlord of samsara. He finds textbook glosses like Huston Smith's misleading, and praises Bertolucci's Little Buddha, where Mara rises from a pool as Siddhartha's mirror twin - 'Oh Lord of my own Ego, you are pure illusion. You do not exist' - a portrayal he reads through Karen Armstrong's Jungian shadow self and Campbell's Freudian eros-and-thanatos frame, concluding that we are Mara/Satan.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 22 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Klein and Fundora trace Jobs's Buddhism from Reed College meditation and the seven-month India pilgrimage (reading Yogananda's Autobiography of a Yogi yearly) to the Zen minimalism of Apple design, arguing his temper tantrums, harsh speech, and reality distortion field do not disqualify him from being 'on the path' since Buddhism is a practice, not a creed test. They expound the Four Noble Truths (dukkha in its three kinds, via Thich Nhat Hanh), the Eightfold Path's Middle Way, and anatta—the non-self they compare to Hume's bundle theory of the self against Descartes's thinking thing—and read Jobs's strip-away-the-essence aesthetics, the three-click intuitive iPod interface that keeps users in the moment, the non-dualist marriage of art and technology, and his Think Different self-reliance as deeply Buddhist authenticity.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 11 "3. Tris Finds Enlightenment" — Rhine argues that Tris's heroism rests on Buddhist practice: her breath-counting on the Ferris wheel and inside Four's fear landscape, her emotional intelligence, and her awareness of the parental 'voices in her head' are classic meditative disciplines for calming the ego whose clinging, on the Buddhist account, is the cause of suffering (dukkha). She reads Abnegation's gray houses, plain food, and four-times-a-year mirror as ritual ego-diminishment - a middle way between indulgence and the extreme asceticism the Buddha rejected - that explains why most Divergent arise from Abnegation. Contemporary neuroscience is then recruited: the amygdala-versus-prefrontal-cortex struggle Will describes, and monks' heightened gamma waves, explain how Tris can see the simulation as a simulation, like Neo in The Matrix, and act while others are paralyzed by fear.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 36 "23. I Fight Crime in My Sleep" — Staged as a Fight Club parody in which a Buddhist psychiatrist, Dr. Quinzel, evaluates a costumed narrator sent to Arkham, the chapter argues neither hero is close to awakening: Batman's crime-fighting is craving that perpetuates dukkha, his secret identities a twice-constructed self that the Buddha's no-self teaching dissolves, and his violence fails the test that 'hostility is never appeased by hostility.' Superman fares no better - his super-intellect imposes illusory order on impermanence, his flight and X-ray vision are distractions beside the Buddha-eye and tapas, and as one of the titans of the six realms he is further from Buddhahood than a human - while the doctor defines justice as karma rather than retaliation and finds Batman one step from American Psycho's Bateman. Only conquering Mara, one's own inner deceiver, is 'the only superpower worth having,' and the closing reveal that the doctor has a plan of her own for 'Mr. Kent' caps the diagnosis.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 17 "6. One Clone from Another" — Asks what metaphysically individuates one Leda clone from another, surveying the tradition: Aristotelian substances bearing properties, Plato's and Descartes's non-repeatable individual essences, Berkeley's and Hegel's soul-substances, Aquinas's matter-based view, Locke's memory-based personal identity (with its sleeping-copy and consciousness-download objections), and Hume's argument that substance is a meaningless idea. It then turns to the Buddhist framework — the Four Noble Truths, anatman (no eternal self), the five skandhas, and dependent origination, illustrated by Alison's soap-and-drug crates — before closing with Nishida Kitaro's logic of contradictory self-identity. Read through that lens, the clone dance party in Felix's loft shows each clone's moves are truly her own precisely because they incorporate and mirror her sisters': identity is relational, not intrinsic.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 31 "17. Dialog with the Buddha" — A Platonic-style fictional dialogue in which a newly enlightened "Canadian Buddha" walks out of the northern Ontario bush to the Prolethean farm and debates Tomas, Henry, and Bonnie over whether clones are abominations. Using karma, rebirth, the gandhabba that carries consciousness-flux to a new embryo, the no-soul doctrine, and the eightfold path, the Buddha argues clones are ordinary beings of the karmic flux — like the split bacterium, nothing unnatural — but that cloning multiplies clinging: hosts crave immortality through copies, each clone inherits the host's whole accumulated karma, and Henry's dream of training an army of Helena-clones would only deepen the unsatisfactoriness the Buddha's mustard-seed lesson says clinging to the dead always brings. Only ending the cycle through enlightenment releases anyone; the clone, like the lost child, is not the one you lost.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 15 "6. Bowie the Buddhist" — Muchall reads 'Quicksand' and 'Where Are We Now?' as suffused with Tibetan Buddhism: 'Don't believe in yourself' voices the anatta teaching Bowie absorbed studying with Chime Rinpoche and from Chogyam Trungpa, whose 'spiritual materialism' warns that ego converts even spirituality and ideologies to its own use. After retelling the Buddha's life, the Four Noble Truths' three kinds of dukkha, and the five aggregates that reveal no permanent self, the chapter maps the song's 'ragged hole' and bardos onto the Tibetan Book of the Dead's after-death journey, and reads Bowie's morphing personas as lived acknowledgment that there is no fixed self - 'there's nothing in here.'
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 25 "14. David Bowie’s Sadness" — Ketcham argues Bowie's sadness is ours: via Deleuze and Guattari's Anti-Oedipus he casts consumer capitalism as a machine producing schizophrenic fad-following (the stuck high-school footballer, the Benetton self), of which Bowie's serial personas are both symptom and escape - 'always crashing in the same car' yet never repeating. Minkowski's lived time and the Buddha's anatman ground the dance as pure becoming without a dancer, while Heidegger's das Man and being-toward-death explain why authentic self-creation - which, unlike Sellers or Williams, Bowie survived - exacts the price Freud's beyond-the-pleasure-principle names as compulsive repetition, turned by Bowie into a life wish.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 36 "22. The Many-Faced God and Indian Philosophy" — Van Eyghen maps the Faceless Men onto Indian philosophy: their one God of many faces parallels Vedanta's Brahman in personal form as Ishvara, and Arya's training to become 'no one' parallels shedding the ego toward identity with Brahman - with Jaqen as guru and the stick-beating ritual as an example of identity fusion in Harvey Whitehouse's cognitive science of religion. But the Faceless Men may go further than Vedanta toward Buddhism, since they worship a god with no face of his own and aim at no-self rather than union, while Arya's pragmatic adoption of the shellfish-merchant disguise echoes the Bhagavad Gita's Krishna: perform your duty without attachment to any self.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 24 "12. A Month from Now, I’ll Be a Balding, Toothless Skeleton" — Reads Fiona Goode's war against fading - the experimental RM47 serum, rejecting the Axeman's escape because he would watch her decay, the Papa Legba bargain that collapses because she has no soul - alongside Delphine LaLaurie's blood facials and Marie Laveau's child sacrifices, as illustrations of Buddhist dukkha and the three thirsts (kama for sense pleasure, bhava for existence, vibhava for annihilation). Legba's 'you don't have a soul' becomes an accidentally liberating glimpse of anatta, and Cordelia's dying advice - 'feel the fear... let it all go' - is the mindfulness, echoing Buddhaghosa's corpse meditations, that might have freed Fiona.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 17 "8. Ode to Joi" — Steve Bein first tests Joi against Mary Anne Warren's five functionalist personhood criteria — consciousness, reason, self-motivated activity, communication, self-awareness — and finds she passes, which makes Luv's stomping of the emanator a murder. The Buddha's no-self doctrine then denies that anyone, Joi included, is an enduring person: we are bundles of fleeting psychophysical processes, 'like tears in rain', which threatens to let Luv plead that the Luv who killed Joi no longer exists. Nagarjuna's two truths resolve the courtroom problem: ultimately there are no persons, but conventionally 'Luv killed Joi' is perfectly true, and the karma ripples through the whole network.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 25 "14. After the Blackout" — Martin Muchall treats the offscreen Blackout as an emblem of the moral catastrophe diagnosed in MacIntyre's After Virtue: our moral vocabulary has shattered into emotivist hissing and clapping, with Roy's murder of Tyrell, his 'God of biomechanics', staging the death of God and the 'everything is permitted' that follows. Utilitarian pleasure and Kantian cold reason (Spock, who must tell the truth to the murderer at the door) have both failed, leaving neoliberal hypercapitalism — corporate psychopathy, the orphanage sweatshop, the Baseline as workplace performance review — as the real villain. Against this, K's ending models the Buddha: everything is impermanent, there is no self to defend, and his selfless, empathetic death points to a morality grounded in evolved and cultivable altruism.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 14 "4. Can We Do Enough Good" — Fetterman argues no one can do enough good to earn The Good Place because the real question is who defines good. Moving from Hobbes's state of nature and Rousseau's innate compassion to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist doctrine of non-self, he shows the four humans' characters were assembled by their formative communities, which is Michael's whole defense before Judge Gen. But Nietzsche's account of how communities christen their own customs 'good' exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife accountants impose their in-group preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's life of point-maximization fails, and why Michael should be asking the Frozen Yogurt Problem instead of blaming demon tampering.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 38 "Fearlessness and Power" — Rebuts Ozai's taunt 'you are still weak' with a Buddhist reading of energybending: Aang wins not by domination but because his unbendable spirit is total vulnerability, a true heart that has abandoned the five hindrances (sensory desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness, doubt — each traced through the chakras, the Serpent's Pass, and 'Nightmares and Daydreams') and a true mind freed from the fundamental delusion of a separate self that 'The Swamp' and 'The Guru' dissolve. The spirit-merging with Ozai is read through Indra's net, and Aang's merciful halt mirrors Indra's Jataka victory where compassion for eagle hatchlings — not force — defeats the demons. Fearlessness, on Sylvia Boorstein's Zen story, is the natural corollary of compassion, so Aang's weakness by Ozai's standard is precisely his power.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 38 "Fearlessness and Power" — Argues that Aang's energybending victory over Ozai vindicates a Buddhist conception of power against Ozai's equation of power with domination: the Lion Turtle's 'unbendable spirit' is not resistance but thorough vulnerability, achieved through the true heart (overcoming the five hindrances mapped onto Aang's sensory desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness, and doubt across the series) and the true mind (overcoming the fundamental delusion of a self separate from others, learned from Huu in 'The Swamp' and Guru Pathik). The merging of Aang's and Ozai's spirits is pictured by the metaphor of Indra's net, and Indra's own Jataka victory, halting his assault to protect eagle hatchlings and disorienting the demons, parallels Aang's refusal to win by killing. Drawing on a Zen story of the abbot who could 'be run through by a sword without batting an eye', the chapter concludes that Aang's fearlessness flows from compassion, so that weakness by Ozai's standard is precisely the power that defeats him.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 40 "Journey’s End and a Vision of a New Community" — Reads Aang's quest through the Karmapa Ogyen Trinley Dorje's book Interconnected: like the seventeenth Karmapa, identified at age seven and taken from his family, Aang learns that an exalted title complicates friendship and that freedom is self-control rather than the rugged individualism of the American hero's quest. Training episodes (Katara's jealous competition in 'The Waterbending Scroll', Jeong Jeong's warnings, the Toph-versus-Katara sifu debate in 'Bitter Work') show moral training as communal, widening from Team Avatar as adoptive family toward universal compassion, with Aang's refusal to open the seventh chakra illustrating how local attachment can obstruct universal love. Zuko's counter-arc from competition, isolation, and betrayal to humility, forgiveness, and contentment shows compassion turning an enemy into a friend, and the finale's simultaneous battles (White Lotus liberating Ba Sing Se, Sokka and Toph destroying the fleet) affirm that Aang wins as an 'interdependent individual', never alone.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 26 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — LoPresti uses 'This Week in God' segments (Ed Helms refereeing a Hindu-versus-Mayan 'faith-off', Colbert's roast line that all religions are infinite paths to accepting Jesus, Rob Corddry's purification rituals and God Exchange stock ticker) to lay out exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism as responses to religious diversity. Inclusivism like Colbert's 'anonymous Christian' logic is exposed as intellectual imperialism that erases genuinely distinct teachings such as the Buddhist non-self and impermanence, while the chapter defends a deep pluralism against the relativism that makes 'all religions equally true' meaningless. Its eulogy for the God Machine borrows Marx's view of religion as an instrument of mass control to explain why religious humor now survives only through a political lens.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 12 "Hakuna Matata, Bodhisattva" — Sets up Disney's maxim 'Hey kid, you can be a hero' as the direct opposite of Zen's 'Hey kid, you can be a buddha': escapism versus liberation, told through the life of Dogen, whose monastic choice parallels Disney hero narratives. Mickey in Steamboat Willie — a bundle of still frames with no sound and no real 'he' — illustrates the Buddha's three marks of existence (emptiness, impermanence, frustration), and the chapter argues Disney products are calibrated distractions from these marks while Dogen counsels facing them, with Ariel's Andersen fate as the price of fantasy. It closes on Disney's merchandising machine (Yoda, Star Wars sequels, direct-to-video cash grabs) as everything the countercultural minimalist Yoda or Baloo's bare necessities stand against, concluding that real hakuna matata is accepting impermanence rather than escaping it.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 14 "4. Can We Do Enough Good" — Interrogates Chidi's question 'why do we choose to be good?' through Hobbes's selfish state of nature, Rousseau's hardwired compassion (Michael's 'little voice' in Eleanor's head), and Hume's bundle theory extended Buddhist-style to a non-self, which grounds Michael's plea to Judge Gen that bad communities made the four humans bad and a better community (Team Cockroach, the Brainy Bunch) can make them good. Nietzsche's account of how communities define their own customs as 'good' then exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife's accountants impose their in-group's preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's point-maximizing life cannot clear the bar. The chapter ends by asking Michael's real question: who gets to decide what's good?
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 21 "a9.xhtml" — The chapter argues Tolkien's clearest moral in The Hobbit is against possessiveness, starting from Aquinas' definition of greed as 'immoderate love of riches': dragon-sickness ruins Thorin and drowns the Master of Lake-town starving in the wilderness with his gold, and Gollum shows the isolating end of a life organized around a 'precious'. Buddhism reframes the diagnosis - Gollum's craving (tanha) is rooted in ignorance (avidya) of the self's illusoriness, since grasping enriches a self that does not exist, per the Four Noble Truths - while Laozi's 'he who knows he has enough is rich' and Thoreau's 'a man is rich in proportion to the things he can afford to let alone' are embodied by Beorn and the gift-giving, nearly government-less hobbits. Bilbo's generosity - giving away the Arkenstone worth 'more than a river of gold', taking only two small chests, later giving Sting and the mithril coat to Frodo - is the book's counter-example to greed.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 29 "Notes" — Kahn argues LEGO play embodies the Buddhist teaching of impermanence that the Buddha states in the Digha Nikaya ('Impermanent are all component things...'): his childhood urge to superglue creations and Finn's father's Kragle dramatize the clinging that produces anxiety when things change, from brick formulations to discontinued sets and even funerals' wilting flowers. The LEGO Star Wars Death Star illustrates non-self — no Death Star exists apart from its 3,803 pieces, and no self apart from shifting aggregates — and the five aggregates (form, sensation, perception, formations, consciousness) are unpacked through building experiences like discovering a daughter has opened the mint Taj Mahal set. Tibetan sand mandalas, painstakingly built then ritually dissolved, model the ceremonial demolition of LEGO creations, teaching acceptance of change without sliding into a nihilistic 'why bother building at all'.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 18 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Godwin reads Spider-Man 3's black-suit episode as a question about the self: with the symbiote amplifying his anger, is Peter still Peter? Against Hume's and the Buddha's bundle theories, on which the self is only an imagined aggregate of thoughts and feelings, and Reid's common-sense simple self, she advances the pragmatist 'social self' of Peirce, James, Dewey, and Mead, updated as Engel's biopsychosocial model: Peter's identity is a shifting web of biology, psyche, and relationships (Aunt May, MJ, Harry) expressed in actions and character. Eddie succumbs to the symbiote because, as Dewey says of the slave to his own blind desires, hatred constitutes who he is, while Peter's thicker web of good relations lets him shed the suit at the church bell.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 36 "23. I Fight Crime in My Sleep" — A Fight Club-style Arkham case study: a patient's hallucinated Superman companion is diagnosed by a Buddhist psychiatrist who explains the three marks of existence—impermanence, non-self, and dissatisfaction—arguing superheroes impose order and a fabricated second self on a world that resists both, so Superman's super-intellect and even flight are distractions (levitation should be ignored; the Buddha-eye beats x-ray vision) while Batman's violence and psychosis, compared to American Psycho's Patrick Bateman, make awakening impossible—both are victims of Mara. A robber literally named David Hume objects that the heroes' law and order is grounded on what ought to be rather than what is, and a Gandhi quote on preferring one's own bad government explains why Batman finally kryptonites his alien 'friend.' The verdict inverts the book's debate: conquering the deceiver within is the only superpower worth having.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 18 "Notes" — Reads Rust's 'dream inside a locked room' and 'everybody is nobody' monologues through the dream-argument and illusion-of-self traditions: the Upanishads and Advaita's atman/brahman, Vasubandhu's Buddhist non-self, Zhuangzi's butterfly dream, Plato's Theaetetus, and Descartes' dream doubt, plus Metzinger's self-model neuroscience. It diagnoses Rust as a neuro-nihilist in Metzinger's sense and defines his predicament with Nietzsche's nihilist, who judges the world as it is that it ought not to be, while noting Schopenhauer misread India's religions as pessimistic. Thompson argues nihilism is a deep insight gone awry — the self is not a thing but an enacted process like dancing — and reads Rust's final near-death experience of love as proof that transcendence of the dream of being a person is possible.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 19 "The Zen Master and the Big Aristotle" — Allhoff and Vaidya argue against the skeptic that philosophy is useless 'bullshit' (nodding to Frankfurt's book) by showing how Phil Jackson's coaching applies it. Jackson's Zen Buddhism, especially zazen meditation and selfless 'triangle offense' play, teaches players to empty the ego and stay in the present, transforming Jordan from point-maker to play-maker; and Jackson's gift of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics to Shaquille O'Neal, who then dubbed himself 'the Big Aristotle,' illustrates Aristotle's doctrine that excellence (his improved free-throw shooting, his generosity) is a habit built by repetition.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 26 "Twelfth Hole Midround and Midlife Defining Moments" — Andy Wible uses defining mid-round shots (the water ball on Augusta's twelfth, the shank that ruins a round) as a way into theories of personal identity, asking why some events make us who we are. He runs through body theory, Descartes's soul theory ('I think, therefore I am'), and Locke's memory theory (the prince-and-cobbler case), refining it with Shoemaker's quasi-memories, to argue that memory is central to identity and explains why a golfer cannot shake a bad shot. He then weighs the Buddhist/Humean/Heraclitean denial of a permanent self as a coping tool ('someone else hit the shank') and debates whether the beta-blocker Propranolol, which dulls adrenaline-fixed memories, could ethically erase the yips much as it treats PTSD.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 21 "Genius All the Time The Beats, Spontaneous Presence, and Primordial Ground" — Marc Olmsted reads Beat spontaneity through Tantric (Vajrayana) Buddhism, arguing that 'first thought, best thought' and Kerouac's 'Mind is shapely, art is shapely' rest on the view that enlightenment/awareness is already present and need only be recognized. He maps Ginsberg's poetics onto the Tantric terms Ground, Path, and Fruition, tying shamatha-vipashyana practice and the doctrine of anatta (no-self) to the poet catching the first pre-conceptual thought. Ginsberg's Blake visions, his study under Trungpa and Gelek Rinpoche, and Burroughs's cut-up 'homemade yankee tantra' are offered as evidence that Beat composition enacts a Buddhist recognition of primordial, empty, self-existing awareness.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 12 "2. Know Thyself, Agent Cooper!" — De Carvalho reads Cooper's ordeal in the Black Lodge as a journey of self-knowledge, distinguishing 'knowing yourself' (your feelings, as Laura sought with Dr. Jacoby) from 'knowing your Self' in the deep sense of Vedanta's Brahman and Tibetan Buddhism's Mind. He sets Hume's bundle theory—the failure to catch a self behind the perceptions—against the Hindu Swami's ocean-and-waves image of an eternal Self beyond thought, and reads Cooper's confrontation with his screaming-Laura and doppelganger visions via the Tibetan Book of the Dead and Jung's shadow: facing his fears with imperfect courage, Cooper fails to integrate his shadow and is split in two.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 44 "“How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons" — James McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism: the fleet's annihilation and constant death illustrate the Four Noble Truths' duhkha, arising from ignorant attachment and violating interdependent arising (no-self and impermanence). Cylon death-and-resurrection parallels karma and rebirth ('all of this has happened before'), Leoben acts as a koan-wielding roshi unsettling Starbuck's assumptions, and Nishida's kenotic God as Absolute Nothingness matches the Cylons' 'we're all God.' Because Cylons feel pain, suffer cognitively, and earn karma, McRae concludes they are persons capable of satori who should seek compassionate reconciliation with humans.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 26 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — LoPresti uses the 'This Week in God' segments (the God Machine, Ed Helms's Hindu-vs-Mayan 'faith-off,' Colbert's inclusivist White House roast) to lay out three responses to religious diversity—exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism—and defends John Cobb's Whiteheadian process-metaphysics pluralism. He insists the distinct concepts of religions be respected rather than collapsed, citing Buddhist impermanence and no-Self and the South Asian Atman/Brahman as unique and non-reducible, and closes by reading the show's turn to political framing of religion through Marx's claim that religion is a mechanism for controlling the masses.
