- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 61 "Unknown" — The chapter argues the film is by no means a Christian movie: Neo is a violent, far-from-sinless mere human savior; the fundamental human problem is ignorance and illusion (Gnostic and Eastern) rather than sin and alienation from God; the rebels' belief that Neo is the reincarnation of the earlier liberator mirrors the Dalai Lama search the Wachowskis cite, though reincarnation is rejected by all major Christian sects; and 'there is no spoon' asserts the illusoriness of empirical reality that Christianity denies. The film's malleable, cyclical time and the Wachowskis' answer that faith is 'in oneself' complete a syncretistic tapestry the essay goes on to examine as religious pluralism.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 81 "Unknown" — The chapter argues the third postulate must be a this-worldly immortality: since no single lifetime suffices to realize the Highest Good, Kant himself (in Universal Natural History) imagined the soul reborn over and over as it climbs the ladder of human perfection, and Mahayana Buddhism's bodhisattva - who chooses to remain on the wheel of rebirth to enlighten all beings - matches the monkish boy 'Potential' and the Oracle's hints. The One accordingly appears in three incarnations: the earlier liberator who freed the first rebels, Neo's second life, and the third life glimpsed at the film's end.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 100 "In It for the Long Run" — Adds Reason Five — being moral always pays in the long run, where the long run includes life after death — arguing that a perfectly good and all-powerful God would not set up a moral order that penalizes virtue, so Peter Parker's virtue is guaranteed its reward beyond this life. It notes that Eastern reincarnation-plus-karma makes the same promise (the more virtuous this life, the better the next), and that since Peter, Uncle Ben and Aunt May would never water morality down, the morally serious are pushed toward these metaphysical guarantees.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 101 "Superheroes, Duty, and the Biggest of Big Pictures" — Argues that non-theistic karma undermines itself: the impersonal moral laws connecting each soul's deeds to its circumstances in the next life would be enormously complex and would serve the moral end of justice, and order that intricate serving a moral end demands an intelligent cause, so reincarnation becomes evidence for God. It closes the chapter by comparing the universe's moral order to a superhero's origin story — it would have to begin with something like a God.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 36 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Observes that only Talking Animals enter Aslan's country when Narnia ends in The Last Battle, then critically examines Lewis's case against wider animal salvation: derivative immortality through human love (Sarah Smith's train of beasts in The Great Divorce), compensation of animal pain in an afterlife, Lewis's follow-Descartes claim that most animals are sentient but not conscious enough to feel pain or have a surviving 'self'. The chapter argues each point fails: the physiological evidence shows animals suffer, resurrection or God-given souls remain possible (Strawberry's transformation into a winged Talking horse), and a compensatory hereafter is still the most promising answer to why a loving God permits the fawn's miserable death. Aquinas's rational-creature hierarchy frames the Talking/Dumb divide, and the Hindu-Buddhist rebirth theodicy is considered and rejected as unbiblical.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 44 "“How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons" — James McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism: the fleet's sleepless FTL jumps in "33" and Roslin's dwindling survivor counts enact the four noble truths, Leoben's interrogation scenes teach that suffering comes from ignorant attachment, and Dogen's no-self and impermanence frame the show's interdependent characters. Cylon resurrection, D'Anna's serial deaths, and the prophecy that "all of this has happened before" model karma and samsara, while Nishida's kenotic God of Absolute Nothingness makes sense of Six and Leoben's God of love. Because Cylons feel pain, fear death away from a resurrection ship, and act volitionally, McRae concludes they are persons in the Buddhist sense, owed the compassion of the Eightfold Path.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 14 "Are We Going Too Far" — David Kyle Johnson distinguishes revenge (personal, emotional, unlimited) from retribution and argues that 'Tarantino's view'—mercy should be common practice yet revenge can be justified—is consistent: Jules buys Pumpkin and Honey Bunny's lives but never waives a right of vengeance, since they never wronged him. He tests the view against Bushido, showing Beatrix's revolt against her lord Bill violates the samurai code, and against karma, which makes revenge unnecessary. After finding that Hobbes, Locke, Nietzsche and Socrates all leave revenge's justification open, he defends it—citing Budd's 'that woman deserves her revenge'—so long as the punishment fits the crime and spares innocents, as when Beatrix refuses to make herself even by killing Vernita's daughter Nikki.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 26 "Sudden Enlightenment" — Luke Cuddy and Michael Bruce ask whether Beatrix Kiddo could reach enlightenment, reading Kill Bill's nonlinear plotting as a Buddhist interconnected web of causes: Pai Mei's Five Point Palm technique causes both the coffin escape and Bill's death, and Budd's degraded trailer life is karma catching up. Beatrix grasps the structure of suffering and its cause—she locates it in Bill and the squad and eliminates them—but mistakes that for ending suffering itself, and her declared lack of 'mercy, compassion, and forgiveness' blocks the compassion enlightenment requires, while Bill's 'natural born killer' story contradicts impermanence and no-self. The chapter closes on her bathroom-floor ecstasy as a candidate case of Zen sudden enlightenment, left to the reader to judge by how she would one day treat a vengeful Nikki.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 19 "Into the Future" — Hanley dismantles the four claimed human/Cylon differences: artificial reproduction is in principle possible for us; prosthetics already blur what we are made of; model copies differ like identical twins (Boomer is not Athena); and resurrection has human analogues — he proposes an SDTR (scanning, death, transmission, replication) model and uses van Inwagen's replica-switch account of bodily resurrection while rejecting soul-based reincarnation on Lockean grounds, since consciousness rather than soul is the criterion of identity. He defends reproductive cloning as reproduction, not replication (a clone is your child, not your copy), and reads Athena's memories of Tyrol as evidence she is a replicated Boomer. The upshot: being a Cylon is nothing to fear — 'I am a Cylon, and so are you.'
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 22 "What Monkey Should Have Known" — Mortensen opens with Monkey from Journey to the West beating six robbers to death despite Tripitaka's protest, and asks whether a practitioner of budo can be a Buddhist. He defends three principles, Take No Life, No First Strike and Stop Before Harm, qualifying them via the Upaya-kausalya Sutra's sea captain, Funakoshi's 'there is no first strike in karate', Ueshiba's purely defensive aikido, the initiator's bad karma, and the exception of multiple attackers; then he applies them to weapons, arguing that wooden weapons (the jo, Musashi's bokken, above all the humble walking stick, the 'last legal weapon') fit the precepts where the katana does not. Monkey, in short, should have carried a stick.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 36 "23. I Fight Crime in My Sleep" — Staged as a Fight Club parody in which a Buddhist psychiatrist, Dr. Quinzel, evaluates a costumed narrator sent to Arkham, the chapter argues neither hero is close to awakening: Batman's crime-fighting is craving that perpetuates dukkha, his secret identities a twice-constructed self that the Buddha's no-self teaching dissolves, and his violence fails the test that 'hostility is never appeased by hostility.' Superman fares no better - his super-intellect imposes illusory order on impermanence, his flight and X-ray vision are distractions beside the Buddha-eye and tapas, and as one of the titans of the six realms he is further from Buddhahood than a human - while the doctor defines justice as karma rather than retaliation and finds Batman one step from American Psycho's Bateman. Only conquering Mara, one's own inner deceiver, is 'the only superpower worth having,' and the closing reveal that the doctor has a plan of her own for 'Mr. Kent' caps the diagnosis.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 31 "17. Dialog with the Buddha" — A Platonic-style fictional dialogue in which a newly enlightened "Canadian Buddha" walks out of the northern Ontario bush to the Prolethean farm and debates Tomas, Henry, and Bonnie over whether clones are abominations. Using karma, rebirth, the gandhabba that carries consciousness-flux to a new embryo, the no-soul doctrine, and the eightfold path, the Buddha argues clones are ordinary beings of the karmic flux — like the split bacterium, nothing unnatural — but that cloning multiplies clinging: hosts crave immortality through copies, each clone inherits the host's whole accumulated karma, and Henry's dream of training an army of Helena-clones would only deepen the unsatisfactoriness the Buddha's mustard-seed lesson says clinging to the dead always brings. Only ending the cycle through enlightenment releases anyone; the clone, like the lost child, is not the one you lost.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 16 "6. The Accidental Hero" — Darian Shump judges Deadpool by Buddhist lights, applying karma as intentional action and skillful means—the permissibility of compassionate killing, after Rupert Gethin—to his Marvel NOW! career: protecting Agent Preston, saving a child and Nightcrawler Kim mid-battle, and the Niagara Bride assisted suicide whose fee he donates to a home for kids with cancer. A hypothetical Hydra spy with a bomb on a S.H.I.E.L.D. helicarrier shows how killing one murderer-to-be can be the compassionate act that saves everyone. He concludes Deadpool is an 'accidental hero'—a mercenary first whose good intentions make him a karmic hero—while Zenpool's failed pacifism in AXIS shows that renouncing violence betrays what makes Deadpool Deadpool.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 23 "11. 999 Fingers" — Voiced by a composite being shredded together from every AHS character, the chapter retells the Buddha's path - Siddhartha sheltered from suffering like a pampered prince, enlightenment as watching 'every episode of American Horror Story', Mara's temptations, and Angulimala with his garland of 999 fingers converted to monkhood - to read Briarcliff's cruelty, Sister Jude's devil, and Bloody Face's son Johnny as suffering born of clinging, in a contingent, moment-to-moment world of karma and rebirth, while Nietzsche's killed God, eternal recurrence, and ressentiment frame the question of who is to blame when there is no creator.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 17 "8. Ode to Joi" — Steve Bein first tests Joi against Mary Anne Warren's five functionalist personhood criteria — consciousness, reason, self-motivated activity, communication, self-awareness — and finds she passes, which makes Luv's stomping of the emanator a murder. The Buddha's no-self doctrine then denies that anyone, Joi included, is an enduring person: we are bundles of fleeting psychophysical processes, 'like tears in rain', which threatens to let Luv plead that the Luv who killed Joi no longer exists. Nagarjuna's two truths resolve the courtroom problem: ultimately there are no persons, but conventionally 'Luv killed Joi' is perfectly true, and the karma ripples through the whole network.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 34 "19. Hinduism Gets More than Five Percent Right" — Kaur and Gupta argue Hinduism got far more than five percent right, mapping the show's points onto karmic theory and the Bhagavad Gita's three kinds of action: right action, inaction, and wrong action. Eleanor's fruitless point-grubbing and selfless departure exemplify nishkama karma, desire-less action, while the 802 reboots and Janet's memory-wiped revivals mirror the birth-death-rebirth cycle on the way to self-realization. Ranking the cast on the Gita's ladder of unfoldment, desire-driven Eleanor and Jason below Tahani and knowledgeable Chidi, with Michael straying from his dharma and detached, duty-bound Janet nearest to Brahman, they show the series dramatizes the Gita's teaching that motivation, not the deed itself, determines an act's worth.
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 24 "The Danger of Thinking “Science Is Whatever We Want It to Be”; or, the" — Barkman reads the 30 Rock cast as prisoners who prefer delusion, using Plato's allegory of the cave and the Upanishadic scheme of samsara, karma, maya, and moksha, in which Atman is realized as one with Brahman, as twin diagnoses. Drew's 'bubble' of good looks, Liz's false memory of being a harmless nerd in 'Reunion' and her belief she can have it all, Jack's pride about his terrible sketch ideas, Kenneth's unexamined dogma ('I can't handle the truth!'), Jenna's age-hiding, and Tracy's white myths about diabetes and Colorado all illustrate ignorance of reality that costs happiness. The Hindu-Platonic lesson is that knowledge of reality, not Dr. Spaceman's 'science is whatever we want it to be', is the route to happiness, because ignorance is not bliss.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 34 "Happily, Ever After" — The chapter asks whether Nish's revenge in 'Black Museum' - poisoning Rolo and downloading his digital self into her father Clayton's eternal-electrocution exhibit - is morally justified. Nussbaum's Anger and Forgiveness condemns payback as sadism plus 'magical thinking' and prescribes transition-anger, then unconditional forgiveness, then best of all unconditional love (the prodigal son); Christian agape commands loving enemies and leaving wrath to God; and the Buddhist analysis of dukkha, karma and non-self shows Nish's hateful revenge generates worse karma than Rolo's greed and deepens the very suffering it means to end. The verdict: revenge, however emotionally satisfying, is never justified - even the tourists zapping Clayton and Nish zapping Rolo fall into the same trap.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 36 "23. I Fight Crime in My Sleep" — A Fight Club-style Arkham case study: a patient's hallucinated Superman companion is diagnosed by a Buddhist psychiatrist who explains the three marks of existence—impermanence, non-self, and dissatisfaction—arguing superheroes impose order and a fabricated second self on a world that resists both, so Superman's super-intellect and even flight are distractions (levitation should be ignored; the Buddha-eye beats x-ray vision) while Batman's violence and psychosis, compared to American Psycho's Patrick Bateman, make awakening impossible—both are victims of Mara. A robber literally named David Hume objects that the heroes' law and order is grounded on what ought to be rather than what is, and a Gandhi quote on preferring one's own bad government explains why Batman finally kryptonites his alien 'friend.' The verdict inverts the book's debate: conquering the deceiver within is the only superpower worth having.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 44 "“How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons" — James McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism: the fleet's annihilation and constant death illustrate the Four Noble Truths' duhkha, arising from ignorant attachment and violating interdependent arising (no-self and impermanence). Cylon death-and-resurrection parallels karma and rebirth ('all of this has happened before'), Leoben acts as a koan-wielding roshi unsettling Starbuck's assumptions, and Nishida's kenotic God as Absolute Nothingness matches the Cylons' 'we're all God.' Because Cylons feel pain, suffer cognitively, and earn karma, McRae concludes they are persons capable of satori who should seek compassionate reconciliation with humans.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 8 "Rāma of Gilead" — Matthew Butkus reads Roland Deschain of The Dark Tower as a parallel to Rama of the Ramayana and Arjuna of the Bhagavad Gita, mapping his cyclical existence onto the Hindu concepts of karma (his coupling with the demon spawning Mordred, letting Jake fall), dharma (the gunslinger's duty to protect the Beams as an avatar restoring cosmic order), samskara (character shaped by all past lives) and samsara (the death-rebirth cycle the Horn of Eld may or may not break). Like Krishna instructing the reluctant Arjuna, the text tells Roland he must 'stand and be true' regardless of misgivings; Butkus concludes the moral for readers is not violence but fulfilling one's own svadharma—to stand and be true in one's own station.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 15 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Geisz reads his daily morning coffee ritual through Buddhist metaphysics: the pre-caffeine grogginess and its transient relief illustrate saṃsāra and duḥkha, the First Noble Truth, driven by self-centered craving (the Second). The transience of the perfect-temperature cup shows impermanence (anitya), and the question of whether a 'self' pre- or post-coffee exists is answered by anatman — he offers three hypotheses (full self dormant, half coffee-cyborg, self created ex Coffea) then dissolves them into no-self plus dependent arising, where the cup and drinker are empty nodes in a web of physical, economic, and karmic conditions. Each intentional sip lays down karma that binds tomorrow's 'me' further into the cycle.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 20 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Deal and Waller use Lakoff and Johnson's conceptual-metaphor theory to explain how we grasp Santa's God-like moral omniscience through human metaphors. Santa 'sees from above' (North Pole, flight), judges with 'cool' reason yet remains jolly, and – echoing Plato's Phaedrus charioteer and Descartes' solitary reasoner – masters his appetites and decides free of bias. His gift-giving runs on a 'moral accounting' metaphor where good deeds are commodities exchanged for presents and 'moral authority is parental authority'; they read A Christmas Story's BB-gun lesson through this frame and finally liken Santa's impartial, dispassionate sorting of naughty and nice to the impersonal law of karma.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 13 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Kieran McManus's travel memoir 'Will I Find My Guru in India?' recounts his search from Kathmandu to Rishikesh and the Agama Yoga School, where teacher Kushru's lectures on karma, breath, and diet finally make asana click for him. His reported insight — that every thought and act moves him toward or away from his sacred potential, and that the yogi transcends suffering by treating each experience as neutral and as an opportunity, remaining present — applies a karmic and present-moment ethic to his own practice rather than expounding doctrine abstractly.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 44 "“How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons" — McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism, using Dogen and the Four Noble Truths. The fleet's relentless suffering (the "33" jumps, the Olympic Carrier), impermanence (Roslin's dwindling headcount), and no-self frame duhkha; Leoben functions as a roshi whose koan-like preaching makes Starbuck and Adama question their false ideals, and the Cylon death-and-resurrection cycle parallels karma and rebirth. Because Cylons feel and are cognitively aware of pain and can accrue karma, McRae concludes they are persons capable of satori, so human and Cylon liberation are intertwined.

### Yin and Yang

Yin and yang name a pair of complementary forces that, in Chinese thought, underlie all change and balance in the natural and social world. Yin is associated with qualities such as darkness, receptivity, and rest, and yang with light, activity, and assertion, but neither is good or evil; each contains a seed of the other and continually gives way to it. This idea offers a way of understanding reality as a dynamic interplay of opposites that must be kept in harmony rather than a battle in which one side must triumph.

- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 29 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Jennifer McMahon and Steve Csaki compare Tolkien with Zen Buddhism and Taoism on four themes while insisting on the real differences. Tolkien's talking trees (Old Man Willow, Treebeard's 'half awake' forest) invite comparison with Buddhist universal sentience and Dogen's walking mountains, but Tolkien anthropomorphizes where Buddhism grants non-human modes of sentience; the hobbits' ties to the Shire echo dependent origination, though Tolkien's stewardship and preference for the domesticated Shire over sinister wild nature remain Western. Frodo's succession of mentors (Bilbo, Gandalf, Aragorn, and the unlikely 'Master Samwise') parallels the Zen master-student relation, while Tolkien's war of light against darkness - nine Walkers against nine Riders - is decisively not the Taoist balance of yin and yang, for Taoists destroying either cosmic force would itself produce evil.
- **The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am**, ch. 14 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" — Argues Tony misappropriates Sun Tzu's Art of War: he applies tactical precepts like deception, formlessness and 'Balk the enemy's power' (citing the book in 'He Is Risen' after Melfi's jab in 'Big Girls Don't Cry'), but ignores the philosophical core. The chapter contrasts Sun Tzu's monistic one-world view of yin-yang interdependence, harmony and winning without fighting with the Greek two-world dualism of Plato and with the Christianity that lets Tony tell Melfi 'soldiers don't go to hell' in 'From Where to Eternity'. Tony's sausage panic attacks in 'Fortunate Son' show his failure to see how his crimes ripple through his family, and because he lacks the commander's exemplary character and harmony, Tony is 'just a soldier', not a ruler.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 11 "“Great Warrior Wars Not Make One Great”" — Robinson (a Zen monk) argues the Force is best understood as ch'i and the Jedi path as philosophical Taoism and Zen: the Light and Dark Sides are the yin-yang polarity whose 'balance' Anakin's prophecy restores, and Anakin's fall is the Buddhist three poisons - clinging attachment to his mother and Padme breeding fear, anger, and hate. Yoda's teaching is Zen practice: 'You must unlearn what you have learned' is wu-wei (effortless action), 'Do or do not' rejects the divided mind of trying, and the Dagobah cave parallels the sword master Tesshu's koan insight that the real enemy is one's own mind ('no-enemy'). The chapter also traces Jedi genealogy to Bodhidharma's Shaolin kung-fu, the Korean Hwa Rang and Japanese Sohei warrior monks, and Bushido's samurai code, noting 'Jedi' derives from 'jidai geki'.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 29 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Jones narrates a day riding a customized Sportster around O'ahu as a lived Daoism that heals the Platonic-Cartesian mind-body split: the ride enacts Zhuangzi's 'rambling without destination' and Cook Ding's effortless wu-wei, rider li (the low hand-greeting among riders) is Confucian ritual propriety, and the island's dry and wet ranges embody yin and yang through whose flow the rider blends. Heraclitus's 'expect the unexpected' and 'the sun is new every day' are vindicated when a container truck stops short and only the disciplined, ego-less low-side, dropping the beloved bike while riding the skid, saves the rider's life, sealing the day's lesson that there is never freedom without discipline. Sartre's hell of other people appears in the cagers' compartmentalized inattention, and the chapter closes with Zhuangzi: 'The way is made by walking it.'
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 29 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Kowalski explains yin-yang cosmology through the Yi Ching and Shu Ching - opposing forces in dynamic harmony, each containing the seed of its opposite, with excess of either bringing destruction - and applies it to the Brosnan-era films, reading Bond himself as the yang force of action. The films improved, he argues, by strengthening yin: Wai Lin as Bond's equal partner in the handcuffed motorcycle chase of Tomorrow Never Dies (each watching the road the other cannot see), Judi Dench's M as the corrective to Admiral Roebuck's hawkish yang ('the advantage is that I don't always have to think with them'), and Elektra King as a genuine yin villainess rather than a damsel. He ends with a Humean caveat that deriving moral conclusions from the natural order is logically suspect, yet endorses the cosmology's practical advice - balance and harmony between opposing forces - as the reason the new millennium Bond films are better.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 46 "Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat" — In a fictional interview with the Taoist sage "Bat-Tzu," Mark White explains Taoism through Batman's circle: Bruce's yang-dominated life of vengeance and paranoia needs the yin that Dick and Tim supply, shown by his forgiveness of Zatanna and tenderness toward Helena's baby, while Jason Todd illustrates the fate of the unbalanced who cannot accept death. Alfred emerges as the Taoist sage practicing wei-wu-wei, effortless service like Chuang Tzu's butcher, balancing right and wrong in Bruce, and the Batman-Joker duality shows yin and yang defining each other. Lao Tzu's sayings on balance, complementary opposites, and water-like yielding organize the whole reading.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 10 "I Still Miss Someone The Self and Its Travels Along the Way" — Geisz explains the Confucian social dao of ritual (li), humaneness (ren), filial piety and the junzi, the Daodejing's metaphysical Dao with its unity of opposites, and Zhuangzi's tales of free wandering, then maps all three onto Cash's songs. Zhuangzi's "Free and Easy Wandering" answers Cash's road songs ("I've Been Everywhere," "The Wanderer"), Cook Ding's effortless carving answers John Henry's hammering in "The Legend of John Henry's Hammer," and the scrambled countdown of "Twenty-Five Minutes to Go" echoes Zhuangzi's logic-bending humor. The payoff is Cash's own country Yin-Yang of interdependent opposites, freedom chained to imprisonment ("Folsom Prison Blues"), sin twinned with redemption ("I Hung My Head"), fidelity with betrayal ("Jackson," "Cocaine Blues"), and a self that, unlike Zhuangzi's self-forgetting sage, must travel a temporal path carrying its guilt, yet stays on what Geisz calls a very wide superhighway of a Dao.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 24 "Alchemic Heroism" — Reads Edward and Alphonse Elric as a single composite 'alchemic hero' who fuses Japanese heroic archetypes: the dual-hero rooted in the Izanami-Izanagi creation myth and yin-yang complementarity (brash yang Ed, calm yin Al whose armored body actually fights better), the student hero forged by Izumi Curtis's brutal island training, and the wandering redemption seeker atoning for the forbidden attempt to resurrect their mother. It argues that the sacrifice built into this fusion — Al's lost senses, puberty, and body — mirrors Japan's own cultural alchemy of absorbing Buddhism, Confucianism, and yin-yang thought while retaining a coherent national identity.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 23 "Living Beauty" — Saltzman explains why a flowing Shaolin Kenpo form is beautiful by way of Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy: the Apollonian geometry of square, triangle and circle fuses with Dionysian power and intention, just as yang hardness needs yin softness. She grounds the body's fitness for this in the Golden Ratio known to Pythagoras, answers 'beauty is in the eye of the beholder' with Clive Bell's 'significant form' as an objective structure that trained judges can recognize, and locates 'living beauty' in the practitioner's own breakthrough, the moment when, as Nietzsche and Yeats agree, the dancer and the dance dissolve into pure mindless movement.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 36 "Psych and Philosophy" — John Thompson argues Psych embodies the Daoist Way of reversal from the Daodejing and Zhuangzi: every episode begins with a death that triggers Shawn and Gus's irreverent, backwards-tracing investigation, their untrained spontaneous 'gifts' exemplify wu wei like Cook Ding carving an ox, and their bickering partnership is yin-yang interplay (as when Gus leads the joking in 'An Evening with Mr. Yang'). Zhuangzi singing at his wife's funeral parallels the Shabby the Sea Lion and 'Dust in the Wind' funeral parodies, the show's blurred TV-versus-fandom reality echoes the butterfly dream, Lassiter succeeds when he relaxes into wu wei ('Feet Don't Kill Me Now'), and the closing bloopers enact Dao's endless reversal - though the chapter ends by conceding Dao defies the very label 'Daoist show.'
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 27 "15. Farts, Butterflies, and Inner Truth" — Franklin Perkins reads Frank's fear that his jewelry business might start World War III — 'you can't fart without changing the balance in the universe' — as the butterfly-effect problem of acting inside a complexity we cannot grasp, from the Roosevelt assassination down to Tagomi's Colt .44. Against the Germans' fatal flight into abstraction (Volk, Blut, Ehre), the chapter presents the I Ching, read through Chinese correlative cosmology of the Tao and yin-yang, as a manual for mole-like, concrete, adaptive interpretation in which each casting (hexagram 11's 'wall falls back into the moat,' the purple knee bands) means only through creative engagement, ending with hexagram 61: our world arose as contingently as a throw of the yarrow stalks.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 12 "The Wisdom of Combination" — Isrow maps each bending art to its real martial art and source philosophy: Katara's Taiji waterbending embodies Daoist wu-wei when she forgoes revenge on Yon Rha ('The Southern Raiders'); Toph's Hong Jia earthbending expresses the Buddhist eightfold path's Right Speech through her insistence on truth; Zuko's Northern Shaolin firebending enacts the Four Noble Truths, his desire-driven suffering ending only when he abandons chasing the Avatar; and Aang's Daoist Baguazhang airbending makes freedom openness to change, shown in his receptivity to Iroh's advice. The Avatar's true power is combining these character strengths, not merely wielding four elements.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 18 "Bending That Saves Life" — Flowers argues bloodbending is morally neutral: like Huu's plantbending ('The Swamp') and taijiquan's qinna joint locks, it is an advanced technique whose harm depends on the practitioner's intention, as Katara's gentle suppression of Hama ('The Puppetmaster') shows against her vengeful contortion of the Southern Raider. Waterbending's Taiji foundation, with the yin-yang harmony of Tui and La's circling koi and the Aikido/Aikijutsu contrast in applying kotegaeshi, grounds his conclusion from Yagyu Munenori's Heiho Kadensho: Hama practiced the sword that takes life, while Katara's compassionate bloodbending is 'bending that saves life'.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 39 "Overcoming Dilemmas" — Frames Aang's dilemma — Avataric duty to stop Ozai by killing versus Air Nomad sanctity of life — as a genuine dilemma only if both duties are non-negotiable, using W.D. Ross and Lisa Tessman's negotiable/non-negotiable duty framework. Air Nomad philosophy is reconstructed as Sublime Ahimsic Practice: the Four Sublime States (loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity) plus ahimsa, grounded in the Buddha's dependent origination that Huu's banyan-grove swamp vision also expresses, which makes everyone 'worth giving a chance'. Because this practice keeps Aang open to the world, he meets the Lion Turtle and learns energybending, so the dilemma's conditions are reshaped rather than solved — the same lesson Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr., and Black Lives Matter teach about nonviolent liberation.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 12 "The Wisdom of Combination" — A martial artist maps each bending style onto the real art it animates and its parent philosophy: Katara's Taiji waterbending embodies wu-wei, shown when she spares Yon Rha in 'The Southern Raiders' as strength rather than weakness; Toph's Hong Jia earthbending grounds her insistence on truth, an example of the Buddhist eightfold path's Right Speech; Zuko's driven Northern Shaolin temperament walks through the first three Noble Truths, from suffering caused by desire for his honor to its cessation when he joins Team Avatar; and Aang's Baguazhang airbending expresses freedom as openness to change and to Iroh's counsel. The Avatar's power is therefore not four bendings but the combination of the four character strengths.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 18 "Bending That Saves Life" — Flowers argues bloodbending is morally neutral by locating it within waterbending's Taiji: its locking motions are qinna, the push-pull art whose harms scale with the practitioner, just as Aikido's kotegaeshi can be gradual or vicious depending on the wielder. Katara's painless suppression of Hama in 'The Puppetmaster' versus her violent contortion of the ship captain in 'The Southern Raiders' shows the technique itself carries no fixed evil, and plantbending's kinship with bloodbending reinforces the point. Yagyū Munenori's distinction between the sword that takes life and the sword that gives life supplies the verdict: Hama's bloodbending takes life, Katara's saves it, so it is people, not the art, that make bloodbending evil.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 28 "What Can We Learn" — Argues that ATLA teaches the rejection of false alternatives by first setting up one-sided stereotypes of earth and then dissolving them: Bumi is both crazy and rational, Toph both tough and sensitive (enjoying the Fancy Lady Day Spa), and earthbending originates in love and secrecy, not rock-throwing, in the tale of Oma and Shu. The chapter explicitly imports the Buddha's first sermon's middle way between sensual indulgence and self-mortification, applying it to Aang's refusal of both killing Ozai and being killed: energybending dissolves the 'kill or be killed' framework rather than picking a side, just as Bumi's 'neutral jing' refuses both attack and retreat. Oma ending the war by building Omashu with both villages, and the compromise over Yu Dao in The Promise, are read as dissolutions of us-vs-them framing, while the duality of Sozin and Roku ('anyone's capable of great good and great evil') shows two-sidedness as the condition of Zuko's redemption.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 39 "Overcoming Dilemmas" — Frames Aang's conflict between his Avataric duty to restore balance even by killing Ozai and his Air Nomad duty of ahimsa as a genuine dilemma only if both obligations are non-negotiable (Tessman's negotiable and non-negotiable duties), then argues the show resolves it because Sublime Ahimsic Practice, the Four Sublime States joined to non-harm, reshapes the very conditions the dilemma rests on. Aang's cultivation of loving-kindness and his grasp of dependent origination (Huu's banyan-grove insight that everything is interconnected) keep him open to the world, which is what leads him to the Lion Turtle; energybending then lets him stop Ozai without killing, dissolving the kill-or-be-killed framework rather than choosing a horn. The Avataric role itself is read as Daoist yin-yang balance-keeping, and the chapter links Aang's triumph to the lessons of Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr., and nonviolent movements: becoming different people changes which options the world affords.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 34 "NOTES" — The book's final chapter is a mock interview in which 'Bat-Tzu' applies Taoism to Bruce Wayne's life: his yang (hard, retributive crime-fighting) has dominated his yin (his tenderness toward Dick, Tim, and Helena), and Robin has always been the yin balancing the Dark Knight. Quoting Lao-Tzu's Tao Te Ching and Chuang-Tzu on duality, acceptance of death (Jason Todd's resurrection), and effortlessness, the piece casts Alfred as the Taoist sage whose help exemplifies wu-wei, like Chuang-Tzu's butcher who cuts without dulling his blade. It even reads Batman's most intimidating feature, his absent shadow, as proof that nothingness can matter more than substance.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 10 "a3.xhtml" — Brannigan reads Bilbo's tug-of-war between Baggins security and Took adventure through Taoism: the two desires are not contradictory but the interplay of yin and yang, and true dwelling is found in the journey itself, as the 'Roads go ever on' song says. Greed is the great weight - Thorin enslaved by the treasure he 'never forgot', Smaug hoarding for hoarding's sake, even the orc-loving of machines - and the cure is the mirror-mind of Empty Mind that reflects without grasping, illustrated by the Taoist masters tale of 'Gold-Is-Heavy' and 'Empty-Mind'. Beorn, who lives on honey indifferent to gold, and Bilbo, who in the spirit of wu-wei sheds his desire for the Arkenstone and finally lets go of the Ring, embody life in harmony with the Tao.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 28 "Notes" — Bein reads the LEGO brick as the Daodejing's 'uncarved block': a single brick is an invitation rather than a toy, and precisely because it is empty of meaning (and mostly empty of plastic — the stud-and-tube marriage of yin and yang) it can become anything, whereas printed, specialized pieces 'are diminished by being added to'. Against the Greek obsession with definition — Socrates refusing sophistry while insisting one cannot rule justly without defining justice, Plato's definition dialogues, Aristotle's inheritance of the precision ideal, and William James's 'think clearly' — Daoist imprecision is defended as a philosophical stance: dao is a way, an activity, not a thing. Wei wu wei ('doing without doing') explains Emmet's winning plan of building the utterly ordinary Octan spaceship, why Lord Business's penny-throw is genius without sagacity (coercive, not water-like), and why governing should be like cooking a small fish — minimal, attentive intervention.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 29 "NOTE" — Shai Biderman and William Devlin argue the character John Locke begins as an empiricist in the mold of his philosophical namesake - his boar hunting, tracking, and trebuchet-building against the hatch all follow the scientific method befitting a tabula rasa mind furnished by experience - but the miracle of his healed legs poses a 'why' that empirical explanation of 'how' cannot answer. He therefore converts to the Taoism of the Tao Te Ching: the moth-cocoon lesson to Charlie, 'I stopped looking' for Sun's ring, reading dreams and signs from the island, and finally his self-sacrifice to stop the time flashes all enact following the Way. The chapter reads the black-and-white backgammon stones, Locke's one-black-one-white eyes in Claire's dream, and Jacob versus the Man in Black as yin-yang complementarity, with empiricism and Taoism finally interdependent like the dots in each half.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 30 "Keep the Needle on the Record" — Donavan Muir argues Lost's narrative world, unlike Jane Eyre's, requires its own metaphysics, and that this metaphysics is an order of balanced binary oppositions: Jacob and the Man in Black as twins diverged at birth, the cave scale's light and dark stones that Locke knocks out of balance in 'The Substitute,' science/faith, with characters like Jack converting from one pole into its opposite. The proper model is the yin-yang in motion - the Tao as a balanced ontological flow in which interdependent opposites wax and wane - so that treating the poles as independent is the delusion that threatens the island's order. The finale, where both Jacob and the Man in Black cease to exist and the castaways are freed, enacts the Mahayana Buddhist Middle Way: enlightenment as letting go of rigid oppositions that interdependence double-negates.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 9 "“Now This Is Podracing!”" — Johnson reads The Phantom Menace as having distinctly Daoist flavors: Shmi's 'you cannot stop the change any more than you can stop the suns from setting,' the Naboo-Gungan 'symbiont circle,' and midi-chlorian symbiosis all express the Daoist unity of opposites and the constant flow of change. He argues Qui-Gon Jinn acts as a Daoist sage practicing wu wei — 'concentrate on the moment,' 'another solution will present itself' — while nearly everyone else in the film makes wrong predictions and grasps at outcomes. Even Anakin's accidental 'Oops!' victory over the Droid Control Ship is presented as success without trying, the practical meaning of 'Do or do not. There is no try.'
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 23 "The Dao of Hoops" — Dirk Dunbar, a former professional player, argues that Daoist concepts illuminate basketball excellence and that the sport can be a path to the Dao. Balancing yin and yang means blending competition with surrender and strategy with spontaneity; Zhuangzi's archer shows how craving victory drains power. Wuwei explains the 'zone' of effortless play Dunbar experienced while scoring sixty-five points in a high school game and seventy-four in Iceland, while qi grounds free-throw breathing and visualization and ziran the discipline of releasing a shot without willing it in. Drawing on Daode jing verses and Phil Jackson's Sacred Hoops, he claims basketball teaches a life of disciplined surrender beyond the ego.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — McRae reads Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon as a dramatization of the tension between Confucian humanism and Daoist naturalism over how to cultivate an authentic 'focus-field' self. Li Mu Bai and Yu Shu Lien are exemplary persons (junzi) bound by the wuxia code and li, unable to voice their love, while Jen rebels into criminal freedom under Jade Fox; Li's use of the green bamboo forest against Jen embodies wu-wei and rou (yielding suppleness). It argues that authentic self-cultivation, and Jen's final leap, require balancing Daoist natural freedom against Confucian roles, since freedom without relationships exacts a fatal price.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 12 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Jameson and Brace read Sense and Sensibility and Brokeback Mountain through Burke's and Gilpin's aesthetics of the sublime, the beautiful and the picturesque, mapped onto the Chinese yin/yang and qi of landscape. In Sense and Sensibility, manicured French/Brownian gardens (beautiful, sanctioned) versus wild picturesque nature (sublime, passionate) mirror Elinor's controlled sense and Marianne's storm-caught sensibility, with Willoughby's rescue and Brandon's steadiness keyed to landscape. In Brokeback Mountain the masculine sublime wilderness (yang) versus feminine confining civilization (yin) is built through tightly framed interiors, sweeping exteriors and an 'aesthetics of isolation' that exposes American freedom as a costly illusion for Ennis and Jack.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 12 "Cherchez la Femme Fatale The Mother of Film Noir" — Read Mercer Schuchardt argues that The Jazz Singer (1927) should be considered the first film noir because it is the first mass-medium announcement of Nietzsche's death of God, staged as the death of Papa Rabinowitz and the old prescriptive Judaism. He reads the film through a three-stage deicide (God as God, then one god among many, then a stage prop for Jakie's voice) and through a Jungian/Neumann anima-animus opposition of the word-based patriarchal religion versus the image-based maternal love that wins out, mirroring film displacing scripture. He ties this to Porfirio's existential pessimism that undercuts happy endings, casting Jakie's blackface Broadway triumph as a bittersweet, angst-ridden creation of meaning after the loss of transcendent value, and traces later 'existential detective' descendants like I Heart Huckabees and Fight Club.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 46 "Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat" — In a mock interview with 'Bat-Tzu' (a disguised Alfred), Mark White explains Taoism through Batman. Bruce is dangerously dominated by yang after his parents' deaths and needs the yin balance that Robin (Dick as the lighthearted 'Batman with a feminine side') and his spiritual quest restore; Batman's fear-inducing shadow illustrates Lao-Tzu's usefulness of nothingness. Alfred is the Taoist sage embodying wei-wu-wei - 'action without action' - quietly serving like Chuang-Tzu's effortless butcher and like water that wears down stone, harmonizing Bruce's warring opposites toward the Way.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 30 "Keep the Needle on the Record" — Donavan S. Muir argues that Lost deliberately withholds its metanarrative so viewers must construct its metaphysics, which he identifies as an order of balanced binary oppositions. Drawing on the spinning Taoist yin-yang, he reads the interdependent, mutually converting poles—Jack from man of science to man of faith, Sawyer from con man to protector—and the light/dark scales in Widmore's painting and the cave (Locke throwing out the white rock) as figures for a Tao whose balance sustains existence. Invoking Derrida's traces and Mahayana Buddhism's Middle Way and emptiness, he reads Jacob and the Man in Black as twins whose oppositions must be annihilated, so that only when both cease to exist in 'The End' are the castaways set free.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 29 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Jennifer McMahon and Steve Csaki test Buddhist and Taoist parallels in the novel and find many only apparent. Tolkien's talking trees and ents anthropomorphize nature and grant it human-like consciousness, whereas Buddhism attributes sentience to all beings without projecting human consciousness, and Tolkien privileges domesticated over wild nature and stewardship over membership in nature. His master-student chain (Bilbo, Gandalf, Aragorn, 'Master Samwise') genuinely echoes the Zen necessity of the right master, as in Dogen's mushroom-cook mentor; but his good-versus-evil war, with light privileged over a personified dark power to be defeated, contradicts Taoism's yin-yang balance in which evil is imbalance, not a force to destroy.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 46 "Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat" — White stages a mock interview with "Bat-Tzu" (revealed to be Alfred) to read Batman through Taoism. Lao-Tzu and Chuang-Tzu supply the ideal of balancing yin and yang: Bruce lets his hard, vengeful yang dominate and needs Robin's yin, while Dick keeps balance and Tim risks losing his. Bruce's intimidating shadow illustrates the usefulness of nothingness, and Chuang-Tzu's teaching on accepting death frames Jason Todd's fate. Alfred embodies the Taoist sage — wei-wu-wei, water-like flexibility, and effortless, unspoken guidance.

### Binary Oppositions

Binary oppositions are the paired, contrasting terms—such as speech and writing, presence and absence, nature and culture, or reason and emotion—through which Western thought has often organized meaning. Jacques Derrida observed that such pairs are rarely equal: one term is typically privileged as primary or natural while the other is treated as derivative or deficient. Deconstruction targets this hierarchy, showing that the favored term secretly depends on the one it subordinates, so the opposition cannot hold as cleanly as it claims. Exposing this instability was central to Derrida's critique of how philosophy establishes and enforces value.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 18 "Possibilities of Postmodern Education Beyond Control" — Toby Daspit reads Season Four as a drama of postmodern education: the Initiative's will to master and dissect — Walsh's Frankenstein-project Adam, who murders a boy to see how he works, fulfilling Wordsworth's 'we murder to dissect' — embodies the Cartesian split and the Hegelian drive to negate the other, while Buffy's world deconstructs fixed identity (Darla reversing the horror-movie opening, the Faith/Buffy body swap in 'Who Are You?', Jonathan's 'Superstar') and thwarts prophecy's metanarrative in 'Prophecy Girl.' Against modernist schooling's 'controlled circumstances' and Freire's banking model (Professor Riegert ejecting Buffy from class, Walsh's transmission lectures), the show models knowledge as collective work — the Scoobies' research sessions in Giles's library, Giles's fluid mentorship versus Kendra's by-the-book training, and the relational magic of 'Primeval' — offering education beyond control in an emergent, postmodern world.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 24 "A Political Philosophy of Vampires" — Phillip Cole takes Rousseau's remark that the eighteenth-century vampire epidemics had complete legal proof - the Arnold Paole exhumations - and argues Rousseau's real point was political: authorities manufacture imaginary monsters, as in the witch craze, to exploit fear and hold power over their own populations. Freud's account of the uncanny explains why the horror is not death itself but the returning dead (the watching eyes of Scratchy in Itchy and Scratchy, versus the serene corpses of Six Feet Under, whose absurdity the show meets with wry amusement), and Julia Kristeva's abjection explains the corpse as the ultimate boundary-breaker. The vampire then resurfaces as the demonized outsider - Stoker's Dracula coded as the unassimilated Jewish immigrant, today's terrorist - exposing political borders as arbitrary fabrications. Buffy completes the collapse of the us/them binary: Angel and Spike join the slayer, and the most shocking killings (Faith's accidental human kill, Warren's stray bullet hitting Tara) are all too human, so the real subject of border policing is the community's own members.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 22 "The Verdict" — Turner runs an ethical audit of iPod use through Levinas's face-to-face: sharing one iPod with his wife forces 'musical justice' negotiations (veto power over a Motörhead cut, gnashing through Bette Midler), his toddler son's listening requires vigilance, and illegal downloading fails Levinas's test that morality begins by ceding 'my place in the sun' to the Other — hence Radiohead's pay-what-you-want release as the Levinasian move, and iPod cafés where strangers DJ for each other while language preserves alterity. Heidegger supplies the counterweight: the shuffle's 'openness to mystery' versus calculative mastery that reduces The Who's Tommy to the 'Pinball Wizard' riff and silences all non-digital media, just as Kant's conditions of possible experience (space, time) would silence things outside them. Derrida's point that categories contain traces of what they exclude illuminates unclassifiable marginal works — bluegrass Pink Floyd, San Francisco Symphony plays Metallica — and the verdict closes with Hölderlin's 'where danger is, grows the saving power also', exiting Plato's cave by thinking the iPod's ethics at all.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 13 "The Postmodern Condition" — Rafe McGregor claims The Hound of the Baskervilles is not a detective story at all: the hound that never bites anyone and Holmes's failure to foresee fog on Dartmoor are, via Derrida's Of Grammatology, the aporia and re-mark where the mystery-horror hierarchy of the text deconstructs. He then applies Noel Carroll's philosophy of horror, the phosphorus-painted hound as a category-crossing monster producing fear plus disgust and Grimpen Mire as horror geography, to reclassify the novel as gothic horror alongside Frankenstein, Jekyll and Hyde and Dracula. The final section ties the book's enduring mass appeal to the postmodern condition, tracing the collapse of certainty from Nietzsche's prophecies about the end of Christian values to Derrida's claim that truth is never finally available, leaving anxiety as the novel's real engine.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 46 "Flowers" — Reads the Flowers album's blooms as dark—'Ruby Tuesday' can't be chained to a life where nothing's gained, and the heliotrope becomes Derrida's figure for philosophy forever turning toward its conceptual sun of truth, knowledge, or the good. That heliotropic bias, the metaphysics of presence, is illustrated by Augustine's treatment of evil as mere privation of good, which Nietzsche's genealogy of slave morality overturns by deriving good and evil from the same source, 'beyond good and evil.'
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 48 "Out of the Cave" — Traces the light-versus-darkness metaphor tradition from Plato's cave and Socrates' unexamined life through medieval 'illumination' and the Enlightenment to St. Paul's glass darkly, then lets Nietzsche ('shadow is as needful as light') and Derrida's deconstruction of presence/absence oppositions overturn it. The Stones do the same work in song: 'Just as every cop is a criminal, and all the sinners saints' in 'Sympathy for the Devil,' with 'Here Comes the Sun' overturned by 'Paint It Black' and 'Let It Be' by 'Let It Bleed.'
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 33 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — William McGinney argues Jerry Goldsmith's modernist score, with its twelve-tone themes, ostinati, cuica, slide whistle, and ram's horn, carries no inherent meaning but acquires it through learned associations: its dissonance recalls Cold War modernist concert music promoted as the high art of Western freedom, while its Stravinsky-like rhythms and 'primitive' timbres mark the apes as other and feed the film's deconstruction of the human-ape, advanced-primitive, civilized-barbaric oppositions. Because Taylor is given no heroic music, the score undercuts identification with him as an anti-hero, and its modernist associations implicate the technocratic, militarized West he represents in Earth's self-destruction. The chapter's machinery is the semiotic view of Kant, Adorno, Cage, Peirce, and Saussure: music modifies a film's images the way adjectives modify nouns.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 30 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Caroline Mosser treats the creature's tragedy as humanist prejudice rather than necessity: the blind De Lacey accepts the eloquent creature sight unseen, so he passes Alan Turing's test, and only the sighted family's terror at his body rejects him - bias against the artificial, not reason. She reads the creature's development through fire, language, and revolution as Rousseau's progression from natural innocence to corruption by society, and Donna Haraway's cyborg as the figure he prefigures: an unfaithful illegitimate offspring who rebels against his father and undermines patriarchal Western self/other dualisms. The chapter concludes that society cannot accept enhanced or posthuman beings until it finds a middle ground beyond its binary grids of good/bad and Self/Other, since otherwise any new life we create will be Othered, hated, and oppressed like Frankenstein's.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 32 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Michael Mendelson rereads James Whale's 1931 Frankenstein as a metaphysics of appearance versus reality: the seemingly monstrous creature killed Fritz only after Fritz tormented him with fire and the whip, killed Dr. Waldman while Waldman was trying to dissect him alive, and drowned Maria in innocent play, expecting her to float like the flowers they had been throwing. The 'criminal brain' was Fritz's accident and explains less than we assume, since the creature spares Henry's fiancée when she screams and faints. The real point is alterity: otherness is a relation, not a property, and individual and social identity are built by excluding an outside where monsters reside - so the horror was inside the well-ordered village all along, the monster is us, and we are its creators.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 36 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Jessie Dern uses Derrida's Rogues and The Animal that Therefore I Am to show that naming is power: Victor cries 'Devil!' before the creature has done anything, and labels like 'monster,' 'rogue,' and 'animal' are performative verdicts that reveal the labeler, who secures his own goodness by negating the Other, more than the labeled. The novel multiplies the pattern, from Justine's confessor making her 'think that I was the monster that he said I was' to Elizabeth's 'men appear to me as monsters thirsting for each other's blood,' while Victor, guarding his self-image, becomes the monster himself. Against the Nietzsche epigraph about fighting monsters, the chapter closes with Derrida's playful self-application ('the animal that therefore I am') as the move the creature never gets to make: contesting the label and claiming a name and a self.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 19 "Walker Bite. Differentiating the Dead" — Di Bernardo argues that the swarm of names for the undead - walkers, roamers, lurkers, biters, empties, geeks - shows the world does not carve itself into pre-existing essences: communities construct their own classifications, as when Alice mocks Rick's group's roamers/lurkers taxonomy ('They all bite. Biters makes a ton more sense') and titles like 'Governor,' 'The Kingdom,' and 'Jesus' are disavowed by their bearers. Naming is a conferral of power that reveals the namers, since without absolute authority every name is a self-authorized exercise of power. Finally the living dead destabilize the strict living/dead opposition, and Rick's dogmatic 'us against them' slips into his own admission 'We are the Walking Dead!', with painful ethical consequences for how we police inclusion and exclusion in our world.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 11 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Donovan and Richardson read the Maltusian split, with the male Guardians banning emotion through the Book of Oa on Oa and the female Zamarons leaving to found the violet light of love on Zamaron, as the Western association of men with reason and women with emotion. They deploy Gilligan's different-voice reply to Kohlberg, the Pythagorean table of opposites via Genevieve Lloyd, Hegel's exclusion of women from the public sphere, and Jaggar's liberal-feminist critique of 'ahistorical' reason, whose comic-book analogue is the third law banning relationships between Lanterns. The chapter ends by arguing the standoff is a false dichotomy the comics themselves begin to dissolve: Kyle's 'Lanterns with heart' speech to the Guardians, the repeal of the third law, and the Indigo Tribe's plan to recombine the seven corps into the white light of creation.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 30 "Keep the Needle on the Record" — Donavan Muir argues Lost's narrative world, unlike Jane Eyre's, requires its own metaphysics, and that this metaphysics is an order of balanced binary oppositions: Jacob and the Man in Black as twins diverged at birth, the cave scale's light and dark stones that Locke knocks out of balance in 'The Substitute,' science/faith, with characters like Jack converting from one pole into its opposite. The proper model is the yin-yang in motion - the Tao as a balanced ontological flow in which interdependent opposites wax and wane - so that treating the poles as independent is the delusion that threatens the island's order. The finale, where both Jacob and the Man in Black cease to exist and the castaways are freed, enacts the Mahayana Buddhist Middle Way: enlightenment as letting go of rigid oppositions that interdependence double-negates.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 32 "Notes" — Pits Donna Haraway's Cyborg Manifesto against Star Trek's horror of the Borg, reading Locutus/Picard, Hugh, and Seven of Nine as tests of the Federation values of autonomy, individuality, and authenticity against the rival Borg values of heteronomy, collectivity, and simulation. Picard's "My culture is based on freedom and self-determination" exchange with the Borg, Hugh's discovery of his name and first-person "I", and Seven's tug-of-war with the Borg Queen in "Dark Frontier" dramatize what assimilation threatens. The chapter then defends a Haraway-inspired feminist reboot: women and minorities were long denied autonomy, individuality, and authenticity by prejudice and stereotype (Seven still must look "warp-core hot" in her catsuit), the human/machine and man/woman binaries were always false, and since we already live as cyborgs of apps, implants, and networks, resistance was negligible - the real Borg problem is their violent means, not their values.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 11 "Mea culpa" — Correcting her own initial dismissal of the show as Nancy Drew redux, the author argues Neptune is structured by a white/Hispanic racial binary laid over the millionaire/work-for-millionaires class binary, enforced through Logan's 'spic and span' jab at Weevil, Mr. Daniels's 'pumping his gas' insult, and the 'coconut' label for Latinos who cross over. Borrowing Saussure's binary oppositions and de Beauvoir's account of how a dominant group constructs a stigmatized Other, she shows the 09-ers defining themselves against everyone else, with teacher Daniels quietly siding with wealth against both boys. Bourdieu's cultural capital then explains why Wallace (basketball, scholarship, colorblind friendships) can cross boundaries that leave Weevil working as a janitor, and she concludes the show keeps race admirably visible in a supposedly postracial era.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Nelson argues that critics forget Soderbergh directed Erin Brockovich because they file his career under the art/commerce binary, and he uses Nietzsche's attack on the 'faith in antithetical values' and Derrida's deconstruction to expose such binaries (art/entertainment, independent/mainstream, activity/passivity) as gendered, hierarchical, and unstable. He then shows the film's real signature is a 'self-centered narration' totally focalized through Julia Roberts's Erin, so that a tension between the movie's altruistic content and its Erin-fixated form never resolves. The chapter treats the binary as a rhetorically useful but collapsing tool rather than a real opposition.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 21 "The Northwestern McCabe and Mrs. Miller" — Deborah Knight and George McKnight read Altman's McCabe and Mrs. Miller as an 'end-of-genre' western in the ironic mode, using Frye's Aristotle-derived mythos to map the classic western's binary oppositions (hero/villain, community/wilderness, virgin/whore) and then show the film collapsing them. Against Nussbaum's and Booth's ethical criticism, which extols works that make us 'finely aware and richly responsible,' they argue irony is itself a moral stance of detached scrutiny: McCabe is no hero but a vulgar, unimaginative businessman crushed by the Harrison Shaughnessy company and shot in the back in the snow while the town obliviously saves its burning church, dramatizing the implosion of the western's moral vision.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 30 "Keep the Needle on the Record" — Donavan S. Muir argues that Lost deliberately withholds its metanarrative so viewers must construct its metaphysics, which he identifies as an order of balanced binary oppositions. Drawing on the spinning Taoist yin-yang, he reads the interdependent, mutually converting poles—Jack from man of science to man of faith, Sawyer from con man to protector—and the light/dark scales in Widmore's painting and the cave (Locke throwing out the white rock) as figures for a Tao whose balance sustains existence. Invoking Derrida's traces and Mahayana Buddhism's Middle Way and emptiness, he reads Jacob and the Man in Black as twins whose oppositions must be annihilated, so that only when both cease to exist in 'The End' are the castaways set free.

### The Tao (the Way)

The Tao, or the Way, is the central notion of Daoism: the nameless, formless source and ordering principle from which all things arise and to which they return. In the Daodejing, associated with Laozi, the Tao is said to be beyond full description or definition—"the Tao that can be spoken is not the eternal Tao"—yet it can be sensed and followed by those who cultivate stillness and simplicity. Living well means aligning oneself with this natural course rather than resisting it through force, ambition, or excessive contrivance.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 14 "Was it a Show about Nothing" — Eric Bronson takes George's NBC pitch for 'a show about nothing' as a live philosophical problem: Parmenides argued we cannot meaningfully speak of what-is-not (so Art Vandelay is unsayable), but Plato's Sophist answers that nothing is 'otherness' with real power - the puffy shirt is something other than beautiful, and 'The Parking Garage' is doing something other than what is interesting or useful. Lao Tzu's Tao Te Ching goes further: the nameless Tao begets the ten thousand things, and wei wu wei (action through non-action) conquers, as in 'The Chinese Restaurant', where a whole episode of standing in line doing nothing is itself something happening.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 29 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Jennifer McMahon and Steve Csaki compare Tolkien with Zen Buddhism and Taoism on four themes while insisting on the real differences. Tolkien's talking trees (Old Man Willow, Treebeard's 'half awake' forest) invite comparison with Buddhist universal sentience and Dogen's walking mountains, but Tolkien anthropomorphizes where Buddhism grants non-human modes of sentience; the hobbits' ties to the Shire echo dependent origination, though Tolkien's stewardship and preference for the domesticated Shire over sinister wild nature remain Western. Frodo's succession of mentors (Bilbo, Gandalf, Aragorn, and the unlikely 'Master Samwise') parallels the Zen master-student relation, while Tolkien's war of light against darkness - nine Walkers against nine Riders - is decisively not the Taoist balance of yin and yang, for Taoists destroying either cosmic force would itself produce evil.
- **The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am**, ch. 14 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" — Argues Tony misappropriates Sun Tzu's Art of War: he applies tactical precepts like deception, formlessness and 'Balk the enemy's power' (citing the book in 'He Is Risen' after Melfi's jab in 'Big Girls Don't Cry'), but ignores the philosophical core. The chapter contrasts Sun Tzu's monistic one-world view of yin-yang interdependence, harmony and winning without fighting with the Greek two-world dualism of Plato and with the Christianity that lets Tony tell Melfi 'soldiers don't go to hell' in 'From Where to Eternity'. Tony's sausage panic attacks in 'Fortunate Son' show his failure to see how his crimes ripple through his family, and because he lacks the commander's exemplary character and harmony, Tony is 'just a soldier', not a ruler.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 29 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Jones narrates a day riding a customized Sportster around O'ahu as a lived Daoism that heals the Platonic-Cartesian mind-body split: the ride enacts Zhuangzi's 'rambling without destination' and Cook Ding's effortless wu-wei, rider li (the low hand-greeting among riders) is Confucian ritual propriety, and the island's dry and wet ranges embody yin and yang through whose flow the rider blends. Heraclitus's 'expect the unexpected' and 'the sun is new every day' are vindicated when a container truck stops short and only the disciplined, ego-less low-side, dropping the beloved bike while riding the skid, saves the rider's life, sealing the day's lesson that there is never freedom without discipline. Sartre's hell of other people appears in the cagers' compartmentalized inattention, and the chapter closes with Zhuangzi: 'The way is made by walking it.'
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 46 "Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat" — In a fictional interview with the Taoist sage "Bat-Tzu," Mark White explains Taoism through Batman's circle: Bruce's yang-dominated life of vengeance and paranoia needs the yin that Dick and Tim supply, shown by his forgiveness of Zatanna and tenderness toward Helena's baby, while Jason Todd illustrates the fate of the unbalanced who cannot accept death. Alfred emerges as the Taoist sage practicing wei-wu-wei, effortless service like Chuang Tzu's butcher, balancing right and wrong in Bruce, and the Batman-Joker duality shows yin and yang defining each other. Lao Tzu's sayings on balance, complementary opposites, and water-like yielding organize the whole reading.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 10 "I Still Miss Someone The Self and Its Travels Along the Way" — Geisz explains the Confucian social dao of ritual (li), humaneness (ren), filial piety and the junzi, the Daodejing's metaphysical Dao with its unity of opposites, and Zhuangzi's tales of free wandering, then maps all three onto Cash's songs. Zhuangzi's "Free and Easy Wandering" answers Cash's road songs ("I've Been Everywhere," "The Wanderer"), Cook Ding's effortless carving answers John Henry's hammering in "The Legend of John Henry's Hammer," and the scrambled countdown of "Twenty-Five Minutes to Go" echoes Zhuangzi's logic-bending humor. The payoff is Cash's own country Yin-Yang of interdependent opposites, freedom chained to imprisonment ("Folsom Prison Blues"), sin twinned with redemption ("I Hung My Head"), fidelity with betrayal ("Jackson," "Cocaine Blues"), and a self that, unlike Zhuangzi's self-forgetting sage, must travel a temporal path carrying its guilt, yet stays on what Geisz calls a very wide superhighway of a Dao.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 38 "Teddy Baseball" — Lee reads Ted Williams's The Science of Hitting as a Daoist skill story from the Zhuangzi: 'get a good ball to hit' matches the cicada-catcher's total absorption in the cicada's wings, hitting 'by feel' like the carpenter's hammer matches Cook Ding carving without looking, and Williams's midnight batting practice after Korea matches the wheelwright grown old at his craft—effortless spontaneity produced by disciplined practice and unified attention, not mere mechanics. Williams's 'proper thinking' is Daoist sorting of objective conditions rather than abstract disputation. The closing tale of the old woman who cannot teach the Way to someone lacking the stuff explains why Williams failed as Senators manager: his players did not have the native talent to receive it.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 20 "The End" — Chan contrasts Zhuangzi's butterfly dream, where dream and reality form one transformable whole and the self is forgotten, with Inception's dreams, which are rigidly structured and must be kept strictly separate from reality for Cobb to function. She shows that the film's motifs (the dream machine, the spinning top, the faceless children) work as narrative codes marking each dream layer, making Inception an example of 'dream explaining' rather than Tarkovsky-style 'dream worshipping'. The chapter concludes that Inception's 'dreams' are really a meta-space narrative device, as in Nolan's short Doodlebug, and that the film lacks the Daoist sense of the whole, so Cobb can never transform into the butterfly.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 36 "Psych and Philosophy" — John Thompson argues Psych embodies the Daoist Way of reversal from the Daodejing and Zhuangzi: every episode begins with a death that triggers Shawn and Gus's irreverent, backwards-tracing investigation, their untrained spontaneous 'gifts' exemplify wu wei like Cook Ding carving an ox, and their bickering partnership is yin-yang interplay (as when Gus leads the joking in 'An Evening with Mr. Yang'). Zhuangzi singing at his wife's funeral parallels the Shabby the Sea Lion and 'Dust in the Wind' funeral parodies, the show's blurred TV-versus-fandom reality echoes the butterfly dream, Lassiter succeeds when he relaxes into wu wei ('Feet Don't Kill Me Now'), and the closing bloopers enact Dao's endless reversal - though the chapter ends by conceding Dao defies the very label 'Daoist show.'
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 36 "22. The Dao of Master Westley" — Doll tests each character against the Dao: Confucius's identification of the Dao with tradition and ritual fails because Florinese tradition is exactly what enables Humperdinck's murder and war plans, so she turns to Laozi's De and wu-wei, diagnosing Vizzini's fatal overconfidence (he lacked Socratic knowledge of his own ignorance), Humperdinck's paranoia, and Buttercup's passivity as failures to sense when to act and when to refrain. Westley emerges as Zhuangzi's ideal - like Cook Ting the butcher, mastering skills until instinct suffices: adapting through the Fire Swamp, treating Vizzini's death as 'an appropriate death', yet sparing Inigo and Fezzik because killing them would be against nature, which is why the giant and the Spaniard accept him as their sage.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 42 "27. The Mystic with the Mouth" — In a lecture Deadpool keeps interrupting, the chapter reads the Merc's violence through Bataille's Theory of Religion: sacrifice as the search for lost intimacy, killing as the moment sacrificer and victim escape the profane world of mere things into sacred immanence, and sovereignty as the freedom glimpsed in destruction, with Rudolf Otto's mysterium tremendum et fascinans naming the awe Deadpool's massacres (the Circle Chase nunchuks, the Ultimate cartoon, the movie's highway slaughter) provoke. His 'dark Dao' of unhappy wandering is then set against the playful ways of the Zhuangzi - Cook Ding's ox-butchering, the Peng bird, the maimed teacher Wang Tai - as a Daoist path of inner-worldly transcendence that is amoral and gore-soaked. The payoff is the human tension of being both animal and angel: Deadpool is 'a savage god of mystical mayhem.'
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 27 "15. Farts, Butterflies, and Inner Truth" — Franklin Perkins reads Frank's fear that his jewelry business might start World War III — 'you can't fart without changing the balance in the universe' — as the butterfly-effect problem of acting inside a complexity we cannot grasp, from the Roosevelt assassination down to Tagomi's Colt .44. Against the Germans' fatal flight into abstraction (Volk, Blut, Ehre), the chapter presents the I Ching, read through Chinese correlative cosmology of the Tao and yin-yang, as a manual for mole-like, concrete, adaptive interpretation in which each casting (hexagram 11's 'wall falls back into the moat,' the purple knee bands) means only through creative engagement, ending with hexagram 61: our world arose as contingently as a throw of the yarrow stalks.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 27 "The Way of the Archer" — White reads Clint Barton through the Tao Te Ching and Chuang Tzu: Hawkeye's instinctive archery—'use your bow gently, naturally, instinctively'—is wei wu wei, while his bragging, his glory-chasing failure against Iron Man, and his attempt to become Goliath all violate it by striving against his own nature, until the Kree-Skrull War teaches him the bow is his way. Chuang Tzu's butcher carves the lesson that the effortless path (the straightforward shot) is the skilled one, and Lao Tzu's sage-leadership—lowering oneself, deflecting praise—is exactly how Captain America handles Clint's insurrections. Lao Tzu on sages putting themselves last illuminates Hawkeye's sacrificial death and his legacy passed to Kate Bishop, while the butterfly dream frames his resurrection and the House of M's rewritten reality: with no way to compare the states, life and death are both to be welcomed as parts of the Way.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 34 "NOTES" — The book's final chapter is a mock interview in which 'Bat-Tzu' applies Taoism to Bruce Wayne's life: his yang (hard, retributive crime-fighting) has dominated his yin (his tenderness toward Dick, Tim, and Helena), and Robin has always been the yin balancing the Dark Knight. Quoting Lao-Tzu's Tao Te Ching and Chuang-Tzu on duality, acceptance of death (Jason Todd's resurrection), and effortlessness, the piece casts Alfred as the Taoist sage whose help exemplifies wu-wei, like Chuang-Tzu's butcher who cuts without dulling his blade. It even reads Batman's most intimidating feature, his absent shadow, as proof that nothingness can matter more than substance.
