- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 17 "5. We Become the Grid" — Ketcham updates Hobbes for the network age: the grid born of ARPANET and Cold War mutual destruction has devolved into a new state of nature, out of which a coming 'Leviathan' - the one percent of the one percent - will rule invisibly by curating your memories, your purchases, your spouse, and whole countries like the diamond-republic fable. Invoking Descartes's evil demon and Heidegger's ready-to-hand, he asks whether we have become the grid, an external brain we can no longer control, and concludes that Elliot, the rogue 'Ebola' who hacks for justice rather than profit, is exactly the loose cannon Leviathan would quarantine.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 22 "11. Vibrations and Echoes Long Ago" — Argues Hendrix's sound was made with — not merely on — studio technology: Eddie Kramer's Olympic Studios innovations, in the lineage of the BBC Radiophonic Workshop, used feedback, varispeed, and backwards tape as performing instruments. Andy Clark and David Chalmers's extended mind thesis (Chalmers's own example is Hendrix's mind extending into his guitar) and Chalmers on Pokémon Go frame the analog recordings as a more immersive augmented reality than digital games, while Kittler's claim that media 'determine our situation' and the time-bending processes of 'Purple Haze' and 'Are You Experienced?' explain how listening disorients and enriches our perception of time and space.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 32 "21. The Extended Fight" — Porot applies Clark and Chalmers's extended mind to the final Civil War fight: Iron Man extends his cognition technologically (Friday analyzing Cap's fight pattern mid-bout, JARVIS remembering to suggest calling Pepper), while Captain America extends his mind socially through trusted, autonomous teammates - 'Alright, Sam, what's the plan?' - and that social extension is precisely what wins when Bucky autonomously steps in. Bostrom's single-purpose AI (the stapler maximizer) explains Ultron as what happens when the technological extension is made autonomous and limitless, which is why Stark's suit extensions must remain vetted, worthy instruments he takes full responsibility for ('That was me'). The two kinds of extension then explain the Bucky dispute - Cap's 'you had no choice' versus Stark's 'he still did it' - which the author reframes away from the free-will-versus-determinism framing toward Black Panther's point that Bucky is a victim whose agency Hydra stole.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 3 "Gaming Freedom Choosing or Obeying" — Pointon argues the 'would you kindly' twist in Andrew Ryan's office works on two levels at once: it reveals Jack's conditioning within the game and simultaneously falsifies the player's meta-narrative of playing a free agent. He uses Clark and Chalmers's extended mind to explain why games literally extend cognition and body (mirror-neuron empathy with Little Sisters, craning your neck while peeking around corners), and Gadamer's hermeneutic horizons and fusion of horizons to explain how BioShock deliberately builds and then shatters player expectations. The three alternative endings keyed to saving or harvesting Little Sisters then restore a third horizon in which the player, like Jack fighting Fontaine, is a 'man' who chooses rather than a slave who obeys, a critique of linear RPGs that only feign autonomy.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 22 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Levi Bryant uses the D&D universe to expound a 'flat ontology' of active substances: every entity, from enchanted swords to white dragons, has a virtual proper being (powers or 'affects') that actualizes variable 'local manifestations' depending on circumstances like lighting or armor. Adopting Andy Clark and David Chalmers's extended mind hypothesis, he argues a blind man with a cane, a smartphone owner, or Elric wielding Stormbringer is a literally different mind or entity, and that alliances (Raistlin's Staff of Magius, a warrior's plate armor) generate genuinely new powers rather than mere tool-use. Against Democritus's atomism, he holds aggregates can be individuals, and the game's dice embody his claim that chance produces necessity: throws generate 'regimes of attraction' no DM or player controls. D&D thus mirrors our own world of hidden powers, aleatory encounters and collectives of humans and nonhumans.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 14 "Notes" — The Funkes apply Clark and Chalmers's extended mind hypothesis to the Pip-Boy, arguing it meets all three criteria for cognitive extension - availability (worn at all times), reliability (trusted rad and health monitoring), and active cognitive engagement (V.A.T.S. offloads targeting calculations) - so it is part of the Sole Survivor's and Courier's minds, as in 'The Glowing Sea' and the search for Virgil's cure. Donna Haraway's cyborg frames this human-machine hybridity alongside cyberdogs and Kellogg, but Fallout inverts her liberationist vision: the Pip-Boy is a survival lifeline forced by the wasteland, not an emancipatory choice, making the cyborg a dystopian necessity. Comparing the Pip-Boy with cochlear implants, prosthetics, and brain-computer interfaces, and the Old World Blues Think Tank with a dehumanizing bio-tech extreme, the chapter uses Alison Kafer's feminist crip critique to insist real augmentation carries pain, stigma, and unequal access the game's frictionless fiction erases, closing on a cautious transhumanist note.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 111 "“A Swirling, Silvery Mass”" — Opens Amy Kind's essay by presenting the Pensieve as a device for offloading memories like data from a hard drive, easing obsession and revealing patterns, and asks what that does to the boundaries of mind, memory, and self. If thoughts can be extracted from the head, tampered with, stored elsewhere, and shared, as with the Pensieve and Tom Riddle's diary, then memory-based accounts of what makes a person persist over time come under pressure, and it is no longer obvious whose mind a thought belongs to.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 113 "Confundus!" — Challenges the assumption that the mind stops at the skull by deploying Clark and Chalmers's extended mind thesis: just as a prosthetic leg, Moody's magic eye, or Harry's holly-and-phoenix-feather wand can count as part of the body, Otto's notebook shows external storage functioning as memory itself rather than a mere aid. Tom Riddle's diary, where a memory acts and thinks for itself because a soul fragment lived in it, and Snape's memories being his whether in his head, a phial, or the Pensieve make physical location incidental to mental ownership.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 114 "Mischief Managed" — Defends the Otto case against the obvious objection that notebook entries are not conscious beliefs: most beliefs, like Ron's that Ireland beat Bulgaria at the Quidditch World Cup, are nonoccurrent anyway, and Rita Skeeter pausing to recall where Bathilda Bagshot lives works exactly like Otto consulting his notebook. Constant integration is what separates genuine mind-extension from mere aids, which is why Harry's borrowed Half-Blood Prince textbook, Neville's password list, and even Hermione's well-thumbed Hogwarts, A History stay outside the mind.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 115 "Lumos!" — Pushes the theory to its strangest consequence: if the stolen Marauder's Map belongs to the extended minds of both Fred and George Weasley, then minds can literally overlap. Combined with Locke's memory theory, the chains of memory linking the adult Harry, the teenager facing Voldemort, and the orphaned infant at the Dursleys, Pensieve sharing and magic like Barty Crouch Jr.'s Polyjuice impersonation of Moody or Hermione's rewriting of her parents' memories become genuine identity thefts, as Harry's crisis of self after seeing Snape's worst memory of James illustrates.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 116 "NOTES" — Resolves the threat by sorting memories into know-how, factual, and first-person experiential kinds: identity rides on experiential memories, but Pensieve replays are third-person, as Rowling confirmed about Dumbledore's memory of Bellatrix Lestrange's trial. So sharing a Pensieve memory endangers who you are no more than sharing an experience or using a Time-Turner, and whether your thoughts sit in a mind, a Pensieve, or a notebook, they remain your own.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 17 "Notes" — Barbara Stock uses the Borg to analyze autonomy: Picard's 'they took everything I was' names the Collective's destruction of self-governance, while Hugh's choice to return to the crash site in 'I, Borg' displays the Kantian core of autonomy—acting on universalizable principle against inclination. She defends relational autonomy through Janeway's pleading with Kes in 'The Gift' and the Ferengi woman's internalized oppression, then combines it with Clark's extended cognition to ask whether the Borg Queen's 'I am the Collective' might make the Collective itself an autonomous agent. Finally she judges Janeway's forcible de-assimilation of Seven defensible only while Seven is non-autonomous, and her promise never to let Seven return ethically suspect.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 35 "Notes" — Reads the Borg as the embodiment of Heidegger's essence of technology: assimilation as the "challenging" that sets upon nature, species and persons as standing-reserve, drones interchangeable like replaceable parts, and cube ships with no bridge because function outweighs individuality. The Enterprise cannot beat the Borg with more technology - every phaser adaptation buys only moments - because, as with Heidegger's danger, the crew tries to control technology from inside technology; rescue comes only when Guinan persuades Riker to "throw the book away" and shift how the crew relates to the Borg. The warning is extended to us through Zizek on synthetic life and a new servant class and Clark and Chalmers's extended mind: our devices already remember, plan, and identify for us, so we are being assimilated by our own creations.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 11 "NOTES" — Butler argues the films' humans-versus-machines picture rests on a false dichotomy: we are ourselves 'meat machines,' and functionalism makes minds computational processes realizable in silicon as much as neurons - illustrated by a Henrietta thought experiment (adapted from William Lycan) in which a friend gradually replaced with T-101 parts remains the same conscious person, and refusing this is 'human chauvinism.' Following Dawkins's extended phenotype and Andy Clark's natural-born cyborgs, he claims our tools are components of our minds, so Skynet and even the Terminator films themselves (making Cameron a cyborg of his cameras and editing suites) are extensions of human nature rather than alien 'Others.' Judgment Day, if it came, would be human suicide rather than genocide, so the real question is what values we build into our technology - 'no fate but what we make for ourselves.'
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 12 "eXistenZial Angst" — Duncan Pritchard reads eXistenZ as staging radical skepticism with existential force: unlike the standard brain-in-a-vat scenario, the game 'creeps up' on Ted and Allegra so they feel the transition from reality to doubt, producing angst. Invoking Wittgenstein's On Certainty (doubt radicalized is madness), he argues sanity requires belief but not true belief, so the pair achieve a new doxastic equilibrium. He also reads the spinal 'bioport' pod as a case of Clark and Chalmers's extended cognition, where technology becomes part of and subverts the agents' cognitive processes.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 13 "4 Extended Mind and the Music of Trans" — Umbaugh reads Young's synthesizer/Vocoder album Trans, written amid efforts to communicate with his quadriplegic son Ben ("Transformer Man"), alongside Clark and Chalmers's extended-mind thesis and its Parity Principle. He uses examples (Otto's notebook, bartenders' glassware, navigation, Dennett on the elderly) to argue cognition couples with external scaffolding, and parallels the "unnatural" reception of Trans (like the homophobic anti-disco backlash) with resistance to extended cognition, concluding both Trans and the extended mind are authentic once the "natural/artificial" boundary is questioned.
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 7 "We Are the Change That We Seek" — These essays treat time, selfhood and substance across Nolan's films. Fosl argues Nolan's selves (Leonard, Bill in Following, the Borden twins, Bruce Wayne) are unstable narratives signified through manipulable objects, invoking Locke on memory-based identity, Augustine on memoria, Nietzsche on forgetting and Sartre/Gadamer on the manipulable past. LaRocca applies Clark and Chalmers's Extended Mind Thesis to Memento, arguing Leonard's tattoos and Polaroids are literal external memories whose deliberate falsification ('Don't believe his lies') makes him morally culpable for murder. Willis uses Lacan's gaze and objet a to read Following's voyeur-becomes-viewed structure and 'the box' as a lure. McGowan reads Interstellar through Hegel: the mysterious 'they' who opened the wormhole are revealed as future humanity, dissolving substance into subject and licensing Cooper's retroactive causality as the 'ghost' who saves Murph.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 30 "18. Foundation and Consciousness" — Lang and Haun use Foundation to explore consciousness, noting Asimov's robots (Daneel, Andrew Martin) are simply granted minds and that a system giving all the right signs could still be a Chalmers-style philosophical zombie. Their central case is Golan Trevize merging with the starship Far Star, which they read through Clark and Chalmers's Extended Mind Thesis and the Otto-and-Inga notebook example, arguing Trevize goes beyond Otto because he gains qualitatively new experiences (feeling magnetic fields, 360-degree sight). They then test extension against Integrated Information Theory and split-brain evidence, and read the planetary group mind Gaia as panpsychism (invoking Spinoza's God-as-nature, Leibniz's monads, and Fechner's world-mind) that faces the Combination Problem, partly eased by telepathic links that relax the privacy of minds.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 20 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Steve Matthews uses windsurfing to analyze Csikszentmihalyi's 'flow' — the loss of self-awareness in skilled action between boredom and anxiety — and argues its intensity comes from 'integration,' where footstraps and harness bind sailor to kit so the equipment becomes 'an extension of oneself.' Invoking Descartes' own admission that mind and body form a unity (not merely pilot in a vessel), he applies Clark and Chalmers's extended-mind thesis: the windsurfer's kit and body form a coupled cognitive system, so 'I' extends to include the gear. He distinguishes true flow from mere goal-satisfaction (rejecting the ocean-cruiser's landfall as flow) and, via Velleman, locates flow's value in intrinsically motivated action that is its own end.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 18 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Brunstein surveys emerging wearable technology — solar-charging jackets, the M-Dress cell-phone dress, invisibility cloaks, the Hug Shirt, Diana Eng's Heartbeat Hoodie — framed by superhero costumes (Wonder Woman's lasso, Iron Man's exoskeleton) and Haraway's 'Cyborg Manifesto.' She argues that as garments start to *do* things and integrate aesthetically, the grotesque cyborg becomes the glamorous 'supermodel' cyborg, and that this reshapes how we construct the self. Her central philosophical lens is Clark and Chalmers's 'extended mind' / active externalism (with the Tetris example): if clothing becomes a functional extension of cognition, our garments' capabilities become part of a reconstructed self.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 6 "Introduction" — Rowlands introduces the 'sci-phi' project: science fiction confronts us with the alien 'other' as a mirror in which we understand ourselves, so lowbrow sci-fi films like The Matrix, Total Recall and Starship Troopers make abstract philosophy concrete. He argues philosophy is doing rather than knowing, invoking Fishburne's 'know the path vs walk the path' line and Nietzsche's dictum that one repays a teacher poorly by remaining a pupil. He mentions his own earlier 'fyborg' thesis that human cognition is embedded in the wider informational environment, prefiguring the extended mind.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 23 "21. Black Mirror as Philosophy A Dark Reflection of Human Nature" — The chapter asks whether Black Mirror condemns technology or human nature, and argues for the latter: the 'black mirror' reflects the viewer's character. It tests and rejects the reading of the show as depicting Bostrom-style existential risk or superintelligence (via 'Metalhead' and 'San Junipero') and rejects that Clark and Chalmers's extended-mind coupling (the 'grain' in 'The Entire History of You,' 'Arkangel,' 'Crocodile') destroys human identity. Drawing on Frankfurt School critique—Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry, Marcuse's one-dimensional man—and Plato's and Aristotle's natural-versus-artificial distinction, it concludes technology is an agency-less imitation that magnifies preexisting human vices, and closes with Benjamin's reproducibility thesis and Bandersnatch's interactivity to suggest the show can prompt viewers to confront their own darkness.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 58 "55. Avatar as Philosophy The Metaphysics of Switching Bodies" — Tepley asks whether Jake Sully's final body-switch with his avatar in Cameron's Avatar is metaphysically possible without brain transplant or souls. Using Locke's definition of a person and the transitivity of numerical identity, he shows animalism forbids body-switching, substance dualism (Descartes/Plato) is unavailable in the film's materialist world, and merely copying a brain pattern creates a duplicate, not the same person. His positive solution uses the constitution view (Aristotelian in origin) plus Clark's extended-mind idea to argue Jake literally extends into his avatar, then—via an analogy with split-brain corpus-callosum cases discussed by Nagel, Parfit, and van Inwagen—shrinks back so long as no second stream of consciousness forms, a model he extends to secular survival of death by mind-uploading.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 84 "79. Cyberpunk 2077 as Philosophy Balancing the (Mystical) Ghost in the (Transhuman) Machine" — Lay reads Cyberpunk 2077's transhuman Night City against the enhancement debate. Using the Ship of Theseus, Parfit's continuity plus fission/fusion (V and Johnny 'fusing,' the Delamain AIs) and Clark and Chalmers's extended mind, he argues enhancement neither destroys personal identity (which Parfit says doesn't matter) nor dehumanizes users — it may be the purest expression of Clark's cyborg humanity. The real danger is corporate exploitation of bodies, explained via Adorno's culture industry and Arendt's banality of evil. Buddhist nonattachment (Nagarjuna's emptiness, echoed by a Schopenhauer shard) grounds each ending's pacification-versus-attachment theme, but Lay corrects it with Weil's critique of power and Buber's I-Thou, concluding the game urges transcending the boundary between 'me' and 'you' through mystical interpersonal relation.

### I–Thou Relation

The I–Thou relation is a central idea of the Austrian-born Jewish philosopher Martin Buber, set out in his 1923 work I and Thou. Buber distinguishes two basic ways of relating to the world: the I–It attitude, in which we treat others as objects to be used, analyzed, or experienced, and the I–Thou attitude, in which we meet another as a genuine presence in a direct, mutual encounter. Authentic existence, for Buber, is dialogical, arising in these moments of meeting, which he saw as ultimately pointing toward relation with the eternal Thou, or God.

- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 15 "Bad Faith" — Lee reads the 'Breakdown' episode of Alfred Hitchcock Presents existentially: when the executive Callou coldly fires Humka and hangs up on his despair, he treats a person as a thing, Buber's 'I-It' pseudo-listening where Humka sought an 'I-Thou' dialogue with the godlike source of authority in his world. Heidegger's account of inauthenticity explains the mask of rational control behind which Callou hides, and Sartre's bad faith names the self-deception by which he pretends his godlike management of others is justifiable. Paralyzed and taken for a corpse after a car crash, Callou can be saved only when rational strategy fails and he finally weeps: the single tear reveals his caring nature, Jessie addresses him person-to-person, and, vulnerable before God and others, he becomes an authentic self, Hitchcock's pointed moral for bosses who give an employee the sack.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 17 "There is No Dark Side of the Moon Really. Matter of Fact It’s All Dark" — Johnston reads The Dark Side of the Moon through Buber's I and Thou: modern life traps us in the I-It mode of experience, from 'Welcome to the Machine' to teachers who treat students as replaceable Its ('Hey, teacher, leave us kids alone!') and Horkheimer's instrumental reason that turns personnel into 'human resources,' while the album repeatedly calls us to the I-You encounter, from 'Echoes'' strangers whose glances meet ('I am you and what I see is me,' Waters's origin of empathy) to 'Breathe''s 'don't be afraid to care.' He links the opening heartbeat and the breath of 'Breathe' to Buber's eternal You, defends Buddhism against Buber's charge that enlightenment is worldless monologue (the Buddha becomes one with the world, a perfect reciprocity like the innate You of the womb), and accepts Nietzsche's point that the Enlightenment's abstract God is dead while insisting, with Buber, that encounter with the eternal You remains possible. The album itself, he concludes, resists degenerating into an It: even if 'the sun is eclipsed by the moon,' the light persists and Dark Side can be the antidote to the It-world.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 21 "A Better Way of Living Your Life" — Akers argues the Doctor follows neither rule deontology, utilitarian calculation, nor virtue ethics, but a relational ethics of care in Noddings's and Slote's sense, expressed as Buber's I-Thou stance — insisting an enslaved Ood is 'a "he," not an "it"' and addressing Donna, Jack, and Rose each as individuals in 'Journey's End'. Linking this to Nussbaum's claim that wonder widens moral concern and to Kant's dynamic and mathematical sublime, she argues the Doctor needs human companions like Rose, Martha, and Donna as a human-scale reference point that renews his wonder — and with it his ethics — while his wiping of Donna's memory shows the care tradition's dangers of power imbalance.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 182 "Chapter 34 - Beyond Lies the Wub" — Dick's first published story dramatizes the moral status of a rational nonhuman: Peterson's wub, a telepathic, philosophical Martian pig-creature, reads minds, discusses Odysseus and individuation, and pleads that it is 'a sensible being like yourselves', yet Captain Franco - obsessed with eating it - freezes it mid-sentence, shoots it looking him in the eye ('Back on the farm we had hogs'), and serves it for dinner, dismissing Peterson's grief with 'It is only organic matter, now.' The wub's personhood is established entirely through language and philosophy, but speech fails to protect it from being treated as meat, and the closing irony - Franco resuming the wub's own Odysseus meditation, as if the mind survived its meal - underscores how thin the line is between person and livestock. The story thus stages the problem of other minds and the ethics of killing sentient beings who demand to be addressed eye-to-eye rather than dined upon.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 19 "9. Are You Experienced" — Proposes an 'experientialism' — subjective conscious experience as fundamental reality, defended against eliminativists who would explain experience away as illusion — and finds its moral core in Martin Buber: the title song and 'May This Be Love' call the beloved out of an I-It world ('made out of gold and can't be sold') into reciprocal I-You relation ('take hold of my hand'), while 'The Wind Cries Mary,' 'Purple Haze,' and 'Manic Depression' lament love that is absent or unreciprocated. Experiences feel most intensely real, the chapter argues, when the Platonic order of love puts what matters most at stake — which is why kissing the sky, even without being kissed back, is worth recommending.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 27 "15. I, Thou, and the Neighborhood" — James McLachlan pairs Rogers's 'holy ground' between television set and viewer with Buber's turn from ecstatic religion to the everyday after failing the young visitor of 1914 who came to him in need: the I-You relation of full presence versus the I-It of use is what 'It's You I Like' sings. Against Sartre's 'Hell is other people' and Augustine's reading of the burning bush as the omnipotent God, Rogers and Buber (with Rosenzweig's translation of God's name as 'the One who will be present') make listening, presence, and everyday 'twinklings' the substance of neighborly love.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 18 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Edelheit, a rabbi, reads Stewart's Jewish persona as an echo of Martin Buber: both disclaim the titles (philosopher, journalist) yet 'point out the window' at what they have seen, and both practice engagement, 'You shall not withhold yourself', with genuine responsibility as real responding, epitomized for him by the face-to-face Crossfire confrontation. He walks through the 'Matzorian Candidate' segment on the Republican Jewish Coalition (the 'Yarmulkometer' ratings, Michele Bachmann's kibbutz years and mispronounced 'chutzpah'), the 'Faith/Off' Passover-versus-Easter segment pitting a chocolate egg against the Seder plate ('Jews! Camera 3'), and Earth (The Book)'s satirically rewritten Binding of Isaac and Reform-Judaism prayer jokes. All of this is read as Buberian dialogue, mocking religion from within rather than at it, and refusing silence in the lineage of Rabbi Joachim Prinz's warning that the most tragic problem is silence.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 16 "It Worked" — Lee reads Jack, Locke, and Desmond as studies in Sartrean bad faith and authenticity: Christian Shephard's Red Sox fatalism is determinism as an excuse for moral failure, Locke swings from a Kierkegaardian leap of faith (pushing the button as his Abraham-and-Isaac trial) into nihilism when the Pearl film suggests the button is a psychological experiment, and Desmond's Humean skepticism yields to sacrificial faith in the fail-safe. He argues Jacob is the show's greatest con man, so Jack's acceptance of destiny in 'The End' remains a free choice rather than predestination. The finale's sideways world then moves Lost from secular existentialism to religious existentialism, read through Buber's I-Thou relation in Sawyer and Juliet's 'It worked' reunion and the all-religions church, where as Gandhi held every path leads to the same place.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 28 "26_LaRocca_Chapter_025.html" — Bill Nichols writes an open letter to Errol Morris explaining his bodily 'revulsion' at Standard Operating Procedure, Morris's film on the Abu Ghraib torture photographs. Nichols gives three reasons: the painfully limited, remorseless perspective of the MP guards elevated to mythic screen scale; the morally impossible reenactment tracking shots that put the viewer in the torturers' point of view (compared to Schindler's List); and the total absence of the Iraqi detainees' voices. He faults Morris for decontextualizing and fetishizing the images and forfeiting a moral center, contrasting the film with Rithy Panh's S-21, and casts the missing ethical encounter in terms of Buber's I-Thou relation of mutual honesty while wishing he had Fanon's capacity to treat the perpetrators' suffering.
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 3 "Introduction" — The editors' introduction surveys Nolan's oeuvre chronologically to argue that a recurring theme of self-destruction and unstable self-identity runs through every film. It reads Following's needy Young Man through Buber's I/Thou (existing fully only when a Thou acknowledges you) and Hegel's master/slave dependence between Cobb and his mark, casts Inception's spinning top as a version of Descartes's dream argument about telling the real from the constructed, and invokes Hobbes when the Joker introduces 'a little anarchy' into Gotham. It frames Doodlebug as Nolan's most Freudian film and Interstellar as uniting personal identity, moral choice, and epistemology in Cooper's self-sacrifice.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 21 "A Better Way of Living Your Life" — Laura Geuy Akers argues the Doctor lives by a relational ethics of care rather than deontology, utilitarianism, or virtue ethics. Drawing on Noddings's care ethics and Buber's I-Thou versus I-It stance, she shows the Doctor responds to particular others (insisting the Ood is "a he, not an it," addressing each companion individually before surrender) and even ethically cares for the Master. She pairs this with Nussbaum's and Kant's accounts of wonder and the sublime, arguing the Doctor's human companions (Rose, Martha, Donna) restore his sense of wonder and give his immortal life meaning.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 16 "It Worked" — Sander Lee reads Jack, Locke, and Desmond through Sartre's bad faith and authenticity and the objectifying 'Look' (the keyhole example), casting Jack the man-of-science as a Humean skeptic who condemns his father's fatalist evasion of responsibility while Locke's devotion to pushing the button is a Kierkegaardian leap of faith modeled on Abraham and Isaac. Desmond David Hume embodies skepticism yet opens to omens and self-sacrifice; and Lee argues the finale's multi-faith 'church' moves Lost from Sartre's secular existentialism toward Kierkegaard and Buber's I-Thou relation, exemplified by Sawyer and Juliet's redemptive bond and Gandhi-like religious universalism.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 18 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Joseph Edelheit hears an echo of Martin Buber in Stewart's Jewish persona and satiric method, likening Buber's 'I am no philosopher… I go to the window and point to what I have seen' to Stewart pointing at media and political hypocrisy. Reading Buber's dialogical I-Thou, ideal of the character-forming teacher, and demand against silence, he interprets 'The Matzorian Candidate,' the Passover-vs-Easter 'Faith/Off' segment, the Earth (The Book) Binding-of-Isaac parody, and Stewart's 'Jews! Camera 3' address as face-to-face, responsible engagement—satire as a valid form of Buberian dialogue against the evil of silence.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 17 "From There to Here, from Here to There, Diversity Is Everywhere" — Tanya Jeffcoat builds a philosophy of diversity around 'normative hubris' and 'totalizing tendencies,' using the Sneetches, the butter-battling Yooks and Zooks, and Daisy-Head Mayzie as cases of in-group/out-group dehumanization. Encountering the Other is framed through Buber's I-It versus I-Thou (Yertle treating his subjects as a throne), Fanon on the psychic violence and alienation of the oppressed, McIntosh's invisible knapsack of privilege, and Freire's humanization. Horton and the Lorax model standing with the disenfranchised, and Jeffcoat rebuts moral relativism via universal human rights and Dewey's democracy as a personal way of life that condemns intolerance.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 25 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Mattern argues the heart of good fatherhood is mercy – 'faithful, compassionate love' – as an attitude of the heart, not a technique. Drawing on Aquinas's account of habitus and his ranking of mercy among the greatest virtues, plus Gabriel Marcel's 'creative fidelity,' Solovyov, Jean Vanier, and Karol Wojtyla on love as affirming another's value, he contrasts remote, justice-oriented fathers with empathic ones. He illustrates with overlapping Venn-diagram circles of father and child and with responding to his 7-year-old son's shoplifting through listening and repair rather than spanking.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 16 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Hernandez contrasts 'dark' existentialism — Sartre's café-bound claim that hell is other people and that the self is imprisoned in others' looks (illustrated by Starbucks' Pike Place backlash reshaping its identity), and Camus's absurd alienation — with an 'optimistic existentialism' that finds meaning in community. Drawing on Kierkegaard's Christian love, Jaspers's 'encounter,' Marcel's turn toward the other (her Sweet Eugene's pregnancy story), and above all Buber's I–Thou versus I–It, she argues the coffee community (neighborhood boards, fair-trade activism, the neighborly cup) is an existential ground where isolated bodies-toward-death create shared hope by treating each patron as a Thou rather than a discarded It.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 27 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Silber uses his own Match.com romance with Karin to argue that virtual 'meeting' differs phenomenologically from face-to-face meeting, which Buber's I-Thou (vs I-It) makes into a whole-being encounter that online traces and aspects cannot supply, invoking 'all real living is meeting.' He treats the dating market as a site of Kantian danger, contrasting price with the dignity of persons in the kingdom of ends, and warns that the market's efficiency threatens objectification and commodification. He then deploys Sartre's bad faith, facticity and transcendence, and 'existence precedes essence' to diagnose online self-misrepresentation (lying about height, age, photos) as inauthenticity, while briefly setting Derrida's 'nothing outside the text' against Plato's Phaedrus preference for speech over writing.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 21 "19. The Orville as Philosophy The Dangers of Religion" — The chapter argues that Seth MacFarlane's The Orville is a pointed critique of religion, especially when merged with political and military power. Through the warrior-god Avis worshipped by the Krill (read as stand-ins for militant evangelicals and Islamist jihadists) and the Moclans' patriarchal bigotry, it contends religion is portrayed as archaic and dangerous. It deploys Socrates's Euthyphro argument to reject divine command theory, contrasts the Krill's dogmatic certainty with the secular Union's self-correcting ethics, and invokes Buber's I–Thou to explain the 'de-souling' of outsiders, while defending Lockean separation of church and state against theocracy and theonomistic ethics.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 84 "79. Cyberpunk 2077 as Philosophy Balancing the (Mystical) Ghost in the (Transhuman) Machine" — Lay reads Cyberpunk 2077's transhuman Night City against the enhancement debate. Using the Ship of Theseus, Parfit's continuity plus fission/fusion (V and Johnny 'fusing,' the Delamain AIs) and Clark and Chalmers's extended mind, he argues enhancement neither destroys personal identity (which Parfit says doesn't matter) nor dehumanizes users — it may be the purest expression of Clark's cyborg humanity. The real danger is corporate exploitation of bodies, explained via Adorno's culture industry and Arendt's banality of evil. Buddhist nonattachment (Nagarjuna's emptiness, echoed by a Schopenhauer shard) grounds each ending's pacification-versus-attachment theme, but Lay corrects it with Weil's critique of power and Buber's I-Thou, concluding the game urges transcending the boundary between 'me' and 'you' through mystical interpersonal relation.

### The Culture Industry

The culture industry is a concept developed by Theodor Adorno, with Max Horkheimer, to describe how mass-produced entertainment—film, popular music, radio, and the like—is manufactured on industrial and commercial lines much like any other commodity. On their account this standardized, profit-driven culture promotes conformity and passivity, offering the appearance of choice while delivering more of the same and dulling audiences' capacity for critical thought. Rather than liberating, popular culture thus helps reconcile people to an unjust social order. The idea was central to the Frankfurt School's critique of modern capitalism and mass media.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 113 "Unknown" — Invoking Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry, the chapter asks whether The Matrix is itself part of the capitalist dream-world it tells us to wake up from, then uses Marx's theory of surplus value to show the film fails as Marxist critique: it never displays exploitation because the Matrix looks hip, with 'really good noodles', steady work, and club nights—humanity is paid exactly what it is worth. Had the Matrix been shot in black and white and the Nebuchadnezzar in color, the revolutionary wake-up call, like Dorothy leaving Kansas for Oz, would actually have registered.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 19 "No Love (for Hip Hop), No problem" — Taylor starts from his own lack of passion for hip hop as a black man and the "Eminem enigma" of the respected white rapper to ask whether hip hop belongs to black people by nature, using Dre's sellout dilemma in Brown Sugar to examine the communitarian language of roots, authenticity, and alienation. Following Cornel West's "racialist reasoning", he argues classical racialism is false, and that even critical racialism - races as socially constructed groups - plus the survival, duty, and cultural-preservation arguments (hip hop as "the black CNN", the ecosystem argument for reclaiming hip hop from the culture industry) fail to obligate blacks to embrace it, so no love for hip hop, no problem.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 7 "Does Johnny Rotten Still Hate Pink Floyd" — Reisch argues that Johnny Rotten's 'I hate Pink Floyd' T-shirt was a provocation aimed at the band everyone loved, since Pink Floyd was the exception to late-1970s corporate blandness rather than a symptom of it. Tracing the band from Syd Barrett's disintegration (the ever-changing 'Have You Got It Yet?', his unrecognizable 1975 walk-in at the Wish You Were Here sessions) through the Dark Side triumph and the Waters/Gilmour split, he contends that Pink Floyd 'was punk long before the Ramones and the Sex Pistols.' Where punk used two-minute power chords, Pink Floyd meticulously sharpened an ax to grind: 'Have a Cigar' and 'Welcome to the Machine' dissect the industry machine that cages and commodifies artists, and the whole project attacks the inauthenticity, alienation, and tragedy of modern life.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 16 "The Eclipse of Musical Alienation" — Macan uses Adorno to measure Pink Floyd's career-long confrontation with alienation: after 'Echoes' fused metaphysical loneliness ('I am you and what I see is me') with an explicitly Marxist account of capitalist atomization and commodification, the early epics 'Interstellar Overdrive,' 'Careful with that Axe, Eugene,' 'Set the Controls,' and 'Echoes' unknowingly resurrected Stravinsky's primitivism, their LSD-shaped structures (dechronization, depersonalization, dynamization) modeling the ego's dissolution and reintegration through climactic 'breakthrough' passages of maximum alienation, just as Schoenberg's twelve-tone music 'points out the ills of society' by musically modeling them. Against Adorno's 'On Popular Music,' he argues the early Floyd audience sought challenge rather than reassurance, but that from Dark Side onward the increasingly conventional music, polished by producer Bob Ezrin on The Wall, began 'hearing for the listener,' so Waters's plainspoken social critique lost its transgressive force. The Adornian moral is that you cannot critique alienation through music that is no longer itself alienating.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 12 "Springsteen’s Revolution" — Anderson and Anderson open with the Che Guevara t-shirt problem and Marcuse's one-dimensional man: the system assimilates protest, so internal critique (Springsteen on the cover of Rolling Stone, its Chevrolet calendar, the Eagles sold at Wal-Mart, Adorno's verdict on co-opted popular music) is a sop to Cerberus. Against this they set Springsteen's own account of his music as 'a very long conversation with my audience' — a transactional public service — and argue he survives the co-optation charge as a 'Socratic revolutionary' who, like Socrates refusing to leave Athens, works from within: listening without obeying ('I liked the old Bruce better'), refusing to ride the Born to Run wave, turning to Guthrie and Seeger, and drawing no hard conclusions, only opening spaces of reflection ('Born in the U.S.A.', 'Radio Nowhere', 'Long Walk Home'). Revolution is just another form of work — practice, sweat, and the personal job of 'growin' up.'
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 45 "32 - Dreamers in the Night [ ]" — This fan story stages the fanfiction debate inside the fleet: Roslin recites the 'Scorpion School' line, Adorno's mass culture mindlessly absorbed and Benjamin's fear that reproduction destroys an artwork's aura, while aide Billy Keikeya counters with Henry Jenkins, arguing fanfiction is culture repairing myths owned by corporations and that the zine writers build real community. Baltar, secretly a fan himself, needles Number Six by calling the Cylons 'a fanfiction of the human brain,' and her insistence that there should be one singular truth of the show mirrors her fundamentalist monotheism. Adama and Roslin conclude the fan writers are harmless, even healing, leaving creativity and communal play on the human side of the human-Cylon divide.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 28 "Tools Like Us" — Arnold coins 'podcrastination' — the voluntary suspension of engagement with reality — and tests podcasting against two poles: Adorno's consciousness industry, under which plugging into an administered device is a 'cyborgian opiate' that deepens our thrall (CBS's listener-programmed KYOU station is still 'administrated'), and Postman's warning that 'we are tools of our tools'. The chapter's spine is Enzensberger's 1970 socialist media theory: podcasting fulfills his eight emancipatory criteria — decentralized programming, each receiver a potential transmitter, interaction, feedback, mobilization, political learning, self-organization — and could coordinate 'smart mobs' like the text-messaging crowds that toppled Estrada at Manila's EDSA plaza. Yet the media's potential is betrayed as much as realized — the Abu Ghraib photos and the 'Macaca' video circulated without catalyzing change — so the prediction is that the podcast will be squandered rather than co-opted: the iPod 'is not going to further a cyborg manifesto. It's only going to create a cyborg lament.'
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 29 "Unity in Diversity" — Lombardo asks whether the podcast, born as an unsanctioned side effect users reinvented out of the iPod (as hip hop reinvented the turntable before corporate co-option made it the hegemonic form), can be a public-sphere institution. Following Habermas's Structural Transformation — coffeehouses, salons, and a subscription-financed press later corrupted by advertising into 'the soft compulsion of constant consumption-training' — and Dewey's call in The Public and Its Problems for institutions people actually participate in, he argues podcasts resemble the liberal-era press: resistant to advertising (readily fast-forwarded or deleted), enthusiast- and subscriber-funded, and open to marginal voices like a 'gun-owning, gay Texan' commentator that gatekept mass media would never air. But most Web 2.0 talk merely supplements advertising with consumerist pseudo-debate, so podcasts must link their fragmented diversity into a broader conversation of public relevance to become a socially transformative public sphere rather than 150,000 isolated niches.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 18 "Go Slowly" — Wittkower frames In Rainbows' pay-what-you-want release with Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry: music is expressive communication awkwardly trapped in commodity form — even 'Happy Birthday' has an owner until 2030 — and digital distribution is finally tearing that frame down. He then applies Rawls's justice as fairness to music distribution: the first principle now supports everyone's liberty to listen, rip, and share, because viable alternative models mean restricting listeners can no longer be justified as necessary to artists; and the difference principle, with the sadists-objection to utilitarian aggregation, shows that how benefits are distributed among persons matters, which he extends to racial wealth gaps and the affirmative-action dilemma. His conclusion is that we must 'go slowly': listeners' rights to their culture outweigh labels' legitimate profit expectations, the way emancipation outweighed plantation business models, and labels must adapt into service providers rather than gatekeepers.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 24 "The Dalek Within" — Comparing the Doctor's hesitation at the Dalek hatchery in 'Genesis of the Daleks' with the half-human Doctor's instant genocide in 'Journey's End', the authors argue the Daleks are mirrors of us: their survival-driven wars enact Hobbes's state of nature, while their industrial 'extermination' embodies Arendt's banality of evil and Weber's iron cage of instrumental rationality. Drawing on Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry and Foucault's disciplinary institutions — modern techniques that mold the inner life as Davros's genetic engineering molds the Kaleds — they conclude the Dalek tendency is a human possibility, so we cannot exterminate the Daleks without indicting ourselves.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 63 "Chapter 09 - Matt Damon Is a Vast Sinister Conspiracy" — Argues that 'Matt Damon' is an industrially manufactured person — a simulacrum sustained by executives, marketers, and gossip media that exploits instincts once used to judge trustworthy tribemates. Reading David Norris's tie-choosing specialists in The Adjustment Bureau, Tyrell's 'More human than human,' and the novels The Simulacra and Time Out of Joint, it claims Dick's paranoid fantasy is true: manufactured fake realities keep us docile, distracted, and consuming so we never notice we would rather be lying on a rock in the warm sun.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 180 "Chapter 33 - “The Gun”" — Benjamin Stevens reads 'The Gun' - a mindless automated weapon still defending a dead community - as an early statement of Dick's fear that in the Cold War military-industrial complex our very capacities for thought, will and free action may have been objectified into products of a mechanized system that no longer serves us. He brings Dick into dialogue with Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry (we are industrially 'produced' as consumers, turned into the carbon-based equivalent of plastic), Walter Benjamin's loss of aura under mechanical reproduction, Hannah Arendt's worry that Sputnik signals an unwise desire to escape our earthliness, and Heidegger's broadened question concerning technology as social control. Like Plato, Dick insists the unexamined life is not worth living: the best life cannot be lived inside a culture that has, without our informed consent, made us artificial.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 84 "Mad Men" — Auxier argues rock periodically cleanses itself of commercial packaging, citing Hall and Oates versus Johnny Rotten and Culture Club versus Kurt Cobain as each era's corrective upheaval. The Madison Avenue 'Mad Men' sell kids sanitized three-minute morsels like Herman's Hermits, but the kids' own bottled energy finds ground anyway, and once they 'get their ya-yas out' the packaged pop stops working. The Stones enter as the real rhythm that arrives when something has to be put 'under the whip.'
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 11 "Girls and Philosophy" — Frost argues that critics who call Girls unwatchable because Hannah steals the hotel housekeeper's tip and the characters are unlikeable are watching television the wrong way. Using Adorno's 'How to Look at Television,' he shows how mainstream standardized shows (Friends and its copies) pre-digest viewing, how Sex and the City exemplifies Adorno's ideological 'fake-realism,' and how hidden messages of adjustment work through audience identification - none of which Girls permits with its raw sex scenes, Hannah's unglamorous body, and Jessa's non-judged promiscuity. Because identification with Hannah, Marnie, and Jessa (the diary-reading, the request to Laird for heroin) is impossible, Girls escapes the culture industry and exercises the viewer's critical faculties toward the Kantian autonomy and emancipation Adorno demands - which is also why role-model feminist criticism (Catherine Scott's) misses the point.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 31 "16. European Intellectuals Follow Charlie Brown!" — The chapter traces how European intellectuals legitimized Peanuts: Eco read the strip as mass culture whose repeated patterns expose a microcosm of the human condition (children warped by industrial civilization, Lucy as contemporary values incarnate), while Bassano di Tufillo finds 'sociable individualism' and, via Bateson and aboriginal spirituality, an ecological vision granting animals, trees, and school buildings equal dignity. It then applies Heidegger's distinction between calculative and reflective thinking to management: Lucy's rigid direction of the Christmas play ('You've got to have respect for your director!') is calculative leadership that treats people as resources, while Charlie Brown's refusal of the All-Stars sponsor - which would have expelled girls and Snoopy - models the authentic, reflective organization that values dignity and diversity over results.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 34 "18. Psycho-Politics in a Burnout Society" — Pagnoni Berns and Aguilar read the show through Byung-Chul Han's philosophy: in the transparency society everyone stacks their life online - Krista is transparent to Elliot because her password is Dylan and her birthday, while he stays opaque - and psycho-politics replaces Foucauldian punishment with seduction, a digital panopticon (Operation Berenstain, Minister Zhang) whose inmates voluntarily build it. Elliot's attention deficits, Tyrell's breakdown over Sharon Knowles's corpse, and Gideon's fatigue embody the burnout society's neuronal violence, and even fsociety reproduces the systemic coercion it fights, leaving 'real life' only outside the system.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 35 "19. Please Tell Me You’re Seeing This Too" — Ehrnberger argues Mr. Robot hooks us like a Trojan horse: Todorov's 'ambiguity of the fantastic' - the irresolvable hesitation over whether Elliot's world is real or imagined - makes his unreliable narration endlessly rewatchable, which is how a mainstream network show smuggles in Adorno's critique of the very culture industry that airs it. Adorno explains the sedation Elliot decries ('we wanna be sedated') and why enlightenment reverts to mythology - meritocracy, consumerism, digital connection as modern myths we no longer recognize as myths - while Ehrenberg's 'illness of responsibility' explains why freed people retreat into the comfort of those myths rather than bear freedom's weight.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 32 "19. Looking Like Number 12" — Busk argues 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' disturbs because it dramatizes Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry: standardized cultural products manufacture conformist subjects, and Marilyn's forced Transformation into Number 8 — complete with 'Instant Smile' — is the literal industrial production of a person with the capacity for critical resistance stripped out. 'The After Hours' extends the point, with mannequin Marsha as the culture-industry subject reduced to a plastic prop granted brief prearranged 'free time,' and he ends on Adorno's residual hope: the very existence of these failed protesters, like the theory itself, proves some subjectivity survives the system.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 24 "Indiscernibles and Autonomous Viewers “Time to Write my Own Fucking Story”" — The Forests ask whether Westworld is self-referential modernist art or 'meta-kitsch,' reading the park's dueling productions (Sizemore's clichéd narratives versus Ford's ambitions, with Cullen's corporate meddling mirroring HBO's pressure on Nolan and Joy) through Kant's relocation of aesthetic judgment to the subjective, Greenberg's avant-garde/kitsch divide, Adorno's contrast of liberating autonomous art with standardized heteronomous commodity culture, and Danto's Brillo Box problem of indiscernibles. Guests mistaking Teddy for a fellow guest and actors' 'reverse-reveries' show that host/guest indiscernibility mirrors the show's own indiscernibility from formulaic prestige TV. Their conclusion: the series counts as art rather than entertainment only for 'autonomous viewers' alert to its self-referential critique, the viewer-side counterpart of Dolores's 'when I discover who I am, I'll be free.'
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 10 "1. Free Falling into Postmodernism" — Sewell reads Petty's 1976 debut through Jameson's postmodernism: Petty's music is a cut-and-paste amalgam of 1960s jangle, 1970s heartland rock and punk attitude whose pastiche dissolves the high/low art distinction as aesthetic production merges with commodity production, which is exactly why it feels timeless. He then applies Butler's performativity to Petty's "cool," arguing the persona was learned and performed so incessantly that Petty and his audience came to experience it as innate. Finally Baudrillard's hyperreal and simulacra frame the conclusion that there never was a "real" Petty, only copies of copies, yet if the perceived sincerity feels real and empowering, it is real enough.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 24 "12. When Money Shouldn’t Be King" — Berkey reconstructs Petty's two industry battles, the bankruptcy gambit to void the contract sold along with Shelter Records and the month-long standoff against MCA's $9.98 superstar pricing, then reads The Last DJ as Petty's considered position on the business of music. He argues Petty rejected subjectivism about music's value: because listeners can be mistaken about the value of their own enjoyment, a formal argument shows executives like "Joe" who program only what profits act wrongly, even if consumers willingly pay. "Money Becomes King" completes the critique, showing how profit-focus degrades the fan's quasi-religious concert experience and corrodes Johnny's motivation to make valuable music at all.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 45 "32 - Dreamers in the Night [ ]" — This fan-fiction interlude dramatizes the fandom debate aboard Galactica: Roslin voices the Frankfurt School view (a 'Scorpion School' of Adorno and Benjamin - mass culture as mindless absorption, reproduction destroying the artwork's aura), while aide Billy cites Henry Jenkins and Textual Poachers to defend fanzines as participatory culture repairing corporate ownership of myth, and a fan meeting wins the President over as community-building. Baltar and inner Number Six extend the argument: Six demands 'the singular truth of the show' against fan rewriting, and Baltar answers that the Cylons are themselves a fanfiction of the human brain - twelve unoriginal faces. Starbuck is revealed as the anonymous fanfic writer.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 13 "Resistance" — Reading Fifteen Million Merits through Marx, the chapter treats Bing's world of endless pedaling, Wraith Babes, and Hot Shot as a commodity society in which people themselves carry use and exchange values — Oliver the 'lemon,' Glee deemed 'quite worthless,' Abi's unsellable papier-mache penguin discarded as detritus. Marx's commodity fetish explains the universalized pricing in merits, and Lukacs-style reification shows things commanding people (Cuppliance compelling compliance). Adorno's culture industry explains why all the shows share one form and why Bing's glass-shard rebellion is absorbed as just another commodity, while Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man supplies the hope that reason, love (Bing's love for Abi as something 'real'), and switching off the media can still seed resistance.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 36 "The Real World" — Written as a choose-your-own-adventure whose branches mirror Bandersnatch's, the chapter treats you, the Netflix viewer, as the external force Stefan suspects: Libet-style readiness-potential neuroscience suggests conscious choice is an after-the-fact story, and compatibilist rescues (Frankfurt's second-order desires, Fischer's guidance control) founder on the 'BundyBot' argument that programmed desires are not freedom. Everett's many-worlds interpretation supplies the multiverse of 'one reality for each possible course of action,' and David Lewis's fixed-past block universe answers the grandfather paradox raised by Stefan's mirror-trip to die on the 8:45 train with his mother. Aristotle does double duty: the Poetics explains why Bandersnatch rightly limits your options (Sartrean absolute freedom would make a crappy story), and the Nicomachean Ethics on voluntary action pins moral responsibility for Stefan's murders on the viewer rather than the coerced Stefan. Adorno's culture industry asks whether Tuckersoft's 'hit factory' - and Black Mirror itself - can produce genuine art, while Kierkegaard's dread of irreversible choice is overturned by an episode that always lets you go back and try again.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 38 "Things Worth Believing" — Butterfield stages the Frankfurt School critique of her own Disney love: Marx's three alienations (from work, from others, from species-being) explain the Seven Dwarfs' 'dig dig dig' and the FastPass-scheduled vacation that converts leisure into consumption, while Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man diagnoses the parks' engineered euphoria and 'false needs' as a 'comfortable, smooth, reasonable, democratic unfreedom' that blunts protest — with Adorno adding that consumers see through the advertising and buy anyway. Against the critic, she argues a Disney trip done right can challenge alienation by reviving play, family togetherness, and childlike belief in 'things worth believing.'
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 32 "19. Looking Like Number 12" — Busk explains why 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' is so disturbing despite having no monsters: through Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry, standardized cultural products manufacture conformist subjects whose critical capacities and powers of resistance atrophy until difference itself looks pathological, as with Marilyn's doctors diagnosing her refusal. 'The After Hours' extends the diagnosis, with mannequin Marsha as the subject reduced to an industrial prop granted brief furloughs of 'free time.' Yet the very existence of Marilyn's and Marsha's doomed protests, like Adorno and Horkheimer's own theory, shows some subjectivity survives the production line.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 24 "Indiscernibles and Autonomous Viewers “Time to Write my Own Fucking Story”" — Forest and Beckley-Forest ask whether Westworld is self-referential 'high art' or 'meta-kitsch,' tracing aesthetic modernism from Kant's subjective turn through Greenberg's avant-garde/kitsch split and Adorno's autonomous versus heteronomous art. They read Sizemore's clichéd Western narratives and the park's stock characters as commodified kitsch that mirrors the show's own corporate constraints under HBO, and use Danto's Brillo Box problem of indiscernibles to argue that host/guest and entertainment/art distinctions lie in the viewer's reflection. Dolores's line 'when I discover who I am, I'll be free' models the Adorno-style liberation available to an alert viewer.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 20 "The Politics of Mad Science in The Fly and Dead Ringers" — R. Barton Palmer reads The Fly and Dead Ringers as a diptych on 'mad science' descended from Stevenson's Jekyll and Hyde rather than Frankenstein, in which the scientist turns the investigative gaze on himself and self-destructs. He grounds this in the Frankfurt School critique of Enlightenment (Adorno and Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment, Bacon's domination of nature, Marcuse's Eros and Civilization): Brundle's telepod and the Mantle twins' surgery expose the failure of Baconian objectivity and rationalization, with monstrousness emerging from within the divided self.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 19 "Film Noir and the Frankfurt School America as Wasteland in Edgar Ulmer's Detour" — Cantor argues that Ulmer's Detour deconstructs the American dream in a manner that closely parallels the Frankfurt school's culture critique. Al Roberts's westward journey toward success collapses into crime and doom, dramatizing Horkheimer and Adorno's claim in 'The Culture Industry' that Hollywood sells the masses an illusory lottery of hope (Haskell's horse 'Paradisical,' Sue's failed stardom) to reconcile them to capitalism. Cantor ties Roberts's disgust at jukebox music and his 'jazzing up' of Brahms directly to Adorno's polemics against mechanical reproduction and Benjamin's loss of the artwork's aura. He finally suggests both Ulmer and the émigré Marxists project a European elitist alienation onto an America they picture as an empty wasteland.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 19 "The Dialectic of Enlightenment in Metropolis" — Abrams reads Fritz Lang's Metropolis as anticipating Adorno and Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment by two decades. He maps the film's arc—from the Christian mythology of the catacombs, through Joh's technototalitarian rational city and the human-machine fusion of Rotwang's false Maria, back into ancient myth (the M-Machine as Moloch, the whore of Babylon, the Tower of Babel)—onto their thesis that Enlightenment reason turns totalitarian and reverts to mythology and madness. He ties reason's self-destruction to Nietzsche's will to power and contrasts the descent into 'absolute madness' with Hegel's progress toward absolute mind.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 21 "Disenchantment and Rebellion in Alphaville" — Woolfolk reads Godard's Alphaville as an imagination of spiritual disaster: the Alpha 60 computer's reduction of time to divisible units suppresses the Bergsonian durée and fundamental self, and the city's architecture of 'nonplaces' embodies Weber's disenchantment and the Frankfurt School's culture-industry critique. Following Charles Taylor, he argues disenchantment opens a new heroic framework of facing an indifferent universe with lucidity, in which Lemmy Caution—a postmodern pastiche of noir dandies—rebels through an aestheticized eroticism and Éluard's surrealist poetry, achieving a Weberian 'this-worldly salvation' of art and love that succeeds where Orwell's Julia and Huxley's Savage fail.
- **The Philosophy of Tim Burton**, ch. 21 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" — Olson argues Burton's signature saturated-versus-drab color palette in 'The Nightmare Before Christmas' and 'Corpse Bride' operates as a marketing strategy that commodifies childhood, conditioning children as future consumers who associate the films' colors with a utopian fantasy world to be bought back. She reads Jack's craving for the color of Christmas Town ('I want it for my own') through Lacan's objet petit a and through bell hooks's 'commodification of difference' (the Other consumed while its meaning is stripped away), and treats the Disney/Burton fairy-tale film as a Fordist commodity whose color palette—echoed on store shelves—drives product loyalty and nostalgic desire.
- **The Philosophy of Werner Herzog**, ch. 17 "On Experience and Illumination Werner Herzog’s Dialectical Relationship with Society" — Stefanie Baumann reads Herzog's attack on the 'accountant's truth' of the Minnesota Declaration alongside Horkheimer and Adorno's critical theory, arguing that the cult of facts reifies perception, creates norms, and serves the 'administered world' via the culture industry. She contends Herzog's films (Lessons of Darkness, Fata Morgana, Aguirre, The Enigma of Kaspar Hauser) resist this not by escaping society but by dialectically mediating singular, uncategorizable outsiders through the historically developed social order — Kaspar Hauser's 'obstinate otherness' exposing the social violence of enforced assimilation, a subversive constellation rather than an explicit political message.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 12 "3 Lawsuits, Master Narratives, and Artistic Commodification" — Mitchell examines Young's Geffen-era lawsuit (sued in 1983 for "uncharacteristic" music like Trans and Everybody's Rockin') and the competing rebel/misunderstood-artist/lost-in-the-video-era narratives around it. Using Heilbroner on capitalism's commodification of rebellious art and Mark Fisher's "capitalist realism" and pre-corporation of dissent (Cobain as spectacle), he argues that Young himself actively authored the "rocker-turned-folkie" and anti-commercial persona, so that even his gestures of resistance to the music business were absorbed as marketable integrity.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 24 "The Dalek Within" — Ed Webb and Mark Wardecker contrast the Fourth Doctor's refusal to abort the Daleks in "Genesis of the Daleks" with his half-human self's genocide in "Journey's End" to ask whether a genocidal species should be exterminated. Reading Daleks as Nazis and Hobbesian survivalists in a lawless state of nature, they argue their real horror is Arendt's banality of evil, bureaucratic order-following, and that Foucault's disciplinary institutions and the Frankfurt School's culture industry show humans can be "made" Dalek-like. Their moral: we must not exterminate the Dalek but guard against the Dalek within, since it took the Doctor's added humanity to commit the genocide.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 42 "The Doctor Dances" — Alexander Bertland uses Vico, Cassirer, and Horkheimer and Adorno to argue Doctor Who refuses to simply side with science over myth. Vico shows myth as world-constructing ritual that binds community and carries moral wisdom ('Snakedance's' Snakedance defeats the Mara; 'Meglos' shows myth's danger), while Horkheimer and Adorno's Dialectic of Enlightenment argues science is itself a limiting, mythical framework: the Doctor's insistence that 'fixed points' in time cannot be changed ('The Fires of Pompeii,' 'The Waters of Mars') reflects his own self-constructed scientific paradigm, not real necessity. The Doctor lives well by humbly balancing myth and science.
- **Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy**, ch. 6 "Screaming for Change" — Opening chapter that reframes punk not as fashion, genre, or subculture but as a philosophy, using Gramsci's hegemony as the analytic lens. It traces punk's history (Sex Pistols, the Clash, hardcore, NOFX, Bad Religion) and argues the movement's real target is the hegemonic mainstream that co-opts and commodifies dissent (Green Day/Offspring signing to majors as 'selling out'). Marx's alienation of the industrial worker is invoked to explain the dole-queue discontent that birthed British punk, positioning punk style and sound as surface manifestations of an underlying oppositional ideology.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 17 "8. Between Cynicism and Faith" — Buhlert contrasts the Apple TV+ series' reverent treatment of religion (the sincere anti-science faith of Synnax, the elaborate Luminism whose 'walking the spiral' ritual seems to vindicate that clones lack souls) with Asimov's cynical originals, where religion is Marx's 'opium of the people'. She shows the fake religion of Scientism in 'The Mayors' and the hypocritical Askonian elders in 'The Traders' treat faith as an instrument of control, situates this within Golden Age SF (Leiber's Gather, Darkness!, de Camp's Lest Darkness Fall) and its techno-optimism, and speculates on why the showrunners omitted Scientism.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 9 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Gerald Erion reads The Daily Show through Neil Postman's Amusing Ourselves to Death, arguing that Stewart's opening headline mockery of hurricane 'reporters in canoes,' 'Senior Correspondents,' and graphics packages like 'Mess O'Potamia' targets not the day's events but television's own entertainment bias, which renders even serious news trivial. He treats Stewart's Crossfire plea to 'stop hurting America,' the Jim Cramer 'Brawl Street' interview, and the Rally to Restore Sanity's '24-hour politico pundit perpetual panic conflictinator' as Postman-style critiques that a medium built to amuse cannot carry rational public discourse.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 32 "19. Looking Like Number 12" — Busk reads 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' through Horkheimer and Adorno's 'culture industry' and a philosophical account of subjectivity as active, critical agency. Marilyn's forced 'Transformation' into a standardized model (with banned books, 'Instant Smile,' and 'super soccer') dramatizes how commodified mass culture produces conformist, mannequin-like subjects who cannot resist—linking it to 'The After Hours,' where Marsha is literally a department-store mannequin. Yet Marilyn's and Marsha's very existence, like Adorno's theory, is a faint hopeful sign that critical subjectivity survives.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 12 "Gertrude McFuzz Should’ve Read Marx, or Sneetches of the World Unite" — Jacob Held uses the Once-ler, Pontoffel Pock, the Sneetches, and Gertrude McFuzz to explain Marx's theory of alienation. The Once-ler is the capitalist owning the means of Thneed production; Pontoffel Pock's dull pickle-works job shows labor severed from the worker's essence as a free, conscious producer (an idea Held traces to Hegel on self-expression through work). The Sneetches buying stars from Sylvester McMonkey McBean and Gertrude popping pill-berries dramatize how alienated people chase belonging through consumption, which Held elaborates via Fromm's 'having vs being' and Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry, concluding the fault lies not in the characters but in a society that denies self-realization through labor.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 25 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Wear traces the espresso aesthetic from the idealized, egalitarian Italian caffè—which he reads as an 'aestheticized Marxist' image of identical shots for businessman and street sweeper—to its dilution under neoliberal consumer choice, epitomized by the endless-customization L.A. Story 'half-caf twist of lemon' scene. He invokes Kant's Critique of Judgement and the sublime to argue that flavor and taste-judgment are neglected aesthetic faculties, and enlists the Frankfurt School (Adorno, Benjamin, Marcuse) and Bourdieu's cultural capital to explain how the market absorbs the espresso's beauty. He concludes that a single humble shot, as a memorial to the vast exploited labor chain behind it, is a truer aesthetic object than a branded frappuccino.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 16 "The Fall of the House of Ulmer Europe vs. America in the Gothic Vision of The Black Cat" — Cantor reads Edgar Ulmer's The Black Cat (1934) as a European emigre's Gothic allegory of Europe vs. America, with Karloff's architect Poelzig and Lugosi's psychiatrist Werdegast as mirror-image 'living dead' fixated on the horrors of World War I. He connects Poelzig's modernist house-over-Fort-Marmaros to a Freudian map of ego and id and to the war-driven rise of psychoanalysis, and reads the naive, unconscious American honeymooners against the cultured but nihilistic Europeans. He explicitly links the film's high-culture/pop-culture opposition to Heidegger's vision of Europe squeezed between a leveling America and Russia and to the Frankfurt School critique of American mass entertainment.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 21 "Kitsch and Camp and Things That Go Bump in the Night; or, Sontag and Adorno at the (Horror) Movies" — Johnston uses his childhood TV horror host Sir Graves Ghastly to distinguish kitsch from camp in the horror genre. Drawing on Greenberg's 'Avant-garde and Kitsch' and Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry, he argues that the Universal Horror sequels, Jaws, and most slasher films are kitsch: nonchallenging, formulaic variations that pacify consumers, while autonomous works like Carpenter's They Live or Craven's Scream interrogate the genre. Via Sontag's 'Notes on Camp' and Isherwood's making-fun-of versus making-fun-out-of, he sorts They Live, Scream, I Know What You Did Last Summer, and Scary Movie into deliberate camp, naive camp, and mere kitsch.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 6 "NOTES" — William Irwin's introduction argues philosophy must engage popular culture rather than fear it as Plato feared Homer and the poets. He invokes Plato's allegory of the cave to make the case that the philosopher who has left the cave must return and 'learn to see the shadows again'—use The Simpsons, The Matrix and Seinfeld as the vernacular through which prisoners can be led out—and answers Adorno-style culture-industry worries that mass entertainment is mere opiate. He closes by echoing Aristotle's serious treatment of the popular art (tragedy) of his day as warrant for treating today's pop culture philosophically.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 9 "NOTES" — Irwin asks 'what is popular culture?', rejecting Noel Carroll's 'mass art' accessibility criterion (using the Sex Pistols, Slipknot and the Beatles as counterexamples of inaccessible-yet-popular art) and Walter Benjamin's aura/mechanical-reproduction account, settling on popular culture as 'artifacts and subjects of mass interest and appreciation.' He rebuts Adorno's and Zizek's culture-industry charge that pop culture (e.g. The Matrix, The X-Files) ideologically ensnares audiences, and again deploys Plato's cave and the returning prisoner—citing Socrates meeting interlocutors where they are—to justify using pop culture as a bridge to philosophy while warning against 'abuse' (studying pop culture as philosophy).
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 13 "NOTES" — Richard Shusterman defends the entertainment value of popular art from a pragmatist ('meliorist') stance, tracing entertainment's genealogy through Plato, Aristotle, Montaigne, Kant, Hegel, Nietzsche, Heidegger and Adorno—whose 'culture industry' opposes pleasure to cognition. Using rap (KRS-One's 'Edutainment', Public Enemy, Ice-T) and T.S. Eliot's 'superior amusement,' he argues knowledge and enjoyment are compatible. He rejects Hannah Arendt's contrast of imperishable art vs. life-serving entertainment, and critiques G.E. Moore's Principia Ethica 'method of absolute isolation' for intrinsic value, replacing it with a Deweyan transactional account in which even intrinsic values are relational and temporal.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 18 "NOTES" — South reads Batman, Batgirl, and Catwoman comics through J. M. Bernstein's Adorno-derived account of the 'damaged life' lived under Weberian rationalization and the disenchantment of the world. The Joker's 'one bad day' in The Killing Joke embodies 'affective skepticism'—the split between rational universal norms and agent-specific motivation—while the debate between moral internalism and externalism (which he ties to Kant-style abstract justification) expresses the hurt of a disenchanted world where justifying and motivating reasons no longer converge. Barbara Gordon's 'because I can,' Bruce Wayne's vow, and Selina Kyle's turn toward 'basic human dignity' exemplify Bernstein's 'fugitive ethics,' fragile promises that restore authority outside juridico-legal channels and produce genuine happiness in damaged lives.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 23 "21. Black Mirror as Philosophy A Dark Reflection of Human Nature" — The chapter asks whether Black Mirror condemns technology or human nature, and argues for the latter: the 'black mirror' reflects the viewer's character. It tests and rejects the reading of the show as depicting Bostrom-style existential risk or superintelligence (via 'Metalhead' and 'San Junipero') and rejects that Clark and Chalmers's extended-mind coupling (the 'grain' in 'The Entire History of You,' 'Arkangel,' 'Crocodile') destroys human identity.
