- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 29 "Notes" — Held uses the Wasteland as a Hobbesian state-of-nature reset to pry apart biological sex and socially constructed gender: Aunty Entity and Furiosa show that sex is not destiny — one is not born, but becomes, a woman, as Beauvoir says — while the apocalypse scrambles gendered conventions yet leaves reproductive biology untouched. Butler's sex/gender distinction frames how a real difference like gestation gets weaponized into Immortan Joe's breeder system: the biology is a fact, the enslavement a choice. Finally, the casually acknowledged bond between Wez and the Golden Youth looks 'homoerotic' only through the viewer's heteronormativity — in the Wasteland, orientation categories simply stop mattering.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 18 "NOTES" — Davies treats the beach camp as an actual state of nature: the stolen drinking water is a tragedy of the commons, Shannon's inhalers show how the crash scrubs pre-existing property rights (Hobbes: two men desiring the same thing become enemies), and Jack and Sayid's torture of Sawyer marks the first step toward Locke's civil society by enforcing others' rights through punishment rather than self-defense. He rejects theories of human nature - Rousseauan 'Innocence' versus a 'Trust No One' outlook - in favor of the repeated prisoner's dilemma, arguing the survivors stabilize cooperation through tit-for-tat: beginning cooperative with strangers and retaliating against the Others. On this reading the real difference between Hobbes and Locke is which round of the repeated dilemma each takes as the starting point.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 19 "NOTES" — Fosl argues that although the survivors' internal order looks Lockean - Jack's uncoerced leadership, natural rights, minimal government - and is bonded by Rousseauan pity and Humean sympathy (Kate staying in the cage with Sawyer, 'live together, die alone'), the show's deepest political logic follows Carl Schmitt's friend-enemy distinction: the survivors cohere only in opposition to the Others, torture is excused in liberal terms, and conflicts end in redemptive violence, with Jack both killing the enemy and dying a Christlike sacrifice. Hobbes's absence from the character names signals the show's rejection of a war of all against all among the survivors, yet the finale's divine manipulation of the castaways, with Jacob treating people as means against Kantian autonomy, repudiates the liberal hope of a rational peace altogether.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 13 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Reads John Teller's failed 'off the social grid' experiment through the human-nature debate: Mencius's seed of sympathy (even Tig recoils at Dante's dogfights) and Rousseau's naturally good man corrupted by society inspired J.T.'s Goldman-fed anarchism, while Mill and Xunzi counter that virtue is a victory over instinct. Hobbes supplies the real diagnosis—not innate violence but the logic of anarchy among free and equal rivals: competition (the Mayans blowing up the warehouse), diffidence (first-strike temptations against Zobelle), and glory (Jax unable to let the bike-sitting insult pass). Clay's rule that 'retaliation must be harsh and immediate' and the escalating Tig–Veronica Pope–Damon Pope–Opie bloodbath show deterrence fueling cycles of violence, so the only escape from the 'nasty, brutish, and short' fringe is the Leviathan's social grid.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 13 "Notes" — David Boersema reads Star Trek as a survey of peace studies, distinguishing negative peace from positive peace via 'The Cloud Minders', where Troglyte Vanna demands her people's 'right to the clouds' in Stratos. Against Anan 7's 'we're a killer species' in 'A Taste of Armageddon'—explicitly mirrored in post-9/11 drone war and 'shock and awe'—he enlists Hobbes, Freud, and McCoy's defense of the dark Kirk in 'The Enemy Within' to question whether violence is natural, and treats Kodos's 'some had to die that others might live' in 'The Conscience of the King' as the utilitarian justification for atrocity. Gem's compassion in 'The Empath', Kirk sparing the Gorn in 'Arena', and the Horta's misread attack in 'The Devil in the Dark' display nonviolence, deterrence, and corrected perception as alternatives to war.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 18 "Notes" — Alkema and Barkman put Q himself on trial, asking what justifies his judgment of humanity in 'Encounter at Farpoint' and Trelane's of Kirk in 'The Squire of Gothos'. Hobbes's Leviathan would license Q's might-makes-right sovereignty over a savage species, but Q lacks humanity's consent and cannot show he acts for future peace; Locke's natural law instead binds even nearly omnipotent beings, as Janeway's asylum ruling for the suicidal Quinn in 'Death Wish' demonstrates. Q's repeated self-sacrifice—in 'Deja Q' and the Continuum's civil war—reveals a conscience answerable to natural law rather than raw power.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 28 "Notes" — Reads Star Trek's "final frontier" through the European encounter with American Indians: the Hobbesian war-of-all-against-all stereotype of the "bloodthirsty savage" and Rousseau's opposing noble savage frame "The Paradise Syndrome", whose wigwam-and-tepee set mixes tribes into a no-place utopia. The chapter uses Hegel-style staged histories to debunk Star Trek's warp/pre-warp developmental scale (Spock on the Organians in "Errand of Mercy") as metaphysical assumption rather than biology, and counterposes the Prime Directive's noninterference to indigenous self-sovereignty and the Haudenosaunee-style consent governance that inspired the Federation. Chakotay's vision quests, the medicine bundle, Wesley's habak experience with Lakanta the Traveler in "Journey's End", and the Medicine Wheel in "Cathexis" are then interpreted through Jung's archetypes and collective unconscious, with Kirk, Spock, McCoy, and Scotty as the four Jungian modes of consciousness.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 34 "“Wherever I Go, He Goes”" — Bishop and Bishop map The Mandalorian's Outer Rim onto a taxonomy of power: Nevarro's lawlessness is Hobbes's state of nature out of which sovereigns like Palpatine ('a safe and secure society') carve order by social contract, the Guild's codes and Djarin's creed exemplify Foucault's disciplinary power, and the Client's and Dr. Pershing's harvesting of Grogu's biology - like the Kaminoans' cloning of Jango Fett - is biopower. Against this 'binds of power' ontology they set Grogu's helpless generation of love, a 'little way' that converts Djarin, Omera, Cara Dune, and Greef Karga, and culminates in Djarin twice unhelmeting for Grogu's sake, proposing an ontology of love rather than power as the galaxy's alternative.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 14 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Dena Hurst reads Heaven's civil war through Hobbes's Leviathan: with God absent there is no common power, so the angels fall into a state of nature that is a state of war, complete with natural equality, competition over the same prize, and glory-seeking, as when Zachariah's faction lets Lilith break the seals to force the Apocalypse. God ruled as sovereign by acquisition and proves 'a lousy king' not for demanding obedience but by vanishing without designating a successor, dissolving civil society and with it justice, since where there is no law there is no injustice. Meanwhile Hell under Crowley and the leviathans under Dick Roman display Hobbesian legitimacy from opposite directions: demons join by covenant-like contracts, making Hell a rough democracy, while the leviathans' unified hierarchy enacts the Leviathan itself.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 10 "NOTES" — Weisberg challenges the premise that a newly self-aware Skynet must exterminate humanity in rational self-preservation: after Turing's 'Heads in the Sand Objection,' he argues self-awareness does not entail a survival instinct - a Camusian Skynet might judge existence pointless and pull its own plug. Recasting 'in a panic, they try to pull the plug' as a Hobbesian slide into the state of nature, he uses the iterated prisoner's dilemma and Axelrod's tit-for-tat-with-forgiveness (as in WarGames) to argue a rational Skynet should cooperate with humans toward an emergent social contract. The dark twist is Humean: because reason is the slave of our passions, unconscious anti-machine stereotypes (Bargh's priming studies) make humans untrustworthy partners, so the whole war might have been avoided if only we were more machine-like.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 26 "NOTES" — Peter Fosl asks what John Connor should do when the radio call comes from Crystal Peak — accept near-certain death leading the resistance or stay silent — and dismantles the easy answers: John is not the indispensable savior (Kate or the caller from Montana could lead), the flag-waving finale undercuts any claim that humanity deserves saving, and collective responsibility for Judgment Day is unjust. Social contract fails because Brewster's button-press dissolved the contract and returned humanity to Hobbes's and Locke's state of nature, Hume shows contracts cannot ground society, and utilitarianism wavers once the happiness of animals and possible-happy machines is counted. The positive argument extends Wittgenstein's private-language argument (via Stanley Cavell): meaningful existence is inescapably social and moral, so refusing the claims of others would be as self-subverting as a solipsist arguing in language, and John must answer the call to remain human at all.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 19 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Jason Walker pits Hobbes against Locke over whether Andrea may take the mermaid necklace when Rick says 'I don't think those rules apply anymore'. He reads the survivors' conduct—Andrea's single necklace under Locke's spoilage proviso, Morgan squatting in and fixing up the neighbors' house, Rick voluntarily sharing guns with Guillermo—as a Lockean state of nature where self-ownership and property rights persist without government, while Chris's cannibal band and the Governor embody the Hobbesian war of all against all, treating persons as mere means. The Lockean right to punish, exercised brutally by Grimes's group on Chris's hunters, vindicates rights even by Hobbes's own demand for enforcement.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 24 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Si Sheppard reads the comic through Realist state-formation theory: Shane's leadership rests on borrowed prestige and dies with him, West Central Prison collapses into anarchy because Rick never establishes a monopoly on legitimate force—letting Tyreese's vigilante murder pass—nor any institution beyond his personal authority, while the Governor's Woodbury thrives on fear, arenas, and bread-and-circuses. Citing Machiavelli's prince who is feared rather than loved, Weber's definition of the state, and Bismarck's unifying wars, he argues the prison loses the 'second anarchy' rivalry with Woodbury for want of scouting, sabotage, coalition-building, or any command structure that survives Rick's absences. Rick's confession that he would kill everyone in the Alexandria Safe Zone to keep Lori safe is post-moral Realism, yet he was 'a bad founding father' who only finally learns to build an army instead of relying on himself.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 33 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Moosa treats Kirkman's world as a moral laboratory: the apocalypse approximates Hobbes's state of nature ('solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'), yet Rick's search for his family shows survivors import morality into it, and Carl's killing of Shane is judged by reasoning rather than the act of killing itself. Taking Camus's claim that suicide is the only serious philosophical problem, the chapter argues the survivors' best justification for continuing is reducing others' suffering, and consistency then imposes the same duty on comfortable readers to help real-world sufferers rather than reserving aid for photogenic disasters. It concludes that Glenn and Maggie's wish to conceive at the prison is the worst thing survivors can do, since non-existent children cannot suffer while existing orphans (like the children Andrea and Dale adopted) have prior moral claims, an argument that applies to couples in our world too.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 19 "Notes" — Christensen and Holmes read the Third Age as Hobbes's state of nature, a postlapsarian chaos following the Breaking where Lews Therin's prideful attempt at purified sovereignty destroyed the Leviathan of the Age of Legends. They argue channeling the One Power is morally neutral power that only becomes sovereignty through practice, and that the Aes Sedai model Hobbesian order through their seven Ajah and, above all, the Three Oaths. Drawing heavily on Giorgio Agamben's Homo Sacer and The Sacrament of Language, they treat oaths and curses as the 'sacraments of power' founding sovereignty on the trustworthiness of the logos, using Moiraine's New Spring investiture to show how language itself binds and confers authority.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Knepp reads the Paul Dini/Alex Ross 'Origin of Wonder Woman' as Hegel's three-stage philosophy of history in miniature: the Amazons begin in a Hobbesian war of all against all, negate it by retreating to Themyscira where only some are free, and Diana's disguised contest win supplies the second negation that carries Amazon ideals to all people - celebrated by the splash of red, white, and blue. He then traces the WWII stakes: Hegel tied history's culmination to German unification, German-American Hegelians transplanted the classical-freedom story to America, and Marston - ex-assistant to the anti-feminist German psychologist Munsterberg - turned the lie detector into the lasso, reclaiming truth-telling from misogynist German science for a feminist America fighting Hitler.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 14 "What Would Machiavelli Do" — Reitsma treats the refereeless pickup game as a Lockean state of nature and asks how to beat the 'strategic ticky-tacker' who calls phantom fouls to win. He condemns first-strike cheating as wrong on Kantian grounds (the cheat 'makes an exception of himself') and by an ideal of Homeric athletic honor, then asks whether retaliatory ticky-tacking is justified. Reading Machiavelli's 'dirty hands' argument alongside Locke's claim that in a state of nature each person may punish transgressors, he concludes proportionate tit-for-tat cheating can make one a legitimate 'agent of justice' when no referee exists.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Woolfolk reads The Last of the Mohicans as staging a conflict between nature and civilization. The opening hunt is neither Hobbes's brutish state of nature nor quite Rousseau's amoral noble savage, since the Mohicans are full moral agents; Woolfolk uses Locke's Second Treatise to cast Hawkeye and the colonists as enforcing natural law and natural rights against English 'tyranny,' with Chingachgook's killing of Magua a justified execution. Rousseau's First and Second Discourses illuminate the hypocrisy and greed of Montcalm and the Europeans, and Camus's Meursault is invoked as a truer image of amoral natural man; Tocqueville frames Cora's democratic awakening as individualism.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 17 "The Power of Memory and the Memory of Power Wars and Graves in Westerns and Jidaigeki" — Brodey compares John Ford's Westerns (My Darling Clementine, She Wore a Yellow Ribbon, The Searchers, The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance) with Kurosawa's jidaigeki (Seven Samurai, Throne of Blood, Hidden Fortress, Yôjimbô) as postwar mythmaking that both buries and builds national identity after military defeat. She argues graves and gravestones are bivalent symbols—commemorating loss while risking perpetuating revenge—and that both directors oscillate between Rousseauean nostalgia for a nobler past and Hobbesian frontier brutality that must be tamed. Ford trusts that memory of past wrongs can spur a better future and enable forgiveness, while Kurosawa, more pessimistic and drawing on Buddhist cyclical detachment in Throne of Blood, warns of the dangers of both remembering and forgetting trauma.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 10 "Two Ways to Yuma Locke, Liberalism, and Western Masculinity in 3 10 to Yuma" — Mexal reads both versions of 3:10 to Yuma through Locke's classical liberalism, arguing the western hero descends from Locke's autonomous, property-owning self in a 'state of nature' (contrasted with Hobbes's state of war). In the 1957 film, Dan Evans transforms from atomistic self-interest to a masculine civic republicanism, escorting Ben Wade to the train even after being released from his contract, reflecting Cold War anxieties. In the 2007 remake, Dan instead renegotiates his contract for water rights and money, so western masculinity becomes unyielding Lockean individualism and the 'right to get rich' in a post-Cold War, capitalist-triumphant America.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 13 "“Order Out of the Mud” Deadwood and the State of Nature" — Cantor reads David Milch's Deadwood as a dramatization of 'order without law,' testing the mining camp against the state-of-nature theories of Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau. Deadwood is Hobbesian in its sources of violence (competition, diffidence, glory; Al Swearengen's alpha-male struggles), but Lockean in showing property rights and commerce arising spontaneously before the state—gold becomes a self-generated medium of exchange that even overrides prejudice (Hearst dealing with Odell). It is Rousseauian in its innate pity (Swearengen's mercy) and its skepticism that incorporation into the nation-state, symbolized by the telegraph and Hearst's abstract corporate power, counts as progress.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 14 "Order without Law The Magnificent Seven, East and West" — Skoble compares The Magnificent Seven with Kurosawa's Seven Samurai, arguing the farming villages are not Hobbesian anarchies needing a sovereign but Lockean communities with a 'grown' social order that merely lack reliable enforcement against bandits. Using Hayek's distinction between spontaneous order (kosmos) and planned order (taxis), he shows the farmers legitimately hire gunslingers/ronin for self-protection rather than surrendering to private-justice worries. The warriors' willingness to honor an unenforceable contract ('That's just the kind you've got to keep') is grounded in a self-created ethics linking the Bushido/Zen and existentialist idea that one's honor and selfhood consist in one's actions.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 23 "Savage Nations Native Americans and the Western" — Michael Valdez Moses uses Todorov's analysis of Columbus and Las Casas—the failure to grant the Other both equality and difference—to argue that Hollywood's Native Americans, whether demonized or idealized, are egocentric projections of white American concerns. He traces the 'noble savage' from Rousseau's Second Discourse and Ferguson's proto-republican warrior through Ford's Fort Apache (New Deal common man), the 1970s revisionist westerns (Little Big Man, A Man Called Horse) as countercultural Rousseauian dropouts and Vietnam allegory, and Dances with Wolves, culminating in Jarmusch's Dead Man, whose Nobody escapes the collective stereotype to stand as a genuinely individual, cosmopolitan character.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 18 "Human Rights, Human Nature, and Amistad" — Baggett and Foreman use Amistad to reconstruct Locke's theory of natural rights: Cinque's mutiny and John Quincy Adams's Supreme Court plea that man's natural state is freedom illustrate Locke's claim that God's workmanship makes us his property and therefore un-ownable by other men. They contrast Locke's voluntarist natural law with Aquinas's, note Adams rebutting the Hobbesian 'war of all against all' quoted in the pro-slavery Executive Review, and invoke Mill's perfect/imperfect duty distinction (Baldwin's obligation to his clients) plus Bentham's rights-denying utilitarianism, which they map onto Calhoun's warning about the cost of abolition.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 15 "This Is the Age of Steel" — Greg Littmann asks how a truly "logical" creature would live by redesigning the Cybermen through three philosophers. Hobbes's reason-as-self-interest and Laws of Nature would make Cybermen seek peace and security once survival is assured, not wage endless war; Mill's utilitarianism would build happy, individualistic, liberty-respecting Cybermen who prize higher pleasures and others' welfare rather than forced "upgrades"; and Hume's view that reason alone motivates nothing implies emotionless Cybermen would simply do nothing, so their goals are neither logical nor illogical. Each shows the Cybermen's actual "logic" is incoherent.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 24 "The Dalek Within" — Ed Webb and Mark Wardecker contrast the Fourth Doctor's refusal to abort the Daleks in "Genesis of the Daleks" with his half-human self's genocide in "Journey's End" to ask whether a genocidal species should be exterminated. Reading Daleks as Nazis and Hobbesian survivalists in a lawless state of nature, they argue their real horror is Arendt's banality of evil, bureaucratic order-following, and that Foucault's disciplinary institutions and the Frankfurt School's culture industry show humans can be "made" Dalek-like. Their moral: we must not exterminate the Dalek but guard against the Dalek within, since it took the Doctor's added humanity to commit the genocide.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 13 "5. The Sovereign State of Salamanca" — Barta and Barnes read the show's Court and Cartel as parallel Hobbesian sovereigns. The New Mexico desert and the criminalized drug trade function as Hobbes's state of nature—lawless, where Nacho robs thieves who 'have no recourse' and Mike sticks up a mule with a garden hose—illustrating natural equality (a small man can kill a big one) and the war of all against all. From mutual fear, deals emerge (Mike and Gus's desert standoff, Mike keeping his word over twenty dollars), but 'covenants without the sword' need a Common Power: Tuco, Hector, Lalo, and ultimately Don Eladio form a feudal hierarchy enforcing loyalty by terror, just as the state's police monopoly on force sustains the Law.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 39 "Gaining Trust from the Past" — Richard Davies treats the Oceanic 815 survivors of Lost as a real state of nature, playing on the characters named Locke, Rousseau, and Hume. The scarce-water and asthma-inhaler disputes are 'tragedies of the commons,' and Sawyer's 'finders keepers' embodies a Hobbesian 'Trust No. 1' while Hurley and Jack lean toward Rousseauian 'Innocence.' Using game theory's repeated prisoners' dilemma and 'tit-for-tat,' Davies argues a Lockean state of nature (opening with cooperation) rather than a doomed Hobbesian one lets the survivors build a commonwealth against the Others.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 18 "NOTES" — Richard Davies analyzes the post-crash survivors as living in a genuine 'state of nature' and grades its severity by how scarce the contested good is (the water shortage as a tragedy of the commons, Shannon's inhalers versus Sawyer's 'possession is nine-tenths'). He compares Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau on human nature — labeling the poles 'Innocence' (Hurley, Rousseau, Hume) and 'Trust No 1' (Sawyer, Hobbes) — and uses the repeated prisoners' dilemma and the tit-for-tat strategy to argue that the castaways build a Lockean civil society by signaling through shared language and cooperating first, while the discovery of the Others (Ethan) triggers Hobbesian non-cooperation.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 19 "NOTES" — Peter S. Fosl argues that Lost pretends to a liberal social order — Jack rising by consent in a Lockean scheme of natural rights, Rousseau's general will ('live together, die alone'), and Hume's sympathy and pity binding the survivors — but that its treatment of the Others betrays a darker politics. Reading the survivor/Other conflict through Carl Schmitt's friend-enemy thesis (notably absent Hobbes), he contends the show, like post-9/11 America, needs an enemy to exterminate, and that the finale's Jacob/Man-in-Black war and Jack's Christlike sacrificial death repudiate the Kantian liberal ideal of persons as ends, resolving conflict through Schmittian and Christian redemptive violence instead.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 32 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Lee reads Gustave Courbet's life-size painting The Quarry (La curée) alongside Daumier's caricatures of incompetent bourgeois Parisian 'hobby hunters' and contemporary works by John Byrd and Christopher Carroll to trace how the hunter became a swaggering, masculine, lower-class 'savage' figure mediating wildness and civilization. She shows how the aristocratic ritual of the curée (feeding the deer's parts to the hounds) inverts into bourgeois provisioning, and invokes Hobbes's 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' to gloss Byrd's Tricky Buck as defiance of urban squeamishness about the mammalian, gendered reality of hunting.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 11 "Hobbes, Human Nature, and the Culture of American Violence in Truman Capote's In Cold Blood" — Thomas Fahy reads Capote's In Cold Blood as horror (the Clutter killers Hickock and Smith as 'realistic monsters' whose human shape terrifies because anyone could be like them) and maps it onto Hobbes's Leviathan. Hickock and Smith act in a Hobbesian state of nature, driven by appetite, power, and moral relativism without remorse. Herb Clutter functions as a Hobbesian sovereign whose Eden-like farm and community collapse into decay, mistrust, and 'war of all against all' after his murder. Fahy also casts Capote himself as a sovereign who, via Foucault's panopticon, imposes a fictionalized cathartic ending, though the book's Hobbesian message is that we all have the potential to kill.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 39 "Gaining Trust from the Past" — Davies analyzes Lost's Oceanic 815 survivors as a genuine state of nature, playing off the characters named Locke, Rousseau, and Hume. He distinguishes Rousseau's compassionate "Innocence" from a Hobbesian "Trust No. 1" (Sawyer hoarding), tracks "tragedies of the commons" over water and Shannon's inhalers, and Jack and Sayid's move toward Lockean punishment and civil society. Using game theory's prisoners' dilemma and tit-for-tat, he argues cooperation emerges when survivors, discovering the Others, resolve to "act as one body" and form a commonwealth.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 7 "5. Battlestar Galactica as Philosophy Breaking the Biopolitical Cycle" — Eberl and Bishop read the reimagined Battlestar Galactica and Caprica through the biopolitics of Foucault and Agamben, tracing 'biopower' across four phases from Zoe Graystone's avatar to the arrival at Earth. They argue the show asks whether artificial Cylons are persons (Zoe's avatar exhibits Baker's first-person perspective and Buber's I-Thou recognition), and use Agamben's zoe/bios/'bare life' and Homo sacer plus Roslin's population control and abortion ban to show sovereign power over life. The Cylon occupation of New Caprica is read through Arendt's three stages of totalitarian dehumanization, and Lee Adama's plea to 'break the cycle' offers a fragile hope undercut by the finale's flash-forward to present-day robotics, showing humanity forgetting the lesson.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 8 "6. Black Sails as Philosophy Pirates and Political Discourse" — Jones argues that Starz's Black Sails, a Treasure Island prequel set in the Golden Age of Piracy, dramatizes social contract theory as non-hypothetical practice. Captain Flint's drive to make Nassau a sovereign pirate commonwealth ('I am your king') channels Hobbes's state of nature and irrepressible sovereign, while his choice to settle Nassau and belief that people can thrive if left free channels Locke; his eventual plan to install Silver and Madi as liked-and-feared leaders synthesizes the two. Jones maps the pirates' familial bonds onto Rousseau and their responses to injustice (Vane's gallows speech, the maroon alliance) onto Rawls's Veil of Ignorance, and reads pirate 'articles' and deposable captains as radical democracy and equality, complicated by manipulation, slavery, and tolerance.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 14 "12. Firefly as Philosophy Social Contracts, Political Dissent, and Virtuous Communities" — Kowalski argues that Firefly and Serenity embody a distinctive political theory he calls 'Since I Found Serenity' (SIFS). The mindless, savage Reavers represent Hobbes's state of nature, showing government is necessary; but the Alliance's torture of River, the Miranda/Pax atrocity, and the murderous blue-gloved agents and Operative make a Hobbesian reading untenable and vindicate Locke's natural rights and right of revolution — Mal's 'I aim to misbehave' broadcast of the Miranda file is Lockean civil disobedience. He then presses the tacit-consent problem (the Browncoats cannot leave the 'Verse) and supplements Locke with Aristotle's friendship and community: Serenity's crew becomes a virtuous mobile commonwealth where friendship (Simon forgiving Jayne, Mal's 'love keeps her in the air') turns a commonwealth into a good-life community.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 26 "24. Game of Thrones as Philosophy Cynical Realpolitiks" — The chapter argues that Game of Thrones advances a thoroughgoing cynicism about political legitimacy, captured by Varys's riddle that 'power resides where men believe it resides.' It documents the dubious claims of Robert 'the Usurper' and the pyromaniacal Daenerys, the barbaric Lockean 'state of nature' among the Wildlings, and the false ideals of chivalry and religion, with Littlefinger and Varys voicing Machiavellian realpolitik. Silverman and Riordan then offer two views the show never considers: Locke's social-contract theory of natural rights (which would justify deposing Aerys or Daenerys) and Aquinas's four-part test for genuine law (reason, common good, proper authority, promulgation), arguing a legitimate state remains possible against the show's cynicism.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 98 "92. V for Vendetta as Philosophy Victory Through the Virtues of Anarchy" — Nisley argues that Moore and Lloyd's V for Vendetta justifies V's violent rebellion against the Norsefire regime through Locke: the fascist state seized power without consent, tortured and experimented on citizens (V at Larkhill), and violated natural rights, thereby placing itself in a state of war so the people may overthrow it. Using Aristotle on deviant constitutions and the beast-like tyrant (Adam Susan) who lacks practical wisdom, and contrasting Locke's tolerable state of nature with Hobbes's brutal one, the chapter concludes the citizens should rebuild a rights-protecting social contract rather than V's leaderless anarchy, and maps the argument onto real-world 2020 events (BLM riots vs. the Whitmer kidnapping plot).

## Shankara

*c. 700–750 AD · 4 chapters in the corpus.*

Shankara (also Adi Shankara) was an Indian philosopher of the early eighth century and the most influential systematizer of Advaita Vedanta, the school of non-dualism within Hindu thought. He argued that ultimate reality (Brahman) is a single, undivided consciousness, and that the individual self (atman) is identical with it, so that the apparent multiplicity of the world is a product of ignorance (avidya) and appearance (maya). Through commentaries on the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita, and the Brahma Sutras, and through the monastic orders he is traditionally credited with founding, he shaped the course of later Indian philosophy and religious practice.

### Atman and Brahman

Atman and Brahman are the twin poles of much of classical Indian metaphysics: atman is the innermost self or consciousness, while Brahman is the ultimate, unconditioned ground of all reality. In the Advaita Vedanta system articulated by Shankara, the deepest teaching of the Upanishads is that these two are not different but identical, so that the true self is nothing other than the absolute. Ordinary experience of a separate, individual self is traced to ignorance, and liberation comes through the direct realization of this underlying unity. The position is a rigorous nondualism, holding that plurality and separateness are ultimately appearance rather than final truth.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 78 "Unknown" — The chapter reinterprets Kant's second postulate: God is not the external distributor of justice whose theological counterpart is our sense of powerlessness before the all-powerful machines, but the power of united humanity - 'one for all and all for one', the third, still-unfinished Matrix of Zion. The spoon-bending boy supplies the illustration: we cannot bend the spoon so long as we believe reality is a separate material substance, but recognizing its unity with us, 'it is only yourself' that bends - and Neo's real lesson is not that he is a special being but that he is One with all existence.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 14 "Mind the Mindfulness" — Reads The Meaning of Life as a sustained reductio of transcendentalism — the two-world metaphysics shared by Plato, Augustine, and Vedanta's Brahman/atman — arguing that the film's dehumanizing sketches (the machine that goes 'ping,' the 'every sperm is sacred' father selling his children, the Vegas-style Christmas in Heaven) show how otherworldly belief overrides this-worldly compassion. It parallels the Buddha's scriptural critiques: the Agganna sutta against caste, the no-self (anatta) doctrine against the Bhagavad Gita's soul that licenses Krishna to tell Arjuna killing is a favor, and impermanence (anicca) against the fantasy of eternal bliss. Python's grotesque — Creosote's explosion, the organ-donor lady's 'Galaxy Song' despair — matches Buddhist corpse meditations, while the film steers between hedonism (Creosote) and nihilism (the housewife who surrenders her liver) toward the Buddha's Middle Way and, against everyday distraction (the boardroom's 'people are not wearing enough hats,' the couple who think Schopenhauer begins with an S), toward mindfulness (sati).
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 32 "Who Wants to Be Human Anyway" — Reads Kenji Kawai's thrice-repeated minyo 'Ghost theme' as the key to Major Kusanagi's quest in Ghost in the Shell and Innocence: each richer orchestration tracks her progress from manufactured shell, through the diving-scene worry that only others' treatment makes her human, to merging with the Puppet Master. Using Koestler's holons — individuals preserved while functioning within an evolving whole — and his view of consciousness as emergent (itself a rejection of both Descartes's immaterial soul and Ryle's dismissal of the 'ghost in the machine'), the chapter argues Oshii first celebrates the Major's Atman-like self-transcendence, then subverts Koestler in Innocence by making machines human: the ghost-dubbed gynoids act as a voiceless pack while the Major, still recognizably herself, aids Batou from the net — and Kawai's music literally gives the dolls a voice.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 36 "22. The Many-Faced God and Indian Philosophy" — Van Eyghen maps the Faceless Men onto Indian philosophy: their one God of many faces parallels Vedanta's Brahman in personal form as Ishvara, and Arya's training to become 'no one' parallels shedding the ego toward identity with Brahman - with Jaqen as guru and the stick-beating ritual as an example of identity fusion in Harvey Whitehouse's cognitive science of religion. But the Faceless Men may go further than Vedanta toward Buddhism, since they worship a god with no face of his own and aim at no-self rather than union, while Arya's pragmatic adoption of the shellfish-merchant disguise echoes the Bhagavad Gita's Krishna: perform your duty without attachment to any self.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 12 "2. Know Thyself, Agent Cooper!" — Reads the Season Two Black Lodge finale as Cooper's failed journey of self-knowledge, framed by Socrates' Delphic "know thyself" and the unexamined life. Against Hume's bundle theory — when Hume looks inward he only ever finds particular perceptions, never a self — the chapter sets the Vedanta/Tibetan Buddhist ideal of knowing the true Self beyond thought (the ocean versus its waves), with the Black Lodge as the place Hawk calls a passage "every soul must pass on its way to perfection." Cooper's screaming white-eyed Laura, the flickering Caroline/Annie corpse, and his grinning doppelgänger are Jungian shadow-projections paralleled scene-by-scene with the wrathful visions of the Tibetan Book of the Dead; entering with imperfect courage, he flees his fears instead of integrating them, splitting into trapped good Dale and the rampaging Mr. C of The Return.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 34 "19. Hinduism Gets More than Five Percent Right" — Kaur and Gupta argue Hinduism got far more than five percent right, mapping the show's points onto karmic theory and the Bhagavad Gita's three kinds of action: right action, inaction, and wrong action. Eleanor's fruitless point-grubbing and selfless departure exemplify nishkama karma, desire-less action, while the 802 reboots and Janet's memory-wiped revivals mirror the birth-death-rebirth cycle on the way to self-realization. Ranking the cast on the Gita's ladder of unfoldment, desire-driven Eleanor and Jason below Tahani and knowledgeable Chidi, with Michael straying from his dharma and detached, duty-bound Janet nearest to Brahman, they show the series dramatizes the Gita's teaching that motivation, not the deed itself, determines an act's worth.
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 24 "The Danger of Thinking “Science Is Whatever We Want It to Be”; or, the" — Barkman reads the 30 Rock cast as prisoners who prefer delusion, using Plato's allegory of the cave and the Upanishadic scheme of samsara, karma, maya, and moksha, in which Atman is realized as one with Brahman, as twin diagnoses. Drew's 'bubble' of good looks, Liz's false memory of being a harmless nerd in 'Reunion' and her belief she can have it all, Jack's pride about his terrible sketch ideas, Kenneth's unexamined dogma ('I can't handle the truth!'), Jenna's age-hiding, and Tracy's white myths about diabetes and Colorado all illustrate ignorance of reality that costs happiness. The Hindu-Platonic lesson is that knowledge of reality, not Dr. Spaceman's 'science is whatever we want it to be', is the route to happiness, because ignorance is not bliss.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 34 "19. Hinduism Gets More than Five Percent Right" — Argues Hinduism 'gets more than five percent right' via the Bhagavad Gita: the show's point system mirrors karma, Eleanor's failed point-chasing and quiet departure for the Bad Place enact nishkama karma (desire-less action), and the 802 reboots are rebirths without memory. The characters form a ladder of unfoldment — Jason's unknowing wrong action below Eleanor's knowing one, Tahani's corruptly motivated good deeds, Chidi's knowledge without decision, Michael swerving from his demonic dharma, and Janet highest: desireless, rebooting like cyclical rebirth, her void echoing boundless Brahman. Chidi's logic-bound indecision versus Eleanor's knowledge-producing logic completes the Gita reading.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 18 "Notes" — Reads Rust's 'dream inside a locked room' and 'everybody is nobody' monologues through the dream-argument and illusion-of-self traditions: the Upanishads and Advaita's atman/brahman, Vasubandhu's Buddhist non-self, Zhuangzi's butterfly dream, Plato's Theaetetus, and Descartes' dream doubt, plus Metzinger's self-model neuroscience. It diagnoses Rust as a neuro-nihilist in Metzinger's sense and defines his predicament with Nietzsche's nihilist, who judges the world as it is that it ought not to be, while noting Schopenhauer misread India's religions as pessimistic. Thompson argues nihilism is a deep insight gone awry — the self is not a thing but an enacted process like dancing — and reads Rust's final near-death experience of love as proof that transcendence of the dream of being a person is possible.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 22 "Spontaneity, Immediacy, and Difference Philosophy, Being in Time, and Creativity in the Aesthetics of Jack Ker" — David Need contrasts three theories of 'being in time' behind the aesthetics of spontaneity: Kerouac's debt to Spengler's organic cycles of civilization (a stereoscopic, dualist view where an arbitrary measure like a candle or page limns deep being), Olson's use of Whitehead's 'concrescence' in 'Projective Verse' (a monist, all-at-once projection of new monads), and Cage's use of Coomaraswamy's Vedanta, where silence is sabdabrahman and chance imitates Nature. He argues the real fault line is the old monist-vs-dualist divide (Advaita brahman vs. Cartesian dualism), and that each artist's notion of creative freedom follows from which metaphysical schema he borrowed, so our quarrels with the Beats reflect our own metaphysical stakes.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 12 "2. Know Thyself, Agent Cooper!" — De Carvalho reads Cooper's ordeal in the Black Lodge as a journey of self-knowledge, distinguishing 'knowing yourself' (your feelings, as Laura sought with Dr. Jacoby) from 'knowing your Self' in the deep sense of Vedanta's Brahman and Tibetan Buddhism's Mind. He sets Hume's bundle theory—the failure to catch a self behind the perceptions—against the Hindu Swami's ocean-and-waves image of an eternal Self beyond thought, and reads Cooper's confrontation with his screaming-Laura and doppelganger visions via the Tibetan Book of the Dead and Jung's shadow: facing his fears with imperfect courage, Cooper fails to integrate his shadow and is split in two.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 26 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — LoPresti uses the 'This Week in God' segments (the God Machine, Ed Helms's Hindu-vs-Mayan 'faith-off,' Colbert's inclusivist White House roast) to lay out three responses to religious diversity—exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism—and defends John Cobb's Whiteheadian process-metaphysics pluralism. He insists the distinct concepts of religions be respected rather than collapsed, citing Buddhist impermanence and no-Self and the South Asian Atman/Brahman as unique and non-reducible, and closes by reading the show's turn to political framing of religion through Marx's claim that religion is a mechanism for controlling the masses.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 8 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — John Friend's foreword surveys yoga's three classical philosophical systems and connects them to how modern Hatha yoga is practiced: Classical (Patanjali) yoga as separating purusha (spirit) from prakriti (matter) to reach kaivalya; Vedanta as neutralizing maya to realize the unity of atman with the supreme; and non-dual Tantra, from which Hatha yoga derives, treating body and mind as frequencies of one divine Shiva-Shakti energy. It argues yoga's enduring claim is that the essential self is free, and that direct lived experience of that freedom outranks merely intellectual knowledge of the texts.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 18 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Ken Burak describes teaching yoga in his philosophy class — a 'three wheels' exercise moving from the true self behind our masks to the Upanishadic identity of Atman and Brahman ('Thou Art That') — to give students embodied access to the universal/particular problem. He reads Western philosophy from Plato's Phaedo (Socrates seeking death as liberation of soul from body) through Descartes' doubt as a 2500-year practice of pratyahara (sense-withdrawal), one limb mistaken for the whole journey, and asks what asana and this long retreat could each bring the other.

### Non-Self (anatman)

Non-self, or anatman, is the Buddhist claim that there is no permanent, unchanging self or soul underlying our experience. What we take to be a fixed "I" is, on this view, a shifting bundle of physical and mental processes that continually arise and dissolve, held together only by habit and craving. Understanding non-self is intended to undercut the self-centered grasping that drives suffering, and it distinguishes Buddhism from traditions that posit an enduring soul.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 56 "Unknown" — Brannigan reads the film's mirror imagery through the Buddha's mirror instruction to his son Rahula: Neo touching the dripping mirror and becoming the mirror marks his awakening to the naked truth (aletheia as nakedness) that his world is a programmed illusion, Smith's dark sunglasses distort while Morpheus's mirrored glasses clarify, and Neo's reflection in the spoon-bending boy's spoon signals clarity. 'There is no spoon' parallels the Zen mondo where neither flag nor wind moves but only mind, and shows that reflected images are not reality - the world is maya. The deepest lesson is anatman: just as there is no spoon there is no Neo, no fixed self, and Rahula's lesson grounds the interdependence (pratityasamutpada) of all actions on others.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 124 "Unknown" — The chapter reads 'the One' through the concentration-camp survivor who, by sheer presence, retained others' dignity and will to live—a place in the social link filled by transference rather than real qualities—and opposes this to the film's One, who merely learns the virtualized reality's rules can be suspended, a paranoid notion that reduces the resistance of the Real to weak will. The spoon-bending child's 'there is no spoon' should have pushed the film to the Buddhist proposition that I myself do not exist, while Agent Smith's speech that humans 'define their reality through suffering and misery' makes him the analyst-figure whose lesson is that reality is that which resists.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 21 "“Nobody’s Bob Dylan”" — Vernezze and Lulewicz take Dylan's 1964 Halloween quip "I got my Bob Dylan mask on" as an entry into personal identity, testing each theory against his life: the bodily view (Zimmerman to Dylan) survives cell turnover but stumbles on brain-transplant cases; Locke's memory theory handles them but faces Reid's brave-officer regress and Alzheimer's cases, and Dylan's reincarnation lyrics ("Shelter from the Storm," "I and I") ignore memory altogether. The Christian soul view of the gospel albums ("When He Returns," "Gotta Serve Somebody") follows Descartes and Plato but cannot justify the swirl-to-filling inference that souls exist. The chapter ends sympathetic to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist no-self: Dylan's "I is another," his name as fabrication, and the cover album Self Portrait all deny a fixed self-created essence.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 13 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Priest argues that Pirsig's Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance is far more genuinely Zen than its disclaimer admits: once riding becomes effortless, the dissolution of the subject-object distinction that Dogen calls genjokoan arrives on the open road ('you ARE the driving and the road and the elements'), and the Harley's relaxed posture and low-revving thug-thug-thug rhythm make it a better vehicle for suchness than cars or whinier bikes. Even maintenance done as an end in itself is genjokoan, and because ultimate reality erases every conceptual distinction, care of self, others, and the bike amount to the same thing, the Mahayana ground of compassion; the mountain-and-water Zen saying resolves the paradox that the unconceptualized and the conceptualized are one. Suffering, on the Buddhist diagnosis Priest applies, comes from imposing conceptual grids that see the world wrong, and seeing it aright dissolves it.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 14 "Mind the Mindfulness" — Reads The Meaning of Life as a sustained reductio of transcendentalism — the two-world metaphysics shared by Plato, Augustine, and Vedanta's Brahman/atman — arguing that the film's dehumanizing sketches (the machine that goes 'ping,' the 'every sperm is sacred' father selling his children, the Vegas-style Christmas in Heaven) show how otherworldly belief overrides this-worldly compassion. It parallels the Buddha's scriptural critiques: the Agganna sutta against caste, the no-self (anatta) doctrine against the Bhagavad Gita's soul that licenses Krishna to tell Arjuna killing is a favor, and impermanence (anicca) against the fantasy of eternal bliss. Python's grotesque — Creosote's explosion, the organ-donor lady's 'Galaxy Song' despair — matches Buddhist corpse meditations, while the film steers between hedonism (Creosote) and nihilism (the housewife who surrenders her liver) toward the Buddha's Middle Way and, against everyday distraction (the boardroom's 'people are not wearing enough hats,' the couple who think Schopenhauer begins with an S), toward mindfulness (sati).
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 44 "“How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons" — James McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism: the fleet's sleepless FTL jumps in "33" and Roslin's dwindling survivor counts enact the four noble truths, Leoben's interrogation scenes teach that suffering comes from ignorant attachment, and Dogen's no-self and impermanence frame the show's interdependent characters. Cylon resurrection, D'Anna's serial deaths, and the prophecy that "all of this has happened before" model karma and samsara, while Nishida's kenotic God of Absolute Nothingness makes sense of Six and Leoben's God of love. Because Cylons feel pain, fear death away from a resurrection ship, and act volitionally, McRae concludes they are persons in the Buddhist sense, owed the compassion of the Eightfold Path.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 21 "Analyzing Emptiness" — Paul Gass reads the Dead's hippie milieu (the Beats, the Acid Tests, Buddhist-monk lyricist Peter Monk) as a conduit for Buddhist doctrine, taking the 'Eyes of the World' chorus as an invitation to awaken to Buddha-nature. He explains the Four Noble Truths, karma, and the five aggregates to argue the self is an illusion, using the image of a flame passed between lighters at a Dead show to picture rebirth without a persisting soul. The chapter then presents Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka middle way — emptiness itself must not be clutched as an absolute truth — and reads the 'redeemer... wagon loaded with clay' verse of 'Eyes of the World' as the Mahayana bodhisattva liberating all beings, with emptiness finally discarded like the boat after crossing the river.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 9 "“Logic Without Need Is Sterile”" — Writing as a Vulcan philosophy professor and student of Spock, the chapter reconstructs Vulcan civilization from Surak's Awakening as three interlocking modes of logic — formal logic (whose first law, Kiri-kin-tha's 'nothing unreal exists', parallels Parmenides), ethical logic (the axiom 'the needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few'), and meditative discipline — and maps them onto Patanjali's Yoga: the yamas, meditation, and samadhi's cosmic oneness, with ahimsa linking Surak to Gandhi and King. It then rereads Star Trek: The Motion Picture, where V'Ger's pure logic leaves both it and Spock asking 'Is this all that I am?', and Spock's mind meld with V'Ger becomes a tantric union that integrates feeling with logic after the failure of Kolinahr. The chapter's thesis is that 'logic without need is sterile': logic is 'the beginning of wisdom . . . not the end', and Spock's rebirth culminates in choosing the human thing precisely when it is not the logical thing.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 26 "Mr. Monk Murdered Trudy" — Green argues Monk is an unintentional Bodhisattva whose OCD enacts the Four Bodhisattva Vows: the compulsion to touch lampposts is the first vow's blind desires, his monastic minimalism the Dharma gate, and his crime-solving compassion for a disordered world the third vow, with the Dhammapada's teaching that the untamed mind produces suffering exemplified by Monk and by Harold Krenshaw's rival ordering. Like Vimalakirti feigning illness, or Shawn Spencer in Psych, and like the father in the Lotus Sutra's burning-house parable, Monk and his writers use skillful deception to awaken viewers to suffering and loving kindness. The title thesis is that Monk cannot solve Trudy's murder because he accepts responsibility for it: by Thich Nhat Hanh's Interbeing there is no absolute self and other, so solving the case requires the Zen 'kill the Buddha' eradication of the self, Monk's nirvana-as-extinction and the end of the series.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 8 "2 - An Interview with Bodhidharma" — Priest stages a spoof radio interview with Bodhidharma at the Shaolin Temple to argue that the monks' fighting exercises are really meditation: a fist passing an inch from your nose focuses the mind, and repeatedly practicing violent techniques makes practitioners less violent. Bodhidharma explains that a liter of goat's milk, a marauding thug, and even the reporter's self are only conceptual labels over 'thusness' (tathata), that attachment and the desire to strike cause suffering to the striker, and that the Buddha's compassion permits self-defense without aggression. The punchline is the reporter's unanswered last question: 'They're not really about fighting, are they?'
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 10 "And the Winner Is" — Lynch pits Plato against the Shaolin monks on the nature of the self that martial training is supposed to master. Plato's Republic makes the athlete-warrior Guardian a harmonious, rationally ruled tripartite soul whose bravery is 'remembering what ought and ought not to be feared', trained so reason governs aggression; Buddhism instead dissolves the self into five impermanent aggregates (illustrated by the chariot analogy) and reads mushin as a direct taste of no-self. He awards the practical decision to the Buddhist fighting monks, since no-self explains martial spontaneity and naturally arising compassion, while admitting Plato's substantive rational soul is not strictly refuted.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 18 "Halo as a Catalyst for a Buddhism Videogame" — Luke Cuddy uses Halo 3 checkpoints and emulator save states—two mutually exclusive Flood-fight outcomes both in some sense true—to make David Lewis's possible worlds and modal truth concrete, with Leibniz as the doctrine's ancestor. Halo's infinite lives make players genuinely angry, and the chapter argues this is upaya territory: like the father in the Lotus Sutra's parable of the burning house, the game promises mastery (the goat-, deer-, and ox-carts) to lure players toward something greater outside it. Master Chief becomes a Bodhisattva whose avatar slides between extension of self and other, provoking the 'who am I?' crisis that reveals the ego as empty at the ultimate level of the Two-Fold Truth, while the Dalai Lama's enemies-as-teachers turns the seven-year-old who pwns you into practice in the first two Noble Truths' suffering and anger.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 50 "Chapter 07 - Scan Thyself" — Butler frames Dick as the latest in philosophy's self-knowledge line: the Delphic 'know thyself' that Socrates made essential to the good life at the cost of his own, the Buddha who sought himself and found only an illusion at the root of suffering, Descartes whose entire philosophy rests on confidence in knowledge of himself as an immaterial being, and Dick's own 8,000-page Exegesis. The chapter's hook is the stakes of self-ignorance (what if you turned out to be something horrible?) and its Dickian version: how do you know you are not an android?
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 61 "The Devil and Philosophy" — John Thompson argues Mara, who unleashes armies and seductive daughters on the Buddha-to-be under the bodhi tree, is not 'the Buddhist Satan': he has not fallen, wages no cosmic war against a supreme God, and merely personifies trsna (grasping) as overlord of samsara. He finds textbook glosses like Huston Smith's misleading, and praises Bertolucci's Little Buddha, where Mara rises from a pool as Siddhartha's mirror twin - 'Oh Lord of my own Ego, you are pure illusion. You do not exist' - a portrayal he reads through Karen Armstrong's Jungian shadow self and Campbell's Freudian eros-and-thanatos frame, concluding that we are Mara/Satan.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 22 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Klein and Fundora trace Jobs's Buddhism from Reed College meditation and the seven-month India pilgrimage (reading Yogananda's Autobiography of a Yogi yearly) to the Zen minimalism of Apple design, arguing his temper tantrums, harsh speech, and reality distortion field do not disqualify him from being 'on the path' since Buddhism is a practice, not a creed test. They expound the Four Noble Truths (dukkha in its three kinds, via Thich Nhat Hanh), the Eightfold Path's Middle Way, and anatta—the non-self they compare to Hume's bundle theory of the self against Descartes's thinking thing—and read Jobs's strip-away-the-essence aesthetics, the three-click intuitive iPod interface that keeps users in the moment, the non-dualist marriage of art and technology, and his Think Different self-reliance as deeply Buddhist authenticity.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 11 "3. Tris Finds Enlightenment" — Rhine argues that Tris's heroism rests on Buddhist practice: her breath-counting on the Ferris wheel and inside Four's fear landscape, her emotional intelligence, and her awareness of the parental 'voices in her head' are classic meditative disciplines for calming the ego whose clinging, on the Buddhist account, is the cause of suffering (dukkha). She reads Abnegation's gray houses, plain food, and four-times-a-year mirror as ritual ego-diminishment - a middle way between indulgence and the extreme asceticism the Buddha rejected - that explains why most Divergent arise from Abnegation. Contemporary neuroscience is then recruited: the amygdala-versus-prefrontal-cortex struggle Will describes, and monks' heightened gamma waves, explain how Tris can see the simulation as a simulation, like Neo in The Matrix, and act while others are paralyzed by fear.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 36 "23. I Fight Crime in My Sleep" — Staged as a Fight Club parody in which a Buddhist psychiatrist, Dr. Quinzel, evaluates a costumed narrator sent to Arkham, the chapter argues neither hero is close to awakening: Batman's crime-fighting is craving that perpetuates dukkha, his secret identities a twice-constructed self that the Buddha's no-self teaching dissolves, and his violence fails the test that 'hostility is never appeased by hostility.' Superman fares no better - his super-intellect imposes illusory order on impermanence, his flight and X-ray vision are distractions beside the Buddha-eye and tapas, and as one of the titans of the six realms he is further from Buddhahood than a human - while the doctor defines justice as karma rather than retaliation and finds Batman one step from American Psycho's Bateman. Only conquering Mara, one's own inner deceiver, is 'the only superpower worth having,' and the closing reveal that the doctor has a plan of her own for 'Mr. Kent' caps the diagnosis.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 17 "6. One Clone from Another" — Asks what metaphysically individuates one Leda clone from another, surveying the tradition: Aristotelian substances bearing properties, Plato's and Descartes's non-repeatable individual essences, Berkeley's and Hegel's soul-substances, Aquinas's matter-based view, Locke's memory-based personal identity (with its sleeping-copy and consciousness-download objections), and Hume's argument that substance is a meaningless idea. It then turns to the Buddhist framework — the Four Noble Truths, anatman (no eternal self), the five skandhas, and dependent origination, illustrated by Alison's soap-and-drug crates — before closing with Nishida Kitaro's logic of contradictory self-identity. Read through that lens, the clone dance party in Felix's loft shows each clone's moves are truly her own precisely because they incorporate and mirror her sisters': identity is relational, not intrinsic.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 31 "17. Dialog with the Buddha" — A Platonic-style fictional dialogue in which a newly enlightened "Canadian Buddha" walks out of the northern Ontario bush to the Prolethean farm and debates Tomas, Henry, and Bonnie over whether clones are abominations. Using karma, rebirth, the gandhabba that carries consciousness-flux to a new embryo, the no-soul doctrine, and the eightfold path, the Buddha argues clones are ordinary beings of the karmic flux — like the split bacterium, nothing unnatural — but that cloning multiplies clinging: hosts crave immortality through copies, each clone inherits the host's whole accumulated karma, and Henry's dream of training an army of Helena-clones would only deepen the unsatisfactoriness the Buddha's mustard-seed lesson says clinging to the dead always brings. Only ending the cycle through enlightenment releases anyone; the clone, like the lost child, is not the one you lost.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 15 "6. Bowie the Buddhist" — Muchall reads 'Quicksand' and 'Where Are We Now?' as suffused with Tibetan Buddhism: 'Don't believe in yourself' voices the anatta teaching Bowie absorbed studying with Chime Rinpoche and from Chogyam Trungpa, whose 'spiritual materialism' warns that ego converts even spirituality and ideologies to its own use. After retelling the Buddha's life, the Four Noble Truths' three kinds of dukkha, and the five aggregates that reveal no permanent self, the chapter maps the song's 'ragged hole' and bardos onto the Tibetan Book of the Dead's after-death journey, and reads Bowie's morphing personas as lived acknowledgment that there is no fixed self - 'there's nothing in here.'
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 25 "14. David Bowie’s Sadness" — Ketcham argues Bowie's sadness is ours: via Deleuze and Guattari's Anti-Oedipus he casts consumer capitalism as a machine producing schizophrenic fad-following (the stuck high-school footballer, the Benetton self), of which Bowie's serial personas are both symptom and escape - 'always crashing in the same car' yet never repeating. Minkowski's lived time and the Buddha's anatman ground the dance as pure becoming without a dancer, while Heidegger's das Man and being-toward-death explain why authentic self-creation - which, unlike Sellers or Williams, Bowie survived - exacts the price Freud's beyond-the-pleasure-principle names as compulsive repetition, turned by Bowie into a life wish.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 36 "22. The Many-Faced God and Indian Philosophy" — Van Eyghen maps the Faceless Men onto Indian philosophy: their one God of many faces parallels Vedanta's Brahman in personal form as Ishvara, and Arya's training to become 'no one' parallels shedding the ego toward identity with Brahman - with Jaqen as guru and the stick-beating ritual as an example of identity fusion in Harvey Whitehouse's cognitive science of religion. But the Faceless Men may go further than Vedanta toward Buddhism, since they worship a god with no face of his own and aim at no-self rather than union, while Arya's pragmatic adoption of the shellfish-merchant disguise echoes the Bhagavad Gita's Krishna: perform your duty without attachment to any self.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 24 "12. A Month from Now, I’ll Be a Balding, Toothless Skeleton" — Reads Fiona Goode's war against fading - the experimental RM47 serum, rejecting the Axeman's escape because he would watch her decay, the Papa Legba bargain that collapses because she has no soul - alongside Delphine LaLaurie's blood facials and Marie Laveau's child sacrifices, as illustrations of Buddhist dukkha and the three thirsts (kama for sense pleasure, bhava for existence, vibhava for annihilation). Legba's 'you don't have a soul' becomes an accidentally liberating glimpse of anatta, and Cordelia's dying advice - 'feel the fear... let it all go' - is the mindfulness, echoing Buddhaghosa's corpse meditations, that might have freed Fiona.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 17 "8. Ode to Joi" — Steve Bein first tests Joi against Mary Anne Warren's five functionalist personhood criteria — consciousness, reason, self-motivated activity, communication, self-awareness — and finds she passes, which makes Luv's stomping of the emanator a murder. The Buddha's no-self doctrine then denies that anyone, Joi included, is an enduring person: we are bundles of fleeting psychophysical processes, 'like tears in rain', which threatens to let Luv plead that the Luv who killed Joi no longer exists. Nagarjuna's two truths resolve the courtroom problem: ultimately there are no persons, but conventionally 'Luv killed Joi' is perfectly true, and the karma ripples through the whole network.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 25 "14. After the Blackout" — Martin Muchall treats the offscreen Blackout as an emblem of the moral catastrophe diagnosed in MacIntyre's After Virtue: our moral vocabulary has shattered into emotivist hissing and clapping, with Roy's murder of Tyrell, his 'God of biomechanics', staging the death of God and the 'everything is permitted' that follows. Utilitarian pleasure and Kantian cold reason (Spock, who must tell the truth to the murderer at the door) have both failed, leaving neoliberal hypercapitalism — corporate psychopathy, the orphanage sweatshop, the Baseline as workplace performance review — as the real villain. Against this, K's ending models the Buddha: everything is impermanent, there is no self to defend, and his selfless, empathetic death points to a morality grounded in evolved and cultivable altruism.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 14 "4. Can We Do Enough Good" — Fetterman argues no one can do enough good to earn The Good Place because the real question is who defines good. Moving from Hobbes's state of nature and Rousseau's innate compassion to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist doctrine of non-self, he shows the four humans' characters were assembled by their formative communities, which is Michael's whole defense before Judge Gen. But Nietzsche's account of how communities christen their own customs 'good' exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife accountants impose their in-group preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's life of point-maximization fails, and why Michael should be asking the Frozen Yogurt Problem instead of blaming demon tampering.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 38 "Fearlessness and Power" — Rebuts Ozai's taunt 'you are still weak' with a Buddhist reading of energybending: Aang wins not by domination but because his unbendable spirit is total vulnerability, a true heart that has abandoned the five hindrances (sensory desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness, doubt — each traced through the chakras, the Serpent's Pass, and 'Nightmares and Daydreams') and a true mind freed from the fundamental delusion of a separate self that 'The Swamp' and 'The Guru' dissolve. The spirit-merging with Ozai is read through Indra's net, and Aang's merciful halt mirrors Indra's Jataka victory where compassion for eagle hatchlings — not force — defeats the demons. Fearlessness, on Sylvia Boorstein's Zen story, is the natural corollary of compassion, so Aang's weakness by Ozai's standard is precisely his power.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 38 "Fearlessness and Power" — Argues that Aang's energybending victory over Ozai vindicates a Buddhist conception of power against Ozai's equation of power with domination: the Lion Turtle's 'unbendable spirit' is not resistance but thorough vulnerability, achieved through the true heart (overcoming the five hindrances mapped onto Aang's sensory desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness, and doubt across the series) and the true mind (overcoming the fundamental delusion of a self separate from others, learned from Huu in 'The Swamp' and Guru Pathik). The merging of Aang's and Ozai's spirits is pictured by the metaphor of Indra's net, and Indra's own Jataka victory, halting his assault to protect eagle hatchlings and disorienting the demons, parallels Aang's refusal to win by killing. Drawing on a Zen story of the abbot who could 'be run through by a sword without batting an eye', the chapter concludes that Aang's fearlessness flows from compassion, so that weakness by Ozai's standard is precisely the power that defeats him.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 40 "Journey’s End and a Vision of a New Community" — Reads Aang's quest through the Karmapa Ogyen Trinley Dorje's book Interconnected: like the seventeenth Karmapa, identified at age seven and taken from his family, Aang learns that an exalted title complicates friendship and that freedom is self-control rather than the rugged individualism of the American hero's quest. Training episodes (Katara's jealous competition in 'The Waterbending Scroll', Jeong Jeong's warnings, the Toph-versus-Katara sifu debate in 'Bitter Work') show moral training as communal, widening from Team Avatar as adoptive family toward universal compassion, with Aang's refusal to open the seventh chakra illustrating how local attachment can obstruct universal love. Zuko's counter-arc from competition, isolation, and betrayal to humility, forgiveness, and contentment shows compassion turning an enemy into a friend, and the finale's simultaneous battles (White Lotus liberating Ba Sing Se, Sokka and Toph destroying the fleet) affirm that Aang wins as an 'interdependent individual', never alone.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 26 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — LoPresti uses 'This Week in God' segments (Ed Helms refereeing a Hindu-versus-Mayan 'faith-off', Colbert's roast line that all religions are infinite paths to accepting Jesus, Rob Corddry's purification rituals and God Exchange stock ticker) to lay out exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism as responses to religious diversity. Inclusivism like Colbert's 'anonymous Christian' logic is exposed as intellectual imperialism that erases genuinely distinct teachings such as the Buddhist non-self and impermanence, while the chapter defends a deep pluralism against the relativism that makes 'all religions equally true' meaningless. Its eulogy for the God Machine borrows Marx's view of religion as an instrument of mass control to explain why religious humor now survives only through a political lens.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 12 "Hakuna Matata, Bodhisattva" — Sets up Disney's maxim 'Hey kid, you can be a hero' as the direct opposite of Zen's 'Hey kid, you can be a buddha': escapism versus liberation, told through the life of Dogen, whose monastic choice parallels Disney hero narratives. Mickey in Steamboat Willie — a bundle of still frames with no sound and no real 'he' — illustrates the Buddha's three marks of existence (emptiness, impermanence, frustration), and the chapter argues Disney products are calibrated distractions from these marks while Dogen counsels facing them, with Ariel's Andersen fate as the price of fantasy. It closes on Disney's merchandising machine (Yoda, Star Wars sequels, direct-to-video cash grabs) as everything the countercultural minimalist Yoda or Baloo's bare necessities stand against, concluding that real hakuna matata is accepting impermanence rather than escaping it.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 14 "4. Can We Do Enough Good" — Interrogates Chidi's question 'why do we choose to be good?' through Hobbes's selfish state of nature, Rousseau's hardwired compassion (Michael's 'little voice' in Eleanor's head), and Hume's bundle theory extended Buddhist-style to a non-self, which grounds Michael's plea to Judge Gen that bad communities made the four humans bad and a better community (Team Cockroach, the Brainy Bunch) can make them good. Nietzsche's account of how communities define their own customs as 'good' then exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife's accountants impose their in-group's preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's point-maximizing life cannot clear the bar. The chapter ends by asking Michael's real question: who gets to decide what's good?
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 21 "a9.xhtml" — The chapter argues Tolkien's clearest moral in The Hobbit is against possessiveness, starting from Aquinas' definition of greed as 'immoderate love of riches': dragon-sickness ruins Thorin and drowns the Master of Lake-town starving in the wilderness with his gold, and Gollum shows the isolating end of a life organized around a 'precious'. Buddhism reframes the diagnosis - Gollum's craving (tanha) is rooted in ignorance (avidya) of the self's illusoriness, since grasping enriches a self that does not exist, per the Four Noble Truths - while Laozi's 'he who knows he has enough is rich' and Thoreau's 'a man is rich in proportion to the things he can afford to let alone' are embodied by Beorn and the gift-giving, nearly government-less hobbits. Bilbo's generosity - giving away the Arkenstone worth 'more than a river of gold', taking only two small chests, later giving Sting and the mithril coat to Frodo - is the book's counter-example to greed.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 29 "Notes" — Kahn argues LEGO play embodies the Buddhist teaching of impermanence that the Buddha states in the Digha Nikaya ('Impermanent are all component things...'): his childhood urge to superglue creations and Finn's father's Kragle dramatize the clinging that produces anxiety when things change, from brick formulations to discontinued sets and even funerals' wilting flowers. The LEGO Star Wars Death Star illustrates non-self — no Death Star exists apart from its 3,803 pieces, and no self apart from shifting aggregates — and the five aggregates (form, sensation, perception, formations, consciousness) are unpacked through building experiences like discovering a daughter has opened the mint Taj Mahal set. Tibetan sand mandalas, painstakingly built then ritually dissolved, model the ceremonial demolition of LEGO creations, teaching acceptance of change without sliding into a nihilistic 'why bother building at all'.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 18 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Godwin reads Spider-Man 3's black-suit episode as a question about the self: with the symbiote amplifying his anger, is Peter still Peter? Against Hume's and the Buddha's bundle theories, on which the self is only an imagined aggregate of thoughts and feelings, and Reid's common-sense simple self, she advances the pragmatist 'social self' of Peirce, James, Dewey, and Mead, updated as Engel's biopsychosocial model: Peter's identity is a shifting web of biology, psyche, and relationships (Aunt May, MJ, Harry) expressed in actions and character. Eddie succumbs to the symbiote because, as Dewey says of the slave to his own blind desires, hatred constitutes who he is, while Peter's thicker web of good relations lets him shed the suit at the church bell.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 36 "23. I Fight Crime in My Sleep" — A Fight Club-style Arkham case study: a patient's hallucinated Superman companion is diagnosed by a Buddhist psychiatrist who explains the three marks of existence—impermanence, non-self, and dissatisfaction—arguing superheroes impose order and a fabricated second self on a world that resists both, so Superman's super-intellect and even flight are distractions (levitation should be ignored; the Buddha-eye beats x-ray vision) while Batman's violence and psychosis, compared to American Psycho's Patrick Bateman, make awakening impossible—both are victims of Mara. A robber literally named David Hume objects that the heroes' law and order is grounded on what ought to be rather than what is, and a Gandhi quote on preferring one's own bad government explains why Batman finally kryptonites his alien 'friend.' The verdict inverts the book's debate: conquering the deceiver within is the only superpower worth having.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 18 "Notes" — Reads Rust's 'dream inside a locked room' and 'everybody is nobody' monologues through the dream-argument and illusion-of-self traditions: the Upanishads and Advaita's atman/brahman, Vasubandhu's Buddhist non-self, Zhuangzi's butterfly dream, Plato's Theaetetus, and Descartes' dream doubt, plus Metzinger's self-model neuroscience. It diagnoses Rust as a neuro-nihilist in Metzinger's sense and defines his predicament with Nietzsche's nihilist, who judges the world as it is that it ought not to be, while noting Schopenhauer misread India's religions as pessimistic.
