The five levels of awareness collapse too: level-four skeptics are just people who trust reliable methods, and the Avatar's claim that the mind is an illusion generator is self-defeating, since his own omniscience presupposes objective truth.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 19 "8. Tom Petty Didn’t Really Need to Know" — Zelinski and Fallis chart Petty's epistemic arc. His early songs ("I Need to Know," "Fooled Again," "Shadow of a Doubt") crave certainty about lovers' fidelity, a Desmond-free obsession closest to Descartes' quest for certainty beyond doubt, except Petty's problem is other minds, not the external world, and his trust that eyes directly reveal feeling sides with Moore's common-sense perception; Sartre's "hell is other people" names why another free person's future love can never be certain. From Full Moon Fever onward ("Into the Great Wide Open," "Time to Move On," "Learning to Fly") Petty instead embodies Pyrrhonian suspension of judgment and the Buddha's "don't know mind" and Daoist farmer's "we'll see," finding tranquility in uncertainty, craving nothing, flying with eyes open.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 13 "3. The M. Night Sh-imulation Hypothesis" — The chapter runs Bostrom's simulation argument against 'M. Night Shaym-Aliens!', where the Zigerions trap Rick in simulations-within-simulations to steal his concentrated dark matter formula, and reads their cheap shortcuts ('My man!' NPCs, human music, Jerry's Appley award) as the glitches and shadow-people Bostrom predicts. It presses the epistemological problem that any evidence for the simulation equally supports its denial, an underdetermination that devastates the theory, and traces the lineage of 'the real world isn't real' through Plato's summoners and allegory of the cave, Descartes's dream doubt, and Paley's design analogy (Morty as the beautiful machine), ending with the microverse battery of 'The Ricks Must Be Crazy': this is the universe we live in, so get used to it.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 22 "11. Are You Imagining That Poopybutthole" — Reading 'Total Rickall' as an evil-genius scenario, the chapter treats the memory parasites (Uncle Steve, Sleepy Gary, Reverse Giraffe) as Descartes's deceiving demon lodged in the Smiths' reconstructive memories, with Rick's written headcount an empirical defense that methodical doubt undermines. Morty's formula that parasites implant only good memories is shown to be merely inductive rather than certain like the cogito, so Beth's shooting of Mr. Poopybutthole becomes the test case: applying Aquinas's three kinds of ignorance, the chapter argues she remains morally responsible despite genuine remorse because she neglected the chance to reconsider Morty's probabilistic rule. The upshot is Descartes's advice to restrain the will beyond what the intellect certifies: shoot for the arm, not the head.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 22 "“I knew I’d know it when I knew it” (King Bumi, “Sozin's Comet, Part 2 The Old Masters”)" — Skirry and Skirry read the Gaang's journey as building 'ethical-epistemological maps' in the manner of Native American and Inuit Traditional Knowledge (pijitsirniq, respect for land and community), against the Fire Nation's epistemology of control that pollutes rivers and brainwashes schoolchildren ('The Headband'). Where Descartes' lone meditator says 'I think, therefore I am' and uses dreams to cast doubt on experience, the Gaang's Native-style epistemology holds 'We think, therefore I am': Aang's prophetic dreams ('The Avatar and the Fire Lord'), his vision of Toph ('The Swamp'), spirit-world journeys, and the counsel of past Avatars and the Lion Turtle are genuine knowledge that resolves his dilemma about killing Ozai.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 22 "“I knew I’d know it when I knew it” (King Bumi, “Sozin's Comet, Part 2 The Old Masters”)" — The Skirrys read the Gaang's knowledge-building as Inuit Traditional Knowledge: Aang's adoption into the Water Tribe enacts pijitsirniq, and the team's 'ethical-epistemological maps' grow communally and through dreams, visions, and spirit journeys, from Roku's dream in 'The Avatar and the Fire Lord' to the swamp vision that identifies Toph and the past Avatars consulted on the Lion Turtle's back. Against this stands the Fire Nation's closed 'epistemology of control,' shown in 'The Headband' classroom and in Sozin letting Roku die rather than revising his map, and the Western model of Descartes, whose cogito makes knowledge individual and whose dream skepticism excludes exactly the experiences Native epistemology counts as real. Where Descartes doubts, Katara and Sokka investigate, as in 'Avatar Day.'
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 13 "No Reason to Get Excited" — The chapter turns the Final Five reveal (Tigh, Tyrol, Anders, Foster) and Boomer's sleeper activation into a skeptical problem about self-knowledge: Descartes's dreaming doubt (Roslin's Opera House dream) and the cogito show we can know that we exist but not what we are, and Baltar's rigged 'bright green' Cylon test destroys testimonial assurance. G.E. Moore's common-sense realism fails to engage the skeptic's special standards, and contextualism and Dretske's relevant-alternatives theory cannot help because in a world of sleeper Cylons the possibility 'I might be one' is always relevant. The answer is Hume's: like Tigh declaring 'I am an officer in the Colonial Fleet' and Anders repeating 'I am Samuel T. Anders' before his first combat mission, we banish skeptical paralysis by carrying on with life, dining and playing backgammon.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 46 "Heaven is a Place on Earth" — The chapter argues Black Mirror's perception tech works because the brain constructs experience top-down (predictive coding), so implants like Playtest's mushroom, Arkangel's filter, and Men Against Fire's MASS can inject perceptions and suppress error signals - and Cooper's total VR illusion defeats every one of Descartes's strategies (memory continuity, cross-checking the senses, reason) for telling dream from reality, killing him seconds after implantation. Nozick's experience machine illuminates Danny's preference for Striking Vipers X over his marriage and Arkangel's lesson that filtering Sara's childhood perceptions left her unable to read danger or emotion. Foucault's panopticon (via Bentham) frames White Christmas's cookie interrogation modeled on real police deception (Frazier v. Cupp), the MASS implant's manufacture of 'roach' targets for killing, and Nosedive's self-imposed social ratings as modern perceptual discipline - with only trusted others (Catarina, Susan, Kelly) punching through the manipulation.
- **Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality**, ch. 27 "Black sabbath & philosophy" — Kevin McCain turns Ozzy's "Am I Going Insane?" into a lived version of Descartes' skeptical scenarios, the madman who cannot trust his senses, the dream argument, the deceiving demon, and asks whether Ozzy can know anything at all. Using inference to the best explanation, he argues the commonsense external-world view beats skeptical scenarios because it predicts experiences (drop the book on your toe) and raises fewer unanswerable questions, so Ozzy keeps knowledge in the no-answer and "no" cases, but if he has reason to think he is insane and everyone tells him "yes", his reasons are defeated and he cannot even know their answers, leaving him, like the rest of us, one testimonial crisis from the void.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 20 "Happily Ever After" — Runs Descartes' dreaming argument and evil-genius doubt on Aurora, for whom the scenario is literal: Maleficent is an actually existing deceiver who could have enchanted her whole life in a dungeon. G. E. Moore's common-sense proof — 'here is a hand,' dubbed the Pinocchio test after the real boy — and the Moorean shift answer the skeptic, illustrated by Maleficent deploying Zeno's paradox to stop Prince Phillip's sword, where Phillip rightly clings to the more certain premise that motion is possible. Nozick's experience machine explains why Aurora should care: we want to actually be good and live real lives rather than merely experience them, so authentic 'happily ever after' requires knowing our experiences are backed by reality.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 8 "Out of the Orb" — Boudreaux maps Strange's comic-book journey into the Orb of Agamotto (dragged in by the Silver Dagger, greeted by a hookah-smoking caterpillar, tempted by counterfeit heroes like the Silver Surfer and Hulk) onto Descartes's Meditations. Empiricism (Locke's tabula rasa, Hume's sense-data) collapses when the senses are so thoroughly deceived inside the Orb, and innate ideas plus the Law of Non-Contradiction are not enough, so Strange reasons his way to the cogito — 'Nothing merits belief here — except oneself!' — just as Descartes doubts the evil demon. The caterpillar is revealed as Agamotto, playing the role of Descartes's non-deceiving God whose guidance lets Strange escape, and Strange's astral projections are offered as dramatic proof of mind-body dualism.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 29 "“What happens to us now ”" — Tests the moral limits of science against Dresden's defense of Eros ('hardly a rounding error', 'we become our own gods'): Descartes' evil demon explains why Holden can never verify the protomolecule-ghost Miller — or even the Roci's bulkhead — is real; Baconian induction and mastery of nature explain why Protogen feeds biomass to the protomolecule ('we can only learn by letting it learn'), though Bacon himself demanded knowledge be shared for universal good; Peirce's pragmatism explains how the Donnager infers stealth ships from their effects and why protomolecule victims count as no longer human; and Dewey's inseparability of means and ends indicts Fred Johnson's readiness to negotiate with Dresden. It culminates in Miller shooting Dresden — 'I killed him because he was making sense' — as the straightest critique of utilitarian calculation, concluding that when empathy is excised (Cortázar's stimulation) or ignored, even science aimed at saving humanity produces Eros, Project Caliban, and the Earth-Mars war.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 25 "NOTES" — Distinguishes Matt Parkman's supernatural telepathy from the 'mundane mind reading' everyone performs, then argues even Matt's power cannot solve the problem of other minds: the suicidal woman's thoughts he hears in the bar ('One Giant Leap') could be part of a Maury-Parkman-style illusion, and a brain-to-brain link could never rule out that others are Chalmers-style philosophical zombies. After grounding the skepticism in Descartes' cogito and method of doubt, it defends our everyday attribution of minds by analogy (Audrey Hanson reading Claire's insincerity) on pragmatic grounds, and maps Matt's progression from hearing thoughts to nightmare manipulation and compulsion onto the four adaptive functions philosophers assign to mind reading: interpretation, prediction, coordination, and influence. It closes by showing why neuroimaging-based technological mind reading remains a pipe dream, since brain recordings are quantitative syntax without semantics.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 9 "Does the Top Fall Does It Matter in the End" — Andersen argues Inception goes one step deeper than Descartes's dream argument: where Descartes doubted the world but kept ownership of his thoughts, the film imagines an identity-defining conviction — Fischer's sense of his father's judgment — being implanted so it never occurs to the victim to question it, which is to co-opt subjectivity itself. He reads Nolan's whole oeuvre (Following, Memento, The Prestige, Batman Begins) as variations on manipulation by misdirection, and diagnoses Cobb's inception on Mal in Limbo as the infection of her mind with Cartesian doubt, a philosophy impossible to live by. Since a totem guards against others' dreams but not self-deception, the film's answer is not universal doubt but trust: only by opening himself to Ariadne and choosing intimacy can Cobb go home and spin the top without looking.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 17 "Do We Give Shakespeare the Last Word" — Kapper treats Inception as a hip epistemological puzzle — unlike The Matrix, the question is not what is real but how we could know — and follows Ariadne's thread (her mythological clue-giving names the chapter) through the tradition: Plato's Theaetetus and Descartes's supremely cunning deceiver pose 'Am I dreaming now?', Wittgenstein shows the doubt is senseless since 'if I am dreaming, this remark is being dreamed as well', Freud makes dreams the royal road to the unconscious, and Heraclitus says only the waking share a common cosmos. The payoff is Eastern: Zhuangzi's butterfly, Indra's net of mutually reflected jewels, and Schopenhauer's single-dreamer universe turn waking up into an endless regress, so the Buddhist ideal of the awakened one — nirvana, where the ideas of real and dream cease to pertain — becomes the reading of Cobb turning away from the top.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 22 "The Kick—Back to ‘Reality’" — Richardson and McWilliams read Inception as an 'existential heist film' by diving through four layers of meaning. At the layer of reality they use Descartes's dream skepticism and wax argument, Hume on belief as custom and cause-effect, and Goffman on being shocked between frames to argue the film makes touch — the fall that wakes, pain ('pain is in the mind'), Saito's wrong-textured polyester carpet, the broken totems (Cobb's top, Arthur's loaded die, Ariadne's holed chess piece) — the only semi-trustworthy sense, while Mal, who locks her totem in the dollhouse safe and picks the dream, replays the cave prisoner who chooses the shadows. The car-chase layer ('downwards is the only way forwards'), Saito's 'old man filled with regrets' limbo, and the pharmacy dreamers who 'come to be woken up' are read through existentialism (Beckett's Waiting for Godot, Jaspers on loneliness and nothingness) and Peirce on the continuity of consciousness, with Cobb cast as the ideological existentialist who chooses action and reality where Cypher in The Matrix and Vanilla Sky's David face the same choice. The chapter then treats the film's reflexivity — the team as screenwriter/producer/director, the Escher-esque Penrose stairs, cross-cut dream time à la Peckinpah — as a lesson in film theory, and finally reaches phenomenology: Cobb's angry projection of Mal shows the dream world displaying his subjective meanings, against Arthur's calm, orderly hotel mindscape.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 23 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Blackmon and Foresman ask what makes ghosts, spells, and holy water supernatural, rejecting definitions based on fiction, disbelief, or weirdness, and using Quine's point about the circularity of dictionary definitions to show lexicography cannot settle the question. Definitions keyed to current science or to the causal nexus fail because ghosts in Supernatural and in Hamlet causally interact, Bobby's ghost talks, moves objects, and possesses a maid, so the authors define the supernatural as what can on occasion transcend the world of material interaction. Descartes' interactionist substance dualism supplies the model: the cogito (even a djinn cannot make you falsely believe you exist), the pineal gland as the soul's point of causal contact, and a testable hypothesis that makes the supernatural scientifically investigable and implies that we, as spirits, are supernatural too.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 10 "Notes" — Tests whether Rust's pessimism is a principled rationalist philosophy (Dienstag's view, versus Ligotti's temperament view) by mapping the Descartes-style rationalist and Hume-style empiricist opposition onto the partners: principled, deductive Rust versus impulse-driven Marty, including Rust's religion debate at the tent revival. It then reads the death of Sophia — Greek for wisdom, root of 'philosophy' — as symbolism suggesting Rust's pessimism stems from the death of wisdom rather than rational reflection, especially since Rust holds that the suffering of growing up is needed to become a pessimist. The finale's experience of Sophia's love is taken as a pure philosophical experience that collapses the reason/emotion distinction, so that pessimism belongs to both sides of the opposition at once.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 18 "Notes" — Reads Rust's 'dream inside a locked room' and 'everybody is nobody' monologues through the dream-argument and illusion-of-self traditions: the Upanishads and Advaita's atman/brahman, Vasubandhu's Buddhist non-self, Zhuangzi's butterfly dream, Plato's Theaetetus, and Descartes' dream doubt, plus Metzinger's self-model neuroscience. It diagnoses Rust as a neuro-nihilist in Metzinger's sense and defines his predicament with Nietzsche's nihilist, who judges the world as it is that it ought not to be, while noting Schopenhauer misread India's religions as pessimistic. Thompson argues nihilism is a deep insight gone awry — the self is not a thing but an enacted process like dancing — and reads Rust's final near-death experience of love as proof that transcendence of the dream of being a person is possible.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 21 "11. The Truth about Lying" — Fallis treats the Zone as a seminar in the philosophy of testimony: truth-tellers like Bob Wilson warning of a gremlin get dismissed as insane ('The Whole Truth' forces truth-telling as a curse), while convincing liars like Arch Hammer come to bad ends, so Kant's letter recommending reticence, saying true things but not the whole truth, looks like the best policy. On the receiving end, Descartes's malicious demon returns as aliens and devils ('To Serve Man,' 'The Howling Man,' 'Printer's Devil'), and Hume's advice to reject miracle-like testimony fails because in the Zone crazy stuff is often true. The chapter ends by endorsing Pascal's wager through 'The Big Tall Wish' and Jeff Myrtlebank's threat: believe the incredible witness just in case.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 27 "Kickstarting Inductive Inference" — Daniel Wilkenfeld analyzes Veronica's 'magic trick' in the 'One Angry Veronica' juryroom and her season-long bus-crash solution as Peter Lipton's inference to the best explanation: the hypothesis 'Beaver is a killer' wins by consilience (explaining the explosion, the dead rat, Curly Moran, even her chlamydia), simplicity, and completeness. But the criteria face Hume's problem of induction — why think the future will resemble the past, when yesterday's popular girl is today's pariah? — and Descartes's evil demon undermines even what Veronica 'sees,' since Curly Moran could fake a bus crash, leaving no non-circular justification for inferential habits none of us can live without. Following Nelson Goodman, Wilkenfeld concludes the demand for justification is misplaced: what matters is that Veronica reasons consistently, in the juryroom as at the cliff.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 3 "The Ethics of Pretending to Be a Cowboy" — Don Fallis uses Westworld to work out definitions of pretense and deception, testing successive accounts (acting-as-if, Austin's intend-to-deceive, Langland-Hassan's believe-P-is-false) against cases like guests playing cowboys, Ford passing off Bernard as human, and Maeve and Hector pretending to be deactivated. He adopts a Cartesian evil-demon model of deception but rejects the claim that deception must manipulate perceived evidence, arguing Ford's direct implanting of Teddy's Wyatt backstory still counts. He concludes, citing Kant on autonomy and Walzer on foreseen collateral harm, that staff who intend to deceive the hosts and even guests who foreseeably contribute to it act wrongly, since deceived hosts suffer real harm to their agency.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 12 "Inside the Helmet What Do Football Players Know" — Geivett uses football to illustrate epistemology, distinguishing factual (propositional) from competence (skill) knowledge through what running backs and quarterbacks must know and enact under split-second pressure, including 'football physics' vectors on a rollout pass. He treats the athlete's need to be mindful of knowledge amid stadium noise as a lesson in reliable belief, then critiques classroom skeptics who deploy Descartes's evil-demon and the brain-in-a-vat thought experiment, arguing mere logical possibility is no evidence for skepticism.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 22 "The Matrix, the Cave, and the Cogito" — Conard argues that The Matrix alludes to Plato's cave (the pod-bound humans mistaking the program for reality, Neo's painful ascent) and to Descartes' dream argument and evil-genius doubt (the singular consciousness generating the Matrix), but betrays their spirit by rejecting transcendence and the a priori. Because the film is 'Christianity without God'—Neo can only remake the shadow-world of the Matrix, not touch ultimate reality—it grounds knowledge in a subjective gut feeling ('being the One is just like being in love') rather than Descartes' intellectual intuition of God or Plato's rational grasp of the Forms, leaving no answer to whether life outside the Matrix is itself another illusion.
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 8 "Sherlock's Reasoning Toolbox" — Pigliucci shows that Holmes's celebrated 'deduction' is really a mix of induction and abduction, contrasting Aristotelian syllogism and Cartesian rationalism (with its failed Cartesian circle) against the fallibility of real investigation. He walks through Hume's problem of induction (Russell's inductivist chicken), the Mill-Whewell 'great induction debate,' and Popper's falsificationism—qualified by the Neptune/Uranus episode where scientists shielded Newton. Using 'Thor Bridge' and 'The Three Students,' he concludes Holmes is a pragmatic scientist wielding a whole toolbox, since there is no single scientific method.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Rodriguez-Ruiz argues that Schizopolis and sex, lies, and videotape function as everyday 'thought experiments' about knowledge, contrasting them with Descartes's evil-genius and dream arguments and Dretske's disguised-zebra case. Fletcher must literally become his wife's lover's double to know she is cheating, and Ann pieces together John's affair from a stray earring, dramatizing how high the bar for knowledge of others is and how much depends on lucky accident. The trashcan-music scene stages the problem of induction and Lehrer's Mr. Truetemp. Soderbergh's boss's 'confirm nor deny' speech and Lester's preventable death show the films endorse a moderate skepticism that still affirms nature and power as real, rejecting full relativism and dogmatism.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 7 "“Do Not Forsake Me, Oh, My Darling” Loneliness and Solitude in Westerns" — Biderman argues that the western hero's solitude carries philosophical benefits, distinguishing being alone from feeling lonely (McCauley in Heat: 'I'm alone, I'm not lonely'). Epistemically he likens the silent, self-reliant hero (Kane in High Noon, Shane, Munny in Unforgiven, Blondie) to Descartes retreating into methodological doubt and solipsistic solitude to secure knowledge. Ethically he sets Aristotle's claim that man is a social animal (so the friendless hero cannot flourish) against Stoic detachment and Sartrean/existentialist authenticity, concluding the hero must be 'lone' because his heroism is inseparable from his chosen solitude.
- **The Philosophy of Werner Herzog**, ch. 10 "Filmmaking and Philosophizing against the Grain of Theory Herzog and Wittgenstein" — Mihai Ometita pairs Herzog's anti-intellectualism with Wittgenstein's later philosophy, arguing that the obstinacy of Herzog's protagonists (Aguirre, Fitzcarraldo) and the dogmatism of Wittgenstein's interlocutors are two faces of an unbounded attachment to a single theory. Herzog's dictum 'An ape is an ape' echoes Wittgenstein's motto that everything is what it is, warning against forced metaphor (the smoking monkey in Echoes from a Somber Empire). Citing the Big Typescript and On Certainty, Ometita reads philosophy's difficulty as one of the will, and treats Aguirre's 'delirium' and Fitzcarraldo's 'dream' as quasi-nonsense that resists hasty diagnoses of madness; he invokes Descartes's window and Merleau-Ponty on film being perceived, not thought.
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 3 "Introduction" — The editors' introduction surveys Nolan's oeuvre chronologically to argue that a recurring theme of self-destruction and unstable self-identity runs through every film. It reads Following's needy Young Man through Buber's I/Thou (existing fully only when a Thou acknowledges you) and Hegel's master/slave dependence between Cobb and his mark, casts Inception's spinning top as a version of Descartes's dream argument about telling the real from the constructed, and invokes Hobbes when the Joker introduces 'a little anarchy' into Gotham. It frames Doodlebug as Nolan's most Freudian film and Interstellar as uniting personal identity, moral choice, and epistemology in Cooper's self-sacrifice.
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 6 "Spinning Tops and Brains in Vats" — This bundle of essays reads Memento and Inception as epistemology. Knepp uses Peirce's icon/index/symbol triad and Plato's Phaedrus critique of writing to show Leonard Shelby's tattoos and Polaroids give a false illusion of permanent truth (he tattoos Teddy as 'John G.' on purpose). Hoffman uses Kierkegaard's subjective truth to contrast Leonard, who lies to himself while pretending to gather objective 'facts', with Cobb, who takes a Kierkegaardian leap of faith and walks away from the spinning totem to embrace his children. Watson runs the Cartesian/Pyrrhonist dream argument against Inception's totems, arguing beliefs can be valuable via intellectual virtue even if unverifiable, and Lindenmuth pits Nozick's experience machine against Cobb's choice of real children over the dream-shade of Mal to argue reality matters more than pleasure.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 14 "6. The Foundations of Psychohistory" — Irish roots psychohistory in the seventeenth- and eighteenth-century clash between rationalism and empiricism over whether history can be a science. Descartes's mathematical, a priori method (which bred an 'anti-historical skepticism') is the ancestor of Seldon's dream of mathematizing human behavior, while Locke's empiricism and probabilistic knowledge inspired Gibbon's defense of historical evidence. Irish stages the Ancients-versus-Moderns debate through the Lord Dorwin / Salvor Hardin exchange over first-hand versus armchair scholarship, and contrasts Gibbon's moral, backward-looking history with Seldon's amoral, forward-looking prediction.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 14 "Skepticism Outside the Matrix" — Lawrence uses The Matrix to raise Cartesian skepticism: Neo's deception dramatizes Descartes's dream argument and evil demon, the computer-run Matrix being a technological version of the demon. He argues even Morpheus cannot be certain he has truly awakened ('the Matrix within the Matrix'), so the only certainty is Descartes's cogito. Drawing on Russell's 'Appearance and Reality,' he then argues that even setting aside Matrix scenarios, naive realism fails, since a chair's color, texture, solidity and shape are all perception-relative, leaving the external world's nature deeply uncertain.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 10 "2. Where Is the Twilight Zone" — Scalambrino argues the Twilight Zone is a televised expression of surrealist philosophy (Breton, Dalí) that provokes the Freudian 'uncanny.' He traces a line from Descartes—whose cogito and 'clear and distinct' rational mind produced the mind–body problem that lets surrealists destabilize waking reality—through psychoanalysis to Breton's 'point' where real and imagined cease to be contradictions. Episodes like 'A World of His Own' (automatic writing), 'The Mirror' (Dalí's paranoiac-critical method), 'Shadow Play,' 'The Shelter,' and 'The Lonely' unleash the imagination unbound by reason and provoke the uncanny in viewers.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 15 "McElligot’s Pool Epistemology (with Fish!)" — Ron Novy uses Marco's faith that unseen fish swim in McElligot's Pool to survey theories of knowledge as justified true belief. The farmer's empiricism and Marco's inference from a book frame a tour through Descartes's evil-genius doubt and skepticism, Locke's primary/secondary qualities (indirect realism), Berkeley's idealism ('to be is to be perceived'), and rationalist a priori knowledge, before turning to feminist epistemology (Schott, Kant's 'intuitions without concepts are blind,' Nietzsche on perspectival seeing) and Quine's naturalized epistemology to argue knowers are situated and the pool may indeed be 'bigger than you or I know.'
- **Food & Philosophy - Eat, Think, and Be Merry**, ch. 10 "Chapter 4" — Verene frames the two great cookbooks, Apicius's De Re Coquinaria and Artusi's La scienza in cucina, through a contrast between a 'Cartesian' and a 'Vichian' epistemology of cookery: Descartes' Discourse on Method, which discards custom for clear-and-distinct reasoning, is blamed for the restaurant chef's invented 'stacked food,' while Vico's New Science, which grounds knowledge in historical tradition, underwrites the trattoria and the home kitchen. Reading Apicius's garum and dormice and Artusi's health-and-economy motto (glossed via Aristotle's Economics as household management), he defends recipes as repeatable topoi like songs rather than one-off novelties. He closes by tying table manners to Rousseau's moeurs and to Socrates' claim in the Phaedo that speaking (and by extension cooking and eating) badly does harm to the soul.
- **Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low**, ch. 23 "BLUES" — Jesse Steinberg argues that doubt — a pervasive blues theme (B. B. King's 'nobody loves me but my momma,' Otis Spann's 'another mule kickin' in my stall,' Buddy Guy's 'I Smell a Rat') — supports Descartes's external-world skepticism, since knowledge would require ruling out the dreaming hypothesis. Against the 'I don't care' hedonistic reply he deploys Nozick's experience machine to show we value authentic reality over mere pleasant appearance, and he rejects contextualism as a solution. Endorsing Socrates' examined life, he settles for strong justification rather than certainty, reading Charley Patton's 'can't tell my future, can't tell my past' as the blues' honest coping with irreducible doubt.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 8 "Horror and the Idea of Everyday Life On Skeptical Threats in Psycho and The Birds" — Philip J. Nickel argues horror has an epistemological value structurally parallel to philosophical skepticism: it maliciously rips away the tacit 'cognitive trust' backing our everyday actions. In The Birds, the diner 'symposium' where Mrs. Bundy's confident science that birds cannot coordinate an attack is refuted moments later dramatizes a paranoid scenario we cannot rationally rule out. In Psycho, Marion Crane's isolation and misplaced trust in the seemingly normal Norman Bates enacts the skeptical premise that the ordinary person you rely on could murder you. Like Hume returning to backgammon, viewers can only resume everyday life, which Nickel says horror exposes as a necessary but insecure construction.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 8 "2. The Matrix" — Rowlands reads The Matrix as a vivid staging of Cartesian skepticism: Neo's pod-world is Descartes's dream and evil-demon conjectures (AI plays the demon) plus the modern brain-in-a-vat, showing we cannot be certain the external world exists. He uses the 'there is no air/muscles' and 'twin buildings' variant of Putnam's Twin Earth to argue we cannot even be certain which thoughts we think. The Hume-Nietzsche bundle critique undermines even the cogito, and the spoon-bending boy ('there is no spoon') illustrates Berkeley's idealism as the endpoint of skepticism about the physical world.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 8 "NOTES" — Carolyn Korsmeyer uses Aristotle's Poetics dictum that the 'probable impossible' beats the possible improbable to argue popular narrative can actually conduct philosophy, not merely illustrate it. Her central case is that the TV series Angel—the ensouled, guilt-cursed vampire who concludes 'if nothing we do matters, then all that matters is what we do'—independently arrives at the same existentialist position as Simone de Beauvoir's The Ethics of Ambiguity, with no textual borrowing. She contrasts The Matrix's dramatically sustained Cartesian dream-doubt against the 'improbable impossible' Dallas dream-season, showing why one is a philosophical vehicle and the other bankrupt.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 14 "Skepticism Outside the Matrix" — Matt Lawrence uses The Matrix to stage the skeptical problem, running Descartes's dream argument and evil-demon method of doubt (the Matrix as a technological demon) and even a 'Matrix within the Matrix' to show Morpheus cannot know he is awake. Descartes's cogito supplies the one certainty that survives radical deception. Lawrence then draws on Russell's analysis of the red chair to argue against naive realism: color, texture, solidity, and shape are appearances, so even setting aside the Matrix we cannot know the world in itself.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 4 "2. Twilight Zone as Philosophy 101" — Marinucci uses The Twilight Zone as a triple introduction to philosophy, the show, and the handbook, arguing that philosophy is defined not by necessary-and-sufficient conditions but by Wittgensteinian family resemblance and salient features (curiosity, depth, abstraction, controversy) learned through MacIntyre-style immersion in a practice. She reads episodes as thought experiments: the amnesiac astronaut in 'Where Is Everybody?' and living-doll/robot episodes echo Plato's cave and Descartes's Method of Doubt about appearance versus reality, Nagel's 'what is it like to be a bat?' frames the problem of other minds, and episodes like 'The Shelter' and 'It's a Good Life' dramatize the tension between egoism and altruism and social conformity, including feminist gaslighting in 'Twenty Two.'
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 34 "31. Inception as Philosophy Choose Your Dreams or Seek Reality" — Johnson uses Nolan's Inception—Cobb's dream-heists, the ambiguous spinning top, and the case that the whole film may be a dream—to test the moral Todd McGowan draws from it: that since we can't be sure what is real, we should abandon the quest for reality and choose the dream (his object of desire, his children) as Cobb does at the end. He evaluates six defenses of that moral, rejecting Descartes' skeptical dream/evil-demon problem (answered by abduction and by Plato's cave and Nozick's experience machine showing true belief is valuable), Baudrillard's denial of reality, Locke/Kant on the unknowable noumenal world, and Kierkegaard's leap of faith and Pascal's Wager, before softening it with Hume's return from skepticism to backgammon: entertain the doubt, then walk away when your children walk in.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 51 "48. The Matrix as Philosophy Understanding Knowledge, Belief, Choice, and Reality" — Perez reads the Matrix trilogy as a sustained argument about how choosing what to believe and 'know' shapes the reality we live in. He opens with Descartes' dream problem and cogito, contrasting Descartes' foundationalism with Rorty's anti-foundationalism to explain Cypher's choice to reject reality for the Matrix's certitude, and uses Searle's brute vs. institutional facts (the cookies, the steak, 'there is no spoon') to show social reality is constructed. Against the fatalism of the Oracle, Architect, and Merovingian, he argues nearly every character makes free choices, and resolves the tension via Hume's compatibilism — liberty requires necessity, and choices gain meaning only in response to causality — while noting agent-causation objections (Reid, O'Connor, Rowe) that make Neo's 'Because I choose to' significant. Gettier's justified-true-belief critique and Plato's Cave frame the knowledge and enlightenment themes.

### Duration (durée)

Duration (durée) is Henri Bergson's name for time as it is actually lived and felt, as opposed to time as measured by clocks. Real duration is a continuous, qualitative flow in which past and present interpenetrate and each moment is genuinely new, unlike the homogeneous, divisible instants that science treats as spatial units laid side by side. Bergson argued that intellect and physics distort time by spatializing it, and that only intuition grasps duration from within. The idea grounds his views on memory, freedom, and creativity, and shaped much of early twentieth-century thought.

- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 31 "Does the Totem Tumble" — Auxier brings Bergson's memory theory, the past gnawing into the present, all dreaming as remembering, and Whitehead's process philosophy to Nolan's 'pathologies of temporal experience', defending the film's supposedly selective physics: with each deeper level the same five minutes disperses across a larger dream space, diluting the carry-over of effects while time expands geometrically, because 'space is frozen time'. He then re-reads the ending through the narrative gaps the audience was lured across: the top was Mal's totem, which Cobb spin as an act of mourning after handling it and betraying her, and Cobb's real totem is his gun, which Saito uses to shoot them both out of Limbo. The top's tumbling in the finale matters only as a sign that Cobb, the coward who once needed total control over Mal, has finally learned the leap of faith of trusting another person.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 154 "Chapter 24 - I Know What You Did Next Summer" — Paul Atkinson's introduction to Chapter 24 frames 'The Minority Report' and 'Paycheck', together with their film adaptations, as explorations of the many different ways of knowing the future. He proposes Henri Bergson - who denied the future can be known and explained why we sometimes think we can - as the philosopher perfectly placed to 'write the rules' for the time-travel game these stories play. It also contrasts philosophy's umpire-like settling of issues with the films' urge to literally show us the future rather than merely predict it.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 155 "Pay Now, Live Later" — This section reads Precrime through Bergson's duree: in Dick's story the precogs are 'monkeys' and 'idiots' emitting snippets that investigators must analyze, while the film shows a precog immersed in and living through the future visually. It explains Bergson's claim that clocks and timelines falsify time, which is really lived duration in which the past endures as memory and actively directs us toward an open future, and rehearses his reunion thought experiment: imagined futures are mere sketches, while the actual future arrives with the unique specificity of the Mona Lisa. No one, on this view, can know the future as if living it.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 156 "I Can Predict What You (Don’t) Do Next Summer" — Using Bergson's imprevisible and 'The Possible and the Real', this section argues that the story's Precrime works by prediction-as-elimination: investigators discard the precogs' babblings that do not fit the world, 'closing the gate' on the impossible to leave only a statistically possible future. Bergson's gate metaphor shows prediction never yields the real future, only the negatively 'not impossible', yet Precrime arrests people for an abstract possible event they have never actually lived. It ends by asking whether Anderton, accused of a future murder in advance, would still commit it, since ever-changing memory and knowledge make a possible future never identical to the actual one.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 157 "Living in the Time of the Crime" — A close reading of the film's opening murder contrasts cinematic precognition with the story's: the camera moves from Sarah Marks's terrified face and dilated pupil to the precog Agatha's watery blue eye as she utters 'murder', making Agatha an empathetic witness immersed in the scene. Anderton then pieces the moving images together like a film editor working with rushes, so no analytic machinery connects present to future - the future is simply given in visual detail. In the film, precognition is the foreseeable rather than the predictable: precogs and audience alike live in the time of the crime.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 158 "Always Invest in the Future" — This section retells 'Paycheck' in story and John Woo film versions: engineer Jennings trades two memory-wiped years for a cloth sack of ordinary objects - a piece of wire, a bus token - which his erased past self chose as tools for future crises, from breaking out of a police cell to paying a robot ticket inspector. It explains the story's time machine, a 'mirror' that images the future and a 'scoop' that extracts objects from it, a significant difference from the movie. The section shows how past-Jennings exists for present-Jennings only through these leftovers, which prove more valuable than money.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 159 "Summarizing the Future" — Applying Bergson's Time and Free Will claim that recalling the past shortens it into a 'thing', the section uses the curriculum-vitae metaphor: like a CV or Facebook page, we imagine the future as a summary compiled from the past. In 'Paycheck', Jennings's sack becomes a plan only when he reflects - the wire at the police station, the token on the bus - until past, present and future fuse and he feels 'a strange elation' at fulfilling his past self's design, raising again whether awareness of the future changes what we do. The film diverges by having Jennings sabotage the atomic-bomb future he foresees, echoing Minority Report's contest between an inevitable future and present action.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 160 "The Future as Predictive Text" — The section develops a 'predictive text' metaphor: once Jennings's past is constructed as a narrative by past-Jennings, the future merely mirrors it, filling in missing letters like autocorrect - as in the ticket-stub passage where Jennings deduces where he 'had been' and concludes 'he had foreseen this too.' It contrasts the short stories, where a possible future only guides present action, with both films' screens - rewinding videotape, headline videos of an exploding city, the Minority Report editing suite - that render the future almost indistinguishable from the present. For Bergson the future can never appear on a television screen, since that would require a camera living in the time of the event; at most the future is a gate closing or a frame narrowing to a vague sketch.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 22 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Randall Auxier explains Jeopardy!'s appeal through Bergson's Matter and Memory: memory is a relation - the past acting in the present - along a continuum of matter (repetition of what was) and memory (variation), and the show strips contestants of bodily action so that what we watch is pure 'recollection', the instantaneous summoning of subtle structures from the flux. Providing the question instead of the answer forces a tiny temporal reversal, a six-step durational epoch he calls (after Edgar Sheffield Brightman) a 'shining present', which is why Jeopardy! outshines College Bowl, why champions like Ken Jennings fascinate as savants of immediate recollection, and why the slow clock music of Final Jeopardy! is the show's most exquisite torture and catharsis.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 25 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Through a hot-tub dialogue in Prismo's Time Room, the chapter walks Jake through the main theories of time: McTaggart's A-theory versus B-theory, plus presentism, the growing block, eternalism and four-dimensionalism, illustrated with the mirror-Finn dream, Farmworld Finn, Jake's unchangeable croak dream, and the Ancient Psychic Tandem War Elephant as a thing stretched across past, present and future selves. Booko's description of the multiverse becomes a springboard for David Lewis's possible-worlds realism and Everett's many-worlds reading of Prismo's 'alternate wish worlds'. Finally, quotes from McTaggart and Bergson delivered as Finn's Glasses of Nerdicon rant argue that time resists spatial and scientific analysis and must be lived, which the authors tie to relativity, black-hole cosmology and Prismo's Time Room as the one dimension outside time.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 22 "Deleuze Jam Today" — Walks Alice through four theories of time: Augustine's three presents in Confessions (Alice 'was a different person then'; the past exists only as present memory), Kant's time as a subjective form of intuition presupposed by experience (the White Rabbit's anxiety about being late already requires it), Bergson's indivisible duration against spatialized clock time (running fastest with the Red Queen yet ending under the same tree; the Hatter stuck at six o'clock; Zeno's Achilles resolved by indivisible acts), and Deleuze's chronos and aion from The Logic of Sense. Mark W. Westmoreland reads 'jam to-morrow and jam yesterday—but never jam to-day' as pure aion: the present never arrives, only an endlessly subdividing past-future.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 16 "Only Time Will Tell" — Latta reads the film through Bergson's distinction between clock time and duration: Strange is introduced as pure quantitative multiplicity — identifying Chuck Mangione's 'Feels So Good' (1977) mid-surgery, surrounding himself with watches, including Christine Palmer's inscribed 'Time will tell how much I love you' — while the Ancient One lives duration, surrendering to the river's current. Kaecilius embodies 'chronological nihilism' ('time is an insult'), and his and Dormammu's timeless Dark Dimension is existentially impossible for Bergson, since life only progresses and endures in time. The climax shows Strange recreating the present in the endless looped bargain with Dormammu ('pain is an old friend'), growing through qualitative multiplicity and élan vital, until the shattered watch — hands broken, inscription intact — marks his conversion from counting time to living it.
- **Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test**, ch. 9 "H E N R I B E R G S O N" — Three Part Three essays on Dr. Manhattan's strange relation to time and fate. Christopher Drohan reads Manhattan's simultaneous 'intricately structured jewel' of time through Bergson's Matter and Memory — perception interlaced with memory, the pure past persisting in every act, time as lived duration — so that 'Nothing ever ends, Adrian' becomes a Bergsonian insight and the thermodynamic-miracle speech an intuition of life's creative improbability. Arthur Ward argues theological fatalism (Boethius and Aquinas placing a timeless God outside time, Paley's watchmaker behind Jon the watchmaker's son with his clock-shaped Martian palace) does not doom Laurie's free will, because Jon's own claims are inconsistent — he is surprised by the cancer rumors, misses Veidt's tachyon-shielded plan, and acts drugged — so either his foresight or his fatalism must be false. Andrew Terjesen reads Manhattan as a Stoic sage: Seneca and Epictetus on emotions as false judgments explain his 'a live body and a dead body contain the same number of particles,' his Mars epiphany is the sage's 'good emotion' of joy at the thermodynamic miracle, and his impersonal 'clock without a craftsman' completes a Neo-Stoic line running through Descartes to Spinoza's God-who-is-Nature.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 22 "Spontaneity, Immediacy, and Difference Philosophy, Being in Time, and Creativity in the Aesthetics of Jack Ker" — David Need contrasts three theories of 'being in time' behind the aesthetics of spontaneity: Kerouac's debt to Spengler's organic cycles of civilization (a stereoscopic, dualist view where an arbitrary measure like a candle or page limns deep being), Olson's use of Whitehead's 'concrescence' in 'Projective Verse' (a monist, all-at-once projection of new monads), and Cage's use of Coomaraswamy's Vedanta, where silence is sabdabrahman and chance imitates Nature. He argues the real fault line is the old monist-vs-dualist divide (Advaita brahman vs. Cartesian dualism), and that each artist's notion of creative freedom follows from which metaphysical schema he borrowed, so our quarrels with the Beats reflect our own metaphysical stakes.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 21 "Disenchantment and Rebellion in Alphaville" — Woolfolk reads Godard's Alphaville as an imagination of spiritual disaster: the Alpha 60 computer's reduction of time to divisible units suppresses the Bergsonian durée and fundamental self, and the city's architecture of 'nonplaces' embodies Weber's disenchantment and the Frankfurt School's culture-industry critique. Following Charles Taylor, he argues disenchantment opens a new heroic framework of facing an indifferent universe with lucidity, in which Lemmy Caution—a postmodern pastiche of noir dandies—rebels through an aestheticized eroticism and Éluard's surrealist poetry, achieving a Weberian 'this-worldly salvation' of art and love that succeeds where Orwell's Julia and Huxley's Savage fail.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Palmer argues that The Underneath and The Limey fuse film noir's obsession with the untranscendable past with Alain Resnais's Bergsonism, mediated by Deleuze's account of the time-image. In The Limey, career criminal Wilson's consciousness accumulates recollection-images (including Poor Cow footage of a young Stamp) and prospective imaginings (the two visualized shootings), building toward a Bergsonian intuition: confronting Terry Valentine, Wilson recognizes himself as the same kind of selfish betrayer and spares him, achieving a redemption denied noir predecessors like Get Carter's Carter and Point Blank's Walker. The Underneath, by contrast, uses achronic color-coded structure only to define Michael from the outside, which Palmer counts a partial failure of the same interior ambition.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — King analyzes The Limey as 'Get Carter as made by Alain Resnais,' using Bordwell's fabula/syuzhet distinction to show how its nonlinear editing renders what Soderbergh calls the nonlinear nature of thought. Dialogue continuity is stretched across discontinuous spaces (the Wilson-Elaine 'embarrassed/ashamed/disappointed' exchange), flash-forwards precede events, and the party shooting is replayed three times as Wilson's fantasy. King argues the whole film reads as Wilson's subjective reconstruction on the plane home, grounded in Bergson (via Deleuze's time-image) yet, unlike Resnais's Marienbad, never producing real ontological or epistemological doubt because the revenge-thriller backbone and color-coding keep it legible. The film's dominant note is nostalgia for a past that, because of Wilson's imprisonments, never really was.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 12 "10_LaRocca_Chapter_009.html" — William Day argues that Herzog's Cave of Forgotten Dreams, filming the 32,000-year-old Chauvet Cave paintings in 3D, works not by preserving a past but by transfiguring the present, placing the viewer in a 'mythological relation to time.' He reads three literary precursors to this cinematic 'doubleness'—Emerson's 'History' and 'The American Scholar' (the past made 'now'), Thoreau's spectator-self in Walden's 'Solitude,' and Weil's 'renunciation of time'—as antecedents to Cavell's ontology of film. The Fred Astaire shadow-dance from Swing Time, spliced into the cave footage, becomes Day's emblem of what becomes of things on film: the shadows dance on after Astaire stops.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 17 "15_LaRocca_Chapter_014.html" — Bernadette Wegenstein examines her own cinema-verite practice in The Good Breast (and See You Soon Again), arguing that verite 'provokes' rather than merely produces truth through the filmmaker's participatory presence. She grounds this in Italian neorealism via Bazin (the real 'aimed at,' not re-presented) and Deleuze's Cinema II 'time-image'—a Bergsonian cinema 'of the seer' attuned to lived duration. Through her breast-cancer patient-characters (Doris, Carol, Debra, Shelia) and the surgeon Dr. Schnaper's trip to Saint Agatha's Catania, she shows how editing calls forth an 'alternate reality' and an existential (Kracauerian) realism.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 20 "18_LaRocca_Chapter_017.html" — Selmin Kara reads Victor Erice's Dream of Light (The Quince Tree Sun), about the painter Antonio Lopez trying to capture a quince tree in shifting autumn light, as a case for a 'new materialist' ontology of documentary against Bill Nichols-style representationalism. Drawing on Deleuze via De Landa's actual/virtual continuum, Spinoza's and Bergson's vital-matter lineage, and Bennett's 'vibrant matter,' she argues the film's dream sequence of the operator-less camera, dimmer and rotting fruit foregrounds the mediation rather than the mastery of light. She proposes updating Grierson's 'creative treatment of actuality' to 'the creative treatment of actuality and virtuality,' treating filmic and profilmic matter as intra-acting agents.

### Faith and Reason

The relationship between faith and reason concerns how religious belief stands in relation to rational argument and evidence. Positions range from rationalism, which holds that belief must be justified by reason, to fideism, which maintains that faith is independent of or even opposed to rational proof, with many thinkers seeking a middle path in which faith and reason are complementary. The debate runs throughout the history of philosophy and theology, from medieval attempts to demonstrate God's existence to modern discussions of whether religious commitment can be reasonable without conclusive proof.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 62 "Unknown" — Taking the film's cafeteria religion seriously as 'Neo-pluralism', the chapter distinguishes four varieties of religious pluralism and finds each wanting: extreme pluralism dies by simple logic since of 100,000 religions many contradict one another; fundamental-teachings pluralism fails because the great religions differ on genuinely fundamental doctrines (Islam's personal God versus Theravada's non-theism versus the Trinity); cafeteria pluralism produces incoherent transplantings (reincarnation fits Hinduism but not Buddhism or Christianity) and lacks any rational justification short of wishful thinking; and Hick's Kantian transcendental pluralism posits an unintelligible, wholly unknowable Real while demanding the doublethink - highlighted by Alvin Plantinga - of continuing to hold beliefs one recognizes as literally false.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 63 "Unknown" — The chapter rebuts three pluralist objections to religious exclusivism: the 'equal fruits' argument confuses hard exclusivism with the common soft (inclusivist) form that freely admits salvation and authentic experience outside one tradition; the arrogance charge rests on a principle that would condemn every political and moral conviction held in the face of reasonable disagreement, and is self-refuting - Plantinga's 'philosophical tar baby'; and the arbitrariness charge begs the question, since pluralists assume rather than argue that no religion could have better evidence, which is precisely the point at issue between exclusivism and pluralism.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 77 "Unknown" — This section explains why the moral quest needs faith: because the ideal Matrix of morality seems powerless against the hard world built on separation and egotism, Kant postulates freedom, God, and immortality as what we must believe to remain faithful to our basic moral choice. It develops the first postulate - freedom: the essence of moral experience is anti-deterministic, scientific knowledge consists in deterministic explanation and so cannot know free will without reducing it to its opposite, therefore we must have faith in our power to choose - the creed of liberators on the way to 'the promised land of Zion, the kingdom of heaven on earth'.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 13 "Who Should Be Committed" — Thomas Senor argues that rooting for the perennially losing Cubs is rationally and morally on a par with religious commitment: genuine fandom, like faith, is loyalty that survives repeated disappointment (distinguished from the zealot's 'my team right or wrong' via the Portland Trailblazers' 'Jailblazers' era). Since beliefs and fan loyalties are not under direct voluntary control, he rereads Pascal's wager not as choosing to believe but as cultivating belief indirectly: attending Mass the way moving to Chicago and following the Cubs daily can make you a fan. The believer's epistemic optimism toward religious experience and the devout's second-order hope in dark times mirror the Cubs fan's springtime optimism, so neither Cubs fans nor the religious should be committed.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 12 "From Knowledge to Faith" — Lawler reads Crimes and Misdemeanors through Kant's problem of the Highest Good: Judah's unpunished murder of Dolores shows a world where the wicked prosper and the good (Cliff, the blind Ben) suffer, the scandal Job complains of, while Levy's suicide shows that a bare existentialist 'yes' to life fails without love. Kant's 'I had to deny knowledge to make room for faith' is applied to the film's two visions: the deterministic, dog-eat-dog world of science and Adam Smith's economic egoism (with Hobbes's war of all against all) is only appearance, not reality. Kant's gallows example shows Judah could have discovered authentic freedom by respecting Dolores's dignity rather than seeing 'the black eyes of an insect', and the postulates of freedom, God, and immortality ground Ben's not-really-blind faith — so it is Judah who is truly blind.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 7 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Editor Jorge Gracia's preface frames The Passion as a phenomenon that stirs people too deeply for indifference (a minister's fatal heart attack in a Brazilian cinema, reviews ranging from zero to five stars) and argues its religious stakes give its questions more bite than those of The Matrix or The Lord of the Rings. It lays out the book's five controversies: whether Christ had to suffer violently and what atonement means, whether the film is anti-Semitic, how faith relates to truth and to reading the Gospels as God's word, why Christ was killed, and whether Judas can be morally responsible for a betrayal God foreknew and redemption required. Gracia insists the collection takes no side and offers only a point of departure.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 9 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — McInerny argues Gibson's film works like Kierkegaard's indirect communication: its shocking graphic realism, against the tamed stations of the cross and serene crucifixes of Catholic churches, targets nominal Christians and forces each viewer to hear Jesus's 'I want you' and confront the scandal of the Incarnation rather than domesticate it. He reads the film alongside Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions as embroidery with no meaning apart from the Gospels, and invokes Aquinas on the Eucharist as the continuing memorial of the passion in which Christ is hidden under bread and wine. The film is 'a sign of contradiction' that, like Nietzsche's self-declared Antichrist, divides humanity into acceptance or rejection, so that efforts to keep religion within the bounds of reason alone must distort it.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 12 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Walls argues the controversy lies not in the gore but in who died on the cross and why, and shows Gibson weaving the three classic atonement theories: Christ crushing the serpent in Gethsemane as the Christus-Victor ransom (with Augustine's mousetrap image), the Isaiah 53 scourging and Gibson's own hand driving the nail as Anselm-style penal substitution in which the innocent dies so the guilty Barabbas in each of us goes free, and the transformed characters (Mary Magdalene, Simon of Cyrene, the good thief, the kneeling soldier) as Abelard's moral influence. Against Kant's charge that atonement is a superstitious substitute for moral transformation, he cites Swinburne and Quinn: pleading the atonement requires repentance, and the tens of thousands of reported conversions and confessions show it transforms lives. He concludes that any adequate account needs all three theories, objective payment and subjective transformation alike, and that atonement aims at mercy and reconciliation rather than retribution.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 18 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Kurtz, the secular humanist, argues the film is a political weapon of the Religious Right (O'Reilly, Dobson, Gingrich) that presents fantasy as fact: Gibson claims fidelity to the Gospels while borrowing torture scenes such as the bridge plunge and the savage flogging from Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions, whitewashing the historical Pilate, and erasing that Jesus, Mary, and the disciples were themselves Jews. Applying historical criticism, he contends the Gospels are anonymous, second- and third-hand missionary propaganda written forty to seventy years after Jesus, shaped by the rivalry between rabbinic Judaism and Gentile-seeking Jewish Christianity and canonized politically at Nicaea under Constantine. He concludes by defending the freedom of inquiry, skeptical scrutiny of all sacred texts, and the First Amendment's separation of church and state against the film's power to inflame anti-Semitism and the American culture war.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 20 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Bronson argues Gibson's fixation on Jesus's suffering is not a Christian oddity but a deeply Jewish mystical one: using William James's four marks of mystical experience (ineffability, noetic quality, transiency, passivity), he reads the Gethsemane opening, where Jesus crushes Satan's serpent and receives a vision of the Father, as a classic mystical trial in the line of Moses at Sinai, Daniel's chariot-throne vision, Elijah's fiery ascent, John the Baptist, Paul's blinding light, and later the Kabbalah and Hasidic masters whose path to God runs through anguish. The Platonic Socrates of the Symposium and Phaedrus (wisdom arriving through the madness of love) and the medieval agreement of al-Ghazali, Maimonides, and Aquinas that reason cannot reach God frame his philosophy-versus-mysticism contrast, including the film's mother-son floorboard scene as love but not full mystical contact. The added scene where Pilate's wife tells him 'If you will not hear the truth, no one can tell you' shows Gibson siding with the mystical path to truth over Pilate's pragmatic one.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 23 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Jorge Gracia reframes the fidelity controversy as a problem in the theory of interpretation: Gibson had to make countless choices the Gospels leave silent (Christ's worn clothing, the Italian landscape, Jesus staring into the camera at the Last Supper, added scenes like Satan raging and demon children haunting Judas), so the film is unavoidably an interpretation. He surveys five criteria interpreters of Scripture have used — personal intuition (illustrated by Augustine's 'take and read' in the Confessions), ecclesial authority and the visions of nuns Emmerich and Agreda, sola scriptura, historical scholarship, and tradition (Aquinas's camp; Veronica's veil, the Shroud, the virgin Mary's prominence) — and argues each is inadequate alone because every one rests on prior theology. Hence disputes about the film are really disputes between theologies, and the film makes sense only within Gibson's Catholic view of Jesus as the Messiah announced by Isaiah 53.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 26 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Dallas Willard defends the film's excess of violence as its whole point: it visualizes human evil as beyond the remedies of education, law, or counseling (the route Plato and Aristotle tried), with Satan — the androgynous figure carrying the smug dwarf through the scourging crowd — explaining why only Christ's non-resistant embrace of the cross can break evil's grip. Against the passive reading of 'the Passion,' he argues Jesus 'played' his judges, deliberately laying down his life to inaugurate the kingdom of God. The argument leans on the hidden God (deus absconditus): God stays hidden, contra Sartre's 'no nature' self-creation and closer to Pico della Mirandola, so that we can freely make ourselves, which is also why demanding 'more evidence' misses what belief in God requires.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 29 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Paul Moser answers the objection that an all-loving God could not plan His Son's torture by arguing the cross is God's scandalous self-giving love: Jesus is no mere moral guru but the unique atoning sacrifice (the mad/Satanic/Son-of-God trilemma, 'he who delivered me to you has the greater sin'), and the crucifixion is God's grand reversal where self-giving love defeats death. He attacks the 'nice god' of natural theology as domesticating idolatry — God hides His plans from 'the wise and the intelligent' — and holds that we know God not by philosophical evidence but through Gethsemane-style filial obedience ('not my will but yours'), noting that Gibson himself appears in the film driving a nail, casting all of us as the crucifiers whom God forgives.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 33 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Bassham and Bagget observe that amid the film's unscriptural brutality Jesus never resists — he stops Peter's sword, heals Malchus's ear, and climbs back up for a second scourging — and ask whether this nonviolence can be rationally grounded without theological premises. They reject four classic readings of 'resist not evil' (Catholic counels-of-perfection, Schweitzer's interim ethics, Luther's penitential ethic, Tolstoy's absolute pacifism, noting Jesus himself used force against the money-changers) in favor of a hyperbole-plus-implicit-qualifier reading; then they show act utilitarianism licenses atrocities, rule utilitarianism at best yields an unpalatable absolute pacifism, and Kantian single-principle deontology preserves a right of self-defense Jesus's ethic calls us to lay aside — closing with a 'character model' of the Passion (duty vs freedom vs character) on which nonviolence is becoming the kind of person for whom violence is no longer an option, justified ultimately only by the cross.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 34 "The Man and His Faith" — Morris argues Daredevil is the rare mainstream hero with a religious interior life: raised nominally Catholic in Hell's Kitchen, his absent mother a nun who calls him 'a servant of God', he prays, thinks in religious categories, and complains to God like King David in the Psalms ('Why do the wicked prosper?'). Distinguishing mere outward religiosity from authentic faith, he proposes his 'Double Power Principle' - whatever has power for ill has equal power for good, religion included - and asks whether faith is blind like Matt Murdock or perceptive like his radar sense: a source of strength or of weakness for a costumed vigilante.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 35 "Faith and Fear" — Against Quentin Beck's claim that 'a man without fear is a man without faith', Morris argues the fear-based account of religion (Freud's) mistakes superstition for faith: authentic faith is a commitment of the heart rather than intellectual certitude, so the truly fearless are likely people of strong faith, as the martyrs show. He then distinguishes paralyzing self-referential 'fear of' from motivating 'fear that' (better called concern), concluding Daredevil genuinely is the Man Without Fear precisely because his deep-down faithfulness sustains him - he lives 'by faith and not by sight'.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 106 "Gloom, Doom, and Morality" — Works out naturalism's moral cost: no purpose behind our existence, no blueprint for life, Russell's hope that sensitive souls can love the tragic beauty of it anyway, and the Wilson-Ruse claim that ethics is "an illusion fobbed off on us by our genes," which loses its grip once seen through — like Macbeth's dagger. Against this it sets Kant's moral faith: morality makes rational sense only if we postulate God and immortality so virtue is finally rewarded, and the chapter concludes naturalism offers no deep basis for the life-risking duties a hero like Superman faces.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 108 "A Theological Basis for Super-Heroics" — Proposes that Christian theism's doctrines of heaven, hell and Christ's return resolve the truth/justice tension by grounding moral obligation in God's perfectly moral nature and guaranteeing that justice prevails. It rebuts Maggin's claim that faith in a power greater than ours breeds inaction: God works through human co-creators, so Superman still has a duty to do what he can, and the objective hope of ultimate justice is exactly the corrective that despairing Superman and tyrannical, fear-ruling Batman in Kingdom Come both lack.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 109 "Hope and the Human Challenge" — Reads Superman's return — "Up in the sky!", the crowd hailing "the second coming of Superman" at the UN — as the enacted theology of Kingdom Come: hope in a greater power revives a world "hungry for hope" and draws the other heroes back to the fray. The Spectre's charge to the preacher Norman McCay, "you exist to give hope," voices the chapter's conclusion that a supernatural eschatology holds hope, truth, and individual responsibility together in a way naturalism's unyielding despair cannot.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 15 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Steven Lovell reads the Green Witch's enchantment in The Silver Chair (the sun is only a copy of the lamp, Aslan only a bigger cat, Narnia a children's tale) as Lewis's staging of the Freudian critique of religion, and answers that similarity cannot tell copy from original, that the genetic fallacy vitiates arguing from a belief's origin, and that Aslan is 'not safe,' so Christianity is hardly wish-fulfillment (Augustine's restless heart and Pascal's God-shaped hole point the other way). Puddleglum's stamping out the fire and vow to live 'as like a Narnian as I can even if there isn't any Narnia' is defended through Pascal's Wager and James's 'The Will to Believe': the reality of Narnia is a live, forced, and momentous option that may legitimately be decided on passional grounds.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 35 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Debunks the 'Anscombe legend' that Lewis abandoned rational apologetics for children's stories after his 1948 Socratic Club defeat by Elizabeth Anscombe over the argument that naturalism is self-refuting. It shows Lewis revised and expanded the argument in the 1960 Miracles, incorporating Anscombe's reasons/causes distinction, and kept writing apologetic essays, while the Professor's trilemma about Lucy (liar, lunatic, or truthful) mirrors the Trilemma of Mere Christianity and shows Narnia using logic, not fleeing it. It rejects A.N. Wilson's identification of the Green Witch with Anscombe and argues the Chronicles teach that prudence and faith are compatible virtues: Edmund's rationalizing, Trumpkin's honest skepticism, and Puzzle's blind trust in Shift all show that fideistic faith is a vice, not what Lewis asks of children.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 17 "Prayer (A Euphemism for Butt-Kissing and Begging)" — Argues the Pythons' religious gags perform philosophy's preliminary job of challenging doctrine: the 'every sperm is sacred' family makes God a voyeur of contraception, the Life of Brian stoning (rocks flying each time anyone utters 'Jehovah') shows blasphemy law run absurd, and 'Christmas in Heaven' exposes heavenly reward as material compensation. Deploying Socrates and Plato — the Republic's ban on portraying pettiful gods, the Apology on why the virtuous need not fear death, and above all the Euthyphro — the chapter reads the witch-weighing and the Holy Hand Grenade as the ancient problem whether acts are just because God sanctions them, and the chaplain's toadying prayer against God's own 'don't grovel' as proof that sacrifice and prayer are bargaining a perfect being has no need of. The upshot is not atheism but the Socratic verdict that the mobs punishing blasphemy, not the mocked, are the real blasphemers.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 17 "U2 and Philosophy" — Merrick sets XTC's 'Dear God' - being 'just struck' that no loving, all-powerful God rules this world - against U2's laments ('Wake Up Dead Man', 'Peace on Earth', '40') and Bono's reading of the Psalms as the blues shouted at God: both share outrage, but U2 adds yearning for the redemption promised in 'the story about eternity' plus Jubilee 2000-style action against debt and AIDS. He then argues the atheistic reaction to evil cannot be reason-producing, since neither divine design nor unguided evolution would give us a faculty that 'just sees' atheism from evil, any more than one that just sees there is no plant life on Mars. If God instead made us so that outrage at evil can trigger conviction that he will make all right, U2's reaction - 'Grace makes beauty out of ugly things' - can be as reasonable as visual perception.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 24 "U2 and Philosophy" — Cleveland sorts the knowing and feeling of U2's lyrics ('Vertigo', 'Beautiful Day', 'Staring at the Sun', 'Daddy's Gonna Pay for Your Crash Car') into Russell's varieties of knowledge - propositional, acquaintance, know-how - and argues that the feeling U2 champions against thought is knowledge by acquaintance: direct, concept-free awareness that, in religious cases, just is Jamesian mystical revelation as against revelation as a set of propositional truths, which is why Bono tells his father he 'hears something back from the silence' rather than holding doctrines. James supplies both the view that feeling is the deeper source of religion and the pragmatist answer to the problem of origins - 'by their fruits ye shall know them', so religious feeling is vindicated by moral transformation. Hume's slave-of-the-passions thesis explains why such feeling, not inert moral knowledge, moves Bono's social justice work: 'God is love, and as much as I respond... in acting in that love, that's my religion'.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 13 "Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress" — Jacoby reads Stan Marsh as W.K. Clifford's ethics of belief in action: from 'All About the Mormons' ('you better have something to back it up') to 'The Biggest Douche in the Universe,' Stan insists the burden of proof lies with claimants and that faith used as a fallback is no evidence at all. 'Cartmanland' and the story of Job serve to criticize Pascal's Wager — a good God would not eternally torment the virtuous nonbeliever, and the Wager simply assumes its afterlife payoff — while the harms of Miss Information's holistic healers, David Blaine's cult suicide, and Scientology show Clifford was right that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken minds and, as Stan tells John Edward, slow down the progress of all mankind.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 21 "Introduction" — Frames Part IV's philosophy of religion chapters. Johnson's chapter sets Cartman's million-dollar theme park against God's goodness, with South Park characters giving answers echoing Calvin, Hick, and Job; Gallagher's uses Rose's 'I just know' on Lost and Aquinas' distinctions between knowledge, opinion, and faith to argue that faith is not knowledge; and Eberl and Vines' uses Battlestar Galactica's Cylon monotheism versus Colonial religion and atheism to ask whether God can be proven, whether evil disproves him, and whether life is meaningful without God.
